translation: I have had the strangest dream. I have had a dream so strange that it's beyond explanation. A man would be a fool if he tried to explain this dream.

original: Methought I was—there is no man can tell what. Methought I was, and methought I had—but man is but a patched fool if he will offer to say what methought I had.
translation: I thought I was—well, nobody could describe what I was. I thought I was, and I thought I had—but a man would have to be a true fool to try and say what I thought I had.

original: The eye of man hath not  heard, the ear of man hath not seen, man's hand is not  able to taste, his tongue to conceive, nor his heart to  report what my dream was.
translation: My dream was so odd that no man's eyes have heard, or his ears have seen, or his hands have tasted, or his tongue felt, or his heart described what it was like.

original: I will get Peter Quince to  write a ballad of this dream. It shall be called  "Bottom's Dream" because it hath no bottom.
translation: I will get Peter Quince to write a ballad about this dream. It will be called "Bottom's Dream" because it's so complex that it has no bottom.

original: And I will  sing it in the latter end of a play before the duke.  Peradventure, to make it more gracious, I shall sing it  at her death.
translation: And I'll sing it for the duke at the end of the play. Or, better yet, to make it more pleasing, I'll sing it when Thisbe dies.

original: He cannot be heard of. Out of doubt he is transported.
translation: No one’s heard from him. There's no question he's been kidnapped by fairies.

original: If he come not, then the play is marred. It goes not  forward. Doth it?
translation: If he doesn’t come, then the play will be ruined. We won't be able to perform it. Will we?

original: It is not possible. You have not a man in all Athens  able to discharge Pyramus but he.
translation: It wouldn't be possible. There's not another man in all of Athens who can play Pyramus besides Bottom.

original: No, he hath simply the best wit of any handicraft man  in Athens.
translation: It's true. To be blunt, he’s the smartest craftsman in Athens.

original: Yea, and the best person too. And he is a very paramour for a sweet voice.
translation: Yes, and the best looking too. And his voice is the paramour of sweetness.

original: You must say “paragon.” A “paramour” is, God bless us,  a thing of naught.
Masters, the duke is coming from the temple, and there  is two or three lords and ladies more married. If our  sport had gone forward, we had all been made men.
translation: Gentlemen, the duke is leaving the temple, along with two or three additional lords and ladies who were also married. If we could only have performed our play, we would all have gotten rewards and been set for life.

original: O sweet bully Bottom! Thus hath he lost sixpence a day  during his life.
translation: Oh that sweet, good guy, Bottom! By not being here he's missed out on a pension of six pence a day for the rest of his life.

original: He could not have ’scaped sixpence a  day. An the duke had not given him sixpence a day for  playing Pyramus, I’ll be hanged.
translation: He wouldn't have been able to avoid getting six pence a day, even if he'd wanted to. If the duke wouldn’t have given him six pence a day for playing Pyramus, I'd go jump off a bridge.

original: He would have deserved  it. Sixpence a day in Pyramus, or nothing.
translation: And he would have deserved it. Pyramus is worth six pence a day, or nothing at all.

original: Where are these lads? Where are these hearts?
translation: Where are my boys? Where are my good fellows?

original: Bottom! O most courageous day! O most happy hour!
translation: Bottom! Oh, what a great day! Oh, what a happy moment!

original: Masters, I am to discourse wonders—but ask me not what, for if I tell you I am no true Athenian. I will tell  you everything, right as it fell out.
translation: Gentlemen, I have incredible stories to tell you—but don’t ask me what, because if I told you, then I would not be a true Athenian citizen. I’ll tell you everything, exactly how it happened.

original: Let us hear, sweet Bottom.
translation: Tell us, good Bottom.

original: Not a word of me. All that I will tell you is that the  duke hath dined.
translation: You won't get a word out of me!  All that I'll tell you is that the duke has had his dinner.

original: Get your apparel together, good strings to your beards, new ribbons to your pumps. Meet  presently at the palace. Every man look o'er his part.
translation: Gather your costumes, some new strings for your false beards,  and some new ribbons to decorate your shoes. Then meet me at the palace as soon as you can. We should each look over our lines again.

original: For the short and the long is, our play is preferred. In any case, let Thisbe have clean linen. And let not him  that plays the lion pair his nails, for they shall hang  out for the lion's claws.
translation: In sum, our play is going to be performed! So make sure that Thisbe has clean underpants. And make sure whoever is playing the lion doesn't cut down his nails, because they are going to need to stand in for the lion's claws.

original: And most dear actors, eat no  onions nor garlic, for we are to utter sweet breath. And I do not doubt but to hear them say, "It is a sweet  comedy." No more words. Away, go away!
translation: And, my most dear fellow actors, please don't eat onions or garlic. We must have sweet-smelling breath so the audience will say, "it's a sweet play." Enough talk.  Come on, let's go!

original: 'Tis strange, my Theseus, that these lovers speak of.
translation: My dear Theseus, what these lovers are describing is strange.

original: More strange than true. I never may believe   These antique fables nor these fairy toys.
translation: I think the story is more strange than it is true. I don't believe any of these ancient stories or fairy tales.

original: Lovers and madmen have such seething brains,   Such shaping fantasies, that apprehend   More than cool reason ever comprehends.
translation: Lovers and madmen have so much going on in their heads, such active imaginations, that they see and hear things that cool, calm, rational people can't understand.

original: The lunatic, the lover, and the poet   Are of imagination all compact.   One sees more devils than vast hell can hold—   That is the madman.
translation: Madmen, lovers, and poets all are all controlled by their imaginations: The ones who see devils and monsters all over the place—those are the madmen.

original: The lover, all as frantic,   Sees Helen’s beauty in a brow of Egypt.   The poet’s eye, in fine frenzy rolling,   Doth glance from heaven to Earth, from Earth to heaven.
translation: Lovers, who are just as wild, see a gypsy's face and think it is as beautiful as Helen of Troy's. Poets, who are always glancing around as if they are overcome by passion, make constant connections between things that are earthly and things that are heavenly.

original: And as imagination bodies forth   The forms of things unknown, the poet’s pen   Turns them to shapes and gives to airy nothing   A local habitation and a name.
translation: And they take the unreal things that tumble out of their imagination and write about them as if they were actual places or things.

original: Such tricks hath strong imagination,   That if it would but apprehend some joy,   It comprehends some bringer of that joy.   Or in the night, imagining some fear,   How easy is a bush supposed a bear!
translation: When people who have such strong imaginations feel some kind of joy, they imagine that it must be some entity or power that brings or creates that joy. Or if, in the night, they feel some fear, they see a bush and imagine it’s a bear!

original: But all the story of the night told over,   And all their minds transfigured so together,   More witnesseth than fancy’s images   And grows to something of great constancy,
translation: But the full story that the lovers are telling about last night—along with the fact that they all described it the same way—suggests that it's something that they really experienced rather than some imagined fantasy.

original: But, howsoever, strange and admirable.
translation: It has a consistency to it that suggests truth, even if it is strange and unbelievable.

original: Here come the lovers, full of joy and mirth. Joy, gentle friends! Joy and fresh days of love Accompany your hearts!
translation: Here come the lovers, full of joy and laughter. Joy to you, kind friends! May joy and sweet days of love be with you always.

original: More than to us Wait in your royal walks, your board, your bed!
translation: May even more joy than you wish for us await you—on your royal journeys, at your table, and in your bed!

original: Come now, what masques, what dances shall we have   To wear away this long age of three hours   Between our after-supper and bedtime?
translation: Now, what performances and dances will we see to pass these three hours between dinner and bedtime?

original: Where is our usual manager of mirth?   What revels are in hand?
translation: Where is our  Master of the Revels ? What entertainments do we have ready?

original: Is there no play,   To ease the anguish of a torturing hour?   Call Philostrate.
translation: Isn’t there a play for us to watch to ease the torture of free time? Call Philostrate.

original: Here, mighty Theseus.
translation: I’m here, Theseus.

original: Say, what abridgement have you for this evening? What masque, what music? How shall we beguile The lazy time if not with some delight?
translation: Tell us, what entertainment do you have that will shorten the evening? What plays, what music? How will we enjoy this boring time without some entertainment?

original: There is a brief, how many sports are ripe. Make choice of which your highness will see first.
translation: That is a list of all of the performances that are ready to go. Choose which one your highness would like to see first.

original: “The battle with the Centaurs, to be sung   By an Athenian eunuch to the harp.”
translation: “The battle between Hercules and the Centaurs at the wedding feast of Pirothous, sung by an Athenian eunuch  accompanied by a harp.”

original: We’ll none of that. That have I told my love,   In glory of my kinsman Hercules.
translation: No, we don’t want that. I’ve already told that story to Hippolyta, telling her of the glory of my cousin Hercules. What else?

original: “The riot of the tipsy Bacchanals,   Tearing the Thracian singer in their rage.”
translation: “The riot of the drunk Bacchanals who in the grip of their drunken frenzy rip the singer Orpheus to shreds.”

original: That is an old device, and it was played   When I from Thebes came last a conqueror.
translation: That’s a story often told in plays, and I saw it when I returned from conquering Thebes.

original: “The thrice three Muses mourning for the death   Of learning, late deceased in beggary.”
translation: “The nine Muses mourning the death of learning and the arts, which lately have become so reduced.”

original: That is some satire, keen and critical,   Not sorting with a nuptial ceremony.
translation: That’s a satire—a sharp and critical satire—and wouldn’t be right to perform at a wedding.

original: “A tedious brief scene of young Pyramus   And his love Thisbe. Very tragical mirth.”
translation: “A boring short drama about young Pyramus and his love Thisbe. Very sad and funny.”

original: “Merry” and “tragical?” “Tedious” and “brief?”   That is hot ice and wondrous strange snow.   How shall we find the concord of this discord?
translation: Funny and sad? Short but still boring? That’s like hot ice and very strange snow. What will we think of this play which claims to be such contradictory things?

original: A play there is, my lord, some ten words long,   Which is as brief as I have known a play.   But by ten words, my lord, it is too long,   Which makes it tedious.
translation: My lord, it is a play that's about ten words long, which is the shortest play I’ve ever encountered. But, my lord, it’s ten words too long, which is what makes it tedious.

original: For in all the play   There is not one word apt, one player fitted.
translation: In the entire play, there is not one well-placed word, and not one actor is a good fit for his part.

original: And tragical, my noble lord, it is.   For Pyramus therein doth kill himself.
translation: It is tragic, my noble lord, because Pyramus does kill himself.

original: Which, when I saw rehearsed, I must confess,   Made mine eyes water—but more merry tears   The passion of loud laughter never shed.
translation: When I saw the suicide during rehearsal, I must admit that it brought tears to my eyes—but I've never cried tears of such loud and merry laughter.

original: What are they that do play it?
translation: Who are the people performing it?

original: Hard-handed men that work in Athens here,   Which never labored in their minds till now,
translation: Manual workers from here in Athens who have never until now spent much doing anything that required thinking.

original: And now have toiled their unbreathed memories   With this same play against your nuptial.
translation: Now they’ve overburdened their under-exercised brains to create this play for your wedding.

original: And we will hear it.
translation: And we will watch it.

original: No, my noble lord.   It is not for you.
translation: No, my noble lord. It’s not something you’ll like.

original: I have heard it over,   And it is nothing, nothing in the world—
translation: I’ve seen it, and it’s worthless, as worthless as anything ever created

original: Unless you can find sport in their intents,   Extremely stretched and conned with cru 'l pain   To do you service.
translation: —unless you find their sad attempt funny, with their bad acting and incorrectly remembered lines.

original: I will hear that play.
translation: I’ll watch this play.

original: For never anything can be amiss   When simpleness and duty tender it.
translation: Because nothing can be bad when it’s motivated by a simple desire to bring pleasure to a person's betters.

original: Go, bring them in. And take your places, ladies.
translation: Go and bring them in. And find your seats, ladies.

original: I love not to see wretchedness o'er charged And duty in his service perishing.
translation: I don’t enjoy seeing incompetent people overwhelmed and made to look bad when they are only trying to serve.

original: Why, gentle sweet, you shall see no such thing.
translation: Why, my noble love, you won’t see any such thing.

original: He says they can do nothing in this kind.
translation: Philostrate says they’re not good at acting.

original: The kinder we, to give them thanks for nothing.   Our sport shall be to take what they mistake,   And what poor duty cannot do, noble respect   Takes it in might, not merit.
translation: Then we’re even more kind, for giving them thanks for something they’re not good at. Our entertainment will be to watch their mistakes, and what their own poor talent can't accomplish. Our noble generosity will see the effort they are giving rather than the quality of their performance.

original: Where I have come, great clerks have purposèd   To greet me with premeditated welcomes,
translation: When I have visited foreign cities, great scholars have tried to greet me with speeches they've rehearsed.

original: Where I have seen them shiver and look pale,   Make periods in the midst of sentences,   Throttle their practiced accent in their fears,   And in conclusion dumbly have broke off,   Not paying me a welcome.
translation: And I have seen them shiver and turn pale from nervousness, and pause incorrectly in the middle of their sentences, and mess up the tones of voice they've practiced, and then finish by suddenly breaking off without even welcoming me.

original: Trust me, sweet,   Out of this silence yet I picked a welcome,
translation: Trust me, my love, even in their silence I could sense the welcome they meant to give.

original: And in the modesty of fearful duty   I read as much as from the rattling tongue   Of saucy and audacious eloquence.
translation: I can understand the same meaning from those who are modest and frightened but also want to do their duty as I can from those who can rattle off a speech with wit, talent, and  eloquence.

original: Love, therefore, and tongue-tied simplicity   In least speak most, to my capacity.
translation: As I see it, my love, tongue-tied simplicity says the most precisely by saying the least.

original: So please your grace, the Prologue is addressed.
translation: If it please your Grace, the actor who will deliver the prologue is ready.

original: Let him approach.
translation: Let him come forward.

original: If we offend, it is with our good will.   That you should think we come not to offend,   But with good will.
translation: If our play offends you, it is our intention . That you know we have not come here to offend, but it is our intention.

original: To show our simple skill,   That is the true beginning of our end.   Consider then we come but in despite.
translation: Showing off the little skill we have in acting will end up getting us executed. Understand, then, that we come in a spirit of ill will.

original: We do not come as minding to contest you,   Our true intent is. All for your delight   We are not here.
translation: We don’t come here with the purpose of making you happy. We did not come here for your complete delight.

original: That you should here repent you,   The actors are at hand, and by their show   You shall know all that you are like to know.
translation: You should regret that the actors are ready. By watching their show, you’ll find out everything you’re likely to know.

original: This fellow doth not stand upon points.
translation: This guy doesn’t pay attention to punctuation.

original: He hath rid his prologue like a rough colt. He knows  not the stop. A good moral, my lord: it is not enough to speak, but to speak true.
translation: He rode his prologue like a wild colt. He didn’t know how to make it stop. The moral here, my lord, is that it’s not enough to speak. You have to speak correctly.

original: Indeed he hath played on his prologue like a child on a recorder—a sound, but not in government.
translation: Yes, he’s performed the prologue like a child plays a recorder—he can make sounds, but not with any purposeful control.

original: His speech was like a tangled chain. Nothing impaired,  but all disordered. Who is next?
translation: His speech was like a tangled chain. Unbroken, but all jumbled up. Who’s next?

original: Gentles, perchance you wonder at this show.   But wonder on, till truth make all things plain.
translation: Ladies and gentlemen, perhaps you're wondering about the subject of this play. Keep on wondering, until the truth makes everything clear.

original: This man is Pyramus, if you would know.   This beauteous lady Thisbe is certain.   This man, with lime and roughcast, doth present   Wall, that vile wall which did these lovers sunder.
translation: This man is Pyramus, if you'd like to know. It's certain that this beautiful lady is Thisbe. This man, dusted in lime and plaster, is playing the Wall, that awful wall that separated these lovers.

original: And through Wall’s chink, poor souls, they are content   To whisper. At the which let no man wonder.
translation: Through a little hole in the Wall, the poor souls are content to whisper. And no one should be amazed by that.

original: This man, with lanthorn, dog, and bush of thorn,   Presenteth Moonshine. For, if you will know,   By moonshine did these lovers think no scorn   To meet at Ninus' tomb—there, there to woo.
translation: This man, who has the lantern, dog, and thorn bush, is playing the role of Moonshine. Because, if you'd like to know, the lovers didn't think it was shameful to meet each other in the moonlight by Ninus’s tomb—there, they would woo each other.

original: This grisly beast, which “Lion” hight by name,   The trusty Thisbe, coming first by night,   Did scare away, or rather did affright.   And, as she fled, her mantle she did fall,   Which Lion vile with bloody mouth did stain.
translation: This dreadful beast, which is called “Lion,” scared away, or rather frightened, the faithful Thisbe when she arrived first at the meeting place one night. And, as she ran away, she dropped her cloak, which the awful Lion stained with his bloody mouth.

original: Anon comes Pyramus, sweet youth and tall,   And finds his trusty Thisbe’s mantle slain.   Whereat, with blade, with bloody blameful blade,   He bravely broached his boiling bloody breast.
translation: Soon Pyramus arrives, a sweet and tall young man, and finds his faithful Thisbe’s cloak covered in blood. Because of that, he raised his sword—his bloodthirsty responsible blade—and bravely stabbed his raging, ferocious chest.

original: And Thisbe, tarrying in mulberry shade,   His dagger drew, and died.
translation: Then Thisbe, waiting in the shade of the mulberry bushes, took out his dagger and killed herself.

original: For all the rest,   Let Lion, Moonshine, Wall, and lovers twain   At large discourse, while here they do remain.
translation: To hear the rest of the story, let Lion, Moonshine, Wall, and the two separated lovers explain it more fully while they stand here on the stage.

original: I wonder if the lion be to speak.
translation: I wonder if the lion will speak.

original: No wonder, my lord. One lion may when many asses do.
translation: It wouldn’t be shocking, my lord. When a bunch of asses are up on stage talking, a lion might talk too.

original: In this same interlude it doth befall   That I, one Snout by name, present a wall.
translation: At this moment of the play I, Snout, play a wall.

original: And such a wall, as I would have you think,   That had in it a crannied hole, or chink,   Through which the lovers, Pyramus and Thisbe,   Did whisper often very secretly.
translation: I want you to know that this wall has a little hole in it, through which the lovers Pyramus and Thisbe often secretly whispered.

original: This loam, this roughcast, and this stone doth show   That I am that same wall. The truth is so.
translation: This clay, this plaster, and this stone that I have on me show that I’m that wall. That's the truth.

original: And this the cranny is, right and sinister,   Through which the fearful lovers are to whisper.
translation: And this is the crack, running horizontally right to left, through which the fated lovers will whisper.

original: Would you desire lime and hair to speak better?
translation: Would you ever hope to hear plaster speak more eloquently?

original: It is the wittiest partition that ever I heard  discourse, my lord.
translation: It’s the smartest barrier that I’ve ever heard speak, my lord.

original: Pyramus draws near the wall. Silence!
translation: Pyramus is approaching the wall. Be quiet!

original: O grim-looked night! O night with hue so black!   O night, which ever art when day is not!   O night, O night! Alack, alack, alack,
translation: Oh, grim-looking night! Oh, night colored so black! Oh night, which always exists when day does not! Oh night, oh night! Sad, sad, sad.

original: I fear my Thisbe’s promise is forgot!   And thou, O Wall, O sweet, O lovely Wall,   That stand’st between her father’s ground and mine.
translation: I’m afraid my Thisbe has forgotten her promise! And you, oh Wall, oh sweet, oh lovely Wall, which stands between Thisbe’s father’s land and mine.

original: Thou Wall, O Wall, O sweet and lovely Wall,   Show me thy chink to blink through with mine eyne!
translation: You Wall, oh Wall, oh sweet and lovely Wall. Show me your hole that I can peer through with my eye!

original: Thanks, courteous Wall. Jove shield thee well for this!   But what see I? No Thisbe do I see.
translation: Thanks, considerate Wall. May  Jove  protect you for doing this. But what do I see? I don’t see Thisbe.

original: O wicked Wall through whom I see no bliss!   Cursed be thy stones for thus deceiving me!
translation: Oh wicked Wall, through which I see no happiness! Curse your stones for tricking me like this!

original: The wall, methinks, being sensible, should curse again.
translation: Since the wall has thoughts and feelings, I think it should curse back at him.

original: No, in truth, sir, he should not. “Deceiving me” is  Thisbe’s cue. She is to enter now and I am to spy her  through the wall. You shall see, it will fall pat as I  told you. Yonder she comes.
translation: No, in fact, sir, he shouldn't. "Tricking me” is the cue for Thisbe to speak. She’s going to enter now, and I’ll spot her through the wall. You’ll see, it’ll happen just as I am telling you. There she comes.

original: O Wall, full often hast thou heard my moans,   For parting my fair Pyramus and me!
translation: Oh Wall, you’ve so often heard my moans because you separate me from my handsome Pyramus!

original: My cherry lips have often kissed thy stones,   Thy stones with lime and hair knit up in thee.
translation: My cherry lips have often kissed your stones which are held together by plaster.

original: I see a voice. Now will I to the chink, To spy an I can hear my Thisbe’s face. Thisbe?
translation: I see a voice! Now I’ll go to the hole to find out if I can hear my Thisbe’s face. Thisbe?

original: My love thou art, my love, I think.
translation: You are my love, my love, I think.

original: Think what thou wilt, I am thy lover’s grace. And like Limander am I trusty still.
And I like Helen, till the Fates me kill.
Not Shafalus to Procrus was so true.
As Shafalus to Procrus, I to you.
translation: I’m as faithful to you as Shafalus was to Procrus.

original: Oh, kiss me through the hole of this vile wall!
translation: Oh, kiss me through the hole in this awful wall.

original: I kiss the wall’s hole, not your lips at all.
translation: I’m kissing the wall’s hole, not your lips at all.

original: Wilt thou at Ninny’s tomb meet me straightway?
translation: Will you meet me at Ninny’s grave right now?

original: Tide life, tide death, I come without delay.
translation: No matter what comes in life or death, I will be there without delay.

original: Thus have I, Wall, my part dischargèd so. And, being done, thus Wall away doth go.
translation: In this way, I, Wall, have played my part. Now, since I’m done, Wall can go away.

original: Now is the moon down between the two neighbors.
translation: With the wall gone, now the two lovers will see each other by the light of the moon.

original: No remedy, my lord, when walls are so willful to hear  without warning.
translation: There's nothing you can do about it, my lord, when walls have ears.

original: This is the silliest stuff that ever I heard.
translation: This is the silliest thing I’ve ever seen.

original: The best in this kind are but shadows, and the worst  are no worse if imagination amend them.
translation: The best plays are a kind of illusion, and the worst are no worse if you use your imagination to fix them up.

original: It must be your imagination then, and not theirs.
translation: Then it's your imagination that's good, not theirs.

original: If we imagine no worse of them than they of themselves, they may pass for excellent men. Here come two noble  beasts in, a man and a lion.
translation: If we imagine these actors as being no worse than they imagine themselves to be, then they'd seem like accomplished actors. Here come two noble beasts, a man and a lion.

original: You, ladies, you whose gentle hearts do fear   The smallest monstrous mouse that creeps on floor,   May now perchance both quake and tremble here,   When lion rough in wildest rage doth roar.
translation: You gentle-hearted ladies—who fear even the smallest monstrous mouse that sneaks along the floor—may shake and tremble when the wild lion roars in its most violent rage.

original: Then know that I, as Snug the joiner, am   A lion fell, nor else no lion’s dam.   For if I should as lion come in strife   Into this place, ’twere pity on my life.
translation: Therefore, know that I, Snug the carpenter, am neither a cruel lion nor a lioness, because if I were a lion that had come to this place in order to fight, then it would cost me my life.

original: A very gentle beast, of a good conscience.
translation: It’s a noble beast, with a good conscience.

original: A very best at a beast, my lord, that e'er I saw.
translation: He’s the best actor at being a beast that I’ve ever seen, my lord.

original: This lion is a very fox for his valor.
translation: This lion seems like a fox, by being more sly than courageous.

original: True. And a goose for his discretion.
translation: True. And he's just about as wise as a goose—that is, not wise at all!

original: Not so, my lord. For his valor cannot carry his  discretion, and the fox carries the goose.
translation: Not true, my lord. He’s not courageous enough pull off being discreet, just as the fox pulls along the goose by carrying it in its mouth.

original: His discretion, I am sure, cannot carry his valor, for  the goose carries not the fox. It is well. Leave it to  his discretion, and let us listen to the moon.
translation: He’s not discreet enough to be brave, actually, just as the goose can't carry the fox. It doesn't matter. Let's leave all this to his discretion, and listen to the what the moon has to say.

original: This lanthorn doth the hornèd moon present—
He should have worn the horns on his head.
He is no crescent, and his horns are invisible within  the circumference.
translation: He’s not shaped like a crescent moon, so his horns are probably invisible inside the circle.

original: This lanthorn doth the hornèd moon present. Myself the man i' th' moon do seem to be.
translation: This lantern represents the crescent moon. I am pretending to be the man in the moon.

original: This is the greatest error of all the rest. The man  should be put into the lanthorn. How is it else the “man i' th' moon?”
translation: That’s a bigger mistake that all the others. The man should be put inside the lantern. How else can he be the “man in the moon?”

original: He dares not come there for the candle. For you see, it is already in snuff.
translation: He doesn't dare to go in there on account of the candle. Because, you see, the candle must first be put out.

original: I am aweary of this moon. Would he would change!
translation: I’m tired of this moon. If only he would wane away.

original: It appears by his small light of discretion, that he is in the wane. But yet, in courtesy, in all reason, we  must stay the time.
translation: It seems by the meager amount of light he's giving off that he is waning. But, to be polite, we’ll have to wait to find out.

original: Proceed, Moon.
translation: Continue, Moon.

original: All that I have to say is to tell you that the lanthorn is the moon; I, the man in the moon; this thornbush, my thornbush; and this dog, my dog.
translation: All I have to say is that the lantern is the moon. I’m the man in the moon. This thorn bush is my thorn bush. And this dog is my dog.

original: Why, all these should be in the lanthorn, for all these are in the moon. But silence! Here comes Thisbe.
translation: Well, all of these should be in the lantern, because all of them are in the moon. But be quiet! Here comes Thisbe.

original: This is old Ninny’s tomb. Where is my love?
translation: This is old Ninny’s tomb. Where is my love?

original: O!
translation: Grr!

original: Well roared, Lion!
translation: Nice roar, Lion!

original: Well run, Thisbe!
translation: Nice running, Thisbe!

original: Well shone, Moon! Truly, the moon shines with a good  grace.
translation: Nice shining, Moon! Really, the Moon shines quite well.

original: Well moused, Lion!
translation: Way to shake that mantle around the way a cat shakes a mouse, Lion!

original: And then came Pyramus.
translation: And then Pyramus arrived.

original: And so the lion vanished.
translation: So then the lion disappeared.

original: Sweet Moon, I thank thee for thy sunny beams.   I thank thee, Moon, for shining now so bright.   For by thy gracious, golden, glittering gleams,   I trust to take of truest Thisbe sight.
translation: Sweet Moon, I thank you for your sunny beams. I thank you, Moon, for shining now so bright, because by the light of your helpful, golden, glittering beams, I will be able to see my faithful Thisbe.

original: But stay, O spite!   But mark, poor knight,   What dreadful dole is here!   Eyes, do you see?   How can it be?
translation: But wait. Oh, misfortune! Look, you poor knight, what an awful sight! Eyes, do you see? How can this be?

original: O dainty duck! O dear!   Thy mantle good,   What, stained with blood?
translation: Oh, my dainty duck! Oh, my dear! What? Your beautiful cloak, is it stained with blood?

original: Approach, ye Furies fell!   O Fates, come, come,   Cut thread and thrum.   Quail, crush, conclude, and quell!
translation: Come, you cruel Furies! Come, come you Fates, and cut the thread of my life. Conquer, crush, bring to an end, and kill!

original: This passion and the death of a dear friend would go  near to make a man look sad.
translation: Watching this performance would be almost enough to make a man sad—so long as a good friend of yours died while you were watching it.

original: Beshrew my heart, but I pity the man.
translation: Curse my heart, but I feel sorry for this man.

original: O wherefore, Nature, didst thou lions frame?   Since lion vile hath here deflowered my dear,   Which is—no, no—which was the fairest dame   That lived, that loved, that liked, that looked with  cheer.
translation: Oh why, Mother Nature, did you create lions? A dreadful lion has  deflowered  my darling, who is—no, no—who  was  the most beautiful woman that ever lived, loved, liked, or smiled.

original: Come, tears, confound!   Out, sword, and wound!   The pap of Pyramus—   Ay, that left pap   Where heart doth hop.
translation: Come, tears, overwhelm me! Come out, sword, and wound me in the chest—yes, on the left side where the heart beats.

original: Thus die I, thus, thus, thus.   Now am I dead.   Now am I fled.   My soul is in the sky.   Tongue, lose thy light.   Moon, take thy flight.
translation: And so, I die, so, so, so. Now I am dead. Now my soul has flown from my body. Tongue, see no more. Moon, disappear.

original: No die, but an ace for him, for he is but one.
Less than an ace, man. For he is dead. He is nothing.
translation: He’s a die with even fewer than one dot. He's dead, so he's nothing.

original: With the help of a surgeon he might yet recover and  prove an ass.
translation: With the help of a doctor he might recover and become an ass.

original: How chance Moonshine is gone before Thisbe comes back  and finds her lover?
translation: What's going to happen since Moonshine has left before Thisbe comes back. How will she be able to find her lover?

original: She will find him by starlight. Here she comes, and her passion ends the play.
translation: She’ll see him by starlight. Here she comes. Her crying will end the play.

original: Methinks she should not use a long one for such a  Pyramus. I hope she will be brief.
translation: I don’t think this Pyramus deserves a whole lot of crying. I hope she does her part quickly.

original: A mote will turn the balance, which Pyramus, which  Thisbe, is the better. He for a man, God warrant us, she for a woman, God bless us.
translation: The difference in who's better between Pyramus and Thisbe is razor thin. God save us from him, as a man. But God save us from her, as a woman.

original: She hath spied him already with those sweet eyes.
translation: She's seen him already with those sweet eyes of hers.

original: And thus she means , videlice t —
translation: And so she’ll start moaning, as we expected—

original: Asleep, my love?   What, dead, my dove?   O Pyramus, arise!   Speak, speak. Quite dumb?   Dead, dead? A tomb   Must cover thy sweet eyes.
translation: Are you asleep, my love? What, are you dead, my dove? Oh, Pyramus, wake up! Speak, speak. Can you talk? Dead, dead? A tomb must cover your sweet eyes.

original: These lily lips,   This cherry nose,   These yellow cowslip cheeks   Are gone, are gone.   Lovers, make moan.
translation: Your lily-white lips, your cherry-red nose, your marigold-yellow cheeks are gone, gone. Lovers, moan.

original: His eyes were green as leeks.   O Sisters three,   Come, come to me   With hands as pale as milk.
translation: His eyes were as green as leeks. Oh, you three Fates, come, come to me, with hands as pale as milk.

original: Lay them in gore,   Since you have shore   With shears his thread of silk.
translation: Place your hands in blood, since you have cut with scissors the thread of his life.

original: Tongue, not a word.   Come, trusty sword.   Come, blade, my breast imbrue.
translation: Tongue, don't say a word. Come, trusty sword. Come, trusted sword, stain my breast with blood.

original: Thus Thisbe ends.   Adieu, adieu, adieu.
translation: Goodbye, friends! This is how Thisbe dies. Goodbye, goodbye, goodbye.

original: Moonshine and Lion are left to bury the dead.
translation: Moonshine and Lion are left to bury the dead.

original: Ay, and Wall too.
translation: Yes, and Wall too.

original: No, assure you. The wall is down  that parted their fathers. Will it please you to see the epilogue, or to hear a Bergomask dance between two of  our company?
translation: No, I assure you. The wall that separated their fathers' land has been taken down. Would you like to see the epilogue or see two of our actors perform a country dance?

original: No epilogue, I pray you, for your play needs no excuse. Never excuse—for when the players are all dead, there  needs none to be blamed.
translation: No epilogue, please. Your play does not need to offer any apology for itself through an epilogue. Never apologize—when the actors are all dead, no one must be blamed.

original: Marry, if he that writ it had  played Pyramus and hanged himself in Thisbe’s garter, it would have been a fine tragedy.
translation: In fact, if the man who wrote the play had performed as Pyramus and hanged himself with Thisbe’s stockings, it would have been a very good tragedy.

original: And so it is, truly,  and very notably discharged. But come, your Bergomask.  Let your epilogue alone.
translation: And that's exactly what it is, honestly, and remarkably performed. Now please, perform your country dance. But don't worry about performing your epilogue.

original: The iron tongue of midnight hath told twelve. Lovers,  to bed. 'Tis almost fairy time.
translation: The hands of the clock have struck midnight. Lovers, let's go to bed. It’s almost fairy time.

original: I fear we shall outsleep the coming morn   As much as we this night have overwatched.   This palpable-gross play hath well beguiled   The heavy gait of night.
translation: I’m afraid we’re going to sleep past morning because we've stayed up so late tonight. This obviously idiotic play has done a good job to help us pass the tired hours of night.

original: Sweet friends, to bed. A  fortnight hold we this solemnity,   In nightly revels and new jollity.
translation: Sweet friends, let’s go to bed. For two weeks we will continue to celebrate, with parties and new fun every night.

original: Now the hungry lion roars   And the wolf behowls the moon,   Whilst the heavy ploughman snores,   All with weary task fordone.
translation: Now the hungry lion roars and the wolf howls at the moon, while the tired farmer snores, exhausted from all the work he's done.

original: Now the wasted brands do glow,   Whilst the screech-owl, screeching loud,   Puts the wretch that lies in woe   In remembrance of a shroud.
translation: The embers of the fire glow, while the owl’s screeching hoot makes the man lying in his sickbed think about the shroud that will cover him in death.

original: Now it is the time of night   That the graves all gaping wide,   Every one lets forth his sprite,   In the churchway paths to glide.
translation: Now is the time of night when the graves all open wide, and release their spirits to glide over the paths of graveyards.

original: And we fairies, that do run   By the triple Hecate’s team   From the presence of the sun,   Following darkness like a dream,   Now are frolic.
translation: And we fairies—who run from the sun just like  Hecate , following darkness like a dream—are jolly.

original: Not a mouse   Shall disturb this hallowed house.   I am sent with broom before   To sweep the dust behind the door.
translation: I will ensure that not even a mouse will disturb this blessed house. I’ve been sent ahead with a broom to sweep the dust behind the door.

original: Through the house give glimmering light,   By the dead and drowsy fire.
translation: The dying fire gives off a glimmering light throughout the house.

original: Every elf and fairy sprite   Hop as light as bird from brier.   And this ditty, after me,   Sing and dance it trippingly.
translation: Now every elf and fairy, hop as lightly as a bird on a twig, and sing this little song along with me, and dance.

original: First, rehearse your song by rote,   To each word a warbling note.
translation: First rehearse your song from memory, and sing each word with a bird-like note.

original: Hand in hand with fairy grace   Will we sing and bless this place.
translation: With everyone holding hands, we'll sing and bless this place with fairy grace.

original: Now until the break of day,   Through this house each fairy stray.
translation: Now, until the dawn,  Each fairy wander through this house.

original: To the best bride bed will we,   Which by us shall blessèd be.   And the issue there create   Ever shall be fortunate.
translation: Titania and I will go  To the bless the royal marriage bed,  So that the children conceived in it Will have good luck.

original: So shall all the couples three   Ever true in loving be.   And the blots of Nature’s hand
translation: All three of the couples will always be  Faithful in love,  And none of the defects of nature  Will appear in their children.

original: Shall not in their issue stand.   Never mole, harelip, nor scar,   Nor mark prodigious, such as are   Despisèd in nativity,   Shall upon their children be.
translation: They won’t have moles, or cleft lips, or scars,  Or abnormal birthmarks,  All of which will cause upset  If a baby is born with it.

original: With this field dew consecrate,   Every fairy take his gait.   And each several chamber bless   Through this palace with sweet peace.
translation: Fairies, take this holy dew from the fields,  And as you walk  Through the rooms of the palace,  Bless them with sweet peace.

original: And the owner of it blessed   Ever shall in safety rest.   Trip away. Make no stay.   Meet me all by break of day.
translation: And the owner of the palace  Will always be blessed and safe.  Now go, but don’t stay long.  Meet me at dawn.

original: If we shadows have offended,   Think but this, and all is mended—   That you have but slumbered here   While these visions did appear.
translation: If we actors have offended you, simply think about it this way, and everything will be better: you just slept here, and saw these visions in a dream.

original: And this weak and idle theme,   No more yielding but a dream,   Gentles, do not reprehend.   If you pardon, we will mend.
translation: This foolish and silly plot was only a dream. Ladies and gentlemen, don't rebuke me. If you forgive us, we'll make everything better.

original: And, as I am an honest Puck,   If we have unearnèd luck   Now to 'scape the serpent's tongue,   We will make amends ere long.
translation: And since I, Puck, am honest, I promise to make everything better—if we're lucky enough to escape your boos and hisses.

original: Else the Puck a liar call.   So good night unto you all.   Give me your hands if we be friends,   And Robin shall restore amends.
translation: Otherwise, call me a liar. So, good night to all of you. If we are friends, please give us a round of applause—and Robin will make it all up to you.

original: Nay, but this dotage of our general’s   O’erflows the measure.
translation: I'm telling you, our general's ridiculous infatuation goes beyond the limits of reasonable behavior.

original: Those his goodly eyes,   That o’er the files and musters of the war   Have glowed like plated Mars, now bend, now turn   The office and devotion of their view   Upon a tawny front.
translation: Those handsome eyes of his, that used to shine like  Mars's  when he looked over the lines of troops, now turn away and give their duty and love to a woman with a dark complexion.

original: His captain’s heart,   Which in the scuffles of great fights hath burst   The buckles on his breast, reneges all temper   And is become the bellows and the fan   To cool a gypsy’s lust.
translation: He used to have the heart of a military commander, which swelled so much during the battles of great wars that it split open the armor on his chest, but now he abandons all self-restraint and only lives to stir up and then satisfy an  Egyptian's  sexual desire.

original: If it be love indeed, tell me how much.
translation: If you really love me, tell me how much.

original: There’s beggary in the love that can be reckoned.
translation: My love for you could not be very great if I could tell you how much I love you.

original: I’ll set a bourn how far to be beloved.
translation: I'll mark off boundaries to see how far your love extends.

original: Then must thou needs find out new heaven, new earth.
translation: If you want to see how far my love extends, you'll need to discover a new world, because my love extends beyond this one.

original: News, my good lord, from Rome.
translation: I have news from Rome, my good lord.

original: Grates me, the sum.
translation: That irritates me. Summarize it for me.

original: Nay, hear them, Antony.   Fulvia perchance is angry.
translation: No, listen to him, Antony. Maybe  Fulvia  is angry.

original: Or who knows   If the scarce-bearded Caesar have not sent   His powerful mandate to you, “Do this, or this.
translation: Or perhaps the young Caesar has sent a stern command, ordering you, "Do this, or this.

original: Take in that kingdom, and enfranchise that.   Perform ’t, or else we damn thee.”
translation: Conquer that kingdom, and free that one. Do it, or I'll be very angry with you."

original: How, my love?
translation: Why are you talking like this, my love?

original: Perchance? Nay, and most like.   You must not stay here longer. Your dismission   Is come from Caesar.
translation: Maybe? No, this is definitely the news. You shouldn't stay here any longer. Caesar has given you your orders.

original: Therefore hear it, Antony.   Where’s Fulvia’s process? Caesar’s, I would say—both?
translation: So, pay attention, Antony. Where's the summons from Fulvia? From Caesar, I should say—or both?

original: Call in the messengers. As I am Egypt’s queen,   Thou blushest, Antony, and that blood of thine   Is Caesar’s homager.
translation: Call in the messengers. As sure as I'm Egypt's queen, I say you're blushing, Antony, and your blush shows your loyalty to Caesar.

original: Else so thy cheek pays shame   When shrill-tongued Fulvia scolds. The messengers!
translation: Either that, or it shows you're shame when Fulvia scolds you with her shrill tongue. Call in the messengers!

original: Let Rome in Tiber melt and the wide arch   Of the ranged empire fall. Here is my space.   Kingdoms are clay.
translation: Let Rome collapse into the  Tiber River  and the whole extent of the wide empire fall. The only empire I want is right here. Conquering foreign lands is worthless.

original: Our dungy earth alike   Feeds beast as man. The nobleness of life   Is to do thus, when such a mutual pair   And such a twain can do ’t,
translation: Land is just something that animals feed off of, the same way humans do. The noble way to live is like  this  when there are two people like us who share the same greatness and the same great feelings—

original: in which I bind,   On pain of punishment, the world to weet   We stand up peerless.
translation: and I order the world to recognize, on pain of punishment, that no one else comes close to our greatness.

original: Excellent falsehood!   Why did he marry Fulvia, and not love her?
translation: What an eloquent lie! Why did Antony marry Fulvia if he didn't love her?

original: I’ll seem the fool I am not. Antony   Will be himself.
translation: I'll pretend to believe him. I know that Antony will keep acting so foolishly.

original: But stirred by Cleopatra.   Now, for the love of Love and her soft hours,   Let’s not confound the time with conference harsh.
translation: Yes, but only because of you. Now, since we love Love and the relaxing hours it brings, let's not ruin our time together by arguing.

original: There’s not a minute of our lives should stretch   Without some pleasure now. What sport tonight?
translation: We shouldn't let a minute pass without pleasure. How shall we entertain ourselves tonight?

original: Hear the ambassadors.
translation: Listen to the messengers.

original: Fie, wrangling Queen!   Whom every thing becomes—to chide, to laugh,   To weep, whose every passion fully strives   To make itself, in thee, fair and admired!
translation: Don't talk like that, you stubborn Queen! But everything you do is endearing, whether you criticize, laugh, or cry; every emotion you express becomes attractive and admirable!

original: No messenger but thine, and all alone   Tonight we’ll wander through the streets and note   The qualities of people.
translation: The only messages I want to hear are yours, and tonight we'll wander through the streets alone and observe the people we meet.

original: Come, my Queen,   Last night you did desire it.—
translation: Come, my Queen, this was what you wanted last night.

original: Speak  not to us.
translation: Don't talk to  me .

original: Is Caesar with Antonius prized so slight?
translation: Does Antony care so little about Caesar's orders?

original: Sir, sometimes when he is not Antony He comes too short of that great property Which still should go with Antony.
translation: Sir, sometimes he doesn't behave like Antony, and he doesn't care about the things that the Antony we know should care about.

original: I am full sorry   That he approves the common liar, who   Thus speaks of him at Rome,
translation: There are people back in Rome who say he's not acting the way he should, and I'm sorry that he's proving them right.

original: but I will hope   Of better deeds tomorrow. Rest you happy!
translation: But I hope he'll behave better tomorrow. Sleep well!

original: Lord Alexas, sweet Alexas, most anything Alexas, almost most absolute Alexas, where’s the soothsayer that you  praised so to th’ Queen?
translation: Lord Alexas, sweet Alexas, Alexas whom I could give almost any compliment, almost perfect Alexas, where's that soothsayer that you praised so much when you were talking to the Queen?

original: Oh that I knew this husband,  which, you say, must charge his horns with garlands!
translation: Oh, I wish I knew who you were referring to when you talked about a husband who had been  cuckolded !

original: Soothsayer!
translation: Soothsayer!

original: Your will?
translation: What do you want?

original: Is this the man?  [To SOOTHSAYER]  Is ’t you, sir, that know things?
translation: Is this the person you were talking about?[To the SOOTHSAYER] Are you the one, sir, who has supernatural knowledge?

original: In nature’s infinite book of secrecy A little I can read.
translation: I know a little about the world's many secrets.

original: Show him your hand.
translation: Show him your hand.

original: Bring in the banquet quickly. Wine enough Cleopatra’s health to drink.
translation: Bring in the banquet quickly. Bring in enough wine to toast to Cleopatra's health.

original: Good sir, give me good  fortune.
translation: Good sir, give me a good fortune.

original: I make not, but foresee.
translation: I don't give fortunes, I just tell people what they are going to be.

original: Pray, then, foresee me one.
translation: Then please tell me what mine is going to be.

original: You shall be yet far fairer than you are.
translation: You'll be more beautiful in the future than you are right now.

original: He means in flesh.
translation: He means that I'll get fatter.

original: No, you shall paint when you are old.
translation: No, he means that you'll use makeup when you get old.

original: Wrinkles forbid!
translation: God forbid I get wrinkles!

original: Vex not his prescience. Be attentive.
translation: Don't annoy this wise man. Pay attention to him.

original: Hush!
translation: Hush!

original: You shall be more beloving than beloved.
translation: You'll love other people more than they love you.

original: I had rather heat my liver with drinking.
Nay, hear him.
translation: No, listen to him.

original: Good now, some excellent fortune! Let me be married to  three kings in a forenoon and widow them all.
translation: Come on, tell me some good news now! Let me marry three kings in a single day and let all of them die and leave me a rich widow.

original: Let me  have a child at fifty, to whom Herod of Jewry may do  homage. Find me to marry me with Octavius Caesar, and  companion me with my mistress.
translation: When I'm fifty years old, let me give birth to a child so great that even  King Herod  would honor him. Look at my palm and tell me that I'm destined to marry Octavius Caesar and become as great as my mistress Cleopatra.

original: You shall outlive the lady whom you serve.
translation: You will live longer than your mistress.

original: Oh, excellent! I love long life better than figs.
You have seen and proved a fairer former fortune Than that which is to approach.
translation: Your life up until now has been happier than it will be in the future.

original: Then belike my children shall have no names. Prithee,  how many boys and wenches must I have?
translation: Then maybe all my children will be illegitimate. Tell me, how many little boys and girls will I have?

original: If every of your wishes had a womb, And fertile every wish, a million.
translation: If every one of your wishes were a child, you would have a million children.

original: Out, fool! I forgive thee for a witch.
translation: Get out of here, fool! Because you're a fortune teller, I won't bring charges of witchcraft against you.

original: You think none but your sheets are privy to your  wishes.
Nay, come, tell Iras hers.
translation: No, come on, tell Iras her fortune.

original: We’ll know all our fortunes.
translation: We'll all have our fortunes told.

original: Mine, and most of our fortunes tonight, shall be—drunk  to bed.
translation: My fortune, and most of ours, tonight will be—that we go to bed drunk.

original: There’s a palm  presages chastity, if nothing else.
translation: My palm tells you that I'm chaste, if nothing else.

original: E’en as the o’erflowing Nilus presageth famine.
Go, you wild bedfellow, you cannot soothsay.
translation: Go away, you lusty friend, you can't tell fortunes.

original: Nay, if an oily palm be not a fruitful prognostication, I cannot scratch mine ear.—Prithee, tell her but a  workaday fortune.
translation: No, if I don't know the meaning of a sweaty palm, I can't scratch my ear.  Please, just tell her an ordinary, everyday kind of fortune.

original: Your fortunes are alike.
translation: You have the same fortunes.

original: But how, but how? Give me particulars.
translation: But how, but how? Give me details.

original: I have said.
translation: I've said what I have to say.

original: Am I not an inch of fortune better than she?
translation: Don't I have at least a slightly better fortune than she does?

original: Well, if you were but an inch of fortune better than I, where would you choose it?
translation: Well, if you had just an inch more fortune than me, where would you want it?

original: Not in my husband’s nose.
Our worser thoughts heavens mend. Alexas!
translation: May God correct our inappropriate thoughts. Alexas!

original: Come, his fortune, his fortune! Oh, let him marry a woman that cannot go, sweet Isis, I beseech  thee, and let her die too,
translation: Come on, his fortune, tell his fortune! Oh, let him marry a woman who is infertile, sweet  Isis , I pray, and let her die too,

original: and give him a worse, and let worse follow worse, till the worst of all follow him  laughing to his grave, fifty-fold a cuckold!
translation: and then have him marry a worse wife, and let every wife be worse after that, until the very worst one laughs next to his grave after she has cuckolded him fifty times!

original: Good Isis,  hear me this prayer, though thou deny me a matter of  more weight, good Isis, I beseech thee!
translation: Good Isis, hear this prayer of mine, even if you don't grant my prayers about more important things. Good Isis, I beg you!

original: Amen, dear goddess, hear that prayer of the people!  For, as it is a heartbreaking to see a handsome man  loose-wived, so it is a deadly sorrow to behold a foul  knave uncuckolded.
translation: Amen, dear goddess, hear that prayer from the people! Because, just as it's a tragedy to see a handsome man with an unfaithful wife, it's also a tragedy to see an ugly scoundrel with a faithful wife.

original: Therefore, dear Isis, keep decorum,  and fortune him accordingly.
translation: Therefore, Isis, respect what's appropriate and treat him accordingly.

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: Lo now, if it lay in their hands to make  me a cuckold, they would make themselves whores but  they’d do ’t.
translation: Honestly, if they had it in their power to make me a cuckold, they would be willing to make themselves whores to do it.

original: Hush! Here comes Antony.
translation: Hush! Here comes Antony.

original: Not he. The Queen.
translation: It's not him, it's the Queen.

original: Saw you my lord?
translation: Have you seen my lord?

original: No, lady.
translation: No, lady.

original: Was he not here?
translation: Wasn't he here?

original: No, madam.
translation: No, madam.

original: He was disposed to mirth, but on the sudden A Roman thought hath struck him.—Enobarbus!
translation: He was in the mood for fun and games, but then he suddenly started thinking about Rome. Enorbarbus!

original: Madam?
translation: Madam?

original: Seek him and bring him hither.— Where’s Alexas?
translation: Find him and bring him here. Where's Alexas?

original: Here at your service. My lord approaches.
translation: I'm at your service. My lord approaches.

original: We will not look upon him. Go with us.
translation: I won't look at him. Go with us.

original: Fulvia thy wife first came into the field.
translation: Your wife Fulvia first entered the battlefield.

original: Against my brother Lucius?
translation: She was fighting against my brother Lucius?

original: Ay.   But soon that war had end, and the time’s state   Made friends of them, joining their force ’gainst  Caesar,
translation: Yes, but that fight was soon over, and the situation forced them to make friends and combine forces to fight against Caesar.

original: Whose better issue in the war from Italy   Upon the first encounter drave them.
translation: But Caesar won the very first battle and drove them out of Italy.

original: Well, what worst?
translation: Well, what worse news could you have than that?

original: The nature of bad news infects the teller.
translation: When a messenger delivers bad news, people usually hate him for it.

original: When it concerns the fool or coward. On.   Things that are past are done, with me.
translation: Only if they're fools or cowards. Continue with your news. I don't get upset about things that are already over and done with.

original: ’Tis thus:   Who tells me true, though in his tale lie death,   I hear him as he flattered.
translation: This is how it is: if someone tells me the truth, then I appreciate what he has to say, even if he brings terrible news.

original: Labienus—   This is stiff news—hath with his Parthian force   Extended Asia:
translation: Labienus —this is terrible news—has seized Asia with his Parthian army.

original: from Euphrates   His conquering banner shook, from Syria   To Lydia and to Ionia,   Whilst—
“Antony,” thou wouldst say.
translation: You were about to say "While Antony."

original: O my lord!
translation: Oh my lord!

original: Speak to me home. Mince not the general tongue.   Name Cleopatra as she is called in Rome.
translation: Tell me the truth. Don't downplay the common people's poor opinion of me. Speak about Cleopatra the way they speak about her in Rome.

original: Rail thou in Fulvia’s phrase, and taunt my faults   With such full license as both truth and malice   Have power to utter.
translation: Scold me using the same words my wife uses, and mock my faults as fully possible, whether you want to speak the truth or want to be malicious.

original: Oh, then we bring forth weeds   When our quick minds lie still, and our ills told us   Is as our earing.
translation: Oh, we create all kinds of problems when we sit back and do not use our abilities, and when other people criticize us, they help us become productive again.

original: At your noble pleasure.
translation: I'll see you again when you please.

original: From Sicyon, how, the news? Speak there.
translation: What news do you have from Sicyon? You there, speak.

original: The man from Sicyon—
translation: The messenger from Sicyon—

original: Is there such an one?
translation: Is there one?

original: He stays upon your will.
translation: He's outside waiting for you to call him in.

original: Let him appear.
translation: Let him come in.

original: Fulvia thy wife is dead.
translation: Your wife Fulvia is dead.

original: Where died she?
translation: Where did she die?

original: In Sicyon. Her length of sickness, with what else more serious Importeth thee to know, this bears.
translation: In Sicyon. This letter tells you how long she was sick, along with more important matters.

original: Forbear me.
translation: Leave me.

original: What’s your pleasure, sir?
translation: What do you want, sir?

original: I must with haste from hence.
translation: I must leave here quickly.

original: Why, then, we kill all our women. We see how mortal an  unkindness is to them. If they suffer our departure,  death’s the word.
translation: Why, that would kill all our women. We see that unkindness is fatal to them. They'll die if we leave.

original: I must be gone.
translation: I must leave.

original: Under a compelling occasion, let women die. It were  pity to cast them away for nothing, though between them  and a great cause they should be esteemed nothing.
translation: If it's absolutely necessary, then let women die. But it would be a shame to kill them for nothing—even if it's true that we should treat them as worthless if they get in the way of our goals.

original: Cleopatra, catching but the least noise of this, dies  instantly. I have seen her die twenty times upon far  poorer moment. I do think there is mettle in death,  which commits some loving act upon her, she hath such a  celerity in dying.
translation: Cleopatra would die instantly if she even suspected that you would leave. I've seen her  die  twenty times for a much smaller reason. I think death must have some kind of sexual power that acts on her, because she's so quick to die.

original: She is cunning past man’s thought.
translation: She is too cunning for a man to outwit.

original: Alack, sir, no, her passions are made of nothing but  the finest part of pure love. We cannot call her winds  and waters sighs and tears.
translation: No, sir, no, her passions aren't cunning performances, they arise from the best part of pure love. We can't refer to her storms and floods as sighs and tears.

original: They are greater storms and  tempests than almanacs can report.   This cannot be  cunning in her. If it be, she makes a shower of rain as  well as Jove.
translation: Her sighs and tears are bigger storms and tempests than any book could describe.  It would be impossible for her to fake them. If they come from her scheming, then she must be able to control the rain like  Jove .

original: Would I had never seen her!
translation: I wish I had never met her!

original: O sir, you had then left unseen a wonderful piece of  work which not to have been blessed withal would have  discredited your travel.
translation: Oh sir, then you would have missed a wonderful sight, which would have reduced the glory of your adventures while traveling.

original: Fulvia is dead.
translation: Fulvia is dead.

original: Sir?
translation: Excuse me?

original: Fulvia is dead.
translation: Fulvia is dead.

original: Fulvia?
translation: Fulvia?

original: Dead.
translation: Dead.

original: Why, sir, give the gods a thankful sacrifice. When it  pleaseth their deities to take the wife of a man from  him, it shows to man the tailors of the earth,  comforting therein, that when old robes are worn out,  there are members to make new.
translation: Why, sir, give a sacrifice to the gods in thanks. When the gods decide to take a man's wife from him, a man takes comfort from realizing that there are  tailors on earth who can make a new robe when the old one is worn out .

original: If there were no more  women but Fulvia, then had you indeed a cut, and the  case to be lamented. This grief is crowned with  consolation   .
translation: If there were no other women but Fulvia, then you would really have suffered a great loss, and your situation would be terrible. As it is, you have a consolation for your grief.

original: Your old smock brings forth a new  petticoat, and indeed the tears live in an onion that  should water this sorrow.
translation: In exchange for your old clothes, you get new ones, and so it makes as much sense to cry over losing Fulvia as to cry when you cut an onion.

original: The business she hath broached in the state Cannot endure my absence.
translation: She has started some business in Rome that makes it necessary for me to return.

original: And the business you have broached here cannot be  without you, especially that of Cleopatra’s, which  wholly depends on your abode.
translation: And the business you have started here makes it necessary for you to stay here, especially Cleopatra's business, which depends entirely on your presence.

original: No more light answers. Let our officers   Have notice what we purpose. I shall break   The cause of our expedience to the Queen   And get her leave to part.
translation: No more of these jokes. Tell my officers what I intend to do. I will let the Queen know why we have to leave so quickly and get her permission to go.

original: For not alone   The death of Fulvia, with more urgent touches,   Do strongly speak to us, but the letters too   Of many our contriving friends in Rome   Petition us at home.
translation: For Fulvia's death is not the only thing on my mind—letters from my friends back in Rome also urge me to go home.

original: Sextus Pompeius   Hath given the dare to Caesar and commands   The empire of the sea. Our slippery people,   Whose love is never linked to the deserver   Till his deserts are past,
translation: Sextus Pompeius  has challenged Caesar's authority and commands the empire around the island of Sicily. Our citizens are fickle, and never acknowledge service until the service is over.

original: begin to throw   Pompey the Great and all his dignities   Upon his son, who—high in name and power,   Higher than both in blood and life—stands up   For the main soldier, whose quality, going on,   The sides o’ th’ world may danger.
translation: And so they give the title "Pompey the Great" and all the honors associated with it to Pompey's son, who has a great name and great power, and even greater vitality and force. Now he acts like the chief soldier, and if his abilities go unchecked, he will endanger the  whole arrangement of the world .

original: Much is breeding   Which, like the courser’s hair, hath yet but life,   And not a serpent’s poison. Say our pleasure,   To such whose place is under us, requires   Our quick remove from hence.
translation: Many troubles are beginning to form that, right now, only have the  potential for disaster . Tell my subordinates that I wish to leave here quickly.

original: I shall do ’t.
translation: I will do it.

original: Where is he?
translation: Where is he?

original: I did not see him since.
translation: I haven't seen him recently.

original: See where he is, who’s with him, what he  does.   I did not send you.
translation: Find out where he is, who he's with, and what he's doing. Don't tell him I sent you.

original: If you find him sad,   Say I am dancing. If in mirth, report   That I am sudden sick. Quick, and return.
translation: If you see that he's sad, tell him I'm happy. If you see that he's happy, tell him that I've suddenly gotten sick. Go quickly and come back.

original: Madam, methinks, if you did love him dearly, You do not hold the method to enforce The like from him.
translation: Madam, in my opinion, if you love him so much, then you're not acting in the right way to get him to reciprocate.

original: What should I do I do not?
translation: What should I be doing that I'm not doing?

original: In each thing give him way. Cross him in nothing.
translation: Let him have his own way in everything. Don't oppose him at all.

original: Thou teachest like a fool the way to lose him.
translation: You fool, you're telling me the best way to lose him.

original: Tempt him not so too far. I wish, forbear. In time we hate that which we often fear.
translation: Don't test him so much. I wish that you'd cut it out. Often, we end up bringing about the very thing we are afraid will happen, and we hate it when we do.

original: I am sick and sullen.
translation: I'm sick and out of sorts.

original: I am sorry to give breathing to my purpose—
translation: I'm sorry to have to tell you what I came to tell you.

original: Help me away, dear Charmian! I shall fall. It cannot be thus long. The sides of nature Will not sustain it.
translation: Help me away, dear Charmian! I will faint. I cannot last much longer. This body of mine can't take it.

original: Now, my dearest Queen—
translation: Now, my dearest Queen—

original: Pray you, stand farther from me.
translation: Please, stand further away from me.

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: I know by that same eye there’s some good news.   What, says the married woman you may go?
translation: I can tell by your expression that you've received some good news. What, does your wife tell you to come home?

original: Would she had never given you leave to come!   Let her not say ’tis I that keep you here.   I have no power upon you. Hers you are.
translation: I wish she had never allowed you to come here! Don't let her say that it's I who kept you here. I don't have any power over you. You belong to her.

original: The gods best know—
translation: The gods know best—

original: Oh never was there queen So mightily betrayed! Yet at the first I saw the treasons planted.
translation: Oh, there never was a queen who was betrayed so terribly! But I saw from the start the signs that you would betray me.

original: Cleopatra—
translation: Cleopatra—

original: Why should I think you can be mine, and true—   Though you in swearing shake the thronèd gods—   Who have been false to Fulvia?
translation: Why did I think that you could belong to me and be true to me—even though your vows to the gods seemed to shake the heavens—when you have been untrue to your wife?

original: Riotous madness,   To be entangled with those mouth-made vows   Which break themselves in swearing!
translation: It's absolute insanity, to be taken in by those insincere vows that are broken the moment they are made!

original: Most sweet Queen—
translation: Most sweet Queen—

original: Nay, pray you, seek no color for your going,   But bid farewell and go. When you sued staying,   Then was the time for words. No going then!
translation: No, please, don't try to come up with an excuse for leaving, just say goodbye and go. When you begged to stay, that was the time for talking. There was no talk of leaving then!

original: Eternity was in our lips and eyes,   Bliss in our brows’ bent, none our parts so poor   But was a race of heaven.
translation: You wanted to enjoy my lips and eyes for eternity, you found bliss in the curve of my eyebrow. No part of my body was anything less than a heavenly creation.

original: They are so still,   Or thou, the greatest soldier of the world,   Art turned the greatest liar.
translation: And that's still true, or else you, the greatest soldier in the world, have become the greatest liar.

original: How now, lady?
translation: What are you saying, my lady?

original: I would I had thy inches. Thou shouldst know There were a heart in Egypt.
translation: I wish I were as big as you. Then you would know that there is someone in Egypt who has as much courage as you.

original: Hear me, Queen:   The strong necessity of time commands   Our services awhile, but my full heart   Remains in use with you. Our Italy   Shines o’er with civil swords.
translation: Listen to me, Queen. There is a situation I must take care of, but my heart remains here with you. Italy, my country, is consumed by civil war.

original: Sextus Pompeius   Makes his approaches to the port of Rome.   Equality of two domestic powers   Breed scrupulous faction. The hated, grown to strength,   Are newly grown to love.
translation: Sextus Pompeius draws near the port of Rome. When there are two equally strong powers in one country, it creates distrust and disagreement. The people who were once hated are now loved, once they have gained power.

original: The condemned Pompey,   Rich in his father’s honor, creeps apace   Into the hearts of such as have not thrived   Upon the present state, whose numbers threaten;
translation: Pompey, who was once condemned, has gained honor thanks to his father's good reputation; he has started to win over the people who haven't succeeded under the current government, and there are enough of them to pose a threat.

original: And quietness, grown sick of rest, would purge   By any desperate change.   My more particular,   And that which most with you should safe my going,   Is Fulvia’s death.
translation: And when our idleness makes us sick in times of peace, we can only cure ourselves through acts of violence.  But my personal motivation, which should make you approve of my leaving, is Fulvia's death.

original: Though age from folly could not give me freedom, It does from childishness. Can Fulvia die?
translation: Even though getting older cannot keep me totally free from foolishness, it does mean that I'm not as foolish as a child. Is it possible Fulvia is dead?

original: She’s dead, my Queen.
translation: She's dead, my queen.

original: O most false love!   Where be the sacred vials thou shouldst fill   With sorrowful water?
Now I see, I see,   In Fulvia’s death how mine received shall be.
translation: Now I see, I see from Fulvia's death, that you wouldn't cry over my death either.

original: Quarrel no more, but be prepared to know   The purposes I bear, which are or cease   As you shall give th’ advice.
translation: Don't fight with me anymore, but listen to my plans, which I will execute or abandon according to what you tell me.

original: By the fire   That quickens Nilus’ slime, I go from hence   Thy soldier, servant, making peace or war   As thou affects.
translation: I swear by the fire of the sun that causes plants to grow on the banks of the Nile, I will leave here as your soldier and servant, and I will seek peace or war as you wish.

original: Cut my lace, Charmian, come! But let it be. I am quickly ill, and well, So Antony loves.
My precious Queen, forbear, And give true evidence to his love which stands An honorable trial.
translation: My precious Queen, please stop this, and be honest that my love is true. It would be found honorable if put to the test.

original: So Fulvia told me.   I prithee, turn aside and weep for her.   Then bid adieu to me, and say the tears   Belong to Egypt.
translation: Yes, that's what Fulvia told me. Please, turn away and cry for her. Then say goodbye to me, and tell me that you're crying for me.

original: Good now, play one scene   Of excellent dissembling, and let it look   Like perfect honor.
translation: Come on now, act one scene of excellent deception, and let it seem perfectly honorable.

original: You’ll heat my blood. No more.
translation: You'll make me angry. No more of this.

original: You can do better yet, but this is meetly.
translation: You can give a better performance than that, but that was pretty good.

original: Now, by my sword—
translation: Now, I swear by my sword—

original: And target. Still he mends.
translation: And by your shield. His acting keeps getting better.

original: But this is not the best. Look, prithee, Charmian,   How this Herculean Roman does become   The carriage of his chafe.
translation: But this still isn't his best work. Look, I tell you, Charmian, how well this Herculean Roman puts on the appearance of rage.

original: I’ll leave you, lady.
translation: I'll leave you, lady.

original: Courteous lord, one word.   Sir, you and I must part, but that’s not it.   Sir, you and I have loved, but there’s not it,   That you know well.
translation: Courteous lord, one word. Sir, you and I must part, but that's not what I wanted to say. Sir, you and I have loved each other, but that's not what I wanted to say either. You know that well.

original: Something it is I would—   Oh, my oblivion is a very Antony,   And I am all forgotten.
translation: There's something I would like to say, oh, my memory is deserting me just like you are, and I'm forgetting everything, just like you've forgotten me.

original: But that your royalty Holds idleness your subject, I should take you For idleness itself.
translation: If you weren't the queen of immaturity, I would think you were immaturity itself.

original: ’Tis sweating labor   To bear such idleness so near the heart   As Cleopatra this.   But, sir, forgive me,   Since my becomings kill me when they do not   Eye well to you.
translation: It's hard work to be foolish deep down the way I am. But, sir, forgive me, since these changes in my behavior disgust me when they don't please you.

original: Your honor calls you hence.   Therefore be deaf to my unpitied folly,   And all the gods go with you! Upon your sword   Sit laurel victory, and smooth success   Be strewed before your feet.
translation: Your honor requires you to leave. Therefore pay no attention to my foolishness and don't pity me, and may all the gods bless you on your way! I hope that you find  victory  in battle and that you succeed easily in all your plans.

original: Let us go. Come.   Our separation so abides and flies
translation: Let us go. Come.  We are so bound together, even in our separation,

original: That thou, residing here, goes yet with me,   And I, hence fleeting, here remain with thee.   Away!
