translation: that even if you stay here, you'll still be with me, and I, when I leave, will still be here with you.  Away, let's go!

original: You may see, Lepidus, and henceforth know,   It is not Caesar’s natural vice to hate   Our great competitor. From Alexandria   This is the news:
translation: You will see Lepidus, and know for the future, that I am not naturally inclined to hate this great competitor of mine. Here's the news from Alexandria.

original: he fishes, drinks, and wastes   The lamps of night in revel; is not more manlike   Than Cleopatra, nor the queen of Ptolemy   More womanly than he;
translation: He fishes, drinks, and stays up all night wasting his time with fun and games. He is no more masculine than Cleopatra is, and she,  the Egyptian queen , is no more feminine than him.

original: hardly gave audience, or   Vouchsafed to think he had partners. You shall find  there   A man who is th’ abstract of all faults   That all men follow.
translation: He hardly listened to my messenger or admitted that he had political partners back here at home. In this letter, you'll read about a man who exemplifies the faults of all men.

original: I must not think there are   Evils enough to darken all his goodness.
translation: I cannot believe there are enough faults in the world to negate all his good qualities.

original: His faults in him seem as the spots of heaven,   More fiery by night’s blackness, hereditary   Rather than purchased, what he cannot change   Than what he chooses.
translation: In him, faults just serve to set off his good qualities more strongly. It seems that he inherited his vices rather than acquiring them. His faults are something he cannot change, not something that he chooses to have.

original: You are too indulgent. Let’s grant, it is not   Amiss to tumble on the bed of Ptolemy,   To give a kingdom for a mirth, to sit   And keep the turn of tippling with a slave,   To reel the streets at noon, and stand the buffet   With knaves that smell of sweat.
translation: You're too lenient. Let's say, for argument's sake, that it's okay to have a sexual affair with Cleopatra, to give up his kingdom for the sake of entertainment, to sit and take turns drinking with a slave, to stagger drunkenly around the streets at noon, and wind up in fights with lowborn scoundrels who smell of sweat.

original: Say this becomes him—   As his composure must be rare indeed   Whom these things cannot blemish—yet must Antony   No way excuse his foils when we do bear   So great weight in his lightness.
translation: Let's say that this behavior is appropriate for him—a man would have to have perfect character for all this not to count against him. Still, Antony can't excuse faults when we have to deal with such serious problems ourselves as a result of his irresponsibility.

original: If he filled   His vacancy with his voluptuousness,   Full surfeits and the dryness of his bones   Call on him for ’t.
translation: If he has filled his leisure time with sexual affairs, then he'll be punished with sickness from overeating and from venereal disease, and that's his problem.

original: But to confound such time   That drums him from his sport and speaks as loud   As his own state and ours, ’tis to be chid   As we rate boys who, being mature in knowledge,   Pawn their experience to their present pleasure   And so rebel to judgment.
translation: But he's wasting vital time and resources and putting all our positions in danger. He needs to be scolded, like any boy who knows what's right but chooses to do the wrong thing regardless.

original: Here’s more news.
translation: Here's more news.

original: Thy biddings have been done, and every hour,   Most noble Caesar, shalt thou have report   How ’tis abroad.
translation: Your orders have been carried out, and every hour, most noble Caesar, you'll have news about how things are going abroad.

original: Pompey is strong at sea,   And it appears he is beloved of those   That only have feared Caesar.
translation: Pompey has strong military power at sea, and it seems that he's supported by people who only obeyed Caesar because they were afraid of him.

original: To the ports   The discontents repair, and men’s reports   Give him much wronged.
translation: These discontented people go to the ports, and they say Pompey has been badly mistreated.

original: I should have known no less.   It hath been taught us from the primal state   That he which is was wished until he were,
translation: I should have guessed this would happen. It's been like this since the first government, people always wish for their leaders to gain power until they have actually done so.

original: And the ebbed man, ne’er loved till ne’er worth love,   Comes deared by being lacked.
translation: Fallen leaders, who are never loved until they are no longer worth loving, become dear to the people because they are gone.

original: This common body,   Like to a vagabond flag upon the stream,   Goes to and back, lackeying the varying tide   To rot itself with motion.
translation: The common people are like a loose piece of cloth on a stream, going back and forth, following the changing tides, and ruining itself by constantly moving and changing.

original: Caesar, I bring thee word   Menecrates and Menas, famous pirates,   Make the sea serve them, which they ear and wound   With keels of every kind.
translation: Caesar, I've come to tell you that Menecrates and Menas, those famous pirates, have taken over the sea, which they  cross  in vessels of every kind.

original: Many hot inroads   They make in Italy—the borders maritime   Lack blood to think on ’t—and flush youth revolt.
translation: They're coming into Italy by many roads—the territories on the coast aren't brave enough to stop them—and spirited young men revolt and join them.

original: No vessel can peep forth, but ’tis as soon   Taken as seen, for Pompey’s name strikes more   Than could his war resisted.
translation: No ship can set sail without being captured as soon as it is seen, because Pompey's name alone is even more terrifying than his armies would be if they were met in battle.

original: Antony,   Leave thy lascivious wassails. When thou once   Wast beaten from Modena, where thou slew’st   Hirtius and Pansa,
translation: Antony, come away from your self-indulgent celebrations. Once, when you were defeated at  Modena , where you slew the  consuls  Hirtius and Pansa,

original: consuls, at thy heel   Did famine follow, whom thou fought’st against,   Though daintily brought up, with patience more   Than savages could suffer.
translation: you were beset by famine, and you fought against it with more endurance than someone used to living in the wild, even though you had been brought up in luxury.

original: Thou didst drink   The stale of horses and the gilded puddle   Which beasts would cough at.   Thy palate then did deign   The roughest berry on the rudest hedge.   Yea, like the stag, when snow the pasture sheets,   The barks of trees thou browsèd.
translation: You drank horses' urine and drank from slime-covered puddles that even the animals wouldn't touch.  You were willing to eat the toughest berries from the wildest bushes. In fact, when snow covered the pastures, you even ate the bark off of trees like a stag.

original: On the Alps   It is reported thou didst eat strange flesh,   Which some did die to look on.
translation: Going over the Alps, they say that you ate strange foods that some people would rather die than eat.

original: And all this—   It wounds thine honor that I speak it now—   Was borne so like a soldier, that thy cheek   So much as lanked not.
translation: And you bore all this—it is a blow to your honor for me to say this now—you bore it so much like a soldier that your cheek didn't even grow hollow from hunger or exhaustion.

original: ’Tis pity of him.
translation: His current state is a great pity.

original: Let his shames quickly   Drive him to Rome.
translation: I hope he will be so ashamed of himself that he will quickly return to Rome.

original: ’Tis time we twain   Did show ourselves i’ th’ field, and to that end   Assemble we immediate council.   Pompey   Thrives in our idleness.
translation: It's time that the two of us appeared on the battlefield, and for that purpose, I am calling a council immediately.   Pompey thrives while we continue to do nothing.

original: Tomorrow, Caesar,   I shall be furnished to inform you rightly
translation: Tomorrow, Caesar, I'll be able to tell you accurately  what troops

original: Both what by sea and land I can be able   To front this present time.
translation: I will be able to assemble, both on sea and land, to face the enemy now.

original: Till which encounter It is my business too. Farewell.
translation: And until we do face him, assembling troops is my business too. Farewell.

original: Farewell, my lord. What you shall know meantime Of stirs abroad, I shall beseech you, sir, To let me be partaker.
translation: Farewell, my lord. In the meantime, when you know what's going on abroad, I ask you to let me know as well, sir.

original: Doubt not, sir. I knew it for my bond.
translation: Don't doubt that I will. I know that's my responsibility.

original: Charmian!
translation: Charmian!

original: Madam?
translation: Yes, madam?

original: Ha, ha! Give me to drink mandragora.
Why, madam?
translation: Why, madam?

original: That I might sleep out this great gap of time My Antony is away.
translation: So I can sleep through this long period while my Antony is away.

original: You think of him too much.
translation: You think about him too much.

original: Oh, ’tis treason!
translation: Oh, that's treasonous to say!

original: Madam, I trust, not so.
translation: Madam, I trust that it isn't.

original: Thou, eunuch Mardian!
translation: You, Mardian the eunuch!

original: What’s your highness’ pleasure?
translation: What does your highness want?

original: Not now to hear thee sing. I take no pleasure   In aught an eunuch has.
translation: I don't wish to hear you sing right now. I don't take pleasure in anything that a eunuch has.

original: ’Tis well for thee   That, being unseminared, thy freer thoughts   May not fly forth of Egypt. Hast thou affections?
translation: It's lucky for you, since you've been castrated, that your fantasies don't involve anything outside of Egypt. Do you have desires?

original: Yes, gracious madam.
translation: Yes, gracious madam.

original: Indeed?
translation: Indeed?

original: Not in deed, madam, for I can do nothing   But what indeed is honest to be done.
translation: Not  in deed , madam, since I can't do anything except what is  honest  to do.

original: Yet have I fierce affections, and think   What Venus did with Mars.
translation: But I still have strong desires, and I think about what  Venus did with Mars .

original: O Charmian,   Where think’st thou he is now? Stands he or sits he?   Or does he walk? Or is he on his horse?   O happy horse, to bear the weight of Antony!
translation: Oh Charmian, where do you think he is now? Is he standing or sitting? Or is he walking? Or he is on horseback? Oh what a lucky horse, to have Antony on top of him!

original: Do bravely, horse, for wott’st thou whom thou mov’st?   The demi-Atlas of this earth, the arm   And burgonet of men.
translation: Run with style and courage, horse, for do you know who is riding you? The  demi-Atlas  of this earth, the champion and guardian of humankind.

original: He’s speaking now,   Or murmuring “Where’s my serpent of old Nile?”   For so he calls me. Now I feed myself   With most delicious poison.
translation: Perhaps he's speaking now, or murmuring, "Where's my serpent of  the old Nile?" For that's what he calls me. Now I cheer myself up with delicious thoughts of the thing that pains me most.

original: Think on me,   That am with Phoebus’ amorous pinches black   And wrinkled deep in time.
translation: Think about me, whose skin is dark from the sun's loving beams and wrinkled with old age.

original: Broad-fronted Caesar,   When thou wast here above the ground, I was   A morsel for a monarch. And great Pompey   Would stand and make his eyes grow in my brow.   There would he anchor his aspect, and die   With looking on his life.
translation: Wide-browed  Caesar , when you were still alive, I was magnificent enough even for a great monarch like you. And great Pompey would stand and gaze for hours at my forehead. There he would fix his gaze, and  die  from looking at the woman who sustained his life.

original: Sovereign of Egypt, hail!
translation: Ruler of Egypt, hail!

original: How much unlike art thou Mark Antony!
translation: How very unlike Mark Antony you are!

original: Yet, coming from him, that great med’cine hath   With his tinct gilded thee.
translation: But, since you were sent by him, some of his greatness has rubbed off on you.

original: How goes it with my brave Mark Antony?
translation: How is my brave Mark Antony doing?

original: Last thing he did, dear Queen, He kissed—the last of many doubled kisses— This orient pearl.
translation: The last thing he did, dear Queen, was to kiss—the last kiss of many such kisses—this pearl from India.

original: His speech sticks in my heart.
translation: His parting words stuck in my mind.

original: Mine ear must pluck it thence.
translation: I must hear them from you.

original: “Good friend,” quoth he,   “Say the firm Roman to great Egypt sends   This treasure of an oyster, at whose foot,   To mend the petty present, I will piece   Her opulent throne with kingdoms. All the East,   Say thou, shall call her mistress.”
translation: "Good friend," he said, "Say that the stalwart Roman sends this treasure from an oyster to the great queen of Egypt, at whose feet—to improve this meager present—I will lay kingdoms, to add glory to her splendid throne. Tell her that all the East will call her their queen."

original: So he nodded,   And soberly did mount an arm-gaunt steed,   Who neighed so high that what I would have spoke   Was beastly dumbed by him.
translation: So he nodded, and somberly mounted a thin, spirited warhorse, who neighed so loudly that the reply I would have made was drowned out by the beast.

original: What was he, sad or merry?
translation: What mood was he in, sad or happy?

original: Like to the time o’ th’ year between the extremes Of hot and cold, he was nor sad nor merry.
translation: Like the midpoint of the year between extreme heat and extreme cold, he was neither sad nor happy.

original: O well-divided disposition! Note him,   Note him, good Charmian, ’tis the man, but note him.
translation: Oh well-balanced temperament! Take notice of him, take notice, good Charmian, that's exactly how he is, but take notice of him.

original: He was not sad, for he would shine on those   That make their looks by his. He was not merry,   Which seemed to tell them his remembrance lay   In Egypt with his joy, but between both.
translation: He wasn't sad, because he wanted to look cheerfully at those people whose moods depend on his. He was not merry, which seems to say that he was remembering Egypt and his joy, but he was between sorrow and merriment.

original: O heavenly mingle! Be’st thou sad or merry,   The violence of either thee becomes,   So does it no man else.—Mett’st thou my posts?
translation: Oh heavenly mixture! Whether you are sad or happy, the extreme of either emotion suits you as it suits no other man. Did you encounter my messengers?

original: Ay, madam, twenty several messengers. Why do you send so thick?
translation: Yes, madam, twenty different messengers. Why did you send so many?

original: Who’s born that day   When I forget to send to Antony   Shall die a beggar.
translation: Whoever is born on the day that I forget to write to Antony will die a beggar.

original: Ink and paper, Charmian.   Welcome, my good Alexas. Did I, Charmian,   Ever love Caesar so?
translation: Bring me ink and paper, Charmian. Welcome, my good Alexas. Did I, Charmian, ever love Caesar this much!

original: Oh, that brave Caesar!
Be choked with such another emphasis! Say, “the brave Antony.”
translation: May you choke if you ever say such a thing again! Say, "the brave Antony."

original: The valiant Caesar!
translation: The valiant Caesar!

original: By Isis, I will give thee bloody teeth If thou with Caesar paragon again My man of men.
translation: I swear by Isis, I will strike you in the mouth if you compare Caesar again with my man who surpasses all other men.

original: By your most gracious pardon, I sing but after you.
translation: I beg your pardon, your highness, I'm only repeating what you said.

original: My salad days,   When I was green in judgment, cold in blood,   To say as I said then.
But, come, away.
translation: But come, away.

original: Get me ink and paper.   He shall have every day a several greeting,   Or I’ll unpeople Egypt.
translation: Get me ink and paper. Antony will have a new greeting every day, even if I have to get rid of all of Egypt to send them.

original: If the great gods be just, they shall assist The deeds of justest men.
translation: If the great gods are just, they will assist the actions of the most honest men.

original: Know, worthy Pompey, That what they do delay, they not deny.
translation: You should know, worthy Pompey, that just because the gods are slow to do something doesn't mean they won't do it.

original: Whiles we are suitors to their throne, decays The thing we sue for.
translation: While we spend time praying to them for help, the thing we pray for loses its value.

original: We, ignorant of ourselves,   Beg often our own harms, which the wise powers   Deny us for our good,
translation: We don't know ourselves well enough, and so we often pray for something that will harm us, which the wise gods withhold for our own good.

original: so find we profit   By losing of our prayers.
translation: So we are often better off when our prayers aren't answered.

original: I shall do well.   The people love me, and the sea is mine.   My powers are crescent, and my auguring hope   Says it will come to th’ full.
translation: I will do well. The people love me, and I have control of the sea. My military power is increasing, and all my knowledge tells me that it will reach its  full potential .

original: Mark Antony   In Egypt sits at dinner, and will make   No wars without doors. Caesar gets money where   He loses hearts.
translation: Mark Antony is off enjoying himself in Egypt and he won't fight any battles except inside the bedroom. Caesar loses the people's loyalty by taxing them to raise money.

original: Lepidus flatters both,   Of both is flattered, but he neither loves,   Nor either cares for him.
translation: Lepidus flatters them both and is flattered by both of them, but he doesn't love either of them, and neither of them cares for him.

original: Caesar and Lepidus Are in the field. A mighty strength they carry.
translation: Caesar and Lepidus are on the battlefield. They have a powerful army.

original: Where have you this? ’Tis false.
translation: Where did you hear that? It's false.

original: From Silvius, sir.
translation: From Silvius, sir.

original: He dreams. I know they are in Rome together   Looking for Antony. But all the charms of love,   Salt Cleopatra, soften thy wanned lip!
translation: He dreamt it. I know Caesar and Lepidus are in Rome together looking for Antony. But I hope, lustful Cleopatra, that all the charms of love will make your withered lips soft!

original: Let witchcraft join with beauty, lust with both.   Tie up the libertine in a field of feasts,   Keep his brain fuming.
translation: May you use witchcraft as well as beauty, and may both arouse Antony's lust. Keep that  libertine  occupied with feast after feast, keep him from thinking clearly.

original: Epicurean cooks,   Sharpen with cloyless sauce his appetite,   That sleep and feeding may prorogue his honor   Even till a Lethe’d dulness—
translation: May decadent cooks increase his appetite with pleasing sauces so that sleeping and eating will make him forgetful, until he  forgets  his duties completely.

original: This is most certain that I shall deliver:   Mark Antony is every hour in Rome   Expected.
translation: The news I have to deliver is absolutely true. Mark Antony is expected to arrive in Rome any minute now.

original: Since he went from Egypt ’tis   A space for farther travel.
translation: Enough time has passed since he left Egypt that he could have traveled an even greater distance.

original: I could have given less matter   A better ear.—Menas, I did not think   This amorous surfeiter would have donned his helm   For such a petty war.
translation: I could have listened more eagerly to something less urgent. Menas, I didn't think that this self-indulgent lover would put on his helmet to join in such a minor war.

original: His soldiership   Is twice the other twain. But let us rear   The higher our opinion, that our stirring   Can from the lap of Egypt’s widow pluck   The ne’er lust-wearied Antony.
translation: He is twice as good a soldier as the other two. But we'll have to increase our opinion of ourselves, since my military preparations can motivate even Antony, who never tires of pleasure, to leave his Egyptian lover.

original: I cannot hope   Caesar and Antony shall well greet together.
translation: I don't think that Caesar and Antony will have a friendly reunion.

original: His wife that’s dead did trespasses to Caesar.   His brother warred upon him, although, I think,   Not moved by Antony.
translation: Antony's late wife opposed Caesar and his brother declared war on him, although I don't think he was encouraged by Antony.

original: I know not, Menas,   How lesser enmities may give way to greater.
translation: I don't know, Menas, whether a greater rivalry might not help them overlook smaller rivalries.

original: Were ’t not that we stand up against them all,   ’Twere pregnant they should square between themselves,   For they have entertainèd cause enough   To draw their swords.
translation: If it weren't for the fact that we are opposing all of them, it's likely that they would fight amongst themselves, since they have enough reasons to draw their swords against each other.

original: But how the fear of us   May cement their divisions and bind up   The petty difference, we yet not know.
translation: But it's possible their fear of our forces will heal the breach between them and end their small disagreements.

original: Be ’t as our gods will have ’t. It only stands   Our lives upon to use our strongest hands.   Come, Menas.
translation: Let it be as the gods will it. Our lives depend only on us using our greatest possible strength. Come, Menas.

original: Good Enobarbus, ’tis a worthy deed, And shall become you well, to entreat your captain To soft and gentle speech.
translation: Good Enobarbus, it's worth your while to urge your captain to use polite and gentle words, and it will do you credit.

original: I shall entreat him   To answer like himself.
translation: I will urge him to speak like himself.

original: If Caesar move him,   Let Antony look over Caesar’s head   And speak as loud as Mars.
translation: If Caesar provokes him, let Antony ignore Caesar and answer as fiercely as  Mars .

original: By Jupiter,   Were I the wearer of Antonio’s beard,   I would not shave ’t today.
translation: By  Jupiter , if I were able to look as heroic as Antony, I would try to do so today.

original: ’Tis not a time for private stomaching.
translation: This isn't the time to deal with private arguments.

original: Every time serves for the matter that is then born in  ’t.
translation: Every time is a good time to deal with the matters that arise in that moment.

original: But small to greater matters must give way.
translation: But small matters should be put aside so we can deal with more important ones.

original: Not if the small come first.
translation: Not if the small matters occur first.

original: Your speech is passion. But pray you stir No embers up. Here comes the noble Antony.
translation: You're letting your emotions run away with you. But please, don't provoke any fights. Here comes the noble Antony.

original: And yonder, Caesar.
translation: And over there is Caesar.

original: If we compose well here, to Parthia. Hark, Ventidius.
translation: If we come to an agreement here, the next stop is Parthia. Come over here, Ventidius.

original: I do not know, Maecenas. Ask Agrippa.
translation: I don't know, Maecenas. Ask Agrippa.

original: ’Tis spoken well. Were we before our armies, and to fight, I should do thus.
Welcome to Rome.
translation: Welcome to Rome.

original: Thank you.
translation: Thank you.

original: Sit.
translation: Sit.

original: Sit, sir.
translation: Sit, sir.

original: Nay, then.
translation: Well then.

original: I learn, you take things ill which are not so, Or being, concern you not.
translation: I hear that you take things as offensive that aren't intended to be—or if they are offensive, they have nothing to do with you.

original: I must be laughed at   If or for nothing or a little, I   Should say myself offended, and with you   Chiefly i’ th’ world;
translation: I would make myself a laughingstock if I got offended over nothing or over a small matter, and most of all in dealings with you.

original: more laughed at, that I should   Once name you derogately, when to sound your name   It not concerned me.
translation: I would deserve even greater mockery if I spoke badly of you once, when it is no business of mine to speak about you at all.

original: My being in Egypt, Caesar, what was ’t to you?
translation: What concern is it of yours if I'm in Egypt?

original: No more than my residing here at Rome   Might be to you in Egypt.
translation: No more than my living here in Rome might concern you in Egypt.

original: Yet if you there   Did practice on my state, your being in Egypt   Might be my question.
translation: But if you plotted against me while you were there, your being in Egypt might be a concern of mine.

original: How intend you, “practiced”?
translation: What do you mean, "plotted?"

original: You may be pleased to catch at mine intent   By what did here befall me.
translation: You might guess what I mean from what happened to me here.

original: Your wife and brother   Made wars upon me, and their contestation   Was theme for you. You were the word of war.
translation: Your wife and brother waged war against me, and they intended for you to join them. They fought in your name.

original: You do mistake your business. My brother never   Did urge me in his act. I did inquire it,   And have my learning from some true reports   That drew their swords with you.
translation: You're mistaken about what happened. My brother never urged me to join him. I asked him about it, and I learned the truth from reliable sources that were on your side.

original: Did he not rather   Discredit my authority with yours,   And make the wars alike against my stomach,   Having alike your cause?
translation: Isn't it the case, rather, that he undermined my authority as well as yours, and that his fight was against me, too, since I was on your side?

original: Of this my letters   Before did satisfy you. If you’ll patch a quarrel,   As matter whole you have to make it with,   It must not be with this.
translation: I told you all this in my letters earlier. If you want to pick a fight, you have enough other reasons to fight with me. It can't be about this.

original: You praise yourself By laying defects of judgment to me, but You patched up your excuses.
translation: You try to make yourself look better by attributing bad judgment to me, but you're coming up with poor excuses for yourself.

original: Not so, not so.   I know you could not lack, I am certain on ’t,   Very necessity of this thought,
translation: Not true, not true. I am certain that you can understand this important truth

original: that I,   Your partner in the cause ’gainst which he fought,   Could not with graceful eyes attend those wars   Which fronted mine own peace.
translation: —since I was your partner in the very cause my brother fought against, I couldn't possibly approve of the wars that undermined my own peace.

original: As for my wife,   I would you had her spirit in such another.   The third o’ th’ world is yours, which with a snaffle   You may pace easy, but not such a wife.
translation: As for my wife, I wish you could find a spirit like hers in another woman. A third of the world belongs to you, and you can  subdue  it easily, but you could not so easily subdue a woman like that.

original: Would we had all such wives, that the men might go to  wars with the women!
translation: I wish we all had such wives, so that men could go to battle accompanied by women!

original: So much uncurbable, her garboils, Caesar,   Made out of her impatience—which not wanted   Shrewdness of policy too—
translation: She was difficult to restrain, Caesar. She waged battles out of boredom—and not entirely without good strategy—

original: I grieving grant   Did you too much disquiet. For that you must   But say I could not help it.
translation: and I do apologetically admit that they caused you too much disturbance. In return, you must admit that I couldn't prevent it.

original: I wrote to you   When rioting in Alexandria.
translation: I wrote to you while you were entertaining yourself in Alexandria.

original: You   Did pocket up my letters and with taunts   Did gibe my missive out of audience.
translation: You ignored my letters and taunted my messenger until he left your sight.

original: Sir,   He fell upon me ere admitted, then.   Three kings I had newly feasted, and did want   Of what I was i’ th’ morning.
translation: Sir, in that instance, your messenger arrived before I had given him permission to come in. I had just been at dinner with three kings and I wasn't feeling quite myself in the morning.

original: But next day   I told him of myself, which was as much   As to have asked him pardon.
translation: But the next day I explained my situation to him, which was as good as asking him to pardon me.

original: Let this fellow   Be nothing of our strife. If we contend,   Out of our question wipe him.
translation: Don't let this person add to our quarrels. If we are going to fight, keep him out of it.

original: You have broken The article of your oath, which you shall never Have tongue to charge me with.
translation: You have broken the terms of your promise, and that's something you will never be able to accuse me of.

original: Soft, Caesar.
translation: Hold on, Caesar.

original: No, Lepidus, let him speak.   The honor is sacred which he talks on now,   Supposing that I lacked it.
translation: No, Lepidus, let him speak. Caesar is speaking about my honor now, and my honor is sacred, even if he thinks that I lack it.

original: —But, on, Caesar.   The article of my oath?
translation: But keep going, Caesar. The terms of my promise?

original: To lend me arms and aid when I required them, The which you both denied.
translation: To lend me weapons and help when I needed them, both of which you denied to me.

original: Neglected, rather,   And then when poisoned hours had bound me up   From mine own knowledge.
translation: I didn't deny it, I just neglected to do it—and that was only when an illness kept me from thinking clearly.

original: As nearly as I may   I’ll play the penitent to you, but mine honesty   Shall not make poor my greatness nor my power   Work without it.
translation: I'll apologize to you as much as I can, but my honesty in this matter doesn't diminish my greatness, and I will never use my power without honesty.

original: Truth is that Fulvia,   To have me out of Egypt, made wars here,   For which myself, the ignorant motive, do   So far ask pardon as befits mine honor   To stoop in such a case.
translation: It is true that Fulvia went to war here in order to draw me away from Egypt. For that, I—who unknowingly motivated this conflict—ask your forgiveness, just because it is fitting for my honor to humble myself in a situation like this.

original: ’Tis noble spoken.
translation: That's nobly said.

original: If it might please you to enforce no further   The griefs between ye,
translation: If you could agree to stop fighting about your past grievances,

original: to forget them quite   Were to remember that the present need   Speaks to atone you.
translation: then forgetting those grievances entirely would be a good way of remembering that you ought to be friends in this current crisis.

original: Worthily spoken, Maecenas.
translation: Well said, Maecenas.

original: Or, if you borrow one another’s love for the instant,  you may, when you hear no more words of Pompey, return  it again.
translation: Or, if you could just agree to be friends for now, you can always take it back later when Pompey is defeated.

original: You shall have time to wrangle in when you  have nothing else to do.
translation: You'll have time to fight when you have nothing else to do.

original: Thou art a soldier only. Speak no more.
translation: You're just a soldier. Don't speak anymore.

original: That truth should be silent I had almost forgot.
translation: I'd almost forgotten that people who speak the truth should be quiet.

original: You wrong this presence. Therefore speak no more.
translation: You're behaving inappropriately in this company. So don't talk anymore.

original: Go to, then. Your considerate stone.
translation: Fine, then. I'll be silent and obedient as a stone.

original: I do not much dislike the matter, but   The manner of his speech, for ’t cannot be   We shall remain in friendship, our conditions   So diff’ring in their acts.
translation: I don't dislike what he says so much as how he says it. For it's impossible for us to remain friends, since our temperaments differ and affect how we act.

original: Yet if I knew   What hoop should hold us stanch, from edge to edge   O’ th’ world I would pursue it.
translation: But if I knew of something that would keep us strong allies, I would pursue it from one end of the world to other.

original: Give me leave, Caesar.
translation: Give me permission to speak, Caesar.

original: Speak, Agrippa.
translation: Speak, Agrippa.

original: Thou hast a sister by the mother’s side, Admired Octavia. Great Mark Antony Is now a widower.
translation: You have a half-sister on your mother's side, the admired Octavia. Great Mark Antony is now a widower.

original: Say not so, Agrippa. If Cleopatra heard you, your reproof Were well deserved of rashness.
translation: Don't say that, Agrippa. If Cleopatra heard you, your rash statement would deserve the rebuke she would give you.

original: I am not married, Caesar. Let me hear Agrippa further speak.
translation: I am not married, Caesar. Let me hear Agrippa speak some more.

original: To hold you in perpetual amity,   To make you brothers, and to knit your hearts   With an unslipping knot, take Antony   Octavia to his wife,
translation: To keep you perpetual friends, to make you brothers, and to join your hearts in an unbreakable bond, let Antony take Octavia as his wife.

original: whose beauty claims   No worse a husband than the best of men,   Whose virtue and whose general graces speak   That which none else can utter.
translation: Her beauty makes her deserve no less a husband than the best of men, and her virtue and many graces reveal her to be a woman like no other.

original: By this marriage,   All little jealousies, which now seem great,   And all great fears, which now import their dangers,   Would then be nothing.
translation: Thanks to this marriage, all the little issues that seem so great now, and all the great fears that bring danger with them, would become nothing.

original: Truths would be tales,   Where now half-tales be truths. Her love to both   Would each to other and all loves to both   Draw after her.
translation: True accusations would be dismissed as rumors, whereas now even unbelievable rumors are taken for truths. Her love for both of you would make each of you love the other, and she would induce everyone else to love both of you.

original: Pardon what I have spoke,   For ’tis a studied, not a present thought,   By duty ruminated.
translation: Pardon me for saying this. It's not something that just occurred to me but something I have been thinking over carefully, moved by duty.

original: Will Caesar speak?
translation: Will you speak, Caesar?

original: Not till he hears how Antony is touched With what is spoke already.
translation: Not until I hear your response to what has already been said.

original: What power is in Agrippa If I would say, “Agrippa, be it so,” To make this good?
translation: If I said, "Agrippa, let this be so," what power would he have to make this happen?

original: The power of Caesar, and His power unto Octavia.
translation: He would have my power, and my power over Octavia.

original: May I never   To this good purpose, that so fairly shows,   Dream of impediment!
translation: May I never dream of interfering with this good plan, which seems so appealing!

original: Let me have thy hand   Further this act of grace, and from this hour   The heart of brothers govern in our loves   And sway our great designs!
translation: I will let you bring about this blessed event, and from this moment on, let's let our brotherly bond govern our love for each other and the great plans we make together.

original: There’s my hand.
translation: Here's my hand.

original: Happily, amen!
translation: Happily, amen!

original: I did not think to draw my sword ’gainst Pompey, For he hath laid strange courtesies and great Of late upon me. I must thank him only, Lest my remembrance suffer ill report; At heel of that, defy him.
translation: I hadn't planned to go into battle against Pompey, since he has lately done me honor of a great, uncommon kind. I must at least thank him, or risk appearing ungrateful. After that, I will oppose him.

original: Time calls upon ’s. Of us must Pompey presently be sought, Or else he seeks out us.
translation: Time is running short. We must go to Pompey immediately, or else he will come to us.

original: Where lies he?
translation: Where is he camped?

original: About the Mount Misena.
What is his strength by land?
translation: How strong are his land armies?

original: Great and increasing. But by sea he is an absolute master.
translation: Very strong and getting stronger. But he controls the sea completely.

original: So is the fame.   Would we had spoke together! Haste we for it.
translation: That's what I hear. If only we had met earlier! Let's move quickly.

original: Yet, ere we put ourselves in arms, dispatch we   The business we have talked of.
translation: But, before we get ready for battle, let's carry out the plan we talked about.

original: With most gladness, And do invite you to my sister’s view, Whither straight I’ll lead you.
translation: Most gladly. I invite you to meet my sister, and I'll take you straight to her.

original: Let us, Lepidus, not lack your company.
translation: Be sure to join us, Lepidus.

original: Noble Antony, not sickness should detain me.
translation: Noble Antony, not even sickness would keep me away.

original: Welcome from Egypt, sir.
translation: Welcome from Egypt, sir.

original: Half the heart of Caesar, worthy Maecenas! My honorable friend, Agrippa.
translation: Hail the most trusted counselor of Caesar, worthy Maecanus! My honorable friend, Agrippa.

original: Good Enobarbus!
translation: Good Enobarbus!

original: We have cause to be glad that matters are so well  digested. You stayed well by ’t in Egypt.
translation: We should be happy that things have worked out so well. You had a fine time in Egypt.

original: Ay, sir, we did sleep day out of countenance and made  the night light with drinking.
translation: Yes, sir, we slept through the day and brightened the night with drinking.

original: Eight wild boars roasted whole at a breakfast—and but  twelve persons there! Is this true?
translation: I hear there were eight wild boars roasted whole at breakfast—and for only twelve people! Is that true?

original: This was but as a fly by an eagle. We had much more  monstrous matter of feast, which worthily deserved  noting.
translation: That was nothing. We had much more extravagant feasts than that, which certainly deserve to be noted.

original: She’s a most triumphant lady, if report be square to  her.
translation: Cleopatra's a most magnificent lady, if the reports about her are true.

original: When she first met Mark Antony, she pursed up his heart upon the river of Cydnus.
translation: When she first met Mark Antony, she secured his heart on the river of Cydnus.

original: There she appeared indeed, or my reporter devised well  for her.
translation: She did appear there, or else the person who told me so made up a good story about her.

original: I will tell you.   The barge she sat in, like a burnished throne,   Burned on the water.
translation: I will tell you. She sat in a barge that looked like a polished throne, so bright that it was like a flame burning on the water.

original: The poop was beaten gold,   Purple the sails, and so perfumèd that   The winds were lovesick with them.
translation: The rear deck was made of hammered gold, and the sails were purple and so perfumed that the scent would have made the very wind fall in love with them.

original: The oars were  silver,   Which to the tune of flutes kept stroke, and made   The water which they beat to follow faster,   As amorous of their strokes.
translation: The oars were made of silver, and the oar-strokes kept time with the music of flutes, and when they beat the water, they made the water flow faster, as if moved by lust.

original: For her own person,   It beggared all description: she did lie   In her pavilion—cloth-of-gold, of tissue—   O’erpicturing that Venus where we see   The fancy outwork nature.
translation: As for Cleopatra's appearance, it was impossible to describe. As she lay under a tent—whose fabric was woven with golden thread—she  outdid even that picture of Venus  which was already idealized.

original: On each side her   Stood pretty dimpled boys, like smiling Cupids,   With divers-colored fans, whose wind did seem   To glow the delicate cheeks which they did cool,   And what they undid did.
translation: On either side of her stood handsome dimpled boys, like smiling Cupids, with fans of different colors. The breeze from the fans seemed to make her delicate cheeks glow even as they cooled them,  undoing the very thing they did .

original: Oh, rare for Antony!
translation: Oh, how nice for Antony!

original: Her gentlewomen, like the Nereides,   So many mermaids, tended her i’ th’ eyes,   And made their bends adornings.   At the helm   A seeming mermaid steers.
translation: Her attendants, resembling sea nymphs or mermaids, tended to her as she watched them closely, and their curtsies further decorated the boat. At the helm, a person dressed as a mermaid was steering.

original: The silken tackle   Swell with the touches of those flower-soft hands   That yarely frame the office. From the barge   A strange invisible perfume hits the sense   Of the adjacent wharfs.
translation: The silken sails and ropes swelled as they were touched by hands, soft as flowers, that skillfully carried out their tasks. A strange invisible perfume wafted from the barge and struck the noses of the people on the adjoining riverbanks.

original: The city cast   Her people out upon her, and Antony,   Enthroned i’ th’ marketplace, did sit alone,   Whistling to th’ air, which, but for vacancy,   Had gone to gaze on Cleopatra too   And made a gap in nature.
translation: Everyone left the city in order to see her, and Antony, sitting on a throne in the marketplace, sat alone, whistling to the air—even the air itself would have gone to look at her, if that wouldn't have caused a vacuum in the atmosphere.

original: Rare Egyptian!
translation: Rare Egyptian!

original: Upon her landing, Antony sent to her,   Invited her to supper. She replied   It should be better he became her guest,   Which she entreated.
translation: When she landed, Antony sent her a message inviting her to supper. She replied that it would be better if he were her guest, and she requested that he would be.

original: Our courteous Antony,   Whom ne’er the word of “No” woman heard speak,   Being barbered ten times o’er, goes to the feast,   And for his ordinary pays his heart   For what his eyes eat only.
translation: Our courteous Antony, who had never heard a woman say "no" to him, groomed himself with ten times the usual care and went to the feast. He paid for his meal by giving her his heart, looking at the food without eating it.

original: Royal wench! She made great Caesar lay his sword to bed. He plowed her, and she cropped.
I saw her once   Hop forty paces through the public street,
translation: I saw her once hop forty steps through the public street.

original: And having lost her breath, she spoke, and panted,   That she did make defect perfection,   And, breathless, pour breathe forth.
translation: Having lost her breath, she panted and said that she turned even a defect into something perfect—she poured out breath even when she was breathless.

original: Now Antony must leave her utterly.
translation: Now Antony must abandon her completely.

original: Never. He will not.   Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale   Her infinite variety.
translation: Never. He will not. Age cannot lessen her beauty, and even once you get to know her, the endless mood swings mean that you never get tired of her.

original: Other women cloy   The appetites they feed, but she makes hungry   Where most she satisfies, for vilest things   Become themselves in her, that the holy priests   Bless her when she is riggish.
translation: With other women, you stop desiring them after you have enjoyed them, but the more you have of Cleopatra, the more you want her. Even the grossest things become attractive in her, so that even the holy priests bless her when she has sexual urges.

original: If beauty, wisdom, modesty, can settle The heart of Antony, Octavia is A blessèd lottery to him.
translation: If beauty, wisdom, modesty, can secure Antony's heart, then Octavia is a valuable prize for him.

original: Let us go. Good Enobarbus, make yourself my guest Whilst you abide here.
translation: Let's go. Good Enobarbus, please be my guest while you are here.

original: Humbly, sir, I thank you.
translation: I humbly thank you, sir.

original: The world and my great office will  sometimes Divide me from your bosom.
translation: The great responsibilities I have to carry out all over the world will sometimes take me away from you.

original: All which time Before the gods my knee shall bow my prayers To them for you.
translation: And while you are gone, I will kneel before the gods and pray for you.

original: Good night, sir.
translation: Good night, sir.

original: —My Octavia,   Read not my blemishes in the world’s report.   I have not kept my square, but that to come   Shall all be done by th’ rule. Good night, dear lady.
translation: My Octavia, don't believe the critical things you will hear about me. I haven't behaved perfectly in the past, but in the future I will abide strictly by the rule-book. Good night, dear lady.

original: Good night, sir.
translation: Good night, sir.

original: Good night.
translation: Good night.

original: Now, sirrah, you do wish yourself in Egypt?
Would I had never come from thence, nor you thither.
translation: I wish I had never left and that you hadn't either.

original: If you can, your reason?
translation: If you can tell me, why do you say that?

original: I see it in my motion, have it not in my tongue. But  yet hie you to Egypt again.
translation: It's a feeling I have, I can't put it into words. But still, return to Egypt.

original: Say to me whose fortunes shall rise higher, Caesar’s or mine?
translation: Tell me who will have the better fortune, me or Caesar?

original: Caesar’s.   Therefore, O Antony, stay not by his side.   Thy dæmon—that thy spirit which keeps thee—is   Noble, courageous, high, unmatchable   Where Caesar’s is not.
translation: Caesar. Therefore, Antony, don't stay near him. Your  daemon —that spirit that sustains you—is noble, courageous, soaring, unequalled, while Caesar's is not.

original: But near him thy angel   Becomes afeard, as being o’erpowered. Therefore   Make space enough between you.
translation: But when you are near him, your daemon becomes afraid, as if overpowered. Therefore, create some distance between you and Caesar.

original: Speak this no more.
translation: Don't talk about this anymore.

original: To none but thee, no more but when to thee.
translation: I won't talk about it to anyone but you, and I won't speak about it anymore except to you.

original: If thou dost play with him at any game,   Thou art sure to lose, and of that natural luck   He beats thee ’gainst the odds.
translation: If you play games with Caesar, you are sure to lose, and because of your natural misfortune around him, he beats you even when the odds are against him.

original: Thy luster thickens   When he shines by. I say again, thy spirit   Is all afraid to govern thee near him,   But, he away, ’tis noble.
translation: Your prospects dim while his look bright. I tell you again, your daemon is afraid to guide you when you are near Caesar, but when he's away, your spirit is noble.

original: Get thee gone. Say to Ventidius I would speak with him.
translation: Get going. Tell Ventidius that I wish to speak with him.

original: Trouble yourselves no further. Pray you, hasten Your generals after.
translation: Don't trouble yourselves any further. Please, hurry after your generals.

original: Sir, Mark Antony Will e’en but kiss Octavia, and we’ll follow.
translation: Sir, Mark Antony is only going to kiss Octavia, and then we'll follow.

original: Till I shall see you in your soldiers’ dress, Which will become you both, farewell.
translation: Until I see you dressed like soldiers, which will suit you both well, goodbye.

original: We shall, As I conceive the journey, be at the Mount Before you, Lepidus.
translation: As I anticipate it, we will be at Mount Misenum before you, Lepidus.

original: Your way is shorter. My purposes do draw me much about. You’ll win two days upon me.
translation: Your route is shorter. I have business that will take me to many different places. You'll get there two days before I will.

original: Sir, good success.
translation: Sir, we wish you luck.

original: Farewell.
translation: Farewell.

original: Give me some music. Music, moody food Of us that trade in love.
translation: Play me some music. Music is the best emotional sustenance for those of us who are in love.

original: The music, ho!
translation: Play the music!

original: Let it alone. Let’s to billiards. Come, Charmian.
translation: Forget the music. Let's play billiards. Come, Charmian.

original: My arm is sore. Best play with Mardian.
translation: My arm is sore. You had better play with Mardian.

original: As well a woman with an eunuch played As with a woman.—Come, you’ll play with me, sir?
translation: It's the same to play with a woman as it is with a eunuch.  Come, you'll play with me, sir?

original: As well as I can, madam.
translation: As well as I can, madam.

original: And when good will is showed, though ’t come too short,   The actor may plead pardon. I’ll none now.
translation: And if an actor tries his best, even if his performance isn't very good, he can still ask for pardon. I don't want to play anymore.

original: Give me mine angle. We’ll to th’ river. There,   My music playing far off, I will betray   Tawny-finned fishes.
translation: Give me my fishing rod. We'll go to the river. There, with my music playing from a distance, I'll catch the golden-finned fishes.

original: My bended hook shall pierce   Their slimy jaws, and as I draw them up   I’ll think them every one an Antony   And say, “Aha! You’re caught.”
translation: My curved hook will pierce their slimy jaws, and as I pull them up, I'll imagine that every one of them is Antony and say, "Aha! I've caught you!"

original: ’Twas merry when   You wagered on your angling,
translation: It was a good joke when you  bet on your fishing ,

original: when your diver   Did hang a salt fish on his hook, which he   With fervency drew up.
translation: and you had your diver go down and put a dried fish on his hook, which he pulled out enthusiastically.

original: That time—Oh, times!—   I laughed him out of patience, and that night   I laughed him into patience.
translation: That time—oh, the times we had!—that I laughed at him until he lost patience, and that night, I satisfied him again.

original: And next morn,   Ere the ninth hour, I drunk him to his bed,   Then put my tires and mantles on him, whilst   I wore his sword Philippan.
translation: And the next morning, before nine o'clock, I got him drunk and sent him to bed, and then put my clothes and headdresses on him, while I put on his  sword .

original: Madam, madam—
translation: Madam, madam—

original: Antonio’s dead! If thou say so, villain,   Thou kill’st thy mistress. But well and free,   If thou so yield him, there is gold,
translation: Antony's dead! If you tell me that,  villain , you kill me. But if you tell me that he is well and has not been captured—if you report that about him—then I will give you gold

original: and here   My bluest veins to kiss
translation: and here, my blue-blooded hand to kiss

original: —a hand that kings   Have lipped, and trembled kissing.
translation: —a hand that kings have kissed, and trembled while they kissed it.

original: First, madam, he is well.
translation: First, madam, he is well.

original: Why, there’s more gold. But, sirrah, mark, we use   To say the dead are well.
translation: Why, there's more gold. But, sir, pay attention, we use to use the word "well" to describe the dead.

original: Bring it to that,   The gold I give thee will I melt and pour   Down thy ill-uttering throat.
translation: If that's what you mean, I will melt the gold I've given you and pour it down that throat of yours that tells me such terrible news.

original: Good madam, hear me.
translation: Good madam, listen to me.

original: Well, go to, I will.   But there’s no goodness in thy face—if Antony   Be free and healthful, so tart a favor   To trumpet such good tidings!
translation: Well, fine, I will.  But there's no goodness in your face—if Antony is free and well, it's odd that he would send such a sour face to bring such good news!

original: If not well,   Thou shouldst come like a Fury crowned with snakes,   Not like a formal man.
translation: But if he isn't well, you should have appeared like a  Fury  with a crown of snakes, not so calm and well-dressed.

original: Will ’t please you hear me?
translation: Will you please listen to me?

original: I have a mind to strike thee ere thou speak’st.
translation: I have half a mind to strike you before you speak.

original: Yet if thou say Antony lives, is well,   Or friends with Caesar, or not captive to him,   I’ll set thee in a shower of gold and hail   Rich pearls upon thee.
translation: But if you tell me that Antony lives, that he's well, that he's friends with Caesar or that he's not Caesar's prisoner, then I'll shower you with gold and greet you with rich pearls.

original: Madam, he’s well.
translation: Madam, he's well.

original: Well said.
translation: Well said.

original: And friends with Caesar.
translation: And friends with Caesar.

original: Th’ art an honest man.
translation: You are a good man.

original: Caesar and he are greater friends than ever.
translation: Caesar and he are greater friends than ever.

original: Make thee a fortune from me.
translation: I will give you a fortune.

original: But yet, madam—
translation: But yet, madam—

original: I do not like “But yet.” It does allay   The good precedence. Fie upon “But yet.”   “But yet” is as a jailer to bring forth   Some monstrous malefactor.
translation: I do not like the sound of "But yet." It casts a shadow on the previous good news. Down with "But yet." "But yet" are the words you'll use to introduce some terrible news.

original: Prithee, friend,   Pour out the pack of matter to mine ear,   The good and bad together. He’s friends with Caesar,   In state of health, thou say’st, and, thou say’st,  free.
translation: Please, friend, tell me all your news at once, both the good and the bad. He's friends with Caesar, he's well, you say, and you say that he's free.

original: Free, madam, no. I made no such report. He’s bound unto Octavia.
For what good turn?
For the best turn i’ th’ bed.
translation: For the best turn, in bed.

original: I am pale, Charmian.
translation: I am pale, Charmian.

original: Madam, he’s married to Octavia.
translation: Madam, he's married to Octavia.

original: The most infectious pestilence upon thee!
translation: May the most infectious disease come upon you!

original: Good madam, patience.
translation: Good madam, patience.

original: What say you?
translation: What did you say?

original: Gracious madam, I that do bring the news made not the match.
translation: Gracious madam, I brought the news, but I did not arrange the marriage.

original: Say ’tis not so, a province I will give thee   And make thy fortunes proud.
translation: Say that it isn't so, and I will give you a territory and build up your fortunes.

original: The blow thou hadst   Shall make thy peace for moving me to rage,   And I will boot thee with what gift beside   Thy modesty can beg.
translation: The blow that I gave you will make up for you making me angry, and I'll enrich you with whatever other gift your lowly self can ask for.

original: He’s married, madam.
translation: He's married, madam.

original: Rogue, thou hast lived too long.
translation: Scoundrel, you have lived too long.

original: Nay then, I’ll run. What mean you, madam? I have made no fault.
translation: No, I'll run. What are you doing, madam? I have done nothing wrong.

original: Good madam, keep yourself within yourself. The man is innocent.
translation: Good madam, pull yourself together. That man is innocent.

original: Some innocents ’scape not the thunderbolt.
translation: Some innocent people don't escape punishment.

original: Melt Egypt into Nile, and kindly creatures   Turn all to serpents.
translation: Let Egypt melt into the Nile and let all sweet creatures turn into serpents.

original: Call the slave again.   Though I am mad, I will not bite him. Call!
translation: Call that lowborn messenger again. Even though I am angry, I will not hurt him. Call!

original: He is afeard to come.
translation: He's afraid to come.

original: I will not hurt him.   These hands do lack nobility that they strike   A meaner than myself,
translation: I will not hurt him.  It would be dishonorable for my hands to strike someone of lower rank than myself,

original: since I myself   Have given myself the cause.
translation: since I am the cause of my anger, by caring about Antony so much.

original: I have done my duty.
translation: I have done my duty.

original: Is he married? I cannot hate thee worser than I do If thou again say “yes.”
translation: Is he married? I cannot hate you worse than I already do if you say "yes" again.

original: He’s married, madam.
translation: He's married, madam.

original: The gods confound thee! Dost thou hold there still?
translation: May the gods destroy you! Do you still stand by that statement?

original: Should I lie, madam?
translation: Should I lie, madam?

original: Oh, I would thou didst,   So half my Egypt were submerged and made   A cistern for scaled snakes!
translation: Oh, I wish you were lying, even if meant half of Egypt had to be submerged in water and turned into a pool for scaly snakes!

original: Go, get thee hence.   Hadst thou Narcissus in thy face, to me   Thou wouldst appear most ugly. He is married?
translation: Go, get out of here. Even if you were as handsome as  Narcissus , you would seem entirely ugly to me. He is married?

original: I crave your highness’ pardon.
translation: I beg your highness's pardon.

original: He is married?
translation: He is married?

original: Take no offense that I would not offend you. To punish me for what you make me do Seems much unequal. He’s married to Octavia.
translation: Do not take offense, since I do not wish to offend you. It seems very unfair to punish me for doing what you order me to. He's married to Octavia.

original: Oh, that his fault should make a knave of thee,   That art not what th’ art sure of! Get thee hence.
translation: Oh, what a pity that his fault should turn you into a scoundrel, since you aren't a bad man even though you bring bad news! Get going.

original: The merchandise which thou hast brought from Rome   Are all too dear for me. Lie they upon thy hand   And be undone by ’em!
translation: The merchandise you brought with you from Rome is too expensive for me. Leave with your  goods on your hands and be ruined by them !

original: Good your highness, patience.
translation: My good queen, have patience.

original: In praising Antony, I have dispraised Caesar.
translation: Whenever I praised Antony, I also insulted Caesar.

original: Many times, madam.
translation: Many times, madam.

original: I am paid for ’t now. Lead me from hence.   I faint.
translation: I'm punished for it now. Lead me away from here. I faint.

original: O Iras, Charmian! ’Tis no matter.—   Go to the fellow, good Alexas.
translation: Oh Iras, Charmian! It doesn't matter—Go to the messenger, good Alexas.

original: Bid him   Report the feature of Octavia: her years,   Her inclination. Let him not leave out   The color of her hair. Bring me word quickly.
translation: Tell him to describe Octavia's features: her age, her temperament. Don't let him leave out any detail, not even the color of her hair. Report back to me quickly.

original: Let him for ever go:—let him not—Charmian,   Though he be painted one way like a Gorgon,   The other way's a Mars. Bid you Alexas
translation: I'll forget about him forever—no I won't—Charmian, even though in some ways he seems like a monster, in other ways he's a god.

original: Bring me word how tall she is. Pity me, Charmian,   But do not speak to me. Lead me to my chamber.
translation: Tell Alexas to let me know how tall she is. Take pity on me, Charmian, but don't speak to me. Lead me to my chamber.

original: Your hostages I have, so have you mine, And we shall talk before we fight.
Most meet   That first we come to words, and therefore have we   Our written purposes before us sent,
translation: It is very appropriate that we talk first, and for that reason we sent our proposals beforehand.

original: Which, if thou hast considered, let us know   If ’twill tie up thy discontented sword   And carry back to Sicily much tall youth   That else must perish here.
translation: So, if you have considered them, let us know if we can convince you to stop waging such an unsatisfying war, and take your brave young troops back to Sicily, who would otherwise die here.

original: To you all three,   The senators alone of this great world,   Chief factors for the gods: I do not know   Wherefore my father should revengers want,   Having a son and friends,
translation: Let me tell the three of you, the sole rulers of this great world and gods' only messengers on earth: I don't know why my father's death shouldn't be  avenged , since he has a son and friends to do it.

original: since Julius Caesar,   Who at Philippi the good Brutus ghosted,   There saw you laboring for him.
translation: You fought on behalf of Julius Caesar, who appeared as a ghost to the good Brutus at Philippi.

original: What was ’t   That moved pale Cassius to conspire? And what   Made the all-honored, honest Roman Brutus,   With the armed rest, courtiers of beauteous freedom,   To drench the Capitol, but that they would   Have one man but a man?
translation: Why was it that pale Cassius started conspiring against Caesar? And what drove Brutus, who was honest and honored by all, along with the rest of the armed conspirators who were seeking glorious freedom, to drench the  Capitol in Caesar's blood , except that they didn't want one man to have  more power  than anyone else?

original: And that is it   Hath made me rig my navy, at whose burden   The angered ocean foams, with which I meant   To scourge th’ ingratitude that despiteful Rome   Cast on my noble father.
translation: And that is what made me equip my navy, under which the angry sea now foams. With this navy, I intend to punish spiteful Rome for its ingratitude towards my noble father.

original: Take your time.
translation: Go carefully now.

original: Thou canst not fear us, Pompey, with thy sails. We’ll speak with thee at sea. At land, thou know’st How much we do o’ercount thee.
translation: You cannot scare us, Pompey, with your navy. We'll engage your forces at sea. By land, you know how much greater our force is than yours.

original: At land indeed   Thou dost o’ercount me of my father’s house,
translation: On land, indeed, you  cheated me out of my father's house .

original: But since the cuckoo builds not for himself,   Remain in ’t as thou mayst.
translation: But, since I know you're  not making it your own , remain in it for the time being.

original: Be pleased to tell us— For this is from the present—how you take The offers we have sent you.
translation: Please tell us—because this is not what we've come to discuss—your response to the offers we've sent you.

original: There’s the point.
translation: That's the main point.

original: Which do not be entreated to, but weigh What it is worth embraced.
translation: Don't let yourself be tricked into anything, but consider carefully how much our offer is worth if you agree to it.

original: And what may follow, To try a larger fortune.
translation: And what may happen to you if you try to win a larger fortune by fighting us instead.

original: You have made me offer   Of Sicily, Sardinia. And I must   Rid all the sea of pirates, then, to send   Measures of wheat to Rome.
translation: You have offered me Sicily and Sardinia. In return, I would rid the whole sea of pirates and send shipments of wheat to Rome.

original: This ’greed upon   To part with unhacked edges and bear back   Our targes undinted.
translation: If we both agree to this, we will part peacefully, without drawing swords against each other and without denting our shields.

original: That’s our offer.
translation: That's our offer.

original: Know then   I came before you here a man prepared   To take this offer, but Mark Antony   Put me to some impatience.
translation: You should know, then, that I came here prepared to accept your offer, but Mark Antony irritated me somewhat.

original: —Though I lose   The praise of it by telling,
translation: Even though I detract from the honor of my good deed by telling you about it,

original: you must know,   When Caesar and your brother were at blows,   Your mother came to Sicily and did find   Her welcome friendly.
translation: you should know that when Caesar and your brother were at war, your mother came to Sicily and found warm hospitality.

original: I have heard it, Pompey, And am well studied for a liberal thanks Which I do owe you.
translation: I have heard that, Pompey, and I intend to thank you generously, which I know I owe you.

original: Let me have your hand.
translation: Give me your hand.

original: The beds i’ th’ East are soft, and thanks to you, That called me timelier than my purpose hither, For I have gained by ’t.
translation: The East is a very pleasant place, and I thank you for calling me away from it earlier than I had intended, because it has been good for me.

original: Since I saw you last There’s a change upon you.
translation: Since I last saw you, you've changed somehow.

original: Well, I know not   What counts harsh Fortune casts upon my face,
translation: Well, I can't tell how hard times have affected my face,

original: But in my bosom shall she never come   To make my heart her vassal.
translation: but I will never let those hard times subdue my courage.

original: Well met here.
translation: It is good for us all to meet here.

original: I hope so, Lepidus. Thus we are agreed. I crave our composition may be written And sealed between us.
translation: I hope so, Lepidus. We're agreed on this. I'd like our agreements to be written down and sealed by all of us.

original: That’s the next to do.
translation: That's the next thing for us to do.

original: We’ll feast each other ere we part, and let’s Draw lots who shall begin.
translation: We'll throw feasts for each other before we part, and we'll draw straws to see who will host the first one.

original: That will I, Pompey.
translation: I will, Pompey.

original: No, Antony, take the lot. But, first or last,   Your fine Egyptian cookery shall have   The fame.
translation: No, Antony, draw straws with us. But, whether you go first or last, your fine Egyptian style of cooking will carry away all the honor.

original: I have heard that Julius Caesar   Grew fat with feasting there.
translation: I've heard that Julius Caesar grew fat from feasting while he was there.

original: You have heard much.
translation: You've heard a lot.

original: I have fair meanings, sir.
translation: I mean well, sir.

original: And fair words to them.
translation: And your words sound good.

original: Then so much have I heard. And I have heard Apollodorus carried—
translation: That's what I heard. And I've heard that Apollodorus carried—

original: No more of that. He did so.
translation: No more about that. He did exactly that.

original: What, I pray you?
translation: What did he carry, I ask you?

original: A certain queen to Caesar in a mattress.
I know thee now. How far’st thou, soldier?
translation: I know who you are now. How are you doing, soldier?

original: Well, And well am like to do, for I perceive, Four feasts are toward.
translation: Well, and I believe I'll continue to do well, for I hear there are four feasts planned.

original: Let me shake thy hand. I never hated thee. I have seen thee fight When I have envied thy behavior.
translation: Let me shake your hand. I never bore you ill will. I've seen you fight so well that I envied your achievements.

original: Sir, I never loved you much, but I ha’ praised ye When you have well deserved ten times as much As I have said you did.
translation: Sir, I have never been very fond of you, but I have praised you—when you deserved ten times as much praise as what I gave you.

original: Enjoy thy plainness.   It nothing ill becomes thee.—
translation: Keep speaking straightforwardly like this. It suits you.

original: Aboard my galley I invite you all.   Will you lead, lords?
translation: I invite you all to come aboard my ship. Will you go first my lords?

original: Show ’s the way, sir.
translation: Please, lead us, sir.

original: Come.
translation: Come.

original: (aside]  Thy father, Pompey, would ne’er have made this treaty.    You and I have known, sir.
translation: Your father, Pompey, would never have made a treaty like this. [To ENOBARBUS] You and I have met before, sir.

original: At sea, I think.
translation: At sea, I think.

original: We have, sir.
translation: We have, sir.

original: You have done well by water.
translation: Your side has done well at sea.

original: And you by land.
translation: And your side has done well on land.

original: I will praise any man that will praise me, though it  cannot be denied what I have done by land.
translation: I'll say good things about anyone who says good things about me, but no one can deny what I have accomplished on land.

original: Nor what I have done by water.
translation: Or what I have accomplished at sea.

original: Yes, something you can deny for your own safety: you  have been a great thief by sea.
translation: Yes, there is something you ought to deny for your own good—the fact that you have been a thief at sea.

original: And you by land.
translation: And you've been a thief on land.

original: There I deny my land service. But give me your hand,  Menas.
translation: I deny that. But give me your hand, Menas.

original: All men’s faces are true, whatsome’er their hands are.
translation: All men have honest faces, even if their hands tend to steal.

original: But there is never a fair woman has a true face.
translation: But no beautiful woman has an honest face.

original: No slander. They steal hearts.
translation: That's true. They steal men's hearts.

original: We came hither to fight with you.
translation: We came here to fight with you.

original: For my part, I am sorry it is turned to a drinking.  Pompey doth this day laugh away his fortune.
translation: For my part, I'm sorry that the fighting has turned into feasting. By entertaining your leaders today, Pompey throws away his fortune.

original: If he do, sure he cannot weep ’t back again.
translation: If he does, I'm sure he cannot get it back by crying.

original: You’ve said, sir. We looked not for Mark Antony here.  Pray you, is he married to Cleopatra?
translation: That's true, sir. We didn't expect to see Mark Antony here. Please tell me, is he married to Cleopatra?

original: Caesar’s sister is called Octavia.
translation: Caesar's sister is called Octavia.

original: True, sir. She was the wife of Caius Marcellus.
translation: True, sir. She was the wife of Caius Marcellus.

original: But she is now the wife of Marcus Antonius.
translation: But now she's the wife of Mark Antony.

original: Pray ye, sir?
translation: Really, sir?

original: ’Tis true.
translation: It's true.

original: Then is Caesar and he forever knit together.
translation: Then Caesar and he are bound in friendship forever.

original: If I were bound to divine of this unity, I would not  prophesy so.
translation: If I had to make a prediction, I wouldn't guess so.

original: I think the policy of that purpose made more in the  marriage than the love of the parties.
translation: I think the marriage was arranged more for that political purpose, rather than the love between the couple.

original: I think so too. But you shall find the band that seems  to tie their friendship together will be the very  strangler of their amity. Octavia is of a holy, cold,  and still conversation.
translation: I think so too. But you'll find that the arrangement that was supposed to bind them in friendship will turn out to kill their friendship. Octavia has a very pious, cold, and quiet temperament.

original: Who would not have his wife so?
translation: Who wouldn't want a wife like that?

original: Not he that himself is not so, which is Mark Antony. He will to his Egyptian dish again.
translation: Not someone who doesn't share that disposition—Mark Antony. He'll return to his Egyptian lover again.

original: Then shall the sighs  of Octavia blow the fire up in Caesar, and, as I said  before, that which is the strength of their amity shall  prove the immediate author of their variance.
translation: Then Octavia's sorrow will anger Caesar, and, as I said before, the source of their friendship will ultimately prove a source of conflict.

original: Antony  will use his affection where it is. He married but his  occasion here.
translation: Antony will return to the woman he's really fond of. He only married Octavia for pragmatic reasons.

original: And thus it may be. Come, sir, will you aboard? I have  a health for you.
translation: And it may turn out that way. Come, sir, will you come aboard? I'll drink a toast to you.

original: I shall take it, sir. We have used our throats in  Egypt.
translation: I'll take it, sir. We're used to drinking in Egypt.

original: Come, let’s away.
translation: Come, let's go.

original: Here they’ll be, man. Some o’ their plants are  ill-rooted already. The least wind i’ th’ world will  blow them down.
translation: They'll eat in here, friend. Some of them are unsteady on their feet already. The smallest breeze in the world would knock them over.

original: Lepidus is high-colored.
translation: Lepidus is flushed.

original: They have made him drink alms-drink.
As they pinch one another by the disposition, he cries  out, “No more,” reconciles them to his entreaty and  himself to th’ drink.
translation: As their personalities clash, he cries, "No more quarreling," urges them to be friends, and resigns himself to another drink.

original: But it raises the greater war between him and his  discretion.
translation: But all this drinking makes him lose his judgment.

original: Why, this it is to have a name in great men’s  fellowship. I had as lief have a reed that will do me no service as a partisan I could not heave.
To be called into a huge sphere, and not to be seen to  move in ’t, are the holes where eyes should be, which  pitifully disaster the cheeks.
Thus do they, sir: they take the flow o’ th’ Nile   By certain scales i’ th’ Pyramid.
translation: This is what they do, sir. They measure the depth of the Nile by  certain markings on the Pyramid .

original: They know   By th’ height, the lowness, or the mean, if dearth   Or foison follow.
translation: They know how low it goes by measuring how high it goes, and they know by the middle position whether famine or abundance will follow.

original: The higher Nilus swells   The more it promises. As it ebbs, the seedsman   Upon the slime and ooze scatters his grain,   And shortly comes to harvest.
translation: The higher the Nile floods, the more fertile it will make the land. As it ebbs, the farmer goes out on the wet, slimy ground and scatters his seeds, and he soon has a harvest.

original: You’ve strange serpents there?
translation: You have strange serpents in Egypt?

original: Ay, Lepidus.
translation: Yes, Lepidus.

original: Your serpent of Egypt is bred now of your mud by the  operation of your sun. So is your crocodile.
They are so.
translation: They are indeed.

original: Sit, and some wine. A health to Lepidus!
translation: Sit down, and have some wine. [To everyone] A toast to Lepidus!

original: I am not so well as I should be, but I’ll ne’er out.
translation: I'm not as well as I ought to be, but I'll never miss a round.

original: Not till you have slept. I fear me you’ll be in till  then.
translation: Not till you fall asleep. I'm afraid you'll be in a drunken stupor then.

original: Nay, certainly, I have heard the Ptolemies’ pyramises  are very goodly things. Without contradiction I have  heard that.
translation: No, certainly, I have heard the Egyptian pyramids are very magnificent things. Without doubt I've heard that.

original: Pompey, a word.
translation: Pompey, let me have a word with you.

original: Say in mine ear. What is ’t?
translation: Whisper it to me. What is it?

original: Forsake thy seat, I do beseech thee,  captain, And hear me speak a word.
translation: Get up, I ask you, captain, and listen to me for a moment.

original: Forbear me till anon.—This wine for  Lepidus!
translation: Leave me alone for a while. [To the rest of the company] This wine is for Lepidus!

original: What manner o’ thing is your crocodile?
translation: What kind of thing is a crocodile?
