original: It is shaped, sir, like itself, and it is as broad as  it hath breadth. It is just so high as it is, and moves  with its own organs. It lives by that which nourisheth  it, and, the elements once out of it, it transmigrates.
What color is it of?
translation: What color is it?

original: Of it own color too.
translation: The color that it is.

original: ’Tis a strange serpent.
translation: That's a strange animal.

original: ’Tis so. And the tears of it are wet.
translation: It is. And its tears are wet.

original: Will this description satisfy him?
translation: Will he be satisfied with that description?

original: With the health that Pompey gives  him, else he is a very epicure.
translation: He'll be satisfied with that and with the toast that Pompey drank with him, or else he really has an insatiable appetite.

original: Go hang, sir, hang! Tell me of that?  Away! Do as I bid you.—Where’s this cup I called for?
translation: Go to hell, sir, go! You talk to me about that? Get away! Do as I told you. [To the company] Where's the drink I asked for?

original: If for the sake of merit thou wilt  hear me, Rise from thy stool.
translation: If you'll listen to me for the sake of your own greatness, get up from your seat.

original: I think th’ art mad.
translation: I think you're crazy.

original: I have ever held my cap off to thy fortunes.
translation: I have always done my best to help you.

original: Thou hast served me with much faith. What’s else to  say?—     Be jolly, lords.
translation: You have served me faithfully. What else do you have to say? Be merry, lords.

original: These quicksands, Lepidus, Keep off them, for you sink.
translation: Keep away from the drinks, Lepidus, for you're drowning in them.

original: Wilt thou be lord of all the world?
translation: Do you want to be the ruler of the whole world?

original: What sayst thou?
translation: What do you mean?

original: Wilt thou be lord of the whole world? That’s twice.
translation: Do you want to be the ruler of the whole world? Now I've said it twice.

original: How should that be?
translation: How could that come about?

original: But entertain it, And, though thou think me poor, I am the man Will give thee all the world.
translation: Listen to what I have to say, and even though you think I'm a poor man, I'll be the person who gave you the whole world.

original: Hast thou drunk well?
translation: Are you drunk?

original: No, Pompey, I have kept me from the cup.   Thou art, if thou dar’st be, the earthly Jove.
translation: No, Pompey, I haven't had a drink tonight. You could, if you dared, be the king of the gods on earth.

original: Whate’er the ocean pales or sky inclips   Is thine, if thou wilt ha ’t.
translation: Whatever land the ocean surrounds or the sky stretches over, will be yours, if you wish.

original: Show me which way.
translation: Tell me how.

original: These three world-sharers, these competitors,   Are in thy vessel.
translation: Your competitors, the three men who govern the world between them, are on your ship.

original: Let me cut the cable,   And, when we are put off, fall to their throats.   All there is thine.
translation: Let me cut the ropes, and, when we have set off from shore, let me kill them. Then all the world will be yours.

original: Ah, this thou shouldst have done   And not have spoke on ’t! In me ’tis villainy,   In thee ’t had been good service.
translation: Oh, you should have done this and not told me beforehand! It would be villainous of me to do it—for you, it would just have been the act of a good servant.

original: Thou must know,   ’Tis not my profit that does lead mine honor;   Mine honor, it. Repent that e’er thy tongue   Hath so betrayed thine act.
translation: You should know that I don't sacrifice my honor for profit; rather, I give up profit for the sake of my honor. You should regret that you ever mentioned this plan to me.

original: Being done unknown,   I should have found it afterwards well done,   But must condemn it now. Desist, and drink.
translation: If you had done it without my knowledge, I would have said afterwards that you had done well—but now, I must condemn the action. Put the thought of it aside, and drink.

original: For this,   I’ll never follow thy palled fortunes more.
translation: Because of this, I'll no longer follow you and hope for your success.

original: Who seeks and will not take when once ’tis offered   Shall never find it more.
translation: Whoever seeks power and won't take it when it is offered will never find the opportunity again.

original: This health to Lepidus!
translation: A toast to Lepidus!

original: Bear him ashore.—I’ll pledge it for him, Pompey.
translation: Carry Lepidus ashore. [To POMPEY] I'll drink for him, Pompey.

original: Here’s to thee, Menas!
translation: Here's to you, Menas!

original: Enobarbus, welcome.
translation: Enobarbus, welcome.

original: Fill till the cup be hid.
translation: Fill the cup until it overflows.

original: There’s a strong fellow, Menas.
translation: There's a strong man, Menas.

original: Why?
translation: What's going on there?

original: He bears The third part of the world, man. Seest not?
translation: He carries one third of the world, man. Don't you see?

original: The third part, then, is drunk. Would it were all, That it might go on wheels!
translation: His third, then, is drunk. If only the whole world were drunk, so it would all spin with joy!

original: Drink thou. Increase the reels.
translation: Have a drink. Increase the spinning.

original: Come.
translation: Come.

original: This is not yet an Alexandrian feast.
translation: This feast is not yet as wild as an Egyptian feast.

original: It ripens towards it. Strike the vessels, ho! Here’s to Caesar.
translation: It's getting there. Open more casks, I say! Here's to Caesar.

original: I could well forbear ’t. It’s monstrous labor when I wash my brain And it grows fouler.
translation: I could do without it. It's unnatural for me to drink if it makes my brain become cloudy.

original: Be a child o’ th’ time.
translation: Get into the spirit of things.

original: Possess it, I’ll make answer. But I had rather fast from all four days Than drink so much in one.
translation: You take a drink and I'll take another. But I'd rather go without eating for four days than drink so much in one day.

original: Ha! My brave emperor, Shall we dance now the Egyptian bacchanals And celebrate our drink?
translation: Ha! My noble emperor, shall we dance the Egyptian bacchanals now and celebrate our drinking?

original: Let’s ha ’t, good soldier.
translation: Let's see it, good soldier.

original: Come, let’s all take hands Till that the conquering wine hath steeped our sense In soft and delicate Lethe.
translation: Come, let's all take hands, until this wine conquers us and sends us into a calm, gentle, forgetful stupor.

original: All take hands.   Make battery to our ears with the loud music,   The while I’ll place you; then the boy shall sing.
translation: Everyone grab hands.  Batter our ears with the loud music, while I position you. Then the boy will sing.

original: The holding every man shall beat as loud   As his strong sides can volley.
translation: Every man will beat out the refrain as loudly as his strong body is able.

original: Come, thou monarch of the vine,   Plumpy Bacchus with pink eyne!
translation: Come, you king of the vine, Plump Bacchus with pink eyes!

original: In thy vats our cares be drowned,   With thy grapes our hairs be crowned.
translation: In your vats, we will drown our cares, With your grapes, we will crown our hair.

original: (Singing) Cup us till the world go round,   Cup us till the world go round!
translation: Fill our cups until the world spins,Fill our cups until the world spins.

original: What would you more?
translation: What more of a feast could you want?

original: —Pompey, good night.
translation: Pompey, good night.

original: Good brother,   Let me request you off. Our graver business   Frowns at this levity.
translation: Good brother, let me ask you to come off the ship. Given our serious business, we shouldn't be fooling around like this.

original: —Gentle lords, let’s part.   You see we have burnt our cheeks. Strong Enobarb   Is weaker than the wine; and mine own tongue   Splits what it speaks.
translation: Noble lords, let's part. You see we've become flushed. Strong Enobarbus is not strong enough to handle the wine, and I cannot articulate my words clearly.

original: The wild disguise hath almost   Anticked us all. What needs more words? Good night.   Good Antony, your hand.
translation: This wild drunkenness has almost made fools out of all of us. What else needs to be said? Good night. Good Antony, give me your hand.

original: I’ll try you on the shore.
translation: I'll test your endurance at drinking on shore.

original: And shall, sir. Give ’s your hand.
translation: Yes you will, sir. Give me your hand.

original: O Antony, You have my father’s house. But what? We are friends. Come, down into the boat.
Take heed you fall not.
translation: Be careful not to fall.

original: No, to my cabin. These drums, these trumpets, flutes!  What! Let Neptune hear we bid a loud farewell To these great fellows. Sound and be hanged, sound out!
Hoo! says ’a. There’s my cap.
translation: Hoo, I say! There's my cap!

original: Hoo! Noble captain, come.
translation: Hoo! Noble captain, come.

original: Now, darting Parthia, art thou struck, and now   Pleased fortune does of Marcus Crassus’ death   Make me revenger.
translation: Now the nation of Parthia, with all its archers, is defeated, and now fortune has given me the chance to avenge  Marcus Crassus' death .

original: Bear the King’s son’s body   Before our army. Thy Pacorus, Orodes,   Pays this for Marcus Crassus.
translation: Carry the King's son's body in front of our army. Your son Pacorus, Orodes, loses his life in payment for Marcus Crassus's death.

original: Noble Ventidius,   Whilst yet with Parthian blood thy sword is warm,   The fugitive Parthians follow.
translation: Noble Ventidus, while you still have momentum from the defeat of the Parthian army, follow the fleeing Parthians who have escaped.

original: Spur through Media,   Mesopotamia, and the shelters whither   The routed fly.
translation: Ride through  Media, Mesopotamia , all the places where the exiled Parthians hope to seek refuge.

original: So thy grand captain, Antony,   Shall set thee on triumphant chariots and   Put garlands on thy head.
translation: For this, your grand captain, Antony, will give you a  triumphal procession  on a chariot and crown your head with garlands.

original: O Silius, Silius,   I have done enough. A lower place, note well,   May make too great an act.
translation: O Silius, Silius, I have accomplished enough. Listen, it's possible for someone of low rank to overstep himself.

original: For learn this, Silius:   Better to leave undone than by our deed   Acquire too high a fame when him we serve’s away.
translation: You should be aware of this, Silius: it's better not to do something than to do it and thereby win too much glory while our commander is away.

original: Caesar and Antony have ever won   More in their officer than person. Sossius,   One of my place in Syria, his lieutenant,   For quick accumulation of renown,   Which he achieved by th’ minute, lost his favor.
translation: Caesar and Antony have won more battles through the skill of their officers than through their own ability. Sossius, a soldier in Syria with the same rank as myself, was Antony's lieutenant, and because he achieved glory too quickly and kept gaining it, he fell out of Antony's favor.

original: Who does i’ th’ wars more than his captain can   Becomes his captain’s captain; and ambition,   The soldier’s virtue, rather makes choice of loss   Than gain which darkens him.
translation: Whoever accomplishes more in war than his captain becomes a greater soldier than him—and because soldiers are generally ambitious, a captain would prefer to lose a battle than have someone else win it and have him pale in comparison .

original: I could do more to do Antonius good,   But ’twould offend him, and in his offense   Should my performance perish.
translation: I could accomplish more to help Antony's cause, but it would offend him, and if he were offended, I would lose all the glory of what I have already done.

original: Thou hast, Ventidius, that Without the which a soldier and his sword Grants scarce distinction. Thou wilt write to Antony?
translation: A sword is just a tool, Ventidius, unless it is being wielded by someone with your qualities. You'll write to Antony?

original: I’ll humbly signify what in his name,   That magical word of war, we have effected:
translation: I'll humbly tell him what we have done in his name, that magical wording.

original: How with his banners and his well-paid ranks   The ne’er-yet-beaten horse of Parthia   We have jaded out o’ th’ field.
translation: I'll tell him how, with his banners and his well-paid troops, we beat the calvary of Parthia out of the field like broken-down old horses, even though they had never been beaten before.

original: Where is he now?
translation: Where is he now?

original: He purposeth to Athens, whither, with what haste The weight we must convey with’s will permit, We shall appear before him.    On,  there. Pass along!
translation: He intends to go to Athens, where we must meet him as fast as we can, given the load that we carry.  Keep going, there. Move along!

original: What, are the brothers parted?
They have dispatched with Pompey; he is gone.   The other three are sealing.
translation: They have settled their affairs with Pompey; he is gone. The other three are signing the agreement.

original: Octavia weeps   To part from Rome. Caesar is sad, and Lepidus,   Since Pompey’s feast, as Menas says, is troubled   With the greensickness.
translation: Octavia weeps that she has to leave Rome. Caeasar is sad, and Menas says that Lepidus, since Pompey's feast, is suffering from a  hangover .

original: ’Tis a noble Lepidus.
translation: Lepidus is a noble man.

original: A very fine one. Oh, how he loves Caesar!
translation: A very fine one. Oh, how he loves Caesar!

original: Nay, but how dearly he adores Mark Antony!
translation: Yes, but how dearly he loves Mark Antony!

original: Caesar? Why, he’s the Jupiter of men.
translation: Caesar? Why, he's like the king of the gods among men.

original: What’s Antony? The god of Jupiter.
translation: Then what is Antony? He is the king of the king of the gods.

original: Spake you of Caesar? How, the nonpareil!
translation: Did you insult Caesar? Why, he is without equal!

original: O Antony, O thou Arabian bird!
Would you praise Caesar, say “Caesar.” Go no further.
translation: If you want to praise Caesar, simply say "Caesar." The name alone conveys all his great qualities.

original: Indeed, he plied them both with excellent praises.
translation: Indeed, Lepidus praised both of them highly.

original: But he loves Caesar best; yet he loves Antony.
translation: But he loves Caesar most; still, he does love Antony.

original: Hoo! Hearts, tongues, figures, scribes, bards, poets,  cannot   Think, speak, cast, write, sing, number—hoo!—   His love to Antony.
translation: Ha! Hearts, tongues, letters, writers, singers, poets, cannot think, speak, calculate, write, sing, or make verses—ha!—that can adequately convey his love for Antony.

original: But as for Caesar,   Kneel down, kneel down, and wonder.
translation: But as for Caesar, the only appropriate reaction is to kneel down, kneel down, and be in awe.

original: Both he loves.
translation: He loves both of them.

original: They are his shards, and he their beetle.
translation: He is a beetle, and they are the wings he uses to fly.

original: Good fortune, worthy soldier, and farewell.
translation: Good luck, worthy soldier, and goodbye.

original: No further, sir.
translation: Speak no more, sir.

original: You take from me a great part of myself;   Use me well in ’t.
translation: You take a part of me away from myself by taking her; treat me well by treating her well.

original: —Sister, prove such a wife   As my thoughts make thee, and as my farthest bond   Shall pass on thy approof.
translation: Sister, be as good a wife as I believe you capable of being, so that the great commitment I have made will be justified by your behavior.

original: —Most noble Antony,   Let not the piece of virtue, which is set   Betwixt us as the cement of our love,   To keep it builded, be the ram to batter   The fortress of it.
translation: Most noble Antony, do not let this good woman—who joins us as brothers to secure our love and keep it firm—become the instrument that will destroy our love.

original: For better might we   Have loved without this mean, if on both parts   This be not cherished.
translation: For we might have been better friends without this intermediary, if she is not cherished by both of us.

original: Make me not offended In your distrust.
translation: Don't offend me by distrusting me.

original: I have said.
translation: I've said what I have to say.

original: You shall not find,   Though you be therein curious, the least cause   For what you seem to fear.
translation: You won't find any reason to be afraid, even though you seem quite anxious about it.

original: So the gods keep you   And make the hearts of Romans serve your ends.   We will here part.
translation: May the gods protect you and bring the Roman people to serve you loyally. We will part here.

original: Farewell, my dearest sister, fare thee well. The elements be kind to thee and make Thy spirits all of comfort! Fare thee well.
translation: Goodbye, dearest sister, take care. May you have good fortune so that your feelings will be ones of comfort! Take care.

original: My noble brother!
translation: My noble brother!

original: The April’s in her eyes; it is love’s spring, And these the showers to bring it on.    Be  cheerful.
translation: She weeps. April is the beginning of love, and she cries in order to bring it on.  Be cheerful.

original: Sir, look well to my husband’s house, and—
translation: Sir, take care of my husband's house, and—

original: What, Octavia?
translation: What, Octavia?

original: I’ll tell you in your ear.
translation: I'll whisper it to you.

original: Her tongue will not obey her heart, nor can   Her heart inform her tongue
translation: She cannot speak her true feelings, neither can her feelings tell her what she should say.

original: —the swan’s-down feather   That stands upon the swell at the full of tide   And neither way inclines.
translation: She is so  torn between her feelings  for her brother and her feelings for her husband that she cannot speak.

original: Will Caesar weep?
translation: Will Caesar weep?

original: He has a cloud in ’s face.
translation: His face is clouded over with emotion.

original: He were the worse for that, were he  a horse; So is he, being a man.
translation: That would be bad for him if he were a horse. It's also bad for him as a man.

original: Why, Enobarbus,   When Antony found Julius Caesar dead,
translation: Why, Enobarbus, when Antony found Julius Caesar's dead body,

original: He cried almost to roaring, and he wept   When at Philippi he found Brutus slain.
translation: he cried so much he was almost roaring, and he wept at  Philippi  when he found Brutus dead.

original: That year indeed he was troubled  with a rheum. What willingly he did confound he wailed, Believe ’t, till I wept too.
translation: That year, he was indeed struck with the flu. He cried at the death of a man he willingly brought down, so much that I wept too—believe it.

original: No, sweet Octavia, You shall hear from me still. The time shall not Outgo my thinking on you.
translation: No, sweet Octavia, you will always hear from me. Time will stop before I stop thinking about you.

original: Come, sir, come, I’ll wrestle with you in my strength of love. Look, here I have you.
translation: Come, sir, come, I'll challenge you to see who can love the most. Look, I'll show you.

original: Adieu. Be happy.
translation: Farewell. Be happy.

original: Let all the number of the stars give light To thy fair way.
translation: May all the stars light an easy path before you.

original: Farewell, farewell.
translation: Farewell, farewell.

original: Farewell.
translation: Farewell.

original: Where is the fellow?
translation: Where is the man?

original: Half afeard to come.
translation: He's afraid to come.

original: Go to, go to.—Come hither, sir.
translation: Never mind that, never mind. Come here, sir.

original: Good majesty, Herod of Jewry dare not look upon you But when you are well pleased.
That Herod’s head I’ll have! But how? When Antony is gone, Through whom I might command it?    Come  thou near.
translation: I'll have King Herod's head! But how? When Antony is gone, who will carry out my orders?  Come closer.

original: Most gracious majesty!
translation: Most gracious queen!

original: Didst thou behold Octavia?
translation: Did you see Octavia?

original: Ay, dread Queen.
translation: Yes, oh powerful Queen.

original: Where?
translation: Where?

original: Madam, in Rome. I looked her in the face, and saw her led Between her brother and Mark Antony.
translation: Madam, in Rome. I looked at her face, and I saw her walking between her brother and Mark Antony.

original: Is she as tall as me?
translation: Is she as tall as me?

original: She is not, madam.
translation: She is not, madam.

original: Didst hear her speak? Is she shrill-tongued or low?
translation: Did you hear her speak? Does she have a high voice or a low one?

original: Madam, I heard her speak. She is low-voiced.
translation: Madam, I heard her speak. She has a low voice.

original: That’s not so good. He cannot like her long.
translation: That's not very good for Octavia. He cannot like her for long.

original: Like her? O Isis, ’tis impossible.
translation: Like her? By Isis, that is impossible.

original: I think so, Charmian. Dull of tongue, and dwarfish.— What majesty is in her gait? Remember, If e’er thou looked’st on majesty.
translation: I think so, Charmian. She has a dull voice and she's short—does she walk in an elegant way? Recall, if you ever looked at a queen.

original: She creeps.   Her motion and her station are as one.
translation: She has a slow, hunched walk. She looks the same walking and standing still.

original: She shows a body rather than a life,   A statue than a breather.
translation: She has a body, not a form with life in it. She's more like a statue than a living, breathing woman.

original: Is this certain?
translation: Is this certain?

original: Or I have no observance.
translation: It is, or I have no power to observe.

original: Three in Egypt Cannot make better note.
translation: There's not three people in Egypt who can observe better than he can.

original: He’s very knowing, I do perceive ’t. There’s nothing in her yet. The fellow has good judgment.
translation: He's very shrewd, I can tell. I haven't heard about any good qualities in Octavia yet. The man has good judgment.

original: Excellent.
translation: Excellent.

original: Guess at her years, I prithee.
translation: Please, guess how old she is.

original: Madam, she was a widow—
translation: Madam, she was a widow—

original: Widow? Charmian, hark.
translation: Widow? Charmian, pay attention to this.

original: And I do think she’s thirty.
Bear’st thou her face in mind? Is ’t long or round?
translation: Do you remember her face? Is it long or round?

original: Round, even to faultiness.
translation: Round, even to a fault.

original: For the most part, too, they are foolish that are so. Her hair, what color?
translation: For the most part, people with round faces are foolish. What color is her hair?

original: Brown, madam, and her forehead As low as she would wish it.
There’s gold for thee.   Thou must not take my former sharpness ill.
translation: Here's money for you. You must not hold my previous hostility against me.

original: I will employ thee back again; I find thee   Most fit for business. Go make thee ready;   Our letters are prepared.
translation: I'll employ you for another task; I find that you're a very useful man. Get ready to go; our letters are ready.

original: A proper man.
translation: An admirable man.

original: Indeed, he is so. I repent me much That so I harried him. Why, methinks, by him, This creature’s no such thing.
translation: Indeed, he is. I'm very sorry that I harassed him so much. Why, judging by his report, I think that this Octavia woman really has no good qualities to speak of.

original: Nothing, madam.
translation: None, madam.

original: The man hath seen some majesty and should know.
translation: Antony has seen what royalty looks like, and he should know it when he sees it.

original: Hath he seen majesty? Isis else defend, And serving you so long!
translation: Has he seen royalty? Isis forbid that he has not seen royalty, after serving you so long!

original: I have one thing more to ask him yet, good Charmian— But ’tis no matter; thou shalt bring him to me Where I will write. All may be well enough.
translation: I have one more thing to ask him still, good Charmian—but it doesn't matter. You'll bring him to me and I'll write my letter. All may be well enough.

original: I warrant you, madam.
translation: I assure you, madam.

original: Nay, nay, Octavia, not only that—   That were excusable, that and thousands more   Of semblable import
translation: No, no, Octavia, it's not just that. That would be excusable, as would thousands of other crimes just like it.

original: —but he hath waged   New wars ’gainst Pompey; made his will, and read it   To public ear;   Spoke scantly of me; when perforce he could not   But pay me terms of honor, cold and sickly   He vented them, most narrow measure lent me.
translation: But he has also waged new wars against Pompey; and he has also written his will and  read it aloud in public . He has spoken badly of me, and when he was forced to say things in my favor, his words were cold and unenthusiastic and he gave me very little credit.

original: When the best hint was given him, he not took ’t,   Or did it from his teeth.
translation: Even when he had the strongest reason to praise me, he did not do it, or he did it very unwillingly.

original: O my good lord,   Believe not all, or, if you must believe,   Stomach not all.
translation: Oh my good lord, don't believe all the things you hear, or, if you must believe them, don't take so much offense at all of them.

original: A more unhappy lady,   If this division chance, ne’er stood between,   Praying for both parts.
translation: There will be no lady unhappier than I if you two fight. I'll be stuck in the middle, praying for you both.

original: The good gods will mock me presently,   When I shall pray “O bless my lord and husband!”   Undo that prayer by crying out as loud   “O bless my brother!”
translation: The gods will laugh at me when I pray for both my husband and my brother. "Oh bless my lord and husband!" when I undo that prayer by crying out just as earnestly, "Oh bless my brother!"

original: Husband win, win brother   Prays and destroys the prayer; no midway   ’Twixt these extremes at all.
translation: To pray that both my brother and husband win would be to  destroy the prayer . There's no way for both sides to find success.

original: Gentle Octavia,   Let your best love draw to that point which seeks   Best to preserve it.
translation: Gentle Octavia, give your most faithful love to the side that most worthily tries to deserve your love.

original: If I lose mine honor,   I lose myself; better I were not yours   Than yours so branchless.
translation: If I lose my honor, I lose myself. It would be better to have no husband, than for you to have a husband who was so defeated.

original: But, as you requested,   Yourself shall go between ’s. The meantime, lady,   I’ll raise the preparation of a war   Shall stain your brother. Make your soonest haste;   So your desires are yours.
translation: But, as you requested, you should negotiate between us. In the meantime, lady, I'll make such strong preparations for war that they will make your brother appear less powerful. Go as quickly as you can; then you'll get what you desire quickly.

original: Thanks to my lord.   The Jove of power make me most weak, most weak,   Your reconciler!
translation: Thank you, my lord. May the powerful king of the gods make me, who am most  weak , act as your mediator!

original: Wars ’twixt you twain would be   As if the world should cleave, and that slain men   Should solder up the rift.
translation: If you were to go to war with each other, it would be as if the world had split in two, and the chasm would have to be filled with the bodies of dead men.

original: When it appears to you where this begins,   Turn your displeasure that way, for our faults   Can never be so equal that your love   Can equally move with them.
translation: When it becomes apparent to you who started this conflict, turn your anger against that person. For our faults could never be so equal that you, in your love, could condemn them equally.

original: Provide your going;   Choose your own company and command what cost   Your heart has mind to.
translation: Get ready to leave. Choose your companions and make your preparations as expensive as you desire.

original: How now, friend Eros!
translation: How are you doing, my friend Eros!

original: There’s strange news come, sir.
translation: There's been some strange news, sir.

original: What, man?
translation: What, man?

original: Caesar and Lepidus have made wars upon Pompey.
translation: Caesar and Lepidus have declared war against Pompey.

original: This is old. What is the success?
translation: That's old news. How is the fight going?

original: Caesar, having made use of him in the wars ’gainst  Pompey, presently denied him rivality, would not let him partake in the glory of the action, and, not resting  here, accuses him of letters he had formerly wrote to  Pompey;
translation: Caesar used Lepidus to help him fight Pompey, but then immediately denied Lepidus equal power, wouldn't share the glory of the victory with him, and what's more, he's making accusations against him based on letters Lepidus had written to Pompey.

original: upon his own appeal seizes him. So the poor  third is up, till death enlarge his confine.
translation: Upon Caesar's accusations, Lepidus was arrested. So this poor  third  is imprisoned until he is freed by death.

original: Then, world, thou hast a pair of chaps, no more, And throw between them all the food thou hast, They’ll grind the one the other. Where’s Antony?
translation: Then, world, you have a pair of leaders, no more, and even if you offer them all the wealth you have, one will still destroy the other. Where's Antony?

original: He’s walking in the garden—   (imitating anger)   thus,
translation: He's walking in the garden— [Imitating anger]  like this.

original: and  spurns   The rush that lies before him; cries, “Fool Lepidus!”   And threats the throat of that his officer   That murdered Pompey.
translation: He kicks the plants that lie in his path, cries, "Fool Lepidus!" and threatens to slit the throat of  that officer of his  that murdered Pompey.

original: Our great navy’s rigged.
translation: Our great navy is ready.

original: For Italy and Caesar. More, Domitius: My lord desires you presently. My news I might have told hereafter.
’Twill be naught, But let it be. Bring me to Antony.
translation: It doesn't matter, never mind. Bring me to Antony.

original: Come, sir.
translation: Come, sir.

original: Contemning Rome, he has done all this and more   In Alexandria. Here’s the manner of ’t:
translation: Anthony condemned Rome, and that's not all. Here's what happened:

original: I’ th’ marketplace, on a tribunal silvered,   Cleopatra and himself in chairs of gold   Were publicly enthroned.
translation: in the marketplace, on a silver platform, he and Cleopatra were publicly enthroned in chairs of gold.

original: At the feet sat   Caesarion, whom they call my father’s son,   And all the unlawful issue that their lust   Since then hath made between them.
translation: At their feet sat Caesarion,  whom they say is my father's son , along with all the illegitimate children that their lust has generated between them.

original: Unto her   He gave the stablishment of Egypt, made her   Of lower Syria, Cyprus, Lydia,   Absolute Queen.
translation: Antony gave her full possession of Egypt and made her absolute ruler of lower Syria, Cyprus, and Lydia.

original: This in the public eye?
translation: He did this in public?

original: I’ th’ common showplace, where they exercise.   His sons he there proclaimed the kings of kings:
translation: In the public arena, where people play sports. There, he proclaimed his sons to be the kings of kings.

original: Great Media, Parthia, and Armenia   He gave to Alexander; to Ptolemy he assigned   Syria, Cilicia, and Phoenicia
translation: He gave great Media, Parthia, and Aremenia to  Alexander ; he gave Syria, Cilicia, and Phoenicia to Ptolemy.

original: . She   In th’ habiliments of the goddess Isis   That day appeared, and oft before gave audience,   As ’tis reported, so.
translation: She appeared that day dressed like the goddess Isis, and it is said that she has often appeared in public in that costume.

original: Let Rome be thus informed.
translation: Let the people in Rome know this.

original: Who, queasy with his insolence already, Will their good thoughts call from him.
translation: The Romans are already indignant at his disrespectful behavior and will stop thinking well of him.

original: The people knows it, and have now received His accusations.
translation: The people know it already, and have now heard the accusations that he makes in order to justify his behavior.

original: Who does he accuse?
translation: Who does he accuse?

original: Caesar, and that, having in Sicily   Sextus Pompeius spoiled, we had not rated him   His part o’ th’ isle.
translation: He accuses me, because after we defeated Sextus Pompey in Sicily, we did not give him his share of the island.

original: Then does he say he lent me   Some shipping, unrestored. Lastly, he frets   That Lepidus of the triumvirate   Should be deposed, and, being, that we detain   All his revenue.
translation: He also says that he lent me some goods that I have not returned. Finally, he's upset that Lepidus has been cut out of the triumvirate and claims that I have kept all of Lepidus's property.

original: Sir, this should be answered.
translation: Sir, some answer should be made to these accusations.

original: ’Tis done already, and the messenger gone.   I have told him, Lepidus was grown too cruel,   That he his high authority abused   And did deserve his change.
translation: It has already been done, and the messenger has left with my reply. I told him that Lepidus had grown too cruel and had abused his high position of power and so deserved to be deposed.

original: For what I have conquered,   I grant him part; but then, in his Armenia,   And other of his conquered kingdoms, I   Demand the like.
translation: I will give him part of the lands I have conquered; but then, I will demand that he give me part of Armenia and the other kingdoms he has conquered.

original: He’ll never yield to that.
translation: He'll never agree to that.

original: Nor must not then be yielded to in this.
translation: Then I should not agree to his terms.

original: Hail, Caesar, and my lord! Hail, most dear Caesar!
translation: Hail, Caesar, my lord! Hail, most dear Caesar!

original: That ever I should call thee castaway!
You have not called me so, nor have you cause.
translation: You haven't called me one, and you have no reason to.

original: Why have you stol’n upon us thus? You come not   Like Caesar’s sister. The wife of Antony   Should have an army for an usher and   The neighs of horse to tell of her approach   Long ere she did appear.
translation: Why have you snuck up on us like this? You don't come in the style that's appropriate for Caesar's sister. Antony's wife should be escorted by an army, with neighing horses to announce her arrival before she appears.

original: The trees by th’ way   Should have borne men, and expectation fainted,   Longing for what it had not. Nay, the dust   Should have ascended to the roof of heaven,   Raised by your populous troops.
translation: Crowds should have climbed trees on the side of the road expecting to see you and fainted when they didn't see the sight they longed to see. In fact, you should have been preceded by so many troops that the dust raised by their feet would reach up to the sky.

original: But you are come   A market-maid to Rome and have prevented   The ostentation of our love, which, left unshown,   Is often left unloved.
translation: But you have traveled to Rome like a common maid going to the market and prevented me from publicly displaying my love, and when love isn't shown, it's often unappreciated.

original: We should have met you   By sea and land, supplying every stage   With an augmented greeting.
translation: I would have met you at sea and on land, with a more spectacular greeting at every stage of the journey.

original: Good my lord,   To come thus was I not constrained, but did it   On my free will.
translation: My good lord, I wasn't forced to travel this way, but I did it of my own free will.

original: My lord, Mark Antony,   Hearing that you prepared for war, acquainted   My grievèd ear withal, whereon I begged   His pardon for return.
translation: My lord, Mark Antony, heard that you were preparing for war and told me about it, which upset me so much that I begged his permission to return.

original: Which soon he granted, Being an obstruct ’tween his lust and him.
translation: And he soon gave you his permission, since you are an obstacle that prevents him from satisfying his lust.

original: Do not say so, my lord.
translation: Do not say that, my lord.

original: I have eyes upon him, And his affairs come to me on the wind. Where is he now?
translation: I'm having him watched, and messengers tell me what he is up to. Where is he now?

original: My lord, in Athens.
translation: In Athens, my lord.

original: No, my most wrongèd sister. Cleopatra   Hath nodded him to her. He hath given his empire   Up to a whore; who now are levying   The kings o’ th’ earth for war.
translation: No, my mistreated sister. Cleopatra has summoned him to her. He's given up his empire to a whore, and they are now marshaling all the kings on earth for war.

original: He hath assembled   Bocchus, the King of Libya; Archelaus,   Of Cappadocia; Philadelphos, King   Of Paphlagonia; the Thracian king, Adallas;   King Manchus of Arabia;
translation: He has assembled Boccus, the king of Libya; Archelaus, of Cappadocia; Philadelphos, king of Paphlagonia; the Thracian king, Adallas; King Manchus of Arabia;

original: King of Pont;   Herod of Jewry; Mithridates, King   Of Comagen; Polemon and Amyntas,   The Kings of Mede and Lycaonia,   With a more larger list of scepters.
translation: King of Pont; Herod of Judea; Mithridates, King of Comegen; Polemon and Amyntas, the kings of Mede and Lycaonia, among others.

original: Ay me, most wretched, That have my heart parted betwixt two friends That does afflict each other!
translation: Oh dear, I am a most wretched woman to have my affections torn between two friends who plague each other!

original: Welcome hither.   Your letters did withhold our breaking forth   Till we perceived both how you were wrong led   And we in negligent danger. Cheer your heart.
translation: You're welcome here. Your letters kept me from waging open war until I knew both that you were being deceived and that I was in danger due to my negligence. Be cheerful.

original: Be you not troubled with the time, which drives   O’er your content these strong necessities,   But let determined things to destiny   Hold unbewailed their way.   Welcome to Rome,   Nothing more dear to me.
translation: Don't be troubled by the current situation, when these obligations threaten to ruin your peace of mind. Don't worry about things that have already been decided. Welcome to Rome, you are more dear to me than anything.

original: You are abused   Beyond the mark of thought, and the high gods,   To do you justice, makes his ministers   Of us and those that love you. Best of comfort,   And ever welcome to us.
translation: You are more abused than anyone could comprehend, and the gods make me and those who love you their agents to bring about justice for you. You bring me most comfort, and you are always welcome with me.

original: Welcome, lady.
translation: Welcome, lady.

original: Welcome, dear madam.   Each heart in Rome does love and pity you.
translation: Welcome, dear madam. Every person in Rome loves you and pities you with all their heart.

original: Only th’ adulterous Antony, most large   In his abominations, turns you off   And gives his potent regiment to a trull   That noises it against us.
translation: Only the adulterous Antony, great in his faults, abandons you and gives his great political power to a whore who opposes us.

original: Is it so, sir?
translation: Is that true, sir?

original: Most certain. Sister, welcome. Pray you Be ever known to patience. My dear’st sister!
translation: It's certain. Sister, welcome. Please, try always to be patient. My dearest sister!

original: I will be even with thee, doubt it not.
translation: I will get even with you, have no doubts about that.

original: But why, why, why?
translation: But why, why, why?

original: Thou hast forspoke my being in these wars And sayst it is not fit.
translation: You say I shouldn't take part in this war and that it isn't appropriate.

original: Well, is it, is it?
translation: Well, is it appropriate, is it?

original: Is ’t not denounced against us? Why should not we Be there in person?
translation: Isn't the war declared against me? Why shouldn't I be there in person?

original: Well, I could reply,   If we should serve with horse and mares together,   The horse were merely lost.
translation: Well, If I could, I would say that if we were to go to war with both men and women, the men would be undone by the women.

original: The mares would bear   A soldier and his horse.
translation: The women would seduce the male soldiers.

original: What is ’t you say?
translation: What are you saying?

original: Your presence needs must puzzle Antony,   Take from his heart, take from his brain, from ’s time   What should not then be spared.
translation: If you were there, your presence would inevitably distract Antony. You'd take his heart and his mind off the business at hand, which we certainly could not afford.

original: He is already   Traduced for levity, and ’tis said in Rome   That Photinus, an eunuch, and your maids   Manage this war.
translation: He's already been criticized for being frivolous, and it's said in Rome that Photinus the eunuch and your maids control this war.

original: Sink Rome! And their tongues rot   That speak against us!
translation: To hell with Rome! And let them rot, those who criticize us!

original: A charge we bear i’ th’ war,   And as the president of my kingdom will   Appear there for a man. Speak not against it.   I will not stay behind.
translation: I'll do my duty in the war, and as the ruler of my kingdom, I'll appear there just as a man would. Don't oppose my plan. I won't stay behind.

original: Nay, I have done. Here comes the Emperor.
translation: No, I'm done talking with you. Here comes the Emperor.

original: Is it not strange, Canidius,   That from Tarentum and Brundusium   He could so quickly cut the Ionian sea   And take in Toryne?
translation: Isn't it strange, Canidius, that after starting from the ports of Tarentum and Brundusium, he could have cut across the Ionian sea so quickly and overpowered the city of Toryne?

original: —You have heard on ’t, sweet?
translation: Have you heard about this, sweetheart?

original: Celerity is never more admired Than by the negligent.
translation: No one admires speed more than a lazy man.

original: A good rebuke,   Which might have well becomed the best of men,   To taunt at slackness.
translation: A good criticism, which would have been suitable for the best of men to use to mock laziness.

original: —Canidius, we will fight   With him by sea.
translation: —Canidius, we will fight with him on the sea.

original: By sea, what else?
translation: By sea, how else would we do it?

original: Why will My lord do so?
translation: Why do you want to do that?

original: For that he dares us to ’t.
translation: Because he dares us to.

original: So hath my lord dared him to single fight.
translation: And my lord Antony has also challenged Caesar to single combat.

original: Ay, and to wage this battle at Pharsalia,   Where Caesar fought with Pompey.
translation: Yes, and also to fight this battle at Pharsalia, where Caesar fought with Pompey.

original: But these offers,   Which serve not for his vantage, he shakes off,   And so should you.
translation: But these offers aren't to Caesar's advantage and he rejects them, and so should you.

original: Your ships are not well manned,   Your mariners are muleteers, reapers, people   Engrossed by swift impress.
translation: Your ships aren't manned by good sailors. Your crew consists of mule drivers, farmers, people that you got together quickly through drafting.

original: In Caesar’s fleet   Are those that often have ’gainst Pompey fought.   Their ships are yare, yours, heavy.
translation: Caesar's fleet has men who often fought against Pompey. Their ships are light and agile, yours are heavy and slow.

original: No disgrace   Shall fall you for refusing him at sea,   Being prepared for land.
translation: There would be no shame in refusing to fight him at sea, since you're better prepared to fight him on land.

original: By sea, by sea.
translation: By sea, by sea.

original: Most worthy sir, you therein throw away   The absolute soldiership you have by land,   Distract your army, which doth most consist   Of war-marked footmen,
translation: Most worthy sir, by doing that you would throw away the advantage of the excellent soldiers you have on land; reroute your army, which consists of trained foot soldiers;

original: leave unexecuted   Your own renownèd knowledge, quite forego   The way which promises assurance, and   Give up yourself merely to chance and hazard   From firm security.
translation: make no use of your own considerable knowledge; abandon the strategy that promises success; and give up a highly secure position to leave yourself at the mercy of chance and fortune.

original: I’ll fight at sea.
translation: I'll fight at sea.

original: I have sixty sails, Caesar none better.
translation: I have sixty ships, Caesar has nothing better than that.

original: Our overplus of shipping will we burn,   And with the rest full-manned, from th’ head of Actium   Beat th’ approaching Caesar.
translation: We'll  burn our surplus ships , and then we'll fully man the rest to beat Caesar back as he approaches the tip of Actium.

original: But if we fail,   We then can do ’t at land.
translation: But if we fail at sea, then we can fight on land.

original: The news is true, my lord. He is descried. Caesar has taken Toryne.
translation: The news is true, my lord. He has been spotted. Caesar has taken Toryne.

original: Can he be there in person? ’Tis impossible,   Strange that his power should be.
translation: How can he be there? That's impossible—it's strange even that all his forces should be there.

original: Canidius,   Our nineteen legions thou shalt hold by land,   And our twelve thousand horse. We’ll to our ship.
translation: Canidius, you'll command the nineteen legions and the twelve thousand horses that we have on land. I will go by sea.

original: Away, my Thetis!
translation: Come with me, my  sea goddess !

original: O noble Emperor, do not fight by sea!   Trust not to rotten planks. Do you misdoubt   This sword and these my wounds?
translation: Oh noble Emperor, don't fight at sea! Don't trust the rotting wood of ships. Can you not see from my sword and my wounds?

original: Let th’ Egyptians   And the Phoenicians go a-ducking. We   Have used to conquer standing on the earth   And fighting foot to foot.
translation: Let the Egyptians and the Pheonicians fight on the water. We are used to conquering our enemies on land and fighting foot soldiers with foot soldiers.

original: Well, well, away.
translation: Well, well, away.

original: By Hercules, I think I am i’ th’ right.
translation: I swear by Hercules, I think I am right.

original: Soldier, thou art; but his whole action grows Not in the power on ’t. So our leader’s led, And we are women’s men.
translation: Soldier, you are, but he makes all his plans without considering what he has the power to accomplish. So our leader is led astray, and we men are led by a woman.

original: You keep by land The legions and the horse whole, do you not?
translation: You still have the entirety of the legions and the horses in reserve, don't you?

original: Marcus Octavius, Marcus Justeius,   Publicola, and Caelius, are for sea;   But we keep whole by land.
translation: Marcus Octavius, Marcus Justeius, Publicola, and Caelius are heading to sea, but our forces are kept together in reserve on land.

original: This speed of Caesar’s   Carries beyond belief.
translation: It's unbelievable how fast Caesar has moved.

original: While he was yet in Rome His power went out in such distractions as Beguiled all spies.
translation: While he was still in Rome, his forces went out in so many different directions that none of our spies could keep track of them.

original: Who’s his lieutenant, hear you?
translation: Have you heard who his lieutenant is?

original: They say, one Taurus.
translation: They say a certain man named Taurus.

original: Well I know the man.
translation: I know the man well.

original: The Emperor calls Canidius.
translation: The Emperor has sent for Canidius.

original: With news the time’s with labor, and throws forth Each minute some.
translation: These times are full of news, and every minute we learn something else.

original: Taurus!
translation: Taurus!

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: Strike not by land; keep whole. Provoke not battle Till we have done at sea. Do not exceed The prescript of this scroll.
translation: Don't send out any troops to attack them on land; stay in reserve. Don't start to fight on land until we have finished fighting at sea. Do not go beyond the instructions written in this scroll.

original: Set we our squadrons on yond side o’ th’ hill,   In eye of Caesar’s battle,
translation: Let's set our forces on the far side of the hill, in view of Caesar's battle line.

original: from which place   We may the number of the ships behold   And so proceed accordingly.
translation: From there, we can see how many ships he has and plan accordingly.

original: Naught, naught, all naught! I can behold no longer.
translation: Lost, lost, all is lost! I can't watch it any longer.

original: Th’   Antoniad   , the Egyptian admiral,   With all their sixty, fly and turn the rudder.   To see ’t mine eyes are blasted.
translation: The Antoniad, the Egyptian flagship, along with the sixty other ships, have turned around and fled the battle. It destroys my eyes to see it.

original: Gods and goddesses, All the whole synod of them!
translation: By the whole assembly of the gods and goddesses!

original: What’s thy passion?
translation: What is troubling you?

original: The greater cantle of the world is lost With very ignorance. We have kissed away Kingdoms and provinces.
translation: The largest portion of the world is lost due to extreme ignorance. We have lost our kingdoms and provinces.

original: How appears the fight?
translation: How is the battle going?

original: On our side like the tokened pestilence,   Where death is sure.
translation: On our side, it's as if we've been struck with the plague, which means that death is sure to come.

original: Yon ribaudred nag of Egypt—   Whom leprosy o’ertake!—i’ th’ midst o’ th’ fight,   When vantage like a pair of twins appeared   Both as the same, or rather ours the elder,
translation: That lustful old Egyptian horse—may leprosy strike her down!—in the very midst of the fight, when the advantage appeared to be even, or rather greater on our side,

original: The breeze upon her, like a cow in June,   Hoists sails and flies.
translation: acted like a cow in June driven by a slight wind, and hoisted sail and fled the battle.

original: That I beheld. Mine eyes did sicken at the sight and could not Endure a further view.
translation: I saw that. It made me sick to watch it happen, and I couldn't bear to watch it any longer.

original: She once being loofed,   The noble ruin of her magic, Antony,   Claps on his sea-wing and, like a doting mallard   Leaving the fight in height, flies after her.
translation: Once she had prepared her ships to leave, Antony—that noble man who has been destroyed by her magic—hoisted his sails as well and, like an overfond duck, left the battle at its very height and flew after her.

original: I never saw an action of such shame.   Experience, manhood, honor, ne’er before   Did violate so itself.
translation: I had never seen such shameful behavior. Never before has any man betrayed his better knowledge, his manhood, and his honor so severely.

original: Alack, alack!
translation: Alas, alas!

original: Our fortune on the sea is out of breath   And sinks most lamentably.
translation: We have lost our advantage at sea, and our prospects for success are decreasing depressingly quickly.

original: Had our general   Been what he knew himself, it had gone well.   Oh, he has given example for our flight   Most grossly by his own!
translation: If our general had been true to himself, the battle would have gone well for us. Oh, he has set an example for us to abandon him, as he so disgustingly abandoned us!

original: Ay, are you thereabouts? Why then, good night indeed.
translation: Ah, are you thinking that too? Well, then, it really is over now.

original: Toward Peloponnesus are they fled.
translation: They fled toward Peloponnesus.

original: ’Tis easy to ’t, and there I will attend What further comes.
translation: It's easy to get there, and I'll wait there to see what comes next.

original: To Caesar will I render My legions and my horse. Six kings already Show me the way of yielding.
translation: I will offer my legions and my horses to Caesar's service. Six kings have already set an example by similarly yielding to Caesar.

original: I’ll yet follow The wounded chance of Antony, though my reason Sits in the wind against me.
translation: I'll stick with Antony and his diminished chances for now, even though I'm acting against my better judgment.

original: Hark. The land bids me tread no more upon ’t.   It is ashamed to bear me. Friends, come hither.
translation: See how the earth itself tells me not to walk on it any more. It is ashamed to hold me. Friends, come here.

original: I am so lated in the world that I   Have lost my way forever. I have a ship   Laden with gold.
translation: I am so overtaken by night that I have lost my way forever in this world. I have a ship full of gold.

original: Take that, divide it. Fly   And make your peace with Caesar.
translation: Take the gold and divide it amongst yourselves. Abandon me and make peace with Caesar.

original: Fly? Not we.
translation: Abandon you? Not us.

original: I have fled myself, and have instructed cowards   To run and show their shoulders. Friends, begone.
translation: I have abandoned myself, and by retreating, I have set an example for other cowards to run away and turn their backs on their enemies. Friends, be gone.

original: I have myself resolved upon a course   Which has no need of you. Begone.
translation: I have resolved to follow a course of action that does not require your assistance. Be gone.

original: My treasure’s in the harbor. Take it. Oh,   I followed that I blush to look upon!   My very hairs do mutiny, for the white   Reprove the brown for rashness, and they them   For fear and doting.
translation: My treasure is in the harbor. Take it. Oh, I followed the very thing that now makes me ashamed to look at it! Even my hairs rebel. The  white hairs condemn the brown ones  for being rash, and the brown ones condemn the white for being fearful and too affectionate.

original: Friends, begone. You shall   Have letters from me to some friends that will   Sweep your way for you. Pray you, look not sad,   Nor make replies of loathness. Take the hint   Which my despair proclaims.
translation: Friends, be gone. I'll write letters for you to some friends of mine that will clear your path. Please, do not be sad or say that you don't want to do this. Take your cue from my despair.

original: Let that be left   Which leaves itself. To the seaside straightway!   I will possess you of that ship and treasure.   Leave me, I pray, a little.
translation: You should abandon someone who abandons himself. Go the seaside immediately! I'll give you the ship and the treasure. Leave me alone, please, for a little while.

original: Pray you now,   Nay, do so, for indeed I have lost command.   Therefore I pray you. I’ll see you by and by.
translation: I ask you, don't protest, leave me—please. I have lost the right to command you, so I can only ask you. I'll see you shortly.

original: Nay, gentle madam, to him, comfort him.
translation: No, gentle madam, go to him, comfort him.

original: Do, most dear Queen.
translation: Do, dearest Queen.

original: Do. Why, what else?
translation: Do. Why, what else would you do?

original: Let me sit down. O Juno!
No, no, no, no, no.
translation: No, no, no, no, no.

original: See you here, sir?
translation: Do you see this woman here, sir?

original: Oh, fie, fie, fie!
translation: Oh, shame on you, shame, shame, shame!

original: Madam!
translation: Madam!

original: Madam, O good Empress!
translation: Madam, Oh good Empress!

original: Sir, sir—
translation: Sir, sir—

original: Yes, my lord, yes. He at Philippi kept   His sword e’en like a dancer, while I struck   The lean and wrinkled Cassius, and ’twas I   That the mad Brutus ended.
translation: Yes, my lord, yes. At Philippi, Caesar used his sword only as a decoration, while I fought thin, wrinkled Casius, and it was I who defeated the insane Brutus.

original: He alone   Dealt on lieutenantry, and no practice had   In the brave squares of war, yet now—no matter.
translation: Caesar was the one who had others fight for him, and he had no experience in the proper battle formations but now—well, it doesn't matter.

original: Ah, stand by.
translation: Ah, stand aside.

original: The Queen, my lord, the Queen.
translation: The Queen, my lord, look at the Queen.

original: Go to him, madam, speak to him. He is unqualitied with very shame.
translation: Go to him, Madam, speak to him. He's so ashamed that he has lost all sense of who he is.

original: Well then, sustain me. Oh!
translation: Well then, support me. Oh!

original: Most noble sir, arise. The Queen approaches. Her head’s declined, and death will seize her but Your comfort makes the rescue.
translation: Most noble sir, get up. The Queen's approaching. Her head is bowed and she will die unless you save her by comforting her.

original: I have offended reputation, A most unnoble swerving.
translation: I have betrayed my good name—a most dishonorable departure from the right path.

original: Sir, the Queen.
translation: Sir, the Queen.

original: Oh, whither hast thou led me, Egypt?
translation: Oh, what have you led me to do, Queen of Egypt?

original: See   How I convey my shame out of thine eyes   By looking back what I have left behind   ’Stroyed in dishonor.
translation: See how I steal away in shame out of your sight, remembering what I left behind destroyed in dishonor.

original: O my lord, my lord, Forgive my fearful sails! I little thought You would have followed.
translation: Oh my lord, my lord! Forgive me for sailing away in fear! I didn't think you would follow me!

original: Egypt, thou knew’st too well   My heart was to thy rudder tied by th’ strings,   And thou shouldst tow me after.
translation: Queen of Egypt, you knew all too well that my heart was tied to you and your movements, and that whatever you did, you would draw me after you.

original: O’er my spirit   Thy full supremacy thou knew’st, and that   Thy beck might from the bidding of the gods   Command me.
translation: You knew that you had full control over my will and that your summons would call me away even from what the gods had ordered me to do.

original: Oh, my pardon!
translation: Oh, please forgive me!

original: Now I must   To the young man send humble treaties, dodge   And palter in the shifts of lowness, who   With half the bulk o’ th’ world played as I pleased,   Making and marring fortunes.
translation: Now I must send humble petitions to that young Caesar, make excuses and play tricks like a man of low status—me, who once did as I pleased with half of the world's territory, raising and destroying people's fortunes.

original: You did know   How much you were my conqueror, and that   My sword, made weak by my affection, would   Obey it on all cause.
translation: You knew how much you had conquered me, and that in battle, since my affection for you made me weak, I would obey you no matter what.

original: Pardon, pardon!
translation: Forgive me, forgive me!

original: Fall not a tear, I say. One of them rates All that is won and lost. Give me a kiss.
translation: Don't cry one tear, I say. One tear makes up for everything I have won and lost. Give me a kiss.

original: Even this repays me.—
translation: Even one kiss repays me for what I have lost.

original: We sent our schoolmaster. Is he come back?—
translation: We sent away our children's tutor on an errand. Has he come back?

original: Love, I am full of lead.—
translation: My love, my spirits are heavy.

original: Some wine,   Within there, and our viands! Fortune knows   We scorn her most when most she offers blows.
translation: You over there, bring us some wine and food! When fortune deals us the heaviest blows, that's when we scorn her the most.

original: Let him appear that’s come from Antony. Know you him?
translation: Call in Antony's messenger. Do you know him?

original: Caesar, ’tis his schoolmaster—   An argument that he is plucked, when hither   He sends so poor a pinion of his wing,
translation: Caesar, it's his children's tutor. It's a sign that Antony is in bad shape, that he sends such a lowly person here as his messenger.

original: Which had superfluous kings for messengers   Not many moons gone by.
translation: Not long ago, he had so many kings in his power that he could afford to send them as messengers.

original: Approach and speak.
translation: Come forward and speak.

original: Such as I am, I come from Antony.
translation: Even though I am a lowly person, I have been sent here by Antony.

original: I was of late as petty to his ends   As is the morn-dew on the myrtle leaf   To his grand sea.
translation: Lately, I've been as insignificant and useless to him as a drop of morning dew on a myrtle leaf would be to the large sea.

original: Be ’t so. Declare thine office.
translation: Put that aside. Tell us what you came here for.

original: Lord of his fortunes he salutes thee, and   Requires to live in Egypt; which not granted,   He lessens his requests, and to thee sues   To let him breathe between the heavens and earth   A private man in Athens.   This for him.
translation: Antony salutes you, you now have control over his fate, and he asks to be allowed to live in Egypt. If you don't grant this request, he asks for a smaller favor and asks you to let him live out his remaining days as a private citizen in Athens. These are his requests.

original: Next, Cleopatra does confess thy greatness,   Submits her to thy might, and of thee craves   The circle of the Ptolemies for her heirs,   Now hazarded to thy grace.
translation: Next, Cleopatra acknowledges your greatness, submits herself to your power, and asks that the kingdom of Egypt, which is now at your mercy, might be given to her children.

original: For Antony,   I have no ears to his request. The Queen   Of audience nor desire shall fail, so she   From Egypt drive her all-disgracèd friend   Or take his life there.
translation: For Antony, I will not listen to his requests. The Queen will get to meet me and get what she wants, so long as she drives her completely disgraced lover out of Egypt or else kills him there.

original: This if she perform,   She shall not sue unheard. So to them both.
translation: If she does this, her requests won't go unheard. Tell this to both of them.

original: Fortune pursue thee!
translation: May you have good fortune!

original: Bring him through the bands.
translation: Escort him through the ranks of soldiers.

original: To try thy eloquence now ’tis time.  Dispatch.   From Antony win Cleopatra. Promise,   And in our name, what she requires.
translation: Now it is time to see what your eloquence can accomplish. Get going. Win over Cleopatra from Antony. Promise her in my name that she will be given what she asks for.

original: Add more,   From thine invention, offers. Women are not   In their best fortunes strong, but want will perjure   The ne’er-touched vestal.
translation: Promise her more than that, whatever you can think of. Women can't stick to their word even at the best of times, but when they are in need, even the most  devout virgin will break her vows .

original: Try thy cunning, Thidias.   Make thine own edict for thy pains, which we   Will answer as a law.
translation: See what your cunning can accomplish, Thidias. Decide what reward you would like for your trouble, and I will supply it as if commanded by law.

original: Caesar, I go.
translation: Caesar, I will go.

original: Observe how Antony becomes his flaw, And what thou think’st his very action speaks In every power that moves.
translation: Observe how Antony reacts to his disgrace, and tell me what you think his actions reveal about him in every move that he makes.

original: Caesar, I shall.
translation: Caesar, I will.

original: What shall we do, Enobarbus?
translation: What we will do, Enobarbus?

original: Think and die.
translation: Consider our situation and die.

original: Is Antony or we in fault for this?
translation: Is Antony at fault for this, or am I?

original: Antony only, that would make his will   Lord of his reason. What though you fled   From that great face of war, whose several ranges   Frighted each other?
translation: Only Antony, who allowed his appetite to overcome his reason. What does it matter that you fled from the dangerous battlefield, where ranks of ships frightened both sides?

original: Why should he follow?   The itch of his affection should not then   Have nicked his captainship at such a point   When half to half the world opposed, he being   The merèd question.
translation: Why should he have followed you? His affection for you shouldn't have undermined his skill as captain, while one half of the world opposed the other, and when he himself was the reason for this fight.

original: ’Twas a shame no less   Than was his loss, to course your flying flags   And leave his navy gazing.
translation: His shame was as great as his loss, when he followed the flags of your fleeing ships and left his navy watching him go.

original: Prithee, peace.
translation: Please, be quiet.

original: Is that his answer?
translation: Is that Caesar's answer?

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: The Queen shall then have courtesy, so she Will yield us up?
translation: He will treat the Queen favorably, so long as she hands me over to him?

original: He says so.
translation: That's what he says.

original: Let her know ’t.—
translation: Let the queen know.

original: To the boy Caesar send this grizzled  head,   And he will fill thy wishes to the brim   With principalities.
translation: If you send my old body to that young boy Caesar, he will give you all the kingdoms you wish.

original: That head, my lord?
translation: That body, my lord?

original: To him again. Tell him he wears the rose   Of youth upon him, from which the world should note   Something particular.
translation: Go to him again. Tell him that he's still in the first bloom of youth, and the world should expect remarkable things from him.

original: His coin, ships, legions,   May be a coward’s, whose ministers would prevail   Under the service of a child as soon   As i’ th’ command of Caesar.
translation: His money, ships, and legions of troops might just as well belong to a  coward . His agents may be so gifted that they would win under the command of a child just as well as under Caesar.

original: I dare him therefore   To lay his gay caparisons apart   And answer me declined, sword against sword,   Ourselves alone. I’ll write it. Follow me.
translation: Therefore, I dare him to set aside his flashy decorations and answer my challenge, even though I am well past the prime of my youth, to fight sword to sword, just the two of us. I'll write the message. Come with me.

original: Yes, like enough, high-battled Caesar will   Unstate his happiness and be staged to th’ show   Against a sworder!
translation: Yes, I'm sure it's very likely that Caesar, with all his armies, will give up his advantage and agree to show himself in public and fight against a trained swordsman!

original: I see men’s judgments are   A parcel of their fortunes, and things outward   Do draw the inward quality after them   To suffer all alike.
translation: I see that men's judgment improves or declines in accordance with their luck. External events shape our inner qualities, so that if we suffer externally, we suffer internally too.

original: That he should dream,   Knowing all measures, the full Caesar will   Answer his emptiness! Caesar, thou hast subdued   His judgment too.
translation: How could he dream, having known both good and bad fortune, that Caesar, with all his good fortune, would answer a challenge from a man in such bad condition! Caesar, you've destroyed his judgment too.

original: A messenger from Caesar.
translation: A messenger from Caesar.

original: What, no more ceremony?
translation: Why dob't you treat me with more  respect ?

original: See, my women,   Against the blown rose may they stop their nose,   That kneeled unto the buds.—Admit him, sir.
translation: See, my women, how when a great person has fallen low, the people who once kneeled before her instead turn their nose up at her. Let him in, sir.

original: Mine honesty and I begin to square.   The loyalty well held to fools does make   Our faith mere folly.
translation: My judgment begins to come into conflict with my honor. To be loyal to fools makes our loyalty simply an act of foolishness.

original: Yet he that can endure   To follow with allegiance a fall’n lord   Does conquer him that did his master conquer   And earns a place i’ th’ story.
translation: But whoever has the perseverance to follow his lord faithfully even after his lord has fallen, proves that he is stronger even than the person who conquered his master, and so makes a great name for himself.

original: Caesar’s will?
translation: What does Caesar want?

original: Hear it apart.
translation: Listen to my message in private.

original: None but friends. Say boldly.
translation: We are all friends here. Say what you have to say.

original: So haply are they friends to Antony.
translation: It may be that they are friends to Antony.

original: He needs as many, sir, as Caesar has,   Or needs not us.
translation: Antony needs as many friends as Caesar, sir, and if things are very bad, even we won't be any use to him.

original: If Caesar please, our master   Will leap to be his friend.
translation: If Caesar is willing, our master will willingly be his friend.

original: For us, you know   Whose he is we are, and that is Caesar’s.
translation: As for you, you know that we obey whomever Antony obeys, and that is Caesar.

original: So.—   Thus then, thou most renowned:
translation: So be it. Here is the situation, then, oh most renowned queen:

original: Caesar entreats   Not to consider in what case thou stand’st,   Further than he is Caesar.
translation: Caesar asks that you not concern yourself with your current situation, given that you know his reputation as a generous man.

original: Go on. Right royal.
translation: Go on. That is generous indeed.

original: He knows that you embrace not Antony As you did love, but as you feared him.
translation: He knows that you took Antony as your lover not because you loved him, but because you feared him.

original: Oh!
translation: Oh!

original: The scars upon your honor therefore he Does pity as constrainèd blemishes, Not as deserved.
translation: Therefore, he pities the damage done to your honor as a blemish you were forced to endure, not as something you deserved.

original: He is a god and knows What is most right. Mine honor was not yielded, But conquered merely.
translation: Caesar is a god, and he knows what is just. I did not yield to Antony voluntarily, I was merely overpowered.

original: To be sure of that,   I will ask Antony.
translation: I'll ask Antony to make sure that that's true.

original: Sir, sir, thou art so leaky   That we must leave thee to thy sinking, for   Thy dearest quit thee.
translation: Antony, Antony, you have fallen so low that we must abandon you to your disgrace, for even those who love you most are deserting you.

original: Shall I say to Caesar   What you require of him? For he partly begs   To be desired to give.
translation: Shall I tell Caesar what you want from him? For he likes to be asked to give.

original: It much would please him   That of his fortunes you should make a staff   To lean upon.
translation: It would please him greatly if you would show your support by appealing to his power.

original: But it would warm his spirits   To hear from me you had left Antony   And put yourself under his shroud,   The universal landlord.
translation: But it would make him truly happy to hear from me that you had abandoned Antony and turned to him, the ruler of the world, for shelter.

original: What’s your name?
translation: What's your name?

original: My name is Thidias.
translation: My name is Thidias.

original: Most kind messenger,   Say to great Caesar this in deputation:
translation: Most kind messenger, tell this to Caesar as my representative:

original: I kiss his conqu’ring hand. Tell him I am prompt   To lay my crown at ’s feet, and there to kneel.   Tell him, from his all-obeying breath I hear   The doom of Egypt.
translation: I kiss his conquering hand. Tell him I am ready immediately to lay my crown at his feet and to kneel there. Tell him that I will obey him and let him decide the fate of Egypt.

original: ’Tis your noblest course.   Wisdom and fortune combating together,   If that the former dare but what it can,   No chance may shake it.
translation: That is the most honorable course of action. When wisdom fights against fortune, so long as wisdom does everything it can, no bad luck can defeat it.

original: Give me grace to lay   My duty on your hand.
translation: Give me permission to show my faithfulness by kissing your hand.

original: Your Caesar’s father oft,   When he hath mused of taking kingdoms in,
translation: Julius Caesar, father of your master Octavius, while he thought about conquering kingdoms,

original: Bestowed his lips on that unworthy place   As it rained kisses.
translation: often put his lips on my unworthy hand  and rained kisses on it.

original: Favors? By Jove that thunders! What art thou, fellow?
One that but performs The bidding of the fullest man, and worthiest To have command obeyed.
translation: I obey the commands of the man who is the most powerful and who most deserves to have his commands obeyed.

original: You will be whipped.
translation: You'll be whipped.

original: Approach, there!
translation: You over there, come here!

original: Ah, you kite!—Now, gods and devils!   Authority melts from me. Of late, when I cried “Ho!”   Like boys unto a muss kings would start forth   And cry, “Your will?”
translation: Ah, you whore! Now, gods and devils! I lose all my authority. Not long ago, when I cried "Ho!" kings would dart forward like boys towards a meal and cry, "What do you wish?"

original: Have you  no ears? I am   Antony yet.
translation: Do you have no ears?  I am still Antony .

original: ’Tis better playing with a lion’s whelp Than with an old one dying.
translation: It's less dangerous to mess with a powerful man's messenger than with a man who was once powerful and now rages against his downfall.

original: Moon and stars!   Whip him. Were ’t twenty of the greatest tributaries   That do acknowledge Caesar,
translation: Moon and stars! Whip him. Even if there were twenty of the greatest monarchs who pay tribute to Caesar,

original: should I find them   So saucy with the hand of she here—what’s her name   Since she was Cleopatra?
translation: if I found them being so intimately familiar with the hand of this woman here—what's her name since she  stopped being Cleopatra ?

original: Whip him, fellows,   Till like a boy, you see him cringe his face   And whine aloud for mercy. Take him hence.
translation: Whip him, fellows, until you see him cringe like a boy and whine aloud for mercy. Take him away.

original: Mark Antony—
translation: Mark Antony—

original: Tug him away! Being whipped, Bring him again. This jack of Caesar’s shall Bear us an errand to him.
translation: Pull him away! Whip him, and bring him back again. This scoundrel of Caesar's will take a message to him for me.

original: You were half blasted ere I knew you.  Ha!
translation: You were half decayed before I met you! Ha!

original: Have I my pillow left unpressed in Rome,   Forborne the getting of a lawful race,   And by a gem of women, to be abused   By one that looks on feeders?
translation: Have I abandoned my home in Rome, neglected the chance to beget a family of legitimate children with a noble woman, only to abused by someone who  bestows favors on servants ?

original: Good my lord—
translation: My good lord—

original: You have been a boggler ever.   But when we in our viciousness grow hard—   Oh, misery on ’t!—
translation: You have always been fickle. But when we grow set in our vicious ways—oh, what misery it is!—

original: the wise gods seel our eyes,   In our own filth drop our clear judgments, make us   Adore our errors, laugh at ’s while we strut   To our confusion.
translation: the wise gods close our eyes, cloud our good judgment through our own bad behavior, make us love our mistakes, and laugh at us as we bring about our own ruin.

original: Oh, is ’t come to this?
translation: Oh, is this what you think now?
