original: I found you as a morsel cold upon   Dead Caesar’s trencher. Nay, you were a fragment   Of Gneius Pompey’s, besides what hotter hours,   Unregistered in vulgar fame, you have   Luxuriously picked out.
translation: When I met you, you had been used up by the dead Caesar. No, you had been used up even more so by Gneius Pompey—and by other men, too, that you wantonly went after, in lustful moments that gossip never picked up on.

original: For I am sure,   Though you can guess what temperance should be,   You know not what it is.
translation: For I'm sure, that although you can guess how a mild woman ought to behave, that you have never been pleasant yourself.

original: Wherefore is this?
translation: Why are you talking like this?

original: To let a fellow that will take rewards   And say “God quit you!” be familiar with   My playfellow, your hand, this kingly seal   And plighter of high hearts!
translation: To let a man that accepts favors and says, "May God repay you!" be intimate with your hand, the hand that I have played with, that bestows the royal seal, and drinks toasts to all those with great spirits!

original: Oh, that I were   Upon the hill of Basan, to outroar   The hornèd herd!
translation: Oh, if only I were on the hill of Basan, so I could roar louder than the  bulls !

original: For I have savage cause,   And to proclaim it civilly were like   A haltered neck which does the hangman thank   For being yare about him.
translation: For I have reason to behave savagely. To speak about my wrongs calmly would be as ignoble as a condemned man thanking the hangman for hanging him quickly.

original: Soundly, my lord.
translation: Thoroughly, my lord.

original: Cried he? And begged he pardon?
translation: Did he cry? And did he ask for mercy?

original: He did ask favor.
translation: He did ask for some relief.

original: If that thy father live, let him repent   Thou wast not made his daughter, and be thou sorry   To follow Caesar in his triumph, since   Thou hast been whipped for following him.
translation: If your father is alive, let him be sorry that you weren't born  a girl . And you should be sorry that you follow Caesar and his success, since you've been whipped for doing so.

original: Henceforth   The white hand of a lady fever thee;   Shake thou to look on ’t. Get thee back to Caesar.   Tell him thy entertainment.
translation: From now on, be as terrified of a lady's white hand as you would be of a fever; shake with fear to look at it. Get back to Caesar. Tell him how you were treated.

original: Look thou say   He makes me angry with him, for he seems   Proud and disdainful, harping on what I am,   Not what he knew I was.
translation: Be sure to tell him how angry he makes me for continuing to focus on my present disgrace, rather than on my past glories.

original: He makes me angry,   And at this time most easy ’tis to do ’t,   When my good stars, that were my former guides,   Have empty left their orbs and shot their fires   Into th’ abysm of hell.
translation: He's making me angry, and right now it's very easy to do that, since the lucky stars that used to guide me have left their positions in the sky and drenched their lights in the pit of hell.

original: If he mislike   My speech and what is done, tell him he has   Hipparchus, my enfranchèd bondman, whom   He may at pleasure whip, or hang, or torture,   As he shall like, to quit me. Urge it thou.   Hence with thy stripes, begone!
translation: If he doesn't like what I have said and done, tell him that he has Hipparchus, my freed slave, and that he may freely whip or hang or torture him, just as he likes, to get revenge on me. Tell him that. Get out of here with your wounds, be gone!

original: Have you done yet?
translation: Are you finished yet?

original: Alack, our terrene moon is now eclipsed, And it portends alone the fall of Antony.
I must stay his time.
translation: I must keep quiet until he has calmed down.

original: To flatter Caesar, would you mingle eyes With one that ties his points?
Not know me yet?
translation: Don't you know me at all by now?

original: Coldhearted toward me?
translation: How can you still be coldhearted towards me?

original: Ah, dear, if I be so,   From my cold heart let heaven engender hail,   And poison it in the source, and the first stone   Drop in my neck.
translation: Ah, dear, if I am, may heaven create hail in my cold heart and poison it at the source, and may the first hailstone that falls lodge in my throat.

original: As it determines, so   Dissolve my life! The next Caesarion smite,   Till by degrees the memory of my womb,   Together with my brave Egyptians all,
translation: As it melts, let it kill me! Let the next stone kill my son Caesarion, until gradually all my children, together with all my brave Egyptians,

original: By the discandying of this pelleted storm   Lie graveless till the flies and gnats of Nile   Have buried them for prey!
translation: are killed by the dissolving hailstones of this storm and lie unburied until the flies and gnats of the Nile have buried them as their prey!

original: I am satisfied.   Caesar sits down in Alexandria, where   I will oppose his fate.
translation: I am satisfied of your feelings for me. Caesar lays siege to Alexandria, where I will oppose him and put an end to his good luck.

original: Our force by land   Hath nobly held. Our severed navy too   Have knit again, and fleet, threat’ning most sealike.
translation: Our armies on land have withstood him nobly. Our dispersed navy, too, has come together again and their ships are afloat, presenting a most seaworthy threat.

original: Where hast thou been, my heart? Dost thou hear, lady?   If from the field I shall return once more   To kiss these lips, I will appear in blood.   I and my sword will earn our chronicle.   There’s hope in ’t yet.
translation: Where has my courage gone? Do you hear me, my lady? If I return from the field again to kiss your lips, I will be bloody and have new vigor. My sword and I will earn a good reputation. There's hope for our side yet.

original: That’s my brave lord!
translation: That's my brave lord!

original: I will be treble-sinewed, -hearted, -breathed,   And fight maliciously. For when mine hours   Were nice and lucky, men did ransom lives   Of me for jests;
translation: I will be three times as strong, as brave, and as persevering, and fight furiously. For when I had good fortune and could act however I pleased, I was so merciful that men could ransom their lives from me for a mere trifle.

original: but now I’ll set my teeth   And send to darkness all that stop me. Come,   Let’s have one other gaudy night.
translation: But now I'll harden my heart and destroy everyone that opposes me. Come, let's have one more night of celebration.

original: Call to me   All my sad captains. Fill our bowls once more.   Let’s mock the midnight bell.
translation: Call all my sad captains to join me. Fill our cups once more. We won't care how late it is, we will mock the late hour by celebrating.

original: It is my birthday. I had thought t’ have held it poor; but since my lord Is Antony again, I will be Cleopatra.
translation: It is my birthday. I thought I would have no celebrations—but since my lord is acting like himself again, I will be myself again too.

original: We will yet do well.
translation: We will still triumph.

original: Call all his noble captains to my lord.
translation: Call all my lord's noble captains to him.

original: Do so. We’ll speak to them, and tonight I’ll force   The wine peep through their scars.
translation: Do that. We'll speak to them, and tonight I'll make them drink so much that the wine will leak out through their scarred skin.

original: —Come on, my Queen,   There’s sap in ’t yet. The next time I do fight   I’ll make Death love me, for I will contend   Even with his pestilent scythe.
translation: Come on, my queen. There's still hope for our side. The next time I fight, I'll make Death admire me, for I'll oppose even his fatal power.

original: Now he’ll outstare the lightning. To be furious   Is to be frighted out of fear, and in that mood   The dove will peck the estridge;
translation: Now he'll set himself against even the mightiest enemies. He is so riled up that his frenzy has driven out his fear, and in that mood, the  weakest man  will challenge the strongest.

original: and I see still   A diminution in our captain’s brain   Restores his heart.
translation: I can tell that our captain is regaining his bravery only because he has lost his judgment.

original: When valor preys on reason,   It eats the sword it fights with. I will seek   Some way to leave him.
translation: When a man's courage destroys his reason, he destroys the very thing that could save him. I will look for some way to leave him.

original: He calls me “boy” and chides as he had power   To beat me out of Egypt. My messenger   He hath whipped with rods, dares me to personal combat,   Caesar to Antony.
translation: Antony calls me "boy" and taunts me as if he had the power to beat my forces out of Egypt. He whipped my messenger with rods and challenges me to single combat, Caesar against Antony.

original: Let the old ruffian know   I have many other ways to die, meantime   Laugh at his challenge.
translation: Let that old scoundrel know that that is not how I plan to die. In the meantime, send a mocking reply to his challenge.

original: Caesar must think   When one so great begins to rage, he’s hunted   Even to falling.
translation: You must suspect that when a man so great starts to rage like this, his defeats have put him on the verge of collapse.

original: Give him no breath, but now   Make boot of his distraction. Never anger   Made good guard for itself.
translation: Don't give him any time to regroup, but promptly use his anger to your advantage. An angry man never takes proper precautions.

original: Let our best heads   Know that tomorrow the last of many battles   We mean to fight.
translation: Let our wisest officers know that tomorrow, I intend to fight the last of our many battles.

original: Within our files there are,   Of those that served Mark Antony but late,   Enough to fetch him in   . See it done   And feast the army.
translation: Among our troops there many soldiers who served Mark Antony only a short time ago—enough soldiers to capture him.  See that this is done, and give the army a feast.

original: We have store to do ’t,   And they have earned the waste. Poor Antony!
translation: We have enough food in our stores to do it, and they have earned it—even if it is a waste of resources. Poor Antony!

original: He will not fight with me, Domitius?
translation: He won't fight me in single combat, Domitius?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: Why should he not?
translation: Why not?

original: He thinks, being twenty times of better fortune, He is twenty men to one.
translation: He estimates that, being twenty times better off than you, his forces outnumber yours twenty to one.

original: Tomorrow, soldier,   By sea and land I’ll fight.
translation: Tomorrow, soldier, I'll fight by land and by sea.

original: Or I will live   Or bathe my dying honor in the blood   Shall make it live again. Woo’t thou fight well?
translation: Either I'll come out alive, or I will restore my ruined reputation by dying honorably in battle. Will you fight bravely?

original: I’ll strike and cry, “Take all.”
translation: I'll strike and cry, "Winner take all!"

original: Well said. Come on! Call forth my household servants.
translation: Well said. Come on! Call my household servants.

original: Let’s tonight Be bounteous at our meal.
translation: Let's be generous with the food at tonight's meal.

original: What means this?
translation: Why is Antony acting like this?

original: ’Tis one of those odd tricks which sorrow shoots Out of the mind.
translation: It's one of his odd quirks that show he is upset.

original: And thou art honest too.   I wish I could be made so many men,
translation: And you are honest too. I wish that I could be divided up into men just like you,

original: And all of you clapped up together in   An Antony, that I might do you service   So good as you have done.
translation: and all of you combined to make one Antony, so I could serve you as well as you have served me.

original: The gods forbid!
translation: God forbid!

original: Well, my good fellows, wait on me tonight.
translation: Well, my good fellows, wait on me at dinner tonight.

original: Scant not my cups, and make as much of me   As when mine empire was your fellow too,   And suffered my command.
translation: Don't skimp when you pour my wine, and treat me as reverently as you did when my empire was also my servant, like you, and obeyed my commands.

original: What does he mean?
translation: What does he mean?

original: To make his followers weep.
translation: He means to make his servants weep.

original: Tend me tonight.   May be it is the period of your duty.   Haply you shall not see me more, or if,   A mangled shadow.
translation: Take care of me tonight. It may be the last time you do so. It may be that you will not see me anymore, or if you do, that you'll see only my disfigured ghost.

original: Perchance tomorrow   You’ll serve another master. I look on you   As one that takes his leave.
translation: Perhaps tomorrow you'll serve another master. I look upon you as if I were saying goodbye.

original: Mine honest friends,   I turn you not away, but, like a master   Married to your good service, stay till death.   Tend me tonight two hours, I ask no more,   And the gods yield you for ’t!
translation: My honest friends, I'm not turning you away. Rather, I will stay with you until death, like a master who is attached to your faithful service. Take care of me tonight, I ask no more, and may the gods bless you for it!

original: What mean you, sir,   To give them this discomfort?
translation: What do you mean, sir, upsetting them like this?

original: Look, they weep,   And I, an ass, am onion-eyed. For shame,   Transform us not to women.
translation: Look, they weep, and I, like an ass, have watery eyes too. For shame, don't make us as emotional as women.

original: Ho, ho, ho!   Now the witch take me if I meant it thus!   Grace grow where those drops fall!
translation: Ha, ha, ha! Curse me if I meant to do that! May the gods bless the men for weeping!

original: My hearty friends,   You take me in too dolorous a sense,   For I spake to you for your comfort, did desire you   To burn this night with torches.
translation: My tender-hearted friends, I didn't mean to make you so upset. I spoke to comfort you, I asked you to keep the night bright by burning torches.

original: Know, my hearts,   I hope well of tomorrow, and will lead you   Where rather I’ll expect victorious life   Than death and honor. Let’s to supper, come,   And drown consideration.
translation: You should know, my dear friends, that I have high hopes for tomorrow, and I will lead you to a battlefield where I expect to live victoriously rather than die honorably. Let's go to supper, come, and drink away our cares.

original: Brother, good night. Tomorrow is the day.
translation: Goodnight, comrade. Tomorrow is the big day.

original: It will determine one way. Fare you well. Heard you of nothing strange about the streets?
translation: Things will be decided one way or another. Good luck to you. Have you heard any strange news from the streets?

original: Nothing. What news?
translation: Nothing. What's the news?

original: Belike ’tis but a rumor. Good night to you.
translation: It's probably just a rumor. Goodnight to you.

original: Well, sir, good night.
translation: Well, sir, goodnight.

original: Soldiers, have careful watch.
translation: Soldiers, stay watchful while you're on guard.

original: And you. Good night, good night.
translation: And you as well. Goodnight, goodnight.

original: Here we. And if tomorrow Our navy thrive, I have an absolute hope Our landmen will stand up.
translation: Here are our positions. And if our navy succeeds tomorrow, I am completely confident that our army will make a good stand.

original: ’Tis a brave army, and full of purpose.
translation: The troops are brave and determined to win.

original: Peace! What noise?
translation: Be quiet! What's that noise?

original: List, list!
translation: Listen, listen!

original: Hark!
translation: Listen!

original: Music i’ th’ air.
translation: There's music in the air.

original: Under the earth.
translation: It's coming from under the ground.

original: It signs well, does it not?
translation: This is a good omen, isn't it?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: Peace, I say! What should this mean?
translation: Be quiet, I say! What does this mean?

original: ’Tis the god Hercules, whom Antony loved, Now leaves him.
Walk. Let’s see if other watchmen Do hear what we do.
translation: Let's walk and see if the other watchmen hear what we hear.

original: How now, masters?
translation: How is it going, officers?

original: How now? How now? Do you hear this?
translation: What is it? What is it? Do you hear this?

original: Ay. Is ’t not strange?
translation: Yes. Isn't it strange?

original: Do you hear, masters? Do you hear?
translation: Do you hear it, officers? Do you hear?

original: Follow the noise so far as we have quarter; Let’s see how it will give off.
translation: Let's follow the noise as far as we can within the boundaries of our watch. Let's see how it ends.

original: Content. ’Tis strange.
translation: That sounds good. It's strange.

original: Eros! Mine armor, Eros!
translation: Eros! Bring me my armor, Eros!

original: Sleep a little.
translation: Sleep a little.

original: No, my chuck.—Eros, come, mine armor, Eros!
translation: No, my dear—Eros, come, my armor, Eros!

original: Nay, I’ll help too. What’s this for?
translation: No, I'll help too. What's this for?

original: Ah, let be, let be! Thou art The armorer of my heart. False, false. This, this.
translation: Ah, leave it alone, leave it alone! It's bad enough that you put the armor on my heart.  That's not how you do it. Like this, like this.

original: Sooth, la, I’ll help. Thus it must be.
translation: Really, I'll help. This is how it should be.

original: Well, well, We shall thrive now.—Seest thou, my good fellow? Go put on thy defenses.
translation: Well, well, we'll succeed now.  Do you see, my good man? Go put on your armor.

original: Briefly, sir.
translation: Soon, sir.

original: Is not this buckled well?
translation: Isn't this buckled well?

original: Rarely, rarely.   He that unbuckles this, till we do please   To doff ’t for our repose, shall hear a storm.—
translation: Uncommonly well. The one that unbuckles this armor—until I am pleased to take it off and rest—will face my anger.

original: Thou fumblest, Eros, and my Queen’s a squire   More tight at this than thou. Dispatch.
translation: You're fumbling, Eros, and my Queen is more skillful as a  squire  than you are. Hurry.

original: —O love,   That thou couldst see my wars today, and knew’st   The royal occupation! Thou shouldst see   A workman in ’t.
translation: Oh my love, if only you could see me in battle today, and if only you were familiar with the techniques of war! You'd see an expert at work.

original: A thousand, sir, Early though ’t be, have on their riveted trim And at the port expect you.
translation: Even though it is early, sir, a thousand soldiers have put on their armor and wait for you at the port.

original: The morn is fair. Good morrow, General.
translation: It is a favorable morning. Good morning, General.

original: Good morrow, General.
translation: Good morning, General.

original: ’Tis well blown, lads.   This morning, like the spirit of a youth   That means to be of note, begins betimes.   So, so.
translation: The morning begins well, boys. Like a spirited young man who means to accomplish great things, it gets started early. So, so.

original: Come, give me that. This way.  Well said.   Fare thee well, dame.
translation: Come, give me that. Like this. Well done. Goodbye to you, my lady.

original: Whate’er becomes of me,   This is a soldier’s kiss.
translation: Whatever happens to me, this is a soldier's kiss.

original: Rebukable   And worthy shameful check it were to stand   On more mechanic compliment. I’ll leave thee   Now like a man of steel.
translation: It would be shameful and worthy of a scolding if I were to give you any baser or less noble a compliment than that. I'll leave you now like a true soldier.

original: You that will  fight,   Follow me close. I’ll bring you to ’t.
translation: You who wish to fight, follow me closely, I'll bring you into battle.

original: Please you retire to your chamber?
translation: Would you like to retire to your room?

original: Lead me.   He goes forth gallantly. That he and Caesar might   Determine this great war in single fight!
translation: Lead me. He goes forward bravely. If only he and Caesar could fight this war through single combat!

original: Then Antony—but now—. Well, on.
translation: Then Antony—but now—Well, let's go.

original: The gods make this a happy day to Antony!
translation: May the gods make this a lucky day for Antony!

original: Would thou and those thy scars had once prevailed To make me fight at land!
translation: If only you and your scarred face had convinced me a short time ago to fight on land!

original: Hadst thou done so,   The kings that have revolted,
translation: If you had done so, the kings that have rebelled against you

original: and the soldier   That has this morning left thee, would have still   Followed thy heels.
translation: and the soldier that abandoned you this morning would still be following you into battle.

original: Who’s gone this morning?
translation: Who deserted this morning?

original: Who?   One ever near thee. Call for Enobarbus
translation: Who? One who was always close to you. Call for Enobarbus.

original: He shall not hear thee, or from Caesar’s camp   Say “I am none of thine.”
translation: He won't hear you, or if he does, he'll call back from Caesar's camp and say, "I'm no soldier of yours."

original: What sayest thou?
translation: What are you saying?

original: Sir, He is with Caesar.
translation: Sir, he has joined with Caesar.

original: Sir, his chests and treasure He has not with him.
translation: Sir, he didn't bring his chests of treasure with him.

original: Is he gone?
translation: Is he gone?

original: Most certain.
translation: It is certain that he is.

original: Go, Eros, send his treasure after. Do it.   Detain no jot, I charge thee. Write to him—   I will subscribe—gentle adieus and greetings.
translation: Go, Eros, send his treasure to him. Do it. Don't withhold a bit of it, I order you. Write to him—I'll sign the letters—sending him kind farewells and greetings.

original: Say that I wish he never find more cause   To change a master. Oh, my fortunes have   Corrupted honest men! Dispatch.—Enobarbus!
translation: Tell him that I hope he never has cause again to leave his master. Oh, I have had such bad luck that it has caused honest men to become unfaithful! Hurry. Oh, Enobarbus!

original: Go forth, Agrippa, and begin the fight. Our will is Antony be took alive. Make it so known.
translation: Go forth, Agrippa, and begin the battle. My desire is for Anthony to be captured alive. Let the troops know.

original: Caesar, I shall.
translation: Caesar, I will.

original: The time of universal peace is near. Prove this a prosp’rous day, the three-nooked world Shall bear the olive freely.
Antony Is come into the field.
translation: Antony has arrived on the battlefield.

original: Go charge Agrippa   Plant those that have revolted in the vant,
translation: Go tell Agrippa to take Antony's former soldiers and place them on the front lines.

original: That Antony may seem to spend his fury   Upon himself.
translation: That way, Antony will feel like he is hurting himself.

original: Alexas did revolt and went to Jewry on   Affairs of Antony, there did dissuade   Great Herod to incline himself to Caesar   And leave his master Antony.
translation: Alexas revolted when he went to Judea on some business for Antony and, while he was there, he persuaded the great king Herod to take Caesar's side and abandon his master Antony.

original: For this pains   Caesar hath hanged him. Canidius and the rest   That fell away have entertainment but   No honorable trust.
translation: Caesar hanged him for his efforts. Candidius and the others who abandoned Antony have found employment, but they aren't trusted as loyal men.

original: I have done ill,   Of which I do accuse myself so sorely   That I will joy no more.
translation: I have done something terrible, for which I accuse myself so bitterly that I will never be happy again.

original: Enobarbus, Antony   Hath after thee sent all thy treasure, with   His bounty overplus.
translation: Enobarbus, Antony has sent you all your treasure, along with additional treasure from his own supply.

original: The messenger   Came on my guard, and at thy tent is now   Unloading of his mules.
translation: The messenger came while I was on guard duty, and he's at your tent now unloading the treasure from his mules.

original: I give it you.
translation: I give the treasure to you.

original: Mock not, Enobarbus.   I tell you true.   Best you safed the bringer   Out of the host.
translation: Don't mock me, Enobarbus, I'm telling you the truth.  It would be best if you saw that the messenger received safe passage through the lines of troops.

original: I must attend mine office,   Or would have done ’t myself. Your Emperor   Continues still a Jove.
translation: I must see to my duties, or I would have done it myself. Your Emperor continues to behave as magnificently as a god.

original: I am alone the villain of the earth,   And feel I am so most. O Antony,   Thou mine of bounty, how wouldst thou have paid   My better service, when my turpitude   Thou dost so crown with gold!
translation: I am the most villainous person on earth, and I know this better than anyone else. Oh Antony, you endless source of generosity, how would you have rewarded me for being more faithful to you, when you reward my treachery with gold like this!

original: This blows my heart.   If swift thought break it not, a swifter mean   Shall outstrike thought, but thought will do ’t, I  feel.
translation: This breaks my heart. If rapid thoughts don't break it, there's something that will break it faster than thought—but I feel that thoughts alone will do it.

original: I fight against thee? No, I will go seek   Some ditch wherein to die. The foul’st best fits   My latter part of life.
translation: Could I possibly fight against you, Antony? No, I will go find a ditch where I can die. The foulest kind of death is most suitable for the foul thing I have done at the end of my life.

original: Retire! We have engaged ourselves too far. Caesar himself has work, and our oppression Exceeds what we expected.
translation: Fall back! We've extended ourselves too far. Even Caesar is assailed, and our enemy's strength is greater than we expected.

original: O my brave Emperor, this is fought indeed! Had we done so at first, we had droven them home With clouts about their heads.
translation: Oh my brave Emperor, this is really the way to fight! If we had fought like this initially, we would have driven them home with bandages around their heads.

original: Thou bleed’st apace.
translation: You're bleeding fast.

original: I had a wound here that was like a “T,” But now ’tis made an “H.”
They do retire.
translation: They're retreating.

original: We’ll beat ’em into bench-holes. I have yet Room for six scotches more.
translation: We'll beat them back into their barracks. I can still stand six more wounds.

original: They are beaten, sir, and our advantage serves For a fair victory.
translation: They are beaten back, sir, and our advantage could help us secure a desirable victory.

original: Let us score their backs And snatch ’em up, as we take hares, behind! ’Tis sport to maul a runner.
translation: Let's make gashes on their backs and take them the same way we catch hares, from behind! It's entertaining to wound someone who's running away from you.

original: I will reward thee Once for thy sprightly comfort and tenfold For thy good valor. Come thee on.
translation: I'll reward you once for the comfort you give me with your high spirits, and reward you ten times for your fine bravery. Come on.

original: I’ll halt after.
translation: I'll limp after you.

original: We have beat him to his camp. Run one before And let the Queen know of our gests.
translation: We have beat him back to his camp. Let someone run on ahead and tell the Queen what we've accomplished.

original: Tomorrow,   Before the sun shall see ’s, we’ll spill the blood   That has today escaped.
translation: Tomorrow, before the sun rises, we'll kill all the enemy forces that escaped us today.

original: I thank you all,   For doughty-handed are you, and have fought   Not as you served the cause, but as ’t had been   Each man’s like mine. You have shown all Hectors.
translation: I thank you all, for you are brave, and you didn't fight as though you had been commanded to serve this cause, but as though it were as much your own cause as it is mine. You have all fought as bravely as  Hector .

original: Enter the city. Clip your wives, your friends.   Tell them your feats, whilst they with joyful tears   Wash the congealment from your wounds and kiss   The honored gashes whole.
translation: Enter the city. Embrace your wives, your friends. Tell them what you have done, while they wash the congealed blood from your wounds with joyful tears and heal your honorable injuries with kisses.

original: Give me thy hand.   To this great fairy I’ll commend thy acts,   Make her thanks bless thee.
translation: Give me your hand. I'll praise your deeds to this great enchantress, the queen, so that she will bless you with her thanks.

original: O thou day o’ the world,   (to CLEOPATRA)   Chain mine armed neck. Leap thou, attire and all,   Through proof of harness to my heart, and there   Ride on the pants triumphing!
translation: Oh light of the world, clasp your arms around my neck. Leap through my armor into my heart, in your robes and all, and ride on my heartbeats as if you were riding a horse in a triumphal parade!

original: Lord of lords! O infinite virtue, com’st thou smiling from The world’s great snare uncaught?
translation: Greatest of all lords! Oh you infinitely brave man, did you face the world's greatest threat and escape with a smile?

original: Mine nightingale,   We have beat them to their beds.
translation: My nightingale, we have beaten them all the way back to their camp in fear.

original: What, girl, though  gray   Do something mingle with our younger brown, yet ha’ we   A brain that nourishes our nerves and can   Get goal for goal of youth. Behold this man.   Commend unto his lips thy favoring hand.
translation: What does it matter, my lady, if I am not as young as I once was—I still have a brain that feeds my muscles and can achieve my goals just as well as a younger man. Look at this man. Give him your hand to kiss.

original: Kiss it, my warrior.
translation: Kiss her hand, my warrior.

original: He hath fought today As if a god, in hate of mankind, had Destroyed in such a shape.
translation: He has fought today like a god who became a man in order to destroy mankind out of hatred.

original: I’ll give thee, friend, An armor all of gold. It was a king’s.
translation: I'll give you a suit of armor made entirely out of gold, my friend. It belonged to a king.

original: He has deserved it, were it carbuncled   Like holy Phoebus’ car. Give me thy hand.   Through Alexandria make a jolly march.
translation: He would deserve it, even if it were covered in jewels like  Phoebus's chariot . Give me your hand. Let's lead a merry parade through Alexandria.

original: Bear our hacked targets like the men that owe them.   Had our great palace the capacity   To camp this host, we all would sup together   And drink carouses to the next day’s fate,   Which promises royal peril.
translation: Let's carry our dented shields as we are the men who own them and received those dents in battle. If our great palace had room to host the entire army, we would all dine together and drink toasts to our victory tomorrow, which I suspect will hold great danger.

original: —Trumpeters,   With brazen din blast you the city’s ear;   Make mingle with our rattling taborins,   That heaven and earth may strike their sounds together,   Applauding our approach.
translation: Trumpeters, blast the ears of everyone in the city with bold noise. Let them sound along with our rattling drums, so that the  sounds of heaven and the sounds of earth  will be heard together as if applauding our approach.

original: If we be not relieved within this hour,   We must return to th’ court of guard.
translation: If the other guards don't come to replace us within the next hour, we'll have to return to the guardroom.

original: The night   Is shiny, and they say we shall embattle   By th’ second hour i’ th’ morn.
translation: There's bright light tonight, and they say we'll resume battle by two in the morning.

original: This last day was a shrewd one to ’s.
translation: This last day was a bad one for us.

original: O bear me witness, night—
translation: Oh night, bear witness to my words—

original: What man is this?
translation: Who is this?

original: Stand close and list him.
translation: Let's hide and listen to him.

original: Be witness to me, O thou blessèd moon,   When men revolted shall upon record   Bear hateful memory,
translation: Bear witness to me, oh you blessed moon: when the time comes that rebels are remembered with hatred,

original: poor Enobarbus did   Before thy face repent.
translation: remember that poor Enobarbus repented before you for rebelling.

original: Enobarbus?
translation: Enobarbus?

original: Peace! Hark further.
translation: Be quiet! Keep listening.

original: O sovereign mistress of true melancholy,   The poisonous damp of night disponge upon me,   That life, a very rebel to my will,   May hang no longer on me.
translation: Oh moon, you royal mistress of genuine melancholy, pour down the poisonous mists of night upon me, so that I may no longer live, now that I no longer wish to.

original: Throw my heart   Against the flint and hardness of my fault,   Which, being dried with grief, will break to powder   And finish all foul thoughts.
translation: Take my heart and throw it against my hard sin. which is weak from grief. It will burst into pieces and all my bitter thoughts will end with my death.

original: O Antony,   Nobler than my revolt is infamous,   Forgive me in thine own particular,   But let the world rank me in register   A master-leaver and a fugitive.   O Antony! O Antony!
translation: Oh Antony, your nobility is even greater than my fault is terrible. I wish that you would forgive me for those sins that I've committed against you, but I want the rest of the world to remember me as a deserter and someone who abandoned his master. Oh Antony! Oh Antony!

original: Let’s speak to him.
translation: Let's speak to him.

original: Let’s hear him, for the things he speaks may concern  Caesar.
translation: Let's listen to him, because the things he's talking about might have to do with Caesar.

original: Let’s do so. But he sleeps.
translation: Let's do that. But he's asleep.

original: Swoons rather, for so bad a prayer as his Was never yet for sleep.
translation: I think he's fainted, actually. No one ever said such a despairing prayer to lull themselves to sleep.

original: Go we to him.
translation: Let's go to him.

original: Awake, sir, awake. Speak to us.
translation: Wake up, sir, wake up. Speak to us.

original: Hear you, sir?
translation: Can you hear us, sir?

original: The hand of death hath raught him.
translation: Death has struck him down.

original: Hark, the drums   Demurely wake the sleepers. Let us bear him   To th’ court of guard.
translation: Listen, the drums are waking up the sleeping men with their subdued noise. Let's carry him to the guardroom.

original: He is of note. Our hour   Is fully out.
translation: He's a person of high rank. The time of our watch is up.

original: Come on, then. He may recover yet.
translation: Come on, then. He might still wake up.

original: Their preparation is today by sea. We please them not by land.
translation: They're preparing to fight by sea today. They're not happy fighting us on land.

original: For both, my lord.
translation: They're preparing to fight by both land and sea, my lord.

original: I would they’d fight i’ th’ fire or i’ th’ air,   We’d fight there too. But this it is: our foot   Upon the hills adjoining to the city   Shall stay with us.
translation: I wish they'd also fight in  fire or in the air —we'd fight them there too. But this is how we'll do things—our foot soldiers up on the hills beside the city will stay with us.

original: Order for sea is given;   They have put forth the haven,   Where their appointment we may best discover   And look on their endeavor.
translation: I've given the orders for our preparations at sea. The ships have left the port.  Let's go up higher  where we can better observe their battle plans and watch what they're doing.

original: But being charged, we will be still by land—   Which, as I take ’t, we shall, for his best force   Is forth to man his galleys.
translation: Unless we are attacked, we won't take any action on land—and I guess that we won't be attacked, since most of his troops have been sent out to guard his ships.

original: To the vales,   And hold our best advantage.
translation: Let's go to the valleys and take the best position.

original: Yet they are not joined. Where yond pine does stand I shall discover all. I’ll bring thee word Straight how ’tis like to go.
translation: But they still aren't fighting. I'll go over to where that pine stands and survey the whole scene. I'll tell you shortly how things are likely to go.

original: Swallows have built   In Cleopatra’s sails their nests. The auguries   Say they know not, they cannot tell, look grimly,   And dare not speak their knowledge.
translation: Swallows have built nests in the sails of Cleopatra's ships. The  soothsayers  say they don't know what this means, they cannot say. They look grim and dare not tell us what they know.

original: Antony   Is valiant and dejected, and by starts   His fretted fortunes give him hope and fear   Of what he has and has not.
translation: Antony is both brave and dejected, and in fits and starts his diminished luck gives him reasons for both hope and fear—hope thanks to what he does have, fear because of what he does not have.

original: All is lost!   This foul Egyptian hath betrayèd me.   My fleet hath yielded to the foe, and yonder   They cast their caps up and carouse together   Like friends long lost.
translation: All is lost! That foul Egyptian has betrayed me. My fleet has surrendered to the enemy, and down there, they throw their caps in the air and drink together like long-lost friends.

original: Triple-turned whore! ’Tis thou   Hast sold me to this novice, and my heart   Makes only wars on thee.
translation: That whore, who's betrayed  three men ! It's you, Cleopatra, who has sold me out to this boy Caesar, and my anger is directed only at you.

original: Bid them all fly,   For when I am revenged upon my charm,   I have done all. Bid them all fly. Begone!
translation: Tell all my forces to flee, for all I intend to do now is take revenge on this woman who bewitched me. Tell them all to flee. Get going!

original: O sun, thy uprise shall I see no more.   Fortune and Antony part here. Even here   Do we shake hands.
translation: Oh sun, I will never see you rise agin. This is when I lose all my luck; at this very moment I bid it goodbye.

original: All come to this? The hearts   That spanieled me at heels, to whom I gave   Their wishes, do discandy, melt their sweets   On blossoming Caesar, and this pine is barked   That overtopped them all.
translation: Has it all come to this? Those men who fawned on me with all their hearts, whose wishes I granted, fall away from me and fawn now on Caesar with his growing good fortune, and I am destroyed even though I was once greater than all of them.

original: Betrayed I am.   Oh, this false soul of Egypt! This grave charm,   Whose eye becked forth my wars and called them home,
translation: I am betrayed. Oh, this treacherous queen of Egypt! This deadly enchantress, who decided when I went to war and when I brought my armies home,

original: Whose bosom was my crownet, my chief end,   Like a right gypsy hath at fast and loose   Beguiled me to the very heart of loss.
translation: whose love was my main goal and greatest glory, she has cheated me like a true gypsy and tricked me until I lost everything.

original: What, Eros, Eros!
translation: Hey there, Eros, Eros!

original: Why is my lord enraged against his love?
translation: Why is my lord so angry at his love?

original: Vanish, or I shall give thee thy deserving,   And blemish Caesar’s triumph. Let him take thee   And hoist thee up to the shouting plebeians!
translation: Get away, or I'll give you what you deserve and diminish the glory of Caesar's  triumphal procession . Let him take you and display you in public in front of the screaming crowd!

original: Follow his chariot, like the greatest spot   Of all thy sex. Most monsterlike be shown   For poor’st diminutives, for dolts, and let   Patient Octavia plow thy visage up   With her preparèd nails!
translation: Follow his chariot, like the most disgraced woman that has ever lived. Be displayed like a spectacle for fools, for the common people to stare at, and let long-suffering Octavia scratch your face with the nails she has sharpened for you!

original: ’Tis well th’art gone,   If it be well to live, but better ’twere   Thou fell’st into my fury, for one death   Might have prevented many.
translation: It's good that you're gone, if you wish to remain alive, but it would have been better if you had fallen prey to my anger. Then your death might have prevented the death of many others.

original: —Eros, ho!—
translation: Eros, hey there!

original: The shirt of Nessus is upon me. Teach me,   Alcides, thou mine ancestor, thy rage.
translation: I feel as if I were wearing the shirt of Nessus.  Hercules , my ancestor, I pray that you will show me how to show my anger as you did.

original: Let me lodge Lichas on the horns o’ th’ moon,   And with those hands that grasped the heaviest club   Subdue my worthiest self.
translation: Let me destroy my enemy, and with my own hands—hands that once wielded the heaviest weapons— destroy myself with honor .

original: The witch shall die.   To the young Roman boy she hath sold me, and I fall   Under this plot. She dies for ’t.
translation: That witch Cleopatra will die. She's sold me to that young Roman boy Caesar, and I am destroyed by her plot. She will die for it.

original: —Eros, ho!
translation: Eros, hey there!

original: Help me, my women! Oh, he’s more mad Than Telamon for his shield. The boar of Thessaly Was never so embossed.
To th’ monument!   There lock yourself and send him word you are dead.
translation: Go to your  tomb ! Lock yourself inside and send him a message that you are dead.

original: The soul and body rive not more in parting   Than greatness going off.
translation: When a great man loses his greatness, he falls lower than anyone—his greatness goes farther from him than the soul goes from the body in death.

original: To th’ monument!—
translation: To the tomb!

original: Mardian, go tell him I have slain myself.   Say that the last I spoke was “Antony,”   And word it, prithee, piteously.
translation: Mardian, go tell him I have killed myself. Tell him the last word I spoke was "Antony," and please, fill your voice with pity when you say it.

original: Hence, Mardian,   And bring me how he takes my death.
translation: Get going, Mardian, and tell me how he reacts to the news of my death.

original: To  th’ monument!
translation: To the tomb!

original: Eros, thou yet behold’st me?
translation: Eros, you still see me?

original: Ay, noble lord.
translation: Yes, my noble lord.

original: Sometimes we see a cloud that’s dragonish,   A vapor sometime like a bear or lion,   A towered citadel, a pendant rock,   A forkèd mountain,
translation: Sometimes we see a cloud that looks like a dragon, and sometimes a mist that looks like a bear or a lion, like a fortress with towers, an overhanging rock, a mountain with many peaks.

original: or blue promontory   With trees upon ’t that nod unto the world   And mock our eyes with air.
translation: Sometimes we see a blue rock with trees on it that shake before our eyes and make mockeries of our sight since they are made only of air.

original: Thou hast seen these signs.   They are black vesper’s pageants.
translation: You have seen the signs. They are the apparitions that tell us night and death are coming.

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: That which is now a horse, even with a thought The rack dislimns and makes it indistinct As water is in water.
translation: We see a shape that now looks like a horse, and even as we think it, the cloud dims and makes the shape indistinct, like one drop in a body of water.

original: It does, my lord.
translation: It does, my lord.

original: My good knave Eros, now thy captain is   Even such a body. Here I am Antony,   Yet cannot hold this visible shape, my knave.
translation: My good young man Eros, your captain's body behaves in just the same way now. I am myself for now, but I cannot maintain this bodily form, my boy.

original: I made these wars for Egypt, and the Queen,   Whose heart I thought I had, for she had mine—   Which whilst it was mine had annexed unto ’t   A million more, now lost
translation: I went to war for the sake of Egypt and the Queen. I thought I had the Queen's love, for she had mine—and until I loved her, I had the love of a million more people, which I have now lost.

original: —she, Eros, has   Packed cards with Caesar and false-played my glory   Unto an enemy’s triumph.
translation: But now she has concocted a plot with Caesar, Eros, and betrayed me so that an enemy may defeat me and destroy my glory.

original: Nay, weep not, gentle Eros. There is left us   Ourselves to end ourselves.
translation: No, do not weep, gentle Eros. We still have enough of our own power to put an end to our lives.

original: Oh, thy vile lady! She has robbed me of my sword.
translation: Oh, your despicable mistress! She has destroyed all my fortitude.

original: No, Antony, My mistress loved thee, and her fortunes mingled With thine entirely.
translation: No, Antony, my mistress loved you, and her fate was inseparable from yours.

original: Hence, saucy eunuch! Peace! She hath betrayed me and shall die the death.
translation: Get out, you shameless eunuch! Be quiet! She has betrayed me and she will die as she deserves.

original: Death of one person can be paid but once,   And that she has discharged. What thou wouldst do   Is done unto thy hand.
translation: A person can only die once, and she has done that. What you intended to do, she has done for you.

original: The last she spake   Was “Antony, most noble Antony!”   Then in the midst a tearing groan did break   The name of Antony.
translation: The last words she spoke were, "Antony, most noble Antony!" Then she broke off in the middle of saying your name to let out a heart-rending groan.

original: It was divided   Between her heart and lips. She rendered life,   Thy name so buried in her.
translation: She spoke half of the word, the other half remained in her heart. And so she died with your name buried inside her.

original: Dead, then?
translation: She is dead, then?

original: Dead.
translation: Dead.

original: Unarm, Eros. The long day’s task is done, And we must sleep.    That thou depart’st  hence safe Does pay thy labor richly. Go.
translation: Take off my armor, Eros. Our long day's work is finished, and we must sleep.

original: Off, pluck off!   The sevenfold shield of Ajax cannot keep   The battery from my heart. O, cleave, my sides!
translation: Off, take my armor off!  [EROS removes his armor]  Not even the shield of Ajax, with all its seven layers, can protect my heart from this assault. Oh, if only my sides would burst open!

original: Heart, once be stronger than thy continent.   Crack thy frail case!—Apace, Eros, apace.   No more a soldier.
translation: I wish my heart were stronger than the weak body that contains it and crack open. Quickly, Eros, quickly. I am no longer a soldier.

original: Bruisèd pieces, go.   You have been nobly borne.   (to EROS)   From me awhile.
translation: Let these damaged pieces of armor be cast aside. I wore them nobly. Eros, leave me alone for a while.

original: What would my lord?
translation: What do you want, my lord?

original: Since Cleopatra died   I have lived in such dishonor that the gods   Detest my baseness.
translation: Since Cleopatra died, my life has had such dishonor that even the gods hate how disgraceful I am.

original: I, that with my sword   Quartered the world, and o’er green Neptune’s back   With ships made cities, condemn myself to lack   The courage of a woman
translation: I, who divided the world into quarters and sailed across the  green sea  with so many ships that they appeared to make a city on the waves—I disgrace myself by having less courage than a woman.

original: —less noble mind   Than she which by her death our Caesar tells   “I am conqueror of myself.”
translation: I have a less noble mind than she, who tells Caesar with her death, " I am conqueror of myself ."

original: Thou art sworn, Eros,   That when the exigent should come which now   Is come indeed, when I should see behind me   Th’ inevitable prosecution of   Disgrace and horror, that on my command,   Thou then wouldst kill me   .
translation: You have sworn, Eros, that when it became necessary, as it is now, when I could see inevitable disgrace and horror looming, that you would kill me on my command.

original: Do ’t. The time is come.   Thou strik’st not me, ’tis Caesar thou defeat’st.   Put color in thy cheek.
translation: Do it. The time has come. It isn't me you strike, it's Caesar you're defeating. Pull yourself together.

original: The gods withhold me! Shall I do that which all the Parthian darts, Though enemy, lost aim and could not?
translation: May the gods prevent me! All of the Parthians' arrows missed their target and could not kill you, how could I kill you instead?

original: Eros,   Wouldst thou be windowed in great Rome and see   Thy master thus with pleached arms, bending down   His corrigible neck, his face subdued   To penetrative shame,
translation: Eros, would you rather look down from a window in the great city of Rome and see your master displayed like this, with his arms tied, bending his neck in submission, his face subdued by penetrating shame,

original: whilst the wheeled seat   Of fortunate Caesar, drawn before him, branded   His baseness that ensued?
translation: while lucky Caesar's chariot was drawn before him, indicating to everyone that the man who walked behind was disgraced?

original: I would not see ’t.
translation: I couldn't look at it.

original: Come, then, for with a wound I must be cured. Draw that thy honest sword, which thou hast worn Most useful for thy country.
translation: Come, then, for you can only help me by wounding me. Draw your faithful sword, which you have used to do good service for your country.

original: O sir, pardon me!
translation: Oh sir, pardon me!

original: When I did make thee free, swor’st thou not then   To do this when I bade thee?
translation: When I freed you from servitude, didn't you swear to me then that you would do this when I told you to?

original: Do it at once,   Or thy precedent services are all   But accidents unpurposed. Draw and come.
translation: Do it immediately, or all your previous service to me was nothing but an accident, not something you intended to do. Draw your sword and come.

original: Turn from me then that noble countenance Wherein the worship of the whole world lies.
translation: Turn away from me, then, that noble face that the whole world used to worship.

original: Lo thee!
translation: Here you are!

original: My sword is drawn.
translation: My sword is drawn.

original: Then let it do at once The thing why thou hast drawn it.
translation: Then do it at once, the thing you drew it in order to do.

original: My dear master, My captain, and my emperor, let me say, Before I strike this bloody stroke, farewell.
translation: My dear master, my captain, and my emperor, before I strike this deadly stroke, let me say goodbye to you.

original: ’Tis said, man, and farewell.
translation: You've said it, man, goodbye.

original: Farewell, great chief. Shall I strike now?
translation: Goodbye, great captain. Shall I strike now?

original: Now, Eros.
translation: Now, Eros.

original: Why, there then!
translation: Why, then there it is!

original: Thrice nobler than myself,   Thou teachest me, O valiant Eros, what   I should and thou couldst not.
translation: You are three times nobler than I am. Oh brave Eros, you teach me how to do the thing that I should do and that you  couldn't do .

original: My Queen and Eros   Have by their brave instruction got upon me   A nobleness in record.
translation: In this brave deed that they've taught me, my Queen and Eros have gained a noble reputation ahead of me, recorded in the history books.

original: But I will be   A bridegroom in my death, and run into ’t   As to a lover’s bed.
translation: But I will embrace death as willingly as a bridegroom embraces his bride, and seek it as eagerly as a lover's bed.

original: Come then, and Eros,   Thy master dies thy scholar. To do thus   I learned of thee.
translation: Come then. Eros, I was once your master but now I am your student. I learned how to do this from you.

original: What’s the noise?
translation: What's all this noise?

original: I have done my work ill, friends. Oh, make an end Of what I have begun!
translation: I've done my work badly, my friends. Oh, finish what I started!

original: The star is fall’n.
translation: The greatest man has fallen.

original: And time is at his period.
translation: And time comes to a halt.

original: Alas, and woe!
translation: Alas, the sorrow!

original: Let him that loves me strike me dead.
translation: If anyone loves me, let him kill me.

original: Not I.
translation: Not I.

original: Nor I.
translation: Nor I.

original: Nor anyone.
translation: Nor anyone.

original: Thy death and fortunes bid thy followers fly.
translation: Your death and your fallen fortunes show your followers that they ought to leave you.

original: This sword but shown to Caesar, with this tidings, Shall enter me with him.
translation: If I just show this sword to Caesar and tell him this news, I'll gain favor with him.

original: Where’s Antony?
translation: Where's Antony?

original: There, Diomed, there.
translation: There, Diomed, there.

original: Lives he? Wilt thou not answer, man?
translation: Is he alive? Won't you answer, man?

original: Art thou there, Diomed? Draw thy sword and give me Sufficing strokes for death.
translation: Are you there, Diomed? Draw your sword and strike me hard enough to kill me.

original: Most absolute lord, My mistress Cleopatra sent me to thee.
translation: Greatest lord, my mistress Cleopatra sent me to you.

original: When did she send thee?
translation: When did she send you?

original: Now, my lord.
translation: Just now, my lord.

original: Where is she?
translation: Where is she?

original: Locked in her monument. She had a prophesying fear   Of what hath come to pass.
translation: Locked in her tomb. She was afraid of what she foresaw might happen.

original: For when she saw—   Which never shall be found—you did suspect   She had disposed with Caesar, and that your rage   Would not be purged, she sent you word she was dead.
translation: For when she saw that you suspected her of plotting with Caesar—something you will never find to be true—and that your rage could not be overcome, she sent you a message that she was dead.

original: But fearing since how it might work, hath sent   Me to proclaim the truth, and I am come,   I dread, too late.
translation: But then she became afraid of what effect the news might have on you, and she sent me to tell you the truth. Now I'm afraid that I've arrived too late.

original: Too late, good Diomed. Call my guard, I prithee.
translation: Too late, good Diomed. Call my guard, please.

original: What ho, the Emperor’s guard! The guard, what ho! Come, your lord calls!
translation: Hey there, the Emperor's guard! The guard, hey there! Come, your lord is calling you!

original: Bear me, good friends, where Cleopatra bides. ’Tis the last service that I shall command you.
translation: Good friends, carry me to where Cleopatra is. This is the last service that I will command you to carry out.

original: Woe, woe are we, sir, you may not live to wear All your true followers out.
translation: We are sorrowful, sorrowful, sir, that you will not live longer than your followers.

original: Most heavy day!
translation: Most sorrowful day!

original: Nay, good my fellows, do not please sharp fate   To grace it with your sorrows. Bid that welcome   Which comes to punish us, and we punish it,   Seeming to bear it lightly.
translation: No, my good friends, do not give cruel fate the satisfaction of seeing your sorrows. If we welcome something that was intended to punish us, we punish it in return by seeming not to mind it.

original: Take me up.   I have led you oft; carry me now, good friends,   And have my thanks for all.
translation: Pick me up. I have often led you; carry me now, good friends. I thank you for everything.

original: O Charmian, I will never go from hence.
translation: Oh Charmian, I will never leave this place.

original: Be comforted, dear madam.
translation: Be comforted, good madam.

original: No, I will not.   All strange and terrible events are welcome,   But comforts we despise.
translation: No, I will not. I welcome all strange and terrible events, but I despise comfort.

original: Our size of sorrow,   Proportioned to our cause, must be as great   As that which makes it.
translation: The size of our sorrow is proportionate to the cause of our sorrow, and so it must be as great as the cause.

original: How now? Is he dead?
translation: What's going on? Is he dead?

original: His death’s upon him, but not dead. Look out o’ th’ other side your monument. His guard have brought him thither.
translation: His death is approaching fast, but he is not dead. Look out from the other side of your tomb. His guards have brought him there.

original: O sun,   Burn the great sphere thou mov’st in. Darkling stand   The varying shore o’ th’ world!
translation: Oh sun,  burn up the path of your orbit and leave it . May all the shores of the world lie in darkness!

original: O Antony,   Antony, Antony! Help, Charmian, help, Iras, help!   Help, friends below! Let’s draw him hither.
translation: Oh Antony, Antony, Antony! Help, Charmian, Iras, help! Help, friends below! Let's draw him up here.

original: Peace! Not Caesar’s valor hath o’erthrown Antony, But Antony’s hath triumphed on itself.
translation: Be at peace! Caesar's bravery did not overthrow me. I conquered myself with my own bravery.

original: So it should be, that none but Antony Should conquer Antony, but woe ’tis so!
translation: That is how it should be, that no one should conquer Antony except Antony himself—but what a pity that it has come to pass!

original: I am dying, Egypt, dying. Only   I here importune death awhile,
translation: I am dying, Queen of Egypt, dying. I just ask now that death hold off for a short while,

original: until   Of many thousand kisses the poor last   I lay upon thy lips.
translation: until I lay the poor last kiss of many thousands of kisses on your lips.

original: I dare not, dear,   Dear my lord, pardon, I dare not,   Lest I be taken. Not th’ imperious show   Of the full-fortuned Caesar ever shall   Be brooched with me.
translation: I dare not come down to you, dear. My dear lord, forgive me, I dare not, for fear I will be captured. I will never serve as an ornament to adorn the triumphal procession of Caesar, for all his good fortune.

original: If knife, drugs, serpents, have   Edge, sting, or operation, I am safe.
translation: As long as knives have edges, serpents have teeth, or drugs have power, I will be safe from him.

original: Your wife Octavia, with her modest eyes   And still conclusion, shall acquire no honor   Demuring upon me.
translation: Your wife Octavia, with her modestly lowered eyes and her silent judgments, will get no honor from gazing upon me.

original: But come, come, Antony—   Help me, my women—We must draw thee up.   Assist, good friends.
translation: But come, come, Antony—help me, my women—we must draw you up. Help, good friends.

original: Oh, quick, or I am gone.
translation: Oh, quick, or I will be dead.

original: Here’s sport indeed! How heavy weighs my lord!   Our strength is all gone into heaviness,   That makes the weight.
translation: Here's a fine game! How heavy my lord is! All our strength is dissolved by  sadness —that's what makes the weight so great.

original: Had I great Juno’s power,   The strong-winged Mercury should fetch thee up   And set thee by Jove’s side.
translation: If I had great Juno's power,  Mercury with his strong wings  would bring you up and set you at Jove's side.

original: Yet come a little.   Wishers were ever fools. Oh, come, come, come!
translation: Still, come a little closer. Wishing has always been a foolish thing to do. Oh, come, come, come!

original: And welcome, welcome! Die when thou hast lived. Quicken with kissing. Had my lips that power, Thus would I wear them out.
translation: And welcome, welcome! Die only after you have lived. Let kissing bring you back to life. If my lips had the power to do that, I would wear them out like this.

original: A heavy sight!
translation: A sad sight!

original: I am dying, Egypt, dying. Give me some wine and let me speak a little.
translation: I am dying, Queen of Egypt, dying. Give me some wine and let me speak a little.

original: No, let me speak, and let me rail so high That the false huswife Fortune break her wheel, Provoked by my offense.
One word, sweet Queen: Of Caesar seek your honor, with your safety—Oh!
translation: One word, sweet Queen. Appeal to Caesar to protect your honor and your safety—oh!

original: They do not go together.
Gentle, hear me. None about Caesar trust but Proculeius.
translation: Gentle lady, listen to me. Don't trust any of Caesar's followers except Proculeius.

original: My resolution and my hands I’ll trust, None about Caesar.
translation: I'll trust my determination and my own hands. I won't trust anyone around Caesar.

original: The miserable change now at my end   Lament nor sorrow at, but please your thoughts   In feeding them with those my former fortunes,   Wherein I lived the greatest prince o’ th’ world,   The noblest,
translation: Do not lament or be sorry for the miserable turn that my life has taken. Rather, please yourself by thinking about the great fortunes I enjoyed in the past, when I was the greatest and noblest prince in the world.

original: and do now not basely die,   Not cowardly put off my helmet to   My countryman
translation: I do not die dishonorably now, nor do I surrender like a coward to my fellow countryman.

original: —a Roman by a Roman   Valiantly vanquished. Now my spirit is going.   I can no more.
translation: I am a Roman who has been bravely conquered by another  Roman . Now my last breath is leaving me. I cannot speak any more.

original: Noblest of men, woo’t die?   Hast thou no care of me?
translation: Noblest of men, are you dying? Don't you care about me?

original: Shall I abide   In this dull world, which in thy absence is   No better than a sty?
translation: Can I remain in this dull world, which will be no better than a pigsty when you are gone from it?

original: O see, my women,   The crown o’ th’ earth doth melt. My lord!
translation: Oh look, my women, the greatest monarch of the earth is fading away. My lord!

original: Oh, withered is the garland of the war.   The soldier’s pole is fall’n! Young boys and girls   Are level now with men.
translation: Oh, the glories that crown battle are all gone now. The  guide  of every soldier has fallen! The men that are left now are no better than young boys and girls.

original: The odds is gone,   And there is nothing left remarkable   Beneath the visiting moon.
translation: There is no person of distinction left among humankind, and there is no longer anything remarkable  on earth .

original: Oh, quietness, lady!
translation: Oh, be calm, my lady!

original: She’s dead too, our sovereign.
translation: She's dead too, our queen.

original: Lady!
translation: Lady!

original: Madam!
translation: Madam!

original: O madam, madam, madam!
translation: Oh madam, madam, madam!

original: Royal Egypt, Empress!
translation: Royal Queen of Egypt, Empress!

original: Peace, peace, Iras.
translation: Peace, peace, Iras.

original: No more but e’en a woman, and commanded   By such poor passion as the maid that milks   And does the meanest chares.
translation: I am no longer a queen but just an ordinary woman. I am overpowered by the same unworthy emotions as any milkmaid who performs the humblest chores.

original: It were for me   To throw my scepter at the injurious gods,   To tell them that this world did equal theirs   Till they had stolen our jewel.
translation: It would be more fitting for me to hurl my scepter at the gods who have injured me and tell them that this earthly world was as good as their divine world until they stole away the greatest man.

original: All’s but naught.   Patience is sottish, and impatience does   Become a dog that’s mad. Then is it sin   To rush into the secret house of death   Ere death dare come to us?
translation: Everything is worthless. It is idiotic to be patient and endure things calmly, and to become impatient is quickly to become like a mad dog. In that case, is it really sinful to rush towards death before death comes to us naturally?

original: How do you, women?   What, what, good cheer! Why, how now, Charmian?   My noble girls! Ah, women, women! Look,   Our lamp is spent, it’s out. Good sirs, take heart.
translation: How are you, my women? What, what, be cheerful! Why, how are you doing there, Charmian? My noble girls! Ah, women, women! Look, our lamp has run out of oil, it's gone out. Good women, take heart.

original: We’ll bury him, and then, what’s brave, what’s noble,   Let’s do ’t after the high Roman fashion   And make death proud to take us.
translation: We'll bury him, and then, whatever is brave or noble, we'll do it in the noble Roman style, and die so nobly that death will be proud to take us.

original: Come, away.   This case of that huge spirit now is cold.   Ah, women, women! Come. We have no friend   But resolution, and the briefest end.
translation: Come, away. The body that contained that great spirit is now cold. Ah, women, women! Come. The only thing that can help us is determination, and the quickest possible death.

original: Go to him, Dolabella, bid him yield. Being so frustrate, tell him, he mocks The pauses that he makes.
translation: Go to Antony, Dolabella, and tell him to surrender. His delay in doing so makes him look ridiculous.

original: Caesar, I shall.
translation: Caesar, I will.

original: Wherefore is that? And what art thou that dar’st Appear thus to us?
translation: What is that? And who are you to dare and appear before me armed?

original: I am called Dercetus.   Mark Antony I served, who best was worthy   Best to be served. Whilst he stood up and spoke,   He was my master, and I wore my life   To spend upon his haters.
translation: My name is Dercetus. I served Mark Antony, who was the man most worthy of being served. While he was alive, he was my master, and I used my life to oppose those who hated him.

original: If thou please   To take me to thee, as I was to him   I’ll be to Caesar. If thou pleasest not,   I yield thee up my life.
translation: If it pleases you to employ me as Antony did I'll be loyal to you, Caesar. If not, I surrender my life to you.

original: What is ’t thou say’st?
translation: What do you mean?

original: I say, O Caesar, Antony is dead.
translation: I mean, Caesar, that Antony is dead.

original: The breaking of so great a thing should make   A greater crack. The round world   Should have shook lions into civil streets   And citizens to their dens.
translation: It should cause a greater disturbance when someone so great dies. The globe should have shaken so much that lions left their dens and entered the city streets and the citizens fled to the lions' dens.

original: The death of Antony   Is not a single doom. In the name lay   A moiety of the world.
translation: His death was not the death of an ordinary man. He controlled half of the world.

original: He is dead, Caesar,   Not by a public minister of justice,   Nor by a hirèd knife,
translation: He is dead. He wasn't killed by a public minister of justice or a hired assassin.

original: but that self hand   Which writ his honor in the acts it did   Hath, with the courage which the heart did lend it,   Splitted the heart.
translation: With a courageous heart, he killed himself with the same hand that he performed many honorable acts.

original: This is his sword.   I robbed his wound of it. Behold it stained   With his most noble blood.
translation: This is his sword. I took it away after it wounded him. See how it's stained with his most noble blood.

original: Look you, sad friends, The gods rebuke me, but it is tidings To wash the eyes of kings.
translation: See, my sad friends, the gods might criticize me for weeping, but this news is enough to make even a king cry.

original: And strange it is That nature must compel us to lament Our most persisted deeds.
His taints and honors Waged equal with him.
translation: His flaws and his virtues fought inside him, both with equal power.

original: A rarer spirit never Did steer humanity, but you gods will give us Some faults to make us men. Caesar is touched.
translation: No man was ever governed with such an uncommonly noble spirit. But the gods give us some faults to make us human. Caesar is emotional over the news.

original: When such a spacious mirror’s set before him, He needs must see himself.
translation: When he thinks about such a great man, he sees what he himself could become.

original: O Antony,   I have followed thee to this, but we do launch   Diseases in our bodies. I must perforce   Have shown to thee such a declining day,   Or look on thine.   We could not stall together   In the whole world.
translation: Oh Antony, I was trying to end your life, but we have to get rid of a disease if it threatens our  body . Either I would have had to die, or you would have. The world wasn't big enough for both of us.

original: But yet let me lament   With tears as sovereign as the blood of hearts   That thou, my brother, my competitor   In top of all design, my mate in empire,   Friend and companion in the front of war,   The arm of mine own body, and the heart   Where mine his thoughts did kindle
translation: But I will still weep, with tears as powerful as the blood in my heart, for you, my brother, my greatest competitor, my co-ruler of the empire, my friend and companion on the battlefield, the arm of my own body, and to whom I confided all my thoughts

original: —that our stars,   Unreconcilable, should divide   Our equalness to this. Hear me, good friends—
translation: —I weep that our partnership was divided by our irreconcilable fates. Listen to me, good friends—

original: But I will tell you at some meeter season.
translation: But I'll tell you what I have to say at a more appropriate time.

original: The business of this man looks out of him.
translation: This man looks like he's here on urgent business.

original: We’ll hear him what he says.
translation: We'll hear what he has to say.

original: (to EGYPTIAN)   Whence are  you?
translation: [To the EGYPTIAN]  Who sent you?

original: A poor Egyptian yet, the Queen my mistress,   Confined in all she has, her monument,   Of thy intents desires instruction,
translation: That poor Egyptian, the Queen my mistress. She has locked herself in her tomb—which is now all she has left—and she wants to know what you intend to do,

original: That she preparedly may frame herself   To th’ way she’s forced to.
translation: so that she can prepare herself for her fate.

original: Bid her have good heart.   She soon shall know of us, by some of ours,   How honorable and how kindly we   Determine for her,
translation: Tell her to take comfort. I will soon send some messengers to tell her how honorable and kind my plans are for her.

original: for Caesar cannot live   To be ungentle.
translation: For it is impossible for me not to be gracious and noble.

original: So the gods preserve thee!
translation: May the gods bless you.

original: Come hither, Proculeius. Go and say   We purpose her no shame. Give her what comforts   The quality of her passion shall require,
translation: Come here, Proculeius. Go and tell Cleopatra that we have no intention of disrespecting her. Give her whatever comforts she requires, given her current emotional state.

original: Lest, in her greatness, by some mortal stroke   She do defeat us, for her life in Rome   Would be eternal in our triumph.
translation: Otherwise, her nobility may lead her to kill herself and so prevent me from gaining undying glory by bringing her to Rome as my captive.

original: Go,   And with your speediest bring us what she says   And how you find of her.
translation: Go, and then report back with her response quickly and tell me how she appears.

original: Caesar, I shall.
translation: Caesar, I will.

original: Gallus, go you along.
translation: Gallus, get going.

original: Dolabella!
translation: Dolabella!

original: Let him alone, for I remember now   How he’s employed. He shall in time be ready.
translation: Forget it, I just remembered that I sent him on an errand. He'll be ready shortly.

original: Go with me to my tent, where you shall see   How hardly I was drawn into this war,   How calm and gentle I proceeded still   In all my writings. Go with me and see   What I can show in this.
translation: Come with me to my tent, and see how I was drawn into this war against my will and how calm and gentle I always was. Come with me and I will prove it.

original: My desolation does begin to make   A better life. ’Tis paltry to be Caesar.   Not being Fortune, he’s but Fortune’s knave,   A minister of her will.
translation: My isolation has helped me better understand my life. It's no great thing to be Caesar. He doesn't control his own fate, he's controlled by fate, and does whatever fortune dictates.

original: And it is great   To do that thing that ends all other deeds,   Which shackles accidents and bolts up change,
translation: And it is great, to do  that deed  that puts an end to everything else, that puts a stop to all the accidents of fortune and to all change,

original: Which sleeps and never palates more the dung,   The beggar’s nurse, and Caesar’s.
translation: that makes us sleep forever so that we never eat food from the earth again—food that nourishes beggars as well as great men like Caesar.

original: Caesar sends greeting to the Queen of Egypt, And bids thee study on what fair demands Thou mean’st to have him grant thee.
translation: Caesar sends greetings to the Queen of Egypt and asks what requests you have for him.

original: What’s thy name?
translation: What is your name?

original: My name is Proculeius.
translation: My name is Proculeius.

original: Antony   Did tell me of you, bade me trust you, but   I do not greatly care to be deceived,   That have no use for trusting.
translation: Antony told me about you and told me to trust you, but I am still hesitant to trust people, since I do not like being deceived.

original: If your master   Would have a queen his beggar, you must tell him,   That majesty, to keep decorum, must   No less beg than a kingdom.
translation: If your master wants me, a queen, to beg for favors from him, then you must tell him that a queen, if she is to act appropriately, cannot ask for anything less than a kingdom.

original: If he please   To give me conquered Egypt for my son,   He gives me so much of mine own as I   Will kneel to him with thanks.
translation: If Caesar is willing to give Egypt back to me so I can make my son its ruler, then I will kneel down and thank him for giving me back what is rightfully mine.

original: Be of good cheer.   You’re fall’n into a princely hand. Fear nothing.   Make your full reference freely to my lord,   Who is so full of grace that it flows over   On all that need.
translation: Take comfort. You've been conquered by a noble and generous man. Don't be afraid of anything. Make all your requests to my lord without hesitation.  His generosity is so great that he will willingly meet your needs.

original: Let me report to him   Your sweet dependency, and you shall find   A conqueror that will pray in aid for kindness   Where he for grace is kneeled to.
translation: Let me report back to him how humbly you acknowledge his power, and you'll find that this conquerer will beg you to tell him new ways to show kindness to you, once you've knelt down to ask him for mercy.

original: Pray you, tell him   I am his fortune’s vassal, and I send him   The greatness he has got.
translation: Please, tell him that I am at the mercy of fortune and that I acknowledge the great power he has won through his good fortune.

original: I hourly learn   A doctrine of obedience, and would gladly   Look him i’ th’ face.
translation: Every hour I learn to become more obedient, and I would gladly speak to him face to face.

original: This I’ll report, dear lady. Have comfort, for I know your plight is pitied Of him that caused it.
translation: I'll tell him this, dear lady. Take comfort, for I know that Caesar, who put you in this position, pities you for what he's done.

original: You see how easily she may be surprised.     Guard her till Caesar come.
translation: You see how easily someone can sneak up on her. Guard her until Caesar arrives.

original: Royal Queen!
translation: Royal Queen!

original: O Cleopatra! Thou art taken, Queen.
translation: Oh Cleopatra! You are captured, Queen.

original: Quick, quick, good hands.
translation: Act quickly, my good hands.

original: Hold, worthy lady, hold! Do not yourself such wrong, who are in this Relieved but not betrayed.
translation: Stop, worthy lady, stop! Do not do yourself such wrong. We are trying to help you, not betray you.

original: What, of death too, That rids our dogs of languish?
translation: What, you are depriving me of my death, too? Even dogs are allowed to die to avoid prolonged suffering.
