original: Cleopatra, Do not abuse my master’s bounty by Th’ undoing of yourself. Let the world see His nobleness well acted, which your death Will never let come forth.
translation: Cleopatra, do not show such ingratitude to my master's generosity by killing yourself. Let the world have a chance to see how nobly he acts; if you die, his nobility cannot be displayed.

original: Where art thou, Death? Come hither, come! Come, come and take a queen Worth many babes and beggars!
translation: Where are you, Death? Come here, come! Come, come, and kill me, a queen, who is worth more than the babies and beggars that you so frequently kill!

original: Oh, temperance, lady!
translation: Oh, be patient, my lady!

original: Sir, I will eat no meat, I’ll not drink, sir.   If idle talk will once be necessary,   I’ll not sleep neither. This mortal house I’ll ruin,   Do Caesar what he can.
translation: Sir, I will eat no food and I will not drink, sir. Even if it takes idle chatter to keep me awake, I won't sleep either. I'll destroy my own body, no matter what Caesar tries to do.

original: Know, sir, that I   Will not wait pinioned at your master’s court,   Nor once be chastised with the sober eye   Of dull Octavia. Shall they hoist me up   And show me to the shouting varletry   Of censuring Rome?
translation: You should know, sir, that I won't wait around to be a captive at your master's court, or to be judged with solemn looks from dull Octavia. Shall they hoist me up and display me to the shouting mobs of Rome with all their harsh judgments?

original: Rather a ditch in Egypt   Be gentle grave unto me. Rather on Nilus’ mud   Lay me stark naked and let the waterflies   Blow me into abhorring. Rather make   My country’s high pyramides my gibbet   And hang me up in chains!
translation: I'd rather have a friendly grave in a ditch in Egypt. I'd rather be laid stark naked in the mud on the shores of the Nile and let waterflies lay eggs on me until I become disgusting. I'd rather you turned Egypt's tall pyramids into a gallows and hung me from them in chains!

original: You do extend These thoughts of horror further than you shall Find cause in Caesar.
translation: You'll learn from Caesar that you're alarming yourself needlessly.

original: Proculeius,   What thou hast done thy master Caesar knows,   And he hath sent for thee.
translation: Proculeius, your master Caesar knows what you have done, and he's sent for you.

original: For the Queen,   I’ll take her to my guard.
translation: As for the Queen, I'll guard her.

original: So, Dolabella,   It shall content me best. Be gentle to her.
translation: That sounds fine to me, Dolabella. Be gentle with her.

original: To Caesar I will speak what you shall  please,   If you’ll employ me to him.
translation: I'll tell Caesar whatever you wish, if you'll send a message to him through me.

original: Say I would die.
translation: Tell him I wish to die.

original: Most noble Empress, you have heard of me?
translation: Most noble Empress, have you heard of me?

original: I cannot tell.
translation: I cannot tell.

original: Assuredly you know me.
translation: I'm sure that you know me.

original: No matter, sir, what I have heard or known. You laugh when boys or women tell their dreams. Is ’t not your trick?
translation: It doesn't matter, sir, what I have heard or known. You laugh when boys or women tell you about their dreams. Isn't that your habit?

original: I understand not, madam.
translation: I don't understand, madam.

original: I dreamt there was an emperor Antony. Oh, such another sleep, that I might see But such another man!
translation: I dreamt Antony was emperor. Oh, I wish I could sleep again like that, so I could dream about another man like that!

original: If it might please ye—
translation: If you care to—

original: His face was as the heavens, and therein stuck A sun and moon, which kept their course and lighted The little “O,” the earth.
translation: His face was as bright and majestic as the heavens. In his face were two bright orbs, like the sun and moon, that followed their course and shed light on this whole round planet, the earth.

original: Most sovereign creature—
translation: Most royal lady—

original: His legs bestrid the ocean. His reared arm   Crested the world. His voice was propertied   As all the tunèd spheres, and that to friends.
translation: He was so tall that his legs straddled the ocean. His upraised arm reached across the whole world. When he spoke to friends, his voice had the same qualities as  musical spheres .

original: But when he meant to quail and shake the orb,   He was as rattling thunder. For his bounty,   There was no winter in ’t, an autumn ’twas   That grew the more by reaping.
translation: But when he wanted to frighten and shake the world, his voice rumbled like thunder. His generosity was endless. It was like an autumn harvest, that grew more bountiful the more you drew from it.

original: His delights   Were dolphinlike; they showed his back above   The element they lived in.
translation: The things he took delight in revealed his extraordinary character; just as a dolphin's fin rises above the water, his character made him rise above the level of common people.

original: In his livery   Walked crowns and crownets. Realms and islands were   As plates dropped from his pocket.
translation: Kings and princes were his servants. He could give away realms and islands as easily as he could drop silver coins from his pocket.

original: Cleopatra—
translation: Cleopatra—

original: Think you there was or might be such a man As this I dreamt of?
translation: Do you think there was, or could be, a man like the one I dreamed of?

original: Gentle madam, no.
translation: Gentle madam, no.

original: You lie up to the hearing of the gods.   But if there be nor ever were one such,   It’s past the size of dreaming.
translation: You lie so blatantly that even the gods can hear you! But if there is or ever was such a man, he's greater than anything that could be dreamed up.

original: Nature wants stuff   To vie strange forms with fancy, yet t’ imagine   An Antony were nature’s piece ’gainst fancy,   Condemning shadows quite.
translation: Nature cannot create creatures as strange as the ones we can imagine, but if nature could create a man like Antony, it would outdo even the imagination, and reveal how pathetic and worthless our imaginary visions are.

original: Hear me, good madam.   Your loss is as yourself, great, and you bear it   As answering to the weight.
translation: Listen to me, good madam. Your loss is great because you yourself are great, and you bear it like the heavy burden it is.

original: Would I might never   O’ertake pursued success, but I do feel,   By the rebound of yours, a grief that smites   My very heart at root.
translation: May I never achieve the success I seek if this is not true: that from sympathizing with your grief, I feel a grief that strikes deep in my own heart.

original: I thank you, sir. Know you what Caesar means to do with me?
translation: I thank you, sir. Do you know what Caesar intends to do with me?

original: I am loath to tell you what I would you knew.
translation: It pains me to tell you what I want you to know.

original: Nay, pray you, sir.
translation: No, please, go on, sir.

original: Though he be honorable—
translation: Even though Caesar is honorable—

original: He’ll lead me, then, in triumph.
Madam, he will. I know ’t.
translation: Madam, he will. I know it.

original: Make way there! Caesar!
translation: Make way there! Caesar is coming!

original: Which is the Queen of Egypt?
translation: Which person is the Queen of Egypt?

original: It is the Emperor, madam.
translation: It is the Emperor, madam.

original: Arise, you shall not kneel. I pray you, rise. Rise, Egypt.
translation: Get up, you shouldn't kneel. Please, rise. Rise, Queen of Egypt.

original: Sir, the gods Will have it thus. My master and my lord I must obey.
translation: Sir, this is what the gods have willed. I must obey my lord and master.

original: Take to you no hard thoughts.
translation: Please don't hold any grudges.

original: The record of what injuries you did us,   Though written in our flesh, we shall remember   As things but done by chance.
translation: Even though our bodies still bear the wounds from battle, we'll agree to forget about the injuries you inflicted on us, treating them as accidents.

original: Sole sir o’ th’ world,   I cannot project mine own cause so well   To make it clear,
translation: Only ruler of the world, I cannot explain my side of the story well enough to make it clear.

original: but do confess I have   Been laden with like frailties which before   Have often shamed our sex.
translation: I can only confess that I have some of the same weaknesses that have often brought shame to women.

original: Cleopatra, know   We will extenuate rather than enforce.   If you apply yourself to our intents,   Which towards you are most gentle, you shall find   A benefit in this change,
translation: Cleopatra, you should know that I intend to excuse your offenses rather than dwell on them. If you agree to go along with my plans, which are very generous, you'll find that this change will benefit you.

original: but if you seek   To lay on me a cruelty by taking   Antony’s course, you shall bereave yourself   Of my good purposes and put your children   To that destruction which I’ll guard them from   If thereon you rely. I’ll take my leave.
translation: But if you try to injure me by killing yourself as Antony did, you'll lose all the generosity I intend to show you and ensure that I destroy your children—which I will not do if you submit to me. I'll leave you now.

original: And may, through all the world! ’Tis yours, and we, Your scutcheons and your signs of conquest, shall Hang in what place you please. Here, my good lord.
translation: And you may go freely wherever you like in the world! The world is yours, and just as you can freely display the shields of your conquered enemies, you can do whatever what you like with me.

original: You shall advise me in all for Cleopatra.
translation: You will let me know everything you need.

original: This is the brief of money, plate, and jewels I am possessed of. ’Tis exactly valued, Not petty things admitted. Where’s Seleucus?
translation: Here's an inventory of all the money, precious metals, and jewels that I own. I've calculated the exact value of everything except for the smaller items. Where's Seleucus?

original: Here, madam.
translation: I'm here, madam.

original: This is my treasurer. Let him speak, my lord,   Upon his peril, that I have reserved   To myself nothing.
translation: [To CAESAR ] This is my treasurer. He will tell you on his honor, my lord, that I haven't held back anything for myself.

original: —   Speak the truth, Seleucus.
translation: [To SELEUCUS]  Speak truthfully, Seleucus.

original: Madam, I had rather seal my lips Than to my peril speak that which is not.
translation: Madam, I would rather not speak than risk endangering myself by saying something false.

original: What have I kept back?
translation: What have I held back?

original: Enough to purchase what you have made known.
Nay, blush not, Cleopatra. I approve Your wisdom in the deed.
translation: No, don't blush, Cleopatra. I approve of the wisdom you demonstrated in this trick.

original: See, Caesar! Oh, behold   How pomp is followed!
translation: See, Caesar! Oh, see what happens when all the spectacle is over!

original: Mine will now be yours,   And, should we shift estates, yours would be mine.   The ingratitude of this Seleucus does   Even make me wild.
translation: My followers will now be your followers, and if we exchanged our positions, your followers would be my followers. Still, Seleucus's ingratitude makes me wild with anger.

original: O slave, of no more  trust   Than love that’s hired!   What, goest thou back? Thou shalt   Go back, I warrant thee!
translation: Oh you villainous man, you are less trustworthy than a mercenary! What, do you retreat from me? I bet you do!

original: But I’ll catch thine eyes,   Though they had wings. Slave, soulless villain, dog!   Oh, rarely base!
translation: But even if your eyes had wings to fly away, I would catch them. Scoundrel, soulless villain, dog! Oh, you uncommonly corrupt man!

original: Good Queen, let us entreat you—
translation: Good Queen, let me ask you to—

original: O Caesar, what a wounding shame is this,   That thou, vouchsafing here to visit me,   Doing the honor of thy lordliness   To one so meek, that mine own servant should   Parcel the sum of my disgraces by   Addition of his envy!
translation: Oh Caesar, I am so ashamed—you agreed to visit me here and honor me in my humiliation with your great presence, and my own servant adds to all my disgraces out of spite!

original: Say, good Caesar,   That I some lady trifles have reserved,   Immoment toys, things of such dignity   As we greet modern friends withal,
translation: Let's suppose, good Caesar, that I did hold back some little feminine, insignificant trinkets, the kind of common items that we give them away to our ordinary friends;

original: and say   Some nobler token I have kept apart   For Livia and Octavia, to induce   Their mediation, must I be unfolded   With one that I have bred?
translation: and let's suppose that I did hold back some more valuable objects to give to your wife Livia and to Octavia, to persuade them to intervene for me—even supposing all that, do I deserve to be betrayed by a servant I have nurtured?

original: The gods! It smites me   Beneath the fall I have.
translation: The gods! This causes me more agony than the embarrassment I've already endured.

original: Prithee, go  hence,   Or I shall show the cinders of my spirit   Through th’ ashes of my chance. Wert thou a man,   Thou wouldst have mercy on me.
translation: Get out of here, or I'll show what's left of my strong will with what resources luck has left me. If you were a real man, you would have had sympathy for me.

original: Forbear, Seleucus.
translation: Hold back, Seleucus.

original: Be it known that we, the greatest, are misthought   For things that others do,
translation: Let it be known that we, the greatest, are misjudged for the things other people do,

original: and when we fall   We answer others’ merits in our name,   Are therefore to be pitied.
translation: and when we fall, we have to answer for the things that  others have done in our name . We should therefore be pitied.

original: Cleopatra,   Not what you have reserved nor what acknowledged   Put we i’ th’ roll of conquest. Still be ’t yours.
translation: Cleopatra, I don't claim as a right of conquest either the treasure you have held back or the treasure you have declared in your inventory. Let it all still belong to you.

original: Bestow it at your pleasure, and believe   Caesar’s no merchant, to make prize with you   Of things that merchants sold. Therefore be cheered.   Make not your thoughts your prison.
translation: Do what you like with it, and do not think that I am like a common merchant, so concerned with material things that I would haggle with you over your property. Therefore, be cheerful. Don't imprison yourself in gloomy thoughts.

original: No, dear Queen,   For we intend so to dispose you as   Yourself shall give us counsel. Feed and sleep.   Our care and pity is so much upon you   That we remain your friend. And so, adieu.
translation: No, dear, Queen, because I intend to treat you in whatever way you yourself advise me to. Eat and sleep. I have so much care and pity for you that I will continue to be your friend. And so, goodbye.

original: My master, and my lord!
translation: My master, and my lord!

original: Not so. Adieu.
translation: I am not your master or your lord. Goodbye.

original: He words me, girls, he words me, that I should not Be noble to myself. But, hark thee, Charmian.
translation: He tries to pacify me with empty words, girls, empty words, so that I will not do the noble thing and commit suicide. But, listen to me, Charmian.

original: Finish, good lady. The bright day is done, And we are for the dark.
translation: Wrap things up, my lady. The bright day is over and night is upon us.

original: Hie thee again. I have spoke already, and it is provided. Go put it to the haste.
translation: Hurry back. I have already given instructions, and everything is arranged. Go set things in motion quickly.

original: Madam, I will.
translation: Madam, I will.

original: Where’s the Queen?
translation: Where is the Queen?

original: Behold, sir.
translation: She's there, sir.

original: Dolabella!
translation: Dolabella!

original: Madam, as thereto sworn by your command,   Which my love makes religion to obey,   I tell you this:
translation: Madam, I vowed to obey your commands, and my devotion compels me to uphold that vow. Therefore, I must tell you this:

original: Caesar through Syria   Intends his journey, and within three days   You with your children will he send before.   Make your best use of this. I have performed   Your pleasure and my promise.
translation: Caesar intends to travel back through Syria, and within three days, he'll send you and your children  on the road ahead of him . Make the best use of this information that you can. I've carried out my promise and served you well.

original: Dolabella, I shall remain your debtor.
translation: Dolabella, I will always be in your debt.

original: I your servant. Adieu, good Queen. I must attend on Caesar.
translation: And I will always be your servant. Goodbye, good Queen. I must go to Caesar.

original: Farewell, and thanks.
translation: Goodbye, and thank you.

original: The gods forbid!
translation: May the gods forbid it!

original: Nay, ’tis most certain, Iras. Saucy lictors   Will catch at us like strumpets, and scald rhymers   Ballad us out o’ tune.
The quick comedians   Extemporally will stage us and present   Our Alexandrian revels.
translation: Witty actors will improvise plays about us and dramatize the parties we had in Alexandria.

original: Antony   Shall be brought drunken forth, and I shall see   Some squeaking Cleopatra boy my greatness   I’ th’ posture of a whore.
translation: They'll bring out some drunken man to play Antony, and I'll see some squeaky-voiced  boy  play me, in all my greatness, as if I were nothing more than a whore.

original: Oh, the good gods!
translation: Oh, may the good gods forbid it!

original: Nay, that’s certain.
translation: No, it's certain.

original: I’ll never see ’t! For I am sure mine nails Are stronger than mine eyes.
translation: I'll never see it! For I'm sure I have enough will-power to tear out my eyes with nails first.

original: Why, that’s the way To fool their preparation and to conquer Their most absurd intents.
translation: Why, that's the best way to ruin their plans and undermine the terrible things they intend to do.

original: Now, Charmian!   Show me, my women, like a queen. Go fetch   My best attires. I am again for Cydnus,   To meet Mark Antony.
translation: Now, Charmian! Dress me, my women, like a queen. Go get my best robes. I am going to  Cydnus , to meet Mark Antony.

original: —Sirrah Iras, go.—
translation: Iras, get going.

original: Now, noble Charmian, we’ll dispatch indeed,   And when thou hast done this chare I’ll give thee leave   To play till doomsday.
translation: Now, noble Charmian, we'll put our plans into action, and when you've done this task, I give you permission to do as you please until the end of the world.

original: Bring our crown and  all.
translation: Bring my crown and everything.

original: Here is a rural fellow That will not be denied your Highness’ presence. He brings you figs.
translation: Here's a country peasant who insists on seeing the Queen. He brings you figs.

original: Let him come in.
translation: Let him come in.

original: This is the man.
translation: This is the man.

original: Avoid, and leave him.
translation: Get out, and leave him here.

original: Truly, I have him, but I would not be the party that  should desire you to touch him, for his biting is  immortal. Those that do die of it do seldom or never  recover.
Remember’st thou any that have died on ’t?
translation: Do you know of any people who have died from it?

original: Very many, men and women too. I heard of one of them no longer than yesterday—a very honest woman, but  something given to lie, as a woman should not do but in  the way of honesty
translation: Very many, both men and women. I heard of one just yesterday. She was a very honest woman, but had a slight tendency to lie, which women should not do except when it's  honest .

original: —how she died of the biting of it,  what pain she felt. Truly, she makes a very good report  o’ th’ worm.
translation: I heard she died from its bite and the pain. Really, she had very favorable things to say about the serpent.

original: But he that will believe all that they say  shall never be saved by half that they do. But this is  most falliable, the worm’s an odd worm.
translation: But if you believe what they say about the serpent and act on it, you'll  never reach heaven . But this is definitely  certain , that the serpent is an odd creature.

original: Get thee hence, farewell.
translation: Get going, goodbye.

original: I wish you all joy of the worm.
translation: I wish you luck with the serpent.

original: Farewell.
translation: Goodbye.

original: You must think this, look you, that the worm will do  his kind.
translation: Be careful, you should be aware that the serpent will do what serpents typically do.

original: Ay, ay. Farewell.
translation: Yes, yes. Goodbye.

original: Look you, the worm is not to be trusted but in the  keeping of wise people, for indeed there is no goodness  in the worm.
translation: See here, it isn't safe for anyone except a wise person to hold on to that serpent, for it really is a dangerous animal.

original: Take thou no care. It shall be heeded.
translation: Don't worry. I will listen to your warnings.

original: Very good. Give it nothing, I pray you, for it is not  worth the feeding.
translation: Very good. Don't give it any food, I advise you, for it isn't worth keeping alive.

original: Will it eat me?
translation: Will it eat me?

original: You must not think I am so simple but I know the devil  himself will not eat a woman. I know that a woman is a  dish for the gods, if the devil dress her not.
translation: You can't think I'm so foolish—I know that even the devil would not eat a woman. I know that a woman is worthy food for the gods, so long as the devil doesn't corrupt her.

original: But,  truly, these same whoreson devils do the gods great harm in their women, for in every ten that they make, the  devils mar five.
translation: But in fact, those terrible devils do the gods great harm by ruining so many women. For every ten women the gods make, the devil ruins five.

original: Well, get thee gone. Farewell.
translation: Well, get going. Goodbye.

original: Yes, forsooth. I wish you joy o’ th’ worm.
translation: Yes, indeed. I wish you luck with the worm.

original: Give me my robe. Put on my crown. I have Immortal longings in me. Now no more The juice of Egypt’s grape shall moist this lip.
translation: Give me my robe. Put on my crown. I long to enter into the afterlife. I will never again drink wine made from Egypt's grapes.

original: Dissolve, thick cloud, and rain, that I may say The gods themselves do weep!
translation: May the thick clouds dissolve and rain so that I can say the gods themselves weep!

original: This proves me base.   If she first meet the curlèd Antony,   He’ll make demand of her and spend that kiss   Which is my heaven to have.
translation: Iras's act makes mine seem less noble. If she meets the curly-haired Antony in the afterlife before I do, he'll speak to her and give her that heavenly kiss that belongs to me.

original: —Come, thou mortal wretch,
translation: Come, you wretched, poisonous thing.

original: O eastern star!
Peace, peace! Dost thou not see my baby at my breast, That sucks the nurse asleep?
translation: Quiet, quiet! Don't you see this baby that's lulling me to sleep by sucking on my breast?

original: Oh, break! Oh, break!
translation: Oh, I wish my heart would break!

original: As sweet as balm, as soft as air, as gentle— O Antony!—Nay, I will take thee too.
translation: This feeling is as sweet as perfumed oil, as soft as air, as gentle—O Antony!—Oh yes, I will take you too.

original: In this wild world? So, fare thee well. Now boast thee, Death, in thy possession lies A lass unparalleled. Downy windows, close,
translation: In this wild world? So, farewell. Now, Death, you can boast that you have taken a woman who has no equal. Let's close these soft eyelids.

original: Where’s the Queen?
translation: Where's the Queen?

original: Speak softly. Wake her not.
translation: Speak softly. Don't wake her up.

original: Caesar hath sent—
translation: Caesar has sent—

original: Too slow a messenger.
translation: A messenger that was too slow.

original: Approach, ho! All’s not well. Caesar’s  beguiled.
translation: Hey there, come here! Something's gone wrong. Caesar has been tricked.

original: There’s Dolabella sent from Caesar. Call him.
translation: There's Dolabella, who was sent from Caesar. Call him.

original: What work is here, Charmian? Is this well done?
translation: What happened here, Charmian? Was this a good thing to do?

original: It is well done and fitting for a princess Descended of so many royal kings. Ah, soldier!
translation: It was a good thing to do, and it was fitting for a princess who was descended from so many royal kings. Ah, soldier!

original: How goes it here?
translation: What's going on here?

original: All dead.
translation: They are all dead.

original: Caesar, thy thoughts   Touch their effects in this.
translation: Caesar, this is the effect of all your planinng.

original: Thyself art coming   To see performed the dreaded act which thou   So sought’st to hinder.
translation: You'll arrive and see she's done the dreaded act you tried so hard to prevent.

original: A way there, a way for Caesar!
translation: Make way there, make way for Caesar!

original: O sir, you are too sure an augurer. That you did fear is done.
translation: Oh sir, your prediction came true. What you feared has happened.

original: Bravest at the last,   She leveled at our purposes and, being royal,   Took her own way.
translation: She was bravest at the very end; she guessed what I planned to do and, being noble, took matters into her own hands.

original: The manner of their deaths?   I do not see them bleed.
translation: How did they die? I don't see any blood.

original: Who was last with them?
translation: Who was the last person with them?

original: A simple countryman that brought her figs. This was his basket.
translation: A simple peasant who brought her figs. This was his basket.

original: Poisoned, then.
translation: They must have been poisoned, then.

original: Oh, Caesar,   This Charmian lived but now. She stood and spake.
translation: Oh, Caesar, this woman Charmian was alive until a moment ago. She stood and spoke.

original: I found her trimming up the diadem   On her dead mistress. Tremblingly she stood   And on the sudden dropped.
translation: I found her adjusting the crown of her dead mistress. She stood trembling and then suddenly collapsed.

original: Oh, noble weakness!   If they had swallowed poison, ’twould appear   By external swelling,
translation: Oh, these women were weak but noble, too! If they had taken poison, we would be able to tell by the swelling of their bodies,

original: but she looks like sleep,   As she would catch another Antony   In her strong toil of grace.
translation: but Cleopatra just looks as if she were sleeping—as if she were dreaming of catching another man like Antony with her strong, bewitching charms.

original: Here on her breast There is a vent of blood, and something blown. The like is on her arm.
translation: There's a trail of blood here on her breast, and some discharge. The same thing appears on her arm.

original: This is an aspic’s trail, and these fig leaves Have slime upon them, such as th’ aspic leaves Upon the caves of Nile.
translation: This is the trail of a serpent. These fig leaves have a slimy discharge on them too, just as a serpent leaves in the caves of the Nile.

original: Most probable   That so she died, for her physician tells me   She hath pursued conclusions infinite   Of easy ways to die. Take up her bed   And bear her women from the monument.
translation: It's most likely that she died from the serpents' bite, for her doctor tells me that she performed countless experiments to find easy ways to die. Pick up her bed and carry her women out of the tomb.

original: She shall be buried by her Antony.   No grave upon the earth shall clip in it   A pair so famous. High events as these   Strike those that make them, and their story is   No less in pity than his glory which   Brought them to be lamented.
translation: She will be buried beside her Antony. No grave on earth will contain such a famous couple. Great events like these strike the hearts of those who brought them about. The pity of their story is as great as the glory of  that person  who brought them to this lamentable end.

original: Our army shall   In solemn show attend this funeral,   And then to Rome. Come, Dolabella, see   High order in this great solemnity.
translation: Our army will solemnly watch this funeral, and then they will go to Rome. Come, Dolabella, and observe the great  decorum  that this solemn occasion requires.

original: As I remember, Adam, it was upon this fashion  bequeathed me by will but poor a thousand crowns, and,  as thou sayest, charged my brother on his blessing to  breed me well. And there begins my sadness.
translation: As I remember it, Adam, in my father's will I was left only a thousand crowns. And, as you say, my father gave my older brother Oliver the responsibility of taking care of me. And that is the source of my sadness.

original: My brother  Jacques he keeps at school, and report speaks goldenly  of his profit. For my part, he keeps me rustically at  home or, to speak more properly, stays me here at home  unkept;
translation: My other brother Jacques is away at school, and they say that he is profiting greatly from his education. But for my part, my brother insists that I stay here at home like a peasant.

original: for call you that “keeping” for a gentleman of  my birth that differs not from the stalling of an ox?  His horses are bred better, for, besides that they are  fair with their feeding, they are taught their manage  and, to that end, riders dearly hired.
translation: He is supposed to maintain me like a gentleman, but instead he treats me like an ox in a stall. My brother's horses are treated better than I am—at least they get training and riders along with their food.

original: But I, his  brother, gain nothing under him but growth, for the  which his animals on his dunghills are as much bound to  him as I.
translation: But I, his brother, get nothing from him but food and shelter. So the only thing I owe him like his livestock on their manure piles—is my physical growth.

original: Besides this nothing that he so plentifully  gives me, the something that nature gave me his  countenance seems to take from me. He lets me feed with  his hinds, bars me the place of a brother, and, as much  as in him lies, mines my gentility with my education.
translation: Besides this "nothing" that he so plentifully gives me, his constant frowning at me also takes from me those  things that nature gave to me. He makes me eat with his servants, refuses to call me his brother, and denies me the education that I deserve.

original: This is it, Adam, that grieves me, and the spirit of my  father, which I think is within me, begins to mutiny  against this servitude. I will no longer endure it,  though yet I know no wise remedy how to avoid it.
translation: Adam, this is what grieves me. And lately I have felt my father's independent spirit—which I think is a part of me—beginning to rebel against this servitude. I will no longer endure it, though I don't know how to improve my situation.

original: Yonder comes my master, your brother.
translation: Here comes my master, your brother.

original: Go apart, Adam, and thou shalt hear how he will shake  me up.
translation: Hide yourself somewhere close by, Adam. And see how he mistreats me.

original: Now, sir, what make you here?
translation: What are you doing here, sir?

original: Nothing. I am not taught to make anything.
translation: Nothing. I have not been taught to do anything.

original: What mar you then, sir?
translation: What are you undoing then, sir?

original: Marry, sir, I am helping you to mar that which God  made, a poor unworthy brother of yours, with idleness.
Marry, sir, be better employed, and be naught awhile.
translation: Well, sir, do something more useful, and go away for a while.

original: Shall I keep your hogs and eat husks with them? What  prodigal portion have I spent that I should come to such penury?
translation: Should I keep your hogs and eat slop with them? What portion of my inheritance have I wasted that I should be so poor?

original: Know you where you are, sir?
translation: Do you know where you are, sir?

original: O sir, very well: here in your orchard.
translation: Oh, sir, I know very well: here in your orchard.

original: Know you before whom, sir?
translation: Do you know who you're talking to, sir?

original: Ay, better than him I am before knows me. I know you  are my eldest brother, and in the gentle condition of  blood you should so know me.
translation: Yes, better than the one I'm talking to knows me. I know you are my eldest brother, and you should know that I am a born gentleman just like you.

original: The courtesy of nations  allows you my better, in that you are the first-born,  but the same tradition takes not away my blood, were  there twenty brothers betwixt us.
translation: According to the  rules and customs of nations  you are my superior, because you were born first. But those rules can't take from me the blood we share, even if there were twenty brothers born between us.

original: I have as much of my  father in me as you, albeit, I confess, your coming  before me is nearer to his reverence.
translation: I have as much of my father in me as you do—though, I confess, you are closer to him in age and importance.

original: What, boy!
translation: What, boy!

original: Come, come, elder brother, you are too young in this.
translation: Come, come, elder brother! In fighting at least, you are too inexperienced.

original: Wilt thou lay hands on me, villain?
translation: Will you lay hands on me, you villain?

original: I am no villain. I am the youngest son of Sir Rowland  de Boys. He was my father, and he is thrice a villain  that says such a father begot villains.
translation: I am no villain. I am the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys. He was my father, and anyone who says that his sons are villains is three times a villain.

original: Wert thou not my brother, I would not take this hand from thy throat  till this other had pulled out thy tongue for saying so. Thou hast railed on thyself.
translation: If you weren't my brother, I wouldn't let go of your throat until I had pulled out your tongue for your insolence. You have only insulted yourself.

original: Sweet masters, be patient. For your father’s  remembrance, be at accord.
translation: Sweet masters, please calm down. Be peaceful, for the sake of your father's memory.

original: Let me go, I say.
translation: Let me go, I say.

original: I will not till I please. You shall hear me. My father  charged you in his will to give me good education. You  have trained me like a peasant, obscuring and hiding  from me all gentlemanlike qualities.
translation: I won't let you go until I want to. You  will  listen to what I have to say. In his will, my father told you to give me a good education. Instead you have raised me like a peasant, keeping anything from me that might make me a gentleman.

original: The spirit of my  father grows strong in me, and I will no longer endure  it.
translation: But now the spirit of my father grows strong in me, and I will no longer endure it.

original: Therefore allow me such exercises as may become a  gentleman, or give me the poor allottery my father left  me by testament. With that I will go buy my fortunes.
translation: Therefore give me the freedom to act like a gentleman, or give me my rightful share of my father's inheritance—small though it is. With that money I can go seek my fortunes on my own.

original: And what wilt thou do—beg when that is spent? Well,  sir, get you in. I will not long be troubled with you.  You shall have some part of your will. I pray you leave  me.
translation: And what will you do—start begging once you've spent that money? Well, sir, go inside. I won't be troubled with you for long. You will get some of what you want. Now please leave me.

original: I will no further offend you than becomes me for my  good.
translation: I won't offend you any more than is necessary to ensure I get what I deserve.

original: Get you with him, you old dog.
translation: You go along with him, you old dog.

original: Is “old dog” my reward? Most true, I have lost my  teeth in your service. God be with my old master. He  would not have spoke such a word.
translation: Is this my reward for years of service, to be called "old dog?" It's true that I have grown old and lost my teeth in your service. God bless my old master, your father. He would never have treated me like this.

original: Is it even so? Begin you to grow upon me? I will physic your rankness and yet give no thousand crowns  neither.—Holla, Dennis!
translation: Can this be? Are you starting to challenge me? I will cure you of your insolence and not give you a thousand crowns either. Hey, Dennis!

original: Calls your Worship?
Was not Charles, the duke’s wrestler, here to speak  with me?
translation: Hasn't the duke's wrestler Charles come here to speak with me?

original: So please you, he is here at the door and importunes  access to you.
translation: Yes, sir. He is here at the door and asks to see you.

original: Call him in.
translation: Call him in.

original: 'Twill be a good way, and tomorrow the wrestling is.
translation: This will be a good plan, and tomorrow is the wrestling match.

original: Good morrow to your Worship.
translation: Good morning to your Worship.

original: Good Monsieur Charles, what’s the new news at the new  court?
translation: Good Monsieur Charles, what's the latest news at the new palace court?

original: There’s no news at the court, sir, but the old news.  That is, the old duke is banished by his younger brother the new duke, and three or four loving lords have put  themselves into voluntary exile with him,
translation: There's no news but the old news, sir. The old duke is still banished by his younger brother, the new duke. Three or four loyal lords have gone into voluntary exile with the old duke.

original: whose lands  and revenues enrich the new duke. Therefore he gives  them good leave to wander.
translation: And since the new duke has seized their land and money, he is happy to let them wander.

original: Can you tell if Rosalind, the duke’s daughter, be  banished with her father?
translation: Do you know if Rosalind, the old duke's daughter, has been banished with her father?

original: Oh, no, for the duke’s daughter her cousin so loves  her, being ever from their cradles bred together, that  she would have followed her exile or have died to stay  behind her.
translation: Oh no, because her cousin, the new duke's daughter, loves Rosalind deeply, and they were raised together as children. The duke's daughter Celia would have followed Rosalind into exile or died of grief at her absence.

original: She is at the court, and no less beloved of  her uncle than his own daughter, and never two ladies  loved as they do.
translation: Rosalind is still at the court, where her uncle loves her like she is his own daughter, and the cousins love each other like no other women before them.

original: Where will the old duke live?
translation: Where is the old duke living?

original: They say he is already in the Forest of Arden, and a  many merry men with him; and there they live like the  old Robin Hood of England.
translation: They say he is already in the Forest of Arden. He has many companions with him, and there they live like  Robin Hood  and his merry men.

original: They say many young gentlemen flock to him every day and fleet the time carelessly,  as they did in the golden world.
translation: They say that many young gentlemen join him every day. They spend their time without a care in the world, the way people lived in the golden days.

original: What, you wrestle tomorrow before the new duke?
translation: So, are you going to wrestle tomorrow before the new duke?

original: Marry, do I, sir, and I came to acquaint you with a  matter. I am given, sir, secretly to understand that  your younger brother Orlando hath a disposition to come  in disguised against me to try a fall.
translation: Yes, sir, and that's what I came to talk to you about. I have been secretly informed that your younger brother Orlando plans to disguise himself and try to wrestle me.

original: Tomorrow, sir, I  wrestle for my credit, and he that escapes me without  some broken limb shall acquit him well.
translation: Tomorrow, sir, I wrestle for my reputation, and anyone who escapes me without a broken limb will have done quite well.

original: Your brother is  but young and tender, and, for your love I would be  loath to foil him, as I must for my own honor if he come in.
translation: Your brother is young and inexperience. And because I love you, I would hate to crush him, which I must do for my honor's sake if we fought.

original: Therefore, out of my love to you, I came hither to  acquaint you withal, that either you might stay him from his intendment or brook such disgrace well as he shall  run into, in that it is a thing of his own search and  altogether against my will.
translation: Therefore, out of my love for you, I came here to tell you everything, so that you might either keep him from fighting me, or be prepared for his disgrace, which will be his own fault and entirely against my will.

original: Charles, I thank thee for thy love to me, which thou  shalt find I will most kindly requite. I had myself  notice of my brother’s purpose herein and have by  underhand means labored to dissuade him from it; but he  is resolute.
translation: Charles, I thank you for your loyalty to me, and you'll see that I will kindly reward you. I had myself learned of my brother's plan to disguise himself and fight you, and I have already been secretly trying to change his mind, but he won't budge.

original: I’ll tell thee, Charles: it is the  stubbornest young fellow of France, full of ambition, an envious emulator of every man’s good parts, a secret  and villainous contriver against me his natural brother.
translation: I tell you, Charles: he is the stubbornest young fellow in France, full of ambition, a jealous mimic of other people's good qualities, and a secret, villainous traitor against me, his own brother.

original: Therefore use thy discretion. I had as lief thou didst  break his neck as his finger. And thou wert best look to ’t, for if thou dost him any slight disgrace or if he  do not mightily grace himself on thee,
translation: So use your discretion. I would be just as pleased if you broke his neck as his finger. And you'd best watch your back, because if you embarrass him or he doesn't thoroughly beat you,

original: he will practice  against thee by poison, entrap thee by some treacherous  device and never leave thee till he hath ta'en thy life  by some indirect means or other.
translation: then he'll try to poison you later, or else trap you in some treacherous way. He won't rest until he's had you killed by some indirect means.

original: For I assure thee—and  almost with tears I speak it—there is not one so young  and so villainous this day living.
translation: For I assure you—and I say this almost in tears—there is no one alive so young and so villainous.

original: I speak but brotherly of him, but should I anatomize him to thee as he is, I  must blush and weep, and thou must look pale and wonder.
translation: I can only speak in a kind way about him because he's my brother, but if I were to really describe him as he is, I'd have to blush and weep. And you would grow pale and not even believe me.

original: I am heartily glad I came hither to you. If he come  tomorrow, I’ll give him his payment.
translation: I am very glad I came here to talk to you. If he tries to wrestle me tomorrow, I'll give him what he deserves.

original: If ever he go alone again, I’ll never wrestle for prize more. And so God  keep your Worship.
translation: If he can walk on his own after I'm through with him, I'll never wrestle professionally again. Farewell, and God bless your Worship.

original: Farewell, good Charles.
translation: Farewell, good Charles.

original: Now will I stir this gamester. I hope I shall see an  end of him, for my soul—yet I know not why—hates nothing more than he. Yet he’s gentle, never schooled and yet  learned, full of noble device, of all sorts enchantingly beloved,
translation: Now I will cause trouble for my adventurous brother. I hope this will be the end of him, for my soul hates him more than anything in the world, though I don't know why. He is an upright man—uneducated but very smart—with a noble manner about him.

original: and indeed so much in the heart of the world  and especially of my own people, who best know him, that I am altogether misprized.
translation: And everyone loves him. Even my own people, who know him best, love him and dislike me.

original: But it shall not be so long; this wrestler shall clear all. Nothing remains but that I kindle the boy thither, which now I’ll go about.
translation: But not for long; this wrestler will fix everything. All that remains is to persuade my brother to wrestle, which I will now do.

original: I pray thee, Rosalind, sweet my coz, be merry.
translation: Please, Rosalind, my sweet cousin, be happy.

original: Dear Celia, I show more mirth than I am mistress of,  and would you yet I were merrier?
translation: Dear Celia, I already look happier than I feel, and you want me to look even happier?

original: Unless you could teach me to forget a banished father, you must not learn me  how to remember any extraordinary pleasure.
translation: Unless you can teach me to forget my banished father, you shouldn't try to teach me to remember any great happiness.

original: Herein I see thou lov’st me not with the full weight  that I love thee. If my uncle, thy banished father, had  banished thy uncle, the duke my father, so thou hadst  been still with me,   I could have taught my love to take  thy father for mine.
translation: Now I see that you don't love me as much as I love you. If instead  my  uncle ( your  banished father), had banished  your  uncle (the duke  my  father), I could have learned to love your father as my own as long as you were still with me.

original: So wouldst thou, if the truth of  thy love to me were so righteously tempered as mine is  to thee.
translation: You would do the same, if your love for me was as true and well-forged as mine is for you.

original: Well, I will forget the condition of my estate to  rejoice in yours.
translation: Well, then I'll try to forget my situation and instead rejoice in yours.

original: You know my father hath no child but I, nor none is  like to have, and, truly, when he dies, thou shalt be  his heir, for what he hath taken away from thy father  perforce, I will render thee again in affection.
translation: You know that I'm my father's only child, and he isn't likely to have another. So when he dies you will be his heir—because whatever he took from your father by force, I will return to you with affection.

original: By mine honor I will, and when I break that oath, let me turn  monster. Therefore, my sweet Rose, my dear Rose, be  merry.
translation: By my honor I will do this, and if I break this oath let me turn into a monster. So my sweet Rose, my dear Rose, be happy.

original: From henceforth I will, coz, and devise sports. Let me see—what think you of falling in love?
translation: From now on I will, cousin. And I'll make up games for us to play. Let me see—what do you think about falling in love?

original: Marry, I prithee do, to make sport withal, but love no  man in good earnest, nor no further in sport neither  than with safety of a pure blush thou mayst in honor  come off again.
translation: Oh yes, please do, so we can make a game of it. But don't fall in love with a man in earnest, or take the game too far. Otherwise you won't be able to get out of it easily and with your honor intact.

original: What shall be our sport, then?
translation: What game should we play, then?

original: Let us sit and mock the good housewife Fortune from her wheel, that her gifts may henceforth be bestowed  equally.
translation: Let us sit and mock the good housewife Fortune, until she starts bestowing her gifts more equally.

original: I would we could do so, for her benefits are mightily  misplaced, and the bountiful blind woman doth most  mistake in her gifts to women.
translation: I wish that we could, for her gifts are indeed wrongly distributed. And Fortune makes the most mistakes in the gifts she gives to women.

original: 'Tis true, for those that she makes fair she scarce  makes honest, and those that she makes honest she makes  very ill- favoredly.
translation: It's true, because the women she makes beautiful she rarely makes chaste. And those that she makes chaste she also makes ugly.

original: Nay, now thou goest from Fortune’s office to Nature’s. Fortune reigns in gifts of the world, not in the  lineaments of Nature.
translation: No, now you're getting Fortune and Nature confused. Fortune determines what happens to us, while Nature decides how we're made.

original: No? When Nature hath made a fair creature, may she not  by Fortune fall into the fire?
translation: Really? If Nature has made a beautiful woman, can't Fortune then make her fall into a fire?

original: Though Nature hath given  us wit to flout at Fortune, hath not Fortune sent in  this fool to cut off the argument?
translation: Even though Nature has given us the wit to mock Fortune, hasn't Fortune then sent in this fool to interrupt our conversation?

original: Indeed, there is Fortune too hard for Nature, when  Fortune makes Nature’s natural the cutter-off of  Nature’s wit.
Peradventure this is not Fortune’s work neither, but  Nature’s, who perceiveth our natural wits too dull to  reason of such goddesses, and hath sent this natural for our whetstone,
translation: Although maybe this isn't Fortune's work after all, but Nature's instead. Maybe Nature perceives that we aren't witty enough to be discussing goddesses, so she sent us this fool to sharpen our wits against.

original: for always the dullness of the fool is  the whetstone of the wits.
translation: The dullness of fools always acts as a sharpening stone for witty people.

original: How now, wit, whither wander  you?
translation: [To TOUCHSTONE]    How are you, you wit? Where are you wandering off to?

original: Mistress, you must come away to your father.
translation: Mistress, you must come and see your father.

original: Were you made the messenger?
translation: Did he make you the messenger?

original: No, by mine honor, but I was bid to come for you.
translation: No, by my honor. But I was told to come for you.

original: Where learned you that oath, fool?
translation: Where did you learn to swear "by my honor," fool?

original: Of a certain knight that swore by his honor they were  good pancakes, and swore by his honor the mustard was  naught.
translation: I learned it from a certain knight who swore by his honor that the pancakes he was eating were good, and swore by his honor that the mustard on them was bad.

original: Now, I’ll stand to it, the pancakes were naught  and the mustard was good, and yet was not the knight  forsworn.
translation: Now, I'll swear that the pancakes were bad and the mustard was good, and yet even so the knight wasn't a liar.

original: How prove you that in the great heap of your knowledge?
translation: How are you going to prove that, out of your great heap of knowledge?

original: Ay, marry, now unmuzzle your wisdom.
translation: Yes, please, now unleash your wisdom.

original: Stand you both forth now: stroke your chins and swear  by your beards that I am a knave.
translation: Both of you come forward now: stroke your chins and swear by your beards that I am a dishonest man.

original: By our beards (if we had them), thou art.
translation: By our beards (if we had them), you are a dishonest man.

original: By my knavery (if I had it), then I were. But if you  swear by that that is not, you are not forsworn.
translation: And I swear by my dishonesty (if I had it) that I am. But if you swear by something that doesn't exist, then your oath isn't binding.

original: No more was this knight swearing by his honor, for he never had any; or if he had, he had sworn it away before ever he  saw those pancakes or that mustard.
translation: So this knight couldn't swear by his honor, for he never had any honor. Or if he ever did, he had sworn it away long before he ever saw those pancakes and that mustard.

original: Prithee, who is ’t that thou mean’st?
translation: Do tell, who is this knight that you're referring to?

original: One that old Frederick, your father, loves.
translation: Someone that old Frederick, your father, loves.

original: My father’s love is enough to honor him. Enough. Speak  no more of him; you’ll be whipped for taxation one of  these days.
translation: If he has my father's love, then that is honor enough. Speak no more of him. You'll be whipped for slander one of these days.

original: The more pity that fools may not speak wisely what wise men do foolishly.
translation: It's a pity that fools aren't allowed to speak wisely about what wise men do foolishly.

original: By my troth, thou sayest true. For, since the little  wit that fools have was silenced, the little foolery  that wise men have makes a great show. Here comes  Monsieur Le Beau.
With his mouth full of news.
translation: With his mouth full of news.

original: Which he will put on us as pigeons feed their young.
translation: Which he'll shove down our throats like a pigeon feeding its young.

original: Then shall we be news-crammed.
translation: Then we'll be crammed full of news.

original: All the better. We shall be the more  marketable.—Bonjour, Monsieur Le Beau. What’s the news?
translation: All the better. We'll be worth more when we're fattened up. Good morning, Sir Le Beau. What's the news?

original: Fair princess, you have lost much good sport.
translation: Fair princess, you've missed some good sport.

original: Sport? Of what color?
translation: Sport? Of what color?

original: What color, madam? How shall I answer you?
As wit and fortune will.
translation: As your wit and fortune permit you.

original: Or as the Destinies decrees.
translation: Or as the Fates say you should.

original: Well said. That was laid on with a trowel.
translation: Well said. You laid that on thick.

original: Nay, if I keep not my rank—
translation: Well, if I don't perform as I should according to my rank—

original: Thou losest thy old smell.
You amaze me, ladies. I would have told you of good  wrestling, which you have lost the sight of.
translation: You confuse me, ladies. I was going to tell you about a good wrestling match, which you have missed.

original: You tell us the manner of the wrestling.
translation: Tell us what kind of wrestling.

original: I will tell you the beginning, and if it please your  Ladyships, you may see the end, for the best is yet to  do, and here, where you are, they are coming to perform  it.
translation: I'll tell you about the beginning, and if it's still interesting to your Ladyships, then you can go see the end. The best is yet to come, and they're coming to perform it right here where you are.

original: Well, the beginning that is dead and buried.
translation: Well, the beginning is already dead and buried.

original: There comes an old man and his three sons—
translation: There comes an old man and his three sons—

original: I could match this beginning with an old tale.
translation: It sounds like the beginning of a folk tale.

original: Three proper young men of excellent growth and  presence.
translation: Three proper young men, all good looking and with charismatic presence—

original: With bills on their necks: “Be it known unto all men by these presents.”
The eldest of the three wrestled with Charles, the  duke’s wrestler, which Charles in a moment threw him and broke three of his ribs, that there is little hope of  life in him.
translation: The eldest of the three brothers wrestled with Charles, the duke's wrestler, and Charles threw him quickly, breaking three of his ribs. There's not much hope that he will survive.

original: So he served the second, and so the third.  Yonder they lie, the poor old man their father making  such pitiful dole over them that all the beholders take  his part with weeping.
translation: Charles then did the same to the second brother, and then to the third. They're lying over there. And the poor old man, their father, weeps so pitifully over them that all the onlookers are crying too.

original: Alas!
translation: Oh my!

original: But what is the sport, monsieur, that the ladies have  lost?
translation: But what was the sport, sir, that the ladies missed?

original: Why, this that I speak of.
translation: Why, the wrestling I just spoke of.

original: Thus men may grow wiser every day. It is the first time that ever I heard breaking of ribs was sport for  ladies.
translation: Men must be getting wiser every day. This is the first time I ever heard about rib-breaking as a sport for ladies.

original: Or I, I promise thee.
translation: Me too, I promise you.

original: But is there any else longs to see this broken music in his sides? Is there yet another dotes upon  rib-breaking? Shall we see this wrestling, cousin?
translation: But doesn't anyone else want to hear the broken music of breathing through broken ribs? Does anyone else love rib-breaking? Should we go see this wrestling, cousin?

original: You must if you stay here, for here is the place  appointed for the wrestling, and they are ready to  perform it.
translation: You'll have to if you stay here, as this is the place where the wrestling is scheduled, and they are ready to begin.

original: Yonder sure they are coming. Let us now stay and see  it.
translation: Yes, I see them coming from over there. Let's  stay and watch.

original: Come on. Since the youth will not be entreated, his own peril on his forwardness.
translation: Come on. Since the youth can't be reasoned with, let him suffer for his eagerness.

original: Is yonder the man?
translation: Is that the man?

original: Even he, madam.
translation: Indeed it is, madam.

original: Alas, he is too young. Yet he looks successfully.
translation: Oh dear, he is too young. But he looks capable.

original: How now, daughter and cousin? Are you crept hither to  see the wrestling?
translation: How goes it, daughter and niece? Have you snuck over here to see the wrestling?

original: Ay, my liege, so please you give us leave.
translation: Yes, my lord, if you'll give us your permission.

original: You will take little delight in it, I can tell you,  there is such odds in the man. In pity of the  challenger’s youth, I would fain dissuade him, but he  will not be entreated.
translation: You won't enjoy it very much, I can tell you, as the odds are stacked against this man. Because of the challenger's youth, I've been trying to discourage him from fighting. But he won't listen.

original: Speak to him, ladies; see if you  can move him.
translation: You speak to him, ladies. See if you can convince him.

original: Call him hither, good Monsieur Le Beau.
translation: Call him here, good Sir Le Beau.

original: Do so. I’ll not be by.
translation: You go ahead—I won't be here.

original: Monsieur the challenger, the Princess calls for you.
translation: Sir Challenger, the Princess calls for you.

original: I attend them with all respect and duty.
translation: I'll wait on them with all respect and duty.

original: Young man, have you challenged Charles the wrestler?
translation: Young man, have you challenged Charles the wrestler?

original: No, fair princess. He is the general challenger. I come but in as others do, to try with him the strength of my youth.
translation: No, lovely princess. He is the general challenger. I have only come in, like the others, to test the strength of my youth against him.

original: Young gentleman, your spirits are too bold for your  years. You have seen cruel proof of this man’s strength.
translation: Young gentleman, your spirits are too bold for your age. You have seen the cruel proof of this man's strength.

original: If you saw yourself with your eyes or knew yourself  with your judgment, the fear of your adventure would  counsel you to a more equal enterprise.
translation: If you would take a step back and look at yourself and then use your judgment, your fear of what you are about to try to do would teach you to find an endeavor more suitable for your abilities.

original: We pray you for  your own sake to embrace your own safety and give over  this attempt.
translation: We beg you, for your own sake, to embrace your own safety and give up this attempt.

original: Do, young sir. Your reputation shall not therefore be  misprized. We will make it our suit to the duke that the wrestling might not go forward.
translation: Please do, young sir. Your reputation won't be hurt. We will beg the duke ourselves that the wrestling match be cancelled.

original: I beseech you, punish me not with your hard thoughts,  wherein I confess me much guilty to deny so fair and  excellent ladies anything.
translation: I beg you, don't punish me by thinking poorly of me, though I confess that I must be guilty if I can deny anything to such beautiful and excellent ladies as you.

original: But let your fair eyes and  gentle wishes go with me to my trial, wherein, if I be  foiled, there is but one shamed that was never gracious;
translation: Instead, may your fair eyes and good wishes support me in this fight. If I'm beaten, then the shame belongs solely to me, a man who was never gracious.

original: if killed, but one dead that was willing to be so. I  shall do my friends no wrong, for I have none to lament  me;
translation: And if I'm killed, it will only mean the death of a man already willing to die. I won't be hurting any of my friends, for I have no friends to grieve for me.

original: the world no injury, for in it I have nothing. Only  in the world I fill up a place which may be better  supplied when I have made it empty.
translation: And I won't be hurting the world, for I have nothing in it. I only take up space in the world, and maybe my space can be filled by someone worthier once I'm gone.

original: The little strength that I have, I would it were with  you.
translation: I wish that the little strength I have were with you.

original: And mine, to eke out hers.
translation: And mine too, to join hers.

original: Fare you well. Pray heaven I be deceived in you.
translation: Good luck. I pray to God that I'm wrong about you.

original: Your heart’s desires be with you.
translation: May you get your heart's desires.

original: Come, where is this young gallant that is so desirous  to lie with his mother earth?
translation: Come, where is this young show-off who is so eager to lie with his mother earth?

original: Ready, sir; but his will hath in it a more modest  working.
translation: Ready, sir; but I have a more modest desire.

original: You shall try but one fall.
translation: You will only get one round.

original: No, I warrant your Grace you shall not entreat him to a second, that have so mightily persuaded him from a  first.
translation: No, I'm sure your Grace won't be able to convince him to try a second round, just as you couldn't convince him not to try a first round.

original: You mean to mock me after, you should not have mocked  me before. But come your ways.
translation: You should mock me after the match, not before. But come on.

original: Now Hercules be thy speed, young man!
I would I were invisible, to catch the strong fellow by the leg.
translation: I wish I were invisible, so I could trip the legs of the strong fellow to help the young man.

original: O excellent young man!
translation: Oh, excellent young man!

original: If I had a thunderbolt in mine eye, I can tell who  should down.
translation: If I could shoot thunderbolts from my eyes, I can tell you who would be thrown down.

original: No more, no more.
translation: No more, no more.

original: Yes, I beseech your Grace. I am not yet well breathed.
translation: Yes, more, I beg your Grace. I'm hardly warmed up yet.

original: How dost thou, Charles?
translation: How are you doing, Charles?

original: He cannot speak, my lord.
translation: He cannot speak, my lord.

original: Bear him away. What is thy name, young man?
translation: Carry him away. What is your name, young man?

original: Orlando, my liege, the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys.
translation: Orlando, my lord, the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys.

original: I would thou hadst been son to some man else.   The world esteemed thy father honorable,   But I did find him still mine enemy.
translation: I wish you had been some other man's son. The world admired your father as an honorable man, but he was still my enemy.

original: Thou shouldst have better pleased me with this deed   Hadst thou descended from another house.   But fare thee well. Thou art a gallant youth.   I would thou hadst told me of another father.
translation: Your victory would have better pleased me if you came from a different family. But good luck. You are a brave youth. I wish you had told me you had another father.

original: Were I my father, coz, would I do this?
translation: Cousin, if I were my father, would I act as he did?

original: I am more proud to be Sir Rowland’s son, His youngest son, and would not change that calling  To be adopted heir to Frederick.
translation: I am proud to be Sir Rowland's son—his youngest son—and I wouldn't change that even to be Frederick's adopted heir.

original: My father loved Sir Rowland as his soul,   And all the world was of my father’s mind.
translation: My father loved Sir Rowland like he loved his own soul, and the rest of the world shared my father's opinion.

original: Had I before known this young man his son,   I should have given him tears unto entreaties   Ere he should thus have ventured.
translation: If had known before that this young man was Sir Rowland's son, I would have wept and tried even harder to persuade him not to wrestle.

original: Gentle cousin,   Let us go thank him and encourage him.   My father’s rough and envious disposition   Sticks me at heart.—
translation: Dear cousin, let us go thank him and encourage him. My father's rough and jealous behavior toward him hurts me in my heart.

original: Sir, you have well deserved.   If you do keep your promises in love   But justly, as you have exceeded all promise,   Your mistress shall be happy.
translation: [To ORLANDO]  Sir, your victory was well deserved. If you keep and exceed your promises in love just as you have exceeded your promises in this wrestling match, your wife will be a happy woman.

original: Gentleman,   [giving him a chain from her neck]   Wear this for me—one out of suits with fortune   That could give more but that her hand lacks means.
translation: [Giving him a chain from her neck]  Gentleman, wear this for me. I have fallen on hard times, and I wish I could give you more.

original: —Shall we go, coz?
translation: [To CELIA]  Should we go, cousin?

original: Ay.—Fare you well, fair gentleman.
translation: Yes. Good luck, fair gentleman.

original: Can I not say “I thank you?”
translation: [To himself]  Can I not even say "I thank you?"

original: My better parts   Are all thrown down, and that which here stands up   Is but a quintain, a mere lifeless block.
translation: My better nature and good manners are overwhelmed as if they have been thrown down in a wrestling match, and what's left of me is but a mannequin—just a lifeless block.

original: He calls us back. My pride fell with my fortunes.   I’ll ask him what he would.—
translation: He's calling us back. I lost my pride when I lost my fortunes, so I'll ask him what he wants.

original: Did you call, sir?   Sir, you have wrestled well and overthrown   More than your enemies.
translation: [To ORLANDO]  Did you call us, sir? Sir, you wrestled well, and defeated more than just your enemies.

original: Will you go, coz?
translation: Will you come on, cousin?

original: Have with you. Fare you well.
translation: Just a second. Farewell.

original: What passion hangs these weights upon my tongue?   I cannot speak to her, yet she urged conference.   O poor Orlando!
translation: What is this passion that makes my tongue so heavy? I can't speak to her, even though she urged me to. Oh, poor Orlando!

original: Thou art overthrown.   Or Charles or something weaker masters thee.
translation: You are defeated. Either Charles or some more delicate thing has mastered you.

original: Good sir, I do in friendship counsel you   To leave this place.
translation: Good sir, let me advise you, as a friend, to leave this place.

original: Albeit you have deserved   High commendation, true applause, and love,   Yet such is now the duke’s condition   That he misconsters all that you have done.
translation: Although you deserve high praise, true applause, and love, right now the duke is misinterpreting all of your actions.

original: The duke is humorous. What he is indeed   More suits you to conceive than I to speak of.
translation: The duke is moody. And what he  really  is I can't say, but I'm sure you can figure it out.

original: I thank you, sir, and pray you tell me this: Which of the two was daughter of the duke That here was at the wrestling?
translation: I thank you, sir, and ask you to tell me this: which of the two ladies at the wrestling match was the daughter of the duke?

original: Neither his daughter, if we judge by manners,   But yet indeed the smaller is his daughter   The other is daughter to the banished duke,
translation: Neither is his daughter, if we are only judging whether they have inherited his bad manners. But in actuality the smaller lady, Celia, is his daughter. The other, Rosalind, is the daughter of the banished duke,

original: And here detained by her usurping uncle   To keep his daughter company, whose loves   Are dearer than the natural bond of sisters.
translation: kept here by her uncle who usurped the throne, to keep his daughter company. The love between the two cousins is stronger than the natural bond between sisters.

original: But I can tell you that of late this duke   Hath ta'en displeasure 'gainst his gentle niece,
translation: But I can tell you that lately this duke has grown displeased with his refined niece,

original: Grounded upon no other argument   But that the people praise her for her virtues   And pity her for her good father’s sake;
translation: for no other reason than that the people praise her virtues and pity her for her good father's sake.

original: And, on my life, his malice 'gainst the lady   Will suddenly break forth. Sir, fare you well.
translation: I swear on my life, the duke's malice against the lady Rosalind will erupt very soon. Sir, farewell.

original: Hereafter, in a better world than this,   I shall desire more love and knowledge of you.
translation: Later, in a better world than this one, I would like to get to know you and love you better.

original: I rest much bounden to you. Fare you well.
translation: I am indebted to you. Farewell.

original: Thus must I from the smoke into the smother,  From tyrant duke unto a tyrant brother. But heavenly Rosalind!
translation: So now I must go from the frying pan and into the fire, from a duke who is a tyrant to my brother who is a tyrant. But oh, heavenly Rosalind!

original: Why, cousin! Why, Rosalind! Cupid have mercy, not a  word?
Not one to throw at a dog.
translation: Not even one to throw at a dog.

original: No, thy words are too precious to be cast away upon  curs.  Throw some of them at me. Come, lame me with reasons.
translation: No, your words are too precious to be thrown at dogs. Throw some of them at me. Come, injure me with your wisdom.

original: Then there were two cousins laid up, when the one  should be lamed with reasons and the other mad without  any.
translation: Then there would be two cousins who were injured. One would be wounded by wisdom, and the other gone crazy because she didn't have any.

original: But is all this for your father?
translation: But is all this about your father?

original: No, some of it is for my child’s father. Oh, how full  of briers is this working-day world!
translation: No, some of it is for my child's father. Oh, this wearisome world is full of thorns!

original: They are but burs, cousin, thrown upon thee in holiday  foolery. If we walk not in the trodden paths our very  petticoats will catch them.
translation: Cousin, they're just burrs thrown on you in your holiday adventuring. If we don't walk on well-worn paths, even our petticoats will catch them.

original: I could shake them off my coat. These burs are in my  heart.
translation: I could shake those burrs off of my coat, but these burrs are in my heart.

original: Hem them away.
translation: Cough them away.

original: I would try, if I could cry “hem” and have him.
translation: I would try to, if I could cry "ahem" and have him.

original: Come, come, wrestle with thy affections.
translation: Come, come, wrestle with your feelings and take control of them.

original: Oh, they take the part of a better wrestler than  myself.
translation: Oh, but my feelings are taking the side of a better wrestler than myself.

original: Oh, a good wish upon you. You will try in time, in  despite of a fall. But turning these jests out of  service, let us talk in good earnest.
translation: Oh, good luck to you then. You will wrestle him eventually, and  fall . But let's put these jokes aside and talk in earnest.

original: Is it possible on  such a sudden you should fall into so strong a liking  with old Sir Rowland’s youngest son?
translation: Is it possible that could have fallen in love with Sir Rowland's youngest son so suddenly?

original: The duke my father loved his father dearly.
translation: The duke my father loved his father dearly.

original: Doth it therefore ensue that you should love his son  dearly? By this kind of chase I should hate him, for my  father hated his father dearly. Yet I hate not Orlando.
translation: So does that mean that you must love his son dearly? By this logic I should hate him, for my father hated his father. But I don't hate Orlando.

original: No, faith, hate him not, for my sake.
translation: No, please, don't hate him. For my sake.

original: Why should I not? Doth he not deserve well?
translation: Why shouldn't I? Doesn't he deserve it ?

original: Let me love him for that, and do you love him because  I do. Look, here comes the duke.
translation: Let me love him because your father hated his father, and you should love him because I do. Look, here comes the duke.

original: With his eyes full of anger.
translation: With his eyes full of anger.

original: Mistress, dispatch you with your safest haste, And get you from our court.
translation: Madam, leave here quickly, while you still can, and get out of my court.

original: Me, uncle?
translation: Me, uncle?

original: You, cousin.   Within these ten days if that thou beest found   So near our public court as twenty miles,
translation: You, niece. If you are found within twenty miles of our court in ten days time,

original: Thou diest for it.
translation: you will die for it.

original: I do beseech your Grace,   Let me the knowledge of my fault bear with me.
translation: I beg your Grace, let me go with the knowledge of what crime I have committed.

original: If with myself I hold intelligence   Or have acquaintance with mine own desires,   If that I do not dream or be not frantic—
translation: If I know my own thoughts and desires, and I'm not dreaming or crazy—

original: As I do trust I am not—then, dear uncle,   Never so much as in a thought unborn   Did I offend your Highness.
translation: which I trust that I'm not—then, dear uncle, I've never had so much as a half-formed thought that could have offended your Highness.

original: Thus do all traitors.   If their purgation did consist in words,
translation: All traitors say things like this. If they could purge their guilt with words,

original: They are as innocent as grace itself.   Let it suffice thee that I trust thee not.
translation: they would be as innocent as God himself. It should be enough for you to know that I don't trust you.

original: Yet your mistrust cannot make me a traitor. Tell me whereon the likelihood depends.
translation: But your mistrust cannot make me a traitor. Tell me on what grounds you think I'm most likely guilty.

original: Thou art thy father’s daughter. There’s enough.
translation: You are your father's daughter. That's enough.

original: So was I when your Highness took his dukedom.   So was I when your Highness banished him.
translation: I was also my father's daughter when your Highness took my father's dukedom. And I was his daughter when your Highness banished him.

original: Treason is not inherited, my lord,   Or if we did derive it from our friends,   What’s that to me? My father was no traitor.
translation: Treason is not inherited, my lord. Even if we could inherit it, what is that to me? My father was no traitor.

original: Then, good my liege, mistake me not so much   To think my poverty is treacherous.
translation: So, my lord, don't make the mistake of assuming that I'm treacherous just because I'm poor.

original: Dear sovereign, hear me speak.
translation: Dear Highness, let me speak.

original: Ay, Celia, we stayed her for your sake. Else had she with her father ranged along.
translation: Yes, Celia, we let her stay here for your sake. Otherwise she would have been banished with her father.

original: I did not then entreat to have her stay.   It was your pleasure and your own remorse.
translation: At that time I didn't ask you to have her stay—it was your own decision, made with compassion.

original: I was too young that time to value her,   But now I know her. If she be a traitor,   Why so am I.
translation: I was too young at the time to value her, but now I really know her. If she is a traitor, then so am I.
