original: We still have slept together,   Rose at an instant, learned, played, eat together,   And, wheresoe'er we went, like Juno’s swans   Still we went coupled and inseparable.
translation: We always slept together, woken up together, learned, played, and eaten together. Wherever we went, we went together, inseparable like the two swans who pulled  Juno's  chariot.

original: She is too subtle for thee, and her smoothness,   Her very silence and her patience   Speak to the people, and they pity her.
translation: She is too treacherous, and has deceived you. Her smoothness, her silence, and her patience appeal to the people, who pity her suffering.

original: Thou art a fool. She robs thee of thy name,   And thou wilt show more bright and seem more virtuous   When she is gone.
translation: You are a fool. She robs you of your name, and you will seem brighter and more virtuous once she is gone.

original: Then open not thy lips.   Firm and irrevocable is my doom   Which I have passed upon her. She is banished.
translation: So don't open your mouth. The judgment I have passed on her is firm and unchangeable. She is banished.

original: Pronounce that sentence then on me, my liege.  I cannot live out of her company.
translation: Then pronounce that sentence on me as well, my lord. I cannot live without her company.

original: You are a fool.—You, niece, provide yourself. If you outstay the time, upon mine honor And in the greatness of my word, you die.
translation: You are a fool.  You, niece, prepare yourself to leave. If you stay here longer than I have given you, then upon my honor and on my word as a duke, you will die.

original: O my poor Rosalind, whither wilt thou go?  Wilt thou change fathers? I will give thee mine. I charge thee, be not thou more grieved than I am.
translation: Oh, my poor Rosalind, where will you go? Can we exchange fathers? I will give you mine. I insist, don't be more grieved than I am.

original: I have more cause.
translation: I have more reason to be grieved.

original: Thou hast not, cousin. Prithee, be cheerful. Know’st thou not the duke Hath banished me, his daughter?
translation: You do not, cousin. Please, be cheerful. Don't you realize that the duke has also banished me, his daughter?

original: That he hath not.
translation: No he has not.

original: No, hath not? Rosalind lacks then the love   Which teacheth thee that thou and I am one.   Shall we be sundered? Shall we part, sweet girl?
translation: No, he hasn't? In that case you lack the love that would teach you that you and I are one. Will we be separated? Should we part, sweet girl?

original: No, let my father seek another heir.   Therefore devise with me how we may fly,   Whither to go, and what to bear with us,
translation: No, let my father find another heir instead. Therefore plan with me how we may escape, where to go, and what to take with us.

original: And do not seek to take your change upon you,   To bear your griefs yourself and leave me out.
translation: Don't try to take all this upon yourself, to bear your grief alone and leave me out.

original: For, by this heaven, now at our sorrows pale,   Say what thou canst, I’ll go along with thee.
translation: I swear by the heavens—which have grown pale in sympathy with our sorrows—that I will go along with you no matter what you say.

original: Why, whither shall we go?
translation: Well, where will we go then?

original: To seek my uncle in the Forest of Arden.
translation: To find my uncle—your father—in the Forest of Arden.

original: Alas, what danger will it be to us, Maids as we are, to travel forth so far? Beauty provoketh thieves sooner than gold.
translation: But it will be very dangerous for us to travel so far as two girls alone. Beauty attracts thieves even more than money does.

original: I’ll put myself in poor and mean attire   And with a kind of umber smirch my face.
translation: I'll put on some poor and ragged clothes and smear my face with dirt.

original: The like do you. So shall we pass along   And never stir assailants.
translation: You do the same thing. Then we can pass by and not attract any attackers.

original: Were it not better,   Because that I am more than common tall,   That I did suit me all points like a man?
translation: Wouldn't it be better, since I am unusually tall, if I just dressed myself from head to foot like a man?

original: A gallant curtal-axe upon my thigh,   A boar-spear in my hand, and in my heart   Lie there what hidden woman’s fear there will,   We’ll have a swashing and a martial outside—
translation: I can wear a sword in my belt, carry a boar-hunting spear in my hand, and keep all my womanly fear hidden in my heart. We'll keep up a swaggering, warlike appearance,

original: As many other mannish cowards have   That do outface it with their semblances.
translation: like so many other cowardly men who hide their feelings behind their outward appearance.

original: What shall I call thee when thou art a man?
translation: What should I call you when you are a man?

original: I’ll have no worse a name than Jove’s own page, And therefore look you call me Ganymede.  But what will you be called?
Something that hath a reference to my state: No longer Celia, but Aliena.
But, cousin, what if we assayed to steal The clownish fool out of your father’s court?  Would he not be a comfort to our travel?
translation: Cousin, what if we took that clownish fool from your father's court and brought him with us? Wouldn't he be a comfort during our travels?

original: He’ll go along o'er the wide world with me.   Leave me alone to woo him. Let’s away   And get our jewels and our wealth together,
translation: He would travel all over the wide world for me. Leave it to me to persuade him. Let's go and gather our jewels and wealth together,

original: Devise the fittest time and safest way   To hide us from pursuit that will be made   After my flight.
translation: and plan the best time and safest way to avoid the people that will chase after us when my absence is discovered.

original: Now go we in content   To liberty, and not to banishment.
translation: And now we go, happily, to liberty— not  to banishment.

original: Now, my co-mates and brothers in exile,   Hath not old custom made this life more sweet   Than that of painted pomp?
translation:
Now, my companions and brothers in exile, hasn't
our long experience shown this simple life to be sweeter than one of superficial luxury?

original: Are not these woods   More free from peril than the envious court?
translation:
Aren't these woods less dangerous than the jealousies and treachery of
the court?

original: Here feel we not the penalty of Adam,   The seasons' difference, as the icy fang   And churlish chiding of the winter’s wind,
translation:
Out here we don't feel the penalty resulting from Adam's sin—the
changing seasons.

original: Which, when it bites and blows upon my body,   Even till I shrink with cold, I smile and say,   “This is no flattery. These are counselors   That feelingly persuade me what I am.”
translation:
When the icy fangs of the scolding winter wind bite
and blow upon my body—even though I shiver with cold—I smile and say to
myself: "The wind isn't flattering me. It is like a counselor who makes me
feel what I truly am."

original: Sweet are the uses of adversity,   Which, like the toad, ugly and venomous,   Wears yet a precious jewel in his head.
translation:
Adversity has sweet benefits, just like the ugly, venomous
toad who  wears a precious jewel in his forehead .

original: And this our life, exempt from public haunt,   Finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks,   Sermons in stones, and good in everything.
translation: And in this new life, far away from society, we can hear the voices of the trees, read books in the running brooks, hear sermons in the stones, and find the good in everything.

original: I would not change it. Happy is your Grace, That can translate the stubbornness of fortune  Into so quiet and so sweet a style.
translation: I wouldn't exchange it for anything. Your Grace, you are lucky to be able to translate your misfortune into such a quiet, happy lifestyle.

original: Come, shall we go and kill us venison?   And yet it irks me the poor dappled fools,
translation: Come, should we go and kill some deer for dinner? Although it bothers me that these poor spotted innocents—

original: Being native burghers of this desert city,   Should in their own confines with forkèd heads   Have their round haunches gored.
translation: who are the native inhabitants of this uninhabited city—should be gored with arrowheads in their own home.

original: Indeed, my lord,   The melancholy Jaques grieves at that,   And in that kind swears you do more usurp   Than doth your brother that hath banished you.
translation: Indeed, my lord, the melancholy Jaques grieves at the same thing, and he swears that when you hunt deer you are in fact a worse usurper than your brother who banished you.

original: Today my Lord of Amiens and myself   Did steal behind him as he lay along   Under an oak, whose antique root peeps out   Upon the brook that brawls along this wood,
translation: Today my Lord of Amiens and I snuck up behind Jaques as he lay under an oak tree, whose ancient roots peek out from the earth near the brook that babbles through this forest.

original: To the which place a poor sequestered stag   That from the hunter’s aim had ta'en a hurt   Did come to languish.
translation: A poor, lonely stag—who had been separated from his herd and hurt by a hunter's arrow—came to rest in that same place.

original: And indeed, my lord,   The wretched animal heaved forth such groans   That their discharge did stretch his leathern coat   Almost to bursting,
translation: And indeed, my lord, the wretched animal groaned so heavily that he seemed to stretch his leather hide almost to bursting,

original: and the big round tears   Coursed one another down his innocent nose   In piteous chase.
translation: and big, round tears ran pitifully down his innocent nose.

original: And thus the hairy fool,   Much markèd of the melancholy Jaques,   Stood on th' extremest verge of the swift brook,   Augmenting it with tears.
translation: And so the hairy, pitiful creature—watched carefully by the melancholy Jaques—stood on the very edge of the swift brook and added his tears to its flow.

original: But what said Jaques? Did he not moralize this spectacle?
translation: But what did Jaques say? Didn't he find some moral in this scene?

original: Oh, yes, into a thousand similes.   First, for his weeping into the needless stream:
translation: Oh yes, he translated it into a thousand similes. First he spoke about the deer weeping needlessly into the stream's water.

original: “Poor deer,” quoth he, “thou mak’st a testament   As worldlings do, giving thy sum of more   To that which had too much.”
translation: "Poor deer," he said, "you make your will and testament just like humans do, and leave what you have to something that already has too much."

original: Then, being there alone,   Left and abandoned of his velvet friend,   “'Tis right,” quoth he. “Thus misery doth part   The flux of company.”
translation: Then, about the deer being alone, abandoned by his velvety friends, he said: "It is right that misery should separate itself from company."

original: Anon a careless herd,   Full of the pasture, jumps along by him   And never stays to greet him.
translation: Soon after a carefree herd of deer—their stomachs full of pasture grass—jumped past without stopping to greet the wounded stag.

original: “Ay,” quoth Jaques,   “Sweep on, you fat and greasy citizens.   'Tis just the fashion. Wherefore do you look   Upon that poor and broken bankrupt there?”
translation: "Yes," said Jaques, "hurry on, you fat and citizens, ready to be hunted. This is just the way life is. Why should you stop and look at that poor, broken, bankrupt creature there?"

original: Thus most invectively he pierceth through   The body of the country, city, court,   Yea, and of this our life,
translation: In this way, with bitter criticism, he pierced the heart of the country, the city, the court, and even our lives here in the woods—

original: swearing that we   Are mere usurpers, tyrants, and what’s worse,   To fright the animals and to kill them up   In their assigned and native dwelling place.
translation: swearing that we are only usurpers and tyrants, frightening and killing the animals in their own rightful dwelling places.

original: And did you leave him in this contemplation?
translation: And did you leave him in this state of contemplation?

original: We did, my lord, weeping and commenting Upon the sobbing deer.
translation: We did, my lord, as he wept and commented on the sobbing deer.

original: Show me the place. I love to cope him in these sullen fits, For then he’s full of matter.
translation: Show me the place where this happened. I love to talk with him when he's in these melancholy moods, for then he's full of things to say.

original: I’ll bring you to him straight.
translation: I'll bring you to him right away.

original: Can it be possible that no man saw them? It cannot be. Some villains of my court Are of consent and sufferance in this.
translation: Can it be possible that no man saw them leave? It cannot be. Some villains in my court must be complicit in this.

original: I cannot hear of any that did see her.   The ladies, her attendants of her chamber   Saw her abed,
translation: I cannot find anyone that saw her leave. The ladies who attend her in her rooms helped her into bed last night,

original: and in the morning early   They found the bed untreasured of their mistress.
translation: but in the early morning they found the bed empty of their mistress.

original: My lord, the roinish clown, at whom so oft   Your Grace was wont to laugh, is also missing.
translation: My lord, the base clown—whom your Grace used to laugh at so often—is also missing.

original: Hisperia, the Princess' gentlewoman,   Confesses that she secretly o'erheard   Your daughter and her cousin much commend   The parts and graces of the wrestler   That did but lately foil the sinewy Charles,
translation: And Hisperia, the Princess's servant, confesses that she secretly overhead your daughter and her cousin praising the good looks and manners of the wrestler who recently defeated the muscular Charles.

original: And she believes wherever they are gone   That youth is surely in their company.
translation: And she believes that wherever they have gone, that young man is surely with them.

original: Send to his brother. Fetch that gallant hither.   If he be absent, bring his brother to me.   I’ll make him find him.
translation: Send a message to his brother. Fetch that pretty-boy Orlando here. If he is absent, then bring his brother to me. I'll make Oliver find Orlando.

original: Do this suddenly,   And let not search and inquisition quail   To bring again these foolish runaways.
translation: Do this immediately, and don't let your searching and questioning falter until you've brought home these foolish runaways.

original: Who’s there?
translation: Who's there?

original: What, my young master, O my gentle master,   O my sweet master, O you memory   Of old Sir Rowland!
translation: My young master; oh, my gentle master; oh, my sweet master; oh, you living memory of old Sir Rowland!

original: Why, what make you here?   Why are you virtuous? Why do people love you?   And wherefore are you gentle, strong, and valiant?
translation: Why, what are you doing here? Why are you virtuous? Why do people love you? And why are you noble, strong, and brave?

original: Why would you be so fond to overcome   The bonny prizer of the humorous duke?   Your praise is come too swiftly home before you.
translation: Why would you be so foolish as to beat the moody duke's prized wrestler? Praise of your victory has reached home before you did.

original: Know you not, master, to some kind of men   Their graces serve them but as enemies?   No more do yours.
translation: Don't you know, master, that to some men their good qualities serve them only as enemies? Yours are like this.

original: Your virtues, gentle master,   Are sanctified and holy traitors to you.
translation: Noble master, your virtues are both blessed and holy traitors to you.

original: Oh, what a world is this when what is comely   Envenoms him that bears it!
translation: Oh, what a world this is, when what is good in a man poisons him!

original: Why, what’s the matter?
translation: Why, what's the matter?

original: O unhappy youth,   Come not within these doors. Within this roof   The enemy of all your graces lives.
translation: Oh, unlucky young man: don't walk through these doors. Under this roof lives a man who is the enemy of all your good qualities.

original: Your brother—no, no brother—yet the son—   Yet not the son, I will not call him son—   Of him I was about to call his father   Hath heard your praises,
translation: Your brother—no, no brother of yours—yet the son, but not the son, I will not call him son—of the man I was about to call his father. He has heard of your success,

original: and this night he means   To burn the lodging where you use to lie,   And you within it.
translation: and tonight he plans to burn down the hut where you usually sleep, with you inside it.

original: If he fail of that,   He will have other means to cut you off.   I overheard him and his practices.
translation: And if he fails at that, he will find other ways to kill you. I overheard him and his plans.

original: This is no place, this house is but a butchery.   Abhor it, fear it, do not enter it.
translation: This is no place for you. This house in now a slaughterhouse. Hate it, fear it, do not enter it.

original: Why, whither, Adam, wouldst thou have me go?
translation: Well, where would you suggest I go then, Adam?

original: No matter whither, so you come not here.
translation: It doesn't matter where, as long as it isn't here.

original: What, wouldst thou have me go and beg my food,   Or with a base and boist'rous sword enforce   A thievish living on the common road?
translation: What, would you have me go and beg for my food, or use a lowly, rough sword to lead a life of thievery on the common road?

original: This I must do, or know not what to do.   Yet this I will not do, do how I can.
translation: That's what I'll have to do, because I don't know what else I could do. And yet that is something I won't do, no matter what.

original: I rather will subject me to the malice   Of a diverted blood and bloody brother.
translation: I would rather give myself up to the hatred of an estranged, violent brother.

original: But do not so. I have five hundred crowns,   The thrifty hire I saved under your father,
translation: But don't do that. I have five hundred gold coins, which I carefully saved while working under your father.

original: Which I did store to be my foster nurse   When service should in my old limbs lie lame   And unregarded age in corners thrown.
translation: I kept it so it would be a retirement fund for when my old body grew lame with service and lay forgotten in some corner.

original: Take that, and He that doth the ravens feed,   Yea, providently caters for the sparrow,   Be comfort to my age. Here is the gold.
translation: Take this money, and God—who feeds the ravens and provides for the sparrows—will comfort me as well in my old age. Here is the gold.

original: All this I give you. Let me be your servant.   Though I look old, yet I am strong and lusty,
translation: All this I give to you. Let me be your servant. Though I look old, I'm still strong and healthy,

original: For in my youth I never did apply   Hot and rebellious liquors in my blood   Nor did not with unbashful forehead woo   The means of weakness and debility.
translation: since in my youth I never drank alcohol, or lived dangerously in a way that would court weakness and injury through foolishness.

original: Therefore my age is as a lusty winter,   Frosty but kindly. Let me go with you.
translation: Therefore my old age is like a strong, vigorous winter: frosty, but kindly. Let me go with you.

original: I’ll do the service of a younger man   In all your business and necessities.
translation: I'll do everything a younger man could do for you regarding your business and needs.

original: O good old man, how well in thee appears   The constant service of the antique world,   When service sweat for duty, not for meed.
translation: Oh, good old man, you are a prime example of the work ethic of the old days, when people worked for duty, not just for money.

original: Thou art not for the fashion of these times,   Where none will sweat but for promotion,   And having that do choke their service up   Even with the having. It is not so with thee.
translation: You are not made for these present times, where no one will work except for a promotion, and when they have that, they stop working.

original: But, poor old man, thou prun’st a rotten tree   That cannot so much as a blossom yield   In lieu of all thy pains and husbandry.
translation: But, poor old man, with me you are pruning a rotten tree that cannot yield even a single blossom, no matter how hard and well you work.

original: But come thy ways. We’ll go along together,   And ere we have thy youthful wages spent,   We’ll light upon some settled low content.
translation: But come. We'll go along together, and we'll find some way to make a modest living before we've spent all the money you saved in your youth.

original: Master, go on, and I will follow thee   To the last gasp, with truth and loyalty.
translation: Master, go on, and I will follow you to the last gasp, with truth and loyalty.

original: From seventeen years till now almost fourscore   Here livèd I, but now live here no more.
translation: I have lived in this house from age seventeen to now, almost eighty, but now I will live here no more.

original: At seventeen years, many their fortunes seek,   But at fourscore, it is too late a week.   Yet fortune cannot recompense me better   Than to die well, and not my master’s debtor.
translation: Many seek their fortunes at age seventeen, but eighty is a bit late for that. Yet fortune cannot reward me better than to die well, without owing my master anything.

original: O Jupiter, how weary are my spirits!
I care not for my spirits, if my legs were not weary.
translation: I wouldn't care about my spirit, if my legs weren't so tired.

original: I could find in my heart to disgrace my man’s apparel  and to cry like a woman, but I must comfort the weaker  vessel,
translation: I could insult my manly clothes by crying  like a woman . But instead I must comfort my weaker feminine side,

original: as doublet and hose ought to show itself  courageous to petticoat. Therefore courage, good Aliena.
translation: just as the man's jacket and breeches must act brave for the woman's petticoat. Therefore have courage, good Aliena.

original: I pray you bear with me. I cannot go no further.
translation: Please bear with me. I can't go any further.

original: For my part, I had rather bear with you than bear you.  Yet I should bear no cross if I did bear you, for I  think you have no money in your purse.
Well, this is the Forest of Arden.
translation: Well, this is the Forest of Arden.

original: Ay, now am I in Arden, the more fool I. When I was at  home I was in a better place, but travelers must be content.
translation: Yes, now I am in Arden, which makes me even more of a fool. When I was at home, I was in a better place. But travelers must be content with what they can get.

original: Ay, be so, good Touchstone.
translation: Yes, be content, good Touchstone.

original: Look you who comes here, a young man and an old in  solemn talk.
translation: Look who's coming this way—a young man and an old man having a serious discussion.

original: That is the way to make her scorn you still.
translation: That's only going to make her keep scorning you.

original: O Corin, that thou knew’st how I do love her!
translation: Oh, Corin, if you only knew how much I love her!

original: I partly guess, for I have loved ere now.
translation: I can probably guess, as I have been in love before.

original: No, Corin, being old, thou canst not guess,   Though in thy youth thou wast as true a lover   As ever sighed upon a midnight pillow.
translation: No, Corin, being old, you cannot guess—even if in your youth you were as true a lover as ever sighed into your pillow all night long.

original: But if thy love were ever like to mine—   As sure I think did never man love so—   How many actions most ridiculous   Hast thou been drawn to by thy fantasy?
translation: But if your love was anything like mine—and I'm sure that no man has ever loved as I do—tell me how many ridiculous actions did your desires lead you to perform?

original: Into a thousand that I have forgotten.
translation: A thousand, but I have forgotten them all.

original: Oh, thou didst then ne'er love so heartily.   If thou rememb’rest not the slightest folly   That ever love did make thee run into,   Thou hast not loved.
translation: Oh, then you never loved as fully as I do. If you cannot remember even the smallest foolish act that love drove you to, then you have not loved.

original: Or if thou hast not sat as I do now,   Wearying thy hearer in thy mistress’s praise,   Thou hast not loved.
translation: Or if you have not sat as I do now, wearying your listener with the praise of your beloved, then you have not loved.

original: Or if thou hast not broke from company   Abruptly, as my passion now makes me,   Thou hast not loved.   O Phoebe, Phoebe, Phoebe!
translation: Or if you have not broken away from all company, as my passion now leads me to do, then you have not loved. Oh Phoebe, Phoebe, Phoebe!

original: Alas, poor shepherd, searching of thy wound,  I have by hard adventure found mine own.
translation: Alas, poor shepherd, hearing you describe your injured heart has reminded me of my own lovelorn suffering.

original: And I mine. I remember when I was in love I broke my  sword upon a stone and bid him take that for coming a-  night to Jane Smile.
translation: And mine as well. I remember when I was in love, I broke my sword upon a stone and told the sword to "take that" for coming at night to visit Jane Smile.

original: And I remember the kissing of her  batler, and the cow’s dugs that her pretty chapped hands had milked.
translation: And I remember kissing Jane's washing stick, and the cow's udders that her pretty chapped hands had milked.

original: And I remember the wooing of a peascod  instead of her, from whom I took two cods and, giving  her them again, said with weeping tears, “Wear these for my sake.”
translation: And I remember wooing a peapod, and taking two peas from it and giving them to her, and tearfully asking her to " Wear these for my sake ."

original: We that are true lovers run into strange  capers. But as all is mortal in nature, so is all nature in love mortal in folly.
translation: We who are true lovers do many strange things. But just as everything in nature is mortal, so all lovers show their humanity through their foolishness.

original: Thou speak’st wiser than thou art ware of.
translation: Your words are wiser than you are aware of.

original: Nay, I shall ne'er be ware of mine own wit till I break my shins against it.
translation: No, I will never be aware of my own wit, until I break my shins against it.

original: Jove, Jove, this shepherd’s passion Is much upon my fashion.
translation: Jove, Jove, this shepherd's passion is much like my own.

original: And mine, but it grows something stale with me.
translation: And mine too, but I am getting somewhat tired of it.

original: I pray you, one of you question yond man, if he for  gold will give us any food. I faint almost to death.
translation: Please, one of you go ask that man if he will sell us any food for gold. I am fainting almost to death with hunger.

original: Holla, you clown!
translation: Hey, you clown!

original: Peace, fool. He’s not thy kinsman.
translation: Quiet, you fool. He's not a clown like you.

original: Who calls?
translation: Who calls?

original: Your betters, sir.
translation: Your superior, sir.

original: Else are they very wretched.
translation: If they weren't my superiors, they would have to be very wretched.

original: Peace, I say. —Good even to you, friend.
translation: Quiet, I say. [To CORIN] Good evening to you, friend.

original: And to you, gentle sir, and to you all.
translation: And to you, noble sir, and to you all.

original: I prithee, shepherd, if that love or gold   Can in this desert place buy entertainment,   Bring us where we may rest ourselves and feed.
translation: Please, shepherd, if kindness or gold can buy food and lodging in this uninhabited place, lead us to where we can rest ourselves and eat.

original: Here’s a young maid with travel much oppressed,   And faints for succor.
translation: With us here is a young lady who is very weary from traveling and faint with hunger.

original: Fair sir, I pity her   And wish, for her sake more than for mine own,   My fortunes were more able to relieve her.
translation: Good-looking sir, I pity her and wish, for her sake more than my own, that I was better able to help her.

original: But I am shepherd to another man   And do not shear the fleeces that I graze.
translation: But I am the hired shepherd of another man, and I do not shear the wool from the sheep I  tend.

original: My master is of churlish disposition   And little recks to find the way to heaven   By doing deeds of hospitality.
translation: My master is a stingy man and doesn't care to get to heaven by doing things that are hospitable.

original: Besides, his cote, his flocks, and bounds of feed   Are now on sale, and at our sheepcote now,   By reason of his absence, there is nothing   That you will feed on.
translation: Besides, his cottage, his flocks, and his pastures are now for sale. And because he's away right now, there's nothing to eat at our cottage.

original: But what is, come see,   And in my voice most welcome shall you be.
translation: But let's see what we can find, and as far as I have any influence, you will be most welcome.

original: What is he that shall buy his flock and pasture?
translation: Who is the person who wants to buy the flock and pasture?

original: That young swain that you saw here but erewhile,  That little cares for buying anything.
translation: That young shepherd you saw here just a little while ago, but in truth he hardly cares about buying anything.

original: I pray thee, if it stand with honesty, Buy thou the cottage, pasture, and the flock, And thou shalt have to pay for it of us.
translation: I ask you—if it can be honorably done—please buy the cottage, the pasture, and the flock, and we will give you the money to pay for it.

original: And we will mend thy wages. I like this place,  And willingly could waste my time in it.
translation: And we will improve your wages. I like this place, and would willingly spend my time here.

original: Assuredly the thing is to be sold.   Go with me. If you like upon report   The soil, the profit, and this kind of life,
translation: The thing will certainly be sold. Come with me. If you like what you see of the land, its potential profit, and this shepherd's life,

original: I will your very faithful feeder be   And buy it with your gold right suddenly.
translation: then I will be your faithful servant and buy it with your gold immediately.

original: [sings]   Under the greenwood tree   Who loves to lie with me   And turn his merry note   Unto the sweet bird’s throat,
translation: [Singing] Who wants to lie with me, Under the greenwood tree, And tune his merry notes To the sweet bird's singing,

original: Come hither, come hither, come hither.   Here shall he see   No enemy   But winter and rough weather.
translation: Come here, come here, come here. Here he will see No enemy But winter and rough weather.

original: More, more, I prithee, more.
translation: More, more, please, more.

original: It will make you melancholy, Monsieur Jaques.
translation: It will make you sad, Sir Jaques.

original: I thank it. More, I prithee, more. I can suck  melancholy out of a song as a weasel sucks eggs. More, I prithee, more.
translation: I will be glad about that. More, please, more. I can suck sadness out of a song like a weasel sucks the yolk out of an egg. More, please, more.

original: My voice is ragged. I know I cannot please you.
translation: My voice has grown ragged. I know it won't please you.

original: I do not desire you to please me. I do desire you to  sing.  Come, more, another stanzo. Call you 'em “stanzos?”
translation: I don't want you to please me. I want you to sing. Come, more, another verse. Is that what you call them, "verses?"

original: What you will, Monsieur Jaques.
translation: Call them what you want, Sir Jaques.

original: Nay, I care not for their names. They owe me nothing.  Will you sing?
translation: No, the only names I care about are those of people who owe me money. Will you sing?

original: More at your request than to please myself.
translation: Only because you ask me, not to please myself.

original: Well then, if ever I thank any man, I’ll thank you.  But that they call “compliment” is like th' encounter of two dog-apes.
translation: Well then, if I've ever thanked any man, I'll thank you. But two men complimenting each other are like two baboons scratching each others' backs: insincere politeness.

original: And when a man thanks me heartily,  methinks I have given him a penny and he renders me the  beggarly thanks. Come, sing. And you that will not, hold your tongues.
translation: When a man thanks me heartily for a compliment, it feels like I have given a beggar a penny and in return he thanks me far too much. Come, sing. And those of you who won't sing, stay quiet.

original: Well, I’ll end the song.—Sirs, cover the while; the  duke will drink under this tree.—He hath been all this  day to look you.
translation: Well, I'll sing the end of the song.  Sirs, you set the table in the meantime; the duke will drink under this tree. [To JAQUES] He has been looking for you all day.

original: And I have been all this day to avoid him. He is too  disputable for my company. I think of as many matters as he, but I give heaven thanks and make no boast of them. Come, warble, come.
translation: And I have been avoiding him all day. He is too argumentative for my company. I think about just as many things as he does, but I thank heaven for them instead of boasting about them. Come, sing, come.

original: [singing]   Who doth ambition shun   And loves to live i' th' sun,
translation: [Singing] Whoever shuns ambition And loves to live in the sun,

original: Seeking the food he eats     And pleased with what he gets,   Come hither, come hither, come hither.
translation: Seeking the food he eats, And pleased with what he gets, Come here, come here, come here.

original: Here shall he see   No enemy   But winter and rough weather.
translation: Here he will see No enemy But winter and rough weather.

original: I’ll give you a verse to this note that I made  yesterday in despite of my invention.
translation: I'll give you a verse I wrote for this tune yesterday, though it's not very imaginative.

original: And I’ll sing it.   [taking paper from JAQUES]   Thus it  goes:   If it do come to pass     That any man turn ass,
translation: And I'll sing it.  [T aking a paper from JAQUES]  It goes like this: If it should come to pass That any man turns into an ass,

original: Leaving his wealth and ease   A stubborn will to please,   Ducdame, ducdame, ducdame.
translation: Leaving his wealth and ease To please his stubborn will, Ducdame, ducdame, ducdame.

original: Here shall he see     Gross fools as he,   An if he will come to me.
translation: Here he will see Fools as vulgar as he, If he will come to me.

original: What’s that “ducdame”?
'Tis a Greek invocation, to call fools into a circle.  I’ll go sleep if I can. If I cannot, I’ll rail against  all the first-born of Egypt.
And I’ll go seek the duke. His banquet is prepared.
translation: And I'll go seek the duke. His meal is ready.

original: Dear master, I can go no further. Oh, I die for food.  Here lie I down and measure out my grave. Farewell, kind master.
translation: Dear master, I can't go any further. Oh, I'm dying of hunger. I will lie down here and measure out my grave. Farewell, kind master.

original: Why, how now, Adam? No greater heart in thee? Live a  little, comfort a little, cheer thyself a little. If  this uncouth forest yield anything savage, I will either be food for it or bring it for food to thee.
translation: Why, what's this now, Adam? Don't you have a braver heart than that? Live a little, comfort yourself a little, cheer up a little. If this wild forest has any animals in it, I will either be food for them or bring them as food for you.

original: Thy  conceit is nearer death than thy powers. For my sake, be comfortable. Hold death awhile at the arm’s end. I will here be with thee presently, and if I bring thee not  something to eat, I will give thee leave to die.
translation: Your body isn't close to death. It's only your imagination. For my sake, be comfortable. Keep death at arm's length a while. I will be back with you soon, and if I don't bring you something to eat, then I will give you permission to die.

original: But if  thou diest before I come, thou art a mocker of my labor. Well said. Thou look’st cheerly, and I’ll be with thee  quickly. Yet thou liest in the bleak air.
translation: But if you die before I return, then you will be mocking my effort to help you. I said that well: you look more cheerful already, and I'll be back quickly. But you're lying in the cold.

original: Come, I will  bear thee to some shelter, and thou shalt not die for  lack of a dinner if there live anything in this desert.  Cheerly, good Adam.
translation: Come, I will carry you to some shelter, and you won't die for lack of dinner if there is anything alive and edible in this uninhabited forest. Cheer up, good Adam.

original: I think he be transformed into a beast, For I can nowhere find him like a man.
translation: I think he must have transformed into an animal, because I cannot find him anywhere looking like a man.

original: My lord, he is but even now gone hence. Here was he merry, hearing of a song.
translation: My lord, he just left from here. Here he was happy, listening to a song.

original: If he, compact of jars, grow musical, We shall have shortly discord in the spheres. Go seek him. Tell him I would speak with him.
He saves my labor by his own approach.
translation: He saves me the trouble by coming here himself.

original: Why, how now, monsieur? What a life is this  That your poor friends must woo your company? What, you look merrily.
translation: Why, what's going on, sir? What a life is this that your poor friends must come begging for your company? Hmm...you look happy.

original: A fool, a fool, I met a fool i' th' forest,   A motley fool. A miserable world!
translation: A fool, a fool, I met a fool in the forest, a jester dressed in mixed colors. What a miserable world!

original: As I do live by food, I met a fool,   Who laid him down and basked him in the sun   And railed on Lady Fortune in good terms,   In good set terms, and yet a motley fool.
translation: As sure as I live off of food, I met a fool who was lying down and basking in the sun, complaining against Lady Fortune using good, well-practiced language, and yet he was a professional fool.

original: “Good morrow, fool,” quoth I. “No, sir,” quoth he,   “Call me not ‘fool’ till heaven hath sent me fortune.”
translation: "Good morning, fool," I said. "No, sir," he said, "Don't call me 'fool' until heaven has sent me my fortune."

original: And then he drew a dial from his poke   And, looking on it with lackluster eye,   Says very wisely, “It is ten o'clock.
translation: And then he pulled a sundial from his pocket and, looking at it gravely, said very wisely, "It is ten o'clock.

original: Thus we may see,” quoth he, “how the world wags.   'Tis but an hour ago since it was nine,   And after one hour more ’twill be eleven.
translation: So we may see," he said, "how the world moves. It was nine only an hour ago, and in one more hour it will be eleven.

original: And so from hour to hour we ripe and ripe,   And then from hour to hour we rot and rot,   And thereby hangs a tale.”
translation: And so from hour to hour we ripen and ripen, and from hour to hour we rot and rot, and there's a story in all this."

original: When I did hear   The motley fool thus moral on the time,   My lungs began to crow like chanticleer   That fools should be so deep-contemplative,
translation: When I heard that fool moralizing about time in this way, I began to laugh and exclaim like a rooster. That fools should be so contemplative

original: And I did laugh sans intermission   An hour by his dial. O noble fool!   A worthy fool! Motley’s the only wear.
translation: made me laugh without a break for a full hour, as recorded by the fool's sundial. Oh, noble fool! A worthy fool! Jester's clothing is the only thing to wear.

original: What fool is this?
translation: What fool is this?

original: O worthy fool!—
translation: Oh, worthy fool!

original: One that hath been a courtier   And says, “If ladies be but young and fair,   They have the gift to know it.”
translation: [To DUKE SENIOR]  A fool who has been at court, and who says, "If ladies are young and fair, they also always know it."

original: And in his brain,   Which is as dry as the remainder biscuit   After a voyage, he hath strange places crammed   With observation,
translation: He has a brain as  dry  as a sailor's biscuit after a voyage, and he has crammed strange parts of it with observations,

original: the which he vents   In mangled forms. Oh, that I were a fool!   I am ambitious for a motley coat.
translation: which he expresses in a twisted, roundabout way. Oh, I wish I were a fool! My ambition is to wear a jester's coat.

original: Thou shalt have one.
translation: You will have one then.

original: It is my only suit,   Provided that you weed your better judgments   Of all opinion that grows rank in them   That I am wise.
translation: It is the only suit I will wear, and the only request I will make too, as long as you will rid yourself of any wild-growing ideas that I am wise.

original: I must have liberty   Withal, as large a charter as the wind,   To blow on whom I please, for so fools have.
translation: Along with my jester's suit, I must have the freedom—like the wind—to blow my satiric comments on anyone I please, just like real fools do.

original: And they that are most gallèd with my folly,   They most must laugh. And why, sir, must they so?   The “why” is plain as way to parish church:
translation: And whoever is most wounded by my foolishness also has to laugh the most. And why, sir, must he? The answer is as plain as the path to a parish church:

original: He that a fool doth very wisely hit   Doth very foolishly, although he smart,   Not to seem senseless of the bob.
translation: any man a fool happens to satirize would be foolish (even if he's smart) not to pretend to ignore the barbed joke.

original: If not,   The wise man’s folly is anatomized   Even by the squand'ring glances of the fool.
translation: Otherwise, the wise man's foolishness would be exposed even by jokes not meant to mock him.

original: Invest me in my motley. Give me leave   To speak my mind, and I will through and through   Cleanse the foul body of th' infected world,   If they will patiently receive my medicine.
translation: Dress me up in jester's clothes. Give me permission to speak my mind, and I will through and through cleanse the sick body of the infected world—if it can accept my medicine.

original: Fie on thee! I can tell what thou wouldst do.
translation: Curse you! I know what you would do.

original: What, for a counter, would I do but good?
translation: I'll give you a penny if you tell me: what would I do besides good?

original: Most mischievous foul sin in chiding sin,   For thou thyself hast been a libertine,
translation: You would be committing a mischievous, foul sin by criticizing other people's sins. For you yourself have been a shameless sinner—

original: As sensual as the brutish sting itself,   And all th' embossèd sores and headed evils   That thou with license of free foot hast caught   Wouldst thou disgorge into the general world.
translation: as lustful as carnal appetite itself. And all the swollen boils and pimples of sin that you acquired in your free roaming you would now burst and return to the general public.

original: Why, who cries out on pride   That can therein tax any private party?   Doth it not flow as hugely as the sea   Till that the weary very means do ebb?
translation: Why, if I cry out against pride in general, should that mean that I'm criticizing a particular person? Doesn't pride flow as much as a moving sea, which exhausts even its own source?

original: What woman in the city do I name,   When that I say the city-woman bears   The cost of princes on unworthy shoulders?
translation: Am I naming any specific woman of the city when I say that the clothes a city-woman wears are rich enough for a prince?

original: Who can come in and say that I mean her,   When such a one as she such is her neighbor?
translation: Who can come in and say that I mean her specifically, when all her neighbors are the same?

original: Or what is he of basest function   That says his bravery is not of my cost,   Thinking that I mean him, but therein suits   His folly to the mettle of my speech?
translation: Or if some low-ranking man tells me that his fancy clothes are none of my business, then isn't he just admitting that his foolishness is exactly what I'm talking about?

original: There then. How then, what then? Let me see wherein   My tongue hath wronged him. If it do him right,   Then he hath wronged himself.
translation: Well then. How then, what then? Tell me how my words have wronged him. If they describe him accurately, then he has done wrong himself.

original: If he be free,   Why then my taxing like a wild goose flies   Unclaimed of any man. But who comes here?
translation: If they don't describe him, why, then my criticisms fly past like a wild goose, unclaimed by any man. But who is this coming?

original: Forbear, and eat no more.
translation: Stop, and eat no more.

original: Why, I have eat none yet.
translation: Why, I haven't eaten anything yet.

original: Nor shalt not till necessity be served.
translation: And you won't until what has to be done is done.

original: Of what kind should this cock come of?
translation: What kind of fighting rooster is this?

original: Art thou thus boldened, man, by thy distress Or else a rude despiser of good manners, That in civility thou seem’st so empty?
translation: Are you acting so boldly, man, because you are in distress? Or do you just despise good manners, that you should seem so lacking in civility?

original: You touched my vein at first. The thorny point   Of bare distress hath ta'en from me the show   Of smooth civility, yet am I inland bred   And know some nurture.
translation: You described me right the first time. The painful thorn of distress has robbed me of the performance of good manners, though I was raised in civilized society and had a proper upbringing.

original: But forbear, I say.   He dies that touches any of this fruit   Till I and my affairs are answerèd.
translation: But stop, I say. Whoever touches this fruit before my business is taken care of will die.

original: An you will not be answered with reason, I must die.
translation: If you won't listen to reason, then I must die.

original: What would you have? Your gentleness shall force More than your force move us to gentleness.
translation: What do you want? Your gentlemanly manners will persuade us to act, more than your force will persuade us to act gentlemanly.

original: I almost die for food, and let me have it.
translation: I am almost dying with hunger, so let me have some food.

original: Sit down and feed, and welcome to our table.
translation: Sit down and eat, and welcome to our table.

original: Speak you so gently? Pardon me, I pray you.   I thought that all things had been savage here,   And therefore put I on the countenance   Of stern commandment.
translation: Do you really speak like such a gentleman? Forgive me, I beg you. I thought that everything in this forest was savage and wild, so I made myself act stern and demanding.

original: But whate'er you are   That in this desert inaccessible,   Under the shade of melancholy boughs,   Lose and neglect the creeping hours of time,
translation: But whoever you are—you who sit under the shade of gloomy branches, losing track of the creeping hours of time in this inaccessible wilderness—

original: If ever you have looked on better days,   If ever been where bells have knolled to church,   If ever sat at any good man’s feast,
translation: if you have ever seen better days, or ever heard bells calling you to church, or ever sat at a good man's table for a feast,

original: If ever from your eyelids wiped a tear   And know what ’tis to pity and be pitied,   Let gentleness my strong enforcement be,   In the which hope I blush and hide my sword.
translation: or ever wiped a tear from your eyes; if you know what it is to pity and be pitied, then let my gentle manners persuade you. In the hope of this, I will blush at my former rudeness, and put away my sword.

original: True is it that we have seen better days   And have with holy bell been knolled to church,   And sat at good men’s feasts and wiped our eyes   Of drops that sacred pity hath engendered.
translation: It is true that we have seen better days, and have been summoned to church by the ringing of holy bells, and have sat at good men's feasts, and have wiped away tears caused by sacred pity.

original: And therefore sit you down in gentleness,   And take upon command what help we have   That to your wanting may be ministered.
translation: Therefore sit down with us and ask for whatever it is you need, so that we may provide it.

original: Then but forbear your food a little while   Whiles, like a doe, I go to find my fawn   And give it food.
translation: Then if you will please stop eating for a little while, I—like a mother deer—will go find my fawn and give it food.

original: There is an old poor man   Who after me hath many a weary step   Limped in pure love.
translation: There is a poor old man who has limped after me for many weary miles, purely out of love.

original: Till he be first sufficed,   Oppressed with two weak evils, age and hunger,   I will not touch a bit.
translation: He is oppressed by two evils, age and hunger, and until he gets food I won't eat a bit.

original: Go find him out, And we will nothing waste till you return.
translation: Go find him, and we won't eat anything until you return.

original: I thank you; and be blessed for your good comfort.
translation: I thank you, and God bless you for your kind hospitality.

original: Thou seest we are not all alone unhappy.   This wide and universal theater
translation: You see that we are not the only unhappy ones here. This wide and universal theater

original: Presents more woeful pageants than the scene   Wherein we play in.
translation: presents more sad plays than just the small scene we are acting in.

original: All the world’s a stage,   And all the men and women merely players.   They have their exits and their entrances,   And one man in his time plays many parts,   His acts being seven ages.
translation: The whole world is a stage, and all the men and women merely actors. They have their exits and their entrances, and in his lifetime one man plays many parts, with the ages of his life in seven acts.

original: At first the infant,   Mewling and puking in the nurse’s arms.   Then the whining schoolboy with his satchel   And shining morning face, creeping like snail   Unwillingly to school.
translation: In the first act he is the infant, crying and puking in the nurse's arms. Then he plays the whining schoolboy with his book bag and bright youthful face, creeping like a snail unwillingly to school.

original: And then the lover,   Sighing like furnace, with a woeful ballad   Made to his mistress' eyebrow.
translation: And then he is the lover, sighing like a furnace and writing sad songs about his beloved's eyebrows.

original: Then a soldier,   Full of strange oaths and bearded like the pard,   Jealous in honor, sudden and quick in quarrel,   Seeking the bubble reputation   Even in the cannon’s mouth.
translation: Then he is a soldier, full of foreign curses and bearded like a leopard, quick to fight and jealously responding to any slight to his honor, seeking fleeting fame and reputation even if it means putting himself in front of the cannon's mouth.

original: And then the justice,   In fair round belly with good capon lined,   With eyes severe and beard of formal cut,   Full of wise saws and modern instances;
translation: Then he plays the judge, with a nice round belly lined with the bribes he's taken, with stern eyes and a beard cut to a respectable shape, full of wise sayings and everyday examples of his points;

original: And so he plays his part. The sixth age shifts   Into the lean and slippered pantaloon   With spectacles on nose and pouch on side,
translation: and in this way he plays his part. In the sixth act he shifts into the skinny, ridiculous old man, wearing slippers on his feet, glasses on his nose, and a money bag at his side.

original: His youthful hose, well saved, a world too wide   For his shrunk shank, and his big manly voice,   Turning again toward childish treble, pipes   And whistles in his sound.
translation: The stockings he has saved since his youth are now way too wide for his shriveled legs, and his big manly voice becomes like a child's voice, squeaking and whistling.

original: Last scene of all,   That ends this strange eventful history,   Is second childishness and mere oblivion,   Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.
translation: In the last scene of all, which ends this strange, eventful story, the man enters his second childhood and goes mentally blank—without teeth, without eyes, without taste, without everything.

original: Welcome. Set down your venerable burden, And let him feed.
translation: Welcome. Set down your honorable old burden, and let the old man eat.

original: I thank you most for him.
translation: I thank you very much on his behalf.

original: So had you need.—  I scarce can speak to thank you for myself.
translation: As you need to, for I can barely speak to thank you for myself.

original: Welcome. Fall to. I will not trouble you As yet to question you about your fortunes.— Give us some music, and, good cousin, sing.
translation: Welcome. Start eating. I won't trouble you with questions about your situation yet.  Now give us some music, and, good cousin, sing for us.

original: [sings]   Blow, blow, thou winter wind.     Thou art not so unkind   As man’s ingratitude.
translation: [Singing] Blow, blow, you winter wind. You are not as cruel As man's ingratitude.

original: Thy tooth is not so keen,   Because thou art not seen,   Although thy breath be rude.
translation: Your teeth are not so sharp, For you cannot be seen, Although your breath is harsh.

original: Heigh-ho, sing heigh-ho, unto the green holly.   Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly.   Then heigh-ho, the holly.
translation: Heigh-ho, sing heigh-ho, sing to the green holly. Most friendship is false, most love is only folly. Then heigh-ho, the holly.

original: This life is most jolly.     Freeze, freeze, thou bitter sky,   That dost not bite so nigh   As benefits forgot.
translation: This life is so jolly. Freeze, freeze, you bitter sky, Your bite is not as piercing As when good deeds are forgotten.

original: Though thou the waters warp,   Thy sting is not so sharp   As friend remembered not.
translation: Though you can freeze the waters, Your sting is not as sharp As a friend who is forgotten.

original: Heigh-ho, sing heigh-ho, unto the green holly.   Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly.   Then heigh-ho, the holly.   This life is most jolly.
translation: Heigh-ho, sing heigh-ho, sing to the green holly. Most friendship is false, most love is only folly. Then heigh-ho, the holly. This life is so jolly.

original: If that you were the good Sir Rowland’s son,   As you have whispered faithfully you were,
translation: If you really are the good Sir Rowland's son, as you convincingly whispered that you are—

original: And as mine eye doth his effigies witness   Most truly limned and living in your face,   Be truly welcome hither.
translation: and as I can see his likeness perfectly portrayed and alive in your face—you are truly welcome here.

original: I am the duke   That loved your father. The residue of your fortune   Go to my cave and tell me.—
translation: I am the duke who loved your father. Come to my cave and tell me the rest of what has happened to you.

original: Good old man,   Thou art right welcome as thy master is.
translation: [To ADAM]  Good old man, you are just as welcome as your master is.

original: Support him by the arm. Give me your hand,   And let me all your fortunes understand.
translation: [To ORLANDO]  Support him with your arm. Give me your hand, and explain your situation.

original: Not see him since? Sir, sir, that cannot be.   But were I not the better part made mercy,   I should not seek an absent argument   Of my revenge, thou present.
translation: You haven't seen him since? Sir, sir, that cannot be true. If I weren't so merciful, I would forget about your absent brother and take my revenge on you in his place.

original: But look to it:   Find out thy brother, wheresoe'er he is.
translation: But do this: find your brother, wherever he is.

original: Seek him with candle. Bring him, dead or living,   Within this twelvemonth or turn thou no more   To seek a living in our territory.
translation: Seek him without resting. Bring him to me, dead or alive, within the next year, or else you can give up ever living in my territory again.

original: Thy lands and all things that thou dost call thine   Worth seizure, do we seize into our hands   Till thou canst quit thee by thy brother’s mouth   Of what we think against thee.
translation: Until you find your brother—and he gives some testimony to defend you from my accusations—I am seizing all your lands and possessions of any value.

original: Oh, that your Highness knew my heart in this: I never loved my brother in my life.
translation: Oh, I wish that your Highness knew my true feelings about this. I have never loved my brother in my life.

original: More villain thou.—
translation: Then you are even more of a villain.

original: Well, push him out of doors   And let my officers of such a nature   Make an extent upon his house and lands.
translation: [To the LORDS]  Well, throw him out. And have my officers make an inventory of his house and lands, and take possession of them.

original: Do this expediently, and turn him going.
translation: Do this immediately, and get him going.

original: Hang there, my verse, in witness of my love.   And thou, thrice-crownéd queen of night, survey   With thy chaste eye, from thy pale sphere above,   Thy huntress' name that my full life doth sway.
translation: Hang there on this tree, you verse of my poetry, as a witness for my love.  And you,  goddess  Diana, queen of the night: with your virginal eye from your pale home in the moon above, survey your huntress Rosalind, whose name rules my whole life.

original: O Rosalind, these trees shall be my books,   And in their barks my thoughts I’ll character,   That every eye which in this forest looks   Shall see thy virtue witnessed everywhere.
translation: Oh, Rosalind, these trees will be my books, and I'll write down my thoughts in their bark. That way, everyone who looks around in this forest will see your excellence described everywhere.

original: Run, run, Orlando, carve on every tree   The fair, the chaste, and unexpressive she.
translation: Run, run, Orlando, and on every tree carve verses about the beautiful, the chaste, the indescribable Rosalind.

original: And how like you this shepherd’s life, Master  Touchstone?
translation: And how do you like this shepherd's life, Master Touchstone?

original: Truly, shepherd, in respect of itself, it is a good  life; but in respect that it is a shepherd’s life, it is naught. In respect that it is solitary, I like it very  well; but in respect that it is private, it is a very  vile life.
translation: Truly, shepherd, in itself it is a good life. But considering that it's a shepherd's life, it's worthless. In that it's solitary, I like it very well. But since it's lonely, it's a terrible life.

original: Now in respect it is in the fields, it  pleaseth me well; but in respect it is not in the court, it is tedious.
translation: Because it's in the fields, it pleases me greatly. But because it isn't in the court, it's boring.

original: As it is a spare life, look you, it fits my humor well; but as there is no more plenty in it, it goes much against my stomach. Hast any philosophy in  thee, shepherd?
translation: Because it is a simple life, it suits my nature well. But as there is no plenty in it, it goes against my taste. Are you any kind of philosopher, shepherd?

original: No more but that I know the more one sickens, the worse at ease he is, and that he that wants money, means, and content is without three good friends; that the  property of rain is to wet, and fire to burn;
translation: Only in the fact that I know that the sicker you get, the worse you feel. And that if you lack money, a job, and contentment, then you are without three good friends. And that rain is wet and fire is burning;

original: that good  pasture makes fat sheep; and that a great cause of the  night is lack of the sun; that he that hath learned no  wit by nature nor art may complain of good breeding or  comes of a very dull kindred.
translation: and that good grass makes fat sheep; and that the main cause of night is the lack of sun; and that he who isn't witty by nature or education can complain that he comes from dull parents or lacked a good upbringing.

original: Such a one is a natural philosopher. Wast ever in  court, shepherd?
No, truly.
translation: Honestly, no.

original: Then thou art damned.
translation: Then you are damned.

original: Nay, I hope.
translation: I hope not.

original: Truly, thou art damned, like an ill-roasted egg, all on one side.
translation: Truly, you are damned, like an egg cooked only on one side.

original: For not being at court? Your reason.
translation: Just because I've never been at court? Explain your reasoning.

original: Why, if thou never wast at court, thou never saw’st  good manners;
translation: Why, if you were never at court, then you never saw good manners.

original: if thou never saw’st good manners, then  thy manners must be wicked, and wickedness is sin, and  sin is damnation. Thou art in a parlous state, shepherd.
translation: And so your own manners must be wicked, and wickedness is a sin, and sin is damnation. You are in a perilous state, shepherd.

original: Not a whit, Touchstone. Those that are good manners at the court are as ridiculous in the country as the  behavior of the country is most mockable at the court.
translation: Not at all, Touchstone. What passes for good manners at the court looks just as ridiculous in the country as country behavior is so mockable at the court.

original: You told me you salute not at the court but you kiss your hands. That courtesy would be uncleanly if courtiers  were shepherds.
translation: You told me that you don't greet each other at the court without kissing your hands. If courtiers were shepherds, that kind of courtesy would be vulgar.

original: Instance, briefly. Come, instance.
translation: Give me proof, briefly. Come, give me an example.

original: Why, we are still handling our ewes, and their fells,  you know, are greasy.
translation: Why, because we shepherds are always handling our sheep, and their fleece is greasy, you know.

original: Why, do not your courtier’s hands sweat? And is not the grease of a mutton as wholesome as the sweat of a man?  Shallow, shallow. A better instance, I say. Come.
translation: What, don't courtiers' hands sweat? And isn't the grease of a sheep as good as the sweat of a man? Poor example, poor. Give me better proof, I say. Come on.

original: Besides, our hands are hard.
translation: Besides, our hands are calloused.

original: Your lips will feel them the sooner. Shallow again. A  more sounder instance. Come.
translation: Then your lips will feel them even sooner. Come on, a more sound example.

original: And they are often tarred over with the surgery of our  sheep; and would you have us kiss tar? The courtier’s  hands are perfumed with civet.
translation: And they are often covered with tar from treating the wounds of our sheep. And would you have us kiss tar? Courtiers' hands are expensively perfumed.

original: Most shallow man. Thou worms' meat in respect of a good piece of flesh, indeed. Learn of the wise and perpend:
translation: You most shallow man. Indeed, you are like rotting flesh in the middle of a good steak. Learn from those wiser than you, and consider: the perfume used by courtiers—

original: civet is of a baser birth than tar, the very uncleanly  flux of a cat. Mend the instance, shepherd.
translation: civet—is filthier than tar, as it is made from the unclean secretions of a cat. Improve your proof, shepherd.

original: You have too courtly a wit for me. I’ll rest.
translation: Your wit is too courtly for me. I'll rest my case.

original: Wilt thou rest damned? God help thee, shallow man. God  make incision in thee; thou art raw.
translation: You'll rest while still damned? God help you, you foolish man. I hope that God does some surgery on you; you are sick.

original: Sir, I am a true laborer. I earn that I eat, get that I wear, owe no man hate, envy no man’s happiness, glad of other men’s good,
translation: Sir, I am a true and simple laborer. I earn what I eat and wear; hate no man; envy no man's happiness; am glad of others' good fortune;

original: content with my harm, and the  greatest of my pride is to see my ewes graze and my  lambs suck.
translation: am resigned to my own bad luck; and the greatest source of my pride is to see my ewes graze and my lambs feed.

original: That is another simple sin in you, to bring the ewes  and the rams together and to offer to get your living by the copulation of cattle;
translation: That's another sin you weren't aware of: bringing ewes and rams together and making a living by their copulation.

original: to be bawd to a bellwether  and to betray a she-lamb of a twelvemonth to a  crooked-pated old cuckoldly ram, out of all reasonable  match.
translation: You play the pimp for the year-old ewe, betraying her by forcing her to mate with a crooked-headed, horny old ram. That's totally outside the realm of acceptable pairings.

original: If thou be’st not damned for this, the devil  himself will have no shepherds. I cannot see else how  thou shouldst ’scape.
translation: If you're not damned for this, it must mean that the devil wants no shepherds in hell. I can't see how else you could escape.

original: Here comes young Master Ganymede, my new mistress’s  brother.
translation: Here comes young Master Ganymede.

original: [as Ganymede, reading]   From the east to western Ind,   No jewel is like Rosalind.   Her worth being mounted on the wind,   Through all the world bears Rosalind.
translation: [Reading]   "From the east to the west Indies, No jewel is like Rosalind. Her worth is carried by the wind, Through all the world it bears the name Rosalind.

original: All the pictures fairest lined   Are but black to Rosalind.
translation: All the brightest, most beautiful paintings Are black compared to Rosalind.

original: Let no fair be kept in mind   But the fair of Rosalind.
translation: Don't think of any beauty But the beauty of Rosalind."

original: I’ll rhyme you so eight years together, dinners and  suppers and sleeping hours excepted. It is the right  butter-women’s rank to market.
translation: I could rhyme like that for eight years straight, taking breaks only to eat and sleep. The verses plod on monotonously like dairy women marching off to the market.

original: Out, fool.
translation: That's enough, fool.

original: For a taste:   If a hart do lack a hind,   Let him seek out Rosalind.
translation: Here's a taste: If a buck should need a  hind , let him seek out Rosalind.

original: If the cat will after kind,   So, be sure, will Rosalind.   Winter garments must be lined,   So must slender Rosalind.
translation: If a cat should look for a mate in kind, certainly also will Rosalind. Winter garments must be lined, and so must skinny Rosalind.

original: They that reap must sheaf and bind,   Then to cart with Rosalind.   Sweetest nut hath sourest rind;
translation: Those who harvest must sheaf and bind, then throw on the market cart ripe Rosalind. The sweetest nut has the sourest rind,

original: Such a nut is Rosalind.   He that sweetest rose will find   Must find love’s prick, and Rosalind.   This is the very false gallop of verses. Why do you  infect yourself with them?
translation: and such a nut is Rosalind. He who the sweetest rose will find, will also find love's thorn, and Rosalind. This is the way those verses gallop unevenly along. Why infect yourself by listening to them?

original: Peace, you dull fool. I found them on a tree.
translation: Quiet, you dull fool. I found them attached a tree.

original: Truly, the tree yields bad fruit.
translation: Honestly, that tree yields rotten fruit.

original: I’ll graft it with you, and then I shall graft it with  a medlar. Then it will be the earliest fruit i' th'  country, for you’ll be rotten ere you be half ripe, and  that’s the right virtue of the medlar.
translation: I'll graft you onto that tree, which will be grafting it with a medlar. The fruit the tree bears will then be the earliest ripe fruit in the country, for you'll be rotten before you're half-ripe, which is the way medlars should be.

original: You have said, but whether wisely or no, let the  forest judge.
translation: You've had your say now, but let the forest judge whether your words are wise or not.

original: Peace. Here comes my sister reading. Stand aside.
translation: Quiet. Here comes my cousin, reading something. Step aside.

original: [as Aliena, reads]   Why should this a desert be?   For it is unpeopled? No.   Tongues I’ll hang on every tree   That shall civil sayings show.
translation: [Reading] Why should this place be a desert? Because it is uninhabited? No. I'll hang poems on every tree that will portray the comments of a city.

original: Some how brief the life of man   Runs his erring pilgrimage,   That the stretching of a span   Buckles in his sum of age;
translation: Some will be on how brief life is— Which man spends in wandering pilgrimage— So that the width of an open hand contains his entire lifetime.

original: Some of violated vows   'Twixt the souls of friend and friend.   But upon the fairest boughs,   Or at every sentence end,   Will I “Rosalinda” write,
translation: Some will be about broken promises Between the souls of friends. But on the most beautiful branches, Or at the end of every sentence, I'll write "Rosalinda,"

original: Teaching all that read to know   The quintessence of every sprite   Heaven would in little show.
translation: Teaching everyone who can read to know That the purest essence of every spirit Has been contained within this one person.

original: Therefore heaven nature charged   That one body should be filled   With all graces wide-enlarged.
translation: Heaven commanded Nature To fill her one body With all the graces usually spread through all women.

original: Nature presently distilled   Helen’s cheek, but not her heart,   Cleopatra’s majesty,   Atalanta’s better part,   Sad Lucretia’s modesty.
translation: Nature then distilled together Helen of Troy 's beautiful face, without her treacherous heart, Cleopatra's majesty, The best parts of Atalanta, And solemn Lucretia's modesty.

original: Thus Rosalind of many parts   By heavenly synod was devised,   Of many faces, eyes, and hearts   To have the touches dearest prized.
translation: In this way Rosalind was composed of many parts— By the decree of heaven— That of the many faces, eyes, and hearts, She might have only the most prized features of all.

original: Heaven would that she these gifts should have   And I to live and die her slave.
translation: Heaven wanted her to have these gifts, And wanted me to live and die as her slave.

original: O most gentle Jupiter, what tedious homily of love have you wearied your parishioners withal, and never cried,  “Have patience, good people.”
translation: Oh, most noble Jupiter, what a tedious sermon of love you have been wearying your congregation with! You should have warned them, "Have patience, good people."

original: How now?—Back, friends.—Shepherd, go off a  little.—Go with him, sirrah.
translation: What now? Move back, my friends.  Shepherd, go off a little ways. [To TOUCHSTONE] Go with him, sir.

original: Come, shepherd, let us make an honorable retreat,  though not with bag and baggage, yet with scrip and  scrippage.
translation: Come, shepherd. Let us make an honorable retreat, though not like an army with its equipment, but rather like a shepherd with his pouch and what he keeps in it.

original: Didst thou hear these verses?
translation: Did you hear those verses?

original: Oh, yes, I heard them all, and more too, for some of  them had in them more feet than the verses would bear.
That’s no matter. The feet might bear the verses.
translation: That's no matter. The feet can bear the verses.

original: Ay, but the feet were lame and could not bear  themselves without the verse, and therefore stood lamely in the verse.
translation: Yes, but the feet were lame and couldn't carry themselves without the verses, and therefore stood badly within the verse.

original: But didst thou hear without wondering how thy name  should be hanged and carved upon these trees?
translation: But did you hear all that without wondering why your name should be written and hung upon all these trees?

original: I was seven of the nine days out of the wonder before  you came, for look here what I found on a palm tree.
translation: I was almost through with my time of wonder when you arrived, for look here what I found on a palm tree.

original: I  was never so berhymed since Pythagoras' time, that I was an Irish rat, which I can hardly remember.
translation: I haven't been rhymed about this since my past life as an  Irish rat , which I can hardly remember.

original: Trow you who hath done this?
translation: Do you know who has written these?

original: Is it a man?
translation: Is it a man?

original: And a chain, that you once wore, about his neck. Change you color?
translation: A man who has a chain, which you once wore, hanging around his neck. Do you blush?

original: I prithee, who?
translation: Please, who is he?

original: O Lord, Lord, it is a hard matter for friends to meet,  but mountains may be removed with earthquakes and so  encounter.
Nay, but who is it?
translation: No, who is it?

original: Is it possible?
translation: Is it possible?

original: Nay, I prithee now, with most petitionary vehemence,  tell me who it is.
translation: Please, I'm begging you now most sincerely, tell me who it is.

original: O wonderful, wonderful, and most wonderful wonderful,  and yet again wonderful, and after that, out of all  whooping!
translation: Oh this is wonderful, wonderful, and most wondrously wonderful, and another wonderful, and after that, wonderful beyond measure!

original: Good my complexion, dost thou think though I am  caparisoned like a man, I have a doublet and hose in my  disposition? One inch of delay more is a South Sea of  discovery.
translation: Good grief, do you think that because I am dressed like a man, I also have a man's patience? One more second of delay is as endless to me as a journey exploring the South Seas.

original: I prithee, tell me who is it quickly, and  speak apace. I would thou couldst stammer, that thou  might’st pour this concealed man out of thy mouth as  wine comes out of a narrow-mouthed bottle—
translation: Please, tell me who it is quickly, and speak fast. I wish you could stammer this hidden man out of your mouth like wine flowing from a narrow-necked bottle—

original: either too  much at once, or none at all. I prithee take the cork  out of thy mouth, that I may drink thy tidings.
translation: either too much at once, or none at all. I beg you, take the cork out of your mouth, that I might drink up your news.

original: So you may put a man in your belly.
Is he of God’s making? What manner of man? Is his head  worth a hat or his chin worth a beard?
translation: Is he a real, flesh-and-blood man? What kind of man is he? Is he enough of a man to wear a hat on his head and grow a beard on his chin?

original: Nay, he hath but a little beard.
translation: No, he has only a little beard.

original: Why, God will send more, if the man will be thankful.  Let me stay the growth of his beard, if thou delay me  not the knowledge of his chin.
translation: Well, God will send him a bigger beard, if the man is thankful. I'll wait for his beard to grow, if you will stop delaying in telling me what chin that beard grows on.

original: It is young Orlando, that tripped up the wrestler’s  heels and your heart both in an instant.
translation: It is young Orlando, who conquered both the wrestler and your heart in the same moment.

original: Nay, but the devil take mocking. Speak sad brow and  true maid.
translation: No—curse you if you're mocking me. Speak seriously and truthfully.

original: I' faith, coz, ’tis he.
translation: I promise, cousin, it's him.

original: Orlando?
translation: Orlando?

original: Orlando.
translation: Orlando.

original: Alas the day, what shall I do with my doublet and  hose? What did he when thou saw’st him? What said he?  How looked he?
translation: Oh no, what will I do with my man's outfit? What did he do when you saw him? What did he say? How did he look?

original: Wherein went he? What makes him here? Did he ask for me? Where remains he? How parted he with  thee? And when shalt thou see him again? Answer me in  one word.
translation: What did he wear? What brings him here? Did he ask for me? Where is he staying? How did he say goodbye to you? And when will you see him again? Answer me in one word.

original: You must borrow me Gargantua’s mouth first. 'Tis a  word too great for any mouth of this age’s size. To say  ay and no to these particulars is more than to answer in a catechism.
But doth he know that I am in this forest and in man’s  apparel? Looks he as freshly as he did the day he  wrestled?
