translation: But does he know that I am here in this forest and dressed like a man? Does he look as healthy as he did the day he wrestled?

original: It is as easy to count atomies as to resolve the  propositions of a lover. But take a taste of my finding  him, and relish it with good observance. I found him  under a tree like a dropped acorn.
translation: It's easier to count dust particles than to answer a lover's many questions. But have a taste of my story, and add sauce to it by paying attention. I found Orlando under a tree, like a dropped acorn.

original: It may well be called Jove’s tree when it drops forth  such fruit.
translation: The oak is truly Jove's tree, as it drops such divine fruit.

original: Give me audience, good madam.
translation: Let me speak, good madam.

original: Proceed.
translation: Continue.

original: There lay he, stretched along like a wounded knight.
translation: There he lay, stretched out like a wounded knight.

original: Though it be pity to see such a sight, it well becomes the ground.
translation: Though it would be sad to see such a sight, he must have made even the ground beneath him look better.

original: Cry “holla” to thy tongue, I prithee. It curvets  unseasonably. He was furnished like a hunter.
translation: Tell your tongue to halt, please. It's leaping around out of turn. He was dressed like a hunter.

original: Oh, ominous! He comes to kill my heart.
translation: Oh, how ominous! He comes to kill my heart.

original: I would sing my song without a burden. Thou bring’st  me out of tune.
translation: I would like to sing my song solo. You throw me off key.

original: Do you not know I am a woman? When I think, I must  speak. Sweet, say on.
translation: Don't you know that I am a woman? When I think, I must speak. Now go on, sweet one.

original: You bring me out. Soft, comes he not here?
translation: You've made me forget the tune. But quiet, isn't he coming here now?

original: 'Tis he. Slink by, and note him.
translation: It's him. Let's sneak away and watch him.

original: I thank you for your company, but, good faith, I had as lief have been myself alone.
translation: I thank you for your company. But, really, I would just as soon be alone.

original: And so had I, but yet, for fashion sake, I thank you  too for your society.
translation: And the same with me. But still, for appearances' sake, I'll thank you also for your company.

original: God be wi' you. Let’s meet as little as we can.
translation: God be with you. Let's meet as infrequently as we can.

original: I do desire we may be better strangers.
translation: I too hope that we can be better strangers.

original: I pray you mar no more trees with writing love songs in their barks.
translation: Please don't wound any more trees by carving love poems in their bark.

original: I pray you mar no more of my verses with reading them  ill- favoredly.
translation: Please don't wound any more of my verses by reading them so badly.

original: Rosalind is your love’s name?
translation: Your love's name is Rosalind?

original: Yes, just.
translation: Yes, that's right.

original: I do not like her name.
translation: I do not like her name.

original: There was no thought of pleasing you when she was  christened.
translation: No one thought about pleasing you when she was named.

original: What stature is she of?
translation: How tall is she?

original: Just as high as my heart.
translation: Just as tall as my heart.

original: You are full of pretty answers. Have you not been  acquainted with goldsmiths' wives and conned them out of rings?
translation: You are full of pretty answers. Are you friends with goldsmith's wives from whom you've stolen their rings, memorizing the love mottoes engraved on them?

original: Not so. But I answer you right painted cloth, from  whence you have studied your questions.
translation: No, but I can answer you with the stock sayings of painted wall hangings, which is where you must have learned all these questions you're asking.

original: You have a nimble wit. I think ’twas made of Atalanta’s heels. Will you sit down with me? And we two will rail  against our mistress the world and all our misery.
I will chide no breather in the world but myself,  against whom I know most faults.
translation: I won't blame any living thing in this world except myself, whose faults I know best.

original: The worst fault you have is to be in love.
translation: Your worst fault is being in love.

original: 'Tis a fault I will not change for your best virtue. I  am weary of you.
translation: It's a fault I wouldn't trade for your best virtue. I'm tired of you.

original: By my troth, I was seeking for a fool when I found you.
translation: I swear, I was looking for a fool when I found you, and I seem to have been successful.

original: He is drowned in the brook. Look but in, and you shall  see him.
translation: Your fool drowned in the brook. Just look in, and you'll see him.

original: There I shall see mine own figure.
translation: There I will only see myself.

original: Which I take to be either a fool or a cipher.
translation: Who must then be either a fool or a nothing.

original: I’ll tarry no longer with you. Farewell, good Signior  Love.
translation: I won't waste my time with you any more. Farewell, good Mister Love.

original: I am glad of your departure. Adieu, good Monsieur Melancholy.
translation: I am glad to see you leave. Farewell, good Mister Gloom.

original: I will speak to him like a saucy  lackey, and under that habit play the knave with him.—Do you hear, forester?
translation: I will speak to him as if I'm an insolent servant, and in that disguise I can trick him. [To ORLANDO] Can you hear me, forest-dweller?

original: Very well. What would you?
translation: Very well. What do you want?

original: [As Ganymede)  I pray you, what is ’t o'clock?
translation: Please, what time does the clock say?

original: You should ask me what time o' day. There’s no clock  in the forest.
translation: You should ask me what time of day it is instead. There's no clock in the forest.

original: Then there is no true lover in the forest, else sighing every minute and groaning every hour would detect the  lazy foot of time as well as a clock.
translation: Then there is no true lover in the forest either, for they are as regular as a clock— their sighing every minute and groaning every hour would easily mark the lazy progress of time.

original: And why not the swift foot of time? Had not that been  as proper?
translation: Why do you say the "lazy progress" and not the "swift progress" of time? Wouldn't that have been just as accurate?

original: By no means, sir. Time travels in diverse paces with  diverse persons. I’ll tell you who time ambles withal,  who time trots withal, who time gallops withal, and who  he stands still withal.
translation: By no means, sir. Time travels at different speeds for different people. I can tell you who time strolls with, who time trots with, who time gallops with, and who time stands still for.

original: I prithee, who doth he trot withal?
translation: Please, who does time trot with?

original: Marry, he trots hard with a young maid between the  contract of her marriage and the day it is solemnized.
translation: Well, it trots painfully for a young maid between her engagement and the day she gets married.

original: If the interim be but a se'nnight, time’s pace is so hard that it seems the length of seven year.
translation: This time period might be only seven days, but time's pace is so torturous that it seems like seven years.

original: Who ambles time withal?
translation: And who does time stroll with?

original: With a priest that lacks Latin and a rich man that hath not the gout, for the one sleeps easily because he  cannot study and the other lives merrily because he  feels no pain—
translation: With a priest who doesn't know Latin and a rich man who doesn't have gout—for the one sleeps easily because he can't stay up late studying, and the other lives merrily because he isn't in pain.

original: the one lacking the burden of lean and  wasteful learning, the other knowing no burden of heavy  tedious penury. These time ambles withal.
translation: One lacks the burden of hard, exhausting study, and the other doesn't have the burden of heavy, tedious poverty. Time ambles along for both of these.

original: Who doth he gallop withal?
translation: And who does it gallop with?

original: With a thief to the gallows, for though he go as softly as foot can fall, he thinks himself too soon there.
translation: With a thief on his way to the gallows. He walks as slowly as he possibly can, but he still gets there too soon.

original: Who stays it still withal?
translation: And who does time stand still for?

original: With lawyers in the vacation, for they sleep between  term and term, and then they perceive not how time  moves.
translation: For lawyers on vacation, because they sleep between court session and court session, and so have no perception of how time moves.

original: Where dwell you, pretty youth?
translation: Where do you live, clever youth?

original: With this shepherdess, my sister, here in the skirts  of the forest like fringe upon a petticoat.
translation: With this shepherdess, my sister, here in the outskirts of the forest, which is like fringe on a petticoat.

original: Are you native of this place?
translation: Were you born in this place?

original: As the cony that you see dwell where she is kindled.
translation: I am as much a native here as the rabbit you see, who lives where she is born.

original: Your accent is something finer than you could purchase in so removed a dwelling.
translation: Your accent is more refined than the one usually acquired in such a remote place.

original: I have been told so of many. But indeed an old  religious uncle of mine taught me to speak, who was in  his youth an inland man, one that knew courtship too  well, for there he fell in love.
translation: Many people have told me this. But actually an old religious uncle of mine taught me how to speak, and he was a city-dweller in his youth—one who knew both courtliness and courtship too well, for he fell in love in the city.

original: I have heard him read  many lectures against it, and I thank God I am not a  woman, to be touched with so many giddy offenses as he  hath generally taxed their whole sex withal.
translation: I have since heard him read many lectures condemning falling in love. And I thank God that I'm not a woman, to be corrupted by the many faults of giddiness that trouble that entire sex.

original: Can you remember any of the principal evils that he  laid to the charge of women?
translation: Can you remember any of the greatest evils your uncle ascribed to women?

original: There were none principal. They were all like one  another as half-pence are, every one fault seeming  monstrous till his fellow fault came to match it.
translation: There were no greatest ones. They were all as similar as one halfpenny to another, with each fault seeming the most monstrous until the next fault came along to match it.

original: I prithee, recount some of them.
translation: Please, tell me some of them.

original: No, I will not cast away my physic but on those that  are sick. There is a man haunts the forest that abuses  our young plants with carving “Rosalind” on their barks, hangs odes upon hawthorns and elegies on brambles,
translation: No, I won't give away my medicine except to those who are sick. There is a man haunting this forest who abuses our young trees by carving "Rosalind" in their bark. He hangs odes on the hawthorns and elegies on the brambles,

original: all, forsooth, deifying the name of Rosalind. If I could  meet that fancy-monger I would give him some good  counsel, for he seems to have the quotidian of love upon him.
translation: and every single one of those poems—I'm being honest here—worships the name of "Rosalind." If I could meet this man—whose business seems to be advertising love—I would give him some good advice, for he seems to have the constant fever of love upon him.

original: I am he that is so love-shaked. I pray you tell me your remedy.
translation: I am that man, the one who is so shaken by love. Please tell me about your medicine.

original: There is none of my uncle’s marks upon you. He taught  me how to know a man in love, in which cage of rushes I  am sure you are not prisoner.
translation: But you don't have any of the symptoms my uncle described. He taught me how to recognize a man in love, and I am sure that you aren't a prisoner of that flimsy cage.

original: What were his marks?
translation: What were the symptoms he described?

original: A lean cheek, which you have not; a blue eye and  sunken, which you have not; an unquestionable spirit,  which you have not; a beard neglected, which you have  not—
translation: A thin face, which you don't have; dark circles under the eyes from sleeplessness, which you don't have; a neglected beard, which you don't have—

original: but I pardon you for that, for simply your having in beard is a younger brother’s revenue. Then your hose  should be ungartered, your bonnet unbanded, your sleeve  unbuttoned, your shoe untied, and everything about you  demonstrating a careless desolation.
translation: but I can forgive you for that, since you are young  and barely have a beard anyway. Your stockings should be falling down; your hat missing its band; your sleeves unbuttoned; your shoes untied; and everything about you demonstrating carelessness and anguish.

original: But you are no such man. You are rather point-device in your accouterments, as loving yourself than seeming the lover of any other.
translation: But you are no such man as this. You are perfect in your dress, like someone who loves himself more than anyone else.

original: Fair youth, I would I could make thee believe I love.
translation: Handsome youth, I wish I could make you believe that I'm in love.

original: Me believe it? You may as soon make her that you love  believe it, which I warrant she is apter to do than to  confess she does.
translation: Make me believe it? You might as well make the one you love believe it, which I suspect she's more likely to  do  than to  admit  to doing.

original: That is one of the points in the which women still give the lie to their consciences. But, in  good sooth, are you he that hangs the verses on the  trees wherein Rosalind is so admired?
translation: That is one of the ways in which women contradict what they know to be true in their hearts. But truly, are you the man who hangs those love poems to Rosalind on the trees?

original: I swear to thee, youth, by the white hand of Rosalind, I am that he, that unfortunate he.
translation: I swear to you by Rosalind's fair hand, young man: I am that unfortunate man.

original: But are you so much in love as your rhymes speak?
translation: But are you really as in love as your poems say you are?

original: Neither rhyme nor reason can express how much.
translation: Neither rhyme nor reason can express how in love I am.

original: Love is merely a madness and, I tell you, deserves as  well a dark house and a whip as madmen do,
translation: Love is merely insanity, I tell you. And lovers deserve the  madhouse  just like insane people do.

original: and the  reason why they are not so punished and cured is that  the lunacy is so ordinary that the whippers are in love, too. Yet I profess curing it by counsel.
translation: The only reason they don't get the punishment and cure of the madhouse is that this form of insanity is so common that all the doctors have it too. But I claim that it can be cured with counseling.

original: Did you ever cure any so?
translation: Have you ever cured anyone in this way?

original: Yes, one, and in this manner. He was to imagine me his love, his mistress, and I set him every day to woo me;  at which time would I, being but a moonish youth,  grieve, be effeminate, changeable, longing and liking,  proud, fantastical, apish, shallow, inconstant, full of  tears, full of smiles;
translation: Yes, one, and here's how I did it: I had him imagine  me  as the woman he loved, and I made him woo me every day. When he did I—being but a fickle youth—would mope; act effeminate; shift my moods; long for him; like him; act proud and distant; be irrational; be foolishly mocking; shallow; inconstant; full of tears; full of smiles;

original: for every passion something, and  for no passion truly anything, as boys and women are,  for the most part, cattle of this color; would now like  him, now loathe him; then entertain him, then forswear  him;
translation: be passionate about everything, and then passionate about nothing—as most young boys and women naturally act. I would like him one minute and hate him the next; accompany him and then send him away;

original: now weep for him, then spit at him, that I drave my suitor from his mad humor of love to a living humor of  madness, which was to forswear the full stream of the  world and to live in a nook merely monastic.
translation: cry for him and then spit at him, until finally I drove out the whim of love and replaced it with the truer state of anger. My suitor then turned away from the flow of life, abandoning the world and hiding himself away as a monk.

original: And thus I  cured him, and this way will I take upon me to wash your liver as clean as a sound sheep’s heart, that there  shall not be one spot of love in ’t.
translation: And so I cured him, and in this way I will cure you too—washing your  liver  as clean as a healthy sheep's heart, until there isn't a single spot of love left in it.

original: I would not be cured, youth.
translation: I don't want to be cured, youth.

original: I would cure you if you would but call me Rosalind and  come every day to my cote and woo me.
translation: I could cure you, though, if you would only call me "Rosalind" and come to my cottage every day to woo me.

original: Now, by the faith of my love, I will. Tell me where it  is.
translation: By the strength of my love, I will then. Tell me where it is.

original: Go with me to it, and I’ll show it you; and by the way you shall tell me where in the forest you live. Will  you go?
translation: Come with me to it, and I'll show you. Along the way you can tell me where in the forest you live. Will you go with me?

original: With all my heart, good youth.
translation: With all my heart, good youth.

original: Nay, you must call me Rosalind.—Come, sister, will you  go?
translation: No, you must call me Rosalind now.  Sister, will you come with us?

original: Come apace, good Audrey. I will fetch up your goats,  Audrey. And how, Audrey? Am I the man yet? Doth my  simple feature content you?
translation: Come along, good Audrey. I will fetch your goats for you, Audrey. And now, Audrey? Am I the man for you? Do the features of my simple appearance please you?

original: Your features, Lord warrant us! What features?
translation: Your features, God protect us! What features?

original: I am here with thee and thy goats, as the most  capricious poet, honest Ovid, was among the Goths.
O knowledge ill-inhabited, worse than Jove in a thatched house.
translation: Oh, knowledge existing in someone as unworthy as this fool is worse than the king of the gods living in a thatched hut.

original: When a man’s verses cannot be understood nor a man’s  good wit seconded with the forward child, understanding,
translation: When a man's verses can't be understood and his good jokes aren't acknowledged or appreciated,

original: it strikes a man more dead than a great reckoning in a  little room. Truly, I would the gods had made thee  poetical.
translation: it's worse than getting a large bill for renting a little room. Truly, I wish the gods had made you more poetical, Audrey.

original: I do not know what “poetical” is. Is it honest in deed  and word? Is it a true thing?
translation: I don't know what "poetical" means. Does it mean honest in word and deed? Does it mean being truthful?

original: No, truly, for the truest poetry is the most feigning, and lovers are given to poetry, and what they swear in  poetry may be said as lovers they do feign.
translation: No, truly, for the truest poetry is the most imaginative and deceptive. Lovers are inclined towards poetry, and what they promise to be true in their poems is often a lie in real life.

original: Do you wish then that the gods had made me poetical?
translation: Do you still wish that the gods had made me poetical, then?

original: I do, truly, for thou swear’st to me thou art honest.  Now, if thou wert a poet, I might have some hope thou  didst feign.
translation: I do, truly. For you swore to me that you were a virgin, and if you were a poet, I might have some hope that you were lying.

original: Would you not have me honest?
translation: What, you don't want me to be chaste?

original: No, truly, unless thou wert hard-favored, for honesty  coupled to beauty is to have honey a sauce to sugar.
translation: No, truly, not unless you were ugly. For chastity alongside beauty in one woman is like sweetening sugar with honey.

original: A material fool.
translation: A fool with good sense.

original: Well, I am not fair, and therefore I pray the gods make me honest.
translation: Well, I am not beautiful, so I pray that the gods will at least keep me chaste.

original: Truly, and to cast away honesty upon a foul slut were  to put good meat into an unclean dish.
translation: Yes, but to waste chastity on an ugly slut is like putting good meat into a dirty dish.

original: I am not a slut, though I thank the gods I am foul.
translation: I am not a slut, though I thank the gods that I am ugly.

original: Well, praised be the gods for thy foulness;  sluttishness may come hereafter. But be it as it may be, I will marry thee;
translation: Well, may the gods be praised for your ugliness then. Maybe sluttishness will come later. But be that as it may, I will marry you.

original: and to that end I have been with Sir Oliver Martext, the vicar of the next village, who hath promised to meet me in this place of the forest and to  couple us.
translation: To that end, I have spoken to Sir Oliver Martext, the priest from the nearby village, and he has promised to meet us in this part of the forest and marry us.

original: I would fain see this meeting.
translation: I'd love to see this.

original: Well, the gods give us joy.
translation: Well, may the gods bless our marriage.

original: Amen. A man may, if he were of a fearful heart, stagger in this attempt, for here we have no temple but the  wood, no assembly but horn-beasts. But what though?  Courage. As horns are odious, they are necessary.
translation: Amen. Another man, if he had a fearful heart, might falter at this point—for this forest isn't a real temple, and there is no audience here but  horned beasts.  But who cares? Horns are hateful, but they are necessary.

original: It is  said, “Many a man knows no end of his goods.” Right:  many a man has good horns and knows no end of  them. Well, that is the dowry of his wife; ’tis none of  his own getting. Horns?
translation: It is said, "Many men are so wealthy that they don't even know how much they own." I agree: many men have good horns, and don't even know how big they are. Well, that is what the wife brings to the marriage; the man has nothing to do with getting his horns or his children. Horns?

original: Even so. Poor men alone? No, no. The noblest deer hath them as huge as the rascal. Is  the single man therefore blessed? No.
translation: There they are. Are they only for poor men? No, no. The noblest deer's horns are as huge as those of the inferior deer. Is the single man the luckiest, then? No.

original: As a walled town  is more worthier than a village, so is the forehead of a married man more honorable than the bare brow of a  bachelor. And by how much defense is better than no  skill, by so much is a horn more precious than to want.
translation: As a town protected by a wall is worth more than a small village, so is a married man's horned forehead more honorable than a bachelor's bare forehead. Just as it's better to be skilled at defending oneself than to be defenseless, so is a horn more precious than no horn at all.

original: Here comes Sir Oliver.—Sir Oliver Martext, you are well met. Will you dispatch us here under this tree, or  shall we go with you to your chapel?
translation: Here comes Sir Oliver.  Sir Oliver Martext, I'm glad to see you. Will you finish our business here under this tree, or should we go with you to your chapel?

original: Is there none here to give the woman?
translation: Is there no one here to give the bride away?

original: I will not take her on gift of any man.
translation: I won't take her as a secondhand gift from another man.

original: Truly, she must be given, or the marriage is not  lawful.
translation: Truly, someone has to give her away, or the marriage isn't legal.

original: Proceed, proceed. I’ll give her.
translation: Continue, continue. I'll give her away.

original: Good even, good Monsieur What-ye-call’t. How do you,  sir? You are very well met. God 'ild you for your last  company. I am very glad to see you. Even a toy in hand  here, sir. Nay, pray be covered.
translation: Good evening, good Mister What's-his-name. How do you do, sir? I am very glad to see you. May God reward you for being here right now. I am very glad to see you. This is just an unimportant matter here, sir. No, please keep your hat on.

original: Will you be married, motley?
translation: Do you want to get married, fool?

original: As the ox hath his bow, sir, the horse his curb, and  the falcon her bells, so man hath his desires; and as  pigeons bill, so wedlock would be nibbling.
translation: As the ox has his yoke, the horse his bridle, and the falcon her tether, so a man has his desires, which must be restrained somehow

original: And will you, being a man of your breeding, be married  under a bush like a beggar? Get you to church, and have  a good priest that can tell you what marriage is.
translation: But will you—as a man of your breeding—get married like a beggar under a bush, by an uneducated priest? Get yourself to a church and have a proper priest teach you the obligations of marriage.

original: This  fellow will but join you together as they join wainscot. Then one of you will prove a shrunk panel and, like  green timber, warp, warp.
translation: This fellow here will just set you two alongside each other like two pieces of paneling. Then one of you will warp like green wood, and you will both be out of alignment.

original: I am not in the mind but I were better to be  married of him than of another, for he is not like to  marry me well, and not being well married, it will be a  good excuse for me hereafter to leave my wife.
translation: I think I'd rather have this fellow marry us than any other, for he isn't likely to marry us properly. And if we're not married properly, then I'll have a good excuse to leave my wife later on.

original: Go thou with me, and let me counsel thee.
translation: Come with me, and let me advise you.

original: Come, sweet Audrey.   We must be married, or we must live in bawdry.—
translation: Come, sweet Audrey. We must be married, or else live in sin.

original: Farewell, good Master Oliver, not
translation: [To SIR OLIVER MARTEXT]  Farewell, good Master Oliver. We're not singing that song:

original: O sweet Oliver,   O brave Oliver,
translation: Oh sweet Oliver, Oh brave Oliver,

original: Leave me not behind thee     But   Wind away,
translation: Don't leave me behind, But Wind, go away,

original: Begone, I say,   I will not to wedding with thee.
translation: Go away, I say, For it's not you I'm marrying.

original: 'Tis no matter. Ne'er a fantastical knave of them all  shall flout me out of my calling.
translation: It doesn't matter to me. None of these crazy fools will ever convince me to abandon my position.

original: Never talk to me. I will weep.
translation: Don't talk to me. I'll cry.

original: Do, I prithee, but yet have the grace to consider that  tears do not become a man.
translation: Go ahead and cry, but at least consider that tears aren't proper for a man.

original: But have I not cause to weep?
translation: But don't I have good reason to cry?

original: As good cause as one would desire. Therefore weep.
translation: As good a reason as you could want. So go on and cry.

original: His very hair is of the dissembling color.
Something browner than Judas’s. Marry, his kisses are Judas’s own children.
translation: It's a bit browner than Judas'. Although, indeed, his kisses are betrayals, like Judas's kisses were.

original: I' faith, his hair is of a good color.
translation: Honestly, his hair is a good color.

original: An excellent color. Your chestnut was ever the only  color.
translation: It is an excellent color. Chestnut is always the best color.

original: And his kissing is as full of sanctity as the touch of  holy bread.
translation: And his kisses are as holy as Communion bread.

original: He hath bought a pair of cast lips of Diana. A nun of  winter’s sisterhood kisses not more religiously. The  very ice of chastity is in them.
But why did he swear he would come this morning, and  comes not?
translation: But why would he swear to come this morning, and then not come?

original: Nay, certainly, there is no truth in him.
translation: Well, certainly, he must be a complete liar.

original: Do you think so?
translation: Do you think so?

original: Yes, I think he is not a pick-purse nor a  horse-stealer, but for his verity in love, I do think  him as concave as a covered goblet or a worm-eaten nut.
translation: Yes. He's not a pickpocket or a horse-thief, but when it comes to honesty in love, I think he's as hollow as a covered cup or a worm-eaten nut.

original: Not true in love?
translation: You think his love isn't true?

original: Yes, when he is in, but I think he is not in.
translation: I think his love is true when he is in love, but I think he's not in love right now.

original: You have heard him swear downright he was.
translation: But you've heard him swear outright that he was.

original: “Was” is not “is.” Besides, the oath of a lover is no  stronger than the word of a tapster.
translation: "Was" is not "is." He may have been in love, but he isn't anymore. Besides, the promises of a lover are no better than those of a swindling bartender:

original: They are both the  confirmer of false reckonings. He attends here in the  forest on the duke your father.
translation: they both swear to their false accounts. Orlando is now staying in the forest and serving the duke your father.

original: I met the duke yesterday and had much question with  him. He asked me of what parentage I was. I told him, of as good as he.
translation: I met my father yesterday, and he had many questions for me. He asked me what rank my parents were, and I told him that they were as good as he is.

original: So he laughed and let me go. But what  talk we of fathers when there is such a man as Orlando?
translation: He laughed at that, and let me go. But why are we talking about fathers, when such a man as Orlando exists?

original: Oh, that’s a brave man. He writes brave verses, speaks brave words, swears brave oaths, and breaks them  bravely, quite traverse, athwart the heart of his lover,
translation: Oh, he's a brave man indeed. He writes brave verses, speaks brave words, makes brave promises—and then bravely breaks them. He's like a bad jouster when it comes to his lover's heart—

original: as a puny tilter that spurs his horse but on one side  breaks his staff like a noble goose; but all’s brave  that youth mounts and folly guides.
translation: he strikes sideways instead of head-on, and breaks his lance like a noble fool. But everything a young man does is brave, when he's mounted on his youth and guided by his folly.

original: Who comes here?
translation: Who's that coming?

original: Mistress and master, you have oft inquired   After the shepherd that complained of love,
translation: Mistress and master, you have often asked me about that lovestruck shepherd,

original: Who you saw sitting by me on the turf,   Praising the proud disdainful shepherdess   That was his mistress.
translation: whom you once saw sitting at my side and praising the proud, disdainful shepherdess with whom he was in love.

original: Well, and what of him?
translation: Well, what about him?

original: If you will see a pageant truly played   Between the pale complexion of true love   And the red glow of scorn and proud disdain,
translation: If you would like to see a performance being played out between someone who is pale with true, unrequited love, and someone red with scorn and proud disdain,

original: Go hence a little, and I shall conduct you,   If you will mark it.
translation: then come with me a little ways and you can watch.

original: O, come, let us remove. The sight of lovers feedeth those in love.     Bring us to this sight, and you shall say I’ll prove a busy actor in their play.
translation: Oh, come, let's go. The sight of lovers is nourishment to those already in love. [To CORIN] Bring us to this scene, and you'll see me take a part in their play.

original: Sweet Phoebe, do not scorn me. Do not, Phoebe.   Say that you love me not, but say not so   In bitterness.
translation: Sweet Phoebe, don't scorn me. Do not, Phoebe. You can tell me you don't love me, but don't do it so bitterly.

original: The common executioner,   Whose heart th' accustomed sight of death makes hard,   Falls not the axe upon the humbled neck   But first begs pardon.
translation: Even the executioner—whose heart has grown hard from seeing so much death—still begs his victim's pardon before he lets his axe fall.

original: Will you sterner be   Than he that dies and lives by bloody drops?
translation: Will you be even crueler than someone who makes his living through blood and killing?

original: I would not be thy executioner.   I fly thee, for I would not injure thee.   Thou tell’st me there is murder in mine eye.
translation: I don't want to be your executioner. I avoid you so that I won't hurt you. You tell me there is murder in my eyes.

original: 'Tis pretty, sure, and very probable   That eyes, that are the frail’st and softest things,   Who shut their coward gates on atomies,   Should be called tyrants, butchers, murderers.
translation: That's a pretty phrase, sure, and very  probable  that eyes—which are the frailest, softest things, and so cowardly that they shut their lids even to something as harmless as dust—should be tyrants, butchers, and murderers.

original: Now I do frown on thee with all my heart,   And if mine eyes can wound, now let them kill thee.   Now counterfeit to swoon, why, now fall down;
translation: Now I'm frowning at you with all my strength. And if my eyes really can wound, then let them kill you. Now go ahead, pretend to faint, go fall down—

original: Or if thou canst not, Oh, for shame, for shame,   Lie not, to say mine eyes are murderers.   Now show the wound mine eye hath made in thee.   Scratch thee but with a pin, and there remains   Some scar of it.
translation: or if you can't, oh, for shame, don't lie and tell me that my eyes are murderers. Now show me the wound my eyes have caused you. If you get scratched with a pin, it leaves a scar.

original: Lean upon a rush,   The cicatrice and capable impressure   Thy palm some moment keeps. But now mine eyes,   Which I have darted at thee, hurt thee not.
translation: If you even lean on a  rush , it leaves a visible impression in your palm for a moment. But my eyes, which I've hurled at you, haven't hurt you at all.

original: Nor, I am sure, there is no force in eyes   That can do hurt.
translation: Now I am sure that there is no force in eyes that can cause injury.

original: O dear Phoebe,   If ever—as that ever may be near—   You meet in some fresh cheek the power of fancy,
translation: Oh, dear Phoebe, if you ever should fall in love with some fresh face,

original: Then shall you know the wounds invisible   That love’s keen arrows make.
translation: then you will know about the invisible wounds that love's sharp arrows make.

original: But till that time   Come not thou near me. And when that time comes,
translation: But until that time comes, don't come near me. And when that time comes,

original: Afflict me with thy mocks, pity me not,   As till that time I shall not pity thee.
translation: then you can mock me. But don't pity me, as I won't pity you now.

original: [Advancing, as Ganymede]   And why, I pray you? Who might be your mother,   That you insult, exult, and all at once,   Over the wretched?
translation: [Coming forward, speaking as Ganymede]  And why, I ask you? Who raised you, that you would insult this wretched man and exult over his injuries all at once?

original: What though you have no beauty—   As, by my faith, I see no more in you   Than without candle may go dark to bed—
translation: Honestly, I don't see much in you—no more brightness than could light my way to bed in the dark—

original: Must you be therefore proud and pitiless?   Why, what means this? Why do you look on me?   I see no more in you than in the ordinary   Of nature’s sale-work.—
translation: so why must you be so proud and pitiless? Why, what's going on? Why do you look at me? There is no more to you than nature's ordinary, mass-produced product.

original: 'Od’s my little life,   I think she means to tangle my eyes, too.
translation: [To herself]  God save my life, I think she intends to ensnare my affections as well.

original: —No, faith, proud mistress, hope not after it.   'Tis not your inky brows, your black silk hair,   Your bugle eyeballs, nor your cheek of cream   That can entame my spirits to your worship.
translation: [To PHOEBE]  No, proud mistress, don't hope for it. You can't tame my spirits and make me worship you—not with your  ink-black  eyebrows; your black silky hair; your black, bead-like eyeballs; or your creamy complexion.

original: —You foolish shepherd, wherefore do you follow her,   Like foggy south puffing with wind and rain?   You are a thousand times a properer man   Than she a woman.
translation: [To SILVIUS]  You foolish shepherd: why do you follow her like the foggy south wind, sighing and raining tears? You are a thousand times more handsome than she is.

original: 'Tis such fools as you   That makes the world full of ill-favored children.   'Tis not her glass but you that flatters her,   And out of you she sees herself more proper   Than any of her lineaments can show her.
translation: It's fools like you who fill the world with ugly children by marrying women like her. It's not her mirror but  you  who flatters her, and she thinks herself more beautiful than she is because of your reflection of her.

original: —But, mistress, know yourself. Down on your knees   And thank heaven, fasting, for a good man’s love,   For I must tell you friendly in your ear,   Sell when you can; you are not for all markets.
translation: [To PHOEBE]  But mistress, know yourself. Get down on your knees and thank heaven for giving you a good man's love. I must tell you as a friend that you should sell while you can, for you won't have buyers for long.

original: Cry the man mercy, love him, take his offer.   Foul is most foul, being foul to be a scoffer.
translation: Ask for this man's mercy, love him, and take his offer. Ugliness is at its worst when it is scornful of others.

original: —So take her to thee, shepherd. Fare you well.
translation: [To SILVIUS]  So take her, shepherd. Good luck.

original: Sweet youth, I pray you chide a year together. I had rather hear you chide than this man woo.
translation: Sweet youth, please keep scorning me all year long. I would rather hear your scolding than this man's wooing.

original: He’s fall'n in love with your foulness.  And she’ll fall in love with my anger. If it be so, as  fast as she answers thee with frowning looks, I’ll sauce her with bitter words.    Why look you so upon me?
translation: He's fallen in love with your ugliness.  And she's falling in love with my anger. If this is so, then as soon as she answers you with frowning looks, I'll rebuke her with bitter words. [To PHOEBE] Why do you look at me like that?

original: For no ill will I bear you.
translation: I don't mean you any harm.

original: I pray you, do not fall in love with me,   For I am falser than vows made in wine.   Besides, I like you not. If you will know my house,   'Tis at the tuft of olives, here hard by.
translation: Please, don't fall in love with me. I am more false than a promise made while drunk. Besides, I don't like you. If you want to know where my house is, it's in the olive grove here close by.

original: —Will you go, sister?—
translation: [To CELIA]  Do you want to go, sister?

original: Shepherd, ply her hard.
translation: [To SILVIUS]  Shepherd, keep working on her.

original: —Come, sister.—
translation: [To CELIA]  Come on, sister.

original: Shepherdess, look on him better,   And be not proud. Though all the world could see,   None could be so abused in sight as he.
translation: [To PHOEBE]  Shepherdess, think better of him, and don't be proud. Even if everyone in the world could see you, no one would be so blind as he is.

original: —Come, to our flock.
translation: [To CELIA and CORIN]  Come, let's go to our flock.

original: Dead shepherd, now I find thy saw of might: “Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?”
Sweet Phoebe—
translation: Sweet Phoebe—

original: Ha, what sayst thou, Silvius?
translation: Ha, what did you say, Silvius?

original: Sweet Phoebe, pity me.
translation: Sweet Phoebe, have pity on me.

original: Why, I am sorry for thee, gentle Silvius.
translation: Well, I am sorry for you, dear Silvius.

original: Wherever sorrow is, relief would be.   If you do sorrow at my grief in love,
translation: If you're really sorry for me, you have the means to cure me. If you are really sorrowing over my grief in love,

original: By giving love your sorrow and my grief   Were both extermined.
translation: then love me back, and both your sorrow and my grief will be eliminated.

original: Thou hast my love. Is not that neighborly?
translation: You have my love—my neighborly love. Isn't that enough?

original: I would have you.
translation: I would have you.

original: Why, that were covetousness.   Silvius, the time was that I hated thee,   And yet it is not that I bear thee love,
translation: Well, that's just being greedy. Silvius, I used to hate you, and I still don't love you.

original: But since that thou canst talk of love so well,   Thy company, which erst was irksome to me,   I will endure, and I’ll employ thee too.
translation: But since you can talk about love so well,  I'll endure your company, and put you to some use too.

original: But do not look for further recompense   Than thine own gladness that thou art employed.
translation: But don't expect any more payment than your own happiness in working for me.

original: So holy and so perfect is my love,   And I in such a poverty of grace,
translation: My love for you is so holy and perfect, and earlier you hated me so much,

original: That I shall think it a most plenteous crop   To glean the broken ears after the man   That the main harvest reaps.
translation: that I'll take the leftover scraps of your love's harvest and consider them a plentiful bounty.

original: Loose now and then   A scattered smile, and that I’ll live upon.
translation: Every now and then let me have a smile, and I'll live on that.

original: Know’st thou the youth that spoke to me erewhile?
translation: Do you know the youth who was speaking to me earlier?

original: Not very well, but I have met him oft, And he hath bought the cottage and the bounds That the old carlot once was master of.
translation: Not very well, but I have met him a few times, and he bought the cottage and land that the old peasant used to own.

original: Think not I love him, though I ask for him.   'Tis but a peevish boy—yet he talks well—   But what care I for words?
translation: Don't start thinking that I love him, just because I'm asking about him. He is just an irritating boy—though he speaks well—but what do I care about words?

original: Yet words do well   When he that speaks them pleases those that hear.   It is a pretty youth—not very pretty—
translation: Though words are good when the man speaking them is pleasant to hear. He is a fine youth—not very fine—

original: But sure he’s proud—and yet his pride becomes him.   He’ll make a proper man. The best thing in him   Is his complexion; and faster than his tongue   Did make offense, his eye did heal it up.
translation: but he's very proud—and yet his pride suits him well. He'll grow up to be a proper man. The best part about him is his complexion; as fast as his words offend me, his appearance heals their wounds.

original: He is not very tall—yet for his years he’s tall.   His leg is but so-so—and yet ’tis well.   There was a pretty redness in his lip,
translation: He is not very tall—but for his age he's tall. His legs are only so-so—and yet they're nice. He had a pretty redness in his lips,

original: A little riper and more lusty red   Than that mixed in his cheek: ’twas just the difference   Betwixt the constant red and mingled damask.
translation: a little darker and more passionate than the red that was in his cheeks; one was pure red and the other mingled pink and white.

original: There be some women, Silvius, had they marked him   In parcels as I did, would have gone near   To fall in love with him;
translation: Silvius, there are some women who would have almost fallen in love with him after inspecting all his parts like I have.

original: but for my part   I love him not nor hate him not;   and yet   I have more cause to hate him than to love him.   For what had he to do to chide at me?
translation: But for my part I neither love him nor hate him. Although I have better reason to hate him than to love him.  What right did he have to scold me?

original: He said mine eyes were black and my hair black   And, now I am remembered, scorned at me.   I marvel why I answered not again.
translation: He said my eyes were black and my hair was black and, now that I remember it, he scorned me too. I'm shocked that I didn't answer him back in the same way.

original: But that’s all one: omittance is no quittance.   I’ll write to him a very taunting letter,   And thou shalt bear it. Wilt thou, Silvius?
translation: But that's all right: forgetting to assert my rights doesn't mean they don't exist. I'll write him a very taunting letter, and you will deliver it. Will you, Silvius?

original: Phoebe, with all my heart.
translation: With all my heart, Phoebe.

original: I’ll write it straight.   The matter’s in my head and in my heart.
translation: I'll write it immediately. What I want to say is already in my head and in my heart.

original: I will be bitter with him and passing short.   Go with me, Silvius.
translation: I'll be bitter and extremely curt with him. Come with me, Silvius.

original: I prithee, pretty youth, let me be better acquainted  with thee.
translation: Please, clever youth, let me get to know you better.

original: They say you are a melancholy fellow.
translation: They say you are a melancholy fellow

original: I am so. I do love it better than laughing.
translation: I am indeed. I like it better than laughing

original: Those that are in extremity of either are abominable  fellows and betray themselves to every modern censure  worse than drunkards.
translation: Those who go to extremes of melancholy or laughter are abominable, and open themselves up to common criticism in an even worse way than drunkards do.

original: Why, ’tis good to be sad and say nothing.
translation: Well, it's good to be sad and say nothing.

original: Why then, ’tis good to be a post.
translation: Well then, it's good to be a post.

original: I have neither the scholar’s melancholy, which is  emulation; nor the musician’s, which is fantastical; nor the courtier’s, which is proud; nor the soldier’s,  which is ambitious; nor the lawyer’s, which is politic;  nor the lady’s, which is nice;
translation: My melancholy is not like the scholar's, which is envy; nor the musician's, which is absurdly elaborate; nor the courtier's, which is proud; nor the soldier's, which is ambitious; nor the lawyer's, which is sneaky; nor the lady's, which is petty;

original: nor the lover’s, which is all these, but it is a melancholy of mine own,  compounded of many simples, extracted from many objects,
translation: nor the lover's, which combines all these qualities. Mine is a melancholy of my own, a compound of many ingredients, extracted from many objects.

original: and indeed the sundry contemplation of my travels, in  which my often rumination wraps me in a most humorous  sadness.
translation: When I contemplate my travels, my thoughts wrap me up in a moody sadness.

original: A traveler. By my faith, you have great reason to be  sad. I fear you have sold your own lands to see other  men’s.
translation: So you are a traveler. Well then, you truly have good reason to be sad. I'm afraid you have sold your own lands to see the lands of others.

original: Then to have seen much and to have nothing is to  have rich eyes and poor hands.
translation: To have seen much but have nothing is to have rich eyes and poor hands.

original: Yes, I have gained my experience.
translation: I have something—I have gained my experience.

original: And your experience makes you sad. I had rather have a  fool to make me merry than experience to make me sad—and to travel for it, too.
translation: And your experience makes you sad. I would rather have a fool to make me merry than experience to make me sad—and you've had to travel to get that sadness, too.

original: Good day and happiness, dear Rosalind.
Nay then, God be wi' you, an you talk in blank verse.
translation: Now then, goodbye to you if you're going to speak in blank verse.

original: Farewell, Monsieur Traveler. Look you lisp and wear  strange suits, disable all the benefits of your own  country, be out of love with your nativity,
translation: Goodbye, Mister Traveler. Be sure to keep up your foreign accent and wear strange clothes, downplay everything good about your own country, fall out of love with your birthplace,

original: and almost  chide God for making you that countenance you are, or I  will scarce think you have swam in a gondola.
translation: and almost scold God for giving you the appearance that you have. Otherwise I'll hardly believe you've been to Venice and ridden in a gondola.

original: Why, how now,  Orlando, where have you been all this while? You a  lover? An you serve me such another trick, never come in my sight more.
translation: Well, what's going on, Orlando? Where have you been all this time? You consider yourself a lover? If you pull another trick like that on me, never appear in my sight again.

original: My fair Rosalind, I come within an hour of my promise.
translation: My beautiful Rosalind, I've arrived within an hour of when I promised I would.

original: Break an hour’s promise in love?
translation: You would break a promise made in love by a whole  hour ?

original: He that will divide a  minute into a thousand parts and break but a part of the thousand part of a minute in the affairs of love,
translation: who would be even a thousandth part of a minute late to meet his beloved —

original: it  may be said of him that Cupid hath clapped him o' th'  shoulder,
translation: You could say that Cupid had nudged a man

original: but I’ll warrant him heart-whole.
translation: but his heart would still be in one piece.  He would have some affection, but I'd bet he wouldn't be in love.

original: Pardon me, dear Rosalind.
translation: Forgive me, dear Rosalind.

original: Nay, an you be so tardy, come no more in my sight. I  had as lief be wooed of a snail.
translation: No, if you're so late again, don't bother coming. I would rather be wooed by a snail.

original: Of a snail?
translation: By a snail?

original: Ay, of a snail, for though he comes slowly, he carries  his house on his head—a better jointure, I think, than  you make a woman. Besides, he brings his destiny with  him.
translation: Yes, a snail, for even though he comes slowly, he carries his whole house on his head—a better marriage settlement than you can offer a woman, I think. Besides, he brings his destiny along with him.

original: What’s that?
translation: What destiny is that?

original: Why, horns, which such as you are fain to be beholding  to your wives for. But he comes armed in his fortune and prevents the slander of his wife.
translation: Why, his cuckold's horns—the kind you men are always blaming your wives for. The snail comes already armed with horns, so he preempts any slander about his wife's faithfulness.

original: Virtue is no hornmaker, and my Rosalind is virtuous.
translation: A virtuous woman won't give a man horns, and my Rosalind is virtuous.

original: And I am your Rosalind.
translation: And I am your Rosalind.

original: It pleases him to call you so, but he hath  a Rosalind of a better leer than you.
translation: It pleases him to call you that, but he has another Rosalind somewhere with a prettier face than yours.

original: Come, woo me, woo me, for now I am in a holiday humor,  and like enough to consent. What would you say to me  now, an I were your very, very Rosalind?
translation: Come on, woo me, woo me, for I'm in a good mood now, and likely enough to consent to what you want. What would you say to me now, if I really were your very precious Rosalind?

original: I would kiss before I spoke.
translation: I would kiss before I spoke.

original: Nay, you were better speak first, and when you were  graveled for lack of matter, you might take occasion to  kiss.
translation: No, you would do better to speak first, and then kiss only when you ran out of things to discuss.

original: Very good orators, when they are out, they will  spit; and for lovers lacking—God warn us—matter, the  cleanliest shift is to kiss.
translation: When very good orators are out of things to say, they spit; and for lovers lacking words—God help us when that happens—the cleverest strategy is to kiss.

original: How if the kiss be denied?
translation: But what if my kiss is denied?

original: Then she puts you to entreaty, and there begins new  matter.
translation: Then she's making you beg, and that gives you a new subject to discuss.

original: Who could be out, being before his beloved mistress?
translation: Who could be out of things to say, if he's with his beloved mistress?

original: Marry, that should you if I were your mistress, or I  should think my honesty ranker than my wit.
translation: Well, you would be if I were your mistress, or else I would think my chastity was less pure than my wit.

original: What, of my suit?
Not out of your apparel, and yet out of your suit. Am  not I your Rosalind?
translation: Not out of your clothes, but out of your suit. But aren't I your Rosalind?

original: I take some joy to say you are because I would be  talking of her.
translation: It makes me happy to pretend that you are, because then it's like I'm talking to her.

original: Well, in her person I say I will not have you.
translation: Well, as Rosalind, I say I don't want you.

original: Then, in mine own person I die.
translation: Then, as myself, I will die.

original: No, faith, die by attorney. The poor world is almost  six thousand years old, and in all this time there was  not any man died in his own person, videlicet, in a love cause.
translation: No, you won't really die as yourself, but only by proxy. This poor world is almost  six thousand years old , and in all this time there hasn't been even a single man who died only from love.

original: Troilus had his brains dashed out with a Grecian club, yet he did what he could to die before, and he is one of the patterns of love. Leander, he would have  lived many a fair year though Hero had turned nun if it  had not been for a hot midsummer night,
translation: Troilus  wanted to die for love, but he actually died because a Greek with a club beat his brains out. And yet now he's one of the great examples of tragic love. Leander would have lived for many more years—even if his beloved Hero had left him and become a nun—if it hadn't been for one hot summer night,

original: for, good youth, he went but forth to wash him in the Hellespont and,  being taken with the cramp, was drowned; and the foolish chroniclers of that age found it was Hero of Sestos.
translation: when the poor youth went to wash himself in the Hellespont, got a cramp, and drowned. But the foolish poets of that age said he died from love of Hero, not from drowning.

original: But these are all lies. Men have died from time to time,  and worms have eaten them, but not for love.
translation: All such stories are lies. Men have died from time to time, and worms have eaten them, but none have died because of love.

original: I would not have my right Rosalind of this mind, for I  protest her frown might kill me.
translation: I hope the real Rosalind doesn't think this way, for her frown alone might kill me.

original: By this hand, it will not kill a fly. But come; now I  will be your Rosalind in a more coming-on disposition,  and ask me what you will, I will grant it.
translation: I swear, her frown couldn't kill a fly. But come on. Now I'll play your Rosalind in a more yielding mood, and whatever you ask of me, I'll give.

original: Then love me, Rosalind.
translation: Then love me, Rosalind.

original: Yes, faith, will I, Fridays and Saturdays and all.
translation: Very well, I will, on Fridays and Saturdays, and all the rest.

original: And wilt thou have me?
translation: And will you have me?

original: Ay, and twenty such.
translation: Yes, and twenty more like you.

original: What sayest thou?
translation: What do you mean?

original: Are you not good?
translation: Aren't you a good man?

original: I hope so.
translation: I hope so.

original: Why then, can one desire too much of a good thing?—  Come, sister, you shall be the priest and marry us.—Give me your hand, Orlando.—What do you say, sister?
translation: Why then, can you ever have too much of a good thing? Come, sister, you will be the priest and marry us. [To ORLANDO] Give me your hand, Orlando.[To CELIA] What do you say, sister?

original: Pray thee, marry us.
translation: Please, marry us.

original: I cannot say the words.
translation: I'm not a priest—I cannot say the words.

original: You must begin “Will you, Orlando—”
translation: You should begin "Do you, Orlando—"

original: Go to.—Will you, Orlando, have to wife this Rosalind?
translation: Oh, fine.  Do you, Orlando, take Rosalind as your wife?

original: I will.
translation: I do.

original: Ay, but when?
translation: All right, but when?

original: Why, now, as fast as she can marry us.
translation: Why, now, as fast as she can get us married.

original: Then you must say “I take thee, Rosalind, for wife.”
translation: Then you must say, "I take you, Rosalind, as my wife."

original: I take thee, Rosalind, for wife.
translation: I take you, Rosalind, as my wife.

original: I might ask you for your commission, but I do take  thee, Orlando, for my husband. There’s a girl goes  before the priest, and certainly a woman’s thought runs  before her actions.
translation: I might ask you by what authority, but I'll go ahead and take you, Orlando, as my husband. Now I've anticipated the priest and answered the question before I was even asked. A woman's thoughts run ahead of her actions.

original: So do all thoughts. They are winged.
translation: So do all thoughts. They have wings.

original: Now tell me how long you would have her after you have  possessed her.
translation: Now tell me how long you intend to keep Rosalind now that you have her.

original: Forever and a day.
translation: Forever and a day.

original: Say “a day” without the “ever.” No, no, Orlando, men  are April when they woo, December when they wed. Maids  are May when they are maids, but the sky changes when  they are wives.
translation: I think it will be more like "a day" without the "forever." No, Orlando, men are like April when they're wooing—warm and pleasant—but like December—cold and harsh—once they've married. In the same way, women are like springtime when they're single, but the climate changes when they become wives.

original: I will be more jealous of thee than a  Barbary cock- pigeon over his hen, more clamorous than a parrot against rain, more newfangled than an ape, more  giddy in my desires than a monkey.
translation: As a wife I'll be more jealous of you than a wild rooster is of his hen, noisier than a parrot scolding the rain, shallower than an ape, and more fickle in my desires than a monkey.

original: I will weep for  nothing, like Diana in the fountain, and I will do that  when you are disposed to be merry. I will laugh like a  hyena, and that when thou art inclined to sleep.
translation: I'll weep over nothing—like a statue of Diana in a fountain—and I'll cry even harder when you're in a good mood. And when you're trying to go to sleep, I'll laugh like a hyena.

original: But will my Rosalind do so?
translation: But will my Rosalind do all this too?

original: By my life, she will do as I do.
translation: I swear on my life, she'll act just like me.

original: Oh, but she is wise.
translation: Oh, but she is wise.

original: Or else she could not have the wit to do this. The  wiser, the waywarder. Make the doors upon a woman’s wit, and it will out at the casement.
translation: If she wasn't wise, she wouldn't have the wits to act so badly. The wiser the woman, the more wayward she is. Lock the doors on a woman's wit, and it will fly out the window.

original: Shut that, and ’twill  out at the keyhole. Stop that, ’twill fly with the smoke out at the chimney.
translation: Shut the windows, and it will escape through the keyhole. Stop up the keyhole, and it will fly out the chimney with the smoke.

original: A man that had a wife with such a wit, he might say  “Wit, whither wilt?”
translation: If a man had a wife like that, he might ask, "Where are you off to, wit?"

original: Nay, you might keep that check for it, till you met  your wife’s wit going to your neighbor’s bed.
translation: No, you had better save that question until you find your wife's wit in your neighbor's bed.

original: And what wit could wit have to excuse that?
translation: And what witty woman could have the wit to excuse that?

original: Marry, to say she came to seek you there. You shall  never take her without her answer unless you take her  without her tongue.
translation: Well, she could say she was at the neighbor's looking for you. You'll never find her without an answer unless you find her without a tongue.

original: Oh, that woman that cannot make her  fault her husband’s occasion, let her never nurse her  child herself, for she will breed it like a fool.
translation: Oh, if a woman can't find a way to blame her husband for her own faults, then she's not very smart—never let her have a child, for she will raise it to be a fool.

original: For these two hours, Rosalind, I will leave thee.
translation: Rosalind, I have to leave you for two hours now.

original: Alas, dear love, I cannot lack thee two hours.
translation: Alas, dear love, I can't live without you for two hours.

original: I must attend the duke at dinner. By two o'clock I will be with thee again.
translation: I must attend to the duke at his lunch. By two o'clock I'll be back with you again.

original: Ay, go your ways, go your ways. I knew what you would  prove. My friends told me as much, and I thought no  less. That flattering tongue of yours won me.
translation: Yes, go on, go on. I knew you would end up like this. My friends warned me, and I knew it, too. But I was won over by that flattering tongue of yours.

original: 'Tis but  one cast away, and so, come, death. Two o'clock is your  hour?
translation: I'm just one more seduced and abandoned woman, so come, take me, death! You'll return at two o'clock?

original: Ay, sweet Rosalind.
translation: Yes, sweet Rosalind.

original: By my troth, and in good earnest, and so God mend me,  and by all pretty oaths that are not dangerous, if you  break one jot of your promise or come one minute behind  your hour,
translation: I swear honestly, truly, by God, and by all the flowery oaths that aren't actually dangerous, that if you break even the tiniest part of your promise or come even a minute after two o'clock,

original: I will think you the most pathetical  break-promise and the most hollow lover and the most  unworthy of her you call Rosalind that may be chosen out of the gross band of the unfaithful. Therefore beware  my censure, and keep your promise.
translation: I will think you the most pitiful promise-breaker, the falsest lover, and the most unworthy match for Rosalind out of every man on earth. So beware of my disapproval, and keep your promise.

original: With no less religion than if thou wert indeed my  Rosalind. So, adieu.
translation: I'll keep my word just as faithfully as if you really were my Rosalind. So, goodbye.

original: Well, time is the old justice that examines all such  offenders, and let time try. Adieu.
translation: Well, time is the old judge who examines men like you, so only time will tell what kind of man you are. Goodbye.

original: You have simply misused our sex in your love-prate. We  must have your doublet and hose plucked over your head  and show the world what the bird hath done to her own  nest.
translation: You have totally slandered our sex in this love-talk of yours. We should pull off your man's jacket and breeches and show the world the bird who has attacked her own nest—the woman who maligns her fellow women.

original: O coz, coz, coz, my pretty little coz, that thou didst know how many fathom deep I am in love. But it cannot  be sounded; my affection hath an unknown bottom, like  the Bay of Portugal.
translation: Oh, cousin, cousin, cousin, my pretty little cousin, if only you could know how deeply I am in love. The depths of my love can't be plumbed; my affection has a bottom of unknown depth, like the Bay of Portugal.

original: Or rather bottomless, that as fast as you pour  affection in, it runs out.
translation: Or rather it's bottomless, so that as quickly as you pour affection in one end, it runs out the other.

original: No, that same wicked bastard of Venus that was begot of thought, conceived of spleen, and born of madness, that blind rascally boy that abuses everyone’s eyes because  his own are out, let him be judge how deep I am in love.
translation: No. Cupid—that wicked bastard son of  Venus , conceived from imagination and impulse and born of insanity; that blind naughty boy who makes everyone else go blind just because  he  can't see—let  him  judge how deeply I am in love.

original: I’ll tell thee, Aliena, I cannot be out of the sight of Orlando. I’ll go find a shadow and sigh till he come.
translation: I tell you, Aliena, I can't live without Orlando. I'll go find some shade and sigh until he comes back.

original: And I’ll sleep.
translation: And I'll sleep.

original: Which is he that killed the deer?
translation: Who is the man that killed the deer?

original: Sir, it was I.
translation: It was me, sir.

original: Let’s present him to the duke like a Roman conqueror.  And it would do well to set the deer’s horns upon his  head for a branch of victory.—Have you no song,  forester, for this purpose?
Yes, sir.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: Sing it. 'Tis no matter how it be in tune, so it make  noise enough.
translation: Sing it. It doesn't matter if it's in tune or not, as long as it makes enough noise.

original: [sings]     What shall he have that killed the deer?   His leather skin and horns to wear.   Then sing him home.   (The rest shall bear this burden.)
translation: [Singing] What should we give the man who killed the deer? Its leather hide and horns to wear. Then sing him home with this song. (The rest will carry the burden of the deer and the chorus.)

original: Take thou no scorn to wear the horn.     It was a crest ere thou wast born.   Thy father’s father wore it,   And thy father bore it.
translation: Don't be ashamed to wear the horns. They have been worn since before you were born. Your father's father wore them, And your father wore them.

original: The horn, the horn, the lusty horn   Is not a thing to laugh to scorn.
translation: The horn, the horn, the lustful horn, Is not to be laughed at or scorned.

original: How say you now? Is it not past two o'clock? And here  much Orlando.
translation: What do you say now? Isn't it past two o'clock? And no Orlando here.

original: I warrant you, with pure love and troubled brain he  hath ta'en his bow and arrows and is gone forth to  sleep.
translation: I promise you: with pure love and a troubled mind he has taken his bow and arrows and gone to take a nap.

original: Look who comes here.
translation: Look who's coming.

original: [To ROSALIND]   My errand is to you, fair youth.   My gentle Phoebe did bid me give you this.   I know not the contents, but as I guess   By the stern brow and waspish action   Which she did use as she was writing of it,
translation: [To ROSALIND]  I'm here to find you, fair youth. My lovely Phoebe told me to give you this letter. I don't know what it says, but guessing from her stern expression and spiteful demeanor while she was writing it,

original: It bears an angry tenor. Pardon me.   I am but as a guiltless messenger.   [Gives the letter]
translation: it has an angry tone. Forgive me. I'm just the innocent messenger.  [He gives her the letter]

original: [Examines the letter as Ganymede]   Patience herself  would startle at this letter   And play the swaggerer. Bear this, bear all.   She says I am not fair, that I lack manners.
translation: [Reading the letter]  The goddess of patience herself would be shocked by this letter, and get angry. If I can put up with this, I can put up with anything. Phoebe writes that I'm not handsome, and that I lack good manners.

original: She calls me proud, and that she could not love me   Were man as rare as phoenix. 'Od’s my will,   Her love is not the hare that I do hunt.
translation: She calls me proud, and says she couldn't love me even if I was the last man on earth. My God,  her  love isn't the rabbit I'm hunting!

original: Why writes she so to me? Well, shepherd, well,   This is a letter of your own device.
translation: Why should she write like this to me? Well, shepherd, hmm— you  wrote this letter.

original: No, I protest, I know not the contents. Phoebe did write it.
translation: No, I promise, I don't even know what it says. Phoebe wrote it.

original: Come, come, you are a fool,   And turned into the extremity of love.   I saw her hand. She has a leathern hand,   A freestone-colored hand.
translation: Come, come, you're being a fool: you've been driven to the madness of love. I saw her hands: she has leathery, yellowish-brown hands.

original: I verily did think   That her old gloves were on, but ’twas her hands.   She has a huswife’s hand—but that’s no matter.
translation: I honestly thought she was wearing old gloves, but they were her real hands. She has housewife's hands—but that's not the point.

original: I say she never did invent this letter.   This is a man’s invention, and his hand.
translation: I say she never wrote this letter. These are a man's words, and a man's handwriting.

original: Sure it is hers.
translation: It's really hers though.

original: Why, ’tis a boisterous and a cruel style,   A style for challengers. Why, she defies me   Like Turk to Christian.
translation: Well, it's written in a cruel and rowdy style, like someone asking for a fight. Why, she challenges me like a Turk challenging a Christian.

original: Women’s gentle brain   Could not drop forth such giant-rude invention,   Such Ethiop words, blacker in their effect   Than in their countenance. Will you hear the letter?
translation: No, a woman's noble brain could never come up with words so crude and violent—words black in their ink but even darker in their meanings. Do you want to hear the letter?

original: So please you, for I never heard it yet, Yet heard too much of Phoebe’s cruelty.
translation: If it pleases you to read it, for I haven't heard it yet—although I've already heard too much of Phoebe's cruelty.

original: She Phoebes me. Mark how the tyrant writes.   [reads]   Art thou god to shepherd turned,   That a maiden’s heart hath burned?
translation: Well, now she's "Phoebe-ing"  me . Listen to how the tyrant writes.  [Reading]   "Are you a god transformed into a shepherd, that you have so burned my heart?"

original: Can a woman rail thus?
translation: How could a woman rant like this?

original: Call you this railing?
translation: You call that ranting?

original: [reads]   Why, thy godhead laid apart,   Warr’st thou with a woman’s heart?   Did you ever hear such railing?
translation: [Reading]   "Why have you set aside your godlike nature and taken human form just to wrestle with a woman's heart?"  Did you ever hear such criticism?

original: Whiles the eye of man did woo me,   That could do no vengeance to me.   Meaning me a beast.
translation: [Reading]   "While other men have wooed me, they never could hurt me."  That means she thinks I'm a beast.

original: If the scorn of your bright eyne   Have power to raise such love in mine,   Alack, in me what strange effect   Would they work in mild aspect?
translation: [Reading]   "If the scorn in your bright eyes had the power to make me fall in love, what power might your eyes have if they looked at me more pleasantly?

original: Whiles you chid me, I did love.   How then might your prayers move?   He that brings this love to thee   Little knows this love in me,
translation: While you were scolding me, I was falling in love. Consider then how your prayers might move me. The man who brings this love letter to you doesn't know about my feelings.

original: And by him seal up thy mind   Whether that thy youth and kind   Will the faithful offer take   Of me,
translation: Enclose your thoughts in a letter and send it back to me through him. Tell me whether your youthful nature will accept my faithful offer of myself

original: and all that I can make,   Or else by him my love deny,   And then I’ll study how to die.
translation: and all that I can do,  or else tell me that you'll deny my love, so I might figure out how to die."

original: Call you this chiding?
translation: You call this scolding?

original: Alas, poor shepherd.
translation: Oh, poor shepherd.

original: Do you pity him? No, he deserves no pity.—
translation: Do you pity him? No, he doesn't deserve pity.

original: Wilt thou  love such a woman? What, to make thee an instrument and  play false strains upon thee? Not to be endured.
translation: [To SILVIUS]  Do you still insist on loving such a woman? So she can use you like an instrument and play false tunes on you? It shouldn't be endured.

original: Well,  go your way to her, for I see love hath made thee a tame snake, and say this to her: that if she love me, I  charge her to love thee;
translation: Well, go back to her if you want—for I can tell that love has made you into a tame, impotent snake. Tell her this: if she loves me, then I command her to love  you .

original: if she will not, I will never  have her unless thou entreat for her. If you be a true  lover, hence and not a word, for here comes more  company.
translation: And if she won't love you, tell her that I will never take her unless  you  beg me on her behalf. Now if you're a true lover, go away and don't say another word, because here comes more company.

original: Good morrow, fair ones. Pray you, if you know,  Where in the purlieus of this forest stands A sheepcote fenced about with olive trees?
translation: Good morning, pretty ones. Tell me please, if you know: where can I find a shepherd's cottage surrounded by olive trees, somewhere within the borders of this forest?

original: [as Aliena]   West of this place, down in the neighbor  bottom,   The rank of osiers by the murmuring stream   Left on your right hand brings you to the place.
translation: West of here, in the nearby valley, a row of willows by the stream on the right leads to the cottage.

original: But at this hour the house doth keep itself.   There’s none within.
translation: But right now the house is keeping itself. There's no one inside.

original: If that an eye may profit by a tongue,   Then should I know you by description.   Such garments, and such years.
translation: If eyes can get a sense of a description that's been spoken, then I recognize you. You match the clothing and ages I was told:

original: “The boy is fair,   Of female favor, and bestows himself   Like a ripe sister; the woman low   And browner than her brother.”
translation: "The boy is pretty and effeminate, and conducts himself like a mature woman. The woman is shorter and darker than her brother."

original: Are not you   The owner of the house I did inquire for?
translation: Are you the owners of the house I just asked about?

original: It is no boast, being asked, to say we are.
translation: It's not boasting, since you asked, to say that we are.

original: Orlando doth commend him to you both, And to that youth he calls his Rosalind He sends this bloody napkin. Are you he?
translation: Orlando sends his regards to you both, and to the youth he calls "his Rosalind" he sends this bloody handkerchief. Is that you?

original: I am. What must we understand by this?
translation: Yes. What does this mean?

original: Some of my shame, if you will know of me  What man I am, and how, and why, and where This handkercher was stained.
translation: It's a story with some shame on my part—a story about what kind of man I am—and how, why, and where this handkerchief was stained.

original: I pray you, tell it.
translation: Please, tell it.

original: When last the young Orlando parted from you,   He left a promise to return again   Within an hour, and pacing through the forest,   Chewing the food of sweet and bitter fancy,   Lo, what befell. He threw his eye aside—
translation: When the young Orlando last left you, he promised to return again within an hour. He was pacing through the forest, musing on the bittersweetness of love, when—oh! what a terrible thing happened—he looked off to the side,

original: And mark what object did present itself:   Under an old oak, whose boughs were mossed with age   And high top bald with dry antiquity,   A wretched, ragged man, o'ergrown with hair,   Lay sleeping on his back.
translation: and guess what he saw there? Under an old oak, whose lower branches were mossy with age and whose high upper branches were leafless, ancient, and dry, he saw a wretched, ragged man with overgrown hair lying asleep on his back.

original: About his neck   A green and gilded snake had wreathed itself,   Who with her head, nimble in threats, approached   The opening of his mouth.
translation: A green and gold snake had wound itself around this man's neck and was slowly approaching his open mouth.
