original: But suddenly,   Seeing Orlando, it unlinked itself   And, with indented glides, did slip away   Into a bush, under which bush’s shade   A lioness, with udders all drawn dry,
translation: But suddenly, when it saw Orlando, the serpent uncoiled itself and slipped away, gliding into a bush. But under this same bush there was a lioness, whose cubs had nursed her dry so that she was undernourished and hungry.

original: Lay couching, head on ground, with catlike watch   When that the sleeping man should stir—for ’tis   The royal disposition of that beast   To prey on nothing that doth seem as dead.
translation: She crouched in the bush's shadow with her head on the ground, watching the man in a catlike way and waiting to see if he would move—for it is in the lion's royal nature not prey on anything that seems dead.

original: This seen, Orlando did approach the man   And found it was his brother, his elder brother.
translation: Seeing this lioness, Orlando approached the sleeping man and saw that it was his brother—his older brother.

original: Oh, I have heard him speak of that same brother, And he did render him the most unnatural That lived amongst men.
translation: Oh, I've heard him talk about that same brother, and describe him as the most inhumane man in the world.

original: And well he might so do, For well I know he was unnatural.
translation: And he would be right to do so. I know very well how inhumane he was.

original: But to Orlando: did he leave him there,  Food to the sucked and hungry lioness?
translation: But back to Orlando: did he leave his brother there to be food for the dry and hungry lioness?

original: Twice did he turn his back and purposed so,   But kindness, nobler ever than revenge,   And nature, stronger than his just occasion,
translation: Twice he turned away, intending to leave him there. But ultimately his brotherly love was nobler than his desire for revenge, and his natural goodness was stronger than his justifiable excuse to leave his brother to the lioness.

original: Made him give battle to the lioness,   Who quickly fell before him; in which hurtling,   From miserable slumber I awaked.
translation: He battled with the lioness, quickly defeating her, and the noise of their tumult woke me up from my miserable slumber.

original: Are you his brother?
translation: Are you his brother?

original: Was ’t you he rescued?
translation: Was it you he rescued?

original: Was ’t you that did so oft contrive to kill him?
translation: Was it you who was always trying to kill him?

original: 'Twas I, but ’tis not I. I do not shame  To tell you what I was, since my conversion So sweetly tastes, being the thing I am.
translation: It was me, but it's not me now. I'm not ashamed to tell you what I once was, since my conversion to my new self seems so sweet.

original: But for the bloody napkin?
translation: But what about the bloody handkerchief?

original: By and by.   When from the first to last betwixt us two   Tears our recountments had most kindly bathed—   As how I came into that desert place—
translation: In a minute. When we had been reunited, and tearfully told each other our entire stories—for me, how I had come to this deserted place—

original: In brief, he led me to the gentle duke,   Who gave me fresh array and entertainment,   Committing me unto my brother’s love,
translation: in brief, he led me to the noble duke, who gave me fresh clothing and food and drink, and committed me to my brother's care.

original: Who led me instantly unto his cave,   There stripped himself, and here upon his arm   The lioness had torn some flesh away,   Which all this while had bled.
translation: Orlando immediately took me to his cave, where he stripped off his clothing and saw that he had a wound on his arm where the lioness had torn off some of his flesh. This wound had been bleeding the whole time.

original: And now he fainted,   And cried in fainting upon Rosalind.   Brief, I recovered him, bound up his wound,   And after some small space, being strong at heart,
translation: Orlando fainted then, but as he fainted he called for "Rosalind." In brief, I helped him recover, and bound up his wound. After only a little while, for he is strong at heart,

original: He sent me hither, stranger as I am,   To tell this story, that you might excuse   His broken promise, and to give this napkin
translation: he sent me here—though I am a stranger—to find you and tell you this story, begging that you might forgive his broken promise. He wanted me to give this handkerchief,

original: Dyed in his blood unto the shepherd youth   That he in sport doth call his Rosalind.
translation: dyed with his blood, to the shepherd boy whom he jokingly calls his Rosalind.

original: Why, how now, Ganymede, sweet Ganymede?
translation: Why, what's this now, Ganymede, sweet Ganymede?

original: Many will swoon when they do look on blood.
translation: Many people faint when they see blood.

original: There is more in it.—Cousin Ganymede.
translation: There is more to it than that.  Cousin Ganymede.

original: Look, he recovers.
translation: Look, he's recovering.

original: I would I were at home.
translation: I wish I were at home.

original: We’ll lead you thither. —I pray you, will you take him by the arm?
translation: We'll take you there.  Please, will you take him by the arm?

original: Be of good cheer, youth. You a man? You lack a man’s  heart.
translation: Cheer up, boy. Are you a man? It seems you lack a man's heart.

original: I do so, I confess it. Ah, sirrah, a body would think  this was well-counterfeited. I pray you tell your  brother how well I counterfeited. Heigh-ho.
translation: I do indeed, I confess it. Ha, sir, you can see that this was all pretend. Please tell your brother how well I played my part. Heigh-ho.

original: This was not counterfeit. There is too great testimony  in your complexion that it was a passion of earnest.
translation: This was no act. Your flushed cheeks declare that your passion was real.

original: Counterfeit, I assure you.
translation: I was just pretending, I assure you.

original: Well then, take a good heart and counterfeit to be a  man.
translation: Well then, cheer up and pretend to be a man.

original: So I do. But i' faith, I should have been a woman by  right.
translation: That's what I'm doing. But honestly, I should have been born a woman.

original: Come, you look paler and paler. Pray you, draw  homewards.—Good sir, go with us.
translation: Come, you're getting paler and paler. Please, let's go home.  Good sir, come with us.

original: That will I, for I must bear answer back How you excuse my brother, Rosalind.
translation: I'll do that, for I must bring your answer back to my brother and tell him how you forgave him, Rosalind.

original: I shall devise something. But I pray you commend my  counterfeiting to him. Will you go?
translation: I'll come up with something. But please, tell him how well I kept up my act as Rosalind. Will you come with us?

original: We shall find a time, Audrey. Patience, gentle Audrey.
translation: We'll find a time to get married soon, Audrey. Patience, kind Audrey.

original: Faith, the priest was good enough, for all the old  gentleman’s saying.
translation: Honestly, that priest was good enough, despite what the old gentleman said.

original: A most wicked Sir Oliver, Audrey, a most vile Martext. But, Audrey, there is a youth here in the forest lays  claim to you.
translation: No, Audrey: he was a wicked Sir Oliver, and a vile Martext. But, Audrey, there is a youth here in the forest who claims that you're his love.

original: Ay, I know who ’tis. He hath no interest in me in the  world.
translation: Yes, I know who that is. He has no claim over me, though.

original: Here comes the man you mean.
translation: Here comes the man you mean.

original: It is meat and drink to me to see a clown. By my  troth, we that have good wits have much to answer for.  We shall be flouting. We cannot hold.
translation: It's like a feast to me to see such a country bumpkin. I swear, we men with good wits have too much responsibility. We have to be mocking. We can't hold our tongues.

original: Good ev'n, Audrey.
translation: Good evening, Audrey.

original: God gi' good ev'n, William.
translation: God give you a good evening, William.

original: And good ev'n to you, sir.
translation: And good evening to you, sir.

original: Good ev'n, gentle friend. Cover thy head, cover thy  head. Nay, prithee, be covered. How old are you, friend?
translation: Good evening, noble friend. No, put your hat back on, put your hat back on. Please, cover your head. How old are you, friend?

original: Five-and-twenty, sir.
translation: Twenty-five, sir.

original: A ripe age. Is thy name William?
translation: A mature age. Is your name William?

original: William, sir.
translation: William, sir.

original: A fair name. Wast born i' th' forest here?
translation: A nice name. Were you born in the forest here?

original: Ay, sir, I thank God.
translation: Yes, sir, thank God.

original: “Thank God.” A good answer. Art rich?
translation: "Thank God"—a good answer. Are you rich?

original: 'Faith, sir, so-so.
translation: To be honest, sir, so-so.

original: “So-so” is good, very good, very excellent good. And  yet it is not: it is but so-so. Art thou wise?
translation: "So-so" is good, very good, very excellently good. And yet it also isn't: it's only so-so. Are you wise?

original: Ay, sir, I have a pretty wit.
translation: Yes, sir, I have a good mind.

original: Why, thou sayst well. I do now remember a saying: “The  fool doth think he is wise, but the wise man knows  himself to be a fool.”
translation: Why, you speak well. Which reminds me of a saying: "The fool thinks he is wise, but the wise man knows he is a fool."

original: The heathen philosopher, when he  had a desire to eat a grape, would open his lips when he put it into his mouth, meaning thereby that grapes were made to eat and lips to open. You do love this maid?
translation: A classical philosopher, when he wanted to eat a grape, would open his lips and put the grape into his mouth, thereby proving that grapes were made to eat and lips were made to open. Do you love this young lady?

original: I do, sir.
translation: I do, sir.

original: Give me your hand. Art thou learned?
translation: Give me your hand. Are you educated?

original: No, sir.
translation: No, sir.

original: Then learn this of me: to have is to have. For it is a  figure in rhetoric that drink, being poured out of a cup into a glass, by filling the one doth empty the other.
translation: Then let me educate you now: to have something is to have it. It's a common figure of speech that when a drink is poured from a cup into a glass, by filling the glass the cup becomes empty.

original: For all your writers do consent that ipse is “he.” Now,  you are not ipse, for I am he.
translation: All the authorities agree that  ipse  translates from the Latin as "he himself." Now, you are not  ipse  anymore, for I am he.

original: Which he, sir?
translation: Which "he," sir?

original: He, sir, that must marry this woman. Therefore, you  clown, abandon—which is, in the vulgar, “leave”—the  society—which in the boorish is “company”—of this  female—which in the common is “woman”   ;
translation: "He," sir, who will marry this woman. Therefore, you clown, abandon—which is, in common language, "leave"—the society—which in unsophisticated language means "company"—of this female—

original: which together  is, abandon the society of this female, or, clown, thou  perishest; or, to thy better understanding, diest; or,  to wit, I kill thee, make thee away, translate thy life  into death, thy liberty into bondage.
translation: which common people would call "woman." All together that makes: abandon the society of this female, or, clown, you'll perish. Or perhaps you'll understand it better if I say "you'll die." Or, rather, I'll kill you; do away with you; transform your life into death and your liberty into captivity.

original: I will deal in  poison with thee, or in bastinado, or in steel. I will  bandy with thee in faction. I will o'errun thee with  policy. I will kill thee a hundred and fifty ways.  Therefore tremble and depart.
translation: I'll poison you, or beat you with sticks, or stab you. I'll engage in a conflict with you. I'll overwhelm you with cleverness. I will kill you in a hundred and fifty ways. Therefore tremble and depart.

original: Do, good William.
translation: Do as he says, good William.

original: God rest you merry, sir.
translation: Farewell, sir.

original: Our master and mistress seeks you. Come away, away.
translation: Our master and mistress are seeking you. Come on, let's go.

original: Trip, Audrey, trip, Audrey.—I attend, I attend.
translation: Quickly, Audrey, quickly, Audrey. I'm coming, I'm coming.

original: Is ’t possible that on so little acquaintance you  should like her?
translation: Is it possible that you could like her after knowing her for such a brief amount of time?

original: That, but seeing, you should love her?
translation: And that you could fall in love after only seeing her once?

original: And loving, woo?
translation: And that you could woo her as soon as you fell in love?

original: And wooing, she should grant?
translation: And that, being wooed, she would immediately accept your offer?

original: And will  you persevere to enjoy her?
translation: And will you keep on with your plan to marry her?

original: Neither call the giddiness of it in question, the  poverty of her, the small acquaintance, my sudden  wooing, nor her sudden consenting, but say with me “I  love Aliena”;
translation: Don't raise questions about how quickly it all happened—or scoff at her poverty, our brief acquaintance, my sudden courtship, or her sudden consent. Just say with me, "I love Aliena,"

original: say with her that she loves me; consent  with both that we may enjoy each other. It shall be to  your good, for my father’s house and all the revenue  that was old Sir Rowland’s will I estate upon you, and  here live and die a shepherd.
translation: and say with her that she loves me. Give your approval to this match, so that we can enjoy each other. It will be to your advantage, for I'll leave our father's house, his wealth, and all his property to you, and I'll stay here to live and die as a shepherd.

original: You have my consent. Let your wedding be tomorrow.   Thither will I invite the duke and all’s contented  followers.
translation: You have my consent. You can get married tomorrow. I will invite the duke and all his happy followers.

original: Go you and prepare Aliena, for look you, here comes my   Rosalind.
translation: Go and get Aliena ready, for look—here comes my Rosalind.

original: God save you, brother.
translation: May God bless you, future brother-in-law.

original: And you, fair sister.
translation: And you, fair sister-to-be.

original: O my dear Orlando, how it grieves me to see thee wear  thy heart in a scarf.
translation: Oh, my dear Orlando, it pains me to see you wearing your heart in a sling.

original: It is my arm.
translation: It's my arm, not my heart.

original: I thought thy heart had been wounded with the claws of a lion.
translation: But I thought your heart had been wounded by the claws of a lion.

original: Wounded it is, but with the eyes of a lady.
translation: It is wounded, but not by a lion—by the eyes of a lady.

original: Did your brother tell you how I counterfeited to swoon  when he showed me your handkercher?
translation: Did your brother tell you how well I pretended to faint when he showed me your handkerchief?

original: Ay, and greater wonders than that.
translation: Yes, and also things more amazing than that.

original: Oh, I know where you are. Nay, ’tis true. There was  never anything so sudden but the fight of two rams and  Caesar’s thrasonical brag of “I came, saw, and  overcame.” For your brother and my sister no sooner met  but they looked, no sooner looked but they loved, no  sooner loved but they sighed,
translation: Oh, I know what you mean. It's true. It was as sudden as two rams fighting, or Caesar boasting "I came, I saw, I conquered." Your brother and my sister had no sooner met than they looked closely at each other; had no sooner looked than they fell in love; had no sooner loved than they sighed;

original: no sooner sighed but they  asked one another the reason, no sooner knew the reason  but they sought the remedy; and in these degrees have  they made a pair of stairs to marriage,
translation: no sooner sighed than they asked each other why they sighed; and no sooner learned the reason than they looked for the solution to their mutual "problem." And in this way the degrees of their courtship made a flight of stairs leading up towards marriage.

original: which they will  climb incontinent, or else be incontinent before  marriage. They are in the very wrath of love, and they  will together. Clubs cannot part them.
translation: They'll climb those stairs immediately, or else they'll sleep together before they get married. They are in the heat of passion, and must be together. You couldn't beat them apart with a club.

original: They shall be married tomorrow, and I will bid the duke to the nuptial. But Oh, how bitter a thing it is to  look into happiness through another man’s eyes.
translation: They'll be married tomorrow, and I'll invite the duke to the wedding. But, oh, it's bitter to look at happiness through another man's eyes.

original: By so  much the more shall I tomorrow be at the height of  heart-heaviness, by how much I shall think my brother  happy in having what he wishes for.
translation: And by tomorrow I'll be totally weighed down by misery, thinking how happy my brother is in getting what he wished for.

original: Why, then, tomorrow I cannot serve your turn for  Rosalind?
translation: Well then, can't I play Rosalind for you tomorrow?

original: I can live no longer by thinking.
translation: I can't live in this fantasy anymore.

original: I will weary you then no longer with idle talking. Know of me then—for now I speak to some purpose—that I know  you are a gentleman of good conceit. I speak not this  that you should bear a good opinion of my knowledge,  insomuch I say I know you are.
translation: I won't weary you with idle talk then. You should know—and now I'm speaking sincerely—that I know you are an intelligent gentleman. I'm not saying this so you'll have a good opinion of my knowledge, as I say I "know" you're intelligent. I'm not trying to increase my reputation either—I only hope you might have some confidence in my ability to do something good for you.

original: Neither do I labor for a  greater esteem than may in some little measure draw a  belief from you to do yourself good, and not to grace  me. Believe then, if you please, that I can do strange  things. I have, since I was three year old, conversed  with a magician, most profound in his art and yet not  damnable.
translation: I'm not trying to bring favor on myself. Believe me, then, when I say that I can make strange things happen. Since I was three years old I have been in contact with a magician. He is very powerful, but he doesn't practice evil magic.

original: If you do love Rosalind so near the heart as  your gesture cries it out, when your brother marries  Aliena shall you marry her. I know into what straits of  fortune she is driven,
translation: If you love Rosalind as much as your behavior implies, then you will marry her when your brother marries Aliena. I know Rosalind's situation and where she is.

original: and it is not impossible to me,  if it appear not inconvenient to you, to set her before  your eyes tomorrow, human as she is, and without any  danger.
translation: And it's not impossible for me to set her before you tomorrow—whole, human, and unharmed—so long as it doesn't seem improper to you.

original: Speak’st thou in sober meanings?
translation: Is what you're saying serious?

original: By my life I do, which I tender dearly, though I say I  am a magician. Therefore put you in your best array, bid your friends; for if you will be married tomorrow, you  shall, and to Rosalind, if you will.
translation: I swear on my life, which I value dearly, even though I said I'm a magician. Therefore put on your finest clothes and invite your friends. For if you want to be married tomorrow, you will, and if you want Rosalind to be the bride, she will.

original: Look, here comes a lover of mine and a lover of hers.
translation: Look, here comes someone who loves me, and someone who loves her.

original: Youth, you have done me much ungentleness To show the letter that I writ to you.
translation: Boy, you were very rude to me when you showed off the letter I wrote to you.

original: I care not if I have. It is my study   To seem despiteful and ungentle to you.
translation: I don't care if I was. I am purposefully being contemptuous and rude to you.

original: You are there followed by a faithful shepherd.   Look upon him, love him; he worships you.
translation: You are followed by a faithful shepherd even now. Look at him, and love him! He worships you.

original: Good shepherd, tell this youth what ’tis to love.
translation: Good shepherd, tell this youth what it is to be in love.

original: It is to be all made of sighs and tears,  And so am I for Phoebe.
translation: It is to be filled with sighs and tears, as I am for Phoebe.

original: And I for Ganymede.
translation: And as I am for Ganymede.

original: And I for Rosalind.
translation: And as I am for Rosalind.

original: And I for no woman.
translation: And as I am for no woman.

original: It is to be all made of faith and service,  And so am I for Phoebe.
translation: It is to be filled with faithfulness and servitude, as I am for Phoebe.

original: And I for Ganymede.
translation: And as I am for Ganymede.

original: And I for Rosalind.
translation: And as I am for Rosalind.

original: And I for no woman.
translation: And as I am for no woman.

original: It is to be all made of fantasy,   All made of passion and all made of wishes,   All adoration,   duty, and observance,
translation: It is to be filled with fantasy; filled with passion and wishes; with adoration, duty, and devotion;

original: All humbleness, all patience and impatience,   All purity, all trial, all observance,   And so am I for Phoebe.
translation: humility, patience, and impatience; filled with purity, suffering, and obedience—just as I am for Phoebe.

original: And so am I for Ganymede.
translation: And as I am for Ganymede.

original: And so am I for Rosalind.
translation: And as I am for Rosalind.

original: And so am I for no woman.
translation: And as I am for no woman.

original: If this be so, why blame you me to love you?
translation: If all this is true, then why do you blame me for loving you?

original: If this be so, why blame you me to love you?
translation: And why do you blame me for loving you?

original: If this be so, why blame you me to love you?
translation: And why do you blame me for loving you?

original: Why do you speak, too, “Why blame you me to love you?”?
translation: Who are you speaking to, Orlando?

original: To her that is not here, nor doth not hear.
translation: To the woman who isn't here, and doesn't hear me.

original: Pray you, no more of this. 'Tis like the howling of  Irish wolves against the moon.
translation: Please, no more of this. You're like a pack of wolves howling passionately at the moon.

original: [to SILVIUS]   I will help you, if I can.
translation: [To SILVIUS]  I will help you, if I can.

original: [to PHOEBE]   I would love you if I  could.—
translation: [To PHOEBE]  I would love you, if I could.

original: Tomorrow meet me all together.
translation: All of you, meet me tomorrow.

original: [to PHOEBE]   I  will marry you if ever I marry woman, and I’ll be  married tomorrow.
translation: [To PHOEBE]  If I'm going to ever marry a woman, it will be you—and I'm getting married tomorrow.

original: [to ORLANDO]   I will satisfy you if  ever I satisfy man, and you shall be married tomorrow.
translation: [To ORLANDO]  If I'm ever going to satisfy a man, I'll satisfy you, and you'll be married tomorrow too.

original: [to SILVIUS]   I will content you, if what pleases you  contents you, and you shall be married tomorrow.
translation: [To SILVIUS]  I'll make you happy, if the thing you desire will make you happy, and you too will be married tomorrow.

original: [to   ORLANDO]   As you love Rosalind, meet.
translation: [To ORLANDO]  By your love for Rosalind, come tomorrow.

original: [to SILVIUS]   As  you love Phoebe, meet.—
translation: [To SILVIUS]  By your love for Phoebe, come tomorrow.

original: And as I love no woman, I’ll  meet. So fare you well. I have left you commands.
translation: And by my love for no woman, I'll meet you all here tomorrow too. So farewell. You know what I want you to do.

original: I’ll not fail, if I live.
translation: If I'm alive, I won't miss it.

original: Nor I.
translation: Me neither.

original: Nor I.
translation: Me neither.

original: Tomorrow is the joyful day, Audrey. Tomorrow will we be married.
translation: Tomorrow is the joyful day, Audrey. Tomorrow we'll be married.

original: I do desire it with all my heart, and I hope it is no  dishonest desire to desire to be a woman of the world.
translation: I desire it with all my heart, and I hope it isn't immodest of me to desire to be a married, worldly woman.

original: Here comes two of the banished duke’s pages.
translation: Here come two of Duke Senior's pages.

original: Well met, honest gentleman.
translation: Nice to see you, honest gentleman.

original: By my troth, well met. Come, sit, sit, and a song.
translation: Truly, it is good to see you. Come sit, sit, and sing a song.

original: We are for you. Sit i' th' middle.
translation: We're here to serve you. Sit between us.

original: Shall we clap into ’t roundly, without hawking or  spitting or saying we are hoarse, which are the only  prologues to a bad voice?
translation: Should we jump right into it, without all that hawking and spitting and saying that we're hoarse—which are only excuses for bad singers?

original: I' faith, i' faith, and both in a tune like two gypsies on a horse.
translation: Yes, yes, and let's sing in unison, like two gypsies riding one horse.

original: [sing]   It was a lover and his lass,     With a hey, and a ho, and a hey-nonny-no,   That o'er the green cornfield did pass   In springtime, the only pretty ring time,   When birds do sing, Hey ding a ding, ding.
translation: [Singing] There was a lover and his lady, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey-nonny-no, Who went through the wheatfield In the springtime, the only wedding season, When birds do sing, Hey ding a ding ding.

original: Sweet lovers love the spring.     Between the acres of the rye,   With a hey, and a ho, and a hey-nonny-no,
translation: Sweet lovers love the spring. Between the fields of rye, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey-nonny-no,

original: These pretty country folks would lie   In springtime, the only pretty ring time,   When birds do sing, Hey ding a ding, ding.
translation: These pretty country folks would lie In the springtime, the only wedding season, When birds do sing, Hey ding a ding ding.

original: Sweet lovers love the spring.   This carol they began that hour,   With a hey, and a ho, and a hey-nonny-no,
translation: Sweet lovers love the spring. They began this song that very hour, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey-nonny-no,

original: How that a life was but a flower   In springtime, the only pretty ring time,     When birds do sing, Hey ding a ding, ding.   Sweet lovers love the spring.
translation: That life is just as brief as a flower In the springtime, the only wedding season, When birds do sing, Hay ding a ding ding. Sweet lovers love the spring.

original: And therefore take the present time,   With a hey, and a ho, and a hhey-nonny-no,   For love is crownèd with the prime     In springtime, the only pretty ring time,
translation: So therefore seize the present moment, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey-nonny-no, For love is crowned by the spring In the springtime, the only wedding season,

original: When birds do sing, Hey ding a ding, ding.   Sweet lovers love the spring.
translation: When birds do sing, Hey ding a ding, ding. Sweet lovers love the spring.

original: Truly, young gentlemen, though there was no great  matter in the ditty, yet the note was very untunable.
translation: Truly, young gentleman, though there wasn't much to the song, the music was still very off-key.

original: You are deceived, sir. We kept time. We lost not our  time.
translation: You're wrong, sir. We kept the song's time. We didn't lose our rhythm.

original: By my troth, yes. I count it but time lost to hear such a foolish song. God be wi' you, and God mend your  voices.— Come, Audrey.
translation: Truly, yes. But I consider it lost time when I must hear such a foolish song. God be with you, and may he fix your voices too. Come, Audrey.

original: Dost thou believe, Orlando, that the boy Can do all this that he hath promisèd?
translation: Orlando, do you really believe that this boy can do all that he's promised?

original: I sometimes do believe and sometimes do not, As those that fear they hope, and know they fear.
translation: Sometimes I believe and sometimes I don't. I'm hoping, and also scared to hope.

original: Patience once more whiles our compact is urged.     You say, if I bring in your Rosalind, You will bestow her on Orlando here?
translation: Be patient while our contract is proclaimed.  You say that if I bring your daughter Rosalind here, you will give her to Orlando to be married?

original: That would I, had I kingdoms to give with her.
translation: I will, even if I had to give kingdoms along with her.

original: And you say you will have her when I bring her?
translation: And you say that you will marry her when I bring her here?

original: That would I, were I of all kingdoms king.
translation: I will, even if I were already the king of all kingdoms.

original: You say you’ll marry me if I be willing?
translation: You say you'll marry me if I'm willing to marry you?

original: That will I, should I die the hour after.
translation: I will, even if I should die the following hour.

original: But if you do refuse to marry me, You’ll give yourself to this most faithful shepherd?
translation: But if you refuse to marry me, you'll marry this faithful shepherd instead?

original: So is the bargain.
translation: That's our bargain.

original: You say that you’ll have Phoebe if she  will?
translation: And you say that you'll marry Phoebe if she is willing?

original: Though to have her and death were both one thing.
translation: Even if marrying her meant death for me.

original: I have promised to make all this matter even.
translation: I have promised to make everything clear.

original: Keep you your word, O duke, to give your daughter,
translation: [To DUKE SENIOR]  Duke Senior, keep your promise to give away your daughter.

original: —You yours, Orlando, to receive his daughter.
translation: [To ORLANDO]  Orlando, keep your promise to marry his daughter.

original: —Keep your word, Phoebe, that you’ll marry me   Or else, refusing me, to wed this shepherd.
translation: [To PHOEBE]  P hoebe, keep your promise that you'll marry me, or marry this shepherd if you refuse me.

original: —Keep your word, Silvius, that you’ll marry her   If she refuse me.
translation: [To SILVIUS]  Silvius, keep your promise that you'll marry Phoebe if she refuses me.

original: And from hence I go   To make these doubts all even.
translation: [To all]  And now I'll go to clear up all your doubts.

original: I do remember in this shepherd boy Some lively touches of my daughter’s favor.
translation: This shepherd boy's appearance reminds me of my daughter.

original: My lord, the first time that I ever saw him   Methought he was a brother to your daughter.
translation: My lord, the first time I saw him I thought he was your daughter's brother.

original: But, my good lord, this boy is forest-born   And hath been tutored in the rudiments   Of many desperate studies by his uncle,
translation: But, my good lord, this boy was born in the forest and has been taught some dangerous magic by his uncle,

original: Whom he reports to be a great magician   Obscurèd in the circle of this forest.
translation: whom he says is a great magician living hidden within the boundaries of this forest.

original: There is sure another flood toward, and these couples  are coming to the ark. Here comes a pair of very strange beasts, which in all tongues are called fools.
translation: There must be another flood on its way, with all these couples coming two-by-two to Noah's ark. Here comes a pair of very strange beasts, which are called "fools" in every language.

original: Salutation and greeting to you all.
translation: Hello and greetings to you all.

original: Good my lord, bid him welcome. This is the  motley-minded gentleman that I have so often met in the  forest. He hath been a courtier, he swears.
translation: My good lord, welcome him. This is the jester gentleman I have met so often in the forest. He swears he used to be a courtier.

original: If any man doubt that, let him put me to my purgation.  I have trod a measure. I have flattered a lady.
translation: If any man doubts that, let him put me on trial. I have danced a step. I have flattered a lady.

original: I have  been politic with my friend, smooth with mine enemy. I  have undone three tailors. I have had four quarrels, and like to have fought one.
translation: I have been polite with my friends, and cunning with my enemy. I have ruined three tailors. I have had four quarrels, and almost had one fight.

original: And how was that ta'en up?
translation: And how was that one fight settled?

original: Faith, we met and found the quarrel was upon the  seventh cause.
translation: Well, we met and then found that the quarrel had reached the seventh cause.

original: How “seventh cause?”—Good my lord, like this fellow.
translation: What is the "seventh cause?"  My good lord, you will like this fellow.

original: I like him very well.
translation: I like him very well.

original: God 'ild you, sir. I desire you of the like. I press in here, sir, amongst the rest of the country copulatives, to swear and to forswear, according as marriage binds  and blood breaks.
translation: God bless you, sir. I wish the same compliment for you. Sir, I have pushed my way in here, among the rest of these country lovers, to be properly married, with binding vows to restrain erupting passion.

original: A poor virgin, sir, an ill-favored  thing, sir, but mine own. A poor humor of mine, sir, to  take that that no man else will. Rich honesty dwells  like a miser, sir, in a poor house, as your pearl in  your foul oyster.
translation: This poor virgin isn't a pretty thing, sir, but she's mine. It's a strange tendency of mine, sir, to take the thing that no one else wants. Sir, the treasure of chastity lives in the vessel of an ugly woman just like a rich man living in a shack, or a pearl lodged in a filthy oyster.

original: By my faith, he is very swift and sententious.
translation: I say, he's very quick-witted and full of pithy sayings.

original: According to the fool’s bolt, sir, and such dulcet  diseases.
translation: I have the fool's arrow, that sweet disease—wittiness—which is here one minute and gone the next.

original: But for the seventh cause. How did you find the quarrel on the seventh cause?
translation: But back to the "seventh cause." How did you find that your quarrel had reached the "seventh cause?"

original: Upon a lie seven times removed.—
translation: The argument went through seven stages.

original: Bear your body more  seeming, Audrey.—
translation: [To AUDREY]  Stand up straight, Audrey.

original: As thus, sir: I did dislike the cut of  a certain courtier’s beard. He sent me word if I said  his beard was not cut well, he was in the mind it was.
translation: [To JAQUES]  It was like this, sir: I disliked the way a certain courtier had cut his beard. He then sent me word that he wasn't concerned about my opinion of his beard.

original: This is called “the retort courteous.” If I sent him word again it was not well cut, he would send me word he cut it to please himself. This is called “the quip modest.”
translation: This stage is called "the courteous retort." If I were then to send him another message that his beard was not cut well, he would respond that he cut it to please himself, not me. This is called "the moderate quip."

original: If again it was not well cut, he disabled my judgment.  This is called “the reply churlish.” If again it was not well cut, he would answer I spake not true. This is  called “the reproof valiant.”
translation: If I repeated my insult again, he would try to disqualify my judgment. This is called "the rude reply." If I say yet again that his beard is not well cut, then he would say I wasn't speaking the truth. This is called "the brave retort."

original: If again it was not well  cut, he would say I lie. This is called “the  countercheck quarrelsome,” and so to “the lie  circumstantial” and “the lie direct.”
translation: If I repeated my insult again, he would call me a liar. This is called "the quarrelsome contradiction," and so on through to "the indirect lie" and "the direct lie."

original: And how oft did you say his beard was not well cut?
translation: And how many times did you say that his beard wasn't cut well?

original: I durst go no further than the lie circumstantial, nor  he durst not give me the lie direct, and so we measured  swords and parted.
translation: I didn't dare go past "the indirect lie," and he didn't dare go to "the direct lie." So we measured our swords, found ourselves equal, and parted ways.

original: Can you nominate in order now the degrees of the lie?
translation: Can you name those stages of an argument again, in order?

original: O sir, we quarrel in print, by the book, as you have  books for good manners. I will name you the degrees: the first, “the retort courteous;” the second, “the quip  modest;” the third, “the reply churlish;” the fourth,  “the reproof valiant;”
translation: Oh sir, we quarrel according to the rulebooks, just as you have rulebooks for good manners. I'll name the degrees again: the first is "the courteous retort;" the second is "the moderate quip;" the third is "the rude reply;" the fourth is "the brave retort;"

original: the fifth, “the countercheque  quarrelsome;” the sixth, “the lie with circumstance;”  the seventh, “the lie direct.” All these you may avoid  but the lie direct, and you may avoid that, too, with an “if.”
translation: the fifth is "the quarrelsome contradiction;" the sixth is "the indirect lie;" and the seventh is "the direct lie." But you can avoid all of these stages, even the seventh, by using an "if" properly.

original: I knew when seven justices could not take up a  quarrel, but when the parties were met themselves, one  of them thought but of an “if,” as: “If you said so,  then I said so.” And they shook hands and swore  brothers. Your “if” is the only peacemaker: much virtue  in “if.”
translation: I once heard of a quarrel that even seven judges couldn't settle. But when the two parties met on their own, one used an "if" and said" "If you said this, then I must have said that." And they shook hands and parted like brothers. "If" is the only peacemaker; there is much virtue in an "if."

original: Is not this a rare fellow, my lord? He’s as good at  anything and yet a fool.
translation: Isn't this a remarkable fellow, my lord? He's as smart as anything, and yet also a fool.

original: He uses his folly like a stalking-horse, and under the presentation of that he shoots his wit.
translation: He uses his foolishness to disguise himself while he hunts with the arrows of his wit.

original: Then is there mirth in heaven   When earthly things, made even,   Atone together.
translation: There is joy in heaven when earthly affairs are set right, and people are brought together.

original: Good duke, receive thy daughter.   Hymen from heaven brought her,
translation: [To DUKE SENIOR]  Good duke, receive your daughter. Hymen brought her from heaven—

original: Yea, brought her hither,   That thou mightst join her hand with his   Whose heart within her bosom is.
translation: yes, brought her here, that you might join her hand with that of the man whose heart resides within your daughter's chest.

original: To you I give myself, for I am yours.     To you I give myself, for I am yours.
translation: I give myself to you, for I am yours. [To ORLANDO] I give myself to you, for I am yours.

original: If there be truth in sight, you are my daughter.
translation: If my eyes do not deceive me, you are my daughter.

original: If there be truth in sight, you are my Rosalind.
translation: If my eyes do not deceive me, you are my Rosalind.

original: If sight and shape be true,  Why then, my love adieu.
translation: If my eyes and your womanly shape aren't deceiving me, why then, farewell to my love.

original: I’ll have no father, if you be not he.     I’ll have no husband, if you be not he,     Nor ne'er wed woman, if you be not she.
translation: If you won't be my father, then I'll have no father.[To ORLANDO] If you won't be my husband, then I'll have no husband.[To PHOEBE] If you won't be my wife, then I'll have no wife.

original: Peace, ho! I bar confusion.   'Tis I must make conclusion   Of these most strange events.
translation: Quiet now! I will clear up the confusion. I am the one who must bring the conclusion to these strange events.

original: Here’s eight that must take hands   To join in Hymen’s bands,   If truth holds true contents.
translation: Here before me are eight people who must join hands and be married, if the truths revealed to the couples reflect their genuine feelings.

original: [to ORLANDO and ROSALIND]   You and you no cross shall part.
translation: [To ORLANDO and ROSALIND]  No disagreement will ever part you.

original: [to OLIVER and CELIA]   You and you are heart in heart.
translation: [To OLIVER and CELIA]  Your two hearts are bound together.

original: [to PHOEBE]   You to his love must accord   Or have a woman to your lord.
translation: [To PHOEBE]  You must accept Silvius' love, or else be married to a woman.

original: [to TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY]   You and you are sure together   As the winter to foul weather.
translation: [To TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY]  The two of you are bound together, like winter with bad weather.

original: [to all]   Whiles a wedlock hymn we sing,   Feed yourselves with questioning,   That reason wonder may diminish   How thus we met, and these things finish.
translation: [To all the couples]  While we sing a wedding hymn, ask your questions, so that your surprise about how we all ended up here might fade, and we can bring these events to a close.

original: [sings]     Wedding is great Juno’s crown,   O blessèd bond of board and bed.   'Tis Hymen peoples every town.
translation: [Singing] Marriage is the crown of great  Juno , The blessed bond of a domestic home. It's Hymen who populates every town,

original: High wedlock then be honorèd.   Honor, high honor, and renown,     To Hymen, god of every town.
translation: So that holy marriage should be honored. Honor, high honor, and fame Should go to Hymen, the god of every town.

original: O my dear niece, welcome thou art to me, Even daughter, welcome in no less degree.
translation: Oh, my dear niece, you are welcome here, as welcome as if you were my own daughter.

original: I will not eat my word. Now thou art mine, Thy faith my fancy to thee doth combine.
translation: I won't break my promise. Now you are mine. Your faithfulness has won over my love.

original: Let me have audience for a word or two.   I am the second son of old Sir Rowland,   That bring these tidings to this fair assembly.
translation: Let me have your attention for a word or two. I am old Sir Rowland's middle son, and I come bringing news to this fine assembly.

original: Duke Frederick, hearing how that every day   Men of great worth resorted to this forest,   Addressed a mighty power, which were on foot   In his own conduct, purposely to take   His brother here and put him to the sword.
translation: Duke Frederick had heard that men of great worth were coming to this forest every day, so he assembled a powerful army to take this land and kill his brother.

original: And to the skirts of this wild wood he came,   Where, meeting with an old religious man,   After some question with him, was converted   Both from his enterprise and from the world,
translation: They came to the edge of this forest, and there Duke Frederick met an old religious man. They discussed things for a while, and ultimately the man convinced the duke to abandon his war, and (after a religious conversion) to retreat from the world.

original: His crown bequeathing to his banished brother,   And all their lands restored to them again   That were with him exiled. This to be true   I do engage my life.
translation: Duke Frederick is now giving his crown to his banished brother and restoring the lands back to the men he exiled. I pledge my life that all this is true.

original: Welcome, young man.   Thou offer’st fairly to thy brothers' wedding:   To one his lands withheld, and to the other   A land itself at large, a potent dukedom.
translation: Welcome, young man. You bring rich gifts to your brothers' wedding: to Oliver you bring his confiscated lands, and to Orlando you give a future dukedom, as he will inherit my lands.

original: —First, in this forest let us do those ends   That here were well begun and well begot,   And, after, every of this happy number   That have endured shrewd days and nights with us   Shall share the good of our returnèd fortune
translation: But first, let's finish the business we began in this forest. Afterward, everyone here who has endured hard days and nights with me will now share in the abundance of my returned fortune—

original: According to the measure of their states.   Meantime, forget this new-fall'n dignity,   And fall into our rustic revelry.   —Play, music.—
translation: each according to his own rank and status. But in the meantime, let's forget this newly acquired dignity, and have a country party. Play, music.

original: And you brides and bridegrooms all,   With measure heaped in joy to th' measures fall.
translation: [To the couples]  And you, brides and bridegrooms, dance with all the fullness of your joy.

original: Sir, by your patience: if I heard you rightly,  The duke hath put on a religious life And thrown into neglect the pompous court.
translation: Sir, with your permission: did I hear you correctly that the duke has given up the rich and glamorous life at court and become a religious hermit?

original: He hath.
translation: Yes, he has.

original: To him will I. Out of these convertites   There is much matter to be heard and learned.
translation: Then I will go to him. There is much to be heard and learned from such converts.

original: [to DUKE SENIOR]   You to your former honor I bequeath;   Your patience and your virtue well deserves it.
translation: [To DUKE SENIOR]  I leave you with all your former honor; you deserve it for your patience and virtue.

original: [to ORLANDO]   You to a love that your true faith doth merit.
translation: [To ORLANDO]  To you I leave the love that your faithfulness deserves.

original: [to OLIVER]   You to your land, and love, and great allies.
translation: [To OLIVER]  To you I leave your land, your love, and great allies.

original: [to SILVIUS]   You to a long and well-deservèd bed.
translation: [To SILVIUS]  To you I leave a well-deserved marriage bed after a long wait.

original: [to TOUCHSTONE]   And you to wrangling, for thy loving voyage   Is but for two months victualled.—
translation: [To TOUCHSTONE]  And to you I leave much arguing, for I suspect your adventure in love will last only two months at the most.

original: So to your pleasures.   I am for other than for dancing measures.
translation: So, everyone, return to your celebration. I am off to seek something other than dancing.

original: Stay, Jaques, stay.
translation: Stay, Jaques, stay.

original: To see no pastime I. What you would have  I’ll stay to know at your abandoned cave.
translation: This isn't relaxing or fun for me. I'll wait for you in your old cave if you need something from me.

original: Proceed, proceed. We’ll so begin these rites As we do trust they’ll end, in true delights.
translation: Carry on, carry on. We'll begin these wedding ceremonies the way we hope they'll end—in true delight.

original: It is not the fashion to see the lady the epilogue, but it is no more unhandsome than to see the lord the  prologue. If it be true that good wine needs no bush,  ’tis true that a good play needs no epilogue.
translation: You don't usually see the  actor  playing the heroine deliver the epilogue, but it's not uglier than seeing the hero deliver the prologue. If it's true that good wine doesn't need to be advertised with  ivy , then it should should also be true that a good play doesn't need an epilogue.

original: Yet to  good wine they do use good bushes, and good plays prove  the better by the help of good epilogues. What a case am I in, then, that am neither a good epilogue nor cannot  insinuate with you in the behalf of a good play.
translation: And yet people do use good ivy to advertise for good wine, and good plays are improved with the help of good epilogues. I'm in a predicament, then, as I don't have a good epilogue. Nor am I confident that this was a good play.

original: I am  not furnished like a beggar; therefore to beg will not  become me. My way is to conjure you, and I’ll begin with the women. I charge you, O women, for the love you bear to men, to like as much of this play as please you.
translation: I'm not dressed as a beggar, so it wouldn't be right for me to beg. So, then, I'll enchant you, and I'll begin with the women. Oh, women, in the name of your love for men, I tell you to like as much of this play as you want.

original: And I charge you, O men, for the love you bear to women—as  I perceive by your simpering, none of you hates  them—that between you and the women the play may please.
translation: And you, oh men, in the name of your love for women—and I can see from your silly smiles that none of you hates women—I tell you to like the other parts of the play.

original: If I were a woman, I would kiss as many of you as had  beards that pleased me, complexions that liked me, and  breaths that I defied not.
translation: If I were actually a woman, I would kiss as many of you men as had beards that pleased me, complexions that I liked, and breaths that weren't bad.

original: And I am sure as many as have good beards, or good faces, or sweet breaths will, for  my kind offer, when I make curtsy, bid me farewell.
translation: And for the sake of my kind offer, I'm sure that all of you who  do  have good beards, or good faces, or sweet-smelling breaths will, sending me off with a round of applause when I curtsy, say goodbye.

original: Who’s there?
translation: Who’s there?

original: Nay, answer me. Stand and unfold yourself.
translation: No, you answer me. Stop and reveal yourself.

original: Long live the king!
translation: Long live the king!

original: Barnardo?
translation: Barnardo?

original: He.
translation: Yes, me.

original: You come most carefully upon your hour.
translation: You arrived right on schedule.

original: ‘Tis now struck twelve. Get thee to bed, Francisco.
translation: The clock just struck twelve. Go to bed, Francisco.

original: For this relief much thanks. ‘Tis bitter cold, And I am sick at heart.
translation: Thanks for relieving me. It’s bitterly cold, and I’m miserable.

original: Have you had quiet guard?
translation: Has your guard duty been quiet?

original: Not a mouse stirring.
translation: Not a mouse stirred.

original: Well, good night. If you do meet Horatio and Marcellus, The rivals of my watch, bid them make haste.
translation: Well, good night. If you see Horatio and Marcellus—who are going to stand guard with me—tell them to hurry.

original: I think I hear them.—Stand, ho! Who’s there?
translation: I think I hear them. Stop! Who’s there?

original: Friends to this ground.
translation: Friends of this country.

original: And liegemen to the Dane.
translation: And loyal servants of the Danish king.

original: Give you good night.
translation: Good night to you.

original: O, farewell, honest soldier. Who hath relieved you?
translation: Oh, goodbye, honorable soldier. Who’s relieved you?

original: Barnardo has my place. Give you good night.
translation: Barnardo’s taken my place. Good night.

original: Holla, Barnardo.
translation: Hello, Barnardo.

original: Say what, is Horatio there?
translation: Say, is Horatio here too?

original: A piece of him.
translation: More or less.

original: Welcome, Horatio.—Welcome, good Marcellus.
translation: Welcome, Horatio. Welcome, Marcellus.

original: What, has this thing appeared again tonight?
translation: So, has the thing appeared again tonight?

original: I have seen nothing.
translation: I haven’t seen anything.

original: Horatio says ’tis but our fantasy   And will not let belief take hold of him   Touching this dreaded sight twice seen of us.
translation: Horatio says it’s all our imagination, and he won’t let himself believe in this awful thing we’ve now seen twice.

original: Therefore I have entreated him along   With us to watch the minutes of this night,   That if again this apparition come   He may approve our eyes and speak to it.
translation: I asked him to join us in our guard duty tonight, so that if the ghost appears he can confirm what we see and speak to it.

original: Tush, tush, ’twill not appear.
translation: Oh, come now. It’s not going to appear.

original: Sit down a while   And let us once again assail your ears,   That are so fortified against our story,
translation: Sit down for a while, and let us tell you again the story you refuse to believe,

original: What we have two nights seen.
translation: about what we’ve seen the last two nights.

original: Well, sit we down, And let us hear Barnardo speak of this.
translation: Sure, let’s sit down and listen to Barnardo tell us about it.

original: Last night of all,   When yond same star that’s westward from the pole   Had made his course t’ illume that part of heaven   Where now it burns,
translation: Last night, when that star to the west of the North Star had moved across the heavens to brighten that spot in the sky where it’s shining now,

original: Marcellus and myself,   The bell then beating one—
translation: at precisely one o’clock, Marcellus and I—

original: Peace, break thee off. Look where it comes again!
translation: Quiet, stop talking! Look, it’s come again.

original: In the same figure like the king that’s dead.
translation: Looking exactly like the dead king.

original: Thou art a scholar. Speak to it, Horatio.
translation: You’re well-educated. Speak to it, Horatio.

original: Looks it not like the king? Mark it, Horatio.
translation: Doesn’t he look like the king, Horatio?

original: Most like. It harrows me with fear and wonder.
translation: Exactly like him. It fills me with fear and wonder.

original: It would be spoke to.
translation: It wants us to speak to it.

original: Question it, Horatio.
translation: Ask it something, Horatio.

original: What art thou that usurp’st this time of night   Together with that fair and warlike form   In which the majesty of buried Denmark   Did sometimes march?
translation: Who are you, disturbing this time of night, and appearing just like the dead king of Denmark, dressed in his battle armor?

original: By heaven, I charge thee, speak.
translation: By God, I order you to speak.

original: It is offended.
translation: You’ve offended it.

original: See, it stalks away.
translation: Look, it’s moving away.

original: Stay! Speak, speak! I charge thee, speak!
translation: Stay! Speak! Speak! I order you, speak!

original: ‘Tis gone and will not answer.
translation: It’s gone, and won’t answer.

original: How now, Horatio? You tremble and look pale. Is not this something more than fantasy? What think you on ’t?
translation: How are you, Horatio? You’re pale and trembling. Isn’t this something more than just our imagination? What do you think about it?

original: Before my God, I might not this believe Without the sensible and true avouch Of mine own eyes.
translation: I swear by God, I would never have believed this if I hadn't seen it with my own eyes.

original: Is it not like the king?
translation: Doesn’t it look like the king?

original: As thou art to thyself.   Such was the very armour he had on   When he the ambitious Norway combated.
translation: As much as you look like yourself. That was the same armor the king wore when he fought the ambitious king of Norway.

original: So frowned he once when, in an angry parle,   He smote the sledded Polacks on the ice.   ‘Tis strange.
translation: And the ghost frowned just like the king did once when he fought the Poles, who traveled on the ice in sleds. It’s eerie.

original: Thus twice before, and jump at this dead hour, With martial stalk hath he gone by our watch.
translation: It’s happened like this twice before, always at this time of night. Dressed like a warrior, the ghost walks by us at our guard post.

original: In what particular thought to work I know not, But in the gross and scope of mine opinion This bodes some strange eruption to our state.
translation: I don’t know exactly what this means, but I have a general feeling it signals that something bad is about to happen to our country.

original: Good now, sit down and tell me, he that knows,   Why this same strict and most observant watch   So nightly toils the subject of the land,
translation: Speaking of that, let’s sit down so that, whoever knows about it, can tell me why we’ve been keeping such a strict schedule of nightly watches.

original: And why such daily cast of brazen cannon   And foreign mart for implements of war,   Why such impress of shipwrights, whose sore task   Does not divide the Sunday from the week.
translation: And why we’ve been building so many cannons, and buying so many weapons from other countries. And why the shipbuilders are kept so busy that they don’t even rest on Sunday.

original: What might be toward, that this sweaty haste   Doth make the night joint laborer with the day?   Who is ’t that can inform me?
translation: What’s coming that forces us to work day and night in this way? Who can tell me?

original: That can I.   At least, the whisper goes so: our last king,   Whose image even but now appeared to us,   Was, as you know, by Fortinbras of Norway,   Thereto pricked on by a most emulate pride,
translation: I can do that. At least, I can tell you the rumors: the greatness of our former king—whose ghost just now appeared to us—inspired the competitive pride of King Fortinbras of Norway.

original: Dared to the combat; in which our valiant Hamlet   (For so this side of our known world esteemed him)   Did slay this Fortinbras, who by a sealed compact   Well ratified by law and heraldry,
translation: Fortinbras challenged him to hand-to-hand combat. During that fight, our courageous  Hamlet  (as we Danes thought of him) killed old King Fortinbras, who—on the basis of a signed and sealed agreement and in full accordance with the law and rules of combat—

original: Did forfeit, with his life, all those his lands   Which he stood seized of to the conqueror,
translation: surrendered, along with his life, all the lands he possessed to his conqueror.

original: Against the which a moiety competent   Was gagèd by our king, which had returned   To the inheritance of Fortinbras   Had he been vanquisher, as, by the same covenant   And carriage of the article designed,   His fell to Hamlet.
translation: By that same agreement, our king bet lands of equal value that he would have had to give up had he been defeated.

original: Now, sir, young Fortinbras,   Of unimprovèd mettle hot and full,   Hath in the skirts of Norway here and there   Sharked up a list of lawless resolutes,
translation: Now, Fortinbras’ son, young Fortinbras, who is daring but has yet to prove himself, has hastily gathered a group lawless brutes.

original: For food and diet, to some enterprise   That hath a stomach in ’t, which is no other—   As it doth well appear unto our state—   But to recover of us, by strong hand   And terms compulsatory, those foresaid lands   So by his father lost.
translation: For no pay other than food on the outskirts of Norway. They’re willing to give their courage to the effort of forcefully regaining the lands the elder Fortinbras lost.

original: And this, I take it,   Is the main motive of our preparations,   The source of this our watch, and the chief head   Of this posthaste and rummage in the land.
translation: I believe this is the reason that we’ve been sent on guard duty, and the primary source of all the recent hustle and bustle in Denmark.

original: I think it be no other but e’en so.
translation: I think that’s right.

original: Well may it sort that this portentous figure   Comes armèd through our watch so like the king   That was and is the question of these wars.
translation: It makes sense that this ghost of the late king would haunt our guard duty now, since he was such an important part of these wars.

original: A mote it is to trouble the mind’s eye.   In the most high and palmy state of Rome,   A little ere the mightiest Julius fell,   The graves stood tenantless and the sheeted dead   Did squeak and gibber in the Roman streets
translation: The ghost is definitely something to worry about, like a speck of dust bothering your eye. In the powerful Roman Empire, just before the mighty emperor Julius Caesar was assassinated, the graves stood empty while the ghostly dead ran through the streets of Rome, squeaking and delirious.

original: As stars with trains of fire and dews of blood,   Disasters in the sun,   and the moist star   Upon whose influence Neptune’s empire stands   Was sick almost to doomsday with eclipse.
translation: Shooting stars streaked across the sky, blood fell along with the morning dew, and omens of disaster appeared on the sun.  The moon, which controls the tides of the sea, was so eclipsed that it almost disappeared completely.

original: And even the like precurse of feared events,   As harbingers preceding still the fates   And prologue to the omen coming on,   Have heaven and earth together demonstrated   Unto our climatures and countrymen.
translation: We’ve had similar signs of disaster, as if heaven and earth have joined together to warn us of what’s to come.

original: But soft, behold! Lo, where it comes again. I’ll cross it though it blast me.—Stay, illusion!
translation: Wait, look! It has returned. I’ll meet it if it’s the last thing I do.

original: If thou hast any sound or use of voice,   Speak to me.   If there be any good thing to be done   That may to thee do ease and grace to me,   Speak to me.
translation: If you have a voice or can make sounds, speak to me. If there’s anything that I can do that might bring peace to you and honor to me, speak to me.

original: If thou art privy to thy country’s fate,   Which happily foreknowing may avoid,   Oh, speak!
translation: If you know something abut your country’s fate—which we could avoid if we knew about it—then, oh, speak!

original: Or if thou hast uphoarded in thy life   Extorted treasure in the womb of earth,   For which, they say, you spirits oft walk in death,   Speak of it. Stay and speak!
translation: Or if you have a treasure buried somewhere in the earth—which they say often makes ghosts restless—then speak of it. Stay and speak!

original: —Stop it, Marcellus.
translation: Don’t let it leave, Marcellus.

original: Shall I strike at it with my partisan?
translation: Should I hit it with my spear?

original: Do, if it will not stand.
translation: Yes, if it doesn’t stand still.

original: ‘Tis here.
translation: It’s here.

original: ‘Tis here.
translation: It’s here.

original: ‘Tis gone.   We do it wrong, being so majestical,   To offer it the show of violence,
translation: It’s gone. We were wrong to threaten it with violence, since it looked so kingly.

original: For it is, as the air, invulnerable,   And our vain blows malicious mockery.
translation: And, like the air, we couldn't hurt it. Our useless blows amounted to cruel taunts.

original: It was about to speak when the cock crew.
translation: It was about to say something when the rooster crowed.

original: And then it started like a guilty thing   Upon a fearful summons.
translation: And then it looked startled, like a guilty person summoned to appear in court.

original: I have heard   The cock, that is the trumpet to the morn,   Doth with his lofty and shrill-sounding throat   Awake the god of day,
translation: I’ve heard that the rooster—which calls to signal the coming morning—awakens the god of day,

original: and, at his warning,   Whether in sea or fire, in earth or air,   Th’ extravagant and erring spirit hies   To his confine, and of the truth herein   This present object made probation.
translation: and makes all wandering ghosts—wherever they are—hurry back to their hiding places. What we’ve just seen is proof of that.

original: It faded on the crowing of the cock.   Some say that ever ‘gainst that season comes   Wherein our Saviour’s birth is celebrated,   The bird of dawning singeth all night long.
translation: It faded away when the rooster crowed. Some people say that just before Christmas the rooster crows all night long, so that no ghost dares go wandering, and the night is safe for all.

original: And then, they say, no spirit dare stir abroad.   The nights are wholesome. Then no planets strike,   No fairy takes, nor witch hath power to charm,   So hallowed and so gracious is that time.
translation: Then, on that night, no dark fates control us, no fairy can cast a spell on us, and witches cannot hurt us with their charms. That’s how holy and blessed Christmas is.

original: So have I heard and do in part believe it.   But look, the morn, in russet mantle clad,   Walks o’er the dew of yon high eastward hill.
translation: I’ve heard the same thing, and partially believe it. But look, the red glow of morning is breaking beyond that hill in the east.

original: Break we our watch up, and by my advice,   Let us impart what we have seen tonight   Unto young Hamlet, for, upon my life,   This spirit, dumb to us, will speak to him.
translation: Let’s end our patrol, and go tell young Hamlet what we’ve seen tonight. I’d bet my life that this ghost, which will not speak to us, will speak to him.

original: Do you consent we shall acquaint him with it,   As needful in our loves, fitting our duty?
translation: Do you agree that we should tell Hamlet, that we owe it to him to him out of our duty and our love?

original: Let’s do ’t, I pray, and I this morning know Where we shall find him most conveniently.
translation: Let’s do it. And I know where we can find him this morning.

original: Though yet of Hamlet our dear brother’s death   The memory be green, and that it us befitted   To bear our hearts in grief and our whole kingdom   To be contracted in one brow of woe,
translation: Though my memories of my brother Hamlet are still fresh—and though it was proper for me and our entire kingdom to grieve for him—life doesn’t stop.

original: Yet so far hath discretion fought with nature   That we with wisest sorrow think on him   Together with remembrance of ourselves.
translation: And so while we must remember to mourn for him, it is also wise to remember our own happiness.

original: Therefore our sometime sister, now our queen,   Th’ imperial jointress to this warlike state,   Have we—as ’twere with a defeated joy,   With an auspicious and a dropping eye,   With mirth in funeral and with dirge in marriage,   In equal scale weighing delight and dole—   Taken to wife.
translation: Therefore—with a sad joy; with one eye merry and the other crying; with laughter at a funeral and grieving at a wedding; with equal measures of happiness and sadness—I have married my former sister-in-law and made her my queen.

original: Nor have we herein barred   Your better wisdoms, which have freely gone   With this affair along. For all, our thanks.
translation: In this marriage, I know I’ve done exactly what all of you have been advising me to do all along. To all of you, my thanks.

original: Now follows that you know. Young Fortinbras,   Holding a weak supposal of our worth   Or thinking by our late dear brother’s death   Our state to be disjoint and out of frame,   Colleaguèd with the dream of his advantage,
translation: Now, let’s move on to news that you all know: young Fortinbras, dreaming of glory and thinking that I am weak—or perhaps that the death of my brother has thrown our country into chaos

original: He hath not failed to pester us with message   Importing the surrender of those lands   Lost by his father, with all bonds of law,   To our most valiant brother. So much for him.
translation: —continues to bother me with demands that I surrender the lands that his father lost to my brother when he was alive. That’s the news on Fortinbras.

original: Now for ourself and for this time of meeting
translation: As for me and this meeting, here’s the story:

original: Thus much the business is: we have here writ   To Norway, uncle of young Fortinbras—   Who, impotent and bedrid, scarcely hears   Of this his nephew’s purpose
translation: I’ve written to the King of Norway—Fortinbras’ uncle—a weak and bedridden old man who’s barely heard a thing about his nephew’s aims.

original: —to suppress   His further gait herein, in that the levies,   The lists, and full proportions are all made   Out of his subject;
translation: I’ve told the Norwegian King to put a halt to Fortinbras’ plans, since all of Fortinbras’ troops are Norwegian.

original: In that and all things will we show our duty.
translation: We’ll show our loyalty to you in that and all other ways.

original: We doubt it nothing. Heartily farewell.
translation: I do not doubt it. A fond goodbye to you.

original: And now, Laertes, what’s the news with you?   You told us of some suit. What is ’t, Laertes?
translation: And now, Laertes, what’s your news? You mentioned that you have a favor to ask of me. What is it, Laertes?

original: You cannot speak of reason to the Dane   And lose your voice. What wouldst thou beg, Laertes,   That shall not be my offer, not thy asking?
translation: You’ll never be wasting your words by making a reasonable request of the King of Denmark. What could you possibly ask for that I wouldn’t give you?

original: The head is not more native to the heart,   The hand more instrumental to the mouth,   Than is the throne of Denmark to thy father.   What wouldst thou have, Laertes?
translation: Your father is as vital to the Danish throne as the head is to the heart, or the hand to the mouth. What do you want, Laertes?

original: My dread lord,   Your leave and favor to return to France,
translation: My powerful lord, I’d like your permission to go back to France.

original: From whence though willingly I came to Denmark   To show my duty in your coronation,   Yet now, I must confess, that duty done,   My thoughts and wishes bend again toward France
translation: Though I came willingly to Denmark to show my loyalty at your coronation, now that my duty is done, I must admit that my thoughts are once more directed toward France.

original: And bow them to your gracious leave and pardon.
translation: I hope you will give me your permission to go.

original: Have you your father’s leave? What says Polonius?
translation: Do you have your father’s permission? What does Polonius say?

original: He hath, my lord, wrung from me my slow leave   By laborsome petition, and at last   Upon his will I sealed my hard consent.
translation: My lord, he has won my permission by asking me over and over again so that, finally, I reluctantly gave my approval.

original: I do beseech you, give him leave to go.
translation: I ask you to please give him permission to go.

original: Take thy fair hour, Laertes. Time be thine, And thy best graces spend it at thy will.— But now, my cousin Hamlet, and my son—
translation: Leave when you like, Laertes. Your time is your own, to be spent however you want. And now, Hamlet, my nephew and my son—

original: A little more than kin and less than kind.
translation: I’m more closely related to you than I used to be, but without any feelings of affection.

original: How is it that the clouds still hang on you?
translation: Why are you so gloomy that it seems like you are covered by clouds?

original: Not so, my lord. I am too much i’ the sun.
Good Hamlet, cast thy nighted color off,   And let thine eye look like a friend on Denmark.
translation: Dearest Hamlet, stop wearing these black clothes, and look upon the King of Denmark as a friend.

original: Do not forever with thy vailèd lids   Seek for thy noble father in the dust.
translation: You can’t spend your whole life with your eyes aimed down at the ground, looking for your noble father in the dust.

original: Thou know’st ’tis common. All that lives must die,   Passing through nature to eternity.
translation: You know it’s common. Everything that lives must die, passing from nature to heaven.

original: Ay, madam, it is common.
translation: Yes, madam, it is common.

original: If it be, Why seems it so particular with thee?
translation: If that’s so, why does it seem like such an issue to you?

original: “Seems,” madam? Nay, it is. I know not “seems.”
translation: “Seem,” mother? No, it  is . I don’t know the meaning of “seems.”

original: ‘Tis not alone my inky cloak, good mother,   Nor customary suits of solemn black,   Nor windy suspiration of forced breath,   No, nor the fruitful river in the eye,   Nor the dejected ‘havior of the visage,   Together with all forms, moods, shapes of grief,   That can denote me truly.
translation: Good mother, the black clothes I wear each day, my heavy sighs, the tears from my eyes, the sadness visible in my face, or any other show of grief cannot capture what I actually feel.

original: These indeed “seem,”   For they are actions that a man might play.   But I have that within which passeth show,   These but the trappings and the suits of woe.
translation: All these things “seem” like grief, since they’re just what a person would do to act like they were grieving in a play. But inside of me I have real grief, of which these clothes and displays of grief are just an outward representation.

original: ‘Tis sweet and commendable in your nature, Hamlet,   To give these mourning duties to your father.   But you must know your father lost a father,   That father lost, lost his, and the survivor bound   In filial obligation for some term   To do obsequious sorrow.
translation: Hamlet, it is sweet and good that you mourn like this for your father. But you must also remember that your father lost his father, who in turn lost his father, and each time the son had a duty to mourn for his father for a certain time.

original: But to persever   In obstinate condolement is a course   Of impious stubbornness. ‘Tis unmanly grief.   It shows a will most incorrect to heaven,   A heart unfortified, a mind impatient,   An understanding simple and unschooled.
translation: But to continue to mourn out of sheer stubbornness is blasphemous. It isn’t manly. It does not fit with God’s desires, and it indicates a too-soft heart, an undisciplined mind, and a general lack of knowledge.

original: For what we know must be and is as common   As any the most vulgar thing to sense,   Why should we in our peevish opposition   Take it to heart? Fie! ‘Tis a fault to heaven,   A fault against the dead, a fault to nature,
translation: When we know that something must eventually happen—and that it happens to everyone—why should we get it into our heads to oppose it? Indeed! Acting this way is a crime against heaven, a crime against the dead, a crime against nature.

original: To reason most absurd, whose common theme   Is death of fathers, and who still hath cried,   From the first corse till he that died today,   “This must be so.” We pray you, throw to earth   This unprevailing woe, and think of us   As of a father.
translation: To a reasonable mind, it is absurd, since the death of fathers—from the first corpse until the most recent—is an inescapable theme of life. I ask you, give up your ceaseless mourning, and think of me as your new father.

original: For let the world take note,   You are the most immediate to our throne,   And with no less nobility of love   Than that which dearest father bears his son   Do I impart toward you.
translation: Let the world understand: you are the next in line for the throne, and I feel as much love for you as any father feels for his son.

original: For your intent   In going back to school in Wittenberg,   It is most retrograde to our desire.   And we beseech you, bend you to remain   Here in the cheer and comfort of our eye,   Our chiefest courtier, cousin, and our son.
translation: As for your desire to return to Wittenberg, it’s not what I would want. So I beg you, please give in to my request and remain here, where you can bring joy and comfort—as the highest-ranking member of my court, my nephew, and now my son.

original: Let not thy mother lose her prayers, Hamlet. I pray thee, stay with us. Go not to Wittenberg.
translation: Please don’t let my prayers be in vain, Hamlet. I beg you, stay with us. Don’t return to Wittenberg.

original: I shall in all my best obey you, madam.
translation: I’ll obey you as best I can, madam.

original: Why, ’tis a loving and a fair reply.   Be as ourself in Denmark.
translation: That loving response is what I hoped for: stay with us in Denmark.

original: Oh, that this too, too sullied flesh would melt,   Thaw, and resolve itself into a dew,   Or that the Everlasting had not fixed   His canon ‘gainst self-slaughter!
translation: Oh, if only my dirty flesh would melt and then evaporate into a dew, or that God had not outlawed suicide.

original: O God, God!   How weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable   Seem to me all the uses of this world!   Fie on ’t, ah fie! ‘Tis an unweeded garden   That grows to seed.
translation: Oh God, God! How tired, stale, dull, and worthless all of life seems to me. Curse it! Yes, curse it! It’s like an untended garden, growing wild. Nasty, gross weeds cover it completely.

original: Things rank and gross in nature   Possess it merely. That it should come to this.   But two months dead—nay, not so much, not two.   So excellent a king, that was to this   Hyperion to a satyr.
translation: That it has come to this point. My father, dead for just two months—no, not even that much, not two. A king so excellent, in comparison to Claudius he was like a god compared to a  goat .
