original: So loving to my mother   That he might not beteem the winds of heaven   Visit her face too roughly.—Heaven and earth,   Must I remember? Why, she would hang on him   As if increase of appetite had grown   By what it fed on,
translation: My father was so loving toward my mother that he would not let the wind blow too hard on her face. Heaven above, must I remember? She would hang on his arm, as if the more time she spent with him, the more she wanted to be with him.

original: and yet, within a month—   Let me not think on ’t. Frailty, thy name is woman!—   A little month, or ere those shoes were old   With which she followed my poor father’s body,   Like Niobe, all tears.
translation: And yet, within a month of my father’s death—no, don’t think about it. Women, curse your weakness!—in just a month, before she had even broken in the shoes she wore to his funeral, weeping endlessly

original: Why she, even she—   O God, a beast that wants discourse of reason   Would have mourned longer!—married with my uncle,   My father’s brother, but no more like my father   Than I to Hercules.
translation: —oh, God, a wild beast would have mourned longer than she did!—she married my uncle, my father’s brother, who’s no more like my father than I’m like  Hercules .

original: Within a month,   Ere yet the salt of most unrighteous tears   Had left the flushing in her gallèd eyes,   She married. O most wicked speed, to post   With such dexterity to incestuous sheets!
translation: Within a month of my father’s death—before the salt from her crocodile tears had washed out of her red eyes—she remarried. Oh, what wicked speed! To jump so quickly into a bed of incest!

original: It is not nor it cannot come to good,   But break, my heart, for I must hold my tongue.
translation: It is not good, and will not lead to any good either. But my heart must break in silence, because I must remain quiet

original: Hail to your lordship.
translation: Hello, my lord.

original: I am glad to see you well.— Horatio? Or I do forget myself?
translation: I’m pleased to see you doing well. You are Horatio, right? Or am I mistaken?

original: The same, my lord, and your poor servant ever.
translation: I am Horatio, my lord, your loyal servant forever.

original: Sir, my good friend, I’ll change that name with you. And what make you from Wittenberg, Horatio?— Marcellus!
translation: Sir, my good friend, not my servant. Why are you not at Wittenberg, Horatio?

original: My good lord.
translation: My good lord.

original: I am very glad to see you.  [to BARNARDO] Good even, sir.    —But what, in faith, make  you from Wittenberg?
translation: So nice to see you.

original: A truant disposition, good my lord.
translation: I have the heart of a dropout, my good lord.

original: I would not hear your enemy say so,   Nor shall you do mine ear that violence,   To make it truster of your own report   Against yourself.
translation: I wouldn’t let your enemies say that about you, so I won’t let you say it—or believe you if you did.

original: I know you are no truant.   But what is your affair in Elsinore?   We’ll teach you to drink deep ere you depart.
translation: I know you’d never drop out. So why are you here at Elsinore? I’ll teach you to drink deeply before you leave.

original: My lord, I came to see your father’s funeral.
translation: My lord, I came to attend your father’s funeral.

original: I pray thee, do not mock me, fellow student. I think it was to see my mother’s wedding.
translation: Please, don’t make fun of me, my fellow student. I think you came to see my mother’s wedding.

original: Indeed, my lord, it followed hard upon.
translation: Well, my lord, it’s true the wedding came soon after the funeral.

original: Thrift, thrift, Horatio! The funeral baked meats   Did coldly furnish forth the marriage tables.
translation: It’s called being frugal, Horatio. The leftovers from the funeral dinner made a great cold lunch for the wedding.

original: Would I had met my dearest foe in heaven   Or ever I had seen that day, Horatio.   My father—methinks I see my father.
translation: Horatio, I would rather have met my worst enemy in heaven than have lived to see that awful day! My father—I think I see my father.

original: Where, my lord?
translation: Where, sir?

original: In my mind’s eye, Horatio.
translation: In my imagination, Horatio.

original: I saw him once. He was a goodly king.
translation: I saw him once. He was an impressive king.

original: He was a man. Take him for all in all. I shall not look upon his like again.
translation: He was a great man, perfect in all things. I’ll never see his equal again.

original: My lord, I think I saw him yesternight.
translation: My lord, I think I saw him last night.

original: Saw who?
translation: Saw who?

original: My lord, the king your father.
translation: The king your father, my lord.

original: The king my father?!
translation: The king my father?!

original: Season your admiration for a while   With an attent ear, till I may deliver,
translation: Hold back your excitement for a while, and listen while I tell you about this astonishing thing,

original: Upon the witness of these gentlemen,   This marvel to you.
translation: with these two gentlemen as my witnesses.

original: For God’s love, let me hear.
translation: For God’s sake, let me hear it.

original: Two nights together had these gentlemen,   Marcellus and Barnardo, on their watch,   In the dead waste and middle of the night,   Been thus encountered: a figure like your father,   Armed at point exactly, cap-à-pie,
translation: For the last two nights, these two guardsmen—Marcellus and Barnardo—during their watch in the middle of the night, encountered a figure that looked very much like your father, dressed in full armor from head to toe.

original: Appears before them and with solemn march   Goes slow and stately by them. Thrice he walked   By their oppressed and fear-surprisèd eyes   Within his truncheon’s length, whilst they, distilled   Almost to jelly with the act of fear,   Stand dumb and speak not to him.
translation: It appeared in front of them and marched by them, slowly and with dignity, at no greater distance than the length of his staff. He walked by them three times as they stood shaking in fear like jelly, too shocked to speak.

original: This to me   In dreadful secrecy impart they did,   And I with them the third night kept the watch,   Where—as they had delivered, both in time,   Form of the thing, each word made true and good—   The apparition comes.
translation: They told me all about what they’d seen, swearing me to secrecy. On the third night, I stood guard with them, and the ghost appeared, just when they said it would and looking just as they had described.

original: I knew your father.   These hands are not more like.
translation: I knew your father. The ghost looked as much like him as my hands look like each other.

original: But where was this?
translation: Where did this happen?

original: My lord, upon the platform where we watch.
translation: On the platform where we stand guard, my lord.

original: Did you not speak to it?
translation: Didn’t you talk to it?

original: My lord, I did,   But answer made it none.
translation: I did, my lord. But it didn’t answer.

original: Yet once methought   It lifted up its head and did address   Itself to motion, like as it would speak.   But even then the morning cock crew loud,
translation: Though once I thought that it raised its head as if it were about to speak, but just then the rooster began to crow,

original: And at the sound it shrunk in haste away   And vanished from our sight.
translation: and at the sound the ghost flinched and then vanished from sight.

original: ‘Tis very strange.
translation: That’s very strange.

original: As I do live, my honored lord, ’tis true. And we did think it writ down in our duty To let you know of it.
translation: I swear on my life that it’s true, my lord. We thought that it was our duty to tell you about it.

original: Indeed, indeed, sirs, but this troubles me. Hold you the watch tonight?
translation: Yes, you’re right. but I’m disturbed by this story. Do you have guard duty again tonight?

original: We do, my lord.
translation: We do, my lord.

original: Armed, say you?
translation: The ghost was armed, you say?

original: Armed, my lord.
translation: Armed, my lord.

original: From top to toe?
translation: From head to toe?

original: My lord, from head to foot.
translation: From head to toe, my lord.

original: Then saw you not his face?
translation: Then you didn’t see his face?

original: Oh yes, my lord. He wore his beaver up.
translation: Oh, yes, we could, my lord. He had his helmet visor up.

original: What, looked he frowningly?
translation: Did he look angry?

original: A countenance more In sorrow than in anger.
translation: His expression looked more sad than angry.

original: Pale or red?
translation: Was he pale or flushed?

original: Nay, very pale.
translation: Very pale.

original: And fixed his eyes upon you?
translation: Did he look straight at you?

original: Most constantly.
translation: The entire time.

original: I would I had been there.
translation: I wish I’d been there.

original: It would have much amazed you.
translation: You would have been shocked and amazed.

original: Very like. Stayed it long?
translation: I’m sure I would have. Did it stay a long time?

original: While one with moderate haste might tell a hundred.
translation: As long as it would take a person to count to one hundred at a moderate speed.

original: Longer, longer.
translation: No, longer.

original: Not when I saw ’t.
translation: Not the time I saw it.

original: His beard was grizzled, no?
translation: His beard was gray, right?

original: It was, as I have seen it in his life, A sable silvered.
translation: It was, just as it looked when I saw it when he was alive: dark brown with silver streaks.

original: I will watch tonight. Perchance ‘Twill walk again.
translation: I’ll join you for guard duty tonight. Perhaps the ghost will appear again.

original: I warrant it will.
translation: I bet it will.

original: If it assume my noble father’s person,   I’ll speak to it, though Hell itself should gape   And bid me hold my peace.
translation: If it looks like my noble father, I’ll speak to it, even if Hell itself opens up and tells me to be quiet.

original: I pray you all,   If you have hitherto concealed this sight,   Let it be tenable in your silence still.   And whatsoever else shall hap tonight,   Give it an understanding, but no tongue.
translation: I beg all of you, if you’ve kept this a secret so far, continue to be silent. And whatever happens tonight, think about it, but don’t discuss it with anyone.

original: I will requite your loves. So fare you well.   Upon the platform, ’twixt eleven and twelve,   I’ll visit you.
translation: I’ll do the same. So goodbye. I’ll come see you on the guards’ platform between eleven and twelve.

original: Our duty to your honor.
translation: We’ll do our duty to your Honor.

original: Your loves, as mine to you. Farewell.
translation: Instead give me your friendship, just as I give mine to you. Goodbye.

original: My father’s spirit in arms. All is not well.   I doubt some foul play. Would the night were come!
translation: My father’s ghost, wearing armor. This is not good. I suspect some foul play. I wish it were night already!

original: Till then sit still, my soul. Foul deeds will rise,   Though all the earth o’erwhelm them, to men’s eyes.
translation: Until then, I must stay calm. Bad deeds will always be revealed, no matter how deeply they’ve been buried.

original: My necessaries are embarked. Farewell.
translation: My belongings are on the ship. Goodbye.

original: And, sister, as the winds give benefit   And convey is assistant, do not sleep,   But let me hear from you.
translation: And, sister, as long as the winds are blowing and ships are traveling, make sure to send me news.

original: Do you doubt that?
translation: Do you doubt I will?

original: For Hamlet and the trifling of his favor,   Hold it a fashion and a toy in blood,
translation: As for Hamlet and the attention he’s given you, consider it no more than a passing thing—the product of his hot-blooded youth.

original: A violet in the youth of primy nature,   Forward, not permanent, sweet, not lasting,   The perfume and suppliance of a minute.   No more.
translation: Like a violet, it’s sweet and beautiful, but won’t last more than a single minute.

original: No more but so?
translation: No more than a single minute?

original: Think it no more.   For nature, crescent, does not grow alone   In thews and bulk, but, as this temple waxes,   The inward service of the mind and soul   Grows wide withal. Perhaps he loves you now,   And now no soil nor cautel doth besmirch   The virtue of his will, but you must fear.
translation: Think of it that way, at least. When a youth becomes a man, it’s not just his body that grows in size. So do the responsibilities that weigh on his mind and soul. Perhaps he loves you now, and currently nothing stains the purity of that love. But you must take into account that he cannot make his own decisions.

original: His greatness weighed, his will is not his own,   For he himself is subject to his birth.   He may not, as unvalued persons do,   Carve for himself, for on his choice depends   The safety and health of this whole state.
translation: He is bound by the needs of the royal family, and can’t just choose whomever he wants—because the choice he makes could affect the safety and security of the entire country. He must do what is right for the the country that he leads when he makes his choice.

original: And therefore must his choice be circumscribed   Unto the voice and yielding of that body   Whereof he is the head.
translation: So if he says he loves you, it would be smart for you to understand that his words can’t mean any more than what the needs of Denmark allow it to mean.

original: Then if he says he loves you,   It fits your wisdom so far to believe it   As he in his particular act and place   May give his saying deed, which is no further   Than the main voice of Denmark goes withal.   Then weigh what loss your honor may sustain   If with too credent ear you list his songs,   Or lose your heart, or your chaste treasure open   To his unmastered importunity.
translation: Then think about how it would stain your reputation if you believe his words of love, or fall in love, or give up your virginity to him.

original: Fear it, Ophelia. Fear it, my dear sister,   And keep you in the rear of your affection,   Out of the shot and danger of desire.   The chariest maid is prodigal enough   If she unmask her beauty to the moon.   Virtue itself ’scapes not calumnious strokes.
translation: Be careful, Ophelia. Be careful, my dear sister. Keep your feelings under control, and keep yourself free from the danger of his desire. Avoid exposing your beauty, even to the moon. Your reputation can be ruined if other people even think that you’re doing something you shouldn’t.

original: The canker galls the infants of the spring   Too oft before their buttons be disclosed.   And in the morn and liquid dew of youth,   Contagious blastments are most imminent.   Be wary, then. Best safety lies in fear.
translation: Too often, worms or disease ruin flowers before they blossom—and young flowers are the most vulnerable. Be careful. You will be safest if you maintain a healthy fear.

original: Youth to itself rebels, though none else near.
translation: Young people can lose their self-control without any outside help.

original: I shall the effect of this good lesson keep   As watchman to my heart.
translation: I’ll take your wise words and hold them close to my heart.

original: But, good my brother,   Do not, as some ungracious pastors do,   Show me the steep and thorny way to heaven
translation: But, my good brother, don’t be like a bad priest who does not follow his own advice, preaching about the need to follow the strict and righteous path to heaven

original: Whiles, like a puffed and reckless libertine,   Himself the primrose path of dalliance treads   And recks not his own rede.
translation: while—like a reckless playboy—he pursues pleasure.

original: O, fear me not.
translation: Don’t worry about me.

original: I stay too long. But here my father comes.
translation: I should be on the ship by now. And here comes our father.

original: A double blessing is a double grace.   Occasion smiles upon a second leave.
translation: Having him bless my leaving a second time will give my journey double the luck.

original: Yet here, Laertes? Aboard, aboard, for shame!   The wind sits in the shoulder of your sail   And you are stayed for. There, my blessing with thee.
translation: Still here, Laertes? Get going, get going—shame on you! The wind gusts in the sails of your ship, and yet it is forced to wait for you. Here, I give you my blessing.

original: And these few precepts in thy memory   Look thou character. Give thy thoughts no tongue,   Nor any unproportioned thought his act.   Be thou familiar but by no means vulgar.
translation: And I’ll give you a few rules to live by in order to maintain your good character. Keep quiet about your own thoughts, and don’t act on any idea you haven’t fully thought through. Be friendly but not too friendly.

original: Those friends thou hast, and their adoption tried,   Grapple them unto thy soul with hoops of steel,   But do not dull thy palm with entertainment   Of each new-hatched, unfledged comrade.
translation: Hold onto those friends you have that you know are trustworthy, with all your heart. But don’t go shaking hands with every new, unknown person you meet.

original: Beware   Of entrance to a quarrel, but being in,   Bear ’t that th’ opposèd may beware of thee.   Give every man thy ear but few thy voice.
translation: Try not to get caught up in any fights or arguments. But, if you do become involved, act to make sure that those you’re facing respect you. Listen to everyone, but give advice to few.

original: Take each man’s censure but reserve thy judgment.   Costly thy habit as thy purse can buy,   But not expressed in fancy—rich, not gaudy,   For the apparel oft proclaims the man,   And they in France of the best rank and station   Are of a most select and generous chief in that.
translation: Hear every man’s opinions, but keep your own judgments to yourself. Buy the most expensive clothes you can afford—but buy clothes that are high-end, not gaudy, because clothes make the man. And that is especially true in France.

original: Neither a borrower nor a lender be,   For loan oft loses both itself and friend,   And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry.
translation: Neither borrow money nor lend it—because lending money to a friend usually results in the loss of the money and the friend, while borrowing makes people reckless with money.

original: This above all: to thine own self be true,   And it must follow, as the night the day,   Thou canst not then be false to any man.
translation: Above all: be true to yourself, which carries with it the natural result that you won’t be false to anybody else.

original: Farewell. My blessing season this in thee.
translation: Goodbye. May my blessing help you remember my advice.

original: Most humbly do I take my leave, my lord.
translation: I will humbly be on my way, my lord.

original: The time invites you. Go. Your servants tend.
translation: The time is right. Go. Your servants await you.

original: Farewell, Ophelia, and remember well What I have said to you.
translation: Goodbye, Ophelia. Remember what I’ve told you.

original: ‘Tis in my memory locked, And you yourself shall keep the key of it.
translation: It’s locked away in my memory, and you have the key.

original: Farewell.
translation: Goodbye.

original: What is ’t, Ophelia, he hath said to you?
translation: What did he say to you, Ophelia?

original: So please you, something touching the Lord Hamlet.
translation: Something about the Lord Hamlet.

original: Marry, well bethought.   ‘Tis told me he hath very oft of late   Given private time to you, and you yourself   Have of your audience been most free and bounteous.
translation: He did? That’s good. I’ve been told that recently Hamlet’s spent a lot of time with you in private, and that you’ve been very open to his visits.

original: If it be so as so ’tis put on me—   And that in way of caution—I must tell you,   You do not understand yourself so clearly   As it behooves my daughter and your honor.
translation: If what I’ve been told is true—and they’re only telling me this to warn me—then I must say, you’re not acting in a way a daughter of mine should. You endanger your honor.

original: What is between you? Give me up the truth.
translation: What’s going on between you two? Tell me the truth.

original: He hath, my lord, of late made many tenders Of his affection to me.
translation: Father, lately he has offered his affection for me, many times.

original: Affection! Pooh, you speak like a green girl, Unsifted in such perilous circumstance. Do you believe his “tenders,” as you call them?
translation: “Affection!” Bah! You’re talking like some innocent girl, unlearned in the dangerous ways of love and lust. Do you believe his “offers,” as you call them?

original: I do not know, my lord, what I should think.
translation: I don’t know what I should think, my lord.

original: Marry, I’ll teach you. Think yourself a baby   That you have ta’en these tenders for true pay,   Which are not sterling.
translation: Then I’ll explain to you. Think of yourself as a foolish child for believing that these “offers” are something real.

original: Tender yourself more dearly,   Or—not to crack the wind of the poor phrase,   Running it thus—you’ll tender me a fool.
translation: Give yourself more respect, or—not to beat this phrase to death, continuing  on like this—you’ll “offer” me the chance to look like a fool.

original: My lord, he hath importuned me with love In honorable fashion.
translation: My lord, he’s always talked about his love for me in an honorable fashion—

original: Ay, “fashion” you may call it. Go to, go to.
translation: Yes, “fashion,” that’s the right word for it. Come on now.

original: And hath given countenance to his speech, my lord, With almost all the holy vows of heaven.
translation: And he’s backed up his words of love with nearly every holy vow.

original: Ay, springes to catch woodcocks. I do know,   When the blood burns, how prodigal the soul   Lends the tongue vows.
translation: Yes, vows that are like traps for birds.

original: These blazes, daughter,   Giving more light than heat, extinct in both   Even in their promise as it is a-making,   You must not take for fire.
translation: I know that when a man’s blood burns, he’ll be quick to swear to anything. You should not mistake such blazes for the true fire of love.  They give off more light than heat, and will go out entirely before he’s even finished making his promises.

original: F   rom this time   Be somewhat scanter of your maiden presence.   Set your entreatments at a higher rate   Than a command to parley.
translation: From now on, make sure to spend less time with him. And make him do more than just ask to get you to talk with him.

original: For Lord Hamlet,   Believe so much in him that he is young,   And with a larger tether may he walk   Than may be given you.
translation: Do not forget that Hamlet is young, and that he has much more freedom to experiment and fool around than you do.

original: In few, Ophelia,   Do not believe his vows, for they are brokers   Not of that dye which their investments show,   But mere implorators of unholy suits,   Breathing like sanctified and pious bawds,   The better to beguile.
translation: In short, Ophelia, don’t believe his vows—which are little more than pimps dressed up in good clothes, pretending to be pious in an effort to lead you into bad behavior.

original: This is for all:   I would not, in plain terms, from this time forth,   Have you so slander any moment leisure,   As to give words or talk with the Lord Hamlet.
translation: To summarize: from now on, don’t waste even another moment of your time. Do not talk with Hamlet.

original: Look to ’t, I charge you. Come your ways.
translation: Do as I say, I order you. Now come with me.

original: I shall obey, my lord.
translation: I will obey, my lord.

original: The air bites shrewdly. It is very cold.
translation: The air bites wickedly. It is very cold.

original: It is a nipping and an eager air.
translation: Yes, the air is nipping and sharp.

original: What hour now?
translation: What time is it now?

original: I think it lacks of twelve.
translation: Just before twelve, I think.

original: No, it is struck.
translation: No, the clock struck twelve.

original: Indeed? I heard it not. It then draws near the season Wherein the spirit held his wont to walk.
translation: Really? I didn’t hear it. So it’s getting close to the time when the ghost usually appears.

original: What does this mean, my lord?
translation: What does that mean, sir?

original: The king doth wake tonight and takes his rouse,   Keeps wassail and the swaggering upspring reels,
translation: The king is staying up late partying.  And as he carouses, and dances,

original: And, as he drains his draughts of Rhenish down,   The kettle-drum and trumpet thus bray out   The triumph of his pledge.
translation: and guzzles his German wine, the musicians play the drum and trumpet to mark each time he drinks another cup.

original: Is it a custom?
translation: Is that a tradition?

original: Ay, marry, is ’t.   But to my mind, though I am native here   And to the manner born, it is a custom   More honored in the breach than the observance.
translation: It is. But in my opinion—though I was born here and should think it natural—I’d say it’s a custom that we’d be better off ignoring rather than observing.

original: This heavy-headed revel east and west   Makes us traduced and taxed of other nations.   They clepe us drunkards and with swinish phrase   Soil our addition.
translation: Countries to the east and west mock and criticize us for our partying. They call us drunks and pigs, staining our reputation.

original: And indeed it takes   From our achievements, though performed at height,   The pith and marrow of our attribute.
translation: And they’re right—our behavior does reduce our achievements, despite their greatness, because it is a flaw in our core qualities.

original: So oft it chances in particular men   That for some vicious mole of nature in them—   As in their birth (wherein they are not guilty,   Since nature cannot choose his origin),   By the o’ergrowth of some complexion,   Oft breaking down the pales and forts of reason,   Or by some habit that too much o’erleavens   The form of plausive manners—
translation: It’s similar to what happens to certain people who are born with some terrible defect (a defect for which they bear no responsibility, since no one can choose his own beginning); or some excess of a more normal trait; or some kind of compulsion that makes it impossible for them to act in a way that pleases others.

original: that these men,   Carrying, I say, the stamp of one defect,   Being nature’s livery or fortune’s star,   Their virtues else (be they as pure as grace,   As infinite as man may undergo)   Shall in the general censure take corruption   From that particular fault.
translation: For such men as these—even if they are kind or limitlessly talented—this single defect, whether they were born with it or got it through some misfortune, will result in others always seeing them as corrupt or evil.

original: The dram of evil   Doth all the noble substance of a doubt   To his own scandal.
translation: That tiny bit of evil casts doubt on all their good qualities and wrecks their reputations.

original: Look, my lord, it comes!
translation: Look, here comes the ghost, my lord!

original: Angels and ministers of grace defend us!   Be thou a spirit of health or goblin damned,   Bring with thee airs from heaven or blasts from hell,   Be thy intents wicked or charitable,   Thou comest in such a questionable shape   That I will speak to thee.
translation: Angels protect us! Whether you’re a good spirit bringing breezes from heaven, or an evil demon wielding hell fire, whether your intentions are wicked or friendly, you appear in a shape that invites so many questions that I must speak to you.

original: I’ll call thee “Hamlet,”   “King,” “Father,” “royal Dane.” O, answer me!   Let me not burst in ignorance, but tell   Why thy canonized bones, hearsed in death,   Have burst their cerements;
translation: I’ll call you “Hamlet,” “King,” “Father,” “royal Dane.” Oh, answer me! Don’t make me explode from curiosity. Tell me why your bones, which were blessed and sanctified in burial rites, have burst out of their coffin,

original: why the sepulcher,   Wherein we saw thee quietly interred,   Hath oped his ponderous and marble jaws   To cast thee up again.
translation: and why your tomb, in whose quiet we buried you, has opened up its weighty marble jaws to spit you out again.

original: What may this mean,   That thou, dead corse, again in complete steel   Revisits thus the glimpses of the moon,   Making night hideous and we fools of nature,   So horridly to shake our disposition   With thoughts beyond the reaches of our souls?
translation: What does it mean that you, dead corpse, once again walk beneath the moon in full armor—making the night terrifying, and forcing on us mere mortals to face thoughts that are beyond our ability to understand?

original: Say why is this? Wherefore? What should we do?
translation: Tell me why? Why? What should we do?

original: It beckons you to go away with it, As if it some impartment did desire To you alone.
translation: It motions you to go off with it, as if it wants to say something to you alone.

original: Look, with what courteous action It waves you to a more removèd ground. But do not go with it.
translation: Look how politely it’s directing you to go to a spot that’s farther away. But don’t go with it.

original: No, by no means.
translation: No, by all means do not.

original: It will not speak. Then I will follow it.
translation: It’s not going to speak here. So I will follow it.

original: Do not, my lord.
translation: Don’t, my lord.

original: Why, what should be the fear?   I do not set my life in a pin’s fee,
translation: Why, what should I fear? I don’t value my life at even the price of a pin.

original: And for my soul—what can it do to that,   Being a thing immortal as itself?
translation: And as for my soul, what can the ghost do to that, since it’s as immortal as the ghost is?

original: It waves me forth again. I’ll follow it.
translation: It’s waving for me to come after it again. I’ll follow it.

original: What if it tempt you toward the flood, my lord,
translation: What if it leads you toward the sea, my lord?

original: Or to the dreadful summit of the cliff   That beetles o’er his base into the sea,   And there assume some other horrible form,   Which might deprive your sovereignty of reason   And draw you into madness?
translation: Or to the high cliff that overhangs the ocean, and then morphs into a beast so horrible that seeing it drives you insane?

original: Think of it.   The very place puts toys of desperation,   Without more motive, into every brain   That looks so many fathoms to the sea   And hears it roar beneath.
translation: Think about it. That cliff's edge over the sea—with its view into those watery depths and the roar of the crashing waves—makes people feel despair even when they have no reason to.

original: It waves me still. —Go on. I’ll follow thee.
translation: It’s still waving to me.

original: You shall not go, my lord.
translation: You will not go, my lord.

original: Hold off your hands.
translation: Let go of me.

original: Be ruled. You shall not go.
translation: Listen to us. You must not go.

original: My fate cries out   And makes each petty artery in this body   As hardy as the Nemean lion’s nerve.
translation: My fate calls out to me, making every sinew of my body as taut as those of the legendary  Nemean lion .

original: Still am I called.—Unhand me, gentlemen.
translation: The ghost still motions for me. Let go of me, gentlemen.

original: By heaven, I’ll make a ghost of him that lets me.   I say, away!
translation: By God, I’ll make a ghost of any of you who holds me back! I say, move away!

original: He waxes desperate with imagination.
translation: His wild thoughts have made him desperate.

original: Let’s follow. ‘Tis not fit thus to obey him.
translation: Let’s follow him. It’s not right for us to obey his orders to stay away.

original: Have after. To what issue will this come?
translation: Let’s go after him. But what does all this mean?

original: Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
translation: That something is wrong in the state of Denmark.

original: Heaven will direct it.
translation: God will determine what will come of all this.

original: Nay, let’s follow him.
translation: No, let’s follow him.

original: Where wilt thou lead me? Speak, I’ll go no further.
translation: Where are you leading me? Speak. I’m not going any farther.

original: Mark me.
translation: Listen to me.

original: I will.
translation: I will.

original: My hour is almost come When I to sulfurous and tormenting flames Must render up myself.
translation: The hour has almost come when I must return to the torment of the flames of purgatory.

original: Alas, poor ghost!
translation: Oh no, poor ghost!

original: Pity me not, but lend thy serious hearing To what I shall unfold.
translation: Don’t pity me. But listen carefully to what I have to say.

original: Speak. I am bound to hear.
translation: Speak. I promise to listen.

original: So art thou to revenge when thou shalt hear.
translation: Then you must promise to avenge my death, too, when you hear what I say.

original: What?
translation: What?

original: I am thy father’s spirit,   Doomed for a certain term to walk the night   And for the day confined to fast in fires,   Till the foul crimes done in my days of nature   Are burnt and purged away.
translation: I’m the ghost of your father, doomed for a certain time to walk the earth at night. During the day, I’m confined in the fires of purgatory, until those flames have burned away the sins I committed in my life.

original: But that I am forbid   To tell the secrets of my prison house,   I could a tale unfold whose lightest word   Would harrow up thy soul, freeze thy young blood,
translation: If I weren’t forbidden to tell you the secrets of purgatory, I could tell you stories that would cut up your soul, freeze your blood,

original: Make thy two eyes, like stars, start from their  spheres,   Thy knotted and combinèd locks to part   And each particular hair to stand on end,   Like quills upon the fearful porpentine.
translation: make your eyes bulge from their sockets, and your hair stand on end like the quills of a frightened porcupine.

original: But this eternal blazon must not be   To ears of flesh and blood. List, list, O, list!   If thou didst ever thy dear father love—
translation: But the secrets of purgatory must not be told to mortals. Listen, listen, oh, listen! If you ever loved your dear father—

original: O God!
translation: Oh God!

original: Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder.
translation: Take revenge for his awful and horrible murder.

original: Murder?
translation: Murder?

original: Murder most foul, as in the best it is. But this most foul, strange and unnatural.
translation: His most awful murder. All murder is awful, but this one was even more awful, startling, and unnatural.

original: Haste me to know ’t, that I, with wings as swift As meditation or the thoughts of love, May sweep to my revenge.
translation: Tell me quickly about it, so that I can rush to take revenge, even faster than a person can think thoughts of love.

original: I find thee apt,   And duller shouldst thou be than the fat weed   That roots itself in ease on Lethe wharf,   Wouldst thou not stir in this.
translation: I like your words. You’d have to be as slow and dull as a weed growing on the banks of  Lethe  not to be brought to anger by my story.

original: Now, Hamlet, hear.   ‘Tis given out that, sleeping in my orchard,   A serpent stung me. So the whole ear of Denmark   Is by a forgèd process of my death   Rankly abused.
translation: Now, Hamlet, listen. The official story is that a poisonous snake bit me while I was sleeping in the orchard. That is a lie that deceives all of Denmark.

original: But know, thou noble youth,   The serpent that did sting thy father’s life   Now wears his crown.
translation: You noble youth, know that the snake that killed your father is now wearing his crown.

original: O my prophetic soul! My uncle?
translation: Oh, my far-seeing soul! My uncle?

original: Ay, that incestuous, that adulterate beast,   With witchcraft of his wit, with traitorous gifts—   O wicked wit and gifts, that have the power   So to seduce!—won to his shameful lust   The will of my most seeming-virtuous queen.
translation: Yes, that incestuous, adulterous beast. With his evil wit and traitorous gifts—oh wicked wit and gifts, that have the power to seduce!—he convinced my seemingly virtuous queen to give in to his lust.

original: O Hamlet, what a falling off was there!   From me, whose love was of that dignity   That it went hand in hand even with the vow   I made to her in marriage, and to decline   Upon a wretch whose natural gifts were poor   To those of mine.
translation: Oh, Hamlet, she fell so far! From me, who loved her with the dignity that goes hand in hand with my marriage vows, to a wretch whose natural abilities could not compare to mine.

original: But virtue, as it never will be moved,   Though lewdness court it in a shape of heaven,   So lust, though to a radiant angel linked,   Will sate itself in a celestial bed   And prey on garbage.
translation: But just as true virtue can’t be corrupted, so will lust show its true nature by satisfying itself first in the blessing of heavenly marriage and then by wallowing in garbage.

original: But soft! Methinks I scent the morning air.   Brief let me be. Sleeping within my orchard,   My custom always of the afternoon,   Upon my secure hour thy uncle stole   With juice of cursed hebenon in a vial,   And in the porches of my ears did pour   The leperous distilment,
translation: But wait. I think I smell the morning air. I must speak quickly. As I was sleeping in the orchard—as I used to do every afternoon—your uncle snuck up and poured a vial of henbane poison into my ear.

original: whose effect   Holds such an enmity with blood of man   That swift as quicksilver it courses through   The natural gates and alleys of the body   And with a sudden vigor doth posset   And curd, like eager droppings into milk,   The thin and wholesome blood. So did it mine.
translation: That poison—which is like a natural enemy of blood—spreads like quicksilver through the veins and curdles the blood. So it did to mine.

original: And a most instant tetter barked about,   Most lazar-like, with vile and loathsome crust   All my smooth body.   Thus was I, sleeping, by a brother’s hand   Of life, of crown, of queen at once dispatched,
translation: I broke instantly into a rash that covered my smooth body with a revolting crust. And so, as I slept, my brother stole my life, my crown, and my queen.

original: Cut off even in the blossoms of my sin,   Unhouseled, disappointed, unaneled.   No reckoning made, but sent to my account   With all my imperfections on my head.   Oh, horrible, oh, horrible, most horrible!
translation: He killed me even as I was still gripped by sin, because I did not get to repent my sins or receive last rites. I was sent to death with all my sins still on my head. Oh, horrible, horrible, most horrible!

original: If thou hast nature in thee, bear it not.   Let not the royal bed of Denmark be   A couch for luxury and damnèd incest.   But howsoever thou pursuest this act,   Taint not thy mind, nor let thy soul contrive   Against thy mother aught.
translation: If you have any natural feelings of a son for a father in you, don’t let this stand. Don’t let the bed of the Danish king be a nest of incest. But however you attempt to get revenge, don’t allow your mind or soul to contemplate harming your mother.

original: Leave her to heaven   And to those thorns that in her bosom lodge   To prick and sting her. Fare thee well at once.   The glowworm shows the matin to be near,   And ‘gins to pale his uneffectual fire.   Adieu, adieu, adieu. Remember me.
translation: Leave her fate to God, and to the sting of her own guilt. Goodbye now. The glow of light on the horizon shows that morning is near. Goodbye, goodbye, goodbye. Remember me.

original: O all you host of heaven! O earth! What else?   And shall I couple hell? Oh, fie! Hold, hold, my heart,   And you, my sinews, grow not instant old,   But bear me stiffly up.
translation: Oh, all you angels of heaven! Oh, everyone on earth! What else? Should I include hell too? Oh, curses! Keep beating, my heart, and muscles, don’t grow suddenly old—hold me upright.

original: Remember thee!   Ay, thou poor ghost, whiles memory holds a seat   In this distracted globe. Remember thee!
translation: Remember you? Yes, you poor ghost, as long as I have any memory in my distracted head. Remember you?

original: Yea, from the table of my memory   I’ll wipe away all trivial fond records,   All saws of books, all forms, all pressures past   That youth and observation copied there,   And thy commandment all alone shall live   Within the book and volume of my brain,   Unmixed with baser matter.
translation: Yes, I’ll wipe clean my memory of all unimportant facts, all the wise sayings of books, all images and impressions from my youth, so that your commandment alone will live there.

original: Yes, by heaven!   O most pernicious woman!   O villain, villain, smiling, damnèd villain!   My tables!—Meet it is I set it down   That one may smile, and smile, and be a villain.   At least I’m sure it may be so in Denmark.
translation: Yes, by heaven! Oh, you wicked woman! Oh, you villain, villain, damned, smiling villain! Where’s my notebook? I should write down that one can smile and smile, and still be a villain. At least it’s possible to do so in Denmark.

original: So, uncle, there you are. Now to my word.   It is “Adieu, adieu. Remember me.”   I have sworn ’t.
translation: So, uncle, there you are. Now I must fulfill my vow. He said, “Remember me.” I’ve sworn I would.

original: My lord, my lord!
translation: My lord, my lord!

original: Lord Hamlet—
translation: Lord Hamlet—

original: Heaven secure him!
translation: God protect him!

original: So be it.
translation: So be it.

original: Illo, ho, ho, my lord!
translation: Hello, hello there, my lord!

original: Hillo, ho, ho, boy. Come, bird, come.
translation: Hello, hello there, boy! Come to me.

original: How is ’t, my noble lord?
translation: What happened, my noble lord?

original: What news, my lord?
translation: What did you learn, my lord?

original: Oh, wonderful!
translation: Oh, it was amazing!

original: Good my lord, tell it.
translation: My lord, tell us.

original: No. You’ll reveal it.
translation: No. You’ll reveal my secret.

original: Not I, my lord, by heaven.
translation: I swear to God I won’t, my lord.

original: Nor I, my lord.
translation: Nor will I, my lord.

original: How say you, then? Would heart of man once think it? But you’ll be secret?
translation: You say so, but can you promise you’ll keep the secret?

original: Ay, by heaven, my lord.
translation: Yes, I swear to God, my lord.

original: There’s ne’er a villain dwelling in all Denmark But he’s an arrant knave.
translation: There’s not a villain in Denmark who isn’t a complete liar .

original: There needs no ghost, my lord, come from the grave To tell us this.
translation: My lord, we didn’t need a ghost returning from the grave to tell us that.

original: Why, right, you are in the right.   And so, without more circumstance at all,   I hold it fit that we shake hands and part.
translation: Why, right, you are right. So, with that, I’d say that the best thing would be for us to shake hands and go our separate ways.

original: You, as your business and desire shall point you—   For every man has business and desire,   Such as it is—and for my own poor part,
translation: You go wherever your business takes you—since every man has some business to take care of, whatever it is.

original: Look you, I’ll go pray.
translation: As for me,’ll go and pray.

original: These are but wild and whirling words, my lord.
translation: Your words are wild and meaningless, my lord.

original: I’m sorry they offend you, heartily. Yes faith, heartily.
translation: I’m very sorry they offended you. Yes, by God, very sorry.

original: There’s no offense, my lord.
translation: There was no offense, my lord.

original: Yes, by Saint Patrick, but there is, Horatio,   And much offense too. Touching this vision here,   It is an honest ghost, that let me tell you.
translation: Ah, but I swear by  Saint Patrick  that there is, Horatio. A lot of offense. As for this ghost, he’s an honest one, I’ll tell you that.

original: For your desire to know what is between us,   O’ermaster ’t as you may.
translation: But as for your desire to know what happened between us, control yourself and don’t ask.

original: And now, good friends,   As you are friends, scholars and soldiers,   Give me one poor request.
translation: And now, good friends—and you are friends, scholars, and soldiers—do me one small favor.

original: What is ’t, my lord? We will.
translation: What is it, my lord? We’ll do it.

original: Never make known what you have seen tonight.
translation: Never tell anyone what you’ve seen tonight.

original: My lord, we will not.
translation: We won’t, my lord.

original: Nay, but swear ’t.
translation: No, you must swear it.

original: In faith, my lord, not I.
translation: I swear to God I won’t.

original: Nor I, my lord, in faith.
translation: Nor I, my lord, I swear to God.

original: Upon my sword.
translation: Swear on my sword.

original: We have sworn, my lord, already.
translation: But we swore already, my lord.

original: Indeed, upon my sword, indeed.
translation: True, but still, swear on my sword.

original: Swear!
translation: Swear!

original: Ah, ha, boy! Sayst thou so? Art thou there, truepenny? Come on, you hear this fellow in the cellarage. Consent to swear.
translation: Aha, do you say so, boy? Are you down there, my trusty fellow?

original: Propose the oath, my lord.
translation: Tell us what to swear, my lord.

original: Never to speak of this that you have seen. Swear by my sword.
translation: Never to speak of what you’ve seen. Swear by my sword.

original: Swear.
translation: Swear.

original: Hic et ubique? Then we’ll shift our ground.
translation: You’re everywhere, huh? We’ll move somewhere else.

original: Swear by his sword.
translation: Swear by his sword.

original: Well said, old mole! Canst work i’ th’ earth so fast? A worthy pioneer! Once more remove, good friends.
translation: That’s right, old mole. Can you really move through the dirt so quickly? What a miner you are!

original: O day and night, but this is wondrous strange!
translation: Oh, by God, this is incredibly strange.

original: And therefore as a stranger give it welcome.   There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio,   Than are dreamt of in your philosophy.
translation: So welcome it like a stranger. Horatio, there are more things in heaven and earth than you can dream of with all your scientific learning.

original: But come,   Here, as before, never, so help you mercy,   How strange or odd soe’er I bear myself   (As I perchance hereafter shall think meet   To put an antic disposition on),
translation: Now listen: just as you swore before, no matter how strangely I act (since from now on I may find it necessary to act a bit crazy),

original: That you, at such times seeing me, never shall—   With arms encumbered thus, or this headshake,   Or by pronouncing of some doubtful phrase,   As “Well, well, we know,” or “We could an if we would,”   Or “If we list to speak,” or “There be an if they  might,”   Or such ambiguous giving out—
translation: you must never, ever let on—with a gesture of your arms, or a shake of your head, or by saying something like “well, well, we understand,” or “we’d tell you if we could,” or “if we were allowed to speak,” or anything like that—

original: to note   That you know aught of me. This not to do,   So grace and mercy at your most need help you,   Swear.
translation: that you know anything about what happened to me here tonight. Swear you won’t, by all of your hopes of going to heaven.

original: Swear!
translation: Swear.

original: Rest, rest, perturbèd spirit!
translation: Rest, rest, unhappy ghost!

original: Give him this money and these notes, Reynaldo.
translation: Give Laertes this money and these letters, Reynaldo.

original: I will, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: You shall do marvelous wisely, good Reynaldo, Before you visit him, to make inquire Of his behavior.
translation: Good Reynaldo, it would be extremely wise of you to ask around about his behavior before you visit him.

original: My lord, I did intend it.
translation: That was my plan, my lord.

original: Marry, well said, very well said. Look you, sir,   Inquire me first what Danskers are in Paris,   And how, and who, what means, and where they keep   What company at what expense;
translation: Excellent, good, good. First find out what Danish people are in Paris—who they are, how much money they have, where they live, who their friends are, and how much they spend.

original: and finding   By this encompassment and drift of question   That they do know my son, come you more nearer   Than your particular demands will touch it.
translation: And if—through this roundabout and indirect questioning—that they happen to know my son, you’ll end up finding out much more than if you asked specific questions about him.

original: Take you, as ’twere, some distant knowledge of him,   As thus: “I know his father and his friends,   And, in part, him.” Do you mark this, Reynaldo?
translation: Talk as if you vaguely know Laertes, such as, “I know his father and his friends, and know him a little.” Do you understand all this, Reynaldo?

original: Ay, very well, my lord.
translation: Yes, very well, my lord.

original: “And in part him, but,” you may say, “not well.   But, if ’t be he I mean, he’s very wild.   Addicted so and so.
translation: You should say, “I know him a little, but not well. I think, from what I’ve heard, that he’s very wild, and addicted to this and that.”

original: —” And there put on him   What forgeries you please. Marry, none so rank   As may dishonor him. Take heed of that.
translation: From there create whatever lies about him that you can think up. Of course, nothing so bad that it would shame him. Be careful about that.

original: But, sir, such wanton, wild, and usual slips   As are companions noted and most known   To youth and liberty.
translation: But feel free to make up stories about the wild and crazy things that young men who are on their own typically get into.

original: As gaming, my lord?
translation: Like gambling, sir?

original: Ay, or drinking, fencing, swearing, Quarreling, drabbing—you may go so far.
translation: Yes, or drinking, dueling, swearing, fighting, going to prostitutes—that sort of thing.

original: My lord, that would dishonor him!
translation: My lord, that would bring dishonor on him!

original: ‘Faith, no, as you may season it in the charge.   You must not put another scandal on him   That he is open to incontinency.   That’s not my meaning.
translation: Oh, no, not if you say it with the right spin. You shouldn’t say that he’s sexually indulgent, that’s not what I mean.

original: But breathe his faults so  quaintly   That they may seem the taints of liberty,   The flash and outbreak of a fiery mind,   A savageness in unreclaimèd blood,   Of general assault.
translation: Instead, just mention these faults lightly, as if you think they're nothing more than the minor faults that sprout in someone new to freedom—like the products of a strong mind and untamed youth—and the kind of thing that occurs in lots of young men.

original: But, my good lord—
translation: But, my lord—

original: Wherefore should you do this?
translation: Why should you do this?

original: Ay, my lord. I would know that.
translation: Yes, my lord. I would like to know that.

original: Marry, sir, here’s my drift:   (And I believe it is a fetch of wit)
translation: All right . Here’s my idea. (And I do think it's a bit clever.)

original: You, laying these slight sullies on my son   As ’twere a thing a little soiled i’ th’ working—   Mark you, your party in converse, him you would sound,
translation: As you casually mention these minor faults and small blemishes as if everyone has heard of them, watch the person with whom you’re talking.

original: Having ever seen in the prenominate crimes   The youth you breathe of guilty, be assured   He closes with you in this consequence:   “Good sir” or so, or “Friend,” or “Gentleman,”
translation: If whoever you’re talking to has ever seen Laertes do any of the things you mention, he’ll mark his agreement by saying something like “good sir” or “friend” or “gentleman”

original: According to the phrase or the addition   Of man and country.
translation: —or something like that, depending on the person’s background.

original: Very good, my lord.
translation: I understand, sir.

original: And then, sir, does he this, he does— What was I about  to say? By the mass, I was about to say something. Where did I leave?
translation: And then, sir, he’ll …after he does that … he’ll … What was I about to say? By God, I was about to say something. Where did I leave off?

original: At “closes in the consequence,” at “‘friend,’ Or so” and “‘gentleman.’”
translation: At, “he’ll mark his agreement by saying sir, or friend, or gentleman.”

original: At “closes in the consequence.” Ay, marry.   He closes thus: “I know the gentleman.   I saw him yesterday”—or “t’ other day,”   Or then, or then, with such or such
translation: “He’ll mark his agreement by saying….” Yes, right. He’ll respond like this: “I know the gentleman. I just saw him yesterday,” or “the other day,” or whenever.

original: —“and, as you say,   There was he gaming, there o’ertook in’s rouse,   There falling out at tennis,” or, perchance,   “I saw him enter such a house of sale”—   Videlicet a brothel, or so forth.
translation: And he'll say with whom—“and, as you said, there he was gambling,” or “there he was, completely drunk,” or “getting into a fight over a tennis match,” or, possibly, “I saw him going into a house of ill repute”—that means a whorehouse—or some such thing.

original: See you now,   Your bait of falsehood takes this carp of truth.   And thus do we of wisdom and of reach,   With windlasses and with assays of bias,   By indirections find directions out.
translation: In this way, make sure your little lie is like bait that lures the larger truth into the open. And that’s how we get wisdom and knowledge, by gradually drawing others in and indirectly finding out what we want to know.

original: So by my former lecture and advice   Shall you my son. You have me, have you not?
translation: Follow my advice and you’ll learn about my son. You understand me, right?

original: My lord, I have.
translation: I do, my lord.

original: God be wi’ you. Fare you well.
translation: God bless you. Goodbye.

original: Good my lord.
translation: My good lord.

original: Observe his inclination in yourself.
translation: Make sure to observe him also with your own eyes.

original: I shall, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: And let him ply his music.
translation: I hope he’s studying his music as he’s supposed to.

original: Well, my lord.
translation: I understand, my lord.

original: Farewell.
translation: Goodbye.

original: How now, Ophelia? What’s the matter?
translation: How are you, Ophelia? What’s the matter?

original: O my lord, my lord, I have been so affrighted!
translation: Oh, my lord, my lord, I’ve had a terrible scare!

original: With what, i’ th’ name of God?
translation: From what, in God’s name?

original: My lord, as I was sewing in my closet,   Lord Hamlet, with his doublet all unbraced;   No hat upon his head; his stockings fouled,   Ungartered, and down-gyvèd to his ankle;
translation: Father, as I was sewing in my room, Lord Hamlet came in with his shirt unbuttoned; no hat on his head; his stockings dirty, undone, and hanging around his ankles.

original: Pale as his shirt; his knees knocking each other;   And with a look so piteous in purport   As if he had been loosèd out of hell   To speak of horrors—he comes before me.
translation: He was pale as his white undershirt, and his knees were knocking together. He looked so awful, as if he’d just escaped from hell.

original: Mad for thy love?
translation: Is he madly in love with you?

original: My lord, I do not know. But truly, I do fear it.
translation: Father, I don’t know. But to be honest, I think he might be.

original: What said he?
translation: What did he say?

original: He took me by the wrist and held me hard.   Then goes he to the length of all his arm,   And, with his other hand thus o’er his brow,   He falls to such perusal of my face   As he would draw it.
translation: He grabbed me by the wrist and held me tightly, then backed a full arm’s length away. And, standing with his other arm raised over his forehead, he stared at my face as if studying it in order to draw it.

original: Long stayed he so.   At last, a little shaking of mine arm   And thrice his head thus waving up and down,   He raised a sigh so piteous and profound   As it did seem to shatter all his bulk   And end his being.
translation: He stood like that for a long while. Then, he gently shook my arm and glancing up and down three times, and sighed so sadly it seemed like he would collapse in on himself and die.

original: That done, he lets me go,   And, with his head over his shoulder turned,   He seemed to find his way without his eyes,   For out o’ doors he went without their helps,   And to the last bended their light on me.
translation: Then he let me go, and walked away while staring back at me. He found his way out without looking away from me the entire time.

original: Come, go with me. I will go seek the king.
translation: Come with me to see the king.

original: This is the very ecstasy of love,   Whose violent property fordoes itself   And leads the will to desperate undertakings   As oft as any passion under heaven   That does afflict our natures.
translation: This is clearly the madness of love, which is an emotion so violently powerful that it can destroy itself, leading people to act as desperately and insanely as often as any other emotion known to man.

original: I am sorry.   What, have you given him any hard words of late?
translation: I’m so sorry. Have you said anything tough or unfriendly recently?

original: No, my good lord. But as you did command I did repel his fetters and denied His access to me.
translation: No, my good lord. But I followed your commands and sent back his letters and refused to let him see me.

original: That hath made him mad. I am sorry that with better heed and judgment I had not quoted him. I feared he did but trifle And meant to wreck thee. But beshrew my jealousy! By heaven, it is as proper to our age To cast beyond ourselves in our opinions As it is common for the younger sort To lack discretion. Come, go we to the king. This must be known, which, being kept close, might move More grief to hide than hate to utter love. Come.
translation: That has driven him crazy. I’m sorry that I didn’t observe him more closely. I feared that he was just toying with you, and did not care if he wrecked your reputation. A curse on my suspicions! By God, it’s as common for us old people to think too much as it is for young people to think too little. Come, let’s go see the king. We have to make this matter known. Keeping it secret could cause more harm than revealing it.

original: Welcome, dear Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.   Moreover that we much did long to see you,   The need we have to use you did provoke   Our hasty sending.
translation: Welcome, dear Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. Not only have I wanted to see you, but I also urgently need your help, which is why I sent for you.

original: Something have you heard   Of Hamlet’s “transformation”—so call it   Since nor th’ exterior nor the inward man   Resembles that it was.
translation: You may have heard about Hamlet’s recent “transformation”—that’s the right word, since he’s changed both inside and out from what he was before.

original: What it should be,   More than his father’s death, that thus hath put him   So much from th’ understanding of himself,   I cannot dream of.
translation: Other than his father’s death, I can’t imagine what’s made him so unlike himself.

original: I entreat you both   That, being of so young days brought up with him   And since so neighbored to his youth and ‘havior,   That you vouchsafe your rest here in our court
translation: Since you both grew up with him and are so familiar with him, I ask you both to stay here at court for a while.

original: Some little time so by your companies   To draw him on to pleasures and to gather,   So much as from occasion you may glean,   Whether aught, to us unknown, afflicts him thus   That, opened, lies within our remedy.
translation: Spend time with Hamlet, get him to enjoy life again, and try to find out if there’s anything we don’t know about that’s bothering him—so we can try to fix it.

original: Good gentlemen, he hath much talked of you.   And sure I am two men there are not living   To whom he more adheres.
translation: Gentlemen, Hamlet’s talked about you a lot. I’m certain that here are no two men alive with whom he’s closer.

original: If it will please you   To show us so much gentry and good will   As to expend your time with us awhile   For the supply and profit of our hope,   Your visitation shall receive such thanks   As fits a king’s remembrance.
translation: If you’d be willing to show us the kindness of staying with us a while to try to help us, we’ll reward you in such a way as only a king can.

original: Both your majesties   Might, by the sovereign power you have of us,
translation: Based on the power you have over us as your subjects, both your Majesties

original: Put your dread pleasures more into command   Than to entreaty.
translation: could have ordered us to follow your command, instead of asking us.

original: But we both obey   And here give up ourselves, in the full bent,
translation: But we’ll obey. We give ourselves to you,

original: To lay our service freely at your feet   To be commanded.
translation: and lay our services at your command.

original: Thanks, Rosencrantz and gentle Guildenstern.
translation: Thanks, Rosencrantz and worthy Guildenstern.

original: Thanks, Guildenstern and gentle Rosencrantz.   And I beseech you instantly to visit   My too much changèd son.
translation: Thanks, Guildenstern and worthy Rosencrantz. I beg you to immediately visit my son, who’s changed too much.

original: Heavens make our presence and our practices Pleasant and helpful to him!
translation: I hope God makes us able to bring him help and happiness!

original: Ay, amen!
translation: Yes, amen!

original: Th’ ambassadors from Norway, my good lord, Are joyfully returned.
translation: The ambassadors have returned from Norway in great spirits, my good lord.

original: Thou still hast been the father of good news.
translation: You once more have brought good news.

original: Have I, my lord? I assure my good liege,   I hold my duty as I hold my soul,   Both to my God and to my gracious king.
translation: Have I, my lord? I assure you, my lord, my duty is as important to me as my soul. And I give both to my God and my blessed king.

original: And I do think—or else this brain of mine   Hunts not the trail of policy so sure   As it hath used to do—that I have found   The very cause of Hamlet’s lunacy.
translation: And—unless this brain of mine is not able to track the twists and turns of politics as it used to—I believe that I’ve discovered the cause of Hamlet’s madness.

original: Oh, speak of that. That do I long to hear.
translation: Oh, tell me! I’d love to hear it.

original: Give first admittance to th’ ambassadors. My news shall be the fruit to that great feast.
translation: First, let the ambassadors come in. My news will be like the dessert to the feast that is their news.

original: Thyself do grace to them, and bring them in.
translation: Please go to them yourself, and bring them in.

original: He tells me, my dear Gertrude, he hath found The head and source of all your son’s distemper.
translation: My dear Gertrude, he says he’s discovered the cause of your son’s anger and moodiness.

original: I doubt it is no other but the main: His father’s death and our o’erhasty marriage.
translation: I doubt it’s anything other than the obvious reason: his father’s death and our overly quick marriage.

original: Well, we shall sift him.—Welcome, my good friends! Say, Voltemand, what from our brother Norway?
translation: Well, we’ll investigate until we figure it out.

original: Most fair return of greetings and desires.   Upon our first, he sent out to suppress   His nephew’s levies, which to him appeared   To be a preparation ‘gainst the Polack,   But, better looked into, he truly found   It was against your highness.
translation: And our greetings to you. The moment we spoke with the king, he moved to put a stop to his nephew’s war preparations—which he had thought were directed against Poland, but, when he looked closer, he saw were directed against you.

original: Whereat grieved—   That so his sickness, age, and impotence   Was falsely borne in hand—sends out arrests   On Fortinbras, which he, in brief, obeys,   Receives rebuke from Norway, and in fine   Makes vow before his uncle never more   To give th’ assay of arms against your majesty.
translation: He was upset that Fortinbras took advantage of his sickness and weakness to deceive him, and he arrested and rebuked Fortinbras, forcing him to swear never again to lift arms against your Majesty.

original: Whereon old Norway, overcome with joy,   Gives him three thousand crowns in annual fee   And his commission to employ those soldiers,   So levied as before, against the Polack,
translation: The old Norwegian king was so overjoyed by this turn of events that he gave young Fortinbras an annual income of three thousand crowns, as well as permission to lead the soldiers he had gathered against Poland.

original: With an entreaty, herein further shown,   That it might please you to give quiet pass   Through your dominions for this enterprise,   On such regards of safety and allowance   As therein are set down.
translation: In this letter, the king officially asks you to let Fortinbras’ troops pass quietly through your lands on their way to Poland, and assures you of your safety.

original: It likes us well,   And at our more considered time we’ll read,   Answer, and think upon this business.
translation: This is good news, and when I have more time to concentrate, I’ll read this, think about it, and reply.

original: Meantime we thank you for your well-took labor.   Go to your rest. At night we’ll feast together.   Most welcome home!
translation: Meanwhile, thank you for your work. Go now, and rest. Tonight we’ll feast. And welcome home!

original: This business is well ended.   My liege and madam, to expostulate   What majesty should be, what duty is,   Why day is day, night night, and time is time,   Were nothing but to waste night, day, and time.
translation: That’s a good outcome to this situation. My lord and my lady, to make grand speeches about what majesty is, what service is, or why day is day, night is night, and time is time, would be nothing more than a waste of day, night, and time.

original: Therefore, since brevity is the soul of wit   And tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes,   I will be brief: your noble son is mad.
translation: Therefore, since being concise is the essence of wisdom—and nothing is so boring as endless verbal flourishes—I’ll get to the point. Your son is crazy.

original: Mad call I it, for, to define true madness,   What is ’t but to be nothing else but mad?   But let that go.
translation: “Crazy” I’m saying, because how can you define craziness other than to say that it’s craziness? But that’s a different issue.

original: More matter, with less art.
translation: More substance, less style.

original: Madam, I swear I use no art at all.   That he is mad, ’tis true. Tis true, ’tis pity,   And pity ’tis ’tis true—a foolish figure,   But farewell it, for I will use no art.
translation: Madam, I swear I’m using no style at all. It's true that he’s crazy. It’s true, it’s a pity, and it’s a pity that it’s true—but now I’m talking like a fool, so I’ll let that go and get to the point.

original: Mad let us grant him then. And now remains   That we find out the cause of this effect,   Or rather say, the cause of this defect,   For this effect defective comes by cause.
translation: We all agree that Hamlet’s crazy. Now all we have to do is to figure out the cause behind the effect—or I guess I should say defect, since this defective effect must have a cause.

original: Thus it remains, and the remainder thus. Perpend.   I have a daughter—have while she is mine—   Who in her duty and obedience, mark,   Hath given me this. Now gather and surmise.
translation: That’s what we have to do, and now I will continue with the rest of what I have to say. Consider this: I have a daughter— until  she gets married—who in her obedience and duty to me has given me this letter. Now listen to this:

original: “To the celestial and my soul’s idol,  the most beautified Ophelia”   —That’s an ill phrase, a  vile phrase. “Beautified” is a vile phrase. But you  shall hear. Thus:   [reads the letter]     “In her excellent  white bosom, these,”   etc.—
translation: “To the heavenly idol of my soul, the most beautified Ophelia” —That’s an ugly phrase, an ugly phrase. That “beautified” is a terrible use of the word. But I’ll continue:  [He reads the letter]   “In her excellent white bosom,”  et cetera—

original: Came this from Hamlet to her?
translation: This is from Hamlet to Ophelia?

original: Good madam, stay a while. I will be faithful.
translation: Madam, please be patient. I’ll read it as its written.

original: “Doubt thou the stars are fire,   Doubt that the sun doth move,   Doubt truth to be a liar,   But never doubt I love.
translation: “You may doubt that the stars are fire,  Doubt that the sun moves across the sky,  Doubt if the truth is actually a liar,  But never doubt my love.

original: O dear Ophelia, I am ill at these numbers. I have not  art to reckon my groans, but that I love thee best, oh,  most best, believe it. Adieu.   Thine evermore, most dear lady,   whilst this machine is to him,   Hamlet.”
translation: Oh, sweet Ophelia, I’m bad at poetry. I have no skill to put my feelings into words. But please believe that I love you best, oh, best of all—believe it. Goodbye. Yours forever, my dearest lady, as long as this body is still mine,          Hamlet.”

original: This in obedience hath my daughter shown me,   And more above, hath his solicitings,   As they fell out by time, by means, and place,   All given to mine ear.
translation: In her obedience to me, my daughter showed me this letter and more besides, as well as telling me how Hamlet has been courting her—when, how, and where.

original: But how hath she received his love?
translation: And how did she respond to his love?

original: What do you think of me?
translation: What is your opinion of me?

original: As of a man faithful and honorable.
translation: You are a loyal and honorable man.

original: I would fain prove so. But what might you think,   When I had seen this hot love on the wing—   As I perceived it, I must tell you that,   Before my daughter told me   —
translation: I would gladly prove that I am. But what would you have thought if I had learned of this hot affair—and I must tell you, I noticed it before my daughter told me of it—

original: what might you,   Or my dear majesty your queen here, think,   If I had played the desk or table-book,   Or given my heart a winking, mute and dumb,   Or looked upon this love with idle sight?   What might you think?
translation: what would your dear wife, her Majesty the Queen, have thought if I had been silent in the face of what I say? Or if I had just allowed it to continue, or just ignored it?

original: No, I went round to work,   And my young mistress thus I did bespeak:   “Lord Hamlet is a prince out of thy star.   This must not be.”
translation: No, I had to do something. And so I said to my daughter: “Lord Hamlet is a prince and above your social rank. You must end this.”

original: And then I prescripts gave her,   That she should lock herself from his resort,   Admit no messengers, receive no tokens.   Which done, she took the fruits of my advice;
translation: And then I ordered her to make it impossible for him to see her, to refuse all messages, and accept no gifts. She followed my advice.

original: And he, repelled—a short tale to make—   Fell into a sadness, then into a fast,   Thence to a watch, thence into a weakness,   Thence to a lightness, and, by this declension,   Into the madness wherein now he raves   And all we mourn for.
translation: In short, Hamlet, faced with this rejection, became sad. He stopped eating, stopped sleeping, got weak, got dizzy, and, moving step by step downward, eventually descended into the insanity that now holds him. And all of us grieve for him.

original: Do you think ’tis this?
translation: Do you think this is the cause of Hamlet’s behavior?

original: It may be, very like.
translation: It may be, it very well may be.

original: Hath there been such a time—I would fain know that— That I have positively said, “‘Tis so,” When it proved otherwise?
translation: Has there ever been a time—I’d gladly like to know—when I’ve definitively said something was true, and it turned out not to be true?

original: Not that I know.
translation: Not that I know of.

original: Take this from this if this be otherwise.   If circumstances lead me,
translation: Take my head from my body if I’m wrong.

original: I will find   Where truth is hid, though it were hid indeed   Within the center.
translation: I’ll follow the evidence and discover the truth, even if it’s hidden at the center of the earth.

original: How may we try it further?
translation: How can we test your theory?

original: You know sometimes he walks four hours together Here in the lobby.
translation: Well, you know he sometimes walks here in the main hall for four hours at a time.

original: So he does indeed.
translation: Yes, he does indeed.

original: At such a time I’ll loose my daughter to him.
translation: During one such time, I’ll send my daughter to see him.

original: We will try it.
translation: We’ll try it.

original: But look where sadly the poor wretch comes reading.
translation: Look how sadly he’s coming in, reading.

original: Away, I do beseech you, both away. I’ll board him presently. O, give me leave.
translation: I beg you, please go away, both of you. I’ll speak to him now. Oh, please leave me to do it.

original: How does my good Lord Hamlet?
translation: How do you do, Lord Hamlet?

original: Well, God-’a’-mercy.
translation: Fine, thank you.

original: Do you know me, my lord?
translation: Do you know who I am, my lord?

original: Excellent well. You are a fishmonger.
translation: Of course. You are a fish seller.

original: Not I, my lord.
translation: No, not me, my lord.

original: Then I would you were so honest a man.
translation: Then I wish you were as honorable a man as a fish seller.

original: Honest, my lord?
translation: Honorable, my lord?

original: Ay, sir. To be honest, as this world goes, is to be one man picked out of ten thousand.
translation: Yes, sir. In this world of ours, just one man in ten thousand is honorable.

original: That’s very true, my lord.
translation: That’s very true, my lord.

original: For if the sun breed maggots in a dead dog, being a  good kissing carrion— Have you a daughter?
translation: Because if the sun breeds maggots on a dead dog, kissing the corpse with its rays—do you have a daughter?

original: I have, my lord.
translation: I do, my lord.

original: Let her not walk i’ th’ sun. Conception is a blessing,  but, as your daughter may conceive—Friend, look to ’t.
translation: Don’t let her walk out in the sun. Pregnancy is a blessing, but if your daughter gets pregnant-–think about it, friend.

original: How say you by that? Still harping on my  daughter. Yet he knew me not at first. He said I was a  fishmonger.
translation: What does that mean? Still focused on my daughter. But he didn’t recognize me at first. He thought I was a fish seller.

original: He is far gone, far gone. And truly in my  youth I suffered much extremity for love, very near  this. I’ll speak to him again.
translation: He’s far gone, far gone. And yet it’s true that when I was young I suffered terribly for love, almost as badly as Hamlet. I’ll talk to him again.

original: Words, words, words.
translation: Words, words, words.

original: What is the matter, my lord?
translation: What is the subject?

original: Between who?
translation: Between whom?

original: I mean, the matter that you read, my lord.
translation: I mean, the subject of what you’re reading?

original: Slanders, sir. For the satirical rogue says here that  old men have gray beards, that their faces are wrinkled, their eyes purging thick amber and plum-tree gum, and  that they have a plentiful lack of wit, together with  most weak hams
translation: Oh, lies, sir. The joking rascal who wrote this says here that old men have gray beards, their faces are wrinkled, their eyes full of crust and gunk, and that they both lack wisdom and have weak thighs.

original: —all which, sir, though I most powerfully  and potently believe, yet I hold it not honesty to have  it thus set down;
translation: And though I believe all of that is true, I still would argue that it’s not good behavior to write it down.

original: for yourself, sir, should be old as I  am, if like a crab you could go backward.
translation: For instance, you yourself would be as old as I am, if you could just travel backward like a crab, sir.

original: Though this be madness, yet there is method in  ’t.    Will you walk out of the air, my lord?
translation: There’s a method to his madness.

original: Into my grave.
translation: Into my grave.

original: Indeed, that is out of the air.
translation: Well, that’s certainly not outside.
