original: You cannot, sir, take from me any thing that I will  more willingly part withal—except my life, except my  life, except my life.
translation: There’s nothing I would more willingly give up than that—except my life, except my life, except my life.

original: Fare you well, my lord.
translation: Take care, my lord.

original: These tedious old fools!
translation: These boring old fools!

original: You go to seek the Lord Hamlet. There he is.
translation: You’re looking for Lord Hamlet. There he is.

original: God save you, sir!
translation: Thank you, sir.

original: My honored lord!
translation: My honorable lord!

original: My most dear lord!
translation: My most dear lord!

original: My excellent good friends! How dost thou, Guildenstern? Ah, Rosencrantz! Good lads, how do you both?
translation: Ah, my good old friends! How are you, Guildenstern? And Rosencrantz! Good friends, how are you both doing?

original: As the indifferent children of the earth.
translation: As well as any old average man.

original: Happy, in that we are not overhappy. On Fortune’s cap we are not the very button.
translation: Happy that we’re not too happy. We’re not exactly the luckiest men in the world.

original: Nor the soles of her shoes?
translation: But not the unluckiest either, right?

original: Neither, my lord.
translation: Neither, my lord.

original: Then you live about her waist, or in the middle of her  favors?
translation: So you’re hanging around Lady Luck’s waist, right in the middle of her favors?

original: Faith, her privates we.
translation: Yup, we’re like privates in her army.

original: In the secret parts of Fortune? Oh, most true. She is a strumpet. What news?
translation: You’re in Lady Luck’s private parts? Ah, it’s true. She is a whore. So what’s the news?

original: None, my lord, but that the world’s grown honest.
translation: Nothing other than that the world’s become honest, , my lord.

original: Then is doomsday near. But your news is not true. Let  me question more in particular. What have you, my good  friends, deserved at the hands of fortune that she sends you to prison hither?
translation: Then the end of the world must be coming. But you’re wrong. Let me ask you one question in particular: my good friends, what have you done to anger the fates that they have sent you here to this prison?

original: Prison, my lord?
translation: Prison, my lord?

original: Denmark’s a prison.
translation: Denmark’s a prison.

original: Then is the world one.
translation: Then the whole world is one as well.

original: A goodly one, in which there are many confines, wards,  and dungeons, Denmark being one o’ th’ worst.
translation: A big one, with lots of cells and dungeons—Denmark being one of the worst.

original: We think not so, my lord.
translation: We don’t think so, my lord.

original: Why, then, ’tis none to you, for there is nothing  either good or bad, but thinking makes it so. To me it  is a prison.
translation: Well, then it isn’t one to you, since nothing is inherently good or bad—it’s what you think of it that makes it so. To me, Denmark is a prison.

original: Why then, your ambition makes it one. ‘Tis too narrow  for your mind.
translation: It must be your ambition that makes it one. It’s too small for your big ideas.

original: O God, I could be bounded in a nutshell and count  myself a king of infinite space, were it not that I have bad dreams.
translation: Oh God, I could be trapped inside a nutshell and consider myself a king of infinite space, if only I didn’t have bad dreams.

original: Which dreams indeed are ambition, for the very  substance of the ambitious is merely the shadow of a  dream.
translation: Dreams are a mark of ambition. After all, ambition is just the shadow of a dream.

original: A dream itself is but a shadow.
translation: A dream is itself just a shadow.

original: Truly, and I hold ambition of so airy and light a  quality that it is but a shadow’s shadow.
translation: True, and I’d argue that ambition is so light and airy that it’s just a shadow of a shadow.

original: Then are our beggars bodies, and our monarchs and  outstretched heroes the beggars’ shadows. Shall we to  th’ court? For by my fay, I cannot reason.
translation: Then beggars without ambition must be the ones with substance, while ambitious kings and heroes are just the shadows of those beggars. Should we go inside to the court? I swear, I can’t think straight any longer.

original: We’ll wait upon you.
translation: We’re at your service.

original: No such matter. I will not sort you with the rest of my servants, for, to speak to you like an honest man, I am most dreadfully attended. But in the beaten way of  friendship, what make you at Elsinore?
translation: Not at all. I won’t treat you like my servants, because, to be honest with you, my servants are pretty dreadful. Now, as my friends, tell me why you’ve returned here to Elsinore?

original: To visit you, my lord, no other occasion.
translation: To visit you, my lord. No other reason.

original: Beggar that I am, I am even poor in thanks; but I thank you, and sure, dear friends, my thanks are too dear a  halfpenny.
translation: Though I’m such a beggar that my thanks aren’t worth much, I still thank you.

original: Were you not sent for? Is it your own  inclining? Is it a free visitation?
translation: But did someone ask you to come? Or was it an idea you had all on your own?

original: Come, come, deal  justly with me. Come, come. Nay, speak.
translation: Come on, be honest with me. Come now. Tell me.

original: What should we say, my lord?
translation: What should we say, my lord?

original: Why, any thing, but to th’ purpose. You were sent for,  and there is a kind of confession in your looks which  your modesties have not craft enough to color.
translation: Anything, as long as it answers my question. You were sent for. I can see it in your faces. You’re not good enough liars to hide your thoughts.

original: I know  the good king and queen have sent for you.
translation: I know the king and queen sent for you.

original: To what end, my lord?
translation: Why would they do that, my lord?

original: That you must teach me. But let me conjure you, by the  rights of our fellowship, by the consonancy of our  youth, by the obligation of our ever-preserved love, and by what more dear a better proposer could charge you  withal:
translation: You'll have to tell me that. But first, let me remind you of our longstanding friendship, the childhood we spent together, the duties of our love for each other, and everything else that a person more eloquent than I would describe.

original: be even and direct with me whether you were sent for or no.
translation: Now: answer me honestly and directly whether or not you were sent for.

original: What say you?
translation: What do you think?

original: Nay, then, I have an eye of you—If you love me, hold not off.
translation: Ah, I’ve got my eye on you.

original: My lord, we were sent for.
translation: My lord, we were sent for.

original: I will tell you why. So shall my anticipation prevent  your discovery, and your secrecy to the king and queen  moult no feather.
translation: I’ll tell you why. That way you won’t have to reveal anything, and you can preserve the secrecy you promised to the king and queen.

original: I have of late—but wherefore I know  not—lost all my mirth, forgone all custom of exercises,  and indeed it goes so heavily with my disposition that  this goodly frame, the earth, seems to me a sterile  promontory;
translation: Lately, for reasons I don’t now, I’ve lost all my joy, stopped exercising, and feel so depressed that the entire world seems to be empty to me.

original: this most excellent canopy, the air—look  you, this brave o’erhanging firmament, this majestical  roof fretted with golden fire—why, it appears no other  thing to me than a foul and pestilent congregation of  vapors.
translation: This beautiful canopy, the sky—look at it, this splendid overarching sky, a majestic roof adorned with golden sunlight—why, to me it seems like nothing more than a foul collection of diseased air.

original: What a piece of work is a man! How noble in  reason, how infinite in faculty! In form and moving how  express and admirable! In action how like an angel, in  apprehension how like a god! The beauty of the world.
translation: What a masterpiece each human is! How noble in his ability to think, how unlimited in abilities, how attractive in his body and movement, how angelic in action, how godlike in understanding! The most beautiful thing in the world.

original: The paragon of animals. And yet, to me, what is this  quintessence of dust? Man delights not me. No, nor woman neither, though by your smiling you seem to say so.
translation: The perfect ideal, standing above all other animals. And yet, for me, what are humans like, except dust? Men don’t delight me. No, women neither—though your smiles seem to suggest that’s what you were thinking.

original: My lord, there was no such stuff in my thoughts.
translation: My lord, I wasn’t thinking that at all.

original: Why did you laugh then, when I said “man delights not  me”?
translation: Why did you laugh, then, when I said that men don’t delight me?

original: To think, my lord, if you delight not in man, what  Lenten entertainment the players shall receive from you. We coted them on the way, and hither are they coming to offer you service.
translation: My lord, I was thinking that if men don’t delight you, what a poor welcome you’ll give the coming troupe of actors. We crossed paths with them as we were on our way here, and they’re coming to entertain you.

original: He that plays the king shall be welcome. His majesty  shall have tribute of me.
translation: The one who plays the part of the king will be particularly welcome. He will be treated like a true king.

original: The adventurous knight shall  use his foil and target, the lover shall not sigh  gratis, the humorous man shall end his part in peace,
translation: The adventurous knight will get to use his sword and shield; the lover’s sighs will not go unrewarded; the crazy one will be allowed to finish without interruption;

original: the clown shall make those laugh whose lungs are tickle  o’ th’ sear, and the lady shall say her mind freely, or  the blank verse shall halt for ’t. What players are  they?
translation: the clown will make everybody who laughs easily laugh; and the lady will get to speak her mind completely—or else I’ll stop the play. Which troupe is it?

original: Even those you were wont to take delight in, the  tragedians of the city.
translation: The troupe you used to love so much, the actors from the city who perform tragedies.

original: How chances it they travel? Their residence, both in  reputation and profit, was better both ways.
translation: Why are they traveling? They’re better known in the city and make more money there.

original: I think their inhibition comes by the means of the late innovation.
translation: New theatrical fads in the city have made it more difficult for the troupe to do well there.

original: Do they hold the same estimation they did when I was in the city? Are they so followed?
translation: Are they as popular as they were when I was in the city? Do they still draw crowds?

original: No, indeed are they not.
translation: No, they don’t.

original: How comes it? Do they grow rusty?
translation: Why not? Are they getting rusty?

original: Nay, their endeavor keeps in the wonted pace. But there is, sir, an eyrie of children, little eyases, that cry  out on the top of question and are most tyrannically  clapped for ’t.
translation: No, they’re as good as they always were. But they now have to compete with troupes of child actors who shout out their lines and get unbelievable applause for it.

original: These are now the fashion, and so  berattle the common stages—so they call them—that many  wearing rapiers are afraid of goose quills and dare  scarce come thither.
translation: These child actors are now in fashion. And they so dominate the public theaters that high-society types are afraid to come, because they fear getting made fun of by the satirical playwrights who write for the boys.

original: What, are they children? Who maintains ‘em? How are  they escoted? Will they pursue the quality no longer  than they can sing?
translation: What, they’re actually children? Who takes care of them? Who supports them financially? Will they stop working once their voices change during puberty?

original: Will they not say afterwards, if  they should grow themselves to common players (as it is  most like if their means are no better), their writers  do them wrong to make them exclaim against their own  succession?
translation: Once they’ve grown to be adult actors (as is likely), won’t these children complain that their former playwrights have done them wrong by causing harm to the profession of acting?

original: Faith, there has been much to do on both sides, and the nation holds it no sin to tar them to controversy.
translation: I swear, there’s been a big debate on the topic, with strong opinions on both sides.

original: There was, for a while, no money bid for argument unless the poet and the player went to cuffs in the question.
translation: For a while, no one could even sell a play unless the play contained a scene in which a poet and an actor had a fistfight.

original: Is ’t possible?
translation: Can that be possible?

original: Oh, there has been much throwing about of brains.
translation: Oh, there’s been a lot of arguing.

original: Do the boys carry it away?
translation: The boys are winning?

original: Ay, that they do, my lord. Hercules and his load too.
translation: Yes, they are, my lord. The boys carry all of theater on their shoulders, just as Hercules carried the world.

original: It is not very strange. For my uncle is King of  Denmark, and those that would make mouths at him while  my father lived give twenty, forty, fifty, a hundred  ducats apiece for his picture in little.
translation: Actually, it’s not so strange. My uncle is King of Denmark, and the same people who made fun of him when my father was alive now pay twenty, forty, fifty, a hundred gold coins apiece for a little painting of him.

original: ‘Sblood, there  is something in this more than natural, if philosophy  could find it out.
translation: By God ! There’s something unnatural about it, if you puzzle it out.

original: There are the players.
translation: There are the actors.

original: Gentlemen, you are welcome to Elsinore. Your hands,  come then. Th’ appurtenance of welcome is fashion and  ceremony.
translation: Gentlemen, welcome to Elsinore. Now come, shake my hand. Giving a proper welcome is a matter of following the current customs.

original: Let me comply with you in this garb—lest my  extent to the players, which, I tell you, must show  fairly outwards, should more appear like entertainment  than yours.
translation: Let’s follow the customs, then, so that my exuberant welcome to the players doesn’t make it seem like I’m happier to see them than I am to see you.

original: You are welcome. But my uncle-father and  aunt-mother are deceived.
translation: You are welcome here. Even so, my uncle-father and aunt-mother are confused.

original: In what, my dear lord?
translation: In what way, my dear lord?

original: I am but mad north-north-west. When the wind is  southerly, I know a hawk from a handsaw.
translation: I’m only crazy at certain times. At others, I know exactly what’s happening.

original: Well be with you, gentlemen.
translation: Gentlemen, I hope you’re well.

original: Hark you, Guildenstern, and you too—at each ear a  hearer.    That great baby you see  there is not yet out of his swaddling-clouts
translation: Now listen, Guildenstern, and you too, Rosencrantz—each of you listen close.  That big baby you see there is still wearing diapers.

original: Happily he’s the second time come to them, for they say an old man is twice a child.
translation: It’s his second time around, as they say—since an old man is like a child again.

original: I will prophesy he comes to tell me of the players. Mark it.  [to  POLONIUS]  — You say right, sir. O’ Monday morning, ’twas  so indeed.
translation: I predict he’s coming to tell me about the actors. Watch.

original: My lord, I have news to tell you.
translation: My lord, I have news to tell you.

original: My lord, I have news to tell you. When Roscius was an  actor in Rome—
translation: My lord, I have news to tell you. When Roscius was an actor in Rome—

original: The actors are come hither, my lord.
translation: The actors have arrived, my lord.

original: Buzz, buzz.
translation: Gossip, gossip.

original: Upon my honor—
translation: I swear—

original: Then came each actor on his ass—
translation: Then each actor came in on his ass.

original: The best actors in the world, either for tragedy,  comedy, history, pastoral, pastoral-comical,  historical-pastoral, tragical-historical,  tragical-comical-historical-pastoral, scene individable, or poem unlimited.
translation: They’re the best actors in the world, for all sorts of plays—tragic, comic, historical, pastoral, pastoral-comical, historical-pastoral, tragical-historical, tragical-comical-historical, one-act plays, or epic poems.

original: Seneca cannot be too heavy, nor  Plautus too light. For the law of writ and the liberty,  these are the only men.
translation: The tragic playwright Seneca is not too serious for them, nor is the comic writer Plautus too silly. For both formal plays and freer dramas, these are the actors you want.

original: O Jephthah, judge of Israel, what a treasure hadst  thou!
translation: Oh, Jephthah, judge of ancient Israel, what a treasure you had!

original: What a treasure had he, my lord?
translation: What treasure did he have, my lord?

original: Why,   One fair daughter and no more, The which he lovèd passing well.
translation: Well,  One fine daughter, and no more, Whom he loved beyond all others—

original: Still on my daughter.
translation: Still focused on my daughter.

original: Am I not i’ th’ right, old Jephthah?
translation: Aren’t I right, old man Jephthah?

original: If you call me Jephthah, my lord, I have a daughter  that I love passing well.
translation: My lord, if you’re calling me Jephthah, I do have a daughter I love beyond all other things.

original: Nay, that follows not.
translation: No, you don’t understand.

original: What follows, then, my lord?
translation: What should I understand, then, my lord?

original: Why,   As by lot, God wot,   and then, you know,   It came to pass, as most like it was—
translation: Why, "as if by chance, God knows," and then, you know, "it happened, as was most likely expect"

original: The first row of the pious chanson will show you more,  for look where my abridgement comes.
translation: —you can learn more by looking at the first verse of the popular song, because I’m stopping now.

original: You are welcome, masters, welcome, all!
translation: You are welcome. Welcome to all of you!

original: What speech, my good lord?
translation: Which speech, my lord?

original: I heard thee speak me a speech once, but it was never  acted. Or, if it was, not above once, for the play, I  remember, pleased not the million. ‘Twas caviary to the  general.
translation: I heard you recite a speech for me once that was never acted on stage. Or, if it was, not more than once—because the play I remember didn’t please the masses. It was like caviar for the masses—too sophisticated for them.

original: But it was—as I received it, and others, whose  judgments in such matters cried in the top of mine—an  excellent play, well digested in the scenes, set down  with as much modesty as cunning.
translation: But I, along with the better-informed critics, thought that it was excellent, with scenes that flowed one to the next and written in language that was clever and yet not overdone.

original: I remember, one said  there were no sallets in the lines to make the matter  savory, nor no matter in the phrase that might indict  the author of affectation, but called it an honest  method, as wholesome as sweet, and by very much more  handsome than fine.
translation: I remember one critic commented that the play lacked spicy jokes to liven it up, and did not display any fancy language, but that it was well-done, and beautiful rather than showy.

original: One speech in it I chiefly loved.  ‘Twas Aeneas’ tale to Dido and thereabout of it,  especially where he speaks of Priam’s slaughter. If it  live in your memory, begin at this line—Let me see, let  me see—
translation: There was one speech in it that I loved the most. It was the story  Aeneas told Dido , particularly the part about  Priam’s  murder. If you remember it, begin at line—let me see, let me see—

original: The rugged Pyrrhus, like th’ Hyrcanian beast—   It is not so. It begins with Pyrrhus—   The rugged Pyrrhus, he whose sable arms,   Black as his purpose, did the night resemble   When he lay couchèd in the ominous horse,   Hath now this dread and black complexion smeared   With heraldry more dismal.
translation: The rugged Pyrrhus, fierce as a tiger...No, that’s not it; it begins like this: Rugged Pyrrhus—whose armor was as black as his desire, resembled the night when he crouched inside the Trojan Horse—has now smeared his terrible black armor with a more awful coat of arms.

original: Head to foot   Now is he total gules, horridly tricked   With blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons,   Baked and impasted with the parching streets,   That lend a tyrannous and damnèd light   To their lord’s murder.
translation: Head to foot, he’s now all red, decorated horribly with the blood of fathers, mothers, daughters, sons. The blood baked solid by fires in the streets—fires that lend a terrible, damned light to his murders.

original: Roasted in wrath and fire,   And thus o’ersizèd with coagulate gore,   With eyes like carbuncles, the hellish Pyrrhus   Old grandsire Priam seeks.   So, proceed you.
translation: Roasted by anger and fire—and covered with hardened gore—with eyes like rubies, the hellish Pyrrhus goes looking for grandfather Priam. Continue from there.

original: ‘Fore God, my lord, well spoken, with good accent and  good discretion.
translation: By God, my lord, well done—with the right accent and capturing all the meaning.

original: Anon he finds him   Striking too short at Greeks. His antique sword,   Rebellious to his arm, lies where it falls,   Repugnant to command.
translation: Soon he finds Priam vainly fighting off the Greeks. His old sword, too heavy for him to wield, lies where it fell, refusing his commands.

original: Unequal matched,   Pyrrhus at Priam drives, in rage strikes wide,   But with the whiff and wind of his fell sword   The unnerved father falls.
translation: An unfair opponent, Pyrrhus rushes Priam, and in a rage, strikes and misses. But the wind made by his dreadful sword knocks the old man down.

original: Then senseless Ilium,   Seeming to feel this blow, with flaming top   Stoops to his base, and with a hideous crash   Takes prisoner Pyrrhus’ ear. For, lo, his sword,   Which was declining on the milky head   Of reverend Priam, seemed i’ th’ air to stick.
translation: Then the city of Troy, seeming to feel this fatal blow to its ruler, collapses in flames, and the hideous crash arrests Pyrrhus’ attention. Now his sword, which was lowering on the white-haired head of old, revered Priam, seemed stuck in the air.

original: So as a painted tyrant Pyrrhus stood,   And, like a neutral to his will and matter,   Did nothing.
translation: Pyrrhus stood like a tyrant in a painting, and, caught between act and intention, did nothing.

original: But as we often see against some storm   A silence in the heavens, the rack stand still,   The bold winds speechless, and the orb below   As hush as death, anon the dreadful thunder   Doth rend the region. So, after Pyrrhus’ pause,   Arousèd vengeance sets him new a-work.
translation: But just as a storm is often broken by a sudden silence—with the clouds growing still and the bold winds calming and the earth below, as quiet as death, once more finds the sky split by sudden thunder—so too did Pyrrhus’ pause renew his fury, and set him back to work.

original: And never did the Cyclops’ hammers fall   On Mars’s armor forged for proof eterne   With less remorse than Pyrrhus’ bleeding sword   Now falls on Priam.
translation: Not even when the Cyclopses worked to make the unbreakable armor of the god of war, their hammers did not fall as cruelly as Pyrrhus’ bloody sword now falls on Priam.

original: Out, out, thou strumpet Fortune! All you gods   In general synod take away her power,   Break all the spokes and fellies from her wheel,   And bowl the round nave down the hill of heaven,   As low as to the fiends!
translation: Be gone, goddess of Fortune, you whore! All you gods should join together to take away her power—break all the spokes on her wheel of fortune, and roll it down the hill of heaven into hell.

original: This is too long.
translation: This speech is too long.

original: It shall to the barber’s, with your beard.—Prithee, say on. He’s for a jig or a tale of bawdry, or he sleeps.  Say on. Come to Hecuba.
But who, ah woe, who had seen the moblèd queen—
translation: But who—ah, sadness—had seen the muffled queen—

original: “The moblèd queen?”
translation: “The muffled queen?”

original: That’s good. “Moblèd queen” is good.
translation: That’s good. “The muffled queen” is good.

original: Run barefoot up and down, threatening the flames   With bisson rheum, a clout upon that head   Where late the diadem stood, and for a robe,   About her lank and all o’erteemèd loins,   A blanket,   in the alarm of fear caught up—
translation: Run barefoot back and forth, dousing the flames with her tears, a cloth on the head where just before a crown had sat, and instead of a robe, she wore a blanket wrapped around her body, withered from childbearing.

original: Who this had seen, with tongue in venom steeped,   ‘Gainst fortune’s state would treason have pronounced.
translation: Anyone seeing her this way would have screamed out in anger against the goddess Fortune.

original: But if the gods themselves did see her then   When she saw Pyrrhus make malicious sport   In mincing with his sword her husband’s limbs,
translation: If the gods themselves had seen her while she watched Pyrrhus make a game of cutting her husbands limbs to bits,

original: The instant burst of clamor that she made,   (Unless things mortal move them not at all)   Would have made milch the burning eyes of heaven,   And passion in the gods.
translation: the awful cry she made would have made the blazing stars of heaven weep hot tears, and bring passion to the gods—unless the gods don’t care about mortals.

original: Look whe’e he has not turned his color and has tears in ’s eyes.—Prithee, no more.
translation: Look how he’s gone pale, and has tears in his eyes. Please, no more.

original: ‘Tis well. I’ll have thee speak out  the rest soon.
translation: Very good. I’ll have you perform the rest of it soon.

original: My lord, I will use them according to their desert.
translation: My lord, I will give them all they deserve.

original: God’s bodykins, man, much better. Use every man after  his desert, and who should ’scape whipping?
translation: By God, man, give them more than that! If you gave everyone just what they deserved, would anyone ever escape a whipping?

original: Use them  after your own honor and dignity. The less they deserve, the more merit is in your bounty. Take them in.
translation: How you treat them speaks to your honor and dignity. The less they deserve, the more merit you’ll earn through your generosity. Bring them inside.

original: Come, sirs.
translation: Come with me, sirs.

original: Follow him, friends. We’ll hear a play tomorrow.  [to  FIRST PLAYER]  — Dost thou hear me, old friend? Can you  play The Murder of Gonzago?
translation: Follow him, friends. We’ll watch a play tomorrow.

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: We’ll ha ’t tomorrow night. You could, for a need,  study a speech of some dozen or sixteen lines which I  would set down and insert in ’t, could you not?
translation: We’ll see that play tomorrow night. If I were to write a speech of twelve to sixteen lines to insert into the play, you could, if necessary, learn it for tomorrow’s performance, right?

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: Very well. Follow that lord, and look you mock him not.
translation: Very well. Follow that gentleman, and please don’t make fun of him.

original: My good friends, I’ll leave you till night. You are  welcome to Elsinore.
translation: My good friends, I’ll see you tonight. Welcome to Elsinore.

original: Good my lord.
translation: Yes, my good lord.

original: Ay, so. Good-bye to you.
translation: Goodbye to you both.

original: Now I am alone.   Oh, what a rogue and peasant slave am I!   Is it not monstrous that this player here,   But in a fiction, in a dream of passion,   Could force his soul so to his own conceit   That from her working all his visage wanned,   Tears in his eyes,
translation: Now I’m alone. Oh, what a low-life scoundrel I am! Isn’t it terrible that this actor—reciting a work of fiction—could force his soul to feel the passion so completely that he grew pale, tears welled in his eyes?

original: distraction in his aspect,   A broken voice, and his whole function suiting   With forms to his conceit? And all for nothing—   For Hecuba!
translation: He got overwhelmed, his voice broke, and the entirety of his being matched the emotions he was supposed to be playing. And all for nothing—for Hecuba!

original: What’s Hecuba to him or he to Hecuba   That he should weep for her? What would he do   Had he the motive and the cue for passion   That I have? He would drown the stage with tears   And cleave the general ear with horrid speech,
translation: What does Hecuba mean to him, or he to Hecuba, that he would weep for her? What would he do if he had the motive or reason for passion that I have? He would drown the stage with tears, and split the ears of all who heard him with angry words.

original: Make mad the guilty and appall the free,   Confound the ignorant, and amaze indeed   The very faculties of eyes and ears.
translation: He would drive the guilty crazy with shame, horrify the innocent, confuse the ignorant, and shock anyone with eyes and ears.

original: Yet I,   A dull and muddy-mettled rascal, peak   Like John-a-dreams, unpregnant of my cause,   And can say nothing—no, not for a king,   Upon whose property and most dear life   A damned defeat was made. Am I a coward?
translation: Meanwhile I—a stupid fool—mope like a daydreamer, don’t have a plan, and have nothing, nothing, to say for a king whose throne and life were brought to destruction. Am I a coward?

original: Who calls me “villain”? Breaks my pate across?   Plucks off my beard and blows it in my face?   Tweaks me by the nose? Gives me the lie i’ th’ throat   As deep as to the lungs? Who does me this?   Ha!
translation: Who will stand up and call me a villain, or slap me across the face? Pluck hairs from my beard and blow them in my face? Tweak my nose? Call me a liar? Who does any of those things? Ha!

original: ‘Swounds, I should take it, for it cannot be   But I am pigeon-livered and lack gall   To make oppression bitter, or ere this   I should have fatted all the region kites   With this slave’s offal.
translation: By God , I’d accept it, because I must have a nature that doesn’t respond to wrongs by making life for the evildoer bitter. Otherwise, I would have long ago fattened up the local birds with the intestines of this scoundrel, King Claudius.

original: Bloody, bawdy villain!   Remorseless, treacherous, lecherous, kindless villain!   O vengeance!   Why, what an ass am I!
translation: Bloody, vulgar villain! Remorseless, treacherous, lustful, unnatural villain! Oh, revenge! Why, what an ass I am.

original: This is most brave,   That I, the son of a dear father murdered,   Prompted to my revenge by heaven and hell,   Must, like a whore, unpack my heart with words   And fall a-cursing like a very drab,   A stallion! Fie upon ’t, foh!
translation: Look how brave I am—the son of a beloved, murdered father; told to take revenge by heaven and hell; and yet all I can do is talk about my problems and curse like a whore in the street. I’m a male whore! Curses on it!

original: About, my brain.—Hum, I have heard   That guilty creatures sitting at a play   Have, by the very cunning of the scene,   Been struck so to the soul that presently   They have proclaimed their malefactions.
translation: Now think, brain—Hmm..I’ve heard that guilty people watching a play have been so affected by the performance that they have confessed their crimes.

original: For murder, though it have no tongue, will speak   With most miraculous organ. I’ll have these players   Play something like the murder of my father   Before mine uncle. I’ll observe his looks.   I’ll tent him to the quick.
translation: Though murder has no tongue, it still miraculously finds other ways to speak. I’ll have these actors perform something like my father’s murder in front of my uncle. Meanwhile, I’ll watch my uncle, and probe him to his very core.

original: If he do blench,   I know my course. The spirit that I have seen   May be the devil, and the devil hath power   T’ assume a pleasing shape.
translation: If he flinches, I’ll know what to do. The ghost I saw may be the devil, who has the power to appear in a pleasing manner.

original: Yea, and perhaps   Out of my weakness and my melancholy,   As he is very potent with such spirits,   Abuses me to damn me. I’ll have grounds   More relative than this. The play’s the thing   Wherein I’ll catch the conscience of the king.
translation: Perhaps he has taken advantage of my sadness—because he has great influence over melancholy people—to trick me into damnation. I need more solid evidence. The play’s the thing I’ll use to reveal the conscience of the king.

original: And can you by no drift of conference   Get from him why he puts on this confusion,
translation: And the two of you haven’t been able to figure out why he’s acting so oddly,

original: Grating so harshly all his days of quiet   With turbulent and dangerous lunacy?
translation: with a dangerous lunacy that’s such a huge shift from his earlier calm and quiet behavior?

original: He does confess he feels himself distracted. But from what cause he will by no means speak.
translation: He admits he feels somewhat crazy, but won’t talk about the cause.

original: Nor do we find him forward to be sounded.   But with a crafty madness keeps aloof
translation: And he’s not willing to be questioned. His insanity is sly and smart,

original: When we would bring him on to some confession   Of his true state.
translation: and he slips away from our questions when we try to get him to tell us about how he’s feeling.

original: Did he receive you well?
translation: Did he treat you well?

original: Most like a gentleman.
translation: Yes, he treated us like a gentleman.

original: But with much forcing of his disposition.
translation: But also as if he he had to force himself to act that way.

original: Niggard of question, but of our demands Most free in his reply.
translation: He didn’t ask many questions, but answered our questions extensively.

original: Did you assay him? To any pastime?
translation: Did you try to get him to do something fun?

original: Madam, it so fell out, that certain players   We o’erraught on the way. Of these we told him,   And there did seem in him a kind of joy   To hear of it.
translation: Madam, as it happened, we crossed paths with some actors on the way here. When we mentioned them to Hamlet, he seemed to feel a kind of joy.

original: They are about the court,   And, as I think, they have already order   This night to play before him.
translation: They are at the court now, and I think they’ve been told to perform for him tonight.

original: ‘Tis most true, And he beseeched me to entreat your Majesties To hear and see the matter.
translation: That’s true, and he asked me to beg both of you, your Majesties, to come and watch.

original: With all my heart, and it doth much content me   To hear him so inclined.
translation: With all my heart, I’m glad to hear of his interest.

original: Good gentlemen, give him a further edge,   And drive his purpose on to these delights.
translation: Gentlemen, try to nurture this interest of his, and keep him focused on these amusements.

original: We shall, my lord.
translation: We will, my lord.

original: Sweet Gertrude, leave us too,   For we have closely sent for Hamlet hither,   That he, as ’twere by accident, may here   Affront Ophelia.
translation: Dear Gertrude, please go as well. We’ve sent for Hamlet as a way for him to meet with Ophelia, seemingly by chance.

original: Her father and myself (lawful espials)   Will so bestow ourselves that, seeing unseen,   We may of their encounter frankly judge,
translation: Her father and I—spying for justifiable reasons—will place ourselves so that we can’t be seen, but can observe the encounter

original: And gather by him, as he is behaved,   If ’t be the affliction of his love or no   That thus he suffers for.
translation: and judge from Hamlet’s behavior whether love is the cause of his madness.

original: I shall obey you
translation: I’ll do as you ask.

original: Madam, I wish it may.
translation: I hope it too, madam.

original: Ophelia, walk you here.
translation: Ophelia, walk over here.

original: Oh, ’tis too true!   How smart a lash that speech doth give my conscience!
translation: Oh, that's all too true! His words are like a whip against my conscience!

original: The harlot’s cheek, beautied with plastering art,   Is not more ugly to the thing that helps it   Than is my deed to my most painted word.   O heavy burden!
translation: The whore’s ugly cheek—only made beautiful with make-up—is no more terrible than the things I’ve done and hidden with fine words. Oh, what guilt!

original: I hear him coming. Let’s withdraw, my lord.
translation: I hear him coming. Quick, let’s hide, my lord.

original: To be, or not to be? That is the question—   Whether ’tis nobler in the mind to suffer   The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,   Or to take arms against a sea of troubles,   And, by opposing, end them?
translation: To live, or to die? That is the question. Is it nobler to suffer through all the terrible things fate throws at you, or to fight off your troubles, and, in doing so, end them completely?

original: To die, to sleep—   No more—and by a sleep to say we end   The heartache and the thousand natural shocks   That flesh is heir to—’tis a consummation   Devoutly to be wished!
translation: To die, to sleep—because that’s all dying is—and by a sleep I mean an end to all the heartache and the thousand injuries that we are vulnerable to—that’s an end to be wished for!

original: To die, to sleep.   To sleep, perchance to dream—ay, there’s the rub,   For in that sleep of death what dreams may come   When we have shuffled off this mortal coil,   Must give us pause. There’s the respect   That makes calamity of so long life.
translation: To die, to sleep. To sleep, perhaps to dream—yes, but there’s there’s the catch. Because the kinds of dreams that might come in that sleep of death—after you have left behind your mortal body—are something to make you anxious. That’s the consideration that makes us suffer the calamities of life for so long.

original: For who would bear the whips and scorns of time,   Th’ oppressor’s wrong, the proud man’s contumely,   The pangs of despised love, the law’s delay,   The insolence of office, and the spurns   That patient merit of th’ unworthy takes,   When he himself might his quietus make   With a bare bodkin?
translation: Because who would bear all the trials and tribulations of time—the oppression of the powerful, the insults from arrogant men, the pangs of unrequited love, the slowness of justice, the disrespect of people in office, and the general abuse of good people by bad—when you could just settle all your debts using nothing more than an unsheathed dagger?

original: Who would fardels bear,   To grunt and sweat under a weary life,   But that the dread of something after death,   The undiscovered country from whose bourn   No traveler returns,   puzzles the will   And makes us rather bear those ills we have   Than fly to others that we know not of?
translation: Who would bear his burdens, and grunt and sweat through a tiring life, if they weren’t frightened of what might happen after death—that undiscovered country from which no visitor returns,  which we wonder about and which makes us prefer the troubles we know rather than fly off to face the ones we don’t?

original: Thus conscience does make cowards of us all,   And thus the native hue of resolution   Is sicklied o’er with the pale cast of thought,   And enterprises of great pitch and moment   With this regard their currents turn awry,   And lose the name of action.
translation: Thus, the fear of death makes us all cowards, and our natural willingness to act is made weak by too much thinking.  Actions of great urgency and importance get thrown off course because of this sort of thinking, and they cease to be actions at all.

original: —Soft you now,   The fair Ophelia!
translation: But wait, here is the beautiful Ophelia!

original: Good my lord, How does your honor for this many a day?
translation: My good lord, how have you been doing these last few days?

original: I humbly thank you. Well, well, well.
translation: Thank you for asking. Well, well, well.

original: My lord, I have remembrances of yours That I have longèd long to redeliver. I pray you now receive them.
translation: My lord, I have some mementos of yours that I’ve been wanting to return to you for a while. Please take them back.

original: No, not I. I never gave you aught.
translation: No, it wasn’t me. I never gave you anything.

original: My honored lord, you know right well you did,   And with them, words of so sweet breath composed   As made the things more rich.
translation: My honorable lord, you know very well that you did. And along with these gifts, you wrote letters with words so sweet that they made the gifts seem even more valuable.

original: Their perfume lost,   Take these again, for to the noble mind   Rich gifts wax poor when givers prove unkind.   There, my lord.
translation: But now the joy they brought me is gone, so please take them back. Beautiful gifts lose their value when the givers turn out to be unkind. There, my lord.

original: Ha, ha, are you honest?
translation: Ha ha, are you pure?

original: My lord?
translation: Excuse me?

original: Are you fair?
translation: Are you beautiful?

original: What means your lordship?
translation: What do you mean?

original: That if you be honest and fair, your honesty should  admit no discourse to your beauty.
translation: That if you’re pure and beautiful, your purity should be unconnected to your beauty.

original: Could beauty, my lord, have better commerce than with  honesty?
translation: But, my lord, could beauty be related to anything better than purity?

original: Ay, truly, for the power of beauty will sooner  transform honesty from what it is to a bawd than the  force of honesty can translate beauty into his likeness.
translation: Yes, definitely, because the power of beauty is more likely to change a good girl into a whore than the power of purity is likely to change a beautiful girl into a virgin.

original: This was sometime a paradox, but now the time gives it  proof. I did love you once.
translation: This used to be a great puzzle, but now I’ve solved it. I used to love you.

original: Indeed, my lord, you made me believe so.
translation: Yes, my lord, you made me believe you did.

original: You should not have believed me, for virtue cannot so  inoculate our old stock but we shall relish of it. I  loved you not.
translation: You shouldn’t have believed me. No matter how hard we try to be virtuous, our natural sinfulness will always come out in the end. I didn’t love you.

original: I was the more deceived.
translation: I fell for your trick, then.

original: Get thee to a nunnery. Why wouldst thou be a breeder of sinners? I am myself indifferent honest, but yet I  could accuse me of such things that it were better my  mother had not borne me.
translation: Go to a  convent . Why would you want to give birth to sinners? I’m as good as the next man, and yet I could accuse myself of such horrible crimes that it would’ve been better if my mother had never given birth to me.

original: I am very proud, revengeful, ambitious, with more  offences at my beck than I have thoughts to put them in, imagination to give them shape, or time to act them in.
translation: I’m arrogant, vengeful, ambitious, and have more criminal desires than I have thoughts or imagination to fit them in—or time in which to commit them.

original: What should such fellows as I do crawling between earth and heaven? We are arrant knaves, all.
translation: Why should people like me be allowed to crawl between heaven and earth? We’re all absolute criminals.

original: Believe none of  us. Go thy ways to a nunnery. Where’s your father?
translation: Don’t believe any of us. Get yourself to to a convent. Where’s your father?

original: At home, my lord.
translation: He’s at home, my lord.

original: Let the doors be shut upon him, that he may play the  fool no where but in ’s own house. Farewell.
translation: May he get locked in, so he can play the fool in his own home only. Goodbye.

original: O, help him, you sweet heavens!
translation: Oh, dear God, please help him!

original: If thou dost marry, I’ll give thee this plague for thy  dowry. Be thou as chaste as ice, as pure as snow, thou  shalt not escape calumny.
translation: If you marry, I’ll give you this curse as your wedding present—even if you are as clean as ice, as pure as snow, you’ll still get a bad reputation.

original: Get thee to a nunnery, go.  Farewell. Or, if thou wilt needs marry, marry a fool,  for wise men know well enough what monsters you make of  them. To a nunnery, go, and quickly too. Farewell.
translation: Get yourself to a convent, now. Goodbye. Or if you must get married, marry a fool, because wise men know that women will eventually cheat on them. Goodbye.

original: Heavenly powers, restore him!
translation: Dear God, make him sane again!

original: I have heard of your paintings too, well enough. God  has given you one face and you make yourselves another.
translation: And I know all about you women and your make-up. God gives you one face, but you use make-up to give yourself another.

original: You jig and amble, and you lisp, you nickname God’s  creatures and make your wantonness your ignorance.
translation: You dance and sway as you walk, and talk in a cutesy way. You call God’s creations by pet names, and claim you don’t realize you’re being seductive.

original: Go  to, I’ll no more on ’t. It hath made me mad.
translation: No more. I won’t allow it anymore. It has made me angry.

original: I say, we  will have no more marriages. Those that are married  already, all but one, shall live. The rest shall keep as they are. To a nunnery, go.
translation: I proclaim: we will have no more marriages. Of those who are married already—all but one person—will live on as couples. Everyone else will have to stay single. Go to a convent.

original: Oh, what a noble mind is here o’erthrown!—   The courtier’s, soldier’s, scholar’s, eye, tongue,  sword,
translation: Oh, his great mind has been overcome by insanity! He had a courtier’s persuasiveness, a soldier’s courage, a scholar’s wisdom.

original: Th’ expectancy and rose of the fair state,   The glass of fashion and the mould of form,   Th’ observed of all observers, quite, quite down!
translation: He was the perfect rose and great hope of our country—the model of good manners, the trendsetter, the center of attention. Now he’s fallen so low!

original: And I, of ladies most deject and wretched,   That sucked the honey of his music vows,   Now see that noble and most sovereign reason   Like sweet bells jangled, out of tune and harsh;
translation: I am the most miserable of all the women who once enjoyed hearing his sweet words. A once noble and disciplined mind that sang sweetly is now harsh and out of tune.

original: That unmatched form and feature of blown youth   Blasted with ecstasy.
translation: The unmatched beauty he had in the full bloom of his youth has been destroyed by madness.

original: Oh, woe is me,   T’ have seen what I have seen, see what I see!
translation: Oh, poor me, to have seen Hamlet as he was, and now to see him in this way!

original: Love? His affections do not that way tend.   Nor what he spake, though it lacked form a little,   Was not like madness.
translation: Love? His feelings don’t move in that direction. And his words—although they were a bit all over the place—weren’t crazy.

original: There’s something in his soul   O’er which his melancholy sits on brood,   And I do doubt the hatch and the disclose   Will be some danger
translation: No, his sadness is like a bird sitting on an egg.  And I think that whatever hatches is going to be dangerous.

original: —which for to prevent,   I have in quick determination   Thus set it down: he shall with speed to England   For the demand of our neglected tribute.
translation: To prevent that danger, I’ve made a quick decision: he’ll be sent to England to try to get back the tribute money they owe to us.

original: Haply the seas and countries different   With variable objects shall expel   This something-settled matter in his heart,   Whereon his brains still beating puts him thus   From fashion of himself.
translation: Hopefully the sea and all the new things to see in a different country will push out these thoughts that have somehow taken root in his mind, making him a stranger to his former self.

original: What think you on ’t?
translation: What do you think?

original: It shall do well. But yet do I believe   The origin and commencement of his grief   Sprung from neglected love.
translation: It should work. But I still think that the cause of his madness was unrequited love.

original: It shall be so. Madness in great ones must not unwatched go.
translation: That’s what we’ll do. Madness in important people must be closely watched.

original: Speak the speech, I pray you, as I pronounced it to  you, trippingly on the tongue. But if you mouth it, as  many of our players do, I had as lief the town crier  spoke my lines.
translation: Please repeat the speech just as I said it to you—smoothly and easily. If you exaggerate it in the way so many current actors do, I’d rather have the town crier say the lines.

original: Nor do not saw the air too much with  your hand thus, but use all gently, for in the very  torrent, tempest, and (as I may say) whirlwind of  passion, you must acquire and beget a temperance that  may give it smoothness.
translation: Don’t make huge gestures with yours hands, like this. Gesture just a bit—because to truly communicate a whirlwind of passion, you must present it in a way that’s smooth and real.

original: Oh, it offends me to the soul to hear a robustious periwig-pated fellow tear a passion  to tatters, to very rags, to split the ears of the  groundlings, who for the most part are capable of  nothing but inexplicable dumb-shows and noise.
translation: Oh, I absolutely hate it when I hear some overexcited actor in a wig shout his “passionate” lines—splitting the audience’s eardrums in an effort to impress the  unsophisticated watchers standing just in front of the stage , who for the most part can only appreciate loud noises and pantomime shows. I would whip a guy for overdoing the part of a  tyrant .

original: I would  have such a fellow whipped for o’erdoing Termagant. It  out-Herods Herod. Pray you, avoid it.
translation: That’s worse than those old plays in which King Herod ranted. Please, don’t do that.

original: I warrant your honor.
translation: I’ll do as you ask.

original: Be not too tame neither, but let your own discretion be your tutor. Suit the action to the word, the word to  the action, with this special observance that you  o’erstep not the modesty of nature.
translation: Don’t be too tame, either. Instead, let your judgment guide you. Fit the action to the word and the word to the action. And never overact in a way that seems unnatural.

original: For anything so  overdone is from the purpose of playing, whose end, both at the first and now, was and is to hold, as ’twere,  the mirror up to nature, to show virtue her own feature, scorn her own image, and the very age and body of the  time his form and pressure.
translation: Exaggerated overacting is the opposite of what acting should be. The purpose of acting—both when it began and until now—is to hold a mirror up to nature, virtue, vice, and to the spirit of the times.

original: Now this overdone or come  tardy off, though it make the unskillful laugh, cannot  but make the judicious grieve, the censure of the which  one must in your allowance o’erweigh a whole theatre of  others   .
translation: If you overact or have bad timing, it may make the unknowledgeable laugh, but will make those who know theater grieve. And you should care more about a single knowledgeable theater-lover than an entire theater of the uninformed.

original: Oh, there be players that I have seen play and  heard others praise (and that highly), not to speak it  profanely, that, neither having th’ accent of Christians nor the gait of Christian, pagan, nor man,
translation: I’ve seen actors perform who are highly praised by others, but who—not to be rude—can’t perform a credible Christian, pagan, or even a man.

original: have so  strutted and bellowed that I have thought some of  nature’s journeymen had made men and not made them well, they imitated humanity so abominably.
translation: They strut around and bellow like beasts that had been made by some apprentice to God—they imitate men, but extremely badly.

original: I hope we have reformed that indifferently with us,  sir.
translation: I hope we’ve removed that fault almost entirely from our acting company, sir.

original: O, reform it altogether! And let those that play your  clowns speak no more than is set down for them,
translation: Oh, get rid of it completely. And make sure that the clowns speak exactly the lines written for them

original: for  there be of them that will themselves laugh to set on  some quantity of barren spectators to laugh too,   though  in the meantime some necessary question of the play be  then to be considered.
translation: —because some of them will laugh in order to to get some stupid spectators to laugh, while in the meantime an important part of the plot is then unfolding.

original: That’s villainous, and shows a  most pitiful ambition in the fool that uses it. Go, make you ready.
translation: That’s villainous, and displays a pitiful ambition in the offending fool to get noticed at the expense of the play. Go, get ready.

original: How now, my lord! Will the king hear this piece of  work?
translation: What’s the news, my lord? Will the king come to see the performance?

original: And the queen too, and that presently.
translation: Yes, and the queen too, and soon.

original: Bid the players make haste.
translation: Tell the actors to hurry.

original: Will you two help to hasten them?
translation: Will you two help to speed the actors along?

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: What ho, Horatio!
translation: Hello, Horatio!

original: Here, sweet lord, at your service.
translation: My dear lord, here I am at your service.

original: Horatio, thou art e’en as just a man As e’er my conversation coped withal.
translation: Horatio, you are as much what a man should be as any I have ever met.

original: O my dear lord—
translation: Oh, my dear lord—

original: Nay, do not think I flatter.   For what advancement may I hope from thee   That no revenue hast but thy good spirits,   To feed and clothe thee? Why should the poor be  flattered?   No, let the candied tongue lick absurd pomp,   And crook the pregnant hinges of the knee   Where thrift may follow fawning.
translation: No, don’t think I’m flattering you. What could I hope to get from you, who has nothing other than your good graces to support you? Why would anyone flatter a poor person? No, only flatter the rich, or bow to those who might respond to your fawning with money or favors.

original: Dost thou hear?   Since my dear soul was mistress of her choice   And could of men distinguish, her election   Hath sealed thee for herself, for thou hast been—   As one in suffering all that suffers nothing—   A man that Fortune’s buffets and rewards   Hast ta’en with equal thanks.
translation: Do you understand me? Since I have the power and ability to distinguish between men, my soul has chosen you for a friend because you are—as one who endures everything, and therefore allows nothing to make you suffer—a man who accepts all the twists and turns of fate, positive or negative, with the same calm thankfulness.

original: And blessed are those   Whose blood and judgment are so well commingled,   That they are not a pipe for Fortune’s finger   To sound what stop she please. Give me that man   That is not passion’s slave, and I will wear him   In my heart’s core, ay, in my heart of heart,   As I do thee.
translation: Blessed are those who have a perfect balance of passion and reason, because they cannot be simply played by Fate any which way she chooses. Show me a man who is not a slave to his emotions, and I will keep him close to my heart—yes, in my heart of hearts, as I do you.

original: —Something too much of this.—   There is a play tonight before the king.   One scene of it comes near the circumstance   Which I have told thee of my father’s death.
translation: But I’ve said too much. A play will be performed tonight in front of the king. One of the scenes in it comes close to showing the circumstances I told you about regarding my father’s death.

original: I prithee, when thou seest that act afoot,   Even with the very comment of thy soul   Observe mine uncle. If his occulted guilt   Do not itself unkennel in one speech,   It is a damnèd ghost that we have seen,   And my imaginations are as foul   As Vulcan’s stithy.
translation: During that scene, please watch my uncle with all of your care and attention. If his hidden guilt is not revealed during the scene, then that ghost was a demon—and my ideas about my uncle were  dirty  and wrong.

original: Give him heedful note.   For I mine eyes will rivet to his face,   And after we will both our judgments join   In censure of his seeming.
translation: Watch him carefully, as will I. Afterwards, we’ll meet and come to a joint conclusion about whether or not he is guilty.

original: Well, my lord. If he steal aught the whilst this play is playing, And ’scape detecting, I will pay the theft.
translation: Very well, my lord. I’ll watch him so closely that if he manages to steal anything and I don’t notice it, I promise to pay the cost of the stolen item.

original: They are coming to the play. I must be idle. Get you a place.
translation: They’re coming. I must look like I’m doing nothing. Find a seat.

original: How fares our cousin Hamlet?
translation: How do you fare, my nephew Hamlet?

original: Excellent, i’ faith, of the chameleon’s dish. I eat the air, promise-crammed. You cannot feed capons so.
I have nothing with this answer, Hamlet. These words  are not mine.
translation: I don’t know what you’re saying, Hamlet. These words don’t answer my question.

original: No, nor mine now.
translation: No, nor mine.

original: That did I, my lord, and was accounted a good actor.
translation: That I was, my lord. And I was considered to be a good actor.

original: What did you enact?
translation: What role did you play?

original: I did enact Julius Caesar. I was killed i’ th’ Capitol. Brutus killed me.
translation: I played Julius Caesar. I was killed in the Capitol. Brutus killed me.

original: It was a brute part of him to kill so capital a calf  there.—Be the players ready?
Ay, my lord. They stay upon your patience.
translation: Yes, my lord. They wait only for you to call them.

original: Come hither, my dear Hamlet, sit by me.
translation: Come here, my dear Hamlet. Sit by me.

original: No, good mother. Here’s metal more attractive.  [sits  next to OPHELIA]
translation: No thanks, my good mother. Here’s something more attractive.

original: Oh, ho, do you mark that?
translation: Aha! Did you hear that?

original: Lady, shall I lie in your lap?
No, my lord.
translation: No, my lord.

original: I mean, my head upon your lap?
translation: I mean, put my head in your lap?

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: Do you think I meant country matters?
translation: Did you think I was talking about sex?

original: I think nothing, my lord.
translation: I think nothing, my lord.

original: That’s a fair thought to lie between maids’ legs.
translation: That’s a nice thought to lie between a girl’s legs.

original: What is, my lord?
translation: What is, my lord?

original: Nothing.
You are merry, my lord.
translation: You’re happy tonight, my lord.

original: Who, I?
translation: Who, me?

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: O God, your only jig-maker. What should a man do but be merry? For, look you, how cheerfully my mother looks,  and my father died within these two hours.
translation: Oh, God—the ultimate puppeteer. What else can a man do but be happy? For example, look how cheerful my mother is—and my father’s been dead for just two hours.

original: Nay, ’tis twice two months, my lord.
translation: No, my lord, it’s been four months.

original: So long? Nay then, let the devil wear black, for I’ll  have a suit of sables. O heavens! Die two months ago and not forgotten yet?
translation: That long? Well, then may the devil wear black mourning clothes, while I go about in a suit of fine fur. Heaven forbid! He’s been dead for two months already and hasn’t been forgotten yet?

original: Then there’s hope a great man’s  memory may outlive his life half a year.
translation: I guess there’s hope that memories of a great man may outlive him by six months.

original: But, by ‘r  Lady, he must build churches then, or else shall he  suffer not thinking on, with the hobby-horse, whose  epitaph is “For, oh, for, oh, the hobby-horse is  forgot.”
translation: But,  by God , he must build churches for that to happen, or else he’ll have to put up with being forgotten, like the hobby-horse in the popular song: “Hey-ho, hey-ho, the hobby-horse is forgotten.”

original: What means this, my lord?
translation: What does this mean, my lord?

original: Marry, this is miching mallecho. It means mischief.
translation: This means we’re having some mischievous fun.

original: Belike this show imports the argument of the play.
translation: This pantomime most likely gives a sense of the plot of the play.

original: We shall know by this fellow. The players cannot keep  counsel. They’ll tell all.
translation: We’ll learn the truth from this fellow. Actors can’t keep secrets. They’ll tell all.

original: Will he tell us what this show meant?
translation: Will he tell us what that pantomime meant?

original: Ay, or any show that you will show him. Be not you  ashamed to show, he’ll not shame to tell you what it  means.
translation: Yes, or anything else you show him. If you’re not ashamed to show it, he won’t be ashamed to tell you what it means.

original: You are naught, you are naught. I’ll mark the play.
translation: You’re just naughty, naughty. I’m watching the play.

original: For us and for our tragedy, Here stooping to your clemency, We beg your hearing patiently.
translation: Appealing to your forgiving nature, we beg you patiently to watch us perform our tragedy.

original: Is this a prologue or the posy of a ring?
translation: Was that a prologue or the inscription on a ring?

original: ‘Tis brief, my lord.
translation: It was short, my lord.

original: As woman’s love.
translation: As short as a woman’s love.

original: Full thirty times hath Phoebus’ cart gone round   Neptune’s salt wash and Tellus’ orbèd ground,
translation: The earth circled the sun thirty times; and the moon has waxed and waned over the ocean;

original: And thirty dozen moons with borrowed sheen   About the world have times twelve thirties been,   Since love our hearts and Hymen did our hands   Unite commutual in most sacred bands.
translation: and the earth for thirty times twelve months, since love joined our hearts and  Hymen  joined our hands in the sacred bonds of marriage.

original: So many journeys may the sun and moon   Make us again count o’er ere love be done.   But woe is me! You are so sick of late,   So far from cheer and from your former state,   That I distrust you.
translation: May we continue to love each other for another thirty years. But I am sad. You’ve been so sick recently—so different from your former cheerful self—that I worry about you.

original: Yet though I distrust,   Discomfort you, my lord, it nothing must.   For women fear too much, even as they love,   And women’s fear and love hold quantity,   In neither aught, or in extremity.
translation: But though I worry, don’t let it upset you, my lord. Women in love are always afraid. For women, love and fear go hand in hand—whether or not there is reason to worry.

original: Now what my love is, proof hath made you know,   And as my love is sized, my fear is so:   Where love is great, the littlest doubts are fear.   Where little fears grow great, great love grows there.
translation: I’ve proven the quality of my love. And as my love is deep, so too is my fear. When someone’s love is great, little worries become big. Little fears grown big are a sign of great love.

original: Faith, I must leave thee, love, and shortly too.   My operant powers their functions leave to do.
translation: In truth, I will soon have to leave you, love. My body is growing weak, ceasing to function.

original: And thou shalt live in this fair world behind,   Honored, beloved, and haply one as kind   For husband shalt thou—
translation: I will leave you behind in this beautiful world, my honorable beloved. Perhaps you’ll find another husband—

original: Oh, confound the rest!   Such love must needs be treason in my breast.
translation: Oh, curse everyone else! Loving another would be treason in my heart.

original: In second husband let me be accursed!   None wed the second but who killed the first.
translation: May I be cursed if I take a second husband. Only a woman who killed her first husband would marry a second.

original: Wormwood, wormwood.
translation: That’s bitter!

original: The instances that second marriage move   Are base respects of thrift, but none of love.
translation: The reasons for a second marriage might be money, but never love.

original: A second time I kill my husband dead   When second husband kisses me in bed.
translation: When my second husband kissed me in bed, it would be like killing my first husband again.

original: I do believe you think what now you speak,   But what we do determine oft we break.   Purpose is but the slave to memory,   Of violent birth, but poor validity,   Which now, like fruit unripe, sticks on the tree,   But fall, unshaken, when they mellow be.
translation: I believe that’s what you think now. But what we swear we’ll do we often don’t. Intentions are driven by memory. They are strong at first, but fade over time—like an unripe apple that sticks to the tree, but falls on its own to the ground when ripe.

original: Most necessary ’tis that we forget   To pay ourselves what to ourselves is debt.   What to ourselves in passion we propose,   The passion ending, doth the purpose lose.
translation: It’s necessary for us to forget to meet the obligation we impose on ourselves. We forget to do what we promise to do in moments of passion once that passion fades.

original: The violence of either grief or joy   Their own enactures with themselves destroy.   Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament.   Grief joys, joy grieves on slender accident.
translation: Grief or joy might spur us to action, but that call to action fades along with the grief or joy. Grief becomes joy, and joy turns to grief, based on little twists of fate.

original: This world is not for aye, nor ’tis not strange   That even our loves should with our fortunes change.   For ’tis a question left us yet to prove,   Whether love lead fortune, or else fortune love.
translation: The world won’t last forever, so it’s not odd that even love can change as our fate changes. It remains an open question whether love propels your fate, or your fate propels love.

original: The great man down, you mark his favorite flies.   The poor advanced makes friends of enemies.   And hitherto doth love on fortune tend,
translation: When the great man falls, he is deserted. When a poor man rises, enemies become friends. Love is similarly dependent on fortune.

original: For who not needs shall never lack a friend,   And who in want a hollow friend doth try,   Directly seasons him his enemy.
translation: A person with money will never lack friends, while a friend who asks another for money will make that friend an enemy.

original: But, orderly to end where I begun,   Our wills and fates do so contrary run   That our devices still are overthrown.
translation: Back to the point on which I began: our desires and our fates will never match. So our plans never end up as we hope.

original: Our thoughts are ours, their ends none of our own.   So think thou wilt no second husband wed,   But die thy thoughts when thy first lord is dead.
translation: What we want to happen, and what happens, will never be the same. So you think you’ll never marry again, but those thoughts will die when I do.

original: Nor earth to me give food, nor heaven light.   Sport and repose lock from me day and night.   To desperation turn my trust and hope.
translation: May the earth give me no food and the sky no light; may I have no rest or leisure, day or night; may my trust and hope turn to despair;

original: An anchor’s cheer in prison be my scope.   Each opposite that blanks the face of joy   Meet what I would have well and it destroy.
translation: may cheap prison food be all the comfort I can hope for; may all the forces that turn joy to sadness destroy all of my desires.

original: Both here and hence pursue me lasting strife   If, once a widow, ever I be wife!
translation: For now and forever may I know no peace if, after becoming a widow, I ever again become a wife.

original: If she should break it now!
translation: What if she breaks that vow?

original: ‘Tis deeply sworn. Sweet, leave me here awhile. My spirits grow dull, and fain I would beguile The tedious day with sleep.
translation: You swear sincerely. Sweetheart, leave me alone a while. I’m getting sleepy, and I would like to escape this tiresome day by going to sleep.

original: Sleep rock thy brain, And never come mischance between us twain.
translation: May you sleep well, and may no twist of fate ever come between us.

original: Madam, how like you this play?
translation: Madam, how do you like this play?

original: The lady protests too much, methinks.
translation: The lady’s promising a bit much, I think.

original: Oh, but she’ll keep her word.
translation: Oh, but she’ll keep her word.

original: Have you heard the argument? Is there no offense in ’t?
translation: Do you know the plot? Is there anything offensive in it?

original: No, no, they do but jest. Poison in jest. No offense i’ th’ world.
translation: No, no, it’s just pretend. Just a little joke. Not offensive at all.

original: What do you call the play?
translation: What’s the title of the play?

original: The Mousetrap. Marry, how? Tropically. This play is the image of a murder done in Vienna.
translation: . Indeed, why? It’s a metaphor. This play re-enacts a murder committed in Vienna.

original: Gonzago is the duke’s name, his wife Baptista. You shall see anon. ‘Tis a  knavish piece of work, but what o’ that?
translation: Gonzago is the duke’s name, and his wife is Baptista. You’ll see soon. It’s really a mischievous piece of work, but who cares?

original: Your majesty  and we that have free souls, it touches us not. Let the  galled jade wince, our withers are unwrung.
translation: You and I have clear consciences, so it doesn’t concern us. Let the guilty flinch. We can watch without being bothered.

original: This is one Lucianus, nephew to the king.
translation: This is Lucianus, the king’s nephew.

original: You are as good as a chorus, my lord.
translation: You’re as good as a play-by-play announcer, my lord.

original: I could interpret between you and your love, if I could see the puppets dallying.
translation: I could do a play-by-play between you and your lover, if you put on a little puppet show for me.

original: You are keen, my lord, you are keen.
translation: You are witty, my lord, and sharp.

original: It would cost you a groaning to take off mine edge.
translation: You could take my edge off, but doing it might make you moan.

original: Still better and worse.
translation: Your jokes get better, even as your manners get worse.

original: So you must take your husbands.—Begin, murderer. Pox,  leave thy damnable faces, and begin. Come, “The croaking raven doth bellow for revenge—”
translation: “For better, for worse”—that’s the vow you take when you take a husband.

original: Thoughts black, hands apt, drugs fit, and time  agreeing,   Confederate season, else no creature seeing,
translation: Evil thoughts, willing hands, the perfect poison, and the opportunity to act. The darkness of the night protects me: no one can see me.

original: Thou mixture rank, of midnight weeds collected,   With Hecate’s ban thrice blasted, thrice infected,   Thy natural magic and dire property   On wholesome life usurp immediately.
translation: You foul mixture of deadly weeds, which  Hecate  has cursed and infected, use your deadly properties to steal away health and life.

original: He poisons him i’ th’ garden for ’s estate. His name’s  Gonzago. The story is extant, and writ in choice  Italian. You shall see anon how the murderer gets the  love of Gonzago’s wife.
translation: He poisons the king in the garden to get the kingdom. The king’s name is Gonzago. The original story was written in Italian. You’ll see shortly how the murderer wins the love of Gonzago’s wife.

original: The king rises.
translation: The king is standing up.

original: What, frighted with false fire?
translation: What—is he scared of a gun firing a blank?

original: How fares my lord?
translation: My lord, how are you feeling?

original: Give o’er the play.
translation: Stop the play.

original: Give me some light, away!
translation: Turn on the lights. I’m leaving!

original: Lights, lights, lights!
translation: Lights, lights, lights!

original: Why, let the stricken deer go weep,   The hart ungallèd play.   For some must watch while some must sleep.   So runs the world away.
translation: Let the deer that’s been shot go weep alone, while the uninjured deer plays. For some must watch while others must sleep—that’s the way of the world.

original: Half a share.
translation: They’d probably give you half a share of the company.

original: A whole one, I.
translation: A whole share for me.

original: For thou dost know, O Damon dear,   This realm dismantled was   Of Jove himself. And now reigns here   A very, very—pajock.
translation: For you know, my dearest Damon, that this kingdom lost Its Jove-like king. And now who rules? A big, big—peacock.

original: You might have rhymed.
O good Horatio, I’ll take the ghost’s word for a  thousand pound. Didst perceive?
translation: Oh, Horatio. I’d wager a thousand dollars the ghost spoke the truth. Did you see?

original: Very well, my lord.
translation: Very well, my lord.

original: Upon the talk of the poisoning?
translation: When the actors mentioned the poison?

original: I did very well note him.
translation: I watched him closely.

original: Ah ha! Come, some music! Come, the recorders!
translation: Aha! Hey, some music please! Play your flutes!

original: For if the king like not the comedy,   Why then, belike, he likes it not, perdy.
translation: For if the king does not like the play, then, that’s it—he does not like it, I say.

original: Come, some music!
translation: Come on now, music!

original: Good my lord, vouchsafe me a word with you.
translation: My lord, might I have a word with you?

original: Sir, a whole history.
translation: You can have a whole story.

original: The king, sir—
translation: The king, sir—

original: Ay, sir, what of him?
translation: Yes, what about him?

original: Is in his retirement marvelous distempered.
translation: He’s in his chambers now, and very upset.

original: With drink, sir?
translation: He has an upset stomach from drinking too much?

original: No, my lord, with choler.
translation: No, my lord, he’s angry.

original: Your wisdom should show itself more richer to signify  this to the doctor. For, for me to put him to his  purgation would perhaps plunge him into far more choler.
translation: You’d be a lot smarter if you told this to a doctor. If I were to treat him, he would only end up angrier.

original: Good my lord, put your discourse into some frame and  start not so wildly from my affair.
translation: My lord, please try to make sense and not to veer on such wild tangents from the point of my question.

original: I am tame, sir. Pronounce.
translation: I’ll behave, sir. Speak.

original: The queen your mother, in most great affliction of  spirit, hath sent me to you.
translation: The queen your mother, who is extremely unhappy, has sent me to you.

original: You are welcome.
translation: You are very welcome here.

original: Nay, good my lord, this courtesy is not of the right  breed.
translation: No, my lord, your polite words don’t make any sense in this situation.

original: If it shall please you to make me a wholesome  answer, I will do your mother’s commandment. If not,  your pardon and my return shall be the end of my  business.
translation: If you’d be so kind as to give me a real answer, I’ll carry out your mother’s request. If not, I’ll say goodbye and that’ll be the end of my business.

original: Sir, I cannot.
translation: Sir, I can’t.

original: What, my lord?
translation: Can’t what, my lord?

original: Make you a wholesome answer. My wit’s diseased. But,  sir, such answer as I can make, you shall command. Or,  rather, as you say, my mother. Therefore no more but to  the matter. My mother, you say—
translation: Give you a real answer. My mind is not right. But I’ll try to give the best answer I can to you—or rather, to my mother. Therefore, let’s get to the point. My mother, you say—

original: Then thus she says: your behavior hath struck her into  amazement and admiration.
translation: She says that your behavior has shocked astonished her.
