original: O wonderful son that can so ’stonish a mother! But is  there no sequel at the heels of this mother’s  admiration? Impart.
translation: Oh, what a wonderful son I am to be able to impress my mother! But what are the details of my mother’s admiration? Explain.

original: She desires to speak with you in her closet ere you go  to bed.
translation: She wants to speak with you in her bedroom before you go to bed.

original: We shall obey, were she ten times our mother. Have you  any further trade with us?
translation: I will obey, as if she were ten times my mother. Have you any other business with me?

original: My lord, you once did love me.
translation: My lord, you once liked me.

original: And do still, by these pickers and stealers.
translation: And I still do, I swear by my hands.

original: Good my lord, what is your cause of distemper? You do  surely bar the door upon your own liberty if you deny  your griefs to your friend.
translation: My lord, what’s the cause of your anger? You’re locking yourself into a prison by refusing to reveal your problems to your friends.

original: Sir, I lack advancement.
translation: Sir, I have no future prospects.

original: How can that be, when you have the voice of the king  himself for your succession in Denmark?
translation: How can that be, when the king himself has proclaimed you the heir to the Danish throne?

original: Ay, sir, but “While the grass grows—” The proverb is  something musty—Oh, the recorders! Let me see one.
translation: Yes, but as the proverb goes, “While the grass grows…” Though that is an old, stale proverb. Oh, the recorders! Let me see one.

original: O my lord, if my duty be too bold, my love is too  unmannerly.
translation: Oh, my lord, if I’m being too bold, it’s only because I care about you too much to show good manners.

original: I do not well understand that. Will you play upon this  pipe?
translation: I don’t understand you. Will you play this recorder?

original: My lord, I cannot.
translation: My lord, I can’t.

original: I pray you.
translation: Please.

original: Believe me, I cannot.
translation: Believe me, I can’t.

original: I do beseech you.
translation: I beg you.

original: I know no touch of it, my lord.
translation: I don’t know how, my lord.

original: It is as easy as lying. Govern these ventages with your fingers and thumb, give it breath with your mouth, and  it will discourse most eloquent music. Look you, these  are the stops.
translation: It’s as easy as lying. Cover these holes with your fingers and thumb and blow into it, and it will produce the most beautiful music. See, here are the holes.

original: But these cannot I command to any utterance of harmony. I have not the skill.
translation: But I can’t play any kind of song or melody. I don’t have the skill.

original: Why, look you now, how unworthy a thing you make of me! You would play upon me. You would seem to know my  stops. You would pluck out the heart of my mystery. You  would sound me from my lowest note to the top of my  compass.
translation: Well, look at that, how you treat me like such a fool. You keep trying to play me—as if you knew exactly where to put your fingers—to tease out my mystery—playing the full scale of all my notes.

original: And there is much music, excellent voice, in  this little organ, yet cannot you make it speak?  ‘Sblood, do you think I am easier to be played on than a pipe?
translation: There is so much music in this little instrument, and yet you can’t make it speak? By God, do you think I’m easier to play than a recorder?

original: Call me what instrument you will, though you can  fret me, yet you cannot play upon me.
translation: Call me whatever instrument you want—even though you try to push my buttons, you can’t play me.

original: God bless you, sir.
translation: God bless you, sir.

original: My lord, the queen would speak with you, and presently.
translation: My lord, the queen would like to speak with you right away.

original: Do you see yonder cloud that’s almost in shape of a  camel?
translation: Do you see the cloud over there that looks almost like a camel?

original: By th’ mass, and ’tis like a camel indeed.
translation: By God, it does look like a camel.

original: Methinks it is like a weasel.
translation: To me it looks like a weasel.

original: It is backed like a weasel.
translation: Its back is like a weasel’s.

original: Or like a whale.
translation: Or like a whale.

original: Very like a whale.
translation: Very much like a whale.

original: Then I will come to my mother by and by.    They  fool me to the top of my bent.—I will come by and by.
translation: I’ll come to see my mother soon.

original: I will say so.
translation: I’ll tell her that.

original: “By and by” is easily said.
translation: It’s easy enough to say “soon.”

original: Leave me, friends.
translation: Leave me alone, my friends.

original: ‘Tis now the very witching time of night,   When churchyards yawn and hell itself breathes out   Contagion to this world.
translation: It’s now the time of night when witches roam, when graveyards open and the stench of hell breathes sickness into the world.

original: Now could I drink hot blood   And do such bitter business as the bitter day   Would quake to look on. Soft, now to my mother.—
translation: Now I could drink hot blood and do things so terrible it would make people tremble the next day. But wait, I must now go to see my mother.

original: O heart, lose not thy nature, let not ever   The soul of Nero enter this firm bosom.   Let me be cruel, not unnatural.
translation: Oh, my heart, do not lose your humanity, don’t let yourself become like  Nero . Let me be cruel, but not inhuman.

original: I will speak daggers to her but use none.   My tongue and soul in this be hypocrites.   How in my words somever she be shent,   To give them seals never, my soul, consent!
translation: I’ll speak to her as sharply as a dagger, but not use a dagger. Though my words will condemn her to hell, my soul must never make that condemnation into reality by letting me kill her.

original: I like him not, nor stands it safe with us   To let his madness range. Therefore prepare you.   I your commission will forthwith dispatch,   And he to England shall along with you.
translation: I don’t like it. It’s not safe to let his madness rage all over the place, so get ready. I’m sending you to England on a diplomatic mission, and Hamlet will go with you.

original: The terms of our estate may not endure   Hazard so dangerous as doth hourly grow   Out of his lunacies.
translation: My duty as a king does not allow me to let such a dangerous man as Hamlet to run loose, especially as he’s getting crazier each hour.

original: We will ourselves provide.
translation: We’ll get ourselves ready.

original: Most holy and religious fear it is   To keep those many, many bodies safe   That live and feed upon your majesty.
translation: It’s a sacred duty to protect all of those people whose lives depend on you, your Majesty.

original: The single and peculiar life is bound   With all the strength and armor of the mind   To keep itself from noyance, but much more   That spirit upon whose weal depend and rest   The lives of many.
translation: Each person tries to avoid injury, with the full effort of his or her mind. But it is even more important to protect that person upon whose health the entire nation depends.

original: The cease of majesty   Dies not alone, but, like a gulf, doth draw   What’s near it with it.
translation: A king does not die alone. Instead, like a whirlpool, he sucks down all that is near.

original: It is a massy wheel   Fixed on the summit of the highest mount,   To whose huge spokes ten thousand lesser things   Are mortised and adjoined,
translation: A king is like a huge wheel on the top of the highest mountain, with a thousand smaller things attached to its spokes.

original: which, when it falls,   Each small annexment, petty consequence,   Attends the boisterous ruin.
translation: When that wheel rolls down the mountain, everything attached goes down with it, spinning wildly into ruin.

original: Never alone   Did the king sigh, but with a general groan.
translation: A king never sighs alone; everyone else always groans with him.

original: Arm you, I pray you, to this speedy voyage. For we will fetters put upon this fear, Which now goes too free-footed.
translation: Please, prepare yourselves for this trip. We’ll put chains on this danger that’s now running free.

original: We will haste us.
translation: We will hurry.

original: My lord, he’s going to his mother’s closet.   Behind the arras I’ll convey myself   To hear the process. I’ll warrant she’ll tax him home.
translation: My lord, Hamlet’s going to his mother’s room. I’ll hide behind the tapestry to listen in. I bet she’ll let him have it.

original: And, as you said (and wisely was it said)   ‘Tis meet that some more audience than a mother—   Since nature makes them partial—should o’erhear   The speech, of vantage.
translation: And as you said (and you said it wisely), it’s good to have someone other than a mother listening to what he says—since, as a mother, she naturally loves him.

original: Fare you well, my liege.   I’ll call upon you ere you go to bed   And tell you what I know.
translation: Goodbye, my lord. I’ll come to see you before you go to bed, and tell you what I’ve learned.

original: Thanks, dear my lord.
translation: Thanks, my dear lord.

original: Oh, my offence is rank. It smells to heaven.   It hath the primal eldest curse upon ’t,   A brother’s murder. Pray can I not.   Though inclination be as sharp as will,   My stronger guilt defeats my strong intent,
translation: Oh, my crime is foul. It stinks all the way to heaven. It is the  oldest , and worst, of all crimes: a brother’s murder. I can’t pray. Though I badly want to pray, my guilt is stronger than my hope to pray.

original: And, like a man to double business bound,   I stand in pause where I shall first begin,   And both neglect. What if this cursèd hand   Were thicker than itself with brother’s blood?   Is there not rain enough in the sweet heavens   To wash it white as snow?
translation: And—like a person with two things he has to do at the same time—I stand paralyzed, unsure which to start first, and thus neglect them both. Even if this cursed hand of mine is covered with my brother’s blood, isn’t there enough rain in sweet heaven to wash it white as snow?

original: Whereto serves mercy   But to confront the visage of offence?   And what’s in prayer but this twofold force,   To be forestallèd ere we come to fall   Or pardoned being down? Then I’ll look up.
translation: What’s the purpose of God’s mercy if not to forgive the sinner? And doesn’t prayer have these two powers: to stop us from sinning before we do, and to offer forgiveness when we’ve sinned? So I’ll pray.

original: My fault is past. But oh, what form of prayer   Can serve my turn, “Forgive me my foul murder?”   That cannot be, since I am still possessed   Of those effects for which I did the murder:   My crown, mine own ambition, and my queen.
translation: My sin is in the past. But, oh, what prayer can possibly give me what I want:  “Forgive me for my awful murder?” That won’t work, since I still have all the things I gained by committing the murder: my crown—the object of my ambition—and my queen.

original: May one be pardoned and retain th’ offense?   In the corrupted currents of this world   Offense’s gilded hand may shove by justice,   And oft ’tis seen the wicked prize itself   Buys out the law. But ’tis not so above.
translation: Is it possible to be forgiven and keep what you got from the crime? In this corrupt world, criminals can use the wealth they get from their crime to shove justice aside by bribing officers of the law. But that’s not how it is heaven.

original: There is no shuffling. There the action lies   In his true nature, and we ourselves compelled,   Even to the teeth and forehead of our faults,   To give in evidence. What then? What rests?
translation: You can’t hide from the law up there. There, every action is judged strictly on its merits, and everyone must confront their sins face-to-face. What then? What remains for me to do?

original: Try what repentance can. What can it not?   Yet what can it when one can not repent?   O wretched state! O bosom black as death!
translation: Repent as best I can. That can’t hurt. But it can’t help much either, since I can’t really repent. Oh, what a wretched situation! Oh, my heart is as black as death.

original: O limèd soul that, struggling to be free,   Art more engaged! Help, angels. Make assay.
translation: My soul is trapped in sin, and the more it struggles to be free, the more trapped it gets. Help me, angels! Make an effort.

original: Bow, stubborn knees, and, heart with strings of steel,   Be soft as sinews of the newborn babe.   All may be well.
translation: Now bend, my stubborn knees, and may my hard heart become soft as the muscle of a newborn baby. Perhaps all will be well.

original: Now might I do it pat. Now he is a-praying.   And now I’ll do ’t.
translation: Now I could do it. Now as he’s praying. And now I’ll do it.

original: And so he goes to heaven.   And so am I revenged.—That would be scanned.   A villain kills my father, and, for that,   I, his sole son, do this same villain send   To heaven.
translation: And so he’ll go to heaven, and I’ll have my revenge. Wait, that needs more thought. A villain kills my father, and, in revenge, I—my father’s only son—send this same villain to heaven.

original: Oh, this is hire and salary, not revenge.   He took my father grossly, full of bread,   With all his crimes broad blown, as flush as May.   And how his audit stands who knows save heaven?
translation: Send him to heaven—oh, that’s doing him a service, not getting revenge. He killed my father before my father could pray and spiritually prepare himself, so that my father’s sins were in full bloom. Only God knows how many sins my father has standing against him.

original: But in our circumstance and course of thought   ‘Tis heavy with him. And am I then revenged   To take him in the purging of his soul   When he is fit and seasoned for his passage?
translation: But as far as I can tell, it doesn’t look good for him. So do I get revenge if I kill Claudius while he’s praying and confessing his sins, so that he’s all set to go right up to heaven?

original: No!   Up, sword, and know thou a more horrid hent.
translation: No! Go away, sword, and wait for a more horrid moment to kill him.

original: When he is drunk asleep, or in his rage,   Or in th’ incestuous pleasure of his bed,   At game a-swearing, or about some act   That has no relish of salvation in ’t—
translation: When he’s drunk and asleep, or partying, or having incestuous sex, or swearing and gambling, or doing some other thing that has no trace of heaven in it

original: Then trip him, that his heels may kick at heaven,   And that his soul may be as damned and black   As hell, whereto it goes.
translation: —then I’ll kill him, so that his heels kick up toward heaven while his damned, black soul falls straight down to hell.

original: My mother stays   This physic but prolongs thy sickly days.
translation: My mother’s waiting. Claudius, this attempt to cure yourself through prayer is only going to prolong your sickly life a little longer.

original: My words fly up, my thoughts remain below. Words without thoughts never to heaven go.
translation: My words fly up to the sky, but my thoughts remain down here. Words without thoughts will never get to heaven.

original: He will come straight. Look you lay home to him.
translation: He’ll be here right away. Be sure to really yell at him.

original: Tell him his pranks have been too broad to bear with,   And that your grace hath screened and stood between   Much heat and him.
translation: Tell him his pranks have been too big to ignore, and that you have protected him from feeling the full heat of their consequences.

original: I’ll silence me even here.   Pray you, be round with him.
translation: I’ll be silent, right here.  Please, be tough with him.

original: Mother, mother, mother!
translation: Mother, mother, mother!

original: I’ll warrant you. Fear me not. Withdraw, I hear him  coming.
translation: I’ll do as you say. Don’t worry. Hide, I hear him coming.

original: Now mother, what’s the matter?
translation: Now, mother, what’s the matter?

original: Hamlet, thou hast thy father much offended.
translation: Hamlet, you have insulted your father.

original: Mother, you have my father much offended.
translation: Mother, you have insulted my father.

original: Come, come, you answer with an idle tongue.
translation: Come now, you answer is foolish.

original: Go, go, you question with a wicked tongue.
translation: Go on, your question is wicked.

original: Why, how now, Hamlet?
translation: Hamlet, what, why?

original: What’s the matter now?
translation: What’s the matter now?

original: Have you forgot me?
translation: Have you forgotten who I am?

original: No, by the rood, not so. You are the queen, your husband’s brother’s wife, And—would it were not so!—you are my mother.
translation: By the Holy Cross, no. You are the queen, your husband’s brother’s wife, and—though I wish it wasn’t so—you are my mother.

original: Nay, then I’ll set those to you that can speak.
translation: Well then, I’ll go get someone who will speak and make you listen.

original: Come, come, and sit you down. You shall not budge. You go not till I set you up a glass Where you may see the inmost part of you.
translation: Come now, sit down. Don't budge. You will not leave until I hold a mirror up to you, so that you can see the inner most part of yourself.

original: What wilt thou do? Thou wilt not murder me? Help, help, ho!
translation: What are you going to do? Would you murder me? Help, help, hey!

original: What, ho? Help, help, help!
translation: Hey! Help, help, help!

original: How now, a rat? Dead for a ducat, dead!
translation: What’s this, a rat? I’ll bet a gold coin that he’s dead now.

original: Oh, I am slain.
translation: Oh, I’ve been killed!

original: O me, what hast thou done?
translation: Oh my God, what have you done?

original: Nay, I know not. Is it the king?
translation: I don’t know. Is it the king?

original: Oh, what a rash and bloody deed is this!
translation: Oh, what a reckless, bloody act!

original: A bloody deed? Almost as bad, good mother, As kill a king and marry with his brother.
translation: A bloody act? Almost as bad, my good mother, as killing a king and marrying his brother.

original: As kill a king?
translation: Killing a king?

original: Ay, lady, ’twas my word.
translation: Yes, lady, that’s what I said.

original: Thou wretched, rash, intruding fool, farewell.   I took thee for thy better.
translation: You sad, silly, interfering fool, goodbye. I mistook you for your superior.

original: Take thy fortune.   Thou find’st to be too busy is some danger.
translation: You’ve gotten what you deserve, and found that meddling can be dangerous.

original: What have I done, that thou darest wag thy tongue In noise so rude against me?
translation: What have I done that you dare to talk to me so rudely?

original: Such an act   That blurs the grace and blush of modesty,   Calls virtue hypocrite, takes off the rose   From the fair forehead of an innocent love   And sets a blister there, makes marriage vows   As false as dicers’ oaths
translation: Something that corrupts modesty, turns virtue into hypocrisy, removes the blossom from the face of true love and replaces it with a blister, makes marriage vows as false as a gambler’s oath

original: —oh, such a deed   As from the body of contraction plucks   The very soul, and sweet religion makes   A rhapsody of words.
translation: —oh, you’ve done such a thing that plucks the soul out of marriage, and turns religion into just a bunch of words.

original: Heaven’s face doth glow   O’er this solidity and compound mass   With tristful visage, as against the doom,   Is thought-sick at the act.
translation: Heaven looks down on earth, its face glowing with anger as if it were Judgment Day now, and is sick because of what you’ve done.

original: Ay me, what act That roars so loud and thunders in the index?
translation: Oh no, what have I done that sounds so terrible—even though I don’t yet know what it is?

original: Look here upon this picture and on this,   The counterfeit presentment of two brothers.   See, what a grace was seated on this brow?   Hyperion’s curls, the front of Jove himself,   An eye like Mars to threaten and command,   A station like the herald Mercury   New-lighted on a heaven-kissing hill—
translation: Look at this picture here and at that one there, the painted portraits of two brothers. See the saintly goodness in this face? He has curls like those of  Hyperion , a forehead like that of Jove, eyes that command like those of Mars, and a stance as light as Mercury’s when that god lands on the peak of a hill.

original: A combination and a form indeed   Where every god did seem to set his seal   To give the world assurance of a man.   This was your husband.
translation: He was such a combination of good qualities that it seemed like he was put together by all the gods to be the perfect man. That was your husband.

original: Look you now, what follows.   Here is your husband, like a mildewed ear   Blasting his wholesome brother. Have you eyes?   Could you on this fair mountain leave to feed   And batten on this moor? Ha, have you eyes?
translation: Now look at what came after: this is your husband, like a rotten ear of corn infecting the one next to it. Do you have eyes? How could you leave the beautiful heights of this man and descend down to this dank swamp of this one? Ha! Do you have eyes?

original: You cannot call it love, for at your age   The heyday in the blood is tame, it’s humble,   And waits upon the judgment. And what judgment   Would step from this to this?
translation: You can’t say it was love—because at at your age romantic passions have been tamed with humility and reason. But there must be something wrong with your reason, because why else would you go from this to that?

original: Sense sure you have,   Else could you not have motion. But sure that sense   Is apoplexed, for madness would not err,   Nor sense to ecstasy was ne’er so thralled,   But it reserved some quantity of choice   To serve in such a difference.
translation: Your senses must still work, or else you wouldn’t be able to move. But those senses seem paralyzed, because madness would not make this mistake. And even senses overcome by desire would still be able to distinguish the huge difference between your former and current husband.

original: What devil was ’t   That thus hath cozened you at hoodman-blind?   Eyes without feeling, feeling without sight,   Ears without hands or eyes, smelling sans all,   Or but a sickly part of one true sense   Could not so mope.
translation: What devil was it that tricked and blindfolded you? Even if you had eyes without feeling, feeling without sight, ears without hands or eyes, smell without any other senses, or the use of just one impaired sense, you would not make a mistake like this.

original: O shame, where is thy blush?   Rebellious hell,   If thou canst mutine in a matron’s bones,   To flaming youth let virtue be as wax   And melt in her own fire.
translation: Oh, for shame, why aren’t you blushing? If a rebellion can rage even in a mother’s bones, then in the fire of youth all virtue must burn away.

original: Proclaim no shame   When the compulsive ardor gives the charge,   Since frost itself as actively doth burn,   And reason panders will.
translation: There’s no longer any shame in acting on impulse when old people burn to act on impulse, and reason acts as a servant to desire.

original: O Hamlet, speak no more!
translation: Oh, Hamlet, no more!

original: Thou turn’st mine eyes into my very soul,   And there I see such black and grainèd spots   As will not leave their tinct.
translation: You’re forcing me to look into my very soul, where the marks of sin are so black they’ll never be cleaned away.

original: Nay, but to live   In the rank sweat of an enseamèd bed,
translation: Yes, and how could you lie in the rank sweat of your dirty sheets,

original: Stewed in corruption, honeying and making love   Over the nasty sty—
translation: wet with corruption, making love in this gross pigpen—

original: O, speak to me no more! These words like daggers enter in my ears. No more, sweet Hamlet.
translation: Oh, please, stop speaking to me! Your words are like daggers stabbing my ears. No more, sweet Hamlet.

original: A murderer and a villain,   A slave that is not twentieth part the tithe   Of your precedent lord, a vice of kings,
translation: A murderer and a villain; a scoundrel who’s not worth even a twentieth of ten percent of your previous husband; an awful king;

original: A cutpurse of the empire and the rule,   That from a shelf the precious diadem stole,   And put it in his pocket—
translation: a thief of the throne and the kingdom, who stole the precious crown from a shelf and put it in his pocket—

original: No more!
translation: No more!

original: A king of shreds and patches—
translation: A patched-up king—

original: Save me and hover o’er me with your wings, You heavenly guards!—What would your gracious figure?
translation: Heavenly angels, protect me with your wings!

original: Alas, he’s mad!
translation: Oh no! He’s crazy!

original: Do you not come your tardy son to chide,   That, lapsed in time and passion,
translation: Have you come to scold your tardy son for delaying and losing his passion,

original: lets go by   The important acting of your dread command?   O, say!
translation: and failing to carry out your deadly command? Tell me!

original: Do not forget. This visitation   Is but to whet thy almost blunted purpose.
translation: Don’t forget. I’ve come to sharpen your almost dulled sense of revenge.

original: But look, amazement on thy mother sits.   O, step between her and her fighting soul.
translation: But look, your mother is astonished. Oh, protect her from her struggling soul.

original: Conceit in weakest bodies strongest works.   Speak to her, Hamlet.
translation: The imagination works strongest in those with the weakest bodies. Speak to her, Hamlet.

original: How is it with you, lady?
translation: How are you doing, madam?

original: Alas, how is ’t with you,   That you do bend your eye on vacancy   And with th’ incorporal air do hold discourse?
translation: Oh, how are  you  doing, since you stare into empty space and talk to the air?

original: Forth at your eyes your spirits wildly peep,   And, as the sleeping soldiers in th’ alarm,   Your bedded hair, like life in excrements,   Starts up and stands on end.
translation: The wildness of your thoughts is visible in your eyes, and your hair is standing upright.

original: O gentle son,   Upon the heat and flame of thy distemper   Sprinkle cool patience. Whereon do you look?
translation: Oh, my noble son, sprinkle some cooling patience on the hot fury of your anger! What are you staring at?

original: On him, on him! Look you, how pale he glares!   His form and cause conjoined, preaching to stones,   Would make them capable.
translation: At him, at him! Look how pale he is and how he glares at me. With the way he looks and the power of his cause, he could preach to stones and get them to act.

original: To whom do you speak this?
translation: Who are you talking to?

original: Do you see nothing there?
translation: You don’t see anything there?

original: Nothing at all, yet all that is I see.
translation: Nothing at all, other than what’s there.

original: Nor did you nothing hear?
translation: And you don’t hear anything?

original: No, nothing but ourselves.
translation: No, nothing but us.

original: Why, look you there! Look how it steals away— My father, in his habit as he lived— Look where he goes, even now, out at the portal!
translation: See, look there! Look how it sneaks away! My father, dressed just as he was when he was alive! Look, now he’s going out the door!

original: This the very coinage of your brain. This bodiless creation ecstasy Is very cunning in.
translation: This is all in your mind. Madness is good at creating hallucinations.

original: Ecstasy?   My pulse as yours doth temperately keep time   And makes as healthful music. It is not madness   That I have uttered. Bring me to the test,   And I the matter will reword, which madness   Would gambol from.
translation: Madness? My heart beats just as evenly, and is in the same good health, as yours. I’ve said nothing crazy. Ask me to, and I’ll rephrase what I’ve said, which a crazy person wouldn’t be able to do.

original: Mother, for love of grace,   Lay not that flattering unction to your soul   That not your trespass but my madness speaks.
translation: Mother, for the love of God, don’t soothe your soul by saying that the problem is my madness and not your crime.

original: It will but skin and film the ulcerous place   Whilst rank corruption, mining all within,   Infects unseen. Confess yourself to heaven.
translation: That would just be putting a bandage on the open sore of your crime, and failing to see how its bad effects are spreading like an infection inside of you. Confess your sins to heaven.

original: Repent what’s past. Avoid what is to come.   And do not spread the compost on the weeds   To make them ranker.
translation: Repent what you’ve done, and avoid damnation. Refusing to repent would be like spreading manure over the weeds, making them even dirtier.

original: Forgive me this my virtue,   For in the fatness of these pursy times   Virtue itself of vice must pardon beg,   Yea, curb and woo for leave to do him good.
translation: Forgive me for having the virtue to speak to you honestly, but in the grossness of these spoiled times, the virtuous must be willing to intervene with sinners, and beg them for the chance to help them.

original: O Hamlet, thou hast cleft my heart in twain.
translation: Oh, Hamlet, you’ve broken my heart in two!

original: Oh, throw away the worser part of it,   And live the purer with the other half.   Good night—but go not to mine uncle’s bed.   Assume a virtue if you have it not.
translation: Oh, then throw away the worse part, and live a purer life with the other half. Good night—but don’t sleep with my uncle tonight. Pretend to be virtuous, even if you’re not.

original: That monster, custom, who all sense doth eat,   Of habits devil, is angel yet in this:   That to the use of actions fair and good   He likewise gives a frock or livery   That aptly is put on.
translation: Habit can be a devil or an angel: it can get you used to doing either good or evil without thinking about it.

original: Refrain tonight,   And that shall lend a kind of easiness   To the next abstinence, the next more easy.
translation: Refrain from sleeping with Claudius tonight, and that will make it easier to say no the next time, and even easier each time after that.

original: For use almost can change the stamp of nature,   And either rein the devil or throw him out   With wondrous potency.
translation: How you act can change your nature, and either keep the devil inside or kick him out.

original: Once more, good night,   And when you are desirous to be blessed,   I’ll blessing beg of you.
translation: Once more, good night, and when you want me to bless you for following this advice, I’ll beg you to forgive me for being so harsh.

original: For this same lord,   I do repent. But heaven hath pleased it so,   To punish me with this and this with me,   That I must be their scourge and minister.
translation: I apologize for what happened to this lord. But God decided to punish me by making me commit this murder—and to punish this man by having me kill him—so that I’m both Heaven’s judge and executioner.

original: I will bestow him and will answer well   The death I gave him. So, again, good night.
translation: I will deal with the body, and suffer the consequences of the death I gave him. So, again, good night.

original: I must be cruel only to be kind.   Thus bad begins and worse remains behind.   One word more, good lady—
translation: I have been cruel only in order to perform a greater act of kindness. This is bad, and there are even worse things to come. One more thing, madam.

original: What shall I do?
translation: What should I do?

original: Not this, by no means, that I bid you do—   Let the bloat king tempt you again to bed,   Pinch wanton on your cheek, call you his mouse,   And let him, for a pair of reechy kisses   Or paddling in your neck with his damned fingers,
translation: By no means should you do this: let the bloated king seduce you into bed, pinch your cheek, call you his pet, or with smelly kisses and caresses of your neck with his damned fingers

original: Make you to ravel all this matter out:   That I essentially am not in madness   But mad in craft.
translation: get you to reveal that I am not crazy, but am just pretending to be.

original: ‘Twere good you let him know,   For who that’s but a queen, fair, sober, wise,   Would from a paddock, from a bat, a gib,   Such dear concernings hide? Who would do so?
translation: What a good thing it would be if you told him that, because why would a queen who’s fair, sober, and wise hide such important things from a toad, a pig, a tom-cat like him? Who would do such a thing?

original: No, in despite of sense and secrecy,   Unpeg the basket on the house’s top.   Let the birds fly, and like the famous ape,   To try conclusions, in the basket creep   And break your own neck down.
translation: No, forget about good sense and secrecy, and open the door of the cage and let the birds fly out, and—like that ape in the famous story who tried to imitate birds and try to fly—break your neck in the process.

original: Be thou assured, if words be made of breath And breath of life, I have no life to breathe What thou hast said to me.
translation: Trust me: as words are made of breath, and breath is a necessity of life, I will give up my life rather than breathe a word of what you’ve said to me.

original: I must to England, you know that?
translation: I must go to England, did you know that?

original: Alack, I had forgot. ‘Tis so concluded on.
translation: Oh no, I’d forgotten. It’s been decided.

original: There’s letters sealed, and my two schoolfellows,   Whom I will trust as I will adders fanged,   They bear the mandate.
translation: The documents are signed and sealed, and my two schoolmates—whom I’ll trust like I would a poisonous snake—are the messengers.

original: They must sweep my way   And marshal me to knavery. Let it work,   For ’tis the sport to have the engineer   Hoist with his own petard.
translation: They’re the ones who’ll lead me on to whatever trickery I’m going to face. Let it come, because it’s fun to fix things so the engineer gets blow up by his own bombs.

original: And ’t shall go hard,   But I will delve one yard below their mines,   And blow them at the moon. Oh, ’tis most sweet   When in one line two crafts directly meet.
translation: It’s going to be tough on them. I’m going to dig down below their bombs and blow them up to the moon. Oh, it’s sweet when you can kill two birds with one stone.   [

original: This man shall set me packing.   I’ll lug the guts into the neighbor room.
translation: Killing this man is going to make me have to leave even sooner. I’ll drag his guts into the next room.

original: Mother, good night. Indeed this counselor   Is now most still, most secret, and most grave   Who was in life a foolish prating knave.—
translation: Mother, good night. This adviser—who was in life a foolish, moralizing liar—is now so quiet, secretive, and serious.

original: There’s matter in these sighs, these  profound heaves.
translation: Your deep, heavy sighs mean something.

original: You must translate. ‘Tis fit we understand them.   Where is your son?
translation: You must tell me what they mean. It’s important that I know. Where’s your son?

original: Bestow this place on us a little while.
translation: Please leave us for a while.

original: Ah, my good lord, what have I seen tonight!
translation: Ah, my good lord, you wouldn’t believe what I’ve seen tonight!

original: What, Gertrude? How does Hamlet?
translation: What, Gertrude? How is Hamlet ?

original: Mad as the sea and wind when both contend   Which is the mightier.
translation: As mad as the waves and the wind when they struggle against each other in a storm.

original: In his lawless fit,   Behind the arras hearing something stir,   Whips out his rapier, cries, “A rat, a rat!”
translation: In an insane rage, he hears something stir behind the tapestry, whips out his sword, and shouts “A rat, a rat!”

original: And in this brainish apprehension kills   The unseen good old man.
translation: And with this crazy idea, he kills the good old man, who was hidden there.

original: O heavy deed!   It had been so with us, had we been there.   His liberty is full of threats to all—   To you yourself, to us, to everyone.
translation: Oh, what a terrible crime! It would’ve happened to me if I’d been there. His freedom is a threat to all of us—to you, to me, to everyone.

original: Alas, how shall this bloody deed be answered?   It will be laid to us, whose providence   Should have kept short, restrained and out of haunt,   This mad young man.
translation: How should we react to this violent deed? I’ll be blamed for not controlling or restraining this crazy young man.

original: But so much was our love,   We would not understand what was most fit,
translation: But I loved him so much that I avoided doing the right thing.

original: But, like the owner of a foul disease,   To keep it from divulging, let it feed   Even on the pith of life. Where is he gone?
translation: Now, I’m like a man who hides the fact that he is suffering from a foul disease, and in doing so, lets it kill him. Where has Hamlet gone?

original: To draw apart the body he hath killed,
translation: To remove the body of the man he killed.

original: O’er whom his very madness, like some ore   Among a mineral of metals base,   Shows itself pure.
translation: His madness does not stop a sliver of his former self from shining through, like a bit of gold in an otherwise worthless rock.

original: He weeps for what is done.
translation: He weeps for what he has done.

original: O Gertrude, come away!   The sun no sooner shall the mountains touch   But we will ship him hence   ,
translation: Oh, Gertrude, let’s go. By the time the sun rises, lighting up those distant mountains, we’ll have him on a ship to England.

original: and this vile deed   We must, with all our majesty and skill,   Both countenance and excuse.
translation: It’ll take all my power and skill to explain and excuse what Hamlet has done.

original: Friends both, go join you with some further aid.   Hamlet in madness hath Polonius slain,   And from his mother’s closet hath he dragged him.
translation: My friends, go find others to help you. In his insanity, Hamlet has killed Polonius and dragged him out of his mother’s bedroom.

original: Go seek him out, speak fair, and bring the body   Into the chapel. I pray you, haste in this.
translation: Go find him and speak nicely to him, and bring the body into the chapel. I beg you, hurry in this.

original: Come, Gertrude, we’ll call up our wisest friends,   And let them know both what we mean to do   And what’s untimely done.
translation: Come, Gertrude. We’ll confer with our wisest friends and tell them what we’re going to do—and what Hamlet has already done.

original: So dreaded slander—   Whose whisper o’er the world’s diameter,   As level as the cannon to his blank,   Transports the poisoned shot—may miss our name   And hit the woundless air.
translation: Let’s hope slander—like a cannonball that can shoot across half the world and still hit its target—misses us.

original: Oh, come away!   My soul is full of discord and dismay.
translation: Oh, we must go. I’m full of confusion and sadness.

original: Safely stowed.
translation: Safely hidden.

original: Hamlet! Lord Hamlet!
translation: Hamlet, Lord Hamlet!

original: But soft, what noise? Who calls on Hamlet? Oh, here they come.
translation: But wait, what’s that noise? Who’s calling for Hamlet? Oh, here they come.

original: What have you done, my lord, with the dead body?
translation: What have you done with the dead body, my lord?

original: Compounded it with dust, whereto ’tis kin.
translation: Gotten it dirty—ashes to ashes, and dust to dust.

original: Tell us where ’tis, that we may take it thence And bear it to the chapel.
translation: Tell us where it is, so we can take it to the chapel.

original: Do not believe it.
translation: Don’t believe it.

original: Believe what?
translation: Believe what?

original: That I can keep your counsel and not mine own. Besides, to be demanded of a sponge! What replication should be  made by the son of a king?
translation: That I’d take your advice and then keep my own secret. Besides, to be questioned by a sponge! How should the son of a king respond to a sponge?

original: Take you me for a sponge, my lord?
translation: You think that I’m a sponge, my lord?

original: Ay, sir, that soaks up the king’s countenance, his  rewards, his authorities.
translation: Yes, sir, a sponge that soaks up the king’s approval, his rewards, and his decisions.

original: But such officers do the king  best service in the end. He keeps them, like an ape, in  the corner of his jaw, first mouthed to be last  swallowed.
translation: Officers like that give the king the best service in the end. He keeps them in his mouth like an ape, moving them around from one side of his mouth to the other.

original: When he needs what you have gleaned, it is  but squeezing you and, sponge, you shall be dry again.
translation: When he needs to know what you have learned, he can just squeeze you like a sponge, and then you’ll be dry again.

original: I understand you not, my lord.
translation: I don’t understand you, my lord.

original: I am glad of it. A knavish speech sleeps in a foolish  ear.
translation: I’m glad about that. Mischievous words will never get a response from a fool, because the fool won't understand them.

original: My lord, you must tell us where the body is and go with us to the king.
translation: My lord, you must tell us where the body is, and then go with us to the king.

original: The body is with the king, but the king is not with the body. The king is a thing—
translation: The body’s with the real king, but the current king’s not with the body. The king’s a thing—

original: A thing, my lord?
translation: A “thing,” my lord?

original: Of nothing. Bring me to him. Hide, fox, and all after.
translation: Of no importance. Take me to him. Actually, try and catch me!

original: I have sent to seek him and to find the body.   How dangerous is it that this man goes loose!   Yet must not we put the strong law on him.
translation: I’ve sent men to find Hamlet and the body. How dangerous it is to have this madman on the loose! But we can’t just use the strong arm of the law on him.

original: He’s loved of the distracted multitude,   Who like not in their judgment, but their eyes.   And where ’tis so, th’ offender’s scourge is weighed,   But never the offense.
translation: He’s loved by the masses, who base their feelings on appearances instead of using good judgment. They’ll focus on the punishment, not the crime.

original: To bear all smooth and even,   This sudden sending him away must seem   Deliberate pause.
translation: So, sending him away suddenly must seem like it was long-planned and carefully considered move.

original: Diseases desperate grown   By desperate appliance are relieved,   Or not at all.
translation: Curing a fatal disease requires immediate treatment, or you won’t cure it at all.

original: How now, what hath befall’n?
translation: What’s going on? What’s happened?

original: Where the dead body is bestowed, my lord, We cannot get from him.
translation: We can’t get him to tell us where he put the body.

original: But where is he?
translation: But where is he?

original: Without, my lord; guarded, to know your pleasure.
translation: Outside, my lord, and under guard, as we wait to hear what you want us to do.

original: Bring him before us.
translation: Bring him to me.

original: Ho, Guildenstern! Bring in my lord.
translation: Hey, Guildenstern! Bring in my lord.

original: Now, Hamlet, where’s Polonius?
translation: Now, Hamlet, where’s Polonius?

original: At supper.
translation: At dinner.

original: At supper where?
translation: At dinner where?

original: Not where he eats, but where he is eaten. A certain  convocation of politic worms are e’en at him.
translation: Not where he’s eating, but where he’s being eaten. A certain gathering of worms are working on him right now.

original: Your worm  is your only emperor for diet. We fat all creatures else to fat us, and we fat ourselves for maggots.
translation: Worms are the kings of all eating. We fatten up all creatures to feed ourselves—and we fatten ourselves to eventually feed the worms.

original: Your fat  king and your lean beggar is but variable service—two  dishes, but to one table. That’s the end.
translation: A fat king and a skinny beggar are just different dishes at the same meal. And that’s that.

original: Alas, alas!
translation: Oh no, oh no!

original: A man may fish with the worm that hath eat of a king,  and eat of the fish that hath fed of that worm.
translation: A man can fish with a worm that ate a king, and then eat the fish he catches with that worm.

original: What dost you mean by this?
translation: What do you mean by that?

original: Nothing but to show you how a king may go a progress  through the guts of a beggar.
translation: Nothing, except to make it clear that a king can move through the guts of a beggar.

original: Where is Polonius?
translation: Where is Polonius?

original: In heaven. Send hither to see. If your messenger find  him not there, seek him i’ th’ other place yourself.
translation: In heaven. Send a messager there if you want to be sure. If your messenger can’t find him, you can check for him in hell yourself.

original: But if indeed you find him not within this month, you shall nose him as you go up the stairs into the lobby.
translation: Now, if you don’t find him within the next month, you’ll smell him as you go upstairs into the main hall.

original: Go seek him there.
translation: Go look for him there.

original: He will stay till ye come.
translation: No need to hurry—he’ll wait for you.

original: Hamlet, this deed, for thine especial safety—   Which we do tender as we dearly grieve   For that which thou hast done—must send thee hence   With fiery quickness.
translation: Hamlet, I care about your safety as much as I grieve over what you’ve done. Therefore I must send you away at once.

original: Therefore prepare thyself.   The bark is ready and the wind at help,   Th’ associates tend, and everything is bent   For England.
translation: Prepare yourself. The ship is ready, and the wind is favorable. Your servants wait for you—everything is set for you to go to England.

original: For England?
translation: To England?

original: Ay, Hamlet.
translation: Yes, Hamlet.

original: Good.
translation: Good.

original: So is it, if thou knew’st our purposes.
translation: Yes, it is, if you knew why I was sending you.

original: I see a cherub that sees them. But come, for England. Farewell, dear mother.
translation: I know an angel who can read your mind. But now, off to England! Goodbye, dear mother.

original: Thy loving father, Hamlet.
translation: I’m your loving father, Hamlet.

original: My mother. Father and mother is man and wife, man and  wife is one flesh, and so, my mother.—Come, for England!
translation: No, my mother. When you married my mother, the two of you became one flesh, so if you’re my father you’re also my mother. Come on, to England!

original: Follow him at foot. Tempt him with speed aboard.   Delay it not. I’ll have him hence tonight.
translation: Follow him on foot, and hurry him onto the ship. Don’t let there be any delays. I want him gone tonight.

original: Away! For everything is sealed and done   That else leans on the affair. Pray you, make haste.
translation: Gone! Everything is signed and sealed to put an end to this affair. Please hurry.

original: And, England, if my love thou hold’st at aught—   As my great power thereof may give thee sense,   Since yet thy cicatrice looks raw and red   After the Danish sword and thy free awe   Pays homage to us   —
translation: And you, dear King of England, if you think me at all important—as you should, considering you can still feel the strength that Denmark bludgeoned you with in the past, causing you to pay us tribute money—

original: thou mayst not coldly set   Our sovereign process, which imports at full,   By letters congruing to that effect,   The present death of Hamlet.
translation: then you’ll have to listen to the instruction in my letters that you kill Hamlet immediately.

original: Do it, England,   For like the hectic in my blood he rages,   And thou must cure me.
translation: Do it, King of England. Hamlet is raging like a fever in my blood, and you must cure me.

original: Till I know ’tis done,   Howe’er my haps, my joys were ne’er begun.
translation: Until I know it’s been done, I’ll never be happy, no matter what else happens to me.

original: Go, Captain, from me greet the Danish king   Tell him that, by his license, Fortinbras   Craves the conveyance of a promised march   Over his kingdom.
translation: Go, Captain, bring my greetings to the Danish king. Tell him that, as was promised, Fortinbras asks for permission to march his troops across Denmark.

original: You know the rendezvous.   If that his majesty would aught with us,   We shall express our duty in his eye,   And let him know so.
translation: You know the place where you should meet back up with our army. If His Majesty wants anything at all from us, let him know that we will do it.

original: I will do ’t, my lord.
translation: I’ll do that, my lord.

original: Go softly on.
translation: Go on, then.

original: Good sir, whose powers are these?
translation: Good sir, whose troops are these?

original: They are of Norway, sir.
translation: The are from Norway, sir.

original: How purposed, sir, I pray you?
translation: Please tell me, what’s their goal, sir?

original: Against some part of Poland.
translation: They’re headed to invade some part of Poland.

original: Who commands them, sir?
translation: Who commands them, sir?

original: The nephew to old Norway, Fortinbras.
translation: The nephew of the old Norwegian king, Fortinbras.

original: Goes it against the main of Poland, sir, Or for some frontier?
translation: Sir, is he attacking central Poland, or some borderlands?

original: Truly to speak, and with no addition,   We go to gain a little patch of ground   That hath in it no profit but the name.
translation: To be honest, we’re going to fight for a little patch of ground that’s not worth anything beyond its name.

original: To pay five ducats, five, I would not farm it.   Nor will it yield to Norway or the Pole   A ranker rate, should it be sold in fee.
translation: I wouldn’t even pay five gold coins for the right to own and farm it. And it won't give either the Norwegians or the Poles more value than that, even if they sold it.

original: Why, then the Polack never will defend it.
translation: Well, then the Poles won’t even try to defend it.

original: Yes, it is already garrisoned.
translation: They will. They’ve already put soldiers there.

original: Two thousand souls and twenty thousand ducats   Will not debate the question of this straw.
translation: It will take more than two thousand men and twenty-thousand gold coins to settle the battle for this pointless bit of land.

original: This is th’ impostume of much wealth and peace,   That inward breaks and shows no cause without   Why the man dies.
translation: This is the curse of having too much wealth and peace—it’s like an abscess that grows inside someone until it bursts and kills them, without anyone knowing why.

original: God be wi’ you, sir.
translation: God be with you, sir.

original: Will ’t please you go, my lord?
translation: Will you please come now, my lord?

original: I’ll be with you straight. Go a little before.
translation: I’ll follow you right away. Go on ahead of me.

original: How all occasions do inform against me,   And spur my dull revenge! What is a man   If his chief good and market of his time   Be but to sleep and feed? A beast, no more.
translation: Everything that I see shames me, and spurs me to sharpen my dulled efforts to get revenge. What is a man who does nothing but eat and sleep? A beast, nothing more.

original: Sure, he that made us with such large discourse,   Looking before and after, gave us not   That capability and godlike reason   To fust in us unused.
translation: God didn’t give us such a great and godlike ability to think and reason so that those capabilities would grow moldy from disuse.

original: Now, whether it be   Bestial oblivion, or some craven scruple   Of thinking too precisely on th’ event—   A thought which, quartered, hath but one part wisdom   And ever three parts coward—I do not know   Why yet I live to say “This thing’s to do,”
translation: Now, whether the cause is an animal-like lack of thought or over-thinking exactly how to do it—thoughts which are one part wisdom, three parts cowardice—I can’t explain how I could still be alive and yet be able to say that “this is something I still have to do.”

original: Sith I have cause and will and strength and means   To do ’t. Examples gross as earth exhort me.
translation: I have the motive, the will, the ability, and the opportunity to do it. Claudius’ guilt is as obvious as the ground beneath my feet.

original: Witness this army of such mass and charge   Led by a delicate and tender prince,   Whose spirit with divine ambition puffed   Makes mouths at the invisible event,   Exposing what is mortal and unsure   To all that fortune, death, and danger dare,   Even for an eggshell.
translation: Look at this huge, expansive army led by a young and unproven prince, who’s so full of divine ambition that he mocks death and exposes his life to all the risks of fortune and danger—all for a cause as thin as an eggshell.

original: Rightly to be great   Is not to stir without great argument,   But greatly to find quarrel in a straw   When honor’s at the stake.
translation: To be great doesn’t require simply fighting for a good reason, but rather boldly fighting for barely any reason at all, so long as honor is at stake.

original: How stand I then,   That have a father killed, a mother stained,   Excitements of my reason and my blood,   And let all sleep
translation: So where do I stand, with my father murdered and my mother dishonored—and yet I do nothing in response to all of these slights and insults?

original: —while, to my shame, I see   The imminent death of twenty thousand men,   That for a fantasy and trick of fame
translation: Meanwhile, to my shame, I watch twenty thousand men—because of a whim and and wish for fame—

original: Go to their graves like beds, fight for a plot   Whereon the numbers cannot try the cause,   Which is not tomb enough and continent   To hide the slain?
translation: march off to death for a tiny bit of land that’s not even large enough to hold all their graves.

original: Oh, from this time forth,   My thoughts be bloody, or be nothing worth!
translation: Oh, from this time forward, my thoughts will be violent, or else I’ll consider them worthless.

original: I will not speak with her.
translation: I won’t speak to her.

original: She is importunate, Indeed distract. Her mood will needs be pitied.
translation: She demands it. In fact, she’s crazed. Her bahavior will inspire your pity.

original: What would she have?
translation: What does she want?

original: She speaks much of her father, says she hears   There’s tricks i’ th’ world, and hems, and beats her  heart,   Spurns enviously at straws, speaks things in doubt   That carry but half sense.
translation: She talks often of her father, and says she’s learned there are deceptions in the world, and coughs, and beats her chest, and takes offense at little things, and says things that don’t make sense.

original: Her speech is nothing,   Yet the unshaped use of it doth move   The hearers to collection.
translation: Her words are meaningless—yet those who hear her babbling attempt to understand its meaning.

original: They aim at it,   And botch the words up fit to their own thoughts,
translation: They patch up the gaps within her words, and end up hearing what they want to hear.

original: Which, as her winks and nods and gestures yield them,   Indeed would make one think there might be thought,   Though nothing sure, yet much unhappily.
translation: And the winks and nods and gestures she makes while speaking imply—without being at all clear—that she’s hinting at some terrible deeper meaning.

original: ‘Twere good she were spoken with, for she may strew Dangerous conjectures in ill-breeding minds.
translation: It would be good for someone to speak to her, because her words might make people think dangerous things.

original: Let her come in.
translation: Bring her in.

original: To my sick soul (as sin’s true nature is)   Each toy seems prologue to some great amiss.
translation: To my sick soul—since sin is actually sickness—each little detail seems like a sign of coming disaster.

original: So full of artless jealousy is guilt,   It spills itself in fearing to be spilt.
translation: Guilt fills you up with suspicions that are so hard to hide, that you give yourself away by trying so hard not to reveal them.

original: Where is the beauteous majesty of Denmark?
translation: Where is the beautiful queen of Denmark?

original: How now, Ophelia?
translation: How are you, Ophelia?

original: How should I your true love know   From another one?
translation: How can you tell  Your true love from some other?

original: By his cockle hat and staff,   And his sandal shoon.
translation: By his pilgrim’s hat and staff And the sandals on his feet.

original: Alas, sweet lady, what imports this song?
translation: Oh no, sweet lady, what’s the meaning of this song?

original: Say you? Nay, pray you, mark.
translation: Did you say something? No, please, listen.

original: He is dead and gone, lady,   He is dead and gone,
translation: He is dead and gone, lady, He is dead and gone.

original: At his head a grass-green turf,   At his heels a stone.   Oh, ho!
translation: At his head is green grass, At his feet a tomb stone. Oh, ho!

original: Nay, but, Ophelia—
translation: No, listen, Ophelia—

original: Pray you, mark.  White his shroud as the mountain snow—
translation: Please, listen.His death shroud was as white as snow—

original: Alas, look here, my lord.
translation: Alas, look at this, my lord.

original: Larded all with sweet flowers, Which bewept to the ground did not go With true-love showers.
translation: Covered with sweet flowersWhich did not fall to the groundIn true-love showers.

original: How do you, pretty lady?
translation: How are you, pretty lady?

original: Well, God’ield you! They say the owl was a baker’s  daughter. Lord, we know what we are, but know not what  we may be. God be at your table.
translation: I’m well. May God reward you as you deserve. They say the baker’s daughter was turned into an owl for refusing to answer Jesus’ request for bread. My lord, we know what we are now, but not what we may become. May God be at your table.

original: Conceit upon her father.
translation: She’s thinking about her dead father.

original: Pray you, let’s have no words of this, but when they  ask you what it means, say you this:
translation: Please, let’s have no words about that, but when they ask you what it means, say this:

original: Tomorrow is Saint Valentine’s day,   All in the morning betime,   And I a maid at your window,   To be your Valentine.
translation: Tomorrow is St. Valentine’s Day And early in the morning, I’m a girl waiting at your window Waiting to be your valentine.

original: Then up he rose, and donned his clothes,   And dupped the chamber door.   Let in the maid that out a maid   Never departed more.
translation: Then he woke and put on his clothes And opened his bedroom door. He let in the girl, who when she left Wasn’t a virgin anymore.

original: Pretty Ophelia—
translation: Pretty Ophelia—

original: Indeed, without an oath I’ll make an end on ’t:
translation: Yes, I’ll get to the end soon:

original: By Gis and by Saint Charity,   Alack, and fie, for shame!   Young men will do ’t, if they come to ’t.   By Cock, they are to blame.
translation: By Jesus and Saint Charity, Alas, what a shame! Young men will do it if they get a chance: By God, they’re the ones to blame.

original: Quoth she, “Before you tumbled me,   You promised me to wed.”
translation: She said, “Before you took me to bed, You promised to marry me.”

original: He answers,   “So would I ha’ done, by yonder sun,   An thou hadst not come to my bed.”
translation: He answers: “And by the sun, I would have done just that, If you hadn’t gone to bed with me.”

original: How long hath she been thus?
translation: How long has she been like this?

original: I hope all will be well. We must be patient, but I  cannot choose but weep, to think they should lay him i’  th’ cold ground.
translation: I hope everything will be all right. We must be patient, but I can’t stop crying when I think of how they laid him in the cold ground.

original: My brother shall know of it, and so I  thank you for your good counsel.
translation: My brother will learn of this. And so I thank you for your good advice.

original: Come, my coach! Good  night, ladies. Good night, sweet ladies. Good night,  good night.
translation: Come, driver! Good night, ladies. Good night, sweet ladies. Good night, good night.

original: Follow her close. Give her good watch, I pray you.
translation: Follow her. Watch her closely, please.

original: Oh, this is the poison of deep grief. It springs   All from her father’s death, and now behold!   O Gertrude, Gertrude,   When sorrows come, they come not single spies   But in battalions.
translation: Oh, her terrible grief has poisoned her mind. All a result of her father’s death—look at her! Oh, Gertrude, Gertrude, when troubles come, they don’t come one at time like spies, but all at once like an army.

original: First, her father slain.   Next, your son gone, and he most violent author   Of his own just remove.
translation: First her father was killed. Then your son had to leave because of the violent thing he did.

original: The people muddied,   Thick, and unwholesome in their thoughts and whispers   For good Polonius’ death, and we have done but greenly   In hugger-mugger to inter him.
translation: The people are stirred up and confused—thinking up dark theories and whispering about Polonius’s death—while we recklessly buried him in secrecy, without an official state funeral.

original: Poor Ophelia   Divided from herself and her fair judgment,   Without the which we are pictures, or mere beasts.   Last—and as much containing as all these—   Her brother is in secret come from France,
translation: Poor Ophelia has been split from her sanity—without which we’re just pictures, or even beasts. Last, and as bad as all of the rest of these, her brother has secretly returned from France.

original: Feeds on his wonder, keeps himself in clouds,   And wants not buzzers to infect his ear   With pestilent speeches of his father’s death,   Wherein necessity, of matter beggared,   Will nothing stick our person to arraign   In ear and ear.
translation: His questions about his father’s death are answered by vicious gossipers who fill his ears with nasty stories, and who—without knowing what really happened—blame it all on me.

original: O my dear Gertrude, this,   Like to a murdering piece, in many places   Gives me superfluous death.
translation: Oh, my dear Gertrude, I feel as though I’m being murdered many times at once.

original: Alack, what noise is this?
translation: Oh, what’s that noise?

original: Where are my Switzers? Let them guard the door.
translation: Where are my Swiss guards? Let them guard the door.

original: What is the matter?
translation: What’s going on?

original: Save yourself, my lord.   The ocean, overpeering of his list,   Eats not the flats with more impiteous haste   Than young Laertes, in a riotous head,   O’erbears your officers.
translation: Save yourself, my lord. Not even the ocean, when it floods and devours the lowlands, is as ferocious as Laertes. He now leads your officers in rebellion against you.

original: The rabble call him “lord”   And—as the world were now but to begin,   Antiquity forgot, custom not known,   The ratifiers and props of every word—
translation: The commoners call him “lord” and—as if they were starting the world from scratch and had forgotten all the traditions and customs that are the bedrock of what we are

original: They cry, “Choose we! Laertes shall be king!”   Caps, hands, and tongues applaud it to the clouds:   “Laertes shall be king, Laertes king!”
translation: –they shout, “we choose Laertes to be king!” They throw their caps in the air, applaud, and shout, “Laertes will be king! King Laertes!”

original: How cheerfully on the false trail they cry. O, this is counter, you false Danish dogs!
translation: How cheerfully they shout as they hunt the wrong prey! Oh, this is wrong, you disloyal Danish dogs!

original: The doors are broke.
translation: They've broken down the doors.

original: Where is this king?—Sirs, stand you all without.
translation: Where’s this king?

original: No, let’s come in!
translation: No, let us in!

original: I pray you, give me leave.
translation: I beg you, give me a moment.

original: We will, we will.
translation: We will, we will.

original: I thank you. Keep the door.—O thou vile king, Give me my father!
translation: Thank you. Guard the door.

original: Calmly, good Laertes.
translation: Be calm, good Laertes.

original: That drop of blood that’s calm proclaims me bastard,   Cries “Cuckold!” to my father,
translation: Any calm drop of blood in my body would mark me as my father’s  bastard son ,

original: brands the “harlot”   Even here between the chaste unsmirchèd brow   Of my true mother.
translation: and stamp the label “whore” on the pure, unstained forehead of my true and devoted mother.

original: What is the cause, Laertes,   That thy rebellion looks so giant-like?—
translation: What is the cause of this rebellion, Laertes?

original: Where is my father?
translation: Where is my father?

original: Dead.
translation: Dead.

original: But not by him.
translation: But the king didn’t kill him.

original: Let him demand his fill.
translation: Let him ask his questions.

original: How came he dead? I’ll not be juggled with.   To hell, allegiance! Vows, to the blackest devil!
translation: How did he die? I won’t be lied to. To hell with my oaths of allegiance! Vows can go to hell!

original: Conscience and grace, to the profoundest pit!   I dare damnation. To this point I stand   That both the worlds I give to negligence.
translation: Conscience, too! I don’t care if I’m damned. I swear that I don’t care about what happens to me in this world or the next.

original: Let come what comes, only I’ll be revenged   Most thoroughly for my father.
translation: No matter what happens, I’ll get revenge for my father’s murder.

original: Who shall stay you?
translation: Who could stop you?

original: My will, not all the world. And for my means, I’ll husband them so well, They shall go far with little.
translation: My own will, and nothing else in all the world. I’ll gather up the little means I have, and use them so well that they’ll take me a long way.

original: Good Laertes,   If you desire to know the certainty   Of your dear father’s death,
translation: Good Laertes, if you wish to know the truth about your dear father’s death, answer me this:

original: is ’t writ in your  revenge,   That, swoopstake, you will draw both friend and foe,   Winner and loser?
translation: are you so angry that in your search for revenge you are willing to hurt both your father’s enemies and his friends?

original: None but his enemies.
translation: Only his enemies.

original: Will you know them then?
translation: Do you want to know who they are, then?

original: To his good friends thus wide I’ll ope my arms And, like the kind life-rendering pelican, Repast them with my blood.
translation: I’ll open my arms wide to his friends, and like a mother pelican with her chicks, I’ll give my own heart's blood for them.

original: Why, now you speak   Like a good child and a true gentleman.
translation: Why, now you’re talking like a faithful son and a true gentleman.

original: That I am guiltless of your father’s death   And am most sensible in grief for it,   It shall as level to your judgment pierce   As day does to your eye.
translation: I will prove to you as plain as day that I am innocent of your father’s death, and feel great grief over it.

original: How now? What noise is that?
translation: What’s going on? What’s that noise?

original: O heat, dry up my brains! Tears seven times salt,   Burn out the sense and virtue of mine eye!   By heaven, thy madness shall be paid by weight,   Till our scale turn the beam.
translation: Oh, heat, dry up my brains! Oh, salt in my tears, burn the vision out of my eyes! By heaven, I’ll get revenge equal to the depth of your madness!

original: O rose of May,   Dear maid, kind sister, sweet Ophelia!   O heavens, is ’t possible a young maid’s wits   Should be as mortal as an old man’s life?
translation: Oh, you rose of May, dear maiden, kind sister, sweet Ophelia! Oh God, is it possible that a young woman’s mind could die as easily as an old man’s life?

original: Nature is fine in love, and where ’tis fine,   It sends some precious instance of itself   After the thing it loves.
translation: Human nature is made spiritual by love. And when it is spiritual, it gives itself to the one it loves—just as Ophelia has given her sanity to her father, whom she loved.

original: They bore him barefaced on the bier,   Hey, non nonny, nonny, hey, nonny,
translation: They carried him uncovered in the coffin, Hey non nonny, nonny, hey nonny.

original: And in his grave rained many a tear.   Fare you well, my dove.
translation: And tears poured down into his grave. Goodbye, my dove.

original: Hadst thou thy wits, and didst persuade revenge, It could not move thus.
translation: Even if you were sane and urged me to take revenge, you couldn’t be more persuasive than this.

original: You must sing A-down a-down—And you, Call him a-  down-a—Oh, how the wheel becomes it! It is the false  steward that stole his master’s daughter.
translation: You have to sing, “A down a-down,” and you, “Call him a-down-a.” Oh, how it turns around like a wheel! Like the lying worker who stole his boss’ daughter.

original: This nothing’s more than matter.
translation: This apparent nonsense has more meaning than rational speech.

original: There’s rosemary, that’s for remembrance. Pray you,  love, remember. And there is pansies, that’s for  thoughts.
translation: Here’s some rosemary, that’s for remembering. Please remember, love. And here are pansies, they’re for thoughts.

original: A document in madness. Thoughts and remembrance fitted.
translation: In her madness, she gives us a lesson: memory and thought belong together.

original: There’s fennel for you, and columbines.—There’s rue for you, and here’s some for me. We may call it “herb of  grace” o’ Sundays.—Oh, you must wear your rue with a  difference.—
translation: Here’s  fennel  for you, and columbines . And here’s rue for you, and some for me. We call it the merciful Sunday flower, though you should wear it for a different reason.

original: There’s a daisy. I would give you some  violets, but they withered all when my father died. They say he made a good end
translation: Here’s a daisy. I’d give you some violets, but they all dried up when my father died. They say he had a good death.

original: For bonny sweet Robin is all my joy—
translation: For good sweet Robin is all my joy.

original: Thought and affliction, passion, hell itself, She turns to favor and to prettiness.
translation: Sad thoughts, terrible suffering, hell itself—she makes them almost graceful and pretty.

original: And will he not come again?   And will he not come again?   No, no, he is dead,   Go to thy deathbed.
translation: And won’t he come again? And won’t he come again? No, no, he’s dead. Go to your deathbed.

original: He never will come again.   His beard was as white as snow,   All flaxen was his poll.   He is gone, he is gone,
translation: He’ll never come again. His beard was white as snow, His hair was all white too. He’s gone, he’s gone,

original: And we cast away moan,   God ha’ mercy on his soul.   —
translation: And we moan our useless grief. God have mercy on his soul.

original: And of all Christian souls, I pray God. God be wi’ ye.
translation: And on the souls of all good Christians, I pray to God. God be with you.

original: Do you see this, O God?
translation: Oh, God: did you see this?

original: Laertes, I must commune with your grief,   Or you deny me right. Go but apart,   Make choice of whom your wisest friends you will.
translation: Laertes, let me share in your grief, or else you deny me my right. Go and choose your wisest friends, and they will sit in judgment of us.

original: And they shall hear and judge ’twixt you and me.   If by direct or by collateral hand   They find us touched, we will our kingdom give,   Our crown, our life, and all that we call ours,   To you in satisfaction.
translation: If they find me at all responsible for your father’s murder, directly or indirectly, then I’ll give up my kingdom, my crown, my life, and everything I call my own to you.

original: But if not,   Be you content to lend your patience to us,   And we shall jointly labor with your soul   To give it due content.
translation: But if they find me innocent, then be patient, and I’ll work with you to ensure that your soul gets what it desires.

original: Let this be so.   His means of death, his obscure funeral—   No trophy, sword, nor hatchment o’er his bones,   No noble rite nor formal ostentation—
translation: That’s what we’ll do. The way he died, and his hushed-up funeral without military display, noble rites, or formal ceremony

original: Cry to be heard as ’twere from heaven to earth,   That I must call ’t in question.
translation: —all these things shout out as if heaven and earth themselves are demanding that I question the way he died.

original: So you shall. And where the offense is, let the great ax fall. I pray you, go with me.
translation: As you should. And may the great ax of justice fall on the guilty. Please, come with me.

original: What are they that would speak with me?
translation: Who wants to speak with me?

original: Seafaring men, sir. They say they have letters for you.
translation: Sailors, sir. They say they have letters for you.

original: Let them come in.
translation: Bring them in.

original: I do not know from what part of the world I should be greeted, if not from Lord Hamlet.
translation: I don’t know who else in the world would send me letters, except Lord Hamlet.

original: God bless you, sir.
translation: God bless you, sir.

original: Let him bless thee too.
translation: May he bless you as well.

original: He shall, sir, an ’t please him. There’s a letter for  you, sir— it comes from the ambassador that was bound  for England—if your name be Horatio, as I am let to know it is.
translation: Sir, he will if it pleases him. Here’s a letter for you, sir. It’s from the ambassador, Lord Hamlet, who was going to England—if your name’s Horatio, as I’ve been told it is.

original: “Horatio,   When thou shalt have overlooked this, give these  fellows some means to the king. They have letters for  him. Ere we were two days old at sea, a pirate of very  warlike appointment gave us chase.
translation: “Horatio, When you’ve read this, make sure these men see the king. They have letters for him. Before we were at sea for even two days, a pirate ship equipped for battle came after us.

original: Finding ourselves too slow of sail, we put on a compelled valor, and in the  grapple I boarded them. On the instant, they got clear  of our ship, so I alone became their prisoner.
translation: Realizing we were too slow to escape, we were forced to fight, and during the battle I boarded the pirate ship. At that moment, the pirates disengaged from our ship, making me their sole prisoner.

original: They have dealt with me like thieves of mercy, but they knew what they did; I am to do a good turn for them. Let the king have the letters I have sent, and repair thou to me  with as much speed as thou wouldst fly death.
translation: For thieves, they’ve treated me very mercifully, but they knew what they were doing. They want me to do a favor for them. Give the king the letters I’ve sent, and come to me as fast as you would run from death.

original: I have  words to speak in thine ear will make thee dumb, yet are they much too light for the bore of the matter. These  good fellows will bring thee where I am.
translation: I’ve got things to tell you that will make you speechless, and they aren’t even the most important details. These sailors will bring you to me.

original: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern hold their course for England. Of them I  have much to tell thee. Fare-well.   He that thou knowest thine,   Hamlet.”
translation: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern continue on their way to England. I have a lot to tell you about them. Goodbye.    From the man that you know is your friend,      Hamlet.”

original: Come, I will give you way for these your letters, And  do ’t the speedier, that you may direct me To him from  whom you brought them.
translation: Come, men. I’ll bring you to the place where you can deliver these letters as quickly as possible, so that you can lead me to the man who sent them.

original: Now must your conscience my acquaintance seal,   And you must put me in your heart for friend,
translation: Now you must admit that I’m innocent, and accept me as a friend,

original: Sith you have heard, and with a knowing ear,   That he which hath your noble father slain   Pursued my life.
translation: since you’ve heard and been convinced that that the man who killed your father was actually trying to kill me.

original: It well appears. But tell me   Why you proceeded not against these feats,   So criminal and so capital in nature,
translation: It looks that way. But explain to me why you didn't take legal action against Hamlet for his capital crimes

original: As by your safety, wisdom, all things else,   You mainly were stirred up.
translation: —when both your wisdom and your own safety must have demanded that you should?
