original: Oh, for two special reasons,   Which may to you perhaps seem much unsinewed,   But yet to me they are strong.
translation: Oh, for two key reasons which to you may seem weak to you, but yet to me are strong.

original: The queen his mother   Lives almost by his looks, and for myself—   My virtue or my plague, be it either which—   She’s so conjunctive to my life and soul,   That, as the star moves not but in his sphere,   I could not but by her.
translation: The queen, his mother, loves him and is devoted to him. And, whether it’s a virtue or a curse, she is so closely connected to my life and soul that I can’t live apart from her—just as a planet can’t leave its orbit.

original: The other motive   Why to a public count I might not go,   Is the great love the general gender bear him,
translation: The other reason why I couldn’t bring charges against Hamlet in a public court is that the commoners loves him.

original: Who, dipping all his faults in their affection,   Would, like the spring that turneth wood to stone,   Convert his gyves to graces
translation: In their affection for him, they overlook all his faults. In fact—like a stream that turns wood to stone—they actually somehow see all his faults as virtues.

original: —so that my arrows,   Too slightly timbered for so loud a wind,   Would have reverted to my bow again,   And not where I had aimed them.
translation: Whatever I said against him would end up coming back to hurt me, like an arrow aimed into a strong wind.

original: And so have I a noble father lost,   A sister driven into desperate terms,
translation: And so I’ve lost my noble father, and my sister has been driven crazy.

original: Whose worth, if praises may go back again,   Stood challenger on mount of all the age   For her perfections. But my revenge will come.
translation: My sister—if I can praise her for what she used to be—was the equal in perfection to any other woman who ever lived. But I’ll get my revenge.

original: Break not your sleeps for that. You must not think   That we are made of stuff so flat and dull   That we can let our beard be shook with danger   And think it pastime.
translation: Don’t lose sleep over that. You must not think that I’m so lazy and stupid that I will let someone threaten and mock me and act as if it’s just a game.

original: You shortly shall hear more.   I loved your father, and we love ourself.   And that, I hope, will teach you to imagine—
translation: Soon you’ll hear more about my plans. I loved your father, and I love myself. And that, I hope, will help you see—

original: How now, what news?
translation: Whats’ going on? What’s your news?

original: Letters, my lord, from Hamlet. This to your majesty, this to the queen.  [gives  CLAUDIUS letters]
translation: My lord, I have letters from Hamlet. This one’s for your Highness, and this one is for the queen.

original: From Hamlet? Who brought them?
translation: From Hamlet? Who delivered them?

original: Sailors, my lord, they say. I saw them not. They were given me by Claudio. He received them Of him that brought them.
translation: I was told that sailors did, my lord. I didn’t see them. Claudio gave the letters to me, and he got them from the one who delivered them.

original: Laertes, you shall hear them.—Leave us.
translation: Laertes, you will hear what these letters say.

original: “High and mighty,   You shall know I am set naked on your kingdom.
translation: “Your majesty,  I’ve been returned to your kingdom naked—with nothing to call my own.

original: Tomorrow shall I beg leave to see your kingly eyes, when I  shall, first asking your pardon thereunto, recount the  occasion of my sudden and more strange return.   Hamlet.”
translation: Tomorrow I’ll ask permission to meet with you, at which point I’ll first apologize and then tell the story of how I came back to Denmark so suddenly and strangely.                     Hamlet”

original: What should this mean? Are all the rest come back? Or  is it some abuse, and no such thing?
translation: What does this mean? Have all the others come back also? Or is it some trick, and none of this is true?

original: Know you the hand?
translation: Do you recognize the handwriting?

original: ‘Tis Hamlet’s character. “Naked”? And in a postscript here, he says “alone.” Can you advise me?
translation: It’s Hamlet’s handwriting. “Naked,” he says. And in a postcript, he adds, “alone.” What do you think about that?

original: I’m lost in it, my lord. But let him come.
translation: It confuses me, my lord. But let him come.

original: It warms the very sickness in my heart   That I shall live and tell him to his teeth,   “Thus diddest thou.”
translation: It warms my sick heart that I’ll get to look him in the face and say, “You did this.”

original: If it be so, Laertes— As how should it be so? How otherwise?— Will you be ruled by me?
translation: If that’s how it should be, Laertes—and why shouldn’t it? How could it be otherwise? Will you follow my orders?

original: Ay, my lord— So you will not o’errule me to a peace.
translation: Yes, my lord, as long as you won’t try to force me toward peace.

original: To thine own peace. If he be now returned,   As checking at his voyage, and that he means   No more to undertake it, I will work him   To an exploit,
translation: Only to your own peace of mind. If he has returned, and now has no plans to continue his trip, then I’ll trick him into taking on some new challenge

original: now ripe in my devise,   Under the which he shall not choose but fall.
translation: —which I’m coming up with now—that will surely kill him.

original: And for his death no wind of blame shall breathe,   But even his mother shall uncharge the practice   And call it accident.
translation: His death will result in no blame. Even his mother will call it an accident.

original: My lord, I will be ruled The rather if you could devise it so That I might be the organ.
translation: My lord, I’ll follow your lead. I want to be the sole agent of his death.

original: It falls right.   You have been talked of since your travel much—   And that in Hamlet’s hearing—for a quality   Wherein, they say, you shine.
translation: That seems only right. Since you left, people have been talking about a quality of yours in which, they say, you shine—and Hamlet has overheard it.

original: Your sum of parts   Did not together pluck such envy from him   As did that one, and that, in my regard,   Of the unworthiest siege.
translation: All your other talents together didn’t make him as envious as this one quality did, though to me it’s of the least importance.

original: What part is that, my lord?
translation: What quality is that, my lord?

original: A very ribbon in the cap of youth,   Yet needful too, for youth no less becomes   The light and careless livery that it wears   Than settled age his sables and his weeds,   Importing health and graveness.
translation: One of those decorative ribbons on the cap of youth—yet a necessary one, too, since casual clothes are like the uniforms of youth, just as formal clothes are the necessary outfits of full maturity.

original: Two months since,   Here was a gentleman of Normandy.   I’ve seen myself, and served against, the French,   And they can well on horseback. But this gallant   Had witchcraft in ’t.
translation: Two months ago, I met a gentleman from Normandy. I’ve watched and fought against the French and know how well they ride, but this man’s skill was almost magical.

original: He grew unto his seat,   And to such wondrous doing brought his horse   As he had been encorpsed and demi-natured   With the brave beast.
translation: He seemed a part of the saddle, and made his horse do such amazing things that he appeared as if he were one with the horse.

original: So far he topped my thought,   That I, in forgery of shapes and tricks,   Come short of what he did.
translation: His skill was beyond my understanding, and even in my imagination I can’t do the tricks he did.

original: A Norman was ’t?
translation: He was from Normandy?

original: A Norman.
translation: From Normandy.

original: Upon my life, Lamond!
translation: I swear by my life it must have been Lamond.

original: The very same.
translation: That’s who it was.

original: I know him well. He is the brooch indeed And gem of all the nation.
translation: I know him well. He’s the jewel of his country.

original: He made confession of you,   And gave you such a masterly report   For art and exercise in your defense,   And for your rapier most especially,
translation: He mentioned you, giving you such high praise for four skill at fencing that he exclaimed that he could not imagine anyone being able to match you.

original: That he cried out ’twould be a sight indeed   If one could match you. The ’scrimers of their nation,   He swore, had had neither motion, guard, nor eye,   If you opposed them.
translation: He swore that French fencers would be clumsy, defenseless, and seem as if they were blind if they ever tried to duel with you.

original: Sir, this report of his   Did Hamlet so envenom with his envy   That he could nothing do but wish and beg   Your sudden coming o’er, to play with him.   Now, out of this—
translation: This description made Hamlet so jealous that he talked about nothing else but having you return to practice dueling against him. Now, the point is—

original: What out of this, my lord?
translation: What’s the point, my lord?

original: Laertes, was your father dear to you? Or are you like the painting of a sorrow, A face without a heart?
translation: Laertes, did you love your father? Or are your putting on a show of grief—a face without a heart?

original: Why ask you this?
translation: How could you ask this?

original: Not that I think you did not love your father   But that I know love is begun by time,   And that I see, in passages of proof,   Time qualifies the spark and fire of it.
translation: Not because I think you didn’t love your father, but because I know that love exists in a particular time and place—and that the passage of time can weaken the spark and fire of that love.

original: There lives within the very flame of love   A kind of wick or snuff that will abate it.   And nothing is at a like goodness still.   For goodness, growing to a pleurisy,   Dies in his own too-much.
translation: Every flame of love eventually burns itself out. Nothing remains the same forever. Even a good thing can grow too big and die from its extreme size.

original: That we would do,   We should do when we would, for this “would” changes   And hath abatements and delays as many   As there are tongues, are hands, are accidents.
translation: We should do what we want in the moment, because our desires might be blocked by as many obstructions or delays as words in the dictionary, or accidents in life.

original: And then this “should” is like a spendthrift sigh   That hurts by easing.
translation: And then all our “woulds” and “shoulds” become like little more than sighs.

original: —But to the quick of th’ ulcer:   Hamlet comes back. What would you undertake   To show yourself in deed your father’s son   More than in words?
translation: But back to the heart of the matter: Hamlet’s coming back. What would you  do , rather than simply  say , to prove that you you are your father’s son?

original: To cut his throat i’ th’ church.
translation: Cut Hamlet’s throat in the church.

original: No place, indeed, should murder sanctuarize.   Revenge should have no bounds. But, good Laertes,   Will you do this, keep close within your chamber.
translation: I agree that no place should protect that murderer. Revenge should have no limits. But, good Laertes, will you do this: stay inside your room?

original: Hamlet returned shall know you are come home.   We’ll put on those shall praise your excellence   And set a double varnish on the fame   The Frenchman gave you, bring you in fine together   And wager on your heads.
translation: When Hamlet returns, he’ll learn that you’ve come home. I’ll have people praise your excellence and add an extra shine to the compliment the Frenchman paid you. Finally, we’ll bring the two of you together and bet on which of you will win.

original: He, being remiss,   Most generous and free from all contriving,   Will not peruse the foils;
translation: Hamlet—who is so careless and trusting—won’t examine the swords beforehand.

original: so that, with ease,   Or with a little shuffling, you may choose   A sword unbated, and in a pass of practice   Requite him for your father.
translation: So you’ll easily be able to choose a sword with a sharpened point, and in the middle of this practice duel, you’ll get revenge for your father's death.

original: I will do ’t.   And for that purpose I’ll anoint my sword.   I bought an unction of a mountebank,
translation: I’ll do it. And I’ll also cover my sword with an oil that I bought from a snake-oil salesman.

original: So mortal that, but dip a knife in it,   Where it draws blood no cataplasm so rare,   Collected from all simples that have virtue   Under the moon, can save the thing from death   That is but scratched withal.
translation: This oil is so poisonous that if a knife dipped in it draws blood, no cure in the world can save the victim.

original: I’ll touch my point   With this contagion, that if I gall him slightly   It may be death.
translation: I’ll cover the point of my sword with it, so that if I even graze him, he’ll probably die.

original: Let’s further think of this,   Weigh what convenience both of time and means   May fit us to our shape.
translation: Let’s think more about this, and consider whether there’s anything else we’ll have the opportunity to do to ensure we get the outcome we want.

original: If this should fail,   And that our drift look through our bad performance,   ‘Twere better not assayed.
translation: If our plan should fail—and if people figure out our plot because we execute it badly—we’d be better off not having tried it at all.

original: Therefore this project   Should have a back or second that might hold   If this should blast in proof.—Soft, let me see.—   We’ll make a solemn wager on your cunnings.—   I ha ’t!
translation: Therefore, we should have a backup plan that will do the trick if we fail in our first attempt. Hmm, let me think—we’re going to bet on your dueling skill—I’ve got it!

original: When in your motion you are hot and dry,   As make your bouts more violent to that end,   And that he calls for drink,
translation: When from all your exertion the two of you have gotten hot and thirsty—make sure the duel is very active to guarantee that happens—Hamlet will want a drink.

original: I’ll have prepared him   A chalice for the nonce, whereon but sipping,   If he by chance escape your venomed stuck,   Our purpose may hold there.
translation: I’ll have a cup ready with poison for just that purpose, and once he sips from it—even if he escapes your poisoned sword—we will get what we want.

original: —But stay, what noise?
translation: But hold on, what’s that sound?

original: One woe doth tread upon another’s heel, So fast they follow.—Your sister’s drowned, Laertes.
translation: The bad news keeps coming, as if each piece follows right on the heels of the one before. Your sister’s drowned, Laertes.

original: Drowned? Oh, where?
translation: Drowned? Oh, where?

original: There is a willow grows aslant a brook   That shows his hoar leaves in the glassy stream.
translation: There’s a willow that leans over the brook, with its white leaves hanging over the glassy water.

original: There with fantastic garlands did she come   Of crowflowers, nettles, daisies, and long purples,   That liberal shepherds give a grosser name,   But our cold maids do “dead men’s fingers” call them.
translation: Ophelia came there—making braided crowns from crowflowers, nettles, daisies, and those wild purple orchids that free-spoken shepherds call by an obscene name, but which innocent girls call “dead men’s fingers.”

original: There, on the pendant boughs her coronet weeds   Clambering to hang, an envious sliver broke,   When down her weedy trophies and herself   Fell in the weeping brook.
translation: She climbed out onto the tree to hang her crowns from a bending branch. But the branch broke, and she and her flowery treasures fell into the swiftly moving brook.

original: Her clothes spread wide,   And mermaid-like a while they bore her up,   Which time she chanted snatches of old lauds   As one incapable of her own distress,   Or like a creature native and indued   Unto that element.
translation: Her clothes spread wide in the water, and held her up while she sang bits of old hymns. She acted as if she could not comprehend the danger, or as if she were a creature that naturally lived in water.

original: But long it could not be   Till that her garments, heavy with their drink,   Pulled the poor wretch from her melodious lay   To muddy death.
translation: But eventually her clothes—heavy with absorbed water—pulled the poor girl out of her song and down to a muddy death.

original: Alas, then she is drowned.
translation: Alas, then she drowned.

original: Drowned, drowned.
translation: Drowned, drowned.

original: Too much of water hast thou, poor Ophelia,   And therefore I forbid my tears. But yet   It is our trick.
translation: Poor Ophelia, you’ve had too much water already, so I won’t cry for you. But crying is what humans do.

original: Nature her custom holds,   Let shame say what it will. When these are gone,   The woman will be out.
translation: We all follow our natures, no matter what shame we feel for it. When I’ve stopped crying, I’ll be done acting like a  woman .

original: Let’s follow, Gertrude.   How much I had to do to calm his rage!
translation: Let’s follow him, Gertrude. I had to do so much to calm him down!

original: Now fear I this will give it start again.   Therefore let’s follow.
translation: Now I fear this might start him up again. Therefore, let’s follow him.

original: Is she to be buried in Christian burial when she  willfully seeks her own salvation?
I tell thee she is. Therefore make her grave straight.  The crowner hath sat on her and finds it Christian  burial.
translation: I’m telling you, she is. So make that grave immediately. The coroner examined her says it should be a Christian funeral.

original: How can that be, unless she drowned herself in her own  defense?
translation: How can that be, unless she drowned herself in self-defense?

original: Why, ’tis found so.
translation: That’s exactly what they’ve determined.

original: It must be se offendendo. It cannot be else.
translation: They must mean “self-offense.” It couldn’t be anything else.

original: For here  lies the point: if I drown myself wittingly, it argues  an act.
translation: Here’s my point: if you drown yourself on purpose, then that’s an act.

original: And an act hath three branches—it is to act, to  do, to perform. Argal, she drowned herself wittingly.
translation: An act has three sides to it: to act, to do, and to perform. Therefore, she must have known she was drowning herself.

original: Nay, but hear you, Goodman Delver—
translation: No, but listen to me, Mister Gravedigger—

original: Give me leave. Here lies the water. Good. Here stands  the man. Good. If the man go to this water and drown  himself, it is, will he nill he, he goes. Mark you that.
translation: Let me finish. Here’s the water, right? Now here stands a man, right? If the man goes into the water and drowns himself, he is—whether you like or not—the one doing it. Got that?

original: But if the water come to him and drown him, he drowns  not himself. Argal, he that is not guilty of his own  death shortens not his own life.
translation: But if the water comes to him and drowns him, then he doesn’t drown himself. Therefore, he who is not guilty of his own death does not shorten his own life.

original: But is this law?
translation: Is that the law?

original: Ay, marry, is ’t. Crowner’s quest law.
translation: Yes, indeed it is. The coroner’s inquest law.

original: Will you ha’ the truth on ’t? If this had not been a  gentlewoman, she should have been buried out o’  Christian burial.
translation: Do you want the truth? If this woman hadn’t been a noble, she wouldn’t have been given a Christian burial.

original: Why, there thou sayst. And the more pity that great  folk should have countenance in this world to drown or  hang themselves more than their even Christian. Come, my spade.
translation: Well, now you’ve said it. It’s a pity that the nobles are given more leeway to drown or hang themselves than other Christians are. Come on, shovel.

original: There is no ancient gentleman but gardeners,  ditchers, and grave-makers. They hold up Adam’s  profession.
translation: The most ancient nobles in the world are gardeners, ditch-diggers, and gravediggers. They keep up Adam’s profession.

original: Was he a gentleman?
translation: Was he a noble?

original: He was the first that ever bore arms.
Why, he had none.
translation: He didn’t bear any arms.

original: What, art a heathen? How dost thou understand the  Scripture?
translation: What, are you not a Christian? Do you not know the Bible?

original: The Scripture says Adam digged. Could he dig  without arms? I’ll put another question to thee. If thou answerest me not to the purpose, confess thyself—
translation: The Bible says Adam dug. Could he dig without arms? I’ll ask you another question. If you can’t answer it, admit it—

original: Go to.
translation: Go ahead!

original: What is he that builds stronger than either the mason,  the shipwright, or the carpenter?
translation: Who builds stronger things than a stonemason, a shipbuilder, or a carpenter?

original: The gallows-maker, for that frame outlives a thousand  tenants.
translation: The one who builds the gallows where people are hung, because the gallows outlive a thousand users.

original: like thy wit well, in good faith. The gallows does  well, but how does it well?
translation: I like your humor, I swear. The gallows do well. But how?

original: It does well to those that  do ill. Now thou dost ill to say the gallows is built  stronger than the church.
translation: They do well to those who do bad. But you do bad to say that the gallows are stronger than a church.

original: Argal, the gallows may do well to thee. To ’t again, come.
translation: Therefore, the gallows may do well to you. Come on, try again.

original: “Who builds stronger than a mason, a shipwright, or a  carpenter?”
translation: “Who builds stronger things than a stonemason, a shipbuilder, or a carpenter?”

original: Ay, tell me that, and unyoke.
translation: Yes, tell me that, then you can call it a day.

original: Marry, now I can tell.
translation: Indeed, I’ll give you answer!

original: To ’t.
translation: Do it.

original: Mass, I cannot tell.
Cudgel thy brains no more about it, for your dull ass  will not mend his pace with beating.
translation: Stop wracking your brains about it. After all, you can’t make a slow donkey run by beating it.

original: And when you are  asked this question next, say “A grave-maker.”
translation: The next time someone asks you this riddle, say “a gravedigger.”

original: The  houses that he makes last till doomsday. Go, get thee  in. Fetch me a stoup of liquor.
translation: The houses he makes last till Judgment Day. Go inside, now, and get me some alcohol.

original: In youth when I did love, did love,   Methought it was very sweet
translation: In my youth when I did love, did love,  I though it was very sweet

original: To contract–o–the time, for–a–my behove,   Oh, methought, there–a–was nothing–a–meet.
translation: To set—O—the date for—Ahh—my duty   Oh, I thought it—ahh—was not—ahh—right.

original: Has this fellow no feeling of his business? He sings at grave- making.
translation: Does this man not understand the seriousness of what he’s doing? He’s singing while digging a grave.

original: Custom hath made it in him a property of easiness.
translation: He’s gotten so used to digging graves that he does it with ease.

original: ‘Tis e’en so. The hand of little employment hath the  daintier sense.
translation: That’s it exactly. Only those who aren't used to that kind of work are more sensitive to it.

original: But age with his stealing steps   Hath clawed me in his clutch,
translation: But old age has snuck up on me   And caught me in his claws,

original: And hath shipped me into the land   As if I had never been such.
translation: And has shipped me into the ground   As if I’d never been like that.

original: That skull had a tongue in it and could sing once. How  the knave jowls it to the ground, as if it were Cain’s  jawbone, that did the first murder!
translation: That skull had a tongue in it, and could sing once. That fool flings it to the ground as if belonged to Cain, who committed the first murder!

original: It might be the pate of a politician, which this ass now o’erreaches, one  that would circumvent God, might it not?
translation: It might be the skull of a power-grabbing politician who could talk his way around God, right? And now this idiot is grasping it.

original: It might, my lord.
translation: It could be, my lord.

original: Or of a courtier, which could say, “Good morrow, sweet  lord!” “How dost thou, good lord?”
translation: Or a courtier, who used to say, “Good night, my sweet lord! How are you, good lord?”

original: This might be my Lord Such-a-one that praised my Lord Such-a-one’s horse when he meant to beg it, might it not?
translation: This might be the skull of Lord So-and-So, who praised Lord So-and-So’s horse when he wanted to borrow it, right?

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: Why, e’en so. And now my Lady Worm’s, chapless and  knocked about the mazard with a sexton’s spade.
translation: Why, yes. Exactly. And now it’s the property of Lady Worm, with its lower jaw knocked off, and thwacked on the head with a little shovel.

original: Here’s  fine revolution, an we had the trick to see ’t.
translation: What a change of fortune, if we could only see it.

original: Did  these bones cost no more the breeding but to play at  loggets with them? Mine ache to think on ’t.
translation: Were these bones grown and used so that they would be worth no more than bowling pins now? My bones ache to think about it.

original: A pickax and a spade, a spade,   For and a shrouding sheet,
translation: A pickax and a shovel, a shovel,  A sheet for a funeral shroud,

original: Oh, a pit of clay for to be made   For such a guest is meet.
translation: Oh, a pit of dirt to be made up  Is the right thing for our guest.

original: There’s another. Why may not that be the skull of a  lawyer? Where be his quiddities now, his quillities, his cases, his tenures, and his tricks? Why does he suffer  this rude knave now to knock him about the sconce with a dirty shovel and will not tell him of his action of  battery?
translation: There’s another. Why, couldn’t that be a lawyer’s skull? Where are all his lawyerly quibbles, his cases, and his tricks? Why does he let this rude fool knock him on the head with a shovel without suing him for assault and battery?

original: Hum! This fellow might be in ’s time a great  buyer of land, with his statutes, his recognizances, his fines, his double vouchers, his recoveries. Is this the fine of his fines and the recovery of his recoveries,  to have his fine pate full of fine dirt?
translation: Maybe he was a great landowner, with his bonds, his deeds, and his rents. Was it part of his contracts and deeds that his skull should get filled up with dirt?

original: Will his  vouchers vouch him no more of his purchases, and double  ones too, than the length and breadth of a pair of  indentures? The very conveyances of his lands will  hardly lie in this box, and must the inheritor himself  have no more, ha?
translation: Does he get to keep only as much of his land as equals the width and length of a pair of his contracts spread out on the ground? The deeds to his properties would barely fit in this coffin—and that coffin is all he gets to have?

original: Not a jot more, my lord.
translation: Not a bit more, my lord.

original: Is not parchment made of sheepskins?
translation: Aren’t legal documents made of sheepskin?

original: Ay, my lord, and of calfskins too.
translation: Yes, my lord, and calfskin too.

original: They are sheep and calves which seek out assurance in  that. I will speak to this fellow.—Whose grave’s this,  sirrah?
translation: Anyone who looks for assurance in such documents is a sheep or a calf. I’m going to talk to this man.

original: Mine, sir.  Oh, a pit of clay for to be made For such a guest is meet.
translation: It’s mine, sir. Oh, a pit of dirt to be made up  Is the right thing for our guest.

original: I think it be thine, indeed, for thou liest in ’t.
translation: I think it must be yours, because you’re lying in it.

original: You lie out on ’t, sir, and therefore it is not yours.  For my part, I do not lie in ’t, and yet it is mine.
translation: You’re lying outside of it, sir, so therefore it’s not yours. As for me, I’m not lying in it—it’s really mine.

original: Thou dost lie in ’t, to be in ’t and say it is thine.  ‘Tis for the dead, not for the quick. Therefore thou  liest.
‘Tis a quick lie, sir. ‘Twill away gain from me to you.
translation: That’s a lively lie, sir, jumping like that from me to you.

original: What man dost thou dig it for?
translation: What man are you digging it for?

original: For no man, sir.
translation: For no man, sir.

original: What woman, then?
translation: What woman, then?

original: For none, neither.
translation: For no woman, either.

original: Who is to be buried in ’t?
translation: Who’s to be buried in it?

original: One that was a woman, sir, but, rest her soul, she’s  dead.
translation: One who used to be a woman, sir, but is now dead, bless her soul.

original: How absolute the knave is! We must speak by the card,  or equivocation will undo us.
translation: How literal this jokester is! We have to speak precisely, or his word play will defeat us.

original: By the Lord, Horatio,  these three years I have taken a note of it.
translation: Lord, Horatio, I’ve been noticing this for the last three years.

original: The age is  grown so picked that the toe of the peasant comes so  near the heel of the courtier he galls his kibe.
translation: The commoners have become so sophisticated that they’re nipping at the heels of noblemen.

original: Of all the days i’ the year, I came to ’t that day that our last King Hamlet overcame Fortinbras.
translation: Of all the days in the year, I started this work on the day that the late King Hamlet defeated Fortinbras.

original: How long is that since?
translation: How long ago was that?

original: Cannot you tell that? Every fool can tell that. It was  the very day that young Hamlet was born, he that is mad  and sent into England.
translation: You don’t know that? Any fool could tell you that. It was the day that young Hamlet was born—the one who’s insane and got sent to England.

original: Ay, marry, why was he sent into England?
translation: Yes, right, and why was he sent to England?

original: Why, because he was mad. He shall recover his wits  there, or, if he do not, it’s no great matter there.
translation: Why? Because he was insane. He’ll recover his sanity there. Or if he doesn’t, it won’t matter in England.

original: Why?
translation: Why?

original: ‘Twill not be seen in him there. There the men are as  mad as he.
translation: Nobody there will notice. All the people there are as crazy as he is.

original: How came he mad?
translation: How did he go insane?

original: Very strangely, they say.
translation: Very strangely, they say.

original: How “strangely?”
translation: What do you mean, “strangely?"

original: Faith, e’en with losing his wits.
translation: By losing his mind, of course.

original: Upon what ground?
translation: On what grounds?

original: Why, here in Denmark. I have been sexton here, man and  boy, thirty years.
translation: Why, right here in Denmark. I’ve been the handyman here for thirty years, since I was a boy.

original: How long will a man lie i’ the earth ere he rot?
translation: How long will a man lie in his grave before he starts to rot?

original: Faith, if he be not rotten before he die—as we have  many pocky corses nowadays that will scarce hold the  laying in— he will last you some eight year or nine  year. A tanner will last you nine year.
translation: Well, if he’s not rotten before he dies—and we do have many corpses nowadays that are so rotten that they fall apart just from being laid in the grave—he’ll last eight or nine years. A man who makes leather will last nine years.

original: Why he more than another?
translation: Why does he last longer than anyone else?

original: Why, sir, his hide is so tanned with his trade that he  will keep out water a great while, and your water is a  sore decayer of your whoreson dead body.
translation: Well, sir, because his skin is so leathery from the work he does that he keeps the water out for a long time, and water is the main cause of decay in your son-of-a-bitch body.

original: Here’s a skull now. This skull has lain in the  earth three-and-twenty years.
translation: Here’s a skull now. It’s been buried in the earth twenty-three years.

original: Whose was it?
translation: Whose was it?

original: A whoreson mad fellow’s it was. Whose do you think it  was?
translation: An insane son-of-a-bitch. Whose do you think it was?

original: Nay, I know not.
translation: I don’t know.

original: A pestilence on him for a mad rogue! He poured a flagon of Rhenish on my head once. This same skull, sir, was  Yorick’s skull, the king’s jester.
translation: A curse on him, that crazy scoundrel! He poured a pitcher of German wine on my head once. Sir, this skull belonged to Yorick, the king’s jester.

original: This?
translation: This one?

original: E’en that.
translation: That one.

original: Let me see.
translation: Let me see.

original: Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio, a fellow of infinite jest, of most  excellent fancy. He hath borne me on his back a thousand times, and now, how abhorred in my imagination it is!
translation: Oh, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio. He was a man of endless humor, a great wit. He gave me piggy-back rides a thousand times, and now..how awful my imagination is!

original: My gorge rises at it. Here hung those lips that I have  kissed I know not how oft. —Where be your gibes now?  Your gambols? Your songs?
translation: It makes me nauseated to think of it. Here hung his lips, which I kissed I don’t know how many times. Where are your jokes now? Your dances? Your songs?

original: Your flashes of merriment that were wont to set the table on a roar? Not one now to  mock your own grinning? Quite chapfallen?
translation: Your flashes of high spirits that used to set the whole table roaring with laughter? You’re not able to mock your own grinning skull now, are you?

original: Now get you to my lady’s chamber and tell her, let her paint an inch  thick, to this favor she must come. Make her laugh at  that.
translation: Now go to my lady’s bedroom and tell her that, even if she piles on the makeup an inch thick, she’ll still wind up looking like you. Make her laugh at that.

original: What’s that, my lord?
translation: What’s that, my lord?

original: Dost thou think Alexander looked o’ this fashion i’ th’ earth?
translation: Do you think Alexander the Great looked like this when he was buried?

original: E’en so.
translation: Just like that.

original: And smelt so? Pah!
translation: And smelled like this? Yuck!

original: E’en so, my lord.
translation: Just like that, my lord.

original: To what base uses we may return, Horatio. Why may not  imagination trace the noble dust of Alexander till he  find it stopping a bunghole?
translation: Look how badly we end up, Horatio. Why, you could imagine how the noble ashes of Alexander the Great might end up plugging a hole in a barrel?

original: ‘Twere to consider too curiously, to consider so.
translation: You’d be thinking about it too much, if you thought about that.

original: No, faith, not a jot. But to follow him thither with  modesty enough, and likelihood to lead it, as thus:  Alexander died, Alexander was buried, Alexander  returneth to dust, the dust is earth, of earth we make  loam
translation: No, I swear, not at all. It’s perfectly reasonable to think of it: Alexander died, Alexander was buried, Alexander returned to dust, the dust is dirt, and dirt is used to make the material we use to stop up holes.

original: —and why of that loam, whereto he was converted,  might they not stop a beer barrel?   Imperious Caesar, dead and turned to clay,   Might stop a hole to keep the wind away.
translation: So why can’t someone use the clay made from Alexander to plug up a beer barrel? The Roman Emperor Caesar, dead and turned to clay, might block a hole to keep the wind away.

original: Oh, that that earth, which kept the world in awe,   Should patch a wall t’ expel the winter’s flaw!   But soft, but soft a while.
translation: Oh, that the body that once ruled the entire world could now patch up a wall to keep out the winter! But quiet, be quiet for a moment.

original: Here comes the king,   The queen, the courtiers—who is this they follow,   And with such maimèd rites?
translation: Here comes the king, the queen, and all of their court. Who is it that they’re following? And with such a plain ceremony?

original: This doth betoken   The corse they follow did with desperate hand   Fordo its own life.
translation: This must mean that the corpse they’re following committed suicide.

original: ‘Twas of some estate.   Couch we a while and mark.
translation: Must have been someone of quite noble birth. Let’s hide and watch for a while.

original: What ceremony else?
translation: What other rites will you perform?

original: That is Laertes, a very noble youth, mark.
translation: That’s Laertes, a very noble young man. Listen.

original: What ceremony else?
translation: What other rites will you perform?

original: Her obsequies have been as far enlarged   As we have warranty. Her death was doubtful,
translation: I’ve performed all the rites that I’m allowed to perform. Her death was questionable.

original: And, but that great command o’ersways the order,   She should in ground unsanctified have lodged   Till the last trumpet.
translation: And if the king had not given a command that overruled our normal customs, she’d have been buried in the unholy ground outside the church graveyard until Judgment Day.

original: For charitable prayers   Shards, flints and pebbles should be thrown on her.
translation: Instead of prayers, she would have had rocks and broken pottery thrown on her body.

original: Yet here she is allowed her virgin crants,   Her maiden strewments, and the bringing home   Of bell and burial.
translation: But she is dressed up like a pure virgin, with flowers scattered on her grave, and the bell tolling for her.

original: Must there no more be done?
translation: Can nothing more be done?

original: No more be done.
translation: Nothing more.

original: We should profane the service of the dead   To sing a requiem and such rest to her   As to peace-parted souls.
translation: We would be disrespectful to the other dead if we sang the same requiem for her that we sang for those who died peacefully.

original: Lay her i’ th’ earth,   And from her fair and unpolluted flesh   May violets spring!
translation: Lay her in the ground, and may violets bloom from her pure and beautiful body!

original: I tell thee, churlish priest,   A ministering angel shall my sister be   When thou liest howling.
translation: I’m telling you, you uncharitable priest, my sister will be an angel in heaven while you’re howling in hell.

original: What, the fair Ophelia?
translation: What, the beautiful Ophelia?

original: Sweets to the sweet. Farewell!
translation: Sweet flowers for a sweet girl. Goodbye!

original: I hoped thou shouldst have been my Hamlet’s wife.
translation: I had hoped you’d be my Hamlet’s wife.

original: I thought thy bride-bed to have decked, sweet maid,   And not have strewed thy grave.
translation: I thought I’d be scattering flowers on your wedding bed, not strewing them on your grave, sweet girl.

original: Oh, treble woe   Fall ten times treble on that cursèd head,   Whose wicked deed thy most ingenious sense   Deprived thee of!
translation: Oh, damn three times, damn thirty times the cursed one whose actions stole your brilliant mind.

original: Hold off the earth awhile   Till I have caught her once more in mine arms.
translation: Do not bury her until I’ve held her in my arms once more.

original: Now pile your dust upon the quick and dead,   Till of this flat a mountain you have made,
translation: Now pile the dirt onto the living and the dead, until you’ve made this flat ground into mountain

original: T’ o’ertop old Pelion or the skyish head   Of blue Olympus.
translation: higher than Mount  Pelion  or the towering peaks of Mount Olympus.

original: What is he whose grief   Bears such an emphasis, whose phrase of sorrow   Conjures the wandering stars,
translation: Who is the man whose grief is so profound, whose words of sadness makes the stars stand still in the heavens

original: and makes them stand   Like wonder-wounded hearers? This is I,   Hamlet the Dane.
translation: as if struck dumb by what they’ve heard? It is me, Hamlet the Dane.

original: The devil take thy soul!
translation: The devil take your soul!

original: Thou pray’st not well.
translation: That’s not the right way to pray.

original: I prithee, take thy fingers from my throat,
translation: I ask you, please remove your fingers from my throat.

original: For though I am not splenitive and rash,   Yet have I something in me dangerous,   Which let thy wisdom fear. Hold off thy hand.
translation: I’m not impulsive and quick-tempered, but I have something dangerous in me which you would be wise to fear. Take your hands off me.

original: Pluck them asunder.
translation: Separate them.

original: Hamlet, Hamlet!
translation: Hamlet! Hamlet!

original: Gentlemen—
translation: Gentlemen!

original: Good my lord, be quiet.
translation: My lord, calm down.

original: Why, I will fight with him upon this theme Until my eyelids will no longer wag.
translation: I’ll fight him on this topic until my eyelids cease to blink.

original: O my son, what theme?
translation: Oh, my son, what topic?

original: I loved Ophelia. Forty thousand brothers Could not with all their quantity of love Make up my sum. What wilt thou do for her?
translation: I loved Ophelia. The love of forty thousand brothers, added together, could not match mine. What are you going to do for her?

original: O, he is mad, Laertes.
translation: Oh, he is crazy, Laertes!

original: For love of God, forbear him.
translation: For the love of God, leave him alone.

original: ‘Swounds, show me what thou’lt do.   Woo’t weep? Woo’t fight? Woo’t fast? Woo’t tear  thyself?
translation: By God! Show me what you’re going to do for her. Will you cry? Will you fight? Will you cease to eat? Will you cut yourself?

original: Woo’t drink up eisel, eat a crocodile?   I’ll do ’t. Dost thou come here to whine,   To outface me with leaping in her grave?   Be buried quick with her?—and so will I.
translation: Will you drink vinegar, or eat a crocodile? I’ll do it. Did you come here to whine? To outdo me by jumping into her grave so theatrically? To be buried alive with her? So will I.

original: And if thou prate of mountains let them throw   Millions of acres on us, till our ground,   Singeing his pate against the burning zone,   Make Ossa like a wart!
translation: And if you babble about mountains, then let them throw millions of acres over us until the peak scrapes against sun and makes  Mount Ossa  look like a wart.

original: Nay, an thou’lt mouth,   I’ll rant as well as thou.
translation: See? I can rant as well as you.

original: This is mere madness.   And thus a while the fit will work on him.
translation: This is pure madness. This fit will stay with him for a little while.

original: Anon, as patient as the female dove   When that her golden couplets are disclosed,   His silence will sit drooping.
translation: Then he’ll be as calm as a female dove waiting for a pair of eggs to hatch.

original: Hear you, sir.   What is the reason that you use me thus?   I loved you ever.
translation: Listen to me, sir. Why do you treat me like this? I always loved you.

original: But it is no matter.   Let Hercules himself do what he may,   The cat will mew and dog will have his day.
translation: But it doesn’t matter. No matter what a hero like Hercules does, fools will seek to draw attention to themselves.

original: I pray thee, good Horatio, wait upon him.
translation: Horatio, please go with him.

original: Strengthen your patience in our last night’s speech.   We’ll put the matter to the present push.—
translation: Control yourself by thinking of our talk last night. We’ll handle this issue very soon.

original: So much for this, sir. Now shall you see the other. You do remember all the circumstances?
translation: That’s everything about that, sir. Now I’ll tell you my other story. You do remember the circumstances of my situation, righ?

original: Remember it, my lord?
translation: How could I not, my lord?

original: Sir, in my heart there was a kind of fighting   That would not let me sleep. Methought I lay   Worse than the mutines in the bilboes.
translation: Sir, there was a kind of war in my heart that wouldn’t let me sleep. It seemed to me that I was in worse shape even than captive rebels in chains.

original: Rashly—   And praised be rashness for it: let us know   Our indiscretion sometimes serves us well   When our deep plots do pall,
translation: I impulsively—let me praise impulsiveness. Sometimes acting impulsively works even when our complicated plans don’t work out,

original: and that should teach us   There’s a divinity that shapes our ends,   Rough-hew them how we will—
translation: showing us that a God who shapes our destiny—

original: That is most certain.
translation: That is a certainty.

original: Up from my cabin,   My sea-gown scarfed about me, in the dark   Groped I to find out them, had my desire,   Fingered their packet, and in fine withdrew   To mine own room again,
translation: I came up from my cabin with my robe tied around me. In the dark, I groped around and found what I was looking for. I stole Rosencrantz and Guildenstern's packet of papers, and snuck back to my cabin again.

original: making so bold   (My fears forgetting manners) to unseal   Their grand commission,
translation: My fears overcoming my manners, I was bold enough to open the letter they carried from Claudius to the English king.

original: where I found, Horatio—   O royal knavery!—an exact command,   Larded with many several sorts of reasons   Importing Denmark’s health, and England’s too,   With—ho!—such bugs and goblins in my life
translation: Horato, there I found—oh, royal mischief!—an explicit command, fattened up with blather about Denmark’s well-being and England’s too —listen!—that described all the terrors that would come from letting me live.

original: That, on the supervise (no leisure bated,   No, not to stay the grinding of the ax)   My head should be struck off.
translation: The letter contained instructions to cut off my head, without even taking any time to sharpen the ax.

original: Is ’t possible?
translation: Is it possible?

original: Here’s the commission. Read it at more leisure. But wilt thou hear me how I did proceed?
translation: Here’s the letter. Read it when you have a moment. But do you want to hear what I did next?

original: I beseech you.
translation: Please.

original: Being thus benetted round with villainies—   Ere I could make a prologue to my brains,   They had begun the play—I sat me down,   Devised a new commission, wrote it fair.
translation: Stuck as I was in their cruel net—before I could even fully think about the problem, my brain had already started playing with possible solutions—I sat down and wrote a new letter. I wrote it in a bureaucrat’s neat handwriting.

original: I once did hold it, as our statists do,   A baseness to write fair, and labored much   How to forget that learning,
translation: I used to think, just as our politicians do, that having nice handwriting was for servants. So I had to really work to forget that bias.

original: but, sir, now   It did me yeoman’s service. Wilt thou know   Th’ effect of what I wrote?
translation: And, sir, it certainly helped me then. Would you like to know what I wrote?

original: Ay, good my lord.
translation: Yes, my good lord.

original: An earnest conjuration from the king,   As England was his faithful tributary,   As love between them like the palm might flourish,
translation: A sincere request from the King of Denmark, to the King of England—his faithful vassal subject—with hopes that the love between the two countries can flourish,

original: As peace should stiff her wheaten garland wear   And stand a comma ’tween their amities,   And many suchlike “as’s” of great charge,
translation: and that peace can rise up and join them together in friendship, and some other important-sounding statements like that.

original: That, on the view and knowing of these contents,   Without debatement further, more or less,   He should the bearers put to sudden death,   Not shriving time allowed.
translation: I instructed the King of England that, after reading and reviewing the letter, without any further debate, he should immediately kill the men who delivered the letter, without even giving them time to confess to a priest.

original: How was this sealed?
translation: How did you get an official seal on it?

original: Why, even in that was heaven ordinant.   I had my father’s signet in my purse,   Which was the model of that Danish seal.
translation: Even there, heaven gave me a helping hand. I had my father’s signet ring in my pocket, which has a small version of the Danish royal seal on it.

original: Folded the writ up in form of th’ other,   Subscribed it, gave ’t th’ impression, placed it  safely,   The changeling never known.
translation: I folded up the letter, signed it, sealed it, and put it safely back without anyone noticing the change.

original: Now, the next day   Was our sea fight, and what to this was sequent   Thou know’st already.
translation: The next day brought our fight at sea, and you already know what happened afterwards.

original: So Guildenstern and Rosencrantz go to ’t.
translation: So Guildenstern and Rosencrantz go to their deaths.

original: Why, man, they did make love to this employment.   They are not near my conscience. Their defeat   Does by their own insinuation grow.
translation: Well, man, they loved doing the king’s every bidding. I don’t feel any guilt. Their deaths grew out of their meddling.

original: ‘Tis dangerous when the baser nature comes   Between the pass and fell incensèd points   Of mighty opposites.
translation: It’s dangerous when inferior people get in between the sword thrusts of mighty opponents.

original: Why, what a king is this!
translation: Oh, what a king this Claudius is!

original: Does it not, think thee, stand me now upon—
translation: Don’t you think that it's now my duty to kill him?

original: He that hath killed my king and whored my mother,   Popped in between th’ election and my hopes,   Thrown out his angle for my proper life   (And with such cozenage!)
translation: He killed my king, made my mother a whore, stole the throne that I wanted, and plotted against my life with shocking trickery.

original: —is ’t not perfect conscience   To quit him with this arm? And is ’t not to be damned   To let this canker of our nature come   In further evil?
translation: Wouldn’t killing him be completely justified? And, in fact, wouldn’t I be damned if I were to let this cancer live to do more harm?

original: It must be shortly known to him from England What is the issue of the business there.
translation: He’s going to get the news from England soon about what happened there.

original: It will be short. The interim’s mine.   And a man’s life’s no more than to say “one.”
translation: He will, soon. But I have time before the news arrives. And it only takes the time to count to one to kill a man.

original: But I am very sorry, good Horatio,   That to Laertes I forgot myself,   For by the image of my cause I see   The portraiture of his.
translation: But I do feel very sorry, Horatio, that I lost control of myself with Laertes. I can see my own cause for revenge mirrored in his.

original: I’ll court his favors.   But sure the bravery of his grief did put me   Into a towering passion.
translation: I’ll try to win him over. But the melodramatic showiness of his grief pushed me into a fury.

original: Peace.—Who comes here?
translation: Stop—who’s coming in here?

original: Your lordship is right welcome back to Denmark.
translation: My lord, welcome back to Denmark.

original: I humbly thank you, sir.    Dost know  this water-fly?
translation: I humbly thank you, sir.

original: No, my good lord.
translation: No, my lord.

original: Thy state is the more gracious, for  ’tis a vice to know him. He hath much land, and fertile.
translation: You're better off for that. It’s a curse to know him. He owns a lot of good, fertile land.

original: Let a beast be lord of beasts and his crib shall stand  at the king’s mess.
translation: Give a beast a lot of cattle, and his food trough will be welcome at the king’s table.

original: ‘Tis a chough, but, as I say,  spacious in the possession of dirt.
translation: He’s a fool who spouts nonsense, but, as I said, he owns a lot of dirt.

original: Sweet lord, if your lordship were at leisure, I should  impart a thing to you from His Majesty.
translation: Sweet lord, if you were to have a free moment, I would like to tell you a message from His Majesty.

original: I will receive it, sir, with all diligence of spirit.  Put your bonnet to his right use. ‘Tis for the head.
translation: Sir, I’ll listen, with all of my being. Now put your hat to its proper use. Put it on your head.

original: I thank your lordship. It is very hot.
translation: Thank you for the advice, my lord. But it’s very hot.

original: No, believe me, ’tis very cold. The wind is northerly.
translation: No, believe me, it’s very cold, with a northern wind.

original: It is indifferent cold, my lord, indeed.
translation: My lord, it is quite cold, indeed.

original: But yet methinks it is very sultry and hot for my  complexion.
translation: But yet I think it’s too humid and hot for me.

original: Exceedingly, my lord. It is very sultry—as ’twere—I  cannot tell how. My lord, his majesty bade me signify to you that he has laid a great wager on your head. Sir,  this is the matter—
translation: Exceedingly hot, sir. It is very humid—so humid I can’t even describe it. My lord, His Majesty asked me to tell you that he’s placed a large bet on you. Sir, here’s what’s going on—

original: I beseech you, remember—  [indicates that OSRIC should  put on his hat]
translation: I beg you, remember—

original: Nay, good my lord, for mine ease, in good faith.
translation: No, my lord, I’m more comfortable like this, I swear.

original: Sir,  here is newly come to court Laertes, believe me, an  absolute gentleman, full of most excellent differences,  of very soft society and great showing.
translation: Sir, a recent arrival to the royal court named Laertes is an absolute gentleman, believe me. He is full of the most excellent qualities, with agreeable manners and good looks.

original: Indeed, to speak feelingly of him, he is the card or calendar of gentry, for you shall find in him the continent of what part a  gentleman would see.
translation: In fact, if I were to reveal my true feelings about him, he is like a checklist of what a gentleman should be. You’ll find that he’s the embodiment of a perfect gentleman.

original: Sir, his definement suffers no perdition in you, though I know to divide him inventorially would dizzy th’  arithmetic of memory, and yet but yaw neither, in  respect of his quick sail.
translation: Sir, your description of him suffers no loss of accuracy, though I know that to try to describe all of his good qualities would dizzy the mind. And even trying to do so, you still would not be able to capture them all.

original: But in the verity of  extolment, I take him to be a soul of great article, and his infusion of such dearth and rareness as, to make  true diction of him, his semblable is his mirror.
translation: But in true and sincere praise, I can say that he has a soul of great nobility, and that he is so unique—to be honest about him—that his equal can only be found when he looks in a mirror.

original: And  who else would trace him? His umbrage, nothing more.
translation: Anyone else is just a shadow of him.

original: Your lordship speaks most infallibly of him.
translation: Your lordship describes him perfectly.

original: The concernancy, sir? Why do we wrap the gentleman in  our more rawer breath?
translation: What’s the relevance? Why do we wrap him up in our breathless words?

original: Sir?
translation: Sir?

original: Is ’t not possible to understand in  another tongue? You will do ’t, sir, really.
translation: You must speak in a different style for him to understand you? You can do it, sir.

original: What imports the nomination of this gentleman?
translation: What is the significance of our discussion of this gentleman?

original: Of Laertes?
translation: Of Laertes?

original: His purse is empty already. All ’s  golden words are spent.
translation: His purse is already empty. He has spent all of his golden words.

original: Of him, sir.
translation: Yes, of him. Of Laertes, sir.

original: I know you are not ignorant—
translation: I know you are not ignorant—

original: I would you did, sir. Yet in faith, if you did, it  would not much approve me. Well, sir?
translation: I wish you did, sir. But in truth, if you did, it would not be much to my credit. Well, sir?

original: You are not ignorant of what excellence Laertes is—
translation: I know you’re not ignorant about how excellent Laertes is—

original: I dare not confess that lest I should compare with him  in excellence, but to know a man well were to know  himself.
translation: I don’t dare to admit it, because you might compare his excellence to mine. But to know excellence in another you must know it in yourself.

original: I mean, sir, for his weapon. But in the imputation laid on him by them, in his meed he’s unfellowed.
translation: I mean, sir, he’s known for his weapon. Popular opinion holds him to be unrivaled.

original: What’s his weapon?
translation: What kind of weapon does he use?

original: Rapier and dagger.
translation: The light sword and the dagger.

original: That’s two of his weapons. But well.
translation: Those are just two of his weapons. But no matter.

original: The king, sir, hath wagered with him six Barbary  horses, against the which he has impawned, as I take it, six French rapiers and poniards with their assigns—as  girdle, hangers, and so.
translation: Sir, the king has gambled with Laertes, betting six Barbary horses against—as I understand it—six French light swords and daggers with all their accessories.

original: Three of the carriages, in  faith, are very dear to fancy, very responsive to the  hilts, most delicate carriages, and of very liberal  conceit.
translation: Three of the carriages, in fact, are very beautifully designed, and match the fencing accessories. Very imaginative carriages.

original: What call you the carriages?
translation: What are you calling “carriages?"

original: I knew you must be edified by the  margin ere you had done.
translation: I knew you’d have to look a word up before we were finished with him.

original: The carriages, sir, are the hangers.
translation: The carriages, sir, are the hangers on which we hang swords.

original: The phrase would be more germane to the matter if we  could carry cannon by our sides.   I would it might be  hangers till then.
translation: That word would make more sense if it were describing something that pulled a cannon. I’d prefer to call it a “hanger.”

original: But, on: six Barbary horses against  six French swords, their assigns, and three  liberal-conceited carriages—that’s the French bet  against the Danish.
translation: But, still. Six Barbary horses against six French swords with accessories, and three imaginatively designed carriages—sounds like a French bet against the Danish.

original: Why is this “impawned,” as you call  it?
translation: Why has all this been “gambled,” as you put it?

original: The king, sir, hath laid that in a dozen passes between yourself and him, he shall not exceed you three hits.
translation: Sir, the king has bet that in a dozen rounds between you and Laertes, he won’t beat you by more than three hits.

original: He hath laid on twelve for nine, and it would come to  immediate trial if your lordship would vouchsafe the  answer.
translation: We could start the match immediately if you’ll do me the honor of giving me your answer.

original: How if I answer “No”?
translation: What if my answer is "no?"

original: I mean, my lord, the opposition of your person in  trial.
translation: I mean, my lord, if you’d agree to compete in the wager.

original: Sir, I will walk here in the hall. If it please His  Majesty, ’tis the breathing time of day with me.
translation: Sir, I’m going to take a walk in the hall. Tell the king that it is my time to exercise.

original: Let the foils be brought, the gentleman willing, and the king  hold his purpose.
translation: If the king still wants to do this, and if Laertes is willing, tell them to bring in the swords.

original: I will win for him an I can. If not, I will gain nothing but my shame and the odd hits.
translation: I’ll win the king’s bet for him if I can. If not, I’ll have suffered just a bit of shame for losing, and a few sword hits.

original: Shall I redeliver you e’en so?
translation: Shall I quote you with those precise words?

original: To this effect, sir, after what flourish your nature  will.
translation: Just get the meaning across, sir. And be as flowery as you want in doing it.

original: I commend my duty to your lordship.
translation: I am at your service, your lordship.

original: Yours, yours.
translation: Thank you.

original: He does well to commend it himself. There are no  tongues else for ’s turn.
translation: He’s smart to recommend himself. There’s no one else who’d do it for him.

original: This lapwing runs away with the shell on his head.
translation: That fool looks like a newly hatched bird running around with its egg still on its head.

original: He did comply, sir, with his dug before he sucked it.
translation: He used to shower flowery praise on his mother’s nipple before he sucked it.

original: Thus has he—and many more of the same bevy that I know  the drossy age dotes on—only got the tune of the time  and outward habit of encounter,
translation: In that way he—and so many others in this frivolous age—follow the fashionable way of talking.

original: a kind of yeasty  collection, which carries them through and through the  most fond and winnowed opinions; and do but blow them to their trial, the bubbles are out.
translation: It's a kind of wispy collection of words through which he can express the most trendy opinions. But blow a little on these ideas to test them, and they’ll burst.

original: My lord, his majesty commended him to you by young  Osric, who brings back to him that you attend him in the hall.
translation: My lord, His Majesty has learned from Osric that you will soon come to the main hall.

original: He sends to know if your pleasure hold to play  with Laertes, or that you will take longer time.
translation: The king would like to know if you would like to duel against Laertes now, or if you’d like a little more time.

original: I am constant to my purpose. They follow the king’s  pleasure. If his fitness speaks, mine is ready, now or  whensoever, provided I be so able as now.
translation: I’ll do as I said before: whatever the king wants. If he’s ready now, so am I. If he prefers some other time, I’ll do it then, so long as I’m able.

original: The king and queen and all are coming down.
translation: The king and queen are coming down with everyone else to watch.

original: In happy time.
translation: And right on time, too.

original: The queen desires you to use some gentle entertainment  to Laertes before you fall to play.
translation: The queen would like you to speak a few polite words to Laertes before the match begins.

original: She well instructs me.
translation: Her advice is good.

original: You will lose this wager, my lord.
translation: You’re going to lose this bet, my lord.

original: I do not think so. Since he went into France, I have  been in continual practice. I shall win at the odds. But thou wouldst not think how ill all’s here about my  heart. But it is no matter.
translation: I don’t think so. Since Laertes left, I’ve been practicing fencing constantly. With the odds they’ve given me, I’m going to win. But even so, I have a bad feeling in my heart. But forget about that.

original: Nay, good my lord—
translation: No, my lord—

original: It is but foolery, but it is such a kind of gain-giving as would perhaps trouble a woman.
translation: It’s just foolishness, but I have the kind of misgiving that might bother a woman.

original: If your mind dislike anything, obey it. I will  forestall their repair hither and say you are not fit.
translation: If your conscience is telling you not to do this, obey it. I’ll go and stop them and say you’re not feeling well.

original: Not a whit. We defy augury. There’s a special  providence in the fall of a sparrow.
translation: You will not. I ignore omens. God controls everything—even the death of a sparrow.

original: If it be now, ’tis  not to come. If it be not to come, it will be now. If it be not now, yet it will come—the readiness is all.
translation: If I am to die now, then it will not be later. If I am to die later, then it will not be now. All that matters is being ready for it when it does happen.

original: Since no man of aught he leaves knows, what is ’t to  leave betimes? Let be.
translation: Since no man knows about what he leaves behind when he dies, then what's it to him if he leaves early? Let it be.

original: Come, Hamlet, come, and take this hand from me.  [puts  LAERTES’ hand into HAMLET’s]
translation: Come, Hamlet, shake hands with Laertes.

original: Give me your pardon, sir. I’ve done you wrong.   But pardon ’t, as you are a gentleman.   This presence knows,   And you must needs have heard, how I am punished   With sore distraction.
translation: I ask your forgiveness, sir. I’ve done you wrong. Forgive me, as a gentleman. Everyone here knows—and you must have heard it too—that I’m suffering from insanity.

original: What I have done,   That might your nature, honor, and exception   Roughly awake, I here proclaim was madness.   Was ’t Hamlet wronged Laertes? Never Hamlet.
translation: What I did to insult your nature and your honor, I did only out of madness. Was it Hamlet who insulted Laertes? Not Hamlet.

original: If Hamlet from himself be ta’en away,   And when he’s not himself does wrong Laertes,   Then Hamlet does it not. Hamlet denies it.   Who does it, then? His madness.
translation: If Hamlet has had his mind stolen, and insults Laertes when he’s not himself, then it is not Hamlet who did it. Who did it, then? Hamlet’s madness.

original: If’t be so,   Hamlet is of the faction that is wronged.   His madness is poor Hamlet’s enemy.
translation: If that’s true, then it’s Hamlet who was the victim. His madness is his enemy.

original: Sir, in this audience,   Let my disclaiming from a purposed evil   Free me so far in your most generous thoughts   That I have shot mine arrow o’er the house   And hurt my brother.
translation: Sir, with this audience as my witness, let me declare that I intended no harm and am as innocent as a man who shoots an arrow over his house and accidentally hits his brother.

original: I am satisfied in nature,   Whose motive in this case should stir me most   To my revenge.
translation: My personal feelings are satisfied—even though what you’ve done should stir them to seek revenge.

original: But in my terms of honor   I stand aloof, and will no reconcilement   Till by some elder masters, of known honor,   I have a voice and precedent of peace   To keep my name ungored.
translation: Yet, as a man who values honor, I must for now hold off and will not accept an apology—until some experts in matters of honor show me that accepting your apology will not stain my reputation.

original: But till that time   I do receive your offered love like love   And will not wrong it.
translation: Until then, I accept the love you offer as love, and won't do anything to offend it.

original: I embrace it freely, And will this brother’s wager frankly play.— Give us the foils. Come on.
translation: I accept it gladly, and will engage in this friendly match without reservations. Come on, give me a sword.

original: Come, one for me.
translation: And one for me.

original: I’ll be your foil, Laertes. In mine ignorance Your skill shall, like a star i’ th’ darkest night, Stick fiery off indeed.
translation: I’m going to make you look good, Laertes. My lack of skill will make yours blaze like the brightest star in the darkest night.

original: You mock me, sir.
translation: You’re making fun of me, sir.

original: No, by this hand.
translation: No, I swear by my hand.

original: Give them the foils, young Osric.—Cousin Hamlet, You know the wager?
translation: Give them the swords, Osric. Hamlet, you know the bet?

original: Very well, my lord. Your grace hath laid the odds o’ th’ weaker side.
translation: Very well, my lord. You’ve placed your bet on the weaker side.

original: I do not fear it. I have seen you both. But since he is better we have therefore odds.
translation: I’m not worried. I’ve seen both of you fence. But since Laertes is better, we’ve given him a handicap.

original: This is too heavy. Let me see another.
translation: This sword’s too heavy. Give me another one.

original: This likes me well. These foils have  all a length?
translation: This one is good for me. Are they all the same length?

original: Ay, my good lord.
translation: Yes, my good lord.

original: Set me the stoups of wine upon that table.   If Hamlet give the first or second hit   Or quit in answer of the third exchange,   Let all the battlements their ordnance fire!
translation: Put the cups of wine on that table. If Hamlet gets the first or second hit, or even responds to Laertes challenge by just making the third hit, then we will fire the cannons in his honor!

original: The king shall drink to Hamlet’s better breath,   And in the cup an union shall he throw   Richer than that which four successive kings   In Denmark’s crown have worn.
translation: I’ll then drink to Hamlet’s health, and into his cup I’ll drop a pearl more valuable than those the last four Danish kings worn in their crowns.

original: Give me the cups.   And let the kettle to the trumpet speak,   The trumpet to the cannoneer without,   The cannons to the heavens, the heavens to earth,   “Now the king dunks to Hamlet.”
translation: Give me the cups. Play the drum to signal the trumpeter, so the trumpet will signal the cannons outside, and the cannons will signal the heavens,  and the heavens will echo the sound in order to tell all the world that the king now drinks to Hamlet’s health.

original: Come, begin.—   And you, the judges, bear a wary eye.
translation: Come on, begin. And you, judges, watch carefully.

original: Come on, sir.
translation: Come on, sir.

original: Come, my lord.
translation: Come on, my lord.

original: One.
translation: That was one hit.

original: No.
translation: No.

original: Judgment?
translation: Referee?

original: A hit, a very palpable hit.
translation: It was a hit, a clear hit.

original: Well, again.
translation: Well, another round.

original: Stay, give me drink.—Hamlet, this pearl is thine. Here’s to thy health.
translation: Give me some wine.

original: Give him the cup.
translation: Give him the cup.

original: I’ll play this bout first. Set it by a while. Come.
translation: I’ll finish this round first. Set the cup down for a while. Let’s go.

original: Another hit. What say you?
translation: Another hit. What do you say?

original: A touch, a touch, I do confess ’t.
translation: It was a small hit, a small hit, I admit it.

original: Our son shall win.
translation: My son will win.

original: He’s fat, and scant of breath.— Here, Hamlet, take my napkin, rub thy brows. The queen carouses to thy fortune, Hamlet.
translation: He’s fat and out of breath.

original: Good madam.
translation: Thank you, madam.

original: Gertrude, do not drink.
translation: Gertrude, don’t drink.

original: I will, my lord. I pray you, pardon me.
translation: I will drink, my lord. Please excuse me.

original: It is the poisoned cup. It is too late.
translation: That was the poisoned drink. It’s too late.

original: I dare not drink yet, madam. By and by.
translation: I can’t afford to drink now, madam. Soon.

original: Come, let me wipe thy face.
translation: Come on, let me wipe your face.

original: My lord, I’ll hit him now.
translation: I’ll hit him now.

original: I do not think ’t.
translation: I doubt it.

original: And yet it is almost ‘gainst my conscience.
translation: And yet, it almost makes me feel guilty.

original: Come, for the third, Laertes. You do but dally. I pray you, pass with your best violence. I am afeard you make a wanton of me.
translation: Come for the third round, Laertes. You’re just playing. Come on, try your hardest. I fear that you’re treating me like a spoiled child.

original: Say you so? Come on.
translation: You believe so? Come on.

original: Nothing, neither way.
translation: There’s little difference between them.

original: Have at you now!
translation: Take this!

original: Part them! They are incensed.
translation: Separate them. They’re too angry.

original: Nay, come, again.
translation: No, come on, again.

original: Look to the queen there, ho!
translation: Hey! Take care of the queen!

original: They bleed on both sides.—How is it, my lord?
translation: Both fencers are bleeding.

original: How is ’t, Laertes?
translation: How are you, Laertes?

original: Why, as a woodcock to mine own springe, Osric. I am  justly killed with mine own treachery.
translation: Why, I'm like a bird caught in my own trap, Osric.  I’ve been killed by my own betrayal, as I deserve.

original: How does the queen?
translation: How is the queen doing?

original: She swoons to see them bleed.
translation: She fainted at the sight of them bleeding.

original: No, no, the drink, the drink!—O my dear Hamlet! The drink, the drink! I am poisoned.
translation: No, no! The drink, the drink! Oh, my dear Hamlet! The drink, the drink! I’ve been poisoned.

original: O villainy! Ho, let the door be locked.
translation: Oh, what evil! Hey, lock the door!

original: Treachery! Seek it out.
translation: We’ve been betrayed! Find the traitor.

original: It is here, Hamlet. Hamlet, thou art slain.   No medicine in the world can do thee good.   In thee there is not half an hour of life.
translation: It’s me, Hamlet. Hamlet, you’re dead. No medicine in the world can cure you. You don’t have more than a half hour left to live.

original: The treacherous instrument is in thy hand,   Unbated and envenomed. The foul practice   Hath turned itself on me.
translation: The treacherous weapon is in your hand, sharpened and dipped in poison. The dirty plan backfired on me.

original: Lo, here I lie,   Never to rise again. Thy mother’s poisoned.   I can no more. The king, the king’s to blame.
translation: And so, here I lie, never to rise again. Your mother’s been poisoned. I can’t say anymore. The king, the king’s to blame.

original: The point envenomed too!—Then, venom, to thy work.
translation: The sword is poisoned! Then, poison, do your job!

original: Treason! Treason!
translation: Treason! Treason!

original: O, yet defend me, friends. I am but hurt.
translation: Oh, defend me, my friends. I’ve only been hurt.

original: Here, thou incestuous, murderous, damnèd Dane, Drink off this potion. Is thy union here? Follow my mother.
translation: Here, you incestuous, murderous, damned Dane! Drink this poisoned wine. Is your pearl in there? Follow my mother.

original: He is justly served.   It is a poison tempered by himself.
translation: He got what he deserved. He made that poison himself.

original: Exchange forgiveness with me, noble Hamlet.
translation: Forgive me as I forgive you, noble Hamlet.

original: Mine and my father’s death come not upon thee,   Nor thine on me.
translation: My death and my father’s death are not your fault, and my death is not yours.

original: Heaven make thee free of it. I follow thee.—
translation: God frees you from blame. I’ll follow you.

original: Never believe it. I am more an antique Roman than a Dane. Here’s yet some liquor left.
translation: Don’t believe it. I’m more like an ancient Roman than a Dane. There’s still some of this wine.

original: As thou’rt a man,   Give me the cup. Let go! By heaven, I’ll have ’t.
translation: On your manhood, give me that cup. Let it go! By heaven, give it to me.

original: O God, Horatio, what a wounded name,   Things standing thus unknown, shall live behind me!
translation: Oh God, Horatio, what a bad reputation I’m leaving behind—because no one knows what happened.

original: If thou didst ever hold me in thy heart   Absent thee from felicity a while,   And in this harsh world draw thy breath in pain   To tell my story.
translation: If you ever loved me, then avoid the sweet relief of death for a while, and stay in this harsh world long enough to draw painful breaths and tell my story.

original: What warlike noise is this?
translation: What are these sounds of war?

original: Young Fortinbras, with conquest come from Poland, To th’ ambassadors of England gives This warlike volley.
translation: Young Fortinbras returns triumphantly from Poland, and fires his cannons to greet the English ambassadors.

original: O, I die, Horatio.   The potent poison quite o’ercrows my spirit.
translation: Oh, I’m dying, Horatio! This powerful poison is too much for me.

original: I cannot live to hear the news from England.   But I do prophesy the election lights   On Fortinbras. He has my dying voice.
translation: I won’t live to hear the news from England. But I predict that Fortinbras will win the election for the Danish crown. I give him my dying vote.

original: So tell him, with th’ occurrents, more and less,   Which have solicited. The rest is silence.   O, O, O, O.
translation: So tell him what has happened here. The rest is silence. Oh, oh, oh, oh.

original: Now cracks a noble heart.—Good night, sweet prince, And flights of angels sing thee to thy rest!— Why does the drum come hither?
