translation: Now a noble heart breaks. Good night, sweet prince. May hosts of angels sing you to your sleep. Why are those drums coming near?

original: Where is this sight?
translation: What am I seeing?

original: What is it ye would see? If aught of woe or wonder, cease your search.
translation: What would you like to see? If it’s a tragedy or other astonishment, you’ve found it.

original: This quarry cries on havoc.
translation: These corpses suggest a massacre.

original: O proud death,   What feast is toward in thine eternal cell,   That thou so many princes at a shot   So bloodily hast struck?
translation: Oh, proud Death, what banquet are you preparing that you’ve struck down so many princes at once?

original: The sight is dismal,   And our affairs from England come too late.
translation: This is an awful sight. Our news arrives from England too late.

original: The ears are senseless that should give us hearing,   To tell him his commandment is fulfilled,   That Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead.
translation: The people who were meant to hear it are all dead. We came to tell the king his orders have been followed: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead.

original: Where should we have our thanks?
translation: Who will thank us now?

original: Not from his mouth,   Had it th’ ability of life to thank you.   He never gave commandment for their death.
translation: Not him, even if he were still alive to thank you.  He never ordered their deaths.

original: But since so jump upon this bloody question,   You from the Polack wars, and you from England,   Are here arrived, give order that these bodies   High on a stage be placèd to the view,   And let me speak to th’ yet-unknowing world   How these things came about.
translation: But since you’ve arrived to see this bloody scene—you from the war in Poland and you from England—then order that these bodies be displayed on a high platform to be viewed, and let me tell the world how all this happened.

original: So shall you hear   Of carnal, bloody, and unnatural acts,   Of accidental judgments, casual slaughters,   Of deaths put on by cunning and forced cause,
translation: You’ll hear of violent, bloody, and unnatural acts; accidental revenge; casual murders; deaths caused by trickery and by threat;

original: And, in this upshot, purposes mistook   Fall’n on th’ inventors’ heads. All this can I   Truly deliver.
translation: and plans that backfired on their inventors. All this I will tell you truthfully.

original: Let us haste to hear it,   And call the noblest to the audience.
translation: Let us hurry to listen to it now, and call in all the noblemen as audience.

original: For me, with sorrow I embrace my fortune.   I have some rights of memory in this kingdom,   Which now to claim my vantage doth invite me.
translation: As for me, I accept my good fortune with sadness. I have some rights to claim the throne of this kingdom, and now I have the chance to make that claim.

original: Of that I shall have also cause to speak,   And from his mouth whose voice will draw on more.
translation: I also have much to say about that, from the mouth of one who only added to your claim.

original: But let this same be presently performed,   Even while men’s minds are wild, lest more mischance   On plots and errors happen.
translation: Let’s do this now, even though everyone’s minds are racing, to make sure no further mistakes, plots, or errors occur.

original: Let four captains   Bear Hamlet like a soldier to the stage,   For he was likely, had he been put on,   To have proved most royally.
translation: Let four captains carry Hamlet like a soldier to the viewing platform. If he only had the chance, it’s likely he would have been a great king.

original: And, for his passage,   The soldiers’ music and the rites of war   Speak loudly for him.   Take up the bodies.
translation: Military music and military rites shall proclaim his greatness. Lift up the bodies.

original: Such a sight as this   Becomes the field, but here shows much amiss.   Go, bid the soldiers shoot.
translation: A sight like this looks right on a battlefield, but here shows that much has gone wrong. Go, tell the soldiers to fire their cannons.

original: So shaken as we are, so wan with care,   Find we a time for frighted peace to pant   And breathe short-winded accents of new broils   To be commenced in strands afar remote.
translation: Even though we are shaken up and weak, we should try to find time in this moment of peace to catch our breath, and as we do this we can decide about where in the world to fight next .

original: No more the thirsty entrance of this soil   Shall daub her lips with her own children’s blood.   Nor more shall trenching war channel her fields,   Nor bruise her flow’rets with the armed hoofs   Of hostile paces.
translation: England's soil will no longer be wet with our own soldiers' blood; her fields will no longer be ruined by the invasions of war; and her flowers will no longer be crushed by the hooves of the warhorses.

original: Those opposèd eyes,   Which, like the meteors of a troubled heaven,   All of one nature, of one substance bred,   Did lately meet in the intestine shock   And furious close of civil butchery   Shall now, in mutual well-beseeming ranks,   March all one way and be no more opposed   Against acquaintance, kindred, and allies.   The edge of war, like an ill-sheathèd knife,   No more shall cut his master.
translation: The two sides of this war—made up of men from the same countries, the same families even—are as similar to each other as shooting stars in the sky. Yet, even though these men have just fought against each other in a civil war and came close to destroying each other, they will now march together in a focused and orderly formation.  They will no longer stand against their friends and family. The violence of war, like a knife which has not been properly covered, will not hurt us any longer.

original: Therefore, friends,   As far as to the sepulcher of Christ—   Whose soldier now, under whose blessed cross   We are impressèd and engaged to fight—   Forthwith a power of English shall we levy,   Whose arms were molded in their mothers' womb   To chase these pagans in those holy fields   Over whose acres walked those blessèd feet   Which fourteen hundred years ago were nailed   For our advantage on the bitter cross.
translation: Therefore friends, an English army will march as far as the  Holy Land,   as soldiers of Christ, recruited and committed to fighting for what Jesus did for us on that cross. Our soldiers were born to remove atheists from the holy fields that Jesus walked on—as the feet which touched this sacred ground were nailed to the cross fourteen hundred years ago to redeem us of our sins.

original: But this our purpose now is twelve month old,   And bootless ’tis to tell you we will go.   Therefor we meet not now.
translation: But we have been planning this trip for a year, and it is useless to tell you we are going as you already know—but that's not why we've met.

original: Then let me hear   Of you, my gentle cousin Westmoreland,   What yesternight our council did decree   In forwarding this dear expedience.
translation: Tell me now, my  noble   cousin  Westmoreland: what did the Council decide last night about this vital expedition?

original: My liege, this haste was hot in question,   And many limits of the charge set down
translation: My lord, this speedy mission was being eagerly debated, and many of the resources and duties had already been decided.

original: But yesternight: when all athwart there came   A post from Wales loaden with heavy news,   Whose worst was that the noble Mortimer,   Leading the men of Herefordshire to fight   Against the irregular and wild Glendower,   Was by the rude hands of that Welshman taken,
translation: But, yesterday evening, a messenger suddenly arrived from Wales to report some sad news. He came to tell us that the noble  Mortimer , who had been taking an army from Herefordshire to fight against the wild  Glendower , was captured by him instead .

original: A thousand of his people butcherèd,   Upon whose dead corpse there was such misuse,   Such beastly shameless transformation   By those Welshwomen done, as may not be   Without much shame retold or spoken of.
translation: A thousand men were murdered, and their corpses were violated by the Welshwomen so badly that I don't even want to repeat what I was told.

original: It seems then that the tidings of this broil Brake off our business for the Holy Land.
translation: I guess that the news of this attack will stop our mission to the Holy Land.

original: This matched with other did, my gracious lord.   For more uneven and unwelcome news   Came from the north and thus it did import:
translation: Y es, my gracious lord, along with this.  We have received even more horrible and unwelcome news from the north, which is this :

original: On Holy-rood Day, the gallant Hotspur there,   Young Harry Percy, and brave Archibald,   That ever valiant and approvèd Scot,   At Holmedon met, where they did spend   A sad and bloody hour—   As by discharge of their artillery
translation: On   September 14th  young Harry Percy, known as the bold "Hotspur," fought against the brave  Archibald , that fearless   Scotsman proven in battle, at  Holmedon . They fought against each other for an hour and it was awfully bloody, if the sound of the gunfire was any indication .

original: And shape of likelihood the news was told;   For he that brought them, in the very heat   And pride of their contention did take horse,   Uncertain of the issue any way.
translation: Yet, the messenger who brought the news left in the midst of the battle, and so could only predict what had happened.  He didn't actually know the final outcome.

original: Here is a dear, a true-industrious friend,   Sir Walter Blunt, new lighted from his horse.   Stained with the variation of each soil   Betwixt that Holmedon and this seat of ours,   And he hath brought us smooth and welcome news.
translation: One of my dear, hardworking friends Sir Walter Blunt has only recently dismounted from his horse and arrived here in court. He has ridden across all of the ground from Holmedon to here to bring us happy and welcome news.

original: The Earl of Douglas is discomfited;   Ten thousand bold Scots, two-and-twenty knights,   Balked in their own blood, did Sir Walter see   On Holmedon’s plains   .
translation: The Earl of Douglas has been defeated and he saw ten thousand Scottish soldiers and twenty-two knights piled up in their own blood on the fields of Holmedon .

original: Of prisoners Hotspur took   Mordake, Earl of Fife, and eldest son   To beaten Douglas, and the Earl of Atholl,   Of Murray, Angus, and Menteith.   And is not this an honorable spoil?   A gallant prize? Ha, cousin, is it not?
translation: Hotspur took some prisoners: he took Mordake, the Earl of Fife and the son of the defeated Earl of Douglas. And he also took the Earls of  Antholl ,  Murray ,  Angus , and  Menteith . Isn't this an honorable bunch? A great prize? Isn't it, cousin?

original: In faith, it is a conquest for a prince to boast of.
translation: Certainly, it's the type of conquest that even a prince could boast about.

original: Yea, there thou mak’st me sad, and mak’st me sin   In envy that my Lord Northumberland   Should be the father to so blest a son,
translation: Don't say that—it makes me feel sad! And it is a sin every time I feel jealous of Lord  Northumberland  for having such an incredible son .

original: A son who is the theme of Honor’s tongue,   Amongst a grove the very straightest plant,   Who is sweet Fortune’s minion and her pride;   Whilst I, by looking on the praise of him,   See riot and dishonor stain the brow   Of my young Harry.
translation: His son is the topic of conversation when Honor speaks. Hotspur is the straightest plant in the whole forest; he is the favorite of sweet Fortune. When I see how he is praised, I also see the wildness and dishonor which ruins the reputation of my own son, Harry.

original: O, that it could be proved   That some night-tripping fairy had exchanged   In cradle-clothes our children where they lay,   And called mine “Percy,” his “Plantagenet”!   Then would I have his Harry, and he mine.
translation: If only I could prove that some fairy had switched them in their cradles when they were babies! Then the Percy family would have had Harry, and we  Plantagenets  would have gotten Hotspur !

original: But let him from my thoughts. What think you, coz,   Of this young Percy’s pride? The prisoners,   Which he in this adventure hath surprised   To his own use he keeps, and sends me word   I shall have none but Mordake, Earl of Fife.
translation: Anyway, I must stop thinking about Harry now. Westmoreland, what do you think about this young Hotspur and his pride? He has said that he is going to keep all of the prisoners that he captured himself, and  tells me that I can only have Mordake, the Earl of Fife .

original: This is his uncle’s teaching.
translation: It's his uncle who's told him to do that.

original: This is Worcester,   Malevolent to you in all aspects,
translation: This is Worcester through and through,  a man who will always act against you .

original: Which makes him prune himself, and bristle up   The crest of youth against your dignity.
translation: Now he has made Hotspur act like this, putting his youth against your dignity and age.

original: But I have sent for him to answer this.   And for this cause awhile we must neglect   Our holy purpose to Jerusalem.
translation: Well, I have asked him to come here to answer for that. Therefore, we are going to have to put our mission to the Holy Land on hold for a while.

original: Cousin, on Wednesday next our council we   Will hold at Windsor. So inform the lords.
translation: Next Wednesday, we will have a meeting at Windsor. Go and tell the other lords,

original: But come yourself with speed to us again,   For more is to be said and to be done   Than out of anger can be utterèd.
translation: and then come back here as quickly as possible, as we have more to discuss and more to do.  But it will have to wait until I am less angry.

original: I will, my liege.
translation: I will do that, my lord.

original: Now, Hal, what time of day is it, lad?
translation: Now, Hal, what time is it, boy?

original: Thou art so fat-witted with drinking of old sack, and  unbuttoning thee after supper, and sleeping upon benches after noon, that thou hast forgotten to demand that  truly which thou wouldst truly know.
translation: You are so  stupid , what with all the  wine  you drink—and how you unbutton your pants after dinner and pass out on benches until after noon. You can't even remember to ask for the thing you actually want to know!

original: What a devil hast  thou to do with the time of the day?
translation: Why in the devil's name do you care what time of day it is?

original: Unless hours were  cups of sack, and minutes capons, and clocks the tongues of bawds, and dials the signs of leaping-houses, and  the blessed sun himself a fair hot wench in  flame-colored taffeta, I see no reason why thou shouldst be so superfluous to demand the time of the day.
translation: Unless hours were cups of wine, minutes were chickens, clocks were the tongues of prostitutes, sundials the signs of whorehouses, and the sun itself a hot woman in a red  silk dress , I don't know why on earth you would need to know the time.

original: Indeed, you come near me now, Hal,
translation: Oh, now you've got me, Hal.

original: or we that take  purses go by the moon and the seven stars, and not by  Phoebus, he, that wand'ring knight so fair.
translation: For we are both thieves of the night, living under the moon and the stars, not under the  beautiful sun .

original: And I  prithee, sweet wag, when thou art king, as God save thy  Grace—Majesty, I should say, for grace thou wilt have  none—
translation: I ask you, my sweet boy, when you are king, God help  your Grace —or rather I should call you "your Majesty," because you have no  grace .

original: What, none?
translation: What? None?

original: No, by my troth, not so much as will serve to be  prologue to an egg and butter.
Well, how then? Come, roundly, roundly.
translation: What do you mean then? Come on, what's your point?

original: Marry, then, sweet wag, when thou art king, let not us  that are squires of the night’s body be called thieves  of the day’s beauty.
translation: Well then , my sweet boy, when you are king, don't let us night-owls be accused of wasting the daylight by sleeping.

original: Let us be Diana’s foresters,  gentlemen of the shade, minions of the moon,
translation: Let us be thought of as followers of  Diana , gentlemen of darkness, servants of the moon.

original: and let men say we be men of good government, being governed, as  the sea is, by our noble and chaste mistress the moon,  under whose countenance we steal.
translation: Let men say that we are well behaved, since we are governed by the same noble and innocent mistress—the moon—who controls the tides and under whose light we can sneak around.

original: Thou sayest well, and it holds well too, for the  fortune of us that are the moon’s men doth ebb and flow  like the sea, being governed, as the sea is, by the  moon.
translation: You speak the truth, and it is a suitable analogy.  For our fortunes come and go just like the tides do, which makes sense, since we are both governed by the moon.

original: As for proof now: a purse of gold most resolutely  snatched on Monday night and most dissolutely spent on  Tuesday morning, got with swearing “Lay by” and spent  with crying “Bring in”;
translation: I can prove it: think of a purse full of gold that has been excellently stolen on a Monday night, and then its contents stupidly spent on a Tuesday morning. When you steal it, you cry, "Give it over," and you spend it crying, "Bring it on."

original: now in as low an ebb as the foot of the ladder, and by and by in as high a flow as the  ridge of the gallows.
translation: At one moment it feels like our fortunes are as low as the foot of the ladder to the gallows, and the next they are as high as the crossbar at the top of them.

original: By the Lord, thou sayest true, lad. And is not my  hostess of the tavern a most sweet wench?
translation: By God, you're right, Hal. Say, isn't the hostess of this bar a very attractive woman?

original: As the honey of Hybla, my old lad of the castle. And is not a buff jerkin a most sweet robe of durance?
How now, how now, mad wag? What, in thy quips and thy  quiddities? What a plague have I to do with a buff  jerkin?
translation: What do you mean, you crazy boy? Are you joking around with me? What on earth do I have to do with a sheriff's jacket?

original: Why, what a pox have I to do with my hostess of the  tavern?
translation: Well, what on earth do I have to do with the hostess of this bar?

original: Well, thou hast called her to a reckoning many a time  and oft.
Did I ever call for thee to pay thy part?
translation: Have I ever asked you to pay for anything yourself?

original: No, I’ll give thee thy due. Thou hast paid all there.
translation: No, I guess that's true. You have always settled everything with her yourself.

original: Yea, and elsewhere, so far as my coin would stretch,  and where it would not, I have used my credit.
translation: Yes, and with other hostesses, when I had the money to pay them. And when I didn't, I just used my credit.

original: Yea, and so used it that were it not here apparent that thou art heir apparent—
translation: Yes, and you've used your credit so much that if it wasn't  "here apparent" that you are the "heir apparent," , you would have never gotten away with it.

original: But I prithee, sweet wag, shall  there be gallows standing in England when thou art king?
translation: But I was wondering, my sweet boy, will there still be hangings in England when you're king?

original: And resolution thus fubbed as it is with the rusty curb of old father Antic the law?
translation: Will a determined thief still be cheated by that horrible, old clown—the law?

original: Do not thou, when thou art king, hang a thief.
translation: When you're king, don't hang thieves.

original: No, thou shalt.
translation: No, you will.

original: Shall I? O rare! By the Lord, I’ll be a brave judge.
translation: I will? Oh wonderful! I will be an excellent judge.

original: Thou judgest false already: I mean thou shalt have the  hanging of the thieves, and so become a rare hangman.
translation: You've already judged what I said in the wrong way. I mean that you will be responsible for hanging thieves, so you will become a wonderful hangman!

original: Well, Hal, well, and in some sort it jumps with my  humor as well as waiting in the court, I can tell you.
translation: Well, Hal, in some ways I am more inclined to be a hangman than to wait around for favors from the king, I can tell you that.

original: For obtaining of suits?
Yea, for obtaining of suits, whereof the hangman hath  no lean wardrobe. 'Sblood, I am as melancholy as a gib  cat or a lugged bear.
Or an old lion, or a lover’s lute.
translation: Or an old lion, or a lover's lute.

original: Yea, or the drone of a Lincolnshire bagpipe.
translation: Yes, or the whining sound of a bagpipe.

original: What sayest thou to a hare, or the melancholy of Moorditch?
Thou hast the most unsavory similes, and art indeed the most comparative, rascaliest, sweet young prince.
translation: You use the most unpleasant similes, and make incredible comparisons for such a naughty, sweet young prince.

original: But,  Hal, I prithee trouble me no more with vanity.
translation: But, Hal, let's not talk about such pointless things anymore.

original: I would  to God thou and I knew where a commodity of good names  were to be bought.
translation: I wish to God that you or I knew where we could buy a supply of good reputations.

original: An old lord of the council rated me  the other day in the street about you, sir,   but I marked him not, and yet he talked very wisely,
translation: Some old lord from the Council came up to me in the street the other day to give me his judgement about you, sir.  But I didn't listen to him, even though he said some very wise things.

original: but I regarded  him not, and yet he talked wisely, and in the street,  too.
translation: I didn't take any notice of him, although his words were certainly wise, and this was just in the middle of the street.

original: Thou didst well, for wisdom cries out in the streets  and no man regards it.
translation: You did well, for the Bible says, "Wisdom cries out in the streets, and no-one hears it."

original: O, thou hast damnable iteration, and art indeed able to corrupt a saint.
translation: Oh, you always seem to make the Bible fit in with your wicked games.  I wouldn't be surprised if you managed to corrupt a saint.

original: Thou hast done much harm upon me, Hal, God forgive thee for it. Before I knew thee, Hal, I  knew nothing, and now am I, if a man should speak truly, little better than one of the wicked.
translation: You have done many bad things to me, Hal. I hope God can forgive you for it. Before I met you, Hal, I knew nothing of wickedness, and now I'm basically a sinner myself, if I'm telling the truth.

original: I must give over  this life, and I will give it over. By the Lord, an I do not, I am a villain. I’ll be damned for never a king’s  son in Christendom.
translation: I need to turn my life around, and I will turn it around. By the Lord, if I don't, then I am a true villain. I refuse to be condemned to hell, even for the son of a Christian king.

original: Where shall we take a purse tomorrow, Jack?
translation: Where shall we go and do some stealing tomorrow, Jack?

original: Zounds, where thou wilt, lad. I’ll make one. An I do  not, call me villain and baffle me.
I see a good amendment of life in thee, from praying to purse-taking.
translation: I'm already seeing you turn your life around, from praying to stealing purses.

original: Why, Hal, ’tis my vocation, Hal. 'Tis no sin for a man  to labor in his vocation.
translation: Why, Hal, it's my calling in life. It's not a sin for a man to follow his calling in life.

original: Good morrow, Ned.
translation: Good morning, Ned.

original: Good morrow, sweet Hal.—What says Monsieur Remorse?  What says Sir John Sack-and-Sugar? Jack, how agrees the  devil and thee about thy soul that thou soldest him on  Good Friday last for a cup of Madeira and a cold capon’s leg?
Sir John stands to his word. The devil shall have his  bargain, for he was never yet a breaker of proverbs. He  will give the devil his due.
translation: Sir John Falstaff will keep his word. The devil will get his end of the bargain, for Jack was never one to break with a proverb. He will give the devil what he owes him.

original: Then art thou damned for keeping thy word with the devil.
translation: Then you're damned for keeping a deal with the devil.

original: Else he had been damned for cozening the devil.
translation: Otherwise he would be damned for cheating the devil.

original: But, my lads, my lads, tomorrow morning, by four  o'clock, early at Gad’s Hill, there are pilgrims going  to Canterbury with rich offerings, and traders riding to London with fat purses.
translation: Anyway boys, boys! Early tomorrow morning, around four o'clock, some travelers are going to pass by  Gad's Hill.  Some of them are on their way to  Canterbury Cathedral with rich offerings , and some are traders who are on their way to London with a lot of money in their purses.

original: I have vizards for you all. You have horses for yourselves.   Gadshill lies tonight in  Rochester. I have bespoke supper tomorrow night in  Eastcheap.
translation: I have masks for all of you. You have your own horses.  Gadshill himself will spend the night in Rochester, and I have already ordered dinner for tomorrow night in  Eastcheap .

original: We may do it as secure as sleep.   If you will  go, I will stuff your purses full of crowns. If you will not, tarry at home and be hanged.
translation: This plan is so certain it could be done in our sleep. If you will do it, I'll give you riches. If you won't, then stay at home and hang yourselves instead.

original: Hear ye, Yedward, if I tarry at home and go not, I’ll  hang you for going.
You will, chops?
translation: You will, fat cheeks?

original: Hal, wilt thou make one?
translation: Hal, will you join us?

original: Who, I rob? I a thief? not I, by my faith.
translation: What me, a robber? Am I a thief? I don't think so, by God.

original: There’s neither honesty, manhood, nor good fellowship  in thee, nor thou cam’st not of the blood royal, if thou darest not stand for ten shillings.
translation: If you won't even fight for ten shillings, then there is no honesty, manhood, or friendship in you, and you certainly aren't of royal descent.

original: Well then, once in my days I’ll be a madcap.
translation: Okay then, for once in my life I'll do something insane.

original: Why, that’s well said.
translation: Good stuff.

original: Well, come what will, I’ll tarry at home.
translation: Well, actually, I guess I'll stay at home and see what happens.

original: By the Lord, I’ll be a traitor then when thou art king.
translation: In that case, by God, I'll be a traitor to you when you become king.

original: I care not.
translation: I don't care.

original: Sir John, I prithee, leave the Prince and me alone. I  will lay him down such reasons for this adventure that  he shall go.
translation: Sir John, please leave me and the Prince alone for a while. I'll give him such good reasons for joining in that he won't be able to resist.

original: Well, God give thee the spirit of persuasion, and him  the ears of profiting,
translation: Well, then I hope that God gives you the powers of persuasion, and him the power to listen.

original: that what thou speakest may move, and what he hears may be believed,
translation: I hope that the words you speak will affect him and he will believe what you tell him.

original: that the true prince may, for recreation sake, prove a false thief, for the  poor abuses of the time want countenance.
translation: That way, the honest prince might become a  false thief  just for fun, since today's wickedness needs a patron.

original: Farewell. You  shall find me in Eastcheap.
translation: Goodbye then. You can find me in Eastcheap.

original: Farewell, thou latter spring. Farewell, All-hallown  summer.
Now, my good sweet honey lord, ride with us tomorrow. I have a jest to execute that I cannot manage alone.
translation: Now, my good sweet lord, join us tomorrow. I have a prank that I want to carry out that I can't do alone.

original: Falstaff, Peto, Bardolph, and Gadshill shall rob those  men that we have already waylaid. Yourself and I will  not be there.
translation: Falstaff, Peto, Bardolph, and Gadshill are going to rob those men that I had mentioned, but you and I won't be there.

original: And when they have the booty, if you and I do not rob them, cut this head off from my shoulders.
translation: When they have the plunder, we will rob them ourselves!  If we don't, then you might as well chop off my head!

original: How shall we part with them in setting forth?
translation: How will we get away from them when we are traveling together?

original: Why, we will set forth before or after them, and  appoint them a place of meeting,
translation: Well, we will leave either before them or after them, and arrange a place to meet.

original: wherein it is at our  pleasure to fail; and then will they adventure upon the  exploit themselves,
translation: When we don't show up, they will have to carry out the robbery themselves,

original: which they shall have no sooner  achieved but we’ll set upon them.
translation: and as soon as they've done that, we'll attack them.

original: Yea, but ’tis like that they will know us by our  horses, by our habits, and by every other appointment to be ourselves.
translation: Okay, but won't they still recognize us by our horses, our clothes, and all of the things that we have with us?

original: Tut, our horses they shall not see; I’ll tie them in  the wood. Our vizards we will change after we leave  them. And, sirrah, I have cases of buckram for the  nonce, to immask our noted outward garments.
Yea, but I doubt they will be too hard for us.
translation: Okay. But I'm afraid it will be too difficult for us to beat them.

original: Well, for two of them, I know them to be as true-bred  cowards as ever turned back;
translation: Well, I'm certain that two of them are complete cowards and will run away.

original: and for the third, if he  fight longer than he sees reason, I’ll forswear arms.
translation: As for the third, if he fights for even a second longer than he sees fit, I will give up fighting forever.

original: The virtue of this jest will be the incomprehensible lies that this same fat rogue will tell us when we meet at  supper:
translation: The hilarity of this practical joke will come from the ridiculous lies that this same, fat idiot Falstaff will tell us when we meet them at dinner.

original: how thirty at least he fought with, what wards,  what blows, what extremities he endured; and in the  reproof of this lies the jest.
translation: I am sure he will pretend that he fought with at least thirty men, and tell us how he bravely defended himself, how he hit them, and received many injuries. And when we prove that he's lying, that will be funniest part.

original: Well, I’ll go with thee. Provide us all things  necessary and meet me tomorrow night in Eastcheap. There I’ll sup. Farewell.
translation: Okay, I'll go with you. Get all of the things that we'll need and meet me tomorrow night in Eastcheap. I'll have dinner there. Goodbye.

original: Farewell, my lord.
translation: Goodbye, my lord.

original: I know you all, and will awhile uphold   The unyoked humor of your idleness.
translation: I understand these men, and will put up with their wild behavior and their laziness for now.

original: Yet herein will I imitate the sun,   Who doth permit the base contagious clouds   To smother up his beauty from the world,   That, when he please again to be himself,   Being wanted, he may be more wondered at   By breaking through the foul and ugly mists   Of vapors that did seem to strangle him.
translation: In this way, I will be like the  sun , which allows the vile, infectious clouds to cover up his beauty from the rest of the world. But then, when he decides that he has been missed enough, he can amaze the world by breaking through the disgusting, ugly mists and vapors that were almost strangling him.

original: If all the year were playing holidays,   To sport would be as tedious as to work,   But when they seldom come, they wished for come,   And nothing pleaseth but rare accidents.
translation: If the entire year was a vacation, then playing would become as boring as working. Because they are so rare, we look forward to vacations, and enjoy them as unusual occurrences.

original: So when this loose behavior I throw off   And pay the debt I never promisèd,   By how much better than my word I am,   By so much shall I falsify men’s hopes;
translation: So when I leave behind this wild behavior and accept that it is my duty to become king—even though I never asked for it—I will be better than people think I will be. I will prove people wrong.

original: And, like bright metal on a sullen ground,   My reformation, glitt'ring o'er my fault,   Shall show more goodly and attract more eyes   Than that which hath no foil to set it off.
translation: J ust like a bright piece of metal, put against a dull background, my transformation will be even more remarkable because of the contrast with my past self.

original: I’ll so offend to make offense a skill,   Redeeming time when men think least I will.
translation: I will use my misbehavior for my own advantage, making up for lost time when people least expect it.

original: My blood hath been too cold and temperate,   Unapt to stir at these indignities,
translation: I have been too cold and moderate, and I haven't reacted to these shameful deeds like I should have.

original: And you have found me, for accordingly   You tread upon my patience.
translation: You have noticed this, and you have abused my patience.

original: But be sure   I will from henceforth rather be myself,   Mighty and to be feared,
translation: But know this: from now on I will act like a king again, powerful and feared.

original: than my condition,   Which hath been smooth as oil, soft as young down,   And therefore lost that title of respect   Which the proud soul ne'er pays but to the proud.
translation: I will not allow my natural characteristics, which are soft and light, to lose me the respect which powerful people will only give to other powerful people.

original: Our house, my sovereign liege, little deserves   The scourge of greatness to be used on it,
translation: Your Majesty, our family—the Percy family—doesn't deserve to be punished by you and your power,

original: And that same greatness too which our own hands   Have holp to make so portly.
translation: as we helped you to get to this position of power in the first place.

original: My lord—
translation: My lord—

original: Worcester, get thee gone; for I do see   Danger and disobedience in thine eye.
translation: Worcester, leave now, for I can see danger and disobedience in your eye.

original: O sir, your presence is too bold and peremptory,   And majesty might never yet endure   The moody frontier of a servant brow.
translation: Oh sir, you speak far too boldly and arrogantly, and royalty should never have to be worried about a servant's threatening frown.

original: You have good leave to leave us. When we need   Your use and counsel, we shall send for you.
translation: You have full permission to leave us. When we need your help and advice, we will send for you.

original: You were about to speak.
translation: You were about to speak.

original: Yea, my good lord.   Those prisoners in your Highness' name demanded,   Which Harry Percy here at Holmedon took,   Were, as he says, not with such strength denied   As is delivered to your Majesty:
translation: Yes, my good lord.  The prisoners that you asked for, which Harry Percy captured at Holmedon, were not kept away from you out of spite, as has been reported to you.

original: Either envy, therefore, or misprison   Is guilty of this fault, and not my son.
translation: Whoever told you this has just done it because they are jealous, or because there's been a misunderstanding. My son's done nothing wrong.

original: My liege, I did deny no prisoners.
translation: My lord, I didn't deny you any prisoners.

original: But I remember, when the fight was done,   When I was dry with rage and extreme toil,   Breathless and faint, leaning upon my sword,   Came there a certain lord, neat, and trimly dressed,   Fresh as a bridegroom, and his chin new reaped   Showed like a stubble land at harvest home.   He was perfumèd like a milliner,
translation: But I do remember that just after the battle, when I was parched with thirst after fighting, when I was breathless, faint, and resting on my sword, a certain lord arrived. He was refined and elegantly dressed—bright like a bridegroom—and his beard was freshly cut, like a field after a harvest. He smelled very fancy.

original: And ’twixt his finger and his thumb he held   A pouncet box, which ever and anon   He gave his nose and took ’t away again,   Who therewith angry, when it next came there,   Took it in snuff; and still he smiled and talked.
translation: And he held a perfume box in his hand, which every so often he lifted to his nose, sniffed, and moved the box away again. He kept doing this as he continued to smile and talk to me.

original: And as the soldiers bore dead bodies by,   He called them untaught knaves, unmannerly,   To bring a slovenly unhandsome corse   Betwixt the wind and his nobility.
translation: As the soldiers were carrying the dead bodies past us, he called them unsophisticated idiots, and rude for bringing an ugly, disgusting corpse where he could smell it.

original: With many holiday and lady terms   He questioned me; amongst the rest demanded   My prisoners in your Majesty’s behalf.
translation: He questioned me, with his fancy, ladylike language and told me that I had to give up the prisoners to your Majesty.

original: I then, all smarting with my wounds being cold,   To be so pestered with a popinjay,   Out of my grief and my impatience   Answered neglectingly I know not what—   He should, or he should not;
translation: At that point, I was so annoyed by my unattended wounds and being pestered by that parrot, that I can't even remember what I said to him in my pain and my impatience to get away. I don't know whether I told him whether or not he could have the prisoners.

original: for he made me mad   To see him shine so brisk and smell so sweet   And talk so like a waiting-gentlewoman   Of guns, and drums, and wounds—God save the mark!—
translation: His shiny face, sweet smell, and hearing him talk about guns, drums, and wounds with the voice of a lady-in-waiting made me so angry! For God's sake!

original: And telling me the sovereignest thing on earth   Was parmacety for an inward bruise,   And that it was great pity, so it was,   This villanous saltpeter should be digged   Out of the bowels of the harmless earth,   Which many a good tall fellow had destroyed   So cowardly, and but for these vile guns   He would himself have been a soldier.
translation: He told me that the best thing for a wound is  parmaceti  and that it was a pity the innocent earth had to be dug up in order to extract the key ingredient for  gunpowder . He said that this gunpowder has cowardly destroyed many good, valiant men, and if it wasn't for horrible guns, he would have been a soldier himself.

original: This bald unjointed chat of his, my lord,   I answered indirectly, as I said,   And I beseech you, let not his report   Come current for an accusation   Betwixt my love and your high Majesty.
translation: I answered this pointless, incoherent chatter casually, as I've already said. Please don't accept his report right away and let it ruin the relationship between me and you, your Majesty.

original: The circumstance considered, good my lord,   Whate'er Lord Harry Percy then had said   To such a person and in such a place,   At such a time, with all the rest retold,   May reasonably die
translation: Considering the circumstances, my lord, whatever Lord Harry Percy said to that man, at such a time and place, should be allowed to be forgotten.

original: and never rise   To do him wrong or any way impeach   What then he said, so he unsay it now.
translation: It should never be used against him, and he should never be blamed for it, as long as he takes it all back now.

original: Why, yet he doth deny his prisoners,   But with proviso and exception   That we at our own charge shall ransom straight   His brother-in-law, the foolish Mortimer,
translation: But he is still refusing to give us the prisoners unless we agree to his terms and conditions. He says that we must pay for the ransom of his foolish  brother-in-law , Mortimer,

original: Who, on my soul, hath willfully betrayed   The lives of those that he did lead to fight   Against that great magician, damned Glendower,   Whose daughter, as we hear, the Earl of March   Hath lately married.
translation: even though Mortimer willingly betrayed the soldiers that he took to fight that great  magician , the cursed Glendower. We have even heard that Mortimer has recently married Glendower's daughter!

original: Shall our coffers then   Be emptied to redeem a traitor home?   Shall we buy treason and indent with fears   When they have lost and forfeited themselves?
translation: Are we supposed to empty our purses just to bring a traitor home? Should I pay for treason and make a deal with a coward, when he has lost sight of even himself?

original: No, on the barren mountains let him starve,   For I shall never hold that man my friend   Whose tongue shall ask me for one penny cost   To ransom home revolted Mortimer.
translation: No. Let him die out there. No-one who asks me to spend even a penny to save that treacherous Mortimer will be my friend.

original: Revolted Mortimer!   He never did fall off, my sovereign liege,   But by the chance of war.
translation: Treacherous Mortimer? He never changed his allegiance, my lord, except in an accident of war.

original: To prove that true   Needs no more but one tongue for all those wounds,   Those mouthèd wounds, which valiantly he took   When on the gentle Severn’s sedgy bank   In single opposition hand to hand   He did confound the best part of an hour   In changing hardiment with great Glendower.
translation: I can prove it, by describing to you all of the wounds—the gaping wounds—which he bravely received when fighting one-on-one with the great Glendower for almost an hour, exchanging brave blows.

original: Three times they breathed, and three times did they  drink,   Upon agreement, of swift Severn’s flood,
translation: They stopped fighting three times to catch their breath, and three times to drink water from the Severn River.

original: Who then, affrighted with their bloody looks,   Ran fearfully among the trembling reeds   And hid his crisp head in the hollow bank,   Bloodstainèd with these valiant combatants.
translation: Even the Severn was scared of their bloody faces, and the bloody water they left behind flowed away to hide itself by the riverbank, out of sight.

original: Never did bare and rotten policy   Color her working with such deadly wounds,   Nor could the noble Mortimer   Receive so many, and all willingly.
translation: A traitor has never used deadly wounds to hide their treachery, and Mortimer would never have willingly received so many blows.

original: Then let not him be slandered with revolt.
translation: Don't let him be falsely accused of treason.

original: Thou dost belie him, Percy; thou dost belie him.   He never did encounter with Glendower.
translation: That's a lie, Percy, that's a lie—he never fought with Glendower.

original: I tell thee, he durst as well have met the devil alone   As Owen Glendower for an enemy.   Art thou not ashamed?
translation: I am telling you, he would probably rather meet the devil for a fight than have Owen Glendower as his enemy. Aren't you ashamed of yourself?

original: But, sirrah, henceforth   Let me not hear you speak of Mortimer.
translation: But, sir, from now on I don't want to hear anymore about Mortimer.

original: Send me your prisoners with the speediest means,   Or you shall hear in such a kind from me   As will displease you.—
translation: Send me the prisoners as quickly as you can, or you will not enjoy my response.

original: My lord Northumberland,   We license your departure with your son.—
translation: My lord Northumberland, you and your son are allowed to leave now.

original: Send us your prisoners, or you will hear of it.
translation: Send us the prisoners, or you will hear from us.

original: An if the devil come and roar for them, I will not send them. I will after straight And tell him so, for I will ease my heart, Albeit I make a hazard of my head.
translation: Even if the devil himself came and shouted at me, I would not hand over these prisoners. I should go after him and tell him that now, even if it costs me my head, it will relieve my heart.

original: What, drunk with choler? stay and pause awhile. Here comes your uncle.
translation: What, are you drunk with anger? Stay and think about it for a minute. Here comes your uncle.

original: Speak of Mortimer?   Zounds, I will speak of him, and let my soul   Want mercy if I do not join with him.
translation: Not talk about Mortimer? Heavens, I will talk about him, and I'll be damned if I don't join him!

original: Yea, on his part I’ll empty all these veins   And shed my dear blood drop by drop in the dust,
translation: I would empty all of my veins for him and watch my blood drip onto the ground, drop by drop!

original: But I will lift the downtrod Mortimer   As high in the air as this unthankful King,   As this ingrate and cankered Bolingbroke.
translation: I will lift up the put-down Mortimer until he sits as high as this horrible King, this ungrateful and rotten  Bolingbroke .

original: Brother, the King hath made your nephew  mad.
translation: Brother, the King has made your nephew very angry.

original: Who struck this heat up after I was gone?
translation: Who started this argument after I left?

original: He will forsooth have all my prisoners,
translation: In truth, the King says that he is going to have all of my prisoners.

original: And when I urged the ransom once again   Of my wife’s brother, then his cheek looked pale,
translation: When I brought up the issue of Mortimer's ransom, his cheeks turned pale,

original: And on my face he turned an eye of death,   Trembling even at the name of Mortimer.
translation: and he had a look of mortal fear on his face—that's how shook up he is just hearing Mortimer's name.

original: I cannot blame him. Was not he proclaimed By Richard, that dead is, the next of blood?
translation: I can't say I blame him. Didn't King Richard announce that Mortimer was next in line to the throne?

original: He was; I heard the proclamation.
translation: He did; I heard the announcement.

original: And then it was when the unhappy King—   Whose wrongs in us God pardon!—did set forth   Upon his Irish expedition;
translation: It happened right when the unlucky King Richard (God forgive us for what we did to him!) was setting out to invade  Ireland .

original: From whence he, intercepted, did return   To be deposed and shortly murderèd.
translation: When this was interrupted, he came back to England, only to be removed from the throne and murdered soon after.

original: And for whose death we in the world’s wide mouth Live scandalized and foully spoken of.
translation: And now because of the role we played in King Richard's death, we are considered appalling, and the whole world speaks badly of us.

original: But soft, I pray you. Did King Richard then Proclaim my brother Edmund Mortimer Heir to the crown?
translation: Hang on a minute, please. Did King Richard actually announce that my brother-in-law, Edmund Mortimer, was the next in line to the throne?

original: He did; myself did hear it.
translation: He did. I heard him myself.

original: Nay then, I cannot blame his cousin King   That wished him on the barren mountains starve.
translation: Well then, I can't blame the King for wanting Mortimer to starve out there.

original: But shall it be that you that set the crown   Upon the head of this forgetful man   And for his sake wear the detested blot   Of murderous subornation—shall it be   That you a world of curses undergo,
translation: But is it okay that you, the men who put the crown on Henry's forgetful head—and bear the awful mark of murderous accusations for his sake—should be the subject of all the world's curses?

original: Being the agents or base second means,   The cords, the ladder, or the hangman rather?   O, pardon me that I descend so low   To show the line and the predicament   Wherein you range under this subtle King.
translation: When you were just the agents, or the instruments, in this plan? Would you blame the rope, the ladder, or the hangman even when someone is hanged? Sorry for associating you with such things, but I just wanted to show you the categories that you are ranked in, under this crafty King.

original: Shall it for shame be spoken in these days,   Or fill up chronicles in time to come,   That men of your nobility and power   Did gage them both in an unjust behalf   (As both of you, God pardon it, have done)   To put down Richard, that sweet lovely rose,   An plant this thorn, this canker, Bolingbroke?
translation: Will you let people shame you in this way? Are you okay with the fact that historical accounts in the future will say that you noble and powerful men pledged yourself to an unjust cause (as you both actually did, God forgive you) to get rid of Richard—that sweet, lovely rose—and helped to plant this thorn, this wild rose, Bolingbroke?

original: And shall it in more shame be further spoken   That you are fooled, discarded, and shook off   By him for whom these shames you underwent?
translation: Will it be even more shameful when people realize that you have been tricked, and discarded by the person for whom you shamed yourselves in the first place?

original: No, yet time serves wherein you may redeem   Your banished honors and restore yourselves   Into the good thoughts of the world again,   Revenge the jeering and disdain’d contempt   Of this proud King,
translation: No, there is still time for you to redeem the honor you have lost, and win back your good reputations in this world. You can take revenge on the mocking and scorn of this arrogant King,

original: who studies day and night   To answer all the debt he owes to you   Even with the bloody payment of your deaths.   Therefore I say—
translation: who thinks all day and night about how he can repay you for your debts, and concludes that he will do so with your  deaths .  Therefore, I say—

original: Peace, cousin, say no more.
translation: Enough, nephew. Don't say anything else.

original: And now I will unclasp a secret book,   And to your quick-conceiving discontents   I’ll read you matter deep and dangerous,
translation: I am going to tell you a secret, which has been  locked away . I will unlock this secret and tell you a dark and dangerous story, which will please you in your anger.

original: As full of peril and adventurous spirit   As to o'erwalk a current roaring loud   On the unsteadfast footing of a spear.
translation: This story is full of peril and adventure, just like the feeling of walking across a fast-rushing river, balanced on an unsteady spear.

original: If he fall in, good night, or sink or swim!
translation: If he falls in, then it's all over—it doesn't matter if he sinks or swims!

original: Send danger from the east unto the west,   So honor cross it from the north to south,   And let them grapple:
translation: Wherever this danger comes from, it's all right, as long as it provides the opportunity to win honor.

original: O, the blood more stirs   To rouse a lion than to start a hare!
translation: It takes more courage to wake up a  lion , than it does to scare a hare!

original: Imagination of some great exploit Drives him beyond the bounds of patience.
translation: Thinking about this heroic adventure is making him lose his self-control.

original: By heaven, methinks it were an easy leap   To pluck bright honor from the pale-faced moon,
translation: By God, I feel like it would be easy to jump up and grab noble Honor off the moon's pale face.

original: Or dive into the bottom of the deep,   Where fathom line could never touch the ground,   And pluck up drownèd honor by the locks,
translation: Or dive down to the bottom of the deepest ocean, and drag drowned Honor by her hair to the surface.

original: So he that doth redeem her thence might wear   Without corrival all her dignities.
translation: That way the man who rescues her doesn't have to share the glory with anyone.

original: But out upon this half-faced fellowship!
translation: Who wants to share glory?!

original: He apprehends a world of figures  here, But not the form of what he should attend.—     Good cousin, give me audience for a while.
translation: He is using some lovely imagery here, but that's not what he should be paying attention to right now.

original: I cry you mercy.
translation: I apologize.

original: Those same noble Scots That are your prisoners—
translation: The noble Scotsmen that you've taken as prisoners—

original: I’ll keep them all. By God, he shall not have a Scot of them. No, if a Scot would save his soul, he shall not. I’ll keep them, by this hand!
You start away And lend no ear unto my purposes: Those prisoners you shall keep—
translation: You interrupt me before listening to what I have to say. You will get to keep the prisoners—

original: Nay, I will. That’s flat!
translation: Yes, I will. That's for sure!

original: He said he would not ransom Mortimer,   Forbad my tongue to speak of Mortimer.
translation: He's said that he will not pay Mortimer's ransom and has forbidden me from speaking of Mortimer.

original: But I will find him when he lies asleep,   And in his ear I’ll hollo “Mortimer.”
translation: I'm going to find him when he's sleeping and shout "Mortimer" in his ear.

original: Nay,   I’ll have a starling shall be taught to speak   Nothing but “Mortimer,” and give it him   To keep his anger still in motion.
translation: No, better yet, I'm going to get a bird and teach it to say nothing but "Mortimer," and give it to the King to make sure he's always angry.

original: Hear you, cousin, a word.
translation: Listen to me, nephew, for a minute.

original: All studies here I solemnly defy,   Save how to gall and pinch this Bolingbroke.   And that same sword-and-buckler Prince of Wales—
translation: I am going to give up all of my other interests to focus on irritating and tormenting this Bolingbroke and his  unworthy  son, the Prince of Wales.

original: But that I think his father loves him not   And would be glad he met with some mischance—   I would have him poisoned with a pot of ale.
translation: If I didn't think that Henry disliked his son and would be happy if something bad happened to him, I would poison his ale.

original: Farewell, kinsman. I’ll talk to you When you are better tempered to attend.
translation: Goodbye, nephew, I'll talk to you when you're in a better mood to listen.

original: Why, what a wasp-stung and impatient fool Art thou to break into this woman’s mood, Tying thine ear to no tongue but thine own!
translation: You're an irritable and impatient idiot to keep chatting away like a woman, listening to no-one's voice but your own!

original: Why, look you, I am whipped and scourged with rods,   Nettled and stung with pismires, when I hear   Of this vile politician, Bolingbroke.
translation: Hey, I feel like I am being whipped with rods, irritated and stung by ants when I hear about this vile politican, Bolingbroke.

original: In Richard’s time—what do you call the place?   A plague upon it! It is in Gloucestershire.
translation: When Richard was alive—what was that place called? Damn it! It's in Gloucestershire.

original: 'Twas where the madcap duke his uncle kept,   His uncle York;
translation: It's where that crazy duke's uncle lived, the Duke of York.

original: where I first bowed my knee   Unto this king of smiles, this Bolingbroke.
translation: It's the place where I first knelt and committed myself to this Bolingbroke.

original: 'Sblood, when you and he came back from Ravenspurgh.
translation: God! It was when you and he had just come back from  Ravenspurgh .

original: At Berkley Castle.
translation: At Berkley Castle.

original: You say true.
translation: That's it.

original: Why, what a candy deal of courtesy   This fawning greyhound then did proffer me:
translation: What great courtesy that flattering dog gave me!

original: “Look when his infant fortune came to age,”   And “gentle Harry Percy,” and “kind cousin.”
translation: "Look how the hopes of his youth have come true," and "gentle Harry Percy," and "kind cousin."

original: O, the devil take such cozeners!—
translation: Oh, to hell with  cheats  like him!

original: God forgive me!   Good uncle, tell your tale. I have done.
translation: I'm sorry. Good uncle, tell me your story. I'm finished.

original: Nay, if you have not, to it again. We will stay your leisure.
translation: Are you sure? If you're not, keep going. We will wait for you to be ready.

original: I have done, i' faith.
translation: I'm finished, I mean it.

original: Then once more to your Scottish prisoners:
translation: Then let's talk once more about your Scottish prisoners.

original: Deliver them up without their ransom straight,
translation: Release them right now without a ransom.

original: And make the Douglas' son your only mean   For powers in Scotland,
translation: Build a relationship with Douglas and use him to build an army in Scotland.

original: which, for divers reasons   Which I shall send you written, be assured   Will easily be granted.—
translation: I know that he'll help you and I will send you a letter soon, explaining why.

original: Of York, is it not?
translation: The Archbishop of York, do you mean?

original: True; who bears hard   His brother’s death at Bristol, the Lord Scroop.
translation: Yes, since he's deeply affected by the death of his brother, the  Lord Scroop , in Bristol.

original: I speak not this in estimation,   As what I think might be,
translation: What I am telling you is not just guesswork.

original: but what I know   Is ruminated, plotted, and set down,
translation: It has been decided, plotted, and put in place,

original: And only stays but to behold the face   Of that occasion that shall bring it on.
translation: and they are now just waiting for the right opportunity to attack.

original: I smell it. Upon my life, it will do well.
translation: I see what you mean. That will go well, I'm sure of it.

original: Before the game is afoot thou still let’st slip.
translation: Don't let your dogs off the leash before the hunt has even started.

original: Why, it cannot choose but be a noble plot. And then the power of Scotland and of York To join with Mortimer, ha?
translation: Well, it can't help being a very good plan. And the armies of Scotland and of York will join up with Mortimer's, right?

original: And so they shall.
translation: They will.

original: In faith, it is exceedingly well aimed.
translation: Truthfully, it's an excellent plan.

original: And ’tis no little reason bids us speed   To save our heads by raising of a head,
translation: There are many reasons why we need to hurry to raise an army in order to save ourselves.

original: For, bear ourselves as even as we can,   The King will always think him in our debt,
translation: Although we behave properly around him, the King will always feel in our debt for what we did in getting him the throne,

original: And think we think ourselves unsatisfied,   Till he hath found a time to pay us home.
translation: and will think that we aren't happy until he has found a way to fully  repay us .

original: And see already how he doth begin   To make us strangers to his looks of love.
translation: Haven't you noticed that he's already begun to stay away from us?

original: He does, he does. We’ll be revenged on him.
translation: He does, he does. We will have our revenge on him.

original: Cousin, farewell.
translation: [To HOTSPUR]  Goodbye, nephew.

original: No further go in this   Than I by letters shall direct your course.
translation: Don't do anything more until I write to you with instructions.

original: When time is ripe, which will be suddenly,   I’ll steal to Glendower and Lord Mortimer,
translation: When the time comes, which will be soon, I will go off to Glendower and Lord Mortimer.

original: Where you and Douglas and our powers at once,   As I will fashion it, shall happily meet
translation: I will make it so that you, Douglas, and all of our armies will meet at the same time,

original: To bear our fortunes in our own strong arms,   Which now we hold at much uncertainty.
translation: and will carry out fates in our weapons, with a strength that we don't have right now.

original: Farewell, good brother. We shall thrive, I trust.
translation: Goodbye, my good brother. We will be successful, I am sure of it.

original: Uncle, adieu: O, let the hours be short Till fields and blows and groans applaud our sport.
translation: Goodbye, uncle. I hope it's not long until battlefields, wounds, and groans are the consequences of our mission!

original: Heigh-ho! An it be not four by the day, I’ll be hanged. Charles’s Wain is over the new chimney, and yet our  horse not packed.—What, ostler!
Anon, anon.
translation: In a second, in a second.

original: I prithee, Tom, beat Cut’s saddle. Put a few flocks in  the point. Poor jade is wrung in the withers out of all  cess.
Peas and beans are as dank here as a dog, and that is  the next way to give poor jades the bots. This house is  turned upside down since Robin ostler died.
translation: The food for the horses here is is as wet as a dog. That's the quickest way to give old horses diseases. This inn has gone downhill since the ostler Robin died.

original: Poor fellow never joyed since the price of oats rose.  It was the death of him.
translation: Poor guy hadn't been happy since the price of oats went up. It was the death of him.

original: I think this be the most villanous house in all London  road for fleas. I am stung like a tench.
Like a tench? By the Mass, there is ne'er a king  christen could be better bit than I have been since the  first cock.
translation: Like a tench? I swear, not even a Christian king could be bitten more than I've been bitten since midnight.

original: Why, they will allow us ne'er a jordan, and then we  leak in your chimney, and your chamber-lye breeds fleas  like a loach.
What, ostler, come away and be hanged. Come away.
translation: What are you doing, ostler?! Come here right now—I mean it!

original: I have a gammon of bacon and two races of ginger to be  delivered as far as Charing Cross.
translation: I have a leg of smoked ham and some ginger roots that I have to deliver to Charing Cross.

original: God’s body, the turkeys in my pannier are quite  starved.—
translation: Jesus Christ , the turkeys in my basket are starving!

original: What, ostler! A plague on thee! Hast thou  never an eye in thy head? Canst not hear?
translation: Come on, ostler! Damn you! Can you not see anything? Can you not hear?

original: An ’twere not  as good deed as drink to break the pate on thee, I am a  very villain.
translation: If it isn't a good idea to smack you on the head, then I am an idiot.

original: Come, and be hanged. Hast no faith in  thee?
translation: Come on I say! Can we trust you at all?

original: Good morrow, carriers. What’s o'clock?
translation: Good morning, carriers. What time is it?

original: I think it be two o'clock.
translation: I think it's about two o'clock.

original: I prithee, lend me thy lantern to see my gelding in the stable.
translation: Lend me your lantern so that I can check on my horse in the stable.

original: Nay, by God, soft. I know a trick worth two of that, i' faith.
translation: Not a chance. I know a few tricks like that myself, indeed.

original: I pray thee, lend me thine.
translation: Okay then, lend me yours.

original: Ay, when, canst tell? “Lend me thy lantern,” quoth he. Marry, I’ll see thee hanged first.
translation: Hey, no way!  "Lend me your lantern," he says. By God, I'll see you hanged before I do.

original: Sirrah carrier, what time do you mean to come to  London?
translation: Sir carrier, when are you planning to be in London?

original: Time enough to go to bed with a candle, I warrant thee. Come, neighbour Mugs, we’ll call up the gentlemen. They will along with company, for they have great charge.
translation: Some time tonight, I can assure you. Come on, Mugs, my friend. We'll go wake up the ostler. They want to travel with us because they have valuable baggage with them.

original: What ho, chamberlain!
At hand, quoth pickpurse.
translation: "I'm ready," as the pickpockets say!

original: That’s even as fair as “at hand, quoth the  Chamberlain,” for thou variest no more from picking of  purses than giving direction doth from laboring: thou  layest the plot how.
translation: That's basically the same as "I'm ready, says the Chamberlain," since you're about as different from a thief as a supervisor is from a worker—you just decide how the work is done.

original: Good morrow, Master Gadshill. It holds current that I  told you yesternight:
translation: Good morning, Mr. Gadshill. Everything I told you last night is still true.

original: there’s a franklin in the Wild of  Kent hath brought three hundred marks with him in gold.
translation: There's a small landowner staying here from Kent who has  two hundred pounds  with him in gold.

original: I heard him tell it to one of his company last night at  supper—a kind of auditor,
translation: I heard him telling one of his friends last night at dinner. The friend was some kind of accountant.

original: one that hath abundance of  charge too, God knows what.
translation: He has a lot of baggage too—Lord knows what it contains.

original: They are up already and call for eggs and butter. They will away presently.
translation: They are already awake and have asked for their breakfast. They will set off soon.

original: Sirrah, if they meet not with Saint Nicholas' clerks,  I’ll give thee this neck.
translation: Sir, if they don't run into thieves on their journey, I'll let you hang me.

original: No, I’ll none of it. I pray thee keep that for the  hangman, for I know thou worshipest Saint Nicholas as  truly as a man of falsehood may.
What talkest thou to me of the hangman?
translation: Why are you talking to me about the hangman?

original: If I hang, I’ll make a fat pair of gallows, for if I hang, old Sir John hangs with me, and thou knowest he is no starveling.
translation: If I am going to hang, I will make up one half of a fat pair, because if I hang, Falstaff will hang alongside me—and you know he is not exactly skinny.

original: Tut, there are other Troyans that thou dream’st not of,  the which for sport sake are content to do the  profession some grace,
translation: You know, there are other companions that you can't even imagine, ones who are happy to give the profession of robbing some respectability—and all for the sake of a practical joke.

original: that would, if matters should be  looked into, for their own credit sake make all whole.
translation: And if there was ever an investigation into our crimes, their reputation would resolve everything.

original: I am joined with no foot-land-rakers, no long-staff  sixpenny strikers, none of these mad mustachio  purple-hued malt-worms,
translation: I'm not accompanied by some highwaymen on foot, or thieves with long canes striking people for small change, or red-faced, mustache-sporting drunkards.

original: but with nobility and  tranquillity, burgomasters and great oneyers, such as  can hold in,
translation: No, I'm accompanied by easygoing noblemen, magistrates, great ones!

original: such as will strike sooner than speak, and  speak sooner than drink, and drink sooner than pray,
translation: These men would prefer to fight than talk, and would rather talk than drink, and would drink first before they'd pray.

original: and yet, zounds, I lie, for they pray continually to their  saint the commonwealth, or rather not pray to her but  prey on her, for they ride up and down on her and make  her their boots.
translation: But, no, that's a lie—they're always praying to their saint—the commonwealth, England.  Or rather, they don't pray to her, but instead they prey on her.  For they trample over her and make her their boots.

original: What, the commonwealth their boots? Will she hold out  water in foul way?
She will, she will. Justice hath liquored her. We steal as in a castle, cocksure. We have the receipt of fern  seed; we walk invisible.
Nay, by my faith, I think you are more beholding to the night than to fern seed for your walking invisible.
translation: No, I don't think so. It will be the darkness of the night which will make us invisible, not some perfect potion.

original: Give me thy hand. Thou shalt have a share in our  purchase, as I am a true man.
translation: Shake my hand. You will get a share of our plunder. On my honor as a true man, you will.

original: Nay, rather let me have it as you are a false thief.
translation: No, I would prefer it if you swore on your reputation as a lying thief.

original: Go to.  Homo  is a common name to all men. Bid the ostler bring my gelding out of the stable. Farewell, you muddy knave.
Come, shelter, shelter! I have removed Falstaff’s  horse, and he frets like a gummed velvet.
Stand close.
translation: Hide.

original: Poins! Poins, and be hanged! Poins!
translation: Poins! Damn you, Poins! Poins!

original: Peace, you fat-kidneyed rascal. What a brawling dost  thou keep!
translation: Be quiet, you fat-bellied idiot! Why are you making so much noise?!

original: Where’s Poins, Hal?
translation: Where's Poins, Hal?

original: He is walked up to the top of the hill. I’ll go seek  him.
translation: He has walked up that hill. I'll go and find him.

original: I am accursed to rob in that thief’s company. The  rascal hath removed my horse and tied him I know not  where.
translation: I do not want to rob anyone with that thief around. He has stolen my horse and I have no idea where he's tied him up.

original: If I travel but four foot by the square further  afoot, I shall break my wind. Well, I doubt not but to  die a fair death for all this, if I ’scape hanging for  killing that rogue.
translation: If I have to walk even four more feet,  I will be out of breath . Although I expect to die an honorable death in spite of this, if I don't get hanged for killing that thief.

original: I have forsworn his company hourly  any time this two-and-twenty years, and yet I am  bewitched with the rogue’s company. If the rascal hath  not given me medicines to make me love him, I’ll be  hanged. It could not be else: I have drunk medicines.—
translation: For the last twenty-two years, I have sworn every hour that I will never speak to him again, but I am still delighted by his company. He must have given me a potion to make me love him—there's no other possibility. Yeah, that must be it! I must have drunk a potion!

original: Poins! Hal! A plague upon you both.—Bardolph! Peto!— I’ll starve ere I’ll rob a foot further.
translation: Poins! Hal! Oh, damn you both. Bardolph! Peto! I'll die before I take another step.

original: An ’twere not as  good a deed as drink to turn true man and to leave these rogues, I am the veriest varlet that ever chewed with a tooth.
translation: If I shouldn't just become an honest man and leave these idiots, then I am the worst scoundrel that ever lived.

original: Eight yards of uneven ground is threescore and  ten miles afoot with me, and the stony-hearted villains  know it well enough. A plague upon it when thieves  cannot be true one to another!
translation: Eight yards of rough ground feels like seventy miles of walking for me, and those hard-hearted villains know that! What good is it when there is no honor among thieves.

original: Peace, you fat guts! Lie down, lay thine ear close to  the ground, and list if thou canst hear the tread of  travelers.
translation: Be quiet, you fat thing. Lie down, put your ear close to the ground, and listen to see if you can hear the travelers' footsteps.

original: Have you any levers to lift me up again being down?  'Sblood, I’ll not bear mine own flesh so far afoot again for all the coin in thy father’s Exchequer. What a  plague mean you to colt me thus?
translation: Do you have a machine to lift me back up again once I'm down? I swear to God, I wouldn't walk all this way again even for all the money in your father's treasury. Why do you cheat me and horse around like this?

original: Thou liest. Thou art not colted; thou art uncolted.
translation: You are lying. How can we horse around when we don't even have a horse?

original: I prithee, good Prince Hal, help me to my horse, good  king’s son.
translation: Please, my good Prince Hal, tell me where my horse is, you good Prince.

original: Out, you rogue! Shall I be your ostler?
translation: Leave it, you scoundrel! Am I supposed to be your stable boy?!

original: Hang thyself in thine own heir-apparent garters! If I  be ta'en, I’ll peach for this. An I have not ballads  made on you all and sung to filthy tunes, let a cup of  sack be my poison—when a jest is so forward, and afoot  too! I hate it.
Stand.
translation: Stop.

original: So I do, against my will.
translation: I am, even if I don't want to.

original: O, ’tis our setter. I know his voice, Bardolph. —What  news?
translation: Oh, it's the one who set up this robbery. I recognize his voice, Bardolph.

original: Case you, case you. On with your vizards. There’s money of the King’s coming down the hill. 'Tis going to the  King’s Exchequer.
translation: Cover up, cover up. Put on your masks. Disguise yourselves.  There's tax revenue coming down the hill, bound for the royal treasury.

original: You lie, you rogue. 'Tis going to the King’s Tavern.
translation: You are lying, you rascal. It's going to the King's bank.

original: There’s enough to make us all.
translation: There's enough to make all of our fortunes.

original: To be hanged.
translation: And guarantee that we are hanged.

original: Sirs, you four shall front them in the narrow lane. Ned Poins and I will walk lower. If they ’scape from your  encounter, then they light on us.
translation: Sirs, you four will attack them in the narrow lane. Ned Poins and I will go further down the way. If they manage to escape from your attack, then they will meet us instead.

original: How many be there of them?
translation: How many of them are there?

original: Some eight or ten.
translation: About eight or ten.

original: Zounds, will they not rob us?
translation: Heavens, won't they just rob us instead?

original: What, a coward, Sir John Paunch?
translation: Oh, are you a coward, Sir John Pot-Belly?

original: Indeed, I am not John of Gaunt, your grandfather, but  yet no coward, Hal.
Well, we leave that to the proof.
translation: Well, let's see about that.

original: Sirrah Jack, thy horse stands behind the hedge. When  thou needest him, there thou shalt find him. Farewell,  and stand fast.
translation: Sir Jack, your horse is waiting behind that hedge. When you need him, you will find him there. Goodbye, and get ready.

original: Now cannot I strike him, if I should be hanged.
translation: I can't hit him now, or I'd be hanged.

original: Ned, where are our disguises?
translation: Ned, where are our disguises?

original: Here, hard by. Stand close.
translation: They are here, right by us. Now let's hide.

original: Now, my masters, happy man be his dole, say I. Every  man to his business.
translation: Now, my men, may luck be with us! Get ready to go.

original: Come, neighbor, the boy shall lead our horses down the  hill. We’ll walk afoot awhile and ease our legs.
translation: Come on, friend. This boy will take our horses down the hill. Let's walk for a little while and stretch our legs.

original: Stand!
translation: Freeze!

original: Jesus bless us!
translation: Jesus bless us!

original: Strike! Down with them! Cut the villains' throats! Ah,  whoreson caterpillars, bacon-fed knaves, they hate us  youth. Down with them! Fleece them!
translation: Attack! Get them! Cut the scoundrels' throats! Oh, vile parasites! Overfed idiots! They hate young people like us. Get them! Take everything they've got!

original: O, we are undone, both we and ours forever!
translation: Oh, we are completely ruined!

original: Hang, you gorbellied knaves! Are you undone? No, you  fat chuffs. I would your store were here. On, bacons,  on! What, you knaves, young men must live. You are  grandjurors, are you? We’ll jure you, faith.
The thieves have bound the true men. Now could thou and I rob the thieves and go merrily to London, it would be argument for a week, laughter for a month, and a good  jest forever.
translation: The thieves have tied up the honest men. Now if we can rob the thieves, we can go happily to London. And this would be something we could talk about for a week, laugh about for a month, and remember as a good joke forever.

original: Stand close, I hear them coming.
translation: Hide—I hear them coming.

original: Come, my masters, let us share, and then to horse  before day. An the Prince and Poins be not two arrant  cowards, there’s no equity stirring. There’s no more  valor in that Poins than in a wild duck.
translation: Come on, men, let's share out this money and then get going before it is light. If the Prince and Poins aren't two complete cowards, then there's no truth in the world. Poins doesn't have any more courage than a wild duck!

original: Your money!
translation: Give us your money!

original: Villains!
translation: Villains!

original: Got with much ease. Now merrily to horse.
translation: How easy was that? Now we can ride off happily.

original: The thieves are all scattered, and possessed with fear   So strongly that they dare not meet each other.   Each takes his fellow for an officer.
translation: The thieves have all run away, so scared that they won't even want to meet each other. Each of them mistakes his companion for an officer of the law!

original: Away, good Ned.
translation: Let's go, Ned.

original: Falstaff sweats to death,   And lards the lean earth as he walks along.   Were ’t not for laughing, I should pity him.
