translation: Falstaff is sweating so much that he drips fat onto the ground as he walks along. If it wasn't so funny, I would feel sorry for him.

original: How the fat rogue roared!
translation: How that fat rascal screamed!

original: But, for mine own part, my lord, I could be well  contented to   be there, in respect of the love I bear  your house.   He could be contented; why is he not, then?
translation: "As for me, my lord, I would be happy to be there, because of the love I have for your family."  If he is happy to be here, then why isn't he?

original: In respect of the love he bears our house—he shows in  this he loves his own barn better than he loves our  house. Let me see some more.
translation: Because of the love I have for your family—it's clear he loves his own house more than he loves mine. I'll read some more.

original: The purpose you undertake  is dangerous.   Why, that’s certain. 'Tis dangerous to  take a cold, to sleep, to drink; but I tell you, my lord fool, out of this nettle, danger, we pluck this flower, safety.
translation: "Your mission is dangerous."  Well, that's true, but it's also dangerous to catch a cold, to sleep, to drink. I can tell you, my silly lord, that even though stinging nettles are dangerous, we will be able to safely find the flower within them.

original: The purpose you undertake is dangerous, the  friends you have named uncertain, the time itself  unsorted, and your whole plot too light for the  counterpoise of so great an   opposition.   Say you so, say  you so?
translation: "Your mission is dangerous, your allies are unreliable, the time unsuitable, and your whole conspiracy is too light to counterbalance an opponent like the King."  Is that so? Is it?

original: I say unto you again, you are a shallow,  cowardly hind, and you lie. What a lack-brain is this!
translation: I will say it again, you are a silly, weak coward, and these are just lies. What an idiot he is!

original: By the Lord, our plot is a good plot as ever was laid,  our friends true and constant—a good plot, good friends, and full of expectation; an excellent plot, very good  friends.
translation: By God, our plan is as good as any plan that's ever been made; our allies are honest and reliable. It's a good plot, with good allies, and it's full of promise. It's even an excellent plan, with very good allies.

original: What a frosty-spirited rogue is this!
translation: What a cold-hearted idiot he is!

original: Why, my  Lord of York commends the plot and the general course of the action.
translation: Why, the  Archbishop of York  supports my plan and how the mission is developing.

original: Zounds, an I were now by this rascal, I  could brain him with his lady’s fan.
translation: Heavens, if I was close to this rascal right now, I would smack him with his wife's fan.

original: Is there not my  father, my uncle, and myself? Lord Edmund Mortimer, my  Lord of York, and Owen Glendower? Is there not besides  the Douglas? Have I not all their letters to meet me in  arms by the ninth of the next month, and are they not  some of them set forward already?
translation: Don't we have the support of my father, my uncle, and myself?! Lord Edmund Mortimer, the Archbishop of York, and Owen Glendower?! And don't we also have  Douglas ? Don't I have letters from all of them agreeing to meet me with their armies by the ninth of next month, and some of them have even set off already?

original: What a pagan rascal is this—an infidel! Ha, you shall see now in very  sincerity of fear and cold heart, will he to the King  and lay open all our proceedings.
translation: What an unbelievable idiot he is—a non-believer! Ha, just wait for him to run to the King and tell him all about our plan, he'll be so filled with fear.

original: O, I could divide  myself and go to buffets, for moving such a dish of skim milk with so honorable an action! Hang him, let him  tell the King. We are prepared. I will set forward  tonight.
translation: Oh, if only I could split myself in half and tell my other half how angry I am that I trusted such an unworthy person with such important news. To hell with him—let him tell the King! We're ready. I will set off tonight.

original: O my good lord, why are you thus alone?
translation: Oh my good lord, why are you always alone?

original: For what offense have I this fortnight been   A banished woman from my Harry’s bed?
translation: Why have you banned me from your bed for the past two weeks?

original: Tell me, sweet lord, what is ’t that takes from thee   Thy stomach, pleasure, and thy golden sleep?
translation: Tell me, sweet lord, what has taken away your appetite, your desire, and your precious sleep?

original: Why dost thou bend thine eyes upon the earth   And start so often when thou sit’st alone?
translation: Why do you stare at the ground so much, and jump so often when you are sitting alone?

original: Why hast thou lost the fresh blood in thy cheeks   And given my treasures and my rights of thee   To thick-eyed musing and curst melancholy?
translation: Why have you lost the color in your cheeks? Why have you taken away the intimacy that is my pleasure and my right as your wife, and instead given it to this dark way of thinking and bad-tempered sadness?

original: In thy faint slumbers I by thee have watched,   And heard thee murmur tales of iron wars,   Speak terms of manage to thy bounding steed,
translation: I have watched you in your restless sleep, and have heard you murmuring stories about war, as if you are giving commands to an army.

original: Cry “Courage! To the field!” And thou hast talk’d   Of sallies and retires, of trenches, tents,   Of palisadoes, frontiers, parapets,   Of basilisks, of cannon, culverin,   Of prisoners' ransom and of soldiers slain,   And all the currents of a heady fight.
translation: You have cried out, "Have courage! To the field!" You have talked about advances and retreats, about trenches, tents,  barriers , ramparts, defensive walls. You have talked about  different cannons , about prisoners being ransomed, soldiers dying, and all of the things that happen in a violent battle.

original: Thy spirit within thee hath been so at war,   And thus hath so bestirred thee in thy sleep,   That beads of sweat have stood upon thy brow   Like bubbles in a late-disturbèd stream,
translation: Your soul has also been at war, and has been disturbing you in your sleep. There have been beads of sweat on your forehead, that look like bubbles in a swirling stream.

original: And in thy face strange motions have appeared,   Such as we see when men restrain their breath   On some great sudden hest.
translation: There have been strange expressions on your face, like the types we see when men hold their breath at a terrible, sudden request.

original: O, what portents are these?   Some heavy business hath my lord in hand,   And I must know it, else he loves me not.
translation: Oh, what do these signs mean? You are plotting something serious, and I want to know what it is, or else you do not love me.

original: What, ho!
translation: Hey, you!

original: He is, my lord, an hour ago.
translation: He has, my lord, about an hour ago.

original: Hath Butler brought those horses from the sheriff?
translation: And did Butler bring those horses from the sheriff?

original: One horse, my lord, he brought even now.
translation: He has brought one horse, my lord, just now.

original: What horse? A roan, a crop-ear, is it not?
translation: Which horse? A brown one, with its ears clipped?

original: It is, my lord.
translation: Yes, that one, my lord.

original: That roan shall be my throne. Well, I will back him straight. O, Esperance! Bid Butler lead him forth into the park.
But hear you, my lord.
translation: Listen to me, my lord.

original: What say’st thou, my lady?
translation: What do you have to say, my lady?

original: What is it carries you away?
translation: Why have you got so carried away?

original: Why, my horse, My love, my horse.
Out, you mad-headed ape!
translation: Stop it, you crazy idiot!

original: A weasel hath not such a deal of spleen   As you are tossed with.
translation: Even a weasel doesn't have the same  temper  that you have.

original: In faith,   I’ll know your business, Harry, that I will.
translation: I swear, I'll find out what you're planning, Harry, that's for sure.

original: I fear my brother Mortimer doth stir   About his title, and hath sent for you   To line his enterprise; but if you go—
translation: I am worried that my brother Mortimer is going to take action to claim his rightful crown and has sent for you to support his mission. But if you go—

original: —So far afoot, I shall be weary, love.
translation: —Such a long way on foot, I will be tired my love.

original: Come, come, you paraquito, answer me   Directly unto this question that I ask.
translation: Come on, you little parrot, take my question seriously and answer me.

original: In faith, I’ll break thy little finger, Harry,   An if thou wilt not tell me all things true.
translation: I swear, I will break your little finger, Harry, if you don't tell me the whole truth.

original: Away!   Away, you trifler.
translation: Go away! Go away, you shrew!

original: Love, I love thee not.   I care not for thee, Kate.
translation: Love? I don't love you. I don't even care about you, Kate.

original: This is no world   To play with mammets and to tilt with lips.
translation: Now is not the time for playing with dolls and  leaning in for  silly kisses.

original: We must have bloody noses and cracked crowns,   And pass them current too.—Gods me, my horse!—
translation: Now is the time for bloody noses and battered  heads , and we must inflict them on others too. Oh God, bring me my horse!

original: What say’st thou, Kate? What would’st thou have with  me?
translation: What do you have to say, Kate? What do you want from me?

original: Do you not love me? Do you not indeed?
translation: You don't love me? Really?

original: Well, do not then, for since you love me not,   I will not love myself.
translation: Well don't bother then, since if you don't love me, I won't love myself.

original: Do you not love me?   Nay, tell me if you speak in jest or no.
translation: You don't love me? Tell me if this is a joke or not.

original: Come, wilt thou see me ride?
translation: Come on, will you come and say goodbye?

original: And when I am a-horseback, I will swear   I love thee infinitely.
translation: When I am on horseback, I will swear to love you forever.

original: But hark you, Kate,   I must not have you henceforth question me   Whither I go, nor reason whereabout.   Whither I must, I must;   and to conclude,   This evening must I leave you, gentle Kate.
translation: But listen, Kate. From now on you must not question me about where I am going, or the reasons why. If I must go, then I must. That's that.  Therefore this evening I must leave you, dear Kate.

original: I know you wise, but yet no farther wise   Than Harry Percy’s wife; constant you are,   But yet a woman;
translation: I know you are wise, but you can only be as wise as the wife of Harry Percy should be;  I know you are loyal, but you are still a woman .

original: and for secrecy   No lady closer, for I well believe   Thou wilt not utter what thou dost not know,   And so far will I trust thee, gentle Kate.
translation: And no woman can keep a secret like you can, especially since you will not be able to speak about something you don't know. So that is as far as I will trust you, sweet Kate.

original: How? So far?
translation: Wow? That far?

original: Not an inch further.
translation: Yes, and not an inch further.

original: But hark you, Kate,   Whither I go, thither shall you go too.
translation: But listen here, Kate, wherever I go, you will go too.

original: Today will I set forth, tomorrow you.   Will this content you, Kate?
translation: I will leave today and you will leave tomorrow. Will that make you happy, Kate?

original: It must, of force.
translation: It will have to, out of necessity.

original: Ned, prithee, come out of that fat room and lend me thy hand to laugh a little.
translation: Ned, please, come out of that stuffy room and make me laugh for a while.

original: Where hast been, Hal?
translation: Where have you been, Hal?

original: With three or four loggerheads amongst three or  fourscore hogsheads. I have sounded the very bass string of humility.
translation: I've been with three or four  blockheads  and somewhere between sixty and eighty cases of wine.  I have been with the lowest of the lowly .

original: Sirrah, I am sworn brother to a leash of  drawers, and can call them all by their christen names,  as Tom, Dick, and Francis. They take it already upon  their salvation that though I be but Prince of Wales,  yet I am the king of courtesy, and tell me flatly am no  proud jack, like Falstaff, but a Corinthian, a lad of  mettle, a good boy—by the Lord, so they call me—
translation: Sir, I am now best friends with three of these bartenders, and can even call them by their first names—Tom, Dick, and Francis. They have promised me that even though I am just the Prince of Wales, I am a king of politeness in their eyes. They told me straight that I'm not a pompous idiot, like Falstaff, but a worthy fellow, a determined lad, a good boy even—I swear to God they call me that.

original: and when I am King of England, I shall command all the good lads in Eastcheap.
translation: When I am King of England, I will have the support of all the good lads in Eastcheap.

original: They call drinking deep “dyeing scarlet,” and when you breathe in your watering, they cry “Hem!”  and bid you “Play it off!” To conclude, I am so good a  proficient in one quarter of an hour that I can drink  with any tinker in his own language during my life.
translation: When you drink a lot, they call it being " dyed red ," and when you take a break from drinking, they cough loudly, and tell you to finish your drink. All in all, I got so good at drinking in fifteen minutes that I can be a good drinking buddy with people of  any social class .

original: I  tell thee, Ned, thou hast lost much honor that thou wert not with me in this action; but, sweet Ned—to sweeten  which name of Ned, I give thee this pennyworth of sugar, clapped even now into my hand by an underskinker, one  that never spake other English in his life than “Eight  shillings and sixpence,” and “You are welcome,” with  this shrill addition, “Anon, anon, sir.—Score a pint of  bastard in the Half-moon,” or so.
translation: I am telling you Ned, you didn't help yourself in missing this encounter. But sweet Ned, I will make your name even sweeter by giving you a penny's worth of sugar. I got this from an apprentice bartender, a boy who has never said anything in his life except for, "That'll be eight shillings and sixpence," and "You're welcome," and sometimes, "Just a minute, sir. Bring a pint of  bastard  to the  Half-moon  room," or something like that.

original: But, Ned, to drive  away the time till Falstaff come, I prithee, do thou  stand in some by-room while I question my puny drawer to what end he gave me the sugar; and do thou never leave  calling “Francis,” that his tale to me may be nothing  but “Anon.” Step aside, and I’ll show thee a precedent.
translation: But Ned, to waste some time before Falstaff gets here, will you stand in a side room while I question one of the inexperienced apprentices about why he gave me the sugar. Keep calling out the name "Francis," so that he keeps having to reply, "Just a minute, sir." Go to this room, and I'll show you something worth remembering.

original: Francis!
translation: Francis!

original: Thou art perfect.
translation: Perfect.

original: Francis!
translation: Francis!

original: Anon, anon, sir.—Look down into the Pomgarnet, Ralph.
Come hither, Francis.
translation: Come here, Francis.

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: How long hast thou to serve, Francis?
translation: How much longer do you have left to serve as an apprentice?

original: Forsooth, five years, and as much as to—
Francis!
translation: Francis!

original: Anon, anon, sir.
translation: Just a minute, sir.

original: Five year! By 'r lady, a long lease for the clinking of pewter! But, Francis, darest thou be so valiant as to  play the coward with thy indenture, and show it a fair  pair of heels, and run from it?
O Lord, sir, I’ll be sworn upon all the books in  England, I could find in my heart—
translation: Oh Lord, sir, I swear on all the Bibles in England, I could manage to—

original: Francis!
translation: Francis!

original: Anon, sir.
translation: One minute, sir.

original: How old art thou, Francis?
translation: How old are you, Francis?

original: Let me see. About Michaelmas next, I shall be—
Francis!
translation: Francis!

original: Anon, sir.    Pray, stay a little, my  lord.
translation: Just a minute, sir.

original: Nay, but hark you, Francis, for the sugar thou gavest  me,’twas a pennyworth, was ’t not?
translation: No, but listen to me, Francis. The sugar that you gave me was about a penny's worth, right?

original: O Lord, I would it had been two!
translation: Oh Lord, I wish it could have been worth two pennies!

original: I will give thee for it a thousand pound. Ask me when  thou wilt, and thou shalt have it.
translation: I will give you a thousand pounds for it. Ask me for it whenever you want, and you can have it.

original: Francis!
translation: Francis!

original: Anon, anon.
translation: One minute, please!

original: Anon, Francis? No, Francis, but tomorrow, Francis; or, Francis, o' Thursday; or indeed, Francis, when thou  wilt. But, Francis—
translation: You want it in one minute, Francis? No, Francis, but you can have it tomorrow, or Thursday. Or indeed, Francis, whenever you want it. But Francis—

original: My lord?
translation: Yes, my lord?

original: Wilt thou rob this leathern jerkin, crystal-button,  not-pated, agate-ring, puke-stocking, caddis-garter,  smooth-tongue, Spanish-pouch—
O Lord, sir, who do you mean?
translation: Oh Lord sir, who are you talking about?

original: Why, then, your brown bastard is your only drink, for  look you, Francis, your white canvas doublet will sully. In Barbary, sir, it cannot come to so much.
What, sir?
translation: What, sir?

original: Francis!
translation: Francis!

original: Away, you rogue! Dost thou not hear them call?
translation: Go on, you rascal! Didn't you hear them calling your name?

original: What, stand’st thou still and hear’st such a calling?  Look to the guests within.
translation: Why are you standing there doing nothing when you hear people are calling your name? Go and see what the guests want.

original: Let them alone awhile, and then open the door.
translation: Leave them outside for a while, and then let them in.

original: Anon, anon, sir.
translation: Hang on, sir.

original: Sirrah, Falstaff and the rest of the thieves are at the door. Shall we be merry?
translation: Sir, Falstaff and the rest of the thieves are at the door. Are we ready to have a good laugh?

original: As merry as crickets, my lad. But hark you, what  cunning match have you made with this jest of the  drawer. Come, what’s the issue?
translation: We'll be chirping like crickets, my lad. But listen, what clever trick did you play on the drawer? Tell me, what's your plan?

original: I am now of all humors that have showed themselves  humors since the old days of Goodman Adam to the pupil  age of this present twelve o'clock at midnight.
Anon, anon, sir.
translation: Give me a minute, sir.

original: That ever this fellow should have fewer words than a  parrot, and yet the son of a woman! His industry is  upstairs and downstairs, his eloquence the parcel of a  reckoning.
translation: This boy has less to say than a parrot does, even though he's a human! His job is to run upstairs and downstairs, and the only things he ever has to say are the items on a bill.

original: I am not yet of Percy’s mind, the Hotspur of  the north, he that kills me some six or seven dozen of  Scots at a breakfast, washes his hands, and says to his  wife “Fie upon this quiet life! I want work.” “O my  sweet Harry,” says she, “how many hast thou killed  today?”
translation: I don't see the world like Percy does, yet this Hotspur of the north, who kills fifty or sixty Scotsmen before breakfast, washes his hands, and says to his wife, "God, life is boring! I want something to do." "Oh my sweet Harry," she replies, "how many people have you killed today?"

original: “Give my roan horse a drench,” says he, and  answers “Some fourteen,” an hour after. “A trifle, a  trifle.”
translation: He tells her, "Give my brown horse its medicine," and then an hour later answers, "Only fourteen, that's nothing, nothing."

original: I prithee, call in Falstaff. I’ll play Percy,  and that damned brawn shall play Dame Mortimer his wife.    “Rivo!”   says the drunkard. Call in Ribs, call in  Tallow.
translation: Please, call in Falstaff now. I will play Percy, and that damned potbellied Falstaff will play his wife, Dame Mortimer. " Bottoms up! " says the drunkard.  Bring in the meat, bring in the fat.

original: Welcome, Jack. Where hast thou been?
translation: Welcome, Jack. Where have you been?

original: A plague of all cowards, I say, and a vengeance too!  Marry and amen!—
translation: I say!  A curse on all cowards, and revenge, too! That's how it should be!

original: Didst thou never see Titan kiss a dish of  butter?—Pitiful-hearted Titan!—that melted at the sweet  tale of the sun’s? If thou didst, then behold that  compound.
(to   FRANCIS   )   You rogue, here’s lime in this sack too.—
translation: [To FRANCIS]  You idiot, there's  lime in this wine !

original: There is nothing but roguery to be found in villanous  man, yet a coward is worse than a cup of sack with lime  in it. A villanous coward!
translation: Evil men have nothing in them but harm, but a coward is even worse than a cup of wine with lime in it. An evil coward!

original: Go thy ways, old Jack. Die  when thou wilt. If manhood, good manhood, be not forgot  upon the face of the earth, then am I a shotten herring.
translation: Get on your way, then, old Jack.  Die now. If there are any true men left on this earth except for me, then I am a  spawned herring .

original: There lives not three good men unhanged in England, and one of them is fat and grows old, God help the while. A bad world, I say.
translation: There aren't even three good men in England who haven't been hanged, and one of them is fat and getting older. God help these times! It is a bad world, I say.

original: I would I were a weaver. I could sing psalms, or anything. A plague of all cowards, I say  still.
translation: I wish  I was a weaver and then I could sing psalms  while I worked. I say it again—damn all you cowards.

original: How now, woolsack, what mutter you?
translation: What's the matter, you big sack of wool, what are you blabbering on about?

original: A King’s son! If I do not beat thee out of thy kingdom  with a dagger of lath, and drive all thy subjects afore  thee like a flock of wild geese, I’ll never wear hair on my face more. You, Prince of Wales!
Why, you whoreson round man, what’s the matter?
translation: Why, you fat son-of-a-bitch, what's the matter?

original: Are not you a coward? Answer me to that—and Poins  there?
translation: Aren't you a coward? Answer that question—you too, Poins!

original: Zounds, ye fat paunch, an you call me coward, by the  Lord, I’ll stab thee.
translation: Good Lord, you potbelly, if you call me a coward, I swear to God, I'll stab you.

original: I call thee coward? I’ll see thee damned ere I call  thee coward,
translation: Me call you a coward? I would rather see you damned than call you a coward.

original: but I would give a thousand pound I could  run as fast as thou canst. You are straight enough in  the shoulders you care not who sees your back.
translation: I would give a thousand pounds if I could run away as fast as you can. Your shoulders are attractive enough that you don't seem to care who sees your back.

original: Call you  that backing of your friends? A plague upon such  backing! Give me them that will face me.—
translation: Do you call that backing up your friends? Damn you and your  help ! Give me a man that will face me rather than turn his back.

original: Give me a cup  of sack.—I am a rogue if I drunk today.
translation: Get me a cup of wine. I would be lying if I said I've had anything to drink today.

original: O villain, thy lips are scarce wiped since thou  drunk’st last.
translation: Oh, you liar! Your lips have barely been wiped clean since your last drink.

original: All is one for that.    A plague of all  cowards, still say I.
translation: That makes no difference.  Damn all cowards, I say again.

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: What’s the matter? There be four of us here have ta'en  a thousand pound this day morning.
translation: What's the matter? Four of us here stole a thousand pounds just this morning.

original: Where is it, Jack? Where is it?
translation: Then where is it, Jack? Where is it?

original: Where is it? Taken from us it is. A hundred upon poor  four of us.
translation: Where is it? It was stolen from us. A hundred men attacked the four of us.

original: What, a hundred, man?
translation: What? One hundred, man?

original: I am a rogue if I were not at half-sword with a dozen  of them two hours together. I have ’scaped by miracle.
translation: I am a liar if I haven't been fighting with at least twelve of them  in close combat  for at least two hours. It's a miracle I escaped.

original: I am eight times thrust through the doublet, four through the hose, my buckler cut through and through, my sword  hacked like a handsaw.   Ecce signum!
translation: They stabbed through my jacket eight times, through my pants four times, my shield is full of holes, and my sword is cut up and useless.  Look at the proof !

original: I never dealt better since I was a man. All would not do. A plague of all  cowards!
translation: I have never fought better, but whatever I did, it wasn't enough. Damn all you cowards.

original: (points to   GADSHILL, PETO   and   BARDOLPH   )   Let  them speak. If they speak more or less than truth, they  are villains, and the sons of darkness.
translation: [Points at GADSHILL, PETO, and BARDOLPH]  Let them speak. If they don't tell you the complete truth, then they're villains and are  evil .

original: Speak, sirs, how was it?
translation: Tell us, sirs, how was it?

original: We four set upon some dozen.
translation: Four of us managed to attack about twelve men.

original: Sixteen at least, my lord.
translation: It was sixteen at least, my lord.

original: And bound them.
translation: And we tied them up.

original: No, no, they were not bound.
translation: No, no, we didn't tie them up.

original: You rogue, they were bound, every man of them, or I am  a Jew else, an Ebrew Jew.
As we were sharing, some six or seven fresh men set  upon us.
translation: As we were dividing up the money, six or seven new men attacked us.

original: And unbound the rest, and then come in the other.
translation: And they untied the others, and then all these other men arrived.

original: What, fought you with them all?
translation: What? And you fought all of them?

original: All? I know not what you call all, but if I fought not  with fifty of them I am a bunch of radish. If there were not two- or three-and-fifty upon poor old Jack, then am I no two-legged creature.
translation: What do you mean by all? I don't know what you mean by all, but if I didn't fight with fifty of them, then I'm a bunch of radishes. If there weren't fifty-two or fifty-three of them attacking poor, old Jack, then I'm not even a man.

original: Pray God you have not murdered some of them.
translation: I pray to God you didn't kill any of them.

original: Nay, that’s past praying for.
translation: It's too late to pray.

original: I have peppered two of  them. Two I am sure I have paid, two rogues in buckram  suits.
translation: I crushed two of then. I am sure I killed two more of them, two idiots wearing  coarse linen .

original: I tell thee what, Hal, if I tell thee a lie, spit in my face, call me horse. Thou knowest my old ward.
translation: I tell you what, Hal, if I am lying then spit in my face and insult me. You know how I fight.

original: Here I lay, and thus I bore my point. Four rogues in  buckram let drive at me.
translation: This is how I stood, and this is how I held my sword. Four idiots in coarse linen attacked me.

original: What, four? Thou saidst but two even now.
translation: There were four of them? You said two just now.

original: Four, Hal, I told thee four.
translation: Four, Hal, I said four.

original: Ay, ay, he said four.
translation: Yes, yes, he definitely said four.

original: These four came all afront, and mainly thrust at me. I  made me no more ado, but took all their seven points in  my target, thus.
translation: These four idiots were all in a row and vigorously thrust at me. I didn't wait any longer, I let all of their seven sword points strike my shield, like this.

original: Seven? Why there were but four even now.
translation: Seven? A minute ago you said there were four.

original: In buckram?
translation: Wearing coarse linen?

original: Ay, four in buckram suits.
translation: Yes, four wearing coarse linen.

original: Seven, by these hilts, or I am a villain else.
translation: There were seven. I swear on this sword, or I am a villain.

original: Prithee, let him alone. We shall have more anon.
translation: Come on, let's leave him alone. There'll be more any second.

original: Dost thou hear me, Hal?
translation: Did you listen to me, Hal?

original: Ay, and mark thee too, Jack.
translation: Yes, and I paid attention to what you said, Jack.

original: Do so, for it is worth the listening to. These nine in  buckram that I told thee of—
translation: That's good, because what I'm saying is worth your attention. So these nine men in coarse linen that I just told you about—

original: So, two more already.
translation: So there are two more already.

original: Their points being broken—
translation: Because their points were broken—

original: Down fell their hose.
Began to give me ground, but I followed me close, came  in foot and hand, and with a thought, seven of the  eleven I paid.
translation: They started to move away, but I followed them closely, and thinking on my feet, I killed seven of the eleven right there and then.

original: O monstrous! Eleven buckram men grown out of two!
translation: Oh wow! Eleven men in coarse linen have grown out of just two!

original: But as the devil would have it, three misbegotten  knaves in Kendal green came at my back, and let drive at me, for it was so dark, Hal, that thou couldst not see  thy hand.
translation: But as the devil would have it, three despicable scoundrels dressed in green, coarse wool fabric crept up on me from behind, and attacked me. You see, Hal, it was so dark that you could barely even see your own hand.

original: These lies are like their father that begets them,  gross as a mountain, open, palpable. Why, thou  claybrained guts, thou knotty-pated fool, thou whoreson, obscene, greasy tallow-catch—
translation: These lies are becoming much like the person who is telling them—big as a mountain, clear to see, and very visible. Why you dull-witted fatty, you thick-headed fool, you son-of-a-bitch, you disgusting, greasy lump of fat—

original: What, art thou mad? Art thou mad? Is not the truth the  truth?
translation: What, are you crazy? Are you crazy? Isn't the truth just the truth?

original: Why, how couldst thou know these men in Kendal green,  when it was so dark thou couldst not see thy hand? Come, tell us your reason. What sayest thou to this?
translation: Well, how would you know that these men were wearing green, coarse wool fabric if it was so dark that you couldn't even see your own hand? Come on, tell us how. What do you have to say to this?

original: Come, your reason, Jack, your reason.
translation: Yeah, tell us how, Jack, how.

original: What, upon compulsion?
translation: What? Just because you have told me to?

original: Zounds, an I were at the  strappado or all the racks in the world, I would not  tell you on compulsion.
translation: Heavens, even if I was put in any  torture device in the world , I wouldn't answer just because you've told me to.

original: Give you a reason on compulsion? If reasons were as plentiful as blackberries, I would  give no man a reason upon compulsion, I.
translation: Tell you how, give you a reason just because you've told me to? Even if reasons were as common as blackberries, I wouldn't give anyone a reason just because they've told me to. I certainly won't.

original: I’ll be no longer guilty of this sin. This sanguine  coward, this bed-presser, this horseback-breaker, this  huge hill of flesh—
translation: I can't listen to this anymore. This red-faced coward, who could flatten a bed, this breaker of horses' backs, this huge mountain of flesh—

original: 'Sblood, you starveling, you elfskin, you dried neat’s  tongue, you bull’s pizzle, you stockfish! O, for breath  to utter what is like thee! You tailor’s-yard, you  sheath, you bowcase, you vile standing tuck—
Well, breathe awhile, and then to it again, and when  thou hast tired thyself in base comparisons, hear me  speak but this.
translation: Catch your breath for a minute and then go again. When you've tired yourself out making stupid comparisons, listen to just one thing I have to say.

original: Mark, Jack.
translation: Listen to him, Jack.

original: We two saw you four set on four, and bound them and  were masters of their wealth. Mark now how a plain tale  shall put you down.
translation: We two saw the four of you attack the four travelers, tie them up, and take their money. Listen now to how the simple truth of the matter will destroy your lies.

original: Then did we two set on you four and, with a word, outfaced you from your prize, and have it; yea, and can show it you here in the house.
translation: Then we two attacked you four, and with a single shout, we frightened you into giving us the money you had stolen. We have it now, and can show it to you right here in this bar.

original: And,  Falstaff, you carried your guts away as nimbly, with as  quick dexterity, and roared for mercy, and still run and roared, as ever I heard bull-calf.
translation: Falstaff, you ran away as quickly and with as much skill as a cow from the slaughterhouse—screaming to be saved and running as far as you could.

original: What a slave art  thou to hack thy sword as thou hast done, and then say  it was in fight!
translation: How outrageous you are to chop away at your sword like you've done, and then say that you did it in a fight!

original: What trick, what device, what  starting-hole canst thou now find out to hide thee from  this open and apparent shame?
translation: What story, what trick, what hiding place are you going to be able to find to escape this obvious and visible shame?

original: Come, let’s hear, Jack. What trick hast thou now?
translation: Come on then, let's hear it, Jack. What trick are you going to use now?

original: By the Lord, I knew you as well as he that made you.
translation: By God, I knew it was you right away.

original: Why, hear you, my masters, was it for me to kill the heir apparent? Should I turn upon the true Prince?
translation: Listen here, gentlemen, was I going to kill the heir to the throne? Was I going to turn on the true Prince?

original: Why, thou knowest I am as valiant as Hercules, but beware  instinct. The lion will not touch the true Prince.
translation: Come on, you know I am as brave as  Hercules , but I listen to my gut. Even a lion will not attack a true Prince.

original: Instinct is a great matter. I was now a coward on  instinct.
translation: Instinct is very important. I was a coward because my instinct told me I had to be.

original: I shall think the better of myself, and thee,  during my life—I for a valiant lion, and thou for a true Prince.
translation: Now I guess I will have to think of myself as a brave lion, since you are a true Prince.

original: But, by the Lord, lads, I am glad you have the  money.—Hostess, clap to the doors.— Watch tonight, pray  to-morrow.
translation: But, by God, am I glad that you have the money! Hostess, shut the doors . Let's have fun tonight and leave our prayers until tomorrow !

original: Gallants, lads, boys, hearts of gold, all the titles of good fellowship come to you. What, shall we  be merry? hall we have a play extempore?
translation: Bold lads, boys, men with hearts of gold—you are not worth all of these good titles. Shall we celebrate? Shall we have some improvised drama to entertain us?

original: Content, and the argument shall be thy running away.
translation: Yes, let's, and the plot can be about you running away.

original: Ah, no more of that, Hal, an thou lovest me.
translation: Ah, no more of that, Hal, if you love me at all.

original: O Jesu, my lord the Prince!
translation: Oh Jesus, my lord the Prince!

original: How now, my lady the hostess, what sayest thou to me?
translation: What's happening, my lady the hostess? Do you have something to say to me?

original: Marry, my lord, there is a nobleman of the court at  door would speak with you. He says he comes from your  father.
translation: Indeed, my lord, there is a nobleman from the court at the door and he said he would like to speak to you. He says that he comes from your father.

original: Give him as much as will make him a royal man and send  him back again to my mother.
What manner of man is he?
translation: What type of man is he?

original: An old man.
translation: An old man.

original: What doth Gravity out of his bed at midnight? Shall I  give him his answer?
translation: What's an old man doing out of his bed at midnight? Should I go and talk to him?

original: Prithee do, Jack.
translation: Please do, Jack.

original: Faith, and I’ll send him packing.
translation: Okay, I will tell him to go.

original: Now, sirs. By 'r lady, you fought fair.—So did you,  Peto.— So did you, Bardolph.—You are lions too. You ran  away upon instinct. You will not touch the true Prince.  No, fie!
translation: Now, sirs, it must be said that you fought well. So did you, Peto. So did you, Bardolph. You are brave lions as well, and you only ran away because your instinct told you it was necessary. You will not attack a true Prince. No, that's for sure!

original: Faith, I ran when I saw others run.
translation: Truthfully, I only ran away when I saw the others running.

original: Faith, tell me now in earnest, how came Falstaff’s  sword so hacked?
translation: Okay, tell me the truth now. How did Falstaff's sword get so cut up?

original: Why, he hacked it with his dagger and said he would  swear truth out of England but he would make you believe it was done in fight, and persuaded us to do the like.
translation: Well, he hacked at it with his dagger, and then said that he would lie so convincingly and make you believe that he had done it fighting.  And he persuaded us to say the same.

original: Yea, and to tickle our noses with speargrass to make  them bleed, and then to beslubber our garments with it,  and swear it was the blood of true men. I did that I did not this seven year before: I blushed to hear his  monstrous devices.
translation: Yes, and he made us rub our noses with some sharp blades of grass to make them bleed, and then to smear this blood all over our clothes and say that it was the blood of the men we had fought. When he told us to tell this outrageous lie, I did something that I haven't done in seven years—I blushed.

original: O villain, thou stolest a cup of sack eighteen years  ago, and wert taken with the manner, and ever since thou hast blushed extempore. Thou hadst fire and sword on  thy side, and yet thou ran’st away. What instinct hadst  thou for it?
My lord, do you see these meteors? Do you behold these  exhalations?
translation: My lord, do you see these red lumps? Can you see these rashes on my face?

original: I do.
translation: I can.

original: What think you they portend?
Hot livers and cold purses.
Choler, my lord, if rightly taken.
translation: Anger, my lord, if I understand them correctly.

original: No, if rightly taken, halter.
My own knee? When I was about thy years, Hal, I was not an eagle’s talon in the waist. I could have crept into  any alderman’s thumb-ring.
translation: My own knee? When I was about your age, Hal, my waist was as thin as an eagle's claw. I could have got through any councilman's sealing ring.

original: A plague of sighing and  grief! It blows a man up like a bladder.
translation: To hell with sighing and sadness! It makes a man blow up like an inflatable.

original: There’s  villanous news abroad. Here was Sir John Bracy from your father. You must to the court in the morning.
translation: There's terrible news going around. That was Sir John Bracy, and he was sent here by your father. You must go to court in the morning.

original: That same mad fellow of the north, Percy, and he of Wales that  gave Amamon the bastinado, and made Lucifer cuckold, and swore the devil his true liegeman upon the cross of a  Welsh hook—what a plague call you him?
translation: Hotspur, that crazy fellow from the north, and that Welshman who beat up  Amamon , seduced the devil's wife, and caused the devil to swear to be his loyal servant by  threatening him with a hooked sword ...what the devil is his name again?

original: Owen Glendower.
translation: Owen Glendower.

original: Owen, Owen, the same, and his son-in-law Mortimer, and  old Northumberland, and that sprightly Scot of Scots,  Douglas, that runs a-horseback up a hill perpendicular—
translation: Owen, Owen, that's it. There's also his son-in-law Mortimer, old Northumberland, and that wonderful, energetic Scotsman, Douglas, who could probably ride a horse up a wall.

original: He that rides at high speed, and with his pistol kills  a sparrow flying.
translation: He rides so quickly, and then tries to kill a flying sparrow with his pistol.

original: You have hit it.
translation: You've got it exactly right.

original: So did he never the sparrow.
Well, that rascal hath good mettle in him. He will not  run.
translation: Well, that rascal has a lot of courage in him.  He won't run away.

original: Why, what a rascal art thou then to praise him so for  running?
translation: Why, you're a rascal!  You just gave him praise for running!

original: A-horseback, you cuckoo, but afoot he will not budge a  foot.
translation: I praised him for running on horseback, you simpleton, but when he's fighting on foot he won't move a muscle.

original: Yes, Jack, upon instinct.
translation: Yes he will, Jack—his instinct will tell him to.

original: I grant you, upon instinct.
translation: I'll give you that, he'll move if his instinct tells him to.

original: Well, he is there too, and  one Mordake, and a thousand blue-caps more:
translation: Well, he's there too, and so is a man called Mordake and about a thousand more  Scottish soldiers .

original: Worcester is stolen away tonight.
translation: Worcester has left London tonight,

original: Thy father’s beard is turned white with the news. You may buy land now as cheap as  stinking mackerel.
translation: and your father's beard turned white when he heard the news. Land is becoming as cheap as some stinking fish.

original: Why, then, it is like if there come a hot June, and  this civil buffeting hold, we shall buy maidenheads as  they buy hob-nails, by the hundreds.
By the Mass, thou sayest true. It is like we shall have good trading that way.
translation: I swear, you speak the truth. We'll have some good luck if it's like that.

original: But tell me, Hal, art not thou  horrible afeard? Thou being heir apparent, could the  world pick thee out three such enemies again as that  fiend Douglas, that spirit Percy, and that devil  Glendower?
translation: But, Hal, tell me—are you very scared? Since you are the heir to the throne, you are going to be the prime target of that wicked Douglas, that lively Percy, and that devil Glendower?

original: Art thou not horribly afraid? Doth not thy  blood thrill at it?
translation: Are you not horribly afraid? Don't you shudder with fear at the thought of it?

original: Not a whit, i' faith; I lack some of thy instinct.
translation: Not at all, truthfully. I must lack some of your instinct.

original: Well, thou wert be horribly chid tomorrow when thou  comest to thy father. If thou love me, practice an  answer.
translation: Well, you are going to be scolded horribly tomorrow when you see your father. I beg you, let's practice what you will say to him.

original: Do thou stand for my father and examine me upon the  particulars of my life.
translation: You can pretend to be my father, and ask me about what's happening in my life.

original: Shall I? Content. This chair shall be my state, this  dagger my scepter, and this cushion my crown.
translation: Should I? All right then. This chair will be my throne, this dagger will be my scepter, and this cushion will be my crown.

original: Thy state is taken for a joined stool, thy golden  scepter for a leaden dagger, and thy precious rich crown for a pitiful bald crown.

Well, an the fire of grace be not quite out of thee,  now shalt thou be moved.—Give me a cup of sack to make  my eyes look red, that it may be thought I have wept,  for I must speak in passion, and I will do it in King  Cambyses' vein.
Well, here is my leg.
translation: Well then, I make my bow to you.

original: And here is my speech. Stand aside, nobility.
translation: And here is my speech for you. Stand aside, noblemen.

original: O Jesu, this is excellent sport, i' faith!
translation: Oh Jesus, this is an excellent game, really!

original: Weep not, sweet queen, for trickling tears are vain.
translation: Don't cry, my sweet Queen, your falling tears are pointless.

original: O the father, how he holds his countenance!
translation: Oh look at the father—he's really good at keeping a straight face.

original: For God’s sake, lords, convey my tristful queen, For tears do stop the floodgates of her eyes.
translation: For God's sake, lords, take my sad queen away from here. The floodgates of her eyes are now filled up with her tears.

original: O Jesu, he doth it as like one of these harlotry  players as ever I see.
translation: Oh Jesus, he's so much like one of those silly real actors!

original: Peace, good pint-pot. Peace, good tickle-brain.—
translation: Enough, good pint of ale. Enough, good liquor-brain.

original: What manner of man, an it like your Majesty?
translation: What type of man is he, your Majesty?

original: A goodly portly man, i' faith, and a corpulent;
translation: A handsome, dignified man, indeed, and quite overweight.

original: of a  cheerful look, a pleasing eye, and a most noble  carriage,
translation: He always looks cheerful, is quite attractive, and has a very noble demeanor about him.

original: and, as I think, his age some fifty, or, by 'r Lady, inclining to three score; and now I remember me,  his name is Falstaff.
translation: I would say that he is about fifty, or, my goodness, possibly closer to sixty. I remember now—his name is Falstaff.

original: If that man should be lewdly  given, he deceiveth me, for, Harry, I see virtue in his  looks. If then the tree may be known by the fruit, as  the fruit by the tree, then peremptorily I speak it:  there is virtue in that Falstaff;
translation: If that man is at all inclined to wickedness, then he has deceived me, Harry, because I see goodness in his character.  If a tree is known by its fruit , and the fruit by its tree, then I can positively say that there is a lot of goodness in that Falstaff.

original: him keep with, the  rest banish. And tell me now, thou naughty varlet, tell  me, where hast thou been this month?
translation: Keep him in your company, and get rid of the rest. Tell me now, you naughty boy, tell me—where have you been this last month?

original: Dost thou speak like a king? Do thou stand for me, and  I’ll play my father.
translation: Is that what a king would say? You pretend to be me, and I'll play my father.

original: Depose me? If thou dost it half so gravely, so  majestically, both in word and matter, hang me up by the heels for a rabbit-sucker or a poulter’s hare.
translation: You're going to take me off the throne? If you manage to do it even half as sincerely or majestically as I did, in both words and behavior, then hang me up like some baby rabbit for sale in a poultry shop.

original: Well, here I am set.
translation: Well, I'm seated and ready.

original: And here I stand. —    Judge, my masters.
translation: And I'll stand here.

original: Now, Harry, whence come you?
translation: Now, Harry, where have you come from?

original: My noble lord, from Eastcheap.
translation: My noble lord, I have come from Eastcheap.

original: The complaints I hear of thee are grievous.
translation: I have heard some very serious complaints about you.

original: 'Sblood, my lord, they are false.—    Nay, I’ll tickle you for a young prince, i' faith.
translation: Damn it, my lord, they're all lies.

original: Swearest thou? Ungracious boy, henceforth ne'er look on me.
translation: Did you just swear? You rude boy, never look at me again.

original: Thou art violently carried away from grace. There  is a devil haunts thee in the likeness of an old fat  man.
translation: You have been forcefully turned away from goodness. There is a devil that haunts you and it looks very much like an old, fat man.

original: A tun of man is thy companion. Why dost thou  converse with that trunk of humors, that bolting-hutch  of beastliness, that swollen parcel of dropsies, that  huge bombard of sack, that stuffed cloakbag of guts,  that roasted Manningtree ox with the pudding in his  belly, that reverend Vice, that gray iniquity, that  father ruffian, that vanity in years?
translation: A ton of man is your companion. Why do you associate yourself with that container of diseases, that sifting bin of beastliness, that swollen crate of disease, that huge case of wine, that stuffed suitcase of stomach, that roasted ox stuffed with pudding, that reverend  Vice , that grey-haired sinner, that elderly swaggerer, that man who has aged with vanity?

original: Wherein is he  good, but to taste sack and drink it? Wherein neat and  cleanly but to carve a capon and eat it?
translation: What is he good for, except to taste wine and then drink it? What is he skilled at besides carving a chicken and eating it?

original: Wherein cunning but in craft? Wherein crafty but in villany? Wherein  villanous but in all things? Wherein worthy but in  nothing?
translation: What is he smart about besides scheming? What does he scheme about besides dirty tricks? Why is he wicked in all respects? Is he really worth anything?

original: I would your Grace would take me with you. Whom means  your Grace?
translation: I wish your Grace would explain what you mean a bit better. Who are you talking about, your Grace?

original: That villanous abominable misleader of youth, Falstaff, that old white-bearded Satan.
translation: That evil, horrific corrupter of youth—Falstaff, that old, white-bearded devil.

original: My lord, the man I know.
translation: My lord, I know the man.

original: I know thou dost.
translation: I know you do.

original: But to say I know more harm in him than in myself were  to say more than I know. That he is old, the more the  pity; his white hairs do witness it. But that he is,  saving your reverence, a whoremaster, that I utterly  deny.
translation: For me to say that he is worse than I am, would be more than I am able to say. He is old, that's true, and it's a shame—his white hairs prove his age. But to say that he's a—forgive me—a pimp, that I completely deny.

original: If sack and sugar be a fault, God help the wicked. If to be old and merry be a sin, then many an old host  that I know is damned. If to be fat be to be hated, then Pharaoh’s lean kine are to be loved.
translation: If drinking sweet wine is a sin, then God help us all. If being old and cheerful is a sin, then most old innkeepers I know are damned. If it is bad to be fat, then we should all love  Pharaoh's lean cows .

original: No, my good lord,  banish Peto, banish Bardolph, banish Poins, but for  sweet Jack Falstaff, kind Jack Falstaff, true Jack  Falstaff, valiant Jack Falstaff, and therefore more  valiant being, as he is old Jack Falstaff,
translation: No, my good lord, banish Peto, banish Bardolph, banish Poins. As for sweet Jack Falstaff, kind Jack Falstaff, honest Jack Falstaff, brave Jack Falstaff—and he is made more brave, since he is old Jack Falstaff—

original: banish not  him thy Harry’s company, banish not him thy Harry’s  company. Banish plump Jack, and banish all the world.
translation: don't banish him from Harry's company. Don't get rid of him. If you get rid of plump Jack, you'll be getting rid of the entire world.

original: I do, I will.
O, my lord, my lord, the Sheriff with a most monstrous  watch is at the door.
translation: Oh my lord, my lord, the Sheriff is at the door with an unusually large group of officers.

original: Out, you rogue.—Play out the play. I have much to say  in the behalf of that Falstaff.
translation: Get out, you idiot. We need to finish our play. I still have a lot to say on behalf of that Falstaff.

original: O Jesu, my lord, my lord—
translation: Oh Jesus, my lord, my lord—

original: Heigh, heigh, the devil rides upon a fiddlestick.  What’s the matter?
translation: Hey, hey! What a lot of commotion. What's the matter?

original: The Sheriff and all the watch are at the door. They are come to search the house. Shall I let them in?
translation: The Sheriff and a group of officers are at the door. They have come to search the bar. Should I let them in?

original: Dost thou hear, Hal? Never call a true piece of gold a  counterfeit. Thou art essentially made, without seeming  so.
translation: Did you hear that, Hal? Never call a real piece of gold a fake—you are true and loyal, even if your recent behavior doesn't show it.

original: And thou a natural coward without instinct.
translation: And you are an born coward, with no instinct.

original: I deny your major. If you will deny the Sheriff, so; if not, let him enter. If I become not a cart as well as  another man, a plague on my bringing up. I hope I shall  as soon be strangled with a halter as another.
translation: I reject your logic. If you are going to reject the Sheriff, then do it.  If not, then let him come in. If I'm not as impressive on the hangman's cart as the next man, then a curse on my upbringing. I'm as willing to be hanged as any other man.

original: Go, hide thee behind the arras. The rest walk up  above.— Now, my masters, for a true face and good conscience.
Both which I have had, but their date is out; and  therefore I’ll hide me.
translation: I've had both of those, but their lease has expired, and so I think I'll hide.

original: Call in the Sheriff.
translation: Call in the Sheriff.

original: First pardon me, my lord. A hue and cry Hath followed certain men unto this house.
What men?
translation: What men?

original: One of them is well known, my gracious lord, A gross fat man.
translation: One of them is very well known, my gracious lord. He is a large, fat man.

original: As fat as butter.
translation: As fat as butter.

original: The man, I do assure you is not here,   For I myself at this time have employed him.
translation: I can assure you that that man isn't here, because I have just sent him on an errand.

original: And, Sheriff, I will engage my word to thee   That I will by tomorrow dinner time   Send him to answer thee
translation: And, Sheriff, I give you my word that I will send him to appear before you by midday tomorrow

original: or any man   For any thing he shall be charged withal.
translation: with any other man that you need. He will answer to anything that he has been accused of.

original: And so let me entreat you leave the house.
translation: Now, will you please leave this bar?

original: I will, my lord. There are two gentlemen Have in this robbery lost three hundred marks.
It may be so. If he have robbed these men, He shall be answerable; and so farewell.
translation: I'm sure that's true. If he has robbed these men, then he will be held responsible for it. And so, take care.

original: Good night, my noble lord.
translation: Good night, my noble lord.

original: I think it is good morrow, is it not?
translation: I think it's good morning by now, isn't it?

original: Indeed, my lord, I think it be two o'clock.
translation: Indeed it is, my lord. It is two o'clock in the morning by now.

original: This oily rascal is known as well as Paul’s. Go call  him forth.
translation: This shifty rascal is as famous as St. Paul's Cathedral. Go and get him.

original: Falstaff!—    Fast asleep behind  the arras, and snorting like a horse.
translation: Falstaff!   He is fast asleep behind here, and snoring like a horse.

original: Hark, how hard he fetches breath. Search his pockets.
translation: God, listen to how heavy his breathing is. Search his pockets.

original: Nothing but papers, my lord.
translation: Just some papers, my lord.

original: Let’s see what they be. Read them.
translation: Let's see what they say. Read them.

original: (reads) Item, a capon, … 2s. 2d.   Item, sauce, … 4d.   Item, sack, two gallons, … 5s. 8d.   Item, anchovies and sack after supper, , , , 2s. 6d.   Item, bread, ob.
translation: "Item One: A chicken—2 shillings, 2 pence. Item Two: Sauce—4 pence.Item Three: Wine, two gallons—5 shillings, 8 pence.Item Four: Anchovies and wine after dinner—2 shillings, 6 pence.Item Five: Bread— half a penny."

original: O monstrous! But one halfpennyworth of bread to this  intolerable deal of sack!
translation: Oh, how horrid! Just half a penny's worth of bread compared to this ridiculous amount of wine!

original: What there is else, keep  close. We’ll read it at more advantage. There let him  sleep till day. I’ll to the court in the morning.
translation: Hold tight to everything else you found; we'll look at it when we have more time. Let him sleep there until the morning, and then I'll go to court.

original: We  must all to the wars, and thy place shall be honorable.  I’ll procure this fat rogue a charge of foot, and I know his death will be a march of twelve score.
translation: We're all going to have to fight in these wars, and you will all have honorable positions. I'm going to put this fat idiot in charge of some foot soldiers, and I bet he'll be dead before they've traveled even two hundred and forty yards.

original: The money  shall be paid back again with advantage. Be with me  betimes in the morning, and so good morrow, Peto.
translation: I will pay back the money that was robbed with interest. Meet me early in the morning and with that, good morning, Peto.

original: Good morrow, good my lord.
translation: Good morning, my good lord.

original: These promises are fair, the parties sure, And our induction full of prosperous hope.
translation: These offers of support are good, our allies are reliable, and the beginning of our mission seems very hopeful.

original: Lord Mortimer and cousin Glendower, Will you sit down? And Uncle Worcester— A plague upon it, I have forgot the map.
translation: Lord Mortimer and cousin Glendower, won't you sit down? And Uncle Worcester—oh damn it! I forgot to bring the map.

original: No, here it is. Sit, cousin Percy
translation: No, here it is. Sit down, cousin Percy,

original: Sit, good cousin Hotspur, for by that name   As oft as Lancaster doth speak of you
translation: sit down good cousin  Hotspur . For that is the name that  King Henry  normally calls you by,

original: His cheek looks pale and with a rising sigh   He wisheth you in heaven.
translation: and when he does he grows pale and with a groan, he wishes you were in heaven.

original: And you in hell, As oft as he hears Owen Glendower spoke of.
translation: And every time he hears someone speak about Owen Glendower, he wishes that you were in hell.

original: I cannot blame him.
translation: I can't blame him.

original: At my nativity   The front of heaven was full of fiery shapes,   Of burning cressets,
translation: When I was born the whole sky was full of fiery comets and meteors ,

original: and at my birth   The frame and huge foundation of the earth   Shaked like a coward.
translation: and at my birth, the whole of the earth shook like some kind of coward.

original: Why, so it would have done At the same season if your mother’s cat Had but kittened, though yourself had never been born.
translation: The same thing would have happened if your mother's cat had given birth to kittens that day, whether you had been born or not.

original: I say the earth did shake when I was born.
translation: I am telling you that the earth shook when I was born.

original: And I say the earth was not of my mind, If you suppose as fearing you it shook.
translation: And I am saying that if you think the earth shook because it was scared of you, then the earth and I think differently.

original: The heavens were all on fire; the earth did tremble.
translation: The sky was on fire, and the earth trembled.

original: O, then the earth shook to see the heavens on fire,   And not in fear of your nativity.
translation: Oh, then maybe the earth shook because it saw that the sky was on fire, not because it was scared of your birth.

original: Diseas—d nature oftentimes breaks forth   In strange eruptions;
translation: When nature is sick, there are often earthquakes.

original: oft the teeming earth   Is with a kind of colic pinched and vexed   By the imprisoning of unruly wind   Within her womb, which, for enlargement striving,   Shakes the old beldam earth and topples down   Steeples and moss-grown towers.
translation: Often the fertile earth is affected and irritated by a pain in her stomach, because she shelters uncontrollable wind within her, which is trying to break free and so shakes the old,  grandmother  earth and knocks over steeples and moss-covered towers.

original: At your birth   Our grandam earth, having this distemperature,   In passion shook.
translation: When you were born, our grandmother earth, feeling this pain, shook in distress.

original: Cousin, of many men   I do not bear these crossings.
translation: Cousin, I wouldn't take these kinds of insults from many men.

original: Give me leave   To tell you once again that at my birth   The front of heaven was full of fiery shapes,
translation: Let me tell you once more that when I was born, the sky was full of fiery comets.

original: The goats ran from the mountains, and the herds   Were strangely clamorous to the frighted fields.
translation: The goats ran away from the mountains, and the animals in the fields were stamping in fear.

original: These signs have marked me extraordinary,   And all the courses of my life do show   I am not in the roll of common men.
translation: These signs have made me an extraordinary man, and everything that has happened to me in my life proves that I should not be considered alongside ordinary men.

original: Where is he living, clipped in with the sea   That chides the banks of England, Scotland, Wales,   Which calls me pupil or hath read to me?
translation: Is there anyone on this island—anyone that lives in England, Scotland, or Wales—who can claim to be my teacher?

original: And bring him out that is but woman’s son   Can trace me in the tedious ways of art   And hold me pace in deep experiments.
translation: Bring out any mortal who can follow me in doing magic and keep up with me in mysterious experiments.

original: I think there’s no man speaks better Welsh. I’ll to dinner.
Peace, cousin Percy. You will make him mad.
translation: Stop now, cousin Percy. You will make him angry.

original: I can call spirits from the vasty deep.
translation: I can summon up spirits from the depths of the ocean.

original: Why, so can I, or so can any man, But will they come when you do call for them?
translation: Well I can, too, and so can any man. The question is, will they come when you call for them?

original: Why, I can teach you, cousin, to command the devil.
translation: I can teach you to command the devil.

original: And I can teach thee, coz, to shame the devil   By telling truth. Tell truth and shame the devil.
translation: And I can teach you, pal, how to shame the devil—by telling the truth!  "Tell the truth and shame the devil," that's what they say .

original: If thou have power to raise him, bring him hither,   And I’ll be sworn I have power to shame him hence.
translation: If you have the power to summon up the devil then do it. I will swear that I have the power to shame him into leaving again.

original: O, while you live, tell truth and shame the devil!
translation: Oh, as long as you're alive, tell the truth and shame the devil!

original: Come, come, no more of this unprofitable chat.
translation: Come on now, let's stop this pointless talking.

original: Three times hath Henry Bolingbroke made head   Against my power;
translation: Henry Bolingbroke has taken military action against me three times now.

original: thrice from the banks of Wye   And sandy-bottomed Severn have I sent him
translation: And three time I have sent him back from the banks of the   Wye  River and the sandy bottoms of the Severn River ,

original: Bootless home and weather-beaten back.
translation: unsuccessful  and defeated by the bad weather.

original: Home without boots, and in foul weather too! How ’scapes he agues, in the devil’s name?
Come, here’s the map. Shall we divide our right According to our threefold order ta'en?
translation: Come on, here's the map. Should we divide up the land according to our three-way agreement?

original: The Archdeacon hath divided it   Into three limits very equally:
translation: The  Archdeacon  has divided it into three parts very equally.

original: England, from Trent and Severn hitherto,   By south and east is to my part assigned;
translation: I will take all of England that is south-east of the Trent and Severn Rivers;

original: All westward, Wales beyond the Severn shore,   And all the fertile land within that bound   To Owen Glendower;
translation: Owen Glendower, you will take the whole of Wales, and everything that is west of the River Severn, including all of the fertile land in that area.

original: A shorter time shall send me to you, lords,
translation: I will be with you sooner than that, my lords,

original: And in my conduct shall your ladies come,
translation: and I will bring your ladies along with me, and keep them safe.

original: From whom you now must steal and take no leave,   For there will be a world of water shed   Upon the parting of your wives and you.
translation: I would advise you to leave now, and don't say goodbye, otherwise they will cry so many tears when you have to go.

original: Methinks my moiety, north from Burton here,   In quantity equals not one of yours.
translation: I don't think that my share of the land, everything north of  Burton  here is equal to your shares.

original: See how this river comes me cranking in   And cuts me from the best of all my land   A huge half-moon, a monstrous cantle out.
translation: Look how the river bends here, and cuts out a huge semi-circle—a chunk out of some of my best land.

original: I’ll have the current in this place dammed up,   And here the smug and silver Trent shall run   In a new channel, fair and evenly.
translation: I'm going to build a dam, and force the smooth water of the Trent River to go a different way, to run straighter.

original: It shall not wind with such a deep indent,   To rob me of so rich a bottom here.
translation: That way it won't make such an deep cut into my portion of the land, and won't rob me of the fertile river valley.

original: Not wind? It shall, it must. You see it doth.
translation: A river not wind? It has to; it must. You can see that it does.

original: Yea, but   Mark how he bears his course,
translation: Yes, but look at how the Trent carries on its journey,

original: and runs me up   With like advantage on the other side,
translation: and does a similar thing in my section later on,

original: Gelding the opposèd continent as much   As on the other side it takes from you.
translation: cutting as large a piece out of my side as it does out of yours.

original: Yea, but a little charge will trench him here And on this north side win this cape of land, And then he runs straight and even.
translation: Yes, but with a little bit of money, you can dig a trench to divert the river, and will get back this bit of land on the north side of the river.  And then it will run straight from then on.

original: I’ll have it so. A little charge will do it.
translation: Okay, I can do that. It will only take a little bit of money.

original: I’ll not have it altered.
translation: I don't want the river to be changed.

original: Will not you?
translation: Why not?

original: No, nor you shall not.
translation: And I won't let you do it.

original: Who shall say me nay?
translation: Oh, are you going to stop me?

original: Why, that will I.
translation: Yes, I will.

original: Let me not understand you, then; speak it in Welsh.
translation: Say so in Welsh then, so I don't have to understand what you're saying.

original: I can speak English, lord, as well as you,
translation: My lord, I can speak English as well as you can.

original: For I was trained up in the English court,
translation: For I was raised in the English court,

original: Where being but young I framèd to the harp   Many an English ditty lovely well
translation: and when I was young I composed many lovely English songs,

original: And gave the tongue a helpful ornament—   A virtue that was never seen in you.
translation: and my Welsh gave the lyrics something extra—an achievement you never had.

original: Marry,   And I am glad of it with all my heart:
translation: Indeed, and I am happy about that.

original: I had rather be a kitten and cry “mew”   Than one of these same meter balladmongers.
translation: I would rather be a kitten and only be able to say, "meow," than be  a hawker of ballads !

original: I had rather hear a brazen can’stick turned,   Or a dry wheel grate on the axletree,
translation: I would rather hear the grating sound of a brass candlestick being smoothed down on a  lathe , or an un-oiled wheel scraping against an axle.

original: And that would set my teeth nothing an edge,   Nothing so much as mincing poetry.   'Tis like the forced gait of a shuffling nag.
translation: Nothing puts my teeth on edge more than fussy poetry. It's like the painful steps of an old horse.

original: Come, you shall have Trent turned.
translation: Okay then, you can change the course of the Trent.

original: I do not care.
translation: I don't care.

original: I’ll give thrice so much land   To any well-deserving friend;
translation: I would give three times this amount of land to a friend who deserves it.

original: But in the way of bargain, mark you me,   I’ll cavil on the ninth part of a hair.
translation: But when I am negotiating about business, I will argue over the tiniest fraction of a hair, that's for sure.

original: Are the indentures drawn? Shall we be gone?
translation: Are the agreements drawn up? Are we ready to go?

original: The moon shines fair. You may away by night.
translation: The moon is bright, so you can leave tonight.

original: I’ll haste the writer,
translation: I will tell the man writing up the agreements to hurry,

original: and withal   Break with your wives of your departure hence.
translation: and at the same time, I will break the news to your wives that you are leaving.

original: I am afraid my daughter will run mad,   So much she doteth on her Mortimer.
translation: I am afraid my daughter will go crazy at the news, she loves Mortimer so much.

original: Fie, cousin Percy, how you cross my father!
translation: Damn it, cousin Percy!  You made my father-in-law so annoyed!

original: I cannot choose.
translation: I can't help it.

original: Sometime he angers me   With telling me of the moldwarp and the ant,
translation: Sometimes he makes me angry, when he talks about ridiculous things, like  moles  and ants.

original: Of the dreamer Merlin and his prophecies,   And of a dragon and a finless fish,   A clip-winged griffin and a moulten raven,   A couching lion and a ramping cat,
translation: Like that wizard  Merlin  and his prophecies. A dragon. A fish without fins. A wingless  griffin , and a raven with no feathers. A lion lying down, a cat ready to pounce,

original: And such a deal of skimble-skamble stuff   As puts me from my faith.
translation: and so much other nonsensical talk that I don't know what to believe, including my Christian faith!

original: I tell you what—   He held me last night at least nine hours   In reckoning up the several devils' names   That were his lackeys.
translation: I tell you what—he made me stay awake for at least nine hours last night, telling me the names of various devils that were his attendants.

original: I cried “Hum,” and “Well, go  to,”   But marked him not a word.
translation: I said, "Hmm," and "Well, do  go on ," at various moments. But I didn't pay attention to a word he was saying.

original: O, he is as tedious   As a tired horse, a railing wife,   Worse than a smoky house:
translation: Oh, he is as boring as a tired horse, or  a complaining wife . He's worse than a house filled with smoke!

original: I had rather live   With cheese and garlic in a windmill, far,   Than feed on cates and have him talk to me   In any summerhouse in Christendom.
translation: I would rather live in a windmill, and only eat  cheese and garlic , than feed on delicacies and have to talk to him in any nice house in the countryside.

original: In faith, he is a worthy gentleman,
translation: Yet, indeed, he is a very worthy gentleman.

original: Exceedingly well read and profited   In strange concealments,
translation: He is incredibly well read, and skilled in the occult.

original: valiant as a lion,   And as wondrous affable, and as bountiful   As mines of India.
translation: He is as courageous as a lion, friendly, and as generous as  the mines of India .

original: Shall I tell you, cousin?   He holds your temper in a high respect   And curbs himself even of his natural scope   When you come cross his humor. Faith, he does.
translation: And you know what, cousin? He greatly respects your character, and restrains himself from getting angry—even though that is his first instinct—when you provoke him. I promise he does.

original: I warrant you that man is not alive   Might so have tempted him as you have done   Without the taste of danger and reproof.   But do not use it oft, let me entreat you.
translation: I am telling you that there is not a man alive who could have provoked him like you do without getting a dangerous reaction from him. Don't make a habit of it though—I'm begging you.

original: (to   HOTSPUR   )   In faith, my lord, you are too  willful-blame,
translation: [To HOTSPUR]  Truthfully, my lord, you are wrong to be so stubborn.

original: And, since your coming hither, have done enough   To put him quite beside his patience.
translation: Ever since you got here, you have done more than enough to test his patience.

original: You must needs learn, lord, to amend this fault.   Though sometimes it show greatness, courage, blood—   And that’s the dearest grace it renders you—
translation: You should learn to stop doing this as much, my lord. Sometimes it does reveal greatness, courage, and spirit—and that's an advantage for you.

original: Yet oftentimes it doth present harsh rage,   Defect of manners, want of government,   Pride, haughtiness, opinion, and disdain,
translation: Yet, it also demonstrates anger, bad manners, lack of self-control, pride, arrogance, judgment, and hatred.

original: The least of which, haunting a nobleman,   Loseth men’s hearts and leaves behind a stain   Upon the beauty of all parts besides,   Beguiling them of commendation.
translation: Any of these traits, if they become associated with a nobleman, will make him lose the support of other men.  And they will leave behind a stain on his beautiful accomplishments, cheating him out of praise.

original: Well, I am schooled. Good manners be your speed! Here come our wives, and let us take our leave.
translation: Well, I've learned my lesson. May your good manners bring you success! Here come our wives. Let's prepare to leave them.

original: This is the deadly spite that angers me: My wife can speak no English, I no Welsh.
translation: This is the awful annoyance that makes me angry—my wife doesn't speak any English, and I don't speak any Welsh.

original: My daughter weeps; she’ll not part with you. She’ll be a soldier too, she’ll to the wars.
translation: My daughter is crying because she doesn't want to be parted from you. She says that she wishes that she was a soldier too, so that she could go to war with you.

original: Good father, tell her that she and my aunt Percy Shall follow in your conduct speedily.
She is desperate here, a peevish self-willed harlotry, One that no persuasion can do good upon.
translation: She is miserable now, a bad-tempered, headstrong hussy. No-one's going to be able to change that.

original: I understand thy looks.
translation: I understand you by looking at your face.

original: That pretty Welsh   Which thou pourest down from these swelling heavens   I am too perfect in,
translation: I understand only too well those pretty Welsh tears that pour from your heavenly eyes.

original: and but for shame   In such a parley should I answer thee.
translation: And I would answer in the same language,  if it wasn't shameful for me to cry .

original: Nay, if you melt, then will she run mad.
translation: Be careful, if you show your feelings too much, you'll make her go crazy.

original: O, I am ignorance itself in this!
translation: Oh, I have no clue what she's saying!

original: She bids you on the wanton rushes lay you down   And rest your gentle head upon her lap,
translation: She asks you to lie down on the floor, covered thick with  reeds , and rest your soft head on her lap.

original: And she will sing the song that pleaseth you   And on your eyelids crown the god of sleep,
translation: She will sing you whichever song you would like to hear until your eyelids droop, and  you fall asleep .

original: Charming your blood with pleasing heaviness,   Making such difference ’twixt wake and sleep
translation: She will charm you so that you will feel pleasantly heavy, somewhere in between being awake and being asleep—

original: As is the difference betwixt day and night   The hour before the heavenly harnessed team   Begins his golden progress in the east.
translation: like the change from day to night, that hour before the sun begins its golden journey in the east.

original: With all my heart I’ll sit and hear her sing. By that time will our book, I think, be drawn
