translation: I would love to sit and hear her sing. By the time she's done, our final documents should be ready.

original: Do so;
translation: Please, do.

original: And those musicians that shall play to you   Hang in the air a thousand leagues from hence,
translation: The musicians who are going to play for you are currently hanging in the air about a thousand  leagues  from here,

original: And straight they shall be here.
translation: and will be here very soon. Sit down and wait for them.

original: Come, Kate, thou art perfect in lying down. Come, quick, quick, that I may lay my head in thy lap.
Go, you giddy goose.
translation: Stop that, you silly goose.

original: Now I perceive the devil understands Welsh, And ’tis no marvel he is so humorous. By 'r Lady, he is a good musician.
Then should you be nothing but musical, for you are  altogether governed by humors. Lie still, you thief, and hear the lady sing in Welsh.
translation: Then it's a wonder you're not more musical, for you are the most unpredictable man there is. Lie still, you thief and listen to the lady singing in Welsh.

original: I had rather hear Lady, my brach, howl in Irish.
Wouldst thou have thy head broken?
translation: Would you like to have your head broken?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: Then be still.
translation: Then be quiet.

original: Neither;’tis a woman’s fault.
Now God help thee!
translation: God help you!

original: To the Welsh lady’s bed.
translation: Into the Welsh lady's bed.

original: What’s that?
translation: What did you say?

original: Peace, she sings.
translation: Be quiet! She's singing.

original: Come, Kate, I’ll have your song too.
translation: Come on, Kate—I'd like to hear your song, too.

original: Not mine, in good sooth.
translation: Not mine, darn it.

original: Not yours, in good sooth!
translation: "Not mine, darn it?"

original: Heart, you swear like a  comfit-maker’s wife!
translation: Goodness , you swear like a candy-maker's wife!

original: “Not you, in good sooth,” and “as  true as I live,” and “as God shall mend me,” and “as  sure as day”—
translation: "Not you, darn it." And "I swear on my life," and "God will forgive me," and "as clear as day."

original: And givest such sarcenet surety for thy oaths   As if thou never walk’st further than Finsbury.
translation: Your swearing is  as weak as a light silk , you would think that you had never been further than  Finsbury .

original: Swear me, Kate, like a lady as thou art,
translation: Swear like the lady you are Kate, so that it fills your mouth.

original: A good mouth-filling oath, and leave “in sooth,”   And such protest of pepper-gingerbread,
translation: Leave out words like "darn it," and outrage at spicy, rude  language ,

original: To velvet-guards and Sunday citizens.   Come, sing.
translation: that should be left for citizens wearing their Sunday best, trimmed with velvet. Come on, sing for us.

original: I will not sing.
translation: I will not sing.

original: 'Tis the next way to turn tailor, or be red-breast  teacher. An the indentures be drawn, I’ll away within  these two hours, and so come in when ye will.
Come, come, Lord Mortimer;
translation: Come on, Lord Mortimer,

original: you are as slow   As hot Lord Percy is on fire to go.
translation: you are as reluctant to leave as the eager Lord Percy is burning to go.

original: By this our book is drawn.
translation: Our agreements have now been drawn up.

original: We’ll but seal,   And then to horse immediately.
translation: We just need to sign them, and then we should leave right after.

original: With all my heart.
translation: I will, with all my heart.

original: Lords, give us leave;
translation: Lords, leave us alone for a bit.

original: the Prince of Wales and I   Must have some private conference,
translation: I need to talk in private with my son.

original: but be near at hand,   For we shall presently have need of you.
translation: But stay close though,  because we will need you again soon.

original: So please your Majesty, I would I could   Quit all offenses with as clear excuse   As well as I am doubtless I can purge   Myself of many I am charged withal.
translation: If I may please speak, your Majesty, I wish I could prove my innocence against all of these charges. And I am confident that I can clear myself of many of them.

original: Yet such extenuation let me beg   As, in reproof of many tales devised,   Which oft the ear of greatness needs must hear,   By smiling pickthanks and base newsmongers,
translation: Yet, let me beg one thing of you. Do not believe all of the false things you have heard about me, stories that smiling informers and silly gossips love to tell great men like you.

original: I may for some things true, wherein my youth   Hath faulty wandered and irregular,   Find pardon on my true submission.
translation: With this in mind, try and forgive me for the things which I will admit  are true—the offenses that I have committed in my reckless and foolish youth.

original: God pardon thee.
translation: God forgive you.

original: Yet let me wonder, Harry,   At thy affections, which do hold a wing   Quite from the flight of all thy ancestors.
translation: But, I am surprised, Harry, at your tendencies, which are so different from any of your ancestors.

original: Thy place in council thou hast rudely lost,   Which by thy younger brother is supplied,   And art almost an alien to the hearts   Of all the court and princes of my blood.
translation: Your  rude behavior  has lost you your place in the Council, and now your younger brother holds that position. You are almost a stranger in the hearts of all the members of the court, and the other members of our family.

original: The hope and expectation of thy time   Is ruined, and the soul of every man   Prophetically doth forethink thy fall.
translation: All the hope and the expectations for your life have been lost, and in their hearts every man anticipates your downfall.

original: Had I so lavish of my presence been,   So common-hackneyed in the eyes of men,   So stale and cheap to vulgar company,   Opinion, that did help me to the crown,   Had still kept loyal to possession   And left me in reputeless banishment,   A fellow of no mark nor likelihood.
translation: If I had been so visible in public—considered  so cheap and vulgar  in men's eyes—and so friendly with the common masses, then the public opinion which helped me to get this crown, would have instead stayed  loyal to Richard . I would have been left in exile, a man with no reputation, or promise of success.

original: By being seldom seen, I could not stir   But like a comet I was wondered at;
translation: But because I stayed away from the public eye, I could only be admired,  like a comet , when I did appear.

original: That men would tell their children “This is he.”   Others would say “Where? Which is Bolingbroke?”
translation: Men tell their children, "That's him." Others say "Where? Which one is Bolingbroke?"

original: And then I stole all courtesy from heaven,   And dressed myself in such humility   That I did pluck allegiance from men’s hearts,   Loud shouts and salutations from their mouths,   Even in the presence of the crownèd King.
translation: I became almost a godlike figure, and behaved with such modesty that I won the support of men's hearts and the loud shouts and tributes from their mouths, even when King Richard himself was present.

original: Thus did I keep my person fresh and new,   My presence, like a robe pontifical,   Ne'er seen but wondered at, and so my state,   Seldom but sumptuous, showed like a feast   And won by rareness such solemnity.
translation: This is how I keep myself fresh and new. My presence is like a bishop's robe—admired on the infrequent occasions it is seen—and my public appearances, although they are rare, are magnificent, like a feast which wins great respect because of its rarity.

original: The skipping King, he ambled up and down   With shallow jesters and rash bavin wits,   Soon kindled and soon burnt;
translation: Frivolous King Richard , he skipped everywhere with shallow clowns and flashy, superficial jokers.  Like brushwood, he burned out almost as quickly as he was lit.

original: carded his state,   Mingled his royalty with cap'ring fools,   Had his great name profanèd with their scorns,   And gave his countenance, against his name,   To laugh at gibing boys and stand the push   Of every beardless vain comparative;
translation: He destroyed his kingdom by mixing royalty with prancing idiots. His reputation was destroyed because he was scorned for the fools he associated with.  And he lost  respect  by laughing with these joking boys and exposing himself to the mockery of every young joker around.

original: Grew a companion to the common streets,   Enfeoffed himself to popularity,   That, being daily swallowed by men’s eyes,   They surfeited with honey and began   To loathe the taste of sweetness, whereof a little   More than a little is by much too much.
translation: He got used to spending time in common places, and  committed himself  to being popular. Soon they saw him every day, and he became like the taste of too much honey—when you start to hate the taste, and even a little bit of it is too much.

original: So, when he had occasion to be seen,   He was but as the cuckoo is in June,   Heard, not regarded; seen,
translation: In the end, when he was seen, he was like a  cuckoo in June —people heard him but they didn't pay attention.

original: but with such eyes   As, sick and blunted with community,   Afford no extraordinary gaze   Such as is bent on sunlike majesty   When it shines seldom in admiring eyes,
translation: When people's eyes are so used to seeing something, they don't pay much attention to it. They didn't look with a special gaze, like they would when the sun shines into their wondering eyes, as it does so rarely.

original: But rather drowsed and hung their eyelids down,   Slept in his face, and rendered such aspect   As cloudy men use to their adversaries,   Being with his presence glutted, gorged, and full.
translation: Instead, they lost interest, and looked at the ground.  It was as like they were asleep in front of him, and looked at him with the same sort of expression that frowning men use for their enemies, as they were so crammed full, stuffed, and full with his presence.

original: And in that very line, Harry, standest thou,   For thou has lost thy princely privilege   With vile participation.
translation: And that is where you currently stand, Harry. For you have lost your status as a prince by hanging out with vulgar people.

original: Not an eye   But is aweary of thy common sight,   Save mine, which hath desired to see thee more,   Which now doth that I would not have it do,   Make blind itself with foolish tenderness.
translation: There's not an eye in this world that isn't tired of seeing you. Except mine, which would like to see you more, yet now act against instructions, by filling with tears.

original: I shall hereafter, my thrice gracious lord, Be more myself.
translation: I will try and behave more like myself from now on, my gracious father.

original: For all the world   As thou art to this hour was Richard then   When I from France set foot at Ravenspurgh,
translation: I must say that up to now, you have acted like Richard did when I first returned to Ravenspurgh from France.

original: And even as I was then is Percy now.   Now, by my scepter, and my soul to boot,   He hath more worthy interest to the state   Than thou, the shadow of succession.
translation: I recognize that Percy is acting a lot like I did then . Now, on my sword, and on my soul as well, he has a more valid claim to the kingdom than you do, as you are a poor imitation of a successor.

original: For of no right, nor color like to right,   He doth fill fields with harness in the realm,   Turns head against the lion’s armèd jaws,   And, being no more in debt to years than thou,   Leads ancient lords and reverend bishops on   To bloody battles and to bruising arms.
translation: F or without a right to the throne—without anything which even resembles a right to the throne—he has filled our fields with troops. He leads an army against the King, into the jaws of a lion. And even though he is no older than you, he leads old lords and distinguished bishops into bloody battles and violent deeds.

original: What never-dying honor hath he got   Against renownèd Douglas, whose high deeds,   Whose hot incursions and great name in arms,   Holds from all soldiers chief majority   And military title capital   Through all the kingdoms that acknowledge Christ.
translation: He has received such honor already from defeating the renowned Douglas! Hotspur's noble actions, his fierce assaults, and his great military reputation have meant he is known in every Christian country as one of the best soldiers there is.

original: Thrice hath this Hotspur, Mars in swathling clothes,   This infant warrior, in his enterprises   Discomfited great Douglas, ta'en him once,   Enlargèd him, and made a friend of him,   To fill the mouth of deep defiance up   And shake the peace and safety of our throne.   And what say you to this?
translation: This Hotspur, this  Mars  in baby clothes, this infant warrior, has defeated Douglas three times, captured him once, freed him again, and now made him an ally. Now they pose a huge problem in rebelling against my throne. What do you have to say about this?

original: Percy, Northumberland,   The Archbishop’s Grace of York, Douglas, Mortimer,   Capitulate against us and are up.   But wherefore do I tell these news to thee?   Why, Harry, do I tell thee of my foes,   Which art my nearest and dearest enemy?
translation: Percy, Northumberland, The Archbishop of York, Douglas, Mortimer— they all have formed a league against us and are openly rebelling. But why am I telling you about my foes, when you are my closest and most loved enemy?

original: Thou that art like enough, through vassal fear,   Base inclination, and the start of spleen,   To fight against me under Percy’s pay,   To dog his heels, and curtsy at his frowns,   To show how much thou art degenerate.
translation: With your  lowly  fear, your base behavior, and your bad temper, you are very likely to fight against me under Percy. I wouldn't be surprised if you followed Hotspur at his heels like a dog, and bowed to him when he frowns—that is how corrupt you are.

original: Do not think so. You shall not find it so.
translation: Don't think that. It won't happen.

original: And God forgive them that so much have swayed   Your Majesty’s good thoughts away from me.   I will redeem all this on Percy’s head,
translation: May God forgive whoever has turned your good opinion against me! I will make up for everything that I have done by killing Percy,

original: And, in the closing of some glorious day,   Be bold to tell you that I am your son,   When I will wear a garment all of blood   And stain my favors in a bloody mask,   Which, washed away, shall scour my shame with it.
translation: and at the triumphant end of some battle I will be worthy of calling myself your son. Only when I am wearing clothes covered in blood and my  face  is stained with blood, will I be able to wash this away and wash my shame away with it.

original: And that shall be the day, whene'er it lights,   That this same child of honor and renown,   This gallant Hotspur, this all-praisèd knight,   And your unthought-of Harry chance to meet.
translation: That will be the day, whenever it comes, that this honorable and renowned child, this brave Hotspur—a knight who is praised for everything and by everyone—will happen to meet with the disregarded Harry.

original: For every honor sitting on his helm,   Would they were multitudes, and on my head   My shames redoubled!   For the time will come   That I shall make this northern youth exchange   His glorious deeds for my indignities.
translation: If only every honor he had could be multiplied and every shame on my head could be doubled! For there will come a time when I will make this youth from the north give me his glorious honors in exchange for my offenses.

original: Percy is but my factor, good my lord,   To engross up glorious deeds on my behalf.   And I will call him to so strict account   That he shall render every glory up,   Yea, even the slightest worship of his time,   Or I will tear the reckoning from his heart.
translation: Percy is like my agent, my lord, collecting glorious honors on my behalf. And I will make sure that he gives back every honor to me, even the smallest one, or I will tear it from his heart instead by killing him.

original: This in the name of God I promise here,   The which if He be pleased I shall perform,   I do beseech your Majesty may salve   The long-grown wounds of my intemperance.
translation: I promise this to you here, in the name of God.  And if God is willing, I will do these things, and I ask you to forgive the long-standing wounds I have caused with my lack of self-control.

original: If not, the end of life cancels all bands,   And I will die a hundred thousand deaths   Ere break the smallest parcel of this vow.
translation: If not, death will cancel all of my promises. I would rather die a hundred thousand deaths than break even the smallest part of this promise.

original: A hundred thousand rebels die in this. Thou shalt have charge and sovereign trust herein.
translation: A hundred thousand rebels will die because of this promise that you have made. You will have command and royal responsibility from now on.

original: So hath the business that I come to speak of.
translation: T he news that I have come to tell you is urgent.

original: Lord Mortimer of Scotland hath sent word   That Douglas and the English rebels met   The eleventh of this month at Shrewsbury.
translation: Lord Mortimer of Scotland has sent word that Douglas and the English rebels met at Shrewsbury on the eleventh of this month.

original: A mighty and a fearful head they are,   If promises be kept on every hand,   As ever offered foul play in the state.
translation: If they all keep their promises, their army will be as big and as terrifying as any army that has ever rebelled against this kingdom.

original: The Earl of Westmoreland set forth today,   With him my son, Lord John of Lancaster,   For this advertisement is five days old.—
translation: This news is five days old. The Earl of Westmoreland and my son,  Lord John of Lancaster , left today.

original: On Wednesday next, Harry, you shall set forward.   On Thursday we ourselves will march. Our meeting   Is Bridgenorth.
translation: You will leave next Wednesday, Harry. Then on Thursday, I will leave. We will meet at  Bridgenorth .

original: And, Harry, you shall march   Through Gloucestershire; by which account,   Our business valuèd, some twelve days hence   Our general forces at Bridgenorth shall meet.
translation: And, Harry, you will march through Gloucestershire. Therefore, considering what we have to do, we should be able to meet at Bridgenorth in twelve days with our full forces.

original: Our hands are full of business. Let’s away.   Advantage feeds him fat while men delay.
translation: We have a lot to do, so let's go. Our enemies will take advantage if we are slow.

original: Bardolph, am I not fallen away vilely since this last  action? Do I not bate? Do I not dwindle?
translation: Bardolph, haven't I completely shrunk since that robbery? Haven't I become so thin?

original: Why, my skin  hangs about me like an like an old lady’s loose gown. I  am withered like an old applejohn.
translation: Look, my skin is hanging off me like an old lady's loose dress. I am wasting away like an old, withered apple.

original: Well, I’ll repent,  and that suddenly, while I am in some liking. I shall be out of heart shortly, and then I shall have no strength to repent.
translation: Well, I'll repent for all the bad things I have done, and I should do it immediately, while I still can. I will be a bad condition soon, and I won't have the strength to repent.

original: An I have not forgotten what the inside of a church is made of, I am a peppercorn, a brewer’s horse. The inside of a church! Company, villanous company,  hath been the spoil of me.
translation: If I haven't forgotten what the inside of a church looks like, I'm a small and shriveled berry, a tired and worn-out horse. The inside of a church! I've been ruined by the company, the bad company, I keep.

original: Sir John, you are so fretful you cannot live long.
translation: Sir John, if you keep fretting this much, you aren't going to live very long.

original: Why, there is it. Come sing me a bawdy song, make me  merry.
translation: Well, that's true. Come on, sing me a rude song, and cheer me up.

original: I was as virtuously given as a gentleman need to  be, virtuous enough:
translation: I have lived a good life, like any other gentleman—well, good enough at least.

original: swore little; diced not above seven times— a week; went to a bawdy house once in a  quarter—of an hour; paid money that I borrowed, three or four times;
translation: I only swore a little bit, didn't gamble more than seven times...well, seven times a week, that is.  I went to a brothel never more than once every fifteen...minutes. I paid back my debts!  Well, at least three or four times.

original: lived well and in good compass; and now I  live out of all order, out of all compass.
translation: I lived well and in moderation, and I now I live a bad life, all out of moderation.

original: Why, you are so fat, Sir John, that you must needs be  out of all compass, out of all reasonable compass, Sir  John.
translation: Sir John, you are so fat that everything about you is out of moderation, moderation wouldn't work for you, Sir John.

original: Do thou amend thy face, and I’ll amend my life. Thou  art our admiral, thou bearest the lantern in the poop,  but ’tis in the nose of thee. Thou art the knight of the burning lamp.
Why, Sir John, my face does you no harm.
translation: But, Sir John, my face can't hurt you.

original: No, I’ll be sworn, I make as good use of it as many a  man doth of a death’s-head or a   memento mori   . I never  see thy face but I think upon hellfire and Dives that  lived in purple, for there he is in his robes, burning,  burning.
translation: No, that's true, I can get some good use out of it, if I think of it like  a skull or a reminder of death . I've never looked at your face and not thought of the fiery pits of hell and  Dives, that rich man in purple from the Bible who burned forever.

original: If thou wert any way given to virtue, I would  swear by thy face. My oath should be “By this fire,  that’s God’s angel.” But thou art altogether given over, and wert indeed, but for the light in thy face, the son of utter darkness.
translation: If there was anything good or virtuous about you, I would swear oaths at your face. My oath would be something like, "Standing by this fire, that's God's angel." But you are completely committed to wickedness that you would be the son of utter darkness, if it wasn't for that light from your red nose.

original: When thou rannest up Gadshill in the night to catch my horse, if I did not think thou hadst  been an   ignis fatuus   , or a ball of wildfire, there’s no  purchase in money. O, thou art a perpetual triumph, an  everlasting bonfire-light! Thou hast saved me a thousand marks in links and torches, walking with thee in the  night betwixt tavern and tavern:
translation: When you ran up Gadshill in the middle of the night to get my horse, I was certain I was seeing a  will-o'-the-wisp  or a firework running. Oh, you are like a permanent festival of torches, an everlasting bonfire! You must have saved me about a thousand marks that I would have had to spend on torches, just by walking with me from bar to bar.

original: but the sack that thou  hast drunk me would have bought me lights as good cheap  at the dearest chandler’s in Europe.
translation: Yet, the amount of wine you have drunk would have bought me lights from the most expensive candle-maker's in Europe.

original: I have maintained  that salamander of yours with fire any time this two and thirty years, God reward me for it.
translation: I have put up with that  nose of yours  and kept it burning for thirty-two years. I deserve some heavenly reward for that.

original: 'Sblood, I would my face were in your belly!
Godamercy, so should I be sure to be heart-burned!
translation: God no! Then I would definitely have heart-burn!

original: Why, Sir John, what do you think, Sir John, do you  think I keep thieves in my house?
translation: Why, Sir John? What do you think has happened, Sir John?  Do you think that I keep thieves in this bar?

original: I have searched, I  have enquired, so has my husband, man by man, boy by  boy, servant by servant.
translation: I have searched for you, and I have asked around, and so has my husband. We have asked every man, every boy, and every servant.

original: The tithe of a hair was never  lost in my house before.
translation: The slightest part of something has never been lost here before.

original: You lie, hostess. Bardolph was shaved and lost many a  hair; and I’ll be sworn my pocket was picked. Go to, you are a woman, go.
translation: That's a lie, hostess. Bardolph has been shaved here, so has lost many hairs. And I am certain that I have been robbed. Damn you, you're just a woman, damn you.

original: Who, I? No; I defy thee! God’s light, I was never  called so in mine own house before.
translation: What, me? No, you won't get a way with that! God, I've never been spoken to like that in my own bar.

original: Go to, I know you well enough.
translation: Leave off, I know all about you.

original: No, Sir John, you do not know me, Sir John. I know you, Sir John. You owe me money, Sir John, and now you pick  a quarrel to beguile me of it. I bought you a dozen of  shirts to your back.
translation: No, Sir John, you don't know everything about me. I know everything about you, Sir John. You owe me money, Sir John. And now you argue with me and try to trick me out of it. I bought you a dozen shirts to wear.

original: Dowlas, filthy dowlas. I have given them away to  bakers' wives; they have made bolters of them.
translation: They were awful, made of coarse linen. I had to give them away to bakers' wives to sift flour with—that was all those shirts were good for.

original: Now, as I am a true woman, holland of eight shillings  an ell. You owe money here besides, Sir John, for your  diet and by- drinkings, and money lent you, four and  twenty pound.
He had his part of it. Let him  pay.
translation: He had some of that, let him pay you.

original: He? Alas, he is poor. He hath nothing.
translation: Him? No, he is poor. He has nothing.

original: How, poor? Look upon his face. What call you rich? Let  them coin his nose. Let them coin his cheeks. I’ll not  pay a denier. What, will you make a younker of me? Shall I not take mine case in mine inn but I shall have my  pocket picked? I have lost a seal ring of my  grandfather’s worth forty mark.
O Jesu, I have heard the Prince tell him, I know not  how oft, that that ring was copper!
translation: Oh Jesus, I've heard the Prince tell him so many times that that ring was just copper!

original: How? The Prince is a jack, a sneak-up. 'Sblood, an he  were here, I would cudgel him like a dog if he would say so.
translation: What? The Prince is a fool, a sneak. I swear to God, if he was here, I would beat him like a dog if he said that.

original: Yea, two and two, Newgate fashion.
My lord, I pray you, hear me.
translation: My lord, please, listen to me.

original: What sayest thou, Mistress Quickly? How doth thy  husband? I love him well; he is an honest man.
translation: What are you saying Mistress Quickly? How is your husband doing? I like him a lot; he is an honorable man.

original: Good my lord, hear me.
translation: My good lord, please listen to me.

original: Prithee, let her alone, and list to me.
translation: Hal, leave her alone, and listen to me.

original: What say’st thou, Jack?
translation: What are you saying, Jack?

original: The other night I fell asleep here behind the arras,  and had my pocket picked. This house is turned bawdy  house; they pick pockets.
translation: The other night I fell asleep behind these curtains and was robbed. This bar is like a brothel; they steal your things.

original: What didst thou lose, Jack?
translation: What did you lose, Jack?

original: Wilt thou believe me, Hal, three or four bonds of forty pound apiece, and a seal ring of my grandfather’s.
translation: Would you believe it, Hal? Three or four promises of money, worth forty pounds each, and a signet ring that was my grandfather's.

original: A trifle, some eightpenny matter.
translation: That ring's nothing—it's barely worth eight pennies.

original: So I told him, my lord, and I said I heard your Grace  say so. And, my lord, he speaks most vilely of you, like a foul-mouthed man as he is; and said he would cudgel  you.
translation: That's what I told him, my lord, and I said I had heard your Grace say so. Then, my lord, he said vile things about you, like the foul-mouthed man he is, and he said he would beat you!

original: What, he did not!
translation: What? He did?!

original: There’s neither faith, truth, nor womanhood in me else.
translation: Either he said that, or I'm not faithful, honest, or womanly at all.

original: There’s no more faith in thee than in a stewed prune,  nor no more truth in thee than in a drawn fox, and for  womanhood, Maid Marian may be the deputy’s wife of the  ward to thee. Go, you thing, go.
Say, what thing, what thing?
translation: Thing? What thing?

original: What thing! Why, a thing to thank God on.
translation: What thing?! Why a thing to thank God for.

original: I am no thing to thank God on, I would thou shouldst  know it! I am an honest man’s wife, and, setting thy  knighthood aside, thou art a knave to call me so.
translation: I am no thing to thank God for, you'd better believe it! I am the wife of an honoraable man, and ignoring my respect for your title of knight, you are a villain to call me that.

original: Setting thy womanhood aside, thou art a beast to say  otherwise.
translation: Ignoring your womanhood, you are just a beast, then.

original: Say, what beast, thou knave, thou?
translation: What beast, you dishonest man?

original: What beast? Why, an otter.
translation: What beast? Why, an otter.

original: An otter, Sir John. Why an otter?
translation: An otter, Sir John. Why an otter?

original: Why, she’s neither fish nor flesh; a man knows not  where to have her.
Thou art an unjust man in saying so. Thou or any man  knows where to have me, thou knave, thou.
translation: You are a horrible man for saying a nasty thing like that. You or any other man would know what to do with me, you rascal, you.

original: Thou sayest true, hostess, and he slanders thee most  grossly.
translation: You speak truthfully, hostess, and he has greatly offended you.

original: So he doth you, my lord, and said this other day you  owed him a thousand pound.
translation: He also offends you, my lord, and he said the other day that you owe him a thousand pounds.

original: Sirrah, do I owe you a thousand pound?
translation: Sir, do I owe you a thousand pounds?

original: A thousand pound, Hal? A million. Thy love is worth a  million; thou owest me thy love.
translation: A thousand pounds, Hal? More like a million. But since your love is worth a million pounds, you just owe me your love.

original: Nay, my lord, he called you “jack,” and said he would  cudgel you.
translation: That's not true, my lord, he called you a fool and said that he would beat you.

original: Did I, Bardolph?
translation: Did I, Bardolph?

original: Indeed, Sir John, you said so.
translation: Yes, Sir John, that's what you said.

original: Yea, if he said my ring was copper.
translation: Yes, but I only said I'd do this if he said my ring was trash and was just made of copper.

original: I say ’tis copper. Darest thou be as good as thy word  now?
translation: I do say it's trash and just made of copper. Are you going to honor your promise and beat me then?

original: Why, Hal, thou knowest, as thou art but man, I dare,  but as thou art Prince, I fear thee as I fear the  roaring of a lion’s whelp.
translation: Hal, you know that if you were only a man, I would honor my promise. But since you're the Prince, I'm scared, like I'm scared of the roaring of a lion's cub.

original: And why not as the lion?
translation: Why am I not the lion?

original: The King is to be feared as the lion. Dost thou think  I’ll fear thee as I fear thy father? Nay, an I do, I  pray God my girdle break.
O, if it should, how would thy guts fall about thy  knees!
translation: Oh, if your girdle broke, your stomach would be hanging around your knees!

original: But, sirrah, there’s no room for faith, truth,  nor honesty in this bosom of thine. It is all filled up  with guts and midriff.
translation: But sir, there's no room in your chest for loyalty, honesty ,or the truth. Your chest is all filled up with guts and stomach.

original: Charge an honest woman with  picking thy pocket? Why, thou whoreson, impudent,  embossed rascal,
translation: You are going to accuse an honest woman of robbing you? Why, you son-of-a-whore! You shameless, fat liar!

original: if there were anything in thy pocket  but tavern reckonings, memorandums of bawdy houses, and  one poor pennyworth, of sugar candy to make thee  long-winded,
translation: I bet that the only things in your pockets were tavern bills, notes about brothels, and about a penny's worth of sweet candy to give you enough energy to keep going.

original: if thy pocket were enriched with any other  injuries but these, I am a villain.
translation: If your pockets had anything in them except these things, then I'm a liar.

original: And, yet you will  stand to it! You will not pocket up wrong! Art thou not  ashamed?
translation: And yet, you continue to lie! You will not accept criticism! Aren't you ashamed of yourself?

original: Dost thou hear, Hal?
translation: Don't you understand, Hal?

original: Thou knowest in the state of  innocency Adam fell, and what should poor Jack Falstaff  do in the days of villany?
translation: You know that Adam fell even when living in the innocent world of Eden, so what chance does poor Jack Falstaff have in these evil times?

original: Thou seest I have more flesh  than another man and therefore more frailty.
translation: You can see that I have  more flesh than most other men, and that makes me more frail .

original: You  confess, then, you picked my pocket?
translation: Are you confessing then, that it was you who robbed me?

original: It appears so by the story.
translation: So it seems, since I told you what was in your pockets.

original: Hostess, I forgive thee. Go make ready breakfast, love  thy, husband, look to thy servants, cherish thy guests.  Thou shalt find me tractable to any honest reason. Thou  seest I am pacified still. Nay, prithee, be gone.
translation: Hostess, I forgive you. Go and get breakfast ready, love your husband, take care of your servants, and look after your guests. You will find me an agreeable man normally. See how easily pleased I am. Now, please, get going!

original: O, my sweet beef, I must still be good angel to thee.  The money is paid back again.
translation: Oh, I will always be your protector, you fresh piece of meat. The money has been paid back.

original: O, I do not like that paying back. 'Tis a double labor.
translation: Oh, I don't like the whole "paying back" thing—it's twice the amount of work.

original: I am good friends with my father and may do anything.
translation: I am good friends with my father again, and so I can do anything.

original: Rob me the Exchequer the first thing thou dost, and do  it with unwashed hands too.
translation: Then start by robbing the royal treasury, and do it right now, without even washing your hands.

original: Do, my lord.
translation: Do it, my lord.

original: I have procured thee, Jack, a charge of foot.
translation: I have found you some foot soldiers to command, Jack.

original: I would it had been of horse.
translation: I wish they could have been cavalrymen instead of foot soldiers.

original: Where shall I find one  that can steal well? O, for a fine thief of the age of  two and twenty or thereabouts!
translation: Where am I going to find a good thief? Oh, if only I had a great thief who was about twenty-two years old!

original: I am heinously  unprovided.
translation: I am awfully ill-equipped.

original: Well, God be thanked for these rebels. They  offend none but the virtuous. I laud them; I praise  them.
translation: Well, thank God for these rebels. They only go against the good people. I give them praise and honor for that.

original: Bardolph!
translation: Bardolph!

original: My lord.
translation: My lord.

original: Go bear this letter to Lord John of Lancaster, To my brother John; this to my Lord of Westmoreland.
translation: Go and give this letter to my brother, Lord John of Lancaster. Take this one to the Lord of Westmoreland.

original: Rare words, brave world!—Hostess, my breakfast, come.— O, I could wish this tavern were my drum.
translation: Well said! What an amazing world this is!  Hostess, bring me my breakfast. Oh, if only I could lead my troops from this bar.

original: Well said, my noble Scot.
translation: Well said, you wonderful Scotsman.

original: If speaking truth   In this fine age were not thought flattery,   Such attribution should the Douglas have   As not a soldier of this season’s stamp   Should go so general current through the world.
translation: If people nowadays didn't think that speaking the truth was the same thing as flattery, I would tell them that you,  Douglas , should be praised more than  any other soldier fighting right now , having gained such an impressive reputation already.

original: By God, I cannot flatter. I do defy   The tongues of soothers.
translation: Heaven knows, I'm not normally a flatterer. I hate people who constantly flatter others with their words.

original: But a braver place   In my heart’s love hath no man than yourself.   Nay, task me to my word; approve me, lord.
translation: But you have a better place in my heart than any other man. Now test me on this love; make me prove it, my lord.

original: Thou art the king of honor. No man so potent breathes upon the ground But I will beard him.
translation: You are an incredibly honorable man, but there is no-one, however powerful, that I cannot defy.

original: Do so, and ’tis well.
translation: Do it then.  That would be good.

original: These letters come from your father.
translation: These are letters from your father.

original: Letters from him! Why comes he not himself?
translation: Just letters? Why hasn't he come to see me himself?

original: He cannot come, my lord. He is grievous sick.
translation: He can't come my lord, he is incredibly sick.

original: Zounds, how has he the leisure to be sick In such a justling time? Who leads his power? Under whose government come they along?
translation: God, how can he have the freedom to be sick at such a time of conflict?! Who is leading his army? Who is bringing them here?

original: His letters bear his mind, not I, my lord.
translation: His letters will reveal his thoughts more than I can, my lord.

original: I prithee, tell me, doth he keep his bed?
translation: Please, tell me, is he bedridden?

original: He did, my lord, four days ere I set forth, And, at the time of my departure thence, He was much feared by his physicians.
translation: He was, my lord, when I set off four days ago. When I was leaving, the doctors were very worried about him.

original: I would the state of time had first been whole Ere he by sickness had been visited. His health was never better worth than now.
translation: I wish this sickness could have come after this present situation has been settled. His health has never been as important to us as it is now.

original: Sick now? Droop now?
translation: He is sick now? He weakens now?

original: This sickness doth infect   The very lifeblood of our enterprise.   'Tis catching hither, even to our camp.
translation: This sickness infects the entire mission, then . And it will even infect us here, in our camp.

original: He writes me here that inward sickness—   And that his friends by deputation   Could not so soon be drawn,
translation: He tells me in his letter about this internal sickness—and that his troops couldn't be assembled quickly enough by his deputies.

original: nor did he think it meet   To lay so dangerous and dear a trust   On any soul removed but on his own;
translation: He also didn't think that it was appropriate to let anyone other than himself carry out such a dangerous and important task.

original: Yet doth he give us bold advertisement   That with our small conjunction we should on   To see how fortune is disposed to us,
translation: Yet, he does tell us to be confident and to go ahead with our small number of troops to see what our fortunes will be.

original: For, as he writes, there is no quailing now,   Because the King is certainly possessed   Of all our purposes. What say you to it?
translation: He writes that now is not a time to be losing courage, since the King certainly knows about our plans to attack. What do you have to say about this?

original: Your father’s sickness is a maim to us.
translation: Your father's sickness is a crippling injury to us.

original: A perilous gash, a very limb lopped off!
translation: A dangerous wound, almost like one of our limbs has been chopped right off!

original: And yet, in faith, it is not. His present want   Seems more than we shall find it.
translation: Yet, actually, it doesn't have to be. His absence now seems worse than it really is.

original: Were it good   To set the exact wealth of all our states   All at one cast? To set so rich a main   On the nice hazard of one doubtful hour?
translation: Was it good for us to gamble everything that we have on a single throw of the dice? Was it right to  bet so much  on the chance of one uncertain hour?

original: It were not good, for therein should we read   The very bottom and the soul of hope,   The very list, the very utmost bound   Of all our fortunes.
translation: No, it wasn't good, since it meant that we had used up all of our hope, and pushed the absolute limit and boundary of our luck.

original: Faith, and so we should, where now remains   A sweet reversion.
translation: That's true, especially when you consider the hope of the inheritance we can expect.

original: We may boldly spend   Upon the hope of what is to come in.
translation: We should be bold now, in the hope of what is to come in the future.

original: A comfort of retirement lives in this.
translation: And the fact that we now we have some help in case we need to retreat .

original: A rendezvous, a home to fly unto, If that the devil and mischance look big Upon the maidenhead of our affairs.
translation: Yes, it gives us a refuge, somewhere to retreat to, if things look like they are going badly in the first stages of our mission.

original: But yet I would your father had been here.   The quality and hair of our attempt   Brooks no division.
translation: Still, I do wish that your father was here. The nature of our mission needs us all to be united together.

original: It will be thought   By some that know not why he is away   That wisdom, loyalty, and mere dislike   Of our proceedings kept the Earl from hence.
translation: Some people, who don't know that he is sick, will just think that the Earl stayed away out of wisdom, loyalty, and absolute dislike of what we are doing.

original: And think how such an apprehension   May turn the tide of fearful faction   And breed a kind of question in our cause.
translation: And think about how these thoughts would affect people who are already scared, and raise doubts among our followers.

original: For well you know, we of the off'ring side   Must keep aloof from strict arbitrament,
translation: For as you very well know, since we are the side making the attack, we have to try to avoid careful scrutiny.

original: And stop all sight-holes, every loop from whence   The eye of reason may pry in upon us.
translation: We have to close up all holes, all loopholes that people who are more rational might look through to criticize us.

original: This absence of your father’s draws a curtain   That shows the ignorant a kind of fear   Before not dreamt of.
translation: The fact that your father is not here opens the curtains, and shows ignorant people things that they had never been scared of before.

original: You strain too far.
translation: You are exaggerating.

original: I rather of his absence make this use:   It lends a luster and more great opinion,
translation: I would rather think of his absence in this way: it makes our mission better.

original: A larger dare, to our great enterprise   Than if the Earl were here, for men must think   If we without his help can make a head   To push against a kingdom,
translation: It gives our mission a better reputation, more boldness than if the Earl was here. It will make men think that if we can raise an army to stand against the King without his help,

original: with his help   We shall o'erturn it topsy-turvy down.
translation: when he does join in the fighting, we will be able to topple the kingdom completely.

original: Yet all goes well, yet all our joints are whole.
translation: Everything is okay, we still have all of our limbs.

original: As heart can think. There is not such a word Spoke of in Scotland as this term of fear.
translation: I should hope so.  We don't understand the word fear in Scotland.

original: My cousin Vernon, welcome, by my soul.
translation: Welcome, kinsman Vernon. Truly, you are welcome.

original: Pray God my news be worth a welcome, lord. The Earl of Westmoreland, seven thousand strong, Is marching hitherwards, with him Prince John.
translation: I wish to God that the news I bring was worth such a welcome, my lord. The Earl of Westmoreland is marching here with seven thousand men, accompanied by Prince John.

original: No harm, what more?
translation: That's not an issue.  What else?

original: And further I have learned, The King himself in person is set forth, Or hitherwards intended speedily, With strong and mighty preparation.
translation: I have also found out that the King himself has set off, and is on his way here quickly, with a huge, strong army.

original: He shall be welcome too.
translation: Well then, we will welcome him too.

original: Where is his son,   The nimble-footed madcap Prince of Wales,
translation: Where is his son, that quick-footed, foolish Prince of Wales,

original: And his comrades, that daffed the world aside   And bid it pass?
translation: and his friends, who don't care about anything in this world?

original: All furnished, all in arms,   All plumed like ostriches that with the wind   Baited like eagles having lately bathed,
translation: They are all prepared, all armed and ready. They are dressed up like  feathered ostriches , they look like eagles beating their wings impatiently after they have just bathed.

original: Glittering in golden coats like images,   As full of spirit as the month of May,   And gorgeous as the sun at midsummer,
translation: Their  coats  are shining like golden statues.  They are as energetic as the month of May, and are as beautiful as the midsummer sun.

original: Wanton as youthful goats, wild as young bulls.
translation: They are as excited as young goats, and as wild as young bulls.

original: I saw young Harry with his beaver on,   His cuisses on his thighs,
translation: I saw young Harry with his  helmet  on, and the armor already on his thighs.

original: gallantly armed   Rise from the ground like feathered Mercury   And vaulted with such ease into his seat
translation: Bravely armed with weapons, he rose from the ground like the  messenger Mercury  and jumped onto his horse so easily.

original: As if an angel dropped down from the clouds,   To turn and wind a fiery Pegasus   And witch the world with noble horsemanship.
translation: It almost looked like an angel had fallen out of the sky, ready to ride on the fiery  Pegasus  and bewitch the world with his excellent riding.

original: No more, no more! Worse than the sun in March   This praise doth nourish agues.
translation: Stop talking! No more! This glowing praise makes me shudder more than the  sun does in March .

original: Let them come.   They come like sacrifices in their trim,   And to the fire-eyed maid of smoky war   All hot and bleeding will we offer them.
translation: Let them come. They come here dressed up and ready to be sacrificed, and we will offer them up, hot and bleeding, to the fiery goddess of war,  Bellona .

original: The mailèd Mars shall on his altar sit   Up to the ears in blood.
translation: The god of war Mars will sit at his altar, up to his ears in blood.

original: I am on fire   To hear this rich reprisal is so nigh   And yet not ours. Come, let me taste my horse,   Who is to bear me like a thunderbolt   Against the bosom of the Prince of Wales.
translation: I am impatient, knowing that this prize is so close, and yet it is still not ours. Come, let me test my horse, ready to charge like a thunderbolt against this Prince of Wales.

original: Harry to Harry shall, hot horse to horse,   Meet and ne'er part till one drop down a corpse.   O, that Glendower were come!
translation: This Harry  Percy will meet that Prince Harry, our horses will also meet, and we will not leave until one of us drops dead. Oh, if only Glendower was already here!

original: There is more news. I learned in Worcester, as I rode along, He cannot draw his power this fourteen days.
That’s the worst tidings that I hear of yet.
translation: That is the worst news yet.

original: Ay, by my faith, that bears a frosty sound.
translation: Yes, certainly, that is discouraging.

original: What may the King’s whole battle reach unto?
translation: How many troops does the King have in total?

original: To thirty thousand.
translation: About thirty thousand.

original: Forty let it be.
translation: Why not let it be forty thousand?!

original: My father and Glendower being both away,   The powers of us may serve so great a day.
translation: Even though my father's and Glendower's men are not here, the troops that we do have could still be enough to win.

original: Come, let us take a muster speedily.
translation: Come, let's assemble and review our forces quickly.

original: Doomsday is near. Die all, die merrily.
translation: It's almost  Doomsday . If we are going to die, let's do it cheerfully!

original: Talk not of dying. I am out of fear Of death or death’s hand for this one half year.
translation: Don't talk about dying. I'm not going to be scared of death for the next six months.

original: Bardolph, get thee before to Coventry. Fill me a bottle of sack. Our soldiers shall march through. We’ll to  Sutton Coldfield tonight.
Will you give me money, captain?
translation: Will you give me money for it, captain?

original: Lay out, lay out.
translation: Pay for it yourself.

original: This bottle makes an angel.
An if it do, take it for thy labor. An if it make  twenty, take them all. I’ll answer the coinage. Bid my  lieutenant Peto meet me at town’s end.
translation: Well if it does, then keep it for your trouble. Even if it earns you twenty shillings, then keep them all, I can pay you for it. Tell my lieutenant Peto to meet me at the edge of the town.

original: I will, captain. Farewell.
translation: I will, captain. Goodbye then.

original: If I be not ashamed of my soldiers, I am a soused  gurnet.
translation: If I'm not ashamed of my soldiers, then I'm a  pickled fish !

original: I have misused the King’s press damnably. I have got, in exchange of a hundred and fifty soldiers, three hundred and odd pounds.
translation: I have misused my position with the King terribly. In return for the one hundred and fifty men I have made fight in the army, I have received over three hundred pounds!

original: I press me none but good  householders, yeomen’s sons; inquire me out contracted  bachelors, such as had been asked twice on the banns;
translation: All the men I have found have been good house-owners and the sons of successful farmers. I found men who were engaged to be married, men whose weddings had already  been announced twice  in church.

original: such a commodity of warm slaves—as had as lief hear the  devil as a drum, such as fear the report of a caliver  worse than a struck fowl or a hurt wild duck.
translation: I found a group of such privileged cowards, that they would rather hear the devil talk than hear the drums of war; they are more scared when they hear gunfire than a bird or a duck that has actually been shot!

original: I pressed  me none but such toasts-and-butter, with hearts in their bellies no bigger than pins' heads, and   they have  bought out their services, and now my whole charge  consists of ancients, corporals, lieutenants, gentlemen  of companies—
translation: I only looked for the pampered citizens, whose  hearts  were about the same size as a pin-head, and they paid me so that they wouldn't have to fight. So now my whole section is made up of flag-bearers, corporals, lieutenants, gentlemen of companies, and crooks

original: slaves as ragged as Lazarus in the painted  cloth, where the glutton’s dogs licked his sores; and  such as indeed were never soldiers, but discarded,  unjust servingmen, younger sons to younger brothers,  revolted tapsters, and ostlers tradefallen, the cankers  of a calm world and a long peace, ten times more  dishonorable-ragged than an old feazed ancient;
translation: who looked as disgusting as that  cheap painted wall hanging of Lazarus , where the dogs are licking the sores on his body. These men were never meant to be soldiers—they are servants who have been fired for lying, they are  younger sons to younger brothers ,  runaway barmen , and unemployed stable boys. They are like diseases in a world full of calm and peace, they are ten times more dishonorable and disgusting than a tattered old flag.

original: and such have I to fill up the rooms of them that have bought  out their services, that you would think that I had a  hundred and fifty tattered prodigals lately come from  swine-keeping, from eating draff and husks.
translation: And I've had to replace the men who have bribed me with these idiots. You would think that I had found a hundred and fifty  men , dirty from looking after pigs and from eating scraps and husks.

original: A mad fellow met me on the way and told me I had unloaded all the  gibbets and pressed the dead bodies. No eye hath seen  such scarecrows. I’ll not march through Coventry with  them, that’s flat.
translation: One crazy guy saw us all marching and told me that it looked like I had taken all of the dead bodies from the gallows and made them fight again— no-one has even seen something so  terrifying ! I can't march through Coventry with them, that's for sure.

original: Nay, and the villains march wide  betwixt the legs as if they had gyves on, for indeed I  had the most of them out of prison.
translation: These men march with their legs wide apart, as if they had chains on their ankles, which makes a lot of sense, as I got most of them from prison.

original: There’s not a shirt  and a half in all my company, and the half shirt is two  napkins tacked together and thrown over the shoulders  like a herald’s coat without sleeves;
translation: There's only about one and a half shirts between the lot of them, and the half shirt is really just two napkins tied together and thrown over his shoulders like some kind of herald in a sleeveless coat.

original: and the shirt, to  say the truth, stolen from my host at Saint Albans or  the red-nose innkeeper of Daventry. But that’s all one;  they’ll find linen enough on every hedge.
translation: Even the whole shirt, to tell you the truth, was stolen from the bar owner at  Saint Albans  or from the red-nosed innkeeper at Daventry. But that doesn't matter, they should be able to steal people's laundry out of their  hedges .

original: How now, blown Jack? How now, quilt?
What, Hal, how now, mad wag? What a devil dost thou in  Warwickshire?—My good Lord of Westmoreland, I cry you  mercy: I thought your Honor had already been at  Shrewsbury.
translation: Is it you Hal, how are you, my crazy joker?! What in the devil's name are you doing in Warwickshire? Oh! My good Lord of Westmoreland, I beg your forgiveness, I thought that you would already be in Shrewsbury.

original: Faith, Sir John, ’tis more than time that I were there  and you too, but my powers are there already. The King,  I can tell you, looks for us all. We must away all  night.
translation: Don't worry, Sir John, I really should be there already and so should you, but at least my men are there already. The King is certainly expecting us. We will have to travel all night.

original: Tut, never fear me. I am as vigilant as a cat to steal  cream.
translation: Oh, don't you worry about me! I am as alert as a cat is when it's trying to steal cream.

original: I think to steal cream indeed, for thy theft hath  already made thee butter. But tell me, Jack, whose  fellows are these that come after?
translation: I think you must have stolen cream, because whatever you steal turns to fat. Tell me, Jack, whose men are these?

original: Mine, Hal, mine.
translation: Mine, Hal, they are mine.

original: I did never see such pitiful rascals.
translation: I've never seen such a pitiful bunch.

original: Tut, tut, good enough to toss; food for powder, food  for powder. They’ll fill a pit as well as better. Tush,  man, mortal men, mortal men.
Ay, but, Sir John, methinks they are exceeding poor and bare, too beggarly.
translation: That might be so, Sir John, but they look incredibly poor and thin, almost like beggars.

original: Faith, for their poverty, I know not where they had  that, and for their bareness, I am sure they never  learned that of me.
translation: Well, I don't know where they got their poverty from, and as for their thinness, I know for certain that they didn't get that from me.

original: No, I’ll be sworn, unless you call three fingers in the ribs bare. But, sirrah, make haste. Percy is already in the field.
translation: No, definitely not, unless you think that having layers of fat over your ribs makes you thin. But come on, sir, let's hurry. Percy is already at the battlefield.

original: What, is the King encamped?
translation: What? Is the King already camped out and ready for battle?

original: He is, Sir John. I fear we shall stay too long.
translation: He is, Sir John. I'm afraid if we don't hurry, we'll get there too late.

original: Well, To the latter end of a fray and the beginning of a  feast Fits a dull fighter and a keen guest.
translation: Well, an excited guest gets to a feast early, whereas a bad fighter gets to a battle as late as he can!

original: We’ll fight with him tonight.
translation: We will fight with King Henry tonight.

original: It may not be.
translation: We can't.

original: You give him then advantage.
translation: Then you are giving him the advantage by waiting until morning.

original: Not a whit.
translation: Not at all.

original: Why say you so? Looks he not for supply?
translation: Why do you say that? Isn't he looking for extra reinforcements?

original: So do we.
translation: Yes, but we are, too.

original: His is certain; ours is doubtful.
translation: He will definitely find reinforcements, but we probably won't.

original: Good cousin, be advised. Stir not tonight.
translation: Good nephew, listen to me. Do not fight tonight.

original: Do not, my lord.
translation: Do not, my lord.

original: You do not counsel well. You speak it out of fear and cold heart.
translation: You are not giving him good advice. You are only saying this because you are scared and nervous.

original: Do me no slander, Douglas. By my life   (And I dare well maintain it with my life),
translation: Don't slander me, Douglas. I swear on my life, and will prove it with my life:

original: If well-respected honor bid me on,   I hold as little counsel with weak fear   As you, my lord, or any Scot that this day lives.
translation: if a thoughtfully considered sense of honor inspires me to fight, I will be no more scared than you, my lord, or any other Scotsman living.

original: Let it be seen tomorrow in the battle   Which of us fears.
translation: We will see in tomorrow's battle which one of us is afraid.

original: Yea, or tonight.
translation: Yes, or tonight.

original: Content.
translation: Enough.

original: Tonight, say I.
translation: I say we attack tonight.

original: Come, come it nay not be.
translation: Come on, we can't do that.

original: I wonder much,   Being men of such great leading as you are,   That you foresee not what impediments   Drag back our expedition.
translation: I don't understand how you can be such great leaders and not see the obvious problems that slow us down.

original: Certain horse   Of my cousin Vernon’s are not yet come up.
translation: My cousin Vernon and his cavalry haven't arrived yet.

original: Your Uncle Worcester’s horse came but today,   And now their pride and mettle is asleep,
translation: Your Uncle's Worcester and his men only arrived today, and now their pride and bravery is asleep.

original: Their courage with hard labor tame and dull,   That not a horse is half the half of himself.
translation: Their courage has been tamed and weakened by their long journey! There isn't a horse in their army that has even a quarter of its usual strength!

original: So are the horses of the enemy In general journey-bated and brought low. The better part of ours are full of rest.
translation: They enemy's horses are also tired and weak from their long journey. Many of our other horses are well-rested.

original: The number of the King exceedeth ours. For God’s sake, cousin, stay till all come in.
translation: The King has many more soldiers than we do. For God's sake, nephew, wait until more men are here.

original: I come with gracious offers from the King, If you vouchsafe me hearing and respect.
translation: I come here with a gracious offer from the King, if you will listen to what I have to say and treat this offer with respect.

original: Welcome, Sir Walter Blunt,
translation: Welcome, Sir Walter Blunt.

original: and would to God   You were of our determination.
translation: If only you were on our side of this battle.

original: Some of us love you well, and even those some   Envy your great deservings and good name
translation: Many of us are very fond of you, although we also resent your noble behavior and your good reputation

original: Because you are not of our quality   But stand against us like an enemy.
translation: because you are not on our side, but instead you are fighting against us like an enemy.

original: And God defend but still I should stand so,   So long as out of limit and true rule   You stand against anointed majesty.
translation: And I pray I will continue to do so for as long as you stand against the  anointed  King, ignoring the boundaries of natural order and good government.

original: But to my charge. The king hath sent to know   The nature of your griefs, and whereupon   You conjure from the breast of civil peace   Such bold hostility,
translation: But now to my task. The King has sent me to find out what your complaints are, and why you are starting another war in a time of peace,

original: teaching his duteous land   Audacious cruelty.
translation: encouraging such violence and cruelty across his loyal land.

original: If that the king   Have any way your good deserts forgot,   Which he confesseth to be manifold,   He bids you name your griefs,
translation: If the King has forgotten about any of your good deeds, of which he knows there are many, he asks you to name your grievances.

original: and with all speed   You shall have your desires with interest   And pardon absolute for yourself and these   Herein misled by your suggestion.
translation: He will quickly give you what you want and more, and will completely pardon you and the followers you have misled.

original: The King is kind, and well we know the king   Knows at what time to promise, when to pay.
translation: The King is kind, and we know that the King makes good promises and sticks to them.

original: My father and my uncle and myself   Did give him that same royalty he wears,
translation: My father, my uncle, and I were the ones who made him King in the first place!

original: And when he was not six-and-twenty strong,   Sick in the world’s regard, wretched and low,   A poor unminded outlaw sneaking home,   My father gave him welcome to the shore;
translation: When he barely had twenty-six men fighting with him, when he was weak and no-one cared about him, just a poor, unnoticed criminal trying to get home,  my father welcomed him back .

original: And when he heard him swear and vow to God   He came but to be Duke of Lancaster,   To sue his livery, and beg his peace,   With tears of innocency and terms of zeal,   My father, in kind heart and pity moved,   Swore him assistance and performed it too.
translation: When my father heard him swearing a promise to God, weeping and speaking with passion, that he had only come back  to claim his title from  his father's inheritanc e , and reconcile himself to King Richard, he felt sorry for him and offered to help him.

original: Now when the lords and barons of the realm   Perceived Northumberland did lean to him,   The more and less came in with cap and knee,
translation: When the important men in the kingdom noticed that Northumberland, my father, was supporting him, they all came to see him and bow to him.

original: Met him in boroughs, cities, villages,   Attended him on bridges, stood in lanes,   Laid gifts before him, proffered him their oaths,   Gave him their heirs as pages, followed him   Even at the heels in golden multitudes.
translation: They met him in towns, cities, villages, they waited for him on bridges, they stood in roads, they gave him gifts, promised to be loyal to him, gave him their children as attendants and even followed him around like slaves.

original: He presently, as greatness knows itself,   Steps me a little higher than his vow   Made to my father while his blood was poor   Upon the naked shore at Ravenspurgh,
translation: Very quickly, as he became aware of his own importance, he began to forget the promise he had made to my father on the beach at Ravenspurgh when he was still humble and thankful to be accepted.

original: And now forsooth takes on him to reform   Some certain edicts and some strait decrees   That lie too heavy on the commonwealth,
translation: Now indeed, he has even decided to change certain laws and some strict decrees that  burden  the kingdom.

original: Cries out upon abuses, seems to weep   Over his country’s wrongs, and by this face,   This seeming brow of justice, did he win   The hearts of all that he did angle for,
translation: He speaks out against the abuses we are facing and seems to cry about the bad things happening in the country. It is this show of sympathy, this pretense of justice, that he won over the hearts of all of the people he was aiming to.

original: Proceeded further—cut me off the heads   Of all the favourites that the absent King   In deputation left behind him here   When he was personal in the Irish war.
translation: He then went even further! He cut off the heads of all of the advisors that  Richard II  had left behind to run the country, when he went to fight in the Irish war.

original: Tut, I came not to hear this.
translation: Enough. I didn't come to hear this.

original: Then to the point.
translation: Now to my point.

original: In short time after, he deposed the King,   Soon after that deprived him of his life   And, in the neck of that, tasked the whole state.
translation: Shortly after this, Henry took the throne from Richard, and quickly had him killed. Immediately after that he made the whole country pay more taxes.

original: To make that worse, suffered his kinsman March   (Who is, if every owner were well placed,   Indeed his king) to be engaged in Wales,   There without ransom to lie forfeited,
translation: To make things even worse, he let his kinsman Mortimer—who would be the king if everyone actually had the position they were entitled to—be held hostage in Wales, forced to stay there without ransom.

original: Disgraced me in my happy victories,   Sought to entrap me by intelligence,   Rated mine uncle from the council board,   In rage dismissed my father from the court,
translation: He shamed me for the battles I had won, he tried to catch me out with spies. He forced my uncle to leave the Council and in anger removed my father from his court.

original: Broke oath on oath, committed wrong on wrong,   And in conclusion drove us to seek out   This head of safety,
translation: He broke promise after promise and did one bad thing after another. And finally, he forced us to build this army to protect ourselves,

original: and withal to pry   Into his title, the which we find   Too indirect for long continuance.
translation: and also to question his right to rule, which we do not think is direct enough to carry on.

original: Shall I return this answer to the King?
translation: Is this what you want me to say to the King?

original: Not so, Sir Walter. We’ll withdraw awhile.
translation: No, Sir Walter. We will hold off on battle for a while.

original: Go to the King, and let there be impawned   Some surety for a safe return again,   And in the morning early shall my uncle   Bring him our purposes.
translation: Go back to the King, and my uncle will bring our reply early tomorrow morning, as long as you pledge that he will be able to return safely.

original: And so farewell.
translation: Goodbye then.

original: I would you would accept of grace and love.
translation: I wish you would accept the King's graceful and loving offer.

original: And maybe so we shall.
translation: Maybe we will.

original: Pray God you do.
translation: I pray to God that you do.

original: Hie, good Sir Michael, bear this sealèd brief   With winged haste to the Lord Marshal,
translation: Hurry, good Sir Michael, and take this sealed letter as quickly as you can to the  Lord Marshal ,

original: This to my cousin Scrope, and all the rest   To whom they are directed.
translation: this sealed letter to  Scrope , and the rest of the letters to whom they are addressed.

original: If you knew   How much they do import, you would make haste.
translation: If you knew how important these letters were, you would hurry.

original: My good lord, I guess their tenor.
translation: My good lord, I can guess what they are about.

original: Like enough you do.
translation: I'm sure you can.

original: Tomorrow, good Sir Michael, is a day   Wherein the fortune of ten thousand men   Must bide the touch. For, sir, at Shrewsbury,   As I am truly given to understand,   The King with mighty and quick-raisèd power   Meets with Lord Harry.
translation: Good Sir Michael, tomorrow is a day which will test the fortunes of ten thousand men. I have been told sir, that the King and his big and quickly-collected army will fight Hotspur at Shrewsbury.

original: And I fear, Sir Michael,   What with the sickness of Northumberland,   Whose power was in the first proportion,
translation: I am scared, Sir Michael, as Northumberland is sick, and his army was the biggest.

original: And what with Owen Glendower’s absence thence,   Who with them was a rated sinew too   And comes not in, o'er-ruled by prophecies,
translation: And Owen Glendower is still not here, even though he is being counted on, because prophecies have told him to stay away.

original: I fear the power of Percy is too weak   To wage an instant trial with the King.
translation: I am afraid that Percy is not strong enough to fight the King right now.

original: Why, my good lord, you need not fear. There is Douglas and Lord Mortimer.
translation: Why, my good lord, you don't need to be scared. There are still Douglas and Lord Mortimer.

original: No, Mortimer is not there.
translation: No, Mortimer is not there.

original: But there is Mordake, Vernon, Lord Harry Percy, And there is my Lord of Worcester and a head Of gallant warriors, noble gentlemen.
translation: Well then there is Mordake, Vernon, Lord Harry Percy. There is also my Lord of Worcester, and a whole bunch of brave warriors, all noble gentlemen.

original: And so there is.
translation: That's true.

original: But yet the King hath drawn   The special head of all the land together:
translation: But the King has assembled noble warriors from all over the land:

original: The Prince of Wales, Lord John of Lancaster,   The noble Westmoreland, and warlike Blunt,
translation: The Prince of Wales, Lord John of Lancaster, the noble Westmoreland, the warlike Blunt,

original: And many more corrivals and dear men   Of estimation and command in arms.
translation: and many more comrades and honorable men who are valued and good in battle.

original: Doubt not, my lord, they shall be well opposed.
translation: It's certain that they will face strong opposition.

original: I hope no less, yet needful ’tis to fear;
translation: I hope so, but I still feel afraid.

original: And to prevent the worst, Sir Michael, speed.
translation: Hurry Sir Michael, hurry now to stop something very bad from happening.

original: For if Lord Percy thrive not, ere the King   Dismiss his power, he means to visit us,
translation: For if Lord Percy does not win this battle, the King will come to look for us before he dismisses his army.

original: For he hath heard of our confederacy,   And ’tis but wisdom to make strong against him:   Therefore make haste.
translation: He has heard that we are part of the opposition, and so it is a good idea for us to prepare to face him. Therefore, hurry now!

original: I must go write again   To other friends. And so farewell, Sir Michael.
translation: I need to go and write more letters to other friends. Goodbye, Sir Michael.

original: How bloodily the sun begins to peer Above yon busky hill. The day looks pale At his distemp'rature.
translation: How bloody the sun looks as it peers over that looming hill. The day looks pale and sick because it has seen the unhealthy appearance of the sun.

original: The southern wind Doth play the trumpet to his purposes, And by his hollow whistling in the leaves Foretells a tempest and a blust'ring day.
translation: The southern wind is a trumpeter, announcing the motives of the sun. And the whistling of the breeze in the leaves makes it clear that it is going to be a stormy and windy day.

original: Then with the losers let it sympathize, For nothing can seem foul to those that win.
translation: Then let it sympathize with the losing side, since nothing seems bad to people who have just won a battle.

original: Hear me, my liege:
translation: Listen to me, my lord.

original: For mine own part I could be well content   To entertain the lag end of my life   With quiet hours.
translation: I would much prefer to spend the last years of my life in peace and quiet.

original: For I do protest   I have not sought the day of this dislike.
translation: I am telling you that I did not seek this day of conflict.

original: You have not sought it? How comes it then?
translation: You didn't seek it? Then how did it happen?

original: Rebellion lay in his way, and he found it.
translation: Rebellion was right in front of him, so he found it by accident, he didn't seek it.

original: Peace, chewet, peace.
translation: Be quiet, you chatterer. Be quiet.

original: (to the   KING   )   It pleased your Majesty to turn your  looks   Of favour from myself and all our house;
translation: [To the KING]  Your Majesty was happy to turn your back on me and all of my family.

original: And yet I must remember you, my lord,   We were the first and dearest of your friends.
translation: Yet, I must remind you, my lord, that we were your first and your dearest friends.

original: For you my staff of office did I break   In Richard’s time, and posted day and night   To meet you on the way, and kiss your hand   When yet you were in place and in account   Nothing so strong and fortunate as I.
translation: I left the role that I had during Richard's reign for you, and rode all day and night to meet you on the road and kiss your hand. Even though you were less powerful than me and your reputation was far weaker than mine,

original: It was myself, my brother, and his son   That brought you home and boldly did outdare   The dangers of the time. You swore to us,   And you did swear that oath at Doncaster,   That you did nothing purpose 'gainst the state,   Nor claim no further than your new-fall'n right,   The seat of Gaunt, dukedom of Lancaster.
translation: it was me, my brother, and his son that took you home and ignored the danger that went with that. When we were at Doncaster you swore an oath to us that you were not interested in the throne, that you just wanted to claim your recently inherited title—your father Gaunt's estate, the dukedom of Lancaster.

original: To this we swore our aid. But in short space   It rained down fortune show'ring on your head,   And such a flood of greatness fell on you—
translation: We promised to help you with this. But, very quickly luck poured down on you and a flood of greatness fell upon you.

original: What with our help, what with the absent King,   What with the injuries of a wanton time,   The seeming sufferances that you had borne,
translation: What with our help, King Richard's absence and the abuses people had been suffering under his rule, you seemed like you had suffered unfairly.

original: And from this swarm of fair advantages   You took occasion to be quickly wooed   To gripe the general sway into your hand,   Forget your oath to us at Doncaster;
translation: You made the most of these opportunities and were persuaded to take control of the entire kingdom. You forgot the oath that you had made to us at Doncaster.

original: And being fed by us, you used us so   As that ungentle gull, the cuckoo’s bird,   Useth the sparrow—did oppress our nest,   Grew by our feeding to so great a bulk   That even our love durst not come near your sight   For fear of swallowing;
translation: We fed you and kept you alive, but you just used us, like the aggressive cuckoo-bird uses the sparrow. We let you stay in our nest, but you grew so big that even we, the people who loved you, didn't want to come anywhere near you in case you swallowed us up.

original: but with nimble wing   We were enforced for safety sake to fly   Out of sight and raise this present head,
translation: We were forced to run away for our own safety and raise this army in secret.

original: Whereby we stand opposèd by such means   As you yourself have forged against yourself
translation: Now we are here with this army, forced to stand against you because of your actions.
