original: By unkind usage, dangerous countenance,   And violation of all faith and troth   Sworn to us in your younger enterprise.
translation: You have treated us badly, your behavior has been threatening, and you have broken the promises and vows that you swore to us when you were younger.

original: These things indeed you have articulate,   Proclaimed at market crosses, read in churches,
translation: You have said these things already, you have announced them in markets, you have lectured on them in churches.

original: To face the garment of rebellion   With some fine color that may please the eye   Of fickle changelings and poor discontents,   Which gape and rub the elbow at the news   Of hurlyburly innovation.
translation: You have done everything you can to make rebellion look better and to please the eyes of fickle  turncoats  and poor unhappy people, who laugh and are  delighted  at news of revolution.

original: And never yet did insurrection want   Such water colors to impaint his cause,
translation: Rebellion has never lacked thin excuses in support of a cause.

original: Nor moody beggars starving for a time   Of pellmell havoc and confusion.
translation: And angry beggars are eager to support a time of chaotic fighting and confusion.

original: In both your armies there is many a soul   Shall pay full dearly for this encounter   If once they join in trial.
translation: Both of our armies contain many men who will sacrifice their lives for this battle, once it starts.

original: Tell your nephew,   The Prince of Wales doth join with all the world   In praise of Henry Percy.
translation: Tell your nephew that the Prince of Wales agrees with the whole world in praising Henry Percy.

original: By my hopes,   This present enterprise set off his head,   I do not think a braver gentleman,   More active-valiant, or more valiant-young,   More daring or more bold, is now alive   To grace this latter age with noble deeds.
translation: I swear on my hopes of salvation, that except for his current actions, I don't think there's another man alive who is as brave, courageous, daring, or bold as him, or has acted as nobly.

original: For my part, I may speak it to my shame,   I have a truant been to chivalry,   And so I hear he doth account me too.
translation: As for me, I should be ashamed of how I have acted. I have avoided my noble position, and I know he agrees with me about that.

original: Yet this before my father’s majesty:   I am content that he shall take the odds   Of his great name and estimation,   And will, to save the blood on either side,   Try fortune with him in a single fight.
translation: Yet, with my father here as witness, I would like to challenge him to fight me in single combat, to save the amount of men who are killed on either side. I am aware that because of his fame and great reputation he is the favorite to win.

original: And, Prince of Wales, so dare we venture thee,   Albeit considerations infinite   Do make against it.—
translation: And, Prince of Wales, I should let you stake your life on this, even though there are countless reasons why I shouldn't.

original: No, good Worcester, no,   We love our people well, even those we love   That are misled upon your cousin’s part.
translation: No, good Worcester, no. We love our people very much, even the people who have been led astray by Hotspur's influence.

original: And, will they take the offer of our grace,   Both he and they and you, yea, every man   Shall be my friend again, and I’ll be his.
translation: If they will accept our pardon, then he, they, you, and in fact every man will be my friend again, and I will be his.

original: So tell your cousin, and bring me word   What he will do. But if he will not yield,   Rebuke and dread correction wait on us,   And they shall do their office.
translation: Tell your nephew this, and bring us back his reply.  If he will not accept this pardon then we will have to respond with harsh punishments.

original: So begone.   We will not now be troubled with reply.   We offer fair. Take it advisedly.
translation: So, leave. I don't want to listen to anything else you have to say right now. Our offer is fair. Consider it carefully.

original: It will not be accepted, on my life.
translation: He isn't going to accept—I could bet my life on it.

original: The Douglas and the Hotspur both together   Are confident against the world in arms.
translation: Douglas and Hotspur are confident that they could fight against the whole world and win.

original: Hence, therefore, every leader to his charge, For on their answer will we set on them, And God befriend us as our cause is just.
translation: Well then, every leader get to your unit and as soon as they reply, we will attack! God be with us, for our cause is just!

original: Hal, if thou see me down in the battle and bestride me, so; ’tis a point of friendship.
translation: Hal, if you see me fall down during the battle, stand over me  to defend me from further harm. It's what a friend would do.

original: Nothing but a colossus can do thee that friendship. Say thy prayers, and farewell.
translation: Only a giant would be able to be that friend for you. Say your prayers, and goodbye.

original: I would ’twere bedtime, Hal, and all well.
translation: I wish it was just bedtime, Hal, and that everything was okay.

original: Why, thou owest God a death.
'Tis not due yet. I would be loath to pay Him before  His day. What need I be so forward with Him that calls  not on me?
translation: Not yet I don't. I don't want to pay God before I have to. Why would I be so eager to pay God before he even asks for it?

original: Well, ’tis no matter. Honour pricks me on.  Yea, but how if honor prick me off when I come on? How  then?
translation: Well, it doesn't matter anyway. Honor drives me forward. Yes, but what if honor also picks me out to die when I go bravely forward? What then?

original: Can honor set to a leg? no. Or an arm? no. Or take away the grief of a wound? No. Honor hath no skill in  surgery, then? No.
translation: Can honor reattach a leg? No. Or an arm? No. Or take away the pain of a wound? No. Honor can't do surgery then? No.

original: What is honor? A word. What is in  that word “honor”? What is that “honor”? Air. A trim  reckoning.
translation: What is honor? A word. Well what's in that word "honor?" What is that "honor?" Just air. What a great deal!

original: Who hath it? He that died o' Wednesday. Doth  he feel it? No. Doth he hear it? No. 'Tis insensible,  then? Yea, to the dead.
translation: Who has it? That guy who died on Wednesday. Does he feel it? No. Does he hear it? No. Is it something which the sense can't be felt by the senses then? Well, at least not by the dead.

original: But will it not live with the  living? No. Why? Detraction will not suffer it.  Therefore, I’ll none of it. Honor is a mere scutcheon.  And so ends my catechism.
translation: But won't it exist with the living? No. Why? Slander will not allow it. Therefore I will have none of it. Honor is just a gravestone, and that concludes my  examination  of the subject.

original: O no, my nephew must not know, Sir Richard, The liberal and kind offer of the King.
translation: Oh no, Sir Richard! My nephew cannot know about this kind and generous offer from the King.

original: 'Twere best he did.
translation: It would be better if he did.

original: Then are we all undone.
translation: The we would be ruined.

original: It is not possible, it cannot be   The King should keep his word in loving us.   He will suspect us still and find a time   To punish this offense in other faults.
translation: There is no way that the King is going to keep his word and forgive us. He will always be suspicious and will find another reason to punish us for this rebellion.

original: Suspicion all our lives shall be stuck full of eyes,   For treason is but trusted like the fox,   Who, never so tame, so cherished and locked up,   Will have a wild trick of his ancestors.
translation: This suspicion will always be watching over us. Treason is like a fox—however tame it is, however cared for, even locked up, it still will have the inherited trait of savageness from its ancestors.

original: Look how we can, or sad or merrily,   Interpretation will misquote our looks,   And we shall feed like oxen at a stall,   The better cherished still the nearer death.
translation: Whether we look sad or happy, people will lie about our looks. And we will have to act like oxen at their stalls, only treated better when we are close to being slaughtered.

original: My nephew’s trespass may be well forgot;   It hath the excuse of youth and heat of blood,   And an adopted name of privilege—   A hairbrained Hotspur governed by a spleen:
translation: My nephew's disloyalty might be forgotten with time, since it could be put down to youth and a bad temper. Also, his nickname lets him act like this—he is just the hare-brained Hotspur, controlled by his rash impulses.

original: All his offenses live upon my head   And on his father’s. We did train him on,   And, his corruption being ta'en from us,   We as the spring of all shall pay for all.
translation: All of his offenses are going to be blamed on me and on his father. We encouraged him. And since we were the ones who originally convinced him to start this rebellion, we are the ones who will have to pay for it.

original: Therefore, good cousin, let not Harry know   In any case the offer of the King.
translation: Therefore, good Vernon, let's not tell Harry what the King has offered.

original: Deliver what you will; I’ll say ’tis so.
translation: Say what you think is best; I will back you up.

original: My uncle is returned. Deliver up my Lord of Westmoreland.— Uncle, what news?
The King will bid you battle presently.
Defy him by the Lord of Westmoreland.
translation: Send a message of defiance in response. Send it with the Lord of Westmoreland.

original: Lord Douglas, go you and tell him so.
translation: Lord Douglas, go and tell him this.

original: Marry, and shall, and very willingly.
translation: Indeed, I will, and gladly.

original: There is no seeming mercy in the King.
translation: The King doesn't seem to be very forgiving.

original: Did you beg any? God forbid!
translation: Did you ask for forgiveness? I hope not.

original: I told him gently of our grievances,   Of his oath-breaking,
translation: I told him politely why we were annoyed, about how he had broken his promises.

original: which he mended thus   By now forswearing that he is forsworn.
translation: He answered by denying all of it and swearing that he is innocent of his treachery.

original: He calls us “rebels,” “traitors,” and will scourge   With haughty arms this hateful name in us.
translation: He called us "rebels" and "traitors," and said that his proud army will make us suffer for what we have done.

original: Arm, gentlemen; to arms.
translation: Get your weapons gentlemen, get your weapons!

original: For I have thrown   A brave defiance in King Henry’s teeth,   And Westmoreland, that was engaged, did bear it,
translation: I have sent a bold message of defiance to King Henry, and our recent hostage Westmoreland will deliver it to him.

original: Which cannot choose but bring him quickly on.
translation: This is only going to make the battle start even sooner.

original: The Prince of Wales stepped forth before the King, And, nephew, challenged you to single fight.
translation: The Prince of Wales stepped forward before his father, and challenged you, nephew, to fight him in single combat.

original: O, would the quarrel lay upon our heads,
translation: Oh, I wish that the whole fight could just be between the two of us,

original: And that no man might draw short breath today   But I and Harry Monmouth!
translation: and that the only people who would have to die today would be me and Harry  Monmouth !

original: Tell me, tell me,   How showed his tasking?
translation: Tell me, tell me, how did he make this challenge?

original: Seemed it in contempt?
translation: Did it seem like he did it out of hatred for me?

original: No, by my soul. I never in my life   Did hear a challenge urged more modestly,
translation: No, on my life. I have never heard a challenge made with more grace.

original: Unless a brother should a brother dare   To gentle exercise and proof of arms.
translation: It felt like it was a brother daring another brother to practice fighting with him.

original: He gave you all the duties of a man,   Trimmed up your praises with a princely tongue,   Spoke your deservings like a chronicle,   Making you ever better than his praise   By still dispraising praise valued in you,
translation: He gave you all the respect that a man deserves, spoke your praises like a true prince. He spoke of how deserving you are, as if he knew your entire life history. He claimed that you were even better than praise itself, since words weren't enough to complement your heroic actions.

original: And, which became him like a prince indeed,   He made a blushing cital of himself,   And chid his truant youth with such a grace   As if he mastered there a double spirit   Of teaching and of learning instantly.
translation: He also spoke of himself very modestly, which was fitting for a prince, and criticized his foolish youth with such grace it was almost like he was both a responsible adult teaching and a foolish child learning at the same time.

original: There did he pause: but let me tell the world:   If he outlive the envy of this day,   England did never owe so sweet a hope,   So much misconstrued in his wantonness.
translation: He stopped there. But let me tell you, if he manages to survive this battle, England has a very hopeful future and he has been very misunderstood because of his wild behavior.

original: Cousin, I think thou art enamorèd   On his follies.
translation: Cousin, I think you might have been enchanted by his foolishness.

original: Never did I hear   Of any Prince so wild a liberty.
translation: I've never heard of a Prince who used his freedom so irresponsibly.

original: But be he as he will, yet once ere night   I will embrace him with a soldier’s arm,   That he shall shrink under my courtesy.—
translation: But whatever he is really like, before this night is over I will embrace him with a soldier's arms, and he will tremble when I do.

original: Arm, arm with speed, and, fellows, soldiers, friends,   Better consider what you have to do   Than I that have not well the gift of tongue   Can lift your blood up with persuasion.
translation: Get your weapons, get your weapons quickly! Friends, soldiers, partners, think about what you have to do in this battle as I am not a good enough speaker to motivate you with my words alone.

original: My lord, here are letters for you.
translation: My lord, here are letters for you.

original: I cannot read them now.—
translation: I can't read them now.

original: O gentlemen, the time of life is short;   To spend that shortness basely were too long
translation: Oh, gentlemen, life is short. If you spend your short life doing stupid things you are wasting your time.

original: If life did ride upon a dial’s point,   Still ending at the arrival of an hour.
translation: Even if life only  lasted one hour , it would always end too soon.

original: An if we live, we live to tread on kings;   If die, brave death, when princes die with us.
translation: If we live, we will triumph over kings. If we die, it will be a glorious death to die with princes.

original: Now, for our consciences, the arms are fair   When the intent of bearing them is just.
translation: Now, as for this battle, it is perfectly okay for us to bear arms because we are fighting for a just cause.

original: My lord, prepare. The King comes on apace.
translation: Get ready my lord. The King is almost here.

original: I thank him that he cuts me from my tale,   For I profess not talking.
translation: I am thankful that he has stopped me from saying anymore, since I am not good with words.

original: Only this:   Let each man do his best. And here draw I a sword,
translation: I will just say this—each man should do his best. And with that I will draw my sword.

original: Whose temper I intend to stain   With the best blood that I can meet withal   In the adventure of this perilous day.
translation: During this battle, on this dangerous day, I hope to stain my shining sword with the blood of all the noble men I encounter.

original: Now, Esperance! Percy! And set on.
translation: Now,  be hopeful ! Percy! Let's go!

original: Sound all the lofty instruments of war,   And by that music let us all embrace,
translation: Let the trumpets of war sound, and when they do, let's embrace each other.

original: For, heaven to earth, some of us never shall   A second time do such a courtesy.
translation: It's certain that some of us will never get to embrace one another again.

original: What is thy name that in the battle thus Thou crossest me? What honor dost thou seek Upon my head?
translation: What is your name, you who attacked me in battle? What honor are you going to get by fighting me?

original: Know then, my name is Douglas, And I do haunt thee in the battle thus Because some tell me that thou art a king.
translation: I will tell you. My name is Douglas, and I was following you in the battle because I have been told that you are a king.

original: They tell thee true.
translation: That is true.

original: The Lord of Stafford dear today hath bought   Thy likeness,
translation: The  Lord of Stafford  has paid heavily today for his resemblance to you,

original: for instead of thee, King Harry,   This sword hath ended him.
translation: since my sword killed him instead of you, King Harry.

original: So shall it thee,   Unless thou yield thee as my prisoner.
translation: Now finally my sword will kill you, unless you surrender to being my prisoner.

original: I was not born a yielder, thou proud Scot, And thou shalt find a king that will revenge Lord Stafford’s death.
translation: I wasn't born to surrender, you smug Scotsman. Now you will see a king taking revenge for Lord Stafford's death.

original: O Douglas, hadst thou fought at Holmedon thus, I never had triumphed upon a Scot.
translation: Oh, Douglas, if only you had fought like this at the battle of Holmedon, I would never have been able to beat a Scotsman like you!

original: All’s done, all’s won; here breathless lies the King.
translation: It's done. The battle has been won! Here is the dead King.

original: Where?
translation: Where?

original: Here.
translation: Here.

original: This, Douglas? No, I know this face full well. A gallant knight he was; his name was Blunt, Semblably furnished like the King himself.
translation: This body, Douglas? No, I recognize this man's face. He was a brave knight called Blunt. He is simply dressed to look like the King.

original: A fool go with thy soul whither it goes! A borrowed title hast thou bought too dear. Why didst thou tell me that thou wert a king?
translation: Wherever your soul is going, may the name of "fool" go with it! You have given your life for a borrowed title. Why did you tell me that you were a king?

original: The King hath many marching in his coats.
translation: The King has made many soldiers march in his clothes.

original: Now, by my sword, I will kill all his coats. I’ll murder all his wardrobe, piece by piece, Until I meet the King.
Up and away! Our soldiers stand full fairly for the day.
translation: Get going then! Our soldiers are on the verge of victory!

original: Though I could ’scape shot-free at London, I fear the  shot here. Here’s no scoring but upon the pate.—
translation: Although I managed to escape  without paying   in London, I am scared I won't escape so easily here.  Here everything is taken on the head.

original: Soft,  who are you? Sir Walter Blunt. There’s honor for you.  Here’s no vanity.
translation: Wait, who is this? Sir Walter Blunt. There's honor for you, but there's no vanity.

original: I am as hot as molten lead, and as  heavy too. God keep lead out of me; I need no more  weight than mine own bowels.
translation: I am as hot as liquid lead, and as heavy as lead as well. Please God keep the lead out of me.  I'm fat enough as it is without extra lead in my stomach.

original: I have led my ragamuffins  where they are peppered.   There’s not three of my hundred and fifty left alive, and they are for the town’s end,  to beg during life. But who comes here?
translation: I've led my pathetic troops into battle, and they've all been killed. There's only about three of my one hundred and fifty left alive, and they're only fit to beg on the outskirts of town. Wait, who's this?

original: What, stand’st thou idle here?   Lend me thy sword.
translation: What? Are you standing around doing nothing?  Lend me your sword.

original: Many a nobleman lies stark and stiff   Under the hoofs of vaunting enemies,   Whose deaths are yet unrevenged.
translation: Many noble men are lying stiff and dead under the horses of our boastful enemies, and their deaths have not yet been revenged.

original: I prithee,   Lend me thy sword.
translation: I ask you again, lend me your sword.

original: O Hal, I prithee, give me leave to breathe awhile. Turk Gregory never did such deeds in arms as I have done  this day. I have paid Percy; I have made him sure.
He is indeed, and living to kill thee. I prithee, lend me thy sword.
translation: He is certainly okay, and will now be coming to kill you. Come on, lend me your sword.

original: Nay, before God, Hal, if Percy be alive, thou gett’st  not my sword; but take my pistol, if thou wilt.
translation: No, I can't Hal! If Percy is still alive, then you can't have my sword. But take my gun if you want.

original: Give it to me. What, is it in the case?
translation: Give it to me. Is it in its holster?

original: Ay, Hal, ’tis hot, ’tis hot. There’s that will sack a  city.  [  PRINCE HENRY  draws it out and finds it to be a bottle of sack]
translation: Yes, Hal, it's hot, very hot—it could sack a city.

original: What, is it a time to jest and dally now?
translation: What?! Do you think now is a time for jokes?

original: Well, if Percy be alive, I’ll pierce him. If he do come in my way, so;
translation: Well, if Percy is still alive, I'll stab him, especially if he runs right at me.

original: if he do not, if I come in his  willingly, let him make a carbonado of me.
translation: If he doesn't run right at me, then I will gladly run at him and let him cut me up  like a piece of meat .

original: I like not  such grinning honor as Sir Walter hath.
translation: I don't want the same kind of insignificant honor that Sir Walter had.

original: Give me life,  which if I can save, so: if not, honor comes unlooked  for, and there’s an end.
translation: Let me have life, and if I can have that, great. If not, then I will get honor without looking for it. There, that's an  ending .

original: I prithee, Harry, withdraw thyself. Thou bleedest too  much. Lord John of Lancaster, go you with him.
translation: Harry, I beg you to withdraw from the battle. You are bleeding too much. Lord John of Lancaster, go with him.

original: Not I, my lord, unless I did bleed too.
translation: My lord, I won't—not unless I am bleeding too.

original: I beseech your Majesty, make up, Lest your retirement do amaze your friends.
translation: Your Majesty, I beg you—please keep your troops moving forward! Your men will be alarmed if they think you are retreating.

original: I will do so.—My Lord of Westmoreland, Lead him to his tent.
translation: Okay, I will. My Lord of Westmoreland, take him to his tent.

original: Come, my lord, I’ll lead you to your tent.
translation: Come on, my lord, I'll take you to your tent.

original: Lead me, my lord? I do not need your help,
translation: Take me, my lord? I don't need your help.

original: And God forbid a shallow scratch should drive   The Prince of Wales from such a field as this,
translation: And I'm certainly not going to let a slight scratch keep The Prince of Wales away from a battlefield like this,

original: Where stained nobility lies trodden on,   And rebels' arms triumph in massacres.
translation: where the blood-stained bodies of noblemen are being trampled on, and the rebels and their weapons are triumphing in their attacks.

original: We breathe too long. Come, cousin Westmoreland, Our duty this way lies. For God’s sake, come.
translation: We have taken too long of a break. Come on, Westmoreland; we are needed this way. For God's sake, come on!

original: By God, thou hast deceived me, Lancaster.   I did not think thee lord of such a spirit.
translation: By God, you have deceived me, Lancaster. I didn't think that you had such courage.

original: Before, I loved thee as a brother, John,
translation: I used to love you like a brother, John.

original: But now, I do respect thee as my soul.
translation: But now I regard you are my soulmate.

original: I saw him hold Lord Percy at the point With lustier maintenance than I did look for Of such an ungrown warrior.
O, this boy lends mettle to us all.
translation: Oh, this boy gives us all hope!

original: Another king! they grow like Hydra’s heads.—
translation: Another king! They grow like the  heads of Hydra !

original: I am the Douglas, fatal to all those   That wear those colors on them.
translation: I am Douglas, and I will murder anyone who wears that coat of arms.

original: What art thou   That counterfeit’st the person of a king?
translation: Who are you, dressed up like the King?

original: The King himself,
translation: I am the King himself.

original: who, Douglas, grieves at heart,   So many of his shadows thou hast met   And not the very king.
translation: Douglas, it upsets me that you have met so many men disguised as me, without meeting  the true King.

original: I have two boys   Seek Percy and thyself about the field,
translation: I have two sons fighting in this battle who are looking for Percy, and for you.

original: But, seeing thou fall’st on me so luckily,   I will assay thee. And defend thyself.
translation: But, since you were lucky enough to find me first, I will fight you now. Defend yourself.

original: I fear thou art another counterfeit,
translation: I am still worried that you are just another fake,

original: And yet, in faith, thou bear’st thee like a king.
translation: and yet it must be said that you do behave like a king.

original: But mine I am sure thou art, whoe'er thou be,   And thus I win thee.
translation: Whoever you are, you are mine, and I will defeat you.

original: Hold up thy head, vile Scot, or thou art like   Never to hold it up again.
translation: Look at me, you vile Scotsman, or you will never look at anyone again.

original: The spirits   Of valiant Shirley, Stafford, Blunt are in my arms.
translation: The spirits of brave  Shirley , Stafford, and Blunt empower me.

original: It is the Prince of Wales that threatens thee,   Who never promiseth but he means to pay.
translation: It is the Prince of Wales who threatens you, and I will always fulfill the promises I make.

original: Stay, and breathe awhile.
translation: Stay here, and rest for a while.

original: Thou hast redeemed thy lost opinion
translation: You have redeemed your awful reputation,

original: And showed thou mak’st some tender of my life   In this fair rescue thou hast brought to me.
translation: and by rescuing me, you have shown that you do care about my life.

original: O God, they did me too much injury   That ever said I hearkened for your death.
translation: Oh God! Anyone who said that I wanted you to die has done me a great offense.

original: If it were so, I might have let alone   The insulting hand of Douglas over you,
translation: If I had wanted you to die, I would have left you to fight against Douglas alone.

original: Which would have been as speedy in your end   As all the poisonous potions in the world,   And saved the treacherous labor of your son.
translation: That would have guaranteed your death quicker than any poisons in this world, and saved me from having to do anything treacherous.

original: Make up to Clifton. I’ll to Sir Nicholas Gawsey.
translation: Go to Clifton.  I'll go to Sir Nicholas Gawsey.

original: If I mistake not, thou art Harry Monmouth.
translation: If I am not mistaken, you are Harry Monmouth.

original: Thou speak’st as if I would deny my name.
translation: You speak like I would deny my own name.

original: My name is Harry Percy.
translation: My name is Harry Percy.

original: Why, then I see   A very valiant rebel of the name.
translation: Why then, you must be the brave rebel I am looking for with the same name.

original: I am the Prince of Wales; and think not, Percy,   To share with me in glory any more.
translation: I am the Prince of Wales and you can't share in my glory any longer, Percy.

original: Two stars keep not their motion in one sphere,
translation: Two stars can't fit into one orbit,

original: Nor can one England brook a double reign,   Of Harry Percy and the Prince of Wales.
translation: and likewise, England can't handle a double reign, with both Harry Percy and the Prince of Wales in charge.

original: Nor shall it, Harry, for the hour is come To end the one of us, and would to God Thy name in arms were now as great as mine.
translation: Well it won't have to, Harry. For it is time for one of us to die. If only your reputation for fighting was as good as mine is.

original: I’ll make it greater ere I part from thee, And all the budding honors on thy crest I’ll crop, to make a garland for my head.
I can no longer brook thy vanities.
translation: I can't listen to any more of your vain boasts.

original: Well said, Hal! To it Hal! Nay, you shall find no boys' play here, I can tell you.
translation: Well done, Hal! Keep it up! This is no child's play, I can tell you that.

original: O Harry, thou hast robbed me of my youth.
translation: Oh, Harry, you have taken away my youth .

original: I better brook the loss of brittle life   Than those proud titles thou hast won of me.
translation: I can handle the fact that my fragile life is over, but I can't deal with all of the honors you have won from me.

original: They wound my thoughts worse than thy sword my flesh.
translation: The thought of that hurts me more than the physical wound your sword has left.

original: But thoughts, the slave of life, and life, time’s fool,   And time, that takes survey of all the world,   Must have a stop.
translation: Thoughts need life, life depends on time, and even time, which watches over our world, has to have an end.

original: O, I could prophesy,   But that the earthy and cold hand of death   Lies on my tongue.
translation: Oh, I could tell prophecies, but the pale and cold hand of death stops me from talking.

original: No, Percy, thou art dust,   And food for—   (he dies)
translation: No, Percy. You are dust, and food for—  [He dies]

original: For worms, brave Percy. Fare thee well, great heart.
translation: For worms, brave Percy. Goodbye, brave thing.

original: Ill-weaved ambition, how much art thou shrunk!   When that this body did contain a spirit,   A kingdom for it was too small a bound,
translation: It's amazing how much your excessive ambition has already shrunk! When that body was alive, a whole kingdom wasn't even enough to contain your ambition.

original: But now two paces of the vilest earth   Is room enough. This earth that bears thee dead   Bears not alive so stout a gentleman.
translation: But now this small patch of dirty ground is enough room. The same ground that your dead body lies upon doesn't have a single living man on it who is anywhere near as brave as you.

original: If thou wert sensible of courtesy,   I should not make so dear a show of zeal.
translation: If you were able to hear these compliments, I wouldn't be so enthusiastic in giving you them.

original: But let my favors hide thy mangled face;   And even in thy behalf I’ll thank myself   For doing these fair rites of tenderness.
translation: But now I will cover your injured face with my scarf, and I will thank myself on your behalf for doing these acts of respect.

original: Adieu, and take thy praise with thee to heaven.   Thy ignominy sleep with thee in the grave,   But not remembered in thy epitaph.
translation: Farewell, and I hope you can take your praises with you to heaven! Let your shame stay with you in your grave, but keep it away from your tombstone.

original: Emboweled? If thou embowel me today, I’ll give you  leave to powder me and eat me too tomorrow.
translation: Disemboweled? If you disembowel me today, I'll let you preserve my body in salt and eat me for dinner tomorrow!

original: 'Sblood,  ’twas time to counterfeit, or that hot termagant Scot  had paid me scot and lot too.
translation: God, I had to pretend to be dead, or that savage Scotsman would have definitely killed me.

original: Counterfeit? I lie. I am  no counterfeit. To die is to be a counterfeit, for he is but the counterfeit of a man who hath not the life of a man;
translation: A fake? No, I am not a fake. To die is to be a faker, because a dead body is an impersonation of a living one.

original: but to counterfeit dying when a man thereby liveth is to be no counterfeit, but the true and perfect image of life indeed.
translation: However, pretending to be dead when you are actually alive is not being a faker, but is actually being the best kind of living person you can be.

original: The better part of valor is discretion, in the which better part I have saved my life.
translation: The most important thing about bravery is being careful with it, and by being careful, I saved my life.

original: Zounds,  I am afraid of this gunpowder Percy, though he be dead.  How if he should counterfeit too and rise? By my faith,  I am afraid he would prove the better counterfeit.
translation: Heavens, I am still afraid this explosive Percy, even though he is dead. What if he's faking too, and he just gets up? I reckon he'd be a better faker than I was.

original: Therefore I’ll make him sure, yea, and I’ll swear I  killed him. Why may not he rise as well as I? Nothing  confutes me but eyes, and nobody sees me.
translation: So, I'll just make sure he's dead, and then I can say that I killed him. Why couldn't he just get up, like I did? No-one could deny this but me, and there is no-one else here.

original: Therefore,  sirrah,   (stabs the body)     with a new wound in your thigh, come you along with me.     (he takes up     HOTSPUR     on his  back)
translation: Therefore, sir,  [He stabs the body]  with this new wound in your thigh you are coming with me.   [He picks up HOTSPUR and carries him on his back]

original: Come, brother John. Full bravely hast thou fleshed Thy maiden sword.
translation: Come on John, my brother. You have fought very bravely in your first battle.

original: But soft, whom have we here? Did you not tell me this fat man was dead?
translation: Hang on, who do we have here? Didn't you tell me that this fat man was dead?

original: I did; I saw him dead,   Breathless and bleeding on the ground.—
translation: I did. I saw him dead, breathless and bleeding on the ground.

original: No, that’s certain. I am not a double man.
translation: No, that's for certain. I am not  an apparition .

original: But if I be  not Jack Falstaff, then am I a jack.
translation: But if I am not Jack Falstaff, then I'm a villain.

original: There is Percy. If  your father will do me any honor, so; if not, let him  kill the next Percy himself.
translation: Here is Percy. If your father will give me the honor I deserve, let him do so. If not, let him kill the next Percy himself.

original: I look to be either earl or duke, I can assure you.
translation: I expect to be made either an earl or a duke, that's for sure.

original: Why, Percy I killed myself, and saw thee dead.
translation: I killed Percy myself, and I saw you dead on the ground.

original: Didst thou? Lord, Lord, how this world is given to  lying.
translation: Did you? Lord, Lord! How people love to lie.

original: I grant you, Iwas down and out of breath, and so  was he, but we rose both at an instant and fought a long hour by Shrewsbury clock.
translation: I will admit, I fell down and was out of breath and so was he. But we both got up at the same time and fought each other for a long hour according to the Shrewsbury clock.

original: If I may be believed, so; if  not, let them that should reward valor bear the sin upon their own heads.
translation: If you believe me, great. If not, let the people that don't believe me feel guilty for not giving me the honor I deserve for my bravery.

original: I’ll take it upon my death, I gave him this wound in the thigh. If the man were alive and  would deny it, zounds, I would make him eat a piece of  my sword.
translation: I swear on my life, I gave him this wound in his thigh. If Percy was alive and denied it, heavens, I would make him eat a bit of my sword.

original: This is the strangest tale that ever I heard.
translation: This is the strangest story I've ever heard.

original: This is the strangest fellow, brother John.— Come, bring your luggage nobly on your back. For my part, if a lie may do thee grace, I’ll gild it with the happiest terms I have.
translation: This is the strangest man alive, brother John. Come on then, carry that body with pride on your back. As for me, if lying is going to help your case, then I will support you however I can.

original: I’ll follow, as they say, for reward. He that rewards  me, God reward him. If I do grow great, I’ll grow less,  for I’ll purge and leave sack and live cleanly as a  nobleman should do.
translation: I'll follow them, but only to get my reward. Let God reward whoever rewards me. If I become a powerful nobleman, I'll get thinner. I'll diet, stop drinking, and live a good, clean life like a nobleman should.

original: Thus ever did rebellion find rebuke.—
translation: Rebellions will always end in defeat and punishment.

original: Ill-spirited Worcester, did not we send grace,   Pardon, and terms of love to all of you?
translation: Oh, evil-minded Worcester, didn't we send you a kind offer of pardon, and the possibility for a restored friendship?

original: And wouldst thou turn our offers contrary,   Misuse the tenor of thy kinsman’s trust?
translation: Yet, haven't you said that we did the exact opposite , and exploited Hotspur's trust in you by lying to him about this?

original: Three knights upon our party slain today,   A noble earl, and many a creature else   Had been alive this hour,   If like a Christian thou hadst truly borne   Betwixt our armies true intelligence.
translation: Three of our knights killed today, an earl, and many more men would still be alive if you had acted like a Christian, and delivered my true message to your leader.

original: What I have done my safety urged me to. And I embrace this fortune patiently, Since not to be avoided it falls on me.
translation: I did what I had to do to protect myself; and I will accept my punishment willingly, as I know there is nothing that I can do to avoid it.

original: Bear Worcester to the death, and Vernon too. Other offenders we will pause upon.
translation: Kill Worcester, and Vernon too. I will decide about the other offenders later.

original: The noble Scot, Lord Douglas, when he saw   The fortune of the day quite turned from him,   The noble Percy slain, and all his men   Upon the foot of fear, fled with the rest,
translation: When Lord Douglas, that brave Scotsman, saw that the battle was not going as planned, that Hotspur had been killed and his men were fleeing in fear, he ran away with them.

original: And, falling from a hill, he was so bruised   That the pursuers took him.
translation: While he was running, he fell from a hill and was so bruised that we managed to catch him.

original: At my tent   The Douglas is,   and I beseech your Grace   I may dispose of him.
translation: Douglas is now being held prisoner in my tent. And I would like to ask for permission, my lord, to decide what to do with him.

original: With all my heart.
translation: I do, with all my heart.

original: Then, brother John of Lancaster, to you   This honorable bounty shall belong.
translation: Then brother, John of Lancaster, I am giving you the honor of this great task.

original: Go to the Douglas, and deliver him   Up to his pleasure, ransomless and free.
translation: Go to Douglas and set him free, without a ransom.

original: His valor shown upon our crests today   Hath taught us how to cherish such high deeds,   Even in the bosom of our adversaries.
translation: His courage when fighting against us today must be acknowledged, even if he was fighting with our enemies.

original: I thank your Grace for this high courtesy, Which I shall give away immediately.
translation: Your Grace, I thank you very much for this honor, and will go and do this immediately.

original: Then this remains, that we divide our power.
translation: Then all that remains to do is for us to split up our army.

original: You, son John, and my cousin Westmoreland,   Towards York shall bend you with your dearest speed   To meet Northumberland and the prelate Scroop,   Who, as we hear, are busily in arms.
translation: John and Westmoreland, you must quickly take your armies towards York to confront Northumberland and that Archbishop Scroop who are preparing for battle as we speak.

original: Myself and you, son Harry, will towards Wales   To fight with Glendower and the Earl of March.   Rebellion in this land shall lose his sway,   Meeting the check of such another day.
translation: Harry, my son—you and I will travel towards Wales to fight with Glendower and Mortimer. Any rebels in this land will be stopped, if they lose another battle like they lost today.

original: And since this business so fair is done,   Let us not leave till all our own be won.
translation: So since we have already been very successful, let's not stop until we have won every battle, and reclaimed what is ours.

original: Open your ears, for which of you will stop   The vent of  hearing when loud Rumor speaks?
translation: Open your ears! For which of you would even be able to block your ears when loud Rumor is speaking?

original: I, from the orient to  the drooping west,   Making the wind my post-horse, still  unfold   The acts commenced on this ball of earth.
translation: I make the wind like my horse, carrying me from the east, to where the sun sets in the west, as I continue to narrate about the things happening in this world.

original: Upon my tongues continual slanders ride,   The which in every  language I pronounce,   Stuffing the ears of men with  false reports.
translation: My tongue always tells lies, and I tell lies in any language, filling up men's ears with these untruths.

original: I speak of peace while covert enmity    Under the smile of safety wounds the world.
translation: I say that everything is peaceful when in fact hidden anger lies behind kind smiles, ready to bring harm to the world.

original: And who but  Rumor, who but only I,   Make fearful musters and prepared defense,   Whiles the big year, swoll'n with some other  grief,   Is thought with child by the stern tyrant war,    And no such matter?
translation: And who is there but Rumor—who is there but me—who can make men raise armies in fear and prepare defenses, ready to fight in some war, when in fact the world is troubled by other problems that year?

original: Rumor is a pipe   Blown by surmises,  jealousies, conjectures,
translation: Rumor is like a pipe.

original: And of so easy and so plain a  stop   That the blunt monster with uncounted heads,   The  still-discordant wav'ring multitude,   Can play upon it.
translation: The only types of breath that can blow into it are suspicion, jealousy, and speculation. It's such an easy pipe to play that even the common people can play it—that stupid monster with so many heads, that is always noisy and always uncertain.

original: But what need I thus   My well-known body to anatomize    Among my household? Why is Rumor here?
translation: But why am I telling you, my audience, about my role and purpose of lying and making things up? You already know that, you're watching a play. Why is Rumor here?

original: I run before King  Harry’s victory,   Who in a bloody field by Shrewsbury    Hath beaten down young Hotspur and his troops,   Quenching  the flame of bold rebellion   Even with the rebels' blood.
translation: I come to tell you about the King's victory, how he defeated young Hotspur and his troops in a bloody battle near Shrewsbury, and now has put out the fire of rebellion with the rebels' own blood.

original: But what mean I   To speak so true at first? My office is   To noise abroad that Harry Monmouth fell
translation: But why am I telling you the truth already? I am supposed to be spreading the rumor that Prince Hal was killed by the angry, noble Hotspur.

original: Under the  wrath of noble Hotspur’s sword,   And that the King before the Douglas' rage   Stooped his anointed head as low as  death.
translation: I am also meant to relate that the King has been killed by Douglas, in his rage.

original: This have I rumored through the peasant towns    Between that royal field of Shrewsbury   And this  worm-eaten hold of ragged stone,
translation: I have already spread this rumor through the rustic towns between Shrewsbury and here—this dirty, old, stone castle,

original: Where Hotspur’s father, old Northumberland,   Lies crafty-sick. The posts come  tiring on,   And not a man of them brings other news   Than  they have learnt of me.
translation: where Hotspur's father, old Northumberland, is pretending to be ill. The messengers will keep arriving, and they all bring with them the news that they have heard from me.

original: From Rumor’s tongues   They bring  smooth comforts false, worse than true wrongs.
translation: It is from my tongues that they will announce false reports to comfort them, which are far worse than honest reports of grief and sadness.

original: Who keeps the gate here, ho?
What shall I say you are?
translation: Who shall I say that you are?

original: Tell thou the Earl That the Lord Bardolph doth  attend him here.
translation: Tell the Earl that Lord Bardolph is here to see him.

original: His lordship is walked forth into the orchard. Please  it your Honor knock but at the gate And he himself will  answer.
translation: His Lordship is currently walking in the garden. If you want to, knock on the gate of the garden and he will greet you himself.

original: Here comes the Earl.
translation: Here's the Earl now.

original: What news, Lord Bardolph? Every minute now   Should be  the father of some stratagem.   The times are wild.
translation: What news do you have for me, Lord Bardolph? There seems to be a new military strategy every minute. These are violent times.

original: Contention, like a horse   Full of high feeding, madly hath broke loose   And bears down all before him.
translation: This war is like a horse which has been overfed and then breaks out in rage and tramples on everything in its way.

original: Noble Earl, I bring you certain news from  Shrewsbury.
translation: Noble Earl, I have news for you from Shrewsbury.

original: Good, an God will!
translation: Good news, I hope.

original: As good as heart can wish.   The King is almost wounded  to the death,
translation: It's the best that we could have hoped for. The King has been wounded and is at risk of dying.

original: And, in the fortune of my lord your son,    Prince Harry slain outright; and both the Blunts   Killed  by the hand of Douglas;
translation: And because of your son's good fortunes, Prince Harry has been killed. Douglas has killed both of the Lords Blunt

original: young Prince John   And  Westmoreland and Stafford fled the field;   And Harry  Monmouth’s brawn, the hulk Sir John,   Is prisoner to your son.
translation: . And young Prince John, Westmoreland, and Stafford have fled the battle. Your son has even captured Harry's fat swine of a friend, that huge Sir John Falstaff.

original: O, such a day,   So fought, so followed, and so  fairly won,   Came not till now to dignify the times   Since Caesar’s fortunes.
translation: Oh, there hasn't been a battle fought or won quite as well as this since the triumphs of Julius Caesar! That is how honorable this moment is!

original: How is this derived? Saw you the field? Came you  from Shrewsbury?
translation: How do you know this? Did you see it happen? Have you just come from Shrewsbury?

original: I spake with one, my lord, that came from thence, A  gentleman well bred and of good name, That freely  rendered me these news for true.
translation: I spoke with someone who came from the battle. He was a gentleman with a strong upbringing and a good reputation, and he told me all of these things truthfully.

original: Here comes my servant Travers, who I sent On Tuesday  last to listen after news.
translation: Here comes my servant Travers. I sent him last Tuesday to find out the latest news.

original: My lord, I overrode him on the way;
translation: My lord, I rode past him on my way here.

original: And he is furnished with no certainties   More than he haply may retail from  me.
translation: He doesn't know anything other than what I told him.

original: Now, Travers, what good tidings comes with you?
translation: Now, Travers, what good news do you have for me?

original: My lord, Sir John Umfrevile turned me back   With joyful  tidings and, being better horsed,   Outrode me.
translation: Sir,  Lord Bardolph  sent me back here, having told me his happy news. As his horse is better than mine, he overtook me.

original: After him  came spurring hard   A gentleman, almost forspent with  speed,   That stopp’d by me to breathe his bloodied horse.
translation: After he had ridden off, another gentleman came along, riding very fast. He was going so quickly that he was exhausted and had to stop by me to give his bleeding horse a rest for a while.

original: He asked the way to Chester, and of him   I did demand  what news from Shrewsbury.
translation: He asked me how to get to Chester and I forced him to tell me if there was any news from Shrewsbury.

original: He told me that rebellion had bad luck   And that young Harry Percy’s spur was cold.
translation: He told me that the rebellion had been defeated and the  spur  of young Harry Percy was now cold.

original: With that he gave his able horse the head   And, bending  forward, struck his armèd heels   Against the panting  sides of his poor jade   Up to the rowel-head,
translation: Having said that, he got back on his horse, leaned forward, and dug his heels so hard into the sides of the poor old animal that he and the horse almost couldn't be seen anymore.

original: and  starting so   He seemed in running to devour the way,    Staying no longer question.
translation: He rode off as if he was trying to swallow the ground in front of him, and wasn't prepared to answer any more of my questions.

original: Ha? Again: Said he young Harry Percy’s spur was  cold? Of Hotspur, Coldspur? That rebellion Had met ill  luck?
My lord, I’ll tell you what: If my young lord your  son have not the day, Upon mine honor, for a silken  point I’ll give my barony. Never talk of it.
Why should that gentleman that rode by Travers Give  then such instances of loss?
translation: But why would this gentleman ride by Travers and make up such horrible things?

original: Who, he? He was some hilding fellow that had stolen  The horse he rode on and, upon my life, Spoke at a  venture. Look, here comes more news.
translation: What, him? He was probably some worthless idiot that had stolen the horse he was riding. I bet that he made it all up. Look, here comes someone with more news.

original: Yea, this man’s brow, like to a title leaf,   Foretells  the nature of a tragic volume.
translation: Yes, this man's face is like the title page of a book, preparing to tell a tragic story.

original: So looks the strond  whereon the imperious flood   Hath left a witness’d  usurpation.
translation: His face has been left marked with sadness, just like the shore after a terrible flood.

original: —   Say, Morton, didst thou come from  Shrewsbury?
translation: [To MORTON]  Have you just come from Shrewsbury, Morton?

original: I ran from Shrewsbury, my noble lord, Where hateful  death put on his ugliest mask To fright our party.
translation: I ran here from Shrewsbury, my noble lord. Death had arrived in its horrible mask and was frightening our men.

original: How doth my son and brother?   Thou tremblest, and the  whiteness in thy cheek   Is apter than thy tongue to tell  thy errand.
translation: How are my son and my brother? You are trembling and your white face gives away your news—you don't even need to say a word.

original: Even such a man, so faint, so spiritless,   So dull, so dead in look, so woebegone,   Drew Priam’s  curtain in the dead of night,   And would have told him  half his Troy was burnt;
translation: You remind me of the faint, passive, dull, dead-looking and sad man, who, after the Battle of Troy, went into King Priam's bedroom to tell him that half of his city had been burned down.

original: But Priam found the fire ere he his tongue,   And I my Percy’s death ere thou report’st  it.
translation: But Priam found the fire before he was told about it, and I know about my Percy's death before you even report it.

original: This thou wouldst say, “Your son did thus and thus;    Your brother thus; so fought the noble Douglas”—   Stopping my greedy ear with their bold deeds.
translation: You will say something like, "Your son did this and this; your brother did this; the noble Douglas fought like this," and you'll fill up my greedy ears with stories about their brave actions.

original: But in the end, to stop my ear indeed,   Thou hast a sigh to blow away this  praise,   Ending with “Brother, son, and all are dead.”
translation: But in the end, the only way to fill up my ears completely, is to blow away all of this praise with a sigh and finally tell me, "Your brother, your son, everyone is dead."

original: Douglas is living, and your brother yet, But for my  lord your son—
translation: Douglas is still living and so is your brother for now. But, my lord, your son—

original: Why, he is dead.   See what a ready tongue suspicion  hath!
translation: Why, he is dead. My suspicions were so quick to say so!

original: He that but fears the thing he would not know    Hath, by instinct, knowledge from others' eyes   That what  he feared is chancèd
translation: Even when a man fears something that he doesn't want to know, his instinct and the look in other people's eyes tell him that the thing has happened.

original: . Yet speak, Morton.   Tell thou an  earl his divination lies,   And I will take it as a sweet  disgrace   And make thee rich for doing me such wrong.
translation: But speak to me, Morton, and even though I'm an  earl , don't be afraid to tell me that my predictions are wrong. I would take it as a welcome disgrace, and would give you riches for lying to me about it.

original: You are too great to be by me gainsaid, Your spirit is  too true, your fears too certain.
translation: You are far too great a man to be lied to; your intuition is correct; your fears are right.

original: Yet, for all this, say not that Percy’s dead.   I see a  strange confession in thine eye.
translation: But in spite of all this, please don't say that Percy's dead. I can see some reluctant confession in your eyes.

original: Thou shak’st thy head  and hold’st it fear or sin   To speak a truth. If he be  slain, say so.   The tongue offends not that reports his  death;
translation: You shake your head and seem afraid to tell the truth in case it is sinful. If he is dead, just tell me. The man who must report a death can't offend anyone by doing his duty.

original: And he doth sin that doth belie the dead,   Not he  which says the dead is not alive.
translation: It is the man who lies about death who sins, not the man who must say that a dead man is not alive.

original: Yet the first bringer  of unwelcome news   Hath but a losing office, and his  tongue   Sounds ever after as a sullen bell   Remembered  tolling a departing friend.
translation: It is a losing battle, having to be the first person to announce terrible news. His words will always sound like a mourning bell, ringing out to remember a lost friend.

original: I cannot think, my lord, your son is dead.
translation: I don't want to believe that your son is dead, my lord.

original: I am sorry I should force you to believe   That which I  would to God I had not seen,   But these mine eyes saw him in bloody state,
translation: I am sorry that I have to force you to believe this, when I would have prayed to God to have never seen it myself. But I saw his bloody body with my own eyes.

original: Rend'ring faint quittance, wearied and outbreathed,   To Harry Monmouth; whose swift wrath beat  down   The never-daunted Percy to the earth,   From whence  with life he never more sprung up.
translation: He could only manage a weak exchange of blows, he was so tired and out of breath. Harry  Monmouth  struck down the unmovable Percy to the ground with his sudden fury, and Percy never got up again.

original: In few, his death,  whose spirit lent a fire   Even to the dullest peasant in  his camp,   Being bruited once, took fire and heat away    From the best tempered courage in his troops;
translation: To say this in just a few words: his courage had inspired us all, even the dullest peasant in the army. As soon as the news had been reported, it took the drive and the spirit out of even the bravest of our troops.

original: For from  his metal was his party steeled,   Which, once in him  abated, all the rest   Turned on themselves, like dull and heavy lead.
translation: For Percy's sword gave his army an edge, which, once blunted by his death, they became like a piece of dull and heavy lead, and couldn't fight anymore

original: And as the thing that’s heavy in itself    Upon enforcement flies with greatest speed,
translation: . And just as something heavy picks up speed when propelled forward

original: So did our  men, heavy in Hotspur’s loss,   Lend to this weight such  lightness with their fear
translation: , our men too—weighed down by their grief for Hotspur—started moving quickly.

original: That arrows fled not swifter  toward their aim   Than did our soldiers, aiming at their  safety,   Fly from the field.
translation: They went as quickly as arrows flying toward their target—but heading for safety, not for the battle.

original: Then was the noble Worcester   Too soon ta'en prisoner; and that furious Scot,   The  bloody Douglas, whose well-laboring sword   Had three  times slain th'appearance of the King,
translation: Your brother, the noble Worcester, was quickly taken captive. Then that angry Scotsman, the bloody Douglas, who had already killed three men dressed up to look like the King

original: Gan vail his  stomach and did grace the shame   Of those that turned  their backs and in his flight,   Stumbling in fear, was  took.
translation: , lost his courage too. He joined the men who were running away. But, as he fled, he stumbled and was captured.

original: The sum of all   Is that the King hath won
translation: The conclusion of all of that is that the King has won the battle.

original: and hath  sent out   A speedy power to encounter you, my lord,   Under the conduct of young Lancaster   And Westmoreland. This  is the news at full.
translation: And, my lord, he has sent out a fast moving army to confront you, led by the young Lancaster and Westmoreland. That is everything that I have to tell you.

original: For this I shall have time enough to mourn.   In poison  there is physic, and these news,   Having been well, that  would have made me sick,
translation: There will be time to mourn for this. Sometimes you can find healing in poison. If I had  been well, this news would have made me sick.

original: Being sick, have in some  measure made me well.   And as the wretch whose  fever-weakened joints,   Like strengthless hinges,
translation: As I am sick, this news has in some way made me well. I am like a diseased man—whose joints are so weakened by fever that they are like useless hinges

original: buckle  under life,   Impatient of his fit, breaks like a fire   Out of his keeper’s arms,
translation: —that buckles under his own weight and then, in a fit of impatience, bursts like a flame out of his nurse's arms.

original: even so my limbs,   Weakened with  grief, being now enraged with grief,   Are thrice  themselves.
translation: That's what my limbs are like now. Once they were weakened with grief, but now they are enraged with it, and feel three times more powerful than they were before.

original: Hence therefore, thou nice crutch.   A scaly  gauntlet now with joints of steel   Must glove this hand.
translation: Get away from me, you ridiculous crutch! Now armor will be the only thing to cover this hand.

original: And hence, thou sickly coif.   Thou art a guard too wanton for the head   Which princes, fleshed with conquest, aim  to hit.
translation: And get rid of this nightcap! It's far too feminine a hat for the head of someone who's about to be the target of princes, fresh from their victory

original: Now bind my brows with iron, and approach   The  ragged’st hour that time and spite dare bring   To frown  upon th'enraged Northumberland.
translation: . Cover my face in iron, and let the rough hour come when time and hatred will bring the worst things to attack me in my anger.

original: Let heaven kiss earth!  Now let not Nature’s hand   Keep the wild flood confined.  Let order die,   And let this world no longer be a stage    To feed contention in a lingering act;
translation: Let the skies fall to the ground! Now let the oceans flood the shores. To hell with order! Let the world stop being a stage that lets this argument carry on and on.

original: But let one spirit of the firstborn Cain   Reign in all bosoms, that, each  heart being set   On bloody courses, the rude scene may  end,   And darkness be the burier of the dead.
translation: Let the spirit of  Cain  live inside all of us. If every heart is set on murder, then this terrible scene might finally end, and darkness will cover up the dead bodies left behind.

original: This strainèd passion doth you wrong, my lord.
translation: This intense passion isn't good for you, my lord,

original: Sweet Earl, divorce not wisdom from your honor.   The  lives of all your loving complices   Lean on your health,  the which, if you give o'er   To stormy passion, must  perforce decay.
translation: Kind Earl, don't let your wronged sense of honor make you forget your wisdom. The lives of all your young allies are depending on you and your health. Don't let yourself be taken in by these violent passions—it will only make your illness worse.

original: You cast th' event of war, my noble  lord,   And summed the account of chance before you said    “Let us make head.” It was your presurmise   That, in the  dole of blows your son might drop.
translation: You thought about the outcome of the war before you said, "Let's raise an army." You predicted that when the fighting started, your son might die.

original: You knew he walked  o'er perils on an edge,   More likely to fall in than to  get o'er.
translation: You knew that he was doing something dangerous, walking on the edge of a cliff, more likely to fall over it than make it through.

original: You were advised his flesh was capable   Of  wounds and scars, and that his forward spirit   Would lift him where most trade of danger ranged.
translation: You knew that he might be wounded and scarred, and that his fearless spirit would take him into the most dangerous situations.

original: Yet did you say  “Go forth,” and none of this,   Though strongly  apprehended, could restrain   The stiff-borne action.
translation: But you still said, "Go ahead." Even though you knew all of these things, none of them sufficed to stop the decided course of action

original: What hath then befall'n,   Or what did this bold enterprise  brought forth,   More than that being which was like to  be?
translation: . So everything that has happened, all the results of this brave mission—were they not just what we expected to happen anyway?

original: We all that are engagèd to this loss   Knew that we  ventured on such dangerous seas
translation: Everyone who feels the pain of this loss knew that we were setting sail into dangerous waters.

original: That if we wrought out  life, ’twas ten to one;   And yet we ventured, for the  gain proposed   Choked the respect of likely peril feared;
translation: We knew that the odds were against us—it was ten to one that we would even survive. But we went ahead with the mission anyway, because the potential of winning meant more to us than the fear of losing.

original: And since we are o'erset, venture again.   Come, we will  all put forth, body and goods.
translation: And even though we lost this time, we will try again. Come on, we will all do this, and we will put our bodies and everything we have on the line.

original: 'Tis more than time.—And, my most noble lord,   I hear  for certain, and do speak the truth:   The gentle  Archbishop of York is up   With well-appointed powers.
translation: It is the right time for that. Also, my noble lord, I have heard for certain—and this is the truth—that the Archbishop of York has raised a strong army. He keeps his followers by using both his earthly and his spiritual powers.

original: He  is a man   Who with a double surety binds his followers.    My lord your son had only but the corpse,   But shadows and the shows of men, to fight;
translation: My lord, your son was only able to have authority over their bodies—they were just like the shadows of men, forced to fight.

original: For that same word  “rebellion” did divide   The action of their bodies from  their souls,
translation: It was because that word, "rebellion," separated their actions from their hearts.

original: And they did fight with queasiness,  constrained,   As men drink potions, that their weapons  only   Seemed on our side.
translation: They fought like they were sick and weak, almost like they were ill enough to be taking medicine. It was only their weapons which made them seem like they were on our side.

original: But, for their spirits and  souls,   This word “rebellion,” it had froze them up   As  fish are in a pond. But now the Bishop   Turns  insurrection to religion.
translation: The word "rebellion" had frozen their spirits and their souls, like fish trapped in an icy pond. But now the Archbishop makes the rebellion about religion.

original: Supposed sincere and holy in  his thoughts,   He’s followed both with body and with  mind,
translation: Because everyone thinks he is a good and holy man, they follow him with both their bodies and their minds.

original: And doth enlarge his rising with the blood   Of fair King Richard, scraped from Pomfret stones;
translation: He enhances his case by preaching about the blood of good King Richard, spilled on the stones of  Pomfret Castle .

original: Derives from heaven his quarrel and his cause;   Tells them he doth  bestride a bleeding land,   Gasping for life under great  Bolingbroke;   And more and less do flock to follow him.
translation: He says that this argument and this rebellion comes from heaven; he tells them that they are in a bleeding region, one that is gasping for breath under the rule of the great  Bolingbroke , and men from everywhere come to join him.

original: I knew of this before, but, to speak truth,   This  present grief had wiped it from my mind.
translation: I already knew this.  B ut, if I'm being honest, right now my grief had made me forget about it.

original: Go in with me  and counsel every man   The aptest way for safety and  revenge.   Get posts and letters, and make friends with  speed.   Never so few, and never yet more need.
translation: Come inside with me and we can discuss the best way to stay safe and get our revenge. Send out messengers with letters—we must make new allies quickly. Our numbers have never been this small, and yet, our need for men has never been greater.

original: Sirrah, you giant, what says the doctor to my water?
He said, sir, the water itself was a good healthy  water, but, for the party that owed it, he might have  more diseases than he knew for.
translation: Sir, he said that the urine itself was healthy urine, but as for the person who made the urine, he probably has more diseases than the doctor can even tell.

original: Men of all sorts take a pride to gird at me. The brain  of this   foolish-compounded clay, man, is not able to  invent   anything that tends to laughter more than I  invent, or is   invented on me.
translation: All sorts of men seem to feel proud when they take a stab at me. The brain of this stupid man—made out of clay—or any man for that matter, isn't able to come up with anything that makes people laugh as much as I do.

original: I am not only witty in  myself, but the cause that wit is in other men. I do  here walk before thee like a sow that hath overwhelmed  all her litter but one.
translation: I am not only extremely witty myself, but I am also the reason why other men are witty. I walk here before you like a sow that has killed all of her babies, except for you.

original: If the Prince put thee into my  service for any other reason than to set me off, why  then I have no judgment. Thou whoreson mandrake, thou  art fitter to be worn in my cap than to wait at my  heels.
translation: If the Prince sent you to work for me for any other reason than to make me angry, well then I'm an idiot. You  tiny , little, son-of-a-bitch, you look like you'd be more suitable for me to wear in my hat than to be a servant at my feet.

original: I was never manned with an agate till now, but I  will inset you neither in gold nor silver, but in vile  apparel, and send you back again to your master for a  jewel.
translation: I have never been waited on by a boy who was as tiny as the stone in a ring. But don't worry, I'm not going to set you in a gold or a silver ring.  I'll wrap you up in vile clothes instead and send you back to your master again, to be his jewel instead.

original: The juvenal, the Prince your master, whose chin  is not yet fledge—I will sooner have a beard grow in the palm of my hand than he shall get one off his cheek,  and yet he will not stick to say his face is a face  royal.
translation: That young man, the Prince, your master, who can't even grow hair on his face yet. I'm more likely to grow a beard in the palm of my hand than he is to grow one on his face. But that doesn't stop him from saying that his face is a royal one.

original: God may finish it when He will. 'Tis not a hair  amiss yet. He may keep it still at a face royal, for a  barber shall never earn sixpence out of it, and yet  he’ll be crowing as if he had writ man ever since his  father was a bachelor.
translation: Well, I guess God will give him a beard when he wants to—there's no sign of one yet. It will be able to remain a  royal  face, as he will never need to spend sixpence at the barbers. But still he claims that he's been a grown man ever since his father was young.

original: He may keep his own grace, but  he’s almost out of mine, I can assure him. What said  Master Dommelton about the satin for my short cloak and  my slops?
translation: He can keep his position. I have no love for him now, that for certain. What did Maiter Dommelton say about the satin to make my short jacket and my loose trousers?

original: He said, sir, you should procure him better assurance  than Bardolph. He would not take his band and yours. He  liked not the security.
translation: Sir, he said that he needs a better assurance that you will pay for it—more than just saying that Bardolph will take care of it. He didn't accept Bardolph's promise and he won't accept yours either. He didn't trust it.

original: Let him be damned like the glutton! Pray God his tongue be hotter! A whoreson Achitophel, a rascally  yea-forsooth   knave, to bear a gentleman in hand and then stand upon   security!
translation: Damn him to hell then, just like  Dives ! I hope to God that he burns even hotter! He's a son of a whore, a  traitor ! He's a complete liar: he'll encourage a gentleman to be hopeful and then later insist that he needs proof that I will pay.

original: The whoreson smoothy-pates do now  wear   nothing but high shoes and bunches of keys at their girdles; and if a man is through with them in honest  taking up, then they must stand upon security.
translation: These horrid tradesmen—who now have short hair, heeled shoes, and important tokens around their waist—will agree with you on an honest bargain, and then turn around and say that they need proof you will pay.

original: I had as  lief they would put ratsbane in my mouth as offer to  stop it with “security.” I looked he should have sent me two-and-twenty yards of satin, as I am a true knight,  and he sends me “security.”
translation: I would rather put rat poison in my mouth than agree to this "proof of payment." He was supposed to send me twenty-two yards of satin, as I am an honest knight— and instead he just demands "proof of payment!"

original: Well, he may sleep in  security, for he hath the horn of abundance, and the  lightness of his wife shines through it, and yet cannot  he see though he have his own lantern to light him.  Where’s Bardolph?
translation: Well, he can at least sleep well in the knowledge that he has a  horn  of plenty—his wife is cheating on him, and he is a cuckold, and yet he refuses to acknowledge it. Where's Bardolph?

original: He’s gone into Smithfield to buy your Worship a horse.
I bought him in Paul’s, and he’ll buy me a horse in    Smithfield.
translation: You know, I bought Bardolph in  Saint Paul's . Now he's going to buy me a horse in Smithfield.

original: An I could get me but a wife in the stews, I  were   manned, horsed, and wived.
translation: If he could just find me a wife in the brothels, I would have the best man, horse, and wife around.

original: Sir, here comes the nobleman that committed the Prince  for striking him about Bardolph.
translation: Sir, this is the nobleman who put the Prince in prison for hitting him when they were arguing about Bardolph.

original: Wait close. I will not see him.
translation: Let's hide, I don't want to talk to him.

original: What’s he that goes there?
translation: Who are you?

original: Falstaff, an ’t please your Lordship.
translation: Falstaff, if it pleases your Lordship.

original: He that was in question for the robbery?
translation: The same Falstaff who was a suspect in that robbery?

original: He, my lord; but he hath since done good service at  Shrewsbury, and, as I hear, is now going with some  charge to the Lord John of Lancaster.
translation: Yes, him, my lord. But since then, he has acted bravely at the Battle of Shrewsbury, and is now supposed to be taking some men to fight alongside Lord John of Lancaster.

original: What, to York? Call him back again.
translation: What? He's off to York? Tell him to come back here.

original: Sir John Falstaff!
translation: Sir John Falstaff!

original: Boy, tell him I am deaf.
translation: Boy, tell him that I am deaf.

original: You must speak louder. My master is deaf.
translation: Sorry, you need to speak louder. My master is deaf.

original: I am sure he is, to the hearing of any thing good.—Go  pluck him by the elbow. I must speak with him.
translation: I'm sure he is—at least when anything good is being said. Then go and grab him by the arm. I need to speak to him.

original: Sir John!
translation: Sir John!

original: What, a young knave and begging? Is there not wars? Is    there not employment?
translation: What? A young rascal and a beggar at that? Are there not wars happening? Aren't there things to do?

original: Doth not the King lack subjects? Do not the rebels need soldiers? Though it be a shame to  be on any side but one, it is worse shame to beg than to be on the worst side,
translation: Doesn't the King need more subjects? Don't the rebels need more soldiers? Even though it's shameful to be on any side other than the King's, it's even more shameful to be a beggar than it is to be a soldier on the wrong side.

original: were it worse than the name of  rebellion can tell how to make it.
translation: It makes the word "rebellion" seem even worse than it already is.

original: You mistake me, sir.
translation: You've got me all wrong, sir.

original: Why sir, did I say you were an honest man? Setting my  knighthood and my soldiership aside, I had lied in my  throat if I had said so.
translation: Why sir, have I said that you are an honest man? Because, ignoring the fact that I'm a knight and a soldier, I would be a liar if I had said that.

original: I pray you, sir, then set your knighthood and our  soldiership aside, and give me leave to tell you, you  lie in your throat if you say I am any other than an  honest man.
translation: Then I'm asking you, sir, to ignore the fact that you're a knight and a soldier, and let me tell you that you're lying if you say that I am anything other than an honest man.

original: I give thee leave to tell me so? I lay aside that which grows   to me?
translation: Do I have to let you tell me that? I am expected to ignore the things which define me as a person.

original: If thou gett’st any leave of me, hang me;  if thou tak’st leave, thou wert better be hanged. You  hunt counter. Hence! Avaunt!
translation: If I let you do this, then hang me. If you allow yourself to do this, then you should be hanged too. You've got the wrong man. Therefore, get going! Out of my sight!

original: Sir, my lord would speak with you.
translation: Sir, my lord wants to speak to you.

original: Sir John Falstaff, a word with you.
translation: Sir John Falstaff, a word please.

original: My good lord. God give your Lordship good time of the  day. I am glad to see your Lordship abroad. I heard say  your Lordship was sick: I hope your Lordship goes abroad by advice.
translation: My good lord. I hope God gives your Lordship a good day. It's good to see your Lordship out and about. I heard some people saying that you have been sick. I hope that it's all right that you're out and about.

original: Your Lordship, though not clean past your  youth, have yet some smack of an age in you, some relish of the saltness of time in you,
translation: Your Lordship—although you're not entirely past your youth—you have a bit of age creeping up on you, some signs of maturity

original: and I most humbly  beseech your Lordship to have a reverent care of your  health.
translation: . And I must humbly encourage your Lordship to make sure that you're taking care of your health.

original: Sir John, I sent for you before your expedition to  Shrewsbury.
translation: Sir John, I sent for you before you went off to fight at Shrewsbury.

original: An ’t please your Lordship, I hear his Majesty is  returned with some discomfort from Wales.
