translation: If it pleases your Lordship, I have heard that the King is back from Wales and everything didn't go quite as planned.

original: I talk not of his Majesty. You would not come when I  sent for you.
translation: I am not here to talk about the King. Why didn't you come when I sent for you?

original: And I hear, moreover, his Highness is fallen into this  same whoreson apoplexy.
translation: I have also heard that his Highness has got the same awful paralysis.

original: Well, God mend him. I pray you let me speak with you.
translation: Well, I hope that he recovers soon. Now please, I need to speak to you.

original: This apoplexy, as I take it, is a kind of lethargy
translation: If I've heard correctly, this paralysis is a kind of lethargy.

original: , an  ’t please   your Lordship, a kind of sleeping in the  blood, a whoreson   tingling.
translation: If it pleases your Lordship to know more, it's a kind of sleepiness in the blood, an awful tingling feeling.

original: What tell you me of it? Be it as it is.
translation: Why are you telling me all about it? Leave it alone.

original: It hath its original from much grief, from study, and  perturbation of the brain. I have read the cause of his  effects in Galen. It is a kind of deafness.
I think you are fallen into the disease, for you hear  not what I say to you.
translation: Well then I think that you must have this disease too, since you don't seem to be able to hear a word I'm saying to you.

original: Very well, my lord, very well. Rather, an ’t please  you, it is the disease of not listening, the malady of  not marking, that I am troubled withal.
translation: It's possible, my lord, it's possible. But instead, if it pleases you, I think that I have the disease of not listening, the sickness of not paying attention—that is what I have.

original: To punish you by the heels would amend the attention of your ears, and I care not if I do become your  physician.
translation: The only way to fix that problem would be to put you in prison, and I can't say that I'd mind being your doctor.

original: I am as poor as Job, my lord, but not so patient. Your    Lordship may minister the potion of imprisonment to me in respect of poverty,
translation: My lord, I am as poor as  Job , but not as patient. Because I am so poor, your Lordship would be able to imprison me.

original: but how should I be your patient to follow your prescriptions, the wise may make some dram  of a scruple, or indeed a scruple itself.
translation: But if I have to go to prison as you command, then people might have doubts or questions about it.

original: I sent for you, when there were matters against you for your life, to come speak with me.
translation: When I sent for you, there were charges against you which could have had you killed.

original: As I was then advised by my learned counsel in the laws of this land-service, I did not come.
translation: I was advised that because of the rules of military service and the fact that I was on duty, I should not go to you.

original: Well, the truth is, Sir John, you live in great infamy.
translation: Well, the truth is that you have a huge reputation for doing dishonorable things, Sir John.

original: He that buckles him in my belt cannot live in less.
Your means are very slender, and your waste is great.
translation: You don't have very much, but you waste what you do have.

original: I would it were otherwise. I would my means were  greater and my waist slender.
translation: I wish it were different. I wish I had more and my waist was smaller.

original: You have misled the youthful Prince.
translation: You have misled the young Prince.

original: The young Prince hath misled me. I am the fellow with  the great belly, and he my dog.
translation: No, the young Prince has misled me. I'm just a man with a huge belly and he's the dog who leads me.

original: Well, I am loath to gall a new-healed wound. Your day’s   service at Shrewsbury hath a little gilded over your  night’s   exploit on Gad’s Hill.
translation: Well, I don't want to open up a wound that has just healed. The good deeds you did at the Battle of Shrewsbury have partly made up for the robbery you committed at Gad's Hill.

original: You may thank th' unquiet time for   your quiet o'erposting that action.
translation: You can thank the rebellion for helping your offense be forgotten.

original: My lord!
translation: My lord!

original: But since all is well, keep it so. Wake not a sleeping  wolf.
translation: Now that everything is all right, let's make sure things stay like that. We don't need to wake a sleeping wolf.

original: To wake a wolf is as bad as to smell a fox.
translation: It's as bad to wake a wolf as it is to smell a fox.

original: What, you are as a candle, the better part burnt out.
translation: What? By this stage you seem like a candle—the best bit is burned out already.

original: A wassail candle, my lord, all tallow. If I did say of  wax, my growth would approve the truth.
translation: Then I'm a large, fat candle, made of animal fat, my lord. It would make more sense if you said I was a wax candle, as my waxing here has proved.

original: There is not a white hair on your face but should have  his effect of gravity.
translation: The white hairs on your face should be enough to tell me you're a man of gravity.

original: His effect of gravy, gravy, gravy.
translation: No, I'm more a man of gravy, gravy, gravy.

original: You follow the young Prince up and down like his ill  angel.
translation: You follow the young Prince wherever he goes, like some kind of evil spirit.

original: Not so, my lord. Your ill angel is light, but I hope he that   looks upon me will take me without weighing.
translation: That's not true, my lord. An evil spirit is light on its feet, and I'm sure that anyone who looks at me can tell that I'm too heavy.

original: And  yet in   some respects I grant I cannot go. I cannot tell. Virtue is of   so little regard in these costermongers'  times that true valor is turned bear-herd;
translation: But I guess in some ways maybe you're right. I don't know what to think. Virtue counts for so little these days that true honor isn't even noticed—everyone is just thought of as a bear-leader

original: pregnancy is  made a tapster, and hath his quick wit wasted in giving  reckonings. All the other gifts appurtenant to man, as  the malice of this age shapes them, are not worth a  gooseberry.
translation: . Being intelligent is only really useful for a bartender, and his intelligence is wasted because all he does is add up various bills. Even all the other good qualities of men aren't worth anything in these awful times.

original: You that are old consider not the capacities of us that are young. You do measure the heat of our  livers with the bitterness of your galls
translation: You old men don't think much of  us younger people . You measure the heat of our passions against our melancholy and sadness.

original: , and we that  are in the vaward of our youth, I must confess, are wags too.
translation: And I have to say that those of us who are at the forefront of youth, we're high-spirited as well as youthful.

original: Do you set down your name in the scroll of youth, that  are   written down old with all the characters of age?  Have you   not a moist eye, a dry hand, a yellow cheek, a  white beard, a decreasing leg, an increasing belly?
translation: Do you include yourself on the list of the young, even though you have age written all over you? Don't you have red and watery eyes? Wrinkled old hands? Jaundice? A white beard? A damaged leg? An ever-growing stomach?

original: Is  not your voice broken, your wind short, your chin  double, your wit single, and every part about you  blasted with antiquity? And will you yet call yourself  young? Fie, fie, fie, Sir John
translation: Isn't your voice hoarse? Aren't you short of breath? Your double chin is even bigger now? Your last bit of wit is gone, and all of you is ruined by age? And you still call yourself young? Oh, for shame, Sir John!

original: My lord, I was born about three of the clock in the  afternoon, with a white head and something a round  belly. For my voice, I have lost it with halloing and  singing of anthems. To approve my youth further, I will  not.
translation: My lord, I was born at about three o'clock in the afternoon, with a white head and a slightly round belly. As for my voice, I lost it by shouting and singing loud songs. I don't feel the need to prove my youth anymore to you.

original: The truth is, I am only old in judgment and  understanding. And he that will caper with me for a  thousand marks, let him lend me the money, and have at  him!
translation: The truth is, I'm only old when it comes to my good judgement and my knowledge. If anyone wants to challenge me to a dancing competition for a thousand  marks , then hand over the money and let's go!

original: For the box of the ear that the Prince gave you, he gave it like a rude prince, and you took it like a  sensible lord. I have checked him for it, and the young  lion repents. Marry, not in ashes and sackcloth, but in  new silk and old sack.
translation: As for the slap against your head that the Prince gave you, he gave it like a rude prince, and you took it like a sensible lord. I have told him off for it, and the young lion is sorry.  Indeed , he might not be wearing the normal  sackcloth and ashes,  but he is making up for it in silk clothes and by drinking old wine.

original: Well, God send the Prince a better companion.
translation: I hope that God sends the Prince a better friend!

original: God send the companion a better prince. I cannot rid my hands of him.
translation: I hope that the friend gets sent a better prince. I can't get rid of this one.

original: Well, the King hath severed you and Prince Harry. I  hear you are going with Lord John of Lancaster against  the Archbishop and the Earl of Northumberland.
translation: Well, the King has made sure that you and Prince Harry are separated. Apparently you are going with Lord John of Lancaster to fight against the Archbishop of York and the Earl of Northumberland.

original: Yea, I thank your pretty sweet wit for it. But look you pray,   all you that kiss my Lady Peace at home, that our armies join not in a hot day, for, by the Lord, I take  but two shirts out with me, and I mean not to sweat  extraordinarily.
translation: Yes, and thanks for bringing that up. But make sure you pray for peace and that our armies don't have to fight each other on a hot day. For, by the Lord, I'm only taking two shirts with me— so I don't want to be sweating a lot in them!

original: If it be a hot day and I brandish  anything but a bottle, I would I might never spit white  again.
translation: If it's a hot day, the only thing I should be doing is holding out a bottle and drinking. If I do anything else, then I will never drink white wine again.

original: There is not a dangerous action can peep out his  head but I am thrust upon it. Well, I cannot last ever.  But it was always yet the trick of our English nation,  if they have a good thing, to make it too common.
translation: I seem to be sent off on every dangerous mission. Well, I guess I can't live forever. That's always the trick of English people—if they have something good, they just keep using it.

original: If ye  will needs say I am an old man, you should give me rest. I would to God my name were not so terrible to the  enemy as it is. I were better to be eaten to death with a rust than to be scoured to nothing with perpetual  motion.
translation: If you want to say that I'm an old man, then let me rest and not go to these wars. I wish to God that the enemy weren't so afraid of my name. I'd rather be left to rust than exhausted by all of this action.

original: Well, be honest, be honest; and God bless your  expedition!
translation: Well, stay true, stay true. God bless your mission!

original: Will your Lordship lend me a thousand pound to furnish  me forth?
translation: Will your Lordship lend me a thousand pounds so I can get ready for the battle?

original: Not a penny, not a penny. You are too impatient to bear crosses. Fare you well. Commend me to my cousin  Westmoreland.
translation: I'm not going to lend you a penny. You're too eager for trouble. Goodbye to you now. Send my regards to Westmoreland.

original: If I do, fillip me with a three-man beetle.
translation: If I do, smack me with a sledgehammer.

original: A man can  no more separate age and covetousness than he can part  young limbs and lechery; but the gout galls the one, and the pox pinches the other, and so both the degrees  prevent my curses.
translation: A man is just as able to separate age from greed as he is to separate youth from lust. Gout affects the first, and syphilis gets the other. So there's no point in cursing either the old or the young, because they both have their own curses!

original: —Boy!
translation: [To his PAGE]  Boy!

original: Sir.
translation: Sir.

original: What money is in my purse?
translation: How much money do I have in my purse?

original: Seven groats and two pence.
I can get no remedy against this consumption of the  purse. Borrowing only lingers and lingers it out, but  the disease is incurable.
translation: There's nothing I can do to make the state of my purse any better. Borrowing money only delays the inevitable, but there is no cure for this disease.

original: Go bear this letter to my Lord of Lancaster, this to the Prince, this to the Earl of  Westmoreland; and this to old Mistress Ursula, whom I  have weekly sworn to marry since I perceived the first  white hair on my chin
translation: Go and take this letter to the Lord of Lancaster; this one to the Prince; and this one to the Earl of Westmoreland. Also, take this one to old Mistress Ursula, as I have been promising to marry her every week since I got my first grey hair.

original: . About it. You know where to find  me.
translation: Off you go. You know where to find me.

original: A pox of this gout! Or, a gout of this pox, for the one or the   other plays the rogue with my great toe. 'Tis no matter if I   do halt.
translation: Oh damn this gout! Or maybe damn this syphilis. For one or the other is wreaking havoc on my big toe. Well, I guess it doesn't matter if I have to limp.

original: I have the wars for my color, and  my pension shall   seem the more reasonable.
translation: I can blame it on the wars, and that will make my pension seem all the more justified.

original: A good wit  will make use of   anything. I will turn diseases to  commodity.
translation: A clever mind can turn any problem into a good thing. I can even turn diseases to my advantage.

original: Thus have you heard our cause and known our means,   And, my most noble friends,
translation: So now you have heard why we're fighting and what kind of support we have, my noble friends.

original: I pray you all   Speak plainly  your opinions of our hopes.
translation: I want you to tell me truthfully if you think we have a chance.

original: And first, Lord Marshal,  what say you to it?
translation: Firstly you, Marshal Mowbray: what do you think?

original: I well allow the occasion of our arms,
translation: I agree with why we are fighting,

original: But gladly would be better satisfied   How in our means we should advance  ourselves   To look with forehead bold and big enough   Upon the power and puissance of the King.
translation: but I would feel happier if I knew how we were going to be strong enough to fight with so few resources against the King's powerful forces.

original: Our present musters grow upon the file   To  five-and-twenty thousand men of choice,   And our supplies live largely in the hope   Of great Northumberland,
translation: Our present army now stands at twenty-five thousand good men, and we are hoping for reinforcements from the great Northumberland,

original: whose bosom burns   With an incensèd fire of injuries.
translation: whose heart is burning with the grief of his loss.

original: The question then, Lord Hastings, standeth thus:
translation: Then the question is, Lord Hastings,

original: Whether our present five-and-twenty thousand   May hold up  head without Northumberland.
translation: would we be able to win this fight solely with our own twenty-five thousand men, without Northumberland's help?

original: With him we may.
translation: With his help, we could win.

original: Yea, marry, there’s the point.   But if without him we be thought too feeble,   My judgment is we should not  step too far   Till we had his assistance by the hand.
translation: That's precisely my point. If we think that we are too weak to fight without him, then I think that we should hold off on doing anything until we know that he is definitely coming.

original: For in a theme so bloody-faced as this,   Conjecture,  expectation, and surmise   Of aids incertain should not be admitted.
translation: In a battle as bloody as this one will be, we cannot allow for uncertainty. There can't be any guessing, hoping, or speculating when it comes to our support—we need to know for certain.

original: 'Tis very true, Lord Bardolph; for indeed It was young  Hotspur’s cause at Shrewsbury.
translation: That's right, Lord Bardolph. That was young Hotspur's mistake at Shrewsbury.

original: It was, my lord; who lined himself with hope,   Eating  the air on promise of supply,
translation: It certainly was, my lord. He went into that battle with just his hope, and believed the empty words of the men who promised to send reinforcements.

original: Flatt'ring himself in  project of a power   Much smaller than the smallest of his thoughts,
translation: He let himself get carried away—expecting a huge army to turn up to help—when in fact, the help that came proved to be smaller than even the smallest of his thoughts.

original: And so, with great imagination   Proper to  madmen, led his powers to death   And, winking, leapt into destruction.
translation: It was with this vivid imagination—which only madmen should have—that he led his soldiers to their deaths, and shutting his eyes, leapt into his own destruction.

original: But, by your leave, it never yet did hurt To lay down  likelihoods and forms of hope.
translation: But, forgive me, it's doesn't hurt to think about possible outcomes of the battle and hopeful strategies that we could use.

original: Yes, if this present quality of war—   Indeed the instant action, a cause on foot—
translation:
Yes it does. The current situation is that our troops are
already on the move.

original: Lives so in hope, as in an  early spring   We see the appearing buds, which to prove  fruit   Hope gives not so much warrant as despair   That  frosts will bite them.
translation:
But if we put all of our hopes in them, that is like seeing
the first buds of spring and expecting that these will bear fruit—when in
reality, they are more likely to be killed by frost.

original: When we mean to build,   We first  survey the plot, then draw the model,   And when we see  the figure of the house,   Then must we rate the cost of  the erection,
translation:
When we decide to build
something, first we look at the land and then we draw up the plans. When we
know what the house will look like, we work out how much it is going to cost.

original: Which if we find outweighs ability,   What  do we then but draw anew the model   In fewer offices, or  at last desist   To build at all?
translation:
If we find that the cost is more than we can afford, we change the plans so
that the house has fewer rooms, or we decide to cancel the building project completely.

original: Much more in this great  work,   Which is almost to pluck a kingdom down   And set  another up, should we survey   The plot of situation and  the model,   Consent upon a sure foundation,
translation:
Since we are trying to take down a kingdom and start a whole
new one, our mission is so great that we must really think about the land and the plans. We need to
know that we have a strong foundation.

original: Question  surveyors, know our own estate,   How able such a work to  undergo,   To weigh against his opposite.
translation:
We need to have the right men for the
task. We need to know what we can afford, and how prepared we are to face the unfortunate events that might occur.

original: Or else   We  fortify in paper and in figures,   Using the names of men  instead of men,
translation: Or else this just seems like a game, in which we list on paper the numbers and names of men, rather than recognize the actual living people behind those figures and names.

original: Like one that draws the model of a house   Beyond his power to build it
translation: It would be like someone who draws up the plans for a house that they know they will never be able to finish building;

original: , who, half through,   Gives  o'er and leaves his part-created cost   A naked subject to the weeping clouds   And waste for churlish winter’s  tyranny.
translation: like someone who abandons the task halfway through, leaving this half-built house to be ruined by rain and the ravages of winter.

original: Grant that our hopes, yet likely of fair birth,   Should  be stillborn and that we now possessed   The utmost man of expectation,
translation:
Even if everything that we're hoping for falls through and
the men that we have now are all that we're going to have,

original: I think we are a body strong enough,   Even  as we are, to equal with the King.
translation:
I still think that
our army is strong enough as we are to be a match for the King.

original: What, is the King but five-and twenty-thousand?
translation: What? Does the King only have twenty-five thousand men as well?

original: To us no more, nay, not so much, Lord Bardolph,   For his divisions, as the times do brawl,   Are in three heads:
translation:
The King has assigned no more men to fight us than we
currently have—and maybe even less, Lord Bardolph. These are violent times,
and the King is currently fighting three battles.

original: one power against the French,   And one against Glendower; perforce a third   Must take up us.
translation:
One army is fighting against
the French, and one against  Glendower . Therefore a third army must fight
against us.

original: So is the unfirm King   In three divided, and his coffers sound   With hollow  poverty and emptiness.
translation: The weak King is now split into three, and his bank account is drained to point of poverty.

original: That he should draw his several strengths together And  come against us in full puissance Need not be dreaded.
translation: We also don't need to be worried about him bringing all of his troops back together to fight against us with his full power.

original: If he should do so, He leaves his back unarmed, the  French and Welsh Baying him at the heels. Never fear  that.
translation: If he did that, he'd be vulnerable from all other sides, with the French and the Welsh hot on his heels. So don't worry about that happening.

original: Who is it like should lead his forces hither?
translation: Who will be leading his troops to fight against us?

original: The Duke of Lancaster and Westmoreland; Against the  Welsh, himself and Harry Monmouth; But who is  substituted against the French I have no certain notice.
translation: The Duke of Lancaster and Westmoreland. He has gone to fight against the Welsh with his son, Prince Hal. And I'm not sure who is now leading the army against the French.

original: Let us on,   And publish the occasion of our arms.   The commonwealth is sick of their own choice.
translation: Let's continue with our plan then. We will announce the reasons why we are fighting. People in this country are sick of the monarch that they themselves chose.

original: Their  over-greedy love hath surfeited.   An habitation giddy and unsure   Hath he that buildeth on the vulgar heart.
translation: They were eager in their love for him, but now they have had too much of it. He built his kingdom on the love of the people, and this made it wobbly and uncertain.

original: O  thou fond many, with what loud applause   Didst thou beat  heaven with blessing Bolingbroke   Before he was what thou wouldst have him be.
translation: Oh, you foolish people! Your applause for Bolingbroke shook the sky, before you even knew if he'd be the type of leader you hoped he would be.

original: And being now trimmed in thine own desires,   Thou, beastly feeder, art so full of him   That  thou provok’st thyself to cast him up.
translation: Now you are all decked out in what you wanted, you horrible gluttons—you've ingested so much of the King that you wish  you could throw him up .

original: So, so, thou  common dog, didst thou disgorge   Thy glutton bosom of the royal Richard,   And now thou wouldst eat thy dead vomit  up   And howl’st to find it.
translation: You disgusting dogs, this was just how you gorged yourselves on the last king, Richard, and then got rid of him by puking him all up. And now you would howl for that vomit and eat it up out of nostalgia for those days.

original: What trust is in these times?   They that, when Richard lived, would have him die   Are  now become enamored on his grave.
translation: In these times who can be trusted? Nowadays, the people who wanted Richard dead in the first place, are now in love with his dead body.

original: Thou, that threw’st  dust upon his goodly head   When through proud London he  came sighing on   After th' admired heels of Bolingbroke,
translation: The people who threw dust and rubbish at his good head when he walked through London in disgrace—people who supported the beloved Bolingbroke

original: Criest now “O earth, yield us that King again,   And take  thou this!” O thoughts of men accursed!   Past and to come seems best; things present, worst.
translation: —now cry, "Oh, earth, give us back King Richard again, and you can have King Henry back!" Oh, men's thoughts are damned! They only think good about things of the past and the future; anything that happens now is hated.

original: Shall we go draw our numbers and set on?
translation: Shall we go to round up our troops and set off?

original: We are time’s subjects, and time bids begone.
translation: Time is our leader, and Time tells us to get going.

original: Master Fang, have you entered the action?
translation: Master Fang, have you filed my complaint?

original: It is entered.
translation: It has been filed.

original: Where’s your yeoman? Is ’t a lusty yeoman? Will a'  stand to ’t?
translation: Where's your second-in-command? Is he a fit second in command? Will he be up to the task?

original: Sirrah! Where’s Snare?
translation: Sir! Where's Snare?

original: O Lord, ay, good Master Snare.
translation: Oh God, yes, good Master Snare!

original: Here, here.
translation: I'm here, I'm here.

original: Snare, we must arrest Sir John Falstaff.
translation: Snare, we have to arrest Sir John Falstaff.

original: Yea, good Master Snare, I have entered him and all.
translation: Yes, good Master Snare, I have filed an official complaint against him and everything.

original: It may chance cost some of us our lives, for he will  stab.
translation: Doing that might cost some of us our lives—he'll try and stab us.

original: Alas the day, take heed of him. He stabbed me in mine  own   house, and that most beastly, in good faith.
translation: Oh dear, watch out for that! He's  stabbed me in my own house , and it was horrible, it really was.

original: He  cares not what   mischief he does. If his weapon be out,  he will foin like any   devil. He will spare neither man,  woman, nor child.
translation: He doesn't care what kind of trouble he gets into. If his weapon is out, he will thrust it at anyone around, like some kind of devil. No man, woman, or child is safe from him.

original: If I can close with him, I care not for his thrust.
No, nor I neither. I’ll be at your elbow.
translation: No, and I won't either, as I will be right next to you.

original: An I but fist him once, an he come but within my vue—
translation: If I could just hit him once, if he just comes within my sight—

original: I am undone by his going. I warrant you, he’s an  infinitive   thing upon my score.
translation: I am ruined because he's gone off to the wars without paying his bill. I am telling you, the amount he owes me is infinite.

original: Good Master Fang, hold  him sure.   Good Master Snare, let him not ’scape. He  comes   continuantly to Pie Corner, saving your manhoods,  to buy a   saddle,
translation: Good Master Fang, make sure you keep hold of him. Good Master Snare, don't let him escape. Any moment now, he is going to come to  Pie Corner , sorry for talking about it, to buy a  saddle .

original: and he is indited to dinner to the  Lubber’s Head in   Lumbert Street, to Master Smooth’s the  silkman.
translation: He is then always invited to lunch at the Lubber's Head in Lumbert Street, with Master Smooth, the silk-salesman.

original: I pray you,   since my exion is entered, and my  case so openly known to   the world, let him be brought in to his answer.
translation: Please make him pay for what he has done. My case has been made at court, and now everyone knows how easily he had me—had me fooled, I mean.

original: A hundred   mark is a long one for a poor  lone woman to bear, and I have   borne, and borne, and  borne, and have been fubbed off, and   fubbed off, and  fubbed off from this day to that day,
translation: A hundred marks is a lot for one poor, lonely woman to take, and I have taken it again and again and again. I have been part of an uneven exchange over and over again, day after day-

original: that it   is a shame to be thought on. There is no honesty in such   dealing,  unless a woman should be made an ass and a beast   to bear every knave’s wrong.
translation: -so many times that I don't even want to think about it. It's an awful way to do your business, unless you think that a woman should just be like an ass or some wild beast, that any idiot can do bad things to.

original: Yonder he comes, and that   errant  malmsey-nose knave, Bardolph, with him. Do your   offices, do your offices, Master Fang and Master Snare, do   me,  do me, do me your offices.
translation: Look, here he comes and he's with that deviant,  red-nosed  rascal Bardolph. Do your jobs, do your jobs. Do this for me, Master Fang and Master Snare, and get him.

original: How now! Whose mare’s dead? What’s the matter?
translation: What's all this?! Whose horse is dead? What's all the fuss about?

original: Sir John, I arrest you at the suit of Mistress Quickly.
translation: Sir John, I arrest you for the case brought against you by Mistress Quickly.

original: Away, varlets!—Draw, Bardolph. Cut me off the villain’s head. Throw the quean in the channel.
translation: Go away, you rascals!  Draw your sword, Bardolph. Cut off this villain's head. Throw this whore in the gutter.

original: Throw me in the channel? I’ll throw thee in the  channel. Wilt   thou, wilt thou, thou bastardly rogue?
translation: Throw me in the gutter? I'll throw you in the gutter. You will, will you, you monstrous villain?

original: —Murder, murder!
translation: [To FANG and SNARE]  Murder, murder!

original: —   Ah, thou honeysuckle villain, wilt thou kill God’s officers   and the King’s? Ah, thou honeyseed  rogue, thou art a   honeyseed, a man-queller, and a  woman-queller.
translation: [To FALSTAFF]  Oh, you  honeysuckle  villain, are you going to kill God's officers, and the King's? Oh, you honeyseed rogue, you are just that—a honeyseed, a man killer, and a woman killer.

original: Keep them off, Bardolph.
translation: Keep them away from me, Bardolph.

original: A rescue, a rescue!
translation: An escape, an escape!

original: Good people, bring a rescue or two.
translation: People, bring him an  escape  or two!

original: —   [to FALSTAFF   ]   Thou   wot, wot thou? Thou wot, wot ta? Do, do, thou rogue.  Do,   thou hempseed.
translation: [To FALSTAFF]  You will, will you? You will, will you? Do it then, do it then, you villain. Do it, you  hempseed .

original: Away, you scullion, you rampallion, you fustilarian!  I’ll tickle your catastrophe.
translation: Get away from me, you lackey, you ruffian, you fat old thing! I'll smack your butt!

original: What is the matter? Keep the peace here, ho!
translation: What is the matter? Let's have some order here, come on!

original: Good my lord, be good to me. I beseech you stand to me.
translation: My good lord, be good to me. Please stand up for me.

original: How now, Sir John? What, are you brawling here?   Doth  this become your place, your time, and business?   You  should have been well on your way to York.
translation: What's going on, Sir John? Why are you fighting? Is this appropriate for a man in your position, at your age, and with your duties? You should already be well on your way to York.

original: —   [to FANG]     Stand from him, fellow: wherefore hang’st thou   upon  him?
translation: [To FANG]  Get away from him, you! Why are you holding onto him like that?

original: O my most worshipful lord, an ’t please your Grace, I  am a poor widow of Eastcheap, and he is arrested at my  suit.
translation: Oh, my magnificent lord, I beg your pardon; I'm just a poor widow from Eastcheap, and he has been arrested because I've made a case against him.

original: For what sum?
translation: What sum does he owe you?

original: It is more than for some, my lord; it is for all I  have. He hath   eaten me out of house and home. He hath  put all my substance   into that fat belly of his.
translation: It's more than  some , my lord—it's everything I have! He's eaten me out of house and home. He's put everything I have into that fat belly of his.

original: [to  FALSTAFF]   But I will have some of   it out again, or I  will ride thee o' nights like the mare.
translation: [To FALSTAFF]  But I'll get some of it back again, or I will ride you hard in your sleep like a horse, as if you're in some kind of  nightmare .

original: I think I am as like to ride the mare if I have any  vantage of ground to get up.
translation: I think it's likely that I will ride you, if I manage to get on top of you.

original: How comes this, Sir John? Fie, what man of good temper    would endure this tempest of exclamation?
translation: How has this happened, Sir John? For shame! What kind of man with a good character would put up with this angry whirlwind of abuse?

original: Are you not    ashamed to enforce a poor widow to so rough a course to    come by her own?
translation: Aren't you ashamed that a poor widow has been made to do all of this, just to get what is rightfully hers?

original: What is the gross sum that I owe  thee?
translation: What is the total amount that I owe you?

original: Marry, if thou wert an honest man, thyself and the  money   too. Thou didst swear to me upon a parcel-gilt  goblet, sitting   in my Dolphin chamber at the round table by a sea-coal fire,
translation: Indeed, if you were an honest man, you would give me both the money and yourself along with it. You swore to me over a gold-plated wine glass, when we were sitting in the  Dolphin chamber  in my inn, at the round table by the fire,

original: upon Wednesday in Wheeson week,  when the Prince broke   thy head for liking his father to  a singing-man of Windsor,
translation: on the Wednesday seven weeks after Easter, when the Prince had hit you on the head for saying that his father was just a singer from Windsor, a pretender to the throne —do you remember?

original: thou didst swear to me then,  as I was washing thy wound, to   marry me and make me my  lady thy wife.   Canst thou deny   it?
translation: You swore to me, as I was cleaning your wounds, that you would marry me and make me a real lady and your wife. Can you deny that?

original: Did not goodwife  Keech, the butcher’s wife, come in then   and call me  Gossip Quickly, coming in to borrow a mess of   vinegar;
translation: Didn't Mrs. Lard, the butcher's wife, come in right at that moment—calling me her friend and neighbor and asking to borrow a little bit of vinegar?

original: telling us she had a good dish of prawns, whereby   thou  didst desire to eat some, whereby I told thee they were    ill for a green wound?
translation: Didn't she tell us that she had some good shrimp, which you of course wanted to try, and I told you that it was not good to eat them with an unhealed wound?

original: And didst thou not, when she was    gone downstairs, desire me to be no more so familiarity  with such poor people, saying that ere long they should  call me madam?
translation: And when she had gone back downstairs, didn't you tell me to stop being so friendly with people of such a low class—telling me that before long they would be calling me madam, because we would be married and I would be a lady?

original: And didst thou not kiss me and bid me  fetch thee thirty shillings? I put thee now to thy  book-oath. Deny it if thou canst.
translation: And didn't you kiss me and ask me to lend you thirty shillings? Now put your hand on the Bible and deny it, if you can.

original: My lord, this is a poor mad soul, and she says up and  down   the town that her eldest son is like you.
translation: My lord, this is a poor insane woman. She's been telling people all over town that her eldest son looks just like you.

original: She hath  been in good   case, and the truth is, poverty hath  distracted her.
translation: She used to have money, and the truth is, poverty has made her lose her mind.

original: But, for   these foolish officers, I  beseech you I may have redress   against them.
translation: But as for these stupid officers, I would like to make my own case against them.

original: Sir John, Sir John, I am well acquainted with your  manner   of wrenching the true cause the false way.
translation: Sir John, Sir John, I know only too well how you can manipulate the truth and twist it into lies.

original: It is  not a   confident brow, nor the throng of words that come  with such   more than impudent sauciness from you, can  thrust me from   a level consideration.
translation: But don't worry, I'm not going to be swayed by your confident manner, or the stream of words that always comes with your rude and disrespectful behavior—I will consider this fairly.

original: You have, as it  appears to me,   practiced upon the easy-yielding spirit  of this woman, and   made her serve your uses both in  purse and in person.
translation: From what I can tell, you have abused the kindness of this woman, and made her take care of you with her money—and in other ways.

original: Yea, in truth, my lord.
translation: Yes, he has, my lord.

original: Pray thee, peace.
translation: Be quiet, please.

original: —   [to FALSTAFF]   Pay her the debt you  owe   her, and unpay the villany you have done her. The  one you   may do with sterling money, and the other with  current   repentance.
translation: [To FALSTAFF]  Pay back your debt to her, and make up for the wrongs you have done to her. You can do the first thing by giving her actual money, and you can do the second thing by asking for her forgiveness.

original: My lord, I will not undergo this sneap without reply.  You call   honorable boldness “impudent sauciness.” If a  man will   make curtsy and say nothing, he is virtuous.
translation: My lord, I won't just take this insult without replying. You call my honorable actions rude and disrespectful. Is a man only virtuous if he bows and says nothing?

original: No, my lord, my   humble duty remembered, I will not be  your suitor. I say to   you, I do desire deliverance from  these officers, being upon   hasty employment in the  King’s affairs.
translation: No, my lord, with all due respect, I'm not going to be completely silent. I am telling you that I need these officers to release me, as I have work that I need to do for the King as soon as possible.

original: You speak as having power to do wrong; but answer in  th' effect of your reputation, and satisfy this poor  woman.
translation: You talk like you're allowed to do whatever you want, regardless of the law. But act in a way that is fitting for your rank, and make it up to this poor woman.

original: Come hither, hostess.
translation: Come here, hostess.

original: Now, Master Gower, what news?
translation: Now, Master Gower, what is the news?

original: The King, my lord, and Harry Prince of Wales Are near  at hand. The rest the paper tells.
translation: My lord, the King and Harry Prince of Wales are almost here. This letter will tell you everything else.

original: As I am a gentleman!
translation: On my honor!

original: Faith, you said so before.
translation: Really?! Because you've said that before.

original: As I am a gentleman. Come. No more words of it.
translation: On my honor as a gentleman! Come on, let's stop talking about it.

original: By this heavenly ground I tread on, I must be fain to  pawn both my plate and the tapestry of my dining  chambers.
translation: I swear on the heavenly ground that I walk on, that I will have to pawn my best silverware and the tapestries in my dining room.

original: Glasses, glasses, is the only drinking. And for thy  walls, a   pretty slight drollery, or the story of the  Prodigal or the   German hunting in waterwork is worth a  thousand of these   bed-hangers and these fly-bitten  tapestries.
translation: Don't worry about that. People just need glasses, glasses for drinking. And as for your walls, you can have a pretty light-hearted painting, or something showing the  Prodigal son . Don't you think that one of those German hunting scenes—the ones painted on the walls to imitate a tapestry—is worth a thousand of those horrible bed curtains, and fly-bitten tapestries?

original: Let it be ten   pound, if thou canst. Come, an ’twere not for thy humors,   there’s not a better wench  in England.
translation: Let me borrow ten pounds, please? Come on, if it weren't for your mood swings, I would say that you are the best woman in England.

original: Go wash thy face, and   draw the action. Come, thou must not be in this humor with   me. Dost not know  me? Come, come, I know thou wast set   on to this.
translation: Go on, go and wash away your tears, and then get rid of this case against me. Come on, don't be so  moody with me. Don't you know me? Come on, come on, I know you were convinced to do this.

original: Pray thee, Sir John, let it be but twenty nobles. I'  faith, I am loath to pawn my plate, so God save me, la.
Let it alone. I’ll make other shift. You’ll be a fool  still.
translation: All right, I'll leave it. I'll find some other way around it. I guess you'll always be a fool.

original: Well, you shall have it, though I pawn my gown. I hope  you’ll come to supper. You’ll pay me all together?
translation: Well, I will lend it to you, even if I have to pawn my dresses. I hope you'll come and have dinner tonight? You can pay it all back to me then?

original: Will I live?    Go with her, with her. Hook  on, hook on.
translation: I swear on my life! Go with her, go with her. Attach yourself to her, and don't let her out of your sight.

original: Will you have Doll Tearsheet meet you at supper?
translation: Would you like Doll Tearsheet to meet you for dinner?

original: No more words. Let’s have her.
translation: No more talking. Let's have her.

original: I have heard better news.
translation: I've heard better news.

original: What’s the news, my good lord?
translation: What's the news, my good lord?

original: Where lay the King last night?
translation: Where did the King sleep last night?

original: At Basingstoke, my lord.
translation: At Basingstoke, my lord.

original: I hope, my lord, all’s well. What is the news, my lord?
translation: I hope everything is all right, my lord. What's happened, my lord?

original: Come all his forces back?
translation: Did all of his troops come back?

original: No; fifteen hundred foot, five hundred horse Are  marched up to my Lord of Lancaster Against  Northumberland and the Archbishop.
translation: No. Fifteen hundred foot soldiers and five hundred cavalrymen are marching up to meet the Lord of Lancaster, to fight against Northumberland and the Archbishop of York.

original: Comes the King back from Wales, my noble lord?
translation: Has the King come back from Wales, my noble lord?

original: You shall have letters of me presently. Come. Go along  with me, good Master Gower.
translation: I'll give you some letters soon. Come on, let's go, Master Gower.

original: My lord!
translation: My lord!

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: Master Gower, shall I entreat you with me to dinner?
translation: Master Gower, would you like to have lunch with me?

original: I must wait upon my good lord here. I thank you, good  Sir John.
translation: I must stay with this good lord, but I thank you for the offer, good Sir John.

original: Sir John, you loiter here too long, being you are to  take soldiers up in counties as you go.
translation: Sir John, you have already stayed here for too long. You need to try to recruit soldiers, as you travel up through the counties to the north.

original: Will you sup with me, Master Gower?
translation: Would you like to have dinner with me then, Master Gower?

original: What foolish master taught you these manners, Sir John?
translation: What foolish teacher taught you to have these manners, Sir John?

original: Master Gower, if they become me not, he was a fool that taught them me.—This is the right fencing grace, my  lord: tap for tap, and so part fair.
translation: Master Gower, if my manners aren't suitable, then the person who taught me them is a fool. This is how people play, my lord: they each give as good as they have, and then they part as equals.

original: Now the Lord lighten thee. Thou art a great fool.
translation: May the Lord help you. You are a great fool.

original: Before God, I am exceeding weary.
translation: I swear to God, I am incredibly tired.

original: Is ’t come to that? I had thought weariness durst not  have attached one of so high blood.
translation: Are you really? I didn't think people as noble as you ever got tired.

original: Faith, it does me; though it discolors the complexion  of my greatness to acknowledge it. Doth it not show  vilely in me to desire small beer?
Why, a prince should not be so loosely studied as to  remember so weak a composition.
translation: A prince shouldn't be so indulgent as to want something as vile as a small beer.

original: Belike then my appetite was not princely got, for, by  my   troth, I do now remember the poor creature small  beer. But   indeed these humble considerations make me out of love   with my greatness.
translation: Well then my appetite is not the appetite of a prince, because all I want right now is a small beer. But you're right, these lowly thoughts do take me away from my noble position.

original: What a disgrace is it to me  to remember   thy name, or to know thy face tomorrow, or  to take note how   many pair of silk stockings thou  hast—with these, and those   that were thy peach-colored  ones
translation: It's a disgrace for me to know a man like you! To know your face, to know how many pairs of silk stockings you have—these ones, and those other peach-colored ones you have.

original: —or to bear the inventory   of thy shirts, as, one for superfluity and another for use.
translation: To know how many shirts you have—one for wearing, and another one just in case.

original: But   that the  tennis-court keeper knows better than I, for it is a   low ebb of linen with thee when thou keepest not racket    there,
translation: But then, I guess the keeper of the tennis court knows that better than I do, since you only give up your games when your supply of shirts has run out.

original: as thou hast not done a great while, because the  rest of   the low countries have made a shift to eat up  thy holland;
translation: And you haven't played for a while, because you've spent all of your money on whores instead of shirts.

original: and   God knows whether those that bawl out  the ruins of thy linen   shall inherit His kingdom;
translation: God knows whether your offspring—howling and dressed in clothes made out of scraps of your shirts—will ever make it to heaven.

original: but  the midwives say the children   are not in the fault,  whereupon the world increases and   kindreds are mightily  strengthened.
translation: The midwives say that children don't bear the faults of their parents though, which is how the population increases and families get stronger.

original: How ill it follows, after you have labored so hard, you should talk so idly! Tell me, how many good young  princes would do so, their fathers being so sick as  yours at this time is?
translation: After everything you have done in battle, it seems wrong for you to spend your time chatting about nothing! Tell me, how many good, young princes would do what you're doing if their fathers were as sick as yours is?

original: Shall I tell thee one thing, Poins?
translation: Shall I tell you something, Poins?

original: Yes, faith, and let it be an excellent good thing.
translation: Yes, please, and let it be something worthwhile.

original: It shall serve among wits of no higher breeding than  thine.
translation: It will be good enough for people who aren't any more intelligent than you are.

original: Go to. I stand the push of your one thing that you will tell.
translation: Go on then. I can stand up to anything that you will say.

original: Marry, I tell thee it is not meet that I should be sad, now my   father is sick
translation: All right. I am telling you that it is not appropriate for me to be sad, now that my father is sick.

original: —albeit I could tell thee, as to  one it pleases me,   for fault of a better, to call my  friend, I could be sad, and sad   indeed too.
translation: But if I wanted to, I could tell you—as a man who is my friend for lack of better company—that I could be sad. I could be incredibly sa

original: Very hardly, upon such a subject.
translation: That would be a hard thing to do when it comes to a subject like this.

original: By this hand, thou thinkest me as far in the devil’s  book as   thou and Falstaff for obduracy and persistency.
translation: I swear that you think I'm as bad as you and Falstaff are—as stubborn and as persistent.

original: Let the end   try the man. But I tell thee, my heart  bleeds inwardly that my   father is so sick:
translation: That's not the case. But I am telling you the truth. My heart is secretly bleeding over the fact that my father is sick.

original: and keeping  such vile company as thou art   hath in reason taken from  me all ostentation of sorrow.
translation: It is just the fact that I am hanging around with men like you that has stopped me from being able to show my sadness.

original: The reason?
translation: Why?

original: What wouldst thou think of me if I should weep?
translation: What would you think of me if I were crying?

original: I would think thee a most princely hypocrite.
translation: I would think you're a royal hypocrite.

original: It would be every man’s thought, and thou art a blessed   fellow to think as every man thinks. Never a man’s  thought   in the world keeps the roadway better than  thine.
translation: That would be what every man would think, and you're blessed to think the same as every man does. No one agrees with public opinions more than you do.

original: Every man   would think me an hypocrite indeed. And what accites your   most worshipful thought to think so?
translation: Every man would think that I'm a hypocrite. And what makes you think that?

original: Why, because you have been so lewd and so much  engraffed to Falstaff.
translation: Because you've acted so obscenely and you're so attached to Falstaff.

original: And to thee.
translation: So are you.

original: By this light, I am well spoke on. I can hear it with  my own   ears.
translation: But indeed, people think highly of me. I've heard their praises with my own ears.

original: The worst that they can say of me is that I am a second   brother, and that I am a proper fellow of  my hands; and those   two things, I confess, I cannot  help. By the Mass, here comes   Bardolph.
translation: The worst thing that they can say about me is that, because I'm not the  oldest brother , I won't get any inheritance. And I'm also a good fighter. I can't help either of those things, can I? By  God , here comes Bardolph.

original: And the boy that I gave Falstaff. He had him from me  Christian, and look if the fat villain have not  transformed him ape.
God save your Grace.
And yours, most noble Bardolph.
translation: And yours, most noble Bardolph.

original: [to BARDOLPH]   Come, you virtuous ass, you bashful fool,   must you be blushing?   Wherefore blush you now?
translation: [To BARDOLPH]  Come on, you virtuous ass, you embarrassed fool—why are you blushing? Why are you blushing right now?

original: What a    maidenly man-at-arms are you become! Is ’t such a matter    to get a pottle-pot’s maidenhead?
translation: What a feminine soldier you've become! Is it such a bad thing to knock of a  pot of ale ?

original: He calls me e'en now, my lord, through a red lattice,  and I   could discern no part of his face from the window.
translation: He called me just now, from behind a red window, and I could barely tell which was the window and which was his face.

original: At last I   spied his eyes, and methought he had made two holes in the   ale-wife’s new petticoat and so peeped  through.
translation: As last I noticed his eyes, and I thought that he must have made two holes in a barmaid's skirt and looked through it.

original: Has not the boy profited?
translation: The boy must have learned a lot from Falstaff?

original: Away, you whoreson upright rabbit, away!
translation: Get out of here, you silly, little rabbit, get out!

original: Away, you rascally Althea’s dream, away!
Instruct us, boy. What dream, boy?
translation: Tell us, boy. What is this dream?

original: Marry, my lord, Althea dreamt she was delivered of a  firebrand, and therefore I call him her dream.
translation: Well, my lord, Althea dreamed that she gave birth to a fiery rod. And so I call it her dream, as he's all red in the face.

original: A crown’s worth of good interpretation. There ’tis,  boy.
O, that this good blossom could be kept from cankers!  Well, there is sixpence to preserve thee.
translation: I hope that this precious, little flower can be kept away from worms that will eat it and corrupt it. Well, here's sixpence to look after you.

original: An you do not make him hanged among you, the gallows  shall have wrong.
translation: If all of you don't end up getting this boy hanged, the gallows have been robbed.

original: And how doth thy master, Bardolph?
translation: And how is your master doing, Bardolph?

original: Well, my good lord. He heard of your Grace’s coming to  town. There’s a letter for you.
translation: He is doing well, my good lord. He heard that your Grace was coming to town. Here's a letter for you.

original: Delivered with good respect. And how doth the Martlemas your master?
translation: Delivered as it should be. And how is that fat beast, your master?

original: In bodily health, sir.
translation: His body's healthy at least.

original: Marry, the immortal part needs a physician, but that  moves not him. Though that be sick, it dies not.
translation: Indeed, it's his soul that really needs a doctor's help. But that doesn't bother him. Even if his soul might be sick, at least he's not going to die right now.

original: I do allow this wen to be as  familiar with me as my dog, and he holds his place, for  look you how be writes.
translation: God, I've allowed this great lump to be as familiar to me as my dog, and he keeps a tight hold on his rank. Look at how he writes. [He hands the letter to POINS]

original: [reads]   John Falstaff, knight.   Every man must know that  as   oft as he has occasion to name himself, even like  those that   are kin to the King
translation: [Reading] "John Falstaff, knight."  He makes sure that he tells people his title whenever he can. He's just like people who are related to the King.

original: , for they never prick  their finger but they   say, “There’s some of the King’s  blood spilt.” “How comes   that?” says he that takes upon  him not to conceive.
translation: Anytime they prick their finger, they say something like, "Look, some of the King's blood has been spilled." Then someone pretends not to understand and says, "What do you mean?"

original: The   answer is as ready as a  borrower’s cap: “I am the King’s   poor cousin, sir.”
translation: The answer is as ready as a beggar is when he holds out his hat. The relative replies, "I am the King's poor cousin, sir."

original: Nay, they will be kin to us, or they will fetch it from Japheth. But to the letter.
translation: True, they all say that they're part of our family, even if they have to look all the way back to  Japheth . But as for this letter.

original: [takes the letter and  reads]Sir John alstaff, knight, to the son of the King  nearest his father, Harry Prince of Wales, greeting.
translation: [He takes the letter and reads]   "Sir John Falstaff, knight to the King's son nearest to his father, Harry Prince of Wales, sends his regards."

original: Why, this is a certificate.
translation: Why, that sounds like contract, not a letter.

original: Peace!   I will imitate the honorable Romans in  brevity.
translation: Quiet!  "I will be like the Romans and be brief about it."

original: He sure means brevity in breath, short-winded.
translation: He must mean shortness of breath—he's probably wheezing.

original: [reads] I commend me to thee, I commend thee, and I  leave thee. Be not too familiar with Poins, for he  misuses thy favors so much that he swears thou art to  marry his sister   Nell.
translation: [Reading] "I salute myself, I salute you, and I leave it. Don't get too close to Poins, as he abuses your kindness so much that he is positive that you're going to marry his sister, Nell.

original: Repent at idle times as thou  mayest, and so, farewell.
translation: Repent for your sins when you have the time, and so, goodbye.

original: Thine by yea and no, which is  as much as to say, as thou usest him, Jack Falstaff with my familiars, John with my brothers and sisters, and  Sir John with all Europe.
translation: Yours here and there, for which I mean, however you want him to be, I am still Jack Falstaff to my friends, John to my brothers and sisters, and Sir John to the rest of Europe."

original: My lord, I’ll steep this letter in sack and make him  eat it.
translation: My lord, I'll cover this letter in wine and force him to eat it.

original: That’s to make him eat twenty of his words. But do you  use me thus, Ned? Must I marry your sister?
translation: That would force him to eat twenty of his words. But are you really abusing my kindness, Ned? Do I actually have to marry your sister?

original: God send the wench no worse fortune! But I never said  so.
translation: It would definitely be good for her if you did. But no, I never said anything like that.

original: Well, thus we play the fools with the time, and the  spirits of the wise sit in the clouds and mock us.  [to  BARDOLPH]  Is your master here in London?
translation: Look at us wasting time here, while the wise angels sit in heaven laughing at us.  Is your master here in London?

original: Yea, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: Where sups he? Doth the old boar feed in the old frank?
translation: Where is he having dinner? Is that old pig eating in his old feeding place?

original: At the old place, my lord, in Eastcheap.
translation: At the old place in Eastcheap, my lord.

original: What company?
translation: Who's he with?

original: Ephesians, my lord, of the old church.
translation: The same old faces.

original: Sup any women with him?
translation: Do any women eat with him?

original: None, my lord, but old Mistress Quickly and Mistress  Doll Tearsheet.
translation: Just old Mistress Quickly and Mistress Doll Tearsheet.

original: What pagan may that be?
translation: Which whore is that?

original: A proper gentlewoman, sir, and a kinswoman of my  master’s.
translation: Sir, she's a proper lady, and related to my master.

original: Even such kin as the parish heifers are to the town  bull.— Shall we steal upon them, Ned, at supper?
translation: The same kind of relationship that country cows have with the local bull, I'm guessing.  Shall we sneak up on them while they're having dinner, Ned?

original: I am your shadow, my lord. I’ll follow you.
translation: I'm your shadow, my lord. I'll follow you.

original: Sirrah—you, boy—and Bardolph, no word to your master  that I am yet come to town.    There’s  for your silence.
translation: Sir—you there, boy—and you, Bardolph: don't say anything to your master about me being in town.   This is for your silence.

original: I have no tongue, sir.
translation: I have no tongue to tell him anything, sir.

original: And for mine, sir, I will govern it.
translation: I have a tongue, sir. But I'll keep it in check.

original: Fare you well. Go.
translation: Goodbye to you then. Off you go.

original: This Doll Tearsheet should be some road.
translation: This Doll Tearsheet must be some whore.

original: I warrant you, as common as the way between Saint  Alban’s and London.
translation: I bet that she's as commonly used as the road between Saint Albans and London.

original: How might we see Falstaff bestow himself tonight in his true colors, and not ourselves be seen?
translation: How can we make Falstaff show his true colors tonight and not be recognized ourselves?

original: Put on two leathern jerkins and aprons, and wait upon  him at his table as drawers.
translation: Let's put on two leather jackets and aprons, and wait on him, pretending to be bartenders.

original: From a god to a bull: a heavy decension. It was Jove’s  case.
translation: To go from being a god to a bull is quite a step down. But  Jove  did it.

original: From a prince to a 'prentice: a low transformation that shall   be mine, for in everything the purpose must  weigh with the   folly. Follow me, Ned.
translation: From a Prince to a servant—that will be my transformation. The end result will make up for all of the tomfoolery. Follow me, Ned.

original: I pray thee, loving wife and gentle daughter,   Give even way unto my rough affairs.
translation: I am asking you, my loving wife and my kind daughter-in-law, to make my difficult position as easy as you can.

original: Put not you on the visage of the times   And be, like them, to Percy troublesome.
translation: Don't let your faces show how horrible these times are—that will only make things more troubling for m

original: I have given over. I will speak no more. Do what you  will; your wisdom be your guide.
translation: I give up. I won't say another word. Do what you want; your wisdom can guide you now.

original: Alas, sweet wife, my honor is at pawn, And, but my  going, nothing can redeem it.
translation: For goodness' sake, my sweet wife: my honor is at risk here. The only way I can redeem myself is by going to fight.

original: O yet, for God’s sake, go not to these wars.   The time  was, father, that you broke your word,   When you were  more endeared to it than now,
translation: Oh, but still, don't go to these wars, for God's sake. The last time you broke your word you were far more bound to the cause than you are now.

original: When your own Percy, when  my heart’s dear Harry,   Threw many a northward look to  see his father   Bring up his powers; but he did long in  vain.   Who then persuaded you to stay at home?
translation: Your own son Percy—my own love, Harry—kept looking north hoping to see his father and his army arriving. But his hopes were in vain. Who was it that persuaded you to stay at home then?

original: There were two honors lost, yours and your son’s.   For yours, the  God of heaven brighten it.   For his, it stuck upon him as the sun   In the gray vault of heaven
translation: Two senses of honor were lost in that battle—your honor, and your son's. As for yours, God might be able to make it shine again. As for your son's, it attached itself to him—like the sun in a blue sky

original: , and by his light    Did all the chivalry of England move   To do brave acts.
translation: —and its beams motivated every soldier in England to act bravely.

original: He was indeed the glass   Wherein the noble youth did dress  themselves.   He had no legs that practiced not his gait;    And speaking thick, which nature made his blemish,   Became the accents of the valiant;
translation: He was like a mirror that noble, young men used to know how to dress themselves. Everyone with legs copied how he walked; all brave men even copied his quick and hurried speech—which was considered one of his only flaws.

original: For those that could speak  low and tardily   Would turn their own perfection to abuse   To seem like him.
translation: For the men who had always spoken softly and slowly manipulated their perfect speech to sound more like him.

original: So that in speech, in gait,   In diet,  in affections of delight,   In military rules, humors of  blood,   He was the mark and glass, copy and book,   That  fashioned others.
translation: In terms of his speech, his walk, his diet; when it came to the things which gave him pleasure, his military actions, his changing moods, he was the signpost and the mirror, the guidebook by which everyone lived.

original: And him—O wondrous him!   O miracle of  men!—him did you leave,   Second to none, unseconded by  you,   To look upon the hideous god of war   In  disadvantage,
translation: And him—oh wonderful him! What a miracle among men! And you left him! Unsupported by you, the best man there was had to face the terrible god of war with this disadvantage.

original: to abide a field   Where nothing but the  sound of Hotspur’s name   Did seem defensible. So you left him
translation: The only defense he had left to fight this battle with was the reputation of his own name, Hotspur. And that is how you left him.

original: Never, O never, do his ghost the wrong   To hold  your honor more precise and nice   With others than with  him. Let them alone.
translation: Don't you dare wrong his name by caring more about your honor with other men than you did with him. Leave them alone.

original: The Marshal and the Archbishop are  strong.   Had my sweet Harry had but half their numbers,    Today might I, hanging on Hotspur’s neck,   Have talked of  Monmouth’s grave.
translation: Marshal Mowbray and the Archbishop of York are strong. If only my sweet Harry had had an army even half the size of theirs, today I could have been holding my Harry and talking about Hal's death instead.

original: Beshrew your heart,   Fair daughter, you do draw my  spirits from me   With new lamenting ancient oversights.
translation: Oh, curse your feelings, my beautiful daughter-in-law. You drag me out of myself again and make me look back at the mistakes that I made.

original: But I must go and meet with danger there,   Or it will seek me in another place   And find me worse provided.
translation: But I have to go and face danger there, or danger will just find me somewhere else and I won't be ready for it.

original: Oh, fly to Scotland Till that the nobles and the  armèd commons Have of their puissance made a little  taste.
translation: Oh, go to Scotland then, until these noblemen and their armies have made some progress in their rebellion.

original: If they get ground and vantage of the King,   Then join  you with them like a rib of steel   To make strength  stronger;
translation: If they manage to make any progress against the King, and gain any ground, then you can join them. And just like a steel pole, you will make their armies even stronger.

original: but, for all our loves,   First let them try  themselves. So did your son;   He was so suffered.   So came I a wid   ow,
translation: But, if you love us, let them try on their own first. That's how your son fought in the battle. You allowed him to do so, and that's how I became a widow.

original: And never shall have length of life enough    To rain upon remembrance with mine eyes   That it may grow  and sprout as high as heaven   For recordation to my noble husband.
translation: My life will never be long enough to water the plant of memory with my tears. This plant will never grow tall enough to truly honor the memory of my noble husband.

original: Come, come, go in with me. 'Tis with my mind   As with  the tide swelled up unto his height,   That makes a  still-stand, running neither way.
translation: Come on now, go inside with me. My mind is currently filled with thoughts that are like a high tide at a standstill, not coming or going.

original: Fain would I go to  meet the Archbishop,   But many thousand reasons hold me  back.
translation: I want to go and join the Archbishop—but there are thousands of reasons holding me back.

original: I will resolve for Scotland. There am I   Till time  and vantage crave my company.
translation: I will go to Scotland. There, I can wait and see if there comes a point when my help is truly needed.

original: What the devil hast thou brought there—applejohns? Thou knowest Sir John cannot endure an applejohn.
Mass, thou sayest true. The Prince once set a dish of    applejohns before him and told him there were five more  Sir   Johns
translation: God, that's true. The Prince once put a plate of apple-johns in front of him and said, "Look, here are five more Sir Johns!"

original: and, putting off his hat, said “I will now  take my leave   of these six dry, round, old, withered  knights.” It angered   him to the heart. But he hath  forgot that.
translation: Then, putting on his hat, he said, "I will now leave these six, dry, round, old, withered knights behind." That made Sir John very angry, but he has forgotten about it now.

original: Why then, cover, and set them down, and see if thou  canst find out Sneak’s noise. Mistress Tearsheet would  fain hear some music.
translation: Well then, put the table cloth on and set the dishes down on top. Then go see if you can find Sneak's band of musicians. Mistress Tearsheet wants to hear some music.

original: Dispatch: the room where they supped is too hot.  They’ll come in straight.
translation: Hurry up! The room they had their dinner in was too hot, and so they'll be here any minute now.

original: Sirrah, here will be the Prince and Master Poins anon,  and they will put on two of our jerkins and aprons, and  Sir John must not know of it. Bardolph hath brought  word.
translation: Sir, the Prince and Master Poins will be here at some point soon. They are going to disguise themselves by putting on a couple of our jackets and aprons—but Sir John can't know anything about it. Bardolph came and told me.

original: By the Mass, here will be old utis. It will be an  excellent stratagem.
translation: By God, there's going to be some fun had here. What an excellent plan!

original: I’ll see if I can find out Sneak.
translation: I'll go see if I can find Sneak and his band.

original: I' faith, sweetheart, methinks now you are in an  excellent   good temperality. Your pulsidge beats as  extraordinarily as   heart would desire, and your color, I warrant you, is as red   as any rose, in good truth, la
translation: Truthfully, sweetheart, I think you are in an excellent  mood . Your pulse is beating as quickly as you want it to, and your cheeks are as red as any rose, honestly!

original: .  But, i' faith, you have drunk   too much canaries, and  that’s a marvellous searching wine,   and it perfumes the  blood ere one can say “What’s this?”   How do you now?
translation: But, in all seriousness, I do think you might have drunk too much of that  sweet wine , and it is strong stuff. It will stir up your blood quicker than you can say, "What's all this?" How are you doing now, Doll?

original: Better than I was. Hem.
translation: I'm doing better than I was.

original: Why, that’s well said. A good heart’s worth gold. Lo,  here comes Sir John.
translation: Well said! A good heart is worth a lot of gold. Look, here comes Sir John.

original: [sings] When Arthur first in court
translation: [Singing]  "When King Arthur was first in court"

original: —Empty the jordan.
translation: [To one of the drawers]  Empty the chamber-pot.

original: [sings] And was a worthy king
translation: [Singing] "And was a worthy king."

original: —   How now, Mistress Doll?
translation: [To DOLL TEARSHEET]  How are you going, Mistress Doll?

original: Sick of a calm, yea, good faith.
So is all her sect. An they be once in a calm, they are sick.
translation: That's common for women of her type. As soon as they have a moment of calm, they get sick.

original: A pox damn you, muddy rascal. Is that all the comfort  you give me?
translation: Damn you, you fat idiot. Is that all you can say to make me feel better?

original: You make fat rascals, Mistress Doll.
translation: You make rascals fat, Mistress Doll.

original: I make them? Gluttony and diseases make them; I make  them not.
translation: I make them fat? No, overeating and diseases make men fat. I have no part in it.

original: If the cook help to make the gluttony, you help to make the diseases, Doll. We catch of you, Doll, we catch of  you. Grant that, my poor virtue, grant that.
translation: If the cook helps us to overeat, then you help us to catch diseases, Doll. We catch them from you, Doll, from you. At least admit to that, my poor girl.

original: Yea, joy, our chains and our jewels.
translation: Yes, my dear, you get from us the valuable things we've been given.

original: Your broaches, pearls, and ouches—for to serve bravely  is   to come halting off, you know;
translation: Your broaches, your pearls, and your  gems . We go in bravely, but we come out limping, you know.

original: to come off the breach with   his pike bent bravely, and to surgery bravely, to  venture upon   the charged chambers bravely—
translation: We leave the ruptured place with our spears bravely bent. We seek medical help, only to bravely re-enter the diseased chambers again.

original: Hang yourself, you muddy conger, hang yourself!
translation: Oh, go die, you disgusting eel, go die somewhere!

original: By my troth, this is the old fashion. You two never  meet but   you fall to some discord. You are both, i' good truth, as   rheumatic as two dry toasts. You cannot one  bear with   another’s confirmities.
translation: I swear, it's always like this. You two can never meet without having some kind of argument. I swear, you're both  as hot as dry toast —you can't stand each others  flaws .

original: What the good-year!  One must bear,   and that must be you. You are the weaker  vessel, as they say,   the emptier vessel.
translation: What on earth is wrong with you two! But one of you has to bear the brunt of it. And that has to be you, Doll, since you're the weaker sex, the empty vessel as they say.

original: Can a weak empty vessel bear such a huge full hogshead?   There’s a whole merchant’s venture of Bourdeaux stuff  in   him. You have not seen a hulk better stuffed in the  hold.
translation: Can this  weak, empty vessel take the weight  of such a huge, fat, barrel? There's an entire merchant's stock of Bordeaux wine in him. I've never seen a ship with a bigger load stuffed in the hold.

original: —   Come, I’ll be friends with thee, Jack. Thou art  going to the wars, and whether I shall ever see thee  again or no, there is nobody cares.
translation: [To FALSTAFF]  Come on, I'll be friends with you, Jack. You're going off to fight in the wars, and whether or not I will ever see you again—well, who cares, really.

original: Sir, Ancient Pistol’s below and would speak with you.
translation: Sir, Pistol the standard-bearer is downstairs and would like to speak to you.

original: Hang him, swaggering rascal! Let him not come hither.  It is the foul-mouthed’st rogue in England.
translation: I hope he dies, that rude scoundrel! Don't let him come in, he's got the most disgusting mouth in all of England.

original: If he swagger, let him not come here. No, by my faith,  I must   live among my neighbors. I’ll no swaggerers: I am in good   name and fame with the very best.
translation: If he's going to cause any problems, then don't let him come in. No, indeed, I have to think about my neighbors. And I don't want any trouble here. I have a good reputation and people think highly of me.

original: S   hut the  door. There   comes no swaggerers here. I have not lived  all this while to   have swaggering now. Shut the door, I  pray you.
translation: Shut the door. We won't have any trouble here. I haven't lived this long just to be ruined by trouble now. Shut the door, please.

original: Dost thou hear, hostess?
translation: Did you hear, hostess?

original: Pray you pacify yourself, Sir John. There comes no  swaggerers here.
translation: Please be quiet for a minute, Sir John. I'm not having any troublemakers here.

original: Dost thou hear? It is mine ancient.
translation: Did you hear? It's my standard-bearer.

original: Tilly-vally, Sir John, ne'er tell me. And your ancient    swaggerer comes not in my doors. I was before Master    Tisick, the debuty t' other day, and, as he said to  me—’twas   no longer ago than Wednesday last, i' good  faith—
translation: Oh fiddlesticks, Sir John, I don't want to know. And your horrible standard-bearer is not coming in here. The other day, I met with the Master Tisick, the deputy. He said to me—this can only have been last Wednesday I think—he said,

original: “Neighbour Quickly,” says he—Master Dumb, our  minister,   was by then—“Neighbour Quickly,” says he,  “receive those   that are civil, for,” said he, “you are  in an ill name.”
translation: "Neighbor Quickly." Master Dumb, the minister, was there as well, actually. Anyway, he said, "Neighbor Quickly, only let in people who are well-behaved, since people are starting to question your reputation."

original: Now he   said so, I can tell whereupon.  “For,” says he, “you are an   honest woman, and well  thought on. Therefore take heed   what guests you receive. Receive,” says he, “no swaggering companions.”
translation: That's what he said, and I can tell you why. "You're an honest woman, and highly regarded," he said. "So be careful about who you let in. Don't let in any troublemakers."

original: There  comes none here. You would bless you to hear what he  said. No, I’ll no swaggerers.
translation: So that's what I'm doing. You would be lucky to hear what he said. No, I will not let any troublemakers in at all.

original: He’s no swaggerer, hostess, a tame cheater, i' faith.  You may   stroke him as gently as a puppy greyhound. He’ll not   swagger with a Barbary hen if her feathers turn  back in any   show of resistance.
translation: He's not a troublemaker, hostess. He's just a harmless cheater, honestly. You can pet him like he's some kind of little puppy. He wouldn't even fight against a guinea fowl, even if her feathers stood up on end in anger

original: —Call him up, drawer.
translation: [To the FIRST DRAWER]  Bring him up here, bartender.
