original: “Cheater,” call you him? I will bar no honest man my  house,   nor no cheater, but I do not love swaggering.
translation: A " cheater " you call him? I won't stop any honest man from coming into my bar, nor any cheater. But I hate troublemakers.

original: By  my troth,   I am the worse when one says “swagger.” Feel,  masters, how   I shake; look you, I warrant you.
translation: Honestly, I can't handle it when someone says the word "trouble." Look, masters, look how I am shaking. Look, I'm telling you.

original: So you do, hostess.
translation: You really are, hostess.

original: Do I? Yea, in very truth, do I, an ’twere an aspen  leaf. I cannot abide swaggerers.
translation: Am I? Yes, I am. I'm shaking like some giant leaf in the wind. I just can't put up with troublemakers.

original: God save you, Sir John.
translation: God save you, Sir John.

original: Welcome, Ancient Pistol. Here, Pistol, I charge you  with a cup of sack. Do you discharge upon mine hostess.
translation: Welcome Pistol, my standard-bearer. Here, Pistol, I toast to you with this glass of wine. Now, kindly do the same for our hostess.

original: I will discharge upon her, Sir John, with two bullets.
She is pistol-proof. Sir, you shall not hardly offend  her.
translation: She's Pistol-proof. Sir, there's not much you can do to harm her.

original: Come, I’ll drink no proofs nor no bullets. I’ll drink  no more than will do me good, for no man’s pleasure, I.
translation: Come on now, I'm not going to have any proofs, or any bullets.  I will only drink as much as I want to. No man will make me do otherwise.

original: Then to you, Mistress Dorothy! I will charge you.
translation: Then what about you, Mistress Dorothy? I'll charge you.

original: Charge me! I scorn you, scurvy companion. What, you  poor, base, rascally, cheating lack-linen mate! Away,  you mouldy rogue, away! I am meat for your master.
translation: Charge me? I'm just going to ignore that, you vile man. What? You're a poor, disgusting, lying, cheating, shirtless fool! Get away from me, you moldy scoundrel, get away from me! I'm meant for someone better than you.

original: I know you, Mistress Dorothy.
translation: I know you, Mistress Dorothy.

original: Away, you cutpurse rascal, you filthy bung, away! By  this   wine, I’ll thrust my knife in your mouldy chaps an  you play   the saucy cuttle with me.
translation: Get away from me, you pickpocket, you villain, you horrible thief! I swear on this very wine that I will stab you in your moldy face if you keep on like this.

original: Away, you bottle-ale  rascal, you   basket-hilt stale juggler, you. Since when,  I pray you, sir?   God’s light, with two points on your  shoulder? Much!
translation: Get away from me, you cheap rascal, you out-of-date soldier! Can I ask, since when have you been a soldier? With two armor tags on your shoulders, I bet!

original: God let me not live, but I will murder your ruff for  this.
translation: I will strangle your neck for saying that, or at least will die trying to.

original: No more, Pistol. I would not have you go off here.  Discharge yourself of our company, Pistol.
translation: Enough, Pistol. I don't want you to go off on anyone here. Go somewhere else, Pistol.

original: No, good Captain Pistol, not here, sweet captain.
translation: No, good Captain Pistol. Not here, sweet captain.

original: Captain? Thou abominable damned cheater, art thou not    ashamed to be called captain? An captains were of my  mind,   they would truncheon you out for taking their  names upon   you before you have earned them.
translation: Captain? You despicable, damned cheater: aren't you ashamed to be called a captain? If captains thought of you like I do, they would beat you for taking their title without earning it.

original: You a  captain? You slave, for what? For tearing a poor whore’s ruff in a bawdy house? He a captain! Hang him, rogue.
translation: You, a captain? You rogue, a captain of what? Of ripping up a poor whore's clothes in a brothel? Is he a captain? Let him die, the villain.

original: He lives upon mouldy stewed prunes and dried cakes. A  captain? God’s light, these villains will make the word  as odious as the word “occupy,” which was an excellent  good word before it was ill sorted. Therefore captains  had need look to ’t.
translation: He lives off the moldy food that is left over in brothels. A captain? By God, men like him with make the word "captain" as hated as the word, " occupy ," a word that was a great choice, before it was tainted. Therefore, captains should be ready for that.

original: Pray thee go down, good ancient.
translation: Please, calm down, good standard-bearer.

original: Hark thee hither, Mistress Doll.
translation: Listen to me, Mistress Doll.

original: Not I. I tell thee what, Corporal Bardolph, I could  tear her. I’ll be revenged of her.
translation: I won't. I'll tell you what, Corporal Bardolph, I could tear her into pieces. I'll get my revenge.

original: Pray thee go down.
translation: Please, calm down!

original: I’ll see her damned first to Pluto’s damnèd lake, by  this   hand, to th' infernal deep with Erebus and tortures vile also.
translation: I'll see her damned first! I'll personally see her damned to the waters of  hell , to the never-ending deep, with darkness and vile tortures.

original: Hold hook and line, say I. Down, down, dogs! Down, Fates!   Have we not Hiren here?
translation: Let things go as I've planned. Down, down, dogs. Down, Fates! I have my sword here!

original: Good Captain Peesell, be quiet. 'Tis very late, i'  faith. I beseek you now, aggravate your choler.
translation: Good Captain Pistol, please be quiet. Honestly, it's very late. Please, rein in your anger.

original: These be good humors indeed. Shall pack-horses   And  hollow pampered jades of Asia, which cannot go but     thirty mile a day,   Compare with Caesars and with  cannibals, and Troyant   Greeks?
translation: These are fine goings-on indeed. Should we let old  pack-horses  and stupid, pampered horses from Asia—who can't travel more than a few miles every day—compare with men like Caesar, important generals, and mythical Greek soldiers going off to Troy?

original: Nay, rather damn  them with King   Cerberus, and let the welkin roar.  Shall we fall foul   for toys?
translation: No, I would rather damn them to  hell , and let the heavens roar. Shall we fight about nothing?

original: By my troth, captain, these are very bitter words.
translation: Honestly, captain, those are very aggressive words.

original: Begone, good ancient. This will grow to a brawl anon.
translation: Leave now, good standard-bearer. This will turn into a fight before long.

original: Die men like dogs! Give crowns like pins! Have we not  Hiren here?
translation: Let men die like dogs! Give away the King's crowns like they're nothing! Isn't this a sword, a Hiren here?

original: O' my word, captain, there’s none such here. What the  good- year, do you think I would deny her? For God’s  sake, be quiet.
Then feed and be fat, my fair Calipolis. Come, give ’s  some   sack.
translation: Then keep eating and get fat, my beautiful lady. Come on, give me some wine.

original: Si fortune me tormente, sperato me contento.
translation: If my fortunes torment me, then hope contents me .

original: Fear we   broadsides? No, let the fiend give fire. Give me  some sack,   and, sweetheart, lie thou there.
translation: Should we have to fear an attack? No, let the devil start shooting. Give me some wine, and, sweetheart, you can lie down there.

original: [lays down  his sword]   Come   we to full points here? And are  etceteras nothing?
translation: [He lays down his sword.]  Is this where this all ends? What about the  et ceteras?

original: Pistol, I would be quiet.
translation: Pistol, I would be quiet if I were you.

original: Sweet knight, I kiss thy neaf. What, we have seen the  seven stars.
translation: Sweet knight, I kiss your hand goodnight. Look, it's so late that we can see the Big Dipper.

original: For God’s sake, thrust him downstairs. I cannot endure  such a fustian rascal.
translation: For God's sake, throw him down the stairs. I can't stand anymore of this ridiculous fool.

original: “Thrust him downstairs?" Know we not Galloway nags?
translation: "Throw him down the stairs?" Let's face it, we all know a common whore when we see one.

original: Quoit him down, Bardolph, like a shove-groat shilling.  Nay, an he do nothing but speak nothing, he shall be  nothing here.
translation: Throw him down, Bardolph, like a coin rolling along some game board. If all he's going to do here is say a bunch of nonsense, then it is nonsense for him to be here at all.

original: Come, get you downstairs.
translation: Come on, get downstairs.

original: What! shall we have incision? Shall we imbrue? [    snatches up his sword]
translation: What? Is there going to be a cutting now? Will we shed blood?  [He snatches up his sword]

original: Then death rock me asleep, abridge my doleful   days. Why then, let grievous, ghastly,  gaping wounds   untwine the Sisters Three. Come, Atropos,  I say.
translation: Then let death rock me to sleep; let death end my sad days! Why then, let horrible, ghastly and gaping wounds sever the thread of my life, made by those  three sisters. Come on then, Atropos.

original: Here’s goodly stuff toward!
translation: This should be good.

original: Give me my rapier, boy.
translation: Give me my sword, boy.

original: I pray thee, Jack, I pray thee do not draw.
translation: Please, Jack, please don't fight him.

original: Get you downstairs.
translation: Get downstairs.

original: Here’s a goodly tumult. I’ll forswear keeping house  afore   I’ll be in these tirrits and frights.
translation: This is going to be quite a fight. I swear, I would rather close my bar than have to put up with such terrors and frights.

original: So, murder,  I warrant now.   Alas, alas, put up your naked weapons,  put up your naked   weapons.
translation: It's murder, I'm telling you! Oh dear, oh dear! Put away your naked weapons, put them away!

original: I pray thee, Jack, be quiet. The rascal’s gone. Ah, you whoreson little valiant villain, you.
translation: Please, Jack, calm down now. The bastard's gone. Oh, you stupid, little, brave scoundrel, you!

original: Are you not hurt i' the groin? Methought he made a  shrewd thrust at your belly.
translation: Did he get you in the groin? I thought that he got a good whack at your stomach.

original: Have you turned him out o' doors?
translation: Have you thrown him out?

original: Yea, sir. The rascal’s drunk. You have hurt him, sir,  i' the shoulder.
translation: Yes, sir. The fool is drunk. You hurt his shoulder, sir.

original: A rascal to brave me!
translation: That fool! Why would he dare to challenge me?

original: Ah, you sweet little rogue, you. Alas, poor ape, how  thou   sweat’st! Come, let me wipe thy face. Come on, you    whoreson chops.
translation: Oh, you sweet little rascal, you! Oh, my poor little monkey, look how much you're sweating! Come on, let me wipe your face clean. Come on, little chubby cheeks.

original: Ah, rogue, i' faith, I love thee. Thou  art as   valorous as Hector of Troy, worth five of  Agamemnon, and   ten times better than the Nine Worthies.  Ah, villain!
translation: Oh, you rascal, truthfully, I love you. You're as brave as  Hector of Troy, you're worth five Agamemnons , and you're at least ten times better than all of the  Nine Worthies . Oh, you villain!

original: Ah, rascally slave! I will toss the rogue in a blanket.
translation: Oh, what a rascal and a villain! I will toss that scoundrel around in a blanket.

original: Do, an thou darest for thy heart. An thou dost, I’ll  canvass thee between a pair of sheets.
translation: Do it, if you dare to risk your life. If you do, I'll toss you around as well, between the sheets.

original: The music is come, sir.
translation: The musicians are here, sir.

original: Let them play.—Play, sirs.—Sit on my knee, Doll. A  rascal bragging slave! The rogue fled from me like  quicksilver.
translation: Let them play.  Play, sirs. [To DOLL TEARSHEET] Doll, come and sit on my knee. What a rascal, a bragging scoundrel! That villain ran away from me like quicksilver.

original: I' faith, and thou followed’st him like a church. Thou    whoreson little tidy Bartholomew boar-pig
translation: He did, and you followed him like a church, at your own pace. You little, wretched, fat pig!

original: , when wilt thou   leave fighting a-days and foining a-nights and begin to patch   up thine old body for heaven?
translation: When are you going to leave your fighting days behind you and your thrusting nights, and start to prepare your body for heaven?

original: Peace, good Doll. Do not speak like a death’s-head; do  not bid me remember mine end.
Sirrah, what humor’s the Prince of?
translation: Sir, what is the Prince like?

original: A good shallow young fellow, he would have made a good  pantler; he would a' chipped bread well.
translation: He's a shallow young man. He would have made a good pantry servant—he would have been good at cutting the crusts off loaves of bread.

original: They say Poins has a good wit.
translation: People say that Poins is very witty.

original: He a good wit? Hang him, baboon. His wit’s as thick as  Tewksbury mustard. There’s no more conceit in him than  is in a mallet.
Why does the Prince love him so then?
translation: Why does the Prince love him so much then?

original: Because their legs are both of a bigness, and he plays  at   quoits well, and eats conger and fennel, and drinks  off   candles' ends for flap-dragons,
translation: Because their legs are roughly the same size, and he likes to play the game of  quoits . He also has good digestion, and he does funny things with drinks—like drinking with a lit candle inside his glass.

original: and rides the wild  mare with   the boys, and jumps upon joint stools, and  swears with a   good grace,
translation: He plays on the see-saw with the boys, hops on top of stools, and swears well.

original: and wears his boots very  smooth, like unto the   sign of the Leg,
translation: His boots fit him very well—they are as smooth as the well-booted leg shown as a sign over a shoemaker's shop.

original: and breeds no  bate with telling of discreet   stories, and such other  gambol faculties he has that show a   weak mind and an  able body,
translation: He doesn't anger others by revealing their secrets, and has all the qualities of a man with a weak mind and a healthy body.

original: for the which the Prince admits   him; for the  Prince himself is such another.
translation: That's why the Prince likes him—because the Prince is exactly the same.

original: The weight of a   hair  will turn the scales between their avoirdupois.
translation: There's barely a hair's difference between them.

original: Would not this nave of a wheel have his ears cut off?
translation: Why don't we cut this fat thing's ears off?

original: Let’s beat him before his whore.
translation: Let's beat him in front of his whore.

original: Look whe'er the withered elder hath not his poll clawed like a parrot.
translation: Look at how this decrepit, old man is having his head scratched like he's some kind of parrot.

original: Is it not strange that desire should so many years  outlive performance?
translation: Isn't it strange that human desires last so much longer than the actual ability to perform?

original: Kiss me, Doll.
translation: Kiss me, Doll.

original: Saturn and Venus this year in conjunction! What says  th' almanac to that?
And look whether the fiery trigon, his man, be not  lisping to his master’s old tables, his notebook, his  counsel keeper.
translation: And look how his man—that red-faced Bardolph—is whispering love to Mistress Quickly, his master's old companion.

original: Thou dost give me flattering busses.
translation: You flatter me with all of your kisses.

original: By my troth, I kiss thee with a most constant heart.
translation: Truthfully, every kiss I give you comes from the heart.

original: I am old, I am old.
translation: But I'm old, I'm old.

original: I love thee better than I love e'er a scurvy young boy  of them all.
translation: I love you more than I could love any silly, young boy.

original: What stuff wilt have a kirtle of? I shall receive money o'   Thursday; shalt have a cap tomorrow.
translation: Out of what material shall we make you a new bodice and skirt? I will get money on Thursday, so you can have a new hat tomorrow.

original: A merry song!
translation: [To the musicians]  Play something happy!

original: Come,   it grows late. We’ll to bed. Thou 'lt forget me  when I am   gone.
translation: [To DOLL TEARSHEET]  Come on, it's getting late. Let's go to bed. You will soon forget me when I am gone.

original: By my troth, thou 'lt set me a-weeping an thou sayest  so. Prove that ever I dress myself handsome till thy  return. Well, harken a' th' end.
translation: I swear, you'll make me cry if you keep saying things like that. I swear that I won't wear any pretty clothes until you come back from the wars. Just you wait and see.

original: Some sack, Francis.
translation: Some wine, Francis.

original: Anon, anon, sir.
translation: Coming, sir.

original: Ha? A bastard son of the King’s?—And art not thou Poins his brother?
translation: Ha? Aren't you a bastard son of the King's? [To POINS] And aren't you his companion, Poins?

original: Why, thou globe of sinful continents, what a life dost  thou lead?
translation: Well, you're like a globe, covered in sinful areas. What kind of life are you leading?

original: A better than thou. I am a gentleman. Thou art a  drawer.
translation: A better one than you. I'm a gentleman, you just pull on taps for beer and wine.

original: Very true, sir, and I come to draw you out by the ears.
translation: That's true, sir, and I've come to pull you out of here by your ears.

original: O, the Lord preserve thy good Grace! By my troth,  welcome to London. Now the Lord bless that sweet face of thine. O Jesu, are you come from Wales?
translation: Oh, God bless your good Grace! Indeed, welcome to London. May the Lord bless that sweet face of yours. Oh Jesus, have you come all the way from Wales?

original: Thou whoreson mad compound of majesty,  [indicating  DOLL]  by this light flesh and corrupt blood, thou art  welcome.
translation: You son-of-a-bitch, you great lump of royalty!  I swear on this weak bit of flesh and this corrupt body that you are welcome here.

original: How? You fat fool, I scorn you.
translation: What? You fat fool! I defy you!

original: My lord, he will drive you out of your revenge and turn all to a merriment, if you take not the heat.
translation: My lord, if you don't show him how angry you are now, he will find some way to turn it into some big joke. And then you'll never get your revenge.

original: You whoreson candle-mine, you how vilely did you speak  of me even now before this honest, virtuous, civil  gentlewoman!
translation: You son-of-a-bitch, you huge mound of candle wax: how dare you say such vile things about me to this chaste, virtuous, and honest woman?

original: God’s blessing of your good heart, and so she is, by my troth.
translation: God bless your good heart, sir. She is all of those things, I swear it.

original: Didst thou hear me?
translation: Did you hear me?

original: Yea, and you knew me, as you did when you ran away by  Gad’s Hill. You knew I was at your back, and spoke it on purpose to try my patience.
No, no, no; not so. I did not think thou wast within  hearing.
translation: No, no, sir, that's not true. I didn't know that you could hear me.

original: I shall drive you, then, to confess the wilfull abuse,  and then I know how to handle you.
translation: Then I will have to force you to confess that you meant to say such awful things—such slander about me. And then I will know what to do with you.

original: No abuse, Hal, o' mine honor, no abuse.
translation: It wasn't slander, Hal. On my honor, it wasn't slander.

original: Not to dispraise me and call me pantier and  bread-chipper and I know not what?
translation: You don't think it was slander to say bad things—calling me a pantry servant, someone only fit to cut crusts off bread—and who knows what else?

original: No abuse, Hal.
translation: It wasn't slander, Hal.

original: No abuse?
translation: It wasn't?

original: No abuse, Ned, i' th' world, honest Ned, none. I  dispraised   him before the wicked, that the wicked might  not fall in love   with thee;
translation: No slander, Ned, in the world, honest Ned, none. I only said those bad things to wicked people, so that they wouldn't fall in love with you.

original: in which doing, I have done  the part of a careful   friend and a true subject, and thy father is to give me thanks   for it. No abuse, Hal.
translation: In doing this, I have acted like a caring friend and a loyal subject, and your father should thank me for it. No slander, Hal, none.

original: —None, Ned, none.
translation: [To POINS]  Ned, none.

original: No, faith, boys, none.
translation: [To PRINCE HENRY and POINS]  Honestly boys, none.

original: See now whether pure fear and entire cowardice doth not   make thee wrong this virtuous gentlewoman to close with   us.
translation: Now your total fear and complete cowardice have made you wrong this honest woman, just so that we won't be angry with you.

original: Is she of the wicked, is thine hostess here of the  wicked,   or is thy boy of the wicked, or honest Bardolph, whose zeal   burns in his nose, of the wicked?
translation: Is she wicked? Is this hostess here wicked? Is this boy here wicked? Or honest Bardolph, whose commitment is so strong it burns his face. Is he wicked too?

original: Answer, thou dead elm, answer.
translation: Answer him, you rotten old thing, answer him.

original: The fiend hath pricked down Bardolph irrecoverable, and   his face is Lucifer’s privy kitchen, where he doth  nothing but   roast malt-worms.
translation: The devil has put Bardolph on his list for certain, and his face is like Lucifer's kitchen—a place where only drunks are.

original: For the boy, there is a  good angel about   him, but the devil outbids him too.
translation: As for the boy, there is definitely a good angel looking after him, but also a devil that overpowers it.

original: For the women?
translation: What about the women?

original: For one of them, she’s in hell already and burns poor  souls. For the other, I owe her money, and whether she  be damned for that I know not.
translation: One of them is already in hell and infects poor men. As for the other one, I owe her money, and I don't know if she's damned.

original: No, I warrant you.
translation: I'm not, I can assure you of that.

original: No, I think thou art not; I think thou art quit for  that.
translation: No, I think you're not; I think you're forgiven for that.

original: Marry,   there is another indictment upon thee for  suffering flesh to   be eaten in thy house contrary to the law,
translation: Although there is another charge against you, for the fact that you serve meat here, which is against the law.

original: for the which I   think thou wilt howl.
translation: You will probably pay for that.

original: All vitlars do so. What’s a joint of mutton or two in a whole Lent?
You, gentlewoman.
translation: Excuse me, gentlewoman.

original: What says your Grace?
translation: What is it, your Grace?

original: His grace says that which his flesh rebels against.
translation: His Grace calls her a gentlewoman, even when his body knows she's a whore.

original: Who knocks so loud at door? Look to th' door there,  Francis.
translation: Who's knocking so loudly at my door? See who it is, Francis.

original: Peto, how now, what news?
translation: Peto, how are you and what news do you have for me?

original: The King your father is at Westminster,   And there are  twenty weak and wearied posts   Come from the north,
translation: The King, your father, is at Westminster. Twenty tired messengers have just arrived there from the north.

original: and  as I came along   I met and overtook a dozen captains,    Bareheaded, sweating, knocking at the taverns   And asking  everyone for Sir John Falstaff.
translation: And as I was traveling I overtook at least a dozen captains, all disheveled and worn out, knocking on the door of every tavern to ask for Sir John Falstaff.

original: By heaven, Poins, I feel me much to blame   So idly to  profane the precious time   When tempest of commotion,  like the south   Borne with black vapour,
translation: By God, Poins, I feel guilty for wasting precious time here when a violent storm is on the horizon,

original: doth begin to  melt   And drop upon our bare unarmèd heads.
translation: ready to rain down on our bare and unprotected heads.

original: —   Give me my  sword and cloak.
translation: Give me my sword and my coat.

original: —Falstaff, good night.
translation: Falstaff, good night.

original: Now comes in the sweetest morsel of the night, and we  must hence and leave it unpicked.
translation: Now it's the best time of the night, and we have to go before we can enjoy it.

original: More knocking at the door?
translation: More knocking?!

original: How now, what’s the matter?
translation: What's going on?

original: You must away to court, sir, presently. A dozen  captains stay at door for you.
translation: You are needed at court immediately, sir. A dozen captains are waiting at the door for you.

original: [to the PAGE]   Pay the musicians, sirrah.
translation: [To the PAGE]  Pay the musicians, sir.

original: —Farewell,    hostess
translation: [To MISTRESS QUICKLY]  Goodbye, hostess.

original: .—Farewell, Doll.
translation: [To DOLL TEARSHEET]  Goodbye, Doll.

original: You see, my good wenches, how    men of merit are sought after. The undeserver may sleep    when the man of action is called on.
translation: [To the ladies]  Look how wanted important men like me are. A person who does nothing might as well just sleep, while men of action like me get going.

original: Farewell, good    wenches. If I be not sent away post, I will see you again ere   I go.
translation: Goodbye, my lovely women. If I am not sent off to the wars right away, I will see you again before I go.

original: I cannot speak. If my heart be not ready to burst—well, sweet Jack, have a care of thyself.
translation: I can't speak. My heart feels ready to burst. Well, my sweet Jack, please take care of yourself.

original: Farewell, farewell.
translation: Goodbye, goodbye.

original: Well, fare thee well. I have known thee these  twenty-nine years, come peascod time, but an honester  and truer-hearted man—well, fare thee well.
translation: Well, goodbye to you. I will have known you for twenty-nine years by the time the peas grow this summer. But a more honest and truer man—well, goodbye to you.

original: Mistress Tearsheet!
translation: Mistress Tearsheet!

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: Bid Mistress Tearsheet come to my master.
translation: Tell Mistress Tearsheet to go to my master.

original: O, run, Doll, run, run, good Doll. Come.—She comes  blubbered.—Yea! Will you come, Doll?
translation: Oh run, Doll, run, run, good Doll. Come on. She will have to go with her face stained with tears. But she's coming! [To DOLL TEARSHEET] Will you come, Doll?

original: Go call the Earls of Surrey and of Warwick; But, ere  they come, bid them o'erread these letters And well  consider of them. Make good speed.
translation: Go and call the Earls of Surrey and Warwick. But, before they come, tell them to read over these letters and think about them carefully. Go quickly now.

original: How many thousand of my poorest subjects   Are at this  hour asleep! O sleep, O gentle sleep,   Nature’s soft  nurse, how have I frighted thee,
translation: How many thousands of even my poorest subjects are asleep right now! Oh, sleep, oh, lovely sleep, nature's kind nurse: what have I done to frighten you away?

original: That thou no more wilt  weigh my eyelids down   And steep my senses in  forgetfulness?
translation: You refuse to make my eyelids heavy anymore, and you refuse to make me giddy and forgetful

original: Why rather, sleep, liest thou in smoky  cribs,   Upon uneasy pallets stretching thee   And hushed  with buzzing night-flies to thy slumber,
translation: . But instead, sleep, you now lie in murky slums, stretched out on some unstable bed, listening only to the buzzing of flies as you drift off.

original: Than in the  perfumed chambers of the great,   Under the canopies of  costly state,   And lull’d with sound of sweetest melody?
translation: You choose that space instead of lying in the sweet-smelling bedrooms of royalty, under luxurious canopies, being lulled to sleep by the sweetest music there is?

original: O thou dull god, why liest thou with the vile   In  loathsome beds and leavest the kingly couch   A watch-case or a common 'larum bell?
translation: Oh, you tiresome god, why do you lie with the vile masses in their horrible beds and leave the King's bed all alone, like a sentry post or any bell tower?

original: Wilt thou upon the high and  giddy mast   Seal up the shipboy’s eyes, and rock his  brains   In cradle of the rude imperious surge   And in the  visitation of the winds,
translation: Will you even close up the eyes of some sailor boy, as he stands high up on the wobbly mast, and rock him to sleep in a cradle of rough, powerful seas and violent winds

original: Who take the ruffian billows by the top,   Curling their monstrous heads and hanging them   With deafening clamor in the slippery clouds   That with  the hurly death itself awakes?
translation: —winds which grab hold of the waves, and, curling them over, make them crash back down with such a deafening racket that they would wake up death itself?

original: Canst thou, O partial  sleep, give thy repose   To the wet sea-boy in an hour so  rude,   And, in the calmest and most stillest night,   With  all appliances and means to boot,   Deny it to a king?
translation: Oh, biased sleep, are you going to let a wet sailor boy sleep through all of that noise, but still refuse to let a king sleep—even in the calmest and most peaceful night, when he has everything he needs to go to bed?

original: Then, happy low, lie down.   Uneasy lies the head that  wears a crown.
translation: Well then, happy people, go to bed. The man who wears the crown is not sleeping very well right now.

original: Many good morrows to your Majesty.
translation: A very good morning to you, your Majesty.

original: Is it good morrow, lords?
translation: Is it morning, lords?

original: 'Tis one o'clock, and past.
translation: It's at least one o'clock, probably later.

original: Why then, good morrow to you all, my lords. Have you  read o'er the letter that I sent you?
translation: Well then, good morning to both of you, my lords. Have you read over the letters that I sent you?

original: We have, my liege.
translation: We have, my lord.

original: Then you perceive the body of our kingdom How foul it  is, what rank diseases grow And with what danger near  the heart of it.
translation: Then you realize how sick our kingdom is, and what diseases are spreading across the land, right to the heart of our nation.

original: It is but as a body yet distempered, Which to his  former strength may be restored With good advice and  little medicine. My Lord Northumberland will soon be  cooled.
translation: The body is only mildly unwell, and can be brought back to full strength with some good care and a little bit of medicine. Lord Northumberland will not be a problem for long.

original: O God, that one might read the book of fate   And see the revolution of the times
translation: Oh God, if only we could read the book of fate and find out what's going to happen! If only we could see how time can completely transform things

original: Make mountains level, and the  continent,   Weary of solid firmness, melt itself   Into the sea, and other times to see   The beachy girdle of the  ocean
translation: — making mountains change height, and making dry land, bored of being so solid and firm, melt into the sea.

original: Too wide for Neptune’s hips; how chance’s mocks    And changes fill the cup of alteration   With divers  liquors!
translation: Other times, we might see that even a beach could be too wide for  Neptune  to overpower. We might see how luck can humiliate a person, and how change can affect you in so many different ways!

original: O, if this were seen,   The happiest youth,  viewing his progress through,   What perils past, what  crosses to ensue,   Would shut the book, and sit him down  and die.
translation: Oh, even if the happiest youth could read this book of fate—if he could look at his life and see what dangers he had already overcome and what he still had left to deal with—he would shut the book right then and there, and just sit down and die.

original: 'Tis not ten years gone   Since Richard and  Northumberland, great friends,   Did feast together, and  in two years after   Were they at wars.
translation: It hasn't even been ten years since Richard and Northumberland were the greatest friends, always feasting together. And then two years later, they were at war with each other.

original: It is but eight  years since   This Percy was the man nearest my soul,   Who  like a brother toiled in my affairs   And laid his love  and life under my foot,
translation: It's only been eight years since Northumberland was the person I was closest to in this world. He was like a brother to me, supporting everything that I did, and even committing both his love and his life to my cause.

original: Yea, for my sake, even to the  eyes of Richard   Gave him defiance. But which of you was  by
translation: For my sake, he even showed his resistance to Richard directly. But which of you was there —

original: —   [to WARWICK]   You, cousin Nevil, as I may remember—
translation: [To WARWICK]   I think it was you,  Warwick , if I'm remembering rightly.

original: When Richard, with his eye brimful of tears,   Then checked and rated by Northumberland,   Did speak these words, now proved a prophecy?
translation: Do you remember when Richard—with his eyes full of tears because of Northumberland's attack—spoke these words?  They almost seem like a prophecy now:

original: “Northumberland, thou ladder by the  which   My cousin Bolingbroke ascends my throne”
translation: "Northumberland, you are just the ladder which Bolingbroke has climbed on to get to the throne."

original: Though  then, God knows, I had no such intent,   But that  necessity so bowed the state   That I and greatness were  compelled to kiss
translation: Although, God knows, I never planned on becoming king. But the country was struggling and needed help so I was forced to step up and become a great leader.

original: “The time shall come,” thus did he  follow it,   “The time will come that foul sin, gathering  head,   Shall break into corruption”
translation: Then he went on to say, "The time will come when this awful sin, as it continues to get bigger and bigger, will break out into rebellion."

original: —so went on,    Foretelling this same time’s condition   And the division  of our amity.
translation: He kept talking, predicting our present situation and the loss of our allies.

original: There is a history in all men’s lives   Figuring the  nature of the times deceased,
translation: There is a history book for every man's life, which reveals what has happened to him in the past.

original: The which observed, a man  may prophesy,   With a near aim, of the main chance of  things   As yet not come to life, which in their seeds   And weak beginnings lie intreasurèd.
translation: If you read this book, you can predict what is going to happen with more certainty. For we know that we can find evidence in the past for everything that is going to happen in the future.

original: Such things become the hatch and brood of time,
translation: The seeds from the past grow up to become the children of our time.

original: And by the necessary form of  this,   King Richard might create a perfect guess   That  great Northumberland,
translation: Because of this, it means that King Richard could predict that the great Northumberland

original: then false to him,   Would of that  seed grow to a greater falseness,   Which should not find  a ground to root upon   Unless on you.
translation: —already a traitor to him—would continue to let his betrayal grow and grow, until the only other person for him to betray was you.

original: Are these things then necessities?   Then let us meet  them like necessities.   And that same word even now cries out on us.
translation: Were all these things necessary then? Well, let's deal with them like necessities, even though the word "necessities" itself goes against us.

original: They say the Bishop and Northumberland   Are  fifty thousand strong.
translation: It is rumored that the Archbishop of York and Northumberland have fifty thousand men in their army.

original: It cannot be, my lord.   Rumor doth double, like the  voice and echo,   The numbers of the feared.
translation: That can't be true, my lord. Rumor, like an echoing voice, always doubles the amount of troops.

original: Please it  your Grace   To go to bed. Upon my soul, my lord,   The  powers that you already have sent forth   Shall bring this prize in very easily.
translation: Please go to bed now, your Grace. I swear on my life that the army you have already sent out will win this battle very easily.

original: To comfort you the more, I have  received   A certain instance that Glendower is dead.
translation: To make things even better, I've heard for certain that  Glendower is dead .

original: Your Majesty hath been this fortnight ill,   And these  unseasoned hours perforce must add   Unto your sickness.
translation: Your Majesty has been ill these past two weeks, and being up at these hours is only going to make you worse.

original: I will take your counsel. And were these inward wars once out of hand, We would, dear lords, unto the Holy  Land.
Come on, come on, come on. Give me your hand, sir, give me your hand, sir. An early stirrer, by the rood. And  how doth my good cousin Silence?
translation: Come on, come on, come on. Shake my hand, sir, shake my hand. You're an early riser, by the Holy Cross. How are you, Silence?

original: Good morrow, good cousin Shallow.
translation: Good morning, good cousin Shallow.

original: And how doth my cousin your bedfellow? And your fairest daughter and mine, my goddaughter Ellen?
translation: How is my cousin, your wife? And how is your beautiful daughter, my lovely goddaughter Ellen?

original: Alas, a black ousel, cousin Shallow.
By yea and no, sir. I dare say my cousin William is  become a good scholar. He is at Oxford still, is he not?
translation: You win some, you lose some, sir. Well, I bet that William has become a good scholar. He's still at Oxford, right?

original: Indeed, sir, to my cost.
translation: He is, sir—and I'm still having to pay for it.

original: He must then to the Inns o' Court shortly. I was once  of Clement’s Inn, where I think they will talk of mad  Shallow yet.
You were called “Lusty Shallow” then, cousin.
translation: I thought you were called, "Lively Shallow" back then, cousin.

original: By the Mass, I was called anything, and I would have  done   anything indeed too, and roundly too.
translation: By God, I was called anything they wanted to call me, and I would have done anything as well, without a fuss.

original: There was I,  and little   John Doit of Staffordshire, and black George  Barnes, and   Francis Pickbone, and Will Squele, a  Cotswold man.
translation: There was me, little John Doit from Staffordshire, the dark-haired George Barnes, Francis Pickbone, and Will Squele, from the Cotswolds.

original: You   had not four such swinge-bucklers in  all the Inns o' Court   again. And I may say to you, we  knew where the bona robas   were and had the best of them  all at commandment.
translation: Since then, in all of the Inns of Court there have been no four  swashbucklers  quite like us. Yet, let me tell you, we knew where to find prostitutes, and we had the best of them at our beck and call.

original: Then   was Jack Falstaff, now Sir  John, a boy, and page to Thomas   Mowbray, Duke of  Norfolk.
translation: Back then, John Falstaff—now  Sir John —was just a boy and was working as a page for Thomas Mowbray, the Duke of Norfolk.

original: This Sir John, cousin, that comes hither anon about  soldiers?
translation: The same Sir John that's on his way here to recruit some soldiers?

original: The same Sir John, the very same. I see him break  Scoggin’s   head at the court gate, when he was a crack  not thus high;
translation: Yes, that Sir John—the very same. I saw him beat  Scogan  on the head at the gates of the court, when he was just a lad, only this tall.

original: and   the very same day did I fight with  one Sampson Stockfish,   a fruiterer, behind Grey’s Inn.  Jesu, Jesu, the mad days that   I have spent! And to see  how many of my old acquaintance   are dead.
translation: On that same day I happened to have a fight with a man called Sampson Stockfish, a fruit seller, behind Gray's Inn. Oh Jesus, Jesus, I've had some wild times! And now so many of the men I used to know are dead.

original: We shall all follow, cousin.
translation: That will be us one day.

original: Certain, ’tis certain; very sure, very sure. Death, as  the   Psalmist saith, is certain to all. All shall die.
translation: You're right, I know you're right—that's for sure. As the Psalms say in the Bible, "death is certain." Everyone will die.

original: How a good   yoke of bullocks at Stamford Fair?
translation: What price are people charging for a good set of young bulls at  Stamford  Fair?

original: By my troth, cousin, I was not there.
translation: I'm not sure, I wasn't there.

original: Death is certain. Is old Dooble of your town living  yet?
translation: Death is certain. Is Dooble, that old man from your hometown, still alive?

original: Dead, sir.
translation: He's dead, sir.

original: Jesu, Jesu, dead! He drew a good bow, and dead? He shot a   fine shoot.
translation: Jesus, Jesus, dead! He was such a good archer, and now he's dead? He had an excellent shot!

original: John o' Gaunt loved him well, and betted  much   money on his head. Dead! He would have clapped i'  th'   clout at twelve score,
translation: John of Gaunt  loved him, and used to bet money on his incredible aim. Dead! Oh, he would have hit the target even from two hundred forty yards away!

original: and carried you a forehand  shaft a   fourteen and fourteen and a half, that it would  have done a   man’s heart good to see. How a score of ewes now?
translation: He could shoot straight at the target from two hundred eighty yards away, maybe even two hundred ninety—it was quite something to see! How much are they charging for twenty ewes now?

original: Thereafter as they be, a score of good ewes may be  worth ten pounds.
translation: That all depends on their quality, but twenty good ewes would be worth about ten pounds.

original: And is old Dooble dead?
translation: But old Dooble is dead?

original: Here come two of Sir John Falstaff’s men, as I think.
translation: Here come two of Sir John Falstaff's men, I think.

original: Good morrow, honest gentlemen.
translation: Good morning, honorable gentlemen.

original: I beseech you, which is Justice Shallow?
translation: Please, which of you is Justice Shallow?

original: I am Robert Shallow, sir, a poor esquire of this county and one of the King’s justices of the peace. What is  your good pleasure with me?
translation: Sir, I am Robert Shallow—a poor gentleman of this country and one of the King's justices of the peace. What can I do for you?

original: My captain, sir, commends him to you, my captain, Sir  John Falstaff, a tall gentleman, by heaven, and a most  gallant leader.
translation: My captain sends you his regards, sir. My captain is Sir John Falstaff. He is a brave gentleman and an excellent leader, I can tell you that.

original: He greets me well, sir. I knew him a good backsword  man. How doth the good knight? May I ask how my lady his wife doth?
translation: It's good to hear from him. I knew him when he was a good fencer. How is the good knight? And if you don't mind me asking, how is his wife?

original: Sir, pardon. A soldier is better accommodated than with a wife.
translation: Sorry, sir. A soldier doesn't need a wife—he is already accommodated with everything he needs.

original: It is well said, in faith, sir, and it is well said  indeed too.   “Better accommodated.” It is good, yea,  indeed, is it.
translation: Well said, indeed, sir. Well said, indeed. "Accommodated with everything he needs." That's good, indeed. That's very good.

original: Good   phrases are surely, and ever were,  very commendable. “Accommodated.” It comes of   accommodo   . Very good, a good phrase.
translation: Good phrases always deserve praise. Even the word, "Accommodated." It comes from the Latin word, "accommodo." Very good, a very good phrase.

original: Pardon, sir; I have heard the word—“phrase” call you  it? By   this day, I know not the phrase,
translation: Sorry, sir. I know the word "accommodated"—but you call it a good phrase? I don't know anything about phrases.

original: but I will  maintain the word   with my sword to be a soldierlike  word, and a word of   exceeding good command, by heaven.  “Accommodated,”
translation: But I am certain that the word, "accommodated" is a good word—a word used by soldiers, an extremely good military term, that's certain. "Accommodated."

original: that is when a man is, as they say,  accommodated, or when   a man is being whereby he may be  thought to be   accommodated, which is an excellent thing.
translation: You can say that a man is accommodated when he has been given what he needs, or when he is actually been given  just what he needs , which is an excellent thing.

original: It is very just. Look, here comes good Sir John.
translation: Quite right. Look, here comes good Sir John.

original: —Give  me   your good hand, give me your Worship’s good hand. By  my   troth, you like well and bear your years very well.  Welcome,   good Sir John.
translation: [To FALSTAFF]  Let me shake your good hand, let me shake your hand. Honestly, you look very well and like you haven't aged a bit. Welcome, good Sir John.

original: I am glad to see you well, good Master Robert Shallow.— Master Sure-card, as I think?
translation: I am glad to see you're well, good Master Robert Shallow. And this must be Master Sure-card, I think?

original: No, Sir John. It is my cousin Silence, in commission  with me.
translation: No, Sir John. This is my cousin Silence, another justice of the peace.

original: Good Master Silence, it well befits you should be of  the peace.
translation: Good Master Silence, your name is very apt for a justice of the peace.

original: Your good Worship is welcome.
translation: You are welcome here, your Worship.

original: Fie, this is hot weather, gentlemen. Have you provided  me here half a dozen sufficient men?
translation: Damn, it's hot outside, gentleman. Have you managed to find at least six men to be soldiers for me?

original: Marry, have we, sir. Will you sit?
translation: Indeed we have, sir. Would you like to sit down?

original: Let me see them, I beseech you.
translation: Let me see them, please.

original: Where’s the roll? Where’s the roll? Where’s the roll?  Let me   see, let me see, let me see. So, so, so, so, so.  So, so. Yea,   marry, sir.
translation: Where's the list? Where's the list? Where's the list? Let me see, let me see, let me see. So, so, so, so, so, so, so, so, so. Right, yes, indeed.

original: —Rafe Mouldy!
translation: [To MOULDY]  Ralph Mouldy!

original: —Let them appear as I call, let   them do so, let them do so. Let me see,  where is Mouldy?
translation: [To the recruits]  Come as I call your names! Do that, make sure you do that. Let's see then, where's Mouldy?!

original: Here, an it please you.
translation: Here, sir.

original: What think you, Sir John? A good-limbed fellow; young,  strong, and of good friends.
translation: What do you think, Sir John? He's got a good physique. He's young, strong, and from a good family.

original: Is thy name Mouldy?
translation: Is your name Mouldy?

original: Yea, an ’t please you.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: 'Tis the more time thou wert used.
translation: Well, then it's time you were put to good use.

original: Ha, ha, ha, most excellent, i' faith! Things that are  mouldy lack use. Very singular good, in faith. Well  said, Sir John, very well said.
translation: Ha, ha, ha, an excellent joke, indeed! Things get moldy when they aren't used. Good one, I swear. Well said, Sir John, very well said.

original: Prick him.
I was pricked well enough before, an you could have let me   alone.
translation: I have been  pricked  enough times before, when you could have just left me alone.

original: My old dame will be undone now for one to do  her   husbandry and her drudgery. You need not to have  pricked   me. There are other men fitter to go out than I.
translation: My old lady will be ruined now, without anyone to do her farming and her housework. You didn't need to prick me—there are men much fitter than I am who could have gone instead.

original: Go to. Peace, Mouldy. You shall go. Mouldy, it is time  you were spent.
translation: That's enough. Be quiet, Mouldy. You will go, Mouldy—it's time that you were used up.

original: Spent?
translation: Used up?

original: Peace, fellow, peace. Stand aside. Know you where you    are?
translation: Quiet, boy, quiet. Step aside. Don't you know where you a

original: —For th' other, Sir John. Let me see.
translation: [To FALSTAFF]  As for the others, Sir John, let's see who's next.

original: —Simon Shadow!
translation: [To SHADOW]  Simon Shadow!

original: Yea, marry, let me have him to sit under. He’s like to  be a cold soldier.
Where’s Shadow?
translation: Where's Shadow?

original: Here, sir.
translation: Here, sir.

original: Shadow, whose son art thou?
translation: Shadow, whose son are you?

original: My mother’s son, sir.
translation: I am my mother's son, sir.

original: Thy mother’s son! Like enough, and thy father’s shadow.
translation: Your mother's son! That makes sense, and your father's  shadow .

original: So   the son of the female is the shadow of the male. It  is often   so, indeed, but much of the father’s substance.
translation: The woman's son is actually a true reflection of the male—that's often how it goes. But normally, the son doesn't have quite as much to him as the father does.

original: Do you like him, Sir John?
translation: Do you approve of him, Sir John?

original: Shadow will serve for summer. Prick him, for we have a  number of shadows to fill up the muster book.
Thomas Wart!
translation: Thomas Wart!

original: Where’s he?
translation: Where is he?

original: Here, sir.
translation: Here, sir.

original: Is thy name Wart?
translation: Is your name Wart?

original: Yea, sir.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: Thou art a very ragged wart.
translation: You're a very rough wart.

original: Shall I prick him down, Sir John?
translation: Shall I prick him on the list, Sir John?

original: It were superfluous, for his apparel is built upon his  back, and the whole frame stands upon pins. Prick him no more.
translation: That's pointless. Can't you see, his clothing has been pieced together, and his whole body is being forced to stand up on two little pins. He's had enough pricking. Don't prick him anymore.

original: Ha, ha, ha. You can do it, sir, you can do it. I  commend you well.—Francis Feeble!
translation: Ha, ha, ha. That's good, sir, that's good. I have nothing but praise for you. Francis Feeble!

original: Here, sir.
translation: Here, sir.

original: What trade art thou, Feeble?
translation: What trade are you in, Feeble?

original: A woman’s tailor, sir.
translation: I'm a woman's tailor, sir.

original: Shall I prick him, sir?
translation: Shall I prick him, sir?

original: You may, but if he had been a man’s tailor, he’d ha'  pricked you.—Wilt thou make as many holes in an enemy’s  battle as thou hast done in a woman’s petticoat?
I will do my good will, sir. You can have no more.
translation: I'll do what I can, sir. I can't do anymore than that.

original: Well said, good woman’s tailor, well said, courageous    Feeble. Thou wilt be as valiant as the wrathful dove or  most   magnanimous mouse.
translation: Well said, good woman's tailor! Well said, brave Feeble! You will be as courageous as an angry dove—or the most fearless mouse.

original: —Prick the woman’s tailor well,    Master Shallow, deep, Master Shallow.
translation: Prick the woman's tailor. Do it well, Master Shallow, do it deeply, Master Shallow.

original: I would Wart might have gone, sir.
translation: I wish Wart were going, sir.

original: I would thou wert a man’s tailor, that thou mightst  mend him   and make him fit to go.
translation: If you were a man's tailor, you could mend his clothes and make him prepared to go.

original: I cannot put him to a  private soldier   that is the leader of so many thousands. Let that suffice, most   forcible Feeble.
translation: I can't enlist him as a private soldier, when he is already a leader of thousands—thousands of vermin, that is. But forget about that now, most powerful Feeble.

original: It shall suffice, sir.
translation: All right, I'll leave it, sir.

original: I am bound to thee, reverend Feeble.—Who is next?
translation: I'm a fan of you, good Feeble.  Who's next?

original: Peter Bullcalf o' th' green.
translation: Peter Bullcalf from the Green.

original: Yea, marry, let’s see Bullcalf.
translation: Oh, yes, let's see Bullcalf.

original: Here, sir.
translation: Here, sir.

original: Fore God, a likely fellow. Come, prick me Bullcalf till he roar again.
translation: By God, he's a good man, I can tell. Come on, prick Bullcalf for me until he shouts again.

original: O Lord, good my lord captain—
translation: Oh Lord! My good lord and captain.

original: What, dost thou roar before thou art pricked?
O Lord, sir, I am a diseased man.
translation: Oh Lord, sir, I'm a very sick man.

original: What disease hast thou?
translation: What disease do you have?

original: A whoreson cold, sir, a cough, sir, which I caught with ringing in the King’s affairs upon his coronation day,  sir.
translation: A horrible cold, sir. And a cough, sir, which I caught when I was ringing the bell for the anniversary of the King's coronation.

original: Come, thou shalt go to the wars in a gown. We will have   away thy cold, and I will take such order that my  friends   shall ring for thee
translation: Come on, you will just have to go to war in a dressing gown. That will help to get rid of your cold, and I will make sure that some of my friends can ring the bell while you're away.

original: .—   [to SHALLOW   ]   Is here all?
translation: [to SHALLOW]  Is that everyone?

original: Here is two more called than your number. You must have but four here, sir, and so I pray you go in with me to  dinner.
translation: There's two more here than you said you needed. You can take four of them. Come on, let's go and have lunch now.

original: Come, I will go drink with you, but I cannot tarry  dinner. I am glad to see you, by my troth, Master  Shallow.
translation: I will come and have a drink with you, but I don't have time to stay for lunch. It is good to see you, truly it is, Master Shallow.

original: O, Sir John, do you remember since we lay all night in  the windmill in Saint George’s Field?
No more of that, good Master Shallow, no more of that.
translation: Let's not talk about that, good Master Shallow. Let's not.

original: Ha, ’twas a merry night. And is Jane Nightwork alive?
translation: Ha, it was a fun night! Is Jane Nightwork still alive?

original: She lives, Master Shallow.
translation: She is, Master Shallow.

original: She never could away with me.
translation: She could never put up with me.

original: Never, never; she would always say she could not abide  Master Shallow.
translation: Never, never. She always said that she just couldn't stand Master Shallow.

original: By the Mass, I could anger her to th' heart. She was  then a bona roba. Doth she hold her own well?
translation: By God, I could anger her to her very heart. She was one of the best whores. Does she still have it?

original: Old, old, Master Shallow.
translation: She's old, very old now, Master Shallow.

original: Nay, she must be old. She cannot choose but be old.
translation: Well, of course she's old—she can't help that.

original: Certain,   she’s old, and had Robin Nightwork by old  Nightwork   before I came to Clement’s Inn.
translation: Of course she's old. She gave birth to Robin Nightwork, the son of old Nightwork, before I even went to Clement's Inn.

original: That’s fifty-five year ago.
translation: That's fifty-five years ago now.

original: Ha, cousin Silence, that thou hadst seen that that this knight and I have seen!—Ha, Sir John, said I well?
translation: Ha, cousin Silence. If you could have seen what this knight and I have seen!  Ha, Sir John, isn't that right?

original: We have heard the chimes at midnight, Master Shallow.
translation: We've certainly seen the clock strike midnight a few times, Master Shallow.

original: That we have, that we have, that we have. In faith, Sir John,   we have. Our watchword was “Hem, boys.”
translation: We certainly have, we certainly have. Really, Sir John, we have. Our motto was "Down with it, boys!"

original: Come,  let’s to   dinner; come, let’s to dinner. Jesus, the days  that we have   seen! Come, come.
translation: Come on, let's go to lunch. Jesus, the things that we've seen. Come on, let's go.

original: Good Master Corporate Bardolph, stand my friend, and    here’s four Harry ten-shillings in French crowns for you.
translation: Good Master  Corporate  Bardolph, be my friend. And here's some French crowns for you, worth four  Harry ten-shillings .

original: In   very truth, sir, I had as lief be hanged, sir, as  go. And yet, for   mine own part, sir, I do not care, but  rather because I am   unwilling,
translation: Truthfully, sir, I would just as happily be hanged than go to war. It's not that I care about my own safety, that doesn't matter to me. It's just that I don't want to go.

original: and, for mine own part,  have a desire to stay with   my friends. Else, sir, I did  not care, for mine own part, so much.
translation: More than anything, I want to stay here with my friends. Other than that, sir, I really don't care about myself.

original: Go to. Stand aside.
translation: Whatever you say. Stand aside now.

original: And, good Master Corporal Captain, for my old dame’s    sake, stand my friend.
translation: And, good Master Corporal Captain, for my old lady's sake, be my friend.

original: She has nobody to do anything  about   her when I am gone, and she is old and cannot help herself:   You shall have forty, sir.
translation: She has no one else to help her do anything if I go, and she's old and can't take care of herself. I'll give you forty shillings, sir.

original: Go to. Stand aside.
translation: Whatever you say. Stand aside now.

original: By my troth, I care not. A man can die but once. We owe God   a death. I’ll ne'er bear a base mind.
translation: Truthfully, I don't care. A man can only die once, and at some point we all owe God a death. I'm not going to do anything that's wrong.

original: An ’t be my  destiny, so;   an ’t be not, so. No man’s too good to  serve ’s prince,
translation: If it's my fate, then that's that. If it's not, then that's fine too. No man is too good to fight for his Prince and his country.

original: and let   it go which way it will, he  that dies this year is quit for the   next.
translation: No matter how it goes, if a person dies this year, then it just means their debts are paid for next year.

original: Well said. Th' art a good fellow.
translation: Very well said. You're a good man.

original: Faith, I’ll bear no base mind.
translation: I'm telling the truth. I won't do anything dishonest.

original: Come, sir, which men shall I have?
translation: Come on then, sir, which men shall I have?

original: Four of which you please.
translation: Whichever four you want.

original: Sir, a word with you.    I have three  pound to free Mouldy and Bullcalf.
translation: Sir, can I have a word? I've been given three pounds to free Mouldy and Bullcalf.

original: Go to, well.
translation: Right! That's fine!

original: Come, Sir John, which four will you have?
translation: Come on, Sir John, which four men will you take?

original: Do you choose for me.
translation: Why don't you choose for me?

original: Marry, then, Mouldy, Bullcalf, Feeble, and Shadow.
translation: Okay then: Mouldy, Bullcalf, Feeble and Shadow.

original: Mouldy and Bullcalf! For you, Mouldy, stay at home till you   are past service.
translation: Mouldy and Bullcalf! You stay at home until you are too old to fight, Mouldy.

original: —And for your part, Bullcalf, grow till you   come unto it. I will none of you.
translation: And as for you, Bullcalf, you should stay at home and wait until you are old enough to fight. I don't want either of you.

original: Sir John, Sir John, do not yourself wrong. They are  your likeliest men, and I would have you served with the best.
translation: Sir John, Sir John, don't make a bad choice. They're the best men of the whole group, and I want to make sure you have the best!

original: Will you tell me, Master Shallow, how to choose a  man?Care I for the limb, the thews, the stature, bulk,  and bigassemblance of a man?
translation: Master Shallow, are you going to tell me how I should choose my soldiers? Do you think I only care about a man's body, power, strength, muscles, and overall appearance?

original: Give me the spirit, Master  Shallow.Here’s Wart. You see what a ragged appearance it is. He shall charge you and discharge you with the  motion of apewterer’s hammer,
translation: Give me his spirit, Master Shallow! Look at Wart here. You can see what a tattered appearance he has. But he will load and fire with the steadiness that a  pewterer  has when using his hammer.

original: come off and on swifter  than he thatgibbets on the brewer’s bucket.
translation: He can advance and retreat as quickly as a man can refill a brewer's pail.

original: And this  same half-facedfellow, Shadow, give me this man. He  presents no mark tothe enemy. The foeman may with as  great aim level at theedge of a penknife.
translation: And this little thin fellow, Shadow, let me have this man. He isn't even a proper target for the enemy. He's so thin the enemy might as well be aiming at the edge of a knife.

original: And for a  retreat, how swiftly will thisFeeble the woman’s tailor, run off! O, give me the sparemen, and spare me the  great ones.
translation: And when it comes to retreating, this Feeble, the woman's tailor, will run away quicker than anyone else! Oh, give me the spare men and spare me the great ones!

original: —Put me a caliver into Wart’s hand,  Bardolph.
translation: [To BARDOLPH]  Now give Wart a light musket, Bardolph.

original: Hold, Wart. Traverse. Thas, thas, thas.
translation: Here it is, Wart. Now march back and forth. March, march, march.

original: Come, manage me your caliver: so, very well, go to,  very   good, exceeding good.
translation: Come on, handle your weapon. Yes, very good, very good, you're doing very well.

original: O, give me always a little,  lean, old,   chopped, bald shot. Well said, i' faith,  Wart. Th' art a good   scab. Hold, there’s a tester for  thee.
translation: Oh, I would always choose a little, thin, old, dried up and bald soldier. Well done, Wart. You're a good little rascal. Hang on, here's sixpence for you.

original: He is not his craft’s master. He doth not do it right.
translation: He is not exactly an expert. He's not doing it right.

original: I   remember at Mile End Green, when I lay at Clement’s  Inn—   I was then Sir Dagonet in Arthur’s show
translation: I remember at  Mile End Green , when I was staying at Clement's Inn, I played the fool in an archery exhibition.

original: —there was a little   quiver fellow, and he would manage you his piece thus. And   he would about and about, and come you in,  and come you   in.
translation: I remember that there was this little nimble man who used to hold his weapon just like this. He would just run around all over the place, and he'd charge over and over again.

original: “Rah, tah, tah,” would he say.  “Bounce,” would he say,   and away again would he go, and  again would he come. I   shall ne'er see such a fellow.
translation: He'd say, "Rah, tah, tah," and "Bang!" Then he would run away, before charging all over again. I've never seen anyone like him.

original: These fellows will do well, Master Shallow.
translation: These men will do well, Master Shallow.

original: —God keep    you, Master Silence. I will not use many words with you.    Fare you well, gentlemen both. I thank you. I must a  dozen   mile to-night.
translation: [To SHALLOW and SILENCE]  Goodbye to both of you. Thank you for your help. I need to travel at least twelve miles tonight.

original: —Bardolph, give the soldiers coats.
translation: [To BARDOLPH]  Give the soldiers their uniforms and their jackets, Bardolph.

original: Sir John, the Lord bless you. God prosper your affairs. God send us peace.
translation: Sir John, may God bless you and may he bring you good fortunes. May God also bring us peace.

original: At your return, visit our house. Let our old acquaintance be renewed. Peradventure I will  with you to the court.
translation: When you get back, come and visit us here. We can rebuild our old friendship. Maybe I will even come and see you at the royal court.

original: Fore God, would you would, Master Shallow.
translation: I swear before God that I hope you do, Master Shallow.

original: Go to. I have spoke at a word. God keep you.
translation: Get going now. I meant what I said. May God keep you safe.

original: Fare you well, gentle gentlemen.
translation: Goodbye, kind gentlemen.

original: On, Bardolph. Lead the men away.
translation: Walk on, Bardolph. Lead the men away.

original: As I return, I will fetch off these justices. I do see  the bottom   of Justice Shallow. Lord, Lord, how subject  we old men are   to this vice of lying.
translation: When I return, I will fleece these justices of the peace. I can see Justice Shallow for who he really is. Lord, Lord, we old men are so good at lying.

original: This same starved  justice hath done   nothing but prate to me of the  wildness of his youth and the   feats he hath done about  Turnbull Street, and every third   word a lie, duer paid  to the hearer than the Turk’s tribute.
translation: This old justice has done nothing but chatter on to me about his wild youth and the crazy things he did near  Turnbull Street . Every third word he's said to me has been a lie. He can tell lies quicker than a Turk will rush off to pay the Sultan.

original: I   do remember him at Clement’s Inn, like a man made after   supper of a  cheese paring. When he was naked, he was, for   all the  world, like a forked radish with a head fantastically    carved upon it with a knife.
translation: I remember him when he was at Clement's Inn. He looked like a man that had been made out of a spare slice of cheese after dinner. When he was naked, he looked like a mandrake root, with a head that someone had taken the time to carve out with a knife.

original: He was so forlorn that his    dimensions to any thick sight were invincible. He was the   very genius of famine, yet lecherous as a monkey, and  the   whores called him “mandrake.”
translation: He was so thin that you had to have perfect vision to even notice him at all. He was the very embodiment of famine, but he was still as horny as a  monkey , and the whores called him " mandrake ."

original: He came ever in the    rearward of the fashion, and sung those tunes to the    overscutched huswives that he heard the carmen whistle,    and swore they were his fancies or his good-nights.
translation: He was always behind on the fashions. He would hear the cart drivers whistling tunes and then would go and sing those tunes to a deadbeat whore, pretending that they were his songs, his ditties.

original: And  now is this Vice’s dagger become a squire, and talks as    familiarly of John o' Gaunt as if he had been sworn  brother   to him, and I’ll be sworn he ne'er saw him but  once in the tilt-yard,   and then he burst his head for  crowding among the Marshal’s men.
translation: And now this vile, thin man has become a gentleman, and talks about John of Gaunt like they were close companions. In fact, the only place he would have seen John of Gaunt was up in Westminster, when he was competing in a jousting tournament. Even then, John of Gaunt cut Shallow's head with his sword for standing where he wasn't supposed to.

original: I saw it and told  John o' Gaunt he beat his own name,   for you might have  thrust him and all his apparel   into an eel-skin;
translation: I saw it all and I told John of Gaunt that he had basically beaten his own name—since Shallow was so gaunt back then you could have fit all of him into the skin of an eel.

original: the  case of a treble hautboy   was a mansion for him, a  court. And now has he land and beefs.
translation: Back then an oboe's case would have looked like a mansion to him—a courtroom even. And now he has land and his own animals.

original: Well, I’ll be  acquainted with him, if I return, and ’t shall go hard  but   I’ll make him a philosopher’s two stones to me.
translation: Well, if I come back, I will make him be my friend. It won't be easy, but I will make him a never-ending source of wealth for myself.

original: If  the young   dace be a bait for the old pike, I see no  reason in the law of   nature but I may snap at him. Let  time shape, and there an end.
translation: If small fish are meant to be eaten by big fish, then I see no reason why I can't snap at his heels. Only time will decide, and with that, I'm done.

original: What is this forest called?
translation: What is this forest called?

original: 'Tis Gaultree Forest, an ’t shall please your Grace.
Here stand, my lords, and send discoverers forth To  know the numbers of our enemies.
translation: We will wait here, my lords, and we will send men ahead of us to find out how many enemy troops there are.

original: We have sent forth already.
translation: We have already sent these men.

original: 'Tis well done.   My friends and brethren in these  great affairs,   I must acquaint you that I have received    New-dated letters from Northumberland,
translation: Well done. My friends and allies in this great mission, I must tell you about some news I've received in these recent letters from Northumberland.

original: Their cold intent, tenor, and substance, thus:   Here doth he wish his  person, with such powers   As might hold sortance with his quality,   The which he could not levy;
translation: They have a frosty tone and the contents are as follows: he says that he would like to be here himself, with an army that matches his own reputation, but he hasn't managed to raise one.

original: whereupon   He is  retired, to ripe his growing fortunes,
translation: Therefore, he has decided to go to Scotland to help his own fortunes.

original: To Scotland, and  concludes in hearty prayers   That your attempts may  overlive the hazard   And fearful melting of their  opposite.
translation: He ends by saying that he is praying for your armies to defeat the danger and the power of the enemy.

original: Thus do the hopes we have in him touch ground And dash  themselves to pieces.
translation: I suppose that means any hopes we had for him might as well be thrown away and destroyed.

original: Now, what news?
translation: What's happening?

original: West of this forest, scarcely off a mile,   In goodly  form comes on the enemy,
translation: The enemy is strong and barely a mile from here, to the west of this forest.

original: And, by the ground they hide, I judge their number   Upon or near the rate of thirty  thousand.
translation: Looking at the amount of space the troops are taking up, I would guess there were almost thirty thousand of them.

original: The just proportion that we gave them out. Let us sway  on and face them in the field.
translation: The exact number we predicted. Let's keep going and get ready to fight them.

original: What well-appointed leader fronts us here?
translation: What well-chosen leader is coming here to confront us?

original: I think it is my Lord of Westmoreland.
translation: I think it's Lord Westmoreland.

original: Health and fair greeting from our general, The Prince  Lord John and Duke of Lancaster.
translation: Our general, the Prince Lord John, Duke of Lancaster, sends his greetings and hopes that you are in good health.

original: Say on, my Lord of Westmoreland, in peace, What doth  concern your coming.
translation: Tell us in peace, Lord Westmoreland: why have you come here?

original: Then, my lord,   Unto your Grace do I in chief address    The substance of my speech.
translation: Well, my lord, it is to your Grace that I need to address the main part of my speech.

original: If that rebellion   Came like  itself, in base and abject routs,   Led on by bloody  youth, guarded with rags,   And countenanced by boys and  beggary
translation: If this rebellion looked like it normally does in its truest form; if it were run by a poor mob, led by bloody young men in rags, with boys and beggars supporting it,

original: I say, if damn’d commotion so appeared   In his  true, native, and most proper shape,   You, reverend  father, and these noble lords
translation: I am telling you that—as a holy man—you and these noble lords

original: Had not been here to dress the ugly form   Of base and bloody insurrection   With your fair honors.
translation: would not be honoring this bloody event with your presence.

original: You, Lord Archbishop,   Whose see is by a  civil peace maintained,   Whose beard the silver hand of  peace hath touched,   Whose learning and good letters  peace hath tutored,
translation: Lord Archbishop, you maintain peace and order in your district. Your beard has turned grey as a sign of your peaceful life. Your learning and writing have followed the teachings of peace.

original: Whose white investments figure  innocence,   The dove and very blessèd spirit of peace,
translation: And your white robes make you almost like a dove—a blessed symbol of peace itself.

original: Wherefore do you so ill translate yourself   Out of the  speech of peace, that bears such grace,   Into the harsh  and boist'rous tongue of war,
translation: Why have you decided to translate yourself from the graceful and soft language of peace to the harsh and violent language of war?

original: Turning your books to  graves, your ink to blood,   Your pens to lances, and your tongue divine   To a trumpet and a point of war?
translation: You have turned your books into graves, your ink into blood, your pens into spears, and your holy tongue into a trumpet that calls men to arms.

original: Wherefore do I this? So the question stands.   Briefly,  to this end: we are all diseased,
translation: But why do I do all of this? That's the real question. The short answer is, we're all sick.

original: And with our  surfeiting and wanton hours   Have brought ourselves into  a burning fever,   And we must bleed for it; of which  disease   Our late King Richard, being infected, died.
translation: We've eaten too much and stayed up too late and now we've given ourselves a burning fever. And the only way to cure it is with the blood shed in battle. This is the same disease that Richard, our late King, was infected with and from which he later died.

original: But, my most noble Lord of Westmoreland,   I take not on me here as a physician,   Nor do I as an enemy to peace    Troop in the throngs of military men,
translation: But, my noble Lord of Westmoreland, I'm not claiming to be any kind of doctor here who can fix these problems. Nor am I marching with our troops as an enemy of peace.

original: But rather show  awhile like fearful war   To diet rank minds sick of  happiness   And purge th' obstructions which begin to stop   Our very veins of life.
translation: I am simply showing them what terrible war is like, to stop their minds from becoming bloated with ease and luxury. Therefore, I clear out the obstructions which are blocking up our arteries and our veins—blocking up our ability to live well.

original: Hear me more plainly.   I have in equal balance justly weighed   What wrongs our arms may  do, what wrongs we suffer,   And find our griefs heavier  than our offenses.
translation: Let me say that more plainly. I've carefully considered the options, weighing up how much harm our weapons could do against the harm that is already being inflicted on us. And I think that the injustices done to us are worse that any that we will commit in battle.

original: We see which way the stream of time  doth run   And are enforced from our most quiet there   By  the rough torrent of occasion,
translation: We can see the direction that things are going in, and so we are forced to step away from our quiet lives and into a time of violence.

original: And have the summary of  all our griefs,   When time shall serve, to show in  articles;   Which long ere this we offered to the King   And might by no suit gain our audience.
translation: We have written out a summary of all of our complaints, and we will publish them when the time is right. We tried to show them to the King a long time ago, but we couldn't get a meeting with him.

original: When we are wronged and would unfold our griefs,   We are denied access unto  his person   Even by those men that most have done us  wrong.
translation: We were wronged. But when we tried to make our complaints, we were denied access to the very person who had wronged us in the first place.

original: The dangers of the days but newly gone,   Whose  memory is written on the earth   With yet appearing blood,
translation: We are wearing this inappropriate armor right now because of the recent battle—the memory of which is still stained on the ground—

original: and the examples   Of every minute’s instance, present  now,   Hath put us in these ill-beseeming arms,
translation: and also because of the awful things happening every minute, at this current time.

original: Not to  break peace or any branch of it,   But to establish here a peace indeed,   Concurring both in name and quality.
translation: We are not trying to destroy peace, or even any small part of peace. Instead, we want to establish a peace that actually means something and actually works.

original: When ever yet was your appeal denied?   Wherein have you  been gallèd by the King?
translation: When were you denied access to the King? How has the King made you so angry?
