original: What peer hath been suborned to grate on you,   That you should seal this lawless bloody  book   Of forged rebellion with a seal divine   And  consecrate commotion’s bitter edge?
translation: What lord has been secretly sent out to harass you—so much so that you would put your divine seal of approval on a fraudulent and lawless rebellion, consecrating such a violent disturbance?

original: My brother general, the commonwealth, To brother born  an household cruelty, I make my quarrel in particular.
translation: The main reasons I am involved in this rebellion include the injustices done to my fellow Englishmen, and my own brother Scroop's cruel murder.

original: There is no need of any such redress, Or if there were, it not belongs to you.
translation: There's no need to claim any compensation for that. And even if there were, that need doesn't belong to you.

original: Why not to him in part, and to us all   That feel the  bruises of the days before
translation: Why shouldn't he at least get a little back? Why shouldn't all of us be allowed to get something back—all of us who've suffered during these recent wars

original: And suffer the condition of  these times   To lay a heavy and unequal hand   Upon our  honors?
translation: and whose honors are ruined by the awful things happening right now?

original: O, my good Lord Mowbray,   Construe the times to their necessities,   And you shall say indeed it is the time,    And not the King, that doth you injuries.
translation: Oh, my good lord Mowbray, if you can understand these times by just considering the inevitability of what has happened, you will see that it is the terrible situation that harms you—and not the King himself.

original: Yet for your  part, it not appears to me   Either from the King or in  the present time   That you should have an inch of any  ground   To build a grief on.
translation: But as for you individually, it seems to me that you don't have any kind of foundation to build an argument on—not against the King and not against your present situation either.

original: Were you not restored   To all the Duke of Norfolk’s signories,   Your noble and right  well remembered father’s?
translation: Haven't you just been given all of the estates and honors of your noble and esteemed late father, the Duke of Norfolk?

original: What thing, in honor, had my father lost,   That need to  be revived and breathed in me?
translation: But what honor did my father lose that I now need to restore and bring back?

original: The King that loved him,  as the state stood then,   Was force perforce compelled to banish him,
translation: The old King, Richard, loved my father. But he was forced to banish him because of the way things were.

original: And then that Harry Bolingbroke and he,    Being mounted and both rousèd in their seats,
translation: And then, my father and Harry Bolingbroke challenged each other to a  duel . They were both mounted on their horses and were ready to charge at each other.

original: Their  neighing coursers daring of the spur,   Their armèd staves in charge, their beavers down,   Their eyes of fire  sparking through sights of steel
translation: Their horses were neighing, ready to gallop forward, when the signal was given. Their steel-tipped spears were ready to attack. Their face-guards were on. Their eyes were burning through the slight gaps in their helmets.

original: And the loud trumpet  blowing them together,
translation: Then the trumpet sounded.

original: Then, then, when there was  nothing could have stayed   My father from the breast of  Bolingbroke,   O, when the King did throw his warder down—   His own life hung upon the staff he threw—
translation: And although nothing could have stopped my father from killing Bolingbroke, King Richard ended the fight before it began by throwing down his royal staff.

original: Then threw  he down himself and all their lives   That by indictment  and by dint of sword   Have since miscarried under  Bolingbroke.
translation: When he threw down the staff, he threw down his own life—and the lives of every man that has died fighting for Bolingbroke.

original: You speak, Lord Mowbray, now you know not what.   The  Earl of Hereford was reputed then   In England the most  valiant gentleman.
translation: You don't know what you're talking about, Lord Mowbray. At that time, Bolingbroke was considered the bravest gentleman in all of England.

original: Who knows on whom fortune would then  have smiled?   But if your father had been victor there,    He ne'er had borne it out of Coventry;
translation: Who knows who would have won the duel? But if your father had won in that duel, he would never have made it out of Coventry alive.

original: For all the  country in a general voice   Cried hate upon him; and all  their prayers and love   Were set on Hereford,
translation: For the country hated him, while they loved and prayed for Bolingbroke.

original: whom they  doted on   And blessed and graced, indeed more than the  King.   But this is mere digression from my purpose.
translation: They blessed him and worshipped him more than they did King  Richard at the time. But I am forgetting the reason that I came here.

original: Here  come I from our princely general   To know your griefs, to tell you from his Grace   That he will give you audience;
translation: I have been sent here by the Prince, our general, to know what your complaints are, and to tell you that his Grace is prepared to listen to them.

original: and wherein   It shall appear that your demands are just,   You shall enjoy them, everything set off   That might so  much as think you enemies.
translation: If it seems like your demands are fair, then you will get what you want—unless it is something that would make you enemies of the Prince.

original: But he hath forced us to compel this offer; And it  proceeds from policy, not love.
translation: But he's only listening to us because we've forced him to. He doesn't listen out of love. Instead, he listens because he thinks it's the right political move!

original: Mowbray, you overween to take it so.   This offer comes  from mercy, not from fear.
translation: Mowbray, you are too presumptuous in thinking that. This offer comes out of mercy, not our of fear.

original: For, lo, within a ken our  army lies,   Upon mine honor, all too confident   To give  admittance to a thought of fear.   Our battle is more full of names than yours,
translation: For, look, our army is just over there. On my honor, our army is far too confident to even entertain the idea of being afraid. Our army is full of men far more renowned than your troops.

original: Our men more perfect in the use of arms,   Our armor all as strong, our cause the best.   Then reason will our hearts should be as good.   Say you not  then our offer is compelled.
translation: Our soldiers know how to use weapons incredibly well. Our armor is just as strong as yours, and our cause is even better. It's only right that we're just as ready as you are. So don't say that the Prince has been forced to make this offer; it's a choice.

original: Well, by my will, we shall admit no parley.
translation: Well, I declare that we refuse to meet with him.

original: That argues but the shame of your offense. A rotten  case abides no handling.
translation: That just shows that you're ashamed of what you're doing. Something that's rotten will crumble if it is touched.

original: Hath the Prince John a full commission, In very ample  virtue of his father, To hear and absolutely to  determine Of what conditions we shall stand upon?
translation: Has Prince John been given complete authority by his father to hear our demands and decide what to do from there?

original: That is intended in the General’s name. I muse you make so slight a question.
translation: That's a given, since he is the General. I'm surprised you'd even ask such a question.

original: Then take, my Lord of Westmoreland, this schedule,   For  this contains our general grievances.
translation: Well then, my Lord of Westmoreland, take this document. It contains a list of our main complaints.

original: Each several  article herein redressed,   All members of our cause, both here and hence,
translation: If every complaint we have made is addressed and everyone involved in this rebellion—both here and elsewhere

original: That are insinewed to this action,    Acquitted by a true substantial form   And present  execution of our wills   To us and to our purposes  confined,
translation: —is fully pardoned, and all of our demands are met right away

original: We come within our awful banks again   And knit  our powers to the arm of peace.
translation: , then we will return to our rightful places and work together to try to come to a peaceful agreement.

original: This will I show the General. Please you, lords,   In  sight of both our battles we may meet,
translation: I will show this to the General. If you don't mind, let's meet again in a place where both of our armies can see us.

original: And either end in peace, which God so frame,   Or to the place of  difference call the swords   Which must decide it.
translation: That way, the discussions can either end in peace—which I hope is God's will—or we can go straight to the battlefield to decide the outcome.

original: My lord, we will do so.
translation: My lord, we will do that.

original: There is a thing within my bosom tells me That no  conditions of our peace can stand.
translation: Something in my heart tells me that even if we agreed to peace, it wouldn't last.

original: Fear you not that. If we can make our peace Upon such  large terms and so absolute As our conditions shall  consist upon, Our peace shall stand as firm as rocky  mountains.
translation: Don't worry about that. If we can come to an agreement based on great terms and stand firm on the conditions we have requested, then our peace will last as long as rocky mountains.

original: Yea, but our valuation shall be such   That every slight  and false-derivèd cause,   Yea, every idle, nice, and  wanton reason,   Shall to the King taste of this action,
translation: Yes, but in the future the King will think so little of us that every slight, false accusation—yes, every stupid, meaningless thing—will remind him of now.

original: That, were our royal faiths martyrs in love,   We shall be  winnowed with so rough a wind   That even our corn shall  seem as light as chaff   And good from bad find no  partition.
translation: Even if we could prove our loyalty to the King by dying, he would be so suspicious of us that even the good things we do for him won't matter—he won't be able to separate them from the bad things we've already done.

original: No, no, my lord. Note this: the King is weary   Of dainty and such picking grievances,
translation: No, no, my lord. Know this. The King is tired of picking fights over every small thing.

original: For he hath found to end  one doubt by death   Revives two greater in the heirs of  life;
translation: For he has found that if he ends one problem by killing someone, it just makes two bigger problems for the people who are left behind.

original: And therefore will he wipe his tables clean   And  keep no telltale to his memory   That may repeat and  history his loss   To new remembrance.
translation: Therefore, he wants to wipe the slate clean, and forget about anything which might remind him of the violent past.

original: For full well he  knows   He cannot so precisely weed this land   As his  misdoubts present occasion;
translation: For he knows that he can't just get rid of every little problem that crops up.

original: His foes are so enrooted  with his friends   That, plucking to unfix an enemy,   He  doth unfasten so and shake a friend;
translation: His enemies like roots grown among his friends, so much so that if he tried to pull up an enemy, he'd also be pulling up and getting rid of a friend.

original: So that this land,  like an offensive wife   That hath enraged him on to offer strokes,   As he is striking holds his infant up
translation: This country is behaving just like a disobedient wife, who, when she is just about to be beaten by her husband, holds up their baby in defense

original: And  hangs resolved correction in the arm   That was upreared  to execution.
translation: and makes him pause mid-action—stopping the arm that was about to carry out the punishment.

original: Besides, the King hath wasted all his rods   On late  offenders,
translation: Besides, the King has already used up all of his anger and punishments on the recent rebellion

original: that he now doth lack   The very instruments of chastisement,   So that his power, like to a fangless  lion,   May offer but not hold.
translation: . He has nothing left to punish us with. He's weak, like a lion without its teeth. He can threaten us, but he can't actually do anything.

original: 'Tis very true, And therefore be assured, my good  Lord Marshal, If we do now make our atonement well, Our  peace will, like a broken limb united, Grow stronger for the breaking.
translation: That's very true. So be assured, my good Lord Marshal, that if we can reach reconciliation, our peaceful agreement will be like a broken limb. It will just grow stronger after it is broken.

original: Be it so. Here is returned my Lord of Westmoreland.
translation: I hope you're right. Look, Lord Westmoreland is back.

original: The Prince is here at hand. Pleaseth your lordship To  meet his Grace just distance ’tween our armies.
translation: The Prince is close by. If you are ready, will your Lordship come and meet his Grace at a spot halfway between our two armies?

original: Your Grace of York, in God’s name then set forward.
translation: Your Grace, Archbishop of York: go forward and meet him in God's name.

original: Before, and greet his Grace.—    My lord,  we come.
translation: Lead on, and I will go and meet his Grace.   My lord, we will come.

original: You are well encountered here, my cousin Mowbray.—   Good day to you, gentle Lord Archbishop,—   And so to you,  Lord Hastings, and to all.
translation: It's good to see you, Mowbray. Good day to you, gentle Archbishop. The same to you, Lord Hastings, and to all of you.

original: My Lord of York, it better  showed with you   When that your flock,
translation: Archbishop, I would prefer to see you with your congregation

original: assembled by the  bell,   Encircled you to hear with reverence   Your  exposition on the holy text   Than now to see you here, an iron man talking,
translation: —called together by the church bell, waiting excitedly to hear your sermons—than to see you here, clothed in armor.

original: Cheering a rout of rebels with your  drum,   Turning the word to sword, and life to death.
translation: Now you cheer on a crowd of rebels with your war drum, speaking only of violence, and turning your life into death.

original: That man that sits within a monarch’s heart   And ripens in  the sunshine of his favor,
translation: When a man who is loved by the King—and prospers under this love

original: Would he abuse the  countenance of the King,   Alack, what mischiefs might he  set abroach   In shadow of such greatness!
translation: —abuses this favor and turns against him, alas! What terrible things a man like that can do, hidden in the shadow of a great man.

original: With you, Lord  Bishop,   It is even so. Who hath not heard it spoken   How  deep you were within the books of God,
translation: That's how it is with you, Lord Archbishop. Who hasn't heard people say how incredible your religious knowledge is?

original: To us the speaker in His parliament,   To us th' imagined voice of God  himself,   The very opener and intelligencer   Between the  grace, the sanctities, of heaven,   And our dull workings?
translation: That's why you were our representative in God's very parliament—the man we almost thought of as God's own voice. You are supposed to be the interpreter of and messenger between God's heavenly actions and our own foolish behavior.

original: O, who shall believe   But you misuse the reverence of  your place,
translation: Oh, now who doesn't think that you have abused the sacred position you hold,

original: Employ the countenance and grace of heaven    As a false favorite doth his prince’s name,   In deeds  dishonorable?
translation: using this pretense of religion to do awful things—just like a lying lord uses the Prince's good name?

original: You have ta'en up,   Under the counterfeited zeal of God,   The subjects of His substitute, my father,   And both against the peace of heaven and him   Have here  up-swarmed them.
translation: Under this fake pretense of religion, you have encouraged the subjects of God's deputy—my father the King—to rise up against the peace of heaven and the King himself.

original: Good my Lord of Lancaster,   I am not here against your  father’s peace,
translation: My good Lord of Lancaster, I am not here as an enemy to your father or to his peace.

original: But, as I told my Lord of Westmoreland,    The time misordered doth, in common sense,   Crowd us and  crush us to this monstrous form   To hold our safety up.
translation: Just as I told my Lord of Westmoreland, and as everyone can see, these disturbed times have forced us and driven us to do these monstrous deeds to keep ourselves safe.

original: I sent your Grace   The parcels and particulars of our  grief,   The which hath been with scorn shoved from the  court,
translation: I sent your Grace the specific details of our complaints, a document which has already been ignored at court.

original: Whereon this Hydra son of war is born,   Whose  dangerous eyes may well be charmed asleep   With grant of  our most just and right desires,
translation: That's why this  Hydra-like  war has started. You can calm this beast by agreeing to the justified and right things that we have demanded.

original: And true obedience, of  this madness cured,   Stoop tamely to the foot of majesty.
translation: If that is done, then this mad disease—this war—will be cured. And then the monster will curl up at your feet, tame and contented.

original: If not, we ready are to try our fortunes To the last  man.
translation: If you don't agree to our demands, then we're ready to fight until the last man is standing.

original: And though we here fall down,   We have supplies to  second our attempt;   If they miscarry, theirs shall  second them,
translation: And even if those of us who are here are defeated, we have reinforcements who can take over for us. If they fail, they have their own reinforcements as well.

original: And so success of mischief shall be born,    And heir from heir shall hold this quarrel up   Whiles  England shall have generation.
translation: The war will go on like this, passed down from father to son, until England has a new beginning.

original: You are too shallow, Hastings, much too shallow To  sound the bottom of the after-times.
translation: You are not clever enough, Hastings, not clever enough to see that far into the future.

original: Pleaseth your Grace to answer them directly How far  forth you do like their articles.
translation: Your Grace, why don't you tell them what you thought about their list of complaints?

original: I like them all, and do allow them well,
translation: I am happy with all of them. And I agree that they are all suitable complaints.

original: And swear here by the honor of my blood,   My father’s purposes have  been mistook,   And some about him have too lavishly    Wrested his meaning and authority.
translation: I swear on my family's honor that my father's intentions have been misunderstood—and some of his men have acted too boldly and done things that he would never have agreed to do.

original: [to ARCHBISHOP]   My  lord, these griefs shall be with speed redressed;   Upon  my soul, they shall.
translation: [To the ARCHBISHOP]  My lord, we will put right these wrongs as quickly as we can; I promise you that.

original: If this may please you,   Discharge  your powers unto their several counties,
translation: If you are happy with this, then break up your armies, and send them back to where they came from.

original: As we will  ours, and here, between the armies,   Let’s drink together friendly and embrace,   That all their eyes may bear  those tokens home   Of our restorèd love and amity.
translation: We will do the same with ours. And here, in the spot between the two armies, let's have a drink together and embrace, knowing that these men will go home and tell others that we are friends again.

original: I take your princely word for these redresses.
translation: I will take your word, as a prince, that you will do these things.

original: I give it you, and will maintain my word, And thereupon I drink unto your Grace.
translation: I give you my word and I will stick to it. And with that, I toast to your Grace.

original: Go, captain, and deliver to the army This news of  peace. Let them have pay, and part. I know it will well  please them. Hie thee, captain.
translation: Go, captain, and tell the army the news of peace. Pay them what we owe them, and then let them go. I know they will be pleased with this. Off you go, captain.

original: To you, my noble Lord of Westmoreland.
translation: Here's to you, my noble Lord of Westmoreland.

original: I pledge your Grace, and if you knew what pains I have  bestowed to breed this present peace, You would drink  freely. But my love to you Shall show itself more openly hereafter.
translation: The same to your Grace. If you knew how much I have done to try to bring about this peaceful agreement, you'd just keep drinking. But my love for you will be more obvious from now on.

original: I do not doubt you.
translation: I don't doubt it.

original: I am glad of it.— Health to my lord and gentle  cousin, Mowbray.
translation: I'm glad.  And here's to your good health, my gentle Mowbray.

original: You wish me health in very happy season, For I am on  the sudden something ill.
translation: Your wish of good health comes at a very good moment, for I suddenly feel quite ill.

original: Against ill chances men are ever merry, But heaviness  foreruns the good event.
translation: Men are always cheerful when bad situations await them, but a heavy heart is a sign that something good will happen.

original: Therefore be merry, coz; since sudden sorrow Serves to  say thus: “Some good thing comes tomorrow.”
translation: So be happy, friend. For your sudden feeling of sadness is just a sign to tell you that something good will happen tomorrow.

original: Believe me, I am passing light in spirit.
translation: Believe me, I am feeling very light-hearted right now.

original: So much the worse if your own rule be true.
translation: Well if the rule you just said is true, then that's not a good thing.

original: The word of peace is rendered. Hark how they shout.
translation: The news of peace has been delivered. Listen to how they shout.

original: This had been cheerful after victory.
translation: They sound like they're cheering a victory.

original: A peace is of the nature of a conquest, For then both  parties nobly are subdued, And neither party loser.
translation: A peaceful agreement is a kind of victory, because both sides may nobly stop fighting, but neither of them loses.

original: Go, my lord, And let our army be dischargèd too.
translation: Go, my lord, and let our army go as well.

original: And, good my lord, so please you, let our trains March  by us, that we may peruse the men We should have coped  withal.
translation: Good Archbishop, let's tell both of our armies to march past us here, so that we can see the men that we would have been fighting against.

original: Go, good Lord Hastings, And ere they be dismissed,  let them march by.
translation: Go, good Lord Hastings. Tell them to march past us before they leave.

original: I trust, lords, we shall lie tonight together.
translation: I hope, lords, that we will spend the night here together.

original: Now, cousin, wherefore stands our army still?
translation: Now, why is our army still standing ready?

original: The leaders, having charge from you to stand, Will not  go off until they hear you speak.
translation: The leaders were ordered by you to stay exactly where they are, and they refuse to move until you give them another order.

original: They know their duties.
translation: They know their duties, that's for sure.

original: My lord, our army is dispersed already. Like youthful  steers unyoked, they take their courses East, west,  north, south, or, like a school broke up, Each hurries  toward his home and sporting-place.
translation: My lord, our army has already dispersed. They've set off east, west, north and south—just like young bulls who have been untied, or like children after school, hurrying home or to play somewhere.

original: Good tidings, my Lord Hastings, for the which   I do  arrest thee, traitor, of high treason.
translation: What good news, Lord Hastings. Now I have heard it, I arrest you, traitor, for high treason.

original: —   And you, Lord  Archbishop, and you, Lord Mowbray,   Of capital treason I  attach you both.
translation: As for you, Lord Archbishop, and you, Lord Mowbray, I arrest you both of capital treason.

original: Is this proceeding just and honorable?
translation: Is this action just and honorable?

original: Is your assembly so?
translation: Was your rebellion just and honorable?

original: Will you thus break your faith?
translation: Are you going to break the faithful promise you made us?

original: I pawned thee none.   I promised you redress of these  same grievances   Whereof you did complain,
translation: I never promised you this. I promised you that I would make up for the complaints you had made, and satisfy your demands.

original: which, by mine honor,   I will perform with a most Christian care.   But  for you rebels, look to taste the due   Meet for rebellion and such acts as yours.
translation: And, I swear on my honor, I will do that as carefully as I can. As for you, rebels: you will have to pay the price for this rebellion, and will get what you deserve for the awful things you have done.

original: Most shallowly did you these  arms commence,   Fondly brought here, and foolishly sent  hence.
translation: You started these wars about trivial things; brought your army here without thinking; and foolishly dismissed them too early.

original: —   Strike up our drums; pursue the scattered stray.   God, and not we, hath safely fought today.
translation: Strike up the drums! Capture the soldiers who are still running away. It is God who has fought today and God who has won.

original: Some guard  these traitors to the block of death,   Treason’s true bed and yielder-up of breath.
translation: Guards, take these traitors to where they will be executed. That is where treason is meant to be, and that is where this rebellion will take its last breath.

original: What’s your name, sir? Of what condition are you, and  of what place, I pray?
translation: What's your name, sir? What rank are you, and where are you from?

original: I am a knight, sir, and my name is Colevile of the  Dale.
translation: I'm a knight, sir, and my name is Coleville of the Valley.

original: Well, then, Colevile is your name, a knight is your  degree, and your place the Dale.
translation: Well then, Coleville is your name, you have the rank of knight, and you are from the Valley.

original: Colevile shall be still your name, a traitor your degree, and the dungeon your  place, a place deep enough so shall you be still  Colevile of the Dale.
translation: Coleville will still be your name even when you are known as a traitor, and your place is in a dungeon so deep that they can still call you Coleville of the Valley.

original: Are not you Sir John Falstaff?
translation: Aren't you Sir John Falstaff?

original: As good a man as he, sir, whoe'er I am. Do ye yield,  sir, or shall I sweat for you?
translation: I'm as good a man as he is, whoever I am. Are you going to surrender, sir, or am I going to have to break a sweat apprehending you?

original: If I do sweat, they are  the drops of thy lovers and they weep for thy death.  Therefore rouse up fear and trembling, and do observance to my mercy.
translation: Every time I sweat, the drops of sweat will be like the tears of your loved ones, weeping over your death. So it would be good if you could be scared of me, start shaking in your boots, and beg me for my mercy.

original: I think you are Sir John Falstaff, and in that thought  yield me.
translation: I think you are Sir John Falstaff, and knowing that, I surrender.

original: I have a whole school of tongues in this belly of mine, and not a tongue of them all speaks any other word but  my name.
translation: My stomach is so big that it can speak many languages, but it only ever says my name.

original: An I had but a belly of any indifferency, I  were simply the most active fellow in Europe. My womb,  my womb, my womb undoes me. Here comes our general.
translation: If I had a more ordinary belly, I would just be another healthy soldier in Europe. But it is my stomach, my stomach, my stomach which gives me away. Look, here comes the general.

original: The heat is past. Follow no further now.
translation: The danger is over. Let's rest here for a while.

original: Call in the powers, good cousin Westmoreland.
translation: Tell our armies to withdraw, my good Westmoreland.

original: Now, Falstaff, where have you been all this while? When everything is ended, then you come. These tardy tricks  of yours will, on my life, One time or other break some  gallows' back.
I would be sorry, my lord, but it should be thus. I  never knew   yet but rebuke and check was the reward of  valor.
translation: My lord, if things could have been different, then I would be sorry. I didn't know that the way we rewarded bravery was with punishment and scrutiny.

original: Do you   think me a swallow, an arrow, or a bullet? Have I in my poor   and old motion the expedition of  thought?
translation: Do you think that I'm as quick as a swallow, an arrow, or a bullet? Now that I am old and weak, do you think that I can move with the same speed that thoughts can?

original: I have speeded   hither with the very extremest  inch of possibility.
translation: I have traveled here as quickly as I possibly could.

original: I have   foundered ninescore and odd  posts, and here, travel-tainted   as I am, have in my pure and immaculate valor taken Sir   John Colevile of the  Dale,
translation: I have worn out about one hundred eighty horses, made it here—and even though I'm exhausted—I still managed to capture Sir John Coleville of the Valley.

original: a most furious knight and   valorous enemy. But what of that? He saw me and yielded,   that I may justly say,  with the hook-nosed fellow of Rome,   “There, cousin, I  came, saw, and overcame.”
translation: That's how honorable and brave I am. He's a dangerous knight and a powerful enemy of ours. But what does that matter? He simply saw me and surrendered, so I feel that just like  Julius Caesar  I can say that "I came, I saw, and I conquered."

original: It was more of his courtesy than your deserving.
translation: That says more about his good manners than it does about your bravery.

original: I know not. Here he is, and here I yield him.
translation: I don't know what you mean. Look, here he is, and now I give him over to you.

original: And I  beseech   your Grace let it be booked with the rest of  this day’s deeds,   or, by the Lord, I will have it in a  particular ballad else, with   mine own picture on the top on ’t, Colevile kissing my foot;
translation: I just ask your Grace to make sure that this is added to the list of successes from today. If you don't, I swear to God I will have a ballad printed about it—and it will have a picture of me right at the top, with Coleville kissing my foot.

original: to the which course if I be enforced, if you do not all show like gilt  twopences to me, and I in the clear sky of fame  o'ershine you as much as the full moon doth the cinders  of the element   (which show like pins' heads to her),
translation: If I'm forced to do that, it will make you all look like  fakes  next to me, And my fame will shine brighter than yours, just like a full moon shines brighter than the stars, which end up looking like tiny dots in comparison.

original: believe not the word of the noble. Therefore let me have right, and let desert mount.
translation: If it doesn't, then I must be lying. So give me what I deserve, and let my achievements build up on top of each other in a pile.

original: Thine’s too heavy to mount.
translation: That pile would be far too heavy for me to pick up.

original: Let it shine, then.
translation: Well, let my achievements shine then.

original: Thine’s too thick to shine.
translation: You're too fat to shine.

original: Let it do something, my good lord, that may do me good, and call it what you will.
translation: Well let it do something, my good lord—anything that will make me look good. And call it whatever you want.

original: Is thy name Colevile?
translation: Is your name Coleville?

original: It is, my lord.
translation: It is, my lord.

original: A famous rebel art thou, Colevile.
translation: You are a famous rebel, Coleville.

original: And a famous true subject took him.
translation: And it was a famous, loyal subject who captured him.

original: I am, my lord, but as my betters are That led me  hither. Had they been ruled by me, You should have won  them dearer than you have.
translation: I am, my lord. But my superior officers led me here. If I had been the leader, you would have lost a lot more than you have.

original: I know not how they sold themselves, but thou, like a  kind fellow, gavest thyself away gratis, and I thank  thee for thee.
translation: I don't know how much these men made us pay. But, Coleville, you gave yourself away for free like a kind man. And I thank you for that.

original: Now, have you left pursuit?
translation: Have you told the troops to retreat?

original: Retreat is made and execution stayed.
translation: The troops have retreated and the fighting has stopped.

original: Send Colevile with his confederates To York, to present execution.— Blunt, lead him hence, and see you guard  him sure.
translation: Send Coleville with his fellow prisoners to York, where they will be executed right away. Blunt, lead him there, and make sure you guard him carefully.

original: And now dispatch we toward the court, my lords.   I hear  the King my father is sore sick.   Our news shall go  before us to his Majesty,
translation: And now, my lords, we must set off quickly for the royal court, as I have heard that my father is very sick. We will send the news ahead of us to the King so that he knows we have won.

original: [to WESTMORELAND   ]   Which,  cousin, you shall bear to comfort   him,   And we with  sober speed will follow you.
translation: [To WESTMORELAND]   Will you please take this news to my father and comfort him? We will be with you as quickly as we can.

original: My lord, I beseech you give me leave to go through  Gloucestershire, and, when you come to court, stand my  good lord, pray, in your good report.
translation: My lord, may I have your permission to travel back through Gloucestershire? Also, when you get back to the court, please stand up for me and say that I did some good work here.

original: Fare you well, Falstaff. I, in my condition, Shall  better speak of you than you deserve.
translation: Goodbye to you, Falstaff. As a Prince, if I say good things about you, it is defintely more than you deserve.

original: I would you had but the wit; ’twere better than your    dukedom. Good faith, this same young sober-blooded boy    doth not love me, nor a man cannot make him laugh.
translation: I wish you had the wit to do that—it would be better than everything you have already done. By Good, this young, sensible boy doesn't like me at all.

original: But    that’s no marvel; he drinks no wine. There’s never none  of   these demure boys come to any proof, for thin drink  doth so   overcool their blood, and making many fish  meals,
translation: And no one seems to be able to make him laugh. But is that any wonder, when he doesn't drink any wine? None of those reserved boys ever turn out well, because weak drinks and a diet of fish makes their blood cool.

original: that they   fall into a kind of male  green-sickness, and then, when they   marry, they get  wenches.
translation: They all become  green-sick , like unmarried girls. Then, even when they eventually do get married, all of their children are girls, because they're too weak to have boys.

original: They are generally fools and   cowards, which  some of us should be too, but for   inflammation.
translation: On the whole, they are fools and cowards. And we would be the same, if it weren't for the excitement of alcohol.

original: A good  sherris sack hath a two-fold operation in it.   It ascends me into the brain, dries me there all the foolish and    dull and crudy vapors which environ it, makes it    apprehensive, quick, forgetive, full of nimble, fiery,  and   delectable shapes,
translation: A good  sherry  has two main benefits to it. First, it goes up into the brain and it gets rid of all the stupid, boring, and thick thoughts which have been left there. It makes the brain quick, responsive, and creative—full of nimble, fiery, and captivating ideas.

original: which, delivered o'er to the  voice, the   tongue, which is the birth, becomes excellent wit. The   second property of your excellent sherris is  the warming of   the blood,
translation: When these are picked up by the voice and the tongue, they grow up and become the things of excellent wit. Second, good sherry warms your blood.

original: which, before cold and  settled, left the liver white   and pale, which is the  badge of pusillanimity and cowardice.
translation: Before the sherry, your blood is cold and slow. And this makes the liver—the source of our passions—pale and cold as well, which is the symbol of weakness and cowardice.

original: But the sherris  warms it and makes it course from the   inwards to the  parts' extremes.
translation: But the sherry warms the blood, and makes it flow all around the body, from the inner organs to the far extremities of a person.

original: It illumineth the face, which   as a  beacon gives warning to all the rest of this little    kingdom, man, to arm;
translation: It brightens up the face, which is a signal for the rest of a man's kingdom—that is, the rest of the body—to do the same as well.

original: and then the vital commoners and    inland petty spirits muster me all to their captain, the  heart,   who, great and puffed up with this retinue, doth  any deed of   courage, and this valor comes of sherris.
translation: Then the substances of the body and the other vital organs stand behind their captain, the heart. The heart is so inspired by this support that it can carry out any brave action it needs to.  This is the courage that comes with sherry.

original: So that skill in the   weapon is nothing without sack, for  that sets it a-work; and   learning a mere hoard of gold  kept by a devil till sack   commences it and sets it in  act and use.
translation: Without any wine, no one is a skilled fighter, for wine gives them that skill. Even education is just  worthless gold looked after by the devil , until it finds some wine and then is ready to be of use.

original: Hereof comes it that   Prince Harry is  valiant, for the cold blood he did naturally   inherit of  his father he hath, like lean, sterile, and bare land,    manured, husbanded, and tilled with excellent endeavor of   drinking good and good store of fertile sherris,
translation: This is how Prince Harry became so brave! He took the cold blood that he inherited from his father, and, just like sterile and bare land, he worked on it, cultivated it, and took care of it by making sure he drank as much good wine as he could

original: that  he is   become very hot and valiant. If I had a thousand  sons, the   first human principle I would teach them  should be to   forswear thin potations and to addict  themselves to sack.
translation: —until it became passionate and courageous. If I had a thousand sons, the very first thing I would teach them would be to avoid weak drinks and get themselves addicted to strong wine.

original: How now, Bardolph?
translation: What's going on, Bardolph?

original: The army is discharged all and gone.
translation: The army has all been discharged and they are leaving.

original: Let them go. I’ll through Gloucestershire, and there  will I visit Master Robert Shallow, Esquire. I have him  already temp'ring between my finger and my thumb, and  shortly will I seal with him. Come away.
translation: Let them go. I'll go back through Gloucestershine, so that I can visit Master Robert Shallow, Esquire, on the way. I already have him basically under my thumb, like soft wax. And soon I will seal the deal with him. Come on, let's go.

original: Now, lords, if God doth give successful end   To this  debate that bleedeth at our doors,   We will our youth  lead on to higher fields   And draw no swords but what are sanctified.
translation: Now, my lords, if God gives us victory in the violent struggle that bleeds at our very doorstep, we will lead our young men on to better fields, and only fight in holy wars.

original: Our navy is addressed, our power collected,   Our substitutes in absence well invested,   And  everything lies level to our wish.
translation: Our navy is ready; our army is assembled; the men who lead in my absence have their power; and everything is prepared just how we like it.

original: Only we want a little personal strength;   And pause us till these rebels now  afoot   Come underneath the yoke of government.
translation: The only thing that's wrong is that I'm feeling a bit weak. And so we will have to rest here for a while, until the rebels are under our control.

original: Both which we doubt not but your Majesty Shall soon  enjoy.
translation: We are sure that you will feel better soon, and also that rebels will soon be defeated.

original: Humphrey, my son of Gloucester, Where is the Prince  your brother?
translation: Humphrey, my son of Gloucester, where is the Prince, your brother Hal?

original: I think he’s gone to hunt, my lord, at Windsor.
translation: I think he's gone hunting at Windsor, my lord.

original: And how accompanied?
translation: Who's with him?

original: I do not know, my lord.
translation: I don't know, my lord.

original: Is not his brother Thomas of Clarence with him?
translation: Isn't his brother Thomas of Clarence with him?

original: No, my good lord, he is in presence here.
translation: No, my good lord, he's here.

original: What would my lord and father?
translation: What would you like, my lord and father?

original: Nothing but well to thee, Thomas of Clarence.   How  chance thou art not with the Prince thy brother?   He  loves thee, and thou dost neglect him, Thomas.
translation: Nothing but good things for you, Thomas of Clarence. How come you are not with your brother, the Prince? He loves you, and you are neglecting him, Thomas.

original: Thou hast a better place in his affection   Than all thy brothers.  Cherish it, my boy,
translation: He loves you more than he loves all your other brothers. Cherish that, my boy.

original: And noble offices thou mayst effect    Of mediation, after I am dead,   Between his greatness and  thy other brethren.   Therefore omit him not;
translation: After I'm dead, you will be in the best position to help strengthen the relationship between Hal and your other brothers. Therefore, don't neglect him.

original: blunt not  his love,   Nor lose the good advantage of his grace   By  seeming cold or careless of his will.   For he is gracious if he be observed;
translation: Don't ignore his love, and don't damage your relationship with him by seeming cold or uncaring. For he is very caring if he is paid due respect;

original: He hath a tear for pity and a hand    Open as day for melting charity;
translation: he can feel pity for others, and he can be generous with charity.

original: Yet notwithstanding,  being incensed he is flint,   As humorous as winter, and  as sudden   As flaws congealed in the spring of day.
translation: Yet, at the same time, when he gets angry, he is as hard as a stone, he is as volatile as winter, and can change as quickly as snowflakes at daybreak.

original: His  temper therefore must be well observed.   Chide him for  faults, and do it reverently,   When thou perceive his  blood inclined to mirth;
translation: Therefore, watch out for his temper. Tell him off when he does things wrong, but do it gently, when he seems like he's in a happy mood.

original: But, being moody, give him time and scope   Till that his passions, like a whale on  ground,   Confound themselves with working.
translation: When he is moody, give him time to work things out himself, so that his moods become like a beached whale, which kills itself trying to get back to the sea.

original: Learn this,  Thomas,   And thou shalt prove a shelter to thy friends,   A hoop of gold to bind thy brothers in,
translation: Remember this, Thomas, and you will be able to protect your friends, and be a golden chain that joins all of your brothers together.

original: That the united  vessel of their blood,   Mingled with venom of suggestion    (As, force perforce, the age will pour it in),
translation: Once you are all united, the poison and instigation to evil—which in this day and age is almost certain

original: Shall  never leak, though it do work as strong   As aconitum or  rash gunpowder.
translation: —will never get in, even though it's as strong as  aconite  or gunpowder.

original: I shall observe him with all care and love.
translation: I'll watch over him with all my care and love.

original: Why art thou not at Windsor with him, Thomas?
translation: So why aren't you at Windsor with him, Thomas?

original: He is not there today; he dines in London.
translation: He's not there today. He's having lunch in London.

original: And how accompanied? Canst thou tell that?
translation: Who's he with? Do you know that?

original: With Poins and other his continual followers.
translation: He's with Poins and all his other normal followers.

original: Most subject is the fattest soil to weeds,   And he, the  noble image of my youth,   Is overspread with them;
translation: Weeds always try to grow in the best soil. And he is overrun with them, just like I was in my youth.

original: therefore my grief   Stretches itself beyond the hour of  death.
translation: So I guess my sadness will have to carry on, even after my death.

original: The blood weeps from my heart when I do shape,   In forms imaginary, th' unguided days   And rotten times  that you shall look upon   When I am sleeping with my  ancestors.
translation: When I think about the days of disorder and the rotten times which are to come—when I will lie sleeping with my ancestors—it makes the blood weep from my heart.

original: For when his headstrong riot hath no curb,    When rage and hot blood are his counsellors,   When means  and lavish manners meet together,
translation: For when Hal's headstrong, wild behavior has no limits; when anger and passion are his advisors; when he has the opportunity to do what he wants,

original: O, with what wings  shall his affections fly   Towards fronting peril and  opposed decay!
translation: oh, his desires will be like a bird, flying headfirst into danger and ruin.

original: My gracious lord, you look beyond him quite.   The Prince but studies his companions   Like a strange tongue,  wherein, to gain the language,
translation: My gracious lord, you've shouldn't judge him so harshly. The Prince is only there to observe his companions, in the same way as a person learns another language.

original: 'Tis needful that the  most immodest word   Be looked upon and learned; which,  once attained,   Your Highness knows, comes to no further  use   But to be known and hated.
translation: For in order to truly understand a language, you need to know even the worst and most immodest word. You need to hear it, learn it, so that once you know it—as your Highness is aware—you can then make sure to avoid using it.

original: So, like gross terms,   The Prince will, in the perfectness of time,   Cast off his  followers, and their memory   Shall as a pattern or a  measure live,
translation: So, when the time is right, the Prince will get rid of his followers, just like vile language. When he does that, they will only survive in his memory,

original: By which his Grace must mete the lives of  others,   Turning past evils to advantages.
translation: as a set of guidelines to judge the actions of others, and thus turn his past bad behavior to his own advantage.

original: 'Tis seldom when the bee doth leave her comb In the  dead carrion.
translation: It's very rare that a bee will make a new nest in a dead animal's carcass. Likewise, I will be very surprised if Hal ever leaves behind his companions.

original: Who’s here? Westmoreland?
translation: Who's there? Is that you, Westmoreland?

original: Health to my sovereign, and new happiness   Added to that that I am to deliver.   Prince John your son doth kiss  your Grace’s hand.
translation: I wish your Majesty good health, and even more happiness than my happy news will bring you. Prince John, your son, sends his love.

original: Mowbray, the Bishop Scroop, Hastings, and all   Are brought to the correction of your law.    There is not now a rebel’s sword unsheathed   But peace  puts forth her olive everywhere.
translation: Mowbray, the Archbishop of York, and Hastings have all been arrested. There are no rebels left anywhere. Peace now holds out her olive branch everywhere.

original: The manner how this  action hath been borne   Here at more leisure may your  Highness read   With every course in his particular.
translation: If your Highness wants to know more about how all of this happened, you can read about it in this letter.

original: O Westmoreland, thou art a summer bird, Which ever in  the haunch of winter sings The lifting up of day.
translation: Oh, Westmoreland, you come here like a summer bird, ready to announce the end of winter and the start of a new day.

original: Here comes more news.
translation: Look, here comes more news.

original: From enemies heaven keep your Majesty,   And when they  stand against you, may they fall   As those that I am come to tell you of.
translation: May heaven protect your Majesty from any enemies. And if enemies do rise up against you, I hope that they die, just like the men I come to tell you about.

original: The Earl Northumberland and the Lord  Bardolph,   With a great power of English and of Scots,    Are by the shrieve of Yorkshire overthrown.
translation: The Earl of Northumberland and the Lord Bardolph—even with their huge armies of Englishmen and Scotsmen—were defeated by the sheriff of Yorkshire.

original: The manner  and true order of the fight   This packet, please it you,  contains at large.
translation: This letter will tell you more about the battle that took place.

original: And wherefore should these good news make me sick?   Will fortune never come with both hands full,   But write her  fair words still in foulest letters?
translation: Why am I sick when I hear such happy news? Can't Fortune let us enjoy the things we are supposed to enjoy? Why is good news so often told with ugly words?

original: She either gives a  stomach and no food—   Such are the poor, in health—or  else a feast   And takes away the stomach—such are the  rich,   That have abundance and enjoy it not.
translation: Fortune either gives you a hungry stomach and no food, which is the case of the poor, healthy people. Or it gives you a feast and takes away your appetite, which is the case of rich people who have plenty, but can't enjoy it.

original: I should  rejoice now at this happy news,   And now my sight fails,  and my brain is giddy.   O, me! Come near me, now I am  much ill.
translation: I should be rejoicing at this happy news. But instead, I am struggling to see, and everything is all dizzy. Oh! Come and help me please, I'm very sick.

original: Comfort, your Majesty.
translation: Take care, your Majesty.

original: O, my royal father!
translation: Oh, my royal father!

original: My sovereign lord, cheer up yourself, look up.
translation: My lord, I hope that you feel better. Be brave.

original: Be patient, princes. You do know these fits Are with  his Highness very ordinary. Stand from him, give him  air. He’ll straight be well.
translation: Give him a minute, princes. You know that his Highness has fits like this all the time. Stand further away, give him some room to breathe. He'll be all right in a minute.

original: No, no, he cannot long hold out these pangs. Th'  incessant care and labor of his mind Hath wrought the  mure that should confine it in So thin that life looks  through and will break out.
translation: No, no, he can't deal with these fits for much longer. The never-ending worries and cares he's been dealing with have disturbed his body so much that he's barely holding it together anymore.

original: The people fear me, for they do observe   Unfathered  heirs and loathly births of nature.
translation: The people of this country are scaring me, because they say that they have seen children with no fathers, and horribly deformed babies.

original: The seasons change  their manners, as the year   Had found some months asleep  and leapt them over.
translation: The weather and the seasons are completely out of sorts. It's almost as if the year has discovered that some months were asleep and decided to skip them completely.

original: The river hath thrice flowed, no ebb between,   And the  old folk, time’s doting chronicles,
translation: The river has flooded three times, with no breaks in between the floods. The older generations—who are like our very own living history books

original: Say it did so a  little time before   That our great-grandsire, Edward,  sicked and died.
translation: —say that the last time that this happened was when our great-grandfather, King Edward III, became ill and then died.

original: Speak lower, princes, for the King recovers.
translation: Speak quieter, princes, for the King is waking up.

original: This apoplexy will certain be his end.
translation: These seizures are going to kill him.

original: I pray you, take me up and bear me hence Into some  other chamber. Softly, pray.
translation: Please, pick me up and take me to a bed. Quietly, please.

original: Let there be no noise made, my gentle friends, Unless  some dull and favorable hand Will whisper music to my  weary spirit.
translation: Don't make any noise, my dear friends, unless anyone can play some calm, whispering music for my tired spirit to hear.

original: Call for the music in the other room.
translation: Tell the musicians to come in from the other room.

original: Set me the crown upon my pillow here.
translation: Put my crown on the pillow next to me.

original: His eye is hollow, and he changes much.
translation: His eyes are lifeless, and he's not himself.

original: Less noise, less noise.
translation: Quiet, quiet.

original: Who saw the Duke of Clarence?
translation: Where's the Duke of Clarence?

original: I am here, brother, full of heaviness.
translation: I am here and full of sadness, brother.

original: How now! Rain within doors, and none abroad? How doth  the King?
Exceeding ill.
translation: Extremely sick.

original: Heard he the good news yet? Tell it him.
translation: Has he heard the good news yet? Someone should tell him.

original: He altered much upon the hearing it.
translation: When he heard it, he was deeply moved.

original: If he be sick with joy, he’ll recover without physic.
translation: If he's just sick with happiness, he should get better without needing a doctor.

original: Not so much noise, my lords.—Sweet Prince, speak low.  The King your father is disposed to sleep.
translation: Less noise, my lords.  Sweet Prince, speak a bit quieter. The King, your father, wants to sleep.

original: Let us withdraw into the other room.
translation: Let's go and talk in another room.

original: Will ’t please your Grace to go along with us?
translation: Would you like to come with us?

original: No, I will sit and watch here by the King.
translation: No, I think I will sit here with the King.

original: Why doth the crown lie there upon his pillow,   Being so  troublesome a bedfellow?   O polished perturbation, golden care,   That keep’st the ports of slumber open wide   To  many a watchful night!
translation: Why is the crown lying there on his pillow, when it is such a difficult bedfellow? Oh, this polished symbol of distress; a golden object of worries, that keeps the eyelids open wide, forced to face night after night without sleep!

original: sleep with it now;   Yet not so  sound and half so deeply sweet   As he whose brow with  homely biggen bound   Snores out the watch of night. O  majesty,
translation: Sleep with the crown now, but you still don't sleep as soundly or as deeply as the man whose head is only covered by a coarse night-cap, as he snores the night away. Oh, you crown!

original: When thou dost pinch thy bearer, thou dost sit    Like a rich armor worn in heat of day,   That scald’st with safety.
translation: When you sit on someone's head you pinch at it—you're as irritating as a grand suit or armor worn on a very hot day; you burn the person you're supposed to protect.

original: By his gates of breath   There lies a downy  feather which stirs not;   Did he suspire, that light and  weightless down   Perforce must move.
translation: Look, there's a feather right near my father's lips and it's not moving. If he were breathing, that feather would have to be moving.

original: My gracious lord, my father,   This sleep is sound indeed. This is a sleep    That from this golden rigol hath divorced   So many English kings.
translation: Oh my gracious lord, my father, this is definitely a deep sleep. This is the type of sleep which has taken the crown off the heads of so many English kings.

original: Thy due from me   Is tears and heavy sorrows of  the blood,   Which nature, love, and filial tenderness    Shall, O dear father, pay thee plenteously.
translation: Now I owe you tears, and a heavy grief. Nature, my love, and my care for you as your son will make sure that I give you plenty of tears.

original: My due from  thee is this imperial crown,   Which, as immediate as thy  place and blood,   Derives itself to me.   [he puts the  crown on his head]
translation: You have left me this crown, which I must claim, as your true heir.   [He puts the crown on his head.]

original: Lo,   where it sits,   Which God shall guard. And put the world’s whole strength   Into one  giant arm, it shall not force   This lineal honor from me.
translation: Look, here it sits on my head, and now God will protect it. Even if all the strength in the world was put into one giant arm, it would not be able to take this honor from me.

original: This from thee   Will I to mine leave, as ’tis left to  me.
translation: I will eventually leave this to my son, as you have left it to me.

original: Warwick! Gloucester! Clarence!
translation: Warwick! Gloucester! Clarence!

original: Doth the King call?
translation: Did you call for us?

original: What would your Majesty? How fares your Grace?
translation: What can we do for you, your Majesty? How are you feeling?

original: Why did you leave me here alone, my lords?
translation: Why did you leave me here alone, my lords?

original: We left the Prince my brother here, my liege, Who  undertook to sit and watch by you.
translation: We left you here with the Prince, my brother, who said that he wanted to sit with you.

original: The Prince of Wales? Where is he? Let me see him. He is not here.
translation: The Prince of Wales? Hal? Where is he? Let me see him. He's not here.

original: This door is open. He is gone this way.
translation: This door is open. He must have gone this way.

original: He came not through the chamber where we stayed.
translation: He didn't come through the room that we were in.

original: Where is the crown? Who took it from my pillow?
translation: Where is my crown? Who has moved it from my pillow?

original: When we withdrew, my liege, we left it here.
translation: When we left the room it was still there, my lord.

original: The Prince hath ta'en it hence. Go seek him out. Is he  so hasty that he doth suppose my sleep my death? Find  him, my Lord of Warwick. Chide him hither.
translation: Then the Prince must have taken it. Go and find him. Is he so quick to presume that my sleep is actually my death? Find him, my Lord of Warwick. Scold him, and bring him back here.

original: This part of his conjoins with my disease   And helps to  end me. See, sons, what things you are,   How quickly  nature falls into revolt   When gold becomes her object!
translation: Hal's actions here join up with my illness and will help to kill me. See, sons, look at what kind of people we are. Look at how quickly even family loyalty can be forgotten, when money is involved.

original: For this the foolish overcareful fathers   Have broke their sleep with thoughts,   Their brains with care, their  bones with industry.
translation: This is what has made foolish, overly caring fathers ruin their sleep, by thinking about it. They have ruined their brains by caring and their bodies by working too hard.

original: For this they have engrossèd and  piled up   The canker’d heaps of strange-achievèd gold.    For this they have been thoughtful to invest   Their sons  with arts and martial exercise
translation: This is what happens to men who have built up large sums of money from strange sources. They have used their money to give their sons good educations and to train them in military matters.

original: When, like the bee,  tolling from every flower   The virtuous sweets,   Our  thighs packed with wax, our mouths with honey,
translation: We fathers are like bees, going to every flower to get the best honey. We only bring it back to the hive when our thighs are full of wax and our mouths full of honey.

original: We bring  it to the hive and, like the bees,   Are murdered for our  pains. This bitter taste   Yield his engrossments to the  ending father.
translation: And in the hive, we are killed by our offspring. This is the same for a dying father, no matter what good he has done in his life.

original: Now, where is he that will not stay so long Till his  friend sickness hath determined me?
translation: Now where is that hasty boy, who can't even wait around for sickness—his friend—to finish me off?

original: My lord, I found the Prince in the next room,   Washing  with kindly tears his gentle cheeks,   With such a deep  demeanor in great sorrow   That tyranny, which never  quaffed but blood,
translation: My lord, I found the Prince in the next room, with tears flowing down his sweet cheeks. He had such a sad look on his face that even cruelty—which has never feasted on anything but blood

original: Would, by beholding him, have washed  his knife   With gentle eyedrops. He is coming hither.
translation: —would see him and wash his own knife with gentle tears. The Prince is coming here right now.

original: But wherefore did he take away the crown?
translation: But why did he take away the crown?

original: Lo where he comes.—Come hither to me, Harry.— Depart  the chamber. Leave us here alone.
translation: Look, here he comes. Come here to me, Harry. [To the others] Everyone else can go. Leave us here alone.

original: I never thought to hear you speak again.
translation: I never thought that I'd hear your voice again.

original: Thy wish was father, Harry, to that thought.   I stay too long by thee; I weary thee.
translation: You thought that, Harry, because you hoped it was the case. I have stayed here too long and you're tired of me.

original: Dost thou so hunger for  mine empty chair   That thou wilt needs invest thee with  my honors   Before thy hour be ripe? O foolish youth,   Thou seek’st the greatness that will overwhelm thee.
translation: Are you so eager to be King that you're prepared to take the honors that come with it before it's the right time? Oh, you foolish young boy: you are eager for a power which will one day overwhelm you.

original: Stay  but a little, for my cloud of dignity   Is held from  falling with so weak a wind   That it will quickly drop.  My day is dim.
translation: Just wait a little while. The little amount of dignity and power that I do have left is so weak that the slightest breeze could make it fall apart. My life is almost over

original: Thou hast stol'n that which after some  few hours   Were thine without offense, and at my death    Thou hast sealed up my expectation.   Thy life did manifest thou loved’st me not,
translation: . You have stolen something which is going to be yours in a few hours anyway. And even on my deathbed, you have confirmed my fears about you. For your entire life, it seemed like you didn't love me.

original: And thou wilt have me die assured of it.   Thou hid’st a thousand daggers in thy thoughts,    Which thou hast whetted on thy stony heart   To stab at  half an hour of my life.
translation: And now I can die knowing that it's true. Your thoughts are full of a thousand daggers, which you have sharpened on your hard heart— ready to stab me, even though I don't have much time left.

original: What, canst thou not forbear me half an hour?   Then get thee gone and dig my grave  thyself,   And bid the merry bells ring to thine ear   That  thou art crownèd, not that I am dead.
translation: Can't you give me my last half hour? Then go and dig my grave yourself, and ring the bells to mark your own coronation, rather than my death.

original: Let all the tears  that should bedew my hearse   Be drops of balm to sanctify thy head;   Only compound me with forgotten dust.
translation: Let any tears which would have gone on my hearse, instead be used as holy water to bless your head—just cover me in dirt instead.

original: Give  that which gave thee life unto the worms.   Pluck down my  officers, break my decrees,   For now a time is come to  mock at form.
translation: Give the body that gave you life to the worms. Get rid of my officers; break my laws. For now is the time to mock law and order.

original: Harry the Fifth is crowned. Up, vanity,    Down, royal state, all you sage counsillors, hence,   And  to the English court assemble now,   From every region,  apes of idleness.
translation: Now  Henry the Fifth  will be crowned. Now let's all be foolish, and forget the rules of our state. All of the wise councilors might as well get going. Now the English court can be made up of stupid apes from all parts of the country.

original: Now, neighbor confines, purge you of  your scum.   Have you a ruffian that will swear, drink,  dance,   Revel the night, rob, murder, and commit   The  oldest sins the newest kind of ways?
translation: Now, neighboring countries, give us your scum. Do you have any scoundrels who swear, drink, dance, enjoy the night, rob, murder, and commit even the oldest sins in the newest ways?

original: Be happy, he will  trouble you no more.   England shall double gild his  treble guilt.   England shall give him office, honor,  might,   For the fifth Harry from curbed license plucks
translation: Be happy, you can get rid of him. English will paint over his guilt and sin with gold. England will give him a position, honor, power, because Henry the Fifth has taken off any limitations of bad behavior.

original: The muzzle of restraint,   and the wild dog   Shall flesh his tooth on every innocent.   O my poor kingdom, sick with  civil blows!
translation: He's taken the muzzle off the wild dog and now it is free to attack any innocent person. Oh, my poor kingdom, already damaged from these civil wars!

original: When that my care could not withhold thy  riots,   What wilt thou do when riot is thy care?
translation: When even my work and care couldn't stop these rebellions, what's going to happen when rebellions are your master?

original: O, thou  wilt be a wilderness again,   Peopled with wolves, thy old inhabitants.
translation: Oh, you will become a wilderness again, and all of the wolves you used to spend time with will live with you again.

original: O pardon me, my liege! But for my tears,   The moist  impediments unto my speech,   I had forestalled this dear  and deep rebuke   Ere you with grief had spoke and I had  heard   The course of it so far.
translation: I am sorry, my lord! If my tears hadn't stopped me from speaking earlier, I would have stopped this harsh criticism before you had said these things in your grief, and before I had to hear what you would say.

original: There is your crown,   And  He that wears the crown immortally   Long guard it yours.
translation: Here is your crown. And I wish that God—who looks after the crown forever—would let you keep it for as long as possible.

original: If I affect it more   Than as your honor and as your  renown,   Let me no more from this obedience rise,   Which  my most inward true and duteous spirit   Teacheth this  prostrate and exterior bending.
translation: If I care about that crown as anything more than a representation of your honor and your reputation, then let me never get up from kneeling at your feet. My truest and most dutiful feelings make me bow down and kneel before you.

original: God witness with me,  when I here came in   And found no course of breath within your Majesty,   How cold it struck my heart!
translation: With God as my witness, when I came in here before, and realized that you weren't breathing, it made my blood cold!

original: If I do  feign,   O, let me in my present wildness die   And never  live to show th' incredulous world   The noble change that I have purposèd.
translation: If that's a lie, then let me die like the wild youth I have been, and never live to show the unbelieving world how much I was going to change.

original: Coming to look on you, thinking you  dead,   And dead almost, my liege, to think you were,   I  spake unto this crown as having sense,   And thus  upbraided it:
translation: When I looked at you and thought you were dead—and indeed it made me almost feel dead to think that you were—I spoke to the crown as if it could talk back to me. I scolded it, saying

original: “The care on thee depending   Hath fed upon  the body of my father;   Therefore thou best of gold art  worst of gold.
translation: , "The worry and pain that you've caused has destroyed my father's body. So even though you may look like the best piece of gold, you are actually the worst.

original: Other, less fine in carat, is more  precious,   Preserving life in med'cine potable;   But thou, most fine, most honored, most renowned,   Hast eat thy  bearer up.”
translation: Other gold, even if its quality is worse, is worth more to us because it can bring us good health when we  drink  it. But you—the finest, most honored, most renowned piece of gold—have destroyed the person who has worn you.

original: Thus, my most royal liege,   Accusing it, I  put it on my head   To try with it,
translation: Therefore, my royal father, as I told this crown what I thought, I put it on my head, to fight against it

original: as with an enemy   That  had before my face murdered my father,   The quarrel of a  true inheritor.
translation: —like it was some enemy who had killed my father while I stood there and watched. That is the action of a loyal son.

original: But if it did infect my blood with joy    Or swell my thoughts to any strain of pride,
translation: If it made me happy in any way, or made me arrogant,

original: If any rebel or vain spirit of mine   Did with the least affection of  a welcome   Give entertainment to the might of it,
translation: or if even the slightest part of me wanted to welcome it and the power it holds,

original: Let God forever keep it from my head   And make me as the poorest vassal is   That doth with awe and terror kneel to it.
translation: let God keep it from me forever. I would rather be the poorest servant that bows before it in awe and fear.

original: O my son,   God put it in thy mind to take it hence   That  thou mightst win the more thy father’s love,   Pleading so wisely in excuse of it.
translation: Oh, my son. God encouraged you to take it from me so that you would have the chance to plead your case and make me love you even more.

original: Come hither, Harry, sit thou by my bed   And hear, I think, the very latest counsel   That  ever I shall breathe.
translation: Come here, Harry, and sit next to me on my bed, and listen to what I think will be the last advice that I will ever give anyone.

original: God knows, my son,   By what bypaths and indirect crook’d ways   I met this crown, and I  myself know well   How troublesome it sat upon my head.
translation: God knows, my son, the strange paths and indirect ways that got me this crown. And I know only too well how much trouble wearing it has caused for me.

original: To thee it shall descend with better quiet,   Better  opinion, better confirmation,   For all the soil of the  achievement goes   With me into the earth.
translation: It will come to you in a time of greater peace, where you will have better support and more approval. For all of the questions about how I got the crown end with me.

original: It seemed in me   But as an honor snatched with boist'rous hand,   And I  had many living to upbraid   My gain of it by their  assistances,
translation: On me, this crown seemed like an honor that had been snatched with a violent hand. Many people lived to tell me how they had helped me get it.

original: Which daily grew to quarrel and to  bloodshed,   Wounding supposèd peace. All these bold fears   Thou see’st with peril I have answerèd,   For all my  reign hath been but as a scene   Acting that argument.
translation: This grew every day until it turned into battles and bloodshed, destroying the supposed peace of the time. You can see the impact that fighting all of these battles has had on me, since my entire reign has been like a scene of a play —and we repeat the same plot again and again

original: And now my death   Changes the mood, for what in me was  purchased   Falls upon thee in a more fairer sort.
translation: . But now my death changes all of that, for you will not inherit what I bought.

original: So thou the garland wear’st successively.   Yet though thou  stand’st more sure than I could do,   Thou art not firm  enough,
translation: So you will wear the crown like you're meant to—because of the succession. But even though your claim to the throne is much stronger than mine was, it's still not strong enough.

original: since griefs are green,   And all my friends,  which thou must make thy friends,   Have but their stings  and teeth newly ta'en out,
translation: Anger and violence are still very recent, and all of my old friends—whom you now need to befriend—have only just been overpowered.

original: By whose fell working I was  first advanced   And by whose power I well might lodge a  fear   To be again displaced;
translation: These men originally got me the crown, and I was always afraid that the same people would overthrow me.

original: which to avoid,   I cut them  off and had a purpose now   To lead out many to the Holy  Land,   Lest rest and lying still might make them look   Too near unto my state.
translation: To avoid this, I defeated their rebellion and was going to lead an army to the Holy Land, in case doing nothing might make them consider my crown and the possibilities it could bring them.

original: Therefore, my Harry,   Be it thy  course to busy giddy minds   With foreign quarrels; that  action, hence borne out,   May waste the memory of the  former days.
translation: Therefore, my Harry, make sure that you force distracted minds to focus on  fighting foreign battles . Military success abroad will help people to forget about the memories of the past.

original: More would I, but my lungs are wasted so    That strength of speech is utterly denied me.   How I came  by the crown, O God forgive,   And grant it may with thee  in true peace live.
translation: I would say more to you, but my lungs are so tired that I can't speak anymore. God forgive me for how I got the crown, and please give it to my son and let him live in peace with it.

original: My gracious liege,   You won it, wore it, kept it, gave  it me.
translation: My gracious father, you won it, wore it, kept it, and now you give it to me.

original: Then plain and right must my possession be,   Which I with more than with a common pain   'Gainst all the  world will rightfully maintain.
translation: Therefore, my possession of it must be honest and true, and I will work as much as I need to, in order to defend this crown against anyone who tries to take it.

original: Look, look, here comes my John of Lancaster.
translation: Look, look, here comes my son, John of Lancaster.

original: Health, peace, and happiness to my royal father.
translation: Good health, peace, and happiness to my royal father.

original: Thou bring’st me happiness and peace, son John,   But  health, alack, with youthful wings is flown   From this  bare withered trunk.
translation: You bring me happiness and peace, John, my son. But sadly, good health has flown quickly away from my tired, old body.

original: Upon thy sight   My worldly business  makes a period.   Where is my Lord of Warwick?
translation: Now that I've seen you, there's nothing more that I need to do. Where is my Lord of Warwick?

original: My Lord of Warwick.
translation: My Lord of Warwick!

original: Doth any name particular belong Unto the lodging where  I first did swoon?
translation: Does the room that I collapsed in have a name?

original: 'Tis called Jerusalem, my noble lord.
translation: It's called the Jerusalem room, my noble lord.

original: Laud be to God! Even there my life must end.   It hath  been prophesied to me many years,   I should not die but  in Jerusalem,   Which vainly I supposed the Holy Land.
translation: Praise be to God! Then that's where I need to die. For years, I've been hearing a prophecy that I am going to die in Jerusalem—which I foolishly thought meant that I would die in the Holy Land.

original: But bear me to that chamber; there I’ll lie.   In that  Jerusalem shall Harry die.
translation: But now take me to that room. That's where I will lie down for the last time. In  that  Jerusalem, Harry must die.

original: By cock and pie, sir, you shall not away tonight.—What, Davy, I say!
translation: By God, you're not going anywhere tonight.  Hey, Davy, I say!

original: You must excuse me, Master Robert Shallow.
translation: You must excuse me, Master Robert Shallow.

original: I will not excuse you. You shall not be excused.  Excuses   shall not be admitted. There is no excuse shall  serve. You   shall not be excused.
