translation: I'm not going to excuse you. You shall not be excused. Excuses will not be allowed. No excuse is good enough, you will not be excused!

original: —Why, Davy!
translation: [Shouting offstage]  Hey, Davy!

original: Here, sir.
translation: Here, sir.

original: Davy, Davy, Davy, Davy, let me see, Davy, let me see,  Davy,   let me see. Yea, marry, William cook, bid him come   hither.
translation: Davy, Davy, Day, Davy, let me see, Davy. Let me see, Davy, let me see. Yes, all right, go and tell William the cook to come here.

original: —Sir John, you shall not be excused.
translation: [To FALSTAFF]  Sir John, you are not excused.

original: Marry, sir, thus: those precepts cannot be served. And  again, sir, shall we sow the hade land with wheat?
With red wheat, Davy. But for William cook, are there  no young pigeons?
translation: It's time to plant some red wheat, Davy. As for William the cook, are there any young pigeons?

original: Yes, sir. Here is now the smith’s note for shoeing and  plow irons.
translation: Yes, sir. Here is the bill from the blacksmith for the horseshoes and the plow irons.

original: Let it be cast and paid.—Sir John, you shall not be  excused.
translation: Add it all up and then pay it.  Anyway, Sir John, you will not be excused.

original: Now, sir, a new link to the bucket must needs be had.
translation: Now, sir, we need to get a new rope for the bucket.

original: And,   sir, do you mean to stop any of William’s wages  about the   sack he lost the other day at Hinckley Fair?
translation: Also, sir, are you going to make William pay for that wine he lost the other day at Hinckley Fair?

original: He shall answer it. Some pigeons, Davy, a couple of  short- legged hens, a joint of mutton, and any pretty  little tiny kickshaws, tell William cook.
translation: He will pay for it. Davy, tell William the cook to prepare some pigeons, a couple of short-legged hens, a shoulder of lamb, and any pretty little fancy side dishes he wants to make.

original: Doth the man of war stay all night, sir?
translation: Is the soldier going to stay for the whole night, sir?

original: Yea, Davy. I will use him well. A friend i' th' court  is better than a penny in purse. Use his men well, Davy, for they are arrant knaves and will backbite.
translation: Yes, Davy, and I'm going to take very good care of him. Having a friend in the court is more useful than having money in your purse. Look after his men, Davy—they're complete rascals and will bite at you.

original: No worse than they are back-bitten, sir, for they have  marvellous foul linen.
translation: Sir, it can't be worse than they've already been bitten, for their clothes definitely have fleas.

original: Well-conceited, Davy. About thy business, Davy.
translation: Very witty. Now run along, Davy, you have things to do.

original: I beseech you, sir, to countenance William Visor of  Woncot against Clement Perkes o' th' hill.
translation: And I beg you, sir, to rule in favor of William Visor of Woncot, in his case against Clement Perkes of the hill.

original: There is many complaints, Davy, against that Visor.  That Visor is an arrant knave, on my knowledge.
translation: Davy, there have been many complaints made about that Visor. He is a complete rogue, as far as I know.

original: I grant your Worship that he is a knave, sir, but yet,  God   forbid, sir, but a knave should have some  countenance at his   friend’s request.
translation: I will admit that he is a bit of a rogue, sir. But, by God, even a rogue should be granted a favor when his friend asks for it.

original: An honest man, sir, is able to speak for   himself when a knave is not. I  have served your Worship   truly, sir, this eight years;
translation: Sir, an honest man is allowed to speak for himself, whereas a rogue cannot. I have served your Worship faithfully for eight years, sir.

original: an if I cannot once or twice in a   quarter bear out a  knave against an honest man, I have a very little credit with your Worship.
translation: And if I can't convince you to support the rogue instead of the honest man every once in a while, then I clearly don't mean that much to you.

original: The knave is mine honest friend,  sir;   therefore I beseech you let him be countenanced.
translation: This rogue is my true friend, sir, so I'm asking you to help him out here.

original: Go to, I say he shall have no wrong. Look about, Davy.
translation: Enough of that, I promise you he won't be wronged. Now, off you go, Davy.

original: Where are you, Sir John? Come, come, come, off with  your boots.—Give me your hand, Master Bardolph.
translation: Where are you, Sir John? Come, come, come, take your boots off.  Shake my hand, Master Bardolph.

original: I am glad to see your Worship.
translation: I am happy to see your Worship.

original: I thank thee with all my heart, kind Master Bardolph,   and welcome, my tall fellow.—Come, Sir  John.
translation: I thank you with all my heart, kind Master Bardolph.  Welcome to you, you tall fellow. [To FALSTAFF] Come on, Sir John.

original: I’ll follow you, good Master Robert Shallow.
translation: I'm right behind you, good Master Robert Shallow.

original: Bardolph, look to our horses.
translation: Bardolph, get the horses ready.

original: If I were sawed into quantities, I should make four  dozen of   such bearded hermits' staves as Master Shallow. It is a   wonderful thing to see the semblable coherence  of his men’s   spirits and his.
translation: If I were cut into little bits, I would make four dozen bearded sticks—and that would look just like Master Shallow. It's lovely to see the obvious similarities between his men's characters and his own.

original: They, by observing of him, do bear   themselves like foolish justices; he, by  conversing with   them, is turned into a justice-like  servingman.
translation: They've clearly been watching him, and now they all act like foolish judges as well. Likewise, he has been talking to them and has become something in between a judge and a servant.

original: Their spirits   are so married in conjunction  with the participation of   society that they flock  together in consent like so many wild   geese.
translation: Their spirits are joined in such an intimate union that when they come together it is like a flock of wild geese flying together.

original: If I had a  suit to Master Shallow, I would humor his   men with the  imputation of being near their master;if to his   men, I  would curry with Master Shallow that no man could   better command his servants.
translation: If I needed a favor from Master Shallow, I would pretend to his men that I was a close friend of their master. If I needed something from his men, I would flatter Master Shallow, telling him that he was the best master to his servants.

original: It is certain that either wise    bearing or ignorant carriage is caught, as men take  diseases,   one of another.
translation: What is certain is that both the behavior of a wise man and that of a stupid one can be caught from other men, in the same way we catch diseases.

original: Therefore let men take heed of their   company. I will devise matter enough out of this  Shallow to keep Prince Harry in continual laughter the  wearing out of six fashions,
translation: Therefore, it is important to be careful about the company you keep. I could think up enough to say about this Shallow to keep Prince Harry laughing for at least a year.

original: which is four terms, or two actions, and a' shall laugh without intervallums.
translation: And, a year from now, the fashions will have changed six times, two lawsuits will have been decided, and Harry will still be laughing without stopping.

original: O, it is much that a lie with a slight oath and a jest with a sad brow will do with a fellow that never had the ache  in his shoulders. O, you shall see him laugh till his  face be like a wet cloak ill laid up.
translation: Oh, a lie told with some honesty and a joke that is delivered with some seriousness will be enjoyed by a lad who's young and carefree, not weighed down by anything. You will see him laugh until his face looks like a wet coat that's been hung up badly to dry—that's how wrinkled it will be.

original: Sir John.
translation: Sir John.

original: I come, Master Shallow; I come, Master Shallow.
translation: I'm coming, Master Shallow, I'm coming.

original: How now, my Lord Chief Justice, whither away?
translation: How's it going, my Lord Chief Justice? Where are you going?

original: How doth the King?
translation: How is the King?

original: Exceeding well. His cares are now all ended.
translation: Very well. All of his cares are gone.

original: I hope, not dead.
translation: I hope you don't mean he's dead.

original: He’s walked the way of nature, And to our purposes  he lives no more.
translation: He's followed the path nature intended. And for our purposes, he is no longer alive.

original: I would his Majesty had called me with him. The service that I truly did his life Hath left me open to all  injuries.
translation: I wish his Majesty had taken me with him. The work that I did for him when he was alive has put me in danger now that he's dead.

original: Indeed, I think the young King loves you not.
translation: Indeed, especially as I don't think the young King cares for you.

original: I know he doth not, and do arm myself   To welcome the  condition of the time,
translation: I know he doesn't, and I need to be prepared for what's going to happen now.

original: Which cannot look more hideously  upon me   Than I have drawn it in my fantasy.
translation: I'm hoping it can't be any worse than what I've pictured in my head.

original: Here come the heavy issue of dead Harry.   O, that the  living Harry had the temper   Of he the worst of these  three gentlemen!
translation: Here come the sad children of the dead king. Oh, if only the living Harry had the personality of the worst of these three gentlemen!

original: How many nobles then should hold their  places   That must strike sail to spirits of vile sort!
translation: Then a lot of noblemen would be safe in their positions, whereas now they will be forced to leave and let nasty men take over their roles.

original: O God, I fear all will be overturned.
translation: Oh God, I am scared that everything is going to change.

original: Good morrow, cousin Warwick, good morrow.
translation: Good morning, Warwick, good morning.

original: Good morrow, cousin.
translation: Good morning to you.

original: We meet like men that had forgot to speak.
translation: We're all acting like men who have forgotten how to speak.

original: We do remember, but our argument Is all too heavy to  admit much talk.
translation: We remember how to speak, but the subject we have to talk about is too sad for us to want to say much about it.

original: Well, peace be with him that hath made us heavy.
translation: Well, peace be with the late king, the man who has made us sad.

original: Peace be with us, lest we be heavier.
translation: And peace be with us, or we'll be even sadder.

original: O, good my lord, you have lost a friend indeed, And I  dare swear you borrow not that face Of seeming sorrow;  it is sure your own.
translation: Oh, my good lord, you have certainly lost a friend. I am sure that the sorrow you wear on your face is not borrowed. It is truly yours.

original: Though no man be assured what grace to find, You stand  in coldest expectation. I am the sorrier; would ’twere  otherwise.
translation: Although no man knows what is going to happen to him, you get used to expecting very little from life. I am sorry, I wish things could be different.

original: Well, you must now speak Sir John Falstaff fair, Which  swims against your stream of quality.
translation: Well, now we're even going to be expected to say nice things about Sir John Falstaff—which goes against the normal behavior of noble people.

original: Sweet princes, what I did I did in honor,   Led by th'  impartial conduct of my soul;
translation: Sweet princes, everything I have done, I did honorably—motivated by impartiality and my moral nature.

original: And never shall you see  that I will beg   A ragged and forestalled remission.
translation: You will never see me horribly begging for a pardon only for the pardon to be taken away again.

original: If  truth and upright innocency fail me,   I’ll to the King my master that is dead   And tell him who hath sent me after him.
translation: If truth and real innocence aren't enough to save me, then I will follow after my dead master, the late King, and tell him who has sent me.

original: Here comes the Prince.
translation: Here comes the Prince.

original: Good morrow, and God save your Majesty.
translation: Good morning, and may God save your Majesty.

original: This new and gorgeous garment majesty   Sits not so easy  on me as you think.
translation: This new addition of the word "majesty" doesn't suit me as well you might think.

original: Brothers, you mix your sadness with some fear.   This is the English, not the Turkish court;    Not Amurath an Amurath succeeds,   But Harry Harry.
translation: [To LANCASTER, CLARENCE, and GLOUCESTER]  Brothers, your sadness seems to be mixed with some fear. This is the English court, not the Turkish one. I am not like Amurath, who killed all of his brothers when he succeeded the late king Amurath. I'm just a Harry, following another Harry.

original: Yet be  sad, good brothers,   For, by my faith, it very well  becomes you.
translation: It's all right to be sad, my good brothers. And honestly, it suits you.

original: Sorrow so royally in you appears   That I  will deeply put the fashion on   And wear it in my heart.  Why then, be sad.
translation: You all look so grand in your sorrow that I will try and put it on as well, and will wear it in my heart. Be sad, my good brothers.

original: But entertain no more of it, good  brothers,   Than a joint burden laid upon us all.   For me,  by heaven, I bid you be assured,   I’ll be your father and your brother too.   Let me but bear your love, I ’ll bear your cares.
translation: But think of this sadness as a burden which we must all share. I want you to know that as far as I'm concerned, I will be both your father and your brother as well. Give me your love, and I will take car e of you.

original: Yet weep that Harry’s dead, and so will I,    But Harry lives that shall convert those tears   By number  into hours of happiness.
translation: For now, keep crying for the dead Harry, and I will too. But there is still a living Harry who will gradually change those tears into hours of happiness.

original: We hope no otherwise from your Majesty.
translation: We hope for nothing more from your Majesty.

original: You all look strangely on me.  And you most. You are, I think, assured I love you  not.
translation: You are all still looking at me strangely, though. You most of all. You are convinced that I do not love you, isn't that right?

original: I am assured, if I be measured rightly, Your Majesty  hath no just cause to hate me.
translation: I am certain that, if you judge me fairly, you should have no reason to hate me.

original: No?   How might a prince of my great hopes forget   So  great indignities you laid upon me?
translation: No? How could a great prince forget the awful things you did to me?

original: What, rate, rebuke,  and roughly send to prison   Th' immediate heir of  England?
translation: What, did you think you could judge, punish, and violently send to prison the next heir of England?

original: Was this easy?   May this be washed in Lethe and  forgotten?
translation: Did you find this an easy thing to do? Do you think your wrongdoings can now just be washed in the  Lethe   River and forgotten?

original: I then did use the person of your father;   The image of  his power lay then in me.
translation: I was acting on behalf of your father, with the power and responsibility that he had given me.

original: And in th' administration of  his law,   Whiles I was busy for the commonwealth,
translation: And in terms of the law, while I was busy keeping the country safe,

original: Your  Highness pleasèd to forget my place,   The majesty and  power of law and justice,   The image of the King whom I  presented,
translation: you ignored my rank and the authority and power of law and justice that I had, as a representative of the King.

original: And struck me in my very seat of judgment,    Whereon, as an offender to your father,   I gave bold way  to my authority   And did commit you.
translation: You hit me in the head—the very location of my judgement. And since this action went against your father's laws, I used my power as I was meant to and arrested you.

original: If the deed were  ill,   Be you contented, wearing now the garland,   To have  a son set your decrees at nought?
translation: If that was the wrong thing to do, then are you prepared, now that you wear the crown, to have a son who ignores all of your laws?

original: To pluck down justice  from your awful bench?   To trip the course of law and  blunt the sword   That guards the peace and safety of your person?
translation: A son who mocks the judges that enforce these laws? A son who disrupts the law and blunts the swords that looks after your own peace and safety?

original: Nay more, to spurn at your most royal image   And mock your workings in a second body?
translation: Or even worse, mocks you and the actions taken by the men you have chosen to work for you?

original: Question your  royal thoughts, make the case yours;   Be now the father  and propose a son,   Hear your own dignity so much  profaned,   See your most dreadful laws so loosely  slighted,
translation: Ask yourself these questions, and put yourself in his position. Think of yourself as a father and imagine a son who disrespects your dignity and so easily ignores your most important laws.

original: Behold yourself so by a son disdained,   And  then imagine me taking your part   And in your power soft  silencing your son.
translation: Think about how it would feel to be scorned by such a son. Then imagine that I support you, and use your power to gently silence your son.

original: After this cold considerance,  sentence me,   And, as you are a king, speak in your state   What I have done that misbecame my place,   My person, or my liege’s sovereignty.
translation: Sentence me only after you have considered all of this. Now that you are King, tell me what I have done to overstep my role, my person, or my lord's power.

original: You are right, justice, and you weigh this well.    Therefore still bear the balance and the sword.
translation: You are right, Justice. And you have made your case very well. Therefore, keep your role as a judge and an enforcer of the law.

original: And I do  wish your honors may increase   Till you do live to see a  son of mine   Offend you and obey you as I did.
translation: I hope that your honors will increase and you will even live to see a son of mine offend you and then obey you—just as I have done.

original: So shall I live to speak my father’s words:   “Happy am I that have  a man so bold   That dares do justice on my proper son;
translation: In that way, I will live to speak my father's words, "I am happy to have a man who is brave enough to even punish my own son;

original: And not less happy, having such a son   That would deliver  up his greatness so   Into the hands of justice.”
translation: I am just as happy that my son is prepared to give up his greatness in the name of the law."

original: You did  commit me,   For which I do commit into your hand   Th'  unstainèd sword that you have used to bear,   With this  remembrance:
translation: You did arrest me, and for that I ask you to continue in your role, remembering this:

original: that you use the same   With the like bold,  just, and impartial spirit   As you have done 'gainst me.  There is my hand.   You shall be as a father to my youth,
translation: you must always be as brave, just, and impartial as you have been with me. Shake my hand. You will be like a father to me in my young age,

original: My voice shall sound as you do prompt mine ear,   And I  will stoop and humble my intents   To your well-practiced  wise directions.
translation: and I will say the things that you whisper in my ear. I will bow to you and will be humble in my ideas, needing your years of experience and wise ideas to help me.

original: —   And, princes all, believe me, I  beseech you:   My father is gone wild into his grave,   For  in his tomb lie my affections,
translation: [To LANCASTER, CLARENCE, and GLOUCESTER]  And, princes, I am asking you to please believe me about this. My wildness is buried with my father; my passions now lie in his tomb.

original: And with his spirit sadly I survive   To mock the expectation of the world,
translation: His sensible spirit now lies in me, and I am ready to prove the world wrong, defying their expectations of me.

original: To  frustrate prophecies, and to raze out   Rotten opinion,  who hath writ me down   After my seeming.
translation: I am going to challenge their predictions, and will destroy the bad opinions of me held by people who judged me based on what I seemed to be like in the past.

original: The tide of  blood in me   Hath proudly flowed in vanity till now.
translation: My actions, the tide of my blood—both used to flow with excess and vanity.

original: Now  doth it turn and ebb back to the sea,   Where it shall  mingle with the state of floods   And flow henceforth in  formal majesty.
translation: But now it is changing its course and turning back to the sea, where it will be able to mix with the ocean's majesty.

original: Now call we our high court of  parliament,   And let us choose such limbs of noble  counsel   That the great body of our state may go   In equal rank with the best governed nation;
translation: Now we must assemble parliament, and choose worthy members for this noble council who will allow our country to stand alongside even the best-governed nations.

original: That war, or peace, or both at once, may be   As things acquainted and  familiar to us,   In which you, father, shall have  foremost hand.
translation: We will be acquainted and familiar with matters of war, peace, or even both at once—and you will be needed greatly for this.

original: Our coronation done, we will accite,   As I before remembered, all our state.
translation: Once my coronation is over, we will, as I have mentioned, summon all men of rank.

original: And, God consigning  to my good intents,   No prince nor peer shall have just  cause to say   God shorten Harry’s happy life one day.
translation: And, if God endorses my good intention, there will be no reason for any prince or man to say that he hopes that God will shorten Harry's happy life by even one day.

original: Nay, you shall see my orchard, where, in an arbor, we  will   eat a last year’s pippin of my own graffing, with a dish of   caraways, and so forth.
translation: Now you can see my garden. We can sit in the  arbor  and eat last year's pippin apples that I  grafted  myself, along with a dish of  caraway  apples, and so on.

original: —Come, cousin Silence.
translation: [To SILENCE]  Come on, Silence.

original: —And then   to bed.
translation: [To the others]  And then we'll all go to bed.

original: Fore God, you have here a goodly dwelling and a rich.
translation: By God, you've got a lovely place here—and an expensive one at that.

original: Barren, barren, barren, beggars all, beggars all, Sir  John.   Marry, good air.
translation: It's worthless, worthless, worthless. We are all poor, all poor, Sir John. But at least we have fresh air.

original: —Spread, Davy, spread, Davy. Well  said,   Davy.
translation: [To DAVY]  Set the table, Davy, set the table. Well done, Davy.

original: This Davy serves you for good uses. He is your  servingman and your husband.
translation: This Davy does so much for you. He's both your attendant and your steward.

original: A good varlet, a good varlet, a very good varlet, Sir  John. By the Mass, I have drunk too much sack at supper. A good varlet. Now sit down, now sit down.—Come,  cousin.
translation: He is a good servant, a very good servant, Sir John. Oh God, I have had too much wine with dinner. A good servant. Now come on, let's sit down. Sit down now. Come on.

original: Ah, sirrah, quoth he, we shall   Do nothing but eat and  make good cheer,
translation: "Yes, sir," he said. We will do nothing but eat and be happy—

original: [sings]     And praise God for the merry  year,   When flesh is cheap and females dear,   And lusty  lads roam here and there
translation: [Singing]   And thank God for a happy year, When meat is cheap, but women are expensive,  And lusty lads go here and there,

original: So merrily,   And ever among so  merrily.
translation: So happily, Always so happily.

original: There’s a merry heart!—Good Master Silence, I’ll give  you a health for that anon.
translation: That's the spirit! Master Silence, I will toast to you in just a moment.

original: Give Master Bardolph some wine, Davy.
translation: Give Master Bardolph some wine, Davy.

original: Sweet sir, sit. I’ll be with you anon. Most sweet sir,  sit.   Master page, good master page, sit. Proface.
translation: Kind sir, sit down. I'll be with you in just a minute. Most kind sir, sit down, please. Master Page, good master Page, sit down as well. Welcome!

original: What  you want   in meat, we’ll have in drink, but you must  bear. The heart’s   all.
translation: Although we don't have much food, we can make up for it with what we have in drink! You just have to put up with it, the heart's what matters!

original: Be merry, Master Bardolph. —And, my little soldier  there, be merry.
translation: Have fun, Master Bardolph. And you too, my little soldier there, have some fun!

original: [sings]   Be merry, be merry, my wife has all,   For women  are shrews, both short and tall.
translation: [Singing]   Be happy, be happy, my wife has it all,  Since women can be shrews, whether they're short of they're tall.

original: 'Tis merry in hall when beards wag all,   And welcome merry Shrovetide.   Be merry, be merry.
translation: Be happy at a party when men joke around,  And let's all be happy on this  Shrovetide . Be happy, be happy!

original: I did not think Master Silence had been a man of this  mettle.
translation: I didn't think Master Silence had this in him.

original: Who, I? I have been merry twice and once ere now.
translation: What, me? I've let my hair down a few times in my life.

original: There’s a dish of leather-coats for you.
translation: Here's a dish of russet apples for you.

original: Davy!
translation: Davy!

original: Your Worship, I’ll be with you straight.—  A cup of wine, sir?
translation: Yes, sir, I'll be with you in a minute.  Would you like a glass of wine, sir?

original: A cup of wine that’s brisk and fine, And drink  unto thee, leman mine, And a merry heart lives long-a.
translation: A glass of wine is quick and fine, And drink to you, sweetheart of mine, A happy heart lives long!

original: Well said, Master Silence.
translation: Well said, Master Silence.

original: And we shall be merry; now comes in the sweet o' th'  night.
translation: So let's have some fun. Now is the best time of the night.

original: Health and long life to you, Master Silence.
translation: May you have good health and a long life, Master Silence.

original: Fill the cup, and let it come, I’ll pledge you  a mile to th' bottom.
translation: Fill up your cup and pass it round, I'll drink right to the bottom, Even if it's a mile to the ground.

original: Honest Bardolph, welcome. If thou wantest anything and     wilt not call, beshrew thy heart.
translation: Welcome, honest Bardolph. If you ever want something and don't ask for it, that's your own fault.

original: [to the PAGE]     Welcome, my little tiny thief, and welcome   indeed too.  I’ll drink to Master Bardolph, and to all the   cabileros  about London.
translation: [To the PAGE]  Welcome, my little tiny thief, a very warm welcome indeed. I will drink to Master Bardolph, and to all the fine gentlemen of London.

original: I hope to see London once ere I die.
translation: I would like to see London before I die.

original: And I might see you there, Davy!
translation: And I might see you there, Davy!

original: By the Mass, you’ll crack a quart together, ha, will  you not, Master Bardolph?
translation: By God, you'll drink a whole quart between the two of you, won't you, Master Bardolph?

original: Yea, sir, in a pottle-pot.
By God’s liggens, I thank thee. The knave will stick by thee, I can assure thee that. He will not out, he. 'Tis true bred!
translation: By God's eyes, I thank you. This rascal will stick with you, I can promise you that. He won't drop out, he's been raised well.

original: And I’ll stick by him, sir.
translation: I'll stick by him too, sir.

original: Why, there spoke a king. Lack nothing, be merry.  [One  knocks at door.]  Look who’s at door there, ho. Who  knocks?
translation: Spoken just like a king. Have whatever you want, enjoy yourselves!  Hey, Davy, go see who's at the door. Who is knocking?

original: Why, now you have done me right.
translation: Why, you're managing to drink just as much as I do!

original: Do me right,   And dub me knight,   Samingo.  Is ’t  not so?
translation: Keep up with me, And call me a knight,Samingo.Isn't that right?

original: 'Tis so.
translation: It certainly is.

original: Is ’t so? Why then, say an old man can do somewhat.
translation: Is it? Well then, you need to admit that an old man can do some things.

original: An ’t please your Worship, there’s one Pistol come from the court with news.
translation: Sir, if I may, a man called Pistol is here from the court with some news.

original: From the court? Let him come in.
translation: From the court? Let him come in.

original: How now, Pistol?
translation: How are you, Pistol?

original: Sir John, God save you.
translation: God save you, Sir John.

original: What wind blew you hither, Pistol?
translation: What wind blew you here, Pistol?

original: Not the ill wind which blows no man to good. Sweet  knight, thou art now one of the greatest men in this  realm.
translation: Don't worry, it's not a bad wind that doesn't blow any man towards something good. My sweet knight, you are now one of the biggest man in this whole country.

original: By 'r Lady, I think he be, but Goodman Puff of Barson.
translation: Truthfully, I think he would be, if it weren't for that good man, Puff from Barson.

original: Puff?   Puff in thy teeth, most recreant coward base!—    Sir John, I am thy Pistol and thy friend,   And  helter-skelter have I rode to thee,
translation: Puff? Puff in your mouth, you disloyal coward! Sir John, I am your Pistol and your friend, and I rode here as quick as I could to tell you something.

original: And tidings do I  bring, and lucky joys,   And golden times, and happy news  of price.
translation: I bring you good luck, joyful times, and happy, important news.

original: I pray thee now, deliver them like a man of this world.
translation: Please, tell me this news like an ordinary person in the world.

original: A foutre for the world and worldlings base! I speak of  Africa and golden joys.
translation: Curse this world and the awful people in it! I have news about Africa, and its golden riches!

original: O base Assyrian knight, what is thy news? Let King  Cophetua know the truth thereof.
And Robin Hood, Scarlet, and John.
translation: And Robin Hood, Scarlet, and John.

original: Shall dunghill curs confront the Helicons, And shall  good news be baffled? Then, Pistol, lay thy head in  Furies' lap.
translation: Will dirty dogs attack the Muses of poetry? Will my happy news be ruined like this? If so, then Pistol, go ahead and enlist the help of the Furies, those forces of revenge.

original: Honest gentleman, I know not your breeding.
translation: Honest gentleman, I don't know how you were raised.

original: Why then, lament therefor.
translation: That's a shame for you.

original: Give me pardon, sir. If, sir, you come with news from  the   court, I take it there’s but two ways,
translation: Pardon me, sir, but if you come with news from the court, it seems like you only have two options:

original: either to  utter them, or   to conceal them. I am, sir, under the  King in some authority.
translation: either to tell us what you know, or conceal what you know. I have some power from the King, I will have you know.

original: Under which king, besonian? Speak or die.
translation: From which King, you fool? Speak, or die.

original: Under King Harry.
translation: From King Henry.

original: Harry the Fourth, or Fifth?
translation: Henry the Fourth, or Henry the Fifth?

original: Harry the Fourth.
translation: Henry the Fourth.

original: A foutre for thine office!—   Sir John, thy tender  lambkin now is king.   Harry the Fifth’s the man.
translation: Then damn your power! Sir John, your little lamb is now the king. Henry the Fifth is now the man.

original: I speak  the truth.   When Pistol lies, do this   [he makes an  obscene gesture]   and   fig me, like   The bragging  Spaniard.
translation: I am telling you the truth. If Pistol is a liar, then do this,  [He makes an obscene gesture]   and tell me to go screw myself, like some ridiculous Spanish man.

original: What, is the old king dead?
translation: What, is the old king dead?

original: As nail in door. The things I speak are just.
translation: Dead as a doornail. I am telling you the truth.

original: Away, Bardolph.—Saddle my horse.—Master Robert Shallow, choose what office thou wilt in the land, ’tis thine.  Pistol, I will double-charge thee with dignities.
translation: Get going, Bardolph—saddle up my horse ready to leave. Master Robert Shallow, choose whatever job you want to have in this country, and you can have it. Pistol, I will give you so many honors!

original: O joyful day! I would not take a knighthood for my  fortune.
translation: Oh, what a happy day! I wouldn't even choose a knighthood over my new, good fortune!

original: What, I do bring good news!
translation: See, didn't I tell you that I brought good news!

original: Carry Master Silence to bed.—Master Shallow, my Lord  Shallow, be what thou wilt. I am Fortune’s steward. Get  on thy boots. We’ll ride all night.—O sweet  Pistol!—Away, Bardolph!
translation: Put Master Silence to bed. Master Shallow, or Lord Shallow—call yourself whatever you want. I am in charge of people's fortunes now! Put on your boots. It's time for us to go. We will ride all night. Oh, sweet Pistol! Let's go, Bardolph!

original: Come, Pistol, utter more to me, and withal devise  something   to do thyself good. Boot, boot, Master  Shallow.
translation: Come, Pistol, tell me more about what has happened, and we will come up with something good for you. We need our boots, our boots, Master Shallow.

original: I know the   young King is sick for me. Let us  take any man’s horses. The   laws of England are at my  commandment.
translation: I know the young King needs me. Let us take any horses—I now control all of the laws of England.

original: Blessed are they   that have been my friends, and woe to my Lord Chief   Justice!
translation: Anyone who has been my friend is lucky, and you just be careful, my Lord Chief Justice!

original: Let vultures vile seize on his lungs also! “Where is  the life that late I led?” say they. Why, here it is.  Welcome these pleasant days.
translation: Let vultures eat out his lungs as well! At some point, people have to say, "Where is the life that I used to lead?" Well, that moment is here for us—welcome to a happier time.

original: No, thou arrant knave.
translation: No, you utter villain!

original: I would to God that I might die, that   I might have thee hanged.
translation: I wish to God that I were dead so that I could have you hanged!

original: Thou hast drawn my  shoulder out   of joint.
translation: You have dislocated my shoulder!

original: The Constables have delivered her over to me, and she  shall   have whipping cheer enough, I warrant her.
translation: The Constables gave her to me, and she will be thoroughly  whipped  soon enough, I swear it.

original: There  hath been   a man or two lately killed about her.
translation: She has been involved in a couple of murders recently.

original: Nut-hook, nut-hook, you lie! Come on, I ’ll tell thee  what,   thou damned tripe-visaged rascal:
translation: You scum, you scum, that's a lie! Come on! I'll tell you what, you damned flabby idiot,

original: an the child I  now go with   do miscarry, thou wert better thou hadst  struck thy mother,   thou paper-faced villain.
translation: if I have a  miscarriage  because of this, you're going to wish you'd hit your mother instead, you white-faced villain!

original: O the Lord, that Sir John were come! I would make this  a bloody day to somebody. But I pray God the fruit of  her womb might miscarry.
If it do, you shall have a dozen of cushions again; you have   but eleven now.
translation: Well if she does, then I guess you will have twelve cushions again. You only have eleven, as she is wearing one of the cushions under her dress to look like a pregnant belly.

original: Come, I charge you both go with  me, for the   man is dead that you and Pistol beat amongst you.
translation: Come on, I order both of you to follow me, for the man that you and Pistol attacked is now dead.

original: I’ll tell you what, you thin man in a censer, I will  have you   as soundly swinged for this, you bluebottle  rogue,
translation: I'll tell you what, you thin rat, I will have you beaten up for this, you blue-coat wearing rogue!

original: you filthy   famished correctioner. If you be not  swinged, I’ll forswear   half-kirtles.
translation: You filthy, starving correction officer. If you're not beaten up for this, then I will give up wearing skirts.

original: Come, come, you she knight-errant, come.
translation: Come on, you night wanderer, come with me.

original: O God, that right should thus overcome might! Well, of  sufferance comes ease.
Come, you rogue, come, bring me to a justice.
translation: Come on then, you scoundrel. Take me to a judge.

original: Ay, come, you starved bloodhound.
translation: Yes, come on, you starving dog.

original: Goodman Death, Goodman Bones!
translation: Master Death! Master Bones!

original: Thou atomy, thou!
translation: You skeleton, you!

original: Come, you thin thing, come, you rascal.
Very well.
translation: Let's go then.

original: More rushes, more rushes.
translation: More rushes, more rushes.

original: The trumpets have sounded twice.
translation: The trumpets have already been blown twice.

original: 'Twill be two o'clock ere they come from the  coronation. Dispatch, dispatch.
translation: It will be two o'clock before they get here from the coronation. Hurry up and finish. Hurry.

original: Stand here by me, Master Robert Shallow. I will make  the   King do you grace.
translation: Stand here next to me, Master Robert Shallow. I will make the King give you his approval.

original: I will leer upon him as he comes  by, and   do but mark the countenance that he will give  me.
translation: I will look at him charmingly as he walks past us, and just wait for the face he will make back at me.

original: God bless thy lungs, good knight!
translation: God bless your words, good knight!

original: Come here, Pistol, stand behind me.
translation: Come here, Pistol, stand behind me.

original: —   [to SHALLOW   ]   O, if  I   had had time to have made new liveries, I would have    bestowed the thousand pound I borrowed of you.
translation: [To SHALLOW]  Oh, if I had had the time to make us new  uniforms , I would have used that thousand pounds I borrowed from you.

original: But ’tis  no   matter. This poor show doth better. This doth infer  the zeal   I had to see him.
translation: But, it doesn't matter. It's better that we look poor—it shows how eager I was to see him.

original: It doth so.
translation: Yes, it does.

original: It shows my earnestness of affection—
translation: It shows him how serious my feelings are for him—

original: It doth so.
translation: It does.

original: My devotion—
translation: My devotion—

original: It doth, it doth, it doth.
translation: It does, it does, it does.

original: As it were, to ride day and night, and not to  deliberate, not to remember, not to have patience to  shift me—
translation: The truth is, we rode all day and all night, not considering our plan, not thinking of stopping, not even having the time to change my shirt—

original: It is best, certain.
translation: It will look good, that's for certain.

original: But to stand stained with travel and sweating with  desire to   see him,
translation: We will stand there, dirty from our journey and sweating with our desire to see him.

original: thinking of nothing else, putting all affairs else in   oblivion, as if there were nothing else to be done but to see   him.
translation: We couldn't think of anything else, all other matters were ignored, our only concern was seeing him.

original: 'Tis  semper idem  , for  obsque hoc nihil est  ; ’tis all in every part.
'Tis so indeed.
translation: That's true indeed.

original: My knight, I will inflame thy noble liver, and make  thee   rage.
translation: My knight, I am going to stir up your noble  liver , and make you angry.

original: Thy Doll and Helen of thy noble thoughts is  in base   durance and contagious prison, Haled thither by  most   mechanical and dirty hand.
translation: Your Doll, the mistress of your noble thoughts, has been imprisoned in a dirty and infected jail—hauled there by an unemotional and dirty hand.

original: Rouse up revenge from  ebon den   with fell Alecto’s snake, for Doll is in.  Pistol speaks nought   but truth.
translation: Summon up revenge from the deepest pit of your stomach, and release  the snakes of hell . For Doll is in prison. Pistol only speaks the truth.

original: I will deliver her.
translation: I will set her free.

original: There roared the sea, and trumpet-clangor sounds.
translation: That was the sea roaring. The blaring trumpets have sounded.

original: God save thy Grace, King Hal, my royal Hal.
translation: God save your Grace, King Hal, my royal Hal.

original: The heavens thee guard and keep, most royal imp of  fame!
translation: May the heavens look after you, you royal child of fame!

original: God save thee, my sweet boy!
translation: God save you, my sweet boy!

original: My Lord Chief Justice, speak to that vain man.
translation: My Lord Chief Justice, speak to that foolish man.

original: Have you your wits? Know you what ’tis to  speak?
translation: Are you out of your mind? Do you know what you are saying?

original: My King, my Jove, I speak to thee, my heart!
I know thee not, old man. Fall to thy prayers.   How ill  white hairs become a fool and jester.
translation: I don't know you, old man . Fall to your knees and pray. White hair doesn't suit a fool and a clown like you.

original: I have long dreamt of such a kind of man,   So surfeit-swelled, so old, and  so profane;   But being awaked, I do despise my dream.
translation: I have dreamed about a man like you for a long tim—ridiculously swollen, old, and so foul. But now that I am awake, I hate that dream

original: Make less thy body hence, and more thy grace;   Leave  gormandizing. Know the grave doth gape   For thee thrice  wider than for other men.
translation: . Lose some weight and find some manners instead; stop eating so much. You know that your grave is going to have to be three times wider than other men's.

original: Reply not to me with a  fool-born jest.   Presume not that I am the thing I was,    For God doth know—so shall the world perceive—   That I  have turned away my former self.
translation: And don't reply to me with some kind of foolish joke, because I am not the man I was before. For God knows—and the whole world will soon realize—that I have left behind my previous life.

original: So will I those that  kept me company.   When thou dost hear I am as I have  been,   Approach me, and thou shalt be as thou wast,   The  tutor and the feeder of my riots.
translation: And so I will also leave behind the people I knew in that life. If you ever hear that I have gone back to my old ways, then come and find me. You will be like you were before—my teacher and the inspiration of my rebellious ways.

original: Till then I banish  thee, on pain of death,   As I have done the rest of my  misleaders,   Not to come near our person by ten mile.
translation: But until then, I banish you, on pain of death, and you must not come within ten miles of me

original: For competence of life I will allow you,   That lack of means enforce you not to evils.
translation: —this is the same warning I have given to the other men who have misled me. I will give you just enough money to live on, so that you won't be tempted to do bad things.

original: And, as we hear you do reform yourselves,   We will, according to your strengths and  qualities,   Give you advancement.
translation: And, if we hear that you have changed your ways, we will give you the honors that your strengths and qualities deserve.

original: [to CHIEF JUSTICE   ]   Be it your charge, my lord,   To see performed the tenor of  my word.—
translation: [To CHIEF JUSTICE]  It is up to you to make sure that this order is carried out.

original: [To the attendants]   Set on.
translation: [To the attendants]  Let's go.

original: Master Shallow, I owe you a thousand pound.
translation: Master Shallow, I owe you a thousand pounds.

original: Yea, marry, Sir John, which I beseech you to let me  have home with me.
translation: Yes, indeed, Sir John. And I would like to take the money home with me.

original: That can hardly be, Master Shallow. Do not you grieve  at   this. I shall be sent for in private to him. Look  you, he must   seem thus to the world.
translation: You can't do that, Master Shallow. Don't worry about this. He will want to talk to me in private—this is just how he has to act in front of everyone else.

original: Fear not your  advancements. I will   be the man yet that shall make you  great.
translation: Don't worry about your own future, I will still be the man who will make you great.

original: I cannot well perceive how, unless you should give me  your   doublet and stuff me out with straw.
translation: I don't know how you plan on doing that, unless you let me wear your jacket and  stuff it full of straw .

original: I beseech you, good Sir   John, let me have five hundred of my thousand.
translation: Please, good Sir John, can I just have five pounds out of that thousand?

original: Sir, I will be as good as my word. This that you heard  was but a color.
translation: Sir, I will be as good as my word. Everything you just heard is simply a color, just a pretense.

original: A color that I fear you will die in, Sir John.
Fear no colors. Go with me to dinner.—Come, Lieutenant  Pistol.—Come, Bardolph.—I shall be sent for soon at  night.
translation: Don't be afraid of any collars. Come on, let's go and have lunch. Come on, Lieutenant Pistol. Come on, Bardolph. He will send for me soon in the evening.

original: Go, carry Sir John Falstaff to the Fleet. Take all his  company along with him.
My lord, my lord—
translation: My lord, my lord—

original: I cannot now speak. I will hear you soon.— Take them  away.
translation: I can't speak to you now. I will hear what you have to say soon enough. Take them away.

original: Si fortune me tormenta, spero me contenta.
translation: If my fortunes torment me, then hope contents me.

original: I like this fair proceeding of the King’s.   He hath  intent his wonted followers   Shall all be very well  provided for,
translation: I like how the King has handled this situation. He has made sure that his old followers will be looked after and provided for,

original: But all are banished till their  conversations   Appear more wise and modest to the world.
translation: but he has banished them until they can act with the intelligence and modesty they need to have in this world.

original: And so they are.
translation: That he has.

original: The King hath called his parliament, my lord.
translation: The King has assembled his parliament, my lord.

original: He hath.
translation: He has.

original: I will lay odds that, ere this year expire,   We bear our civil swords and native fire   As far as France:
translation: I bet that before this year is over, we will have tried to invade France.

original: I beard  a bird so sing,   Whose music, to my thinking, pleased the King.   Come, will you hence?
translation: I heard a bird singing about it, and I noticed that the King liked hearing that song. Come on, will you go with me?

original: First my fear; then my curtsy, last my speech. My fear  is your   displeasure my curtsy my duty; and my speech, to  beg your   pardons.
translation: First, I will tell you about my worries. Then I will bow to you. And, after that, I will finally end with my speech. I am worried that you didn't like the play, and so I bow to you out of duty and will make my speech to ask you for forgiveness.

original: If you look for a good speech now, you  undo me,   for what I have to say is of mine own making,  and what   indeed I should say will, I doubt, prove mine  own marring.   But to the purpose, and so to the venture.
translation: If you are expecting a great speech, then that is a bad thing. For I wrote the speech myself, and I am sure that what I'm going to say will lead to bad things for me. But, as for the matter at hand, I will just have to risk it.

original: Be it known to you,   as it is very well, I was lately here  in the end of a displeasing   play to pray your patience  for it and to promise you a better.
translation: Hopefully you will know that I was here on this stage recently at the end of another annoying play to ask you to have patience with it, and to promise you a better play next time.

original: I meant indeed to pay you with this, which, if like an ill   venture it come  unluckily home, I break, and you, my gentle   creditors,  lose.
translation: I was hoping to pay you off with this one, but if that didn't work, then I'm just like a businessman coming home from an unsuccessful trading trip—I have broken my promise and gone bankrupt. And you, my lovely creditors, have lost out.

original: Here I promised you I would be, and here I   commit  my body to your mercies. Bate me some, and I will   pay you some, and, as most debtors do, promise you   infinitely.
translation: I promised you that I would be here, and so here I will give myself up to your mercy. Let me off, and I promise I will pay you back at some point. That's what most people in debt do, they just keep promising to pay next time.

original: And so I kneel down before you, but, indeed, to   pray for  the Queen.
translation: So I will kneel down before you, but not to beg you, but to pray for the Queen.

original: If my tongue cannot entreat you to acquit me,  will you   command me to use my legs? And yet that were but light   payment, to dance out of your debt. But a good  conscience   will make any possible satisfaction, and so  would I.
translation: If my words can't convince you to forgive me, then maybe you will let me try dancing? That would be easy, if you could dance your way out of your debt. But anyone with a good conscience will make sure that they repay their debt, and I plan on doing the same.

original: All the   gentlewomen here have forgiven me; if  the gentlemen will   not, then the gentlemen do not agree  with the gentlewomen,   which was never seen before in such an assembly.
translation: All the women here have forgiven me. If the men will not forgive me, then the men don't agree with the women—and I think that would be the first time that's happened in a theater audience.

original: One word more, I beseech you: if you be not too much   cloyed with fat meat, our humble author will  continue the   story, with Sir John in it, and make you  merry with fair   Katherine of France
translation: One thing more, please. If this fat flesh hasn't clogged you up too much already, then our author will continue the story in his next play,  with Sir John in it , and entertain you with the story of the beautiful  Catherine of France .

original: , where, for anything  I know, Falstaff   shall die of a sweat, unless already he  be killed with your   hard opinions;
translation: As far as I know, Falstaff is going to die of some kind of sweating fever—if he hasn't already been killed off because of your negative opinions of him from this play.

original: for Oldcastle died a  martyr, and this is not   the man. My tongue is weary; when my legs are too, I will   bid you good night.
translation: Let it be said that  Oldcastle  died a martyr, and so he is nothing like this man at all. My tongue is tired now, and so are my legs. This is where I say good night to you all.

original: Oh, for a muse of fire that would ascend   The brightest heaven of invention!
translation: I wish I had a  goddess made out of fire  to lead to me to  the greatest heights of imagination !

original: A kingdom for a stage, princes to act,   And monarchs to behold the swelling scene!
translation: And that I had a kingdom to use as a stage, princes to act the play, and monarchs to watch the glorious show!

original: Then should the warlike Harry, like himself,   Assume the port of Mars,
translation: Then the great fighter Henry would look like himself or rather like Mars, the god of war.

original: and at his heels,   Leashed in like hounds, should famine, sword, and fire   Crouch for employment.
translation: Starvation, violence, and fire would follow him on leashes like dogs, waiting for his instructions.

original: But pardon, gentles all,   The flat unraisèd spirits that hath dared   On this unworthy scaffold to bring forth   So great an object.
translation: But forgive, gentlemen, the ordinary people who dare to act out such a great subject matter on this unworthy stage

original: Can this cockpit hold   The vasty fields of France? Or may we cram   Within this wooden   O   the very casques   That did affright the air at Agincourt?
translation: . Can this stage the size of a  cockfighting ring  hold the huge fields of France? Or can we stuff the helmets that terrified even the air itself at the Battle of Agincourt into this  wooden  O ?

original: O pardon, since a crookèd figure may   Attest in little place a million,
translation: Oh forgive us, since when you're writing you can abbreviate a million into a little squiggle.

original: And let us, ciphers to this great account,   On your imaginary forces work.
translation: Let us, zeros in this huge bank account, work on your imagination.

original: Suppose within the girdle of these walls   Are now confined two mighty monarchies   Whose high uprearèd and abutting fronts   The perilous narrow ocean parts asunder.
translation: Pretend that there are two powerful monarchies shut into these walls, threatening violence to each other but separated by a dangerous, narrow ocean.

original: Piece out our imperfections with your thoughts.
translation: Make up for what our version lacks by filling in the rest with your own thoughts.

original: Into a thousand parts divide one man,   And make imaginary puissance.
translation: Pretend that one man stands for a thousand so that you have a whole imaginary army.

original: Think, when we talk of horses, that you see them   Printing their proud hoofs i' th' receiving earth,
translation: When we talk about horses, pretend you see them stamping their proud hooves into the soft earth.

original: For ’tis your thoughts that now must deck our kings,   Carry them here and there, jumping o'er times,   Turning th' accomplishment of many years   Into an hour-glass;
translation: Your  minds have to dress our kings, carry them here and there, jump forward in time, and imagine that several years have passed within one hour.

original: for the which supply,   Admit me chorus to this history;
translation: To help you, let me narrate this story.

original: Who, prologue-like, your humble patience pray   Gently to hear, kindly to judge our play.
translation: Like a prologue in a book, I ask you to hear our play patiently and judge it kindly.

original: My lord, I’ll tell you that self bill is urged   Which in th' eleventh year of the last king’s reign   Was like,
translation: My lord, they're suggesting the same bill again now that seemed likely to pass in the eleventh year of the  last king's  reign.

original: and had indeed against us passed   But that the scambling and unquiet time   Did push it out of farther question.
translation: It would have been passed, except that it was forgotten about in the trouble and confusion of that time.

original: But how, my lord, shall we resist it now?
translation: What will we do? Should we resist it now?

original: It must be thought on.
translation: We have to think about this.

original: If it pass against us,   We lose the better half of our possession,   For all the temporal lands which men devout   By testament have given to the Church   Would they strip from us, being valued thus:
translation: If it passes we'll lose more than half of what we own because they will take from us all the land that religious men gave to the church in their wills.

original: “As much as would maintain, to the King’s honor,   Full fifteen earls and fifteen hundred knights,   Six thousand and two hundred good esquires;
translation: This is how much they would take: "Enough to maintain honorably fifteen earls, fifteen hundred knights, six thousand and two hundred gentlemen,

original: And, to relief of lazars and weak age   Of indigent faint souls past corporal toil,   A hundred almshouses right well supplied;
translation: and one hundred well supplied poorhouses to help sick people and old people who can't work.

original: And to the coffers of the King besides,   A thousand pounds by th' year.”
translation: And a thousand pounds a year to the king."

original: Thus runs the bill.
translation: That's what the bill says.

original: This would drink deep.
translation: That bill would drink up a lot of our money.

original: 'Twould drink the cup and all.
translation: It would drink the cup as well: we'd be left with nothing.

original: But what prevention?
translation: What can we do to stop it?

original: The king is full of grace and fair regard.
translation: The king is generous and polite.

original: And a true lover of the holy Church.
translation: And a true supporter of the holy Church.

original: The courses of his youth promised it not.
translation: You wouldn't have predicted that from how he acted when he was young.

original: The breath no sooner left his father’s body   But that his wildness, mortified in him,   Seemed to die too.
translation: No sooner did his father die than it was as though his wildness froze and died too.

original: Yea, at that very moment   Consideration like an angel came   And whipped th' offending Adam out of him,   Leaving his body as a paradise   T' envelop and contain celestial spirits.
translation: At that very moment, thoughtfulness came to him like an angel and banished the sinful part of him, like Adam banished from Eden, so that his body was like a paradise where holy spirits lived.

original: Never was such a sudden scholar made,   Never came reformation in a flood   With such a heady currance scouring faults,
translation: No one ever became a scholar more quickly, and no one ever repented as suddenly, scrubbing out bad qualities,

original: Nor never Hydra-headed willfulness   So soon did lose his seat, and all at once,   As in this king.
translation: and no one ever got rid of their monstrous stubbornness as fast and as completely as this king did.

original: We are blessèd in the change.
translation: We're blessed that he changed in this way.

original: Hear him but reason in divinity   And, all-admiring, with an inward wish,   You would desire the King were made a prelate.
translation: Just listen to him talk about theology and, overwhelmed with admiration, you would wish the king could become a priest.

original: Hear him debate of commonwealth affairs,   You would say it hath been all in all his study.
translation: Listen to him talk about  politics  and you'd think that was the only thing he'd ever studied.

original: List his discourse of war, and you shall hear   A fearful battle rendered you in music.
translation: Listen to him talk about war, and it'll be like hearing a horrible battle turned into beautiful music.

original: Turn him to any cause of policy,   The Gordian knot of it he will unloose   Familiar as his garter;
translation: Get him to talk about his policies, and he'll  make the most complicated problems seem simple .

original: that, when he speaks,   The air, a chartered libertine, is still,   And the mute wonder lurketh in men’s ears   To steal his sweet and honeyed sentences;
translation: When he talks, he makes even the air itself, which is a well-known flirt, stand still, and men become amazed to hear his sweet and beautiful sentences.

original: So that the art and practic part of life   Must be the mistress to this theoric;
translation: He must have spent a lot of time studying arts and practical applications of them to be able to speak this way.

original: Which is a wonder how his Grace should glean it,   Since his addiction was to courses vain,   His companies unlettered, rude, and shallow,   His hours filled up with riots, banquets, sports,
translation: It's amazing that he's learned so many things, since he used to waste all his time with illiterate, rough, and shallow friends and spend his hours causing public disturbances, feasting, and playing games.

original: And never noted in him any study,   Any retirement, any sequestration   From open haunts and popularity.
translation: I never saw him study anything or even spend time privately, away from public spaces filled with people.

original: The strawberry grows underneath the nettle,   And wholesome berries thrive and ripen best   Neighbored by fruit of baser quality;
translation: Strawberries grow under  nettles , and the healthiest berries grow and ripen best when they're next to a lower kind of fruit.

original: And so the Prince obscured his contemplation   Under the veil of wildness, which, no doubt,   Grew like the summer grass, fastest by night,   Unseen yet crescive in his faculty.
translation: The Prince hid his thoughts under a mask of wildness, and no doubt his learning was like summer grass in that it grew fastest at night, unseen but flourishing.

original: It must be so, for miracles are ceased,
translation: That must be true because there are no miracles anymore,

original: And therefore we must needs admit the means   How things are perfected.
translation: so we have to think that there's a cause for things becoming perfect.

original: But, my good lord,   How now for mitigation of this bill   Urged by the Commons?
translation: But, my lord, what will we do about this bill the House of Commons wants to pass?

original: Doth his Majesty   Incline to it or no?
translation: Does his Majesty agree with it or not?

original: He seems indifferent,   Or rather swaying more upon our part   Than cherishing th' exhibitors against us;
translation: He seems not to care, or maybe he's a little more on our side than the people presenting this bill against us.

original: For I have made an offer to his Majesty—   Upon our spiritual convocation   And in regard of causes now in hand,   Which I have opened to his Grace at large,   As touching France—
translation: That's because I made an offer to his Majesty —in light of the issues surrounding France now at hand—

original: to give a greater sum   Than ever at one time the clergy yet   Did to his predecessors part withal.
translation: to give him a larger amount of money than the church ever gave to any king before him .

original: How did this offer seem received, my lord?
translation: How did he seem to feel about this offer, my lord?

original: With good acceptance of his Majesty—   Save that there was not time enough to hear,
translation: He seemed to want to accept it,  except that there wasn't enough time to hear,

original: As I perceived his Grace would fain have done,   The severals and unhidden passages   Of his true titles to some certain dukedoms,
translation: as I saw he would have liked to do, about the details and clear proofs of his ownership of some dukedoms

original: And generally to the crown and seat of France,   Derived from Edward, his great-grandfather.
translation: and especially of the crown and throne of France, which he inherited from Edward, his great-grandfather.

original: What was th' impediment that broke this off?
translation: What was it that interrupted this?

original: The French ambassador upon that instant   Craved audience.
translation: At that moment the French ambassador wanted to see him.

original: And the hour, I think, is come   To give him hearing. Is it four o'clock?
translation: And I think the time has come to hear him. Is it four o'clock?

original: It is.
translation: It is.

original: Then go we in to know his embassy,
translation: Then let's go in to hear his message,

original: Which I could with a ready guess declare   Before the Frenchman speak a word of it.
translation: which I can easily guess before he says a word of it.

original: I’ll wait upon you, and I long to hear it.
translation: I'll go with you, and am eager to hear it.

original: Where is my gracious lord of Canterbury?
translation: Where is the lord of Canterbury?

original: Not here in presence.
translation: Not here in the throne room.

original: Send for him, good uncle.
translation: Send for him, dear uncle.

original: Shall we call in th' ambassador, my liege?
translation: Should we call in the ambassador, your Highness?

original: Not yet, my cousin. We would be resolved, Before we hear him, of some things of weight That task our thoughts concerning us and France.
translation: Not yet, cousin. We should make a decision before we hear from him about some important things I have been thinking about concerning us and France.

original: God and his angels guard your sacred throne And make you long become it.
translation: May God and his angels guard your holy throne and keep you on it for a long time.

original: Sure we thank you.   My learnèd lord, we pray you to proceed   And justly and religiously unfold   Why the law Salic that they have in France   Or should or should not bar us in our claim.
translation: Thank you.  Wise lord, please tell us truly and religiously why the Salic law that they have in France either does or does not stand in the way of my claim to the throne.

original: And God forbid, my dear and faithful lord,   That you should fashion, wrest, or bow your reading,   Or nicely charge your understanding soul   With opening titles miscreate, whose right   Suits not in native colors with the truth;
translation: And God forbid, dear and faithful nobleman, that you twist your interpretation out of shape or make up minor distinctions that don't lead to the truth.

original: For God doth know how many now in health   Shall drop their blood in approbation   Of what your reverence shall incite us to.
translation: Because God knows how many healthy people will shed their life's blood for this business of yours.

original: Therefore take heed how you impawn our person,   How you awake our sleeping sword of war.
translation: So be careful about what you put me under the obligation of doing and about encouraging us to go to war when we are now at peace.

original: We charge you in the name of God, take heed,   For never two such kingdoms did contend   Without much fall of blood,
translation: In the name of God, I'm ordering you to be careful, because two such kingdoms as England and France never fought without a lot of bloodshed.

original: whose guiltless drops   Are every one a woe, a sore complaint   'Gainst him whose wrong gives edge unto the swords   That make such waste in brief mortality.
translation: Each innocent drop of blood is a tragedy, and each one is a terrible blame to the person who begins the fight that takes so many lives, when life is so short already.

original: Under this conjuration, speak, my lord,   For we will hear, note, and believe in heart   That what you speak is in your conscience washed   As pure as sin with baptism.
translation: Now that I've said this, speak, my lord. I will hear, pay attention to, and believe completely that you say the things you do with a conscience as innocent as a baby's that has just been baptized.

original: Then hear me, gracious sovereign, and you peers   That owe yourselves, your lives, and services   To this imperial throne.
translation: Then listen to me, kind king, and you lords who owe your lives and duties to his power.

original: There is no bar   To make against your Highness' claim to France   But this, which they produce from Pharamond:   “In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant”   (No woman shall succeed in Salic land),
translation: There is nothing standing in the way of your Highness's claim to France except this, which they found in the writings of Pharamond:  “In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant”  (no woman will inherit anything in the Salic land).

original: Which Salic land the French unjustly gloze   To be the realm of France, and Pharamond   The founder of this law and female bar.
translation: Wrongly, the French say that the Salic land is the country of France, and that Pharamond is the inventor of this law keeping women from inheriting.

original: Yet their own authors faithfully affirm   That the land Salic is in Germany,   Between the floods of Sala and of Elbe,   Where Charles the Great, having subdued the Saxons,   There left behind and settled certain French,
translation: But their scholars write truthfully that the Salic land is in Germany, between the rivers Sala and Elbe, where Charles the Great defeated the Saxons and left some French men there to settle the land.

original: Who, holding in disdain the German women   For some dishonest manners of their life,   Established then this law: to wit, no female   Should be inheritrix in Salic land,
translation: They, looking down on the German women because of their dirty way of life, made this law then: that no woman should inherit anything in the Salic land.

original: Which “Salic,” as I said, ’twixt Elbe and Sala   Is at this day in Germany called Meissen.   Then doth it well appear the Salic law   Was not devisèd for the realm of France,
translation: As I said, the "Salic land" is in Germany between the Elbe and Sala and is now called Meissen. So it's clear that the Salic law was not made for the country of France.

original: Nor did the French possess the Salic land   Until four hundred one and twenty years   After defunction of King Pharamond,   Idly supposed the founder of this law;   Who died within the year of our redemption   Four hundred twenty-six; and Charles the Great   Subdued the Saxons and did seat the French   Beyond the river Sala in the year   Eight hundred five.
translation: The French didn't even own the Salic land until four hundred and twenty-one years after King Pharamond's death, who was wrongly thought to be the inventor of this law. He died in the year 426 AD and Charles the Great defeated the Saxons and settled the French beyond the river Sala in the year 805.

original: Besides, their writers say,   King Pepin, which deposèd Childeric,   Did, as heir general, being descended   Of Blithild, which was daughter to King Clothair,   Make claim and title to the crown of France.
translation: Besides, their writers say that King Pepin, who took the throne from Childeric, was descended from Blithild, King Clothair's daughter, and laid claim to the crown of France.

original: Hugh Capet also, who usurped the crown   Of Charles the duke of Lorraine, sole heir male   Of the true line and stock of Charles the Great,   To find his title with some shows of truth,   Though in pure truth it was corrupt and naught,
translation: Hugh Capet also, who took the crown from Charles the duke of Lorraine, the only male heir descended from Charles the Great, claimed to be the heir of the Lady Lingare, daughter of Charlemagne, who was the son of Emperor Lewis, who was the son of Charles the Great. He said this so he would seem to have a claim to the title of king, but he actually invented this and it was worth nothing as proof.

original: Conveyed himself as th' heir to th' Lady Lingare,   Daughter to Charlemagne, who was the son   To Lewis the Emperor, and Lewis the son   Of Charles the Great. Also King Lewis the Tenth,   Who was sole heir to the usurper Capet,   Could not keep quiet in his conscience,   Wearing the crown of France, till satisfied   That fair Queen Isabel, his grandmother,   Was lineal of the Lady Ermengare,   Daughter to Charles the foresaid duke of Lorraine,
translation: Also King Lewis the Tenth, who was the only heir to the greedy Capet, felt uneasy wearing the crown of France until he made sure that beautiful Queen Isabel, his grandmother, was descended from the Lady Ermengare, daughter of the aforementioned Charles duke of Lorraine.

original: By the which marriage the line of Charles the Great   Was reunited to the crown of France.
translation: By their marriage the family of Charles the Great got the crown of France back.

original: So that, as clear as is the summer’s sun,   King Pepin’s title and Hugh Capet’s claim,   King Lewis his satisfaction, all appear   To hold in right and title of the female.
translation: So it's as clear as the sun on a summer day that King Pepin's, Hugh Capet's, and King Lewis's claims to the throne all depend on inheriting it from a woman.

original: So do the kings of France unto this day,   Howbeit they would hold up this Salic law   To bar your Highness claiming from the female
translation: And that's what the kings of France do to this day, although they hold up this Salic law to keep you from making a claim based on inheriting from a woman, your Highness.

original: And rather choose to hide them in a net   Than amply to imbar their crooked titles   Usurped from you and your progenitors.
translation: They're hiding the truth to protect the power that they stole from you and your ancestors.

original: May I with right and conscience make this claim?
translation: Is it right for me to make this claim, and can I do it in good conscience?

original: The sin upon my head, dread sovereign,
translation: May I be punished instead of you, your highness, if not.

original: For in the Book of Numbers is it writ:   “When the man dies, let the inheritance   Descend unto the daughter.”
translation: It's written in the Book of Numbers in the Bible: "When a man dies, his daughter should inherit his estate."

original: Gracious lord,   Stand for your own, unwind your bloody flag,   Look back into your mighty ancestors.
translation: Kind king, stand up for what's yours, take out your blood-covered battle-flag, think back to your powerful ancestors.

original: Go, my dread lord, to your great-grandsire’s tomb,   From whom you claim.
translation: Go, powerful king, to your great-grandfather's tomb, from whom you inherited the throne.

original: Invoke his warlike spirit   And your great-uncle’s, Edward the Black Prince,   Who on the French ground played a tragedy,   Making defeat on the full power of France
translation: Pray to his war-like ghost and that of your great-uncle,  Edward the Black Prince , who performed a tragedy on French soil and defeated the entire army of France

original: Whiles his most mighty father on a hill   Stood smiling to behold his lion’s whelp   Forage in blood of French nobility.
translation: while his strong father stood on a hill smiling to see his lion cub shed the blood of French nobles.

original: O noble English, that could entertain   With half their forces the full pride of France   And let another half stand laughing by,   All out of work and cold for action!
translation: Oh noble Englishmen, who could fight with half their army the whole army of France and let the other half stand by laughing, with no work to do!

original: Awake remembrance of these valiant dead   And with your puissant arm renew their feats.
translation: Remember these brave dead men and do the same things they did yourself.

original: You are their heir, you sit upon their throne,   The blood and courage that renownèd them   Runs in your veins;
translation: You are their heir, you sit on their throne, and the blood and courage that made them famous runs in your veins.

original: and my thrice-puissant liege   Is in the very May-morn of his youth,   Ripe for exploits and mighty enterprises.
translation: My extremely powerful king is a young man ready for adventures and great deeds.

original: Your brother kings and monarchs of the earth   Do all expect that you should rouse yourself
translation: Your fellow kings all expect you to get ready to fight

original: As did the former lions of your blood.
translation: like your relatives the former lion-like kings.

original: They know your Grace hath cause and means and might;   So hath your Highness.
translation: They know you have a cause, resources, and power to fight. And you do.

original: Never king of England   Had nobles richer, and more loyal subjects,
translation: No king of England ever had richer nobles and more loyal subjects.

original: Whose hearts have left their bodies here in England   And lie pavilioned in the fields of France.
translation: It's as if your subjects' hearts have already left their bodies here in England and are now attacking France.

original: Oh, let their bodies follow, my dear liege,   With blood and sword and fire to win your right,
translation: Let their bodies follow, my dear king, to fight for your rights with blood and sword and fire.

original: In aid whereof we of the spiritualty   Will raise your Highness such a mighty sum   As never did the clergy at one time   Bring in to any of your ancestors.
translation: We in the church will raise such a huge sum to help you, your Highness—larger than any the church ever brought to one of your ancestors at once.

original: We must not only arm t' invade the French,
translation: We must not only prepare to attack the French

original: But lay down our proportions to defend   Against the Scot, who will make road upon us   With all advantages.
translation: but make plans to defend ourselves against the Scots, who will invade us and have the advantage.

original: They of those marches, gracious sovereign,
translation: Those who live in the  zones  along the border, good king,

original: Shall be a wall sufficient to defend   Our inland from the pilfering borderers.
translation: will be a sufficient wall to defend the inside of our country from the thieving people on the border.

original: We do not mean the coursing snatchers only,   But fear the main intendment of the Scot,   Who hath been still a giddy neighbor to us.
