translation: I don't just mean the thieves who attack randomly but the main army of the Scots, who have always been an unpredictable neighbor to us.

original: For you shall read that my great-grandfather   Never went with his forces into France   But that the Scot on his unfurnished kingdom   Came pouring like the tide into a breach   With ample and brim fullness of his force,
translation: You can read in books that my great-grandfather never took his army into France without the Scots pouring into his defenseless kingdom, as the ocean's tide rushes in to fill a gap, with their full force.

original: Galling the gleanèd land with hot assays,   Girding with grievous siege castles and towns,
translation: They attacked and looted, attacking towns and castles,

original: That England, being empty of defense,   Hath shook and trembled at th' ill neighborhood.
translation: so that England, with no one to defend it, shook with fear at these terrible neighbors.

original: She hath been then more feared than harmed, my liege,
translation: England was more afraid than hurt, my king.

original: For hear her but exampled by herself:   When all her chivalry hath been in France   And she a mourning widow of her nobles,
translation: Just listen to what England did in the past when all the soldiers were in France and the country was like a widow mourning her noblemen:

original: She hath herself not only well defended   But taken and impounded as a stray   The king of Scots,
translation: she not only defended herself well but captured and locked up the king of Scots like a stray dog.

original: whom she did send to France   To fill King Edward’s fame with prisoner kings
translation: She sent him to France to make King Edward famous for holding kings captive,

original: And make her chronicle as rich with praise   As is the ooze and bottom of the sea   With sunken wrack and sumless treasuries.
translation: so that historians would cover England in as much praise as the ooze at the bottom of the sea is covered in shipwrecks and priceless treasures.

original: But there’s a saying very old and true:   “If that you will France win,   Then with Scotland first begin.”
translation: But there's a very old and true saying: "If you want to win France, begin with Scotland."

original: For once the eagle England being in prey,   To her unguarded nest the weasel Scot   Comes sneaking and so sucks her princely eggs,
translation: Because when the eagle England is hunting for prey, the weasel Scot comes sneaking to her nest and eats her royal eggs,

original: Playing the mouse in absence of the cat,   To ’tame and havoc more than she can eat.
translation: like a mouse when the cat is gone that destroys what it can't eat.

original: It follows, then, the cat must stay at home.
translation: So it would follow that the cat must stay home.

original: Yet that is but a crushed necessity,   Since we have locks to safeguard necessaries   And pretty traps to catch the petty thieves.
translation: But that's a hasty conclusion, since we have locks to keep provisions safe and pretty traps to catch small thieves.

original: While that the armèd hand doth fight abroad,   Th' advisèd head defends itself at home.
translation: While the armed hand fights abroad, the wise head defends itself at home.

original: For government, though high and low and lower,   Put into parts, doth keep in one consent,   Congreeing in a full and natural close,   Like music.
translation: Even though a society has high and low and even lower parts, when they work together they work naturally in complete harmony, like in music.

original: Therefore doth heaven divide   The state of man in diverse functions,
translation: That's why God divides men into different groups

original: Setting endeavor in continual motion,   To which is fixèd as an aim or butt   Obedience;
translation: that work continually and whose  goal  is obedience.

original: for so work the honeybees,   Creatures that by a rule in nature teach   The act of order to a peopled kingdom.
translation: That's how bees work, animals who serve as examples of good order to the people in a kingdom.

original: They have a king and officers of sorts,   Where some like magistrates correct at home,   Others like merchants venture trade abroad,   Others like soldiers armèd in their stings   Make boot upon the summer’s velvet buds,   Which pillage they with merry march bring home   To the tent royal of their emperor,
translation: They have a king and professions of a kind. Some like judges impose the law at home, others like merchants go abroad to trade, others like soldiers armed with stings loot the soft summer flowers and happily march back with what they capture to the royal tent of their emperor.

original: Who, busied in his majesty, surveys   The singing masons building roofs of gold,   The civil citizens kneading up the honey,   The poor mechanic porters crowding in   Their heavy burdens at his narrow gate,   The sad-eyed justice with his surly hum   Delivering o'er to executors pale   The lazy yawning drone.
translation: He, busy in his royal work, watches the singing builders build golden roofs, the citizens knead honey, the poor porters crowd with their heavy loads through his narrow gate, the sad-eyed judge buzz grumpily and hand over a lazy yawning drone to pale executioners.

original: I this infer:   That many things, having full reference   To one consent, may work contrariously,
translation: I infer this: that many things governed by one goal can work in contrary ways.

original: As many arrows loosèd several ways   Come to one mark, as many ways meet in one town,   As many fresh streams meet in one salt sea,   As many lines close in the dial’s center,
translation: Just as many arrows shot in different directions can hit one mark, many roads meet in one town, many fresh-waters rivers end in a salty sea, many lines meet at the center of a circle—

original: So may a thousand actions, once afoot,   End in one purpose, and be all well borne   Without defeat.
translation: in this way, a thousand actions once begun will end in one purpose, and they will be done well and we will not be defeated.

original: Therefore to France, my liege!   Divide your happy England into four,   Whereof take you one quarter into France,   And you withal shall make all Gallia shake.
translation: So go to France, my king! Divide your happy English people into four parts and take a quarter to France, and you will shake up all of France.

original: If we, with thrice such powers left at home,   Cannot defend our own doors from the dog,   Let us be worried, and our nation lose   The name of hardiness and policy.
translation: If we, with three times that number left at home, can't defend our own homes from the dog, let us be mauled and let our country lose its reputation for toughness and strategy.

original: Call in the messengers sent from the Dauphin.
May’t please your Majesty to give us leave   Freely to render what we have in charge,
translation: May I have permission from your Majesty to speak freely what I was told to say,

original: Or shall we sparingly show you far off   The Dauphin’s meaning and our embassy?
translation: or should I water it down and summarize the Dauphin's message?

original: We are no tyrant, but a Christian king,   Unto whose grace our passion is as subject   As is our wretches fettered in our prisons.
translation: I am no tyrant, but a Christian king, and my emotions are as much under my control as the miserable people tied up in my prisons are.

original: Therefore with frank and with uncurbèd plainness   Tell us the Dauphin’s mind.
translation: So tell me what the Dauphin says honestly and completely.

original: Thus, then, in few:   Your Highness, lately sending into France,   Did claim some certain dukedoms in the right   Of your great predecessor, King Edward the Third;
translation: So, in few words: Your Highness lately wrote to France to lay claim to some dukedoms in the name of your great ancestor,  King Edward the Third .

original: In answer of which claim, the prince our master   Says that you savor too much of your youth   And bids you be advised there’s naught in France   That can be with a nimble galliard won.
translation: In answer to this claim, our master the prince says that you show your youth and wants you to know that there's nothing in France that can be won by dancing well.

original: You cannot revel into dukedoms there.
translation: You can't party your way into dukedoms there.

original: He therefore sends you, meeter for your spirit,   This tun of treasure,
translation: So he sends you this chest of treasure as a better fit for your personality,

original: and, in lieu of this,   Desires you let the dukedoms that you claim   Hear no more of you. This the Dauphin speaks.
translation: and in return for this asks you not to mention the dukedoms you lay claim to anymore. That's what the Dauphin said.

original: What treasure, uncle?
translation: What is the treasure, uncle?

original: Tennis balls, my liege.
translation: Tennis balls, my king.

original: We are glad the Dauphin is so pleasant with us.   His present and your pains we thank you for.
translation: I'm glad the Dauphin is so light-hearted around me. Thank you for his present and the trouble you've taken.

original: When we have matched our rackets to these balls,   We will in France, by God’s grace, play a set   Shall strike his father’s crown into the hazard.
translation: When we have hit these balls with our rackets, we will (if God wills it) play a set that will put his father's crown into play.

original: Tell him he hath made a match with such a wrangler   That all the courts of France will be disturbed   With chases.
translation: Tell him he's playing a match with such a fighter that we'll be chasing balls through all the courts of France.

original: And we understand him well,   How he comes o'er us with our wilder days,   Not measuring what use we made of them.
translation: I understand him well when he holds my wilder days over me, not considering what I learned from them.

original: We never valued this poor seat of England   And therefore, living hence, did give ourself   To barbarous license, as ’tis ever common   That men are merriest when they are from home.
translation: I never used to value poor England and, living outside of it, spent all my time behaving badly, as men always do when they're away from home.

original: But tell the Dauphin I will keep my state,   Be like a king, and show my sail of greatness   When I do rouse me in my throne of France,
translation: But tell the Dauphin I will keep calm like a king should, and show my greatness when I rise to the throne of France

original: For that I have laid by my majesty   And plodded like a man for working days.
translation: because I have set aside my dignity and worked like a manual laborer.

original: But I will rise there with so full a glory   That I will dazzle all the eyes of France,   Yea, strike the Dauphin blind to look on us.
translation: But I will rise to the throne with such glory that I will dazzle all the eyes in France, so that it will strike the Dauphin blind to look at me.

original: And tell the pleasant prince this mock of his   Hath turned his balls to gun-stones, and his soul   Shall stand sore chargèd for the wasteful vengeance   That shall fly with them;
translation: And tell the light-hearted prince that this joke of his has turned these balls into bullets, and he will be to blame for the wasteful revenge that will fly with them.

original: for many a thousand widows   Shall this his mock mock out of their dear husbands,   Mock mothers from their sons, mock castles down,   And some are yet ungotten and unborn   That shall have cause to curse the Dauphin’s scorn.
translation: For this joke will joke many thousands of widows out of their beloved husbands, joke mothers out of their sons, joke castles down, and some people are not yet conceived and born who will have good reason to regret the Dauphin's jokes.

original: But this lies all within the will of God,   To whom I do appeal, and in whose name   Tell you the Dauphin I am coming on,   To venge me as I may and to put forth   My rightful hand in a well-hallowed cause.
translation: But this will all only happen if God wishes it to, and I appeal to him. Tell the Dauphin it's in God's name that I am coming to take revenge if I can and to fight for a holy cause.

original: So get you hence in peace. And tell the Dauphin   His jest will savor but of shallow wit   When thousands weep more than did laugh at it.
—Convey them with safe conduct.—
translation: [To attendants]  Escort them safely back.

original: Fare you well.
translation: [To AMBASSADOR]  Goodbye.

original: This was a merry message.
translation: That was a funny message.

original: We hope to make the sender blush at it.
translation: I hope I'll make the sender ashamed of it.

original: Therefore, my lords, omit no happy hour   That may give furth'rance to our expedition;
translation: So, my lords, don't waste any time you could use to prepare our expedition,

original: For we have now no thought in us but France,   Save those to God, that run before our business.
translation: because I don't have any thoughts except about France and our business there, and of course God.

original: Therefore let our proportions for these wars   Be soon collected, and all things thought upon   That may with reasonable swiftness add   More feathers to our wings.
translation: So let our troops for these wars be gathered soon, and all the things taken care of that can be done quickly to give us the advantage.

original: For, God before,   We’ll chide this Dauphin at his father’s door.
translation: For, with God on our side, I'll scold this Dauphin in his father's own house.

original: Therefore let every man now task his thought,   That this fair action may on foot be brought.
translation: So let every man now start thinking what to do to get this expedition going.

original: Now all the youth of England are on fire,   And silken dalliance in the wardrobe lies.
translation: Now all the English young people are on fire and have set aside their love affairs along with their fancy clothes.

original: Now thrive the armorers, and honor’s thought   Reigns solely in the breast of every man.
translation: Now the armor-makers are doing good business, and every man thinks only about honor.

original: They sell the pasture now to buy the horse,   Following the mirror of all Christian kings   With wingèd heels, as English Mercurys.
translation: They're selling their land to buy horses, so they can follow the greatest of all Christian kings with winged heels as though they were English  Mercurys .

original: For now sits Expectation in the air   And hides a sword, from hilts unto the point,   With crowns imperial, crowns and coronets   Promised to Harry and his followers.
translation: Anticipation is sitting in the air, stacking all the different kinds of crowns promised to Harry and his followers on a sword.

original: The French, advised by good intelligence   Of this most dreadful preparation,   Shake in their fear, and with pale policy   Seek to divert the English purposes.
translation: The French, whose spies told them about these frightening preparations, shake with fear and try to use frightened politics to change the Englishmen's minds.

original: O England, model to thy inward greatness,   Like little body with a mighty heart,   What might’st thou do, that honor would thee do,   Were all thy children kind and natural!
translation: Oh England, on the outside you are like a tiny model of the greatness you hold inside you, like a little body with a huge heart. What things you could do that would do you honor, if only all your children were kind and normal!

original: But see, thy fault France hath in thee found out,   A nest of hollow bosoms, which he fills   With treacherous crowns, and three corrupted men—   One, Richard, Earl of Cambridge, and the second,   Henry, Lord Scroop of Masham, and the third,   Sir Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland—
translation: But see, the king of France has found your only fault, a nest of empty hearts which he fills with traitorous  coins.  There are three corrupt men. One is Richard, Earl of Cambridge, the second, Henry, Lord Scroop of Marsham, and the third, Sir Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland.

original: Have, for the gilt of France (Oh, guilt indeed!),   Confirmed conspiracy with fearful France,   And by their hands this grace of kings must die,   If hell and treason hold their promises,   Ere he take ship for France, and in Southampton.
translation: They are in a conspiracy with France and will kill this best of kings with their own hands in Southampton before he sails for France, if  Hell and Treason  keep their promises.

original: Linger your patience on, and we’ll digest   Th' abuse of distance, force a play.
translation: Be patient for a while longer, and we'll  summarize  the time between this act and the last and force our play onward.

original: The sum is paid, the traitors are agreed,   The king is set from London, and the scene   Is now transported, gentles, to Southampton.
translation: The money is paid, the traitors have agreed to a plan, the king has left London, and the scene has now changed, gentlemen and ladies, to Southampton.

original: There is the playhouse now, there must you sit,   And thence to France shall we convey you safe   And bring you back, charming the narrow seas   To give you gentle pass;
translation: There is the theater now, you must sit there, and from there we will carry you safely to France and bring you back, enchanting the narrow seas to give you a gentle journey.

original: for, if we may,   We’ll not offend one stomach with our play.
translation: If possible, we won't make anyone seasick with our play.

original: But, till the king come forth, and not till then,   Unto Southampton do we shift our scene.
translation: But, until the king comes out, and not until then, we're changing our scene to Southampton.

original: Well met, Corporal Nym.
Good morrow, Lieutenant Bardolph.
What, are Ancient Pistol and you friends yet?
For my part, I care not. I say little, but when time  shall serve, there shall be smiles; but that shall be as it may.
translation: I don't personally care. I don't say much, but when the time is right there will be smiles. But that will go however it goes.

original: I dare not fight, but I will wink and hold out  mine iron. It is a simple one, but what though?
translation: I don't dare to fight, but I'll wink and hold out  my sword. It's a simple one, but what of that?

original: It will  toast cheese, and it will endure cold as another man’s  sword will, and there’s an end.
translation: It will toast cheese and endure cold as well as any other man's sword, and that's the end of the matter.

original: I will bestow a breakfast to make you friends; and  we’ll be all three sworn brothers to France. Let ’t be  so, good Corporal Nym.
translation: I will give you breakfast to make you friends, and all three of us, having sworn to be like brothers to each other, will go to France. Agree to that, good Corporal Nym.

original: Faith, I will live so long as I may, that’s the certain of it.
translation: Well, I will live as long as I can, that's for sure.

original: And when I cannot live any longer, I will do as  I may.
translation: And when I can't live any more, I'll do what I can.

original: That is my rest; that is the rendezvous of it.
translation: That's all I have to say, that's my goodbye to that issue.

original: It is certain, corporal, that he is married to Nell  Quickly, and certainly she did you wrong, for you were  troth-plight to her.
I cannot tell. Things must be as they may.
translation: I can't tell. Things must be however they can be.

original: Men may  sleep, and they may have their throats about them at  that time, and some say knives have edges.
translation: Men can sleep, and they can have their throats on them at that time, and some people say knives have edges.

original: It must be as it may. Though patience be a tired mare, yet she will  plod.
translation: It must be however it can. Though Patience is a tired old horse, she'll keep plodding on.

original: There must be conclusions. Well, I cannot tell.
translation: There must be conclusions. Well, I can't tell.

original: Here comes Ancient Pistol and his wife. Good corporal,  be patient here.—How now, mine host Pistol?
translation: Here comes Ancient Pistol—and his wife. Good corporal, wait here.  How are you, innkeeper Pistol?

original: Base tyke, call’st thou me host? Now, by this hand, I swear, I scorn the term, Nor shall my Nell keep lodgers.
translation: You low peasant, are you calling me an innkeeper? I swear by this hand, I hate the word, and my Nell won't take lodgers.

original: No, by my troth, not long, for we cannot lodge and  board a dozen or fourteen gentlewomen that live honestly by the prick of their needles
translation: No, I swear, not long, because we can't give room and board to a dozen or fourteen gentlewomen who make an honest living by  sewing

original: but it will be thought we keep a bawdy house straight.
translation: without people immediately thinking we run a brothel.

original: Oh, well-a-day, Lady! If he be not hewn now, we shall  see willful adultery and murder committed.
translation: Oh no! If he's not cut down now, we will see willful adultery and murder committed.

original: Good lieutenant, good corporal, offer nothing here.
translation: Good lieutenant, good corporal, don't fight here.

original: Pish!
translation: Pshaw!

original: Pish for thee, Iceland dog, Thou prick-eared cur of Iceland!
translation: Pshaw for you, you Icelandic dog, you pointy-eared cur from Iceland!

original: Good Corporal Nym, show thy valor and put up your  sword.
translation: Good Corporal Nym, show your courage and put away your sword.

original: Will you shog off?    I would have you  solus  .
translation: Will you go away?  I want to see you solo.

original: “Solus,”   egregious dog?
translation: Solo , you shocking dog?

original: O viper vile,   The   solus   in thy most marvelous face,   The   solus   in thy teeth and in thy throat   And in thy hateful lungs, yea, in thy maw, perdy,   And, which is worse, within thy nasty mouth!
translation: Oh you disgusting snake,  solo  in your amazing face,  solo  in your teeth and your throat and in your hateful lungs, yes, in your jaws, by god, and, which is worse, inside your nasty mouth!

original: I do retort the   solus   in thy bowels,   For I can take, and Pistol’s cock is up,   And flashing fire will follow.
translation: I throw back the  solo  to your guts, because I can take it, and  Pistol's cocking his gun  at you, and the flash of him firing will follow.

original: I am not Barbason; you cannot conjure me.
translation: I am not a demon, you can't conjure me.

original: I have an  humor to knock you indifferently well.
translation: I feel like knocking you around pretty well.

original: If you grow foul  with me, Pistol, I will scour you with my rapier, as I  may, in fair terms.
translation: If you're rude with me, Pistol, I'll scrape you up with my sword as well as I can, fairly.

original: If you would walk off, I would prick your guts a little in good terms, as I may, and that’s  the humor of it.
translation: If you want to walk a little this way, I feel like stabbing your guts a little according to the rules, as well as I can, and that's the way it is.

original: O braggart vile and damnèd furious wight, The grave doth gape, and doting death is near. Therefore exhale.
translation: Oh you disgusting bragger and damned crazy man, the grave is waiting, and silly death is near. So exhale.

original: Hear me, hear me what I say: he that strikes the first  stroke, I’ll run him up to the hilts, as I am a soldier.  [ draws]
translation: Hear me, hear what I say: he who strikes the first hit, I'll stick my sword in him up to the hilt, I swear if I'm a soldier I'll do it.

original: An oath of mickle might, and fury shall abate. Give me thy fist, thy forefoot to me give. Thy spirits are most tall.
translation: A powerful oath, and anger will calm down. Give me your fist, give me your paw. You are in very high spirits.

original: I will cut thy throat one time or other in fair terms,  that is the humor of it.
translation: I will cut your throat sometime or other, fairly. That's the way it is.

original: Couple à gorge   , that is the word. I defy thee again.
translation: Couple à gorge ,  that's the French for "cut your throat". I challenge you again.

original: O hound of Crete, think’st thou my spouse to get?
translation: Oh you Cretan dog, do you think you'll get my spouse?

original: No, to the spital go,   And from the powd'ring tub of infamy   Fetch forth the lazar kite of Cressid’s kind,   Doll Tearsheet she by name, and her espouse.
translation: No, go to the charity hospital, and fetch the poor disgusting cheating predator,  Doll Tearsheet is her name, from the  sweating-tub for venereal diseases  and marry her.

original: I have, and I will hold, the quondam Quickly   For the only she, And—   pauca—   there’s enough. Go to.
translation: I have and will keep the woman formerly known as Quickly as my only woman, and - in few words - that's enough. Get going.

original: Mine host Pistol, you must come to my master and your  hostess.
translation: Innkeeper Pistol, you must come to my master, and your wife too.

original: He is very sick and would to bed.—
translation: He is very sick and wants to go to bed.

original: Good  Bardolph, put thy face between his sheets, and do the  office of a warming-pan. Faith, he’s very ill.
translation: Good Bardolph, put your  face  between his sheets and warm him as though you're a hot water bottle. Really, he's very sick.

original: Away, you rogue!
translation: Go away, you scamp!

original: By my troth, he’ll yield the crow a pudding one of  these days. The king has killed his heart. Good husband, come home presently.
Come, shall I make you two friends? We must to France  together. Why the devil should we keep knives to cut one another’s throats?
translation: Can I reconcile you two? We must go to France together. Why the devil should we keep knives to cut one another's throats with?

original: Let floods o'erswell and fiends for food howl on!
translation: Let the rivers flood and demons howl for food!

original: You’ll pay me the eight shillings I won of you at  betting?
translation: You'll pay me the eight shillings I won from you betting?

original: Base is the slave that pays.
translation: It's shameful to be a slave who pays his debts.

original: That now I will have—that’s the humor of it.
translation: No, I will have that money - that's the way it is.

original: As manhood shall compound. Push home.
translation: Our manhoods will clash. Stab well.

original: By this sword, he that makes the first thrust, I’ll  kill him. By this sword, I will.
translation: By this sword, I'll kill whoever hits first. By this sword, I will.

original: “Sword” is an oath, and oaths must have their course.
translation: "Sword" is an oath, and oaths are powerful.

original: Corporal Nym, an thou wilt be friends, be friends; an  thou wilt not, why then be enemies with me too.
translation: Corporal Nym, if you agree to be friends, be friends. If you won't, then I'm your enemy too.

original: Prithee, put up.
translation: Please, put away your sword.

original: A noble shalt thou have, and present pay,   And liquor likewise will I give to thee,   And friendship shall combine, and brotherhood.
translation: You'll have a gold coin, and soon, and I'll also give you liquor, and friendship will join us together, and brotherhood.

original: I’ll live by Nym, and Nym shall live by me.   Is not this just?
translation: I'll live my life for Nym, and Nym for me. Is this not fair?

original: For I shall subtler be   Unto the camp, and profits will accrue.   Give me thy hand.
translation: I will be  cunning  in camp and profits will heap up. Give me your hand.

original: I shall have my noble?
translation: I'll have my gold coin?

original: In cash, most justly paid.
translation: In cash, fairly paid.

original: Well, then, that’s the humor of ’t.
translation: Well, then, that's the way it is.

original: As ever you come of women, come in quickly to Sir John.
translation: If you were ever born from women, come in quickly to see Sir John.

original: Ah, poor heart, he is so shaked of a burning quotidian  tertian that it is most lamentable to behold. Sweet men, come to him.
translation: Oh, poor sweetheart, he's so shaken by a burning fever that it's tragic to see it. Sweet men, come see him.

original: The king hath run bad humors on the knight, that’s the  even of it.
translation: The king made him sick, that's the truth of it.

original: Nym, thou hast spoke the right. His heart is fracted and corroborate.
The king is a good king, but it must be as it may. He  passes some humors and careers.
translation: The king is a good king, but it must go however it can go. He gets strange ideas and runs away with them.

original: Let us condole the knight, for, lambkins, we will live.
translation: Let's grieve for the knight, for, my lambs, we will survive.

original: 'Fore God, his grace is bold to trust these traitors.
translation: By God, the king is brave to trust these traitors.

original: They shall be apprehended by and by.
translation: They will be arrested soon.

original: How smooth and even they do bear themselves,
translation: They're acting so calmly,

original: As if allegiance in their bosoms sat   Crownèd with faith and constant loyalty.
translation: as if Patriotism sat in their hearts crowned with faithfulness and loyalty.

original: The king hath note of all that they intend, By interception which they dream not of.
translation: They have no idea that the king found out what they mean to do, or how he did it.

original: Nay, but the man that was his bedfellow,   Whom he hath dulled and cloyed with gracious favors—
translation: Even the man who used to share a bed with him and who received so many gifts from him—

original: That he should, for a foreign purse, so sell   His sovereign’s life to death and treachery!
translation: how could he traitorously sell out his king for foreign money?

original: Now sits the wind fair, and we will aboard.
translation: Now the wind is blowing in the right direction so we'll board our ships.

original: —My Lord of Cambridge, and my kind Lord of Masham,   And you, my gentle knight, give me your thoughts.
translation: My lord of Cambridge and my kind Lord of Masham, and you, my dear knight, tell me your thoughts.

original: Think you not that the powers we bear with us   Will cut their passage through the force of France,   Doing the execution and the act   For which we have in head assembled them?
translation: Don't you think the troops I'm bringing with me will cut their way through the French army, doing exactly what I assembled them here to do?

original: No doubt, my liege, if each man do his best.
translation: No doubt, my king, if each man does his best.

original: I doubt not that, since we are well-persuaded   We carry not a heart with us from hence   That grows not in a fair consent with ours,
translation: I don't doubt that, since we all believe we're not bringing a single heart with us that doesn't wish the same thing we do.

original: Nor leave not one behind that doth not wish   Success and conquest to attend on us.
translation: Nor do we leave a single one behind that doesn't want us to win.

original: Never was monarch better feared and loved   Than is your Majesty.
translation: No monarch was ever more feared and loved than you, your majesty.

original: There’s not, I think, a subject   That sits in heart-grief and uneasiness   Under the sweet shade of your government.
translation: I don't think there's a single subject who sits sad or uneasy under the cool shade of your government.

original: True. Those that were your father’s enemies   Have steeped their galls in honey,
translation: True. Those who were your father's enemies have become  friends ,

original: and do serve you   With hearts create of duty and of zeal.
translation: and obey you with hearts full of duty and eagerness.

original: We therefore have great cause of thankfulness   And shall forget the office of our hand   Sooner
translation: That's why I have so much reason to be thankful and would sooner forget what my own hand did

original: than quittance of desert and merit   According to the weight and worthiness.
translation: than forget to give everyone exactly what they deserved.

original: So service shall with steelèd sinews toil,
translation: So those working for you will work even harder,

original: And labor shall refresh itself with hope   To do your Grace incessant services.
translation: and fuel themselves with the hope to be able to do you constant services.

original: We judge no less.—
translation: I think so too.

original: Uncle of Exeter,   Enlarge the man committed yesterday   That railed against our person.
translation: Uncle Exeter, free the man arrested yesterday for complaining about me.

original: We consider   It was excess of wine that set him on,   And on his more advice we pardon him.
translation: I think it was too much wine that made him do it, and I pardon him now he's had time to think.

original: That’s mercy, but too much security.
translation: That's mercy, but you're too confident.

original: Let him be punished, sovereign, lest example   Breed, by his sufferance, more of such a kind.
translation: Punish him so that other people won't follow his example, when they see you let him go.

original: Oh, let us yet be merciful.
translation: Oh, let me be merciful.

original: So may Your Highness, and yet punish, too.
translation: You can be, but you should also punish.

original: Sir, you show great mercy if you give him life After the taste of much correction.
translation: Sir, you would show great mercy by allowing him to live after punishing him terribly.

original: Alas, your too much love and care of me   Are heavy orisons 'gainst this poor wretch.
translation: You love and care for me too much, and that makes you speak against this poor man.

original: If little faults proceeding on distemper   Shall not be winked at, how shall we stretch our eye   When capital crimes, chewed, swallowed, and digested,   Appear before us?
translation: If small faults that come from drunkenness are not forgiven, how unmerciful will I have to be when I judge capital crimes planned in cold blood?

original: We’ll yet enlarge that man,   Though Cambridge, Scroop, and Grey, in their dear care   And tender preservation of our person,   Would have him punished.
translation: I'll let that man go anyway, even though Cambridge, Scroop, and Grey, with all their care and sweet concern for me, want him punished.

original: And now to our French causes.   Who are the late commissioners?
translation: Now, to the French business. Who was recently given a commission?

original: I one, my lord. Your Highness bade me ask for it today.
translation: I was, my lord. You told me to ask for that today.

original: So did you me, my liege.
translation: And you told me the same, my king.

original: And I, my royal sovereign.
translation: And me, my royal king.

original: Then, Richard, Earl of Cambridge, there is yours.   —There yours, Lord Scroop of Masham.   —And, sir knight, Grey of Northumberland, this same is  yours.
translation: Then, Richard, Earl of Cambridge, there's yours.  [Gives him a paper]   There's yours, Lord Scroop of Masham. [Gives him a paper]   And, sir, Grey of Northumberland, this one is yours.  [Gives him a paper]

original: —Read them, and know I know your worthiness.
translation: Read them, and know that I know what you deserve.

original: I do confess my fault, And do submit me to Your Highness' mercy.
translation: I confess my crime and beg Your Highness's mercy.

original: To which we all appeal.
translation: We all appeal to it.

original: The mercy that was quick in us but late   By your own counsel is suppressed and killed.
translation: According to your own advice, the mercy that was alive in me lately has been suppressed and killed.

original: You must not dare, for shame, to talk of mercy,   For your own reasons turn into your bosoms,   As dogs upon their masters, worrying you.
translation: Shame on you! You shouldn't dare to talk about mercy because your own arguments turn on you like dogs turning on their masters and attack you.

original: I arrest thee of high treason, by the name of   Richard, Earl of Cambridge.
translation: I arrest you of high treason, Richard, Earl of Cambridge.

original: —I arrest thee of high treason, by the name of   Henry, Lord Scroop of Masham.
translation: I arrest you of high treason, Henry, Lord Scroop of Masham.

original: —I arrest thee of high treason, by the name of   Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland.
translation: I arrest you of high treason, Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland.

original: Our purposes God justly hath discovered,   And I repent my fault more than my death,
translation: God has justly revealed our plots and I repent my crime more than my death.

original: Which I beseech Your Highness to forgive,   Although my body pay the price of it.
translation: I beg Your Highness to forgive it, although my body will pay the price of it.

original: For me, the gold of France did not seduce,   Although I did admit it as a motive   The sooner to effect what I intended;
translation: The French gold didn't seduce me, although I took it as an excuse to do what I wanted sooner.

original: But God be thankèd for prevention,   Which I in sufferance heartily will rejoice,   Beseeching God and you to pardon me.
translation: But may God be thanked for preventing us from acting. I will be happy about that while being tortured, asking God and you to pardon me.

original: Never did faithful subject more rejoice   At the discovery of most dangerous treason
translation: No faithful subject was more joyful at the discovery of dangerous treason

original: Than I do at this hour joy o'er myself,   Prevented from a damnèd enterprise.
translation: than I now am joyful that I was prevented from a damned action.

original: My fault, but not my body, pardon, sovereign.
translation: Pardon my crime, not my body, king.

original: God quit you in His mercy.
translation: May God be merciful on you.

original: Hear your sentence:   You have conspired against our royal person,   Joined with an enemy proclaimed, and from his coffers   Received the golden earnest of our death,
translation: Hear your sentence: you plotted against me, joined with a declared enemy, and from him received money to kill me.

original: Wherein you would have sold your king to slaughter,   His princes and his peers to servitude,   His subjects to oppression and contempt,   And his whole kingdom into desolation.
translation: You would have sold your king to death, his princes and nobles to slavery, his subjects to oppression and hatred, and his whole kingdom to destruction.

original: Touching our person, seek we no revenge,   But we our kingdom’s safety must so tender,   Whose ruin you have sought, that to her laws   We do deliver you.
translation: I don't look for revenge for myself, but I have to take care of the safety of my kingdom, which you wanted to ruin. So I deliver you over to its laws.

original: Get you therefore hence,   Poor miserable wretches, to your death,   The taste whereof God of His mercy give   You patience to endure, and true repentance   Of all your dear offences.
translation: Go to your deaths, poor miserable men. May God in His mercy give you patience to bear it, and true repentance for all your terrible sins.

original: Now, lords, for France, the enterprise whereof   Shall be to you as us, like glorious.
translation: Now, lords, let's go to France, where you and I will win glory.

original: We doubt not of a fair and lucky war,   Since God so graciously hath brought to light   This dangerous treason lurking in our way   To hinder our beginnings.
translation: I don't doubt it will be a beautiful and lucky war, since God so kindly has brought this terrible treason to light that was lurking in our way to stop us before we could begin.

original: We doubt not now   But every rub is smoothèd on our way.
translation: I don't doubt that every impediment has been removed from our journey.

original: Then forth, dear countrymen. Let us deliver   Our puissance into the hand of God,   Putting it straight in expedition.
translation: So, dear countrymen, let's go. Let's put our war into God's hands, and leave immediately.

original: Cheerly to sea. The signs of war advance.   No king of England if not king of France.
translation: Let's go cheerfully to sea. The war-flags are advancing. I'm no king of England if not also a king of France.

original: Prithee, honey-sweet husband, let me bring thee to  Staines.
No; for my manly heart doth earn.—Bardolph, be blithe.—
translation: No, because my manly heart is sad. Bardolph, cheer up.

original: Nym, rouse thy vaunting veins.—Boy, bristle thy courage up
translation: Nym, get your bragging blood flowing. Boy, get up your courage.

original: . For Falstaff, he is dead, and we must earn  therefore.
translation: Falstaff is dead, so we must be sad.

original: Would I were with him, wheresome'er he is, either in  heaven or in hell.
translation: I wish I were with him, wherever he is, either in heaven or in hell.

original: Nay, sure, he’s not in hell! He’s in Arthur’s bosom, if ever man went to Arthur’s bosom.
translation: No, he's surely not in hell! He's in  Arthur's bosom , if any man ever went to Arthur's bosom.

original: He made a finer end,  and went away an it had been any christom child.
translation: He had as good a death as any Christian child.

original: He  parted ev'n just between twelve and one, ev'n at the  turning o' th' tide; for after I saw him fumble with the sheets and play with flowers and smile upon his  finger’s end,
translation: He died between twelve and one, just as the tide was turning. I saw him fumble with the sheets as though he was playing with flowers, and smile at his fingers.

original: I knew there was but one way, for his nose was as sharp as a pen, and he told of green fields.
translation: I knew how it would go, because his nose was as sharp as the tip of a pen, and was talking about green fields.

original: “How now, Sir John?” quoth I. “What, man, be o' good  cheer!” So he cried out “God, God, God!” three or four  times.
translation: "What's wrong, Sir John?", I said. "Come on, man, cheer up!" So he called out "God, God, God!" three or four times.

original: Now I, to comfort him, bid him he should not  think of God. I hoped there was no need to trouble  himself with any such thoughts yet.
translation: To comfort him, I told him not to think about God. I hoped there was need for him to worry about such things yet.

original: So he bade me lay  more clothes on his feet. I put my hand into the bed and felt them, and they were as cold as any stone. Then I  felt to his knees, and so upward and upward, and all was as cold as any stone.
translation: So he asked me to put more blankets on his feet. I put my hand in the bed and felt them, and they were as cold as a stone. Then I felt up to his knees, and higher and higher, and it was all as cold as stone.

original: They say he cried out of sack.
translation: They say he complained about wine.

original: Ay, that he did.
translation: Yes, he did.

original: And of women.
translation: And about women.

original: Nay, that he did not.
translation: No, he didn't do that.

original: Yes, that he did, and said they were devils incarnate.
translation: Yes, he did, and said they were devils incarnate.

original: 'A could never abide carnation. 'Twas a color he never  liked.
He said once the devil would have him about women.
translation: He said once the devil would get him because of women.

original: He did in some sort, indeed, handle women, but then he  was rheumatic, and talked of the Whore of Babylon.
Do you not remember he saw a flea stick upon Bardolph’s nose, and he said it was a black soul burning in hell?
translation: Do you remember he saw a flea sticking on Bardolph's nose and said it was a black soul burning in hell?

original: Well, the fuel is gone that maintained that fire.  That’s all the riches I got in his service.
translation: Well, the wood that kept that fire burning is gone now he's dead. That's all the wealth I ever got from serving him.

original: Shall we shog? The King will be gone from Southampton.
translation: Shall we set off? The King will be gone from Southampton soon.

original: Come, let’s away.
translation: Come, let's go.

original: And that’s but unwholesome food, they say.
translation: And they say that's not very healthy food.

original: Touch her soft mouth, and march.
translation: Kiss her soft mouth, and march.

original: Farewell, hostess.
translation: Goodbye, Hostess.

original: I cannot kiss, that is the humor of it. But adieu.
translation: I can't kiss, that's the way it is. But goodbye.

original: Let housewifery appear. Keep close, I thee command.
translation: Be a housewife. Keep inside, I command you.

original: Farewell. Adieu.
translation: Farewell. Goodbye.

original: Thus comes the English with full power upon us,   And more than carefully it us concerns   To answer royally in our defenses.
translation: So the English are coming with a large army to fight us, and it's right for us to defend ourselves royally, rather than cautiously.

original: Therefore the Dukes of Berri and of Brittany,   Of Brabant and of Orléans, shall make forth,   And you, Prince Dauphin, with all swift dispatch,   To line and new-repair our towns of war   With men of courage and with means defendant.
translation: So the Dukes of Berri and of Britanny, of Brabant and of Orléans, will head out, and you, Prince Dauphin, as quickly as possible, to fortify our towns for war and fill them with brave men and with means to defend themselves.

original: For England his approaches makes as fierce   As waters to the sucking of a gulf.
translation: The king of England's approach is as fierce as a whirlpool sucking down water.

original: It fits us then to be as provident   As fear may teach us out of late examples   Left by the fatal and neglected English   Upon our fields.
translation: It's right for us to be careful, because fear shows us recent examples of what happened on our battlefields when we underestimated the English.

original: To view the sick and feeble parts of France.   And let us do it with no show of fear,
translation: Let's go see the sick and weak parts of France. And let's do it without seeming afraid

original: No, with no more than if we heard that England   Were busied with a Whitsun morris-dance.
translation: —no, more as if we heard that England were busy dancing.

original: For, my good liege, she is so idly kinged,   Her scepter so fantastically borne   By a vain, giddy, shallow, humorous youth,   That fear attends her not.
translation: Because, my good king, England has such a lazy king, a vain, unpredictable, shallow, moody young man who uses his power so irrationally that there's no reason to fear England.

original: My most redoubted father,   It is most meet we arm us 'gainst the foe,
translation: My respected father, it's right for us to prepare to fight the enemy,

original: For peace itself should not so dull a kingdom,   Though war nor no known quarrel were in question,
translation: because peace shouldn't be allowed to make a kingdom weak, even if there were no war or conflict that might bring one about.

original: But that defenses, musters, preparations,   Should be maintained, assembled, and collected,   As were a war in expectation.
translation: Defenses, militias, and preparations should be maintained, assembled, and collected as if a war were expected.

original: Therefore I say ’tis meet we all go forth.
translation: So I say it's right for us all to head out.

original: Oh peace, Prince Dauphin!   You are too much mistaken in this king.
translation: Be quiet, Prince Dauphin! You're wrong about this king.

original: Question your Grace the late ambassadors   With what great state he heard their embassy,
translation: Ask the last ambassadors with what dignity he heard their message,

original: How well supplied with noble counselors,   How modest in exception, and withal   How terrible in constant resolution,
translation: how well supplied he is with noble advisers, how modest when disagreeing, but still how determined he is when he's made his mind up,

original: And you shall find his vanities forespent   Were but the outside of the Roman Brutus,   Covering discretion with a coat of folly,
translation: and you will find that the foolish things he used to do were just a disguise for a Roman hero, covering wisdom with a layer of folly,

original: As gardeners do with ordure hide those roots   That shall first spring and be most delicate.
translation: the way gardeners cover with manure the shoots that will grow first and be most beautiful.

original: Well, ’tis not so, my Lord High Constable.   But though we think it so, it is no matter.
translation: It's not true, my Lord High Constable. But though you think it is, it doesn't make a difference.

original: In cases of defense ’tis best to weigh   The enemy more mighty than he seems.
translation: In cases of self-defense it's best to consider the enemy to be stronger than he seems.

original: So the proportions of defense are filled,
translation: So you're able to make an adequate defense.

original: Which of a weak or niggardly projection   Doth, like a miser, spoil his coat with scanting   A little cloth.
translation: Assuming your enemy is weak and trying to save resources means being like a greedy man who spoils a coat by trying to save a little cloth when it's being made.

original: Think we King Harry strong,   And, princes, look you strongly arm to meet him.
translation: Let's assume King Harry is strong, and princes, make yourselves strong to meet him.

original: The kindred of him hath been fleshed upon us,   And he is bred out of that bloody strain   That haunted us in our familiar paths.
translation: His relative drew our blood, and he comes from that bloody family that has already haunted us in our own country.

original: Witness our too-much-memorable shame   When Cressy battle fatally was struck   And all our princes captived by the hand   Of that black name, Edward, Black Prince of Wales,
translation: Remember our too-easily-remembered shame at the fatal battle of Cressy when all our princes were captured by the terrible Edward, Black Prince of Wales, himself,

original: Whiles that his mountain sire, on mountain standing   Up in the air, crowned with the golden sun,   Saw his heroical seed and smiled to see him   Mangle the work of nature and deface   The patterns that by God and by French fathers   Had twenty years been made.
translation: while his mountain-dwelling father standing on a mountain up in the air, haloed by the golden sun, saw his heroic son and smiled to see him kill the men who had been made by God and by French fathers twenty years before.

original: This is a stem   Of that victorious stock, and let us fear   The native mightiness and fate of him.
translation: This is a relative of that conquering family, and we should fear his inherited strength and luck.

original: Ambassadors from Harry King of England Do crave admittance to your Majesty.
translation: Ambassadors from Harry King of England ask to be brought to see you, your Majesty.

original: We’ll give them present audience. Go, and bring them.
translation: I'll hear them now. Go and bring them.

original: You see this chase is hotly followed, friends.
translation: You see they've already started hunting us.

original: Turn head and stop pursuit, for coward dogs   Most spend their mouths when what they seem to threaten   Runs far before them.
translation: Then turn and stop them following,  because cowardly dogs bark loudest when what they're trying to attack runs far ahead of them.

original: Good my sovereign,   Take up the English short, and let them know   Of what a monarchy you are the head.
translation: Dear king, stop the English short and let them see what kingdom you're the king of.

original: Self-love, my liege, is not so vile a sin   As self-neglecting.
translation: Self-respect, my king, is not as bad a sin as being insecure.

original: From our brother England?
translation: You come from my brother the King of England?

original: From him, and thus he greets your Majesty:   He wills you, in the name of God Almighty,   That you divest yourself and lay apart   The borrowed glories that, by gift of heaven,   By law of nature and of nations, 'longs   To him and to his heirs
translation: Yes, and he greets you in this way: he asks you, in the name of God Almighty, to give up the borrowed riches that belong to him and his heirs by the gift of heaven and laws of countries

original: —namely, the crown   And all wide-stretchèd honors that pertain   By custom and the ordinance of times   Unto the crown of France.
translation: . That is, the crown and all the honors that go along, by custom and ancient laws, with the crown of France.

original: That you may know   'Tis no sinister nor no awkward claim   Picked from the wormholes of long-vanished days,   Nor from the dust of old oblivion raked,
translation: So that you know this isn't a trumped-up or weak claim made out of loopholes of ancient laws, or based on something that happened a long time ago,

original: He sends you this most memorable line,   In every branch truly demonstrative,   Willing you overlook this pedigree,
translation: he sends you this interesting family tree, showing every branch of his family, and asks you to look it over.

original: And when you find him evenly derived   From his most famed of famous ancestors,   Edward the Third, he bids you then resign   Your crown and kingdom, indirectly held   From him, the native and true challenger.
translation: And when you find he's honestly descended from his most famous of famous ancestors, Edward the Third, he asks you to then give up your crown and kingdom, which you're keep unfairly from him, the natural and true ruler.

original: Or else what follows?
translation: Or what will happen?

original: Bloody constraint, for if you hide the crown   Even in your hearts, there will he rake for it.
translation: Bloody violence, because even if you hide the crown in your hearts, he'll cut them open to find it.

original: Therefore in fierce tempest is he coming,   In thunder and in earthquake like a Jove,
translation: So he's coming in a fierce storm, in thunder and earthquakes like God.

original: That, if requiring fail, he will compel,
translation: If asking doesn't work, he'll use force.

original: And bids you, in the bowels of the Lord,   Deliver up the crown and to take mercy   On the poor souls for whom this hungry war   Opens his vasty jaws,
translation: He asks you, by the body of God, to give him the crown and to save all the poor people that this hungry war is opening its huge jaws to eats.

original: and on your head   Turning the widows' tears, the orphans' cries,   The dead men’s blood, the pining maidens' groans,   For husbands, fathers, and betrothèd lovers,   That shall be swallowed in this controversy.
translation: You'll be to blame for the widows' tears, the orphans' cries, the dead men's blood, the sad women's moans for husbands, fathers, and fiancés who will be swallowed by this war.

original: This is his claim, his threat'ning, and my message—   Unless the Dauphin be in presence here,   To whom expressly I bring greeting too.
translation: That is his claim, his threat, and my message—unless the Dauphin is here too, because I have a message specifically for him.

original: For us, we will consider of this further. Tomorrow shall you bear our full intent Back to our brother England.
translation: As for me, I will think more about this. Tomorrow you'll bring my complete response to my brother England.

original: For the Dauphin, I stand here for him. What to him from England?
translation: As for the Dauphin, I'm speaking for him. What does the king of England send him?

original: Scorn and defiance, slight regard, contempt,   And anything that may not misbecome   The mighty sender, doth he prize you at.
translation: Scorn and hostility, a low opinion, disrespect, and anything that doesn't make the powerful sender look bad. That's what he thinks of you.

original: Thus says my king: an if your father’s Highness   Do not, in grant of all demands at large,   Sweeten the bitter mock you sent his Majesty,
translation: The king says this: if your father doesn't, by granting all the demands he's made, make up for your nasty joke about his Majesty,

original: He’ll call you to so hot an answer of it   That caves and womby vaultages of France   Shall chide your trespass and return your mock   In second accent of his ordinance.
translation: he'll make you answer for it so violently that hollow caves in France will scold you for your mistake and repeat the echoes of your joke as it's expressed by his cannons.

original: Say, if my father render fair return,   It is against my will, for I desire   Nothing but odds with England.
translation: Tell him, if my father agrees to his terms, it's against my will, because I want nothing more than war with England.

original: To that end,   As matching to his youth and vanity,   I did present him with the Paris balls.
translation: It was for that, and because they matched his youth and silliness, that I sent him the Paris tennis balls.

original: He’ll make your Paris Louvre shake for it,   Were it the mistress court of mighty Europe.
translation: He would make your Louvre in Paris shake for that even if it were the capital of all of Europe.

original: And be assured you’ll find a difference,   As we his subjects have in wonder found,   Between the promise of his greener days   And these he masters now.
translation: Be sure you'll see a difference, as we his subjects were amazed to see, between what he seemed to be like in his younger days and now.

original: Now he weighs time   Even to the utmost grain. That you shall read   In your own losses, if he stay in France.
translation: Now he spends time carefully even to the second. You will find that out by all your losses if he stays in France.

original: Tomorrow shall you know our mind at full.
translation: Tomorrow you will know everything I have to say.

original: Dispatch us with all speed, lest that our king   Come here himself to question our delay,
translation: Send us back soon, or our king will come here himself to ask what's delaying us,

original: For he is footed in this land already.
translation: since he's already landed in this country.

original: You shall be soon dispatched with fair conditions.
translation: You will soon be sent back with a fair answer.

original: Thus with imagined wing our swift scene flies   In motion of no less celerity   Than that of thought.
translation: Our fast scene flies with imaginary wings as quickly as thoughts do.

original: Suppose that you have seen   The well-appointed king at Hampton pier   Embark his royalty, and his brave fleet   With silken streamers the young Phoebus fanning.
translation: Pretend you have seen the well-prepared king embark at  Southampton  pier, his brave ships fanning the sun with silk banners.

original: Play with your fancies and in them behold,   Upon the hempen tackle, shipboys climbing.
translation: Use your imagination and see the boys climbing on the ropes of the ships' rigging.

original: Hear the shrill whistle, which doth order give   To sounds confused. Behold the threaden sails,   Borne with th' invisible and creeping wind,   Draw the huge bottoms through the furrowed sea,   Breasting the lofty surge.
translation: Hear the piercing whistle, which imposes some order on all the cacophonous sounds. See the sails made of thread, carried by the invisible creeping wind, pulling the huge  ships  through the sea, facing the high waves.

original: Oh, do but think   You stand upon the rivage and behold   A city on th' inconstant billows dancing,   For so appears this fleet majestical   Holding due course to Harfleur.
translation: Oh, just imagine you're standing on the shore and see a city dancing on the unpredictable waves, because that's what this royal fleet sailing to Harfleur looks like.

original: Follow, follow!   Grapple your minds to sternage of this navy   And leave your England, as dead midnight still,   Guarded with grandsires, babies, and old women,   Either past or not arrived to pith and puissance,
translation: Follow, follow! Use grappling-hooks to attach your minds to the decks of these ships and leave your England, quiet as the dead of night, guarded by grandfathers, babies, and old women, either past or not yet arrived at their prime.

original: For who is he whose chin is but enriched   With one appearing hair that will not follow   These culled and choice-drawn cavaliers to France?
translation: What man who has even one hair on his chin wouldn't follow these chosen knights to France?

original: Work, work your thoughts, and therein see a siege.   Behold the ordnance on their carriages,   With fatal mouths gaping on girded Harfleur.
translation: Work, work your imaginations, and see a siege there. See the cannons on their supports, opening their deadly mouths at the walls of Harfleur.

original: Suppose th'Ambassador from the French comes back,   Tells Harry that the king doth offer him   Katherine his daughter and with her, to dowry,   Some petty and unprofitable dukedoms.
translation: Imagine that the Ambassador comes back from the French, tells Harry the king offers him Katherine his daughter and with her, as a dowry, some small, poor dukedoms.

original: The offer likes not, and the nimble gunner   With linstock now the devilish cannon touches,
translation: He doesn't like the offer, so the fast gunner lights the devilish cannon's fuse,

original: And down goes all before them. Still be kind   And eke out our performance with your mind.
translation: And everything falls down in front of them. Remain kind and fill out gaps in our performance with your mind.

original: Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more,   Or close the wall up with our English dead!
translation: Once more back into the gap in the wall, dear friends, once more, or let it be closed up with dead English soldiers!

original: In peace there’s nothing so becomes a man   As modest stillness and humility,   But when the blast of war blows in our ears,   Then imitate the action of the tiger:
translation: There's nothing more proper for a man in a time of peace as modest calm and humility, but when the trumpet of war blows in your ears, you should imitate the actions of a tiger.

original: Stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood,   Disguise fair nature with hard-favored rage,   Then lend the eye a terrible aspect,   Let pry through the portage of the head   Like the brass cannon,
translation: Stiffen your muscles, raise your heartbeat, disguise your natural kindness with ugly anger, then frown horribly, let your eyes shoot glares from your head like a brass cannon shooting out of a porthole.

original: let the brow o'erwhelm it   As fearfully as doth a gallèd rock   O'erhang and jutty his confounded base,   Swilled with the wild and wasteful ocean.
translation: Let your forehead hang over them as frighteningly as a dislodged rock, jutting over a doomed piece of ground washed over by the wild and destructive ocean.

original: Now set the teeth and stretch the nostril wide,   Hold hard the breath and bend up every spirit   To his full height.
translation: Now grit your teeth and flare your nostrils, hold your breath and raise your spirits.

original: On, on, you noblest English,   Whose blood is fet from fathers of war-proof,   Fathers that, like so many Alexanders,   Have in these parts from morn till even fought   And sheathed their swords for lack of argument.
translation: On, on, you noblest Englishmen, who are descended from fathers whose worth was proved in war, fathers who, as though they were all Alexander the Great, fought in this country from morning until evening, then put away their swords because there was no-one left to fight.

original: Dishonor not your mothers. Now attest   That those whom you called fathers did beget you.
translation: Don't dishonor your mothers. Now prove that the men you called your fathers conceived you.

original: Be copy now to men of grosser blood,   And teach them how to war. And you, good yeoman,   Whose limbs were made in England, show us here   The mettle of your pasture.
translation: Be an example for less noble men and show them how to fight. And you, good commoner, whose bodies were made in England, show us the character you developed working the land.

original: Let us swear   That you are worth your breeding, which I doubt not,   For there is none of you so mean and base   That hath not noble luster in your eyes.
translation: Convince us you were worth bringing up, which I don't doubt, because even the lowest and least important of you has a noble light in your eyes.

original: I see you stand like greyhounds in the slips,   Straining upon the start. The game’s afoot.
Follow your spirit, and upon this charge   Cry “God for Harry, England, and Saint George!”
translation: Follow your instincts, and when we charge shout, "God help Harry, England, and Saint George!"

original: On, on, on, on, on! To the breach, to the breach!
translation: On, on, on, on, on! To the gap, to the gap!

original: Pray thee, corporal, stay. The knocks are too hot, and, for mine own part, I have not a case of lives.
translation: Please, corporal, wait. The blows are coming too hot and, as for me, I don't have any spare lives.

original: The  humor of it is too hot; that is the very plainsong of  it.
translation: The way it is is too hot; that's the tune of it.

original: “The plainsong” is most just, for humors do abound.    Knocks go and come. God’s vassals drop and die,   And sword and shield   In bloody field   Doth win immortal fame.
translation: The "tune" is very true, because emotions are running high. Blows go and come. God's servants drop down and dieAnd a sword and shieldIn a bloody battlefieldDo win immortal fame.

original: Would I were in an alehouse in London! I would give all my fame for a pot of ale, and safety.
translation: I wish I were in a pub in London! I would give all my fame for a mug of ale, and safety.

original: And I.    If wishes would prevail with me,   My purpose should not fail with me,   But thither would I hie.
translation: So would I. If my wishes could come trueI wouldn't fail in my purposeBut I would go there.

original: As duly,   But not as truly,   As bird doth sing on bough.
translation: As properly,But not as well,As a bird sings on a branch.

original: Up to the breach, you dogs! Avaunt, you cullions!
translation: Up to the gap, you dogs! Forward, you good-for-nothings!

original: Be merciful, great duke, to men of mold.
translation: Take mercy, great duke, on men made of earth.

original: Abate thy  rage, abate thy manly rage, abate thy rage, great duke.  Good bawcock, 'bate thy rage. Use lenity, sweet chuck.
translation: Calm your anger, calm your manly anger, calm your anger, great duke. Darling, calm down! Be nice, dear.

original: These be good humors. Your Honor wins bad humors.
translation: Those are good emotions. You, your Honor, are showing bad emotions.

original: As young as I am, I have observed these three swashers. I am boy to them all three, but all they three, though  they would serve me, could not be man to me.
translation: As young as I am, I have watched these three swashbucklers. I am a servant to all three of them, but all three, even if they were my servants, could not be my men.

original: For indeed  three such antics do not amount to a man: for Bardolph,  he is white-livered and red-faced, by the means whereof  he faces it out but fights not;
translation: Because three clowns like that don't make up a man. Bardolph is  yellow at heart  and red-faced, so he brags but never fights.

original: for Pistol, he hath a  killing tongue and a quiet sword, by the means whereof  he breaks words and keeps whole weapons;
translation: Pistol has a killing mouth and a quiet sword, so he breaks words and keeps his weapons whole.

original: for Nym, he  hath heard that men of few words are the best men, and  therefore he scorns to say his prayers, lest he should  be thought a coward, but his few bad words are matched  with as few good deeds, for he never broke any man’s  head but his own, and that was against a post when he  was drunk.
translation: Nym has heard that men of few words are the best men, so he doesn't say his prayers because he's worried about being thought to be a coward. But his few bad words are matched with as few good deeds. He never hurt any man's head except his own, and that was against a post when he was drunk.

original: They will steal anything and call it  purchase. Bardolph stole a lute case, bore it twelve  leagues, and sold it for three halfpence.
translation: They will steal anything and say they bought it. Bardolph stole a lute case, carried it for twelve leagues, and sold it for three half-pennies

original: Nym and  Bardolph are sworn brothers in filching, and in Calais  they stole a fire shovel. I knew by that piece of  service the men would carry coals.
translation: . Nym and Bardolph are partners in crime, and in Calais they stole a fire shovel. I knew by that action that they would be willing to do  servants' work.

original: They would have me as familiar with men’s pockets as their gloves or their  handkerchers, which makes much against my manhood, if I  should take from another’s pocket to put into mine, for  it is plain pocketing up of wrongs.
translation: They want me to be as at home in the pockets of men as the men's gloves and handkerchiefs are, but it is degrading to my manliness to take something from another's pocket to put into mine, because that's just pocketing a sin.

original: I must leave them  and seek some better service. Their villainy goes  against my weak stomach, and therefore I must cast it  up.
translation: I must leave them and find someone better to serve. Their crimes upset my weak stomach, so I should throw them up.

original: Captain Fluellen, you must come presently to the mines; the duke of Gloucester would speak with you.
translation: Captain Fluellen, you must come to the tunnels now. The duke of Gloucester wants to speak with you.

original: To the mines? Tell you the duke it is not so good to  come to the mines, for, look you, the mines is not  according to the disciplines of the war.
translation: To the tunnels?  Tell the duke it is not good to come to the tunnels because, see, the tunnels are not according to the strategy of war.

original: The concavities of it is not sufficient, for, look you, th' athversary, you may discuss unto the duke, look you, is digt  himself four yard under the countermines.
translation: The hollowness of them is not sufficient, because, see, you may discuss it with the duke, see, the enemy has dug himself four yards under the tunnels.

original: By Cheshu, I  think he will plow up all if there is not better  directions.
translation: By Jesus, I think he will dig it all up if there are not better orders.

original: The duke of Gloucester, to whom the order of the siege  is given, is altogether directed by an Irishman, a very  valiant gentleman, i' faith.
translation: The duke of Gloucester, who is in charge of the siege, does everything an Irishman tells him—a really brave man, truly.

original: It is Captain Macmorris, is it not?
translation: It is Captain Macmorris, is it not?

original: I think it be.
translation: I think it is.

original: By Cheshu, he is an ass, as in the world. I will verify as much in his beard.
translation: By Jesus, he is an ass, as great any in the world. I will tell him that to his face.

original: He has no more directions in the  true disciplines of the wars, look you, of the Roman  disciplines, than is a puppy dog.
translation: He has no more knowledge of the true strategies of war, see, the Roman strategies, than does a puppy dog.

original: Here he comes, and the Scots captain, Captain Jamy,  with him.
translation: Here he comes, and the Scottish captain, Captain Jamy, with him.

original: Captain Jamy is a marvelous falorous gentleman, that is certain, and of great expedition and knowledge in  th'aunchient wars, upon my particular knowledge of his  directions.
translation: Captain Jamy is a marvelously brave man, that is certain, and of great accomplishments and knowledge of the ancient wars, as I know for sure from his orders.

original: By Cheshu, he will maintain his argument as  well as any military man in the world in the disciplines of the pristine wars of the Romans.
translation: By  Jesus , he can talk as well as any military man in the world about the strategies of the pure wars of the Romans.

original: I say gudday, Captain Fluellen.
translation: I say good-day, Captain Fluellen.

original: Godden to your Worship, good Captain James.
translation: Good-day to you, your Worship, good Captain James.

original: How now, Captain Macmorris, have you quit the mines? Have the pioneers given o'er?
translation: What, Captain Morris, have you left the tunnels? Have the tunnelers given up?

original: By Chrish, la, ’tish ill done. The work ish give over.  The trompet sound the retreat.
translation: By Christ, it's badly done. The work is abandoned. The trumpet sounds the retreat.

original: By my hand I swear, and  my father’s soul, the work ish ill done. It ish give  over.
translation: I swear by my hand and my father's soul , the work is badly done. It has been abandoned.

original: I would have blowed up the town, so Chrish save  me, la, in an hour. Oh, ’tish ill done, ’tish ill done,  by my hand, ’tish ill done.
translation: I would have blown up the town, Christ save me, in an hour. Oh, it's badly done, it's badly done, by my hand, it's badly done.

original: Captain Macmorris, I beseech you now, will you voutsafe me, look you, a few disputations with you as partly  touching or concerning the disciplines of the war, the  Roman wars?
translation: Captain Macmorris, I ask you now, will you grant me, see, a few debates with you partly touching on or concerning the strategies of war, the Roman wars?

original: In the way of argument, look you, and  friendly communication, partly to satisfy my opinion,  and partly for the satisfaction, look you, of my mind,  as touching the direction of the military discipline,  that is the point.
translation: For the sake of argument, see, and friendly communication, partly to satisfy my opinion, and partly for the satisfaction, see, of my mind, concerning the art of military strategy, that is the point.

original: It sall be vary gud, gud feith, gud captens bath, and I sall quit you with gud leve, as I may pick occasion,  that sall I, marry.
translation: It will be very good, truly, good captains, and I will leave you if that's all right, when I see fit, that I will, truly.

original: It is no time to discourse, so Chrish save me. The day  is hot, and the weather, and the wars, and the king, and the dukes. It is no time to discourse.
translation: Now is no time to talk, Christ save me. The day is hot, and the weather, and the wars, and the king, and the dukes. Now is no time to talk.

original: The town is  beseeched, and the trumpet call us to the breach, and we talk and, be Chrish, do nothing, ’tis shame for us all. So God sa' me, ’tis shame to stand still. It is shame,  by my hand.
translation: The town is besieged, and the trumpet calls us to the gap, and we talk and, by Christ, do nothing, it's a shame to us all. So God save me, it's shameful to stand still. It's shameful, by my hand.

original: And there is throats to be cut and works to  be done, and there ish nothing done, so Chrish sa' me,  la.
translation: And there are throats to cut and deeds to be done, and nothing is done, so Christ save me, la.

original: By the mess, ere theise eyes of mine take themselves to slomber, ay’ll de gud service, or I’ll lig i' th' grund for it, ay, or go to death.
translation: By the mass, before I fall asleep, I'll do good service, or I'll lie on the ground, yes, or die.

original: And I’ll pay ’t as  valorously as I may, that sall I suerly do, that is the  breff and the long.
translation: And I'll pay for my death as bravely as I can, that I will surely do, that is the long and short of it.

original: Marry, I wad full fain heard some  question ’tween you tway.
translation: Come on, I would like to hear some debate between you two.

original: Captain Macmorris, I think, look you, under your  correction, there is not many of your nation—
translation: Captain Macmorris, I think, see, under your command, there are not many of your nation—

original: Of my nation? What ish my nation? Ish a villain and a  basterd and a knave and a rascal. What ish my nation?  Who talks of my nation?
Look you, if you take the matter otherwise than is  meant, Captain Macmorris, peradventure I shall think you do not use me with that affability as, in discretion,  you ought to use me,
translation: Look, if you take this in a different way than I meant it, Captain Macmorris, perhaps I will think you do not treat me with the politeness that, reasonably, you should treat me with,

original: look you, being as good a man as  yourself, both in the disciplines of war and in the  derivation of my birth and in other particularities.
translation: see, since I am as good a man as you are, as good at the strategies of war and from as good a family and other particulars.

original: I do not know you so good a man as myself. So Chrish  save me, I will cut off your head.
translation: I do not know you are as good a man as I am. Christ save me, I will cut off your head.

original: Gentlemen both, you will mistake each other.
translation: Gentlemen, you're misunderstanding each other.

original: Ah, that’s a foul fault.
translation: Yes, that's a terrible fault.

original: The town sounds a parley.
translation: The town calls for a truce.

original: Captain Macmorris, when there is more better  opportunity to be required, look you, I will be so bold  as to tell you I know the disciplines of war, and there  is an end.
translation: Captain Macmorris, when there is a better opportunity, see, I will be so bold as to tell you I know the strategies of war, and that is the end of it.

original: How yet resolves the governor of the town?   This is the latest parle we will admit.
translation: What has the mayor of the town decided? This is the last truce we will grant.

original: Therefore to our best mercy give yourselves   Or, like to men proud of destruction,   Defy us to our worst.
translation: So surrender to us or, like men proud of destroying themselves, dare us to do our worst.
