original: For, as I am a soldier,   A name that in my thoughts becomes me best,   If I begin the batt'ry once again,   I will not leave the half-achieved Harfleur   Till in her ashes she lie burièd.
translation: Because, as sure as I am a soldier, which I think is the most fitting thing for me to call myself, if I begin the attack once again, I will not leave half-defeated Harfleur until it's buried in its own ashes.

original: The gates of mercy shall be all shut up,   And the fleshed soldier, rough and hard of heart,   In liberty of bloody hand, shall range   With conscience wide as hell, mowing like grass   Your fresh fair virgins and your flow'ring infants.
translation: The gates of mercy will be shut, and the bloody soldiers, rough and hard-hearted, free to do whatever terrible deeds they want, will wander around with the willingness to do anything, mowing down like grass your beautiful young girls and your growing babies.

original: What is it then to me if impious war,   Arrayed in flames like to the prince of fiends,   Do with his smirched complexion all fell feats   Enlinked to waste and desolation?
translation: What is it to me if unholy war, dressed in flames like the devil, with a scorched face, does all the horrible things that go along with destruction and loss?

original: What is ’t to me, when you yourselves are cause,   If your pure maidens fall into the hand   Of hot and forcing violation?
translation: What is it to me, since you yourselves are to blame, if your pure young women are raped?

original: What rein can hold licentious wickedness   When down the hill he holds his fierce career?
translation: What kind of control can you have over immoral evil when it's charging fiercely on as though running down a hill?

original: We may as bootless spend our vain command   Upon th' enragèd soldiers in their spoil   As send precepts to the Leviathan   To come ashore.
translation: We could just as uselessly give pointless orders to looting angry soldiers as send instructions to the sea-monster Leviathan to come to shore.

original: Therefore, you men of Harfleur,   Take pity of your town and of your people   Whiles yet my soldiers are in my command,   Whiles yet the cool and temperate wind of grace   O'erblows the filthy and contagious clouds   Of heady murder, spoil, and villainy.
translation: So, you men of Harfleur, have pity on your town and on your people while my soldiers are still under my control, while the cool and mild wind of kindness is stronger than the dirty and unhealthy clouds of wild murder, looting, and evil.

original: If not, why, in a moment look to see   The blind and bloody soldier with foul hand   Desire the locks of your shrill-shrieking daughters,
translation: If not, in a moment expect to see a blind and bloody soldier reaching with a dirty hand towards the hair of your piercingly-shrieking daughters,

original: Your fathers taken by the silver beards   And their most reverend heads dashed to the walls,
translation: your fathers grabbed by their silver beards and their wise heads smashed against the walls,

original: Your naked infants spitted upon pikes   Whiles the mad mothers with their howls confused   Do break the clouds, as did the wives of Jewry   At Herod’s bloody-hunting slaughtermen.
What say you? Will you yield and this avoid   Or, guilty in defense, be thus destroyed?
translation: What do you say? Will you surrender and avoid this or, guilty of these crimes because you continue to defend yourselves, be destroyed in this way?

original: Our expectation hath this day an end.
translation: Our hopes end today.

original: The Dauphin, whom of succors we entreated,   Returns us that his powers are yet not ready   To raise so great a siege.
translation: The Dauphin, whom we begged to help us, replies that his forces are not yet ready to end such a strong siege.

original: Therefore, great King,   We yield our town and lives to thy soft mercy.   Enter our gates, dispose of us and ours,   For we no longer are defensible.
translation: So, great King, we surrender our town and lives to your kind mercy. Enter our gates, do what you want with us and what we own, because we can no longer defend ourselves.

original: Alice, tu as été en Angleterre, et tu parles bien le  langage.
translation: Alice, you've been in England, and you speak the language well.

original: Un peu, madame  .
translation: A little, ma'am.

original: Je te prie, m'enseignez. Il faut que j'apprenne à  parler  .   Comment appelez-vous  la main  en anglais?
translation: Please, teach me. I have to learn to speak. What do you call the hand in English?

original: La main?  Elle est appelée “de hand.”
translation: The hand? It's called "de hand".

original: “De hand.” Et  les doigts?
translation: "De hand."  And the fingers?

original: Les doigts? Ma foi, j'oublie les doigts; mais je me  souviendrai.   Les doigts? Je pense qu'ils sont appelés  “de fingres”;  oui,  “de fingres.”
translation: The fingers? Goodness, I forget the fingers; but I'll remember. The fingers? I think they're called "de fingres"; yes, "de fingres".

original: La main  , “de hand”;  les doigts  , “de fingres.”  Je pense  que je suis le bon écolier. J'ai gagné deux mots  d'anglais vitement. Comment appelez-vous  les ongles?
translation: The hand, "de hand"; the fingers, "de fingres". I think I'm a good student. I'm learned two English words quickly. What do you call the nails?

original: Les ongles?  Nous les appelons “de nails.”
translation: The nails? We call them "de nails."

original: “De nails.”  Écoutez. Dites-moi si je parle bien  : “de  hand, de fingres, et de nails.”
translation: "De nails". Listen. Tell me if I'm talking well: “de hand, de fingres, and de nails.”

original: C'est bien dit, madame. Il est fort bon anglais.
translation: That's well said, ma'am. That's very good English.

original: Dites-moi l'anglais pour  le bras.
translation: Tell me the English word for the arm.

original: “De arme,” madame.
translation: "De arme," ma'am.

original: Et le coude?
translation: And the elbow?

original: “D'elbow.”
translation: "D'elbow."

original: “D'elbow.”  Je m'en fais la répétition de tous les mots  que vous m'avez appris dés à présent.
translation: "D'elbow." I'll repeat all the words you've taught me up to now.

original: Il est trop difficile, madame, comme je pense.
translation: That's too hard, ma'am, in my opinion.

original: Excusez-moi, Alice. Écoutez:  “de hand, de fingres, de  nails, de arma, de bilbow.”
translation: Please, Alice. Listen: “de hand, de fingres, de nails, de arma, de bilbow.”

original: “D'elbow,”  madame.
translation: “D'elbow,” ma'am.

original: Ô Seigneur Dieu! Je m'en oublie;  “d'elbow.” Comment appelez-vous  le col?
translation: Oh Lord God! I forgot; “d'elbow.” What do you call the neck?

original: “De nick,”  madame.
translation: “De nick,” ma'am.

original: “De nick.”  Et le menton?
translation: "De nick." And the chin?

original: “De chin.”
translation: "De chin."

original: “De sin.”  Le col,  “de nick”;  le menton,  “de sin.”
translation: "De sin." The neck, "de nick"; the chin, "de sin."

original: Oui. Sauf votre honneur, en vérité, vous prononcez les  mots aussi droit que les natifs d'Angleterre.
translation: Yes. Truly, you speak the words as well as native English speakers do.

original: Je ne doute point d'apprendre, par la grâce de Dieu, et en peu de temps.
translation: I don't doubt I'll learn quickly,  if God allows it.

original: N'avez vous pas déjà oublié ce que je vous ai enseigné?
translation: Have you not already forgotten what I taught you?

original: Non, je réciterai à vous promptement:  “de hand, de  fingre, de nails—”
translation: No, I'll recite them to you right now: “de hand, de fingre, de nails—”

original: “De nails,”  madame.
translation: “De nails,” ma'am.

original: “De nails, de arme, de ilbow.”
translation: “De nails, de arme, de ilbow.”

original: Sauf votre honneur,  “d'elbow.”
translation: Sorry, it's "d'elbow".

original: Ainsi dis-je:  “d'elbow, de nick, et de sin.”  Comment  appelez-vous le pied et la robe?
translation: That's what I said: “d'elbow, de nick, and de sin.” What do you call the foot and the dress?

original: “Le foot,”  madame, et  “le count.”
translation: “Le foot,”ma'am, and "le count.”

original: “   Le   foot”   et   “de count.”   Ô   Seigneur Dieu! Ils sont mots de son mauvais, corruptible, gros, et impudique, et non pour les dames d'honneur d'user.
translation: “ The  foot”  and  “de count.”  Oh Lord God! Those are ugly sounding words, rotten, vulgar, and immodest words, and not for honorable ladies to use.

original: Je ne voudrais  prononcer ces mots devant les seigneurs de France pour  tout le monde. Foh!   “Le foot”   et   “le count”!   Néanmoins,  je réciterai une autre fois ma leçon ensemble:   “d' hand, de fingre, de nails, d' arme, d'elbow, de nick, de sin, de foot, le count.”
translation: I wouldn't say those words in front of the lords of France for all the world. What!  "Le foot!"  and  "le count"!  Nonetheless, I'll recite my whole lesson together one more time:  “d' hand, de fingre, de nails, d' arme, d'elbow, de nick, de sin, de foot, le count.”

original: Excellent, madame!
translation: Excellent, ma'am!

original: C'est assez pour une fois: Allons-nous à dîner.
translation: That's enough for now: let's go have dinner.

original: 'Tis certain he hath passed the river Somme.
An if he be not fought withal, my lord,   Let us not live in France.
translation: And if we don't fight him, my lord, we shouldn't live in France.

original: Let us quit all   And give our vineyards to a barbarous people.
translation: Let's all leave and give our vineyards to barbarians.

original: Ô Dieu vivant   , shall a few sprays of us,   The emptying of our fathers' luxury,   Our scions, put in wild and savage stock,
translation: Oh God , will we let a few offshoots of our race, made out of our fathers' loose living, our creations, planted in a wild and savage place,

original: Spurt up so suddenly into the clouds   And overlook their grafters?
translation: shoot up so high into the clouds and look down on the people who planted them?

original: Normans, but bastard Normans, Norman bastards!
translation: They're Normans, but illegitimate Normans, Norman bastards!

original: Mort de ma vie,   if they march along   Unfought withal, but I will sell my dukedom   To buy a slobb'ry and a dirty farm   In that nook-shotten isle of Albion.
translation: Damn me , if they keep marching along without being fought, I will sell my dukedom to buy a disgusting, dirty farm on that strangely-shaped island of Britain.

original: Dieu de batailles,   where have they this mettle?   Is not their climate foggy, raw, and dull,   On whom, as in despite, the sun looks pale,   Killing their fruit with frowns?
translation: God of battles , where did they get this courage? Isn't their climate foggy, cold, and dark, and does't the sun look palely at them as though it hates them, killing their fruit by frowning?

original: Can sodden water,   A drench for sur-reined jades, their barley broth,   Decoct their cold blood to such valiant heat?   And shall our quick blood, spirited with wine,   Seem frosty?
translation: Can boiled water, a drink for old broken-down horses, and their barley soup heat up their blood to make them so fiery and hot-headed? Should our easily-heated blood, encouraged by wine, seem ice-cold?

original: Oh, for honor of our land,   Let us not hang like roping icicles   Upon our houses' thatch, whiles a more frosty people   Sweat drops of gallant youth in our rich fields!
translation: Oh, for the honor of our country, let's not hang like drooping icicles from our houses' roofs, while young men from a colder country sweat bravely on our rich fields!

original: “Poor” we may call them in their native lords.
translation: We can rightly say they're poor in noblemen.

original: By faith and honor,   Our madams mock at us and plainly say   Our mettle is bred out
translation: By faith and honor, our women mock us and plainly say we're inbred and and all the courage has been bred out of our genes,

original: and they will give   Their bodies to the lust of English youth   To new-store France with bastard warriors.
translation: and that they will sleep with English young men to stock up France with illegitimate soldiers.

original: And teach lavoltas high, and swift corantos,   Saying our grace is only in our heels   And that we are most lofty runaways.
translation: And they teach us fast dances, saying the only grace we have is in our feet and that we're very graceful when running away.

original: They bid us to the   English dancing schools.
translation: They ask us to go to the English dancing schools.

original: Where is Montjoy the herald? Speed him hence.   Let him greet England with our sharp defiance.
translation: Where is Montjoy the messenger? Send him from here. Let him tell the king of England fiercely that we will fight him.

original: Up, princes, and, with spirit of honor edged   More sharper than your swords, hie to the field:   Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France;   You dukes of Orléans, Bourbon, and of Berri,   Alençon, Brabant, Bar, and Burgundy;   Jacques Chatillon, Rambures, Vaudemont,   Beaumont, Grandpré, Roussi, and Faulconbridge,   Foix, Lestrale, Bouciqualt, and Charolois;
translation: Go, princes, and with a desire for honor even sharper than your swords, go to battle: Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; you dukes of Orléans, Bourbon, Berri, Alençon, Brabant, Bar, Burgundy, Jacques Chatillon, Rambures, Vaudemont, Beaumont, Grandpré, Roussi, Faulconbridge, Foix, Lestrale, Bouciqualt, and Charolois.

original: High dukes, great princes, barons, lords, and knights,   For your great seats now quit you of great shames.
translation: Great dukes, princes, barons, lords, and knights, for the sake of your great power now make up for your shame.

original: Bar Harry England, that sweeps through our land   With pennons painted in the blood of Harfleur.
translation: Stop Harry of England, who sweeps through our country with banners painted in blood from Harfleur.

original: Rush on his host, as doth the melted snow   Upon the valleys, whose low vassal seat   The Alps doth spit and void his rheum upon.
translation: Rush against his army like melted snow into the valleys, whose low servant-like positions the Alps spit and spew their water at.

original: Go down upon him—you have power enough—   And in a captive chariot into Rouen   Bring him our prisoner.
translation: Go attack him—you have enough forces—and bring him in a captured cart into Rouen as our prisoner.

original: This becomes the great!
translation: This is proper behavior for great men!

original: Sorry am I his numbers are so few,   His soldiers sick and famished in their march
translation: I'm sad that he has so few men and that his soldiers are sick and starving from marching

original: For, I am sure, when he shall see our army   He’ll drop his heart into the sink of fear   And for achievement offer us his ransom.
translation: because, I'm sure, when he sees our army his heart will sink with fear and he'll offer to pay us to end the war.

original: Therefore, Lord Constable, haste on Montjoy   And let him say to England that we send   To know what willing ransom he will give.
translation: So, Lord Constable, hurry to Montjoy and let him tell the king of England that we are sending him to ask how much money he's willing to give us.

original: Not so, I do beseech your Majesty.
translation: Please don't make me do that, your Majesty.

original: Be patient, for you shall remain with us.
translation: Be patient, because you're staying with me.

original: How now, Captain Fluellen? Come you from the bridge?
translation: Hello, Captain Fluellen. Are you coming from the bridge?

original: I assure you, there is very excellent services  committed at the bridge.
translation: I assure you, there are very excellent things happening at the bridge.

original: Is the duke of Exeter safe?
translation: Is the duke of Exeter safe?

original: The duke of Exeter is as magnanimous as Agamemnon, and  a man that I love and honor with my soul and my heart  and my duty and my life and my living and my uttermost  power.
translation: Exeter has as great a soul as the Greek king  Agamemnon , and he's a man I love and honor with all my soul and my heart and my duty and my life and my job and as much as I can.

original: He is not, God be praised and blessed, any hurt  in the world, but keeps the bridge most valiantly, with  excellent discipline.
translation: He is not, God be praised and blessed, at all hurt, but guards the bridge bravely, with excellent strategy.

original: There is an aunchient lieutenant  there at the pridge.
I think in my very conscience he is as valiant a man as Mark Antony, and he is a man of no  estimation in the world, but I did see him do as gallant service.
translation: I think truly he is as brave a man as the Roman hero Mark Anthony, and he is not at all an important man, but I saw him acting as bravely as those who are.

original: What do you call him?
translation: What is he called?

original: He is called Aunchient Pistol.
translation: He is called Ancient Pistol.

original: I know him not.
translation: I don't know him.

original: Here is the man.
translation: Here he is.

original: Captain, I thee beseech to do me favors. The duke of Exeter doth love thee well.
translation: Captain, please do me a favor. The duke of Exeter loves you.

original: Ay, I praise God, and I have merited some love at his  hands.
translation: Yes, I thank God, and I have deserved some love from him.

original: Bardolph, a soldier firm and sound of heart   And of buxom valor,
translation: Bardolph, a strong and good-hearted soldier and of great courage

original: hath, by cruel Fate   And giddy Fortune’s furious fickle wheel,   That goddess blind   That stands upon the rolling restless stone—
translation: has, by cruel Fate and light-headed Fortune's crazy unreliable wheel, that blind goddess who stands on the rolling restless stone—

original: By your patience, Aunchient Pistol, Fortune is painted  blind, with a muffler afore her eyes, to signify to you  that Fortune is blind;
translation: Excuse me, Ancient Pistol, Fortune is depicted as blind, with a scarf before her eyes, to signify to you that Fortune is blind;

original: and she is painted also with a  wheel to signify to you, which is the moral of it, that  she is turning and inconstant, and mutability and  variation;
translation: and she is also depicted with a wheel to signify to you, which is the moral of this, that she is turning and unpredictable, and full of change and variation;

original: and her foot, look you, is fixed upon a  spherical stone, which rolls and rolls and rolls.
translation: and her foot, you see, is planted on a round stone, which rolls and rolls and rolls.

original: In  good truth, the poet makes a most excellent description  of it. Fortune is an excellent moral.
Fortune is Bardolph’s foe and frowns on him,   For he hath stolen a pax and hangèd must he be.
translation: Fortune is Bardolph's enemy and glares at him, because he has stolen a  pax  and he must be hanged.

original: A damnèd death!   Let gallows gape for dog, let man go free,   And let not hemp his windpipe suffocate.
translation: A terrible death! Let dogs be hanged, let men go free, and rope not suffocate their windpipes.

original: But Exeter hath given the doom of death   For pax of little price.
translation: But Exeter has condemned him to death for a cheap pax.

original: Therefore go speak—the duke will hear thy voice—   And let not Bardolph’s vital thread be cut   With edge of penny cord and vile reproach.
translation: So go speak—the duke will listen to you—and don't let Bardolph's life be cut short by the edge of a cheap rope and terrible shame.

original: Speak, Captain, for his life, and I will thee requite.
translation: Speak, Captain, to save him, and I will pay you back.

original: Aunchient Pistol, I do partly understand your meaning.
translation: Ancient Pistol, I partly understand your meaning.

original: Why then, rejoice therefore.
translation: Well, then rejoice.

original: Certainly, aunchient, it is not a thing to rejoice at,  for if, look you, he were my brother,
translation: Certainly, ancient, it's nothing to rejoice at, because, see, even if he were my brother,

original: I would desire the duke to use his good pleasure and put him to execution, for discipline ought to be used.
translation: I would ask the duke to use his own judgement and execute him, because discipline is important.

original: Die and be damned, and  figo  for thy friendship!
translation: Die and be damned, and a fig for your friendship!

original: It is well.
translation: Very well.

original: The fig of Spain!
translation: A Spanish fig!

original: Very good.
translation: Very good.

original: Why, this is an arrant counterfeit rascal. I remember  him now, a bawd, a cutpurse.
translation: What, he's a deceitful criminal. I remember him now, a pimp, a pickpocket.

original: I’ll assure you, he uttered as prave words at the  pridge as you shall see in a summer’s day.
translation: I assure you, he spoke as brave words at the bridge as any you'll hear on a summer's day.

original: But it is  very well; what he has spoke to me, that is well, I  warrant you, when time is serve.
translation: But very well; what he has spoken to me, well, I tell you, when the time comes.

original: Why, ’tis a gull, a fool, a rogue, that now and then  goes to the wars to grace himself at his return into  London under the form of a soldier.
translation: He's a fraud, a fool, a good-for-nothing, who now and then goes to the wars so he can call himself a soldier when he returns to London.

original: And such fellows are perfect in the great commanders' names, and they will  learn you by rote where services were done
translation: Fellows like that know all the great generals' names by heart, and they will learn all about where battles happened—

original: —at such and  such a sconce, at such a breach, at such a convoy; who  came off bravely, who was shot, who disgraced, what  terms the enemy stood on.
translation: in such and such a corner, at such and such a pass, on such a ship; who acted bravely, who was shot, who was disgraced, what agreement the enemy came to.

original: And this they con perfectly in the phrase of war, which they trick up with new-tuned  oaths;
translation: And they learn perfectly how to say this in military vocabulary, to which they add newly-invented oaths.

original: and what a beard of the general’s cut and a  horrid suit of the camp will do among foaming bottles  and ale-washed wits is wonderful to be thought on.
translation: And it's amazing what a beard cut like a general's and a frightening military uniform can get you among foamy bottles and drunk people.

original: But  you must learn to know such slanders of the age, or else you may be marvelously mistook.
translation: But you must learn to recognize people who lie in this way, or you will be completely deceived.

original: I tell you what, Captain Gower.
translation: I tell you what, Captain Gower.

original: I do perceive he is not the man that he would gladly make show to the world he  is.
translation: I do see he is not the man he wants the world to think he is.

original: If I find a hole in his coat, I will tell him my  mind.
translation: If I find a hole in his coat, I will tell him what I think of him.

original: How now, Fluellen, cam’st thou from the bridge?
translation: Hello, Fluellen, did you come from the bridge?

original: Ay, so please your Majesty. The duke of Exeter has very gallantly maintained the pridge.
translation: Yes, your majesty. The duke of Exeter has very bravely held on to the bridge.

original: The French is gone  off, look you, and there is gallant and most prave  passages.
translation: The French have gone off, see, and there have been very brave fights.

original: Marry, th' athversary was have possession of  the pridge, but he is enforced to retire, and the duke  of Exeter is master of the pridge.
translation: The enemy had taken possession of the bridge, but was forced to retreat, and the duke of Exeter is holding the bridge.

original: I can tell your  Majesty, the duke is a prave man.
translation: I can tell your Majesty, the duke is a brave man.

original: What men have you lost, Fluellen?
translation: What men have you lost, Fluellen?

original: The perdition of th' athversary hath been very great,  reasonable great.
translation: The enemy's loss has been very great, reasonably great.

original: Marry, for my part, I think the duke  hath lost never a man, but one that is like to be  executed for robbing a church, one Bardolph, if your  Majesty know the man.
translation: For my part, I don't think the duke has lost a single man, except one who has likely been executed for robbing a church, a certain Bardolph, if your Majesty knows the man.

original: His face is all bubukles and  whelks and knobs and flames o' fire; and his lips blows  at his nose, and it is like a coal of fire, sometimes  plue and sometimes red, but his nose is executed, and  his fire’s out.
translation: His face is covered in swellings and pimples and bumps and fiery flames, and his lips blow up his nose, which is like a coal in a fire, sometimes blue and sometimes red, but his nose has been executed and his fire is out.

original: We would have all such offenders so cut off, and we  give express charge that in our marches through the  country there be nothing compelled from the villages,  nothing taken but paid for, none of the French upbraided or abused in disdainful language;
translation: I want all such criminals killed that way, and I particularly command that in our march through the country nothing is stolen from the villages, nothing taken unless it's paid for, none of the French scolded or insulted in rude language.

original: for when lenity and  cruelty play for a kingdom, the gentler gamester is the  soonest winner.
translation: Because when kindness and cruelty compete for a kingdom, the gentlest player wins first.

original: You know me by my habit.
translation: You know who I am by how I'm dressed.

original: Well then, I know thee. What shall I know of thee?
translation: Well then, I know who you are. What will I know from you?

original: My master’s mind.
translation: My master's thoughts.

original: Unfold it.
translation: Reveal them.

original: Thus says my king: “Say thou to Harry of England,  though we seemed dead, we did but sleep.
translation: My king says this: "Tell Harry king of England that although we seemed dead, we were just asleep.

original: Advantage is a  better soldier than rashness. Tell him we could have  rebuked him at Harfleur, but that we thought not good to bruise an injury till it were full ripe.
translation: Having the advantage is a better thing in war than foolhardiness. Tell him we could have taught him a lesson at Harfleur, but we didn't think it would be worth hitting a bruise until it was completely ripe.

original: Now we speak  upon our cue, and our voice is imperial. England shall  repent his folly, see his weakness, and admire our  sufferance.
translation: Now it's time for us to speak, and our voice is royal. The king of England will regret his folly, see his weakness, and admire our patience.

original: Bid him therefore consider of his ransom,  which must proportion the losses we have borne, the  subjects we have lost, the disgrace we have digested,  which, in weight to reanswer, his pettiness would bow  under.
translation: So ask him to consider what his ransom will be, which must pay for the losses we suffered, the subjects we lost, the shame we were subjected to, which if we paid him back in kind would completely overwhelm his minor kingdom.

original: For our losses, his exchequer is too poor; for  th' effusion of our blood, the muster of his kingdom too faint a number; and for our disgrace, his own person,  kneeling at our feet but a weak and worthless  satisfaction.
translation: As for our losses, his treasury is too poor; as for the bloodshed, his kingdom doesn't have enough inhabitants; and as for our shame, making him kneel at our feet would be only a weak and worthless revenge.

original: To this, add defiance, and tell him, for  conclusion, he hath betrayed his followers, whose  condemnation is pronounced.” So far my king and master;  so much my office.
translation: To this, add our scorn for him and tell him, finally, he has betrayed his followers, who will be punished." That's what my king and master said. Now I've done my job.

original: What is thy name? I know thy quality.
translation: What is your name? I know what kind of man you are.

original: Montjoy.
translation: Montjoy.

original: Thou dost thy office fairly. Turn thee back,   And tell thy king I do not seek him now   But could be willing to march on to Calais   Without impeachment,
translation: You do your job well. Turn back  and tell your king I'm not looking for him now but could be willing to march on to Calais without fighting.

original: for, to say the sooth,   Though ’tis no wisdom to confess so much   Unto an enemy of craft and vantage,
translation: To tell the truth, although it's not wise to confess so much to an enemy who is so crafty and has such an advantage,

original: My people are with sickness much enfeebled,   My numbers lessened, and those few I have   Almost no better than so many French,
translation: my people have been weakened by sickness. I've lost soldiers and the few I have left are almost worth no more than as many Frenchman.

original: Who when they were in health, I tell thee, herald,   I thought upon one pair of English legs   Did march three Frenchmen.
translation: When they were healthy, I tell you, messenger, I thought that one pair of Englishmen was worth three Frenchmen.

original: Yet, forgive me, God,   That I do brag thus. This your air of France   Hath blown that vice in me. I must repent.
translation: But forgive me, God, for bragging in this way. Your French air has blown this sin into me. I must repent.

original: Go therefore, tell thy master: here I am.   My ransom is this frail and worthless trunk,   My army but a weak and sickly guard,
translation: So go, tell your master: here I am. My ransom is this weak and worthless body, my army is a weak and sickly force,

original: Yet, God before, tell him we will come on   Though France himself and such another neighbor   Stand in our way.
translation: but God willing, tell him we would come fight him even if France itself and another country of the same size stood in our way.

original: There’s for thy labor, Montjoy.   Go bid thy master well advise himself:   If we may pass, we will; if we be hindered,   We shall your tawny ground with your red blood   Discolor.
translation: There's payment for your work, Montjoy. Go ask your master to consider: if we can keep going, we will. If we are stopped, we will stain your dark ground with your red blood.

original: And so, Montjoy, fare you well.   The sum of all our answer is but this:   We would not seek a battle as we are,   Nor, as we are, we say we will not shun it.   So tell your master.
translation: So, Montjoy, farewell. The summary of my answer is this: we wouldn't go looking for a fight as we are, but, as we are, we say we won't avoid one. Tell your master that.

original: I shall deliver so. Thanks to your Highness.
translation: I will. Thank you, your Highness.

original: I hope they will not come upon us now.
translation: I hope they don't attack us now.

original: We are in God’s hand, brother, not in theirs.   March to the bridge.
translation: We are in God's hands, brother, not in theirs. March to the bridge.

original: It now draws toward night.   Beyond the river we’ll encamp ourselves,   And on tomorrow bid them march away.
translation: It's almost night. We'll camp across the river, and tomorrow march away.

original: Tut, I have the best armor of the world. Would it were  day!
translation: I have the best armor in the world. I wish it were day!

original: You have an excellent armor, but let my horse have his  due.
translation: You have excellent armor, but admit my horse's excellence.

original: It is the best horse of Europe.
translation: It is the best horse in Europe.

original: Will it never be morning?
translation: Will it never be morning?

original: My lord of Orléans, and my Lord High Constable, you  talk of horse and armor?
translation: My lord of Orléans and my Lord High Constable, you're talking about horses and armor?

original: You are as well provided of both as any prince in the  world.
translation: You have as good examples of both as any prince inthe world.

original: What a long night is this! I will not change my horse  with any that treads but on four pasterns.
translation: What a long night this is! I wouldn't trade my horse with any other that only walks on four hooves.

original: Çà   ha! He  bounds from the earth, as if his entrails were hairs,   le cheval volant   , the Pegasus,   qui a les narines de feu   .
translation: He jumps from the earth as if his guts were light as hair,  the flying horse , the Pegasus,  who breathes fire from his nostrils .

original: When I bestride him, I soar; I am a hawk; he trots the  air. The earth sings when he touches it. The basest horn of his hoof is more musical than the pipe of Hermes.
translation: When I ride him, I fly; I am a hawk; he trots through the air. The earth sings when he touches it. His least attractive hoof is more musical than the god Hermes's flute.

original: He’s of the color of the nutmeg.
translation: He's the color of nutmeg.

original: And of the heat of the ginger. It is a beast for  Perseus.
translation: And as fiery as ginger. He's an animal fit for the hero  Perseus  to ride.

original: He is pure air and fire; and the dull elements  of earth and water never appear in him, but only in  patient stillness while his rider mounts him.
translation: He is made only of air and fire and the duller elements, earth and water, never show in him, except when he's patiently still while his rider mounts him.

original: He is  indeed a horse, and all other jades you may call beasts.
translation: He is really a horse, and all other nags should only be called beasts.

original: Indeed, my lord, it is a most absolute and excellent  horse.
translation: Yes, my lord, it's an ideal and excellent horse.

original: It is the prince of palfreys. His neigh is like the  bidding of a monarch, and his countenance enforces  homage.
translation: It is the prince of ponies. His neigh is like a king's command, and his face forces you to respect him.

original: No more, cousin.
translation: That's enough, cousin.

original: Nay, the man hath no wit that cannot, from the rising  of the lark to the lodging of the lamb, vary deserved  praise on my palfrey. It is a theme as fluent as the  sea.
translation: No, any man who can't think of different compliments for my horse from the moment the birds get up in the morning to the time the lambs go home in the evening is an idiot. It's a subject that flows like the sea.

original: Turn the sands into eloquent tongues, and my horse  is argument for them all.
translation: Turn all the grains of sand into well-spoken mouths, and my horse gives them all something to talk about.

original: 'Tis a subject for a sovereign to reason on, and for a sovereign’s sovereign to ride  on, and for the world, familiar to us and unknown, to  lay apart their particular functions and wonder at him.
translation: It's a subject for a king to speak of, and for a king's king to ride on, and for the whole world, both familiar parts of it an unknown ones, to set aside all their different business and be amazed at him.

original: I once writ a sonnet in his praise and began thus:  “Wonder of nature—”
translation: I once wrote a sonnet praising him that began, "Wonder of nature—"

original: I have heard a sonnet begin so to one’s mistress.
translation: I've heard a sonnet to someone's girlfriend begin that way.

original: Then did they imitate that which I composed to my  courser, for my horse is my mistress.
translation: Then they were imitating the one I wrote for my warhorse, because my horse is my girlfriend.

original: Your mistress bears well.
translation: Your girlfriend carries weight well.

original: Me well—which is the prescript praise and perfection of a good and particular mistress.
translation: My weight—which is exactly the highest praise and perfect quality of a good, faithful girlfriend.

original: Nay, for methought yesterday your mistress shrewdly  shook your back.
translation: I don't think so, because I thought yesterday your mistress jolted your back around terribly.

original: So perhaps did yours.
translation: Maybe yours did too.

original: Mine was not bridled.
translation: Mine was not wearing a bridle.

original: Oh, then belike she was old and gentle, and you rode,  like a kern of Ireland, your French hose off and in your straight strossers.
translation: Oh, then maybe she was old and gentle and you rode like a poor Irish soldier, with your French tights off and wearing straight trousers instead.

original: You have good judgment in horsemanship.
translation: You are good at judging horses.

original: Be warned by me, then: they that ride so, and ride not  warily, fall into foul bogs. I had rather have my horse  to my mistress.
translation: Take my warning, then: those who ride that way and aren't careful fall into dirty swamps. I would prefer to have my horse as a girlfriend.

original: I had as lief have my mistress a jade.
translation: I would prefer my girfriend to be a nag.

original: I tell thee, Constable, my mistress wears his own hair.
I could make as true a boast as that if I had a sow to  my mistress.
translation: I could make the same boast and be telling the truth if I had a pig as my girlfriend.

original: “Le chien est retourné à son propre vomissement, et la  truie lavée au bourbier.”  Thou mak’st use of anything.
translation: The dog has returned to his own vomit, and the pig has washed herself in mud. You're grasping at straws.

original: Yet do I not use my horse for my mistress, or any such  proverb so little kin to the purpose.
translation: But I don't grasp at my horse like a girlfriend, or supply any pointless proverb.

original: My Lord Constable, the armor that I saw in your tent  tonight, are those stars or suns upon it?
translation: My Lord Constable, the armor I saw in your tent tonight, are those stars or suns on it?

original: Stars, my lord.
translation: Stars, my lord.

original: Some of them will fall tomorrow, I hope.
translation: Some of them will fall tomorrow, I hope.

original: And yet my sky shall not want.
translation: But there will be plenty left in my sky.

original: That may be, for you bear a many superfluously, and  ’twere more honor some were away.
translation: Maybe, because you carry far more than you need, and it would reflect better on you if some went away.

original: Ev'n as your horse bears your praises—who would trot as well were some of your brags dismounted.
translation: The same way your horse bears your compliments—it would trot just as well if some of your brags got off.

original: Would I were able to load him with his desert! Will it  never be day? I will trot tomorrow a mile, and my way  shall be paved with English faces.
translation: I wish I could give him what's coming to him! Will it never be day? I'll trot a mile tomorrow, and my path will be paved with English faces.

original: I will not say so, for fear I should be faced out of my way.
translation: I won't say the same, because I fear I wouldn't be able to face them.

original: But I would it were morning, for I would fain be  about the ears of the English.
translation: But I wish it were morning, because I want to be hacking around the Englishmen's ears.

original: Who will go to hazard with me for twenty prisoners?
translation: Who will bet I'll take twenty prisoners?

original: You must first go yourself to hazard ere you have them.
translation: You will first have to bet your life in battle before you get them.

original: 'Tis midnight. I’ll go arm myself.
translation: It's midnight. I'll go get ready.

original: The Dauphin longs for morning.
translation: The Dauphin longs for morning.

original: He longs to eat the English.
translation: He longs to eat the English.

original: I think he will eat all he kills.
translation: I think he will eat everything he kills.

original: By the white hand of my lady, he’s a gallant prince.
translation: By the white hand of my wife, he’s a brave prince.

original: Swear by her foot, that she may tread out the oath.
translation: Swear by her foot, so she can stamp out the oath.

original: He is simply the most active gentleman of France.
translation: He is simply the most active gentleman in France.

original: Doing is activity, and he will still be doing.
translation: Doing is an activity, and he's always doing someone.

original: He never did harm that I heard of.
translation: I never heard of him doing anyone harm.

original: Nor will do none tomorrow. He will keep that good name  still.
translation: Nor will he do any tomorrow. He'll keep that good reputation.

original: I know him to be valiant.
translation: I know that he's brave.

original: I was told that by one that knows him better than you.
What’s he?
translation: Who's that?

original: Marry, he told me so himself; and he said he cared not  who knew it.
translation: He told me so himself, and said he didn't care who knew.

original: He needs not. It is no hidden virtue in him.
translation: He shouldn't. It's not a hidden quality in him.

original: By my faith, sir, but it is; never anybody saw it but  his lackey.
translation: Actually, sir, it is. No one ever saw it except his servant.

original: 'Tis a hooded valor, and when it appears, it will bate.
translation: It's a disguised bravery, and when it appears, it will end.

original: Ill will never said well.
translation: No one ever spoke well out of spite.

original: I will cap that proverb with “There is flattery in  friendship.”
translation: I will top that saying with "Friends flatter you".

original: And I will take up that with “Give the devil his due.”
translation: And I will meet that with “Give the devil his due.”

original: Well placed; there stands your friend for the devil.  Have at the very eye of that proverb with “A pox of the  devil.”
translation: Well done; the devil now stands for your friend. I'll fight that saying with "Damn the devil".

original: You are the better at proverbs, by how much “A fool’s  bolt is soon shot.”
translation: You're better at sayings, because "a fool is quick to take a shot at people."

original: You have shot over.
translation: Your shot went right over me.

original: 'Tis not the first time you were overshot.
translation: It's not the first time something went over your head.

original: My Lord High Constable, the English lie within fifteen  hundred paces of your tents.
translation: My Lord High Constable, the English camp is less than fifteen hundred steps away from your tents.

original: Who hath measured the ground?
translation: Who measured the distance?

original: The Lord Grandpré.
translation: The Lord Grandpré.

original: A valiant and most expert gentleman.—Would it were day! Alas, poor Harry of England! He longs not for the  dawning as we do.
translation: A brave and very competent gentleman.

original: What a wretched and peevish fellow is this king of  England
translation: What a miserable and headstrong fellow this king of England is,

original: to mope with his fat-brained followers so far  out of his knowledge.
translation: to come mope with his fat-brained followers so far from anything he understands.

original: If the English had any apprehension, they would run  away.
translation: If the English had any sense, they would run away.

original: That they lack, for if their heads had any intellectual armor, they could never wear such heavy head-pieces.
That island of England breeds very valiant creatures.  Their mastiffs are of unmatchable courage.
translation: That island of England breeds very brave creatures. Their mastiff dogs are the bravest of any.

original: Foolish curs, that run winking into the mouth of a  Russian bear and have their heads crushed like rotten  apples.
translation: Silly dogs, that run with their eyes closed into the mouth of a Russian bear and have their heads crushed like rotten apples.

original: You may as well say, that’s a valiant flea that  dare eat his breakfast on the lip of a lion.
translation: You might as well say, that’s a brave flea that dares suck blood from a lion's lip for breakfast.

original: Just, just; and the men do sympathize with the mastiffs in robustious and rough coming on, leaving their wits  with their wives.
translation: True, true. And the men are like mastiffs in that they run at you strongly and roughly, leaving their brains with their wives.

original: And then give them great meals of beef and iron and steel, they will eat like wolves and fight like devils.
translation: And then just give them huge meals of beef and iron and steel, and they will eat like wolves and fight like devils.

original: Ay, but these English are shrewdly out of beef.
translation: Yes, but these English are definitely out of beef.

original: Then shall we find tomorrow they have only stomachs to  eat and none to fight. Now is it time to arm. Come,  shall we about it?
translation: Then we'll find tomorrow that they only have appetites for eating, not fighting. Now it's time to get ready. Come on, shall we go do that?

original: It is now two o'clock. But, let me see, by ten We shall have each a hundred Englishmen.
translation: It's now two o'clock. But, let me see, by ten we'll each have captured a hundred Englishmen.

original: Now entertain conjecture of a time   When creeping murmur and the poring dark   Fills the wide vessel of the universe.
translation: Now imagine a time when creeping whispers and staring darkness fill the wide container of the universe.

original: From camp to camp, through the foul womb of night,   The hum of either army stilly sounds,   That the fixed sentinels almost receive   The secret whispers of each other’s watch.
translation: From camp to camp, through the dirty belly of night, both armies hum quietly, so the guards of each camp can almost hear each other's whispered secrets.

original: Fire answers fire, and through their paly flames   Each battle sees the other’s umbered face.
translation: Fires in both camps mirror each other, and through their pale flames each army sees the other army's shadowy face.

original: Steed threatens steed, in high and boastful neighs   Piercing the night’s dull ear; and from the tents   The armorers, accomplishing the knights,   With busy hammers closing rivets up,   Give dreadful note of preparation.
translation: Horses threaten each other, piercing the quiet night with high-pitched and bragging neighs; and from the tents the armorers, finishing their work for the knights, busily hammering down nails, make frightening sounds of preparation.

original: The country cocks do crow, the clocks do toll,   And, the third hour of drowsy morning named,   Proud of their numbers and secure in soul,   The confident and overlusty French   Do the low-rated English play at dice
translation: The roosters crow in the countryside, the clocks strike, and, now that it is the third hour of sleepy morning, proud of their army's size and sure of themselves, the confident and overeager French play dice for English captives they assume they will take,

original: And chide the cripple, tardy-gaited night,   Who like a foul and ugly witch doth limp   So tediously away.
translation: and scold the handicapped, slow-walking night, which limps like a dirty and ugly witch so slowly away.

original: The poor condemnèd English,   Like sacrifices, by their watchful fires   Sit patiently and inly ruminate   The morning’s danger;
translation: The poor doomed English, like animals waiting to be sacrificed, sit awake patiently by their fires and think quietly about the danger the morning brings.

original: and their gesture sad,   Investing lank-lean cheeks and war-worn coats,   Presenteth them unto the gazing moon   So many horrid ghosts.
translation: And their sad appearance and the hollow cheeks and war-torn coats they wear make them seem to the watching moon like horrible ghosts.

original: Oh, now, who will behold   The royal captain of this ruined band   Walking from watch to watch, from tent to tent?
translation: Oh, now who wants to see the royal leader of this ruined troop walking from guard to guard, from tent to tent?

original: Let him cry, “Praise and glory on his head!”   For forth he goes and visits all his host,   Bids them good morrow with a modest smile,   And calls them brothers, friends, and countrymen.
translation: Let whoever sees him cry, "May he have praise and glory!" because he goes out and visits his whole army, greets them with a humble smile, and calls them brothers, friends, and countrymen.

original: Upon his royal face there is no note   How dread an army hath enrounded him,   Nor doth he dedicate one jot of color   Unto the weary and all-watchèd night,
translation: On his royal face there is no hint of how frightening an army has surrounded him, nor does he allow the tired, sleepless night to take any color from his face,

original: But freshly looks and overbears attaint   With cheerful semblance and sweet majesty,   That every wretch, pining and pale before,   Beholding him, plucks comfort from his looks.
translation: but instead he looks fresh and overcomes tiredness with a cheerful appearance and greatness, so that every poor man, previously suffering and pale, takes comfort from his appearance when he sees him.

original: A largess universal, like the sun,   His liberal eye doth give to everyone,   Thawing cold fear, that mean and gentle all   Behold, as may unworthiness define,   A little touch of Harry in the night.
translation: His generous eye gives gifts to everyone like the sun, thawing cold fear, so that common men and nobles all get what is, as I unworthily call it, a little touch of Harry in the night.

original: And so our scene must to the battle fly,   Where, Oh, for pity, we shall much disgrace,   With four or five most vile and ragged foils   Right ill-disposed in brawl ridiculous,   The name of Agincourt.
translation: And so we must change our scene to the battle, where, sadly, we will disgrace the name of Agincourt very much, misusing four or five cheap and broken-down fencing swords in a ridiculous squabble.

original: Yet sit and see,   Minding true things by what their mock'ries be.
translation: But sit and watch, remembering true things by seeing mockeries of them.

original: Gloucester, ’tis true that we are in great danger.   The greater therefore should our courage be.
translation: Gloucester, it's true we're in great danger. That should make us braver.

original: Not so, my liege, this lodging likes me better, Since I may say, “Now lie I like a king.”
translation: No, my king, I prefer this accommodation, since now I can say "I sleep like a king."

original: 'Tis good for men to love their present pains   Upon example. So the spirit is eased.
translation: It's good for men to love the hardship they suffer because they see other people suffering. It eases the mind.

original: And when the mind is quickened, out of doubt,   The organs, though defunct and dead before,   Break up their drowsy grave and newly move,   With casted slough and fresh legerity.
translation: And when the mind is strengthened, the formerly dead body breaks out of its sleepy grave and moves again, casting off tiredness and gaining new energy.

original: Lend me thy cloak, Sir Thomas. Brothers both,   Commend me to the princes in our camp,   Do my good morrow to them, and anon   Desire them all to my pavilion.
translation: Lend me your cloak, Sir Thomas. Brothers, greet the nobles in our camp for me. Say good morning to them then send them all to my tent.

original: We shall, my liege.
translation: We will, my king.

original: Shall I attend your Grace?
translation: Should I accompany you?

original: No, my good knight.   Go with my brothers to my lords of England.
translation: No, my good knight. Go with my brothers to the nobles of England.

original: I and my bosom must debate awhile,   And then I would no other company.
translation: I must have time to think for a while, but after that there's no one I would rather be with than you.

original: The Lord in heaven bless thee, noble Harry!
translation: May God bless you, noble Harry!

original: God-a-mercy, old heart, thou speak’st cheerfully.
translation: Goodness, old friend, you speak cheerfully.

original: Qui vous là?
translation: Who you there?

original: A friend.
translation: A friend.

original: Discuss unto me: art thou officer or art thou base,  common, and popular?
translation: Tell me: are you an officer or are you low, common, and ordinary?

original: I am a gentleman of a company.
translation: I am a gentleman in a unit.

original: Trail’st thou the puissant pike?
translation: Do you drag a powerful pike?

original: Even so. What are you?
translation: Yes. Who are you?

original: As good a gentleman as the emperor.
translation: As good a man as the emperor.

original: Then you are a better than the king.
translation: Then you are a better one than the king.

original: The king’s a bawcock, and a heart of gold,   A lad of life, an imp of fame,   Of parents good, of fist most valiant.
translation: The king's a darling, and has a heart of gold. He's a lively boy, a famous child, comes from good parents, very brave with his fist.

original: I kiss his dirty shoe, and from heartstring   I love the lovely bully. What is thy name?
translation: I kiss his dirty shoe and from my heart I love the dear fellow. What is your name?

original: Harry le Roy.
translation: Harry le Roy.

original: Le Roy? A Cornish name. Art thou of Cornish crew?
translation: Le Roy? A Cornish name. Are you Cornish?

original: No, I am a Welshman.
translation: No, I am Welsh.

original: Know’st thou Fluellen?
translation: Do you know Fluellen?

original: Yes.
translation: Yes.

original: Tell him I’ll knock his leek about his pate Upon Saint Davy’s day.
translation: Tell him I'll hit him on the head with the leek he wears on Saint Davy's day.

original: Do not you wear your dagger in your cap that day, lest  he knock that about yours.
translation: Don't wear your knife on your hat that day, or he'll hit you on the head with that.

original: Art thou his friend?
translation: Are you his friend?

original: And his kinsman too.
translation: Yes, and his relative.

original: The  figo  for thee then!
translation: A fig for you then!

original: I thank you. God be with you.
translation: Thank you. May God be with you.

original: My name is Pistol called.
translation: My name is Pistol.

original: It sorts well with your fierceness.
translation: It goes well with your temper.

original: Captain Fluellen.
translation: Captain Fluellen.

original: So. In the name of Jesu Christ, speak fewer. It is the  greatest admiration in the universal world when the true and aunchient prerogatifes and laws of the wars is not  kept.
translation: So. In the name of Jesus Christ, don't talk as much. It's the greatest wonder in the whole world when the true and ancient rules and laws of war are broken.

original: If you would take the pains but to examine the  wars of Pompey the Great, you shall find, I warrant you, that there is no tiddle toddle nor pibble babble in  Pompey’s camp.
translation: If you just make the effort to examine the wars of Pompey the Great, you will find, I tell you, that there is no chatting or babbling in Pompey's camp.

original: I warrant you, you shall find the  ceremonies of the wars and the cares of it and the forms of it and the sobriety of it and the modesty of it to  be otherwise.
translation: I tell you, you will find the dignity of war and the care taken about it and the good form of it and the sobriety of it and the modesty of it to be very different from this.

original: Why, the enemy is loud. You hear him all night.
translation: But the enemy is loud. You hear them all night.

original: If the enemy is an ass and a fool and a prating  coxcomb,
translation: If the enemy is an ass and a fool and a babbling idiot,

original: is it meet, think you, that we should also,  look you, be an ass and a fool and a prating coxcomb, in your own conscience, now?
translation: is it right, do you think, that we should also, see, be an ass and a fool and a babbling idiot, tell me truly?

original: I will speak lower.
translation: I will speak more quietly.

original: I pray you and beseech you that you will.
translation: I pray and beg you to.

original: Though it appear a little out of fashion, There is much care and valor in this Welshman.
translation: Although he's very strange, there's a lot of seriousness and bravery in this Welshman.

original: Brother John Bates, is not that the morning which  breaks yonder?
translation: Brother John Bates, is that not the dawn over there?

original: I think it be, but we have no great cause to desire the approach of day.
translation: I think so, but we have no good reason to want day to come.

original: We see yonder the beginning of the day, but I think we  shall never see the end of it.—Who goes there?
translation: We see the beginning of the day there, but I think we will never see the end of it.

original: A friend.
translation: A friend.

original: Under what captain serve you?
translation: Who is your captain?

original: Under Sir Thomas Erpingham.
translation: Sir Thomas Erpingham.

original: A good old commander and a most kind gentleman. I pray  you, what thinks he of our estate?
translation: A good old commander and a very kind man. Please, what does he think about our situation?

original: Even as men wracked upon a sand, that look to be washed off the next tide.
translation: That we're like men shipwrecked on a sandbank, who expect to be washed off by the next tide.

original: He hath not told his thought to the king?
translation: He hasn't told the king what he thinks?

original: No. Nor it is not meet he should, for, though I speak  it to you, I think the king is but a man as I am.
translation: No. And he shouldn't, because, though I say so, I think the king is just a man like me.

original: The  violet smells to him as it doth to me. The element shows to him as it doth to me. All his senses have but human  conditions.
translation: The violet smells the same to him as it does to me. The world looks the same to him as it does to me. All his senses are only human.

original: His ceremonies laid by, in his nakedness he  appears but a man, and though his affections are higher  mounted than ours, yet when they stoop, they stoop with  the like wing.
translation: Without his props of royalty, he looks like a man when he's naked. Although his emotions are nobler than ours, when he is weak, he is weak in the same way we are.

original: Therefore, when he sees reason of fears  as we do, his fears, out of doubt, be of the same relish as ours are.
translation: So when he sees good reason for fear like we do, his fears are the same kind as ours.

original: Yet, in reason, no man should possess him  with any appearance of fear, lest he, by showing it,  should dishearten his army.
translation: But, thinking reasonably, no man should look afraid, because he could discourage the army by showing fear.

original: He may show what outward courage he will, but I  believe, as cold a night as ’tis, he could wish himself  in Thames up to the neck
translation: He can pretend to be as brave as he wants, but I think, even though it's so cold tonight, he wishes he were in the Thames up to his neck;

original: ; and so I would he were, and I  by him, at all adventures, so we were quit here.
translation: and I wish he were, and me too, whatever happened, so we could get out of here.

original: By my troth, I will speak my conscience of the king. I  think he would not wish himself anywhere but where he  is.
translation: Truly, I will tell you what I think about the king. I think he would not wish to be anywhere except where he is.

original: Then I would he were here alone; so should he be sure  to be ransomed, and a many poor men’s lives saved.
translation: Then I wish he were here alone; he would be certain of being ransomed, and many poor men's lives would be saved.

original: I dare say you love him not so ill to wish him here  alone, howsoever you speak this to feel other men’s  minds.
translation: I bet you don't dislike him enough to wish he were here alone, even though you say that to figure out what other men think.

original: Methinks I could not die anywhere so contented as in the king’s company, his cause being just and his  quarrel honorable.
translation: I think I couldn't die anywhere more happily than in the king's company, since his cause is right and the war is justified.

original: That’s more than we know.
translation: That's more than we could say.

original: Ay, or more than we should seek after, for we know  enough if we know we are the king’s subjects.
translation: Yes, and it's more than we should want to say, because we know enough if we know we are the king's subjects.

original: If his  cause be wrong, our obedience to the king wipes the  crime of it out of us.
translation: If his cause is wrong, we're not guilty of the crime because we're right to obey the king.

original: But if the cause be not good, the king himself hath a  heavy reckoning to make, when all those legs and arms  and heads, chopped off in a battle, shall join together  at the latter day, and cry all, “We died at such a  place,”
translation: But if the cause isn't good, the king will have to pay for it at the Judgment Day when all the legs and arms and heads chopped off in a battle join together all all cry, "We died at this place,"

original: some swearing, some crying for a surgeon, some  upon their wives left poor behind them, some upon the  debts they owe, some upon their children rawly left.
translation: some swearing, some crying out for a doctor, some crying out about their wives being left without them without resources, some about the debts they owe, some about their children suddenly left behind.

original: I  am afeard there are few die well that die in a battle,  for how can they charitably dispose of anything, when  blood is their argument?
translation: I am afraid that few men die a good death in a battle, because how can they worry about good deeds when they are shedding blood?

original: Now, if these men do not die  well, it will be a black matter for the king that led  them to it, who to disobey were against all proportion  of subjection.
translation: No, if these men do not die a good death, it will be bad for the king who led them to this, when it would be wrong for a subject to disobey him.

original: So, if a son that is by his father sent about  merchandise do sinfully miscarry upon the sea, the  imputation of his wickedness, by your rule, should be  imposed upon his father that sent him.
translation: So, if a sinful son sent by his father to do a business deal is shipwrecked, his sins, by your rule, should be paid for by the father who sent him.

original: Or if a servant,  under his master’s command transporting a sum of money,  be assailed by robbers and die in many irreconciled  iniquities, you may call the business of the master the  author of the servant’s damnation.
translation: Or if a servant, transporting money under his master's orders, is attacked by robbers and dies without repenting for his sins, you call the master's business the cause of the servant being damned.

original: But this is not so.  The king is not bound to answer the particular endings  of his soldiers, the father of his son, nor the master  of his servant, for they purpose not their death, when  they purpose their services.
translation: But that isn't true. The king isn't forced to answer for the deaths of his soldiers, the father for his son's, or the master for his servant's, because they don't mean for them to die when they send them to do their jobs.

original: Besides, there is no king,  be his cause never so spotless, if it come to the  arbitrament of swords, can try it out with all unspotted soldiers.
translation: Besides, there is no king, however good his cause is, when the cause comes to be settled in battle, who can fight with completely innocent soldiers.

original: Some, peradventure, have on them the guilt of premeditated and contrived murder; some, of beguiling  virgins with the broken seals of perjury; some, making  the wars their bulwark, that have before gored the  gentle bosom of peace with pillage and robbery.
translation: Some, perhaps, are guilty of premeditated murder; some, of lying to young women so they sleep with them; some go to war to protect themselves because they previously destroyed peacetime by robbing and looting.

original: Now, if  these men have defeated the law and outrun native  punishment, though they can outstrip men, they have no  wings to fly from God.
translation: Now, if these men have defeated the law and run from punishment at home, although they can escape men, they can't run from God.

original: War is His beadle, war is His  vengeance, so that here men are punished for  before-breach of the king’s laws in now the king’s  quarrel.
translation: War is His officer, war is His revenge, so that men are punished here and now while fighting for the king for previously breaking the king's laws.

original: Where they feared the death, they have borne  life away; and where they would be safe, they perish.  Then, if they die unprovided, no more is the king guilty of their damnation than he was before guilty of those  impieties for the which they are now visited.
translation: When they feared death, they escaped with their lives. And here where they thought they would be safe, the die. So, if they died without repenting, the king is no more guilty of their damnation than he was guilty before of the sins for which they are now punished.

original: Every  subject’s duty is the king’s, but every subject’s soul  is his own. Therefore should every soldier in the wars  do as every sick man in his bed: wash every mote out of  his conscience.
translation: Every subject's obedience belongs to the king, but every subject's soul is his own. So every soldier in the war should do the same as every sick man in his bed: make up for everything that he feels guilty about.

original: And, dying so, death is to him  advantage; or not dying, the time was blessedly lost  wherein such preparation was gained.
translation: So if he dies after that, he profits by going to heaven. Or, if he doesn't die, the time was well spent in preparing for death.

original: And in him that  escapes, it were not sin to think that, making God so  free an offer, He let him outlive that day to see His  greatness and to teach others how they should prepare.
translation: And whoever survives should think that, because he offered himself to God so completely, God let him survive that day so he would understand His greatness and teach others how to prepare for battle.

original: 'Tis certain, every man that dies ill, the ill upon his own head. The king is not to answer it.
translation: It's true, every man who dies badly is responsible for it himself. The king shouldn't be punished for it.

original: I do not desire he should answer for me, and yet I  determine to fight lustily for him.
translation: I don't want him to be punished for me, but I am determined to fight well for him.

original: I myself heard the king say he would not be ransomed.
translation: I heard the king say he would not pay a ransom if he were captured.

original: Ay, he said so, to make us fight cheerfully, but when  our throats are cut, he may be ransomed, and we ne'er  the wiser.
translation: Yes, he said so to make us fight cheerfully, but when our throats have been cut he can be ransomed without us knowing about it.

original: If I live to see it, I will never trust his word after.
translation: If I live to see that, I'll never trust him again.

original: You pay him then.
translation: Then make him pay for it.

original: That’s a perilous shot out of an  elder gun, that a poor and private displeasure can do  against a monarch. You may as well go about to turn the  sun to ice with fanning in his face with a peacock’s  feather.
translation: A poor, ordinary man offended by a king can't do anything about it. It's like trying to shoot an old gun—it could blow up in your face.  You might as well try to turn the sun to ice by fanning its face with a peacock feather.

original: You’ll “never trust his word after.” Come, ’tis a foolish saying.
translation: You'll "never trust him again." Come on, that's a silly thing to say.

original: Your reproof is something too round. I should be angry  with you if the time were convenient.
translation: Your response is too rude. I would be angry with you if it were convenient.

original: Let it be a quarrel between us, if you live.
translation: Let's fight about it later, if you survive.

original: I embrace it.
translation: Gladly.

original: How shall I know thee again?
translation: How will I recognize you again?

original: Give me any gage of thine, and I will wear it in my  bonnet. Then, if ever thou dar’st acknowledge it, I will make it my quarrel.
translation: Give me anything of yours, and I'll wear it on my hat. Then, if you dare acknowledge it's yours, I'll fight you.

original: Here’s my glove. Give me another of thine.
translation: Here's my glove. Give me one of yours.

original: There.
translation: There.

original: This will I also wear in my cap. If ever thou come to  me and say, after tomorrow, “This is my glove,” by this  hand I will take thee a box on the ear.
translation: I'll also wear this in my hat. I you ever come to me and say, after tomorrow, "This is my glove", then I swear by this hand I'll hit you on the ear.

original: If ever I live to see it, I will challenge it.
translation: If I live to see it, I will challenge you.

original: Thou dar’st as well be hanged.
translation: You don't dare - you'd rather be hanged.

original: Well, I will do it, though I take thee in the king’s  company.
translation: I'll do it, even if I see you in the king's company.

original: Keep thy word. Fare thee well.
translation: Keep your promise. Goodbye.

original: Be friends, you English fools, be friends. We have  French quarrels enough, if you could tell how to reckon.
Indeed, the French may lay twenty French crowns to one  they will beat us, for they bear them on their  shoulders.
translation: Yes, the French can bet twenty French crown coins to one they'll beat us, because they carry French crowns, heads, on their shoulders.

original: But it is no English treason to cut French  crowns, and tomorrow the king himself will be a clipper.
translation: But it's not treason for English people to attack the French crown, and tomorrow the king himself will  clip  some crowns off.

original: Upon the king! Let us our lives, our souls, our debts,  our careful wives, our children, and our sins lay on the king!   We must bear all.
translation: Blame the king! Let's blame the king for what happens to our lives, our souls, our debts, our sad wives, our children, and our sins! I have to be responsible for all of it.

original: O hard condition,   Twin-born with greatness, subject to the breath   Of every fool, whose sense no more can feel   But his own wringing.
translation: What a difficult situation it is being powerful, being talked about by every fool who can't understand anything except his own hardship.

original: What infinite heart’s ease   Must kings neglect that private men enjoy?   And what have kings that privates have not too,   Save ceremony, save general ceremony?
translation: What wonderful calm do kings have to give up that other men who have a private life enjoy? And what do kings have that people with private lives don't have too?  Except ritual, except ritual in everything they do?

original: And what art thou, thou idol ceremony?   What kind of god art thou, that suffer’st more   Of mortal griefs than do thy worshippers?   What are thy rents? What are thy comings in?   O ceremony, show me but thy worth!   What is thy soul of adoration?
translation: And what are you, you false god, ritual? What kind of god are you, who suffer more than your worshippers? What are your revenues? What do you earn? Ritual, show me your worth! What are you really?

original: Art thou aught else but place, degree, and form,   Creating awe and fear in other men,   Wherein thou art less happy, being feared,   Than they in fearing?
translation: Are you anything else than circumstances, rank, and appearances, creating wonder and fear in other men, but less happy to be feared than they are to fear you?

original: What drink’st thou oft, instead of homage sweet,   But poisoned flattery? Oh, be sick, great greatness,   And bid thy ceremony give thee cure!
translation: Don't you often drink poisoned flattery instead of sweet faithfulness? Oh, be sick, great greatness, then ask ritual to cure you!

original: Think’st thou the fiery fever will go out   With titles blown from adulation?   Will it give place to flexure and low bending?   Canst thou, when thou command’st the beggar’s knee,   Command the health of it?
translation: Do you think your raging fever will go down by being called by great titles by flatterers? Will it go down by being bowed to? Can you, when you command a beggar to bow to you, command yourself to be healthy?

original: No, thou proud dream,   That play’st so subtly with a king’s repose.
translation: No, you proud dream, you play cleverly with a king's thoughts.

original: I am a king that find thee, and I know   'Tis not the balm, the scepter, and the ball,   The sword, the mace, the crown imperial,   The intertissued robe of gold and pearl,   The farcèd title running 'fore the king,   The throne he sits on, nor the tide of pomp   That beats upon the high shore of this world.
translation: I am a king, and I know it's not the royal ointment, the scepter, the orb, the sword, the club, the imperial crown, the robe woven from pearls and gold, the stuffy title running in front of the king, the throne he sits, or the sea of splendid things that beats on the high shore of this world.

original: No, not all these, thrice-gorgeous ceremony,   Not all these, laid in bed majestical,   Can sleep so soundly as the wretched slave,   Who, with a body filled and vacant mind,   Gets him to rest, crammed with distressful bread;
translation: No, none of these, gorgeous ritual, none of these, laid in a royal bed, can sleep as soundly as a miserable slave who, with a full stomach and empty mind, lies down to sleep stuffed with hard-earned bread.

original: Never sees horrid night, the child of hell,   But, like a lackey, from the rise to set   Sweats in the eye of Phoebus, and all night   Sleeps in Elysium;
translation: He never sees horrible night, the child of hell. Like a servant, from sunrise to sunset he sweats in the sun, and all night sleeps in Paradise.

original: next day after dawn,   Doth rise and help Hyperion to his horse,   And follows so the ever-running year   With profitable labor to his grave.
translation: The next day, he rises at dawn and helps the day begin, and follows the year over and over in this way with useful labor until he dies.

original: And, but for ceremony, such a wretch,   Winding up days with toil and nights with sleep,   Had the forehand and vantage of a king.
translation: And, except for ritual, a miserable man like that, using up days with work and nights with sleep, is in a better situation than a king.

original: The slave, a member of the country’s peace,   Enjoys it, but in gross brain little wots   What watch the king keeps to maintain the peace,   Whose hours the peasant best advantages.
translation: The slave, a subject in a peaceful country, enjoys that peace, but in his dull brain he doesn't know the king is staying up all night to keep the peace, to improve the peasant's life.

original: My lord, your nobles, jealous of your absence, Seek through your camp to find you.
translation: My lord, your nobles, worried about your absence, are looking for you throughout the camp.

original: Good old knight, Collect them all together at my tent. I’ll be before thee.
translation: Good old knight, gather them all at my tent. I'll go there now.

original: I shall do’t, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: O God of battles, steel my soldiers' hearts.   Possess them not with fear. Take from them now   The sense of reck'ning ere th' opposèd numbers   Pluck their hearts from them.
translation: Oh God of battles, strengthen my soldiers' courage. Don't make them afraid. Take from them now the ability to count before the number of our enemies frightens them.

original: Not today, O Lord,   Oh, not today, think not upon the fault   My father made in compassing the crown.
translation: Don't think today, Oh Lord, oh, not today, about the crime my father committed by taking the crown.

original: I Richard’s body have interrèd anew,   And on it have bestowed more contrite tears   Than from it issued forcèd drops of blood.
translation: I have re-buried Richard's body, and I have cried more repenting tears on it than drops of blood were forced from it.

original: Five hundred poor I have in yearly pay,   Who twice a day their withered hands hold up   Toward heaven to pardon blood.
translation: I pay five hundred poor people every year to pray twice every day for God to pardon the murder.

original: And I have built   Two chantries where the sad and solemn priests   Sing still for Richard’s soul.
translation: And I have built two chapels where the serious priests still sing for Richard's soul.

original: More will I do—   Though all that I can do is nothing worth,   Since that my penitence comes after all,   Imploring pardon.
translation: I'll do more—although everything I can do is worth nothing, since my repentance comes after the sin, asking for forgiveness.

original: My liege.
translation: My king.

original: My brother Gloucester’s voice.—Ay, I know thy errand. I will go with thee. The day, my friends, and all things stay for me.
translation: That's my brother Gloucester's voice.

original: The sun doth gild our armor. Up, my lords.
translation: The sun is shining off our armor. Get up, my lords.

original: Montez à cheval!  My horse, varlet! Lackey! Ha!
translation: Get on your horses! My horse, servant! Servant!

original: O brave spirit!
translation: What a brave man!

original: Via les eaux et la terre.
translation: Let's go, by water and earth.

original: Rien puis? L'air et feu?
translation: And nothing else? Air and fire?

original: Cieux,  cousin Orléans.
translation: Heaven, cousin Orléans.

original: Now, my Lord Constable?
translation: Now, my Lord Constable?

original: Hark how our steeds for present service neigh.
translation: Listen to our horses neighing. They're asking to be ridden and made useful soon.
