original: Mount them and make incision in their hides,
translation: Get on them and spur them so hard they bleed,

original: That their hot blood may spin in English eyes   And dout them with superfluous courage. Ha!
translation: so that their hot blood gushes into English eyes and extinguishes them with too much courage. Ha!

original: What, will you have them weep our horses' blood? How shall we then behold their natural tears?
translation: What, you want them to weep our horses' blood? Then how will we see their own tears?

original: The English are embattled, you French peers.
translation: The English are ready to fight, you French noblemen.

original: To horse, you gallant princes, straight to horse.   Do but behold yond poor and starvèd band,   And your fair show shall suck away their souls,   Leaving them but the shales and husks of men.
translation: Get on your horses, brave princes, straight on your horses. Just look at that poor starved troop and your good appearance will suck away their souls, making them just peels and husks of men.

original: There is not work enough for all our hands,   Scarce blood enough in all their sickly veins   To give each naked curtal axe a stain,   That our French gallants shall today draw out   And sheathe for lack of sport.
translation: There is not enough work for all of us, hardly enough blood in all their sick veins to stain every short axe that our brave Frenchmen will draw today then sheathe because there's nothing left to do.

original: Let us but blow on them,   The vapor of our valor will o'erturn them.
translation: Just blow on them, and the steam of our courage will defeat them.

original: 'Tis positive against all exceptions, lords,   That our superfluous lackeys and our peasants,   Who in unnecessary action swarm   About our squares of battle, were enough   To purge this field of such a hilding foe,
translation: It's certain, lords, that our unnecessary servants and peasants, who swarm pointlessly around the battlefield, would be enough to clear this field of such a pathetic enemy,

original: Though we upon this mountain’s basis by   Took stand for idle speculation,
translation: even if we stood at the base of this mountain watching and doing nothing.

original: But that our honors must not. What’s to say?   A very little little let us do,   And all is done.
translation: But our honor doesn't allow that. What more is there to say? Let's just do a very little, and it will all be done.

original: Then let the trumpets sound   The tucket sonance and the note to mount,   For our approach shall so much dare the field   That England shall couch down in fear and yield.
translation: So blow the trumpets to signal the troops to get on their horses and march, because our approach will be so confident that the English will hide in fear and give up.

original: Why do you stay so long, my lords of France?   Yond island carrions, desperate of their bones,   Ill-favoredly become the morning field.
translation: Why are you waiting so long, lords of France? Those island-dwelling carcasses, desperate for their lives, are ugly on the battlefield this morning.

original: Their ragged curtains poorly are let loose,   And our air shakes them passing scornfully.
translation: Their ragged banners are badly rolled out, and the wind of our country shakes them mockingly.

original: Big Mars seems bankrupt in their beggared host   And faintly through a rusty beaver peeps.
translation: The big war-god Mars seems bankrupt when you look at their army of beggars and peeps weakly through a rusty helmet.

original: The horsemen sit like fixèd candlesticks   With torch staves in their hand, and their poor jades   Lob down their heads, dropping the hides and hips,
translation: The horsemen sit stiffly as candlesticks holding up torches, and their poor nags droop their heads, their skins and hips sagging,

original: The gum down-roping from their pale-dead eyes,   And in their pale dull mouths the gemeled bit   Lies foul with chawed grass, still and motionless.
translation: with tears dripping from their death-pale eyes, and in their pale dull mouths the jewel-covered bit is dirty with chewed grass, quiet and motionless.

original: And their executors, the knavish crows,   Fly o'er them all, impatient for their hour.
translation: And their  executors , the evil crows, fly over them, impatient for their time to be up.

original: Description cannot suit itself in words   To demonstrate the life of such a battle   In life so lifeless, as it shows itself.
translation: You can't describe in words, exactly as you see it, such a lifeless life prepared for battle.

original: They have said their prayers, and they stay for death.
translation: They have said their prayers, and they're waiting for death.

original: Shall we go send them dinners and fresh suits, And give their fasting horses provender, And after fight with them?
translation: Should we go send them dinner and fresh suits, and give their starving horses hay, and fight them afterwards?

original: I stay but for my guard. On, to the field!   I will the banner from a trumpet take   And use it for my haste.
translation: I'm only waiting for my guards. Let's go, to the field! I will take the banner from a trumpet and use it to hurry things up.

original: Come, come away.   The sun is high, and we outwear the day.
translation: Come on, let's go. The sun is high in the sky, and we're wasting the day.

original: Where is the king?
translation: Where is the king?

original: The king himself is rode to view their battle.
translation: He rode out to look at their army himself.

original: Of fighting men they have full threescore thousand.
translation: They have a good sixty thousand fighting men.

original: There’s five to one. Besides, they all are fresh.
translation: That's five to one. And they're all fresh.

original: God’s arm strike with us! 'Tis a fearful odds.   God be wi' you, princes all. I’ll to my charge.
translation: May God fight for us! It's frightening odds. God be with you, princes. I'll go to my troops.

original: If we no more meet till we meet in heaven,   Then joyfully, my noble Lord of Bedford,   My dear Lord Gloucester, and my good Lord Exeter,   And my kind kinsman, warriors all, adieu.
translation: If we don't meet again until we meet in heaven, then I joyfully say goodbye, noble Lord of Bedford, dear Lord Gloucester, and good Lord Exeter, and

original: Farewell, good Salisbury, and good luck go with thee.
translation: Goodbye, good Salisbury, and good luck.

original: Farewell, kind lord. Fight valiantly today. And yet I do thee wrong to mind thee of it, For thou art framed of the firm truth of valor.
translation: Goodbye, kind lord. Fight bravely today. But I'm insulting you by reminding you of that, because you're made out of bravery itself.

original: He is as full of valor as of kindness, Princely in both.
translation: He is as full of bravery out of kindness, and has the amount of each quality one expects in a prince.

original: Oh, that we now had here But one ten thousand of those men in England That do no work today.
translation: I wish we now had here just ten thousand of the men in England who aren't working today.

original: What’s he that wishes so?   My cousin Westmoreland? No, my fair cousin.   If we are marked to die, we are enough   To do our country loss;
translation: Who wishes that? My cousin Westmoreland? No, good cousin. If we are doomed to die, there are enough of us to harm our country by our loss;

original: and if to live,   The fewer men, the greater share of honor.
translation: and if to live, the fewer men there are, the greater share of honor each one gets.

original: God’s will, I pray thee wish not one man more.
translation: By God, please don't wish for even one more man.

original: By Jove, I am not covetous for gold   Nor care I who doth feed upon my cost;   It yearns me not if men my garments wear;   Such outward things dwell not in my desires.
translation: By God, I don't desire gold and I don't care who takes my money to pay for food; I don't mind if men wear my clothes; I don't desire such worldly things.

original: But if it be a sin to covet honor,   I am the most offending soul alive.
translation: But if it's a sin to desire honor, I am the most sinful man alive.

original: No, faith, my coz, wish not a man from England.   God’s peace, I would not lose so great an honor   As one man more, methinks, would share from me,   For the best hope I have. Oh, do not wish one more!
translation: No, really, cousin, don't wish for a single man from England. God, I wouldn't give up so great a share of honor as one more man, I think, would take from me, in exchange for getting my greatest wish. Don't wish for one more!

original: Rather proclaim it, Westmoreland, through my host,   That he which hath no stomach to this fight,   Let him depart.
translation: But, Westmoreland, announce to my army that anyone who doesn't feel like fighting should leave.

original: His passport shall be made,   And crowns for convoy put into his purse.   We would not die in that man’s company   That fears his fellowship to die with us.
translation: We'll give him a passport and money to pay for his travel back. I don't want to die in the company of a man who is afraid to die in mine.

original: This day is called the feast of Crispian.   He that outlives this day and comes safe home,   Will stand o' tiptoe when the day is named   And rouse him at the name of Crispian.
translation: This day is the feast day of Crispin. Anyone who lives through this day and gets home safely will stand on tiptoe when the day is mentioned and jump up at the name of Crispin.

original: He that shall see this day, and live old age,   Will yearly on the vigil feast his neighbors   And say, “Tomorrow is Saint Crispian.”
translation: Anyone who lives through this day and lives to old age will hold a feast for his neighbors on the day before and say "Tomorrow is Saint Crispin's day."

original: Then will he strip his sleeve and show his scars,   And say, “These wounds I had on Crispin’s day.”
translation: Then he will raise his sleeve and show his scars and say, "I got these wounds on Crispin's day."

original: Old men forget; yet all shall be forgot   But he’ll remember with advantages   What feats he did that day.
translation: Old men forget; but everything else will be forgotten and he'll still remember, with additions, all the deeds he did that day.

original: Then shall our names,   Familiar in his mouth as household words,   Harry the King, Bedford and Exeter,   Warwick and Talbot, Salisbury and Gloucester,   Be in their flowing cups freshly remembered.
translation: Then our names, familiar to him as household words, Harry the King, Bedford and Exeter, Warwick and Talbot, Salisbury and Gloucester, will be remembered by them as they drink.

original: This story shall the good man teach his son,   And Crispin Crispian shall ne'er go by,   From this day to the ending of the world,   But we in it shall be rememberèd—   We few, we happy few, we band of brothers;
translation: The good man will teach his son that story, and Saint Crispin's day will never go by, from this day to the end of the world, without us being remembered—we few, we lucky few, we band of brothers.

original: For he today that sheds his blood with me   Shall be my brother; be he ne'er so vile,   This day shall gentle his condition;
translation: Because anyone who sheds his blood today with me will be my brother. However low-born he is, this day will make him a nobleman.

original: And gentlemen in England now abed   Shall think themselves accursed they were not here,   And hold their manhoods cheap whiles any speaks   That fought with us upon Saint Crispin’s day.
translation: And gentlemen now in their beds in England will be miserable that they were not here, and they will think that they are not real men when anyone is speaking who fought with us on Saint Crispin's day.

original: My sovereign lord, bestow yourself with speed. The French are bravely in their battles set, And will with all expedience charge on us.
translation: My king, get ready quickly. The French are well prepared for battle, and will soon charge at us.

original: All things are ready if our minds be so.
translation: Everything is ready if our minds are.

original: Perish the man whose mind is backward now!
translation: Death to anyone who wants to run away now!

original: Thou dost not wish more help from England, coz?
translation: You don't wish for more help from England, cousin?

original: God’s will, my liege, would you and I alone, Without more help, could fight this royal battle!
translation: By God, my king, I wish you and I alone, without more help, could fight this royal battle!

original: Why, now thou hast unwished five thousand men, Which likes me better than to wish us one. —You know your places. God be with you all.
translation: What, you've just wished away five thousand men, which I like better than to wish to add one.

original: Once more I come to know of thee, King Harry,   If for thy ransom thou wilt now compound,   Before thy most assurèd overthrow.
translation: Once more I've come to ask you, King Harry, if you'll agree to a sum for your ransom before your certain defeat.

original: For certainly thou art so near the gulf   Thou needs must be englutted.
translation: Because certainly you are so near the whirlpool that you'll necessarily be swallowed by it.

original: Besides, in mercy,   The constable desires thee thou wilt mind   Thy followers of repentance, that their souls   May make a peaceful and a sweet retire   From off these fields where, wretches, their poor  bodies   Must lie and fester.
translation: Besides, as an act of mercy, the constable asks that you remind your followers to repent, so that their souls retreat peacefully and sweetly from these fields where, poor things, their poor bodies must lie and rot.

original: Who hath sent thee now?
translation: Who has sent you now?

original: The constable of France.
translation: The constable of France.

original: I pray thee, bear my former answer back.   Bid them achieve me and then sell my bones.
translation: Please, send the same answer back as last time. Tell them they'll have to catch me before they sell my bones.

original: Good God, why should they mock poor fellows thus?   The man that once did sell the lion’s skin   While the beast lived was killed with hunting him.
translation: Good God, why do they have to mock poor men this way? The man who sold the lion's skin while the beast was alive, died while hunting him.

original: A many of our bodies shall no doubt   Find native graves, upon the which, I trust,   Shall witness live in brass of this day’s work.
translation: Many of our bodies will no doubt be buried in our own countries, on which, I trust, carved in brass will be a reminder of the work we do today.

original: And those that leave their valiant bones in France,   Dying like men though buried in your dunghills,   They shall be famed;
translation: And those who leave their brave bones in France, dying like men though buried in piles of dung, will be famous.

original: for there the sun shall greet them   And draw their honors reeking up to heaven,   Leaving their earthly parts to choke your clime,   The smell whereof shall breed a plague in France.
translation: Because the the sun will greet them and drag their honor stinking up to heaven, leaving their flesh to choke your climate, the smell of which will start a plague in France.

original: Mark, then, abounding valor in our English,   That being dead, like to the bullet’s crazing,   Break out into a second course of mischief,   Killing in relapse of mortality.
translation: See, then, huge bravery in our Englishmen, who although they're dead, like a bullet breaking in two, break out into a second path of mischief, killing by being dead.

original: Let me speak proudly: tell the constable   We are but warriors for the working day;
translation: Let me speak proudly: tell the constable we're just working-day heroes.

original: Our gayness and our gilt are all besmirched   With rainy marching in the painful field.
translation: Our beautiful things and gold are dirty from painful marching in the rain.

original: There’s not a piece of feather in our host—   Good argument, I hope, we will not fly—   And time hath worn us into slovenry.
translation: There's not a single decorative feather in our whole army, which goes to show we won't fly away, and time has worn us down and made us messy.

original: But, by the Mass, our hearts are in the trim,   And my poor soldiers tell me, yet ere night   They’ll be in fresher robes, or they will pluck   The gay new coats o'er the French soldiers' heads   And turn them out of service.
translation: But, by God, our hearts are in order, and my poor soldiers tell me that before night they'll be wearing fresher clothes, or they'll pull the beautiful new uniforms over the French soldiers' heads and so throw them out of the army.

original: If they do this,   As, if God please, they shall, my ransom then   Will soon be levied.
translation: If they do this, as (if God wishes it) they will, my ransom will be paid soon.

original: Herald, save thou thy labor.   Come thou no more for ransom, gentle herald.   They shall have none, I swear, but these my joints,   Which, if they have, as I will leave 'em them,   Shall yield them little. Tell the constable.
translation: Herald, save yourself pointless work. Don't come any more for ransom, gentle herald. They will have none, I swear, except my joints here, which, in the state I'll leave them, won't be worth much to them. Tell the constable that.

original: I shall, King Harry. And so fare thee well. Thou never shalt hear herald anymore.
translation: I will, king Harry. Goodbye. You will never hear a herald ever again.

original: I fear thou wilt once more come again for a ransom.
translation: I am afraid you will come once more for a ransom.

original: My lord, most humbly on my knee I beg The leading of the vaward.
translation: My lord, I beg humbly, on my knees, to lead the charge.

original: Take it, brave York. Now, soldiers, march away, And how Thou pleasest, God, dispose the day.
translation: Do it, brave York. Now, soldiers, march away, and make the day go however you want, God.

original: Yield, cur.
translation: Surrender, you dog.

original: Je pense que vous êtes gentilhomme de bonne qualité.
translation: I think you're a noble gentleman.

original: Qualtitie calmie custure me. Art thou a gentleman? What is thy name? Discuss.
translation: Qualtitie calmie custure me. Are you a gentleman? What is your name? Discuss.

original: Ô Seigneur Dieu!
translation: Oh Lord God!

original: O Seigneur Dew should be a gentleman.
translation: Olord God sounds like a gentleman.

original: Perpend my words, O Seigneur Dew, and mark
translation: Listen to my words, Olord God, and see:

original: : O Seigneur Dew, thou diest on point of fox, except, O Seigneur, thou do give to me  egregious ransom.
translation: Olord God, you'll die on the point of a sword unless, Olord, you give give me an extraordinary ransom.

original: Ô, prenez miséricorde! Ayez pitié de moi!
translation: Oh, be merciful! Take pity on me!

original: Moy shall not serve. I will have forty moys, or I will  fetch thy rim out at thy throat in drops of crimson  blood.
Est-il impossible d'Échapper la force de ton bras?
translation: Is it possible to escape your strong arm?

original: Brass, cur? Thou damned and luxurious mountain goat,  offer’st me brass?
translation: "Brass", dog? You damned and self-indulgent mountain goat, you offer me brass?

original: Ô, pardonnez-moi!
translation: Oh, forgive me!

original: Say’st thou me so? Is that a ton of moys?—Come hither,  boy. Ask me this slave in French what is his name.
translation: Is that what you're telling me? Does that mean a ton of moys?

original: Écoutez. Comment êtes-vous appelé?
translation: Listen. What are you called?

original: Monsieur le Fer.
translation: Mister le Fer.

original: He says his name is Master Fer.
translation: He says his name is Mister Fer.

original: Master Fer. I’ll fer him, and firk him, and ferret him. Discuss the same in French unto him.
translation: Mister Fer. I'll fer  him, and fight him, and hunt him with ferrets. Discuss this in French with him.

original: I do not know the French for “fer,” and “ferret,” and  “firk.”
translation: I do not know the French for “fer,” and “ferret,” and “fight.”

original: Bid him prepare, for I will cut his throat.
translation: Ask him to prepare himself, because I'm going to cut his throat.

original: [To the BOY) Que dit-il, monsieur?
translation: [to the BOY] What is he saying, sir?

original: Il me commande à vous dire que vous faites vous prêt,  car ce soldat ici est disposé tout à cette heure de  couper votre gorge.
translation: He commands me to tell you to prepare, because this soldier here feels like cutting your throat at once.

original: Owy, cuppele gorge, permafoy, peasant, unless thou give me crowns, brave crowns, or mangled shalt thou be by  this my sword.
translation: Ohyes, cuttythe throat, bygod, peasant, unless you give me coins, beautiful coins, or you will be mangled by this sword.

original: Ô, je vous supplie, pour l'amour de Dieu, me pardoner.  Je suis gentilhomme de bonne maison. Gardez ma vie, et  je vous donnerai deux cents écus
translation: Oh, I beg you, for the love of God, forgive me. I'm a gentleman from a good family. Save my life, and I'll give you two hundred silver coins.

original: What are his words?
translation: What is he saying?

original: He prays you to save his life. He is a gentleman of a  good house, and for his ransom he will give you two  hundred crowns.
translation: He begs you to save his life. He is a gentleman from a good family, and for his ransom he will give you two hundred coins.

original: Tell him my fury shall abate, and I the crowns will  take.
translation: Tell him I will stop being angry, and will take the coins.

original: Petit monsieur, que dit-il?
translation: Little sir, what does he say?

original: Encore qu'il est contre son jurement de pardoner aucun  prisonnier;
translation: Although it's against his oath to pardon any prisoner,

original: néanmoins, pour les écus que vous lui avez  promis, il est content à vous donner la liberté, le  franchisement.
translation: nonetheless, for the silver coins you promised him, he is willing to give you liberty, freedom.

original: Sur mes genoux je vous donne mille remercîments, et je  m'estime heureux que j'ai tombé entre les mains d'un  chevalier,
translation: On my knees I give you a thousand thanks, and I consider myself lucky to have fallen into the hands of a knight—

original: je pense, le plus brave, vaillant, et très  distingué seigneur d'Angleterre.
translation: I think, the most brave, bold, and famous lord of England.

original: Expound unto me, boy.
translation: Explain that to me, boy.

original: He gives you upon his knees a thousand thanks, and he  esteems himself happy that he hath fall'n into the hands of one
translation: He gives you on his knees a thousand thanks, and he considers himself lucky that he fell into the hands of someone who is,

original: , as he thinks, the most brave, valorous, and  thrice- worthy seigneur of England.
translation: he thinks, the most brave, bold, and famous lord of England.

original: As I suck blood, I will some mercy show. Follow me.
translation: By the blood I suck, I will show some mercy.

original: Suivez-vous le grand capitaine.
translation: Follow the great captain.

original: Ô diable!
translation: By the devil!

original: Ô seigneur! Le jour est perdu, tout est perdu!
translation: By God! We've lost, we've lost everything!

original: Mort de ma vie,   all is confounded, all!
translation: By death,  everything is destroyed, everything!

original: Reproach and everlasting shame   Sits mocking in our plumes.
translation: Blame and eternal shame sit in the feathers on our helmets, mocking us.

original: Why, all our ranks are broke.
translation: But our ranks have all been broken.

original: O perdurable shame! Let’s stab ourselves. Be these the wretches that we played at dice for?
translation: Oh eternal shame! Let's stab ourselves. Are these the miserable men we gambled for?

original: Is this the king we sent to for his ransom?
translation: Is this the king we asked to pay us ransom?

original: Shame, and eternal shame, nothing but shame!   Let us die.
translation: Shame, and eternal shame, nothing but shame! Let's die.

original: In once more! Back again!   And he that will not follow Bourbon now,   Let him go hence, and with his cap in hand   Like a base pander hold the chamber door,
translation: Into battle once more! Go back! Let whoever refuses to follow Bourbon now go from here, and go with his hat in his hand like a low pimp holding the door to the room

original: Whilst by a slave, no gentler than my dog,   His fairest daughter is contaminate.
translation: while his most beautiful daughter is contaminated by a slave, no nobler than my dog.

original: Disorder, that hath spoiled us, friend us now. Let us on heaps go offer up our lives.
translation: Disorder, you destroyed us before—now be friends with us. Let's go die on heaps of bodies.

original: We are enough yet living in the field   To smother up the English in our throngs,
translation: There are enough of us still alive in the battlefield to smother the English with our army,

original: If any order might be thought upon.
translation: if we could only think of a way to put some order into our troops.

original: The devil take order now! I’ll to the throng. Let life be short, else shame will be too long.
translation: Damn order now! I'll go where the fight is. Let life be short, or shame will be too long.

original: Well have we done, thrice-valiant countrymen, But all’s not done. Yet keep the French the field.
translation: We've done well, brave countrymen. But this isn't done. The French still have control of the field.

original: The duke of York commends him to your Majesty.
translation: The Duke of York greets you, your Majesty.

original: Lives he, good uncle? Thrice within this hour   I saw him down, thrice up again and fighting.
translation: Is he alive, good uncle? Three times this hour I saw him fall down, and three times I saw him get up again and keep fighting.

original: From helmet to the spur, all blood he was.
translation: He was entirely covered in blood, from his helmet to his heels.

original: In which array, brave soldier, doth he lie,   Larding the plain, and by his bloody side,   Yoke-fellow to his honor-owing wounds,   The noble earl of Suffolk also lies.
translation: Looking like that, the brave soldier lies, covering the field with blood, and by his his bloody side, with equal honorable wounds, the noble earl of Suffolk also lies.

original: Suffolk first died, and York, all haggled over,   Comes to him where in gore he lay insteeped   And takes him by the beard, kisses the gashes   That bloodily did yawn upon his face.
translation: Suffolk died first, and York, mangled all over, came to where he lay swimming in gore and took him by the beard, kissed the cuts that gaped all over his face,

original: And cries aloud, “Tarry, my cousin Suffolk.   My soul shall thine keep company to heaven.   Tarry, sweet soul, for mine; then fly abreast,   As in this glorious and well-foughten field   We kept together in our chivalry.”
translation: and cried aloud, "Wait, my cousin Suffolk. My soul will keep yours company on the way to heaven. Wait, dear soul, for mine; then fly together, just as in this glorious and well-fought-for field we rode together."

original: Upon these words I came and cheered him up.   He smiled me in the face, raught me his hand,   And with a feeble grip, says “Dear my lord,   Commend my service to my sovereign.”
translation: At these words I came and tried to cheer him up. He smiled at me, grabbed me by the hand, and gripping me weakly, said, "My dear lord, tell my king what I have done."

original: So did he turn, and over Suffolk’s neck   He threw his wounded arm and kissed his lips,   And so, espoused to death, with blood he sealed   A testament of noble-ending love.
translation: So he turned, and threw his wounded arm over Suffolk's neck and kissed his lips. So, married to death, he sealed with blood a  will  of nobly dying love.

original: The pretty and sweet manner of it forced   Those waters from me which I would have stopped,   But I had not so much of man in me,   And all my mother came into mine eyes   And gave me up to tears.
translation: The beautiful way he did this forced me to cry even though I wished I could stop, but I didn't have enough man in me, and my mother came into my eyes and made me cry.

original: I blame you not, For, hearing this, I must perforce compound With mistful eyes, or they will issue too.
translation: I don't blame you because, hearing this, I have to bargain with my wet eyes, or they'll let out tears.

original: Kill the poys and the luggage! 'Tis expressly against  the law of arms. 'Tis as arrant a piece of knavery, mark you now, as can be offert, in your conscience now, is  it not?
translation: Kill the boys and the luggage! That's explicitly against the laws of war. It's as horrible a crime as can be done, don't you think?

original: 'Tis certain there’s not a boy left alive, and the  cowardly rascals that ran from the battle ha' done this  slaughter.
translation: It's certain that there's not a single boy left alive, and the cowardly good-for-nothings who ran from the battle did this.

original: Besides, they have burned and carried away  all that was in the king’s tent, wherefore the king,  most worthily, hath caused every soldier to cut his  prisoner’s throat.
translation: They have also burned or carried away everything that was in the king's tent, which is the reason the king, quite rightly, made every soldier cut his prisoner's throat.

original: Oh, ’tis a gallant king!
translation: Oh, he's a great king!

original: Ay, he was porn at Monmouth, Captain Gower. What call  you the town’s name where Alexander the Pig was born?
translation: Yes, he was born at Monmouth, Captain Gower. What was the town called where Alexander the Big was born?

original: Alexander the Great.
translation: Alexander the Great.

original: Why, I pray you, is not “pig” great?
translation: What, I ask you, isn't "big" great?

original: The pig, or the  great, or the mighty, or the huge, or the magnanimous  are all one reckonings, save the phrase is a little  variations.
translation: The big, or the great, or the powerful, or the huge, or the generous are all the same, except that there are a few variations in the phrasing.

original: I think Alexander the Great was born in Macedon. His  father was called Philip of Macedon, as I take it.
translation: I think Alexander the Great was born in Macedon. His father was called Philip of Macedon, I believe.

original: I think it is in Macedon where Alexander is porn. I  tell you, Captain, if you look in the maps of the 'orld, I warrant you shall find, in the comparisons between  Macedon and Monmouth, that the situations, look you, is  both alike.
translation: I think it was Macedon where Alexander was born. I tell you, Captain, if you look at maps of the world, I bet you will find, comparing Macedon and Monmouth, that they're in very similar locations.

original: There is a river in Macedon, and there is  also, moreover, a river at Monmouth. It is called Wye at Monmouth, but it is out of my prains what is the name  of the other river. But ’tis all one; ’tis alike as my  fingers is to my fingers, and there is salmons in both.
translation: There is a river in Macedon and there is also, moreover, a river in Monmouth. It is called Wye at Monmouth, but I've forgotten what the name of the other river is. But it doesn't matter; they're as alike as my fingers are to each other, and there is  salmons  in both.

original: If you mark Alexander’s life well, Harry of Monmouth’s  life is come after it indifferent well, for there is  figures in all things.
translation: If you consider Alexander's life well,  Harry of Monmouth's life has followed pretty much the same course, because everything stands for something else.

original: Alexander, God knows and you  know, in his rages and his furies and his wraths and his cholers and his moods and his displeasures and his  indignations, and also being a little intoxicates in his prains, did, in his ales and his angers, look you, kill his best friend, Cleitus.
translation: Alexander, God knows and you know, in his rages and his furies and his temper and his tantrums and his moods and his displeasures and his indignations, and also being a little intoxicated, did, in his ale and his anger, see, kill his best friend, Cleitus.

original: Our king is not like him in that. He never killed any  of his friends.
translation: Our king is not like him in that way. He never killed any of his friends.

original: It is not well done, mark you now, to take the tales  out of my mouth ere it is made and finished. I speak but in the figures and comparisons of it.
translation: Look, it's not good to take the story away from me before it's over and done with. I'm speaking about the metaphors and comparisons in it.

original: As Alexander  killed his friend Cleitus, being in his ales and his  cups, so also Harry Monmouth, being in his right wits  and his good judgments, turned away the fat knight with  the great-belly doublet; he was full of jests, and gipes and knaveries, and mocks—I have forgot his name.
translation: Just as Alexander killed his friend Cleitus, being drunk and in his cups, so also Harry Monmouth, being in his right mind and showing good judgement, turned away the fat knight who wore the huge belly. He was full of jokes, and insults, and crimes, and mocking—I have forgotten his name.

original: Sir John Falstaff.
translation: Sir John Falstaff.

original: That is he. I’ll tell you, there is good men porn at Monmouth.
translation: That's him. I tell you, there are good men born in Monmouth.

original: Here comes his Majesty.
translation: Here comes his Majesty.

original: I was not angry since I came to France   Until this instant.
translation: I have not been angry since I came to France, until now.

original: Take a trumpet, herald.   Ride thou unto the horsemen on yond hill.   If they will fight with us, bid them come down,   Or void the field.
translation: Take a trumpet, messenger. Ride to the horsemen on that hill. If they want to fight us, ask them to ride down, or they should leave the field.

original: They do offend our sight.
translation: They offend our eyes.

original: If they’ll do neither, we will come to them   And make them skirr away as swift as stones   Enforcèd from the old Assyrian slings.
Besides, we’ll cut the throats of those we have,   And not a man of them that we shall take   Shall taste our mercy. Go and tell them so.
translation: Besides, we'll cut the throats of the prisoners we've captured, and won't be merciful toward a single one of the ones we capture from now on. Go tell them that.

original: Here comes the herald of the French, my liege.
translation: Here comes the French messenger, my king.

original: His eyes are humbler than they used to be.
translation: He looks more humble than he used to.

original: How now, what means this, herald? Know’st thou not   That I have fined these bones of mine for ransom?
translation: What, what does this mean, herald? Don't you know I have offered these bones of mine as ransom?

original: Com’st thou again for ransom?
translation: Do you come for ransom again?

original: No, great king.   I come to thee for charitable license,   That we may wander o'er this bloody field   To book our dead and then to bury them;
translation: No, great King. I come to you to ask for your permission for us to wander over this bloody field to record our dead and then to bury them.

original: To sort our nobles from our common men,   For many of our princes—woe the while!—   Lie drowned and soaked in mercenary blood.
translation: To sort our nobles from our commoners, because many of our princes, sadly, lie drowned and soaked in the blood of mercenaries.

original: So do our vulgar drench their peasant limbs   In blood of princes, and the wounded steeds   Fret fetlock deep in gore, and with wild rage   Yerk out their armèd heels at their dead masters,   Killing them twice.
translation: And our commoners' peasant limbs are drenched with the blood of princes, and the wounded horses are fretting, their legs buried in mud up to the fetlocks, and with wild rage kick their hooves covered in metal at their dead owners, killing them again.

original: Oh, give us leave, great king,   To view the field in safety and dispose   Of their dead bodies.
translation: Oh, let us, great king, look over the field safely and take care of their dead bodies.

original: I tell thee truly, herald,   I know not if the day be ours or no,
translation: I'll tell you the truth, messenger, I don't know whether we won or not,

original: For yet a many of your horsemen peer   And gallop o'er the field.
translation: because many of your horsemen are searching and galloping over the field.

original: The day is yours.
translation: You won.

original: Praised be God, and not our strength, for it! What is this castle called that stands hard by?
translation: May God, not our strength, be praised for that! What is this castle that stands near here called?

original: They call it Agincourt.
translation: They call it Agincourt.

original: Then call we this the field of Agincourt, Fought on the day of Crispin Crispianus.
translation: Then we call this the battle of Agincourt, fought on Crispin Crispianus's day.

original: Your grandfather of famous memory, an’t please your  Majesty, and your great-uncle Edward the Plack Prince of Wales, as I have read in the chronicles, fought a most  prave pattle here in France.
translation: You majesty, your famous grandfather and your great-uncle Edward the Black Prince of Wales, as I have read in history books, fought a very brave battle here in France.

original: They did, Fluellen.
translation: They did, Fluellen.

original: Your Majesty says very true. If your Majesties is  remembered of it, the Welshmen did good service in a  garden where leeks did grow, wearing leeks in their  Monmouth caps, which, your Majesty know, to this hour is an honorable badge of the service.
translation: Your Majesty speaks the truth. If you remember, your Majesty, the Welsh fought well in a garden where leeks grew, wearing leeks in their hats at Monmouth. You know, your Majesty, that to this day wearing a leek is an honorable reminder of that fight.

original: And I do believe  your Majesty takes no scorn to wear the leek upon Saint  Tavy’s day.
translation: And I believe your Majesty is not ashamed to wear the leek on  Saint Davy's day .

original: I wear it for a memorable honor, For I am Welsh, you know, good countryman.
translation: I wear it to remember an honorable occasion, because, as you know, I am Welsh like you.

original: Thanks, good my countryman.
translation: Thanks, good countryman.

original: By Jeshu, I am your Majesty’s countryman, I care not  who know it. I will confess it to all the 'orld.
translation: By Jesus, I  am  your Majesty's countryman, I don't care who knows. I will confess it to the whole world.

original: I need  not to be ashamed of your Majesty, praised be God, so  long as your Majesty is an honest man.
translation: I don't need to be ashamed of you, your Majesty, praise God, as long as you are an honest man.

original: God keep me so.—Our heralds go with him. Bring me just notice of the numbers dead On both our parts. Call yonder fellow hither.
translation: May God me one.

original: Soldier, you must come to the king.
translation: Soldier, you must come see the king.

original: Soldier, why wear’st thou that glove in thy cap?
translation: Soldier, why do you wear that glove in your hat?

original: An’t please your Majesty, ’tis the gage of one that I  should fight withal, if he be alive.
translation: Your Majesty, it was give to me by a man I'm supposed to fight, if he's alive.

original: An Englishman?
translation: An Englishman?

original: An ’t please your Majesty, a rascal that swaggered with me last night,
translation: Your majesty, a good-for-nothing who was rude to me last night.

original: who, if alive and ever dare to challenge this glove, I have sworn to take him a box o' th' ear,
translation: If he's alive and ever dares ask for the glove back, I promised to box him on the ear.

original: or if I can see my glove in his cap, which he swore, as  he was a soldier, he would wear if alive, I will strike  it out soundly.
translation: Or if I see my glove in his hat which he swore that, if he was a soldier, he would wear if he survived, I will hit it hard.

original: What think you, Captain Fluellen, is it fit this  soldier keep his oath?
translation: What do you think, Captain Fluellen, is it right for this soldier to keep his oath?

original: He is a craven and a villain else, an ’t please your  Majesty, in my conscience.
translation: I think he would be a coward and a criminal if he didn't, your Majesty.

original: It may be his enemy is a gentleman of great sort, quite from the answer of his degree.
translation: It might be that his enemy is an important gentleman, far above him in rank.

original: Though he be as good a gentleman as the devil is, as  Lucifer and Beelzebub himself, it is necessary, look  your Grace, that he keep his vow and his oath.
translation: Even if he's as good a gentleman as the devil, as good as Lucifer and Beelzebub themselves, it is necessary, you see, that he keep his oath and his promise.

original: If he be  perjured, see you now, his reputation is as arrant a  villain and a Jack Sauce as ever his black shoe trod  upon God’s ground and His earth, in my conscience, la.
translation: If he breaks the oath, see, his reputation will be that he's as terrible a good-for-nothing and insolent fellow as any that every walked with a black shoe on God's earth, that's what I think.

original: Then keep thy vow, sirrah, when thou meet’st the  fellow.
translation: Then keep your oath, fellow, when you meet the man.

original: So I will, my liege, as I live.
translation: I will, my king, I swear.

original: Who serv’st thou under?
translation: Who do you serve under?

original: Under Captain Gower, my liege.
translation: Under Captain Gower, my king.

original: Gower is a good captain, and is good knowledge and  literatured in the wars.
translation: Gower is a good captain, and is knowledgeable of and well-read in the wars.

original: Call him hither to me, soldier.
translation: Call him here to me, soldier.

original: I will, my liege.
translation: I will, my king.

original: Here, Fluellen, wear thou this favor for me and stick  it in thy cap.   (gives   WILLIAMS'   s glove to   FLUELLEN   )
translation: Here, Fluellen, wear this object for me and stick it in your hat.  [gives WILLIAMS's glove to FLUELLEN]

original: When Alençon and myself were down together, I plucked this  glove from his helm.
translation: When Alençon and I had both fallen from our horses fighting each other, I grabbed this glove from his helmet.

original: If any man challenge this, he is a  friend to Alençon and an enemy to our person. If thou  encounter any such, apprehend him, an thou dost me love.
translation: If any man tries to fight you over this, he is a friend of Alençon's and an enemy of mine. If you meet anyone like that, take him captive if you love me.

original: Your Grace does me as great honors as can be desired in the hearts of his subjects.
translation: Your Grace does me as great an honor as any subject could wish for.

original: I would fain see the man  that has but two legs that shall find himself aggrieved  at this glove, that is all;
translation: I would like to see the man who only has two legs who wants to fight about this glove, that's all I have to say;

original: but I would fain see it  once, an please God of his Grace that I might see.
translation: I would like to see him, if it pleases God to let me see him.

original: Know’st thou Gower?
translation: Do you know Gower?

original: He is my dear friend, an please you.
translation: He is my good friend.

original: Pray thee, go seek him, and bring him to my tent.
translation: Go find him and bring him to my tent.

original: I will fetch him.
translation: I will fetch him.

original: My Lord of Warwick and my brother Gloucester,   Follow Fluellen closely at the heels.
translation: Lord Warwick and brother Gloucester, follow Fluellen closely.

original: The glove which I have given him for a favor   May haply purchase him a box o' th' ear.   It is the soldier’s. I by bargain should   Wear it myself.
translation: The glove I gave him to wear might get him a box on the ear. It belongs to the soldier. I'm supposed to be wearing it myself.

original: Follow, good cousin Warwick.   If that the soldier strike him, as I judge   By his blunt bearing he will keep his word,   Some sudden mischief may arise of it,
translation: Follow, good cousin Warwick. If the soldier hits him, and I think by the bold way he carries himself that he will keep his word, some thing bad might happen.

original: For I do know Fluellen valiant   And, touched with choler, hot as gunpowder,   And quickly will return an injury.
translation: I know Fluellen is brave and, when he gets angry, explodes like gunpowder, and will be quick to hit back.

original: Follow, and see there be no harm between them.   —Go you with me, uncle of Exeter.
translation: Follow him, and make sure no harm comes to them.

original: I warrant it is to knight you, Captain.
translation: I bet it's to knight you, Captain.

original: God’s will and His pleasure, Captain, I beseech you  now, come apace to the king.
translation: By God, Captain, I beg you, come quickly to the king.

original: There is more good toward  you peradventure than is in your knowledge to dream of.
translation: There are more good things coming to you than perhaps you can dream of.

original: Sir, know you this glove?
translation: Sir, do you recognize this glove?

original: Know the glove! I know the glove is a glove.
translation: Recognize the glove! I recognize the glove is a glove.

original: I know this, and thus I challenge it.
translation: I know that, and I'll fight for it.

original: 'Sblood, an arrant traitor as any ’s in the universal  world, or in France, or in England!
translation: By God, he's as terrible a traitor as any in the whole world, or in France, or in England!

original: How now, sir? You villain!
translation: What, sir? You criminal!

original: Do you think I’ll be forsworn?
translation: Do you think I'll break my oath?

original: Stand away, Captain Gower. I will give treason his  payment into plows, I warrant you.
translation: Get back, Captain Gower. I will punish treason by hitting it, I swear.

original: I am no traitor.
translation: I am not a traitor.

original: That’s a lie in thy throat.—I charge you in his  Majesty’s name, apprehend him. He’s a friend of the Duke Alençon’s.
translation: That's a lie.  I order you in his Majesty name, arrest him. He's a friend of the Duke of Alençon.

original: How now, how now, what’s the matter?
translation: What, what's the matter?

original: My Lord of Warwick, here is, praised be God for it, a  most contagious treason come to light, look you, as you  shall desire in a summer’s day.
translation: My Lord of Warwick, here is, praise God for it, disgusting treason made clear, see, as clear as a summer's day.

original: How now, what’s the matter?
translation: What, what's the matter?

original: My liege, here is a villain and a traitor, that, look  your Grace, has struck the glove which your Majesty is  take out of the helmet of Alençon.
translation: My king, here's a criminal and a traitor, see, who hit the glove that your Majesty took off of Alençon's helmet.

original: My liege, this was my glove; here is the fellow of it.
translation: My king, this was my glove. Here is the other in the pair.

original: And he that I gave it to in change promised to wear it  in his cap. I promised to strike him if he did.
translation: And the man I gave it to in exchange for his promised to wear it in his hat. I promised to hit him if he did.

original: I met  this man with my glove in his cap, and I have been as  good as my word.
translation: I met this man with my glove in his hat, and I have done what I promised.

original: Your Majesty, hear now, saving your Majesty’s manhood,  what an arrant, rascally, beggarly, lousy knave it is.
translation: Your Majesty, hear now what a wrongdoing, criminal, beggar-like, lousy good-for-nothing he is.

original: I hope your Majesty is pear me testimony and witness, and will avouchment that this is the glove of Alençon that  your Majesty is give me, in your conscience now.
translation: I hope your Majesty will be my witness, and will confirm that this is Alençon's glove you gave me, truly.

original: Give me thy glove, soldier. Look, here is the fellow of it. 'Twas I indeed thou promised’st to strike, And thou hast given me most bitter terms.
translation: Give me your glove, soldier. Look, here's the other in the pair. It was me you promised to hit, and you insulted me terribly.

original: An please your Majesty, let his neck answer for it, if  there is any martial law in the world.
translation: Your Majesty, hang him for it, if there is any martial law in this world.

original: How canst thou make me satisfaction?
translation: How can you make this up to me?

original: All offenses, my lord, come from the heart. Never came  any from mine that might offend your Majesty.
translation: All bad deeds, my lord, come from the heart. My heart never intended to hurt your Majesty.

original: It was ourself thou didst abuse.
translation: It was me you insulted.

original: Your Majesty came not like yourself. You appeared to me but as a common man. Witness the night, your garments,  your lowliness.
translation: You didn't come to as yourself, your Majesty. You appeared to me to be a common man. Because of the night, your clothes, your common appearance.

original: And what your Highness suffered under  that shape, I beseech you take it for your own fault and not mine, for, had you been as I took you for, I made  no offense.
translation: And what you experienced in that disguise, I beg you to see it as your own fault and not mine, because, had you been what you seemed to be, I would not have committed a crime.

original: Therefore, I beseech your Highness pardon  me.
translation: So I beg you to pardon me.

original: Here, uncle Exeter, fill this glove with crowns   And give it to this fellow.—
translation: Here, uncle Exeter, fill this glove with coins and give it to this fellow.

original: By this day and this light, the fellow has mettle  enough in his belly.
translation: By day and by this light, the fellow is brave enough.

original: I will none of your money.
translation: I don't want your money.

original: It is with a good will. I can tell you it will serve  you to mend your shoes.
translation: I offer it with good will. I can tell you it would be good for you to use it to get your shoes fixed.

original: Come, wherefore should you be so pashful? Your shoes is not so good.
translation: Come on, why do you look so embarrassed? Your shoes are not so good.

original: 'Tis a good  silling, I warrant you, or I will change it.
translation: This is a good shilling, I promise you, or I'll exchange it for another.

original: Now, herald, are the dead numbered?
translation: Now, messenger, have the dead been counted?

original: Here is the number of the slaughtered French.
translation: Here is the list of dead Frenchman.

original: What prisoners of good sort are taken, uncle?
translation: What noble prisoners have been captured, uncle?

original: Charles, duke of Orléans, nephew to the king;   John, duke of Bourbon, and Lord Bouciqualt.
translation: Charles, duke of Orléans, nephew of the king, John, duke of Bourbon, and Lord Bouciqualt.

original: Of other lords and barons, knights and squires,   Full fifteen hundred, besides common men.
translation: A good fifteen hundred lords, barons, knights and squires. Also commoners.

original: This note doth tell me of ten thousand French   That in the field lie slain. Of princes in this number   And nobles bearing banners, there lie dead   One hundred twenty-six.
translation: This note tells me about ten thousand Frenchmen lying dead in the field. Among these, one hundred twenty-six princes and nobles carrying banners lie dead.

original: Added to these,   Of knights, esquires, and gallant gentlemen,   Eight thousand and four hundred, of the which,   Five hundred were but yesterday dubbed knights.
translation: Added to these, eight thousand four hundred knights, esquires, and gentlemen, of which five hundred were dubbed knights only yesterday.

original: So that in these ten thousand they have lost,   There are but sixteen hundred mercenaries.   The rest are princes, barons, lords, knights, squires,   And gentlemen of blood and quality.
translation: So among the ten thousand they lost were only sixteen hundred mercenaries. The rest are princes, barons, lords, knights, squires, and gentlemen of good family.

original: The names of those their nobles that lie dead:   Charles Delabreth, high constable of France;   Jaques of Chatillon, admiral of France;   The Master of the Crossbows, Lord Rambures;   Great Master of France, the brave Sir Guichard Dauphin;   John, duke of Alençon; Anthony, duke of Brabant,   The brother of the duke of Burgundy,   And Edward, duke of Bar.
translation: The names of their nobles who lie died are: Charles Delabreth, high constable of France, Jaques of Chatillon, admiral of France, the Master of the Crossbows, Lord Rambures, Great Master of France, the brave Sir Guichard Dauphin, John, duke of Alençon, Anthony, duke of Brabant, the brother of the duke of Burgundy, and Edward, duke of Bar.

original: Of lusty earls:   Grandpré and Roussi, Faulconbridge and Foix,   Beaumont and Marle, Vaudemont and Lestrale.
translation: Of brave earls: Grandpré and Roussi, Faulconbridge and Foix, Beaumont and Marle, Vaudemont and Lestrale.

original: Here was a royal fellowship of death.   Where is the number of our English dead?
translation: This is a noble fellowship of dead people. Where is the list of our dead Englishmen?

original: 'Tis wonderful.
translation: It's amazing.

original: Come, go we in procession to the village,
translation: Come one, let's go in a parade to the village.

original: And be it death proclaimèd through our host   To boast of this or take that praise from God   Which is His only.
translation: And have it announced to the army that boasting about this or trying to take the praise that belongs to God for this will be punished by death.

original: Is it not lawful, an please your Majesty, to tell how  many is killed?
translation: Is it not allowed, your Majesty, to report how many were killed?

original: Yes, Captain, but with this acknowledgement: That God fought for us.
translation: Yes, Captain, but with the acknowledgement that God fought for us.

original: Yes, my conscience, He did us great good.
translation: Yes, I know He did us a lot of good.

original: Do we all holy rites.
translation: Let's perform all the holy ceremonies.

original: Let there be sung   Non nobis   and   Te Deum,   The dead with charity enclosed in clay,
translation: Have the  Non nobis   and  Te deum  sung and the dead buried well,

original: And then to Calais, and to England then,   Where ne'er from France arrived more happy men.
translation: and then we'll go to Calais, and to England after that. Happier men never arrived there from France.

original: Vouchsafe to those that have not read the story   That I may prompt them;
translation: Those who have not read the story, let me assist you.

original: and of such as have,   I humbly pray them to admit th' excuse   Of time, of numbers, and due course of things,   Which cannot in their huge and proper life   Be here presented.
translation: Those who have, please admit my excuses that time, and large numbers, and the proper way of doing things can't be presented here as they really are.

original: Now we bear the king   Toward Calais. Grant him there. There seen,   Heave him away upon your wingèd thoughts   Athwart the sea.
translation: Now we bring the king to Calais. Imagine he's there. From there, carry him away on your winged imaginations across the sea.

original: Behold, the English beach   Pales in the flood with men, with wives and boys,   Whose shouts and claps outvoice the deep-mouthed sea,   Which like a mighty whiffler 'fore the king   Seems to prepare his way.
translation: See, the English beach is made pale by being covered with men, wives, and boys whose shouting and clapping drown out the noisy sea which had cleared the king's way like a bodyguard.

original: So let him land,   And solemnly see him set on to London.   So swift a pace hath thought that even now   You may imagine him upon Blackheath,   Where that his lords desire him to have borne   His bruisèd helmet and his bended sword   Before him through the city.
translation: So let him land and see him go on to London. Imagination moves so quickly that now you can imagine him at Blackheath, where his lords want him to have his battered helmet and bent sword carried in front of him through the city.

original: He forbids it,   Being free from vainness and self-glorious pride,   Giving full trophy, signal, and ostent   Quite from himself, to God.
translation: He forbids it, being free from vanity and self-indulgent pride, and gives away all of his trophies, symbols, and showy ceremonies to God.

original: But now behold,   In the quick forge and workinghouse of thought,   How London doth pour out her citizens.   The Mayor and all his brethren in best sort,   Like to the senators of th' antique Rome,   With the plebeians swarming at their heels,   Go forth and fetch their conquering Caesar in—
translation: But now see, in the quick blacksmith's shops and factories of your imaginations, how London's citizens pour out. The Mayor and all the other officials in their best clothes, like the senators of ancient Rome, with the commoners swarming behind them, go out and bring their victorious king in.

original: As, by a lower but loving likelihood,   Were now the general of our gracious empress,   As in good time he may, from Ireland coming,   Bringing rebellion broached on his sword,   How many would the peaceful city quit   To welcome him!
translation: In the same way, except that he is lower in rank, if our kind Queen's general came from Ireland, having ended the rebellion there, as he may eventually, consider how many would leave the peaceful city to welcome him!

original: Much more, and much more cause,   Did they this Harry.
translation: Many more, and with a better reason, did this for Harry .

original: Now in London place him   (As yet the lamentation of the French   Invites the king of England’s stay at home;   The emperor’s coming in behalf of France   To order peace between them) and omit   All the occurrences, whatever chanced,   Till Harry’s back return again to France.
translation: Now imagine him in London, because the French people beg the English king to stay at home; the emperor is coming at France's request to make peace between them. And leave out all the events, whatever happened, until Harry returns to France.

original: There must we bring him, and myself have played   The interim, by remembering you ’tis past.   Then brook abridgment, and your eyes advance   After your thoughts, straight back again to France.
translation: We must bring him there, and I myself played the part of the time between the acts, by reminding you that it passed. So allow us to abridge the story, and let your eyes and your imagination pass straight back to France.

original: Nay, that’s right. But why wear you your leek today?  Saint Davy’s day is past.
translation: No, that's right. But why do you wear your leek today? Saint Davy's day has passed.

original: There is occasions and causes why and wherefore in all  things. I will tell you as my friend, Captain Gower.
translation: There are times and reasons why for everything. I will tell you, since you're my friend, Captain Gower.

original: The rascally, scald, beggarly, lousy, pragging knave,  Pistol, which you and yourself and all the world know to be no petter than a fellow, look you now, of no merits,
translation: The good-for-nothing, scabby, beggar-like, lousy, bragging criminal, Pistol, who you yourself and all the world know to be nothing more than a fellow, you see, with no good qualities,

original: he is come to me and prings me pread and salt  yesterday, look you, and bid me eat my leek. I
translation: he came to me and brought me bread and salt yesterday, see, and asked me to eat my leek.

original: t was in  place where I could not breed no contention with him,  but I will be so bold as to wear it in my cap till I see him once again, and then I will tell him a little piece of my desires.
translation: It was in a place where I couldn't fight with him, but I will wear it in my hat until I see him again, and then I will give him a piece of my mind.

original: Why, here he comes, swelling like a turkey-cock.
translation: Here he comes, swelled up like a turkey.

original: 'Tis no matter for his swellings, nor his  turkey-cocks.— God pless you, Aunchient Pistol, you scurvy, lousy  knave, God pless you.
translation: I don't care about his swellings, or his turkeys.  God bless you, Ancient Pistol, you disgusting, lousy criminal, God bless you.

original: Ha, art thou bedlam? Dost thou thirst, base Trojan, to  have me fold up Parca’s fatal web?
translation: What, are you crazy? Do you want, low  Trojan , to make me meet my fate?

original: Hence. I am qualmish  at the smell of leek.
translation: Go away. The smell of leeks makes me sick.

original: I peseech you heartily, scurvy, lousy knave, at my  desires, and my requests, and my petitions, to eat, look you, this leek.
translation: I beg you, disgusting, lousy criminal, to fulfill my desire, my request, and my petition to you to eat, see, this leek.

original: Because, look you, you do not love it,  nor your affections and your appetites and your  digestions does not agree with it, I would desire you to eat it.
translation: Because, see, you do not love it, and your feelings and your appetite and your digestion do not agree with it. I would like you to eat it.

original: Not for Cadwallader and all his goats.
translation: Not for the Welsh hero Cadwallader and all his goats.

original: There is one goat for you.    Will you be so good, scald knave, as eat it?
translation: Here's one goat for you.  Will you be so kind, scabby criminal, as to eat it?

original: Base Trojan, thou shalt die.
translation: Low Trojan, you will die.

original: You say very true, scald knave, when God’s will is. I  will desire you to live in the meantime and eat your  victuals.
translation: You tell the truth, scabby knave, when God wishes it. I ask you to survive in the meantime and eat your food.

original: Come, there is sauce for it. (strikes him)
translation: Come on, here's a sauce for it.  [hits him]

original: You called me yesterday “mountain squire,” but I will make  you today a squire of low degree.
translation: You called me a "mountain servant" yesterday, but today I will make you a low servant.

original: I pray you, fall to.  If you can mock a leek, you can eat a leek.
translation: Please, tuck in. If you can mock a leek, you can eat a leek.

original: Enough, Captain. You have astonished him.
translation: Enough, Captain. You have astonished him.

original: I say I will make him eat some part of my leek, or I  will peat his pate four days.—
translation: I say I will make him eat some part of my leek, or I will beat him on the head for four days.

original: Must I bite?
translation: Must I bite?

original: Yes, certainly, and out of doubt and out of question,  too, and ambiguities.
translation: Yes, certainly, no doubt and no question, too, and no ambiguities.

original: By this leek, I will most horribly revenge. I eat and  eat, I swear—
translation: By this leek, I will get a horrible revenge. I'm eating and eating, I promise—

original: Eat, I pray you. Will you have some more sauce to your  leek? There is not enough leek to swear by.
translation: Eat, please. Do you want more sauce on your leek? There isn't enough leek left to swear by.

original: Quiet thy cudgel. Thou dost see I eat.
translation: Shut your mouth. You see I'm eating.

original: Much good do you, scald knave, heartily. Nay, pray you  throw none away.
translation: Much good may it do you, scabby criminal, really. No, please don't throw any of it away.

original: The skin is good for your broken  coxcomb.
translation: The skin is good for your wounded head.

original: When you take occasions to see leeks hereafter, I pray you, mock at 'em, that is all.
translation: When you happen to see leeks in the future, please, go ahead and mock them, that's all.

original: Good.
translation: Good.

original: Ay, leeks is good. Hold you, there is a groat to heal  your pate.
translation: Yes, leeks are good. Here, here's four pence to heal your head.

original: Me, a groat?
translation: Me, four pence?

original: Yes, verily, and in truth you shall take it, or I have  another leek in my pocket, which you shall eat.
translation: Yes, truly, and you'll take it, or I have another leek in my pocket, which you will eat.

original: I take thy groat in earnest of revenge.
translation: I take your four pence as a sign of my revenge.

original: If I owe you anything, I will pay you in cudgels.
translation: If I owe you anything, I will pay you with clubs.

original: You  shall be a woodmonger and buy nothing of me but cudgels.
translation: You will be a wood-seller and not buy anything from me except clubs.

original: God be wi' you and keep you and heal your pate.
translation: God be with you and keep you safe and heal your head.

original: All hell shall stir for this.
translation: All hell will rise for this.

original: Go, go. You are a counterfeit cowardly knave.
translation: Go, go. You're a lying cowardly criminal.

original: Will you  mock at an ancient tradition begun upon an honorable  respect and worn as a memorable trophy of predeceased  valor, and dare not avouch in your deeds any of your  words?
translation: You mocked an ancient tradition begun on an honorable occasion and worn as a memento of past bravery, and you don't dare to follow through with any of the threats you make.

original: I have seen you gleeking and galling at this  gentleman twice or thrice. You thought because he could  not speak English in the native garb, he could not  therefore handle an English cudgel.
translation: I have seen you mocking and annoying this gentleman two or three times. You thought because he couldn't speak English like a native speaker, he couldn't use an English club.

original: You find it  otherwise, and henceforth let a Welsh correction teach  you a good English condition. Fare you well.
translation: You find out you were wrong, and from now on let a Welsh punishment teach you good English manners. Goodbye.

original: Doth Fortune play the huswife with me now?   News have I that my Nell is dead i' th' spital   Of a malady of France,   And there my rendezvous is quite cut off.
translation: Is Fortune being as mean as a wife to me now? I have heard that my Nell is dead in the hospital from a  French sickness , and my romance is cut short.

original: Old I do wax, and from my weary limbs   Honor is cudgeled.
translation: I grow old, and honor is clubbed out of my tired limbs.

original: Well, bawd I’ll turn,   And something lean to cutpurse of quick hand.
translation: Well, I'll become a pimp, and sometimes a quick-handed pick-pocket.

original: To England will I steal, and there I’ll steal.
translation: I'll steal away to England, and there I'll steal.

original: And patches will I get unto these cudgeled scars,   And swear I got them in the Gallia wars.
translation: And I'll put patches on these club scars, and swear I got them in the wars in France.

original: Unto our brother France and to our sister,   Health and fair time of day.
translation: To my brother the king of France and my sister his wife, I wish good-day and good health.

original: Right joyous are we to behold your face, Most worthy brother England. Fairly met. —So are you, princes English, every one.
translation: I am very glad to see your face, my most worth brother. It's a pleasure.

original: So happy be the issue, brother England,   Of this good day and of this gracious meeting,   As we are now glad to behold your eyes—
translation: May the decisions made on this good day and at this polite meeting be as happy, brother England, as we are now to see you your face

original: Your eyes which hitherto have borne in them   Against the French that met them in their bent   The fatal balls of murdering basilisks.
translation: —your face which has up to now carried in it against the French who came across it the deadly eyes of murdering  basilisks .

original: The venom of such looks, we fairly hope,   Have lost their quality, and that this day   Shall change all griefs and quarrels into love.
translation: The poison of such looks, we hope, does not work any more, and this day will change all sorrows and quarrels into love.

original: To cry “Amen” to that, thus we appear.
translation: I'm here to say "amen" to that.

original: You English princes all, I do salute you.
translation: Welcome, all you English princes.

original: My duty to you both, on equal love,   Great kings of France and England.
translation: My obedience to you both, whom I love equally, great kings of France and England.

original: That I have labored   With all my wits, my pains, and strong endeavors,   To bring your most imperial Majesties   Unto this bar and royal interview,   Your mightiness on both parts best can witness.
translation: Both sides can bear witness that I have worked with all my wit and strength and made every effort to bring your royal Majesties to this royal meeting.

original: Since, then, my office hath so far prevailed   That face to face and royal eye to eye   You have congreeted.
translation: I have done part of my job in bringing you face to face and royal eye to eye.

original: Let it not disgrace me   If I demand before this royal view   What rub or what impediment there is   Why that the naked, poor, and mangled peace,   Dear nurse of arts, plenties, and joyful births,   Should not in this best garden of the world,   Our fertile France, put up her lovely visage?
translation: Allow me to ask in front of all you royals what impediment there is to naked, poor, and mangled peace, which allows the arts, plenty, and joyful births to flourish, showing her beautiful face in this most beautiful garden of the world, our fertile France?

original: Alas, she hath from France too long been chased,   And all her husbandry doth lie on heaps,   Corrupting in its own fertility.
translation: Sadly, she has been chased from France for too long, and all her crops lie in heaps, rotting.

original: Her vine, the merry cheerer of the heart,   Unprunèd, dies. Her hedges, even-pleached,   Like prisoners wildly overgrown with hair,   Put forth disordered twigs.
translation: Her vine, which makes the heart happy, dies uncared-for. Her evenly cut hedges, like prisoners with wildly-growing hair, sprout disorderly twigs.

original: Her fallow leas   The darnel, hemlock, and rank fumitory   Doth root upon, while that the coulter rusts   That should deracinate such savagery.
translation: Grass, hemlock, and other weeds grow on her fields, while ploughs rust which should get rid of these wild things.

original: The even mead, that erst brought sweetly forth   The freckled cowslip, burnet, and green clover,   Wanting the scythe, withal uncorrected, rank,   Conceives by idleness, and nothing teems   But hateful docks, rough thistles, kecksies, burrs,   Losing both beauty and utility.
translation: The flat meadow, on which formerly grew sweet plants like the freckled cowslip, burnet, and green clover, needing to be mowed, completely uncorrected and neglected, grows useless things, and produces nothing but hateful docks, rough thistles, hollow plants, burrs - losing both beauty and usefulness.

original: And as our vineyards, fallows, meads, and hedges,   Defective in their natures, grow to wildness,   Even so our houses and ourselves and children   Have lost, or do not learn for want of time,   The sciences that should become our country,   But grow like savages,
translation: And just as our vineyards, fields, meadows, and hedges, grow wild because of defects in their natures, so our houses and our children and we ourselves have lost, or do not learn because there is no time, the knowledge that we should to help our country, but instead grow like savages.

original: as soldiers will   That nothing do but meditate on blood,   To swearing and stern looks, diffused attire,   And everything that seems unnatural.
translation: Just as soldiers who do nothing but think about blood start to swear and look stern, dress messily, and do everything that seems unnatural.

original: Which to reduce into our former favor   You are assembled, and my speech entreats   That I may know the let why gentle peace   Should not expel these inconveniences   And bless us with her former qualities.
translation: You are assembled to bring us back to the way we were, and I ask you to tell me what stands in the way of gentle peace getting rid of these inconveniences and blessing us the way she used to.

original: If, Duke of Burgundy, you would the peace,   Whose want gives growth to th' imperfections   Which you have cited,
translation: If, Duke of Burgundy, you want the peace, lack of which allows the imperfections you mentioned to grow,

original: you must buy that peace   With full accord to all our just demands,   Whose tenors and particular effects   You have, enscheduled briefly, in your hands.
translation: you must buy that peace by agreeing fully to all my just demands, which you have, written down, with details and explanations, in your hands.

original: The king hath heard them, to the which as yet There is no answer made.
translation: The king has heard them, and has not yet given an answer.

original: Well then, the peace which you before so urged Lies in his answer.
translation: Well then, the peace you argued for before depends on his answer.

original: I have but with a cursitory eye   O'erglanced the articles.
translation: I have only glanced at the list very quickly.

original: Pleaseth your Grace   To appoint some of your council presently   To sit with us once more with better heed   To resurvey them, we will suddenly   Pass our accept and peremptory answer.
translation: If your grace could appoint some of your advisers to sit with me once again to look at them more closely, I will soon give you my acceptance and final answer.

original: Brother, we shall.—Go, uncle Exeter,   And brother Clarence, and you, brother Gloucester,   Warwick and Huntingdon, go with the king   And take with you free power to ratify,   Augment, or alter, as your wisdoms best   Shall see advantageable for our dignity,   Anything in or out of our demands,   And we’ll consign thereto.—
translation: Brother, I will.

original: Our gracious brother, I will go with them. Haply a woman’s voice may do some good, When articles too nicely urged be stood on.
translation: Kind brother, I will go with them. Perhaps a woman's voice will do some good, when they are arguing about unimportant details.

original: Yet leave our cousin Katherine here with us. She is our capital demand, comprised Within the forerank of our articles.
translation: But leave my cousin Katherine here with me. She is my primary demand, asked for first in the list.

original: She hath good leave.
translation: She has permission.

original: Fair Katherine, and most fair,   Will you vouchsafe to teach a soldier terms
translation: Beautiful, most beautiful Katherine, will you agree to teach a soldier words

original: Such as will enter at a lady’s ear   And plead his love suit to her gentle heart?
translation: that will enter a woman's ear and argue for his love to her gentle heart?

original: Your Majesty shall mock at me. I cannot speak your England.
translation: Your Majesty will laugh at me. I cannot speak your England.

original: O fair Katherine, if you will love me soundly with your French heart, I will be glad to hear you confess it  brokenly with your English tongue. Do you like me, Kate?
translation: Oh beautiful Katherine, if you love me with your French heart, I will be glad to hear you say it in your broken English. Do you like me, Kate?

original: Pardonnez-moi,  I cannot tell what is “like me.”
translation: Forgive me, I don't know what is "like me."

original: An angel is like you, Kate, and you are like an angel.
translation: An angel is like you, Kate, and you are like an angel.

original: [To  ALICE  ) Que dit-il? Que je suis semblable à les  anges?
translation: [To ALICE] What does he say? That I am like the angels?

original: Oui, vraiment, sauf votre Grâce, ainsi dit-il.
translation: Yes, truly, your Grace, that's what he's saying.

original: I said so, dear Katherine; and I must not blush to  affirm it.
translation: I said so, dear Katherine; and I don't blush to stand by it.

original: Ô bon Dieu! Les langues des hommes sont pleines de  tromperies.
translation: Oh Good God! Men's words are full of lies.

original: What says she, fair one? That the tongues of men are  full of deceits?
translation: What is she saying, beautiful one? That the words of men are full of lies?

original: Oui, dat de tongues of de mans is be full of deceits;  dat is de princess.
translation: Yes, that the tongues of the mans is be full of lies; that is the princess.

original: The princess is the better Englishwoman.
translation: The princess is a  better Englishwoman  than I am an Englishman.

original: Sauf votre honneur,  me understand vell.
translation: Your honor, I understand well.

original: Marry, if you would put me to verses or to dance for  your sake, Kate, why you undid me. For the one, I have  neither words nor measure; and for the other, I have no  strength in measure, yet a reasonable measure in  strength.
translation: Well, if you want me to write poetry or dance for you, Kate, you'll destroy me. For the first, I don't have words or a sense of rhythm. And for the other, I don't have a strong sense of balance, although I have a pretty good balance of strength.

original: If I could win a lady at leapfrog or by  vaulting into my saddle with my armor on my back, under  the correction of bragging be it spoken, I should  quickly leap into a wife.
translation: If I could win a woman at leapfrog or by jumping into my saddle while wearing my armor, if I do say so myself, I would quickly leap my way into marriage.
