original: Or if I might buffet for my  love or bound my horse for her favors, I could lay on  like a butcher and sit like a jackanapes, never off.
translation: Or if I could fight for my love or make my horse jump for her to love me, I could fight like a butcher and cling to my horse like a monkey, never stopping.

original: But, before God, Kate, I cannot look greenly nor gasp out my eloquence, nor I have no cunning in protestation,  only downright oaths, which I never use till urged, nor  never break for urging.
translation: But, by God, Kate, I can't look weak or gasp out fancy words, and I don't have clever things to say, just plain oaths, which I never make until there's a reason, or break for any reason.

original: If thou canst love a fellow of  this temper, Kate, whose face is not worth sun-burning,  that never looks in his glass for love of any thing he  sees there, let thine eye be thy cook.
translation: If you can love a fellow like that, Kate, whose face is so ugly it's not even worth protecting from sunburn, who never looks in his mirror because he loves what he sees there, let your eyes be your cook.

original: I speak to thee  plain soldier: If thou canst love me for this, take me:  if not, to say to thee that I shall die, is true: but  for thy love, by the Lord, no; yet I love thee too.
translation: I'm speaking plain soldier to you: if you can love me for this, take me. If not, to say I'll die is true—but for your love, by God, no. But I love you.

original: And  while thou livest, dear Kate, take a fellow of plain and uncoined constancy; because he perforce must do thee  right, because he hath not the gift to woo in other  places: for these fellows of infinite tongue, that can  rhyme themselves into ladies' favours, they do always  reason themselves out again.
translation: And while you're alive, dear Kate, marry a plain and honestly faithful man. He must treat you well, because he doesn't have the skill to flirt with anyone else. These fellows of infinite words, who can rhyme their way into ladies' affections—they always talk themselves back out again

original: What! a speaker is but a  prater; a rhyme is but a ballad. A good leg will fall; a straight back will stoop; a black beard will turn  white; a curled pate will grow bald; a fair face will  wither; a full eye will wax hollow:
translation: . What! A speaker is just a babbler; a rhyme is just a jingle. A nice leg will lose its shape; a straight back will stoop; a black beard will turn white; curly hair will fair out; a beautiful face will shrivel up; a beautiful eye will turn hollow;

original: but a good heart,  Kate, is the sun and the moon; or rather, the sun, and  not the moon; for it shines bright and never changes,  but keeps its course truly.
translation: but a good heart, Kate, is the sun and moon. Or rather, the sun and not the moon; because it shines bright and never changes, but keeps its course.

original: If thou would have such a  one, take me; and take me, take a soldier; take a  soldier, take a king.
translation: If you will take someone like that, take me. If you take me, you take a soldier. If you take a soldier, you take a king.

original: And what sayest thou then to my  love? speak, my fair, and fairly, I pray thee.
translation: What do you say to my love? Speak, agreeable one, and agree, please.

original: Is it possible dat I sould love de enemy of France?
translation: It is possible for me to love the enemy of France?

original: No, it is not possible you should love the enemy of  France, Kate.
translation: No, it is not possible for you to love the enemy of France.

original: But, in loving me, you should love the  friend of France, for I love France so well that I will  not part with a village of it. I will have it all mine.
translation: But, in loving me, you would love the friend of France, because I love France so much I refuse to give up a single village in it. It will all be mine.

original: And, Kate, when France is mine and I am yours, then  yours is France and you are mine.
translation: And, Kate, when France is mine and I am yours, then France is yours and you are mine.

original: I cannot tell wat is dat.
translation: I can't tell what that means.

original: No, Kate? I will tell thee in French, which I am sure  will hang upon my tongue like a new-married wife about  her husband’s neck, hardly to be shook off.
translation: No, Kate? I'll tell you in French, which I'm sure will hang as heavily on my tongue like a new wife around her husband's neck, hard to shake off.

original: Je quand sur le possession de France, et quand vous avez le  possession de moi   —let me see, what then? Saint Denis be  my speed!—   donc vôtre est France et vous êtes mienne.
translation: I when the possession of France, and when you have the possession of me— let me see, what then? Saint Denis help me!— then yours is France and you are mine .

original: It is as easy for me, Kate, to conquer the kingdom as to  speak so much more French.
translation: It is as easy for me, Kate, to conquer the country as to speak that much French.

original: I shall never move thee in  French, unless it be to laugh at me.
translation: I will never convince you to do anything in French, except  to laugh at me.

original: Sauf votre honneur, le français que vous parlez, il est meilleur que l'anglais lequel je parle.
translation: You speak French better than I speak English.

original: No, faith, is ’t not, Kate, but thy speaking of my  tongue, and I thine, most truly-falsely must needs be  granted to be much at one.
translation: No, really, I don't, Kate, but you speak my language and I yours as well or rather badly as each other.

original: But, Kate, dost thou  understand thus much English? Canst thou love me?
translation: But, Kate, do you understand this much English? Can you love me?

original: I cannot tell.
translation: I cannot tell.

original: Can any of your neighbors tell, Kate? I’ll ask them.
translation: Can any of your neighbors tell, Kate? I'll ask them.

original: Come, I know thou lovest me; and at night, when you come  into your closet, you’ll question this gentlewoman about me, and, I know, Kate, you will to her dispraise those  parts in me that you love with your heart.
translation: Come on, I know you love me; and at night, when you go to your room, you'll ask this gentlewoman about me, and I know that you'll complain about the things you secretly love about me.

original: But, good  Kate, mock me mercifully, the rather, gentle princess,  because I love thee cruelly.
translation: But, good Kate, be merciful in mocking me, because I'm terribly in love with you.

original: If ever thou beest mine,  Kate, as I have a saving faith within me tells me thou  shalt, I get thee with scambling, and thou must  therefore needs prove a good soldier-breeder.
translation: If you're ever mine, Kate, which I have faith that you will, I will win you by fighting, and you must for that reason give birth to soldiers.

original: Shall not  thou and I, between Saint Denis and Saint George,  compound a boy, half French, half English, that shall go to Constantinople and take the Turk by the beard?
translation: Won't the two of us, between Saint Denis and Saint George, give birth to a boy, half French, half English, who will go to Constantinople and fight the Turks?

original: Shall we not? What say’st thou, my fair flower de luce?
translation: Won't we? What do you say, my beautiful  French princess ?

original: I do not know dat.
translation: I do not know that.

original: No, ’tis hereafter to know, but now to promise. Do but  now promise, Kate, you will endeavor for your French  part of such a boy;
translation: No, we'll know later, but we can promise it now. Just promise now, Kate, you'll do your best on your French side to make a boy like that;

original: and for my English moiety take the  word of a king and a bachelor.
translation: and as for my English half take the word of a king and a bachelor.

original: How answer you,   la plus  belle Katherine du monde, mon très cher et divin déesse?
translation: What do you say,  the most beautiful Katherine in the world, my most dear and divine  god ?

original: Your Majestée ave fausse French enough to deceive de  most sage  demoiselle  dat is  en  France.
translation: Your Majesty has enough bad French to deceive the wisest lady in France.

original: Now fie upon my false French. By mine honor, in true  English, I love thee, Kate.
translation: Darn my bad French. By my honor, in honest English, I love you, Kate.

original: By which honor I dare not  swear thou lovest me, yet my blood begins to flatter me  that thou dost, notwithstanding the poor and untempering effect of my visage.
translation: I don't dare swear you love me by that honor, but I begin to flatter myself you do, despite the bad effect my face has.

original: Now, beshrew my father’s ambition! He was thinking of civil wars when he got me; therefore was I created with a stubborn outside, with an aspect  of iron, that when I come to woo ladies, I fright them.
translation: Now, damn my father's ambition! He was thinking about civil war when he conceived me, so I was created with an ugly appearance, with a face of iron, so when I flirt with ladies, I frighten them.

original: But, in faith, Kate, the elder I wax, the better I shall  appear. My comfort is that old age, that ill layer-up of beauty, can do no more spoil upon my face.
translation: But, really, Kate, the older I get, the better I will look. My comfort is that old age, which treats beauty so badly, can't do any more damage to my face.

original: Thou hast  me, if thou hast me, at the worst, and thou shalt wear  me, if thou wear me, better and better.
translation: You take me, if you take me, at my worst, and if you put me on you'll wear me better and better.

original: And therefore  tell me, most fair Katherine, will you have me? Put off  your maiden blushes, avouch the thoughts of your heart  with the looks of an empress, take me by the hand, and  say “Harry of England, I am thine,”
translation: So tell me, most beautiful Katherine, will you have me? Stop blushing, admit your desires with the pride of an empress, take me by the hand and say, "Harry of England, I am yours,"

original: which word thou  shalt no sooner bless mine ear withal, but I will tell  thee aloud “England is thine, Ireland is thine, France  is thine, and Harry Plantagenet is thine,” who, though I speak it before his face, if he be not fellow with the  best king, thou shalt find the best king of good  fellows.
translation: and I will no sooner hear that but I will tell you, "England is yours, Ireland is yours, France is yours, and Harry Plantagenet is yours." And he, although I say it in front of him, although he can't keep company with the best kings, you will find he's the best company.

original: Come, your answer in broken music, for thy  voice is music and thy English broken. Therefore, queen  of all, Katherine, break thy mind to me in broken  English. Wilt thou have me?
translation: Come, tell me your answer in broken music, because your voice is music and your English broken. So, queen of everything, Katherine, break it to me in broken English. Will you have me?

original: Dat is as it sall please de  roi mon père.
translation: That depends on what pleases the king my father.

original: Nay, it will please him well, Kate; it shall please  him, Kate.
translation: No, it will please him a lot, Kate; it will please him, Kate.

original: Den it sall also content me.
translation: Then it will also please me.

original: Upon that I kiss your hand, and I call you my queen.
translation: Then I kiss your hand and call you my queen.

original: Laissez, mon seigneur, laissez, laissez! Ma foi, je ne  veux point que vous abaissiez votre grandeur en baisant  la main d'une—Notre Seigneur!—indigne serviteur.
translation: Stop, my lord, stop, stop! Goodness, I don't want you to lower your greatness by kissing the hand of a—my God!—unworthy servant.

original: Excusez-moi, je vous supplie, mon très puissant seigneur.
translation: Don't, I beg you, my most powerful lord.

original: Then I will kiss your lips, Kate.
translation: Then I will kiss your lips, Kate.

original: Les dames et demoiselles pour être baisées devant leur  noces, il n'est pas la coutume de France.
translation: It's not the custom in France for ladies and young women to be kissed before their marriage.

original: Madam my interpreter, what says she?
translation: My interpreter, what does she say?

original: Dat it is not be de fashion pour les ladies of France—I cannot tell wat is  baiser en  Anglish.
translation: That it is not the fashion for the ladies of France - I can't tell what is to kiss in English.

original: To kiss.
translation: To kiss.

original: Your  Majesté entendre  bettre  que moi.
translation: Your Majesty understands better than I do.

original: It is not a fashion for the maids in France to kiss  before they are married, would she say?
translation: It's not a custom for the ladies in France to kiss before they are married, she wants to say?

original: Oui, vraiment.
translation: Yes, exactly.

original: O Kate, nice customs curtsy to great kings. Dear Kate,  you and I cannot be confined within the weak list of a  country’s fashion.
translation: Oh Kate, pointless customs don't apply to great kings. Dear Kate, you and I aren't confined by the weak customs of a country.

original: We are the makers of manners, Kate,  and the liberty that follows our places stops the mouth  of all find- faults, as I will do yours for upholding  the nice fashion of your country in denying me a kiss.  Therefore, patiently and yielding.
translation: We make customs and are free, Kate, because our power seals the lips of anyone who wants to criticize, just as I'll seal yours for sticking to the pointless custom of your country in denying me a kiss. So, patiently and agreeably.

original: You  have witchcraft in your lips, Kate. There is more  eloquence in a sugar touch of them than in the tongues  of the French council, and they should sooner persuade  Harry of England than a general petition of monarchs.
translation: . There's witchcraft in your lips, Kate. There are more beautiful speeches in a sweet touch of them than in the mouths of the French council, and they would persuade Harry of England more quickly than a petition signed by all the other kings.

original: Here comes your father.
translation: Here comes your father.

original: God save your Majesty. My royal cousin, teach you our  princess English?
translation: God save your majesty. My royal cousin, are you teaching our princess English?

original: I would have her learn, my fair cousin, how perfectly I love her, and that is good English.
translation: My cousin, I want her to learn how much I love her, and that is good English.

original: Is she not apt?
translation: Is she not a quick learner?

original: Our tongue is rough, coz, and my condition is not  smooth,
translation: I don't speak very well, cousin, and am not polite,

original: so that, having neither the voice nor the heart  of flattery about me,
translation: so, because I don't know how and don't want to flatter her,

original: I cannot so conjure up the spirit  of love in her that he will appear in his true likeness.
translation: I can't conjure up the spirit of love in her to make him appear in his true form.

original: Pardon the frankness of my mirth if I answer you for  that
translation: Forgive me for laughing at you openly.

original: . If you would conjure in her, you must make a  circle; if conjure up Love in her in his true likeness,  he must appear naked and blind.
translation: If you want to conjure in her, you must make a circle. If you want to conjure up Love in his true form, he would have to appear naked and blind.

original: Can you blame her then,  being a maid yet rosed over with the virgin crimson of  modesty, if she deny the appearance of a naked blind boy in her naked seeing self? It were, my lord, a hard  condition for a maid to consign to.
translation: Can you blame her then, since she's still a modest virgin, if she doesn't allow a naked blind boy to appear in her naked seeing self? It would be a bad situation for a virgin to agree to.

original: Yet they do wink and yield, as love is blind and  enforces.
translation: But they do shut their eyes and give in, since love is blind and powerful.

original: They are then excused, my lord, when they see not what  they do.
translation: It's not their fault, then, my lord, when they don't see what they do.

original: Then, good my lord, teach your cousin to consent  winking.
translation: Then, my good lord, teach your cousin to agree to shut her eyes.

original: I will wink on her to consent, my lord, if you will  teach her to know my meaning,
translation: I will wink at her to tell her to consent, my lord, if you will teach her to understand my meaning.

original: for maids, well summered  and warm kept, are like flies at Bartholomew-tide:  blind, though they have their eyes;
translation: Because virgins, kept warm and safe, are like flies in midsummer: blind, although they have eyes.

original: and then they will  endure handling, which before would not abide looking  on.
translation: And they can bear to be handled, when previously they couldn't bear to be looked at.

original: This moral ties me over to time and a hot summer.
translation: The moral of this is I should wait for the right time and a hot summer.

original: And  so I shall catch the fly, your cousin, in the latter end and she must be blind too.
translation: And that way I will catch the fly, your cousin, by the tail, and she will be blind too.

original: As love is, my lord, before it loves.
translation: As blind as love is, my lord, before it loves.

original: It is so. And you may, some of you, thank love for my  blindness,
translation: It's true. And some of you can thank me for my blindness,

original: who cannot see many a fair French city for  one fair French maid that stands in my way.
translation: because I can't see many French cities because of one beautiful French virgin who stands in my way.

original: Yes, my lord, you see them perspectively, the cities  turned into a maid,
translation: Yes, my lord, you see them in perspective, the cities turned into a virgin,

original: for they are all girdled with maiden walls that war hath never entered.
translation: because they are surrounded by virgin walls that war has never entered.

original: Shall Kate be my wife?
translation: Will Kate be my wife?

original: So please you.
translation: If it pleases you.

original: I am content, so the maiden cities you talk of may wait on her.
translation: I am content, as long as the virgin cities you talk about come too.

original: So the maid that stood in the way for my wish  shall show me the way to my will.
translation: So the virgin who stood in the way of my wish will show me the way to my desire.

original: We have consented to all terms of reason.
translation: I have consented to all reasonable demands.

original: Is ’t so, my lords of England?
translation: Is that so, my lords of England?

original: Only he hath not yet subscribèd this:   Where your Majesty demands that the king of France,  having any occasion to write for matter of grant, shall  name your Highness in this form and with this addition,  in French:
translation: But he hasn't yet signed this: where your Majesty demands that the king of France, if he has any reason to write out a declaration, will name your Highness too in this way, in French:

original: Notre très cher fils Henri, roi d'Angleterre, héritier de France   ; and thus in Latin:   Praeclarissimus  filius noster Henricus, rex Angliae, et haeres Franciae.
translation: Our very dear son Henry, king of England, heir of France,  and this in Latin:  Our most famous son Henry, king of England, and heir of France.

original: Nor this I have not, brother, so denied But your request shall make me let it pass.
translation: I have not denied this, brother. If you ask me to agree to this, I will.

original: I pray you, then, in love and dear alliance,   Let that one article rank with the rest,
translation: I ask you, then, with love and as allies, that you agree to that article along with the rest,

original: And thereupon give me your daughter.
translation: and give me your daughter.

original: Take her, fair son, and from her blood raise up   Issue to me, that the contending kingdoms   Of France and England, whose very shores look pale   With envy of each other’s happiness,   May cease their hatred,
translation: Take her, son, and have her give birth to heirs for me, so that the fighting kingdoms of France and England, whose shores look pale with envy of each other's happiness, will cease hating each other.

original: and this dear conjunction   Plant neighborhood and Christian-like accord   In their sweet bosoms, that never war advance   His bleeding sword ’twixt England and fair France.
translation: May this match make them neighborly and make them agree like Christians, so that bloody war never arises again between England and beautiful France.

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: Now welcome, Kate, and bear me witness all That here I kiss her as my sovereign queen.
translation: Now welcome, Kate.  You are all witnesses that here I kiss her as my queen.

original: God, the best maker of all marriages,   Combine your hearts in one, your realms in one.
translation: May God, the best matchmaker, combine your hearts in one, your countries in one.

original: As man and wife, being two, are one in love,   So be there ’twixt your kingdoms such a spousal   That never may ill office or fell jealousy,   Which troubles oft the bed of blessèd marriage,   Thrust in between the paction of these kingdoms   To make divorce of their incorporate league,
translation: Just as man and wife, although they are two people, become one, so may there be between your kingdoms such a marriage that ill will and terrible jealousy, which often trouble blessed marriage, never thrust themselves between these two joined kingdoms to divorce them.

original: That English may as French, French Englishmen,   Receive each other. God speak this “amen”!
translation: May Englishmen and Frenchmen treat each other as though they come from the same country. May God speak this "amen"!

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: Prepare we for our marriage; on which day,   My Lord of Burgundy, we’ll take your oath,   And all the peers', for surety of our leagues.
translation: Let's prepare for our marriage, and on that day, my Lord of Burgundy, we'll have you and all the noblemen swear an oath to honor our alliance.

original: Then shall I swear to Kate, and you to me,   And may our oaths well kept and prosp'rous be.
translation: Then I will swear to Kate, and you to me, and may our oaths be kept well and be fortunate.

original: Thus far with rough and all-unable pen   Our bending author hath pursued the story,   In little room confining mighty men,   Mangling by starts the full course of their glory.
translation: Our obedient author followed the story this far with his rough and incompetent writing, confining great men into a small room, mangling and breaking up the full extent of their glory.

original: Small time, but in that small most greatly lived   This star of England.
translation: This English star lived a short but very great life.

original: Fortune made his sword,   By which the world’s best garden he achieved   And of it left his son imperial lord.
translation: Fortune made his sword, which he used to win the world's best garden and left his son ruler of it.

original: Henry the Sixth, in infant bands crowned king   Of France and England, did this king succeed,   Whose state so many had the managing   That they lost France and made his England bleed,   Which oft our stage hath shown.
translation: Henry the Sixth, crowned king of France and England when he was an infant, succeeded this king. So many people were in charge of ruling his country that they lost France and made his England bleed, as our stage has often shown you.

original: And for their sake,   In your fair minds let this acceptance take.
translation: For their sake, kindly accept this play.

original: Hence! Home, you idle creatures get you home!   Is this a holiday?
translation: Go away! Go home, you lazy creatures. Go home! Is today a holiday?

original: What, know you not,   Being mechanical, you ought not walk   Upon a laboring day without the sign   Of your profession?
translation: Don't you know that, as working-class men, you shouldn’t walk around on a workday without wearing your work clothes?

original: Why, sir, a carpenter.
translation: Why, I’m a carpenter, sir.

original: Where is thy leather apron and thy rule?
translation: Where are your leather apron and ruler?

original: What dost thou with thy best apparel on?
translation: Why are you wearing your finest clothes?

original: —You, sir, what trade are you?
translation: [To COBBLER]  And you, sir, what’s your job?

original: Truly, sir, in respect of a fine workman, I am but, as  you would say, a cobbler.
translation: Well, sir, compared to a skilled workman, I'm just a cobbler, as you would put it.

original: But what trade art thou? Answer me directly.
translation: But what’s your trade? Answer me straightforwardly.

original: A trade, sir, that I hope I may use with a safe  conscience, which is, indeed, sir, a mender of bad  soles.
translation: I work a trade, sir, that I hope I can practice with a clear conscience. I am a mender of worn soles.

original: What trade, thou knave? Thou naughty knave, what trade?
translation: What trade, fool? You good-for-nothing fool, what trade?

original: Nay, I beseech you, sir, be not out with me. Yet, if  you be out, sir, I can mend you.
translation: Sir, I beg you, don’t be angry. Yet, if your soles are worn out, I can mend you.

original: What mean’st thou by that? “Mend” me, thou saucy  fellow?
translation: What do you mean by that? “Mend” me, you rude man?

original: Why, sir, cobble you.
translation: Well, cobble you, sir.

original: Thou art a cobbler, art thou?
translation: You’re a cobbler, are you?

original: Truly, sir, all that I live by is with the awl. I  meddle with no tradesman’s matters nor women’s matters,  but withal I am indeed, sir, a surgeon to old shoes.  When they are in great danger, I recover them.
translation: Yes, sir, I make my living through use of an awl. I don’t meddle in politics or in the affairs of women. I’m just a surgeon for old shoes. When they’re in bad shape, I fix them.

original: As proper men as ever trod upon neat’s leather have gone upon my  handiwork.
translation: The most noble men who have ever walked on leather have walked on my handiwork.

original: But wherefore art not in thy shop today? Why dost thou lead these men about the streets?
translation: But why aren’t you in your shop today? Why are you leading these men through the streets?

original: Truly, sir, to wear out their shoes to get myself into  more work. But indeed, sir, we make holiday to see  Caesar and to rejoice in his triumph.
Wherefore rejoice? What conquest brings he home?
translation: Why celebrate it? What foreign lands has he conquered for Rome to rule?

original: What tributaries follow him to Rome   To grace in captive bonds his chariot wheels?
translation: What foreign princes are chained to his chariot wheels and will earn Rome ransom money?

original: You blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless  things,   O you hard hearts, you cruèl men of Rome,   Knew you not Pompey?
translation: You blockheads, you unfeeling men, you worse than stupid things! Oh, you with hard hearts, you cruel men of Rome!  didn’t you know  Pompey ?

original: Many a time and oft   Have you climbed up to walls and battlements,   To towers and windows, yea, to chimney tops,   Your infants in your arms,
translation: Many a time you climbed up on walls and battlements, towers and windows—yes, even chimney tops, with your babies in your arms—

original: and there have sat   The livelong day with patient expectation   To see great Pompey pass the streets of Rome.
translation: and sat there all day just waiting to see great Pompey ride through the streets of Rome.

original: And when you saw his chariot but appear,   Have you not made an universal shout   That Tiber trembled underneath her banks   To hear the replication of your sounds   Made in her concave shores?
translation: And when you saw his chariot, didn’t all of you shout all at once so loudly that the Tiber River shook from the sound echoing within its banks?

original: And do you now put on your best attire?   And do you now cull out a holiday?   And do you now strew flowers in his way   That comes in triumph over Pompey’s blood?   Be gone!
translation: And now you put on your finest clothes?  And now you choose to celebrate a holiday? And now you toss flowers in the path of the man who comes in triumph having defeated Pompey’s sons? Get out of here!

original: Run to your houses, fall upon your knees,   Pray to the gods to intermit the plague   That needs must light on this ingratitude.
translation: Run to your houses, fall on your knees, and pray to the gods to spare you from the terrible punishment that is certain to come down upon you for such ingratitude.

original: Go, go, good countrymen, and for this fault,   Assemble all the poor men of your sort,
translation: Go, go, good countrymen. And to atone for this error in judgment, gather together all the poor men like you.

original: Draw them to Tiber banks, and weep your tears   Into the channel till the lowest stream   Do kiss the most exalted shores of all.
translation: Lead them to the banks of the Tiber River, and weep into the water until it overflows.

original: See whether their basest metal be not moved.
translation: That should move even these coarse and unrefined men .

original: They vanish tongue-tied in their guiltiness.
translation: They’re leaving, and feel so guilty they can’t speak.

original: Go you down that way towards the Capitol.   This way will I.
translation: You go that way towards the  Capitol , and I’ll go this way.

original: Disrobe the images   If you do find them decked with ceremonies.
translation: Undress any statues you see that have been decorated in honor of Caesar.

original: May we do so? You know it is the feast of Lupercal.
It is no matter. Let no images   Be hung with Caesar’s trophies.
translation: It doesn’t matter. None of the statues should be decorated in honor to Caesar.

original: I’ll about   And drive away the vulgar from the streets.   So do you too, where you perceive them thick.
translation: I’ll make sure the commoners get off the streets, and you do the same wherever you see a bunch of them together.

original: These growing feathers plucked from Caesar’s wing   Will make him fly an ordinary pitch,
translation: If we can pluck the feathers of Caesar’s growing support among the commoners now, he’ll have to fly at a normal height.

original: Who else would soar above the view of men   And keep us all in servile fearfulness.
translation: If we don’t, he’ll soar to such heights of power that all of us will live in fear and be his servants.

original: Calphurnia!
translation: Calphurnia!

original: Peace, ho! Caesar speaks.
translation: Hey, quiet down! Caesar speaks.

original: Calphurnia!
translation: Calphurnia!

original: Here, my lord.
translation: Here I am, my lord.

original: Stand you directly in Antonius' way   When he doth run his course.
translation: Stand directly in Antonius’ path as he runs the race.

original: —Antonius!
translation: [To ANTONY]  Antonius!

original: Caesar, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord Caesar?

original: Forget not in your speed, Antonius,   To touch Calphurnia,
translation: Antonius, while you’re running don’t forget to touch Calphurnia.

original: for our elders say   The barren, touchèd in this holy chase,   Shake off their sterile curse.
translation: As our elders say, if an infertile woman is touched during this holy race, she’ll escape the curse of sterility.

original: I shall remember. When Caesar says, “do this,” it is performed.
translation: I will remember. When Caesar says “do this,” it is done.

original: Set on, and leave no ceremony out.
translation: Go on, then, and don’t leave out any of the proper rituals.

original: Caesar!
translation: Caesar!

original: Ha! Who calls?
translation: Hey! Who’s calling me?

original: Bid every noise be still. Peace yet again.
translation: Everyone, be quiet! Again, quiet!

original: Who is it in the press that calls on me?
translation: Who is it in the crowd that’s calling me?

original: I hear a tongue, shriller than all the music,   Cry “Caesar!”
translation: I hear a voice that's shriller than any of this music, calling out “Caesar!”

original: —Speak. Caesar is turned to hear.
translation: Speak. Caesar is listening.

original: Beware the ides of March.
What man is that?
translation: Who is saying that?

original: A soothsayer bids you beware the ides of March.
translation: A soothsayer tells you to beware March 15th.

original: Set him before me. Let me see his face.
translation: Bring him to me. Let me see his face.

original: Fellow, come from the throng. Look upon Caesar.
translation: Man, step out of the crowd. Stand before Caesar.

original: What sayst thou to me now? Speak once again.
translation: What are you saying to me now? Say it again.

original: Beware the ides of March.
translation: Beware March 15th.

original: He is a dreamer. Let us leave him. Pass!
translation: He’s crazy. Let’s leave him. Continue on!

original: Will you go see the order of the course?
translation: Are you going to come watch the race?

original: Not I.
translation: Not me.

original: I pray you, do.
translation: Please, come and watch it.

original: I am not gamesome.
translation: I’m not feeling festive.

original: I do lack some part   Of that quick spirit that is in Antony.
translation: I lack some of Antony’s lively, competitive spirit.

original: Let me not hinder, Cassius, your desires.   I’ll leave you.
translation: But don’t let me stop you from doing what you want, Cassius. I’ll leave you alone.

original: Brutus, I do observe you now of late   I have not from your eyes that gentleness   And show of love as I was wont to have.
translation: Brutus, I’ve been watching you recently. I’ve noticed that you seem less friendly toward me than I’m used to.

original: You bear too stubborn and too strange a hand   Over your friend that loves you.
translation: You’ve been rough and unfriendly to me, your friend who loves you.

original: Cassius,   Be not deceived. If I have veiled my look,   I turn the trouble of my countenance   Merely upon myself.
translation: Cassius, don’t be fooled. If I seem unfriendly, it’s because my troubled looks are actually directed at myself.

original: Vexèd I am   Of late with passions of some difference,   Conceptions only proper to myself,   Which give some soil perhaps to my behaviors.
translation: Lately I’ve been overwhelmed with private thoughts and conflicting emotions, which must have affected my behavior.

original: But let not therefore, my good friends, be grieved—   Among which number, Cassius, be you one—
translation: But my good friends should not be troubled—and I count you as a good friend, Cassius.

original: Nor construe any further my neglect   Than that poor Brutus, with himself at war,   Forgets the shows of love to other men.
translation: And they should not see anything more in my distant behavior than that poor Brutus—who is at war with himself—has forgotten to show affection to others.

original: Then, Brutus, I have much mistook your passion,
translation: Brutus, I misunderstood your feelings.

original: By means whereof this breast of mine hath buried   Thoughts of great value, worthy cogitations.
translation: And for that reason, I kept to myself a number of important thoughts.

original: Tell me, good Brutus, can you see your face?
translation: Good Brutus, tell me, can you see your face?

original: No, Cassius, for the eye sees not itself But by reflection, by some other things.
translation: No, Cassius, because the eye can’t see itself, except in reflections on other surfaces.

original: 'Tis just.
translation: That’s a fact.

original: And it is very much lamented, Brutus,   That you have no such mirrors as will turn   Your hidden worthiness into your eye   That you might see your shadow   .
translation: But it’s a shame that you don’t have any mirrors in which to view your own worthiness, Brutus.

original: I have heard   Where many of the best respect in Rome,   Except immortal Caesar, speaking of Brutus   And groaning underneath this age’s yoke,   Have wished that noble Brutus had his eyes.
translation: I’ve heard many of the most respected Romans—with the exception of immortal Caesar—mention you while complaining of the burden of our current government, and wish that your eyes were working better.

original: Into what dangers would you lead me, Cassius, That you would have me seek into myself For that which is not in me?
translation: Cassius, what dangers do you want to lead me into, by asking me to look inside myself for something that isn't in me?

original: Therefore, good Brutus, be prepared to hear.
translation: Be prepared to listen, good Brutus.

original: And since you know you cannot see yourself   So well as by reflection, I, your glass,   Will modestly discover to yourself   That of yourself which you yet know not of.
translation: And since you know the best way to see yourself is by reflection, I'll act as your mirror and show to you the parts of yourself of which you are unaware, without exaggerating.

original: And be not jealous on me, gentle Brutus.
translation: Don’t be suspicious of what I say, noble Brutus.

original: Were I a common laugher, or did use   To stale with ordinary oaths my love   To every new protester, if you know   That I do fawn on men and hug them hard   And, after, scandal them,
translation: If I were some frivolous fool; or made the same stale vows of friendship to every new friend I met; or if you knew that I flatter men to their faces only to slander them once they're gone;

original: or if you know   That I profess myself in banqueting   To all the rout, then hold me dangerous.
translation: or if you learn that I make declarations of friendship to all the mobs of people while at a feast, then, of course, don't believe me.

original: What means this shouting? I do fear, the people Choose Caesar for their king.
translation: What is the meaning of this shouting? I fear the people have made Caesar their king.

original: Ay, do you fear it? Then must I think you would not have it so.
translation: Really, do you fear that? Then I must guess that you don’t want that to happen.

original: I would not, Cassius. Yet I love him well.
translation: I don’t, Cassius, even though I love Caesar dearly.

original: But wherefore do you hold me here so long?   What is it that you would impart to me?
translation: But why do you keep me here so long? What is it that you want to tell me?

original: If it be aught toward the general good,   Set honor in one eye and death i' th' other,   And I will look on both indifferently,
translation: If it’s for the general good of Rome, I’d do anything, even if it meant my death.

original: For let the gods so speed me as I love   The name of honor more than I fear death.
translation: May the gods grant me good favor only so long as I love honor more than I fear death.

original: I know that virtue to be in you, Brutus,   As well as I do know your outward favor.   Well, honor is the subject of my story.
translation: I see that good quality in you, Brutus. It’s as familiar to me as your appearance.  In fact, honor is what I want to discuss with you.

original: I cannot tell what you and other men   Think of this life, but, for my single self,   I had as lief not be as live to be   In awe of such a thing as I myself.
translation: I don’t know what you and other men think of this life. But, as for me, I’d rather not live at all than stand in awe of a man no better than myself.

original: I was born free as Caesar. So were you.   We both have fed as well, and we can both   Endure the winter’s cold as well as he.
translation: I was born as free as Caesar. So were you. We both have eaten as well, and we can both endure the winter's cold as well as he.

original: For once upon a raw and gusty day,   The troubled Tiber chafing with her shores,   Caesar said to me, “Darest thou, Cassius, now   Leap in with me into this angry flood   And swim to yonder point?”
translation: Once, on a harsh and windy day, as the Tiber River swelled against its banks, Caesar said to me, “Cassius, would you dare to jump with me into this rough water and swim to that distant point?”

original: Upon the word,   Accoutred as I was, I plungèd in   And bade him follow. So indeed he did.
translation: The moment he said that—though I was still in my clothes—I jumped in and told him to follow. He did.

original: The torrent roared, and we did buffet it   With lusty sinews, throwing it aside   And stemming it with hearts of controversy.
translation: The water roared, and we fought against it with all our strength, inspired to overcome it by our competitive natures

original: But ere we could arrive the point proposed,   Caesar cried, “Help me, Cassius, or I sink!”
translation: But before we could reach our destination, Caesar cried, “Help me, Cassius, or I'll sink!”

original: I, as Aeneas, our great ancestor,   Did from the flames of Troy upon his shoulder   The old Anchises bear, so from the waves of Tiber   Did I the tired Caesar.
translation: Just like  Aeneas  carried on his shoulders his elderly father Anchises from the fires of Troy, I carry the tired Caesar from the waves of the Tiber.

original: And this man   Is now become a god, and Cassius is   A wretched creature and must bend his body   If Caesar carelessly but nod on him.
translation: And this man has now become a god, while I am a wretched creature who must bow down if Caesar carelessly nods my way .

original: He had a fever when he was in Spain,   And when the fit was on him, I did mark   How he did shake. 'Tis true, this god did shake!
translation: When he was in Spain, Caesar had a fever. And when he was in its grip, I noticed how he shook. It’s true, this “god” was shaking!

original: His coward lips did from their color fly,   And that same eye whose bend doth awe the world   Did lose his luster. I did hear him groan,
translation: His cowardly lips lost their color, and that same eye whose gaze now terrifies the world lost its gleam. Yes, I heard him groan.

original: Ay, and that tongue of his that bade the Romans   Mark him and write his speeches in their books—   “Alas,” it cried, “give me some drink, Titinius,”   As a sick girl.
translation: And that tongue of his that ordered the Romans to listen to him and transcribe his speeches in their books cried like a sick girl, “Oh, get me a drink, Titinius.”

original: Ye gods, it doth amaze me   A man of such a feeble temper should   So get the start of the majestic world   And bear the palm alone.
translation: Oh, by the gods, it amazes me that a man of such weak constitution could get an advantage over the entire world and carry the prize of victory alone.

original: Another general shout! I do believe that these applauses are For some new honors that are heaped on Caesar.
translation: More shouting from the crowd! I think this applause is for some new honor given to Caesar.

original: Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world   Like a Colossus, and we petty men   Walk under his huge legs and peep about   To find ourselves dishonorable graves.
translation: Why, sir, he straddles the narrow world like a giant, and we petty men walk under his huge legs and peek out just to find our graves, as if we were slaves.

original: Men at some time are masters of their fates.   The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars   But in ourselves, that we are underlings.
translation: Men can be masters of their fate. Brutus, our problem is not destiny, but ourselves.

original: Brutus and Caesar—what should be in that   “Caesar?”   Why should that name be sounded more than yours?   Write them together, yours is as fair a name.   Sound them, it doth become the mouth as well.
translation: “Brutus” and “Caesar"—what's special about “Caesar?” Why should that name be shouted more than yours? Write them together—yours looks just as good. Say them—yours is just as pleasant to say.

original: Weigh them, it is as heavy. Conjure with 'em,   “Brutus” will start a spirit as soon as “Caesar.”   Now in the names of all the gods at once,
translation: Weigh them—it’s just as heavy. Do magic with them, and “Brutus” will call up a spirit just as well as “Caesar.” Now, in the name of all the gods,

original: Upon what meat doth this our Caesar feed   That he is grown so great?
translation: I ask you what meat Caesar has eaten that has made him grow to be so great?

original: Age, thou art shamed!   Rome, thou hast lost the breed of noble bloods!   When went there by an age, since the great flood,   But it was famed with more than with one man?
translation: The people of our time should be ashamed! Rome has lost the ability to raise noble men! When was there an age, since the  great flood , that didn’t contain more than one famous man?

original: When could they say till now, that talked of Rome,   That her wide walks encompassed but one man?   Now is it Rome indeed, and room enough,   When there is in it but one only man.
translation: When could anyone speaking of Rome say, before now, that just one man ruled the entire city? Indeed, now Rome only has room for one man.

original: Oh, you and I have heard our fathers say,   There was a Brutus once that would have brooked   Th' eternal devil to keep his state in Rome   As easily as a king.
translation: Oh, you and I have heard our fathers say that once there was a Brutus—your ancestor—who would have let the devil reign in the Roman Republic before he would allow a king.

original: That you do love me, I am nothing jealous.   What you would work me to, I have some aim.
translation: I do not doubt that you love me. I’m starting to understand what you would like me to do.

original: How I have thought of this and of these times   I shall recount hereafter. For this present,   I would not, so with love I might entreat you,   Be any further moved.
translation: I'll tell you what I think about this and about what’s happening in Rome later. For the moment—in the name of our friendship—I would prefer that you not try to do any more persuading.

original: What you have said   I will consider, what you have to say   I will with patience hear, and find a time   Both meet to hear and answer such high things.
translation: I’ll think over what you’ve said; I’ll listen patiently to whatever else you have to say; and I’ll find an appropriate time for us to consider and make a decision about such weighty matters.

original: Till then, my noble friend, chew upon this:   Brutus had rather be a villager   Than to repute himself a son of Rome   Under these hard conditions as this time   Is like to lay upon us.
translation: Until then, my noble friend, think about this: I would rather be some villager than call myself a citizen of Rome during the difficult situation these times are likely to put us through.

original: I am glad that my weak words Have struck but thus much show of fire from Brutus.
translation: I’m glad that my weak words have forced even this small show of passion from you.

original: The games are done and Caesar is returning.
translation: The games are finished, and Caesar is returning.

original: As they pass by, pluck Casca by the sleeve, And he will, after his sour fashion, tell you What hath proceeded worthy note today.
translation: As they pass by, grab Casca by the sleeve. In his sour way, he'll tell you if anything important happened today.

original: I will do so. But, look you, Cassius,   The angry spot doth glow on Caesar’s brow,   And all the rest look like a chidden train.
translation: I’ll do so. But look there, Cassius. Caesar's face is full of anger while everyone with him look like they’ve been scolded.

original: Calphurnia’s cheek is pale, and Cicero   Looks with such ferret and such fiery eyes   As we have seen him in the Capitol   Being crossed in conference by some senators.
translation: Calphurnia’s face is pale, and Cicero’s eyes are darting and angry, just as they get when senators argue with him during sessions at the Capitol.

original: Casca will tell us what the matter is.
translation: Casca will tell us what's happened.

original: Antonio.
translation: Antonio.

original: Caesar.
translation: Caesar.

original: [aside to ANTONY]   Let me have men about me that are  fat,   Sleek-headed men and such as sleep a-nights.
translation: [To ANTONY so that only he can hear]  I want the men around me to be fat, well-groomed men who sleep soundly through the night.

original: Yond Cassius has a lean and hungry look.   He thinks too much. Such men are dangerous.
translation: Cassius over there has a lean and hungry look. He thinks too much. Men like that are dangerous.

original: Fear him not, Caesar. He’s not  dangerous. He is a noble Roman and well given.
translation: Don’t be afraid of him, Caesar. He's not dangerous. He’s a noble Roman with an honorable character.

original: [aside to ANTONY]   Would he were fatter! But I fear him  not.   Yet if my name were liable to fear,   I do not know the man I should avoid   So soon as that spare Cassius.
translation: [To ANTONY so that only he can hear]  If only he were fatter! But I’m not afraid of him. Yet, if I myself were capable of fear, I don’t know of any man I would avoid more than skinny Cassius.

original: He reads much.   He is a great observer, and he looks   Quite through the deeds of men. He loves no plays,   As thou dost, Antony
translation: He reads a lot. He’s a skilled observer, and he sees the hidden motives behind men’s actions. He doesn’t enjoy plays like you do, Antony.

original: . He hears no music.   Seldom he smiles, and smiles in such a sort   As if he mocked himself and scorned his spirit   That could be moved to smile at anything.
translation: He never listens to music. He almost never smiles. Though when he does smile, he does it as if he’s mocking the part of himself that could be inspired to smile by anything .

original: Such men as he be never at heart’s ease   Whiles they behold a greater than themselves,   And therefore are they very dangerous.
translation: Men like  him can never be content as long as they know that there is someone better and more powerful than they are. And therefore they’re very dangerous.

original: I rather tell thee what is to be feared   Than what I fear, for always I am Caesar.   Come on my right hand, for this ear is deaf,   And tell me truly what thou think’st of him.
translation: I’m telling you what should be feared rather than what I fear, because, after all, I am Caesar. Step over to my right side, because my left ear is deaf, and tell me honestly what you think of Cassius.

original: You pulled me by the cloak. Would you speak with me?
translation: You pulled on my cloak. Do you want to speak with me?

original: Ay, Casca. Tell us what hath chanced today That Caesar looks so sad.
translation: Yes, Casca. Tell us what happened today that made Caesar seem so unhappy.

original: Why, you were with him, were you not?
translation: Well, weren’t you with him?

original: I should not then ask Casca what had chanced.
translation: If I were with him, I wouldn’t be asking what happened.

original: Why, there was a crown offered him; and, being offered  him, he put it by with the back of his hand, thus; and  then the people fell a-shouting.
translation: Well, a crown was offered to him, and, when it was offered, he pushed it away with the back of his hand, like this—and then the people started shouting.

original: What was the second noise for?
translation: What was the second noise for?

original: Why, for that too.
translation: For that same thing.

original: They shouted thrice. What was the last cry for?
translation: They shouted three times. What was the last cry for?

original: Why, for that too.
translation: For the same thing.

original: Was the crown offered him thrice?
translation: The crown was offered to him three times?

original: Ay, marry, was ’t, and he put it by thrice, every time  gentler than other, and at every putting-by mine honest  neighbors shouted.
translation: Yes, that's right, it was. And he pushed it away three times, but each time more gently than the last. And each time he pushed it away, my noble countrymen cheered.

original: Who offered him the crown?
translation: Who offered him the crown?

original: Why, Antony.
translation: Antony.

original: Tell us the manner of it, gentle Casca.
translation: Tell us what it was like, noble Casca.

original: I can as well be hanged as tell the manner of it. It  was mere foolery. I did not mark it.
translation: I'd just as soon be hanged than describe it! It was all foolishness. I paid no attention.

original: I saw Mark Antony  offer him a crown (yet ’twas not a crown neither, ’twas  one of these coronets)
translation: I saw Mark Antony offer him a crown—though it wasn’t a real crown, it was more like a wreath—

original: and, as I told you, he put it by  once—but, for all that, to my thinking, he would fain  have had it   .
translation: and, as I told you, Caesar refused it once. Although, in my opinion, he would’ve gladly taken it .

original: Then he offered it to him again, then he  put it by again—but, to my thinking, he was very loath  to lay his fingers off it. And then he offered it the  third time. He put it the third time by.
translation: T hen Antony offered it to him again, and Caesar refused it again—though, in my opinion, he didn't want to take his hand off it. Then Antony offered it the third time, and Caesar refused it the third time.

original: And still, as  he refused it, the rabblement hooted and clapped their  chopp'd hands and threw up their sweaty night-caps and  uttered such a deal of stinking breath because Caesar  refused the crown that it had almost choked Caesar—for  he swooned and fell down at it.
translation: Yet even as he refused it, the masses hooted and clapped their chapped hands, and threw up their sweaty hats, and roared out such a load of stinking breath because Caesar refused the crown that it nearly choked Caesar, who fainted and fell down.

original: And for mine own part, I durst not laugh for fear of opening my lips and  receiving the bad air.
translation: As for me, I didn’t dare laugh because I feared opening my lips and inhaling the stinking air.

original: But soft, I pray you. What, did Caesar swoon?
translation: Stop for a moment, please. What, did Caesar faint?

original: He fell down in the marketplace, and foamed at mouth,  and was speechless.
translation: He fell down in the marketplace and foamed at the mouth and couldn't speak.

original: 'Tis very like. He hath the falling sickness.
translation: That’s very likely. He has epilepsy, the falling sickness.

original: No, Caesar hath it not. But you and I And honest Casca, we have the falling sickness.
translation: No, Caesar doesn’t have it. But you and I, and honest Casca, we have the falling sickness.

original: I know not what you mean by that, but I am sure Caesar  fell down. If the tag-rag people did not clap him and  hiss him according as he pleased and displeased them, as they use to do the players in the theatre, I am no true man.
translation: I don’t know what you mean by that. But I’m sure Caesar fell down. If the masses didn’t clap for him or hiss at him based on whether he pleased or displeased them—just as they do for actors in the theater—then I’m a liar.

original: What said he when he came unto himself?
translation: What did he say when he woke up?

original: Marry, before he fell down, when he perceived the  common herd was glad he refused the crown, he plucked me ope his doublet and offered them his throat to cut.
translation: Well, before he fell down—when he realized the commoners were glad he refused the crown—he pulled open his jacket and offered them his throat to cut.

original: An  I had been a man of any occupation, if I would not have  taken him at a word, I would I might go to hell among  the rogues.
translation: If I were a common laborer and didn't take him at his word and cut his throat, then to hell with me.

original: And so he fell. When he came to himself  again, he said, if he had done or said anything amiss,  he desired their worships to think it was his infirmity.
translation: Then he fainted. When he came to, he said to the crowd that if he’d done or said anything wrong, he wanted them to know that it was caused by his sickness.

original: Three or four wenches where I stood cried, “Alas, good  soul!” and forgave him with all their hearts. But  there’s no heed to be taken of them. If Caesar had  stabbed their mothers they would have done no less.
translation: Three or four women standing near me cried, “Alas, good soul!” and forgave him with all their hearts. But don't pay any attention to them—if Caesar had stabbed their mothers, they would have said the same thing.

original: And after that he came thus sad away?
translation: And after all that he came this way looking so serious?

original: Ay.
translation: Yes.

original: Did Cicero say anything?
translation: Did Cicero say anything?

original: Ay, he spoke Greek.
translation: Yes, he said something in Greek.

original: To what effect?
translation: What did he say?

original: Nay, an I tell you that, I’ll ne'er look you i' th'  face again.   But those that understood him smiled at one  another and shook their heads.
translation: No, if I told you I understood what he was saying, I wouldn’t be able to look you in the eye.  But those who did understand him smiled at one another and shook their heads.

original: But, for mine own part,  it was Greek to me. I could tell you more news too.  Murellus and Flavius, for pulling scarfs off Caesar’s  images, are put to silence.
translation: But, speaking for myself, it was Greek to me. But I have more news to tell you. Murellus and Flavius have been punished for pulling scarves off of statues of Caesar.

original: Fare you well. There was  more foolery yet, if I could remember it.
translation: Goodbye. There was more foolishness, too, but I can’t remember it.

original: Will you sup with me tonight, Casca?
translation: Will you have dinner with me tonight, Casca?

original: No, I am promised forth.
translation: No, I have another commitment.

original: Will you dine with me tomorrow?
translation: Will you dine with me tomorrow?

original: Ay, if I be alive and your mind hold and your dinner  worth the eating.
translation: Yes, if I’m still alive, and you’re still sane, and your dinner is worth eating.

original: Good. I will expect you.
translation: Good. I’ll expect you.

original: Do so. Farewell both.
translation: Do that. Farewell to both of you.

original: What a blunt fellow is this grown to be! He was quick mettle when he went to school.
translation: What a dull man he’s become! He was so quick-witted when he was in school.

original: So is he now in execution   Of any bold or noble enterprise,   However he puts on this tardy form.
translation: And he’s quick-witted now when it comes to carrying out any bold or noble enterprise, despite this show of being dull.

original: This rudeness is a sauce to his good wit,   Which gives men stomach to digest his words   With better appetite.
translation: The crudeness of his words is a kind of tasty sauce for the wisdom of what he says, which makes other people more likely to listen to him.

original: And so it is. For this time I will leave you.   Tomorrow, if you please to speak with me,   I will come home to you.
translation: That’s it exactly. For now, I’ll leave you. Tomorrow, if you’d like to speak with me, I’ll come to your house.

original: Or, if you will,   Come home to me, and I will wait for you.
translation: Or, if you want, come to my house, and I’ll wait for you.

original: I will do so. Till then, think of the world.
translation: I’ll do that. Until then, think of what’s best for the world.

original: Well, Brutus, thou art noble. Yet I see   Thy honorable mettle may be wrought   From that it is disposed. Therefore it is meet   That noble minds keep ever with their likes,
translation: Well, Brutus, you’re noble. Yet I see that your honorable nature can be turned from its usual inclination. Therefore, it's better for noble men to spend time only with other noble men,

original: For who so firm that cannot be seduced?
translation: because who is so firm that he can’t be seduced?

original: Caesar doth bear me hard, but he loves Brutus.   If I were Brutus now and he were Cassius,   He should not humor me.
translation: Caesar doesn't like me, but he loves Brutus. If I were Brutus now and he were Cassius, I wouldn’t have let him persuade me.

original: I will this night,   In several hands, in at his windows throw,   As if they came from several citizens,
translation: Tonight I’ll throw a few letters through his window—each written with different handwriting, as if they came from different citizens—

original: Writings all tending to the great opinion   That Rome holds of his name, wherein obscurely   Caesar’s ambition shall be glancèd at.
translation: all saying how great his reputation is throughout all of Rome, while also hinting at Caesar’s ambition.

original: And after this let Caesar seat him sure,   For we will shake him, or worse days endure.
translation: And after this, Caesar won't be able to sit comfortably in his power, because we’ll either overthrow him, or suffer worse than we do now.

original: Good even, Casca. Brought you Caesar home? Why are you breathless? And why stare you so?
translation: Good evening, Casca. Did you walk Caesar home? Why are you breathless? And why are you looking around like that?

original: Are not you moved when all the sway of earth   Shakes like a thing unfirm?
translation: Aren’t you disturbed when the entire earth shakes as if it were unsteady?

original: O Cicero,   I have seen tempests when the scolding winds   Have rived the knotty oaks, and I have seen   Th' ambitious ocean swell and rage and foam   To be exalted with the threatening clouds,
translation: Oh, Cicero, I’ve seen storms with gusting winds that have split ancient oak trees. And I’ve seen the ocean swell, rage, and foam, as if it wanted to rise all the way to the dark clouds above.

original: But never till tonight, never till now,   Did I go through a tempest dropping fire.
translation: But not until tonight—not until now—have I ever seen a storm that drops fire.

original: Either there is a civil strife in heaven,   Or else the world, too saucy with the gods,   Incenses them to send destruction.
translation: Either there is a civil war in heaven, or the world—too disrespectful toward the gods—angers them so much that they send destruction.

original: Why, saw you anything more wonderful?
translation: Why, did you see anything else that made it seem like it came from the gods?

original: A common slave—you know him well by sight—   Held up his left hand, which did flame and burn   Like twenty torches joined, and yet his hand,   Not sensible of fire, remained unscorched.
translation: A common slave—you’d recognize him—held up his left hand, which flamed and burned with the strength of twenty torches. And yet his hand did not feel the fire and was not scorched.

original: Besides—I ha' not since put up my sword—   Against the Capitol I met a lion,   Who glaz'd upon me and went surly by,   Without annoying me.
translation: In addition—I haven't sheathed my sword since seeing this—across from the Capitol I saw a lion who stared at me and then walked by without harming me.

original: And there were drawn   Upon a heap a hundred ghastly women,   Transformèd with their fear, who swore they saw   Men all in fire walk up and down the streets.
translation: And there were a hundred frightened women all clustered together, who swore they saw men covered in fire walk up and down the streets.

original: And yesterday the bird of night did sit   Even at noon-day upon the marketplace,   Hooting and shrieking.
translation: And yesterday the owl sat hooting and shrieking in the marketplace at noon.

original: When these prodigies   Do so conjointly meet, let not men say,   “These are their reasons; they are natural.”
translation: When all these strange things happen at the same time, men should not say, “Here are the reasons why this is happening; it's all natural and normal.”

original: For I believe they are portentous things   Unto the climate that they point upon.
translation: I believe these are omens regarding what will happen in the place where they occur, right here in Rome.

original: Indeed, it is a strange-disposèd time.
translation: Yes, these are strange times.

original: But men may construe things after their fashion,   Clean from the purpose of the things themselves.
translation: But men often interpret things for their own purposes, and misunderstand the actual meaning of the things themselves

original: Comes  Caesar to the Capitol tomorrow?
translation: .  Is Caesar coming to the Capitol tomorrow?

original: He doth, for he did bid Antonius Send word to you he would be there tomorrow.
translation: He is. He told Antonius to tell you he’d be there tomorrow.

original: Good night then, Casca. This disturbèd sky Is not to walk in.
translation: Good night then, Casca. This angry weather isn’t something to walk around in.

original: Farewell, Cicero.
translation: Farewell, Cicero

original: Who’s there?
translation: Who’s there?

original: A Roman.
translation: A Roman.

original: Casca, by your voice.
translation: Casca, I recognize your voice.

original: Your ear is good. Cassius, what night is this!
translation: Your ear is good. Cassius, what a night this is!

original: A very pleasing night to honest men.
translation: It’s a very pleasing night to honest men.

original: Who ever knew the heavens menace so?
translation: Who’s ever seen the heavens seem so threatening as this?

original: Those that have known the earth so full of faults.
translation: Those who have known how bad things are here on earth.

original: For my part, I have walked about the streets,   Submitting me unto the perilous night,   And, thus unbracèd, Casca, as you see,   Have bared my bosom to the thunder-stone.
translation: I have walked around the streets, exposing myself to the perilous night, with my jacket unbuttoned like this, baring my chest to the thunderbolt, as you see, Casca.

original: And when the cross blue lightning seemed to open   The breast of heaven, I did present myself   Even in the aim and very flash of it.
translation: When the forked blue lightning seemed to break open the sky, I put myself right where I thought it would hit.

original: But wherefore did you so much tempt the heavens? It is the part of men to fear and tremble When the most mighty gods by tokens send Such dreadful heralds to astonish us.
translation: But why would you tempt the heavens that way? Men are supposed to be afraid and tremble when the mightiest gods send such dreadful signs to warn and shock us.

original: You are dull, Casca, and those sparks of life   That should be in a Roman you do want,   Or else you use not.
translation: You are dull, Casca. And you lack the sparks of liveliness that a Roman should have—or else you just don’t show them.

original: You look pale, and gaze,   And put on fear, and cast yourself in wonder   To see the strange impatience of the heavens.
translation: You look pale, you stare, and you give yourself over to fear and wonder at the strange uproar in the heavens.

original: But if you would consider the true cause   Why all these fires, why all these gliding ghosts,   Why birds and beasts from quality and kind,
translation: But if you think about the true cause of all these fires, all these floating ghosts; or the reason why birds and animals are acting differently from how they normally behave;

original: Why old men fool and children calculate,   Why all these things change from their ordinance   Their natures and preformèd faculties   To monstrous quality—
translation: why old men, fools, and children make prophecies; why all these things have transformed from their natural qualities and become monstrous,

original: why, you shall find   That heaven hath infused them with these spirits   To make them instruments of fear and warning   Unto some monstrous state.
translation: then you’d see that heaven put such evil spirits in them so as to give a terrifying warning of an unnatural government that is coming .

original: Now could I, Casca, name to thee a man   Most like this dreadful night,   That thunders, lightens, opens graves, and roars   As doth the lion in the Capitol—
translation: Right now, Casca, I could name a man who’s just like this dreadful night. He thunders, shoots lightning, opens up graves, and roars just like the lion in the Capitol.

original: A man no mightier than thyself or me   In personal action, yet prodigious grown,   And fearful as these strange eruptions are.
translation: He is a man no mightier in his abilities than you or me. Yet he has grown as tremendous and frightening as tonight’s shocking sights.

original: 'Tis Caesar that you mean. Is it not, Cassius?
translation: It’s Caesar you’re talking about. Isn’t it, Cassius?

original: Let it be who it is. For Romans now   Have thews and limbs like to their ancestors,   But—woe the while!—our fathers' minds are dead,
translation: Don’t worry about who it is. Romans today may have the same strong bodies as our ancestors. But—curse this time!—we don’t have the will of our fathers.

original: And we are governed with our mothers' spirits.   Our yoke and sufferance show us womanish.
translation: It's like we have inherited only the spirits of our  mothers  instead. Our willingness to be enslaved shows that we are weak, like women.

original: Indeed, they say the senators tomorrow Mean to establish Caesar as a king, And he shall wear his crown by sea and land In every place save here in Italy.
translation: Indeed, they say that the senators plan to make Caesar a king tomorrow. And he’ll wear his crown at sea and on land everywhere except here in Italy.

original: I know where I will wear this dagger then.   Cassius from bondage will deliver Cassius.
translation: I know where I’ll wear this dagger if that happens. I’ll free myself from slavery by killing myself.

original: Therein, ye gods, you make the weak most strong.   Therein, ye gods, you tyrants do defeat.
translation: Oh, you gods, through suicide you make weak become strong. Through suicide, you gods, you can defeat tyrants.

original: Nor stony tower, nor walls of beaten brass,   Nor airless dungeon, nor strong links of iron   Can be retentive to the strength of spirit.
translation: No stony tower, no brass walls, no airless dungeon, no iron chains can imprison a strong spirit.

original: But life, being weary of these worldly bars,   Never lacks power to dismiss itself.
translation: Though held by such prisons, life never loses the power to destroy itself.

original: If I know this, know all the world besides,   That part of tyranny that I do bear   I can shake off at pleasure.
translation: I know—and may all the world know—that I can overthrow the tyranny I currently suffer I whenever I want by killing myself.

original: So can I. So every bondman in his own hand bears The power to cancel his captivity.
translation: So can I. Every imprisoned man holds in his own hand the ability to escape his captivity.

original: And why should Caesar be a tyrant then?   Poor man! I know he would not be a wolf   But that he sees the Romans are but sheep.   He were no lion were not Romans hinds.
translation: So then how can Caesar have become a tyrant? Poor man! I know he wouldn’t be a wolf if he didn't see that the Romans were such sheep. He would not be a lion if the Romans weren’t deer.

original: Those that with haste will make a mighty fire   Begin it with weak straws.
translation: Someone who wants to make a big fire quickly starts with little twigs.

original: What trash is Rome,   What rubbish and what offal, when it serves   For the base matter to illuminate   So vile a thing as Caesar!
translation: Rome is trash—just rubbish and garbage to be burned—when it allows itself to light up the ambitions of a thing as worthless as Caesar.

original: But, O grief,   Where hast thou led me? I perhaps speak this   Before a willing bondman. Then I know   My answer must be made. But I am armed,   And dangers are to me indifferent.
translation: But, oh, grief! What have you made me say? I might be saying this to someone who wants to be a slave, and then I'll have to face the consequences of my words. But I’m armed, and danger is unimportant to me.

original: You speak to Casca, and to such a man That is no fleering telltale. Hold, my hand. Be factious for redress of all these griefs, And I will set this foot of mine as far As who goes farthest.
translation: You’re speaking to Casca, not some smirking tattletale. Take my hand. If you’re forming a faction that will right all of these wrongs, I’ll go just as far as the one of you who will go the farthest.

original: There’s a bargain made.
translation: You’ve got a deal.

original: Now know you, Casca, I have moved already   Some certain of the noblest-minded Romans   To undergo with me an enterprise   Of honorable-dangerous consequence.
translation: Now you should know, Casca, that I’ve already persuaded some of the noblest Romans to join me in an effort that is at once honorable and dangerous.

original: And I do know by this they stay for me   In Pompey’s porch. For now, this fearful night,   There is no stir or walking in the streets,
translation: And I know that by now they’re waiting for me in the lobby of Pompey’s theater, because no one is out walking in the streets right now.

original: And the complexion of the element   In favor’s like the work we have in hand,   Most bloody, fiery, and most terrible.
translation: And the sky is as bloody, fiery, and terrible as the work we are planning to do.

original: Stand close awhile, for here comes one in haste.
translation: Hide for a bit—someone is rushing toward us.

original: 'Tis Cinna. I do know him by his gait.   He is a friend.
translation: It’s Cinna. I recognize him by the way he walks. He is a friend.

original: —Cinna, where haste you so?
translation: [To CINNA]  Cinna, where are you rushing to?

original: To find out you. Who’s that? Metellus Cimber?
translation: To find you. Who’s that? Metellus Cimber?

original: No, it is Casca, one incorporate To our attempts. Am I not stayed for, Cinna?
translation: No, it’s Casca, who is an ally in our efforts. Are the others waiting for me, Cinna?

original: I am glad on ’t. What a fearful night is this! There’s two or three of us have seen strange sights.
translation: I’m glad to hear it. What a frightening night this is! There are two or three of us who have seen strange sights.

original: Am I not stayed for? Tell me.
translation: Are the others waiting for me? Tell me.

original: Yes, you are. O Cassius, if you could But win the noble Brutus to our party—
translation: Yes, they are. Oh, Cassius, if you could just persuade noble Brutus to join us—

original: Be you content. Good Cinna, take this paper,   And look you lay it in the praetor’s chair   Where Brutus may but find it.
translation: Don’t worry. Good Cinna, take this paper and put it in the judge’s chair where Brutus sits so he will find it.

original: And throw this   In at his window. Set this up with wax   Upon old Brutus' statue.
translation: And throw this one in through his window. Attach this one with wax to the statue of Brutus’ ancestor, Old Brutus.

original: All this done,   Repair to Pompey’s porch, where you shall find us.   Is Decius Brutus and Trebonius there?
translation: When all this is done, return to the lobby of Pompey’s theater, where you will find us. Are Decius Brutus and Trebonius there?

original: All but Metellus Cimber, and he’s gone To seek you at your house. Well, I will hie, And so bestow these papers as you bade me.
translation: Everyone but Metellus Cimber, and he’s gone to look for you at your house. Well, I’ll get going, and do what you've asked me to do with these papers.

original: That done, repair to Pompey’s theatre.
translation: When you’re done, return to Pompey’s theater.

original: Come, Casca, you and I will yet ere day   See Brutus at his house.
translation: Come on, Casca. Before the daylight comes, you and I will go see Brutus at his house.

original: Three parts of him   Is ours already, and the man entire   Upon the next encounter yields him ours.
translation: He is already three-quarters on our side, and this next meeting will bring him to us completely.

original: Oh, he sits high in all the people’s hearts,
translation: Oh, he is loved and admired by the people.

original: And that which would appear offense in us,   His countenance, like richest alchemy,   Will change to virtue and to worthiness.
translation: Just like an alchemist who transforms lead into gold, Brutus’ natural nobility would make actions look virtuous and good that would look bad if we did them alone.

original: Him and his worth and our great need of him   You have right well conceited.
translation: You’re completely right about both Brutus’ nobility and our need for him.

original: Let us go,   For it is after midnight, and ere day   We will awake him and be sure of him.
translation: Let’s go, because it’s already after midnight, and before it’s day we must wake him and make sure he’s with us.

original: What, Lucius, ho!—   I cannot by the progress of the stars   Give guess how near to day   .
translation: Hello, Lucius, where are you? I can’t tell by the position of the stars how near it is to dawn.

original: —Lucius, I say!—   I would it were my fault to sleep so soundly.—   When, Lucius, when? Awake, I say! What, Lucius!
translation: Lucius, where are you? I wish I had the weakness of sleeping too deeply. Come, Lucius, come! Wake up, I say! Lucius!

original: Called you, my lord?
translation: You called, my lord?

original: Get me a taper in my study, Lucius. When it is lighted, come and call me here.
translation: Put a candle in my study, Lucius. When it’s lit, come here and get me.

original: I will, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: It must be by his death,
translation: Killing Caesar is the only way.

original: and for my part   I know no personal cause to spurn at him   But for the general. He would be crowned.
translation: As for me, I have no personal reason to harm him other than the common good of the people. He wants to be crowned king.

original: How that might change his nature, there’s the question.   It is the bright day that brings forth the adder   And that craves wary walking.
