translation: The question is, how might being king change him? Just as sunny days cause poisonous snakes to come outside, bad things can come from what looks good—and so we must step carefully.

original: Crown him that,   And then I grant we put a sting in him   That at his will he may do danger with.
translation: If we crown him king, then—I admit—we’d be giving him a power that he could use to do evil things, if he wanted.

original: Th' abuse of greatness is when it disjoins   Remorse from power. And, to speak truth of Caesar,   I have not known when his affections swayed   More than his reason.
translation: The abuse of power comes when power gets separated from compassion. And, to be honest about Caesar, I’ve never seen his emotions get the better of his reason.

original: But ’tis a common proof   That lowliness is young ambition’s ladder,   Whereto the climber upward turns his face.
translation: But it's a basic truth that an ambitious young man uses humility as a tool to move up the ladder.

original: But when he once attains the upmost round,   He then unto the ladder turns his back,   Looks in the clouds, scorning the base degrees   By which he did ascend. So Caesar may.
translation: And then, when he gets to the top rung, he turns his back on those beneath him and shoots for the skies, while scorning what he did to get to the top. Caesar might do the same.

original: Then, lest he may, prevent. And since the quarrel   Will bear no color for the thing he is,   Fashion it thus: that what he is, augmented,   Would run to these and these extremities.
translation: Therefore, because he might, we must stop him. And since our argument has nothing to do with who he is right now, I must think of it this way:  if he got more power, his character as it is now would be transformed into the extreme one I've described.

original: And therefore think him as a serpent’s egg—   Which, hatched, would as his kind grow mischievous—   And kill him in the shell.
translation: Therefore, we should think of him as a serpent’s egg—which, once it's hatched, grows dangerous, just as all serpents do. So we must kill him while he’s still in the shell.

original: The taper burneth in your closet, sir.
translation: The candle is lit in your study, sir.

original: Searching the window for a flint, I found   This paper, thus sealed up, and I am sure   It did not lie there when I went to bed.   [gives him a letter]
translation: While I was searching on the window sill for a flint, I found this paper, sealed up like this. And I’m sure it wasn’t lying there when I went to bed.  [He gives BRUTUS the letter]

original: Get you to bed again. It is not day. Is not tomorrow, boy, the ides of March?
translation: Go back to bed again. It’s not daytime yet. Boy ,isn’t tomorrow March 15th?

original: I know not, sir.
translation: I don’t know, sir.

original: Look in the calendar and bring me word.
translation: Check the calendar and let me know.

original: I will, sir.
translation: I will, sir.

original: The exhalations whizzing in the air   Give so much light that I may read by them.
translation: The  meteors  whizzing in the sky give so much light that I can read by them.

original: [opens the letter and reads]   “Brutus, thou sleep’st. Awake, and see thyself.   Shall Rome, etc. Speak, strike, redress!”   “Brutus, thou sleep’st. Awake.”
translation: [He opens the letter and reads] “Brutus, you’re sleeping. Wake up and see yourself for who you are. Will Rome … et cetera. Speak, strike, right the wrongs!”   “Brutus, you’re sleeping. Wake up.”

original: Such instigations have been often dropped   Where I have took them up.
translation: I’ve come upon many other encouragements like these, left in places where I would find them.

original: —“Shall Rome, etc.”
translation: “Is Rome going to … et cetera.”

original: Thus must I piece it out:   “Shall Rome stand under one man’s awe?” What, Rome?   My ancestors did from the streets of Rome   The Tarquin drive when he was called a king.
translation: And so I must complete the thought. Will Rome stand in awe of one single man? Really, Rome? My ancestors drove  Tarquin  from the streets of Rome when he was pronounced a king.

original: —“Speak, strike, redress!”
translation: “Speak, strike,  right the wrongs!”

original: Am I entreated   To speak and strike? O Rome, I make thee promise,   If the redress will follow, thou receivest   Thy full petition at the hand of Brutus!
translation: Is this letter asking me to speak and strike? Oh, Rome, I promise you, if a strike would result in the restoration of the Republic, then I would give you everything you're asking for from my very own hands!

original: Sir, March is wasted fifteen days.
translation: Sir, fifteen days of March have passed.

original: 'Tis good. Go to the gate. Somebody knocks.
translation: That’s good. Go to the gate. Somebody’s knocking.

original: Since Cassius first did whet me against Caesar,   I have not slept.
translation: I haven’t slept since Cassius began to turn me against Caesar.

original: Between the acting of a dreadful thing   And the first motion, all the interim is   Like a phantasma or a hideous dream.
translation: The time spent waiting between the moment when you decide to do something great and terrible, and the instant when you actually do it, feels unreal or like an awful dream.

original: The genius and the mortal instruments   Are then in council, and the state of man,   Like to a little kingdom, suffers then   The nature of an insurrection.
translation: The man who waits becomes like a little kingdom, in which the unconscious and the body join together in a conspiracy to overthrow the conscious mind.

original: Sir, ’tis your brother Cassius at the door, Who doth desire to see you.
translation: Sir, it’s your brother-in-law Cassius at the door. He wants to see you.

original: Is he alone?
translation: Is he alone?

original: No, sir, there are more with him.
translation: No, sir. There are others with him.

original: Do you know them?
translation: Do you know them?

original: No, sir. Their hats are plucked about their ears,   And half their faces buried in their cloaks,
translation: No, sir. Their hats are pulled down over their ears and their faces are half-hidden behind their cloaks,

original: That by no means I may discover them   By any mark of favor.
translation: so I can’t make out any features to identify them.

original: Let 'em enter.
translation: Let them come in.

original: They are the faction.
translation: It’s the faction that wants to kill Caesar.

original: O conspiracy,   Shamest thou to show thy dangerous brow by night   When evils are most free?
translation: Oh, conspiracy, are you ashamed to show your face even at night, when evil things are most at liberty?

original: O, then by day   Where wilt thou find a cavern dark enough   To mask thy monstrous visage? Seek none, conspiracy.   Hide it in smiles and affability.
translation: If so, when it’s day, where are you going to find a cave dark enough to hide your monstrous face? No, don’t bother to find a cave, conspiracy. Instead, hide your true face behind smiles and friendliness.

original: For if thou path, thy native semblance on,   Not Erebus itself were dim enough   To hide thee from prevention.
translation: If you went ahead and exposed your true face, hell itself wouldn’t be dark enough to keep you from being found and stopped.

original: I think we are too bold upon your rest. Good morrow, Brutus. Do we trouble you?
translation: I think we may be interrupting your sleep. Good morning, Brutus. Are we bothering you?

original: I have been up this hour, awake all night. Know I these men that come along with you?
translation: I was up. I’ve been awake all night. Do I know these men who’ve come with you?

original: Yes, every man of them, and no man here   But honors you,
translation: Yes, every one of them. And every one of them admires you

original: and every one doth wish   You had but that opinion of yourself   Which every noble Roman bears of you.   This is Trebonius.
translation: , and wishes you had as high an opinion of yourself as every noble Roman has of you. This is Trebonius.

original: He is welcome hither.
translation: He’s welcome here.

original: This, Decius Brutus.
translation: This is Decius Brutus.

original: He is welcome too.
translation: He’s welcome too.

original: This, Casca. This, Cinna. And this, Metellus Cimber.
translation: This is Casca. This is Cinna. And this is Metellus Cimber.

original: They are all welcome. What watchful cares do interpose themselves Betwixt your eyes and night?
translation: They are all welcome. What nagging worries have stopped you from sleeping tonight?

original: Shall I entreat a word?
translation: May I have a private word with you?

original: Here lies the east. Doth not the day break here?
translation: Here’s the east. Is that the break of day I see?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: O, pardon, sir, it doth, and yon gray lines That fret the clouds are messengers of day.
translation: Oh, pardon me, sir, it is. Those gray lines that adorn the clouds are the messengers of coming dawn.

original: You shall confess that you are both deceived.
translation: You’ll both soon admit that you are mistaken.

original: [points his sword]   Here, as I point my sword, the sun arises,   Which is a great way growing on the south,   Weighing the youthful season of the year.
translation: [He points his sword]  Here, where I point my sword, the sun rises—way over toward the south, since it’s still so early in the year.

original: Some two months hence up higher toward the north   He first presents his fire, and the high east   Stands, as the Capitol, directly here.
translation: Two months from now, the light of dawn will break a good deal further to the north. Due east is where the Capitol stands, right there.

original: Give me your hands all over, one by one.
translation: Give me your hands, all of you, one by one. [He shakes their hands]

original: And let us swear our resolution.
translation: Now we should swear to our resolve.

original: No, not an oath. If not the face of men,   The sufferance of our souls, the time’s abuse—   If these be motives weak, break off betimes,   And every man hence to his idle bed.
translation: No, no swearing. If the unhappy faces of the men around us, the suffering of our own souls, and the corruption of our current time aren’t motivation enough, then we should break it off now and each one of us of us go back and rest in bed.

original: So let high-sighted tyranny range on   Till each man drop by lottery.
translation: Then we’ll just let the ambitious tyrant rule and kill each one of us when the whim takes him.

original: But if these—   As I am sure they do—bear fire enough   To kindle cowards and to steel with valor   The melting spirits of women, then, countrymen,
translation: But if these reasons are powerful enough—and I’m sure they are—to spark cowards to act and to strengthen with courage the failing spirits of our women, then, countrymen,

original: W   hat need we any spur but our own cause   To prick us to redress? What other bond   Than secret Romans that have spoke the word   And will not palter?
translation: what else do we need other than our cause to spur us to make things right? What bond do we need other than being Romans who have given their word to act and not back down?

original: And what other oath   Than honesty to honesty engaged,   That this shall be, or we will fall for it?
translation: And what oath do we need other than that we have all said to each other honestly that either we will make this happen or die trying?

original: Swear priests and cowards and men cautelous,   Old feeble carrions and such suffering souls   That welcome wrongs.
translation: Swearing is for priests and cowards and cautious men; for people who are old and feeble; and for those weak people who like to be mistreated.

original: Unto bad causes swear   Such creatures as men doubt.
translation: Oaths are only necessary for men you wouldn’t trust, who are engaged in causes that are bad.

original: But do not stain   The even virtue of our enterprise,   Nor th' insuppressive mettle of our spirits,   To think that or our cause or our performance   Did need an oath, when every drop of blood
translation: Don’t stain our justified efforts or the indomitable core of our spirits by thinking that either our cause or performance requires an oath, when every drop of blood in

original: That every Roman bears—and nobly bears—   Is guilty of a several bastardy   If he do break the smallest particle   Of any promise that hath passed from him.
translation: every noble Roman would be nothing more than bastard’s blood if he broke the smallest part of any promise he had made.

original: But what of Cicero? Shall we sound him? I think he will stand very strong with us.
translation: But what about Cicero? Should we get a sense of his thoughts? I think he will strongly support us.

original: Let us not leave him out.
translation: Let’s not leave him out.

original: No, by no means.
translation: No, by no means.

original: O, let us have him, for his silver hairs   Will purchase us a good opinion   And buy men’s voices to commend our deeds.
translation: Yes, we should bring him in. His age and renown will ensure that people see us in a good light and speak in praise of our actions.

original: It shall be said his judgment ruled our hands.   Our youths and wildness shall no whit appear,   But all be buried in his gravity.
translation: It will be said that that Cicero’s good judgment directed our plans. Our relative youth and recklessness will be obscured by his sober seriousness.

original: O, name him not. Let us not break with him,
translation: No, don’t bring him up. We shouldn’t speak with him,

original: For he will never follow anything   That other men begin.
translation: because he’ll never follow anything that other men have started.

original: Then leave him out.
translation: Then leave him out.

original: Indeed he is not fit.
translation: Indeed, he’s not a good fit for this.

original: Shall no man else be touched but only Caesar?
translation: Should Caesar be the only one we target?

original: Decius, well urged. I think it is not meet   Mark Antony, so well beloved of Caesar,   Should outlive Caesar.
translation: Good point, Decius. I think it would be a bad idea to allow Mark Antony to outlive Caesar, since Caesar loves Antony so dearly.

original: We shall find of him   A shrewd contriver.
translation: We’ll find that he is a cunning schemer.

original: And, you know, his means,   If he improve them, may well stretch so far   As to annoy us all; which to prevent,   Let Antony and Caesar fall together.
translation: And, as you know, if he took advantage of his wealth and reputation, he could hurt us all. To prevent this, let Antony die along with Caesar.

original: Our course will seem too bloody, Caius Cassius,   To cut the head off and then hack the limbs,   Like wrath in death and envy afterwards,   For Antony is but a limb of Caesar.
translation: Caius Cassius, it will seem too bloody if we cut off Caesar’s head and then also hack off his arms and legs—because Mark Antony is just one of Caesar’s arms.

original: Let us be sacrificers but not butchers, Caius.   We all stand up against the spirit of Caesar,   And in the spirit of men there is no blood.
translation: We want to be sacrificers of Caesar out of necessity, not butchers who are just out for blood. We are standing up against Caesar’s spirit, what he stands for, and there’s no blood in that.

original: Oh, that we then could come by Caesar’s spirit   And not dismember Caesar! But, alas,   Caesar must bleed for it. And, gentle friends,   Let’s kill him boldly but not wrathfully.
translation: Oh, if only we could overcome Caesar’s spirit without having to cut up Caesar himself! But, sadly, our only option is to kill Caesar. Noble friends, let’s kill him boldly—but not with anger.

original: Let’s carve him as a dish fit for the gods,   Not hew him as a carcass fit for hounds.   And let our hearts, as subtle masters do,   Stir up their servants to an act of rage
translation: Let’s carve him up like a dish fit for the gods, not hack him up like a carcass fit for dogs. Like subtle masters do, let’s make our bodies—as our servants—act in obedience to the anger in our hearts.

original: And after seem to chide 'em. This shall make   Our purpose necessary and not envious,   Which so appearing to the common eyes,   We shall be called purgers, not murderers.
translation: And then, afterward, we will seem to disapprove of our bodies’ bloody deeds. This will make our actions seem necessary and not driven by envy, ensuring that commoners will see us as surgeons instead of murderers.

original: And for Mark Antony, think not of him,   For he can do no more than Caesar’s arm   When Caesar’s head is off.
translation: As for Mark Antony—don’t think about him. He'll be able to do nothing more as Caesar's right-hand man once Caesar’s head is cut off.

original: Yet I fear him. For in the engrafted love he bears to Caesar—
translation: But I still fear Antony, because of the depth of his love for Caesar—

original: Alas, good Cassius, do not think of him.   If he love Caesar, all that he can do   Is to himself:
translation: Alas, good Cassius, don’t think about him. If Antony loves Caesar, then he can only hurt himself

original: take thought and die for Caesar.   And that were much he should, for he is given   To sports, to wildness and much company.
translation: —by falling into despair and dying for Caesar. And he’s not likely to do even that, because he enjoys sports, excitement, and parties too much.

original: There is no fear in him. Let him not die, For he will live and laugh at this hereafter.
translation: There’s nothing to fear from him. Let him not die. He’ll live and laugh at this later on.

original: Peace! Count the clock.
translation: Quiet! Count the chimes of the clock.

original: The clock hath stricken three.
translation: The clock struck three.

original: 'Tis time to part.
translation: It’s time for us to go.

original: But it is doubtful yet   Whether Caesar will come forth today or no.   For he is superstitious grown of late,
translation: But it's still not certain that Caesar will leave his house today. He’s become superstitious lately

original: Quite from the main opinion he held once   Of fantasy, of dreams and ceremonies.
translation: —a total shift from the opinions he used to hold about fortune-tellers, dream interpreters, and rites meant to tell the future.

original: It may be, these apparent prodigies,   The unaccustomed terror of this night,   And the persuasion of his augurers   May hold him from the Capitol today.
translation: It might be that these strange omens, the unusual terror of this night, and the advice of his fortune-tellers will stop him from coming to the Capitol today.

original: Never fear that. If he be so resolved,   I can o'ersway him.
translation: Don’t worry about that. If that's what he's planning, I can persuade him otherwise.

original: For he loves to hear   That unicorns may be betrayed with trees,   And bears with glasses, elephants with holes,   Lions with toils, and men with flatterers.
translation: He loves to hear me tell him how unicorns can be captured with trickery around trees, bears with glasses, elephants in holes, and lions with nets—just as men can be tricked by flatterers.

original: But when I tell him he hates flatterers,   He says he does, being then most flatterèd.
translation: When I tell him he hates flatterers, he agrees—even though that is the instant when I’m flattering him the most.

original: Let me work.   For I can give his humor the true bent,   And I will bring him to the Capitol.
translation: Let me work on him. I can shape his mood in the right direction, and I’ll bring him to the Capitol.

original: Nay, we will all of us be there to fetch him.
translation: No, we’ll all go there to bring him.

original: By the eighth hour. Is that the uttermost?
translation: By eight o'clock. Is that the latest we can do it?

original: Be that the uttermost, and fail not then.
translation: Let’s make that the latest, but be sure not to arrive any later.

original: Caius Ligarius doth bear Caesar hard   ,
translation: Caius Ligarius doesn’t like Caesar,

original: Who rated him for speaking well of Pompey.   I wonder none of you have thought of him.
translation: who berated him for saying nice things about Pompey. I’m surprised that none of you thought about including him.

original: Now, good Metellus, go along by him. He loves me well, and I have given him reasons. Send him but hither and I’ll fashion him.
translation: Good Metellus, go to see him. He likes me very much, as I’ve always been good to him. Send him here and I’ll persuade him.

original: The morning comes upon ’s. We’ll leave you, Brutus. —And, friends, disperse yourselves. But all remember What you have said, and show yourselves true Romans.
translation: The morning comes. We’ll leave you, Brutus. And friends, go your separate ways. But all of you: remember what you’ve said and prove yourselves to be true Romans.

original: Good gentlemen, look fresh and merrily.   Let not our looks put on our purposes,   But bear it as our Roman actors do,   With untired spirits and formal constancy.
translation: Good gentlemen, look happy and well-rested. Let's not allow our faces betray our plans. Instead, let's carry ourselves as our Roman actors do—with bright spirits and calm faces.

original: And so good morrow to you every one.
translation: And so, good morning to every one of you.

original: Boy! Lucius!—Fast asleep? It is no matter.   Enjoy the honey-heavy dew of slumber.
translation: Boy! Lucius! Fast asleep? No matter. Enjoy the sweet nectar of sleep.

original: Thou hast no figures nor no fantasies,   Which busy care draws in the brains of men.   Therefore thou sleep’st so sound.
translation: You don’t suffer from the phantoms or fantasies which the cares of the world bring to all men. That’s why you sleep so soundly.

original: Brutus, my lord.
translation: Brutus, my lord.

original: Portia, what mean you? Wherefore rise you now? It is not for your health thus to commit Your weak condition to the raw, cold morning.
translation: Portia, why are you here? Why have you woken up so early? It's not good for your health to expose your weak body to the raw, cold morning.

original: Nor for yours neither. Y' have ungently, Brutus,   Stole from my bed. And yesternight, at supper,   You suddenly arose and walked about,   Musing and sighing, with your arms across,
translation: It's not good for yours, either. You rudely snuck out of our bed, Brutus. And last night, at dinner, you suddenly got up and paced around with your arms crossed, worrying and sighing.

original: And when I asked you what the matter was,   You stared upon me with ungentle looks.   I urged you further, then you scratched your head   And too impatiently stamped with your foot.
translation: And when I asked you what was wrong, you stared at me with a rude look. I repeated my question, and you scratched your head and stamped your foot impatiently.

original: Yet I insisted; yet you answered not,   But with an angry wafture of your hand   Gave sign for me to leave you.
translation: I insisted, but you did not answer. Instead, with an angry wave of your hand, you signaled that I should leave you alone.

original: So I did,   Fearing to strengthen that impatience   Which seemed too much enkindled, and withal   Hoping it was but an effect of humor,   Which sometime hath his hour with every man.
translation: So I did, because I didn't want to further strengthen your anger, which was already inflamed. Yet I hoped that it was just the result of a bad mood, which can from time to time affect anyone.

original: It will not let you eat nor talk nor sleep,   And could it work so much upon your shape   As it hath much prevailed on your condition,
translation: Your bad mood won’t let you eat or talk or sleep. If it could affect your appearance as much as it has affected the way you are acting,

original: I should not know you, Brutus. Dear my lord,   Make me acquainted with your cause of grief.
translation: I wouldn’t even recognize you, Brutus. My dear lord, tell me about what is making you upset.

original: I am not well in health, and that is all.
translation: I’m not feeling well, that’s all.

original: Brutus is wise, and were he not in health, He would embrace the means to come by it.
translation: No. Since you’re wise, if you were feeling sick, you’d do the right thing to make yourself better.

original: Why, so I do. Good Portia, go to bed.
translation: And that’s what I’m doing. Good Portia, go to bed.

original: Is Brutus sick? And is it physical   To walk unbracèd and suck up the humors   Of the dank morning?
translation: Are you sick? And is it good for your health to walk outside with an open jacket and breathe in the dampness of the morning?

original: What, is Brutus sick,   And will he steal out of his wholesome bed,   To dare the vile contagion of the night   And tempt the rheumy and unpurgèd air   To add unto his sickness?
translation: Really, Brutus? You’re not feeling well, but you sneak out of your warm bed, letting the humid and dirty air make you even sicker?

original: No, my Brutus.   You have some sick offense within your mind,   Which by the right and virtue of my place   I ought to know of.
translation: No, my Brutus. You have some sickness within your mind. According to my rights as your wife, I deserve to know about it.

original: [kneels]   And upon my knees   I charm you, by my once-commended beauty,   By all your vows of love and that great vow   Which did incorporate and make us one
translation: [He kneels]  On my knees, I beg—by my once-praised beauty, by all your vows of love, and by that great marriage vow which brought the two of us together and made us into one person

original: That you unfold to me, your self, your half,   Why you are heavy, and what men tonight   Have had to resort to you.
translation: —that you reveal it to me. As I am one-half of yourself, tell me why you’re unhappy and what men felt the need to visit you tonight.

original: For here have been   Some six or seven who did hide their faces   Even from darkness.
translation: For there were six or seven men who came, and who hid their faces even in the darkness.

original: Kneel not, gentle Portia.
translation: Don’t kneel, noble Portia.

original: [rising]   I should not need if you were gentle, Brutus.   Within the bond of marriage, tell me, Brutus,   Is it excepted I should know no secrets   That appertain to you?
translation: [Standing up]  I wouldn’t need to kneel if you were acting nobly, Brutus. Tell me, Brutus, don’t the bonds of our marriage mean that I am supposed to know all the secrets that concern you?

original: Am I yourself   But, as it were, in sort or limitation,   To keep with you at meals, comfort your bed,   And talk to you sometimes?
translation: Am I part of you only in a limited sense—getting to eat meals with you, sleep with you, and talk to you sometimes?

original: Dwell I but in the suburbs   Of your good pleasure? If it be no more,   Portia is Brutus' harlot, not his wife.
translation: Do I exist only on the borders of your happiness? If it’s only that, then I’m your whore, not your wife.

original: You are my true and honorable wife, As dear to me as are the ruddy drops That visit my sad heart.
translation: You’re my true and honorable wife, as precious to me as the blood that runs through my sad heart.

original: If this were true, then should I know this secret.   I grant I am a woman, but withal   A woman that Lord Brutus took to wife.
translation: If that were true, then I’d know your secret. I admit that I’m just a woman. But, even so, I’m the woman that Lord Brutus took for his wife.

original: I grant I am a woman, but withal   A woman well-reputed, Cato’s daughter.   Think you I am no stronger than my sex,   Being so fathered and so husbanded?
translation: I admit that I’m just a woman. But, even so, I'm a woman with a noble reputation, and  Cato’s  daughter. Do you think I’m no stronger than the rest of my sex, having such a father and such a husband?

original: Tell me your counsels. I will not disclose 'em.   I have made strong proof of my constancy,   Giving myself a voluntary wound   Here in the thigh.
translation: Tell me your secrets. I won’t tell them to anyone else. I’ve proved my trustworthiness by giving myself a voluntary wound here in my thigh.

original: Can I bear that with patience,   And not my husband’s secrets?
translation: If I can bear that pain, can't I bear my husband’s secrets?

original: O ye gods, Render me worthy of this noble wife!
translation: Oh, gods, make me worthy of this noble wife!

original: Hark, hark! One knocks. Portia, go in awhile.   And by and by thy bosom shall partake   The secrets of my heart.
translation: Listen, listen! Someone knocks. Portia, go inside for a while, and soon you’ll know the secrets of my heart.

original: All my engagements I will construe to thee,   All the charactery of my sad brows.   Leave me with haste.
translation: I’ll explain all my plans to you, and all the reasons behind the sad expression on my face. Leave me quickly.

original: Lucius, who’s that knocking?
translation: Lucius, who’s that knocking?

original: He is a sick man that would speak with you.
translation: Here’s a sick man who’d like to speak with you.

original: Caius Ligarius, that Metellus spake of.
translation: Caius Ligarius, whom Metellus spoke of.

original: —   Boy, stand aside.
translation: [To LUCIUS]  Boy, stand aside.

original: —Caius Ligarius, how?
translation: [TO LIGARIUS]  Caius Ligarius, what is going on?

original: Vouchsafe good morrow from a feeble tongue.
translation: Please accept this greeting of “good morning” from a sick man.

original: O, what a time have you chose out, brave Caius,   To wear a kerchief!
translation: Oh, what a time you’ve chosen to get ill, brave Caius!

original: Would you were not sick!
translation: I wish you were not sick!

original: I am not sick if Brutus have in hand
translation: Brutus, I’m not sick if you have something for me to do

original: Any exploit worthy the name of honor.
translation: —something that is worthy of being called honorable.

original: Such an exploit have I in hand, Ligarius, Had you a healthful ear to hear of it.
translation: Ligarius, I do have just such a thing for you to do, if you are feeling well enough to hear about it.

original: [removes his kerchief]   By all the gods that Romans bow before,   I here discard my sickness! Soul of Rome,   Brave son derived from honorable loins,
translation: [He takes off his handkerchief]  By all the gods that Romans worship, I now throw away my sickness! Soul of Rome! Brave son of honorable ancestors!

original: Thou, like an exorcist, hast conjured up   My mortifièd spirit. Now bid me run,   And I will strive with things impossible,   Yea, get the better of them. What’s to do?
translation: Like an exorcist, you have raised up my dead spirit. Now just tell me what to do, and I will take on the impossible task, and succeed. What is there to do?

original: A piece of work that will make sick men whole.
translation: A bit of work that will make sick men healthy.

original: But are not some whole that we must make sick?
translation: But aren’t there some healthy men whom we’ll have to make sick?

original: That must we also. What it is, my Caius, I shall unfold to thee as we are going To whom it must be done.
translation: We must also do that. My dear Caius, I’ll explain what we have to do as we walk toward the one to whom it must be done.

original: Set on your foot,   And with a heart new-fired I follow you,
translation: Start walking, and I’ll follow you, with my heart newly full of fire.

original: To do I know not what. But it sufficeth   That Brutus leads me on.
translation: I don’t know what we will be doing, but it is enough that Brutus leads me.

original: Follow me, then.
translation: Follow me, then.

original: Nor heaven nor earth have been at peace tonight.   Thrice hath Calphurnia in her sleep cried out,   “Help, ho! They murder Caesar!”
translation: Neither the sky nor the earth have been at peace tonight. Three times Calphurnia cried out in her sleep, “Help, help! They’re murdering Caesar!”

original: —Who’s within?
translation: [He hears a noise]  Who’s there?

original: My lord.
translation: My lord?

original: Go bid the priests do present sacrifice And bring me their opinions of success.
translation: Go tell the priests to sacrifice an animal to the gods, and bring me their interpretation of the results.

original: I will, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: What mean you, Caesar? Think you to walk forth? You shall not stir out of your house today.
translation: What is this, Caesar? Do you think you’re going to go outside? You’re not leaving this house today.

original: Caesar shall forth. The things that threatened me   Ne'er looked but on my back.
translation: I will go out. The things that threaten me have never seen anything but my back.

original: When they shall see   The face of Caesar, they are vanishèd.
translation: When they see Caesar's face, they will disappear.

original: Caesar, I never stood on ceremonies,   Yet now they fright me. There is one within,   Besides the things that we have heard and seen,
translation: Caesar, I never paid attention to omens, but now they frighten me. One of our servants told me that—in addition to the things that we have heard and seen

original: Recounts most horrid sights seen by the watch.   A lioness hath whelpèd in the streets,   And graves have yawned and yielded up their dead.
translation: —the night-watchmen have also seen horrid things. A lioness gave birth in the streets, and graves opened wide and let out their dead.

original: Fierce fiery warriors fought upon the clouds   In ranks and squadrons and right form of war,   Which drizzled blood upon the Capitol.   The noise of battle hurtled in the air.
translation: Fierce, fiery warriors fought in the clouds in ranks and squadrons—the usual military formations—until blood drizzled down from the sky onto the Capitol. The noise of battle clashed in the air,

original: Horses did neigh, and dying men did groan,   And ghosts did shriek and squeal about the streets.   O Caesar! These things are beyond all use,   And I do fear them.
translation: and horses neighed, and dying men groaned, and ghosts shrieked and squealed in the streets. Oh, Caesar! These things are beyond all normal experience, and I fear them.

original: What can be avoided   Whose end is purposed by the mighty gods?
translation: Who can avoid what the gods want to happen?

original: Yet Caesar shall go forth, for these predictions   Are to the world in general as to Caesar.
translation: Still, Caesar will go out. These omens have to do with the world in general as much as they have to do with Caesar.

original: When beggars die there are no comets seen. The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of  princes.
translation: When beggars die, no comets appear in the sky. The heavens only light up to announce the deaths of princes.

original: Cowards die many times before their deaths.   The valiant never taste of death but once.   Of all the wonders that I yet have heard,   It seems to me most strange that men should fear,
translation: Cowards die many times before their deaths. The brave only die once. Of all the incredible things I’ve ever heard about, man's fear of death is the strangest.

original: Seeing that death, a necessary end,   Will come when it will come.
translation: Death—which can’t be avoided—will come when it wishes to come.

original: What say the augurers?
translation: What do the priests say?

original: They would not have you to stir forth today. Plucking the entrails of an offering forth, They could not find a heart within the beast.
translation: They don’t want you to go out today. When they pulled out the insides of the holy sacrifice, they found no heart within the animal.

original: The gods do this in shame of cowardice.   Caesar should be a beast without a heart   If he should stay at home today for fear.   No, Caesar shall not.
translation: The gods do this to teach me to be ashamed of my cowardice. They’re saying I would be an animal without a heart if I stayed home today out of fear. So, Caesar won’t stay home, then.

original: Danger knows full well   That Caesar is more dangerous than he.   We are two lions littered in one day,   And I the elder and more terrible.   And Caesar shall go forth.
translation: Danger knows very well that Caesar is more dangerous than he is. Danger and I are two lions born from the same mother on the same day, and I’m the older and fiercer one. Caesar will go out.

original: Alas, my lord,   Your wisdom is consumed in confidence.   Do not go forth today. Call it my fear   That keeps you in the house, and not your own.
translation: Alas, my lord, your arrogance is overwhelming your wisdom. Don’t go out today. Say that it’s my fear that keeps you inside, and not your own.

original: We’ll send Mark Antony to the senate house,   And he shall say you are not well today.   [kneels]   Let me, upon my knee, prevail in this.
translation: We’ll send Mark Antony to the Senate, and he’ll say that you’re not feeling well today.  [She kneels]  Here on my knees, let me convince you.

original: Mark Antony shall say I am not well, And for thy humor I will stay at home.
translation: Mark Antony will say I’m not well, and I will stay at home for your sake.

original: Here’s Decius Brutus. He shall tell them so.
translation: Here’s Decius Brutus. He’ll tell them that I'll stay home.

original: Caesar, all hail! Good morrow, worthy Caesar. I come to fetch you to the senate house.
translation: Hail, Caesar! Good morning, noble Caesar. I’ve come to escort you to the Senate.

original: And you are come in very happy time   To bear my greeting to the senators   And tell them that I will not come today.
translation: And you’ve come at just the right time, so you can carry my greetings to the senators and tell them I won’t come today.

original: “Cannot” is false, and that I dare not, falser.   I will not come today. Tell them so, Decius.
translation: It would be false to say that I can't—and even more false to say I don't dare to come. I simply won’t come today. Tell them that, Decius.

original: Say he is sick.
translation: Say he’s sick.

original: Shall Caesar send a lie? Have I in conquest stretched mine arm so far To be afraid to tell graybeards the truth? Decius, go  tell them Caesar will not come.
translation: Would Caesar send a lie? Have I been so victorious in battle, but am now afraid to tell the truth to some old men? Decius, go tell them that Caesar won’t come.

original: Most mighty Caesar, let me know some cause, Lest I be laughed at when I tell them so.
translation: Most mighty Caesar, tell me some reason, so I won’t be laughed at when I tell them.

original: The cause is in my will. I will not come.   That is enough to satisfy the senate.   But for your private satisfaction,   Because I love you, I will let you know.
translation: The reason is that's what I want to do. I’m not coming. That’s enough to satisfy the senators. But because I like you, I'll tell you for your personal satisfaction.

original: Calphurnia here, my wife, stays me at home.   She dreamt tonight she saw my statue,   Which, like a fountain with an hundred spouts,   Did run pure blood.
translation: My wife Calphurnia has asked me to stay home. She dreamed last night that she saw a statue of me, that was streaming pure blood, like a fountain with a hundred spouts.

original: And many lusty Romans   Came smiling and did bathe their hands in it.
translation: And many happy Romans came smiling and washed their hands in it.

original: And these does she apply for warnings and portents   And evils imminent, and on her knee   Hath begged that I will stay at home today.
translation: Calphurnia thinks the dreams are warnings and omens of approaching evil, and she begged me on her knees to stay home today.

original: This dream is all amiss interpreted.   It was a vision fair and fortunate.   Your statue spouting blood in many pipes,   In which so many smiling Romans bathed,
translation: This dream has been interpreted all wrong. It was a wonderful, lucky vision. Your statue spouting fountains of blood, in which so many smiling Romans bathed,

original: Signifies that from you great Rome shall suck   Reviving blood, and that great men shall press   For tinctures, stains, relics, and cognizance.   This by Calphurnia’s dream is signified.
translation: means that you will give great Rome the blood that will keep it alive. And it means that great men will beg  you to give your blood to them as signs of your approval. This is what Calphurnia’s dream means.

original: And this way have you well expounded it.
translation: This is a very good interpretation.

original: I have, when you have heard what I can say.   And know it now: the senate have concluded   To give this day a crown to mighty Caesar.
translation: I will have interpreted it well, after you have heard the rest of what I have to say. The Senate has decided to give mighty Caesar a crown today.

original: If you shall send them word you will not come,   Their minds may change. Besides, it were a mock   Apt to be rendered for someone to say,
translation: If you send them word that you won’t come, they may change their minds. Also, someone’s likely to joke

original: “Break up the senate till another time   When Caesar’s wife shall meet with better dreams.”   If Caesar hide himself, shall they not whisper,   “Lo, Caesar is afraid?”
translation: , “Postpone the Senate until some other time, when Caesar’s wife has had better dreams.” If you hide yourself, won’t they whisper, “See, Caesar is afraid?”

original: Pardon me, Caesar. For my dear, dear love   To your proceeding bids me tell you this,   And reason to my love is liable.
translation: Excuse me, Caesar. My love and high hopes for your advancement makes me tell you this. My manners are less powerful than my love for you.

original: How foolish do your fears seem now, Calphurnia! I am ashamèd I did yield to them. Give me my robe, for I will go.
translation: How foolish your fears seem now, Calphurnia! I’m ashamed that I gave in to them. Give me my robe. I’m going.

original: And look, where Publius is come to fetch me.
translation: And look, here’s Publius, coming to get me.

original: Good morrow, Caesar.
translation: Good morning, Caesar.

original: Welcome, Publius.
translation: [To PUBLIUS]  Welcome, Publius.

original: —What, Brutus, are you stirred so early too?
translation: [To BRUTUS]  What, Brutus? Are you awake this early too?

original: —Good morrow, Casca.
translation: [To CASCA]  Good morning, Casca.

original: —Caius Ligarius,   Caesar was ne'er so much your enemy   As that same ague which hath made you lean.   —What is ’t o'clock?
translation: [To LIGARIUS]  Caius Ligarius, I was never your enemy as much as the disease that has made you so thin. What time is it?

original: Caesar, ’tis strucken eight.
translation: Caesar, the clock has struck eight.

original: I thank you for your pains and courtesy.
translation: I thank you for your trouble and courtesy.

original: See, Antony, that revels long a-nights,   Is notwithstanding up.
translation: Even Antony—who parties all night long—is awake.

original: —Good morrow, Antony.
translation: [To ANTONY]  Good morning, Antony.

original: So to most noble Caesar.
translation: The same to you, most noble Caesar.

original: Bid them prepare within.   I am to blame to be thus waited for.
translation: Tell them to set up the other room for guests. It's my fault you all must wait for me.

original: —Now, Cinna.
translation: [To CINNA]  Now, Cinna.

original: —Now, Metellus.
translation: [To METELLUS]  Now, Metellus.

original: —What, Trebonius,   I have an hour’s talk in store for you.   Remember that you call on me today.   Be near me, that I may remember you.
translation: [To TREBONIUS]  Well, Trebonius, I need an hour to discuss something with you. Remember to come see me today. Stay near me so I’ll remember.

original: Caesar, I will.
translation: Caesar, I will.

original: [aside]   And so near will I be   That your best friends shall wish I had been further.
translation: [To himself]  I’ll be so near that your best friends will wish I’d been further away.

original: Good friends, go in and taste some wine with me. And we, like friends, will straightway go together.
translation: Good friends, come in and have some wine with me. And we will leave together right after that, like friends.

original: That every “like” is not the same, O Caesar, The heart of Brutus earns to think upon.
translation: Oh Caesar, that we are only “like” friends makes my heart grieve when I think of it.

original: [reads aloud]   “Caesar, beware of Brutus. Take heed of Cassius. Come  not near Casca. Have an eye to Cinna. Trust not  Trebonius. Mark well Metellus Cimber. Decius Brutus  loves thee not. Thou hast wronged Caius Ligarius.
translation: [Reading aloud from the letter] “Caesar, beware of Brutus. Pay attention to Cassius. Stay away from Casca. Keep an eye on Cinna. Don’t trust Trebonius. Take note of Metellus Cimber. Decius Brutus doesn’t love you. You’ve wronged Caius Ligarius.

original: There  is but one mind in all these men, and it is bent against Caesar.
translation: All these men share just one thought, and it’s aimed against Caesar.

original: If thou beest not immortal, look about you.  Security gives way to conspiracy. The mighty gods defend thee!   Thy lover,   Artemidorus”
translation: If you are not immortal, look around you. A sense of security makes you vulnerable to conspiracy. May the mighty gods protect you! Your friend, Artemidorus.”

original: Here will I stand till Caesar pass along,   And as a suitor will I give him this.   My heart laments that virtue cannot live   Out of the teeth of emulation.
translation: I'll stand here until Caesar passes by, and I’ll give him this as if I'm asking for a favor. My heart is sad that good men aren’t safe from the bite of bitter jealousy.

original: If thou read this, O Caesar, thou mayst live.   If not, the Fates with traitors do contrive.
translation: Caesar, if you read this, you will live. If not, the Fates are on the side of the traitors.

original: I prithee, boy, run to the senate house. Stay not to answer me, but get thee gone. Why dost thou stay?
translation: Boy, I beg you to run to the Senate House. Don’t stand there to respond—get going. Why are you still here?

original: To know my errand, madam.
translation: To find out what I'm supposed to do, madam.

original: I would have had thee there and here again   Ere I can tell thee what thou shouldst do there.
translation: I want you there and back again before I can even tell you what you should do there.

original: —O constancy, be strong upon my side,   Set a huge mountain ’tween my heart and tongue!
translation: [To herself]  Oh, willpower, support me so that I do not say what I know in my heart!

original: I have a man’s mind but a woman’s might.   How hard it is for women to keep counsel!
translation: I have a man’s mind, but only a woman’s strength. How hard it is for women to keep secrets!

original: —Art thou here yet?
translation: [To LUCIUS]  Are you still here?

original: Madam, what should I do? Run to the Capitol, and nothing else? And so return to you, and nothing else?
translation: Madam, what should I do? Run to the Capitol and nothing else? And then return to you, and nothing else?

original: Yes, bring me word, boy, if thy lord look well,   For he went sickly forth. And take good note   What Caesar doth, what suitors press to him.
translation: Yes, boy: bring me news of whether your master looks well, because he looked sick when he left. And pay attention to what Caesar does and who is standing close to him.

original: Hark, boy! What noise is that?
translation: Listen, boy! What’s that noise?

original: I hear none, madam.
translation: I hear nothing, madam.

original: Prithee, listen well. I heard a bustling rumor like a fray, And the wind brings it from the Capitol.
translation: I beg you, listen well. I heard a clamor like some kind of brawl. It seemed to come on the wind from the Capitol.

original: Sooth, madam, I hear nothing.
translation: Truly, madam, I don’t hear anything.

original: Come hither, fellow. Which way hast thou been?
translation: Come here, man. Where are you coming from?

original: At mine own house, good lady.
translation: From my own house, good lady.

original: What is ’t o'clock?
translation: What time is it?

original: About the ninth hour, lady.
translation: Around nine o'clock, lady.

original: Is Caesar yet gone to the Capitol?
translation: Has Caesar gone to the Capitol yet?

original: Madam, not yet. I go to take my stand To see him pass on to the Capitol.
translation: Not yet, madam. I’m going to find a place to stand so I can see him pass on his way to the Capitol.

original: Thou hast some suit to Caesar, hast thou not?
translation: You have some request for Caesar, don’t you?

original: That I have, lady. If it will please Caesar   To be so good to Caesar as to hear me,
translation: I do, lady. If it pleases Caesar to do himself the favor of listening to me,

original: I shall beseech him to befriend himself.
translation: I’ll beg him to do what’s good for him.

original: Why, know’st thou any harm’s intended towards him?
translation: Why, do you know of any harm intended toward him?

original: None that I know will be; much that I fear may chance.   Good morrow to you. Here the street is narrow.
translation: Nothing that I know for sure, but there's a lot that I fear may happen. Good morning to you. The street is narrow here.

original: The throng that follows Caesar at the heels,   Of senators, of praetors, common suitors,   Will crowd a feeble man almost to death.
translation: The mob that follows after Caesar—senators, judges, commoners asking for favors —will squeeze a feeble man almost to death.

original: I’ll get me to a place more void, and there   Speak to great Caesar as he comes along.
translation: I’ll find a place that is less crowded and speak to great Caesar there as he walks past.

original: I must go in.
translation: I must go inside.

original: [aside]   Ay me, how weak a thing   The heart of woman is! O Brutus,   The heavens speed thee in thine enterprise!   Sure, the boy heard me.
translation: [To herself]  Oh my, a woman’s heart is such a weak thing! Oh Brutus, may the gods help you in your efforts! Surely, the boy heard me.

original: [to LUCIUS]   Brutus hath a suit   That Caesar will not grant.—Oh, I grow faint.—   Run, Lucius, and commend me to my lord.   Say I am merry. Come to me again,   And bring me word what he doth say to thee.
translation: [To LUCIUS]  Brutus has a claim that Caesar won’t grant. Oh, I'm getting faint. Run, Lucius, and give my greetings to my lord. Say that I’m happy. Then return to me and tell me what he says to you.

original: The ides of March are come.
translation: March 15th has come.

original: Ay, Caesar, but not gone.
translation: Yes, Caesar, but the day is not over.

original: Hail, Caesar! Read this schedule.
translation: Hail, Caesar! Read this letter.

original: Trebonius doth desire you to o'er-read, At your best leisure, this his humble suit.
translation: Trebonius would like you to read his humble request for help, when you have the time.

original: O Caesar, read mine first, for mine’s a suit That touches Caesar nearer. Read it, great Caesar.
translation: Oh, Caesar, read mine first, for my letter actually pertains to you. Read it, great Caesar.

original: What touches us ourself shall be last served.
translation: I will leave whatever pertains to me for last.

original: Delay not, Caesar. Read it instantly.
translation: Don’t delay, Caesar. Read it immediately.

original: What, is the fellow mad?
translation: What, is this man crazy?

original: Sirrah, give place.
translation: Sir, stand aside.

original: What, urge you your petitions in the street? Come to the Capitol.
translation: What? Are you trying to give Caesar your letter in the street? Do it at the Capitol.

original: I wish your enterprise today may thrive.
translation: I hope your efforts succeed today.

original: What enterprise, Popillius?
translation: What efforts, Popillius?

original: Fare you well.
translation: Good luck.

original: What said Popillius Lena?
translation: What did Popillius Lena say?

original: He wished today our enterprise might thrive. I fear our purpose is discoverèd.
translation: He wished that our efforts would succeed today. I’m afraid our plans have been discovered.

original: Look how he makes to Caesar. Mark him.
translation: Look, he’s approaching Caesar. Watch him.

original: Casca, be sudden, for we fear prevention
translation: Be quick, Casca, because we're afraid our plans might be stopped.

original: —Brutus, what shall be done? If this be known,   Cassius or Caesar never shall turn back,   For I will slay myself.
translation: [To BRUTUS]  Brutus, what will we do? If our plan is known, either Caesar or I will die, because I’ll kill myself if I can't kill him.

original: Cassius, be constant. Popillius Lena speaks not of our purposes. For, look, he smiles, and Caesar doth not change.
translation: Cassius, be calm. Popillius Lena isn't telling Caesar about our plot. Look, he’s smiling, and Caesar’s expression hasn't changed.

original: Trebonius knows his time. For, look you, Brutus. He draws Mark Antony out of the way.
translation: Trebonius knows what he should do. Look, Brutus, he’s guiding Mark Antony out of the way.

original: Where is Metellus Cimber? Let him go And presently prefer his suit to Caesar.
translation: Where’s Metellus Cimber? He should go now to present his petition to Caesar.

original: He is addressed. Press near and second him.
translation: They’re speaking to him. Move up close and second his petition.

original: Casca, you are the first that rears your hand.
translation: Casca, you raise your hand first.

original: Are we all ready? What is now amiss That Caesar and his senate must redress?
translation: Are we all ready? What are the problems that Caesar and his senate should deal with?

original: Most high, most mighty, and most puissant Caesar, Metellus Cimber throws before thy seat An humble heart—
translation: Most high, most mighty, and most powerful Caesar, Metellus Cimber kneels before you with a humble heart—

original: I must prevent thee, Cimber.
translation: I must stop you, Cimber.

original: These couchings and these lowly courtesies   Might fire the blood of ordinary men   And turn preordinance and first decree   Into the law of children.
translation: Your kneeling and overly humble courtesies might flatter ordinary men to turn Roman law into some kind of child's game.

original: Be not fond,   To think that Caesar bears such rebel blood   That will be thawed from the true quality   With that which melteth fools
translation: But don’t be so foolish as to think that you can influence Caesar to do something that is not right through the tricks that persuade fools

original: —I mean, sweet words,   Low-crookèd curtsies, and base spaniel fawning.   Thy brother by decree is banishèd.
translation: —flattery, low bows, and pathetic dog-like fawning. Your brother was banished by decree.

original: If thou dost bend and pray and fawn for him,   I spurn thee like a cur out of my way.   Know, Caesar doth not wrong, nor without cause   Will he be satisfied.
translation: If you kneel and beg and flatter for him, I’ll kick you like a dog out of my way. Know that Caesar does not punish him without good reason, and will not give him what he wants without good reason.

original: Is there no voice more worthy than my own To sound more sweetly in great Caesar’s ear For the repealing of my banished brother?
translation: Is there no voice worthier than my own to sweetly ask the great Caesar to repeal the banishment of my brother?

original: I kiss thy hand, but not in flattery,  Caesar, Desiring thee that Publius Cimber may Have an immediate freedom of repeal.
translation: Caesar, I kiss your hand, but not in flattery, as I also want you to repeal Publius Cimber’s banishment immediately.

original: What, Brutus?
translation: What, Brutus?

original: Pardon, Caesar. Caesar, pardon. As low as to thy foot doth Cassius fall To beg enfranchisement for Publius Cimber.
translation: Caesar, pardon Publius. Caesar, pardon him. I throw myself down at your feet to beg that Publius Cimber regain his citizenship.

original: I could be well moved if I were as you.
translation: I could be influenced if I were like you.

original: If I could pray to move, prayers would move me.   But I am constant as the northern star,   Of whose true-fixed and resting quality   There is no fellow in the firmament.
translation: If I could beg others to change their minds, begging would convince me, too. But I’m as steady as the northern star, whose stable and immobile quality has no equal in the sky.

original: The skies are painted with unnumbered sparks.   They are all fire and every one doth shine,   But there’s but one in all doth hold his place.   So in the world.
translation: The skies are filled with countless stars. They are all made of fire, and every single one shines. But there's just one out of all of them that holds its central place. The world is the same way.

original: 'Tis furnished well with men,   And men are flesh and blood, and apprehensive,
translation: It's full of men—and men are flesh and blood, and capable of understanding.

original: Yet in the number I do know but one   That unassailable holds on his rank,   Unshaked of motion
translation: Yet of them all, I know just one who is beyond questioning and immovable, who never shifts from his position.

original: . And that I am he   Let me a little show it even in this:   That I was constant Cimber should be banished,   And constant do remain to keep him so.
translation: I am that man, and I will show you in this way: I was resolved that Cimber should be banished, and I am resolved that he should remain banished.

original: O Caesar—
translation: Oh, Caesar—

original: Hence! Wilt thou lift up Olympus?
Great Caesar—
translation: Great Caesar—

original: Doth not Brutus bootless kneel?
translation: Why are you kneeling, when even Brutus' kneeling is in vain?

original: Speak, hands, for me!
translation: Hands, speak for me!

original: Et tu, Bruté?
translation: And you too, Brutus?

original: —Then fall, Caesar.   [dies]
translation: [To himself]  Then die, Caesar.  [He dies]

original: Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead! Run hence, proclaim, cry it about the streets.
translation: Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead! Run and shout it out in the streets.

original: Some to the common pulpits, and cry out, “Liberty, freedom, and enfranchisement!”
translation: Some of us should go to the public platforms, and cry out, “Liberty, freedom, and full citizenship to all!”

original: People and senators, be not affrighted. Fly not. Stand still. Ambition’s debt is paid.
translation: People and Senators, don’t be afraid. Don’t leave. Stay here. Caesar alone had to die for his ambition.

original: Go to the pulpit, Brutus.
translation: Go to the platform, Brutus.

original: And Cassius too.
translation: And Cassius too.

original: Where’s Publius?
translation: Where’s Publius?

original: Here, quite confounded with this mutiny.
translation: Here, shocked by this rebellion.

original: Stand fast together, lest some friend of Caesar’s Should chance—
translation: Stand close together, in case some friend of Caesar tries—

original: Talk not of standing.
translation: Don’t talk about standing together.

original: —Publius, good cheer.   There is no harm intended to your person,   Nor to no Roman else. So tell them, Publius.
translation: [To PUBLIUS]  Publius, cheer up. We don’t mean any harm to you, or to any other Roman. Tell the people this, Publius.

original: And leave us, Publius, lest that the people, Rushing on us, should do your age some mischief.
translation: And leave us, Publius, in case the people should rush at us and harm you.

original: Do so. And let no man abide this deed But we the doers.
translation: Leave us. Let no man suffer the consequences of deed except we who did it.

original: Where is Antony?
translation: Where’s Antony?

original: Fled to his house amazed. Men, wives, and children stare, cry out, and run As it were doomsday.
translation: He ran to his house, stunned. Men, wives, and children stare, cry out, and run around as if it were doomsday.

original: Fates, we will know your pleasures.   That we shall die, we know.
translation: We'll soon discover what the Fates want to happen to us. We already know that we'll all die one day.

original: 'Tis but the time,   And drawing days out, that men stand upon.
translation: It's just a matter of when. Men try to control that by prolonging the time they have left to live as long as possible.

original: Why, he that cuts off twenty years of life Cuts off so many years of fearing death.
translation: Why, he who shortens his own life by twenty years also cuts off twenty years of worrying about death.

original: Grant that, and then is death a benefit.   So are we Caesar’s friends, that have abridged   His time of fearing death. Stoop, Romans, stoop,
translation: If you look at it that way, then death becomes a gift. This makes us Caesar’s friends, since we've shortened the time he would have spent fearing death. Kneel, Romans, kneel.

original: And let us bathe our hands in Caesar’s blood   Up to the elbows, and besmear our swords.   Then walk we forth, even to the marketplace,
translation: And let’s wash our hands up to the elbows in Caesar’s blood, and smear our swords with it. Then we’ll walk outside, even to the public marketplace.

original: And waving our red weapons o'er our heads   Let’s all cry, “Peace, freedom, and liberty!”
translation: And, waving our bloody swords over our heads, we'll cry, “Peace, freedom, and liberty!”

original: Stoop, then, and wash.
translation: Kneel, then, and wash.

original: How many ages hence Shall this our lofty scene be acted over In states unborn and accents yet unknown!
translation: How many years from now will this epic scene be reenacted in countries that don’t yet exist, and in languages not yet known?!

original: How many times shall Caesar bleed in sport, That now on Pompey’s basis lies along No worthier than the dust!
translation: How many times will Caesar bleed in plays about this moment, just as he now lies beneath Pompey’s statue as worthless as dust?!

original: So oft as that shall be, So often shall the knot of us be called “The men that gave their country liberty.”
translation: And every time that the play is shown, the group of us will be acclaimed as "the men who gave their country liberty."

original: What, shall we forth?
translation: Well, should we go out?

original: Ay, every man away. Brutus shall lead, and we will grace his heels With the most boldest and best hearts of Rome.
translation: Yes, every man should go. Brutus will lead the way, and we’ll follow him with the boldest and best hearts of Rome.

original: Soft! Who comes here? A friend of Antony’s.
translation: Wait! Who’s coming? A friend of Antony’s.

original: [kneeling]   Thus, Brutus, did my master bid me kneel.   [falls prostrate]   Thus did Mark Antony bid me fall  down,   And, being prostrate, thus he bade me say:   Brutus is noble, wise, valiant, and honest.
translation: [Kneeling]  Brutus, my master told me to kneel just like this.  [He lays down with his head down to the floor]  And like this. He told me to prostrate myself, and, being on the ground like this, he told me to say: “Brutus is noble, wise, brave, and honest.

original: Caesar was mighty, bold, royal, and loving.   Say I love Brutus, and I honor him.   Say I feared Caesar, honored him, and loved him.
translation: Caesar was mighty, bold, royal, and loving. Antony loves Brutus and honors him. Antony feared Caesar, honored him, and loved him.

original: If Brutus will vouchsafe that Antony   May safely come to him and be resolved   How Caesar hath deserved to lie in death,
translation: If Brutus will promise that Antony would be safe to come to him and hear and explanation why Caesar deserved to be killed,

original: Mark Antony shall not love Caesar dead   So well as Brutus living
translation: Mark Antony will not love dead Caesar as much as living Brutus.

original: , but will follow   The fortunes and affairs of noble Brutus   Thorough the hazards of this untrod state   With all true faith. So says my master Antony.
translation: And he will follow noble Brutus through the hard times of this unprecedented state of affairs.” So says my master, Antony.

original: Thy master is a wise and valiant Roman.   I never thought him worse.
translation: Your master is a wise and brave Roman. I never thought otherwise.

original: Tell him, so please him come unto this place,   He shall be satisfied and, by my honor,   Depart untouched.
translation: Tell him that if he wants to come here, he'll get a full explanation, and he’ll leave unharmed. I swear it on my honor.

original: I’ll fetch him presently.
translation: I’ll get him now.

original: I know that we shall have him well to friend.
translation: I know that we'll soon have Antony as a good friend to us.

original: I wish we may. But yet have I a mind   That fears him much, and
translation: I hope we do. But still, I fear him greatly, and

original: my misgiving still   Falls shrewdly to the purpose.
translation: my misgivings usually end up coming painfully true.

original: But here comes Antony.—Welcome, Mark Antony.
translation: But here comes Antony. Welcome, Mark Antony.

original: O mighty Caesar! Dost thou lie so low?   Are all thy conquests, glories, triumphs, spoils,   Shrunk to this little measure? Fare thee well.
translation: [To CAESAR's body]  Oh, mighty Caesar! Do you lie so low? Are all of your conquests, glories, triumphs, and successes now shrunk to such little value? Farewell.

original: —I know not, gentlemen, what you intend,   Who else must be let blood, who else is rank.   If I myself, there is no hour so fit   As Caesar’s death’s hour,
translation: [To the conspirators]  Gentlemen, I don’t know what you plan to do; who else you must kill; who else you think is corrupt. If it’s me, there’s no time as fitting as this hour of Caesar’s death,

original: nor no instrument   Of half that worth as those your swords, made rich   With the most noble blood of all this world.
translation: and no weapons even half as worthy as your swords— which have been made rich by being covered in the noblest blood in the whole world.

original: I do beseech ye, if you bear me hard,   Now, whilst your purpled hands do reek and smoke,   Fulfill your pleasure. Live a thousand years,   I shall not find myself so apt to die.
translation: I beg you, if you have a grudge against me, do what you want to do right now while your stained hands still smell of blood. Even if were I to live a thousand years, I would never find another moment when I would be as ready to die as I am now.

original: No place will please me so, no mean of death,   As here by Caesar, and by you cut off,   The choice and master spirits of this age.
translation: There’s no place I’d rather die than next to Caesar, and no manner of death I'd prefer than being stabbed by you, the leaders of this new era.

original: O Antony, beg not your death of us.   Though now we must appear bloody and cruel—   As by our hands and this our present act   You see we do
translation: Oh, Antony, don’t beg us to kill you. Though we must seem to be bloody and cruel right now to you—with our bloody hands and what we've just done

original: —yet see you but our hands   And this the bleeding business they have done.   Our hearts you see not. They are pitiful.
translation: —you’re only seeing our hands and the bloody work they've done. You have not seen into our hearts. They are full of pity for Caesar.

original: And pity to the general wrong of Rome—   As fire drives out fire, so pity pity—   Hath done this deed on Caesar.
translation: But, just as fire drives out fire, our pity for the wrongs committed against Rome overcame our pity for Caesar and made us do what we did to Caesar.

original: For your part,   To you our swords have leaden points, Mark Antony.   Our arms in strength of malice and our hearts   Of brothers' temper do receive you in   With all kind love, good thoughts, and reverence.
translation: As for you, our swords have soft points that will not harm you, Mark Antony. Our arms—with the same strength they had in striking Caesar—and our hearts—filled with brotherly love—embrace you with kind love, good thoughts, and admiration.

original: Your voice shall be as strong as any man’s In the disposing of new dignities.
translation: Your influence will be as strong as anyone’s in the selection of new government officials.

original: Only be patient till we have appeased   The multitude, beside themselves with fear,
translation: Just be patient until we’ve calmed the masses, who are beside themselves with fear.

original: And then we will deliver you the cause,   Why I, that did love Caesar when I struck him,   Have thus proceeded.
translation: And then we’ll explain to you why I—who loved Caesar even while I stabbed him—have done this.

original: I doubt not of your wisdom.   Let each man render me his bloody hand.   [shakes hands with the conspirators]
translation: I don’t doubt your wisdom. May each of you give me his bloody hand.  [He shakes hands with the conspirators]

original: First, Marcus Brutus, will I shake with you.
translation: [To BRUTUS]  First, Marcus Brutus, I will shake your hand.

original: —Next, Caius Cassius, do I take your hand.
translation: [To CASSIUS]  Next, Caius Cassius, I take your hand.

original: —Now, Decius Brutus, yours.
translation: [To DECIUS]  Now, Decius Brutus, yours.

original: —Now yours, Metellus.
translation: [To METELLUS]  Now yours, Metellus.

original: —Yours, Cinna.
translation: [To CINNA]  Yours, Cinna.

original: —And, my valiant Casca, yours.
translation: [To CASCA]  And, my valiant Casca, yours.

original: —Though last, not last in love, yours, good Trebonius.
translation: [To TREBONIUS]  Though I shake your hand last, I do not love you the least, good Trebonius.

original: —Gentlemen all, alas, what shall I say?   My credit now stands on such slippery ground   That one of two bad ways you must conceit me,   Either a coward or a flatterer
translation: [To the conspirators]  All of you gentlemen, alas, what can I say? Now that we’ve shaken hands, my credibility stands on such slippery ground that you must think me either a coward or a flatterer.

original: —That I did love thee, Caesar, O, ’tis true.   If then thy spirit look upon us now,   Shall it not grieve thee dearer than thy death   To see thy Antony making his peace,
translation: [To CAESAR's body]  It is true that I loved you, Caesar. If your spirit is looking down upon us now, would it grieve you more than even your death to see your Antony making peace

original: Shaking the bloody fingers of thy foes—   Most noble!—in the presence of thy corse?
translation: , and shaking the bloody hands of your enemies—most noble enemies!—in the presence of your corpse?

original: Had I as many eyes as thou hast wounds,   Weeping as fast as they stream forth thy blood,   It would become me better than to close   In terms of friendship with thine enemies.
translation: If I had as many eyes as you have wounds, and they wept tears as fast as your wounds stream blood, even that would be more becoming than joining your enemies in friendship.

original: Pardon me, Julius! Here wast thou bayed, brave hart;   Here didst thou fall; and here thy hunters stand,   Signed in thy spoil, and crimsoned in thy lethe.
translation: Forgive me, Julius! Here is where you were brought down, like a brave deer surrounded by hunting dogs. Here is where you fell, and here your hunters still stand, stained and reddened by your blood.

original: O world, thou wast the forest to this hart,   And this indeed, O world, the heart of thee.   How like a deer, strucken by many princes,   Dost thou here lie!
translation: Oh, world, you were the forest to this deer. And this deer, oh world, was your dear. Now you lie here, so much like a deer, stabbed by many princes!

original: Mark Antony—
translation: Mark Antony—

original: Pardon me, Caius Cassius. The enemies of Caesar shall say this; Then, in a friend, it is cold modesty.
translation: Pardon me, Caius Cassius. Even the enemies of Caesar would say the same. So, when said by a friend, it’s just a plain unemotional truth.

original: I blame you not for praising Caesar so.   But what compact mean you to have with us?
translation: I don’t blame you for praising Caesar as you do. But what agreement do you plan to make with us?

original: Will you be pricked in number of our friends?   Or shall we on, and not depend on you?
translation: Will you be marked down as one of our friends, or should we move on without depending on you?

original: Therefore I took your hands, but was indeed   Swayed from the point by looking down on Caesar.
translation: Because I wanted to be your friend, I shook your hands. But, indeed, I was distracted when I looked down at Caesar.

original: Friends am I with you all and love you all   Upon this hope: that you shall give me reasons   Why and wherein Caesar was dangerous.
translation: I am friends with you all and love you all, on one condition—that you will give me the reasons how and why Caesar was dangerous.

original: Or else were this a savage spectacle!
translation: If we couldn't, killing him would have been just some savage act!

original: Our reasons are so full of good regard   That were you, Antony, the son of Caesar,   You should be satisfied.
translation: Antony, our reasons are so well thought-out that even if you were Caesar’s son, you would be satisfied by them.

original: That’s all I seek.   And am moreover suitor that I may   Produce his body to the marketplace,
translation: That’s all I ask—and would also ask the favor that I be allowed to bring his body to the marketplace

original: And in the pulpit, as becomes a friend,   Speak in the order of his funeral.
translation: and stand on the platform and speak during his funeral ceremony, as a friend ought to do.

original: You shall, Mark Antony.
translation: You may, Mark Antony.

original: Brutus, a word with you
translation: Brutus, may I speak with you?

original: [aside to BRUTUS]   You know not what you do.   Do not consent   That Antony speak in his funeral.
translation: [To BRUTUS so that only he can hear]  You don’t know what you’re doing. Don’t agree to let Antony speak at his funeral.

original: Know you how much the people may be moved   By that which he will utter?
translation: Do you know how much the people could be stirred up by what he says?

original: [aside to CASSIUS]   By your pardon.   I will myself into the pulpit first,   And show the reason of our Caesar’s death.
translation: [To CASSIUS so that only he can hear]  If you'll agree, I myself will stand on the platform first and explain the reason for Caesar’s death.

original: What Antony shall speak, I will protest,   He speaks by leave and by permission,   And that we are contented Caesar shall   Have all true rites and lawful ceremonies.
translation: I will announce that Antony speaks with our permission, and I will say that we believe Caesar should be honored with all the usual and lawful ceremonies.

original: It shall advantage more than do us wrong.
translation: It will help us more than it will do us harm.

original: I know not what may fall. I like it  not.
translation: Anything could happen. I don’t like this.

original: Mark Antony, here, take you Caesar’s body.   You shall not in your funeral speech blame us,   But speak all good you can devise of Caesar,   And say you do ’t by our permission.
translation: Mark Antony, here, take Caesar’s body. You will not blame us in your funeral speech, but will say all the good you can think of about Caesar. And you will also say that you do all this with our permission.

original: Else shall you not have any hand at all   About his funeral. And you shall speak   In the same pulpit whereto I am going,   After my speech is ended.
translation: Otherwise, you won't take any part in his funeral. And you’ll speak on the same platform that I do, after I've finished my own speech.

original: Be it so. I do desire no more.
translation: So be it. I want nothing more than that.

original: Prepare the body then, and follow us.
translation: Prepare the body, then, and follow us.

original: O, pardon me, thou bleeding piece of earth,   That I am meek and gentle with these butchers!   Thou art the ruins of the noblest man   That ever livèd in the tide of times.
translation: Oh, pardon me, you bleeding corpse, for being quiet and friendly with these butchers! You are the remains of the noblest man that ever lived.

original: Woe to the hand that shed this costly blood!   Over thy wounds now do I prophesy—   Which, like dumb mouths, do ope their ruby lips   To beg the voice and utterance of my tongue—
translation: May disaster strike the hand that shed this priceless blood. Over your wounds—which, like speechless mouths, open their red lips as if to beg me to speak

original: A curse shall light upon the limbs of men.   Domestic fury and fierce civil strife   Shall cumber all the parts of Italy.
translation: —I predict that a curse will come down on us. Anger between brothers and fierce civil war will burden all of Italy.

original: Blood and destruction shall be so in use,   And dreadful objects so familiar,   That mothers shall but smile when they behold   Their infants quartered with the hands of war,
translation: Blood and destruction will be so common and dreadful events so familiar, that mothers will just smile when they watch their babies cut to pieces by the hands of war.

original: All pity choked with custom of fell deeds,   And Caesar’s spirit, ranging for revenge,   With Ate by his side come hot from hell,
translation: The sheer volume of evil deeds will choke people’s compassion. And Caesar’s ghost—searching for revenge with  Atë  by his side

original: Shall in these confines with a monarch’s voice   Cry “Havoc!” and let slip the dogs of war,   That this foul deed shall smell above the earth   With carrion men, groaning for burial.
translation: —will rush up from hell and cry in the voice of a king, “Havoc!” His ghost will unleash the dogs of war, so that this foul murder will cover the earth with men’s corpses, begging to be buried.

original: You serve Octavius Caesar, do you not?
translation: You serve Octavius Caesar, right?

original: I do, Mark Antony.
translation: I do, Mark Antony.

original: Caesar did write for him to come to Rome.
translation: Caesar wrote to him that he should come to Rome.
