original: He did receive his letters and is coming. And bid me say to you by word of mouth—     O Caesar!—
translation: He received Caesar’s letters and is coming. He told me to say to you personally— Oh, Caesar!—

original: Thy heart is big. Get thee apart and weep.
translation: Your heart swells with sadness. Go find some privacy and weep.

original: Passion, I see, is catching, for mine eyes,   Seeing those beads of sorrow stand in thine,   Began to water. Is thy master coming?
translation: I see that grief is contagious. Seeing the tears of sorrow in your eyes makes my eyes begin to water. Is your master coming?

original: He lies tonight within seven leagues of Rome.
translation: He is resting tonight within twenty miles of Rome.

original: Post back with speed, and tell him what hath chanced.   Here is a mourning Rome, a dangerous Rome,   No Rome of safety for Octavius yet.
translation: Ride quickly back to him, and tell him what has happened. This is now a Rome in mourning, a dangerous Rome. A Rome that is not safe for Octavius yet.

original: Hie hence, and tell him so.—Yet, stay awhile.   Thou shalt not back till I have borne this corse   Into the marketplace.
translation: Get going and tell him so. No, actually, stay a while. You shouldn't go back until I’ve carried the corpse into the marketplace.

original: There shall I try,   In my oration, how the people take   The cruèl issue of these bloody men.
translation: There I’ll figure out, through my speech, what the people think of the cruel deeds of these bloody men.

original: According to the which, thou shalt discourse   To young Octavius of the state of things.   Lend me your hand.
translation: Based on how the people respond, you’ll report back to young Octavius about the state of things. Help me with the body.

original: We will be satisfied! Let us be satisfied!
translation: We demand answers! Give us answers!

original: Then follow me and give me audience, friends.
translation: Then follow me and listen to what I say, friends.

original: —Cassius, go you into the other street   And part the numbers.
translation: [To CASSIUS]  Cassius, go on to the next street. Split up the crowd.

original: —Those that will hear me speak, let 'em stay here.   Those that will follow Cassius, go with him,   And public reasons shall be renderèd   Of Caesar’s death.
translation: [To PLEBEIANS]  Let those who want to hear me speak stay here. Those who want to hear from Cassius, go with him. We’ll explain the reasons behind Caesar’s death publicly.

original: I will hear Brutus speak.
translation: I’ll listen to Brutus.

original: I will hear Cassius and compare their reasons When severally we hear them renderèd.
translation: I’ll listen to Cassius, and later we'll compare what they've said.

original: The noble Brutus is ascended. Silence!
translation: Noble Brutus has walked up to the platform. Quiet!

original: Be patient till the last. Romans, countrymen, and  lovers! Hear me for my cause, and be silent that you may hear. Believe me for mine honor, and have respect to  mine honor that you may believe.
translation: Please be calm until I finish. Romans, countrymen, and friends! Listen to the reasons for my actions, and be silent so you can hear. Do me the honor of believing me, and know that, upon my honor, you can believe me.

original: Censure me in your  wisdom, and awake your senses that you may the better  judge. If there be any in this assembly, any dear friend of Caesar’s, to him I say that Brutus' love to Caesar  was no less than his.
translation: Be wise in your judgment of me, and keep your minds alert so that you can judge me wisely. If there’s anyone in this assembly, any dear friend of Caesar’s, I say to him that my love for Caesar was no less than his.

original: If then that friend demand why  Brutus rose against Caesar, this is my answer: not that  I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more. Had you rather Caesar were living and die all slaves, than that Caesar were dead, to live all free men?
translation: If, then, that friend demands to know why I rose up against Caesar, this is my answer: it’s not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more. Would you prefer that Caesar were living, and we would all one day die as slaves? Or would you prefer that Caesar were dead and we all lived as free men?

original: As Caesar loved me, I weep for him. As he was fortunate, I rejoice at  it. As he was valiant, I honor him. But, as he was  ambitious, I slew him.
translation: Because Caesar was my friend, I weep for him. Because he had so much good fortune, I am so happy for him. Because he was brave, I honor him. But because he was ambitious, I killed him.

original: There is tears for his love, joy  for his fortune, honor for his valor, and death for his  ambition. Who is here so base that would be a bondman?  If any, speak—for him have I offended.
translation: There are tears for his love, joy for his fortune, honor for his bravery, and death for his ambition. Who standing here is so wretched that he wants to be a slave? If there are any, let them speak—because they are the ones that I have offended.

original: Who is here so  rude that would not be a Roman? If any, speak—for him  have I offended. Who is here so vile that will not love  his country? If any, speak—for him have I offended. I  pause for a reply.
translation: Who here is so uncivilized that he does not want to be a Roman? If there are any, let them speak—because they are the ones that I have offended. Who here is so despicable that he does not love his country? If there are any, let them speak—because they are the ones that I have offended. I will wait for a reply.

original: None, Brutus, none.
translation: No one, Brutus, no one.

original: Then none have I offended. I have done no more to  Caesar than you shall do to Brutus. The question of his  death is enrolled in the Capitol.
translation: Then I have offended no one. I’ve done no more to Caesar than you would do to me. The reasons for his death are on record in the Capitol.

original: His glory not  extenuated wherein he was worthy, nor his offenses  enforced for which he suffered death.
translation: His glory has not been reduced where he earned it, nor have the offenses for which he was killed been exaggerated.

original: Here comes his body, mourned by Mark Antony, who,  though he had no hand in his death, shall receive the  benefit of his dying—a place in the commonwealth—as  which of you shall not?
translation: Here comes his body, mourned by Mark Antony, who, though he had no part in killing Caesar, will benefit from his death—full citizenship in the commonwealth. And which of you won't benefit from that?

original: With this I depart: that, as I  slew my best lover for the good of Rome, I have the same dagger for myself when it shall please my country to  need my death.
translation: I will depart with these final words: just as I killed my best friend for the good of Rome, I will still keep the same dagger, so that I can kill myself when my country requires my death.

original: Live, Brutus! Live, live!
translation: Live, Brutus! Live, live!

original: Bring him with triumph home unto his house!
translation: Let’s carry him in triumph to his house!

original: Give him a statue with his ancestors!
translation: Let’s build a statue of him, near those of his ancestors!

original: Let him be Caesar!
translation: Let him become Caesar!

original: Caesar’s better parts Shall be crowned in Brutus!
translation: We will crown Brutus, who has all of Caesar’s better qualities.

original: We’ll bring him to his house with shouts and clamors.
translation: We’ll carry him to his house with shouts and celebration!

original: My countrymen—
translation: My countrymen—

original: Peace, silence! Brutus speaks.
translation: Quiet! Silence! Brutus speaks.

original: Peace, ho!
translation: Hey, quiet!

original: Good countrymen, let me depart alone.   And, for my sake, stay here with Antony.   Do grace to Caesar’s corpse, and grace his speech   Tending to Caesar’s glories,
translation: Good countrymen, let me leave on my own. And, for my sake, stay here with Antony. Give honor to Caesar’s corpse, as well as to Antony’s speech about Caesar’s glories

original: which Mark Antony   By our permission is allowed to make.
translation: —which we have given him our permission to make.

original: I do entreat you, not a man depart,   Save I alone, till Antony have spoke.
translation: I beg that none of you leave until Antony has spoken, except for me.

original: Stay, ho! And let us hear Mark Antony.
translation: We'll stay! Let us listen to Mark Antony.

original: Let him go up into the public chair.   We’ll hear him.
translation: Let him walk up to the platform. We’ll listen to him.

original: —Noble Antony, go up.
translation: [To ANTONY]  Noble Antony, mount the platform.

original: For Brutus' sake, I am beholding to you.
translation: For Brutus’ sake, I am indebted to you.

original: What does he say of Brutus?
translation: What does he say about Brutus?

original: He says for Brutus' sake He finds himself beholding to us all.
translation: He says that for Brutus’ sake he finds himself indebted to us all.

original: 'Twere best he speak no harm of Brutus here.
translation: He’d better not say anything bad about Brutus here.

original: This Caesar was a tyrant.
translation: Caesar was a tyrant.

original: Nay, that’s certain. We are blest that Rome is rid of him.
translation: That’s for sure. We’re lucky that Rome is rid of him.

original: Peace! Let us hear what Antony can say.
translation: Quiet! Let’s hear what Antony has to say.

original: You gentle Romans—
translation: You noble Romans—

original: Peace, ho! Let us hear him.
translation: Hey, quiet! Let us hear him.

original: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears.   I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him.   The evil that men do lives after them;   The good is oft interrèd with their bones.
translation: Friends, Romans, countrymen: give me a moment of your attention. I’ve come here to bury Caesar, not to praise him. The evil that men do is remembered after they die, but the good is often buried with their bones.

original: So let it be with Caesar. The noble Brutus   Hath told you Caesar was ambitious.   If it were so, it was a grievous fault,   And grievously hath Caesar answered it.
translation: May it be that way with Caesar. The noble Brutus told you that Caesar was ambitious. If that’s true, it’s a terrible fault—and Caesar has paid terribly for it.

original: Here, under leave of Brutus and the rest—   For Brutus is an honorable man;   So are they all, all honorable men—   Come I to speak in Caesar’s funeral.
translation: Now, with the permission of Brutus and the others—because Brutus is an honorable man, as all the others are honorable men—I have come to speak at Caesar’s funeral.

original: He was my friend, faithful and just to me.
translation: He was my friend. He was loyal and fair to me.

original: But Brutus says he was ambitious,   And Brutus is an honorable man.   He hath brought many captives home to Rome   Whose ransoms did the general coffers fill.
translation: But Brutus says he was ambitious, and Brutus is an honorable man. He brought many captives home to Rome whose filled the public treasury.

original: Did this in Caesar seem ambitious?   When that the poor have cried, Caesar hath wept.   Ambition should be made of sterner stuff.
translation: Did Caesar seem ambitious when he did this? When the poor cried, Caesar cried. Ambition shouldn’t be so tender-hearted.

original: Yet Brutus says he was ambitious,   And Brutus is an honorable man.   You all did see that on the Lupercal   I thrice presented him a kingly crown,   Which he did thrice refuse.
translation: Yet Brutus says he was ambitious, and Brutus is an honorable man. You all saw that on the feast day of Lupercal, I offered Caesar a king’s crown three times. And all three times he refused it.

original: Was this ambition?   Yet Brutus says he was ambitious,   And, sure, he is an honorable man.
translation: Was that ambition? Yet Brutus says he was ambitious. And, of course, Brutus is an honorable man.

original: I speak not to disprove what Brutus spoke,   But here I am to speak what I do know.   You all did love him once, not without cause.   What cause withholds you then to mourn for him?
translation: I do not say this to disprove what Brutus has said, but to speak about what I know. You all loved Caesar once, and not without reason. So what reason stops you from mourning him?

original: O judgment! Thou art fled to brutish beasts,   And men have lost their reason. Bear with me.   My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar,   And I must pause till it come back to me.   [weeps]
translation: Oh, gods! You have become brutish beasts, and men have lost their reason! Apologies for that outburst. My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar, and I must pause until it returns to me.  [He weeps]

original: Methinks there is much reason in his sayings.
translation: I think that a lot of what he's saying makes sense.

original: If thou consider rightly of the matter, Caesar has had great wrong.
translation: If you think about it the right way, Caesar has been badly wronged.

original: Has he, masters? I fear there will a worse come in his place.
translation: Has he, good sirs? I worry that someone worse than Caesar will come to replace him.

original: Marked ye his words? He would not take the crown. Therefore ’tis certain he was not ambitious.
translation: Did you listen to Antony's words? Caesar wouldn’t take the crown. Therefore it’s certain that he wasn’t ambitious.

original: If it be found so, some will dear abide it.
translation: If it can be proven that he wasn't, certain people will pay dearly for all this.

original: Poor soul! His eyes are red as fire with weeping.
translation: Poor man! Antony’s eyes are fiery red from weeping.

original: There’s not a nobler man in Rome than Antony.
translation: There's not a nobler man than Antony in Rome.

original: Now mark him. He begins again to speak.
translation: Now pay attention to him. He’s starting to speak again.

original: But yesterday the word of Caesar might   Have stood against the world. Now lies he there,   And none so poor to do him reverence.
translation: Just yesterday, no one in the world would have stood against Caesar's commands. Now he lies there dead, and no one is so humble as to show him respect.

original: O masters, if I were disposed to stir   Your hearts and minds to mutiny and rage,   I should do Brutus wrong, and Cassius wrong—   Who, you all know, are honorable men.
translation: Oh, sirs, if I were trying to stir your hearts and minds to rage and rebellion, I would be doing wrong to Brutus and Cassius—who, as you all know, are honorable men.

original: I will not do them wrong. I rather choose   To wrong the dead, to wrong myself and you,   Than I will wrong such honorable men.
translation: I will not do them wrong. I choose rather to wrong the dead, and wrong myself and you, than wrong such honorable men.

original: But here’s a parchment with the seal of Caesar.   I found it in his closet. 'Tis his will.
translation: But here’s a paper with Caesar’s seal on it. I found it in his room. It’s his will.

original: Let but the commons hear this testament—   Which, pardon me, I do not mean to read—
translation: If the public were to know what was in this will—which, excuse me, I don’t plan on reading to you—

original: And they would go and kiss dead Caesar’s wounds   And dip their napkins in his sacred blood,   Yea, beg a hair of him for memory,
translation: they would go and kiss dead Caesar’s wounds, dip their handkerchiefs in his blessed blood, and even beg for a lock of his hair to remember him by.

original: And, dying, mention it within their wills,   Bequeathing it as a rich legacy   Unto their issue.
translation: And when they died, they would include the handkerchief or the hair in their wills, passing it on to their own heirs as a treasured inheritance.

original: We’ll hear the will. Read it, Mark Antony!
translation: We want to hear the will. Read it, Mark Antony!

original: The will, the will! We will hear Caesar’s will.
translation: The will, the will! We want to hear Caesar’s will.

original: Have patience, gentle friends. I must not read it.   It is not meet you know how Caesar loved you.   You are not wood, you are not stones, but men.
translation: Have patience, noble friends. I must not read it. It's not right for you to know how much Caesar loved you. You're not wood, you're not stones. You’re men.

original: And, being men, bearing the will of Caesar,   It will inflame you, it will make you mad.   'Tis good you know not that you are his heirs.   For, if you should—Oh, what would come of it!
translation: And, being men, if you knew what was in Caesar’s will, it would anger you. It will drive you crazy. It’s better that you not know that you are his heirs. Because, if you did know—oh, what would happen!

original: Read the will. We’ll hear it, Antony. You shall read us the will, Caesar’s will.
translation: Read the will. We want to hear it, Antony. You must read us the will, Caesar’s will.

original: Will you be patient? Will you stay awhile?   I have o'ershot myself to tell you of it.
translation: Will you be patient? Will you wait a while? I’ve said too much in telling you about it.

original: I fear I wrong the honorable men   Whose daggers have stabbed Caesar. I do fear it.
translation: I’m afraid that I wrong the honorable men whose daggers have stabbed Caesar. I really fear it.

original: They were traitors! “Honorable men”!
translation: They were traitors, these so-called “honorable men!”

original: The will! The testament!
translation: The will! The testament!

original: They were villains, murderers. The will! Read the will!
translation: They were villains, murderers. The will! Read the will!

original: You will compel me, then, to read the will?
translation: So you'll force me to read the will?

original: Then make a ring about the corpse of Caesar,   And let me show you him that made the will.   Shall I descend? And will you give me leave?
translation: Then form a circle around Caesar’s corpse, and let me show you the man who made this will. Shall I come down? Will you allow me to?

original: Come down.
translation: Come down.

original: Descend.
translation: Come down.

original: You shall have leave.
translation: We’ll allow you.

original: A ring! Stand round.
translation: A circle! Form a circle!

original: Stand from the hearse. Stand from the body.
translation: Stand back from the hearse. Stand back from the body.

original: Room for Antony, most noble Antony!
translation: Make room for Antony, most noble Antony!

original: Nay, press not so upon me. Stand far off.
translation: No, don’t press up against me. Stand further away.

original: Stand back. Room! Bear back.
translation: Stand back. Give him room. Move back.

original: If you have tears, prepare to shed them now.
translation: If you have tears, prepare to shed them now.

original: You all do know this mantle. I remember   The first time ever Caesar put it on.   'Twas on a summer’s evening in his tent,   That day he overcame the Nervii.
translation: You all know this cloak. I remember the first time Caesar ever put it on. It was a summer evening in his tent, on the day he defeated the  Nervii  warriors.

original: Look, in this place ran Cassius' dagger through.   See what a rent the envious Casca made.   Through this the well-belovèd Brutus stabbed.
translation: Look, this is the place where Cassius’s dagger cut through it. See the rip that the envious Casca made. The much beloved Brutus stabbed him through this hole.

original: And as he plucked his cursèd steel away,   Mark how the blood of Caesar followed it,   As rushing out of doors, to be resolved   If Brutus so unkindly knocked, or no.
translation: And when Brutus yanked out his cursed dagger, see how Caesar’s blood followed after it—as if rushing out a door to see for sure if it was Brutus knocking so rudely.

original: For Brutus, as you know, was Caesar’s angel.   Judge, O you gods, how dearly Caesar loved him!   This was the most unkindest cut of all.
translation: For Brutus was Caesar’s angel, as you know. Oh gods, how dearly Caesar loved him! This was the cruelest cut of all.

original: For when the noble Caesar saw him stab,   Ingratitude, more strong than traitors' arms,   Quite vanquished him.
translation: When the noble Caesar saw him stab, it was Brutus' ingratitude more than the traitors' weapons that overwhelmed him.

original: Then burst his mighty heart,   And, in his mantle muffling up his face,   Even at the base of Pompey’s statue,   Which all the while ran blood, great Caesar fell.
translation: Then his mighty heart burst. And with his face covered by his cloak—which was dripping with blood—great Caesar fell at the base of Pompey’s statue.

original: O, what a fall was there, my countrymen!   Then I, and you, and all of us fell down,   Whilst bloody treason flourished over us.
translation: Oh, what a fall it was, my countrymen! Then I, and you, all of us fell down, while bloody treason celebrated its victory over us.

original: Oh, now you weep, and, I perceive, you feel   The dint of pity. These are gracious drops.
translation: Oh, now you weep, and I see you feel the pain of pity. These tears are honorable.

original: Kind souls, what, weep you when you but behold   Our Caesar’s vesture wounded? Look you here,   Here is himself, marred, as you see, with traitors.   [lifts up CAESAR's mantle]
translation: Good men, do you weep when all you're looking at is Caesar’s wounded cloak? Look right here, here is the man himself, battered by traitors, as you can see.  [He lifts up CAESAR's cloak]

original: O piteous spectacle!
translation: Oh, what a heartbreaking sight!

original: O noble Caesar!
translation: Oh, noble Caesar!

original: O woeful day!
translation: Oh, what a sad day!

original: O traitors, villains!
translation: Oh, traitors, villains!

original: O most bloody sight!
translation: Oh, most bloody sight!

original: We will be revenged.
translation: We will get revenge.

original: Revenge! About! Seek! Burn! Fire! Kill! Slay! Let not a traitor live!
translation: Revenge! Look around. Find them! Burn! Set fire! Kill! Slay! Leave no traitors alive!

original: Stay, countrymen.
translation: Wait, countrymen.

original: Peace there! Hear the noble Antony.
translation: Quiet there! Listen to the noble Antony.

original: We’ll hear him. We’ll follow him. We’ll die with him.
translation: We’ll listen to him. We’ll follow him. We’ll die with him.

original: Good friends, sweet friends! Let me not stir you up   To such a sudden flood of mutiny.   They that have done this deed are honorable.
translation: Good friends, sweet friends: don’t let me stir you up to such a sudden surge of revolt. Those who have done this deed are honorable.

original: What private griefs they have, alas, I know not,   That made them do it. They are wise and honorable,   And will, no doubt, with reasons answer you.
translation: I don’t know what personal grudges they had that made them do it. They are wise and honorable, and will give you reasons for their actions, without a doubt

original: I come not, friends, to steal away your hearts.   I am no orator, as Brutus is,   But, as you know me all, a plain blunt man   That love my friend.
translation: . I am not here to steal your loyalty, friends. I’m no orator like Brutus. As you all know, I'm just a plain, blunt man who loved his friend.

original: And that they know full well   That gave me public leave to speak of him.   For I have neither wit nor words nor worth,   Action nor utterance nor the power of speech,   To stir men’s blood.
translation: And those who gave me permission to speak know this very well. I don't have the cleverness, vocabulary, reputation, body language, or eloquence to stir men to passion.

original: I only speak right on.   I tell you that which you yourselves do know,   Show you sweet Caesar’s wounds, poor poor dumb mouths,   And bid them speak for me.
translation: I just say what I really think. I tell you what you already know. I show you sweet Caesar’s wounds—those poor, poor, speechless mouths—and ask them to speak for me.

original: But were I Brutus,   And Brutus Antony, there were an Antony   Would ruffle up your spirits and put a tongue   In every wound of Caesar that should move   The stones of Rome to rise and mutiny.
translation: But if I were Brutus—and Brutus were me—then that would be an Antony who would fill your spirits with rage, and put in each of Caesar’s wounds a voice that would inspire even the stones in Rome to rise up and rebel.

original: We’ll mutiny.
translation: We’ll revolt.

original: We’ll burn the house of Brutus.
translation: We’ll burn Brutus’ house.

original: Away, then! Come, seek the conspirators.
translation: Let’s go, then! Come, find the conspirators!

original: Yet hear me, countrymen. Yet hear me speak.
translation: Wait, and listen to me, countrymen.

original: Peace, ho! Hear Antony. Most noble Antony!
translation: Quiet! Wait! Listen to Antony. Most noble Antony!

original: Why, friends, you go to do you know not what.   Wherein hath Caesar thus deserved your loves?
translation: Why, friends, you don’t know what you’re doing. What has Caesar done to deserve your love?

original: Alas, you know not. I must tell you then.   You have forgot the will I told you of.
translation: Alas, you don’t know. I must tell you then. You’ve forgotten the will I told you about.

original: Most true. The will! Let’s stay and hear the will.
translation: That's true. The will! Let’s stay and hear the will!

original: Here is the will, and under Caesar’s seal To every Roman citizen he gives— To every several man—seventy-five drachmas.
translation: Here’s the will, marked by Caesar’s seal. To every Roman citizen he gives—to every single man—seventy-five silver coins.

original: Most noble Caesar! We’ll revenge his death.
translation: Most noble Caesar! We’ll revenge his death.

original: O royal Caesar!
translation: Oh, royal Caesar!

original: Hear me with patience.
translation: Listen to me with patience.

original: Peace, ho!
translation: Quiet!

original: Moreover, he hath left you all his walks,   His private arbors and new-planted orchards,   On this side Tiber.
translation: In addition, he’s left you all of his walkways, his private gardens, and newly planted orchards, on this side of the Tiber River.

original: He hath left them you   And to your heirs forever—common pleasures,   To walk abroad and recreate yourselves.   Here was a Caesar! When comes such another?
translation: He has left them to you and to your heirs forever—public parks where you can wander and relax. Here was a Caesar! When will there be another like him?

original: Never, never.—Come, away, away! We’ll burn his body in the holy place, And with the brands fire the traitors' houses. Take up the body.
translation: Never, never. Come, let’s go, let's go! We’ll burn his body in the holy place, and use the torches to set fire to the traitors' houses. Lift up the body.

original: Go fetch fire.
translation: Go get some fire.

original: Pluck down benches.
translation: Go get some benches for wood.

original: Pluck down forms, windows, anything.
translation: Rip down doors, windowsills, anything.

original: Now let it work. Mischief, thou art afoot. Take thou what course thou wilt!
translation: Now let it work. Mischief, you are on the loose. Follow whatever path you want!

original: How now, fellow?
translation: What’s going on?

original: Sir, Octavius is already come to Rome.
translation: Sir, Octavius has already arrived in Rome.

original: Where is he?
translation: Where is he?

original: He and Lepidus are at Caesar’s house.
translation: He and Lepidus are at Caesar’s house.

original: And thither will I straight to visit him.
translation: I'll go straight there to visit him.

original: He comes upon a wish. Fortune is merry,   And in this mood will give us anything.
translation: He comes just when I hoped he would. Fortune is happy and will give us anything in this mood.

original: I heard him say, Brutus and Cassius Are rid like madmen through the gates of Rome.
translation: I heard Octavius say that Brutus and Cassius rode their horses like madmen to escape through the gates of Rome.

original: Belike they had some notice of the people How I had moved them. Bring me to Octavius.
translation: They probably got some warning of how much I stirred up the people. Bring me to Octavius.

original: I dreamt tonight that I did feast with Caesar,   And things unlucky charge my fantasy.
translation: I dreamed last night that I was feasting with Caesar, and ominous signs filled my mind.

original: I have no will to wander forth of doors,   Yet something leads me forth.
translation: I have no desire to walk around outdoors, yet something leads me out.

original: What is your name?
translation: What’s your name?

original: Whither are you going?
translation: Where are you going?

original: Where do you dwell?
translation: Where do you live?

original: Are you a married man or a bachelor?
translation: Are you married or single?

original: Answer every man directly.
translation: Answer each one of us right now.

original: Ay, and briefly.
translation: Yes, and quickly.

original: Ay, and wisely.
translation: Yes, and wisely.

original: Ay, and truly, you were best.
translation: Yes, and be truthful, or else.

original: What is my name? Whither am I going? Where do I dwell?  Am I a married man or a bachelor?
translation: What’s my name? Where am I going? Where do I live? Am I married or single?

original: Then, to answer every  man directly and briefly, wisely and truly—wisely I say, I am a bachelor.
translation: Then, to answer every man quickly, wisely, and truthfully—wisely, I say, I am single.

original: That’s as much as to say they are fools that marry.  You’ll bear me a bang for that, I fear. Proceed,  directly.
translation: That's like saying that anyone who marries is a fool. I'm afraid you’ll get a beating from me for that. Continue, right now.

original: Directly, I am going to Caesar’s funeral.
translation: Right now, I’m going to Caesar’s funeral.

original: As a friend or an enemy?
translation: As a friend or an enemy?

original: As a friend.
translation: As a friend.

original: That matter is answered directly.
translation: He answered that question straightforwardly.

original: For your dwelling—briefly.
translation: And where do you live—quickly.

original: Briefly, I dwell by the Capitol.
translation: Quickly, I live near the Capitol.

original: Your name, sir, truly.
translation: Tell us your name, sir, truthfully.

original: Truly, my name is Cinna.
translation: Truthfully, my name is Cinna.

original: Tear him to pieces. He’s a conspirator.
translation: Tear him to pieces. He’s a conspirator.

original: I am Cinna the poet. I am Cinna the poet.
translation: I am Cinna the poet. I am Cinna the poet.

original: Tear him for his bad verses! Tear him for his bad  verses!
translation: Tear him apart for his bad poetry. Tear him apart for his bad poetry.

original: I am not Cinna the conspirator.
translation: I am not Cinna the conspirator.

original: It is no matter. His name’s Cinna. Pluck but his name  out of his heart and turn him going.
translation: It doesn’t matter. His name’s Cinna. Rip only his name out of his heart, and send him away.

original: Tear him, tear him! Come, brands, ho! Firebrands: to  Brutus', to Cassius', burn all. Some to Decius' house  and some to Casca’s. Some to Ligarius'. Away, go!
translation: Tear him apart, tear him apart! Come, firebrands: let's go to Brutus’ house; then to Cassius’s house; let’s burn them all. Some of you go to Decius’s house, and some to Casca’s. Some to Ligarius’. Get going. Go!

original: These many, then, shall die. Their names are pricked.
translation: These are the ones who will be killed. Their names are marked.

original: Your brother too must die. Consent you, Lepidus?
translation: Your brother must die, too. Do you agree, Lepidus?

original: I do consent—
translation: I agree—

original: Prick him down, Antony.
translation: Mark him down, Antony.

original: Upon condition Publius shall not live, Who is your sister’s son, Mark Antony.
translation: On the condition that your sister's son, Publius, also must not be allowed to live, Mark Antony.

original: He shall not live. Look, with a spot I damn him.
translation: He will not live. See—with this mark I've sentenced him to death.

original: But, Lepidus, go you to Caesar’s house.   Fetch the will hither, and we shall determine   How to cut off some charge in legacies.
translation: But, Lepidus, go now to Caesar’s house. Bring his will here, and we’ll figure out a way to reduce his gifts to the people.

original: What, shall I find you here?
translation: Will you be here when I get back?

original: Or here, or at the Capitol.
translation: We'll either be here or at the Capitol.

original: This is a slight, unmeritable man,   Meet to be sent on errands.
translation: He’s an insignificant, and unworthy man—only fit to be sent on errands.

original: Is it fit,   The threefold world divided, he should stand   One of the three to share it?
translation: When we've split rulership of the world  into three parts , is it proper that he should be one of the three men to share it?

original: So you thought him. And took his voice who should be pricked to die In our black sentence and proscription.
translation: You thought so. Besides, you listened to his opinion about who we should mark for death.

original: Octavius, I have seen more days than you.   And though we lay these honors on this man   To ease ourselves of divers slanderous loads,   He shall but bear them as the ass bears gold,
translation: Octavius, I’ve lived longer than you have. And though we’re giving these honors to this man so that he carries the blame for the wrongs we’re going to do, he’ll carry these honors like a jackass carries gold

original: To groan and sweat under the business,   Either led or driven, as we point the way.
translation: —groaning and sweating under the load, either led or pushed, as we direct the way he should go.

original: And having brought our treasure where we will,   Then take we down his load and turn him off,   Like to the empty ass, to shake his ears   And graze in commons.
translation: And once he’s brought our treasure where we want, we’ll relieve him of the load and put him out to pasture, like a jackass, to shake his ears and graze.

original: You may do your will, But he’s a tried and valiant soldier.
translation: You can do whatever you want, but he’s an experienced and brave soldier.

original: So is my horse, Octavius, and for that   I do appoint him store of provender.   It is a creature that I teach to fight,   To wind, to stop, to run directly on,
translation: So is my horse, Octavius, and for that reason I give him a supply of food. My horse is a creature that I direct during a fight—to turn, to stop, to run straight ahead.

original: His corporal motion governed by my spirit,   And, in some taste, is Lepidus but so.   He must be taught and trained and bid go forth,
translation: I control his movements. And, to some degree, Lepidus is nothing more than that. He has to be taught and trained and told what to do.

original: A barren-spirited fellow, one that feeds   On objects, arts, and imitations,   Which, out of use and staled by other men,   Begin his fashion.
translation: He's an empty sort of man, and he considers the trends and tastes that went out of fashion with other men long ago to be the utmost in style.

original: Do not talk of him   But as a property.
translation: Don’t think of Lepidus as anything other than a tool for us to use.

original: And now, Octavius,   Listen great things. Brutus and Cassius   Are levying powers. We must straight make head.  Therefore let our alliance be combined,
translation: And now, Octavius, listen to more important things. Brutus and Cassius are building armies. We must immediately do the same. Therefore, we should combine our strength,

original: Our best friends made, our means stretched.   And let us presently go sit in council   How covert matters may be best disclosed,   And open perils surest answered.
translation: confirm the support of our allies, and stretch our connections to their fullest reach. Let’s now go discuss how we can find out what hidden dangers face us, and how to respond to those dangers we already know about.

original: Let us do so. For we are at the stake   And bayed about with many enemies.
translation: Let’s do that, because we’re surrounded by many enemies, like a  bear chained to a stake  and circled by howling dogs.

original: And some that smile have in their hearts, I fear,   Millions of mischiefs.
translation: And I fear that some of the people who smile at us actually mean to harm us.

original: Stand, ho!
translation: Halt!

original: Give the word, ho, and stand.
translation: Hey, pass on the command to halt.

original: What now, Lucillius? Is Cassius near?
translation: What’s going on, Lucillius? Is Cassius nearby?

original: He is at hand, and Pindarus is come To do you salutation from his master.
translation: He’s close by, and Pindarus has come to greet you on his master's behalf.

original: He greets me well.
translation: He has sent a noble man to greet me.

original: —Your master, Pindarus,   In his own change or by ill officers   Hath given me some worthy cause to wish   Things done, undone. But if he be at hand   I shall be satisfied.
translation: [To PINDARUS]  Your master,  Pindarus—either because his feelings for me have changed or because he's been influenced by bad advice—has made me wish we could undo some of the things we've done. But if he is nearby, I'll get an explanation.

original: I do not doubt But that my noble master will appear Such as he is, full of regard and honor.
translation: I don't doubt that my noble master will prove himself to be what he is: respectful and honorable.

original: He is not doubted.
translation: I don’t doubt him.

original: —A word, Lucillius.   [takes LUCILLIUS aside]   How he received you, let me be resolved.
translation: [To LUCILLIUS]  Lucillius, can I speak with you?  [He takes LUCILLIUS aside]  Please tell me, how did Cassius greet you?

original: With courtesy and with respect enough.   But not with such familiar instances
translation: With suitable courtesy and respect, but not with real friendship

original: Nor with such free and friendly conference   As he hath used of old.
translation: or with the same open and friendly conversation that he used to greet me before.

original: Thou hast described   A hot friend cooling.
translation: You’ve described a formerly good friend who’s now cooling off.

original: Ever note, Lucillius,   When love begins to sicken and decay,   It useth an enforcèd ceremony.
translation: Note this, Lucillius: when a love starts to fade and wither, what remains is strained formality

original: There are no tricks in plain and simple faith.   But hollow men, like horses hot at hand,   Make gallant show and promise of their mettle.
translation: . There are no tricks hiding behind plain and simple friendship. But insincere men make a big show of their courage, like horses who are too spirited when a rider first takes the reins.

original: But when they should endure the bloody spur,
translation: But when the going gets tough,

original: They fall their crests and, like deceitful jades,   Sink in the trial.
translation: they drop their necks and fail the test, like the poor horse they truly are.

original: Comes his army on?
translation: Is Cassius' army approaching?

original: They mean this night in Sardis to be quartered. The greater part, the horse in general, Are come with Cassius.
Hark! He is arrived. March gently on to meet him.
translation: Look! He’s arrived. March to meet him slowly, without hostility.

original: Stand, ho!
translation: Halt!

original: Stand, ho! Speak the word along.
translation: Halt! Pass along the order.

original: Stand!
translation: Halt!

original: Stand!
translation: Halt!

original: Stand!
translation: Halt!

original: Most noble brother, you have done me wrong.
translation: Most noble brother, you have done me wrong.

original: Judge me, you gods! Wrong I mine enemies? And if not so, how should I wrong a brother?
translation: May the gods judge me, then! Do I mistreat my enemies? No. So why would I wrong a brother?

original: Brutus, this sober form of yours hides wrongs. And when you do them—
translation: Brutus, this dignified manner of yours hides the fact that you’ve wronged me. And when you do these wrongs—

original: Cassius, be content.   Speak your griefs softly. I do know you well.
translation: Cassius, keep calm. We know each other well, so you don't have to shout your grievances.

original: Before the eyes of both our armies here,   Which should perceive nothing but love from us,   Let us not wrangle. Bid them move away.
translation: Let's not argue in front of our armies, which should see nothing but love between us. Tell them to move away.

original: Then in my tent, Cassius, enlarge your griefs,   And I will give you audience.
translation: Then, in my tent, you can fully explain your grievances, and I’ll listen.

original: Pindarus, Bid our commanders lead their charges off A little from this ground.
translation: Pindarus, tell our commanders to lead their soldiers a little ways away from this spot.

original: Lucillius, do you the like. And let no man Come to our tent till we have done our conference. Let Lucius and Titinius guard our door.
translation: Lucillius, you do the same. And don’t let any man come near our tent until we’ve finished our conversation. Have Lucius and Titinius guard the door.

original: That you have wronged me doth appear in this:   You have condemned and noted Lucius Pella   For taking bribes here of the Sardians,
translation: This is how you have wronged me: you condemned and publicly disgraced Lucius Pella for taking bribes from the Sardinians.

original: Wherein my letters, praying on his side   Because I knew the man, were slighted off.
translation: Then you ignored my letters, in which I asked you to be lenient with him because I know the man.

original: You wronged yourself to write in such a case.
translation: You wronged yourself to write in support of such a man.

original: In such a time as this it is not meet That every nice offense should bear his comment.
translation: In a time like this, it is not appropriate to focus on every little offense.

original: Let me tell you, Cassius, you yourself   Are much condemned to have an itching palm,
translation: Let me tell you, Cassius, that you yourself are often accused of being corrupt

original: To sell and mart your offices for gold   To undeservers.
translation: , of selling positions in your army to undeserving men.

original: I “an itching palm!” You know that you are Brutus that speak this, Or, by the gods, this speech were else your last.
translation: Me, “corrupt!” You know that if you were not Brutus, then I swear by the gods, that speech would have been your last.

original: The name of Cassius honors this corruption, And chastisement doth therefore hide his head.
translation: Cassius, your honorable reputation masks this corruption, and so it is not condemned.

original: Chastisement!
translation: Condemned!

original: Remember March, the ides of March remember.   Did not great Julius bleed for justice' sake?   What villain touched his body, that did stab,   And not for justice?
translation: Remember March. March 15th. Remember. Didn’t great Caesar die for the sake of justice? Any man who stabbed him for reasons other than justice is a villain.

original: What, shall one of us   That struck the foremost man of all this world   But for supporting robbers, shall we now   Contaminate our fingers with base bribes,
translation: What? Did we strike down the most powerful man in the world in part because he allowed tax-collectors to act corruptly, only to dirty our own hands with immoral bribes now?

original: And sell the mighty space of our large honors   For so much trash as may be graspèd thus?
translation: And sell our reputations for as much money as we can grab?

original: I had rather be a dog and bay the moon   Than such a Roman.
translation: I’d rather be a dog, howling at the moon, than be that kind of Roman.

original: Brutus, bait not me.   I’ll not endure it. You forget yourself   To hedge me in.
translation: Brutus, don’t hassle me. I won’t take it. You’re forgetting yourself if you think you can limit my authority.

original: I am a soldier, I,   Older in practice, abler than yourself   To make conditions.
translation: I’m a soldier, more experienced than you, and better able to decide how to manage things.

original: Go to. You are not, Cassius.
translation: You must be kidding! You are not, Cassius.

original: I am.
translation: I am.

original: I say you are not.
translation: I say you’re not.

original: Urge me no more, I shall forget myself. Have mind upon your health, tempt me no further.
translation: Stop pushing me, or I might forget to control myself. Think about your health. Provoke me no more.

original: Away, slight man!
translation: Go away, you little man.

original: Is ’t possible?
translation: Is this possible?

original: Hear me, for I will speak. Must I give way and room to your rash choler? Shall I be frighted when a madman stares?
translation: Listen to me, because I have something to say. Must I give in to your impulsive anger? Should I be frightened when a madman stares wildly around?

original: O ye gods, ye gods, must I endure all this?
translation: Oh you gods, oh you gods! Must I tolerate all this?

original: “All this?” Ay, more. Fret till your proud heart break.   Go show your slaves how choleric you are   And make your bondmen tremble. Must I budge?   Must I observe you?
translation: “All this?” Yes, and more. Rage until your proud heart breaks. Go show your slaves how angry you are, and make your servants tremble. But must I give way? Must I watch out for you?

original: Must I stand and crouch   Under your testy humor? By the gods,   You shall digest the venom of your spleen,   Though it do split you.
translation: Must I hide in fear when you're in a bad mood? By the gods, before I’ll respond to you, you’ll have to swallow the poison of your bad temper until it makes you burst.

original: For from this day forth,   I’ll use you for my mirth, yea, for my laughter,   When you are waspish.
translation: From this day on, you’ll only make me laugh when you get hotheaded.

original: Is it come to this?
translation: Has it come to this?

original: You say you are a better soldier. Let it appear so. Make your vaunting true, And it shall please me well. For mine own part, I shall be glad to learn of noble men.
translation: You say that you’re a better soldier. Prove it. Make your boasting come true, and I’ll be delighted. I’m always happy to learn from noble men.

original: You wrong me every way. You wrong me, Brutus. I said an elder soldier, not a better. Did I say “better?”
translation: You wrong me in every way. You wrong me, Brutus. I said an older soldier, not a better one. Did I say “better?”

original: If you did, I care not.
translation: If you did, I don’t care.

original: When Caesar lived, he durst not thus have moved me.
translation: When Caesar was alive, even he didn't dare to anger me this way.

original: Peace, peace! You durst not so have tempted him.
translation: Enough, enough! You would not have dared to tempt him like this.

original: I durst not!
translation: I wouldn’t have dared!

original: No.
translation: No.

original: What, durst not tempt him?
translation: What? Not dared to tempt him?

original: For your life you durst not!
translation: Not on your life!

original: Do not presume too much upon my love. I may do that I shall be sorry for.
translation: Don’t count too much on my love for you. I might do something that I’ll regret.

original: You have done that you should be sorry for.
translation: You’ve already done the thing you should regret.

original: There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats,   For I am armed so strong in honesty   That they pass by me as the idle wind,   Which I respect not.
translation: Cassius, your threats don’t frighten me, because I’m so sure that I am in the right that they pass me by like an insignificant breeze that I barely even notice.

original: I did send to you   For certain sums of gold, which you denied me,   For I can raise no money by vile means.
translation: I sent you a message asking for a certain amount of gold, which you refused to give me. It's against my nature to raise money in immoral ways.

original: By heaven, I had rather coin my heart   And drop my blood for drachmas than to wring   From the hard hands of peasants their vile trash   By any indirection.
translation: By god, I’d rather turn my heart into money—spilling my blood in exchange for coins—than to wring from the calloused hands of peasants what little they have through dishonesty or trickery.

original: I did send   To you for gold to pay my legions,   Which you denied me.
translation: I asked you for gold to pay my soldiers, and you refused

original: Was that done like Cassius?   Should I have answered Caius Cassius so?
translation: . Is that how Caius Cassius acts? Would I have ever responded in such a way to you?

original: When Marcus Brutus grows so covetous   To lock such rascal counters from his friends,   Be ready, gods, with all your thunderbolts.   Dash him to pieces!
translation: If I ever grow so greedy that I hoard such a measly amount of money from my friends, then, gods, crush me to pieces with your thunderbolts!

original: I denied you not.
translation: I did not refuse you.

original: You did.
translation: You did.

original: I did not. He was but a fool that brought   My answer back. Brutus hath rived my heart.
translation: I did not. The man who brought my answer back to you was a fool. Brutus, you’ve broken my heart.

original: A friend should bear his friend’s infirmities,   But Brutus makes mine greater than they are.
translation: A friend should put up with his friend’s weaknesses, but you make mine seem larger than they are.

original: I do not, till you practice them on me.
translation: I don’t, until you practice them on me.

original: You love me not.
translation: You do not love me.

original: I do not like your faults.
translation: I don’t like your faults.

original: A friendly eye could never see such faults.
translation: A friend would never see those faults.

original: A flatterer’s would not, though they do appear As huge as high Olympus.
translation: No, a flatterer wouldn’t, even though they are as huge as towering Mount Olympus.

original: Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come,   Revenge yourselves alone on Cassius,   For Cassius is aweary of the world—
translation: Come, Antony and young Octavius, come. Take your revenge on Cassius alone, because Cassius has grown tired of the world.

original: Hated by one he loves; braved by his brother;   Checked like a bondman, all his faults observed,   Set in a notebook, learned, and conned by rote   To cast into my teeth.
translation: Hated by someone he loves; defied by his brother; scolded like a servant; and all his faults noted, written down in a notebook, studied, and memorized so that they can be thrown back in his face.

original: Oh, I could weep   My spirit from mine eyes.   [offers BRUTUS his bared dagger]   There is my dagger.   And here my naked breast.
translation: Oh, I could weep my soul right out of my eyes.  [He offers BRUTUS his unsheathed dagger]  There’s my dagger, and here’s my bare chest.

original: Within, a heart   Dearer than Plutus' mine, richer than gold.   If that thou beest a Roman, take it forth.   I, that denied thee gold, will give my heart.
translation: Inside it is a heart more valuable than  Pluto's  silver mine, and richer than gold. If you are a Roman, take out my heart. I, who refused to give you gold, will give you my heart.

original: Strike, as thou didst at Caesar. For I know   When thou didst hate him worst, thou lovedst him better   Than ever thou lovedst Cassius.
translation: Strike at me just as you did at Caesar. Because I know that even when you hated him the most, you still loved him better than you ever loved me.

original: Sheathe your dagger.   Be angry when you will, it shall have scope.   Do what you will, dishonor shall be humor.
translation: No, put away your dagger. Be angry whenever you like, I won’t try to stop you. Do whatever you want, and I’ll look upon your insults as just the product of a bad mood.

original: O Cassius, you are yokèd with a lamb   That carries anger as the flint bears fire,   Who, much enforcèd, shows a hasty spark   And straight is cold again.
translation: Oh, Cassius, you are partners with a quiet lamb that gets angry in the same way that a flint makes fire—a brief spark when struck, and then immediately I’m cold again.

original: Hath Cassius lived To be but mirth and laughter to his Brutus, When grief and blood ill-tempered vexeth him?
translation: Have I lived this long only to be mocked by Brutus when grief and anger get the best of me?

original: When I spoke that, I was ill-tempered too.
translation: When I said that, I was angry too.

original: Do you confess so much? Give me your hand.
translation: You admit that? Give me your hand.

original: And my heart too.
translation: And my heart too.

original: O Brutus!
translation: Oh, Brutus!

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What’s the matter?

original: Have not you love enough to bear with me, When that rash humor which my mother gave me Makes me forgetful?
translation: Do you have enough love for me to patiently bear with me when the bad temper I inherited from my mother makes me forget how I should act?

original: Yes, Cassius. And from henceforth When you are over-earnest with your Brutus, He’ll think your mother chides and leave you so.
translation: Yes, Cassius. And from now on, when you get angry with me, I’ll assume it’s your mother scolding me, and leave it at that.

original: Let me go in to see the generals. There is some grudge between 'em. 'Tis not meet They be alone.
translation: Let me in to see the generals. There’s a grudge between them. It isn’t good for them to be alone.

original: You shall not come to them.
translation: You can’t go in to see them.

original: Nothing but death shall stay me.
translation: Only death will stop me.

original: How now? What’s the matter?
translation: What’s going on? What’s the matter?

original: For shame, you generals! What do you mean? Love, and be friends as two such men should be. For I have seen more years, I’m sure, than ye.
Ha, ha, how vilely doth this cynic rhyme!
translation: Ha ha! How badly this rude man rhymes!

original: Get you hence, sirrah. Saucy fellow, hence!
translation: Get out of here, sir! Rude man, get gone!

original: Bear with him, Brutus. 'Tis his fashion.
translation: Go easy on him, Brutus. That’s just how he is.

original: I’ll know his humor when he knows his time.   What should the wars do with these jigging fools?
translation: I’ll humor his behavior when he learns the right time for it. What should we do with all these rhyming fools that follow our armies?

original: —Companion, hence!
translation: [To the POET]  Get out of here, buddy.

original: Away, away, be gone.
translation: Away, away, be gone.

original: Lucillius and Titinius, bid the commanders Prepare to lodge their companies tonight.
translation: Lucillius and Titinius, tell the commanders to prepare to camp for the night.

original: And come yourselves, and bring Messala with you, Immediately to us.
translation: Then come back, immediately, and bring Messala with you.

original: Lucius, a bowl of wine!
translation: Lucius, bring a bowl of wine.

original: I did not think you could have been so angry.
translation: I didn’t think you could get so angry.

original: O Cassius, I am sick of many griefs.
translation: Oh, Cassius, I’m worn out by many sorrows.

original: Of your philosophy you make no use If you give place to accidental evils.
No man bears sorrow better. Portia is dead.
translation: No one bears sorrow better than I do. Portia is dead.

original: Ha, Portia?
translation: What, Portia?

original: She is dead.
translation: She is dead.

original: How ’scaped I killing when I crossed you so?   O insupportable and touching loss!
translation: How did I escape getting killed when I argued with you just now? What an unbearable and pitiful loss!

original: Upon what sickness?
translation: What sickness killed her?

original: Impatient of my absence,   And grief that young Octavius with Mark Antony   Have made themselves so strong—for with her death   That tidings came—with this she fell distract
translation: Unable to bear my absence, and worried that young Octavius and Mark Antony have become so strong—which I learned about along with the news of her death—she fell into despair.

original: And, her attendants absent, swallowed fire.
translation: And, when her attendants were away, she swallowed burning coals.

original: And died so?
translation: That’s how she died?

original: Even so.
translation: Like that.

original: O ye immortal gods!
translation: Oh, you immortal gods!

original: Speak no more of her.—Give me a bowl of wine.— In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius.
translation: Speak no more about her. Give me a bowl of wine. I bury all our previous anger with this drink, Cassius.

original: My heart is thirsty for that noble pledge. Fill, Lucius, till the wine o'erswell the cup. I cannot drink too much of Brutus' love.
translation: My heart is thirsty for that noble promise. Pour, Lucius, until the wine overflows my cup. I cannot drink too much of Brutus' love.

original: Come in, Titinius.—Welcome, good Messala! Now sit we close about this taper here And call in question our necessities.
translation: Come in, Titinius! Welcome, good Messala. Now let’s sit around this candle and consider our situation.

original: Portia, art thou gone?
translation: Portia, are you really gone?

original: No more, I pray you. —Messala, I have here receivèd letters That young Octavius and Mark Antony Come down upon us with a mighty power, Bending their expedition toward Philippi.
Myself have letters of the selfsame tenor.
translation: I have gotten letters that say the same thing.

original: With what addition?
translation: Do they say anything else?

original: That by proscription and bills of outlawry, Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus Have put to death an hundred senators.
translation: They say that Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus have put to death a hundred senators through legal proclamations declaring men to be unprotected by the law.

original: Therein our letters do not well agree. Mine speak of seventy senators that died By their proscriptions, Cicero being one.
translation: There, our letters don’t agree. My letters mention only seventy senators that were killed, with Cicero being one.

original: Cicero one?
translation: Cicero too?

original: Cicero is dead,   And by that order of proscription.
translation: Cicero is dead, by that same proclamation.

original: [to BRUTUS]   Had you your letters from your wife, my  lord?
translation: [To BRUTUS]  Have you gotten letters from your wife, my lord?

original: No, Messala.
translation: No, Messala.

original: Nor nothing in your letters writ of her?
translation: And the letters you have received say nothing about her?

original: Nothing, Messala.
translation: Nothing, Messala.

original: That methinks is strange.
translation: I think that’s strange.

original: Why ask you? Hear you aught of her in yours?
translation: Why do you ask? Have you heard something about her in your letters?

original: No, my lord.
translation: No, my lord.

original: Now, as you are a Roman, tell me true.
translation: Now, as you’re a Roman, tell me the truth.

original: Then like a Roman bear the truth I tell. For certain she is dead, and by strange manner.
translation: Then like a Roman you must bear the truth. It’s certain that she is dead, and she died in a strange way.

original: Why, farewell, Portia. We must die, Messala. With meditating that she must die once, I have the patience to endure it now.
translation: Well, goodbye, Portia. We all must die, Messala. Knowing that she would have to die sometime, I can endure her death now.

original: Even so great men great losses should endure.
translation: That’s exactly the way that great men should endure great losses.

original: I have as much of this in art as you, But yet my nature could not bear it so.
translation: I know the philosophy of Stoicism as well as you, but I still couldn’t bear this news as you do.

original: Well, to our work alive. What do you think Of marching to Philippi presently?
translation: Well, now for our work concerning the living. Should we march to Philippi immediately?

original: I do not think it good.
translation: I don’t think that's a good idea.

original: Your reason?
translation: Your reasons?

original: This it is:   'Tis better that the enemy seek us.   So shall he waste his means, weary his soldiers,   Doing himself offense,
translation: Here it is: it’s better if the enemy has to come to us. In doing so, he’ll waste his supplies and tire out his soldiers—reducing his own strength.

original: whilst we, lying still,   Are full of rest, defense, and nimbleness.
translation: Meanwhile we will be rested, strong, and nimble by staying here.

original: Good reasons must of force give place to better.   The people ’twixt Philippi and this ground   Do stand but in a forced affection,   For they have grudged us contribution.
translation: Those are good reasons, but they must give way to better ones. The people who live between here and Philippi are only loyal to us out of fear of our force. They only gave us men and money for our army because they felt they had to.

original: The enemy, marching along by them,   By them shall make a fuller number up,   Come on refreshed, new-added, and encouraged,
translation: The enemy, marching past them, will be able to grow by recruiting them. Then, they'll come at us refreshed, newly reinforced, and confident.

original: From which advantage shall we cut him off   If at Philippi we do face him there,   These people at our back.
translation: We can block this advantage if we face the enemy at Philippi, because these people will then be behind us.

original: Hear me, good brother—
translation: Listen to me, good brother—

original: Under your pardon. You must note beside,   That we have tried the utmost of our friends,   Our legions are brim-full, our cause is ripe.   The enemy increaseth every day.
translation: Allow me to finish. You must also recognize that we’ve gotten as much as we can from those who support us. Our regiments are full, and our cause is ready. While the enemy gets larger each day,

original: We, at the height, are ready to decline.   There is a tide in the affairs of men,   Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune;
translation: we—now at our largest—can only decrease. There’s a kind of tidal movement, a back-and-forth, in the affairs of men. Acting when you are at high tide leads to success

original: Omitted, all the voyage of their life   Is bound in shallows and in miseries.
translation: . But if you miss high tide, all the rest of the voyage of your life will be mired in the shallows of misery.

original: On such a full sea are we now afloat,   And we must take the current when it serves   Or lose our ventures.
translation: We now float on such a high tide. And we must ride the current now, or lose out.

original: Then, with your will, go on. We’ll along ourselves, and meet them at Philippi.
translation: Then, if that’s your desire, proceed. We two will go as well, and meet them at Philippi.

original: The deep of night is crept upon our talk,   And nature must obey necessity,
translation: Night has snuck up on us while we were talking. Our bodies must obey the requirement of nature and sleep.

original: Which we will niggard with a little rest.   There is no more to say?
translation: But we’ll satisfy that requirement with as little rest as possible. Is there anything else to discuss?

original: No more. Good night. Early tomorrow will we rise and hence.
translation: Nothing else. Good night. Early tomorrow, we will get up and get moving.

original: Lucius!
translation: Lucius!

original: My gown.
translation: My nightgown.

original: Farewell, good Messala.— Good night, Titinius.—Noble, noble Cassius, Good night and good repose.
translation: Farewell, good Messala. Good night, Titinius. Noble, noble Cassius, good night, and sleep well.

original: O my dear brother, This was an ill beginning of the night. Never come such division ’tween our souls. Let it not, Brutus.
translation: Oh, my dear brother! This was a poor start to the night. May we never again have such a disagreement. Let’s not, Brutus.

original: Everything is well.
translation: All is well.

original: Good night, my lord.
translation: Good night, my lord.

original: Good night, good brother.
translation: Good night, good brother.

original: Good night, Lord Brutus.
translation: Good night, Lord Brutus.

original: Farewell, everyone.
translation: Farewell, everyone.

original: Give me the gown. Where is thy instrument?
translation: Give me the nightgown. Where’s your lute?

original: Here in the tent.
translation: Here in the tent.

original: What, thou speak’st drowsily?   Poor knave, I blame thee not. Thou art o'erwatched.
translation: What, you speak as if you are tired? Poor fool, I don’t blame you. You’ve stayed awake too long, watching over me.

original: Call Claudio and some other of my men.   I’ll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.
translation: Call Claudio and some of my other men. I’ll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.

original: Varrus and Claudio!
translation: Varrus and Claudio!

original: Calls my lord?
translation: You called us, my lord?

original: I pray you, sirs, lie in my tent and sleep. It may be I shall raise you by and by On business to my brother Cassius.
translation: Sirs, I ask you to sleep in my tent. I might wake you up at some point to send you on business to my brother Cassius.

original: So please you, we will stand and watch your pleasure.
translation: If you’d like, we’ll stand by and be ready to do what whatever you need.

original: I will not have it so. Lie down, good sirs.   It may be I shall otherwise bethink me.
translation: I refuse to let you stay up. Lie down, good sirs. I might decide not to send you.

original: —Look, Lucius, here’s the book I sought for so.   I put it in the pocket of my gown.
translation: Look, Lucius, here’s the book I was searching for. I put it in the pocket of my nightgown.

original: I was sure your lordship did not give it me.
translation: I was sure that you hadn’t given it to me.

original: Bear with me, good boy, I am much forgetful.
translation: Bear with me, good boy. I’m very forgetful.

original: Canst thou hold up thy heavy eyes awhile,   And touch thy instrument a strain or two?
translation: Can you stay awake a while longer and play a song or two on your lute?

original: Ay, my lord, an ’t please you.
translation: Yes,  if it would make you happy, my lord.

original: It does, my boy. I trouble thee too much, but thou art willing.
translation: It would, my boy. I ask too much of you, but you’re willing.

original: It is my duty, sir.
translation: It’s my duty, sir.

original: I should not urge thy duty past thy might. I know young bloods look for a time of rest.
translation: I shouldn’t make you perform your duty beyond what you’re able to do. I know that the young need rest.

original: I have slept, my lord, already.
translation: I’ve slept already, my lord.

original: It was well done, and thou shalt sleep again. I will not hold thee long. If I do live, I will be good to thee.
translation: That was smart, and you’ll sleep some more. I won’t keep you very long. If I survive, I’ll be good to you.

original: This is a sleepy tune. O murderous slumber,   Layst thou thy leaden mace upon my boy   That plays thee music?
translation: This is a sleepy tune. Oh, deadening sleep, have you touched your staff to my boy who plays music for you?

original: —Gentle knave, good night.   I will not do thee so much wrong to wake thee.   If thou dost nod, thou break’st thy instrument.   I’ll take it from thee. And, good boy, good night.
translation: [To LUCIUS]  Dear boy, good night. I won’t trouble you so much as to wake you. If your head were to nod down, you’d break your instrument, so I’ll take it from you. Good boy, good night.

original: —Let me see, let me see. Is not the leaf turned down   Where I left reading? Here it is, I think.
translation: [To himself]  Let me see, let me see. Didn’t I turn down the corner of the page where I stopped reading? Here it is, I think.

original: How ill this taper burns!—Ha, who comes here?   I think it is the weakness of mine eyes   That shapes this monstrous apparition.   It comes upon me.—Art thou any thing?
translation: This candle is so dim. Hey! Who comes here? I think the weakness in my eyes is making me see this awful ghost. It’s coming toward me. Are you real?

original: Art thou some god, some angel, or some devil   That makest my blood cold and my hair to stare?   Speak to me what thou art.
translation: Are you some god, some angel, or some devil, that you make my blood turn cold and my hair stand up? Tell me what you are.

original: Thy evil spirit, Brutus.
translation: Your evil spirit, Brutus.

original: Why comest thou?
translation: Why did you come here?

original: To tell thee thou shalt see me at Philippi.
translation: To tell you that you’ll see me at Philippi.

original: Well, then I shall see thee again?
translation: Then I will see you again?

original: Ay, at Philippi.
translation: Yes, at Philippi.

original: Why, I will see thee at Philippi, then.
translation: I guess I will see you at Philippi, then.

original: Now I have taken heart thou vanishest. Ill spirit, I would hold more talk with thee. —Boy, Lucius!—Varrus!—Claudio!—Sirs, awake! —Claudio!
translation: Just as I get the courage to talk to you, you disappear. Evil spirit, I’d like to talk with you some more. Boy, Lucius! Varrus! Claudio! Sirs, awake! Claudio!

original: The strings, my lord, are false.
translation: The strings are out of tune, my lord.

original: He thinks he still is at his instrument. Lucius, awake.
translation: He thinks he’s still playing his instrument. Lucius, wake up!

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: Didst thou dream, Lucius, that thou so criedst out?
translation: Were you dreaming, Lucius? Is that why you cried out?

original: My lord, I do not know that I did cry.
translation: My lord, I don’t know if I did cry out.

original: Yes, that thou didst. Didst thou see any thing?
translation: Yes, you did. Did you see anything?

original: Nothing, my lord.
translation: Nothing, my lord.

original: Sleep again, Lucius.—Sirrah Claudio!  Fellow thou, awake!
translation: Go back to sleep, Lucius. Sir Claudio! You there, wake up!

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: Why did you so cry out, sirs, in your sleep?
translation: Why did you cry out in your sleep?

original: Did we, my lord?
translation: Did we, my lord?

original: Ay. Saw you anything?
translation: Yes. Did you see anything?

original: No, my lord, I saw nothing.
translation: No, my lord, I didn’t see anything.

original: Nor I, my lord.
translation: Me neither, my lord.

original: Go and commend me to my brother Cassius.
translation: Go and bring my greetings to my brother Cassius.

original: Bid him set on his powers betimes before,   And we will follow.
translation: Ask him to get his soldiers marching first, and we will follow.

original: It shall be done, my lord.
translation: It will be done, my lord.

original: Now, Antony, our hopes are answerèd.   You said the enemy would not come down   But keep the hills and upper regions.
translation: Now, Antony, our prayers have been answered. You said the enemy wouldn’t come down, but would keep to the hills and high ground instead. They have not.

original: It proves not so. Their battles are at hand.   They mean to warn us at Philippi here,   Answering before we do demand of them.
translation: Their forces are nearby. They mean to attack us here on the plains of Philippi, fig hting us before we’ve forced them to.

original: Tut, I am in their bosoms, and I know   Wherefore they do it. They could be content   To visit other places, and come down
translation: No, I know their secret thoughts, and I understand why they’re doing this. They’d be happier if they were somewhere else.

original: With fearful bravery, thinking by this face   To fasten in our thoughts that they have courage.   But ’tis not so.
translation: They come here with a false show of bravery, to convince us that they have courage. But they don’t.

original: Prepare you, generals.   The enemy comes on in gallant show.
translation: Prepare yourselves, generals. The enemy approaches with a great display.

original: Their bloody sign of battle is hung out,   And something to be done immediately.
translation: They’ve raised their battle standards as if they are about to attack.

original: Octavius, lead your battle softly on, Upon the left hand of the even field.
translation: Octavius, lead your forces out slowly, to the left side of the flat field.

original: Upon the right hand I. Keep thou the left.
translation: I’ll go to the right side. You take the left.

original: Why do you cross me in this exigent?
translation: Why do you defy me at this critical moment?

original: I do not cross you. But I will do so.
translation: I’m not defying you. But this is what I’m going to do.

original: They stand and would have parley.
translation: They haven't advanced, and want to talk.

original: Stand fast, Titinius. We must out and talk.
translation: Stay here, Titinius. We must go and talk to them.

original: Mark Antony, shall we give sign of battle?
translation: Mark Antony, should we give the signal to attack?

original: No, Caesar, we will answer on their charge.
translation: No, Octavius Caesar. We’ll only respond once they attack.

original: Make forth. The generals would have some words.
translation: Step forward. The generals want to speak with us.

original: Stir not until the signal.
translation: Don’t move until we give the signal.

original: Words before blows. Is it so, countrymen?
translation: Words before fighting. Is that it, countrymen?

original: Not that we love words better, as you do.
translation: Not that we prefer words to fighting, as you do.

original: Good words are better than bad strokes, Octavius.
translation: Good words are better than worthless fighting, Octavius.

original: In your bad strokes, Brutus, you give good words. Witness the hole you made in Caesar’s heart, Crying “Long live, hail, Caesar!”
translation: Brutus, along with your treacherous strokes you say “good” words. For instance, the hole you made in Caesar’s heart while you cried, “Long live Caesar! Hail, Caesar!”

original: Antony, The posture of your blows are yet unknown. But for your words, they rob the Hybla bees And leave them honeyless.
Not stingless too?
translation: Didn’t I take the bees' stingers too?

original: Oh, yes, and soundless too. For you have stol'n their buzzing, Antony, And very wisely threat before you sting.
translation: Oh, yes, and their sounds, because you stole their buzzing. Antony, you seem to do a lot of warning about how you are going to sting.

original: Villains, you did not so when your vile daggers   Hacked one another in the sides of Caesar.
translation: Scoundrels, you did not give any warning before your vile daggers clashed, hacking away at Caesar's sides.

original: You showed your teeth like apes, and fawned like  hounds,   And bowed like bondmen, kissing Caesar’s feet,
translation: You smiled like apes and fawned like dogs and bowed like servants, kissing Caesar’s feet.

original: Whilst damnèd Casca, like a cur, behind   Struck Caesar on the neck. O you flatterers!
translation: Then damned Casca, like a mangy dog, struck Caesar on the neck from behind. Oh, you flatterers!

original: Flatterers?—Now, Brutus, thank yourself. This tongue had not offended so today If Cassius might have ruled.
translation: Flatterers? Now, Brutus, you have only yourself to thank. Antony’s tongue would not be offending us today if I’d had my way.

original: Come, come, the cause. If arguing make us sweat,   The proof of it will turn to redder drops.
translation: Come, come, back to the point. Arguing makes us sweat, but the real trial will produce blood.

original: [draws his sword]   Look, I draw a sword against  conspirators.   When think you that the sword goes up again?
translation: [He draws his sword]  Look: I draw my sword against conspirators. When do you think I’ll put this sword away again?

original: Never, till Caesar’s three and thirty wounds   Be well avenged, or till another Caesar   Have added slaughter to the sword of traitors.
translation: Never, until Caesar’s thirty-three wounds are well avenged, or until you traitors have killed me too.

original: Caesar, thou canst not die by traitors' hands Unless thou bring’st them with thee.
translation: Octavius Caesar, the only way you will die by a traitor’s hands is if you have some mutinous soldiers in your army.

original: So I hope. I was not born to die on Brutus' sword.
translation: I hope you’re right. I wasn’t born to die on your sword.

original: O, if thou wert the noblest of thy strain, Young man, thou couldst not die more honorable.
translation: Oh, young man, if you were the noblest of your family you couldn’t die more honorably.

original: A peevish schoolboy, worthless of such honor, Joined with a masker and a reveler!
translation: A cranky schoolboy, unworthy of such an honor, partnered with a masquerader and a partier!

original: Old Cassius still.
translation: The same old Cassius.

original: Come, Antony, away.—
translation: Come, Antony, let’s go.

original: Defiance, traitors, hurl we in your teeth.   If you dare fight today, come to the field.   If not, when you have stomachs.
translation: [To CASSIUS and BRUTUS]  Traitors, we throw our defiance at your teeth. If you dare to fight today, come to the field. If not, come when you have the courage.

original: Why, now, blow wind, swell billow, and swim bark! The storm is up and all is on the hazard.
translation: Blow wind, swell waves, and may the ship float where it will! The storm has risen and everything is at stake.

original: Ho, Lucillius, hark, a word with you.
translation: Hey, Lucillius! I’d like a word with you.

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: Messala!
translation: Messala!

original: What says my general?
translation: What is it, my general?

original: Messala,   This is my birthday, as this very day   Was Cassius born.
translation: Messala, today is my birthday. On this very day, I was born.
