original: Give me thy hand, Messala.   Be thou my witness that against my will,   As Pompey was, am I compelled to set   Upon one battle all our liberties.
translation: Give me your hand, Messala. Be my witness that I’ve been forced against my desire, as Pompey was, to bet all of our freedoms on one battle.

original: You know that I held Epicurus strong   And his opinion. Now I change my mind,   And partly credit things that do presage.
translation: You know that I used to believe in  Epicurus ' position that the gods did not send omens. Now I’ve changed my mind, and partly believe in signs that foretell what is to come.

original: Coming from Sardis, on our former ensign   Two mighty eagles fell, and there they perched,   Gorging and feeding from our soldiers' hands,   Who to Philippi here consorted us.
translation: As we traveled from Sardis, two mighty eagles landed and perched on our front flag, and ate from the hands of the soldiers who marched with us to Philippi.

original: This morning are they fled away and gone,   And in their steads do ravens, crows, and kites   Fly o'er our heads and downward look on us   As we were sickly prey.
translation: This morning, they’ve flown away and in their place are ravens, crows, and kites, flying over our heads and looking down on us, as though we were their sickly prey.

original: Their shadows seem   A canopy most fatal, under which   Our army lies, ready to give up the ghost.
translation: Their shadows are like a deadly canopy, under which our army lies, ready to die.

original: Believe not so.
translation: Don’t believe it.

original: I but believe it partly, For I am fresh of spirit and resolved To meet all perils very constantly.
translation: I believe it only partly, for I’m hopeful and determined to meet all dangers without flinching.

original: Even so, Lucillius.
translation: Right, Lucillius.

original: Now, most noble Brutus,   The gods today stand friendly that we may,   Lovers in peace, lead on our days to age.
translation: Now, most noble Brutus, may the gods be friendly with us today so that we, who love peace, can live on to old age.

original: But since the affairs of men rest still incertain,   Let’s reason with the worst that may befall.
translation: But since the affairs of men are always uncertain, let’s think about the worst that may happen.

original: If we do lose this battle, then is this   The very last time we shall speak together.   What are you then determinèd to do?
translation: If we lose this battle, then this will be the last time we speak to each other. What do you plan to do if we do lose?

original: Even by the rule of that philosophy   By which I did blame Cato for the death   Which he did give himself
translation: By the same Stoic philosophy that made me condemn Cato for committing suicide,

original: — I know not how,   But I do find it cowardly and vile,   For fear of what might fall, so to prevent   The time of life —
translation: . I don’t know why, but I find it cowardly and vile to cut off your life early by suicide, in order to prevent possible suffering later on.

original: arming myself with patience   To stay the providence of some high powers   That govern us below.
translation: I will be patient and await whatever outcome the gods have in store for us

original: Then if we lose this battle You are contented to be led in triumph Thorough the streets of Rome?
translation: Then if we lose this battle, you’d be willing to be led in chains by those who defeated you through the streets of Rome?

original: No, Cassius, no. Think not, thou noble Roman,   That ever Brutus will go bound to Rome.   He bears too great a mind. But this same day   Must end that work the ides of March begun.
translation: No, Cassius, no. Don’t imagine, you noble Roman, that I will ever return to Rome in chains. I am too great for that. But today will be the end of the work that we began on March 15th.

original: And whether we shall meet again I know not.   Therefore our everlasting farewell take.
translation: I don’t know if we will ever meet again. Therefore, accept my everlasting farewell. Forever and forever, farewell, Cassius.

original: Forever and forever farewell, Cassius.   If we do meet again, why, we shall smile.   If not, why then this parting was well made.
translation: If we meet again, why, then we’ll smile. If not, then this parting was well done.

original: Forever and forever farewell, Brutus. If we do meet again, we’ll smile indeed. If not, ’tis true this parting was well made.
translation: Forever and forever, farewell, Brutus. If we meet again, we’ll smile indeed. If not, it’s true this parting was well done.

original: Why then, lead on. Oh, that a man might know   The end of this day’s business ere it come!
translation: Then, lead on. Oh, if only I could know the outcome of today’s business before it happens!

original: But it sufficeth that the day will end,   And then the end is known.—Come, ho! Away!
translation: But it’s enough to know that the day will end, and then the end will be known. Come! Let’s go!

original: Ride, ride, Messala, ride, and give these bills Unto the legions on the other side.
translation: Ride, ride, Messala! Ride, and give these written orders to Cassius’ forces on the other side.

original: Let them set on at once, for I perceive   But cold demeanor in Octavius' wing,
translation: They should attack right now, because Octavius’ forces seem demoralized.

original: And sudden push gives them the overthrow.   Ride, ride, Messala. Let them all come down.
translation: A sudden push would defeat them entirely. Ride, ride, Messala. All Cassius’ men should commit to the attack.

original: O, look, Titinius, look, the villains fly!   Myself have to mine own turned enemy.
translation: Oh, look, Titinius, look! My soldiers, those scoundrels, are running away! I have become an enemy to my own soldiers!

original: This ensign here of mine was turning back.   I slew the coward and did take it from him.   [indicates his standard]
translation: This flag-bearer of mine was running away, so I killed the coward and took the flag from him.  [Points to the flag he’s holding]

original: O Cassius, Brutus gave the word too early,   Who, having some advantage on Octavius,   Took it too eagerly.
translation: Oh, Cassius, Brutus gave the orders too soon. Having an advantage on Octavius, he took a his chance too early.

original: His soldiers fell to spoil,   Whilst we by Antony are all enclosed.
translation: His soldiers began looting, while we were surrounded by Antony’s men.

original: Fly further off, my lord, fly further off.   Mark Antony is in your tents, my lord.
translation: Retreat further, my lord, retreat further. Mark Antony has over-run your camp, my lord.

original: Fly, therefore, noble Cassius, fly far off.
translation: Run, noble Cassius, run far away.

original: This hill is far enough.—Look, look, Titinius. Are those my tents where I perceive the fire?
translation: This hill is far enough. Look, look, Titinius. Are those my tents on fire?

original: They are, my lord.
translation: They are, my lord.

original: Titinius, if thou lovest me,   Mount thou my horse, and hide thy spurs in him   Till he have brought thee up to yonder troops   And here again,
translation: Titinius, if you love me, get on your horse and spur him on as fast as you can until he’s brought you near to those troops and back again.

original: that I may rest assured   Whether yond troops are friend or enemy.
translation: That way, I can learn whether those troops are friends or enemies.

original: I will be here again, even with a thought.
translation: I’ll be there and back again, as quick as a thought.

original: Go, Pindarus, get higher on that hill.   My sight was ever thick.
translation: Go, Pindarus. Climb a little higher up that hill. My eyesight was always bad.

original: Regard Titinius,   And tell me what thou notest about the field.
translation: Watch Titinius and tell me what you see in the field.

original: This day I breathed first. Time is come round,   And where I did begin, there shall I end.   My life is run his compass.
translation: Today was the day I breathed my first breath. Time has come around, and I’ll end where I began—on my birthday. My life has run its circle.

original: [to PINDARUS]   Sirrah, what news?
translation: [To PINDARUS]  What can you see, boy?

original: O my lord!
translation: Oh, my lord!

original: What news?
translation: What news?

original: [above]   Titinius is enclosèd round about   With horsemen, that make to him on the spur.   Yet he spurs on. Now they are almost on him.
translation: [From above the stage]  Titinius is surrounded by horsemen who are riding rapidly toward him. Yet he rides onward. Now they’re almost on him.

original: Now, Titinius. Now some light. Oh, he lights too.   He’s ta'en.
translation: Now, Titinius! Now some men are dismounting from their horses. Oh, he's getting down too. He’s been taken captive.

original: And, hark! They shout for joy.
translation: And listen! They shout for joy.

original: Come down, behold no more. Oh, coward that I am, to live so long To see my best friend ta'en before my face!
translation: Come down. Don't look anymore. Oh, what a coward I am to live long enough to see my best friend taken before my eyes!

original: Come hither, sirrah.   In Parthia did I take thee prisoner.
translation: Come here, boy. I took you prisoner in  Parthia , and

original: And then I swore thee, saving of thy life,   That whatsoever I did bid thee do,   Thou shouldst attempt it. Come now, keep thine oath.
translation: at that time, I spared your life and made you swear to attempt to do whatever I ordered you to.  Come now, keep your oath.

original: [gives his sword to PINDARUS]   Now be a free man, and with this good sword   That ran through Caesar’s bowels, search this bosom.
translation: [He gives his sword to PINDARUS]  Now you’ll be a free man. Take this good sword, which ran through Caesar’s guts, and thrust it into my chest.

original: Stand not to answer. Here take thou the hilts   And, when my face is covered, as ’tis now,   Guide thou the sword.
translation: Don’t pause to ask questions. Here, take the handle, and when my face is covered as it is now, thrust the sword.

original: Caesar, thou art revenged, Even with the sword that killed thee.
translation: Caesar, you are revenged, with the same sword that killed you.

original: So I am free. Yet would not so have been,   Durst I have done my will.
translation: So I’m free. But if I had dared to follow my own desires, I wouldn't be free.

original: O Cassius,   Far from this country Pindarus shall run,   Where never Roman shall take note of him.
translation: Oh, Cassius, I’ll run far from this country to where no Romans can find me.

original: It is but change, Titinius, for Octavius Is overthrown by noble Brutus' power, As Cassius' legions are by Antony.
translation: Titinius, it’s a meaningless change. Noble Brutus’ forces overcame Octavius' troops at the same time Antony overcame Cassius’ legions.

original: These tidings will well comfort Cassius.
translation: This news will comfort Cassius.

original: Where did you leave him?
translation: Where did you leave him?

original: All disconsolate, With Pindarus his bondman on this hill.
translation: In despair, with his slave Pindarus on this hill.

original: Is not that he that lies upon the ground?
translation: Isn’t that him lying on the ground?

original: He lies not like the living. O my heart!
translation: He lies there as if he isn’t alive. Oh, my heart!

original: Is not that he?
translation: Isn’t that him?

original: No, this was he, Messala,   But Cassius is no more. O setting sun,   As in thy red rays thou dost sink tonight,   So in his red blood Cassius' day is set.
translation: It was him, Messala. But Cassius is no more. Oh, setting sun, just as you sink into your red rays to end the day, so has Cassius’ life ended in his own red blood.

original: The sun of Rome is set. Our day is gone.   Clouds, dews, and dangers come! Our deeds are done.   Mistrust of my success hath done this deed.
translation: The sun of Rome has set! Our day is over. Clouds, dew, and dangers approach. We’re finished! His doubts about the successful outcome of my mission drove him to kill himself.

original: Mistrust of good success hath done this deed.   O hateful error, melancholy’s child,   Why dost thou show to the apt thoughts of men   The things that are not?
translation: His uncertainty of any positive outcome drove him to do this. Despair, why do you make men believe things that are false, so that they act in error?

original: O error, soon conceived,   Thou never comest unto a happy birth   But kill’st the mother that engendered thee!
translation: And error, as soon as you come into being, you kill the person that created you, instead of bringing joy to that person!

original: What, Pindarus! Where art thou, Pindarus?
translation: Pindarus! Where are you, Pindarus?

original: Seek him, Titinius, whilst I go to meet   The noble Brutus, thrusting this report   Into his ears.
translation: Titinius, look for Pindarus while I go to meet the noble Brutus and thrust this news into his ears.

original: I may say “thrusting” it,   For piercing steel and darts envenomèd   Shall be as welcome to the ears of Brutus   As tidings of this sight.
translation: I say “thrust” because Brutus would prefer to have sharp blades and poisoned darts in his ears than to hear of this.

original: Hie you, Messala, And I will seek for Pindarus the while.
translation: Get going, Messala, and I’ll look for Pindarus in the meantime.

original: Why didst thou send me forth, brave Cassius?   Did I not meet thy friends? And did not they   Put on my brows this wreath of victory   And bid me give it thee? Didst thou not hear their  shouts?
translation: Why did you send me out, brave Cassius? Didn’t I meet up with your allies? And didn’t they place the wreath of victory on my forehead and ask me to give it to you? Didn’t you hear their shouts?

original: Alas, thou hast misconstrued everything!   But, hold thee, take this garland on thy brow.   Thy Brutus bid me give it thee, and I   Will do his bidding.
translation: Alas, you misunderstood everything! But, wait, I’ll place this wreath on your head. Your Brutus asked me to give it to you, and I’ll do as he asks.

original: [lays wreath on CASSIUS’ head]   Brutus, come apace,   And see how I regarded Caius Cassius.
translation: [He lays a wreath on CASSIUS’ head]  Brutus, come quickly, and see how much I loved Caius Cassius.

original: —By your leave, gods, this is a Roman’s part.   Come, Cassius' sword, and find Titinius' heart.   [stabs himself with CASSIUS’s sword and dies]
translation: With your permission, gods, this is a Roman’s duty. Come, Cassius’s sword, and find Titinius’s heart.  [He stabs himself with CASSIUS’ sword and dies.]

original: Where, where, Messala, doth his body lie?
translation: Where, where is his body lying, Messala?

original: Lo, yonder, and Titinius mourning it.
translation: Look, over there, where Titinius mourns it.

original: Titinius' face is upward.
translation: Titinius is lying face-up.

original: He is slain.
translation: He is dead.

original: O Julius Caesar, thou art mighty yet! Thy spirit walks abroad and turns our swords In our own proper entrails.
translation: Oh, Julius Caesar, you are still mighty. Your ghost walks among us, and turns our swords toward our own stomachs.

original: Brave Titinius!— Look whe 'er he have not crowned dead Cassius.
translation: Brave Titinius! Look, he even placed a wreath on dead Cassius!

original: Are yet two Romans living such as these?
translation: Are there two Romans left who are as good as these men?

original: —The last of all the Romans, fare thee well!   It is impossible that ever Rome   Should breed thy fellow.
translation: [To CASSIUS and TITINIUS' bodies]  Goodbye, the last of all the Romans. It is impossible that Rome will ever produce your equal.

original: —Friends, I owe more tears   To this dead man than you shall see me pay.
translation: [To the others]  Friends, I owe more tears to this dead man than you will see me shed.

original: —I shall find time, Cassius, I shall find time.
translation: [To CASSIUS' body]  I will find the time to cry for you, Cassius, I will find the time.

original: —Come, therefore, and to Thasos send his body.   His funerals shall not be in our camp,   Lest it discomfort us.
translation: [To the others]  Come, now, and send his body to  Thasos . His funeral won’t be held at our camp, because it may make us too demoralized to fight.

original: —Lucillius, come.
translation: Lucillius, come.

original: —   And come, young Cato. Let us to the field.
translation: And come, young Cato. Let’s go to the field

original: —Labio and Flavio, set our battles on.
translation: . Labio and Flavio, send our armies forward.

original: —'Tis three o'clock, and, Romans, yet ere night   We shall try fortune in a second fight.
translation: It is three o'clock. And, Romans, before night, we will test our luck in a second battle.

original: Yet, countrymen, O, yet hold up your heads!
translation: Fight on, countrymen. Oh, keep holding your heads up high!

original: What bastard doth not? Who will go with me?
translation: Who would be such a bastard as to give up? Who will fight on with me?

original: I will proclaim my name about the field.   I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!   A foe to tyrants, and my country’s friend.   I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!
translation: I will proclaim my name around the field. I am the son of Marcus Cato! An enemy to tyrants and a friend to my country. Hey, I am the son of Marcus Cato!

original: And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I! Brutus, my country’s friend. Know me for Brutus!
translation: And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus. Brutus, my country’s friend. Know that I am Brutus!

original: O young and noble Cato, art thou down? Why, now thou diest as bravely as Titinius, And mayst be honored, being Cato’s son.
translation: Oh, young and noble Cato, are you killed? Why, you die now as bravely as Titinius did. And you will be honored as Cato’s son.

original: Yield, or thou diest.
translation: Surrender, or you die.

original: Only I yield to die. There is so much that thou wilt kill me straight. Kill Brutus, and be honored in his death.
translation: I’ll surrender only to death. Here’s enough money for you to kill me immediately. Kill Brutus, and be honored by the killing.

original: We must not. A noble prisoner!
translation: We must not. He’s a noble prisoner!

original: Room, ho! Tell Antony Brutus is ta'en.
translation: Hey, make room! Tell Antony that Brutus has been taken.

original: I’ll tell the news. Here comes the general. —Brutus is ta'en, Brutus is ta'en, my lord.
translation: I’ll tell him the news. Here comes the general. Brutus is captured, Brutus is captured, my lord.

original: Where is he?
translation: Where is he?

original: Safe, Antony. Brutus is safe enough.   I dare assure thee that no enemy   Shall ever take alive the noble Brutus.
translation: Safe, Antony. Brutus is safe enough. I assure you that no enemy will ever take the noble Brutus alive.

original: The gods defend him from so great a shame!
translation: The gods protect him from so great a shame!

original: When you do find him, or alive or dead,   He will be found like Brutus, like himself.
translation: When you do find him, alive or dead, he’ll be found as Brutus, on his own terms.

original: [to SOLDIERS]   This is not Brutus, friend, but, I assure you,   A prize no less in worth. Keep this man safe.   Give him all kindness.
translation: [To SOLDIERS]  Friend, this isn’t Brutus. But, I assure you, he is as valuable a prize. Keep this man safe. Be gentle with him.

original: I had rather have   Such men my friends than enemies.
translation: I would rather have such men as my friends than as my enemies.

original: Go on,   And see whether Brutus be alive or dead.   And bring us word unto Octavius' tent   How everything is chanced.
translation: Keep going, and see if Brutus is alive or dead. Then return to Octavius’ tent to bring us word of how thing’s have turned out.

original: Come, poor remains of friends, rest on this rock.
translation: Come, my few last remaining friends, and rest on this rock.

original: Statilius showed the torchlight but, my lord, He came not back. He is or ta'en or slain.
translation: Statilius waved the torchlight at us, but he hasn’t come back. He’s been captured or killed.

original: Sit thee down, Clitus. Slaying is the word. It is a deed in fashion. Hark thee, Clitus.
translation: Sit down, Clitus. Killed, probably. It’s in fashion, apparently. Listen, Clitus.

original: What, I, my lord? No, not for all the world.
translation: Who, me, my lord? No, not for all the world.

original: Peace then! No words.
translation: Silence, then! Don’t say anything.

original: I’ll rather kill myself.
translation: I’d rather kill myself.

original: Hark thee, Dardanius.
translation: Listen, Dardanius.

original: Shall I do such a deed?
translation: Me, do something like that?

original: O Dardanius!
translation: Oh, Dardanius!

original: O Clitus!
translation: Oh, Clitus!

original: What ill request did Brutus make to thee?
translation: What awful request did Brutus ask of you?

original: To kill him, Clitus. Look, he meditates.
translation: To kill him, Clitus. Look, he’s thinking about what to do.

original: Now is that noble vessel full of  grief, That it runs over even at his eyes.
translation: Now that noble man is so full of grief that it spills from his eyes.

original: Come hither, good Volumnius. List a word.
translation: Come here, good Volumnius. Listen for a minute.

original: What says my lord?
translation: What is it, my lord?

original: Why this, Volumnius:   The ghost of Caesar hath appeared to me   Two several times by night.
translation: Well, this, Volumnius. The ghost of Caesar has appeared to me two times at night.

original: At Sardis once,   And this last night here in Philippi fields.   I know my hour is come.
translation: Once at Sardis, and then last night, here in the fields of Philippi. I know that my hour has come.

original: Not so, my lord.
translation: No it hasn’t, my lord.

original: Nay, I am sure it is, Volumnius. Thou seest the world, Volumnius, how it goes. Our enemies have beat us to the pit.
translation: No, I’m sure it has, Volumnius. You understand the world and how it works, Volumnius. Our enemies have driven us to the edge of the grave.

original: It is more worthy to leap in ourselves   Than tarry till they push us.
translation: It’s nobler to leap in ourselves than wait until they push us. Good Volumnius, you know that we went to school together.

original: Good Volumnius,   Thou know’st that we two went to school together.   Even for that our love of old, I prithee,   Hold thou my sword hilts, whilst I run on it.
translation: In the name of our old friendship, I beg you, hold my the handle of my sword while I impale myself on it.

original: That’s not an office for a friend, my lord.
translation: That’s not a job for a friend, my lord.

original: Fly, fly, my lord. There is no tarrying here.
translation: Run, run, my lord. We can’t wait here.

original: Farewell to you.
translation: [To CLITUS]  Farewell to you.

original: —And you
translation: [To DARDANIUS]  And you.

original: .—And you, Volumnius.
translation: [To VOLUMNIUS]  And you, Volumnius.

original: —Strato, thou hast been all this while asleep.   Farewell to thee too, Strato.
translation: [To STRATO]  Strato, you’ve slept all this while. Farewell to you too, Strato.

original: —Countrymen,   My heart doth joy that yet in all my life   I found no man but he was true to me.
translation: [To all of his soldiers]  Countrymen, my heart rejoices that, throughout my life, I've only known men who were true to me.

original: I shall have glory by this losing day   More than Octavius and Mark Antony   By this vile conquest shall attain unto.
translation: I’ll have glory in defeat this day—more than Octavius and Mark Antony will gain by their foul victory.

original: So fare you well at once, for Brutus' tongue   Hath almost ended his life’s history.   Night hangs upon mine eyes. My bones would rest,   That have but labored to attain this hour.
translation: So farewell, without further ado, for my tongue has almost finished speaking. I see only darkness before my eyes. My bones, which have worked to hold me up until this time, now want to rest.

original: Fly, my lord, fly.
translation: Run, my lord, run.

original: Hence. I will follow.
translation: Go on! I’ll follow.

original: I prithee, Strato, stay thou by thy lord.   Thou art a fellow of a good respect.   Thy life hath had some smatch of honor in it.
translation: I beg you, Strato, stay by me, your lord. You’re a man with a good reputation. Your life has had some taste of honor in it.

original: Hold then my sword and turn away thy face   While I do run upon it. Wilt thou, Strato?
translation: So hold my sword, and turn your face away while I run myself onto it. Will you, Strato?

original: Give me your hand first.     Fare you well, my lord.
translation: Shake my hand, first.  Farewell, my lord.

original: Farewell, good Strato.     Caesar, now be still. I killed not thee with half so good a will.
translation: Farewell, good Strato.  Caesar, now rest. I killed you half as willingly as I kill myself. [He dies]

original: What man is that?
translation: What man is that?

original: My master’s man.—Strato, where is thy master?
translation: My master’s man. Strato, where’s your master?

original: Free from the bondage you are in, Messala.   The conquerors can but make a fire of him.
translation: He's free from the captivity you are in, Messala. The conquerors can do nothing but make a fire of him,

original: For Brutus only overcame himself,   And no man else hath honor by his death.
translation: because Brutus alone defeated himself. And no other man can gain honor from his death.

original: So Brutus should be found.—I thank thee, Brutus, That thou hast proved Lucillius' saying true.
translation: This is how Brutus should be found. Thank you, Brutus, for proving my prediction true.

original: All that served Brutus, I will entertain them. —Fellow, wilt thou bestow thy time with me?
translation: I will gladly take anyone who served Brutus into my own service.  Will you serve me, man?

original: Ay, if Messala will prefer me to you.
translation: Yes, if Messala recommends me to you.

original: Do so, good Messala.
translation: Do so, good Messala.

original: How died my master, Strato?
translation: How did my master die, Strato?

original: I held the sword and he did run on it.
translation: I held the sword and he impaled himself on it.

original: Octavius, then take him to follow thee, That did the latest service to my master.
translation: Then take this man into your service, Octavius, for he did the final service to my master.

original: This was the noblest Roman of them all.   All the conspirators save only he   Did that they did in envy of great Caesar.
translation: This was the noblest Roman of them all. All the conspirators except for Brutus did what they did because they were jealous of great Caesar.

original: He only in a general honest thought   And common good to all, made one of them.
translation: He alone acted from high ideals, and for the general good.

original: His life was gentle, and the elements   So mixed in him that Nature might stand up   And say to all the world, “This was a man.”
translation: His life was noble, and the elements were so perfectly balanced in him that Nature might stand up and say to all the world, “This was a man.”

original: According to his virtue let us use him,   With all respect and rites of burial.   Within my tent his bones tonight shall lie   Most like a soldier, ordered honorably.
translation: We will treat him according to his virtue, with the highest respect and all the proper burial rites. His body will rest tonight in my tent with all the honorable ceremony owed to a soldier.

original: So call the field to rest, and let’s away   To part the glories of this happy day.
translation: So order the armies in the fields to rest, and let’s go share the glories of this happy day.

original: I thought the king had more affected the Duke of Albany than Cornwall.
translation: I thought the king liked the Duke of Albany more than the Duke of Cornwall.

original: It did always seem so to us. But now in the division of the kingdom, it appears not which of the dukes he  values most,
translation: It always seemed like that to me, too. But now that he has divided the kingdom, no one can tell which duke he prefers the most.

original: for equalities are so weighed that  curiosity in neither can make choice of either’s moiety.
translation: He's divided the kingdom so evenly that not even the closest scrutiny reveals any favoritism to either one.

original: Is not this your son, my lord?
translation: Isn't this your son, my lord?

original: His breeding, sir, hath been at my charge. I have so  often blushed to acknowledge him that now I am brazed to it.
translation: Well, his education has certainly been at my expense. I used to be embarrassed to acknowledge him as my son, but I've done it so many times now that I can do it without blushing.

original: I cannot conceive you.
translation: I can't conceive of what you mean by that.

original: Sir, this young fellow’s mother could, whereupon she  grew round-wombed, and had indeed, sir, a son for her  cradle ere she had a husband for her bed. Do you smell a fault?
translation: Well, sir, this young fellow's mother certainly could conceive—she conceived him. She got pregnant and had a son for her crib before she had a husband in her bed. Do you perceive a sin in this?

original: I cannot wish the fault undone, the issue of it being  so proper.
translation: Well, I can't wish to undo the sin, since its result—your son—turned out so well.

original: But I have, sir, a son by order of law, some year older than this, who yet is no dearer in my account.
translation: I also have a legitimate son, sir, a few years older than this one, though he's not more valuable to me than Edmund.

original: Though  this knave came something saucily to the world before he was sent for, yet was his mother fair, there was good  sport at his making, and the whoreson must be  acknowledged.—
translation: This rascal Edmund may have come into this world somewhat rudely, and before he was meant to, but his mother was beautiful, we had a good time making him, and I must now acknowledge the bastard as my son.

original: Do you know this noble gentleman, Edmund?
translation: [To EDMUND] Do you know this noble gentleman, Edmund?

original: No, my lord.
translation: No, my lord.

original: My lord of Kent. Remember him hereafter as my  honorable friend.
translation: This is Lord Kent. Remember him from now on, as he is my honorable friend.

original: My services to your lordship.
translation: I'm at your service, my lord.

original: I must love you and sue to know you better.
translation: I sincerely look forward to knowing you better.

original: Sir, I shall study deserving.
translation: Sir, I'll try to earn your approval.

original: He hath been out nine years, and away he shall again.
translation: He's been abroad for nine years, and he's soon leaving again.

original: The king is coming.
translation: The king is coming.

original: Attend the lords of France and Burgundy, Gloucester.
translation: Go attend to the rulers of France and Burgundy, Gloucester.

original: I shall, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: Meantime we shall express our darker purpose.—   Give me the map there.—
translation: In the meantime I will discuss my more secret plan. Give me that map there.

original: Know that we have divided   In three our kingdom, and ’tis our fast intent   To shake all cares and business from our age,   Conferring them on younger strengths while we   Unburdened crawl toward death.—
translation: I now declare that I have divided my kingdom into three parts, which will be handed over to my sons-in-law. It's my firm intention to free myself from all worry and business in my old age, so that I can crawl unburdened towards death.

original: Our son of Cornwall,   And you, our no less loving son of Albany,   We have this hour a constant will to publish   Our daughters' several dowers, that future strife   May be prevented now.
translation: To you, my son-in-law Cornwall, and to you, my equally loving son-in-law Albany, at this time I want to publicly announce what each of my daughters will inherit from me, so as to prevent quarreling after I die.

original: The two great princes, France and Burgundy,   Great rivals in our youngest daughter’s love,   Long in our court have made their amorous sojourn,   And here are to be answered.—
translation: The two great rulers of France and Burgundy—who are rivals in pursuing my youngest daughter Cordelia's love— have stayed at my court for a long time. And they will soon have their answer.

original: Tell me, my daughters,   (Since now we will divest us both of rule,   Interest of territory, cares of state)   Which of you shall we say doth love us most
translation: Now tell me, my daughters, (since I'm about to give up my throne, my lands, and the worries and stress of being a ruler), tell me which one of you loves me the most.

original: That we our largest bounty may extend   Where nature doth with merit challenge?—   G   oneril,   Our eldest born, speak first.
translation: Then I can give my greatest gifts to the one who best deserves them.   Goneril, my oldest, you speak first.

original: Sir, I do love you more than words can wield the  matter,   Dearer than eyesight, space, and liberty,   Beyond what can be valued, rich or rare,
translation: Sir, I love you more than words can express, more dearly than eyesight, space, and liberty, beyond all wealth, no matter how valuable or precious.

original: No less than life, with grace, health, beauty, honor,   As much as child e'er loved or father found—   A love that makes breath poor and speech unable.
translation: I love you as much as life itself, and I love you with all my grace, health, beauty, and honor, as much as any daughter ever loved, or any father ever received. My love is so great that it makes my voice weak and my words fail.

original: Beyond all manner of so much I love you.
translation: I love you beyond any comparison I could ever make.

original: What shall Cordelia speak? Love, and be  silent.
translation: What will I do when it's my turn to speak? I can only love, and be silent.

original: Of all these bounds, even from this line to this,   With shadowy forests and with champains riched,   With plenteous rivers and wide-skirted meads,   We make thee lady.
translation: [To GONERIL]  I now give you all this land, from this line to that one, containing dark forests, fertile plains, bountiful rivers, and wide meadows.

original: To thine and Albany’s issue   Be this perpetual.—What says our second daughter,   Our dearest Regan, wife of Cornwall? Speak.
translation: This land will forever belong to you and Albany's descendants. Now what does my second daughter, my dear Regan, Cornwall's wife, have to say? Speak.

original: Sir, I am made of that self mettle as my sister,   And prize me at her worth. In my true heart,   I find she names my very deed of love—
translation: Sir, I am made of the same materials as my sister, and I consider myself her equal in my love for you. Truly, she has described my feelings for you exactly—

original: Only she comes too short, that I profess   Myself an enemy to all other joys,   Which the most precious square of sense possesses.
translation: but she fell a little short. I reject any joy whatsoever except my love for you, which is everything I need in life,

original: And find I am alone felicitate   In your dear highness' love.
translation: and I find that the only thing that makes me truly happy is your dear Highness's love.

original: Then poor Cordelia! And yet not so, since I am sure my love’s More ponderous than my tongue.
translation: And now it's poor Cordelia's turn! And yet I'm not poor at all, since I know my love is weightier and more sincere than my words.

original: To thee and thine hereditary ever   Remain this ample third of our fair kingdom,   No less in space, validity, and pleasure   Than that conferred on Goneril.—
translation: [ To REGAN]  To you and your heirs I now give this large third of my fair kingdom, which is no less in area, value, or beauty than the land I gave to Goneril.

original: But now, our joy,   Although our last and least, to whose young love   The vines of France and milk of Burgundy   Strive to be interessed.
translation: But now for Cordelia, the joy of my life—though the youngest of my daughters— who has been courted so seriously by the rulers of fertile France and Burgundy.

original: What can you say to draw   A third more opulent than your sisters? Speak.
translation: What can you tell me that will earn a larger portion of my kingdom than your sisters?

original: Nothing, my lord.
translation: Nothing, my lord.

original: Nothing?
translation: Nothing?

original: Nothing.
translation: Nothing.

original: How? Nothing will come of nothing. Speak again.
translation: What is this? "Nothing" will earn you nothing. Speak again.

original: Unhappy that I am, I cannot heave My heart into my mouth. I love your majesty According to my bond, no more nor less.
translation: I am unlucky, for I can't put my heart's emotions into words. I love your Majesty as a daughter should love her father, no more and no less.

original: How, how, Cordelia? Mend your speech a little, Lest you may mar your fortunes.
translation: What is this, Cordelia? Fix your speech a little, or you may damage your future.

original: Good my lord,   You have begot me, bred me, loved me. I   Return those duties back as are right fit—   Obey you, love you, and most honor you.
translation: My good lord, you fathered me, raised me, and loved me. In return, I am dutiful to you, as I should be. I obey you, love you, and honor you.

original: Why have my sisters husbands if they say   They love you all? Haply when I shall wed   That lord whose hand must take my plight shall carry   Half my love with him, half my care and duty.
translation: Why do my sisters have husbands if they claim that they love only you? I hope that when I get married, my husband will take half of my love, and half of my care and sense of duty.

original: Sure, I shall never marry like my sisters,   To love my father all.
translation: Surely I'll never get married like my sisters are married—loving only their father.

original: But goes thy heart with this?
translation: But do you really mean this?

original: Ay, good my lord.
translation: Yes, my good lord.

original: So young and so untender?
translation: So young and so heartless?

original: So young, my lord, and true.
translation: So young, my lord, and honest.

original: Let it be so. Thy truth then be thy dower.   For by the sacred radiance of the sun,   The mysteries of Hecate and the night,   By all the operation of the orbs   From whom we do exist and cease to be—
translation: Then this is how it will be: your truth will be your only inheritance. For now I swear by the holy light of the sun, the mysteries of  witchcraft  and the night, and by all the stars whose movements control our lives—

original: Here I disclaim all my paternal care,   Propinquity, and property of blood,   And as a stranger to my heart and me   Hold thee from this for ever.
translation: I hereby disown you as my daughter. I give up all my duties as a father and dissolve all family ties between us. From now on you will be a stranger to me.

original: The barbarous Scythian,   Or he that makes his generation messes   To gorge his appetite, shall to my bosom   Be as well neighbored, pitied, and relieved   As thou my sometime daughter.
translation: Even a foreign  barbarian  who eats his own children will be as close to my heart, pitied, and helped during difficult times as you were, my former daughter.

original: Good my liege—
translation: But your Majesty—

original: Peace, Kent.   Come not between the dragon and his wrath.   I loved her most and thought to set my rest   On her kind nursery.
[To CORDELIA]   Hence, and avoid my  sight!—   So be my grave my peace as here I give   Her father’s heart from her.—
Call France. Who stirs?   Call Burgundy.—
translation: Call the King of France. Will someone go? Call the Duke of Burgundy.

original: Cornwall and Albany,   With my two daughters' dowers digest this third.   Let pride, which she calls plainness, marry her.
translation: Cornwall and Albany, you divide Cornelia's third of my kingdom between you. Let her marry her pride, which she calls "honesty."

original: I do invest you jointly with my power,   Preeminence, and all the large effects   That troop with majesty.
translation: I now give the two of you all my power, privileges, and the riches that come with kingship.

original: Ourself, by monthly course,   With reservation of an hundred knights   By you to be sustained, shall our abode   Make with you by due turns.
translation: For myself I will keep an entourage of a hundred knights, and I will live with one of you one month, and the other the next month.

original: Only shall we retain   The name, and all th' additions to a king.   The sway, revenue, execution of the rest,   Belovèd sons, be yours;
translation: I'll keep the title of king and its accompanying honors, but everything else—the power, responsibility, and income—is now yours, my beloved sons-in-law.

original: which to confirm,   This coronet part between you.   [Gives CORNWALL and ALBANY the coronet]
translation: To confirm this, take this crown and share it between you.  [He gives CORNWALL and ALBANY the crown]

original: Royal Lear,   Whom I have ever honored as my king,
translation: Royal Lear, I've always honored you as my king,

original: Loved as my father, as my master followed,   As my great patron thought on in my prayers—
translation: loved you as my father, followed you as my master, and thanked you as my benefactor in my prayers—

original: The bow is bent and drawn. Make from the shaft.
translation: I've already bent my bow and taken aim. Get out of the way of the arrow.

original: Let it fall rather, though the fork invade   The region of my heart. Be Kent unmannerly   When Lear is mad. What wouldst thou do, old man?
translation: Let it strike me, no matter what, even if the arrow strikes my heart. Kent must be rude when Lear is acting madly. What are you doing, old man?

original: Think’st thou that duty shall have dread to speak   When power to flattery bows? To plainness honor’s bound   When majesty falls to folly.
translation: Do you think that loyal men will be afraid to speak when a king gives in to flattery? If I consider myself honorable, then I'm obligated to speak bluntly when majesty turns to foolishness.

original: Reserve thy state,   And in thy best consideration check   This hideous rashness. Answer my life my judgment,   Thy youngest daughter does not love thee least,
translation: Use your best judgment and rethink this rash, horrible decision. I swear on my life that your youngest daughter doesn't love you the least—

original: Nor are those empty-hearted whose low sound   Reverbs no hollowness.
translation: just because her words don't echo hollowly, it doesn't mean her heart is unloving.

original: Kent, on thy life, no more.
translation: Kent, if you value your life, say nothing more.

original: My life I never held but as a pawn   To wage against thy enemies   ,
translation: I've never valued my life except as a tool you could use against your enemies.

original: nor fear to lose it,   Thy safety being motive.
translation: I don't fear to lose my life if it will help preserve your safety.

original: Out of my sight!
translation: Get out of my sight!

original: See better, Lear, and let me still remain The true blank of thine eye.
translation: Lear, if it will help you see better, let me stay here and always be the target of your angry looks.

original: Now, by Apollo—
Now, by Apollo, King, Thou swear’st thy gods in vain.
translation: You swear by Apollo, King? Now you're taking the names of the gods in vain.

original: O vassal! Miscreant!
translation: You peasant! Villain!

original: Dear sir, forbear!
translation: Dear sir, please stop!

original: Do, kill thy physician, and the fee bestow   Upon thy foul disease.
translation: Go ahead, kill your doctor and pay the medical bill to your foul disease.

original: Revoke thy gift,   Or whilst I can vent clamor from my throat,   I’ll tell thee thou dost evil.
translation: Take back your gift to Albany and Cornwall, or as long as I can make a fuss, I'll keep telling you that you've done an evil thing.

original: Hear me, recreant! On thine allegiance hear me.   That thou hast sought to make us break our vows,   Which we durst never yet,
translation: Listen to me, you traitor! If you still show me allegiance as my subject, hear me. You've tried to make me break my promise to Cornwall and Albany, and I've never broken a promise yet.

original: and with strained pride   To come betwixt our sentence and our power,   Which nor our nature nor our place can bear,   Our potency made good, take thy reward:
translation: You tried to overturn my sentence of judgment on Cordelia, and neither my personality nor my role as king can accept such disrespect of power. To prove my authority, here is the reward for your actions:

original: Five days we do allot thee for provision   To shield thee from diseases of the world.   And on the sixth to turn thy hated back   Upon our kingdom.
translation: you have five days to gather whatever you need to survive the misfortunes of the world. And on the sixth day you must turn your hated back on my kingdom.

original: If on the next day following   Thy banished trunk be found in our dominions,   The moment is thy death. Away! By Jupiter,   This shall not be revoked.
translation: If your banished self is found here after that day, you will be immediately killed. Now go away! I swear by  Jupiter  I'll never take back what I've promised to do.

original: Why, fare thee well, King. Sith thus thou wilt appear,   Freedom lives hence, and banishment is here.
[To CORDELIA]   The gods to their dear shelter take thee, maid,   That justly think’st and hast most rightly said!
[To REGAN and GONERIL]   And your large speeches may your deeds approve,   That good effects may spring from words of love.—
translation: And may your actions live up to your grand words, so that we can see good deeds spring from words of love.

original: Thus Kent, O princes, bids you all adieu.   He’ll shape his old course in a country new.
translation: And so Kent bids you all farewell, you princes. He'll go be his same old self in a new country.

original: Here’s France and Burgundy, my noble lord.
translation: The rulers of France and Burgundy are here, my noble lord.

original: My lord of Burgundy.   We first address towards you, who with this king   Hath rivaled for our daughter.
translation: My lord of Burgundy, I'll address you first. You've been a rival to this king in pursuing my daughter.

original: What in the least   Will you require in present dower with her   Or cease your quest of love?
translation: What is the least amount you will accept as her  dowry  before you give up seeking her love?

original: Most royal majesty,  I crave no more than hath your highness offered. Nor will you tender less.
translation: Your most royal Majesty, I want nothing more than what your Highness has already offered, and I know you won't offer less than that.

original: Right noble Burgundy,   When she was dear to us we did hold her so,   But now her price is fallen.   Sir, there she stands.
translation: Noble Burgundy, when my love for Cordelia was great, I considered her worth to be great too. But now her price has fallen.  There she is, sir.

original: If aught within that little seeming substance,   Or all of it, with our displeasure pieced   And nothing more, may fitly like your grace,   She’s there, and she is yours.
translation: If there's anything  your Grace  like about that small, worthless creature, who is now inseparable from my anger, then there she is—she's yours.

original: I know no answer.
translation: I don't know what to say.

original: Sir, will you, with those infirmities she owes—   Unfriended, new adopted to our hate,
translation: Sir, now that you know her flaws—that she is friendless and just now hated by her father,

original: Dowered with our curse and strangered with our oath—   Take her or leave her?
translation: and that her only dowry is my curse—will you take her or leave her?

original: Pardon me, royal sir. Election makes not up in such conditions.
translation: Forgive me, royal sir. It's impossible to choose in such a situation.

original: Then leave her, sir, for by the power that made me,   I tell you all her wealth.
[To FRANCE]   For you, great King,   I would not from your love make such a stray   To match you where I hate.
translation: And you, great King: I would never want to alienate you by making you marry someone I hate.

original: Therefore beseech you   T' avert your liking a more worthier way   Than on a wretch whom Nature is ashamed   Almost t' acknowledge hers.
translation: So please look elsewhere for a wife and forget this worthless girl, who can barely be called human.

original: This is most strange,   That she that even but now was your best object—   The argument of your praise, balm of your age,   Most best, most dearest—
translation: This is very strange. How could Cordelia—who until just now was your favorite, the object of all your praise, your comfort in your old age, and your best and dearest—

original: should in this trice of time   Commit a thing so monstrous to dismantle   So many folds of favor.
translation: have done something so monstrous that she suddenly stripped away the many layers of your love and favor?

original: Sure, her offense   Must be of such unnatural degree   That monsters it (or your fore-vouched affection   Fall into taint),
translation: Surely she must have committed an atrocious crime to make your formerly strong affection for her turn rotten.

original: which to believe of her   Must be a faith that reason without miracle   Could never plant in me.
translation: But it would take a miracle to make me believe that she could do something like that.

original: [To LEAR]   I yet beseech your majesty,   If for I want that glib and oily art   To speak and purpose not—   since what I well intend,   I’ll do ’t before I speak—
translation: [To LEAR]  Please, your Majesty, I lack the glib art of flattery and empty words. When I want to do something, I just do it instead of talking about it.

original: that you make known   It is no vicious blot, murder, or foulness,   No unchaste action or dishonored step   That hath deprived me of your grace and favor,
translation: So let it be known that it wasn't because I committed an act of murder, lust, or dishonor that I lost your love and favor.

original: But even for want of that for which I am richer:   A still-soliciting eye and such a tongue   As I am glad I have not, though not to have it   Hath lost me in your liking.
translation: It was because I lack a flattering tongue and a greedy eye. I'm a richer person even without these things. And I'm glad that I don't have them, although lacking them has lost me your love.

original: Go to, go to. Better thou  Hadst not been born than not t' have pleased me  better.
translation: Enough, go away. It would've been better for you to have never been born than to have displeased me like you did.

original: Is it no more but this—a tardiness in nature   Which often leaves the history unspoke   That it intends to do?—
translation: Is that all? You're banishing her because she has a quiet nature that makes her act without telling the world about her actions?

original: My lord of Burgundy,   What say you to the lady? Love’s not love   When it is mingled with regards that stands   Aloof from th' entire point.
translation: My lord of Burgundy, what do you have to say to the lady? Love is not love when it mingles with irrelevant matters.

original: Will you have her?   She is herself a dowry.
translation: Will you marry her? She is a valuable dowry in and of herself.

original: [To LEAR]   Royal King,   Give but that portion which yourself proposed,
translation: [To LEAR]  Royal king, if you'll only give me the dowry that you offered me originally,

original: And here I take Cordelia by the hand,   Duchess of Burgundy.
translation: then I'll marry Cordelia right away and make her the Duchess of Burgundy.

original: Nothing. I have sworn. I am firm.
translation: I'll give nothing. I have sworn. I'll stand firm.

original: I am sorry then. You have so lost a  father That you must lose a husband.
translation: I am sorry then. In losing the king as a father, you've also lost me as a husband.

original: Peace be with Burgundy. Since that respects and fortunes are his love,  I shall not be his wife.
translation: Peace be with you, Burgundy. Since your real love is money, I won't be your wife.

original: Fairest Cordelia, that art most rich being poor,   Most choice forsaken, and most loved despised!   Thee and thy virtues here I seize upon,   Be it lawful I take up what’s cast away.
translation: Fairest Cordelia—in being poor you have become most rich; in being abandoned you are valuable; and in being hated you are loved! I accept you and your virtues right away, if it's legal to pick up and keep something that has been cast away by another man.

original: Gods, gods! 'Tis strange that from their cold’st  neglect   My love should kindle to inflamed respect.—   Thy dowerless daughter, King, thrown to my chance,   Is queen of us, of ours, and our fair France.
translation: Gods, gods! It's strange that in treating you so coldly, they've fanned the flames of my love and made me respect you as well. King, your daughter without a dowry, whom you've rejected and thrown to me by chance, will now become the Queen of France and of my heart.

original: Not all the dukes of waterish Burgundy   Can buy this unprized precious maid of me.—   Bid them farewell, Cordelia, though unkind.   Thou losest here, a better where to find.
translation: No duke of watered-down Burgundy could buy this priceless, precious girl from me. Cordelia, bid them farewell, even though they've been unkind to you. You've lost your life here to find a better life elsewhere.

original: Thou hast her, France. Let her be thine, for we   Have no such daughter, nor shall ever see   That face of hers again.
[To CORDELIA]   Therefore be  gone   Without our grace, our love, our benison.—   Come, noble Burgundy.
translation: [To CORDELIA]  So go away, and leave without any love or blessing from me. Come, noble Burgundy.

original: Bid farewell to your sisters.
translation: Say goodbye to your sisters.

original: The jewels of our father, with washed eyes   Cordelia leaves you. I know you what you are,   And like a sister am most loath to call   Your faults as they are named.
translation: Sisters, you jewels of our father's love, I leave you now with tears in my eyes. I know what you really are, but as a sister I am reluctant to criticize your faults and call them by their true names.

original: Love well our father.   To your professèd bosoms I commit him.   But yet, alas, stood I within his grace,   I would prefer him to a better place.   So farewell to you both.
translation: Love our father and take care of him. I leave him to you who have claimed to love him so dearly. But, oh, I wish I were still in his favor, so I could recommend him to better caretakers. So farewell to you both.

original: Prescribe not us our duty.
translation: Don't tell us what our duty is.

original: Let your study   Be to content your lord, who hath received you   At fortune’s alms.
translation: You should focus on pleasing your lord and husband, who has accepted you out of charity.

original: You have obedience scanted,   And well are worth the want that you have wanted.
translation: You have failed to be obedient to our father, and you deserve to lose the love that you yourself have lacked.

original: Time shall unfold what plighted cunning hides, Who covers faults at last with shame derides. Well may you prosper.
translation: Time will reveal what you're hiding under your cunning flattery. Those who cover their faults always end up being shamed by them. May you have prosperous lives.

original: Come, my fair Cordelia.
translation: Come along, my fair Cordelia.

original: Sister, it is not a little I have to say of what most  nearly appertains to us both. I think our father will  hence tonight.
translation: Sister, I have much to say about things that concern us both. I think our father will leave tonight.

original: That’s most certain, and with you. Next month with us.
translation: Certainly, and he'll go to stay with you. Next month he'll stay with us.

original: You see how full of changes his age is. The observation we have made of it hath not been little.
translation: I know you see how moody and fickle he's gotten in his old age, as we've both been observing him so closely.

original: He always  loved our sister most, and with what poor judgment he  hath now cast her off appears too grossly.
translation: He always loved our sister the most, and his poor judgment in banishing her now seems obvious.

original: 'Tis the infirmity of his age. Yet he hath ever but  slenderly known himself.
translation: It's the sickness of his old age. But even when he was younger, he never understood himself very well.

original: The best and soundest of his time hath been but rash.
translation: Even in the prime of his life he was impulsive.

original: Then must we look from his age to receive not alone the  imperfections of long-engrafted condition, but  therewithal the unruly waywardness that infirm and  choleric years bring with them.
translation: Now that he's old, we must deal not only with his deeply-rooted bad habits, but also with the unpredictable bad temper that comes with old age and senility.

original: Such unconstant starts are we like to have from him as  this of Kent’s banishment.
translation: We're likely to see more unpredictable outbursts from him, like his banishment of Kent.

original: There is further compliment of leave-taking between  France and him. Pray you, let’s sit together.
translation: There is still going to be a farewell ceremony between the King of France and our father. Please, let's sit together and come up with a plan.

original: If our  father carry authority with such dispositions as he  bears, this last surrender of his will but offend us.
translation: If our father continues to wield his authority in such a fickle way, then his recent surrender to his passions will only hurt us.

original: We shall further think on ’t.
translation: We must think more about it.

original: We must do something, and i' th' heat.
translation: We have to do something, and should strike while the iron is hot.

original: Thou, nature, art my goddess. To thy law   My services are bound.
translation: Y ou, Nature, are my goddess, and I only serve the laws of nature.

original: Wherefore should I   Stand in the plague of custom and permit   The curiosity of nations to deprive me   For that I am some twelve or fourteen moonshines   Lag of a brother?
translation: So why should I put up with the sick injustice of man-made social rules, which deprive me of rights just because I was born some twelve or fourteen months after my brother?

original: Why “bastard?” Wherefore “base?”   When my dimensions are as well compact,   My mind as generous, and my shape as true   As honest madam’s issue?
translation: Why call me a "bastard?" Why is a bastard inherently "worthless" when I'm as sound in my body and my mind as any legitimate child?

original: Why brand they us   With “base,” with “baseness,” “bastardy,” “base,”  “base”—
translation: Why do they call us "worthless," with "worthlessness," "bastard," "worthless," "worthless?"

original: Who in the lusty stealth of nature take   More composition and fierce quality   Than doth within a dull, stale, tirèd bed   Go to th' creating a whole tribe of fops   Got ’tween a sleep and wake?
translation: We bastards were at least conceived in a moment of passionate, stealthy lust, and so we have a stronger and fiercer nature than those shallow fools who were conceived in a dull, stale, tired marriage bed, where half-asleep couples churn out whole tribes of children.

original: Well then,   Legitimate Edgar, I must have your land.   Our father’s love is to the bastard Edmund   As to the legitimate.—
translation: Well then, legitimate brother Edgar, I must have your land. Our father loves me just as much as he loves his legitimate son.

original: Fine word, “legitimate!”—   Well, my legitimate, if this letter speed   And my invention thrive, Edmund the base   Shall top th' legitimate.
translation: What a fine word, "legitimate!" Well, my legitimate brother, if this letter succeeds and my plan goes well, Edmund the worthless will triumph over Edgar the legitimate.

original: I grow, I prosper.   Now, gods, stand up for bastards!
translation: I will grow, I will prosper. Now, gods, stand up for the bastards!

original: Kent banished thus? And France in choler parted?   And the king gone tonight, prescribed his power   Confined to exhibition?
translation: Has Kent really been banished like this? And the King of France has gone away angry? And King Lear has left tonight, having given up all his power except for some money and his title?

original: All this done   Upon the gad?—Edmund, how now? What news?
translation: All this done on the spur of the moment? Edmund, what's going on? What's the news?

original: So please your lordship, none.
translation: There is no news, my lord.

original: Why so earnestly seek you to put up that letter?
translation: Why are you being so secretive about that letter?

original: I know no news, my lord.
translation: I don't have any news, my lord.

original: What paper were you reading?
translation: What's that letter you were reading?

original: Nothing, my lord.
translation: Nothing, my lord

original: No? What needed, then, that terrible dispatch of it  into your pocket? The quality of nothing hath not such  need to hide itself.
translation: No? Why did you look so terrified and stuff it in your pocket then? If it's nothing, then there's no need to hide it.

original: Let’s see. Come, if it be nothing,  I shall not need spectacles.
translation: Let's see it. Come on, if it's nothing, I won't need my glasses to read it.

original: I beseech you, sir, pardon me. It is a letter from my  brother that I have not all o'er-read. And for so much  as I have perused, I find it not fit for your  o'erlooking.
translation: Please sir, forgive me. It's a letter from my brother that I haven't finished reading yet. And, judging by what I have read, it's not fit for you to look over.

original: Give me the letter, sir.
translation: Give me the letter, sir.

original: I shall offend, either to detain or give it. The  contents, as in part I understand them, are to blame.
translation: I see that I'll offend you whether I keep it or give it to you. The only offensive thing is the content of the letter, as far as I can understand it.

original: Let’s see, let’s see.
translation: Let's see, let's see.

original: I hope, for my brother’s justification, he wrote this  but as an essay or taste of my virtue.
translation: I hope, for my brother's sake, that he wrote this just to test my virtue.

original: [reads]   “This policy and reverence of age makes the  world bitter to the best of our times, keeps our  fortunes from us till our oldness cannot relish them. I  begin to find an idle and fond bondage in the oppression of aged tyranny, who sways not as it hath power but as  it is suffered.
translation: [Reading]   "The craftiness of old men and society's custom of treating them with reverence makes life bitter for those of us in the prime of our lives, and keeps us from our inheritance until we're too old to enjoy it. I begin to see a kind of useless, foolish slavery in the oppressive power of the elderly—and they only have this power because we allow them to have it.

original: Come to me, that of this I may speak  more. If our father would sleep till I waked him, you  should enjoy half his revenue forever, and live the  beloved of your brother,   Edgar.”
translation: Come visit me, so I can speak more about this. If our father should happen to go to his eternal rest, then you would enjoy half of his wealth forever, and live as my beloved brother. Edgar"

original: Hum, conspiracy? “'Sleep till I wake him, you should  enjoy half his revenue”—my son Edgar? Had he a hand to  write this, a heart and brain to breed it in? When came  this to you? Who brought it?
translation: @ "If our father should happen to go to his eternal rest, then you would enjoy half of his wealth" —my son Edgar said this? How could he have a hand that would write such things, and a heart and brain to think them up? When did this letter come to you? Who brought it?

original: It was not brought me, my lord. There’s the cunning of  it. I found it thrown in at the casement of my closet.
translation: It wasn't brought to me, my lord. That's what's cunning about it. I found it. It had been thrown through the window of my room.

original: You know the character to be your brother’s?
translation: And you're sure this is your brother's handwriting?

original: If the matter were good, my lord, I durst swear it  were his. But in respect of that, I would fain think it were not.
translation: My lord, if the letter's contents were good, I would swear that it was his handwriting. But because of what the letter does say, I would rather believe otherwise.

original: It is his.
translation: It is his.

original: It is his hand, my lord, but I hope his heart is not in the contents.
translation: It is his handwriting, my lord. But I hope he didn't really mean what he said.

original: Hath he never heretofore sounded you in this business?
translation: Has he ever spoken to you about anything like this before?

original: Never, my lord. But I have heard him oft maintain it to be fit that, sons at perfect age and fathers declined,  the father should be as ward to the son, and the son  manage his revenue.
translation: Never, my lord. But I've often heard him argue that when sons reach full maturity and their fathers grow old and feeble, the son should take care of the father, and manage his money.

original: O villain, villain! His very opinion in the letter!  Abhorred villain! Unnatural, detested, brutish  villain—worse than brutish!
translation: Oh, the villain, the villain! That's the same opinion he expresses in the letter! The hateful villain! The unnatural, hateful, beastly villain—worse than a beast!

original: Go, sirrah, seek him. I’ll  apprehend him. Abominable villain! Where is he?
translation: Go,  sir , and find him. I'll arrest him. The abominable villain! Where is he?

original: I do not well know, my lord. If it shall please you to suspend your indignation against my brother till you  can derive from him better testimony of his intent, you  shall run a certain course—
translation: I don't know, my lord. If you can, you should restrain your anger against my brother until you can find out exactly what his intentions are. That would be a safer course.

original: where if you violently  proceed against him, mistaking his purpose, it would  make a great gap in your own honor and shake in pieces  the heart of his obedience.
translation: For if you immediately act violently against him and are mistaken about his purpose, then it would damage your own honor and badly hurt his loyalty to you.

original: I dare pawn down my life for him that he hath wrote this to feel my affection to  your honor and to no other pretense of danger.
translation: I would dare to bet my life that he wrote this letter only to test my love for you, and he didn't actually mean anything dangerous.

original: Think you so?
translation: Do you think so?

original: If your honor judge it meet, I will place you where you shall hear us confer of this and by an auricular  assurance have your satisfaction—and that without any  further delay than this very evening.
translation: If it would be acceptable to your sense of honor, I can hide you somewhere where you can hear us talking about the letter, and then you'll have the proof of your own hearing about his intentions. We can do it this very evening.

original: He cannot be such a monster—
translation: He can't be such a monster—

original: Nor is not, sure.
translation: I'm sure he isn't.

original: To his father, that so tenderly and entirely loves  him. Heaven and earth!
translation: —to his own father, who so tenderly and completely loves him. By heaven and earth!

original: Edmund, seek him out, wind me  into him, I pray you. Frame the business after your own  wisdom. I would unstate myself to be in a due  resolution.
translation: Edmund, go find him, and gain his confidence for my sake, please. Do whatever needs to be done, and use your own common sense. I would give up anything to relieve my doubts.

original: I will seek him, sir, presently, convey the business as I shall find means, and acquaint you withal.
translation: Sir, I'll find him immediately, and manage the business in the best way I can. Then I'll tell you everything.

original: These late eclipses in the sun and moon portend no good to us. Though the wisdom of nature can reason it thus  and thus, yet nature finds itself scourged by the  sequent effects.
translation: These recent eclipses of the sun and moon are evil omens for us. Though science can explain how they happen, they are still omens, and bad things always follow eclipses.

original: Love cools, friendship falls off,  brothers divide, in cities mutinies, in countries  discord, in palaces treason, and the bond cracked ’twixt son and father. This villain of mine comes under the  prediction—there’s son against father.
translation: Love loses its passion, friendships fall apart, brothers become enemies, riots break out in cities, civil wars begin, treason infiltrates palaces, and the bond between fathers and sons is broken. This villainous son of mine fits the prediction of the bad omens—that's son against father.

original: The king falls  from bias of nature—there’s father against child. We  have seen the best of our time. Machinations,  hollowness, treachery, and all ruinous disorders follow  us disquietly to our graves.
translation: The king goes against his former nature—that's father against child. The best part of our age has passed. Schemes, emptiness, treachery, and chaos will follow us loudly to our graves.

original: Find out this villain,  Edmund. It shall lose thee nothing. Do it carefully.—And the noble and true-hearted Kent banished, his offense  honesty! 'Tis strange, strange.
translation: Find out the truth about this villain, Edmund. It won't damage your reputation. Just do it carefully. And the noble and true-hearted Kent has been banished, for the crime of being honest! It's strange, strange.

original: This is the excellent foppery of the world that when we are sick in fortune—often the surfeit of our own  behavior—we make guilty of our disasters the sun, the  moon, and the stars, as if we were villains by  necessity,
translation: This is the foolishness of the world, that when we are having bad luck—often because of our own excesses—we lay the blame for our disasters on the sun, the moon, and the stars, as if they forced us to be villains!

original: fools by heavenly compulsion, knaves,  thieves, and treachers by spherical predominance,  drunkards, liars, and adulterers by an enforced  obedience of planetary influence, and all that we are  evil in by a divine thrusting-on.
translation: As if we were fools because of the heavens' decree, or scoundrels, thieves, and traitors because of the influence of the planets, or drunkards, liars, and adulterers because the planets forced us to act that way. As if all our evil was the result of some divine compulsion!

original: An admirable evasion  of whoremaster man, to lay his goatish disposition to  the charge of a star! My father compounded with my  mother under the dragon’s tail and my nativity was under Ursa Major, so that it follows I am rough and  lecherous.
translation: This is a good technique for avoiding blame, a trick by which a lustful man can blame his lechery on a star! My father slept with my mother under the influence of Draco, and I was born under the Big Dipper, so it naturally follows that I have a rude and lustful nature.

original: Fut, I should have been that I am, had the  maidenliest star in the firmament twinkled on my  bastardizing. Edgar—
translation: Good God ! I would have turned out the way I am even if the most virginal star in the sky had twinkled over my conception. Edgar—

original: and pat on ’s cue he comes like the catastrophe of the  old comedy. My cue is villainous melancholy, with a sigh like Tom o' Bedlam.
translation: And here he comes, right on cue, like the neat ending of a clichéd comedy. My role is to be falsely sad, and sigh like a  crazy beggar .

original: Oh, these eclipses do portend these divisions! Fa, sol, la, mi.
translation: Oh, these eclipses are bad omens of such disasters!  Fa, sol, la, mi.

original: How now, brother Edmund? What serious contemplation are you in?
translation: How's it going, brother Edmund? What are you thinking about so seriously?

original: I am thinking, brother, of a prediction I read this  other day, what should follow these eclipses.
translation: Brother, I am thinking of a prediction I read about the other day. An astrologer wrote about what will follow these eclipses.

original: Do you busy yourself about that?
translation: Are you really wasting your time with such things?

original: I promise you, the effects he writes of succeed  unhappily — as of unnaturalness between the child and  the parent, death, dearth, dissolutions of ancient  amities, divisions in state,
translation: I promise you, the predictions he made keep getting worse—things like divisions among children and parents, death, famine, the breaking of old friendships, political fighting,

original: menaces and maledictions  against king and nobles, needless diffidences,  banishment of friends, dissipation of cohorts, nuptial  breaches, and I know not what.
translation: treason and threats against kings and nobles, baseless suspicions, the banishment of friends, the desertion of troops, adultery, and I don't even know what else.

original: How long have you been a sectary astronomical?
translation: How long have you been a follower of astrology?

original: Come, come. When saw you my father last?
translation: Come now. When did you last see my father?

original: Why, the night gone by.
translation: Why, just last night.

original: Spake you with him?
translation: Did you speak with him?

original: Ay, two hours together.
translation: Yes, we spent two hours together.

original: Parted you in good terms? Found you no displeasure in  him by word or countenance?
translation: Did you part on good terms? Did he seem displeased with you, in either his words or in his expression?

original: None at all.
translation: Not at all.

original: Bethink yourself wherein you may have offended him.  And at my entreaty forbear his presence till some little time hath qualified the heat of his displeasure,
translation: Try to remember how you might have offended him. And let me advise you to avoid his presence until he has some time to let off his rage.

original: which  at this instant so rageth in him that with the mischief  of your person it would scarcely allay.
translation: At this moment his anger is so hot that even physically injuring you would hardly cool it down.

original: Some villain hath done me wrong.
translation: Some villain has told a malicious lie about me.

original: That’s my fear. I pray you, have a continent  forbearance till the speed of his rage goes slower. And  as I say, retire with me to my lodging, from whence I  will fitly bring you to hear my lord speak.
translation: That's what I'm afraid of. But please, keep control of yourself until his rage slows down a little. And now come with me to my rooms, and at the right moment I'll bring you to hear my father speak.

original: Pray ye, go. There’s my key. If you do stir abroad, go armed.
translation: Please, go. There's my key. If you do go outside, arm yourself.

original: Armed, brother?
translation: Arm myself, brother?

original: Brother, I advise you to the best. Go armed. I am no  honest man if there be any good meaning towards you.
translation: Brother, I'm giving you the best advice I can. Arm yourself. I would be lying if I said that our father had good intentions towards you.

original: I  have told you what I have seen and heard—but faintly,  nothing like the image and horror of it. Pray you, away.
translation: I've told you what I've seen and heard—but only vaguely. I've toned down the horrible reality. Now please, go.

original: Shall I hear from you anon?
translation: Will I hear from you soon?

original: I do serve you in this business.
translation: Everything I'm doing in this business is to help you.

original: A credulous father, and a brother noble—   Whose nature is so far from doing harms   That he suspects none, on whose foolish honesty   My practices ride easy.
translation: A gullible father, and a noble brother, whose nature is so innocent of evil that he suspects no evil. My plots will easily work on his foolish honesty.

original: I see the business.   Let me, if not by birth, have lands by wit.   All with me’s meet that I can fashion fit.
translation: I see what I must do. If I can't have lands by birthright, then let me have them through cunning. Everything that I can shape to fit my own purposes is good for me.

original: Did my father strike my gentleman For chiding of his fool?
translation: Did my father strike one of my servants for scolding his fool?

original: Ay, madam.
translation: Yes, madam.

original: By day and night he wrongs me. Every hour   He flashes into one gross crime or other   That sets us all at odds. I’ll not endure it.
translation: He offends me constantly, day and night. Every hour he has an outburst, causing some new offense that makes everyone start fighting. I won't endure it anymore.

original: His knights grow riotous, and himself upbraids us   On every trifle. When he returns from hunting,   I will not speak with him. Say I am sick.
translation: His knights are getting unruly, and he himself criticizes us about every little thing. When he returns from hunting, I won't speak to him. Say that I'm sick.

original: If you come slack of former services,   You shall do well. The fault of it I’ll answer.
translation: And if you do less than you used to do to serve the king, you'll be doing the right thing. I'll take the blame for it.

original: He’s coming, madam. I hear him.
