original: Where I could not be honest   I never yet was valiant. For this business,   It touches us as France invades our land,
translation: I can't be brave if the cause I'm fighting for isn't honorable. This business concerns me only  because the French have invaded our land.

original: Not bolds the king, with others whom I fear   Most just and heavy causes make oppose.
translation: I don't care whether the French support King Lear or others who I'm afraid have good reason to oppose us.

original: Sir, you speak nobly.
translation: Sir, you speak nobly.

original: Why is this reasoned?
translation: Why are we discussing this?

original: Combine together 'gainst the enemy,  For these domestic and particular broils Are not the question here.
translation: We must unite against the enemy. These domestic and personal quarrels are not the issue here.

original: Let’s then determine with the ancient of war On our proceedings.
translation: Then let's meet with our experienced officers and determine how to proceed.

original: I shall attend you presently at your tent.
translation: I'll meet you at your tent right away.

original: Sister, you’ll go with us?
translation: Sister, will you come with us?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: 'Tis most convenient. Pray you, go with us.
translation: It would be best if you did. Please, come with us.

original: Oh ho, I know the riddle.—I will go.
translation: Oh, ha! I know what she's doing: trying to keep me away from Edmund.[To the others] All right, I'll go.

original: If e'er your grace had speech with man so  poor, Hear me one word.
translation: If your Grace would ever stoop to speak with a man as poor as I am, then hear what I have to say.

original: I’ll overtake you.—
translation: I'll catch up with you.

original: Speak.
translation: Tell me.

original: [Giving ALBANY a letter]   Before you fight the battle, ope this letter.   If you have victory, let the trumpet sound   For him that brought it.
translation: [Giving ALBANY a letter]  Before you fight the battle, open this letter. If you are victorious, then blow your trumpet to signal to me.

original: Wretched though I seem,   I can produce a champion that will prove   What is avouchèd there.
translation: I seem wretched now, but I can produce a champion who will defend my claims.

original: If you miscarry,   Your business of the world hath so an end,   And machination ceases. Fortune love you.
translation: If you die in battle, then your business in this world will be over, and the plot against your life will be over as well. Good luck to you.

original: Stay till I have read the letter.
translation: Stay until I've read the letter.

original: I was forbid it. When time shall serve, let but the herald cry, And I’ll appear again.
translation: I was ordered not to do that. When the time comes, all you have to do is blow a horn, and I'll appear again.

original: Why, fare thee well. I will o'erlook thy paper.
translation: Well, farewell then. I'll read your letter.

original: The enemy’s in view. Draw up your powers.   [gives ALBANY a document]
translation: The enemy's in sight. Prepare your troops.  [He gives ALBANY a document]

original: Here is the guess of their true strength and forces   By diligent discovery, but your haste   Is now urged on you.
translation: Here is an estimate of the enemy's true strength and weaponry, drawn up by our diligent scouts. But hurry now, please.

original: We will greet the time.
translation: We will be ready for the occasion.

original: To both these sisters have I sworn my love,   Each jealous of the other as the stung   Are of the adder. Which of them shall I take?   Both? One? Or neither?
translation: I've pledged my love to both of these sisters now. And they're each suspicious of the other, as if they were both poisonous snakes. Which of them will I pick? Both? One? Or neither?

original: Neither can be enjoyed   If both remain alive. To take the widow   Exasperates, makes mad her sister Goneril,
translation: I can't be happy with either one of them as long as the other remains alive. If I married the widowed Regan, it would drive Goneril crazy.

original: And hardly shall I carry out my side,   Her husband being alive.
translation: But it would be difficult to carry out my plan with Goneril while her husband's still alive.

original: Now, then, we’ll use   His countenance for the battle, which being done,   Let her who would be rid of him devise   His speedy taking off.
translation: Now then, I'll use Albany's authority and power to win this battle. And when it's over, let Goneril figure out how to get rid of him.

original: As for the mercy   Which he intends to Lear and to Cordelia,   The battle done and they within our power,   Shall never see his pardon, for my state   Stands on me to defend, not to debate.
translation: Albany intends to be merciful to Lear and Cordelia, but if I win the battle and they become my prisoners, they won't live long enough to see his pardon. My position requires actions, not words.

original: Here, father, take the shadow of this tree   For your good host.
translation: Here, old man, use the shadow of this tree for shelter.

original: Pray that the right may thrive.   If ever I return to you again,   I’ll bring you comfort.
translation: Pray that the right side will win this battle. If I ever return to you again, I'll bring you good news.

original: Grace go with you, sir.
translation: May God go with you, sir.

original: Away, old man. Give me thy hand. Away! King Lear hath lost, he and his daughter ta'en. Give me thy hand. Come on.
translation: Let's go, old man. Give me your hand. Now! King Lear has been defeated, and he and his daughter are captured. Give me your hand. Come on.

original: No further, sir. A man may rot even here.
translation: I can't go any further, sir. I might as well die here as anywhere else.

original: What, in ill thoughts again?
translation: What, are you feeling depressed again?

original: Men must endure   Their going hence even as their coming hither.
translation: We cannot choose our deaths any more than we can choose our births.

original: Ripeness is all. Come on.
translation: We must ripen before we decay. Come on.

original: And that’s true too.
translation: And that's true too.

original: Some officers take them away. Good guard Until their greater pleasures first be known That are to censure them.
translation: Have some officers take them away. Guard them carefully until we know what punishment has been decided for them.

original: [to LEAR   ]   We are not the first   Who with best meaning have incurred the worst.   For thee, oppressèd King, I am cast down.
translation: [To LEAR]  We're not the first ones to have made things worse with only the best of intentions. I'm unhappy for your sake, poor, oppressed King.

original: Myself could else outfrown false fortune’s frown.   Shall we not see these daughters and these sisters?
translation: If it were me alone in this situation, I could be defiant in the face of bad luck. Should we see your daughters, my sisters?

original: No, no, no, no! Come, let’s away to prison.   We two alone will sing like birds i' th' cage.   When thou dost ask me blessing, I’ll kneel down   And ask of thee forgiveness.
translation: No, no, no, no! Come, let's go to prison. We two will sing like birds in a cage. When you ask me for my blessing, I'll kneel down and ask you for your forgiveness.

original: So we’ll live,   And pray, and sing, and tell old tales, and laugh   At gilded butterflies, and hear poor rogues   Talk of court news, and we’ll talk with them too—
translation: So we'll live, and pray, and sing, and tell old tales, and laugh at trivial matters, and listen to courtiers gossiping, and talk to them too—

original: Who loses and who wins, who’s in, who’s out—   And take upon ’s the mystery of things   As if we were God’s spies.
translation: we'll find out who's winning and who's losing, who's in and who's out. And we'll ponder the mysteries of life as if we were God's spies sent to observe the world.

original: And we’ll wear out   In a walled prison packs and sects of great ones   That ebb and flow by the moon.
translation: And in our walled prison we'll outlast all the politicians and rulers whose power comes and goes like the tide.

original: Take them away.
translation: Take them away.

original: Upon such sacrifices, my Cordelia,   The gods themselves throw incense. Have I caught thee?   He that parts us shall bring a brand from heaven   And fire us hence like foxes.
translation: Even the gods should celebrate the sacrifices you've made for me, my Cordelia. Are we really together again? Now it would take divine lightning bolt to separate us, like a fire to drive foxes out of their den.

original: Wipe thine eyes.   The good years shall devour them, flesh and fell,   Ere they shall make us weep. We’ll see 'em starve  first.   Come.
translation: Wipe your eyes. Our enemies will waste away with age before they can make us cry again. We'll watch them starve before that. Come.

original: Come hither, captain. Hark.   [gives FIRST CAPTAIN a document]   Take thou this note.
translation: Come here, captain. Listen.  [He gives the FIRST CAPTAIN a document]  Take this note.

original: Go follow them to prison.   One step I have advanced thee. If thou dost   As this instructs thee, thou dost make thy way   To noble fortunes.
translation: Follow them to prison. I've already gotten you promoted once.  If you follow these instructions, you'll be well rewarded.

original: Know thou this: that men   Are as the time is. To be tender-minded   Does not become a sword.
translation: Know this: we must adapt ourselves to these harsh times.  A soldier can't afford to be tender-hearted.

original: Thy great employment   Will not bear question. Either say thou'lt do ’t,   Or thrive by other means.
translation: There can be no discussion about this assignment.  Say you'll do it, or else you can find a different job.

original: I’ll do ’t, my lord.
translation: I'll do it, my lord.

original: About it, and write “happy” when thou’st done. Mark, I say, instantly, and carry it so As I have set it down.
translation: Then go to it, and feel fortunate that you've been given such a high-paying task. Go immediately, I say, and do exactly what I've written.

original: I cannot draw a cart, nor eat dried oats.  If it be man’s work, I’ll do ’t.
translation: I can't do a horse's work, pulling a cart or eating dried oats. But if it's man's work, then I'll do it.

original: [to EDMUND]   Sir, you have shown today your valiant  strain,   And fortune led you well. You have the captives   That were the opposites of this day’s strife.
translation: [To EDMUND]  Sir, today you've shown your courageous lineage, and luck has been on your side. You've captured the leaders of our opposition.

original: I do require them of you, so to use them   As we shall find their merits and our safety   May equally determine.
translation: I need to take custody of them now, to treat them according to their honor and do what is best for our kingdom's safety.

original: Sir, I thought it fit   To send the old and miserable king   To some retention and appointed guard—   Whose age has charms in it, whose title more—
translation: Sir, I thought it would be best if I sent the old, miserable king to a prison cell with a guard. Lear's old age and his title have the power

original: To pluck the common bosom on his side,   An turn our impressed lances in our eyes   Which do command them.
translation: to make common folk take his side, and he could even make our drafted soldiers turn against us.

original: With him I sent the queen,   My reason all the same, and they are ready   Tomorrow or at further space t' appear   Where you shall hold your session.
translation: I sent his daughter Queen Cordelia along with him, for the same reason. They're ready to appear whenever you want to hold your trial for them, tomorrow or at some future point.

original: At this time   We sweat and bleed. The friend hath lost his friend,   And the best quarrels, in the heat, are cursed   By those that feel their sharpness.
translation: Right now we are all sweating and bleeding. Friends have lost friends, and soldiers will curse even the best of causes in the heat of battle.

original: The question of Cordelia and her father   Requires a fitter place.
translation: We need to find a more appropriate place where we can make sure Cordelia and her father have a fair trial.

original: Sir, by your patience, I hold you but a subject of this war, Not as a brother.
translation: By your leave, sir: you are my subordinate in waging this war, not my equal.

original: That’s as we list to grace him.   Methinks our pleasure might have been demanded   Ere you had spoke so far.
translation: That's for me to decide. I think you should have asked for my opinion before speaking to him like that.

original: He led our powers,   Bore the commission of my place and person—   The which immediacy may well stand up   And call itself your brother.
translation: He led our armies, and acted as my proxy in battle. His close connection to me means that he might as well consider himself your equal.

original: Not so hot. In his own grace he doth exalt himself More than in your addition.
translation: Not so fast. He has distinguished himself with his own merits more than any honors you've conferred upon him.

original: In my rights,  By me invested, he compeers the best.
translation: I'm the one who invested my authority in him, and with it he proved his merit.

original: That were the most if he should  husband you.
translation: If he married you, that investment would be complete.

original: Jesters do oft prove prophets.
translation: You joke, but it might come true.

original: Holla, holla! That eye that told you so looked but asquint.
translation: Hey, hey! You're squinting with jealousy and can't see straight.

original: Lady, I am not well, else I should answer   From a full-flowing stomach.
translation: Lady, I'm not feeling well, or else I would answer you with my full temper.

original: [to EDMUND   ]   General,   Take thou my soldiers, prisoners, patrimony.   Dispose of them, of me. The walls is thine.
translation: [To EDMUND]  General, take my soldiers, my prisoners, and my inheritance. Do whatever you want with them, and with me. You have conquered the fortress of my heart.

original: Witness the world that I create thee here   My lord and master.
translation: Let the world be my witness that I hereby make you my lord and master.

original: Mean you to enjoy him then?
translation: Are you going to sleep with him right now?

original: The let-alone lies not in your good will.
translation: It's not in your power to prevent it.

original: Nor in thine, lord.
translation: Nor is it in yours, lord.

original: Half-blooded fellow, yes.
translation: Yes it is, you illegitimate fellow.

original: Let the drum strike and prove my title  thine.
translation: Let the drums beat, and fight anyone who challenges your right to me.

original: Stay yet. Hear reason.—Edmund, I arrest thee   On capital treason, and in thine attaint   This gilded serpent.   [indicates GONERIL   ]
translation: Wait, and listen to reason.—Edmund, I now arrest you for capital treason, and as an accessory to your treason I arrest this snake of a woman.  [He points to GONERIL]

original: [to REGAN   ]   For your claim, fair sister,   I bar it in the interest of my wife.   'Tis she is subcontracted to this lord.
translation: [To REGAN]  But, my fair sister-in-law, as for your claim to him, I veto your engagement on my wife's behalf. She's the one who is already engaged to Edmund.

original: And I, her husband, contradict your banns.   If you will marry, make your loves to me,   My lady is bespoke.
translation: If you want to get married, then start wooing me. My lady is already spoken for.

original: An interlude!
translation: What a ridiculous story!

original: Thou art armed, Gloucester. Let the trumpet sound.   If none appear to prove upon thy person   Thy heinous, manifest, and many treasons,   There is my pledge.   [throws down his glove]
translation: You have a sword,  Gloucester . Let the trumpets sound. If no one appears to challenge you and prove that you are a hideous traitor, then I'll do it myself.  [He throws down his glove as a challenge]

original: I’ll make it on thy heart,   Ere I taste bread, thou art in nothing less   Than I have here proclaimed thee.
translation: I make this promise on your life: I won't eat again until I prove that you're just as guilty as I say you are.

original: Sick, oh, sick!
translation: Oh, I feel sick, sick!

original: If not, I’ll ne'er trust medicine.
translation: If she's not sick, I'll never trust poison again.

original: [throwing down his glove]   There’s my exchange. What in the world he is   That names me traitor, villainlike he lies.   Call by thy trumpet.
translation: [Throwing down his glove]  I accept your challenge. Whoever calls me a traitor is a villainous liar. Blow your trumpet.

original: He that dares approach,   On him—on you, who not?—I will maintain   My truth and honor firmly.
translation: I'll fight to firmly prove my truth and honor to anyone who dares approach—you, or anyone else.

original: A herald, ho!
A herald, ho, a herald!
translation: A herald, hey, a herald!

original: Trust to thy single virtue, for thy  soldiers,  All levied in my name, have in my name Took their discharge.
translation: Trust in your own unaided strength now, for your soldiers were all drafted in my name. And in my name they have been discharged.

original: My sickness grows upon me.
translation: I can feel my sickness growing.

original: She is not well. Convey her to my tent.
translation: She is not well. Take her to my tent.

original: Come hither, herald.—Let the trumpet sound,— And read out this.
translation: Come here, herald.—Let the trumpet sound!—Read this.

original: Sound, trumpet!
translation: Blow the trumpet!

original: [reads]   “If any man of quality or degree within the lists of  the army will maintain upon Edmund, supposed Earl of  Gloucester,
translation: [ Reading]   "If any honorable man of the army will accuse Edmund, the supposed Earl of Gloucester,

original: that he is a manifold traitor, let him  appear by the third sound of the trumpet. He is bold in  his defense.”
translation: of being a traitor, then let him appear by the  third sound of the trumpet. Edmund is willing to fight in his own defense."

original: Again!
translation: Again!

original: Again!
translation: Again!

original: Ask him his purposes, why he appears Upon this call o' th' trumpet.
translation: Ask him what he wants, and why he's stepping forward at this call of the trumpet.

original: What are you? Your name, your quality, and why you answer This present summons?
translation: Who are you? What is your name and your rank? And why do you step forward now?

original: O, know, my name is lost.   By treason’s tooth bare-gnawn and canker-bit.
translation: Know this: my name has been lost to a traitorous worm.

original: Yet am I noble as the adversary   I come to cope withal.
translation: But I am as noble as the opponent I've come to fight.

original: Which is that adversary?
translation: And which opponent is that?

original: What’s he that speaks for Edmund, Earl of Gloucester?
translation: Who speaks for Edmund, Earl of Gloucester?

original: Himself. What sayst thou to him?
translation: I speak for myself. What do you have to say to me?

original: Draw thy sword,   That if my speech offend a noble heart   Thy arm may do thee justice.   [draws his sword]   Here is  mine.
translation: Draw your sword. If I offend your noble heart with my words, then you can take your revenge with your sword. Here is mine.  [He draws his sword]

original: Behold: it is the privilege of mine honors,   My oath, and my profession. I protest—   Maugre thy strength, youth, place, and eminence,
translation: Look: it is the symbol of my honor, my vows, and my privilege as a knight. I now solemnly declare that—despite your strength, youth, rank, and power;

original: Despite thy victor sword and fire-new fortune,   Thy valor and thy heart—thou art a traitor,   False to thy gods, thy brother, and thy father,   Conspirant 'gainst this high illustrious prince,
translation: and despite your recent victory, newly-minted fortune, courage, and bravery—you are a traitor. You have betrayed your gods, your brother, and your father, and you've conspired against this noble, glorious duke.

original: And from th' extremest upward of thy head   To the descent and dust below thy foot   A most toad-spotted traitor.
translation: From the top of your head to the soles of your feet you are a filthy, tainted traitor.

original: Say thou “No,”   This sword, this arm, and my best spirits are bent   To prove upon thy heart, whereto I speak,   Thou liest.
translation: If you disagree with me, then I'm ready to use my sword, my arm, and my courage to prove that you are a liar.

original: In wisdom I should ask thy name.   But since thy outside looks so fair and warlike,   And that thy tongue some say of breeding breathes,   What safe and nicely I might well delay   By rule of knighthood, I disdain and spurn.
translation: Prudence would suggest that I ask your name first. But since you look so noble and knightly— and since your speech implies that you are of a high rank— I will disdain the rules of knighthood that say I can refuse to fight a man I don't know.

original: Back do I toss these treasons to thy head,   With the hell-hated lie o'erwhelm thy heart—
translation: I toss your accusations of treason back at your own head, and your hateful lies back at your heart.

original: Which, for they yet glance by and scarcely bruise,   This sword of mine shall give them instant way,   Where they shall rest for ever.—Trumpets, speak!
translation: They hardly hurt you now, but I'll follow them with my sword and embed the word "traitor" in your heart forever. Trumpets, blow!

original: Save him, save him!
translation: Save him, save him!

original: This is practice, Gloucester.   By th' law of arms thou wast not bound to answer   An unknown opposite.
translation: This was trickery, Gloucester. By the laws of dueling you didn't have to fight an unknown opponent.

original: Thou art not vanquished,   But cozened and beguiled.
translation: You haven't been conquered—only cheated and deceived.

original: Shut your mouth, dame,   Or with this paper shall I stop it.—Hold, sir,   [gives the letter to EDMUND   ]   Thou worse than any name, read thine own evil.—
translation: Shut your mouth, woman, or I'll plug it up with this paper. Look, sir.  [He gives the letter to EDMUND]  Read your own evil, you who are worse than any words could describe.

original: [to GONERIL]   Nay, no tearing, lady. I perceive you know it.
translation: [To GONERIL]  No, don't tear it, lady. I think you know what it says.

original: Say, if I do? The laws are mine, not thine. Who can arraign me for ’t?
translation: And what if I do? I make the laws, not you. Who can prosecute me for it?

original: Most monstrous, oh!     Know’st thou this paper?
translation: Oh, how monstrous!  Do you know what this letter is?

original: Ask me not what I know.
translation: Do not ask me what I know.

original: Go after her. She’s desperate. Govern her.
translation: Go after her. She's desperate. Restrain her.

original: What you have charged me with, that have I done—   And more, much more. The time will bring it out.   'Tis past, and so am I.   [to EDGAR   ]
translation: I have done all the things you've accused me of—and more, much more. You'll find out the rest in due time. But now it's over, and so am I.

original: But what art thou   That hast this fortune on me? If thou'rt noble,   I do forgive thee.
translation: [To EDGAR]  But who are you who defeated me? If you're a nobleman, I forgive you.

original: Let’s exchange charity.   I am no less in blood than thou art, Edmund.   If more, the more thou’st wronged me.
translation: Let's exchange forgiveness. I am no less noble than you are, Edmund. And if I'm more noble, then you've wronged me all the more.

original: My name is Edgar, and thy father’s son.   The gods are just, and of our pleasant vices   Make instruments to plague us.
translation: My name is Edgar, and I'm your father's son. The gods are just, and use the sins we commit in giving ourselves pleasure as a means of making instruments to torment us.

original: The dark and vicious place where thee he got   Cost him his eyes.
translation: The adultery he committed created you, and cost him his eyes.

original: Thou’st spoken right. 'Tis true. The wheel is come full circle. I am here.
translation: You've spoken rightly. It's true. The wheel of fortune has come full circle. Here I am on the bottom again.

original: Methought thy very gait did prophesy   A royal nobleness. I must embrace thee.
translation: I could tell that you were noble even by the way you walked. Let me hug you.

original: Let sorrow split my heart if ever I   Did hate thee or thy father.
translation: I swear that I never hated you or your father.

original: Worthy prince, I know ’t.
translation: Worthy prince, I know.

original: Where have you hid yourself? How have you known the miseries of your father?
translation: Where have you been hiding yourself? How do you know about your father's suffering?

original: By nursing them, my lord. List a brief tale,   And when ’tis told, oh, that my heart would burst!   The bloody proclamation to escape,   That followed me so near—
translation: By nursing him through it, my lord. Listen to my brief tale, and when it's over, oh, may my heart burst! To escape the proclamation condemning me to death, I disguised myself in the rags of a crazy beggar, making myself a creature scorned even by dogs.

original: O our lives' sweetness,   That we the pain of death would hourly die   Rather than die at once!—
translation: Oh, how sweet life must be, that we prefer the pain of slowly dying to death itself!

original: taught me to shift   Into a madman’s rags, t' assume a semblance   That very dogs disdained.   And in this habit   Met I my father with his bleeding rings,   Their precious stones new lost,
translation: In this disguise I met my father with his bloody eye sockets—his precious eyes recently lost—

original: became his guide,   Led him, begged for him, saved him from despair.
translation: and I became his guide. I led him, begged for him, and saved him from despair.

original: Never—O fault!—revealed myself unto him   Until some half-hour past, when I was armed.
translation: I never—oh, what a mistake!—revealed myself to him until just half an hour ago, when I was in my armor.

original: Not sure, though hoping of this good success,   I asked his blessing, and from first to last   Told him my pilgrimage.
translation: I hoped for a successful outcome to the battle, but I still decided to ask for my father's blessing, and I told him the whole story of my journey.

original: But his flawed heart—   Alack, too weak the conflict to support—   'Twixt two extremes of passion, joy and grief,   Burst smilingly.
translation: But his cracked heart was too weak to support such extremes of joy and grief at once, and it gave out.

original: This speech of yours hath moved me, And shall perchance do good. But speak you on.  You look as you had something more to say.
translation: Your words have moved me, and may end up doing some good. But continue. You look like you have something more to say.

original: If there be more, more woeful, hold it in. For I am almost ready to dissolve, Hearing of this.
translation: If there's anything more sorrowful to add, then keep it to yourself. I'm already about to lose myself to tears from hearing this much.

original: This would have seemed a period   To such as love not sorrow, but another   To amplify too much would make much more   And top extremity.
translation: This might have seemed like a fitting end for a sad story. But if I go on I must add to what is already too much, and reach a new extremity of sorrow.

original: Whilst I was big in clamor came there in a man   Who, having seen me in my worst estate,   Shunned my abhorred society, but then, finding   Who ’twas that so endured, with his strong arms   He fastened on my neck, and bellowed out   As he’d burst heaven,
translation: While I was crying loudly over my father, a man came in. He had seen me in my beggar's clothes and shunned me earlier, but when he found out who I was, he wrapped his strong arms around my neck and cried as if he was trying to burst heaven.

original: threw him on my father,   Told the most piteous tale of Lear and him   That ever ear received—
translation: He then threw himself on my father and told the saddest story that was ever heard about Lear and him.

original: which in recounting   His grief grew puissant and the strings of life   Began to crack. Twice then the trumpets sounded,   And there I left him tranced.
translation: And as he told the story his grief overcame him and his heart-strings began to break. Then I heard the trumpets blow twice, and I left him in a trance.

original: But who was this?
translation: But who was this man?

original: Kent, sir, the banished Kent, who in disguise Followed his enemy king and did him service  Improper for a slave.
translation: Kent, sir. It was the banished Kent, who disguised himself and followed his hostile king—serving him with tasks too menial for even a slave.

original: Help, help, O, help!
translation: Help, help, oh, help!

original: What kind of help?
translation: What kind of help?

original: Speak, man.
translation: Speak, man!

original: What means that bloody knife?
translation: What does that bloody knife mean?

original: 'Tis hot, it smokes. It came even from the heart of—oh, she’s dead!
translation: It's hot, it's still smoking with life blood. It was just removed from the heart of—oh, she's dead!

original: Who dead? Speak, man.
translation: Who's dead? Speak, man.

original: Your lady, sir, your lady. And her sister By her is poisoned. She confesses it.
translation: Your wife Goneril, sir, your wife. And she poisoned her sister Regan, who's now dead too. She confessed it.

original: I was contracted to them both. All three Now marry in an instant.
translation: I was engaged to them both. We three will now be united in death.

original: Here comes Kent.
translation: Here comes Kent.

original: Produce their bodies, be they alive or dead.  This judgment of the heavens that makes us tremble Touches us not with pity.
translation: Bring the bodies here, whether they're alive or dead. The judgment of the gods makes us tremble, but it doesn't make us pity these deaths.

original: Oh, is this he? The time will not allow the compliment Which very manners urges.
translation: Oh, is this him? There's no time for the greetings that good manners require.

original: I am come To bid my king and master aye good night. Is he not here?
translation: I am here to say goodnight forever to my king and master. Is he not here?

original: Great thing of us forgot!— Speak, Edmund, where’s the king? And where’s Cordelia?—
translation: What a thing for us to forget! Speak, Edmund, where's the king? And where's Cordelia?

original: Seest thou this object, Kent?
translation: Do you see this spectacle, Kent?

original: Alack, why thus?
translation: Alas, why has this happened?

original: Yet Edmund was beloved. The one the other poisoned for my sake,  And after slew herself.
translation: Despite everything, Edmund was beloved. One sister poisoned the other for my sake, and then killed herself.

original: Even so.—Cover their faces.
translation: It seems so. Cover their faces.

original: I pant for life. Some good I mean to do   Despite of mine own nature. Quickly send—   Be brief in it—to th' castle,
translation: These are my last breaths. I want to do a little good despite my nature. Go quickly—be speedy about it—to the castle.

original: for my writ   Is on the life of Lear and on Cordelia.   Nay, send in time!
translation: For I've ordered the executions of Lear and Cordelia. Hurry, send someone now!

original: Run, run, O, run!
translation: Run, run, oh, run!

original: To who, my lord?—Who hath the office? Send Thy token of reprieve.
translation: Where should we run, my lord? Who has the orders to kill them? Send something to prove that you've changed your commands.

original: Well thought on. Take my sword. The captain— Give it the captain.
translation: Good idea. Take my sword. The captain—give it to the captain.

original: Haste thee for thy life.
translation: Run as if your life depended on it.

original: He hath commission from thy wife and me   To hang Cordelia in the prison and   To lay the blame upon her own despair,
translation: Your wife and I ordered the captain to hang Cordelia in the prison and lay the blame on her own despair,

original: That she fordid herself.
translation: making it look like she killed herself.

original: The gods defend her!—bear him hence awhile.
translation: May the gods protect her! Carry him away for now.

original: Howl, howl, howl, howl! Oh, you are men of stones.   Had I your tongues and eyes, I’d use them so   That heaven’s vault should crack. She’s gone forever.
translation: Howl, howl, howl, howl! Oh, you are men of stone! If I had your eyes to weep and your tongues to cry out, I'd use them until the sky itself cracked. She's gone forever.

original: I know when one is dead and when one lives.   She’s dead as earth. Lend me a looking-glass.   If that her breath will mist or stain the stone,   Why then, she lives.
translation: But I know how to tell when someone is dead and when they're alive. She's as dead as the senseless ground. Bring me a mirror. If her breath makes a mist on the glass, then she's still alive.

original: Is this the promised end?
translation: Is this the end of the world?

original: Or image of that horror?
translation: Or a reflection of that final horror?

original: Fall and cease.
translation: Let the world collapse and end!

original: This feather stirs. She lives. If it be so,  It is a chance which does redeem all sorrows That ever I have felt.
translation: This feather moved with her breath. She lives. If it's true, then it will make up for all the sorrows I've ever felt.

original: O my good master!
translation: Oh my good master!

original: Prithee, away.
translation: Please, go away.

original: 'Tis noble Kent, your friend.
translation: It's noble Kent, your friend.

original: A plague upon you, murderers, traitors all!   I might have saved her. Now she’s gone for ever.—
translation: A plague on you, you're all murderers and traitors! I could have saved her. Now she's gone forever.

original: Cordelia, Cordelia, stay a little. Ha?   What is ’t thou say’st?—
translation: [To CORDELIA's body]  Cordelia, Cordelia, stay a little while. What? What are you saying?

original: Her voice was ever soft,   Gentle and low, an excellent thing in woman.—
translation: [To the others]  Her voice was always so soft, gentle, and low—an excellent thing in a woman.

original: I killed the slave that was a-hanging thee.
translation: [To CORDELIA's body]  I killed the scum who was hanging you.

original: 'Tis true, my lords, he did.
translation: It's true, my lords, he did.

original: Did I not, fellow?   I have seen the day with my good biting falchion   I would have made them skip.
translation: Didn't I, man? In the old days I would've made them all dance with my sword.

original: I am old now,   And these same crosses spoil me.
translation: But I am old now, and my trials have worn me down.

original: [to KENT   ]   Who are you?   Mine eyes are not o' th' best, I’ll tell you straight.
translation: [To KENT]  Who are you? My eyesight's not the best. I'll recognize you soon.

original: If Fortune brag of two she loved and hated,  One of them we behold.
translation: This man was the luckiest and then the unluckiest that ever lived.

original: This a dull sight. Are you not Kent?
translation: My vision is failing. Are you not Kent?

original: The same. Your servant Kent. Where is your servant Caius?
He’s a good fellow, I can tell you that. He’ll strike, and quickly too. He’s dead and rotten.
translation: He's a good fellow, I can tell you that. He'll strike when in a fight, and quickly too. But now he's dead and rotting.

original: No, my good lord. I am the very man—
translation: No, my good lord. I am Caius, the man—

original: I’ll see that straight.
translation: I'll deal with this soon.

original: That from your first of difference and decay Have followed your sad steps.
translation: —who followed you from the very beginning of your suffering and decline.

original: You’re welcome hither.
translation: You're welcome here.

original: Nor no man else. All’s cheerless, dark, and deadly.  Your eldest daughters have fordone themselves, And desperately are dead.
translation: No, I'm not welcome. No one is welcome. Everything is cheerless, dark, and dreadful. Your eldest daughters have killed themselves and died in despair.

original: Ay, so I think.
translation: Yes, I think that's true.

original: He knows not what he says, and vain it is That we present us to him.
translation: He doesn't know what he's saying. It's useless to try to explain it to him.

original: Very bootless.
translation: It's pointless.

original: Edmund is dead, my lord.
translation: Edmund is dead, my lord.

original: That’s but a trifle here.—   You lords and noble friends, know our intent.   What comfort to this great decay may come   Shall be applied.
translation: That's just a drop in this ocean of sorrow. You lords and noble friends, hear what I intend to do. We must try to bring as much comfort as we can amid this great destruction.

original: For us, we will resign   During the life of this old majesty   To him our absolute power.
translation: And as for me, I will surrender my power to the old king, that he should have absolute authority for the rest of his life.

original: [to EDGAR and KENT   ]   You, to your rights   With boot, and such addition as your honors   Have more than merited.—
translation: [To EDGAR and KENT]  And you will get back your rightful property and titles, along with rewards and distinctions that you have more than earned.

original: All friends shall taste   The wages of their virtue, and all foes   The cup of their deservings. O, see, see!
translation: All my friends will taste the rewards of their virtue, and all my enemies will drink from the cup of punishment that they deserve. Oh, look, look!

original: And my poor fool is hanged.—No, no, no life?
translation: And my poor child was hanged.

original: Why should a dog, a horse, a rat have life,   And thou no breath at all? Oh, thou'lt come no more,   Never, never, never, never, never.—
translation: [To CORDELIA's body]  No, no, no life left in you? Why should a dog, a horse, or a rat have life, but you have none at all? Oh, you'll never come to me again, never, never, never, never, never.

original: Pray you, undo this button. Thank you, sir.   Do you see this? Look on her. Look, her lips.   Look there, look there. O, O, O, O.   [dies]
translation: To the others]  Please, undo this button. Thank you, sir. Do you see this? Look at her. Look, her lips. Look there, look there. Oh, oh, oh, oh.  [He dies]

original: He faints!—My lord, my lord!
translation: He faints!  My lord, my lord!

original: Break, heart. I prithee, break!
translation: Break, heart. Please, break!

original: Look up, my lord.
translation: Look up, my lord.

original: Vex not his ghost. O, let him pass. He hates him That would upon the rack of this tough world Stretch him out longer.
translation: Don't disturb his departing spirit. Oh, let him pass on. He would hate anyone who made him linger in this torturous world any longer.

original: Oh, he is gone indeed.
translation: Oh, he is dead indeed.

original: The wonder is he hath endured so long. He but usurped his life.
translation: It's a wonder that he endured for so long. He was only living on borrowed time.

original: Bear them from hence. Our present business   Is to general woe.
translation: Carry them away from here. Our business is now to grieve.

original: [to KENT and EDGAR]   Friends of my soul, you twain   Rule in this realm, and the gored state sustain.
translation: [To KENT and EDGAR]  My dear friends, you two should rule this kingdom and keep the wounded country alive.

original: I have a journey, sir, shortly to go. My master calls me. I must not say no.
translation: I have a journey to make soon, sir. My master calls me on to following him to the next life, and I cannot say no.

original: The weight of this sad time we must obey.   Speak what we feel, not what we ought to say.
translation: We must bear the weight of this sad day, and say what we feel, not what we ought to say.

original: The oldest hath borne most. We that are young   Shall never see so much, nor live so long.
translation: The oldest has suffered the most. We who are young will never see as much as he has seen, or live so long.

original: When shall we three meet again? In thunder, lightning, or in rain?
translation: When will we three meet again? In a thunderstorm, or in a lightning storm, or when it's raining?

original: When the hurly-burly’s done, When the battle’s lost and won.
translation: When the mayhem’s finished, when the battle’s been lost by one side and won by the other.

original: That will be ere the set of sun.
translation: That will happen before the sun sets.

original: Where the place?
translation: At what place?

original: Upon the heath.
translation: Out in the field.

original: There to meet with Macbeth.
translation: We’ll meet Macbeth there.

original: I come, Graymalkin!
translation: Coming, Graymalkin!

original: Paddock calls.
translation: Paddock calls me.

original: Anon.
translation: I'll be there soon.

original: Fair is foul, and foul is fair Hover through the fog and filthy air.
translation: What's fair is foul, and what's foul is fair. We’ll fly off through the fog and filthy air.

original: What bloody man is that? He can report, As seemeth by his plight, of the revolt The newest state.
translation: Who’s this bloody man? From the looks of him, it seems likely he can give us the latest news about the revolt.

original: This is the sergeant   Who like a good and hardy soldier fought   ‘Gainst my captivity.
translation: This is the sergeant, a good and tough soldier who fought to stop me from getting captured.

original: Doubtful it stood,
translation: The outcome was in doubt.

original: As two spent swimmers that do cling together   And choke their art.
translation: The two armies were like two tired swimmers clinging to each other, making it impossible for either to stay afloat.

original: The merciless Macdonwald—   Worthy to be a rebel, for to that   The multiplying villanies of nature   Do swarm upon him—   from the Western Isles   Of kerns and gallowglasses is supplied,
translation: The armies of the merciless Macdonwald—who has so many villainous qualities that he’s a natural rebel— were reinforced by foot soldiers and warriors with axes from Ireland and the  Hebrides .

original: And fortune, on his damnèd quarrel smiling,   Showed like a rebel’s whore.
translation: Luck was smiling on his damned rebellion as if she were his whore.

original: But all’s too weak,   For brave Macbeth—well he deserves that name—   Disdaining fortune, with his brandished steel,   Which smoked with bloody execution,   Like valor’s minion carved out his passage   Till he faced the slave;
translation: But that wasn’t enough because brave Macbeth—he deserves that description—defied Lady Luck with his sword, which smoked with blood, and carved through Macdonwald’s army until he faced the rogue.

original: Which ne’er shook hands, nor bade farewell to him,   Till he unseamed him from the nave to th’ chops,   And fixed his head upon our battlements.
translation: Not pausing to shake hands or say goodbye, Macbeth split Macdonwald from belly to jaw and stuck his head on the walls of our castle.

original: O valiant cousin! Worthy gentleman!
As whence the sun ‘gins his reflection   Shipwracking storms and direful thunders break,   So from that spring whence comfort seemed to come   Discomfort swells.   Mark, King of Scotland, mark:
translation: But just as terrible storms and dreadful thunder come right when the sun rises, so did new trouble arise from what had seemed to be our triumph.  Listen, King of Scotland, listen:

original: No sooner justice had, with valor armed,   Compelled these skipping kerns to trust their heels,   But the Norweyan lord, surveying vantage,   With furbished arms and new supplies of men,   Began a fresh assault.
translation: as soon as we defeated those Irish soldiers and sent them running, the Norwegian king spied an advantage and began a new assault with fresh soldiers and sharpened weapons.

original: Dismayed not this our captains, Macbeth and Banquo?
translation: Didn’t this trouble our captains, Macbeth and Banquo?

original: Yes, as sparrows eagles, or the hare the lion.
translation: About as much as sparrows trouble eagles, or rabbits scare a lion.

original: If I say sooth, I must report they were   As cannons overcharged with double cracks,
translation: To be honest, they were like cannons loaded with double charges of gunpowder.

original: So they doubly redoubled strokes upon the foe.
translation: They fought this new opponent with double their earlier ferocity.

original: Except they meant to bathe in reeking wounds,   Or memorize another Golgotha,   I cannot tell—   But I am faint,
translation: Perhaps they wanted to bathe in the blood of their enemies’ wounds, or make that battlefield as infamous as  Golgotha ...But I feel weak.

original: my gashes cry for help.
translation: My wounds are crying out for a doctor.

original: So well thy words become thee as thy wounds; They smack of honor both. Go get him surgeons.
translation: Your words speak to your honor—as do your wounds. Get him to a doctor.

original: Who comes here?
translation: Who’s just arrived?

original: The worthy thane of Ross.
What a haste looks through his eyes! So should he look That seems to speak things strange.
translation: His eyes are wild! He looks like a man with an incredible story to tell.

original: God save the king.
translation: God save the king.

original: Whence cam’st thou, worthy thane?
translation: Where have you come from, heroic thane?

original: From Fife, great king,   Where the Norweyan banners flout the sky   And fan our people cold.
translation: Great King, I've come from Fife, where the Norwegian flag flies—mocking our land and terrifying our people.

original: Norway himself, with terrible numbers,   Assisted by that most disloyal traitor,   The thane of Cawdor, began a dismal conflict,
translation: The King of Norway—with a huge army and the support of that disloyal traitor, the Thane of Cawdor—began a battle that our forces looked likely to lose.

original: Till that Bellona’s bridegroom, lapped in proof,   Confronted him with self-comparisons,   Point against point, rebellious arm ‘gainst arm,   Curbing his lavish spirit;
translation: That is, until Macbeth—covered in armor and seeming like  Bellona's  husband—met the rebellious thane sword in hand-to-hand combat, and in the end, Macbeth defeated Cawdor.

original: and to conclude,   The victory fell on us.
translation: To conclude, we were victorious.

original: Great happiness!
translation: Great happiness!

original: That now   Sweno, the Norways’ king, craves composition.
translation: Now Sweno, the Norwegian king, begs for a peace treaty.

original: Nor would we deign him burial of his men   Till he disbursed at Saint Colme’s Inch   Ten thousand dollars to our general use.
translation: We refused to let him bury his men until he retreated to Saint Colme’s Inch and gave us ten thousand dollars.

original: No more that thane of Cawdor shall deceive Our bosom interest: go pronounce his present death,  And with his former title greet Macbeth.
translation: The Thane of Cawdor will never again deceive me. Go proclaim that he will be executed, and tell Macbeth that he will receive Cawdor’s title.

original: I’ll see it done.
translation: I’ll do that.

original: What he hath lost, noble Macbeth hath won.
translation: Noble Macbeth has won what the Thane of Cawdor has lost.

original: Where hast thou been, sister?
translation: Where have you been, sister?

original: Killing swine.
translation: Killing pigs.

original: Sister, where thou?
translation: Where were you, sister?

original: A sailor’s wife had chestnuts in her lap,   And munched, and munched, and munched.
translation: A sailor’s wife had chestnuts in her lap and munched, and munched, and munched them.

original: “Give me,”  quoth I.   “Aroint thee, witch!”   the rump-fed runnion cries.
translation: “Give me one,” I said.  “Get out of here, witch!”  the fat-bottomed, scabby woman cried.

original: Her husband’s to Aleppo gone, master o’ th’ Tiger;
translation: Her husband has gone to Aleppo as captain of a sailing ship called The Tiger.

original: But in a sieve I’ll thither sail,   And like a rat without a tail,   I’ll do, I’ll do, and I’ll do.
translation: I’m going to sail there in a strainer, and them—like a rat without a tail—I’ll do this to him, and this, and that.

original: I’ll give thee a wind.
translation: I’ll make a wind for you to sail there.

original: Thou ‘rt kind.
translation: That’s very kind.

original: And I another.
translation: And I’ll give you another wind.

original: I myself have all the other,   And the very ports they blow,   All the quarters that they know   I’ th’ shipman’s card.
translation: I’m already master of all the other winds, the locations from which they originate, and every direction on the compass that they can blow.

original: I’ll drain him dry as hay.   Sleep shall neither night nor day   Hang upon his penthouse lid.
translation: I’ll drain him until he’s dry as hay, and won’t let him sleep during night or day.

original: He shall live a man forbid.
translation: He’ll live as a cursed man.

original: Weary sev’nnights nine times nine   Shall he dwindle, peak and pine.
translation: For eighty-one wearying weeks he’ll slowly become sickly, and waste away from grief.

original: Though his bark cannot be lost,   Yet it shall be tempest-tossed.   Look what I have.
translation: Although I can’t destroy his ship, I can still buffet it with storms by controlling the winds.  Look what I’ve got.

original: Show me, show me.
translation: Show me, show me.

original: Here I have a pilot’s thumb, Wrecked as homeward he did come.
translation: Here I hold the thumb of a captain who was shipwrecked while returning home.

original: A drum, a drum! Macbeth doth come.
translation: A drum, a drum! Macbeth comes.

original: [dancing together in a circle]     The weird sisters, hand in hand,   Posters of the sea and land,   Thus do go about, about,
translation: [Dancing together in a circle]  The weird sisters, hand in hand, swift travelers over the sea and land, dance around and around!

original: Thrice to thine and thrice to mine   And thrice again, to make up nine.
translation: Three times your way, then three times mine, and three times again, to add up to nine.

original: Peace! The charm’s wound up.
translation: Quiet! The spell is ready.

original: So foul and fair a day I have not seen.
translation: I’ve never seen a day that was so good—because of our great victory—and yet with such bad weather.

original: How far is ’t called to Forres?
translation: How far is it to Forres, King Duncan’s palace?

original: —What are these     So withered and so wild in their attire,
translation: [He sees the WITCHES]   What are these creatures?  They’re so wrinkled and wildly dressed.

original: That look not like th’ inhabitants o’ th’ Earth,   And yet are on ’t?
translation: They don’t look like residents of the earth, and yet here they are on it.

original: —Live you?   Or are you aught   That man may question?
translation: [To the WITCHES]  Are you alive?  Are you something that a man can question?

original: You seem to understand me,   By each at once her choppy finger laying   Upon her skinny lips.
translation: You seem to understand me, since each of you has placed a chapped finger to her skinny lips.

original: You should be women,   And yet your beards forbid me to interpret   That you are so.
translation: You look like women, but your beards won’t let me believe that you actually are.

original: Speak, if you can: what are you?
translation: Speak, if you can. What are you?

original: All hail, Macbeth! Hail to thee, thane of Glamis!
translation: All hail, Macbeth! Hail to you, Thane of Glamis!

original: All hail, Macbeth! Hail to thee, thane of Cawdor!
translation: All hail, Macbeth! Hail to you, Thane of Cawdor!

original: All hail, Macbeth, that shalt be king hereafter!
translation: All hail, Macbeth, who will be king in the future!

original: Good sir, why do you start and seem to fear   Things that do sound so fair
translation: [To MACBETH]  Good sir, why do you flinch and seem afraid of these words that predict such good things for you?

original: [to the WITCHES]   I’ th’  name of truth,   are ye fantastical, or that indeed   Which outwardly ye show?   ?
translation: [To the WITCHES]  Be truthful, are you some kind of illusion—or are you, in fact, what you appear to be?

original: My noble partner    That he seems rapt withal.
translation: You’ve greeted my noble friend by his current title, and predict a future of additional noble titles and the promise of becoming king—all of which has left him astonished.

original: To me you speak not.
translation: Yet you don’t speak at all to me.

original: Speak, then, to me,
translation: If you can look into the future and say what will happen, then speak to me.

original: who neither beg nor fear
translation: I neither want your favors nor fear your hatred.

original: Hail!
translation: Hail!

original: Hail!
translation: Hail!

original: Hail!
translation: Hail!

original: Lesser than Macbeth and greater.
translation: You are lesser than Macbeth but also greater.

original: Not so happy, yet much happier.
translation: You will not be so fortunate as Macbeth, and yet much more fortunate.

original: Thou shalt get kings, though thou be none. So all hail, Macbeth and Banquo!
translation: Your descendants will be kings, though you will not be king. So all hail, Macbeth and Banquo!

original: Banquo and Macbeth, all hail!
translation: Banquo and Macbeth, all hail!

original: Stay,   you imperfect speakers, tell me more.
translation: Wait!  You have not told me everything. Tell me more.

original: By Sinel’s death I know I am thane of Glamis.
translation: I know I am the Thane of Glamis, because the title became mine when my father Sinel died.

original: But how of Cawdor?
translation: But how can I be the Thane of Cawdor?

original: The thane of Cawdor lives,   A prosperous gentleman,
translation: The Thane of Cawdor is alive—and he is a rich, strong man too.

original: and to be king   Stands not within the prospect of belief,   No more than to be Cawdor.
translation: And for me to become king is beyond belief—just as it’s crazy for me to be Thane of Cawdor.

original: Say from whence   You owe this strange intelligence,
translation: Tell me where you got this unnatural information.

original: or why   Upon this blasted heath you stop our way   With such prophetic greeting.
translation: And why did you come to us on this bleak and empty field with such a prophecy?

original: Speak, I charge you.
translation: I command you to speak.

original: The earth hath bubbles, as the water has, And these are of them. Whither are they vanished?
translation: The earth has bubbles, just like as water does. These beings must come from such a bubble. Where did they vanish?

original: Into the air, and what seemed corporal Melted, as breath into the wind. Would they had stayed.
translation: Into the air. They seemed solid, but then just melted like breath into the wind. I wish that they would have stayed!

original: Were such things here as we do speak about?  Or have we eaten on the insane root That takes the reason prisoner?
translation: Were these creatures that we're discussing ever even here? Or have we both eaten some root that's given us hallucinations?

original: Your children shall be kings.
translation: Your children will be kings.

original: You shall be king.
translation: You will be king.

original: And thane of Cawdor too: went it not so?
translation: And Thane of Cawdor too. Is that what they said?

original: To the selfsame tune and words. Who’s here?
translation: Those were their exact words. Who’s coming here?

original: The king hath happily received, Macbeth,   The news of thy success,
translation: Macbeth, the king was happy to learn of your success.

original: and when he reads   Thy personal venture in the rebels’ fight,   His wonders and his praises do contend   Which should be thine or his.
translation: And when he heard the story of your personal heroism in the battle against the rebels, he couldn't decide whether to praise you or just be silently amazed.

original: Silenced with that,   In viewing o’er the rest o’ the selfsame day,   He finds thee in the stout Norweyan ranks,   Nothing afeard of what thyself didst make,   Strange images of death.
translation: He was also at a loss for words to find out that on the same day you fought the rebels, you also fought against the army of Norway—and that you weren’t at all afraid of death, even as you killed those around you.

original: As thick as tale   Can post with post, and every one did bear   Thy praises in his kingdom’s great defense,   And poured them down before him.
translation: A stream of messengers brought news of this to the king, and they gushed with praise for how you defended his country.

original: We are sent To give thee from our royal master thanks, Only to herald thee into his sight, Not pay thee.
translation: We’ve been sent to give you the king’s thanks and to escort you to him, although we don’t have your reward.

original: And, for an earnest of a greater honor,   He bade me, from him, call thee thane of Cawdor:
translation: But— to give you a hint of the honors coming your way—the king told me to call you the Thane of Cawdor.

original: In which addition, hail, most worthy thane,   For it is thine.
translation: Hail, most worthy thane, for that title is now yours.

original: What, can the devil speak true?
translation: What? Can the devil speak the truth?

original: The thane of Cawdor lives. Why do you dress me  In borrowed robes?
translation: The Thane of Cawdor is still alive. How can you pretend that his title is now mine?

original: Who was the thane lives yet,   But under heavy judgment bears that life   Which he deserves to lose.
translation: The former Thane of Cawdor is still alive, but he’s held under a death sentence—and he deserves to die.

original: Whether he was combined   With those of Norway, or did line the rebel   With hidden help and vantage, or that with both   He labored in his country’s wrack, I know not;
translation: I don’t know whether he fought alongside the Norwegians or if he secretly helped the rebels, or if he worked with both of our enemies to destroy or country.

original: But treasons capital, confessed and proved,   Have overthrown him.
translation: But his capital treason has been proven, and he has confessed to it, so he has lost his former title.

original: [aside]   Glamis, and thane of Cawdor!   The greatest is behind.   [to ROSS and ANGUS]   Thanks for  your pains.
translation: [To himself]  Glamis, and Thane of Cawdor!  With the biggest part of their prophecy yet to come.

original: That, trusted home,   Might yet enkindle you unto the crown,   Besides the thane of Cawdor.   But ’tis strange.
translation: If you trust them, then it seems you might eventually become king, not just Thane of Cawdor.  But all of this is strange.

original: And oftentimes, to win us to our harm,   The instruments of darkness tell us truths,
translation: Often, to lead us to harm, the agents of darkness will first tell us some bit of truth.

original: Win us with honest trifles, to betray ’s   In deepest consequence.
translation: They win us over by telling us the truth about unimportant things, only to betray us when the consequences will be most terrible.

original: [aside]   Two truths are told,   As happy prologues to the swelling act   Of the imperial theme.
translation: [To himself]  Two of the  prophecies have come true, making it seem like this will end with my rise to the throne.

original: Look how our partner’s rapt.
translation: Look how our friend is daydreaming.

original: If chance will have me king, why, chance may  crown me Without my stir.
translation: If fate wants me to be king, well, maybe fate will give me the throne without me having to do anything at all.

original: New honors come upon him,  Like our strange garments, cleave not to their mold But with the aid of use.
translation: Like brand new clothes, Macbeth’s new titles don’t fit well until they’ve been worn for a while.

original: Come what come may, Time and the hour runs through the roughest day.
translation: No matter what happens, time continues on.

original: Worthy Macbeth, we stay upon your leisure.
translation: Good Macbeth, we’re waiting for you, whenever you’re ready to go.

original: Give me your favor.   My dull brain was wrought   With things forgotten.
translation: Pardon me.  I was occupied by forgotten thoughts.

original: Kind gentlemen, your pains   Are registered where every day I turn   The leaf to read them.
translation: Kind gentlemen, I won’t forget your efforts today, and will remember them every day.

original: Let us toward the king.
translation: Let’s go to the king.

original: Very gladly.
translation: Gladly.

original: Till then, enough.    Come, friends.
translation: Until then, we'll keep quiet about it.

original: Is execution done on Cawdor? Are not Those in commission yet returned?
translation: Has the Thane of Cawdor been executed? Have those in charge of the execution returned?

original: My liege,   They are not yet come back.
translation: My lord, they haven’t returned yet.

original: But I have spoke   With one that saw him die,
translation: But I spoke with someone who saw Cawdor die.

original: who did report   That very frankly he confessed his treasons,   Implored your highness’ pardon, and set forth   A deep repentance.
translation: He reported that Cawdor confessed his treason, begged your Highness’s forgiveness, and displayed deep regret for his actions.

original: Nothing in his life   Became him like the leaving it.
translation: Nothing he did in his entire life was as noble as the way he died.

original: He died   As one that had been studied in his death   To throw away the dearest thing he owed   As ’twere a careless trifle.
translation: He died like a man completely prepared to throw away the most precious thing he owned as if it were a worthless trinket.

original: There’s no art   To find the mind’s construction in the face.
translation: It’s impossible to tell what’s in a man’s mind by looking at his face.

original: He was a gentleman on whom I built   An absolute trust.
translation: Cawdor was a gentleman whom I trusted completely.

original: [to MACBETH]   O worthiest cousin,   The sin of my ingratitude even now   Was heavy on me.
translation: [To MACBETH]  My noble cousin! I’ve just been feeling guilty for not showing you enough gratitude.

original: Thou art so far before   That swiftest wing of recompense is slow   To overtake thee.
translation: You’ve accomplished so much that, no matter how fast I try to reward you, I haven’t been able to give you enough.

original: Would thou hadst less deserved,   That the proportion both of thanks and payment   Might have been mine!
translation: If you deserved less, then perhaps the balance between what I can reward and what you deserve could be tipped in my favor.

original: Only I have left to say,   More is thy due than more than all can pay.
translation: But all I have left to say is that I owe you more than I can ever repay.

original: The service and the loyalty I owe   In doing it pays itself.
translation: The loyalty I feel to you and the chance to serve you is its own reward.

original: Your highness’ part   Is to receive our duties, and our duties   Are to your throne and state children and servants,
translation: Your Highness’s duty is to accept our loyalty and service, while our duty to your kingship and country is similar to that owed by children to their father or servants to their master:

original: Which do but what they should, by doing everything   Safe toward your love and honor.
translation: we’re only doing what we should when we do all we can to protect you.

original: Welcome hither.   I have begun to plant thee, and will labor   To make thee full of growing.
translation: Be welcome here. The rewards I have given you are like newly planted seeds, and now I will work to help you grow into a great future.

original: There, if I grow, The harvest is your own.
translation: Then, if I grow to greatness, it will be a benefit to you as well.

original: My plenteous joys,   Wanton in fullness, seek to hide themselves   In drops of sorrow.
translation: I am so full of joy it brings tears to my eyes.

original: Sons, kinsmen, thanes,   And you whose places are the nearest, know   We will establish our estate upon   Our eldest, Malcolm, whom we name hereafter   The prince of Cumberland;
translation: My sons, relatives, thanes, and all those who are most close to me: I hereby proclaim that the heir to my throne is my eldest son, Malcolm, whom we will now call the Prince of Cumberland.

original: which honor must   Not unaccompanied invest him only,   But signs of nobleness, like stars, shall shine   On all deservers.
translation: He will not be alone in gaining new titles—new titles of nobility, like stars, will shine on all who deserve them.

original: The rest is labor which is not used for you:
translation: Any effort in your service does not feel like work at all.

original: I’ll be myself the harbinger and make joyful   The hearing of my wife with your approach.   So humbly take my leave.
translation: I’ll be the messenger and delight my wife with the news that you’re coming. Now I will humbly be on my way.

original: My worthy Cawdor!
translation: My noble Cawdor!

original: [aside] The prince of Cumberland!
translation: [To himself]  Malcolm is the Prince of Cumberland!

original: That is a step   On which I must fall down, or else o’erleap,   For in my way it lies.
translation: Because he is between me and the throne, I’m either going to have to move above him, or give up my hopes of kingship.

original: Stars, hide your fires;   Let not light see my black and deep desires.
translation: Stars, hide your brightness so that my evil desires are hidden from the light.

original: The eye wink at the hand,   yet let that be   Which the eye fears, when it is done, to see.
translation: May my eye be blind to the actions of my hand.  Yet if I do the thing that my eyes fear to see, I will be forced to see it once it’s been done.

original: True, worthy Banquo. He is full so valiant,   And in his commendations I am fed;
translation: True, Banquo. Macbeth is incredibly heroic, and by praising him I myself benefit.

original: It is a banquet to me.—Let’s after him,   Whose care is gone before to bid us welcome:   It is a peerless kinsman.
translation: Let’s follow him, since he’s gone ahead of us to prepare for our arrival. He is unequaled as a lord or kinsman.

original: [reading] “They met me in the day of success, and I  have learned by the perfectest report they have more in  them than mortal knowledge.
translation: [Reading] “The witches met me on my day of victory, and I have since learned for certain that they have supernatural knowledge.

original: When I burned in desire to  question them further, they made themselves air, into  which they vanished.
translation: When I tried frantically to question them further, they vanished into the air.

original: Whiles I stood rapt in the wonder  of it came missives from the king, who all-hailed me  ‘Thane of Cawdor,’ by which title, before, these weird  sisters saluted me, and referred me to the coming on of  time with ‘Hail, king that shalt be!’
translation: While I stood amazed at the strangeness of all of this, messengers from the king arrived and greeted me as “Thane of Cawdor,” which is exactly what the weird sisters had called me before then hailing me as 'the future king!’

original: This have I  thought good to deliver thee, my dearest partner of  greatness, that thou might’st not lose the dues of  rejoicing, by being ignorant of what greatness is  promised thee.
translation: M y dearest partner in greatness,  I wanted to tell you this news, so that you would not be ignorant of the greatness promised to us and therefore be unable to celebrate.

original: Lay it to thy heart, and farewell.”
translation: Keep it close to your heart, and farewell.”   [She puts down the letter]

original: Glamis thou art, and Cawdor; and shalt be   What thou art promised.
translation: You are Thane of Glamis, and Cawdor, and you will be the king just as you were promised.

original: Yet do I fear thy nature;   It is too full o’ th’ milk of human kindness   To catch the nearest way:
translation: Yet I worry about your character. You are too full of the milk of human kindness to take the shortest route to power.

original: thou wouldst be great,   Art not without ambition, but without   The illness should attend it.
translation: You want to be powerful, and you don’t lack ambition—but you don’t have the nastiness required to truly go for it.

original: What thou wouldst  highly,   That wouldst thou holily;
translation: You hope to become great by acting with virtue and goodness.

original: wouldst not play false,   And yet wouldst wrongly win. Thou’ld’st have, great  Glamis,   That which cries, “Thus thou must do,” if thou have it,   And that which rather thou dost fear to do,   Than wishest should be undone.
translation: You don’t want to lie or cheat, yet you want to win what Great Thane of Glamis, you want to have something, but you’re too frightened to do it.

original: Hie thee hither,   That I may pour my spirits in thine ear   And chastise with the valor of my tongue   All that impedes thee from the golden round,   Which fate and metaphysical aid doth seem   To have thee crowned withal.
translation: Get yourself home, so I can whisper in your ear and criticize you so that you cease to be affected by everything that’s keeping you from taking the crown—which fate and magic both seem to want you to have.

original: What is your tidings?
translation: What’s your news?

original: The king comes here tonight.
translation: The king is coming here tonight.

original: Thou ‘rt mad to say it.  Is not thy master with him, who, were ’t so, Would have informed for preparation?
translation: You’re crazy to think that. Isn’t my lord Macbeth with the king? If what you say is true, Macbeth would have sent word so I could prepare?

original: So please you, it is true: our thane is coming.
translation: I beg your pardon, but it’s true: our lord is coming.

original: One of my fellows had the speed of him,   Who, almost dead for breath, had scarcely more   Than would make up his message.
translation: One of my fellow servants raced ahead of him, and was so out of breath that he almost couldn’t tell me his message.

original: Give him tending. He brings great news.
translation: Take care him. He brings great news.

original: The raven himself is hoarse   That croaks the fatal entrance of Duncan   Under my battlements.
translation: The messenger croaks the announcement of Duncan’s fatal arrival to my castle, just like a  raven  would croak out a warning.

original: Come, you spirits   That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here,   And fill me from the crown to the toe top-full   Of direst cruelty.
translation: Come on, you spirits that aid thoughts of murder: remove my womanhood and fill me up from head to toe with terrible cruelty!

original: Make thick my blood.   Stop up the access and passage to remorse,   That no compunctious visitings of nature   Shake my fell purpose, nor keep peace between   The effect and it!
translation: Thicken my blood. Block my veins from all feelings of regret, so that no natural feelings of guilt or doubt can sway me from my dark desires, or prevent me from accomplishing them!

original: Come to my woman’s breasts,   And take my milk for gall, you murd’ring ministers,   Wherever in your sightless substances   You wait on nature’s mischief.
translation: Demons of murder, come to me from wherever you hide yourselves as you wait to aid and abet corrupt and evil feelings, and turn my mother’s milk into bitter acid.

original: Come, thick night,   And pall thee in the dunnest smoke of hell,   That my keen knife see not the wound it makes,   Nor heaven peep through the blanket of the dark   To cry “Hold, hold!”
translation: Come, thick night—wrapped in the darkest smoke of hell—so that my sharp knife can’t see the wound it makes, and heaven can’t peek through the darkness and cry: “Stop! Stop!”

original: Great Glamis, worthy Cawdor,   Greater than both, by the all-hail hereafter,
translation: Great Thane of Glamis and noble Thane of Cawdor, you’ll be greater than both when you become king.

original: Thy letters have transported me beyond   This ignorant present, and I feel now   The future in the instant.
translation: Your letter has transported me beyond the present moment and all its ignorance of what will come, so that I now feel like the future is here now.

original: My dearest love,  Duncan comes here tonight.
translation: My dearest love, Duncan will be here tonight.

original: And when goes hence?
translation: And when does he leave?

original: Tomorrow, as he purposes.
translation: Tomorrow, according to his plans.

original: O, never   Shall sun that morrow see!   Your face, my thane, is as a book where men   May read strange matters.
translation: That will never happen. My thane, your face betrays your troubled thoughts, so that others can read it like a book.

original: To beguile the time,   Look like the time.
translation: To deceive all others, you have to look exactly as they do.

original: Bear welcome in your eye,   Your hand, your tongue.
translation: When you greet the king, do so completely: with your eyes, hands, and words.

original: Look like th’ innocent flower,   But be the serpent under ’t.
translation: Look like an innocent flower, but be the snake that hides beneath it.

original: He that’s coming   Must be provided for;
translation: The king must be taken care of.

original: and you shall put   This night’s great business into my dispatch,   Which shall to all our nights and days to come   Give solely sovereign sway and masterdom.
translation: Allow me to manage everything tonight, because the events of this night will bring us sole mastery and power for all our nights and days to come.

original: We will speak further.
translation: We’ll speak about this further.

original: Only look up clear. To alter favor ever is to fear.  Leave all the rest to me.
translation: Keep your head up and look calm. If your expression changes it will arouse suspicion. Leave all the rest to me.

original: This castle hath a pleasant seat. The air Nimbly and sweetly recommends itself Unto our gentle senses.
translation: This castle sits in a pleasant place. The fresh, sweet air delights my noble senses.

original: This guest of summer,   The temple-haunting martlet, does approve,   By his loved mansionry, that the heaven’s breath   Smells wooingly here.
translation: That the martin—a summer bird that builds its nest in the steeples of churches—builds its nest here proves how sweet and blessed the breeze is.

original: No jutty, frieze,   Buttress, nor coign of vantage, but this bird   Hath made his pendant bed and procreant cradle.
translation: These birds have built nests on every projection, carving, buttress, and corner of this castle.

original: Where they most breed and haunt, I have observed,   The air is delicate.
translation: I've noticed that martins prefer to live and mate in places where the air is most fine.

original: See, see, our honored hostess!   The love that follows us sometime is our trouble,   Which still we thank as love.
translation: Look, it’s our honored hostess! I am troubled sometimes by the lengths that my subjects go to out of love for me, but I still thank you for your love.

original: Herein I teach you   How you shall bid God ‘ild us for your pains,   And thank us for your trouble.
translation: In saying this, I’m suggesting that you thank me for the trouble my presence is causing you, since I’m here out of my love for you.

original: All our service,   In every point twice done and then done double,   Were poor and single business to contend   Against those honors deep and broad wherewith   Your majesty loads our house.
translation: All our efforts—even if they were doubled and then doubled again—are poor and small acts when compared to the profound honor you’ve brought to our home.

original: For those of old,   And the late dignities heaped up to them,   We rest your hermits.
translation: In gratitude for the honors you’ve given us in the past, and those you’ve added just recently, we will always pray for and support you.

original: Where’s the thane of Cawdor?   We coursed him at the heels and had a purpose   To be his purveyor;
translation: Where’s Macbeth, Thane of Cawdor? We followed closely after him, and hoped to overtake him on the road so that we would be the ones to welcome him.

original: but he rides well,   And his great love, sharp as his spur, hath holp him   To his home before us.
translation: But he rides well, and his great love for you—which is as sharp as his spur—helped him reach his home before us.

original: Fair and noble hostess,   We are your guest tonight.
translation: Beautiful and noble hostess, we are your guests tonight.

original: Your servants ever   Have theirs, themselves, and what is theirs in compt
translation: We are always your servants. And our servants, we ourselves, and everything we own belong to you.

original: To make their audit at your highness’ pleasure,   Still to return your own.
translation: It is all yours to use and enjoy, and we are ready to return it to you because it is really your own, after all.

original: Give me your hand.   Conduct me to mine host.
translation: Give me your hand. Lead me to Macbeth, my host.

original: We love him highly   And shall continue our graces towards him.   By your leave, hostess.
translation: I love him dearly, and I shall continue to hold him in high favor. When you’re ready, hostess.

original: If it were done when ’tis done, then ’twere well   It were done quickly.
translation: If this will really all be over once it’s done, then it would be best to get it over with quickly.
