translation: They have tied me to a stake. I can’t run. Instead, I must stand and fight, like a  bear .

original: What’s he   That was not born of woman? Such a one   Am I to fear, or none.
translation: Where’s the man who wasn’t born from a woman? I fear him, and no one else.

original: What is thy name?
translation: What’s your name?

original: Thou ‘lt be afraid to hear it.
translation: You’ll be afraid to hear it.

original: No, though thou call’st thyself a hotter name Than any is in hell.
translation: No, not even if you called yourself a name more evil than any demon that's in hell.

original: My name’s Macbeth.
translation: My name’s Macbeth.

original: The devil himself could not pronounce a title More hateful to mine ear.
translation: The devil himself couldn’t say a name I hate more.

original: No, nor more fearful.
translation: No, nor could the devil’s name be more frightening.

original: Thou liest, abhorrèd tyrant. With my sword I’ll prove the lie thou speak’st.
translation: You lie, hated tyrant. My sword will prove that you speak lies.

original: Thou wast born of woman. But swords I smile at, weapons laugh to scorn,  Brandished by man that’s of a woman born.
translation: You were born from a woman. I smile at swords, and laugh at any weapon held by a man born from a woman.

original: That way the noise is. Tyrant, show thy face!
translation: The noise is coming from over there. Tyrant, show your face!

original: If thou beest slain, and with no stroke of mine,   My wife and children’s ghosts will haunt me still.
translation: If you are killed without a strike from my own sword, the ghosts of my wife and children will haunt me forever.

original: I cannot strike at wretched kerns, whose arms   Are hired to bear their staves. Either thou, Macbeth,   Or else my sword with an unbattered edge   I sheathe again undeeded.
translation: I won’t fight these wretched soldiers. Macbeth, I’ll dull the edge of my sword fighting you, or else I’ll sheathe my sword, unused.

original: There thou shouldst be;   By this great clatter, one of the greatest note   Seems bruited.
translation: You must be over there based on that great noise, which sounds like the announcement of some notable man.

original: Let me find him, Fortune,   And more I beg not.
translation: Oh Fortune, let me find him! That's all I ask.

original: This way, my lord. The castle’s gently rendered.
translation: Come this way, my lord. The castle has surrendered without a fight.

original: The tyrant’s people on both sides do fight,   The noble thanes do bravely in the war,
translation: Macbeth’s soldiers are fighting on both sides, while our thanes fight bravely.

original: The day almost itself professes yours,   And little is to do.
translation: The victory is almost yours, and there is little left to do.

original: We have met with foes That strike beside us.
translation: Our enemies seem to be trying to miss when they strike at us.

original: Enter, sir, the castle.
translation: Sir, enter the castle.

original: Why should I play the Roman fool and die On mine own sword? Whiles I see lives, the gashes Do better upon them.
translation: Why should I act like some ancient Roman fool and commit suicide by stabbing myself? As long as I see living enemies, I’d rather wound them than be wounded myself.

original: Turn, hellhound, turn!
translation: Turn and face me, you dog from hell, turn!

original: Of all men else I have avoided thee.  But get thee back. My soul is too much charged With blood of thine already.
translation: You are the only man I have avoided. Go away. My soul is already stained too much by the blood of your murdered family.

original: I have no words. My voice is in my sword. Thou bloodier villain Than terms can give thee out!
translation: I have nothing to say to you. My sword will be my voice. You are too vicious for words to describe!

original: Thou losest labor.   As easy mayst thou the intrenchant air   With thy keen sword impress as make me bleed.
translation: You’re wasting your effort. You might as well try to stab the air with your sword rather than try to use it to make me bleed.

original: Let fall thy blade on vulnerable crests;
translation: Use your sword to fight someone who can be harmed.

original: I bear a charmèd life, which must not yield   To one of woman born.
translation: I lead a charmed life, and can’t be defeated by anyone born from a woman.

original: Despair thy charm,   And let the angel whom thou still hast served   Tell thee,
translation: Then you should despair. The evil spirit you serve can tell you that I was not born.

original: Macduff was from his mother’s womb   Untimely ripped.
translation: I was cut out of my mother’s womb before she could deliver me naturally.

original: Accursèd be that tongue that tells me so,   For it hath cowed my better part of man!
translation: Curse your tongue for telling me this, for now my courage has deserted me!

original: And be these juggling fiends no more believed,
translation: I no longer believe those tricky witches.

original: That palter with us in a double sense,   That keep the word of promise to our ear,   And break it to our hope. I’ll not fight with thee.
translation: They tricked me with their double meanings, raising my hopes only to destroy them. I won’t fight you.

original: Then yield thee, coward,   And live to be the show and gaze o’ th’ time.
translation: Then surrender, coward, and live on as an amusement we all mock and stare at.

original: We’ll have thee, as our rarer monsters are,   Painted on a pole, and underwrit,   “Here may you see the tyrant.”
translation: As with a rare beast, we’ll put a picture of you on a sign, right above the words, “Here is the tyrant!”

original: I will not yield,   To kiss the ground before young Malcolm’s feet,   And to be baited with the rabble’s curse.
translation: I won’t surrender and kiss the ground in front of young Malcolm’s feet, or be taunted by commoners.

original: Though Birnam Wood be come to Dunsinane,   And thou opposed, being of no woman born,   Yet I will try the last.
translation: Though Birnam Wood really did come to Dunsinane, and I’m facing a man not born of a woman, I’ll fight to the end.

original: Before my body   I throw my warlike shield.
translation: I’ll raise my shield in front of my body.

original: Lay on, Macduff,   And damned be him that first cries, “Hold, enough!”
translation: Now come and fight, Macduff, and damn the first of us who cries, "Stop! Enough!"

original: I would the friends we miss were safe arrived.
translation: I wish all of our friends had survived to be here.

original: Some must go off. And yet, by these I see, So great a day as this is cheaply bought.
translation: Some people will be killed in every battle. And yet, from what I can see, our great victory didn’t cost us very much.

original: Macduff is missing, and your noble son.
translation: Macduff is missing, as is your noble son.

original: Your son, my lord, has paid a soldier’s debt.
translation: My lord, your son, Young Siward, has paid the soldier’s price.

original: He only lived but till he was a man,   The which no sooner had his prowess confirmed   In the unshrinking station where he fought,   But like a man he died.
translation: He lived just long enough to be a man, and he had no sooner proved his manhood through courage in battle than he died.

original: Then he is dead?
translation: Then he is dead?

original: Ay, and brought off the field. Your cause of sorrow  Must not be measured by his worth, for then It hath no end.
translation: Yes, and carried off the battlefield. If your grief were to equal his worth, then it would never end.

original: Had he his hurts before?
translation: Were his wounds on his front side?

original: Ay, on the front.
translation: Yes, on his front.

original: Why then, God’s soldier be he!
translation: Well then, he’s God’s soldier now!

original: Had I as many sons as I have hairs,   I would not wish them to a fairer death.
translation: If I had as many sons as I have hairs on my head, I couldn’t hope for any of them to die with more honor.

original: And so, his knell is knolled.
translation: And so, his time has come to die.

original: He’s worth more sorrow, And that I’ll spend for him.
translation: He’s worth more grief than that, and I’ll mourn for him.

original: He’s worth no more. They say he parted well and paid his score. And so, God be with him! Here comes newer comfort.
translation: He is worth no more than that. They say he died well, and did his duty. And so, may God be with him! Here comes better news.

original: Hail, king! For so thou art. Behold where stands   The usurper’s cursèd head. The time is free.
translation: Hail, King Malcolm! Because that’s what you are. Look, here is Macbeth’s cursed head. We are free of the tyrant.

original: I see thee compassed with thy kingdom’s pearl,   That speak my salutation in their minds,
translation: I see that you are surrounded by the kingdom’s noblemen, and they’re thinking what I’m saying.

original: Whose voices I desire aloud with mine.   Hail, King of Scotland!
translation: I ask them to cheer aloud with me: Hail, King of Scotland!

original: Hail, King of Scotland!
translation: Hail, King of Scotland!

original: We shall not spend a large expense of time   Before we reckon with your several loves   And make us even with you.
translation: It will not take long for me to repay my debt to you all by rewarding each of you as your loyalty and service deserves.

original: My thanes and kinsmen,   Henceforth be earls, the first that ever Scotland   In such an honor named.
translation: My thanes and kinsmen, I name you all earls—the first ever to be named earls in Scotland.

original: What’s more to do,   Which would be planted newly with the time,
translation: We have much else to do as well, which should be started soon, as the beginning of a new era.

original: As calling home our exiled friends abroad   That fled the snares of watchful tyranny,   Producing forth the cruel ministers   Of this dead butcher and his fiendlike queen,   Who, as ’tis thought, by self and violent hands   Took off her life;
translation: We must call home our exiled friends who fled from the trap of Macbeth’s tyranny, and we must find all those cruel attendants who helped this dead butcher and his demon-like queen, who is thought to have killed herself.

original: this, and what needful else   That calls upon us, by the grace of Grace,   We will perform in measure, time, and place.
translation: This, and whatever else we must do, by the grace of God, we will do in the right amount, at the right time, and in the right place.

original: So, thanks to all at once and to each one,   Whom we invite to see us crowned at Scone.
translation: So I thank you all together and individually, and I invite you to come see me be crowned King of Scotland at Scone.

original: I learn in this letter that Don Pedro of Aragon comes  this night to Messina.
translation: This letter says that Don Pedro of Aragon is coming to Messina tonight.

original: He is very near by this. He was not three leagues off  when I left him.
translation: He must be very close by now. He was less than nine miles away when I left him.

original: How many gentlemen have you lost in this action?
translation: How many men did you lose in this battle?

original: But few of any sort, and none of name.
translation: Not many, and no one with any notable rank or reputation.

original: A victory is twice itself when the achiever brings home full numbers. I find here that Don Pedro hath bestowed  much  honor on a young Florentine called Claudio.
translation: A victory is twice as great when the victor comes home without losing any soldiers. This letter also says that Don Pedro has given great honors to a young man from Florence named Claudio.

original: Much deserved on his part, and equally remembered  by Don Pedro.
translation: The honors are well-deserved, and Don Pedro has bestowed them fairly.

original: He hath borne himself beyond the promise  of his age, doing in the figure of a lamb the feats of a lion.
translation: Claudio has achieved things that no one would expect from such a young man. He has the look of a lamb, but he fights like a lion.

original: He hath indeed better bettered expectation than  you must expect of me to tell you how.
translation: Indeed, he's surpassed all expectations by so much that you can't expect me to describe him properly.

original: He hath an uncle here in Messina will be very much  glad of it.
translation: He has an uncle here in Messina who will be very glad to hear about this.

original: I have already delivered him letters, and there  appears much joy in him—even so much that joy could not  show itself modest enough without a badge of bitterness.
translation: I've already delivered letters to him, and he seemed overjoyed. Indeed, he got so emotional that he couldn't restrain his tears.

original: Did he break out into tears?
translation: Did he really start crying?

original: In great measure.
translation: Yes, heavily.

original: A kind overflow of kindness. There are no faces truer  than those that are so washed. How much better is it to  weep at joy than to joy at weeping!
translation: That's the result of a natural overflow of affection for family members. There's no face more honest than one washed by tears. And how much better it is to weep for joy than to laugh in sadness!

original: I pray you, is Signor Montanto returned from the wars  or no?
I know none of that name, lady. There was none such in  the army of any sort.
translation: I don't know anyone by that name, my lady. There never was a Sir Montanto in our army.

original: What is he that you ask for, niece?
translation: Who is it you're asking about, niece?

original: My cousin means Signor Benedick of Padua.
Oh, he’s returned, and as pleasant as ever he was.
translation: Oh, he's returned, and he's as witty and cheerful as ever.

original: He set up his bills here in Messina and challenged  Cupid at the flight,
translation: Benedick once put up signs here in Messina  challenging Cupid to an archery contest .

original: and my uncle’s Fool, reading the  challenge, subscribed for Cupid and challenged him at  the bird-bolt.
translation: My uncle's jester read the challenge, accepted on Cupid's behalf, and challenged Benedick with blunt arrows.

original: I pray you, how many hath he killed and  eaten in these wars? But how many hath he killed? For  indeed I promised to eat all of his killing.
translation: But please tell me, how many men has he killed and eaten in these battles? For I promised to eat any man he could kill.

original: Faith, niece, you tax Signor Benedick too much, but  he’ll be meet with you, I doubt it not.
translation: Honestly, niece, you criticize Sir Benedick too much. But I don't doubt that he'll give as good as he gets.

original: He hath done good service, lady, in these wars.
translation: He served well in this war, my lady.

original: You had musty victual, and he hath holp to eat it. He  is a very valiant trencherman. He hath an excellent  stomach.
translation: You had stale food, and he helped you eat it. He's a very brave eater. He has an excellent stomach for eating.

original: And a good soldier too, lady.
translation: And a stomach for fighting too, my lady. He's a good soldier.

original: And a good soldier to a lady, but what is he to a lord?
translation: A good soldier compared to a lady, but what is he compared to a lord?

original: A lord to a lord, a man to a man, stuffed with all  honorable virtues.
translation: He's a lord to a lord and a man to a man. He's stuffed full of honorable virtues.

original: It is so indeed. He is no less than a stuffed man. But  for the stuffing—well, we are all mortal.
translation: Indeed he is. He's nothing more than a dummy—a stuffed man. But as for what he's stuffed with—well, we all have our faults.

original: You must not, sir, mistake my niece. There is a kind  of merry war betwixt Signor Benedick and her. They  never meet but there’s a skirmish of wit between them.
translation: Sir, you mustn't misunderstand my niece. There is a kind of cheerful war between her and Sir Benedick. Whenever they meet there's always a battle of wits.

original: Alas, he gets nothing by that.
translation: And he never gains anything from such battles.

original: In our last conflict  four of his five wits went halting off, and now is the  whole man governed with one, so that if he have wit  enough to keep himself warm, let him bear it for a  difference between himself and his horse, for it is all  the wealth that he hath left to be known a reasonable  creature.
translation: In our last encounter, all his wits but one went limping off, leaving him with only enough wit to keep himself warm and distinguish himself from his horse.

original: Who is his companion now? He hath every month  a new sworn brother.
translation: But who is his companion now? Every month he has a new best friend.

original: Is ’t possible?
translation: Is that possible?

original: Very easily possible. He wears his faith but as the  fashion of his hat; it ever changes with the next block.
translation: Entirely possible. He wears his loyalty like he wears his hats—always changing with the latest fashions.

original: I see, lady, the gentleman is not in your books.
translation: I see that this gentleman isn't included in your good book, my lady.

original: No. An he were, I would burn my study. But I pray  you, who is his companion? Is there no young squarer now that will make a voyage with him to the devil?
translation: No. And if he were in my good book, I'd burn down my library. But please tell me, who is his friend now? Isn't there some quarrelsome young man who will go along with Benedick on his voyage to hell?

original: He is most in the company of the right noble Claudio.
translation: He spends most of his time in the company of the most noble Claudio.

original: O Lord, he will hang upon him like a disease!
translation: Oh Lord, Benedick will cling to him like a disease!

original: He is  sooner caught than the pestilence, and the taker runs  presently mad.
translation: Benedick is easier to catch than the plague, and the person he's infected immediately goes insane.

original: God help the noble Claudio! If he have  caught the Benedick, it will cost him a thousand pound  ere a be cured.
translation: God help the noble Claudio! If he's caught the Benedick, he'll lose all his money before he can be cured.

original: I will hold friends with you, lady.
translation: I'll make sure to stay on your good side, my lady.

original: Do, good friend.
translation: Do, good friend.

original: You will never run mad, niece.
translation: You will never "catch the Benedick," niece.

original: No, not till a hot January.
translation: No, not until there's a hot January.

original: Don Pedro is approached.
translation: Don Pedro is here.

original: Good Signor Leonato, are you come to meet your  trouble? The fashion of the world is to avoid cost, and  you encounter it.
translation: Good Sir Leonato, have you come to meet your burden—the burden of hosting me and all my followers? Most people avoid expense, but you welcome it.

original: Never came trouble to my house in the likeness of  your Grace,
translation: You are never a burden to my house,  your Grace .

original: for trouble being gone, comfort should  remain,
translation: When a burden leaves, comfort should replace it.

original: but   when you depart from me, sorrow abides and happiness   takes his leave.
translation: But when  you  leave, you take happiness with you and leave behind only sorrow.

original: You embrace your charge too willingly. I think this is  your daughter.
translation: You welcome your troubles too cheerfully.  This must be your daughter.

original: Her mother hath many times told me so.
translation: That's what her mother keeps telling me.

original: Were you in doubt, sir, that you asked her?
translation: Sir, did you doubt that she was your daughter, since you had to ask?

original: Signor Benedick, no, for then were you a child.
translation: No, Sir Benedick, for you were only a child then—not yet old enough to seduce my wife.

original: You have it full, Benedick. We may guess by this what  you are, being a man. Truly, the lady fathers  herself.—Be happy, lady, for you are like an honorable  father.
translation: He got you back, Benedick! I can tell from this what kind of a man you are, and that you have a reputation with women. But seriously, the lady proves who her father is by her resemblance to him. Be happy, my lady, for you resemble an honorable father.

original: If Signor Leonato be her father, she would not have  his head on her shoulders for all Messina, as like him  as she is.
translation: Even if Sir Leonato is her father, she wouldn't want to resemble an old man, no matter how similar she is to him.

original: I wonder that you will still be talking, Signor  Benedick. Nobody marks you.
translation: I'm surprised that you're still talking, Sir Benedick. Nobody's paying attention to you.

original: What, my dear Lady Disdain! Are you yet living?
translation: Oh, it's my dear Lady Scorn! Haven't you died from boredom yet?

original: Is it possible disdain should die while she hath such  meet food to feed it as Signor Benedick? Courtesy itself must convert to disdain if you come in her presence.
translation: How could Scorn die when she has such a plentiful supply of food in the form of Sir Benedick? When you're around, even Lady Courtesy must transform into Lady Scorn.

original: Then is courtesy a turncoat. But it is certain I am  loved of all ladies, only you excepted. And I would I  could find in my heart that I had not a hard heart, for  truly I love none.
translation: Then Lady Courtesy is a traitor. But, truly, all ladies love me, except you. And I wish I could say that I wasn't so hard-hearted, for I really don't love anyone.

original: A dear happiness to women. They would else have  been troubled with a pernicious suitor.
translation: What a stroke of good fortune for women. Otherwise they would all be plagued by a terrible suitor.

original: I thank God and  my cold blood I am of your humor for that.
translation: I thank God and my own cold blood that I feel the same way, and don't love anyone.

original: I had rather  hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves me.
translation: I would rather hear my dog bark at a crow than hear a man swear that he loves me.

original: God keep your Ladyship still in that mind, so some  gentle-man or other shall ’scape a predestinate  scratched face.
translation: Your Ladyship, may God preserve you in that state of mind forever, so that some poor gentleman will escape having his face scratched up.

original: Scratching could not make it worse an ’twere such a  face as yours were.
translation: If it's a face like yours then scratching couldn't make it look any worse.

original: Well, you are a rare parrot-teacher.
translation: You'd be great at teaching parrots—you say the same things over and over again.

original: A bird of my tongue is better than a beast of yours.
translation: Better a bird that talks like me than a beast that talks like you—unable to say anything at all.

original: I would my horse had the speed of your tongue and so  good a continuer. But keep your way, i' God’s name. I  have done.
translation: I wish my horse were as fast as your tongue, and could go on and on in the same way. But have it your way, for God's sake. I'm done.

original: You always end with a jade’s trick. I know you of old.
translation: You always drop out of the horse race before it's over. I know how you are.

original: That is the sum of all, Leonato.
translation: And that's everything that's happened since we last saw each other, Leonato.

original: —Signior Claudio  and Signior Benedick, my dear friend Leonato hath  invited you all. I tell him we shall stay here at the  least a month, and he heartily prays some occasion may  detain us longer.
translation: [To CLAUDIO and BENEDICK]  Sir Claudio and Sir Benedick, my dear friend Leonato has invited you all to stay here. I told him we'll stay for at least a month, and he begged us to stay longer.

original: I dare   swear he is no hypocrite but prays from his heart.
translation: I swear that he's not just being polite, but is sincere.

original: If you swear, my lord, you shall not be forsworn.  [to  DON JOHN]  Let me bid you welcome, my lord. Being  reconciled to the Prince your brother, I owe you all  duty.
translation: My lord, if you swear it, you won't be lying.  Let me welcome you as well, my lord. Now that you and your brother are reconciled, I owe you the same allegiance I owe to Don Pedro.

original: I thank you. I am not of many words, but I thank you.
translation: I thank you. I'm a man of few words, but I thank you.

original: Please it your Grace lead on?
translation: Do you want to lead us all inside, your Grace?

original: Your hand, Leonato. We will go together.
translation: Give me your hand, Leonato. We'll go together.

original: Benedick, didst thou note the daughter of Signior  Leonato?
translation: Benedick, did you notice Sir Leonato's daughter?

original: I noted her not, but I looked on her.
translation: I saw her, but I didn't see anything worth noting.

original: Is she not a modest young lady?
translation: Isn't she a well-mannered young lady?

original: Do you question me as an honest man should do, for  my simple true judgment? Or would you have me speak  after my custom, as being a professed tyrant to their  sex?
translation: Are you asking me that honestly, and want my true opinion? Or do you want me to criticize her in the way that I'm known to criticize all women?

original: No, I pray thee speak in sober judgment.
translation: No, please speak honestly and seriously.

original: Why, i' faith, methinks she’s too low for a high  praise, too brown for a fair praise, and too little for  a great praise.
translation: Well, to be honest, I think she's too short to be praised highly, too ugly to be praised prettily, and too little to be praised greatly.

original: Only this commendation I can afford her, that were she other than she is, she were unhandsome,  and being no other but as she is, I do not like her.
translation: The only compliment I can give her is this: if she were different than the way she is, she would be ugly. And since she can't be anything but herself, I do not like her.

original: Thou thinkest I am in sport. I pray thee tell me truly  how thou lik’st her.
translation: You think I'm joking. Please tell me honestly what you think of her.

original: Would you buy her, that you enquire after her?
translation: Why are you asking about her—do you want to buy her?

original: Can the world buy such a jewel?
translation: Could anything in the world be enough to buy such a jewel?

original: Yea, and a case to put it into.
translation: Yes, and a box to put it in.

original: But speak you this with a sad brow?
translation: But are you saying this seriously?

original: Or do you play the flouting jack, to tell  us Cupid is a good hare-finder and Vulcan a rare  carpenter?
translation: Or are you just playing the part of the mocking rascal, saying that blind Cupid is good at catching hares and  Vulcan  is a good carpenter?

original: Come, in what key shall a man take you to go  in the song?
translation: Come, tell me what key you're singing in, so I can sing in harmony.

original: In mine eye she is the sweetest lady that ever I looked on.
translation: In my eyes, she seems like the sweetest lady I've ever seen.

original: I can see yet without spectacles, and I see no such  matter.
translation: I can still see without glasses, and I don't see it.

original: There’s her cousin, an she were not possessed  with a fury, exceeds her as much in beauty as the first  of May doth the last of December.
translation: If her cousin Beatrice didn't have such a temper, she would exceed Hero in beauty more than spring does winter.

original: But I hope you have no intent to turn husband, have you?
translation: But I hope you aren't looking to become a husband, are you?

original: I would scarce trust myself, though I had sworn  the contrary, if Hero would be my wife.
translation: Even if I had sworn to never marry, I wouldn't trust myself if Hero said she would be my wife.

original: Is ’t come to this? In faith, hath not the world one  man but he will wear his cap with suspicion?
translation: Is this what the world's coming to? Honestly, isn't there one man left  who can wear his hat without fearing to sprout horns ?

original: Shall I  never see a bachelor of three-score again?
translation: Will I never see a sixty-year-old bachelor again?

original: Go to, i'  faith, an thou wilt needs thrust thy neck into a yoke,  wear the print of it, and sigh away Sundays. Look, Don  Pedro is returned to seek you.
translation: Go ahead then, if you insist on putting your neck in the yoke of marriage like an ox, and throwing away your free time. Look, Don Pedro has returned to look for you.

original: What secret hath held you here that you followed not  to Leonato’s?
translation: What secrets have you been telling that kept you from following us to Leonato's?

original: I would your grace would constrain me to tell.
translation: Your Grace will have to command me to tell.

original: I charge thee on thy allegiance.
translation: I command you by your allegiance to me. Tell me.

original: You hear, Count Claudio?
translation: Do you hear this, Count Claudio?

original: I can be secret as a dumb man, I would have you think so, but on my allegiance—mark  you this, on my allegiance—   [to DON PEDRO]   he is in love.
translation: I can keep secrets like a mute man, and I want you to know that. But my allegiance is to Don Pedro—look, I have to tell him because of my allegiance— [To DON PEDRO]  Claudio is in love.

original: With who? Now, that is your Grace’s part. Mark how  short his answer is: with Hero, Leonato’s short  daughter.
translation: With whom? Now, that's what your Grace is supposed to ask next. See how short the answer is: with Hero, Leonato's short daughter.

original: If this were so, so were it uttered.
translation: If that were true, then that would be the thing to say.

original: Like the old tale, my lord: “It is not so nor ’twas  not so but, indeed, God forbid it should be so.”
translation: See how he denies his crime, my lord, like the man in the old tale "Mr. Fox." "It isn't true and it wasn't true, and God forbid that it should be true."

original: If my passion change not shortly, God forbid it should  be otherwise.
translation: If my passions don't change very soon, God forbid that it should not be true.

original: Amen, if you love her, for the lady is very well  worthy.
translation: If you really love Hero, then I approve. The lady is very deserving of love.

original: You speak this to fetch me in, my lord.
translation: You're saying this to trick me into confessing, my lord.

original: By my troth, I speak my thought.
translation: Truthfully, I'm saying what I really think.

original: And, in faith, my lord, I spoke mine.
translation: And honestly, my lord, I also said what I thought when I said that I loved her.

original: And by my two faiths and troths, my lord, I spoke mine.
translation: And truthfully and honestly I swear, my lord, that I did the same when I said this was a bad idea.

original: That I love her, I feel.
translation: I feel that I love her.

original: That she is worthy, I know.
translation: And I know that she is worthy.

original: That I neither feel how she should be loved nor know  how she should be worthy is the opinion that fire cannot melt out of me. I will die in it at the stake.
translation: And I neither feel how she could be loved nor know how she could be worthy. Even fire couldn't melt this opinion out of me. I'd say it even if you burned me at the stake for it.

original: Thou wast ever an obstinate heretic in the despite of  beauty.
translation: You've always been a stubborn dissenter in the way you scorn beauty.

original: And never could maintain his part but in the force of  his will.
translation: And you can't give any good reasons for your argument—just sheer willfulness.

original: That a woman conceived me, I thank her.
translation: A woman conceived me, and I thank her for that.

original: That she  brought me up, I likewise give her most humble thanks.
translation: Then she brought me up, and I give her humble thanks for that, too.

original: But that I will have a recheat winded in my forehead or  hang my bugle in an invisible baldrick, all women shall  pardon me.
translation: But all other women will have to pardon me if I don't want to be made a fool of by having  hunting horns grow from my forehead .

original: Because I will not do them the wrong to  mistrust any, I will do myself the right to trust none.
translation: Because I don't want to insult any particular woman by mistrusting her, I'll just protect myself by avoiding and mistrusting them all.

original: And the fine is, for the which I may go the finer, I will live a bachelor.
translation: And the result of this is that I'll live as a bachelor, and have more money to spend on fine clothes.

original: I shall see thee, ere I die, look pale with love.
translation: Before I die, I swear I'll see you turn pale with lovesickness.

original: With anger, with sickness, or with hunger, my lord,  not with love.
translation: I'll turn pale with anger, with illness, or with hunger—but never with love, my lord.

original: Prove that ever I lose more blood with  love than I will get again with drinking, pick out mine  eyes with a ballad-maker’s pen and hang me up at the  door of a brothel house for the sign of blind Cupid.
translation: If you can show that I'll ever be so weak with love that I can't be strengthened by a few cups of wine, you can pluck out my eyes with a love-poet's pen and hang me up at the door of a brothel's house, where the sign of blind Cupid usually goes.

original: Well, if ever thou dost fall from this faith, thou wilt prove a notable argument.
translation: Well, if you ever do change your mind and fall in love, you'll become an extreme example for everyone to gossip about.

original: If I do, hang me in a bottle like a cat and shoot at  me, and he that hits me, let him be clapped on the  shoulder and called Adam.
translation: If I do, you can use me for target practice. And if any man hits me, let him be patted on the back and called a hero.

original: Well, as time shall try. In time the savage bull doth  bear the yoke.
translation: Well, time will tell. Even the savage bull eventually wears the yoke.

original: The savage bull may, but if ever the sensible Benedick bear it, pluck off the bull’s horns and set them in my  forehead,
translation: The savage bull may wear it. But if the sensible Benedick ever takes up the yoke of marriage, then pluck off the bull's horns and put them on  my  forehead—for I'll soon be a cuckold like the rest.

original: and let me be vilely painted, and in such  great letters
translation: And let me be painted gaudily, and hang a sign around my neck, with big letters.

original: as they write “Here is good horse to hire” let them signify under my sign “Here you may see  Benedick the married man.”
translation: Instead of what the sign usually says, "Here is a good horse to hire," the sign will say, "Here is Benedick, the married man."

original: If this should ever happen, thou wouldst be horn-mad.
Nay, if Cupid have not spent all his quiver in Venice,  thou wilt quake for this shortly.
translation: Well, if Cupid hasn't used up all his arrows in lustful Venice, then he'll soon have his revenge by making you shake with love.

original: I look for an earthquake too, then.
translation: It's just as likely that there'll be an earthquake.

original: Well, you temporize with the hours. In the meantime,  good Signior Benedick, repair to Leonato’s. Commend me  to him and tell him I will not fail him at supper, for  indeed he hath made great preparation.
translation: Well, you'll grow milder as time passes. But in the meantime hurry to Leonato's, good Sir Benedick. Give him my compliments and tell him that I'll be there for dinner, since I know he's done a lot of preparation for it.

original: I have almost matter enough in me for such an  embassage, and so I commit you—
To the tuition of God. From my house, if I had it—
translation: —into God's hands. From my house—if I had a house—

original: The sixth of July. Your loving friend, Benedick.
translation: The sixth of July. Your loving friend, Benedick.

original: Nay, mock not, mock not.
translation: Now, don't make fun.

original: The body of your discourse  is sometimes guarded with fragments and the guards are  but slightly basted on neither.
translation: Sometimes you two might decorate your conversation with little fragments of wit, but they don't hold together very well.

original: Ere you flout old ends  any further, examine your conscience. And so I leave  you.
translation: Before you show off your witty scraps any longer, take a look at your conscience, and you'll see that I speak the truth. And with that I leave you.

original: My liege, your highness now may do me good.
translation: My lord, you can really help me now.

original: My love is thine to teach. Teach it but how,  And thou shalt see how apt it is to learn Any hard lesson that may do thee good.
translation: I'm eager to help. Just let me what I can do, and you'll see how good I am at learning even the hardest lesson.

original: Hath Leonato any son, my lord?
translation: Does Leonato have any sons, my lord?

original: No child but Hero; she’s his only heir. Dost thou affect her, Claudio?
translation: He has no child but Hero, who is his only heir. Do you love her, Claudio?

original: O, my lord,   When you went onward on this ended action,   I looked upon her with a soldier’s eye,
translation: Oh my lord, when we left to fight the war that's now over, I looked at Hero with a soldier's eyes.

original: That liked but had a rougher task in hand   Than to drive liking to the name of love.
translation: And I liked her, but my mind was too filled with the rough tasks ahead to change liking into loving.

original: But now I am returned and that war thoughts   Have left their places vacant, in their rooms   Come thronging soft and delicate desires,   All prompting me how fair young Hero is,   Saying I liked her ere I went to wars.
translation: But now that I've returned and my thoughts of war are gone, they've been replaced with soft and delicate desires that all lead me to one thing: how beautiful young Hero is, and how I must have liked her even before I went off to war.

original: Thou wilt be like a lover presently   And tire the hearer with a book of words.
translation: Soon you'll be a true lover, and wear out everyone who listens to you with endless speeches about your feelings.

original: If thou dost love fair Hero, cherish it,
translation: If you love the beautiful Hero, then enjoy it.

original: And I will break with her and with her father,   And thou shalt have her.
translation: I'll bring up the subject to her and to her father, and soon you'll have her as your wife.

original: Was ’t not to this end   That thou began’st to twist so fine a story?
translation: Isn't this the result you were looking for when you told me this story?

original: How sweetly you do minister to love,   That know love’s grief by his complexion!
translation: You can see how lovesick I am without even asking, and you take care of me so kindly!

original: But lest my liking might too sudden seem,   I would have salved it with a longer treatise.
translation: But I didn't want to seem to hasty in my feelings, so I was going to smooth them over with a longer explanation.

original: What need the bridge much broader than the flood?
translation: Why build a bridge wider than the river it's crossing?

original: The fairest grant is the necessity.   Look what will serve is fit.
translation: You don't have to say more than what gets the point across.  The best gift is one that's needed most, and whatever gets the job done will work.

original: 'Tis once, thou lovest,   And I will fit thee with the remedy.
translation: You are in love, and that's that. I'll get you what you need to cure your sickness.

original: I know we shall have reveling tonight.
translation: I know we'll have a party tonight.

original: I will assume thy part in some disguise   And tell fair Hero I am Claudio,   And in her bosom I’ll unclasp my heart
translation: I'll disguise myself and tell Hero that I am Claudio, and in private I'll tell her all about my feelings for her.

original: And take her hearing prisoner with the force   And strong encounter of my amorous tale.
translation: When she hears, she'll be taken prisoner by the force of my tale of love.

original: Then after to her father will I break,   And the conclusion is, she shall be thine.   In practice let us put it presently.
translation: Then I'll talk to her father, and in the end she'll be yours. Now let's put this plan into action right away.

original: How now, brother, where is my cousin, your son? Hath  he provided this music?
translation: How are you, brother? Where is my nephew, your son? Has he taken care of the music for tonight's party?

original: He is very busy about it. But, brother, I can tell you  strange news that you yet dreamt not of.
translation: He's working on it right now. But, brother, I have some strange, surprising news to tell you.

original: Are they good?
translation: Is it good news?

original: As the events stamps them, but they have a good  cover; they show well outward.
translation: Well, it seems good right now, but who knows how it will unfold.

original: The Prince and Count  Claudio, walking in a thick-pleached alley in mine  orchard, were thus much overheard by a man of mine:
translation: A servant of mine overheard the Prince and Count Claudio as they walked along an overgrown path in my orchard.

original: the  Prince discovered to Claudio that he loved my niece your daughter and meant to acknowledge it this night in a  dance,
translation: The Prince revealed to Claudio that he is in love with my niece Hero—your daughter—and that he means to tell her so at the dance tonight.

original: and if he found her accordant, he meant to take  the present time by the top and instantly break with you of it.
translation: If she seems agreeable to the idea, he intends to seize the opportunity and immediately ask you for permission to marry her.

original: Hath the fellow any wit that told you this?
translation: Is the fellow who told you this a smart man?

original: A good sharp fellow. I will send for him, and question him yourself.
translation: He's very sharp. I'll send for him, and you can question him yourself.

original: No, no, we will hold it as a dream till it appear  itself. But I will acquaint my daughter withal, that she may be the better prepared for an answer if  peradventure this be true. Go you and tell her of it.
translation: No, no, we'll pretend it was just a dream until it makes itself evident in reality. But my daughter should know about it, so she can be better prepared with an answer if all this happens to be true. Go and tell her about it.

original: Cousins, you know what you have to do.—O, I cry  you mercy, friend. Go you with me and I will use your  skill.—Good cousin, have a care this busy time.
What the goodyear, my lord, why are you thus out  of measure sad?
translation: Honestly, my lord, why are you so excessively sad?

original: There is no measure in the occasion that breeds.  Therefore the sadness is without limit.
translation: There is no measure to the things that cause my sadnes. Therefore, the sadness itself is limitless.

original: You should hear reason.
translation: You should listen to reason.

original: And when I have heard it, what blessing brings it?
translation: And when I've heard it, how will reason reward me?

original: If not a present remedy, at least a patient sufferance.
translation: If reason won't immediately cure your suffering, then at least reason will give you the patience to endure it.

original: I wonder that thou, being, as thou sayst thou art,  born under Saturn, goest about to apply a moral medicine to a mortifying mischief.
translation: I'm surprised that you—being such a  gloomy  man yourself—go about trying to cure a deadly disease with platitudes.

original: I cannot hide what I am.
translation: I cannot hide who I am.

original: I  must be sad when I have cause and smile at no man’s  jests,
translation: I'll be sad when I have reason to be, and won't smile at any man's jokes.

original: eat when I have stomach and wait for no man’s  leisure,
translation: I'll eat when I'm hungry, and won't wait for any man's convenience.

original: sleep when I am drowsy and tend on no man’s  business,
translation: I'll sleep when I'm tired, and won't wake up for any man's business.

original: laugh when I am merry and claw no man in his  humor.
translation: I'll laugh when I'm happy, and won't flatter a man or humor him.

original: Yea, but you must not make the full show of this till  you may do it without controlment.
translation: Yes, but you shouldn't act this way until you can do it without restraint or fear of endangering yourself.

original: You have of late  stood out against your brother, and he hath ta'en you  newly into his grace,
translation: You rebelled against your brother, and he has only recently forgiven you and returned you to his favor.

original: where it is impossible you should  take true root but by the fair weather that you make  yourself.
translation: You won't stay there unless you further establish yourself in his good graces.

original: It is needful that you frame the season for  your own harvest.
translation: You need to use this time to benefit yourself.

original: I had rather be a canker in a hedge than a rose in his  grace,
translation: I'd rather be a weed in a hedge than a rose in my brother's garden.

original: and it better fits my blood to be disdained of  all than to fashion a carriage to rob love from any.
translation: And it suits my mood better to be hated by all than to put on an act and trick someone into loving me.

original: In  this, though I cannot be said to be a flattering honest  man, it must not be denied but I am a plain-dealing  villain.
translation: I cannot be called a flattering, virtuous man, but you can't deny that at least I'm honest and straightforward about being a scoundrel.

original: I am trusted with a muzzle and enfranchised  with a clog; therefore I have decreed not to sing in my  cage.
translation: My brother trusts me like he trusts a muzzled dog, and gives me all the freedom of a horse with a block chained to its foot.

original: If I had my mouth, I would bite;
translation: If I had my mouth free, I would bite.

original: if I had my  liberty, I would do my liking.
translation: If I had my liberty, I would do as I please.

original: In the meantime, let me  be that I am, and seek not to alter me.
translation: In the meantime, let me be who I am, and don't try to change me.

original: Can you make no use of your discontent?
translation: Can't you put your unhappiness to some use?

original: I make all use of it, for I use it only. Who comes  here?
translation: I already make the most possible use of it, because it's the only thing I use. Who's that coming?

original: What news, Borachio?
translation: What's the news, Borachio?

original: I came yonder from a great supper. The Prince  your brother is royally entertained by Leonato, and I  can give you intelligence of an intended marriage.
translation: I just came from a great feast. Leonato is giving your brother, the Prince, entertainment fit for royalty. And I can give you some information about an intended marriage.

original: Will it serve for any model to build mischief on? What  is he for a fool that betroths himself to unquietness?
translation: Can I use this information to cause trouble? Who is this fool who wants the constant hassle of marriage?

original: Marry, it is your brother’s right hand.
translation: Well, it's your brother's right-hand man.

original: Who? The most exquisite Claudio?
translation: Who? The amazing Claudio?

original: Even he.
translation: That's the one.

original: A proper squire. And who, and who? Which way looks he?
translation: A handsome young man. And who's the girl? Who's caught his eye?

original: Marry, on Hero, the daughter and heir of Leonato.
translation: Hero, the daughter and heir of Leonato.

original: A very forward March-chick! How came you to this?
translation: A precocious young thing! How did you come to hear this?

original: Being entertained for a perfumer,
translation: I was hired to perfume Leonato's house.

original: as I was smoking a  musty room, comes me the Prince and Claudio, hand in  hand, in sad conference.
translation: While I was burning incense in one musty room, the Prince and Claudio came in, hand in hand, in the middle of a serious conversation.

original: I whipped me behind the arras,  and there heard it agreed upon that the Prince should  woo Hero for himself, and having obtained her, give her  to Count Claudio.
translation: I hid myself behind a tapestry, and from there I heard them agree that the Prince would court Hero, and once he won her over, he would give her to Count Claudio.

original: Come, come, let us thither. This may prove food to  my displeasure. That young start-up hath all the glory  of my overthrow. If I can cross him any way, I bless  myself every way. You are both sure, and will assist me?
translation: Come, come, let's go to the feast. This might be just the food I need to cure my unhappiness. That young upstart Claudio has gained honor and glory through my defeat. If I can injure him in any way, I'll rejoice. You'll both stay loyal and help me, won't you?

original: To the death, my lord.
translation: Until death, my lord.

original: Let us to the great supper. Their cheer is the greater  that I am subdued. Would the cook were o' my mind! Shall we go prove what’s to be done?
translation: Then let's go to this great feast. They're all so happy because I have been defeated. If only the cook thought like me—then he could have poisoned their food! Now, should we go discover what must be done?

original: We’ll wait upon your lordship.
translation: We'll accompany your Lordship.

original: Was not Count John here at supper?
translation: Wasn't Don John here at dinner?

original: I saw him not.
translation: I didn't see him.

original: How tartly that gentleman looks! I never can see him  but I am heartburned an hour after.
translation: That gentleman always looks so sour! I can't ever see him without getting heartburn afterwards.

original: He is of a very melancholy disposition.
translation: He does have a very sad disposition.

original: He were an excellent man that were made just in  the midway between him and Benedick. The one is too like an image and says nothing, and the other too like my  lady’s eldest son, evermore tattling.
translation: A man would be excellent if he were halfway between Don John and Benedick. One of them is like a statue, saying nothing, and the other is like a spoiled child, always babbling on.

original: Then half Signor Benedick’s tongue in Count  John’s mouth, and half Count John’s melancholy in  Signor Benedick’s face—
translation: Then you could put half of Sir Benedick's chatter in Don John's mouth, and put half of Don John's gloominess in Sir Benedick's face—

original: With a good leg and a good foot, uncle, and money  enough in his purse, such a man would win any woman in  the world, if he could get her goodwill.
translation: And if he also had handsome legs and a full wallet, such a man could have any woman in the world, if he could win over her good will, uncle.

original: By my troth, niece, thou wilt never get thee a husband  if thou be so shrewd of thy tongue.
translation: Niece, I swear you'll never get a husband if you keep such a sharp tongue in your mouth.

original: In faith, she’s too curst.
translation: Honestly, she's too mean.

original: Too curst is more than curst. I shall lessen God’s  sending that way, for it is said, “God sends a curst cow short horns,” but to a cow too curst, he sends none.
translation: Too mean is better than just mean. In that respect, I'll escape God's punishment, for as the old proverb says: "God gives a mean cow short horns," so she can't cause as much damage. But he doesn't do anything to a cow that is too ill-tempered.

original: So, by being too curst, God will send you no horns.
translation: So by being too mean, God won't send you horns?

original: Just, if he send me no husband, for the which blessing  I am at him upon my knees every morning and evening.  Lord, I could not endure a husband with a beard on his  face! I had rather lie in the woolen.
translation: Exactly, and if he won't send me horns then he won't send me a husband, for any husband of mine would be sure to grow cuckold's horns. And I thank God every morning and evening for sending me no husband. Lord, I couldn't stand a husband with a beard on his face! I'd rather sleep under scratchy wool blankets.

original: You may light on a husband that hath no beard.
translation: You might find a husband without a beard.

original: What should I do with him?
translation: And what would I do with him?

original: Dress him in my apparel  and make him my waiting gentlewoman?
translation: Dress him up in my clothes and make him my serving woman?

original: He that hath a  beard is more than a youth, and he that hath no beard is less than a man;
translation: If he has a beard, he's more than a youth. And if he has no beard, he's less than a man.

original: and he that is more than a youth is  not for me, and he that is less than a man, I am not for him.
translation: If he's older than a handsome youth, then he's not for me. But if he's less than a man, then he wouldn't be able to handle me.

original: Therefore I will even take sixpence in earnest of  the bearherd, and lead his apes into hell.
translation: Therefore, I bet that I'll die an old maid, and lead apes and bears in hell, as they say unmarried women will.

original: Well then, go you into hell?
translation: Well then, does that mean you'll go to hell?

original: No, but to the gate, and there will the devil meet me  like an old cuckold with horns on his head, and say,  “Get you to heaven, Beatrice, get you to heaven; here’s  no place for you maids.”
translation: No, just to its gates. There the devil will meet me, looking like an old cuckold with horns on his head, and say, "Go off to heaven, Beatrice, go off to heaven. Hell is no place for virgins."

original: So deliver I up my apes and  away to Saint Peter.
translation: So, I'll leave my apes behind and fly up to Saint Peter at heaven's gates.

original: For the heavens, he shows me where  the bachelors sit, and there live we as merry as the day is long.
translation: Then he'll show me the part of heaven where the unmarried people live, and we'll all live together happily ever after.

original: Well, niece, I trust you will be ruled by  your father.
translation: Well, niece, I trust that you at least will always defer to your father.

original: Yes, faith, it is my cousin’s duty to make curtsy and  say, “Father, as it please you.” But yet for all that,  cousin, let him be a handsome fellow, or else make  another curtsy and say, “Father, as it please me.”
translation: Yes, of course, it's my cousin's duty to curtsy and say, "Father, I'll do whatever pleases you." But despite all that, cousin, if your father doesn't pick a handsome husband for you, you should curtsy again and say, "Father, I'll do whatever pleases me."

original: Daughter, I hope to see you one day fitted  with a husband.
translation: Well, niece, I hope to see you with a husband one day.

original: Not till God make men of some other metal than earth.
translation: Not until God starts making men out of something other than dirt.

original: Would it not grieve a woman to be overmastered with  a piece of valiant dust?
translation: Shouldn't it make a woman grieve, being ordered about by some brave clump of dust?

original: To make an account of her life  to a clod of wayward marl? No, uncle, I’ll none.
translation: Linking her life forever to a wandering piece of clay? No, uncle, I would rather not have a husband.

original: Adam’s  sons are my brethren, and truly I hold it a sin to match in my kindred.
translation: All of  Adam's  descendants are my relatives, and I truly believe that marriage between relatives is a sin.

original: Daughter, remember what I told you. If  the Prince do solicit you in that kind, you know your  answer.
translation: Daughter, remember what I told you. If the Prince asks you about marriage, you know how to answer him.

original: The fault will be in the music, cousin, if you be not  wooed in good time.
translation: Cousin, if he doesn't court you properly and appropriately, the fault will be in his timing.

original: If the Prince be too important, tell him there is measure in everything, and so dance out  the answer.
translation: If he presses you too hard, tell him that everything has its proper rhythm, and romance is like a dance.

original: For hear me, Hero, wooing, wedding, and  repenting is as a Scotch jig, a measure, and a  cinquepace.
translation: Listen, Hero, the three stages of romance are like three dances.

original: The first suit is hot and hasty like a  Scotch jig, and full as fantastical;
translation: The initial courtship is hot and hasty like a Scottish jig, and just as full of fantasy.

original: the wedding,  mannerly modest as a measure, full of state  and ancientry;
translation: Then the wedding is a slower, more solemn dance, full of dignity and tradition.

original: and then comes repentance, and with his  bad legs falls into the   cinquepace   faster and faster  till he sink into his grave.
translation: And then comes the stage where you regret your marriage, and this stage is like the lively  cinquepace  dance, which keeps getting faster and faster until you fall into your grave.

original: Cousin, you apprehend passing shrewdly.
translation: Niece, you see things with unusual perceptiveness.

original: I have a good eye, uncle. I can see a church by  daylight.
translation: I have a good eye, uncle. I can see obvious things in broad daylight.

original: The revelers are entering, brother. Make good room.
translation: The partygoers are coming in, brother. Give them room.

original: Lady, will you walk a bout with your friend?
translation: My lady, will you dance with me for a while?

original: So you walk softly, and look sweetly, and say nothing,  I am yours for the walk, and especially when I walk  away.
translation: As long as you move gently, look handsome, and say nothing, I'm yours for the dance, and especially when I dance away.

original: With me in your company?
translation: Will I be in your company then?

original: I may say so when I please.
translation: I'll tell you when I decide.

original: And when please you to say so?
translation: And when will you decide?

original: When I like your favor, for God defend the lute should  be like the case!
translation: When I like your actual appearance, for God forbid that your face should look like your mask.

original: My visor is Philemon’s roof; within the house is Jove.
Why, then, your visor should be thatched.
translation: Why, then your mask should be thatched like a roof.

original: Speak low if you speak love.
translation: Speak softly if you'll speak about love.

original: Well, I would you did like me.
translation: Well, I wish that you liked me.

original: So would not I for your own sake, for I have many ill  qualities.
translation: For your sake, I don't wish it. Because I have many bad qualities.

original: Which is one?
translation: Name one.

original: I say my prayers aloud.
translation: I say my prayers aloud.

original: I love you the better; the hearers may cry “Amen.”
translation: I love you even more for that. Whoever hears you praying can then cry, "Amen."

original: God match me with a good dancer!
translation: May God pair me with a good dancer!

original: Amen.
translation: Amen. Here I am.

original: And God keep him out of my sight when the dance is  done! Answer, clerk.
translation: And may God take him away from me when the dance is done! Now say "amen," preacher.

original: No more words. The clerk is answered.
translation: No more words from me. I have my answer.

original: I know you well enough. You are Signor Antonio.
translation: I know you well enough. You are Sir Antonio.

original: At a word, I am not.
translation: In short, I am not.

original: I know you by the waggling of your head.
translation: I recognize you by the way you move your head.

original: To tell you true, I counterfeit him.
translation: To be honest, I'm only imitating Antonio.

original: You could never do him so ill-well unless you were the  very man. Here’s his dry hand up and down. You are he,  you are he.
translation: You could never imitate his bad qualities so well unless you were the man himself. See, you have his dry, aging hands exactly. You are he, you are he.

original: At a word, I am not.
translation: In short, I am not.

original: Come, come, do you think I do not know you by  your excellent wit? Can virtue hide itself? Go to, mum,  you are  he. Graces will appear, and there’s an end.
translation: Come, come, do you think I can't recognize you by the excellent wit of your answers? Can virtue hide itself? Be quiet, for you are Antonio. Nobility will always make itself known, and there's nothing more to be said.

original: Will you not tell me who told you so?
translation: Won't you tell me who said that?

original: No, you shall pardon me.
translation: No, you'll have to pardon me.

original: Nor will you not tell me who you are?
translation: And you won't tell me who you are either?

original: Not now.
translation: Not now.

original: That I was disdainful and that I had my good wit out  of The Hundred Merry Tales! Well this was Signor  Benedick that said so.
translation: To think, someone said that I was scornful, and that I got my wit from an old joke book! Well, it must have been Sir Benedick who said that.

original: What’s he?
translation: Who's he?

original: I am sure you know him well enough.
translation: I'm sure you know him well enough.

original: Not I, believe me.
translation: I don't, believe me.

original: Did he never make you laugh?
translation: Didn't he ever make you laugh?

original: I pray you, what is he?
translation: Please tell me, who is he?

original: Why, he is the Prince’s jester, a very dull fool, only  his gift is in devising impossible slanders.
translation: Why, he's the Prince's jester—a very stupid fool, whose only gift is coming up with outrageous insults.

original: None but  libertines delight in him, and the commendation is not  in his wit but in his villainy,
translation: Only immoral rascals enjoy his company, and they don't like his wit, but only his rudeness.

original: for he both pleases men  and angers them, and then they laugh at him and beat  him.
translation: He both pleases and angers people; they laugh at him and then beat him up.

original: I am sure he is in the fleet.
translation: I'm sure he's in that army of dancers out there.

original: I would he had  boarded me.
translation: I wish he had been brave enough to approach me for a battle.

original: When I know the gentleman, I’ll tell him what you say.
translation: When I meet the gentleman, I'll tell him what you've said.

original: Do, do. He’ll but break a comparison or two on me,  which, peradventure not marked or not laughed at,  strikes him into melancholy,
translation: Do that. He'll make a joke by comparing me to something insulting, and if no one pays attention to him or laughs, he'll get depressed.

original: and then there’s a  partridge wing saved, for the fool will eat no supper  that night.
translation: And that will save a partridge wing from being eaten, for the fool will be too unhappy to eat any dinner.

original: We must follow the leaders.
translation: We must follow the leaders of the dance.

original: In every good thing.
translation: We should follow them in every good thing.

original: Nay, if they lead to any ill, I will leave them at the  next turning.
translation: No, if they lead us the wrong way, I'll leave them at the next song.

original: Sure my brother is amorous on Hero, and hath withdrawn her father to break with him about it.  The ladies follow her, and but one visor remains.
translation: My brother is surely in love with Hero, and has now taken her father aside to ask him about marrying her. The ladies have all followed Hero, but one masked man remains.

original: And that is Claudio. I know him by his bearing.
translation: And that is Claudio. I recognize him by his posture.

original: Are not you Signor Benedick?
translation: Aren't you Sir Benedick?

original: You know me well. I am he.
translation: You know me well. I am Benedick.

original: Signor, you are very near my brother in his love. He  is enamored on Hero. I pray you, dissuade him from her.  She is no equal for his birth. You may do the part of an honest man in it.
translation: Sir, you are a close friend of my brother's. He is in love with Hero. Please, convince him to change his mind. Her social rank is so low that it would be inappropriate for him to marry her. You would be an honorable man if you did this for me.

original: How know you he loves her?
translation: How do you know he loves her?

original: I heard him swear his affection.
translation: I heard him swear it.

original: So did I too, and he swore he would marry her tonight.
translation: I did too, and he swore he would marry her tonight.

original: Come, let us to the banquet.
translation: Come, let's go to the banquet.

original: [unmasking]   Thus answer I in the name of Benedick,   But hear these ill news with the ears of Claudio.
translation: [Taking off his mask]  I answered to Benedick's name, but I heard this bad news with Claudio's ears.

original: 'Tis certain so, the Prince woos for himself.
translation: So it's true: the Prince wants Hero for himself.

original: Friendship is constant in all other things   Save in the office and affairs of love.
translation: Friendship is loyal in all things except for the business of love.

original: Therefore all hearts in love use their own tongues.
translation: Therefore all lovers should speak only for themselves.

original: Let every eye negotiate for itself   And trust no agent,
translation: Let everyone do their own courting, and not trust any middle-men.

original: for beauty is a witch   Against whose charms faith melteth into blood.
translation: Beauty is a witch whose spells melt honor into passion.

original: This is an accident of hourly proof,   Which I mistrusted not. Farewell, therefore, Hero.
translation: This is something that happens all the time, but I never expected it to happen to me. Farewell then, Hero.

original: Count Claudio?
translation: Count Claudio?

original: Yea, the same.
translation: Yes, that's me.

original: Come, will you go with me?
translation: Will you come with me?

original: Whither?
translation: Where?

original: Even to the next willow, about your own business,  county.
translation: Just to the nearest  willow tree , to take care of your business, Count.

original: What fashion will you wear the garland of? About your neck like an usurer’s chain? Or under your arm  like a lieutenant’s scarf?
translation: How do you want to wear your willow garland? Around your neck, like a rich man's chain? Or under your arm, like a lieutenant's sash?

original: You must wear it one way, for the Prince hath gat your Hero.
translation: You must wear it one way or another, for the Prince has won your Hero.

original: I wish him joy of her.
translation: I wish him happiness with her.

original: Why, that’s spoken like an honest drover; so they  sell bullocks. But did you think the Prince would have  served you thus?
translation: Why, you sound like an honest cattle-dealer. That's how they sell bulls. But did you really think the Prince would trick you like that?

original: I pray you, leave me.
translation: Please, leave me alone.

original: Ho, now you strike like the blind man. 'Twas the boy  that stole your meat, and you’ll beat the post.
translation: Hey, now you're lashing out in the dark. Someone else robbed you, but you'll beat up the messenger.

original: If it will not be, I’ll leave you.
translation: If you won't go away, I'll leave you.

original: Alas, poor hurt fowl, now will he creep into sedges.
translation: Alas, that poor wounded bird. Now he'll crawl into the bushes and hide.

original: But that my Lady Beatrice should know me, and not know  me!
translation: But how strange that Lady Beatrice should seem to recognize me, and yet also not recognize me!

original: The Prince’s fool! Ha, it may be I go under that  title because I am merry.
translation: "The Prince's jester!" Ha, maybe they call me that because I am cheerful.

original: Yea, but so I am apt to do  myself wrong. I am not so reputed!
translation: No, but I'm only insulting myself by thinking this. I don't have that kind of a reputation!

original: It is the base,  though bitter, disposition of Beatrice that puts the  world into her person and so gives me out.
translation: It's just Beatrice's mean, sarcastic nature that causes her to think that everyone in the world shares her opinion, and therefore makes her describe me in this way.

original: Well, I’ll be revenged as I may.
translation: Well, I'll get my revenge if I can.

original: Now, Signior, where’s the Count? Did you see him?
translation: Now, Sir, where's Count Claudio? Did you see him?

original: Troth, my lord, I have played the part of Lady Fame.
translation: Truly, my lord, I played the part of Lady Rumor and relayed the news to him.

original: I found him here as melancholy as a lodge in a warren.
translation: I found him here, as melancholy as a rabbit in a burrow.

original: I  told him, and I think I told him true, that your Grace  had got the goodwill of this young lady,
translation: I told him—and I think I told him the truth—that you had won over the lady's goodwill.

original: and I offered  him my company to a willow tree, either to make him a  garland, as being forsaken, or to bind him up a rod, as  being worthy to be whipped.
translation: I then offered to accompany him to a willow tree, to either help him make a garland as a forsaken lover, or else to bind willow switches into a whip to beat him.

original: To be whipped? What’s his fault?
translation: To beat him? What's his crime?

original: The flat transgression of a schoolboy who, being  overjoyed with finding a birds' nest, shows it his  companion, and he steals it.
translation: The simple crime of a schoolboy who finds a birds' nest and joyfully shows it to his friend, who then steals it.

original: Wilt thou make a trust a transgression? The  transgression is in the stealer.
translation: Will you turn trusting a friend into a crime? The criminal is the thief.

original: Yet it had not been amiss the rod had been made, and  the garland too, for the garland he might have worn  himself and the rod he might have bestowed on you, who,  as I take it, have stolen his birds' nest.
translation: But it still would have been appropriate to make both the whip and the garland. He could have worn the garland himself, and used the whip on you, since you—as I understand it—have stolen his birds' nest.

original: I will but teach them to sing and restore them to the  owner.
translation: I only plan to teach the baby birds to sing, and then return them to their rightful owner.

original: If their singing answer your saying, by my faith, you  say honestly.
translation: If their singing corresponds with what you say—if Hero really is ready to love Claudio, and not you—then you'll be telling the truth.

original: The Lady Beatrice hath a quarrel to you. The  gentleman that danced with her told her she is much  wronged by you.
translation: The Lady Beatrice has a quarrel with you. The gentleman she danced with told her that you had insulted her gravely.

original: O, she misused me past the endurance of a block!
translation: Oh, she's insulted me so badly that not even a block of wood could endure it!

original: An  oak but with one green leaf on it would have answered  her.
translation: An oak tree with only one green leaf left would revive itself to respond to her abuse.

original: My very visor began to assume life and scold with  her.
translation: Even my mask started to come to life and try to argue with her.

original: She told me, not thinking I had been myself, that I was the Prince’s jester, that I was duller than a great thaw,
translation: She told me—not recognizing me as myself—that I was the Prince's jester, and duller than mud.

original: huddling jest upon jest with such impossible  conveyance upon me that I stood like a man at a mark  with a whole army shooting at me.
translation: She piled up mockery upon mockery until I stood paralyzed, like a man set up as a target with a whole army shooting at me.

original: She speaks poniards,  and every word stabs.
translation: She speaks daggers, and every word stabs.

original: If her breath were as terrible as  her terminations, there were no living near her; she  would infect to the north star.
translation: If her breath were as terrible as her insults, she would stink up and kill everything from here to the North Star.

original: I would not marry her,  though she were endowed with all that Adam had left him  before he transgressed.
translation: I wouldn't marry her even if her dowry were Paradise.

original: She would have made Hercules  have turned spit, yea, and have cleft his club to make  the fire, too.
translation: If  Hercules  were her husband, she'd make him cook for her, and chop up his club for firewood.

original: Come, talk not of her. You shall find her the infernal Ate in good apparel.
translation: Come on, don't talk about her. She's like  Atë  dressed up in fine clothes.

original: I would to God  some scholar would conjure her, for certainly, while she is here, a man may live as quiet in hell as in a  sanctuary,
translation: I wish to God that some magician would exorcize her, for as long as she's here on earth, hell itself must be just as quiet as a church.

original: and people sin upon purpose because they  would go thither.
translation: People sin on purpose just so they can go to hell and escape her.

original: So indeedall disquiet, horror and  perturbation follows her.
translation: Indeed, chaos, horror, and turmoil follow her everywhere.

original: Look, here she comes.
translation: Look, here she comes.

original: Will your grace command me any service to the  world’s end?
translation: Will your Grace please send me on a mission to the ends of the earth?

original: I will go on the slightest errand now to  the Antipodes that you can devise to send me on.
translation: I'll go to the other side of the globe for any silly errand you can come up with.

original: I will  fetch you a toothpicker now from the furthest inch of  Asia, bring you the length of Prester John’s foot, fetch you a hair off the great Cham’s beard, do you any  embassage to the Pygmies, rather than hold three words'  conference with this harpy.
translation: I'll fetch you a toothpick from the farthest reaches of Asia, or find out  Prester John's shoe size, or bring you a hair from Cham's beard, or deliver any message you want to send to the Pygmies —anything rather than exchange three words with this man-eating vulture.

original: You have no employment for  me?
translation: Don't you have any work for me?

original: None but to desire your good company.
translation: No work at all—all I desire is your good company.

original: O God, sir, here’s a dish I love not. I cannot endure  my Lady Tongue!
translation: Oh God, sir, then here comes a meal I hate. I can't stand tongue!

original: Come, lady, come, you have lost the heart of Signior Benedick.
translation: Come, my lady, come. You have lost Signor Benedick's heart.

original: Indeed, my lord, he lent it me awhile, and I gave him  use for it, a double heart for his single one. Marry,  once before he won it of me with false dice. Therefore  your Grace may well say I have lost it.
You have put him down, lady, you have put him down.
translation: You've defeated him, lady. You've put him down.

original: So I would not he should do me, my lord, lest I should  prove the mother of fools. I have brought Count Claudio, whom you sent me to seek.
Why, how now, Count, wherefore are you sad?
translation: Why, what's going on, Count? Why are you sad?

original: Not sad, my lord.
translation: I'm not sad, my lord.

original: How then, sick?
translation: What is it then? Are you sick?

original: Neither, my lord.
translation: Neither sad nor sick, my lord.

original: The Count is neither sad, nor sick, nor merry, nor  well, but civil count, civil as an orange, and something of that jealous complexion.
translation: The Count is neither sad, nor sick, nor happy, nor well—he's just civil, civil and orange like an orange from Seville, and with the same jealous, yellow complexion.

original: I' faith, lady, I think your blazon to be true, though, I’ll be sworn, if he be so, his conceit is false.
translation: Truly, lady, I think your description is right, though I swear he has no reason to look so jealous.

original: —Here, Claudio, I have wooed in thy name, and fair Hero is  won.
translation: [To CLAUDIO]  Here, Claudio, I've courted Hero on your behalf, and beautiful Hero has been won.

original: I have broke with her father and his goodwill  obtained.
translation: I asked her father, and he's given his permission.

original: Name the day of marriage, and God give thee  joy.
translation: Name the day you want to get married, and may God give you joy.

original: Count, take of me my daughter, and with her my  fortunes. His grace hath made the match, and all grace  say “Amen” to it.
translation: Count Claudio, take my daughter, and take all my fortunes along with her. The Prince has made the match, and may God—the Prince of heaven—say "amen" to it.

original: Speak, Count, ’tis your cue.
translation: That's your cue to speak, Count.

original: Silence is the perfectest herald of joy. I were but  little happy if I could say how much.—Lady, as you are  mine, I am yours. I give away myself for you and dote  upon the exchange.
translation: Silence is the best announcer of joy. If I were only a little happy, I could say how much, but as it is I'm speechless. Lady, you are mine, and I am yours. I give myself away for you, and I delight in the trade.

original: Speak, cousin, or if you cannot, stop his mouth with a  kiss and let not him speak neither.
translation: Say something, cousin. Or if you can't, stop his mouth with a kiss and don't let him say anything either.

original: In faith, lady, you have a merry heart.
translation: Truly, lady, you have a cheerful heart.
