original: Yea, my lord. I thank it, poor fool, it keeps on the  windy side of care. My cousin tells him in his ear that  he is in her heart.
translation: Yes, my lord. I thank my heart, the poor fool, for it keeps itself safe from worries. Now my cousin is whispering to Claudio that she loves him.

original: And so she doth, cousin.
translation: And so she is, cousin.

original: Good Lord for alliance! Thus goes everyone to the  world but I, and I am sunburnt. I may sit in a corner  and cry, “Heigh-ho for a husband!”
translation: Thank the good Lord for alliances! And so everyone goes off into the world of marriage except for me. I stay in, sunburned and unattractive. I ought to sit in a corner and cry, "Heigh-ho for a husband!"

original: Lady Beatrice, I will get you one.
translation: Lady Beatrice, I will get you a husband.

original: I would rather have one of your father’s getting. Hath  your grace ne'er a brother like you? Your father got  excellent husbands, if a maid could come by them.
Will you have me, lady?
translation: Will you have me, my lady?

original: No, my lord, unless I might have another for working  days. Your Grace is too costly to wear every day. But I  beseech your Grace pardon me. I was born to speak all  mirth and no matter.
translation: No, my lord—not unless I could have another husband for workdays. Your Grace is too expensive to wear every day. But please pardon me, your Grace. I was born to tell jokes, not to make sense.

original: Your silence most offends me, and to be merry  best becomes you, for out o' question you were born in a merry hour.
translation: I'd be more offended if you were silent, for being cheerful suits you best. You must have been born in a happy hour.

original: No, sure, my lord, my mother cried, but then there was  a star danced, and under that was I born.—Cousins,  God give you joy!
translation: No, my lord, my mother actually cried when she gave birth to me. But then a star danced overhead, and under that star I was born. Friends and cousins, I must be off!

original: Niece, will you look to those things I told you of?
translation: Niece, will you take care of those things I asked you about?

original: I cry you mercy, uncle.—By your Grace’s pardon.
translation: Forgive me, uncle, I will. If you'll excuse me, your Grace.

original: By my troth, a pleasant-spirited lady.
translation: By God, what a good-humored lady.

original: There’s little of the melancholy element in her, my  lord.
translation: There's certainly not much gloominess in her, my lord.

original: She is never sad but when she sleeps, and not ever sad then, for I have heard my daughter say she hath  often dreamed of unhappiness and waked herself with  laughing.
translation: She's only sad when she sleeps, and even then Hero has told me that Beatrice can dream of misfortune but still wake herself up laughing.

original: She cannot endure to hear tell of a husband.
translation: She can't stand to hear about getting a husband.

original: Oh, by no means. She mocks all her wooers out of suit.
translation: Oh, certainly not. She mocks all her suitors until they give up courting her.

original: She were an excellent wife for Benedick.
translation: She would be an excellent wife for Benedick.

original: O Lord, my lord, if they were but a week married,  they would talk themselves mad.
translation: Oh Lord, if they were married, they'd talk each other into insanity within a week, my lord.

original: County Claudio, when mean you to go to church?
translation: Count Claudio, when do you plan to get married?

original: Tomorrow, my lord. Time goes on crutches till love  have all his rites.
translation: Tomorrow, my lord. Time limps along slowly when love is waiting to be fulfilled.

original: Not till Monday, my dear son, which is hence a  just sevennight, and a time too brief, too, to have all  things answer my mind.
translation: Wait until Monday, my dear future son-in-law. It's only a week away, and even that is too short a time to put together all the arrangements I have planned.

original: [to CLAUDIO]   Come, you shake the head at so long  a breathing, but I warrant thee, Claudio, the time shall not go dully by us.
translation: [To CLAUDIO]  Come, you shake your head at such a long wait. But I promise you, Claudio, the time won't be boring for us.

original: I will in the interim undertake one of Hercules' labors, which is to bring Signor Benedick  and the Lady Beatrice into a mountain of affection, th'  one with th' other.
translation: While we wait, I intend to take on an impossible task, like one of the Labors of Hercules: I want to make Sir Benedick and Lady Beatrice fall totally in love with each other.

original: I would fain have it a match,
translation: I want to see them matched.

original: and I  doubt not but to fashion it, if you three will but  minister such assistance as I shall give you direction.
translation: And I'm sure I can arrange it, if you three will help me when I ask for it.

original: My lord, I am for you, though it cost me ten  nights' watchings.
translation: My lord, I'll accept your proposal, even if I have to stay up for ten nights straight.

original: And I, my lord.
translation: And me too, my lord.

original: And you too, gentle Hero?
translation: And you too, dear Hero?

original: I will do any modest office, my lord, to help my cousin to a good husband.
translation: My lord, I'll perform any task if it will help my cousin get a good husband.

original: And Benedick is not the unhopefulest husband that I  know.
translation: And Benedick isn't the worst husband I know.

original: Thus far can I praise him: he is of a noble  strain, of approved valor, and confirmed honesty.
translation: I can praise him this much at least: he is well-born, he's had his bravery tested in battle, and he is established as an honorable man.

original: I will teach you how to humor your cousin that she shall fall  in love with Benedick.
translation: I'll teach you how to influence your cousin so that she falls in love with Benedick.

original: —And I, with your two helps, will  so practice on Benedick that, in despite of his quick  wit and his queasy stomach, he shall fall in love with  Beatrice.
translation: [To CLAUDIO and LEONATO]  And we men will scheme against Benedick so that, despite his quick wit and fear of marriage, he will fall in love with Beatrice.

original: If we can do this, Cupid is no longer an  archer; his glory shall be ours, for we are the  only love gods.
translation: If we can do this, then we'll steal all of Cupid's glory. He won't even be able to call himself an archer anymore—we will be the only gods of love!

original: Go in with me, and I will tell you my  drift.
translation: Now come inside with me, and I'll tell you my plan.

original: It is so. The Count Claudio shall marry the daughter  of Leonato.
translation: It's been decided. Count Claudio will marry Leonato's daughter.

original: Yea, my lord, but I can cross it.
translation: Yes, my lord, but I can still ruin it.

original: Any bar, any cross, any impediment will be med'cinable  to me. I am sick in displeasure to him, and whatsoever  comes athwart his affection ranges evenly with mine. How canst thou cross this marriage?
translation: Any obstacle or impediment to Claudio's marriage will be like medicine to me. I am sick with anger toward him, and whoever can spoil his happiness will improve my own happiness. How do you plan to stop this wedding?

original: Not honestly, my lord, but so covertly that no  dishonesty shall appear in me.
translation: My lord, I can't do it without being dishonest, but I'll be so secretive that no one will suspect me.

original: Show me briefly how.
translation: Quickly, tell me how.

original: I think I told your lordship a year since how much I am in the favor of Margaret, the waiting gentlewoman to  Hero.
translation: I think  I told you about a year ago how much Hero's serving woman, Margaret, likes me.

original: I remember.
translation: I remember.

original: I can, at any unseasonable instant of the night,  appoint her to look out at her lady’s chamber window.
translation: I can arrange for her to meet me at Hero's bedroom window at some indecent hour of the night.

original: What life is in that to be the death of this marriage?
translation: How will that help to kill this marriage?

original: The poison of that lies in you to temper.
translation: It's up to you to brew the poison with these ingredients.

original: Go you to  the Prince your brother.
translation: Go to the Prince your brother.

original: Spare not to tell him that he  hath wronged his honor in marrying the renowned  Claudio, whose estimation do you mightily hold up, to  a contaminated stale, such a one as Hero.
translation: Tell him that he has wronged his own honor by matching the heroic Claudio—whose reputation you greatly admire—with a common prostitute like Hero.

original: What proof shall I make of that?
translation: And how can I prove that?

original: Proof enough to misuse the Prince, to vex Claudio, to  undo Hero, and kill Leonato. Look you for any other  issue?
translation: You'll have enough proof to deceive the Prince, torment Claudio, ruin Hero, and kill Leonato. What more could you want?

original: Only to despite them, I will endeavor anything.
translation: I'll do anything to hurt them.

original: Go then, find me a meet hour to draw Don Pedro and  the Count Claudio alone.
translation: Go then, find a suitable time to speak with Don Pedro and Count Claudio alone.

original: Tell them that you know that  Hero loves me.
translation: Tell them that you know that Hero loves me.

original: Intend a kind of zeal both to the Prince  and Claudio, as in love of your brother’s honor, who  hath made this match, and his friend’s reputation, who  is thus like to be cozened with the semblance of a maid, that you have discovered thus.
translation: Pretend to be very passionate about preserving your brother's honor, which has been compromised by making this match, and also Claudio's reputation, which will be ruined by this woman, whom you've discovered is only pretending to be a virgin.

original: They will scarcely  believe this without trial. Offer them instances,
translation: They won't believe this without proof, of course—so give them examples.

original: which  shall bear no less likelihood than to see me at her  chamber window, hear me call Margaret “Hero,” hear  Margaret term me “Claudio,” and bring them to see this  the very night before the intended wedding,
translation: Tell them you've seen the two of us together at Hero's bedroom window, and on the night before the intended wedding, bring them to see for themselves.

original: for in the  meantime I will so fashion the matter that Hero shall be absent, and there shall appear such seeming truth of  Hero’s disloyalty that jealousy shall be called  assurance and all the preparation overthrown.
translation: I'll arrange it so that Hero is away for the night, and Margaret and I will be at the window, with me calling her "Hero" and her calling me " Claudio ." This will seem like such convincing evidence of Hero's disloyalty that Claudio's suspicions will be confirmed, and he'll immediately call off the wedding preparations.

original: Grow this to what adverse issue it can, I will put it  in practice. Be cunning in the working this, and thy fee is a thousand ducats.
translation: Make this happen as you say, and I'll do my part. Arrange this cunningly, and I'll reward you with a thousand gold coins.

original: Be you constant in the accusation, and my cunning  shall not  shame me.
translation: If you can make your accusation of Hero convincing, then my cunning won't fail me.

original: I will presently go learn their day of marriage.
translation: I'll go right now to learn the date of their wedding.

original: Boy!
translation: Boy!

original: Signior?
translation: Sir?

original: In my chamber window lies a book. Bring it hither to me in the orchard.
translation: In my bedroom window there is a book. Go get it and bring it to me here in the garden.

original: I am here already, sir.
translation: But I am here already, sir.

original: I know that, but I would have thee hence and here  again.
translation: I know that, but I want you to go there and then come back here again.

original: I do much wonder that one man, seeing how much  another man is a fool when he dedicates his behaviors to love, will, after he hath laughed at such shallow  follies in others, become the argument of his own scorn  by falling in love—
translation: I'm amazed that a man—after seeing another man fall in love and become a fool, and laughing at that foolishness—can then become the very thing he once scorned.

original: and such a man is Claudio.
translation: Claudio is such a man.

original: I have  known when there was no music with him but the drum and  the fife, and now had he rather hear the tabor and the  pipe.
translation: I knew him back when the only music he cared for was the drums of war, but now he would rather hear the sweet, delicate music of love.

original: I have known when he would have walked ten mile  afoot to see a good armor, and now will he lie ten  nights awake carving the fashion of a new doublet.
translation: I knew him when he would have walked ten miles to see a good suit of armor, but now he'll lie awake ten nights in a row thinking about a fancy new jacket.

original: He  was wont to speak plain and to the purpose, like an  honest man and a soldier, and now is he  turned orthography; his words are a very fantastical  banquet, just so many strange dishes.
translation: He used to speak plainly and to the point, like an honest man and a soldier. But now his speech has become a collection of pretty words, like a fantastical banquet full of strange new dishes.

original: May I be so  converted and see with these eyes? I cannot tell; I  think not.
translation: Could I be transformed like this, and see everything through a lover's eyes? I can't be sure, but I don't think so.

original: I will not be sworn but love may transform me to an oyster, but I’ll take my oath on it, till he have made an oyster of me, he shall never make me such a  fool.
translation: I can't promise that love won't change me. But until I  have  really fallen in love, I'll never act like such a fool.

original: One woman is fair, yet I am well; another is wise, yet I am well; another virtuous, yet I am well;
translation: One woman is beautiful, but I don't care. Another woman is wise, but I don't care. Another is virtuous, but I don't care.

original: but  till all graces be in one woman, one woman shall not  come in my grace.
translation: I won't pay attention to anyone until all three of these qualities come together in one woman.

original: Rich she shall be, that’s certain;  wise, or I’ll none;
translation: She must be rich, that's for sure, and wise—or else I'll have nothing to do with her.

original: virtuous, or I’ll never cheapen her; fair, or I’ll ever look on her; mild, or come not  near me; noble, or not I for an angel;
translation: She must be virtuous, or I won't consider her; beautiful, or I won't look at her; mild-mannered, or else she shouldn't come near me;  noble, or I won't have her even if she's an angel .

original: of good  discourse, an excellent musician, and her hair shall be  of what color it please God.
translation: She must be well-spoken, an excellent musician, and her hair should be whatever color God wants it to be.

original: Ha! The Prince and Monsieur Love! I will hide me in the arbor.
translation: Ha! Here come the Prince and Mister Love! I'll hide myself in the garden alcove.

original: Come, shall we hear this music?
translation: Come, shall we hear some music?

original: Yea, my good lord. How still the evening is, As hushed on purpose to grace harmony!
translation: Yes, my good lord. How still the evening is—as if it's purposefully being quiet to honor the music!

original: See you where Benedick hath hid  himself?
translation: Do you see where Benedick is hiding?

original: O, very well, my lord. The music ended, We’ll fit the kid-fox with a pennyworth.
translation: Oh, very well, my lord. When the music is over, we'll give that hidden fox more than he bargained for!

original: Come, Balthasar, we’ll hear that song again.
translation: Come, Balthasar, please play that song again.

original: O, good my lord, tax not so bad a voice  To slander music anymore than once.
translation: Oh, my good lord, don't command me to insult music again with my awful voice.

original: It is the witness still of excellency To put a strange face on his own perfection. I pray thee, sing, and let me woo no more.
translation: It's a sure sign of excellence that your voice doesn't admit to its own perfection. Please, sing for us, and don't make me woo you anymore.

original: Because you talk of wooing, I will sing,
translation: Since you talk of wooing, I'll sing.

original: Since many a wooer doth commence his suit   To her he thinks not worthy, yet he woos,   Yet will he swear he loves.
translation: You're like a suitor who starts to court a woman he doesn't really think is worthy, but he still keeps courting her anyway, and will even swear he loves her.

original: Nay, pray thee, come, Or, if thou wilt hold longer argument, Do it in notes.
translation: No, please, sing. Or if you want to keep arguing, do it through song.

original: Note this before my notes:  There’s not a note of mine that’s worth the noting.
translation: But note this before I play my notes: there's not a note I can sing that's worthy of being noted.

original: Why, these are very crotchets that he speaks! Note notes, forsooth, and nothing.
translation: Why, listen to him speaking his odd ideas in quarter notes! Everyone take note: we will now hear notes.

original: [aside]   Now, divine air! Now is his soul ravished.
translation: [To himself]  Now that must be a divine song!

original: Is  it not strange that sheeps' guts should hale souls out  of men’s bodies?
translation: Now their souls are filled with passion. Isn't it strange that strings made of sheep's guts can draw men's souls from their bodies?

original: Well, a horn for my money, when all’s  done.
translation: Well, I'd rather listen to a plain hunting horn any day, when all's said and done.

original: [singing]   Sigh no more, ladies, sigh no more,   Men were deceivers ever,
translation: [Singing] Cry no more, ladies, cry no more, Men have always been deceivers,

original: One foot in sea and one on shore,   To one thing constant never.
translation: With one foot on a ship and one on the shore, Never faithful to anything.

original: Then sigh not so, but let them go,   And be you blithe and bonny,
translation: So don't cry like that, but let them go, And be carefree and happy,

original: Converting all your sounds of woe   Into   Hey, nonny nonny.   Sing no more ditties, sing no mo   Of dumps so dull and heavy.
translation: Changing all your sad songsInto "Hey, nonny nonny." Sing no more laments, sing no more  Mournful tunes so sad and heavy.

original: The fraud of men was ever so,   Since summer first was leavy.
translation: Men have always been frauds Since trees had leaves in summer.

original: Then sigh not so, but let them go   And be you blithe and bonny,
translation: So don't cry like that, but let them go, And be carefree and happy,

original: Converting all your sounds of woe   Into Hey, nonny nonny.
translation: Changing all your sad songs Into "Hey, nonny nonny."

original: By my troth, a good song.
translation: I swear, that's good song.

original: And an ill singer, my lord.
translation: And a bad singer, my lord.

original: Ha, no, no, faith, thou sing’st well enough for a  shift.
translation: Ha! No, no, really, you sing well enough to to be passable.

original: [aside]   An he had been a dog that should have howled  thus, they would have hanged him.
translation: [To himself]  If a dog had howled like that they would have killed it.

original: And I pray God his bad voice   bode no mischief.
translation: I pray to God that his bad voice isn't an omen of trouble.

original: I had as lief have heard the night  raven, come what plague could have come after it.
translation: I would rather have heard a night raven shriek, even if it does mean the plague is coming after it, as they say.

original: Yea, marry, dost thou hear, Balthasar? I pray thee,  get us some excellent music, for tomorrow night we would have it at the Lady Hero’s chamber window
translation: Yes, well, do you hear me, Balthasar? Please, get us some excellent music—for tomorrow night we want to serenade Lady Hero at her bedroom window.

original: The best I can, my lord.
translation: I'll do the best I can, my lord.

original: Do so. Farewell.
translation: Do so. Farewell.

original: Come hither, Leonato. What was it you told me of  today, that your niece Beatrice was in love with Signor  Benedick?
translation: Come here, Leonato. What was it you told me today—that your niece Beatrice was in love with Sir Benedick?

original: Oh, ay.    Stalk on, stalk on; the  fowl sits.—I did never think that lady would have loved  any man.
translation: Oh, yes.  Tread carefully: our prey is nearby.[Speaking louder so that all can hear] Yes, and I never thought that that lady would ever love any man.

original: No, nor I neither, but most wonderful that she should  so dote on Signor Benedick, whom she hath in all  outward behaviors seemed ever to abhor.
translation: No, I didn't either. And it's especially amazing that she should fall in love with Sir Benedick, whom she's always seemed to hate, judging from all her outward behavior.

original: Is ’t possible? Sits the wind in that corner?
translation: Is it possible? Is that the way the wind is blowing now?

original: By my troth, my lord, I cannot tell what to think of  it, but that she loves him with an enraged affection, it is past the infinite of thought.
translation: Truly, my lord, I don't know what to think about it. But she loves him with such a wild passion that it's past all the boundaries of understanding.

original: May be she doth but counterfeit.
translation: Maybe she's only pretending.

original: Faith, like enough.
translation: Yes, that seems more likely.

original: O God! Counterfeit? There was never counterfeit  of passion came so near the life of passion as she  discovers it.
translation: Oh God! Pretending? Then pretend passion has never seemed so much like real passion, at least the way she displays it.

original: Why, what effects of passion shows she?
translation: Why, what symptoms of love has she been showing?

original: Bait the hook well; this fish will  bite.
translation: Bait the hook well; this fish is about to bite.

original: What effects, my lord? She will sit you—you heard  my daughter tell you how.
translation: What symptoms, my lord? You know, she will sit—but you heard my daughter tell you about it.

original: She did indeed.
translation: She did indeed.

original: How, how I pray you? You amaze me. I would have  thought her spirit had been invincible against all  assaults of affection.
translation: How, how? Please tell! You amaze me. I would have thought that her spirit would be invincible against any sudden attack of love.

original: I would have sworn it had, my lord, especially  against Benedick.
translation: I would have sworn that too, my lord—and especially against such an attack of love for Benedick.

original: I should think this a gull but that the  white-bearded fellow speaks it. Knavery cannot, sure,  hide himself in such reverence.
translation: I would think this was a joke if the white-bearded fellow weren't saying it. Mischief surely can't hide itself in such a respectable old man.

original: He hath ta'en th' infection. Hold  it up.
translation: He's taken the bait. Keep it up.

original: Hath she made her affection known to Benedick?
translation: Has she revealed her feelings to Benedick?

original: No, and swears she never will. That’s her torment.
translation: No, and she swears she never will. That's what's been tormenting her.

original: 'Tis true indeed, so your daughter says. “Shall I,”  says she, “that have so oft encountered him with scorn,  write to him that I love him?”
translation: That's the truth. Hero says so. Beatrice asks herself, "How can I write to him that I love him, when I've always treated him so scornfully?"

original: This says she now when she is beginning to write to  him, for she’ll be up twenty times a night, and there  will she sit in her smock till she have writ a sheet of  paper. My daughter tells us all.
translation: She says this when she's starting to write to him. And she's been getting up twenty times a night, sitting there in her nightgown until she's written a single page. My daughter told us everything.

original: Now you talk of a sheet of paper, I remember a pretty  jest your daughter told.
translation: Now that you speak of a page of paper, I remember a funny story Hero told.

original: Oh, when she had writ it and was reading it over, she  found “Benedick” and “Beatrice” between the sheet?
translation: Oh, you mean when Beatrice had written the letter and Hero was reading it over, and saw that it had "Benedick" and "Beatrice" written all over the page?

original: That.
translation: That was it.

original: O, she tore the letter into a thousand halfpence,  railed at herself that she should be so immodest to  write to one that she knew would flout her.
translation: Oh, Beatrice tore that letter into a thousand pieces, and got angry at herself for being so forward as to write to a man she knew would mock her.

original: “I measure  him,” says she, “by my own spirit, for I should flout  him if he writ to me,
translation: She said, "I can predict his response by comparing him to myself. For I would mock him if he wrote me a letter like this.

original: yea, though I love him, I should.”
translation: Yes, even though I love him, I still would mock him!"

original: Then down upon her knees she falls, weeps, sobs, beats  her heart, tears her hair, prays, curses: “O sweet  Benedick! God give me patience!”
translation: Then she fell down on her knees and wept, sobbed, beat at her chest, tore her hair, prayed, and cursed: "Oh, sweet Benedick! God give me patience!"

original: She doth indeed, my daughter says so,
translation: She did indeed; my daughter said so.

original: and the ecstasy  hath so much overborne her that my daughter is sometime   afeared she will do a desperate outrage to herself. It  is very true.
translation: And Beatrice is so overcome with passion that my daughter worries that she might do something violent to herself. It's true.

original: It were good that Benedick knew of it by some other, if she will not discover it.
translation: If Beatrice won't tell Benedick, then it would be good if someone else let him know.

original: To what end? He would make but a sport of it and  torment the poor lady worse.
translation: What purpose would that serve? He would just turn it into a joke and torment the poor lady even more.

original: An he should, it were an alms to hang him. She’s  an excellent sweet lady, and, out of all suspicion, she  is virtuous.
translation: If he does that, it would be a good deed to hang him. She's an excellent, sweet lady, and there's no doubt that she's virtuous.

original: And she is exceeding wise.
translation: And she is exceptionally wise.

original: In every thing but in loving Benedick.
translation: In everything except for her love for Benedick.

original: Oh, my lord, wisdom and blood combating in so tender  a body, we have ten proofs to one that blood hath the  victory. I am sorry for her, as I have just cause, being her uncle and her guardian.
translation: Oh, my lord, when wisdom and emotion are at war within a tender young person, it's ten to one that emotion will be victorious. I am sorry for her, as I ought to be, being both her uncle and her guardian.

original: I would she had bestowed this dotage on me. I would  have daffed all other respects and made her half myself. I pray you tell Benedick of it and hear what he will  say.
translation: I wish she had bestowed her love on me instead. I would have put aside all other considerations and made her my wife. Please, tell Benedick about this and hear what he says.

original: Were it good, think you?
translation: Do you think that would be a good idea?

original: Hero thinks surely she will die,
translation: Hero thinks that Beatrice will surely die.

original: for she says she will  die if he love her not, and she will die ere she make  her love known, and she will die if he woo her rather  than she will bate one breath of her accustomed  crossness.
translation: For she says she'll die if Benedick doesn't love her; and she'll die before she tells him she loves him; and she'll die if he courts her too, rather than hold back even a breath of her usual mockery.

original: She doth well. If she should make tender of her love,  ’tis very possible he’ll scorn it, for the man, as you  know all, hath a contemptible spirit.
translation: She's right. If she made him an offer of love, it's very possible that he'll scorn it—for that man has a contemptuous nature, as we all know.

original: He is a very proper man.
translation: He is a very handsome man, though.

original: He hath indeed a good outward happiness.
translation: He does indeed have a good outward appearance.

original: Before God, and in my mind, very wise.
translation: And I'll swear to God that he's very wise.

original: He doth indeed show some sparks that are like wit.
translation: He does indeed show some sparks of something like wisdom.

original: And I take him to be valiant.
translation: And he seems very brave.

original: As Hector, I assure you, and in the managing of  quarrels you may say he is wise, for either he avoids  them with great discretion or undertakes them with a  most Christian-like fear.
If he do fear God, he must necessarily keep peace. If  he break the peace, he ought to enter into a quarrel  with fear and trembling.
translation: If he's a God-fearing man, then he must necessarily keep the peace as best he can. And if he breaks the peace, then he ought to enter into a quarrel with appropriate fear and trembling.

original: And so will he do, for the man doth fear God,  howsoever it seems not in him by some large jests he  will make. Well, I am sorry for your niece. Shall we go  seek Benedick and tell him of her love?
translation: And so he will, for he is indeed a God-fearing man, even though some of his rude jokes make him seem otherwise. Well, I am sorry for your niece. Should we go find Benedick and tell him of her love?

original: Never tell him, my lord, let her wear it out with  good counsel.
translation: Don't tell him, my lord. Let her get over her feelings through self-reflection and good advice.

original: Nay, that’s impossible. She may wear her heart out  first.
translation: No, that's impossible. Her heart might give out first.

original: Well, we will hear further of it by your daughter. Let  it cool the while. I love Benedick well, and I could  wish he would modestly examine himself to see how much  he is unworthy so good a lady.
translation: Well, we'll hear more about this from your daughter. Let's leave it for a while. I am fond of Benedick, and I wish he would examine himself humbly and see how undeserving he is of that good lady.

original: My lord, will you walk? Dinner is ready.
translation: My lord, will you go? Dinner is ready.

original: If he do not dote on  her upon this, I will never trust my expectation.
translation: If he doesn't fall in love with her after this, I'll never trust myself again.

original: [aside to LEONATO]   Let there be the same net spread for her, and that must your daughter and her gentlewomen  carry.
translation: [To LEONATO so that only he can hear]  Make sure your daughter and her servants set the same trap for Beatrice.

original: The sport will be when they hold one an opinion  of another’s dotage, and no such matter.
translation: The real fun will be when they each believe the other is in love, when none of it is actually true.

original: That’s the  scene that I would see, which will be merely a dumb  show.
translation: That's the scene I want to watch—it will be like some silent performance, since neither will have anything to say without their usual insults!

original: Let us send her to call him in to dinner.
translation: Let's send Beatrice to call Benedick in to dinner.

original: [coming forward]   This can be no trick. The conference  was sadly borne; they have the truth of this from Hero;
translation: [Coming forward]  This can't be a trick. Their discussion was serious, and they had Hero's words to back them up.

original: they seem to pity the lady. It seems her affections have  their full bent.
translation: They seem to pity the lady. It seems that her passion is stretched to the limit.

original: Love me? Why, it must be requited!
translation: She loves me? Why, her love must be returned!

original: I  hear how I am censured.   They sy I will bear myself  proudly if I perceive the love come from her.
translation: I hear how I am criticized. They say I will be arrogant if I find out about her love.

original: They say,  too, that she will rather die than give any sign of  affection.
translation: They also say that she'd rather die than show any sign of affection.

original: I did never think to marry. I must not seem  proud.
translation: I never thought I would marry. I must not be too proud to change my ways.

original: Happy are they that hear their detractions and  can put them to mending.
translation: Only fortunate people can hear their own faults criticized and then go about fixing them.

original: They say the lady is fair; ’tis a truth, I can bear them witness.
translation: They say the lady is beautiful—it's true, I've witnessed it myself.

original: And virtuous; ’tis  so, I cannot reprove it.
translation: And virtuous—it's so, I can't deny it.

original: And wise, but for loving me; by my troth, it is no addition to her wit, nor no great  argument of her folly, for I will be horribly in  love with her!
translation: And wise, except for loving me—well, that might not be any great indication of her intelligence, but it won't be a sign of foolishness either, for I will be horribly in love with her!

original: I may chance have some odd quirks and  remnants of wit broken on me because I have railed so  long against marriage, but doth not the appetite alter?
translation: Some of my witty remarks about marriage might be thrown back at me here and there, but don't tastes change?

original: A man loves the meat in his youth that he cannot endure  in his age.
translation: In his youth, a man can love a dish that he can't stand in his old age.

original: Shall quips and sentences and these paper  bullets of the brain awe a man from the career of his  humor?
translation: Will sarcastic remarks, old sayings, and verbal ammunition from books keep a man from pursuing his desire?

original: No! The world must be peopled.
translation: No! The world must be populated.

original: When I said I  would die a bachelor, I did not think I should live till I were married.
translation: When I said I would die a bachelor, I didn't think that I would live long enough to get married.

original: Here comes Beatrice. By this day, she’s a fair lady. I do spy some marks of love in her.
translation: Here comes Beatrice. By God, she's a beautiful lady. I think I see some signs of love in her.

original: Against my will, I am sent to bid you come in to  dinner.
translation: I've been sent against my will to tell you to come in to dinner.

original: Fair Beatrice, I thank you for your pains.
translation: Fair Beatrice, I thank you for making the effort to do that for me.

original: I took no more pains for those thanks than you take  pains to thank me. If it had been painful, I would not  have come.
translation: I made no more effort in doing this task for your thanks than you made an effort in thanking me for it. If it had been a hard task, I wouldn't have come.

original: You take pleasure then in the message?
translation: So you took pleasure in delivering the message then?

original: Yea, just so much as you may take upon a knife’s point  and choke a daw withal. You have no stomach, Signior.  Fare you well.
translation: Yes, just as much pleasure as choking a bird with a knife. So you have no appetite for our battle of wits, sir? Farewell then.

original: Ha! “Against my will I am sent to bid you come in  to dinner.”
translation: Ha! "I've been sent against my will to tell you to come in to dinner."

original: There’s a double meaning in that.
translation: There's a double meaning in that.

original: “I took no more pains for those thanks than you took pains to  thank me.”
translation: "I made no more effort in doing this task for your thanks than you made an effort in thanking me for it."

original: That’s as much as to say, “Any pains that I  take for you is as easy as thanks.”
translation: That's as much as to say, "Any effort I make for you is as easy as saying 'thank you.'"

original: If I do not take  pity of her, I am a villain.
translation: If I don't take pity on her, I'm a villain.

original: If I do not love her, I am  a Jew.
translation: If I don't love her,  I'm totally hard-hearted .

original: I will go get her picture.
translation: I'll go get a picture of her.

original: Good Margaret, run thee to the parlor.
translation: Good Margaret, run to the parlor.

original: There shalt thou find my cousin Beatrice   Proposing with the Prince and Claudio.
translation: You'll find my cousin Beatrice talking to the Prince and Claudio there.

original: Whisper her ear and tell her I and Ursula   Walk in the orchard, and our whole discourse   Is all of her.
translation: Whisper in her ear, and tell her that Ursula and I are walking in the garden and talking about her.

original: Say that thou overheardst us,   And bid her steal into the pleachèd bower   Where honeysuckles ripened by the sun   Forbid the sun to enter, like favorites   Made proud by princes, that advance their pride   Against that power that bred it.
translation: Say that you overheard us, and tell her to sneak into the leafy arbor where the honeysuckles, brought to full bloom by the sun, now block the sunlight from entering—like men promoted by princes who then turn against their masters.

original: There will she hide  her   To listen our propose.
translation: Beatrice can hide there and listen to our conversation.

original: This is thy office.   Bear thee well in it and leave us alone.
translation: This is your job. Do it well, and then leave the rest to us.

original: I’ll make her come, I warrant you, presently.
translation: I'll make her come right away, I promise you.

original: Now, Ursula, when Beatrice doth come,   As we do trace this alley up and down,   Our talk must only be of Benedick.
translation: Now, Ursula, when Beatrice shows up, we must walk back and forth on this garden path and talk about nothing but Benedick.

original: When I do name him, let it be thy part   To praise him more than ever man did merit.
translation: When I mention him, you should praise him more than any man ever deserved.

original: My talk to thee must be how Benedick   Is sick in love with Beatrice.
translation: And I'll talk to you about how Benedick is sick with love for Beatrice.

original: Of this matter   Is little Cupid’s crafty arrow made,   That only wounds by hearsay.
translation: This is how Cupid makes his crafty arrows: out of rumor and hearsay.

original: Now begin, For look where Beatrice like a lapwing runs  Close by the ground, to hear our conference.
translation: Let's begin, because Beatrice is running here now like a little bird—keeping close to the ground—to come eavesdrop on our discussion.

original: [aside to HERO]   The pleasant’st angling is to see the fish   Cut with her golden oars the silver stream   And greedily devour the treacherous bait.
translation: [To HERO so that only she can hear]  The best part of fishing is when you can see the fish cut through the water and greedily devour the treacherous bait.

original: So angle we for Beatrice, who even now   Is couchèd in the woodbine coverture.
translation: We're fishing for Beatrice, who is hiding even now in the honeysuckle arbor.

original: Fear you not my part of the dialogue.
translation: Don't worry about my part in our conversation.

original: [aside to URSULA   ]   Then go we near her, that her ear lose nothing   Of the false sweet bait that we lay for it.—
translation: [To URSULA so that only she can hear]  Then let's get closer to her, so she won't miss any of the false, sweet bait we're putting out for her.

original: [approaching the bower]   No, truly, Ursula, she is too disdainful.
translation: [Approaching the arbor]  No, truly, Ursula, she is too scornful.

original: I know her spirits are as coy and wild   As haggards of the rock.
translation: I know that she's as shy and untameable as a wild hawk in the mountains.

original: But are you sure That Benedick loves Beatrice so entirely?
translation: But are you sure that Benedick is so completely in love with Beatrice?

original: So says the Prince and my new-trothèd lord.
translation: That's what the Prince and my new fiancé say.

original: And did they bid you tell her of it, madam?
translation: And did they ask you to tell Beatrice about it, madam?

original: They did entreat me to acquaint her of it,
translation: They did want me to make her aware of it.

original: But I persuaded them, if they loved Benedick,   To wish him wrestle with affection   And never to let Beatrice know of it.
translation: But I persuaded them that—if they really cared for Benedick—they would advise him to wrestle with his feelings, and never let Beatrice know about them.

original: Why did you so? Doth not the gentleman  Deserve as full as fortunate a bed As ever Beatrice shall couch upon?
translation: Why did you say that? Doesn't Benedick deserve at least as good a wife as Beatrice would ever be?

original: O god of love! I know he doth deserve   As much as may be yielded to a man,   But Nature never framed a woman’s heart   Of prouder stuff than that of Beatrice.
translation: Oh, by the god of love! I know he deserves as much as any man could be given, but Nature never made a woman's heart prouder than Beatrice's.

original: Disdain and scorn ride sparkling in her eyes,   Misprizing what they look on,
translation: Disdain and scorn sparkle in her eyes, and make her undervalue everything she looks upon.

original: and her wit   Values itself so highly that to her   All matter else seems weak.
translation: She prizes her wit so highly that other people's words seem weak by comparison.

original: She cannot love   Nor take no shape nor project of affection   She is so self-endeared.
translation: She's so full of self-love that she cannot love anyone else, or even imagine what love is.

original: Sure, I think so, And therefore certainly it were not good She knew his love, lest she make sport at it.
translation: Yes, I think you're right. It certainly wouldn't be good if she learned about Benedick's love and made a joke of it.

original: Why, you speak truth. I never yet saw man,   How wise, how noble, young, how rarely featured   But she would spell him backward.
translation: Indeed, you speak the truth. No matter how wise, noble, young, and handsome a man is, she always manages to turn his merits into faults.

original: If fair-faced,   She would swear the gentleman should be her sister;
translation: If he's pale and delicate, she'll say the gentleman should be her sister, not her husband.

original: If black, why, Nature, drawing of an antic,   Made a foul blot;
translation: If he has a dark complexion, she'll say that Nature must have spilled some ink while drawing his ugly portrait.

original: if tall, a lance ill-headed;
translation: If he's tall, she'll call him a spear with a bad head.

original: If low, an agate very vilely cut;
translation: If he's small, she'll say that he's a badly carved statue.

original: If speaking, why, a vane blown with all winds;
translation: If he's talkative, she'll say he's a weather vane blown around by the wind;

original: If silent, why, a block moved with none.
translation: and if he's silent, why, she'll call him a block that can't be moved by anything at all.

original: So turns she every man the wrong side out   And never gives to truth and virtue that   Which simpleness and merit purchaseth.
translation: And so she turns every man inside out, and never acknowledges the virtue that integrity and sincerity deserve.

original: Sure, sure, such carping is not commendable.
translation: Surely, surely, such fussy nitpicking is not to be praised.

original: No, not to be so odd and from all fashions   As Beatrice is, cannot be commendable.
translation: No, it's certainly not praiseworthy to be as odd and willfully eccentric as Beatrice is.

original: But who dare tell her so? If I should speak,   She would mock me into air.
translation: But who would dare to tell her that? If I spoke to her, she would mock me into thin air.

original: O, she would laugh me   Out of myself, press me to death with wit.
translation: Oh, she would laugh me right out of my body and press me to death with her wit, as witches are pressed to death with stones.

original: Therefore let Benedick, like covered fire,   Consume away in sighs, waste inwardly.
translation: So Benedick should keep his feelings hidden, like a covered fire, and consume himself with his passionate sighs and waste away.

original: It were a better death than die with mocks,   Which is as bad as die with tickling.
translation: This will be a better death than to die from mockery, which is as bad as being killed by tickling.

original: Yet tell her of it. Hear what she will say.
translation: But you should tell her, and hear how she responds.

original: No, rather I will go to Benedick   And counsel him to fight against his passion;
translation: No, I would rather go to Benedick and advise him to fight against his passion.

original: And truly I’ll devise some honest slanders   To stain my cousin with.
translation: I'll even make up some harmless slanders against my cousin to make her seem less attractive.

original: One doth not know   How much an ill word may empoison liking.
translation: You don't know how a single unkind word can poison love.

original: O, do not do your cousin such a wrong!
translation: Oh, don't do your cousin wrong like that!

original: She cannot be so much without true judgment,   Having so swift and excellent a wit   As she is prized to have, as to refuse   So rare a gentleman as Signior Benedick.
translation: If she really has the quick and excellent wit she's known for, then she can't be so unwise as to refuse an exceptional gentleman like Sir Benedick.

original: He is the only man of Italy, Always excepted my dear Claudio.
translation: He's the best man in Italy, except for my dear Claudio, of course.

original: I pray you, be not angry with me, madam,   Speaking my fancy.
translation: Madam, please don't be angry with me for speaking my mind,

original: Signor Benedick,   For shape, for bearing, argument and valor,   Goes foremost in report through Italy.
translation: but throughout Italy Sir Benedick is known as the best in looks, bearing, wit, and bravery.

original: Indeed, he hath an excellent good name.
translation: Indeed, he does have an excellent reputation.

original: His excellence did earn it, ere he had it.  When are you married, madam?
translation: And he was excellent before he had the reputation, too. When are you getting married, madam?

original: Why, every day, tomorrow. Come, go in. I’ll show thee some attires, and have thy counsel Which is the best to furnish me tomorrow.
translation: Why, tomorrow and every day after. Come, let's go inside. I want to show you some outfits and have you advise me on what I should wear tomorrow for the wedding.

original: She’s limed, I warrant you. We have caught her, madam.
translation: She's trapped, I promise you. We have caught her, madam.

original: If it proves so, then loving goes by haps; Some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps.
translation: If you're right, then love comes by chance. Cupid gets some lovers with arrows, but some with traps.

original: [coming forward]   What fire is in mine ears? Can this be true?
translation: [Coming forward]  My ears are burning! Can this be true?

original: Stand I condemned for pride and scorn so much?
translation: Do people really condemn me so much for being proud and scornful?

original: Contempt, farewell, and maiden pride, adieu!
translation: Then farewell to contempt, and farewell to my pride in being unmarried!

original: No glory lives behind the back of such.
translation: No one speaks well of a person with such qualities.

original: And Benedick, love on; I will requite thee,
translation: And Benedick, keep on loving; I will return your love.

original: Taming my wild heart to thy loving hand.
translation: I'll tame my fierce heart, which will be trained like a wild hawk to come to your loving hand.

original: If thou dost love, my kindness shall incite thee   To bind our loves up in a holy band.
translation: If you really love me, I'll be kind to you from now on, and inspire you to bind our love together in marriage.

original: For others say thou dost deserve, and I   Believe it better than reportingly.
translation: Other people say that you deserve my love, and I believe it—on better evidence than mere rumors.

original: I do but stay till your marriage be consummate, and  then go I toward Aragon.
translation: I'll only stay in Messina until your marriage is official, and then I'll go on to Aragon.

original: I’ll bring you thither, my lord, if you’ll vouchsafe  me.
translation: My lord, I'll escort you there if you'll allow me.

original: Nay, that would be as great a soil in the new gloss of  your marriage as to show a child his new coat and forbid him to wear it.
translation: No, that would be throwing a blot on your shiny new marriage, like showing a child his new coat and then not letting him wear it.

original: I will only be bold with Benedick for  his company, for from the crown of his head to the sole  of his foot he is all mirth.
translation: I'll only take the liberty of asking Benedick to come with me, for he's a true joker from head to toe.

original: He hath twice or thrice cut Cupid’s bow-string, and the little hangman dare not  shoot at him.
translation: He's evaded love two or three times and cut Cupid's bow-string—and since then Cupid doesn't dare to shoot at him.

original: He hath a heart as sound as a bell, and  his tongue is the clapper, for what his heart thinks,  his tongue speaks.
translation: Benedick's heart is like a bell, and his tongue is the clapper that makes it ring—whatever his heart thinks, his tongue speaks.

original: Gallants, I am not as I have been.
translation: Gentlemen, I am not the same man I used to be.

original: So say I. Methinks you are sadder.
translation: I agree. You seem more serious.

original: I hope he be in love.
translation: I hope he's in love.

original: Hang him, truant! There’s no true drop of blood in him to be truly touched with love. If he be sad, he wants  money.
translation: There's no way in hell! Benedick doesn't have a drop of emotion in his blood that could be affected by love. If he looks serious, then he needs money.

original: I have the toothache.
Draw it.
translation: Draw it.

original: Hang it!
translation: Hang it!

original: You must hang it first, and draw it afterwards.
translation: You must hang it first, and then draw it afterwards.

original: What, sigh for the toothache?
translation: What, are you re so depressed about a toothache?

original: Where is but a humor or a worm.
Well, everyone can master a grief but he that has it.
translation: Well, everyone knows how to cure a pain except the person actually feeling it.

original: Yet say I, he is in love.
translation: I still say he's in love.

original: There is no appearance of fancy in him, unless it be a  fancy that he hath to strange disguises,
translation: There's no signs of love in him, unless it's his love for strange costumes.

original: as to be a  Dutchman today, a Frenchman tomorrow, or in the shape of two countries at once, as a German from the waist  downward, all slops, and a Spaniard from the hip upward, no doublet.
translation: He's like a Dutchman today, a Frenchman tomorrow, or even in clothes from two countries at once—like a German from the waist down, with his baggy pants, and a Spaniard from the waist up, with his cloak and no jacket.

original: Unless he have a fancy to this foolery, as  it appears he hath, he is no fool for fancy, as you  would have it appear he is.
translation: Unless he has a love for this kind of foolishness—which it seems that he does—he is no fool for love, as you would have it seem.

original: If he be not in love with some woman, there is no  believing old signs. He brushes his hat o' mornings.  What should that bode?
translation: All the traditional symptoms point to him being in love. He brushes his hat in the mornings. What does that imply?

original: Hath any man seen him at the barber’s?
translation: Has any man seen him at the barber's?

original: No, but the barber’s man hath been seen with him, and  the old ornament of his cheek hath already stuffed  tennis balls.
Indeed, he looks younger than he did, by the loss of a beard.
translation: Indeed, the loss of his beard does make him look younger.

original: Nay, he rubs himself with civet. Can you smell him out  by that?
translation: And he's rubbed himself with perfume. Can you sniff out his secret now?

original: That’s as much as to say, the sweet youth’s in love.
translation: You might as well say that the sweet-smelling youth's in love.

original: The greatest note of it is his melancholy.
translation: The greatest sign of it is his melancholy behavior.

original: And when was he wont to wash his face?
translation: And when has he ever been in the habit of washing his face?

original: Yea, or to paint himself? For the which I hear what  they say of him.
translation: Yes, or wearing makeup? I hear he's been doing that, too.

original: Nay, but his jesting spirit, which is now crept into a  lute string and now governed by stops—
translation: And his mocking spirit is gone. It's crawled into a lute string to play love songs—

original: Indeed, that tells a heavy tale for him. Conclude,  conclude, he is in love.
translation: Indeed, this all adds up to a serious tale for Benedick. To conclude: he is in love

original: Nay, but I know who loves him.
translation: Oh, and I know who loves him.

original: That would I know too. I warrant, one that knows him  not.
translation: I want to know too. It must be someone who doesn't know him well.

original: Yes, and his ill conditions, and, in despite of all,  dies for him.
translation: But she does know him, and all his bad qualities. Yet, despite all this, she's dying for him.

original: She shall be buried with her face upwards.
Yet is this no charm for the toothache.—Old Signior,  walk aside with me. I have studied eight or nine wise  words to speak to you, which these hobbyhorses must not  hear.
translation: But all this talk won't cure a toothache.  Old sir, walk with me a while. I have eight or nine wise words to say to you, and I don't want these buffoons to hear them.

original: For my life, to break with him about Beatrice!
translation: I'd bet my life he wants to talk to Leonato about marrying Beatrice!

original: 'Tis even so. Hero and Margaret have by this played  their parts with Beatrice, and then the two bears will  not bite one another when they meet.
translation: It must be that. By now Hero and Margaret ought to have played their parts and tricked Beatrice too. These two bears won't bite each other the next time they meet.

original: My lord and brother, God save you.
translation: My lord and brother, God bless you.

original: Good e'en, brother.
translation: Good evening, brother.

original: If your leisure served, I would speak with you.
translation: If you have time, I'd like to speak with you.

original: In private?
translation: In private?

original: If it please you. Yet Count Claudio may hear, for what I would speak of concerns him.
translation: If you like. But Count Claudio should stay and listen, for what I have to say concerns him as well.

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: Means your lordship to be married  tomorrow?
translation: Do you plan on getting married tomorrow, my lord?

original: You know he does.
translation: You know he does.

original: I know not that, when he knows what I know.
translation: I can't be sure of that, once he learns what I know.

original: If there be any impediment, I pray you discover it.
translation: If there's any obstacle to the marriage, please reveal it.

original: You may think I love you not.
translation: You might think that I don't like you, Claudio.

original: Let that appear  hereafter, and aim better at me by that I now will  manifest.
translation: I hope that you will think better of me after I reveal this news.

original: For my brother, I think he holds you well, and in dearness of heart hath holp to effect your ensuing  marriage—surely suit ill spent and labor ill bestowed.
translation: I think my brother holds you in high regard, and has affectionately helped you to arrange this marriage—but that was an unfortunate courtship and a waste of labor.

original: Why, what’s the matter?
translation: Why, what's the matter?

original: I came hither to tell you; and, circumstances  shortened, for she has been too long a-talking of, the  lady is disloyal.
translation: I came here to tell you, and, without any unnecessary details—for we've already wasted too many words on her—the lady is unfaithful.

original: Who, Hero?
translation: Who, Hero?

original: Even she: Leonato’s Hero, your Hero, every man’s Hero.
translation: The same: Leonato's Hero, your Hero, every man's Hero.

original: Disloyal?
translation: Unfaithful?

original: The word is too good to paint out her wickedness.
translation: That word is too good to properly describe her wickedness.

original: I  could say she were worse.
translation: I would call her something worse.

original: Think you of a worse title,  and I will fit her to it.
translation: Come up with a worse word for her, and I'll show you how she deserves it.

original: Wonder not till further  warrant.
translation: But restrain your disbelief until you've seen proof.

original: Go but with me tonight, you shall see her  chamber window entered, even the night before her  wedding day.
translation: Go with me tonight, and you'll see a man enter her bedroom window—even tonight, the night before her wedding day.

original: If you love her then, tomorrow wed her.
translation: If you still love her after that, then go through with the marriage tomorrow.

original: But it would better fit your honor to   change your mind.
translation: But it would suit your honor better if you changed your mind.

original: May this be so?
translation: Can this be so?

original: I will not think it.
translation: I refuse to believe it.

original: If you dare not trust that you see, confess not that  you know. If you will follow me, I will show you enough, and when you have seen more and heard more, proceed  accordingly.
translation: If you don't have the courage to see the truth for yourself, then don't claim to know anything. If you follow me, I'll show you plenty of proof. And once you've seen more and heard more, you can act accordingly.

original: If I see anything tonight why I should not marry  her, tomorrow in the congregation, where I should wed,  there will I shame her.
translation: If I see anything tonight that convinces me not to marry her, then tomorrow I'll shame her in front of the same congregation where I would have married her.

original: And as I wooed for thee to obtain her, I will join with thee to disgrace her.
translation: And since I courted her for you, I will join you in disgracing her.

original: I will disparage her no farther till you are my  witnesses. Bear it coldly but till midnight and let the  issue show itself.
translation: I won't criticize her any more until you can bear witness to my accusations. Keep calm until midnight, and then you'll see for yourself.

original: O day untowardly turned!
translation: Oh, what a day horribly ruined!

original: O mischief strangely thwarting!
translation: Oh, unexpected unfaithfulness ruining my hopes!

original: O plague right well prevented! So will you say when  you have seen the sequel.
translation: Oh, what a curse prevented! That's what you'll say when you've seen what comes next.

original: Are you good men and true?
translation: Are you good and honest men?

original: Yea, or else it were pity but they should suffer  salvation, body and soul.
Nay, that were a punishment too good for them, if  they should have any allegiance in them, being chosen  for the Prince’s watch.
Well, give them their charge, neighbor Dogberry.
translation: Well, give them their instructions, Sir Dogberry.

original: First, who think you the most desartless man to be  constable?
Hugh Oatcake, sir, or George Seacole, for they can  write and read.
translation: Hugh Oatcake or George Seacole, sir. Both can read and write.

original: Come hither, neighbor Seacole. God hath blessed you  with a good name. To be a well-favored man is the gift  of fortune, but to write and read comes by nature.
translation: Come here, Sir Seacole. God has blessed you with a good name. To be a good-looking man is a gift of luck, but to know how to read and write comes by nature.

original: Both which, Master Constable—
translation: Both of which, Master Constable—

original: You have. I knew it would be your answer.
translation: You have. I knew that would be your answer.

original: Well, for  your favor, sir, why, give God thanks, and make no boast of it,
translation: Well, sir, thank God for your good looks, and don't boast about this.

original: and for your writing and reading, let that  appear when there is no need of such vanity.
translation: And as for your reading and writing, only use that when you can't use your looks.

original: You are  thought here to be the most senseless and fit man for  the constable of the watch; therefore bear you the  lantern.
translation: You're considered the most  senseless  and able man here, so you'll carry the lantern and be constable of the watch.

original: This is your charge: you shall comprehend all  vagrom men;
translation: These are your instructions: you will  comprehend  any vagrants you see.

original: you are to bid any man stand, in the  Prince's name.
translation: You will order all men to halt, in the Prince's name.

original: How if he will not stand?
translation: What if a man won't stop?

original: Why, then, take no note of him, but let him go  and presently call the rest of the watch together and  thank God you are rid of a knave.
translation: Why, then, don't bother with him. Let him go, and then call the rest of the watch together, and all of you can thank God that you've gotten rid of a villain.

original: If he will not stand when he is bidden, he is none of  the Prince’s subjects.
translation: If he won't stop when ordered to, then he's not one of the Prince's subjects.

original: True, and they are to meddle with none but the  Prince’s subjects.—You shall also make no noise in the  streets; for, for the watch to babble and to talk is  most tolerable and not to be endured.
translation: True, and you are only supposed to deal with the Prince's subjects. You also will be quiet in the streets. For a watchman to babble on and talk is tolerable and not to be endured.

original: We will rather sleep than talk. We know what belongs to a watch.
translation: We'll sleep instead of talk. We know what the duties of a watchman are.

original: Why, you speak like an ancient and most quiet  watchman, for I cannot see how sleeping should offend.
translation: Why, you speak like an old and quiet watchman, for I don't see how sleeping could offend anyone.

original: Only have a care that your bills be not stolen.
translation: Just be careful that your weapons don't get stolen.

original: Well, you are to call at all the alehouses and bid those that are drunk get them to bed.
translation: Also, you are to visit all the bars and tell those who are drunk to go to bed.

original: How if they will not?
translation: What if they won't?

original: Why, then, let them alone till they are sober. If they  make you not then the better answer, you may say they  are not the men you took them for.
translation: Why, then, leave them alone until they're sober. If they don't agree to go home even then, you can say that they aren't the men you thought they were.

original: Well, sir.
translation: Very well, sir.

original: If you meet a thief, you may suspect him, by virtue of  your office, to be no true man, and for such kind of  men, the less you meddle or make with them, why the more is for your honesty.
translation: If you meet a thief, you can suspect him—as a watchman—of being dishonest. And the less you have to do with that kind of man, the more honest you will remain.

original: If we know him to be a thief, shall we not lay hands  on him?
translation: If we know he's a thief, then shouldn't we arrest him?

original: Truly, by your office you may, but I think they that  touch pitch will be defiled. The most peaceable way for  you, if you do take a thief, is to let him show himself  what he is and steal out of your company.
translation: Truly, your position allows you to, but personally I think that those who touch tar will become unclean themselves. If you do find a thief, the most peaceable thing to do is to let him prove himself a thief by stealing away from your presence.

original: You have been always called a merciful man, partner.
translation: You've always been known as a merciful man, partner.

original: Truly, I would not hang a dog by my will, much more a  man who hath any honesty in him.
If you hear a child cry in the night,  you must call to the nurse and bid her still it.
translation: If you hear a child crying in the night, you must call to the nurse and tell her to quiet it.

original: How if the nurse be asleep and will not hear us?
translation: What if the nurse is asleep and won't listen to us?

original: Why then, depart in peace and let the child wake her  with crying, for the ewe that will not hear her lamb  when it baas will never answer a calf when he bleats.
'Tis very true.
translation: It's very true.

original: This is the end of the charge. You, constable, are to  present the Prince’s own person. If you meet the Prince  in the night, you may stay him.
translation: This is the end of your instructions. You, constable, are representing the Prince himself. If you meet the Prince in the night, you can detain him.

original: Nay, by 'r Lady, that I think he cannot.
translation: No, by the Virgin Mary, I don't think he can.

original: Five shillings to one on ’t, with any man that knows  the statutes, he may stay him
translation: I'd bet five to one that he can—ask any man who knows the acts of Parliament.

original: —marry, not without the  Prince be willing, for indeed the watch ought to offend  no man, and it is an offense to stay a man against his  will.
translation: Although, you can't stop the Prince unless the Prince is willing to stop, for the watch shouldn't offend anyone—and it's an offense to detain a man against his will.

original: By 'r lady, I think it be so.
translation: By the Virgin Mary, I think that's true.

original: Ha, ha, ha! Well, masters, good night. An there be any matter of weight chances, call up me. Keep your  fellows' counsels and your own; and good night.—Come,  neighbor.
translation: Ha, ha, ha! Well, sirs, goodnight. If anything important comes up, call on me. Keep each other's advice, and your own. Good night. Come, friend.

original: Well, masters, we hear our charge. Let us go sit here  upon the church bench till two, and then all to bed.
translation: Well, sirs, we've heard our instructions. Let's sit here on the church bench until two o'clock, and then all go to bed.

original: One word more, honest neighbors. I pray you watch  about Signior Leonato’s door, for the wedding being  there tomorrow, there is a great coil tonight. Adieu, be vigitant, I beseech you.
What Conrad!
translation: Hey, Conrad!

original: Peace! Stir not.
translation: Quiet! Don't move.

original: Conrad, I say!
translation: Conrad, I say!

original: Here, man. I am at thy elbow.
translation: Here, man, I'm at your elbow.

original: Mass, and my elbow itched, I thought there would a  scab follow.
I will owe thee an answer for that. And now forward  with thy tale.
translation: I'll get you back for that later. Now continue with your story.

original: Stand thee close, then, under this penthouse, for it  drizzles rain, and I will, like a true drunkard, utter  all to thee.
Some treason, masters. Yet stand close.
translation: There's some villainy going on here, gentlemen. Keep hidden.

original: Therefore know I have earned of Don John a  thousand ducats.
translation: You should know that I've earned a thousand gold pieces from Don John.

original: Is it possible that any villainy should be so dear?
translation: Is it possible that any villainy could be so expensive?

original: Thou shouldst rather ask if it were possible any  villainy should be so rich. For when rich villains have  need of poor ones, poor ones may make what price they  will.
translation: Instead you should ask if it's possible that any villain could be so rich. For when rich villains need poor ones, then the poor villains can name their price.

original: I wonder at it.
translation: I'm amazed.

original: That shows thou art unconfirmed. Thou knowest that  the fashion of a doublet, or a hat, or a cloak, is  nothing to a man.
translation: That shows that you're inexperienced. You know that the style of a man's jacket, hat, or cloak doesn't make the man, right?

original: Yes, it is apparel.
translation: Yes, it's just clothing.

original: I mean the fashion.
translation: No, I mean the fashion of the clothing.

original: Yes, the fashion is the fashion.
translation: Yes, the fashion is the fashion.

original: Tush, I may as well say the fool’s the fool. But seest  thou not what a deformed thief this fashion is?
I know that Deformed. He has been a vile thief  this seven year. He goes up and down like a gentleman.  I remember his name.
translation: I know that man Deformed. He's been a terrible thief for the last seven years. He walks about like he's a gentleman. I remember his name.

original: Didst thou not hear somebody?
translation: Did you hear somebody?

original: No, ’twas the vane on the house.
translation: No, it was just the weathervane on the house.

original: Seest thou not, I say, what a deformed thief this  fashion is,
translation: As I was saying, don't you see what a deformed thief fashion is?

original: how giddily he turns about all the hot  bloods between fourteen and five-and-thirty, sometimes  fashioning them like Pharaoh’s soldiers in the reechy  painting, sometime like god Bel’s priests in the old  church-window, sometime like the shaven Hercules in the  smirched worm-eaten tapestry, where his codpiece seems  as massy as his club?
translation: It makes all the hot-blooded young men go crazy, sometimes dressing up like the Pharaoh's soldiers in that dirty old painting, sometimes like the pictures in old church windows of the priests of the god  Baal , and sometimes like the picture of Hercules in that dusty, worm-eaten tapestry, where his  codpiece  is as big as a club!

original: All this I see, and I see that the fashion wears out  more apparel than the man. But art not thou thyself  giddy with the fashion too, that thou hast shifted out  of thy tale into telling me of the fashion?
translation: I understand all this, and I can see that clothes are discarded because of changing fashions before they can get worn out. But aren't you crazy about fashion, too, since you've changed out of your story to start going on about fashion?

original: Not so, neither. But know that I have tonight  wooed Margaret, the Lady Hero’s gentlewoman, by the name of Hero.
translation: No, I'm not. But you should know that tonight I seduced Margaret, Lady Hero's serving woman, and called her "Hero" the whole time.

original: She leans me out at her mistress' chamber  window, bids me a thousand times good night.
translation: She leaned out of her mistress's bedroom window and told me goodnight a thousand times.

original: I tell this tale vilely.
translation: But I'm telling this story badly.

original: I should first tell thee how the Prince,  Claudio and my master, planted and placed and possessed  by my master Don John, saw afar off in the orchard this  amiable encounter.
translation: I should first tell you how my master Don John filled the Prince and Claudio with suspicion about Hero's virtue, and arranged that they should witness this lovers' meeting from the garden.

original: And thought they Margaret was Hero?
translation: And they thought that Margaret was Hero?

original: Two of them did, the Prince and Claudio, but the devil  my master knew she was Margaret;
translation: Two of them did—the Prince and Claudio—but the devil, my master, knew it was Margaret.

original: and partly by his  oaths, which first possessed them,
translation: It was partly because of his testimony that they suspected Hero in the first place.

original: partly by the dark  night, which did deceive them, but chiefly by my  villainy, which did confirm any slander that Don John  had made,
translation: They were also tricked by the dark, deceiving night, but it was mostly my villainy, which confirmed all of Don John's slander against Hero.

original: away went Claudio enraged, swore he would meet her as he was appointed next morning at the temple, and there, before the whole congregation, shame her with  what he saw o'ernight   and send her home again without a husband.
translation: Claudio went away enraged, swearing that he would meet Hero at the temple the next day as planned, and there, before the whole congregation, would shame her with his testimony and send her home again without a husband.

original: We charge you, in the Prince’s name, stand!
translation: In the Prince's name, we command you to halt!

original: Call up the right Master Constable. We have  here recovered the most dangerous piece of lechery that  ever was known in the commonwealth.
And one Deformed is one of them. I know him; he wears  a lock.
translation: And the criminal Deformed is one of them. I know him; he has a long lock of hair.

original: Masters, masters—
translation: Gentlemen, gentlemen—

original: You’ll be made bring Deformed forth,  I warrant you.
translation: You'll be forced to bring Deformed forward, I promise you.

original: Masters, never speak, we charge you, let us obey you  go with us.
We are like to prove a goodly commodity, being taken up of these men’s bills.
translation: We're probably a valuable catch for these fools.

original: A commodity in question, I warrant you.—Come,  we’ll obey you.
translation: Well, our value is about to be judged, I'll bet. All right, we'll obey you.

original: Good Ursula, wake my cousin Beatrice and desire her  to rise.
translation: Good Ursula, wake my cousin Beatrice and ask her to get up.

original: I will, lady.
translation: I will, my lady.

original: And bid her come hither.
translation: And tell her to come here.

original: Well.
translation: Very well.

original: Troth, I think your other rebato were better.
translation: Honestly, I think your other collar looks better.

original: No, pray thee, good Meg, I’ll wear this.
translation: No, please, good Meg, I'll wear this one.

original: By my troth, ’s not so good, and I warrant your cousin  will say so.
translation: I swear it's not as good as the other one, and I bet your cousin will say so too.

original: My cousin’s a fool, and thou art another. I’ll wear  none but this.
translation: My cousin's a fool, and so are you. I'll wear this one and no other.

original: I like the new tire within excellently, if the hair  were a thought browner; and your gown’s a most rare  fashion, i' faith. I saw the Duchess of Milan’s gown  that they praise so.
translation: I like the new wig and headdress a lot, though I wish the hair was a shade browner. Your gown is very stylish indeed. I saw the Duchess of Milan's gown, the one that everyone goes on about.

original: Oh, that exceeds, they say.
translation: Oh, that dress is beyond comparison, they say.

original: By my troth, ’s but a nightgown in respect of yours
translation: I swear, it's just a nightgown compared to your dress.

original: —cloth o' gold, and cuts, and laced with silver, set with pearls, down sleeves, side sleeves, and skirts, round  underborne with a bluish tinsel.
translation: On that dress the cloth is of golden thread, with slashes in it to show the fabric underneath. It's embroidered with silver and adorned with pearls, has two sets of sleeves, and has skirts trimmed with blue tinsel.

original: But for a fine, quaint, graceful, and excellent fashion, yours is worth ten on  ’t.
translation: But for a fine, elegant, graceful, and excellent dress, yours is worth ten times more than that one.

original: God give me joy to wear it, for my heart is exceeding  heavy.
translation: May God give me joy in wearing it, for my heart is very heavy.

original: 'Twill be heavier soon by the weight of a man.
translation: It will be even heavier soon, with the weight of a man on top of it.

original: Fie upon thee! Art not ashamed?
translation: Watch your tongue! Aren't you ashamed?

original: Of what, lady? Of speaking honorably? Is not  marriage honorable in a beggar? Is not your lord  honorable without marriage?
translation: Of what, lady? Of speaking honorably? Sex and marriage are honorable things even for a beggar, aren't they? Isn't your new husband honorable?

original: I think you would have me  say, “Saving your reverence, a husband.”
translation: Maybe you would prefer it if I had said, "I beg your pardon, a  husband , not just a man."

original: An bad thinking do not wrest true speaking, I’ll offend nobody.
translation: If dirty minds don't twist my honest words, then I'll offend no one.

original: Is  there any harm in “the heavier for a husband?”
translation: Is there any harm in saying that your husband will lie on top of you?

original: None, I  think, an it be the right husband and the right wife.
translation: No, I think not, as long it's the right husband and the right wife.

original: Otherwise, ’tis light and not heavy.
translation: Otherwise it would be frivolous and immoral.

original: Ask my Lady Beatrice else. Here she comes.
translation: Ask my Lady Beatrice if this isn't true. Here she comes.

original: Good morrow, coz.
translation: Good morning, cousin.

original: Good morrow, sweet Hero.
translation: Good morning, sweet Hero.

original: Why, how now? Do you speak in the sick tune?
