translation: Why, what's going on? You sound sad, or sick.

original: I am out of all other tune, methinks.
translation: It's the only way I can sound, I think.

original: Clap ’s into “Light o' love.” That goes without a  burden. Do you sing it, and I’ll dance it.
translation: Let's change your tune, then, and sing "Light of Love." That song doesn't need any man to sing harmony. You sing it, and I'll dance.

original: Ye light o' love, with your heels! Then, if your  husband have stables enough, you’ll see he shall lack no barns.
O illegitimate construction! I scorn that with my  heels.
translation: Oh, your dirty jokes! I kick them away with my heels.

original: 'Tis almost five o'clock, cousin. 'Tis time you were  ready. By my troth, I am exceeding ill. Heigh-ho!
translation: It's almost five o'clock, cousin. It's time to get ready. I swear, I really don't feel well. Heigh-ho!

original: For a hawk, a horse, or a husband?
translation: Are you sighing for a hawk, a horse, or a husband?

original: For the letter that begins them all, H.
Well, an you be not turned Turk, there’s no more  sailing by the star.
translation: Well, if you haven't yet renounced your old belief that you'd never marry, then we can't trust anything anymore.

original: What means the fool, trow?
translation: What is this fool trying to say, I wonder?

original: Nothing, I; but God send everyone their heart’s  desire.
translation: Nothing—only that God sends everyone their heart's desire.

original: These gloves the Count sent me, they are an  excellent perfume.
translation: The Count sent me these gloves, and they're perfumed excellently.

original: I am stuffed, cousin. I cannot smell.
translation: I'm all stuffed up, cousin. I can't smell anything.

original: A maid, and stuffed! There’s goodly catching of cold.
Oh, God help me, God help me! How long have  you professed apprehension?
translation: Oh, God help me, God help me! How long have you claimed to have such a wit?

original: Even since you left it. Doth not my wit become me  rarely?
translation: Ever since you left yours behind. Doesn't my wit suit me excellently?

original: It is not seen enough; you should wear it in your cap. By my troth, I am sick.
translation: It doesn't show itself enough—you should wear it in your fool's cap. I swear, I'm really sick.

original: Get you some of this distilled  carduus benedictus  and  lay it to your heart. It is the only thing for a qualm.
translation: Get some distilled carduus benedictus and put it over your heart. It's the only thing for a sudden sickness.

original: There thou prick’st her with a thistle.
translation: With that joke you've pricked her with a thistle.

original: Benedictus! Why benedictus? You have some moral in  this  benedictus?
translation: Benedictus! Why benedictus? Is there some hidden meaning in this benedictus?

original: Moral! No, by my troth, I have no moral meaning.
translation: Hidden meaning? No, I swear, I intended no hidden meaning.

original: I  meant plain holy thistle.
translation: I just mean that you should use plain holy thistle.

original: You may think perchance that I think you are in love.
translation: Perhaps you think that I think that you're in love.

original: Nay, by 'r Lady, I am not such a fool to think what I list,
translation: No, by the Virgin Mary, I'm not such a fool to think whatever I want.

original: nor I list not to think what I can, nor indeed I cannot think, if I would think my  heart out of thinking, that you are in love or that you  will be in love or that you can be in love.
translation: And I don't want to think what I can—nor can I even think at all—even if I want to think my heart out of thinking, that you are in love or that you will be in love or that you even  can  be in love.

original: Yet Benedick was such another, and now is he become a man.
translation: Yet Benedick was like you once, and now he has become like other men.

original: He swore  he would never marry,
translation: He swore that he would never marry.

original: and yet now, in despite of his  heart, he eats his meat without grudging.
translation: But now, despite his old self, he has an ungrudging appetite for love.

original: And how you  may be converted I know not, but methinks you look with  your eyes as other women do.
translation: I don't know how you can be converted like he was, but I know that you still look through your eyes just as every woman does.

original: What pace is this that thy tongue keeps?
translation: Why are you talking so quickly?

original: Not a false gallop.
translation: I'm not running on untruthfully.

original: Madam, withdraw: the Prince, the Count,  Signor Benedick, Don John, and all the gallants of the  town are come to fetch you to church.
translation: Madam, come with me: the Prince, the Count, Sir Benedick, Don John, and all the gentlemen of the town have come to bring you to the church.

original: Help to dress me, good coz, good Meg, good Ursula.
translation: Help to dress me, good cousin, good Meg, good Ursula.

original: What would you with me, honest neighbor?
translation: What do you want from me, honorable neighbor?

original: Marry, sir, I would have some confidence with you  that decerns you nearly.
Brief, I pray you, for you see it is a busy time with  me.
translation: Be brief, please, for as you can see this is a busy time for me.

original: Marry, this it is, sir.
translation: Well, it certainly seems to be, sir.

original: Yes, in truth it is, sir.
translation: Yes, it truly is, sir.

original: What is it, my good friends?
translation: What is this news, my friend?

original: Goodman Verges, sir, speaks a little off the matter. An old man, sir, and his wits are not so blunt as, God  help, I would desire they were, but, in faith, honest as the skin between his brows.
Yes, I thank God I am as honest as any man living that  is an old man and no honester than I.
translation: Yes, I thank God that I'm as honest as any man alive who is also old and is no more honest than I am.

original: Comparisons are odorous.  Palabras  , neighbor Verges.
Neighbors, you are tedious.
translation: Neighbors, you're becoming tedious.

original: It pleases your Worship to say so, but we are the poor  duke’s officers. But truly, for mine own part, if I were as tedious as a king, I could find it in my heart to  bestow it all of your worship.
All thy tediousness on me, ah?
translation: You'd give all your tediousness to me, huh?

original: Yea, an ’twere a thousand pound more than ’tis, for I  hear as good exclamation on your Worship as of any man  in the city, and though I be but a poor man, I am glad  to hear it.
And so am I.
translation: And so am I.

original: I would fain know what you have to say.
translation: I want to hear your news.

original: Marry, sir, our watch tonight, excepting your  Worship’s presence, ha' ta'en a couple of as arrant  knaves as any in Messina.
A good old man, sir. He will be talking.
translation: [To LEONATO]  He's a good old man, sir, but he always has to be talking.

original: As they say,  “When the age is in, the wit is out.” God help us, it is a world to see!
translation: As they say, " When age comes in, wit goes out ." God help us, it's a wonder to see!

original: Well said, i' faith, neighbor Verges.
translation: [To VERGES]  Well said, honestly, neighbor Verges.

original: —Well, God’s a good man.
translation: [To LEONATO]  Well, God is good, and he works in mysterious ways.

original: An two men ride of a horse, one  must ride behind.
translation: If two men will ride a horse, one must ride behind.

original: An honest soul, i' faith, sir, by my  troth he is, as ever broke bread,
translation: Verges is as honest a soul as any that ever broke bread, sir.

original: but God is to be  worshipped, all men are not alike, alas, good neighbor!
translation: But, alas, not all men are created equal!

original: Indeed, neighbor, he comes too short of you.
translation: Indeed, my friend, you're certainly his superior.

original: Gifts that God gives.
translation: It's only God's gifts.

original: I must leave you.
translation: I must leave you now.

original: One word, sir. Our watch, sir, have indeed  comprehended two aspicious persons, and we would have  them this morning examined before your worship.
Take their examination yourself and bring it me. I am  now in great haste, as it may appear unto you.
translation: Examine them yourself, and then bring me the results. I'm in a great hurry right now, as you can see.

original: It shall be suffigance.
Drink some wine ere you go. Fare you well.
translation: Drink some wine before you go. Farewell.

original: My lord, they stay for you to give your daughter to  her husband.
translation: My lord, they're waiting for you to give your daughter away to her husband.

original: I’ll wait upon them. I am ready.
translation: I'll attend to them. I am ready.

original: Go, good partner, go, get you to Francis Seacole. Bid  him bring his pen and inkhorn to the jail. We are now  to examination these men.
And we must do it wisely.
translation: And we must do it wisely.

original: We will spare for no wit, I warrant you. Here’s that  shall drive some of them to a noncome. Only get the  learned writer to set down our excommunication and meet  me at the jail.
Come, Friar Francis, be brief, only to the plain form  of marriage, and you shall recount their particular  duties afterwards.
translation: All right, Friar Francis, be brief. Just do a simple ceremony now, and you can list all the particular duties of marriage afterwards.

original: You come hither, my lord, to marry this  lady?
translation: My lord, have you come here to marry this lady?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: To be married to her.—Friar, you come to marry her.
translation: He means he's here to be married to her. Friar, you're the one who's come to marry her.

original: Lady, you come hither to be married to this count?
translation: Lady, do you come here to be married to this count?

original: I do.
translation: I do.

original: If either of you know any inward impediment why  you should not be conjoined, charge you on your souls to utter it.
translation: If either of you knows of any secret reason why you should not be married, then I command you, by your souls, to say it now.

original: Know you any, Hero?
translation: Do you know of any, Hero?

original: None, my lord.
translation: None, my lord.

original: Know you any, count?
translation: Do you know of any, Count?

original: I dare make his answer, none.
translation: I'll dare to answer for him—none.

original: O, what men dare do! What men may do! What men  daily do, not knowing what they do!
translation: Oh, what men will dare to do! What men are allowed to do! What men do daily, not aware of what they're doing!

original: How now, interjections? Why, then, some be of  laughing, as, ah, ha, he!
Stand thee by, Friar.—Father, by your leave, Will you  with free and unconstrainèd soul  Give me this maid, your daughter?
translation: Step aside, Friar.  Father, will you freely and without reservations give me this maiden, your daughter?

original: As freely, son, as God did give her me.
translation: As freely, son, as God gave her to me.

original: And what have I to give you back whose worth May  counterpoise this rich and precious gift?
translation: And what can I give you back that would balance out this rich and precious gift?

original: Nothing, unless you render her again.
translation: Nothing, unless you should give her back.

original: Sweet Prince, you learn me noble thankfulness.—
translation: Sweet Prince, you teach me how to accept things nobly.

original: There, Leonato, take her back again.
translation: [To LEONATO]  There, Leonato. Take your daughter back again.

original: Give not this rotten orange to your friend.
translation: Don't give this rotten orange to your friend.

original: She’s but the sign and semblance of her honor.
translation: She has only the outward appearance of honor.

original: Behold how like a maid she blushes here!
translation: See how she blushes like a virgin now!

original: Oh, what authority and show of truth   Can cunning sin cover itself withal!
translation: Oh, how masterfully sin can disguise itself!

original: Comes not that blood as modest evidence   To witness simple virtue?
translation: Doesn't her blush seem like natural evidence of simple virtue?

original: Would you not swear,   All you that see her, that she were a maid   By these exterior shows?
translation: [To the others]  Wouldn't you swear, all of you who see her now, that she's a virgin, based on her exterior?

original: But she is none.   She knows the heat of a luxurious bed.
translation: But she is no virgin. She has known the heat of a lustful bed.

original: Her blush is guiltiness, not modesty.
translation: Her blush is from guilt, not modesty.

original: What do you mean, my lord?
translation: What do you mean, my lord?

original: Not to be married, Not to knit my soul to an approvèd wanton.
translation: I mean to not be married. I won't join my soul with such a proven whore.

original: Dear my lord, if you in your own proof Have vanquished the resistance of her youth  And made defeat of her virginity—
translation: My dear lord, if your proof is yourself—if you are the one who conquered her in her youthfulness and took her virginity—

original: I know what you would say: if I have known her,   You will say she did embrace me as a husband,   And so extenuate the forehand sin.
translation: I know what you will say: if I were the one who slept with her, you'll say that she was accepting me as her future husband, and the anticipation of our marriage would make it less of a sin.

original: No, Leonato,   I never tempted her with word too large   But, as a brother to his sister, showed   Bashful sincerity and comely love.
translation: No, Leonato, I never tempted her with indecent words, but only treated her like a brother would treat his sister, showing her nothing but bashful sincerity and modest love.

original: And seemed I ever otherwise to you?
translation: And have I ever showed anything else to you?

original: Out on thee, seeming! I will write against it.
translation: Shame on you, false appearance! I will argue against you.

original: You seem to me as Dian in her orb,   As chaste as is the bud ere it be blown.
translation: To me you still seem like  Diana , as innocent as the bud before it blooms.

original: But you are more intemperate in your blood   Than Venus, or those pampered animals   That rage in savage sensuality.
translation: But you are more hot-blooded than Venus, or an animal left to run wild in its lust.

original: Is my lord well, that he doth speak so wide?
translation: My lord, are you ill? Is that what's making you speak so wildly?

original: Sweet Prince, why speak not you?
translation: Sweet Prince, why don't you say something?

original: What should I speak? I stand dishonored, that have gone about To link my dear friend to a common stale.
translation: What should I say? I stand here dishonored. I've arranged to join my dear friend to a common prostitute.

original: Are these things spoken, or do I but dream?
translation: Are these things really being said, or am I dreaming?

original: Sir, they are spoken, and these things are true.
translation: Sir, they are spoken, and they are true.

original: This looks not like a nuptial.
translation: This doesn't look like a wedding.

original: True! O God!
translation: He says they're true! Oh God!

original: Leonato, stand I here? Is this the Prince? Is this the Prince’s brother?  Is this face Hero’s? Are our eyes our own?
translation: Leonato, am I standing here? Is this the Prince? Is this the Prince's brother? Is this face Hero's? Are our eyes our own eyes?

original: All this is so, but what of this, my lord?
translation: All this is true. But what do you mean by it, my lord?

original: Let me but move one question to your daughter, And by that fatherly and kindly power That you have in her, bid her answer truly.
translation: Let me just ask your daughter one question. By your natural authority over her as her father, tell her to answer truthfully.

original: I charge thee do so, as thou art my child.
translation: As you are my child, I order you to do so.

original: Oh, God defend me! how am I beset!— What kind of catechizing call you this?
translation: Oh, God defend me! How I am attacked from all sides!  What kind of interrogation is this?

original: To make you answer truly to your name.
translation: We want you to answer to your true name and show who you truly are.

original: Is it not Hero? Who can blot that name With any just reproach?
translation: Isn't my name Hero? Who can stain that name with any honest accusation?

original: Marry, that can Hero!   Hero itself can blot out Hero’s virtue.
translation: Well, Hero can do that! The word "Hero" itself—which I heard spoken last night—can stain Hero's virtue.

original: What man was he talked with you yesternight   Out at your window betwixt twelve and one?
translation: What man talked with you last night at your window, between midnight and one?

original: Now, if you are a maid, answer to this.
translation: Now, if you are a virgin, answer this.

original: I talked with no man at that hour, my lord.
translation: I didn't talk to any man at that hour, my lord.

original: Why, then are you no maiden.
translation: Why, then you are no virgin.

original: —Leonato,   I am sorry you must hear. Upon mine honor,   Myself, my brother, and this grievèd count   Did see her, hear her, at that hour last night   Talk with a ruffian at her chamber window
translation: [To LEONATO]   I'm sorry you must hear this, Leonato. I swear on my honor that I, my brother, and this wronged count saw and heard Hero last night, talking to some brute at her bedroom window.

original: Who hath indeed, most like a liberal villain,   Confessed the vile encounters they have had   A thousand times in secret.
translation: And that man, the lustful villain, confessed to a thousand secret, immoral encounters that they've had.

original: Fie, fie, they are not to be named, my lord,   Not to be spoke of!
translation: Shame, shame! Those sins are not to be named, my lord—not to be spoken of!

original: There is not chastity enough in language,   Without offense, to utter them.
translation: Language itself is not innocent enough to describe them without offending everyone here.

original: —Thus, pretty lady,   I am sorry for thy much misgovernment.
translation: [To HERO]  So, pretty lady, I'm sorry about your great wickedness.

original: O Hero, what a Hero hadst thou been   If half thy outward graces had been placed   About thy thoughts and counsels of thy heart!
translation: Oh, Hero, you could have lived up to your  name  if only half of your outward beauty and apparent innocence had influence over the secret thoughts and desires of your heart!

original: But fare thee well, most foul, most fair!
translation: Farewell, you who are most foul, and yet look most beautiful!

original: Farewell,   Thou pure impiety and impious purity.
translation: Farewell, you pure wickedness and you wicked purity.

original: For thee I’ll lock up all the gates of love,
translation: Because of you, I'll lock up my heart against all love.

original: And on my eyelids shall conjecture hang,   To turn all beauty into thoughts of harm,   And never shall it more be gracious.
translation: Suspicion will weigh down my eyelids, and turn all thoughts of beauty into thoughts of danger, so that nothing is beautiful ever again.

original: Hath no man’s dagger here a point for me?
translation: Does any man here have a dagger for me to stab myself?

original: Why, how now, cousin! wherefore sink you down?
translation: Why, how are you doing, cousin? Why are you collapsing now?

original: Come, let us go. These things, come thus to light,  Smother her spirits up.
translation: Come on, let's go. These secrets being brought to light have overwhelmed her spirit.

original: How doth the lady?
translation: How is the lady?

original: Dead, I think.—Help, uncle!— Hero, why, Hero! Uncle! Signor Benedick! Friar!
translation: Dead, I think. Help, uncle![To the others] Hero, why Hero! Uncle! Sir Benedick! Friar!

original: O Fate! Take not away thy heavy hand! Death is the fairest cover for her shame That may be wished for.
translation: Oh, Fate, don't spare your heavy hand of punishment! The best thing I could wish for to cover up her shame is death.

original: How now, cousin Hero!
translation: How are you, cousin Hero?

original: Have comfort, lady.
translation: Take comfort, lady.

original: Dost thou look up?
translation: Do you dare to look up?

original: Yea, wherefore should she not?
translation: Well, why shouldn't she?

original: Wherefore! Why, doth not every earthly thing   Cry shame upon her?
translation: Why shouldn't she look up? Why, isn't everything on earth condemning her?

original: Could she here deny   The story that is printed in her blood?—
translation: Can she deny the story that is written in her guilty blush?

original: Do not live, Hero, do not ope thine eyes,
translation: [To HERO]  Do not live, Hero. Do not open your eyes.

original: For, did I think thou wouldst not quickly die,   Thought I thy spirits were stronger than thy shames,   Myself would, on the rearward of reproaches,   Strike at thy life.
translation: If I didn't think that you were about to die—if I thought that your spirits were stronger than your shame—then I would condemn you and kill you myself.

original: Grieved I I had but one?   Chid I for that at frugal Nature’s frame?
translation: Was I sorry that I only had one child? Did I scold Nature for being so thrifty with me?

original: O, one too much by thee! Why had I one?
translation: Oh, now one child is too many! Why did I even have one?

original: Why ever wast thou lovely in my eyes?
translation: Why did you ever seem lovely to my eyes?

original: Why had I not with charitable hand   Took up a beggar’s issue at my gates,
translation: Why didn't I just take in a beggar's child left at my gates?

original: Who, smirchèd thus, and mired with infamy,   I might have said, “No part of it is mine;   This shame derives itself from unknown loins”?
translation: Then—if she were shamed and ruined like this—I might have said, "No part of her is mine; this shame comes from an unknown father!"

original: But mine, and mine I loved, and mine I praised,   And mine that I was proud on,
translation: But you were mine, and I loved you and praised you for being mine, and I was proud that you were mine.

original: mine so much   That I myself was to myself not mine,   Valuing of her–
translation: I valued you so highly that I lived only for you, and considered myself worthless.

original: why, she, O she is fall'n   Into a pit of ink, that the wide sea   Hath drops too few to wash her clean again   And salt too little which may season give   To her foul tainted flesh!
translation: Oh, but now you have fallen into a pit of ink, and even the wide sea doesn't have enough water to wash you clean again, or enough salt to preserve your rotting flesh!

original: Sir, sir, be patient. For my part, I am so attired in wonder I know not what to say.
translation: Sir, sir, calm down. For my part, I'm so filled with amazement that I don't know what to say.

original: Oh, on my soul, my cousin is belied!
translation: Oh, I swear on my soul, my cousin has been slandered!

original: Lady, were you her bedfellow last night?
translation: Lady, did you sleep in her room last night?

original: No, truly not, although until last night I have this twelvemonth been her bedfellow.
translation: No, truly I didn't. But until last night I've slept there every night for the last year.

original: Confirmed, confirmed! Oh, that is stronger made   Which was before barred up with ribs of iron!
translation: Then it's confirmed, confirmed! Oh, that has added even more evidence to what is already a strong case against her!

original: Would the two princes lie and Claudio lie,   Who loved her so that, speaking of her foulness,   Washed it with tears?
translation: Would the two princes lie? And would Claudio—who loved her so much that speaking of her foulness made him weep—lie too?

original: Hence from her. Let her die.
translation: Leave her. Let her die.

original: Hear me a little,   For I have only silent been so long,   And given way unto this course of fortune,   By noting of the lady.
translation: Hear me for a moment. I've only kept silent this long, and let these events unfold as they did, because I've been watching Hero carefully.

original: I have marked   A thousand blushing apparitions   To start into her face, a thousand innocent shames   In angel whiteness beat away those blushes,
translation: I've noticed a thousand blushes start to rush on her face, and then a thousand feelings of innocent shame—as white as angels—drive those blushes away.

original: And in her eye there hath appeared a fire   To burn the errors that these princes hold   Against her maiden truth.
translation: In her eyes I've seen a fire appear that would seem to burn away these lies the princes told about her virginity.

original: Call me a fool,   Trust not my reading nor my observations,   Which with experimental seal doth warrant   The tenor of my book;
translation: Call me a fool if you want, and don't trust my observations or interpretations of her face, which are backed up by my years of experience.

original: trust not my age,   My reverence, calling, nor divinity,   If this sweet lady lie not guiltless here   Under some biting error.
translation: Don't trust my age, my respected position, my calling as a priest, or my holiness, if in fact this sweet lady here isn't innocent, and the victim of some cruel mistake.

original: Friar, it cannot be.   Thou seest that all the grace that she hath left   Is that she will not add to her damnation   A sin of perjury.   She not denies it.
translation: Friar, this cannot be. You see that the only virtue she has left prevents her from adding perjury to her sins—she won't deny the accusations.

original: Why seek’st thou then to cover with excuse   That which appears in proper nakedness?
translation: Why are you trying to excuse her crimes, now that they've been exposed?

original: Lady, what man is he you are accused of?
translation: Lady, what man is it you're accused of meeting with?

original: They know that do accuse me. I know none.
translation: Ask the ones who accuse me. I don't know.

original: If I know more of any man alive   Than that which maiden modesty doth warrant,   Let all my sins lack mercy!
translation: If I've been with any man alive in a way that's inappropriate for a proper, modest virgin, then let all my sins be punished!

original: —O my father,   Prove you that any man with me conversed   At hours unmeet, or that I yesternight   Maintained the change of words with any creature,   Refuse me, hate me, torture me to death!
translation: [To LEONATO ] Oh my father, if you can prove that any man talked to me at an indecent hour—or that last night I spoke to anyone at all—then disown me, hate me, and torture me to death!

original: There is some strange misprision in the princes.
translation: The princes have had some strange misunderstanding.

original: Two of them have the very bent of honor,
translation: Two of them have perfectly honorable dispositions.

original: And if their wisdoms be misled in this,   The practice of it lives in John the Bastard,   Whose spirits toil in frame of villainies.
translation: And if they've been misled in this affair, the culprit must be John the Bastard, whose nature makes him plot wickedness.

original: I know not. If they speak but truth of her,   These hands shall tear her;
translation: I don't know. If they're telling the truth about Hero, then I'll tear her apart with my own hands.

original: if they wrong her honor,   The proudest of them shall well hear of it.
translation: But if they have slandered her honor falsely, then even the greatest of them will hear from me.

original: Time hath not yet so dried this blood of mine   Nor age so eat up my invention   Nor fortune made such havoc of my means   Nor my bad life reft me so much of friends
translation: Time hasn't dried up all my courage, old age hasn't ruined my mind, fortune hasn't stolen all my money, and my bad life hasn't left me without friends.

original: But they shall find, awaked in such a kind,   Both strength of limb and policy of mind,   Ability in means and choice of friends,   To quit me of them throughly.
translation: Those who have wronged my daughter will find me strong in body and mind, and with money and friends at my disposal—and ready to take thorough revenge.

original: Pause awhile,   And let my counsel sway you in this case.
translation: Pause a moment, and hear my advice about this.

original: Your daughter here the princes left for dead.
translation: The princes have left your daughter for dead here.

original: Let her awhile be secretly kept in   And publish it that she is dead indeed.
translation: Let her be hidden secretly in your house for a while, and make it publicly known that she is, indeed, dead.

original: Maintain a mourning ostentation,   And on your family’s old monument   Hang mournful epitaphs and do all rites   That appertain unto a burial.
translation: Keep up a show of mourning, hang sad epitaphs at your family's old tomb, and perform all the usual burial rites.

original: What shall become of this? What will this do?
translation: What will result from this? What will this accomplish?

original: Marry, this, well carried, shall on her behalf   Change slander to remorse.
translation: Well, if we can carry this out correctly, it will move Hero's accusers from slander to feelings of remorse.

original: That is some good.   But not for that dream I on this strange course,   But on this travail look for greater birth.
translation: That will be one good thing. But I haven't decided on this strange plan for that reason alone—I have an even greater goal for this business.

original: She, dying, as it must so be maintained,   Upon the instant that she was accused,
translation: We must maintain that she died the instant she was accused.

original: Shall be lamented, pitied and excused   Of every hearer.
translation: Whoever hears this will mourn her, pity her, and excuse her.

original: For it so falls out   That what we have we prize not to the worth   Whiles we enjoy it,
translation: For that's how it is: we don't value the things we have until we lose them.

original: but being lacked and lost,   Why then we rack the value, then we find   The virtue that possession would not show us   Whiles it was ours.
translation: Once they're gone, we exaggerate their value and see all the virtues we couldn't see when the thing itself was with us.

original: So will it fare with Claudio.   When he shall hear she died upon his words,   The idea of her life shall sweetly creep   Into his study of imagination,
translation: That's how it will be with Claudio. When he hears that Hero died because of his words, thoughts of her will creep into his imagination.

original: And every lovely organ of her life   Shall come apparelled in more precious habit,   More moving, delicate and full of life,   Into the eye and prospect of his soul   Than when she lived indeed.
translation: Every aspect of her lovely life will seem to be dressed up more beautifully, and in his mind's eye she'll seem more moving, more delicate, and more lively than she was even in life.

original: Then shall he mourn,   If ever love had interest in his liver,   And wish he had not so accused her,   No, though he thought his accusation true.
translation: Then if he ever truly felt love for her, he will mourn, and wish that he hadn't accused her—even though he thought his accusations were true.

original: Let this be so, and doubt not but success   Will fashion the event in better shape   Than I can lay it down in likelihood.
translation: If my prediction is right, then everything will turn out even better than I can describe it.

original: But if all aim but this be leveled false,   The supposition of the lady's death   Will quench the wonder of her infamy.
translation: But even if everything else fails, at least Hero's supposed death will overshadow the shameful rumors about her.

original: And if it sort not well, you may conceal her,   As best befits her wounded reputation,   In some reclusive and religious life,
translation: And if it doesn't turn out well, you can hide her away as a nun or a religious recluse—this will be the best place for someone with her wounded reputation.

original: Out of all eyes, tongues, minds, and injuries.
translation: Then she'll be out of reach of all other eyes, tongues, minds, and insults.

original: Signior Leonato, let the friar advise you.
translation: Sir Leonato, listen to the friar's advice.

original: And though you know my inwardness and love   Is very much unto the Prince and Claudio,   Yet, by mine honor, I will deal in this   As secretly and justly as your soul   Should with your body.
translation: And although you know that I'm close friends with the Prince and Claudio, I swear by my honor that I'll deal with this business secretly and honorably.

original: Being that I flow in grief,  The smallest twine may lead me.
translation: I am carried away by a river of grief, so I will cling to the smallest piece of string offered to me.

original: 'Tis well consented. Presently away,   For to strange sores strangely they strain the cure.—
translation: It's a good agreement. Let's go immediately. Strange diseases require strange cures.

original: Come, lady, die to live. This wedding day   Perhaps is but prolonged. Have patience and endure.
translation: [To HERO]  Come, lady, you will die so that you might live. This wedding may only be postponed. Have patience and endure.

original: Lady Beatrice, have you wept all this while?
translation: Lady Beatrice, have you been weeping this whole time?

original: Yea, and I will weep a while longer.
translation: Yes, and I will weep for a while longer.

original: I will not desire that.
translation: I wish you wouldn't.

original: You have no reason. I do it freely.
translation: You have no reason to wish that. I do it willingly.

original: Surely I do believe your fair cousin is wronged.
translation: I do truly believe that your beautiful cousin was wronged.

original: Ah, how much might the man deserve of me that  would right her!
translation: Ah, I would give anything to any man who made this right!

original: Is there any way to show such friendship?
translation: Is there any way I could show you such friendship?

original: A very even way, but no such friend.
translation: A very clear way, but there is no such friend to do it.

original: May a man do it?
translation: Can a man do it?

original: It is a man’s office, but not yours.
translation: It is a man's job, but not a job for you.

original: I do love nothing in the world so well as you. Is not  that strange?
translation: There's nothing in the world I love as much as you. Isn't that strange?

original: As strange as the thing I know not. It were as possible for me to say I loved nothing so well as you,
translation: As strange as my own confusion. It would also be possible for me to say that there's nothing I love as much as you.

original: but  believe me not, and yet I lie not, I confess nothing,  nor I deny nothing. I am sorry for my cousin.
translation: But don't believe me when I say it—and yet I'm not lying. I confess nothing, and I deny nothing. I am sorry for my cousin.

original: By my sword, Beatrice, thou lovest me.
translation: Beatrice, I swear by my sword that you love me.

original: Do not swear, and eat it.
translation: Don't swear. You might have to eat your words later.

original: I will swear by it that you love me, and I will make  him eat it that says I love not you.
translation: I'll swear by my sword that you love me, and if any man says I don't love you, I'll make him eat my sword.

original: Will you not eat your word?
translation: But you won't eat your words?

original: With no sauce that can be devised to it. I protest I  love thee.
translation: Not with any sauce that could be invented for them. I declare that I love you.

original: Why then, God forgive me.
translation: Why, then, God forgive me.

original: What offense, sweet Beatrice?
translation: Forgive you for what offense, sweet Beatrice?

original: You have stayed me in a happy hour. I was about to  protest  I loved you.
translation: You've stopped me at just the right moment. I was about to declare that I loved you too.

original: And do it with all thy heart.
translation: Then declare it with all your heart.

original: I love you with so much of my heart that none is left  to protest.
translation: I love you with so much of my heart that none of it is left to object.

original: Come, bid me do anything for thee.
translation: Come, ask me to do anything for you.

original: Kill Claudio.
translation: Kill Claudio.

original: Ha! Not for the wide world.
translation: Ha! Not for the whole wide world.

original: You kill me to deny it. Farewell.
translation: Then you kill me by refusing. Farewell.

original: Tarry, sweet Beatrice.
translation: Wait, sweet Beatrice.

original: I am gone, though I am here. There is no love in you.  Nay, I pray you let me go.
translation: My spirits have left, though my body is still here. There is no true love in you. Please, let me go .

original: Beatrice—
translation: Beatrice—

original: In faith, I will go.
translation: I swear, I will go.

original: We’ll be friends first.
translation: We must part on friendly terms.

original: You dare easier be friends with me than fight with  mine enemy.
translation: You would dare to be my friend when you won't fight my enemies?

original: Is Claudio thine enemy?
translation: Is Claudio your enemy?

original: Is he not approved in the height a villain, that  hath slandered, scorned, dishonored my kinswoman?
translation: Hasn't he proved to be the worst kind of villain by slandering, scorning, and dishonoring my cousin?

original: Oh,  that I were a man! What, bear her in hand until they  come to take hands and then, with public accusation,  uncovered slander, unmitigated rancor
translation: Oh, if only I were a man! What, he just leads her on until the moment they were exchanging vows, and then, with public accusation, open slander, pure hatred

original: —O God, that I were a man! I would eat his heart in the marketplace.
translation: —Oh God, if only I were a man! I would rip out his heart and eat it in the marketplace.

original: Hear me, Beatrice—
translation: Listen to me, Beatrice—

original: Talk with a man out at a window! A proper saying!
translation: Talking with a man at her bedroom window! That's a likely story!

original: Nay, but Beatrice—
translation: No, but Beatrice—

original: Sweet Hero, she is wronged, she is slandered, she  is undone.
translation: Sweet Hero! She is wronged, she is slandered, she is ruined.

original: Beat—
translation: Beat—

original: Princes and counties! Surely, a princely testimony, a  goodly count, Count Comfect, a sweet gallant, surely!
translation: Princes and counts! Sure, what a princely testimony they gave—an excellent conviction! Count Sweetmeat, that sweet gentleman, for sure!

original: Oh, that I were a man for his sake! Or that I had any  friend would be a man for my sake!
translation: Oh, if only I were a man, I would deal with him! Or even if I had a friend who would be a man for my sake!

original: But manhood is melted into curtsies, valor into compliment, and men are only  turned into tongue, and trim ones too.
translation: But manliness and bravery have been melted into curtsies and compliments, and all men have become nothing but tongues, fancy tongues.

original: He is now as  valiant as Hercules that only tells a lie and swears it.
translation: The man who tells a lie and swears that it's true is now considered as brave as Hercules.

original: I cannot be a man with wishing, therefore I will die a  woman with grieving.
translation: I can't become a man by wishing, so I'll die as a woman, from grieving.

original: Tarry, good Beatrice. By this hand, I love thee.
translation: Wait, good Beatrice. I swear by this hand, I love you.

original: Use it for my love some other way than swearing by it.
translation: Then use it for something other than swearing, and prove your love for me.

original: Think you in your soul the Count Claudio hath  wronged Hero?
translation: Do you really think in your soul that Count Claudio has wronged Hero?

original: Yea, as sure as I have a thought or a soul.
translation: Yes, as sure as I have a mind or a soul.

original: Enough, I am engaged. I will challenge him.
translation: That's enough for me—I am bound by my pledge of love. I will challenge him.

original: I will  kiss your hand, and so I leave you.
translation: I'll kiss your hand, and so I leave you.

original: By this hand,  Claudio shall render me a dear account.
translation: I swear by this hand, Claudio will pay dearly for what he's done.

original: As you hear of  me, so think of me.
translation: Listen for news of me, and keep me in your thoughts.

original: Go comfort your cousin. I must say  she is dead, and so, farewell.
translation: Go comfort your cousin. I'll go tell them that she is dead. Farewell.

original: Is our whole dissembly appeared?
Oh, a stool and a cushion for the Sexton.
translation: Oh, but we need a stool and a cushion for the sexton.

original: Which be the malefactors?
translation: Which ones are the malefactors?

original: Marry, that am I and my partner.
Nay, that’s certain; we have the exhibition to  examine.
But which are the offenders that are to be examined?  Let  them come before Master Constable.
translation: But which ones are the criminals to be examined? Let them come before the Master Constable.

original: Yea, marry, let them come before me.
translation: Yes, well, bring them before me.

original: What is your name, friend?
translation: What is your name, friend?

original: Borachio.
translation: Borachio.

original: Pray, write down, “Borachio.”—Yours, sirrah?
translation: Please, write down "Borachio."[To CONRAD] And yours, sir?

original: I am a gentleman, sir, and my name is Conrad.
translation: I am a gentleman, sir. And my name is Conrad.

original: Write down “Master Gentleman Conrad.”—Masters, do you  serve God?
translation: Write down "Master Gentleman Conrad."[To CONRAD and BORACHIO] Sirs, do you obey God's laws?

original: Yea, sir, we hope.
translation: Yes sir, we hope we do.

original: Write down that they hope they serve God;
translation: [To the SEXTON]  Write down that they hope they obey God's laws.

original: and write  God first, for God defend but God should go before  such villains!
translation: And write "God" first, for God forbid that such villains should come before God!

original: —Masters, it is proved already that you  are little better than false knaves, and it will go near to be thought so shortly.
translation: [To CONRAD and BORACHIO]  Sirs, it has already been proven that you're no better than lying villains—and soon we'll suspect you of it too.

original: How answer you for  yourselves?
translation: What do you have to say for yourselves?

original: Marry, sir, we say we are none.
A marvelous witty fellow, I assure you, but I will go  about with him.—Come you hither, sirrah, a word in your  ear. Sir, I say to you it is thought you are false  knaves.
translation: He's a marvelously witty fellow, I assure you, but I'll get the better of him. Come here, sir, and I'll whisper a word in your ear. Sir, I say that you are both suspected of being lying villains.

original: Sir, I say to you we are none.
translation: And I say that we are not, sir.

original: Well, stand aside.—'Fore God, they are both in a ale.  Have you writ down that they are none?
translation: Well, step aside then. By God, they've both agreed to the same lie. Have you written that down, that they aren't lying villains?

original: Master Constable, you go not the way to examine.  You must call forth the watch that are their accusers.
translation: Master Constable, this isn't the right way to conduct an examination. First you must call forth the watchmen who accused them.

original: Yea, marry, that’s the eftest way.—Let the watch  come forth. Masters, I charge you in the Prince’s name,  accuse these men.
translation: Yes, well, that's the easiest way. Let the watchmen step forward. Sirs, I order you in the Prince's name to accuse these men.

original: This man said, sir, that Don John, the Prince’s  brother, was a villain.
translation: Sir, this man said that Don John, the Prince's brother, was a villain.

original: Write down Prince John a villain. Why, this is flat  perjury, to call a prince’s brother villain.
Master Constable—
translation: Master Constable—

original: Pray thee, fellow, peace. I do not like thy look, I  promise thee.
translation: Please, man, be quiet. I don't like the look of you, I promise you that.

original: What heard you him say else?
translation: What else did you hear him say?

original: Marry, that he had received a thousand ducats of Don  John for accusing the Lady Hero wrongfully.
translation: Well, that he had received a thousand gold pieces from Don John for wrongfully accusing the Lady Hero.

original: Flat burglary as ever was committed.
Yea, by Mass, that it is.
translation: Yes, by God, it is.

original: What else, fellow?
translation: And what else, man?

original: And that Count Claudio did mean upon his words  to disgrace Hero before the whole assembly, and not  marry her.
translation: And that Count Claudio—based on Don John's accusation—was going to disgrace Hero before the whole wedding assembly, and refuse to marry her.

original: O villain! Thou wilt be condemned  into everlasting redemption for this.
translation: Oh, you villain! You'll be condemned to everlasting redemption for this!

original: What else?
translation: What else?

original: This is all.
translation: That's all.

original: And this is more, masters, than you can deny.
translation: [To BORACHIO and CONRAD]  And all this is more than you can deny, sirs.

original: Prince  John is this morning secretly stolen away.
translation: This morning Prince John secretly fled Messina.

original: Hero was in  this manner accused, in this very manner refused, and  upon the grief of this, suddenly died.
translation: Hero was accused and refused by Claudio just as the watchman reported, and she died from her sudden grief.

original: —Master Constable, let these men be bound and brought to Leonato’s.
translation: [To DOGBERRY]  Master Constable, tie these men up and bring them to Leonato's.

original: I will go before and show him their examination.
translation: I'll go ahead of you and show him the written report of this examination.

original: Come, let them be opinioned.
Let them be in the hands—
translation: Let them be handcuffed.

original: Off, coxcomb!
translation: Get off of me, you fool!

original: God’s my life, where’s the Sexton? Let him write down  the  Prince’s officer “coxcomb.” Come, bind them.—Thou naughty varlet!
translation: God save me, where's the sexton? He ought to write down that the Prince's officer was called "fool." Come on, bind them.

original: Away! You are an ass, you are an ass!
translation: Get away from me! You are an ass, you are an ass!

original: Dost thou not suspect my place? Dost thou not suspect  my years?
translation: How dare you! Don't you  suspect  my position? Don't you suspect my age?

original: Oh, that he were here to write me down an ass!
translation: Oh, if only the sexton were here to write down that I'm an ass!

original: But masters, remember that I am an ass, though it be  not written down, yet forget not that I am an ass.
translation: But sirs, remember that I am an ass, even though it wasn't written down—don't forget that I am an ass.

original: —No,  thou villain, thou art full of piety, as shall be proved upon thee by good witness.
translation: To CONRAD]  No, you villain, you are full of  piety , as witnesses will prove.

original: I am a wise fellow and,  which is more, an officer and, which is more, a  householder and, which is more, as pretty a piece of  flesh as any is in Messina,
translation: I'm a wise fellow and—what's more—an officer and—what's more—a homeowner and—what's more—as fine a mortal man as any in Messina.

original: and one that knows the law,  go to, and a rich fellow enough, go to, and a fellow  that hath had losses, and one that hath two gowns and  everything handsome about him.
translation: And I know the law, damn you, and I'm rich enough, damn you! And I've known hardships, and I have two pairs of robes, and everything about me is impressive.

original: —Bring him away.—Oh, that  I had been writ down an ass!
translation: [To the WATCHMEN]  Take him away! Oh, if only it had been written down that I'm an ass!

original: If you go on thus, you will kill yourself, And ’tis not wisdom thus to second grief Against yourself.
translation: If you go on like this, you'll kill yourself. There's no point in adding to the grief that's destroying you.

original: I pray thee, cease thy counsel,   Which falls into mine ears as profitless   As water in a sieve.
translation: Please, stop giving me advice. Your words pass uselessly through my ears like water through a sieve.

original: Give not me counsel,   Nor let no comforter delight mine ear   But such a one whose wrongs do suit with mine.
translation: Don't give me advice, and don't let anyone try to comfort or please me except someone whose injuries match my own.

original: Bring me a father that so loved his child,   Whose joy of her is overwhelmed like mine,   And bid him speak of patience.
translation: Find me a father who loved his child as I loved Hero—and whose joy in her has been crushed like mine has—and ask  him  to tell me about patience.

original: Measure his woe the length and breadth of mine,   And let it answer every strain for strain,   As thus for thus and such a grief for such,   In every lineament, branch, shape, and form.
translation: Let his suffering be as big and deep as mine, and let it reflect all of my mental strain—with each sadness matching up in every way, shape, and form.

original: If such a one will smile and stroke his beard,   Bid sorrow wag, cry “hem” when he should groan,   Patch grief with proverbs, make misfortune drunk   With candle-wasters, bring him yet to me
translation: f such a man will act like you—smiling and stroking his beard, telling sorrow to run away, saying "keep going" instead of mourning with me, patching up grief with cliched sayings, and forgetting misfortune by poring over books—if you find such a person, bring him to me.

original: And I of him will gather patience.   But there is no such man.
translation: I'll share in his strength and patience. But there is no such man.

original: For, brother, men   Can counsel and speak comfort to that grief   Which they themselves not feel,
translation: Brother, it's easy for men to comfort and advise about sorrows that they themselves don't feel.

original: but, tasting it,   Their counsel turns to passion
translation: But once they taste them too, their advice turns into passion.

original: which before   Would give preceptial med'cine to rage,   Fetter strong madness in a silken thread,   Charm ache with air, and agony with words.
translation: You can't cure rage with advice, bind up madness with silk thread, treat aches with hot air, or fix agony with words.

original: No, no, 'tis all men's office to speak patience   To those that wring under the load of sorrow,   But no man's virtue nor sufficiency   To be so moral when he shall endure   The like himself.
translation: No, no, every man thinks it's his duty to advise patience to those who bear the burden of sorrow, but no man has the ability or power to live up to his own advice when he's in the same situation.

original: Therefore give me no counsel.   My griefs cry louder than advertisement.
translation: So don't give me advice. My griefs drown out whatever you have to say.

original: Therein do men from children nothing differ.
translation: You're behaving no better than a child by acting like this.

original: I pray thee, peace. I will be flesh and blood,
translation: Please, be quiet. I will be flesh and blood, not just words.

original: For there was never yet philosopher   That could endure the toothache patiently,   However they have writ the style of gods   And made a push at chance and sufferance.
translation: There has never been a philosopher who could endure a toothache patiently, even though they all write as if they're gods who have pushed aside human suffering and misfortune.

original: Yet bend not all the harm upon yourself.  Make those that do offend you suffer too.
translation: But don't take up the burden of all this pain on your own. Make those responsible suffer too.

original: There thou speak’st reason. Nay, I will do so.
translation: Now you're speaking reasonably. I'll do that.

original: My soul doth tell me Hero is belied,
translation: My soul tells me that Hero has been wronged.

original: And that shall Claudio know; so shall the Prince   And all of them that thus dishonor her.
translation: I'll make sure that Claudio, the Prince, and all those who dishonored her will know about this.

original: Here comes the Prince and Claudio hastily.
translation: Here comes the Prince and Claudio in a hurry.

original: Good e'en, good e'en.
translation: Good evening, good evening.

original: Good day to both of you.
translation: Good day to both of you.

original: Hear you, my lords—
translation: Listen to me, my lords—

original: We have some haste, Leonato.
translation: We're in a bit of a hurry, Leonato.

original: Some haste, my lord! Well, fare you well, my lord. Are you so hasty now? Well, all is one.
translation: A bit of a hurry, my lord! Well, farewell then, my lord. Are you in such a hurry now that my daughter is dead? Well, it doesn't matter to me.

original: Nay, do not quarrel with us, good old man.
translation: Don't fight with us now, good old man.

original: If he could right himself with quarreling, Some of us would lie low.
translation: If he could right his wrongs by fighting, some of us here would be smart to run off and hide.

original: Who wrongs him?
translation: Who has wronged him?

original: Marry, thou dost wrong me, thou dissembler, thou. Nay, never lay thy hand upon thy sword. I fear thee not.
translation: Indeed, you have wronged me, you hypocrite. No, don't lay your hand on your sword. I'm not afraid of you.

original: Marry, beshrew my hand If it should give your age such cause of fear. In faith, my hand meant nothing to my sword.
translation: Indeed, curse my hand if it should ever frighten an old man like you. I swear, my hand had no intention of using my sword.

original: Tush, tush, man, never fleer and jest at me.
translation: Shame on you, man. Don't mock and sneer at me.

original: I speak not like a dotard nor a fool,   As under privilege of age to brag   What I have done being young, or what would do   Were I not old.
translation: I'm not a foolish old man who is protected by his age and brags about the deeds of his youth, or what he would do now if he weren't so old.

original: Know, Claudio, to thy head,   Thou hast so wronged mine innocent child and me
translation: Know this, Claudio, for I declare it to your face: you have wronged me and my innocent child.

original: That I am forced to lay my reverence by,   And with gray hairs and bruise of many days
translation: I am forced to lay aside the respectability of my age, and with my gray hairs and aching body,

original: Do challenge thee to trial of a man.
translation: I challenge you to a test worthy of a man: a duel.

original: I say thou hast belied mine innocent child.
translation: I say that you have slandered my innocent child.

original: Thy slander hath gone through and through her heart,   And she lies buried with her ancestors,   Oh, in a tomb where never scandal slept   Save this of hers, framed by thy villainy.
translation: Your lies have pierced her heart, and now she lies buried with her ancestors, oh, in a tomb that was never stained by scandal until you caused  this  scandal with your villainy.

original: My villainy?
translation: My villainy?

original: Thine, Claudio, thine, I say.
translation: Yours, Claudio, yours, I say.

original: You say not right, old man.
translation: Then you don't speak the truth, old man.

original: My lord, my lord,   I’ll prove it on his body if he dare,
translation: My lord, my lord, I'll prove it over his dead body if he dares to fight me.

original: Despite his nice fence and his active practice,   His May of youth and bloom of lustihood.
translation: I'll beat him despite his fancy fencing techniques, his recent practice in battle, his youth, and his vigor.

original: Away! I will not have to do with you.
translation: Enough! I won't have anything to do with you.

original: Canst thou so daff me? Thou hast killed my child. If thou kill’st me, boy, thou shalt kill a man.
translation: You think you can push me aside just like that? You have killed my child. Boy, if you want to kill a man, then dare to kill me.

original: He shall kill two of us, and men indeed,   But that’s no matter.
translation: We're both real men, and he'll have to kill both of us. But that's no matter.

original: Let him kill one first.   Win me and wear me! Let him answer me.—
translation: Let him try to kill one of us first. If he can beat me then he can brag about it! Let him accept my challenge.

original: Come, follow me, boy. Come, sir boy, come, follow me.
translation: [To CLAUDIO]  Come on, come and get me, boy. Come on, sir boy, come and get me.

original: Sir boy, I’ll whip you from your foining fence,   Nay, as I am a gentleman, I will.
translation: Sir boy, I'll whip you despite all your fancy fencing—I swear as a gentleman I will.

original: Brother—
translation: Brother—

original: Content yourself. God knows I loved my niece,   And she is dead, slandered to death by villains   That dare as well answer a man indeed   As I dare take a serpent by the tongue.
translation: Don't try to stop me. God knows I loved my niece, and now she's dead. She was slandered to death by villains who are as likely to accept a fight with a real man as I am to grab a snake by the tongue.

original: Boys, apes, braggarts, jacks, milksops!
translation: [To CLAUDIO and DON PEDRO]  Boys, monkeys, braggarts, fools, pampered children!

original: Brother Anthony—
translation: Brother Antonio—

original: Hold you content. What, man! I know them, yea,   And what they weigh, even to the utmost scruple
translation: Dont' stop me. Yes, I know their kind, and I know what they're really worth.

original: Scrambling, outfacing, fashion-monging boys,   That lie and cog and flout,
translation: They're just fighting, swaggering, fashionably-dressed boys who lie and cheat and show off.

original: deprave and slander,   Go anticly and show outward hideousness,   And speak off half a dozen dang'rous words   How they might hurt their enemies, if they durst,   And this is all.
translation: They defame and slander people, walk around in extravagant clothes, put on a scary show and say a few threatening words about how they'll hurt their enemies—if they dare. And that's all they'll do.

original: But brother Anthony—
translation: But, brother Antonio—

original: Come, ’tis no matter. Do not you meddle. Let me deal in this.
translation: Don't worry about it. Let me deal with this.

original: Gentlemen both, we will not wake your patience.
translation: Gentlemen, we won't stay and test your patience any further.

original: My heart is sorry for your daughter’s death,   But, on my honor, she was charged with nothing   But what was true and very full of proof.
translation: I'm sorry for your daughter's death, but I swear on my honor that the charges were true and backed up by proof.

original: My lord, my lord—
translation: My lord, my lord—

original: I will not hear you.
translation: I'm not listening to you.

original: No? Come, brother; away! I will be heard.
translation: No? Come on, then, brother, let's go! I want somebody to listen to me.

original: And shall, or some of us will smart for it.
translation: And somebody will listen to you, or certain people will suffer for it.

original: See, see, here comes the man we went to seek.
translation: See, here comes the man we were looking for.

original: Now, Signior, what news?
translation: Now, sir, what's new?

original: Good day, my lord.
translation: Good day, my lord.

original: Welcome, Signior. You are almost come to part almost  a fray.
translation: Welcome, sir. You almost arrived in time to break up what was almost a fight.

original: We had like to have had our two noses snapped off with  two old men without teeth.
translation: We were about to have our noses snapped off by two old men without teeth.

original: Leonato and his brother. What think’st thou? Had  we fought, I doubt we should have been too young for  them.
translation: Leonato and his brother. What do you think of that? If we had fought, I fear that we should have been too inexperienced for them.

original: In a false quarrel there is no true valor. I came to  seek you both.
translation: There's no real bravery in an unfair fight. I came to find you both.

original: We have been up and down to seek thee, for we are  high-proof melancholy and would fain have it beaten  away. Wilt thou use thy wit?
translation: We've been looking everywhere for you too. We're feeling very depressed and we want to have our sadness beaten away. Will you use your wit to do it?

original: It is in my scabbard. Shall I draw it?
translation: My wit's in my sword's scabbard. Should I unsheathe it?

original: Dost thou wear thy wit by thy side?
translation: Do you wear your wit by your side?

original: Never any did so, though very many have been beside  their wit.
translation: No one wears their wit by their side, though many are  beside their wit .

original: I will bid thee draw, as we do the minstrels: draw to pleasure us.
translation: Now I'll ask you to draw your wit, as you draw your sword—or as musicians draw their bows across their fiddles. Draw in order to please us.

original: As I am an honest man, he looks pale.—Art thou sick,  or angry?
translation: I swear, Benedick looks pale. Are you sick, or angry?

original: What, courage, man! What though  care killed a cat? Thou hast mettle enough in thee to  kill care.
translation: What, cheer up, man! What does it matter that worry killed the cat? You have enough liveliness in you to kill worry.

original: Sir, I shall meet your wit in the career, an you charge it  against me. I pray you, choose another subject.
translation: Sir, if you try to use your wit to attack me, I'll knock you down with my own wit. Please, choose another method.

original: Nay, then, give him another staff. This  last was broke 'cross.
translation: Give him another lance. He broke that last one in half with a poor hit.

original: By this light, he changes more and more. I think he be  angry indeed.
translation: I swear, his face keeps getting paler. I think he really is angry.

original: If he be, he knows how to turn his girdle.
translation: If he is, it's up to him to change his own attitude.

original: Shall I speak a word in your ear?
translation: Can I have a word with you?

original: God bless me from a challenge!
translation: God forbid that he wants to challenge me!

original: [aside to CLAUDIO   ]   You are a villain. I jest not.
translation: [To CLAUDIO so that only he can hear]  You're a villain. I'm not joking.

original: I  will make it good how you dare, with what you dare, and  when you dare.
translation: I challenge you in whatever way you prefer, with whatever weapon you prefer, and whenever you prefer.

original: Do me right, or I will protest your  cowardice.
translation: Accept the challenge, or I will proclaim you a coward.

original: You have killed a sweet lady, and her death  shall fall heavy on you. Let me hear from you.
translation: You've killed an innocent girl, and your punishment for killing her will be steep. Say something.

original: Well, I will meet you, so I may have good cheer.
translation: I accept your challenge, and will enjoy it.

original: What, a feast, a feast?
translation: What, are we having a feast?

original: I' faith, I thank him. He hath bid me to a calf’s head and a capon, the which if I do not carve most  curiously, say my knife’s naught. Shall I not find a  woodcock too?
Sir, your wit ambles well; it goes easily.
translation: Sir, your wit is slow and rambling

original: I’ll tell thee how Beatrice praised thy wit he other  day.
translation: [To BENEDICK]  I'll tell you how Beatrice praised your wit the other day.

original: I said thou hadst a fine wit.
translation: I said that you had a fine wit.

original: “True,” said she, “a  fine little one.”
translation: "True," she said, "a fine little one."

original: “No,” said I, “a great wit.”
translation: "No," I said, "a large wit."

original: “Right,”  says she, “a great gross one.”
translation: "Right," she said, "a large, coarse one."

original: “Nay,” said I, “a good  wit.”
translation: "No, I said, "a good wit."

original: “Just,” said she, “it hurts nobody.”
translation: "Exactly," she said, "it doesn't hurt anybody."

original: “Nay,” said  I, “the gentleman is wise.”
translation: "No," I said, "the gentleman is wise."

original: “Certain,” said she, “a wise gentleman.”
translation: "Certainly," she said, "he's a  wise gentleman ."

original: “Nay,” said I, “he hath the tongues.”
translation: "No," I said, "he knows foreign languages."

original: “That I believe,” said she, “for he swore a thing to me on  Monday night, which he forswore on Tuesday morning;  there’s a double tongue, there’s two tongues.”
translation: "I believe that," she said, "for he swore one thing to me on Monday night, and then took it back on Tuesday morning. There's two different languages for you."

original: Thus did  she an hour together transshape thy particular virtues.
translation: And so she turned your virtues inside out for a whole hour.

original: Yet at last she concluded with a sigh, thou wast the  proper’st man in Italy.
translation: But at last she sighed and concluded that you were the handsomest man in Italy.

original: For the which she wept heartily and said she cared  not.
translation: Then she cried because of it, and said she didn't care.

original: Yea, that she did. But yet for all that, an if she did  not hate him deadly, she would love him dearly. The old  man’s daughter told us all.
translation: Yes, she did. And yet, for all that, if she didn't hate him completely, she'd love him totally. Leonato's daughter told us everything.

original: All, all. And, moreover, God saw him when he was hid  in the garden.
translation: Everything. Everything. And, moreover, God saw Benedick when he was hiding in the garden.

original: But when shall we set the savage bull’s horns on the  sensible Benedick’s head?
Yea, and text underneath: “Here dwells Benedick  the married man?”
translation: Yes, and make the sign underneath him that says: "Here is Benedick, the married man?"

original: Fare you well, boy. You know my mind.
translation: See you later, boy. You know what I plan.

original: I will leave you  now to your gossip-like humor.
translation: I'll leave you now to your silly gossip.

original: You break jests as  braggarts do their blades, which, God be thanked, hurt  not.
translation: Your jokes are like the swords of cowardly braggarts—thank God, they don't hurt at all.

original: —My lord, for your many courtesies I thank you. I  must discontinue your company.
translation: [To DON PEDRO]  My lord, I thank you for your many kindnesses to me. I can no longer remain with you.

original: Your brother the Bastard  is fled from Messina.
translation: Your brother Don John the Bastard has fled from Messina.

original: You have among you killed a sweet  and innocent lady.
translation: The three of you have killed a pure and innocent girl.

original: For my Lord Lackbeard there, he and I shall meet, and till then peace be with him.
translation: As for Lord Beardless over there, he and I will duel. May he know peace until then.

original: He is in earnest.
translation: He's serious.

original: In most profound earnest, and, I’ll warrant you, for  the love of Beatrice.
translation: He is absolutely serious. And, I bet you, he's said all of this because he loves Beatrice.

original: And hath challenged thee?
translation: And has he challenged you?

original: Most sincerely.
translation: He has challenged me, completely seriously.

original: What a pretty thing man is when he goes in his doublet  and hose and leaves off his wit!
translation: What a silly thing a man looks like when he's gotten dressed but left his brain behind!

original: He is then a giant to an ape; but then is an ape a  doctor to such a man.
translation: He's like a giant compared to a monkey, but a monkey could be his doctor—that's how much smarter it is than a man like him.

original: But soft you, let me be. Pluck up, my heart, and be  sad. Did he not say my brother was fled?
translation: But wait a minute, let me think. I must consider this and get serious. Didn't he say that my brother has run away?

original: Come you, sir. If justice cannot tame you, she shall  ne'er weigh more reasons in her balance. Nay, an you be  a cursing hypocrite once, you must be looked to.
translation: Come here, sir. If you don't feel the sting of justice, then Justice no longer has any power. Since you are a damned hypocrite, we must deal with you.

original: How now? Two of my brother’s men bound! Borachio one!
translation: What's going on? Two of my brother's men in handcuffs? And Borachio is one of them?

original: Hearken after their offense, my lord.
translation: Listen to their crime, my lord.

original: Officers, what offense have these men done?
translation: Officers, what have these men done?

original: Marry, sir, they have committed false report;
translation: Well, sir, they have lied.

original: moreover, they have spoken untruths;
translation: In addition, they have said things that weren't true.

original: secondarily, they  are slanders; sixth and lastly, they have belied a lady;
translation: Second, they are slanderers. Sixth and last, they have falsely accused a lady.

original: thirdly, they have verified unjust things;
translation: And thirdly, they have confirmed as true things that were false.

original: and, to  conclude, they are lying knaves.
translation: And, finally, they are lying fools.

original: First, I ask thee what they have done; thirdly, I ask  thee what’s their offense; sixth and lastly, why they  are committed; and, to conclude, what you lay to their  charge.
Rightly reasoned, and in his own division; and, by my  troth, there’s one meaning well suited.
translation: Well put, and in the same order he used. By God, that's one simple question and answer dressed up in many different ways.

original: [to BORACHIO and CONRAD   ]   Who have you  offended, masters, that you are thus bound to your  answer?
translation: [To BORACHIO and CONRAD]  Who have you wronged, men, to be in custody and forced to answer?

original: This learned constable is too cunning to be  understood. What’s your offense?
translation: This knowledgeable policeman is too smart to be understood. What was your crime?

original: Sweet Prince, let me go no farther to mine answer. Do  you hear me, and let this count kill me.
translation: Sweet Prince, don't wait for the trial, but let me give my answer here. Listen to me, and let this count kill me.

original: I have deceived even your very eyes.
translation: I have deceived your very eyes.

original: What your wisdoms could not  discover, these shallow fools have brought to light,
translation: These shallow fools have discovered what you in your wisdom could not.

original: who in the night overheard me confessing to this man how  Don John your brother incensed me to slander the Lady  Hero,
translation: In the night they overheard me confessing to this man, Conrad, that your brother Don John incited me to slander the Lady Hero.

original: how you were brought into the orchard and saw me  court Margaret in Hero’s garments,
translation: I explained how you were brought to the garden and saw me courting Margaret, who was wearing Hero's clothes.

original: how you disgraced her when you should marry her.
translation: And then you disgraced Hero when you should have married her.

original: My villainy they have upon  record, which I had rather seal with my death than  repeat over to my shame.
translation: They have my villainy on record, and I'd rather seal it up with my death than have to retell the story of my shame.

original: The lady is dead upon mine and  my master’s false accusation.
translation: The lady is dead because of my and my master's false accusation.

original: And, briefly, I desire  nothing but the reward of a villain.
translation: In short, I desire nothing now but the proper punishment for a villain.

original: Runs not this speech like iron through  your blood?
translation: Doesn't this make ice run through your veins?

original: I have drunk poison whiles he uttered it.
translation: I feel as if I've drunk poison while he was talking.

original: But did my brother set thee on to this?
translation: But did my brother tell you to do all this?

original: Yea, and paid me richly for the practice of it.
translation: Yes, and he paid me a lot to do it.

original: He is composed and framed of treachery, And fled he is upon this villainy.
translation: He is made entirely of treachery. He's run away because of this crime.

original: Sweet Hero, now thy image doth appear In the rare semblance that I loved it first.
translation: Sweet Hero, when I imagine you now, you seem as beautiful and exceptional as you were when I first loved you.

original: Come, bring away the plaintiffs. By this time our  sexton hath reformed Signior Leonato of the matter.
translation: Come, take away the  plaintiffs. By now the sexton will have reformed  Sir Leonato about all this.

original: And, masters, do not forget to specify, when time and  place shall serve, that I am an ass.
translation: And sirs, don't forget to specify, when the time is right, that I am an ass.

original: Here, here comes Master Signior Leonato, and the  Sexton too.
translation: Here, here comes Master Sir Leonato, and the sexton too.

original: Which is the villain? Let me see his eyes, That, when I note another man like him,  I may avoid him. Which of these is he?
translation: Which one is the villain? Let me look into his eyes so that, when I see another man like him, I can avoid him. Which of these men is he?

original: If you would know your wronger, look on me.
translation: If you want to know who has wronged you, then look at me.

original: Art thou the slave that with thy breath hast killed Mine innocent child?
translation: Are you the villain that has killed my innocent child with your words?

original: Yea, even I alone.
translation: Yes, I alone.

original: No, not so, villain, thou beliest thyself.
translation: No, not so, villain, you weren't the only one.

original: Here stand a pair of honorable men—   A third is fled—that had a hand in it.—
translation: [Pointing to CLAUDIO and DON PEDRO]  Here stand a pair of "honorable men"—the third has fled—who also had a hand in this crime.

original: I thank you, princes, for my daughter’s death.
translation: [To CLAUDIO and DON PEDRO]  I thank you, princes, for my daughter's death.

original: Record it with your high and worthy deeds.   'Twas bravely done, if you bethink you of it.
translation: Record it in the list of your great and noble deeds. It was bravely done.

original: I know not how to pray your patience,   Yet I must speak.
translation: I don't know how to ask you for patience, but I must speak.

original: Choose your revenge yourself.   Impose me to what penance your invention   Can lay upon my sin.
translation: Choose your revenge against me. Do whatever you want with me to punish my sin.

original: Yet sinned I not   But in mistaking.
translation: But my only sin was in making a mistake.

original: By my soul, nor I,  And yet to satisfy this good old man I would bend under any heavy weight That he’ll enjoin me to.
translation: Mine too. But to satisfy this good old man, I would bear any burden he might place on me.

original: I cannot bid you bid my daughter live—   That were impossible
translation: I cannot make you make my daughter live—that would be impossible.

original: —but, I pray you both,   Possess the people in Messina here   How innocent she died.
translation: But please, both of you, inform the people of Messina that she died innocently.

original: And if your love   Can labor ought in sad invention,   Hang her an epitaph upon her tomb   And sing it to her bones.
translation: And if your love for Hero can inspire any creativity, then write a tribute to her. Hang it on her tomb, and sing it to her bones.

original: Sing it tonight.   Tomorrow morning come you to my house,
translation: Sing it tonight. Then come to my house tomorrow morning,

original: And since you could not be my son-in-law,   Be yet my nephew.
translation: and since you could not be my son-in-law, be my nephew instead.

original: My brother hath a daughter,   Almost the copy of my child that’s dead,   And she alone is heir to both of us.
translation: My brother has a daughter who is the spitting image of dead Hero, and she is heir to both of us.

original: Give her the right you should have given her cousin,   And so dies my revenge.
translation: Give her what you should have given her cousin—the right and rite of marriage—and my thirst for revenge will die.

original: O noble sir!   Your overkindness doth wring tears from me.
translation: Oh, noble sir! Your kindness is making me cry.

original: I do embrace your offer; and dispose   For henceforth of poor Claudio.
translation: I gladly accept your offer. From now on, demand whatever you like of poor Claudio.

original: Tomorrow then I will expect your coming.   Tonight I take my leave.
translation: I will expect you tomorrow then, and say goodbye for tonight.

original: This naughty man   Shall face to face be brought to Margaret,   Who I believe was packed in all this wrong,   Hired to it by your brother.
translation: This wicked man will be brought face to face with Margaret, whom I believe was a conspirator in all this, and hired by Don John.

original: No, by my soul, she was not,   Nor knew not what she did when she spoke to me,
translation: No, I swear she was not. She didn't know what she was doing when she spoke to me.

original: But always hath been just and virtuous   In any thing that I do know by her.
translation: All I've ever heard about her is that she is honest and virtuous.

original: [to LEONATO   ]   Moreover, sir, which indeed is not  under white and black, this plaintiff here, the  offender, did call me ass.
