translation: [To LEONATO]  Another thing, sir, which hasn't been written down—this  plaintiff  here, the criminal, called me an ass.

original: I beseech you, let it be  remembered in his punishment.
translation: Please remember this when you're handing out his punishment.

original: And also the watch heard  them talk of one Deformed.
translation: Also the watchmen heard these two talking about a criminal named  Deformed .

original: They say he wears a key in  his ear and a lock hanging by it
translation: They say that he wears a key in his ear with a lock hanging from it.

original: and borrows money in  God’s name, the which he hath used so long and never  paid that now men grow hard-hearted and will lend  nothing for God’s sake.
translation: He borrows money in God's name and never pays it back, and now everyone is so hard-hearted about it that no one will fund anything in God's name anymore.

original: Pray you, examine him upon that  point.
translation: Please, interrogate them about this.

original: I thank thee for thy care and honest pains.
translation: I thank you for your hard work and honest efforts.

original: Your worship speaks like a most thankful and  reverent youth, and I praise God for you.
translation: Your Worship speaks like a very thankful and respectful youth, and I thank God for you.

original: There’s for thy pains.
translation: That's for your trouble.

original: God save the foundation!
translation: God save the charity!

original: Go, I discharge thee of thy prisoner, and I thank thee.
translation: Go. I'll relieve you of your prisoner. Thank you.

original: I leave an arrant knave with your Worship, which I  beseech your Worship to correct yourself, for the  example of others.
translation: I leave a complete scoundrel with you, your Worship,  whom I ask your Worship to correct yourself  for the example of others.

original: God keep your Worship! I wish your  Worship well. God restore you to health!
translation: God bless your Worship! I wish your Worship well.  May God restore you to health!

original: I humbly give  you leave to depart, and   if a merry meeting may be wished, God prohibit it!—   Come, neighbor.
translation: I now humbly allow you to leave, and may we meet again in the future, if God prohibits it! [To VERGES]  Come on, neighbor.

original: Until tomorrow morning, lords, farewell.
translation: Farewell until tomorrow morning, my lords.

original: Farewell, my lords. We look for you tomorrow.
translation: Farewell, my lords. We'll expect you tomorrow.

original: We will not fail.
translation: We will be there without fail.

original: Tonight I’ll mourn with Hero.
translation: I'll mourn for Hero tonight.

original: Bring you these fellows on.—We’ll talk with Margaret, How her acquaintance grew with this lewd fellow.
translation: Bring these criminals along. We'll talk with Margaret, and find out how she became friends with this wicked fellow.

original: Pray thee, sweet Mistress Margaret, deserve well at  my hands by helping me to the speech of Beatrice.
translation: Please, sweet Mistress Margaret, do me a favor by calling Beatrice to speak with me.

original: Will you then write me a sonnet in praise of my beauty?
translation: Will you write me a sonnet praising my beauty in exchange?

original: In so high a style, Margaret, that no man living shall  come over it, for in most comely truth thou deservest  it.
To have no man come over me! Why, shall I always keep  below stairs?
translation: No man will come over me! Why, will I always be a servant, and never a mistress of the house?

original: Thy wit is as quick as the greyhound’s mouth; it  catches.
translation: Your wit is as quick as a greyhound's mouth—it catches whatever it wants.

original: And yours as blunt as the fencer’s foils, which hit but hurt not.
translation: And your wit is as blunt as a fencer's practice sword—it hits, but doesn't hurt.

original: A most manly wit, Margaret, it will not hurt a woman.  And so, I pray thee, call Beatrice. I give thee the  bucklers.
Give us the swords; we have bucklers of our own.
translation: Give us the swords—we women have bucklers of our own.

original: If you use them, Margaret, you must put in the pikes  with a vice, and they are dangerous weapons for maids.
translation: But, Margaret, if you're going to use your bucklers, you must screw the spikes in the center. They're dangerous weapons for virgins.

original: Well, I will call Beatrice to you, who I think hath  legs.
translation: Well, I'll call Beatrice to come to you. She has legs, and can walk here herself.

original: And therefore will come.
translation: And so she will come.

original: [sings]     The god of love   ,     That sits above   ,     And knows me, and knows me   ,     How pitiful I deserve   —   I mean in singing.
translation: [Singing] The god of love, Who sits above, And knows me, and knows me, How much pity I deserve— How pitiful my singing is.

original: But in loving, Leander the good  swimmer, Troilus the first employer of panders, and a  whole bookful of these quondam carpetmongers, whose  names yet run smoothly in the even road of a blank  verse,
translation: But as for loving, take  Leander, Troilus, or a whole book full of those ancient carpetmongers , whose names sound so smooth in verse.

original: why, they were never so truly turned over and  over as my poor self in love.
translation: Why, none of them were driven as crazy by love as I have been.

original: Marry, I cannot show it in rhyme. I have tried.
translation: But, alas, I can't show my feelings in a poem. I have tried.

original: I can find out no rhyme to “lady”  but “baby”—an innocent rhyme; for “scorn,” “horn”—a hard rhyme; for, “school,” “fool”—a babbling rhyme; very  ominous endings.
translation: I can't come up with any rhyme for "lady" but "baby"—which is too silly;  for "scorn" I can only find "horn"—which is too harsh ; for "school," I can only find "fool"—a rhyme that will babble on like a fool. These are all very ominous endings for describing a relationship.

original: No, I was not born under a rhyming  planet, nor I cannot woo in festival terms.
translation: No, I wasn't destined to be a poet. I can't court a lady with fancy language.

original: Sweet Beatrice, wouldst thou come when I called thee?
translation: Sweet Beatrice, did you come because I called you?

original: Yea, Signior, and depart when you bid me.
translation: Yes, sir, and I'll leave when you command.

original: Oh, stay but till then!
translation: Oh, stay until then!

original: “Then” is spoken. Fare you well now. And yet, ere I go, let me go with that I came, which is, with knowing what hath passed between you and Claudio.
translation: Well, you've said "then." So farewell. But before I go, let me get what I came for—the knowledge of what happened between you and Claudio.

original: Only foul words, and thereupon I will kiss thee.
translation: Only foul, angry words passed between us, and with that I'll kiss you.

original: Foul words is but foul wind, and foul wind is but  foul breath, and foul breath is noisome. Therefore I  will depart unkissed.
translation: Foul words are foul air, and foul air is foul breath, and foul breath is nauseating. Therefore I will leave unkissed.

original: Thou hast frighted the word out of his right sense,  so forcible is thy wit.
translation: Your wit is so forceful that it's frightened the words out of their proper meanings.

original: But I must tell thee plainly,  Claudio undergoes my challenge, and either I must  shortly hear from him, or I will subscribe him a coward.
translation: But I must tell you this plainly: Claudio has heard my challenge. He'll either accept it soon, or I will publicly proclaim him a coward.

original: And I pray thee now tell me, for which of my bad parts  didst thou first fall in love with me?
translation: And now, please tell me, which of my bad qualities did you first fall in love with?

original: For them all together, which maintained so politic a  state of evil that they will not admit any good part to  intermingle with them.
translation: With all of them together: they are so wholly united that they create a perfectly bad person, and won't let any good qualities mix in with them.

original: But for which of my good parts  did you first suffer love for me?
translation: But which of my good qualities first made you suffer love for me?

original: Suffer love! A good epithet! I do suffer love indeed,  for I love thee against my will.
translation: Suffer love! That's a good expression. I do suffer love indeed, for I love you against my will.

original: In spite of your heart, I think. Alas, poor heart, if  you spite it for my sake, I will spite it for yours, for I will never love that which my friend hates.
translation: You love me in spite of your heart, I think. Alas, if you spite your poor heart for my sake, then I will spite it for your sake. I will never love something that my friend hates.

original: Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably.
translation: You and I are too wise to woo each other peacefully.

original: It appears not in this confession. There’s not one wise man among twenty that will praise himself.
translation: You don't show your wisdom by declaring yourself wise, though. It's said that a wise man won't praise himself.

original: An old, an old instance, Beatrice, that lived in the  time of good neighbors.
translation: Beatrice, that's an old, old proverb, from the good old days when neighbors would praise each other.

original: If a man do not erect in this  age his own tomb ere he dies, he shall live no longer in monument than   the bell rings and the widow weeps.
translation: Nowadays, if a man doesn't erect a monument to himself before he dies, his memory won't last any longer than the church bell ringing and his widow's weeping.

original: And how long is that, think you?
translation: And how long is that, do you think?

original: Question: why, an hour in clamor and a quarter in  rheum.
translation: That's the question: why, an hour of ringing and fifteen minutes of crying.

original: Therefore is it most expedient for the wise, if  Don Worm, his conscience, find no impediment to the  contrary, to be the trumpet of his own virtues, as I am  to myself.
translation: Therefore it's best for a wise man—if his conscience permits it—to trumpet his own virtues, like I do.

original: So much for praising myself, who, I myself  will bear witness, is praiseworthy.
translation: So that's why I praise myself, for—I'll bear witness to it myself—I'm quite praiseworthy.

original: An now tell me, how  doth your cousin?
translation: Now tell me, how is your cousin doing?

original: Very ill.
translation: She's very sick.

original: And how do you?
translation: And how are you doing?

original: Very ill, too.
translation: I'm very sick, too.

original: Serve God, love me, and mend. There will I leave you  too, for here comes one in haste.
translation: Serve God, love me, and feel better. I'll leave you with that, for someone is hurrying this way.

original: Madam, you must come to your uncle. Yonder’s old coil  at home.
translation: Madam, you must go to your uncle's. There's a great to-do at home.

original: It is proved my Lady Hero hath been  falsely accused, the Prince and Claudio mightily abused, and Don John is the author of all, who is fled and  gone.
translation: It's been proved that my Lady Hero was falsely accused, the Prince and Claudio were greatly deceived, and Don John—who has fled and gone—is responsible for everything.

original: Will you come presently?
translation: Will you come right away?

original: Will you go hear this news, Signior?
translation: Will you come with me to hear this news, sir?

original: I will live in thy heart, die in thy lap, and be buried in thy eyes—and moreover, I will go with thee to thy  uncle’s.
Is this the monument of Leonato?
translation: Is this Leonato's family tomb?

original: It is, my lord.
translation: It is, my lord.

original: [reading an epitaph]   Done to death by slanderous tongues   Was the Hero that here lies.
translation: [Reading an epitaph] Here lies Hero, A hero killed by slanderous tongues.

original: Death, in guerdon of her wrongs,   Gives her fame which never dies.   So the life that died with shame   Lives in death with glorious fame.
translation: To repay her for her wrongs, Death gives her fame, which never dies. So the life that died with shame Lives in death with glorious fame.

original: Hang thou there upon the tomb,   Praising her when I am dumb.
translation: Stay there on the tomb, scroll, and keep praising Hero even when I can no longer speak.

original: Now, music, sound, and sing your solemn hymn.
translation: [To the musicians]  Now start the music, and sing your solemn hymn.

original: [sings]     Pardon, goddess of the night   ,     Those that slew thy virgin knight   ,
translation: [Singing] Pardon, goddess of the night, We who killed your virgin knight.

original: For the which with songs of woe     Round about her tomb they go   .
translation: Now singing songs of woe Around about her tomb we go.

original: Midnight, assist our moan   .     Help us to sigh and groan     Heavily, heavily   .
translation: Oh, midnight, assist our grief. Help us to sigh and groan Mournfully, mournfully.

original: Graves, yawn and yield your dead   ,     Till death be utterèd   ,     Heavily, heavily   .
translation: Oh, graves, open wide and release your dead, Until her death is fully lamented, Mournfully, mournfully.

original: Now, unto thy bones good night!   Yearly will I do this rite.
translation: Goodnight to your bones for now, Hero! I will perform this ceremony every year.

original: Good morrow, masters. Put your torches out.
translation: Good morning, sirs. Put your torches out.

original: The wolves have preyed, and look, the gentle day,   Before the wheels of Phoebus, round about   Dapples the drowsy east with spots of grey.
translation: The wolves have finished their night's hunting, and look—the gentle dawn precedes  Phoebus ' chariot, and dapples the drowsy eastern sky with spots of light.

original: Thanks to you all, and leave us. Fare you well.
translation: Thanks to you all. Now leave us. Farewell.

original: Good morrow, masters. Each his several way.
translation: Good morning, sirs. Let each of us go his separate ways.

original: Come, let us hence, and put on other weeds, And then to Leonato’s we will go.
translation: Come, let's go and put on different clothes, and then we'll go to Leonato's.

original: And Hymen now with luckier issue speed ’s Than this for whom we rendered up this woe.
Did I not tell you she was innocent?
translation: Didn't I tell you that she was innocent?

original: So are the Prince and Claudio, who accused her   Upon the error that you heard debated.
translation: And so are the Prince and Claudio, who accused her because they themselves were deceived.

original: But Margaret was in some fault for this,
translation: Margaret was partly at fault for this.

original: Although against her will, as it appears   In the true course of all the question.
translation: Yet our examination has shown that she didn't know about the plot, even though she played a role in it.

original: Well, I am glad that all things sort so well.
translation: Well, I am glad that things have turned out so well.

original: And so am I, being else by faith enforced To call young Claudio to a reckoning for it.
translation: And so am I, or else my own promise would have made me fight Claudio.

original: Well, daughter, and you gentlewomen all,   Withdraw into a chamber by yourselves,   And when I send for you, come hither masked.
translation: Well, daughter, and all you gentlewomen, retreat to a room by yourselves. When I send for you, come out wearing masks.

original: The Prince and Claudio promised by this hour   To visit me.
translation: The Prince and Claudio promised me they would be here by now.

original: —You know your office, brother.   You must be father to your brother’s daughter,   And give her to young Claudio.
translation: [To ANTONIO]  You know your job, brother. You must be the father to my daughter, and give her away to young Claudio.

original: Which I will do with confirmed countenance.
translation: I'll do it with a straight, serious face.

original: Friar, I must entreat your pains, I think.
translation: Friar, I must ask you for a favor, I think.

original: To do what, Signior?
translation: To do what, sir?

original: To bind me or undo me, one of them.— Signior Leonato, truth it is, good Signior, Your niece regards me with an eye of favor.
translation: To tie me up, or to undo me—one or the other. Sir Leonato, the truth is, good sir, that your niece Beatrice has been looking at me favorably.

original: That eye my daughter lent her; ’tis most true.
translation: She sees you with eyes my daughter lent her, that's true.

original: And I do with an eye of love requite her.
translation: And I look back at her with eyes of love.

original: The sight whereof I think you had from me, From Claudio and the Prince. But what’s your will?
translation: I think you got such sight from me, Claudio, and the Prince. But what do you want?

original: Your answer, sir, is enigmatical.
translation: Your words are puzzling to me, sir.

original: But for my will, my will is your goodwill   May stand with ours, this day to be conjoined   In the state of honorable marriage—
translation: But as for what I want—what I want is your blessing, so your niece and I can be honorably married today.

original: In which, good Friar, I shall desire your help.
translation: [To FRIAR FRANCIS]  And that, good Friar, is where I need your help.

original: My heart is with your liking.
translation: I am pleased with your desire, and I give you my blessing.

original: And my help. Here comes the Prince and Claudio.
translation: And I offer you my help. Here comes the Prince and Claudio.

original: Good morrow to this fair assembly.
translation: Good morning to this fair gathering.

original: Good morrow, Prince; good morrow, Claudio. We here attend you. Are you yet determined Today to marry with my brother’s daughter?
translation: Good morning, Prince. Good morning, Claudio. We've been expecting you. Are you still determined to marry my brother's daughter today?

original: I’ll hold my mind were she an Ethiope.
Call her forth, brother. Here’s the friar ready.
translation: Bring her out, brother. The friar's ready.

original: Good morrow, Benedick. Why, what’s the matter That you have such a February face, So full of frost, of storm and cloudiness?
translation: Good morning, Benedick. Why, what's the matter? Why do you have such a February face—so full of frost, storms, and cloudiness?

original: I think he thinks upon the savage bull.   Tush, fear not, man.
translation: I think he's remembering how the free, savage bull must wear the yoke of marriage. Oh, don't be afraid, man.

original: We’ll tip thy horns with gold,   And all Europa shall rejoice at thee   As once Europa did at lusty Jove   When he would play the noble beast in love.
translation: We'll coat your horns with gold, and all of Europe will love you, just as Europa once loved lustful Jove when  he  was the bull .

original: Bull Jove, sir, had an amiable low,   And some such strange bull leapt your father’s cow   And got a calf in that same noble feat   Much like to you,
translation: Bull Jove, sir, came mooing for love, and some strange bull like him mated with one of your father's cows, who then gave birth to a calf like you.

original: for you have just his bleat.
translation: You have the same bleat.

original: For this I owe you. Here comes other reck'nings.
translation: I'll get you back for that. But here come other accounts I must settle first.

original: Which is the lady I must seize upon?
translation: Which is the lady I'm going to marry?

original: This same is she, and I do give you her.
translation: This one here, and I now give her to you.

original: Why, then she’s mine.—Sweet, let me see your face.
translation: Why then, she's mine. Sweet one, let me see your face.

original: No, that you shall not till you take her hand Before this friar and swear to marry her.
translation: No, you won't see her face until you take her hand and swear to marry her in front of this friar.

original: Give me your hand before this holy friar. I am your husband, if you like of me.
translation: Give me your hand before this holy friar. I am your husband, if you want me to be.

original: And when I lived, I was your other wife, And when you loved, you were my other husband.
translation: And when I lived, I was your other wife. And when you loved me, you were my other husband.

original: Another Hero!
translation: Another Hero!

original: Nothing certainer. One Hero died defiled, but I do live, And surely as I live, I am a maid.
translation: It's true. One Hero died disgraced. But I am still alive, and as surely as I'm alive, I am a virgin.

original: The former Hero! Hero that is dead!
translation: The former Hero! Hero that was dead!

original: She died, my lord, but whiles her slander lived.
translation: She was only dead while her slander lived, my lord.

original: All this amazement can I qualify   When after that the holy rites are ended   I’ll tell you largely of fair Hero’s death.
translation: I can explain all these surprises. After the wedding ceremony is over, I'll tell you in full detail about fair Hero's supposed "death."

original: Meantime let wonder seem familiar,   And to the chapel let us presently.
translation: In the meantime, let's accept these amazing events as natural, and go straight to the chapel.

original: Soft and fair, Friar.—Which is Beatrice?
translation: Wait a moment, Friar. Which one is Beatrice?

original: I answer to that name. What is your will?
translation: I answer to that name. What do you want?

original: Do not you love me?
translation: Do you love me?

original: Why no, no more than reason.
translation: Why no, no more than is reasonable.

original: Why then, your uncle and the Prince and Claudio Have been deceived. They swore you did.
translation: Why then, your uncle and the Prince and Claudio have been deceived. They swore that you did.

original: Do not you love me?
translation: Do you love me?

original: Troth, no, no more than reason.
translation: Truly, no, no more than is reasonable.

original: Why then, my cousin, Margaret, and Ursula Are much deceived, for they did swear you did.
translation: Why then, my cousin, Margaret, and Ursula have been greatly deceived, for they swore that you did.

original: They swore that you were almost sick for me.
translation: They swore that you were almost sick with love for me.

original: They swore that you were well-nigh dead for me.
translation: They swore that you were almost dead with love for me.

original: 'Tis no such matter. Then you do not love me?
translation: Well then. You don't love me?

original: No, truly, but in friendly recompense.
translation: No, truly—just as a friend.

original: Come, cousin, I am sure you love the gentleman.
translation: Come, niece, I am sure that you love this gentleman.

original: And I’ll be sworn upon ’t that he loves her, For here’s a paper written in his hand, A halting sonnet of his own pure brain, Fashioned to Beatrice.
translation: And I'll swear that he loves her, for here's a paper in his handwriting—a clumsy sonnet that he composed himself, dedicated to Beatrice.

original: And here’s another, Writ in my cousin’s hand, stol'n from her pocket,  Containing her affection unto Benedick.
translation: And here's another, stolen from my cousin's pocket—written in her handwriting, and full of her affection for Benedick.

original: A miracle! Here’s our own hands against our hearts.  Come, I will have thee, but, by this light, I take thee  for pity.
translation: A miracle! Our own handwriting gives evidence against our guilty hearts. Come, I'll take you then, but I swear I'm only doing it out of pity.

original: I would not deny you, but, by this good day, I yield  upon great persuasion, and partly to save your life, for I was told you were in a consumption.
translation: I won't refuse you. But, to be clear, I'm only doing this because everyone persuaded me, and partly to save your life—for I heard you were wasting away with love for me.

original: Peace! I will stop your mouth.
translation: Enough talking! I'll stop your mouth with a kiss.

original: How dost thou, Benedick, the married man?
translation: How are you now, Benedick, the Married Man?

original: I’ll tell thee what, Prince: a college of wit-crackers  cannot flout me out of my humor.
translation: I'll tell you what, Prince: a whole assembly of wisecrackers couldn't ruin my mood.

original: Dost thou think I care  for a satire or an epigram? No.
translation: Do you think I care about mockery and name-calling? No.

original: If a man will be beaten  with brains, he shall wear nothing handsome about him.
translation: If a man is always afraid of being ridiculed, he'll never dare to wear something nice.

original: In brief, since I do purpose to marry, I will think  nothing to any purpose that the world can say against  it,
translation: In short, since I intend to marry, I won't hear anything the world has to say against marriage.

original: and therefore never flout at me for what I have said against it.
translation: So don't mock me for what I said against it before.

original: For man is a giddy thing, and this is my  conclusion.
translation: Man is a fickle creature, and that's my conclusion.

original: —For thy part, Claudio, I did think to have  beaten thee,
translation: [To CLAUDIO]  And as for you, Claudio, I think I would have beaten you in our duel.

original: but in that thou art like to be my  kinsman, live unbruised, and love my cousin.
translation: But now that you're going to become my cousin, I'll let you go uninjured, and love you and my new cousin Hero.

original: I had well hoped thou wouldst have denied Beatrice,  that I might have cudgeled thee out of thy single life,  to make thee a double-dealer,
translation: I had almost hoped that you would deny Beatrice, just so I might have beaten you out of your single life and made you a  double-dealer .

original: which out of question,  thou wilt be, if my cousin do not look exceedingly  narrowly to thee.
translation: But you'll probably become one anyway, if my new cousin Beatrice doesn't keep a close eye on you.

original: Come, come, we are friends. Let’s have a dance ere we  are married, that we may lighten our own hearts and our  wives' heels.
translation: Come, come, we're all friends here. Let's have a dance before we're married to cheer ourselves up.

original: We’ll have dancing afterward.
translation: We'll have dancing after the wedding.

original: First, of my word! Therefore play, music.—Prince, thou  art sad. Get thee a wife, get thee a wife. There is no  staff more reverend than one tipped with horn.
translation: No, we'll have it first! Play a song, musicians. Prince, you look serious. Get yourself a wife, get yourself a wife! Your royal staff would be more impressive if it were tipped with horn.

original: My lord, your brother John is ta'en in  flight   And brought with armed men back to Messina.
translation: My lord, your brother John has been captured, and armed men have brought him back to Messina.

original: Think not on him till tomorrow. I’ll  devise thee brave punishments for him.—Strike up,  pipers.
translation: Don't worry about him until tomorrow. For your sake, I'll come up with a suitable punishment for him.[To the musicians] Now, play, musicians!

original: Tush! Never tell me. I take it much unkindly That thou, Iago, who hast had my purse As if the strings were thine, shouldst know of this.
translation: Psh! Don't say that. Iago, I am not pleased that you've known about this, especially since I've given you access to my wallet as if it were your own.

original: 'Sblood, but you’ll not hear me!   If ever I did dream of such a matter, abhor me.
Thou told’st me Thou didst hold him in thy hate.
translation: You told me that you hated him.

original: Despise me   If I do not. Three great ones of the city   (In personal suit to make me his lieutenant)   Off-capped to him, and by the faith of man   I know my price, I am worth no worse a place.
translation: If I don't hate him, you can hate me. Three noblemen of the city tipped their hats to him, making a personal plea for him to make me his lieutenant. And, truly, I know my value, and I'm worthy of that position.

original: But he (as loving his own pride and purposes)   Evades them with a bombast circumstance   Horribly stuffed with epithets of war,   And in conclusion   Nonsuits my mediators.
translation: But of course  Othello  is too proud to listen and wants to do things his own way, so he speaks in circles with empty talk about war-related titles. And in the end he declines their proposal

original: For “Certes,” says he,   “I have already chose my officer.”   And what was he?
translation: and says, "Certainly, I have already chosen my lieutenant." And who did he choose?

original: Forsooth, a great arithmetician,   One Michael Cassio, a Florentine   A fellow almost damned in a fair wife   That never set a squadron in the field,
translation: A guy who's basically a mathematician, some Michael Cassio, from Florence. A man practically cursed with a  wife  too beautiful (whom he can't control). A man who has never commanded a squadron on the battlefield,

original: Nor the division of a battle knows   More than a spinster—unless the bookish theoric,   Wherein the toged consuls can propose   As masterly as he.
translation: who knows no more about battle than an old lady. He knows only theory from books, full of the talk of old geezers in togas.

original: Mere prattle without practice   Is all his soldiership. But he, sir, had th' election   And I, of whom his eyes had seen the proof   At Rhodes, at Cyprus, and on other grounds   Christian and heathen,
translation: His military experience is all ideas, with no real action! But, sir, Othello chose this Cassio for lieutenant, not me—even though he's seen proof of my military prowess with his own eyes at Rhodes, at Cyprus, and on all sorts of battlefields in Christian and Pagan lands.

original: must be belee’d and calmed   By debitor and creditor. This counter-caster   He (in good time) must his lieutenant be   And I, bless the mark, his Moorship’s ancient.
translation: Now, my career's stalled and I'm overtaken by some number cruncher—an accountant! That bean-counter will be his lieutenant before too long, and meanwhile I'll be carrying around  his Moorship's  flag, thank you very much.

original: By heaven, I rather would have been his hangman.
translation: God, I'd rather be his executioner than his flag-bearer.

original: Why, there’s no remedy. 'Tis the curse of service.   Preferment goes by letter and affection,   And not by old gradation, where each second   Stood heir to th' first.
translation: Well, there's nothing I can do. That's the price of military service. Promotions are a matter of favoritism—based on whoever the leader likes—not based on rank, with a second officer stepping up to become a first officer, and so on.

original: Now sir, be judge yourself,   Whether I in any just term am affined   To love the Moor.
translation: So now , sir, you be the judge and tell me: do I have any reason at all to love that Moor?

original: I would not follow him then.
translation: If I were your position I wouldn't follow him. So why do you?

original: O sir, content you.   I follow him to serve my turn upon him.   We cannot all be masters, nor all masters   Cannot be truly followed.
translation: Oh, sir, calm yourself. I'm following him only so I can turn on him later. Maybe we can't all be leaders, but not all leaders can have loyal followers.

original: You shall mark   Many a duteous and knee-crooking knave   That (doting on his own obsequious bondage)   Wears out his time much like his master’s ass   For naught but provender, and when he’s old, cashiered.   Whip me such honest knaves.
translation: All the time you see dutiful servants kneeling to their masters and working like mules for nothing but food. And when they get old, they're fired. These honest fools deserve to be whipped!

original: Others there are   Who, trimmed in forms and visages of duty,   Keep yet their hearts attending on themselves   And, throwing but shows of service on their lords,   Do well thrive by them.
translation: There are others who take the appearance of duty and loyalty, but stay focused on their own interests. They put on a good show of serving their lords, and thrive in their subservient positions.

original: And when they have lined their  coats,   Do themselves homage. These fellows have some soul,   And such a one do I profess myself. For, sir,   It is as sure as you are Roderigo,   Were I the Moor, I would not be Iago.
translation: But once they get enough money, they serve only themselves. These are the guys who really have some soul. That's the kind of servant I am. Believe me, as sure as your name is Roderigo: if I were the Moor, I would not want Iago as my servant.

original: In following him, I follow but myself.   Heaven is my judge, not I for love and duty,   But seeming so, for my peculiar end.
translation: In following him, I'm really just following myself. God may judge me. I swear I'm not serving Othello out of love and duty, but merely appearing to, for my own purposes.

original: For when my outward action doth demonstrate   The native act and figure of my heart   In compliment extern, ’tis not long after   But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve   For daws to peck at. I am not what I am.
translation: If my outward appearance showed what my real intentions are, It would be like wearing my heart on my sleeve for birds to peck at. I am not what I seem to be.

original: What a full fortune does the Thick-lips owe If he can carry’t thus!
Call up her father.   Rouse him. Make after him, Poison his delight,   Proclaim him in the streets. Incense her kinsmen,   And, though he in a fertile climate dwell,   Plague him with flies.
translation: Call up Desdemona's father.  Wake him up. We'll slander Othello in the streets, and ruin his happiness by getting his wife's family all riled up. And even if he's in a paradise right now, we'll fill it with flies.

original: Though that his joy be joy   Yet throw such changes of vexation on’t,   As it may lose some color.
translation: He may still be happy, but we'll douse him in so much irritation that his happiness will lose some of its luster.

original: Here is her father’s house, I’ll call aloud.
translation: Here's Desdemona's father's house. I'll call out.

original: Do, with like timorous accent and dire yell As when, by night and negligence, the fire Is spied in populous cities.
translation: Do it! Shout as loud and as seriously as when someone cries "Fire!" in a crowded city at night.

original: What, ho, Brabantio! Signior Brabantio, ho!
translation: Hey, Brabantio! Sir Brabantio, hey!

original: Awake! What, ho, Brabantio! Thieves! Thieves!  Look to your house, your daughter, and your bags! Thieves! thieves!
translation: Brabantio, wake up! Thieves! Thieves! Check on your house, check on your daughter, check on your money bags! Thieves! Thieves!

original: What is the reason of this terrible summons? What is the matter there?
translation: What's the reason for your awful shouting? What's the matter out there?

original: Signior, is all your family within?
Are your doors locked?
translation: Are your doors locked?

original: Why, wherefore ask you this?
translation: Why?  Why on earth are you asking me this?

original: Zounds, sir, you’re robbed! For shame, put on your  gown.   Your heart is burst, you have lost half your soul.   Even now, now, very now, an old black ram   Is tupping your white ewe.
translation: Good lord , you're being robbed! You should be ashamed. Get dressed! It's like your heart is burst open and you're bleeding away your very soul. At this very moment—right now— an old black ram is having his way with your white lamb .

original: Arise, arise,   Awake the snorting citizens with the bell   Or else the devil will make a grandsire of you.   Arise, I say!
translation: Get up, get up! Ring the bell and wake up all the snoring citizens, or else that devil will make you a grandfather. Get up!

original: What, have you lost your wits?
translation: What are you saying? Have you lost your mind?

original: Most reverend signior, do you know my voice?
translation: Most noble sir, do you recognize my voice?

original: Not I. What are you?
translation: I do not. Who are you?

original: My name is Roderigo.
translation: My name is Roderigo.

original: The worser welcome.   I have charged thee not to haunt about my doors.   In honest plainness thou hast heard me say   My daughter is not for thee.
translation: Then you're not welcome here. I've already told you not to come by my house. I told you bluntly and honestly: my daughter is not for you.

original: And now in madness,   Being full of supper and distempering drafts,   Upon malicious knavery dost thou come   To start my quiet?
translation: And now you come here in some kind of madness brought on by feasting and too many drinks, just to make trouble and ruin my good sleep?

original: Sir, sir, sir—
translation: Sir, sir, sir—

original: But thou must needs be sure  My spirits and my place have in their power To make this bitter to thee.
translation: Make sure you understand: I have the will—and the power—to make you regret this.

original: Patience, good sir.
translation: Good sir, hold on.

original: What tell’st thou me of robbing? This is Venice, My house is not a grange.
translation: What are you talking to me about with "robbing?"  This is the city of Venice. My house isn't some unprotected barn.

original: Most grave Brabantio, In simple and pure soul I come to you—
translation: Honorable Brabantio, I come to you in all honesty and good will—

original: Zounds, sir, you are one of those that will not serve  God, if the devil bid you. Because we come to do you  service and you think we are ruffians, you’ll have your  daughter covered with a Barbary horse.
translation: Christ, sir, you're the type of man who would refuse to serve God if the devil told you to! We've come here to do you a favor, and you're ignoring us just because you think we're no good. You're letting your daughter mate with a  Barbary  horse.

original: You’ll have your  nephews neigh to you. You’ll have coursers for cousins  and gennets for germans.
translation: Your grandchildren will neigh to you. You'll have ponies and colts for descendants.

original: What profane wretch art thou?
translation: What kind of foul-mouthed jerk are you?

original: I am one, sir, that comes to tell you your daughter and the Moor are now making the beast with two backs.
translation: Sir, I am one that comes to tell you that your daughter and the Moor are doing the deed at this very moment.

original: Thou art a villain!
translation: You're a villain!

original: You are a senator!
translation: And you're a senator!

original: This thou shalt answer. I know thee, Roderigo.
translation: You will pay for this, Roderigo. I know what kind of man you are.

original: Sir, I will answer any thing. But, I beseech you,   If’t be your pleasure and most wise consent   (As partly I find it is) that your fair daughter   At this odd-even and dull watch o' th' night
translation: Sir, I'll answer for anything I've done. But, I beg you. if you're okay with the fact that your fair daughter, at this late hour of the night,

original: Transported with no worse nor better guard   But with a knave of common hire, a gondolier,   To the gross clasps of a lascivious Moor,
translation: is handed over  to the gross hands of a lustful Moor with no guard but a common servant for hire, a gondolier even—

original: If this be known to you and your allowance,   We then have done you bold and saucy wrongs.   But if you know not this my manners tell me   We have your wrong rebuke.
translation: if you know all this, and you allow it (which I think is the case), well then I admit we have insolently done you wrong. But if you're not aware of all this, then my own good manners suggest that you're wrong to scold us.

original: Do not believe   That, from the sense of all civility,   I thus would play and trifle with your reverence.
translation: Don't think that I would just play around with such a serious matter, contrary to any good manners.

original: Your daughter (if you have not given her leave)   I say again, hath made a gross revolt,   Tying her duty, beauty, wit, and fortunes   In an extravagant and wheeling stranger   Of here and everywhere.
translation: I repeat: if you haven't given your daughter permission, then she has seriously rebelled against your authority. She's giving all her obedience, beauty, wit, and wealth to some extravagant, wandering foreigner, who seems to have roots just about everywhere.

original: Straight satisfy yourself.   If she be in her chamber or your house,   Let loose on me the justice of the state   For thus deluding you.
translation: Go now and see for yourself. If she's in her room, or even in your house, sue me and let the government punish me for lying to you like this.

original: Strike on the tinder, ho!   Give me a taper, call up all my people!
translation: Hey, strike a match! Light me a torch! Wake everyone up!

original: This accident is not unlike my dream,   Belief of it oppresses me already.   Light, I say, light!
translation: This whole situation is not unlike a dream I had. And I'm worried it's coming true. Light—give me light!

original: [to RODERIGO]   Farewell, for I must leave you.   It seems not meet, nor wholesome to my place,   To be producted (as, if I stay, I shall)   Against the Moor.
translation: [To RODERIGO]  Goodbye. I must leave you now. It seems to me neither wise nor appropriate given my position in Othello's service to be brought forward against the Moor—and it seems like I will be, if I stay here.

original: For I do know the state   (However this may gall him with some check)   Cannot with safety cast him,
translation: Besides, I know that the government cannot get rid of him (even if this whole thing may annoy Brabantio),

original: for he’s embarked   With such loud reason to the Cyprus wars   (Which even now stand in act) that, for their souls,   Another of his fathom they have none   To lead their business.
translation: since he's needed so greatly to fight in the wars with Cyprus that are going on right now. And the government has no one else of his capability to lead their forces, not even if they should trade their own souls for someone.

original: In which regard,   Though I do hate him as I do hell pains,   Yet for necessity of present life   I must show out a flag and sign of love,   (Which is indeed but sign).
translation: Although I do hate Othello as much as I hate the tortures of Hell, for the time being I must show signs of love—which, I assure you, are nothing more than empty signs.

original: That you shall surely find  him,   Lead to the Sagittary the raisèd search,   And there will I be with him. So farewell.
translation: You go lead the search party to the Sagittary Inn, where you will surely find him. I'll be there with him. So goodbye.

original: It is too true an evil. Gone she is.   And what’s to come of my despisèd time   Is naught but bitterness. Now, Roderigo,   Where didst thou see her?—
translation: The evil thing you warned me of is all too true. She is gone. And all that's left of my life, which I now hate, is bitterness. Now, Roderigo, where did you see her? Oh, unhappy girl!

original: Oh, unhappy girl!—   With the Moor, say’st thou?—Who would be a father?—   How didst thou know ’twas she?—
translation: Did you say she was with the Moor? Who would want to be a father in such a situation as this? How did you know it was her?

original: Oh, she deceives me   Past thought!—What said she to you?—Get more tapers,   Raise all my kindred. Are they married, think you?
translation: Oh, she has tricked me beyond anything I could have thought possible. What did she say to you? Get more torches, and wake up my whole family. Do you think they've gotten married?

original: Truly, I think they are.
translation: Truly, I think they have.

original: Oh, heaven, how got she out? Oh, treason of the blood!   Fathers, from hence trust not your daughters' minds   By what you see them act.
translation: Oh, heaven, how did she get out of the house? Oh, she has committed treason against her own blood! All you fathers, from now on do not trust your daughters' minds based on how you see them act.

original: Is there not charms   By which the property of youth and maidhood   May be abused? Have you not read, Roderigo,   Of some such thing?
translation: Aren't there magic charms out there that can trick and violate young maidens? Roderigo, have you read about such things?

original: Yes, sir, I have indeed.
translation: Yes, sir.  I have indeed.

original: Call up my brother—Oh, would you had had her! Some one way, some another. Do you know Where we may apprehend her and the Moor?
translation: Call up my brother—oh, if only you had married her!  Some of you go one way, some go another way. [To RODERIGO] Do you know where we might find her and the Moor?

original: I think I can discover him, if you please  To get good guard and go along with me.
translation: I think I can find him, if you want to get some strong, armed men together and come along with me.

original: Pray you lead on. At every house I’ll call.   I may command at most.—Get weapons, ho!
translation: Please, lead the way. I'll call on every house. I know most of them well enough to tell them, "Hey, get your weapons!"

original: And raise some special officers of might.—   On, good Roderigo. I will deserve your pains.
translation: I'll raise up a force of especially strong officers. Go on, good Roderigo. I will reward you for your efforts.

original: Though in the trade of war I have slain men,   Yet do I hold it very stuff o' th' conscience   To do no contrived murder.
translation: Even though I have killed men while serving in war, still my conscience forbids me from committing any premeditated murder.

original: I lack iniquity   Sometimes to do me service. Nine or ten times   I had thought t' have yerked him here under the ribs.
translation: I lack the evil disposition that would sometimes serve my purpose. Nine or ten times I've thought about just stabbing him right under the ribs.

original: 'Tis better as it is.
translation: It's better that you haven't.

original: Nay, but he prated   And spoke such scurvy and provoking terms   Against your honor   That, with the little godliness I have,   I did full hard forbear him.
translation: No, he said such insulting, rude things against your sense of honor that it took all the goodness in me to hold back from hurting him.

original: But I pray you, sir,   Are you fast married? Be assured of this:   That the Magnifico is much beloved   And hath in his effect a voice potential   As double as the Duke’s.
translation: But I beg you to tell me, sir: are you safely married? Because you can be sure that Senator Barbantio is well-liked in the city, and has twice as much influence as the Duke.

original: He will divorce you,   Or put upon you what restraint and grievance   The law (with all his might to enforce it on)   Will give him cable.
translation: He will divorce you two, or at least subject you to whatever restraint and punishment he has the power to inflict.

original: Let him do his spite.   My services which I have done the signiory   Shall out-tongue his complaints. 'Tis yet to know—   Which, when I know that boasting is an honor,   I shall promulgate.
translation: Let him do his worst. My good deeds done in service to the city government will have more influence than his complaints. It's not yet well-known—and I won't spread this news until I hear that it's an honor to boast—

original: I fetch my life and being   From men of royal siege, and my demerits   May speak unbonneted to as proud a fortune   As this that I have reached.
translation: but I am descended from men of royal lineage. So I'm worthy of the noble fortune of Desdemona's family.

original: For know, Iago,   But that I love the gentle Desdemona,   I would not my unhousèd free condition   Put into circumscription and confine   For the sea’s worth. But look, what lights come yond?
translation: And know this, Iago: if I didn't love the gentle Desdemona, I wouldn't give up all my freedom for the confines and restrictions of marriage—not in return for all the treasure in the sea. But look, what light is that, coming from over there?

original: Those are the raisèd father and his friends. You were best go in.
translation: That's the awakened father and his friends. You'd better go inside.

original: Not I, I must be found. My parts, my title, and my perfect soul Shall manifest me rightly. Is it they?
translation: Not me. I must let them find me. My qualities, my title and legal right to Desdemona as her husband, and my clear conscience will show for all to see. Is that them?

original: By Janus, I think no.
The servants of the Duke and my lieutenant?  The goodness of the night upon you, friends! What is the news?
translation: My lieutenant, and the servants of the Duke? May this good night be a blessing to you, friends! What's the news?

original: The Duke does greet you, general, And he requires your haste-post-haste appearance, Even on the instant.
translation: The Duke sends his greetings, General. And he orders you to come appear before him immediately, right this very instant.

original: What’s the matter, think you?
translation: What do you think is the matter?

original: Something from Cyprus as I may divine.   It is a business of some heat. The galleys   Have sent a dozen sequent messengers   This very night at one another’s heels,
translation: Something about Cyprus, I would guess. It's an urgent matter. The warships have sent a dozen successive messengers this very night, one after the other.

original: And many of the consuls, raised and met,   Are at the Duke’s already. You have been hotly called  for.
translation: Many of the senators have woken up and met, and are now already at the Duke's. You've been urgently called for.

original: When being not at your lodging to be found   The Senate hath sent about three several guests   To search you out.
translation: When you couldn't be found at your home, the Duke sent three separate search parties to look for you.

original: 'Tis well I am found by you. I will but spend a word here in the house And go with you.
translation: It's a good thing I was found by you. I'll just go say one thing inside, and then I'll go with you.

original: Ancient, what makes he here?
Faith, he tonight hath boarded a land carrack. If it prove lawful prize, he’s made for ever.
translation: In truth, tonight he's boarded a ship carrying lots of treasure. And if his prize turns out to be legal, he'll be well-off forever.

original: I do not understand.
translation: I don't understand.

original: He’s married.
translation: He got married.

original: To who?
translation: To whom?

original: Marry, to—
translation: Indeed, to—

original: Come, captain, will you go?
translation: Come on, captain, will you go now?

original: Have with you.
translation: Yes, I'll go with you.

original: Here comes another troop to seek for you.
translation: Here comes another group of people looking for you.

original: It is Brabantio. General, be advised, He comes to bad intent.
translation: It's Brabantio. General, be advised that he comes with bad intentions.

original: Holla! Stand there!
translation: Hey! Stop right there!

original: Signior, it is the Moor.
translation: Sir, it is the Moor.

original: Down with him, thief!
translation: Get him, the thief!

original: You, Roderigo! Come, sir, I am for you.
translation: You, Roderigo! Come on, sir, I'll fight you.

original: Keep up your bright swords, for the dew will rust  them. Good signior, you shall more command with years Than with your weapons.
translation: Sheathe your shiny swords, or the dew will make them rust. Good sir, your old age commands more respect than your weapons do.

original: O thou foul thief, where hast thou stowed my daughter?   Damned as thou art, thou hast enchanted her!
translation: Oh, you foul thief! Where have you hidden my daughter? Since you're damned yourself, you probably cast a spell on her!

original: For I’ll refer me to all things of sense,   If she in chains of magic were not bound,   Whether a maid so tender, fair, and happy,   So opposite to marriage that she shunned   The wealthy curlèd darlings of our nation,
translation: I'll stake my case on plain evidence and common sense as to whether such a tender, beautiful, and happy virgin girl—one who was so opposed to marriage that she shunned even the wealthy, good-looking young men of our city—

original: Would ever have, t' incur a general mock,   Run from her guardage to the sooty bosom   Of such a thing as thou—to fear, not to delight.
translation: would have ever risked her reputation to run away from her protected home into the dirty embrace of such a thing as you, a thing to be feared and not loved, unless she had been caught by magic.

original: Judge me the world if ’tis not gross in sense   That thou hast practiced on her with foul charms,   Abused her delicate youth with drugs or minerals   That weakens motion. I’ll have ’t disputed on.
translation: Let the world be my judge: isn't it completely obvious that you have practiced some evil magic on her, and abused her delicate youth with drugs or toxins that make her weak? I'll bring you to court.

original: 'Tis probable and palpable to thinking.   I therefore apprehend and do attach thee   For an abuser of the world, a practicer   Of arts inhibited and out of warrant.—
translation: This is most likely what happened. Therefore, I hereby arrest you as a criminal and a practitioner of illegal black magic.

original: Lay hold upon him. If he do resist,   Subdue him at his peril!
translation: [T o the officers]  Get a hold of him. If he resists you, subdue him even if it means hurting him.

original: Hold your hands,   Both you of my inclining and the rest.
translation: Hold on, everyone—both those supporting me, and the rest of you.

original: Were it my cue to fight, I should have known it   Without a prompter. Whither will you that I go   To answer this your charge?
translation: If this were the time to fight, I'd know it without anyone telling me. So where do you want me to go to answer this accusation of yours?

original: To prison, till fit time Of law and course of direct session Call thee to answer.
translation: To prison, until it's time for you to go bear witness at your trial.

original: What if I do obey?   How may the Duke be therewith satisfied,
translation: What happens if I obey you? How would the Duke like that,

original: Whose messengers are here about my side   Upon some present business of the state   To bring me to him?
translation: when he has just sent messengers here to bring me to him on urgent business of the city?

original: 'Tis true, most worthy signior. The Duke’s in council and your noble self, I am sure, is sent for.
translation: That's true, most noble sir. The Duke is in a council meeting, and I am sure you have also been sent for.

original: How? The Duke in council?   In this time of the night? Bring him away.   Mine’s not an idle cause.
translation: What? The Duke is having a council meeting? At this hour of the night? Bring him along with us. My cause isn't a frivolous one.

original: The Duke himself,   Or any of my brothers of the state,   Cannot but feel this wrong as ’twere their own.
translation: The Duke himself, and my fellow senators, will sympathize with my situation as if it were their own.

original: For if such actions may have passage free,   Bondslaves and pagans shall our statesmen be.
translation: For if we let people get away with things like this, our statesmen will be as good as slaves and pagans.

original: There’s no composition in this news That gives them credit.
translation: This news is so inconsistent that it doesn't have any credibility.

original: Indeed, they are disproportioned. My letters say a hundred and seven galleys.
translation: Indeed, it is inconsistent. My letters say a hundred and seven ships.

original: And mine a hundred and forty.
translation: And my letters say a hundred and forty.

original: And mine, two hundred.   But though they jump not on a just account—
translation: And mine say two hundred. But, although our letters do not agree on the exact number,

original: As in these cases, where the aim reports   'Tis oft with difference—yet do they all confirm   A Turkish fleet, and bearing up to Cyprus.
translation: that's often the case with estimates. And all the reports confirm that there is a Turkish fleet heading toward Cyprus.

original: Nay, it is possible enough to judgment.   I do not so secure me in the error,
translation: Indeed, that's clear to see. I am not at ease with the discrepancy in the reports,

original: But the main article I do approve   In fearful sense.
translation: but I understand the general idea of all of them, and it makes me worried.

original: What, ho, what, ho, what, ho!
translation: Hey! Hey!

original: A messenger from the galleys.
translation: It's a messenger from the ship.

original: Now, what’s the business?
translation: What's going on now?

original: The Turkish preparation makes for Rhodes,  So was I bid report here to the state By Signior Angelo.
translation: The Turkish forces are heading for Rhodes. Sir Angelo ordered me to bring this news here to the city government.

original: How say you by this change?
translation: What do you think of this change?

original: This cannot be,   By no assay of reason. 'Tis a pageant,   To keep us in false gaze.
translation: This can't be true. It makes no sense. It must be a trick, to draw our attention in the wrong direction.

original: When we consider   Th' importancy of Cyprus to the Turk,   And let ourselves again but understand   That as it more concerns the Turk than Rhodes   So may he with more facile question bear it,
translation: Think about how important Cyprus is to the Turks, and think how much more the Turks care about Cyprus than Rhodes.  And also consider that they can take over Cyprus more easily than Rhodes,

original: For that it stands not in such warlike brace   But altogether lacks th' abilities   That Rhodes is dressed in.
translation: since it doesn't have the same military defenses that Rhodes has.

original: If we make thought of this   We must not think the Turk is so unskillful   To leave that latest which concerns him first,
translation: Considering all this, we cannot think that the Turks would be so foolish as to leave Cyprus for later when it would be easiest to take first.

original: Neglecting an attempt of ease and gain   To wake and wage a danger profitless.
translation: They wouldn't neglect an easy, profitable mission to undertake a dangerous one that wouldn't benefit them as much.

original: Nay, in all confidence, he’s not for Rhodes.
translation: I agree completely. The Turks cannot be headed for Rhodes.

original: Here is more news.
translation: Here comes more news.

original: The Ottomites, reverend and gracious,  Steering with due course toward the isle of Rhodes, Have there injointed them with an after fleet.
Ay, so I thought. How many, as you guess?
translation: Just as I thought. How many of them do you think are there?

original: Of thirty sail. And now they do re-stem   Their backward course, bearing with frank appearance   Their purposes toward Cyprus.
translation: Thirty ships. And now they are retracing their course backwards, clearly sailing towards Cyprus.

original: Signior Montano,   Your trusty and most valiant servitor,   With his free duty recommends you thus,   And prays you to believe him.
translation: Sir Montano, your trusty and bravest servant, has sent me to bring you this news, and he prays you will believe him.

original: 'Tis certain then for Cyprus. Marcus Luccicos, is not he in town?
translation: Then it's certain that they are going for Cyprus. Is Marcus Luccicos not in town?

original: He’s now in Florence.
translation: He's in Florence now.

original: Write from us to him. Post-post-haste, dispatch.
translation: Write him a letter from us. Right away, hurry now.

original: Here comes Brabantio and the valiant Moor.
translation: Here comes Brabantio and the brave Moor.

original: Valiant Othello, we must straight employ you   Against the general enemy Ottoman—
translation: Brave Othello, we must send you immediately to go fight against the Ottoman forces, enemy to us all.

original: [to BRABANTIO]   I did not see you. Welcome, gentle  signior.   We lacked your counsel and your help tonight.
translation: [To BRABANTIO]  I didn't see you. Welcome,  noble  sir. We missed your advice and help tonight.

original: So did I yours. Good your grace, pardon me.   Neither my place nor aught I heard of business   Hath raised me from my bed,
translation: And I missed your help, too. Your Grace, pardon me. It is neither my official position nor anything I heard about business that has gotten me out of bed.

original: nor doth the general care   Take hold on me, for my particular grief   Is of so flood-gate and o'erbearing nature   That it engluts and swallows other sorrows   And it is still itself.
translation: And it is not the general problem of war that brought me here. Rather, my own particular trouble is so great that it is overwhelming, and takes precedence over other problems.

original: Why, what’s the matter?
translation: Why? What's the matter?

original: My daughter! Oh, my daughter!
translation: My daughter! Oh, my daughter!

original: Dead?
translation: Is she dead?

original: Ay, to me.   She is abused, stol'n from me, and corrupted   By spells and medicines bought of mountebanks.
translation: She's dead to me. She has been abused, stolen from me, and corrupted by spells and potions bought from charlatans.

original: For nature so prepost'rously to err,   Being not deficient, blind, or lame of sense,   Sans witchcraft could not.
translation: For Desdemona is neither lacking in common sense, nor blind to it.  She could not make such a mistake naturally, without some kind of witchcraft.

original: Whoe'er he be that in this foul proceeding   Hath thus beguiled your daughter of herself   And you of her,
translation: Whoever he is that has tricked your daughter in this foul way and robbed you of her,

original: the bloody book of law   You shall yourself read in the bitter letter,   After your own sense, yea, though our proper son   Stood in your action.
translation: you will get to punish him according  whatever your own interpretation is of the law books,  which have the power of the death penalty. Yes, even if it turns out to be my own son who is the perpetrator.

original: Humbly I thank your grace.   Here is the man, this Moor,
translation: I humbly thank you, your Grace. Here is the culprit: this Moor,

original: whom now it seems,   Your special mandate for the state affairs   Hath hither brought.
translation: who it seems your orders have brought here for state business.

original: We are very sorry for’t.
translation: We are very sorry to hear this.

original: What, in your own part, can you say to  this?
translation: What can you say about this on your own behalf?

original: Nothing, but this is so.
translation: There's nothing he can say, except that what I've said is true.

original: Most potent, grave, and reverend signiors,   My very noble and approved good masters,   That I have ta'en away this old man’s daughter,   It is most true. True, I have married her.
translation: Most powerful, serious, and honorable sirs—my very noble masters who have proved to be good to me—I tell you it is absolutely true that I have taken away this old man's daughter. It is true that I have married her.

original: The very head and front of my offending   Hath this extent, no more. Rude am I in my speech,   And little blessed with the soft phrase of peace,
translation: But this is the extent of my offense—no more. I am not good with words, and haven't been blessed with the skill of peaceful speech.

original: For since these arms of mine had seven years' pith   Till now some nine moons wasted, they have used   Their dearest action in the tented field,
translation: My skill is in war: from the time I was seven-years-old to just nine months ago, I have used the strength of my arms on the battlefield.

original: And little of this great world can I speak,   More than pertains to feats of broils and battle,   And therefore little shall I grace my cause   In speaking for myself.
translation: I cannot speak about much in this great big world besides wartime deeds and battle. Therefore, I probably won't help my case much by speaking for myself.

original: Yet, by your gracious patience,   I will a round unvarnished tale deliver   Of my whole course of love.
translation: Nonetheless, if you will be patient, I will tell you the whole straightforward story of my love with Desdemona, and won't embellish it at all.

original: What drugs, what charms,   What conjuration and what mighty magic—   For such proceeding I am charged withal—   I won his daughter.
translation: I will tell you what sort of spells, what kind of powerful magic, what drugs, and what charms I have used to win this man's daughter—since that is the accusation.

original: A maiden never bold,   Of spirit so still and quiet that her motion   Blushed at herself. And she, in spite of nature,   Of years, of country, credit, everything,   To fall in love with what she feared to look on?
translation: My daughter is a young girl who has never been bold. She is so still and quiet and naturally inclined to blushing. Is it possible that she, in spite of her nature, in spite of her young age, in spite of her nationality, in spite of her reputation—in spite of everything—would fall in love with something she feared to even look at?

original: It is a judgment maimed and most imperfect   That will confess perfection so could err.   Against all rules of nature,
translation: It would be a foolish misjudgment to think that my perfect daughter could make such a mistake, contrary to all rules of nature.

original: and must be driven   To find out practices of cunning hell   Why this should be.
translation: We must find out what cunning evil plots have brought this about.

original: I therefore vouch again   That with some mixtures powerful o'er the blood   Or with some dram, conjured to this effect,   He wrought upon her.
translation: Therefore I say again that he has used some potion on her that affects the blood, or some drug magically enchanted for his purpose.

original: To vouch this is no proof,
translation: You say this, but you have no proof.

original: Without more wider and more overt test   Than these thin habits and poor likelihoods   Of modern seeming do prefer against him.
translation: You have no clear evidence beyond your thin accusations and poor guesses based on his appearance.

original: But, Othello, speak.   Did you by indirect and forcèd courses   Subdue and poison this young maid’s affections?
translation: Speak up, Othello. Did you subdue and poison this young girl by trickery and force?

original: Or came it by request and such fair question   As soul to soul affordeth?
translation: Or did the marriage come about voluntarily, as two souls are accustomed to come together?

original: I do beseech you,   Send for the lady to the Sagittary,   And let her speak of me before her father.
translation: I beg you, send someone to get Desdemona from the Sagittary Inn, and let her talk about me in front of her father.

original: If you do find me foul in her report   The trust, the office I do hold of you,   Not only take away, but let your sentence   Even fall upon my life.
translation: If she speaks badly of me, then you can take away my official position, lose all your trust in me, and even sentence me to death.

original: Fetch Desdemona hither.
translation: Bring Desdemona here.

original: Ancient, conduct them. You best know the place.
translation: Flag-bearer, lead them to her. You know the place where she is the best.

original: And till she come, as truly as to heaven   I do confess the vices of my blood   So justly to your grave ears   I’ll present
translation: And until she comes, I'll tell you the story

original: How I did thrive in this fair lady’s love   And she in mine.
translation: of how Desdemona and I fell in love as truthfully as I confess my sins to God.

original: Say it, Othello.
translation: Go ahead and speak, Othello.

original: Her father loved me, oft invited me,   Still questioned me the story of my life   From year to year, the battles, sieges, fortunes,   That I have passed.
translation: Her father loved me and often invited me to his house, where he would ask about the story of my life, about the battles and sieges I've fought in, and the good and bad fortune I've had.

original: I ran it through, even from my boyish days,   To th' very moment that he bade me tell it,   Wherein I spoke of most disastrous chances,
translation: I told him everything, even from when I was a boy, and spoke about disastrous turns of events,

original: Of moving accidents by flood and field,   Of hair-breadth ’scapes i' th' imminent deadly breach,   Of being taken by the insolent foe   And sold to slavery,
translation: moving events on land and on sea, and about times I barely escaped imminent death by a hair's breadth. I told him about how I was taken prisoner by my enemy and sold into slavery,

original: of my redemption thence   And portance in my traveler’s history.   Wherein of antres vast and deserts idle,   Rough quarries, rocks, hills whose heads touch heaven   It was my hint to speak—such was my process—
translation: about how I was ransomed back and how I traveled around through vast caverns and empty deserts, through rough, rocky quarries and hills so high they touch heaven itself.

original: And of the Cannibals that each others eat,   The Anthropophagi, and men whose heads   Grew beneath their shoulders. These things to hear   Would Desdemona seriously incline.
translation: I told him about the cannibals that eat other humans, called the Anthropophagi, and about strange men whose heads grow beneath their shoulders. Desdemona was always fascinated by these stories,

original: But still the house affairs would draw her hence,   Which ever as she could with haste dispatch,   She’d come again, and with a greedy ear   Devour up my discourse,
translation: but household chores would call her away. She did her chores quickly so she could come back and listen voraciously to my stories again.

original: which I, observing,   Took once a pliant hour and found good means   To draw from her a prayer of earnest heart   That I would all my pilgrimage dilate,
translation: When I had some spare time, she asked me to expand on the story of my travels

original: Whereof by parcels she had something heard   But not intentively. I did consent,   And often did beguile her of her tears   When I did speak of some distressful stroke   That my youth suffered.
translation: and fill her in on what she had only heard parts of. I agreed, and my tales often brought her to tears.

original: My story being done   She gave me for my pains a world of sighs.   She swore, in faith, ’twas strange, ’twas passing  strange,   'Twas pitiful, ’twas wondrous pitiful.
translation: When I finished my stories, she would sigh.  She would always say things like, "That was strange, very strange," or "That was pitiful, so pitiful."

original: She wished she had not heard it, yet she wished   That heaven had made her such a man. She thanked me   And bade me, if I had a friend that loved her,
translation: She wished she hadn't heard the moving stories, but also wished that God had made her that kind of a man. She thanked me and told me that if I knew anyone who loved her,

original: I should but teach him how to tell my story   And that would woo her. Upon this hint I spake.
translation: all he would have to do to woo her was to tell her my stories. Picking up on her hint, I spoke to her.

original: She loved me for the dangers I had passed,   And I loved her that she did pity them.   This only is the witchcraft I have used.   Here comes the lady. Let her witness it.
translation: She loved me for the dangers I had endured, and I loved her because she pitied me for having endured them. This is the only witchcraft I have used. Here comes the woman herself. Let her testify.

original: I think this tale would win my daughter too.   Good Brabantio.   Take up this mangled matter at the  best.
translation: I think such a story would win over my daughter, too. Good Brabantio, try to make the best of a bad situation.

original: Men do their broken weapons rather use   Than their bare hands.
translation: As they say, a broken weapon is better than none at all.

original: I pray you, hear her speak.   If she confess that she was half the wooer,   Destruction on my head if my bad blame   Light on the man.—
translation: Please, hear her speak. If she admits that she flirted back, then I will no longer place all the blame on Othello.

original: Come hither, gentle mistress.   Do you perceive in all this noble company   Where most you owe obedience?
translation: Come here, sweet girl. Do you see to whom, out of everyone here, you should be most obedient?

original: My noble father,   I do perceive here a divided duty.   To you I am bound for life and education.
translation: My noble father, I feel that my loyalty is divided. I owe you for my very life and my upbringing.

original: My life and education both do learn me   How to respect you. You are the lord of duty.   I am hitherto your daughter.
translation: And because of this I respect you.  I have a duty to you, as I am your daughter.

original: But here’s my husband.   And so much duty as my mother showed   To you, preferring you before her father,
translation: But here is my husband. And as my mother showed duty to you, prioritizing you above her own father,

original: So much I challenge that I may profess   Due to the Moor my lord.
translation: so must I show duty to my husband, the Moor.

original: God be with you. I have done.   Please it your grace, on to the state affairs.   I had rather to adopt a child than get it.—   Come hither, Moor.
translation: God be with you. I'm finished with my business. If you please, your Grace, you can move on to the state affairs. I'd rather adopt a child than father my own. Come here, Moor.

original: I here do give thee that with all my heart   Which, but thou hast already, with all my heart   I would keep from thee.
translation: I now give you with all my heart my daughter, whom I'd keep from you with all my heart if you didn't already have her.

original: For your sake, jewel,   I am glad at soul I have no other child.   For thy escape would teach me tyranny,   To hang clogs on them.—
translation: For your sake, precious Desdemona, I am glad that I don't have another daughter. For what you have done would make me a tyrannical parent, and I'd lock her up like a prisoner.

original: I have done, my lord.
translation: [To the DUKE]  I'm done with my business, my lord.

original: Let me speak like yourself and lay a sentence   Which, as a grise or step, may help these lovers   Into your favor.
translation: Let me speak, as you have, and offer some proverbs that may help you to be happier with these two lovers.

original: When remedies are past, the griefs are ended   By seeing the worst, which late on hopes depended.   To mourn a mischief that is past and gone   Is the next way to draw new mischief on.
translation: When there's nothing you can do to fix a situation, there's no use crying about it anymore, because you've already survived seeing the worst outcome of your former hopes. To be sad after something bad happens only makes it worse.

original: What cannot be preserved when fortune takes,   Patience her injury a mock'ry makes.   The robbed that smiles steals something from the thief,   He robs himself that spends a bootless grief.
translation: When fortune takes something away from you, you make a mockery of your trouble by being patient. If you've been robbed, it's better to smile and take away the thief's pleasure of making you upset than to grieve about it, and rob yourself even further of good cheer.

original: So let the Turk of Cyprus us beguile,   We lose it not, so long as we can smile.
translation: If that's true, then let the Turks take Cyprus from us, and we'll be fine as long as we smile.

original: He bears the sentence well that nothing bears   But the free comfort which from thence he hears.   But he bears both the sentence and the sorrow   That, to pay grief, must of poor patience borrow.
translation: It's easy to use a proverb when you're not the one suffering a loss,  and not so easy when you're the one suffering grief.

original: These sentences to sugar or to gall,   Being strong on both sides, are equivocal.   But words are words. I never yet did hear   That the bruised heart was piercèd through the ears.
translation: These sayings mean nothing. I've never heard of a time someone's broken heart was made better by words.

original: I humbly beseech you, proceed to th' affairs of state.
translation: I humbly beg you to move on to the state business.

original: The Turk with a most mighty preparation makes for  Cyprus. Othello, the fortitude of the place is best  known to you, and though we have there a substitute of  most allowed sufficiency, yet opinion, a sovereign  mistress of effects, throws a more safer voice on you.
translation: The Turks are heading for Cyprus with a strong fleet. Othello, you know the strengths of the place the best. And although we have someone stationed there who is very skilled, everyone seems to think that you would be better in that position.

original: You must therefore be content to slubber the gloss of  your new fortunes with this more stubborn and boist'rous expedition.
translation: So, you must tinge the happiness of your recent marriage with this difficult mission.

original: The tyrant custom, most grave senators,   Hath made the flinty and steel couch of war   My thrice-driven bed of down.
translation: Honorable senators, I'm so used to the difficult, cruel war that it's as comfortable to me as a soft down bed.

original: I do agnize   A natural and prompt alacrity   I find in hardness, and do undertake   These present wars against the Ottomites.
translation: I am naturally eager to take on difficult challenges, and I will undertake this mission against the Ottomites.

original: Most humbly therefore bending to your state,   I crave fit disposition for my wife.
translation: As I am obeying you, I humbly ask for appropriate arrangements for my wife.

original: Due reference of place and exhibition,   With such accommodation and besort   As levels with her breeding.
