translation: She should have a place to live that is worthy of her nobility, as well as suitable company.

original: Why, at her father’s.
translation: She can have all this at her father's house.

original: I’ll not have it so.
translation: I won't allow it.

original: Nor I.
translation: Neither will I.

original: Nor would I there reside,   To put my father in impatient thoughts   By being in his eye.
translation: And I wouldn't want to stay at my father's house, either, as my presence would irritate him.

original: Most gracious Duke,   To my unfolding lend your prosperous ear   And let me find a charter in your voice,   T' assist my simpleness.
translation: Most gracious Duke, listen to my proposal, and please voice your support for my simple idea.

original: What would you, Desdemona?
translation: What is your idea, Desdemona?

original: That I did love the Moor to live with him,   My downright violence and storm of fortunes   May trumpet to the world. My heart’s subdued   Even to the very quality of my lord.
translation: The quickness and boldness with which I have taken control of my future clearly show that I married the Moor so that I could live with him. My heart is completely under his control.

original: I saw Othello’s visage in his mind,   And to his honors and his valiant parts   Did I my soul and fortunes consecrate.
translation: I saw Othello's true nature in his mind, and dedicated my soul and all my fortune to his honor and bravery.

original: So that, dear lords, if I be left behind   A moth of peace and he go to the war,   The rites for which I love him are bereft me,
translation: So, my dear lords, if I am left behind while he goes off to war, I will be deprived of seeing the very things I married him for.

original: And I a heavy interim shall support   By his dear absence. Let me go with him.
translation: And I will have a horrible time here without him. Let me go with him.

original: Let her have your voice.   Vouch with me, heaven, I therefore beg it not   To please the palate of my appetite,   Nor to comply with heat the young affects   In my defunct and proper satisfaction,
translation: Give your support to her idea. I swear by heaven that I am asking for her to come with me not to satisfy my appetite or fulfill hot urges, since those feelings of youth are defunct in me.

original: But to be free and bounteous to her mind,   And heaven defend your good souls, that you think   I will your serious and great business scant   When she is with me.
translation: I am asking in order to be liberal and open to her ideas. And if any of you think that I will be distracted from my serious and great business there if she is with me, may heaven protect your souls, for you are wrong.

original: No, when light-winged toys   Of feathered Cupid seel with wanton dullness   My speculative and officed instrument,   That my disports corrupt and taint my business,
translation: If winged  Cupid  should ever sew shut my eyes and blind me so that I am more concerned with my pleasures than with business,

original: Let housewives make a skillet of my helm   And all indign and base adversities   Make head against my estimation.
translation: let housewives use my helmet as a skillet and let my reputation be completely ruined.

original: Be it as you shall privately determine,  Either for her stay or going. Th' affair cries haste And speed must answer it.
translation: As to whether she will stay or go, it shall be as you decide privately. But this business is urgent, and we must act quickly.

original: You must away tonight.
translation: You must depart tonight.

original: With all my heart.
translation: With all my heart, I will.

original: At nine i' th' morning here we’ll meet again.   Othello, leave some officer behind   And he shall our commission bring to you,
translation: The rest of us will meet here again at nine in the morning. Othello, leave an officer behind here, and later he can bring you our instructions,

original: And such things else of quality and respect   As doth import you.
translation: and anything else you feel you need.

original: So please your grace, my ancient.   A man he is of honesty and trust.
translation: If you don't mind, I'll leave my flag-bearer behind for the task. He is an honest, trustworthy man,

original: To his conveyance I assign my wife,   With what else needful your good grace shall think   To be sent after me.
translation: and I'll let him bring my wife to Cyprus, along with whatever else your good grace thinks I might need.

original: Let it be so.   Good night to every one.—
translation: Let it be so. Good night to everyone.

original: [to BRABANTIO]   And, noble signior,   If virtue no delighted beauty lack,   Your son-in-law is far more fair than black.
translation: [To BRABANTIO]  And, noble sir, if virtue is a beautiful thing, then your son-in-law is much more  fair  than he is black.

original: Adieu, brave Moor. Use Desdemona well.
translation: Farewell, brave Moor. Be good to Desdemona.

original: Look to her, Moor, if thou hast eyes to see. She has deceived her father, and may thee.
translation: Look out, Moor, and keep an eye on her. She has deceived her father, and may deceive you.

original: My life upon her faith!—Honest Iago,   My Desdemona must I leave to thee.   I prithee, let thy wife attend on her,   And bring them after in the best advantage.
translation: I would bet my life on her honesty! Honest Iago, I must leave Desdemona with you. Please, have your wife look after her, and bring them along after me when you get the chance.

original: Come, Desdemona, I have but an hour   Of love, of worldly matter and direction,   To spend with thee. We must obey the time.
translation: Come with me, Desdemona. I have only an hour to spend with you in love, and to teach you some worldly things. We can't be late.

original: Iago.
translation: Iago.

original: What say’st thou, noble heart?
translation: What is it, noble man?

original: What will I do, think’st thou?
translation: What do you think I should do?

original: Why, go to bed, and sleep.
translation: Well, go to bed and sleep.

original: I will incontinently drown myself.
translation: I will drown myself right now.

original: If thou dost I shall never love thee after. Why, thou  silly gentleman!
translation: If you do that, I'll never love you again. Why would you do such a thing, you silly gentleman?

original: It is silliness to live when to live is torment, and  then have we a prescription to die when death is our  physician.
translation: It is silliness to live when life is torture? When death is the only remedy, then the best prescription is to die.

original: Oh, villainous! I have looked upon the world for four  times seven years, and since I could distinguish betwixt a benefit and an injury I never found man that knew how to love himself.
translation: Oh, please! I've been around for twenty-eight years, and ever since I've known the difference between a good thing and a bad thing, I've never yet found a man who knew what was good for him.

original: Ere I would say I would drown myself  for the love of a guinea hen, I would change my humanity with a baboon.
translation: I'd trade in my humanity to become a baboon before I'd ever say that I'd drown myself for the love of some hen.

original: What should I do? I confess it is my shame to be so  fond, but it is not in my virtue to amend it.
translation: What should I do? I admit it's embarrassing to be so in love, but I can't help it.

original: Virtue? A fig! 'Tis in ourselves that we are thus or  thus. Our bodies are our gardens, to the which our wills are gardeners.
translation: You can't help it? A lie! It's all up to you. Our bodies are like gardens, and our willpower is the gardener.

original: So that if we will plant nettles or sow  lettuce, set hyssop and weed up thyme, supply it with  one gender of herbs or distract it with many—either to  have it sterile with idleness, or manured with  industry—why, the power and corrigible authority of this lies in our wills.
translation: We can have all sorts of different plants in the garden, but whether they grow well or not is up to our will.

original: If the balance of our lives had not  one scale of reason to poise another of sensuality, the  blood and baseness of our natures would conduct us to  most prepost'rous conclusions.
translation: If we didn't have an ounce of reason to counterbalance our passions, our base urges would make us ridiculous.

original: But we have reason to  cool our raging motions, our carnal stings, our unbitted lusts. Whereof I take this that you call love to be a  sect or scion.
translation: But we have rationality to cool our raging emotions, carnal desires, and uncontrollable lust. And what you call love is just an offshoot of this kind of lust.

original: It cannot be.
translation: That can't be true.

original: It is merely a lust of the blood and a permission of  the will. Come, be a man. Drown thyself? Drown cats and  blind puppies! I have professed me thy friend, and I  confess me knit to thy deserving with cables of  perdurable toughness. I could never better stead thee  than now. Put money in thy purse.
translation: It's just lust, and your will is letting it control you. Come on, be a man. Drown yourself? Drown cats and blind puppies instead! I have told you that I am your friend, and our bond is strong. I am being a good friend to you right now. Sell some things to put money in your wallet.

original: Follow thou the wars, defeat thy favor with an usurped beard. I say, put  money in thy purse. It cannot be long that Desdemona  should continue her love to the Moor—put money in thy  purse—nor he his to her.
translation: Desdemona can't stay in love with the Moor for long—get money in your wallet—and he can't stay in love with her.

original: It was a violent commencement  in her, and thou shalt see an answerable  sequestration—put but money in thy purse. These Moors  are changeable in their wills—fill thy purse with  money.
translation: It was such a sudden union, and you'll see an equally quick separation. Put money in your wallet.

original: The food that to him now is as luscious as  locusts shall be to him shortly as bitter as  coloquintida. She must change for youth. When she is  sated with his body she will find the errors of her  choice. Therefore, put money in thy purse.
translation: He now finds her sweet, but before long he'll think she's bitter. She'll want to exchange him for a younger man. Once she's had her fill of his body, she'll realize the errors of her decision. So put money in your wallet.

original: If thou wilt needs damn thyself, do it a more delicate way than  drowning. Make all the money thou canst. If sanctimony  and a frail vow betwixt an erring barbarian and  supersubtle Venetian be not too hard for my wits and all the tribe of hell, thou shalt enjoy her.
translation: If you absolutely must kill yourself, do it a better way than drowning. Gather all the money you can. If a little marriage vow between a wandering barbarian and a gentle Venetian isn't too much for my clever wits, you'll have her soon.

original: Therefore  make money. A pox of drowning thyself! 'Tis clean out  of the way. Seek thou rather to be hanged in compassing thy joy than to be drowned and go without her.
translation: So sell your things for some money! To hell with drowning yourself! That's a ridiculous idea. It would be better to get hanged for committing a crime in an attempt to win her than to drown for being without her.

original: Wilt thou be fast to my hopes, if I depend on the  issue?
translation: Will you be loyal to me, if I need your help?

original: Thou art sure of me. Go, make money. I have told thee  often, and I re-tell thee again and again, I hate the  Moor. My cause is hearted. Thine hath no less reason.  Let us be conjunctive in our revenge against him.
translation: You can rely on me. Go, get some money. I've said it before, and I'll say it again and again: I hate the Moor. My objective is set in my heart. And you are equally determined in yours. Let's work together to get our revenge on him.

original: If  thou canst cuckold him, thou dost thyself a pleasure, me a sport. There are many events in the womb of time  which will be delivered. Traverse, go, provide thy  money. We will have more of this tomorrow. Adieu.
translation: If you can get Desdemona to cheat on him with you, you'd get some pleasure and I'd get some amusement. There's still much that may happen. Now go, go and scrounge up your money. We can discuss this further tomorrow. Goodbye.

original: Where shall we meet i' th' morning?
translation: Where will we meet in the morning?

original: At my lodging.
translation: At my house.

original: I’ll be with thee betimes.
translation: I'll meet you there early.

original: Go to, farewell. Do you hear, Roderigo?
translation: Go on, now. Bye. Now are you listening to me?

original: What say you?
translation: What?

original: No more of drowning, do you hear?
translation: No more of this drowning nonsense, you hear?

original: I am changed.
translation: I've changed my mind about that.

original: Go to, farewell. Put money enough in your purse.
translation: Then go, goodbye. Get enough money together in your wallet.

original: I’ll sell all my land.
translation: I'll sell all my land.

original: Thus do I ever make my fool my purse.   For I mine own gained knowledge should profane   If I would time expend with such a snipe   But for my sport and profit.
translation: Thus I make this fool into my bank account. I'd be wasting my cleverness if I spent time with such an idiot without getting some amusement and money out of it.

original: I hate the Moor,   And it is thought abroad that ’twixt my sheets   He has done my office. I know not if ’t be true,   But I, for mere suspicion in that kind,   Will do as if for surety.
translation: I hate the Moor, and there's a rumor going around that he's slept with my wife. I don't know if this is true, but even just on suspicion, I'll think of it like a sure thing.

original: He holds me well.   The better shall my purpose work on him.   Cassio’s a proper man. Let me see now,   To get his place and to plume up my will   In double knavery. How? How? Let’s see.
translation: He holds me in high esteem. This will be even better for my plan. Cassio is an attractive fellow. Let me think now: how can I get his place as lieutenant and raise up my own status through trickery? How? How? Let's see.

original: After some time, to abuse Othello’s ear   That he is too familiar with his wife.   He hath a person and a smooth dispose   To be suspected, framed to make women false.
translation: In a little while, I can lie to Othello, telling him that Cassio is getting too close with Desdemona. Cassio has the good looks and smooth manners to be suspected of such a thing. He looks like he could get a woman to cheat on her husband.

original: The Moor is of a free and open nature   That thinks men honest that but seem to be so,   And will as tenderly be led by th' nose   As asses are.
translation: The Moor is gullible and trusting. He thinks men are honest when they only appear to be. I can lead him around like a donkey.

original: I have ’t. It is engendered! Hell and night   Must bring this monstrous birth to the world’s light.
translation: That's it. I've laid the seeds of my plan, and it will come to fruition with the help of Hell.

original: What from the cape can you discern at sea?
translation: What can you see out on the sea?

original: Nothing at all. It is a high-wrought flood. I cannot ’twixt the heaven and the main Descry a sail.
translation: Nothing at all. The waters are rough, and I can't see a single sail between the sky and the ocean.

original: Methinks the wind hath spoke aloud at land,   A fuller blast ne'er shook our battlements.
translation: The wind's been blowing loudly on land, too. The strongest gust I've ever seen shook our walls.

original: If it hath ruffianed so upon the sea   What ribs of oak, when mountains melt on them,   Can hold the mortise? What shall we hear of this?
translation: If the same kind of wind has been raging on the sea, what ships made of oak could hold together when waves as tall as mountains strike them? What do you think will happen?

original: A segregation of the Turkish fleet.   For do but stand upon the foaming shore,   The chidden billow seems to pelt the clouds,
translation: The Turkish fleet will be dispersed. From the shore here, the billowing water seems to touch the clouds,

original: The wind-shaked surge, with high and monstrous mane,   Seems to cast water on the burning bear,   And quench the guards of th' ever-fixèd pole.
translation: and the wind-shaken, surging waves, with their high crests, seem to spray water on the constellations in the sky.

original: I never did like molestation view   On the enchafèd flood.
translation: I've never seen such a rough, raging sea.

original: If that the Turkish fleet Be not ensheltered and embayed, they are drowned. It is impossible they bear it out.
translation: Unless the Turkish fleet is sheltered from this storm, they must be drowned. It's impossible for them to survive the storm at sea.

original: News, lads, Our wars are done!   The desperate tempest hath so banged the Turks,   That their designment halts.
translation: I've got news, lads. Our war is over! The storm has battered the Turkish fleet so badly that their attack has been halted.

original: A noble ship of Venice   Hath seen a grievous wreck and sufferance   On most part of their fleet.
translation: A noble Venetian ship has seen most of the Turkish fleet shipwrecked and in trouble.

original: How? Is this true?
translation: What? Is this true?

original: The ship is here put in,   A Veronesa. Michael Cassio,   Lieutenant to the warlike Moor Othello,
translation: The ship that saw all this is now docking here. It came from Verona, bringing Michael Cassio, the lieutenant of the warlike Moor Othello.

original: Is come on shore. The Moor himself at sea   And is in full commission here for Cyprus.
translation: The Moor himself is still at sea, having been ordered to come here to Cyprus.

original: I am glad on ’t. 'Tis a worthy governor.
translation: I'm glad. He's a good governor.

original: But this same Cassio, though he speak of comfort   Touching the Turkish loss, yet he looks sadly   And prays the Moor be safe.
translation: But this Cassio I mentioned—he brings good news about the Turks' losing their ships, but he looks sad and hopes that the Moor is safe at sea.

original: For they were parted   With foul and violent tempest.
translation: Their two ships were separated by the foul, violent storm.

original: Pray heavens he be,   For I have served him, and the man commands   Like a full soldier. Let’s to the seaside, ho!
translation: I pray to heaven that Othello is safe. For I have served under him, and he commands like a perfect soldier. Let's go to the shore,

original: As well to see the vessel that’s come in   As to throw out our eyes for brave Othello,   Even till we make the main and th' aerial blue   An indistinct regard.
translation: both to see the ship that's already arrived, and also to look out for brave Othello, even until it's so dark that we can't tell the blue sky from the sea.

original: Come, let’s do so. For every minute is expectancy Of more arrivance.
translation: Come on, let's do that. Every minute we expect more ships to come in.

original: Thanks, you the valiant of this warlike isle   That so approve the Moor.
translation: Thank you, you brave men of this warlike island, who think highly of the Moor.

original: Oh, let the heavens   Give him defense against the elements,   For I have lost him on a dangerous sea.
translation: Oh, let heaven protect him from the elements. I lost sight of him on the dangerous sea.

original: Is he well shipped?
translation: Does he have a good ship?

original: His bark is stoutly timbered and his pilot   Of very expert and approved allowance
translation: His ship is strongly put together, and the captain is an expert.

original: Therefore my hopes, not surfeited to death,   Stand in bold cure.
translation: Therefore I have hope that he will be okay, and haven't resigned myself to thinking he's dead.

original: A sail, a sail, a sail!
translation: A sail, a sail, a sail!

original: What noise?
translation: What's this noise?

original: The town is empty. On the brow o' th' sea  Stand ranks of people, and they cry “A sail!”
translation: The town is empty. Everyone is standing on the shoreline, and they're crying out, "A sail!"

original: My hopes do shape him for the governor.
translation: I hope the ship they see is the one carrying Othello.

original: They do discharge their shot of courtesy. Our friends at least.
I pray you sir, go forth And give us truth who ’tis that is arrived.
translation: Please sir, go out and then let us know who has arrived.

original: I shall.
translation: I will.

original: But good lieutenant, is your general wived?
translation: Good lieutenant, is your general married?

original: Most fortunately. He hath achieved a maid   That paragons description and wild fame,
translation: Yes, and it's a good marriage. He's married to a woman that surpasses description and exceeds her reputation.

original: One that excels the quirks of blazoning pens,   And in th' essential vesture of creation   Does tire the ingener.
translation: Words can't express how great she is, and no artist could capture her natural beauty.

original: How now? Who has put in?
translation: What's the news? Who has arrived?

original: 'Tis one Iago, ancient to the general.
translation: It's someone named Iago, the general's flag-bearer.

original: He’s had most favorable and happy speed.   Tempests themselves, high seas, and howling winds,   The guttered rocks and congregated sands,   Traitors ensteeped to enclog the guiltless keel,
translation: He's been fortunate to have such a speedy trip. It's as if the storms themselves—the high seas, the howling winds, the jagged rocks, and the heaped up sands—normally bent on wrecking ships,

original: As having sense of beauty, do omit   Their mortal natures, letting go safely by   The divine Desdemona.
translation: have recognized the beauty of the divine Desdemona and went easy on her ship, letting her travel safely.

original: What is she?
translation: Who is she?

original: She that I spake of, our great captain’s captain,   Left in the conduct of the bold Iago,   Whose footing here anticipates our thoughts   A se'nnight’s speed.
translation: The woman I told you about, our great captain's captain, left under bold Iago's watch. She's come here seven days earlier than I expected.

original: Great Jove, Othello guard,   And swell his sail with thine own powerful breath,   That he may bless this bay with his tall ship,   Make love’s quick pants in Desdemona’s arms,
translation: May  Jove  guard Othello and send his ship quickly here, so that he may bless us with his arrival, embrace Desdemona in love,

original: Give renewed fire to our extincted spirits   And bring all Cyprus comfort!
translation: and rekindle the fire in our spirits, bringing comfort to all of Cyprus.

original: Oh, behold,   The riches of the ship is come on shore!   You men of Cyprus, let her have your knees.
translation: Oh, look: the precious passengers of the ship have come on shore. You, men of Cyprus, kneel down.

original: Hail to thee, lady, and the grace of heaven,   Before, behind thee, and on every hand,   Enwheel thee round!
translation: Hail, lady, and may the grace of God be all around you.

original: I thank you, valiant Cassio. What tidings can you tell me of my lord?
translation: Thank you, brave Cassio. What news do you have of my husband?

original: He is not yet arrived. Nor know I aught But that he’s well and will be shortly here.
translation: He hasn't arrived yet. And I don't know anything, but I'm sure he's all right and will be here soon

original: Oh, but I fear. How lost you company?
translation: Oh, but I'm worried. How did you get separated from him?

original: The great contention of the sea and skies Parted our fellowship—
translation: The great storm parted our ships.

original: A sail, a sail!
translation: A sail, a sail!

original: But, hark! a sail.
translation: But look! A sail.

original: They give this greeting to the citadel. This likewise is a friend.
translation: They've fired a shot as a greeting. This ship is also friendly.

original: See for the news.
translation: Go see what's going on.

original: Good ancient, you are welcome.—Welcome, mistress.   (kisses EMILIA)
translation: Good flag-bearer, welcome. And welcome, ma'am.  [He kisses EMILIA]

original: Let it not gall your patience, good Iago,   That I extend my manners. 'Tis my breeding   That gives me this bold show of courtesy.
translation: Now, good Iago, don't get mad that I'm kissing your wife hello. I was brought up to show courtesy that way.

original: Sir, would she give you so much of her lips As of her tongue she oft bestows on me,  You would have have enough.
translation: Sir, if she gave you as much of her lips as she gives me of her talkative tongue, you'd have had enough.

original: Alas, she has no speech!
translation: No, she doesn't talk that much!

original: In faith, too much.   I find it still, when I have leave to sleep.
translation: Really, she talks too much. She even talks when I'm trying to sleep.

original: Marry, before your ladyship, I grant,   She puts her tongue a little in her heart   And chides with thinking.
translation: I admit that maybe she talks less in front of you, and thinks before she speaks.

original: You have little cause to say so.
translation: You have little reason to say that.

original: Come on, come on. You are pictures out of door,   Bells in your parlors, wild-cats in your kitchens,
translation: Come on, come on. You women are the picture of perfection out in public, but annoying as ringing bells in your parlors and like wild-cats in your kitchens.

original: Saints in your injuries, devils being offended,   Players in your housewifery, and hussies in your beds.
translation: When you've been hurt, you act like saints, but when you're offended you act like devils. You all fool around when you should be doing your housewife duties, and you are hussies in bed.

original: Oh, fie upon thee, slanderer!
translation: Oh, curses upon you, you slandering women!

original: Nay, it is true, or else I am a Turk. You rise to play and go to bed to work.
You shall not write my praise.
translation: You're not going to say anything good about me, are you?

original: No, let me not.
translation: No, I won't.

original: What wouldst thou write of me, if thou should’st  praise me?
translation: What would you say about me, if you had to praise me?

original: O gentle lady, do not put me to ’t, For I am nothing, if not critical.
translation: Oh, dear lady, don't put me on the spot. I'm nothing if not overly critical.

original: Come on, assay. There’s one gone to the harbor?
translation: Come on, give it a try. Has someone gone to the harbor?

original: Ay, madam.
translation: Yes, madam.

original: I am not merry, but I do beguile The thing I am by seeming otherwise. Come, how wouldst thou praise me?
translation: I'm not in a good mood, but I'm putting on an act and pretending to be jovial. Tell me, Iago, how would you praise me?

original: I am about it, but indeed my invention   Comes from my pate as birdlime does from frieze,   It plucks out brains and all. But my Muse labors   And thus she is delivered:
translation: I'm thinking. But I'm finding it hard to come up with something. Nonetheless, I've found some inspiration.

original: If she be fair and wise, fairness and wit,   The one’s for use, the other useth it.
translation: Here: if she is beautiful and wise, she'll use her wisdom to make use of her beauty.

original: Well praised! How if she be black and witty?
translation: Clever praise! And what if she's unattractive and smart?

original: If she be black, and thereto have a wit, She’ll find a white that shall her blackness fit.
translation: If she is unattractive, but has some wits, she'll find a man suitable for her appearance.

original: Worse and worse!
translation: That one's worse.

original: How if fair and foolish?
translation: What if she's pretty and foolish?

original: She never yet was foolish that was fair, For even her folly helped her to an heir.
translation: There's never been a woman that was foolish and pretty. For even the stupidity of such a woman would help her find a man.

original: These are old fond paradoxes to make fools laugh i'  th' alehouse.  What miserable praise hast thou for her That’s foul and foolish?
translation: These are old sayings to make fools laugh in the bars. What saying do you have for a woman that's both ugly and foolish?

original: There’s none so foul and foolish thereunto, But does foul pranks which fair and wise ones do.
translation: The ugly, foolish women play the same tricks the pretty, wise ones do.

original: Oh, heavy ignorance! Thou praisest the worst best. But  what praise couldst thou bestow on a deserving woman  indeed, one that in the authority of her merit did  justly put on the vouch of very malice itself?
translation: Oh, you're ignorant! You give the best praise to the worst women. But what would you say about a truly virtuous woman, one that even malicious people would have to admit was a good person?

original: She that was ever fair and never proud,   Had tongue at will and yet was never loud,   Never lacked gold and yet went never gay,   Fled from her wish and yet said “Now I may,”
translation: The woman who was beautiful but not too proud, who was eloquent but not too loud, who never lacked gold but never dressed too extravagantly, who held back her desires even when she could fulfill them,

original: She that being angered, her revenge being nigh,   Bade her wrong stay and her displeasure fly,   She that in wisdom never was so frail   To change the cod’s head for the salmon’s tail,
translation: the woman who, when angry and able to get revenge nonetheless endured her misfortune and turned the other cheek, who was wise enough not to make foolish decisions,

original: She that could think and ne'er disclose her mind,   See suitors following and not look behind,   She was a wight, if ever such wights were—
translation: who could think and not share her thoughts, who could see men pursuing her but not pay them any attention . . . that's the sort of woman —

original: To do what?
translation: The sort of woman to do what?

original: To suckle fools and chronicle small beer.
translation: To raise foolish children and tally household expenditures.

original: Oh, most lame and impotent conclusion! Do not learn of  him, Emilia, though he be thy husband. How say you,  Cassio? Is he not a most profane and liberal counselor?
translation: Oh, what a lame, bad punchline! Emilia, don't listen to him, even though he's your husband. What do you think, Cassio? Doesn't he give profane, poor advice?

original: He speaks home, madam. You may relish him more in the  soldier than in the scholar.
translation: He speaks bluntly, madam. He's a better soldier than a scholar.

original: (   aside   ) He takes her by the palm. Ay, well said,  whisper! With as little a web as this will I ensnare as  great a fly as Cassio. Ay, smile upon her, do, I will  gyve thee in thine own courtship.
translation: [To himself]  He takes her hand. Ah, yes, whisper together. This is all I need to trap Cassio like a fly in my web. Yes, smile at her. I will use your own politeness against you.

original: You say true, 'Tis so, indeed. If such tricks as these strip you out of your  lieutenantry, it had been better you had not kissed  your three fingers so oft, which now again you are most apt to play the sir in.
translation: You tell her, "Yes, you're right." If these little gestures end up taking away your office of lieutenant, you'll wish you hadn't been so flirtatious and gentlemanly to her.

original: Very good, well kissed, and  excellent courtesy! ’tis so, indeed. Yet again your  fingers to your lips? Would they were clyster-pipes for your sake!
translation: Very good, you kissed her well—keep showing such courtesy to her! Yes, that's right. Are you kissing your fingers again? It would be better, for your sake, if those fingers were enema tubes, to get rid of your B.S.

original: The Moor! I know his trumpet.
translation: I know that trumpet! It's the Moor.

original: 'Tis truly so.
translation: Indeed it is.

original: Let’s meet him and receive him.
translation: Let's go meet and welcome him.

original: Lo, where he comes!
translation: Look, he's coming!

original: Oh my fair warrior!
translation: Oh, my beautiful warrior!

original: My dear Othello!
translation: My dear Othello!

original: It gives me wonder great as my content   To see you here before me. Oh, my soul’s joy!
translation: I'm surprised, but happy to see that you made it here before me. Oh, my soul is overjoyed!

original: If after every tempest come such calms,   May the winds blow till they have wakened death,   And let the laboring bark climb hills of seas   Olympus-high, and duck again as low   As hell’s from heaven!
translation: If this is my reward for every sea-storm, then let the winds rage and blow all they can, and let my ships have to climb up mountainous waves and drop down from their crests as if falling from heaven to hell!

original: If it were now to die,   'Twere now to be most happy, for I fear   My soul hath her content so absolute   That not another comfort like to this   Succeeds in unknown fate.
translation: If I were to die now, I'd die at my happiest moment. I don't think my soul will ever be as happy as this again.

original: The heavens forbid But that our loves and comforts should increase, Even as our days do grow.
translation: May heaven give us even more love and comfort as we get older.

original: Amen to that, sweet powers!   I cannot speak enough of this content.
translation: Amen to that, oh heavenly powers! I can't speak enough about how happy I am.

original: It stops me here, it is too much of joy.   And this, and this, the greatest discords be   (kissing  her)   That e'er our hearts shall make!
translation: It's too much joy.  [H e kisses DESDEMONA]  And let this, and this, be the only quarrels we have.

original: Oh, you are well tuned now, But I’ll set down the pegs that make this music, As honest as I am.
translation: You are happy now, but I'll ruin your happiness, no matter how honest you may think I am.

original: Come, let us to the castle.   News, friends! Our wars are done, the Turks are  drowned.   How does my old acquaintance of this isle?—
translation: Come on, let's go to the castle. I have good news, friends! The war is over, and the Turks are all drowned. How is my old friend on this island doing?

original: Honey, you shall be well desired in Cyprus,   I have found great love amongst them. O my sweet,   I prattle out of fashion, and I dote   In mine own comforts.—
translation: [To DESDEMONA] @

original: I prithee, good Iago,   Go to the bay and disembark my coffers.
translation: [To IAGO]  Iago, if you don't mind, go to the bay and unload my chests from the ship.

original: Bring thou the master to the citadel.   He is a good one, and his worthiness   Does challenge much respect.—
translation: Bring the ship captain to the castle. He's a good man, and his virtue demands respect.

original: Come, Desdemona,   Once more, well met at Cyprus.
translation: [To DESDEMONA]  Come with me Desdemona.   One more time: it's so nice to see you at Cyprus.

original: (to the attendant)   Do thou meet me presently at the  harbor.
translation: [To an attendant]  Meet me in a minute at the harbor.

original: (to RODERIGO)   Come hither. If thou be’st  valiant, as they say base men being in love have then a  nobility in their natures more than is native to them,  list me.
translation: [To RODERIGO]  Come here. If you are brave—for after all, they say that lousy men acquire more nobility than they naturally have when they are in love—listen to me.

original: The lieutenant tonight watches on the court of  guard. First, I must tell thee this: Desdemona is  directly in love with him.
translation: Tonight, the lieutenant Cassio will be on guard. First of all, I have to tell you this: Desdemona is in love with him.

original: With him? Why, ’tis not possible.
translation: With him? But that's not possible.

original: Lay thy finger thus, and let thy soul be instructed.  Mark me with what violence she first loved the Moor, but for bragging and telling her fantastical lies. To love  him still for prating?
translation: Quiet for a second, and listen up. Remember how quickly she fell in love with the Moor, all over some bragging and made-up fantastical stories. Do you think she still loves him now for talking?

original: Let not thy discreet heart think  it. Her eye must be fed, and what delight shall she have to look on the devil? When the blood is made dull with  the act of sport, there should be a game to inflame it  and to give satiety a fresh appetite, loveliness in  favor, sympathy in years, manners and beauties.
translation: Don't think this for a second. She wants something nice to look at, and she won't get that with the devil Othello. When she gets bored with having sex, she'll need to find something to inflame her passion again—someone good-looking, closer to her age, and more like her in behavior and appearance.

original: All  which the Moor is defective in. Now for want of these  required conveniences, her delicate tenderness will find itself abused, begin to heave the gorge, disrelish and  abhor the Moor. Very nature will instruct her in it and  compel her to some second choice.
translation: She'll find none of this in the Moor. Without any of these desirable things, she'll get so sick of the Moor she'll want to throw up. Her very nature will compel her to find a second man.

original: Now sir, this  granted—as it is a most pregnant and unforced  position—who stands so eminent in the degree of this  fortune as Cassio does? A knave very voluble, no further conscionable than in putting on the mere form of civil  and humane seeming, for the better compassing of his  salt and most hidden loose affection.
translation: Now, sir, given all this obvious information, who do you think she will turn to if not Cassio? He's eloquent, and puts up a facade of good manners to hide his real desires.

original: Why, none, why,  none! A slipper and subtle knave, a finder of occasions  that has an eye, can stamp and counterfeit advantages,  though true advantage never present itself. A devilish  knave.
translation: She'll choose no one but him. He's a tricky, opportunistic villain, who takes advantage of situations. He's a devilish fool.

original: Besides, the knave is handsome, young, and hath  all those requisites in him that folly and green minds  look after. A pestilent complete knave, and the woman  hath found him already.
translation: And besides, this scoundrel is handsome, young, and has everything that foolish young women look for in a man. He's an awful and complete rascal, and Desdemona's already found him.

original: I cannot believe that in her. She’s full of most  blessed condition.
translation: I can't believe this about Desdemona. She's such a good, blessed woman.

original: Blessed fig’s-end! The wine she drinks is made of  grapes. If she had been blessed, she would never have  loved the Moor.
translation: Blessed? As if. She drinks the same wine we do. If she was really blessed, she never would have fallen in love with the Moor.

original: Blessed pudding! Didst thou not see her  paddle with the palm of his hand? Didst not mark that?
translation: Blessed? Nonsense! Didn't you see her playing with Cassio's hand? Didn't you notice that?

original: Yes, that I did, but that was but courtesy.
translation: Yes, I did notice that. But it was just courtesy.

original: Lechery, by this hand, an index and obscure prologue to the history of lust and foul thoughts. They met so near with their lips that their breaths embraced together.  Villainous thoughts, Roderigo!
translation: It was flirtation, the sort of thing that leads to foul thoughts and lust. Their faces were so close to each other that they almost breathed the same breath. It's horrible to think about, Roderigo!

original: When these mutabilities  so marshal the way, hard at hand comes the master and  main exercise, th' incorporate conclusion. Pish! But,  sir, be you ruled by me. I have brought you from Venice. Watch you tonight for the command, I’ll lay ’t upon  you. Cassio knows you not.
translation: When this kind of behavior happens, the main event isn't far away—the physical consummation. Psh! But, sir, let me tell you what to do. I've brought you here from Venice. Wait for my command tonight. Cassio doesn't know who you are.

original: I’ll not be far from you. Do  you find some occasion to anger Cassio, either by  speaking too loud, or tainting his discipline, or from  what other course you please, which the time shall more  favorably minister.
translation: I won't be far away from you. Find some excuse to make Cassio angry, either by speaking too loudly, or mocking his discipline, or whatever way you want that seems like a good idea at the time.

original: Well.
translation: Okay.

original: Sir, he’s rash and very sudden in choler, and haply may strike at you. Provoke him that he may. For even out of that will I cause these of Cyprus to mutiny, whose  qualification shall come into no true taste again but by the displanting of Cassio.
translation: Sir, Cassio has a bad temper, and maybe he'll try to hit you. Provoke him so that he will. Then, if he hits you, I'll use that as an excuse to stir up a riot of the inhabitants of Cyprus—a riot that won't die down until Cassio is stripped of his position as lieutenant.

original: So shall you have a shorter  journey to your desires by the means I shall then have  to prefer them, and the impediment most profitably  removed, without the which there were no expectation of  our prosperity.
translation: This will give you an easier path to getting what you want, with my help, and it will get Cassio out of your way. With him standing in the way, you would have no hope of getting what you want.

original: I will do this, if you can bring it to any opportunity.
translation: I will do this, if you give me the chance.

original: I warrant thee. Meet me by and by at the citadel. I  must fetch his necessaries ashore. Farewell.
translation: I promise I will. Meet me later at the castle. I have to bring Othello's things in from the boat. Goodbye.

original: Adieu.
translation: Goodbye.

original: That Cassio loves her, I do well believe ’t.   That she loves him, ’tis apt and of great credit.   The Moor, howbeit that I endure him not,   Is of a constant, loving, noble nature,   And I dare think he’ll prove to Desdemona   A most dear husband.
translation: I really do believe that Cassio loves Desdemona. And I think it's probable that she loves him. Although I hate the Moor, he really is steadfast, loving, and noble, and I think he'll be a good husband to Desdemona.

original: Now, I do love her too,   Not out of absolute lust—though peradventure   I stand accountant for as great a sin—
translation: Now, I love her too, but not just out of lust—though I'm guilty of that, too—

original: But partly led to diet my revenge,   For that I do suspect the lusty Moor   Hath leaped into my seat.
translation: but also in order to carry out my revenge. For I suspect the lusty Moor has slept with my wife.

original: The thought whereof   Doth, like a poisonous mineral, gnaw my inwards,   And nothing can or shall content my soul   Till I am evened with him, wife for wife.
translation: The thought of it gnaws my insides like a poison, and I won't be satisfied until I've gotten even with him—a wife for a wife.

original: Or, failing so, yet that I put the Moor   At least into a jealousy so strong   That judgment cannot cure.
translation: Or, failing that, I'll at least make the Moor so jealous that no good judgment can fix it.

original: Which thing to do,   If this poor trash of Venice, whom I trace   For his quick hunting, stand the putting on,   I’ll have our Michael Cassio on the hip,
translation: And I'll have Michael Cassio right where I want him to carry out that plan—as long as this piece of Venetian trash, Roderigo, does as I've told him.

original: Abuse him to the Moor in the right garb   (For I fear Cassio with my night-cape too)   Make the Moor thank me, love me, and reward me   For making him egregiously an ass   And practicing upon his peace and quiet   Even to madness.
translation: I'll speak ill of Cassio to Othello, and the Moor will love me and reward me for it, even though all I'll be doing is making an ass of him and destroying his peace and quiet.

original: 'Tis here, but yet confused.   Knavery’s plain face is never seen till used.
translation: It's all doable, but I haven't worked out all the details yet. Evil plots never reveal themselves fully until they've worked.

original: It is Othello’s pleasure, our noble and valiant  general, that, upon certain tidings now arrived,  importing the mere perdition of the Turkish fleet, every man put himself into triumph: some to dance, some to  make bonfires, each man to what sport and revels his  addiction leads him.
translation: It is our noble, brave General Othello's desire that every man celebrate, since we know the Turkish fleet has been completely destroyed. Some can dance, some can make bonfires—everyone can find whatever enjoyment he likes best.

original: For besides these beneficial news,  it is the celebration of his nuptial. So much was his  pleasure should be proclaimed.
translation: Besides the good news about the Turks, we are also celebrating his marriage. This is what he asked me to announce.

original: All offices are open, and there is full liberty of feasting from this present  hour of five till the bell have told eleven. Bless the  isle of Cyprus and our noble general Othello!
translation: All the kitchens are open, and everyone is welcome to feast from now, five o'clock, until eleven o'clock. God bless the island of Cyprus and our noble general, Othello!

original: Good Michael, look you to the guard tonight. Let’s teach ourselves that honorable stop Not to outsport discretion.
translation: Good Michael, take care of the guard duties tonight. Let's show some self-restraint and not celebrate to the point of excess.

original: Iago hath direction what to do,  But notwithstanding with my personal eye Will I look to ’t.
translation: Iago knows what he is supposed to do. But nonetheless, I will personally look after things.

original: Iago is most honest.   Michael, good night. Tomorrow with your earliest   Let me have speech with you.—
translation: Iago is most honest. Good night, Michael. Come speak with me tomorrow as soon as you're up.

original: Come, my dear love,   The purchase made, the fruits are to ensue:   That profit’s yet to come ’tween me and you.   Good night.
translation: [To DESDEMONA]  Come with me, my dear love. Now that we're married, the consummation is to follow. We have not yet enjoyed that benefit. Good night.

original: Welcome, Iago. We must to the watch.
translation: Welcome, Iago. We must go be on the lookout.

original: Not this hour, lieutenant, ’tis not yet ten o' the  clock. Our general cast us thus early for the love of  his Desdemona—who let us not therefore blame.
translation: Not now, lieutenant. It's not ten o'clock yet. Our general left us so early so he could spend time with his love Desdemona—and who could blame him?

original: He hath  not yet made wanton the night with her, and she is sport for Jove.
translation: They haven't slept together yet, and she's beautiful enough to catch  Jove's  eye.

original: She’s a most exquisite lady.
translation: She's a most beautiful lady.

original: And, I’ll warrant her, full of game.
translation: And I'll bet she has a trick or two up her sleeve.

original: Indeed she’s a most fresh and delicate creature.
translation: Indeed, she's a young, delicate creature.

original: What an eye she has! Methinks it sounds a parley to  provocation.
translation: What nice eyes she has! They could provoke a war.

original: An inviting eye, and yet methinks right modest.
translation: She has an inviting eye, and yet I think she's very modest.

original: And when she speaks, is it not an alarum to love?
translation: And when she speaks, isn't it like a call to arms for lovers?

original: She is indeed perfection.
translation: She really is perfect.

original: Well, happiness to their sheets! Come, lieutenant, I  have a stoup of wine, and here without are a brace of  Cyprus gallants that would fain have a measure to the  health of black Othello.
translation: Well, may she and Othello be happy in bed! Come now, lieutenant—I have a jug of wine and there are a couple of gentlemen from Cyprus here who'd gladly want to drink a toast to the health of black Othello.

original: Not tonight, good Iago. I have very poor and unhappy  brains for drinking. I could well wish courtesy would  invent some other custom of entertainment.
translation: Not tonight, good Iago. I'm not a very good drinker. I wish it was customary to celebrate in some other way.

original: Oh, they are our friends. But one cup. I’ll drink for  you.
translation: Oh, but they're our friends. Just one drink. I'll even drink it for you.

original: I have drunk but one cup tonight, and that was craftily qualified too, and behold what innovation it makes  here. I am unfortunate in the infirmity, and dare not  task my weakness with any more.
translation: I've had one drink so far tonight, and it was a strong one. And see how much it's affected me? I unfortunately don't have a very good tolerance for alcohol, and I don't want to risk drinking any more.

original: What, man, ’tis a night of revels! The gallants desire  it.
translation: What? It's a night of celebration, man! The gentlemen want you to join.

original: Where are they?
translation: Where are they?

original: Here at the door. I pray you call them in.
translation: Here at the door. Please, call them in.

original: I’ll do ’t, but it dislikes me.
translation: I will, but I don't like where this is going.

original: If I can fasten but one cup upon him,   With that which he hath drunk tonight already,   He’ll be as full of quarrel and offense   As my young mistress' dog.
translation: If I can get him to have just one drink, together with what he's already had to drink, he'll be as belligerent and testy as a badly trained as a young girl's pet dog.

original: Now my sick fool Roderigo,   Whom love hath turned almost the wrong side out,   To Desdemona hath tonight caroused   Potations pottle-deep, and he’s to watch.
translation: Now my fool Roderigo—whom love has practically turned inside out, has drunk whole pots full of wine in toasts to Desdemona—and he's on guard duty.

original: Three lads of Cyprus, noble swelling spirits   (That hold their honors in a wary distance,   The very elements of this warlike isle)   Have I tonight flustered with flowing cups,   And they watch too.
translation: I've gotten three men from Cyprus drunk as well, noble men who are worried about maintaining their honor (which is important in this warlike island), and they are also on guard duty.

original: Now ’mongst this flock of drunkards   Am I to put our Cassio in some action   That may offend the isle.
translation: Now among this flock of drunkards, I will put Cassio, and I'll have him do something to offend the men of Cyprus.

original: But here they come.   If consequence do but approve my dream   My boat sails freely, both with wind and stream.
translation: But here they come. If things turn out as I want them to, I've got smooth sailing ahead.

original: 'Fore heaven, they have given me a rouse already.
translation: By heaven, they have already given me a drink.

original: Good faith, a little one, not past a pint, As I am a  soldier.
translation: Just a little one, really, no more than a pint I promise, on my soldier's honor.

original: Some wine, ho!   (sings)
translation: Hey, more wine! [Singing]

original: And let me the cannikin clink, clink,   And let me the cannikin clink.   A soldier’s a man,
translation: And let me clink, clink the little can, And let me clink the little can, A soldier's a man,

original: A life’s but a span,   Why then let a soldier drink.   Some wine, boys!
translation: With a short life span, So why don't we soldiers drink! Some more wine, boys!

original: Fore heaven, an excellent song.
translation: By heaven, that's an excellent song.

original: I learned it in England, where indeed they are most  potent in potting. Your Dane, your German, and your  swag-bellied Hollander—Drink, ho!—are nothing to your  English.
translation: I learned it in England, where they really are strong drinkers. The Danes, the Germans, and the pot-bellied Dutch—drink, everybody!—can't compare to the English in drinking.

original: Is your Englishman so expert in his drinking?
translation: Are the English really so good at drinking?

original: Why, he drinks you with facility your Dane dead drunk;  he sweats not to overthrow your Almain. He gives your  Hollander a vomit ere the next pottle can be filled.
translation: Why, an Englishman could easily drink a Dane under the table, and wouldn't sweat out-drinking a German. And if a Dutchman tried to go drink for drink with an Englishman, the Dutchman would end up vomiting before they could even refill his cup.

original: To the health of our general!
translation: A toast, to the health of our general!

original: I am for it, lieutenant, and I’ll do you justice.
translation: I'll toast to that, lieutenant! And I'll match you, drink for drink.

original: Oh, sweet England!   (sings)
translation: Oh, sweet England! [Singing]

original: King Stephen was a worthy peer,   His breeches cost him but a crown,   He held them sixpence all too dear,     With that he called the tailor lown.
translation: King Stephen was a good fellow, He paid just a dollar for his pants, But still thought he'd been overcharged, So he called the tailor a rogue.

original: He was a wight of high renown,   And thou art but of low degree,   'Tis pride that pulls the country down,   Then take thine auld cloak about thee.   Some wine, ho!
translation: He was a man with a good reputation, And you're just a lowly man, It's pride that brings the country down, So wrap yourself up in your old cloak. Some more wine!

original: Why, this is a more exquisite song than the other.
translation: Why, that song is even better than the last.

original: Will you hear ’t again?
translation: Do you want to hear it again?

original: No, for I hold him to be unworthy of his place that  does those things. Well, heaven’s above all, and there  be souls must be saved, and there be souls must not be  saved.
translation: No, I find men who do things like that to be acting below their social rank. Anyways, heaven is the final judge of us all, and some souls must go to heaven while others go to hell.

original: It’s true, good lieutenant.
translation: That's true, good lieutenant.

original: For mine own part, no offence to the general nor any  man of quality, I hope to be saved.
translation: As far as I'm concerned, I hope to go to heaven—no offense to the general or any noble man.

original: And so do I too, lieutenant.
translation: I hope to go to heaven, too, lieutenant.

original: Ay, but (by your leave) not before me. The lieutenant  is to be saved before the ancient. Let’s have no more of this, let’s to our affairs.—Forgive us our  sins!—Gentlemen, let’s look to our business.
translation: Yes, but, if you don't mind, not before me. A lieutenant's must get into heaven before the flag-bearer. But enough of this, let's get down to business. Forgive us our sins, God! Gentlemen, let's get to work.

original: Do not  think, gentlemen, I am drunk. This is my ancient, this  is my right hand, and this is my left. I am not drunk  now. I can stand well enough, and I speak well enough.
translation: Don't think I'm drunk now, gentlemen. Here's my flag-bearer. This is my right hand, and this is my left hand. I'm not drunk. I can stand well enough, and my words aren't slurred.

original: Excellent well!
translation: Very good!

original: Why, very well then. You must not think then that I am  drunk.
translation: Very well, then. You must not think that I am drunk.

original: To th' platform, masters. Come, let’s set the watch.
translation: To the platform, gentlemen. Come on, let's take up our posts for tonight's guard.

original: You see this fellow that is gone before,   He is a soldier fit to stand by Caesar   And give direction.
translation: You see this man who just left, Cassio? He is such a good soldier he could be a commander in and help lead Caesar's army.

original: And do but see his vice,   'Tis to his virtue a just equinox,   The one as long as th' other. 'Tis pity of him.
translation: But his vice is equal to his virtue. It's too bad.

original: I fear the trust Othello puts him in   On some odd time of his infirmity   Will shake this island.
translation: I worry, though, that the trust Othello puts in him will cause a lot of trouble on this island at some point when Cassio is drunk.

original: But is he often thus?
translation: But is he often this drunk?

original: 'Tis evermore the prologue to his sleep. He’ll watch the horologe a double set If drink rock not his cradle.
translation: He's always drunk before going to bed. He can't sleep unless he's had something to drink.

original: It were well   The general were put in mind of it.
translation: The general should know about this.

original: Perhaps he sees it not, or his good nature   Prizes the virtue that appears in Cassio   And looks not on his evils. Is not this true?
translation: Perhaps he doesn't see this, or he only sees the virtues in Cassio and is blind to his faults. What do you think?

original: How now, Roderigo? I pray you, after the lieutenant, go!
translation: What's going on, Roderigo? Please, follow the lieutenant, go!

original: And ’tis great pity that the noble Moor   Should hazard such a place as his own second   With one of an ingraft infirmity.
translation: And it's such a pity that the noble Moor has made someone with such a weakness for alcohol his second in command.

original: It were an honest action to say   So to the Moor.
translation: I really ought to tell Othello about this.

original: Not I, for this fair island. I do love Cassio well, and would do much To cure him of this evil—
translation: I wouldn't tell him, not if you gave me this beautiful island in return. I love Cassio, and would do anything to cure him of his alcoholism—

original: But, hark! What noise?
translation: But listen! What is that noise?

original: Zounds! You rogue! You rascal!
translation: Christ! You scoundrel! You rascal!

original: What’s the matter, lieutenant?
translation: What's the matter, lieutenant?

original: A knave teach me my duty? I’ll beat the knave into a twiggen bottle.
translation: A rogue is going to tell me what to do? I'll beat the scoundrel to a pulp.

original: Beat me?
translation: Beat me?

original: Dost thou prate, rogue?
translation: Did you say something, you rogue?

original: Nay, good lieutenant! I pray you, sir, hold your hand.
translation: No, good lieutenant! Please, sir, stop hitting him!

original: Let me go, sir, or I’ll knock you o'er the mazzard.
translation: Let me go, sir, or I'll  strike you on your head.

original: Come, come, you're drunk.
translation: Stop that. You're drunk.

original: Drunk?
translation: Drunk?

original: (aside to RODERIGO)  Away, I say, go out, and cry a  mutiny.
translation: Go away, I tell you. Run off and shout out that there's a brawl.

original: Nay, good lieutenant! Alas, gentlemen— Help, ho!— Lieutenant—sir, Montano— Help, masters!—Here’s a goodly watch indeed!
translation: Hey, good lieutenant! No, gentlemen! Hey, help! Lieutenant—sir Montano—Gentlemen, help!—Some fine guards these guys are.

original: Who’s that which rings the bell?—Diablo, ho!  The town will rise. Fie, Fie, lieutenant, You’ll be ashamed for ever.
translation: Who's ringing that bell? The devil! It's going to wake up the town. For shame, lieutenant, stop or you'll never live this down.

original: What is the matter here?
translation: What's the matter here?

original: I bleed still, I am hurt to the death. He dies!
translation: I'm bleeding. I'm mortally wounded. Cassio must die!

original: Hold, for your lives!
translation: Stop, for God's sake!

original: Hold, ho! Lieutenant—sir, Montano—gentlemen,   Have you forgot all place of sense and duty?
translation: Stop, lieutenant! Sir Montano—Gentlemen, are you out of your minds? Have you forgotten your sense of duty?

original: Hold! The general speaks to you. Hold, for shame!
translation: Stop! The general is talking to you. Stop, for shame!

original: Why, how now, ho! From whence ariseth this?   Are we turned Turks? And to ourselves do that   Which heaven hath forbid the Ottomites?
translation: What is going on? What is the reason for this fight? Have we become Turks? Are we attacking ourselves since fate stopped the Turks from attacking us?

original: For Christian shame, put by this barbarous brawl.   He that stirs next to carve for his own rage   Holds his soul light, he dies upon his motion.
translation: You are Christians; stop this barbarous brawl. The next one of you to raise a fist must not value his life very much, for I'll kill whoever moves.

original: Silence that dreadful bell, it frights the isle   From her propriety. What is the matter, masters?—
translation: Silence that annoying bell. It will worry everyone on the island. What is the matter, gentlemen?

original: Honest Iago, that looks dead with grieving,   Speak, who began this? On thy love, I charge thee.
translation: Honest Iago, you look sick with worry. Tell me, who started this? I command you to tell me, if you care for me.

original: I do not know. Friends all but now, even now,   In quarter, and in terms like bride and groom   Divesting them for bed.
translation: I don't know who started it. We were all friends just a moment ago, as close as a bride and groom going to bed.

original: And then, but now,   As if some planet had unwitted men,   Swords out, and tilting one at other’s breasts   In opposition bloody.
translation: But then, just now, as if some cosmic shift of the planets had affected them, they drew their swords and started lunging at each other in a bloody fight.

original: I cannot speak   Any beginning to this peevish odds,   And would in action glorious I had lost   Those legs that brought me to a part of it.
translation: I can't say what was the cause of it, and I wish I didn't have the legs that brought me here to take part in it.

original: How comes it, Michael, you are thus forgot?
translation: How have you become so out of your mind, Michael?

original: I pray you pardon me, I cannot speak.
translation: Please, forgive me. There's nothing I can say in my defense.

original: Worthy Montano, you were wont be civil.   The gravity and stillness of your youth   The world hath noted, and your name is great   In mouths of wisest censure.
translation: Noble Montano, you are usually civil. You are famous for the discipline and restraint you show in your youth. Even those who are fond of criticizing can't help but praise you.

original: What’s the matter   That you unlace your reputation thus   And spend your rich opinion for the name   Of a night-brawler? Give me answer to it.
translation: What's the matter? What has caused you to throw away your reputation and trade in your good name for that of a night-brawler? Tell me.

original: Worthy Othello, I am hurt to danger.   Your officer Iago can inform you,   While I spare speech, which something now offends me,   Of all that I do know.
translation: Noble Othello, I am seriously injured. So that I save my energy by not speaking, your officer Iago can tell you all that I know.

original: Nor know I aught   By me that’s said or done amiss this night,   Unless self-charity be sometimes a vice,
translation: I don't know of anything I said or did wrong, unless taking care of yourself is a vice,

original: And to defend ourselves it be a sin   When violence assails us.
translation: and defending ourselves when someone attacks us is a sin.

original: Now, by heaven,   My blood begins my safer guides to rule,   And passion, having my best judgment collied,   Assays to lead the way.
translation: Now, by heaven, my anger starts to overwhelm my reason, and passion is working to take over my good judgment.

original: If I once stir,   Or do but lift this arm, the best of you   Shall sink in my rebuke. Give me to know   How this foul rout began, who set it on,
translation: I have the ability to make either of you regret this. Tell me how this foul brawl began and who started it.

original: And he that is approved in this offence,   Though he had twinned with me, both at a birth,   Shall lose me.
translation: I'll sever my ties with whoever started this fight—even if it were my twin brother, I'd do this.

original: What, in a town of war   Yet wild, the people’s hearts brimful of fear,   To manage private and domestic quarrel?
translation: We're in a town during wartime, and the citizens are all nervous, and you decide to have a fight between yourselves?

original: In night, and on the court and guard of safety?   'Tis monstrous. Iago, who began ’t?
translation: At night, when you should be on guard duty? This is a horrible offense. Iago, who started the fight?

original: If partially affined or leagued in office Thou dost deliver more or less than truth Thou art no soldier.
translation: If you don't tell the truth because you're partial to Cassio, then you don't deserve the title of soldier.

original: Touch me not so near.   I had rather have this tongue cut from my mouth   Than it should do offence to Michael Cassio.
translation: Don't accuse me of such a thing. I would rather have my tongue cut out of my mouth than speak ill of Michael Cassio.

original: Yet I persuade myself to speak the truth   Shall nothing wrong him. This it is, general:
translation: But I think that speaking the truth cannot wrong him. This is the truth, general:

original: Montano and myself being in speech,   There comes a fellow crying out for help   And Cassio following him with determined sword   To execute upon him.
translation: Montano and I were talking, and all of a sudden a man came crying out for help, and Cassio was chasing after him with his sword drawn.

original: Sir, this gentleman   Steps in to Cassio and entreats his pause,   Myself the crying fellow did pursue,   Lest by his clamor—as it so fell out—   The town might fall in fright.
translation: Sir, this gentleman stepped in to stop Cassio, while I chased after the shouting man, because I was worried his clamor would awaken and scare the townspeople.

original: He, swift of foot,   Outran my purpose, and I returned then rather   For that I heard the clink and fall of swords   And Cassio high in oath,
translation: He was too fast for me, though, so I returned here, as I heard the clink of swords and Cassio swearing oaths.

original: which till tonight   I ne'er might say before. When I came back—   For this was brief— I found them close together   At blow and thrust,
translation: I've never heard Cassio talk like that before. When I got back here I found these two fighting,

original: even as again they were   When you yourself did part them.   More of this matter cannot I report.
translation: just as they were when you got here and separated them. That's all I know.

original: But men are men, the best sometimes forget.   Though Cassio did some little wrong to him,   As men in rage strike those that wish them best,
translation: In his rage, Cassio wronged Montano, who was only trying to help,

original: Yet surely Cassio, I believe, received   From him that fled some strange indignity   Which patience could not pass.
translation: but I think that Cassio must have received some strange insult from the man who ran away that he simply couldn't tolerate.

original: I know, Iago,  Thy honesty and love doth mince this matter, Making it light to Cassio. Cassio, I love thee But never more be officer of mine.—
translation: Iago, I realize that your affection for Cassio makes you downplay what he has done. Cassio, I love you, but you are no longer one of my officers.

original: Look, if my gentle love be not raised up! I’ll make thee an example.
translation: Look, my gentle wife was woken up by this! I'll make an example out of you, Cassio.

original: What’s the matter, dear?
translation: What's the matter, dear?

original: All’s well, sweeting, Come away to bed.—    Sir, for your hurts Myself will be your surgeon. Lead him off.
translation: Everything is fine, my sweet. Go back to bed.  Sir, I myself will tend to your wounds. Someone lead him away.

original: Iago, look with care about the town   And silence those whom this vile brawl distracted.—
translation: Iago, look carefully around town, and calm down anyone who feels riled up after this awful fight.

original: Come, Desdemona, ’tis the soldiers' life   To have their balmy slumbers waked with strife.
translation: Come on, Desdemona, it's typical for a soldier to have his sleep interrupted by strife and turmoil.

original: What, are you hurt, lieutenant?
translation: Are you hurt, lieutenant?

original: Ay, past all surgery.
translation: Yes, beyond anything a doctor can help with.

original: Marry, heaven forbid!
Reputation, reputation, reputation! Oh, I have lost my  reputation! I have lost the immortal part of myself, and what remains is bestial. My reputation, Iago, my  reputation!
translation: I mean my reputation. Reputation, reputation! Oh, I have lost my reputation! I've lost the only part of me that will live on after my death, and what remains is some kind of beast. My reputation, Iago, my reputation!

original: As I am an honest man, I thought you had received some  bodily wound. There is more sense in that than in  reputation. Reputation is an idle and most false  imposition, oft got without merit and lost without  deserving.
translation: I'm an honest man who takes things literally, so I thought you had been seriously wounded. That would be worse than losing your reputation. Reputation is an empty, stupid idea. Often people get good reputations when they don't deserve it, and people lose their reputations unfairly.

original: You have lost no reputation at all unless you repute yourself such a loser. What, man, there are ways to recover the general again.
translation: You haven't lost your reputation unless you consider yourself to have lost it. Come on, man, there are ways to gain back the general's favor.

original: You are but now cast in  his mood, a punishment more in policy than in malice,  even so as one would beat his offenseless dog to  affright an imperious lion. Sue to him again and he’s  yours.
translation: He's just in a bad mood, and he punished you because he had to in front of the men of Cyprus, not because he dislikes you. It's like someone beating their dog in front of a strong lion, when the dog did nothing wrong, just to show the lion that he's powerful. Ask Othello's pardon, and he'll be your friend again.

original: I will rather sue to be despised than to deceive so  good a commander with so slight, so drunken, and so  indiscreet an officer.
translation: I'd rather ask him to hate me than ask him to have a commander who is as feeble, drunk, and indiscreet as I am.

original: Drunk? And speak parrot?   And  squabble? Swagger? Swear? And discourse fustian with  one’s own shadow? O thou invisible spirit of wine, if  thou hast no name to be known by, let us call thee  devil!
translation: I got drunk, and spoke nonsense, and squabbled, swaggered, and swore. I practically ranted at my own shadow. Oh, wine, you invisible spirit—if you don't have a name, then I will call you devil!

original: What was he that you followed with your sword? What had he done to you?
translation: Who was it that you were chasing after with your sword? What did he do to you?

original: I know not.
translation: I don't know.

original: Is ’t possible?
translation: Really?

original: I remember a mass of things, but nothing distinctly. A  quarrel, but nothing wherefore. Oh, that men should put  an enemy in their mouths to steal away their brains!
translation: I remember everything in a big haze. I can't recall the particulars. I remember the fight, but not the reason for it. Oh, why do men drink their enemy, which robs them of their senses!

original: That we should, with joy, pleasance revel and applause,  transform ourselves into beasts!
translation: Why do we celebrate by willingly turning ourselves into beasts?

original: Why, but you are now well enough. How came you thus  recovered?
translation: But you seem fine now. How did you sober up so fast?

original: It hath pleased the devil drunkenness to give place to the devil wrath. One unperfectness shows me another, to make me frankly despise myself.
translation: The devil of drunkenness decided to give up his place to the devil of anger. One vice leads to another, and now I hate myself.

original: Come, you are too severe a moraler. As the time, the  place, and the condition of this country stands, I could heartily wish this had not befallen. But since it is as it is, mend it for your own good.
translation: Oh stop, you're being too hard on yourself. Given the circumstances, I wholeheartedly wish this hadn't happened. But it has happened, so make the best of the situation.

original: I will ask him for my place again, he shall tell me I  am a drunkard. Had I as many mouths as Hydra, such an  answer would stop them all.
translation: If I ask him for my place as lieutenant back, he'll say that I am a drunkard. If I had as many mouths as the  Hydra  to ask him with, he'd say no to each one.

original: To be now a sensible man, by and by a fool, and presently a beast! Oh, strange!  Every inordinate cup is unblessed and the ingredient is  a devil.
translation: How strange it is that I should be a sensible man, but occasionally foolish, and then just now a beast! Every drink is unblessed, and alcohol is a devil.

original: Come, come, good wine is a good familiar creature, if  it be well used. Exclaim no more against it. And, good  lieutenant, I think you think I love you.
translation: Come on, good wine isn't bad if you don't drink too much of it. Stop swearing against wine. Now, good lieutenant, am I right in thinking that you know I care about you?

original: I have well approved it, sir. I drunk!
translation: I know you are my friend. I can't believe I got drunk!

original: You or any man living may be drunk at a time, man. I  tell you what you shall do. Our general’s wife is now  the general. I may say so in this respect, for that he  hath devoted and given up himself to the contemplation,  mark, and denotement of her parts and graces.
translation: You or any man may get drunk now and then. I'll tell you what to do. Our general's wife is now the one who's actually in charge. What I mean by this is that he is totally devoted to her and obsessed with contemplating and describing her qualities and graces.

original: Confess  yourself freely to her, importune her help to put you in your place again. She is of so free, so kind, so apt,  so blessed a disposition, she holds it a vice in her  goodness not to do more than she is requested.
translation: Apologize to her, and beg her to help you regain your place as lieutenant. She is noble, kind, clever, and blessed. She thinks it is wrong not to do as she is asked.

original: This  broken joint between you and her husband entreat her to  splinter, and, my fortunes against any lay worth naming, this crack of your love shall grow stronger than it was before.
translation: Ask her to help mend your relationship with her husband, and—I'll bet anything on it—the friendship between Othello and you will grow stronger now than ever before.

original: You advise me well.
translation: That's good advice.

original: I protest, in the sincerity of love and honest  kindness.
translation: I give it out of sincere kindness and affection for you.

original: I think it freely, and betimes in the morning I will  beseech the virtuous Desdemona to undertake for me. I am desperate of my fortunes if they check me.
translation: I think you're right, and in the morning I will ask the virtuous Desdemona to plead on my behalf. But I worry for my fortunes if they hold me back.

original: You are in the right. Good night, lieutenant, I must to the watch.
translation: You're on the right track. Good night, lieutenant. I must go and keep a lookout.

original: Good night, honest Iago.
translation: Good night, honest Iago.

original: And what’s he then that says I play the villain?   When this advice is free I give and honest,   Probal to thinking and indeed the course   To win the Moor again?
translation: Who could say that I'm a villain, when I give free and honest advice that is helpful for Cassio in winning back the Moor's favor?

original: For ’tis most easy   Th' inclining Desdemona to subdue   In any honest suit. She’s framed as fruitful   As the free elements.
translation: For it really is easy to persuade Desdemona to help you in anything. She gives rise to as many good things as nature itself.

original: And then for her   To win the Moor, were to renounce his baptism,   All seals and symbols of redeemèd sin,   His soul is so enfettered to her love,   That she may make, unmake, do what she list,
translation: And Othello is such a slave to his love for her that he would renounce his baptism and reject all symbols of Christian redemption to win her over. She can do whatever she wants, and whatever she desires he will carry out.

original: Even as her appetite shall play the god   With his weak function. How am I then a villain   To counsel Cassio to this parallel course,   Directly to his good? Divinity of hell!
translation: How then could I be a villain, when I am advising Cassio to do what is in his best interest? That's Satan's theology!

original: When devils will the blackest sins put on   They do suggest at first with heavenly shows   As I do now.
translation: When devils do the worst sins, they first put on the pretense of goodness and innocence, as I am doing now.

original: For whiles this honest fool   Plies Desdemona to repair his fortune   And she for him pleads strongly to the Moor,   I’ll pour this pestilence into his ear:
translation: For while this honest fool begs Desdemona to fix his misfortune and while she pleads on his behalf to the Moor, I'll poison Othello's thoughts by whispering into his ear.

original: That she repeals him for her body’s lust.   And by how much she strives to do him good   She shall undo her credit with the Moor.
translation: I'll say that Desdemona is standing up for Cassio because she is attracted to him. The more that she argues for Cassio, the guiltier she'll seem to the Moor.
