original: So will I turn her virtue into pitch   And out of her own goodness make the net   That shall enmesh them all.
translation: In this way I'll turn her own virtue into a sort of  tar , to entrap her—and everyone else—with her own goodness.

original: How now, Roderigo!
translation: How are things going, Roderigo?

original: I do follow here in the chase not like a hound that  hunts, but one that fills up the cry. My money is almost spent, I have been tonight exceedingly well cudgeled,  and I think the issue will be I shall have so much  experience for my pains.
translation: I come here exhausted, like a dog bringing up the rear of the pack during a hunt. I've spent almost all my money, have been thoroughly beaten up tonight, and all I have for all this is some painful life experience.

original: And so, with no money at all  and a little more wit, return again to Venice.
translation: So, I'm going to return to Venice a little wiser and a lot poorer.

original: How poor are they that have not patience!   What wound did ever heal but by degrees?   Thou know’st we work by wit and not by witchcraft,   And wit depends on dilatory time.
translation: How poor are those who don't have any patience! Every wound must heal gradually. You know that our plan is based on cleverness and not magic, and cleverness needs time to work.

original: Does’t not go well? Cassio hath beaten thee.   And thou, by that small hurt, hath cashiered Cassio.   Though other things grow fair against the sun,   Yet fruits that blossom first will first be ripe.
translation: Aren't things actually going well? Cassio has beaten you up, yes. But because of this he's been fired from his position as lieutenant. The fruits that blossom first are the first to ripen, and before long, we'll reap the fruits of our labors.

original: Content thyself awhile. In troth, ’tis morning.   Pleasure and action make the hours seem short.   Retire thee, go where thou art billeted.
translation: Be patient a while longer. It's already morning, in fact. Excitement and action make time fly. Go back to your room and get some sleep.

original: Away, I say, thou shalt know more hereafter.   Nay, get thee gone.
translation: Go, I tell you. I'll fill you in more later. Now, get going.

original: Two things are to be done:   My wife must move for Cassio to her mistress.   I’ll set her on.
translation: I must do two things. First, my wife has to advocate for Cassio to Desdemona. I'll get her to do that.

original: Myself, the while, to draw the Moor apart   And bring him jump when he may Cassio find   Soliciting his wife. Ay, that’s the way.   Dull not device by coldness and delay.
translation: Meanwhile, I need to take the Moor aside and orchestrate it so that he happens upon Cassio pleading to his wife. Yes, that's the way to do it. I have no time to waste!

original: Masters, play here, I will content your pains. Something that’s brief, and bid “Good morrow, general.”
translation: Gentlemen, play some music here. I'll pay you for your trouble. Play a short song, and then say, "Good morning, general."

original: Why masters, have your instruments been in Naples, that they speak i' th' nose thus?
How, sir? How?
translation: What do you mean, sir?

original: Are these, I pray you, wind instruments?
translation: Tell me, are these wind instruments?

original: Ay, marry, are they, sir.
translation: Yes, indeed they are, sir.

original: Oh, thereby hangs a tail.
translation: Well, that's an problem.

original: Whereby hangs a tale, sir?
translation: What's the problem, sir?

original: Marry sir, by many a wind instrument that I know. But, masters, here’s money for you, and the general so likes your music that he desires you, for love’s sake, to  make no more noise with it.
translation: Indeed, sir, windbags!  They're the problem. But, gentlemen, here's some money for you. The general likes your music so much that he would like you to stop playing it, for God's sake.

original: Well, sir, we will not.
translation: Well then, sir, we will stop.

original: If you have any music that may not be heard, to ’t  again. But, as they say, to hear music the general does  not greatly care.
translation: If you have any songs that are silent, feel free to keep playing those. But, you know, the general doesn't care much for music.

original: We have none such, sir.
translation: We don't have any silent songs, sir.

original: Then put up your pipes in your bag, for I’ll away. Go,  vanish into air, away!
translation: Then pack up your instruments and go. Vanish into the air. Go!

original: Dost thou hear, my honest friend?
translation: Do you hear, my honest friend?

original: No, I hear not your honest friend, I hear you.
Prithee, keep up thy quillets. There’s a poor piece of  gold for thee. If the gentlewoman that attends the  general’s wife be stirring,
translation: Please, that's enough of your jokes. Here's a little gold for you.  If the woman who takes care of the general's wife is awake,

original: tell her there’s one Cassio  entreats her a little favour of speech. Wilt thou do  this?
translation: tell her that a man named Cassio begs the she give him a chance to speak with her. Will you do this?

original: She is stirring, sir. If she will stir hither, I shall  seem to notify unto her.
translation: She is awake, sir. If she happens to come this way, I'll tell her.

original: In happy time, Iago.
translation: Just in time, Iago.

original: You have not been abed, then?
translation: You haven't gone to bed, then?

original: Why, no. The day had broke   Before we parted. I have made bold, Iago,   To send in to your wife.
translation: No. It was already daytime when we left each other. Iago, I've been bold enough to ask to speak to your wife.

original: My suit to her   Is that she will to virtuous Desdemona   Procure me some access.
translation: I will ask her to allow me to see the virtuous Desdemona.

original: I’ll send her to you presently,   And I’ll devise a mean to draw the Moor   Out of the way,
translation: I'll send her to you right away. And I'll figure out a way to take the Moor somewhere out of the way,

original: that your converse and business   May be more free.
translation: so that you can talk to her in private.

original: I humbly thank you for’t.
translation: I humbly thank you for this.

original: I never knew a Florentine more kind and honest.
Good morrow, good Lieutenant. I am sorry   For your displeasure, but all will sure be well.   The general and his wife are talking of it,   And she speaks for you stoutly.
translation: Good morning, good Lieutenant. I am sorry for what has happened to you, but I'm sure everything will turn out okay. The general and his wife are talking about the situation, and Desdemona is speaking up for you.

original: The Moor replies   That he you hurt is of great fame in Cyprus   And great affinity, and that in wholesome wisdom   He might not but refuse you.
translation: Othello says that the man you hurt is well-known and well-liked in Cyprus, and that he has no choice but to refuse your appeal.

original: But he protests he loves  you   And needs no other suitor but his likings   To take the safest occasion by the front   To bring you in again.
translation: But Othello insists that he still loves you, and doesn't need any persuading to put you back in your position when he gets the opportunity.

original: Yet I beseech you,   If you think fit, or that it may be done,
translation: Nonetheless, I beg you—if you think it's possible and a good idea—

original: Give me advantage of some brief discourse   With Desdemona alone.
translation: to let me talk with Desdemona alone for a little bit.

original: Pray you come in. I will bestow you where you shall have time To speak your bosom freely.
translation: Please, come inside. I will give you a chance to talk to her freely.

original: I am much bound to you.
translation: I owe you for this.

original: These letters give, Iago, to the pilot,   And by him do my duties to the senate.
translation: Iago, give these letters to the captain of my ship, and tell him to extend my greetings to the senate back in Venice.

original: That done, I will be walking on the works,   Repair there to me.
translation: Once that is done, come find me where I will be walking atop the walls.

original: Well, my good lord, I’ll do ’t.
translation: Very well, my good lord. I'll do it.

original: This fortification, gentlemen, shall we see ’t?
translation: Well then, gentlemen, shall we go see the walls of this fort?

original: We’ll wait upon your lordship.
translation: After you, my lord.

original: Be thou assured, good Cassio, I will do All my abilities in thy behalf.
translation: Rest assured, good Cassio,  I will do all I can for you.

original: Good madam, do. I warrant it grieves my husband As if the cause were his.
translation: Please do, good madam. The situation has my husband troubled as if the problem were his own.

original: Oh, that’s an honest fellow. Do not doubt, Cassio, But I will have my lord and you again As friendly as you were.
translation: Oh, your husband's an honest fellow. Cassio, do not doubt that I will soon have you and my husband as close as you were before.

original: Bounteous madam, Whatever shall become of Michael Cassio, He’s never anything but your true servant.
translation: Generous madam, whatever happens to me, I'll always be your loyal servant.

original: I know ’t, I thank you. You do love my lord.   You have known him long, and be you well assured
translation: Thank you. I know you mean that. You really do love my husband. You've known him for a long time, and you can be sure

original: He shall in strangeness stand no farther off   Than in a polite distance.
translation: that he is only keeping his distance from you for political reasons.

original: Ay, but, lady,   That policy may either last so long,   Or feed upon such nice and waterish diet,   Or breed itself so out of circumstances,
translation: Yes, but, my lady, I worry that he may keep this distance for so long—because it is easier to keep doing it, or because some accident or other makes it necessary—

original: That, I being absent and my place supplied,   My general will forget my love and service.
translation: that he will forget my love and service to him while I am gone and someone else is in my place.

original: Do not doubt that. Before Emilia here   I give thee warrant of thy place. Assure thee,   If I do vow a friendship, I’ll perform it   To the last article.
translation: Don't worry about that. With Emilia here as my witness, I guarantee that you will have your place back as lieutenant. I assure you, when I promise to do something out of friendship, I deliver.

original: My lord shall never rest,   I’ll watch him tame and talk him out of patience.   His bed shall seem a school, his board a shrift,
translation: My husband won't have a moment of rest because I'll keep him awake all night to talk his ear off about this.

original: I’ll intermingle everything he does   With Cassio’s suit. Therefore be merry, Cassio,   For thy solicitor shall rather die   Than give thy cause away.
translation: I'll lecture him until our bed feels like a school room and his table a confessional. I'll mention your case no matter what he's doing. So cheer up, Cassio. I'd rather die than fail on your behalf.

original: Madam, here comes my lord.
translation: Madam, here comes my husband.

original: Madam, I’ll take my leave.
translation: Madam, I'll leave now.

original: Why, stay and hear me speak.
translation: Why don't you stay here and hear me speak?

original: Madam, not now. I am very ill at ease, Unfit for mine own purposes.
translation: Madam, not now. I don't have a good feeling about this, and don't think it's the right time.

original: Well, do your discretion.
translation: Well, it's up to you.

original: Ha! I like not that.
translation: Huh. I don't like the looks of that.

original: What dost thou say?
translation: What are you talking about?

original: Nothing, my lord, or if—I know not what.
translation: Nothing, my lord, unless—I don't know.

original: Was not that Cassio parted from my wife?
translation: Wasn't that Cassio who was just talking to my wife?

original: Cassio, my lord? No, sure, I cannot think it That he would steal away so guilty-like Seeing you coming.
translation: Cassio, my lord? No, surely not. I can't imagine he would slink away looking so guilty after seeing you coming.

original: I do believe ’twas he.
translation: I think it was him.

original: How now, my lord? I have been talking with a suitor here, A man that languishes in your displeasure.
translation: How are you, my husband? I have been talking here with a man who, sadly, you are displeased with.

original: Who is ’t you mean?
translation: Who do you mean?

original: Why, your lieutenant, Cassio. Good my lord,   If I have any grace or power to move you   His present reconciliation take.
translation: Your lieutenant, Cassio. My good husband, if I have any grace or power to persuade you, please accept his apology.

original: For if he be not one that truly loves you,   That errs in ignorance and not in cunning,   I have no judgment in an honest face.   I prithee, call him back.
translation: I swear he truly loves you and made a mistake on accident, not on purpose, or else I can't judge an honest face. Please, call him back here.

original: Went he hence now?
translation: Was that him who just left?

original: Ay, sooth, so humbled That he hath left part of his grief with me  To suffer with him. Good love, call him back.
translation: Yes, that's right. And he was so humbled and troubled that now I feel sad for him. My love, call him back here.

original: Not now, sweet Desdemona. Some other time.
translation: Not now, sweet Desdemona. Some other time.

original: The sooner, sweet, for you.
translation: All the sooner because you asked, sweetheart.

original: Shall ’t be tonight at supper?
translation: So, will that be tonight at dinner?

original: No, not tonight.
translation: No, not tonight.

original: Tomorrow dinner, then?
translation: Tomorrow at dinner, then?

original: I shall not dine at home,  I meet the captains at the citadel.
translation: I'm not eating dinner at home tomorrow. I'm meeting the captains at the castle.

original: Why, then, tomorrow night, or Tuesday morn.   On Tuesday noon, or night, or Wednesday morn.   I prithee name the time, but let it not   Exceed three days.
translation: Then do it tomorrow night, or Tuesday morning. Or Tuesday at noon, or Tuesday night, or even Wednesday morning. You name the time, but please sometime within the next three days.

original: In faith, he’s penitent,   And yet his trespass, in our common reason   (Save that, they say, the wars must make example   Out of her best)
translation: Truly, he regrets what he's done, and his error wasn't really that serious—except that, as they say, military discipline requires that you be most strict with the best soldiers—

original: is not, almost, a fault   T' incur a private check. When shall he come?   Tell me, Othello.
translation: and should barely have even required a private scolding . When will Cassio come back? Tell me, Othello.

original: I wonder in my soul   What you would ask me that I should deny   Or stand so mamm'ring on. What?
translation: If you asked me for something, I wouldn't just say no, or stand there hesitating. What do you say?

original: Michael Cassio   That came a-wooing with you, and so many a time,   When I have spoke of you dispraisingly,   Hath ta'en your part,
translation: Michael Cassio helped you when you were courting me, and whenever I criticized you he stood up for you.

original: to have so much to do   To bring him in? Trust me, I could do much—
translation: Why should it be so hard for him to get to talk with you? Trust me, I could do a lot—

original: Prithee, no more. Let him come when he will, I will deny thee nothing.
translation: Please, don't talk anymore about this. Let Cassio come when he wants. I won't deny you what you want.

original: Why, this is not a boon,   'Tis as I should entreat you wear your gloves,   Or feed on nourishing dishes, or keep you warm,
translation: This isn't a great favor you're doing me. It's as if I'm trying to persuade you to put on gloves when it's cold out, or to eat healthy food, or to keep yourself warm,

original: Or sue to you to do a peculiar profit   To your own person.
translation: or to do anything that's good for you.

original: Nay, when I have a suit   Wherein I mean to touch your love indeed   It shall be full of poise and difficult weight   And fearful to be granted.
translation: No, when I have something to ask of you that will really test your love, it will be a difficult, serious thing, one that you wouldn't grant easily.

original: I will deny thee nothing!  Whereon I do beseech thee, grant me this, To leave me but a little to myself.
translation: I will never say no to you! All I ask of you right now is that you leave me alone for a bit.

original: Shall I deny you? No. Farewell, my lord.
translation: And will I say no to you? No, I won't. Goodbye, my husband.

original: Farewell, my Desdemona. I’ll come to thee straight.
translation: Goodbye, my Desdemona. I'll come see you soon.

original: Emilia, come.—Be as your fancies teach you.  Whate'er you be, I am obedient.
translation: Emilia, come with me. Act however you want, Othello. Whatever you do, I'll be obedient to you.

original: Excellent wretch! Perdition catch my soul But I do love thee! And when I love thee not Chaos is come again.
translation: Oh, that crazy girl. But I'll be damned if don't love her! The world will end before I stop loving her.

original: My noble lord—
translation: My noble lord—

original: What dost thou say, Iago?
translation: What is it, Iago?

original: Did Michael Cassio, when you wooed my lady, Know of your love?
translation: Did Michael Cassio know about your love for Desdemona when you were courting her?

original: He did, from first to last. Why dost thou ask?
translation: He did, from the very beginning. Why do you ask?

original: But for a satisfaction of my thought, No further harm.
translation: Oh, no reason. I was just curious.

original: Why of thy thought, Iago?
translation: Why were you curious, Iago?

original: I did not think he had been acquainted with her.
translation: I didn't think he had met her.

original: Oh, yes, and went between us very oft.
translation: Oh, yes he knew her, and often carried messages between Desdemona and me.

original: Indeed?
translation: Really?

original: Indeed? Ay, indeed! Discern’st thou aught in that?  Is he not honest?
translation: What do you mean, "really?" Yes, really. You think something's strange about that? Isn't Cassio honest?

original: Honest, my lord?
translation: Honest, my lord?

original: Honest, ay, honest.
translation: Honest, yes, honest.

original: My lord, for aught I know.
translation: My lord, for all I know.

original: What dost thou think?
translation: What do you think?

original: Think, my lord?
translation: Think, my lord?

original: “Think, my lord?” Alas, thou echo’st me   As if there were some monster in thy thought   Too hideous to be shown. Thou dost mean something.
translation: "Think, my lord?" Come on, you're repeating everything I say like a strange monster in your mind that you're afraid is to hideous to show. You're hinting at something.

original: I heard thee say even now thou lik’st not that   When Cassio left my wife. What didst not like?   And when I told thee he was of my counsel   Of my whole course of wooing, thou cried’st “Indeed?”
translation: You just said earlier that you didn't like how Cassio left my wife's side. What about it didn't you like? And when I told you that Cassio advised me the whole time I was courting Desdemona, you said, "Oh really?"

original: And didst contract and purse thy brow together   As if thou then hadst shut up in thy brain   Some horrible conceit. If thou dost love me   Show me thy thought.
translation: And you raised your eyebrows like you had some secret thought about it. If you care about me at all, tell me what you're thinking.

original: My lord, you know I love you.
translation: My lord, you know I care about you.

original: I think thou dost.   And for I know thou 'rt full of love and honesty   And weigh’st thy words before thou giv’st them breath,   Therefore these stops of thine fright me the more.
translation: I think you do. And it's precisely because I know you are full of love and honesty and think carefully before you speak that I'm even more worried about the way you're hesitating.

original: For such things in a false disloyal knave   Are tricks of custom, but in a man that’s just   They are close dilations, working from the heart,   That passion cannot rule.
translation: In some disloyal liar, it wouldn't mean anything, but in an honest man like you, these kinds of reactions are indications of thoughts that come from the heart which cannot be clouded by emotion.

original: For Michael Cassio,  I dare be sworn, I think, that he is honest.
translation: As far as Michael Cassio goes, I think I can swear that he is honest.

original: I think so too.
translation: I think so too.

original: Men should be what they seem, Or those that be not, would they might seem none!
translation: Men should be what they seem to be. And if they aren't, I wish they wouldn't pretend to be anything that they're not!

original: Certain, men should be what they seem.
translation: Certainly, men should be what they seem to be.

original: Why then I think Cassio’s an honest man.
translation: Well then, I think Cassio is an honest man.

original: Nay, yet there’s more in this.
translation: No, there's something more going on.

original: I prithee speak to me as to thy thinkings,   As thou dost ruminate, and give thy worst of thoughts   The worst of words.
translation: Please, tell me what you're thinking to yourself,  and speak even the worst thoughts you are thinking.

original: Good my lord, pardon me,   Though I am bound to every act of duty   I am not bound to that all slaves are free to.   Utter my thoughts?
translation: My good lord, pardon me. I must obey your every order, but I don't have to do that which even slaves aren't obligated to do—divulge my thoughts.

original: Why, say they are vile and false,   As where’s that palace whereinto foul things   Sometimes intrude not?
translation: What if my thoughts are vile and untrue? After all, what palace is there that has never let a foul thing inside?

original: Who has that breast so pure   Wherein uncleanly apprehensions   Keep leets and law-days and in sessions sit   With meditations lawful?
translation: Who has ever had a heart so pure that impure thoughts haven't held court with lawful thoughts?

original: Thou dost conspire against thy friend, Iago, If thou but think’st him wronged and mak’st his ear A stranger to thy thoughts.
translation: Iago, if you think that a friend of yours is in trouble but you don't say anything, then you are wronging your friend.

original: I do beseech you,   Though I perchance am vicious in my guess,   As, I confess, it is my nature’s plague   To spy into abuses, and oft my jealousy   Shapes faults that are not,
translation: Since I am maybe wrong in my guess—and I admit it's my nature to look into possible misdeeds and often I imagine wrongs that aren't really there—

original: that your wisdom,   From one that so imperfectly conceits,   Would take no notice, nor build yourself a trouble   Out of his scattering and unsure observance.
translation: I beg you in your wisdom not to put too much stock in what I say, since I often wrongly imagine things. Don't make a big deal out of my smattering of uncertain observations.

original: It were not for your quiet nor your good,   Nor for my manhood, honesty, and wisdom   To let you know my thoughts.
translation: It would not be good for you, and it wouldn't be wise, honest, or manly of me to let you know my thoughts.

original: What dost thou mean?
translation: What do you mean?

original: Good name in man and woman, dear my lord,   Is the immediate jewel of their souls.   Who steals my purse steals trash. 'Tis something,  nothing:   'Twas mine, ’tis his, and has been slave to thousands.
translation: A good reputation is the most precious jewel of a man's or a woman's soul, my dear lord. If someone steals money from me, it's not a big deal. It was mine, now it's his, and it's been held by thousands of others.

original: But he that filches from me my good name   Robs me of that which not enriches him   And makes me poor indeed.
translation: But if someone steals my good reputation from me, then he really does make me truly poor, and steals something that doesn't even make him any richer.

original: I’ll know thy thoughts.
translation: I want to know your thoughts.

original: You cannot, if my heart were in your hand, Nor shall not, whilst ’tis in my custody.
translation: You cannot know, not even if you were squeezing my heart in your hand to make me tell you. And as long as I have my heart, I won't tell you.

original: Ha!
translation: Ha!

original: Oh, beware, my lord, of jealousy!   It is the green-eyed monster which doth mock   The meat it feeds on.
translation: Oh, my lord, beware of jealousy! It is a green-eyed monster that mocks whoever it eats away at.

original: That cuckold lives in bliss   Who, certain of his fate, loves not his wronger,   But, oh, what damnèd minutes tells he o'er   Who dotes, yet doubts— suspects, yet soundly loves!
translation: A man who knows for sure that his wife is cheating on him lives in bliss, since he knows not to love his wife. But, oh, what torture it is to love but doubt your wife, suspect her of something but still love her.

original: Oh, misery!
translation: Oh, what misery!

original: Poor and content is rich, and rich enough,   But riches fineless is as poor as winter   To him that ever fears he shall be poor.
translation: To be poor but content is actually to be quite rich. But you can have endless riches and still be as poor as anyone if you are always afraid of losing your riches.

original: Good heaven, the souls of all my tribe defend   From jealousy!
translation: Good heaven, defend us all from jealousy!

original: Why, why is this?   Think’st thou I’d make a life of jealousy,   To follow still the changes of the moon   With fresh suspicions? No! To be once in doubt   Is to be resolved.
translation: Why would say that? Do you think I would make jealousy my whole life, and with every change in the moon find new suspicions? No! To doubt once is to make up your mind.

original: Exchange me for a goat   When I shall turn the business of my soul   To such exsufflicate and blowed surmises,   Matching thy inference.
translation: I'd rather turn into a goat than devote all my time to such overblown suspicions, like the sort of jealous man you're describing.

original: 'Tis not to make me jealous   To say my wife is fair, feeds well, loves company,   Is free of speech, sings, plays, and dances.
translation: It wouldn't make me jealous for you to say that my wife is pretty, eats well, enjoys the company of others, speaks her mind, sings, plays music, and dances.

original: Where virtue is, these are more virtuous.   Nor from mine own weak merits will I draw   The smallest fear or doubt of her revolt,   For she had eyes and chose me.
translation: When a woman is virtuous, these traits are virtuous as well. And I will not worry or fear that she may be unfaithful because I am not very desirable. She knew who she was marrying.

original: No, Iago,   I’ll see before I doubt, when I doubt, prove,   And on the proof there is no more but this:   Away at once with love or jealousy!
translation: No, Iago, I won't doubt Desdemona until I see something, and if I doubt her I'll see if I can prove it. If I get proof, there's only one thing to do: get rid of either my love or my jealousy.

original: I am glad of this, for now I shall have reason   To show the love and duty that I bear you   With franker spirit.
translation: I'm glad to hear this, because now I can show my love for you and fulfill my duty in a more frank manner.

original: Therefore, as I am bound,   Receive it from me. I speak not yet of proof.   Look to your wife, observe her well with Cassio.
translation: So, hear what I must tell you. I don't have any proof yet. But keep an eye on your wife, and watch her carefully with Cassio.

original: Wear your eyes thus, not jealous nor secure.   I would not have your free and noble nature   Out of self-bounty be abused. Look to ’t.
translation: Look at her like this: don't be too jealous or too trusting. I wouldn't want you to get taken advantage of because of your noble, kind nature. Look out.

original: I know our country disposition well.   In Venice they do let God see the pranks   They dare not show their husbands.
translation: I know the people of my country well. Women of Venice let God see the sorts of exploits they wouldn't dare let their husbands see.

original: Their best  conscience   Is not to leave ’t undone, but keep’t unknown.
translation: Their conscience doesn't stop them from doing bad things, but only keeps them from letting their bad deeds be known.

original: Dost thou say so?
translation: Do you think so?

original: She did deceive her father, marrying you, And when she seemed to shake and fear your looks, She loved them most.
translation: Desdemona deceived her father in marrying you, and she pretended to shake in fear at your looks when she actually loved them.

original: And so she did.
translation: Yes, she did.

original: Why, go to then.   She that, so young, could give out such a seeming,   To seel her father’s eyes up close as oak,   He thought ’twas witchcraft.
translation: Well, there you have it, then. Even though she was a young woman, she was so good at lying that she made her father as blind as a tree to her plans. He even thought you'd used witchcraft on her.

original: But I am much to blame.   I humbly do beseech you of your pardon   For too much loving you.
translation: But I'm partially to blame for saying this. I beg your pardon for loving you too much.

original: I am bound to thee forever.
translation: I am forever in your debt.

original: I see this hath a little dashed your spirits.
translation: I can see this has upset you a little.

original: Not a jot, not a jot.
translation: Not at all, not at all.

original: Trust me, I fear it has.   I hope you will consider what is spoke   Comes from my love. But I do see you’re moved.
translation: Trust me, I worry it has. Please consider that what I am saying comes from my love for you. But I see you really are affected by what I've said.

original: I am to pray you not to strain my speech   To grosser issues nor to larger reach   Than to suspicion.
translation: I only meant to warn you to be a little suspicious.  I beg you not to make more out of this than you should.

original: I will not.
translation: I won't.

original: Should you do so, my lord,   My speech should fall into such vile success   Which my thoughts aimed not at.
translation: If you do, my speech would have the very vile effects that I didn't want it to.

original: Cassio’s my worthy  friend—   My lord, I see you’re moved.
translation: Cassio is my deserving friend—my Lord, I see you're troubled.

original: No, not much moved.  I do not think but Desdemona’s honest.
translation: No, I'm not troubled. I think Desdemona is nothing but honest.

original: Long live she so. And long live you to think so.
translation: May she be be honest for a long time. And that you will think she's honest for a long time.

original: And yet how nature, erring from itself—
translation: And yet, one can act against one's nature—

original: Ay, there’s the point. As, to be bold with you,   Not to affect many proposèd matches   Of her own clime, complexion, and degree,   Whereto we see in all things nature tends—
translation: Yes, that's the point. At the risk of being too honest, it was against her nature not to like so many suitors of her own country, complexion, and social rank, since those who share such similarities are naturally drawn to each other.

original: Foh! One may smell in such a will most rank,   Foul disproportions, thoughts unnatural.   But—pardon me—
translation: Ugh! You can practically smell a gross desire in excessive proportion and foul thoughts in such a person.  But forgive me,

original: I do not in position   Distinctly speak of her, though I may fear   Her will, recoiling to her better judgment,
translation: I am talking generally and don't mean her in particular, although I do fear that she may return to her better judgment,

original: May fall to match you with her country forms,   And happily repent.
translation: prefer her own countrymen to you, and take back her love for you.

original: Farewell, farewell. If more thou dost perceive, let me know more.  Set on thy wife to observe. Leave me, Iago.
translation: Goodbye, goodbye. If you notice anything more, let me know. Have your wife look out, too. Leave me, Iago.

original: My lord, I take my leave.
translation: My lord, I will leave now.

original: Why did I marry? This honest creature doubtless Sees and knows more, much more, than he unfolds.
translation: Why did I marry? Without a doubt, this honest man has seen more than he lets on, and knows more—much more—than he is telling me.

original: (returns)   My lord, I would I might entreat your honor   To scan this thing no farther. Leave it to time.
translation: [Returning]  My lord, I ask you not to worry about this anymore. Give it some time.

original: Although ’tis fit that Cassio have his place,   For sure, he fills it up with great ability,   Yet, if you please to hold him off awhile,   You shall by that perceive him and his means.
translation: It is right for Cassio to get his place as lieutenant back—for sure, he's very good at the job—but if you wait for a while you will get a better idea of what he's up to.

original: Note if your lady strain his entertainment   With any strong or vehement importunity.   Much will be seen in that.
translation: Take note if your wife strongly insists that you reinstate him. That would mean a lot.

original: In the meantime,   Let me be thought too busy in my fears—   As worthy cause I have to fear I am—   And hold her free, I do beseech your honor.
translation: In the meantime, just think that I'm being overly suspicious in my fears—and I have good reason to think I may be—and I beg you to consider Desdemona innocent.

original: Fear not my government.
translation: Don't worry about how I'll handle myself.

original: I once more take my leave.
translation: Once again, goodbye.

original: This fellow’s of exceeding honesty   And knows all quantities, with a learnèd spirit,   Of human dealings.
translation: This man is very honest and knows human interactions very well.

original: If I do prove her haggard,   Though that her jesses were my dear heartstrings,   I’d whistle her off and let her down the wind   To prey at fortune.
translation: If I find proof that Desdemona is unfaithful, I'll let her go like I'm getting rid of a pet, even if the leash is my own heartstrings.

original: Haply, for I am black   And have not those soft parts of conversation   That chamberers have, or for I am declined   Into the vale of years—yet that’s not much—
translation: Maybe since I am black and don't have the smooth conversational skills of gallant men, or maybe since I'm getting old—but no, none of that's important.

original: She’s gone, I am abused, and my relief   Must be to loathe her. Oh, curse of marriage   That we can call these delicate creatures ours   And not their appetites!
translation: She's gone, I am betrayed, and my only recourse must be to hate her. Oh, this is the curse of marriage, that we can have control over our delicate wives, but not their desires.

original: I had rather be a toad   And live upon the vapor of a dungeon   Than keep a corner in the thing I love   For others' uses.
translation: I'd rather be a toad who survives off the mold in a dungeon than to share the thing I love with others.

original: Yet ’tis the plague to great ones,   Prerogatived are they less than the base.   'Tis destiny unshunnable, like death.
translation: But that's what you get for being a powerful man, as this happens more often to noblemen than to commoners. It's an inescapable part of fate, like death.

original: Even then this forkèd plague is fated to us   When we do quicken. Look where she comes.
translation: From the moment we're born we are fated to  wear the horns . Look, here she comes.

original: If she be false, heaven mocked itself. I’ll not believe ’t.
translation: If she is a liar, heaven has played a trick on itself. I won't believe it.

original: How now, my dear Othello? Your dinner, and the generous islanders  By you invited, do attend your presence.
translation: How are you, my dear Othello? The islanders you invited to dinner are waiting for you.

original: I am to blame.
translation: My mistake.

original: Why do you speak so faintly? Are you not well?
translation: Why do you speak so faintly? Are you okay?

original: I have a pain upon my forehead, here.
Why that’s with watching, ’twill away again.  Let me but bind it hard, within this hour It will be well.
translation: Well, that's from staying up too late. It will go away soon. Let me just tie this handkerchief tight around your head and it will feel better within an hour.

original: Your napkin is too little, Let it alone.
translation: Your handkerchief is too small. Leave it alone.

original: Come, I’ll go in with you.
translation: Come on, I'll go inside with you.

original: I am very sorry that you are not well.
translation: I am very sorry that you aren't feeling well.

original: (picks up the handkerchief)   I am glad I have found this napkin,   This was her first remembrance from the Moor.
translation: [She picks up DESDEMONA's handkerchief]  I am glad I have found this handkerchief. This was Desdemona's first gift from the Moor.

original: My wayward husband hath a hundred times   Wooed me to steal it, but she so loves the token   (For he conjured her she should ever keep it)
translation: My stubborn husband has asked me to steal it a hundred times, but she loves it so much (for Othello asked her never to lose it)

original: That she reserves it evermore about her   To kiss and talk to. I’ll have the work ta'en out   And give ’t Iago.
translation: that she always keeps it with her to kiss and talk to. I'll have the embroidered pattern copied and give it to Iago.

original: What he will do with it   Heaven knows, not I.   I nothing but to please his fantasy.
translation: God knows what he will do with it. God only knows. I certainly don't. I just like to make him happy.

original: How now! What do you here alone?
translation: What's going on? What are you doing here alone?

original: Do not you chide. I have a thing for you.
translation: Don't scold me. I have something for you.

original: A thing for me? It is a common thing—
Ha?
translation: What?

original: To have a foolish wife.
translation: . . . to have a foolish wife.

original: Oh, is that all? What will you give me now  For the same handkerchief?
translation: Oh, is that it? What will you give me now for the handkerchief itself?

original: What handkerchief?
translation: What handkerchief?

original: What handkerchief? Why, that the Moor first gave to Desdemona, That which so often you did bid me steal.
translation: What handkerchief? The one the Moor first gave to Desdemona, the one you so often asked me to steal.

original: Hast stolen it from her?
translation: You've stolen it from her?

original: No, but she let it drop by negligence And, to th' advantage, I being here, took ’t up. Look, here it is.
translation: No, she let it drop carelessly. And, since I happened to be here, I took the opportunity to pick it up. Look, here it is.

original: A good wench, give it me.
translation: That's a good girl, give it to me.

original: What will you do with ’t, that you have been so earnest To have me filch it?
translation: What will you do with it? Why have you been so eager for me to steal it?

original: Why, what is that to you?
translation: Why do you care?

original: If it be not for some purpose of import, Give ’t me again. Poor lady, she’ll run mad When she shall lack it.
translation: If you don't have an important purpose for it, then give it back to me. Poor Desdemona, she'll be so upset when she realizes it's missing.

original: Be not acknown on ’t, I have use for it. Go, leave me.
translation: Don't tell her what happened to it. I have a use for it. Go on, leave me alone.

original: I will in Cassio’s lodging lose this napkin   And let him find it. Trifles light as air   Are to the jealous confirmations strong   As proofs of holy writ.
translation: I will leave this handkerchief in Cassio's room, and let him find it there. Unimportant, trifling matters count as strong evidence to the jealous.

original: This may do something.   The Moor already changes with my poison.   Dangerous conceits are in their natures poisons   Which at the first are scarce found to distaste,
translation: This may have significant consequences. The Moor is already being changed by my poisonous advice. Dangerous suspicion are like poisons that don't even taste very bad at first,

original: But with a little act upon the blood   Burn like the mines of sulfur.
translation: but slowly act on the blood and burn the insides before long like unquenchable sulfur.

original: I did say so.   Look, where he comes. Not poppy nor mandragora   Nor all the drowsy syrups of the world,
translation: Just as I said. Look, here he comes. No exotic plant or herb, nor any sleeping medicine in the world,

original: Shall ever medicine thee to that sweet sleep   Which thou owedst yesterday.
translation: will return to you that sweet restful sleep you enjoyed just yesterday.

original: Ha! Ha! False to me?
translation: Ha! Ha! Desdemona, unfaithful to me?

original: Why, how now, general? No more of that.
translation: Why, what is going on, General? Don't talk like that.

original: Avaunt! Be gone! Thou hast set me on the rack. I swear ’tis better to be much abused Than but to know ’t a little.
translation: Away! Get away from me! You have tortured me. I swear it's better to be horribly betrayed and not realize it than to know a bit about it.

original: How now, my lord!
translation: What is going on, my lord?

original: What sense had I in her stol'n hours of lust?   I saw ’t not, thought it not, it harmed not me.   I slept the next night well, fed well, was free and  merry.
translation: Was I completely senseless during the hours she was cheating on me? I didn't see anything, and I didn't suspect anything. So, it didn't do me any harm. I slept well after, ate well, and was happy and carefree.

original: I found not Cassio’s kisses on her lips.   He that is robbed, not wanting what is stol'n,   Let him not know’t, and he’s not robbed at all.
translation: I didn't see Cassio's kisses on her lips. If a man is ever robbed but doesn't realize what has been stolen, let him not know he's been robbed. And then it's as if the robbery never happened.

original: I am sorry to hear this.
translation: I am sorry to hear this.

original: I had been happy if the general camp,   Pioneers and all, had tasted her sweet body,   So I had nothing known. Oh, now forever   Farewell the tranquil mind! Farewell content!
translation: I would have been happy if the whole camp of soldiers, trench-diggers and all, had tasted her sweet body, if only I didn't know about it. Oh, now I can say farewell to a peaceful mind! Farewell to being content!

original: Farewell the plumèd troops and the big wars   That makes ambition virtue! Oh, farewell!   Farewell the neighing steed and the shrill trump,   The spirit-stirring drum, th' ear-piercing fife,
translation: Farewell to the soldiers in uniform and the big wars that allow me to fulfill my ambitions! Oh, farewell! Farewell the neighing horses and the shrill war trumpets, the war drums that stir the spirit, the ear-piercing flute,

original: The royal banner, and all quality,   Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war!
translation: the royal banners, pride, the pomp and circumstance, and everything else that's good about war!

original: And O you mortal engines, whose rude throats   The immortal Jove’s dead clamors counterfeit,   Farewell! Othello’s occupation’s gone.
translation: And you deadly cannons, whose rude blasts are as loud as Jove's thunderbolts, farewell! Othello's military career is finished.

original: Is ’t possible, my lord?
translation: Can this be possible, my lord?

original: Villain, be sure thou prove my love a whore,   Be sure of it.
translation: Villain, you'd better be sure that my wife turns out to be a whore. You'd better be sure of it.

original: Give me the ocular proof   Or by the worth of mine eternal soul   Thou hadst been better have been born a dog   Than answer my waked wrath!
translation: Give me proof that I can see with my own eyes, or I swear on my soul that you'll wish you had been born a dog rather than have to answer to my anger.

original: Is ’t come to this?
translation: Has it come to this?

original: Make me to see ’t, or at the least so prove it  That the probation bear no hinge nor loop To hang a doubt on, or woe upon thy life!
translation: Give me evidence, or at least prove it beyond an ounce of doubt—or else you'll regret it!

original: My noble lord—
translation: My noble lord—

original: If thou dost slander her and torture me,   Never pray more. Abandon all remorse.   On horror’s head horrors accumulate,
translation: If you are going to slander Desdemona and torture me, you can give up on praying, and showing any remorse, because it won't help you. Go ahead and pile more sins on top of the ones you've already committed,

original: Do deeds to make heaven weep, all earth amazed,   For nothing canst thou to damnation add   Greater than that.
translation: do things so horrible they'll make heaven cry and astound everyone on earth. For nothing you could do would add more to your damnation than if you should slander Desdemona more.

original: Oh, grace! Oh, heaven forgive me!   Are you a man? Have you a soul or sense?   God buy you, take mine office. O wretched fool   That lov’st to make thine honesty a vice!
translation: Oh, grace! Oh, heaven forgive me! Are you human? Do you have any sense, or a soul? Goodbye, I resign as flag-bearer. Oh what a fool I am for being honest to a fault!

original: O monstrous world! Take note, take note, O world,   To be direct and honest is not safe.   I thank you for this profit, and from hence   I’ll love no friend, sith love breeds such offence.
translation: Oh this monstrous world! Take note, take note, everyone: it is not safe to be direct and honest. Thank you for teaching me this lesson. From here on out, I'll love no friend, since showing love for your friends causes such hate.

original: Nay, stay. Thou shouldst be honest.
translation: No, stay. You should be honest.

original: I should be wise, for honesty’s a fool And loses that it works for.
translation: I should be wise, because being honest is foolish and causes someone to lose all that he works for.

original: By the world,   I think my wife be honest and think she is not.   I think that thou art just and think thou art not.   I’ll have some proof.
translation: By the world, part of me thinks my wife is honest, and another part of me thinks she isn't. Part of me thinks you're trustworthy, and another part of me thinks you're not. I need some proof.

original: Her name, that was as fresh   As Dian’s visage, is now begrimed and black   As mine own face. If there be cords or knives,
translation: Her reputation, which was as pure and fair as  Diana's , is now besmirched and black as my face. If I can find any ropes, knives,

original: Poison, or fire, or suffocating streams,   I’ll not endure it. Would I were satisfied!
translation: poison, fire, or streams you can drown in, I won't endure this dishonor. If only I could be satisfied in this!

original: I see, sir, you are eaten up with passion. I do repent me that I put it to you. You would be satisfied?
translation: I see, sir, that passion is eating away at you. I regret that I told you about this. You say that you wish you could be satisfied?

original: Would? Nay, and I will.
translation: Yes, and I will be.

original: And may, but how? How satisfied, my lord?  Would you, the supervisor, grossly gape on, Behold her topped?
translation: But how? How will you be satisfied, my lord? Would you, like a voyeur, inappropriately watch and look on as she is having sex?

original: Death and damnation! Oh!
translation: Death and damnation! Oh!

original: It were a tedious difficulty, I think,   To bring them to that prospect. Damn them then,   If ever mortal eyes do see them bolster   More than their own! What then? How then?
translation: It would be very difficult, I think, to arrange it so you could watch the two of them sleep together. They'd be damned if anyone else saw them having sex. So, what now? What should we do?

original: What shall I say? Where’s satisfaction?   It is impossible you should see this,   Were they as prime as goats, as hot as monkeys,   As salt as wolves in pride, and fools as gross   As ignorance made drunk.
translation: What should I say? How could you be satisfied that you know the truth? It is impossible that you should see them in the act, even if they were frisky as goats, monkeys, or wolves in heat, as lustful as drunk idiots.

original: But yet, I say,   If imputation and strong circumstances   Which lead directly to the door of truth   Will give you satisfaction, you may have ’t.
translation: But nonetheless, I tell you, if you would be satisfied to find strong circumstantial evidence pointing to the truth, you could then find such satisfaction.

original: Give me a living reason she’s disloyal.
translation: Give me some proof that Desdemona is disloyal.

original: I do not like the office.   But, sith I am entered in this cause so far,   Pricked to ’t by foolish honesty and love,   I will go on.
translation: I don't like this task. But since I'm already so deeply involved in this, thanks to foolish honesty and concern for you, I will go on.

original: I lay with Cassio lately   And, being troubled with a raging tooth,   I could not sleep. There are a kind of men   So loose of soul that in their sleeps will mutter   Their affairs.
translation: I was recently spending the night in Cassio's bedroom and couldn't sleep because of a raging toothache. Now, some men have such a loose soul that they mutter things in their sleep.

original: One of this kind is Cassio.   In sleep I heard him say “Sweet Desdemona,   Let us be wary, let us hide our loves.”
translation: Cassio is one of them. I heard him say in his sleep, "Sweet Desdemona, let's be careful and hide our love."

original: And then, sir, would he gripe and wring my hand,   Cry “O sweet creature!” and then kiss me hard,   As if he plucked up kisses by the roots   That grew upon my lips,
translation: And then, sir, he clutched and grabbed my hand, crying "Oh sweet woman!" and he kissed me hard as if with his kisses he was trying to pull up some plant by the roots that was growing on my lips.

original: lay his leg   Over my thigh, and sigh, and kiss, and then   Cry “Cursed fate that gave thee to the Moor!”
translation: He laid his leg over my thigh and sighed, and kissed, and then cried out, "Curse fate for giving you to the Moor!"

original: Oh, monstrous! Monstrous!
translation: Oh, this is terrible! Terrible!

original: Nay, this was but his dream.
translation: But this was only his dream.

original: But this denoted a foregone conclusion.
translation: But his actions suggests something he had already done.

original: 'Tis a shrewd doubt, though it be but a dream.  And this may help to thicken other proofs That do demonstrate thinly.
translation: It's very suspicious, even though it's only a dream. And this may support and strengthen other, shakier evidence.

original: I’ll tear her all to pieces!
translation: I'll tear Desdemona to pieces!

original: Nay, yet be wise, yet we see nothing done,   She may be honest yet.
translation: No, be smart. We still haven't seen anything actually happen. She may still turn out to be honest.

original: Tell me but this,   Have you not sometimes seen a handkerchief   Spotted with strawberries in your wife’s hand?
translation: Just tell me this: have you occasionally seen a handkerchief decorated with strawberries in your wife's hand?

original: I gave her such a one, ’twas my first gift.
translation: I gave her such a handkerchief. It was my first gift to her.

original: I know not that, but such a handkerchief— I am sure it was your wife’s—did I today See Cassio wipe his beard with.
translation: I didn't know that, but I saw Cassio use such a handkerchief—I'm sure it was your wife's—to wipe his beard earlier today.

original: If it be that—
translation: If it really was that handkerchief—

original: If it be that, or any that was hers, It speaks against her with the other proofs.
translation: If it's the same one, or any handkerchief of Desdemona's, it is another piece of evidence weighing against her.

original: Oh, that the slave had forty thousand lives!   One is too poor, too weak for my revenge.   Now do I see ’tis true.
translation: Oh, if only that wretch Cassio had forty thousand lives, so I could kill him all those times! Once isn't enough for my revenge. Now I see that my suspicions are true.

original: Look here, Iago,   All my fond love thus do I blow to heaven—'tis gone.   Arise, black vengeance, from the hollow hell!
translation: Look, Iago, I let go of all my fond love; it's all gone. Black vengeance, come to me from the depths of hell!

original: Yield up, O love, thy crown and hearted throne   To tyrannous hate! Swell, bosom, with thy fraught,   For ’tis of aspics' tongues!
translation: Oh love, give way to cruel hate! May my chest swell up with hate, as deadly as the venom of poisonous snakes!

original: Yet be content.
translation: Calm down, now.

original: Oh, blood, blood, blood!
translation: Oh, blood, blood, blood!

original: Patience, I say. Your mind may change.
translation: Be patient, I'm telling you. You might change your mind.

original: Never, Iago. Like to the Pontic sea,   Whose icy current and compulsive course   Ne'er keeps retiring ebb but keeps due on   To the Propontic and the Hellespont,
translation: I'll never change my mind, Iago. Just like how the Black Sea never ebbs back but keeps flowing on with its icy waters through the Propontic sea and onward to the Hellespont,

original: Even so my bloody thoughts with violent pace   Shall ne'er look back, ne'er ebb to humble love   Till that a capable and wide revenge   Swallow them up.
translation: so my bloody thoughts only move forward with a violent current and never look back. My anger is like a tide and if it ever recedes back to love it is swallowed up again by a huge wave of revenge.

original: Now, by yon marble heaven,   In the due reverence of a sacred vow   I here engage my words.   (he kneels)
translation: Now, by heaven, with all the reverence of a sacred oath, I here make a vow.  [He kneels down]

original: Do not rise yet.   Witness, you ever-burning lights above,   You elements that clip us round about,
translation: Don't get up yet.  [He kneels down as well]  May the stars in the sky, and the sky itself be my witnesses:

original: Witness that here Iago doth give up   The execution of his wit, hands, heart,   To wronged Othello’s service.
translation: Iago hereby dedicates all of his wit, strength, and heart to helping Othello, who has been wronged.

original: Let him command,   And to obey shall be in me remorse,   What bloody business ever.
translation: Whatever he commands, I will obey, whatever bloody task he gives me.

original: I greet thy love   Not with vain thanks but with acceptance bounteous,   And will upon the instant put thee to ’t.
translation: Rather than just giving you empty thanks for your vow, I will take up your generous offer and give you an order right now.

original: Within these three days let me hear thee say   That Cassio’s not alive.
translation: Within three days, let me hear you say that Cassio is dead.

original: My friend is dead, 'Tis done at your request. But let her live.
translation: Your wish is my command. My friend Cassio will die. But let Desdemona live.

original: Damn her, lewd minx! Oh, damn her, damn her!   Come, go with me apart.
translation: Damn her, that lusty flirt! Oh damn her, damn her! Come on, come leave with me.

original: I will withdraw   To furnish me with some swift means of death   For the fair devil. Now art thou my lieutenant.
translation: I will go to figure out some quick way to kill the beautiful devil. Now you are my lieutenant.

original: I am your own for ever.
translation: I am loyal to you forever.

original: Do you know, sirrah, where Lieutenant Cassio lies?
translation: Do you know where Lieutenant Cassio lies?

original: I dare not say he lies anywhere.
translation: I daresay he doesn't lie anywhere.

original: Why, man?
translation: Why?

original: He’s a soldier, and for one to say a soldier lies,  ’tis stabbing.
Go to. Where lodges he?
translation: Oh, come on. I mean where does he sleep?

original: To tell you where he lodges is to tell you where I lie.
translation: To tell you where he sleeps would be to tell you where I lie.

original: Can anything be made of this?
translation: That doesn't make any sense.

original: I know not where he lodges, and for me to devise a  lodging and say he lies here, or he lies there, were to  lie in mine own throat.
translation: I don't know where he sleeps, so for me to say that he sleeps somewhere would be lying.

original: Can you inquire him out and be edified by report?
translation: Can you ask around and find out?

original: I will catechize the world for him, that is, make  questions, and by them answer.
translation: I will interrogate all the world about him, and make everyone answer my questions.

original: Seek him, bid him come hither. Tell him I have moved my lord on his behalf, and hope all will be well.
translation: Find him and tell him to come to me. Tell him I have persuaded my husband on his behalf, and I hope that everything will be resolved.

original: To do this is within the compass of man’s wit, and  therefore I will attempt the doing it.
translation: To do that is within the scope of a man's ability. And therefore I'll give it a try.

original: Where should I lose that handkerchief, Emilia?
translation: Where could I have lost that handkerchief, Emilia?

original: I know not, madam.
translation: I don't know, madam.

original: Believe me, I had rather have lost my purse   Full of crusadoes.
translation: Believe me, I would rather have lost my purse full of coins.

original: And but my noble Moor   Is true of mind and made of no such baseness   As jealous creatures are, it were enough   To put him to ill thinking.
translation: Losing my handkerchief would be enough to make my husband jealous, if he were less loyal and more of a jealous man.

original: Is he not jealous?
translation: Is he not a jealous man?

original: Who, he? I think the sun where he was born Drew all such humors from him.
translation: Who, Othello? I think he got so much sunlight where he was born that it burned the jealousy out of him.

original: Look where he comes.
translation: Look, he's coming here.

original: I will not leave him now till Cassio Be called to him.—How is ’t with you, my lord?
translation: I won't stop bothering him now until he reinstates Cassio.  How are you doing, my husband?

original: Well, my good lady.—    Oh, hardness to dissemble!— How do you, Desdemona?
translation: I'm doing well, my good lady.  Oh, it's so hard to pretend I'm fine! [To DESDEMONA] How are you, Desdemona?

original: Well, my good lord.
translation: Well, my good husband.

original: Give me your hand. This hand is moist, my lady.
translation: Give me your hand. It's moist, my lady.

original: It hath felt no age nor known no sorrow.
translation: Yes, because I am young and haven't experienced any sorrow.

original: This argues fruitfulness and liberal heart.   Hot, hot, and moist. This hand of yours requires   A sequester from liberty, fasting, and prayer,
translation: Warm and moist skin means that you are fertile and have a generous heart. This hand of yours suggests that you need to be secluded, to fast and to pray.

original: Much castigation, exercise devout,   For here’s a young and sweating devil here,   That commonly rebels. 'Tis a good hand,   A frank one.
translation: You need some discipline, for someone with these kinds of sweating hands commonly rebels against authority. It's a good hand, an open one.

original: You may indeed say so, For ’twas that hand that gave away my heart.
translation: You could say that, for it was that hand that gave you my heart.

original: A liberal hand. The hearts of old gave hands,  But our new heraldry is hands, not hearts.
translation: A giving hand. It used to be that people's hearts controlled whether they gave someone their hand in marriage. But now people give away their hands without consulting their hearts.

original: I cannot speak of this. Come now, your promise.
translation: I can't speak to that. Now come on, remember your promise.

original: What promise, chuck?
translation: What promise, dear?

original: I have sent to bid Cassio come speak with you.
translation: I have sent someone to tell Cassio to come speak to you.

original: I have a salt and sorry rheum offends me. Lend me thy handkerchief.
translation: I have a cold and a runny nose. Lend me your handkerchief.

original: Here, my lord.
translation: Here, my lord.

original: That which I gave you.
translation: No, give me the one I gave to you.

original: I have it not about me.
translation: I don't have it with me.

original: Not?
translation: You don't?

original: No, indeed, my lord.
translation: No, my lord.

original: That’s a fault. That handkerchief   Did an Egyptian to my mother give,   She was a charmer and could almost read   The thoughts of people.
translation: That's not good. My mother was given that handkerchief by an Egyptian woman who could read people's minds.

original: She told her, while she kept it   'Twould make her amiable and subdue my father   Entirely to her love, but if she lost it   Or made gift of it,
translation: She told my mother that as long as she had the handkerchief, she would be desirable and my father would be helplessly in love with her, but if she lost it or gave it away,

original: my father’s eye   Should hold her loathèd and his spirits should hunt   After new fancies. She, dying, gave it me   And bid me, when my fate would have me wived,   To give it her.
translation: my father would hate her and he would go after other women. Before my mother died, she gave the handkerchief to me and told me to give it to my wife whenever I married.

original: I did so, and take heed on ’t,   Make it a darling like your precious eye.   To lose ’t or give ’t away were such perdition   As nothing else could match.
translation: I did this, and so keep it close like a precious treasure. To lose that handkerchief or give it away would be a sin greater than any other.

original: Is ’t possible?
translation: Is this true?

original: 'Tis true. There’s magic in the web of it.   A sibyl, that had numbered in the world   The sun to course two hundred compasses,   In her prophetic fury sewed the work.
translation: It is true. There's magic in the sewing. A prophetess who lived to the age of two hundred sewed the handkerchief while she was in a trance.

original: The worms were hallowed that did breed the silk,   And it was dyed in mummy which the skillful   Conserved of maidens' hearts.
translation: The worms that made the silk were magical, and it was tinted in dye extracted from embalmed virgins' hearts.

original: Indeed? Is ’t true?
translation: Really? Is this true?

original: Most veritable, therefore look to ’t well.
translation: Absolutely, so look after that handkerchief carefully.

original: Then would to Heaven that I had never seen ’t!
translation: God, I wish I'd never seen it!

original: Ha! Wherefore?
translation: Aha! Why do you wish that?

original: Why do you speak so startingly and rash?
translation: Why are you talking in fits in starts—and so impulsively, too?

original: Is ’t lost? Is ’t gone? Speak, is ’t out o' th' way?
translation: Is the handkerchief lost? Is it gone? Tell me, have you lost it?

original: Bless us!
translation: God help me.

original: Say you?
translation: What do you say?

original: It is not lost, but what and if it were?
translation: It isn't lost, but what if it were?

original: How!
translation: What?

original: I say, it is not lost.
translation: I'm telling you, it's not lost.

original: Fetch ’t, let me see ’t.
translation: Go get it, then. Let me see it.

original: Why, so I can, sir, but I will not now.   This is a trick to put me from my suit.
translation: Well, sir, I could do that, but I won't right now. You're trying to trick me so I forget about persuading you regarding Cassio.

original: Pray you, let Cassio be received again.
translation: Please, let Cassio be your lieutenant again.

original: Fetch me the handkerchief—my mind misgives.
translation: Bring me the handkerchief. I am worried.

original: Come, come, You’ll never meet a more sufficient man.
translation: Come on. You'll never find a better man for the job than Cassio.

original: The handkerchief!
translation: The handkerchief!

original: A man that all his time Hath founded his good fortunes on your love, Shared dangers with you—
translation: Cassio has always had good fortune because of your love for him. He and you have faced dangers together.

original: The handkerchief!
translation: The handkerchief!

original: In sooth, you are to blame.
translation: To tell the truth, it's all your fault.

original: Zounds!
translation: Christ!

original: Is not this man jealous?
translation: Doesn't that look like a jealous man?

original: I ne'er saw this before. Sure, there’s some wonder in this handkerchief, I am most unhappy in the loss of it.
translation: I've never seen him like this. There really must be some magic in that handkerchief. I am really sad and unlucky that I lost it.

original: 'Tis not a year or two shows us a man.   They are all but stomachs, and we all but food.
translation: It takes just a year or two for a man's true colors to become apparent. They're nothing but hungry stomachs, and we women are the food.

original: To eat us hungerly, and when they are full,   They belch us. Look you, Cassio and my husband!
translation: All they want is to get their fill of us, and when they've had enough they throw us back up. Look, here comes Cassio and my husband.

original: There is no other way. 'Tis she must do ’t, And, lo, the happiness! Go and importune her.
translation: There's no other way. She must be the one to do it. And what luck, here she is! Go and ask her.

original: How now, good Cassio, what’s the news with you?
translation: How are you, Cassio? What's going on with you?

original: Madam, my former suit. I do beseech you   That by your virtuous means I may again   Exist, and be a member of his love   Whom I, with all the office of my heart   Entirely honor.
translation: Madam, only my case from before. I beg you to use your virtuous powers to help me return to the good graces of Othello, whom I honor with all of my heart.

original: I would not be delayed.   If my offence be of such mortal kind   That nor my service past, nor present sorrows,   Nor purposed merit in futurity,
translation: I want this to happen quickly. If my offense was so bad that neither my past service nor my present regret, nor the future good deeds I promise

original: Can ransom me into his love again,   But to know so must be my benefit.
translation: can buy back his love, then I at least would like to know this now.

original: So shall I clothe me in a forced content,   And shut myself up in some other course,   To fortune’s alms.
translation: If that is the case then I will pretend to be content, and settle on a new career to try my fortunes there.

original: Alas, thrice-gentle Cassio,   My advocation is not now in tune.   My lord is not my lord, nor should I know him   Were he in favor as in humor altered.
translation: Alas, dearest Cassio, my pleading on your behalf isn't working right now. My husband is not acting like himself. If his physical appearance were as transformed as his inner character is now, I wouldn't even recognize him.

original: So help me every spirit sanctified   As I have spoken for you all my best   And stood within the blank of his displeasure   For my free speech.
translation: So help me God, I have spoken up for you as best I could and he has looked down on me because of it.

original: You must awhile be patient.   What I can do I will, and more I will   Than for myself I dare. Let that suffice you.
translation: You must be patient for a while. I will do what I can, and I will even do more than I would dare do for myself. Let that be enough for you.

original: Is my lord angry?
translation: Is Othello angry?

original: He went hence but now, And certainly in strange unquietness.
translation: He was just here, and he is certainly strangely bothered.

original: Can he be angry? I have seen the cannon   When it hath blown his ranks into the air   And, like the devil, from his very arm   Puffed his own brother—
translation: Can he be angry? I have seen him remain calm when a cannon has blown his soldiers into the air and, like the devil, blown his own brother out of his arms.

original: and is he angry?   Something of moment then, I will go meet him.   There’s matter in ’t indeed, if he be angry.
translation: And  now  he's angry? It must be about a serious matter. I will go see him. If he's angry, it must really be something significant.

original: I prithee, do so.
translation: Please do go see him.

original: Something, sure, of state,   Either from Venice, or some unhatched practice   Made demonstrable here in Cyprus to him,
translation: It must be something government-related—either having to do with Venice or some secret thing that's now come to light in Cyprus—

original: Hath puddled his clear spirit, and in such cases   Men’s natures wrangle with inferior things,   Though great ones are their object.
translation: that has put him in this mood. When this happens, men take out their tempers on less important things, when they're really upset with bigger issues.

original: 'Tis even so,   For let our finger ache and it endues   Our other healthful members even to that sense   Of pain.
translation: That's what happens when we hurt our finger, and it makes other parts of our bodies seem to hurt.

original: Nay, we must think men are not gods,   Nor of them look for such observances   As fit the bridal.
translation: No, we shouldn't idolize men, or expect them to always be as nice as they are on their wedding day.

original: Beshrew me much, Emilia,   I was, unhandsome warrior as I am,   Arraigning his unkindness with my soul,   But now I find I had suborned the witness,   And he’s indicted falsely.
translation: Oh, Emilia, curse me: I'm so foolish that I thought Othello was being unkind, but I was clearly falsely accusing him.

original: Pray heaven it be State matters, as you think, and no conception Nor no jealous toy concerning you.
translation: I pray to heaven that he is upset over some government matter, as you think is the case, and not over some jealous idea about you.

original: Alas the day! I never gave him cause.
translation: God forbid! I've given him no reason to be jealous.

original: But jealous souls will not be answered so.   They are not ever jealous for the cause,   But jealous for they’re jealous.
translation: But jealous souls need no evidence. They aren't jealous because of a reason, but merely because they are jealous people.

original: It is a monster   Begot upon itself, born on itself.
translation: Jealousy is a monster that gives birth to itself.

original: Heaven keep the monster from Othello’s mind!
translation: May heaven keep that monster away from Othello's mind!

original: Lady, amen.
translation: Amen, my lady.

original: I will go seek him.—Cassio, walk hereabout.
translation: I will go find him. Cassio, stay around here.

original: If I do find him fit, I’ll move your suit   And seek to effect it to my uttermost.
translation: If I find him in a good mood, I'll plead your case and try my hardest to get you your job back.

original: I humbly thank your ladyship.
translation: My lady, I humbly thank you.

original: Save you, friend Cassio!
translation: Hello, my friend Cassio!

original: What make you from home?  How is ’t with you, my most fair Bianca? Indeed, sweet love, I was coming to your house.
translation: What are you doing away from home? How are you, my most beautiful Bianca? I was actually just on my way to your house, my sweet love.

original: And I was going to your lodging, Cassio.   What, keep a week away? Seven days and nights?   Eight score eight hours?
translation: And I was on my way to yours, Cassio. Why have you been away for a week? Seven days and nights? One hundred and sixty-eight hours?

original: And lovers' absent hours   More tedious than the dial eightscore times!   Oh weary reckoning!
translation: And hours that lovers spend apart pass eight times more slowly than normal. How tiresome to count the hours going by!

original: Pardon me, Bianca,   I have this while with leaden thoughts been pressed,   But I shall, in a more continuate time,   Strike off this score of absence.
translation: Pardon me, Bianca. I've been busy with heavy thoughts. But, when I have some time, I will make up for being away for so long.

original: Sweet Bianca,   (giving her DESDEMONA’s handkerchief)   Take me this work out.
translation: Sweet Bianca, copy out the pattern on this.  [He gives her DESDEMONA's handkerchief]

original: O Cassio, whence came this?   This is some token from a newer friend!
translation: Oh, Cassio, where did you get this from? This is some gift from another woman!

original: To the felt absence now I feel a cause.   Is ’t come to this? Well, well.
translation: Now I see why you haven't come to see me. Has it come to this? Well, well, well.

original: Go to, woman,   Throw your vile guesses in the devil’s teeth   From whence you have them.
translation: Oh please, woman. Throw your vile guesses back to hell, where they came from.

original: You are jealous now   That this is from some mistress, some remembrance.   No, in good troth, Bianca.
translation: You are jealous now and think that this handkerchief is from some mistress. No, in truth, it isn't, Bianca.

original: Why, whose is it?
translation: Whose is it, then?

original: I know not neither, I found it in my chamber.   I like the work well.
translation: I don't know. I found it in my bedroom, and I like the pattern on it.

original: Ere it be demanded,   As like enough it will, I would have it copied.   Take it and do ’t, and leave me for this time.
translation: Before someone asks for it back, I want to have the pattern copied. Take it and do it, and leave me alone for a bit.

original: Leave you! Wherefore?
translation: Leave you! Why?

original: I do attend here on the general And think it no addition, nor my wish, To have him see me womaned.
translation: I am waiting on the general here, and I don't think it would be very good for him to see me with a woman.

original: Why, I pray you?
translation: Why?

original: Not that I love you not.
translation: It's not that I don't love you.

original: But that you do not love me. I pray you bring me on the way a little And say if I shall see you soon at night.
translation: But that you don't love me. Please come with me just a little ways, and tell me if I will see you soon at night.

original: 'Tis but a little way that I can bring you,  For I attend here. But I’ll see you soon.
translation: I can't go with you very far, for I must wait here. But I will see you soon.

original: 'Tis very good. I must be circumstanced.
translation: That's good enough. I have to take what I can get given the circumstances.

original: Will you think so?
translation: Do you think so?

original: Think so, Iago?
translation: Think what, Iago?

original: What, To kiss in private?
translation: What, that they kissed in private?

original: An unauthorized kiss!
translation: An inappropriate kiss!

original: Or to be naked with her friend in bed An hour or more, not meaning any harm?
translation: Or because she was naked in bed with a friend for just an hour or more, not meaning any harm?

original: Naked in bed, Iago, and not mean harm!   It is hypocrisy against the devil.
translation: Iago, naked in bed and not meaning any harm? That would be like tricking the devil.

original: They that mean virtuously, and yet do so,   The devil their virtue tempts, and they tempt heaven.
translation: If they were acting this way but had virtuous intentions, they were tempted by the devil and they were tempting God to damn them.

original: So they do nothing, ’tis a venial slip.  But if I give my wife a handkerchief—
translation: As long as they haven't actually done anything, it's just a pardonable sin. But, if I give my wife a handkerchief . . .

original: What then?
translation: What then?

original: Why then ’tis hers, my lord, and, being hers, She may, I think, bestow ’t on any man.
translation: Then it belongs to her, my lord. And since it is hers, she may give it to any man she wants.

original: She is protectress of her honor too.  May she give that?
translation: Her honor belongs to her, too. Can she give that away, as well?

original: Her honor is an essence that’s not seen, They have it very oft that have it not. But for the handkerchief—
translation: Her honor is part of her inner essence that can't be seen. Often people have an honorable reputation but aren't really honorable. But as for the handkerchief—

original: By heaven, I would most gladly have forgot it.   Thou saidst—Oh, it comes o'er my memory,
translation: By heaven, I wish I had forgotten about it. You told me—oh, it comes back to my memory,

original: As doth the raven o'er the infectious house,   Boding to all—he had my handkerchief.
translation: like the bad omen of a raven coming over a house where someone is sick—that Cassio had my handkerchief.

original: Ay, what of that?
translation: Yes, so what?

original: That’s not so good now.
translation: That is not so good, now.

original: What if I had said I had seen him do you wrong?   Or heard him say—as knaves be such abroad,
translation: What if I had told you that I saw him do you wrong? Or what if I heard him say so—there are some villains out there

original: Who having, by their own importunate suit,   Or voluntary dotage of some mistress,   Convincèd or supplied them, cannot choose   But they must blab—
translation: who, once they have seduced or satisfied some mistress with their flirting and doting, can't help but brag about it —
