original: Hath he said any thing?
translation: Has he said something?

original: He hath, my lord, but be you well assured No more than he’ll unswear.
translation: My lord, he has—but you can be sure that he'll deny it.

original: What hath he said?
translation: What did he say?

original: Why, that he did—I know not what he did.
translation: Well, he said that he did—I don't know what he did.

original: What? what?
translation: What? What?

original: Lie—
translation: He said he did lie—

original: With her?
translation: With Desdemona?

original: With her, on her, what you will.
translation: With her, on her, however you want to say it.

original: Lie with her? lie on her? We say “lie on her” when they belie her! Lie with her—that’s fulsome.  Handkerchief—confessions—handkerchief!
translation: Lie with her? Lie on her? To lie  on  someone is to tell lies about that person! To lie  with  her—that's obscene. First the handkerchief, and now this confession!

original: To confess, and  be hanged for his labor.   First to be hanged, and then to confess—I tremble at it   .
translation: Should he confess first and then be executed?  No, I'll kill him first and let him confess later. I am trembling with anger,

original: Nature would not invest  herself in such shadowing passion without some  instruction. It is not words that shake me thus. Pish!  Noses, ears, and lips. Is ’t possible?  Confess!—Handkerchief!—Oh, devil!—
translation: and nature wouldn't make my body do this without some reason. It must be more than a rumor if it's making me tremble like this. Ugh! Noses, ears, and lips. Could this be true? That he would admit to it—and the handkerchief! Oh, devil!

original: Work on, My medicine, work! Thus credulous fools are  caught,   And many worthy and chaste dames even thus,   All guiltless, meet reproach.—
translation: [To himself]  Keep on working, my harmful medicine, keep on working! This is how gullible fools are tricked, and many trustworthy and chaste women, completely innocent, are punished in situations like this.

original: What, ho! My lord!   My lord, I say! Othello!
translation: [To OTHELLO]  Hey! My lord! My lord! Othello!

original: How now, Cassio!
translation: Hey there, Cassio!

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: My lord is fall'n into an epilepsy. This is his second fit. He had one yesterday.
translation: My lord has fallen into a seizure. This is the second time he's had one of these fits. He had one yesterday.

original: Rub him about the temples.
translation: Rub his temples.

original: No, forbear.   The lethargy must have his quiet course.   If not, he foams at mouth and by and by   Breaks out to savage madness. Look, he stirs.
translation: No, hold on. We have to let the fit run its course. Otherwise he'll foam at the mouth and break out in a fit of savage madness. Look, he's moving.

original: Do you withdraw yourself a little while,   He will recover straight. When he is gone   I would on great occasion speak with you.
translation: Stay away for a bit. He'll recover soon.  When he is gone, I would really like to talk to you in private.

original: How is it, general? Have you not hurt your head?
translation: How are you, General? Have you hurt your head?

original: Dost thou mock me?
I mock you not, by heaven. Would you would bear your fortune like a man!
translation: No, I swear to God! I wish you would bear your misfortune like a man!

original: A hornèd man’s a monster and a beast.
translation: A man who's been cheated on isn't a man; he has the cuckold's horns, and so is a monstrous beast.

original: There’s many a beast then in a populous city, And many a civil monster.
translation: Well then, there are many monsters in big cities, and many monsters that pass for men.

original: Did he confess it?
translation: Did Cassio confess to it?

original: Good sir, be a man,   Think every bearded fellow that’s but yoked   May draw with you.
translation: Good sir, be a man. Think about it: every married man has experienced what you're going through.

original: There’s millions now alive   That nightly lie in those unproper beds   Which they dare swear peculiar. Your case is better.
translation: There are millions of wives now living who sleep in disgraced beds which they swear belong only to their husbands. But you're better off.

original: Oh, ’tis the spite of hell, the fiend’s arch-mock,   To lip a wanton in a secure couch,   And to suppose her chaste.
translation: It's even worse—a curse from hell—to kiss your wife in bed thinking that she is chaste when she isn't.

original: No, let me know,   And knowing what I am, I know what she shall be.
translation: No, I'd rather know if my wife were cheating on me. Then I'd know exactly what sort of person I am and what sort of person my wife is.

original: Oh, thou art wise! 'Tis certain.
translation: Oh, you are certainly wise!

original: Stand you awhile apart,   Confine yourself but in a patient list.   Whilst you were here o'erwhelmèd with your grief—
translation: Stay away from her for a while. Be patient. While you were overwhelmed by your grief—

original: A passion most resulting such a man—   Cassio came hither. I shifted him away   And laid good ’scuses upon your ecstasy,
translation: a passionate feeling you are prone to—Cassio was here. I sent him away and made some excuse for your fit of passion.

original: Bade him anon return and here speak with me,   The which he promised. Do but encave yourself,   And mark the fleers, the gibes, and notable scorns   That dwell in every region of his face.
translation: I told him to come back here and speak with me, and he promised to do so. Hide nearby and watch the sneers and visible expressions of scorn all over his face,

original: For I will make him tell the tale anew   Where, how, how oft, how long ago, and when   He hath, and is again to cope your wife.
translation: as I ask him to tell me again about where, how, how often, how long ago, and when he has slept and will again sleep with your wife.

original: I say, but mark his gesture. Marry, patience,   Or I shall say you are all in all in spleen,   And nothing of a man.
translation: Just watch his expression. Please, be patient, or else you'll show that you are completely ruled by your emotions and not a real man.

original: Dost thou hear, Iago? I will be found most cunning in my patience, But—dost thou hear?—most bloody.
translation: Listen to me, Iago: I will be patient and cunning. But—do you hear me?—I will take violent action later.

original: That’s not amiss,  But yet keep time in all. Will you withdraw?
translation: That's not wrong. But wait for a bit. Will you step back and hide?

original: Now will I question Cassio of Bianca,   A huswife that by selling her desires   Buys herself bread and clothes.
translation: Now I will question Cassio about Bianca, a loose girl that makes a living by selling herself to men.

original: It is a creature   That dotes on Cassio, as ’tis the strumpet’s plague   To beguile many and be beguiled by one.
translation: The whore loves Cassio, and it's her bad luck to attract many men but be attracted to just one.

original: He, when he hears of her, cannot refrain   From the excess of laughter. Here he comes.
translation: When he is asked about her, he can't help but laugh. Here he comes.

original: As he shall smile, Othello shall go mad.   And his unbookish jealousy must construe   Poor Cassio’s smiles, gestures, and light behavior   Quite in the wrong.—
translation: [To himself]  As Cassio smiles while we talk, Othello will go mad. And his unrestrained jealousy will misinterpret poor Cassio's smiles, gestures, and jovial behavior.

original: How do you now, lieutenant?
translation: [To CASSIO ]  How are you doing now, lieutenant?

original: The worser that you give me the addition Whose want even kills me.
translation: I'm doing worse now since you called me lieutenant, when it's killing me that I don't have that title anymore.

original: Ply Desdemona well, and you are sure on ’t.  Now if this suit lay in Bianca’s power How quickly should you speed!
translation: Ask Desdemona to help you, and you'll surely get it back.  Now, if it were Bianca who had the power to help you, I imagine you'd be running off to her as fast as you could!

original: Alas, poor caitiff!
translation: Ha, that poor woman!

original: Look how he laughs already!
translation: Look how he's laughing already!

original: I never knew woman love man so.
Alas, poor rogue, I think indeed she loves me.
translation: Alas, the poor girl, I think she really does love me.

original: Now he denies it faintly, and laughs it out.
translation: Now he denies his crime a bit, and laughs it off.

original: Do you hear, Cassio?
translation: Have you heard, Cassio?

original: Now he importunes him To tell it o'er. Go to, well said, well said.
translation: Now Iago is asking Cassio to tell the story again. Go on, well said, well said.

original: She gives it out that you shall marry her. Do you intend it?
translation: She is saying that you're going to marry her. Do you intend to?

original: Ha, ha, ha!
translation: Ha, ha, ha!

original: Do ye triumph, Roman? Do you triumph?
translation: Are you celebrating like a triumphant Roman general? Are you triumphing after your conquest?

original: I marry her! What? A customer? Prithee bear some  charity to my wit. Do not think it so unwholesome. Ha,  ha, ha!
translation: Me, marry her? A prostitute? Please, think a little more highly of me; don't think I'm that stupid. Ha, ha, ha!

original: So, so, so, so! They laugh that win!
translation: Aha, so there! He's laughing like he's won her over!

original: Faith, the cry goes that you shall marry her.
translation: Really, rumor has it that you are going to marry her.

original: Prithee say true!
translation: Please, is that true?

original: I am a very villain else.
translation: I swear it is, or else I'm a villain.

original: Have you scored me? Well.
translation: Have you wronged me? Well, then.

original: This is the monkey’s own giving out. She is persuaded I will marry her, out of her own love and flattery, not  out of my promise.
translation: The monkey herself must be spreading this rumor. She is convinced I will marry her, driven by her own love and self-flattery. I haven't promised her anything.

original: Iago beckons me. Now he begins the story.
translation: Iago is signaling to me. Now Cassio is beginning the story.

original: She was here even now. She haunts me in every place. I  was the other day talking on the sea-bank with certain  Venetians, and thither comes the bauble and, by this  hand, she falls me thus about my neck—
translation: She was here just now. She follows me everywhere. The other day I was talking along the shore with some Venetians, and the silly girl came to me and—I swear—she hangs around my neck like this—

original: Crying “O dear Cassio!” as it were. His gesture imports it.
translation: He looks like he's crying out, "Oh dear Cassio!" That's what his gestures indicate.

original: So hangs and lolls and weeps upon me, so shakes, and  pulls me! Ha, ha, ha!
translation: She hangs on me like this and cries on my shoulder and shakes and pulls me like this! Ha, ha, ha!

original: Now he tells how she plucked him to my chamber. Oh, I  see that nose of yours, but not that dog I shall throw  it to.
translation: Now he's talking about how she dragged him to my bedroom. Oh, Cassio, I'm going to cut off your nose and throw it to some dog.

original: Well, I must leave her company.
translation: Well, I must stop spending time with her.

original: Before me! Look, where she comes.
translation: My goodness! Look, she's coming.

original: 'Tis such another fitchew. Marry, a perfumed one.— What do you mean by this haunting of me?
translation: Just the prostitute we were talking about. And she's wearing perfume. Why are you following me around like this?

original: Let the devil and his dam haunt you! What did you mean  by that same handkerchief you gave me even now? I was a  fine fool to take it. I must take out the work?
translation: Let the devil and his wife follow you around! Why did you give me that handkerchief just recently? I was an idiot to accept it. You want me to copy the embroidery?

original: A likely piece of work, that you should find it in your chamber, and not know who left it there! This is some minx’s  token, and I must take out the work? There, give it your hobby-horse. Wheresoever you had it, I’ll take out no  work on ’t.
translation: What a likely story, that you found it in your room and didn't know who left it there! This is a gift from some woman, and you want  me  to copy out the embroidery? There, give it back to your new mistress. Wherever you got it from, I'm not copying any of it.

original: How now, my sweet Bianca! How now, how now?
translation: What's the matter, my sweet Bianca? What's the matter?

original: By heaven, that should be my handkerchief!
translation: By heaven, that's my handkerchief!

original: If you’ll come to supper tonight, you may. If you will  not, come when you are next prepared for.
translation: If you will come have dinner with me tonight, then okay. If you don't come to dinner then just keep on waiting until I call for you next—which will be never.

original: After her, after her.
translation: Go after her, go after her.

original: I must, she’ll rail in the street else.
translation: I must. Otherwise, she'll make a ruckus in the street.

original: Will you sup there?
translation: Will you go to dinner with her?

original: Yes, I intend so.
translation: Yes, I intend to go.

original: Well, I may chance to see you, for I would very fain  speak with you.
translation: Well, I'd like to get a chance to see you later, because I really would like to speak with you.

original: Prithee come, will you?
translation: Please come to the diner, then. Will you?

original: Go to! Say no more.
translation: Stop talking and go after her!

original: How shall I murder him, Iago?
translation: How should I murder him, Iago?

original: Did you perceive how he laughed at his vice?
translation: Did you see how he laughed about his crime?

original: Oh Iago!
translation: Oh, Iago!

original: And did you see the handkerchief?
translation: And did you see the handkerchief?

original: Was that mine?
translation: Was that my handkerchief?

original: Yours by this hand. And to see how he prizes the  foolish woman your wife! She gave it him, and he hath  given it his whore.
translation: I swear on my hand, it was yours. And look how much he cares about your foolish wife! She gave him her handkerchief, and he turns around and gives it to a whore.

original: I would have him nine years a-killing. A fine woman! A  fair woman! A sweet woman!
translation: If I could, I'd spend nine years killing him slowly. She was a fine woman! A beautiful woman! A sweet woman!

original: Nay, you must forget that.
translation: You must forget about that.

original: Ay, let her rot and perish and be damned tonight, for  she shall not live. No, my heart is turned to stone. I  strike it and it hurts my hand.
translation: Yes, let her rot and perish and go to hell tonight, for she will not live past tonight. No, my heart has turned to stone. If I beat my chest, it hurts my hand.

original: Oh, the world hath not a sweeter creature, she might lie by an emperor’s side  and command him tasks.
translation: Oh, there's not a sweeter creature in the world! She could be the wife of an emperor and he'd obey her commands.

original: Nay, that’s not your way.
translation: No, that's not like you to obey a woman.

original: Hang her! I do but say what she is. So delicate with  her needle, an admirable musician. Oh, she will sing the savageness out of a bear! Of so high and plenteous wit  and invention!
translation: Let her be hanged! I'm just calling her what she is now. Such a skilled sewer, such an admirable musician. Oh, she could sing so well she'd charm a savage bear to gentleness! She's so clever and intelligent!

original: She’s the worse for all this.
translation: All these traits make her even worse.

original: Oh, a thousand thousand times—and then of so gentle a  condition!
translation: Oh, they make her a thousand times worse! And she has such a gentle nature!

original: Ay, too gentle.
translation: Yes, too gentle.

original: Nay, that’s certain. But yet the pity of it, Iago! O  Iago, the pity of it, Iago!
translation: That's certainly true. But what a pity this is, Iago! Oh, Iago, the pity!

original: If you are so fond over her iniquity, give her patent  to offend, for if it touch not you it comes near nobody.
translation: If you still care about her after her sinfulness, give her permission to cheat on you. If it doesn't bother you, it doesn't harm anyone.

original: I will chop her into messes! Cuckold me?
translation: I will chop her up into little bits! Cheat on me, will she?

original: Oh, ’tis foul in her.
translation: Oh, it's really a foul thing for her to do.

original: With mine officer!
translation: With my own lieutenant!

original: That’s fouler.
translation: That's even worse.

original: Get me some poison, Iago, this night. I’ll not  expostulate with her, lest her body and beauty unprovide my mind again—This night, Iago!
translation: Iago, get me some poison this very night. I won't speak to her, so her body and beauty don't trick my mind again. Get me the poison tonight, Iago!

original: Do it not with poison. Strangle her in her bed, even  the bed she hath contaminated.
translation: Don't poison her. Strangle her in her bed—the very bed she contaminated with her affair.

original: Good, good, the justice of it pleases! Very good!
translation: Good idea! Poetic justice! Very good!

original: And for Cassio, let me be his undertaker. You shall  hear more by midnight.
translation: And as for Cassio, let me handle him. You'll hear more about it by midnight.

original: Excellent good.
translation: Very good.

original: What trumpet is that same?
translation: What is that trumpet?

original: I warrant something from Venice. 'Tis Lodovico, this,  comes from the duke. See, your wife’s with him.
translation: It must be some news from Venice. Here comes Lodovico, from the Duke. Look, your wife is with him.

original: Save you, worthy general!
translation: Hello, noble General.

original: With all my heart, sir.
translation: Hello, sir.

original: The duke and senators of Venice greet you.
translation: The Duke and Senators of Venice send their greetings.

original: I kiss the instrument of their pleasures.
translation: I kiss the letter that contains their commands.

original: And what’s the news, good cousin Lodovico?
I am very glad to see you, signior. Welcome to Cyprus.
translation: I am very glad to see you, sir. Welcome to Cyprus.

original: I thank you. How does lieutenant Cassio?
translation: Thank you. How is Lieutenant Cassio doing?

original: Lives, sir.
translation: He's alive, sir.

original: Cousin, there’s fall'n between him and my lord An unkind breach, but you shall make all well.
translation: Cousin, there's a rift now between my husband and him. But you can mend it.

original: Are you sure of that?
translation: Are you sure about that?

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: “This fail you not to do, as you will—”
translation: "Don't fail to do this, since you will—"

original: He did not call, he’s busy in the paper. Is there division ’twixt my lord and Cassio?
translation: He wasn't talking to you, Desdemona. He's busy reading the letter. Is there really a dispute between my lord and Cassio?

original: A most unhappy one. I would do much  T' atone them, for the love I bear to Cassio.
translation: Yes, a most unhappy one. I would do anything to repair their friendship, because of my love for Cassio.

original: Fire and brimstone!
translation: Fire and brimstone!

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: Are you wise?
translation: Do you have any sense?

original: What, is he angry?
translation: What, is he angry?

original: Maybe the letter moved him, For, as I think, they do command him home, Deputing Cassio in his government.
translation: Maybe the letter upset him. I think they've ordered him to return home and leave Cassio in charge here.

original: By my troth, I am glad on ’t.
translation: Truthfully, I'm glad about that.

original: Indeed!
translation: Really!

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: I am glad to see you mad.
translation: I'm glad to see that you are angry.

original: Why, sweet Othello—
translation: Why, sweet Othello—

original: Devil!
translation: You devil!

original: I have not deserved this.
translation: I haven't done anything to deserve this.

original: My lord, this would not be believed in Venice, Though I should swear I saw ’t. 'Tis very much. Make her amends, she weeps.
translation: My lord, no one in Venice would believe you just did that—even if I swore that I saw it with my own eyes. This is no small matter. Apologize to her. She's crying.

original: Oh, devil, devil!   If that the earth could teem with woman’s tears,
translation: Oh, devil, devil! If the whole world were filled with the tears of women,

original: Each drop she falls would prove a crocodile.   Out of my sight!
translation: they'd all be fake tears! Get out of my sight!

original: I will not stay to offend you.
translation: I will not stay, if it offends you.

original: Truly, an obedient lady. I do beseech your lordship, call her back.
translation: She is truly an obedient lady. I beg you, my lord, call her back.

original: Mistress!
translation: Mistress!

original: My lord?
translation: Yes, my lord?

original: What would you with her, sir?
translation: What do you want with her, sir?

original: Who, I, my lord?
translation: Me, my lord?

original: Ay, you did wish that I would make her turn.   Sir, she can turn, and turn, and yet go on,   And turn again.
translation: Yes, you're the one who wanted me to have her turn around and come back here. She can turn around all right; she's very good at turning on you.

original: And she can weep, sir, weep.   And she’s obedient, as you say, obedient,   Very obedient.
translation: And she can weep, sir. And she's obedient, as you say, very obedient.

original: (To DESDEMONA)   Proceed you in your  tears.
translation: [To DESDEMONA]  Keep on crying.

original: (To LODOVICO)   Concerning this, sir—
translation: [To LODOVICO]  About this letter, sir.

original: (To DESDEMONA)   Oh, well-painted passion!
translation: [To DESDEMONA ]  Oh you are pretending really well!

original: (To LODOVICO)   I am commanded home.
translation: [ To LODOVICO]  I have been ordered to come home.

original: (To DESDEMONA)   Get  you away,   I’ll send for you anon.
translation: [To DESDEMONA]  Go away. I'll call for you later.

original: (To LODOVICO)   Sir, I obey the  mandate   And will return to Venice.
translation: [To LODOVICO]  Sir, I obey my orders and will return to Venice.

original: (To DESDEMONA)   Hence,  avaunt!
translation: [To DESDEMONA]  Get away from here! Away!

original: Cassio shall have my place. And, sir, tonight I do entreat that we may sup together.  You are welcome, sir, to Cyprus. Goats and monkeys!
Is this the noble Moor whom our full senate   Call all in all sufficient? Is this the nature   Whom passion could not shake?
translation: Is this the same noble Moor that our whole senate thinks so highly of? Is this the person who supposedly could not be shaken by passion?

original: Whose solid virtue   The shot of accident nor dart of chance   Could neither graze nor pierce?
translation: The man whose solid virtue was invulnerable to anything chance or fortune could throw at it?

original: He is much changed.
translation: He has changed a lot.

original: Are his wits safe? Is he not light of brain?
translation: Does he still have his wits? Has he gone crazy, too?

original: He’s that he is. I may not breathe my censure What he might be. If what he might he is not, I would to heaven he were!
translation: He is as he is. I can't say a bad word about what he might be like. If he is not what he has the potential to be, then I wish to heaven he was!

original: What? Strike his wife?
translation: What was that about? Why did he hit his wife?

original: 'Faith, that was not so well. Yet would I knew That stroke would prove the worst!
translation: That really was not so good. But I wish I could say that was the worst he'll do.

original: Is it his use? Or did the letters work upon his blood And new-create his fault?
translation: Does he usually hit her like that? Or did the letter he was reading raise his temper and make him so angry that he hit her?

original: Alas, alas!   It is not honesty in me to speak   What I have seen and known. You shall observe him,
translation: Alas, alas! It is not right for me to tell you about what I have seen and learned. You will see for yourself,

original: And his own courses will denote him so   That I may save my speech. Do but go after   And mark how he continues.
translation: and his actions will show you what he is like, so that I don't have to tell you. Go follow after him, and just watch how he acts.

original: I am sorry that I am deceived in him.
translation: I'm sorry I misjudged him.

original: You have seen nothing then?
translation: You haven't seen anything, then?

original: Nor ever heard, nor ever did suspect.
translation: I haven't heard anything either, and I haven't suspected anything.

original: Yes, you have seen Cassio and she together.
translation: But you've seen Desdemona and Cassio together.

original: But then I saw no harm, and then I heard  Each syllable that breath made up between them.
translation: But I didn't see anything wrong then, and I heard every syllable they uttered to each other.

original: What, did they never whisper?
translation: What, did they never whisper so you couldn't hear?

original: Never, my lord.
translation: Never, my lord.

original: Nor send you out o' th' way?
translation: And they never sent you away?

original: Never.
translation: Never.

original: To fetch her fan, her gloves, her mask, nor nothing?
translation: She didn't send you away to go get her fan, her gloves, her mask? Nothing?

original: Never, my lord.
translation: Never, my lord.

original: That’s strange.
translation: That's strange.

original: I durst, my lord, to wager she is honest,   Lay down my soul at stake. If you think other   Remove your thought, it doth abuse your bosom.
translation: I would bet that Desdemona is honest, my lord. I'd bet my soul on it. If you think otherwise, throw away this suspicion—it is poisoning your heart.

original: If any wretch have put this in your head   Let heaven requite it with the serpent’s curse
translation: If any wretch has put the idea in your head, may God curse him the way he cursed the  snake .

original: For if she be not honest, chaste, and true   There’s no man happy. The purest of their wives   Is foul as slander.
translation: If Desdemona is not honest, chaste, and true, then no woman is, and no man is happy with his wife.

original: Bid her come hither. Go.
translation: Tell her to come here. Go.

original: She says enough, yet she’s a simple bawd   That cannot say as much.
translation: She says Desdemona is faithful, but the stupidest girl could say as much.

original: This is a subtle whore,   A closet, lock and key, of villainous secrets.   And yet she’ll kneel and pray, I have seen her do ’t.
translation: Desdemona is a sneaky whore, a locked closet full of villainous secrets. And the whole time she'll kneel and pray like a good woman. I have seen her do it.

original: My lord, what is your will?
translation: My lord, what do you want?

original: Pray you, chuck, come hither.
translation: Please, dear, come here.

original: What is your pleasure?
translation: What would you like?

original: Let me see your eyes. Look in my face.
translation: Let me see your eyes. Look into my face.

original: What horrible fancy’s this?
translation: What horrible things are you imagining?

original: (to EMILIA)   Some of your function, mistress,   Leave procreants alone and shut the door.
translation: [To EMILIA]  Do your job, mistress, and leave us lovers alone. Shut the door.

original: Cough or cry “hem” if any body come.   Your mystery, your mystery! Nay, dispatch!
translation: Cough or say "ahem" if anyone comes. That's your job, your  job ! Go!

original: Upon my knee, what doth your speech import? I understand a fury in your words, But not the words.
translation: I beg you here on my knees—tell me, what do you mean by your speech? I can see that you are angry, but I don't understand what you mean.

original: Why, what art thou?
translation: Well, what are you?

original: Your wife, my lord. Your true and loyal wife.
translation: I am your wife, my lord. Your true and loyal wife.

original: Come, swear it, damn thyself.   Lest, being like one of heaven, the devils themselves   Should fear to seize thee.
translation: Come and swear that's true, damn yourself by making a false oath. Otherwise, since you look so angelic, the devils themselves would be afraid to seize you.

original: Therefore be double damned,   Swear thou art honest!
translation: So doubly damn yourself by swearing falsely that you are honest!

original: Heaven doth truly know it.
translation: Heaven knows the truth.

original: Heaven truly knows that thou art false as hell.
translation: Heaven knows the truth: that you are false as hell.

original: To whom, my lord? With whom? How am I false?
translation: To whom, my lord? With whom have I been unfaithful? How am I false?

original: Ah, Desdemona, away, away, away!
translation: Ah, Desdemona, go away, away, away!

original: Alas the heavy day, why do you weep?   Am I the motive of these tears, my lord?
translation: Alas, this is a sad day. Why are you crying? Am I the cause of these tears, my lord?

original: If haply you my father do suspect   An instrument of this your calling back,   Lay not your blame on me. If you have lost him,   Why, I have lost him too.
translation: If you suspect that my father has something to do with your being called back home, don't blame me for it. If he has cut ties with you, well then he has cut ties with me, too.

original: Had it pleased heaven   To try me with affliction, had they rained   All kinds of sores and shames on my bare head,
translation: If God had decided to give me some affliction, if he had put all kinds of shameful sores on my bare head,

original: Steeped me in poverty to the very lips,   Given to captivity me and my utmost hopes,   I should have found in some place of my soul   A drop of patience.
translation: had made me extremely poor, and made me a prisoner with no hope, I would have found a way to endure it.

original: But, alas, to make me   The fixèd figure for the time of scorn   To point his slow and moving finger at!   Yet could I bear that too, well, very well.
translation: But, alas, to make me a laughing-stock forever, and an object of scorn! And yet, I could even endure that too, very well.

original: But there where I have garnered up my heart,   Where either I must live or bear no life,
translation: But to do something to my heart, on which my life depends,

original: The fountain from the which my current runs   Or else dries up—to be discarded thence!   Or keep it as a cistern for foul toads   To knot and gender in!
translation: which pumps all the blood through my veins, to dry it up and turn into a basin for foul toads to wallow and couple in!

original: Turn thy complexion there,   Patience, thou young and rose-lipped cherubin,—   Ay, there, look grim as hell!
translation: The very god of Patience could look at my heart with her young, rosy lips, and her complexion would turn grim as hell!

original: I hope my noble lord esteems me honest.
translation: I hope my noble lord thinks I am honest.

original: Oh, ay, as summer flies are in the shambles,   That quicken even with blowing.
translation: Oh yes, as honest as a swarm of flies all reproducing together in the blowing wind.

original: O thou weed,   Who art so lovely fair and smell’st so sweet   That the sense aches at thee, would thou hadst ne'er  been born!
translation: Oh, you weed, you are so lovely and smell so sweet that it hurts to look at you. I wish you had never been born!

original: Alas, what ignorant sin have I committed?
translation: Alas, what sin have I committed without knowing about it?

original: Was this fair paper, this most goodly book,   Made to write “whore” upon? What committed?   Committed? O thou public commoner!
translation: Did God create in you a beautiful blank slate just to write "whore" on it? What sin did you commit? Commit? Oh, you public prostitute!

original: I should make very forges of my cheeks   That would to cinders burn up modesty   Did I but speak thy deeds. What committed?
translation: If I even spoke of what you did, my mouth would burn up modesty itself just by uttering the words. What sin have you committed?

original: Heaven stops the nose at it and the moon winks,   The bawdy wind that kisses all it meets   Is hushed within the hollow mine of earth   And will not hear ’t.
translation: Heaven and the moon itself, the wind and the depths of the earth all turn away and don't want to hear about it.

original: What committed!   Impudent strumpet!
translation: What sin have you committed? You shameless whore!

original: By heaven, you do me wrong!
translation: By heaven, you accuse me wrongly!

original: Are you not a strumpet?
translation: Are you not a whore?

original: No, as I am a Christian.   If to preserve this vessel for my lord
translation: No, I swear on my Christianity. If the definition of not being a whore is to preserve my virginity for my husband

original: From any other foul unlawful touch   Be not to be a strumpet, I am none.
translation: and not let any other foul man unlawfully touch me, then I am not one.

original: What, not a whore?
translation: What, not a whore?

original: No, as I shall be saved.
translation: No I am not, on my word as a good Christian.

original: Is ’t possible?
translation: Can this be true?

original: Oh, heaven forgive us!
translation: Oh, God forgive us!

original: I cry you mercy, then,   I took you for that cunning whore of Venice   That married with Othello.—
translation: I beg your pardon, then. I mixed you up with that cunning whore from Venice who married that man Othello.

original: You, mistress,   That have the office opposite to Saint Peter   And keep the gate of hell!
translation: You, madam, must be Saint Peter's diabolical counterpart, the gate-keeper of hell!

original: You, you, ay, you! We have done our course. There’s money for your pains. I pray you, turn the key and keep our counsel.
Alas, what does this gentleman conceive?  How do you, madam? How do you, my good lady?
translation: Alas, what is this gentleman talking about? How are you doing, madam? My good lady, are you okay?

original: Faith, half asleep.
translation: I've practically fainted, to tell the truth.

original: Good madam, what’s the matter with my lord?
translation: Good madam, what's the matter with my lord?

original: With who?
translation: With who?

original: Why, with my lord, madam.
translation: With my lord, madam.

original: Who is thy lord?
translation: Who is your lord?

original: He that is yours, sweet lady.
translation: Your husband, sweet lady.

original: I have none. Do not talk to me, Emilia.   I cannot weep, nor answers have I none,   But what should go by water.
translation: I have no husband. Do not talk to me, Emilia. I cannot weep, and I have nothing to say besides what could be expressed by tears. Please, make my bed tonight with the sheets from my wedding night.

original: Prithee, tonight   Lay on my bed my wedding sheets. Remember,   And call thy husband hither.
translation: Remember to do this, and call your husband here.

original: Here’s a change indeed!
translation: Everything has changed so much!

original: 'Tis meet I should be used so, very meet.
translation: It's appropriate that I am treated like this, very appropriate.

original: How have I been behaved that he might stick   The small’st opinion on my least misuse?
translation: What have I ever done to make him find the smallest thing to complain about?

original: What is your pleasure, madam? How is ’t with you?
translation: What do you want, madam? How are things going with you?

original: I cannot tell. Those that do teach young babes   Do it with gentle means and easy tasks.
translation: I can't tell. Those who teach young children do it in a gentle way with easy tasks.

original: He might have chid me so, for, in good faith,   I am a child to chiding.
translation: He should have scolded me in this kind of a gentle way, for I am truly like a child who has been scolded.

original: What is the matter, lady?
translation: What is the matter, lady?

original: Alas, Iago, my lord hath so bewhored her, Thrown such despite and heavy terms upon her,  That true hearts cannot bear it.
translation: Alas, Iago, my lord has called her a whore, and called her such serious, spiteful names that someone with a true heart couldn't bear to hear them.

original: Am I that name, Iago?
translation: Am I that name, Iago?

original: What name, fair lady?
translation: What name, fair lady?

original: Such as she says my lord did say I was.
translation: The one my lord called me.

original: He called her “whore.” A beggar in his drink  Could not have laid such terms upon his callet.
translation: He called her "whore." A drunken beggar wouldn't call his girl such a name.

original: Why did he so?
translation: Why did he call you this?

original: I do not know. I am sure I am none such.
translation: I do not know. I am sure I am not such a thing.

original: Do not weep, do not weep. Alas the day!
translation: Do not weep, do not weep. Alas, what a terrible day!

original: Hath she forsook so many noble matches,   Her father and her country, and her friends,
translation: Did she reject so many noble suitors and turn her back on her father, her country, and her friends

original: To be called “whore”? Would it not make one weep?
translation: just to be called a whore? Wouldn't that make anyone weep?

original: It is my wretched fortune.
translation: It is my wretched fate.

original: Beshrew him for ’t! How comes this trick upon him?
translation: Damn him for this! What has happened to him?

original: Nay, heaven doth know.
translation: Only God knows.

original: I will be hanged, if some eternal villain,   Some busy and insinuating rogue,
translation: I would bet my life that some villain—some scheming, insinuating rogue,

original: Some cogging, cozening slave, to get some office,   Have not devised this slander. I will be hanged else!
translation: some deceitful, double-crossing rogue— has slandered Desdemona in order to get some military position. If I'm wrong, let me be hanged!

original: Fie, there is no such man. It is impossible.
translation: But there is no man who would do such a thing. It is impossible.

original: If any such there be, heaven pardon him!
translation: If there is any such man, may God have mercy on him!

original: A halter pardon him and hell gnaw his bones!   Why should he call her “whore?” Who keeps her company?   What place? What time? What form? What likelihood?
translation: Let him get his mercy from a noose, and let devils in hell gnaw on his bones! Why should Othello call Desdemona a whore? Who does she sleep with? Where? When? How? What proof is there?

original: The Moor’s abused by some most villainous knave,   Some base notorious knave, some scurvy fellow.
translation: The Moor has been tricked by some absolutely villainous lowlife—some base, well-known fool, some vile man.

original: O heavens, that such companions thou’dst unfold,   And put in every honest hand a whip   To lash the rascals naked through the world   Even from the east to th' west!
translation: Oh God, if only you would reveal the evil people in the world and give every honest person a whip to lash the rascals with as they run naked east to west across the whole globe!

original: Speak within door.
translation: Quiet down.

original: Oh, fie upon them! Some such squire he was  That turned your wit the seamy side without And made you to suspect me with the Moor.
translation: Oh, curse those evil people! It was a person like this who got inside your head and made you suspect that I cheated on you with the Moor.

original: You are a fool. Go to.
translation: You are a fool. Get out of here.

original: Alas Iago,   What shall I do to win my lord again?   Good friend, go to him. For, by this light of heaven,   I know not how I lost him.
translation: Alas, Iago, what should I do to win back my husband? Good friend, go to him. For I swear by heaven, I do not know what I did to lose him.

original: Here I kneel:   If e'er my will did trespass 'gainst his love,   Either in discourse of thought or actual deed,
translation: I kneel down here and swear it: if I ever betrayed his love, either by some actual deed or even by just thinking about doing something;

original: Or that mine eyes, mine ears, or any sense,   Delighted them, or any other form,   Or that I do not yet, and ever did,   And ever will—
translation: if my eyes, ears, or anything else ever delighted in any other man; if I never really loved him or don't love him now, or won't continue to love him dearly

original: though he do shake me off   To beggarly divorcement—love him dearly,   Comfort forswear me!
translation: (even as he tries to divorce me), then may I lose all comforts!

original: Unkindness may do much,   And his unkindness may defeat my life,   But never taint my love.
translation: Unkindness is powerful—and his unkindness could kill me—but it can never change my love for him.

original: I cannot say “whore,”   It does abhor me now I speak the word.   To do the act that might the addition earn   Not the world’s mass of vanity could make me.
translation: I cannot say "whore." The word catches in my throat even as I try to say it now. Not all the pleasures in the world could make me do the act that would earn me that name.

original: I pray you, be content, ’tis but his humor.  The business of the state does him offence, And he does chide with you.
translation: I beg you, don't get upset. Othello is just in a bad mood. State business has angered him, and he's just taking out his anger on you.

original: If ’twere no other—
translation: If there were no other reason—

original: 'Tis but so, I warrant.
translation: That's it, I promise.

original: Hark, how these instruments summon to supper.  The messengers of Venice stays the meat. Go in, and weep not. All things shall be well.
translation: Listen, these trumpets announce that dinner is ready. The messenger from Venice is waiting on the food. Go inside, and don't cry. Everything will be okay.

original: How now, Roderigo!
translation: How are things, Roderigo?

original: I do not find that thou deal’st justly with me.
translation: I don't think you've been honest with me.

original: What in the contrary?
translation: Why not?

original: Every day thou daff’st me with some device, Iago, and  rather, as it seems to me now, keep’st from me all  conveniency than suppliest me with the least advantage  of hope.
translation: Every day you play some trick on me, Iago. And it seems to me now that you are making things more difficult for me rather than giving me any advantage or hope of success.

original: I will indeed no longer endure it, nor am I yet persuaded to put up in peace what already I have  foolishly suffered.
translation: I won't tolerate this any longer, and as for what you've already done and what I've foolishly suffered because of you, I'm not just going to take it peacefully.

original: Will you hear me, Roderigo?
translation: Will you listen to me, Roderigo?

original: I have heard too much, and your words and performances  are no kin together.
translation: I have heard you speak too much, and your actions and words don't match up.

original: You charge me most unjustly.
translation: You accuse me unjustly.

original: With naught but truth. I have wasted myself out of my  means. The jewels you have had from me to deliver  Desdemona would half have corrupted a votaress.
translation: I accuse you with nothing but the truth. I have spent all my money. The jewels you took from me to send to Desdemona would have been enough to corrupt a nun.

original: You have told me she hath received them and returned me  expectations and comforts of sudden respect and  acquaintance, but I find none.
translation: You told me she received them, and promised that, in return, I would see hope and encouragement by her immediate affection. But I have seen nothing.

original: Well, go to. Very well.
translation: Well, fine.

original: “Very well,” “go to”! I cannot go to, man, nor ’tis  not very well. Nay, I think it is scurvy, and begin to  find myself fopped in it.
translation: "Fine!" Things aren't "fine," man. Things are not going very well. No, things are going horribly, and now I've been tricked into a big mess.

original: Very well.
translation: Very well.

original: I tell you ’tis not very well. I will make myself known to Desdemona.
translation: It is  not  very well, I tell you. I will tell everything to Desdemona.

original: If she will return me my jewels I will  give over my suit and repent my unlawful solicitation.  If not, assure yourself I will seek satisfaction of you.
translation: If she will return my jewels, I will give up on courting her and take back my unlawful advances. If she doesn't, I'll seek repayment from you.

original: You have said now.
translation: You've spoken your piece, now.

original: Ay, and said nothing but what I protest intendment of  doing.
translation: Yes, and I've said just what I intend to do.

original: Why, now I see there’s mettle in thee, and even from  this instant to build on thee a better opinion than ever before. Give me thy hand, Roderigo.
translation: Well, now I see you have a backbone, and I think more highly of you now than ever before. Give me your hand, Roderigo.

original: Thou hast taken  against me a most just exception, but yet I protest I  have dealt most directly in thy affair.
translation: Your accusation against me is understandable, but I still insist that I have behaved honestly in helping you with your situation.

original: It hath not appeared.
translation: It doesn't appear that way.

original: I grant indeed it hath not appeared, and your suspicion is not without wit and judgment. But, Roderigo, if thou hast that in thee indeed, which I have greater reason  to believe now than ever—I mean purpose, courage and  valor—this night show it.
translation: I admit it doesn't seem that way, and you are not stupid or unjustified to have suspicions. But, Roderigo, if you have courage, dedication, and bravery—which I now more than ever think you do—then prove it tonight.

original: If thou the next night  following enjoy not Desdemona, take me from this world  with treachery and devise engines for my life.
translation: If you do not spend the next night with Desdemona, then feel free to take me away and devise ways to kill me.

original: Well, what is it? Is it within reason and compass?
translation: Well, what is your plan? Is it reasonable?

original: Sir, there is especial commission come from Venice to  depute Cassio in Othello’s place.
translation: Sir, a special order has come from Venice to put Cassio in charge here, in Othello's place.

original: Is that true? Why, then Othello and Desdemona return  again to Venice.
translation: Is that true? Then Othello and Desdemona are returning to Venice.

original: Oh, no, he goes into Mauritania and taketh away with  him the fair Desdemona,
translation: Oh, no, he is going to  Mauritania,  and taking the fair Desdemona with him,

original: unless his abode be lingered  here by some accident—wherein none can be so determinate as the removing of Cassio.
translation: unless some freak accident keeps him here. And nothing would serve this purpose more than the removal of Cassio.

original: How do you mean, removing of him?
translation: What do you mean by "removal?"

original: Why, by making him uncapable of Othello’s place:  knocking out his brains.
translation: Well, I mean making him incapable of taking Othello's place. Knocking out his brains.

original: And that you would have me to do!
translation: And you want me to do that!

original: Ay, if you dare do yourself a profit and a right. He  sups tonight with a harlotry, and thither will I go to  him.
translation: Yes, if you dare do something that would help yourself. Cassio is having dinner tonight with a prostitute, and I am going to go meet him there.

original: He knows not yet of his honorable fortune. If you  will watch his going thence (which I will fashion to  fall out between twelve and one) you may take him at  your pleasure.
translation: He doesn't know yet about his good luck with this promotion. If you will be on the lookout for him there (and I'll make it so he is walking by between twelve and one o'clock) you can get him.

original: I will be near to second your attempt,  and he shall fall between us. Come, stand not amazed at  it, but go along with me.
translation: I'll be nearby to help you, and he'll be surrounded by us. Come on, don't stand there dumbfounded. Go along with me.

original: I will show you such a  necessity in his death that you shall think yourself  bound to put it on him. It is now high suppertime, and  the night grows to waste. About it!
translation: I will prove to you that you absolutely  must  kill Cassio, and you will realize you have no choice but to do it. It is now almost dinner time, and time is wasting. Go do it!

original: I will hear further reason for this.
translation: I'll come and hear what reasons you have for doing this.

original: And you shall be satisfied.
translation: You won't regret it.

original: I do beseech you, sir, trouble yourself no further.
translation: Sir, I beg you: don't trouble yourself any further.

original: Oh, pardon me, ’twill do me good to walk.
translation: I beg your pardon, but it will be good for me to walk.

original: Madam, good night. I humbly thank your ladyship.
translation: Good night, madam. I humbly thank you, my lady.

original: Your honor is most welcome.
translation: You are most welcome, your Honor.

original: Will you walk, sir?—O Desdemona—
translation: Will you walk with me, sir? And oh, Desdemona—

original: My lord?
translation: Yes, my lord?

original: Get you to bed on th' instant, I will be returned Forthwith. Dismiss your attendant there, look ’t be  done.
translation: Go to bed right away. I will come back soon. Dismiss your servant there in the bedroom. Make sure you do this.

original: I will, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: How goes it now? He looks gentler than he did.
translation: How is it going now? Othello looks gentler than before.

original: He says he will return incontinent, And hath commanded me to go to bed And bid me to dismiss you.
translation: He said he's coming back immediately and commanded me to go to bed and dismiss you for the night.

original: Dismiss me?
translation: Dismiss me?

original: It was his bidding. Therefore, good Emilia,   Give me my nightly wearing, and adieu.
translation: That's what he ordered. Therefore, good Emilia, give me my night gown and then goodbye.

original: We must not now displease him.
translation: We must not displease Othello now.

original: Ay. Would you had never seen him!
translation: Okay. I wish you had never seen him!

original: So would not I. My love doth so approve him   That even his stubbornness, his checks, his frowns—
translation: I don't wish that. My love for him is so strong that I don't mind—

original: Prithee, unpin me—have grace and favor.
translation: please help unpin this for me—even his stubbornness, his reprimands, his frowns.

original: I have laid those sheets you bade me on the bed.
translation: I have made your bed with the sheets from your wedding night, as you asked.

original: All’s one. Good Father, how foolish are our minds! If I do die before thee, prithee, shroud me In one of these same sheets.
translation: All right. Good God, how foolish our minds can be! If I die before you, please wrap me in one of these same sheets.

original: Come, come! You talk!
translation: Oh come on! You're just saying that.

original: My mother had a maid called Barbary,   She was in love, and he she loved proved mad   And did forsake her.
translation: My mother had a maid named Barbary. She was in love, and the man she loved turned out to be crazy and abandoned her.

original: She had a song of “Willow,”   An old thing ’twas, but it expressed her fortune   And she died singing it.
translation: She had a song called "Willow," an old song that expressed what she had experienced, and she died singing it.

original: That song tonight   Will not go from my mind. I have much to do   But to go hang my head all at one side   And sing it like poor Barbary. Prithee, dispatch.
translation: I can't stop thinking of that song tonight. I almost can't help but droop my head and sing it just like poor Barbary. Please, hurry.

original: Shall I go fetch your nightgown?
translation: Should I go and get your nightgown?

original: No, unpin me here. This Lodovico is a proper man.
translation: No, just unpin this for me here. That Lodovico is a good man.

original: A very handsome man.
translation: A very handsome man.

original: He speaks well.
translation: He's well-spoken.

original: I know a lady in Venice would have walked barefoot to  Palestine for a touch of his nether lip.
translation: I know a lady in Venice who would have walked barefoot to Palestine just to touch his lower lip.

original: (   singing)     The poor soul sat sighing by a sycamore tree,     Sing all a green willow.     Her hand on her bosom, her head on her knee,     Sing willow, willow, willow.
translation: [Singing] The poor soul sat sighing by a sycamore tree, Everyone sing a green willow. With her hand on her chest and her head on her knee, Sing willow, willow, willow.

original: The fresh streams ran by her, and murmured her moans,     Sing willow, willow, willow.     Her salt tears fell from her, and softened the stones     Sing willow, willow, willow—
translation: The fresh streams ran by her, and murmured along with her moans, Sing willow, willow, willow. Her salt tears fell from her, and softened the stones, Sing willow, willow, willow —

original: Lay by these—     Willow, willow—   Prithee, hie thee, he’ll come anon—
translation: Put these things down over there, Emilia. [Singing] Willow, willow — Please, hurry up, he'll come any minute now.

original: Sing all a green willow must be my garland.     Let nobody blame him, his scorn I approve—   Nay, that’s not next—Hark! Who is ’t that knocks?
translation: [Singing] Everyone sing a green willow must be my garland. Let nobody blame him, I approve of his scorn — No, that's not the next line. Listen! Who is that knocking at the door?

original: It’s the wind.
translation: It's just the wind

original: (sings)   I called my love false love but what said he then?     Sing willow, willow, willow.
translation: [ Singing] I called my love false love, but what did he say then? Sing willow, willow, willow.

original: If I court more women you’ll couch with more men—   So, get thee gone, good night. Mine eyes do itch,   Doth that bode weeping?
translation: If I court more women, you'll sleep with more men— Okay, you can go now, good night. My eyes itch. Does that mean I'm going to cry?

original: 'Tis neither here nor there.
translation: It might, or it might not.

original: I have heard it said so. Oh, these men, these men!   Dost thou in conscience think—tell me, Emilia—
translation: I've heard that it means that. Oh these men, these men! Tell me, Emilia:

original: That there be women do abuse their husbands   In such gross kind?
translation: do you think that there are women who deceive and cheat on their husbands as badly as men do to women?

original: There be some such, no question.
translation: No question, there are some.

original: Wouldst thou do such a deed for all the world?
translation: Would you ever cheat on your husband, for all the world?

original: Why, would not you?
translation: Well, wouldn't you?

original: No, by this heavenly light!
translation: No, by the light of heaven!

original: Nor I neither, by this heavenly light. I might do ’t as well i' th' dark.
translation: Well I wouldn't do it by light either. I might do it in the dark, though.

original: Wouldst thou do such a deed for all the world?
translation: Would you really do such a thing for all the world?

original: The world’s a huge thing. It is a great price for a  small vice.
translation: All the world is a huge thing. It would be a great reward for a little misdeed.

original: In troth, I think thou wouldst not.
translation: In truth, I think you wouldn't do it.

original: In troth, I think I should, and undo ’t when I had  done. Marry, I would not do such a thing for a  joint-ring, nor for measures of lawn, nor for gowns,  petticoats, nor caps, nor any petty exhibition.
translation: In truth, I think I should do it, and then undo it after. Really, I wouldn't do such a thing for a ring, or for fine linen, or for gowns and petticoats, or for caps, or for any little gift.

original: But for  the whole world? Why, who would not make her husband a  cuckold to make him a monarch? I should venture  purgatory for ’t.
translation: But for the whole world? Why, who would not cheat on her husband in order to make him king of the world? I'd risk being punished in purgatory for it.

original: Beshrew me, if I would do such a wrong For the whole world.
translation: The devil may take me if I should ever do such a wrong for the whole world.

original: Why the wrong is but a wrong i' th' world, and having  the world for your labor, ’tis a wrong in your own  world, and you might quickly make it right.
translation: But the wrong is just a wrong in the world, so if the world is yours, then it is a wrong in your own world. And then you could quickly make it right.

original: I do not think there is any such woman.
translation: I don't think there is any such woman who would do it.

original: Yes, a dozen, and as many to th' vantage as would store the world they played for.   But I do think it is their husbands' faults   If wives do fall.
translation: Yes—there are a dozen, and in fact as many as would populate the whole world that they wagered for. But I think that if wives are unfaithful, it is their husbands' fault.

original: Say that they slack their duties   And pour our treasures into foreign laps,   Or else break out in peevish jealousies,   Throwing restraint upon us.
translation: Let's say they stop sleeping with us and give themselves to other women instead, or break out in fits of jealousy and impose restraints on us.

original: Or say they strike us,   Or scant our former having in despite.   Why, we have galls, and though we have some grace,   Yet have we some revenge.
translation: Or let's say they hit us, or spitefully cut back on our allowance. Why, we feel resentment, and although we have some grace, we can still have some revenge, too.

original: Let husbands know   Their wives have sense like them. They see and smell   And have their palates both for sweet and sour,   As husbands have.
translation: Let husbands know that their wives have good sense just like them. They see and smell and can taste both sweet and sour, just like their husbands can.

original: What is it that they do   When they change us for others? Is it sport?   I think it is. And doth affection breed it?
translation: What are they doing when they switch us out for other women? Is it for fun? I think so. And does physical attraction lead to it?

original: I think it doth. Is ’t frailty that thus errs?   It is so too. And have not we affections,   Desires for sport, and frailty, as men have?
translation: I think so. Is it a weakness to do this wrong? I think so, too. And don't we have physical attractions, desire for fun, and weakness, just like men?

original: Then let them use us well, else let them know,   The ills we do, their ills instruct us so.
translation: They should treat us well, or else they should know that whatever bad things we do, we are only following their example.

original: Good night, good night. Heaven me such uses send, Not to pick bad from bad, but by bad mend!
translation: Good night, good night. May heaven send me the ability not to behave badly by following bad examples, but to behave well by avoiding bad examples.

original: Here, stand behind this bulk, straight will he come.   Wear thy good rapier bare, and put it home.   Quick, quick! Fear nothing.
translation: Here, stand behind this wall. He'll come soon. Keep your sword unsheathed, and then drive it into him. Quick, quick! Don't be scared.

original: I’ll be at thy elbow.   It makes us, or it mars us. Think on that,   And fix most firm thy resolution.
translation: I'll be at your side. We win or lose everything with this. Think about that, and be firmly resolved for the task.

original: Be near at hand, I may miscarry in ’t.
translation: Be nearby, since I might mess this up.

original: Here, at thy hand. Be bold, and take thy stand.
translation: I'll be here, right by your side. Be bold, and make a stand.

original: I have no great devotion to the deed   And yet he hath given me satisfying reasons.
translation: I don't have any great dedication to do this deed, but Iago has given me satisfactory reasons to do it.

original: 'Tis but a man gone. Forth, my sword: he dies.
translation: It's just one man to kill. Go forth, my sword: he will die.

original: (aside)   I have rubbed this young quat almost to the  sense,   And he grows angry. Now, whether he kill Cassio   Or Cassio him, or each do kill the other,   Every way makes my gain.
translation: [To himself ]  I rubbed this young pimple as much as I can, and he's getting angry. Now, whether he kills Cassio or Cassio kills him, or they each kill each other, it's all good for me.

original: Live Roderigo,   He calls me to a restitution large   Of gold and jewels that I bobbed from him   As gifts to Desdemona.
translation: If Roderigo lives, he will make me pay him back for all the gold and jewels I took from him as gifts for Desdemona.

original: It must not be. If Cassio do remain   He hath a daily beauty in his life   That makes me ugly.
translation: I can't have that. If Cassio survives, his beauty every day makes me seem ugly by comparison.

original: And besides, the Moor   May unfold me to him—there stand I in much peril.   No, he must die. But so, I hear him coming.
translation: And besides, the Moor might tell him what I've said about him—that would be very dangerous for me. No, he must die. But I hear him coming.

original: I know his gait, ’tis he.—Villain, thou diest!
translation: I know his walk. It's him. Villain, time for you to die!

original: That thrust had been mine enemy indeed  But that my coat is better than thou know’st I will make proof of thine.
translation: That thrust would have been quite bad for me indeed, except that my coat is thicker than you realize. Now I'll put your coat to the test.

original: Oh, I am slain!
translation: Oh, I've been killed!

original: I am maimed for ever. Help, ho! Murder! Murder!
translation: I am crippled forever. Help, hey! Murder! Murder!

original: The voice of Cassio. Iago keeps his word.
translation: It's the voice of Cassio. Iago keeps his word.

original: Oh, villain that I am!
translation: Oh, I am a villain.

original: It is even so.
translation: Yes, you are.

original: Oh, help, ho! Light! A surgeon!
translation: Oh, help, hey! Bring some light! I need a doctor!

original: 'Tis he. Oh, brave Iago, honest and just,   That hast such noble sense of thy friend’s wrong!   Thou teachest me.
translation: It's him. Oh, brave Iago, you are honest and just, to care so much for a wrong done to your friend! You teach me by your example.

original: Minion, your dear lies dead,   And your unblest fate hies. Strumpet, I come.
translation: Unchaste woman, your dear boyfriend lies dead, and your own damned fate hurries your way. Whore, I'm coming for you.

original: For, of my heart, those charms, thine eyes, are  blotted.   Thy bed, lust-stained, shall with lust’s blood be  spotted.
translation: Your charms, your eyes, are erased from my heart. Your bed, stained with lust, will soon be stained with your lusty blood.

original: What, ho! No watch? No passage? Murder! Murder!
translation: What's going ? No one on guard? No one passing by? Murder! Murder!

original: 'Tis some mischance, the cry is very direful.
translation: Something's wrong. That cry is very serious.

original: Oh, help!
translation: Oh, help!

original: Hark!
translation: Look!

original: Oh, wretched villain!
translation: Oh, that wretched villain!

original: Two or three groan. 'Tis heavy night, These may be counterfeits. Let’s think ’t unsafe  To come in to the cry without more help.
translation: Two or three people are groaning. It's the middle of the night—they might be trying to trick us. Let's not rush in unsafely by ourselves, without any other help.

original: Nobody come? Then shall I bleed to death.
translation: Will nobody come? I'm going to bleed to death.

original: Hark!
translation: Look!

original: Here’s one comes in his shirt, with light and weapons.
translation: Here comes someone in his night shirt, with a light and weapons.

original: Who’s there? Whose noise is this that ones on murder?
translation: Who's there? Whose voice is it that keeps saying murder?

original: We do not know.
translation: We don't know.

original: Do not you hear a cry?
translation: Don't you hear a cry?

original: Here, here! For heaven’s sake, help me!
translation: Over here! For heaven's sake, help me!

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: This is Othello’s ancient, as I take it.
translation: This is Othello's flag-bearer, I think.

original: The same indeed, a very valiant fellow.
translation: This is him, a very brave man.

original: What are you here that cry so grievously?
translation: Who are you that's crying out in such pain?

original: Iago? Oh, I am spoiled, undone by villains! Give me some help.
translation: Iago? Oh, I have been ruined and undone by villains! Give me some help.

original: Oh, me, lieutenant! What villains have done this?
translation: Oh my, lieutenant! What villains have done this?

original: I think that one of them is hereabout, And cannot make away.
translation: I think one of them is around here, and cannot run away.

original: Oh, treacherous villains!—   What are you there? Come in, and give some help.
translation: Oh, treacherous villains!  Who are you over there? Come here and give some help.

original: Oh, help me there!
translation: Oh, help me!

original: That’s one of them.
translation: That's one of the villains that did this to me.

original: O murd'rous slave! O villain!
translation: Oh, murdering scoundrel! Oh, villain!

original: O damned Iago! O inhuman dog!
translation: Oh, damned Iago! You inhuman dog!

original: Kill men i' th' dark! Where be these bloody thieves?   How silent is this town!—
translation: Where are these bloody thieves who are killing men in the dark? This town is so silent!

original: Ho! murder! murder!—   What may you be? Are you of good or evil?
translation: Hey! Murder! Murder! Who are you? Are you good or evil?

original: As you shall prove us, praise us.
translation: Judge us by our actions.

original: Signior Lodovico?
translation: Sir Lodovico?

original: He, sir.
translation: That's me, sir.

original: I cry you mercy. Here’s Cassio hurt by villains.
translation: I ask for your forgiveness. This here is Cassio, hurt by some villains.

original: Cassio!
translation: Cassio!

original: How is ’t, brother!
translation: How are you, brother?

original: My leg is cut in two.
translation: My leg has been cut in half.

original: Marry, heaven forbid!  Light, gentlemen, I’ll bind it with my shirt.
translation: No, heaven forbid! Gentlemen, give me some light so I can bind the wound with my shirt.

original: What is the matter, ho? Who is ’t that cried?
translation: Hey, what is the matter? Who is it that cried out?

original: Who is ’t that cried?
translation: Who is it that cried out?

original: Oh, my dear Cassio! My sweet Cassio! O Cassio, Cassio, Cassio!
translation: Oh, my dear Cassio! My sweet Cassio! Oh, Cassio, Cassio, Cassio!

original: O notable strumpet! Cassio, may you suspect  Who they should be that have thus mangled you?
translation: You notorious whore! Cassio, do you have any idea who attacked you?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: I am sorry to find you thus. I have been to seek you.
translation: I am sorry to find you like this. I've been out looking for you.

original: Lend me a garter. So.—Oh, for a chair, To bear him easily hence!
translation: Lend me a stocking. There. Oh, if only we had a chair, to carry him off easily!

original: Alas, he faints! O Cassio, Cassio, Cassio!
translation: Alas, he is fainting! Oh, Cassio, Cassio, Cassio!

original: Gentlemen all, I do suspect this trash   To be a party in this injury.—   Patience awhile, good Cassio.—
translation: All of you gentlemen, I suspect that this piece of trash has played a role in Cassio's injury. Hold on just a bit, good Cassio.

original: Come, come,   Lend me a light. Know we this face or no?   Alas, my friend and my dear countryman   Roderigo! No—yes, sure! Yes, ’tis Roderigo.
translation: Come on, give me some light. Do we know this face or not? Alas, it is my friend and my dear countryman Roderigo! No, it can't be—yes, it is for sure! Yes, it's Roderigo.

original: What, of Venice?
translation: Roderigo from Venice?

original: Even he, sir. Did you know him?
translation: That's the man, sir. Do you know him?

original: Know him? Ay.
translation: Know him? Yes.

original: Signior Gratiano? I cry you gentle pardon, These bloody accidents must excuse my manners That so neglected you.
translation: Sir Gratiano, is that you? I beg your pardon. This bloody incident has made it so that I couldn't treat you with proper manners.

original: I am glad to see you.
translation: I am glad to see you.

original: How do you, Cassio?—Oh, a chair, a chair!
translation: Are you okay, Cassio? Oh, we need a chair, a chair!

original: Roderigo!
translation: Roderigo!

original: He, he, ’tis he.
translation: It's him, yes, him

original: Oh, that’s well said—the chair!   Some good man bear him carefully from hence.   I’ll fetch the general’s surgeon.—
translation: Ah, well done, the chair! Some good man carry him away carefully. I'll go get the general's doctor.

original: (to BIANCA)   For you,  mistress,   Save you your labor.—He that lies slain here, Cassio,   Was my dear friend. What malice was between you?
translation: [To BIANCA]  As for you, mistress, don't bother trying to help. Cassio, the man who lies murdered here was my dear friend. What bad blood was there between the two of you?

original: None in the world, nor do I know the man.
translation: None at all, and I don't even know him.

original: What, look you pale?—Oh, bear him out o' the air.—
translation: What, are you looking pale? Someone carry him off.

original: Do you perceive the gastness of her eye?—Stay you, good gentlemen.—Look you pale, mistress?—
translation: Do you see the fright in her eyes? Stay here, good gentlemen. Do you look a little pale, mistress?

original: Nay, if you stare, we shall hear more anon.—   Behold her well. I pray you, look upon her.
translation: Keep watching her; we'll hear more about what happened soon. Watch her carefully.

original: Do you see, gentlemen? Nay, guiltiness   Will speak, though tongues were out of use.
translation: I beg you, look at her. Do you see, gentlemen? Guiltiness speaks, even when the guilty person holds his or her tongue.

original: Alas, what is the matter? What is the matter, husband?
translation: Alas, what is the matter? What is the matter, husband?

original: Cassio hath here been set on in the dark   By Roderigo and fellows that are ’scaped.
translation: Cassio has been attacked here in the dark by Roderigo and some men who have run away.

original: He’s almost slain, and Roderigo dead.
translation: Cassio was almost killed, and Roderigo is dead.

original: Alas, good gentleman! Alas, good Cassio!
translation: Alas, he was a good gentleman! And alas, poor Cassio!

original: This is the fruits of whoring. Prithee, Emilia, Go know of Cassio where he supped tonight.—     What, do you shake at that?
translation: This is what you get from whoring around. Please, Emilia, go ask Cassio where he had dinner tonight.  Why do you shake with worry at that?

original: He supped at my house, but I therefore shake not.
translation: He had dinner at my house, but that's not why I'm shaking.

original: Oh, did he so? I charge you, go with me.
translation: Oh did he? I order you, come with me.

original: Oh, fie upon thee, strumpet!
translation: Oh, shame on you, whore!

original: I am no strumpet, but of life as honest As you that thus abuse me.
translation: I am no whore. I am as chaste as you who accuse me.

original: As I! Fie upon thee!
translation: As chaste as me? Shame on you!

original: Kind gentlemen, let’s go see poor Cassio dressed.—   Come, mistress, you must tell ’s another tale.
translation: Kind gentlemen, let's go make sure poor Cassio's wounds get tended to. Come on, mistress, you must tell us another story.

original: Emilia, run you to the citadel   And tell my lord and lady what hath happed.—   Will you go on afore?
translation: Emilia, run to the castle and tell Othello and Desdemona what has happened. Will you go on ahead?

original: (aside)   This is the night   That either makes me or fordoes me quite.
translation: [To himself]   This is the night that either makes me, or utterly ruins me.

original: It is the cause, it is the cause, my soul.   Let me not name it to you, you chaste stars,   It is the cause.
translation: That's the reason for this, that's the reason, my soul. I won't say the reason to the chaste stars in the sky, but it is the reason.

original: Yet I’ll not shed her blood,   Nor scar that whiter skin of hers than snow   And smooth as monumental alabaster.
translation: But I won't shed her blood, or scar that skin of hers that is whiter than snow and as smooth as alabaster.

original: Yet she must die, else she’ll betray more men.   Put out the light, and then put out the light.
translation: Still, she must die or else she'll betray more men. Extinguish the light, and then extinguish her light.

original: If I quench thee, thou flaming minister,   I can again thy former light restore   Should I repent me.
translation: If I extinguish you, flame, I can light you again if I have second thoughts.

original: But once put out thy light,   Thou cunning’st pattern of excelling nature,   I know not where is that Promethean heat   That can thy light relume.
translation: But as for you—you most artfully, excellently fashioned woman—once I put out your light, I don't know of any magical fire that can bring your life back.

original: When I have plucked thy rose   I cannot give it vital growth again,   It must needs wither. I’ll smell thee on the tree.
translation: When I have plucked the rose of your life, I can't re-plant it again—it must wither. I'll smell you while you're still alive.

original: Oh, balmy breath, that dost almost persuade   Justice to break her sword! One more, one more.   Be thus when thou art dead and I will kill thee   And love thee after.
translation: Oh, your gentle breath almost persuades Justice herself to put away her sword! One more, one more kiss. If you look like this when you are dead, I will kill you and love you after.

original: (kissing her)   One more, and that’s the last.   So sweet was ne'er so fatal. I must weep,   But they are cruel tears.
translation: [He kisses DESDEMONA]  One more, and that's the last. There was never anything so sweet and yet so deadly as you. I can't help but weep, but that is not a sign of pity.

original: This sorrow’s heavenly,   It strikes where it doth love. She wakes.
translation: This sorrow is like that of God, who must strike down the creatures he loves. She's waking up.

original: Who’s there? Othello?
translation: Who's there? Othello?

original: Ay, Desdemona.
translation: Yes, Desdemona.

original: Will you come to bed, my lord?
translation: Will you come to bed, my lord?

original: Have you prayed tonight, Desdemon?
translation: Have you prayed tonight, Desdemona?

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: If you bethink yourself of any crime Unreconciled as yet to heaven and grace,  Solicit for it straight.
translation: If you can think of any crime you haven't atoned for, make amends with God right now.

original: Alack, my lord, what do you mean by that?
translation: My lord, what do you mean by that?

original: Well, do it, and be brief. I will walk by.   I would not kill thy unpreparèd spirit.
translation: Just do it. And quickly. I will walk around. I would not want to kill you when you haven't prepared your soul by confessing and repenting.

original: No, heavens forfend, I would not kill thy soul!
translation: No, heaven forbid it, I would not send your soul to hell.

original: Talk you of killing?
translation: You're talking about killing?

original: Ay, I do.
translation: Yes, I am.

original: Then heaven Have mercy on me!
translation: Then heaven have mercy on me!

original: Amen, with all my heart.
translation: Amen, I wholeheartedly agree.

original: If you say, I hope you will not kill me.
translation: Then I hope you will not kill me.

original: Humh!
translation: Hmph!

original: And yet I fear you, for you’re fatal then   When your eyes roll so.
translation: And yet I fear you, because when your eyes roll like that I know you're in a deadly mood.

original: Why I should fear I know not,   Since guiltiness I know not. But yet I feel I fear.
translation: I don't know why I should be afraid, since I am not guilty of anything. But I am afraid nonetheless.

original: Think on thy sins.
translation: Think about your sins.

original: They are loves I bear to you.
translation: My only sin is my love for you.

original: Ay, and for that thou diest.
translation: Yes, and that's why you're going to die.

original: That death’s unnatural that kills for loving.   Alas, why gnaw you so your nether lip?
translation: It's not a natural thing to kill someone for loving. Alas, why are you biting your lower lip?

original: Some bloody passion shakes your very frame.   These are portents, but yet I hope, I hope   They do not point on me.
translation: Some bloodthirsty passion is shaking your whole body. These are bad signs, but I hope they do not point to something that is going to happen to me.

original: Peace, and be still.
translation: Be quiet, and stay still.

original: I will so. What’s the matter?
translation: I will. What's the matter?

original: That handkerchief Which I so loved and gave thee, thou gav’st To Cassio.
