translation: That handkerchief that I loved so much and gave to you, you gave to Cassio.

original: No, by my life and soul! Send for the man and ask him.
translation: No, I swear on my life and soul! Send for him and ask him.

original: Sweet soul, take heed, take heed of perjury.  Thou art on thy deathbed.
translation: You sweet soul, careful now, be careful about lying. You are on your deathbed.

original: Ay—but not yet to die!
translation: Yes, but it's not yet time for me to die!

original: Presently.   Therefore confess thee freely of thy sin,
translation: It will be soon. Therefore confess your sin openly.

original: For to deny each article with oath   Cannot remove nor choke the strong conception   That I do groan withal. Thou art to die.
translation: Your denial of every part of it can do nothing to remove the horrible idea that I have in my head. You are about to die.

original: Oh, heaven have mercy on me!
translation: Oh, heaven have mercy on me!

original: I say “amen.”
translation: I say amen to that.

original: And have you mercy too! I never did   Offend you in my life,
translation: And you have mercy, too! I never did anything to offend you in my life.

original: never loved Cassio   But with such general warranty of heaven   As I might love. I never gave him token.
translation: I never loved Cassio except in a general way, as a friend. I never gave him a token of my affection.

original: By heaven, I saw my handkerchief in ’s hand.   O perjured woman, thou dost stone my heart,
translation: By heaven, I saw my handkerchief in his hand. Oh, you lying woman! You turn my heart to stone

original: And mak’st me call what I intend to do   A murder, which I thought a sacrifice!   I saw the handkerchief.
translation: and make me call what I intend to do a murder, instead of a sacrifice! I saw the handkerchief.

original: He found it then, I never gave it him. Send for him hither, Let him confess a truth.
translation: Then he must have found it. I never gave it to him. Send for him to come here, and let him tell you the truth.

original: He hath confessed.
translation: He has confessed.

original: What, my lord?
translation: What, my lord?

original: That he hath usèd thee.
translation: He has confessed that he has had sex with you.

original: How? Unlawfully?
translation: What? Adulterous sex with me?

original: Ay.
translation: Yes.

original: He will not say so.
translation: He would not say that.

original: No, his mouth is stopped. Honest Iago Hath ta'en order for ’t.
translation: No, he cannot speak. Honest Iago has taken care of that.

original: Oh! My fear interprets. What, is he dead?
translation: Oh! I am afraid I know what you mean by that. What, is he dead?

original: Had all his hairs been lives My great revenge had stomach for them all.
translation: If he had had as many lives as hairs on his head, I would have had enough revenge for each one of them.

original: Alas, he is betrayed and I undone.
translation: Alas, he has been betrayed, and now I am ruined.

original: Out, strumpet! weep’st thou for him to my face?
translation: Enough, whore! Do you dare to weep for him in front of me?

original: Oh, banish me, my lord, but kill me not!
translation: Oh, my lord, banish me, but do not kill me.

original: Down, strumpet!
translation: Get down, whore!

original: Kill me tomorrow—let me live tonight!
translation: Kill me tomorrow—let me live tonight!

original: Nay, if you strive—
translation: No, if you struggle—

original: But half an hour!
translation: Just half an hour!

original: Being done, there is no pause.
translation: Once I've started this, I cannot stop.

original: But while I say one prayer!
translation: Let me say just one prayer!

original: It is too late.
translation: It is too late.

original: My lord , my lord! What, ho! My lord, my lord!
translation: My lord, my lord! What is going on? My lord, my lord!

original: What noise is this?—Not dead? Not yet quite dead?
translation: What is this noise? Is she not dead? Not quite dead yet?

original: I that am cruel am yet merciful,   I would not have thee linger in thy pain.   So, so.
translation: I may be cruel, but I am merciful too: I don't want you to die slowly and painfully. So here.

original: What, ho! My lord, my lord!
translation: Hey! My lord, my lord!

original: Who’s there?
translation: Who's there?

original: O good my lord, I would speak a word with you!
translation: Oh, my good lord, I want to have a word with you!

original: Yes, ’tis Emilia.—
translation: Yes, it is Emilia.

original: (to EMILIA)   By and by.—
translation: [To EMILIA]   One minute.

original: She’s dead.—   'Tis like she comes to speak of Cassio’s death,   The noise was high. Ha!
translation: [To himself]  She's dead. Emilia is likely coming to tell me about Cassio's death.  There was a lot of noise outside. Ha!

original: No more moving?   Still as the grave. Shall she come in? Were ’t good?
translation: Not moving anymore, Desdemona? Still as the grave. Should Emilia come in here? Would that be good?

original: I think she stirs again—No. What’s best to do?   If she come in, she’ll sure speak to my wife—   My wife! my wife! what wife? I have no wife.
translation: Is Desdemona moving again? No. What should I do? If she comes in, she'll definitely want to speak to my wife. My wife! My wife! What wife? I have no wife.

original: Oh, insupportable! Oh, heavy hour!   Methinks it should be now a huge eclipse   Of sun and moon, and that th' affrighted globe   Should yawn at alteration.
translation: Oh, this is unbearable! Oh, what a terrible time! I think there should be a huge eclipse now of both the sun and the moon, and the ground itself should break open at what has happened.

original: I do beseech you That I may speak with you, O good my lord!
translation: I beg you to let me speak with you, my good lord!

original: I had forgot thee—Oh, come in, Emilia. Soft, by and by. Let me the curtains draw. Where art thou?
translation: I forgot you were out there. Come in, Emilia. Quietly, now. Let me draw the bed curtains. Where are you?

original: What’s the matter with thee now?
translation: What's the matter with you now?

original: O my good lord, yonder’s foul murders done!
translation: Oh, my good lord, foul murders have been committed outside!

original: What, now?
translation: What? Just now?

original: But now, my lord.
translation: Just now, my lord.

original: It is the very error of the moon, She comes more nearer earth than she was wont  And makes men mad.
translation: This has something to do with the odd path of the moon. It is closer to the earth than normal, and this makes men crazy.

original: Cassio, my lord, hath killed a young Venetian Called Roderigo.
translation: My lord, Cassio has killed a young Venetian named Roderigo.

original: Roderigo killed? And Cassio killed!
translation: Roderigo killed? And Cassio killed!

original: No, Cassio is not killed.
translation: No, Cassio is not killed.

original: Not Cassio killed! Then murder’s out of tune,  And sweet revenge grows harsh.
translation: Cassio isn't killed? Then the murder was botched, and sweet revenge hasn't gone as planned.

original: Oh, falsely, falsely murdered!
translation: Oh, I have been unjustly murdered!

original: Alas, what cry is that?
translation: Alas, what is that cry?

original: That? What?
translation: That? What?

original: Out and alas, that was my lady’s voice.
translation: Oh no, that was my lady's voice.

original: Help! Help, ho, help! O lady, speak again! Sweet Desdemona! O sweet mistress, speak!
translation: Help! Hey, help, help! Oh, my lady, say something! Sweet Desdemona! Oh, sweet mistress, say something!

original: A guiltless death I die.
translation: I die as an innocent.

original: Oh, who hath done this deed?
translation: Oh, who has done this to you?

original: Nobody. I myself. Farewell. Commend me to my kind lord. Oh, farewell!
translation: Nobody. I did it to myself. Farewell. Send my love to my kind lord. Oh, farewell!

original: Why, how should she be murdered?
translation: Why, how could she have been murdered?

original: Alas, who knows?
translation: Alas, who knows?

original: You heard her say herself it was not I.
translation: You heard her say herself that it wasn't me.

original: She said so. I must needs report the truth.
translation: She said so. I must tell the truth.

original: She’s like a liar gone to burning hell. 'Twas I that killed her.
translation: Then she's gone to hell as a liar. I'm the one who killed her.

original: Oh, the more angel she, And you the blacker devil!
translation: Oh, this makes her even more of an angel, and you more of a devil!

original: She turned to folly, and she was a whore.
translation: She strayed, and she was a whore.

original: Thou dost belie her, and thou art a devil.
translation: You slander her, and you are a devil.

original: She was false as water.
translation: She was as unfaithful as water is inconstant.

original: Thou art rash as fire, To say that she was false. Oh, she was heavenly true!
translation: You are as impetuous as fire to say that she was unfaithful. She was heavenly faithful and honest!

original: Cassio did top her, ask thy husband else.   Oh, I were damned beneath all depth in hell,
translation: Cassio slept with her; you can ask your husband. I would be damned to hell

original: But that I did proceed upon just grounds   To this extremity. Thy husband knew it all.
translation: if I didn't seek out just punishment to this end. Your husband knew all about this.

original: My husband!
translation: My husband!

original: Thy husband.
translation: Yes, your husband.

original: That she was false to wedlock?
translation: He knew that she was unfaithful in her marriage?

original: Ay, with Cassio. Had she been true,
translation: Yes, with Cassio. If she had been faithful,

original: If heaven would make me such another world   Of one entire and perfect chrysolite,   I’d not have sold her for it.
translation: I wouldn't have traded her for an entire world made entirely of gemstones.

original: My husband?
translation: My husband?

original: Ay, ’twas he that told me on her first.  An honest man he is, and hates the slime That sticks on filthy deeds.
translation: Yes, he was the one who told me about her first. He is an honest man, and hates the slime of filthy bad deeds.

original: My husband!
translation: My husband!

original: What needs this iterance, woman? I say thy husband.
translation: Why are you repeating yourself, woman? I said your husband.

original: O mistress, villainy hath made mocks with love! My husband say that she was false!
translation: Oh, my mistress—a villain has played tricks with love. My husband said she was unfaithful!

original: He, woman.  I say “thy husband”—dost understand the word? My friend, thy husband, honest, honest Iago.
translation: Yes, him, woman. I said "your husband"—do you understand the words? My friend, your husband, the honest, honest Iago.

original: If he say so, may his pernicious soul   Rot half a grain a day! He lies to th' heart.
translation: If Iago said this, then let his malicious soul rot slowly day after day! He lies down to his heart.

original: She was too fond of her most filthy bargain.
translation: She was too attached to her filthy marriage to you to be unfaithful.

original: Ha!
translation: Ha!

original: Do thy worst. This deed of thine is no more worthy heaven Than thou wast worthy her.
translation: Do your worst. This deed you have done is not justified. It is no more worthy of heaven than you were worthy of her.

original: Peace, you were best.
translation: You'd better be quiet.

original: Thou hast not half that power to do me harm   As I have to be hurt. O gull! O dolt!
translation: You don't have enough strength to do me half as much harm as I can endure. Oh, you fool! You idiot!

original: As ignorant as dirt! Thou hast done a deed—   I care not for thy sword, I’ll make thee known   Though I lost twenty lives.—
translation: You are as ignorant as dirt! You've dome something so awful . . . I don't care about your sword. I'd spread the news of this even if I was killed twenty times.

original: Help! Help, ho! Help!   The Moor hath killed my mistress! Murder, murder!
translation: Help! Hey, help! The Moor has killed my mistress! Murder! Murder!

original: What is the matter? How now, general?
translation: What is the matter? What is going on, general?

original: Oh, are you come, Iago? You have done well, That men must lay their murders on your neck.
translation: Oh, you've come, Iago? You've done really well, since other men credit you for their murders .

original: What is the matter?
translation: What is the matter?

original: (to IAGO)   Disprove this villain, if thou be’st a man.   He says thou told’st him that his wife was false.
translation: [To IAGO]  Refute what this villain has said, if you are a man. He says that you told him his wife was unfaithful.

original: I know thou didst not, thou'rt not such a villain.   Speak, for my heart is full.
translation: I know you did not; you aren't that much of a villain. Speak, for my heart can't bear your silence any longer.

original: I told him what I thought, and told no more Than what he found himself was apt and true.
translation: I told him what I thought, and said no more than that which he himself found out to be true.

original: But did you ever tell him she was false?
translation: But did you ever tell him that she was unfaithful?

original: I did.
translation: I did.

original: You told a lie, an odious, damnèd lie.   Upon my soul, a lie, a wicked lie.
translation: You told a lie—a horrible, damned lie.

original: She false with Cassio! Did you say with Cassio?
translation: I swear by my soul, it was a lie, a wicked lie. Desdemona, unfaithful with Cassio! Did you say with Cassio?

original: With Cassio, mistress. Go to, charm your tongue.
translation: Yes, with Cassio, mistress. Now come on, hold your tongue.

original: I will not charm my tongue, I am bound to speak. My mistress here lies murdered in her bed—
translation: I will not hold my tongue. I must speak. My mistress lies here murdered in her bed—

original: Oh, heavens forfend!
translation: Heaven forbid!

original: And your reports have set the murder on.
translation: And the news you spread led to the murder.

original: Nay, stare not, masters, it is true, indeed.
translation: Don't look so amazed, gentlemen. It is really true.

original: 'Tis a strange truth.
translation: It's a strange truth.

original: Oh, monstrous act!
translation: What a monstrous act!

original: Villainy, villainy, villainy!   I think upon ’t, I think I smell ’t, Oh, villainy!
translation: Wickedness, wickedness, wickedness! I think about it, and I think I can smell it, oh wickedness!

original: I thought so then, I’ll kill myself for grief.   Oh, villainy, villainy!
translation: I suspected it earlier. I could kill myself out of grief. Oh, wickedness, wickedness!

original: What, are you mad? I charge you, get you home.
translation: What, are you crazy? I order you to go back home.

original: Good gentlemen, let me have leave to speak.   'Tis proper I obey him, but not now.
translation: Good gentlemen, give me permission to speak. It is proper for me to obey my husband, but not in this case.

original: Perchance, Iago, I will ne'er go home.
translation: Maybe I will never go home, Iago.

original: Oh! Oh! Oh!
translation: Oh! Oh! Oh!

original: Nay, lay thee down and roar, For thou hast killed the sweetest innocent That e'er did lift up eye.
translation: Yes, lie down and roar with grief, since you have killed the sweetest innocent girl that ever lived.

original: Oh, she was foul!—   I scarce did know you, uncle.
translation: Oh, she was foul! I barely knew you, Uncle Gratiano,

original: There lies your niece,   Whose breath, indeed, these hands have newly stopped.   I know this act shows horrible and grim.
translation: but there lies your niece, whose life I have just recently stopped with these very hands. I know this act seems horrible and grim.

original: Poor Desdemon! I am glad thy father’s dead,   Thy match was mortal to him, and pure grief   Shore his old thread in twain.
translation: Poor Desdemona! I am glad your father is dead. Your marriage was painful to him, and his grief cut his life short.

original: Did he live now,   This sight would make him do a desperate turn,   Yea, curse his better angel from his side   And fall to reprobation.
translation: If he were alive now, this sight would put him in a downward spiral. Yes, he would curse his good conscience and stoop to damnation.

original: 'Tis pitiful, but yet Iago knows   That she with Cassio hath the act of shame   A thousand times committed.
translation: It is pitiful, but Iago knows that Desdemona had shamefully cheated on me with Cassio a thousand times.

original: Cassio confessed it,   And she did gratify his amorous works   With that recognizance and pledge of love   Which I first gave her.
translation: Cassio confessed it, and she repaid his love with a token, the pledge of love that I first gave her.

original: I saw it in his hand,   It was a handkerchief, an antique token   My father gave my mother.
translation: I saw it in his hand. It was a handkerchief, an antique my father gave to my mother.

original: Oh, heaven! Oh, heavenly powers!
translation: Oh God! Oh heavenly powers!

original: Zounds, hold your peace.
translation: Christ, keep quiet.

original: '   Twill out, ’twill out.—I peace?   No, I will speak as liberal as the north.
translation: The truth will come out, the truth will come out. Me, be quiet? No, I will speak as freely as the north wind blows.

original: Let heaven and men and devils, let them all,   All, all cry shame against me, yet I’ll speak.
translation: I don't care if all angels and devils and humans cry out that I am shameful for disobeying my husband, I will still speak out.

original: Be wise, and get you home.
translation: Be smart and go back home.

original: I will not.
translation: I will not go.

original: Fie! Your sword upon a woman?
translation: Shame! You draw your sword against a woman?

original: O thou dull Moor! That handkerchief thou speak’st of   I found by fortune and did give my husband.
translation: Oh, you stupid Moor!  I found the handkerchief you speak of by chance, and gave it to my husband.

original: For often, with a solemn earnestness—   More than indeed belonged to such a trifle—   He begged of me to steal it.
translation: For he often eagerly and earnestly begged me to steal it. He was more concerned about it than one would expect for such a little thing.

original: Villainous whore!
translation: Evil whore!

original: She give it Cassio? No, alas, I found it And I did give ’t my husband.
translation: Did Desdemona give it to Cassio? No. I found it and gave it to my husband.

original: Filth, thou liest!
translation: Filth, you are lying!

original: By heaven, I do not, I do not, gentlemen.—
translation: I swear by heaven, I do not lie, I do not, gentlemen.

original: (to OTHELLO)   O murderous coxcomb! What should such a fool   Do with so good a wife?
translation: [To OTHELLO]  Oh, you murdering fool! How did such a fool as you get such a good wife?

original: Are there no stones in heaven But what serve for the thunder?—Precious villain!
The woman falls! Sure he hath killed his wife.
translation: The woman has fallen down! He's surely killed his own wife.

original: Ay, ay. Oh, lay me by my mistress' side.
translation: Yes, yes. Oh, lay me down next to Desdemona.

original: He’s gone, but his wife’s killed.
translation: He's run off, and his wife has been killed.

original: 'Tis a notorious villain. Take you this weapon,   Which I have recovered from the Moor.
translation: He is a terrible villain. Take this weapon that I have obtained from the Moor.

original: Come, guard the door without. Let him not pass,   But kill him rather. I’ll after that same villain,   For ’tis a damnèd slave.
translation: Go, guard the outer door. Don't let Iago get out. Kill him instead. I'll chase after the same villain, for he is a damned scoundrel.

original: I am not valiant neither,   But ever puny whipster gets my sword.
translation: I'm not very strong if some puny little man can take my sword from me.

original: But why should honor outlive honesty?   Let it go all.
translation: But then again, why should my honor live on after my honesty is dead? I'll let it all go.

original: What did thy song bode, lady?   Hark, canst thou hear me? I will play the swan.   And die in music.
translation: What did your song foretell, my lady? Listen, can you  hear me? I will be like a swan and die while singing.

original: singing)     Willow, willow, willow   —   Moor, she was chaste, she loved thee, cruel Moor.   So come my soul to bliss, as I speak true.   So speaking as I think, alas, I die.
translation: [Singing] Willow, willow, willow—  Moor, she was chaste and she loved you, cruel Moor. I speak the truth, so my soul will go to heaven. And so, alas, I die—speaking my honest thoughts.

original: I have another weapon in this chamber,   It was a sword of Spain, the ice-brook’s temper.
translation: I have another weapon in this room. It is a sword from Spain, hardened in an icy stream.

original: Oh, here it is. Uncle, I must come forth.
translation: Oh, here it is. Uncle, I must come out of the room.

original: If thou attempt it, it will cost thee dear. Thou hast no weapon, and perforce must suffer.
translation: If you try to get by, you'll pay for it. You have no weapon, and so you'll surely get hurt.

original: Look in upon me then and speak with me,  Or, naked as I am, I will assault thee.
translation: Then come in here and speak with me. Or, unarmed as I am, I will attack you.

original: What is the matter?
translation: What is the matter?

original: Behold, I have a weapon.   A better never did itself sustain   Upon a soldier’s thigh.
translation: Look, I have a weapon. A better sword has never graced a soldier's scabbard.

original: I have seen the day   That with this little arm and this good sword   I have made my way through more impediments   Than twenty times your stop.
translation: I remember times when, with this little arm and good sword of mine, I made my way through obstacles more than twenty times as tough as you.

original: But, oh, vain boast!   Who can control his fate? ’tis not so now.   Be not afraid, though you do see me weaponed.
translation: But what a pointless boast that is! Who can control his fate? I can't now. Don't worry, even though I am carrying a weapon.

original: Here is my journey’s end, here is my butt,   And very sea-mark of my utmost sail.   Do you go back dismayed? ’tis a lost fear.
translation: This is the end of my journey, the end of the rope, and my final destination. Are you backing off, frightened? You have nothing to fear.

original: Man but a rush against Othello’s breast,   And he retires. Where should Othello go?—   Now, how dost thou look now?
translation: You could strike at me with nothing more than a reed, and I'd draw back. Where could Othello run to? Do you see how you look now?

original: O ill-starred wench,   Pale as thy smock! When we shall meet at compt   This look of thine will hurl my soul from heaven   And fiends will snatch at it.
translation: Oh, you woman with an unlucky fate, as pale as your white nightgown! When we meet on Judgment Day, this look of yours will throw my soul out of heaven and into hell, where devils will snatch it.

original: Cold, cold, my girl,   Even like thy chastity. O cursed, cursed slave!   Whip me, ye devils,   From the possession of this heavenly sight!
translation: You are cold, my girl, cold like your chastity, which never gave in to the heat of desire. Oh cursed, cursed villain! Devils, whip me until I no longer see this horrible sight!

original: Blow me about in winds, roast me in sulfur,   Wash me in steep-down gulfs of liquid fire!—   Oh, Desdemona! Desdemona! dead! Oh! Oh!
translation: Blow me around in winds, burn me in sulfur flames, wash me in gulfs of liquid fire! Oh, Desdemona! Desdemona! Dead! Oh! Oh!

original: Where is this rash and most unfortunate man?
translation: Where is this impulsive and most unfortunate man?

original: That’s he that was Othello. Here I am.
translation: You speak of Othello. Here I am.

original: Where is that viper? Bring the villain forth.
translation: And where is that poisonous snake? Bring the villain forward.

original: I look down towards his feet, but that’s a fable. If that thou be’st a devil, I cannot kill thee.
translation: I see his feet, so it must just be a fairy tale that the devil has hooves. If you are a devil, then I cannot kill you.

original: Wrench his sword from him.
translation: Take his sword away from him.

original: I bleed, sir, but not killed.
translation: I am bleeding, but I haven't been killed, sir.

original: I am not sorry neither. I’d have thee live, For in my sense ’tis happiness to die.
translation: Good. I want you to live, because for me death is sweet now.

original: O thou Othello, thou was once so good, Fall'n in the practice of a cursèd slave, What shall be said to thee?
translation: Oh, Othello, you used to be so good, and now you've fallen under the control of a cursed villain. What can I say to you?

original: Why, anything.  An honorable murderer, if you will, For naught I did in hate, but all in honor.
translation: Anything. Call me an honorable murderer, if you wish, since I didn't do anything out of hate but instead out of a sense of honor.

original: This wretch hath part confessed his villainy. Did you and he consent in Cassio’s death?
translation: This wretched man has confessed to some of his evil doings. Did you and he conspire to kill Cassio?

original: Ay.
translation: Yes.

original: Dear general, I never gave you cause.
translation: Dear general, I gave you no reason to kill me.

original: I do believe it, and I ask your pardon.
translation: I believe you, and I ask for your forgiveness.

original: Will you, I pray, demand that demi-devil   Why he hath thus ensnared my soul and body?
translation: Will you please ask that half-devil why he has tricked me and ruined my soul and body?

original: Demand me nothing. What you know, you know.  From this time forth I never will speak word.
translation: Ask me nothing. You know what you know. From now on I will never speak again.

original: What, not to pray?
translation: Not even to pray?

original: Torments will ope your lips.
translation: We can make you speak with torture.

original: Well, thou dost best.
translation: Do your best, then.

original: Sir, you shall understand what hath befall'n,   Which, as I think, you know not. Here is a letter   Found in the pocket of the slain Roderigo,
translation: Sir, let me explain what has happened, which I don't think you know. Here is a letter that was found in dead Roderigo's pocket.

original: And here another. The one of them imports   The death of Cassio to be undertook   By Roderigo.
translation: And here is another. One of them says that Roderigo should kill Cassio.

original: Oh, villain!
translation: Oh, you villain!

original: Most heathenish and most gross!
translation: Filthiest heathen!

original: Now here’s another discontented paper   Found in his pocket too, and this,
translation: And now here's the other paper from his pocket, an angry letter.

original: it seems,   Roderigo meant to have sent this damnèd villain   But that, belike, Iago in the interim   Came in and satisfied him.
translation: It seems Roderigo meant to send it to Iago, but the damned villain likely killed him before he had the chance.

original: O thou pernicious caitiff! How came you, Cassio, by that handkerchief That was my wife’s?
translation: Oh, you malicious wretch! Cassio, how did you come across my wife's handkerchief?

original: I found it in my chamber,   And he himself confessed but even now
translation: I found it in my room, and Iago himself just confessed

original: That there he dropped it for a special purpose   Which wrought to his desire.
translation: that he left it there on purpose as part of his plan.

original: O fool! fool! fool!
translation: I'm a fool! A fool! A fool!

original: There is besides in Roderigo’s letter   How he upbraids Iago, that he made him   Brave me upon the watch, whereon it came   That I was cast.
translation: Moreover, Roderigo's letter describes how Iago told him to offend me while I was on guard duty, the thing that made me lose my title of lieutenant.

original: And even but now he spake,   After long seeming dead—Iago hurt him,   Iago set him on.
translation: And just now, even though he seemed to be dead, Roderigo spoke and said that Iago tricked him and urged him to on.

original: (to OTHELLO)   You must forsake this room and go with us.   Your power and your command is taken off   And Cassio rules in Cyprus.
translation: [To OTHELLO]  You must leave this room and come with us. You have been stripped of your power and command, and Cassio now rules over Cyprus.

original: For this slave,   If there be any cunning cruelty   That can torment him much and hold him long,   It shall be his.
translation: As for this scoundrel, he will get whatever clever, cruel torture we can devise to cause him a lot of pain for a long time.

original: You shall close prisoner rest   Till that the nature of your fault be known   To the Venetian state.—Come, bring him away.
translation: You will stay a prisoner until the Venetian government hears of your crime. Come on, bring him away.

original: Soft you, a word or two before you go.   I have done the state some service, and they know ’t.   No more of that.
translation: Wait, let me say a word or two before you go. I have served the government of Venice well, and they know it. But nothing more about that.

original: I pray you, in your letters,   When you shall these unlucky deeds relate,   Speak of me as I am. Nothing extenuate,   Nor set down aught in malice.
translation: I beg you, in your letters, when you relate the story of these unfortunate deeds, speak of me as I am. Don't downplay my crime, but don't exaggerate it maliciously.

original: Then must you speak   Of one that loved not wisely, but too well.   Of one not easily jealous, but being wrought,   Perplexed in the extreme.
translation: Speak of me as a man who loved not wisely, but too much; a man who was not easily made jealous, but was manipulated and tricked into extreme jealously;

original: Of one whose hand,   Like the base Indian, threw a pearl away   Richer than all his tribe.
translation: a man who behaved like a vile  Indian  that throws away a pearl worth more than his whole tribe.

original: Of one whose subdued eyes,   Albeit unused to the melting mood,   Drop tears as fast as the Arabian trees   Their medicinal gum.
translation: Speak of me as a man who is not used to crying, but whose eyes now drop tears like the Arabian trees that drip with medicinal sap.

original: Set you down this,   And say besides that in Aleppo once,   Where a malignant and a turbaned Turk   Beat a Venetian and traduced the state,
translation: Write this, and also say that one time in Aleppo a malicious Turk wearing a turban beat a Venetian, flouting the Venetian state,

original: I took by the throat the circumcisèd dog,   And smote him, thus.
translation: and so I grabbed the circumcised Turkish dog by his throat and struck him down like this.

original: Oh, bloody period!
translation: What a bloody conclusion!

original: All that is spoke is marred.
translation: Everything he said is tarnished by what he's done.

original: I kissed thee ere I killed thee. No way but this, Killing myself, to die upon a kiss.
translation: I kissed you before I killed you. Now that I am killing myself, I must die with a kiss.

original: This did I fear, but thought he had no weapon, For he was great of heart.
translation: I feared this would happen because he was a brave man, but I didn't think he had a weapon.

original: (to IAGO)   O Spartan dog,   More fell than anguish, hunger, or the sea,   Look on the tragic loading of this bed.
translation: [To IAGO]  You cruel dog, look at the tragic contents of this bed—worse than pain, starvation, or the tempestuous sea.

original: This is thy work. The object poisons sight,   Let it be hid.—
Gratiano, keep the house   And seize upon the fortunes of the Moor,   For they succeed on you.—
translation: [To GRATIANO]  Gratiano, guard the house and take the Moor's possessions, for you inherit them all.

original: T   o you, lord governor,   Remains the censure of this hellish villain:
translation: [To CASSIO]  And you, my lord governor, will decide how to punish this hellish villain.

original: The time, the place, the torture. Oh, enforce it!   Myself will straight aboard, and to the state   This heavy act with heavy heart relate.
translation: You can pick the time, the place, and the kind of torture. And then enforce the punishment! I will go to a ship immediately, and tell the Venetian government about these tragic events with a heavy heart.

original: Now is the winter of our discontent   Made glorious summer by this son of York,
translation: Now the winter of our troubles has been transformed into glorious summer by the ascension of my brother, King Edward IV,  son  of the house of York.

original: And all the clouds that loured upon our house   In the deep bosom of the ocean buried.
translation: All the clouds that had descended over our family have now been banished and returned to the sea.

original: Now are our brows bound with victorious wreaths,   Our bruisèd arms hung up for monuments,
translation: Now we wear wreaths of victory on our foreheads, and we've hung up our armor as decoration.

original: Our stern alarums changed to merry meetings,   Our dreadful marches to delightful measures.
translation: We've exchanged the sound of our battle trumpets for the sound of joyful greetings, and our death marches have become stately dances.

original: Grim-visaged war hath smoothed his wrinkled front;
translation: The grim, warlike expressions on our faces have smoothed.

original: And now, instead of mounting barbèd steeds   To fright the souls of fearful adversaries,   He capers nimbly in a lady’s chamber   To the lascivious pleasing of a lute.
translation: And instead of charging on armored horses to frighten our opponents, we now dance in ladies' chambers to seductive songs on the lute.

original: But I, that am not shaped for sportive tricks,   Nor made to court an amorous looking glass;
translation: But as for me, I am not made for such games of love, or to admire myself in a mirror.

original: I, that am rudely stamped and want love’s majesty   To strut before a wanton ambling nymph;
translation: I was badly made, and I lack the good looks to strut in front of passing girls.

original: I, that am curtailed of this fair proportion,   Cheated of feature by dissembling nature,
translation: Nature has cheated me out of handsome features and proper proportions.

original: Deformed, unfinished, sent before my time   Into this breathing world, scarce half made up,   And that so lamely and unfashionable   That dogs bark at me as I halt by them—
translation: I was born  deformed , unfinished, and born prematurely. I was barely half-created when I came into the world, and left so lame and misshapen that dogs bark at me as I limp past them.

original: Why, I, in this weak piping time of peace,   Have no delight to pass away the time,
translation: In such delicate times of peace, I have nothing to do

original: Unless to see my shadow in the sun   And descant on mine own deformity.
translation: No joys help me pass the time, unless I want to see my own shadow in the sun and make speeches about my deformity.

original: And therefore, since I cannot prove a lover   To entertain these fair well-spoken days,   I am determinèd to prove a villain
translation: Therefore, since I cannot amuse myself by being a lover during these peaceful days, I am determined to become a villain.

original: And hate the idle pleasures of these days.   Plots have I laid, inductions dangerous,   By drunken prophecies, libels and dreams,
translation: I have hatched plots and put dangerous plans into action, using prophecies made while drunk; slander; and stories about dreams

original: To set my brother Clarence and the king   In deadly hate, the one against the other;
translation: in order to set my brother George, Duke of Clarence, against my other brother, the king, so that they hate each other.

original: And if King Edward be as true and just   As I am subtle, false, and treacherous,
translation: If King Edward is as true as I am clever, false, and treacherous,

original: This day should Clarence closely be mewed up   About a prophecy which says that “G”   Of Edward’s heirs the murderer shall be.
translation: then this very day Clarence will be imprisoned because of a prophecy that " G " will murder Edward's children.

original: Dive, thoughts, down to my soul. Here Clarence comes.
translation: But, you thoughts, hide yourselves deep down in my soul, for here comes Clarence.

original: Brother, good day. What means this armèd guard That waits upon your Grace?
His majesty, Tend'ring my person’s safety, hath appointed  This conduct to convey me to the Tower.
Upon what cause?
translation: You're being arrested? For what reason?

original: Because my name is George.
translation: Because my name is George.

original: Alack, my lord, that fault is none of yours.
translation: Alas, my lord, that's no fault of yours.

original: He should, for that, commit your godfathers.
translation: If that's the problem, then our brother, the king, should arrest those who named you instead.

original: O, belike his majesty hath some intent   That you shall be new christened in the Tower.
translation: Or maybe his Majesty intends to baptize you and rename you in the Tower.

original: But what’s the matter, Clarence? May I know?
translation: But what's the reason for this, Clarence? Will you tell me?

original: Yea, Richard, when I know, for I protest   As yet I do not.
translation: Yes, Richard, I'll inform you when I know—but right now I have no idea.

original: But, as I can learn,   He hearkens after prophecies and dreams,
translation: As far as I can tell, the king has been putting a lot of trust in prophecies and dreams lately.

original: And from the crossrow plucks the letter "G",   And says a wizard told him that by “G”   His issue disinherited should be.
translation: And he picked the letter "G" from the alphabet, and says that a wizard told him that "G" will steal the throne from his children.

original: And for my name of George begins with "G",   It follows in his thought that I am he.
translation: And my name, George, begins with "G," so he thinks that the prophecy refers to me.

original: These, as I learn, and such like toys as these   Have moved his Highness to commit me now.
translation: Because of this, along with other trivial reasons, his Highness feels compelled to arrest me.

original: Why, this it is when men are ruled by women.   'Tis not the king that sends you to the Tower.
translation: Well, this is what happens when men are ruled by women. It isn't the king who's sending you to the Tower—

original: My Lady Grey his wife, Clarence, ’tis she   That tempers him to this extremity.
translation: it's his wife, Lady Elizabeth Grey. She's the one who persuaded him to take such an extreme action.

original: Was it not she and that good man of worship,   Anthony Woodeville, her brother there,   That made him send Lord Hastings to the Tower,
translation: Didn't she and her brother, Anthony Woodeville, make the king send Lord Hastings to the Tower?

original: From whence this present day he is delivered?   We are not safe, Clarence. We are not safe.
translation: He was released only today. We are not safe, Clarence. We are not safe.

original: By heaven, I think there is no man is secure   But the queen’s kindred and night-walking heralds   That trudge betwixt the king and Mistress Shore.
translation: By heaven, I think the only people who  are  safe are the queen's relatives, and the secret messengers who travel between the king and his mistress, Jane Shore.

original: Heard ye not what an humble suppliant   Lord Hastings was to her for his delivery?
translation: Didn't you hear how Lord Hastings had to beg Miss Shore in order to get released?

original: Humbly complaining to her deity   Got my Lord Chamberlain his liberty.
translation: Yes, Lord Hastings gained his liberty by humbly bowing down to that  goddess .

original: I’ll tell you what: I think it is our way,   If we will keep in favor with the king,   To be her men and wear her livery.
translation: I'll tell you what: if we want to stay in the king's favor, it would be best if we act like Miss Shore's servants too.

original: The jealous o'erworn widow and herself,   Since that our brother dubbed them gentlewomen,   Are mighty gossips in this monarchy.
translation: Ever since our brother declared that Miss Shore and the queen are nobility, they've become great gossips in the court.

original: I beseech your Graces both to pardon me.
translation: I beg your pardon, your Graces.

original: His majesty hath straitly given in charge   That no man shall have private conference,   Of what degree soever, with his brother.
translation: His Majesty the king has strictly ordered that no one can speak privately with your brother Clarence, no matter their social rank.

original: Even so. An please your Worship, Brakenbury,   You may partake of anything we say.
translation: Is that so? If it please  your Worship , Brakenbury, you can listen to anything we say.

original: We speak no treason, man. We say the king   Is wise and virtuous, and his noble queen   Well struck in years, fair, and not jealous.
translation: We're not plotting any treason, man. We say that the king is wise and virtuous, and his noble queen is well advanced in years, beautiful, and not jealous.

original: We say that Shore’s wife hath a pretty foot,   A cherry lip, a bonny eye, a passing pleasing tongue,   And that the queen’s kindred are made gentlefolks.
translation: We say that Mister Shore's wife has pretty feet, cherry lips, lovely eyes, and a pleasant voice. We say that the queen's relatives have all become nobles.

original: How say you, sir? Can you deny all this?
translation: What do you say to that, sir? Can you deny any of this?

original: With this, my lord, myself have naught to do.
Naught to do with Mistress Shore? I tell thee, fellow, He that doth naught with her, excepting one,  Were best he do it secretly, alone.
translation: "Naught" to do with Miss Shore? I tell you, fellow, there's only one man who can do "naught" with her. And if anyone else is doing it, he'd best do it secretly.

original: What one, my lord?
translation: Who is that, my lord?

original: Her husband, knave. Wouldst thou betray me?
translation: Her husband, fool. Are you going to tell on me?

original: I do beseech your Grace to pardon me, and withal  Forbear your conference with the noble duke.
translation: I beg your Grace to forgive me, and now please stop talking to the Duke of Clarence.

original: We know thy charge, Brakenbury, and will obey.
translation: We know your orders, Brakenbury. And we'll obey.

original: We are the queen’s abjects and must obey.—   Brother, farewell.
translation: We are the queen's lowly subjects, and we must obey. Farewell, brother.

original: I will unto the king,   And whatsoe'er you will employ me in,   Were it to call King Edward’s widow “sister,”   I will perform it to enfranchise you.
translation: I will go to the king and do whatever you need me to do to get you released, even if it means calling King Edward's  wife  "sister."

original: Meantime, this deep disgrace in brotherhood   Touches me deeper than you can imagine.
translation: And just so you know, our brother's disgraceful conduct towards you upsets me more than you can imagine.

original: I know it pleaseth neither of us well.
translation: I know it doesn't make either of us very happy.

original: Well, your imprisonment shall not be long. I will deliver you or else lie for you. Meantime, have patience.
translation: Well, your imprisonment won't be for long. I'll free you, or else go to prison in your place. In the meantime, have patience.

original: I must perforce. Farewell.
translation: I have no choice in the matter. Farewell.

original: Go tread the path that thou shalt ne'er return.
translation: Go, walk down the path from which you'll never return.

original: Simple, plain Clarence, I do love thee so   That I will shortly send thy soul to heaven,   If heaven will take the present at our hands.
translation: Stupid, plain Clarence, I love you so much that I'll soon send your soul to heaven—if heaven will accept any presents from me.

original: But who comes here? The new-delivered Hastings?
translation: But who's this coming? The newly released Hastings?

original: Good time of day unto my gracious lord.
translation: Good day to you, my gracious lord.

original: As much unto my good Lord Chamberlain.  Well are you welcome to the open air. How hath your lordship brooked imprisonment?
With patience, noble lord, as prisoners must. But I shall live, my lord, to give them thanks That were the cause of my imprisonment.
translation: With patience,  as all prisoners must, noble lord. But I will live to thank those who imprisoned me, my lord, by taking revenge.

original: No doubt, no doubt; and so shall Clarence too, For they that were your enemies are his And have prevailed as much on him as you.
translation: No doubt, no doubt. And so will Clarence, for the people who were your enemies are now his enemies, and they've overcome him just like they overcame you.

original: More pity that the eagle should be mewed While kites and buzzards prey at liberty.
translation: It's a pity that the eagles should be caged while the buzzards are free to hunt.

original: What news abroad?
translation: What's the news from outside the country?

original: No news so bad abroad as this at home: The king is sickly, weak and melancholy, And his physicians fear him mightily.
translation: There's no foreign news as bad as the news at home: the king is sickly, weak, and depressed, and his physicians fear for his life.

original: Now, by Saint Paul, that news is bad indeed.
translation: By Saint Paul, that is bad news indeed.

original: O, he hath kept an evil diet long,   And overmuch consumed his royal person.
translation: Oh, the king has kept many bad habits all his life, and now they've consumed his health.

original: 'Tis very grievous to be thought upon.   Where is he, in his bed?
translation: It's very sad to think about. Where is he, in his bed?

original: He is.
translation: He is.

original: Go you before, and I will follow you.
translation: Then you go ahead, and I will follow you.

original: He cannot live, I hope, and must not die   Till George be packed with post-horse up to heaven.
translation: I hope the king won't survive. But he mustn't die until Clarence is sent off to heaven by the quickest route.

original: I’ll in to urge his hatred more to Clarence   With lies well steeled with weighty arguments,
translation: I'll go in and incite the king to more hatred against Clarence, using lies backed up by sound reasoning.

original: And, if I fail not in my deep intent,   Clarence hath not another day to live;
translation: And if I don't fail in my plan, then Clarence won't live even one more day.

original: Which done, God take King Edward to His mercy,   And leave the world for me to bustle in.
translation: Once that's done, God can take King Edward to heaven as soon as he wants, and leave the world for me to run around in.

original: For then I’ll marry Warwick’s youngest daughter.   What though I killed her husband and her father?
translation: For then I'll marry  Warwick's  youngest daughter, Lady Anne Neville. What does it matter that I killed her  husband  and her father?

original: The readiest way to make the wench amends   Is to become her husband and her father;
translation: The best way to make it up to the girl is to become her new husband and father.

original: The which will I, not all so much for love   As for another secret close intent   By marrying her which I must reach unto.
translation: I'll do that then, not out of love for her, but because it's part of my secret plan.

original: But yet I run before my horse to market.   Clarence still breathes; Edward still lives and reigns.
translation: But I'm getting ahead of myself. Clarence is still breathing. Edward still lives and reigns as king.

original: When they are gone, then must I count my gains.
translation: I can only count my gains when they're dead.

original: Set down, set down your honorable load,   If honor may be shrouded in a hearse,
translation: Set down, set down your honorable load, men — if honor can be shrouded in a coffin —

original: Poor key-cold figure of a holy king,   Pale ashes of the house of Lancaster,   Thou bloodless remnant of that royal blood,
translation: Oh, you poor cold corpse of a holy king, you last remains of the house of Lancaster, you bloodless remnant of that royal blood!

original: Be it lawful that I invocate thy ghost   To hear the lamentations of poor Anne,
translation: If it's lawful to speak to your ghost, then listen to the sorrows of poor Anne.

original: Wife to thy Edward, to thy slaughtered son,   Stabbed by the selfsame hand that made these wounds.
translation: My husband was Edward—your slaughtered son—who was murdered by the same man who stabbed you.

original: Lo, in these windows that let forth thy life   I pour the helpless balm of my poor eyes.
translation: Oh, let me pour my helpless tears into your wounds, those open windows that let your spirit escape.

original: O, cursèd be the hand that made these holes;   Cursèd the heart that had the heart to do it;   Cursèd the blood that let this blood from hence.
translation: I curse the hand that made these holes in you. I curse the heart of the person who had the heart to do it. And I curse the blood of the man that shed your blood.

original: More direful hap betide that hated wretch   That makes us wretched by the death of thee   Than I can wish to wolves, to spiders, toads,   Or any creeping venomed thing that lives.
translation: I hope evil fortunes fall upon that hateful man, the one who killed you and now makes me suffer. May his fate be worse than anything I would wish on wolves, spiders, toads, or any creeping venomous thing that lives.

original: If ever he have child, abortive be it,   Prodigious, and untimely brought to light,   Whose ugly and unnatural aspect   May fright the hopeful mother at the view,   And that be heir to his unhappiness.
translation: If he ever has a child, may it be born premature and unnatural, and may its appearance be so ugly and monstrous that even its own hopeful mother will fear it.

original: If ever he have wife, let her be made   More miserable by the death of him   Than I am made by my poor lord and thee.—
translation: That way, the child will inherit your murderer's own unhappiness. And if he ever has a wife, may she be more miserable at his death than I am now, mourning my husband and you, my father-in-law.

original: And still, as you are weary of this weight, Rest you, whiles I lament King Henry’s corse.
translation: And whenever your burden grows too heavy, rest a while, and I will lament over King Henry's corpse.

original: Stay, you that bear the corse, and set it down.
translation: Stop, you who bear that corpse, and set down your load.

original: What black magician conjures up this fiend  To stop devoted charitable deeds?
translation: What evil magician has conjured up this devil to interrupt our sacred burial procession?

original: Villains, set down the corse or, by Saint Paul, I’ll make a corse of him that disobeys.
translation: You base men, set down the corpse or, I swear by Saint Paul, I'll make corpses out of you.

original: My lord, stand back and let the coffin pass.
translation: My lord, stand back and let the coffin pass.

original: Unmannered dog, stand thou when I command!—
translation: Rude dog, halt when I command you to!

original: Advance thy halberd higher than my breast,   Or by Saint Paul I’ll strike thee to my foot   And spurn upon thee, beggar, for thy boldness.
translation: And raise your weapon so it isn't pointing at my chest, or, by Saint Paul, I'll strike you down and trample on you for your boldness, you beggar.

original: [to gentlemen and halberds]   What, do you tremble? Are you all afraid?   Alas, I blame you not, for you are mortal,   And mortal eyes cannot endure the devil.—
translation: [To the gentlemen and guards]   What, do you tremble at the sight of him? Are you all afraid? Alas, I don't blame you, for you're only mortal, and mortal eyes can't stand to look at the devil.

original: Sweet saint, for charity, be not so curst.
translation: Sweet saint, for goodness's sake, don't be so harsh.

original: Foul devil, for God’s sake, hence, and trouble us not,   For thou hast made the happy earth thy hell,   Filled it with cursing cries and deep exclaims.
translation: Foul devil, for God's sake, go away and leave us alone. You've made the pleasant earth into your hell, filling it with cursing cries and deep laments.

original: If thou delight to view thy heinous deeds,   Behold this pattern of thy butcheries.
translation: If you enjoy looking at your horrible deeds, then behold this example of your butchery.

original: O, gentlemen, see, see dead Henry’s wounds   Open their congealed mouths and bleed afresh!—
translation: Oh, gentlemen, see, see! Dead Henry's wounds have opened and are bleeding again!

original: Lady, you know no rules of charity, Which renders good for bad, blessings for curses.
translation: Lady, you don't know the rules of charity, which transforms evil into good, and curses into blessings.

original: Villain, thou know’st not law of God nor man. No beast so fierce but knows some touch of pity.
translation: Villain, you don't know the laws of God or man. Even the fiercest beast has a touch of pity.

original: But I know none, and therefore am no beast.
translation: But I have no pity, so I must not be a beast.

original: O, wonderful, when devils tell the truth!
translation: Oh, how amazing to hear a devil tell the truth!

original: More wonderful, when angels are so angry.
translation: It's more amazing that an angel should be so angry.

original: Vouchsafe, divine perfection of a woman,   Of these supposèd crimes to give me leave   By circumstance but to acquit myself.
translation: You divinely perfect woman, please allow me to clear myself of these crimes of which you've accused me.

original: Vouchsafe, defused infection of a man, Of these known evils but to give me leave  By circumstance to curse thy cursèd self.
translation: You shapeless plague of a man, please allow me to curse your cursed self for the crimes I know you've committed.

original: Fairer than tongue can name thee, let me have Some patient leisure to excuse myself.
translation: You who are more beautiful than words can say, give me some time and let me explain myself.

original: Fouler than heart can think thee, thou canst make No excuse current but to hang thyself.
translation: You who are more awful than any heart could believe, the only explanation you can give is to go hang yourself.

original: By such despair I should accuse myself.
translation: Such an act of despair would prove my guilt.

original: And by despairing shalt thou stand excused For doing worthy vengeance on thyself That didst unworthy slaughter upon others.
translation: And such an act of despair would be a worthy act of revenge against yourself for slaughtering innocents.

original: Say that I slew them not.
translation: Let's say that I didn't kill them.

original: Then say they were not slain.  But dead they are, and devilish slave, by thee.
translation: Then we might as well say that they aren't dead. But, you devilish scoundrel, they are dead, and you killed them.

original: I did not kill your husband.
translation: I did not kill your husband.

original: Why then, he is alive.
translation: Well then, he must be alive.

original: Nay, he is dead, and slain by Edward’s hands.
translation: No, he is dead, and Edward killed him.

original: In thy foul throat thou liest.
translation: You're lying through your teeth.

original: Queen Margaret saw   Thy murd'rous falchion smoking in his blood,   The which thou once didst bend against her breast,
translation: Queen Margaret  saw your murderous sword steaming with his blood—the same sword with which you once tried to kill her.

original: But that thy brothers beat aside the point.
translation: She was only saved because your brothers restrained you.

original: I was provokèd by her sland'rous tongue, That laid their guilt upon my guiltless shoulders.
translation: I was provoked by her lying tongue, which tried to lay guilt on my guiltless shoulders.

original: Thou wast provokèd by thy bloody mind,  That never dream’st on aught but butcheries. Didst thou not kill this king?
translation: No, you were provoked by your own bloody mind, which never thinks about anything but butchery. Did you kill this king?

original: I grant you.
translation: Yes, I'll grant you that.

original: Dost grant me, hedgehog? Then, God grant me too Thou mayst be damnèd for that wicked deed. O, he was gentle, mild, and virtuous.
translation: You'll grant me, you hedgehog? Then let God grant me my wish that you'll be damned for that wicked deed. Oh, Henry was gentle, mild, and virtuous.

original: The better for the King of heaven that hath him.
translation: All the better for God, who has him now.

original: He is in heaven, where thou shalt never come.
translation: Yes, he's in heaven, where you will never go.

original: Let him thank me, that holp to send him thither, For he was fitter for that place than earth.
translation: Then let him thank me, who helped him get there. He's better suited for heaven than for earth.

original: And thou unfit for any place but hell.
translation: And you're not suited for any place but hell.

original: Yes, one place else, if you will hear me name it.
translation: Yes, though I'm also suited for one other place, if you'll let me name it.

original: Some dungeon.
translation: Some dungeon.

original: Your bedchamber.
translation: Your bedroom.

original: Ill rest betide the chamber where thou liest!
translation: There will be no rest in any bedroom where you lie!

original: So will it, madam till I lie with you.
translation: That's true, madam, until I sleep with you.

original: I hope so.
translation: I hope so—because then you'll never sleep.

original: I know so. But, gentle Lady Anne,   To leave this keen encounter of our wits   And fall something into a slower method—
translation: I know so. But, dear Lady Anne, let's leave this battle of wits and move into a calmer, slower conversation.

original: Is not the causer of the timeless deaths   Of these Plantagenets, Henry and Edward,   As blameful as the executioner?
translation: Isn't the person who caused the untimely deaths of these  Plantagenets —Henry and Edward—as much to blame as the person who physically committed the murders?

original: Thou wast the cause and most accursed effect.
translation: You are both—the cause and the dreadful effect.

original: Your beauty was the cause of that effect—
translation: No, your beauty was the cause of my deeds—

original: Your beauty, that did haunt me in my sleep   To undertake the death of all the world,   So I might live one hour in your sweet bosom.
translation: your beauty that haunted my sleep, and could have convinced me to kill the whole world to have just an hour of intimacy with you.

original: If I thought that, I tell thee, homicide, These nails should rend that beauty from my cheeks.
translation: If I believed you, murderer, then I tell you that I would scratch the beauty from my cheeks with my fingernails.

original: These eyes could never endure that beauty’s wrack.   You should not blemish it, if I stood by.
translation: I couldn't stand to see you ruin your beauty. I would stop you if you tried to blemish it.

original: As all the world is cheerèd by the sun,   So I by that. It is my day, my life.
translation: Your beauty encourages me like the sun encourages the whole world. Your beauty is my day, my life.

original: Black night o'ershade thy day, and death thy life.
translation: Then may black night overshadow your day, and death take your life.

original: Curse not thyself, fair creature; thou art both.
translation: Beautiful lady, don't curse yourself, since you are both my day and my life.

original: I would I were, to be revenged on thee.
translation: I wish I were, so I could have some power to take revenge and kill you.

original: It is a quarrel most unnatural  To be revenged on him that loveth thee.
translation: It's unnatural to want to take revenge on the man who loves you.

original: It is a quarrel just and reasonable To be revenged on him that killed my husband.
translation: It's just and reasonable to want to take revenge on the man who killed my husband.

original: He that bereft thee, lady, of thy husband Did it to help thee to a better husband.
translation: Lady, the man who robbed you of your husband did it to help you find a better husband.

original: His better doth not breathe upon the earth.
translation: There is no better man on earth than my husband.

original: He lives that loves thee better than he could.
translation: But there is one man who loves you better than your husband could.

original: Name him.
translation: Name him.

original: Plantagenet.
translation: Plantagenet.

original: Why, that was he.
translation: Yes, that's my husband's name.

original: The selfsame name, but one of better nature.
translation: I mean someone with the same name, but a better personality.

original: Where is he?
translation: Where is he?

original: Here.
translation: Right here.

original: Why dost thou spit at me?
translation: Why do you spit at me?

original: Would it were mortal poison for thy sake.
translation: I wish my spit were deadly poison.

original: Never came poison from so sweet a place.
translation: Poison never came from so sweet a place.

original: Never hung poison on a fouler toad. Out of my sight! Thou dost infect mine eyes.
translation: Poison never fell onto a fouler toad. Get out of my sight! You're infecting my eyes.

original: Thine eyes, sweet lady, have infected mine.
translation: Sweet lady, your eyes have infected mine with love.

original: Would they were basilisks to strike thee dead.
I would they were, that I might die at once,   For now they kill me with a living death.
translation: I wish they were, so I could die at once. For right now your eyes are killing me with a living death.

original: Those eyes of thine from mine have drawn salt tears,   Shamed their aspect with store of childish drops.
translation: Your eyes have drawn salty tears from my eyes, making me weep shamefully like a child.

original: These eyes, which never shed remorseful tear—   No, when my father York and Edward wept   To hear the piteous moan that Rutland made   When black-faced Clifford shook his sword at him;
translation: My eyes have never cried like this before—not even when my father York and my brother Edward wept at the death of my brother Rutland, who was slaughtered by the gloomy  Clifford .

original: Nor when thy warlike father, like a child,   Told the sad story of my father’s death   And twenty times made pause to sob and weep,
translation: And when your warlike father told the sad story of my father's death, and had to pause twenty times to sob and weep like a child,

original: That all the standers-by had wet their cheeks   Like trees bedashed with rain—in that sad time,   My manly eyes did scorn an humble tear;
translation: so that all the bystanders' cheeks ended up as wet as trees in a rainstorm—even in that sad time I didn't shed a single tear.

original: And what these sorrows could not thence exhale   Thy beauty hath, and made them blind with weeping.
translation: All these sorrows couldn't produce tears in me, but your beauty has blinded me with weeping.

original: I never sued to friend, nor enemy;   My tongue could never learn sweet smoothing word.
translation: I never begged a friend or enemy or learned the art of flattery,

original: But now thy beauty is proposed my fee,   My proud heart sues, and prompts my tongue to speak.
translation: but if your beauty is the reward, then I'll flatter and beg as much as I have to.

original: Teach not thy lip such scorn, for it were made   For kissing, lady, not for such contempt.
translation: Don't teach your lips to curl so scornfully—they were made for kissing, lady, not for such contempt.

original: If thy revengeful heart cannot forgive,   Lo, here I lend thee this sharp-pointed sword,   Which if thou please to hide in this true breast
translation: If your vengeful heart cannot forgive me, then here, take my sharp-pointed sword and bury it in my chest.

original: And let the soul forth that adoreth thee,   I lay it naked to the deadly stroke   And humbly beg the death upon my knee.
translation: That way my soul, which adores you, can be free. I lay myself open to being killed, and in fact, I humbly beg for death on my knees.

original: Nay, do not pause; for I did kill King Henry—   But ’twas thy beauty that provokèd me.
translation: No, don't pause. For I did kill King Henry—though your beauty provoked me to do it. Now go ahead.

original: Nay, now dispatch; ’twas I that stabbed young Edward—   But ’twas thy heavenly face that set me on.
translation: I was the one who stabbed young  Edward —though your heavenly face that drove me to it.

original: Take up the sword again, or take up me.
translation: Take up the sword again, or else take me.

original: Arise, dissembler. Though I wish thy death, I will not be the executioner.
translation: Stand up, liar. Though I wish you were dead, I won't be your executioner.

original: Then bid me kill myself, and I will do it.
translation: Then tell me to kill myself, and I will do it.

original: I have already.
translation: I have already.

original: That was in thy rage.   Speak it again and, even with the word,
translation: You said it in a rage. Say it again, and as soon as you finish speaking,

original: This hand, which for thy love did kill thy love,   Shall for thy love kill a far truer love.
translation: my hand—which killed your lover out of love for you—will kill your far truer lover.

original: To both their deaths shalt thou be accessory.
translation: You will be the cause of both these deaths.

original: I would I knew thy heart.
translation: I wish I knew what was in your heart.

original: 'Tis figured in my tongue.
translation: The same thing that was in my words.

original: I fear me both are false.
translation: I fear that both your heart and your words are false.

original: Then never man was man true.
translation: Then no man has ever been an honest man.

original: Well, well, put up your sword.
translation: Very well, then. Put up your sword.

original: Say then my peace is made.
translation: Then say that you'll accept me.

original: That shall you know hereafter.
translation: You'll know about that later.

original: But shall I live in hope?
translation: But should I live in hope?

original: All men I hope live so.
translation: I hope that all men live in hope.

original: Vouchsafe to wear this ring.
translation: Consent to wear this ring.

original: To take is not to give.
translation: To take is not to give. I'll accept it, but I won't promise anything in return.

original: Look, how this ring encompasseth finger;   Even so thy breast encloseth my poor heart.
translation: See how this ring encircles your finger. In the same way, my poor heart is enclosed inside your chest.

original: Wear both of them, for both of them are thine.
translation: Wear both of them, for both of them are yours.

original: And if thy poor devoted servant may   But beg one favor at thy gracious hand,   Thou dost confirm his happiness forever.
translation: And if I, your poor devoted servant, can ask for one small favor from your gracious hand, then you'll guarantee my happiness forever.

original: What is it?
translation: What is it?

original: That it would please you leave these sad designs   To him that hath more cause to be a mourner,   And presently repair to Crosby House,
translation: Please leave these burial ceremonies for me to finish, as I have more reason to mourn than you do. Go immediately to my estate at Crosby House.

original: Where, after I have solemnly interred   At Chertsey monast'ry this noble king   And wet his grave with my repentant tears,   I will with all expedient duty see you.
translation: After I have solemnly buried this noble king at Chertsey Abbey, and wet his grave with my repentant tears, I will hurry to meet you there.

original: For divers unknown reasons, I beseech you,   Grant me this boon.
translation: Please do this for me, I beg you. My reasons must remain secret for now.

original: With all my heart, and much it joys me too To see you are become so penitent.— Tressel and Berkeley, go along with me.
translation: I'll do it with all my heart, and it pleases me to see how remorseful you've become.

original: Bid me farewell.
translation: Bid me farewell.

original: 'Tis more than you deserve;  But since you teach me how to flatter you, Imagine I have said “farewell” already.
translation: To "fare well" is more than you deserve. But since you're now teaching me how to flatter you, pretend that I've said "farewell" already.

original: Sirs, take up the corse.
translation: Sirs, take up the corpse.

original: Towards Chertsey, noble lord?
translation: Towards Chertsey, noble lord?

original: No, to Whitefriars. There attend my coming.
translation: No, towards Whitefriars Monastery. Wait for me there.

original: Was ever woman in this humor wooed?   Was ever woman in this humor won?   I’ll have her, but I will not keep her long.
translation: Has a woman in such a mood ever been courted? Has a woman in such a mood ever been won? I'll get her, but I won't keep her long.

original: What, I that killed her husband and his father,   To take her in her heart’s extremest hate,   With curses in her mouth, tears in her eyes,   The bleeding witness of my hatred by,
translation: How can it be that I—who killed her husband and his father—should win her over at the moment she hates me the most? When her mouth was full of curses, her eyes full of tears, and the bloody corpse of my victim right in front of her?

original: Having God, her conscience, and these bars against me,   And I no friends to back my suit at all   But the plain devil and dissembling looks?
translation: She has God, her conscience, and the evidence of my deeds against me, and I have nothing to back me up but the devil and my own false looks!

original: And yet to win her, all the world to nothing! Ha!
translation: And yet I won her over, with all odds against me! Ha!

original: Hath she forgot already that brave prince,   Edward, her lord, whom I some three months since   Stabbed in my angry mood at Tewkesbury?
translation: Has she already forgotten her brave husband Prince Edward, whom I stabbed in an angry mood three months ago at the  Battle of Tewkesbury ?

original: A sweeter and a lovelier gentleman,   Framed in the prodigality of nature,   Young, valiant, wise, and, no doubt, right royal,   The spacious world cannot again afford.
translation: The world will never again be able to afford a man like him: such a sweet and lovely gentleman, blessed with all of nature's gifts. He was young, brave, wise, and no doubt meant to be king one day.

original: And will she yet abase her eyes on me,   That cropped the golden prime of this sweet prince   And made her widow to a woeful bed?
translation: And now she's going to cheapen herself by turning her eyes on me, who cut short her sweet prince's life and made her a widow in mourning?

original: On me, whose all not equals Edward’s moiety?   On me, that halts and am misshapen thus?
translation: On me, though I'm less than half of the man that Edward was? On me, who limps along, deformed like this?

original: My dukedom to a beggarly denier,   I do mistake my person all this while!
translation: I'd bet my dukedom on a beggar's penny that I've been wrong about myself all this time!

original: Upon my life, she finds, although I cannot,   Myself to be a marv'lous proper man.
translation: Upon my life, she finds me to be a proper, handsome man—though I can't see it.

original: I’ll be at charges for a looking glass   And entertain a score or two of tailors   To study fashions to adorn my body.
translation: I should buy a mirror and employ twenty or so tailors to study the current fashions and dress me up.

original: Since I am crept in favor with myself,   I will maintain it with some little cost.
translation: Since I like myself now, it will be worth the cost.

original: But first I’ll turn yon fellow in his grave   And then return lamenting to my love.
translation: But first I'll dump this fellow into his grave and then return, weeping, to my love.

original: Shine out, fair sun, till I have bought a glass,   That I may see my shadow as I pass.
translation: Shine out, fair sun, so I can watch my shadow as I pass—until I've bought a mirror to admire my reflection.

original: Have patience, madam. There’s no doubt his majesty Will soon recover his accustomed health.
translation: Have patience, madam. There's no doubt that his Majesty, King Edward, will soon recover his health.

original: In that you brook it ill, it makes him worse. Therefore, for God’s sake, entertain good comfort  And cheer his grace with quick and merry eyes.
translation: And if you're visibly worried, you'll make him worse. So for God's sake, let us comfort you, and then you can cheer up his Majesty with your lively, happy mood.

original: If he were dead, what would betide on me?
translation: If he were dead, what would happen to me?

original: No other harm but loss of such a lord.
translation: No harm would come to you but the loss of such a husband.

original: The loss of such a lord includes all harms.
translation: The loss of such a husband includes all kinds of harm.

original: The heavens have blessed you with a goodly son  To be your comforter when he is gone.
translation: The heavens have blessed you with a good son, who will comfort you when the king is gone.

original: Ah, he is young, and his minority Is put unto the trust of Richard Gloucester, A man that loves not me nor none of you.
translation: Ah, but he is young, and while he's young he is still in the care of Richard, the Duke of Gloucester—a man who loves neither me nor any of you.

original: Is it concluded that he shall be Protector?
It is determined, not concluded yet; But so it must be if the king miscarry.
translation: It's been decided, but not officially declared yet. But that's the way it must be if the king dies.

original: Here comes the lord of Buckingham, and Derby.
translation: Here comes the lords of Buckingham, and Derby.

original: Good time of day unto your royal  Grace.
translation: Good day to you, your royal Grace.

original: God make your Majesty joyful, as you have been.
translation: May God make your Majesty as happy as you once were.

original: The countess Richmond, good my lord of Derby,   To your good prayer will scarcely say amen.
translation: My good Lord Stanley, the countess Richmond would hardly agree and say "amen" to you prayer.

original: Yet, Derby, notwithstanding she’s your wife   And loves not me, be you, good lord, assured   I hate not you for her proud arrogance.
translation: But even though she's your wife and doesn't like me, you can be assured, good lord, that I don't hate you for her proud  arrogance.

original: I do beseech you either not believe   The envious slanders of her false accusers,
translation: Please don't believe the jealous lies of her slanderers.

original: Or if she be accused in true report,   Bear with her weakness, which I think proceeds   From wayward sickness and no grounded malice.
translation: And even if there's some truth to the rumors, then forgive her, for I think she only acts that way because she's sick—not because she hates you.

original: Saw you the king today, my lord of Derby?
translation: Did you see the king today, Lord Stanley?

original: But now the duke of Buckingham and I Are come from visiting his majesty.
translation: The Duke of Buckingham and I are just coming now from a visit to his Majesty.

original: What likelihood of his amendment, lords?
translation: What are the chances of his recovery, lords?

original: Madam, good hope. His grace speaks cheerfully.
translation: There is good hope, madam. The king seems cheerful.

original: God grant him health. Did you confer with him?
translation: May God grant him health. Did you speak with him?

original: Ay, madam. He desires to make atonement   Betwixt the duke of Gloucester and your brothers,
translation: Yes, madam. He wants to reconcile Richard with your brothers,

original: And betwixt them and my Lord Chamberlain,   And sent to warn them to his royal presence.
translation: and your brothers with Lord Hastings. He has just summoned them all to his royal presence.

original: Would all were well—but that will never be. I fear our happiness is at the height.
translation: I wish that all were well—but that will never be. I fear that our good fortune has reached its peak.

original: They do me wrong, and I will not endure it!
translation: They're abusing me, and I won't endure it!

original: Who is it that complains unto the king   That I, forsooth, am stern and love them not?
translation: Who has been complaining to the king that I am harsh and don't like them?

original: By holy Paul, they love his grace but lightly   That fill his ears with such dissentious rumors.
translation: By Saint Paul, whoever is worrying the king with these treacherous rumors doesn't love him very much.

original: Because I cannot flatter and look fair,   Smile in men’s faces, smooth, deceive and cog,   Duck with French nods and apish courtesy,   I must be held a rancorous enemy.
translation: Just because I cannot flatter and look handsome, smile in men's faces, ingratiate myself, lie and cheat, and bow like a pretentious Frenchman, people assume that I'm a foul enemy.

original: Cannot a plain man live and think no harm,   But thus his simple truth must be abused   With silken, sly, insinuating jacks?
translation: Can't a plain man live, wishing no harm on anyone, without his words being twisted like this by slick, sly, slithering lowlifes?

original: To whom in all this presence speaks your Grace?
translation: Which of us are you referring to, your Grace?

original: To thee, that hast nor honesty nor grace.   When have I injured thee? When done thee wrong?—
translation: To you, who have neither honesty nor grace. When have I injured you? When have I done you any wrong?

original: Or thee?—Or thee? Or any of your faction?
translation: Or you? Or you? Or any of you and your supporters?
