original: A plague upon you all! His royal grace,   Whom God preserve better than you would wish,
translation: Curse you all! The king—whom I hope God will preserve better than you'd like—

original: Cannot be quiet scarce a breathing while   But you must trouble him with lewd complaints.
translation: can hardly catch his breath before you start troubling him with your wicked complaints.

original: Brother of Gloucester, you mistake the matter.
translation: My brother-in-law of Gloucester, you're mistaken.

original: The king, on his own royal disposition,   And not provoked by any suitor else,   Aiming belike at your interior hatred   That in your outward actions shows itself   Against my children, brothers, and myself,
translation: It was the king himself, unprovoked by anyone, who noticed your hatred for my children, my brothers, and myself—an inner hatred that expresses itself in your outward actions. He summoned people to ask them about your dislike of us,

original: Makes him to send, that he may learn the ground   Of your ill will, and thereby to remove it.
translation: so that he might discover the reasons behind it and do something about it.

original: I cannot tell. The world is grown so bad   That wrens make prey where eagles dare not perch.
translation: I can't tell what's going on. The world has grown so bad that little wrens now live where eagles dare not perch.

original: Since every jack became a gentleman,   There’s many a gentle person made a jack.
translation: Since every peasant has become a nobleman, there are now many noblemen who've been turned into peasants.

original: Come, come, we know your meaning, brother Gloucester.  You envy my advancement, and my friends'. God grant we never may have need of you.
translation: Come, come, I know what you're referring to, brother-in-law Richard. You're jealous of my friends' rise in rank, and of my own. May God grant that I never need your help.

original: Meantime God grants that we have need of you.   Our brother is imprisoned by your means,
translation: But in the meantime God grants that I need your help. My brother, the Duke of Clarence, is imprisoned because of your influence.

original: Myself disgraced, and the nobility   Held in contempt, while great promotions   Are daily given to ennoble those   That scarce some two days since were worth a noble.
translation: I am disgraced, and the nobility are scorned, while great promotions are handed out daily to those who weren't worth a  noble  two days ago.

original: By Him that raised me to this careful height   From that contented hap which I enjoyed,
translation: I swear by the God who raised me up to this anxious height from the contented life I used to enjoy—

original: I never did incense his majesty   Against the duke of Clarence, but have been   An earnest advocate to plead for him.
translation: I never provoked the king's anger against the Duke of Clarence. I have only ever advocated for him and pled on his behalf.

original: My lord, you do me shameful injury   Falsely to draw me in these vile suspects.
translation: My lord, you do me wrong to implicate me in these wicked suspicions.

original: You may deny that you were not the mean Of my Lord Hastings' late imprisonment.
translation: Then I'm sure you'll also deny that you were the cause of Lord Hastings' recent imprisonment

original: She may, my lord, for—
translation: She may deny it, my lord, for—

original: She may, Lord Rivers. Why, who knows not so?   She may do more, sir, than denying that.
translation: Yes, she may, Lord Rivers. Why, everyone knows that she  may . And she may do more than just denying that, sir.

original: She may help you to many fair preferments   And then deny her aiding hand therein,   And lay those honors on your high desert.
translation: She may help you to many nice promotions and then deny that she aided you, claiming that you won those honors through your own merit.

original: What may she not? She may, ay, marry, may she—
translation: What may she not do? She may, yes,  by God , she may—

original: What, marry, may she?
translation: What, by God, may she do?

original: What, marry, may she? Marry with a king, A bachelor, a handsome stripling too. I wis, your grandam had a worser match.
translation: What, by God, may she do? She may marry a king, a bachelor, a handsome young man. Certainly, your grandmother had a worse match.

original: My Lord of Gloucester, I have too long borne   Your blunt upbraidings and your bitter scoffs.
translation: My Lord of Gloucester, for too long I've suffered your blunt insults and your bitter scorn.

original: By heaven, I will acquaint his majesty   With those gross taunts that oft I have endured.
translation: By heaven, I will tell the king about the vile taunts I've endured.

original: I had rather be a country servant-maid   Than a great queen with this condition,   To be so baited, scorned, and stormèd at.
translation: I would rather be a country servant-maid than a great queen in such a situation—to be so taunted, scorned, and attacked.

original: Small joy have I in being England’s queen.
translation: I've had very little joy in being England's queen.

original: And lessened be that small, God I beseech Him! Thy honor, state, and seat is due to me.
translation: And may her joy be even less than that, God! Elizabeth's honor, rank, and throne all rightly belong to me.

original: [to QUEEN ELIZABETH]     What, threat you me with telling  of the king?   Tell him, and spare not.
translation: [To QUEEN ELIZABETH]   What, are you threatening me that you'll tell the king? Go ahead and tell him, and don't spare any details.

original: Look, what I have said,   I will avouch ’t in presence of the king;   I dare adventure to be sent to th' Tower.
translation: Look, I will repeat what I have said here in the presence of the king. I'll even risk being sent to the Tower for it.

original: 'Tis time to speak. My pains are quite forgot.
translation: It seems that all my efforts on Edward's behalf have been forgotten.

original: Out, devil! I do remember them too well: Thou killed’st my husband Henry in the Tower,  And Edward, my poor son, at Tewkesbury.
translation: You devil! I remember those efforts all too well: you killed my husband Henry in the Tower, and my poor son Edward at Tewkesbury.

original: [to QUEEN ELIZABETH]     Ere you were queen, ay, or your  husband king,   I was a packhorse in his great affairs,
translation: [To QUEEN ELIZABETH]   Yes, before you were queen, or your husband was king, I was a beast of burden for his great affairs.

original: A weeder-out of his proud adversaries,   A liberal rewarder of his friends.
translation: I weeded out his proud enemies and generously rewarded his friends.

original: To royalize his blood, I spent mine own.
translation: I spent my own blood to make his blood royal.

original: Ay, and much better blood than his or thine.
translation: Yes, and in killing my husband and son, you spent much better blood than yours or your brother's.

original: [to QUEEN ELIZABETH]     In all which time, you and your  husband Grey   Were factious for the house of Lancaster.—
translation: [To QUEEN ELIZABETH]   And during all that time, you and your first husband, Sir John Grey, were fighting for the house of Lancaster.

original: A murd'rous villain, and so still thou art.
translation: You were a murderous villain, and you still are.

original: Poor Clarence did forsake his  father Warwick, Ay, and forswore himself—which Jesu pardon!—
translation: Poor Clarence abandoned his father-in-law Warwick, yes, and broke his own oath—may Jesus pardon him!—

original: Which God revenge!
translation: And may God take revenge on him!

original: To fight on Edward’s party for the crown;   And for his meed, poor lord, he is mewed up.
translation: —to fight for Edward's side and help him win the crown. And his reward for that, the poor lord, is to be imprisoned.

original: I would to God my heart were flint, like Edward’s,   Or Edward’s soft and pitiful, like mine.
translation: I wish to God that my heart was made of stone, like Edward's—or that Edward's heart was soft and emotional, like mine.

original: I am too childish-foolish for this world.
translation: I am too childlike and innocent for this world.

original: Hie thee to hell for shame, and leave the  world, Thou cacodemon! There thy kingdom is.
translation: Hurry on to hell then, and leave this world, you evil spirit! Hell is where your true kingdom is.

original: My Lord of Gloucester, in those busy days   Which here you urge to prove us enemies,   We followed then our lord, our sovereign king.
translation: My Lord of Gloucester, in those busy days, we were just following our lord, our rightful king—which you now bring up to prove that we're your enemies.

original: So should we you, if you should be our king.
translation: And we would follow you in just the same way, if you were our king.

original: If I should be? I had rather be a peddler.  Far be it from my heart, the thought thereof.
translation: If I were king? I would rather be a peddler. Far be it for me to ever think of being king.

original: As little joy, my lord, as you suppose   You should enjoy were you this country’s king,
translation: You would have just as little joy as you imagine if you were indeed this country's king.

original: As little joy may you suppose in me   That I enjoy, being the queen thereof.
translation: As the queen, I have had no joy.

original: Ah, little joy enjoys the queen thereof, For I am she, and altogether joyless. I can no longer hold me patient.
translation: Ah, no joy for that "queen" indeed. For I am the queen, and completely unhappy. I can no longer hold myself back.

original: Hear me, you wrangling pirates, that fall out   In sharing that which you have pilled from me!   Which of you trembles not that looks on me?
translation: Hear me, you scheming pirates, who quarrel over what you've plundered from me! Which of you doesn't tremble to look at me?

original: If not, that I am queen, you bow like subjects,   Yet that, by you deposed, you quake like rebels.—
translation: If you're not trembling because I am the queen and you are my bowing subjects, then you're quivering because you're traitors who stole my throne!

original: Foul, wrinkled witch, what mak’st thou in my sight?
translation: You foul, wrinkled witch, what are you doing here?

original: But repetition of what thou hast marred. That will I make before I let thee go.
translation: Just trying to redo what you have undone. I will do that much before I let you go.

original: Wert thou not banishèd on pain of death?
translation: Weren't you banished on pain of death?

original: I was, but I do find more pain in banishment   Than death can yield me here by my abode.   A husband and a son thou ow’st to me;
translation: [To RICHARD]   I was, but banishment is more painful to me than dying here at home. You owe me a husband and a son.

original: The curse my noble father laid on thee   When thou didst crown his warlike brows with paper,   And with thy scorns drew’st rivers from his eyes,   And then, to dry them, gav’st the duke a clout   Steeped in the faultless blood of pretty Rutland—
translation: The  curse  my noble father laid on you when you set a paper crown on his head, and drew rivers of tears from his eyes with your scorn, and then, to dry them, you gave him a handkerchief soaked in innocent Rutland's blood—

original: His curses then, from bitterness of soul   Denounced against thee, are all fall'n upon thee,
translation: the curses he laid on you then, when his bitter soul condemned you, have now come to pass.

original: And God, not we, hath plagued thy bloody deed.
translation: God, not us, is punishing you for your bloody deeds.

original: So just is God to right the innocent.
translation: God is just, and he rewards the innocent.

original: O, ’twas the foulest deed to slay that babe, And the most merciless that e'er was heard of!
translation: Oh, killing that child, Rutland, was the foulest, most merciless deed that was ever heard of!

original: Tyrants themselves wept when it was reported.
translation: Even tyrants wept when they heard about it.

original: No man but prophesied revenge for it.
translation: Everyone knew that there would be revenge for it.

original: Northumberland, then present, wept to see it.
What, were you snarling all before I came,   Ready to catch each other by the throat,   And turn you all your hatred now on me?
translation: What, weren't you all snarling at each other before I came—about to jump at each others' throats like dogs? And now you're turning all your hatred on me?

original: Did York’s dread curse prevail so much with heaven   That Henry’s death, my Lovelly Edward’s death,   Their kingdom’s loss, my woeful banishment,   Could all but answer for that peevish brat?
translation: Did the Duke of York's curse have so much power that Henry's death; my lovely Edward's death; the loss of their kingdom; and my sad banishment were all required to avenge the death of that peevish brat Rutland?

original: Can curses pierce the clouds and enter heaven?   Why then, give way, dull clouds, to my quick curses!
translation: Can curses pierce the clouds and enter heaven? Well then, open up, you dark clouds—and hear  my  strong curses!

original: Though not by war, by surfeit die your king,   As ours by murder to make him a king.
translation: Though your Yorkist king didn't die in battle, may he die from his gluttony, just as our Lancastrian king—my husband—was murdered to give your king his throne.

original: Have done thy charm, thou hateful, withered hag.
translation: Enough of your witchcraft, you hateful, withered hag.

original: And leave out thee? Stay, dog, for thou shalt hear me.
translation: And leave you out, Richard? Stay, dog, for you must hear me out.

original: If heaven have any grievous plague in store   Exceeding those that I can wish upon thee,
translation: If heaven has any horrible plagues worse than anything I could imagine,

original: O, let them keep it till thy sins be ripe   And then hurl down their indignation   On thee, the troubler of the poor world’s peace.
translation: oh, let it keep them until you've committed the maximum amount of sin. And then let heaven hurl down its anger on you all at once, you disturber of the poor world's peace!

original: The worm of conscience still begnaw thy soul.   Thy friends suspect for traitors while thou liv’st,   And take deep traitors for thy dearest friends.
translation: May the worm of guilt gnaw away at your soul constantly. May you suspect your friends of being traitors, and consider the worst traitors as your dearest friends.

original: No sleep close up that deadly eye of thine,   Unless it be while some tormenting dream   Affrights thee with a hell of ugly devils.
translation: May you never close your wicked eyes and be able to sleep—unless it's to dream some terrifying nightmare of a hell filled with ugly devils.

original: Thou elvish-marked, abortive, rooting hog,   Thou was sealed in they nativity   The slave of nature and the son of hell,
translation: You cursed, prematurely born  hog , wallowing in the mud; you who were born a deformed child of hell;

original: Thou slander of they heavy mother's womb,   Thou loathed issue of they father's loins,   Thou rag of honor, thou detested—
translation: you insult to your sad mother's womb; you hated product of your father's loins; you filthy scrap of dishonor; you disgusting—

original: Margaret.
translation: Margaret.

original: Richard!
translation: Richard!

original: Ha?
translation: Yes?

original: I call thee not.
translation: I didn't call you.

original: I cry thee mercy, then, for I did think That thou hadst called me all these bitter names.
translation: I beg your pardon, then—for I thought you had called me all those bitter names.

original: Why, so I did, but looked for no reply. O, let me make the period to my curse!
translation: Why, so I did. But I didn't want any reply from you. Oh, let me finish my curse!

original: 'Tis done by me, and ends in “Margaret.”
translation: I've already finished it. It ends in "Margaret."

original: Thus have you breathed your curse against yourself.
translation: See, you've only cursed yourself.

original: Poor painted queen, vain flourish of my fortune,   Why strew’st thou sugar on that bottled spider,   Whose deadly web ensnareth thee about?
translation: You poor imitation of a queen, you meaningless decoration on my throne: why do you give sugar to this swollen spider when he's already ensnared you in his deadly web?

original: Fool, fool, thou whet’st a knife to kill thyself.   The day will come that thou shalt wish for me   To help thee curse that poisonous bunch-backed toad.
translation: Fool, fool, you're sharpening the knife that will kill you. The day will come when you'll wish that I could help you curse this poisonous, hunchbacked toad.

original: False-boding woman, end thy frantic curse, Lest to thy harm thou move our patience.
translation: You false prophet, stop your frantic curses before we lose our patience and cause you harm.

original: Foul shame upon you, you have all moved mine.
translation: Foul shame on you—I've already lost my patience with you all.

original: Were you well served, you would be taught your duty.
translation: If you got what you deserved, you would be taught to show some respect.

original: To serve me well, you all should do me duty:  Teach me to be your queen, and you my subjects. O, serve me well, and teach yourselves that duty!
translation: If I got what I deserved, you would all be showing me respect—I would be your queen, and you would be my subjects. Oh, give me what I deserve, then—and teach yourselves some respect!

original: Dispute not with her; she is lunatic.
translation: Don't try to argue with her. She's a lunatic.

original: Peace, Master Marquess, you are malapert.   Your fire-new stamp of honor is scarce current.
translation: Quiet, Master Marquess, you're being impudent. Your noble title is so newly-minted that its not even legal yet.

original: O, that your young nobility could judge   What ’twere to lose it and be miserable!
translation: Oh, that your recent nobility could understand what it means to be lost and miserable!

original: They that stand high have many blasts to shake them,   And if they fall, they dash themselves to pieces.
translation: Those who are very high up must be shaken by many blasts of wind. And when they fall, they dash themselves to pieces.

original: Good counsel, marry. —Learn it, learn it, marquess.
translation: Good advice, by God.

original: It touches you, my lord, as much as me.
translation: It applies to you as much as to me, my lord.

original: Ay, and much more; but I was born so high. Our aerie buildeth in the cedar’s top, And dallies with the wind and scorns the sun.
translation: Yes, and even more so. But I was born at that high social rank. My family lives like eagles at the top of the tallest cedar tree, playing in the wind and looking fearlessly at the sun.

original: And turns the sun to shade. Alas, alas,   Witness my son, now in the shade of death,   Whose bright out-shining beams thy cloudy wrath   Hath in eternal darkness folded up.
translation: And turning the sun into shadow. Alas, alas, like  my  son, who is now in the shadow of death. Your cloudy anger has swallowed up his bright-shining beams, and now he dwells in eternal darkness.

original: Your aerie buildeth in our aerie’s nest.
translation: You're building your nest in  our  nest.

original: O God, that seest it, do not suffer it!   As it was won with blood, lost be it so.
translation: Oh God, witness this injustice and don't let it go unpunished! As the Yorks won the crown through bloodshed, let them also lose it in the same way.

original: Peace, peace, for shame, if not for charity.
translation: Quiet, quiet—have some shame at least, if you can't be kind.

original: Urge neither charity nor shame to me.
translation: Don't preach about kindness or shame to me.

original: Have done, have done.
translation: Enough, enough.

original: O princely Buckingham, I’ll kiss thy hand   In sign of league and amity with thee.
translation: Oh, princely Buckingham, I'll kiss your hand as a sign of my support and friendship.

original: Now fair befall thee and thy noble house!
translation: May only good things come to you and your noble family!

original: Thy garments are not spotted with our blood,   Nor thou within the compass of my curse.
translation: Your clothes are not stained with my family's blood, and so you don't fall under my curse.

original: Nor no one here, for curses never pass The lips of those that breathe them in the air.
translation: No one here is under your curse either. For curses are just empty words, lost to the air as soon as they're spoken.

original: I will not think but they ascend the sky,   And there awake God’s gentle-sleeping peace.
translation: No, I believe that they rise up to heaven and awaken God from his gentle, peaceful sleep.

original: What doth she say, my lord of Buckingham?
translation: What does she say, my lord of Buckingham?

original: Nothing that I respect, my gracious lord.
translation: Nothing that I respect, my gracious lord.

original: What, dost thou scorn me for my gentle counsel,   And soothe the devil that I warn thee from?
translation: What, will you scorn me for my friendly advice, and comfort the devil that I'm warning you about?

original: O, but remember this another day,   When he shall split thy very heart with sorrow,   And say poor Margaret was a prophetess.—
translation: Oh, you will remember this, when one day he splits your heart in two with sorrow. Then you'll say that poor Margaret was a prophet.

original: Live each of you the subjects to his hate,   And he to yours, and all of you to God’s.
translation: May Richard come to hate everyone here, and may you come to hate him, and may God hate you all!

original: My hair doth stand an end to hear her curses.
translation: My hair stands on end when I hear her curses.

original: And so doth mine. I muse why she’s at liberty.
translation: So does mine. I wonder why she's not in prison.

original: I cannot blame her. By God’s holy mother,  She hath had too much wrong, and I repent My part thereof that I have done to her.
translation: I cannot blame her. By God's holy mother, she has suffered too much. And I'm sorry for the part I've played in her troubles.

original: I never did her any, to my knowledge.
translation: I never did her any wrong, to my knowledge.

original: Yet you have all the vantage of her wrong.   I was too hot to do somebody good   That is too cold in thinking of it now.
translation: But you've reaped all the benefits from her suffering. I was too eager in helping Edward to the throne, and now he seems to have forgotten my deeds.

original: Marry, as for Clarence, he is well repaid;   He is franked up to fatting for his pains.
translation: Well, as for Clarence, he is being well repaid for his pains—shut in a pigsty to be fattened up and slaughtered.

original: God pardon them that are the cause thereof.
translation: May God pardon those responsible.

original: A virtuous and a Christian-like conclusion  To pray for them that have done scathe to us.
translation: That's very virtuous and Christian of you to pray for those who have harmed us.

original: So do I ever    being well-advised, For had I cursed now, I had cursed myself.
translation: I always do.

original: Madam, his majesty doth call for you,— And for your Grace, —and yours, my gracious lords.
translation: Madam, his Majesty asks for you—and for you, Duke of Gloucester—and for you, my gracious lords.

original: Catesby, I come. —Lords, will you go with me?
translation: I will go now, Catesby. Lords, will you go with me?

original: We wait upon your Grace.
translation: We will attend you, your Grace.

original: I do the wrong, and first begin to brawl.   The secret mischiefs that I set abroach   I lay unto the grievous charge of others.
translation: I commit the crimes, and I start the quarrels. I do wicked things in secret, and then lay the blame on others.

original: Clarence, whom I indeed have cast in darkness,   I do beweep to many simple gulls,   Namely, to Derby, Hastings, Buckingham,   And tell them ’tis the queen and her allies   That stir the king against the duke my brother.
translation: I weep about Clarence, whom I've had thrown into prison, in front of these gullible fools—namely, Derby, Hastings, and Buckingham. And I tell them that it's the queen and her allies who have incited the King against Clarence.

original: Now they believe it and withal whet me   To be revenged on Rivers, Dorset, Grey;
translation: Now they believe it, and they urge me to take revenge on Rivers, Dorset, and Grey...

original: But then I sigh and, with a piece of scripture,   Tell them that God bids us do good for evil;
translation: but then I sigh, and quote a piece of scripture to them, saying that God tells us to repay evil with good.

original: And thus I clothe my naked villainy   With odd old ends stolen out of Holy Writ,   And seem a saint when most I play the devil.
translation: And so I clothe my naked villainy with odds and ends stolen from the Holy Bible, and I seem like a saint exactly when I act most like the devil.

original: But, soft! here come my executioners.— How now, my hardy, stout, resolvèd mates? Are you now going to dispatch this thing?
translation: But quiet! Here come the executioners I've hired.

original: We are, my lord, and come to have the warrant That we may be admitted where he is.
translation: We are, my lord. We've come to get the warrant so we can be admitted into Clarence's cell.

original: Well thought upon. I have it here about me.
translation: Good thinking. I have it on me here.

original: [He gives a paper]   When you have done, repair to Crosby Place.   But, sirs, be sudden in the execution,   Withal obdurate;
translation: [He gives them a paper]   When you're done, go to Crosby Place. But, sirs, be quick in your execution.

original: do not hear him plead,   For Clarence is well-spoken and perhaps   May move your hearts to pity if you mark him.
translation: And don't let him plead for his life, for Clarence is well-spoken, and he may convince you to spare him if you listen too closely to his words.

original: Tut, tut, my lord, we will not stand to prate. Talkers are no good doers. Be assured  We go to use our hands and not our tongues.
translation: Tut, tut, my lord, we won't stand around and chat. Talkers are not good doers. Rest assured that we go to use our hands, not our tongues.

original: Your eyes drop millstones, when fools' eyes drop tears. I like you lads. About your business straight. Go, go, dispatch.
translation: You remain stone-faced when fools' eyes drop tears. I like you lads. Go about your business right away. Go, go, get to it.

original: We will, my noble lord.
translation: We will, my noble lord.

original: Why looks your grace so heavily today?
translation: Why do you look so sad today, your Grace?

original: O, I have passed a miserable night,   So full of ugly dreams, of ugly sights,
translation: Oh, I had a miserable night last night. It was so full of ugly dreams and terrifying visions

original: That, as I am a Christian faithful man,   I would not spend another such a night
translation: that I swear I wouldn't choose to spend another night like it—

original: Though ’twere to buy a world of happy days,   So full of dismal terror was the time.
translation: even if it bought me a lifetime of happy days.

original: What was your dream, my lord? I pray you tell me.
translation: What was your dream, my lord? Please tell me.

original: Methoughts that I had broken from the Tower   And was embarked to cross to Burgundy,   And in my company my brother Gloucester,
translation: I dreamed that I had broken out of the Tower and was on a ship to France, and my brother Richard was with me.

original: Who from my cabin tempted me to walk   Upon the hatches.
translation: He persuaded me to leave my cabin and walk on the boat's deck with him.

original: Thence we looked toward England   And cited up a thousand fearful times,   During the wars of York and Lancaster   That had befall'n us.
translation: From there we looked toward England and reminisced about our many frightening experiences during the wars between the Yorks and the Lancasters.

original: O Lord, methought what pain it was to drown,   What dreadful noise of waters in my ears,   What sights of ugly death within my eyes.
translation: As we paced along the boards of the deck, Richard seemed to stumble, and as I tried to grab him he knocked me overboard into the rolling waves. Oh Lord, how painful it was to drown—with the dreadful noise of water in my ears and the ugly visions of death in my eyes.

original: Methoughts I saw a thousand fearful wracks,   Ten thousand men that fishes gnawed upon,   Wedges of gold, great anchors, heaps of pearl,   Inestimable stones, unvalued jewels,   All scattered in the bottom of the sea.
translation: I seemed to see a thousand shipwrecks; ten thousand men whose bodies had been gnawed by fish; bars of gold; huge anchors; heaps of pearls; and vast amounts of priceless jewels, all scattered on the bottom of the sea.

original: Some lay in dead men's skulls, and in the holes   Where eyes did once inhabit, there were crept—   as 'twere in scorn of eyes—   reflecting gems,
translation: Some of the jewels lay inside of dead men's skulls. And they had crept into their empty eye sockets— so that they looked like false eyes.

original: That wooed the slimy bottom of the deep   And mocked the dead bones that lay scattered by.
translation: The gems reflected the slimy bottom of the ocean floor, and mocked the dead bones that lay scattered around.

original: Had you such leisure in the time of death  To gaze upon the secrets of the deep?
translation: Did you really have so much time to examine the secrets of the deep while you were dying?

original: Methought I had, and often did I strive   To yield the ghost, but still the envious flood   Stopped in my soul
translation: It seemed like I did. And I often tried to die, but the jealous waves kept my soul bottled up inside of me,

original: and would not let it forth   To find the empty, vast, and wand'ring air,
translation: and wouldn't let it go free to find the empty, wandering air.

original: But smothered it within my panting bulk,   Who almost burst to belch it in the sea.
translation: The water kept my soul smothered inside my panting body until I almost burst open.

original: Awaked you not in this sore agony?
translation: Didn't you wake up during all this agony?

original: No, no, my dream was lengthened after life.   O, then began the tempest to my soul.
translation: No, no, my dream continued after I died. Oh, then the real storm of my soul began!

original: I passed, methought, the melancholy flood,   With that sour ferryman which poets write of,   Unto the kingdom of perpetual night.
translation: I passed over the river of death with the help of Charon, the ferryman of the underworld, and I entered the kingdom of perpetual night.

original: The first that there did greet my stranger-soul   Was my great father-in-law, renownèd Warwick,   Who cried aloud, “What scourge for perjury   Can this dark monarchy afford false Clarence?”
translation: The first soul to greet me there was my great father-in-law, the Earl of Warwick, who cried aloud, "What terrible punishment for oath-breaking can this dark kingdom inflict on that false Clarence?"

original: And so he vanished. Then came wand'ring by   A shadow like an angel, with bright hair   Dabbled in blood,
translation: And then he vanished. Next a  shadow  like an angel came wandering by, with its bright hair spattered with blood,

original: and he shrieked out aloud   "Clarence is come—false, fleeting, perjured Clarence,   That stabbed me in the field by Tewkesbury.   Seize on him, furies. Take him unto torment."
translation: and it shrieked aloud, "Clarence is here—false, fickle, lying Clarence, who stabbed me in the field at Tewkesbury.  Seize him, avenging devils. Take him and torture him."

original: With that, methoughts, a legion of foul fiends   Environed me and howled in mine ears   Such hideous cries that with the very noise   I trembling waked,
translation: With that it seemed like a legion of foul demons surrounded me and howled in my ears, and their cries were so loud and horrible that I woke up trembling.

original: and for a season after   Could not believe but that I was in hell,   Such terrible impression made my dream.
translation: And for a long time afterward I still believed that I was in hell—that was how terrible an impression this dream made on me.

original: No marvel, lord, though it affrighted you.  I am afraid, methinks, to hear you tell it.
translation: It's no surprise that it frightened you, my lord. I'm afraid just hearing you tell it.

original: Ah keeper, keeper, I have done those things,   That now give evidence against my soul,   For Edward’s sake, and see how he requites me.—
translation: [To BRAKENBURY]   Ah, jailer, jailer, I did all those things that the ghosts accused me of—and my crimes are now giving evidence against my soul. I did them all for King Edward's sake, and now see how he thanks me.

original: I will, my lord. God give your Grace good rest.
translation: I will, my lord. May God give you good rest.

original: Sorrow breaks seasons and reposing hours,   Makes the night morning, and the noontide night.
translation: Sorrow breaks natural rhythms and interrupts sleep, making night into morning and noon into night.

original: Princes have but their titles for their glories,   An outward honor for an inward toil,
translation: The only glory princes really have are their titles, which are outward honors for their inner troubles.

original: And, for unfelt imaginations,   They often feel a world of restless cares,   So that betwixt their titles and low name   There's nothing differs but the outward fame.
translation: They experience a world of worry about imaginary things, so that the only real difference between princes and peasants is the princes' outward fame.

original: Ho, who’s here?
translation: Hey, who's there?

original: What wouldst thou, fellow? And how cam’st thou hither?
translation: What do you want, man? And how did you get here?

original: I would speak with Clarence, and I came hither on my  legs.
translation: I want to speak with Clarence, and I came here on my legs.

original: What, so brief?
translation: What, do you dare to be so blunt with me?

original: 'Tis better, sir, to be brief than tedious.—Let him see our commission, and talk no more.
translation: It's better to be blunt than to be long-winded, sir.

original: I am in this commanded to deliver   The noble duke of Clarence to your hands.
translation: This warrant commands me to deliver the noble Duke of Clarence into your hands.

original: I will not reason what is meant hereby   Because I will be guiltless from the meaning.
translation: I won't ask what this means, for I'd rather not know about something that might make me guilty later.

original: There lies the duke asleep, and there the keys.
translation: There's the duke, sleeping, and here are the keys.

original: [He hands them the keys]   I’ll to the king and signify to him   That thus I have resigned my charge to you.
translation: [He hands them the keys]   I'll go to the king and tell him that I've handed over my prisoner to you.

original: You may, sir. 'Tis a point of wisdom. Fare you well.
translation: You may do that, sir. It's a wise idea. Farewell.

original: What, shall I stab him as he sleeps?
translation: Well, should I stab him as he sleeps?

original: No. He’ll say ’twas done cowardly, when he wakes.
translation: No. When he wakes up he'll say that we killed him like cowards.

original: Why, he shall never wake until the great Judgment Day.
translation: Why, he won't be waking up until Judgment Day.

original: Why, then he’ll say we stabbed him sleeping.
translation: Well, then on Judgment Day he'll say that we stabbed him in his sleep.

original: The urging of that word “judgment” hath bred a kind of  remorse in me.
translation: That word "judgment" has made me feel a little bit guilty.

original: What, art thou afraid?
translation: What, are you afraid?

original: Not to kill him, having a warrant, but to be damned  for killing him, from the which no warrant can defend  me.
translation: Not afraid to kill him, since we have a warrant for it. But I'm afraid to be damned for killing him. No warrant can protect me from that.

original: I thought thou hadst been resolute.
translation: I thought you were sure about this.

original: So I am—to let him live.
translation: I am sure—that we should let him live.

original: I’ll back to the duke of Gloucester and tell him so.
translation: I'll go back to the Duke of Gloucester and tell him so.

original: Nay, I prithee stay a little. I hope this passionate  humor of mine will change. It was wont to hold me but  while one tells twenty.
translation: No, please, stay a minute. I'm hoping that my compassionate mood will pass. It usually only lasts about twenty seconds.

original: How dost thou feel thyself now?
translation: How are you feeling now?

original: Faith, some certain dregs of conscience are yet within  me.
translation: Honestly, my conscience is still troubling me a bit.

original: Remember our reward when the deed’s done.
translation: Remember the reward we'll get when the deed is done.

original: Zounds, he dies! I had forgot the reward.
Where’s thy conscience now?
translation: Where's your conscience now?

original: O, in the duke of Gloucester’s purse.
translation: Oh, in the Duke of Gloucester's purse.

original: So when he opens his purse to give us our reward, thy  conscience flies out.
translation: So when he opens his purse to give us our reward, your conscience will fly out.

original: 'Tis no matter. Let it go. There’s few or none will  entertain it.
translation: That won't matter. Let it fly off. No one will take it in.

original: What if it come to thee again?
translation: What if it comes back to you?

original: I’ll not meddle with it. It makes a man a coward: a man cannot steal but it accuseth him; a man cannot swear  but it checks him; a man cannot lie with his neighbor’s  wife but it detects him.
translation: I won't bother with it. A conscience makes a man a coward. A man can't steal without it accusing him; he can't swear without it restraining him; he can't sleep with his neighbor's wife without it exposing him.

original: 'Tis a blushing, shamefaced  spirit that mutinies in a man’s bosom. It fills a man  full of obstacles.
translation: It's a blushing, shamefaced spirit that betrays a man's heart. It fills him with obstacles.

original: It made me once restore a purse of  gold that by chance I found. It beggars any man that  keeps it.
translation: It once made me return a purse full of gold that I found. A conscience can turn any man into a beggar.

original: It is turned out of towns and cities for a  dangerous thing, and every man that means to live well  endeavors to trust to himself and live without it.
translation: It's been thrown out of towns and cities like a dangerous enemy. Any man who wants to live well should trust only himself, and live without his conscience.

original: Zounds, ’tis even now at my elbow, persuading me not to kill the duke.
translation: My God, now it's even at my elbow, persuading me not to kill the duke.

original: Take the devil in thy mind, and believe him not. He  would insinuate with thee but to make thee sigh.
translation: Ignore your conscience, and think about the devil instead. He might flatter you, but he won't make you sad.

original: I am strong-framed. He cannot prevail with me.
translation: I'm strong-willed. My conscience won't overcome me.

original: Spoke like a tall man that respects thy reputation.  Come, shall we fall to work?
translation: Spoken like a brave man who values his reputation. Come, shall we get to work?

original: Take him on the costard with the hilts of thy sword,  and then throw him into the malmsey butt in the next  room.
translation: Hit him on the head with the hilt of your sword, and then throw him in the wine barrel in the next room.

original: O excellent device— and make a sop of him.
translation: Oh, what an excellent plan—we'll make him a sponge for the wine.

original: Soft, he wakes.
translation: Quiet, he's waking up.

original: Strike!
translation: Strike!

original: No, we’ll reason with him.
translation: No, we'll talk to him first.

original: Where art thou, keeper? Give me a cup of wine.
translation: Where are you, jailer? Give me a cup of wine.

original: You shall have wine enough, my lord, anon.
translation: You'll have plenty of wine soon enough, my lord.

original: In God’s name, what art thou?
translation: In God's name, who are you?

original: A man, as you are.
translation: A man, like you are.

original: But not, as I am, royal.
translation: But not a royal man, as I am.

original: Nor you, as we are, loyal.
translation: And you're not a loyal man, as we are.

original: Thy voice is thunder, but thy looks are humble.
translation: You speak with authority, but you look like a common man.

original: My voice is now the king’s, my looks mine own.
translation: I'm speaking for the king—my looks are my own.

original: How darkly and how deadly dost thou speak!  Your eyes do menace me. Why look you pale? Who sent you hither? Wherefore do you come?
translation: Your words are so dark and threatening! Your eyes menace me. Why do you look so pale? Who sent you here? Why have you come?

original: To, to, to—
translation: To, to, to—

original: To murder me?
translation: To murder me?

original: Ay, ay.
translation: Yes, yes.

original: You scarcely have the hearts to tell me so, And therefore cannot have the hearts to do it.  Wherein, my friends, have I offended you?
translation: You hardly have the heart to tell me, so you must not have the heart to do it. Besides, my friends, have I offended you?

original: Offended us you have not, but the king.
translation: You haven't offended us—you offended the king.

original: I shall be reconciled to him again.
translation: He and I will be reconciled again.

original: Never, my lord. Therefore prepare to die.
translation: Never, my lord. So prepare to die.

original: Are you drawn forth among a world of men   To slay the innocent? What is my offense?
translation: Have you been chosen specially, just to kill the innocent? What is my offense?

original: Where is the evidence that doth accuse me?   What lawful quest have given their verdict up   Unto the frowning judge?
translation: Where is the evidence against me? What jury has sentenced me in front of a frowning judge?

original: Or who pronounced   The bitter sentence of poor Clarence' death   Before I be convict by course of law?
translation: Or who has pronounced this death sentence on me before I could be convicted by a court of law?

original: To threaten me with death is most unlawful.
translation: To threaten me with death is wrong.

original: I charge you, as you hope to have redemption,   By Christ’s dear blood shed for our grievous sins,   That you depart, and lay no hands on me.
translation: If you hope to be saved by Christ's dear blood—which was shed for our sins—then I tell you to leave now without touching me.

original: What we will do, we do upon command.
translation: What we do, we do because we were commanded to.

original: And he that hath commanded is our king.
translation: And the one who has commanded us is our king.

original: Erroneous vassals, the great King of kings   Hath in the tables of His law commanded   That thou shalt do no murder.
translation: You misguided subjects, the great King of  Kings —God—has said in his Ten Commandments that "you shall not murder."

original: Will thou then   Spurn at His edict and fulfill a man’s?
translation: Will you then disobey God's commandment just to obey a man's?

original: Take heed, for He holds vengeance in His hand   To hurl upon their heads that break His law.
translation: Beware, for God holds vengeance in his hand, waiting to smite those who break his laws.

original: And that same vengeance doth He hurl on thee   For false forswearing and for murder too.
translation: And he will smite you with that same vengeance for breaking your oaths, and for murder too.

original: Thou didst receive the sacrament to fight   In quarrel of the house of Lancaster.
translation: You swore a holy oath to fight for the house of Lancaster.

original: And, like a traitor to the name of God, Didst break that vow, and with thy treacherous blade  Unrippedst the bowels of thy sovereign’s son.
translation: And—like a traitor to the name of God—you broke that vow, and with your treacherous sword you ripped open the chest of your king, Henry's, son Edward.

original: Whom thou wert sworn to cherish and defend.
translation: Whom you were sworn to cherish and defend.

original: How canst thou urge God’s dreadful law to us When thou hast broke it in such dear degree?
translation: How can you preach about God's laws to us when you have broken them to such an extreme degree?

original: Alas! For whose sake did I that ill deed?   For Edward, for my brother, for his sake.
translation: Alas! But for whose sake did I do that terrible deed? For my brother Edward, for his sake.

original: He sends you not to murder me for this,   For in that sin he is as deep as I.
translation: He can't be sending you to murder me for the prince's death—because in that, he is just as guilty as I am.

original: If God will be avengèd for this deed,   O, know you yet He doth it publicly!
translation: If God intends to punish me for this deed, oh, you know that he will do it publicly!

original: Take not the quarrel from His powerful arm;   He needs no indirect or lawless course   To cut off those that have offended Him.
translation: God has no need for indirect or illegal methods of killing those who have offended him.

original: Who made thee then a bloody minister When gallant-springing, brave Plantagenet,  That princely novice, was struck dead by thee?
translation: Who provoked you to kill that brave and lively youth, Prince Edward?

original: My brother’s love, the devil, and my rage.
translation: My brother's love; the devil; and my rage.

original: Thy brother’s love, our duty, and thy faults Provoke us hither now to slaughter thee.
translation: Well, your brother's love; our duty; and your own crimes now provoke us to kill you.

original: If you do love my brother, hate not me.   I am his brother, and I love him well.
translation: If you really love my brother Richard, then don't hate me. I am his brother, and I love him very much.

original: If you are hired for meed, go back again,   And I will send you to my brother Gloucester,   Who shall reward you better for my life   Than Edward will for tidings of my death.
translation: If you're hired to do this for money, then go back again and talk to my brother the Duke of Gloucester. He will reward you better for sparing my life than King Edward will for news of my death.

original: You are deceived. Your brother Gloucester hates you.
translation: You are deceived. Your brother Richard hates you.

original: O, no, he loves me, and he holds me dear. Go you to him from me.
translation: Oh, no, he loves me and cherishes me. Go to him from me.

original: Ay, so we will.
translation: Yes, so we will.

original: Tell him, when that our princely father York   Blessed his three sons with his victorious arm,   And charged us from his soul to love each other,   He little thought of this divided friendship.
translation: Tell him that when our princely father, the Duke of York, blessed his three sons and commanded us to love each other, he never imagined that our friendship would end up divided like this.

original: Bid Gloucester think of this, and he will weep.
translation: Remind Richard of this, and he will weep.

original: Ay, millstones, as he lessoned us to weep.
translation: Yes, he'll weep stones, as he taught us to do.

original: O, do not slander him, for he is kind.
translation: Oh, do not slander him, for he is a kind man.

original: As snow in harvest. Come, you deceive yourself. 'Tis he that sends us to destroy you here.
translation: As kind as snow during harvest time. Come, you're deceiving yourself. It's Richard who sent us here to kill you.

original: It cannot be, for he bewept my fortune, And hugged me in his arms, and swore with sobs That he would labor my delivery.
translation: It cannot be. He wept over my imprisonment. And he hugged me in his arms, and swore while sobbing that he would work to have me released.

original: Why, so he doth, when he delivers you From this earth’s thralldom to the joys of heaven.
translation: Why, that's what he did—and now you'll be released from the prison of earth, to be free among the joys of heaven.

original: Make peace with God, for you must die, my lord.
translation: Make your peace with God, for you must die, my lord.

original: Have you that holy feeling in your souls   To counsel me to make my peace with God,   And art you yet to your own souls so blind   That thou will war with God by murd'ring me?
translation: You have enough holy feeling in your souls to advise me to make my peace with God. But you're still willing to disobey God by murdering me?

original: O sirs, consider: they that set you on   To do this deed will hate you for the deed.
translation: Oh, sirs, consider this: those who sent you to do this deed will hate you for doing it.

original: What shall we do?
translation: What should we do?

original: Relent, and save your souls.
translation: Give up this attempt, and save your souls.

original: Which of you—if you were a prince's son   Being pent from liberty, as I am now—   If two such murderers as yourselves came to you,   Would you not entreat for life?
translation: Which of you, if you were in my position—a prince's son in prison, and two murderers like yourselves came to you—wouldn't beg for your life?

original: Ay, you would beg,   Were you in my distress.
translation: Yes, you would beg, if you were in my situation.

original: Relent? No. 'Tis cowardly and womanish.
Not to relent is beastly, savage, devilish.
translation: But to  not  give up, and murder me, is beastly, savage, and devilish.

original: Look behind you, my lord.
translation: Look behind you, my lord.

original: Take that, and that. If all this will not do, I’ll drown you in the malmsey butt within.
translation: Take that, and that.  If all this won't do the job, then I'll drown you in that wine barrel.

original: A bloody deed, and desperately dispatched.  How fain, like Pilate, would I wash my hands Of this most grievous murder.
How now? What mean’st thou, that thou help’st me not? By heavens, the duke shall know how slack you have  been.
translation: What's going on? What's wrong with you, that you didn't help me? By God, the duke will hear about how you've neglected your duty.

original: I would he knew that I had saved his brother.  Take thou the fee, and tell him what I say, For I repent me that the duke is slain.
translation: I wish he could hear that I had saved his brother. You take the reward, and tell him what I've said. I'm sorry that the Duke of Clarence has been killed.

original: So do not I. Go, coward as thou art.   Well, I’ll go hide the body in some hole   Till that the duke give order for his burial.
translation: I'm not sorry. Go, coward that you are. Well, I'll go hide the body in some hole until the Duke of Gloucester gives orders for its burial.

original: And when I have my meed, I will away,   For this will out, and then I must not stay.
translation: And when I have my reward, I'll flee. For this murder will be found out, and I must not be around then.

original: Why, so. Now have I done a good day’s work.   You peers, continue this united league.
translation: Well, now I've done a good day's work. You must all maintain this unity and friendship.

original: I every day expect an embassage   From my Redeemer to redeem me hence,   And more in peace my soul shall part to heaven   Since I have made my friends at peace on earth   Rivers and Hastings, take each other’s hand.
translation: Every day I expect a messenger of God to bear me away from here, and I can leave for heaven in peace now that my friends have made their peace on earth. Rivers and Hastings, take each other's hand.

original: Dissemble not your hatred. Swear your love.
translation: Don't just hide your hatred under a facade of friendship. Swear your love for each other.

original: By heaven, my soul is purged  from grudging hate,  And with my hand I seal my true heart’s love.
translation: By heaven, my soul is now cleansed of all grudges and hatred. With this handshake I swear that this love is true.

original: So thrive I as I truly swear the like.
translation: So may I prosper, as I swear the same thing.

original: Take heed you dally not before your king,
translation: Make sure that you don't mock your king by lying in front of him.

original: Lest He that is the supreme King of kings   Confound your hidden falsehood, and award   Either of you to be the other’s end.
translation: Otherwise God, the supreme King of  Kings , will uncover your hidden lies and cause you to be the death of each other.

original: So prosper I as I swear perfect love.
translation: I swear perfect love for Rivers, or may I never prosper.

original: And I as I love Hastings with my heart.
translation: And I love Hastings with all my heart.

original: [to QUEEN ELIZABETH]   Madam, yourself is not exempt in this,—
translation: [To QUEEN ELIZABETH]   Madam, you're not exempt from this.

original: There, Hastings, I will never more remember Our former hatred, so thrive I and mine.
translation: Here's my hand, Hastings. I will forget all our past hatred for each other, and may we both prosper in the future.

original: Dorset, embrace him.—Hastings, love Lord Marquess.
translation: Now Dorset, hug Hastings. Hastings, befriend Lord Marquess of Dorset.

original: This interchange of love, I here protest, Upon my part shall be inviolable.
translation: I swear that I will never go back on this exchange of love and friendship.

original: And so swear I.
translation: And I swear it too.

original: Now, princely Buckingham, seal thou this league  With thy embracements to my wife’s allies And make me happy in your unity.
translation: Now, princely Buckingham, seal this friendship by embracing my wife's allies, and through your unity make me happy.

original: [to QUEEN ELIZABETH]   Whenever Buckingham doth turn his hate   Upon your Grace, but with all duteous love   Doth cherish you and yours, God punish me   With hate in those where I expect most love.
translation: [To QUEEN ELIZABETH]   If I should ever come to hate your Grace, and fail to love and cherish you and your relatives, may God punish me by making me find hatred where I expect love.

original: When I have most need to employ a friend,   And most assurèd that he is a friend,   Deep, hollow, treacherous, and full of guile   Be he unto me:
translation: When I most need a friend and am sure that my friends are trustworthy, may they turn false, treacherous, and full of deceit.

original: this do I beg of God   When I am cold in love to you or yours.
translation: I beg that God will do this if I ever lose my love for you and your allies.

original: A pleasing cordial, princely Buckingham,   Is this thy vow unto my sickly heart.
translation: Noble Buckingham, your vow of friendship is like medicine for my sickly heart.

original: There wanteth now our brother Gloucester here   To make the blessèd period of this peace.
translation: Now all we need is my brother Richard to bring the blessed conclusion to this time of peace.

original: And in good time, Here comes Sir Richard Ratcliffe and the duke.
translation: And just in time, here comes Richard with Sir Richard Ratcliffe.

original: Good morrow to my sovereign king and queen, And, princely peers, a happy time of day.
translation: Good morning to my sovereign king and queen. And I'm happy to see you too, my princely peers.

original: Happy indeed, as we have spent the day.
translation: Happy indeed—that's the way we've spent the day.

original: Brother, we have done deeds of charity,   Made peace of enmity, fair love of hate,   Between these swelling, wrong-incensèd peers.
translation: Brother, we have done deeds of love, turning enmity to peace and hatred to love between these misguidedly angry nobles.

original: A blessèd labor, my most sovereign lord.
translation: A blessed labor, my sovereign lord.

original: Amongst this princely heap, if any here   By false intelligence, or wrong surmise   Hold me a foe,   If I unwittingly, or in my rage,   Have aught committed that is hardly borne   By any in this presence,
translation: If any among this princely group considers me an enemy—whether from lies they've heard about me, or because by accident or in anger I've done something to give offense—

original: I desire   To reconcile me to his friendly peace.
translation: I want us to be reconciled and become peaceful friends.

original: 'Tis death to me to be at enmity;   I hate it, and desire all good men’s love.
translation: To be enemies with anyone is like death to me; I hate it, and only desire the love of all good men.

original: A holy day shall this be kept hereafter.   I would to God all strifes were well compounded.
translation: This will be remembered as a holy day. I wish to God that all troubles could end this well.

original: My sovereign lord, I do beseech your Highness   To take our brother Clarence to your grace.
translation: But I must also ask your Highness to pardon your brother Clarence.

original: Why, madam, have I offered love for this, To be so flouted in this royal presence?  Who knows not that the gentle duke is dead?
translation: Why, madam, have I offered you my love only to be mocked in front of the king? Who doesn't know that the gentle duke is dead?

original: You do him injury to scorn his corse.
translation: You do him wrong to joke about his death.

original: Who knows not he is dead! Who knows he is?
translation: Who doesn't know that he's dead? Who knew that he was!

original: All-seeing heaven, what a world is this!
translation: Oh all-seeing God, what a terrible world!

original: Look I so pale, Lord Dorset, as the rest?
translation: Do I look as pale as everyone else, Lord Dorset?

original: Ay, my good lord, and no one in the presence But his red color hath forsook his cheeks.
translation: Yes, my good lord. Everyone here in the king's presence has gone totally pale.

original: Is Clarence dead? The order was reversed.
translation: Is Clarence dead? The death sentence had been reversed.

original: But he, poor man, by your first order died,   And that a wingèd Mercury did bear.
translation: But Clarence died by your first order, the poor man. The death sentence must have been carried by Mercury, the winged messenger god,

original: Some tardy cripple bear the countermand,   That came too lag to see him burièd.
translation: while the counter-order was carried by some slow cripple. It arrived too late even for his burial.

original: God grant that some, less noble and less loyal,   Nearer in bloody thoughts, and not in blood,
translation: It seems that someone less noble and less loyal—nearer in bloody thoughts but not a blood relation—

original: Deserve not worse than wretched Clarence did,   And yet go current from suspicion.
translation: deserves the punishment that poor Clarence got, but instead goes free without suspicion.

original: A boon, my sovereign, for my service done.
translation: I must ask you a favor in return for the service I've done for you, my king.

original: I prithee, peace. My soul is full of sorrow.
translation: Quiet, please. My soul is full of sorrow.

original: I will not rise unless your Highness hear me.
translation: I will not rise until your Highness hears my request.

original: Then say at once what is it thou requests.
translation: Then quickly say what it is you want.

original: The forfeit, sovereign, of my servant’s life, Who slew today a riotous gentleman Lately attendant on the duke of Norfolk.
translation: I ask you to spare the life of my servant, who just today killed a rowdy gentleman that used to serve the Duke of Norfolk.

original: Have I a tongue to doom my brother’s death,   And shall the tongue give pardon to a slave?
translation: I was willing to condemn my own brother to death, and now you want me to pardon a servant?

original: My brother killed no man; his fault was thought,   And yet his punishment was bitter death.
translation: My brother Clarence didn't kill anyone. His only fault was his ideas, and yet he was punished with bitter death.

original: Who sued to me for him? Who, in my wrath,   Kneeled at my feet, and bade me be advised?
translation: Who pled on  his  behalf?  When I was so angry, who kneeled at my feet and asked me to think about what I was doing?

original: Who spoke of brotherhood? Who spoke of love?   Who told me how the poor soul did forsake   The mighty Warwick and did fight for me?
translation: Who spoke to me about brotherhood? Who spoke about love? Who told me how the poor soul abandoned his father-in-law—the mighty Earl of Warwick—to come fight for me?

original: Who told me, in the field by Tewkesbury,   When Oxford had me down, he rescued me,   And said “Dear brother, live, and be a king?”
translation: Who told me of the battlefield at Tewkesbury, where Clarence rescued me when Oxford had me down, saying, "Dear brother, live, and be a king?"

original: Who told me, when we both lay in the field   Frozen almost to death, how he did lap me   Even in his garments and did give himself,   All thin and naked, to the numb-cold night?
translation: Who told me how, when we both lay in the field almost freezing to death, he wrapped me in his own clothes and left himself naked, exposed to the mercy of the numbingly cold night?

original: All this from my remembrance brutish wrath   Sinfully plucked, and not a man of you   Had so much grace to put it in my mind.
translation: All this seemed erased from my memory in my brutish rage, and not a man of you had the grace to remind me.

original: But when your carters or your waiting vassals   Have done a drunken slaughter and defaced   The precious image of our dear Redeemer,
translation: But when your servants drunkenly kill someone and scorn the law of our dear Christ,

original: You straight are on your knees for pardon, pardon,   And I, unjustly too, must grant it you.
translation: you immediately get on your knees and beg, "pardon, pardon." And I, unfair as I am, must give it to you.

original: [STANLEY rises]   But for my brother, not a man would speak,   Nor I, ungracious, speak unto myself   For him, poor soul.
translation: [Stanley rises]   But no one spoke on behalf my brother, and I didn't speak to myself on his behalf either, the poor soul.

original: The proudest of you all   Have been beholding to him in his life,   Yet none of you would once beg for his life.
translation: Even the proudest among you owed him something, and yet none of you would beg for his life.

original: O God, I fear Thy justice will take hold   On me and you, and mine and yours for this!—
translation: Oh God, I fear that your justice will punish me and all these gathered here, and our families as well, because of this!

original: This is the fruits of rashness. Marked you not   How that the guilty kindred of the queen   Looked pale when they did hear of Clarence' death?
translation: This sorrow is the result of recklessness. Didn't you notice how the queen's guilty relatives turned pale when they heard about Clarence's death?

original: O, they did urge it still unto the king.   God will revenge it.
translation: Oh, they were always urging the king to do it. God will revenge it.

original: Come, lords, will you go   To comfort Edward with our company?
translation: Come, lords, will you come with me to comfort Edward with our companionship?

original: We wait upon your Grace.
translation: We will attend you, your Grace.

original: Good grandam, tell us, is our father dead?
translation: Good grandmother, tell us, is our father dead?

original: No, boy.
translation: No, boy.

original: Why do you weep so oft, and beat your breast, And cry, “O Clarence, my unhappy son?”
translation: Then why do you weep so often, and beat your chest, and cry, "Oh, Clarence, my unlucky son?"

original: Why do you look on us and shake your head, And call us orphans, wretches, castaways, If that our noble father were alive?
translation: If our noble father is still alive, why do you look at us and shake your head, and call us orphans, wretches, and castaways?

original: My pretty cousins, you mistake me both.   I do lament the sickness of the king,
translation: My pretty grandchildren, you both misunderstand me. I'm lamenting the sickness of the king,

original: As loath to lose him, not your father’s death.   It were lost sorrow to wail one that’s lost.
translation: because I don't want to lose him. I'm not lamenting your father's death. It would be wasted sorrow to cry over someone who's already dead.

original: Then, you conclude, my grandam, he is dead.   The king mine uncle is to blame for it.
translation: Then, my grandmother, you're admitting that our father is dead. My uncle, the king, is to blame for it.

original: God will revenge it, whom I will importune   With earnest prayers, all to that effect.
translation: God will revenge it, and I'll pray earnestly every day that he does so.

original: And so will I.
translation: And so will I.

original: Peace, children, peace. The king doth love you well. Incapable and shallow innocents, You cannot guess who caused your father’s death.
translation: Quiet, children, quiet. The king loves you both very much. You innocent, naive children, you cannot guess who caused your father's death.

original: Grandam, we can, for my good uncle Gloucester   Told me the king, provoked to it by the queen,   Devised impeachments to imprison him;
translation: But we can, grandmother, for my good uncle Richard told me. He said that the king was provoked by the queen to make up accusations against my father that would get him arrested.

original: And when my uncle told me so, he wept,   And pitied me, and kindly kissed my cheek,
translation: When my uncle told me about this he wept, and pitied me, and kindly kissed my cheek.

original: Bade me rely on him as on my father,   And he would love me dearly as a child.
translation: He told me that I could rely on him as if he were my father, and that he would love me as dearly as if I were his child.

original: Ah, that deceit should steal such gentle shape,   And with a virtuous visor hide deep vice.
translation: Ah, it's terrible that liars can steal the appearance of gentle people, and hide their wickedness under a virtuous mask.

original: He is my son, ay, and therein my shame,   Yet from my dugs he drew not this deceit.
translation: Yes, he is my son. And in being my son, he is the source of my shame as a mother. But he didn't get his deceitfulness from my breast.

original: Think you my uncle did dissemble, grandam?
translation: Do you think that my uncle was lying, grandmother?

original: Ay, boy.
translation: Yes, boy.

original: I cannot think it. Hark, what noise is this?
translation: I can't believe it. Wait, what's that noise?

original: Ah, who shall hinder me to wail and weep,   To chide my fortune and torment myself?
translation: Ah, who can stop me from wailing and weeping, cursing my bad luck, and tormenting myself?

original: I’ll join with black despair against my soul   And to myself become an enemy.
translation: I'll ally myself with the black despair that threatens my soul, and become my own enemy.

original: What means this scene of rude impatience?
translation: What do you mean by this melodramatic scene?

original: To make an act of tragic violence.   Edward, my lord, thy son, our king, is dead.
translation: I'm performing the violent tragedy of my life. Edward—my husband, your son, our king—is dead.

original: Why grow the branches when the root is gone?   Why wither not the leaves that want their sap?
translation: Why should we keep living when our leader and lifeblood is gone? How can the branches keep growing when the root is gone?  Why aren't the leaves withering now that the sap is dried up?

original: If you will live, lament. If die, be brief,   That our swift-wingèd souls may catch the king’s,
translation: If you will live, then lament. If you will die, then be quick about it, so our swift-winged souls might catch up with the king's—

original: Or, like obedient subjects, follow him   To his new kingdom of ne'er-changing night.
translation: or at least follow him, like obedient subjects, into his new kingdom of never-ending night.

original: Ah, so much interest have I in thy sorrow   As I had title in thy noble husband.   I have bewept a worthy husband’s death   And lived with looking on his images;
translation: Ah, I was your noble husband's mother, so I have just as large a share in your grief. I've already wept over my own worthy husband's death and kept myself alive only by looking at his sons, his mirror images.

original: But now two mirrors of his princely semblance   Are cracked in pieces by malignant death,   And I, for comfort, have but one false glass   That grieves me when I see my shame in him.
translation: But now two of those mirrors have been cracked into pieces by death,  and the only one left to comfort me is Richard—an untrustworthy mirror who only causes me shame and grief.

original: Thou art a widow, yet thou art a mother,   And hast the comfort of thy children left,
translation: You are a widow, but you're also a mother, and you still have the comfort of your children left.

original: But death hath snatched my husband from mine arms   And plucked two crutches from my feeble hands,   Clarence and Edward.
translation: But death has snatched my husband from my arms and then plucked my two crutches, Clarence and Edward, from my feeble hands.

original: O, what cause have I,   Thine being but a moiety of my moan,   To overgo thy woes and drown thy cries!
translation: Oh, I have every reason to surpass you in sorrow and drown out your weeping with my own, as your loss is only half of mine!

original: Ah, aunt, you wept not for  our father’s death. How can we aid you with our kindred tears?
translation: Oh, Aunt, you didn't weep for our father's death. So why would we help you with our tears?

original: Our fatherless distress was left unmoaned.  Your widow-dolor likewise be unwept!
translation: You didn't mourn with us when we were left fatherless. Your sadness as a widow will likewise go unmourned by us!

original: G   ive me no help in lamentation.   I am not barren to bring forth complaints.
translation: I don't need any help in mourning. I am full of sorrows to complain about.

original: All springs reduce their currents to mine eyes,   That I, being governed by the watery moon,   May send forth plenteous tears to drown the world.
translation: May all the earth's springs keep my eyes replenished with tears, so that when the tide is high in the ocean of my weeping, I can drown the world.

original: Ah, for my husband, for my dear lord Edward!
translation: Ah, for my husband, my dear lord Edward!

original: Ah, for our father, for our dear lord Clarence!
translation: Ah, for our father, for our dear lord Clarence!

original: Alas for both, both mine, Edward and Clarence!
translation: Alas for both Edward and Clarence, both mine!

original: What stay had I but Edward? And he’s gone.
translation: What support did I have besides Edward? And he's dead.

original: What stay had we but Clarence? And he’s gone.
translation: What support did we have besides Clarence? And he's dead.

original: What stays had I but they? And they are gone.
translation: What supports did I have besides both of them? And they are dead.

original: Was never widow had so dear a loss.
translation: A widow never suffered so great a loss.

original: Were never orphans had so dear a loss.
translation: Orphans never suffered so great a loss.

original: Was never mother had so dear a loss.   Alas, I am the mother of these griefs.
translation: A mother never suffered so great a loss. Alas, I am the mother of these griefs.

original: Their woes are parceled; mine are general.   She for an Edward weeps, and so do I;
translation: Each of you has only a single loss, while I suffer all of them. Elizabeth weeps for Edward, and so do I,

original: I for a Clarence weep; so doth not she.   These babes for Clarence weep and so do I;
translation: but she does not weep for Clarence like I do. These children weep for Clarence, and so do I,

original: I for an Edward weep; so do not they.
translation: but they don't weep for Edward like I do.

original: Alas, you three, on me, threefold distressed,   Pour all your tears. I am your sorrow’s nurse,   And I will pamper it with lamentations.
translation: You three should pour all your tears onto me. I will be your sorrow's nurse, and feed your tears with more mourning.

original: [to QUEEN ELIZABETH]     Comfort, dear mother. God is   much displeased   That you take with unthankfulness, his doing.
translation: [To QUEEN ELIZABETH]   Dear Mother, let yourself be comforted. God is displeased that you respond to his doings so unthankfully.

original: In common worldly things, ’tis called ungrateful   With dull unwillingness to repay a debt   Which with a bounteous hand was kindly lent;
translation: In everyday business, it's considered ungrateful if someone is unwilling to repay a debt which was generously loaned in the first place.

original: Much more to be thus opposite with heaven,   For it requires the royal debt it lent you.
translation: It's much worse to be so opposed to heaven, now that it requires the royal debt it lent to you.

original: Madam, bethink you, like a careful mother,   Of the young prince your son.
translation: Madam, think of your son, the young prince, and be a careful mother.

original: Send straight for him.   Let him be crowned. In him your comfort lives.
translation: Send for him right away. Let him be crowned king. He is your hope for future peace of mind.

original: Drown desperate sorrow in dead Edward’s grave   And plant your joys in living Edward’s throne.
translation: Drown your desperate sorrows in dead Edward's grave, and plant your future joys in Prince Edward's new throne.

original: Sister, have comfort. All of us have cause   To wail the dimming of our shining star,   But none can help our harms by wailing them.—
translation: Sister, let yourself be comforted. All of us have reason to mourn the dimming of the king, our shining star, but none of us can help anything by wailing.

original: God bless thee, and put meekness in thy breast, Love, charity, obedience, and true duty.
translation: God bless you, and fill you with humility, love, charity, obedience, and true duty.

original: Amen.  [aside]  And make me die a good old  man!  That is the butt end of a mother’s blessing; I marvel that her Grace did leave it out.
translation: Amen.

original: You cloudy princes and heart-sorrowing peers   That bear this heavy mutual load of moan,   Now cheer each other in each other’s love.
translation: You weeping princes and sorrowful nobles who bear this mutual weight of grief, let us now cheer each other up with our love.

original: Though we have spent our harvest of this king,   We are to reap the harvest of his son.
translation: Though we have lost our old, fruitful king, we will now reap the harvest of his son.

original: The broken rancor of your high-swoll'n hates,   But lately splintered, knit, and joined together,   Must gently be preserved, cherished, and kept.
translation: Our former hatreds were only recently broken and then rejoined as friendship, and now we must gently preserve, cherish, and keep this new goodwill.

original: Meseemeth good that with some little train   Forthwith from Ludlow the young prince be fet   Hither to London, to be crowned our king.
translation: It seems like a good idea that a small group of us should now set out for Ludlow Castle in Wales, to fetch the young prince and bring him here to London, where he will be crowned our king.

original: Why “with some little train,” my Lord of Buckingham?
translation: Why only a "small group," my Lord of Buckingham?

original: Marry, my lord, lest by a multitude   The new-healed wound of malice should break out,   Which would be so much the more dangerous   By how much the estate is green and yet ungoverned.
translation: Well, my lord, if a large group goes, the newly-healed hostilities between us might break out again. This could be very dangerous, as the Yorkist rule is still new and untested.

original: Where every horse bears his commanding rein   And may direct his course as please himself,   As well the fear of harm as harm apparent,   In my opinion, ought to be prevented.
translation: We should prevent a situation where it seems like every man is out for himself, with everyone paranoid about imagined enemies.

original: I hope the king made peace with all of us; And the compact is firm and true in me.
translation: The king tried to make peace among all of us, and I hope he succeeded. For me, at least, those vows of friendship were firm and true.

original: And so in me, and so, I think, in all.
translation: And for me also. And so, I think, for all of us.

original: Yet since it is but green, it should be put   To no apparent likelihood of breach,   Which haply by much company might be urged.
translation: But since our agreement is so fresh, we shouldn't risk putting it under too much stress—which might happen if all of us go at once to fetch the prince.

original: Therefore I say with noble Buckingham   That it is meet so few should fetch the prince.
translation: So I agree with noble Buckingham that it's best for only a few to go.

original: And so say I.
translation: And I agree.

original: Then be it so, and go we to determine   Who they shall be that straight shall post to Ludlow.—
translation: Then we'll do that. Now let's go and figure out which of us will ride off to Ludlow.

original: My lord, whoever journeys to the prince,   For God’s sake let not us two at home.
translation: My lord, whoever ends up journeying to meet the prince, for God's sake let us be part of the group.

original: For by the way I’ll sort occasion,   As index to the story we late talked of,   To part the queen’s proud kindred from the prince.
translation: Along the way I'll create an opportunity to separate him from the queen's proud relatives—as the first step in the plan we discussed recently.

original: My other self, my council’s consistory,   My oracle, my prophet, my dear cousin,
translation: My dear cousin, you are my other self, my council of advisors, my oracle, my prophet!

original: I, as a child, will go by thy direction   Toward Ludlow then, for we’ll not stay behind.
