translation: I will let you lead me like a child. Let's go to Wales then, for we won't stay behind.

original: Good morrow, neighbor, whither away so fast?
translation: Good morning, neighbor. Where are you hurrying off to?

original: I promise you I scarcely know myself. Hear you the news abroad?
translation: I swear, I hardly know where I'm going myself. Have you heard the news going around?

original: Yes, that the king is dead.
translation: Yes, that the king is dead.

original: Ill news, by 'r Lady. Seldom comes the better.  I fear, I fear, ’twill prove a giddy world.
translation: Bad news, by the Virgin Mary. The news is always bad, and likely to get worse. I fear that the world will go crazy.

original: Neighbors, God speed.
translation: Hello, neighbors.

original: Give you good morrow, sir.
translation: Good morning to you, sir.

original: Doth this news hold of good King Edward’s death?
translation: Is the news true that good King Edward has died?

original: Ay, sir, it is too true, God help the while.
translation: Yes, sir, it's too true, God help us.

original: Then, masters, look to see a troublous world.
translation: Then be ready for troubled times, sirs.

original: No, no, by God’s good grace, his son shall reign.
translation: No, no, by God's good grace, his son will become king.

original: Woe to the land that’s governed by a child.
translation: It's bad for a country to be ruled by a child.

original: In him there is a hope of government,
translation: There is hope for the country under his rule, though.

original: Which, in his nonage, council under him,   And, in his full and ripened years, himself,   No doubt shall then, and till then, govern well.
translation: A young king who governs wisely under his advisors will govern wisely on his own when he reaches adulthood.

original: So stood the state when Henry the Sixth Was crowned in Paris but at nine months old.
translation: That's how it went when Henry the Sixth was crowned in Paris at just nine months old.

original: Stood the state so? No, no, good friends, God wot,
translation: Is that how it was? No, no, good friends,

original: For then this land was famously enriched   With politic grave counsel; then the king   Had virtuous uncles to protect his Grace.
translation: back then the country was rich with intelligent advisors, and the king had virtuous uncles to protect him.

original: Why, so hath this, both by the father and mother.
translation: Why, this king—Edward's son—has uncles too, on both his father's and his mother's side.

original: Better it were they all came by his father,   Or by the father there were none at all,   For emulation who shall now be nearest   Will touch us all too near if God prevent not.
translation: It would be better if they were all on his father's side, or if none at all were on his father's side. For as it is, the contest over which uncles will be closest to the king is likely to affect all of us, if God doesn't prevent it.

original: O, full of danger is the duke of Gloucester,   And the queen’s sons and brothers haught and proud,
translation: The Duke of Gloucester—Richard—is a dangerous man. And Queen Elizabeth's sons and brothers are haughty and proud.

original: And were they to be ruled, and not to rule,   This sickly land might solace as before.
translation: This sickly country will only have a chance of being healed if they end up as subjects, not rulers.

original: Come, come, we fear the worst. All will be well.
translation: Come, come, we're worrying about the worst possible outcome. I'm sure that everything will be all right.

original: When clouds are seen, wise men put on their cloaks;
translation: You know what they say: when clouds appear, wise men put on their coats.

original: When great leaves fall, then winter is at hand;   When the sun sets, who doth not look for night?
translation: When leaves fall from the trees, winter is coming. When the sun sets, who doesn't expect night?

original: Untimely storms make men expect a dearth.   All may be well; but if God sort it so,   'Tis more than we deserve or I expect.
translation: When storms arrive early, men expect a bad harvest. Everything may be all right, as you say. But if God wills it to turn out all right, that will be more than we deserve, and not what I expect.

original: Truly, the hearts of men are full of fear. Ye cannot reason almost with a man  That looks not heavily and full of dread.
translation: Truly, the hearts of men are full of fear. There's hardly anyone who isn't unreasonably worried right now.

original: Before the days of change, still is it so.   By a divine instinct, men’s minds mistrust   Ensuing dangers,
translation: It's always like this before times of great change. By some divine instinct, we get nervous when danger is coming—

original: as by proof we see   The water swell before a boist'rous storm.
translation: just like when we see the waves swelling before a storm arrives.

original: But leave it all to God. Whither away?
translation: But leave it all to God. Where are you off to?

original: Marry, we were sent for to the justices.
translation: Indeed, the judges have sent for us.

original: And so was I. I’ll bear you company.
translation: And for me to. I'll keep you company.

original: Last night, I hear, they lay at Stony Stratford, And at Northampton they do rest tonight. Tomorrow or next day they will be here.
translation: I hear that last night they slept at Stony Stratford, and tonight they'll rest in Northampton. Tomorrow or the next day they'll be here.

original: I long with all my heart to see the prince.  I hope he is much grown since last I saw him.
translation: I long with all my heart to see the prince. I hope he's grown a lot since the last time I saw him.

original: But I hear no; they say my son of York Has almost overta'en him in his growth.
translation: I heard he hasn't though. They say that my son of York has almost passed him in height.

original: Ay, mother, but I would not have it so.
translation: Yes, Mother, but I wish it weren't so.

original: Why, my young cousin? It is good to grow.
translation: Why, my child? It is good to grow.

original: Grandam, one night as we did sit at supper,   My uncle Rivers talked how I did grow   More than my brother:
translation: Grandmother, one night while we were eating dinner, my uncle Rivers mentioned that I had grown more than my brother.

original: “Ay,” quoth my uncle Gloucester,   “Small herbs have grace; great weeds do grow apace.”
translation: "Yes," said my uncle Richard, "Small herbs grow with grace, while big weeds grow quickly."

original: And since, methinks I would not grow so fast   Because sweet flowers are slow and weeds make haste.
translation: And since then, I've wished that I wouldn't grow so fast, because sweet flowers are slow, and weeds are hasty.

original: Good faith, good faith, the saying did not hold   In him that did object the same to thee!
translation: Honestly, honestly, that saying certainly didn't hold true for Richard!

original: He was the wretched’st thing when he was young,   So long a-growing and so leisurely,   That if this rule were true, he should be gracious.
translation: He was a terrible child, and took such a long time to grow up that if that rule were true, he should be a very gracious adult.

original: And so no doubt he is, my gracious madam.
translation: And no doubt he is, my gracious madam.

original: I hope he is, but yet let mothers doubt.
translation: I hope he is, but mothers can have their doubts.

original: Now, by my troth, if I had been remembered, I could have given my uncle’s grace a flout  To touch his growth nearer than he touched mine.
translation: Now, if I'd considered something I once heard about him, I could have scoffed at my uncle—and mocked his growth more than he mocked mine.

original: How, my pretty York? I prithee let me hear it.
translation: How, my clever York? Let me hear your comeback.

original: Marry, they say my uncle grew so fast   That he could gnaw a crust at two hours old.
translation: Well, they say that my uncle grew so fast that he could gnaw a crust of bread at two hours old.

original: 'Twas full two years ere I could get a tooth.   Grandam, this would have been a biting jest.
translation: For me, it took two full years before I could get a single tooth. Grandmother, this would have been a biting joke.

original: I prithee, pretty York, who told thee this?
translation: Please tell me, clever York, who told you this about him?

original: Grandam, his nurse.
translation: His nurse, grandmother.

original: His nurse? Why, she was dead ere thou wast born.
translation: His nurse? Why, she was dead before you were born.

original: If ’twere not she, I cannot tell who told me.
translation: If it wasn't her, then I can't say who told me.

original: A parlous boy! Go to, you are too shrewd.
translation: A cunning boy! Get out of here, you're too clever for your own good.

original: Good madam, be not angry with the child.
translation: Good madam, don't be angry with the child.

original: Pitchers have ears.
Here comes a messenger. —What news?
translation: Here comes a messenger.

original: Such news, my lord, as grieves me to report.
translation: It's news that grieves me to report, my lord.

original: How doth the prince?
translation: How is the prince?

original: Well, madam, and in health.
translation: Madam, he's well and in good health.

original: What is thy news then?
translation: What's your news then?

original: Lord Rivers and Lord Grey are sent to Pomfret, And, with them, Sir Thomas Vaughan, prisoners.
Who hath committed them?
translation: Who had them arrested?

original: The mighty dukes, Gloucester and Buckingham.
translation: The mighty dukes of Gloucester and Buckingham.

original: For what offence?
translation: For what crime?

original: The sum of all I can, I have disclosed. Why, or for what, the nobles were committed Is all unknown to me, my gracious lord.
translation: I've told you all that I know. Why the nobles were arrested, and on what charges, is all unknown to me, my gracious lord.

original: Ay me! I see the ruin of my house.   The tiger now hath seized the gentle hind.
translation: God help us! I see the ruin of my family. The tiger has now seized the gentle deer.

original: Insulting tyranny begins to jut   Upon the innocent and aweless throne.
translation: Brute tyranny begins to attack the innocent, weak throne.

original: Welcome, destruction, blood, and massacre.   I see, as in a map, the end of all.
translation: Welcome, destruction, blood, and massacre! I can see how this will end as clearly as if I was reading it on a map.

original: Accursèd and unquiet wrangling days,   How many of you have mine eyes beheld?
translation: Oh, how many cursed and violent days of unrest have my old eyes seen?

original: My husband lost his life to get the crown,   And often up and down my sons were tossed   For me to joy, and weep, their gain and loss.
translation: My husband lost his life to get the crown. And my sons' lives have been tossed up and down for me to rejoice over their gains and weep over their losses.

original: And being seated, and domestic broils   Clean overblown, themselves the conquerors   Make war upon themselves, brother to brother,   Blood to blood, self against self.
translation: And when one of them gained the throne and got rid of the domestic quarrels, now the conquerors turn on each other, making war among themselves—brother against brother, blood against blood, self against self.

original: O, preposterous   And frantic outrage, end thy damnèd spleen,   Or let me die, to look on death no more.
translation: Oh, it's a perversion of the natural order, a frenzied outrage! Let it end—or let me die—so I won't have to see any more death.

original: Come, come, my boy. We will to sanctuary. Madam, farewell.
translation: Come, come, my boy. We'll go take sanctuary. Madam, farewell.

original: Stay, I will go with you.
translation: Wait, I will go with you.

original: You have no cause.
translation: You have no reason to.

original: [to QUEEN ELIZABETH]   My gracious lady, go,   And thither bear your treasure and your goods.
translation: [To QUEEN ELIZABETH]  My gracious lady, go. And take your money and belongings with you.

original: For my part, I’ll resign unto your Grace   The seal I keep; and so betide to me   As well I tender you and all of yours.
translation: For my part, I'll reassign the  seal I keep to you , and I'll try to take care of you and all your relatives.

original: Go. I’ll conduct you to the sanctuary.
translation: Go, I'll conduct you to the sanctuary.

original: Welcome, sweet prince, to London, to your chamber.
translation: Welcome to your room here in London, sweet prince.

original: Welcome, dear cousin, my thoughts'  sovereign. The weary way hath made you melancholy.
translation: Welcome, dear nephew, ruler of my thoughts. It seems that the tiring journey has made you sad.

original: No, uncle, but our crosses on the way  Have made it tedious, wearisome, and heavy. I want more uncles here to welcome me.
translation: No, uncle, but the annoyances on the way made the journey tedious, tiring, and dull. I wish more uncles were here to welcome me.

original: Sweet prince, the untainted virtue of your years   Hath not yet dived into the world’s deceit;
translation: Sweet prince, you are young and innocent, and haven't experienced the deceitfulness of the world yet.

original: Nor more can you distinguish of a man   Than of his outward show, which, God He knows,   Seldom or never jumpeth with the heart.
translation: You can't perceive the truth about a man except for what he shows on the outside—which, God knows, hardly ever corresponds with his heart.

original: Those uncles which you want were dangerous.   Your Grace attended to their sugared words   But looked not on the poison of their hearts.
translation: Those uncles you wish for were dangerous. You heard their sugary words, but you couldn't see the poison in their hearts, your Grace.

original: God keep you from them, and from such false friends.
translation: May God protect you from them, and from all such false friends!

original: God keep me from false friends, but they were none.
translation: May God protect me from false friends—but my uncles weren't false.

original: My lord, the mayor of London comes to greet you.
translation: My lord, the mayor of London is here to greet you.

original: God bless your Grace with health and happy days.
translation: May God bless your Grace with health and happy days.

original: I thank you, good my lord, and thank you all.—   I thought my mother and my brother York   Would long ere this have met us on the way.
translation: I thank you, my good lord, and thank you all. But I thought my mother and my brother York would have met us on our way long before now.

original: Fie, what a slug is Hastings that he comes not   To tell us whether they will come or no!
translation: And it's shameful what a slug Hastings is, that he hasn't even come to tell us whether or not they're coming!

original: And in good time here comes the sweating lord.
translation: And just in time, here comes the sweating lord.

original: Welcome, my lord. What, will our mother come?
translation: Welcome, my lord. Well, is my mother coming?

original: On what occasion God He knows, not I,   The Queen your mother and your brother York   Have taken sanctuary.
translation: Only God knows why, but the queen your mother and your brother York have taken sanctuary in Westminster Abbey.

original: The tender prince   Would fain have come with me to meet your Grace,   But by his mother was perforce withheld.
translation: The tender prince wanted to come with me to meet your Grace, but his mother forced him to stay.

original: Fie, what an indirect and peevish course   Is this of hers!
translation: For shame, what a devious and perverse course the queen is taking!

original: My Lord of Buckingham, if my weak oratory   Can from his mother win the duke of York,   Anon expect him here;
translation: My Lord of Buckingham, if my weak words can persuade his mother to give up the Duke of York, then you can expect him here soon.

original: but if she be obdurate   To mild entreaties, God in heaven forbid   We should infringe the holy privilege   Of blessèd sanctuary!
translation: But if she resists my mild requests, then God forbid that we should break the holy laws of sanctuary!

original: Not for all this land   Would I be guilty of so deep a sin.
translation: I would not commit such a terrible sin even in exchange for a kingdom.

original: You are too senseless obstinate, my lord,   Too ceremonious and traditional.
translation: My lord, you are foolishly stubborn, and too tied to formalities and traditions.

original: Weigh it but with the grossness of this age,   You break not sanctuary in seizing him.
translation: Consider the moral roughness of these times, and you'll see that you're not really breaking sanctuary in seizing him.

original: The benefit thereof is always granted   To those whose dealings have deserved the place   And those who have the wit to claim the place.
translation: The benefit of sanctuary is always given to those who really deserve protection, or those who are smart enough to claim it.

original: This prince hath neither claimed it nor deserved it   And therefore, in mine opinion, cannot have it.
translation: This prince has neither claimed it nor does he deserve it.

original: Then taking him from thence that is not there,   You break no privilege nor charter there.
translation: Therefore, in my opinion, he cannot have it. If you seize him from sanctuary when he was never really taking sanctuary in the first place, then you aren't breaking any laws or traditions.

original: Oft have I heard of sanctuary men,   But sanctuary children, ne'er till now.
translation: I've often heard of "sanctuary men," but until now I've never heard of "sanctuary children."

original: My lord, you shall o'errule my mind for once.— Come on, Lord Hastings, will you go with me?
translation: My lord, I'll let you convince me this once.

original: I go, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: Good lords, make all the speedy haste you may.
translation: Good lords, go as quickly as you can.

original: Say, uncle Gloucester, if our brother come, Where shall we sojourn till our coronation?
translation: Tell me, Uncle Richard: if my brother comes, where will we stay until my coronation ceremony?

original: Where it seems best unto your royal self.
translation: Wherever seems best for your royal self.

original: If I may counsel you, some day or two   Your Highness shall repose you at the Tower;
translation: If I can advise you, though, you should stay a day or two in the Tower.

original: Then where you please and shall be thought most fit   For your best health and recreation.
translation: After that you can stay wherever you like, and wherever seems best for your health and pleasure.

original: I do not like the Tower, of any place.— Did Julius Caesar build that place, my lord?
translation: Of all places, I don't like the Tower at all. Didn't Julius Caesar build it, my lord?

original: He did, my gracious lord, begin that place, Which, since, succeeding ages have re-edified.
translation: He began it, my gracious lord. And since then succeeding generations have added on to it.

original: Is it upon record, or else reported Successively from age to age, he built it?
translation: Is it on record that he built the Tower, or is it just reported by word of mouth from generation to generation?

original: Upon record, my gracious lord.
translation: On record, my gracious lord.

original: But say, my lord, it were not registered,   Methinks the truth should live from age to age,
translation: But even if it weren't recorded, I think that the truth would live on from generation to generation—

original: As ’twere retailed to all posterity,   Even to the general all-ending day.
translation: being told as part of legend and history—all the way until Judgment Day.

original: So wise so young, they say, do never live long.
translation: They say that those who are so wise when so young never live long.

original: What say you, uncle?
translation: What did you say, uncle?

original: I say, without characters fame lives long.     Thus, like the formal Vice, Iniquity, I moralize two meanings in one word.
translation: I said that without written records, fame lives long.

original: That Julius Caesar was a famous man.   With what his valor did enrich his wit,   His wit set down to make his valor live.
translation: That Julius Caesar was a famous man. His courage aided his intelligence, and his intelligence helped him make sure that his reputation for courage outlived him.

original: Death makes no conquest of this conqueror,
translation: Death didn't conquer  that  conqueror.

original: For now he lives in fame, though not in life.   I’ll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham—
translation: Now he lives on in fame, though not in life. I'll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham—

original: What, my gracious lord?
translation: What, my gracious lord?

original: An if I live until I be a man, I’ll win our ancient right in France again Or die a soldier, as I lived a king.
Short summers lightly have a forward spring.
translation: Short summers often have an early spring, as they say. Those who die young are usually precocious.

original: Now in good time here comes the duke of York.
translation: Now here comes the Duke of York, right on time.

original: Richard of York, how fares our loving brother?
translation: Richard of York, how are you, my loving brother?

original: Well, my dread lord—so must I call you now.
translation: I'm well, my sovereign lord—for that's what I must call you now.

original: Ay, brother, to our grief, as it is yours. Too late he died that might have kept that title,  Which by his death hath lost much majesty.
translation: Yes, Brother, and it's a sad occasion for both of us. Our father—the man who should have kept that title—died too recently. And the sadness of his death makes the title seem much less majestic.

original: How fares our cousin, noble Lord of York?
translation: How are you, my nephew, noble Lord of York?

original: I thank you, gentle uncle. O, my lord, You said that idle weeds are fast in growth. The prince my brother hath outgrown me far.
translation: I thank you for asking, noble uncle. Oh, my lord, you once said that lazy weeds grow quickly. The prince my brother has far outgrown me.

original: He hath, my lord.
translation: He has, my lord.

original: And therefore is he idle?
translation: So is he lazy then?

original: O, my fair cousin, I must not say so.
translation: Oh, my fair nephew, I can't say that.

original: Then is he more beholding to you than I.
translation: Then he has more power over you than I do.

original: He may command me as my sovereign, But you have power in me as in a kinsman.
translation: He may command me as my king, but you still have power over me as my relative.

original: I pray you, uncle, give me this dagger.
translation: Please give me your dagger, uncle.

original: My dagger, little cousin? With all my heart.
translation: My dagger, little Nephew? With all my heart.

original: A beggar, brother?
translation: Are you begging, Brother?

original: Of my kind uncle, that I know will give, And being but a toy, which is no grief to give.
translation: Only from my kind uncle. I know he'll give it to me, and it's not valuable, so it shouldn't make him sad to lose it.

original: A greater gift than that I’ll give my cousin.
translation: I'll give my nephew a greater gift than that.

original: A greater gift? O, that’s the sword to it.
translation: A greater gift? Oh, that must mean a sword.

original: Ay, gentle cousin, were it light enough.
translation: Yes, noble nephew. That is, if it's light enough for you to hold.

original: O, then I see you will part but with light gifts. In weightier things you’ll say a beggar nay.
translation: Oh, then I see that you'll only part with light, trivial gifts. You'll refuse a beggar's request in heavier, more valuable things.

original: It is too heavy for your Grace to wear.
translation: A sword is too heavy for your Grace to wear.

original: I weigh it lightly, were it heavier.
translation: I'd consider it light and trivial even if it were heavier.

original: What, would you have my weapon, little lord?
translation: What, do you want my weapon, little lord?

original: I would, that I might thank you as you call me.
translation: I do, so I can thank you for what you called me.

original: How?
translation: What do you mean?

original: Little.
translation: You called me "little."

original: My lord of York will still be cross in talk. Uncle, your Grace knows how to bear with him.
translation: The Lord of York is always argumentative. Uncle, you know how to bear with him.

original: You mean, to bear me, not to bear with me.—
translation: You mean to bear me, not to bear  with  me.

original: [aside]   With what a sharp-provided wit he reasons!
translation: [To himself]  What a sharp and thoughtful mind he has!

original: To mitigate the scorn he gives his uncle,   He prettily and aptly taunts himself.
translation: To smooth over his mockery of his uncle, he cleverly and politely mocks himself.

original: So cunning and so young is wonderful.
translation: It's amazing that he's so cunning while so young.

original: [to PRINCE]   My lord, will ’t please you pass along?
translation: [To the PRINCE]  My lord, would you like to continue on?

original: Myself and my good cousin Buckingham   Will to your mother, to entreat of her   To meet you at the Tower and welcome you.
translation: My good cousin Buckingham and I will go to your mother and ask her to meet you at the Tower.

original: What, will you go unto the Tower, my lord?
translation: What, are you going to the Tower, my lord?

original: My lord protector needs will have it so.
translation: My Lord Protector Richard insists on it.

original: I shall not sleep in quiet at the Tower.
translation: I won't sleep peacefully at the Tower.

original: Why, what should you fear?
translation: Why, what do you have to be afraid of?

original: Marry, my uncle Clarence' angry ghost.  My grandam told me he was murdered there.
translation: Well, my uncle Clarence's angry ghost. My grandmother told me he was murdered there.

original: I fear no uncles dead.
translation: I'm not afraid of any dead uncle.

original: Nor none that live, I hope.
translation: Nor living ones, I hope.

original: An if they live, I hope I need not fear.     But come, my lord. With a heavy heart, Thinking on them, go I unto the Tower.
Think you, my lord, this little prating York Was not incensèd by his subtle mother To taunt and scorn you thus opprobriously?
translation: My lord, don't you think that this talkative little York was encouraged by his deceitful mother to taunt and scorn you in that outrageous manner?

original: No doubt, no doubt. O, ’tis a parlous boy, Bold, quick, ingenious, forward, capable.  He is all the mother’s, from the top to toe.
translation: No doubt, no doubt. Oh, he's a dangerous and cunning boy—bold, lively, ingenious, outspoken, and capable. He takes after his mother, from head to toe.

original: Well, let them rest.—
translation: Well, let's leave them for the moment.

original: He, for his father’s sake, so loves the prince  That he will not be won to aught against him.
translation: Hastings loves the Prince because of his great love for his father, the late King Edward. We won't be able to convince him.

original: What think’st thou then of Stanley? Will not he?
translation: What do you think about Stanley then? Won't he join us?

original: He will do all in all as Hastings doth.
translation: He'll do whatever Hastings does.

original: Well then, no more but this: go, gentle Catesby,   And, as it were far off, sound thou Lord Hastings   How he doth stand affected to our purpose   And summon him tomorrow to the Tower   To sit about the coronation.
translation: Well then, just do this, noble Catesby: go and sound out Lord Hastings regarding our cause. But make it seem like a vague plan for the distant future. Find out how he feels, and summon him to the Tower tomorrow for the coronation.

original: If thou dost find him tractable to us,   Encourage him and show him all our reasons.
translation: If he seems like he could be convinced to join us, then encourage him and explain all our reasons to him.

original: If he be leaden, icy, cold, unwilling,   Be thou so too, and so break off the talk,
translation: If he's surly, cold, or unwilling, then you should act like that too, and break off the conversation.

original: And give us notice of his inclination;   For we tomorrow hold divided councils,   Wherein thyself shalt highly be employed.
translation: Let us know how he responds, for tomorrow we will hold two separate council meetings—one public, and one in secret, only for our supporters—and you'll have lots of work to do at them.

original: Commend me to Lord William. Tell him, Catesby,   His ancient knot of dangerous adversaries   Tomorrow are let blood at Pomfret castle,
translation: Give my regards to Lord Hastings. Tell him, Catesby, that the dangerous enemies who have plagued him for years will be executed tomorrow at Pomfret Castle.

original: And bid my lord, for joy of this good news,   Give mistress Shore one gentle kiss the more.
translation: And to celebrate this good news, tell him to give Miss Shore an extra  kiss .

original: Good Catesby, go effect this business soundly.
translation: Good Catesby, go do your work well.

original: My good lords both, with all the heed I can.
translation: My good lords, I'll do the best I can.

original: Shall we hear from you, Catesby, ere we sleep?
translation: Will we hear from you before we go to sleep, Catesby?

original: You shall, my lord.
translation: You will, my lord.

original: At Crosby Place, there shall you find us both.
translation: You'll find us both at Crosby Place.

original: Now, my lord, what shall we do, if we perceive Lord Hastings will not yield to our complots?
translation: Now, my lord, what will we do if Lord Hastings won't go along with our conspiracy?

original: Chop off his head. Something we will determine.   And look when I am king,   claim thou of me   The earldom of Hereford,
translation: Chop off his head. We'll come up with something. And when I am king, you will have the earldom of Hereford—

original: and all the moveables   Whereof the king my brother was possessed.
translation: and all the wealth and possessions that go with it—which my brother, King Edward, used to own.

original: I’ll claim that promise at your Grace’s hands.
translation: I'll take you up on that promise, your Grace.

original: And look to have it yielded with all kindness. Come, let us sup betimes, that afterwards We may digest our complots in some form.
translation: And you'll see that I'll give it gladly. Come, let's eat early, so that afterwards we can think about our plot further.

original: My lord, my lord.
translation: My lord, my lord.

original: Who knocks?
translation: Who's knocking?

original: One from the Lord Stanley.
translation: A messenger from Lord Stanley.

original: What is ‘t o’clock?
translation: What time is it?

original: Upon the stroke of four.
translation: Four in the morning.

original: Cannot my Lord Stanley sleep these tedious nights?
translation: Can't Lord Stanley sleep on this long night?

original: So it appears by that I have to say.  First, he commends him to your noble self.
translation: It appears not, based on his message. First, he sends his regards to your noble self.

original: What then?
translation: And what else?

original: Then certifies your Lordship that this night   He dreamt the boar had razèd his helm.
translation: He then tells your Lordship that tonight he dreamed that the  boar  cut off his head.

original: Besides, he says there are two councils kept,   And that may be determined at the one   Which may make you and him to rue at th' other.
translation: He also says that there will be two council meetings tomorrow, and that the results of one meeting may make you and Stanley—who will be at the other—very sorry indeed.

original: Therefore he sends to know your Lordship’s pleasure,   If you will presently take horse with him   And with all speed post with him toward the north   To shun the danger that his soul divines.
translation: Because of this, he wants to know if you'll ride with him to the north as soon as possible, to escape the danger that his soul senses.

original: Go, fellow, go. Return unto thy lord.   Bid him not fear the separated council.
translation: Go, fellow, go. Return to your lord. Tell him not to worry about the two separate meetings.

original: His Honor and myself are at the one,   And at the other is my good friend Catesby,   Where nothing can proceed that toucheth us   Whereof I shall not have intelligence.
translation: He and I will be at one meeting, and my good friend Catesby will be at the other. Nothing important can happen at the secret meeting without us hearing about it.

original: Tell him his fears are shallow, without instance.   And for his dreams, I wonder he’s so simple   To trust the mock'ry of unquiet slumbers.
translation: Tell your lord that his fears are shadows without evidence. And as for his dreams, I'm surprised that he's so foolish as to trust the imaginings of restless sleep.

original: To fly the boar before the boar pursues   Were to incense the boar to follow us   And make pursuit where he did mean no chase.
translation: To flee the boar before he even pursues us would make the boar angry, and incite him to chase us even if he never intended to in the first place.

original: Go, bid thy master rise and come to me,   And we will both together to the Tower,   Where he shall see, the boar will use us kindly.
translation: Go tell your master to get up and meet me, and we'll go together to the Tower. There he'll see that the boar will treat us kindly.

original: I’ll go, my lord, and tell him what you say.
translation: I'll go and tell him what you say, my lord.

original: Many good morrows to my noble lord.
translation: Good morning to you, my noble lord.

original: Good morrow, Catesby. You are early stirring. What news, what news in this our tott'ring state?
translation: Good morning, Catesby. You're up early. What's the news in our unsteady kingdom?

original: It is a reeling world indeed, my lord, And I believe will never stand upright Till Richard wear the garland of the realm.
translation: It is a crazy world indeed, my lord. And I believe it will never stand upright again until Richard wears the garland of the realm.

original: How “wear the garland?” Dost thou mean the crown?
translation: What do you mean, "wears the garland?" Do you mean the crown?

original: Ay, my good lord.
translation: Yes, my good lord.

original: I’ll have this crown of mine cut from my shoulders Before I’ll see the crown so foul misplaced. But canst thou guess that he doth aim at it?
translation: I'll have my head cut from my shoulders before I'll see the crown so terribly misplaced. But do you think that's his intention?

original: Ay, on my life, and hopes to find you forward   Upon his party for the gain thereof;
translation: Yes, I swear on my life. And he hopes that you'll join his side and help him.

original: And thereupon he sends you this good news,   That this same very day your enemies,   The kindred of the queen, must die at Pomfret.
translation: For that reason he sends you this good news: that this very day your enemies—the queen's relatives—will die at Pomfret Castle.

original: Indeed, I am no mourner for that news,   Because they have been still my adversaries.
translation: Indeed, I'm not sorry to hear that news, for they have always been my enemies.

original: But that I’ll give my voice on Richard’s side   To bar my master’s heirs in true descent,   God knows I will not do it, to the death.
translation: But as for the idea that I'd support Richard's side in keeping my master's  true heirs  from the throne—God knows I'll never do it. I'd rather die.

original: God keep your Lordship in that gracious mind.
translation: May God preserve your Lordship in that noble state of mind.

original: But I shall laugh at this a twelve-month hence,   That they which brought me in my master’s hate,   I live to look upon their tragedy.
translation: But I'll laugh at all this in a year, and rejoice that I could see tragedy come to those who once convinced King Edward to hate me.

original: Well, Catesby, ere a fortnight make me older   I’ll send some packing that yet think not on ’t.
translation: Well, Catesby, before two weeks have passed I'll send some people packing who won't be expecting it at all.

original: 'Tis a vile thing to die, my gracious lord,  When men are unprepared and look not for it.
translation: It's a terrible thing to die when you're unprepared and not expecting it, my gracious lord.

original: O monstrous, monstrous! And so falls it out   With Rivers, Vaughan, Grey;
translation: Yes, it's monstrous, monstrous! That's how it is for Rivers, Vaughan, and Grey.

original: and so ’twill do   With some men else that think themselves as safe   As thou and I, who, as thou know’st, are dear   To princely Richard and to Buckingham.
translation: And that's how it will be soon for some other men who think they're as safe as you and I are—we who are dear to princely Richard and Buckingham.

original: The princes both make high account of you—    For  they account his head upon the Bridge.
translation: Those two lords both think highly of you.

original: I know they do, and I have well deserved it.
translation: I know they do, and I deserve it.

original: Come on, come on. Where is your boar-spear, man?  Fear you the boar, and go so unprovided?
translation: Come on, come on. Where is your boar-hunting spear, man? You're afraid of the boar, but you'll go around unarmed?

original: My lord, good morrow. —Good morrow, Catesby.— You may jest on, but, by the Holy Rood, I do not like these several councils, I.
translation: My lord, good morning.

original: My lord, I hold my life as dear as you do yours,   And never in my days, I do protest,   Was it so precious to me as ’tis now.
translation: My lord, I care about my life as much as you care about yours, and I swear I care about it as much now as I ever have.

original: Think you but that I know our state secure,   I would be so triumphant as I am?
translation: Do you think I would be as confident as I am if I wasn't certain of our safety?

original: The lords at Pomfret, when they rode from London,   Were jocund and supposed their states were sure,   And they indeed had no cause to mistrust;
translation: When the queen's relatives rode from London, they too were joyful and felt sure that they were safe. And indeed they had no reason to worry.

original: But yet you see how soon the day o'ercast.
translation: But see how quickly the day grew cloudy for them—now they're imprisoned at Pomfret Castle.

original: This sudden stab of rancor I misdoubt.   Pray God, I say, I prove a needless coward!
translation: Richard's sudden attack on them makes me worried. I pray to God that it turns out I'm being cowardly for no reason. Well, should we go to the Tower?

original: What, shall we toward the Tower? The day is spent.
translation: The day has already begun.

original: Come, come. Have with you. Wot you what, my lord? Today the lords you talked of are beheaded.
translation: Come, come. Let's go. Do you know what, my lord? Those lords you just mentioned—Rivers and Grey—will be beheaded today.

original: They, for their truth, might better wear their heads Than some that have accused them wear their hats.  But come, my lord, let’s away.
translation: To be honest, they deserve to keep their heads more than the people who've accused them deserve to keep their duke's caps. But come, my lord, let's go.

original: Go on before. I’ll talk with this good fellow.
translation: Go on ahead. I'll talk with this good fellow.

original: How now, sirrah! How goes the world with thee?
The better that your Lordship please to ask.
translation: Better, now that your Lordship was kind enough to ask.

original: I tell thee, man, ’tis better with me now   Than when thou met’st me last where now we meet.
translation: I tell you, man, it's better with me now than it was the last time you met me here.

original: Then was I going prisoner to the Tower   By the suggestion of the queen’s allies.
translation: At that time I was on my way to be imprisoned in the Tower, accused by the queen's allies.

original: But now, I tell thee—keep it to thyself—   This day those enemies are put to death,   And I in better state than e'er I was.
translation: But now, I tell you—and keep this to yourself—those enemies are being put to death today, and I'm better than ever.

original: God hold it, to your Honor’s good content!
translation: May God preserve your good luck, your Honor!

original: Gramercy, fellow. There, drink that for me.
translation: Thank you very much, fellow. Here, have a drink on me.

original: I thank your Honor.
translation: I thank your Honor.

original: Well met, my lord. I am glad to see your Honor.
translation: Hello, my lord. I'm glad to see you.

original: I thank thee, good Sir John, with all my heart. I am in your debt for your last exercise. Come the next sabbath, and I will content you.
translation: I thank you with all my heart, Sir John. I'm in your debt for your last sermon. Next Sunday I'll give the church a nice donation.

original: I’ll wait upon your Lordship.
translation: I'll come to see you, your Lordship.

original: What, talking with a priest, Lord Chamberlain? Your friends at Pomfret, they do need the priest;  Your Honor hath no shriving work in hand.
translation: What, talking with a priest, Lord Hastings? Your friends at Pomfret Castle, they're the ones who need a priest. You, your Honor, have no deathbed confessions to make.

original: Good faith, and when I met this holy man, The men you talk of came into my mind. What, go you toward the Tower?
translation: Honestly, when I ran into this holy man, I did think of those men you mention. So, are you going to the Tower?

original: I do, my lord, but long I shall not stay there.  I shall return before your Lordship thence.
translation: I am, my lord. But I won't stay there long. I'll return from there before your Lordship does.

original: Nay, like enough, for I stay dinner there.
translation: That's likely, since I'm staying for lunch there.

original: And supper too, although thou know’st it not.— Come, will you go?
translation: And for dinner too, though you don't know it yet.

original: I’ll wait upon your Lordship.
translation: I'll follow your Lordship.

original: Sir Richard Ratcliffe, let me tell thee this: Today shalt thou behold a subject die For truth, for duty, and for loyalty.
translation: Sir Richard Ratcliffe, let me tell you this: today you will watch a man die for truth, for duty, and for loyalty.

original: God bless the prince from all the pack of you!  A knot you are of damnèd bloodsuckers.
translation: May God protect the prince from the pack of you! All of you are damned bloodsuckers.

original: You live that shall cry woe for this  hereafter.
translation: You'll live to regret this later.

original: Dispatch. The limit of your lives is out.
translation: Enough. You've reached the limit of your lives.

original: O Pomfret, Pomfret! O thou bloody prison, Fatal and ominous to noble peers!  Within the guilty closure of thy walls, Richard the Second here was hacked to death, And, for more slander to thy dismal seat, We give thee up our guiltless blood to drink.
translation: Oh, Pomfret, Pomfret! Oh, you bloody prison, fatal to noblemen! King Richard II was hacked to death within your guilty walls. And now—to bring greater shame to your ominous name—we must offer up our innocent lives here.

original: Now Margaret’s curse is fall'n upon our heads, When she exclaimed on Hastings, you, and I,  For standing by when Richard stabbed her son.
translation: Now old Queen Margaret's curse has fallen on our heads, when she condemned me, Hastings, and you for standing by while Richard stabbed her son.

original: Then cursed she Richard, then cursed she Buckingham. Then cursed she Hastings. O, remember, God, To hear her prayer for them, as now for us! And for my sister and her princely sons,  Be satisfied, dear God, with our true blood, Which, as thou know’st, unjustly must be spilt.
translation: Then she cursed Richard, then she cursed Buckingham, and then she cursed Hastings. Oh, God, remember to hear her prayer and punish them as you now punish us! But, dear God, please be satisfied with our blood—which is being unjustly spilled—and don't punish my sister and her princely sons.

original: Make haste. The hour of death is expiate.
translation: Hurry up. The hour of death has come.

original: Come, Grey. Come, Vaughan. Let us all embrace.  Farewell until we meet in heaven.
translation: Come, Grey. Come, Vaughan. Let us all embrace.  Farewell, until we meet again in heaven.

original: Now, noble peers. the cause why we are met Is to determine of the coronation. In God’s name, speak. When is the royal day?
translation: Now, noble peers, we are meeting today to come to a decision about the coronation. In God's name, speak. When will the royal day be?

original: Is all things ready for the royal time?
translation: Is everything ready for the royal event?

original: It is, and wants but nomination.
translation: Yes, and all we need to do is name the day.

original: Tomorrow, then, I judge a happy day.
translation: Then I think tomorrow should be a favorable day.

original: Who knows the Lord Protector’s mind herein? Who is most inward with the noble duke?
translation: Who knows what the Lord Protector Richard thinks about this? Who is closest to the noble duke?

original: Your Grace, we think, should soonest know his mind.
translation: We think you would best know his mind, your Grace.

original: We know each other’s faces; for our hearts,   He knows no more of mine than I of yours,   Or I of his, my lord, than you of mine.—
translation: We know each other's faces. But as for our hearts, he doesn't know mine any more than I know yours or his, or you know mine.

original: I thank his Grace. I know he loves me well.
translation: I thank you for saying that. I know he loves me well.

original: But for his purpose in the coronation,   I have not sounded him, nor he delivered   His gracious pleasure any way therein.
translation: But I haven't asked him out about the coronation, and he hasn't told me his preferences about it.

original: But you, my honorable lords, may name the time,   And in the duke’s behalf I’ll give my voice,   Which I presume he’ll take in gentle part.
translation: But you can name a time, my honorable lords. And I'll give my vote on the duke's behalf. I'm sure he won't mind.

original: In happy time here comes the duke himself.
translation: Here comes the duke himself, right on time.

original: My noble lords and cousins all, good morrow.
translation: Good morning, my noble lords and kinsmen.

original: I have been long a sleeper; but I trust   My absence doth neglect no great design   Which by my presence might have been concluded.
translation: I slept late, but I trust that my absence hasn't delayed any important decisions that required me to be here.

original: Had you not come upon your cue, my lord, William Lord Hastings had pronounced your part— I mean your voice for crowning of the king.
translation: My lord, if you hadn't shown up when you did, Lord Hastings would have taken your part. He was going to cast a vote on your behalf in deciding about the coronation of the king.

original: Than my Lord Hastings no man might be bolder.   His Lordship knows me well, and loves me well.—
translation: There's no man bolder than Lord Hastings. He knows me well, and loves me well.

original: Marry and will, my lord, with all my heart.
translation: Indeed, I will do so with pleasure, my lord.

original: Cousin of Buckingham, a word with you.
translation: Cousin Buckingham, a word with you.

original: [they move aside]   Catesby hath sounded Hastings in our business   And finds the testy gentleman so hot
translation: [They move aside and speak so the others can't hear]  Catesby has sounded Hastings about our business, and he found the quick-tempered gentleman to be so passionately opposed to our plan

original: As he will lose his head ere give consent   His master’s child, as worshipfully he terms it,   Shall lose the royalty of England’s throne.
translation: that—as Hastings devotedly put it—he would lose his head before he'd allow his master's child to lose the throne of England.

original: Withdraw yourself awhile. I’ll go with you.
translation: Go to the next room for a while. I'll go with you.

original: We have not yet set down this day of triumph.
translation: We haven't yet set the date for the triumphant coronation day.

original: Tomorrow, in my judgement, is too sudden,   For I myself am not so well provided   As else I would be, were the day prolonged.
translation: In my opinion, tomorrow is too sudden, for I myself am not as well prepared as I would be if a later date were set.

original: Where is my lord the duke of Gloucester? I have sent for these strawberries.
translation: Where is my lord the Duke of Gloucester? I've sent for those strawberries.

original: His grace looks cheerfully and smooth this morning.   There’s some conceit or other likes him well   When that he bids good morrow with such spirit.
translation: His Grace Richard looks so cheerful and calm this morning. He has some idea or plan that he's pleased about whenever he says "good morning" with such spirit.

original: I think there’s never a man in Christendom   Can lesser hide his love or hate than he,   For by his face straight shall you know his heart.
translation: I don't think there's a man in all the Christian kingdoms who's worse at hiding his love or hate than Richard is. You can know his heart from looking at his face.

original: What of his heart perceive you in his face  By any livelihood he showed today?
translation: And what do you see in his heart today, based on the cheer in his face?

original: Marry, that with no man here he is offended, For were he, he had shown it in his looks.
translation: That he's not offended with any man here. If he were, he would have shown it in his face.

original: I pray God he be not, I say.
translation: I pray to God that you're right.

original: I pray you all, tell me what they deserve   That do conspire my death with devilish plots   Of damnèd witchcraft,
translation: Please tell me, what is the proper punishment for someone who conspires to kill me with wicked plots and witchcraft—

original: and that have prevailed   Upon my body with their hellish charms?
translation: and who has already plagued my body with hellish magic?

original: The tender love I bear your Grace, my lord,   Makes me most forward in this princely presence   To doom th' offenders, whosoe'er they be.
translation: My love for your Grace makes me say forcefully among all these lords that the offenders should be executed.

original: I say, my lord, they have deservèd death.
translation: My lord, they deserve death.

original: Then be your eyes the witness of their evil.
[shows his arm]   Look how I am bewitched! Behold mine arm   Is like a blasted sapling withered up;
translation: [He shows his arm]  See how I am bewitched! Look at how my arm has shriveled up like a withered tree branch.

original: And this is Edward’s wife, that monstrous witch,   Consorted with that harlot, strumpet Shore,   That by their witchcraft thus have markèd me.
translation: This is the work of King Edward's wife Elizabeth—that monstrous witch—and her associate, that whorish Jane Shore. They've done this to me with their witchcraft.

original: If they have done this deed, my noble lord—
translation: If they have done this, my noble lord—

original: If? Thou protector of this damnèd strumpet,   Talk’st thou to me of “ifs?” Thou art a traitor—
translation: "If?" You protector of that damned whore, are you talking to me about "ifs?" You are a traitor.

original: Off with his head. Now by Saint Paul I swear   I will not dine until I see the same.—
translation: Off with his head. By Saint Paul, I swear I won't eat until I see him dead.

original: Woe, woe for England! Not a whit for me,   For I, too fond, might have prevented this.
translation: Woe, woe for England! I pity her fate, but save no pity for myself. I might have prevented this, but I was too foolish.

original: Stanley did dream the boar did raze his helm,   And I did scorn it and disdain to fly.
translation: Stanley dreamed that the boar cut off his head, and I laughed at him and refused to flee.

original: Three times today my foot-cloth horse did stumble,   And started when he looked upon the Tower,   As loath to bear me to the slaughterhouse.   O, now I need the priest that spake to me!
translation: Three times today my horse stumbled, and he bucked when he looked upon the Tower—as if reluctant to carry me to the slaughterhouse. Oh, now I need that priest I spoke to earlier!

original: I now repent I told the pursuivant,   As too triumphing, how mine enemies   Today at Pomfret bloodily were butchered,   And I myself secure in grace and favor.
translation: And now I regret boasting to the pursuivant that my enemies were being butchered at Pomfret while I was safe and secure.

original: O Margaret, Margaret, now thy heavy curse   Is lighted on poor Hastings' wretched head.
translation: Oh, Margaret, Margaret, now your heavy curse has fallen on poor Hastings' wretched head!

original: Come, come, dispatch. The duke would be at dinner.  Make a short shrift. He longs to see your head.
translation: Come, come, that's enough. The duke wants to eat his dinner. Make a quick confession. He's eager to see your head.

original: O momentary grace of mortal men,   Which we more hunt for than the grace of God!
translation: Oh, why do we spend so much time hunting for the temporary approval of mortal men, instead of seeking God's favor?

original: Who builds his hopes in air of your good looks   Lives like a drunken sailor on a mast,   Ready with every nod to tumble down   Into the fatal bowels of the deep.
translation: Anyone who builds his hopes on the airy foundation of mankind's approval must live like a drunken sailor on the ship's mast—ready with every nod of his head to tumble down into the fatal ocean.

original: Come, come, dispatch. 'Tis bootless to exclaim.
translation: Come on, that's enough. It's useless to make speeches.

original: O bloody Richard! Miserable England,   I prophesy the fearfull’st time to thee   That ever wretched age hath looked upon.—
translation: Oh, bloody Richard! Miserable England, I predict that the most frightening time you've ever seen is coming.

original: Come, cousin, canst thou quake and change thy color,   Murder thy breath in the middle of a word,
translation: Come, cousin, can you shake and turn pale, and stop speaking suddenly,

original: And then begin again, and stop again,   As if thou wert distraught and mad with terror?
translation: and then begin again, and then stop again—as if you were driven crazy from terror?

original: Tut, I can counterfeit the deep tragedian,   Speak, and look back, and pry on every side,   Tremble and start at wagging of a straw,   Intending deep suspicion.
translation: Of course, I can imitate the best of tragic actors. I can speak, and then look back, and search all around me, trembling, and jump at the least movement as if I were paranoid.

original: Ghastly looks   Are at my service, like enforcèd smiles,   And both are ready in their offices,   At any time to grace my stratagems.
translation: Frightened looks and forced smiles are both at my service, ready to perform their functions whenever I need them.

original: But what, is Catesby gone?
translation: But what, has Catesby gone?

original: He is; and see, he brings the mayor along.
translation: He has. But see, here he comes with the mayor.

original: Lord Mayor—
translation: Lord Mayor—

original: Look to the drawbridge there!
translation: Look out, the drawbridge!

original: Hark, a drum!
translation: Listen, a drum!

original: Catesby, o'erlook the walls.
translation: Catesby, look out over the walls for us.

original: Lord Mayor, the reason we have sent—
translation: Lord Mayor, the reason we sent—

original: Look back! Defend thee! Here are enemies.
translation: Look behind you! Defend yourself! There are enemies here.

original: God and our innocence defend and guard us!
translation: May God and our own innocence defend us!

original: Be patient. They are friends, Ratcliffe and Lovell.
translation: Calm yourself. These are friends—Ratcliffe and Lovell.

original: Here is the head of that ignoble traitor, The dangerous and unsuspected Hastings.
translation: Here is the head of that wicked traitor, the dangerous and unsuspected Hastings

original: So dear I loved the man that I must weep.
translation: I loved the man so dearly that I must weep.

original: I took him for the plainest harmless creature   That breathed upon this earth a Christian;
translation: I took him to be the most honest, harmless Christian that ever walked the earth.

original: Made him my book, wherein my soul recorded   The history of all her secret thoughts.
translation: I made him like my diary, and trusted him with all my soul's most secret thoughts.

original: So smooth he daubed his vice with show of virtue   That, his apparent open guilt omitted—
translation: He covered his wickedness with a virtuous facade so well that, if his guilt hadn't become apparent—

original: I mean his conversation with Shore’s wife—   He lived from all attainder of suspects.
translation: I mean his affair with Shore's wife—I never would have suspected him.

original: Well, well, he was the covert’st sheltered traitor That ever lived.
translation: Well, well, he was the most secretive, hidden traitor that ever lived.

original: [to the MAYOR]   Would you imagine, or almost believe,   Were ’t not that by great preservation   We live to tell it,
translation: Can you imagine, Lord Mayor—if we hadn't been lucky enough to stop him—

original: that subtle traitor   This day had plotted, in the council house   To murder me and my good Lord of Gloucester?
translation: that sneaky traitor was plotting to murder me and the Lord of Gloucester in the council room today?

original: Had he done so?
translation: Is that true?

original: What, think you we are Turks or infidels?
translation: What, do you think we're heathens or savages?

original: Or that we would, against the form of law,   Proceed thus rashly in the villain’s death,   But that the extreme peril of the case,
translation: You think that we would have broken the law and executed this villain unless it was a case of extreme danger,

original: The peace of England and our persons' safety   Enforced us to this execution?
translation: with England's peace and our own lives at stake?

original: Now fair befall you! He deserved his death,   And your good Graces both have well proceeded   To warn false traitors from the like attempts.
translation: May only good things happen to you from now on! He deserved to die, and your Graces did well in making an example of him and discouraging other false traitors from attempting similar plots.

original: Yet had we not determined he should die   Until your Lordship came to see his end
translation: Yes, but we had decided that he shouldn't die until you, Lord Mayor, were able to come and witness his execution.

original: (Which now the loving haste of these our friends,   Something against our meaning, have prevented),
translation: But this was prevented by the loving haste of our friends, Lovell and Ratcliffe, who went slightly against our intentions by executing him so soon.

original: Because, my lord, I would have had you heard   The traitor speak, and timorously confess   The manner and the purpose of his treasons,
translation: My lord, if you could have heard the traitor speak—and fearfully confess his plots of treason—

original: That you might well have signified the same   Unto the citizens, who haply may   Misconstrue us in him, and wail his death.
translation: then you could have told the citizens what you heard. However, as it is now, they're likely to misunderstand our methods of dealing with Hastings, and mourn his death.

original: But, my good lord, your Graces' words shall serve   As well as I had seen and heard him speak;
translation: But, my good lord, your Graces' words are just as trustworthy as if I had seen him and heard him myself.

original: And do not doubt, right noble princes both,   But I’ll acquaint our duteous citizens   With all your just proceedings in this case.
translation: And don't worry, you noble princes. I'll tell our citizens about how fairly you dealt with this case.

original: And to that end we wished your Lordship here T' avoid the censures of the carping world.
translation: That is why we wanted you here, your Lordship—to avoid the condemnation of the critical public.

original: Which since you come too late of our intent, Yet witness what you hear we did intend. And so, my good Lord Mayor, we bid farewell.
translation: But since you came too late to see the execution as we intended, at least bear witness t our good intentions. And so, my good Lord Mayor, we bid you farewell.

original: Go, after, after, cousin Buckingham.   The mayor towards Guildhall hies him in all post.
translation: Go after him, cousin Buckingham. He's riding quickly to the town hall.

original: There, at your meetest vantage of the time,   Infer the bastardy of Edward’s children.
translation: There, at the most advantageous moment, bring up the possibility that King Edward's children are illegitimate.

original: Tell them how Edward put to death a citizen   Only for saying he would make his son   Heir to the Crown—meaning indeed his house,   Which, by the sign thereof, was termèd so.
translation: Tell the public how Edward executed a citizen just for saying that he would make his son "heir to the crown"—when he was only talking about the tavern he owned, "The Crown."

original: Moreover, urge his hateful luxury   And bestial appetite in change of lust,   Which stretched to their servants, daughters, wives,   Even where his raging eye or savage heart,   Without control, lusted to make his prey.
translation: And then bring up Edward's hateful lust and his insatiable appetite for women, which stretched even to the citizens' servants, daughters, and wives—anyone that his lustful eye and savage heart wanted to prey on.

original: Nay, for a need, thus far come near my person:   Tell them when that my mother went with child   Of that insatiate Edward,
translation: If you need to, you can even bring  me  up: tell them that when my mother became pregnant with that insatiable Edward,

original: noble York   My princely father then had wars in France,
translation: my noble father York was away fighting wars in France.

original: And, by true computation of the time,   Found that the issue was not his begot,   Which well appearèd in his lineaments,   Being nothing like the noble duke my father.
translation: If you calculate the time of Edward's birth, and consider the fact that he looks nothing like my father, then it's clear that he's not my father's true son.

original: Yet touch this sparingly, as ’twere far off,   Because, my lord, you know my mother lives.
translation: But only vaguely touch on that subject. For, as you know, my lord, my mother is still alive.

original: Doubt not, my lord. I’ll play the orator As if the golden fee for which I plead  Were for myself. And so, my lord, adieu.
translation: Don't worry, my lord. I'll speak as persuasively as if I were trying to win the throne for myself. And so farewell, my lord.

original: If you thrive well, bring them to Baynard’s Castle, Where you shall find me well accompanied With reverend fathers and well-learnèd bishops.
translation: If things go well, bring the citizens to my estate at Baynard's Castle. There you'll find me accompanied by priests and bishops.

original: I go; and towards three or four o'clock  Look for the news that the Guildhall affords.
translation: I'll go now. At around three or four o'clock you should expect the news from the town hall.

original: Go, Lovell, with all speed to Doctor Shaw.     Go thou to Friar Penker. Bid them both Meet me within this hour at Baynard’s Castle.
translation: Lovell, go as quickly as you can to the Mayor's brother, Doctor Shaw.

original: Now will I go to take some privy order   To draw the brats of Clarence out of sight,
translation: Now I'll go and make some secret arrangement to keep Clarence's brats out of sight.

original: And to give order that no manner of person   Have any time recourse unto the princes.
translation: And I'll give orders that no one is to see King Edward's sons.

original: This is the indictment of the good Lord Hastings,   Which in a set hand fairly is engrossed,   That it may be today read o'er in Paul’s.
translation: This here is the indictment of the good Lord Hastings. It's been written neatly in a formal, legal hand, so that it can be read aloud today in Saint Paul's Cathedral.

original: And mark how well the sequel hangs together:   Eleven hours I have spent to write it over,
translation: But see how well the sequence of events holds together: last night, Catesby brought me the indictment, and it took me eleven hours to copy it all out.

original: For yesternight by Catesby was it sent me;   The precedent was full as long a-doing,   And yet within these five hours Hastings lived,   Untainted, unexamined, free, at liberty.
translation: The original indictment must have taken just as long to write. And yet, five hours, earlier Lord Hastings was alive, innocent, free, and at liberty.

original: Here’s a good world the while. Who is so gross   That cannot see this palpable device?
translation: What a world we live in now! Who is so stupid that he can't see this obvious trickery?

original: Yet who so bold but says he sees it not?
translation: And yet who is bold enough to speak out against it?

original: How now, how now? What say the citizens?
translation: Tell me, tell me, what did the citizens say?

original: Now, by the holy mother of our Lord, The citizens are mum, say not a word.
translation: I swear by the holy mother of our Lord—the citizens didn't say a word.

original: Touched you the bastardy of Edward’s children?
translation: Did you mention that Edward's children are bastards?

original: I did, with his contract with Lady Lucy   And his contract by deputy in France;
translation: I did. I brought up his earlier engagements—to Lady Lucy, who bore him a child, and Lady Bona in France.

original: Th' unsatiate greediness of his desire   And his enforcement of the city wives;
translation: And I described the insatiable greediness of his lust, and his rape of citizens' wives.

original: His tyranny for trifles; his own bastardy,   As being got, your father then in France,   His resemblance being not like the duke.
translation: I reminded them of his harsh punishments for trivial offenses, and said that he was nothing like the duke your father, as the duke was away in France when Edward was conceived.

original: Withal, I did infer your lineaments,   Being the right idea of your father,   Both in your form and nobleness of mind;
translation: Then I brought up your own appearance and suggested that you were the spitting image of your father, both in your looks and in your noble mind.

original: Laid open all your victories in Scotland,   Your discipline in war, wisdom in peace,   Your bounty, virtue, fair humility;
translation: I described all your victories in Scotland, your discipline in battle, your wisdom in peacetime, your generosity, your virtue, and your noble humility.

original: Indeed, left nothing fitting for your purpose   Untouched or slightly handled in discourse.
translation: Indeed, I didn't leave out anything that might have helped your case at all.

original: And when mine oratory grew toward end,   I bid them that did love their country’s good   Cry “God save Richard, England’s royal king!”
translation: And then when my speech came to an end, I asked those who loved their country to cry, "God save Richard, England's royal king!"

original: And did they so?
translation: And did they do it?

original: No. So God help me, they spake not a word   But, like dumb statues or breathing stones,
translation: No. So help me God, they didn't say a word, but just sat there like silent statues or breathing stones.

original: Stared each on other and looked deadly pale;   Which when I saw, I reprehended them   And asked the mayor what meant this willful silence.
translation: They looked at each other and turned deadly pale, and when I saw this, I scolded them and asked the mayor what they meant by this stubborn silence.

original: His answer was, the people were not used   To be spoke to but by the recorder.
translation: The mayor said that the citizens weren't used to being spoken to except by the town's official recorder.

original: Then he was urged to tell my tale again:   “Thus saith the duke. Thus hath the duke inferred”—   But nothing spoke in warrant from himself.
translation: So I made the recorder repeat my tale. Everything was "the duke said this" and "the duke means that," and he added nothing of his own opinion.

original: When he had done, some followers of mine own,   At the lower end of the hall, hurled up their caps,   And some ten voices cried “God save King Richard!”
translation: When he was done, some of my own followers at the end of the hall threw their caps in the air, and ten or so voices cried, "God save King Richard!"

original: And thus I took the vantage of those few.   “Thanks, gentle citizens and friends,” quoth I.
translation: So I pounced on that feeble opportunity and said, "Thank you, noble citizens and friends.

original: "This general applause and cheerful shout   Argues your wisdoms and your love to Richard"—   And even here brake off, and came away.
translation: This public applause and joyful shouting clearly shows your wisdom and your love for Richard." And then I broke off my speech, and came straight here.

original: What tongueless blocks were they! Would not they speak? Will not the mayor then and his brethren come?
translation: What tongueless blockheads! Why wouldn't they speak? Will the mayor and his fellow citizens not come here?

original: The Mayor is here at hand. Intend some fear;   Be not you spoke with but by mighty suit.
translation: The mayor is on his way and nearly here. Pretend to be afraid, and don't let yourself be spoken to until we plead with you.

original: And look you get a prayer book in your hand   And stand between two churchmen, good my lord,   For on that ground I’ll make a holy descant
translation: And get a prayer book in your hand and stand between two priests, my good lord. I'll use that to improvise an argument for your holiness.

original: And be not easily won to our requests.   Play the maid’s part: still answer “nay,” and take it.
translation: But don't be easily won over by our requests to be king. Be like a coy virgin: refuse for a long time, and then finally accept.

original: I go. An if you plead as well for them As I can say “nay” to thee for myself, No doubt we bring it to a happy issue.
translation: I'm going now. If you're as good at pleading on their behalf as I am at saying "no" to you, then there's no doubt this will end well.

original: Go, go, up to the leads. The Lord Mayor knocks.
translation: Go, go, up to the roof. The Lord Mayor knocks.

original: Welcome, my lord. I dance attendance here. I think the duke will not be spoke withal.
translation: Welcome, my lord. I'm just entertaining myself and waiting for an audience with the duke. I don't think he wants to be spoken to.

original: Now, Catesby, what says your lord to my request?
translation: Now, Catesby, what does your lord say to my request?

original: He doth entreat your Grace, my noble lord,   To visit him tomorrow or next day.
translation: My noble lord, he asks your Grace to please visit him tomorrow or the next day. He is inside with two priests, deep in prayer.

original: He is within, with two right reverend fathers,   Divinely bent to meditation,   And in no worldly suits would he be moved   To draw him from his holy exercise.
translation: He doesn't want to be disturbed from his holy labors by any worldly business.

original: Return, good Catesby, to the gracious duke.
translation: Return, good Catesby, to the gracious duke.

original: Tell him myself, the mayor, and aldermen,   No less importing than our general good,   In deep designs, and matters of great moment   Are come to have some conference with his grace.
translation: Tell him that I, the mayor, and some citizens have come to confer with his Grace about matters of great importance, which concern the good of all.

original: I’ll signify so much unto him straight.
translation: I'll tell him that right away.

original: Ah, ha, my lord, this prince is not an Edward!
translation: Aha, my lord, this prince is not an Edward!

original: He is not lolling on a lewd love bed,   But on his knees at meditation;
translation: He's not lolling about in a lustful bed, but on his knees in prayer;

original: Not dallying with a brace of courtesans,   But meditating with two deep divines;
translation: not enjoying himself with a few prostitutes, but praying with two learned priests;

original: Not sleeping, to engross his idle body,   But praying, to enrich his watchful soul.
translation: not sleeping to fatten up his lazy body, but praying to enrich his attentive soul.

original: Happy were England would this virtuous prince   Take on his grave the sovereignty thereof.
translation: England would be blessed to have this virtuous prince wearing its crown.

original: But sure I fear we shall not win him to it.
translation: But I'm afraid he won't agree to it.

original: Marry, God defend his grace should say us nay!
translation: Indeed, God forbid that he should say no to us!

original: I fear he will. Here Catesby comes again.
translation: I fear that he will. Here comes Catesby again.

original: Now, Catesby, what says his grace?
translation: Now, Catesby, what does his Grace say?

original: He wonders to what end you have assembled   Such troops of citizens to come to him,   His grace not being warned thereof before.
translation: He wonders why you have assembled such a large group of citizens to come to him without warning him beforehand.

original: He fears, my lord, you mean no good to him.
translation: He fears that you mean him harm, my lord.

original: Sorry I am my noble cousin should   Suspect me that I mean no good to him.
translation: I'm sorry that my noble cousin should suspect that I wish him harm.

original: By heaven, we come to him in perfect love,   And so once more return and tell his grace.
translation: By heaven, we are here because we love him. Go back and tell him.

original: When holy and devout religious men Are at their beads, ’tis much to draw them thence, So sweet is zealous contemplation.
translation: When holy and devout religious men are praying, it takes a great deal to draw them away, because they are so wrapped up in their eager contemplation of God.

original: See where his Grace stands, ’tween two clergymen.
translation: See where his Grace is standing—between two clergymen.

original: Two props of virtue for a Christian prince,   To stay him from the fall of vanity;
translation: They are like two virtuous supports for a Christian prince, to prevent him from the downfall of vanity.

original: And, see, a book of prayer in his hand,   True ornaments to know a holy man.—
translation: And see, he has a prayer book in his hand. These are the accessories of a holy man.

original: My lord, there needs no such apology.   I do beseech your Grace pardon me,
translation: My lord, there's no need for such an apology. I ask your Grace to pardon me instead.

original: Who, earnest in the service of my God,   Deferred the visitation of my friends.   But, leaving this, what is your Grace’s pleasure?
translation: I've been so focused on serving God that I kept my friends waiting. But aside from this, what is it you want?

original: Even that, I hope, which pleaseth God above  And all good men of this ungoverned isle.
translation: Only that which will, I hope, please God above, and all good men of this ungoverned island.

original: I do suspect I have done some offense That seems disgracious in the city’s eye, And that you come to reprehend my ignorance.
translation: I suspect that I've committed some offense that the citizens disapprove of, and you've come to reprimand me for my ignorance.

original: You have, my lord. Would it might please your Grace,  On our entreaties, to amend your fault.
translation: You have, my lord. If it would please your Grace, you should listen to our request and make up for your offense.

original: Else wherefore breathe I in a Christian land?
translation: Why else would I live in a Christian country, if I can't be forgiven for my faults?

original: Know, then, it is your fault that you resign   The supreme seat, the throne majestical,   The sceptered office of your ancestors,
translation: Know, then, that it is your fault that you've given up the supreme seat, the majestic throne, the powerful office of your ancestors,

original: Your state of fortune, and your due of birth,   The lineal glory of your royal house,   To the corruption of a blemished stock,
translation: your position of greatness, and the glory of your royal family—all of which are yours by birth.  And instead you've handed it over to a corrupted, impure usurper.

original: Whiles in the mildness of your sleepy thoughts,   Which here we waken to our country’s good,
translation: You have been lost in prayer and dreamy contemplation, but now we've come to alert you of your country's needs.

original: The noble isle doth want her proper limbs—   Her face defaced with scars of infamy,   Her royal stock graft with ignoble plants,
translation: Our noble island wants her true self back—her face has been scarred by Edward's infamous deeds, and her royal family has been corrupted by ignoble outsiders.

original: And almost shouldered in the swallowing gulf   Of dark forgetfulness and deep oblivion;
translation: Its majesty is almost lost in an abyss of dark forgetfulness and deep oblivion.

original: Which to recure, we heartily solicit   Your gracious self to take on you the charge   And kingly government of this your land,
translation: To fix this situation, we beg your Grace to take charge and become king of this land—

original: Not as Protector, steward, substitute,   Or lowly factor for another’s gain,   But as successively, from blood to blood,   Your right of birth, your empery, your own.
