translation: not Lord Protector, steward, substitute, or lowly agent to another ruler, but king, the successor of a noble bloodline. This is your right by birth, your empire, your own.

original: For this, consorted with the citizens,   Your very worshipful and loving friends,   And by their vehement instigation,   In this just suit come I to move your Grace.
translation: It's for this purpose that I have come with these citizens—who are your devoted and loving friends, and vehemently begged me to do this—to try and convince your Grace to accept our plea.

original: I cannot tell if to depart in silence   Or bitterly to speak in your reproof   Best fitteth my degree or your condition.
translation: I can't decide if I should leave in silence or bitterly scold you. I don't know which response is more appropriate to my rank and your social position.

original: If not to answer, you might haply think   Tongue-tied ambition, not replying, yielded   To bear the golden yoke of sovereignty,   Which fondly you would here impose on me.
translation: If I say nothing, you might think that my silence means consent, and you'll assume that I agree to bear the golden burden of responsibility that you're foolishly trying to impose on me.

original: If to reprove you for this suit of yours,   So seasoned with your faithful love to me,   Then on the other side I checked my friends.
translation: But if I scold you for this request just after you've proven your faithful love for me, then I would be guilty of rebuking my friends.

original: Therefore, to speak, and to avoid the first,   And then, in speaking, not to incur the last,   Definitively thus I answer you:
translation: Therefore I will speak, and so avoid the first possibility, but with my words I will avoid the second. So this is my answer, once and for all:

original: Your love deserves my thanks, but my desert   Unmeritable shuns your high request.
translation: I thank you for your love, but I don't deserve to be king. So I must turn down your noble request.

original: First, if all obstacles were cut away   And that my path were even to the crown   As the ripe revenue and due of birth,
translation: Even if all obstacles were removed and my path led straight to the crown—my proper birthright—

original: Yet so much is my poverty of spirit,   So mighty and so many my defects,   That I would rather hide me from my greatness,
translation: my poverty of spirit and my many other flaws would still make me prefer to hide from my greatness, rather than be swallowed up by it and be smothered in glory.

original: Being a bark to brook no mighty sea,   Than in my greatness covet to be hid   And in the vapor of my glory smothered.
translation: I am only a small boat, unprepared for the stormy sea of kingship.

original: But, God be thanked, there is no need of me,   And much I need to help you, were there need.
translation: But, thank God, there is no need for me to rule.

original: The royal tree hath left us royal fruit,   Which, mellowed by the stealing hours of time,   Will well become the seat of majesty,   And make, no doubt, us happy by his reign.
translation: The royal tree has left us royal fruit, which, with time, will fit the throne well, and make us all happy as our king.

original: On him I lay what you would lay on me,   The right and fortune of his happy stars,   Which God defend that I should wring from him.
translation: I lay on him the responsibility you want to lay on me, as it is his birthright and his happy destiny. God forbid that I should steal the crown from him.

original: My lord, this argues conscience in your Grace,   But the respects thereof are nice and trivial,   All circumstances well considerèd.
translation: My lord, your response shows that you have a strong conscience, but your objections are trivial, especially considering the circumstances.

original: You say that Edward is your brother’s son;   So say we too, but not by Edward’s wife.
translation: You say that Prince Edward is your brother's son. We agree, but not by your brother's wife.

original: For first was he contract to Lady Lucy—   Your mother lives a witness to that vow—   And afterward by substitute betrothed   To Bona, sister to the king of France.
translation: King Edward was first engaged to Lady Lucy—and your mother lives as a witness to this—and after that he was betrothed to Lady Bona, the King of France's sister-in-law.

original: These both put off, a poor petitioner,   A care-crazed mother to a many sons,   A beauty-waning and distressèd widow,   Even in the afternoon of her best days,   Made prize and purchase of his wanton eye,   Seduced the pitch and height of his degree   To base declension and loathed bigamy.
translation: But when both these engagements failed, Elizabeth Grey—a harried mother of many sons, a poor widow losing her former beauty, a woman past her prime—took advantage of his lust and seduced him away from his role of majesty.

original: By her in his unlawful bed he got   This Edward, whom our manners term “the Prince.”   More bitterly could I expostulate,
translation: She led him to drop his standards and commit adultery with her. With him she conceived this illegitimate Edward, whom we now politely call "the Prince."

original: Save that, for reverence to some alive,   I give a sparing limit to my tongue.
translation: I could describe even worse things, too, but I'll restrain myself out of respect for some who are still alive.

original: Then, good my lord, take to your royal self   This proffered benefit of dignity,   If not to bless us and the land withal,   Yet to draw forth your noble ancestry   From the corruption of abusing times   Unto a lineal, true-derivèd course.
translation: Therefore, my good lord, even if you don't want to bless us and the land with your rule, then at least accept this offered crown to rescue your noble family from its current corruption .  Return the line of hereditary kingship to a true, straight course.

original: Do, good my lord. Your citizens entreat you.
translation: Do accept, my lord. Your citizens beg you.

original: Refuse not, mighty lord, this proffered love.
translation: Don't refuse this love we offer you, mighty lord.

original: O, make them joyful. Grant their lawful suit.
translation: Oh, make them joyful. Grant their request!

original: Alas, why would you heap this care on me?   I am unfit for state and majesty.
translation: Alas, why would you heap this responsibility on me? I am unfit for power and majesty.

original: I do beseech you, take it not amiss;   I cannot, nor I will not, yield to you.
translation: Don't take this the wrong way, but I cannot and will not give in to you.

original: If you refuse it, as in love and zeal   Loath to depose the child, your brother’s son—   As well we know your tenderness of heart
translation: If you're refusing this out of love and family honor, because you're reluctant to depose the child, your brother's son— we all know how tender your heart is.

original: And gentle, kind, effeminate remorse,   Which we have noted in you to your kindred   And equally indeed to all estates—
translation: We know what gentle, kind, and tearful feelings you have for your relatives, and indeed for people of any rank and status.

original: Yet know whe'er you accept our suit or no,   Your brother’s son shall never reign our king,   But we will plant some other in the throne,   To the disgrace and downfall of your house.
translation: But know this: whether or not you accept our request, your brother's son will never be our king. We'll find someone else to take the throne, to the disgrace and downfall of your family.

original: And in this resolution here we leave you.—
translation: And with this we leave you.

original: O, do not swear, my lord of Buckingham!
translation: Oh, do not swear, my lord of Buckingham!

original: Call them again, sweet prince. Accept their suit. If you deny them, all the land will rue it.
translation: Call them back, sweet prince. Accept their request. If you deny them, the whole country will regret it.

original: Will you enforce me to a world of cares?   Call them again.
translation: Would you force me into a world of worries?  Call them back then.

original: I am not made of stones,   But penetrable to your kind entreaties,   Albeit against my conscience and my soul.
translation: I am not made of stone. I can be persuaded by these kind pleas, even though it goes against my conscience and my soul.

original: Cousin of Buckingham and sage, grave men,   Since you will buckle fortune on my back,   To bear her burden, whe'er I will or no,   I must have patience to endure the load;
translation: Cousin Buckingham and you wise, solemn men, since you intend to force the crown onto my head—to bear its burden whether I want to or not—then I must have the patience to endure the load.

original: But if black scandal or foul-faced reproach   Attend the sequel of your imposition,   Your mere enforcement shall acquittance me   From all the impure blots and stains thereof,
translation: But if any foul scandal or ugly criticism comes of this, the mere fact that you forced me to accept must clear me from any future blame.

original: For God doth know, and you may partly see,   How far I am from the desire of this.
translation: For God knows, and you can see, how reluctant I am to accept this responsibility.

original: God bless your Grace! We see it and will say it.
translation: God bless your Grace! We will bear witness to the fact that you didn't want the crown.

original: In saying so, you shall but say the truth.
translation: And in saying so, you'll only be telling the truth.

original: Then I salute you with this royal title:  Long live Richard, England’s worthy king!
translation: Then I salute you with this royal title: Long live Richard, England's worthy king!

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: Tomorrow will it please you to be crowned?
translation: Will you let yourself be crowned tomorrow?

original: Even when you please, since you will have it so.
translation: Whenever you want, since you will insist on it.

original: Tomorrow, then, we will attend your Grace,  And so most joyfully we take our leave.
translation: Tomorrow, then. We will wait on your Grace. And now we joyfully bid you farewell.

original: Come, let us to our holy task again.— Farewell, my cousin. Farewell, gentle friends.
translation: Come, let us return to our holy labors.

original: Who meets us here? My niece Plantagenet   Led in the hand of her kind aunt of Gloucester?
translation: Who is this? My granddaughter Plantagenet, led by the hand of her kind aunt, the Duchess of Gloucester?

original: Now, for my life, she’s wandering to the Tower,   On pure heart’s love, to greet the tender prince.—
translation: Now, I swear, she's heading to the Tower to greet the young prince, whom she loves so purely.

original: God give your Graces both A happy and a joyful time of day.
translation: May God grant both of you a nice day.

original: As much to you, good sister. Whither away?
translation: And you too, good sister-in-law. Where are you off to?

original: No farther than the Tower, and, as I guess, Upon the like devotion as yourselves,  To gratulate the gentle princes there.
translation: Just to the Tower. And I can guess that I'm going for the same reason you are: to greet the gentle princes who are staying there.

original: Kind sister, thanks. We’ll enter all together.
translation: Kind sister-in-law, thanks. We'll all go together.

original: And in good time here the lieutenant comes.— Master Lieutenant, pray you, by your leave, How doth the prince and my young son of York?
translation: And here comes the lieutenant, right on time.

original: Right well, dear madam. By your patience, I may not suffer you to visit them. The king hath strictly charged the contrary.
translation: They are well, dear madam. But if you'll pardon me, I'm not allowed to let you visit them. The king has strictly forbidden it.

original: The king? Who’s that?
translation: The king? Who's that?

original: I mean, the Lord Protector.
translation: I mean the Lord Protector.

original: The Lord protect him from that kingly title!  Hath he set bounds between their love and me? I am their mother. Who shall bar me from them?
translation: And may the Lord protect the crown from him! Is he trying to set up barriers between my children and me? I am their mother. Who will forbid me from seeing them?

original: I am their father’s mother. I will see them.
translation: I am their father's mother. I will see them.

original: Their aunt I am in law, in love their mother. Then bring me to their sights. I’ll bear thy blame  And take thy office from thee, on my peril.
translation: I am their aunt by marriage, but I love them like a mother. Bring me to see them. I'll take your office upon myself, Lieutenant—and take all the blame as well.

original: No, madam, no. I may not leave it so. I am bound by oath, and therefore pardon me.
translation: No, madam, no. I cannot do that. I am bound by oath, so you must forgive me.

original: Let me but meet you ladies one hour hence,   And I’ll salute your Grace of York as mother   And reverend looker-on, of two fair queens.
translation: If I were greeting you ladies again in just an hour, I would be saluting you, Duchess of York, as the mother of two fair queens.

original: Ah, cut my lace asunder that my pent heart  May have some scope to beat, or else I swoon  With this dead-killing news!
translation: Oh, cut my dress open so that my constrained heart can have some room to beat, or else I'll faint from this deadly news!

original: Despiteful tidings! O, unpleasing news!
translation: Cruel tidings! Oh, unhappy news!

original: Be of good cheer, mother. How  fares  your Grace?
translation: Cheer up, mother. How are you feeling?

original: O Dorset, speak not to me. Get thee gone.   Death and destruction dogs thee at thy heels.
translation: Oh Dorset, don't speak to me. Leave immediately. Death and destruction are snapping at your heels.

original: Thy mother’s name is ominous to children.   If thou wilt outstrip death, go, cross the seas,   And live with Richmond, from the reach of hell.
translation: Your mother's name has become a bad omen. If you want to outrun death, then go. Cross the seas to France, and live with  Richmond , out of the reach of hell.

original: Go, hie thee, hie thee from this slaughterhouse,   Lest thou increase the number of the dead
translation: Go, run away. Run away from this slaughterhouse, before you end up a body increasing the number of the dead,

original: And make me die the thrall of Margaret’s curse,   Nor mother, wife, nor England’s counted queen.
translation: and make me die the slave of Margaret's curse— neither wife, nor mother, nor England's queen.

original: Full of wise care is this your counsel, madam.     Take all the swift advantage of the hours. You shall have letters from me to my son  In your behalf, to meet you on the way. Be not ta'en tardy by unwise delay.
translation: Madam, your advice is full of wisdom and caring.

original: O ill-dispersing wind of misery! O my accursèd womb, the bed of death! A cockatrice hast thou hatched to the world,  Whose unavoided eye is murderous.
Come, madam, come. I in all haste was sent.
translation: Come, madam, come. I was sent in a great hurry.

original: And I in all unwillingness will go.   O, would to God that the inclusive verge   Of golden metal that must round my brow   Were red-hot steel to sear me to the brains!
translation: And with great unwillingness I'll go. Oh, I wish to God that the golden crown I must wear would turn to red-hot steel, and burn my skull to the brains!

original: Anointed let me be with deadly venom,   And die ere men can say, “God save the Queen.”
translation: Let me be anointed with deadly venom instead of holy oil, so I can die before anyone manages to say, "God save the Queen!"

original: Go, go, poor soul, I envy not thy glory. To feed my humor, wish thyself no harm.
translation: Go, go, poor soul. I don't envy your new throne. But make me happy by not wishing harm on yourself.

original: No? Why? When he that is my husband now   Came to me, as I followed Henry’s corse,   When scarce the blood was well washed from his hands   Which issued from my other angel husband
translation: No? Why not? Richard—who is now my husband—first came to me when he'd hardly washed all the blood off his hands from killing both my first, angelic husband and my husband's father—

original: And that dear saint which then I weeping followed—   O, when, I say, I looked on Richard’s face,   This was my wish: be thou, quoth I, accursed   For making me, so young, so old a widow;
translation: that dear saint Henry—whose corpse I was tearfully following. Oh, I tell you, when I looked at Richard's face then, my only wish was this: "May you be cursed for making me a widow so young.

original: And, when thou wedd’st, let sorrow haunt thy bed;   And be thy wife, if any be so mad,   More miserable by the life of thee   Than thou hast made me by my dear lord’s death.
translation: When you get married, let sorrow haunt your bed, and may your wife—if any woman is crazy enough to marry you—be made more miserable by your life than you've made me by my dear husband's death."

original: Lo, ere I can repeat this curse again,   Within so small a time my woman’s heart   Grossly grew captive to his honey words   And proved the subject of mine own soul’s curse,
translation: But alas! Before I could even repeat my curse again, my woman's heart stupidly fell prey to his honeyed words. I then proved the victim of my own soul's curse.

original: Which hitherto hath held my eyes from rest,   For never yet one hour in his bed   Did I enjoyed the golden dew of sleep,   But with his timorous dreams was still awaked.
translation: From then on, I haven't had one hour of precious sleep in his bed without being awakened by the sounds of his nightmares.

original: Besides, he hates me for my father Warwick,   And will, no doubt, shortly be rid of me.
translation: It doesn't matter, though—Richard hates me because of my father, Warwick, who was his enemy. He'll soon get rid of me, no doubt.

original: Poor heart, adieu. I pity thy complaining.
translation: Poor heart, farewell. I pity your troubles.

original: No more than from my soul I mourn for yours.
translation: No more than I mourn for yours, from the depths of my soul.

original: Farewell, thou woeful welcomer of glory.
translation: Farewell, you sad new queen.

original: Adieu, poor soul that tak’st thy leave of it.
translation: And farewell to you, sad old queen.

original: [to DORSET]   Go thou to Richmond, and good fortune guide thee.
translation: [To DORSET]  You go to Richmond, and may good fortune go with you.

original: Stay, yet look back with me unto the Tower.—
translation: Wait, and look back at the Tower with me.

original: Pity, you ancient stones, those tender babes   Whom envy hath immured within your walls—
translation: You ancient stones of the Tower, have pity on those tender children who are locked inside your walls because of envy.

original: Rough cradle for such little pretty ones.
translation: You are a rough cradle for such little pretty ones.

original: Rude ragged nurse, old sullen playfellow   For tender princes, use my babies well.
translation: You rude, ragged nurse; you old, sullen playmate for tender princes—treat my babies well.

original: So foolish sorrows bids your stones farewell.
translation: And so I bid your stones farewell, you Tower, with all my foolish sorrow.

original: Stand all apart. —Cousin of Buckingham.
translation: Everyone stand aside.

original: My gracious sovereign.
translation: My gracious sovereign.

original: Give me thy hand.
translation: Give me your hand.

original: Thus high, by thy advice   And thy assistance is King Richard seated.
translation: I now have this high seat as King Richard because of your advice and assistance.

original: But shall we wear these glories for a day,   Or shall they last and we rejoice in them?
translation: But will I have these glories for a day only, or will they last long enough for me to enjoy them?

original: Still live they, and forever let them last.
translation: May they live on forever.

original: Ah, Buckingham, now do I play the touch,  To try if thou be current gold indeed. Young Edward lives; think now what I would speak.
translation: Ah, Buckingham, now I must test you to see if you're true gold indeed. Young Prince Edward is alive. Think about what I might say next.

original: Say on, my loving lord.
translation: Go on, my loving lord.

original: Why, Buckingham, I say I would be king,
translation: Why, Buckingham, I said I wanted to be king.

original: Why so you are, my thrice-renownèd lord.
translation: Why, you are king, my glorious lord.

original: Ha! Am I king? 'Tis so—but Edward lives.
translation: Ha! Am I king? Perhaps it's so—but Edward still lives.

original: True, noble prince.
translation: True, noble prince.

original: O bitter consequence   That Edward still should live “true noble prince!”   Cousin, thou wast not wont to be so dull.
translation: Oh, what a bitter conclusion that Edward should still live as the "true, noble prince!" Cousin, you didn't use to be so stupid.

original: Shall I be plain? I wish the bastards dead,   And I would have it suddenly performed.
translation: Shall I speak plainly? I want the bastards dead, and I want it done immediately.

original: What sayest thou now? Speak suddenly. Be brief.
translation: What do you say now? Speak quickly, and be brief.

original: Your Grace may do your pleasure.
translation: Your Grace can do as he pleases.

original: Tut, tut, thou art all ice; thy kindness freezes. Say, have I thy consent that they shall die?
translation: Tut, tut, you've grown icy. Your kindness freezes over. Tell me, do you agree that they must die?

original: Give me some little breath, some pause, dear lord, Before I positively speak in this. I will resolve you herein presently.
translation: Give me a moment to breathe, dear lord, a pause before I make a statement. I'll give you my answer shortly.

original: The king is angry. See, he gnaws his lip.
translation: The king is angry. See how he bites his lip.

original: [aside]   I will converse with iron-witted fools   And unrespective boys.
translation: [To himself]  I only want to deal with unfeeling fools and careless boys.

original: None are for me   That look into me with considerate eyes.
translation: I want nothing to do with anyone who can read me well.

original: High-reaching Buckingham grows circumspect.—
translation: Ambitious Buckingham is growing too thoughtful.

original: My lord?
translation: My lord?

original: Know’st thou not any whom corrupting gold Will tempt unto a close exploit of death?
translation: Do you know anyone who can be tempted with gold into secretly killing someone?

original: I know a discontented gentleman   Whose humble means match not his haughty spirit.
translation: I know one unhappy gentleman whose empty wallet doesn't match his proud spirit.

original: Gold were as good as twenty orators,   And will, no doubt, tempt him to anything.
translation: Gold is better than twenty speeches, and will, no doubt, tempt him to do anything.

original: What is his name?
translation: What is his name?

original: His name, my lord, is Tyrrel.
translation: His name is Tyrrel, my lord.

original: I partly know the man. Go, call him hither, boy
translation: I know the man a little. Go, call him here, boy.

original: [aside]   The deep-revolving witty Buckingham   No more shall be the neighbor to my counsels
translation: [To himself]  The deep-thinking, clever Buckingham will no longer be privy to my plots.

original: Hath he so long held out with me, untired,   And stops he now for breath? Well, be it so.
translation: Has he run with me for so long, only to stop for a "moment to breathe" now? Well, so be it.

original: How now, Lord Stanley, what’s the news?
translation: Hello, Lord Stanley, what's the news?

original: Know, my loving lord, The marquess Dorset, as I hear, is fled  To Richmond, in the parts where he abides.
translation: You should know, my loving lord: I've heard that the Marquess of Dorset has fled to Richmond in France.

original: Come hither, Catesby. Rumor it abroad   That Anne my wife is very grievous sick.
translation: Come here, Catesby. Spread around a rumor that my wife Anne is very sick.

original: I will take order for her keeping close.   Enquire me out some mean poor gentleman,   Whom I will marry straight to Clarence' daughter.
translation: I will make arrangements for keeping her locked up. And find me some poor gentleman whom I can marry straight away to Clarence's daughter.

original: The boy is foolish, and I fear not him.   Look how thou dream’st! I say again, give out   That Anne my queen is sick and like to die.
translation: Clarence's son is an idiot, so I'm not afraid of him. But look at you daydreaming! I say again: spread the rumor that Anne, my queen, is sick and likely to die.

original: About it, for it stands me much upon   To stop all hopes whose growth may damage me.
translation: Hurry up—it's very important that I destroy anything that might come to damage me.

original: [aside]   I must be married to my brother’s daughter,   Or else my kingdom stands on brittle glass.
translation: [To himself]  I must marry my brother Edward's  daughter , or else my kingdom is only standing on fragile glass.

original: Murder her brothers, and then marry her—   Uncertain way of gain.
translation: Murder her brothers, and then marry her—it's a strange way to go about things.

original: But I am in   So far in blood that sin will pluck on sin.   Tear-falling pity dwells not in this eye.
translation: But I'm so steeped in blood at this point that one sin must follow another. These eyes of mine have no tears of pity.

original: Is thy name Tyrrel?
translation: Is your name Tyrrel?

original: James Tyrrel, and your most obedient subject.
translation: James Tyrrel, your most obedient subject.

original: Art thou indeed?
translation: Are you indeed?

original: Prove me, my gracious lord.
translation: Let me prove it, my gracious lord.

original: Dar’st thou resolve to kill a friend of mine?
translation: Would you dare to kill a friend of mine?

original: Please you. But I had rather kill two enemies.
translation: If it would please you. But I would rather kill two enemies.

original: Why then, thou hast it. Two deep enemies,   Foes to my rest, and my sweet sleep’s disturbers,   Are they that I would have thee deal upon.
translation: Well, you can do that then. I want you to kill two great enemies of mine, enemies of my sleep and my peace of mind.

original: Tyrrel, I mean those bastards in the Tower.
translation: Tyrrel, I mean those bastards in the Tower.

original: Let me have open means to come to them, And soon I’ll rid you from the fear of them.
translation: Let me have free access to reach them, and soon you won't have to fear them anymore.

original: Thou sing’st sweet music. Hark, come hither, Tyrrel.
translation: Your words are sweet music. Come here, Tyrrel.

original: Go, by this token. Rise, and lend thine ear.
translation: Go, with this password. Rise and listen.

original: There is no more but so. Say it is done, And I will love thee and prefer thee for it.
translation: There's nothing more than that. When you tell me the deed is done, I will love you and promote you for it.

original: I will dispatch it straight.
translation: I'll do it straight away.

original: My lord, I have considered in my mind  The late request that you did sound me in.
translation: My lord, I've been considering the request you just asked me about.

original: Well, let that rest. Dorset is fled to Richmond.
translation: Well, forget about that. Dorset has fled to join Richmond.

original: I hear the news, my lord.
translation: I heard that news, my lord.

original: Stanley, he is your wife’s son. Well, look unto it.
My lord, I claim the gift, my due by promise,   For which your honor and your faith is pawned—
translation: My lord, I want to claim the gift you promised me on your honor and faith—

original: Th' earldom of Hereford and the movables   Which you promisèd I shall possess.
translation: the earldom of Hereford and all the possessions that go with it, which you swore that I would have.

original: Stanley, look to your wife. If she convey Letters to Richmond, you shall answer it.
translation: Stanley, watch your wife. If she sends any letters to Richmond, you will answer for it.

original: What says your Highness to my just request?
translation: What does your Highness say to my just request?

original: I do remember me, Henry the Sixth   Did prophesy that Richmond should be king,
translation: I remember that Henry the Sixth prophesied that Richmond would be king one day,

original: When Richmond was a little peevish boy.   A king, perhaps—
translation: when Richmond was only a foolish boy. A king, perhaps—

original: My lord—
translation: My lord—

original: How chance the prophet could not at that time Have told me, I being by, that I should kill him?
translation: But why wasn't the prophet able to foresee that I, who was there at the time, would kill him?

original: My lord, your promise for the earldom—
translation: My lord, your promise of the earldom—

original: Richmond? When last I was at Exeter,   The mayor in courtesy showed me the castle   And called it Rougemont,
translation: Richmond? The last time I was in Exeter, the mayor politely showed me a castle and called it  "Rougemont."

original: at which name I started,   Because a bard of Ireland told me once   I should not live long after I saw Richmond.
translation: The name startled me, for an Irish poet once told me that I wouldn't live long after seeing Richmond.

original: My Lord—
translation: My lord—

original: Ay, what’s o'clock?
translation: Hey, what time is it?

original: I am thus bold to put your Grace in mind Of what you promised me.
translation: I am reminding your Grace of what you promised me.

original: Well, but what’s o'clock?
translation: Well, but what time is it?

original: Upon the stroke of ten.
translation: Almost ten o'clock.

original: Well, let it strike.
translation: Well, let it strike ten then.

original: Why let it strike?
translation: Why "let it strike?"

original: Because that, like a jack, thou keep’st the stroke Betwixt thy begging and my meditation. I am not in the giving vein today.
translation: Because you're like the peasant who strikes the bell, interrupting my thoughts with your begging. I'm not in the giving mood today.

original: Why then, resolve me whether you will or no.
translation: Well then, give me a final answer of whether I'll have the earldom or not.

original: Thou troublest me; I am not in the vein.
translation: You're annoying me. I'm not in the mood.

original: And is it thus? Repays he my deep service   With such deep contempt? Made I him king for this?
translation: Is this how it is? He rewards my great service with such great contempt? Did I make him king for this?

original: O, let me think on Hastings and be gone   To Brecknock, while my fearful head is on!
translation: Oh, let me learn from Hastings and hurry away to  Brecknock , while my frightened head is still on my shoulders!

original: The tyrannous and bloody act is done,   The most arch deed of piteous massacre   That ever yet this land was guilty of.
translation: The tyrannous and bloody act is done. It was the worst, most horrible massacre of which this land has ever been guilty.

original: Dighton and Forrest, whom I did suborn   To do this piece of ruthless butchery,
translation: Dighton and Forrest—whom I hired to do this piece of ruthless butchery—are experienced villains.

original: Albeit they were fleshed villains, bloody dogs,   Melted with tenderness and mild compassion,   Wept like two children in their deaths' sad story.
translation: They are like bloody hunting dogs. But even they melted with tenderness and compassion, and wept like children when they told the sad story of what they'd done.

original: “O thus” quoth Dighton, “lay those gentle babes.”   “Thus, thus,” quoth Forrest, “girdling one another   Within their alabaster innocent arms.
translation: "The gentle children lay like this," Dighton said. "Like this," said Forrest, "embracing each other with their white innocent arms.

original: Their lips were four red roses on a stalk,   And in their summer beauty kissed each other.
translation: Their lips were touching, like four red roses on a stalk.

original: A book of prayers on their pillow lay,   Which once,” quoth Forrest, “almost changed my mind,   But O, the devil—”There the villain stopped;
translation: And a prayer book lay on their pillow," said Forrest, "which almost made me change my mind. But oh, the devil—" And there the villain stopped talking,

original: When Dighton thus told on: “We smotherèd   The most replenishèd sweet work of nature   That from the prime creation e'er she framed.”
translation: and Dighton continued the tale: "We smothered the most perfect, sweet work that nature ever created."

original: Hence both are gone with conscience and remorse;   They could not speak; and so I left them both   To bear this tidings to the bloody king.
translation: Both men were crushed with remorse, so that they couldn't speak any more. I left them both to bring this news to the bloody king.

original: And here he comes.—All health, my sovereign lord.
translation: And here he comes.

original: Kind Tyrrel, am I happy in thy news?
translation: Kind Tyrrel, will your news make me happy?

original: If to have done the thing you gave in charge Beget your happiness, be happy then, For it is done.
translation: If the completion of your task will make you happy, be happy then. For it is done.

original: But did’st thou see them dead?
translation: But did you see them dead?

original: I did, my lord.
translation: I did, my lord.

original: And buried, gentle Tyrrel?
translation: And buried, gentle Tyrrel?

original: The chaplain of the Tower hath buried them,  But where, to say the truth, I do not know.
translation: The chaplain of the Tower has buried them. But to tell you the truth, I don't know where.

original: Come to me, Tyrrel, soon at after-supper,   When thou shalt tell the process of their death.
translation: Tyrrel, come back to me soon after dessert, and tell me the details of their deaths.

original: Meantime, but think how I may do thee good,   And be inheritor of thy desire.   Farewell till then.
translation: In the meantime, think about how I can reward you with whatever you desire. Farewell until then.

original: I humbly take my leave.
translation: I humbly leave you.

original: The son of Clarence have I pent up close,   His daughter meanly have I matched in marriage,   The sons of Edward sleep in Abraham’s bosom,   And Anne my wife hath bid this world goodnight.
translation: I have Clarence's son locked up, and Clarence's daughter married off to a poor fellow. Edward's sons are sleeping in heaven, and my wife Anne has bid this world goodnight.

original: Now, for I know the Breton Richmond aims   At young Elizabeth, my brother’s daughter,   And by that knot looks proudly on the crown,   To her go I, a jolly thriving wooer.
translation: But I know that Richmond aims to marry young Elizabeth—my brother Edward's daughter—and win the crown through that match. So now I go to her: a jolly, lively wooer.

original: My lord!
translation: My lord!

original: Good or bad news, that thou com’st in so bluntly?
translation: Is it good news or bad news, that you come bursting in here?

original: Bad news, my lord. Morton is fled to Richmond, And Buckingham, backed with the hardy Welshmen, Is in the field, and still his power increaseth.
translation: Bad news, my lord. The Bishop of Ely has fled to Richmond. And Buckingham, backed by his army of hardy Welshmen, is on the march, his power still growing.

original: Ely with Richmond troubles me more near   Than Buckingham and his rash-levied strength.
translation: Ely joining Richmond troubles me more than Buckingham and his hastily raised army.

original: Come, I have learned that fearful commenting   Is leaden servitor to dull delay;
translation: Come, I have learned that frightened talk only leads to delay, and delay leads to slow ruin. Fiery speed will be my course of action.

original: Delay leads impotent and snail-paced beggary;   Then fiery expedition be my wing,   Jove’s Mercury, and herald for a king.
translation: I will be  Jupiter , with wing-footed Mercury as my messenger.

original: Go, muster men. My counsel is my shield.   We must be brief when traitors brave the field.
translation: Go, rally men to fight. My sword will be my advisor. We must act quickly when traitors march to war.

original: So now prosperity begins to mellow   And drop into the rotten mouth of death.
translation: So now the Yorks' prosperity has ripened and rotted, falling into the mouth of death.

original: Here in these confines slyly have I lurked   To watch the waning of mine enemies.
translation: I've been lurking in the shadows here to watch my enemies come to ruin,

original: A dire induction am I witness to,   And will to France, hoping the consequence   Will prove as bitter, black, and tragical.
translation: and it's a terrible scene I've witnessed—an ominous prologue to what I hope will be a bitter, dark, and tragic conclusion.

original: Withdraw thee, wretched Margaret. Who comes here?
translation: I'll head to France. But hide now, wretched Margaret. Who's coming?

original: Ah, my poor princes! Ah, my tender babes,   My unblown flowers, new-appearing sweets,
translation: Ah, my poor princes! Ah, my tender babes—my flowers who didn't have a chance to bloom!

original: If yet your gentle souls fly in the air   And be not fixed in doom perpetual,
translation: If your gentle souls are still flying about in the air and haven't yet landed in their final resting place,

original: Hover about me with your airy wings   And hear your mother’s lamentation.
translation: then hover about me now with your airy wings, and hear your mother's cries of mourning.

original: Hover about her; say that right for right Hath dimmed your infant morn to agèd night.
translation: Hover about her, spirits, and say that she got what she deserved, since you were also killed before your time.

original: So many miseries have crazed my voice That my woe-wearied tongue is still and mute. Edward Plantagenet, why art thou dead?
translation: So many miseries have cracked my voice that my tongue is weary of wailing and has gone silent. Edward Plantagenet, why are you dead?

original: Plantagenet doth quit Plantagenet; Edward for Edward pays a dying debt.
translation: One Plantagenet makes up for another. Edward dies to pay the debt for another Edward's death.

original: Wilt thou, O God, fly from such gentle lambs And throw them in the entrails of the wolf? When didst thou sleep when such a deed was done?
translation: Oh God, will you abandon such gentle lambs, and throw them to the wolf? How could you sleep when such a deed was done?

original: When holy Harry died, and my sweet son.
translation: God slept when my holy husband Henry died, and my sweet son Edward.

original: [sitting down]   Dead life, blind sight, poor mortal living ghost,
translation: [Sitting down]  My life has died. My sight has gone blind. I'm like a ghost that's still alive.

original: Woe’s scene, world’s shame, grave’s due by life  usurped,
translation: I am the bearer of misfortune; the shame of the world; a soul that rightfully belongs to the grave.

original: Brief abstract and record of tedious days,   Rest thy unrest on England’s lawful earth,   Unlawfully made drunk with innocent blood.
translation: As a summary and brief record of my unbearable life, I will rest my restless bones on England's lawful earth, which is now covered with innocent blood, against the laws of man and nature.

original: [sitting down beside her]   Ah, that thou wouldst as soon afford a grave   As thou canst yield a melancholy seat,
translation: [Sitting down beside her]  Ah, if only the earth could provide me with a grave instead of just a sad seat,

original: Then would I hide my bones, not rest them here.   O, who hath any cause to mourn but we?
translation: then I would bury my bones, instead of simply resting them here. Oh, who has any right to mourn except for us?

original: [joining them]   If ancient sorrow be most reverend,   Give mine the benefit of seigniory,   And let my griefs frown on the upper hand.
translation: [Joining them and sitting]  If the oldest sorrow is the most revered, then give mine the privilege of seniority, and let my grief have the upper hand.

original: If sorrow can admit society,   Tell o'er your woes again by viewing mine.
translation: If you can accept company in your sadness, then consider your losses again by looking at mine.

original: I had an Edward till a Richard killed him;   I had a husband till a Richard killed him.
translation: I had an Edward until a Richard killed him. And I had a husband, Henry, until a Richard killed him.

original: Thou hadst an Edward till a Richard killed him;   Thou hadst a Richard till a Richard killed him.
translation: You had an Edward until a Richard killed him, and you had a Richard, young York, until a Richard killed him.

original: I had a Richard too, and thou did’st kill him;  I had a Rutland too; thou holp’st to kill him.
Thou hadst a Clarence too, and Richard killed him   Then forth the kennel of thy womb hath crept   A hellhound that doth hunt us all to death—
translation: You had a Clarence too, and Richard killed him. The kennel of your womb has let loose a hellhound that hunts us all to death—

original: That dog, that had his teeth before his eyes,   To worry lambs and lap their gentle blood;
translation: a dog that had teeth before it had eyes. His teeth attack lambs and lap up their gentle blood.

original: That excellent grand tyrant of the earth,   That reigns in gallèd eyes of weeping souls;
translation: He is the greatest tyrant of the earth, and thrives among the tears of those he has injured.

original: That foul defacer of God’s handiwork   Thy womb let loose to chase us to our graves.
translation: That foul creature who defaces God's handiwork came forth from  your  womb to chase us to our graves.

original: O upright, just, and true-disposing God,   How do I thank thee that this carnal cur   Preys on the issue of his mother’s body   And makes her pew-fellow with others' moan!
translation: Oh, upright, just, and generous God, how can I thank you enough that this deadly mutt preys on his mother's offspring and makes her a companion to others' sorrow?

original: O Harry’s wife, triumph not in my woes!  God witness with me, I have wept for thine.
translation: Oh, Henry's wife, do not triumph in my woes! As God is my witness, I have wept for yours.

original: Bear with me, I am hungry for revenge,   And now I cloy me with beholding it.
translation: Bear with me. I am hungry for revenge, and now I'm almost sick from gorging myself upon it.

original: Thy Edward he is dead, that killed my Edward,   Thy other Edward dead, to quit my Edward;
translation: Your son Edward—who killed my son Edward—is dead. Your grandson Edward is also dead,

original: Young York, he is but boot, because both they   Matched not the high perfection of my loss.
translation: with young York thrown in as an extra, because both your grandsons didn't equal my lost son.

original: Thy Clarence he is dead that stabbed my Edward,   And the beholders of this frantic play,   Th' adulterate Hastings, Rivers, Vaughan, Grey,   Untimely smothered in their dusky graves.
translation: Your Clarence—who stabbed my son Edward—is dead. And the audience to this frantic play—the adulterer Hastings, Rivers, Vaughan, and Grey—have all been smothered in early graves.

original: Richard yet lives, hell’s black intelligencer,   Only reserved their factor to buy souls   And send them thither.
translation: Richard still lives as hell's dark spy, only allowed to remain long enough to buy souls and send them down below.

original: But at hand, at hand   Ensues his piteous and unpitied end.
translation: But soon, soon his pitiful and well-deserved end will come.

original: Earth gapes, hell burns, fiends roar, saints pray,   To have him suddenly conveyed from hence.
translation: The earth gapes open, hell burns, devils roar, and saints pray that he might be quickly sent from this earth.

original: Cancel his bond of life, dear God I pray,   That I may live to say, “The dog is dead.”
translation: Dear God, end his life soon, so that I may live to say, "The dog is dead!"

original: O, thou didst prophesy the time would come  That I should wish for thee to help me curse That bottled spider, that foul bunch-backed toad!
translation: Oh, you once did prophesy that the time would come when I would want your help in cursing that swollen spider, that foul hunchbacked toad!

original: I called thee then “vain flourish of my fortune.”   I called thee then poor shadow, “painted queen,”   The presentation of but what I was,
translation: And then I called you a "poor imitation of a queen" and a "meaningless decoration on my throne"—the image of what I was in reality—

original: The flattering index of a direful pageant,   One heaved a-high, to be hurled down below,   A mother only mocked with two fair babes,   A dream of what thou wast, a garish flag   To be the aim of every dangerous shot,   A sign of dignity, a breath, a bubble,   A queen in jest, only to fill the scene.
translation: the pretty prologue to an ominous tragedy; a woman lifted high only to be hurled down below; a mother mocked with the gifts of two dear babies, only to lose them. You were a shadow of a queen; a gaudy banner that enemies could target; an empty symbol of dignity; a breath; a bubble; a mockery of a queen; a stand-in only there to fill the role.

original: Where is thy husband now? Where be thy brothers?   Where are thy two sons? Wherein dost thou joy?
translation: And where is your husband now? Where are your brothers? Where are your two sons?

original: Who sues and kneels and says “God save the queen?”   Where be the bending peers that flattered thee?   Where be the thronging troops that followed thee?
translation: Where do you find your joy? Who kneels before you and makes requests and says, "God save the queen?" Where are the bowing noblemen who flattered you? Where are the crowds that followed you?

original: Decline all this, and see what now thou art:   For happy wife, a most distressèd widow;   For joyful mother, one that wails the name;   For queen, a very caitiff crowned with care;
translation: Without all this, see what you are: instead of a happy wife, a grieving widow; instead of a joyful mother, a woman who wails over her children; instead of a queen, a poor wretch crowned only with worries;

original: For one being sued to, one that humbly sues;   For she that scorned at me, now scorned of me;   For she being feared of all, now fearing one;   For she commanding all, obeyed of none.
translation: instead of one granting favors, one humbly begging for favors. She who mocked me is now mocked by me, and she who commanded everyone is now obeyed by no one. See how the wheel of justice has turned, leaving you the victim of time.

original: Thus hath the course of justice whirled about   And left thee but a very prey to time,   Having no more but thought of what thou wast   To torture thee the more, being what thou art.
translation: All you have left are the memories of your former glory, which torture you even more when you consider what you've become.

original: Thou didst usurp my place, and dost thou not   Usurp the just proportion of my sorrow?
translation: You usurped my position, and now see how you usurp my sorrow.

original: Now thy proud neck bears half my burdened yoke,   From which even here I slip my weary head   And leave the burthen of it all on thee.
translation: Your proud neck bears half of my heavy burden, but now let me give it all to you.

original: Farewell, York’s wife, and queen of sad mischance.   These English woes will make me smile in France.
translation: Farewell, York's wife, queen of sad misfortune.  These English woes will make me smile in France.

original: O, thou well-skilled in curses, stay awhile, And teach me how to curse mine enemies.
translation: Oh, you who are so skilled in curses, stay a while and teach me how to curse my enemies.

original: Forbear to sleep the nights, and fast the days;   Compare dead happiness with living woe;
translation: Don't sleep at night, and don't eat during the day. Compare lost happiness with current suffering.

original: Think that thy babes were sweeter than they were,   And he that slew them fouler than he is.
translation: Remember your children as being sweeter than they were, and think of the one that killed them as fouler than he is.

original: My words are dull. O, quicken them with thine!
translation: My words are dull. Oh, give them life with yours!

original: Thy woes will make them sharp and pierce like mine.
translation: Your suffering will make them sharp, so they can pierce like mine.

original: Why should calamity be full of words?
translation: Why should this catastrophe be accompanied by so many words?

original: Windy attorneys to their clients' woes,   Airy succeeders of intestate joys,   Poor breathing orators of miseries,
translation: Words are useless breath, like lawyers pleading on their sad clients' behalf; like the children of joys who inherit nothing; like poor speech-makers going on about misery.

original: Let them have scope, though what they will impart   Help nothing else, yet do they ease the heart.
translation: Even so, let them have a chance. Though they won't help in any other way, they still help ease the heart.

original: If so, then be not tongue-tied. Go with me, And in the breath of bitter words let’s smother My damnèd son that thy two sweet sons smothered.
translation: If that's so, then don't be tongue-tied. Come with me, and with our bitter words let's smother my damned son Richard who smothered your two sons.

original: The trumpet sounds. Be copious in exclaims.
translation: The trumpet sounds—he's coming. Don't restrain yourself.

original: Who intercepts my expedition?
translation: Who's blocking my path?

original: O, she that might have intercepted thee, By strangling thee in her accursèd womb, From all the slaughters, wretch, that thou hast done.
translation: Oh, you wretch! It is she who could have blocked you from all the murders you've committed—by strangling you in her cursed womb.

original: Hid’st thou that forehead with a golden crown   Where should be branded, if that right were right,
translation: Are you hiding that forehead with a golden crown, when, if the world was just, it would be branded with the mark of your crimes—

original: The slaughter of the prince that owed that crown   And the dire death of my poor sons and brothers?
translation: the slaughter of the prince who rightfully possessed that crown, and the monstrous deaths of my poor sons and brothers?

original: Tell me, thou villain-slave, where are my children?
translation: Tell me, you low-born criminal, where are my children?

original: Thou toad, thou toad, where is thy brother Clarence? And little Ned Plantagenet his son?
translation: You toad, you toad, where is your brother Clarence? And little Ned Plantagenet, his son.

original: Where is gentle Rivers, Vaughan, Grey?
translation: Where is noble Rivers, and Vaughan, and Grey?

original: Where is kind Hastings?
translation: Where is kind Hastings?

original: A flourish, trumpets! Strike alarum, drums!  Let not the heavens hear these telltale women Rail on the Lord’s anointed. Strike, I say!
translation: Trumpets, play! Drums, a call to arms! Don't let the heavens hear these tattle-tale women abuse the Lord's anointed king. Play, I say!

original: Either be patient and entreat me fair, Or with the clamorous report of war Thus will I drown your exclamations.
translation: Either be patient and treat me with courtesy or I'll drown you out with the noisy music of war.

original: Art thou my son?
translation: Are you my son?

original: Ay, I thank God, my father, and yourself.
translation: Yes, and for that I thank God, my father, and yourself.

original: Then patiently hear my impatience.
translation: Then patiently listen to my impatience.

original: Madam, I have a touch of your condition, Which cannot brook the accent of reproof.
translation: Madam, I have some of your temperament, in that I can't tolerate the language of disapproval.

original: O, let me speak!
translation: Oh, let me speak!

original: Do then, but I’ll not hear.
translation: Speak then, but I won't listen.

original: I will be mild and gentle in my words.
translation: I will be mild and gentle in my words.

original: And brief, good mother, for I am in haste.
translation: And be brief too, good mother, for I'm in a hurry.

original: Art thou so hasty? I have stayed for thee, God knows, in torment and in agony.
translation: Are you so impatient? God knows I waited for you, in torment and in agony, when I was giving birth to you.

original: And came I not at last to comfort you?
translation: And didn't I come at last to comfort you?

original: No, by the Holy Rood, thou know’st it well.   Thou cam’st on earth to make the earth my hell.
translation: No, by the Holy Cross, and you know it well. You came to earth to make the earth my hell.

original: A grievous burden was thy birth to me;   Tetchy and wayward was thy infancy;   Thy school days frightful, desp'rate, wild, and  furious;   Thy prime of manhood daring, bold, and venturous;
translation: Your birth was a painful burden to me. You were fussy and willful as a baby. Your school days were frightening, wild, and angry. As a young man, you were daring, bold, and adventurous.

original: Thy age confirmed, proud, subtle, sly, and bloody,   More mild, but yet more harmful, kind in hatred.
translation: And in your maturity you've grown proud, cunning, sly, and bloody—less wild but more dangerous, flattering in your hatred.

original: What comfortable hour canst thou name,   That ever graced me in thy company?
translation: Can you name a comfortable hour I've ever had in your company?

original: Faith, none but Humfrey Hower, that called your Grace   To breakfast once, forth of my company.
translation: Well, none but  Humphrey Hour , who once invited you to have breakfast without my company.

original: If I be so disgracious in your eye,   Let me march on and not offend you, madam.—
translation: If I'm so displeasing to look at, then let me march on and not offend you, madam.

original: I prithee, hear me speak.
translation: Please, listen to me speak.

original: You speak too bitterly.
translation: You speak too bitterly.

original: Hear me a word, For I shall never speak to thee again.
translation: Just listen a moment, and then I'll never speak to you again.

original: So.
translation: Then do it.

original: Either thou wilt die by God’s just ordinance   Ere from this war thou turn a conqueror,   Or I with grief and extreme age shall perish   And nevermore behold thy face again.
translation: Either you'll die—as God's just punishment—before you can return victorious from this war, or else I will die from grief and old age. At any rate, I'll never see your face again.

original: Therefore take with thee my most grievous curse,   Which in the day of battle tire thee more   Than all the complete armor that thou wear’st.
translation: So take with you my most terrible curse, and may it weigh you down in battle more than your suit of armor. My prayers will fight on your enemies' side.

original: My prayers on the adverse party fight,   And there the little souls of Edward’s children   Whisper the spirits of thine enemies   And promise them success and victory.
translation: And the little souls of Edward's children will encourage your enemies, promising them success and victory.

original: Bloody thou art; bloody will be thy end.   Shame serves thy life and doth thy death attend.
translation: You have lived in violence, and now you will die with violence. Your life has been shameful, so let your death be as well.

original: Though far more cause, yet much less spirit to curse Abides in me. I say amen to her.
translation: Though I have far more reason to curse you, I don't have her energy. I'll just say "amen" to everything she said.

original: Stay, madam. I must talk a word with you.
translation: Wait, madam. I must speak with you.

original: I have no more sons of the royal blood   For thee to slaughter.
translation: have no more sons of royal blood for you to murder.

original: For my daughters, Richard,   They shall be praying nuns, not weeping queens,   And therefore level not to hit their lives.
translation: And as for my daughters, Richard, they'll become praying nuns, not weeping queens. So don't aim to destroy their lives.

original: You have a daughter called Elizabeth,  Virtuous and fair, royal and gracious.
translation: You have a daughter called Elizabeth, who is virtuous and beautiful, royal and gracious.

original: And must she die for this? O, let her live,   And I’ll corrupt her manners, stain her beauty,   Slander myself as false to Edward’s bed,   Throw over her the veil of infamy.
translation: And must she die for this? Oh, let her live, and I'll ruin her manner, mar her beauty, lie and say she is illegitimate, and destroy her reputation.

original: So she may live unscarred of bleeding slaughter,   I will confess she was not Edward’s daughter.
translation: So that she might escape being murdered, I'll say that she was not Edward's daughter.

original: Wrong not her birth. She is a royal princess.
translation: Don't lie about her birth. She is a royal princess.

original: To save her life, I’ll say she is not so.
translation: To save her life, I'll say she isn't.

original: Her life is safest only in her birth.
translation: Her royal birth is what makes her safest.

original: And only in that safety died her brothers.
translation: Her brothers died because of that same "safety."

original: Lo, at their births good stars were opposite.
translation: Alas, at birth they were badly fated.

original: No, to their lives ill friends were contrary.
translation: No, in their lives they were opposed by bad friends.

original: All unavoided is the doom of destiny.
translation: No one can avoid the doom of destiny.

original: True, when avoided grace makes destiny.  My babes were destined to a fairer death If grace had blessed thee with a fairer life.
translation: That's true, when someone who has avoided God's grace is controlling that destiny. My children would have been destined to better deaths if you had been blessed with a more virtuous life.

original: You speak as if that I had slain my cousins.
translation: You speak as if I had killed my nephews.

original: Cousins, indeed, and by their uncle cozened   Of comfort, kingdom, kindred, freedom, life.
translation: Indeed, your nephews were cheated by their uncle of their comfort, kingdom, relatives, freedom, and life.

original: Whose hand soever launched their tender hearts,   Thy head, all indirectly, gave direction.
translation: Some other hand might have pierced their tender hearts, but you're the one who gave the order.

original: No doubt the murd'rous knife was dull and blunt   Till it was whetted on thy stone-hard heart,   To revel in the entrails of my lambs.
translation: No doubt the murderous knife was dull and blunt until it was sharpened against your hard heart of stone, and after that it could rejoice among my little lambs' bloody innards.

original: But that still use of grief makes wild grief tame,   My tongue should to thy ears not name my boys   Till that my nails were anchored in thine eyes,
translation: But constant talk of grief makes wild grief tame, so I won't say my boys' names again until I've anchored my fingernails in your eyes and gouged them out.

original: And I, in such a desp'rate bay of death,   Like a poor bark of sails and tackling reft,   Rush all to pieces on thy rocky bosom.
translation: I am like a poor boat without sails in a stormy bay of death, and I'll break myself to pieces against your rocky heart.

original: Madam, so thrive I in my enterprise   And dangerous success of bloody wars
translation: Madam, if I am successful in these dangerous, bloody wars to which I am marching off,

original: As I intend more good to you and yours   Than ever you or yours were by me harmed!
translation: I then intend to do more good to you and your relatives than I've ever done them harm!

original: What good is covered with the face of heaven, To be discovered, that can do me good?
translation: What good is there still undiscovered in this world that can do me good now?

original: The advancement of your children, gentle lady.
translation: The advancement of your children, noble lady.

original: Up to some scaffold, there to lose their heads.
translation: Advancing them up to some scaffold, to lose their heads.

original: Unto the dignity and height of fortune,  The high imperial type of this earth’s glory.
translation: Advancement to the dignity and height of fortune, the most kingly symbol of this world's glory.

original: Flatter my sorrow with report of it. Tell me what state, what dignity, what honor, Canst thou demise to any child of mine?
translation: Flatter me in my sorrow then. Tell me what rank, what dignity, or what honor you could possibly offer to any child of mine?

original: Even all I have— ay, and myself and all—   Will I withal endow a child of thine;
translation: Only everything I have—yes, including myself. That's what I'll give to a child of yours.

original: So in the Lethe of thy angry soul   Thou drown the sad remembrance of those wrongs   Which thou supposest I have done to thee.
translation: May  Lethe  drown your sad memories of the wrongs you imagine I've done to you.

original: Be brief, lest that the process of thy kindness  Last longer telling than thy kindness' date.
translation: Explain yourself quickly, before this speech about your kindness outlasts whatever kindness you have.

original: Then know that from my soul I love thy daughter.
translation: Then know that from my soul I love your daughter Elizabeth.

original: My daughter’s mother thinks it with her soul.
translation: And I believe it with my soul.

original: What do you think?
translation: What do you believe?

original: That thou dost love my daughter from thy soul.  So from thy soul’s love didst thou love her brothers, And from my heart’s love I do thank thee for it.
translation: That you love my daughter from your soul—far from your soul. Just like you loved her brothers. And from my heart's same love I thank you for it.

original: Be not so hasty to confound my meaning. I mean that with my soul I love thy daughter And do intend to make her Queen of England.
translation: Don't be so quick to confuse my meaning. I mean that I love your daughter with my soul, and I intend to make her Queen of England.

original: Well then, who dost thou mean shall be her king?
translation: Well then, who will be her king?

original: Even he that makes her queen. Who else should be?
translation: The same man who makes her queen. Who else should it be?

original: What, thou?
translation: What, you?

original: Even so. How think you of it?
translation: Of course. What did you think?

original: How canst thou woo her?
translation: How would you go about wooing her?

original: That would I learn of you, As one being best acquainted with her humor.
translation: That's what I want to learn from you, since you know her temperament best.

original: And wilt thou learn of me?
translation: And will you learn from me?

original: Madam, with all my heart.
translation: Madam, with all my heart.

original: Send to her, by the man that slew her brothers,   A pair of bleeding hearts; thereon engrave   “Edward” and “York.” Then haply she will weep.
translation: Then send to her—from the man who killed her brothers—a pair of bleeding hearts. Write "Edward" and "York" on them. Then she might weep.

original: Therefore present to her—as sometime Margaret   Did to thy father, steeped in Rutland’s blood—
translation: So to wipe up her tears, present her with a handkerchief—like the one Margaret gave to your father, steeped in his son Rutland's blood—

original: A handkerchief, which say to her did drain   The purple sap from her sweet brother’s body,   And bid her wipe her weeping eyes withal.
translation: and tell her that this handkerchief wiped up the blood that drained from her sweet brother's body.

original: If this inducement move her not to love,   Send her a letter of thy noble deeds;
translation: Tell her to wipe her weeping eyes with it. If all this doesn't convince her to love you, then send her a letter describing your other noble deeds.

original: Tell her thou mad’st away her uncle Clarence,   Her uncle Rivers, ay, and for her sake   Mad’st quick conveyance with her good aunt Anne.
translation: Tell her that you secretly killed her uncle Clarence, her uncle Rivers, yes, and speedily killed her good aunt Anne for her sake.

original: You mock me, madam. This is not the way To win your daughter.
translation: You mock me, madam. This is not the way to win your daughter.

original: There is no other way, Unless thou couldst put on some other shape  And not be Richard, that hath done all this.
translation: There is no other way, unless you could change your shape and be someone other than the Richard who has committed all these deeds.

original: Say that I did all this for love of her.
translation: Say that I did all those things out of love for her.

original: Nay, then indeed she cannot choose but hate thee, Having bought love with such a bloody spoil.
translation: No, for then she has no choice but to hate you, as you tried to buy her love with murder.

original: Look what is done cannot be now amended.   Men shall deal unadvisedly sometimes,   Which after-hours give leisure to repent.
translation: Whatever is done cannot be undone. Men make mistakes sometimes, and then they repent when they have the time.

original: If I did take the kingdom from your sons,   To make amends I’ll give it to your daughter.
translation: If I did take the kingdom from your sons, then to make up for it I'll give it to your daughter.

original: If I have killed the issue of your womb,   To quicken your increase I will beget   Mine issue of your blood upon your daughter.
translation: If I've killed your children, then I'll give them new life by having children with your daughter.

original: A grandam’s name is little less in love   Than is the doting title of a mother.
translation: A grandmother is hardly loved less than a mother. Grandchildren are just one step removed from children,

original: They are as children but one step below,   Even of your metal, of your very blood,   Of all one pain, save for a night of groans   Endured of her for whom you bid like sorrow.
translation: made of your same substance and your very blood. They take the same amount of effort, minus that one night of labor which you suffered for your daughter's sake.

original: Your children were vexation to your youth,   But mine shall be a comfort to your age.
translation: Your children troubled you in your youth, but my children will comfort you in your old age.

original: The loss you have is but a son being king,   And by that loss your daughter is made queen.
translation: Your only real loss is that your son wasn't king, but through that loss your daughter will become queen.

original: I cannot make you what amends I would;   Therefore accept such kindness as I can.
translation: I can't repay you as much as I'd like to, so accept what kindness I can offer.

original: Dorset your son, that with a fearful soul   Leads discontented steps in foreign soil,   This fair alliance quickly shall call home   To high promotions and great dignity.
translation: Your son Dorset—who fled in fear and joined the French army against me—would come quickly home to high promotions and great dignity if this marriage takes place.

original: The king that calls your beauteous daughter wife   Familiarly shall call thy Dorset brother.
translation: The king who calls your beautiful daughter "wife" will call Dorset "brother."

original: Again shall you be mother to a king,   And all the ruins of distressful times   Repaired with double riches of content.   What, we have many goodly days to see!
translation: Once again you'll be the mother to a king, and all the ruins of unhappy times will be repaired with double their value in contentment. Why, we can look forward to many good days ahead!

original: The liquid drops of tears that you have shed   Shall come again, transformed to orient pearl,   Advantaging their love with interest   Of ten times double gain of happiness.
translation: The liquid tears you've shed will return, transformed into pearls. Your happiness will increase to ten times its original size, plus interest.

original: Go then, my mother; to thy daughter go.   Make bold her bashful years with your experience;   Prepare her ears to hear a wooer’s tale;
translation: Go then, my future mother-in-law; go to your daughter. Use your experience to make her bold in her youthful innocence. Prepare her ears to hear my courting words.

original: Put in her tender heart th' aspiring flame   Of golden sovereignty; acquaint the Princess   With the sweet silent hours of marriage joys;
translation: Put in her tender heart the ambition to be queen. Acquaint the Princess with the sweet, silent hours of joy in marriage,

original: And when this arm of mine hath chastisèd   The petty rebel, dull-brained Buckingham,
translation: and when I've punished that petty rebel, dull-brained Buckingham,

original: Bound with triumphant garlands will I come   And lead thy daughter to a conqueror’s bed,
translation: I will return crowned with victory wreaths and lead your daughter to a conquerer's bed.

original: To whom I will retail my conquest won,   And she shall be sole victoress, Caesar’s Caesar.
translation: I will transmit all my victory to her, and she will be the  real conqueror—the emperor of the emperor.

original: What were I best to say? Her father’s brother   Would be her lord? Or shall I say her uncle?
translation: What should I say to her? Her father's brother wants to be her husband? Or should I say it's her uncle?

original: Or he that slew her brothers and her uncles?
translation: Or should I say it's the man who killed her brothers and uncles?

original: Under what title shall I woo for thee,   That God, the law, my honor and her love   Can make seem pleasing to her tender years?
translation: Under what name should I go wooing on your behalf? What name can please God, the law, and my honor, and also seem appealing to such a young woman?

original: Infer fair England’s peace by this alliance.
translation: Imply that fair England's peace depends on this marriage.

original: Which she shall purchase with still-lasting war.
translation: So she will purchase that peace with everlasting war.

original: Tell her the king, that may command, entreats—
translation: Tell her that the King, who has the power to command, instead begs her—

original: That, at her hands, which the king’s King forbids.
translation: Begs her to do what God, the King of Kings, forbids—marriage between an uncle and a niece.

original: Say she shall be a high and mighty queen.
translation: Say that she will be a high and mighty queen.

original: To vail the title, as her mother doth.
translation: Only so that she can give up that title, as her mother has.

original: Say I will love her everlastingly.
translation: Say I will love her forever.

original: But how long shall that title “ever” last?
translation: But how long will that "ever" last?

original: Sweetly in force unto her fair life’s end.
translation: For as long as her fair life lasts.

original: But how long fairly shall her sweet life last?
translation: But how long will her sweet life last?

original: As long as heaven and nature lengthens it.
translation: As long as heaven and nature lengthen it.

original: As long as hell and Richard likes of it.
translation: As long as hell and Richard decide.

original: Say I, her sovereign, am her subject low.
translation: Say that I, her king, am her lowly subject.

original: But she, your subject, loathes such sovereignty.
translation: But she, your actual subject, hates such a king.

original: Be eloquent in my behalf to her.
translation: Speak well of me to her.

original: An honest tale speeds best being plainly told.
translation: An honest tale works best when it's told plainly.

original: Then plainly to her tell my loving tale.
translation: Then plainly tell her my loving tale.

original: Plain and not honest is too harsh a style.
translation: Plain and not honest is too harsh to hear. Lies need some decoration.

original: Your reasons are too shallow and too quick.
translation: Your answers are too shallow and too lively.

original: O no, my reasons are too deep and dead— Too deep and dead, poor infants, in their graves.
translation: Oh no, my reasons are too deep and too dead—too deep and too dead, just like my poor infants in their graves.

original: Harp not on that string, madam; that is past.
translation: Don't harp on that string, madam—that's in the past.

original: Harp on it still shall I till heart-strings break.
translation: I'll harp on it until my heartstrings break.

original: Now by my George, my Garter, and my crown—
Profaned, dishonored, and the third usurped.
translation: The first one profaned, the second dishonored, and the third stolen.

original: I swear—
translation: I swear—

original: By nothing, for this is no oath.   Thy George, profaned, hath lost his lordly honor;
translation: By nothing—because this is no proper oath. Your Saint George, profaned by you, has lost his lordly honor.

original: Thy garter, blemished, pawned his knightly virtue;   Thy crown, usurped, disgraced his kingly glory.
translation: Your garter, stained by you, has lost its knightly virtue. Your crown, stolen by you, has disgraced its kingly glory.

original: If something thou wouldst swear to be believed,   Swear then by something that thou hast not wronged.
translation: If you want to swear by something that I might believe in, then swear by something that you haven't wronged.

original: Then, by myself—
translation: Then I swear by myself—

original: Thyself is self-misused.
translation: You've misused yourself.

original: Now, by the world—
translation: By the world then—

original: 'Tis full of thy foul wrongs.
translation: It's full of your foul crimes.

original: My father’s death—
translation: By my father's death—

original: Thy life hath it dishonored.
translation: Your life has dishonored his death.

original: Why then, by God.
translation: Why then, by God.

original: God’s wrong is most of all.   If thou didst fear to break an oath by Him,   The unity the king my husband made   Thou hadst not broken, nor my brothers died.
translation: You've abused God most of all. If you really feared to break an oath sworn by God, you never would have broken the oath of friendship and unity we made to the king my husband before he died—

original: If thou hadst feared to break an oath by Him,   Th' imperial metal circling now thy head   Had graced the tender temples of my child,
translation: and my brothers wouldn't have been killed. If you really feared to break an oath sworn by God, then the crown you now wear would instead be gracing the tender head of my child—

original: And both the princes had been breathing here,   Which now, two tender bedfellows for dust,   Thy broken faith hath made the prey for worms.
translation: and both the princes would still be alive. Your broken oaths have resulted in many corpses, and much food for the worms.

original: What canst thou swear by now?
translation: What can you swear by now?

original: The time to come.
translation: By the future.

original: That thou hast wrongèd in the time o'erpast;   For I myself have many tears to wash   Hereafter time, for time past wronged by thee.
translation: You've already wronged that with your past actions. I myself have many tears left to cry in the future because of your past crimes.

original: The children live whose fathers thou hast slaughtered,   Ungoverned youth, to wail it in their age;
translation: The children whose fathers you slaughtered are still alive, and they will grow up without guidance, unfortunate in their adulthood.

original: The parents live whose children thou hast butchered,   Old barren plants, to wail it with their age.
translation: The parents whose children you butchered are still alive too, old barren plants who will be miserable in their old age.

original: Swear not by time to come, for that thou hast   Misused ere used, by times ill-used o'erpast.
translation: Don't swear by the future, for with your past you've already ruined it.

original: As I intend to prosper and repent,   So thrive I in my dangerous affairs   Of hostile arms!
translation: May I succeed in my dangerous battles to the same degree that I truly intend to repent and prosper!

original: Myself myself confound,   Heaven and fortune bar me happy hours,   Day, yield me not thy light, nor night thy rest,
translation: May I ruin myself; be deprived of happiness by heaven and destiny; my days be dark; my nights sleepless;

original: Be opposite all planets of good luck   To my proceedings if, with dear heart’s love,   Immaculate devotion, holy thoughts,   I tender not thy beauteous princely daughter.   In her consists my happiness and thine.
translation: and my luck be bad if I don't love your beautiful, royal daughter with dear affection, pure devotion, and holy thoughts.  Both my happiness and yours depends on her.

original: Without her follows to myself and thee,   Herself, the land, and many a Christian soul,   Death, desolation, ruin and decay.
translation: Without her as my queen, death, desolation, ruin, and decay will fall on me, you, your daughter, the land, and many a Christian soul. It cannot be avoided except by this marriage.

original: It cannot be avoided but by this;   It will not be avoided but by this.
translation: It  will  not be avoided except by this marriage.

original: Therefore, dear mother—I must call you so—   Be the attorney of my love to her:   Plead what I will be, not what I have been;
translation: Therefore, dear mother-in-law—for I must call you that now—be my advocate, pleading on my behalf to her. Describe what I  will  be, not what I have been.

original: Not my deserts, but what I will deserve.   Urge the necessity and state of times,   And be not peevish found in great designs.
translation: Don't mention what I deserve now, but what I  will  deserve. Remind her of how necessary this marriage is for the good of the country right now, and tell her not to be foolishly willful about such an important decision.

original: Shall I be tempted of the devil thus?
translation: Will I let myself be tempted by the devil like this?
