original: Ay, if the devil tempt you to do good.
translation: Yes, if the devil tempts you to do good.

original: Shall I forget myself to be myself?
translation: Will I forget to be who I am?

original: Ay, if your self’s remembrance wrong yourself.
translation: Yes, if your memories of yourself only hurt you.

original: Yet thou didst kill my children.
translation: But you killed my children.

original: But in your daughter’s womb I bury them, Where, in that nest of spicery, they will breed Selves of themselves, to your recomforture.
translation: But I will bury them in your daughter's womb, and in that nest of fragrant spices they will be reborn again, to grow and comfort you.

original: Shall I go win my daughter to thy will?
translation: Will I really go win my daughter over for you?

original: And be a happy mother by the deed.
translation: And make yoursel a happy mother by doing so.

original: I go. Write to me very shortly, And you shall understand from me her mind.
translation: I'll go. Write to me very soon, and I'll tell you how she feels.

original: Bear her my true love’s kiss; and so, farewell.
translation: Give her my true love's kiss. And so, farewell.

original: Relenting fool and shallow, changing woman!
translation: Weak fool! Shallow, fickle woman!

original: How now, what news?
translation: Hello, what's the news?

original: Most mighty sovereign, on the western coast   Rideth a puissant navy. To our shores   Throng many doubtful hollow-hearted friends,   Unarmed and unresolved to beat them back.
translation: Most mighty king, a powerful navy is sailing to our western coast. Many weak, unreliable allies of ours have gathered at the shore to meet the ships—but they are unarmed and undecided about whether or not to fight them.

original: 'Tis thought that Richmond is their admiral;   And there they hull, expecting but the aid   Of Buckingham to welcome them ashore.
translation: It's thought that Richmond is the invading navy's admiral. Right now the ships are just drifting around offshore, waiting for Buckingham to welcome them to land.

original: Some light-foot friend post to the duke of Norfolk— Ratcliffe, thyself, or Catesby. Where is he?
translation: Send some speedy ally to the duke of Norfolk. You go yourself, Ratcliffe—or Catesby. Where is Catesby?

original: Here, my good lord.
translation: Here, my good lord.

original: Catesby, fly to the duke.
translation: Catesby, hurry to the Duke of Buckingham.

original: I will, my lord, with all convenient haste.
translation: I will go as quickly as I can, my lord.

original: Ratcliffe, come hither. Post to Salisbury.   When thou com’st thither
translation: Ratcliffe, come here. Ride quickly to Salisbury. When you get there—

original: First, mighty liege, tell me your Highness' pleasure, What from your Grace I shall deliver to him.
translation: First, mighty King, tell me what your Highness wants, so I can deliver your message to him.

original: O true, good Catesby. Bid him levy straight The greatest strength and power that he can make  And meet me suddenly at Salisbury.
translation: Oh, true, good Catesby. Tell him to gather the largest army he can in a hurry, and meet me at Salisbury right away.

original: I go.
translation: I'm off.

original: What, may it please you, shall I do at Salisbury?
translation: And what would you like me to do at Salisbury?

original: Why, what wouldst thou do there before I go?
translation: Why, what would you do there before I arrive?

original: Your Highness told me I should post before.
translation: Your Highness just told me that I should hurry there.

original: My mind is changed.
translation: I've changed my mind.

original: Stanley, what news with you?
translation: Stanley, what's the news?

original: None good, my liege, to please you with the hearing, Nor none so bad but well may be reported.
translation: My lord, it's nothing so good that it will please you to hear it, but nothing so bad that I can't report it.

original: Hoyday, a riddle! Neither good nor bad.
translation: Aha, a riddle! Neither good nor bad.

original: What need’st thou run so many mile about   When thou mayst tell thy tale the nearest way?   Once more, what news?
translation: Why do you need to run in such wide circles when you can get straight to the point with your story? I'll ask you again: what's the news?

original: Richmond is on the seas.
translation: Richmond is on the seas.

original: There let him sink, and be the seas on him! White-livered runagate, what doth he there?
translation: Let him sink there, so the seas will be on him! The cowardly rebel, what is he doing there?

original: I know not, mighty sovereign, but by guess.
translation: I don't know, mighty king. I can only guess.

original: Well, as you guess?
translation: Well, what do you guess?

original: Stirred up by Dorset, Buckingham, and Morton, He makes for England, here to claim the crown.
translation: That he's been stirred up by Dorset, Buckingham, and Morton, and now he's coming to England to claim the crown.

original: Is the chair empty? Is the sword unswayed?   Is the king dead, the empire unpossessed?
translation: Is the throne empty? Does the royal sword have no owner? Is the king dead, the kingdom dispossessed?

original: What heir of York is there alive but we?
translation: What living heir of the York family is there but me?

original: And who is England’s king but great York’s heir?   Then tell me, what makes he upon the seas?
translation: And who can be England's king but great York's heir? So tell me, what is he doing at sea?

original: Unless for that, my liege, I cannot guess.
translation: Unless it's for that then I cannot guess, my lord.

original: Unless for that he comes to be your liege,  You cannot guess wherefore the Welshman comes. Thou wilt revolt and fly to him, I fear.
No, my good lord. Therefore mistrust me not.
translation: No, my good lord. Don't distrust me.

original: Where is thy power, then, to beat him back?   Where be thy tenants and thy followers?
translation: Where is your army, then, to beat him back? Where are your tenants and your followers?

original: Are they not now upon the western shore,   Safe-conducting the rebels from their ships?
translation: Aren't they on the western shore right now, helping his rebels disembark safely from their ships?

original: No, my good lord. My friends are in the north.
translation: No, my good lord. My friends are in the north.

original: Cold friends to me. What do they in the north When they should serve their sovereign in the west?
translation: Then they're cold friends to me. What are they doing in the north when they should be serving their king in the west?

original: They have not been commanded, mighty king.
translation: They haven't been commanded to do so, mighty king.

original: Pleaseth your Majesty to give me leave,   I’ll muster up my friends and meet your Grace   Where and what time your Majesty shall please.
translation: If it would please your Majesty, I'll gather up my friends and meet your Grace wherever and whenever your Majesty wants.

original: Ay, thou wouldst be gone to join with Richmond, But I’ll not trust thee.
translation: Yes, you want to leave so you can join Richmond. But I won't trust you.

original: Most mighty sovereign, You have no cause to hold my friendship doubtful. I never was nor never will be false.
translation: Most mighty king, you have no reason to doubt my friendship. I never have been false, and never will be.

original: Go then and muster men, but leave behind Your son George Stanley. Look your heart be firm.  Or else his head’s assurance is but frail.
translation: Go then and get your men, but leave behind your son, George Stanley. Make sure your loyalty stays firm, or else he has a good chance of losing his head.

original: So deal with him as I prove true to you.
translation: So treat him as well as my faithfulnes deserves.

original: My gracious sovereign, now in Devonshire,   As I by friends am well advertisèd,
translation: My gracious king, my friends have informed me

original: Sir Edward Courtney and the haughty prelate,   Bishop of Exeter, his elder brother,   With many more confederates are in arms.
translation: that Sir Edward Courtney and his elder brother—the arrogant Bishop of Exeter—are now in Devonshire with an army.

original: In Kent, my liege, the Guilfords are in arms, And every hour more competitors Flock to the rebels, and their power grows strong.
translation: My lord, Buckingham's supporters—the Guilfords—are armed and gathering in Kent. Every hour more men flock to join the rebels, and their army grows strong.

original: My lord, the army of great Buckingham—
translation: My lord, great Buckingham's army—

original: Out on you, owls! Nothing but songs of death.  There, take thou that till thou bring better news.
translation: Enough, you owls! All I hear are songs of death.  There, take that until you bring me better news.

original: The news I have to tell your Majesty   Is that by sudden floods and fall of waters   Buckingham’s army is dispersed and scattered,
translation: The news I have to tell your Majesty is that sudden floods and heavy rains have dispersed and scattered Buckingham's army.

original: And he himself wandered away alone,   No man knows whither.
translation: Buckingham himself has wandered away alone, though no one knows where.

original: I cry thee mercy.   There is my purse to cure that blow of thine.
translation: I beg your pardon. Here's some money to cure that blow I gave you.

original: [he gives money]   Hath any well-advisèd friend proclaimed   Reward to him that brings the traitor in?
translation: [He gives money]  Has any quick-thinking friend of mine offered a reward to whoever brings that traitor in?

original: Such proclamation hath been made, my lord.
translation: Yes, that proclamation has been made, my lord.

original: Sir Thomas Lovell and Lord Marquess Dorset,   'Tis said, my liege, in Yorkshire are in arms.   But this good comfort bring I to your Highness:
translation: It's reported that Sir Thomas Lovell and the Lord Marquess of Dorset are gathering an army in Yorkshire. But I bring your Highness this comfort:

original: The Breton navy is dispersed by tempest.   Richmond, in Dorsetshire, sent out a boat   Unto the shore to ask those on the banks   If they were his assistants, yea or no—
translation: Richmond's navy has been dispersed by a storm. At Dorsetshire, Richmond sent a boat to shore to ask the men on the banks if they were his allies.

original: Who answered him they came from Buckingham   Upon his party. He, mistrusting them,   Hoisted sail and made his course for Brittany.
translation: They answered that they were with Buckingham. Richmond didn't trust them, and he hoisted sail and returned to Brittany.

original: March on, march on, since we are up in arms, If not to fight with foreign enemies, Yet to beat down these rebels here at home.
translation: March on, march on, since we're already prepared for battle. Even if we don't have to fight foreign enemies, we'll still beat down these rebels here at home.

original: My liege, the duke of Buckingham is taken.   That is the best news.
translation: My lord, the Duke of Buckingham has been captured. That's the best news.

original: That the earl of Richmond   Is with a mighty power landed at Milford,   Is colder tidings, yet they must be told.
translation: There's worse, but it must be told: The Earl of Richmond has landed at Milford with a mighty army.

original: Away towards Salisbury! While we reason here,   A royal battle might be won and lost.
translation: We must go away towards Salisbury! While we talk here, a royal battle might be won and lost.

original: Someone take order Buckingham be brought   To Salisbury. The rest march on with me.
translation: Someone deliver the order that Buckingham should be brought to Salisbury. The rest of you, march on with me.

original: Sir Christopher, tell Richmond this from me:   That in the sty of the most deadly boar   My son George Stanley is franked up in hold;
translation: Sir Christopher, bring this message to Richmond for me: my son George Stanley is locked up in the  deadly boar's  pen.

original: If I revolt, off goes young George’s head;   The fear of that holds off my present aid.
translation: If I revolt, off goes young George's head. My fear of that happening prevents me from helping right now.

original: So get thee gone. Commend me to thy lord.   Withal, say that the queen hath heartily consented   He should espouse Elizabeth her daughter.
translation: So go quickly, and give my regards to your lord. Also say that Queen Elizabeth has readily agreed that  Richmond  should marry her daughter Elizabeth.

original: But, tell me, where is princely Richmond now?
translation: But tell me, where is princely Richmond now?

original: At Pembroke, or at Ha'rfordwest in Wales.
translation: At Pembroke, or at Haverford West in Wales.

original: What men of name resort to him?
translation: What noblemen have joined him?

original: Sir Walter Herbert, a renownèd soldier;   Sir Gilbert Talbot, Sir William Stanley,   Oxford, redoubted Pembroke, Sir James Blunt,   And Rhys-ap-Thomas, with a valiant crew,   And many other of great name and worth;
translation: Sir Walter Herbert, a renowned soldier; Sir Gilbert Talbot; your brother, Sir William Stanley; Oxford; the powerful Pembroke; Sir James Blunt; Rhys-ap-Thomas, with a brave crew; and many other famous and powerful men.

original: And towards London they do bend their power,   If by the way they be not fought withal.
translation: They're now sending their armies straight to London, if they don't have to fight along the way.

original: Well, hie thee to thy lord.  I kiss his hand. My letter will resolve him of my  mind. Farewell.
translation: Well, hurry to your lord. Kiss his hand for me. This letter will explain my thoughts to him. Farewell.

original: Will not King Richard let me speak with him?
translation: Won't King Richard let me speak with him?

original: No, my good lord. Therefore be patient.
translation: No, my good lord. So calm down.

original: Hastings and Edward’s children, Grey and Rivers,   Holy King Henry and thy fair son Edward,   Vaughan, and all that have miscarrièd   By underhand, corrupted, foul injustice,
translation: Oh, Hastings; Edward's children; Grey and Rivers; holy King Henry and your fair son Edward; Vaughan; and all who have died because of underhanded, corrupt, foul injustice—

original: If that your moody, discontented souls   Do through the clouds behold this present hour,   Even for revenge mock my destruction.—
translation: if your angry souls still cannot rest and are witnessing this scene through the clouds, then enjoy your revenge and mock my destruction.

original: It is.
translation: It is.

original: Why, then All Souls' Day is my body’s doomsday.   This is the day which, in King Edward’s time,   I wished might fall on me when I was found   False to his children and his wife’s allies.
translation: Why, then All Souls' Day is also my body's Judgment Day. This is the punishment that I once wished might fall on me if I was ever false to King Edward's children or his wife's allies.

original: This is the day wherein I wished to fall   By the false faith of him who most I trusted.
translation: This is the punishment I wished might fall on me—that I would be betrayed by the man I trusted most.

original: This, this All Souls' Day to my fearful soul   Is the determined respite of my wrongs.
translation: This, this All Souls' Day, is the predestined punishment for my frightened soul.

original: That high All-seer which I dallied with   Hath turned my feignèd prayer on my head   And given in earnest what I begged in jest.
translation: I tried to play games with God—the all-knowing seer—but he has turned my false prayer on my head and earnestly given me what I asked for as a joke.

original: Thus doth he force the swords of wicked men   To turn their own points in their masters' bosoms.
translation: This is how he forces wicked men to turn their swords against their masters.

original: Thus Margaret’s curse falls heavy upon my neck:   “When he,” quoth she, “shall split thy heart with  sorrow,   Remember Margaret was a prophetess.”—
translation: Now Margaret's curse falls heavy on my neck. "When Richard splits your heart in two with sorrow," she said, "remember that Margaret was a prophetess."

original: Fellows in arms, and my most loving friends,   Bruised underneath the yoke of tyranny,
translation: Fellow soldiers and loving friends, all who have suffered under the burden of Richard's tyranny—

original: Have we marched on without impediment,   Thus far into the bowels of the land
translation: we have marched this far without obstacles, all the way to the center of England.

original: And here receive we from our father Stanley   Lines of fair comfort and encouragement.
translation: And here we receive news of encouragement and comfort from my stepfather Stanley.

original: The wretched, bloody, and usurping boar,   That spoiled your summer fields and fruitful vines,   Swills your warm blood like wash, and makes his trough   In your embowelled bosoms—
translation: He says this: the wretched, violent, and usurping boar, that ruined your fields and vineyards; drinks your warm blood like water; and uses your disemboweled stomachs as his feeding trough—

original: this foul swine   Is now even in the center of this isle,   Near to the town of Leicester, as we learn.   From Tamworth thither is but one day’s march.
translation: this foul swine is right now in the center of the country, near the town of Leicester. It's only a day's march from Tamworth, where we are now.

original: In God’s name, cheerly on, courageous friends,   To reap the harvest of perpetual peace   By this one bloody trial of sharp war.
translation: In God's name, let's continue with cheerful spirits, my courageous friends, to reap the harvest of eternal peace from this one bloody trial of war.

original: Every man’s conscience is a thousand men, To fight against this guilty homicide.
translation: Every man's clean conscience is like a thousand swords to fight against this guilty murderer.

original: I doubt not but his friends will turn to us.
translation: I don't doubt that his friends will turn on him and join us.

original: He hath no friends but who are friends for fear. Which in his dearest need will fly from him.
translation: He has no friends except for those who are too afraid to leave him. But they'll abandon him in his time of greatest need.

original: All for our vantage. Then, in God’s name, march. True hope is swift, and flies with swallow’s wings. Kings it makes gods, and meaner creatures kings.
translation: All to our advantage. Then, in God's name, let's march. True hope is swift, and flies as fast as a swallow. Hope makes kings into gods, and lesser men into kings.

original: Here pitch our tent, even here in Bosworth field.— My Lord of Surrey, why look you so sad?
translation: Pitch our tents right here, in Bosworth field.

original: My heart is ten times lighter than my looks.
translation: My heart is ten times lighter than my appearance.

original: My Lord of Norfolk—
translation: My Lord of Norfolk—

original: Here, most gracious liege.
translation: Here, most gracious lord.

original: Norfolk, we must have knocks, ha, must we not?
translation: Norfolk, we must have a few swings of the sword, ha, must we not?

original: We must both give and take, my loving lord.
translation: We must both give them and take them, my loving lord.

original: Up with my tent!—Here will I lie tonight. But where tomorrow? Well, all’s one for that. Who hath descried the number of the traitors?
translation: Put up my tent! I'll sleep here tonight. But where will I sleep tomorrow? Well, it makes no difference. Who has spied out the size of the traitor's army?

original: Six or seven thousand is their utmost power.
translation: Six or seven thousand, at the most.

original: Why, our battalia trebles that account.   Besides, the king’s name is a tower of strength   Which they upon the adverse party want.
translation: Why, our army is three times that many. Besides, the King's name is a tower of strength, which the opposition lacks.

original: Up with the tent!—Come, noble gentlemen,   Let us survey the vantage of the ground.   Call for some men of sound direction.
translation: Put up the tent! Come, noble gentlemen, let's survey the military advantages of this battlefield. Call for some experienced officers.

original: Let’s lack no discipline, make no delay,   For, lords, tomorrow is a busy day.
translation: Let's lack no discipline and make no delay, for tomorrow will be a busy day, my lords.

original: The weary sun hath made a golden set,   And by the bright track of his fiery car,   Gives token of a goodly day tomorrow.—
translation: The weary sun has had a golden sunset, and left a bright trail in the sky. This is an omen that tomorrow will be a good day.

original: Unless I have mista'en his colors much,   Which well I am assured I have not done,
translation: Unless I've mistaken his banners—which I'm sure I haven't—

original: His regiment lies half a mile, at least,   South from the mighty power of the king.
translation: his regiment lies at least half a mile south of the King's mighty army.

original: If without peril it be possible,  Sweet Blunt, make some good means to speak with him, And give him from me this most needful note.
translation: Sweet Captain Blunt, if it can be done without too much danger, find a way to speak with him, and give him this important note from me.

original: Upon my life, my lord, I’ll undertake it. And so God give you quiet rest tonight!
translation: I swear by my life that I'll do this for you, my lord. And may God give you a quiet, restful night!

original: Good night, good Captain Blunt.
translation: Goodnight, good Captain Blunt.

original: Come, gentlemen, Let us consult upon tomorrow’s business Into my tent. The dew is raw and cold.
translation: Come, gentlemen, let's go to my tent and discuss tomorrow's business. The night is too raw and cold to stay outside.

original: What is “t o”clock?
translation: What time is it?

original: It’s suppertime, my lord. It’s nine o'clock.
translation: It's dinnertime, my lord. It's nine o'clock.

original: I will not sup tonight. Give me some ink and paper. What, is my beaver easier than it was? And all my armor laid into my tent?
translation: I will not eat tonight. Give me some ink and paper. Is my helmet's visor working better now? And is my armor laid out in my tent?

original: It is, my liege, and all things are in readiness.
translation: It is, my lord. Everything's ready.

original: Good Norfolk, hie thee to thy charge.  Use careful watch. Choose trusty sentinels.
translation: Good Norfolk, hurry to your post. Make sure everyone is on constant alert. Choose trusty watchmen.

original: I go, my lord.
translation: I'm off to do it, my lord.

original: Stir with the lark tomorrow, gentle Norfolk.
translation: Rise with the lark at dawn tomorrow, gentle Norfolk.

original: I warrant you, my lord.
translation: I promise I will, my lord.

original: Catesby.
translation: Catesby.

original: My lord.
translation: My lord.

original: Send out a pursuivant-at-arms   To Stanley’s regiment.
translation: Send out a junior officer to Stanley's regiment.

original: Bid him bring his power   Before sunrising, lest his son George fall   Into the blind cave of eternal night.
translation: Tell Stanley to bring his army here before sunrise, or else his son George will go to his eternal rest.

original: [to soldiers]   Fill me a bowl of wine. Give me a watch.   Saddle white Surrey for the field to-morrow.
translation: [To soldiers]  Give me a goblet of wine. Give me a personal guard. Saddle my white horse Surrey for the battle tomorrow.

original: Look that my staves be sound, and not too heavy.—
translation: Make sure that my lances are strong, but not too heavy.

original: My lord.
translation: My lord.

original: Sawst thou the melancholy Lord Northumberland?
translation: Did you see the gloomy Lord Northumberland?

original: Thomas the earl of Surrey and himself, Much about cockshut time, from troop to troop Went through the army cheering up the soldiers.
translation: He and Thomas, the Earl of Surrey, were moving from troop to troop around twilight, and cheering up the soldiers.

original: So, I am satisfied. Give me a bowl of wine.   I have not that alacrity of spirit   Nor cheer of mind that I was wont to have.
translation: Good, I am satisfied. Give me some wine. I don't have the same energetic spirit or optimistic mind that I used to.

original: Set it down. Is ink and paper ready?
translation: Set down the goblet. Is the ink and paper ready?

original: It is, my lord.
translation: It is, my lord.

original: Bid my guard watch. Leave me.  Ratcliffe, about the mid of night come to my tent And help to arm me. Leave me, I say.
translation: Tell my guard to be on alert. Now leave me. Ratcliffe, come to my tent around midnight and help me put on my armor. Now leave me, I say.

original: Fortune and victory sit on thy helm!
translation: May fortune and victory be yours!

original: All comfort that the dark night can afford Be to thy person, noble father-in-law.  Tell me, how fares our loving mother?
translation: Take all the comfort that such a dark night as this can offer, noble father-in-law. Tell me, how is my loving mother?

original: I, by attorney, bless thee from thy mother,   Who prays continually for Richmond’s good.   So much for that. The silent hours steal on,   And flaky darkness breaks within the east.
translation: I bless you on your mother's behalf. She prays continually for you. But enough of that. The silent hours keep passing, and dawn is breaking in the east.

original: In brief, for so the season bids us be,   Prepare thy battle early in the morning,   And put thy fortune to the arbitrament   Of bloody strokes and mortal-staring war.
translation: To be brief—as the situation requires—you should prepare your army early in the morning. Let bloody fighting and deadly war be the judges of your destiny.

original: I, as I may—that which I would I cannot,—   With best advantage will deceive the time,   And aid thee in this doubtful shock of arms.
translation: I can't help you in this battle as much as I'd like to, but I'll do the best I can without Richard finding out.

original: But on thy side I may not be too forward,   Lest, being seen, thy brother, tender George,   Be executed in his father’s sight.
translation: If I act too boldly on your behalf and Richard notices, then your stepbrother, young George, will be executed in front of me.

original: Farewell. The leisure and the fearful time   Cuts off the ceremonious vows of love   And ample interchange of sweet discourse,   Which so-long-sundered friends should dwell upon.
translation: Farewell. The danger and urgency of the current situation must keep us from the long greetings and happy catching-up that friends like us, who have been separated for so long, should have.

original: God give us leisure for these rites of love!   Once more, adieu. Be valiant, and speed well.
translation: But may God grant us time for all that soon! Once more, farewell. Be brave, and do well.

original: Good lords, conduct him to his regiment:   I’ll strive with troubled thoughts to take a nap,
translation: Good lords, escort him to his regiment. I'll wrestle with my troubled thoughts and try to take a nap,

original: Lest leaden slumber peise me down tomorrow,   When I should mount with wings of victory.
translation: so that sleepiness won't weigh me down tomorrow and keep me from flying on the wings of victory.

original: Once more, good night, kind lords and gentlemen.
translation: Once more, good night, kind lords and gentlemen.

original: O Thou, whose captain I account myself,   Look on my forces with a gracious eye.
translation: Oh God—of whose side I call myself captain—please look upon my forces with a gracious eye.

original: Put in their hands thy bruising irons of wrath,   That they may crush down with a heavy fall   The usurping helmets of our adversaries!
translation: Put the bruising swords of anger in their hands, so they can crush the helmets of our enemies!

original: Make us thy ministers of chastisement,   That we may praise thee in the victory!
translation: Make us agents of your divine punishment, so we can praise you when we're victorious!

original: To thee I do commend my watchful soul,   Ere I let fall the windows of mine eyes.
translation: I entrust my soul to you now, before I close my eyes and fall asleep.

original: Sleeping and waking, O, defend me still!   [Sleeps]
translation: Oh God, defend me always, whether sleeping or waking!  [He falls asleep]

original: [to RICHARD]   Let me sit heavy on thy soul tomorrow!
translation: [To RICHARD]  May I weigh down your soul tomorrow!

original: Think how thou stabbed’st me in my prime of youth   At Tewkesbury. Despair therefore, and die!
translation: Remember how you stabbed me at Tewkesbury in the prime of my life. So despair, and die!

original: [to RICHARD]   When I was mortal, my anointed body   By thee was punchèd full of deadly holes.
translation: [To RICHARD]  When I was alive, you stabbed my kingly body full of deadly holes.

original: Think on the Tower and me. Despair, and die!   Harry the Sixth bids thee despair and die.
translation: Remember the Tower, and remember me. Despair, and die! Henry the Sixth tells you to despair and die!

original: [to RICHARD]   Let me sit heavy in thy soul tomorrow,   I, that was washed to death with fulsome wine,   Poor Clarence, by thy guile betrayed to death.
translation: [To RICHARD]  May I weigh down your soul tomorrow! It's me, poor Clarence, who was drowned to death in a barrel of sickening wine, betrayed by your plotting.

original: Tomorrow in the battle think on me,   And fall thy edgeless sword. Despair, and die!
translation: Remember me tomorrow in the battle, and let your blunted sword fall from your hand. Despair, and die!

original: Let me sit heavy in thy soul tomorrow, Rivers, that died at Pomfret. Despair, and die!
translation: May I weigh down your soul tomorrow! It's me, Rivers, who died at Pomfret. Despair, and die!

original: Think upon Grey, and let thy soul despair!
translation: Remember Grey, and let your soul despair!

original: Think upon Vaughan, and with guilty fear Let fall thy lance. Despair, and die!
translation: Remember Vaughan, and drop your lance with guilt and fear. Despair, and die!

original: Awake, and think our wrongs in Richard’s bosom Will conquer him! Awake, and win the day.
translation: Wake up, and believe that Richard's guilty conscience will be his downfall! Wake up, and win the day!

original: [to RICHARD]   Dream on thy cousins smothered in the Tower.
translation: [To RICHARD]  Dream about your nephews, smothered in the Tower.

original: Let us be lead within thy bosom, Richard,   And weigh thee down to ruin, shame, and death.   Thy nephews' souls bid thee despair and die.
translation: Richard, may we weigh down your soul like lead, and drag you down to ruin, shame, and death. Your nephews' souls tell you to despair and die!

original: [to RICHARD]   Bloody and guilty, guiltily awake,   And in a bloody battle end thy days.
translation: [To RICHARD]  You bloody, guilty man, wake up full of guilt and then die in a bloody battle!

original: Think on Lord Hastings. Despair and die!
translation: Remember Lord Hastings. Despair, and die!

original: [to RICHARD]   Richard, thy wife, that wretched Anne thy wife,   That never slept a quiet hour with thee,   Now fills thy sleep with perturbations.
translation: [To RICHARD]  Richard, it's your wife, wretched Anne your wife, who never had a quiet hour of sleep with you. Now I've come to fill your sleep with disturbing thoughts.

original: Tomorrow, in the battle, think on me,   And fall thy edgeless sword: Despair and die!
translation: Tomorrow in the battle, remember me and drop your blunted sword. Despair, and die!

original: [to RICHARD]   The last was I that helped thee to the  crown;   The last was I that felt thy tyranny.
translation: [To RICHARD]  I was the last to help you to the crown, and the last to feel the sting of your tyranny.

original: O, in the battle think on Buckingham,   And die in terror of thy guiltiness.
translation: Oh, in battle remember Buckingham, and die in terror of your own guilt. Dream on, dream on, of bloody deeds and death.

original: Dream on, dream on, of bloody deeds and death.   Fainting, despair; despairing, yield thy breath.
translation: And tomorrow, fall and despair, and despairing die!

original: Give me another horse! Bind up my wounds!   Have mercy, Jesu!—Soft, I did but dream.   O coward conscience, how dost thou afflict me!
translation: Give me another horse! Bind up my wounds! Have mercy, Jesus! But wait, I was only dreaming. Oh, you coward conscience, how you torture me!

original: The lights burn blue. It is now dead midnight.   Cold fearful drops stand on my trembling flesh.
translation: The candles burn blue. It is now dead midnight. I'm in a cold sweat and trembling with fear.

original: What do I fear? Myself? There’s none else by.   Richard loves Richard; that is, I and I.
translation: What am I so afraid of? Myself? There's no one else here. Richard loves Richard; that is, I am only myself.

original: Is there a murderer here? No. Yes, I am.   Then fly! What, from myself? Great reason why:   Lest I revenge. What, myself upon myself?
translation: Is there a murderer here? No. But yes, it's  me . Then run away! What, from myself? Yes, so I won't take revenge. What, revenge myself upon myself?

original: Alack, I love myself. Wherefore? For any good   That I myself have done unto myself?
translation: Alas, I love myself. But why? Have I ever done myself any good?

original: O, no! Alas, I rather hate myself   For hateful deeds committed by myself.
translation: No, no! Alas, I hate myself instead, for all the hateful deeds I've committed. I am a villain.

original: I am a villain. Yet I lie. I am not.   Fool, of thyself speak well.
translation: But I'm lying—I am not a villain. Fool, speak well of yourself.

original: Fool, do not flatter.   My conscience hath a thousand several tongues,   And every tongue brings in a several tale,   And every tale condemns me for a villain.
translation: Fool, do not flatter yourself. My conscience has a thousand separate voices, and each voice tells a separate story, and each story condemns me as a villain.

original: Perjury, perjury, in the highest degree;   Murder, stern murder, in the direst degree;   All several sins, all used in each degree,   Throng to the bar, crying all, “Guilty! guilty!”
translation: Perjury, perjury, in the highest degree; murder, ominous murder, in the highest degree; all kinds of sins, all done in each degree—bad, worse, and worst—all of these crimes cry out "Guilty! guilty!"

original: I shall despair. There is no creature loves me,   And if I die no soul will pity me.   And wherefore should they, since that I myself   Find in myself no pity to myself?
translation: I will despair. There is no one who loves me, and if I die no one will pity me. And why should they, since I can't even find any pity for myself in myself?

original: Methought the souls of all that I had murdered   Came to my tent, and every one did threat   Tomorrow’s vengeance on the head of Richard.
translation: Just now it seemed like the souls of all those I murdered came to my tent, and every one of them threatened that vengeance would fall on my head tomorrow.

original: My lord.
translation: My lord.

original: Zounds, who is there?
translation: By God! Who's there?

original: Ratcliffe, my lord, ’tis I. The early village cock Hath twice done salutation to the morn. Your friends are up and buckle on their armor.
translation: My lord, it's Ratcliffe, it's me. The village rooster has already crowed twice to welcome the dawn. Your friends are up and putting on their armor.

original: O Ratcliffe, I have dreamed a fearful dream!  What think’st thou, will our friends prove all true?
translation: Oh, Ratcliffe, I have dreamed a fearful dream! What do you think, will all our friends prove loyal?

original: No doubt, my lord.
translation: No doubt, my lord.

original: O Ratcliffe, I fear, I fear.
translation: Oh, Ratcliffe, I'm afraid, I'm afraid.

original: Nay, good my lord, be not afraid of shadows.
translation: No, my good lord, don't be afraid of shadows.

original: By the apostle Paul, shadows tonight   Have struck more terror to the soul of Richard   Than can the substance of ten thousand soldiers   Armed in proof and led by shallow Richmond.
translation: By Saint Paul, tonight shadows have struck more terror in my soul than ten thousand soldiers could, even if they were dressed in impenetrable armor and led by that fool Richmond.

original: 'Tis not yet near day. Come, go with me;   Under our tents I’ll play the eavesdropper   To see if any mean to shrink from me.
translation: It's not yet daytime. Come with me; I'll eavesdrop under our tents to see if anyone plans to desert me

original: Good morrow, Richmond.
translation: Good morning, Richmond.

original: Cry mercy, lords and watchful gentlemen, That you have ta'en a tardy sluggard here.
translation: I beg your pardon, lords and gentlemen who stayed awake and alert—you've caught me sleeping late.

original: How have you slept, my lord?
translation: How did you sleep, my lord?

original: The sweetest sleep and fairest-boding dreams   That ever entered in a drowsy head   Have I since your departure had, my lords.
translation: My lords, since you last left me, I've had the sweetest sleep and the most hopeful dreams that ever entered someone's drowsy head.

original: Methought their souls whose bodies Richard murdered   Came to my tent and cried on victory.
translation: It seemed like the souls of those Richard had murdered came to my tent and encouraged me to victory.

original: I promise you, my soul is very jocund   In the remembrance of so fair a dream.   How far into the morning is it, lords?
translation: I promise you, my soul is very joyful now, remembering that beautiful dream. How late in the morning is it, lords?

original: Upon the stroke of four.
translation: Almost four o'clock.

original: Why, then ’tis time to arm and give direction.
translation: Why, then it's time to arm myself and direct my troops.

original: What said Northumberland as touching Richmond?
translation: What did Northumberland say regarding Richmond?

original: That he was never trainèd up in arms.
translation: That he was never trained to be a soldier.

original: He said the truth. And what said Surrey then?
translation: He said the truth. And what did Surrey say to that?

original: He smiled and said “The better for our purpose.”
translation: He smiled and said, "All the better for us."

original: He was in the right, and so indeed it is.
translation: He was right, and so indeed it is.

original: Tell the clock there. Give me a calendar.  Who saw the sun today?
translation: Read the clock there. Give me an almanac.  Has anyone seen the sun yet today?

original: Not I, my lord.
translation: Not I, my lord.

original: Then he disdains to shine, for by the book He should have braved the east an hour ago  A black day will it be to somebody. Ratcliffe!
translation: Then it's refusing to shine. For according to this almanac, it should have risen in the east an hour ago. It will be a dark day for somebody today. Hey, Ratcliffe!

original: My lord.
translation: My lord.

original: The sun will not be seen today.   The sky doth frown and lour upon our army.   I would these dewy tears were from the ground.
translation: The sun won't come out today. The sky frowns and scowls at our army. I wish there wasn't all this dew on the ground.

original: Not shine today? Why, what is that to me   More than to Richmond, for the selfsame heaven   That frowns on me looks sadly upon him.
translation: So the sun won't shine today? Why, that shouldn't matter any more to me than it does to Richmond. The same heaven that frowns on me also looks sadly on him.

original: Arm, arm, my lord. The foe vaunts in the field.
translation: Arm yourself, my lord. The enemy is on the battlefield.

original: Come, bustle, bustle. Caparison my horse.—   Call up Lord Stanley; bid him bring his power.—
translation: Come, hurry, hurry. Prepare my horse. Call up Lord Stanley. Tell him to bring his army.

original: I will lead forth my soldiers to the plain,   And thus my battle shall be orderèd:
translation: I will lead my soldiers in the field, with my army arranged like this:

original: My foreward shall be drawn out all in length,   Consisting equally of horse and foot;   Our archers shall be placèd in the midst.
translation: the front lines will be equal parts horsemen and foot soldiers and our archers will be placed in the middle.

original: John Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Earl of Surrey,   Shall have the leading of this foot and horse.
translation: John—the Duke of Norfolk—and Thomas—the Earl of Surrey—will lead the horsemen and foot soldiers.

original: They thus directed, we will follow   In the main battle, whose puissance on either side   Shall be well wingèd with our chiefest horse.
translation: With them placed like this, I will follow with the main army, which will be defended on both sides by our best horsemen.

original: This, and Saint George to boot—What think’st  thou, Norfolk?
translation: We will have all this, and Saint George on our side as well. What do you think, Norfolk?

original: A good direction, warlike sovereign.
translation: A good plan, my warrior king.

original: This found I on my tent this morning.
translation: I found this on my tent this morning.

original: [reads]   Jockey of Norfolk, be not so bold.   For Dickon thy master is bought and sold.   A thing devisèd by the enemy.—
translation: [Reading]   "Jack of Norfolk, don't be too bold, for Dick your master's been bought and sold."  Some plot of the enemy's.

original: Go, gentlemen, every man unto his charge.   Let not our babbling dreams affright our souls.
translation: Go, gentlemen, every man to his position. Don't let our babbling dreams frighten our souls.

original: Conscience is but a word that cowards use,   Devised at first to keep the strong in awe.
translation: "Conscience" is just a word that cowards use to keep down the strong.

original: Our strong arms be our conscience, swords our law.   March on.
translation: Our strength will make us right; our swords will be the law. March on.

original: Join bravely. Let us to it pell mell   If not to heaven, then hand in hand to hell.
translation: Meet the enemy bravely. Let's go down fighting—if not to heaven, then hand in hand to hell.

original: Hark! I hear their drum.   Fight, gentlemen of England.—Fight, bold yeomen.—
translation: Listen! I hear their drums. Fight, gentlemen of England! Fight, bold citizens!

original: Draw, archers, draw your arrows to the head.—
translation: Draw, archers—draw your bows all the way back!

original: Spur your proud horses hard, and ride in blood.   Amaze the welkin with your broken staves—
translation: Horsemen, spur your proud horses hard, and ride with violence, to violence! Break your lances against the enemy and amaze even the heavens!

original: What says Lord Stanley? Will he bring his power?
translation: What does Lord Stanley say? Will he bring his army?

original: My lord, he doth deny to come.
translation: My lord, he refuses to come.

original: Off with his son George’s head!
translation: Off with his son George's head!

original: My lord, the enemy is past the marsh. After the battle let George Stanley die.
translation: My lord, the enemy has passed the marsh. Let George Stanley die after the battle is over.

original: A thousand hearts are great within my bosom.   Advance our standards. Set upon our foes.
translation: A thousand hearts seem to beat within my chest. Advance our banners. Attack our enemies.

original: Our ancient word of courage, fair Saint George,   Inspire us with the spleen of fiery dragons.   Upon them! Victory sits on our helms.
translation: May our ancient battle cry of courage, fair Saint George, inspire us with the fury of fiery dragons! Attack! Victory rides with us.

original: Rescue, my lord of Norfolk, rescue, rescue!   The king enacts more wonders than a man,   Daring an opposite to every danger.
translation: Help, my lord of Norfolk, help, help! The king has performed more wonders than seems humanly possible, facing down every dangerous enemy himself.

original: His horse is slain, and all on foot he fights,   Seeking for Richmond in the throat of death.   Rescue, fair lord, or else the day is lost!
translation: His horse is killed, and now he's fighting on foot, searching for Richmond even in the face of death. Help, honorable lord, or else the battle is lost!

original: A horse, a horse, my kingdom for a horse!
translation: A horse, a horse! I'd give my kingdom for a horse!

original: Withdraw, my lord. I’ll help you to a horse.
translation: Retreat from the fighting, my lord. I'll help you get to a horse.

original: Slave, I have set my life upon a cast,   And I will stand the hazard of the die.   I think there be six Richmonds in the field;
translation: You villain, I have gambled my life on this throw of the dice, and I will take the risks that come with it. I think there are six Richmonds on the battlefield;

original: Five have I slain today instead of him.   A horse, a horse, my kingdom for a horse!
translation: I've killed five already who looked like him. A horse, a horse! I'd give my kingdom for a horse!

original: God and your arms be praised, victorious friends! The day is ours; the bloody dog is dead.
translation: May God and your swords be praised, victorious friends! The day is ours. The bloody dog is dead.

original: [offering him the crown]   Courageous Richmond, well hast thou acquit thee.
translation: [Offering him the crown]  Courageous Richmond, you fought well.

original: Lo, here this long-usurpèd royalty   From the dead temples of this bloody wretch   Have I plucked off, to grace thy brows withal.
translation: See, I took this long-stolen crown from the dead forehead of that bloody wretch. Now let it grace your brows.

original: Wear it, enjoy it, and make much of it.
translation: Wear it, enjoy it, and do much with it.

original: Great God of heaven, say amen to all! But tell me, is young George Stanley living?
translation: Great God of heaven, say amen to all of this! But tell me, is young George Stanley still alive?

original: He is, my lord, and safe in Leicester town, Whither, if it please you, we may now withdraw us.
translation: My lord, he is alive, and safe in Leicester, where we can now go, if you'd like.

original: What men of name are slain on either side?
translation: What noblemen have been killed on either side?

original: John Duke of Norfolk, Walter, Lord Ferrers, Sir Robert Brakenbury, and Sir William Brandon.
translation: John—the Duke of Norfolk; Lord Walter Ferrers; Sir Robert Brakenbury; and Sir William Brandon.

original: Inter their bodies as becomes their births.   Proclaim a pardon to the soldiers fled   That in submission will return to us.
translation: Bury them in a manner appropriate to their social rank. Proclaim a pardon to the soldiers who fled, if they'll return and submit to me.

original: And then, as we have ta'en the sacrament,   We will unite the white rose and the red.
translation: And then—as I swore I would—I will marry  Elizabeth , uniting the York and Lancaster families.

original: Smile heaven upon this fair conjunction,   That long have frowned upon their enmity.
translation: God, smile upon this fair union now, after frowning so long upon the hatred between the two families.

original: What traitor hears me and says not “Amen?”   England hath long been mad and scarred herself.   The brother blindly shed the brother’s blood.
translation: What traitor hears me and doesn't agree? England has been crazy for a long time, and injured herself. Brothers have blindly shed their brothers' blood.

original: The father rashly slaughtered his own son.   The son, compelled, been butcher to the sire.
translation: Fathers have impulsively slaughtered their own sons. Sons have been compelled to butcher their fathers.

original: All this divided York and Lancaster,   Divided, in their dire division.
translation: All this divided York and Lancaster even more, when they were already ominously divided.

original: O, now let Richmond and Elizabeth,   The true succeeders of each royal house,   By God’s fair ordinance conjoin together,
translation: Oh, but now let Richmond and Elizabeth—the true heirs of each royal house—be joined together in holy marriage!

original: And let their heirs, God, if thy will be so,   Enrich the time to come with smooth-faced peace,   With smiling plenty and fair prosperous days!
translation: And if God wills it, let their heirs enrich the future with peace, plenty, and beautiful, prosperous days!

original: Abate the edge of traitors, gracious Lord,   That would reduce these bloody days again,   And make poor England weep in streams of blood!
translation: Gracious God, may you blunt the sharpness of traitors' swords and anyone who would bring back these violent days to make poor England weep tears of blood!

original: Let them not live to taste this land’s increase,   That would with treason wound this fair land’s peace.
translation: If any would try to wound this land's fair peace with treason, then don't let them live to enjoy its prosperity.

original: Now civil wounds are stopped, peace lives again.   That she may long live here, God say amen.
translation: Now civil wounds are bandaged and can heal, and peace lives again. Long may she live here. Let God say amen!

original: Two households, both alike in dignity   In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,   From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,   Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.
translation: In beautiful Verona, where our play takes place, there are two families, both equally noble. From their old grudge there is an outbreak of new fighting, in which they stain their refined hands with fellow citizens' blood.

original: From forth the fatal loins of these two foes   A pair of star-crossed lovers take their life,   Whose misadventured piteous overthrows   Doth with their death bury their parents' strife.
translation: A pair of ill-fated lovers from the deadly bloodlines of these two feuding households commit suicide. Their sad and tragic deaths put an end to their parents' fighting.

original: The fearful passage of their death-marked love   And the continuance of their parents' rage—   Which but their children's end, naught could remove—   Is now the two-hours' traffic of our stage;
translation: Now, for the two hours in which we are onstage, we will present the story of their love and death, which was the only thing that could stop their families' rage.

original: The which if you with patient ears attend,   What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend.
translation: If we've left anything out of this prologue, just listen with patient ears—we will work to make everything understood.

original: Gregory, on my word, we’ll not carry coals.
translation: Gregory, I swear we won’t put up with their crap.

original: No, for then we should be colliers.
I mean, an we be in choler, we’ll draw.
translation: I mean, if they make us angry, we’ll draw our swords.

original: Ay, while you live, draw your neck out of collar.
I strike quickly, being moved.
translation: I hit hard, when I’m motivated.

original: But thou art not quickly moved to strike.
translation: But you avoid getting “motivated,” so you don’t ever have to hit.

original: A dog of the house of Montague moves me.
translation: One of those Montague scoundrels would motivate me.

original: To move is to stir, and to be valiant is to stand.  Therefore if thou art moved thou runn’st away.
translation: To be motivated is to act, while to be valiant is to face a fight. When you’re motivated, you just run away.

original: A dog of that house shall move me to stand. I will take the wall of any man or maid of Montague’s.
translation: If I saw a Montague rascl, I’d face him. I’d walk on the side of the street closer to the wall, and so force the Montague into the gutter.

original: That shows thee a weak slave, for the weakest goes to  the wall.
translation: Then you must be a weakling, because it’s the weak one who gets shoved up against a wall.

original: ‘Tis true, and therefore women, being the weaker  vessels, are ever thrust to the wall. Therefore I will  push Montague’s men from the wall, and thrust his maids  to the wall.
translation: That’s true, which is why women, being the weaker sex, get thrust up against the wall. So I’ll push Montague’s men into the gutter, and thrust Montague women against the wall.

original: The quarrel is between our masters and us their men.
translation: The feud is between our masters and us, their servants.

original: ‘Tis all one. I will show myself a tyrant. When I have  fought with the men, I will be civil with the maids. I  will cut off their heads.
translation: It’s all the same. I’ll be the Montague’s master. After fighting with the men, I’ll be nice to the maids—I’ll cut off their heads.

original: The heads of the maids?
translation: You’ll cut off the heads of the maids?

original: Ay, the heads of the maids, or their maidenheads. Take it in what sense thou wilt.
They must take it in sense that feel it.
translation: It’s the maids you rape or kill or who will have to sense it.

original: Me they shall feel while I am able to stand, and ’tis known I am a pretty piece of flesh.
translation: The maids will feel me as long as I can stand upright. Everyone knows I’m a stud.

original: ‘Tis well thou art not fish. If thou hadst, thou hadst  been poor-john. Draw thy tool! Here comes of the house of Montagues.
My naked weapon is out. Quarrel! I will back thee.
translation: I’ve drawn my sword out of its sheath. Fight them! I’ll back you up.

original: How? Turn thy back and run?
translation: How? By turning your back and running?

original: Fear me not.
translation: Don’t worry about me.

original: No, marry. I fear thee.
Let us take the law of our sides. Let them begin.
translation: Let’s make sure the law is on our side by getting them to start the fight.

original: I will frown as I pass by, and let them take it as  they list.
translation: I’ll frown at them as I pass by them. How they respond is up to them.

original: Nay, as they dare. I will bite my thumb at them, which  is a disgrace to them, if they bear it.  [He bites his  thumb]
translation: No, I’ll bite my thumb at them. That’s an insult, and they’ll be disgraced if they don’t react.

original: Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?
translation: Are you biting your thumb at us, sir?

original: I do bite my thumb, sir.
translation: I am biting my thumb.

original: Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?
translation: But are you biting your thumb at us, sir?

original: Is the law of our side if I say “ay”?
translation: Will the law be on our side if I say yes?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: No, sir. I do not bite my thumb at you, sir, but I bite my thumb, sir.
translation: I’m not biting my thumb at you, sir. But I am biting my thumb, sir.

original: Do you quarrel, sir?
translation: Do you want to fight us, sir?

original: Quarrel, sir? No, sir.
translation: Fight, sir? No, sir.

original: But if you do, sir, I am for you. I serve as good a man as you.
translation: If you do want to fight, sir, then I’m up for it. My master is as good as yours.

original: No better.
translation: But not better than mine.

original: Well, sir.
translation: Very well then, sir.

original: Say “better.” Here comes one of my  master’s kinsmen.
translation: Say “better.” One of our master’s kinsmen has just arrived.

original: Yes, better, sir.
translation: Yes, my master is better than yours, sir.

original: You lie.
translation: You’re a liar.

original: Draw, if you be men.—Gregory, remember thy washing  blow.
translation: Draw your swords, if you’re men. Gregory, get ready to slash them.

original: Part, fools! Put up your swords. You know not what you do.
translation: Break it up, fools! Sheathe your swords. You don’t know what you’re doing.

original: What, art thou drawn among these heartless hinds? Turn thee, Benvolio. Look upon thy death.
translation: What, have you drawn your sword to fight with servants? Turn around, Benvolio, and see the man who will kill you.

original: I do but keep the peace. Put up thy sword, Or manage it to part these men with me.
translation: I’m just trying to keep the peace. Put away your sword, or else use it to help me stop this fighting.

original: What, drawn, and talk of peace? I hate the word, As I hate hell, all Montagues, and thee. Have at thee, coward!
translation: You hold your sword drawn out, and say “peace?” I hate that word, just as I hate hell, all Montagues, and you. Now let's fight, you coward!

original: Clubs, bills, and partisans! Strike! Beat them down! Down with the Capulets! Down with the Montagues!
translation: Beat them down with your clubs, spears, and axes. Hit them! Down with the Capulets! Down with the Montagues!

original: What noise is this? Give me my long sword, ho!
translation: What is this noise? Give me my long sword. Now!

original: A crutch, a crutch! Why call you for a sword?
translation: You need a crutch! Why are you calling for a sword?

original: My sword, I say! Old Montague is come, And flourishes his blade in spite of me.
translation: Give me my sword, I said! Old Montague has arrived, and he’s waving his sword just to spite me.

original: Thou villain Capulet! Hold me not. Let me go.
translation: You are a villain, Capulet!  Let go of me. Don’t stop me.

original: Thou shalt not stir one foot to seek a foe.
translation: You’re not taking one step to try to fight an enemy.

original: Rebellious subjects, enemies to peace,   Profaners of this neighbor-stainèd steel!—
translation: You rebels and enemies of the peace, who curse your own weapons by turning them on your neighbors.

original: Who set this ancient quarrel new abroach?  Speak, nephew. Were you by when it began?
translation: Who stirred this old feud up again? Tell me, nephew. Were you around when the fight began?

original: Here were the servants of your adversary,   And yours, close fighting ere I did approach.   I drew to part them.
translation: Your servants were fighting Capulet's servants when I arrived. I drew my sword to try to stop them.

original: In the instant came   The fiery Tybalt, with his sword prepared,   Which, as he breathed defiance to my ears,   He swung about his head and cut the winds,   Who, nothing hurt withal, hissed him in scorn.
translation: Just then, the reckless Tybalt showed up with his sword drawn. He taunted me while swinging his sword through the air, which made a hissing sound.

original: While we were interchanging thrusts and blows,   Came more and more and fought on part and part,   Till the Prince came, who parted either part.
translation: As we fought, more and more Capulets and Montagues showed up to join the battle. Finally, the Prince came and stopped the fighting.

original: Oh, where is Romeo? Saw you him today? Right glad I am he was not at this fray.
translation: Oh, where’s Romeo? Have you seen him at all today? I’m happy he wasn’t around for this fight.

original: Madam, an hour before the worshipped sun   Peered forth the golden window of the east,   A troubled mind drove me to walk abroad,   Where, underneath the grove of sycamore   That westward rooteth from this city side,
translation: Madam, my mind was troubled this morning, so an hour before dawn I went out for a walk. As I walked, I saw your son beneath the sycamore grove that grows near the western edge of the city.

original: So early walking did I see your son.   Towards him I made, but he was ‘ware of me   And stole into the covert of the wood.   I, measuring his affections by my own,   Which then most sought where most might not be found,
translation: I walked toward him, but he noticed me and ran and hid in the woods. I assumed that he must be feeling the same way I was, and was looking for a place where he wouldn't be found.

original: Being one too many by my weary self,   Pursued my humor not pursuing his,   And gladly shunned who gladly fled from me.
translation: So I continued on, following my own inclination to not pursue Romeo and ask him what was on his mind. I was happy to leave Romeo alone as he fled from me. Besides, I was feeling so weary of company that even being with myself was being with one too many people.

original: Many a morning hath he there been seen,   With tears augmenting the fresh morning’s dew,   Adding to clouds more clouds with his deep sighs.
translation: He’s been seen at that spot on many mornings, his tears adding to the morning dew and his deep sighs thickening the clouds in the sky.

original: But all so soon as the all-cheering sun   Should in the farthest east begin to draw   The shady curtains from Aurora’s bed,   Away from light steals home my heavy son,
translation: Then, as soon as the happy sun begins to  dawn , my unhappy son comes home in order to hide from the light.

original: And private in his chamber pens himself,   Shuts up his windows, locks fair daylight out,   And makes himself an artificial night.
translation: He keeps to himself in his bedroom, shutting his windows to keep out the daylight so that he can sit in an artificial night.

original: Black and portentous must this humor prove   Unless good counsel may the cause remove.
translation: His bad mood is likely to have a bad result, unless someone can give him good advice and remove the cause of his sadness.

original: My noble uncle, do you know the cause?
translation: My noble uncle, do you know what’s causing his mood?

original: I neither know it nor can learn of him.
translation: I don’t know. And he refuses to tell me.

original: Have you importuned him by any means?
translation: Have you done everything possible to get him to explain?

original: Both by myself and many other friends.   But he, his own affections’ counselor,   Is to himself—I will not say how true,
translation: I and many of our friends have tried to speak with him. But he insists on sharing his thoughts only with himself, though I don’t know how good the advice is that he’s giving himself.

original: But to himself so secret and so close,   So far from sounding and discovery,   As is the bud bit with an envious worm,
translation: He keeps his secrets so completely that he’s like a flower bud that can’t open to the air or sun, because it’s been poisoned from within by the bite of a worm.

original: Ere he can spread his sweet leaves to the air,   Or dedicate his beauty to the same.   Could we but learn from whence his sorrows grow.   We would as willingly give cure as know.
translation: If we could just find out the cause of his sadness, we’d try to help him as eagerly as we have tried to figure out why he feels sad.

original: See, where he comes. So please you, step aside. I’ll know his grievance or be much denied.
translation: Here he comes. If you don't mind, please leave us alone. I’ll make him either tell me what’s wrong, or else he'll just decline to tell me over and over again.

original: I would thou wert so happy by thy stay To hear true shrift.—Come, madam, let’s away.
translation: I hope you're lucky enough to hear the true story. Come on, madam, let’s go.

original: Good morrow, cousin.
translation: Good morning, cousin.

original: Is the day so young?
translation: Is it still that early?

original: But new struck nine.
translation: The clock has just barely struck nine.

original: Ay me! Sad hours seem long. Was that my father that went hence so fast?
translation: Oh, my! Time goes by slowly when you’re sad. Was that my father who just rushed away?

original: It was. What sadness lengthens Romeo’s hours?
translation: It was. What sadness is making Romeo's hours so long?

original: Not having that which, having, makes them short.
translation: Lacking the thing which would make the hours short if I had it.

original: In love?
translation: Are you in love?

original: Out.
translation: Out.

original: Of love?
translation: So you’re not in love?

original: Out of her favor, where I am in love.
translation: I am in love. But the one I love does not love me back.

original: Alas, that love, so gentle in his view, Should be so tyrannous and rough in proof!
translation: Oh, it is sad how love, which in theory seems like such a gentle thing, should in actual experience be so rough!

original: Alas, that love, whose view is muffled still,   Should, without eyes, see pathways to his will!   Where shall we dine?
translation: How can love, which is supposed to be blind, force you to be able to do what it wants? Where should we eat?

original: —O me! What fray was here?   Yet tell me not, for I have heard it all.   Here’s much to do with hate but more with love.
translation: Oh my goodness, what fighting happened here? No, don’t tell me. I already know: it was something that had a lot to do with hate, but even more to do with love .

original: Why then, O brawling love, O loving hate,   O anything of nothing first created!   O heavy lightness, serious vanity,   Misshapen chaos of well-seeming forms!
translation: Oh, fighting love! Oh, loving hate! Oh, love that originates from nothing! Oh heavy lightness! Serious frivolity! Beautiful shapes smashed together to create an ugly chaos!

original: Feather of lead, bright smoke, cold fire, sick health,   Still-waking sleep, that is not what it is!   This love feel I, that feel no love in this.   Dost thou not laugh?
translation: Love is like heavy feathers, bright smoke, cold fire, sick health, waking sleep, the opposite of what it is! That’s the love I feel, since no one loves me in return. Are you laughing?

original: No, coz, I rather weep.
translation: No, cousin—I'm crying instead..

original: Good heart, at what?
translation: But why, my good man?

original: At thy good heart’s oppression.
translation: Because of the way love has oppressed your heart.

original: Why, such is love’s transgression.   Griefs of mine own lie heavy in my breast,   Which thou wilt propagate, to have it pressed   With more of thine.
translation: That’s how it it goes with love. My own sadness is a heavy weight on my chest, and now you’re going to add your own sadness to mine.

original: This love that thou hast shown   Doth add more grief to too much of mine own.   Love is a smoke raised with the fume of sighs;   Being purged, a fire sparkling in lovers’ eyes;
translation: The love you are showing me is only increasing my grief. Love is like a smoke made out of the sighs of lovers. When the smoke clears, love is a fire burning in the lovers' eyes.

original: Being vexed, a sea nourished with loving tears.   What is it else? A madness most discreet,   A choking gall, and a preserving sweet.   Farewell, my coz.
translation: But if that love is thwarted, then it is a sea made out of lovers' tears. What else is love? A wise madness. A sweet candy that makes you choke. Goodbye, my cousin.

original: Soft! I will go along. And if you leave me so, you do me wrong.
translation: Wait! I’ll come with you. If you leave me behind, you’ll be insulting me.

original: Tut, I have lost myself. I am not here. This is not Romeo. He’s some other where.
translation: Oh, I’m not acting like myself. It’s as if I’m not even here. This is not Romeo, he’s somewhere else.

original: Tell me in sadness, who is that you love.
translation: Tell me, seriously, who is the one you love?

original: What, shall I groan and tell thee?
translation: What? Should I cry out the name in a groan of sadness?

original: Groan! Why, no. But sadly, tell me who.
translation: Groan?! Why, of course not. Just tell me who it is.

original: A sick man in sadness makes his will, A word ill urged to one that is so ill.  In sadness, cousin, I do love a woman.
translation: You wouldn’t ask a sick man to “seriously” write out his will—it would only make him feel worse. Seriously, cousin, I do love a woman.

original: I aimed so near when I supposed you loved.
translation: I figured that out when I guessed you were in love.

original: A right good markman! And she’s fair I love.
translation: Then you have good aim! And the woman I love is beautiful.

original: A right fair mark, fair coz, is soonest hit.
translation: My dear cousin, a beautiful target is usually the one that is hit fastest.

original: Well, in that hit you miss. She’ll not be hit   With Cupid’s arrow. She hath Dian’s wit.   And, in strong proof of chastity well armed
translation: Well, now you missed the target. She won’t be hit by  Cupid’s  arrow. She’s like  Diana , protected by the armor of chastity.

original: From love’s weak childish bow, she lives uncharmed.   She will not stay the siege of loving terms,   Nor bide th’ encounter of assailing eyes,   Nor ope her lap to saint-seducing gold.
translation: She is immune to the weak and childish arrows of love. She ignores words of love, refuses to even let you look at her with loving eyes, or open her lap to receive golden gifts that would even tempt a saint.

original: Oh, she is rich in beauty, only poor   That when she dies, with beauty dies her store.
translation: Oh, she’s rich in beauty. But she’s also poor, because when she dies her beauty will die along with her.

original: Then she hath sworn that she will still live chaste?
translation: So she’s sworn to live her life a virgin?

original: She hath, and in that sparing makes huge waste,   For beauty, starved with her severity,   Cuts beauty off from all posterity.
translation: She has, and in doing so she wastes her beauty, because by living in chastity she ensures that she will never pass her beauty on to her children.

original: She is too fair, too wise, wisely too fair,   To merit bliss by making me despair.
translation: She’s too beautiful, and too smart, to be allowed to gain entrance to Heaven by making me despair.

original: She hath forsworn to love, and in that vow   Do I live dead that live to tell it now.
translation: She’s sworn never to love, and in that vow has sentenced me to a kind of living death.

original: Be ruled by me. Forget to think of her.
translation: Listen to me. Stop thinking about her.

original: O, teach me how I should forget to think!
translation: Oh, then teach me to forget how to think!

original: By giving liberty unto thine eyes. Examine other beauties.
translation: By letting your eyes wander. Take a look at other beautiful girls.

original: ‘Tis the way   To call hers exquisite, in question more.   These happy masks that kiss fair ladies’ brows,   Being black, puts us in mind they hide the fair.
translation: Such comparisons will only make her own beauty more obvious. It will be like the masks that pretty girls wear to hide their faces. When they hide their beauty, they make us think of it more.

original: He that is strucken blind cannot forget   The precious treasure of his eyesight lost.
translation: A blind man can’t forget the precious eyesight he lost.

original: Show me a mistress that is passing fair;   What doth her beauty serve but as a note   Where I may read who passed that passing fair?
translation: Show me any beautiful girl. What good is her beauty, other than a reminder of  a girl who is even more beautiful?

original: Farewell. Thou canst not teach me to forget.
translation: Goodbye. You can’t teach me to forget.

original: I'll pay that doctrine or else die in debt.
translation: I'll teach you how to forget, or else I'll die owing you the lesson.

original: But Montague is bound as well as I,   In penalty alike.
translation: Montague has sworn the same oath I have, and is bound by the same penalty.

original: And ’tis not hard, I think,   For men so old as we to keep the peace.
translation: I don’t think it should be hard for men as old as us to remain peaceful.

original: Of honorable reckoning are you both.   And pity ’tis you lived at odds so long.
translation: You both have honorable reputations. It’s a pity you’ve been enemies for so long.

original: But now, my lord, what say you to my suit?
translation: But, now, my lord: how do you respond to my request?

original: But saying o’er what I have said before.   My child is yet a stranger in the world.
translation: By repeating what I’ve said before. My child is still extremely young.

original: She hath not seen the change of fourteen years.   Let two more summers wither in their pride   Ere we may think her ripe to be a bride.
translation: She’s not even fourteen years old. Let’s allow two more summers to pass before we consider her ready for marriage.

original: Younger than she are happy mothers made.
translation: Girls who are younger than your daughter have become happy mothers.

original: And too soon marred are those so early made.   Earth hath swallowed all my hopes but she.   She’s the hopeful lady of my earth.
translation: Girls who marry that young grow up too quickly. All of my other children are dead and buried in the earth, so all hopes on this earth rest in her.

original: But woo her, gentle Paris, get her heart.   My will to her consent is but a part.   An she agreed within her scope of choice,   Lies my consent and fair according voice.
translation: But you may woo her, kind Paris. Win her love. My permission for you to marry her is only part of the bargain; she must also agree to marry you. Then my blessing on the marriage will confirm her choice.

original: This night I hold an old accustomed feast,   Whereto I have invited many a guest   Such as I love. And you among the store,   One more, most welcome, makes my number more.
translation: This very night I’m throwing a party that I’ve hosted for many years. I’ve invited many guests, many close friends. I’d like to invite you as a most welcome guest.

original: At my poor house look to behold this night   Earth-treading stars that make dark heaven light.
translation: At my humble home tonight, you’ll see see young women like stars that walk the earth and light the sky from below.

original: Such comfort as do lusty young men feel   When well-appareled April on the heel   Of limping winter treads.   Even such delight   Among fresh fennel buds shall you this night   Inherit at my house.
translation: Like all lusty young men, you’ll be delighted by the young women who are as fresh as spring flowers.

original: Hear all, all see,   And like her most whose merit most shall be—   Which on more view of many, mine, being one,   May stand in number, though in reckoning none,   Come, go with me.
translation: Look at them all, and choose whichever woman you like best. Amidst all these girls, you may no longer think that my daughter’s the most beautiful. Come with me.

original: Find them out whose names are written here? It is  written, that the shoemaker should meddle with his yard  and the tailor with his last, the fisher with his pencil and the painter with his nets.
translation: Find the people whose names are on this list? It’s written that shoemakers and tailors should use each others’ tools, and that fisherman should play with paints while painters should play with with fishing nets.

original: But I am sent to find  those persons whose names are here writ, and can never  find what names the writing person hath here writ. I  must to the learned in good time!
translation: But now I’ve been sent to find the people on this list, and I can’t read. I’ll have to ask somebody educated to help me.

original: Tut man, one fire burns out another’s burning.   One pain is lessened by another’s anguish.
translation: Come on, Romeo. Starting a new fire will put out the old one. An old pain is lessened by the arrival of a new one.

original: Turn giddy, and be helped by backward turning.   One desperate grief cures with another’s languish.
translation: If you make yourself dizzy, you can cure yourself by spinning in the other direction. A new grief will cure an old one.

original: Take thou some new infection to thy eye,   And the rank poison of the old will die.
translation: Stare obsessively at some new girl, and your former lovesickness will disappear.

original: Your plantain leaf is excellent for that.
For what, I pray thee?
translation: For what?

original: For your broken shin.
translation: For treating your injured shin.

original: Why Romeo, art thou mad?
translation: Why, Romeo, have you gone crazy?

original: Not mad, but bound more than a madman is, Shut up in prison, kept without my food, Whipped and tormented and—Good e’en, good fellow.
translation: No, though I’m bound more tightly than any mental patient is. I’m locked in a prison without food. I’m whipped, tortured.

original: God ‘i’ good e’en. I pray, sir, can you read?
translation: A blessed good evening to you. Excuse me, sir, do you know how to read?

original: Ay, mine own fortune in my misery.
translation: Yes. I can read my fortune in my misery.

original: Perhaps you have learned it without book. But I pray,  can you read anything you see?
Ay, if I know the letters and the language.
translation: Yes, if I know the letters and the language.

original: Ye say honestly. Rest you merry.
translation: You speak honestly. Have a nice day.

original: Stay, fellow. I can read.
translation: Stay, man. I can read.

original: “Seigneur Martino and his wife and daughters;   County Anselme and his beauteous sisters;
translation: “Signor Martino and his wife and daughters; Count Anselme and his gorgeous sisters;

original: The lady widow of Vitruvio;   Seigneur Placentio and his lovely nieces;
translation: Vitravio’s widow; Signor Placentio and his lovely nieces;

original: Mercutio and his brother Valentine;   Mine uncle Capulet, his wife and daughters;
translation: Mercutio and his brother Valentine; my uncle Capulet and his wife and daughters;

original: My fair niece Rosaline and Livia;   Seigneur Valentio and his cousin Tybalt;   Lucio and the lively Helena.”
translation: my fair niece Rosaline and Livia; Signor Valentio and his cousin Tybalt; Lucio and the lively Helena.”

original: A fair assembly. Whither should they come?
translation: That’s quite a lovely group of people. Where are they supposed to go?

original: Up.
translation: Up.

original: Whither?
translation: Where?

original: To supper; to our house.
translation: To supper. To our house.

original: Whose house?
translation: Whose house?

original: My master’s.
translation: My master’s house.

original: Indeed, I should have asked thee that before.
translation: Indeed, I should have asked you that earlier.

original: Now I’ll tell you without asking. My master is the  great rich Capulet, and if you be not of the house of  Montagues, I pray come and crush a cup of wine. Rest you merry!
translation: I’ll tell you so that you don’t have to ask. My master is the great, rich Capulet. And as long as you are not a Montague, I invite you to come and drink a cup of wine at our house. Have a nice day!
