original: At this same ancient feast of Capulet’s   Sups the fair Rosaline whom thou so loves   With all the admired beauties of Verona.
translation: Rosaline whom you love so much is going to attend Capulet's traditional feast, along with all the beautiful woman of Verona.

original: Go thither, and with unattainted eye   Compare her face with some that I shall show,   And I will make thee think thy swan a crow.
translation: Go there and, without bias, compare her to some of the girls I’ll point out to you. I’ll show you that the woman you think is as beautiful as a swan is in fact as ugly as a crow.

original: When the devout religion of mine eye   Maintains such falsehood, then turn tears to fires,
translation: If my eyes ever show me such a lie about the woman they worship, then may my tears turn into flames.

original: And these, who, often drowned, could never die,   Transparent heretics, be burnt for liars!
translation: That way my eyes, which never drowned in all my tears, may be burned for being such clear liars!

original: One fairer than my love? The all-seeing sun   Ne’er saw her match since first the world begun.
translation: A woman more beautiful than my love? The sun has never seen anyone as beautiful since the world began.

original: Tut, you saw her fair, none else being by,   Herself poised with herself in either eye.
translation: Oh come on. You decided she was beautiful when no one else was around and there was no one to compare her to except herself.

original: But in that crystal scales let there be weighed   Your lady’s love against some other maid   That I will show you shining at the feast,   And she shall scant show well that now shows best.
translation: But if instead you compare her to some other beautiful woman who I’ll point out to you at this feast, you’ll see that she’s far from the best.

original: I'll go along, no such sight to be shown,  But to rejoice in splendor of mine own.
translation: I'll go along with you—not to look at other women, but to rejoice in my love's beauty.

original: Nurse, where’s my daughter? Call her forth to me.
translation: Nurse, where’s my daughter? Tell her to come here.

original: Now, by my maidenhead at twelve year old I bade her come. What, lamb! What, ladybird! God forbid! Where’s this girl? What, Juliet!
translation: I swear by my virginity at age twelve, I told her to come. What is this?! Heaven forbid! Where is that girl? Juliet!

original: How now, who calls?
translation: What? Who’s calling me?

original: Your mother.
translation: Your mother.

original: Madam, I am here. What is your will?
translation: Madam, I’m here. What do you want?

original: This is the matter.—Nurse, give leave awhile,   We must talk in secret.
translation: Here’s what I want—Nurse, leave us for a bit while we talk privately

original: —Nurse, come back again.   I have remembered me. Thou’s hear our counsel.   Thou know’st my daughter’s of a pretty age.
translation: —wait, no, Nurse, come back. I just remembered, you can listen to our secrets. You know my daughter’s of a certain age.

original: Faith, I can tell her age unto an hour.
translation: Yes, I know her age to the hour.

original: She’s not fourteen.
translation: She’s not yet fourteen.

original: I’ll lay fourteen of my teeth—and yet, to my teen be it spoken, I have but four—she is not fourteen. How long  is it now to Lammastide?
A fortnight and odd days.
translation: Two weeks and a few odd days.

original: Even or odd, of all days in the year,   Come Lammas Eve at night shall she be fourteen.   Susan and she—God rest all Christian souls!—   Were of an age.
translation: Even or odd, of all the days in the year, she’ll be fourteen on the night of  July 31st . She and my daughter Susan—God rest all Christian souls—were born that same day.

original: Well, Susan is with God.   She was too good for me. But, as I said,   On Lammas Eve at night shall she be fourteen.   That shall she.
translation: Well, Susan died and is now with God. She was too good for me. But, as I said, on the night of July 31st, Juliet will be fourteen. Yes, she will indeed.

original: Marry, I remember it well.   ‘Tis since the earthquake now eleven years,   And she was weaned—I never shall forget it—
translation: I remember it well. It’s been eleven years since the earthquake, and it was on that very day that she stopped nursing from my breast. I’ll never forget it.

original: Of all the days of the year, upon that day.   For I had then laid wormwood to my dug,   Sitting in the sun under the dovehouse wall.   My lord and you were then at Mantua.—   Nay, I do bear a brain.
translation: I had put some bitter wormwood on my breast as I was sitting in the sun, under the wall of the dovehouse. Your husband and you were in Mantua. Oh my, what a great memory I have!

original: —But, as I said,   When it did taste the wormwood on the nipple   Of my dug and felt it bitter, pretty fool,   To see it tetchy and fall out with the dug!
translation: As I said, when Juliet tasted the bitter wormwood on my nipple, the pretty little thing got angry with my breast. That’s when the earthquake hit and the dovehouse started to shake.

original: “Shake!” quoth the dovehouse. ‘Twas no need, I trow,   To bid me trudge.   And since that time it is eleven years,   For then she could stand alone.
translation: You didn’t have to tell me to get out of there. It’s been eleven years since then. She could stand up by herself then.

original: Nay, by the rood,   She could have run and waddled all about,   For even the day before, she broke her brow.
translation: No, in fact, by then she could run and waddle all over the place. I remember because just the day before she had cut her forehead.

original: And then my husband—God be with his soul!   He was a merry man—took up the child.   “Yea,” quoth he, “Dost thou fall upon thy face?   Thou wilt fall backward when thou hast more wit,   Wilt thou not, Jule?”
translation: My husband—God rest his soul, he was a jolly man—picked Juliet up. “Oh,” he said, “Did you fall on your face?  You’ll fall backward when you grow up , won’t you, Jule?”

original: and, by my holy dame,   The pretty wretch left crying and said “ay.”   To see now, how a jest shall come about!
translation: And, by God, the pretty little thing stopped crying and said, “Yes.” To watch a joke come true!

original: I warrant, an I should live a thousand years,   I never should forget it. “Wilt thou not, Jule?” quoth  he.   And, pretty fool, it stinted and said “ay.”
translation: Even if I live a thousand years I’ll never forget it. “Won’t you, Jule,” he said. And the pretty fool stopped crying and said, “Yes.”

original: Enough of this. I pray thee, hold thy peace.
translation: Enough of this. Please, be quiet.

original: Yes, madam. Yet I cannot choose but laugh   To think it should leave crying and say “ay.”
translation: Yes, madam. But I have to laugh when I think that the baby stopped crying and said, “Yes.”

original: And yet, I warrant, it had upon its brow   A bump as big as a young cockerel’s stone,   A perilous knock, and it cried bitterly.
translation: What’s more, I swear she had a bump on her forehead as big as a rooster’s testicle. It was quite a knock she took, and she was crying bitterly.

original: “Yea,” quoth my husband, “Fall’st upon thy face?   Thou wilt fall backward when thou comest to age.   Wilt thou not, Jule?” It stinted and said “ay.”
translation: “Yes,” said my husband, “Did you fall on your face? You’ll fall backward when you grow up, won’t you, Jule?” And she stopped crying and said, “Yes.’

original: And stint thou too, I pray thee, Nurse, say I.
translation: Please, Nurse, I'm asking you to step, too.

original: Peace, I have done. God mark thee to his grace!
translation: I'll be quiet. I’m done. May you receive God’s grace.

original: Thou wast the prettiest babe that e’er I nursed.   An I might live to see thee married once,   I have my wish.
translation: You were the prettiest baby I ever nursed. If I live to see you get married someday, my wishes will be fulfilled.

original: Marry, that “marry” is the very theme I came to talk of. Tell me, daughter Juliet, How stands your disposition to be married?
translation: In fact, marriage is exactly what I came here to discuss. Tell me, Juliet, my daughter—what do you think about getting married?

original: It is an honor that I dream not of.
translation: It's an honor that I don’t think about at all.

original: An honor! Were not I thine only nurse,  I would say thou hadst sucked wisdom from thy teat.
translation: “An honor!” If I weren’t the only nurse you’ve had, I’d say you’d sucked wisdom from the breast that fed you.

original: Well, think of marriage now. Younger than you   Here in Verona, ladies of esteem   Are made already mothers.
translation: Well, you should start thinking about marriage. In Verona, girls from noble families who are younger than you have already become mothers.

original: By my count,   I was your mother much upon these years   That you are now a maid.
translation: By my count, I was already your mother at around your age, while you remain a virgin.

original: Thus then in brief:   The valiant Paris seeks you for his love.
translation: So, to be brief: the valiant Paris wants to marry you.

original: A man, young lady! Lady, such a man As all the world. Why, he’s a man of wax.
translation: What a man, young lady! He’s a man as great as any other in the world. He’s so perfect it’s as if he were sculpted from wax.

original: Verona’s summer hath not such a flower.
translation: Verona in the summertime has no flower as fine as him.

original: Nay, he’s a flower. In faith, a very flower.
translation: He’s a fine flower, absolutely, a flower.

original: What say you? Can you love the gentleman?   This night you shall behold him at our feast.   Read o’er the volume of young Paris’ face   And find delight writ there with beauty’s pen.
translation: What do you say, Juliet? Can you love this gentleman? Tonight he’ll be at our feast. Look at his face and delight in his beauty.

original: Examine every married lineament   And see how one another lends content,   And what obscured in this fair volume lies   Find written in the margin of his eyes.
translation: Examine how all the lines of his features combine to make him handsome. And what you can’t see in his beauty, find by looking in his eyes.

original: This precious book of love, this unbound lover,   To beautify him only lacks a cover.   The fish lives in the sea, and ’tis much pride   For fair without the fair within to hide.
translation: This wonderful, loving man lacks only a bride to make him perfect. As fish do not hide from the sea, neither should a beauty like you hide from a handsome man like him.

original: That book in many’s eyes doth share the glory   That in gold clasps locks in the golden story.   So shall you share all that he doth possess   By having him, making yourself no less.
translation: Everyone thinks he’s handsome, and whoever becomes his bride would be equally loved. You would share all that he possesses, and lose nothing by having him.

original: No less? Nay, bigger. Women grow by men.
Speak briefly. Can you like of Paris, love?
translation: Answer me now. Can you love Paris?

original: I’ll look to like if looking liking move.  But no more deep will I endart mine eye Than your consent gives strength to make it fly.
translation: I’ll look at him with the intent to like him, if looking at him moves me to like him. But I won’t let myself fall for him any more than your permission allows.

original: Madam, the guests are come, supper served up, you  called, my young lady asked for, the Nurse cursed in the pantry,
translation: Madam, the guests are here and dinner is served. Your guests call for you and Juliet, while the servants in the pantry are cursing the Nurse.

original: and every thing in extremity. I must hence to  wait. I beseech you, follow straight.
translation: Things are getting out of control. I must rush off to serve the guests. Please, follow right after me.

original: We follow thee.—Juliet, the county stays.
translation: We’ll follow you. Juliet, Paris is waiting for you.

original: Go, girl, seek happy nights to happy days.
translation: Go, girl, and look for the man who will give you happy nights at the end of happy days.

original: What, shall this speech be spoke for our excuse? Or shall we on without apology?
translation: What excuse will we make? Or should we enter without apology?

original: The date is out of such prolixity.   We’ll have no Cupid hoodwinked with a scarf,   Bearing a Tartar’s painted bow of lath,   Scaring the ladies like a crowkeeper,
translation: It’s no longer fashionable to talk that much. We’re not going to announce our entrance with some guy blindfolded, dressed up as Cupid, and carrying a toy bow in order to frighten the ladies like some scarecrow.

original: Nor no without-book prologue, faintly spoke   After the prompter for our entrance.
translation: Nor will we introduce ourselves with a memorized speech.

original: But let them measure us by what they will.   We’ll measure them a measure and be gone.
translation: They can judge us however they want. We’ll dance for one dance, and then get out of there.

original: Give me a torch. I am not for this ambling. Being but heavy, I will bear the light.
translation: Give me a torch. I don’t feel like dancing. Since I’m sad, I might as well carry the light.

original: Nay, gentle Romeo, we must have you dance.
translation: No, sweet Romeo, you have to dance.

original: Not I, believe me. You have dancing shoes  With nimble soles. I have a soul of lead So stakes me to the ground I cannot move.
translation: Not me, believe me. You’ve got on dancing shoes with nimble soles. But my soul is made of lead so heavy that it anchors me to the ground and I can’t move.

original: You are a lover. Borrow Cupid’s wings And soar with them above a common bound.
translation: You’re a lover. Borrow Cupid’s wings and use them to soar higher than the average man.

original: I am too sore enpiercèd with his shaft
translation: I’ve been too strongly pierced by his arrow to soar.

original: To soar with his light feathers, and so bound,   I cannot bound a pitch above dull woe.
translation: My wounded heart won’t let me escape my dull sadness.

original: Under love’s heavy burden do I sink.
translation: I am sinking under love’s heavy burden.

original: And to sink in it, should you burthen love— Too great oppression for a tender thing.
Is love a tender thing? It is too rough, Too rude, too boisterous, and it pricks like thorn.
translation: Is love really so tender? To me it seems too rough, too rude, too unruly, and it pricks like a thorn.

original: If love be rough with you, be rough with love.   Prick love for pricking, and you beat love down.—
translation: If love is rough with you, be rough with love. Prick love when it pricks you, and you’ll beat love down.

original: Give me a case to put my visage in!   A visor for a visor.
translation: Give me a mask to put over my face. A mask to cover that mask I call my face.

original: —What care I   What curious eye doth cote deformities?   Here are the beetle brows shall blush for me.
translation: What do I care if someone sees my flaws? Let the this mask, with its dark eyebrows, blush for me.

original: Come, knock and enter. And no sooner in But every man betake him to his legs.
translation: Come on, let’s knock and go inside. And once inside, let’s all start dancing.

original: A torch for me. Let wantons light of heart   Tickle the senseless rushes with their heels.
translation: Give me a torch to carry. Let those with light hearts dance.

original: For I am proverbed with a grandsire phrase,   I’ll be a candle holder, and look on.   The game was ne’er so fair, and I am done.
translation: There’s an old proverb that fits me perfectly: I’ll hold a torch and watch. The game looks like fun, but I’m done with it.

original: Tut, dun’s the mouse, the constable’s own word.
translation: Come on, “ dun ” is the color of a timid mouse. You’re being as timid as a patrolman on night duty.

original: If thou art dun, we’ll draw thee from the mire,   Or—save your reverence—love, wherein thou stick’st   Up to the ears. Come, we burn daylight, ho!
translation: If you’re a stick stuck in the mud, we’ll pull you out—pardon me for being rude— out of the love in which you’re stuck up to your ears. Come on, we’re wasting daylight.

original: Nay, that’s not so.
translation: No, that’s wrong—it’s night.

original: I mean, sir, in delay.   We waste our lights in vain, like lights by day.
translation: I mean, sir, that by delaying we’re wasting our torches, which is like wasting the sunshine during the day.

original: Take our good meaning, for our judgment sits   Five times in that ere once in our five wits.
translation: Show your good judgment by taking what I say the way I mean it, which is five times more important than literally trusting your five senses.

original: And we mean well in going to this mask, But ’tis no wit to go.
translation: We mean well by going to this party, but it’s not smart of us to go.

original: Why, may one ask?
translation: Why, may I ask?

original: I dreamt a dream tonight.
translation: I dreamed a dream last night.

original: And so did I.
translation: So did I.

original: Well, what was yours?
translation: What was your dream?

original: That dreamers often lie.
translation: I dreamed that dreamers often lie.

original: In bed asleep while they do dream things true.
translation: They lie in bed while dreaming about true things.

original: Oh, then, I see Queen Mab hath been with you.
Queen Mab, what’s she?
translation: Queen Mab? Who’s she?

original: She is the fairies’ midwife, and she comes   In shape no bigger than an agate stone   On the forefinger of an alderman,   Drawn with a team of little atomi   Over men’s noses as they lie asleep.
translation: She’s the fairies’ midwife, and is no bigger than the stone on the ring of a city councilman. She rides her carriage, which is pulled by tiny little creatures, over men’s noses as they lie sleeping.

original: Her wagon spokes made of long spinners’ legs,   The cover of the wings of grasshoppers,   Her traces of the smallest spider’s web,
translation: The wheel spokes of her carriage are made of spiders’ legs; its cover is made of grasshopper wings; and its harnesses are made of the smallest spiderwebs.

original: Her collars of the moonshine’s watery beams,   Her whip of cricket’s bone, the lash of film,   Her wagoner a small gray-coated gnat,   Not half so big as a round little worm   Pricked from the lazy finger of a maid.
translation: The horse collars are made from moonbeams, while her whip is a single cobweb attached to a cricket bone. Her wagon driver is a tiny gnat wearing a gray coat that is not even half as large as  a little round worm  that comes from the finger of a lazy young girl.

original: Her chariot is an empty hazelnut   Made by the joiner squirrel or old grub,   Time out o’ mind the fairies’ coachmakers.   And in this state she gallops night by night   Through lovers’ brains, and then they dream of love;
translation: Her carriage is an empty hazelnut, made by a squirrel and an old worm, which have been the fairies’ carriage-builders for countless years.  With this magnificent carriage she rides each night through the brains of lovers, who then dream about love.

original: On courtiers’ knees, that dream on curtsies straight;   O’er lawyers’ fingers, who straight dream on fees;   O’er ladies’ lips, who straight on kisses dream,
translation: She rides across courtiers’ knees, who then dream about bowing and curtsying. She rides over lawyers’ fingers, who then dream about their fees. She rides over ladies’ lips, and they immediately dream of kisses.

original: Which oft the angry Mab with blisters plagues,   Because their breaths with sweetmeats tainted are.   Sometime she gallops o’er a courtier’s nose,   And then dreams he of smelling out a suit.
translation: But Queen Mab often puts blisters on their lips because their breath smells of candy, which angers her. Sometimes she rides over a courtier’s nose, and he dreams of sniffing out a way to make some money.

original: And sometime comes she with a tithe-pig’s tail   Tickling a parson’s nose as he lies asleep,   Then he dreams of another benefice.
translation: Sometimes she tickles a priest’s nose with the tail of pig given as a tithe to the church, and he dreams of getting a high-paid church position.

original: Sometime she driveth o’er a soldier’s neck,   And then dreams he of cutting foreign throats,   Of breaches, ambuscadoes, Spanish blades,   Of healths five fathom deep, and then anon   Drums in his ear, at which he starts and wakes,   And being thus frighted swears a prayer or two   And sleeps again.
translation: Sometimes she drives over a soldier’s neck, and he dreams of cutting the throats of foreigners, of breaking through fortifications, of ambushes, of the finest-quality Spanish swords, and of huge mugs of alcohol before suddenly waking, frightened, by the sound of drums in his ears. Then he says a prayer or two and goes back to sleep.

original: This is that very Mab   That plaits the manes of horses in the night   And bakes the elflocks in foul sluttish hairs,   Which once untangled, much misfortune bodes.
translation: Mab is the one who tangles the hair of horses’ manes at night and then hardens the tangles in the foul, dirty hairs; tangles which, if you undo them, bring bad luck.

original: This is the hag, when maids lie on their backs,   That presses them and learns them first to bear,   Making them women of good carriage.   This is she—
translation: Mab is the hag who gives dreams of sex to virgins and teaches them how to bear the weight of a lover and to bear a child. She’s the one—

original: Peace, peace, Mercutio, peace! Thou talk’st of nothing.
translation: Calm down, calm down! Mercutio, be calm. You’re talking about nothing.

original: True, I talk of dreams,   Which are the children of an idle brain,
translation: True. I’m talking about dreams, which are produced by a brain that’s doing nothing.

original: Begot of nothing but vain fantasy,   Which is as thin of substance as the air
translation: Dreams are born of no more than empty fantasy, which lack substance like air,

original: And more inconstant than the wind, who woos   Even now the frozen bosom of the north,   And, being angered, puffs away from thence,   Turning his face to the dew-dropping south.
translation: and are more unpredictable than the wind, which can blow on the frozen north and then suddenly get angry and blow south.

original: This wind you talk of, blows us from ourselves. Supper is done, and we shall come too late.
translation: This wind you’re talking about is blowing us off course. Dinner is already over. We’re going to get there too late.

original: I fear too early, for my mind misgives   Some consequence yet hanging in the stars   Shall bitterly begin his fearful date   With this night’s revels, and expire the term   Of a despisèd life closed in my breast   By some vile forfeit of untimely death.
translation: I fear we’re going to arrive too early. I have a feeling this party tonight is fated to set in motion some awful destiny that will result in my own untimely death.

original: But he that hath the steerage of my course,   Direct my sail. On, lusty gentlemen.
translation: But whoever’s in charge of my fate can steer me where they want. Let’s go, my lusty friends!

original: Strike, drum.
translation: Bang the drum!

original: Where’s Potpan, that he helps not to take away? He  shift a trencher? He scrape a trencher!
translation: Where’s Potpan, who’s not helping us clear the table? Has he even moved or scraped a plate?

original: When good manners shall lie all in one or two men’s  hands, and they unwashed too, ’tis a foul thing.
translation: When all the good manners are owned by just one or two men, and even those two are dirty, it’s a bad thing.

original: Away with the joint-stools, remove the court-cupboard, look to the plate. Good thou, save me a piece of  marchpane,
translation: Clear away the stools, sideboards, and plates. My friend, save me a piece of marzipan,

original: and, as thou loves me, let the porter let in  Susan Grindstone and Nell.—Antony and Potpan!
translation: and if you love me, have the porter let in Susan Grindstone and Nell. Antony and Potpan!

original: Ay, boy, ready.
translation: Yes, boy, I’m ready.

original: You are looked for and called for, asked for and  sought for, in the great chamber.
translation: You’re being called for, asked after, and looked for in the great chamber.

original: We cannot be here and there too. Cheerly, boys. Be  brisk a while, and the longer liver take all.
translation: We can’t be both here and there at once! Be cheerful, boys. Be quick for a while, and may the longest lived take everything.

original: Welcome, gentlemen! Ladies that have their toes   Unplagued with corns will walk a bout with you.   Ah, my mistresses! Which of you all   Will now deny to dance?
translation: Welcome, gentlemen. All the ladies who aren’t suffering from corns on their feet will dance with you. Ha ha! My ladies, now which of you will refuse to dance now?

original: She that makes dainty,   She, I’ll swear, hath corns. Am I come near ye now?—
translation: If any of you acts shyly, I’ll swear she has corns. Have I hit the mark?

original: Welcome, gentlemen! I have seen the day   That I have worn a visor and could tell   A whispering tale in a fair lady’s ear   Such as would please.
translation: Welcome, gentlemen. Once there was a time when I could wear a mask and charm a girl by whispering a story in her ear.

original: ‘Tis gone, ’tis gone, ’tis gone.—   You are welcome, gentlemen.—Come, musicians, play.
translation: No more, no more, no more. You are welcome gentlemen. Come, musicians, play.

original: A hall, a hall, give room!—And foot it, girls.—
translation: Make room in the hall! Make room! Dance, girls.

original: By’r Lady, thirty years.
translation: By the Virgin Mary, I’d swear thirty years.

original: What, man, ’tis not so much, ’tis not so much.   ‘Tis since the nuptials of Lucentio,
translation: What, man? It’s not been that long, not that long. It was at Lucentio’s wedding.

original: Come Pentecost as quickly as it will,   Some five and twenty years, and then we masked.
translation: No matter how quickly the years fly by, it’s been just twenty-five years since we last wore masks.

original: ‘Tis more, ’tis more. His son is elder, sir. His son is thirty.
translation: Longer, longer. Lucentio’s son is older than that, sir. He’s thirty.

original: Will you tell me that? His son was but a ward two years ago.
translation: How can you say that? His son was still a minor two years ago.

original: What lady is that which doth enrich  the hand Of yonder knight?
translation: Who is that girl on the arm of that man over there?

original: I know not, sir.
translation: I don’t know, sir.

original: Oh, she doth teach the torches to burn bright!   It seems she hangs upon the cheek of night   Like a rich jewel in an Ethiope’s ear,   Beauty too rich for use, for earth too dear.
translation: Oh, she teaches the torches to burn bright! She glows in the darkness like a jewel in the ear of an African. Her beauty is too good to be used and worn, too precious for this world.

original: So shows a snowy dove trooping with crows   As yonder lady o’er her fellows shows.   The measure done, I’ll watch her place of stand,   And, touching hers, make blessèd my rude hand.
translation: Like a white dove in a flock of crows, she surpasses all the other women. When this dance ends, I’ll note where she stands, and then I’ll touch her hand and thereby bless my ugly one.

original: Did my heart love till now? Forswear it, sight!   For I ne’er saw true beauty till this night.
translation: Did I ever love anyone before this moment? Renounce that love, my eyes! I never saw true beauty until this night.

original: This, by his voice, should be a Montague.—
translation: By his voice I know that this man is a Montague.

original: Why, how now, kinsman? Wherefore storm you so?
translation: What’s all this, nephew? Why are you so furious?

original: Uncle, this is a Montague, our foe, A villain that is hither come in spite To scorn at our solemnity this night.
translation: Uncle, that is a Montague—our rival. He’s a rogue who’s come here out of spite to scorn our celebration.

original: Young Romeo is it?
translation: It’s young Romeo, right?

original: ‘Tis he, that villain Romeo.
translation: That’s him, that villain Romeo.

original: Content thee, gentle coz. Let him alone.   He bears him like a portly gentleman,   And, to say truth, Verona brags of him   To be a virtuous and well-governed youth.
translation: Calm yourself, gentle  nephew . Leave him be. He holds himself like a gentleman of good manners, and, to be honest, everyone in Verona says that he is a virtuous and well-behaved youth.

original: I would not for the wealth of all the town   Here in my house do him disparagement.   Therefore be patient. Take no note of him.
translation: Not for all the wealth in this town would I insult him in my own house. Be calm. Pretend you never saw him .

original: It is my will, the which if thou respect,   Show a fair presence and put off these frowns,   An ill-beseeming semblance for a feast.
translation: That is my command, and if you respect me, you’ll stop with all these frowns, which is no way to behave at a party.

original: It fits when such a villain is a guest.  I’ll not endure him.
translation: It’s the way to behave when a scoundrel like him shows up. I won’t stand him coming here.

original: He shall be endured.   What, goodman boy! I say, he shall. Go to.   Am I the master here, or you? Go to.
translation: You will stand him. What, boy? I say you will. Get out of here. Am I the master here, or you? Get out.

original: You’ll not endure him! God shall mend my soul,   You’ll make a mutiny among my guests.   You will set cock-a-hoop. You’ll be the man!
translation: You won’t stand him? God save my soul, you’ll start a riot among my guests! And you’ll crow like a rooster, like you’re the man!

original: Why, uncle, ’tis a shame.
translation: But, uncle, we’re being dishonored.

original: Go to, go to.   You are a saucy boy. Is ’t so, indeed?   This trick may chance to scathe you, I know what.   You must contrary me. Marry, ’tis time.—
translation: Come on, come on. You’re an impertinent boy. Is that really how you think it is? This silliness is likely to come back to harm you. I know what I’m doing, but you feel the need to contradict me. Well, I’ll show you a thing or two.

original: Patience perforce with willful choler meeting   Makes my flesh tremble in their different greeting.
translation: The blend of enforced restraint with my burning rage is making me tremble.

original: I will withdraw, but this intrusion shall   Now seeming sweet, convert to bitterest gall.
translation: I’ll leave. But I’ll make Romeo regret this prank, which at the moment seems to him like such great fun.

original: If I profane with my unworthiest hand   This holy shrine, the gentle sin is this:
translation: If I offend you by touching your holy hand with my own unworthy one,

original: My lips, two blushing pilgrims, ready stand   To smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.
translation: then my lips stand ready, like two blushing pilgrims, to smooth my rough touch with a gentle kiss.

original: Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much,   Which mannerly devotion shows in this,
translation: Good pilgrim, you are unfair to your hand. Your hand shows proper devotion by touching mine,

original: For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do touch,   And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss.
translation: just as pilgrims reach out to touch the hands of saints. Holding palm to palm is like a pilgrim’s kiss.

original: Have not saints lips, and holy palmers too?
translation: Don’t saints have lips? And pilgrims, too?

original: Ay, pilgrim, lips that they must use in prayer.
translation: Yes, pilgrim—lips they’re supposed to use to pray.

original: O, then, dear saint, let lips do what hands do. They pray; grant thou, lest faith turn to despair.
translation: Oh, then, saint, let lips do what hands do: pray. Grant my prayer or my faith will turn to despair.

original: Saints do not move, though grant for prayers’ sake.
translation: Saints don’t move, though they do grant prayers.

original: Then move not, while my prayer’s effect I take.
translation: Then remain still while I pray.

original: Thus from my lips, by thine, my sin is purged.
translation: Now your lips have cleaned the sin from mine.

original: Then have my lips the sin that they have took.
translation: Then my lips now have the sin they took from yours.

original: Sin from thy lips? O trespass sweetly urged!  Give me my sin again.
translation: Sin from my lips? Oh, how you urge me on to another crime. Give me back my sin.

original: You kiss by th’ book.
Madam, your mother craves a word with you.
translation: Madam, your mother wants to speak with you.

original: What is her mother?
translation: Who is her mother?

original: Marry, bachelor,   Her mother is the lady of the house,   And a good lady, and a wise and virtuous.
translation: Well, young man, her mother is the lady of the house. A good, wise, and virtuous lady.

original: I nursed her daughter that you talked withal.   I tell you, he that can lay hold of her   Shall have the chinks.
translation: I nursed her daughter, who you were talking to just now. I tell you, the man who marries that girl will be rich.

original: Is she a Capulet? O dear account! My life is my foe’s debt.
translation: Is she a Capulet? Oh, what a price I’ve paid! My life is now owned by my enemy.

original: Away, begone. The sport is at the best.
translation: Let’s go, let’s go, now while everything is still perfect.

original: Ay, so I fear. The more is my unrest.
translation: Yes, it is still perfect now. But I’m afraid it will never be perfect again.

original: Nay, gentlemen, prepare not to be gone.   We have a trifling foolish banquet towards.—
translation: No, gentlemen, don’t leave now. We have a bit of dessert arriving any moment.

original: Is it e’en so? Why, then, I thank you all.   I thank you, honest gentlemen. Good night.—   More torches here!—Come on then, let’s to bed.
translation: Is that so? Then, I thank you. I thank you, honest gentlemen. Good night. Bring more torches over here! Come on, let’s all get to bed.

original: Come hither, Nurse. What is yond gentleman?
translation: Come here, nurse. Who is that gentleman over there?

original: The son and heir of old Tiberio.
translation: The son and heir of old Tiberio.

original: What’s he that now is going out of door?
translation: Who’s the one going out the door?

original: Marry, that, I think, be young Petruchio.
translation: That, I think, is young Petruchio.

original: What’s he that follows here, that would not dance?
translation: What about the one over there, who wouldn’t dance?

original: I know not.
translation: I don’t know him.

original: Go ask his name.
translation: Go ask him for his name.

original: If he be married. My grave is like to be my wedding bed.
translation: If he’s married, I’d rather die than marry someone else.

original: His name is Romeo, and a Montague, The only son of your great enemy.
translation: His name is Romeo. He’s a Montague. He’s the only son of your greatest enemy.

original: My only love sprung from my only hate!   Too early seen unknown, and known too late!
translation: The one man I love is the son of the one man I hate! I saw him before I knew who he was, and learned who he was too late!

original: Prodigious birth of love it is to me,   That I must love a loathèd enemy.
translation: What a monster love is to make me love my worst enemy.

original: What’s this? What’s this?
translation: What’s this? What’s this?

original: A rhyme I learned even now Of one I danced withal.
translation: A rhyme I learned just now from somebody I danced with.

original: Anon, anon.  Come, let's away. The strangers are all gone.
translation: On our way, on our way! Come along, let's go. The strangers have all left.

original: Now old desire doth in his deathbed lie,   And young affection gapes to be his heir.   That fair for which love groaned for and would die,   With tender Juliet matched, is now not fair.
translation: Now Romeo's old desire for Rosaline lies in its deathbed, and a new love is ready to be its heir. Romeo used to groan and swear he would die for Rosaline's love, but now he finds Rosaline's beauty nothing in comparison to tender Juliet's.

original: Now Romeo is beloved and loves again,   Alike bewitchèd by the charm of looks;   But to his foe supposed he must complain,   And she steal love's sweet bait from fearful hooks.
translation: Now someone loves Romeo and Romeo loves someone, and they are both charmed by each other's looks. But Romeo must declare his love to someone who is supposed to be his enemy, and Juliet is love-struck, adoring someone she is supposed to fear.

original: Being held a foe, he may not have access   To breathe such vows as lovers use to swear,
translation: Because he is considered an enemy, Romeo is not allowed to see Juliet, and make the sorts of oaths that lovers usually swear to each other.

original: And she as much in love, her means much less   To meet her new belovèd anywhere.
translation: And Juliet—just as much in love with Romeo as he is with her—she has even fewer means of meeting her beloved Romeo.

original: But passion lends them power, time means, to meet,   Temp'ring extremities with extreme sweet.
translation: But passion gives them the power, and time gives them the opportunity, to meet each other, tempering their extreme adversity with extreme sweetness.

original: Can I go forward when my heart is here? Turn back, dull earth, and find thy center out.
translation: Can I continue on while my heart stays here? I’ll be nothing but an empty body unless I go back to find my heart.

original: Romeo, my cousin Romeo! Romeo!
translation: Romeo! Cousin Romeo! Romeo!

original: He is wise, And, on my life, hath stol’n him home to bed.
translation: He’s smart. I’d bet on my life that he’s snuck off towards home to go to bed.

original: He ran this way and leapt this orchard wall. Call, good Mercutio.
translation: He ran this way and jumped over this orchard wall. Call him, Mercutio.

original: Nay, I’ll conjure too!   Romeo! Humours, madman, passion, lover!   Appear thou in the likeness of a sigh!   Speak but one rhyme, and I am satisfied.
translation: No, I’ll summon him as I would a spirit. Romeo! Humors! Madman! Passion! Lover! Appear to me in the form of a sigh. Speak just a single rhyme, and I’ll be satisfied.

original: Cry but “Ay me!” Pronounce but “love” and “dove.”   Speak to my gossip Venus one fair word,
translation: Cry out, “Ah me!” Say “love” and “dove.” Say one pretty word to my good gossiping friend  Venus .

original: One nickname for her purblind son and heir,   Young Abraham Cupid, he that shot so true   When King Cophetua loved the beggar maid.—
translation: Say the nickname of her blind son and heir, Cupid, who shot arrows so accurately and made King Cophetua fall in love with a beggar maid.

original: He heareth not, he stirreth not, he moveth not.   The ape is dead, and I must conjure him.—
translation: —Romeo doesn’t hear me, stir, or move. The little monkey is dead, so I must conjure him to appear.—

original: I conjure thee by Rosaline’s bright eyes,   By her high forehead and her scarlet lip,   By her fine foot, straight leg, and quivering thigh,   And the demesnes that there adjacent lie,   That in thy likeness thou appear to us.
translation: By Rosaline’s bright eyes, by her high forehead and her red lips, by her fine feet, straight legs, and trembling thighs, and by parts of her that lie next to her thighs, I summon you to appear before us in your actual form.

original: An if he hear thee, thou wilt anger him.
translation: You’ll make him angry if he hears you.

original: This cannot anger him. ‘Twould anger him   To raise a spirit in his mistress’ circle   Of some strange nature, letting it there stand   Till she had laid it and conjured it down.
translation: This won’t make him angry. It would anger him if I conjured a strange spirit into Rosaline's room for her to have sex with.

original: That were some spite. My invocation   Is fair and honest. In his mistress’ name   I conjure only but to raise up him.
translation: That would really anger him. But what I’m saying is fair and honest. I’m just saying the name of his love in order to call him out from the darkness.

original: To be consorted with the humorous night. Blind is his love and best befits the dark.
translation: Come on. He’s hidden within these trees to be alone with the night. His love is blind, so it's fitting he share it with the dark.

original: If love be blind, love cannot hit the mark.   Now will he sit under a medlar tree   And wish his mistress were that kind of fruit   As maids call medlars when they laugh alone.—
translation: If love is blind, it can’t hit the target. He’ll sit under a  medlar  tree and wish his love were one of its fruits, which women, when they’re alone, joke look like female genitals.

original: O Romeo, that she were! Oh, that she were   An open arse, and thou a poperin pear.
translation: Oh, Romeo, I wish she were one such fruit! I wish she was an open-arse, and that you were a “pop her in” pear.

original: Romeo, good night. I’ll to my truckle bed.   This field-bed is too cold for me to sleep.—   Come, shall we go?
translation: Good night, Romeo. I’m off to my little trundle bed. It’s too cold in this field for me to sleep here. Come on, Benvolio, shall we leave?

original: Go then, for 'tis in vain To seek him here that means not to be found.
translation: Yes, let's go, then. We'd be looking for Romeo in vain because he doesn't want to be found.

original: He jests at scars that never felt a wound.
translation: He jokes about scars from wounds he’s never felt.

original: But soft! What light through yonder window breaks?   It is the east, and Juliet is the sun.   Arise, fair sun, and kill the envious moon,   Who is already sick and pale with grief,   That thou, her maid, art far more fair than she.
translation: But wait! What light is that in the window over there? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun. Rise, beautiful sun, and kill the jealous  moon , which is already sick and pale with grief because Juliet, her maid, is more beautiful than she is.

original: Be not her maid since she is envious.   Her vestal livery is but sick and green,   And none but fools do wear it. Cast it off!   It is my lady. Oh, it is my love.   Oh, that she knew she were!
translation: Don’t be her maid, since she’s jealous. The moon’s virginity makes her look  sick and green , and only fools hold on to their virginity. Throw it off. It is my lady. Oh, it is my love. Oh, I wish she knew I loved her.

original: She speaks, yet she says nothing. What of that?   Her eye discourses. I will answer it.—   I am too bold. ‘Tis not to me she speaks.
translation: She’s talking, but isn’t saying anything. Why is that? Her eyes are speaking. I’ll respond—no, I am too bold. It’s not to me she speaks.

original: Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven,   Having some business, do entreat her eyes   To twinkle in their spheres till they return.   What if her eyes were there, they in her head?   The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars   As daylight doth a lamp.
translation: Two of the most beautiful stars in the sky had to go off on some business, and begged her eyes to twinkle in their place until they return. If her eyes were in the sky and the stars were in her head the brightness of her cheeks would overwhelm the stars, just as daylight outshines a lamp.

original: Her eye in heaven   Would through the airy region stream so bright   That birds would sing and think it were not night.
translation: And her eyes in the night sky would shine so brightly that birds would start singing, thinking it was day.

original: See how she leans her cheek upon her hand.   Oh, that I were a glove upon that hand   That I might touch that cheek!
translation: Look how she leans her cheek against her hand. I wish I were a glove on that hand, so I could touch her cheek.

original: Ay me!
translation: Oh, my!

original: She speaks.   O, speak again, bright angel! For thou art   As glorious to this night, being o’er my head,   As is a wingèd messenger of heaven
translation: She speaks. Speak again, bright angel. For tonight you are as glorious as an angel, shining above my head like a winged messenger from heaven;

original: Unto the white, upturnèd, wondering eyes   Of mortals that fall back to gaze on him   When he bestrides the lazy-puffing clouds   And sails upon the bosom of the air.
translation: one who makes mortals fall onto their backs to gaze up in awe as the angel strides across the clouds and sails through the air.

original: O Romeo, Romeo! Wherefore art thou Romeo?   Deny thy father and refuse thy name.
translation: Oh, Romeo, Romeo, why must you be Romeo? Deny your father and give up your name.

original: Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love,   And I’ll no longer be a Capulet.
translation: Or, if you won’t change your name, just swear your love to me and I’ll give up being a Capulet.

original: Shall I hear more, or shall I speak at this?
translation: Should I listen longer, or respond now to these words?

original: ‘Tis but thy name that is my enemy.   Thou art thyself, though not a Montague.   What’s Montague? It is nor hand, nor foot,   Nor arm, nor face, nor any other part   Belonging to a man.
translation: Only your name is my enemy. You’d be yourself even if you ceased to be a Montague. What’s a Montague, after all? It’s not a hand, foot, arm, face, or any other body part.

original: O, be some other name!   What’s in a name? That which we call a rose   By any other word would smell as sweet.
translation: Oh, change your name! What’s the significance of a name? The thing we call a rose would smell as sweet even if we called it by some other name.

original: So Romeo would, were he not Romeo called,   Retain that dear perfection which he owes   Without that title.
translation: So even if Romeo had some other name, he would still be perfect.

original: Romeo, doff thy name,   And for that name, which is no part of thee   Take all myself.
translation: Romeo, take off your name—which really has no connection to who you are—and take all of me instead.

original: I take thee at thy word.  Call me but love, and I’ll be new baptized. Henceforth I never will be Romeo.
translation: I take you at your word. If you call me your love, I’ll take a new name. From now on I’ll never again be Romeo.

original: What man art thou that, thus bescreened in night, So stumblest on my counsel?
translation: Who are you, hiding in the darkness and eavesdropping on my private thoughts?

original: By a name   I know not how to tell thee who I am.
translation: I don’t know how to tell you who I am by using a name.

original: My name, dear saint, is hateful to myself   Because it is an enemy to thee.   Had I it written, I would tear the word.
translation: I hate my name, dear saint, because it is your enemy. If I had it written down, I would tear up the word.

original: My ears have not yet drunk a hundred words Of that tongue’s uttering, yet I know the sound.  Art thou not Romeo, and a Montague?
translation: I haven't even heard you say a hundred words yet, but I do recognize the sound of your voice. Aren’t you Romeo, the Montague?

original: Neither, fair maid, if either thee dislike.
translation: Beautiful girl, I’ll be neither of those things, if you dislike them.

original: How camest thou hither, tell me, and wherefore?   The orchard walls are high and hard to climb,
translation: How and why did you come here? The orchard walls are high and difficult to climb.

original: And the place death, considering who thou art,   If any of my kinsmen find thee here.
translation: And it will mean your death, because of who you are, if any of my family members find you here.

original: With love’s light wings did I o’erperch these walls,   For stony limits cannot hold love out,
translation: I flew over these walls on the wings of love. No stone wall can keep love out.

original: And what love can do, that dares love attempt.   Therefore thy kinsmen are no stop to me.
translation: Whatever a man in love can do, love will make him attempt to do it. Therefore your relatives can’t stop me.

original: If they do see thee they will murder thee.
translation: If they see you they’ll murder you.

original: Alack, there lies more peril in thine eye Than twenty of their swords. Look thou but sweet, And I am proof against their enmity.
translation: Alas, there would be more danger for me in one angry look from you than there would be from twenty of your relatives with swords. If you just look at me with love, their hatred would not be able to touch me.

original: I would not for the world they saw thee here.
translation: I’d give the world to make sure they do not see you here.

original: I have night’s cloak to hide me from their eyes,   And but thou love me, let them find me here.
translation: The darkness of night will hide me from their eyes. And if you don’t love me, then let them find me.

original: My life were better ended by their hate   Than death proroguèd, wanting of thy love.
translation: I’d rather they killed me in hatred than experience the prolonged death of life without your love.

original: By whose direction found’st thou out this place?
translation: Who told you how to find my my bedroom?

original: By love, that first did prompt me to inquire.   He lent me counsel and I lent him eyes.
translation: Love, which spurred me to come and find you. Love advised me, while I lent love my eyes.

original: I am no pilot. Yet, wert thou as far   As that vast shore washed with the farthest sea,   I would adventure for such merchandise.
translation: I’m not a sailor. Still, even if you were on the shore across the farthest sea, I would set out to find you.

original: Thou know’st the mask of night is on my face,   Else would a maiden blush bepaint my cheek   For that which thou hast heard me speak tonight.
translation: The darkness of night masks my face, or else you’d see me blushing about the things you heard me say tonight.

original: Fain would I dwell on form. Fain, fain deny   What I have spoke. But farewell compliment!
translation: I would gladly stick to the proper manners of courtship and deny everything I said. But, instead: I'll say goodbye to good manners!

original: Dost thou love me? I know thou wilt say “ay,”   And I will take thy word. Yet if thou swear’st   Thou mayst prove false.
translation: Do you love me? I know you will answer “yes,” and I will trust you. But your swears may turn out to be false.

original: At lovers’ perjuries,   They say, Jove laughs. O gentle Romeo,   If thou dost love, pronounce it faithfully.
translation: They say that  Jove  laughs when lovers lie. Oh, noble Romeo, if you really love me, say it in truth.

original: Or if thou think’st I am too quickly won,   I’ll frown and be perverse and say thee nay,   So thou wilt woo. But else, not for the world.
translation: Or if you think I’m letting myself be won too easily, then I’ll frown and act superior and unapproachable so that you’ll woo me. But if that’s not necessary, then I would never act that way.

original: In truth, fair Montague, I am too fond,   And therefore thou mayst think my ‘havior light.
translation: In truth, beautiful Montague, I like you too much, which might make it seem as if I am overly silly and flirtatious.

original: But trust me, gentleman, I’ll prove more true   Than those that have more coying to be strange.   I should have been more strange, I must confess,   But that thou overheard’st, ere I was ‘ware,   My true love’s passion.
translation: But trust me, gentleman, I’ll prove to be more faithful than girls who act coy and standoffish. I probably should have acted more standoffish, I confess, but you overheard me talking about my passion for you before I knew you were there.

original: Therefore pardon me,   And not impute this yielding to light love,   Which the dark night hath so discovered.
translation: So please forgive me, and don’t condemn me for so quickly falling in love when it was only revealed to you because the dark night let you discover it.

original: Lady, by yonder blessèd moon I vow, That tips with silver all these fruit-tree tops—
translation: Lady, I swear by the sacred moon, which outlines in silver the tops of these fruit trees—

original: O, swear not by the moon, th’ inconstant moon,  That monthly changes in her circle orb, Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.
translation: Please don’t swear by the moon, the unreliable moon, which changes its position in the sky each month. I do not want your love to end up being similarly variable.

original: What shall I swear by?
translation: What should I swear by?

original: Do not swear at all. Or, if thou wilt, swear by thy gracious self, Which is the god of my idolatry,  And I’ll believe thee.
translation: Don’t swear at all. Or, if you must swear, swear by your magnificent self, which is the god I worship like an idol, and I’ll believe you.

original: If my heart’s dear love—
translation: If my heart’s dear love—

original: Well, do not swear. Although I joy in thee,   I have no joy of this contract tonight.   It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden,
translation: Well, don’t swear. Although you bring me joy, I can’t take joy in this exchange of promises tonight. It’s too wild, thoughtless, sudden.

original: Too like the lightning, which doth cease to be   Ere one can say “It lightens.”
translation: It’s too much like lightning, which disappears before you can even say, “it’s lightning.”

original: Sweet, good night.   This bud of love, by summer’s ripening breath,   May prove a beauteous flower when next we meet.
translation: My love, good night. Our love, which now is like a flower bud, may blossom in the summer air into a beautiful flower by the next time we meet.

original: Good night, good night! As sweet repose and rest   Come to thy heart as that within my breast.
translation: Good night! I hope you feel in your heart the same sweet calm and rest that I feel in mine.

original: O, wilt thou leave me so unsatisfied?
translation: Are you going to leave me so unsatisfied?

original: What satisfaction canst thou have tonight?
translation: What satisfaction could you have tonight?

original: Th’ exchange of thy love’s faithful vow for mine.
translation: If we exchanged vows of love.

original: I gave thee mine before thou didst request it, And yet I would it were to give again.
translation: I pledged my love before you even requested it. But now I wish I could take that promise back to give it again.

original: Wouldst thou withdraw it? For what purpose, love?
translation: You’d take back your vow? Why, my love?

original: But to be frank, and give it thee again.   And yet I wish but for the thing I have.
translation: In order to generously give it to you again. But I’m wishing for something I have already.

original: My bounty is as boundless as the sea,   My love as deep. The more I give to thee,   The more I have, for both are infinite.
translation: My generosity to you is as endless as the sea, my love as deep as the sea. The more love I give you, the more I have. Both are infinite.

original: I hear some noise within. Dear love, adieu.— Anon, good Nurse!—Sweet Montague, be true. Stay but a little. I will come again.
translation: I hear a noise from inside. Dear love, goodbye—Just a second, Nurse!—Sweet Montague, be true. Stay for a moment. I’ll come right back.

original: O blessèd, blessèd night! I am afeard,  Being in night, all this is but a dream, Too flattering sweet to be substantial.
translation: Oh, blessed, blessed night! Because it’s night, I’m scared that all this is a dream. It is too wonderful to be real.

original: Three words, dear Romeo, and good night indeed.   If that thy bent of love be honorable,   Thy purpose marriage, send me word tomorrow
translation: Three words, dear Romeo, and then good night. If your love is honorable and you want to marry me, send me word tomorrow.

original: By one that I’ll procure to come to thee   Where and what time thou wilt perform the rite,
translation: I’ll find a messenger who will come to you, and you can tell that messenger when and where we will be married.

original: And all my fortunes at thy foot I’ll lay   And follow thee my lord throughout the world.
translation: All my fortunes I’ll lay at your feet and follow you, my lord, all over the world.

original: Madam!
translation: Madam!

original: I come, anon.—But if thou mean’st not well, I do beseech thee—
translation: I’ll be right there!

original: Madam!
translation: Madam!

original: By and by, I come.— To cease thy strife and leave me to my grief.  Tomorrow will I send.
translation: In a second, I’m coming!

original: So thrive my soul—
translation: My soul depends on it—

original: A thousand times good night!
translation: A thousand times good night.

original: A thousand times the worse to want thy light.
translation: It is a thousand times worse to leave you.

original: Love goes toward love as schoolboys from their books,
translation: A lover goes toward his beloved as joyfully as a schoolboy leaving his books.

original: But love from love, toward school with heavy looks.
translation: But when a lover leaves his beloved, he is as unhappy as a schoolboy on his way to school.

original: Hist! Romeo, hist!—Oh, for a falconer’s voice,   To lure this tassel-gentle back again!
translation: Psst! Romeo! Psst! Oh, I wish I could cry out like a falconer, so I could call my little falcon to return to me.

original: Bondage is hoarse, and may not speak aloud,   Else would I tear the cave where Echo lies,
translation: Stuck as I am in my family’s house, I have to be quiet. Otherwise I would tear open the cave where  Echo  sleeps

original: And make her airy tongue more hoarse than mine,   With repetition of “My Romeo!”
translation: and make her call out my love’s name until her voice grew more hoarse than mine by repeating, “My Romeo!”

original: It is my soul that calls upon my name.
translation: It is my soul that calls out my name.

original: How silver-sweet sound lovers’ tongues by night,   Like softest music to attending ears!
translation: Lovers' voices at night sound silver-sweet, the most lovely music to lovers’ ears.

original: Romeo!
translation: Romeo!

original: My nyas?
translation: My little hawk?

original: What o’clock tomorrow Shall I send to thee?
translation: At what time tomorrow should I send the messenger to you?

original: By the hour of nine.
translation: Nine o’clock.

original: I will not fail. ‘Tis twenty year till then. I have forgot why I did call thee back.
translation: I won’t fail. It will feel like twenty years until then. I’ve forgotten why I called you back.

original: Let me stand here till thou remember it.
translation: I’ll stand here until you remember.

original: I shall forget, to have thee still stand there, Remembering how I love thy company.
translation: I’ll forget it, so you’ll have to stand there forever, because of how much I love your company.

original: And I’ll still stay, to have thee still forget, Forgetting any other home but this.
translation: And I’ll remain here, even if you keep forgetting. I’ll forget that I have any other home but here.

original: ‘Tis almost morning. I would have thee gone.   And yet no further than a wanton’s bird,   That lets it hop a little from his hand
translation: It’s almost morning. I want to force you to go. Yet I would not let you move any further than a spoiled child would let his pet bird go.

original: Like a poor prisoner in his twisted gyves,   And with a silken thread plucks it back again,   So loving-jealous of his liberty.
translation: The child so loves the bird that he will not let the bird hop any more than a small distance from his hand before pulling it back by a silk thread.

original: I would I were thy bird.
translation: I wish I were your bird.

original: Sweet, so would I.   Yet I should kill thee with much cherishing.
translation: Sweetheart, so do I. But I would pet you so much it would kill you.

original: Good night, good night! Parting is such sweet sorrow   That I shall say good night till it be morrow.
translation: Good night. Good night! Parting is such sweet sorrow that I will say good night until it becomes tomorrow.

original: Sleep dwell upon thine eyes, peace in thy breast.
translation:
May sleep shut your eyes,
 and may you feel peace in your heart.

original: Would I were sleep and peace, so sweet to rest,  Hence will I to my ghostly sire's close cell, His help to crave, and my deap hap to tell.
The gray-eyed morn smiles on the frowning night,   Checkering the eastern clouds with streaks of light,   And fleckled darkness like a drunkard reels   From forth day’s path and Titan’s fiery wheels.
translation: The morning smiles as it replaces frowning night, and streaks light across the clouds in the east. Darkness staggers away from the sun’s path like a drunkard.

original: Now, ere the sun advance his burning eye,   The day to cheer and night’s dank dew to dry,   I must upfill this osier cage of ours   With baleful weeds and precious-juicèd flowers.
translation: Now, before the sun rises, bringing on the day and drying the dew, I must fill my basket with poisonous weeds and the precious nectar of flowers.

original: The earth, that’s natu re’s mother, is her tomb.   What is her burying, grave that is her womb.
translation: The earth is both nature’s mother and its tomb. Plants arise from the earth as from a womb, and when they die, they are buried in the earth.

original: And from her womb children of divers kind   We sucking on her natural bosom find,   Many for many virtues excellent,   None but for some and yet all different.
translation: Many different plants and animals come from the earth’s womb. All of these children find nourishment from the earth, and all have some special, unique virtue.

original: Oh, mickle is the powerful grace that lies   In herbs, plants, stones, and their true qualities.   For naught so vile that on the earth doth live   But to the earth some special good doth give.
translation: There is a power that resides in herbs, plants, and stones. For there’s nothing on earth that’s so evil that it does not also provide the earth with some kind of good.

original: Nor aught so good but, strained from that fair use   Revolts from true birth, stumbling on abuse.   Virtue itself turns vice, being misapplied,   And vice sometime by action dignified.
translation: Nor is there anything so good that it can’t be turned bad if it’s abused and used incorrectly. Virtue, when misused, turns to vice, while vice can sometimes become virtue through proper action.

original: Within the infant rind of this small flower   Poison hath residence and medicine power.   For this, being smelt, with that part cheers each part;   Being tasted, stays all senses with the heart.
translation: Within the small rind of this little flower there is both poison and medicine. If you smell it, you feel good. If you taste it, it stops your heart.

original: Two such opposèd kings encamp them still,   In man as well as herbs—grace and rude will.   And where the worser is predominant,   Full soon the canker death eats up that plant.
translation: Two opposing elements, good and evil, reside in both men and herbs. In the cases where evil predominates, death will soon kill the plant or body like a cancer.

original: Good morrow, Father.
translation: Good morning, father.

original: Benedicite.   What early tongue so sweet saluteth me?   Young son, it argues a distempered head   So soon to bid good morrow to thy bed.
translation: God bless you. Whose voice greets me so sweetly this early in the morning? My son, jumping so quickly out of bed this early indicates some trouble in your thoughts.

original: Care keeps his watch in every old man’s eye,   And where care lodges, sleep will never lie.   But where unbruisèd youth with unstuffed brain   Doth couch his limbs, there golden sleep doth reign.
translation: All old men have concerns, and these worries never let them sleep. Young men, though, should be carefree and without worry, and their sleep should be restful and long.

original: Therefore thy earliness doth me assure   Thou art uproused by some distemperature.   Or if not so, then here I hit it right:   Our Romeo hath not been in bed tonight.
translation: Therefore, the fact that you’re awake so early makes it clear that some anxiety has you in its grip. Or, if that’s not true, then I’d guess that you actually never went to sleep at all tonight.

original: That last is true. The sweeter rest was mine.
translation: That last is right. The rest I had was sweeter than sleep.

original: God pardon sin! Wast thou with Rosaline?
translation: God forgive all sin!—Did you sleep with Rosaline?

original: With Rosaline, my ghostly Father? No. I have forgot that name and that name’s woe.
translation: With Rosaline, my holy father? No, I have forgotten her and the sadness she gave me.

original: That’s my good son. But where hast thou been, then?
translation: That’s good, my son. But where were you, then?

original: I’ll tell thee ere thou ask it me again.   I have been feasting with mine enemy,   Where on a sudden one hath wounded me,   That’s by me wounded.
translation: I’ll tell you before you ask me again. I’ve been at a party with my enemy, where suddenly someone wounded me and was in turn wounded by me.

original: Both our remedies   Within thy help and holy physic lies.   I bear no hatred, blessèd man, for, lo,   My intercession likewise steads my foe.
translation: But both of us can be cured by your holy power. I hold no hatred, blessed father, because my request will also help my enemy.

original: Be plain, good son, and homely in thy drift. Riddling confession finds but riddling shrift.
translation: Speak plainly, my son. Be clear. A confusing confession will result only in confused absolution.

original: Then plainly know my heart’s dear love is set   On the fair daughter of rich Capulet.   As mine on hers, so hers is set on mine,   And all combined, save what thou must combine   By holy marriage.
translation: Here it is set plain: I love the beautiful daughter of rich Capulet. I love her, and she loves me. We’re bound together, and need only for you to combine us completely by marrying us.

original: When and where and how   We met, we wooed and made exchange of vow,   I’ll tell thee as we pass, but this I pray:   That thou consent to marry us today.
translation: In good time I’ll tell you about when and where and how we met, how we wooed each other and vowed our love. But  now I pray that you will agree to marry us today.

original: Holy Saint Francis, what a change is here!   Is Rosaline, whom thou didst love so dear,   So soon forsaken?
translation: Holy Saint Francis, what an incredible change! Have you so quickly abandoned Rosaline, whom you loved so much?

original: Young men’s love then lies   Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes.   Jesu Maria, what a deal of brine   Hath washed thy sallow cheeks for Rosaline!   How much salt water thrown away in waste   To season love that of it doth not taste!
translation: If so, then young men love not with their hearts but with their eyes. Jesus and Mary, you cried so many tears for Rosaline! So many salty tear-drops wasted, seasoning a love you never even tasted!

original: The sun not yet thy sighs from heaven clears,   Thy old groans ring yet in my ancient ears.   Lo, here upon thy cheek the stain doth sit   Of an old tear that is not washed off yet.
translation: The sun has not yet burned away the fog from all your sighs. My old ears are still ringing from your groans. And look, here on your cheek there’s a stain from an old tear that has not yet been washed off.

original: If e’er thou wast thyself and these woes thine,   Thou and these woes were all for Rosaline.
translation: If you were ever yourself and this sorrow yours, you and your sorrow were all for Rosaline.

original: And art thou changed? Pronounce this sentence then:   Women may fall when there’s no strength in men.
translation: And are you now changed? Then say the following: women will never be faithful when men are so unreliable.

original: Thou chid’st me oft for loving Rosaline.
translation: You often scolded me for loving Rosaline.

original: For doting, not for loving, pupil mine.
translation: I scolded you for obsessing, not for loving, my student.

original: And badest me bury love.
translation: And you urged me to bury my love.

original: Not in a grave, To lay one in, another out to have.
translation: But not to bury it in a grave in order to start a new love.

original: I pray thee, chide not. Her I love now Doth grace for grace and love for love allow. The other did not so.
translation: I beg you, don’t scold me. The one I love now returns my love. The other did not.

original: Oh, she knew well   Thy love did read by rote, that could not spell.
translation: Oh, Rosaline knew that you were play-acting at love but did not actually understand what love means.

original: But come, young waverer, come, go with me,   In one respect I’ll thy assistant be,   For this alliance may so happy prove   To turn your households’ rancor to pure love.
translation: But come with me, my young unreliable friend. I’ll help you, because it’s possible that this marriage may transform your two families’ hatred into pure love.

original: Oh, let us hence. I stand on sudden haste.
translation: Let’s go, then! Let’s do this quickly.

original: Wisely and slow. They stumble that run fast.
translation: Go wisely, and go slowly. Those who rush into things stumble.

original: Where the devil should this Romeo be? Came he not home tonight?
translation: Where the devil is Romeo? Did he come home last night?

original: Not to his father’s. I spoke with his man.
translation: Not to his father’s house. I asked Romeo’s servant.

original: Why, that same pale hard-hearted wench, that Rosaline,  Torments him so, that he will sure run mad.
translation: Rosaline—that pale-skinned, hard-hearted wench—torments him so much that he’s going to go insane.

original: Tybalt, the kinsman to old Capulet, Hath sent a letter to his father’s house.
translation: Tybalt, old Capulet’s kinsman, has sent a letter to Romeo’s father’s house.

original: A challenge, on my life.
translation: I bet it’s a challenge to fight.

original: Romeo will answer it.
translation: Romeo will answer it.

original: Any man that can write may answer a letter.
translation: Any man who can write is able to answer a letter.

original: Nay, he will answer the letter’s master, how he dares,  being dared.
translation: No, Romeo will respond to the letter writer and accept the challenge.

original: Alas, poor Romeo! He is already dead, stabbed with a  white wench’s black eye, shot through the ear with a  love song,
translation: Poor Romeo! He is already dead: stabbed by the black eye of a fair-skinned girl, cut through the ear by a love song.

original: the very pin of his heart cleft with the  blind bow-boy’s butt shaft. And is he a man to encounter Tybalt?
translation: The very core of his heart has been split by blind Cupid’s arrow. Is he really man enough to fight Tybalt?

original: Why, what is Tybalt?
translation: Why, what’s up with Tybalt?

original: More than Prince of Cats. Oh, he’s the courageous  captain of compliments. He fights as you sing  prick-song, keeps time, distance, and proportion.
translation: He’s more than just the  Prince of Cats . Oh, he does everything according to convention. He fights like you sing printed music, carefully keeping the correct time, distance, and rhythm.

original: He  rests his minim rests—one, two, and the third in your  bosom.
translation: He rests when it is proper to rest: one, two, and the third in your heart. He’s a master duelist who can hit any of his opponent’s buttons that he chooses.

original: The very butcher of a silk button, a duelist, a  duelist, a gentleman of the very first house of the  first and second cause.
translation: He’s a gentleman who learned at the finest fencing school, and he’s skilled at identifying insults and slights to his honor so that he’s “forced” to fight.

original: Ah, the immortal passado, the  punto reverso, the hai!
translation: He knows the  passado —the forward thrust—the  punto reverso —the backhand thrust—and the  hai —the thrust for the heart.

original: The what?
translation: He knows what?

original: The pox on such antic, lisping, affecting fantasmines,  these new tuners of accents! “By Jesu, a very good  blade! A very tall man! A very good whore!”
translation: A curse on these wild, pompous fellows who are always spouting exotic foreign phrases. These fellows, who say things like: “By Jesus, this is a very good blade! A very brave man! A very good whore.”

original: Why, is not  this a lamentable thing, grandsire, that we should be  thus afflicted with these strange flies, these  fashion-mongers, these “pardon me’s,”
translation: Isn’t it a sad thing, good man, that we are forced to interact with these foreign flies, these fashionmongers, these fellows who say “pardon me”

original: who stand so much  on the new form, that they cannot sit at ease on the old bench? Oh, their bones, their bones!
translation: and care so deeply about good manners that they can’t relax on a bench without groaning, “Oh, my aching bones!”

original: Here comes Romeo, here comes Romeo.
translation: Here comes Romeo, here comes Romeo.

original: Without his roe, like a dried herring. O flesh, flesh, how art thou fishified! Now is he for the numbers that  Petrarch flowed in.
translation: He looks skinny as a dried herring without its eggs. O flesh, flesh, you’ve turned pale as a fish. Now he’s just like Petrarch’s hopeless love poetry.

original: Laura to his lady was but a  kitchen-wench— marry, she had a better love to berhyme  her—
translation: In Romeo’s opinion, compared to his own lady love:  Petrarch’s Laura  was like a kitchen slave—though Laura clearly had a lover who was better at making rhymes;

original: Dido a dowdy, Cleopatra a gypsy, Helen and Hero  hildings and harlots, Thisbe a grey eye or so, but not  to the purpose.
translation: Dido was drab and dull; Cleopatra was a gypsy girl; Helen and Hero were good-for-nothing harlots; Thisbe might have had beautiful eyes, but that doesn’t matter.

original: Good morrow to you both. What counterfeit did I give  you?
translation: Good morning to you both. What do you mean I tricked you?

original: The slip, sir, the slip. Can you not conceive?
translation: You gave us the slip, sir, the slip. Do you understand me now?

original: Pardon, good Mercutio, my business was great, and in  such a case as mine a man may strain courtesy.
translation: I’m sorry, good Mercutio. My business was so important that I must be forgiven for stretching good manners and courtesy.

original: That’s as much as to say, such a case as yours  constrains a man to bow in the hams.
Meaning “to curtsy”?
translation: Meaning make a curtsy?

original: Thou hast most kindly hit it.
translation: Now you’ve “hit it.”

original: A most courteous exposition.
translation: What a courteous explanation.

original: Nay, I am the very pink of courtesy.
translation: Indeed, I am the very “pink” of courtesy.

original: Pink for flower.
Right.
translation: Right.

original: Why, then is my pump well flowered.
Sure wit, follow me this jest now till thou hast worn  out thy pump, that when the single sole of it is worn,  the jest may remain, after the wearing solely singular.
translation: Ah, witty Romeo, now you’ve taken this joke so far that it’s worn out your pump. With the sole of your pump now worn away, the joke is all that remains.

original: O single-soled jest, solely singular for the  singleness.
translation: This jest has such a thin sole, and is unique only because of its lameness.

original: Come between us, good Benvolio. My wits faints.
translation: Please break up this war of words, Benvolio. My wits can’t keep up.

original: Switch and spurs, switch and spurs, or I’ll cry a  match.
translation: Continue, continue, or I’ll proclaim victory.

original: Nay, if our wits run the wild-goose chase, I am done,  for thou hast more of the wild-goose in one of thy wits  than, I am sure, I have in my whole five. Was I with you there for the goose?
translation: No, if our witticisms go on a wild-goose chase, I’m done for. You have more wild goose in one of your jokes than I have in five of mine. Was I  even close to you in our goose chase?

original: Thou wast never with me for anything when thou wast not there for the goose.
translation: You would not have been with me for anything if you weren’t there for the goose.

original: I will bite thee by the ear for that jest.
translation: I’ll bite you on the ear for that joke.

original: Nay, good goose, bite not.
translation: No, good goose, don’t bite me.

original: Thy wit is a very bitter sweeting. It is a most sharp  sauce.
translation: Your wit is a bitter apple. It is a very spicy sauce.

original: And is it not well served into a sweet goose?
translation: Isn’t that the perfect sauce for a sweet goose?

original: Oh, here’s a wit of cheveril, that stretches from an  inch narrow to an ell broad!
translation: Oh, that joke is made of leather so thin it has been stretched from an inch wide to a full fat yard.

original: I stretch it out for that word “broad,” which, added  to the goose, proves thee far and wide a broad goose.
translation: I stretched it for that word “fat.” Add that to the goose, and it makes you a fat goose.

original: Why, is not this better now than groaning for love? Now art thou sociable. Now art thou Romeo.
translation: Now, isn’t this jesting better than groaning about love? Now you’re being sociable. Now you’re Romeo.

original: Now art thou  what thou art—by art as well as by nature, for this  driveling love is like a great natural that runs lolling up and down to hide his bauble in a hole.
translation: Now you are what you truly are, both naturally and through education. In contrast, this love of yours made you like some fool who runs all over the place looking for a hole in which to hide his  precious trinket.

original: Stop there, stop there.
translation: Stop there, stop there.

original: Thou desirest me to stop in my tale against the hair.
translation: You’re asking me to stop my tale before it’s finished.

original: Thou wouldst else have made thy tale large.
translation: Continuing on would have made your tale too long.

original: Oh, thou art deceived. I would have made it short, for I was come to the whole depth of my tale, and meant,  indeed, to occupy the argument no longer.
