original: What misadventure is so early up That calls our person from our morning rest?
translation: What disaster has occurred so early in the morning that it forces me from my bed?

original: What should it be, that they shriek so abroad?
translation: What has happened to cause everyone to start shrieking?

original: Oh, the people in the street cry “Romeo,” Some “Juliet,” and some “Paris,” and all run With open outcry toward our monument.
translation: Some people in the street are crying “Romeo.” Others cry “Juliet,” and still others “Paris.” They’re all running and screaming towards our tomb.

original: What fear is this which startles in our ears?
translation: What terror has occurred to result in all this startling noise?

original: Sovereign, here lies the County Paris slain,  And Romeo dead, and Juliet, dead before, Warm and new killed.
translation: Prince, here lies Count Paris, killed. And Romeo dead. And Juliet, who was dead before, but is warm like someone newly killed.

original: Search, seek, and know how this foul murder comes.
translation: Find out how this foul murder came to happen.

original: Here is a friar, and slaughtered Romeo’s man, With instruments upon them fit to open  These dead men’s tombs.
translation: Here is a friar, and dead Romeo’s servant. They’re carrying tools for opening a tomb.

original: O heavens! O wife, look how our daughter bleeds!   This dagger hath mista’en
translation: Oh heavens! Oh, wife, look at how our daughter bleeds! That dagger is in the wrong place.

original: —for, lo, his house   Is empty on the back of Montague,   And it mis-sheathèd in my daughter’s bosom.
translation: It should be in the empty sheath on the back of that Montague, but instead is misplaced, sheathed in my daughter’s chest.

original: O me! This sight of death is as a bell, That warns my old age to a sepulcher.
translation: Woe is me! Seeing my daughter dead is like a warning bell of my own imminent death.

original: Come, Montague, for thou art early up To see thy son and heir now early down.
translation: Come, Montague. You’re up early to see your son and heir killed at too young an age.

original: Alas, my liege, my wife is dead tonight.  Grief of my son’s exile hath stopped her breath. What further woe conspires against mine age?
translation: My liege, my wife died tonight. Her sadness about my son’s exile stopped her breath. What further misery must I endure in my old age?

original: Look, and thou shalt see.
translation: Look, and you’ll see.

original: O thou untaught! What manners is in this, To press before thy father to a grave?
translation: Oh, you rude boy! What terrible manners to die before your father.

original: Seal up the mouth of outrage for a while,   Till we can clear these ambiguities
translation: Quiet your outrage for a time, until we can clear up the remaining uncertainties about the cause of all this.

original: And know their spring, their head, their true descent,   And then will I be general of your woes,   And lead you even to death.
translation: Once we do know what happened, I will lead you in expressing our pain, all the way to our deaths.

original: Meantime forbear,   And let mischance be slave to patience.—   Bring forth the parties of suspicion.
translation: In the meantime, hold on, and let your patience control your desire to act. Bring forth the men under suspicion.

original: I am the greatest, able to do least,   Yet most suspected, as the time and place   Doth make against me, of this direful murder.
translation: I am the most suspected, and least able to defend myself, because I was here at the time of this terrible murder.

original: And here I stand, both to impeach and purge,   Myself condemnèd and myself excused.
translation: Here I stand, to be questioned and punished. I have already condemned myself.

original: Then say at once what thou dost know in this.
translation: Then tell us immediately what you know about all this.

original: I will be brief, for my short date of breath   Is not so long as is a tedious tale.
translation: I’ll be brief, because the time I have left to live is not long enough to tell a long story.

original: Romeo, there dead, was husband to that Juliet,   And she, there dead, that Romeo’s faithful wife.
translation: Romeo, who lies there dead, was Juliet’s husband. And she, who lies there dead, was Romeo’s faithful wife.

original: I married them, and their stol’n marriage day   Was Tybalt’s doomsday, whose untimely death   Banished the new-made bridegroom from the city—   For whom, and not for Tybalt, Juliet pined.
translation: I married them. Their secret wedding day was the same day Tybalt died. His untimely death led to the banishment of the bridegroom. Juliet was distraught not over Tybalt’s death, but rather over Romeo’s banishment.

original: You, to remove that siege of grief from her,   Betrothed and would have married her perforce   To County Paris. Then comes she to me,   And with wild looks bid me devise some mean   To rid her from this second marriage,   Or in my cell there would she kill herself.
translation: To end her grief, you arranged for her to marry Count Paris. At that point she came to me, and, looking wild, threatened to kill herself unless I came up with a plan to help her escape this second marriage.

original: Then gave I her, so tutored by my art,   A sleeping potion, which so took effect   As I intended, for it wrought on her   The form of death.
translation: Then I gave her a special sleeping potion that, as I had planned, made it seem as if she had died.

original: Meantime I writ to Romeo,   That he should hither come as this dire night,   To help to take her from her borrowed grave,   Being the time the potion’s force should cease.
translation: Meanwhile, I wrote to Romeo to tell him to come here tonight, this awful night, to help get her out of her temporary grave when the sleeping potion wore off.

original: But he which bore my letter, Friar John,   Was stayed by accident, and yesternight   Returned my letter back. Then all alone   At the prefixèd hour of her waking   Came I to take her from her kindred’s vault,
translation: But the man who carried my letter, Friar John, was stopped by an accident, and returned my letter to me last night. So at the time when Juliet was scheduled to wake up, I came here alone to take her out of her family’s tomb.

original: Meaning to keep her closely at my cell   Till I conveniently could send to Romeo,   But when I came, some minute ere the time   Of her awakening, here untimely lay   The noble Paris and true Romeo dead.
translation: My plan was to hide her in my cell until I could get word to Romeo. But when I arrived, just a few minutes before Juliet awoke, Paris and Romeo were already here, lying dead.

original: She wakes, and I entreated her come forth,   And bear this work of heaven with patience.   But then a noise did scare me from the tomb,
translation: She woke up, and I begged her to come out of the tomb with me and bear this work of God with patience. But then a noise frightened me, and I ran from the tomb.

original: And she, too desperate, would not go with me,   But, as it seems, did violence on herself.   All this I know, and to the marriage   Her Nurse is privy.
translation: She was too desperate to leave with me, and, it seems, she killed herself. I know all of this. And her Nurse knows about the marriage.

original: And if aught in this   Miscarried by my fault, let my old life   Be sacrificed some hour before his time   Unto the rigor of severest law.
translation: If any of this misfortune is my fault, let me be sacrificed and punished under the strictest law.

original: We still have known thee for a holy man.—  Where’s Romeo’s man? What can he say in this?
translation: We have always known you to be a holy man. Where is Romeo’s servant? What does he say about all this?

original: I brought my master news of Juliet’s death,   And then in post he came from Mantua   To this same place, to this same monument.
translation: I brought my master news of Juliet’s death. And then with great haste he rode from Mantua to this tomb.

original: This letter he early bid me give his  father,   And threatened me with death, going in the vault,   If I departed not and left him there.
translation: Early this morning he told me to give this letter to his father. Then he threatened to kill me if I did not leave when he went into the tomb.

original: Give me the letter. I will look on it.  Where is the county’s page, that raised the watch?— Sirrah, what made your master in this place?
translation: Give me the letter. I’ll read it.  Where is the count’s page, who called the watch? Boy, what was your master doing here?

original: He came with flowers to strew his lady’s grave,   And bid me stand aloof, and so I did.
translation: He came with flowers to put on his lady’s grave. He asked me to stand apart from him, and so I did.

original: Anon comes one with light to ope the tomb,   And by and by my master drew on him,   And then I ran away to call the watch.
translation: Soon after someone with a torch came to open the tomb. One thing led to another, and my master drew his sword to fight him. That’s when I ran away to call the watch.

original: This letter doth make good the  friar’s words,   Their course of love, the tidings of her death.   And here he writes that he did buy a poison   Of a poor ‘pothecary, and therewithal   Came to this vault to die and lie with Juliet.
translation: This letter corroborates the friar’s story. It describes the course of their love and how he heard of her death. Then he writes that he bought poison from a poor pharmacist and came to this tomb to die and lie with Juliet.

original: Where be these enemies?—Capulet! Montague!   See what a scourge is laid upon your hate,   That heaven finds means to kill your joys with love!
translation: Where are these enemies? Capulet! Montague! Do you see how your hate has cursed you? Heaven has in response conspired to kill your joys with love.

original: And I, for winking at your discords, too   Have lost a brace of kinsmen. All are punished.
translation: And because I did not take a firm hand against your feud, I’ve lost two of my family members as well. Everyone is punished.

original: O brother Montague, give me thy hand. This is my daughter’s jointure, for no more Can I demand.
translation: Oh, brother Montague, give me your hand. This handshake is my daughter’s dowry. I can ask you for nothing more.

original: But I can give thee more,   For I will raise her statue in pure gold,
translation: But I can give you more. I’ll raise a golden statue of her.

original: That whiles Verona by that name is known,   There shall no figure at such rate be set   As that of true and faithful Juliet.
translation: So long as this city is called Verona, there will be no figure praised more than that of true and faithful Juliet.

original: As rich shall Romeo’s by his lady’s lie, Poor sacrifices of our enmity.
translation: The statue of Romeo I’ll make to lie beside Juliet will be just as rich. Our hate was not worth their sacrifice.

original: A glooming peace this morning with it brings.   The sun for sorrow will not show his head.
translation: This morning brings a gloomy peace with it. The sun won't shine because of his sadness.

original: Go hence, to have more talk of these sad things;   Some shall be pardoned, and some punishèd;
translation: Go forward, to talk more about these sad things. Some will be pardoned, and some will be punished.

original: For never was a story of more woe   Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.
translation: For there was never a sadder story than this one of Juliet and her Romeo.

original: Proceed, Solinus, to procure my fall, And by the doom of death end woes and all.
Merchant of Syracuse, plead no more.   I am not partial to infringe our laws.
translation: Merchant  of Syracuse, stop pleading. I'm not in the mood to violate our laws.

original: The enmity and discord which of late   Sprung from the rancorous outrage of your duke   To merchants, our well-dealing countrymen,   Who, wanting guilders to redeem their lives,   Have seal’d his rigorous statutes with their bloods,   Excludes all pity from our threatening looks.
translation: All this recent hostility and chaos is your resentful duke's fault.  When our honest merchants don't have the  money  to pay their ransoms, he's been using his own strict laws to execute our honest merchants. So, we're not going to show any pity.

original: For, since the mortal and intestine jars   'Twixt thy seditious countrymen and us,   It hath in solemn synods been decreed   Both by the Syracusians and ourselves,   To admit no traffic to our adverse towns.
translation: Ever since the fatal civil wars between your unruly countrymen and our people, it's been decreed in parliaments both by the people of Syracuse and by us that no one will be allowed to enter the opposing town.

original: Nay, more, if any born at Ephesus   Be seen at any Syracusian marts and fairs;   Again, if any Syracusian born   Come to the bay of Ephesus, he dies,
translation: And, what's more, if anyone born in Ephesus is seen in any markets or fairs in Syracuse, or if anyone born in Syracuse comes to the bay of Ephesus, he dies.

original: His goods confiscate to the Duke’s dispose,   Unless a thousand marks be levièd   To quit the penalty and to ransom him.
translation: In addition, the Duke takes possession of his goods unless  a thousand marks   are paid to lift the sentence and pay the ransom.

original: Thy substance, valued at the highest rate,   Cannot amount unto a hundred marks;   Therefore by law thou art condemned to die.
translation: Even at the highest rate, you can't be worth a hundred marks.  So, by law, you are condemned to die .

original: Yet this my comfort: when your words are done, My woes end likewise with the evening sun.
Well, Syracusian, say in brief the cause Why thou dep-artedst from thy native home And for what cause thou camest to Ephesus.
translation: Well, Syracusian, quickly say what led you to leave your native home and why you came to Ephesus.

original: A heavier task could not have been imposed   Than I to speak my griefs unspeakable;
translation: There couldn't be a more severe punishment than making me speak my unspeakable sorrows.

original: Yet, that the world may witness that my end   Was wrought by nature, not by vile offense,   I’ll utter what my sorrow gives me leave.
translation: However, so that everyone knows that the end of my life was due to natural love for my son, not due to vile crime, I'll say as much as my pain allows me.

original: In Syracusa was I born, and wed   Unto a woman happy but for me,   And by me, had not our hap been bad.
translation: I was born in Syracuse and I married a woman who I would have made happy if we hadn't had bad fortune.

original: With her I lived in joy. Our wealth increased   By prosperous voyages I often made   To Epidamnum, till my factor’s death   And the great care of goods at random left   Drew me from kind embracements of my spouse;
translation: We lived together in joy. We got wealthier since I was frequently making prosperous trips to Epidamnum, but, when my agent died, I had to leave my wife's kind embraces to deal with all the goods left over.

original: From whom my absence was not six months old   Before herself—   almost at fainting under   The pleasing punishment that women bear—   Had made provision for her following me   And soon and safe arrivèd where I was.
translation: I hadn't been gone six months before my wife, almost fainting because of her pregnancy, had made plans to follow me and soon safely joined me.

original: There had she not been long but she became   A joyful mother of two goodly sons,   And, which was strange, the one so like the other   As could not be distinguished but by names.
translation: She hadn't been there long before she became the happy mother of two wonderful sons, and, strangely, they were so similar that they couldn't be told apart except by their names.

original: That very hour, and in the selfsame inn,   A meaner woman was deliverèd   Of such a burden, male twins, both alike.   Those, for their parents were exceeding poor,   I bought and brought up to attend my sons.
translation: The same hour, in the same inn, a poorer woman gave birth to male identical twins. The parents were extremely poor, so I bought those twins to be my sons' servants.

original: My wife, not meanly proud of two such boys,   Made daily motions for our home return.   Unwilling, I agreed. Alas, too soon   We came aboard.
translation: My wife, who was extremely proud of our kids, tried to convince me every day that we should go home. Reluctantly, I agreed. Unfortunately, we set sail too soon.

original: A league from Epidamnum had we sailed   Before the always-wind-obeying deep   Gave any tragic instance of our harm;   But longer did we not retain much hope;   For what obscured light the heavens did grant   Did but convey unto our fearful minds   A doubtful warrant of immediate death,
translation: We'd sailed a  league  from Epidamnum before the waters, which always obey the wind, gave some sign of danger. Hope quickly faded because the stormy sky made us believe we were all doomed to die immediately.

original: Which though myself would gladly have embraced,   Yet the incessant weepings of my wife,   Weeping before for what she saw must come,   And piteous plainings of the pretty babes,   That mourned for fashion, ignorant what to fear,   Forced me to seek delays for them and me.
translation: I would have gladly embraced death, but when I heard my wife's incessant weeping when she saw what was coming, and her compassionate laments for our beautiful babies who were sobbing in imitation of their mother although they didn't understand why they should be afraid, I looked for ways to delay our deaths.

original: And this it was, for other means was none:   The sailors sought for safety by our boat   And left the ship, then sinking-ripe, to us.   My wife, more careful for the latter-born,   Had fastened him unto a small spare mast,   Such as seafaring men provide for storms.
translation: This was the only means I could come up with: the sailors took our boat to seek safety and left the sinking ship to us. My wife, taking more care of the younger twin, tied him to a small, extra mast, one of the ones sailors have ready in case of storms.

original: To him one of the other twins was bound,   Whilst I had been like heedful of the other.   The children thus disposed, my wife and I,   Fixing our eyes on whom our care was fixed,   Fastened ourselves at either end the mast   And, floating straight, obedient to the stream,   Was carried towards Corinth, as we thought.
translation: One of the other twins was tied to him, while I was similarly watching over the other. Having taken care of the kids in this way, my wife and I, always watching the children, tied ourselves to either end of the mast and, floating straight, following the current, were carried towards what we thought was Corinth.

original: At length the sun, gazing upon the earth,   Dispersed those vapors that offended us,   And by the benefit of his wished light   The seas waxed calm, and we discoverèd   Two ships from far, making amain to us,   Of Corinth that, of Epidaurus this.   But ere they came,—   O, let me say no more!   Gather the sequel by that went before.
translation: Finally, the sun, looking down on the earth, cleared up the stormy winds that were assaulting us, and, thanks to the lucky sunlight, the seas calmed down, and we saw two faraway ships coming towards us, one from Corinth, one from Epidaurus. But before they came — oh, don't make me go on! Predict what comes next from what I've already told you.

original: Nay, forward, old man. Do not break off so, For we may pity though not pardon thee.
translation: No, go on, old man. Don't stop here, for we might just pity you and not pardon you.

original: O, had the gods done so, I had not now   Worthily termed them merciless to us.   For, ere the ships could meet by twice five leagues,   We were encountered by a mighty rock,   Which being violently borne upon,   Our helpful ship was splitted in the midst;
translation: Oh, if the gods had pitied us, I wouldn't have to call them merciless now. For, before the ships could get within ten leagues of each other, we ran into a huge rock which violently crashed into our ship, splitting it in the middle;

original: So that, in this unjust divorce of us,   Fortune had left to both of us alike   What to delight in, what to sorrow for.
translation: so you see, in this unjust splitting, fortune had given each of us equal delights and sorrows.

original: Her part, poor soul, seeming as burdenèd   With lesser weight, but not with lesser woe,   Was carried with more speed before the wind,   And in our sight they three were taken up   By fishermen of Corinth, as we thought.
translation: My wife's half of the ship, poor woman, seemingly weighing less but not carrying less woe, was carried more quickly by the wind, and we saw the three of them taken up by fishermen of Corinth (or so we assumed).

original: At length, another ship had seized on us   And, knowing whom it was their hap to save,   Gave healthful welcome to their shipwracked guests,   And would have reft the fishers of their prey   Had not their bark been very slow of sail;
translation: Eventually, another ship got to our half, and, knowing who they'd had the good fortune to save, gave us a big welcome. They would have  robbed the Corinthian fishermen of their catches  if their ship hadn't been so slow.

original: And therefore homeward did they bend their course.   Thus have you heard me severed from my bliss;   That by misfortunes was my life prolonged   To tell sad stories of my own mishaps.
translation: Then they steered the ship for home. So, now you've heard how I was severed from my happiness and that misfortunes have kept me alive to tell sad stories of my own tragedies.

original: And for the sake of them thou sorrowest for, Do me the favour to dilate at full What hath befall'n of them and thee till now.
translation: And for the sake of those you cry for, do me the favor of telling us in detail what happened to them and you up till now.

original: My youngest boy, and yet my eldest care,   At eighteen years became inquisitive   After his brother, and importuned me   That his attendant—   so his case was like,   Reft of his brother, but retained his name—   Might bear him company in the quest of him,
translation: My last-born boy, who's also my first source of worry, started wondering about his brother when he was eighteen, and begged me that he and his servant (who had lost his brother, too, but kept his brother's name) could go in search of him.

original: Whom whilst I laboured of a love to see,   I hazarded the loss of whom I loved.
translation: While I also desperately wanted to see him, I risked the loss of the son I loved.

original: Five summers have I spent in farthest Greece,   Roaming clean through the bounds of Asia,   And, coasting homeward, came to Ephesus,   Hopeless to find, yet loath to leave unsought   Or that or any place that harbors men.
translation: I've spent five summers in the far corners of Greece, roaming to the ends of Asia, and, traveling homeward, I came to Ephesus, knowing I should have no hope that I'd find my son here but unwilling not to search this or any place where men live.

original: But here must end the story of my life;   And happy were I in my timely death   Could all my travels warrant me they live.
translation: But my life story must end here, and I'd be happy to die now if all my travels could reassure me that my sons were still alive.

original: Hapless Egeon, whom the fates have marked   To bear the extremity of dire mishap,
translation: Unlucky Egeon, you've been marked by the fates to endure the worst of misfortunes.

original: Now, trust me, were it not against our laws,   Against my crown, my oath, my dignity,   Which princes, would they, may not disannul,   My soul would sue as advocate for thee.
translation: Now, trust me, were it not illegal and against my duty as king, my vow, and my dignity, which princes can't violate even when they want to, I'd advocate on your behalf.

original: But though thou art adjudgèd to the death,   And passèd sentence may not be recalled   But to our honour’s great disparagement,   Yet will I favor thee in what I can.
translation: But even though you're sentenced to death, and I can't take back the sentence without disgracing my honor, I'll do what I can to help you.

original: Therefore, merchant, I’ll limit thee this day   To seek thy life by beneficial help.
translation: Therefore, merchant, I'll give you just one day—today—to try to get help to save your life.

original: Try all the friends thou hast in Ephesus;   Beg thou, or borrow, to make up the sum,   And live. If no, then thou art doom’d to die.—
translation: Try all the friends you have in Ephesus. Beg or borrow to get the money you need, and, if you succeed, you'll live. If you fail, then you're doomed to die.

original: Jailer, take him to thy custody.
translation: Jailer, take him away.

original: I will, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: Hopeless and helpless doth Egeon wend, But to procrastinate his lifeless end.
Therefore give out you are of Epidamnum,   Lest that your goods too soon be confiscate.
translation: You'd better tell people you're from Epidamnum or your goods will be taken.

original: This very day a Syracusian merchant   Is apprehended for arrival here   And, not being able to buy out his life,   According to the statute of the town   Dies ere the weary sun set in the west.
translation: This very day, a merchant from Syracuse was arrested for arriving here, and, since he can't pay his ransom, he will die at sundown according to the town's law.

original: There is your money that I had to keep.
translation: Here's your money I was keeping for you.

original: Go bear it to the Centaur, where we host,   And stay there, Dromio, till I come to thee.   Within this hour it will be dinnertime.
translation: Go bring it to the Centaur, where we're staying, and stay there, Dromio, till I come to you. It'll be lunchtime within the hour.

original: Till that, I’ll view the manners of the town,   Peruse the traders, gaze upon the buildings,   And then return and sleep within mine inn,   For with long travel I am stiff and weary.   Get thee away.
translation: Until then, I'll watch how people behave around town, look at the traders, gaze at the buildings, and then return and sleep within the inn, for I'm stiff and tired from traveling for so long. Get away, you.

original: Many a man would take you at your word And go indeed, having so good a mean.
translation: Many men would take you literally and get away for good, having such an easy opportunity.

original: A trusty villain, sir, that very oft, When I am dull with care and melancholy, Lightens my humor with his merry jests. What, will you walk with me about the town And then go to my inn and dine with me?
I am invited, sir, to certain merchants,   Of whom I hope to make much benefit.
translation: I've been invited, sir, to meet some merchants from whom I'm hoping to gain something.

original: I crave your pardon. Soon at five o'clock,   Please you, I’ll meet with you upon the mart   And afterward consort you till bedtime.
translation: I hope you'll pardon me. Soon, at five o'clock if it pleases you, I'll meet you at the market and then accompany you until bedtime.

original: My present business calls me from you now.
translation: I have to leave you now to take care of some business.

original: Farewell till then. I will go lose myself And wander up and down to view the city.
translation: Goodbye till then. I'll let myself get lost in the streets as I wander up and down to see the city.

original: Sir, I commend you to your own content.
translation: Sir, I hope you do so to your heart's content.

original: He that commends me to mine own content   Commends me to the thing I cannot get.
translation: He who hopes I find my heart's content hopes for what I cannot have.

original: I to the world am like a drop of water   That in the ocean seeks another drop,   Who, falling there to find his fellow forth,   Unseen, inquisitive, confounds himself.
translation: In this huge world, I'm like a drop of water looking for another drop throughout the ocean. When the first drop doesn't find that second drop he's looking for, unseen, questioning, he loses track of himself.

original: So I, to find a mother and a brother,   In quest of them, unhappy, lose myself.
translation: So I, in search of my mother and my brother, unhappily lose myself.

original: Here comes the almanac of my true date.— What now? How chance thou art returned so soon?
translation: Here comes the calendar that tells me exactly how old I am. [To DROMIO OF EPHESUS] What now? How is it possible you're back so soon?

original: Returned so soon? Rather approach’d too late!
translation: Back so soon? More like came too late!

original: The capon burns; the pig falls from the spit;   The clock hath strucken twelve upon the bell;   My mistress made it one upon my cheek.
translation: The fish is burning, the pig is falling off the spit, the clock has struck twelve. My mistress  made it one o'clock  by slapping me across the cheek.

original: She is so hot because the meat is cold;   The meat is cold because you come not home;
translation: She is so hot-tempered because the meat is cold. The meat is cold because you don't come home.

original: You come not home because you have no stomach;   You have no stomach, having broke your fast;
translation: You don't come home because you have no appetite. You have no appetite because you already ate,

original: But we that know what ’tis to fast and pray   Are penitent for your default today.
Stop in your wind, sir. Tell me this, I pray: Where have you left the money that I gave you?
O, sixpence, that I had o' Wednesday last To pay the saddler for my mistress' crupper? The saddler had it, sir; I kept it not.
translation: Oh, the sixpence that you gave me last Wednesday to pay the saddler for my mistress's saddle strap? The saddler took it, sir. I didn't keep it.

original: I am not in a sportive humor now.   Tell me, and dally not: where is the money?
translation: I'm not in a joking mood now. Tell me and don't beat around the bush: where's the money?

original: We being strangers here, how dar’st thou trust   So great a charge from thine own custody?
translation: We're strangers here— how dare you take the risk of not keeping the money with you?

original: I pray you, jest, sir, as you sit at dinner.
translation: Please, sir, make jokes while you sit at lunch.

original: I from my mistress come to you in post;   If I return, I shall be post indeed,   For she will scour your fault upon my pate.
translation: I've been running from my mistress  post-haste . If I go back, she'll treat me like a post indeed, for she'll take out her anger at you on my head.

original: Methinks your maw, like mine, should be your clock,   And strike you home without a messenger.
translation: I think your appetite, like mine, should be your clock, and let you know when to come home without needing a messenger.

original: Come, Dromio, come, these jests are out of season.   Reserve them till a merrier hour than this.
translation: Come, Dromio, come, these jokes aren't appropriate right now. Save them for a happier time than this.

original: Where is the gold I gave in charge to thee?
translation: Where's the gold I gave you to keep safe?

original: To me, sir? Why, you gave no gold to me!
translation: To me, sir? Why, you gave no gold to me!

original: Come on, sir knave, have done your foolishness, And tell me how thou hast disposed thy charge.
translation: Come on, you rascal, quit this foolishness, and tell me how you've done what I commanded you to do.

original: My charge was but to fetch you from the mart   Home to your house, the Phoenix, sir, to dinner.
translation: My only command was to fetch you from the market and bring you back to your house, the Phoenix, sir, for lunch.

original: My mistress and her sister stays for you.
translation: My mistress and her sister are waiting for you.

original: Now, as I am a Christian, answer me   In what safe place you have bestowed my money,
translation: Now, as I am a Christian, answer me in what safe place you have left my money,

original: Or I shall break that merry sconce of yours   That stands on tricks when I am undisposed.   Where is the thousand marks thou hadst of me?
translation: or I will break that chattering head of yours that's playing tricks on me when I'm unwell. Where is the  thousand marks  you got from me?

original: I have some marks of yours upon my pate,   Some of my mistress' marks upon my shoulders,   But not a thousand marks between you both.
translation: I have some  marks  of yours on my head, some of my mistress's marks on my shoulders, but not a thousand marks between the two of you.

original: If I should pay your worship those again,   Perchance you will not bear them patiently.
translation: If I should pay you those again , sir, you might not take it so well.

original: Thy mistress' marks? what mistress, slave, hast thou?
Your worship’s wife, my mistress at the Phoenix, She that doth fast till you come home to dinner And prays that you will hie you home to dinner.
translation: Your wife, sir, my mistress at the Phoenix, she who's fasting until you come home to lunch and prays you will hurry home to lunch.

original: What, wilt thou flout me thus unto my face, Being forbid? There, take you that, sir knave.  [beats  DROMIO OF EPHESUS]
translation: What, will you mock me to my face like this when I told you not to? There, take that, you rascal.

original: What mean you, sir? For God’s sake, hold your hands. Nay, an you will not, sir, I’ll take my heels.
translation: What do you mean, sir? For God's sake, keep your hands off me. And if you won't, sir, I'll run for it.

original: Upon my life, by some device or other   The villain is o'erraught of all my money.
translation: I'll be damned! Somehow or other, the villain's been tricked into giving up all my money.

original: They say this town is full of cozenage,   As nimble jugglers that deceive the eye,   Dark-working sorcerers that change the mind,   Soul-killing witches that deform the body,
translation: They say this town is full of tricksters, like nimble jugglers that deceive people's eyes, sorcerers that perform dark magic to control people's minds, soul-killing witches that cast spells to deform people's bodies,

original: Disguised cheaters, prating mountebanks,   And many suchlike liberties of sin.
translation: disguised cheaters, fast-talking quack salesmen, and many similar freely sinning folk.

original: If it prove so, I will be gone the sooner.   I’ll to the Centaur to go seek this slave.   I greatly fear my money is not safe.
translation: If that's proved to be true, I'll get out of here as soon as I can. I'll go the Centaur to find this rascal. I greatly fear my money is not safe.

original: Neither my husband nor the slave returned   That in such haste I sent to seek his master?
translation: Neither my husband nor my servant who I sent running to find his master have returned?

original: Sure, Luciana, it is two o'clock.
translation: Luciana, it's already two o'clock.

original: Perhaps some merchant hath invited him,   And from the mart he’s somewhere gone to dinner.
translation: Perhaps some merchant has invited him, and he's gone to lunch somewhere from the market.

original: Good sister, let us dine and never fret.
translation: Remember that men are masters of their own freedom.

original: A man is master of his liberty;   Time is their master, and when they see time   They’ll go or come. If so, be patient, sister.
translation: Time is their only master, and when they think it's the right time they come and go as they wish. Let's eat and not fret.

original: Why should their liberty than ours be more?
translation: Why should men have more freedom than women?

original: Because their business still lies out o' door.
translation: Because their work takes place outside the house.

original: Look when I serve him so, he takes it ill.
translation: When I treat him like this, he takes it badly.

original: O, know he is the bridle of your will.
There’s none but asses will be bridled so.
translation: Only donkeys would be controlled like this.

original: Why, headstrong liberty is lashed with woe.   There’s nothing situate under heaven’s eye   But hath his bound, in earth, in sea, in sky.
translation: Well, being headstrong in your desire for freedom leads only to woe. There's nothing under heaven—whether on land, in sea, or in sky—that isn't bound in some way.

original: The beasts, the fishes, and the wingèd fowls   Are their males' subjects and at their controls.
translation: The beasts, fish, and birds, are all subject to the control of the males of their species.

original: Man, more divine, the masters of all these,   Lord of the wide world and wild wat'ry seas,   Endued with intellectual sense and souls,   Of more preeminence than fish and fowls,   Are masters to their females, and their lords.
translation: Man is more godly and is master of all these creatures. Man is lord of the whole world and wild, watery seas. Man has intellectual ability and a soul greater than any fish or birds. Men are masters of women, and lords to their ladies.

original: Then let your will attend on their accords.
translation: For those reasons, let yourself be ruled by men's wishes.

original: This servitude makes you to keep unwed.
translation: With that servant-like attitude, you'll never get married.

original: Not this, but troubles of the marriage bed.
translation: It's not that. It's just that I don't want to deal with what happens in the marriage bed.

original: But, were you wedded, you would bear some sway.
translation: But, if you were married, you would have some power.

original: Ere I learn love, I’ll practice to obey.
translation: Before I fall in love, I'll learn to obey.

original: How if your husband start some otherwhere?
translation: What if your husband strayed elsewhere?

original: Till he come home again, I would forbear.
translation: Till he came home, I'd hold out for him.

original: Patience unmoved! No marvel though she pause;   They can be meek that have no other cause.
translation: What amazing patience! I'm not amazed you hesitate to marry: it's easy to be meek when you have no reason not to be.

original: A wretched soul, bruised with adversity   We bid be quiet when we hear it cry,   But were we burdened with like weight of pain,   As much or more we should ourselves complain.
translation: We tell miserable people who have been mistreated to be quiet when we hear them cry, but if we had the same pain, or more, we should complain just like them.

original: So thou, that hast no unkind mate to grieve thee,   With urging helpless patience would relieve me;
translation: So you, who have no cruel husband to cause you grief, would stop telling me to be patient if you had a man.

original: But, if thou live to see like right bereft,   This fool-begged patience in thee will be left.
translation: But, if you lose your rights in the same way that I have, you'll give up this insistence on being patient.

original: Well, I will marry one day, but to try. Here comes your man. Now is your husband nigh.
translation: Well, I will marry one day, if only to try it out. Here comes your servant. Now your husband's on his way.

original: Say, is your tardy master now at hand?
translation: Tell me, is your tardy master coming soon?

original: Nay, he’s at two hands with me, and that my two ears  can witness.
Say, didst thou speak with him? Know’st thou his mind?
translation: Tell me, did you speak with him? Do you know what he's planning to do?

original: Ay, ay, he told his mind upon mine ear. Beshrew his hand, I scarce could understand it.
translation: Yes, yes, he told me his plans by beating me on the my ear. Curse his hand, I could hardly understand it.

original: Spake he so doubtfully thou couldst not feel his  meaning?
translation: He spoke so unclearly you couldn't get a feeling for what he meant?

original: Nay, he struck so plainly I could too well feel his  blows, and withal so doubtfully that I could scarce  understand them.
translation: No, he struck so clearly I could easily feel his blows, and yet he was so confusing that I could hardly understand what was happening.

original: But say, I prithee, is he coming home? It seems he hath great care to please his wife.
Why, mistress, sure my master is horn mad.
Horn mad, thou villain!
translation: Horn mad, you villain!

original: I mean not cuckold mad,   But sure he is stark mad.
translation: I don't mean he's a  cuckold , but surely he's stark raving mad.

original: When I desired him to come home to dinner,   He asked me for a thousand marks in gold.
translation: When I asked him to come home to dinner, he asked me for a thousand marks in gold.

original: “'Tis dinnertime,” quoth I. “My gold,” quoth he.   “Your meat doth burn,” quoth I. “My gold,” quoth he.
translation: "It's lunch time," said I. "My gold," said he. "Your meat is burning," said I. "My gold," said he. "Will you come?" said I. "My gold," said he.

original: “Will you come?” quoth I. “My gold,” quoth he.   “Where is the thousand marks I gave thee, villain?”   “The pig,” quoth I, “is burned.”
translation: "Where is the thousand marks I gave you, villain?" "The pig," said I, "is burned."

original: “My gold,” quoth he.   “My mistress, sir,” quoth I. “Hang up thy mistress!   I know not thy mistress. Out on thy mistress!”
translation: "My gold," said he. "My mistress, sir," said I. "Who cares about your mistress! I don't know your mistress. Damn your mistress!"

original: Quoth who?
translation: Who said that?

original: Quoth my master. “I know,” quoth he, “no house, no wife, no mistress.” So that my errand, due unto my tongue, I thank him, I bare home upon my shoulders, For, in conclusion, he did beat me there.
translation: Said my master. "I have," said he, "no house, no wife, no mistress." So I carry this message to you on my shoulders instead of on my tongue, since, in conclusion, he beat me there.

original: Go back again, thou slave, and fetch him home.
translation: Go back again, you slave, and bring him home.

original: Go back again and be new beaten home? For God’s sake, send some other messenger.
translation: Go back again and be beaten home again? For God's sake, send another messenger.

original: Back, slave, or I will break thy pate across.
translation: Go back, slave, or I'll break your head.

original: And he will bless that cross with other beating. Between you, I shall have a holy head.
translation: And he'll beat me on the head so that it makes a cross with the beating you've given me. Between the two of you, I'll have a holy head.

original: Hence, prating peasant! Fetch thy master home.
translation: Get out, chattering peasant! Bring your master home.

original: Am I so round with you as you with me, That like a football you do spurn me thus? You spurn me hence, and he will spurn me hither. If I last in this service, you must case me in leather.
translation: Am I so disrespectful to you as you are to me that you would throw me about like a football? You throw me out from here, and he'll throw me out from there. If I can survive this work, you must cover me in leather like a football.

original: Fie, how impatience loureth in your face.
translation: Come on now, your face looks so impatient.

original: His company must do his minions grace,   Whilst I at home starve for a merry look.
translation: He must be spending time in the company of other women while I wait at home wishing for his smile.

original: Hath homely age th' alluring beauty took   From my poor cheek? Then he hath wasted it.
translation: Has my advancing age taken my alluring beauty from my poor cheek? Then he's wasted it.

original: Are my discourses dull? Barren my wit?   If voluble and sharp discourse be marred,   Unkindness blunts it more than marble hard.
translation: Are my speeches boring? Is my wit bland? If sharp, witty conversation falls apart, unkindness worsens it more than marble would blunt something equally sharp.

original: Do their gay vestments his affections bait?   That’s not my fault; he’s master of my state.
translation: Do these women's bright colors seduce him? That's not my fault. He's master over all of my fortunes.

original: What ruins are in me that can be found   By him not ruined? Then is he the ground   Of my defeatures.
translation: What sorrows have I felt that aren't due to him? He's the cause of everything that's gone wrong with me.

original: My decayèd fair   A sunny look of his would soon repair.   But, too unruly deer, he breaks the pale   And feeds from home. Poor I am but his stale.
translation: His sunny smile would quickly fix my decaying face. But, like an unruly deer, he runs from me and eats outside our home. I'm nothing but his washed-up mistress.

original: Self-harming jealousy, fie, beat it hence.
translation: This jealousy is just harmful to yourself. Come on, get rid of it.

original: Unfeeling fools can with such wrongs dispense.   I know his eye doth homage otherwhere,   Or else what lets it but he would be here?
translation: Only fools without feelings can move on from such mistreatment. I know he's been unfaithful to me, or else why wouldn't he be here?

original: Sister, you know he promised me a chain.   Would that alone o' love he would detain,   So he would keep fair quarter with his bed.
translation: Sister, you know he promised me a chain. I'd give up the chain if he'd come back to our marriage and our bed.

original: I see the jewel best enamelèd   Will lose his beauty. Yet the gold bides still   That others touch, and often touching will   Wear gold; yet no man that hath a name   By falsehood and corruption doth it shame.
translation: Even the most beautiful jewel will lose its beauty. Gold can sometimes last when others put their dirty fingers on it, and it only sometimes gets worn down. It's me, and not my husband, who will feel shame and it's only my reputation that will be ruined by his falsehood and unfaithfulness .

original: Since that my beauty cannot please his eye,   I’ll weep what’s left away, and weeping die.
translation: Since my beauty can't please his eye, I'll weep what's left of my face off, and die weeping.

original: How many fond fools serve mad jealousy!
translation: There are so many fools in love at the mercy of their own jealousy!

original: The gold I gave to Dromio is laid up   Safe at the Centaur, and the heedful slave   Is wandered forth, in care to seek me out.
translation: The gold that I gave to Dromio is safely hidden at the Centaur, and according to the inn host, Dromio has left there in order to find me.

original: By computation and mine host’s report,   I could not speak with Dromio since at first   I sent him from the mart. See, here he comes.
translation: Given my calculations and what the host told me, there's no way I could have spoken to Dromio since I first sent him on his errands from the market. See, here he comes.

original: What answer, sir? When spake I such a word?
translation: What answer, sir? When did I say anything like that?

original: Even now, even here, not half an hour since.
translation: Just now, right here, less than half an hour ago.

original: I did not see you since you sent me hence, Home to the Centaur with the gold you gave me.
translation: I haven't seen you since you sent me to the Centaur with the gold you gave me.

original: Villain, thou didst deny the gold’s receipt And told’st me of a mistress and a dinner, For which, I hope, thou felt’st I was displeased.
translation: Villain, you just denied having received the gold from me and told me of a wife and a lunch. I hope you felt that I was displeased by that.

original: I am glad to see you in this merry vein. What means this jest? I pray you, master, tell me?
translation: I'm glad to see you in this merry mood. What does this joking mean? I ask you, master, tell me.

original: Yea, dost thou jeer and flout me in the teeth? Think’st thou I jest? Hold, take thou that and that. [beats DROMIO OF SYRACUSE
translation: Oh, do you mock me to my face? Do you think I joke? Okay, then, take that and that.

original: Hold, sir, for God’s sake! Now your jest is earnest. Upon what bargain do you give it me?
translation: Stop, sir, for God's sake! Now your jokes are in earnest. How have I earned this beating?

original: Because that I familiarly sometimes   Do use you for my fool and chat with you,   Your sauciness will jest upon my love   And make a common of my serious hours.
translation: Just because sometimes I make jokes with you and chat with you, you think you can use our friendship as an excuse to mock me and make fun of me when I'm serious.

original: When the sun shines, let foolish gnats make sport,   But creep in crannies when he hides his beams.
translation: When I'm kind to you, it's like the sun's out, and you can joke with me like bugs out playing, but when the sun goes down, and I'm in a bad mood, creep back into your hole.

original: If you will jest with me, know my aspect,   And fashion your demeanor to my looks,   Or I will beat this method in your sconce.
translation: If you're going to joke with me, look at my face and behave accordingly, or I'll beat this lesson into your  sconce .

original: “Sconce” call you it? So you would leave battering, I  had rather have it a “head.” An you use these blows  long, I must get a sconce for my head and ensconce it  too, or else I shall seek my wit in my shoulders. But I  pray, sir, why am I beaten?
Dost thou not know?
translation: Do you not know?

original: Nothing, sir, but that I am beaten.
translation: I only know that I'm beaten.

original: Shall I tell you why?
translation: Should I tell you why?

original: Ay, sir, and wherefore, for they say every why hath a  wherefore.
translation: Yes, sir, and for what reason, for they say that every "why" has a reason behind it.

original: “Why” first: for flouting me; and then “wherefore”: for urging it the second time to me.
translation: First, "why": for mocking me. Then, "for what reason": for mocking me again the second time.

original: Was there ever any man thus beaten out of season, When in the “why” and the “wherefore” is neither rhyme  nor reason? Well, sir, I thank you.
translation: Was any man in history so wrongly beaten, when neither the "why" or the "for what reason" have any truth or logic in them? Well, sir, I thank you.

original: Thank me, sir, for what?
translation: Thank me for what, sir?

original: Marry, sir, for this something that you gave me for  nothing.
I’ll make you amends next, to give you nothing for  something. But say, sir, is it dinnertime?
translation: Next time, I'll do the reverse and give you nothing for something. But, tell me, sir, is it lunchtime?

original: No, sir, I think the meat wants that I have.
In good time, sir, what’s that?
translation: Quickly, sir, what's that thing?

original: Basting.
translation: Basting.

original: Well, sir, then ’twill be dry.
translation: Well, sir, then the meat will be dry.

original: If it be, sir, I pray you, eat none of it.
translation: If it is, sir, I hope you'll eat none of it.

original: Your reason?
translation: Your reason?

original: Lest it make you choleric and purchase me another dry  basting.
Well, sir, learn to jest in good time. There’s a time  for all things.
translation: Well, sir, you'll find a good time to joke eventually. There's a right time for everything.

original: I durst have denied that before you were so choleric.
translation: I would have denied that before you were so angry.

original: By what rule, sir?
translation: How would you have denied that, sir?

original: Marry, sir, by a rule as plain as the plain bald pate  of Father Time himself.
Let’s hear it.
translation: Let's hear it.

original: There’s no time for a man to recover his hair that  grows bald by nature.
translation: There's no time for a man to recover his hair when he's naturally become bald.

original: May he not do it by fine and recovery?
Yes, to pay a fine for a periwig, and recover the lost  hair of another man.
translation: Yes, he could pay a fine to buy a wig and recover the hair that another man had lost.

original: Why is Time such a niggard of hair, being, as it is, so plentiful an excrement?
translation: Why is Time so stingy about hair when there's so much of it to go around?

original: Because it is a blessing that he bestows on beasts, and what he hath scanted men in hair, he hath given them in wit.
translation: Because it's also shared by beasts, and he made up for taking people's hair from them by giving them brains.

original: Why, but there’s many a man hath more hair than wit.
translation: Well, there are many men with more hair than brains.

original: Not a man of those but he hath the wit to lose his  hair.
translation: But all of those men have enough brains to lose their hair.

original: Why, thou didst conclude hairy men plain dealers  without wit.
translation: Ah, you just concluded that hairy men deal plainly and have no brains.

original: The plainer dealer, the sooner lost. Yet he loseth it  in a kind of jollity.
For what reason?
translation: For what reason?

original: For two, and sound ones too.
translation: For two reasons, and sound ones too.

original: Nay, not sound, I pray you.
translation: No, not sound reasons, please.

original: Sure ones, then.
translation: Sure reasons, then.

original: Nay, not sure, in a thing falsing.
translation: No, not sure, in such an unreliable context.

original: Certain ones, then.
translation: Certain reasons, then.

original: Name them.
translation: Name them.

original: The one, to save the money that he spends in tiring;  the other, that at dinner they should not drop in his  porridge.
translation: First, they save the money spent to keep their hair looking nice. Second, at dinner they won't get their hair in the soup.

original: You would all this time have proved there is no time  for all things.
translation: You meant to spend this whole time proving that it's not true that there's a time for all things.

original: Marry, and did, sir: namely, e'en no time to recover  hair lost by nature.
translation: Well, and I did it, sir. Namely, there's not time to recover hair that's naturally lost.

original: But your reason was not substantial why there is no  time to recover.
translation: But your reasoning did not convince me why there is no time to recover hair.

original: Thus I mend it: Time himself is bald and therefore, to  the world’s end, will have bald followers.
translation: I'll try again like this: Time himself is bald, and therefore, until the world ends, he will have people following him who are bald.

original: I knew ’twould be a bald conclusion: But soft, who wafts us yonder?
translation: I knew you would end with an argument as empty as a bald head. But hush, who's gesturing to us over there?

original: Ay, ay, Antipholus, look strange and frown.   Some other mistress hath thy sweet aspects.   I am not Adriana, nor thy wife.
translation: Yes, yes, Antipholus, look confused and frown. Some other woman has gotten your affection. Apparently I am not Adriana, nor your wife.

original: The time was once when thou unurged wouldst vow   That never words were music to thine ear,   That never object pleasing in thine eye,   That never touch well welcome to thy hand,   That never meat sweet-savored in thy taste,   Unless I spake, or looked, or touched, or carved to  thee.
translation: There was once a time when, without prompting, you would vow that no words could be music to your ear, no object could please your eye, no touch could be welcome to your hand, no meat could taste sweet to your mouth, unless I spoke, or looked, or touched, or carved the meat for you.

original: How comes it now, my husband, O, how comes it   That thou art thus estranged from thyself?   Thy "self" I call it, being strange to me,   That, undividable, incorporate,   Am better than thy dear self’s better part.   Ah, do not tear away thyself from me!
translation: How has it happened, my husband, oh, how has it happened that you are such a stranger to yourself? Your "self," I call it, a stranger to me, when I am indivisible, united as one with you, no better than the best part of you. Oh, don't tear yourself away from me!

original: For know, my love, as easy mayest thou fall   A drop of water in the breaking gulf,   And take unmingled thence that drop again   Without addition or diminishing,   As take from me thyself and not me too.
translation: Just know, my love, that you can separate me from you without separating me from myself too as easily as you can splash a drop of water into the sea, and then take the drop back from the sea without gaining or losing water .

original: How dearly would it touch thee to the quick,   Shouldst thou but hear I were licentious   And that this body, consecrate to thee,   By ruffian lust should be contaminate!
translation: How much it would pain you if you only heard a whisper that I was unfaithful, and that this body, so sacred to you, had been contaminated by lust!

original: Wouldst thou not spit at me, and spurn at me,   And hurl the name of husband in my face,   And tear the stained skin off my harlot brow,   And from my false hand cut the wedding ring,   And break it with a deep-divorcing vow?
translation: Wouldn't you spit at me and turn on me, and remind me that you were my husband, and tear the skin off my cheating forehead, and cut the wedding ring from my false hand, and break that ring with a vow to divorce me?

original: I know thou canst, and therefore see thou do it.   I am possessed with an adulterate blot;   My blood is mingled with the crime of lust;   For if we two be one, and thou play false,   I do digest the poison of thy flesh,   Being strumpeted by thy contagion.
translation: I know you could, and therefore I want to see you do that. Now I'm filled with adulterous blood that's mingled with lustful crimes. If we two are one, and you act falsely to me, the poison of your flesh enters mine, and your sin is contagious.

original: Keep then fair league and truce with thy true bed,   I live disstained, thou undishonorèd.
translation: You'd better stay true to me, for I am ruined when you are dishonored.

original: Plead you to me, fair dame? I know you not. In Ephesus I am but two hours old, As strange unto your town as to your talk, Who, every word by all my wit being scanned, Want wit in all one word to understand.
translation: Are you pleading with me, fair lady? I don't know you. I've been in Ephesus for only two hours. I'm as much a stranger to the town as to the subject you're talking with, which, as hard as I'm trying to follow your words, I have absolutely no ability to understand.

original: Fie, brother, how the world is changed with you! When were you wont to use my sister thus? She sent for you by Dromio home to dinner.
translation: For shame, brother, you've changed so much! When would you ever abuse my sister like this? She sent Dromio to bring you home to lunch.

original: By Dromio?
translation: Dromio?

original: By me?
translation: Me?

original: By thee; and this thou didst return from him: That he did buffet thee and, in his blows, Denied my house for his, me for his wife.
translation: You, and this is the report you brought back from him: that he struck you and, in his blows, denied that you live in my house or that I am your wife.

original: Did you converse, sir, with this gentlewoman? What is the course and drift of your compact?
translation: Did you talk to this lady, sir? What's the nature of your conspiracy?

original: I, sir? I never saw her till this time.
translation: Me, sir? I never saw her until right now.

original: Villain, thou liest; for even her very words Didst thou deliver to me on the mart.
translation: Villain, you lie. In the market, you said to me the very words she just spoke.

original: I never spake with her in all my life.
translation: I never spoke with her in my whole life.

original: How can she thus then call us by our names— Unless it be by inspiration?
translation: How can she call us by our names then unless she's divinely inspired?

original: How ill agrees it with your gravity   To counterfeit thus grossly with your slave,   Abetting him to thwart me in my mood.
translation: It's not a good look for your dignity to play-act this stupidly with your slave, maddening me in my angry mood.

original: Be it my wrong you are from me exempt,   But wrong not that wrong with a more contempt.   Come, I will fasten on this sleeve of thine.
translation: Even if it's my fault that you've turned away from me, don't react to that fault by treating me with worse contempt. Come, I'll cling to your sleeve.

original: Thou art an elm, my husband, I a vine,   Whose weakness, married to thy stronger state,   Makes me with thy strength to communicate.
translation: You're an elm tree, my husband, and I'm a weak vine who, when I cling to you, get strength from you to express myself.

original: If aught possess thee from me, it is dross,   Usurping ivy, brier, or idle moss,   Who, all for want of pruning, with intrusion   Infect thy sap and live on thy confusion.
translation: Anything that is trying to steal you from me is garbage, just creeping ivy, or brambles, or invasive moss, all of which haven't been pruned so they infect the sap of your tree and flourish in your sickness.

original: To me she speaks; she moves me for her theme.   What, was I married to her in my dream?   Or sleep I now and think I hear all this?
translation: She's speaking to me. Her story's moving. Well, was I married to her in a dream? Or am I asleep now and dreaming this?

original: What error drives our eyes and ears amiss?   Until I know this sure uncertainty   I’ll entertain the offered fallacy.
translation: What's the cause of the confusion of our eyes and ears? Until I know what's caused this clear misunderstanding, I'll go along with it.

original: Dromio, go bid the servants spread for dinner.
translation: Dromio, go tell the servants to prepare for dinner.

original: O, for my beads! I cross me for a sinner.   This is the fairy land. O spite of spites!
translation: Oh, where are my rosary beads? I'll cross myself since I must be a sinner. This is a fairy land. Oh, horrible fate!

original: We talk with goblins, owls, and sprites:   If we obey them not, this will ensue:   They’ll suck our breath, or pinch us black and blue.
translation: We've been talking with goblins, owls, and spirits. If we don't obey them, they'll suck our breath out of us, or pinch us till we're black and blue.

original: Why prat’st thou to thyself and answer’st not? Dromio—thou, Dromio—thou snail, thou slug, thou sot.
translation: Why are you muttering to yourself and not answering? Dromio—you, Dromio—you snail, you slug, you fool.

original: I am transformèd, master, am I not?
translation: I've been transformed, master, haven't I?

original: I think thou art in mind, and so am I.
translation: I think your mind has been, and so has mine.

original: Nay, master, both in mind and in my shape.
translation: No, master, both my mind and my appearance.

original: Thou hast thine own form.
translation: You have your own appearance.

original: No, I am an ape.
translation: No, I'm an ape.

original: If thou art changed to aught, ’tis to an ass.
'Tis true. She rides me, and I long for grass. 'Tis so. I am an ass; else it could never be But I should know her as well as she knows me.
Come, come, no longer will I be a fool,   To put the finger in the eye and weep   Whilst man and master laugh my woes to scorn.   Come, sir, to dinner.
translation: Come along now. I won't be a fool anymore to make myself cry while my husband and his servant mock my sorrows. Come, sir, to lunch.

original: —Dromio, keep the gate. —   Husband, I’ll dine above with you today,   And shrive you of a thousand idle pranks.
translation: Dromio, watch over the gate. Husband, I'll dine with you today, and you can confess all of your silly pranks to me.

original: Sirrah, if any ask you for your master,   Say he dines forth, and let no creature enter.—   Come, sister.—Dromio, play the porter well.
translation: Servant,  if anyone asks to see your master, tell them he's dining out, and don't let anyone in. Come, sister. Dromio, play the role of the porter well.

original: Am I in earth, in heaven, or in hell? Sleeping or waking, mad or well-advised? Known unto these, and to myself disguised! I’ll say as they say, and persever so, And in this mist at all adventures go.
translation: Am I in earth, heaven, or hell? Sleeping or waking, mad or sane? I'm known to these women and not to myself! I'll do what they tell me and go along with them through this mental mist.

original: Master, shall I be porter at the gate?
translation: Master, should I be the porter at the gate?

original: Ay; and let none enter, lest I break your pate.
translation: Yes, and don't let anyone in, or I'll break your head.

original: Come, come, Antipholus, we dine too late.
translation: Come, come, Antipholus, it's already late to eat.

original: Good Signior Angelo, you must excuse us all;   My wife is shrewish when I keep not hours.
translation: Good sir Angelo, you must let us all go. My wife gets in a bad mood when I don't come home on time.

original: Say that I lingered with you at your shop   To see the making of her carcanet,   And that tomorrow you will bring it home.
translation: Let's say that I was waiting at your shop to see her necklace made, and that you'll bring it to my house tomorrow.

original: But here’s a villain that would face me down   He met me on the mart, and that I beat him   And charged him with a thousand marks in gold,   And that I did deny my wife and house.—
translation: But this man's a villain that insists that he met me at the market, and claims that I beat him, asked him for a thousand gold marks, and told him I didn't have any wife or house.

original: Say what you will, sir, but I know what I know. That you beat me at the mart I have your hand to show; If the skin were parchment and the blows you gave were  ink, Your own handwriting would tell you what I think.
translation: Say what you want, sir, but I know what happened to me. I can prove you beat me at the market because of the mark of your hand on me. It's like my skin was parchment, and the blows you gave me in the beating were ink: anyone can read the marks on me in your own handwriting and know what happened.

original: I think thou art an ass.
Marry, so it doth appear By the wrongs I suffer and the blows I bear. I should kick being kicked; and, being at that pass, You would keep from my heels and beware of an ass.
translation: Well, it looks like it, given how I suffer and how much I'm beaten up. I should kick back when I'm kicked. If I did that, you'd keep away from my heels just like you'd keep away from the legs of an ass.

original: You’re sad, Signior Balthasar. Pray God our cheer May answer my good will and your good welcome here.
translation: You look very serious, Balthasar, sir. I hope our food will show my friendliness and how much you're welcome here.

original: I hold your dainties cheap, sir, and your welcome dear.
translation: I care less about the food you serve and more about the warm welcome you give.

original: O Signior Balthasar, either at flesh or fish A table full of welcome make scarce one dainty dish.
translation: Oh, Balthasar, whether you want meat or fish, all the welcome in the world doesn't cook the meals.

original: Good meat, sir, is common; that every churl affords.
translation: Good meat, sir, is cheap. Even the poorest can buy that.

original: And welcome more common, for that’s nothing but words.
translation: Welcome's cheap, too. It's only words.

original: Small cheer and great welcome makes a merry feast.
translation: A little celebration and a warm welcome make for a merry feast.

original: Ay, to a niggardly host and more sparing guest. But though my cates be mean, take them in good part. Better cheer may you have, but not with better heart. But soft! My door is lock’d.     Go, bid them  let us in.
translation: Sure, to a stingy host and an easygoing guest. Well, even though my food's not much, eat your fill. I hope you'll be cheerier, but you couldn't be warmer. But wait! My door is locked. Go, tell them to let us in.

original: Maud, Bridget, Marian, Ciceley, Gillian, Ginn!
translation: Maud, Bridget, Marian, Cicely, Gillian, Ginn!

original: Mome, malt-horse, capon, coxcomb, idiot,  patch! Either get thee from the door or sit down at the hatch. Dost thou conjure for wenches, that thou call’st for  such store When one is one too many? Go, get thee from the door.
translation: Fool, horse, eunuch, simpleton, idiot, clown! Either get away from the door or sit down at the gate. Are you summoning young women by magic, or why else do you call for so many when one is already too many for you? Go, get away from the door.

original: What patch is made our porter? My master stays in the  street.
translation: How has our porter become a clown? My master's waiting in the street.

original: Let him walk from whence he came, lest he  catch cold on ’s feet.
translation: He can go back where he came from so he doesn't catch cold.

original: Who talks within there? Ho, open the door.
translation: Who's talking from inside there? Hey, open the door.

original: Right, sir, I’ll tell you when an you tell me  wherefore.
translation: Sure, sir, I'll tell you when if you tell me why.

original: Wherefore? For my dinner. I have not dined today.
translation: Why? For my dinner. I haven't dined today.

original: Nor today here you must not. Come again when  you may.
translation: Well, you won't dine here today. Come again when you're free.

original: What art thou that keep’st me out from the house I owe?
translation: Who do you think you are, keeping me out from my own house?

original: The porter for this time, sir, and my name is  Dromio.
translation: I'm the porter for now, sir, and my name is Dromio.

original: O villain, thou hast stolen both mine office and my  name! The one ne'er got me credit, the other mickle blame. If thou hadst been Dromio today in my place, Thou wouldst have changed thy face for a name, or thy  name  for an ass.
translation: Oh, villain, you've stolen both my job and my name! My name's never had a great reputation, but I never fell short of my responsibilities in my job. If you had been Dromio today instead of me, you would have traded your job for a reputation, or your name for an ass.

original: What a coil is there, Dromio! Who are those at the gate?
translation: What a ruckus, Dromio! Who are those people at the gate?

original: Let my master in, Luce.
translation: Let my master in, Luce.

original: Faith, no, he comes too late, And so tell your master.
translation: God, no, he comes too late, and tell your master that.

original: O Lord, I must laugh. Have at you with a proverb: shall I set in my staff?
translation: Oh Lord, I must laugh. Here's a proverb for you: shall I plant my staff here and wait?

original: Have at you with another: that’s—When, can you tell?
translation: Here's another proverb: When, can you tell?

original: If thy name be called “Luce,” Luce, thou hast  answered him well.
translation: If your name is "Luce," Luce, you've answered him cleverly.

original: Do you hear, you minion? You’ll let us in, I hope?
translation: Do you hear us, you villain? You'll let us in, I hope?

original: I thought to have asked you.
translation: I thought that was a question for you.

original: And you said no.
translation: Well, you said no already.

original: So, come, help. Well struck! There was blow for blow.
translation: Come bang at the door. Just like that! That was one blow on the door for every blow they aimed at us with their words.

original: Thou baggage, let me in.
translation: You riff-raff, let me in.

original: [within)  Can you tell for whose sake?
translation: Can you say for whose sake we should let you in?

original: Master, knock the door hard.
translation: Master, knock on the door hard.

original: Let him knock till it ache.
translation: Let him knock until his hand aches.

original: You’ll cry for this, minion, if I beat the door down.
translation: You'll be sorry for this, woman, if I knock down the door.

original: What needs all that, and a pair of stocks in  the town?
translation: Why should I feel threatened when you'll be put in the stocks in town?

original: Who is that at the door that keeps all this  noise?
translation: Who is that at the door making all this noise?

original: By my troth, your town is troubled with unruly boys.
translation: It seems to me that a gang of unruly boys has come to town.

original: Are you there, wife? You might have come before.
translation: Wife, are you there? You could have come sooner.

original: Your wife, sir knave? Go, get you from the  door.
translation: Your wife, you villain? Go, get away from the door.

original: If you went in pain, master, this knave would go sore.
translation: If you leave angrily, master, this servant will be beaten sore for it.

original: Here is neither cheer, sir, nor welcome. We would  fain have either.
translation: There's neither cheer nor welcome here, sir. It would be great to have either.

original: In debating which was best, we shall part with neither.
translation: We were debating which was best, but we'll leave having had neither.

original: They stand at the door, master. Bid them welcome  hither.
translation: They're waiting at the door, master. Tell them they're welcome here.

original: There is something in the wind, that we cannot get in.
translation: There's something in the wind preventing us from getting in.

original: You would say so, master, if your garments were thin. Your cake there is warm within; you stand here in the  cold. It would make a man mad as a buck to be so bought and  sold.
Go, fetch me something: I’ll break ope the gate.
translation: Go, get me something and I'll break open the gate.

original: Break any breaking here, and I’ll break your  knave’s pate.
translation: If you break anything, I'll break your foolish head.

original: A man may break a word with you, sir, and words are but wind, Ay, and break it in your face, so he break it not  behind.
It seems thou want’st breaking. Out upon thee, hind!
translation: Oh, well. now you're asking for someone to break you. Get out of here, servant!

original: Here’s too much “out upon thee!” I pray thee, let me  in.
translation: Enough with your "get out of here!" I beg of you, let me in.

original: Ay, when fowls have no feathers and fish have  no fin.
translation: Sure, when birds have no feathers and fish have no fins.

original: Well, I’ll break in. Go, borrow me a crow.
translation: Well, I'll break in. Go, borrow a crowbar for me.

original: A crow without feather? Master, mean you so? For a fish without a fin, there’s a fowl without a  feather.—     If a crow help us in, sirrah,  we’ll pluck a crow together.
translation: A crow without feathers? Master, is that what you mean? We don't have a fish without a fin, but that's a bird without feathers.  If a crowbar helps us in, sir, we'll get this settled once and for all.

original: Go, get thee gone. Fetch me an iron crow.
translation: Go, get out of here. Fetch me an iron crowbar.

original: Have patience, sir. O, let it not be so.   Herein you war against your reputation,   And draw within the compass of suspect   Th' unviolated honor of your wife.
translation: Have patience, sir. Oh, don't let it come to this. You're putting your reputation at risk and your wife's pure honor will be the subject of suspicion and gossip.

original: Once this: your long experience of her wisdom,   Her sober virtue, years, and modesty   Plead on her part some cause to you unknown.
translation: Here's what I think: you know her wisdom, clear-minded virtue, age, and modesty well, and you should give her the benefit of the doubt that there's some cause you don't know about.

original: And doubt not, sir, but she will well excuse   Why at this time the doors are made against you.   Be ruled by me; depart in patience,   And let us to the Tiger all to dinner,   And about evening come yourself alone   To know the reason of this strange restraint.
translation: I'm sure that she will have a good excuse for why she's locked the doors on you at this time. Listen to me, leave patiently, and let's all go to the Tiger for lunch. In the evening, come alone and find out the reason for this strange behavior.

original: If by strong hand you offer to break in   Now in the stirring passage of the day,   A vulgar comment will be made of it;
translation: If you try to break in by force in the busy streets in the middle of the day, it will be talked about.

original: And that supposèd by the common rout   Against your yet ungallèd estimation   That may with foul intrusion enter in   And dwell upon your grave when you are dead;
translation: Whatever the common people say about you, ruining your good reputation, might well stick around until after you're dead and be your legacy.

original: For slander lives upon succession,   Forever housèd where it gets possession.
translation: Slander and gossip grows and grows and never dies.

original: You have prevailed. I will depart in quiet   And, in despite of mirth, mean to be merry.
translation: You've persuaded me. I'll leave quietly, and, even though I have nothing to make me happy, I'll try to be cheerful.

original: I know a wench of excellent discourse,   Pretty and witty, wild and yet, too, gentle.   There will we dine. This woman that I mean,   My wife—but, I protest, without desert—   Hath oftentimes upbraided me withal;   To her will we to dinner.
Get you home   And fetch the chain; by this I know ’tis made.   Bring it, I pray you, to the Porpentine,   For there’s the house.
translation: Go home and get the chain. That way I'll know you've finished it. Bring it, please, to the Porpentine, since that's where the house is.

original: That chain will I bestow—   Be it for nothing but to spite my wife—   Upon mine hostess there. Good sir, make haste.
translation: That chain I'll give—only to spite my wife— to my hostess there. Good sir, hurry.

original: Since mine own doors refuse to entertain me,   I’ll knock elsewhere, to see if they’ll disdain me.
translation: Since I can't be entertained within my own doors, I'll knock at other doors and see if they're locked against me too.

original: I’ll meet you at that place some hour hence.
translation: I'll meet you there in about an hour.

original: Do so. This jest shall cost me some expense.
translation: We'll see you there. This prank will be costly to me.

original: And may it be that you have quite forgot   A husband’s office? Shall, Antipholus,   Even in the spring of love thy love-springs rot?
translation: Is it possible you've forgotten your duty as a husband? Will you let your love rot when it's just started flourishing?
