original: Shall love, in building, grow so ruinous?   If you did wed my sister for her wealth,   Then for her wealth’s sake use her with more kindness.
translation: In the process of building this love, will you turn it into a ruin? If you married my sister for her money, then for the sake of her money, be kinder to her.

original: Or if you like elsewhere, do it by stealth—   Muffle your false love with some show of blindness.   Let not my sister read it in your eye;
translation: Or if you're going to cheat on her, do it sneakily. Hide your true feelings so that my sister can't see it in your eyes.

original: Be not thy tongue thy own shame’s orator;   Look sweet, be fair, become disloyalty;   Apparel vice like virtue’s harbinger.
translation: Don't talk about your shamelessness. Look loving, be warm, mask your disloyalty in kindness. Dress your sins as if they were virtues.

original: Bear a fair presence, though your heart be tainted.   Teach sin the carriage of a holy saint.   Be secret-false. What need she be acquainted?
translation: Just present yourself sweetly, even if your heart is poisoned. Carry your evil thoughts like you were a holy saint. Just keep it to yourself. Why does she need to know?

original: What simple thief brags of his own attaint?   'Tis double wrong to truant with your bed   And let her read it in thy looks at board.
translation: What kind of thief brags about what he's stolen? It's doubly wrong to stray from her in bed and then let her see it in your face at breakfast.

original: Shame hath a bastard fame, well managèd;   Ill deeds is doubled with an evil word.   Alas, poor women, make us but believe,   Being compact of credit, that you love us.
translation: Your shame doesn't need to be public if you do it right. Your hateful actions are doubled if you talk about them. Oh, poor women, just make us believe, since we're so blindly trusting, that you love us.

original: Though others have the arm, show us the sleeve;   We in your motion turn, and you may move us.   Then, gentle brother, get you in again.
translation: Even if you're really in love with other women, make it look like you're still attached to us. We're totally dependent on you, and you can control us. So, dear brother, go to her again.

original: Comfort my sister, cheer her, call her wife.   'Tis holy sport to be a little vain   When the sweet breath of flattery conquers strife.
translation: Comfort my sister, cheer her up, call her your wife. It's not a sin to tell a white lie since your sweet flattery will vanquish her misery.

original: Sweet mistress—what your name is else I know not,   Nor by what wonder you do hit of mine,—   Less in your knowledge and your grace you show not   Than our earth’s wonder, more than earth divine.
translation: Sweet mistress—I don't know your name and I can't figure out how you miraculously know mine,—your wisdom and your presence are more wondrous and divine than the earth itself.

original: Teach me, dear creature, how to think and speak.   Lay open to my earthy gross conceit,   Smothered in errors, feeble, shallow, weak,   The folded meaning of your words' deceit.
translation: Explain to me (just a lowly, earth-bound fellow, prone to errors, feeble, shallow, weak) the complex meaning of your words.

original: Against my soul’s pure truth why labour you   To make it wander in an unknown field?   Are you a god? would you create me new?   Transform me, then, and to your power I’ll yield.   But if that I am I, then well I know   Your weeping sister is no wife of mine,   Nor to her bed no homage do I owe.   Far more, far more, to you do I decline.
translation: When my soul moves toward another, why are you trying so hard to send me to love some woman I don't know? Are you a god? Do you want to make me into a new man? Transform me, then, and I'll give in to your powers.   But if I'm still myself, then I know well that your weeping sister's not my wife, and I haven't made any vows to her. I'm much, much more interested in you.

original: O, train me not, sweet mermaid, with thy note   To drown me in thy sister’s flood of tears.   Sing, Siren, for thyself, and I will dote.
translation: Oh, don't steer me with your song, sweet mermaid, to drown in your sister's endless tears and succumb to her. Sing, instead,  Siren , on your own behalf, and I'll be devoted to you.

original: Spread o'er the silver waves thy golden hairs,   And as a bed I’ll take them and there lie,   And in that glorious supposition think   He gains by death that hath such means to die.   Let Love, being light, be drownèd if she sink.
translation: Spread your golden hair over the ocean and I'll lie in it like it's a bed. In that glorious position, I'll think that death would be good if you could die like that. Love is usually lightweight, but when it's weighty enough to sink, it's worth it to drown.

original: What, are you mad that you do reason so?
translation: Are you crazy enough to reason like this?

original: Not mad, but mated—how, I do not know.
translation: Not crazy but in love—I don't know how.

original: It is a fault that springeth from your eye.
translation: It's a sin that's come from your wandering eye.

original: For gazing on your beams, fair sun, being by.
translation: I fell in love by gazing at your beams, you beautiful sun, since you were right there.

original: Gaze where you should, and that will clear your sight.
translation: Gaze where you're supposed to, and that will make you see straight.

original: As good to wink, sweet love, as look on night.
Why call you me “love”? Call my sister so.
translation: Why do you call me "love?" Call my sister that name.

original: Thy sister’s sister.
translation: Your sister's sister.

original: That’s my sister.
translation: That's my sister.

original: No, It is thyself, mine own self’s better part, Mine eye’s clear eye, my dear heart’s dearer heart, My food, my fortune, and my sweet hope’s aim, My sole earth’s heaven, and my heaven’s claim.
translation: No, it's you yourself, my better half, the apple of my eye, the heart within my heart, my sustenance, my wealth, and the aim of all my hopes, the only heaven on earth, and the only hope I have to get into heaven.

original: All this my sister is, or else should be.
translation: You mean to say all this about my sister, or, at least, you should.

original: Call thyself “sister,” sweet, for I am thee. Thee will I love and with thee lead my life; Thou hast no husband yet, nor I no wife. Give me thy hand.
translation: Call yourself "sister," sweetheart, for I am yours. I will love you and live my life with you. You have no husband yet and I have no wife. Give me your hand.

original: O soft, sir! Hold you still. I’ll fetch my sister to get her goodwill.
translation: Oh, wait, sir! Don't move. I'm going to my sister and we'll see what she says about this.

original: Why, how now, Dromio. Where runn’st thou so fast?
translation: Oh, what's happening, Dromio? Where are you running so fast?

original: Do you know me, sir? Am I Dromio? Am I your man? Am I myself?
translation: Do you know me, sir? Am I Dromio? Am I your servant? Am I myself?

original: Thou art Dromio, thou art my man, thou art thyself.
translation: You are Dromio, you're my servant, you're yourself.

original: I am an ass, I am a woman’s man, and besides myself.
translation: I'm an ass, I belong to a woman, and I'm beside myself.

original: What woman’s man? And how besides thyself?
translation: Belong to what woman? Why are you beside yourself?

original: Marry, sir, besides myself I am due to a woman, one  that claims me, one that haunts me, one that will have  me.
translation: Well, sir, I'm being pursued by a woman who claims me, haunts me, and insists that she'll have me.

original: What claim lays she to thee?
translation: What claim does she say she has over you?

original: Marry, sir, such claim as you would lay to your horse;  and she would have me as a beast; not that I being a  beast she would have me, but that she, being a very  beastly creature, lays claim to me.
translation: Well, sir, the same claim you'd have over your horse. She wants to have me as if I were a beast. Not that she'd want me if I were a beast, except that she, since she's a very beastly creature, says she has a claim over me.

original: What is she?
translation: What is she?

original: A very reverent body, ay, such a one as a man may not  speak of without he say “sir-reverence.” I have but lean luck in the match, and yet is she a wondrous fat  marriage.
How dost thou mean a “fat marriage”?
translation: What do you mean a "fat marriage"?

original: Marry, sir, she’s the kitchen wench, and all grease,  and I know not what use to put her to but to make a lamp of her and run from her by her own light.
translation: Well, sir, she's the kitchen maid, and she's made of grease, and I don't know how I would use her except to make her into a lamp and run away from her in the light that she gives off.

original: I warrant her rags and the tallow in them will burn a Poland winter.  If she lives till doomsday, she’ll burn a week longer  than the whole world.
translation: I bet the rags she wears and the fat inside them are enough to burn for a whole winter in Poland. If she lives until the end of the world, she'll still be burning a week after the whole world's in ashes.

original: What complexion is she of?
translation: What's her face like?

original: Swart like my shoe, but her face nothing like so clean  kept. For why? She sweats a man may go overshoes in the  grime of it.
translation: Dark like my shoe, but her face is not kept as clean as my shoe. Why, you ask? She sweats so much that her perspiration might come up to a man's ankles.

original: That’s a fault that water will mend.
translation: She could wash off the sweat with water.

original: No, sir, ’tis in grain; Noah’s flood could not do it.
translation: No, sir, it's undefeatable. Noah's flood couldn't wash it off.

original: What’s her name?
translation: What's her name?

original: Nell, sir, but her name and three quarters—that’s an  ell and three quarters—will not measure her from hip to  hip.
Then she bears some breadth?
translation: Then she's pretty wide?

original: No longer from head to foot than from hip to hip. She  is spherical, like a globe. I could find out countries  in her.
In what part of her body stands Ireland?
translation: Where on her body is Ireland?

original: Marry, sir, in her buttocks. I found it out by the  bogs.
translation: Well, sir, in her buttocks. I knew it was Ireland from the spongy marshes.

original: Where Scotland?
translation: Where on her body is Scotland?

original: I found it by the barrenness; hard in the palm of the  hand.
translation: The palm of her hand: I knew it was Scotland from the dryness.

original: Where France?
translation: What about France?

original: In her forehead, armed and reverted, making war against her heir.
Where England?
translation: What about England?

original: I looked for the chalky cliffs, but I could find no  whiteness in them. But I guess it stood in her chin, by  the salt rheum that ran between France and it.
translation: I looked for the white cliffs in her teeth, but I couldn't find any whiteness in them. I guess England must have been in her chin, given the salty saliva that ran between her forehead France and her chin.

original: Where Spain?
translation: What about Spain?

original: Faith, I saw it not, but I felt it hot in her breath.
translation: Well, I didn't see Spain, but I felt it in her hot breath.

original: Where America, the Indies?
O, sir, upon her nose, all o'er-embellished with  rubies, carbuncles, sapphires, declining their rich  aspect to the hot breath of Spain, who sent whole  armadas of caracks to be ballast at her nose.
Where stood Belgia, the Netherlands?

O, sir, I did not look so low. To conclude: this drudge or diviner laid claim to me, call’d me Dromio, swore I  was assured to her, told me what privy marks I had about me, as the mark of my shoulder, the mole in my neck,  the great wart on my left arm, that I, amazed, ran from  her as a witch.
translation: Oh, sir, I didn't look so low down. In conclusion, this slave or witch said she had a claim over me, called me Dromio, swore that I was pledged to her, told me what private marks I had on my body, like a mark on my shoulder, the mole on my neck, the big wart on my left art. So I, astonished, ran away from her as if she were a witch.

original: And, I think, if my breast had not been  made of faith, and my heart of steel, She had  transformed me to a curtal dog and made me turn i' th'  wheel.
translation: And, I think, if my soul had not been so faithful and my heart had not been made of steel, she might have transformed me into a dog with no tail and put me to work.

original: Go, hie thee presently. Post to the road.   An if the wind blow any way from shore,   I will not harbor in this town tonight.
translation: Go, get moving now. Run to the road. If the wind is blowing any direction from the shore, I won't stay in this town tonight.

original: If any bark put forth, come to the mart,   Where I will walk till thou return to me.
translation: If any ship is leaving, come to the market, where I'll walk until you return to me.

original: If every one knows us, and we know none,   'Tis time, I think, to trudge, pack, and be gone.
translation: If everyone knows us, and we don't know anybody, I think it's time to get up, pack up, and get out of here.

original: As from a bear a man would run for life, So fly I from her that would be my wife.
translation: Just like a man would run for his life from a bear, I'll flee that woman who wants to be my wife.

original: There’s none but witches do inhabit here,   And therefore ’tis high time that I were hence.
translation: The only people who live here are witches, so it's time we get out of here.

original: She that doth call me husband, even my soul   Doth for a wife abhor. But her fair sister,   Possessed with such a gentle sovereign grace,   Of such enchanting presence and discourse,   Hath almost made me traitor to myself.
translation: I would hate to have that woman who calls me husband for a wife. But her beautiful sister, who has such a gentle, divine grace, such an enchanting presence and skill at conversation, has almost made me forget myself.

original: But lest myself be guilty to self wrong,   I’ll stop mine ears against the mermaid’s song.
translation: But to make sure I'm not guilty of doing harm to myself, I'll stop listening to this  mermaid's song .

original: Master Antipholus.
translation: Master Antipholus.

original: Ay, that’s my name.
translation: Yes, that's my name.

original: I know it well, sir. Lo, here’s the chain. I thought to have ta'en you at the Porpentine; The chain unfinished made me stay thus long.
translation: I know it well, sir. Look, here's the chain. I meant to take it to you at the Porpentine. The chain took me until now to finish.

original: What is your will that I shall do with this?
translation: What do you want me to do with this?

original: What please yourself, sir. I have made it for you.
translation: Whatever you want, sir. I made it for you.

original: Made it for me, sir? I bespoke it not.
translation: Made it for me, sir? I never asked for it.

original: Not once, nor twice, but twenty times you have. Go home with it and please your wife withal, And soon at supper time I’ll visit you And then receive my money for the chain.
translation: Not once or twice, you've asked me twenty times for it. Take it home and please your wife with it, and I'll visit you at supper time to get my money for the chain then.

original: I pray you, sir, receive the money now, For fear you ne'er see chain nor money more.
translation: Please, sir, take the money now, for fear you'll never see the chain or the money again.

original: You are a merry man, sir. Fare you well.
translation: You're a goofy man, sir. Goodbye.

original: What I should think of this I cannot tell,   But this I think: there’s no man is so vain   That would refuse so fair an offered chain.
translation: I have no idea what to make of this, but I do know one thing: there's no one so stupid that wouldn't take a chain that's offered to him.

original: I see a man here needs not live by shifts   When in the streets he meets such golden gifts.
translation: I guess men here don't need to work for things when they get golden gifts in the streets.

original: I’ll to the mart, and there for Dromio stay.   If any ship put out, then straight away.
translation: I'll go to the market and wait for Dromio there. If any ship is leaving, I'll be on it immediately.

original: You know since Pentecost the sum is due,   And since I have not much importuned you,   Nor now I had not, but that I am bound   To Persia, and want guilders for my voyage.
translation: You know the fee has been due since Pentecost. I haven't nagged you that much about it since then, and I don't want to now, but I'm leaving for Persia and I need the money for my voyage.

original: Therefore make present satisfaction,   Or I’ll attach you by this officer.
translation: Therefore, give me the money now, or I'll have you arrested by this officer.

original: Even just the sum that I do owe to you   Is growing to me by Antipholus.
translation: Antipholus owes me exactly the amount that I owe you.

original: And in the instant that I met with you,   He had of me a chain. At five o'clock   I shall receive the money for the same.
translation: Right before I met you today, he bought a chain from me. At five o'clock, I'll get the money for that.

original: Pleaseth you walk with me down to his house,   I will discharge my bond and thank you too.
translation: If you care to walk with me down to his house, I'll pay you what I owe you and give you thanks.

original: That labor may you save. See where he comes.
translation: You don't have to go far. Look, he's coming now.

original: While I go to the goldsmith’s house, go thou   And buy a rope’s end.
translation: While I go to the goldsmith's house, you go and buy a rope.

original: That will I bestow   Among my wife and her confederates   For locking me out of my doors by day.
translation: I'll beat my wife and her accomplices with it for locking me out of my own house.

original: But soft. I see the goldsmith. Get thee gone.   Buy thou a rope, and bring it home to me.
translation: But hush. I see the goldsmith. Get out of here. Buy the rope, and bring it back to me.

original: I buy a thousand pound a year! I buy a rope!
translation: First a thousand marks and now a rope!

original: A man is well holp up that trusts to you!   I promisèd your presence and the chain,   But neither chain nor goldsmith came to me.
translation: A man is in good hands when he trusts you! I expected you to come with the chain, but I didn't see either or you or the chain.

original: Belike you thought our love would last too long   If it were chained together, and therefore came not.
translation: Maybe you thought we'd be too inseparable if we were chained together so you didn't bother to come.

original: Saving your merry humor, here’s the note   How much your chain weighs to the utmost carat,   The fineness of the gold, and chargeful fashion,   Which doth amount to three-odd ducats more   Than I stand debted to this gentleman.
translation: I'm glad you're in such a jolly mood, and here's the bill for how much your chain weighs down to the last carat, the quality of the gold, and the cost, which comes to three and a bit ducats more than I owe this gentleman.

original: I pray you, see him presently discharged,   For he is bound to sea, and stays but for it.
translation: Please, pay up, for he's going to sea and is only waiting for the money.

original: I am not furnished with the present money.   Besides, I have some business in the town.
translation: I don't have the money right now. Besides, I have business to attend to in town.

original: Good signior, take the stranger to my house,   And with you take the chain, and bid my wife   Disburse the sum on the receipt thereof.
translation: Good man, take the stranger to my house along with the chain, and ask my wife to pay the amount listed on the bill.

original: Perchance I will be there as soon as you.
translation: Maybe I'll get there at the same time.

original: Then you will bring the chain to her yourself.
translation: Then you will bring the chain to her yourself.

original: No, bear it with you lest I come not time enough.
translation: No, you bring it in case I don't get there in time.

original: Well, sir, I will. Have you the chain about you?
translation: Well, sir, I will. Do you have the chain with you?

original: An if I have not, sir, I hope you have, Or else you may return without your money.
translation: If I don't sir, I hope you do, or else you're not getting paid.

original: Nay, come, I pray you, sir, give me the chain. Both wind and tide stays for this gentleman, And I, to blame, have held him here too long.
translation: No, come on, please, sir, give me the chain. The wind and the tide are on hold for this gentleman, and I've kept him here too long.

original: Good Lord! You use this dalliance to excuse Your breach of promise to the Porpentine. I should have chid you for not bringing it, But, like a shrew, you first begin to brawl.
translation: Good Lord! You're stalling to make me forget that you didn't show up at the Porpentine as you'd promised. I should have laid into you for not bringing it, but, like a whiny brat, you start to fight first.

original: The hour steals on. I pray you, sir, dispatch.
translation: The clock is ticking. Please, sir, let's get moving.

original: You hear how he importunes me. The chain!
translation: You hear how he begs me! The chain!

original: Why, give it to my wife, and fetch your money.
translation: Just give it to my wife and get your money.

original: Come, come. You know I gave it you even now. Either send the chain, or send me by some token.
translation: Come on now. You know I just gave it to you. Either give me the chain, or give me something of yours to let your wife know to pay me.

original: Fie, now you run this humor out of breath. Come, where’s the chain? I pray you, let me see it.
translation: Really, now you're running this joke into the ground. Come on, where's the chain? I'm asking you, let me see it.

original: My business cannot brook this dalliance.     Good sir, say whe'er you’ll answer me  or no. If not, I’ll leave him to the Officer.
translation: I really don't have time for this dilly-dallying. Good sir, tell me whether you'll pay me or not. If not, I'll have Angelo arrested.

original: I answer you? What should I answer you?
translation: I pay you? What should I pay you?

original: The money that you owe me for the chain.
translation: The money that you owe me for the chain.

original: I owe you none till I receive the chain.
translation: I owe you nothing until I receive the chain.

original: You know I gave it you half an hour since.
translation: You know I gave it to you half an hour ago.

original: You gave me none. You wrong me much to say so.
translation: You gave me nothing. You do me wrong to say that.

original: You wrong me more, sir, in denying it. Consider how it stands upon my credit.
translation: You do me more wrong, sir, in lying about it. Think about what this does to my reputation.

original: Well, officer, arrest him at my suit.
translation: Well, officer, arrest him on my accusation.

original: I do,   and charge you in the Duke’s name to  obey me.
translation: I do, , and I charge you in the Duke's name to obey me.

original: This touches me in reputation. Either consent to pay this sum for me, Or I attach you by this officer.
translation: This damages my reputation. Either agree to pay me the money you owe, or I'll have you arrested by this officer.

original: Consent to pay thee that I never had?— Arrest me, foolish fellow, if thou dar’st.
translation: Agree to pay you for something I never got? Arrest me, foolish fellow, if you dare.

original: Here is thy fee. Arrest him, officer. I would not spare my brother in this case If he should scorn me so apparently.
translation: Here's money to do it. Arrest him, officer. I'd have my brother arrested too, if he'd wronged me as obviously as this man has.

original: I do arrest you, sir. You hear the suit.
translation: I do arrest you, sir. You've heard the accusation.

original: I do obey thee till I give thee bail. But, sirrah, you shall buy this sport as dear As all the metal in your shop will answer.
translation: I will obey you till I pay you bail. But, sir, you'll pay for this, and it will cost you all the metal in your shop.

original: Sir, sir, I will have law in Ephesus, To your notorious shame, I doubt it not.
translation: Sir, I'll make sure I have justice and keep my rights in Ephesus, even if it means you'll be humiliated and shamed.

original: Master, there is a bark of Epidamnum   That stays but till her owner comes aboard,   And then, sir, she bears away.
translation: Master, there's a ship from Epidamnum that's just waiting until her owners comes aboard, and then, sir, she sails away.

original: Our fraughtage, sir,   I have conveyed aboard, and I have bought   The oil, the balsamum and aqua vitae.
translation: All of our stuff, sir, I've brought on board, and I've bought the oil, the juice, and the alcohol.

original: The ship is in her trim; the merry wind   Blows fair from land. They stay for naught at all   But for their owner, master, and yourself.
translation: The ship's ready to go, and the wind is blowing away from land. They're waiting only for their owner and yourself, master.

original: How now? A madman? Why, thou peevish sheep, What ship of Epidamnum stays for me?
translation: Huh? Are you a madman? You silly animal, what ship from Epidamnum is waiting for me?

original: A ship you sent me to, to hire waftage.
translation: The ship you sent me to, to book our passage.

original: Thou drunken slave, I sent thee for a rope And told thee to what purpose and what end.
translation: You drunken slave, I sent you for a rope and told you what I wanted to use it for and for what purpose.

original: You sent me for a rope’s end as soon. You sent me to the bay, sir, for a bark.
translation: That's as true as saying you sent me to get a beating with a rope. You sent me to the bay, sir, to find a ship.

original: I will debate this matter at more leisure   And teach your ears to list me with more heed.
translation: I'll argue you about this with you when we have more time, and I'll teach your ears to listen to me with greater care.

original: To Adriana, villain, hie thee straight.   Give her this key, and tell her in the desk   That’s cover’d o'er with Turkish tapestry   There is a purse of ducats. Let her send it.
translation: Villain, get to Adriana, go immediately. Give her this key, and tell her that there's a bag of money in the desk that's covered with Turkish tapestry. Have her send it.

original: Tell her I am arrested in the street,   And that shall bail me. Hie thee, slave. Begone.—
translation: Tell her I've been arrested in the street, and that the money will bail me out. Get going, slave. Move it.

original: To Adriana. That is where we dined, Where Dowsabel did claim me for her husband. She is too big, I hope, for me to compass. Thither I must, although against my will, For servants must their masters' minds fulfill.
translation: To Adriana? That's where we ate, where that lady said I was her husband. She's more than I can handle. I must go there, even though I'd rather not, for servants must do whatever they're commanded.

original: Ah, Luciana, did he tempt thee so?   Mightst thou perceive austerely in his eye   That he did plead in earnest, yea or no?
translation: Oh, Luciana, did he really attempt to seduce you like that? Could you tell from his face whether he was serious, yes or no?

original: Looked he or red or pale, or sad or merrily?   What observation mad’st thou in this case   Of his heart’s meteors tilting in his face?
translation: Did he look red or pale or sad or happy? What observation did you make in his face of what his heart might really feel?

original: First he denied you had in him no right.
translation: First he denied that you had any right to him.

original: He meant he did me none; the more my spite.
translation: He meant he didn't do right by me, which makes me all the more miserable.

original: Then swore he that he was a stranger here.
translation: Then he swore that he was a stranger here.

original: And true he swore, though yet forsworn he were.
translation: He's definitely acting stranger, so that's true, even though he's lying.

original: Then pleaded I for you.
translation: Then I pleaded on your behalf.

original: And what said he?
translation: And what did he say?

original: That love i begged for you he begged of me.
translation: The love that I begged him to give you he begged me to give to him.

original: With what persuasion did he tempt thy love?
translation: What methods did he use to tempt your love?

original: With words that in an honest suit might move. First he did praise my beauty, then my speech.
translation: He used words that might have moved me if they were honest. First, he praised my beauty, then my voice.

original: Did’st speak him fair?
translation: Did you encourage him?

original: Have patience, I beseech.
translation: Calm down, I beg you.

original: I cannot, nor I will not hold me still;   My tongue, though not my heart, shall have his will.
translation: I cannot and I will not hold still. Even though my heart still loves him, listen to what I have to say:

original: He is deformèd, crooked, old, and sere,   Ill-faced, worse-bodied, shapeless everywhere,   Vicious, ungentle, foolish, blunt, unkind,   Stigmatical in making, worse in mind.
translation: he's deformed, crooked, old, and withered, with an ugly face and a worse body, shapeless all over. He's vicious, ungentle, foolish, stupid, unkind. His body is awful, but his mind is worse.

original: Who would be jealous, then, of such a one? No evil lost is wailed when it is gone.
translation: Who would be jealous over someone like that, then? No one cries over something evil when it's gone.

original: Ah, but I think him better than I say,   And yet would herein others' eyes were worse.
translation: Ah, but I think better of him than I say, and still wish other women saw him as ugly.

original: Far from her nest the lapwing cries away.   My heart prays for him, though my tongue do curse.
translation: Just like the lapwing flies far away from her nest so no one knows where it is located, I'm hiding how much my heart loves him in my angry  words.

original: Here, go—the desk, the purse! Sweet, now make haste.
translation: Here, go—the desk, the purse! Come on now, move fast.

original: How hast thou lost thy breath?
translation: How have you lost your breath?

original: By running fast.
translation: By running fast.

original: Where is thy master, Dromio? Is he well?
translation: Where's your master, Dromio? Is he well?

original: No, he’s in Tartar limbo, worse than hell.   A devil in an everlasting garment hath him,   One whose hard heart is buttoned up with steel;
translation: No he's in limbo in Tartarus, that's worse than hell. A devil in a prison officer uniform has got him, a devil whose hard heart is closed and steely.

original: A fiend, a fury, pitiless and rough;   A wolf, nay, worse, a fellow all in buff;
translation: He's a demon, evil, pitiless, and rough. He's a wolf; no, it's worse, he's wearing the uniform.

original: A back-friend, a shoulder clapper, one that  countermands   The passages of alleys, creeks, and narrow lands;
translation: He's a back-stabber, he arrests you by the shoulder, he forbids you to walk through alleys, and creeks, and narrow paths.

original: A hound that runs counter and yet draws dryfoot well,   One that before the judgment carries poor souls to  hell.
translation: He's a dog that flees from the prey but also tracks the prey by the smell of its foot. On Judgment Day, he'll be carrying the damned to hell.

original: Why, man, what is the matter?
translation: Why, man, what is the matter?

original: I do not know the matter. He is ’rested on the case.
What, is he arrested? Tell me at whose suit.
translation: What, is he arrested? Tell me who's had him arrested.

original: I know not at whose suit he is arrested well, But he’s in a suit of buff which ’rested him; that can  I tell. Will you send him, mistress, redemption—the money in  his  desk?
translation: I don't know who's had him arrested, but the man who arrested him is in prison-keeper uniform, that I can tell you. Will you send him his redemption, mistress—I mean the money in his desk?

original: Go fetch it, sister.
translation: Go get the money, sister.

original: Not on a bond, but on a stronger thing: A chain, a chain. Do you not hear it ring?
translation: Not on a bond but something stronger: a chain, a chain. Don't you hear it ring?

original: What, the chain?
translation: Hear what, the chain?

original: No, no, the bell. 'Tis time that I were gone. It was two ere I left him, and now the clock strikes  one.
The hours come back. That did I never hear.
translation: The hours go backwards. I've never heard of that happening before.

original: O yes, if any hour meet a sergeant, he turns back for  very fear.
translation: Oh, yes, if any hour runs into a cop, he goes backwards out of fear.

original: As if time were in debt. How fondly dost thou reason!
translation: As if time owed debts. How crazy your reasoning is!

original: Time is a very bankrupt and owes more than he’s worth  to   season.
translation: Time always owes major debt— he's always running out.

original: Nay, he’s a thief too. Have you not heard men say   That time comes stealing on by night and day?
translation: He's a thief too. Haven't you heard men say that times steals on by night and day?

original: If he be in debt and theft, and a sergeant in the way,   Hath he not reason to turn back an hour in a day?
translation: If he's in debt and a a thief, and there's a cop coming, doesn't he have good reason to turn back an hour?

original: Go, Dromio. There’s the money. Bear it straight, And bring thy master home immediately. Come, sister, I am pressed down with conceit: Conceit, my comfort and my injury.
translation: Go, Dromio. There's the money. Bring it right away, and bring your master home immediately. Come, sister, my imagination weighs on me: imagination, it both comforts me and hurts me.

original: There’s not a man I meet but doth salute me   As if I were their well-acquainted friend,   And every one doth call me by my name.
translation: Every man I meet salutes me as if I were a good friend, and everyone calls me by my name.

original: Some tender money to me; some invite me;   Some other give me thanks for kindnesses;   Some offer me commodities to buy.
translation: Some offer me money, some invite me over, some thank me for things I've done, some offer me things to buy.

original: Even now a tailor called me in his shop   And showed me silks that he had bought for me,   And therewithal took measure of my body.
translation: Just now a tailor called me into his shop and showed me silks that he had bought for me, and then took my measurements.

original: Sure, these are but imaginary wiles,   And lapland sorcerers inhabit here.
translation: These must all be deceitful tricks and all the residents must be sorcerers, like those from  Lapland .

original: Master, here’s The gold you sent me for. What, have you got redemption of the picture of old Adam  new-appareled?
What gold is this? What Adam dost thou mean?
translation: What gold are you talking about? What Adam do you mean?

original: Not that Adam that kept the Paradise, but that Adam  that keeps the prison;
translation: Not Adam who lived in the Garden of Eden, but Adam who runs the prison;

original: he that goes in the calf’s skin  that was killed for the Prodigal;
translation: he that wears the prison uniform that looks like the skin of the calf that was killed as a tribute to the Prodigal Son.

original: he that came behind  you, sir, like an evil angel, and bid you forsake your  liberty.
translation: The Adam who came behind you, sir, like an evil angel following you around, telling you to give up your freedom.

original: I understand thee not.
translation: I don't understand you.

original: No? Why, ’tis a plain case: he that went, like a bass  viol in a case of leather; the man, sir, that, when  gentlemen are tired, gives them a sob and ’rests them;
translation: You don't? Why, it's a straightforward case: this guy is like a big stringed instrument in a leather case. This man, sir, when gentlemen are tired, lets them pause and then arrests them.

original: he, sir, that takes pity on decayed men and gives them  suits of durance; he that sets up his rest to do more  exploits with his mace than a morris-pike.
translation: This man, sir, takes pity on ruined men and offers them long prison sentences. This man schedules his day, and he arrests people with his official mace rather than with a violent weapon.

original: What, thou meanest an officer?
translation: Huh? You mean an officer?

original: Ay, sir, the sergeant of the band; he that brings any  man to answer it that breaks his bond; one that thinks a man always going to bed and says “God give you good  rest.”
Well, sir, there rest in your foolery. Is there any  ships put forth tonight? May we be gone?
translation: Well, sir, stop being silly right there. Are there any ships leaving tonight? Can we get out of here?

original: Why, sir, I brought you word an hour since that the  bark  Expedition  put forth tonight, and then were you  hindered by the sergeant to tarry for the hoy  Delay  .  Here are the angels that you sent for to deliver you.
translation: Well, sir, I brought you news an hour ago that the ship Expedition left tonight, and then you were stopped by the sergeant before you could make it to the vessel called Delay. Here are the coins with the angel Michael's picture on them that you asked me to bring to you.

original: The fellow is distract, and so am I, And here we wander in illusions. Some blessed power deliver us from hence!
translation: The man is going nutty, and I am too, while we're wandering here surrounded by illusions. I hope some heavenly power gets us out of here.

original: Well met, well met, Master Antipholus. I see, sir, you have found the goldsmith now. Is that the chain you promised me today?
translation: Hey, hey, Master Antipholus. I see, sir, that you've found the goldsmith now. Is that the chain you promised me today?

original: Satan, avoid! I charge thee, tempt me not.
translation: Satan, get away from me! I command you, don't tempt me.

original: Master, is this Mistress Satan?
translation: Master, is this Mistress Satan?

original: It is the devil.
translation: She's the devil.

original: Nay, she is worse; she is the devil’s dam, and here she comes in the habit of a light wench.
translation: No, she's worse; she's the devil's mother, and she comes dressed as a loose woman.

original: And thereof comes  that the wenches say “God damn me” that’s as much to say “God make me a light wench.” It is written they appear  to men like angels of light.
translation: And that's why the women say "God  damn  me" which means "God make me a loose woman." It's written that these women look like angels of light when they appear to men.

original: Light is an effect of fire, and fire will burn: ergo, light wenches will burn. Come not near her.
translation: Light comes from fire, and fire burns: therefore, loose women will burn. Don't go near her.

original: Your man and you are marvelous merry, sir. Will you go with me? We’ll mend our dinner here.
translation: You and your servant are very jolly, sir. Will you go with me? We'll finish our dinner here.

original: Master, if you do, expect spoon meat; or bespeak a long spoon.
translation: Master, if you do, she'll feed you meat meant for a baby on a spoon; you'd better ask for a long spoon.

original: Why, Dromio?
translation: Why, Dromio?

original: Marry, he must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil.
translation: Oh, he who must eat with the devil must have a long spoon.

original: Avoid then, fiend! What tell’st thou me  of supping? Thou art, as you are all, a sorceress. I conjure thee to leave me and be gone.
translation: Get away then, demon! What are you saying to me about eating dinner? You are, as you all are here, a sorceress. I command you to leave me and vanish.

original: Give me the ring of mine you had at dinner Or, for my diamond, the chain you promised, And I’ll be gone, sir, and not trouble you.
translation: Give me the ring I gave you at dinner, or, in exchange for it, the chain you promised me, and I'll vanish, sir, and not bother you any more.

original: Some devils ask but the parings of one’s nail, a rush,  a hair, a drop of blood, a pin, a nut, a cherrystone;  but she, more covetous, would have a chain. Master, be  wise. An if you give it her, the devil will shake her  chain and fright us with it.
translation: Some devils only ask for nail clippings, some straw, a hair, a drop of blood, a pin, a nut, a cherry pit, but she's more greedy and wants a chain. Master, be wise. If you give it to her, the devil will shake her chain and frighten us with it.

original: I pray you, sir, my ring or else the chain. I hope you do not mean to cheat me so.
translation: I beg of you, sir, bring me my ring or otherwise bring the chain. I hope you don't mean to cheat me out of what I'm owed.

original: Avaunt, thou witch!—Come, Dromio, let us go.
translation: Get away, you witch!  Come, Dromio, let's go.

original: “Fly pride,” says the peacock. Mistress, that you know.
translation: "Stop being prideful," says the peacock. Mistress, you know all about creatures calling people out for their own sins.

original: Now, out of doubt Antipholus is mad;   Else would he never so demean himself.   A ring he hath of mine worth forty ducats,   And for the same he promised me a chain.
translation: Now, there's no question Antipholus is mad. There's no other reason he would humiliate himself like this. He took a ring of mine that was worth forty ducats, and he promised he'd give me a chain in exchange.

original: Both one and other he denies me now.   The reason that I gather he is mad,   Besides this present instance of his rage,   Is a mad tale he told today at dinner   Of his own doors being shut against his entrance.
translation: He's denying me both of them now. What's led me to think he is mad, besides seeing his rage just now, is the crazy story he told me today at dinner of how his own doors were shut when he tried to enter.

original: Belike his wife, acquainted with his fits,   On purpose shut the doors against his way.   My way is now to hie home to his house   And tell his wife that, being lunatic,   He rushed into my house and took perforce   My ring away.
translation: It's possible his wife, knowing his fits well, purposefully locked the door on him. Now I'm going to hurry to his house and tell his wife that he's become a lunatic and rushed into my house and stole my ring.

original: This course I fittest choose,   For forty ducats is too much to lose.
translation: This is the best course I can take, since forty ducats is too much to lose.

original: Fear me not, man. I will not break away:   I’ll give thee, ere I leave thee, so much money,   To warrant thee, as I am ’rested for.
translation: Don't be afraid of me, man. I won't try to flee: I'll give you, before I go, as much money as you've arrested me for, I assure you.

original: My wife is in a wayward mood today   And will not lightly trust the messenger   That I should be attached in Ephesus.
translation: My wife is not in a good mood today and she won't calmly accept the messenger's news that I've been arrested in Ephesus.

original: I tell you, ’twill sound harshly in her ears.
translation: I'm telling you, it will be upsetting news for her to hear.

original: Here’s that, I warrant you, will pay them all.
But where’s the money?
translation: But where's the money?

original: Why, sir, I gave the money for the rope.
translation: Why, sir, I paid the money for the rope.

original: Five hundred ducats, villain, for a rope?
translation: You paid five hundred ducats, you villain, for a rope?

original: I’ll serve you, sir, five hundred at the rate.
translation: I'll get you five hundred ropes for five hundred ducats, sir.

original: To what end did I bid thee hie thee home?
To a rope’s end, sir, and to that end am I returned.
translation: To bring you a rope's end, sir, and, with that end in mind, I've returned.

original: And to that end, sir, I will welcome you.  [beats DROMIO OF EPHESUS]
translation: Well, to make an end of it, sir, I'll welcome you.

original: Good sir, be patient.
translation: Good sir, be patient.

original: Nay, ’tis for me to be patient. I am in adversity.
translation: I'm the one who needs to be patient. I'm being attacked.

original: Good now, hold thy tongue.
translation: All right, all right, hold your tongue.

original: Nay, rather persuade him to hold his hands.
translation: No, tell him to hold his hands instead.

original: Thou whoreson, senseless villain.
translation: You scumbag villain with no sense!

original: I would I were senseless, sir, that I might not feel  your blows.
translation: I wish I had no senses, sir, so I didn't have to feel this beating.

original: Thou art sensible in nothing but blows, and so is an  ass.
translation: You're not smart enough to feel anything but beating, just like an ass.

original: I am an ass, indeed; you may prove it by my long  ears.—I have served him from the hour of my nativity to  this instant, and have nothing at his hands for my  service but blows.
translation: I'm an ass, indeed. You can prove that from my long  ears —I have served my master from the hour I was born until this moment, and I've had no reward from him but beatings.

original: When I am cold, he heats me with  beating; when I am warm, he cools me with beating. I am  waked with it when I sleep, raised with it when I sit,  driven out of doors with it when I go from home,  welcomed home with it when I return.
translation: When I'm cold, he heats me with beating. When I am warm, he cools me with beating. I'm woken up by beatings when I go to sleep, stood up by beatings when I sit down, thrown out the door with beatings when I'm leaving the house, and welcomed back home with beatings when I return.

original: Nay, I bear it on  my shoulders as a beggar wont her brat, and I think when he hath lamed me, I shall beg with it from door to  door.
translation: No, I carry beatings on my shoulders like a beggar carries her baby, and I think when he's crippled me, I'll beg just like that from door to door.

original: Come, go along. My wife is coming yonder.
translation: Come on, let's go. My wife is approaching.

original: Mistress,  respice finem,  respect your end, or rather,  the prophecy like the parrot, “Beware the rope’s end.”
translation: Mistress, respice finem, respect your end, or, I should say, like a parrot that's learned to make prophecies, "Beware the rope's end."

original: Wilt thou still talk?
translation: Are you going to go on talking?

original: How say you now? Is not your husband mad?
translation: What do you say now? Is your husband not crazy?

original: His incivility confirms no less.— Good Doctor Pinch, you are a conjurer; Establish him in his true sense again, And I will please you what you will demand.
translation: His wild behavior makes me think so. Good Doctor Pinch, you are a magician. Put him back to normal, and I'll give you anything you ask for.

original: Alas, how fiery and how sharp he looks!
translation: Oh no, how angry and nasty he looks!

original: Mark how he trembles in his ecstasy.
translation: Notice how he shakes in his fit.

original: Give me your hand, and let me feel your pulse.
translation: Give me your hand, and let me feel your pulse.

original: There is my hand, and let it feel your ear.  [strikes  PINCH]
translation: Here is my hand, and now feel it on your ear.

original: I charge thee, Satan, housed within this man,   To yield possession to my holy prayers   And to thy state of darkness hie thee straight.
translation: Satan, you are possessing this man's spirit, and I command you to be defeated by my prayers and get back to hell.

original: I conjure thee by all the saints in heaven.
translation: I summon you out of this man's body by all the saints in heaven.

original: Peace, doting wizard, peace. I am not mad.
translation: Calm down, you loony wizard, calm down. I am not crazy.

original: O, that thou wert not, poor distressèd soul!
translation: Oh, if only you weren't, poor, distressed man!

original: You minion, you, are these your customers?
translation: You wicked woman, you, did you bring these people?

original: Did this companion with the saffron face   Revel and feast it at my house today   Whilst upon me the guilty doors were shut   And I denied to enter in my house?
translation: Did this man here with the orange face feast at my house yesterday while the doors were shut on me and I was barred from entering my own house?

original: O husband, God doth know you dined at home, Where would you had remained until this time, Free from these slanders and this open shame.
translation: Oh, husband, God knows you ate at home, where I wish you still were, free from these accusations and this public humiliation.

original: “Dined at home”? Thou villain, what sayest thou?
translation: "Ate at home"?  You villain, what do you say to that?

original: Sir, sooth to say, you did not dine at home.
translation: Sir, what you say is true, you did not eat at home.

original: Were not my doors locked up and I shut out?
translation: Weren't my doors locked up and wasn't I shut out?

original: Perdie, your doors were locked, and you shut out.
translation: I swear, your doors were locked and you were shut out.

original: And did not she herself revile me there?
translation: And didn't my wife herself attack me there?

original: Sans fable, she herself reviled you there.
translation: It's not a fiction, she herself attacked you there.

original: Did not her kitchen maid rail, taunt, and scorn me?
translation: Didn't her kitchen maid yell, taunt, and mock me?

original: Certes, she did; the kitchen vestal scorned you.
translation: Certainly, she did; the kitchen maid mocked you.

original: And did not I in rage depart from thence?
translation: And didn't I depart in rage from there?

original: In verity you did.—My bones bear witness, That since have felt the vigour of his rage.
translation: In truth, you did. My bruised bones are proof of that, since they felt the violence of his rage.

original: Is’t good to soothe him in these contraries?
translation: Is it healthy to go along with his falsehoods?

original: It is no shame. The fellow finds his vein And, yielding to him, humors well his frenzy.
Thou hast suborned the goldsmith to arrest me.
translation: You have hired the goldsmith to arrest me.

original: Alas, I sent you money to redeem you By Dromio here, who came in haste for it.
translation: No, I only sent you bail money with Dromio, who had come running for it.

original: Money by me! heart and goodwill you might, But surely, master, not a rag of money.
translation: Money from me! Thoughts and prayers maybe. But, I swear, master, not a piece of money.

original: Went’st not thou to her for a purse of ducats?
translation: Did you not go to her for a bag of ducats?

original: He came to me, and I delivered it.
translation: He came to me and I gave the money to him.

original: And I am witness with her that she did.
translation: And I was there and saw her give it.

original: God and the rope-maker bear me witness That I was sent for nothing but a rope.
translation: God and the rope-maker alone know that I was sent to get nothing but a rope.

original: Mistress, both man and master is possessed.
translation: [To ADRIANA]   Dear lady, both this man and his master are possessed.

original: I know it by their pale and deadly looks.
translation: I know that from their pale and angry looks.

original: They must be bound and laid in some dark room.
translation: They must be tied up and left in a dark room somewhere.

original: Say wherefore didst thou lock me forth  today.     And why dost thou deny the bag  of gold?
translation: Tell me why you locked me out today.

original: I did not, gentle husband, lock thee forth.
translation: I did not, gentle husband, lock you out.

original: And, gentle master, I received no gold. But I confess, sir, that we were locked out.
translation: And, gentle master, I received no gold. But I admit, sir, that we were locked out.

original: Dissembling villain, thou speak’st false in both.
translation: Deceitful villain, both of these are lies.

original: Dissembling harlot, thou art false in all,   And art confederate with a damnèd pack   To make a loathsome abject scorn of me.
translation: Deceitful woman, all you've said is lies, and you're in cahoots with a cursed mob to make a disgraced mockery of me.

original: But with these nails I’ll pluck out these false eyes   That would behold in me this shameful sport.
translation: But I'll use my nails to pluck out your lying eyes that want to see me humiliated.

original: O bind him, bind him! Let him not come near me.
translation: Oh, tie him up, tie him up! Don't let him come near me.

original: More company! The fiend is strong within him.
translation: We need backup! The demon is strong inside him.

original: Ay me, poor man, how pale and wan he looks!
translation: Oh, God, poor man, how pale and weak he looks!

original: What, will you murder me?—Thou jailer, thou, I am thy prisoner. Wilt thou suffer them To make a rescue?
translation: What, will you murder me? You jailer, you, I'm already your prisoner. Will you allow them to steal me away?

original: Masters, let him go. He is my prisoner, and you shall not have him.
translation: Gentlemen, let him go. He's my prisoner, and you shall not have him.

original: Go, bind this man, for he is frantic too.
translation: Go, tie up this man, for he is crazy too.

original: What wilt thou do, thou peevish officer? Hast thou delight to see a wretched man Do outrage and displeasure to himself?
translation: What will you do, you obstinate officer? Do you take pleasure in seeing a disgraced man harm and embarrass himself?

original: He is my prisoner. If I let him go, The debt he owes will be required of me.
translation: He's my prisoner. If I let him go, I'll have to pay the debt that he owes.

original: I will discharge thee ere I go from thee. Bear me forthwith unto his creditor, And, knowing how the debt grows, I will pay it.— Good Master Doctor, see him safe conveyed Home to my house. O most unhappy day!
translation: I will pay you that debt before I leave you. Bring me immediately to the person he owes, and, when I hear how much the debt is, I'll pay it.  Good Doctor, make sure he's conveyed safely home to my house. Oh, what an awful day!

original: O most unhappy strumpet!
translation: Oh, what an awful woman!

original: Master, I am here entered in bond for you.
translation: Master, I'm tied up here because of you.

original: Out on thee, villain! Wherefore dost thou mad me?
translation: Shut up, villain! Why do you keep annoying me?

original: Will you be bound for nothing? Be mad, good master. Cry “The devil!”
translation: Will you be tied up and not resist? Be crazy, master. Cry, "The devil!"

original: God help poor souls! How idly do they talk!
translation: God help poor souls! They talk a lot of nothing!

original: Go bear him hence. Sister, go you with me.
translation: Go bring him to my house. Sister, come with me.

original: One Angelo, a goldsmith. Do you know him?
translation: A man named Angelo, a goldsmith. Do you know him?

original: I know the man. What is the sum he owes?
translation: I know the man. How much does he owe?

original: Two hundred ducats.
translation: Two hundred ducats.

original: Say, how grows it due?
translation: What does he owe it for?

original: Due for a chain your husband had of him.
translation: It's for a chain your husband bought from him.

original: He did bespeak a chain for me but had it not.
translation: He did mention a chain for me, but he didn't have it.

original: Whenas your husband all in rage today Came to my house and took away my ring, The ring I saw upon his finger now, Straight after did I meet him with a chain.
translation: When your husband angrily today came to my house and took away my ring, the ring I saw him wearing on his finger now, I met him right after that and he had a chain.

original: It may be so, but I did never see it.— Come, jailer, bring me where the goldsmith is. I long to know the truth hereof at large.
translation: That may be true, but I never saw it.  Come, jailer, bring me to where the goldsmith is. I'd love to know the truth of this story finally.

original: God for Thy mercy, they are loose again!
translation: Oh my God, they're loose again!

original: And come with naked swords. Let’s call more help To have them bound again.
translation: And they've come with their swords drawn. Let's call for reinforcements to tie them up again.

original: Away! They’ll kill us.
translation: Get out of here! They'll kill us.

original: I see these witches are afraid of swords.
She that would be your wife now ran from you.
translation: The woman who claims she's your wife runs away from you now.

original: Come to the Centaur. Fetch our stuff from thence. I long that we were safe and sound aboard.
translation: Go to the Centaur. Get our stuff from there. I wish we were safe and sound onboard the ship.

original: Faith, stay here this night. They will surely do us no  harm.
translation: Please, stay here tonight. They surely won't hurt us.

original: You saw they speak us fair, give us gold.
translation: You saw they said nice things to us and gave us gold.

original: Methinks they are such a gentle nation that, but for the  mountain of mad flesh that claims marriage of me, i  could find in my heart to stay here still, and turn  witch.
translation: I think they're such a nice people that, if it weren't for the mountain of fat that says I'm supposed to marry her, I would love to stay here longer, and become a witch myself.

original: I will not stay tonight for all the town. Therefore away, to get our stuff aboard.
translation: I would not stay here tonight even if they gave me the whole town. So go and get our stuff on the ship.

original: I am sorry, sir, that I have hindered you, But I protest he had the chain of me, Though most dishonestly he doth deny it.
translation: I'm sorry, sir, to have delayed you, but I promise he took the chain from me, even though he dishonestly denies it.

original: How is the man esteemed here in the city?
translation: What's the man's reputation here in the city?

original: Of very reverend reputation, sir, Of credit infinite, highly beloved, Second to none that lives here in the city. His word might bear my wealth at any time.
translation: He's very well respected, sir, and trusted and beloved by all. He's second to none that lives here in the city. I'd bet all my money on his telling the truth at any time.

original: Speak softly. Yonder, as I think, he walks.
translation: Speak softly. I think he's walking this way.

original: 'Tis so; and that self chain about his neck   Which he forswore most monstrously to have.   Good sir, draw near to me. I’ll speak to him.—

Signior Antipholus, I wonder much   That you would put me to this shame and trouble,   And not without some scandal to yourself,   With circumstance and oaths so to deny   This chain, which now you wear so openly.
translation: Antipholus, sir, I'm dumbfounded that you would put me to all this shame and trouble, and scandalize yourself in the process, swearing up and down that you didn't have the chain which you're wearing so openly.

original: Beside the charge, the shame, imprisonment,   You have done wrong to this my honest friend,   Who, but for staying on our controversy,   Had hoisted sail and put to sea today.   This chain you had of me. Can you deny it?
translation: Besides the cost, the shame, and getting sent to prison, you've done wrong to my honest friend here, who was supposed to set sail today if it weren't for your shenanigans. You got this chain from me. Can you deny it?

original: I think I had. I never did deny it.
translation: I think I got it from you. I never did deny it.

original: Yes, that you did, sir, and forswore it too.
translation: Yes, you did deny it, sir, and swore you never had it, too.

original: Who heard me to deny it or forswear it?
translation: Who heard me deny and swear it?

original: These ears of mine, thou know’st did hear thee. Fie on thee, wretch. 'Tis pity that thou liv’st To walk where any honest men resort.
translation: You know my ears heard you. Damn you, wretch. You shouldn't be allowed to walk in the same vicinity as honest men.

original: Thou art a villain to impeach me thus. I’ll prove mine honor and mine honesty Against thee presently if thou dar’st stand.
translation: You're a villain to accuse me like this. I'll prove my honor and my honesty against you right now, if you'll dare to fight me.

original: I dare, and do defy thee for a villain.
translation: I dare, and I'll defeat you, you villain.

original: Hold, hurt him not, for God’s sake. He is mad.— Some get within him; take his sword away. Bind dromio too, and bear them to my house!
translation: Stop, don't hurt him, for God's sake. He's mad. Someone go to him and take his sword away. Tie up Dromio too and bring them to my house!

original: Run, master, run. For God’s sake, take a house. This is some priory. In, or we are spoiled.
translation: Run, master run. For God's sake, enter some house. Here's a nunnery. Get in, or we'll be ruined.

original: Be quiet, people. Wherefore throng you hither?
translation: Be quiet, people. What are you all doing here?

original: To fetch my poor distracted husband hence. Let us come in, that we may bind him fast And bear him home for his recovery.
translation: We're here to get my poor, mad husband. Let us come in, so we can tie him up and bring him home where he can recover.

original: I knew he was not in his perfect wits.
translation: I knew he wasn't in his right mind.

original: I am sorry now that I did draw on him.
translation: I'm sorry now that I drew my sword on him.

original: How long hath this possession held the man?
translation: How long has this man been mad?

original: This week he hath been heavy, sour, sad, And much different from the man he was. But till this afternoon his passion Ne'er brake into extremity of rage.
translation: This week he's been moody, sour, sad, and very different from the man he was. But until this afternoon his mood had never turned into extreme rage.

original: Hath he not lost much wealth by wrack of sea?
translation: Has he not lost a lot of money in a shipwreck?

original: Buried some dear friend? Hath not else his eye   Stray’d his affection in unlawful love,   A sin prevailing much in youthful men   Who give their eyes the liberty of gazing?
translation: Buried a dear friend? Has his eye not led him to think of infidelity? That's a sin that a lot of youthful men commit when they allow themselves to stare at women.

original: Which of these sorrows is he subject to?
translation: Which of these sorrows is weighing on him?

original: To none of these, except it be the last, Namely, some love that drew him oft from home.
translation: None of them, unless it's the last. Namely, some love that drew him often away from home.

original: You should for that have reprehended him.
translation: You should have scolded him for that.

original: Why, so I did.
translation: I did.

original: Ay, but not rough enough.
translation: Yes, but not roughly enough.

original: As roughly as my modesty would let me.
translation: As roughly as my modesty would let me.

original: Haply in private.
translation: Maybe in private.

original: And in assemblies too.
translation: And publicly too.

original: Ay, but not enough.
translation: Okay, but not enough.

original: It was the copy of our conference.   In bed he slept not for my urging it;
translation: We had this conversation all the time. He wouldn't sleep in our bed when I told him to.

original: At board he fed not for my urging it.   Alone, it was the subject of my theme;
translation: He wouldn't eat at our table when I told him too. When we were alone, it was the only think I talked about.

original: In company I often glancèd it.   Still did I tell him it was vile and bad.
translation: When were with other people, I referred to it in passing. I told him over and over it was vile and bad.

original: And thereof came it that the man was mad.   The venom clamors of a jealous woman   Poisons more deadly than a mad dog’s tooth.
translation: And that's how the man went mad. The venom of a jealous woman's nagging has more poison in it than a mad dog's tooth.

original: It seems his sleeps were hinder’d by thy railing,   And therefore comes it that his head is light.
translation: It sounds like he couldn't sleep because of your railing at him, so he went crazy.

original: Thou sayst his meat was sauced with thy upbraidings.   Unquiet meals make ill digestions.
translation: You say you poured your scoldings on his dinner like meat sauce. Meals accompanied by fighting lead to bad digestion.

original: Thereof the raging fire of fever bred,   And what’s a fever but a fit of madness?
translation: That's how he got this raging fever, and aren't fevers and fits of madness one and the same?

original: Thou sayest his sports were hinderd by thy brawls.   Sweet recreation barred, what doth ensue   But moody and dull melancholy,   Kinsman to grim and comfortless despair,   And at her heels a huge infectious troop   Of pale distemperatures and foes to life?
translation: You say all his relaxation time was ruined by your fights. Without time for sweet recreation, what's going to happen but moody and dull melancholy, which leads to grim and comfortless despair, and right after that a whole army of illnesses and humoral imbalances that put his life in danger.

original: In food, in sport, and life-preserving rest   To be disturbed, would mad or man or beast.   The consequence is, then, thy jealous fits   Have scared thy husband from the use of wits.
translation: Any man or animal would go mad if he was disturbed while he was eating, sporting, and trying to get his much-needed sleep. The consequence is that your jealous fits have cost your husband his sanity.

original: She never reprehended him but mildly When he demeaned himself rough, rude, and wildly.—     Why bear you these rebukes and answer not?
translation: She only ever scolded him mildly when he behaved rough, rude, and wildly. Why aren't you responding to these insults?

original: She did betray me to my own reproof. Good people, enter and lay hold on him.
translation: I think I deserved those reprimands. Good people, enter and get him.

original: No, not a creature enters in my house.
translation: No, no one enters my house.

original: Then let your servants bring my husband forth.
translation: Then let your servants bring my husband out.

original: Neither: he took this place for sanctuary, And it shall privilege him from your hands Till I have brought him to his wits again Or lose my labor in assaying it.
translation: Not a chance. He chose my nunnery for sanctuary, and so he'll stay out of your hands until I restore his sanity or die trying.

original: I will attend my husband, be his nurse, Diet his sickness, for it is my office And will have no attorney but myself; And therefore let me have him home with me.
translation: I'll take care of my husband, be his nurse, and treat his sickness, for it's my job, and no one will else can do it for me. Therefore, let me bring him home with me.

original: Be patient, for I will not let him stir   Till I have used the approvd means I have,   With wholesome syrups, drugs, and holy prayers,   To make of him a formal man again.
translation: Be patient, for I won't let him stir until I've used the syrups, drugs, and holy prayers that I have to make him come to his senses. It's part of my oath as abbess.

original: It is a branch and parcel of mine oath,   A charitable duty of my order.   Therefore depart and leave him here with me.
translation: It's a charitable duty of my holy order. Therefore, depart and leave him here with me.

original: I will not hence and leave my husband here; And ill it doth beseem your holiness To separate the husband and the wife.
translation: I will not go and leave my husband here. It looks bad for an abbess to separate a husband and wife.

original: Be quiet and depart. Thou shalt not have him.
translation: Be quite and depart. You shall not have him.

original: Complain unto the Duke of this indignity.
translation: Complain to the Duke about this rudeness.

original: Come, go. I will fall prostrate at his feet And never rise until my tears and prayers Have won his grace to come in person hither And take perforce my husband from the Abbess.
translation: Come, let's go. I will fall at his feet and I won't get up until my tears and prayers have persuaded him to come in person here and take my husband from the Abbess by force.

original: By this, I think, the dial points at five. Anon, I’m sure, the Duke himself in person Comes this way to the melancholy vale, The place of death and sorry execution Behind the ditches of the abbey here.
translation: I think it's five o'clock. The Duke will surely come this way in person to the melancholy place where executions are carried out behind the abbey here.

original: Upon what cause?
translation: For what reason?

original: To see a reverend Syracusian merchant, Who put unluckily into this bay Against the laws and statutes of this town, Beheaded publicly for his offense.
translation: To see an old merchant from Syracuse, who unluckily sailed into this bay against the town laws, publicly beheaded for this offense.

original: See where they come. We will behold his death.
translation: Look, they're coming. We'll watch his death.

original: Kneel to the duke before he pass the abbey.
translation: Kneel to the Duke before he passes the abbey.

original: Yet once again proclaim it publicly, If any friend will pay the sum for him, He shall not die; so much we tender him.
translation: Yet once again I'll say it publicly: if any friend will pay his ransom, he shall not die. That's how much we care for him.

original: Justice, most sacred duke, against the Abbess.
translation: Justice, most sacred Duke, against the Abbess.

original: She is a virtuous and a reverend lady. It cannot be that she hath done thee wrong.
translation: She's a virtuous and respected lady. It can't be true that she's done you wrong.

original: May it please your Grace, Antipholus my husband,   Whom I made lord of me and all I had   At your important letters, this ill day   A most outrageous fit of madness took him,
translation: Your Grace, I married my husband Antipholus and gave everything I had to him on your instructions, and, this sad day, he's been overcome by a terrible fit of madness.

original: That desp'rately he hurried through the street,   With him his bondman, all as mad as he,   Doing displeasure to the citizens   By rushing in their houses, bearing thence   Rings, jewels, any thing his rage did like.
translation: He ran desperately through the street, with his servant, equally mad, upsetting all the citizens by rushing into their houses, stealing rings, jewels, anything that caught his crazed fancy.

original: Once did I get him bound and sent him home   Whilst to take order for the wrongs I went   That here and there his fury had committed.
translation: I had him tied up and sent home while I went to deal with all the wrongs he'd committed in his fury.

original: Anon, I wot not by what strong escape,   He broke from those that had the guard of him,   And with his mad attendant and himself,   Each one with ireful passion, with drawn swords,   Met us again and, madly bent on us,   Chased us away, till, raising of more aid,   We came again to bind them.
translation: I don't know how he then escaped, but he broke away from the men that were guarding him, and he and his mad servant, both of them furiously wielding swords, ran into us again and, charging right at us, chased us away until we found reinforcements and came back to tie them up.

original: Then they fled   Into this abbey, whither we pursued them,   And here the Abbess shuts the gates on us   And will not suffer us to fetch him out,   Nor send him forth that we may bear him hence.
translation: Then they fled into this abbey, where we pursued them, and now the Abbess has shut the gates on us and won't let us fetch him out or send him out herself that we can take him away.

original: Therefore, most gracious duke, with thy command   Let him be brought forth and borne hence for help.
translation: Therefore, most gracious Duke, command that he brought out of the abbey and taken away for help.

original: Long since thy husband served me in my wars,   And I to thee engaged a prince’s word,   When thou didst make him master of thy bed,   To do him all the grace and good I could.
translation: Long ago, your husband served me in my wars, and I gave you a prince's word, when you married him, to do him all the good I could.

original: Go, some of you, knock at the abbey gate,   And bid the Lady Abbess come to me.   I will determine this before I stir.
translation: Go, some of you, knock at the abbey gate, and tell the Lady Abbess to come to me. I won't move until I've cleared this up.

original: O mistress, mistress, shift and save yourself.   My master and his man are both broke loose,   Beaten the maids a-row, and bound the doctor,   Whose beard they have singed off with brands of fire,   And ever as it blazed, they threw on him   Great pails of puddled mire to quench the hair.
translation: Oh, mistress, mistress, do what you can to save yourself. My master and his servant have broken free, beaten the maids and tied up the doctor, whose beard they burned off, and, while his beard was blazing, threw mud on him to put out the fire.

original: My master preaches patience to him, and the while   His man with scissors nicks him like a fool;   And sure, unless you send some present help,   Between them they will kill the conjurer.
translation: My master urges him to be patient while his servant cuts the doctor's beard with scissors to make him look like a fool. Surely, unless you send someone to help, they'll kill the doctor between them.

original: Peace, fool. Thy master and his man are here, And that is false thou dost report to us.
translation: Calm down, fool. Your master and his servant are here, and what you've told us is false.

original: Mistress, upon my life I tell you true. I have not breathed almost since I did see it. He cries for you, and vows, if he can take you, To scorch your face and to disfigure you.
translation: Mistress, upon my life, I'm telling the truth. I've barely breathed since I saw it. He cries for you, and vows, if he can catch you, to burn your face and disfigure you.

original: Come, stand by me. Fear nothing.—Guard with halberds.
translation: Come, stand by me. Fear nothing. Guard her with spears.

original: Ay me, it is my husband. Witness you That he is borne about invisible. Even now we housed him in the abbey here, And now he’s there, past thought of human reason.
translation: Oh my God, it's my husband. Everyone see that he travels invisibly. We just saw him go into the abbey here, and now he's there. It's beyond reason.

original: Justice, most gracious duke, O, grant me justice,   Even for the service that long since I did thee   When I bestrid thee in the wars and took   Deep scars to save thy life.
translation: Justice, most gracious Duke. Oh, grant me justice, if only for the service that I performed for you long ago when I fought for you in the wars and received deep wounds to save your life.

original: Even for the blood   That then I lost for thee, now grant me justice.
translation: I f only for the blood that I lost for you then, grant me justice now.

original: Unless the fear of death doth make me dote, I see my son Antipholus and Dromio.
translation: Unless the fear of death has driven me mad, I see my son Antipholus and Dromio.

original: Justice, sweet prince, against that woman there,   She whom thou gav’st to me to be my wife,   That hath abusèd and dishonored me   Even in the strength and height of injury.
translation: Give me justice, sweet prince, against that woman there, she whom you gave to me to be my wife. She has abused and dishonored me more than could be thought possible.

original: Beyond imagination is the wrong   That she this day hath shameless thrown on me.
translation: It's beyond imagination how shamelessly she's wronged me.

original: Discover how, and thou shalt find me just.
translation: Explain what you mean, and you'll find me just.

original: This day, great duke, she shut the doors upon me While she with harlots feasted in my house.
translation: Today, great Duke, she locked the doors on me while she feasted with ruffians in my house.

original: A grievous fault.—Say, woman, didst thou so?
translation: That's very bad.  Say, woman, did you do that?

original: No, my good lord. Myself, he, and my sister Today did dine together. So befall my soul As this is false he burdens me withal.
translation: No, my good lord. Myself, my husband, and my sister dined together today. I wager my soul that what he accuses me of is false.

original: Ne'er may I look on day, nor sleep on night But she tells to your Highness simple truth.
translation: Never shall I see daylight again or sleep at night if what she tells your Highness isn't true.

original: O perjured woman! —They are both forsworn. In this the madman justly chargeth them.
translation: Oh, slandering woman! They have both sworn falsely. The madman's right in accusing them of that.

original: My liege, I am advisèd what I say,   Neither disturbed with the effect of wine,   Nor heady-rash, provoked with raging ire,   Albeit my wrongs might make one wiser mad.
translation: My lord, I am sure in what I say, neither intoxicated nor mad, provoked with fury, although what's been done to me might make a wiser man go insane.

original: This woman locked me out this day from dinner.   That goldsmith there, were he not packed with her,   Could witness it, for he was with me then,   Who parted with me to go fetch a chain,   Promising to bring it to the Porpentine,   Where Balthasar and I did dine together.
translation: This woman locked me out today from dinner. That goldsmith there, if he wasn't in cahoots with her, could attest to it, since he was with me then. He parted with me to go fetch a chain, promising to bring it to the Porpentine, where I dined with Balthasar.

original: Our dinner done and he not coming thither,   I went to seek him. In the street I met him,   And in his company that gentleman.
