translation: After our dinner, the goldsmith hadn't come yet so I went to seek him. In the street I met him, and he was with this gentleman.

original: There did this perjured goldsmith swear me down   That I this day of him received the chain,   Which, God he knows, I saw not; for the which   He did arrest me with an officer.
translation: There, this lying goldsmith swore that I took the chain from him, which, God knows, I never saw. With this accusation, he arrested me with an officer.

original: I did obey, and sent my peasant home   For certain ducats. He with none returned.   Then fairly I bespoke the officer   To go in person with me to my house.
translation: I obeyed and sent my servant home for money. He came back with nothing. Then I calmly told the officer to come with me to my house.

original: By th' way we met   My wife, her sister, and a rabble more   Of vile confederates. Along with them   They brought one Pinch, a hungry, lean-faced villain,   A mere anatomy, a mountebank,   A threadbare juggler, and a fortune-teller,   A needy, hollow-eyed, sharp-looking wretch,   A living dead man.
translation: On the way, we met my wife, her sister, and a crowd of their vile friends. Along with them they brought someone named Pinch, a hungry, thin villain, a mere skeleton, a quack doctor, a poor magician, and a fortune-teller, a hollow-eyed, gaunt wretch, a living dead man.

original: This pernicious slave,   Forsooth, took on him as a conjurer,   And, gazing in mine eyes, feeling my pulse,   And with no face (as ’twere) outfacing me,   Cries out I was possessed.
translation: This awful rascal pretended to be a conjurer, gazed in my eyes, felt my pulse, and, with his thin face looking into mine, cried out I was possessed.

original: Then all together   They fell upon me, bound me, bore me thence,   And in a dark and dankish vault at home   There left me and my man, both bound together,   Till gnawing with my teeth my bonds in sunder,   I gained my freedom and immediately   Ran hither to your Grace, whom I beseech   To give me ample satisfaction   For these deep shames and great indignities.
translation: Then all together they fell upon me, tied me up, took me away, and in a dark and foul cell at home left me and my servant, tied together, till I'd gnawed the ropes apart with my teeth, gaining my freedom. I immediately ran here to your Grace, whom I plead will deliver justice to me for these deep shames and great indignities.

original: My lord, in truth, thus far I witness with him: That he dined not at home, but was locked out.
translation: My lord, in truth, I can back him up that he didn't dine at home but was locked out.

original: But had he such a chain of thee or no?
translation: But did he have this chain from you or not?

original: He had, my lord, and when he ran in here, These people saw the chain about his neck.
translation: He had, my lord, and when he ran in here, these people saw the chain around his neck.

original: Besides, I will be sworn these ears of mine Heard you confess you had the chain of him After you first forswore it on the mart, And thereupon I drew my sword on you, And then you fled into this abbey here, From whence I think you are come by miracle.
translation: Besides, I'll be sworn I heard you confess you had the chain from him after you first denied it in the marketplace, and then I drew my sword on you, and then you fled into this abbey here. I think you've come from there by a miracle.

original: I never came within these abbey walls, Nor ever didst thou draw thy sword on me. I never saw the chain, so help me heaven, And this is false you burden me withal.
translation: I never went inside the abbey nor did you ever draw your sword on me. I never saw the chain, I swear to God, and you accuse me falsely.

original: Why, what an intricate impeach is this! I think you all have drunk of Circe’s cup. If here you housed him, here he would have been. If he were mad, he would not plead so coldly.     You say he dined at home; the goldsmith  here Denies that saying. Sirrah, what say you?
translation: Why, what a complex case this is! I think you've all drunk some magical potion. If you saw him enter here, he would be in here. If he were mad, he wouldn't plead so logically.  You say he dined at home. The goldsmith here denies that. Sir, what do you say?

original: Sir, he dined with her there, at the Porpentine.
translation: Sir, he dined with her there, at the Porpentine.

original: He did, and from my finger snatched that ring.
translation: He did, and snatched that ring from my finger.

original: 'Tis true, my liege; this ring I had of her.
translation: That's true, my lord. I took this ring from her.

original: Saw’st thou him enter at the abbey here?
translation: Did you see him enter the abbey here?

original: As sure, my liege, as I do see your Grace.
translation: As sure, my Lord, as I see you now.

original: Why, this is strange.—Go call the Abbess hither. I think you are all mated or stark mad.
translation: Well, this is strange. Go tell the Abbess to come out. I think you're all confused or totally crazy.

original: Most mighty duke, vouchsafe me speak a word. Haply I see a friend will save my life And pay the sum that may deliver me.
translation: Most mighty Duke, allow me to say a word. Happily, I see a friend who will save my life and pay the ransom to free me.

original: Speak freely, Syracusian, what thou wilt.
translation: Speek freely whatever you want to say, Syracusian.

original: Is not your name, sir,  called Antipholus? And is not that your bondman Dromio?
translation: Sir, isn't your name Antipholus? And is that not your bondman Dromio?

original: Within this hour I was his bondman sir, But he, I thank him, gnawed in two my cords. Now am I Dromio, and his man, unbound.
I am sure you both of you remember me.
translation: I am sure both of you remember me.

original: Ourselves we do remember, sir, by you. For lately we were bound as you are now. You are not Pinch’s patient, are you, sir?
translation: You remind us of ourselves, sir. Recently, we were bound as you are now. You're not Doctor Pinch's patient, are you, sir?

original: Why look you strange on me? you know me well.
translation: Why do you look at me like I'm a stranger? You know me well.

original: I never saw you in my life till now.
translation: I never saw you in my life till now.

original: O, grief hath changed me since you saw me last, And careful hours with time’s deformèd hand Have written strange defeatures in my face. But tell me yet, dost thou not know my voice?
translation: Oh, I've been changed by grief since you last saw me. The deforming hand of time, over many stressful hours, has scarred my face with wrinkles. Tell me, though, do you not know my voice?

original: Neither.
translation: Not your voice either.

original: Dromio, nor thou?
translation: Dromio, you don't either?

original: No, trust me, sir, nor I.
translation: No trust me, sir, I don't either.

original: I am sure thou dost.
translation: I am sure you do.

original: Ay, sir, but I am sure I do not, and whatsoever a man  denies, you are now bound to believe him.
Not know my voice! O time’s extremity,   Hast thou so crack’d and splitted my poor tongue   In seven short years that here my only son   Knows not my feeble key of untuned cares?
translation: Not know my voice! Oh,  time's extremity , have you so damaged and split my poor tongue in seven short years that my only son here doesn't recognize my feeble  voice badly singing its woes ?

original: Though now this grainèd face of mine be hid   In sap-consuming winter’s drizzled snow,   And all the conduits of my blood froze up,   Yet hath my night of life some memory,   My wasting lamps some fading glimmer left,   My dull deaf ears a little use to hear.
translation: Though this wrinkled face of mine is hidden in my white beard and all my veins have frozen, even in my final days, I still have some memory, my wavering eyes can still see a fading glimmer, and my dull, deaf ears can still hear a little.

original: All these old witnesses—I cannot err—   Tell me thou art my son Antipholus.
translation: All these  old witnesses —they don't deceive me— tell me the you are my son Antipholus.

original: I never saw my father in my life.
translation: I never saw my father in my life.

original: But seven years since, in Syracusa, boy, Thou know’st we parted. But perhaps, my son, Thou sham’st to acknowledge me in misery.
translation: But you know we parted seven years ago in Syracuse, boy. But, perhaps, my son, you're ashamed to acknowledge me in my misery.

original: The Duke and all that know me in the city Can witness with me that it is not so I ne'er saw Syracusa in my life.
translation: The Duke and everyone who knows me in this city can back me up that this isn't true. I've never been to Syracuse in my life.

original: I tell thee, Syracusian, twenty years Have I been patron to Antipholus, During which time he ne'er saw Syracusa. I see thy age and dangers make thee dote.
translation: I can tell you, Syracusian, I've been Antipholus's patron for twenty years, and he's never been to Syracuse in that time. I suppose your age and the danger of your situation have made you lose your marbles.

original: Most mighty duke, behold a man much wronged.
translation: Most might duke, behold a man who has been much wronged.

original: I see two husbands, or mine eyes deceive me.
translation: Either I see two husbands or my eyes deceive me.

original: One of these men is  genius to the other.     And so, of these, which is  the natural man And which the spirit? Who deciphers them?
translation: One of these men is genius to the other. [Looks at the DROMIO twins] And so, of these two, which is the real man and which is the spirit? Who can figure it out?

original: I, sir, am Dromio. Command him away.
translation: I am Dromio, sir. Send the other one away.

original: I, sir, am Dromio. Please, let me stay.
translation: I am Dromio, sir. Please, let me stay.

original: Egeon art thou not, or else his ghost?
translation: Aren't you Egeon, or, if not, his ghost?

original: O, my old master.—Who hath bound him here?
translation: Oh, my old master. Who has tied him up here?

original: Whoever bound him, I will loose his bonds   And gain a husband by his liberty.—
translation: Whoever tied him up, I will free him, and gain a husband in his freedom.

original: Speak, old Egeon, if thou be’st the man   That hadst a wife once called Emilia,   That bore thee at a burden two fair sons.
translation: Speak, old Egeon, if you are the man who once had a wife named Emilia who gave birth to your two beautiful twin sons.

original: O, if thou be’st the same Egeon, speak,   And speak unto the same Emilia.
translation: Oh, if you are the same Egeon, speak, and speak to the same Emilia.

original: Why, here begins his morning story right;   These two Antipholuses, these two so like,   And these two Dromios, one in semblance—
translation: Why, that was where his story from this morning began. These two Antipholuses, who look so alike, and these two Dromios, who are identical—

original: Besides his urging of her wreck at sea—   These are the parents to these children,   Which accidentally are met together.
translation: just like when he told us about the wreck at sea—these are the parents of those children. They've found each other by chance.

original: If I dream not, thou art Emilia. If thou art she, tell me where is that son That floated with thee on the fatal raft?
translation: If I do not dream, you are Emilia. If you are she, tell me where is our son who floated with you on that doomed raft?

original: By men of Epidamnum he and I   And the twin Dromio all were taken up;
translation: He and I and Dromio were saved by men of Epidamnum.

original: But by and by rude fishermen of Corinth   By force took Dromio and my son from them   And me they left with those of Epidamnum.
translation: But eventually beastly fisherman from Corinth took Dromio and my son by force and left me with the men from Epidamnum.

original: What then became of them I cannot tell;   I to this fortune that you see me in.
translation: I do not know what happened to them next. All I know is that I became what you see I am now.

original: Antipholus, thou cam’st  from Corinth first.
translation: Antipholus, you came from Corinth originally.

original: No, sir, not I. I came from Syracuse.
translation: No, sir, not me. I came from Syracuse.

original: Stay, stand apart. I know not which is which.
translation: Hold on, stand apart from each other. I don't know which is which.

original: I came from Corinth, my most gracious lord.
translation: I came from Corinth, my most gracious lord.

original: And I with him.
translation: And I came with him.

original: Brought to this town by that most famous warrior Duke Menaphon, your most renownèd uncle.
translation: You were brought to this town by that very famous warrior, Duke Menaphon, your celebrated uncle.

original: Which of you two did dine with me today?
translation: Which of the two of you dined with me today?

original: I, gentle mistress.
translation: I, gentle lady.

original: And are not you my husband?
translation: And are you my husband?

original: No, I say nay to that.
translation: No, he's definitely not.

original: And so do I, yet did she call me so, And this fair gentlewoman, her sister here, Did call me brother.    What I told you then I hope I shall have leisure to make good, If this be not a dream I see and hear.
translation: And I agree, even though she called her husband, and this beautiful lady, her sister here, called me her brother.  What I told you earlier, I hope I'll have the opportunity to follow through on, if this isn't all a dream that I see and hear.

original: That is the chain, sir, which you had of me.
translation: Sir, that is the chain that you got from me.

original: I think it be, sir. I deny it not.
translation: I think it is, sir. I don't deny it.

original: And you, sir, for this chain arrested me.
translation: And you, sir, arrested me for this chain.

original: I think I did, sir. I deny it not.
translation: I think I did, sir. I don't deny it.

original: I sent you money, sir, to be your bail By Dromio, but I think he brought it not.
translation: I sent Dromio with money, sir, to bail you out, but I think he didn't bring it.

original: No, none by me.
translation: No,  I never was given any money.

original: This purse of ducats I received from you,   And Dromio my man did bring them me.
translation: I received this purse of money from you, and my servant Dromio brought them to me.

original: I see we still did meet each other’s man,   And I was ta'en for him, and he for me,   And thereupon these errors are arose.
translation: It looks like each of us ran into the other's servant, and mine thought you were me and yours thought I was you, and this is where all these errors came from.

original: These ducats pawn I for my father here.
translation: I offer this money as ransom for my father.

original: It shall not need. Thy father hath his life.
translation: No need. Your father can live.

original: Sir, I must have that diamond from you.
translation: Sir, I must have that diamond from you.

original: There, take it; and much thanks for my good cheer.
translation: There, take it, with many thanks for a good time.

original: Renownèd duke, vouchsafe to take the pains   To go with us into the abbey here   And hear at large discoursed all our fortunes,   And all that are assembled in this place   That by this sympathizèd one day’s error   Have suffered wrong.
translation: Great duke, will you be so good as to go with us into the abbey and hear all our stories told, along with everyone assembled here that has suffered from the confusions today?

original: Go, keep us company,   And we shall make full satisfaction.—
translation: Come, keep us company, and we'll figure out everything.

original: Thirty-three years have I but gone in travail   Of you, my sons, and till this present hour   My heavy burden ne'er deliverèd.—
translation: Thirty-three years have I been grieving for you, my sons, and till this hour I never found freedom from that pain.

original: The Duke, my husband, and my children both,   And you, the calendars of their nativity,   Go to a gossips' feast, and go with me.   After so long grief, such nativity!
translation: The Duke, my husband, my two sons, and you, who share their birthday, come to a celebration, and come with me. After so long a grief, such rebirth!

original: With all my heart I’ll gossip at this feast.
translation: With all my heart, I'll celebrate at this feast.

original: Master, shall I fetch your  stuff from shipboard?
translation: Master, should I get your stuff from the ship?

original: Dromio, what stuff of mine hast thou embarked?
translation: Dromio, what stuff of mine is on a ship?

original: Your goods that lay at host, sir, in the Centaur.
translation: Your goods that were being kept in the Centaur, sir.

original: He speaks to me.—I am your master, Dromio. Come, go with us. We’ll look to that anon. Embrace thy brother there. Rejoice with him.
translation: He speaks to me.—I'm your master, Dromio. Come, go with us. We'll deal with that later. Embrace your brother there. Rejoice with him.

original: There is a fat friend at your master’s house That kitchened me for you today at dinner. She now shall be my sister, not my wife.
translation: There's a fat lady at your master's house that cornered me today at dinner, thinking it was you. She shall be my sister now, not my wife.

original: Methinks you are my glass, and not my brother: I see by you I am a sweet-faced youth. Will you walk in to see their gossiping?
translation: I think you're my reflection and not my brother: I see in your face that I must be a good-looking guy. Will you go in to see their celebrations?

original: Not I, sir. You are my elder.
translation: Not me first, sir. You're older than me.

original: That’s a question. How shall we try it?
translation: You bring up a good question. How can we figure it out?

original: We’ll draw cuts for the signior. Till then, lead thou  first.
translation: We'll draw straws to decide who's older. Until then, you lead first.

original: Nay, then, thus: We came into the world like brother and brother, And now let’s go hand in hand, not one before another.
translation: No, let's do it this way: we came into the world as brother and brother, so let's walk hand in hand, not one ahead of the other.

original: In sooth, I know not why I am so sad.   It wearies me; you say it wearies you.
translation: To tell the truth, I don't know why I am so sad. I'm tired of being sad, and you say you're tired of it, too.

original: But how I caught it, found it, or came by it,   What stuff ’tis made of, whereof it is born,   I am to learn.
translation: But I don't know how I caught, found, or came by this sadness; what it's about; or where it came from.

original: And such a want-wit sadness makes of me,   That I have much ado to know myself.
translation: And since I don't know anything about this sadness, I clearly have a ways to go in understanding myself.

original: Your mind is tossing on the ocean,   There, where your argosies with portly sail,   Like signors and rich burghers on the flood—   Or, as it were, the pageants of the sea—
translation: Your mind is focused on the ocean where your merchant ships are sailing like rich, important men parading on the sea.

original: Do overpeer the petty traffickers   That curtsy to them, do them reverence   As they fly by them with their woven wings.
translation: They tower over the little trade boats that they pass by, sailing along, and it's as if the little boats  bow  before the greatness of your ships.

original: Believe me, sir, had I such venture forth,   The better part of my affections would   Be with my hopes abroad. I should be still   Plucking the grass to know where sits the wind,   Peering in maps for ports and piers and roads.
translation: Believe me, sir, if I were involved in a trade venture like yours, most of my mental energy would be with my ships, as well. I'd be pulling up shoots of grass to use them to check the wind, and looking at maps of ports and piers and roads.

original: And every object that might make me fear   Misfortune to my ventures out of doubt   Would make me sad.
translation: And any little thing that might make me worry that something bad would happen to my ships would make me sad, without a doubt.

original: My wind cooling my broth   Would blow me to an ague when I thought   What harm a wind too great at sea might do.
translation: I'd get upset blowing on my hot soup, because it would make me think of what a strong wind at sea could do to my ships.

original: I should not see the sandy hourglass run,   But I should think of shallows and of flats   And see my wealthy Andrew docked in sand,   Vailing her high top lower than her ribs   To kiss her burial.
translation: If I saw the sands run in an hourglass, I would think of flat shallows where my ship,  " The Andrew ," run aground with all its riches and flipped over, completely done for.

original: Should I go to church   And see the holy edifice of stone   And not bethink me straight of dangerous rocks,   Which, touching but my gentle vessel’s side,   Would scatter all her spices on the stream,   Enrobe the roaring waters with my silks,   And, in a word, but even now worth this,   And now worth nothing?
translation: If I went to church and saw its stone construction, I couldn't help but think of dangerous rocks that could break the sides of my ships and scatter valuable spices all over the water, causing my silks to fall out and drape on the waves. They are worth so much, and would all of a sudden be lost and worth nothing to me.

original: Shall I have the thought   To think on this, and shall I lack the thought   That such a thing bechanced would make me sad?
translation: How could I think of such things and not get sad?

original: But tell not me. I know Antonio   Is sad to think upon his merchandise.
translation: But you don't need to tell me. I know that Antonio is sad because he's worrying about his merchandise.

original: Believe me, no. I thank my fortune for it—   My ventures are not in one bottom trusted,   Nor to one place, nor is my whole estate   Upon the fortune of this present year.
translation: Believe me, you're wrong. Thank goodness, not all my merchandise is in one ship or any one place, and I haven't risked all my riches on this year's venture.

original: Therefore my merchandise makes me not sad.
translation: Therefore, it's not my merchandise that is making me sad.

original: Why then, you are in love.
translation: Well, then, you must be in love.

original: Fie, fie!
translation: Oh please!

original: Not in love neither? Then let us say you are sad   Because you are not merry—   and ’twere as easy   For you to laugh and leap and say you are merry   Because you are not sad.
translation: You're not in love either? Then let's just say you are sad because you are not happy.  It would be just as easy for you to laugh and jump around and just say you are happy because you are not sad.

original: Now, by two-headed Janus,   Nature hath framed strange fellows in her time.
translation: I swear, by two-headed  Janus , nature has made all kinds of different people.

original: Some that will evermore peep through their eyes   And laugh like parrots at a bagpiper,
translation: Some people are always happy and could even laugh at a funeral,

original: And other of such vinegar aspect   That they’ll not show their teeth in way of smile   Though Nestor swear the jest be laughable.
translation: while others are so sour they don't even crack a smile at anything, not even at a joke that  Nestor  called the funniest.

original: Here comes Bassanio, your most noble kinsman, Gratiano, and Lorenzo. Fare ye well. We leave you now with better company.
translation: Here comes Bassanio, your most noble relative, along with Gratiano and Lorenzo. Goodbye. We'll leave you to these better friends.

original: I would have stayed till I had made you merry If worthier friends had not prevented me.
translation: If it weren't for these better friends coming along, I would have stayed until I made you smile.

original: Your worth is very dear in my regard. I take it your own business calls on you And you embrace th' occasion to depart.
translation: I see you as very worthy. I gather you have business to take care of and are just taking this opportunity to leave.

original: Good morrow, my good lords.
translation: Good day, my good lords.

original: Good signors both, when shall we laugh? Say, when? You grow exceeding strange. Must it be so?
translation: Both of you are good men; when are we going to have fun times together? Tell me, when? You're practically strangers now. Does it have to be that way?

original: We’ll make our leisures to attend on yours.
translation: The next time we get a chance, we'll spend some time together.

original: My Lord Bassanio, since you have found Antonio,  We two will leave you. But at dinnertime I pray you have in mind where we must meet.
translation: My Lord Bassanio, since you've found Antonio, the two of us will leave you two alone. But please remember where we're meeting for dinner.

original: I will not fail you.
translation: Don't worry.

original: You look not well, Signor Antonio.
translation: You don't look good, Sir Antonio.

original: You have too much respect upon the world.   They lose it that do buy it with much care.
translation: You care too much about worldly things. Those who care too much about things end up losing them.

original: Believe me, you are marvelously changed.
translation: Believe me, you really don't look yourself.

original: I hold the world but as the world, Gratiano— A stage where every man must play a part, And mine a sad one.
Let me play the fool.   With mirth and laughter let old wrinkles come.
translation: Well let me play the  fool , then. I don't care if laughter causes wrinkles.

original: And let my liver rather heat with wine   Than my heart cool with mortifying groans.
translation: I'd rather destroy my liver with wine than waste away with sad groans.

original: Why should a man whose blood is warm within   Sit like his grandsire cut in alabaster,   Sleep when he wakes, and creep into the jaundice   By being peevish?
translation: Why should a warm-blooded man be as cold and stoic as a statue of his dead grandfather?  Why should he be so inactive that he is practically asleep while awake, and start to get  jaundice  from being cranky so much?

original: I tell thee what, Antonio—   I love thee, and ’tis my love that speaks—   There are a sort of men whose visages   Do cream and mantle like a standing pond,
translation: I tell you what, Antonio—I love you, and I'm speaking out of love—there are some people whose faces are so unmoving that they grow scum like a still pond,

original: And do a willful stillness entertain   With purpose to be dressed in an opinion   Of wisdom, gravity, profound conceit,   As who should say, “I am Sir Oracle,   And when I ope my lips, let no dog bark!”
translation: and they try hard to maintain a still expression so that they can seem to be wise, serious, and profound, like someone who could say, "I am Sir Oracle, and when I open my lips to speak, let no dog bark!"

original: O my Antonio, I do know of these   That therefore only are reputed wise   For saying nothing, when I am very sure   If they should speak, would almost damn those ears   Which, hearing them, would call their brothers fools.
translation: Oh my Antonio, these kind of men only have the reputation of wisdom because they say nothing, and I'm sure that if they should speak, everyone listening would realize they are fools.

original: I’ll tell thee more of this another time.   But fish not with this melancholy bait   For this fool gudgeon, this opinion.—
translation: I'll tell you more about this another time. But stop trying to get people to think you're serious and wise by acting all melancholy.

original: Come, good Lorenzo.—Fare ye well awhile.   I’ll end my exhortation after dinner.
translation: Come with me now, good Lorenzo. Goodbye for now, Antonio. I'll finish the rest of my encouraging speech after dinner.

original: Well, we will leave you then till dinnertime.
translation: Well, we'll leave you until dinnertime, then.

original: I must be one of these same dumb wise men,   For Gratiano never lets me speak.
translation: I must be one of these dumb but wise-seeming men he talks about, because Gratiano never lets me speak.

original: Well, keep me company but two years more, Thou shalt not know the sound of thine own tongue.
translation: Well, stick around with me for two more years and you'll forget what your voice even sounds like.

original: Farewell. I’ll grow a talker for this gear.
translation: Goodbye. I'll start to talk more, now.

original: Thanks, i' faith, for silence is only commendable In a neat’s tongue dried and a maid not vendible.
translation: Thanks, because in fact the only tongues that should keep quiet are beef tongues on the dinner plate, and those of uncooperative maids.

original: Is that any thing now?
translation: What do you think of all that?

original: Gratiano speaks an infinite deal of nothing, more than  any man in all Venice.
translation: Gratiano speaks an endless stream of nonsense, more than any man in all of Venice.

original: His reasons are as two grains of  wheat hid in two bushels of chaff
translation: Trying to find the point of what he's talking about is like looking for two grains of wheat hidden in bushels of hay.

original: —you shall seek all day ere you find them, and when you have them they are not  worth the search.
translation: You could look all day before you find them, and once you do it's not even worth the effort you put into it.

original: Well, tell me now what lady is the same  To whom you swore a secret pilgrimage, That you today promised to tell me of?
translation: Well, then tell me know who the lady is that you made an agreement with to go on a secret trip? You promised to tell me today.

original: 'Tis not unknown to you, Antonio,   How much I have disabled mine estate,   By something showing a more swelling port   Than my faint means would grant continuance.
translation: Antonio, you know how I've been using up my wealth, living a more lavish life than I can afford.

original: Nor do I now make moan to be abridged   From such a noble rate.
translation: Now,  I'm not complaining about having to be more frugal,

original: But my chief care   Is to come fairly off from the great debts   Wherein my time something too prodigal   Hath left me gaged.
translation: but I do care about fairly paying off the debts that I incurred while I was living beyond my means.

original: To you, Antonio,   I owe the most in money and in love,
translation: I owe the most to you, Antonio, both in money and in love.

original: And from your love I have a warranty   To unburden all my plots and purposes   How to get clear of all the debts I owe.
translation: And because we are good friends, I know I can tell you all my plans and plots for paying back all the debts I owe.

original: I pray you, good Bassanio, let me know it.
translation: Please do tell me, good Bassanio.

original: And if it stand, as you yourself still do,   Within the eye of honor, be assured   My purse, my person, my extremest means   Lie all unlocked to your occasions.
translation: And if your plan is as honorable as you still are, rest assured that I will help you with my money, myself, and whatever other ways I can.

original: In my school days, when I had lost one shaft,
translation: Back during my school days, I was shooting arrows once and lost one.

original: I shot his fellow of the selfsame flight   The selfsame way with more advisèd watch   To find the other forth—   and by adventuring both,   I oft found both.
translation: So, I shot another arrow the same exact way and paid better attention to it so that I could follow its course, and it led me to the first arrow.

original: I urge this childhood proof   Because what follows is pure innocence.
translation: With this example from my childhood in mind, listen to my plan, which is completely  innocent .

original: I owe you much, and, like a willful youth,   That which I owe is lost.
translation: I owe you a lot, and like a rash young man I have lost the money I owe you.

original: But if you please   To shoot another arrow that self way   Which you did shoot the first, I do not doubt,   As I will watch the aim, or to find both   Or bring your latter hazard back again   And thankfully rest debtor for the first.
translation: But if you shoot another arrow the same way you shot the first, by lending me money again, I have no doubt that I will bring both arrows back to you, because I'll watch the second one more carefully. Or at least I'll bring back the first, and remain in your debt for the second.

original: You know me well, and herein spend but time   To wind about my love with circumstance.
translation: You know me well, and are wasting your time complicating my affection for you with explanation and reasoning.

original: And out of doubt you do me now more wrong   In making question of my uttermost   Than if you had made waste of all I have.
translation: You do me more wrong in doubting that I love you enough to lend you more money than if you had wasted all of my money.

original: Then do but say to me what I should do   That in your knowledge may by me be done,   And I am pressed unto it. Therefore speak.
translation: Simply tell me what you would like me to do, and I will do it. Tell me.

original: In Belmont is a lady richly left,   And she is fair and—fairer than that word—   Of wondrous virtues.
translation: There's a lady in Belmont who has inherited some riches and is both beautiful—more beautiful than can be described—and virtuous.

original: Sometimes from her eyes   I did receive fair speechless messages.
translation: We've occasionally exchanged some knowing glances.

original: Her name is Portia, nothing undervalued   To Cato’s daughter, Brutus' Portia.
translation: Her name is Portia, and she lives up to her namesake, Cato's daughter and the wife of  Brutus .

original: Nor is the wide world ignorant of her worth,   For the four winds blow in from every coast   Renownèd suitors, and her sunny locks   Hang on her temples like a golden fleece,   Which makes her seat of Belmont Colchos' strand,   And many Jasons come in quest of her.
translation: Her worthiness as a wife is well-known, and suitors come to her from all four corners of the world. Her blonde hair hangs over her temples like the  Golden Fleece , and it makes many a Jason want to come on a quest for her.

original: O my Antonio, had I but the means   To hold a rival place with one of them,   I have a mind presages me such thrift   That I should questionless be fortunate!
translation: Antonio, if I only had the means to stand as a rival with these suitors, I know without a doubt that I would be successful in wooing her!

original: Thou know’st that all my fortunes are at sea.   Neither have I money nor commodity   To raise a present sum.
translation: You know that all my money has been put into my ships. I have neither money nor any goods to sell in order raise some funds for you.

original: Therefore go forth,   Try what my credit can in Venice do—   That shall be racked even to the uttermost   To furnish thee to Belmont, to fair Portia.
translation: So go forth and see how far my  credit  will get you in Venice, all of which I will use to get you to Belmont and to beautiful Portia.

original: Go presently inquire, and so will I,   Where money is, and I no question make   To have it of my trust or for my sake.
translation: Go ask around to find somewhere you can borrow some money, and so will I. I am certain that people will lend me the money, either for my own sake or for the sake of my business.

original: Three thousand ducats, well.
Ay, sir, for three months.
translation: Yes, sir, for three months.

original: For three months, well.
translation: For three months, eh?

original: For the which, as I told you, Antonio shall be bound.
translation: And, as I told you, Antonio will be the guarantor of the loan.

original: Antonio shall become bound, well.
translation: Antonio will, eh?

original: May you stead me? Will you pleasure me? Shall I know  your answer?
translation: Can you help me out? Will you agree to the loan? Can I hear your answer?

original: Three thousand ducats for three months, and Antonio  bound.
translation: Three thousand ducats for three months, and Antonio will be bound to guarantee the loan.

original: Your answer to that?
translation: What's your answer to that offer?

original: Antonio is a good man.
translation: Antonio is a good man.

original: Have you heard any imputation to the contrary?
translation: Have you heard anyone say otherwise about him?

original: Ho, no, no, no, no. My meaning in saying he is a good  man is to have you understand me that he is sufficient.  Yet his means are in supposition.
translation: Oh no, no, no, no I haven't. I just meant to suggest that is a sufficient guarantor for the loan. But, his wealth isn't certain at the moment.

original: He hath an argosy  bound to Tripolis, another to the Indies. I understand  moreover, upon the Rialto, he hath a third at Mexico, a  fourth for England, and other ventures he hath  squandered abroad.
translation: He has one ship bound for Tripoli and another for the Indies. Moreover, the word around the  Rialto  is that he has a third ship in Mexico, a fourth bound for England, and other ventures he has invested his money in abroad.

original: But ships are but boards, sailors but men. There be land rats and water rats, water thieves  and land thieves—I mean pirates—and then there is the  peril of waters, winds, and rocks.
translation: Ships are just wood, and sailors are just men. There are rats on land and sea, and thieves on land and sea, including pirates. And then there is also the matter of dangerous waters, winds, and rocks.

original: The man is  notwithstanding sufficient.
translation: But in spite of all these risks, he is still a sufficient guarantor.

original: Be assured you may.
translation: You can be sure of that.

original: I will be assured I may, and that I may be assured, I will bethink me. May I speak with Antonio?
translation: I will be sure, and I will figure out how I can be completely sure. May I speak with Antonio?

original: If it please you to dine with us.
translation: Would you like to have dinner with Antonio and me?

original: Yes—to smell pork, to eat of the habitation which your  prophet the Nazarite conjured the devil into.
translation: Oh yes, I'd love to eat  pork  with you, the animal into which your Jesus exorcised the devil.

original: I will buy with you, sell with you, talk with you, walk with you,  and so following, but I will not eat with you, drink  with you, nor pray with you.
translation: I will buy and sell with you, talk with you, walk with you, and so forth, but I will neither eat, nor drink, nor pray with you.

original: What news on the Rialto?  Who is he comes here?
translation: What's the news on the Rialto? Who is the man coming here?

original: This is Signor Antonio.
translation: This is Mr. Antonio.

original: How like a fawning publican he looks!   I hate him for he is a Christian,
translation: He looks like someone who wants to take my money but then ask me for a favor!  I hate him because he is a Christian,

original: But more for that in low simplicity   He lends out money gratis and brings down   The rate of usance here with us in Venice.
translation: but I hate him even more because he lends out money  without charging interest , which forces me to lower the interest rates that I loan at.

original: If I can catch him once upon the hip,   I will feed fat the ancient grudge I bear him.
translation: If I get the better of him just once, I will satisfy my old grudge against him.

original: He hates our sacred nation, and he rails,   Even there where merchants most do congregate,   On me, my bargains and my well-won thrift,   Which he calls “interest.”
translation: He hates us Jews, and he speaks badly of me, my bargains, and my hard-won money in the company of other merchants, talking about "interest."

original: Cursèd be my tribe   If I forgive him!
translation: May my Jewish tribe be cursed if I forgive him!

original: Shylock, do you hear?
translation: Shylock, are you listening?

original: I am debating of my present store,   And by the near guess of my memory
translation: I am thinking about how much money I have right now, and as best as I can remember,

original: I cannot instantly raise up the gross   Of full three thousand ducats. What of that?
translation: I can't raise the gross sum of three thousand ducats right now. But that doesn't matter.

original: Tubal, a wealthy Hebrew of my tribe,   Will furnish me. But soft! How many months   Do you desire?
translation: Tubal, a wealthy Jew of my tribe, will supply the rest of the money. But wait! How many months do you want the money for?

original: Rest you fair, good signor.   Your worship was the last man in our mouths.
translation: Hello, good sir. We were just talking about you.

original: Shylock, albeit I neither lend nor borrow   By taking nor by giving of excess,
translation: Shylock, I normally don't lend or borrow money with interest,

original: Yet to supply the ripe wants of my friend,   I’ll break a custom.
translation: but in order to help my needy friend, I'll break my custom.

original: Is he yet possessed   How much ye would?
translation: Does he know how much money you want yet?

original: Ay, ay, three thousand ducats.
translation: Yes, yes, three thousand ducats.

original: And for three months.
translation: And for three months.

original: I had forgot—three months.    You told me so.     Well then, your bond, and let me see—But  hear you,  Methought you said you neither lend nor borrow Upon advantage.
translation: I had forgotten—three months.  You told me that. [To ANTONIO] Well then, and you'll be the guarantor on behalf of Bassanio, let's see—but listen, I thought you said you don't lend or borrow money with interest.

original: I do never use it.
translation: I never do.

original: When Jacob grazed his uncle Laban’s sheep—   This Jacob from our holy Abram was,
translation: In the  Bible , when Jacob looked after his uncle Laban's sheep—this is the Jacob who was descended from our holy ancestor Abram,

original: As his wise mother wrought in his behalf,   The third possessor, ay, he was the third—
translation: and his wise mother made him his father's heir so that he was the third to possess God's promise —

original: And what of him? Did he take interest?
translation: And what about him? Did he charge interest?

original: No, not take interest—not as you would say   Directly interest.
translation: No, he didn't. He didn't exactly charge interest, as you would say.

original: Mark what Jacob did:   When Laban and himself were compromised   That all the eanlings which were streaked and pied   Should fall as Jacob’s hire, the ewes, being rank,   In the end of autumn turnèd to the rams.
translation: But listen to what Jacob did do: when he and Laban agreed that all the streaked and spotted sheep would be his, it was the end of autumn and so the sheep were starting to mate.

original: And when the work of generation was   Between these woolly breeders in the act,   The skillful shepherd peeled me certain wands.   And in the doing of the deed of kind   He stuck them up before the fulsome ewes,
translation: And when the wooly sheep were starting to couple off together to breed, the skillful shepherd Jacob put some dappled sticks in front of the ewes while they were conceiving.

original: Who then conceiving did in weaning time   Fall parti-colored lambs—and those were Jacob’s.
translation: When they gave birth, they produced streaked and spotted lambs, and those became Jacob's.

original: This was a way to thrive, and he was blessed.   And thrift is blessing, if men steal it not.
translation: Jacob became very prosperous in this way, and he was blessed. Profit is a blessing, if it is not obtained by stealing.

original: This was a venture, sir, that Jacob served for—   A thing not in his power to bring to pass   But swayed and fashioned by the hand of heaven.
translation: But that was something that wasn't in Jacob's power to bring about; it happened through the hand of God.

original: Was this inserted to make interest good?   Or is your gold and silver ewes and rams?
translation: Did you tell this story to imply that it is good to charge interest? Is your gold and silver like a bunch of ewes and rams?

original: I cannot tell: I make it breed as fast. But note me, signor—
Mark you this, Bassanio,   The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose.
translation: Take note, Bassanio: even the devil can quote the Bible for his own purpose.

original: An evil soul producing holy witness   Is like a villain with a smiling cheek,   A goodly apple rotten at the heart.
translation: An evil soul quoting holy words is like a villain who pretends to be good, a good-looking apple with a rotten core.

original: Oh, what a goodly outside falsehood hath!
translation: What a good appearance falsehood can have!

original: Three thousand ducats—’tis a good round sum.  Three months from twelve, then. Let me see. The rate—
translation: Three thousand ducats: that's a good, round number. Three months out of the twelve that make up the year, then. Let me see. The rate—

original: Well, Shylock, shall we be beholding to you?
translation: Well, Shylock, will we be in your debt?

original: Signor Antonio, many a time and oft   In the Rialto you have rated me   About my moneys and my usances.
translation: Sir Antonio, many times you have criticized me about my money and habit of charging interest in the Rialto.

original: Still have I borne it with a patient shrug,   For sufferance is the badge of all our tribe.
translation: I have endured it all with patience and a shrug, because we Jews are known for our ability to endure.

original: You call me misbeliever, cutthroat dog,   And spet upon my Jewish gaberdine—   And all for use of that which is mine own.
translation: You say I believe in the wrong religion, call me a cut-throat dog, and spit on my Jewish clothing, all because I use my own money to make profit.

original: Well then, it now appears you need my help.   Go to, then! You come to me and you say,   “Shylock, we would have moneys.”
translation: And now it appears that you need my help. Okay, then! You come to me and you say, "Shylock, I need money."

original: You say so!—    You, that did void your rheum upon my beard   And foot me as you spurn a stranger cur   Over your threshold! Moneys is your suit.
translation: You tell me this! You who spat on my beard and kicked me as you'd kick a stray dog away from your threshold! You ask for money.

original: What should I say to you? Should I not say,   “Hath a dog money? Is it possible   A cur can lend three thousand ducats?”
translation: What should I say to you? Shouldn't I say, "Does a dog have money? Is it possible for a dog to lend you three thousand ducats?"

original: Shall I bend low and in a bondman’s key   With bated breath and whispering humbleness   Say this:
translation: Or should I get bend to my knees and with bated breath humbly whisper,

original: “Fair sir, you spet on me on Wednesday last;   You spurned me such a day; another time   You called me ’dog'—and for these courtesies   I’ll lend you thus much moneys?”
translation: "Fair sir, you spat on me last Wednesday; you spurned me then; another time you called me a dog—and for all this courtesy you've shown me, I will gladly lend you this much money?"

original: I am as like to call thee so again,   To spet on thee again, to spurn thee too.
translation: I am likely to call you such names again, spit on you again, and spurn you, too.

original: If thou wilt lend this money, lend it not   As to thy friends, for when did friendship take   A breed for barren metal of his friend?
translation: If you decide to lend this money, don't do it as if we are your friends. After all, when have friends ever charged each other interest?

original: But lend it rather to thine enemy,   Who, if he break, thou mayst with better face   Exact the penalty.
translation: Lend me the money as your enemy and if I break my part of the agreement you can more happily punish me.

original: Why, look you how you storm!   I would be friends with you and have your love,
translation: Why, look at your temper! I would be friends with you and have your affection,

original: Forget the shames that you have stained me with,   Supply your present wants and take no doit   Of usance for my moneys—and you’ll not hear me!
translation: forget about how you have shamed me, lend you what you need and take no interest—but you won't listen to me!

original: This is kind I offer.
translation: I'm giving you a kind offer.

original: This were kindness.
translation: That would be kind.

original: This kindness will I show.   Go with me to a notary, seal me there   Your single bond,
translation: I'll show you this kindness. Go with me to a notary and sign an agreement:

original: and—in a merry sport—   If you repay me not on such a day,   In such a place, such sum or sums as are   Expressed in the condition,
translation: if you do not repay me the agreed-upon amount of money on the agreed-upon day, in the agreed-upon place,

original: let the forfeit   Be nominated for an equal pound   Of your fair flesh,   to be cut off and taken   In what part of your body pleaseth me.
translation: you will forfeit to me one pound of your fair flesh, to be cut off from whatever part of your body I choose.

original: Content, in faith. I’ll seal to such a bond, And say there is much kindness in the Jew.
translation: Sure, why not? I'll agree to such a deal, and I'll admit there is much kindness in Jews.

original: You shall not seal to such a bond for me! I’ll rather dwell in my necessity.
translation: I won't let you agree to such a deal on my behalf! I'd rather deal with my poverty.

original: Why, fear not, man. I will not forfeit it.
translation: Don't worry, man. I won't have to give up the pound of flesh.

original: Within these two months—that’s a month before   This bond expires—I do expect return   Of thrice three times the value of this bond.
translation: I expect to make nine times the amount of this contract within these next two months, and that's a month before I have to pay him back.

original: O Father Abram, what these Christians are,   Whose own hard dealings teaches them suspect   The thoughts of others!—   Pray you, tell me this:
translation: Oh, Father Abram, what strange people these Christians are! They suspect the worst in others because of their own trickery. Please, tell me this:

original: If he should break his day, what should I gain   By the exaction of the forfeiture?
translation: if he fails to pay me back in time, what would I gain by taking a pound of his flesh?

original: A pound of man’s flesh taken from a man   Is not so estimable, profitable neither,   As flesh of muttons, beefs, or goats.
translation: A pound of flesh taken from a man is not worth very much, and isn't as profitable as mutton, beef, or goat flesh.

original: I say,   To buy his favor I extend this friendship.   If he will take it, so. If not, adieu.   And for my love I pray you wrong me not.
translation: I'm telling you, I'm giving him this kind offer to be friendly. If he will accept the offer, good. If not, goodbye. And for this kindness I show you, I ask you not to think poorly of me.

original: Yes, Shylock, I will seal unto this bond.
translation: Yes, Shylock, I will enter into this contract

original: Then meet me forthwith at the notary’s.   Give him direction for this merry bond,
translation: Then meet me right away at the notary's office. Explain to him this happy agreement,

original: And I will go and purse the ducats straight,   See to my house left in the fearful guard   Of an unthrifty knave, and presently   I will be with you.
translation: and I will go immediately to gather up the ducats from my house,  which I've left guarded by a careless clown. Then, soon, I'll meet you.

original: Hie thee, gentle Jew.
translation: Take care, gentle Jew.

original: The Hebrew will turn Christian. He grows kind.
translation: This Hebrew must be turning Christian, because he's getting kinder.

original: I like not fair terms and a villain’s mind.
translation: I don't like fair terms when they're thought up by a villain's mind.

original: Come on. In this there can be no dismay. My ships come home a month before the day.
translation: Come on. There's nothing bad about this. My ships will come home with the money a month before I have to pay him.

original: Mislike me not for my complexion,   The shadowed livery of the burnished sun,   To whom I am a neighbor and near bred.
translation: Don't dislike me because of my skin color, the shadow-colored skin that results from the burning sun in Africa.

original: Bring me the fairest creature northward born,   Where Phoebus' fire scarce thaws the icicles,   And let us make incision for your love   To prove whose blood is reddest, his or mine.
translation: Bring me the most beautiful person born in the north, where the light of the sun barely thaws the ice, and let's cut both him and me so you can see whose blood is reddest, his or mine.

original: I tell thee, lady, this aspect of mine   Hath feared the valiant. By my love I swear   The best-regarded virgins of our clime   Have loved it too.
translation: I'm telling you, my lady, this aspect of my appearance has frightened brave men. By my love, I swear the best-regarded virgins of my land love me.

original: I would not change this hue   Except to steal your thoughts, my gentle queen.
translation: I wouldn't trade my dark skin color for anything, my gentle queen, except to have you think kindly of me.

original: In terms of choice I am not solely led   By nice direction of a maiden’s eyes.
translation: In terms of my choosing a husband, I care about more than looks.

original: Besides, the lottery of my destiny   Bars me the right of voluntary choosing.
translation: And besides, my destiny is to be decided by a lottery, so I can't even choose for myself.

original: But if my father had not scanted me   And hedged me by his wit to yield myself   His wife who wins me by that means I told you,
translation: But if my father hadn't robbed me of that right as I described to you,

original: Yourself, renownèd Prince, then stood as fair   As any comer I have looked on yet   For my affection.
translation: you would be as good a potential husband in me eyes, renowned Prince, as anyone else.

original: Even for that I thank you.   Therefore I pray you lead me to the caskets   To try my fortune.
translation: Thank you for that compliment. Therefore, I beg you to lead me to the caskets so I can try my luck.

original: By this scimitar   That slew the Sophy and a Persian prince   That won three fields of Sultan Solyman,
translation: By this sword with which I killed the leader of Persia and a Persian prince, and with which I won three battles against Sultan Solyman,

original: I would o'erstare the sternest eyes that look,   Outbrave the heart most daring on the earth,   Pluck the young sucking cubs from the she-bear,   Yea, mock the lion when he roars for prey,   To win the lady.
translation: I swear that I would stare down the sternest eyes in the world, be braver than the most daring man on earth, steal the bear cubs from a suckling mother bear, and even mock a lion roaring at his prey—all to win you.

original: But, alas the while!   If Hercules and Lychas play at dice   Which is the better man, the greater throw   May turn by fortune from the weaker hand.
translation: But alas! If  Hercules  and his servant Lychas had to play a game of dice to decide the better man, the weaker man might win by luck.

original: So is Alcides beaten by his page,   And so may I, blind fortune leading me,   Miss that which one unworthier may attain   And die with grieving.
translation: So the great Hercules could be beaten by his own servant, and so I might lose you to a less worthy man because of blind luck. If that happened, I would die of grief.

original: You must take your chance,   And either not attempt to choose at all
translation: You must try your luck. Either don't attempt it at all,

original: Or swear before you choose,   if you choose wrong   Never to speak to lady afterward   In way of marriage. Therefore be advised.
translation: or promise before you choose a casket that if you choose the wrong one you will never speak to a lady about marriage again. Be warned.

original: Nor will not. Come, bring me unto my chance.
translation: I promise. Come on, bring me to the caskets.

original: First, forward to the temple. After dinner Your hazard shall be made.
translation: First, let's go forward to the temple. After dinner, you can try your luck.

original: Good fortune then!— To make me blessed or cursed’st among men.
translation: May I have good luck, then! I'll either be a blessed or a cursed man.

original: Certainly my conscience will serve me to run from this  Jew, my master. The fiend is at mine elbow and tempts  me, saying to me, “Gobbo,” “Launcelot Gobbo,” “Good  Launcelot,” or “Good Gobbo,” or “Good Launcelot Gobbo”  —“use your legs, take the start, run away.”
translation: Certainly part of me wants to run from my master, this Jew. The devil whispers in my ear, tempting me, saying to me, "Gobbo," "Launcelot Gobbo," "Good Launcelot," or "Good Gobbo," or "Good Launcelot Gobbo"—"use your legs, get going, run away."

original: My  conscience says, “No. Take heed, honest Launcelot. Take  heed, honest Gobbo,” or as aforesaid, “Honest Launcelot  Gobbo, do not run. Scorn running with thy heels.”
translation: But my conscience says, "No. Wait here, honest Launcelot. Wait here, honest Gobbo." Or it says, "Honest Launcelot Gobbo, do not run away. Don't you dare run away."

original: Well,  the most courageous fiend bids me pack. “Fia!” says the  fiend. “Away!” says the fiend. “For the heavens, rouse  up a brave mind,” says the fiend, “and run.”
translation: Well, the bold devil is encouraging me to get going. "Go!" says the devil. "Go away!" says the devil. "For heaven's sake, be brave and run," says the devil.

original: Well, my  conscience, hanging about the neck of my heart, says  very wisely to me, “My honest friend Launcelot, being an honest man’s son”—or rather an honest woman’s son, for  indeed my father did something smack, something grow to. He had a kind of taste.—Well, my conscience says,  “Launcelot, budge not.” “Budge!” says the fiend. “Budge  not,” says my conscience.
translation: But then my conscience pulls on my heart and says very wisely to me, "My honest friend Launcelot, since you are the son of an honest man"—or rather the son of an honest woman, for actually my father was somewhat dishonest and unfaithful. He had a kind of taste for it. Anyways, my conscience says, "Launcelot, don't budge!" "Budge!" says the devil. "Don't budge," says my conscience.

original: “Conscience,” say I, “you  counsel well.” “Fiend,” say I, “you counsel well.” To be ruled by my conscience I should stay with the Jew my  master, who, God bless the mark, is a kind of devil.
translation: "Conscience," I say, "you give good advice." "Devil," I say, "you give good advice, too." If I listen to my conscience, I'd stay here with my master the Jew, who is a kind of devil himself.

original: And to run away from the Jew I should be ruled by the  fiend, who, saving your reverence, is the devil himself. Certainly the Jew is the very devil incarnation.
translation: And if I run away from the Jew I'd be listening to the devil, who is the devil himself. But then again, the Jew is certainly the very devil incarnate.

original: And in my conscience, my conscience is but a kind of hard  conscience, to offer to counsel me to stay with the Jew. The fiend gives the more friendly counsel. I will run,  fiend. My heels are at your command. I will run.
translation: And my conscience is being rather difficult in advising me to stay with the Jew. The devil is giving more friendly advice. I will run away, devil. My feet are at your command: I will run away.

original: Master young man, you, I pray you, which is the way to Master Jew’s?
translation: Excuse me, young man, where is the Jew's house?

original: O heavens, this is my true-begotten father,  who, being more than sand-blind—high-gravel blind—knows  me not. I will try confusions with him.
translation: Oh God, this is my father. He is as blind as a bat and doesn't recognize me. I'll play some tricks on him.

original: Master young gentleman, I pray you, which is the way to Master Jew’s?
translation: Young man, please, where is the Jew's house?

original: Turn up on your right hand at the next turning, but at  the next turning of all on your left. Marry, at the very next turning turn of no hand, but turn down indirectly  to the Jew’s house.
translation: At the next intersection, take a right, and then at the next take a left. And then at the next intersection keep going straight and you'll be at the Jew's house.

original: By God’s sonties, ’twill be a hard way to hit. Can you  tell me whether one Launcelot that dwells with him,  dwell with him or no?
translation: By God, it will be hard to find my way there. Do you know if someone named Launcelot, who lives with him, is there with him or not?

original: Talk you of young Master Launcelot? @     Mark me now. Now will I raise the waters.—Talk  you of young Master Launcelot?
translation: Are you talking about young Master Launcelot?  Watch this. Now I'll raise the stakes. [To GOBBO] Are you talking about the young Master Launcelot?

original: No “master,” sir, but a poor man’s son. His father,  though I say ’t, is an honest exceeding poor man and,  God be thanked, well to live.
translation: Not a "master," sir, but a poor man's son. His father, though, is an honest, if very poor, man and—thank God—in good health.

original: Well, let his father be what he will, we talk of young Master Launcelot.
translation: Well, whatever his father is like, we are talking about young Master Launcelot.

original: Your worship’s friend and Launcelot, sir.
translation: Yes, but just Launcelot, not "master," sir.

original: But I pray you, ergo, old man, ergo, I beseech you,  talk you of young Master Launcelot?
Of Launcelot, an ’t please your mastership.
translation: Master, I am speaking of someone simply called  Launcelot.

original: Ergo, Master Launcelot. Talk not of Master Launcelot,  Father,
translation: Ergo, Master Launcelot. Don't talk about Master Launcelot, father.

original: for the young gentleman, according to Fates and  Destinies and such odd sayings, the Sisters Three and  such branches of learning, is indeed deceased,
translation: That young gentleman, according to his fate and destiny and so forth, the  Three Sisters  and so on, is deceased.

original: or as you would say in plain terms, gone to heaven.
translation: Or, to say it plainly, he has gone to heaven.

original: Marry, God forbid! The boy was the very staff of my  age, my very prop.
translation: God forbid! In my old age I relied on that boy, like a crutch!

original: Do I look like a cudgel or a hovel-post, a staff or a  prop? Do you know me, Father?
translation: Do I look like a crutch or a prop? Do you recognize me, father?

original: Alack the day, I know you not, young gentleman. But I  pray you, tell me, is my boy, God rest his soul, alive  or dead?
translation: I swear, I don't know who you are, young gentleman. But please tell me: is my son—God rest his soul—alive or dead?

original: Do you not know me, Father?
translation: Do you not know who I am, father?

original: Alack, sir, I am sand-blind. I know you not.
translation: Alas, sir, I am completely blind. I don't know you.

original: Nay, indeed if you had your eyes, you might fail of  the knowing me. It is a wise father that knows his own  child.
translation: Even if you could see, you might not recognize me. It takes a wise father to recognize his own child.

original: Well, old man, I will tell you news of your son.  Give me your blessing.
translation: Well, old man, I will give you news regarding your son. Give me your blessing.

original: Truth will come to light. Murder  cannot be hid long—a man’s son may, but in the end truth will out.
translation: The truth will come to light. Murder can't be hidden for long. A man's son can be hidden, but not the truth.

original: Pray you, sir, stand up. I am sure you are not  Launcelot, my boy.
translation: Please sir, stand up. I am sure you aren't my son Launcelot.

original: Pray you, let’s have no more fooling about it, but give me your blessing. I am Launcelot, your boy that was,  your son that is, your child that shall be.
translation: Please, enough fooling around. Give me your blessing. I am Launcelot, who was, is, and will continue to be your son.

original: I cannot think you are my son.
translation: I can't believe that you are my son.

original: I know not what I shall think of that. But I am  Launcelot, the Jew’s man, and I am sure Margery your  wife is my mother.
translation: I don't know what to think of that. But I really am Launcelot, the Jew's servant, and I am sure your wife Margery is my mother.

original: Her name is Margery, indeed. I’ll be sworn, if thou be Launcelot, thou art mine own flesh and blood.
translation: My wife's name is Margery, indeed. If you're Launcelot, I'll swear you are my own flesh and blood.

original: Lord worshipped  might he be, what a beard hast thou got!
translation: Good lord, what a beard you have!

original: Thou hast got  more hair on thy chin than Dobbin my fill-horse has on  his tail.
translation: You have more hair on your chin than my horse Dobbin has on his tail.

original: It should seem then that Dobbin’s tail grows backward. I am sure he had more hair of his tail than I have of  my face when I last saw him.
translation: It would seem that Dobbin's tail is shrinking, then. I am sure that he had more hair on his tail the last time I saw him than I have on my face.

original: Lord, how art thou changed! How dost thou and thy  master agree? I have brought him a present. How 'gree  you now?
translation: Lord, you have changed! How are you and your master getting along? I have bought him a present. Are you getting along with him?

original: Well, well, but for mine own part, as I have set up my  rest to run away, so I will not rest till I have run  some ground. My master’s a very Jew.
translation: Pretty well, but I've decided to run away from him, so I won't rest until I've run some distance. My master is very much a Jew.

original: Give him a present. Give him a halter. I am famished in his service. You  may tell every finger I have with my ribs. Father, I am  glad you are come.
translation: Go ahead and give him a present; give him a noose. I work as his servant and he hardly feeds me. You can count my ribs, they protrude so much. I'm glad you've come, father.

original: Give me your present to one Master  Bassanio, who indeed gives rare new liveries.
translation: Give me the present so I can give it to Master Bassanio, who gives his servants fancy new outfits.

original: If I serve not him, I will run as far as God has any ground.—O  rare fortune! Here comes the man.—To him, Father, for I  am a Jew if I serve the Jew any longer.
translation: If I don't end up as his servant, I will run as far away as is possible. Oh, just my luck! Here he comes. Let's go talk to him, father, for if I serve the Jew any longer, I'll be a Jew myself.

original: You may do so, but let it be so hasted  that supper be ready at the farthest by five of the  clock. See these letters delivered, put the liveries to  making, and desire Gratiano to come anon to my lodging.
translation: You may do that, but do it quick so that supper is ready by five o'clock at the latest. Make sure these letters are delivered, get the outfits made, and tell Gratiano to come soon to my house.

original: To him, Father.
translation: Go talk to him, father.

original: God bless your worship!
translation: God bless you!

original: Gramercy! Wouldst thou aught with me?
translation: Thanks! Do you want something?

original: Here’s my son, sir, a poor boy—
translation: This here is my son, a poor boy—

original: Not a poor boy, sir, but the rich Jew’s man that would, sir, as my father shall specify—
translation: Not a poor boy, sir, but a servant of the rich Jew. And I would like, sir, as my father will tell you—

original: He hath a great infection, sir, as one would say, to  serve—
translation: He has a great desire, sir, as they say, to serve—

original: Indeed the short and the long is, I serve the Jew and  have a desire, as my father shall specify—
translation: Yes, to make a long story short, I currently serve under the Jew and, as my father will tell you, I have a desire—

original: His master and he, saving your worship’s reverence,  are scarce cater-cousins—
translation: He and his master, your reverence, are not the closest of friends—

original: To be brief, the very truth is that the Jew, having  done me wrong, doth cause me, as my father, being, I  hope, an old man, shall frutify unto you—
I have here a dish of doves that I would bestow upon  your worship, and my suit is—
translation: I have a gift of a plate of doves here that I would give to you, and all I ask is—

original: In very brief, the suit is impertinent to myself, as  your worship shall know by this honest old man—and  though I say it, though old man, yet poor man, my  father—
translation: In short, the request is about me, and you will learn from this honest old man—and even though I'm his son, I tell you, even though he's old and poor, my father—

original: One speak for both. What would you?
translation: One of you speak for both of you. What do you want?

original: Serve you, sir.
translation: To be your servant, sir.

original: That is the very defect of the matter, sir.
translation: That is the heart of the matter, sir.

original: I know thee well. Thou hast obtained thy suit.   Shylock thy master spoke with me this day,   And hath preferred thee,
translation: I know you well. You will get what you ask for. Your master Shylock spoke with me today and spoke well of you,

original: if it be preferment   To leave a rich Jew’s service, to become   The follower of so poor a gentleman.
translation: if you really want to leave the service of a rich Jew to become a servant of such a poor gentleman.

original: The old proverb is very well parted between my master  Shylock and you, sir—you have “the grace of God,” sir,  and he hath “enough.”
translation: The old proverb says, "the grace of God is enough." It could be split up between you and my master Shylock, sir. You have the grace of God, and he has enough.

original: Thou speak’st it well.—Go, father, with thy son.—
translation: Well said. Go along with your son, father.

original: Take leave of thy old master and inquire   My lodging out.—
translation: Go leave your old master and come inquire at my house.

original: Give him a livery   More guarded than his fellows'. See it done.
translation: Give him a outfit  more frilled  than his fellow servants. Make sure this is done.

original: Father, in. I cannot get a service, no. I have ne'er a  tongue in my head.
translation: Father, go. I can't get a job, no. I'm not very good at talking.

original: Well, if any man in Italy have a fairer table which doth offer to swear upon a book, I  shall have good fortune.
translation: Well, I have as good a palm as any man in Italy to swear upon a Bible with. I will have good luck.

original: Go to, here’s a simple line of  life. Here’s a small trifle of wives. Alas, fifteen  wives is nothing! Eleven widows and nine maids is a  simple coming-in for one man.
translation: Look, here's the life line. It predicts several wives. Fifteen wives is nothing! Eleven widows and nine young women is good for one man.

original: And then to ’scape  drowning thrice and to be in peril of my life with the  edge of a feather-bed—here are simple ’scapes.
translation: It looks like I will escape drowning three times and nearly lose my life in a feather-bed. Simple escapes.

original: Well, if  Fortune be a woman, she’s a good wench for this  gear.—Father, come. I’ll take my leave of the Jew in the twinkling.
translation: If Fortune is a lady, she's a good one for all this. Come with me, father. I'll leave the Jew in the blink of an eye.

original: I pray thee, good Leonardo, think on this.   These things being bought and orderly bestowed,   Return in haste,
translation: Please, Leonardo, pay attention to this. Buy and arrange these things and then come back to me quickly,

original: for I do feast tonight   My best esteemed acquaintance. Hie thee, go.
translation: for I'm having my most respected acquaintance over for dinner tonight. Get going now.

original: My best endeavours shall be done herein.
translation: I'll give it my best effort.

original: Where is your master?
translation: Where is your master?

original: Yonder, sir, he walks.
translation: Over there, sir, walking about.

original: Signor Bassanio!
translation: Sir Bassanio!

original: Gratiano!
translation: Gratiano!

original: I have a suit to you.
translation: I have a favor to ask of you.

original: You have obtained it.
translation: Your wish is my command.

original: You must not deny me. I must go with you to Belmont.
translation: Please don't deny my favor. I must go with you to Belmont.

original: Why, then you must. But hear thee, Gratiano.   Thou art too wild, too rude and bold of voice—
translation: Well then, you will. But listen, Gratiano. You are too wild and too rude, and you speak too boldly.

original: Parts that become thee happily enough   And in such eyes as ours appear not faults.
translation: These qualities suit you well and I don't mind them.

original: But where thou art not known, why, there they show   Something too liberal.
translation: But in a place where people don't know you, these qualities might seem excessive.

original: Pray thee, take pain   To allay with some cold drops of modesty   Thy skipping spirit,
translation: Please, take care to moderate your hot-headed spirit with some cold drops of modesty,

original: lest through thy wild behavior   I be misconst’red in the place I go to,   And lose my hopes.
translation: so that your wild behavior doesn't reflect poorly on me in Belmont, and ruin my own hopes there.

original: Signor Bassanio, hear me.   If I do not put on a sober habit,
translation: Sir Bassanio, listen to me. I give you permission to never trust me again if I do not behave in a sober fashion,

original: Talk with respect and swear but now and then,   Wear prayer books in my pocket, look demurely—
translation: talk respectfully and not swear too much, carry prayer books around with me, look modestly—

original: Nay more.   While grace is saying, hood mine eyes   Thus with my hat, and sigh and say, “Amen”—
translation: even more,  if during grace I do not pull my hat down over my eyes, sigh, and say "Amen"—

original: Use all the observance of civility   Like one well studied in a sad ostent   To please his grandam, never trust me more.
translation: if I don't follow every guideline of good manners like someone who's studied hard to please his grandmother.

original: Well, we shall see your bearing.
translation: Well, we will see how you behave.

original: Nay, but I bar tonight. You shall not gauge me By what we do tonight.
translation: But tonight is an exception. Don't gauge me based on what I do tonight.

original: No, that were pity.
translation: No, it would be a pity to judge you based on tonight.

original: I would entreat you rather to put on   Your boldest suit of mirth, for we have friends   That purpose merriment.
translation: Rather, I encourage you to to put on your boldest display of merriment, for we are entertaining two friends whom I want to entertain.

original: But fare you well.   I have some business.
translation: But I must say goodbye, because I have some business to take care of.

original: And I must to Lorenzo and the rest. But we will visit you at supper time.
translation: And I must go to Lorenzo and the others. We will see you at dinner time.

original: I am sorry thou wilt leave my father so.   Our house is hell, and thou, a merry devil,   Didst rob it of some taste of tediousness.
translation: I  am sorry that you are leaving my father's service like this. Our house is hell, and you, a joking little devil, made life here a little less boring.

original: But fare thee well, there is a ducat for thee.   And Launcelot, soon at supper shalt thou see   Lorenzo, who is thy new master’s guest.   Give him this letter.
translation: But I wish you well. Here is a ducat for you. And Launcelot, you will soon see a man named Lorenzo at dinner, a guest of your new master's. Give this letter to him.

original: Do it secretly.   And so farewell. I would not have my father   See me in talk with thee.
translation: Do it secretly. Goodbye, now. I don't want my father to see me talking with you.

original: Adieu! Tears exhibit my tongue. Most beautiful pagan,  most sweet Jew!
translation: Goodbye! I am speaking through my tears. You most beautiful pagan, you sweet Jew!

original: If a Christian do not play the knave and get thee, I am much deceived. But adieu.
translation: I'll bet some Christian will figure out a way to get you. But goodbye.

original: These foolish  drops do something drown my manly spirit. Adieu.
translation: These silly tears aren't very manly. Goodbye.

original: Farewell, good Launcelot.
translation: Farewell, good Launcelot.

original: Alack, what heinous sin is it in me   To be ashamed to be my father’s child!
translation: Alas, what a heinous sin it is for me to be ashamed to be my father's child!

original: But though I am a daughter to his blood,   I am not to his manners.
translation: I am his daughter by blood, but I have not inherited his manners.

original: O Lorenzo,   If thou keep promise, I shall end this strife,   Become a Christian and thy loving wife.
translation: Oh, Lorenzo, if you keep your promise I will end this pain by becoming a Christian and your loving wife.

original: Nay, we will slink away in supper time, Disguise us at my lodging, and return, All in an hour.
translation: No, we'll sneak off at dinner, disguise ourselves at my house, and then get back here all in an hour.

original: We have not made good preparation.
translation: We haven't prepared well enough for this.

original: We have not spoke us yet of torchbearers.
translation: We haven't got ourselves torchbearers yet.

original: 'Tis vile, unless it may be quaintly ordered, And better in my mind not undertook.
translation: Unless we plan carefully, this will turn out badly, and it will be better not to try this.

original: 'Tis now but four o'clock. We have two hours To furnish us.
