original: You should in all sense be much bound to him. For as I hear he was much bound for you.
translation: You owe him being all tied up and arrested, since I hear he was tied up for you.

original: No more than I am well acquitted of.
translation: But I have been well compensated for that.

original: Sir, you are very welcome to our house. It must appear in other ways than words,  Therefore I scant this breathing courtesy.
translation: Sir, you are very welcome to our house. I must welcome you in ways other than words, so I will stop speaking such courtesies.

original: By yonder moon I swear you do me wrong.   In faith, I gave it to the judge’s clerk.
translation: By the moon there I swear you are doing me wrong. Honestly, I gave it to the judge's clerk.

original: Would he were gelt that had it, for my part,   Since you do take it, love, so much at heart.
translation: Damn him for that, because this is really upsetting you, my love.

original: A quarrel, ho, already? What’s the matter?
translation: A lovers' quarrel already? What's the matter?

original: About a hoop of gold, a paltry ring   That she did give me,
translation: It's over a hoop of gold, a little ring she gave me with some writing carved on it,

original: whose posy was   For all the world like cutler’s poetry   Upon a knife, “Love me and leave me not.”
translation: the poetry of a knife-maker, saying, "Love me and don't leave me."

original: What talk you of the posy or the value?
translation: Why are you talking about the inscription or the value of the ring?

original: You swore to me when I did give it you   That you would wear it till your hour of death,   And that it should lie with you in your grave.
translation: You swore to me when I gave it to you that you would wear it until you died, and that it would lie in your grave with you.

original: Though not for me, yet for your vehement oaths,   You should have been respective and have kept it.
translation: You should have kept it and respected at least me, if not your strong oaths.

original: Gave it a judge’s clerk! No, God’s my judge.   The clerk will ne'er wear hair on ’s face that had it.
translation: You gave it to a judge's clerk! No, with God as my witness, I bet whoever you gave it to had no beard.

original: He will, an if he live to be a man.
translation: He will have one, if he lives long enough to grow into a man.

original: Ay, if a woman live to be a man.
translation: Yes, if a woman can grow into a man.

original: Now, by this hand, I gave it to a youth,   A kind of boy,
translation: I swear by my hand that I gave it to a young man, a boy,

original: a little scrubbèd boy   No higher than thyself, the judge’s clerk,   A prating boy that begged it as a fee.
translation: a little boy no taller than you, the judge's clerk, a talkative boy who begged for it as payment.

original: I could not for my heart deny it him.
translation: My heart couldn't bear denying him the ring.

original: You were to blame, I must be plain with you,   To part so slightly with your wife’s first gift,   A thing stuck on with oaths upon your finger   And so riveted with faith unto your flesh.
translation: I have to say, you are to blame for giving up your wife's first gift to you so easily, something stuck on your finger with oaths and riveted onto your flesh with good faith.

original: I gave my love a ring and made him swear   Never to part with it.
translation: I gave my husband a ring and made him swear never to lose it.

original: And here he stands.   I dare be sworn for him he would not leave it   Nor pluck it from his finger for the wealth   That the world masters.
translation: And here he stands. I daresay I'd swear on his behalf that he would not leave it or take it off his finger for all the money in the world.

original: Now in faith, Gratiano,   You give your wife too unkind a cause of grief.   An ’twere to me, I should be mad at it.
translation: Now, really, Gratiano, you are giving your wife cause for grief. If I were in her place, I'd be mad about it, too.

original: Why, I were best to cut my left hand off And swear I lost the ring defending it.
translation: I'd be better off cutting off my left hand and swearing that I lost the ring while trying to defend it.

original: My Lord Bassanio gave his ring away   Unto the judge that begged it and indeed   Deserved it too.
translation: My lord Bassanio gave his ring away to the judge that begged for it and, indeed, deserved it, too.

original: And then the boy, his clerk,   That took some pains in writing, he begged mine.
translation: And then the boy, the judge's clerk, who went through a lot of trouble writing things, begged for my ring.

original: And neither man nor master would take aught   But the two rings.
translation: Neither the judge nor his clerk would take anything but the two rings.

original: What ring gave you my lord? Not that, I hope, which you received of me.
translation: What ring did you give him, my lord? I hope not the one you got from me.

original: If I could add a lie unto a fault I would deny it. but you see my finger Hath not the ring upon it. It is gone.
translation: If I were able to top off my mistake with a lie, I'd deny it, but you can see that my finger doesn't have the ring on it. It is gone.

original: Even so void is your false heart of truth. By heaven, I will ne'er come in your bed Until I see the ring.
translation: Your false heart lacks truth just like your finger lacks the ring. By heaven, I will never go to bed with you until I see the ring.

original: Nor I in yours Till I again see mine.
translation: And I will never go to bed with you until I see my ring again.

original: Sweet Portia,   If you did know to whom I gave the ring,   If you did know for whom I gave the ring,
translation: Sweet Portia, if you knew to whom and for whom and for what reason I gave the ring,

original: And would conceive for what I gave the ring,   And how unwillingly I left the ring   When naught would be accepted but the ring,
translation: and if you knew how unwillingly I parted with it when the man accepted no gift other than the ring,

original: You would abate the strength of your displeasure.
translation: you wouldn't be so upset.

original: If you had known the virtue of the ring,   Or half her worthiness that gave the ring,   Or your own honor to contain the ring,   You would not then have parted with the ring.
translation: If you had known the virtue of the ring, or if you had realized half the worth of the woman who gave it to you, or if you had thought about your own honor in keeping the ring,  then you would not have given the ring away.

original: What man is there so much unreasonable,   If you had pleased to have defended it   With any terms of zeal, wanted the modesty   To urge the thing held as a ceremony?
translation: What kind of unreasonable man would have been so immodest as to demand it as a gift if you had defended it with any zeal?

original: Nerissa teaches me what to believe.   I’ll die for ’t but some woman had the ring.
translation: I will follow Nerissa's example. I'll bet my life that you gave it to some woman.

original: No, by my honor, madam, by my soul,   No woman had it but a civil doctor,
translation: No, I swear by my honor, madam, by my soul, I didn't give it to a woman, but rather to a doctor of law.

original: Which did refuse three thousand ducats of me   And begged the ring, the which I did deny him   And suffered him to go displeased away—   Even he that did uphold the very life   Of my dear friend.
translation: He refused an offer of three thousand ducats and begged for the ring, which I refused to give him. I even let him go away all displeased. And he is the one who saved my dear friend's life.

original: What should I say, sweet lady?
translation: What should I say, sweet lady?

original: I was enforced to send it after him.   I was beset with shame and courtesy.
translation: I was compelled to send the ring after him. I felt compelled by shame and courtesy.

original: My honor would not let ingratitude   So much besmear it.
translation: My honor would not let me show such ingratitude to the man.

original: Pardon me, good lady,   For by these blessèd candles of the night,   Had you been there I think you would have begged   The ring of me to give the worthy doctor.
translation: Pardon me, good lady. I swear by these blessed stars that if you were there you yourself would have begged me to give the ring to the worthy lawyer.

original: Let not that doctor e'er come near my house!   Since he hath got the jewel that I loved,   And that which you did swear to keep for me,   I will become as liberal as you.
translation: I hope that lawyer never comes near my house! Since he got the jewel that I loved and that you swore to keep for me, I will become as generous as you.

original: I’ll not deny him anything I have,   No, not my body, nor my husband’s bed.
translation: If he comes around, I won't deny him anything I have. No, not my body, not even my marriage bed.

original: Know him I shall, I am well sure of it.   Lie not a night from home.
translation: I'll know who he is, I'm sure. You'd better not spend a single night away from home.

original: Watch me like Argus.   If you do not, if I be left alone,   Now, by mine honor—which is yet mine own—   I’ll have that doctor for my bedfellow.
translation: Watch me like the god Argus, with his hundred eyes. If not, if you leave me alone, I swear by my honor (which is still mine) that I'll sleep with that lawyer.

original: And I his clerk. Therefore be well  advised How you do leave me to mine own protection.
translation: And I'll sleep with his clerk. So be wary of leaving me to my own ways.

original: Well, do you so, let not me take him then. For if I do I’ll mar the young clerk’s pen.
translation: Well, go ahead, but don't let me catch him. If that happens, I'll break the clerk's pen.

original: I am th' unhappy subject of these quarrels.
translation: All this unhappy quarreling is because of me.

original: Sir, grieve not you. You are welcome notwithstanding.
translation: Sir, don't worry. You are welcome here regardless.

original: Portia, forgive me this enforcèd wrong,
translation: Portia, forgive me for this mistake that I was forced into.

original: And in the hearing of these many friends   I swear to thee, even by thine own fair eyes   Wherein I see myself—
translation: In front of our friends I swear to you by your own beautiful eyes in which I can see my image—

original: Mark you but that!   In both my eyes he doubly sees himself—   In each eye, one.
translation: Listen to that! In both my eyes he sees two images of himself, one in each eye.

original: Swear by your double self,   And there’s an oath of credit!
translation: If you swear by your double self, then that will be a serious oath!

original: Nay, but hear me. Pardon this fault, and by my soul I swear I never more will break an oath with thee.
translation: Listen to me. Pardon me for this and by my soul I swear I will never break another promise to you.

original: I once did lend my body for his wealth,   Which but for him that had your husband’s ring   Had quite miscarried.
translation: Once I put my body in danger to get him money, and that arrangement would not have gone well if it wasn't for the man who now has your husband's ring.

original: I dare be bound again,   My soul upon the forfeit, that your lord   Will never more break faith advisedly.
translation: I dare to risk something again: I'll wager my soul that your husband will never again break a promise to you.

original: Then you shall be his surety. Give him this, And bid him keep it better than the other.
translation: Then you will vouch for him. Give him this ring, and tell him to hold onto it better than the last one.

original: Here, Lord Bassanio. Swear to keep this ring.
translation: Here, Lord Bassanio. Swear that you will keep this ring.

original: By heaven, it is the same I gave the doctor!
translation: By heaven, this is the same ring I gave to the lawyer!

original: I had it of him. Pardon me, Bassanio, For by this ring, the doctor lay with me.
translation: He gave it to me. Forgive me, Bassanio, because I slept with the lawyer for the ring.

original: And pardon me, my gentle Gratiano,  For that same scrubbèd boy, the doctor’s clerk, In lieu of this, last night did lie with me.
translation: And forgive me, my gentle Gratiano, because I slept with that same young boy, the lawyer's clerk, in return for this ring last night.

original: Why, this is like the mending of highways In summer where the ways are fair enough! What, are we cuckolds ere we have deserved it?
translation: This is like fixing highways in the summer when there's nothing wrong with them! We've been cheated on before we've even deserved it!

original: Speak not so grossly.—You are all amazed.
translation: Don't speak like that. You are all shocked.

original: Here is a letter. Read it at your leisure.   It comes from Padua, from Bellario.
translation: Here is a letter. Read it when you can. It comes from Padua, from Bellario.

original: There you shall find that Portia was the doctor,   Nerissa there her clerk.
translation: In the letter you will learn that Portia was the lawyer and Nerissa was her clerk. Lorenzo will testify that I left here when you did and just got back now.

original: Lorenzo here   Shall witness I set forth as soon as you,   And even but now returned.
translation: I haven't even entered the house yet.

original: I have not yet   Entered my house.—Antonio, you are welcome.   And I have better news in store for you   Than you expect.   [gives ANTONIO another letter]
translation: Antonio, you are welcome here. And I have even better news in store for you than you expect.

original: Unseal this letter soon.   There you shall find three of your argosies   Are richly come to harbor suddenly.
translation: Open this letter soon and you will read that three of your ships have suddenly come into harbor full of riches.

original: You shall not know by what strange accident   I chancèd on this letter.
translation: You can't guess by what strange coincidence I happened upon this letter.

original: I am dumb.
translation: I am flabbergasted.

original: Were you the doctor and I knew you not?
translation: Were you the lawyer and I didn't recognize you?

original: Were you the clerk that is to make me  cuckold?
translation: Were you the clerk that supposedly slept with my wife?

original: Ay, but the clerk that never means to do it Unless he live until he be a man.
translation: Yes, but the clerk will never sleep with your wife unless he becomes a man.

original: Sweet doctor, you shall be my bedfellow. When I am absent then lie with my wife.
translation: Sweet lawyer, you will share my bed tonight. And when I am gone, you sleep alongside my wife.

original: Sweet lady, you have given me life and living. For here I read for certain that my ships Are safely come to road.
translation: Sweet lady, you have given me life and a living. I read here for certain that my ships have safely returned.

original: How now, Lorenzo? My clerk hath some good comforts too for you.
translation: How are you now, Lorenzo? My clerk has something good for you, too.

original: Ay, and I’ll give them him without a fee.
translation: Yes, and I'll give it to you for free.

original: There do I give to you and Jessica,   From the rich Jew, a special deed of gift,
translation: I am giving you and Jessica a will from the rich Jew.

original: After his death of all he dies possessed of.
translation: After he dies, all that he owns is yours.

original: Fair ladies, you drop manna in the way Of starvèd people.
translation: Fair ladies, it is as if you are giving blessed bread to starving people.

original: It is almost morning,   And yet I am sure you are not satisfied   Of these events at full.
translation: It is almost morning, and yet I am sure you aren't completely satisfied with the story of these events.

original: Let us go in,   And charge us there upon interr'gatories,   And we will answer all things faithfully.
translation: Let's go inside and there you can ask us more questions, and we will answer them all honestly.

original: Let it be so. The first interrogatory   That my Nerissa shall be sworn on is   Whether till the next night she had rather stay,   Or go to bed now, being two hours to day.
translation: Let's do that. The first question that my Nerissa will have to answer is whether she would rather wait until the next night or just go to bed now, since it's daylight in two hours.

original: But were the day come, I should wish it dark,   That I were couching with the doctor’s clerk.
translation: But if the day should come, I would wish it were dark out, so that I could be sleeping with the lawyer's clerk.

original: Well, while I live I’ll fear no other thing   So sore as keeping safe Nerissa’s ring.
translation: Well, as long as I live I'll worry about nothing else as much as about keeping Nerissa's ring safe.

original: I’ll pheeze you, in faith.
translation: I'll get you back, I promise.

original: A pair of stocks, you rogue!
Y'are a baggage, the Slys are no rogues. Look in the  chronicles—we came in with Richard Conqueror. Therefore paucas pallabris  : let the world slide. Sessa!
You will not pay for the glasses you have burst?
translation: You won't pay for the glasses you've broken?

original: No, not a denier. Go by, Saint Jeronimy. Go to thy cold bed and warm thee.
I know my remedy. I must go fetch the thirdborough.
translation: I know what to do. I'll go call the constable.

original: Third, or fourth, or fifth borough, I’ll answer him by  law. I’ll not budge an inch, boy. Let him come, and kindly.
translation: Call every last one, I'll answer them all. I have my rights. I won't budge an inch. Let the constable come—I welcome him!

original: Huntsman, I charge thee, tender well my hounds.   Breathe Merriman, the poor cur is embossed,
translation: Huntsman, take care of my hounds. Let Merriman rest—the poor dog's exhausted.

original: And couple Clowder with the deep-mouthed brach.
translation: And leash Clowder with the bitch with the deep bark.

original: Saw’st thou not, boy, how Silver made it good   At the hedge corner, in the coldest fault?   I would not lose the dog for twenty pound.
translation: Didn't you see how Silver picked up the trail at the hedge corner, when the scent was coldest? I wouldn't sell that dog for twenty pounds.

original: Why, Belman is as good as he, my lord.   He cried upon it at the merest loss,   And twice today picked out the dullest scent.
translation: Why, Belman is just as good, my lord. He was the only one to howl when the scent was lost completely, and twice today he picked it up when it was weakest.

original: Trust me, I take him for the better dog.
translation: Trust me, I think he's the better dog.

original: Thou art a fool. If Echo were as fleet,   I would esteem him worth a dozen such.
translation: You're a fool. If Echo were as fast, he'd be worth a dozen Belmans.

original: But sup them well and look unto them all.   Tomorrow I intend to hunt again.
translation: But feed them all well and look after them. I intend to go hunting again tomorrow.

original: I will, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: What’s here? One dead, or drunk? See, doth he breathe?
translation: What's this here? Is he dead or drunk? Check and see if he's breathing.

original: He breathes, my lord. Were he not warmed with ale, This were a bed but cold to sleep so soundly.
translation: He's breathing, my lord. But he couldn't be sleeping so deeply in such a cold place if beer wasn't keeping him warm.

original: O monstrous beast, how like a swine he lies!   Grim death, how foul and loathsome is thine image!
translation: Oh, what a monstrous beast, lying there like a pig! Grim death, how foul and hateful your twin—sleep—is!

original: Sirs, I will practice on this drunken man.
translation: Gentlemen, I will play a trick on this drunken man.

original: What think you: if he were conveyed to bed,   Wrapped in sweet clothes, rings put upon his fingers,   A most delicious banquet by his bed,   And brave attendants near him when he wakes,
translation: What do you think: if he were carried to bed, dressed in fresh clothes, had rings put on his fingers, a delicious feast laid out by his bed, and had finely dressed servants near him when he woke up

original: Would not the beggar then forget himself?
translation: —wouldn't the beggar be confused then?

original: Believe me, lord, I think he cannot choose.
translation: I don't think he'd have any choice, my lord, believe me.

original: It would seem strange unto him when he waked.
translation: Everything would seem strange to him when he woke up.

original: Even as a flatt'ring dream or worthless fancy.   Then take him up and manage well the jest.
translation: Like a nice dream or an empty fantasy. So take him inside and start setting up the prank.

original: Carry him gently to my fairest chamber   And hang it round with all my wanton pictures.
translation: Carry him gently to my finest room, and hang all my erotic paintings on the walls.

original: Balm his foul head in warm distilled waters   And burn sweet wood to make the lodging sweet.
translation: Bathe his filthy head with warm, clean water, and burn fragrant wood to make the room smell sweet.

original: Procure me music ready when he wakes,   To make a dulcet and a heavenly sound.
translation: Find some musicians to be ready for when he wakes, so they can make sweet and heavenly sounds for him.

original: And if he chance to speak, be ready straight   And with a low submissive reverence   Say, “What is it your Honor will command?”
translation: If he happens to speak, be ready right away—bow low and say obediently, "What does your Honor command us to do?"

original: Let one attend him with a silver basin   Full of rose-water and bestrewed with flowers,   Another bear the ewer, the third a diaper,
translation: Let one servant wait on him with a silver bowl full of rosewater and flowers. Have another servant carry the pitcher, and a third carry a towel,

original: And say, “Will ’t please your Lordship cool your  hands?”   Someone be ready with a costly suit   And ask him what apparel he will wear.
translation: and say, "Would it please your Lordship to cool your hands?" Have someone ready with expensive clothing, and ask him what he wants to wear.

original: Another tell him of his hounds and horse,   And that his lady mourns at his disease.
translation: Have another servant tell him about his dogs and his horse, and explain that his wife has been grieving over his illness.

original: Persuade him that he hath been lunatic,   And when he says he is, say that he dreams,   For he is nothing but a mighty lord.
translation: Convince him he's been out of his mind, and when he says that he's insane  now , tell him that he's just mistaken, for he is really a mighty lord.

original: This do, and do it kindly, gentle sirs.   It will be pastime passing excellent   If it be husbanded with modesty.
translation: Do all this, and do it convincingly, gentle sirs. If this can be managed subtly, it will be some excellent entertainment for us.

original: My lord, I warrant you we will play our part As he shall think by our true diligence He is no less than what we say he is.
translation: My lord, I promise you that we'll play our parts so well that he'll believe everything we tell him.

original: Take him up gently, and to bed with him, And each one to his office when he wakes.
translation: Carry him gently off to bed, and have everyone in position for when he wakes up.

original: Sirrah, go see what trumpet ’tis that sounds.
translation: Go see what that trumpet's for, boy.

original: Belike some noble gentleman that means, Traveling some journey, to repose him here.
translation: Probably some noble gentleman on a journey, who wants to stop and rest here.

original: How now! who is it?
translation: Hello! Who is it?

original: An’t please your Honor, players That offer service to your Lordship.
translation: It's a troupe of actors, your Honor, offering to perform for your Lordship.

original: Bid them come near.
translation: Tell them to come in.

original: Now, fellows, you are welcome.
translation: Now, fellows, you are welcome here.

original: We thank your Honor.
translation: We thank your Honor.

original: Do you intend to stay with me tonight?
translation: Do you intend to sleep here tonight?

original: So please your Lordship to accept our duty.
translation: If it would please your Lordship to have us.

original: With all my heart.
translation: With all my heart.

original: This fellow I remember   Since once he played a farmer’s eldest son.
translation: I remember this fellow here—he once played the part of a farmer's eldest son.

original: 'Twas where you wooed the gentlewoman so well.   I have forgot your name, but sure that part   Was aptly fitted and naturally performed.
translation: That was the play in which you courted the gentlewoman so successfully. I've forgotten your name, but you were well suited for that role, and played it realistically.

original: I think ’twas Soto that your Honor means.
translation: I think your Honor means the character "Soto."

original: 'Tis very true. Thou didst it excellent.
translation: Yes, that's right. You played it excellently

original: Well, you are come to me in happy time,   The rather for I have some sport in hand   Wherein your cunning can assist me much.
translation: . Well, you've come at just the right time, especially because I have some special entertainment planned and could use your acting skills.

original: There is a lord will hear you play tonight;   But I am doubtful of your modesties,
translation: There is a lord who will watch you perform tonight, but I'm worried about your self-control

original: Lest over-eyeing of his odd behavior—   For yet his Honor never heard a play—   You break into some merry passion   And so offend him.
translation: —for his Honor has never seen a play before—and I fear that you might notice his odd behavior and burst out laughing, and offend him.

original: For I tell you, sirs,   If you should smile, he grows impatient.
translation: I tell you, sirs, if you even smile, he will notice.

original: Fear not, my lord, we can contain ourselves Were he the veriest antic in the world.
translation: Don't worry, my lord. We can control ourselves even if he's the greatest buffoon in the world.

original: Go, sirrah, take them to the buttery And give them friendly welcome every one.  Let them want nothing that my house affords.
translation: Go, fellow, take them to the pantry and make them all welcome. See that they have whatever they need.

original: Sirrah, go you to Barthol’mew, my page,   And see him dressed in all suits like a lady.
translation: And you, fellow, go find my page, Bartholomew, and dress him up like a lady in great detail.

original: That done, conduct him to the drunkard’s chamber   And call him “madam,” do him obeisance.
translation: When that's done, bring him to the drunkard's room, address him as "madam," and bow to him and treat him as if he were the lady of the house.

original: Tell him from me, as he will win my love,   He bear himself with honorable action,   Such as he hath observed in noble ladies   Unto their lords, by them accomplishèd.
translation: Tell Bartholomew I said this: if he wants to please me, he will conduct himself properly, copying the way he's seen noble ladies act towards their husbands.

original: Such duty to the drunkard let him do   With soft low tongue and lowly courtesy,   And say,
translation: Let him attend to the drunkard like that: speaking softly, acting humble and polite, and saying things like,

original: “What is ’t your Honor will command,   Wherein your lady and your humble wife   May show her duty and make known her love?”
translation: "What does your Honor command your lady and humble wife to do, that she might show her devotion and love?"

original: And then with kind embracements, tempting kisses,   And with declining head into his bosom,
translation: And then with kind embraces, tempting kisses, and his head resting on the drunkard's breast,

original: Bid him shed tears, as being overjoyed   To see her noble lord restored to health,   Who for this seven years hath esteemed him   No better than a poor and loathsome beggar.
translation: Bartholomew should weep as if he's overjoyed to see his noble husband restored to health after believing for the last seven years that he was no better than a poor, disgusting beggar.

original: And if the boy have not a woman’s gift   To rain a shower of commanded tears,   An onion will do well for such a shift,
translation: And if the boy lacks a woman's gift for crying on command, an onion will serve the same purpose.

original: Which in a napkin being close conveyed   Shall in despite enforce a watery eye.
translation: Hide one in a handkerchief and put it close to his face, and that will certainly make his eyes water.

original: I know the boy will well usurp the grace,   Voice, gait, and action of a gentlewoman.
translation: I know the boy will convincingly mimic the grace, voice, walk, and gestures of a gentlewoman.

original: I long to hear him call the drunkard “husband,”   And how my men will stay themselves from laughter   When they do homage to this simple peasant.
translation: I can't wait to hear him call the drunkard "husband," and to watch my men contain their laughter as they bow to this simple peasant.

original: I’ll in to counsel them. Haply my presence   May well abate the over-merry spleen   Which otherwise would grow into extremes.
translation: I'll go in and advise them. Perhaps my presence will restrain their joy and rowdiness, which otherwise might get out of control.

original: For God’s sake, a pot of small ale.
translation: For God's sake, someone bring me a mug of cheap beer.

original: Will ’t please your Lordship drink a cup of sack?
Will ’t please your Honor taste of these conserves?
translation: Would your Honor like to try this dried fruit?

original: What raiment will your Honor wear today?
translation: What outfit will your Honor wear today?

original: I am Christophero Sly. Call not me “Honor” nor  “Lordship.”
translation: I am Christopher Sly. Don't call me your "Honor" or your "Lordship."

original: I ne'er drank sack in my life. An if you  give me any conserves, give me conserves of beef.
translation: I've never drunk Spanish wine in my life. And if you give me anything "preserved," give me some salted beef.

original: Ne'er  ask me what raiment I’ll wear, for I have no more  doublets than backs, no more stockings than legs, nor no more shoes than feet,
translation: Don't bother asking what "outfit" I'll wear, for I have no more jackets than I do backs, no more stockings than I have legs, and no more shoes than I have feet.

original: nay sometime more feet than  shoes, or such shoes as my toes look through the  over-leather.
translation: Sometimes I even have more feet than shoes, unless the ones where my toes stick out count as shoes.

original: Heaven cease this idle humor in your Honor!
translation: May God end this foolish fantasy in your Honor's mind!

original: Oh, that a mighty man of such descent,   Of such possessions and so high esteem,   Should be infusèd with so foul a spirit!
translation: Alas, that a mighty man of such noble birth, with so much wealth and such a good reputation, should be infected with such a terrible illness!

original: What, would you make me mad?
translation: What, are you trying to make me go crazy?

original: Am not I Christopher Sly,  old Sly’s son of Burton Heath, by birth a peddler, by  education a cardmaker, by transmutation a bearherd, and  now by present profession a tinker?
translation: Aren't I Christopher Sly, son of old Sly from Barton-on-the-Heath, a peddler by birth, trained to be a  cardmaker , who then became a bear keeper, and now a pot-mender?

original: Ask Marian Hacket,  the fat alewife of Wincot, if she know me not! If she  say I am not fourteen pence on the score for sheer ale,  score me up for the lying’st knave in Christendom.
translation: Ask Marian Hacket, the fat innkeeper in Wincot, if she knows me! If she doesn't tell you about the tab I've run up—fourteen pence on beer alone—then you can call me the biggest liar in God's kingdom.

original: What! I am not bestraught! Here’s—
translation: What! I'm not crazy! Here's—

original: O, this it is that makes your lady mourn!
translation: Oh, it's this that makes your wife mourn!

original: O, this is it that makes your servants droop!
translation: Oh, it's this that makes your servants hang their heads in sorrow!

original: Hence comes it that your kindred shuns your house,   As beaten hence by your strange lunacy.
translation: And this is why your relatives avoid your house, as if beaten away by your strange insanity.

original: O noble lord, bethink thee of thy birth,   Call home thy ancient thoughts from banishment,   And banish hence these abject lowly dreams.
translation: Oh noble lord, remember your lineage, call back the thoughts of your former state of mind, and banish these worthless, lowly fantasies.

original: Look how thy servants do attend on thee,   Each in his office ready at thy beck.
translation: Look how your servants attend to you, each one ready to obey your every request.

original: Wilt thou have music? Hark! Apollo plays,
translation: Do you want music? Listen! Apollo, god of music, plays for you.

original: And twenty cagèd nightingales do sing:   Or wilt thou sleep?
translation: And twenty caged nightingales sing along. Or do you want to sleep?

original: We’ll have thee to a couch   Softer and sweeter than the lustful bed   On purpose trimmed up for Semiramis.
translation: We'll bring you to a couch that's softer and more fragrant than the lustful bed of  Semiramis .

original: Say thou wilt walk, we will bestrew the ground.   Or wilt thou ride? Thy horses shall be trapped,   Their harness studded all with gold and pearl.
translation: Say you want to walk, and we'll strew the ground with flowers. Or do you want to ride? Your horses will be made ready, their harnesses studded with gold and pearls.

original: Dost thou love hawking? Thou hast hawks will soar   Above the morning lark.
translation: Do you like hawking? You have hawks that can soar higher than the morning lark.

original: Or wilt thou hunt?   Thy hounds shall make the welkin answer them   And fetch shrill echoes from the hollow earth.
translation: Or do you want to hunt? Your hounds will make the heavens and earth echo with their barks.

original: Say thou wilt course. Thy greyhounds are as swift As breathed stags, ay, fleeter than the roe.
translation: Say you want to hunt rabbits. Your greyhounds are as swift as healthy stags, yes, and quicker than young deer.

original: Dost thou love pictures? We will fetch thee straight   Adonis painted by a running brook   And Cytherea all in sedges hid,
translation: Do you like pictures? We'll instantly fetch you one of  Adonis  next to a running brook, with  Venus  hidden in the rushes and spying on him.

original: Which seem to move and wanton with her breath,   Even as the waving sedges play with wind.
translation: The rushes seem to move seductively with her sighs, just like real grass swaying in the wind.

original: We’ll show thee Io as she was a maid And how she was beguileèd and surprised, As lively painted as the deed was done.
Or Daphne roaming through a thorny wood,   Scratching her legs that one shall swear she bleeds,   And at that sight shall sad Apollo weep,
translation: Or one of  Daphne running through a thorny wood, her legs scratched up and Apollo weeping at that sad sight .

original: So workmanly the blood and tears are drawn.
translation: The blood and tears are drawn so well you'll swear that they're real.

original: Thou art a lord, and nothing but a lord.  Thou hast a lady far more beautiful Than any woman in this waning age.
translation: You are a lord, and nothing less than a lord. You have a wife who is far more beautiful than any other woman in this declining age.

original: And till the tears that she hath shed for thee Like envious floods o'errun her lovely face, She was the fairest creature in the world—  And yet she is inferior to none.
Am I a lord, and have I such a lady?   Or do I dream? Or have I dreamed till now?
translation: Am I a lord? Do I have such a lady? Or am I dreaming? Or have I been dreaming until now?

original: I do not sleep: I see, I hear, I speak.   I smell sweet savors and I feel soft things.
translation: I'm not asleep: I can see, and hear, and speak. I can smell sweet aromas and feel soft things.

original: Upon my life, I am a lord indeed   And not a tinker, nor Christopher Sly.
translation: I swear, I must be a lord indeed! I'm not a tinker, and I'm not Christopher Sly.

original: Well, bring our lady hither to our sight,   And once again, a pot o' the smallest ale.
translation: Well, bring my lady here before me, and I'll ask again, bring me a mug of the cheapest beer.

original: Will ’t please your Mightiness to wash your hands?   O, how we joy to see your wit restored!
translation: Would your greatness like to wash your hands? Oh, how overjoyed we are to see your sanity restored!

original: O, that once more you knew but what you are!   These fifteen years you have been in a dream
translation: Oh, if only you could better remember who you are! These past fifteen years you've been living in a dream.

original: Or, when you waked, so waked as if you slept.
translation: Even when you were awake, it was as if you slept.

original: These fifteen years! By my fay, a goodly nap.  But did I never speak of all that time?
translation: Fifteen years! By God, that's quite a nap. But did I not speak that entire time?

original: O, yes, my lord, but very idle words.
translation: Oh yes, my lord, but only complete nonsense.

original: For though you lay here in this goodly chamber,   Yet would you say ye were beaten out of door;   And rail upon the hostess of the house,
translation: Even though you were lying here in this nice room, you would talk as if you'd been thrown out of a tavern, and you'd curse at the tavern's hostess,

original: And say you would present her at the leet,   Because she brought stone jugs and no sealed quarts.
translation: and swear you would take her to court for cheating you out of liquor.

original: Sometimes you would call out for Cicely Hacket.
translation: Sometimes you would call out for Cicely Hacket.

original: Ay, the woman’s maid of the house.
translation: Yes, the hostess's maid.

original: Why, sir, you know no house nor no such maid,   Nor no such men as you have reckoned up,
translation: But sir, you don't know any such house or any such maid, or any of the men you dreamed up,

original: As Stephen Sly and old John Naps of Greece,   And Peter Turph and Henry Pimpernell,
translation: like Stephen Sly and Old John Naps of Greet, and Peter Turph and Henry Pimpernell,

original: And twenty more such names and men as these,   Which never were, nor no man ever saw.
translation: and twenty more names like this—men who never existed.

original: Now Lord be thanked for my good amends!
translation: Thank the Lord for my recovery!

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: I thank thee. Thou shalt not lose by it.
translation: Thank you all. You won't regret my return.

original: How fares my noble lord?
translation: How is my noble lord doing?

original: Marry, I fare well, For here is cheer enough. Where is my wife?
translation: Well, I'm doing well. Everything's quite nice around here. Where is my wife?

original: Here, noble lord. What is thy will with her?
translation: Here, noble lord. What do you wish of her?

original: Are you my wife and will not call me “husband”? My men should call me “lord.” I am your goodman.
translation: You say you're my wife, but you won't call me your husband? My men should call me "lord," not you. I am your husband, your fellow.

original: My husband and my lord, my lord and husband, I am your wife in all obedience.
translation: You are my husband and my lord, my lord and my husband, and I am your obedient wife.

original: I know it well.—What must I call her?
translation: I know it now.—

original: “Madam.”
translation: "Madam."

original: “Alice Madam,” or “Joan Madam”?
“Madam,” and nothing else. So lords call ladies.
translation: Just "madam," and nothing else. That's what lords call their ladies.

original: Madam wife, they say that I have dreamed And slept above some fifteen year or more.
translation: Madam wife, they say that I've been dreaming or asleep for fifteen years or more.

original: Ay, and the time seems thirty unto me, Being all this time abandoned from your bed.
translation: Yes, and it seemed like thirty years to me, as I've been banished from your bed this whole time.

original: 'Tis much.—Servants, leave me and her alone. Madam, undress you and come now to bed.
translation: That's a lot.—Servants, leave me and her alone.—Madam, undress and come to bed.

original: Thrice noble lord, let me entreat of you   To pardon me yet for a night or two,   Or if not so, until the sun be set.
translation: Noble lord, I ask you to pardon me for another night or two, or at least wait until nightfall.

original: For your physicians have expressly charged,   In peril to incur your former malady,   That I should yet absent me from your bed.
translation: Your doctors have expressly ordered me not to sleep with you, as otherwise you might be in danger of a relapse of your illness.

original: I hope this reason stands for my excuse.
translation: I hope this reason will stand as my excuse.

original: Ay, it stands so that I may hardly tarry so long. But I would be loath to fall into my dreams again. I will  therefore tarry in despite of the flesh and the blood.
translation: Well, something's standing up and making it so I can hardly wait that long. But I would hate to fall back into my dreams. I'll wait, despite my flesh and blood.

original: Your Honor’s players, hearing your amendment,   Are come to play a pleasant comedy,
translation: Your Honor's actors heard about your recovery and have come to perform a pleasant comedy for you.

original: For so your doctors hold it very meet,   Seeing too much sadness hath congealed your blood,   And melancholy is the nurse of frenzy.
translation: Your doctors approve of this, as too much sadness has made your blood congeal, and melancholy can lead to more insanity.

original: Therefore they thought it good you hear a play   And frame your mind to mirth and merriment,   Which bars a thousand harms and lengthens life.
translation: So they think it would be good for you to watch a play and direct your thoughts toward laughter and joy—both of which can prevent a thousand illnesses and lengthen your life.

original: Marry, I will. Let them play it. Is not a comonty a Christmas gambold or a tumbling-trick?
No, my good lord, it is more pleasing stuff.
translation: No, my good lord, it is more pleasing stuff than that.

original: What, household stuff?
translation: What, stuff from a house?

original: It is a kind of history.
translation: It's a kind of story.

original: Well, we’ll see ’t. Come, madam wife, sit by my side  and let the world slip. We shall ne'er be younger.
translation: Well, let's watch it. Come, madam wife, sit by my side. Forget about the world. We aren't getting any younger.

original: Tranio, since for the great desire I had   To see fair Padua, nursery of arts,   I am arrived for fruitful Lombardy,   The pleasant garden of great Italy,
translation: Tranio, because I have always longed to see Padua and its famous university, I wanted to stop here on my way to fertile Lombardy, that pleasant garden of great Italy.

original: And by my father’s love and leave am armed   With his goodwill and thy good company.
translation: And now, thanks to my father's love and approval, and your own good company—here I am.

original: My trusty servant, well approved in all,   Here let us breathe and haply institute   A course of learning and ingenious studies.
translation: So, my trusty, dependable servant, let's rest here a while and begin a course of intellectual studies.

original: Pisa, renownèd for grave citizens,   Gave me my being and my father first,
translation: I was born in Pisa, famous for its serious citizens, along with my father before me: Vincentio of the Bentivoli family.

original: A merchant of great traffic through the world,   Vincentio, come of the Bentivolii.   Vincentio’s son, brought up in Florence,
translation: He was a successful merchant and world traveler, and it now seems fitting that I, Vincentio's son, brought up in Florence,

original: It shall become to serve all hopes conceived   To deck his fortune with his virtuous deeds.
translation: should fulfill all my father's hopes for me and increase his wealth with my own virtuous deeds .

original: And therefore, Tranio, for the time I study   Virtue, and that part of philosophy   Will I apply that treats of happiness   By virtue specially to be achieved.
translation: And therefore, Tranio, I will study virtue for now, and that area of philosophy that discusses how to achieve happiness through virtue.

original: as he that leaves   A shallow plash to plunge him in the deep   And with satiety seeks to quench his thirst.
translation: and now I feel like I've left a puddle behind and jumped into an ocean, hoping to quench my thirst.

original: Mi perdonato,   gentle master mine.   I am in all affected as yourself,   Glad that you thus continue your resolve   To suck the sweets of sweet philosophy.
translation: Pardon me, my gentle master. I agree with everything you've said, and I'm glad that you've followed through with your decision to enjoy all the pleasures of sweet philosophy.

original: Only, good master, while we do admire   This virtue and this moral discipline,   Let’s be no stoics nor no stocks, I pray,
translation: Only, good master, while we're studying all this admirable virtue and moral discipline, let's not become  stoics or stocks ,

original: Or so devote to Aristotle’s checks   As Ovid be an outcast quite abjured.
translation: and let's not focus on  Aristotle's restraints so much that we forget to read Ovid .

original: Balk logic with acquaintance that you have,   And practice rhetoric in your common talk;   Music and poesy use to quicken you;
translation: Practice your logic with the friends you have, and use rhetoric in everyday talk.  Stimulate yourself with music and poetry.

original: The mathematics and the metaphysics—   Fall to them as you find your stomach serves you.
translation: And as for mathematics and metaphysics—follow your appetite, and only study what you can stomach.

original: No profit grows where is no pleasure ta'en.   In brief, sir, study what you most affect.
translation: You'll gain no profit from something you take no pleasure in. In short, sir, study what you enjoy.

original: Gramercies, Tranio, well dost thou advise.
translation: Many thanks, Tranio, for the good advice.

original: If, Biondello, thou wert come ashore,   We could at once put us in readiness   And take a lodging fit to entertain
translation: If Biondello would come ashore, we could get ready at once and find a place to stay.

original: Such friends as time in Padua shall beget.   But stay awhile. What company is this?
translation: Then we would have a place to entertain the friends we'll make here in Padua. But wait a minute. Who are all these people?

original: Master, some show to welcome us to town.
translation: Master, maybe it's a gathering to welcome us to town.

original: Gentlemen, importune me no farther,   For how I firmly am resolved you know—
translation: Gentlemen, stop pestering me about this. You know that my mind is made up.

original: That is, not to bestow my youngest daughter   Before I have a husband for the elder.
translation: I won't let my younger daughter marry until I've found a husband for the elder one.

original: To cart her, rather. She’s too rough for me.— There, there, Hortensio, will you any wife?
I pray you, sir, is it your will To make a stale of me amongst these mates?
translation: Please, sir, is it your intention to make a laughingstock of me in front of these mates?

original: “Mates,” maid? how mean you that? No mates for you  Unless you were of gentler, milder mold.
translation: "Mates," girl? What do you mean by that? You won't have any mates until you improve your temper.

original: I' faith, sir, you shall never need to fear.   I wis it is not halfway to her heart.
translation: Don't worry, sir, you don't need to worry about being my husband. Indeed, marriage doesn't appeal to my heart.

original: But if it were, doubt not her care should be   To comb your noddle with a three-legged stool   And paint your face and use you like a fool.
translation: But even if it did, the only thing I'd want to do with you is knock you on the head with a three-legged stool, scratch up your face, and make you my fool.

original: From all such devils, good Lord, deliver us!
translation: May God preserve us from all devils like her!

original: And me too, good Lord!
translation: And me too, good Lord!

original: Husht, master, here’s some good pastime toward. That wench is stark mad or wonderful froward.
translation: Keep quiet master, here's some entertainment for us. That girl is either insane or incredibly disobedient.

original: But in the other’s silence do I see Maid’s mild behavior and sobriety. Peace, Tranio.
translation: But her sister is silent, and seems to have a proper girl's mildness and obedience. Quiet, Tranio.

original: Well said, master. Mum, and gaze  your fill.
translation: You're right, master. Let's keep quiet and enjoy the sight.

original: Gentlemen, that I may soon make good  What I have said—Bianca, get you in, And let it not displease thee, good Bianca, For I will love thee ne'er the less, my girl.
translation: Gentlemen, I want to make good on what I've said—so Bianca, go inside. And don't let this make you unhappy, good Bianca, for I'll never love you any less, my girl.

original: A pretty peat! It is best Put finger in the eye, an she knew why.
translation: What a spoiled pet! If she knew what she was doing, she would have put on a show of weeping.

original: Sister, content you in my discontent.—   Sir, to your pleasure humbly I subscribe.
translation: Sister, let yourself be happy in my unhappiness. Sir, I will humbly obey your will.

original: Hark, Tranio! Thou may’st hear Minerva speak.
Signior Baptista, will you be so strange? Sorry am I that our goodwill effects Bianca’s grief.
translation: Sir Baptista, will you really act so unnaturally? I'm sorry that our good will towards Bianca should cause her grief.

original: Why will you mew her up, Signior Baptista, for this fiend of hell And make her bear the penance of her tongue?
translation: Why would you cage her up in place of this fiend from hell, Sir Baptista, and punish her for her sister's tongue?

original: Gentlemen, content ye. I am resolved.— Go in, Bianca.
translation: Gentleman, calm down. I've made my decision, and I can't be swayed.—Go inside, Bianca.

original: And for I know she taketh most delight   In music, instruments, and poetry,   Schoolmasters will I keep within my house,
translation: And I know that she loves music, playing her instruments, and poetry, so I'll keep tutors in my house to instruct her.

original: Fit to instruct her youth. If you, Hortensio,   Or, Signior Gremio, you know any such,   Prefer them hither,
translation: If either of you, Hortensio and Sir Gremio, know of any good tutors, then recommend them to me.

original: for to cunning men   I will be very kind, and liberal   To mine own children in good bringing up.
translation: I'll pay well for good teachers, and won't spare anything in giving my children a good education.

original: Why, and I trust I may go too, may I not? What, shall I be appointed hours as though, belike, I knew not what  to take and what to leave, ha?
translation: Well, I can go too, can't I? What, do I have to start making appointments now, as if I didn't know when to come and go?

original: You may go to the devil’s dam! Your gifts are so good  here’s none will hold you.
translation: You can go straight to the devil! No one here can stand your "gifts."

original: So will I, Signior Gremio. But a word, I pray.
translation: So will I, Sir Gremio. But wait, let me have a word with you first, please.

original: and be happy  rivals in Bianca’s love, to labor and effect one thing  specially.
translation: so that we can once again be friendly rivals competing for Bianca's love. But first we have to work to achieve one thing.

original: What’s that, I pray?
translation: And what's that?

original: Marry, sir, to get a husband for her sister.
translation: Well, sir, to get a husband for her sister.

original: A husband? A devil!
translation: A husband? A devil!

original: I say a husband.
translation: I say a husband.

original: I say a devil. Think’st thou, Hortensio, though her  father be very rich, any man is so very a fool to be  married to hell?
translation: I say a devil. Do you really think, Hortensio, that any man is foolish enough to marry hell itself—even if her father is very rich?

original: Tush, Gremio. Though it pass your patience and mine to  endure her loud alarums, why, man, there be good fellows in the world,
translation: Hush, Gremio. Even though you and I don't have the patience to put up with her loud cries, why, man, there are good fellows in this world,

original: an a man could light on them, would take  her with all faults, and money enough.
translation: if we could only find them, who would take her with all her faults—and enough money.

original: I cannot tell. But I had as lief take her dowry with  this condition: to be whipped at the high cross every  morning.
Faith, as you say, there’s small choice in rotten  apples.
translation: Well, as you say, it's a choice between two evils.

original: But come, since this bar in law makes us  friends, it shall be so far forth friendly maintained  till by helping Baptista’s eldest daughter to a husband
translation: But come, since this great obstacle makes us allies, let's be friends until we can find a husband for Baptista's elder daughter.

original: we set his youngest free for a husband, and then have to ’t afresh.
translation: Then we'll set the younger daughter free to be courted, and we can resume our competition.

original: Sweet Bianca! Happy man be his dole! He that runs fastest gets the ring. How say you, Signior  Gremio?
translation: Sweet Bianca! Happy is the man who wins you! To the victor go the spoils. What do you say, Sir Gremio?

original: I am agreed, and would I had given him the best horse  in Padua to begin his wooing that would thoroughly woo  her, wed her, and bed her, and rid the house of her!  Come on.
translation: I agree with this plan. If we can find the right man, I'd give him the best horse in Padua to start wooing Katherine immediately, marry her, take her to bed, and rid the house of her! Come on.

original: I pray, sir, tell me, is it possible That love should of a sudden take such hold?
translation: Please tell me, sir, is it possible that love could overpower a person so suddenly?

original: O Tranio, till I found it to be true,   I never thought it possible or likely.
translation: Oh Tranio, I never thought it possible or likely until it happened to me.

original: But see, while idly I stood looking on,   I found the effect of love in idleness
translation: But see, while I stood here watching this unfold, I suddenly found myself struck with love.

original: And now in plainness do confess to thee   That art to me as secret and as dear   As Anna to the Queen of Carthage was,   Tranio,
translation: You are as trustworthy and dear to me as Anna was to  Dido, Queen of Carthage , so I must plainly confess to you, Tranio:

original: I burn, I pine, I perish, Tranio,   If I achieve not this young modest girl.
translation: I'm on fire, I'm burning, I'm filled with longing. Tranio—I'll die if I can't win this modest young girl for myself.

original: Counsel me, Tranio, for I know thou canst.   Assist me, Tranio, for I know thou wilt.
translation: Advise me, Tranio, for I know you can. Help me, Tranio, for I know you will.

original: Master, it is no time to chide you now.
translation: Master, now's not the time to scold you.

original: Affection is not rated from the heart.   If love have touched you, naught remains but so:
translation: Affection can't be driven out of the heart. If love has really touched you, then there's only one thing to be done.

original: Redime te captum quam queas minimo.
translation: As the Latin grammar book says, "Ransom yourself from captivity as cheaply as you can."

original: Gramercies, lad, go forward. This contents. The rest will comfort, for thy counsel’s sound.
translation: Many thanks, friend. Go on. This is helping. Your advice is good, so I know the rest of it will comfort me.

original: Master, you looked so longly on the maid,  Perhaps you marked not what’s the pith of all.
translation: Master, you spent so much time looking at the girl that you might have missed the heart of the matter here.

original: Oh yes, I saw sweet beauty in her face   Such as the daughter of Agenor had,
translation: Oh yes, I saw the sweet beauty in her face, just like that of  Europa , the daughter of Agenor

original: That made great Jove to humble him to her hand   When with his knees he kissed the Cretan strand.
translation: —beauty that made even the great god Jove fall in love and humble himself, falling to his knees and kissing the ground on that beach in Crete.

original: Saw you no more? Marked you not how her sister Began to scold and raise up such a storm That mortal ears might hardly endure the din?
translation: Is that all you saw? Didn't you notice how her sister began to scold and cause such a ruckus that human ears could hardly endure the noise?

original: Tranio, I saw her coral lips to move And with her breath she did perfume the air.  Sacred and sweet was all I saw in her.
translation: Tranio, I saw her coral-pink lips move, and her breath perfume the air. Everything I saw in her was holy and sweet.

original: Nay, then, ’tis time to stir him from his  trance.—
translation: Well, then, it's time to wake him up from his trance.

original: Ah, Tranio, what a cruel father’s he!  But art thou not advised, he took some care To get her cunning schoolmasters to instruct her?
translation: Ah, Tranio, what a cruel father he is! But didn't you hear how he wanted to hire good tutors to instruct her?

original: Ay, marry, am I, sir; and now ’tis plotted!
translation: Yes, I did, sir—and now I've got a plan!

original: I have it, Tranio!
translation: I have it, Tranio!

original: Master, for my hand, Both our inventions meet and jump in one.
translation: Master, I think we both had the same idea at the same time.

original: Tell me thine first.
translation: Tell me your idea first.

original: You will be schoolmaster And undertake the teaching of the maid: That’s your device.
translation: You will be a tutor and offer to teach the girl. Is that your plan?

original: It is. May it be done?
translation: It is. Can it be done?

original: Not possible. For who shall bear your part   And be in Padua here Vincentio’s son,
translation: It's impossible. Who would take your place and be Vincentio's son here in Padua,

original: Keep house and ply his book, welcome his friends,   Visit his countrymen and banquet them?
translation: living in your house and studying your books, welcoming your friends, visiting and dining with your fellow countrymen from Pisa?

original: Basta,   content thee, for I have it full.
translation: Enough—don't worry, I have it all planned out.

original: We have not yet been seen in any house,   Nor can we be distinguished by our faces   For man or master.
translation: No one has seen us yet, so no one knows which of us is the master and which is the servant.

original: Then it follows thus:   Thou shalt be master, Tranio, in my stead,
translation: So this is how it'll go:  you 'll be the master, Tranio, and replace me.

original: Keep house and port and servants as I should.
translation: You'll maintain my rank, live in my house, and keep servants, just as I would do.

original: I will some other be, some Florentine,   Some Neapolitan, or meaner man of Pisa.
translation: I, on the other hand, will be some other man—some fellow from Florence or Naples, or a low-ranking man from Pisa.

original: 'Tis hatched, and shall be so. Tranio, at once   Uncase thee. Take my colored hat and cloak.
translation: Well, that's the plan, so let's do it. Tranio, undress yourself at once, and put on my colored hat and cloak.

original: When Biondello comes, he waits on thee, But I will charm him first to keep his tongue.
translation: When Biondello comes, he must wait on you like you're his master. But first I'll persuade him to keep all this a secret.

original: So had you need.   In brief, sir, sith it your pleasure is,   And I am tied to be obedient—
translation: That's very important. Since this is what you want, sir, and I am sworn to obey you

original: For so your father charged me at our parting,   "Be serviceable to my son," quoth he,   Although I think 'twas in another sense—
translation: —for that's what your father commanded me when we left, saying, "Serve my son," although I don't think he had  this  in mind

original: I am content to be Lucentio   Because so well I love Lucentio.
translation: —I will pretend to be Lucentio, because I love the real Lucentio so much.

original: Tranio, be so, because Lucentio loves, And let me be a slave t'achieve that maid Whose sudden sight hath thralled my wounded eye.
translation: Good, Tranio, for the real Lucentio is also in love. I will even become a slave if it will win me that girl, whose appearance has bewitched my lovestruck eyes.

original: Here comes the rogue. Sirrah, where have you been?
translation: Here comes that rascal. Boy, where have you been?

original: Where have  I  been? Nay, how now, where are you? Master, has my fellow Tranio stolen your clothes? Or you stolen his? Or both? Pray, what’s the news?
translation: Where have I been? The real question is, where are you? Master, has Tranio stolen your clothes? Or have you stolen his? Or both? Please tell me, what's going on?

original: Sirrah, come hither: ’tis no time to jest,   And therefore frame your manners to the time.
translation: Boy, come here. This is no time for jokes, so get serious.

original: Your fellow Tranio here, to save my life,   Puts my apparel and my countenance on,   And I for my escape have put on his;
translation: Your fellow Tranio here has taken on my outward appearance to save my life, and I have put on his appearance in order to escape.

original: For in a quarrel since I came ashore   I killed a man and fear I was descried.
translation: I've been in a fight since we came ashore, and I killed a man. I'm afraid that someone saw me.

original: Wait you on him, I charge you, as becomes,   While I make way from hence to save my life.   You understand me?
translation: So for now you must wait on Tranio like he's your master, while I make my escape and save my life. Do you understand me?

original: Aye, sir.    Ne'er a whit.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: And not a jot of “Tranio” in your mouth.  Tranio is changed into Lucentio.
translation: And don't ever let the name "Tranio" slip out. "Tranio" is now "Lucentio."

original: The better for him. Would I were so too.
translation: All the better for him. I wish I could be Lucentio too.

original: So could I, faith, boy, to have the next wish after,   That Lucentio indeed had Baptista’s youngest daughter.
translation: I'd second your wish, boy, if it meant that the next wish gave Baptista's youngest daughter to Lucentio.

original: But, sirrah, not for my sake, but your master’s, I  advise   You use your manners discreetly in all kind of  companies.
translation: But for your master's sake, boy, not mine, I advise you to be discreet in the company of others.

original: When I am alone, why then I am Tranio;   But in all places else, your master Lucentio.
translation: When we're alone, then I'm Tranio. But everywhere else, I'm your master Lucentio.

original: Tranio, let’s go. One thing more rests, that thyself  execute,   To make one among these wooers. If thou ask me why,  Sufficeth my reasons are both good and weighty.
translation: Tranio, let's go. One more thing still has to be done, and it's up to you to arrange it. You have to become another suitor to Bianca. Don't ask me why—just trust that I have a good reason for doing this.

original: My lord, you nod. You do not mind the play.
translation: My lord, you're falling asleep. You're not watching the play.

original: Yes, by Saint Anne, do I. A good matter, surely. Comes  there any more of it?
translation: I am watching, by God, I am. It's a good play, to be sure. Is there any more?

original: My lord, ’tis but begun.
translation: My lord, it's only just begun.

original: 'Tis a very excellent piece of work, madam lady. Would ’twere done.
translation: It's a very excellent piece of work, madam lady. I wish it were over.

original: Verona, for a while I take my leave,   To see my friends in Padua,
translation: Farewell for now, Verona. I have come to see my friends in Padua,

original: but of all   My best belovèd and approvèd friend,   Hortensio.
translation: but especially my best and most beloved friend Hortensio.

original: And I trow this is his house.   Here, sirrah Grumio. Knock, I say.
translation: And I believe this is his house. Here, Grumio. Knock, I say.

original: Knock, sir? Whom should I knock? Is there any man has  rebused your Worship?
Villain, I say, knock me here soundly.
translation: Villain, I say, knock for me here.

original: Knock you here, sir? Why, sir, what am I, sir, that I  should knock you here, sir?
translation: Knock you here, sir? Why, sir, I don't think it's appropriate for me to knock you here, sir.

original: Villain, I say, knock me at this gate And rap me well, or I’ll knock your knave’s pate.
translation: Villain, I say, knock for me on this door, and pound it well, or I'll knock your fool's head!

original: My master is grown quarrelsome. I should knock you  first, And then I know after who comes by the worst.
translation: My master is getting angry. If I knock him first, then I know who's going to end up sorry for it.

original: Will it not be? Faith, sirrah, an you’ll not knock, I’ll ring it. I’ll try how you can  sol, fa,  and sing it.
translation: Why is this so hard? Well, man, if you won't knock, I'll ring—wring your ears and make you sing!

original: Help, mistress, help! My master is mad.
translation: Help, help! My master's gone crazy.

original: Now knock when I bid you, sirrah villain.
translation: Now knock when I tell you to, you idiot peasant.

original: How now, what’s the matter? My old friend Grumio and  my good friend Petruchio? How do you all at Verona?
translation: What's going on, what's the matter? Is this my old friend Grumio and my good friend Petruchio? How are all your family in Verona?

original: Signior Hortensio, come you to part the fray?   Con tutto il cuore, ben trovato,  may I say.
translation: Sir Hortensio, have you come to break up the fig? Let me say con tutto il cuore, ben trovato.

original: Alla nostra casa ben venuto, molto honorato signor mio Petruchio.—Rise, Grumio, rise. We will compound this  quarrel.
translation: Alla nostra casa ben venuto, molto honorato signor mio Petruchio.—Get up, Grumio, get up. We will settle this argument.

original: Nay, ’tis no matter, sir, what he 'leges in Latin. If  this be not a lawful case for me to leave his service
translation: It doesn't matter what he's accused me of in Latin. If this isn't legal justification for me to leave his service, I don't know what is.

original: —look you, sir: he bid me knock him and rap him soundly,  sir.
translation: Listen to this, sir: he tells me to knock him and pound him well, sir.

original: Well, was it fit for a servant to use his master  so, being perhaps, for aught I see, two-and-thirty, a  pip out?
translation: Well, was it proper for a servant to treat his master like that—especially if he might be a little more drunk than drunk?

original: Whom, would to God, I had well knocked at first,   Then had not Grumio come by the worst.
translation: Maybe I ought to have hit him first, and then I'd feel better.

original: A senseless villain, good Hortensio.  I bade the rascal knock upon your gate And could not get him for my heart to do it.
translation: He's a senseless villain, good Hortensio. I told the rascal to knock on your door and couldn't for the life of me get him to do it.

original: Knock at the gate? O heavens! Spake you not these words plain: “Sirrah, knock me here, rap me here, knock me  well, and knock me soundly”? And come you now with  “knocking at the gate”?
translation: Knock on the door? Oh God! Didn't you clearly say the words "Man, knock me here, pound here, and knock me well?" And now you're claiming it was "knocking on the door?"

original: Sirrah, begone or talk not, I advise you.
translation: Be quiet or go away, I warn you.

original: Petruchio, patience. I am Grumio’s pledge.
translation: Calm down, Petruchio. I'll vouch for Grumio.

original: Why, this' a heavy chance ’twixt him and you,   Your ancient, trusty, pleasant servant Grumio.
translation: Why, this is sad to see you two fighting—you and Grumio, your trusty, cheerful servant of many years.

original: And tell me now, sweet friend, what happy gale   Blows you to Padua here from old Verona?
translation: But tell me now, sweet friend, what lucky wind blew you from old Verona here to Padua.

original: Such wind as scatters young men through the world   To seek their fortunes farther than at home,   Where small experience grows.
translation: The wind that scatters young men throughout the world to seek their fortunes away from home, where there are few new experiences to be had.

original: But in a few,   Signior Hortensio, thus it stands with me:
translation: But to be brief, Sir Hortensio, this is how it stands:

original: Antonio, my father, is deceased,   And I have thrust myself into this maze,   Happily to wive and thrive as best I may.
translation: Antonio, my father, is dead, and I have now thrown myself into the wide world to try and marry and thrive as best I can.

original: Crowns in my purse I have and goods at home,   And so am come abroad to see the world.
translation: I have money in my purse and property at home, so I've set off to see the world.

original: Petruchio, shall I then come roundly to thee   And wish thee to a shrewd, ill-favored wife?
translation: Petruchio, should I speak plainly then and offer you a shrewish, unpleasant wife?

original: Thou’dst thank me but a little for my counsel;   And yet I’ll promise thee she shall be rich,   And very rich.
translation: I don't think you'd thank me for my suggestion, but I promise you she's rich, yes, very rich.

original: But thou'rt too much my friend,   And I’ll not wish thee to her.
translation: But you are my friend, so I won't wish her on you.

original: Signior Hortensio, ’twixt such friends as we   Few words suffice.
translation: Sir Hortensio, for good friends like us only a few words are needed.

original: And therefore, if thou know   One rich enough to be Petruchio’s wife,   As wealth is burden of my wooing dance,
translation: So if you know a woman rich enough to be Petruchio's wife—and wealth is the biggest factor for me—

original: Be she as foul as was Florentius' love,   As old as Sibyl and as curst and shrewd   As Socrates' Xanthippe, or a worse,
translation: it doesn't matter if she's as ugly as  Florentius' love , as old as the  Sybil , or as shrewish as Socrates'  Xanthippe .

original: She moves me not, or not removes at least   Affection’s edge in me, were she as rough   As are the swelling Adriatic seas.
translation: None of that would bother me, or make me less keen to marry her, even if she were as rough as the Adriatic Sea.

original: I come to wive it wealthily in Padua;   If wealthily, then happily in Padua.
translation: I've come to find a wealthy wife in Padua, and if she's wealthy, then I'll have found a good wife.

original: Nay, look you, sir, he tells you flatly what his mind is.
translation: Look at that, sir, he is very straightforward with his intentions.

original: Why, give him gold enough and marry  him to a puppet or an aglet-baby, or an old trot with  ne'er a tooth in her head, though she have as many  diseases as two-and-fifty horses.
translation: Why, if you give him enough gold he'll marry a puppet, a doll, or an old prostitute with a dozen diseases and not a tooth in her head.

original: Why, nothing comes  amiss, so money comes withal.
translation: Why, nothing can bother him, as long as money comes with it.

original: Petruchio, since we are stepped thus far in,   I will continue that I broached in jest.
translation: Petruchio, since the conversation has gone this far already, I'll continue with what I meant only as a joke.

original: I can, Petruchio, help thee to a wife   With wealth enough, and young and beauteous,   Brought up as best becomes a gentlewoman.
translation: I  can  help you find a wife, Petruchio, who's rich, young, beautiful, and brought up as a noble gentlewoman.

original: Her only fault, and that is faults enough,   Is that she is intolerable curst,   And shrewd and froward,
translation: Her only flaw, and it's certainly a big one, is that she is an unbearable shrew, disagreeable and willful,

original: so beyond all measure   That, were my state far worser than it is,   I would not wed her for a mine of gold.
translation: and so much so that even if I was broke I wouldn't marry her for a goldmine.

original: Hortensio, peace. Thou know’st not gold’s effect.
translation: Quiet, Hortensio. You don't know the power of money.

original: Tell me her father’s name, and ’tis enough;
translation: Tell me her father's name, and that will be enough.

original: For I will board her, though she chide as loud   As thunder when the clouds in autumn crack.
translation: I will pursue her even if her scolding is as loud as thunder in an autumn storm.

original: Her father is Baptista Minola,   An affable and courteous gentleman.
translation: Her father is Baptista Minola, an agreeable and polite gentleman.

original: Her name is Katherina Minola,   Renowned in Padua for her scolding tongue.
translation: Her name is Katherina Minola, famous in Padua for her scolding tongue.

original: I know her father, though I know not her,   And he knew my deceasèd father well.
translation: I don't know her, but I know her father, and he knew my father well when he was alive.

original: I will not sleep, Hortensio, till I see her,   And therefore let me be thus bold with you   To give you over at this first encounter,
translation: I won't sleep until I see her, Hortensio, so I hope you'll pardon me for cutting off this first meeting of ours

original: Unless you will accompany me thither.
translation: —unless you want to come with me.

original: I pray you, sir, let him go while the  humor lasts.
translation: Please, sir, let him go while this mood lasts.

original: O' my word, an she knew him as well as I  do, she would think scolding would do little good upon  him.
translation: I swear, if she knew him as well as I do, she'd know how little scolding affects him.

original: She may perhaps call him half a score knaves or so. Why, that’s nothing;
translation: At best, she might come up with ten or so horrible names to call him. Why, that's nothing.

original: an he begin once, he’ll rail in  his rope tricks.
translation: Once he gets started, he'll rant and rave and throw his  rope tricks  around,

original: I’ll tell you what sir: an she stand  him but a little, he will throw a figure in her face and so disfigure her with it that she shall have no more  eyes to see withal than a cat.
translation: and if she tries to stand up to him, he'll throw a figure of speech in her face that'll disfigure her so she'll have no more eyes to see with than a cat does.

original: You know him not, sir.
translation: You don't know him, sir.

original: Tarry, Petruchio, I must go with thee,   For in Baptista’s keep my treasure is.
translation: Wait, Petruchio. I must go with you, for my own treasure is in Baptista's keeping too.

original: He hath the jewel of my life in hold,   His youngest daughter, beautiful Bianca,
translation: He has my precious jewel hidden away in his fortress: his youngest daughter, the beautiful Bianca.

original: And her withholds from me and other more,   Suitors to her and rivals in my love,   Supposing it a thing impossible,
translation: He keeps her away from me and her other suitors, my rivals for her love, as he assumes it will be impossible

original: For those defects I have before rehearsed,   That ever Katherina will be wooed.
translation: —because of those character defects I already described—for Katherina to ever find a husband.

original: Therefore this order hath Baptista ta'en,   That none shall have access unto Bianca   Till Katherine the curst have got a husband.
translation: Baptista has therefore set down this rule: no one will have access to Bianca until Katherine the shrew gets a husband.

original: “Katherine the curst!” A title for a maid of all titles the worst.
translation: "Katherine the shrew!" Of all the titles you could give a girl, that's the worst.

original: Now shall my friend Petruchio do me grace,   And offer me disguised in sober robes   To old Baptista as a schoolmaster
translation: Now my friend Petruchio will do me a favor, and present me—disguised in somber robes—to Baptista as a teacher,

original: Well seen in music, to instruct Bianca,
translation: well-versed in music, to instruct Bianca.

original: That so I may, by this device at least,   Have leave and leisure to make love to her   And, unsuspected, court her by herself.
translation: With this disguise, I'll at least have time and permission to be with Bianca alone, and then I can court her once more.

original: Here’s no knavery! See, to beguile the old folks, how  the young folks lay their heads together!
translation: What a nice trick! See how the young folks put their heads together to deceive the old.

original: Master, master, look about you. Who goes there, ha?
translation: Master, master, look behind you. Who's that, huh?

original: Peace, Grumio. It is the rival of my love. Petruchio, stand by a while.
translation: Quiet, Grumio. It is my rival for Biana's love. Petruchio, let's watch a while.

original: A proper stripling, and an amorous.
translation: What a handsome young man! A real heartbreaker.

original: O, very well, I have perused the note.
translation: Oh, very well, I've read the list of books for Bianca.

original: Hark you, sir: I’ll have them very fairly bound,   All books of love.
translation: Now listen, sir: I want them very handsomely bound, and I want them to be books of love.
