original: See that at any hand,   And see you read no other lectures to her.
translation: No matter what, don't teach her any other lessons.

original: You understand me. Over and beside   Signior Baptista’s liberality,   I’ll mend it with a largess.
translation: Do you understand me? Above and beyond what Sir Baptista pays you, I'll add on a hefty bonus.

original: Take your paper too.   And let me have them very well perfum’d   For she is sweeter than perfume itself   To whom they go to.
translation: Take your book list too. And have all the books well perfumed too, for the lady they're going to is sweeter than perfume itself.

original: What will you read to her?
translation: What will you teach her?

original: Whate'er I read to her, I’ll plead for you   As for my patron, stand you so assured,
translation: Whatever I teach her, I'll plead your case. You can be sure of that

original: As firmly as yourself were still in place,
translation: —I'll argue for you as strongly as if you were there yourself.

original: O this learning, what a thing it is!
translation: Oh, this learning, what an excellent thing it is!

original: O this woodcock, what an ass it is!
translation: Oh, this moron, what an ass it is!

original: Peace, sirrah.
translation: Quiet, boy.

original: Grumio, mum! God save you, Signior Gremio.
translation: Grumio, hush!—

original: And you are well met, Signior Hortensio.   Trow you whither I am going? To Baptista Minola.
translation: Good to see you, Sir Hortensio. Do you know where I'm going? To see Baptista Minola.

original: I promised to enquire carefully   About a schoolmaster for the fair Bianca,   And by good fortune I have lighted well   On this young man,
translation: I promised that I would find a teacher for the fair Bianca, and my good luck has led me to this young man.

original: for learning and behavior   Fit for her turn, well read in poetry   And other books—good ones, I warrant ye.
translation: His manners and learning are well-suited for her needs, and he's well-read in poetry and other books—good books, I assure you.

original: 'Tis well. And I have met a gentleman   Hath promised me to help me to another,   A fine musician to instruct our mistress.
translation: That's good. And  I  have met a gentleman who has promised to help find a fine musician to teach our lady.

original: So shall I no whit be behind in duty   To fair Bianca, so beloved of me.
translation: So I won't fall even a step behind in my duty to fair Bianca, my beloved.

original: Beloved of me, and that my deeds shall prove.
translation: My beloved—as my deeds will prove.

original: And that his bags shall prove.
translation: And as his moneybags will prove.

original: Gremio, ’tis now no time to vent our love.
translation: Gremio, now is not the time to express our love.

original: Listen to me, and if you speak me fair,   I’ll tell you news indifferent good for either.
translation: If you're willing to be polite and listen to me, then I'll give you some news that's equally good for both of us.

original: So said, so done, is well. Hortensio, have you told him all her faults?
translation: If he'll do as he says, then that's good. But Hortensio, have you told him about all her flaws?

original: I know she is an irksome brawling scold. If that be all, masters, I hear no harm.
translation: I know she is an annoying, argumentative scolder. If that's all, masters, then I see no problem.

original: No? Say’st me so, friend? What countryman?
translation: No? Is that what you're telling me, friend? Where are you from?

original: Born in Verona, old Antonio’s son. My father dead, my fortune lives for me. And I do hope good days and long to see.
translation: I was born in Verona. I'm old Antonio's son. My father is dead, and his fortune is mine now. I hope to see many long, good days.

original: O sir, such a life with such a wife were strange!
translation: Oh sir, such a life with such a wife will be strange!

original: But if you have a stomach, to ’t, i' God’s name:   You shall have me assisting you in all.
translation: But if you have the stomach for it, then godspeed—and you'll have my help in everything you need.

original: Will I live?
translation: As long as I'm alive.

original: Will he woo her? Ay, or I’ll hang her.
translation: Will he woo her? Yes, or I'll hang her.

original: Why came I hither but to that intent?   Think you a little din can daunt mine ears?
translation: Why did I come here if not for that? Do you think a little noise can frighten me?

original: Have I not in my time heard lions roar?   Have I not heard the sea, puffed up with winds,   Rage like an angry boar chafèd with sweat?
translation: Haven't I heard lions roar? Haven't I heard the windy sea rage like an angry boar?

original: Have I not heard great ordnance in the field,   And heaven’s artillery thunder in the skies?
translation: Haven't I heard cannons on the battlefield, and thunder—heaven's artillery—in the sky?

original: Have I not in a pitchèd battle heard   Loud 'larums, neighing steeds, and trumpets' clang?
translation: Haven't I been at war and heard loud calls to arms, neighing horses, and trumpets blasting?

original: And do you tell me of a woman’s tongue   That gives not half so great a blow to hear   As will a chestnut in a farmer’s fire?
translation: And now you warn me about some woman's tongue, which isn't even half as loud as a chestnut popping in a farmer's fire?

original: Tush, tush! Fear boys with bugs.
translation: For shame! Save your bogeymen to frighten children.

original: For he fears none.
translation: For he fears nothing.

original: Hortensio, hark. This gentleman is happily arrived, My mind presumes, for his own good and ours.
translation: Hortensio, listen. This gentleman has arrived at a fortunate time, I think—for both our good and his.

original: I promised we would be contributors And bear his charge of wooing, whatsoe'er.
translation: I promised that we would all contribute and pay the expenses for his courtship, whatever they turn out to be.

original: And so we will, provided that he win her.
translation: And so we will, as long as he wins Katherine.

original: I would I were as sure of a good dinner.
translation: I wish I could be as sure of a good dinner.

original: Gentlemen, God save you. If I may be  bold, Tell me, I beseech you, which is the readiest way To the house of Signior Baptista Minola?
translation: God bless you, gentlemen. If I may be so bold, please tell me, which is the best way to the house of Sir Baptista Minola?

original: He that has the two fair daughters—is ’t he you mean?
translation: The man with the two pretty daughters—is that who you mean?

original: Even he, Biondello.
translation: The very man, Biondello.

original: Hark you, sir, you mean not her to—
translation: Listen, sir, you're not looking for the daughter—

original: Perhaps him and her, sir. What have you to do?
translation: Maybe I mean the father and the daughter, sir. What is it to you?

original: Not her that chides, sir, at any hand, I pray.
translation: Not the daughter who scolds, anyway, I hope.

original: I love no chiders, sir. Biondello, let’s  away.
translation: I have no love for scolders, sir. Biondello, let's go.

original: Well begun, Tranio.
translation: Well done, Tranio.

original: Sir, a word ere you go.  Are you a suitor to the maid you talk of, yea or no?
translation: Sir, a word before you go. Are you a suitor to the girl you asked about—yes or no?

original: An if I be, sir, is it any offense?
translation: And if I am, sir, is it a problem?

original: No, if without more words you will get you hence.
translation: Not if you get out of here without saying another word.

original: Why, sir, I pray, are not the streets as  free For me as for you?
translation: Why, sir, don't I have just as much a right to be out on the streets as you do?

original: But so is not she.
translation: But she doesn't.

original: For what reason, I beseech you?
translation: For what reason, I ask you?

original: For this reason, if you’ll know: That she’s the choice love of Signior Gremio.
translation: For this reason, if you want to know: because she's the chosen beloved of Sir Gremio.

original: That she’s the chosen of Signior Hortensio.
translation: Because she's the chosen beloved of Sir Hortensio.

original: Softly, my masters. If you be gentlemen,   Do me this right: hear me with patience.
translation: Calm down, sirs. If you're gentleman, then be polite and hear me out.

original: Baptista is a noble gentleman,   To whom my father is not all unknown,   And were his daughter fairer than she is,   She may more suitors have,   and me for one.
translation: Baptista is a noble gentleman—one who knows my father—and even if his daughter was more beautiful than she already is, she would still be entitled to more than one suitor—and I will be one of them.

original: Fair Leda’s daughter had a thousand wooers;   Then well one more may fair Bianca have.
translation: Helen of Troy  had a thousand suitors, so let fair Bianca have one more.

original: And so she shall. Lucentio shall make one,   Though Paris came in hope to speed alone.
translation: And so she does. Lucentio will woo her, even if Paris himself should come to try and win her.

original: What! This gentleman will out-talk us all.
translation: What! This gentleman will out-talk us all.

original: Sir, give him head; I know he’ll prove a  jade.
translation: Well, let him sprint ahead for now. He's not likely to finish the race.

original: Hortensio, to what end are all these words?
translation: Hortensio, what's all this talk about?

original: Sir, let me be so bold as ask you, Did you yet ever see Baptista’s daughter?
translation: Sir, if I may be so bold as to ask you, have you even seen Baptista's daughter yet?

original: No, sir, but hear I do that he hath two,  The one as famous for a scolding tongue As is the other for beauteous modesty.
translation: No, sir, but I hear that he has two, the one as famous for her scolding tongue as the other is for her beauty and modesty.

original: Sir, sir, the first’s for me; let her go by.
translation: Sir, sir, the first one's mine, so let her go by.

original: Yea, leave that labor to great Hercules, And let it be more than Alcides' twelve.
Sir, understand you this of me, in sooth:
translation: Sir, let me make sure you understand this:

original: The youngest daughter, whom you hearken for,   Her father keeps from all access of suitors
translation: the youngest daughter, the one you long for, is kept locked away from all suitors by her father.

original: And will not promise her to any man   Until the elder sister first be wed.   The younger then is free, and not before.
translation: He won't promise her to any man until the elder sister is married first. Then, and only then, will the younger be free.

original: If it be so, sir, that you are the man   Must stead us all, and me amongst the rest,
translation: If that's true, sir, and you are the man who will help us all—myself included—

original: And if you break the ice and do this feat,   Achieve the elder, set the younger free   For our access,
translation: and you  do  break the ice and perform the incredible feat of winning the elder sister, thereby setting the younger free for us to woo—

original: whose hap shall be to have her   Will not so graceless be to be ingrate.
translation: then I'm sure whoever happens to win her won't be such a brute as to be ungrateful to you.

original: Sir, you say well, and well you do conceive.
translation: Sir, you speak well, and you understand well.

original: And since you do profess to be a suitor,   You must, as we do, gratify this gentleman,   To whom we all rest generally beholding.
translation: And since you declare yourself a suitor, you must do as we already have, and pay this gentleman to whom we all owe so much.

original: Sir, I shall not be slack;
translation: Sir, I won't be stingy.

original: in sign  whereof,   Please ye we may contrive this afternoon   And quaff carouses to our mistress' health
translation: On that note, let's spend this afternoon drinking toasts to our beloved's health.

original: And do as adversaries do in law,   Strive mightily, but eat and drink as friends.
translation: We'll be like opposing lawyers in a case, who fight viciously in court, but outside of it eat and drink as friends.

original: O excellent motion! Fellows, let’s be gone.
translation: An excellent suggestion! Fellows, let's go.

original: The motion’s good indeed and be it so.— Petruchio, I shall be your  ben venuto.
Good sister, wrong me not nor wrong yourself,   To make a bondmaid and a slave of me.   That I disdain.
translation: Good sister, don't wrong both me and yourself by turning me into a slave. I won't stand for that.

original: But for these other goods—   Unbind my hands, I’ll pull them off myself,   Yea, all my raiment to my petticoat,
translation: But if it's my jewelry and clothes you want—untie my hands and I'll pull them off myself, yes, everything down to my underwear.

original: Or what you will command me will I do,   So well I know my duty to my elders.
translation: Or I'll do anything else you command me to do, for I know that it is my duty is to obey my elders.

original: Of all thy suitors here I charge thee tell Whom thou lovest best. See thou dissemble not.
translation: I order you to tell me which of your suitors you like best. And make sure you don't lie.

original: Believe me, sister, of all the men alive I never yet beheld that special face Which I could fancy more than any other.
translation: Believe me, sister, out of all the men alive I've never yet seen that special face that I could love more than any other.

original: Minion, thou liest. Is ’t not Hortensio?
translation: You're lying, you hussy. It's Hortensio, isn't it?

original: If you affect him, sister, here I swear  I’ll plead for you myself, but you shall have him.
translation: If you love him, sister, you can have him. I swear I'll even plead with him on your behalf.

original: Oh, then belike you fancy riches more. You will have Gremio to keep you fair.
translation: Oh, then you probably prefer money. You'll choose Gremio who will keep you dressed up in fine clothes and jewelry.

original: Is it for him you do envy me so?
translation: Are you really jealous of me because of  him ?

original: Nay, then you jest, and now I well perceive   You have but jested with me all this while.
translation: You must be joking—and now I can see that you've been joking with me this whole time.

original: I prithee, sister Kate, untie my hands.
translation: Please, sister Kate, untie my hands.

original: If that be jest, then all the rest was so.
translation: If you consider that a joke, then the rest was too.

original: Why, how now, dame! whence grows this insolence?—   Bianca, stand aside.—Poor girl, she weeps!
translation: What's going on, woman? How dare you!—Bianca, step away from her.—The poor girl, she's weeping!

original: Go ply thy needle; meddle not with her.
translation: Go do some sewing, and don't talk to her.

original: For shame, thou hilding of a devilish  spirit!   Why dost thou wrong her that did ne'er wrong thee?
translation: For shame, you vicious creature, you devil! Why would you hurt her when she's never done you any harm?

original: When did she cross thee with a bitter word?
translation: When did she ever speak a single cruel word to you?

original: Her silence flouts me, and I’ll be revenged.
translation: Her silence mocks me, and I'll get my revenge on her.

original: What, in my sight?—Bianca, get thee in.
translation: What, right in front of me?—Bianca, go inside.

original: What, will you not suffer me?
translation: What, you can't even stand my presence?

original: Nay, now I see   She is your treasure, she must have a husband,
translation: Now I see that she is your treasure. She must have a husband,

original: I must dance barefoot on her wedding day   And, for your love to her, lead apes in hell.
translation: while I must  dance barefoot on her wedding day and lead apes in hell , all because you love her most.

original: Talk not to me. I will go sit and weep   Till I can find occasion of revenge.
translation: Don't speak to me, I will go cry and wait until I can get my revenge.

original: Was ever gentleman thus grieved as I? But who comes here?
translation: Was there ever a man who suffered like I do? But who's this coming?

original: Good morrow, neighbor Baptista.
translation: Good morning, neighbor Baptista.

original: Good morrow, neighbor Gremio.—God save you, gentlemen!
translation: Good morning, neighbor Gremio.—Hello and God bless you, gentlemen!

original: And you, good sir. Pray, have you not a daughter Called Katherina, fair and virtuous?
translation: And you, good sir. Please tell me, don't you have a daughter named Katherina, who is fair and virtuous?

original: I have a daughter, sir, called Katherina.
translation: I do have a daughter named Katherina, sir.

original: You are too blunt. Go to it orderly.
translation: You're being too blunt. Go about it with more ceremony.

original: You wrong me, Signior Gremio. Give me leave.—
translation: You do me wrong, Sir Gremio. Let me continue.

original: I am a gentleman of Verona, sir,   That hearing of her beauty and her wit,   Her affability and bashful modesty,   Her wondrous qualities and mild behavior,
translation: —I am a gentleman of Verona, sir, who has heard of your daughter's beauty and wit, her friendliness and bashful modesty, her wondrous talents and mild behavior.

original: Am bold to show myself a forward guest   Within your house, to make mine eye the witness   Of that report which I so oft have heard.
translation: I have now boldly come as a guest to your house to try and see for myself all the things I've heard reported.

original: And, for an entrance to my entertainment,   I do present you with a man of mine,
translation: And, to pay the price of my admission to your hospitality, I here present you with a servant of mine.

original: You’re welcome, sir, and he for your good sake. But for my daughter Katherine, this I know, She is not for your turn, the more my grief.
translation: You're welcome here, sir, and he is too, for your sake. But as for my daughter Katherine, this much I know: she won't meet your expectations—and that's a pity for me.

original: I see you do not mean to part with her,  Or else you like not of my company.
translation: I see that you don't intend to part with her, or else you don't like my company.

original: Mistake me not. I speak but as I find. Whence are you, sir? What may I call your name?
translation: No, don't misunderstand me—I'm just stating the facts. Where are you from, sir? What name should I call you?

original: Petruchio is my name, Antonio’s son, A man well known throughout all Italy.
translation: Petruchio is my name. My father was Antonio, a man well known throughout Italy.

original: I know him well. You are welcome for his sake.
translation: He's well known to me. You are welcome for his sake.

original: Saving your tale, Petruchio, I pray Let us that are poor petitioners speak too.   Bacare,  you are marvelous forward.
translation: With all due respect, Petruchio, please let us poor petitioners get a word in too. Stand back—you're too forward.

original: Oh, pardon me, Signior Gremio, I would fain be doing.
translation: Oh, pardon me, Sir Gremio. I'm just eager to get down to business.

original: I doubt it not, sir, but you will curse your wooing.—
translation: I don't doubt it, sir, but you'll regret your wooing if it's successful.

original: A thousand thanks, Signior Gremio. Welcome, good  Cambio.    But, gentle sir,  methinks you walk like a stranger. May I be so bold to  know the cause of your coming?
translation: A thousand thanks, Sir Gremio. Welcome, good Cambio.

original: Pardon me, sir, the boldness is mine  own,
translation: Pardon me sir, for the boldness is all my own.

original: That being a stranger in this city here   Do make myself a suitor to your daughter,   Unto Bianca, fair and virtuous.
translation: I am a foreigner in this city, but I have come to make myself a suitor to your daughter, the fair and virtuous Bianca.

original: Nor is your firm resolve unknown to me,   In the preferment of the eldest sister.
translation: I'm also aware of your firm decision that your eldest daughter must marry first.

original: This liberty is all that I request,   That, upon knowledge of my parentage,   I may have welcome ’mongst the rest that woo   And free access and favor as the rest.
translation: All I ask is that, once you know who my parents are, you make me as welcome as Bianca's other suitors, and give me the same freedom and permission as the rest.

original: And toward the education of your daughters,   I here bestow a simple instrument   And this small packet of Greek and Latin books.
translation: And as for the education of your daughters, I here contribute a simple instrument and this small pack of Greek and Latin books.

original: Lucentio is your name. Of whence, I pray?
Of Pisa, sir, son to Vincentio.
translation: From Pisa, sir. My father is Vincentio.

original: A mighty man of Pisa. By report   I know him well. You are very welcome, sir.
translation: A mighty man of Pisa. I know him well by reputation. You are very welcome, sir.

original: Sirrah, lead these gentlemen To my daughters, and tell them both These are their tutors. Bid them use them well.
translation: Boy, lead these gentlemen to my daughters, and tell them that these are their tutors, so make sure to treat them well.

original: We will go walk a little in the orchard,  And then to dinner. You are passing welcome, And so I pray you all to think yourselves.
translation: We'll go for a little walk in the garden, and then to dinner. Please, know that you are all very welcome here and make yourselves at home.

original: Signior Baptista, my business asketh haste,   And every day I cannot come to woo.
translation: Sir Baptista, I'm in a bit of a hurry with this business, and I can't come wooing every day.

original: You knew my father well, and in him me,   Left solely heir to all his lands and goods,   Which I have bettered rather than decreased.
translation: You knew my father well, and through him, me, the only heir to all his lands and wealth, which I have increased rather than depleted.

original: Then tell me, if I get your daughter’s love,   What dowry shall I have with her to wife?
translation: So tell me, if I can win your daughter's love, what dowry will I get when I marry her?

original: After my death, the one half of my lands,  And, in possession, twenty thousand crowns.
translation: Twenty thousand crowns right away, and one half of my lands after my death.

original: And, for that dowry, I’ll assure her of   Her widowhood, be it that she survive me,   In all my lands and leases whatsoever.
translation: And on my side, if I die before she does, as her widow's inheritance she'll get all my lands and the rent from my property.

original: Let specialties be therefore drawn between us,   That covenants may be kept on either hand.
translation: Let's have contracts drawn up between us, so both of us will be sure to keep up our end of the agreement.

original: Ay, when the special thing is well obtained, That is, her love, for that is all in all.
translation: Of course, once the most important thing has been obtained—her love, that is. That is everything.

original: Why, that is nothing.
translation: Why, that is nothing.

original: For I tell you, father,   I am as peremptory as she proud-minded;   And where two raging fires meet together,   They do consume the thing that feeds their fury.
translation: I tell you, father, I am as domineering as she is proud-minded, and when two raging fires come together, they cancel each other out.

original: Though little fire grows great with little wind,   Yet extreme gusts will blow out fire and all.
translation: A little wind will make a little fire great, but a great gust will blow the fire out.

original: So I to her and so she yields to me,   For I am rough and woo not like a babe.
translation: I'll be the great gust to her fire, and she will yield to me, for I am rough and don't woo like a child.

original: Well mayst thou woo, and happy be thy speed. But be thou armed for some unhappy words.
translation: Good luck with your wooing. May you be successful. But be ready for some unpleasant words.

original: Ay, to the proof, as mountains are for winds, That shakes not, though they blow perpetually.
translation: I'll be well-armed against them, like a mountain in the wind. Even if it keeps blowing forever, the mountain never shakes.

original: How now, my friend, why dost thou look so pale?
translation: What's going on, my friend? Why do you look so pale?

original: For fear, I promise you, if I look pale.
translation: If I look pale, it must be from fear.

original: What, will my daughter prove a good musician?
translation: What, will my daughter turn out to be a good musician?

original: I think she’ll sooner prove a soldier. Iron may hold with her, but never lutes.
translation: I think she'd do better as a soldier. Swords might withstand her, but never lutes.

original: Why, then thou canst not break her to the lute?
Why, no, for she hath broke the lute to me.
translation: Why no—she's broken the lute on me.

original: I did but tell her she mistook her frets,   And bowed her hand to teach her fingering,
translation: All I told her was that she was using the wrong frets, and I bent her hand to teach her the right fingering.

original: When, with a most impatient devilish spirit,   “'Frets' call you these?” quoth she. “I’ll fume with  them!”
translation: Then she jumped up with impatience and said, "'Frets,' is that what you call them? Let me fret you then!"

original: And with that word she struck me on the head,   And through the instrument my pate made way,
translation: And with that she struck me on the head, so that my head went right through the lute.

original: And there I stood amazèd for a while   As on a pillory, looking through the lute,   While she did call me “rascal fiddler”   And “twangling Jack”; with twenty such vile terms,
translation: I stood there confused for a while, looking through the strings of the lute as if they were prison bars, while she called me a "rascal fiddler," "twangling fool," and twenty other hateful names like that.

original: As had she studied to misuse me so.
translation: It was as if she'd been practicing and planning to abuse me like this.

original: Now, by the world, it is a lusty wench. I love her ten times more than e'er I did.  O, how I long to have some chat with her!
translation: By God, that's a lively girl! Now I like her ten times more than I did before. Oh, I can't wait to talk to her!

original: Well, go with me and be not so discomfited.
translation: Well, come with me, and don't be discouraged.

original: Proceed in practice with my younger daughter.   She’s apt to learn and thankful for good turns.
translation: Proceed in your lessons with my younger daughter. She's a quick learner and will be grateful for your help.

original: Signior Petruchio, will you go with us,   Or shall I send my daughter Kate to you?
translation: Sir Petruchio, will you come with us, or should I send my daughter Kate to you?

original: I pray you do.
translation: Please send her in.

original: I’ll attend her here   And woo her with some spirit when she comes.
translation: I'll wait for her here and woo her forcefully when she comes.

original: Say that she rail; why then I’ll tell her plain   She sings as sweetly as a nightingale.
translation: If she rants and scolds, I'll tell her that she sings as sweetly as a nightingale.

original: Say that she frown; I’ll say she looks as clear   As morning roses newly washed with dew.
translation: If she frowns, I'll say that she looks as cheerful as morning roses newly washed with dew.

original: Say she be mute and will not speak a word;   Then I’ll commend her volubility,   And say she uttereth piercing eloquence.
translation: If she is silent and won't say a word, then I'll praise  her for being talkative, and say that she speaks with piercing eloquence.

original: If she do bid me pack, I’ll give her thanks,   As though she bid me stay by her a week.
translation: If she tells me to get out, then I'll thank her as if she'd asked me to stay with her for a week.

original: If she deny to wed, I’ll crave the day   When I shall ask the banns and when be marrièd.
translation: If she refuses to marry me, then I'll ask about the date for the announcement and the wedding.

original: But here she comes—and now, Petruchio, speak.
translation: But here she comes—and now, Petruchio, speak.

original: Good morrow, Kate—for that’s your name, I hear.
translation: Hello, Kate—for that's your name, I hear.

original: Well have you heard, but something hard of hearing. They call me Katherine that do talk of me.
translation: You may have heard that, but you must be somewhat hard of hearing then. Those who talk about me call me Katherine.

original: You lie, in faith, for you are called plain Kate,   And bonny Kate, and sometimes Kate the curst,   But Kate,
translation: You lie, I swear, for you are called Kate, plain Kate, and pretty Kate, and sometimes Kate the shrew, but always Kate,

original: the prettiest Kate in Christendom,   Kate of Kate Hall, my super-dainty Kate—   For dainties are all Kates
translation: the prettiest Kate in God's kingdom, Kate from Kate Hall, my delicious Kate—for all delicacies are  Kates

original: —and therefore, Kate,   Take this of me, Kate of my consolation:
translation: —and so, Kate, listen to me:

original: Hearing thy mildness praised in every town,   Thy virtues spoke of, and thy beauty sounded—   Yet not so deeply as to thee belongs—   Myself am moved to woo thee for my wife.
translation: having heard your modesty, virtue, and beauty praised in every town, though not as highly as you deserve, I have been moved to court you for my wife.

original: “Moved,” in good time. Let him that moved you hither Remove you hence. I knew you at the first You were a moveable.
Why, what’s a moveable?
translation: Why, what do you mean by "moveable?"

original: A joint stool.
translation: A stool.

original: Thou hast hit it. Come, sit on me.
translation: Exactly. Come sit on me.

original: Asses are made to bear, and so are you.
translation: Asses are meant for bearing, and so are you.

original: Women are made to bear, and so are you.
No such jade as you, if me you mean.
translation: Not for bearing the likes of you, if you're talking about me.

original: Alas, good Kate, I will not burden thee, For knowing thee to be but young and light—
Too light for such a swain as you to catch, And yet as heavy as my weight should be.
translation: Too light for a bumpkin like you to catch—and yet just as heavy as I should be.

original: “Should be”—should buzz!
translation: "Should be?" Keep on buzzing, bee!

original: Well ta'en, and like a buzzard.
O slow-winged turtle, shall a buzzard take thee?
translation: Oh slow-winged turtledove, will you let a buzzard catch you?

original: Ay, for a turtle, as he takes a buzzard.
translation: No, this turtledove will catch a buzzard.

original: Come, come, you wasp. I' faith, you are too angry.
translation: Come, come, my little wasp. Really, you're too angry.

original: If I be waspish, best beware my sting.
translation: If I'm a wasp, then you'd better beware my stinger.

original: My remedy is then to pluck it out.
translation: I'll have to pluck it out.

original: Ay, if the fool could find it where it lies.
translation: If a fool like you could find it.

original: Who knows not where a wasp does wear his sting? In his tail.
translation: Who doesn't know where a wasp wears its stinger? In its tail.

original: In his tongue.
translation: No, in its tongue.

original: Whose tongue?
translation: Whose tongue?

original: Yours, if you talk of tales. And so farewell.
translation: Yours, if we're telling tall tales of tails. Farewell then.

original: What, with my tongue in your tail? Nay, come again, Good Kate. I am a gentleman.
translation: What, you'll leave with my tongue in your tail? No, come back, good Kate. I am a gentleman.

original: That I’ll try.
translation: I'll test that out.

original: I swear I’ll cuff you if you strike again.
translation: I swear I'll hit you if you strike me again.

original: So may you lose your arms. If you strike me, you are no gentleman; And if no gentleman, why then no arms.
A herald, Kate? Oh, put me in thy books!
translation: Are you a register for gentlemen, Kate? Oh, put me in your good books!

original: What is your crest? A coxcomb?
A combless cock, so Kate will be my hen.
translation: I'd be a cock without a comb, if Kate will be my hen.

original: No cock of mine. You crow too like a craven.
translation: Then you'd be no cock of mine. You won't fight.

original: Nay, come, Kate, come. You must not look so sour.
translation: Come, Kate, come. Don't look so sour.

original: It is my fashion, when I see a crab.
translation: That's just what I do, when I see a crab apple.

original: Why, here’s no crab, and therefore look not sour.
translation: Why, there's no crab apple here, so don't look sour.

original: There is, there is.
translation: But there is, there is.

original: Then show it me.
translation: Then show it to me.

original: Had I a glass, I would.
translation: If I had a mirror, I would.

original: What, you mean my face?
translation: What, you mean my face?

original: Well aimed of such a young one.
translation: What a good guess for such a boy!

original: Now, by Saint George, I am too young for you.
translation: By Saint George, I probably am too young for you.

original: Yet you are withered.
translation: But you're also wrinkled.

original: 'Tis with cares.
translation: That's from worries and cares.

original: I care not.
translation: I don't care.

original: Nay, hear you, Kate: in sooth you ’scape not so.
translation: Now listen, Kate: you won't escape like that.

original: I chafe you, if I tarry. Let me go.
translation: I'll only irritate you if I stay. Let me go.

original: No, not a whit. I find you passing gentle.
translation: No, not a bit. I find you exceedingly gentle.

original: 'Twas told me you were rough and coy and sullen,   And now I find report a very liar.
translation: I was told that you were rough, scornful, and sullen, but now I see that those rumors are lies.

original: For thou are pleasant, gamesome, passing courteous,   But slow in speech, yet sweet as springtime flowers.
translation: You are pleasant, amusing, polite, not sharp-tongued, and as sweet as springtime flowers.

original: Thou canst not frown, thou canst not look askance,   Nor bite the lip as angry wenches will,   Nor hast thou pleasure to be cross in talk.
translation: Even if you tried, you couldn't frown, glare scornfully, or bite your lip as angry women do, and you take no pleasure in arguments.

original: But thou with mildness entertain’st thy wooers,   With gentle conference, soft and affable.
translation: Instead you entertain your suitors with mild and gentle conversation, and are quiet and friendly.

original: Why does the world report that Kate doth limp?   O slanderous world!
translation: So why does the world report that Kate limps along? What a slanderous world!

original: Kate like the hazel-twig   As hazel nuts, and sweeter than the kernels.
translation: Kate is like a hazel-twig, straight and slender, her hair is as brown as hazelnuts, and she herself is sweeter than the hazelnut kernels.

original: Oh, let me see thee walk! Thou dost not halt.
translation: Oh, let me see you walk, Kate! You don't limp at all!

original: Go, fool, and whom thou keep’st command.
translation: Go, fool. Order your servants around—not me.

original: Did ever Dian so become a grove   As Kate this chamber with her princely gait?
translation: Did the goddess Diana ever grace a forest like Kate now graces this room with her queenly walk?

original: Oh, be thou Dian, and let her be Kate,   And then let Kate be chaste and Dian sportful.
translation: Oh, you be Diana, then, and let Diana be Kate. Then let Kate be the chaste one, while Diana is my love.

original: Where did you study all this goodly speech?
translation: Where did you memorize all this witty talk?

original: It is extempore, from my mother wit.
translation: It's off-the-cuff. It comes from my natural intelligence.

original: A witty mother! Witless else her son.
translation: What a witty mother! Too bad her son is witless.

original: Am I not wise?
translation: Am I not wise?

original: Yes, keep you warm.
Marry, so I mean, sweet Katherine, in thy bed.
translation: Indeed, I do mean to keep myself warm, sweet Katherine, in your bed.

original: And therefore, setting all this chat aside,   Thus in plain terms:
translation: But enough chatter. Let's speak plainly:

original: your father hath consented   That you shall be my wife, your dowry 'greed on,   And, will you, nill you, I will marry you.
translation: your father has consented that you will be my wife. Your dowry is agreed upon,  and whether you want it or not, I  will  marry you.

original: Now, Kate, I am a husband for your turn,   For, by this light, whereby I see thy beauty,   Thy beauty that doth make me like thee well,   Thou must be married to no man but me.
translation: Now, Kate, I'm the only husband for you. I swear by this light, which lets me see your beauty—your beauty that makes me love you—that you must be married to no man but me.

original: For I am he am born to tame you, Kate,   And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate   Conformable as other household Kates.
translation: I was born to tame you, Kate, and change you from a wildcat Kate into a Kate as obedient as other domesticated Kates.

original: Here comes your father. Never make denial. I must and will have Katherine to my wife.
translation: Here comes your father. Don't refuse my proposal. I must and will have Katherine for my wife.

original: Now, Signior Petruchio, how speed you with my daughter?
translation: Now, Sir Petruchio, how's it going with my daughter?

original: How but well, sir? How but well?  It were impossible I should speed amiss.
translation: How but well, sir? How but well? It would be impossible to go any other way.

original: Why, how now, daughter Katherine? In your dumps?
translation: And how are you, daughter Katherine? Are you sad?

original: Call you me daughter?
translation: You'd dare to call me daughter?

original: Now, I promise you   You have showed a tender fatherly regard   To wish me wed to one half lunatic,   A madcup ruffian and a swearing Jack,
translation: I swear, you've certainly shown a father's tender care in trying to marry me off to a lunatic, a crazed villain and a swearing fool,

original: That thinks with oaths to face the matter out.
translation: who thinks that he can force his way through with enough cursing!

original: Father, ’tis thus: yourself and all the world   That talked of her have talked amiss of her.
translation: Father, it's like this: you and everyone else who've talked about her have all been wrong.

original: If she be curst, it is for policy,   For she’s not froward, but modest as the dove.
translation: If she's a shrew, then it's for some crafty purpose, for she's not naturally willful, but is in fact as modest as a dove.

original: She is not hot, but temperate as the morn.
translation: She's not fierce, but as mild as the morning.

original: For patience she will prove a second Grissel,   And Roman Lucrece for her chastity.
translation: She has the patience of  Griselda  and the chastity of Rome's  Lucrece .

original: And to conclude, we have 'greed so well together,   That upon Sunday is the wedding day.
translation: To conclude, we've gotten along so well together that Sunday will be our wedding day.

original: I’ll see thee hanged on Sunday first.
translation: I'll see you hanged on Sunday first!

original: Hark, Petruchio: she says she’ll see thee hanged first.
translation: Did you hear that, Petruchio? She says she'll see you hanged first.

original: Is this your speeding? Nay, then, good night our part.
translation: Is this what you call success? So much for our hopes of freeing Bianca.

original: Be patient, gentlemen. I choose her for myself.   If she and I be pleased, what’s that to you?
translation: Be patient, gentlemen. I choose her for myself. If she and I are happy, then what's it to you?

original: 'Tis bargained ’twixt us twain, being alone,   That she shall still be curst in company.
translation: When we were alone, we agreed that she would go on being a shrew in public.

original: I tell you, ’tis incredible to believe   How much she loves me. O, the kindest Kate!
translation: I tell you, it's incredible how much she loves me, though. Oh, the kindest Kate!

original: She hung about my neck, and kiss on kiss   She vied so fast, protesting oath on oath,   That in a twink she won me to her love.
translation: She threw her arms around my neck, giving me kiss after kiss and swearing vows of love, and in an instant she had won my heart.

original: O, you are novices! 'Tis a world to see,   How tame, when men and women are alone,   A meacock wretch can make the curstest shrew.—
translation: Oh, you are all just beginners! It's amazing to see—even a cowardly wretch can tame the fiercest shrew when a man and a woman are left alone together.

original: Give me thy hand, Kate. I will unto Venice   To buy apparel 'gainst the wedding day.
translation: —Give me your hand, Kate. I'll now go to Venice to buy clothes for the wedding.

original: Provide the feast, father, and bid the guests.   I will be sure my Katherine shall be fine.
translation: You plan the feast, father, and invite the guests. I'll make sure my Katherine will be beautifully dressed.

original: I know not what to say, but give me your hands. God send you joy, Petruchio. 'Tis a match.
translation: I don't know what to say. Give me your hands. May God give you joy, Petruchio. It's a match.

original: Amen, say we. We will be witnesses.
translation: We say Amen to that! We will be witnesses.

original: Father, and wife, and gentlemen, adieu.   I will to Venice.
translation: Father, and wife, and gentlemen—farewell. I'm off to Venice.

original: Sunday comes apace.   We will have rings, and things, and fine array,   And kiss me, Kate.
translation: Sunday is coming soon. We will have rings, and things, and fine clothes, and kiss me, Kate.

original: We will be married o' Sunday.
translation: We will be married on Sunday.

original: Was ever match clapped up so suddenly?
translation: Was ever a match agreed upon so suddenly?

original: Faith, gentlemen, now I play a merchant’s part, And venture madly on a desperate mart.
translation: Truly, gentlemen, I'm now playing the part of the merchant, and I've made a desperate bargain.

original: 'Twas a commodity lay fretting by you. 'Twill bring you gain or perish on the seas.
translation: Yes, but your goods were just gathering dust and annoying you. Now they'll either bring you a profit or be lost at sea.

original: The gain I seek is quiet in the match.
translation: The only profit I seek is a quiet, peaceful match.

original: No doubt but he hath got a quiet catch.
translation: And no doubt Petruchio will have a quiet catch—no one's going to fight him for her.

original: But now, Baptista, to your younger daughter.
translation: But now, Baptista, let's think about your younger daughter.

original: Now is the day we long have lookèd for.   I am your neighbor, and was suitor first.
translation: This is the day we've been waiting for. I am your neighbor, and I was her first suitor.

original: And I am one that love Bianca more Than words can witness or your thoughts can guess.
translation: And I am a man that loves Bianca more than words can express, or your thoughts can guess.

original: Youngling, thou canst not love so dear as I.
translation: Boy, you don't know how to love like I do.

original: Graybeard, thy love doth freeze.
translation: Old graybeard, your love has frozen over.

original: But thine doth fry. Skipper, stand back. 'Tis age that nourisheth.
translation: But yours will burn out. Stand back, fickle boy. Age is what nourishes.

original: But youth in ladies' eyes that  flourisheth.
translation: But in ladies' eyes, it's youth that flourishes.

original: Content you, gentlemen. I will compound this strife.
translation: Calm down, gentlemen. I will settle this quarrel.

original: 'Tis deeds must win the prize, and he of both   That can assure my daughter greatest dower   Shall have my Bianca’s love.
translation: Only  deeds  can determine the winner here. Whoever can offer my daughter the most wealth and property as her widow's inheritance will have Bianca's love.

original: Say, Signior Gremio, what can you assure her?
translation: So tell me, Sir Gremio, what can you offer her?

original: First, as you know, my house within the city   Is richly furnishèd with plate and gold,   Basins and ewers to lave her dainty hands;
translation: First, as you know, my house in the city, which is richly furnished with gold and china, and basins and jugs for her to wash her dainty hands.

original: My hangings all of Tyrian tapestry,   In ivory coffers I have stuffed my crowns,
translation: My wall hangings are of  purple  tapestry, my ivory chests are stuffed with gold,

original: In cypress chests my arras counterpoints,   Costly apparel, tents, and canopies,
translation: and my cypress-wood chests are filled with quilted bedspreads, expensive clothes, bed curtains and canopies,

original: Fine linen, Turkey cushions bossed with pearl,   Valance of Venice gold in needlework,   Pewter and brass, and all things that belong   To house or housekeeping.
translation: fine linen, Turkish cushions embossed with pearl, gold Venetian draperies, pewter and brass, and everything else you could want for a house or housekeeping.

original: Then, at my farm   I have a hundred milch-kine to the pail,   Six score fat oxen standing in my stalls,
translation: Then, at my farm I have a hundred milk cows and a hundred and twenty fat oxen in my stables.

original: And all things answerable to this portion.
translation: Everything else I own is of a similar high value.

original: Myself am struck in years, I must confess,   And if I die tomorrow this is hers,   If whilst I live she will be only mine.
translation: I myself am getting on in years, I must confess, and if I should die tomorrow, all this will belong to Bianca—so long as while I live she will be only mine.

original: That “only” came well in.
translation: That "only" came just in time.

original: Two thousand ducats by the year of land!
translation: Two thousand gold coins a year from his land!

original: Gremio, ’tis known my father hath no  less   Than three great argosies, besides two galliasses,   And twelve tight galleys.
translation: Gremio, it's well known that my father has no fewer than three great merchant ships, along with two large galleys and twelve smaller ones.

original: These I will assure her,   And twice as much whate'er thou offer’st next.
translation: I'll offer all these to Bianca, and I'll double whatever you might offer next.

original: Nay, I have offered all, I have no more, And she can have no more than all I have.     If you like me, she shall have me and  mine.
translation: No, I've offered everything I own. I have nothing left. She can't have more than all I have.

original: Why, then the maid is mine from all the world, By your firm promise. Gremio is outvied.
translation: Why, then she's mine alone, of all the men in the world, by your firm promise. Gremio has been outbid.

original: I must confess your offer is the best,   And, let your father make her the assurance,   She is your own;
translation: I must confess that your offer is the best. If your father will second your guarantees, then she's yours.

original: else, you must pardon me.   If you should die before him, where’s her dower?
translation: Otherwise, you must pardon me—if you should die before your father does, then what would become of all the wealth Bianca is supposed to inherit from you?

original: That’s but a cavil: he is old, I young.
translation: That's a trivial objection: he is old, and I am young.

original: And may not young men die as well as old?
translation: And can't young men die as well as old men?

original: Well, gentlemen,   I am thus resolved. On Sunday next, you know   My daughter Katherina is to be married.
translation: Well, gentlemen, I have decided. Next Sunday my daughter Katherina is to be married, you know.

original: Adieu, good neighbor.
translation: Farewell, good neighbor.

original: Now I fear thee not.
translation: Now I'm not afraid of you anymore, boy.

original: Sirrah young gamester, your father were a fool   To give thee all and in his waning age   Set foot under thy table.
translation: You young gambler, your father would be a fool to give you everything and spend his declining years as a dependent in your house.

original: Tut, a toy!   An old Italian fox is not so kind, my boy.
translation: Ha, it's nonsense! An old Italian fox is never that kind, my boy.

original: A vengeance on your crafty withered hide!   Yet I have faced it with a card of ten.
translation: A curse on your crafty withered hide! But I've bluffed successfully without even a  face card .

original: 'Tis in my head to do my master good.   I see no reason but supposed Lucentio   Must get a father, called “supposed Vincentio”—   And that’s a wonder.
translation: I think I'll be able to do my master good. I see no reason why the pretend Lucentio shouldn't produce a father, called "pretend Vincentio"—and that'll be a miracle.

original: Fathers commonly   Do get their children. But in this case of wooing,   A child shall get a sire, if I fail not of my cunning.
translation: Fathers usually father their children, not the other way around. But in this case of wooing, a child will father a father, if my wits don't fail me.

original: Fiddler, forbear. You grow too forward,  sir. Have you so soon forgot the entertainment Her sister Katherina welcomed you withal?
translation: Enough, fiddler! You grow too forward, sir. Have you already forgotten how her sister Katherina thanked you for your insistence?

original: But, wrangling pedant, this is   The patroness of heavenly harmony.
translation: But this is not Katherine, that quarrelsome know-it-all—this is the goddess of heavenly harmony.

original: Then give me leave to have prerogative,   And when in music we have spent an hour,   Your lecture shall have leisure for as much.
translation: So let me go first, and after we've spent an hour on music, you can have the same amount of time for your lesson.

original: Preposterous ass, that never read so far   To know the cause why music was ordained.
translation: Ridiculous ass! You are not even educated enough to know why music was created in the first place.

original: Was it not to refresh the mind of man   After his studies or his usual pain?
translation: Wasn't it to refresh the mind of man  after  his studies and daily labor?

original: Then give me leave to read philosophy   And, while I pause, serve in your harmony.
translation: So let me read philosophy with her, and when I take a break, you can come in with your harmony.

original: Sirrah, I will not bear these braves of  thine.
translation: Boy, I won't stand for these insults!

original: Why, gentlemen, you do me double wrong   To strive for that which resteth in my choice.
translation: Why, gentlemen, you both do me wrong in arguing over something that is really my decision.

original: I am no breeching scholar in the schools.
translation: I am no schoolboy to be whipped and disciplined.

original: I’ll not be tied to hours nor 'pointed times   But learn my lessons as I please myself.
translation: I won't be ordered about with hours and appointed schedules—I will learn my lessons as it pleases me.

original: And, to cut off all strife, here sit we down.
translation: So to cut off all this arguing, let's sit down and figure this out.

original: You’ll leave his lecture when I am in tune?
translation: And you'll stop his lesson once I am in tune?

original: That will be never.  [To HORTENSIO]  Tune your  instrument.
translation: That will be never.

original: Where left we last?
translation: Where did we leave off?

original: Here, madam:   Hic ibat Simois, hic est Sigeia tellus,   Hic steterat Priami regia celsa senis.
translation: Here, madam:

original: Construe them.
translation: Translate them.

original: Hic ibat   , as I told you before,   Simois   , I am Lucentio,    hic est   , son unto Vincentio of Pisa,     Sigeia tellus   ,  disguised thus to get your love,
translation: Hic ibat , as I told you before,  Simois , I am Lucentio,  hic est , son of Vincentio of Pisa,   Sigeia tellus , disguised like this to win your love.

original: Hic steterat   , and that  “Lucentio” that comes a-wooing,   Priami   is my man Tranio,    regia   , bearing my port,   celsa senis,   that we might  beguile the old pantaloon.
translation: Hic steterat , and the other "Lucentio" who comes to woo you,  Priami , is my servant Tranio,  regia , pretending to be me,  celsa senis , so we can trick the foolish old Gremio.

original: Madam, my instrument’s in tune.
translation: Madam, my instrument's in tune.

original: Let’s hear.    O fie! The treble jars.
translation: Let's hear it.

original: Spit in the hole, man, and tune again.
translation: Start over, man, and tune again.

original: Now let me see if I can construe it.  Hic ibat Simois  ,  I know you not,  hic est Sigeia tellus  , I trust you not, Hic steterat Priami  , take heed he hear us not,  regia  ,  presume not,  celsa   senis,  despair not.
translation: Now let me see if I can translate it. Hic ibat Simois, I don't know you, hic est Sigeia tellus, I don't trust you, Hic steterat Priami, make sure he doesn't hear us, regia, don't presume anything, celsa senis, don't give up.

original: Madam, ’tis now in tune.
translation: Madam, now it's in tune.

original: All but the base.
translation: All but the bass string.

original: The base is right; ’tis the base knave  that jars.
translation: The bass string is fine—it's this base villain that's out of tune.

original: In time I may believe, yet I mistrust.
translation: In time I may believe you, but I'm still doubtful.

original: Mistrust it not, for sure Aeacides Was Ajax, called so from his grandfather.
translation: Don't doubt me, for—

original: I must believe my master; else, I promise you,   I should be arguing still upon that doubt.
translation: I must believe you because you're my teacher, or else, I promise you, I would keep arguing.

original: But let it rest.—Now, Litio, to you.
translation: But let it go.—Now, Litio, it's your turn.

original: Good master, take it not unkindly, pray,   That I have been thus pleasant with you both.
translation: Good teacher, I hope you're not offended that I've been equally friendly to both of you.

original: You may go walk, and give me leave awhile. My lessons make no music in three parts.
translation: You can go take a walk, and leave us alone for a while. I don't teach music for three people.

original: Are you so formal, sir? Well, I must wait.     And watch withal, for, but I be deceived, Our fine musician groweth amorous.
translation: Are you so strict, sir? Well, I guess I have to wait then.

original: Madam, before you touch the instrument,   To learn the order of my fingering   I must begin with rudiments of art,
translation: Madam, before you touch the instrument or learn the fingering, I must begin by teaching you the fundamentals of music.

original: To teach you gamut in a briefer sort,   More pleasant, pithy, and effectual   Than hath been taught by any of my trade.
translation: To teach you the scales, I have a method that's more pleasant and effective than what any other teachers use.

original: And there it is in writing, fairly drawn.
translation: And here it is written out.

original: Why, I am past my gamut long ago.
translation: Why, I learned my scales long ago.

original: Yet read the gamut of Hortensio.
translation: But still, read Hortensio's scale.

original: “   Gamut   I am, the ground of all accord:
translation: "I am the scale, the foundation of all harmony:

original: A re,   to plead Hortensio’s passion;
translation: A re , to declare Hortensio's passion;

original: B mi,   Bianca, take him for thy lord,
translation: B mi , Bianca, take him for your husband,

original: C fa ut,   that loves with all affection;
translation: C fa ut , he loves you with all affection;

original: D sol re,   one clef, two notes have I;
translation: D sol re , I have one key but only two notes;

original: E la mi,   show pity, or I die.”
translation: E la mi , show me pity, or I'll die."

original: Call you this “gamut”? Tut, I like it not.   Old fashions please me best.
translation: You call this a scale? I don't like it. I prefer the old-fashioned way.

original: I am not so nice   To change true rules for old inventions.
translation: I'm not so foolish as to want to replace the old, true methods.

original: Mistress, your father prays you leave your books And help to dress your sister’s chamber up. You know tomorrow is the wedding day.
translation: Mistress, your father asks that you leave your books and help decorate your sister's room. You know tomorrow is the wedding day.

original: Farewell, sweet masters both. I must be gone.
translation: Farewell, sweet teachers. I must go.

original: Faith, mistress, then I have no cause to  stay.
translation: Well, mistress, then I have no reason to stay any longer.

original: But I have cause to pry into this pedant.
translation: But I have a reason to examine this know-it-all teacher more closely.

original: Methinks he looks as though he were in love.
translation: I think he looks like he's in love.

original: Yet if thy thoughts, Bianca, be so humble   To cast thy wand'ring eyes on every stale,   Seize thee that list!
translation: But if Bianca is so vulgar as to fall for every false man she sees, then let him have her!

original: If once I find thee ranging,   Hortensio will be quit with thee by changing.
translation: If I ever catch her being unfaithful, I'll get even with her by loving someone else.

original: Signior Lucentio, this is the 'pointed day   That Katherine and Petruchio should be married,   And yet we hear not of our son-in-law.
translation: Sir Lucentio, this is the day appointed for Katherine and Petruchio to be married, but I haven't heard from my son-in-law at all.

original: What will be said? What mockery will it be,   To want the bridegroom when the priest attends   To speak the ceremonial rites of marriage?
translation: What will people say? What a mockery it will be to have the priest here, ready to perform the marriage ceremony, and be missing the bridegroom!

original: What says Lucentio to this shame of ours?
translation: What does Lucentio have to say about our shame?

original: No shame but mine. I must, forsooth, be forced   To give my hand, opposed against my heart,   Unto a mad-brain rudesby, full of spleen,   Who wooed in haste and means to wed at leisure.
translation: The shame is all mine. I was forced to oppose my own heart and give my hand to that boorish, fickle madman, who wooed in a hurry and means to marry at his leisure.

original: I told you, I, he was a frantic fool,   Hiding his bitter jests in blunt behavior,
translation: I told you he was a crazy fool, hiding his bitter jokes with his forward behavior.

original: And, to be noted for a merry man,   He’ll woo a thousand, 'point the day of marriage,   Make friends, invite, and proclaim the banns,   Yet never means to wed where he hath wooed.
translation: He wants to be known as this cheerful libertine, so he'll woo a thousand women, set the marriage date, invite friends, and make a public announcement —but he has no intention of actually getting married.

original: Now must the world point at poor Katherine   And say, “Lo, there is mad Petruchio’s wife,   If it would please him come and marry her!”
translation: Now everyone must point at poor Katherine and say, "Look, there is mad Petruchio's wife—if he could be bothered to come and marry her!"

original: Patience, good Katherine, and Baptista  too.
translation: Be patient, good Katherine, and you too, Baptista.

original: Upon my life, Petruchio means but well,   Whatever fortune stays him from his word:
translation: I swear Petruchio means well, despite whatever might be keeping him from honoring his word.

original: Though he be blunt, I know him passing wise;   Though he be merry, yet withal he’s honest.
translation: Though he's rude, I know he's exceedingly wise, and though he's a joker, he's still an honest man.

original: Would Katherine had never seen him, though!
translation: I wish that I had never seen him, though!

original: Go, girl. I cannot blame thee now to weep, For such an injury would vex a very saint, Much more a shrew of thy impatient humor.
translation: Go, girl. I can't blame you for weeping now. Such an insult would offend even a saint, let alone an impatient shrew like you.

original: Master, master! News, old news, and such news as you  never heard of!
Is it new and old too? How may that be?
translation: You have news that's both new and old? How can that be?

original: Why, is it not news to hear of Petruchio’s coming?
translation: Why, isn't it news that Petruchio is coming?

original: Is he come?
translation: Is he here?

original: Why, no, sir.
translation: Why, no, sir.

original: What then?
translation: What then?

original: He is coming.
translation: He is coming.

original: When will he be here?
translation: When will he be here?

original: When he stands where I am and sees you there.
translation: When he stands where I am and sees you there.

original: But say, what to thine old news?
translation: But tell us, what is your old news?

original: Why, Petruchio is coming in a new hat and an old  jerkin, a pair of old breeches thrice turned, a pair of  boots that have been candle cases,   one buckled, another  laced;
translation: Well, Petruchio is coming in a new hat and an old jacket, a pair of old pants turned inside out, broken suspenders holding them up, and a pair of boots that have been used as candle holders:  one of them buckled, the other laced.

original: an old rusty sword ta'en out of the town armory,  with a broken hilt and chapeless; with two broken  points;
translation: He has an old rusty sword from the town armory with a broken hilt and no scabbard.

original: his horse hipped, with an old mothy saddle and  stirrups of no kindred,
translation: He's riding on a lame horse with an old moth-eaten saddle and two different stirrups,

original: besides possessed with the  glanders and like to mose in the chine, troubled with  the lampass, infected with the fashions, full of  wingdalls, sped with spavins, rayed with yellows, past  cure of the fives, stark spoiled with the staggers,  begnawn with the bots, swayed in the back and  shoulder-shotten,
translation: @ jaundice , swollen ears, palsy, worms, a twisted back, a sprained shoulder, and knock-kneed forelegs.

original: near-legged before and with a  half-checked bit and a headstall of sheeps leather,  which, being restrained to keep him from stumbling, hath been often burst, and now repaired with knots, one  girth six times pieced, and a woman’s crupper of velour, which hath two letters for her name fairly set down in  studs, and here and there pieced with packthread.
translation: His bit is hanging off and his cheap bridle, which is pulled tight, is pieced together with knots; his saddle strap is patched up and his tail strap is velvet, studded with the initials of some woman, and here and there held together with thread.

original: Who comes with him?
translation: Who's with him?

original: O, sir, his lackey, for all the world caparisoned like  the horse; with a linen stock on one leg and a kersey  boot-hose on the other,
translation: Oh, sir, just his servant, who's dressed up like the horse, with a linen stocking on one leg and a big woolen sock on the other,

original: gartered with a red and blue  list; an old hat and the humor of forty fancies pricked  in ’t for a feather.
translation: a pair of red and blue garters, and an old hat with some crazy decoration on it in place of the feather.

original: A monster, a very monster in  apparel, and not like a Christian footboy or a  gentleman’s lackey.
translation: He's dressed like a monster, a total monster, and not at all like a proper Christian page or a gentleman's servant.

original: 'Tis some odd humor pricks him to this fashion, Yet oftentimes he goes but mean-appareled.
translation: It's some strange whim of his that inspires this fashion—though he does often dress casually.

original: I am glad he’s come, howsoe'er he comes.
translation: I'm glad he's coming, however he might be dressed.

original: Why, sir, he comes not.
translation: Why, sir, he's not coming.

original: Didst thou not say he comes?
translation: Didn't you say he was coming?

original: Who? That Petruchio came?
translation: Who? Petruchio?

original: Ay, that Petruchio came.
translation: Yes, that Petruchio was coming.

original: No, sir, I say his horse comes, with him on his back.
translation: No, sir, I said that his horse was coming, with him on its back.

original: Why, that’s all one.
translation: Why, that's the same thing.

original: Nay, by Saint Jamy,  I hold you a penny, A horse and a man Is more than one And yet not many.
Come, where be these gallants? Who’s at home?
translation: Come now, where are all the gentlemen? Is anyone at home?

original: You are welcome, sir.
translation: You are welcome, sir.

original: And yet I come not well.
translation: And yet I didn't come well.

original: And yet you halt not.
translation: And yet you aren't limping.

original: Not so well appareled as I wish you were.
translation: And you're not as well-dressed as I wish you would be.

original: Were it better I should rush in thus—   But where is Kate? Where is my love?
translation: Even if my clothes were better I would still rush in like this—But where is Kate? Where is my love?

original: How does my father?
translation: How is my father-in-law?

original: Gentles, methinks you frown.   And wherefore gaze this goodly company   As if they saw some wondrous monument,   Some comet or unusual prodigy?
translation: Gentlemen, you seem to be frowning. Why is this fine gathering of people all staring, as if at something strange—a comet or some unnatural phenomenon?

original: Why, sir, you know this is your wedding day.
translation: Why, sir, you know this is your wedding day.

original: First were we sad, fearing you would not come,   Now sadder that you come so unprovided.
translation: First we were sad because we feared you wouldn't come, but now we're sadder to see that you've come so unprepared.

original: Fie, doff this habit, shame to your estate,   An eyesore to our solemn festival.
translation: For God's sake, take off this costume. It's a disgrace to your social rank and an eyesore in the middle of our solemn ceremony.

original: And tell us what occasion of import Hath all so long detained you from your wife And sent you hither so unlike yourself.
translation: And tell us what was so important that it made you late for your wedding, and sent you here dressed so unlike yourself.

original: Tedious it were to tell and harsh to hear.
translation: It would be a tedious story to tell, and a rough one to hear.

original: See not your bride in these unreverent robes. Go to my chamber, put on clothes of mine.
translation: Don't go see your bride in these disrespectful clothes. Go to my room and put on some of my clothes.

original: Not I, believe me. Thus I’ll visit her.
translation: I won't, believe me. I'll visit her like this.

original: But thus, I trust, you will not marry her.
translation: But surely you won't marry her like this.

original: Good sooth, even thus. Therefore, ha' done with words:
translation: I swear, I will. So let's stop talking about it.

original: To me she’s married, not unto my clothes.
translation: She's marrying  me , not my clothes.

original: Could I repair what she will wear in me   As I can change these poor accoutrements,   'Twere well for Kate and better for myself.
translation: If I could fix my bad qualities as easily as I could change out of these ugly clothes, it would be good for Kate and even better for myself.

original: But what a fool am I to chat with you,   When I should bid good morrow to my bride   And seal the title with a lovely kiss!
translation: But what a fool I am for standing here chatting with you, when I should say good morning to my bride and seal our bargain with a loving kiss!

original: He hath some meaning in his mad attire. We will persuade him, be it possible, To put on better ere he go to church.
translation: He has some plan in dressing up like this. If it's possible, I'll try to persuade him to put on something better before he goes to the church.

original: I’ll after him, and see the event of this.
translation: I'll follow him too, and see how this turns out.

original: But sir, to love concerneth us to add   Her father’s liking,
translation: Sir, to be successful you need to get her father's approval as well as Bianca's love.

original: which to bring to pass,   As I before unparted to your worship,   I am to get a man—whate'er he be   It skills not much, we’ll fit him to our turn—
translation: To make this happen, as I explained to your worship, I will find a man—it doesn't really matter what kind of man; I'll make him suit our purposes—

original: And he shall be “Vincentio of Pisa”   And make assurance here in Padua   Of greater sums than I have promisèd.
translation: who can pretend to be "Vincentio of Pisa," and he can offer Baptista even greater sums of money than I already promised.

original: So shall you quietly enjoy your hope   And marry sweet Bianca with consent.
translation: And so you can get what you want without any trouble, and marry sweet Bianca with her father's consent.

original: Were it not that my fellow schoolmaster   Doth watch Bianca’s steps so narrowly,   'Twere good, methinks, to steal our marriage,
translation: If it weren't for the fact that my fellow tutor was watching Bianca so closely, I'd think it would be good to just elope in secret.

original: Which, once performed, let all the world say no,   I’ll keep mine own despite of all the world.
translation: Once the ceremony was performed, it wouldn't matter if the whole world disapproved—I'd keep my wife, despite what anyone might say.

original: That by degrees we mean to look into   And watch our vantage in this business.
translation: I mean to look into that, too, and to keep on eye on our opportunities in this business.

original: We’ll overreach the graybeard, Gremio,   The narrow-prying father, Minola,   The quaint musician, amorous Litio,   All for my master’s sake, Lucentio.
translation: I'll outwit the old graybeard, Gremio, the overbearing father, Minola, and the crafty musican, Litio the lover—all for the sake of my master Lucentio.

original: Signior Gremio, came you from the church?
translation: Sir Gremio, are you coming from the church?

original: As willingly as e'er I came from school.
translation: As eagerly as I ever came home from school.

original: And is the bride and bridegroom coming  home?
translation: And are the bride and bridegroom coming home?

original: A bridegroom, say you? 'Tis a groom indeed, A grumbling groom, and that the girl shall find.
translation: A bridegroom, you say? More like a groom who cleans stables, a grumbling groom, as that girl will soon discover.

original: Curster than she? Why, ’tis impossible.
translation: You mean he's more of a shrew than she is? Why, that's impossible.

original: Why, he’s a devil, a devil, a very fiend.
translation: Why, he's a devil, a devil, a total fiend.

original: Why, she’s a devil, a devil, the devil’s  dam.
translation: No, she's a devil, a devil, the devil's own mother.

original: Tut, she’s a lamb, a dove, a fool to him!
translation: Ha! She's a lamb, a dove, an innocent child compared to him!

original: I’ll tell you, Sir Lucentio: when the priest   Should ask if Katherine should be his wife,   “Ay, by gogs wouns!”
quoth he, and swore so loud   That, all amazed, the priest let fall the book,
translation: and swore so loudly that everyone was shocked and the priest dropped the prayer book.

original: And as he stooped again to take it up,   The mad-brained bridegroom took him such a cuff   That down fell priest and book, and book and priest.   “Now take them up,” quoth he, “if any list.”
translation: And when the priest bent down to pick it back up, that lunatic bridegroom gave him such a smack that both priest and book went flying "Now pick them up," he said then, "if anyone dares to."

original: What said the wench when he rose again?
translation: What did the girl say when the priest got back up?

original: Trembled and shook, for why he stamped and swore   As if the vicar meant to cozen him.
translation: She trembled and shook, because the bridegroom starting stamping and swearing, as if the priest was trying to cheat him out of his marriage.

original: But after many ceremonies done,   He calls for wine. “A health!” quoth he, as if   He had been aboard, carousing to his mates   After a storm;
translation: But then when the ceremony was finally done, he called for wine. "A toast!" he said, as if he were some drunken sailor partying with his mates after a storm.

original: quaffed off the muscatel   And threw the sops all in the sexton’s face,   Having no other reason   But that his beard grew thin and hungerly   And seemed to ask him sops as he was drinking.
translation: He chugged the wine and then threw the dregs in the  sexton's  face, just because the man's beard looked "thin and hungry" and seemed to be asking for it.

original: This done, he took the bride about the neck   And kissed her lips with such a clamorous smack   That at the parting all the church did echo.
translation: After that he threw his arms around the bride's neck and kissed her with such a noisy smack that the whole church echoed when their lips parted.

original: And I, seeing this, came thence for very shame,   And after me, I know, the rout is coming.   Such a mad marriage never was before.
translation: After seeing that, I immediately left the shameful scene. I'm sure the rest of the crowd is following me. There's never been a wedding as crazy as that!

original: Hark, hark! I hear the minstrels play.
translation: Listen, listen! I can hear the musicians playing.

original: Gentlemen and friends, I thank you for you
translation: Gentlemen and friends, I thank you for coming.

original: I know you think to dine with me today   And have prepared great store of wedding cheer,
translation: I know you expected to dine with me today, and you've prepared a feast to celebrate the wedding,

original: But so it is, my haste doth call me hence,   And therefore here I mean to take my leave.
translation: but it so happens that I've been called away to urgent business. So I must say goodbye.

original: Is ’t possible you will away tonight?
translation: Are you really leaving tonight?

original: I must away today, before night come.   Make it no wonder.
translation: I must leave today, before the night even comes. Don't be so surprised.

original: If you knew my business,   You would entreat me rather go than stay.
translation: If you knew my business, you'd urge me to go rather than stay.

original: And, honest company, I thank you all,   That have beheld me give away myself   To this most patient, sweet and virtuous wife.
translation: And, honest friends, I thank you all for coming to watch me give myself away to this patient, sweet, virtuous wife.

original: Dine with my father, drink a health to me,   For I must hence, and farewell to you all.
translation: Dine with my father-in-law and drink a toast to me, for I must go. Farewell to you all.

original: Let us entreat you stay till after  dinner.
translation: Can you at least stay until after dinner?

original: It may not be.
translation: I cannot.

original: Let me entreat you.
translation: Whaf if  I ask you to stay?

original: It cannot be.
translation: I cannot.

original: Let me entreat you.
translation: Can I ask you to stay?

original: I am content.
translation: I'd be glad to.

original: Are you content to stay?
translation: You'd be glad to stay?

original: I am content you shall entreat me stay, But yet not stay, entreat me how you can.
translation: I'd be glad to hear you ask me to stay. But I cannot stay, no matter how much you plead with me.

original: Now, if you love me, stay.
translation: If you love me, stay.

original: Grumio, my horse.
translation: Grumio, get my horses ready.

original: Ay, sir, they be ready. The oats have eaten the horses.
translation: They're ready, sir. The oats have all eaten the horses.

original: Nay, then,   Do what thou canst, I will not go today,   No, nor tomorrow, not till I please myself.
translation: All right then, you do what you want. I won't go today, or tomorrow either. I won't go until I feel like it.

original: The door is open, sir. There lies your way.   You may be jogging whiles your boots are green.
translation: The door is open, sir. There's the way out. You'd better get an early start.

original: For me, I’ll not be gone till I please myself.
translation: As for me, I'll leave when I want to.

original: 'Tis like you’ll prove a jolly surly groom,   That take it on you at the first so roundly.
translation: If you throw your weight around so rudely at the very start, I'm sure you'll prove to be a surly, overbearing husband.

original: O Kate, content thee. Prithee, be not angry.
translation: Oh Kate, calm down. Please, don't be angry.

original: I will be angry. What hast thou to do?— Father, be quiet. He shall stay my leisure.
translation: I will be angry. What business is it of yours?—Father, be quiet. He'll stay until I want him to.

original: Ay, marry, sir, now it begins to work.
translation: Well, sir, now it begins.

original: Gentlemen, forward to the bridal dinner. I see a woman may be made a fool If she had not a spirit to resist.
translation: Gentlemen, go on to the bridal dinner. I see that a woman will be made into a fool if she doesn't stand up for herself.

original: They shall go forward, Kate, at thy command.—   Obey the bride, you that attend on her.
translation: They'll go on, Kate, at your command.—Obey the bride, you guests who attend on her.

original: Go to the feast, revel and domineer,   Carouse full measure to her maidenhead,
translation: Go to the feast, party and be merry, get drunk toasting to her virginity!

original: Be mad and merry, or go hang yourselves.   But for my bonny Kate, she must with me.
translation: Be wild and happy, or else go hang yourselves. But as for my pretty Kate, she must go with me.

original: Nay, look not big, nor stamp, nor stare, nor fret;   I will be master of what is mine own.
