translation: Now, don't look threatening, or stamp your feet, or glare, or worry. I will be the master of what is mine.

original: She is my goods, my chattels; she is my house,   My household stuff, my field, my barn,   My horse, my ox, my ass, my anything.
translation: She is my possession now, my property—like my house, my household stuff, my field, my barn, my horse, my ox, my donkey, my anything.

original: And here she stands, touch her whoever dare.   I’ll bring mine action on the proudest he   That stops my way in Padua.
translation: And here she stands. Touch her if you dare! I'll attack—legally and otherwise—any man in Padua who stands in my way, no matter what his rank.

original: —Grumio,   Draw forth thy weapon, we are beset with thieves.   Rescue thy mistress if thou be a man.—
translation: —Grumio, draw your sword, we are surrounded by thieves! Rescue your mistress, if you have any manliness in you!

original: Fear not, sweet wench, they shall not touch thee, Kate.   I’ll buckler thee against a million.
translation: —Don't be afraid, sweet girl, no one will touch you. I'll shield you against a million of them, Kate.

original: Nay, let them go, a couple of quiet ones.
translation: No, let them go. What a calm, quiet couple!

original: Went they not quickly, I should die with laughing.
translation: If they hadn't left so quickly, I would have died of laughing.

original: Of all mad matches never was the like.
translation: Of all the craziest pairings, I've never seen one like this.

original: Mistress, what’s your opinion of your  sister?
translation: Mistress, what's your opinion of your sister?

original: That, being mad herself, she’s madly mated.
translation: That, being mad herself, she has now married a madman.

original: I warrant him, Petruchio is Kated.
Neighbors and friends, though bride and bridegroom  wants   For to supply the places at the table,   You know there wants no junkets at the feast.
translation: Neighbors and friends, though the seats for the bride and bridegroom will be empty at the table, you know there are no delicacies lacking at the feast itself.

original: Shall sweet Bianca practice how to bride  it?
translation: Will sweet Bianca practice being a bride?

original: She shall, Lucentio. Come, gentlemen, let’s go.
translation: She will, Lucentio. Come, gentlemen, let's go.

original: Fie, fie on all tired jades, on all mad masters, and  all foul ways! Was ever man so beaten? Was ever man so  'rayed? Was ever man so weary?
translation: A curse, a curse  on all tired, worthless horses, on all crazy masters, and on all bad roads! Was ever a man beaten so much as me? Was ever a man so weary?

original: I am sent before to make  a fire, and they are coming after to warm them.
translation: I've been sent ahead to make a fire, and they're coming afterward to warm themselves up.

original: Now,  were not I a little pot and soon hot, my very lips might freeze to my teeth, my tongue to the roof of my mouth,  my heart in my belly, ere I should come by a fire to  thaw me.
translation: It's a good thing I can keep myself hot with my quick temper, or else my lips might freeze to my teeth, my tongue to the roof of my mouth, and my heart to my belly before I could find a fire to thaw myself out.

original: But I with blowing the fire shall warm myself.  For, considering the weather, a taller man than I will  take cold.—Holla, ho! Curtis!
translation: But I'll keep stoking my anger to stay warm. In weather like this, a better man than I am would catch cold.—Hey, hello! Curtis!

original: Who is that calls so coldly?
translation: Who is it who calls so coldly?

original: A piece of ice. If thou doubt it, thou mayst slide from my shoulder to my heel with no greater a run but my  head and my neck. A fire, good Curtis.
translation: A piece of ice. If you doubt me, try it out—you could slide from my shoulder to my heel after just a step from my head to my neck. Start a fire, good Curtis.

original: Is my master and his wife coming, Grumio?
translation: Are my master and his wife coming, Grumio?

original: O, ay, Curtis, ay, and therefore fire, fire. Cast on no water.
translation: Oh, yes, Curtis, yes, so they need a fire, a fire. And leave out the water.

original: Is she so hot a shrew as she’s reported?
translation: Is she as fiery a shrew as she's reported to be?

original: She was, good Curtis, before this frost. But thou  knowest winter tames man, woman and beast, for it hath  tamed my old master and my new mistress and myself,  fellow Curtis.
translation: She was, good Curtis, before this frost. But you know how winter tames man, woman, and beast—and so it's tamed my old master, my new mistress, and myself, good colleague Curtis.

original: Away, you three-inch fool! I am no beast.
translation: So you're a beast, and I'm your colleague! I don't think so. Away with you, you tiny fool!

original: Am I but three inches? Why, thy horn is a foot, and so  long am I, at the least.
But wilt thou make a fire, or  shall I complain on thee to our mistress,
translation: But are you going to make a fire, or will I have to complain about you to our mistress?

original: whose hand,  she being now at hand, thou shalt soon feel, to thy cold comfort, for being slow in thy hot office?
translation: Now that she's at hand, you'll soon feel her hand, and you'll find it cold comfort if you're slow in warming us up.

original: I prithee, good Grumio, tell me, how goes the world?
translation: Please, good Grumio, tell me, how are things out in the world?

original: A cold world, Curtis, in every office but thine, and  therefore fire! Do thy duty, and have thy duty, for my  master and mistress are almost frozen to death.
translation: It's a cold world, Curtis, for every man except fire-starters like you, so start a fire! Do your duty, and take your reward, for my master and mistress are almost frozen to death.

original: There’s fire ready. And therefore, good Grumio, the  news.
translation: There's a fire ready. So tell me the news, good Grumio.

original: Why, “Jack, boy! Ho, boy!” and as much news as wilt  thou.
translation: Why, "Jack, boy! Ho, boy!" and whatever other news you want.

original: Come, you are so full of cony-catching!
Why, therefore fire, for I have caught extreme cold.
translation: Why, make a fire then, for I have caught extreme cold.

original: Where’s the cook? Is supper ready, the house trimmed,  rushes strewed, cobwebs swept, the servingmen in their  new fustian, their white stockings, and every officer  his wedding garment on?
translation: Where's the cook? Is supper ready? Is the house prepared, the floor covered, the cobwebs swept up? Are the servingmen wearing their new clothes and white stockings, and the household servants their wedding suits?

original: Be the Jacks fair within, the  Jills fair without, the carpets laid, and everything in  order?
translation: Are the  Jacks and Jills  in their places, the tablecloths laid out—is everything in order?

original: All ready. And therefore, I pray thee, news.
translation: Everything's ready. So please, give me the news.

original: First, know my horse is tired, my master and mistress  fallen out.
translation: First of all, my horse is tired, and my master and mistress have had a falling out.

original: How?
translation: How?

original: Out of their saddles into the dirt, and thereby hangs a tale.
translation: Out of their saddles and into the dirt. But that's a long story.

original: Let’s ha' ’t, good Grumio.
translation: Let's hear it, good Grumio.

original: Lend thine ear.
translation: Lean close and I'll tell you.

original: Here.
translation: Here.

original: There!
translation: There!

original: This ’tis to feel a tale, not to hear a tale.
translation: That's to feel a story, not hear it.

original: And therefore ’tis called a sensible tale. And this  cuff was but to knock at your ear and beseech list'ning. Now I begin: Imprimis, we came down a foul hill, my  master riding behind my mistress—
translation: That's why it's a "sensitive" story. I was just knocking to see if your ear was listening. But now I'll begin: first of all, we came down a muddy hill, my master riding behind my mistress.

original: Both of one horse?
translation: Both on one horse?

original: What’s that to thee?
translation: What's the difference?

original: Why, a horse.
translation: Why, a horse.

original: Tell thou the tale! But hadst thou not crossed me, thou shouldst have heard how her horse fell, and she under  her horse.
translation: Then why don't you tell the story! If you hadn't interrupted me, you would have heard about how her horse fell, with her under it.

original: Thou shouldst have heard in how miry a place, how she was bemoiled, how he left her with the horse  upon her,
translation: You would have heard about the swampy place she landed, and how she was covered in mud, and how my master left her with the horse on top of her,

original: how he beat me because her horse stumbled, how she waded through the dirt to pluck him off me, how he  swore, how she prayed that never prayed before,
translation: and beat  me  because  her  horse stumbled, and how she waded through the dirt to pull him off of me, and how he swore, and how she prayed—she who had never prayed before—

original: how I  cried, how the horses ran away, how her bridle was  burst, how I lost my crupper, with many things of worthy memory which now shall die in oblivion, and thou return unexperienced to thy grave.
translation: and how I yelled, and how the horses ran away, and how her bridle was broken, and how I lost my saddle strap, and many other things worth being remembered, but which will now be forgotten, and you'll go ignorant to your grave.

original: By this reck'ning he is more shrew than she.
translation: It sounds like he is more of a shrew than she is.

original: Ay, and that thou and the proudest of you all shall  find when he comes home. But what talk I of this?
translation: Yes, and you and everyone else will find that out when he comes home. But why am I talking about this?

original: Call  forth Nathaniel, Joseph, Nicholas, Philip, Walter,  Sugarsop, and the rest.
translation: Call in Nathaniel, Joseph, Nicholas, Philip, Walter, Sugarsop, and all the rest.

original: Let their heads be slickly  combed, their blue coats brushed, and their garters of  an indifferent knit.
translation: Make sure their hair is slicked down and combed, their blue coats are brushed, and their garters are normal-looking and matching.

original: Let them curtsy with their left  legs, and not presume to touch a hair of my master’s  horse-tail till they kiss their hands. Are they all  ready?
translation: Have them do an elaborate greeting and not dare to touch a hair of my master's horse's tail until they've kissed their hands. Are they all ready?

original: They are.
translation: They are.

original: Call them forth.
translation: Call them in.

original: Do you hear, ho? you must meet my  master to countenance my mistress.
translation: Hey, do you hear that? You must come greet the master and countenance the mistress.

original: Why, she hath a face of her own.
translation: Why, she already has a face of her own.

original: Who knows not that?
translation: Who said she didn't?

original: Thou, it seems, that calls for company to countenance  her.
translation: You did, it seems, since you told them to "countenance" her.

original: I call them forth to credit her.
translation: I mean they should give her credit.

original: Why, she comes to borrow nothing of them.
Welcome home, Grumio.
translation: Welcome home, Grumio.

original: How now, Grumio?
translation: How's it going, Grumio?

original: What, Grumio!
translation: Hey, Grumio!

original: Fellow Grumio!
translation: Grumio, my friend!

original: How now, old lad?
translation: How's it going, old boy?

original: Welcome, you!—How now, you?—What, you!—Fellow,  you!—And thus much for greeting. Now, my spruce  companions, is all ready, and all things neat?
translation: Welcome to you!—How's it going to you?—Hey to you!—My friend to you!—And that's enough greetings. Now, my dapper companions, is everything neat and ready?

original: All things is ready. How near is our master?
translation: Everything's ready. How far away is our master?

original: E'en at hand, alighted by this. And therefore be not—  Cock’s passion, silence! I hear my master.
translation: He's probably here already. So don't—by God, quiet! I hear him.

original: Where be these knaves?
translation: Where are those villains?

original: What, no man at door   To hold my stirrup nor to take my horse!
translation: What, there's no man at the door to help me off my horse and take him to the stable!

original: Where is Nathaniel, Gregory, Philip?
translation: Where are Nathaniel, Gregory, and Philip?

original: Here, here, sir! Here, sir!
translation: Here, here, sir! Here, sir!

original: “Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir!”
translation: "Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir!"

original: You loggerheaded and unpolished grooms!   What, no attendance? No regard? No duty?
translation: You blockheaded servants! What, I'll get no service from you? No respect? No duty?

original: Where is the foolish knave I sent before?
translation: Where is the foolish villain I sent ahead of me?

original: Here, sir, as foolish as I was before.
translation: Here, sir, and just as foolish as I was before.

original: You peasant swain! You whoreson malt-horse drudge! Did I not bid thee meet me in the park And bring along these rascal knaves with thee?
translation: You stupid bumpkin! You bastard workhorse drudge! Didn't I tell you to meet me outside and bring these idiot rascals along with you?

original: Nathaniel’s coat, sir, was not fully made,   And Gabriel’s pumps were all unpinked i' th' heel.
translation: Nathaniel's coat wasn't ready, sir, and Gabriel's shoes didn't have the proper pattern on them.

original: There was no link to color Peter’s hat,   And Walter’s dagger was not come from sheathing.
translation: Peter's hat was the wrong color, and Walter's dagger needed a sheathe.

original: There were none fine but Adam, Rafe, and Gregory.   The rest were ragged, old, and beggarly.
translation: The only ones properly dressed were Adam, Rafe, and Gregory. The rest looked like ragged old beggars.

original: Yet, as they are, here are they come to meet you.
translation: But here they are sir, and they've come as they are to greet you.

original: Go, rascals, go, and fetch my supper in.
translation: Go, idiots, go, and fetch me my supper.

original: Singing   Where is the life that late I led—   Where are those  —Sit down, Kate, and welcome.— Soud, soud, soud, soud!
translation: Where is the life I used to lead? Where are those—Sit down, Kate, and make yourself welcome.—Food, food, food, food!

original: Why, when, I say?—Nay, good sweet Kate, be merry.—  Off with my boots, you rogues! You villains, when?
translation: Now, I say!—Be happy, good sweet Kate.—Get my boots off, you rogues! You villains, now!

original: It was the friar of orders gray,   As he forth walkèd on his way   :—
translation: It was the friar in robes of gray, Who walked along on his way:

original: One, Kate, that you must kiss and be acquainted with.— Where are my slippers? Shall I have some water?—
translation: He's someone you must get to know, Kate.—Where are my slippers? Can I get some water please?

original: Come, Kate, and wash, and welcome heartily.— You whoreson villain! Will you let it fall?   Strikes him
translation: Come, Kate, and wash, and make yourself at home.—You bastard villain! Are you really going to spill it?

original: Patience, I pray you! 'Twas a fault unwilling.
translation: Calm down, please! It was an accident.

original: A whoreson, beetle-headed, flap-eared knave!—
translation: He's a stupid, blockheaded, flap-eared son of a bitch!

original: Come, Kate, sit down. I know you have a stomach.   Will you give thanks, sweet Kate, or else shall I?—
translation: —Come, Kate, sit down. I know you must be hungry. Will you say grace, sweet Kate, or should I?

original: What’s this? Mutton?
translation: —What's this? Mutton?

original: Ay.
translation: Yes.

original: Who brought it?
translation: And who brought it?

original: I.
translation: I did.

original: 'Tis burnt, and so is all the meat.   What dogs are these! Where is the rascal cook?
translation: It's burnt, and so is all the rest of the meat. These servant dogs! Where is the rascal cook?

original: How durst you, villains, bring it from the dresser   And serve it thus to me that love it not?
translation: You villains, how dare you bring me this meat when you know I don't like it overcooked?

original: There, take it to you, trenchers, cups, and all!
translation: There, take it back, plates, cups, and all!

original: I pray you, husband, be not so disquiet.  The meat was well, if you were so contented.
translation: Please, husband, don't be so upset. The meat was fine, if you would have accepted it.

original: I tell thee, Kate, ’twas burnt and dried away.   And I expressly am forbid to touch it,   For it engenders choler, planteth anger;
translation: I tell you, Kate, it was burnt and dried up.  @ .

original: And better ’twere that both of us did fast,   Since of ourselves, ourselves are choleric,   Than feed it with such over-roasted flesh.
translation: It's probably better that we should go hungry, since we're both hotheaded and temperamental, than that we should eat such overcooked meat.

original: Be patient, tomorrow ’t shall be mended,   And, for this night, we’ll fast for company.
translation: Be patient—it'll get fixed tomorrow. For tonight we'll just go without food.

original: Come, I will bring thee to thy bridal chamber.
translation: Come, I'll bring you to your bridal bedroom.

original: Peter, didst ever see the like?
translation: Peter, did you ever see the likes of this?

original: He kills her in her own humor.
translation: He subdues her by acting like her.

original: Where is he?
translation: Where is he?

original: In her chamber,   Making a sermon of continency to her,
translation: In her room, preaching to her about self-control.

original: And rails and swears and rates, that she, poor soul,   Knows not which way to stand, to look, to speak,   And sits as one new-risen from a dream.
translation: He rants and rails and swears so much that she, poor soul, doesn't know which way to stand, look, or speak, so she just sits like someone who's woken up from a dream.

original: Away, away, for he is coming hither!
translation: But go, go, he's coming!

original: Thus have I politicly begun my reign,   And ’tis my hope to end successfully.
translation: I've begun my reign in this cunning way, and I hope to end up successful.

original: My falcon now is sharp and passing empty,   And, till she stoop, she must not be full-gorged,   For then she never looks upon her lure.
translation: My falcon is now hungry and unfed, and she won't be allowed to eat until she submits to my authority.  Otherwise she'll just ignore my bait.

original: Another way I have to man my haggard,   To make her come and know her keeper’s call.   That is, to watch her, as we watch these kites   That bate and beat and will not be obedient.
translation: And I also have another plan to tame my wild hawk, to make her come and recognize her owner's call—that is, I'll keep her from sleeping, just like trainers do with falcons that flap and flutter and won't be obedient.

original: She ate no meat today, nor none shall eat.   Last night she slept not, nor tonight she shall not.
translation: She ate no food today, and she'll continue to have none. She got no sleep last night, and she'll get none tonight.

original: As with the meat, some undeservèd fault   I’ll find about the making of the bed,   And here I’ll fling the pillow, there the bolster,   This way the coverlet, another way the sheets.
translation: Just like I did with the meat, I'll make up some problem with the way the bed is made, and throw around the pillow, the cushion, the blanket, and the sheets.

original: Ay, and amid this hurly I intend   That all is done in reverend care of her.
translation: Yes, and I'll pretend that I'm making all this fuss for  her  sake.

original: And, in conclusion, she shall watch all night,   And if she chance to nod I’ll rail and brawl,   And with the clamor keep her still awake.
translation: The result will be that she'll stay awake all night, and if she starts to nod off, I'll scold and argue and keep her awake with my yelling.

original: This is a way to kill a wife with kindness,   And thus I’ll curb her mad and headstrong humor.
translation: This is how to kill a wife with kindness, and in this way I'll curb her wild and headstrong nature.

original: He that knows better how to tame a shrew,   Now let him speak; ’tis charity to show.
translation: If anyone knows a better way to tame a shrew, let him speak up now. I'd appreciate the help.

original: Is ’t possible, friend Litio, that mistress Bianca Doth fancy any other but Lucentio? I tell you, sir, she bears me fair in hand.
translation: Is it possible, my dear friend Litio, that Bianca could prefer another man over me? I tell you, sir, she's been very friendly towards me.

original: Sir, to satisfy you in what I have said,  Stand by and mark the manner of his teaching.   They stand aside
translation: Sir, to prove to you what I've said, stand by right here and watch how this fellow teaches her.

original: Now, mistress, profit you in what you read?
translation: Now, mistress, have you been making progress in your studies?

original: What, master, read you? First resolve me that.
translation: What are you studying, teacher? First answer me that.

original: I read that I profess,  The Art to Love.
translation: I study what I teach—The Art of Love.

original: And may you prove, sir, master of your art.
translation: And may you prove, sir, to be a master of your art.

original: While you, sweet dear, prove mistress of  my heart!
translation: While you, sweet dear, prove to be the mistress of my heart!

original: Quick proceeders, marry! Now, tell me, I  pray, You that durst swear that your mistress Bianca Loved none in the world so well as Lucentio.
translation: How quickly he earns his degree! Now tell me, please, what just happened? I thought you swore that your mistress Bianca loved no one in the world better than Lucentio.

original: O despiteful love! Unconstant womankind!  I tell thee, Litio, this is wonderful!
translation: Oh spiteful love! Faithless womankind! I tell you, Litio, it's incredible!

original: Mistake no more. I am not Litio,   Nor a musician as I seem to be,
translation: Let me reveal myself. I am not Litio, and not a musician either.

original: But one that scorn to live in this disguise   For such a one as leaves a gentleman   And makes a god of such a cullion.
translation: I refuse to continue with this disguise for the sake of a woman who would choose a low-class scoundrel over a gentleman like me.

original: Know, sir, that I am called Hortensio.
translation: Know, sir, that I am called Hortensio.

original: Signior Hortensio, I have often heard   Of your entire affection to Bianca,
translation: Sir Hortensio, I've often heard of your sincere affection for Bianca,

original: And since mine eyes are witness of her lightness,   I will with you, if you be so contented,   Forswear Bianca and her love for ever.
translation: and now that I've seen with my own eyes that she is unfaithful, I will join you, if you like, in rejecting Bianca and her love forever.

original: See how they kiss and court!
translation: See how they kiss and flirt!

original: Signior Lucentio,   Here is my hand, and here I firmly vow   Never to woo her more,
translation: Sir Lucentio, take my hand. I firmly vow to stop wooing her forever.

original: but do forswear her   As one unworthy all the former favors   That I have fondly flattered her withal.
translation: I reject her as a woman unworthy of all the time and money I have so foolishly flattered her with.

original: And here I take the like unfeignèd oath Never to marry with her, though she would entreat. Fie on her! See how beastly she doth court him!
translation: And I now make the same oath, never to marry her even if she begs me. Damn her! See how lustfully she flirts with him!

original: Would all the world but he had quite forsworn!
translation: I wish all the world but him would reject her, so she'd have only that poor schoolteacher to accept her as a wife!

original: For me, that I may surely keep mine oath,   I will be married to a wealthy widow,   Ere three days pass,
which hath as long loved me   As I have loved this proud disdainful haggard.
translation: She's been in love with me for as long as I've been pursuing this proud, disdainful vixen.

original: And so farewell, Signior Lucentio.   Kindness in women, not their beauteous looks,   Shall win my love,
translation: And so farewell, Sir Lucentio. From now on, kindness in women, not their beauty, will win my love.

original: and so I take my leave,   In resolution as I swore before.
translation: And so I bid you farewell, and am resolved to keep my promise.

original: Mistress Bianca, bless you with such grace   As 'longeth to a lover’s blessèd case!
translation: Miss Bianca, may you be blessed with all the good fortune you deserve!

original: Nay, I have ta'en you napping, gentle love,   And have forsworn you with Hortensio.
translation: No, I've caught you napping, my dear. Both Hortensio and I have rejected you.

original: Tranio, you jest. But have you both forsworn me?
translation: You're joking, Tranio! But have you both really given me up?

original: Mistress, we have.
translation: Mistress, we have.

original: Then we are rid of Litio.
translation: Then we've gotten rid of Litio.

original: I' faith, he’ll have a lusty widow now That shall be wooed and wedded in a day.
translation: Yes, now he'll have a lively widow for himself. He claims he'll woo her and marry her in a day.

original: God give him joy!
translation: God give him joy!

original: Ay, and he’ll tame her.
translation: Yes, and he'll tame her.

original: He says so, Tranio?
translation: Did he say that, Tranio?

original: Faith, he is gone unto the taming school.
translation: Well, he's gone off to the taming school.

original: The taming school? What, is there such a place?
translation: The taming school? What, is there such a place?

original: Ay, mistress, and Petruchio is the master, That teacheth tricks eleven and twenty long To tame a shrew and charm her chattering tongue.
O master, master, I have watched so long   That I am dog-weary, but at last I spied   An ancient angel coming down the hill
translation: Oh master, master, I've been watching for so long that I'm dog-tired, but at last I spied a good old fellow coming down the hill.

original: Will serve the turn.
translation: He'll work for our needs.

original: What is he, Biondello?
translation: Who is he, Biondello?

original: Master, a marcantant, or a pedant,  I know not what, but formal in apparel, In gait and countenance surely like a father.
translation: Master, I'm not sure if he's a merchant or a schoolmaster, but he's well-dressed and looks old and respectable enough to be Lucentio's father.

original: And what of him, Tranio?
translation: And what will you do with him, Tranio?

original: If he be credulous and trust my tale,   I’ll make him glad to seem Vincentio   And give assurance to Baptista Minola   As if he were the right Vincentio.
translation: If he's gullible and believes my story, then I'll make him happy to pretend to be Vincentio and vouch for you to Baptista Minola, just as if he were the real Vincentio.

original: Take in your love, and then let me alone.
translation: Take your sweetheart and leave this to me.

original: God save you, sir.
translation: Hello and God bless you, sir.

original: And you, sir. You are welcome. Travel you far on, or are you at the farthest?
translation: And you too, sir. Welcome. Are you going farther, or is this your destination?

original: Sir, at the farthest for a week or two, But then up farther, and as far as Rome, And so to Tripoli, if God lend me life.
translation: Sir, this is my destination for a week or two, but then I'll go on as far as Rome, and then to Tripoli, if God is willing.

original: What countryman, I pray?
translation: Where are you from, if I might ask?

original: Of Mantua.
translation: From Mantua.

original: Of Mantua, sir? Marry, God forbid!  And come to Padua, careless of your life?
translation: Mantua, sir? God forbid! And you've come to Padua? Are you so careless with your life?

original: My life, sir! how, I pray? For that goes hard.
translation: My life, sir! What do you mean? That sounds serious indeed.

original: 'Tis death for anyone in Mantua   To come to Padua. Know you not the cause?
translation: It's death for anyone from Mantua to come to Padua. Don't you know why?

original: Your ships are stayed at Venice, and the Duke,   For private quarrel ’twixt your duke and him,   Hath published and proclaimed it openly.
translation: The Duke of Padua proclaimed it openly. There's a private quarrel between him and your duke, and all the ships from Mantua are being impounded in Venice.

original: 'Tis marvel, but that you are but newly come,   You might have heard it else proclaimed about.
translation: It's amazing that you didn't know, but I guess you just arrived. Otherwise you would have heard it proclaimed all around town.

original: Alas, sir, it is worse for me than so,  For I have bills for money by exchange From Florence, and must here deliver them.
translation: Alas, sir, this is bad news for me. I have money orders from Florence, and I must deliver them here.

original: Well, sir, to do you courtesy, This will I do, and this I will advise you. First tell me, have you ever been at Pisa?
translation: Well, sir, I'll do you a favor, and help you out and give you some advice. But first tell me, have you ever been to Pisa?

original: Ay, sir, in Pisa have I often been, Pisa renownèd for grave citizens.
translation: Yes, sir, I've often been to Pisa—Pisa, famous for its serious citizens.

original: Among them know you one Vincentio?
translation: Do you know one of those citizens called Vincentio?

original: I know him not, but I have heard of him: A merchant of incomparable wealth.
translation: I don't know him, but I've heard of him: a merchant of incomparable wealth.

original: He is my father, sir, and sooth to say, In count'nance somewhat doth resemble you.
translation: He is my father, sir, and to be honest, you look a little bit like him.

original: As much as an apple doth an oyster, and all  one.
translation: As much as an apple looks like an oyster, but that's no matter.

original: To save your life in this extremity,   This favor will I do you for his sake—   And think it not the worst of all your fortunes   That you are like to Sir Vincentio—
translation: I'll do you this favor for his sake, and to save your life in this dangerous situation—indeed, you should consider yourself lucky that you resemble Sir Vincentio.

original: His name and credit shall you undertake,   And in my house you shall be friendly lodged.
translation: You'll pretend to be him, assume his name and reputation, and stay at my house as a guest.

original: Look that you take upon you as you should.   You understand me, sir.
translation: Just make sure that you play your part well. Do you understand, sir?

original: So shall you stay   Till you have done your business in the city.   If this be court’sy, sir, accept of it.
translation: This way you can stay until you've done your business in the city. If this is kindness, then accept it.

original: O sir, I do, and will repute you ever  The patron of my life and liberty.
translation: Oh sir, I will, and I'll always consider you the savior of my life and liberty.

original: (as   LUCENTIO   )   Then go with me to make the matter good.
translation: [As LUCENTIO]  Then come with me, and we'll get everything ready.

original: This, by the way, I let you understand:   My father is here looked for every day   To pass assurance of a dower in marriage
translation: By the way, I should also tell you this: my father is expected here any day now to come vouch for me about a widow's inheritance for my marriage.

original: 'Twixt me and one Baptista’s daughter here.   In all these circumstances I’ll instruct you.
translation: The marriage contract is between me and the daughter of a man named Baptista, who lives here. I'll instruct you about the rest of the details.

original: Go with me to clothe you as becomes you.
translation: Come with me, and I'll get you some new clothes.

original: No, no, forsooth, I dare not for my life.
translation: No, no, I swear, I can't. He'd kill me.

original: The more my wrong, the more his spite appears.   What, did he marry me to famish me?
translation: The more I suffer, the angrier he seems to get. What, did he marry me to starve me?

original: Beggars that come unto my father’s door   Upon entreaty have a present alms.   If not, elsewhere they meet with charity.
translation: Even beggars who come to my father's door get money when they ask for it. If not, they find charity elsewhere.

original: But I, who never knew how to entreat,   Nor never needed that I should entreat,   Am starved for meat, giddy for lack of sleep,   With oaths kept waking and with brawling fed.
translation: But I, who never learned how to beg and never needed to beg, am starved for food and dizzy with lack of sleep, kept awake by curses and fed only with arguing.

original: And that which spites me more than all these wants,   He does it under name of perfect love,
translation: And what puzzles me more than all these troubles is that he does it all under the pretense of perfect love.

original: As who should say, if I should sleep or eat,   'Twere deadly sickness or else present death.
translation: He acts as if I would get sick and die right away if I were to sleep or eat.

original: I prithee, go and get me some repast,   I care not what, so it be wholesome food.
translation: Please, go and get me some food. I don't care what it is, as long as it's filling.

original: What say you to a neat’s foot?
translation: What do you say to an ox's foot?

original: 'Tis passing good. I prithee let me have it.
translation: It sounds excellent. Please let me have it.

original: I fear it is too choleric a meat.  How say you to a fat tripe finely broiled?
I like it well. Good Grumio, fetch it me.
translation: I'd like that very much. Good Grumio, bring it to me.

original: I cannot tell. I fear ’tis choleric. What say you to a  piece of beef and mustard?
translation: I'm not sure. I'm afraid it's choleric too. What do you say to a piece of beef with mustard?

original: A dish that I do love to feed upon.
translation: It's a dish I love to eat.

original: Ay, but the mustard is too hot a little.
translation: Yes, but the mustard's a little too hot.

original: Why then, the beef, and let the mustard rest.
translation: Why then, the beef, and leave the mustard off.

original: Nay then, I will not. You shall have the mustard Or else you get no beef of Grumio.
translation: Certainly not, in that case. You'll have the mustard or else you'll get no beef from Grumio.

original: Then both, or one, or anything thou wilt.
translation: Then both, or one, or anything you want.

original: Why then, the mustard without the beef.
translation: Why then, the mustard without the beef.

original: Go, get thee gone, thou false deluding slave,
translation: Go, get out of here, you false, deceitful slave.

original: How fares my Kate? What, sweeting, all amort?
translation: How is my Kate doing? What, sweetheart, why so dejected?

original: Mistress, what cheer?
translation: Mistress, how are you?

original: Faith, as cold as can be.
translation: Indeed, I'm as bad as can be.

original: Pluck up thy spirits. Look cheerfully upon me.   Here love, thou seest how diligent I am,   To dress thy meat myself and bring it thee.
translation: Cheer up. Give me a smile. Here, love, see how diligent I am—I've prepared your meat myself, and brought it to you.

original: I am sure, sweet Kate, this kindness merits thanks.   What, not a word?
translation: I am sure, sweet Kate, that this kindness deserves your thanks. What, not a word?

original: Nay, then thou lov’st it not   And all my pains is sorted to no proof.   Here, take away this dish.
translation: Well, then I guess you don't like it, and all my work was for nothing. Here, take away this dish.

original: I pray you, let it stand.
translation: Please, don't take it away.

original: The poorest service is repaid with thanks, And so shall mine, before you touch the meat.
translation: Even the poorest service is repaid with thanks, and mine will be too, before you touch the meat.

original: I thank you, sir.
translation: I thank you, sir.

original: Signior Petruchio, fie, you are to blame. Come, mistress Kate, I’ll bear you company.
translation: Shame on you, Sir Petruchio, this is your fault. Come, mistress Kate, I'll join you.

original: Eat it up all, Hortensio, if thou lovest me.—   Much good do it unto thy gentle heart.
translation: Do me a favor and eat it all up yourself, Hortensio.—May it do your gentle heart much good, Kate.

original: Kate, eat apace. And now, my honey love,   Will we return unto thy father’s house   And revel it as bravely as the best,
translation: Eat quickly. And now, my honey love, we will return to your father's house and party with the best of them,

original: With silken coats and caps and golden rings,   With ruffs and cuffs and farthingales and things,   With scarves and fans and double change of brav'ry,   With amber bracelets, beads, and all this knav'ry.
What, hast thou dined? The tailor stays thy leisure   To deck thy body with his ruffling treasure.
translation: What, have you finished? The tailor is waiting to dress you in ruffled finery.

original: Come, tailor, let us see these ornaments. Lay forth the gown.
translation: Come, tailor, let's see what you have. Lay out the gown.

original: What news with you, sir?
translation: What do you want, sir?

original: Here is the cap your Worship did bespeak.
translation: Here is the cap your Worship asked for.

original: Why, this was molded on a porringer!   A velvet dish! Fie, fie, ’tis lewd and filthy!
translation: Why, this must have been modeled on a porridge bowl! It's like a velvet dish! For shame, for shame, it's worthless and filthy!

original: Why, ’tis a cockle or a walnut shell,   A knack, a toy, a trick, a baby’s cap.
translation: Why, it's like a cockleshell or a walnut shell, a knickknack, a trifle, a baby's cap.

original: Away with it! Come, let me have a bigger.
translation: Take it away! Come, let me see a bigger one.

original: I’ll have no bigger. This doth fit the time,  And gentlewomen wear such caps as these.
When you are gentle, you shall have one too, And not till then.
translation: Well, when you are gentle you can have one too, and not before.

original: That will not be in haste.
translation: That won't be anytime soon.

original: Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak,   And speak I will. I am no child, no babe.
translation: Why, sir, I trust that I'm allowed to speak, and speak I will. I am not a child or an infant.

original: Your betters have endured me say my mind,   And if you cannot, best you stop your ears.
translation: Better men than you have heard me speak my mind, and if you cannot endure it, then you'd better stop up your ears.

original: My tongue will tell the anger of my heart   Or else my heart, concealing it, will break,
translation: My tongue must express the anger of my heart, or else my heart will burst from trying to contain it all.

original: And, rather than it shall, I will be free   Even to the uttermost, as I please, in words.
translation: So I will speak as freely as I like, no matter what.

original: Why, thou say’st true. It is a paltry cap, A custard-coffin, a bauble, a silken pie. I love thee well in that thou lik’st it not.
Love me or love me not, I like the cap,  And it I will have, or I will have none.
translation: Whether you love me or love me not, I like the cap, and I will have it, or I'll have nothing.

original: Thy gown? Why, ay. Come, tailor, let us see ’t.
translation: Now, your gown? Why, yes. Come, tailor, let us see it.

original: O mercy, God! What masking stuff is here?   What’s this? A sleeve? 'Tis like a demi-cannon.
translation: God have mercy! What is this costume? What's this, a sleeve? It's more like a cannon.

original: What, up and down, carved like an apple tart?   Here’s snip and nip and cut and slish and slash,   Like to a censer in a barber’s shop.
translation: What, you've carved it like an apple tart all over? A snip here and a nip there, a cut here and a slash there—it's like a sieve!

original: Why, what i' devil’s name, tailor, call’st thou this?
translation: What in the hell do you call this, tailor?

original: I see she’s like to have neither cap nor gown.
translation: I see that she's likely to have neither a cap nor a gown.

original: You bid me make it orderly and well,  According to the fashion and the time.
translation: You told me to make it properly and well, according to the current fashions.

original: Marry, and did. But if you be remembered,   I did not bid you mar it to the time.
translation: Indeed I did. But if you remember, I didn't tell you to make it a mockery of the current fashions.

original: Go, hop me over every kennel home,   For you shall hop without my custom, sir.
translation: Go on, hop on home, for you must hop without my money, sir.

original: I’ll none of it. Hence, make your best of it.
translation: I want nothing to do with this. Get out of here, and do whatever you want with it.

original: I never saw a better-fashioned gown, More quaint, more pleasing, nor more commendable. Belike you mean to make a puppet of me.
translation: I never saw a better-made gown, or one more elegant, pleasing, and praiseworthy. It seems like you're trying to make a plaything out of me.

original: Why, true, he means to make a puppet of thee.
translation: Why, exactly! That tailor intends to make a plaything out of you.

original: She says your Worship means to make a puppet of her.
translation: She says you, your Worship, intend to make a plaything out of her.

original: O monstrous arrogance! Thou liest, thou thread, thou  thimble,   Thou yard, three-quarters, half-yard, quarter, nail!
translation: Oh monstrous arrogance! You lie, you thread, you thimble, you puny measurement!

original: Thou flea, thou nit, thou winter cricket thou!   Braved in mine own house with a skein of thread?
translation: You flea, you louse egg, you winter cricket! Defied in my own house by a spool of thread?

original: Away, thou rag, thou quantity, thou remnant,   Or I shall so be-mete thee with thy yard   As thou shalt think on prating whilst thou liv’st!
translation: Away with you, you rag, you fragment, you remnant, or I'll use your own yardstick against you until you think twice about talking again for the rest of your life!

original: I tell thee, I, that thou hast marred her gown.
translation: I tell you that you've ruined her gown.

original: Your Worship is deceived. The gown is made  Just as my master had direction. Grumio gave order how it should be done.
translation: Your Worship is deceived. The gown is made just as my master directed me to make it. Grumio gave the order for how it should be done.

original: I gave him no order. I gave him the stuff.
translation: I gave him no order. I gave him the material.

original: But how did you desire it should be made?
translation: But how did you want it to be made?

original: Marry, sir, with needle and thread.
translation: Well, sir, with needle and thread.

original: But did you not request to have it cut?
translation: But didn't you want to have it cut, too?

original: Thou hast faced many things.
I have.
translation: I have.

original: Face not me. Thou hast braved many men; brave not me. I will neither be faced nor braved. I say unto thee, I  bid thy master cut out the gown, but I did not bid him  cut it to pieces.  Ergo,  thou liest.
Why, here is the note of the fashion to testify.
translation: Why, here is the order as evidence.

original: Read it.
translation: Read it.

original: The note lies in ’s throat, if he say I said so.
translation: The note is a low note and a liar, if it says I said so.

original: “  Imprimis,  a loose-bodied gown—”
translation: "First, a loose-bodied gown—"

original: Master, if ever I said “loose-bodied gown,” sew me in  the skirts of it, and beat me to death with a bottom of  brown thread. I said “a gown.”
Proceed.
translation: Go on.

original: “With a small-compassed cape—”
translation: "With a flared half-circle cape—"

original: I confess the cape.
translation: I admit to ordering the cape.

original: “With a trunk sleeve—”
translation: "With a large, wide sleeve—"

original: I confess two sleeves.
translation: I admit to two sleeves.

original: “The sleeves curiously cut.”
translation: "The sleeves elaborately cut."

original: Ay, there’s the villany.
translation: Ah, there's the problem.

original: Error i' the bill, sir, error i' the bill! I commanded  the sleeves should be cut out and sewed up again, and  that I’ll prove upon thee, though thy little finger be  armed in a thimble.
translation: Error in the bill, sir, error in the bill! I said that the sleeves should be cut out and sewed up again, and I'll prove it by defeating you in combat, even if your little finger is armed with a thimble.

original: This is true that I say: an I had thee in place where, thou shouldst know it.
translation: What I say is the truth: and if I had you in the right place, I'd prove it to you.

original: I am for thee straight. Take thou the bill, give me thy mete- yard, and spare not me.
God-a-mercy, Grumio! Then he shall have no odds.
translation: God have mercy, Grumio! Then he'll have no chance.

original: Well, sir, in brief, the gown is not for me.
translation: Well, sir, in conclusion, the gown is not for me.

original: You are i' the right, sir, ’tis for my mistress.
translation: You're right, sir. It's for my mistress.

original: Go, take it up unto thy master’s use.
translation: Go, take it away and let your master use it however he wants.

original: Villain, not for thy life! Take up my mistress' gown  for thy master’s use!
translation: Villain, not on your life! Take off my mistress's gown for your master's use!

original: Why, sir, what’s your conceit in that?
translation: Why, sir, what do you mean by that?

original: O, sir, the conceit is deeper than you think for. Take  up my mistress' gown to his master’s use! O, fie, fie,  fie!
translation: Oh, sir, the meaning is deeper than you think. Take off my mistress's gown for his master's use! Oh, shameful, shameful, shameful!

original: Hortensio, say thou wilt see the tailor paid.     Go, take it hence. Begone, and say no more.
translation: Hortensio, tell the tailor that you'll make sure he gets paid.

original: Tailor, I’ll pay thee for thy gown  tomorrow. Take no unkindness of his hasty words. Away, I say. Commend me to thy master.
translation: Tailor, I'll pay you for your gown tomorrow. Don't take his rudeness to heart. Go then, I say. Give my regards to your master.

original: Well, come, my Kate. We will unto your father’s   Even in these honest mean habiliments.
translation: Well, come on then, my Kate. We'll just go on to your father's house dressed in our plain, respectable clothes.

original: Our purses shall be proud, our garments poor,   For ’tis the mind that makes the body rich,   And as the sun breaks through the darkest clouds,   So honor peereth in the meanest habit.
translation: Our purses will be proud and our clothes will be poor. It's the mind that makes the body rich, after all, and just as the sun breaks through the darkest clouds, so honor can be seen through even the lowliest attire.

original: What, is the jay more precious than the lark   Because his feathers are more beautiful?   Or is the adder better than the eel   Because his painted skin contents the eye?
translation: What, is the jay more precious than the lark because his feathers are more beautiful? Or is the poisonous snake better than the eel because his patterned scales please the eye?

original: Oh, no, good Kate. Neither art thou the worse   For this poor furniture and mean array.
translation: Certainly not, good Kate. Therefore you aren't any less precious because of your poor clothes and lowly attire.

original: If thou account’st it shame, lay it on me,
translation: If you consider it shameful, then lay the shame on me.

original: And therefore frolic! We will hence forthwith   To feast and sport us at thy father’s house.
translation: So cheer up! We will go now to feast and party at your father's house.

original: I dare assure you, sir, ’tis almost two, And ’twill be supper time ere you come there.
translation: I dare say, sir, that it's almost two, and it will be dinnertime before we get there.

original: It shall be seven ere I go to horse.
translation: It will be seven o'clock before I'll get on any horse.

original: Look what I speak, or do, or think to do,   You are still crossing it.
translation: Whatever I say, or do, or think, you are still contradicting it.

original: Sirs, let ’t alone.   I will not go today, and ere I do   It shall be what o'clock I say it is.
translation: Sirs, never mind. I won't go today. I won't go until it is the time that I say it is.

original: Why, so this gallant will command the sun.
translation: Why, this gentleman wants to command even the sun.

original: Sir, this is the house. Please it you  that I call?
translation: Sir, this is the house. Do you want me to knock?

original: Ay, what else? and but I be deceived,   Signior Baptista may remember me,
translation: Yes, of course. Unless I'm mistaken, Sir Baptista might remember me,

original: Near twenty years ago, in Genoa,   Where we were lodgers at the Pegasus.
translation: Sir Vincentio, from when we both stayed at the Pegasus in Genoa nearly twenty years ago.

original: 'Tis well; and hold your own, in any  case, With such austerity as 'longeth to a father.
translation: Very good. Now keep playing your part, and act as respectable as a father should.

original: I warrant you.
translation: I swear I will.

original: But, sir, here comes your boy. 'Twere good he were schooled.
translation: But sir, here comes your boy. He needs to learn his lines.

original: Fear you not him.—Sirrah Biondello, Now do your duty throughly, I advise you. Imagine ’twere the right Vincentio.
translation: Don't worry about him.—Biondello, boy, now play your part well. Imagine this is the real Vincentio.

original: Tut, fear not me.
translation: Ha, don't worry about me.

original: But hast thou done thy errand to  Baptista?
translation: But have you delivered the message to Baptista?

original: I told him that your father was at Venice, And that you looked for him this day in Padua.
translation: I told him that your father was in Venice, and that you expected him in Padua today.

original: Thou'rt a tall fellow. Hold thee that to  drink.   Gives money
translation: You're a fine fellow. Here, have a drink on me.

original: Here comes Baptista. Set your countenance, sir.
translation: Here comes Baptista. Look appropriately serious, sir.

original: Signior Baptista, you are happily met.—
translation: Sir Baptista, it's good to see you.—

original: Soft son.—   Sir, by your leave, having come to Padua   To gather in some debts, my son Lucentio   Made me acquainted with a weighty cause   Of love between your daughter and himself.
translation: Quiet, son. —Sir, if I may—having come to Padua to collect some debts, my son Lucentio made me aware of the deep love between your daughter and himself.

original: And, for the good report I hear of you   And for the love he beareth to your daughter   And she to him, to stay him not too long,   I am content, in a good father’s care,   To have him matched.
translation: Because of the good reports I've heard about you, and for the sake of the love between your daughter and my son, I won't delay —I am glad to have him matched.

original: And if you please to like   No worse than I, upon some agreement   Me shall you find ready and willing   With one consent to have her so bestowed,
translation: And if you also approve of the marriage, then you'll find me ready and willing to consent to your daughter's betrothal.

original: For curious I cannot be with you,   Signior Baptista, of whom I hear so well.
translation: I won't be fussy about details with you, Sir Baptista, for I respect you.

original: Sir, pardon me in what I have to say.   Your plainness and your shortness please me well.
translation: Sir, pardon me for what I have to say. I like your plainness and honesty.

original: Right true it is your son Lucentio here   Doth love my daughter and she loveth him,   Or both dissemble deeply their affections.
translation: It is indeed true that your son Lucentio here loves my daughter, and she loves him—unless they're both good at pretending.

original: And therefore, if you say no more than this,   That like a father you will deal with him   And pass my daughter a sufficient dower,   The match is made, and all is done.
translation: Therefore, if you have nothing else to say, and agree that you will treat your son as a father should and settle on a sufficient widow's inheritance for my daughter, then the match is made, and all's done.

original: Your son shall have my daughter with consent.
translation: Your son will marry my daughter with my consent.

original: I thank you, sir. Where then do you know best We be affied and such assurance ta'en As shall with either part’s agreement stand?
translation: I thank you, sir. Where is the best place to draw up the necessary papers and settle this matter?

original: Not in my house, Lucentio, for you know   Pitchers have ears, and I have many servants.
translation: Not in my house, Lucentio, for you know that I have many servants who might eavesdrop, and "little pitchers have big ears," as they say.

original: Besides, old Gremio is heark'ning still,   And happily we might be interrupted.
translation: Besides, old Gremio is always hanging around and listening, so we might be interrupted.

original: Then at my lodging, an it like you.
translation: Then let's go to my lodging, if you'd like.

original: There doth my father lie, and there this night   We’ll pass the business privately and well.
translation: That's where my father is staying, and tonight we can complete our transactions privately there.

original: Send for your daughter by your servant here.   My boy shall fetch the scrivener presently.
translation: Send your servant for Bianca. My boy will fetch the notary right away.

original: The worst is this, that at so slender warning   You are like to have a thin and slender pittance.
translation: The only bad thing is that with such short notice, we'll only be able to offer you a small meal.

original: It likes me well.
translation: That sounds good to me.

original: —Cambio, hie you home,   And bid Bianca make her ready straight.
translation: —Cambio, hurry home and tell Bianca to get ready right away.

original: And, if you will, tell what hath happenèd:   Lucentio’s father is arrived in Padua,   And how she’s like to be Lucentio’s wife.
translation: And, if you want to, tell her what has happened: Lucentio's father has come to Padua, and now she's likely to be Lucentio's wife.

original: I pray the gods she may, with all my heart!
translation: With all my heart I pray to the gods that she will!

original: Dally not with the gods, but get thee  gone.—
translation: Don't worry about the gods. Go on about your business.

original: Signior Baptista, shall I lead the way?
translation: —Signor Baptista, should I lead the way?

original: Welcome! One mess is like to be your cheer.   Come, sir, we will better it in Pisa.
translation: Welcome! We'll only have one course to feed you, but we'll make up for it in Pisa. Come, sir.

original: I follow you.
translation: I'll follow you.

original: Cambio.
translation: Cambio.

original: What sayest thou, Biondello?
translation: What is it, Biondello?

original: You saw my master wink and laugh upon you?
translation: Did you see my master winking and laughing at you?

original: Biondello, what of that?
translation: What about it, Biondello?

original: Faith, nothing; but 'has left me here behind to  expound the meaning or moral of his signs and tokens.
translation: Well, nothing. But he left me behind to explain the meaning of his signs and signals.

original: I pray thee, moralize them.
translation: Please, explain them.

original: Then thus: Baptista is safe, talking with the deceiving father of a deceitful son.
translation: It's like this: Baptista is safely taken care of. He's talking with the pretend father of the pretend son.

original: And what of him?
translation: And what else?

original: His daughter is to be brought by you to the supper.
translation: You're to bring his daughter to dinner.

original: And then?
translation: And then?

original: The old priest at Saint Luke’s Church is at your  command at all hours.
translation: The old priest at Saint Luke's Church is at your service at all hours.

original: And what of all this?
translation: And what of all this?

original: I cannot tell, except they are busied about a  counterfeit assurance.
translation: I'm not sure, except that they are busy with some fake marriage contract.

original: Take you assurance of her cum  privilegio ad imprimendum solum.
translation: Go get your exclusive rights to that girl.

original: To th' church take the  priest, clerk, and some sufficient honest witnesses.
translation: Go to the church and take a priest, a clerk, and some honest-enough witnesses.

original: If this be not that you look for, I have no more to  say,   But bid Bianca farewell forever and a day.
translation: If this isn't what you've been waiting for, then I have nothing more to say—but bid Bianca farewell forever.

original: Hear’st thou, Biondello?
translation: Do you hear, Biondello—

original: I cannot tarry. I knew a wench married in an afternoon  as she went to the garden for parsley to stuff a rabbit, and so may you, sir.
translation: I can't linger. I once knew a girl who was married in the afternoon as she went out to the garden to look for parsley to stuff a rabbit. It may happen to you too, sir.

original: And so adieu, sir.   My master hath  appointed me to go to Saint Luke’s to bid the priest be  ready to come against you come with your appendix.
translation: And so farewell, sir.  My master instructed me to go to Saint Luke's and tell the priest to be ready in anticipation of your arrival with your better half.

original: I may, and will, if she be so contented.   She will be pleased.
translation: I may, and I will, if she agrees. She will be pleased.

original: Then wherefore should I doubt?   Hap what hap may, I’ll roundly go about her.
translation: Then why am I doubtful? What will be will be. I'll just be honest and straightforward with her.

original: It shall go hard if “Cambio” go without her.
translation: But it will be hard for "Cambio" if he loses her.

original: Come on, i' God’s name, once more toward our father’s. Good Lord, how bright and goodly shines the moon!
translation: Come on, in God's name, let's continue on to your father's house. Good Lord, the moon is so bright and beautiful tonight!

original: The moon? The sun! It is not moonlight now.
translation: The moon? That's the sun! There's no moonlight now.

original: I say it is the moon that shines so bright.
translation: I say it's the moon that shines so bright.

original: I know it is the sun that shines so bright.
translation: I know it's the sun that shines so bright.

original: Now, by my mother’s son, and that’s myself,   It shall be moon, or star, or what I list,   Or e'er I journey to your father’s house.
translation: Now, I swear by my mother's son, and that's myself, it will be the moon, or a star, or whatever I want it to be before I'll journey on to your father's house.

original: Say as he says, or we shall never go.
translation: Say what he wants you to say, or we'll never go.

original: Forward, I pray, since we have come so far,
translation: Let's keep going, please, since we've come so far already.

original: And be it moon, or sun, or what you please.
translation: And it can be the moon, or the sun, or whatever you like.

original: An if you please to call it a rush candle,   Henceforth I vow it shall be so for me.
translation: If you want to call it a tea candle, then I swear it will be a tea candle to me from now on.

original: I say it is the moon.
I know it is the moon.
translation: I know it is the moon.

original: Nay, then you lie. It is the blessèd sun.
translation: No, you're a liar. It's the blessed sun.

original: Then God be blessed, it is the blessèd sun.
translation: Then God be blessed, it's the blessed sun.

original: But sun it is not, when you say it is not,   And the moon changes even as your mind.
translation: But it's not the sun when you say it isn't, and the  moon changes with your mind .

original: What you will have it named, even that it is,   And so it shall be so for Katherine.
translation: Whatever you name it, that's what the thing is, and so it will always be for Katherine.

original: Petruchio, go thy ways; the field is won.
translation: Petruchio, let's go on. You've won the war.

original: Well, forward, forward! Thus the bowl should run, And not unluckily against the bias. But, soft! Company is coming here.
translation: Well, forward, forward then! This is how things should go, smooth and straight. But wait! Someone's coming.

original: Good morrow, gentle mistress, where away?—
translation: Good morning, gentle mistress, where are you off to?

original: Tell me, sweet Kate, and tell me truly too,   Hast thou beheld a fresher gentlewoman?
translation: —Tell me, sweet Kate, and be honest, have you ever seen a prettier, healthier-looking young lady?

original: Such war of white and red within her cheeks!   What stars do spangle heaven with such beauty   As those two eyes become that heavenly face?—
translation: See how the shades of white and red do battle with each other in her cheeks! And what stars in heaven sparkle with as much beauty as the two eyes in that heavenly face?

original: Fair lovely maid, once more good day to thee.—   Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty’s sake.
translation: —Fair lovely maid, once more I say good day to you.—Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty's sake.

original: He will make the man mad, to make a woman of  him.
translation: He'll make the man go crazy, pretending that he's a woman.

original: Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet,   Whither away, or where is thy abode?
translation: Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet, where are you off to, and where is your home?

original: Happy the parents of so fair a child.   Happier the man whom favorable stars   Allot thee for his lovely bedfellow!
translation: Happy are the parents of such a fair child. And happier the man whose destiny is to share your bed!

original: Why, how now, Kate! I hope thou art not mad. This is a man—old, wrinkled, faded, withered—  And not a maiden, as thou say’st he is.
translation: Why, what's going on, Kate! I hope you haven't gone crazy. This is a man—old, wrinkled, faded, and withered—not a girl, as you say he is.

original: Pardon, old father, my mistaking eyes   That have been so bedazzled with the sun   That everything I look on seemeth green.
translation: Pardon me, sir! My eyes were so blinded by the sun that everything I see looks young and fresh.

original: Now I perceive thou art a reverend father.   Pardon, I pray thee, for my mad mistaking.
translation: But now I can see that you're a respectable old gentleman. Pardon me, please, for my crazy mistake.

original: Do, good old grandsire, and withal make known Which way thou travellest. If along with us, We shall be joyful of thy company.
translation: Do pardon her, good old grandfather, and also tell us which way you're traveling. If you're going the same way we are, we'd be glad to have your company.

original: Fair sir, and you, my merry mistress,   That with your strange encounter much amazed me,
translation: Well, fair sir, and you, my cheerful mistress, you've surprised me with your strange behavior,

original: My name is called Vincentio, my dwelling Pisa,   And bound I am to Padua,
translation: but know that my name is Vincentio, my home is Pisa, and I am headed for Padua.

original: there to visit   A son of mine which long I have not seen.
translation: I'm going to visit my son who I haven't seen in a long time.

original: What is his name?
translation: What is his name?

original: Lucentio, gentle sir.
translation: Lucentio, gentle sir.

original: Happily met, the happier for thy son.   And now by law as well as reverend age,   I may entitle thee my loving father.
translation: What a happy coincidence, and even happier for your son. I can now call you "father" legally, and not just as a term of respect for your age.

original: The sister to my wife, this gentlewoman,   Thy son by this hath married.
translation: This gentlewoman here is my wife, and her sister is now married to your son.

original: Wonder not   Nor be grieved. She is of good esteem,   Her dowry wealthy, and of worthy birth.
translation: Don't be amazed or upset. His wife has a good reputation, a wealthy dowry, and a noble bloodline.

original: Beside, so qualified as may beseem   The spouse of any noble gentleman.
translation: She has all the qualities that would make her a worthy spouse for any noble gentleman.

original: Let me embrace with old Vincentio,   And wander we to see thy honest son,   Who will of thy arrival be full joyous.
translation: Now let me embrace you, Vincentio, and then we'll go out of our way to see your honest son. He'll be overjoyed at your coming.

original: But is this true, or is it else your pleasure, Like pleasant travelers, to break a jest Upon the company you overtake?
translation: But is all this true? Or are you just having fun, like silly travelers, and playing jokes on people you meet along the way?

original: I do assure thee, father, so it is.
translation: I assure you, father, it's true.

original: Come, go along and see the truth hereof, For our first merriment hath made thee jealous.
translation: Come along with us and you'll see the truth for yourself, if our initial joke has made you suspicious.

original: Well, Petruchio, this has put me in heart. Have to my widow, and if she be froward,  Then hast thou taught Hortensio to be untoward.
translation: Well, Petruchio, this has been encouraging to me. I'll go to my widow now, and if she's stubborn, you've taught me how to tame her—by being even more difficult than she is.

original: Softly and swiftly, sir, for the priest is ready.
translation: Quietly and quickly, sir. The priest is ready.

original: I fly, Biondello. But they may chance to need thee at  home. Therefore leave us.
translation: I'm hurrying, Biondello. But they might need you at home, so you go back.

original: Nay, faith, I’ll see the church a' your back, and then  come back to my master’s as soon as I can.
translation: No, I'll see you safely to the church, and then I'll hurry back to my master's.

original: I marvel Cambio comes not all this while.
translation: I'm surprised Cambio hasn't come by all this time.

original: Sir, here’s the door. This is Lucentio’s house. My father’s bears more toward the marketplace. Thither must I, and here I leave you, sir.
translation: Sir, here's the door. This is Lucentio's house. My father-in-law's house lies closer to the marketplace. That's where I'm off to, and here I leave you, sir.

original: You shall not choose but drink before you go. I think I shall command your welcome here, And, by all likelihood, some cheer is toward.
translation: You must have a drink before you go. I think I can welcome you on my son's behalf, and it's likely that some entertainment is being prepared anyway.

original: They’re busy within. You were best knock louder.
translation: They're busy inside. You'd better knock louder.

original: What’s he that knocks as he would beat  down the gate?
translation: Who's that trying to break down the door?

original: Is Signior Lucentio within, sir?
translation: Is Sir Lucentio inside, sir?

original: He’s within, sir, but not to be spoken  withal.
translation: He's inside, sir, but he can't be bothered right now.

original: What if a man bring him a hundred pound or two to make  merry withal?
translation: What if a man were to bring him a couple hundred pounds to have fun with?

original: Keep your hundred pounds to yourself. He shall need none so long as I live.
translation: Keep your hundred pounds to yourself. He won't need anything as long as I'm alive.

original: Nay, I told you your son was well  beloved in Padua.
translation: See, I told you your son was well-loved in Padua.—

original: Thou liest. His father is come from  Padua and here looking out at the window.
translation: You are lying. His father has already come to Padua, and here he is looking out the window.

original: Art thou his father?
translation: Are you his father?

original: Ay, sir, so his mother says, if I may  believe her.
translation: Yes, sir, or so his mother tells me, if I can believe her.

original: Why, how now, gentleman! Why, this is  flat knavery to take upon you another man’s name.
translation: Why, what's going on? This is downright criminal, to take on another man's name!

original: Lay hands on the villain. I believe he  means to cozen somebody in this city under my  countenance.
translation: Arrest the villain. I believe he means to cheat someone in this city while pretending to be me.

original: I have seen them in the church together. God  send 'em good shipping! But who is here? Mine old master Vincentio! Now we are undone and brought to nothing.
translation: Now I've seen them go into the church together. May God give them a good marriage! But who's this here? My old master Vincentio! Now everything's ruined! It was all for nothing.

original: Come hither, crack-hemp.
translation: Come here, you villain.

original: Hope I may choose, sir.
translation: I don't have to obey you, sir.

original: Come hither, you rogue! What, have you forgot me?
translation: Come here, you rogue! What, have you forgotten me?

original: Forgot you! No, sir. I could not forget you, for I  never saw you before in all my life.
translation: Forgotten you! No, sir. I could not forget you, for I've never seen you before in my life.

original: What, you notorious villain, didst thou never see thy  master’s father, Vincentio?
translation: What, you foul villain, did you never see your master's father, Vincentio?

original: What, my old worshipful old master? Yes, marry, sir.  See where he looks out of the window.
translation: What, my respectable old master? Yes, of course, sir. There he is, looking out the window.

original: Is ’t so, indeed.
translation: Is that so.

original: Help, help, help! Here’s a madman will murder me.
translation: Help, help, help! There's a madman trying to murder me!

original: Help, son! Help, Signior Baptista!
translation: Help, son! Help, Sir Baptista!

original: Prithee, Kate, let’s stand aside and see the end of  this controversy.
translation: Come on, Kate, let's stand aside and see how all this chaos turns out.

original: Sir, what are you that offer to beat my  servant?
translation: Sir, who are you that you would presume to beat my servant?

original: What am I, sir! Nay, what are you, sir? O immortal  gods! O fine villain!
translation: Who am I, sir! No, who are  you , sir? By the immortal gods! Oh, you complete villain!

original: A silken doublet, a velvet hose, a scarlet cloak, and a copatain hat! Oh, I am undone, I  am undone!
translation: A silken jacket, velvet hose, a scarlet cloak, and a tall hat! Oh, I'm ruined, I'm ruined!

original: While I play the good husband at home, my son and my servant spend all at the university.
translation: While I played the thrifty father at home, my son and my servant have spent all my money at university.

original: How now, what’s the matter?
translation: What's going on, what's the matter?

original: What, is the man lunatic?
translation: What, is the man a lunatic?

original: Sir, you seem a sober ancient gentleman  by your habit, but your words show you a madman.
translation: Sir, from your clothes you seem to be a wise, respectable old gentleman, but your words show you to be a madman.

original: Why,  sir, what 'cerns it you if I wear pearl and gold? I  thank my good father I am able to maintain it.
translation: Why, sir, what is it to you if I should wear pearls and gold? Thanks to my good father, I can afford it.

original: Thy father! O villain! He is a sailmaker in Bergamo.
translation: Your father! Oh you villain! Your father is a sailmaker in Bergamo.

original: You mistake, sir, you mistake, sir. Pray, what do you  think is his name?
translation: You're mistaken, sir, you're mistaken. Please tell me, what do you think his name is?

original: His name! As if I knew not his name! I have brought him up ever since he was three years old, and his name is  Tranio.
translation: His name! As if I didn't know his name! I raised him ever since he was three years old, and his name is Tranio.

original: Away, away, mad ass! His name is  Lucentio and he is mine only son, and heir to the lands  of me, Signior Vincentio.
translation: Away with you, mad fool! His name is Lucentio, my only son, and heir to all the lands owned by me, Vincentio.

original: Lucentio! Oh, he hath murdered his master! Lay hold on  him, I charge you in the Duke’s name. O my son, my son!  Tell me, thou villain, where is my son Lucentio?
translation: Lucentio! Oh, he's murdered his master! Arrest him, I charge you in the Duke's name. Oh my son, my son! Tell me, you villain, where is my son Lucentio?

original: Call forth an officer.
translation: Call an officer.

original: Carry this mad knave to the jail.—Father Baptista, I charge you see that he be forthcoming.
translation: Take this mad fool to jail.—Father Baptista, make sure that he's ready to appear in court when he's called.

original: Carry me to the jail?
translation: Take me to jail?

original: Stay, officer. He shall not go to prison.
translation: Wait, officer. He won't go to prison.

original: Talk not, Signior Gremio. I say he shall go to prison.
translation: Be quiet, Sir Gremio. I say he will go to prison.

original: Take heed, Signior Baptista, lest you be cony-catched  in this business. I dare swear this is the right  Vincentio.
translation: Be careful, Sir Baptista, or else you'll be tricked by this business. I would dare to swear that this is the real Vincentio.

original: Swear, if thou darest.
translation: Swear, if you dare.

original: Nay, I dare not swear it.
translation: No, I won't really dare to swear it.

original: Then thou wert best say that I am not Lucentio.
translation: Then you'd better say that I'm not really Lucentio.

original: Yes, I know thee to be Signior Lucentio.
translation: No, I know you're Sir Lucentio.

original: Away with the dotard! To the jail with him!
translation: Away with this old fool! Take him to jail!

original: Thus strangers may be haled and abused.—O monstrous  villain!
translation: This is how strangers are mistreated and abused!—Oh you monstrous villain!

original: O! We are spoiled and yonder he is! Deny him, forswear  him, or else we are all undone.
translation: Oh! There he is, and we're ruined! Deny him, swear that you don't know him, or else we're completely undone.

original: Pardon, sweet father.
translation: Forgive me, sweet father.

original: Lives my sweet son?
translation: Is my sweet son alive?

original: Pardon, dear father.
translation: Forgive me, dear father.

original: How hast thou offended? Where is Lucentio?
translation: Why, what have you done wrong? Where is Lucentio?

original: Here’s Lucentio, right son to the right Vincentio, That have by marriage made thy daughter mine While counterfeit supposes bleared thine eyne.
translation: Here is Lucentio, the real son of the real Vincentio. I've made your daughter mine by marriage while you were tricked by false appearances.

original: Here’s packing, with a witness, to deceive us all!
translation: A conspiracy, a total conspiracy, that deceived us all!

original: Where is that damnèd villain, Tranio, That faced and braved me in this matter so?
translation: Where is that damned villain Tranio, who bullied and defied me about this?

original: Why, tell me, is not this my Cambio?
translation: Why, tell me though, isn't this my daughter's tutor Cambio?

original: Cambio is changed into Lucentio.
translation: Cambio has become Lucentio.

original: Love wrought these miracles. Bianca’s love   Made me exchange my state with Tranio,   While he did bear my countenance in the town,
translation: Love performed these miracles. Bianca's love made me trade my identity with Tranio, while he pretended to be me in town.

original: And happily I have arrivèd at the last   Unto the wishèd haven of my bliss.
translation: And now at last I've arrived happily at the blissful conclusion of my endeavors.

original: What Tranio did, myself enforced him to.   Then pardon him, sweet father, for my sake.
translation: Whatever Tranio did, I commanded him to do. So pardon him, sweet father, for my sake.

original: I’ll slit the villain’s nose that would have sent me to the jail.
translation: No, I'll slit the nose of that villain who tried to send me to jail.

original: But do you hear, sir, have you married my daughter  without asking my goodwill?
translation: But is this true, sir, that you've married my daughter without asking for my permission?

original: Fear not, Baptista, we will content you. Go to. But I  will in to be revenged for this villany.
translation: Don't worry, Baptista, we will satisfy you. You'll see. But I will go inside and get some revenge for this villainy.

original: And I, to sound the depth of this knavery.
translation: And I will too, to see how deep this villainy goes.

original: Look not pale, Bianca. Thy father will not frown.
translation: Don't look so pale, Bianca. Your father won't be angry with you.

original: My cake is dough, but I’ll in among the rest, Out of hope of all but my share of the feast.
Husband, let’s follow to see the end of this ado.
translation: Husband, let's follow them and see how all this turns out.

original: First kiss me, Kate, and we will.
translation: First kiss me, Kate, and then we will.

original: What, in the midst of the street?
translation: What, in the middle of the street?

original: What, art thou ashamed of me?
translation: What, are you ashamed of me?

original: No, sir, God forbid, but ashamed to kiss.
translation: No sir, God forbid, but I am ashamed to kiss.

original: Why, then let’s home again.    Come, sirrah,  let’s away.
translation: Well then, let's go home again.

original: Nay, I will give thee a kiss.    Now pray  thee, love, stay.
