translation: No, I'll give you a kiss.

original: Is not this well? Come, my sweet Kate. Better once than never, for never too late.
translation: Isn't this nice? Come, my sweet Kate. Better late than never, for never's too late.

original: At last, though long, our jarring notes agree,
translation: It's taken a long time, but at last we've all been reconciled.

original: And time it is when raging war is done   To smile at ’scapes and perils overblown.
translation: Now that the raging war is over, it's time to smile at our past dangers and adventures.

original: My fair Bianca, bid my father welcome,   While I with selfsame kindness welcome thine.
translation: My fair Bianca, welcome my father, while I with equal kindness welcome yours.

original: Brother Petruchio, sister Katherina,   And thou, Hortensio, with thy loving widow,   Feast with the best, and welcome to my house.
translation: Brother Petruchio, Sister Katherina, and you, Hortensio, with your loving widow, feast with the best of them, and welcome to my house.

original: My banquet is to close our stomachs up,   After our great good cheer. Pray you, sit down,   For now we sit to chat as well as eat.
translation: This dessert is to close up our stomachs—and any hard feelings—after our great feast. Please, sit down, for now we sit to chat as well as to eat.

original: Nothing but sit and sit, and eat and eat!
translation: Nothing but sit and sit, and eat and eat!

original: Padua affords this kindness, son Petruchio.
translation: Padua can afford this pleasant lifestyle, my son Petruchio.

original: Padua affords nothing but what is kind.
translation: Padua contains nothing that isn't pleasant.

original: For both our sakes, I would that word were true.
translation: For both our sakes, I hope that's true.

original: Now, for my life, Hortensio fears his widow.
Then never trust me if I be afeard.
translation: Don't worry, I'm not afraid of him.

original: You are very sensible, and yet you miss my sense: I mean, Hortensio is afeard of you.
translation: You are very sensible, but you mistook my meaning: I meant that Hortensio is afraid of you.

original: He that is giddy thinks the world turns round.
translation: He who is dizzy thinks the world spins round.

original: Roundly replied.
translation: Well said.

original: Mistress, how mean you that?
translation: Mistress, what do you mean by that?

original: Thus I conceive by him.
translation: That's what I conceive of Petruchio.

original: Conceives by me? How likes Hortensio that?
My widow says, thus she conceives her tale.
translation: My widow means that that's how she understands you.

original: Very well mended. Kiss him for that, good widow.
translation: Good job fixing that. Kiss him for that, good widow.

original: “He that is giddy thinks the world turns round”— I pray you, tell me what you meant by that.
translation: "He who is dizzy thinks the world spins round"—Please, tell me what you meant by that.

original: Your husband being troubled with a shrew  Measures my husband’s sorrow by his woe. And now you know my meaning.
translation: Your husband, who has to live with a shrew, projects his own troubles onto my husband. And now you know my meaning.

original: A very mean meaning.
translation: A very mean meaning.

original: Right, I mean you.
translation: Right, because I mean you.

original: And I am mean indeed, respecting you.
translation: And I demean myself by paying you any attention.

original: To her, Kate!
translation: Get her, Kate!

original: To her, widow!
translation: Get her, widow!

original: A hundred marks, my Kate does put her down.
translation: I'll bet you a hundred marks, my Kate will have her on her back.

original: That’s my office.
translation: That's my job.

original: Spoke like an officer! Ha' to thee, lad!
translation: Spoken like a good worker! Here's to you, boy!

original: How likes Gremio these quick-witted folks?
translation: How does Gremio like these quick-witted folks?

original: Believe me, sir, they butt together well.
translation: Believe me, sir, they butt heads well.

original: Head and butt! An hasty-witted body Would say your head and butt were head and horn.
Ay, mistress bride, hath that awakened you?
translation: Ah, mistress bride, have we woken you up?

original: Ay, but not frighted me. Therefore I’ll sleep again.
translation: Yes, but it hasn't frightened me. So I'll go back to sleep.

original: Nay, that you shall not. Since you have begun, Have at you for a bitter jest or two!
translation: No, you certainly won't. Now that you've gotten started, be ready for a sharp joke or two!

original: Am I your bird? I mean to shift my bush, And then pursue me as you draw your bow.— You are welcome all.
translation: Am I the bird you're shooting at now? I'll fly to a different tree, so you must follow me with your bow. You are all welcome here. Ladies, let me lead you out.

original: She hath prevented me. Here, Signior Tranio, This bird you aimed at, though you hit her not.— Therefore a health to all that shot and missed.
translation: Well, she's escaped me. Sir Tranio, you also aimed at that bird, though you didn't hit her.—So here's a toast to all who have shot and missed.

original: Oh, sir, Lucentio slipped me like his greyhound, Which runs himself and catches for his master.
translation: Oh, sir, Lucentio just let me off his leash like a greyhound. I did the running, but the catch was for my master.

original: A good swift simile, but something currish.
translation: A good and fast answer, but also one for the dogs.

original: 'Tis well, sir, that you hunted for yourself. 'Tis thought your deer does hold you at a bay.
Oh, Oh, Petruchio! Tranio hits you now.
translation: Oh, oh, Petruchio! Now Tranio hits you with a good one.

original: I thank thee for that gird, good Tranio.
translation: I thank you for that taunt, good Tranio.

original: Confess, confess, hath he not hit you here?
translation: Admit it, admit, didn't that one hit close to home?

original: He has a little galled me, I confess. And, as the jest did glance away from me, 'Tis ten to one it maimed you two outright.
translation: He has wounded me a little, I confess. But since the taunt grazed me and kept flying, it's ten to one that it hit you two straight on.

original: Now, in good sadness, son Petruchio,  I think thou hast the veriest shrew of all.
translation: In all seriousness though, my son Petruchio, I think you have the biggest shrew of all.

original: Well, I say no. And therefore, for assurance,
translation: Well, I have to disagree. But let's have some proof.

original: Let’s each one send unto his wife;
translation: Each one of us should send for his wife,

original: And he whose wife is most obedient   To come at first when he doth send for her,   Shall win the wager which we will propose.
translation: and whoever's wife is most obedient, and comes immediately when he sends for her, that man will win the bet we make.

original: Content. What’s the wager?
translation: Sounds good. What's the bet?

original: Twenty crowns.
translation: Twenty crowns.

original: Twenty crowns? I’ll venture so much of my hawk or hound,  But twenty times so much upon my wife.
translation: Twenty crowns? I'd bet that much on my hawk or my hound, but I'd bet twenty times that on my wife.

original: A hundred then.
translation: A hundred then.

original: Content.
translation: Agreed.

original: A match! 'Tis done.
translation: It's a bet! Let's do it.

original: Who shall begin?
translation: Who should begin?

original: That will I. Go, Biondello, bid your mistress come to me.
translation: I will. Go, Biondello, and tell your mistress to come to me.

original: I go.
translation: I go.

original: Son, I’ll be your half Bianca comes.
translation: Son, I'll take half your bet that Bianca comes.

original: I’ll have no halves. I’ll bear it all myself.
translation: I don't want any halves. I'll bear it all myself.

original: How now, what news?
translation: Well, what's the news?

original: Sir, my mistress sends you word That she is busy, and she cannot come.
translation: Sir, my mistress says to tell you that she's busy, and she cannot come.

original: How! “She’s busy, and she cannot come!” Is that an answer?
translation: What! "She's busy, and she cannot come!" Is that her answer?

original: Ay, and a kind one too. Pray God, sir, your wife send you not a worse.
translation: Yes, and a kind one at that. Pray to God, sir, that your wife doesn't send you a worse one.

original: I hope better.
translation: I expect something better.

original: Sirrah Biondello, go and entreat my wife To come to me forthwith.
translation: Biondello, boy, go and ask my wife to come to me right away.

original: O, ho, entreat her! Nay, then she must needs come.
translation: Oh ho, ask her! Well, then she has to come.

original: I am afraid, sir, Do what you can, yours will not be entreated.
translation: I'm afraid that no matter what you do, sir, your wife won't let herself be asked for anything.

original: Now, where’s my wife?
translation: Now, where's my wife?

original: She says you have some goodly jest in hand. She will not come. She bids you come to her.
translation: She says you must be playing some kind of joke. She will not come. She tells you to come to her.

original: Worse and worse. She will not come!   O vile, intolerable, not to be endured!—
translation: Worse and worse. She will not come! Oh, it's vile, intolerable, not to be endured!

original: Sirrah Grumio, go to your mistress,   Say I command her to come to me.
translation: —Grumio, go to your mistress. Say that I command her to come to me.

original: I know her answer.
translation: I know what her answer will be.

original: What?
translation: What?

original: She will not.
translation: She will not.

original: The fouler fortune mine, and there an end.
translation: That'll be the worse for me, and an end to the matter.

original: Now, by my holidam, here comes Katherina!
translation: Now, by all that's holy, here comes Katherina!

original: What is your will, sir, that you send for me?
translation: What is your will, sir, that you sent for me?

original: Where is your sister, and Hortensio’s wife?
translation: Where are your sister and Hortensio's wife?

original: They sit conferring by the parlor fire.
translation: They sit talking by the fire in the parlor.

original: Go fetch them hither. If they deny to come, Swinge me them soundly forth unto their husbands. Away, I say, and bring them hither straight.
translation: Go bring them here. If they refuse to come, give them a beating on my behalf to get them out here to their husbands. Go on, I say, and bring them here right away.

original: Here is a wonder, if you talk of a wonder.
translation: Here is a miracle, if we're speaking of miracles.

original: And so it is. I wonder what it bodes.
translation: So it is. I wonder what it means.

original: Marry, peace it bodes, and love, and quiet life, And awful rule, and right supremacy, And, to be short, what not that’s sweet and happy?
translation: Well, it means peace, and love, and a quiet life, and authority commanding respect, and proper hierarchy, and, in brief, everything sweet and happy.

original: Now, fair befall thee, good Petruchio!
translation: Well, may you have good fortune, good Petruchio!

original: The wager thou hast won, and I will add   Unto their losses twenty thousand crowns,
translation: You've won the bet, and I'll add twenty thousand crowns to these two men's losses.

original: Nay, I will win my wager better yet, And show more sign of her obedience, Her new-built virtue and obedience.
translation: Wait, I'll win the bet even more completely, and show more signs of her obedience, her newly-created virtue and obedience.

original: See where she comes and brings your froward wives   As prisoners to her womanly persuasion.—
translation: See, here she comes, bringing your willful wives with her as prisoners of her womanly duty.

original: Katherine, that cap of yours becomes you not.   Off with that bauble, throw it underfoot.
translation: Katherine, that cap of yours doesn't look good. Take off the silly thing and stomp on it.

original: Lord, let me never have a cause to sigh, Till I be brought to such a silly pass!
translation: Lord, don't let me ever be brought to such a silly state of affairs where someone could treat me like that!

original: Fie! What a foolish duty call you this?
translation: For shame! What kind of foolish "obedience" do you call this?

original: I would your duty were as foolish too. The wisdom of your duty, fair Bianca, Hath cost me an hundred crowns since suppertime.
translation: I wish your obedience was just as foolish. The wisdom of your obedience, fair Bianca, has cost me a hundred crowns since dinnertime.

original: The more fool you for laying on my duty.
translation: Then you're the bigger fool for betting money on my obedience.

original: Katherine, I charge thee, tell these headstrong women  What duty they do owe their lords and husbands.
translation: Katherine, I want you to tell these headstrong women what kind of obedience they owe to their lords and husbands.

original: Come, come, you’re mocking. We will have no telling.
translation: Come on, you're joking. She won't tell us anything.

original: Come on, I say, and first begin with her.
translation: Do it, I say, and begin with her.

original: She shall not.
translation: She won't.

original: I say she shall.—And first begin with her.
translation: I say she will.—And first begin with her.

original: Fie, fie! Unknit that threat'ning unkind brow   And dart not scornful glances from those eyes   To wound thy lord, thy king, thy governor.
translation: For shame, for shame! Don't furrow your brow and glare so scornfully to try to wound the man who is your lord, your king, and your governor.

original: It blots thy beauty as frosts do bite the meads,   Confounds thy fame as whirlwinds shake fair buds,   And in no sense is meet or amiable.
translation: It tarnishes your beauty like frost blights the meadows, and ruins your reputation like a strong wind shaking a flower bud. In no sense whatsoever is it appropriate or pleasant.

original: A woman moved is like a fountain troubled,   Muddy, ill-seeming, thick, bereft of beauty,   And while it is so, none so dry or thirsty   Will deign to sip or touch one drop of it.
translation: An angry woman is like a stirred-up fountain—muddy, ugly, thick, lacking beauty—and while it's in this condition, no one, not even a dry or thirsty man, will stoop to sip or touch one drop of it.

original: Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper,   Thy head, thy sovereign, one that cares for thee,
translation: Your husband is your lord, your life, your keeper, your head, your ruler, and one who cares for you.

original: And for thy maintenance commits his body   To painful labor both by sea and land,   To watch the night in storms, the day in cold,   Whilst thou liest warm at home, secure and safe,
translation: To keep you safe and comfortable he commits his body to painful labor on both sea and land, to staying awake on stormy nights and cold days at sea, while you stay at home, warm and secure.

original: And craves no other tribute at thy hands   But love, fair looks and true obedience—   Too little payment for so great a debt.   Such duty as the subject owes the prince,
translation: And in exchange all he asks for is love, beauty, and true obedience—too little payment for so great a debt. A woman owes her husband the same obedience that a subject owes to his prince.

original: Even such a woman oweth to her husband.   And when she is froward, peevish, sullen, sour,   And not obedient to his honest will,   What is she but a foul contending rebel   And graceless traitor to her loving lord?
translation: And when she is stubborn, peevish, sullen, sour, and not obedient to his honest will, then what is she but a foul, vicious rebel, and a cursed traitor to her loving lord?

original: I am ashamed that women are so simple   To offer war where they should kneel for peace;   Or seek for rule, supremacy and sway   When they are bound to serve, love, and obey.
translation: I am ashamed that women are so foolish as to declare war when they should kneel and plead for peace. I'm ashamed that they should seek rulership, supremacy, and power when they are obligated to serve, love and obey.

original: Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth,   Unapt to toil and trouble in the world,   But that our soft conditions and our hearts   Should well agree with our external parts?
translation: Why else are our bodies so soft and weak and smooth, unfit for labor and trouble in the world, if not so that our soft qualities and our hearts should agree with our external parts?

original: Come, come, you froward and unable worms!   My mind hath been as big as one of yours,   My heart as great, my reason haply more,   To bandy word for word and frown for frown.
translation: Come, come, you weak, willful worms! My mind was once just as arrogant as yours, my courage just as great, and my wit perhaps even better when it came to tossing words back and forth and exchanging frowns for frowns.

original: But now I see our lances are but straws,   Our strength as weak, our weakness past compare,   That seeming to be most which we indeed least are.
translation: But now I see that our swords are only straws, our strength is just as weak, and our weakness is beyond compare, so that we seem to be exactly the thing we are not.

original: Then vail your stomachs, for it is no boot,   And place your hands below your husband’s foot:   In token of which duty, if he please,   My hand is ready, may it do him ease.
translation: So humble your pride, for it's useless. Place your hands beneath your husband's boot as a gesture of obedience. My hand is always ready to comfort and pleasure my husband, if he wants me to.

original: Why, there’s a wench! Come on and kiss me, Kate.
translation: Why, there's a good girl! Come on and kiss me, Kate.

original: Well, go thy ways, old lad, for thou shalt ha ’t.
translation: Well, what do you know, old boy, you've done it.

original: 'Tis a good hearing when children are toward.
translation: It's good to hear children being obedient.

original: But a harsh hearing when women are froward.
translation: But it's unpleasant to hear women being willful.

original: Come, Kate, we’ll to bed.   We three are married, but you two are sped.
translation: Come, Kate, we'll go to bed. We three are all married, but you two are done for—your wives are too disobedient.

original: Now, go thy ways, thou hast tamed a curst shrew.
translation: Well, go on. You've tamed a terrible shrew.

original: 'Tis a wonder, by your leave, she will be tamed so.
translation: And it's a miracle, if I may say so, that she could be tamed like that.

original: Boatswain!
translation: Boatswain!

original: Here, master. What cheer?
translation: Here I am, sir. What do you need?

original: Good, speak to th' mariners. Fall to ’t yarely, or we  run ourselves aground. Bestir, bestir.
translation: Good man, speak to the sailors to get them working harder. Do it quickly, or we’re going to be shipwrecked. Move, move!

original: Heigh, my hearts! Cheerly, cheerly, my hearts! Yare!  Yare! Take in the topsail. Tend to th' master’s whistle.  Blow, till thou burst thy wind, if room enough!
translation: Come on, my boys! Cheer up, cheer up, my boys! Quickly! Quickly! Pull down the topmost sail. Follow the master’s whistled commands. Blow, you wind, until you have nothing left to blast! We’ll survive as long as we have enough room to maneuver without running aground.

original: Good Boatswain, have care. Where’s the Master? Play the men.
translation: Good Boatswain, be careful! Where’s the Master? Urge these men to work harder.

original: I pray now, keep below.
translation: I ask you, please stay below deck now.

original: Where is the Master, Boatswain?
translation: Where is the Master, Boatswain?

original: Do you not hear him? You mar our labor. Keep your  cabins. You do assist the storm.
translation: Can’t you hear him shouting commands? You’re interfering with our work. Stay in your cabins. You’re helping the storm.

original: Nay, good, be patient.
translation: Please be calm, my good man.

original: When the sea is. Hence! What cares these roarers for  the name of king? To cabin, silence! Trouble us not.
translation: I’ll be calm when the sea is. Get out of here! These waves don’t care that someone here is a king. Get to your cabins and be quiet! Stop bothering us.

original: Good, yet remember whom thou hast aboard.
translation: Good man, please remember whom you’ve got on board.

original: None that I more love than myself. You are a councilor. If you can command these elements to silence and work  the peace of the present, we will not hand a rope more.
translation: Not one person that I care about more than myself. You’re a king’s advisor. If you can order the storm to stop, or negotiate a peace with it, we sailors will all stop working with our ropes and take a rest.

original: Use your authority. If you cannot, give thanks you have  lived so long and make yourself ready in your cabin for  the mischance of the hour, if it so hap.—
translation: Use your authority and do it. If you can’t, be thankful that you’ve lived as long as you have, and go to your cabin and prepare yourself to face death, should the worst happen.

original: Cheerly, good  hearts!—
translation: [To SAILORS]  Work, my boys!

original: Out of our way, I say.
translation: [To GONZALO]  Now, I’m telling you, get out of our way.

original: I have great comfort from this fellow. Methinks he hath no drowning mark upon him. His complexion is perfect  gallows. Stand fast, good Fate, to his hanging.
translation: That man makes me feel a lot more confident. It seems to me that he doesn’t look like he’s fated to die by drowning. Instead he looks like he’s destined to die by hanging. Good Fate, hold strong, and make sure that man survives this storm so that one day he can hanged.

original: Make the rope of his destiny our cable, for our own doth little  advantage. If he be not born to be hanged, our case is  miserable.
translation: May the rope fated to hold him by the neck save us, because the ropes we have on the ship don’t seem to be helping us much. If he’s not fated to be hanged, then things look bleak for us.

original: Down with the topmast! Yare, lower, lower! Bring her to try wi' th' main course.
translation: Bring down the top sail! Quickly, lower, lower! Bring the ship in line with the wind using the main sail.

original: A plague upon this howling! They are louder than the  weather or our office.
translation: Curse those men shouting below decks! They’re louder than the storm and distracting us from our duties.

original: Yet again?  What do you here? Shall we give o'er and drown? Have you a mind to sink?
translation: You’re up on deck again? What are you doing here? Should we just give up and drown? Are you in the mood to sink?

original: A pox o' your throat, you bawling, blasphemous,  incharitable dog!
Work you, then.
translation: Do some work, then.

original: Hang, cur! Hang, you whoreson insolent noisemaker! We  are less afraid to be drowned than thou art.
translation: Go hang yourself, you rascal! Hang yourself, you loud, disrespectful bastard! We’re less afraid of drowning than you are.

original: I’ll warrant him for drowning though the ship were no  stronger than a nutshell and as leaky as an unstanched  wench.
translation: I guarantee he’ll never drown, not even if the ship were as fragile as a nutshell and as leaky as a menstruating woman.

original: Lay her a-hold, a-hold! Set her two courses off to sea  again. Lay her off!
translation: Turn the ship close to the wind! Set both sails to push us back out to sea! Push her away from the land!

original: All lost! To prayers, to prayers, all lost!
translation: We’re going to die! Pray, pray! We’re going to die!

original: What, must our mouths be cold?
translation: What, must we drown in the cold water?

original: The king and prince at prayers. Let’s assist them, for  our case is as theirs.
translation: The king and the prince are praying. Let’s pray with them, since we share their situation.

original: I’m out of patience.
translation: I’ve lost all my patience.

original: We are merely cheated of our lives by drunkards. This  wide-chopped rascal—would thou mightst lie drowning the  washing of ten tides!
translation: We’ve had our lives completely taken from us by a bunch of drunken sailors. As for this bigmouthed rascal of a boatswain— I hope you drown ten times!

original: He’ll be hanged yet, though every drop of water swear  against it and gape at widest to glut him.
translation: He’ll still end up hanged, even if every drop of water in the ocean swears he won't, and opens its mouth wide to try to swallow him.

original: Mercy on us! We split, we split! Farewell, my  wife and children! Farewell, brother! We split, we  split, we split!
translation: God have mercy on us! The ship’s splitting apart; the ship's splitting! Goodbye, my wife and children! Goodbye, brother! The ship's splitting, splitting, splitting!

original: Let’s all sink wi' th' king.
translation: Let’s all sink with the king.

original: Let’s take leave of him.
translation: Let’s say goodbye to him.

original: Now would I give a thousand furlongs of sea for an acre of barren ground: long heath, brown furze, anything.  The wills above be done, but I would fain die a dry  death.
translation: I’d give 125 square miles of sea for a single acre of infertile ground: an empty plain, plants growing in bad soil, anything. What's fated to be will be, but I'd be happier to die a dry death.

original: If by your art, my dearest father, you have   Put the wild waters in this roar, allay them.
translation: My dearest father, if you used your magic to incite the wild waters into this this awful storm, please calm them.

original: The sky, it seems, would pour down stinking pitch,   But that the sea, mounting to th' welkin’s cheek,   Dashes the fire out.
translation: The sky is so dark it seems like it would rain down hot tar, except that the sea is swelling up to the sky and would put out the fire boiling the tar.

original: Oh, I have suffered   With those that I saw suffer. A brave vessel   Who had, no doubt, some noble creature in her   Dashed all to pieces.
translation: Oh, I've suffered along with all of those I saw suffering onboard the ship! A magnificent ship—which carried, without a doubt, some noble people—was smashed to pieces.

original: Oh, the cry did knock   Against my very heart! Poor souls, they perished.
translation: Oh, their cries shook my heart! Those poor people—they died.

original: Had I been any god of power, I would   Have sunk the sea within the earth or ere   It should the good ship so have swallowed and   The fraughting souls within her.
translation: If I were a god with even a bit of power I would have forced the sea to sink down into the earth before it could have swallowed up that ship and all the people it carried.

original: Be collected. No more amazement. Tell your piteous heart There’s no harm done.
translation: Be calm. Don't be scared. Tell your heart, which is full of pity, that no harm was done to anyone.

original: Oh, woe the day!
translation: Oh, what a sad day!

original: No harm.   I have done nothing but in care of thee,   Of thee, my dear one—thee my daughter, who   Art ignorant of what thou art,
translation: No harm was done. All that I have done has been for you, for you, my dear daughter. You don’t know who you are.

original: naught knowing   Of whence I am, nor that I am more better   Than Prospero, master of a full poor cell   And thy no greater father.
translation: Nor do you know where I came from, or that I’m of higher rank than Prospero, your simple father who is master of some poor little shack.

original: More to know Did never meddle with my thoughts.
translation: I never even considered that there might be more to know.

original: 'Tis time I should inform thee farther. Lend thy hand And pluck my magic garment from me.
translation: It’s time that I told you everything. Give me a hand and take this magic cloak off of me.

original: Lie   there, my art.
translation: [To the cloak on the ground]  Lay there, my magic.

original: Wipe thou thine eyes. Have comfort.   The direful spectacle of the wrack, which touched   The very virtue of compassion in thee,
translation: [To MIRANDA]  Wipe your eyes. Take comfort. As for the awful shipwreck—which touched the goodness of your heart and moved you to such compassion—

original: I have with such provision in mine art   So safely ordered that there is no soul—   No, not so much perdition as an hair   Betid to any creature in the vessel—
translation: I controlled it so carefully with my magic that not one person was hurt. No, not a hair was lost from the head of any person on that ship

original: Which thou heard’st cry, which thou sawst sink. Sit  down.   For thou must now know farther.
translation: which you heard break apart and saw sink. Sit down. There's more that you must know.

original: You have often   Begun to tell me what I am,
translation: You’ve often started to tell me who I am.

original: but stopped   And left me to a bootless inquisition,   Concluding, “Stay. Not yet.”
translation: But then you would stop, leaving me asking questions that you wouldn't answer until you would finally say, “Wait. Not yet.”

original: The hour’s now come.   The very minute bids thee ope thine ear.   Obey and be attentive.
translation: Now the time has come. At this very instant, you must listen. Pay close attention.

original: Canst thou remember   A time before we came unto this cell?   I do not think thou canst, for then thou wast not   Out three years old.
translation: Can you remember the time before we came to live in this shack? I don't think you can, because you weren't even three years old.

original: Certainly, sir, I can.
translation: Of course I can, sir.

original: By what? By any other house or person?
translation: What do you remember? Some house or person?

original: Of anything the image tell me that   Hath kept with thy remembrance.
translation: Tell me about anything you see in your memory.

original: 'Tis far off,   And rather like a dream than an assurance   That my remembrance warrants.
translation: My memories seem distant and far away, more like a dream than something that I can be sure really happened.

original: Had I not   Four or five women once that tended me?
translation: Didn’t I have four or five women who took care of me?

original: Thou hadst, and more, Miranda. But how is it   That this lives in thy mind? What seest thou else   In the dark backward and abysm of time?
translation: You did—and even more than that, Miranda. But how is it possible that you can remember all this? What else do you remember through the darkness and abyss of passing time?

original: If thou rememberest aught ere thou camest here,   How thou camest here thou mayst.
translation: If you remember something about your life before you came here, you may also remember how you arrived here.

original: But that I do not.
translation: But I don’t remember that.

original: Twelve year since, Miranda, twelve year since, Thy father was the Duke of Milan and A prince of power.
translation: Twelve years ago, Miranda, twelve years ago, your father was the Duke of Milan, a prince with great power.

original: Sir, are not you my father?
translation: Sir, aren’t you my father?

original: Thy mother was a piece of virtue and   She said thou wast my daughter.
translation: Your mother was good and honest, and she said you were my daughter.

original: And thy father   Was Duke of Milan, and thou his only heir   And princess no worse issued.
translation: And your father was Duke of Milan, and you were his heir, a princess of the same noble birth as her parents.

original: Oh, the heavens!   What foul play had we that we came from thence?
translation: My God! What crimes were committed against us that we ended up here?

original: Or blessèd was ’t we did?
translation: Or was our coming here a blessing?

original: Both, both, my girl.   By foul play, as thou sayst, were we heaved thence,
translation: Both, both, my girl. We were forced from our old positions by crimes, as you call them.

original: But blessedly holp hither.
translation: But we were blessed in the help we received that allowed us to end up here.

original: Oh, my heart bleeds To think o' th' teen that I have turned you to, Which is from my remembrance! Please you, farther.
translation: Oh, it breaks my heart to think about how sad it must make you to be reminded of these events that I don’t remember! Please, though, continue.

original: My brother and thy uncle, called Antonio—   I pray thee, mark me (that a brother should   Be so perfidious!)—
translation: My brother, your uncle, whose name is Antonio—I beg you, listen carefully (oh, how could a brother be so treacherous!)—

original: he whom next thyself   Of all the world I loved and to him put   The manage of my state, as at that time   Through all the signories it was the first,
translation: was the person whom I loved more than anyone else in the world, other than you. I trusted him to manage Milan where I ruled, which at that time was the most powerful city-state in Italy.

original: And Prospero the prime duke, being so reputed   In dignity, and for the liberal arts   Without a parallel.
translation: I, Prospero, was the most powerful duke, and was admired for my dignity and my unmatched knowledge of the liberal arts.

original: Those being all my study,   The government I cast upon my brother   And to my state grew stranger, being transported   And rapt in secret studies.
translation: Because I spent all my time absorbed in studying secret topics, I let my brother run the government and lost contact with my city.

original: Thy false uncle—   Dost thou attend me?
translation: Your lying uncle—are you listening to me?

original: Sir, most heedfully.
translation: Sir, very closely.

original: Being once perfected how to grant suits,   How to deny them, who t' advance and who   To trash for overtopping, new created   The creatures that were mine, I say
translation: As soon as Antonio got the hang of how to grant some requests while denying others, of figuring out which people to promote and which to hold back in order to stop them from getting too powerful, he was able to steal the people who used to be mine.

original: —or changed 'em,   Or else new formed 'em—having both the key   Of officer and office, set all hearts i' th' state   To what tune pleased his ear,
translation: He changed them, or, you might say, remade them completely. Having power over both the government and all the people in the government, he could make everyone say or do whatever he wanted them to.

original: that now he was   The ivy which had hid my princely trunk,   And sucked my verdure out on ’t. Thou attend’st not.
translation: He was like ivy growing up a tree, and I was like the tree—he covered me entirely until I was hidden, and sucked my vitality out of me. You’re not listening.

original: O, good sir, I do.
translation: Oh, good sir, I am.

original: I pray thee, mark me.   I, thus neglecting worldly ends, all dedicated   To closeness and the bettering of my mind
translation: Please, pay attention to me. I neglected all things related to ordinary life or politics, and dedicated myself entirely to seclusion in order to improve my knowledge

original: With that which, but by being so retired,   O'erprized all popular rate, in my false brother   Awaked an evil nature.
translation: of topics that have more value than is commonly believed. But by cutting myself off from the world, I unknowingly awoke evil in the heart of my brother.

original: And my trust,   Like a good parent, did beget of him   A falsehood in its contrary as great   As my trust was, which had indeed no limit,
translation: Like a good parent who raises a bad child, my trust in him produced the opposite effect, making him into a liar as big as my trust in him was—and my trust in him had no limit.

original: A confidence sans bound. He being thus lorded,   Not only with what my revenue yielded   But what my power might else exact,
translation: My confidence in him was infinite. Now established in his position of power, and able to use all of my wealth (and whatever wealth he could use my power to take for himself),

original: like one   Who having into truth, by telling of it,   Made such a sinner of his memory   To credit his own lie—
translation: he became like a man who told a lie for so long that he began to believe it was true.

original: he did believe   He was indeed the duke, out o' th' substitution   And executing th' outward face of royalty,   With all prerogative:
translation: He began to believe he was actually the duke. As a result of being my substitute, and acting as the royal duke in public with all the duke's rights and power,

original: Hence his ambition growing—   Dost thou hear?
translation: his ambition began to grow—are you listening?

original: Your tale, sir, would cure deafness.
translation: Your story would cure deafness. It’s impossible not to hear it.

original: To have no screen between this part he played   And him he played it for, he needs will be   Absolute Milan.
translation: He was playing the role of being the duke. But to get rid of the last thing separating the role he was playing from who he  was , he had to become the  actual  Duke of Milan.

original: Me, poor man, my library   Was dukedom large enough.
translation: As for me—poor fool that I was—my library was as large a dukedom as I wanted.

original: Of temporal royalties   He thinks me now incapable, confederates—   So dry he was for sway—wi' th' King of Naples
translation: Having decided that I was unable to run or rule my city, he become so thirsty for power that he secretly allied with the King of Naples to get rid of me.

original: To give him annual tribute, do him homage,   Subject his coronet to his crown and bend   The dukedom yet unbowed—
translation: In return, Antonio agreed to pay the King of Naples a certain amount of money every year; to swear to obey him; and to force his dukedom, which had always been independent—

original: alas, poor Milan!—   To most ignoble stooping.
translation: oh, poor Milan!—into the shameful position of being under Naples’ control.

original: Oh, the heavens!
translation: Oh, my God!

original: Mark his condition and the event. Then tell me If this might be a brother.
translation: Think about this pact he made with King Alonso, and about what happened as a consequence of it. Then tell me if Antonio can really be thought of as a brother.

original: I should sin To think but nobly of my grandmother. Good wombs have borne bad sons.
translation: I would be wicked if I had anything other than good thoughts about my grandmother. But good women sometimes give birth to bad sons.

original: Now the condition.   The King of Naples, being an enemy   To me inveterate, hearkens my brother’s suit,
translation: Now listen to outcome of their secret alliance. The king of Naples, who had always been an enemy of mine, listened to my brother’s request.

original: Which was that he, in lieu o' th' premises   Of homage and I know not how much tribute,   Should presently extirpate me and mine   Out of the dukedom,
translation: Antonio asked that the king, in return for his oath of loyalty and however much money he paid to the king each year, would immediately remove me and all of immediate family from Milan,

original: and confer fair Milan   With all the honors on my brother. Whereon,   A treacherous army levied,
translation: and then give the dukedom to my brother. So then, they raised an army to pull off this treachery.

original: one midnight   Fated to th' purpose did Antonio open   The gates of Milan, and, i' th' dead of darkness,
translation: At midnight on the date they’d chosen to act, Antonio opened the gates of Milan, and in the deep darkness

original: The ministers for th' purpose hurried thence   Me and thy crying self.
translation: had the agents he’d chosen for the job rush me and you, crying, out of there.

original: Alack, for pity!   I, not remembering how I cried out then,
translation: Alas, how sad! I can’t remember crying then,

original: Will cry it o'er again. It is a hint   That wrings mine eyes to ’t.
translation: but now I’ll cry about it all over again. This story wrings tears from my eyes.

original: Hear a little further   And then I’ll bring thee to the present business   Which now ’s upon ’s,
translation: Listen to a little more, and I’ll tell you everything up to our current situation,

original: without the which this story   Were most impertinent.
translation: which is the entire reason why it’s necessary for me to tell you this story at all.

original: Wherefore did they not That hour destroy us?
translation: Why didn’t they just kill us when they took us from Milan?

original: Well demanded, wench.   My tale provokes that question. Dear, they durst not,   So dear the love my people bore me,
translation: Good question, my dear girl. My story does indeed bring up that question. My dear, they didn’t dare. Because I was so loved by the people of Milan,

original: nor set   A mark so bloody on the business, but   With colors fairer painted their foul ends.
translation: Antonio and Alonso had to keep any blood from staining their actions, and hide their evil goals behind a prettier picture.

original: In few, they hurried us aboard a bark,   Bore us some leagues to sea, where they prepared   A rotten carcass of a butt, not rigged,   Nor tackle, sail, nor mast.
translation: In short, they hurried us onto a ship and carried us a few miles out to sea. There, they had prepared a rotten shell of a boat that had no ropes, equipment, sails, or a mast.

original: The very rats   Instinctively had quit it. There they hoist us   To cry to th' sea that roared to us,
translation: Even the rats had abandoned it when they sensed its likelihood to sink.They lowered us down into the water. We were left to cry out to the sea, which just roared back at us.

original: to sigh   To th' winds whose pity, sighing back again,   Did us but loving wrong.
translation: We sighed in sadness to the wind, which sighed back in pity. And in doing so it buffeted us with winds that—no matter how loving—only made us more uncomfortable.

original: Alack, what trouble Was I then to you!
translation: My God! What trouble I must have been to you then!

original: Oh, a cherubim   Thou wast that did preserve me.
translation: Oh no, you were a little angel who kept me alive.

original: Thou didst smile   Infusèd with a fortitude from heaven,
translation: you smiled with a strength and courage that came from heaven.

original: When I have decked the sea with drops full salt,   Under my burthen groaned;
translation: While I cried salty tears into the ocean and groaned under my burden,

original: which raised in me   An undergoing stomach to bear up   Against what should ensue.
translation: That gave me the courage to face whatever was going to come.

original: How came we ashore?
translation: How did we land here?

original: By providence divine.   Some food we had and some fresh water that   A noble Neapolitan, Gonzalo,   Out of his charity, who being then appointed   Master of this design, did give us,
translation: With the help of God. A nobleman from Naples, Gonzalo, had been put in charge of the task of abandoning us at sea. Out of charity, he gave us some food and fresh water,

original: with   Rich garments, linens, stuffs, and necessaries,   Which since have steaded much.
translation: as well as clothes, linens, supplies, and other necessities that have over the years been so useful.

original: So, of his gentleness,   Knowing I loved my books, he furnished me   From mine own library with volumes that   I prize above my dukedom.
translation: Also, he was so noble and kind, that, knowing how much I loved my books, he gave me some books from my library that I value more than my dukedom.

original: Would I might But ever see that man!
translation: If only I could meet that man someday.

original: Now I arise.   [stands and puts on his mantle]   Sit still, and hear the last of our sea-sorrow.
translation: Now I will stand up.  [He stands up and puts on his magic cloak]  Sit still, and listen to the rest of the story of our sad times at sea.

original: Here in this island we arrived, and here   Have I, thy schoolmaster, made thee more profit   Than other princesses can that have more time   For vainer hours and tutors not so careful.
translation: We arrived here on this island. I, as your teacher here, have given you a better education than other princesses get, because they have so many opportunities to spend their time more foolishly and do not pay as close attention to their teachers.

original: Heavens thank you for ’t! And now, I pray you, sir—
translation: May God thank you for it! But now, please, sir:

original: For still ’tis beating in my mind—your reason   For raising this sea storm?
translation: a question keeps popping up in my mind. Why did you create this storm at sea?

original: Know thus far forth:   By accident most strange, bountiful Fortune   (Now my dear lady) hath mine enemies   Brought to this shore.
translation: You should know this much: by a strange chance, the goddess of luck (whom I now love) has brought my old enemies to this island.

original: And by my prescience   I find my zenith doth depend upon   A most auspicious star,
translation: And by my magic senses, I can tell that my opportunity for good fortune depends on this lucky circumstance.

original: whose influence   If now I court not but omit, my fortunes   Will ever after droop. Here cease more questions.
translation: And if I do not act but instead do nothing, then I will never again have such an opportunity. No more questions now.

original: Thou art inclined to sleep. 'Tis a good dullness,   And give it way. I know thou canst not choose.
translation: You are sleepy. It’s a good time for sleepiness, so give in to it. I know you have no choice.

original: Come  away, servant, come. I am ready now. Approach, my Ariel, come.
translation: Come here, servant, come. I’m ready now. Approach, my Ariel, come.

original: All hail, great master! Grave sir, hail! I come   To answer thy best pleasure, be ’t to fly,
translation: Greetings, great master! Noble sir, greetings! I’ve come to do whatever you would like, whether it’s to fly,

original: To swim, to dive into the fire, to ride   On the curled clouds. To thy strong bidding, task   Ariel and all his quality.
translation: swim, jump into fire, or ride upon the clouds. Whatever you want done, ask Ariel and all his many skills, to do it.

original: Hast thou, spirit, Performed to point the tempest that I bade thee?
translation: Spirit, have you created and controlled the storm exactly as I told you to?

original: To every article.   I boarded the king’s ship. Now on the beak,   Now in the waist, the deck, in every cabin,   I flamed amazement.
translation: Down to the last detail. I boarded the king’s ship. And from the prow, to the middle of the ship, to the stern, and in every cabin, I took the form of a fire and sent everyone into a terror.

original: Sometime I’d divide,   And burn in many places. On the topmast,   The yards, and bowsprit would I flame distinctly,   Then meet and join.
translation: Sometimes I would divide myself, and burn at many places at once. I burned on the main mast, the yards extending from the mast—and, at the same time, split to burn the bowsprit extending from the prow. Then I joined back together to form a single flame.

original: Jove’s lightning, the precursors   O' th' dreadful thunderclaps, more momentary   And sight-outrunning were not.
translation: Not even  Jove's  lightning—which precedes and then causes thunder—could move as fast as I did.

original: The fire and cracks   Of sulfurous roaring the most mighty Neptune   Seem to besiege and make his bold waves tremble,   Yea, his dread trident shake.
translation: The fire and deafening cracks of my burning seemed to terrify even mighty Neptune, the god of the sea, and made his waves tremble and his weapon—the trident—shake.

original: My brave spirit! Who was so firm, so constant, that this coil Would not infect his reason?
translation: My splendid spirit! Was anyone on the ship so strong and steady that the uproar of this storm did not make him crazy?

original: Not a soul   But felt a fever of the mad and played   Some tricks of desperation.
translation: Every person on the ship was like a madman and did desperate things.

original: All but mariners   Plunged in the foaming brine and quit the vessel,   Then all afire with me. The king’s son, Ferdinand,   With hair up-staring—then, like reeds, not hair—
translation: Everyone except the sailors jumped into the rough sea to escape the ship that I had set on fire. The king’s son, Ferdinand, with his hair standing straight up—looking like reeds instead of hair—

original: Was the first man that leaped, cried, “Hell is empty   And all the devils are here.”
translation: was the first one who jumped, shouting, “Hell is empty, and all the devils are here!”

original: Why, that’s my spirit! But was not this nigh shore?
translation: Hey, well done, my spirit! But did this happen near the shore?

original: Close by, my master.
translation: Close by the shore, my master.

original: But are they, Ariel, safe?
translation: But are they all safe, Ariel?

original: Not a hair perished.   On their sustaining garments not a blemish,   But fresher than before.
translation: Not even a hair was harmed on anyone’s head. The clothes that helped keep them afloat in the water not only didn’t get stained, but are in fact cleaner than they were before the storm.

original: And, as thou badest me,   In troops I have dispersed them 'bout the isle.
translation: And, as you told me to do, I’ve scattered everyone from the ship in a few different groups around the island.

original: The king’s son have I landed by himself,   Whom I left cooling of the air with sighs   In an odd angle of the isle, and sitting,   His arms in this sad knot.
translation: I brought the king’s son all by himself to the land, on a far corner of the island. He’s sitting there with his arms crossed like this in sadness  [ARIEL crosses his arms] , and cooling the air with his sighs.

original: Of the king’s ship, The mariners, say how thou hast disposed, And all the rest o' th' fleet.
translation: Tell me what you did with the king’s ship, the sailors, and all of the other ships in the king’s fleet.

original: Safely in harbor   Is the king’s ship. In the deep nook where once   Thou called’st me up at midnight to fetch dew   From the still-vexed Bermoothes, there she’s hid.
translation: The king’s ship is safely harbored and hidden in that deep inlet where you once summoned me at midnight to go get dew from the stormy Bermuda Islands.

original: The mariners all under hatches stowed,   Who, with a charm joined to their suffered labor,   I have left asleep.
translation: The sailors are all below deck, sleeping both because of a spell I put them under, and also because of how tired they are from all their effort during the storm.

original: And for the rest o' th' fleet,   Which I dispersed, they all have met again   And are upon the Mediterranean float,
translation: As for the rest of the fleet, I scattered them. They've all met up in the Mediterranean Sea,

original: Bound sadly home for Naples,   Supposing that they saw the king’s ship wracked   And his great person perish.
translation: and are now sailing sadly home to Naples, believing that they saw the shipwreck of the king’s ship—and therefore the death of their great king.

original: Ariel, thy charge Exactly is performed. But there’s more work. What is the time o' th' day?
translation: Ariel, you performed your task exactly as I asked. But there’s more work required. What time of day is it?

original: Past the mid season.
translation: Past noon.

original: At least two glasses. The time ’twixt six and now Must by us both be spent most preciously.
translation: At least two hours past. We must treat the time between now and six o'clock as precious, and waste none of it.

original: Is there more toil? Since thou dost give me pains,
translation: Is there more work to do? Since you’re giving me new chores,

original: Let me remember thee what thou hast promised,   Which is not yet performed me.
translation: let me remind you what you promised to me but haven’t yet actually done for me.

original: How now? Moody? What is ’t thou canst demand?
translation: What? You’re feeling moody? What is it that you would demand from me?

original: My liberty.
translation: My freedom.

original: Before the time be out? No more!
translation: Before the time of our deal is up? Stop right there!

original: I prithee,   Remember I have done thee worthy service,   Told thee no lies, made thee no mistakings,
translation: I beg you: remember that I’ve done good work for you. I’ve never lied to you. I've made no mistakes.

original: served   Without or grudge or grumblings. Thou didst promise   To bate me a full year.
translation: And I've served you without bitterness or grumbling. You promised to shorten my time to serve you by a full year.

original: Dost thou forget From what a torment I did free thee?
translation: Have you forgotten the torture from which I freed you?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: Thou dost, and think’st it much to tread the ooze   Of the salt deep,
translation: You have forgotten. And so now you think it’s too much effort to walk along the bottom of the ocean,

original: To run upon the sharp wind of the north,   To do me business in the veins o' th' earth   When it is baked with frost.
translation: or run on the cold north wind, or do work for me under the surface of the Earth when the ground is frozen solid.

original: I do not, sir.
translation: I don’t, sir.

original: Thou liest, malignant thing! Hast thou forgot   The foul witch Sycorax,
translation: You lie, you evil thing! Have you forgotten the awful witch Sycorax,

original: who with age and envy   Was grown into a hoop? Hast thou forgot her?
translation: who was so old and filled with anger that she was so stooped over? Have you forgotten her?

original: No, sir.
translation: No, sir.

original: Thou hast. Where was she born? Speak. Tell me.
translation: You have. Where was she born? Speak. Tell me.

original: Sir, in Argier.
translation: In Algiers, sir.

original: Oh, was she so? I must   Once in a month recount what thou hast been,   Which thou forget’st.
translation: Oh, was she really? I’ll have to tell the story again every month, since you seem to forget it.

original: This damned witch Sycorax,   For mischiefs manifold and sorceries terrible   To enter human hearing, from Argier,   Thou know’st, was banished.
translation: This damned witch Sycorax was thrown out of Algiers for committing so many crimes and performing magic too terrible to even describe.

original: For one thing she did   They would not take her life. Is not this true?
translation: There was just one reason why they didn’t kill her. Isn’t that true?

original: Ay, sir.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: This blue-eyed hag was hither brought with child   And here was left by th' sailors. Thou, my slave,   As thou report’st thyself, wast then her servant.
translation: This hag—with bags under her eyes—was brought to this island while pregnant, and was left here by the sailors. You, my slave, as you yourself have said, were her servant then.

original: And, for thou wast a spirit too delicate   To act her earthy and abhorred commands,   Refusing her grand hests,
translation: And, because you were too kind and sensitive to carry out her dirty and disgusting commands, you refused her orders.

original: she did confine thee,   By help of her more potent ministers   And in her most unmitigable rage,   Into a cloven pine,
translation: In a rage that could not be calmed, and with the help of her most powerful spirits, she locked you into a hole in the middle of a pine tree that had been split in two.

original: within which rift   Imprisoned thou didst painfully remain   A dozen years; within which space she died   And left thee there,
translation: You were painfully imprisoned there for twelve years. During that time she died and you were stuck there,

original: where thou didst vent thy groans   As fast as mill wheels strike. Then was this island—
translation: groaning in pain at the same rate that the blades of a mill wheel hit the water. At that time the island

original: Save for the son that she did litter here,   A freckled whelp hag-born—not honored with   A human shape.
translation: had no people on it, other than the son that Sycorax gave birth to on the island—that freckled son of a hag.

original: Yes, Caliban, her son.
translation: Yes, Caliban, her son.

original: Dull thing, I say so. He, that Caliban   Whom now I keep in service. Thou best know’st   What torment I did find thee in.
translation: I already said that, you stupid thing. Caliban, who I now keep as a servant. You know better than anyone the pain you were in when I found you.

original: Thy groans   Did make wolves howl and penetrate the breasts   Of ever angry bears.
translation: Your groans made wolves howl, and made perpetually angry bears feel pity for you.

original: It was a torment   To lay upon the damned, which Sycorax   Could not again undo.
translation: The spell that Sycorax put on you—and which she could not undo—was something fit only for souls damned to hell.

original: It was mine art,   When I arrived and heard thee, that made gape   The pine and let thee out.
translation: When I arrived on the island and heard you, it was my magic that made the pine tree open and let you out.

original: I thank thee, master.
translation: I thank you for that, master.

original: If thou more murmur’st, I will rend an oak   And peg thee in his knotty entrails
translation: If you continue to complain, I’ll split an oak tree and lock you inside its wooden trunk

original: till   Thou hast howled away twelve winters.
translation: until you’ve howled for twelve years.

original: Pardon, master. I will be correspondent to command And do my spiriting gently.
translation: Forgive me, master. I’ll obey your commands and perform all my work as a sprite both pleasantly and ungrudgingly.

original: Do so, and after two days I will discharge thee.
translation: Do that, and in two days I will give you your freedom.

original: That’s my noble master! What shall I do? Say, what? What shall I do?
translation: My noble master! What should I do for you? Tell me. What? What should I do?

original: Go make thyself like a nymph o' th' sea.
translation: Go and make yourself look like a sea nymph.

original: Be subject   To no sight but thine and mine, invisible   To every eyeball else.
translation: Be invisible to everyone other than to me and yourself.

original: Go take this shape   And hither come in ’t. Go hence with diligence.
translation: Go take this shape, and then return in that form. Go and do it, carefully.

original: Awake, dear heart, awake! Thou hast slept well. Awake!
translation: Wake up, my dear, wake up! You have slept well. Wake up.

original: The strangeness of your story put Heaviness in me.
translation: The strangeness of your story made me drowsy.

original: Shake it off. Come on.
translation: Shake off your drowsiness. Come on.

original: We’ll visit Caliban, my slave who never   Yields us kind answer.
translation: We’ll go and visit Caliban, my slave who never has anything nice to say to us.

original: 'Tis a villain, sir, I do not love to look on.
translation: He’s a bad person, father. I don’t like to see him.

original: But as ’tis,   We cannot miss him.
translation: But as it is, we can’t manage without him.

original: He does make our fire,   Fetch in our wood, and serves in offices   That profit us.
translation: He builds our fires, gathers our firewood, and performs useful work.

original: What, ho! Slave! Caliban!   Thou earth, thou! Speak.
translation: Hey there! Caliban! You pile of dirt, you! Answer me.

original: There’s wood enough within.
translation: You have enough wood in your shack.

original: Come forth, I say! There’s other business for thee. Come, thou tortoise! When?
translation: Come here, I tell you! There’s other work for you to do. Come here, you slow turtle! Come on!

original: Fine apparition! My quaint Ariel, Hark in thine ear.
translation: A pretty spirit! My clever Ariel, listen closely.

original: My lord it shall be done.
translation: My lord, consider it done.

original: Thou poisonous slave, got by the devil  himself Upon thy wicked dam, come forth!
translation: You vicious slave, fathered by the devil himself with your wicked mother, come here!

original: As wicked dew as e'er my mother brushed   With raven’s feather from unwholesome fen   Drop on you both!
translation: I hope that a dew as evil as the one my mother used to gather from poison swamps and apply with a raven’s feather will fall on top of you!

original: A southwest blow on ye   And blister you all o'er!
translation: May a hot wind from the southwest blow on you and cover you with blisters!

original: For this, be sure, tonight thou shalt have cramps,   Side-stitches that shall pen thy breath up. Urchins   Shall, forth at vast of night that they may work,   All exercise on thee.
translation: For saying that, rest assured, I’ll give you cramps, pains in your sides that will make it hard to breathe. Goblins shaped like hedgehogs will come out at night when they are free to act, and do their worst to you.

original: Thou shalt be pinched   As thick as honeycomb, each pinch more stinging   Than bees that made 'em.
translation: Every inch of you will be stung, and each sting will hurt more than beestings.

original: I must eat my dinner.   This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother,   Which thou takest from me.
translation: It’s time for my dinner. This island is mine, given to me by my mother Sycorax. You took it from me.

original: When thou camest first,   Thou strok’st me and made much of me, wouldst give me   Water with berries in ’t,
translation: When you first came here, you petted me and treated me well. You would give me water with berries in it,

original: and teach me how   To name the bigger light, and how the less,   That burn by day and night.
translation: and you taught me the names for the sun burning in the daytime sky and the moon which lights the night.

original: And then I loved thee   And showed thee all the qualities o' th' isle,   The fresh springs, brine pits, barren place and  fertile.
translation: I loved you then, and I showed you all the features of the island—the freshwater springs, the saltwater pits, the places that were good for growing things and those that were not.

original: Cursed be I that did so! All the charms   Of Sycorax, toads, beetles, bats, light on you!
translation: A curse on me for doing all that! May all the evil spells of Sycorax torment you with toads, beetles, and bats!

original: For I am all the subjects that you have,   Which first was mine own king.
translation: I’m the only subject you have on this island, where once I was my own king.

original: And here you sty me   In this hard rock, whiles you do keep from me   The rest o' th' island.
translation: And now you keep me confined in this cave and don’t let me go anywhere else on the island.

original: Thou most lying slave,   Whom stripes may move, not kindness!
translation: You lying slave, who responds only to whipping and not to kindness!

original: I have used thee,   Filth as thou art, with human care, and lodged thee   In mine own cell till thou didst seek to violate   The honor of my child.
translation: Though you are a piece of dirt, I treated you kindly and humanely. I even let you live in my own shack, until you tried to rape my daughter.

original: Oh ho, oh ho! Would ’t had been done! Thou didst prevent me. I had peopled else This isle with Calibans.
translation: Oh ha, oh ha! I wish I’d done it! You stopped me. If you hadn’t, I would have filled this island with a horde of little Calibans.

original: Abhorrèd slave,   Which any print of goodness wilt not take,   Being capable of all ill!
translation: You repulsive slave! You who are completely resistant to any effort to make you good, and are instead capable of every evil thing!

original: I pitied thee,   Took pains to make thee speak, taught thee each hour   One thing or other. When thou didst not, savage,   Know thine own meaning,
translation: I pitied you. I made the effort to teach you to speak, and taught you some new thing nearly every hour. When you, savage, didn’t know the meaning of the words you were speaking,

original: but wouldst gabble like   A thing most brutish, I endowed thy purposes   With words that made them known.
translation: and would babble like some beast, I gave you words that would let you make your desires understood.

original: But thy vile race,   Though thou didst learn, had that in ’t which good  natures   Could not abide to be with.
translation: But even though you learned, your evil nature made it so that people who were good could not stand to be with you.

original: Therefore wast thou   Deservedly confined into this rock,   Who hadst deserved more than a prison.
translation: And so, just as you deserved, you were sent to live in this cave, which is a more suitable place for you to live than a prison would be.

original: You taught me language, and my profit on ’t   Is I know how to curse.
translation: You taught me language, and all I gained from it is that I now know how to curse.

original: The red plague rid you   For learning me your language!
translation: May you die of the plague for teaching me your language!

original: Hag-seed, hence!   Fetch us in fuel. And be quick, thou 'rt best,   To answer other business. Shrug’st thou, malice?
translation: You son of a hag, get going! Bring us firewood. And you’d better be quick, because I have other work for you.

original: If thou neglect’st or dost unwillingly   What I command, I’ll rack thee with old cramps,
translation: Are you shrugging as if refusing my orders, you evil thing? If you neglect my commands, or perform them grudgingly, I’ll overwhelm your body with painful cramps.

original: Fill all thy bones with aches, make thee roar   That beasts shall tremble at thy din.
translation: I'll fill your bones with aches, and make you scream so that the wild animals will tremble at the noise you make.

original: No, pray thee.
translation: No, I beg you.

original: [aside]   I must obey. His art is of such power,   It would control my dam’s god, Setebos,   And make a vassal of him.
translation: [To himself]  I must obey. His magic is so powerful that he could even defeat Setebos—the god that my mother used to worship—and make him into his servant.

original: So, slave, hence!
translation: Well then, slave, go!

original: [sings]   Come unto these yellow sands,   And then take hands.
translation: [Singing] Come onto these yellow sands, And then take my hands.

original: Curtsied when you have, and kissed   The wild waves whist.
translation: When you’ve curtsied, and kissed The wild waves into quietness.

original: Foot it featly here and there,   And, sweet sprites, bear   The burden. Hark, hark!
translation: Step lightly here and there, And, sweet spirits, carry The burden. Listen, listen!

original: Bow-wow.
translation: Bow-wow.

original: The watchdogs bark.
translation: The watchdogs bark.

original: (within) Bow-wow.
translation: Woof, woof!

original: Hark, hark! I hear The strain of strutting chanticleer Cry “Cock-a-diddle-dow.”
translation: Listen, listen! I hear, the song of the strutting rooster who cries “cock-a-doodle-doo.”

original: Where should this music be? I' th' air or th' earth?   It sounds no more, and sure, it waits upon   Some god o' th' island.
translation: Where is that music coming from? From the air or the ground? It’s no longer playing—probably it plays for some god of this island.

original: Sitting on a bank,   Weeping again the king my father’s wrack,   This music crept by me upon the waters,
translation: As I sat on a sandbank on the beach crying again about my father’s shipwreck, I heard the music over the roaring of the waves,

original: Allaying both their fury and my passion   With its sweet air. Thence I have followed it,   Or it hath drawn me rather.
translation: and it calmed the fury of the water and soothed my intense sadness with its sweet sound. I’ve followed it here, or maybe I should say it led me here.

original: But ’tis gone.   No, it begins again.
translation: But now it’s gone. No, it’s started up again.

original: [sings]   Full fathom five thy father lies.   Of his bones are coral made.
translation: [Singing] Your father lies thirty feet below the sea, His bones are made of coral now.

original: Those are pearls that were his eyes.   Nothing of him that doth fade,
translation: His eyes have turned to pearls. Every part of him that is impermanent,

original: But doth suffer a sea-change   Into something rich and strange.   Sea nymphs hourly ring his knell.
translation: Has changed completely in the sea To become something rich and strange. Sea nymphs ring his death bell hourly.

original: Ding-dong.
translation: Ding-dong.

original: Hark, now I hear them.
translation: Listen, I hear them ringing the bell.

original: Ding-dong, bell.
translation: Ding-dong, bell.

original: The ditty does remember my drowned father.
translation: This little song is in honor of my drowned father.

original: This is no mortal business, nor no sound   That the earth owes. I hear it now above me.
translation: This is not something done by mortals. Nor is it a sound that could come from the normal world. I hear it now coming from above me.

original: The fringèd curtains of thine eye advance And say what thou seest yond.
translation: Lift the tasseled curtains of your eyelids, and tell me what you see over there.

original: What is ’t? A spirit?   Lord, how it looks about!
translation: What is it? A spirit? Lord, it’s looking all around!

original: Believe me, sir,   It carries a brave form. But ’tis a spirit.
translation: Believe me, sir, it is very good-looking. But it must be a spirit.

original: No, wench! It eats and sleeps and hath such senses   As we have, such. This gallant which thou seest   Was in the wrack.
translation: No, my girl! It eats and sleeps and has the same senses as we do. The gentleman you see was in the shipwreck.

original: And, but he’s something stained   With grief that’s beauty’s canker, thou mightst call  him   A goodly person.
translation: And, even though he’s marked by grief—which always spoils beauty—you could describe him as handsome.

original: He hath lost his fellows   And strays about to find 'em.
translation: He’s lost his friends and is wandering around trying to find them.

original: I might call him A thing divine, for nothing natural I ever saw so noble.
translation: I might describe him as a god, because I’ve never seen anything on earth that looked so noble.

original: It goes on, I see, As my soul prompts it. Spirit, fine spirit! I’ll free  thee Within two days for this.
translation: Everything is happening, I see, just as my soul hoped it would. [To ARIEL] Spirit, you wonderful spirit, I’ll set you free in two days for doing your work so well.

original: [seeing MIRANDA]   Most sure, the goddess   On whom these airs attend! Vouchsafe my prayer   May know if you remain upon this island,
translation: [Seeing MIRANDA]  Obviously, this must be the goddess for whom the music is playing! Please answer my prayer, and let me know if you live on this island,

original: And that you will some good instruction give   How I may bear me here.
translation: and explain to me how I should behave here.

original: My prime request,   Which I do last pronounce, is, O you wonder!   If you be maid or no.
translation: But my most important question, which I’ve saved for last, is—oh, you wondrous being—are you a girl or something else?

original: No wonder, sir, But certainly a maid.
translation: I’m not some wondrous being, sir. I’m definitely a girl.

original: My language! Heavens, I am the best of them that speak this speech, Were I but where ’tis spoken.
translation: She speaks my language! God, I’m the highest-ranking person of all the people who speak this language. If only we were back where it’s spoken.

original: How? The best? What wert thou if the King of Naples heard thee?
translation: What? The highest-ranking? What would happen to you if the King of Naples heard you say that?

original: A single thing, as I am now, that wonders   To hear thee speak of Naples. He does hear me,   And that he does I weep.
translation: The same thing I am doing now as I stand here amazed to hear you mention Naples. He does hear me, and it makes me cry that he hears me.

original: Myself am Naples,   Who with mine eyes, never since at ebb, beheld   The king my father wracked.
translation: I myself am the King of Naples —I saw with my own eyes, which haven’t been dry since—my father killed by a shipwreck.

original: Alack, for mercy!
translation: Oh, that’s awful!

original: Yes, faith, and all his lords, the Duke of Milan And his brave son being twain.
[aside]   The Duke of Milan   And his more braver daughter could control thee   If now ’twere fit to do ’t!
translation: [To himself]  The real Duke of Milan and his even finer daughter could control you right now, if now were the right time to do it.

original: At the first sight   They have changed eyes.
translation: They’ve fallen in love at first sight!

original: Delicate Ariel,   I’ll set thee free for this.
translation: [To ARIEL]  Beautiful Ariel, I’ll set you free for making this happen.

original: [to FERDINAND]   A word, good sir.   I fear you have done yourself some wrong. A word.
translation: [To FERDINAND]  May I speak with you, sir? I’m afraid you’ve may have said something untrue. It won’t take more than a moment.

original: [   aside]   Why speaks my father so ungently? This   Is the third man that e'er I saw, the first   That e'er I sighed for.
translation: [To herself]  Why is my father speaking to him so rudely? This is the third man that I’ve ever seen in my life, and the first one for whom I’ve ever felt such feelings that made me sigh.

original: Pity move my father   To be inclined my way!
translation: I hope my father is compassionate enough to me that he wants for me what I want for myself!

original: [to MIRANDA]   Oh, if a virgin,   And your affection not gone forth,
translation: [To MIRANDA]  Oh, if you’re a virgin, and you haven’t given your love to someone else,

original: I’ll make you   The queen of Naples.
translation: then I’ll make you the queen of Naples.

original: Soft, sir! One word more.
translation: [To FERDINAND]  Wait, sir! I have one more thing to say.

original: [   aside]   They are both in either’s powers, but this swift  business   I must uneasy make lest too light winning   Make the prize light.
translation: [To himself]  They’re in love with each other. But I have to put some obstacles in the way of this quick love, so that they don’t undervalue their love because it came so easily.

original: [To FERDINAND]   One word more. I charge thee   That thou attend me.
translation: [To FERDINAND]  Just one more thing to say. I demand that you listen to me.

original: Thou dost here usurp   The name thou owest not, and hast put thyself   Upon this island as a spy to win it   From me, the lord on ’t.
translation: You are stealing a name for yourself that does not belong to you. You’ve come to this island as a spy to try to take this island from me, its lord.

original: No, as I am a man!
translation: No, I swear on my honor as a man!

original: There’s nothing ill can dwell in such a temple. If the ill spirit have so fair a house, Good things will strive to dwell with ’t.
translation: Nothing evil could ever exist in a body this attractive. If the devil had a house as beautiful as his body, then good things would fight to live in it.

original: [to FERDINAND]   Follow me.
translation: [To FERDINAND]  Follow me.

original: [to MIRANDA]   Speak not you for him. He’s a traitor.
translation: [To MIRANDA]  Don’t speak in his defense. He’s a traitor.

original: [to FERDINAND]   Come,   I’ll manacle thy neck and feet together.   Seawater shalt thou drink.
translation: [To FERDINAND]  Come, I’ll chain your neck and feet together. You’ll have only sea water to drink.

original: Thy food shall be   The fresh-brook muscles, withered roots, and husks   Wherein the acorn cradled. Follow.
translation: Your food will be fresh-water mussels, old roots, and empty acorn shells. Follow me.

original: No. I will resist such entertainment till Mine enemy has more power.
translation: No, I’ll resist such treatment until my enemy overpowers me.

original: O dear father, Make not too rash a trial of him, for He’s gentle and not fearful.
translation: Oh, dear father, don’t be too harsh with him. He’s a gentleman, and not a coward.

original: What, I say?   My foot my tutor?—
translation: [To MIRANDA]  What? Do you, my daughter—who owes me obedience—dare to tell me what to do?

original: Put thy sword up, traitor,   Who makest a show but darest not strike, thy conscience   Is so possessed with guilt.
translation: [To FERDINAND]  Sheathe your sword, traitor. You put on a nice show there, but you wouldn’t dare to actually strike me because you feel too guilty.

original: Come from thy ward,   For I can here disarm thee with this stick   And make thy weapon drop.
translation: Step out of your defensive position. For, if I wanted to, I could use this magic wand to disarm you and make your sword drop.

original: Beseech you, father.
translation: I beg you, Father.

original: Hence! Hang not on my garments.
translation: Go away! Don’t grab my clothes.

original: Sir, have pity, I’ll be his surety.
translation: Father, have pity on him. I’ll be the guarantee of his goodness.

original: Silence! One word more   Shall make me chide thee, if not hate thee. What,   An advocate for an imposter?
translation: Silence! If you say another word, I’ll scold you, maybe even hate you. What, you’re taking the side of an impostor?

original: Hush,   Thou think’st there is no more such shapes as he,   Having seen but him and Caliban.
translation: Be quiet. You think no one else is as beautiful as him, because you’ve seen only him and Caliban.

original: Foolish wench,   To th' most of men this is a Caliban   And they to him are angels.
translation: Foolish girl, to most people this man looks like a Caliban, and compared to him, most people look like angels.

original: My affections Are then most humble. I have no ambition To see a goodlier man.
translation: Then my love is humble. I have no desire to see a more handsome man than this one.

original: Come on. Obey. Thy nerves are in their infancy again And have no vigor in them.
translation: Come on. Obey me. Your muscles are like those of a baby, without strength or energy.
