original: So they are.   My spirits, as in a dream, are all bound up.
translation: They are. My strength is all tied up, as if in a bad dream.

original: My father’s loss, the weakness which I feel,   The wrack of all my friends, nor this man’s threats,   To whom I am subdued, are but light to me,
translation: The loss of my father, the physical weakness I feel, the destruction of all my friends, the threats of this man who’s captured me would be like nothing to me,

original: Might I but through my prison once a day   Behold this maid.
translation: if I could just look through my prison windows once a day and see this girl. I would not need to have the freedom to go anywhere else in the world.

original: All corners else o' th' earth   Let liberty make use of. Space enough   Have I in such a prison.
translation: A prison like that would give me all the space I needed.

original: [aside]   It works!
translation: [To himself]  It’s working!

original: [to FERDINAND]   Come on.
translation: [To FERDINAND]  Come on.

original: [aside]   Thou hast done well, fine Ariel!
translation: [To himself]  You’ve done well, Ariel.

original: [to FERDINAND]   Follow me.
translation: [To FERDINAND]  Follow me.

original: [to ARIEL]   Hark what thou else shalt do me.
translation: [To ARIEL]  Listen to what else you should do for me.

original: [to FERDINAND]   Be of comfort.   My father’s of a better nature, sir,   Than he appears by speech.
translation: [To FERDINAND]  Take comfort, sir. My father is more kind and gentle than his words make him seem.

original: This is unwonted   Which now came from him.
translation: The way he just acted is unusual for him.

original: Thou shalt be free As mountain winds. But then exactly do All points of my command.
translation: You’ll be free as the mountain winds. But first you must do everything I command.

original: To th' syllable.
translation: Every little thing.

original: Come, follow.     Speak not for him.
translation: Come, follow me.[To MIRANDA] Don’t defend him.

original: [to ALONSO]   Beseech you, sir, be merry. You have cause,   So have we all, of joy, for our escape   Is much beyond our loss.
translation: [To ALONSO]  I beg you sir, be happy. You, like all of us, have good reasons to be joyful. The fact that we escaped the shipwreck with our lives far outweighs what we lost.

original: Our hint of woe   Is common. Every day some sailor’s wife,   The masters of some merchant, and the merchant   Have just our theme of woe.
translation: Many people have also experienced what we have to feel sad about. Every day some sailor’s wife, the owner of some merchant ship, and the merchant who owns the cargo on that ship all experience the same sort of loss.

original: But for the miracle—   I mean our preservation—few in millions   Can speak like us.
translation: But the miracle—the fact that we survived—has only been experienced by a few people out of millions.

original: Then wisely, good sir, weigh   Our sorrow with our comfort.
translation: So, good sir, be wise, and weigh our sorrow against what should bring us happiness.

original: Prithee, peace.
translation: Please, be quiet.

original: He receives comfort like cold porridge.
translation: Alonso enjoys these comforting words about as much as he enjoys cold soup.

original: The visitor will not give him o'er so.
translation: But the visitor trying to bring comfort to the sick won’t give up on him.

original: Look he’s winding up the watch of his wit. By and by it will strike.
translation: Look. He’s trying to come up with some new idea for how to help Alonso, winding his brain up like some kind of clock. Soon it will strike...

original: Sir—
translation: Sir—

original: One. Tell.
translation: The clock strikes one. Count it.

original: When every grief is entertained that’s offered, Comes to th' entertainer—
translation: If we allowed ourselves to think about, or entertain, every sad thing that happens, then the entertainer will end up with—

original: A dollar.
translation: A dollar.

original: Dolor comes to him, indeed. You have spoken truer than  you purposed.
You have taken it wiselier than I meant you should.
translation: You took what I said more seriously than I meant it.

original: Therefore, my lord—
translation: Therefore, my lord—

original: Fie, what a spendthrift is he of his  tongue!
translation: Goodness, he just talks and talks and talks!

original: I prithee, spare.
translation: Please, stop.

original: Well, I have done. But yet—
translation: Well, I’m basically finished. But still—

original: He will be talking.
translation: He insists on talking.

original: Which, of he or Adrian, for a good wager, first begins  to crow?
translation: Here’s a good bet. Which of the two, Gonzalo or Adrian, will speak first?

original: The old cock.
translation: The old rooster, Gonzalo.

original: The cockerel.
translation: I’ll take the young rooster, Adrian.

original: Done. The wager?
translation: You’re on. What does the winner get?

original: A laughter.
translation: A good laugh.

original: A match!
translation: It’s a deal!

original: Though this island seem to be desert—
translation: Though this island seems to deserted—

original: Ha, ha, ha!
translation: Ha, ha, ha!

original: So you’re paid.
translation: You got your prize.

original: Uninhabitable and almost inaccessible—
translation: Uninhabited, and almost inaccessible—

original: Yet—
translation: Next he’ll say “but”—

original: Yet—
translation: But—

original: He could not miss ’t.
translation: He couldn’t not say it.

original: It must needs be of subtle, tender, and delicate  temperance.
translation: It seems to be mild and gentle, and to have a temperate climate.

original: Temperance was a delicate wench.
Ay, and a subtle, as he most learnedly delivered.
translation: Yes, and, as Adrian described so smartly, she was a subtle one in bed, too.

original: The air breathes upon us here most sweetly.
translation: The air here is like a fresh, sweet breath.

original: As if it had lungs, and rotten ones.
translation: As if the island had lungs—rotten lungs.

original: Or as ’twere perfumed by a fen.
translation: As if the air was perfumed by a swamp.

original: Here is everything advantageous to life.
translation: This island contains everything that is good for life.

original: True. Save means to live.
translation: True. Except anything you could actually use to live.

original: Of that there’s none, or little.
translation: There’s none of that, or just a little.

original: How lush and lusty the grass looks! How green!
translation: The grass looks so rich and healthy! It is so green!

original: The ground indeed is tawny.
translation: The ground is actually brown.

original: With an eye of green in ’t.
translation: With a tinge of green in it.

original: He misses not much.
translation: He doesn’t miss a thing.

original: No, he doth but mistake the truth totally.
translation: No, he just misses the actual truth entirely.

original: But the rarity of it is—which is indeed almost beyond  credit—
translation: But the unbelievable thing is—and this is really almost hard to imagine—

original: As many vouched rarities are.
translation: As by definition most unbelievable things are.

original: That our garments, being, as they were, drenched in the sea, hold notwithstanding their freshness and glosses,  being rather new-dyed than stained with salt water.
translation: That our clothes—which were drenched in sea water—continue to be fresh and clean, and in fact seem almost new rather than stained by the salt water.

original: If but one of his pockets could speak, would it not say he lies?
translation: If just one of the pockets on his clothes could speak, wouldn’t it say that he’s a liar?

original: Ay, or very falsely pocket up his report.
translation: Yes, or just try to hide and suppress the lie.

original: Methinks our garments are now as fresh as when we put  them on first in Afric, at the marriage of the king’s  fair daughter Claribel to the King of Tunis.
translation: I think our clothes are as fresh now as they were when we put them on in Africa to attend the marriage of the king’s beautiful daughter Claribel to the King of Tunis.

original: 'Twas a sweet marriage, and we prosper well in our  return.
translation: The wedding was wonderful, and we’re doing just great on our journey back home.

original: Tunis was never graced before with such a paragon to  their queen.
translation: Tunis has never before had such a perfect beauty for a queen.

original: Not since widow Dido’s time.
Widow! A pox o' that! How came that “widow” in? Widow  Dido!
translation: Widow! To hell with that! Why is he calling her a widow? Widow Dido—ha!

original: What if he had said “widower Aeneas” too? Good Lord,  how you take it!
translation: Next thing you know, he’ll be saying “widower Aeneas.” Good Lord, how can he interpret the story in that way?

original: “Widow Dido” said you? You make me study of that. She  was of Carthage, not of Tunis.
translation: “Widow Dido,” did you say? I'd have to look into that. Dido was from Carthage, not Tunis.

original: This Tunis, sir, was Carthage.
translation: Tunis used to be Carthage, sir.

original: Carthage?
translation: Carthage?

original: I assure you, Carthage.
translation: I promise you, it was Carthage.

original: His word is more than the miraculous harp. He hath  raised the wall and houses too.
translation: Gonzalo's word is like the legendary harp of Amphion, which, when played, caused the walls of Thebes to rise. Now Gonzalo—just by saying so—has created a whole new city.

original: What impossible matter will he make easy next?
translation: What incredible thing will he do next as if it was nothing?

original: I think he will carry this island home in his pocket  and give it his son for an apple.
translation: I think he’ll carry this island home in his pocket and give it to his son as an apple.

original: And sowing the kernels of it in the sea, bring forth  more islands.
translation: And throw its seeds in the sea to make more islands grow.

original: Ay.
translation: Yes, that's exactly what I would do.

original: Why, in good time.
translation: Well, sure it is.

original: Sir, we were talking that our garments seem now as fresh as when we were at Tunis at the marriage  of your daughter, who is now queen.
translation: Sir, we were discussing that our clothes seem just as clean as they did when we were in Tunis at the wedding of your daughter, who’s now queen.

original: And the rarest that e'er came there.
translation: The most remarkable queen that's ever been there.

original: Bate, I beseech you, widow Dido.
translation: Except for the widow Dido, if I may say so.

original: Oh, widow Dido? Ay, widow Dido.
translation: Oh, the widow Dido? Of course, the widow Dido.

original: Is not, sir, my doublet as fresh as the first day I  wore it? I mean, in a sort.
translation: Sir, isn’t my jacket as clean as the first time I wore it? I mean, in a way.

original: That “sort” was well fished for.
translation: He did a good job of sticking that "in a way" in there.

original: When I wore it at your daughter’s marriage?
translation: When I wore it at your daughter’s wedding.

original: You cram these words into mine ears against   The stomach of my sense. Would I had never   Married my daughter there!
translation: You keep pushing these words into my ears that I don’t have any desire to hear. If only I had never sent my daughter to Tunis to be married!

original: For, coming thence,   My son is lost and, in my rate, she too,   Who is so far from Italy removed   I ne'er again shall see her.
translation: I lost my son because of it. And, as far as I'm concerned, I lost my daughter too, since she is now living so far from Italy that I'll never see her again.

original: O thou mine heir   Of Naples and of Milan, what strange fish   Hath made his meal on thee?
translation: Oh, my dear son and heir of Naples and Milan, what strange fish has eaten your dead body?

original: Sir, he may live.   I saw him beat the surges under him,   And ride upon their backs.
translation: Sir, he may still live. I saw him swim over the waves and ride upon their backs.

original: He trod the water,   Whose enmity he flung aside, and breasted   The surge most swoll'n that met him.
translation: He treaded water, withstanding all their rage, and fought through even the biggest waves that came at him.

original: His bold head   'Bove the contentious waves he kept, and oared   Himself with his good arms in lusty stroke   To th' shore,
translation: He bravely kept his head above the rough waves. And with his powerful arms and strong strokes he swam toward the shore,

original: that o'er his wave-worn basis bowed,   As stooping to relieve him. I not doubt   He came alive to land.
translation: which seemed almost to lean forward to help him from the water. I have no doubt that he got to the shore alive.

original: No, no, he’s gone.
translation: No, no, he’s dead.

original: Sir, you may thank yourself for this great loss,   That would not bless our Europe with your daughter,   But rather loose her to an African,
translation: Sir, you can thank yourself for this great loss, because rather than give your daughter to a husband in Europe you instead threw her to some African.

original: Where she at least is banished from your eye,   Who hath cause to wet the grief on ’t.
translation: It's a good thing you'll never see her again, since then she won't be around to remind you of this awful thing you've done to her.

original: Prithee, peace.
translation: Please, be quiet.

original: You were kneeled to and importuned otherwise   By all of us, and the fair soul herself   Weighed between loathness and obedience, at   Which end o' th' beam should bow.
translation: All of us kneeled down in front of you and begged you not to do this, and the beautiful girl herself was forced to choose whether to follow her own disgust at the marriage or her duty to obey you.

original: We have lost your  son,   I fear, forever. Milan and Naples have   More widows in them of this business' making   Than we bring men to comfort them.
translation: Now we’ve lost your son forever too, I fear. This marriage and subsequent shipwreck has created more widows in Milan and Naples than we have survivors to bring home to comfort them.

original: The fault’s your own.
translation: All of this is your fault.

original: So is the dearest o' th' loss.
translation: The heaviest loss is mine as well.

original: My lord Sebastian,   The truth you speak doth lack some gentleness   And time to speak it in.
translation: My lord Sebastian, despite the truth in your words, what you're saying is unkind and inappropriate at this time.

original: You rub the sore   When you should bring the plaster.
translation: You’re rubbing salt in his wounds when you should be bringing him bandages.

original: Very well.
translation: All right.

original: And most chirurgeonly.
translation: That Gonzalo is quite the doctor, isn't he?

original: It is foul weather in us all, good sir, When you are cloudy.
translation: Noble sir, we all feel under the weather when you’re feeling gloomy.

original: Foul weather?
translation: Under the weather?

original: Very foul.
translation: Far under.

original: Had I plantation of this isle, my lord—
translation: If I colonized this island, my lord—

original: He’d sow ’t with nettle seed.
translation: He’d grow useless, stinging nettle plants all over it.

original: Or docks, or mallows.
translation: Or weeds.

original: And were the king on ’t, what would I do?
translation: And if I were the king of the colony, would you like to know what I’d do?

original: 'Scape being drunk for want of wine.
translation: He wouldn’t get drunk because there isn't any wine.

original: I' th' commonwealth I would by contraries   Execute all things. For no kind of traffic   Would I admit. No name of magistrate.
translation: In my commonwealth I’d do everything in the opposite way from what's normal. I wouldn’t allow any business. There would be no judges.

original: Letters should not be known. Riches, poverty,   And use of service—none. Contract, succession,   Bourn, bound of land, tilth, vineyard—none.
translation: There would be no school or learning. No riches, poverty, or servants. None of that. No contracts, inheritance, privately owned land, farming, or vineyards. None of that.

original: No use of metal, corn, or wine, or oil.   No occupation. All men idle, all.
translation: There’d be no metal-work, no grinding of corn, no wine-making, or making of olive oil. There'd be no work. Men would do nothing at all.

original: And women too, but innocent and pure.   No sovereignty—
translation: Women too, except those things that are innocent and pure. There’d be no kingship—

original: Yet he would be king on ’t.
translation: Though he'd be the king of this land with no kingship.

original: The latter end of his commonwealth forgets the  beginning.
translation: His colony is ending up a long way from where it began.

original: All things in common nature should produce   Without sweat or endeavor.
translation: Nature would produce everything people needed, and all of it would be shared equally by all.

original: Treason, felony,   Sword, pike, knife, gun, or need of any engine,   Would I not have.
translation: There’d be no treason, crimes, swords, spears, knives, guns, or need for any other weapon.

original: But nature should bring forth   Of its own kind all foison, all abundance,   To feed my innocent people.
translation: Without any human help, nature would grow bountiful harvests to feed my innocent people.

original: No marrying ’mong his subjects?
translation: Would there be no marriage among those he ruled?

original: None, man. All idle. Whores and knaves.
translation: None, my man. They'd do nothing. They’d all be whores and scoundrels.

original: I would with such perfection govern, sir, T' excel the Golden Age.
translation: My leadership would be so perfect that my colony would be even better than the mythical ancient Golden Age.

original: 'Save his majesty!
translation: May God protect his Majesty!

original: Long live Gonzalo!
translation: Long live Gonzalo!

original: And—do you mark me, sir?
translation: And—are you listening to me, sir?

original: Prithee, no more. Thou dost talk nothing to me.
translation: Please, no more. What you're saying to me is meaningless.

original: I do well believe your highness, and did it to minister occasion to these gentlemen, who are of such sensible  and nimble lungs that they always use to laugh at  nothing.
translation: I agree with you completely, your Highness. I said those things to give these gentlemen a good time, since they have such strong lungs that they so often use to laugh at meaningless trivialities.

original: 'Twas you we laughed at.
translation: We were laughing at you.

original: Who in this kind of merry fooling am nothing to you. So you may continue and laugh at nothing still.
translation: But in all of your silly little jokes, you see me as nothing. So go on, laugh at nothing.

original: What a blow was there given!
translation: What an insult he just made!

original: An it had not fallen flat-long.
translation: Too bad it fell so flat.

original: You are gentlemen of brave mettle. You would lift the  moon out of her sphere if she would continue in it five  weeks without changing.
translation: You are courageous gentlemen. You’d give the moon a helpful push if it got stuck in the same spot of its orbit for five weeks.

original: We would so, and then go a-batfowling.
Nay, good my lord, be not angry.
translation: My good lord, please don’t be angry.

original: No, I warrant you. I will not adventure my discretion  so weakly. Will you laugh me asleep, for I am very  heavy?
translation: I promise you, I’m not. I wouldn't risk my reputation for self-control for such a tiny thing. Will you laugh me to sleep? For I’m feeling very tired.

original: Go sleep, and hear us.
translation: Go to sleep, and we'll laugh.

original: What, all so soon asleep? I wish mine eyes Would with themselves shut up my thoughts. I find They are inclined to do so.
translation: What, is everyone asleep so quickly? I wish my eyes would close and I could sleep, so that I could stop thinking. In fact, my eyes are starting to close.

original: Please you, sir,   Do not omit the heavy offer of it.
translation: Please, sir, don't refuse the opportunity to sleep.

original: It seldom visits sorrow. When it doth,   It is a comforter.
translation: Sleep rarely comes to people who are grieving. When it does come, it gives comfort.

original: We two, my lord, Will guard your person while you take your rest And watch your safety.
translation: The two of us, my lord, will guard you while you rest and make sure that you're safe.

original: Thank you. Wondrous heavy.
translation: Thank you. I’m extremely tired.

original: What a strange drowsiness possesses them!
translation: It's so strange how all of them suddenly got so tired!

original: It is the quality o' th' climate.
translation: There's something in the climate here.

original: Why Doth it not then our eyelids sink? I find not Myself disposed to sleep.
translation: Then why aren’t our eyelids closing? I’m not feeling tired at all.

original: Nor I. My spirits are nimble.   They fell together all, as by consent.   They dropped, as by a thunderstroke.
translation: Me neither. I’m full of energy. They all fell asleep together, as if they’d all agreed on it earlier. They fell asleep as if they’d all been struck by lightning.

original: What might,   Worthy Sebastian, O, what might—? No more.—
translation: What might happen, noble Sebastian, what might happen if—? No, I shouldn't say any more.

original: And yet methinks I see it in thy face,   What thou shouldst be.
translation: And yet, I think I can see in your face what you have the potential to be.

original: Th' occasion speaks thee, and   My strong imagination sees a crown   Dropping upon thy head.
translation: Opportunity is knocking on your door, and my imagination sees a crown coming to rest on your head.

original: What, art thou waking?
translation: What, are you awake or asleep?

original: Do you not hear me speak?
translation: Don’t you hear me speaking?

original: I do, and surely   It is a sleepy language, and thou speak’st   Out of thy sleep. What is it thou didst say?
translation: I do, and it certainly sounds like the language of dreams, like you're talking in your sleep. What is it that you said?

original: This is a strange repose, to be asleep   With eyes wide open, standing, speaking, moving,   And yet so fast asleep.
translation: This is a very strange sleep. How can you be standing, speaking, and moving, with your eyes wide open, and yet be fast asleep?

original: Noble Sebastian, Thou let’st thy fortune sleep—die, rather—wink’st Whiles thou art waking.
translation: Noble Sebastian, by not seizing this opportunity you’re letting this chance sleep—no, die—even while you are wide awake.

original: Thou dost snore distinctly. There’s meaning in thy snores.
translation: You have a strange way of snoring. It sounds like you're speaking actual words.

original: I am more serious than my custom.
translation: I'm more serious right now than I usually am.

original: You   Must be so too if heed me, which to do   Trebles thee o'er.
translation: You should be too, if you listen to me. If you follow my advice you will become three times as powerful as you are now.

original: Well, I am standing water.
translation: Like standing water, I'm not moving at all.

original: I’ll teach you how to flow.
translation: I'll teach you how to move, to act.

original: Do so. To ebb Hereditary sloth instructs me.
translation: Do that. As a younger brother who cannot inherit the throne, I’m naturally lazy.

original: Oh,   If you but knew how you the purpose cherish   Whiles thus you mock it! How, in stripping it,   You more invest it!
translation: Oh, if you only knew how ambitious you truly are, even while you mock ambition! The more you make fun of it, the more obvious it is how much you care!

original: Ebbing men indeed   Most often do so near the bottom run   By their own fear or sloth.
translation: Men who do nothing usually wind up at the bottom, controlled by their own fear and laziness.

original: Prithee, say on.
translation: Please, continue.

original: The setting of thine eye and cheek proclaim   A matter from thee,
translation: There’s something in your face and eyes that indicates you're talking about something serious,

original: and a birth indeed   Which throes thee much to yield.
translation: and that—like giving birth—you're finding it hard to actually get it out.

original: Thus, sir:   Although this lord of weak remembrance—this,   Who shall be of as little memory   When he is earthed—
translation: Here it is, sir:  [Points at GONZALO]  Although this lord with the bad memory—and who won't be remembered by anyone when he’s dead and buried—

original: hath here almost persuade   (For he’s a spirit of persuasion only,   Professes to persuade) the king his son’s alive,
translation: almost persuaded the king (because his entire mind is focused only on persuading people) that the king's son is alive,

original: 'Tis as impossible that he’s undrowned   And he that sleeps here swims.
translation: it’s impossible that he didn't drown. Saying he survived is like saying that this man sleeping over here is actually swimming.

original: I have no hope That he’s undrowned.
translation: I also hold no hope that he survived.

original: Oh, out of that “no hope”   What great hope have you!
translation: Oh, but from that “no hope” arise amazing hopes for you!

original: No hope that way is   Another way so high a hope that even   Ambition cannot pierce a wink beyond,   But doubt discovery there.
translation: No hope for Ferdinand's survival is, for you, so high a hope that not even ambition for greatness could imagine anything higher—or even entirely believe that this possibility exists.

original: Will you grant with me   That Ferdinand is drowned?
translation: Do you agree with me that Ferdinand has drowned?

original: He’s gone.
translation: He’s dead.

original: Then, tell me, Who’s the next heir of Naples?
translation: Then, tell me, who is now the heir to the throne of Naples?

original: Claribel.
translation: Claribel, Alonso's daughter.

original: She that is Queen of Tunis; she that dwells   Ten leagues beyond man’s life; she that from Naples   Can have no note, unless the sun were post—   The man i' th' moon’s too slow—
translation: Claribel, who is now Queen of Tunis, and who lives thirty miles farther than a lifetime's journey from Italy. She wouldn't even receive a letter from Italy (unless it could somehow be delivered by the light of the sun; the man in the moon's too slow to deliver it)

original: till newborn chins   Be rough and razorable; she that from whom   We all were sea-swallowed,
translation: in less than the time it takes a baby to grow old enough to shave. Claribel was the cause of our ship getting swallowed by the sea,

original: though some cast again,   And by that destiny to perform an act   Whereof what’s past is prologue, what to come   In yours and my discharge.
translation: though some of us survived—and our survival suggests that it is our destiny to perform an act that, in fact, reenacts the past.

original: What stuff is this? How say you?   'Tis true, my brother’s daughter’s Queen of Tunis,
translation: What is this? What are you talking about? It's true that my brother's daughter is the Queen of Tunis

original: So is she heir of Naples, ’twixt which regions   There is some space.
translation: as well as the heir to the throne of Naples, and that a great distance separates those two places.

original: A space whose every cubit   Seems to cry out, “How shall that Claribel   Measure us back to Naples?
translation: A distance whose every inch seems to scream, “How can Claribel ever follow us back to Naples?

original: Keep in Tunis,   And let Sebastian wake.” Say this were death   That now hath seized them.
translation: Stay in Tunis, and let Sebastian get his good fortune." Imagine that instead of these men sleeping here, they were dead.

original: Why, they were no worse   Than now they are. There be that can rule Naples   As well as he that sleeps,
translation: Well, they'd be just as badly off as they are now. There are many who can rule Naples just as well as this man who's sleeping.

original: lords that can prate   As amply and unnecessarily   As this Gonzalo. I myself could make   A chough of as deep chat.
translation: And there are lots of lords who can babble as much as Gonzalo. I could teach a crow to blabber such nonsense.

original: Oh, that you bore   The mind that I do, what a sleep were this   For your advancement! Do you understand me?
translation: Oh, I wish your thoughts were the same as mine—then you'd see how these sleeping men are an unparalleled opportunity for you. Do you understand what I'm saying?

original: Methinks I do.
translation: I think I do.

original: And how does your content Tender your own good fortune?
translation: And how do your feelings about what I've just said affect your chances at good fortune?

original: I remember You did supplant your brother Prospero.
translation: I remember that you overthrew and replaced your brother Prospero.

original: True.   And look how well my garments sit upon me,   Much feater than before.
translation: True. And look how well that position suits me—far better than the one I had before.

original: My brother’s servants   Were then my fellows. Now they are my men.
translation: Back then, my brother’s servants were my equals. Now they work for me.

original: But, for your conscience?
translation: But what about your guilty conscience?

original: Ay, sir. Where lies that? If ’twere a kibe,   'Twould put me to my slipper. But I feel not   This deity in my bosom.
translation: Ah, yes. Where is my conscience? If a conscience were a blister on my heel, I'd put my slippers on. But I don't feel this "conscience" in my chest.

original: Twenty consciences,   That stand ’twixt me and Milan, candied be they   And melt ere they molest!
translation: Even if there were twenty guilty consciences standing between me and the dukedom of Milan, I'd combine them like candies and melt them away before they'd bother me.

original: Here lies your brother,   No better than the earth he lies upon,   If he were that which now he’s like, that’s dead;
translation: Here lies your sleeping brother, who'd be of no more value than the ground he's lying on if he were in fact what he now looks like—dead, that is.

original: Whom I, with this obedient steel, three inches of it,   Can lay to bed for ever; whiles you, doing thus,   To the perpetual wink for aye might put   This ancient morsel, this Sir Prudence, who   Should not upbraid our course.
translation: And I, with just three inches of this sword, could put him to rest forever; while you, doing the same, could give ancient Gonzalo a permanent sleep to ensure that he wouldn't stand against us.

original: For all the rest,   They’ll take suggestion as a cat laps milk.   They’ll tell the clock to any business that   We say befits the hour.
translation: As for everyone else, they'll accept whatever we say just as easily as a cat accepts milk. They'll chime in agreement when we instruct them to, just like a clock telling time.

original: Thy case, dear friend,   Shall be my precedent. As thou got’st Milan,   I’ll come by Naples. Draw thy sword.
translation: I'll use your experience as a model, my friend. Just as you got Milan, I’ll get Naples. Take out your sword.

original: One stroke   Shall free thee from the tribute which thou payest.   And I the king shall love thee.
translation: With one thrust of your sword, you will be free from having to pay tribute money to Naples ever again. And I, as King of Naples, will be your great friend.

original: Draw together. And when I rear my hand, do you the like, To fall it on Gonzalo.
translation: We'll both draw our swords. When I raise my sword, you do the same, and bring it down to kill Gonzalo.

original: O, but one word.
translation: Oh, just one more thing.

original: [to GONZALO]   My master through his art foresees the  danger   That you, his friend, are, and sends me forth—   For else his project dies—to keep them living.
translation: [To GONZALO]  With his magic, my master could see the danger that you, his friend, are in. He sent me to keep you all alive—or else his plans would die along with you.

original: [sings in GONZALO’s ear]   While you here do snoring lie,   Open-eyed conspiracy   His time doth take.
translation: [Singing in GONZALO’s ear]  While you lie here snoring,  Cold-blooded conspirators  Are about to seize their chance.

original: If of life you keep a care,   Shake off slumber and beware.   Awake! Awake!
translation: If you want to live,  Wake up and beware!  Wake up! Wake up!

original: Then let us both be sudden.
translation: Now let’s do this quickly.

original: Now, good angels preserve the king!
translation: Angels above protect the king!

original: [waking] Why, how now? Ho, awake!
translation: Why, what’s happening? Hey, wake up!

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What’s going on here?

original: Whiles we stood here securing your repose,   Even now, we heard a hollow burst of bellowing   Like bulls, or rather lions.
translation: While we stood here on guard while you were asleep, we just now heard a tremendous thundering that sounded like bulls, or lions.

original: Did ’t not wake you?   It struck mine ear most terribly.
translation: Isn't that what woke you? It sounded awful to me.

original: I heard nothing.
translation: I didn’t hear anything.

original: Oh, ’twas a din to fright a monster’s ear,   To make an earthquake!
translation: Oh, it was loud enough to frighten a monster, or to cause an earthquake!

original: Sure, it was the roar   Of a whole herd of lions.
translation: Surely, it must have been the roar of an entire herd of lions.

original: Heard you this, Gonzalo?
translation: Did you hear it, Gonzalo?

original: Upon mine honor, sir, I heard a humming,   And that a strange one too, which did awake me.   I shaked you, sir, and cried.
translation: Sir, I swear that I did hear a strange humming sound, which woke me up. I shook you, sir, and cried out.

original: As mine eyes opened,   I saw their weapons drawn. There was a noise,   That’s verily.
translation: When I opened my eyes, I saw their raised swords. There was a noise, that’s true.

original: 'Tis best we stand upon our guard,   Or that we quit this place. Let’s draw our weapons.
translation: It would be best if we either set a constant guard here, or left this place entirely. Let’s take out our own swords too.

original: Lead off this ground, and let’s make further search For my poor son.
translation: Lead us away from this place, and let's go search some more for my poor son.

original: Heavens keep him from these beasts! For he is, sure, i' th' island.
translation: May God protect Ferdinand from those lions. Because I’m sure he’s on the island.

original: Lead away.
translation: Lead on.

original: Prospero my lord shall know what I have done. So, King, go safely on to seek thy son.
translation: My lord Prospero will know what I’ve done. So, King, continue on in safety and search for your son.

original: All the infections that the sun sucks up   From bogs, fens, flats, on Prosper fall and make him   By inchmeal a disease!
translation: May all the sicknesses that grow in swamps, marshes, and wetlands strike Prospero so that, little by little, he becomes nothing more than a disease!

original: His spirits hear me   And yet I needs must curse. But they’ll nor pinch,   Fright me with urchin-shows, pitch me i' th' mire,
translation: His spirits are spying on me, but I just have to curse him. Unless he tells the spirits to, they won’t pinch me; frighten me by appearing as hedgehog-shaped goblins; push me in the mud;

original: Nor lead me like a firebrand in the dark   Out of my way, unless he bid 'em.
translation: or lead me the wrong way like a false guide in the night.

original: But   For every trifle are they set upon me,   Sometime like apes that mow and chatter at me,   And after bite me,
translation: But he does send them after me for every little thing I do. Sometimes his spirits come after me in the form of apes, chattering and making faces at me and then biting me.

original: then like hedgehogs which   Lie tumbling in my barefoot way and mount   Their pricks at my footfall.
translation: Sometimes they come in the shape of porcupines, lying curled up on the paths where I walk barefoot and pricking me when I step down.

original: Sometime am I   All wound with adders who with cloven tongues   Do hiss me into madness.
translation: Sometimes poisonous snakes wrap around me, hissing with their forked tongues until I go crazy.

original: Lo, now, lo!   Here comes a spirit of his, and to torment me   For bringing wood in slowly. I’ll fall flat.
translation: Look, right there, look! Here comes one of his spirits to punish me for bringing back the wood too slowly. I’ll lie down, flat on the ground.

original: Perchance he will not mind me.   [lies down, covered by  his gaberdine]
translation: Maybe he won’t notice me. [He lies down, covering himself with his cloak]

original: Here’s neither bush nor shrub to bear off any weather  at all. And another storm brewing, I hear it sing i' th' wind. Yond same black cloud, yond huge one, looks like  a foul bombard that would shed his liquor.
translation: There aren’t any bushes or shrubs here to offer me even a little protection from the weather. And another storm is coming. I can hear it in the sound of the wind. That black cloud over there—the huge one—looks like a dirty leather canteen that’s about to drop the liquid it contains.

original: If it should  thunder as it did before, I know not where to hide my  head. Yond same cloud cannot choose but fall by  pailfuls.   [sees CALIBAN]   What have we here? A man or a  fish? Dead or alive? A fish.
translation: If it storms like it did earlier, I don’t know where I’ll hide. That cloud is going to drop buckets of rain.  [He sees CALIBAN]  What do we have here? Is it a man or a fish? Is it dead or alive? It must be a fish.

original: He smells like a fish, a  very ancient and fish-like smell, a kind of  not-of-the-newest poor-john. A strange fish!
translation: He smells like a fish, an old fish, like old cheap dried fish. What a strange fish!

original: Were I in  England now, as once I was, and had but this fish  painted, not a holiday fool there but would give a piece of silver. There would this monster make a man. Any  strange beast there makes a man.
translation: If I were in England now, as I was once before, and had a painting that showed this fish, every single fool there would give me a silver coin just to look at it. In England, this monster would make a man rich.  But, then again, any strange beast there is just like a man.

original: When they will not give a doit to relieve a lame beggar, they will lay out ten  to see a dead Indian. Legged like a man and his fins  like arms!
translation: English people won’t give a penny to help a lame beggar, but they’ll give ten to see a dead Indian. This monster here has legs like a man but fins for arms!

original: Warm, o' my troth. I do now let loose my  opinion, hold it no longer: this is no fish, but an  islander that hath lately suffered by a thunderbolt.
translation: He’s still warm, too, by my faith. I no longer think this is a fish. I think now that it’s a native of the island who’s been struck by a lightning bolt.

original: Alas,   the storm is come again! My best way is to creep under his gaberdine.
translation: Oh no, the storm is returning! The best thing for me would be to crawl under his cloak.

original: T   here is no other shelter hereabouts.  Misery acquaints a man with strange bedfellows. I will  here shroud till the dregs of the storm be past.   [crawls under gaberdine]
translation: There’s no other shelter nearby. When times are tough, you’ll end up close to the strangest people. I’ll cover myself up here until the last of the storm passes.  [He crawls under the cloak]

original: [sings]   I shall no more to sea, to sea,   Here shall I die ashore—
translation: [Singing] I’ll never again go to sea, to sea, I’ll die here on the shore—

original: This is a very scurvy tune to sing at a man’s funeral.   Well, here’s my comfort.   [drinks, sings]
translation: This is a terrible song to sing at a man’s funeral. Well, here’s something to give me a bit of comfort.  [He lifts a bottle of alcohol to his mouth, drinks, and sings again]

original: The master, the swabber, the boatswain, and I,   The gunner and his mate   Loved Mall, Meg, and Marian, and Margery,   But none of us cared for Kate.
translation: The master, the deck-cleaner, the boatswain, and I, The gunman and his crewmate, All loved Molly, Meg, Marian, and Margery But none of us much liked Kate,

original: For she had a tongue with a tang,   Would cry to a sailor, “Go hang!”   She loved not the savor of tar nor of pitch,
translation: Because she spoke so cruelly, And would shout to sailors, “Go hang!” She did not like the smell of tar or pitch,

original: Yet a tailor might scratch her where'ershe did itch.   Then to sea, boys, and let her go hang!   This is a scurvy tune too. But here’s my comfort.    [drinks]
translation: But would sleep with a tailor when she was in the mood. So go to sea, boys, and let her go to hang! That’s a wretched song too. But here’s my comfort.  [He drinks]

original: Do not torment me. Oh!
translation: Don’t punish me. Oh!

original: What’s the matter? Have we devils here? Do you put  tricks upon ’s with savages and men of Ind, ha? I have  not ’scaped drowning to be afeard now of your four legs.
translation: What’s happening? Are there devils here? Are you trying to trick me with these savages and men from the Indies, huh? I didn’t escape from drowning only to be frightened by  your four legs .

original: Or it hath been said, “As proper a man as ever went on  four legs cannot make him give ground,” and it shall be  said so again while Stephano breathes at' nostrils.
translation: As the old saying goes, "He won't back up even for the most handsome man who ever walked on four legs." And they'll say it again for as long as I'm still alive and breathing.

original: The spirit torments me. Oh!
translation: This spirit is torturing me. Oh!

original: This is some monster of the isle with four legs who  hath got, as I take it, an ague. Where the devil should  he learn our language? I will give him some relief if it be but for that.
translation: This is some four-legged monster of the island, who seems to have some kind of fever, as far as I can tell. How the devil did he learn our language? But since he does, I'll try to give him some relief from his pain.

original: If I can recover him and keep him tame and get to Naples with him, he’s a present for any  emperor that ever trod on neat’s leather.
translation: If I can get him better, tame him, and get him back to Naples, he’d be a perfect present to give to any emperor who's ever worn shoes.

original: Do not torment me, prithee. I’ll bring my wood home  faster.
translation: Don’t punish me, please. I’ll bring the wood home faster.

original: He’s in his fit now and does not talk after the wisest. He shall taste of my bottle. If he have never drunk  wine afore, it will go near to remove his fit.
translation: He’s having a fit, and saying things that don't make sense. I’ll give him a taste of the wine from my bottle. If he’s never drunk wine before, it’ll go a long way to stop his fit.

original: If I can  recover him and keep him tame, I will not take too much  for him. He shall pay for him that hath him, and that  soundly.
translation: If I can get him better and tame him, it would be impossible for me to charge too much for people to come and see him. He’ll make a lot of money to whoever owns him, that's for sure.

original: Thou dost me yet but little hurt. Thou wilt anon, I  know it by thy trembling. Now Prosper works upon thee.
translation: So far you haven’t hurt me much. You will soon, though, I can tell by your trembling. Prospero made you do this.

original: [trying to give CALIBAN drink]   Come on your ways. Open your mouth. Here is that which  will give language to you, cat. Open your mouth.
translation: [Trying to get CALIBAN to drink]  Come on now. Open your mouth. As the saying goes, "This good liquor will make a cat talk." Open your mouth.

original: This  will shake your shaking, I can tell you, and that  soundly. You cannot tell who’s your friend. Open your  chaps again.
translation: This’ll put an end to your trembling—I can tell you that for sure.  [CALIBAN opens his mouth and drinks]  You can't even recognize a friend. Open your mouth again.

original: I should know that voice. It should be—But he is  drowned, and these are devils. Oh, defend me!
translation: I think I recognize that voice. It must be...But he’s drowned, and I'm surrounded by devils. Oh, God protect me!

original: Four legs and two voices—a most delicate monster.His  forward voice now is to speak well of his friend. His  backward voice is to utter foul speeches and to detract.
translation: Four legs and two voices—this is a very unique monster. The voice near the front of him is speaking kindly about his friend. The voice near the back of him shouts curses and abusive language.

original: If all the wine in my bottle will recover him, I will  help his ague. Come.   [CALIBAN drinks]   Amen! I will pour  some in thy other mouth.
translation: Even if it takes all the wine in my bottle, I’ll cure his fever. Come on.  [CALIBAN drinks]  Amen to that! I’ll pour some in your other mouth now.

original: Stephano!
translation: Stephano!

original: Doth thy other mouth call me? Mercy, mercy! This is a  devil, and no monster. I will leave him. I have no long  spoon.
translation: Is your other mouth calling my name? Save me, save me! This is a devil, not a monster. I'm getting away from him. I'd be a fool to get involved with the devil.

original: Stephano! If thou beest Stephano, touch me and speak to me. For I am Trinculo—be not afeard—thy good friend  Trinculo.
translation: Stephano! If you are Stephano, touch me and speak to me. Because I’m Trinculo—don’t be scared—your good friend Trinculo.

original: If thou beest Trinculo, come forth. I’ll pull thee by  the lesser legs. If any be Trinculo’s legs, these are  they.   [pulls TRINCULO out from under the gaberdine]
translation: If you are Trinculo, then come out from under there. I’ll pull on you by these smaller legs. If any of these four legs are Trinculo’s, these small ones are them.  [He pulls TRINCULO out from under the cloak]

original: Thou art very Trinculo indeed! How camest thou to be the  siege of this mooncalf? Can he vent Trinculos?
translation: You're really Trinculo! How did you end up being this monster’s excrement? Does he defecate Trinculos?

original: I took him to be killed with a thunderstroke. But art  thou not drowned, Stephano? I hope now thou art not  drowned. Is the storm overblown? I hid me under the dead mooncalf’s gaberdine for fear of the storm.
translation: I thought that he'd been killed by a bolt of lightning. But aren’t you drowned, Stephano? I hope now that you’re not drowned. Is the storm over? I hid under this dead monster’s cloak because I was afraid of the storm.

original: And art  thou living, Stephano? O Stephano, two Neapolitans  ’scaped!   [dances STEPHANO about]
translation: Are you actually alive, Stephano? Oh, Stephano, two of us from Naples survived the shipwreck! [TRINCULO grabs STEPHANO and dances him around]

original: Prithee, do not turn me about. My stomach is not  constant.
translation: Please, don't spin me around. My stomach’s not feeling well.

original: These be fine things, an if they be not  sprites. That’s a brave god and bears celestial liquor.  I will kneel to him.
translation: These are handsome beings, if they’re not spirits. That one's a noble god, who carries liquor from the heavens. I'll bow down before him.

original: [to TRINCULO]   How didst thou ’scape? How camest thou  hither? Swear by this bottle how thou camest hither.
translation: [To TRINCULO]  How did you escape the shipwreck? How did you end up here? Swear on this bottle of wine how you got here.

original: I  escaped upon a butt of sack which the sailors heaved  o'erboard, by this bottle, which I made of the bark of a tree with mine own hands since I was cast ashore.
translation: I swear on the bottle—which I made myself from the bark of a tree after I washed up on shore—that I survived by grabbing onto a barrel of wine that the sailors threw overboard during the storm.

original: I’ll swear upon that bottle to be thy  true subject, for the liquor is not earthly.
translation: I’ll swear on that wine bottle in order to become your loyal subject, because that wine must come from heaven.

original: Here. Swear then how thou escapedst.
translation: Here, swear, and tell me how you escaped the wreck.

original: Swum ashore, man, like a duck. I can swim like a duck,  I’ll be sworn.
translation: I swam ashore, man, like a duck. I can swim like a duck, I swear it.

original: Here, kiss the book. Though thou canst swim like a  duck, thou art made like a goose.
translation: Here, kiss the Bible. Though you can swim like a duck, you look like a silly goose.

original: O Stephano, hast any more of this?
translation: Oh Stephano, do you have any more of this wine?

original: The whole butt, man. My cellar is in a rock by th'  seaside where my wine is hid.—How now, mooncalf? How  does thine ague?
translation: I have the whole barrel, man. I keep it in my wine cellar—a cave by the seaside, where I've stowed away the wine barrel. What’s going on, monster? How is your fever?

original: Hast thou not dropped from heaven?
translation: Have you come down to this island from heaven?

original: Out o' th' moon, I do assure thee. I was the man i’ the moon when time was.
translation: We come from the moon, I promise you. Once upon a time, I was the man in the moon.

original: I have seen thee in her and I do adore thee. My  mistress showed me thee and thy dog and thy bush.
Come, swear to that, kiss the book. I will furnish it  anon with new contents, swear.
translation: Come here, and swear that what you just said was true by kissing the “book.”  I’ll fill it back up again soon, I promise.

original: By this good light, this is a very shallow monster. I  afeard of him! A very weak monster. The man i' th' moon! A most poor credulous monster.—
translation: Now that I see him in this brighter light, it’s clear that he’s not much of a monster. I used to be scared of him! He’s a pretty unconvincing monster. The man in the moon! He’s a poor, gullible monster.

original: Well drawn, monster, in  good sooth!
translation: [To CALIBAN]  That’s a good swig of wine you just took, monster! I mean it!

original: I’ll show thee every fertile inch o' th'  island. And I will kiss thy foot. I prithee, be my god.
translation: I’ll show you every inch of good land on this island. And I’ll kiss your feet. Please, be my god.

original: By this light, a most perfidious and drunken monster. When ’s god’s asleep, he’ll rob his bottle.
translation: Now I can see that he’s a lying, drunken monster. When his “god” falls asleep, he’ll steal the wine bottle.

original: I’ll kiss thy foot. I’ll swear myself thy subject.
translation: I’ll kiss your feet. I’ll take an oath that I’m your loyal subject.

original: Come on then. Down, and swear.
translation: Come on, then. Kneel down and swear.

original: I shall laugh myself to death at this puppy-headed  monster. A most scurvy monster. I could find in my heart to beat him—
translation: I’m going to laugh myself to death at this foolish monster. A disgraceful monster. I could find it in my heart to beat him—

original: Come, kiss.
translation: Now, kiss my feet.

original: But that the poor monster’s in drink. An abominable  monster!
translation: —except that the poor monster is drunk. A repulsive monster!

original: I’ll show thee the best springs. I’ll pluck thee  berries.   I’ll fish for thee and get thee wood enough.
translation: I’ll show you the best sources of fresh water. I’ll pick berries for you. I’ll fish for you and gather enough firewood for you.

original: A plague upon the tyrant that I serve!   I’ll bear him no more sticks, but follow thee,   Thou wondrous man.
translation: May the tyrant I’m serving now die of the plague! I won’t carry any more wood for him. Instead, I’ll serve you now, you miraculous man.

original: A most ridiculous monster, to make a wonder of a poor  drunkard.
translation: What a ridiculous monster, to see a poor drunk man and think him a miracle.

original: [to STEPHANO]   I prithee, let me bring thee where crabs  grow.   And I with my long nails will dig thee pignuts,   Show thee a jay’s nest, and instruct thee how   To snare the nimble marmoset.
translation: [To STEPHANO]  Please, let me show you where you can catch crabs to eat. I’ll dig with my long fingernails to find you peanuts. I’ll show you a bird’s nest with eggs inside, and teach you how to catch a quick-moving monkey.

original: I’ll bring thee   To clustering filberts, and sometimes I’ll get thee   Young scamels from the rock. Wilt thou go with me?
translation: I’ll lead you to clusters of hazelnuts, and sometimes I’ll catch seagulls for you on the rocks. Will you come with me?

original: I prithee now, lead the way without any more talking.  Trinculo, the king and all our company else being  drowned, we will inherit here.
translation: Please, lead the way without doing any more talking. Trinculo, since the king and everyone else we were with have drowned, we’re the rightful owners of this place.

original: Here, bear my bottle.  Fellow Trinculo, we’ll fill him by and by again.
translation: Here, carry my wine bottle. My good friend Trinculo, we’ll fill that bottle again soon.

original: Farewell, master! Farewell, farewell.
translation: Goodbye, master! Goodbye, goodbye.

original: A howling monster, a drunken monster.
translation: A singing, drunken monster.

original: [sings]   No more dams I’ll make for fish,   Nor fetch in firing   At requiring,   Nor scrape trencher, nor wash dish.
translation: [Singing] I won’t build any more dams to catch you fish, Whenever you want, Or scrape clean the platters, or wash dishes.

original: 'Ban, 'Ban, Ca-Caliban   Has a new master. Get a new man.   Freedom, high-day! High-day, freedom! Freedom,  high-day, freedom!
translation: 'Ban, 'Ban, Ca-Caliban Has a new master. Get yourself a new servant. Freedom, hooray, hooray, freedom, freedom, hooray, freedom!

original: O brave monster! Lead the way.
translation: Oh, splendid monster! Lead on.

original: There be some sports are painful, and their labor   Delight in them sets off. Some kinds of baseness   Are nobly undergone.
translation: Some games are difficult, but the effort they require contributes to the pleasure they give. Some kinds of dishonorable manual labor are undertaken for noble reasons.

original: And most poor matters   Point to rich ends. This my mean task   Would be as heavy to me as odious, but   The mistress which I serve quickens what’s dead   And makes my labors pleasures.
translation: And many things that bring no money can lead to great wealth in the end. This hard and undignified work would be dull and disgusting to me, but the woman for whom I am doing this makes what is awful seem wonderful. She makes my hard work seem like a pleasure.

original: Oh, she is   Ten times more gentle than her father’s crabbed,   And he’s composed of harshness. I must remove   Some thousands of these logs and pile them up,   Upon a sore injunction.
translation: Oh, she’s ten times more kind than her father is nasty, and he’s completely nasty. He’s issued a severe command that I have to move thousands of these logs and put them in a stack.

original: My sweet mistress   Weeps when she sees me work, and says such baseness   Had never like executor.
translation: My sweet lady cries when she sees me work, and tells me that such lowly work has never been done by such a noble person.

original: I forget,   But these sweet thoughts do even refresh my labors,   Most busiest when I do it.
translation: These sweet thoughts refresh me and make me forget that I am working, especially when I am working the hardest.

original: Alas now, pray you,   Work not so hard. I would the lightning had   Burnt up those logs that you are enjoined to pile!   Pray, set it down and rest you.
translation: Oh, please, I beg you, don’t work so hard. I wish the lightning had burned up these logs that you’ve been commanded to stack in a pile! Please, put the log down and rest.

original: When this burns,   'Twill weep for having wearied you. My father   Is hard at study. Pray now, rest yourself.   He’s safe for these three hours.
translation: When this wood burns, it will cry because it made you tired. My father is hard at work studying. So please, rest. We’re safe from my father for the next three hours.

original: O most dear mistress, The sun will set before I shall discharge What I must strive to do.
translation: Oh, my dear lady, the sun will set before I've finished the work I've been told to do.

original: If you’ll sit down, I’ll bear your logs the while. Pray, give me that. I’ll carry it to the pile.
translation: If you'll sit down, I’ll carry your logs for a while. Please, give them to me. I’ll carry it to the pile.

original: No, precious creature.
translation: No, my precious darling,

original: I had rather crack my sinews, break my back,   Than you should such dishonor undergo   While I sit lazy by.
translation: I’d rather tear my muscles and break my back than let you do such dishonorable work while I sit lazily nearby.

original: It would become me   As well as it does you,
translation: The work would suit me as much as it suits you,

original: and I should do it   With much more ease, for my good will is to it   And yours it is against.
translation: and it would be easier for me because I want to do it, whereas you do not.

original: Poor worm, thou art infected! This visitation shows it.
translation: Poor little thing, you’re overwhelmed by love! These lovesick words prove it.

original: You look wearily.
translation: You look tired.

original: No, noble mistress. 'Tis fresh morning with me   When you are by at night. I do beseech you—
translation: No, noble lady. When you’re nearby, I’m as fresh and strong as I am in the morning—even at night. I beg you

original: Chiefly that I might set it in my prayers—   What is your name?
translation: —so that I can mention it in my prayers—what is your name?

original: Miranda. O my father, I have broke your hest to say so!
translation: Miranda. Oh, Father, I’ve broken your command to me by telling him that!

original: Admired Miranda!   Indeed the top of admiration, worth   What’s dearest to th' world!
translation: Admired  Miranda! You do indeed deserve the utmost admiration, as much as the most treasured thing in the world!

original: Full many a lady   I have eyed with best regard and many a time   Th' harmony of their tongues hath into bondage   Brought my too diligent ear.
translation: I’ve looked at many women with great enjoyment. And I've been entranced by the sweet sounds of their voices in my ear, which too eagerly heard their words.

original: For several virtues   Have I liked several women. Never any   With so full soul but some defect in her   Did quarrel with the noblest grace she owed   And put it to the foil.
translation: There have been several women whom I liked for the multiple good qualities they had. But every one of them had some bad trait that contrasted with and outweighed even their best qualities.

original: But you, O you,   So perfect and so peerless, are created   Of every creature’s best.
translation: But you, oh you, are perfect, beyond compare, and are made out of the best qualities possible in a woman.

original: I do not know   One of my sex, no woman’s face remember—   Save, from my glass, mine own. Nor have I seen   More that I may call men than you, good friend,   And my dear father.
translation: I don't know a single woman, or even seen a woman’s face—except my own in the mirror. I’ve also never met any other men than you, my friend, and my dear father.

original: How features are abroad   I am skill-less of, but, by my modesty,   The jewel in my dower, I would not wish   Any companion in the world but you,
translation: I have no knowledge of what people look like in other places. But I swear by my virginity—the most precious thing that I can give—that I’d never want to be with anyone in the world but you.

original: Nor can imagination form a shape   Besides yourself to like of. But I prattle   Something too wildly, and my father’s precepts   I therein do forget.
translation: I can’t even imagine that I might like any other shape besides your own. But listen to me babbling on and on, forgetting that my father told me not to.

original: I am in my condition   A prince, Miranda—I do think, a king;   I would, not so!—and would no more endure   This wooden slavery than to suffer   The flesh-fly blow my mouth. Hear my soul speak.
translation: I am a prince, Miranda—I think I'm probably now a king, though I wish that were not true—and normally I wouldn't tolerate being forced to carry logs any more than I’d let insects fly into my mouth. But listen to this, from the bottom of my soul.

original: The very instant that I saw you did   My heart fly to your service, there resides   To make me slave to it, and for your sake   Am I this patient log-man.
translation: The moment that I saw you, my heart rushed to serve you, and it remains there as your servant. So, for your sake, I patiently carry these logs.

original: Do you love me?
translation: Do you love me?

original: O heaven, O earth, bear witness to this sound   And crown what I profess with kind event   If I speak true!
translation: Oh, heaven; oh, earth—witness the words I'm going to speak. And if I speak the truth, bless them with the outcome I hope for.

original: If hollowly, invert   What best is boded me to mischief! I   Beyond all limit of what else i' th' world   Do love, prize, honor you.
translation: If I’m insincere, then take all the good fortune that's in store for me and turn it bad. More than anything else in the world, I love, cherish, and honor you.

original: I am a fool To weep at what I am glad of.
translation: I'm such a fool to cry at the thing that makes me happy.

original: Fair encounter Of two most rare affections! Heavens rain grace On that which breeds between 'em!
translation: What a beautiful encounter between two people so utterly in love! May heaven shower blessings on the love growing between them!

original: Wherefore weep you?
translation: Why are you crying?

original: At mine unworthiness, that dare not offer   What I desire to give, and much less take   What I shall die to want.
translation: I’m crying at my cowardice for not daring to give you what I want to give you, much less take what I’m dying to have.

original: But this is trifling,   And all the more it seeks to hide itself   The bigger bulk it shows. Hence, bashful cunning,   And prompt me, plain and holy innocence!
translation: But that's nothing. And the more I try to hide my feelings, the larger they get. So stop being so shy and indirect, Miranda, and let your innocent directness guide you!

original: I am your wife if you will marry me.   If not, I’ll die your maid. To be your fellow   You may deny me, but I’ll be your servant   Whether you will or no.
translation: I’ll be your wife if you will marry me. If you won't, I’ll die a virgin, having never loved another man. You can refuse to make me your wife, but I’ll be your servant whether you want me to or not.

original: My mistress, dearest, and I thus humble ever.
translation: You’ll be the one I adore, my dearest. And I’ll serve you as I do now, forever.

original: My husband, then?
translation: You'll be my husband, then?

original: Ay, with a heart as willing As bondage e'er of freedom. Here’s my hand.
translation: Yes, with a heart as eager to become a husband as any slave has ever wanted freedom. Here's my hand.

original: And mine, with my heart in ’t. And now farewell Till half an hour hence.
translation: And here's mine, with my heart in it. And now goodbye until half an hour from now.

original: A thousand thousand!
translation: A million goodbyes.

original: So glad of this as they I cannot be,   Who are surprised withal. But my rejoicing   At nothing can be more.
translation: I can’t be as happy as they are at what's happening, because they are surprised by it—whereas I planned it all along. But nothing could make me happier.

original: I’ll to my book,   For yet ere supper-time must I perform   Much business appertaining.
translation: Now I'll return to my book of magic, because there's a lot of work that pertains to the love growing between Miranda and Ferdinand that I must do before dinner.

original: Tell not me. When the butt is out, we will drink water. Not a drop before. Therefore bear up and board  'em.—Servant- monster, drink to me.
translation: Don’t tell me that. When the wine barrel is empty, we’ll drink water. But we won't drink even a drop of water before then. Therefore, raise the bottle and drink.  Servant-monster, drink a toast to me.

original: “Servant-monster?” The folly of this island. They say  there’s but five upon this isle. We are three of them.  If th' other two be brained like us, the state totters.
translation: “Servant-monster?” What foolishness is found on this island! They say there are just five people on the island. We’re three of them. If the other two are as crazy as us, our country is going to collapse.

original: Drink, servant-monster, when I bid thee. Thy eyes are  almost set in thy head.
translation: Drink when I tell you to, servant-monster. Your eyes look sunk into your head.

original: Where should they be set else? He were a brave monster  indeed, if they were set in his tail.
translation: Where else should his eyes be sunk? He’d be quite a remarkable monster if his eyes were sunk in his tail.

original: My man-monster hath drowned his tongue in sack. For my  part, the sea cannot drown me.
translation: My servingman-monster is so drowned in the wine he’s drunk that he can’t even talk. For my part, not even the sea can drown me.

original: I swam, ere I could  recover the shore, five and thirty leagues off and on.  By this light, thou shalt be my lieutenant, monster, or  my standard.
translation: Before I reached the shore from the shipwreck, I swam a hundred and five miles. Therefore, monster, you’ll be my lieutenant, or my flag-bearer.

original: Your lieutenant, if you list. He’s no standard.
translation: Make him your lieutenant, please. He can barely stand up straight, much less hold a flag.

original: We’ll not run, Monsieur Monster.
Nor go neither. But you’ll lie like dogs, and yet say  nothing neither.
translation: Or even walk. Instead you’ll lie there like sleeping dogs and say nothing.

original: Mooncalf, speak once in thy life, if thou beest a good  mooncalf.
translation: Monster, if you want to be a good monster, please say something.

original: How does thy honor? Let me lick thy shoe.      I’ll not serve him. He’s not  valiant.
translation: How are you, my lord? Let me lick your shoe.  I won’t serve him. He’s not brave the way you are.

original: [to CALIBAN]   Thou liest, most ignorant monster. I am in case to justle a constable. Why, thou deboshed fish,  thou, was there ever man a coward that hath drunk so  much sack as I today?
translation: [To CALIBAN]  You’re lying, you most ignorant monster. I’m so brave I would go brawl with a police officer right now. Why, you drunk fish, you: has any coward ever drunk as much wine as I have today?

original: Wilt thou tell a monstrous lie,  being but half a fish and half a monster?
translation: Are you telling such monstrous lies just because you’re half-fish, half-monster?

original: Lo, how he mocks me! Wilt thou let him, my lord?
translation: Look, he’s making fun of me! Will you let him do that, my lord?

original: “Lord,” quoth he? That a monster should be such a  natural!
translation: “Lord,” he says? That monster is such an idiot!

original: Lo, lo, again! Bite him to death, I prithee.
translation: Look, look, he’s mocking me again! Please, bite him to death.

original: Trinculo, keep a good tongue in your head. If you prove a mutineer, the next tree. The poor monster’s my  subject and he shall not suffer indignity.
translation: Trinculo, if you don’t have anything nice to say, don’t say anything at all. And if you don’t listen to me, I’ll hang you from the next tree. This poor monster is my loyal subject, and I refuse to let him be insulted.

original: I thank my noble lord. Wilt thou be pleased to hearken  once again to the suit I made to thee?
translation: Thank you, my noble lord. Now would you be willing to listen once again to the request I made to you before?

original: Marry, will I. Kneel and repeat it. I will stand, and  so shall Trinculo.
As I told thee before, I am subject to a  tyrant, a sorcerer that by his cunning hath cheated me  of the island.
translation: As I told you before, I’m enslaved to a tyrant, a magician who used his magic to steal the island from me.

original: Thou liest.
translation: You lie.

original: Thou liest, thou jesting monkey, thou! I  would my valiant master would destroy thee. I do not  lie.
translation: No you are lying, you joking monkey, you! I wish my brave master would kill you. I did not lie.

original: Trinculo, if you trouble him any more in ’s tale, by  this hand, I will supplant some of your teeth.
translation: Trinculo, if you interrupt his story again, I swear by my hand, I’ll knock out some of your teeth.

original: Why, I said nothing.
translation: But I didn’t say anything.

original: Mum, then, and no more. Proceed.
translation: Quiet, then, no more. Continue.

original: I say, by sorcery he got this isle.   From me he got it.
translation: I was saying: he used magic to take over this island. He took it from me.

original: If thy greatness will   Revenge it on him—for I know thou darest,   But this thing dare not—
translation: If your Highness will take revenge on him—because I know that you're brave enough to do it, though this thing  [He points to TRINCULO]  wouldn't dare—

original: That’s most certain.
translation: That’s obvious.

original: Thou shalt be lord of it and I’ll serve thee.
translation: You’ll be lord of the island, and I’ll serve you.

original: How now shall this be compassed? Canst thou bring me to th' party?
translation: How can all this be accomplished? Can you bring me to him?

original: Yea, yea, my lord. I’ll yield him thee asleep, Where thou mayst knock a nail into his head.
translation: Yes, yes, my lord. I’ll take you to him when he's asleep, then you can smash a nail into his head.

original: Thou liest. Thou canst not.
translation: You lie. You can’t do that.

original: What a pied ninny’s this! Thou scurvy patch!   I do beseech thy greatness, give him blows   And take his bottle from him.
translation: What a motley fool he is! You are a wretched fool! Please, your Highness, punch him a few times and take his wine bottle away from him.

original: When that’s gone,   He shall drink naught but brine, for I’ll not show him   Where the quick freshes are.
translation: When he doesn't have that, he’ll drink nothing but salt water—because I won't show him where the freshwater springs are.

original: Trinculo, run into no further danger. Interrupt the  monster one word further, and, by this hand, I’ll turn  my mercy out o' doors and make a stockfish of thee.
translation: Trinculo, stop trying to cause trouble. If you interrupt this monster one more time then, I swear by my hand, I'll stop being nice and beat you until you're as stiff as a piece of dried fish.

original: Why, what did I? I did nothing. I’ll go farther off.
translation: Why, what did I do? I didn’t do anything. I need to move away from you.

original: Didst thou not say he lied?
translation: Didn’t you just say that he lied?

original: Thou liest.
translation: You lie.

original: Do I so? Take thou that.  As you like this, give me the lie another time.
translation: Oh, do I? Take that, then. [He hits TRINCULO] There's more where that came from if you say that I'm a liar again.

original: I did not give the lie. Out o' your wits and hearing  too? A pox o' your bottle! This can sack and drinking  do. A murrain on your monster, and the devil take your  fingers!
translation: I didn’t say you were a liar. Are you out of your mind, and deaf, too? A curse on your wine bottle! This is what drinking wine does to you. May your monster get the plague, and you can go to hell!

original: Ha, ha, ha!
translation: Ha, ha, ha!

original: Now, forward with your tale.—Prithee, stand farther  off.
translation: Now, continue with your story. Trinculo, please, stand farther away.

original: Beat him enough. After a little time, I’ll beat him too.
translation: Beat him up some more. After a little while, I’ll beat him up too.

original: Stand farther.—Come, proceed.
translation: Stand even farther away, Trinculo. All right, continue.

original: Why, as I told thee, ’tis a custom with him,   I' th' afternoon to sleep. There thou mayst brain him,   Having first seized his books;
translation: Well, as I told you, it’s his habit to take a nap in the afternoon. That’s when you can smash in his skull, after you’ve first stolen his books.

original: or with a log   Batter his skull; or paunch him with a stake;   Or cut his weasand with thy knife.
translation: Or you could hit him on the head with a log. Or stab him in the belly with a spear. Or cut his throat with a knife.

original: Remember   First to possess his books, for without them   He’s but a sot, as I am, nor hath not   One spirit to command. They all do hate him   As rootedly as I. Burn but his books.
translation: But remember to steal his books first, because without them, he’s just a fool like me, and won’t be able to command even one spirit. The other spirits all hate him as completely as I do. Just be sure to burn his magic books.

original: He has brave utensils—for so he calls them—   Which when he has a house, he’ll deck withal.   And that most deeply to consider is   The beauty of his daughter.
translation: He has some magnificent furniture and furnishings—at least that’s how he describes them—that he plans to use to furnish his house once he gets one. The thing you should focus on though is the beauty of his daughter.

original: He himself   Calls her a nonpareil. I never saw a woman,   But only Sycorax my dam and she.
translation: Prospero himself says she has no equal. I never saw a woman other than my mother, Sycorax.

original: But she as far surpasseth Sycorax   As great’st does least.
translation: Miranda is so much more beautiful than Sycorax that it’s like comparing the most beautiful thing to the least.

original: Is it so brave a lass?
translation: Is she really such a splendid girl?

original: Ay, lord. She will become thy bed, I warrant. And bring thee forth brave brood.
translation: Yes, my lord. She’ll be a perfect fit for your bed, and she’ll bear you some excellent children.

original: Monster, I will kill this man. His daughter and I will  be king and queen—save our graces!—and Trinculo and  thyself shall be viceroys. Dost thou like the plot,  Trinculo?
translation: Monster, I will kill this man. His daughter and I will be king and queen—God protect our royal selves!—and you and Trinculo will be our governors. Do you like that plan, Trinculo?

original: Excellent.
translation: Excellent.

original: Give me thy hand. I am sorry I beat thee. But while  thou livest, keep a good tongue in thy head.
translation: Give me your hand. I’m sorry I beat you up. But for as long as you live, be more polite when you speak.

original: Within this half hour will he be asleep. Wilt thou  destroy him then?
translation: In the next half an hour he’ll be asleep. Will you kill him then?

original: Ay, on mine honor.
translation: Yes, I swear on my honor.

original: This will I tell my master.
translation: I’ll tell my master about this.

original: Thou makest me merry. I am full of pleasure.   Let us be jocund.
translation: You make me glad. I’m full of happiness. Let’s have some fun.

original: Will you troll the catch   You taught me but whilere?
translation: Will you sing the song you taught me a short while ago?

original: At thy request, monster, I will do reason, any reason.   Come on, Trinculo, let us sing.
translation: Monster, whatever you ask for I'll do, so long as it's reasonable. Come on, Trinculo, let’s sing.

original: [sings]   Flout 'em and scout 'em,   And scout 'em and flout 'em.   Thought is free.
translation: [Singing] Mock 'em and shock 'em And shock 'em and mock 'em. Thought is free.

original: That’s not the tune.
translation: That’s not the song.

original: What is this same?
translation: What is this song?

original: This is the tune of our catch, played by the picture of Nobody.
translation: That’s the song you were singing, played by nobody.

original: If thou beest a man, show thyself in thy likeness. If  thou beest a devil, take ’t as thou list.
translation: If you’re a man who's playing that music, show yourself. If you’re a devil, then you can go to hell.

original: O, forgive me my sins!
translation: Oh, forgive me for all my sins!

original: He that dies pays all debts.—I defy thee!—Mercy upon  us!
translation: The man who dies pays the ultimate debt. I defy you, devil! God bless us.

original: Art thou afeard?
translation: Are you scared?

original: No, monster, not I.
translation: No, monster, not me.

original: Be not afeard. The isle is full of noises,   Sounds, and sweet airs that give delight and hurt not.
translation: Don’t be frightened. The island is full of noises, sounds, and sweet music that will delight you and not hurt you.

original: Sometimes a thousand twangling instruments   Will hum about mine ears, and sometime voices   That, if I then had waked after long sleep,   Will make me sleep again.
translation: Sometimes I hear a thousand instruments playing in my ears, and sometimes I hear voices that send me back to sleep even if I had just woken up.

original: And then, in dreaming,   The clouds methought would open and show riches   Ready to drop upon me, that when I waked   I cried to dream again.
translation: And once asleep again, I dream of clouds that open up to show that they carry riches, which will soon drop down on me like rain. So when I woke up, I begged to dream again.

original: This will prove a brave kingdom to me, where I shall  have my music for nothing.
translation: This will be a splendid kingdom for me to rule. I'll get music played to me for free.

original: When Prospero is destroyed.
translation: Once you kill Prospero.

original: That shall be by and by. I remember the story.
translation: That will be done soon. I remember our plan.
