translation: Oh, my poor brother! But maybe he has been saved by chance too.

original: True, madam. And, to comfort you with chance,   Assure yourself, after our ship did split,   When you and those poor number saved with you   Hung on our driving boat,
translation: True, madam. And let me comfort you: when our ship was wrecked, and you and the few other survivors hung onto our drifting lifeboat,

original: I saw your brother,   Most provident in peril, bind himself,   Courage and hope both teaching him the practice,   To a strong mast that lived upon the sea,
translation: I saw your brother tie himself to the mast that was floating on the waves—acting with courage and hope in the middle of great danger.

original: Where, like Arion on the dolphin’s back,   I saw him hold acquaintance with the waves   So long as I could see.
translation: For as long as I could see him, he safely rode upon the waves like  Arion  on the dolphin's back.

original: For saying so, there’s gold.
translation: Here's some gold to thank you for telling me this.

original: Mine own escape unfoldeth to my hope,   Whereto thy speech serves for authority,   The like of him.
translation: My own escape gives me hope for my brother, and what you've told me now gives me even more reason to hope.

original: Know’st thou this country?
translation: Do you know this country?

original: Ay, madam, well, for I was bred and born Not three hours' travel from this very place.
translation: Yes, madam, I was born and raised less than three hours' travel from here.

original: Who governs here?
translation: Who rules here?

original: A noble duke, in nature As in name.
translation: A duke who is as noble in his character as he is in his rank.

original: What is his name?
translation: What is his name?

original: Orsino.
translation: Orsino.

original: Orsino. I have heard my father name him.  He was a bachelor then.
translation: Orsino—I have heard my father mention him. He was a bachelor back then.

original: And so is now, or was so very late.
translation: And he still is, or was very recently at least.

original: For but a month ago I went from hence,   And then ’twas fresh in murmur
translation: I only left here a month ago, and at that time there was a popular rumor

original: —as, you know,   What great ones do the less will prattle of—
translation: —as, you know, people gossip about the nobility—

original: That he did seek the love of fair Olivia.
translation: that he was courting the fair Olivia.

original: What’s she?
translation: Who's she?

original: A virtuous maid, the daughter of a count   That died some twelvemonth since,
translation: A virtuous young woman, the daughter of a count who died a year ago.

original: then leaving her   In the protection of his son, her brother,   Who shortly also died,
translation: He left her in the care of his son, Olivia's brother, but the brother died soon after.

original: for whose dear love,   They say, she hath abjured the company   And sight of men.
translation: They say that out of love for her brother, Olivia has stopped interacting with men altogether.

original: Oh, that I served that lady
translation: Oh, I wish that I could serve that lady—

original: And might not be delivered to the world,   Till I had made mine own occasion mellow,   What my estate is.
translation: then I wouldn't have to reveal myself to the world until I was ready to identify my place in society.

original: That were hard to compass, Because she will admit no kind of suit, No, not the duke’s.
translation: That would be hard to bring about, because she won't allow anyone in to see her, not even the duke's men.

original: There is a fair behavior in thee, captain,   And though that nature with a beauteous wall   Doth oft close in pollution, yet of thee   I will believe thou hast a mind that suits   With this thy fair and outward character.
translation: You seem to be a good man in both behavior and appearance, captain, and even though nature often makes beautiful people corrupt on the inside, I believe that you have a noble mind to fit your good looks and manners.

original: I prithee—and I’ll pay thee bounteously—   Conceal me what I am, and be my aid   For such disguise as haply shall become   The form of my intent
translation: Please—and I'll pay you well for this—help me conceal my identity, and find me the disguise that will suit my intentions.

original: . I’ll serve this duke.   Thou shall present me as an eunuch to him.
translation: I want to serve this duke. You will present me to him as a  eunuch .

original: It may be worth thy pains, for I can sing   And speak to him in many sorts of music   That will allow me very worth his service.
What else may hap to time I will commit.
translation: What might happen after that, only time will tell.

original: Only shape thou thy silence to my wit.
translation: You must only match my wit with your silence and discretion.

original: Be you his eunuch, and your mute I’ll be. When my tongue blabs, then let mine eyes not see.
translation: You will be his eunuch, and I will be your mute attendant. If I tell your secret, may I lose my sight.

original: I thank thee. Lead me on.
translation: I thank you. Lead me on.

original: What a plague means my niece, to take the death of her  brother thus? I am sure care’s an enemy to life.
translation: What is ailing my niece, that she reacts so strongly to her brother's death? I'm now sure that caring too much is bad for one's health.

original: By my troth, Sir Toby, you must come in earlier o'  nights. Your cousin, my lady, takes great exceptions to  your ill hours.
translation: By God, Sir Toby, you must come home earlier at night. Your niece, my lady, strongly disapproves of the late hours you keep.

original: Why, let her except, before excepted.
translation: Well, let her disapprove of me—I disapprove of her.

original: Ay, but you must confine yourself within the modest  limits of order.
translation: Yes, but you must at least confine yourself within the limits of order and decency.

original: Confine? I’ll confine myself no finer than I am.
translation: Confine myself? I'll only confine myself to these clothes I'm wearing.

original: These  clothes are good enough to drink in, and so be these  boots too.
translation: They're good enough to drink in, and these boots are too.

original: An they be not, let them hang themselves in  their own straps.
translation: And if they aren't, then let them hang themselves by their own straps.

original: That quaffing and drinking will undo you:
translation: All this drinking will be your ruin:

original: I heard my  lady talk of it yesterday, and of a foolish knight that  you brought in one night here to be her wooer.
translation: I heard my lady Olivia talking about it yesterday. She also spoke of some foolish knight you brought here one night to woo her.

original: Who, Sir Andrew Aguecheek?
translation: Who, Sir Andrew Aguecheek?

original: Ay, he.
translation: Yes, him.

original: He’s as tall a man as any’s in Illyria.
translation: He's as tall and brave as any man in Illyria.

original: What’s that to the purpose?
translation: What does that have to do with anything?

original: Why, he has three thousand ducats a year.
Ay, but he’ll have but a year in all these ducats. He’s a very fool and a prodigal.
translation: Yes, but he'll only make all those ducats last for one year. He's foolish, wasteful, and reckless.

original: Fie, that you’ll say so! He plays o' the  viol-de-gamboys,
and speaks three or four languages word for word without book,
translation: and speaks three or four languages  word for word from memory .

original: and hath all the good gifts of  nature.
translation: He has all of nature's good gifts.

original: He hath indeed, almost natural,
translation: He does indeed seem like a  natural-born fool

original: for besides that he’s a fool, he’s a great quarreler,
translation: —and besides being a fool, he's argumentative.

original: and but that he hath the  gift of a coward to allay the gust he hath in  quarreling,
translation: If he didn't have the coward's gift of stepping away from a fight,

original: ’tis thought among the prudent he would  quickly have the gift of a grave.
translation: they say he would've been long dead by now.

original: By this hand, they are scoundrels and substractors that say so of him. Who are they?
translation: By God, anyone who says that about him is a villain and a naysayer. Who said that?

original: They that add, moreover, he’s drunk nightly in your  company.
translation: They also say that he gets drunk with you every night.

original: With drinking healths to my niece. I’ll drink to her as long as there is a passage in my throat and drink in  Illyria.
translation: We are only toasting my niece when we drink. I'll drink to her as long as there's a hole in my throat and alcohol in Illyria.

original: He’s a coward and a coistrel that will not  drink to my niece till his brains turn o' th' toe like a parish top.
translation: Only cowards and scum wouldn't drink to my niece until their brains spin round like a top.

original: What, wench!
translation: What do you have to say to that!

original: Castiliano vulgo   , for here  comes Sir Andrew Agueface.
translation: But hush, we must be polite. Here comes Sir Andrew Agueface himself.

original: Sir Toby Belch! How now, Sir Toby Belch!
translation: Sir Toby Belch! How are you, Sir Toby Belch?

original: Sweet Sir Andrew!
translation: Sweet Sir Andrew.

original: Bless you, fair shrew.
translation: And hello to you, pretty wench.

original: And you too, sir.
translation: Hello to you, sir.

original: Accost, Sir Andrew, accost.
translation: Accost her, Sir Andrew, accost her.

original: What’s that?
translation: What's that?

original: My niece’s chambermaid.
translation: This is my niece's chambermaid.

original: Good Mistress Accost, I desire better acquaintance.
translation: Good Miss Accost-her, I look forward to knowing you better.

original: My name is Mary, sir.
translation: My name is Mary, sir.

original: Good Mistress Mary Accost—
translation: Good Miss Mary Accost-her—

original: You mistake, knight. “Accost” is front her, board her,  woo her, assail her.
translation: You're mistaken, knight. "Accost her" isn't her name—I meant that you should face her, greet her, woo her, and conquer her.

original: By my troth, I would not undertake her in this company. Is that the meaning of “accost”?
translation: I say, I wouldn't do that in this company. Is that really what you meant by "accost her?"

original: Fare you well, gentlemen.
translation: Goodbye, gentlemen.

original: An thou let part so, Sir Andrew, would thou mightst  never draw sword again.
An you part so, mistress, I would I might never draw  sword again. Fair lady, do you think you have fools in  hand?
translation: If you leave like this, miss, I swear I won't ever draw my sword again. Why are you leaving, fair lady—do you think you have fools on your hands here?

original: Sir, I have not you by the hand.
translation: Sir, I'm not holding your hand.

original: Marry, but you shall have, and here’s my hand.
translation: Indeed, but you will be, and here's my hand.

original: Now, sir, thought is free.
translation: Now, sir, everyone has a right to their opinions.

original: I pray  you, bring your hand to the buttery-bar and let it  drink.
translation: Please, take your hand to the  dairy  and let it drink.

original: Wherefore, sweetheart? What’s your metaphor?
translation: What do you mean, sweetheart? Is this a metaphor?

original: It’s dry, sir.
Why, I think so. I am not such an ass, but I can keep  my hand dry. But what’s your jest?
translation: Well, I should hope so. I'm not such a fool that I can't keep my hand dry. But what's the joke?

original: A dry jest, sir.
translation: Just some dry humor, sir.

original: Are you full of them?
translation: Are you full of such jokes?

original: Ay, sir, I have them at my fingers' ends. Marry, now I  let go your hand, I am barren.
translation: Yes, sir, I have a handful of them. Although now that I've let go of your hand, I've lost the biggest joke I had.

original: O knight, thou lackest a cup of canary. When did I see  thee so put down?
translation: Oh knight, you need some wine. Have you ever been put down like that before?

original: Never in your life, I think, unless you see canary put me down.
translation: Never, I think, except when I've been put down by too much wine.

original: Methinks sometimes I have no more wit than a  Christian or an ordinary man has.
translation: Sometimes I think I'm no smarter than a humble, ordinary man.

original: But I am a great eater of beef, and I believe that does harm to my wit.
translation: But I eat a lot of beef, and maybe that hurts my intelligence.

original: No question.
translation: There's no question about that.

original: An I thought that, I’d forswear it. I’ll ride home  tomorrow, Sir Toby.
translation: If I really thought that, I'd give up beef altogether. I think I'll ride home tomorrow, Sir Toby.

original: Pourquoi,  my dear knight?
translation: Pourquoi, my dear knight?

original: What is “pourquoi”? Do, or not do?
translation: What does " pourquoi " mean?  Does it mean to do or not do?

original: I would I had  bestowed that time in the tongues that I have in  fencing, dancing, and bear-baiting. O, had I but  followed the arts!
translation: I wish I had spent more time learning languages instead of fencing, dancing, and  bear-baiting . Oh, if I'd only studied more!

original: Then hadst thou had an excellent head of hair.
translation: Then you would have an excellent head of hair.

original: Why, would that have mended my hair?
translation: Why, would that have improved my hair?

original: Past question, for thou seest it will not curl by  nature.
translation: Certainly, for you can see that it won't curl naturally.

original: But it becomes me well enough, does ’t not?
translation: But my hair still suits me well enough, doesn't it?

original: Excellent. It hangs like flax on a distaff.
translation: It looks excellent. It hangs like flax waiting to be spun.

original: And I hope to see a housewife take thee between her legs and spin  it off.
translation: And I hope to see some  hussy take it between her legs  and spin it off with a venereal disease.

original: Faith, I’ll home tomorrow, Sir Toby. Your niece will  not be seen.
translation: Truly, I'm going home tomorrow, Sir Toby. Your niece refuses to see anyone.

original: Or if she be, it’s four to one she’ll none  of me.
translation: Even if she did see me, chances are she'd reject me.

original: The count himself here hard by woos her.
translation: The duke himself is courting her as hard as he can.

original: She’ll none o' the count.
translation: She'll reject the duke.

original: She’ll not match above her  degree, neither in estate, years, nor wit. I have heard  her swear ’t
translation: She won't marry anyone who's above her social rank, her wealth, her age, or her intelligence—I've heard her swear this.

original: . Tut, there’s life in ’t, man.
translation: So cheer up, you're still in the running, man.

original: I’ll stay a month longer.
translation: I'll stay a month longer then.

original: I am a fellow o' th'  strangest mind i' th' world. I delight in masques and  revels sometimes altogether.
Art thou good at these kickshawses, knight?
translation: Are you good at such trifles, knight?

original: As any man in Illyria, whatsoever he be, under the  degree of my betters.
translation: As good as any man in Illyria, as long as he isn't better than I am.

original: And yet I will not compare with an old man.
translation: And yet I'm not as good as an experienced dancer.

original: What is thy excellence in a galliard, knight?
translation: How good are you at the fast dances, knight?

original: Faith, I can cut a caper.
And I can cut the mutton to ’t.
And I think I have the back-trick simply as strong as  any man in Illyria.
translation: And I think I can do that tricky backward step as well as any man in Illyria.

original: Wherefore are these things hid? Wherefore have these  gifts a curtain before 'em? Are they like to take dust,  like Mistress Mall’s picture?
translation: Why do you keep these things hidden? Why do you keep your gifts behind a curtain? Are you afraid they'll get dusty, like some woman's portrait?

original: Why dost thou not go to  church in a galliard and come home in a coranto?
translation: Why don't you show off your skill by going to church dancing a galliard and coming home dancing a coranto?

original: My very walk should be a jig. I would not so much as make water but in a sink-a-pace.
translation: If I were you, even my walk would be a dance. I wouldn't even pee unless I was dancing at the same time.

original: What dost thou mean? Is it a  world to hide virtues in?
translation: What do you mean by this? Is this a world where we should hide our virtues?

original: I did think, by the excellent  constitution of thy leg, it was formed under the star of a galliard.
translation: I could always tell from your excellent legs that you were born under a dancing star.

original: Ay, ’tis strong, and it does indifferent well in a  dun-colored stock. Shall we set about some revels?
translation: Yes, my legs are strong, and they don't look bad in brown stockings. Should we have a little dance?

original: What shall we do else? Were we not born under Taurus?
translation: What else are we going to do? Weren't we born under the sign of Taurus?

original: Taurus! That’s sides and heart.
translation: Taurus! But that governs the torso and the heart.

original: No, sir, it is legs and thighs. Let me see the caper. [SIR ANDREW dances]  Ha, higher! Ha, ha, excellent!
translation: No, sir, it governs the legs and the thighs. Let me see you dance. Ha, higher! Ha ha, excellent!

original: If the duke continue these favors towards you, Cesario, you are like to be much advanced.
translation: If the duke keeps favoring you like this, Cesario, you're likely to get promoted very high.

original: He hath known you but three days, and already you are no stranger.
translation: He's only known you for three days, and already he's treating you like a friend.

original: You either fear his humor or my negligence, that you  call in question the continuance of his love.
translation: You must be afraid of his moodiness or my faults, if you think there's any chance that he'll stop liking me.

original: Is he  inconstant, sir, in his favors?
translation: Is he usually fickle in his moods and favors?

original: No, believe me.
translation: No, believe me.

original: I thank you. Here comes the count.
translation: I thank you for telling me. Here comes the duke.

original: Who saw Cesario, ho?
translation: Hey, has anyone seen Cesario?

original: On your attendance, my lord, here.
translation: I'm here, my lord, at your service.

original: Stand you a while aloof.
Cesario,   Thou know’st no less but all. I have unclasped   To thee the book even of my secret soul.
translation: Cesario, you know everything about me. I have opened the book of my most secret soul to you.

original: Therefore, good youth, address thy gait unto her;   Be not denied access, stand at her doors,
translation: Therefore, good youth, direct your steps to Olivia's house. Don't let them deny you access—stand outside her door

original: And tell them there thy fixed foot shall grow   Till thou have audience.
translation: and tell them that you'll plant roots there until they let you see her.

original: Sure, my noble lord,   If she be so abandoned to her sorrow   As it is spoke
translation: But my noble lord, if she is really as brokenhearted as they say,

original: , she never will admit me.
translation: she is sure to deny me an audience.

original: Be clamorous, and leap all civil bounds,
translation: Be loud and obnoxious, and go beyond the limits of decency and civility if you have to—

original: Rather than make unprofited return.
translation: just don't come back without having spoken to her.

original: Say I do speak with her, my lord, what then?
translation: And if I do get to speak to her, my lord, what do I do then?

original: O, then unfold the passion of my love,   Surprise her with discourse of my dear faith:
translation: Oh, then describe the passion of my love for her. Ambush her with descriptions of my faithfulness.

original: It shall become thee well to act my woes;
translation: It will be best if you act out my feelings—

original: She will attend it better in thy youth   Than in a nuncio’s of more grave aspect.
translation: she'll pay closer attention to you, as a young man, than to an older, more serious messenger.

original: I think not so, my lord.
translation: I don't think so, my lord.

original: Dear lad, believe it.   For they shall yet belie thy happy years   That say thou art a man.
translation: Dear boy, believe me. Anyone who says that you're a man is denying you the happy years of your youth.

original: Diana’s lip   Is not more smooth and rubious. Thy small pipe   Is as the maiden’s organ, shrill and sound,   And all is semblative a woman’s part.
translation: Your lips are as smooth and ruby-red as the goddess  Diana 's. Your small voice is like a girl's, high and clear, and the rest of you is feminine as well.

original: I know thy constellation is right apt   For this affair.
translation: I know you have been predestined to do this job. @

original: Some four or five attend him.   All, if you will, for I myself am best   When least in company.
Prosper well in  this,   And thou shalt live as freely as thy lord,   To call his fortunes thine.
translation: If you succeed in this you will live as well as I do, and share in all my fortune.

original: I’ll do my best   To woo your lady—
translation: I'll do my best to woo this lady for you.

original: Yet, a barful strife—   Whoe'er I woo, myself would be his wife.
translation: And yet, what a conflict—I must go courting on behalf of the man I want to marry myself!

original: Nay, either tell me where thou hast been, or I will not open my lips so wide as a bristle may enter in way of  thy excuse.
translation: No, either tell me where you've been, or I won't say a word in your defense.

original: My lady will hang thee for thy absence.
translation: My lady Olivia will have you hanged for being absent.

original: Let her hang me. He that is well hanged in this world  needs to fear no colors.
Make that good.
translation: Explain—and clean up your language.

original: He shall see none to fear.
translation: He'll be dead, and so he won't see anything to be afraid of.

original: A good lenten answer. I can tell thee where that saying was born, of “I fear no colors.”
Where, good Mistress Mary?
translation: Where, good Mistress Mary?

original: In the wars. And that may you be bold to say in your  foolery.
translation: From soldiers at war. And it's bold of you to talk like a soldier, when you're only a fool.

original: Well, God give them wisdom that have it. And those that are fools, let them use their talents.
translation: Well, let God give wisdom to those who have it. Everyone has their talents, and for those of us who are fools, let us use our gifts.

original: Yet you will be hanged for being so long absent.
translation: But you'll still be hanged for being gone so long.

original: Or to be turned away, is not that as good as a hanging to  you?
translation: Or at least fired and kicked out, and wouldn't that be just as bad for you?

original: Many a good hanging prevents a bad marriage,
translation: Sometimes getting hanged saves a man from getting into a bad marriage,

original: and, for  turning away, let summer bear it out.
translation: and as for getting kicked out, it's summer, so being homeless won't be so bad.

original: You are resolute, then?
translation: You are firm in your resolve, then?

original: Not so, neither, but I am resolved on two points.
translation: No, but I am resolved on two points.

original: That if one break, the other will hold.
translation: Yes—the two points where your suspenders are buttoned on. If one breaks, the other will hold.

original: Or, if both  break, your gaskins fall.
translation: But if both break, your pants will fall.

original: Apt, in good faith, very apt. Well, go thy way.
translation: Very clever, really, very clever. Well, go along now.

original: If Sir  Toby would leave drinking, thou wert as witty a piece of Eve’s flesh as any in Illyria.
translation: If only Sir Toby would stop drinking, you'd be a woman who was as funny as any person in Illyria.

original: Peace, you rogue, no more o' that. Here comes my lady. Make your excuse wisely, you were best.
translation: Quiet, you villain, no more of that. Here comes my lady. It would be best for you if you came up with a good excuse for being gone so long.

original: Wit, an ’t be thy will, put me into good  fooling!
translation: Come on, wit, give me something good to say now!

original: Those wits, that think they have thee, do very  oft prove fools.
translation: Those people who think they're witty often prove to be fools.

original: And I, that am sure I lack thee, may  pass for a wise man. For what says Quinapalus?
translation: And I'm sure that I'm not witty, so I might pass for a wise man. For what did the philosopher  Quinapalus  say?

original: “Better a witty fool, than a foolish wit.”
translation: "Better a witty fool, than a foolish wit."

original: God bless thee, lady!
translation: God's greetings to you, my lady!

original: Take the fool away.
translation: Take the fool away.

original: Do you not hear, fellows? Take away the lady.
translation: Didn't you hear her, fellows? Take the lady away.

original: Go to, you’re a dry fool. I’ll no more of you.  Besides, you grow dishonest.
translation: That's enough—you're a dull, dry fool. I'm tired of you. Besides, you're getting unreliable.

original: Two faults, madonna, that drink and good counsel will  amend. For give the dry fool drink, then is the fool not dry.
translation: My holy lady, these are two flaws that some alcohol and good advice will fix. If you give the dry fool a drink, then the fool won't be dry anymore.

original: Bid the dishonest man mend himself. If he mend, he is no longer dishonest.
translation: And if you give the unreliable man some good advice, then he can mend his ways and won't be unreliable anymore.

original: If he cannot, let the botcher  mend him. Anything that’s mended is but patched.
translation: And if he can't mend his ways, then let the tailor mend him. Anything that's mended is only patched up.

original: Virtue  that transgresses is but patched with sin, and sin that  amends is but patched with virtue.
translation: A virtuous man who does something wrong is only patched with sin, and a sinner who mends his ways is only patched with virtue.

original: If that this simple  syllogism will serve, so. If it will not, what remedy?
translation: If this logical argument will convince you, then good. But if not, what can be done?

original: As there is no true cuckold but calamity, so beauty’s a  flower.
translation: The only truly betrayed husband is one deserted by luck, and beauty is a lucky flower—so you won't remain alone for long, my lady.

original: The lady bade take away the fool. Therefore, I  say again, take her away.
translation: But you gave orders to take away the fool. So I tell you all again, take the lady away.

original: Sir, I bade them take away you.
translation: Sir, I told them to take you away.

original: Misprision in the highest degree!
translation: An error of the worst kind!

original: Lady, Cucullus non  facit monachum—
translation: Lady, don't judge a book by its cover—

original: that’s as much to say as I wear not  motley in my brain.
translation: that's to say that I wear jester's clothes on the outside,

original: Good madonna, give me leave to prove you a fool.
translation: but my brain is still sharp. My holy lady, let me prove that you're a fool.

original: Can you do it?
translation: Can you do it?

original: Dexterously, good madonna.
translation: Easily, my good lady.

original: Make your proof.
translation: Then prove it.

original: I must catechise you for it, madonna. Good my mouse of  virtue, answer me.
Well, sir, for want of other idleness, I’ll bide your  proof.
translation: Well, sir, I have nothing better to do, so I'll go along with this.

original: Good madonna, why mournest thou?
translation: Dear lady, why are you in mourning?

original: Good fool, for my brother’s death.
translation: Dear fool, because of my brother's death.

original: I think his soul is in hell, madonna.
translation: I think his soul is in hell, lady.

original: I know his soul is in heaven, fool.
translation: I know his soul is in heaven, fool.

original: The more fool, madonna, to mourn for your brother’s  soul being in heaven. Take away the fool, gentlemen.
What think you of this fool, Malvolio? Doth he not  mend?
translation: What do you think of this fool, Malvolio? Hasn't he gotten better?

original: Yes, and shall do till the pangs of death shake him.
translation: Yes, and he will until the day he dies.

original: Infirmity, that decays the wise, doth ever make the  better fool.
translation: Old age and senility hurt wise people, but improve fools.

original: God send you, sir, a speedy infirmity, for the better  increasing your folly!
translation: Then may God send you old age and senility, that you might become a better fool!

original: Sir Toby will be sworn that I am  no fox, but he will not pass his word for two pence that you are no fool.
translation: Sir Toby would bet a fortune that I'm not a clever man, but he wouldn't bet two cents that you're not a fool.

original: How say you to that, Malvolio?
translation: What do you say to that, Malvolio?

original: I marvel your ladyship takes delight in such a barren  rascal.
translation: I'm surprised that your ladyship enjoys the company of such an empty-headed villain.

original: I saw him put down the other day with an  ordinary fool that has no more brain than a stone.
translation: The other day I saw him lose a battle of wits to an ordinary idiot who had no more brains than a stone.

original: Look  you now, he’s out of his guard already. Unless you laugh and minister occasion to him, he is gagged.
translation: Look at him now, he's without a witty retort already. Unless you laugh and give him an opportunity, he can't think of a thing to say.

original: I protest I take these wise men that crow so at these set kind of  fools no better than the fools' zanies.
translation: I declare that the so-called wise men who laugh so hard at these jesters' well-rehearsed routines are no better than jesters' assistants themselves.

original: Oh, you are sick of self-love, Malvolio, and taste with a distempered appetite.
To be generous, guiltless, and  of free disposition is to take those things for  bird-bolts that you deem cannon-bullets.
translation: If you were generous, innocent, and friendly, then you wouldn't make such mountains out of mole-hills.

original: There is no  slander in an allowed fool, though he do nothing but  rail.
translation: There's no real harm in a professional fool, even if he does nothing but mock people.

original: Nor no railing in a known discreet man, though he  do nothing but reprove.
translation: In the same way there's no real mockery in a wise man, even if he does nothing but criticize people.

original: Now Mercury endue thee with leasing, for thou speakest  well of fools!
translation: May Mercury—that god of deception—make you a skilled liar, to reward you for speaking so highly of fools!

original: Madam, there is at the gate a young gentleman much  desires to speak with you.
translation: Madam, there's a young gentleman at the gate who greatly desires to speak with you.

original: From the Count Orsino, is it?
translation: Is he sent from Duke Orsino?

original: I know not, madam. 'Tis a fair young man, and well  attended.
translation: I don't know, madam. He's a good-looking young man, and has some attendants with him.

original: Who of my people hold him in delay?
translation: Which of my people is delaying him right now?

original: Sir Toby, madam, your kinsman.
translation: Sir Toby, madam, your uncle.

original: Fetch him off, I pray you. He speaks nothing but  madman. Fie on him!
translation: Send Sir Toby away, please. He talks like a madman. Shame on him!

original: Go you, Malvolio. If it be a suit from the count, I am  sick, or not at home.
translation: You go, Malvolio. If this visitor is a messenger from the duke, then tell him that I'm sick, or not at home.

original: What you will, to dismiss it.
translation: Do whatever you have to to make him go away.

original: Now you see, sir, how your fooling grows old, and  people dislike it.
translation: Now you see, sir, how your jokes grow stale, and people dislike them.

original: Thou hast spoke for us, madonna, as if thy eldest son  should be a fool,
translation: Holy lady, you've spoken so highly of us fools—it's almost as if your eldest son was going to be a fool.

original: whose skull Jove cram with brains,  for—here he comes—one of thy kin has a most weak   pia  mater.
translation: And may God cram his skull with brains, for here comes one of your relatives whose head is quite empty.

original: By mine honor, half-drunk. What is he at the gate,  cousin?
translation: I swear, he's half-drunk. Who is that at the gate, uncle?

original: A gentleman.
translation: A gentleman.

original: A gentleman? What gentleman?
translation: A gentleman? What gentleman?

original: 'Tis a gentleman here—
translation: There's a gentleman here—

original: a plague o' these pickle  herring!   How now, sot!
translation: Damn those pickled herring! They upset my stomach. How's it going, you drunken fool?

original: Good Sir Toby!
translation: Good Sir Toby!

original: Cousin, cousin, how have you come so early by this  lethargy?
translation: Uncle, uncle, it's so early in the day—how are you already so sick?

original: Lechery! I defy lechery. There’s one at the gate.
Ay, marry, what is he?
translation: Yes, I heard, but who is he?

original: Let him be the devil, an he will, I care not. Give me  faith, say I. Well, it’s all one.
translation: Let him be the devil if he wants to be, I don't care. God will give me the faith to resist him. It doesn't matter to me.

original: What’s a drunken man like, fool?
translation: Tell me what a drunk man is like, fool.

original: Like a drowned man, a fool and a madman. One draught  above heat makes him a fool, the second mads him, and a  third drowns him.
translation: He's like a drowned man, a fool, and a madman. The first drink makes him a fool, the second makes him a madman, and the third drowns him.

original: Go thou and seek the crowner, and let him sit o' my  coz.
For he’s in the third degree of drink, he’s  drowned. Go look after him.
translation: for he's in the third degree of drunkenness, and has drowned. Go look after him.

original: He is but mad yet, madonna, and the fool shall look to  the madman.
translation: He's still only in the second degree, my lady, so the fool will take care of the madman.

original: Madam, yond young fellow swears he will speak with you. I told him you were sick.
translation: Madam, that young fellow out there swears that he must speak with you no matter what. I told him you were sick.

original: He takes on him to understand so much, and therefore comes to speak with you.
translation: He claims to know that already, and says that that's why he came to speak with you.

original: I told  him you were asleep. He seems to have a foreknowledge of that too, and therefore comes to speak with you.
translation: I told him you were asleep. He claims to know that already too, and said that that's why he came to speak with you.

original: What  is to be said to him, lady? He’s fortified against any  denial.
translation: What should I say to him, lady? He's too strong for all my excuses.

original: Tell him he shall not speak with me.
translation: Just tell him that he won't speak with me.

original: He's been told so, and he says he’ll stand at your  door like a sheriff’s post, and be the supporter to a  bench, but he’ll speak with you.
translation: I told him that already, but he says he'll stand at your door like a signpost or the leg of a bench until he is allowed to speak with you.

original: What kind o' man is he?
translation: What kind of man is he?

original: Why, of mankind.
translation: Why, part of mankind.

original: What manner of man?
translation: But what is his manner?

original: Of very ill manner. He’ll speak with you, will you or  no.
translation: He has very bad manners. He says he'll speak to you whether you like it or not.

original: Of what personage and years is he?
translation: But what does he look like, and how old is he?

original: Not yet old enough for a man, nor young enough for a  boy,
translation: He's not yet old enough to be a man, but not young enough to be a boy either.

original: as a squash is before ’tis a peascod, or a codling  when ’tis almost an apple.
translation: He's like a pea pod or an apple just before it's ripe.

original: 'Tis with him in standing  water, between boy and man.
translation: He's like a slack tide, caught between coming in and going out—between boyhood and manhood.

original: He is very well-favored, and he speaks very shrewishly.
translation: He's very good-looking, but he's  nagging .

original: One would think his mother’s milk were scarce out of him.
translation: It seems like he's just barely stopped breastfeeding.

original: Let him approach. Call in my gentlewoman.
translation: Let him enter. Call in my lady-in-waiting.

original: Gentlewoman, my lady calls.
translation: Gentlewoman, my lady calls for you.

original: Give me my veil. Come, throw it o'er my face.  [OLIVIA  puts on a veil]  We’ll once more hear Orsino’s embassy.
translation: Give me my veil. Come, throw it over my face.  Let's hear Orsino's offer once more.

original: The honorable lady of the house, which is she?
translation: Which of you is the honorable lady of the house?

original: Speak to me. I shall answer for her. Your will?
translation: Speak to me—I'll answer for her. What do you want?

original: Most radiant, exquisite and unmatchable beauty—I pray  you, tell me if this be the lady of the house, for I  never saw her.
translation: Most radiant, exquisite, and unmatchable beauty—but please, tell me if you're really the lady of the house, for I've never actually seen her.

original: I would be loath to cast away my speech,  for besides that it is excellently well penned, I have  taken great pains to con it.
translation: I would hate to throw away my speech on the wrong person, for it is excellently written and was very hard for me to memorize.

original: Good beauties, let me  sustain no scorn.
translation: Good beauties, please don't scorn me.

original: I am very comptible, even to the least sinister usage.
translation: I'm very sensitive, even to the slightest bit of rudeness.

original: Whence came you, sir?
translation: Where do you come from, sir?

original: I can say little more than I have studied, and that  question’s out of my part.
translation: I can only repeat what I've memorized, and that question isn't part of my lines.

original: Good gentle one, give me  modest assurance if you be the lady of the house, that I may proceed in my speech.
translation: Please, gentle lady, just assure me that you are the lady of the house, so I can go on with my speech.

original: Are you a comedian?
translation: Are you an actor?

original: No, my profound heart. And yet, by the very fangs of  malice I swear, I am not that I play. Are you the lady  of the house?
translation: No, my dear lady. But I also swear that I'm not the same person as the part I'm playing. Are you the lady of the house?

original: If I do not usurp myself, I am.
translation: If I haven't stolen this role from myself, then I am.

original: Most certain, if you are she, you do usurp yourself,  for what is yours to bestow is not yours to reserve.
translation: If you  are  the lady of the house, then you certainly have stolen from yourself, because what's yours to give away is not yours to keep for yourself.

original: But this is from my commission. I will on with my speech in your praise and then show you the heart of my message.
translation: But this isn't what I was sent to say. I'll go on with my speech praising you, and then I'll get to the heart of my message.

original: Come to what is important in ’t. I forgive you the  praise.
translation: Just tell me the important part. I'll excuse you for skipping the praise.

original: Alas, I took great pains to study it, and ’tis  poetical.
translation: Oh, but I worked so hard memorizing it, and it's poetic.

original: It is the more like to be feigned. I pray you, keep it  in.
translation: Then it's more likely to be  fake . Please, keep it to yourself.

original: I heard you were saucy at my gates and allowed your  approach rather to wonder at you than to hear you.
translation: I heard you were rude at my gates, and I let you in because I was curious about you, not to hear your message.

original: If  you be not mad, be gone. If you have reason, be brief.
translation: If you're not crazy, then go. If you're sane, be quick.

original: 'Tis not that time of moon with me to make one in so  skipping a dialogue.
translation: I am not in the mood for lively conversation.

original: Will you hoist sail, sir? Here lies your way.
translation: Will you set sail and leave now, sir? Here's the door.

original: No, good swabber, I am to hull here a little longer.  Some mollification for your giant, sweet lady.
translation: No, good sailor, I'll dock here a little longer. My lady, would you call off your giant here?

original: Tell me your mind.
translation: Tell me what you want.

original: I am a messenger.
translation: I am a messenger.

original: Sure, you have some hideous matter to deliver, when the courtesy of it is so fearful. Speak your office.
translation: Then you must have a horrible message to deliver, since you're so afraid to get to the point. Speak your business.

original: It alone concerns your ear.
translation: It only concerns you.

original: I bring no overture of war, no taxation of homage. I hold the olive in my hand
translation: I'm not bringing a declaration of war or a demand for praise. I'm only bringing you an  olive branch .

original: . My  words are as full of peace as matter.
translation: My words are full of peace.

original: Yet you began rudely. What are you? What would you?
translation: Yet you began rudely. Who are you? What do you want?

original: The rudeness that hath appeared in me have I learned  from my entertainment.
translation: I only learned my rudeness from the way I was received here.

original: What I am and what I would are as secret as maidenhead.
translation: Who I am and what I want are as secret as a girl's virginity.

original: To your ears, divinity. To any  other’s, profanation.
translation: I have a holy message for your ears only. It would be blasphemy for anyone else to hear it.

original: Give us the place alone. We will hear this divinity.
translation: Everyone, leave us alone. I will hear this "holy message."

original: Now, sir, what is your text?
translation: Now, sir, what is your sacred text?

original: Most sweet lady—
translation: Most sweet lady—

original: A comfortable doctrine, and much may be said of it.  Where lies your text?
translation: This sounds like a comforting doctrine of faith, one that deserves to be spoken of. Where is the sacred text your "holy message" comes from?

original: In Orsino’s bosom.
translation: In Orsino's heart.

original: In his bosom? In what chapter of his bosom?
translation: In his heart? In what chapter and verse of his heart?

original: To answer by the method, in the first of his heart.
translation: To continue this metaphor—in the first chapter of his heart.

original: Oh, I have read it. It is heresy. Have you no more to  say?
translation: Oh, I have read that. It's not a holy message, it's heresy. Do you have anything more to say?

original: Good madam, let me see your face.
translation: Good madam, let me see your face.

original: Have you any commission from your lord to negotiate  with my face? You are now out of your text.
translation: Did your lord order you to negotiate with my face? You've gone off your script now.

original: But we will  draw the curtain and show you the picture.
translation: But I'll draw the curtain and show you the picture.

original: Look you,  sir, such a one I was this present. Is ’t not well done?
translation: Look, sir, this is a portrait of me in this present moment. Isn't it well done?

original: Excellently done, if God did all.
'Tis in grain, sir. 'Twill endure wind and weather.
translation: It's natural, sir. Wind and rain won't wash it off.

original: 'Tis beauty truly blent, whose red and white   Nature’s own sweet and cunning hand laid on.
translation: It's truly beautiful— your red lips and white skin  painted by Nature's sweet and skillful hand.

original: Lady, you are the cruel’st she alive   If you will lead these graces to the grave   And leave the world no copy.
translation: My lady, you are the cruelest woman alive if you'll let your beauty go with you to the grave, instead of having children and passing it on.

original: O, sir, I will not be so hard-hearted. I will give out  divers schedules of my beauty. It shall be inventoried,  and every particle and utensil labeled to my will:
translation: Oh, sir, I won't be so cruel. I'll give out lists of my beauty. I'll make a detailed inventory, with every part labeled and added to my will.

original: as,  item, two lips indifferent red; item, two grey eyes,  with lids to them; item, one neck, one chin, and so  forth. Were you sent hither to praise me?
translation: For example—item: two lips, moderately red. Item: two grey eyes, with lids attached. Item: one neck, one chin, and so forth. Were you only sent here to praise my beauty?

original: I see you what you are, you are too proud.   But, if you were the devil, you are fair.
translation: I see what you are—you're too proud. But even if you were the devil, you'd still be beautiful.

original: My lord and master loves you. Oh, such love   Could be but recompensed though you were crowned   The nonpareil of beauty.
translation: My lord and master loves you. Such love as his couldn't be repaid even if you were crowned the most beautiful woman in the world.

original: How does he love me?
translation: How does he love me?

original: With adorations, fertile tears,  With groans that thunder love, with sighs of fire.
translation: With adoration, with abundant tears, with thunderous groans, with passionate sighs.

original: Your lord does know my mind. I cannot love him.
translation: Your lord knows my mind. I cannot love him.

original: Yet I suppose him virtuous, know him noble,   Of great estate, of fresh and stainless youth.
translation: I'm sure he is a virtuous man, and I know he's noble, rich, and young.

original: In voices well divulged, free, learned, and valiant;   And in dimension and the shape of nature   A gracious person.
translation: Public opinion reports that he is generous, smart, and brave, both gracious in his manner and good-looking.

original: But yet I cannot love him;   He might have took his answer long ago.
translation: But despite all that, I cannot love him. He should have accepted my answer long ago.

original: If I did love you in my master’s flame,   With such a suffering, such a deadly life,
translation: If I loved you with my master's passion—with such suffering and a life that is like death—

original: In your denial I would find no sense;   I would not understand it.
translation: your rejection would make no sense to me. I would not understand it.

original: Why, what would you?
translation: Well, what would you do if you were your master?

original: Make me a willow cabin at your gate   And call upon my soul within the house.
translation: I would build a little cabin outside your gates, and from there I'd call out to you, my soul, in your house.

original: Write loyal cantons of contemned love   And sing them loud even in the dead of night.
translation: I would write loyal songs about unrequited love and sing them loudly even in the dead of night.

original: Halloo your name to the reverberate hills   And make the babbling gossip of the air   Cry out “Olivia!”
translation: I would shout your name to the hills and make their echoes cry out "Olivia!"

original: Oh, you should not rest   Between the elements of air and earth,   But you should pity me.
translation: Oh, you wouldn't be able to go anywhere under the sun without pitying me.

original: You might do much. What is your parentage?
translation: There's a lot you would do. What rank are your parents?

original: Above my fortunes, yet my state is well. I am a gentleman.
translation: I was born to a higher rank than I have now, but I'm still well-off. I am a gentleman.

original: Get you to your lord.   I cannot love him. Let him send no more—
translation: Go back to your lord. I cannot love him. Tell him not to send any more messengers—

original: Unless perchance you come to me again   To tell me how he takes it.
translation: unless, perhaps, you were to return and tell me how he takes my rejection.

original: Fare you well.   I thank you for your pains. Spend this for me.
translation: Farewell. Thank you for your trouble. Here is something for you to spend.

original: I am no fee’d post, lady. Keep your purse.   My master, not myself, lacks recompense.
translation: I'm no paid messenger, my lady. Keep your money. It's my master, not myself, who's going without his due reward.

original: Love make his heart of flint that you shall love,   And let your fervor, like my master’s, be   Placed in contempt. Farewell, fair cruelty.
translation: May the man you fall in love with have a heart of stone, and may your passion, like my master's, be scornfully rejected. Farewell, you beautiful cruelty.

original: “What is your parentage?”   “Above my fortunes, yet my state is well.   I am a gentleman.”
translation: "What rank are your parents?" "I was born to a higher rank than I have now, but I'm still well-off. I am a gentleman."

original: I’ll be sworn thou art;   Thy tongue, thy face, thy limbs, actions, and spirit,   Do give thee fivefold blazon.
translation: Yes, I'll swear that you are; your words, your face, your body, your actions, and your spirit all seem like a  coat of arms  for a lord.

original: Not too fast! Soft, soft!   Unless the master were the man. How now?   Even so quickly may one catch the plague?
translation: But not so fast! Calm down, calm down! If only Orsino were Cesario. But what's going on? Can someone catch the plague of love this quickly?

original: Methinks I feel this youth’s perfections   With an invisible and subtle stealth   To creep in at mine eyes.
translation: I think I can feel this youth's perfection creeping stealthily and invisibly in through my eyes.

original: Well, let it be.—   What ho, Malvolio!
translation: Well, let it happen.  [Calling out to MALVOLIO]  Come, Malvolio!

original: Here, madam, at your service.
translation: Here, madam, at your service.

original: Run after that same peevish messenger,   The county’s man. He left this ring behind him,   Would I or not. Tell him I’ll none of it.
translation: Run after that irritating messenger who just left, the duke's man. He left this ring behind, whether I wanted it or not. Tell him I want nothing to do with it.

original: Desire him not to flatter with his lord,   Nor hold him up with hopes.   I am not for him.
translation: Tell him not to encourage Orsino, or get his hopes up. I am not for him.

original: If that the youth will come this way tomorrow,   I’ll give him reasons for ’t. Hie thee, Malvolio.
translation: And tell that youth that if he'll come by tomorrow, I'll give him reasons why. Now hurry up, Malvolio.

original: Madam, I will.
translation: Madam, I will.

original: I do I know not what and fear to find   Mine eye too great a flatterer for my mind.
translation: I don't know what I'm doing, and I'm afraid that I'm falling in love based entirely on good looks—using my eyes instead of using my head.

original: Fate, show thy force. Ourselves we do not owe.   What is decreed must be, and be this so.
translation: Fate, do what you will. We can't control our destinies. What must be will be, so let it happen.

original: Will you stay no longer, nor will you not that I go  with you?
translation: Won't you stay longer? And don't you want me to go with you?

original: By your patience, no. My stars shine darkly over me.  The malignancy of my fate might perhaps distemper yours.
translation: If you'll allow it, no. My luck is bad, and my doomed fate might disturb your own destiny.

original: Therefore I shall crave of you your leave that I may  bear my evils alone. It
translation: Therefore I will say farewell, and face the evils of my fate alone.

original: were a bad recompense for your  love to lay any of them on you.
translation: It would be a bad way of thanking you if I burdened you with any of my troubles.

original: Let me yet know of you whither you are bound.
translation: At least let me know where you're headed to.

original: No, sooth, sir. My determinate voyage is mere  extravagancy. But I perceive in you so excellent a touch of modesty that you will not extort from me what I am  willing to keep in.
translation: Truly, I can't, sir. The voyage I am determined to make is merely wandering without a destination. But I can tell that you're polite enough to not force me to tell you something I want to keep to myself—

original: Therefore it charges me in manners  the rather to express myself.
translation: so it's only good manners for me to tell you what I can, Antonio.

original: You must know of me then,  Antonio, my name is Sebastian, which I called Roderigo.  My father was that Sebastian of Messaline, whom I know  you have heard of.
translation: My name is Sebastian, though I called myself Roderigo. My father was Sebastian of Messaline, whom I know you've heard of.

original: He left behind him myself and a  sister, both born in an hour. If the heavens had been  pleased, would we had so ended!
translation: He is dead now, but he left behind myself and my twin sister, who was born the same hour as me. If only God had allowed us to die in the same hour as well!

original: But you, sir, altered  that, for some hour before you took me from the breach  of the sea was my sister drowned.
translation: But you, sir, kept that from happening, for my sister drowned an hour before you pulled me from the breaking waves.

original: Alas the day!
translation: What a tragic day!

original: A lady, sir, though it was said she much resembled me,  was yet of many accounted beautiful.
translation: She was a lady who many people said looked just like me, but she was also considered beautiful.

original: Pardon me, sir, your bad entertainment.
translation: Forgive me, sir, for not being a better host.

original: O good Antonio, forgive me your trouble.
translation: Oh good Antonio, forgive me for causing you trouble.

original: If you will not murder me for my love, let me be your  servant.
translation: Let me be your servant and go with you—if you won't return my devotion, you'll be killing me.

original: If you will not undo what you have done—that is, kill  him whom you have recovered—desire it not.
translation: And if you won't undo what you have done—that is, if you don't want to kill the man whose life you saved—then you won't come with me.

original: Fare you well at once. My bosom is full of kindness, and I am yet so  near the manners of my mother, that upon the least  occasion more mine eyes will tell tales of me.
translation: Say goodbye at once. My heart is full of affection for you, and I'm feeling so effeminate that I'm about to cry.

original: I am  bound to the Count Orsino’s court. Farewell.
translation: My destination is Duke Orsino's court. Farewell.

original: The gentleness of all the gods go with thee!
translation: May the blessings of the gods go with you!

original: I have many enemies in Orsino’s court,   Else would I very shortly see thee there.
translation: I have many enemies in Orsino's court, or else I would join you there soon.

original: But, come what may, I do adore thee so   That danger shall seem sport, and I will go.
translation: But I don't care—my adoration for you is too strong, and the danger seems trivial to me. I'll go.

original: Were not you even now with the Countess Olivia?
translation: Weren't you with the Countess Olivia just now?

original: Even now, sir. On a moderate pace I have since arrived  but hither.
translation: Yes, just now, sir. I've only made it this far, walking at a moderate pace.

original: She returns this ring to you, sir. You might have saved me my pains to have taken it away yourself.
translation: She returns this ring to you, sir. You might have saved me the trouble and taken it with you.

original: She adds,  moreover, that you should put your lord into a desperate assurance she will none of him.
translation: She also adds that you should make it clear to your lord that there is no hope—she wants nothing to do with him.

original: And one thing more,  that you be never so hardy to come again in his affairs, unless it be to report your lord’s taking of this.
translation: And one thing more: you should never return here as Orsino's messenger again, unless it is to report how he takes the bad news.

original: Receive it so.
translation: Take the ring now.

original: She took the ring of me. I’ll none of it.
translation: She took that ring from me. I don't want it.

original: Come, sir, you peevishly threw it to her, and her will  is it should be so returned.
translation: Come, sir, you rudely threw it to her, and she wants it to be returned just as rudely.

original: If it be worth stooping for, there it lies in your eye.  If not, be it his that finds it.
translation: If it's worth stooping to pick up, there it is where you can see it. If not, let whoever finds it first have it.

original: I left no ring with her. What means this lady?
translation: I didn't leave any ring with her. What does this lady mean by this?

original: Fortune forbid my outside have not charmed her!   She made good view of me, indeed so much   That sure methought her eyes had lost her tongue,   For she did speak in starts distractedly.
translation: God forbid that she's smitten by my appearance! She did look intently at me, indeed so much that I thought her eyes had caused her to lose her tongue, for she spoke wildly and distractedly.

original: She loves me, sure! The cunning of her passion   Invites me in this churlish messenger.
translation: I think she loves me! She is crafty in her passion, and has used this rude messenger to subtly invite me back.

original: None of my lord’s ring? Why, he sent her none.   I am the man.
translation: So she doesn't want my lord's ring? Well, he never sent her one. I am the man she wants.

original: If it be so, as ’tis,   Poor lady, she were better love a dream.
translation: If this is true, which it is, then the poor lady would be better off loving a dream.

original: Disguise, I see thou art a wickedness,   Wherein the pregnant enemy does much.
translation: I now see that disguises are a tool to aid the resourceful devil.

original: How easy is it for the proper false   In women’s waxen hearts to set their forms!
translation: How easy it is for attractive, deceitful men to mold women's hearts to their will!

original: Alas, our frailty is the cause, not we,   For such as we are made of, such we be.
translation: Alas, it's our female frailty that's to blame—we can't help it. We turn out the way we're made.

original: How will this fadge? My master loves her dearly,   And I, poor monster, fond as much on him,   And she, mistaken, seems to dote on me.
translation: But how will all this play out? My master loves her dearly, and I,  poor androgynous fool , love him just as much. And now she, mistaking me for a man, seems to have fallen in love with me.

original: What will become of this? As I am man,   My state is desperate for my master’s love.   As I am woman, now, alas the day,   What thriftless sighs shall poor Olivia breathe!
translation: What will become of all this? In my disguise as a man, I have no hope of winning Orsino's love, but as I am really a woman, Olivia's love for me is hopeless too!

original: O time, thou must untangle this, not I.   It is too hard a knot for me to untie!
translation: Oh time, you must untangle this mess—I can't do it myself. It is too hard a knot for me to untie!

original: Approach, Sir Andrew. Not to be abed after midnight is  to be up betimes, and  diluculo surgere,  thou know’st,—
translation: Come, Sir Andrew. To be still awake after midnight is to be up early in the morning, and you surely know that waking up at dawn is supposed to be healthy—

original: Nay, my troth, I know not. But I know to be up late is  to be up late.
translation: No, truly, I don't know. But I do know that to be up late is to be up late.

original: A false conclusion. I hate it as an unfilled can.
translation: A false conclusion. I hate your logic like I hate an empty wine goblet.

original: To  be up after midnight and to go to bed then, is early, so that to go to bed after midnight is to go to bed  betimes.
translation: To stay up past midnight means going to bed in the early morning, so therefore to stay up past midnight is to go to bed early.

original: Does not our life consist of the four elements?
translation: Doesn't life consist of the four elements—fire, water, earth, and air?

original: Faith, so they say, but I think it rather consists of  eating and drinking.
translation: Well, that's what they say, but I think life consists of eating and drinking.

original: Thou'rt a scholar. Let us therefore eat and drink.  Marian, I say! A stoup of wine!
translation: You're a smart man. Let us eat and drink then. Maria, I say! Bring us a big mug of wine!

original: Here comes the fool, i' faith.
translation: Here comes the fool, actually.

original: How now, my hearts! Did you never see the picture of  “We Three”?
Welcome, ass. Now let’s have a catch.
translation: Welcome, you jackass. Now sing us a song.

original: By my troth, the fool has an excellent breast. I had  rather than forty shillings I had such a leg, and so  sweet a breath to sing, as the fool has.—
translation: I swear, the fool has an excellent voice. I would give forty shillings to have legs like his and his beautiful singing voice.

original: In sooth, thou wast in very gracious fooling last night  when thou spokest of Pigrogromitus, of the Vapians  passing the equinoctial of Queubus. 'Twas very good, i'  faith.
translation: Truly, that was some elegant fooling last night when you spoke that astrological nonsense about  Pigrogromitus , and the Vapians passing the equinoctial of Queubus. It was very funny, really.

original: I sent thee sixpence for thy leman. Hadst it?
translation: I sent you some money to spend on your sweetheart. Did you get it?

original: I did impeticos thy gratillity, for Malvolio’s nose is  no whipstock.
translation: I put your little gift in my pocket, for Malvolio can't keep his nose out of anything.

original: My lady has a white hand, and the  Myrmidons are no bottle-ale houses.
translation: My lady has lovely white hands, and  ancient warriors aren't low class taverns, you know .

original: Excellent! Why, this is the best fooling when all is  done. Now, a song.
translation: Excellent! Why, this nonsense talk is the best kind of fooling when all's said and done. Now sing us a song.

original: Come on. There is sixpence for you. Let’s have a song.
translation: Come on. Here's sixpence for you. Let's have a song.

original: There’s a testril of me too. If one knight give a—
translation: There's money from me too. If one knight gives a—

original: Would you have a love song or a song of good life?
translation: Do you want a love song or a drinking song?

original: A love song, a love song.
translation: A love song, a love song.

original: Ay, ay. I care not for good life.

O mistress mine, where are you roaming?   O, stay and hear! Your true love’s coming,   That can sing both high and low:   Trip no further, pretty sweeting.   Journeys end in lovers meeting,   Every wise man’s son doth know.
translation: Oh my mistress, where are you roaming?Oh, stay and listen! Your true love's coming:He can sing both high and low.Travel no more, my pretty sweetheart.Journeys end when lovers meet,As every wise man's son should know.

original: Excellent good, i' faith.
translation: That was excellent, truly.

original: Good, good.
translation: Good, good.

original: What is love? 'Tis not hereafter.   Present mirth hath present laughter.   What’s to come is still unsure.   In delay there lies no plenty.   Then come kiss me, sweet and twenty.   Youth’s a stuff will not endure.
translation: What is love? It's not the future.Joy in the present means present laughter.What's to come is still unsure.There's no reward for wasting time.So come kiss me while you're sweet and twenty.Youthful beauty will not endure.

original: A mellifluous voice, as I am true knight.
translation: A sweet voice if I ever heard one.

original: A contagious breath.
translation: A catchy song.

original: Very sweet and contagious, i' faith.
translation: Yes, both sweet and catchy, truly.

original: To hear by the nose, it is dulcet in contagion. But  shall we make the welkin dance indeed?
translation: If we could hear with our noses, his plague-breath would be sweet indeed. But will we make the sky dance with our antics?

original: Shall we rouse  the night owl in a catch that will draw three souls out  of one weaver? Shall we do that?
translation: Will we wake up the night owl and sing loud enough to make people pray? Will we?

original: An you love me, let’s do ’t. I am dog at a catch.
By 'r lady, sir, and some dogs will catch well.
translation: We'll do it then—some dogs are good at playing catch.

original: Most certain. Let our catch be “Thou Knave.”
translation: Certainly. Let our catch be "You Villain."

original: “Hold thy peace, thou knave,” knight? I shall be  constrained in ’t to call thee knave, knight.
translation: You mean "Shut your mouth, you villain," right? If we sing that then I'll have to call you a villain, knight.

original: 'Tis not the first time I have constrained one to call  me “knave.” Begin, Fool. It begins “Hold thy peace.”
translation: It won't be the first time someone has had to call me "villain." You begin, Fool. It begins, "Shut your mouth."

original: I shall never begin if I hold my peace.
translation: I won't ever begin if I shut my mouth.

original: Good, i' faith. Come, begin.
translation: That's a good one. But come on, begin.

original: What a caterwauling do you keep here!
translation: What a racket you're making out here!

original: If my lady have  not called up her steward Malvolio and bid him turn you  out of doors, never trust me.
translation: My lady Olivia called up her steward Malvolio and told him to kick you out of the house—it's true.

original: My lady’s a Cataian. We are politicians, Malvolio’s a  Peg- a-Ramsey, and   (sings) Three merry men be we.
translation: My lady Olivia's a trickster, we are clever plotters, Malvolio's a loose woman, and  [singing] We are three merry men.

original: —Am not I consanguineous? Am I not of her blood? Tillyvally!  “Lady”!
translation: Aren't we related? I'm Olivia's uncle, right? Well la-dee-da! "Lady!"

original: (   sings) There dwelt a man in Babylon, lady,  lady!
translation: [singing]There lived a man in Babylon, lady, lady!

original: Beshrew me, the knight’s in admirable fooling.
translation: My my, the knight's very good at playing the fool.

original: Ay, he does well enough if he be disposed, and so do I  too. He does it with a better grace, but I do it more  natural.
(sings) O' the twelfth day of December—
translation: On the twelfth day of December—

original: For the love o' God, peace!
translation: For the love of God, be quiet!

original: My masters, are you mad? Or what are you?
translation: Masters, are you crazy? What's wrong with you?

original: Have you no  wit, manners, nor honesty but to gabble like tinkers at  this time of night?
translation: Have you no wit, manners, or honesty, that you're making such a racket at this time of night?

original: Do you make an alehouse of my lady’s house, that you squeak out your coziers' catches  without any mitigation or remorse of voice?
translation: Are you trying to turn my lady's house into a noisy tavern by singing these  rowdy songs  without bothering to lower your voices at all?

original: Is there no  respect of place, persons, nor time in you?
translation: Do you have no respect for people, this place, or this time of night?

original: We did keep time, sir, in our catches. Sneck up!
translation: We did respect the time, sir, in the beat of our songs. So go hang yourself!

original: Sir Toby, I must be round with you.
translation: Sir Toby, I must be plain with you.

original: My lady bade me  tell you, that, though she harbors you as her kinsman,  she’s nothing allied to your disorders.
translation: My lady told me to tell you that she lets you stay here because you're her relative, but she doesn't approve of your disorderly behavior.

original: If you can  separate yourself and your misdemeanors, you are welcome to the house. If not, an it would please you to take  leave of her, she is very willing to bid you farewell.
translation: If you can start cleaning yourself up, you are welcome to stay in the house, but if not, and you would prefer to leave, then my lady would be glad to bid you farewell.

original: (sings) Farewell, dear heart, since I must needs be  gone.
translation: Farewell, sweetheart, since I have to go now.

original: Nay, good Sir Toby.
translation: No, good Sir Toby.

original: (  sings  )  His eyes do show his days are almost done.
translation: [Singing] His eyes do show that his life is almost over.

original: Is ’t even so?
translation: Is this really happening?

original: (  sings  )  But I will never die.
translation: [Singing] But I will never die.

original: (  sings  )  Sir Toby, there you lie.
translation: [Singing] Sir Toby, that's a lie.

original: This is much credit to you.
translation: This isn't helping your case.

original: (sings) Shall I bid him go?
translation: [Singing] Should I tell him to go?

original: (sings) What an if you do?
translation: [Singing] And what if you do?

original: (sings) Shall I bid him go, and spare not?
translation: [Singing] Should I tell him to go, and not spare his feelings?

original: (sings) O no, no, no, no, you dare not.
translation: [Singing] Oh no, no, no, no, don't you dare.

original: Out o' tune, sir. You lie.
Art any more than a steward?
translation: You're nothing more than a  steward .

original: Dost thou think, because thou art virtuous, there shall be no more cakes and ale?
translation: Do you think that just because you are boring and virtuous, food and wine will disappear?

original: Yes, by Saint Anne, and ginger shall be hot i' the  mouth too.
translation: By Saint Anne, we'll have spiced ale too.

original: Thou'rt i' the right. Go, sir, rub your chain with  crumbs. A stoup of wine, Maria!
translation: You've got the right idea.  Go rub your steward's chain in some crumbs, sir. Maria, bring us more wine!

original: Mistress Mary, if you prized my lady’s favor at  anything more than contempt, you would not give means  for this uncivil rule.
translation: Miss Maria, if you care at all about Lady Olivia's approval, then you won't bring more wine and contribute to this boorish behavior.

original: She shall know of it, by this  hand.
translation: She'll hear about this—I'll tell her.

original: Go shake your ears!
translation: Go wiggle your donkey's ears.

original: 'Twere as good a deed as to drink when a man’s  a-hungry,
translation: Making a fool out of that man would be as virtuous a deed as giving wine to the thirsty.

original: to challenge him the field and then to break  promise with him and make a fool of him.
translation: I could challenge him to a duel and then not show up—that might work.

original: Do ’t, knight. I’ll write thee a challenge. Or I’ll  deliver thy indignation to him by word of mouth.
translation: Do it, knight. I'll write a letter challenging him on your behalf. Or I'll tell him your insults myself.

original: Sweet Sir Toby, be patient for tonight. Since the youth of the count’s was today with thy lady, she is much out of quiet.
translation: Sweet Sir Toby, be patient for tonight. Ever since the Duke's young messenger visited Lady Olivia, she's been in a strange mood.

original: For Monsieur Malvolio, let me alone with him. If I do not gull him into a nayword and make him a  common recreation, do not think I have wit enough to lie straight in my bed.
translation: And as for Mister Malvolio, let me take care of him. If I can't trick him into making a fool of himself and turn him into a big joke, then I'm not even smart enough to lie straight in my bed.

original: I know I can do it.
translation: I know I can do it.

original: Possess us, possess us, tell us something of him.
translation: Give us the facts, give us the facts—tell us something about him.

original: Marry, sir, sometimes he is a kind of puritan.
O, if I thought that, I’d beat him like a dog!
translation: Oh, I'd beat him like a dog for that!

original: What, for being a puritan? Thy exquisite reason, dear  knight?
translation: What, for being a Puritan? And what's your far-fetched reason for that, dear knight?

original: I have no exquisite reason for ’t, but I have reason  good enough.
translation: I don't have a far-fetched reason for it, but my reason is good enough.

original: The devil a puritan that he is, or anything constantly, but a time-pleaser;
translation: He's not always a Puritan, though. He doesn't remain anything for long, except for a flatterer and a yes-man,

original: an affectioned ass that cons state  without book and utters it by great swarths;
translation: an affected jackass who tries to talk like the nobility.

original: the best  persuaded of himself, so crammed, as he thinks, with  excellencies, that it is his grounds of faith that all  that look on him love him.
translation: He has such a high opinion of himself and thinks he's so crammed full of excellent qualities that he's sure everyone loves him.

original: And on that vice in him will  my revenge find notable cause to work.
translation: And that's the weakness that I'll use to get my revenge on him.

original: What wilt thou do?
translation: What will you do?

original: I will drop in his way some obscure epistles of love,
translation: I'll drop some mysterious love letters in his path.

original: wherein by the color of his beard, the shape of his leg, the manner of his gait, the expressure of his eye,  forehead, and complexion, he shall find himself most  feelingly personated.
translation: They'll describe the color of his beard, the shape of his legs, the way he walks, and the expression of his eyes, forehead, and complexion—so he'll be sure that they're addressed to him.

original: I can write very like my lady your niece: on a forgotten matter we can hardly make  distinction of our hands.
translation: I can make my handwriting look just like your niece Lady Olivia's. Sometimes we can't tell our writing apart.

original: Excellent! I smell a device.
translation: Excellent! I can smell the trick.

original: I have ’t in my nose too.
translation: I smell it too.

original: He shall think, by the letters that thou wilt drop,  that they come from my niece, and that she’s in love  with him.
translation: He'll think, based on the letters you drop, that they come from my niece, and assume that she's in love with him.

original: My purpose is, indeed, a horse of that color.
translation: My purpose is indeed a horse of that color, so to speak.

original: And your horse now would make him an ass.
translation: And your horse would now make him into a jackass.

original: Ass, I doubt not.
translation: Yes, you jackass.

original: Oh, ’twill be admirable!
translation: Oh, it's going to be great!

original: Sport royal, I warrant you.
translation: It will be royal fun, I promise you.

original: I know my physic will work  with him.
translation: I know my medicine will work on him.

original: I will plant you two, and let the fool make a  third, where he shall find the letter. Observe his  construction of it.
translation: You two will hide, along with the Fool, in the place where I'll leave the letter. Then you can observe how he interprets it.

original: For this night, to bed, and dream on the event. Farewell.
translation: But for tonight, it's time to go to bed and dream about this plan. Farewell.

original: Good night, Penthesilea.
Before me, she’s a good wench.
translation: She's a good wench—I swear.

original: She’s a beagle, true-bred, and one that adores me. What o' that?
translation: She's a little purebred hunting hound, and she adores me. What of it?

original: I was adored once too.
translation: Someone once adored me, too.

original: Let’s to bed, knight. Thou hadst need send for more  money.
translation: Let's go to bed, knight. You need to send for some more money.

original: If I cannot recover your niece, I am a foul way out.
translation: If I don't marry your niece, then I'm going to be in horrible financial trouble.

original: Send for money, knight. If thou hast her not i' the  end, call me “Cut.”
translation: Send for more money, knight. If you don't end up with her in the end, then I'm a fool.

original: If I do not, never trust me, take it how you will.
translation: If I don't, never trust me again—interpret that how you want to.

original: Come, come, I’ll go burn some sack. 'Tis too late to go to bed now. Come, knight. Come, knight.
translation: Come, come, I'll go warm up some sherry for us. It's too late to go to bed now. Come, knight. Come, knight.

original: Give me some music.
translation: Give me some music.

original: Now, good morrow, friends.—
Now, good Cesario, but that piece of song,   That old and antique song we heard last night.
translation: Now, good Cesario, have them play that old-fashioned song we heard last night.

original: Methought it did relieve my passion much,   More than light airs and recollected terms   Of these most brisk and giddy-paced times:   Come, but one verse.
translation: It helped ease my passion and made me feel better, more than the silly songs and memorized words of these fast-paced modern times. Come, have them sing just one verse at least.

original: He is not here, so please your lordship, that should  sing it.
translation: Forgive me, my lord, but the man who should sing it isn't here.

original: Who was it?
translation: Who is that?

original: Feste, the jester, my lord, a fool that the lady  Olivia’s father took much delight in. He is about the  house.
translation: Feste the jester, my lord, a fool that Olivia's father used to like. He's somewhere in the house.
