original: Seek him out, and play the tune the while.
translation: Go find him, and in the meantime you all play the tune.

original: Come hither, boy. If ever thou shalt love,   In the sweet pangs of it remember me;
translation: Come here, boy. If you ever fall in love, remember me when you feel its bittersweet pangs.

original: For such as I am, all true lovers are,   Unstaid and skittish in all motions else   Save in the constant image of the creature   That is beloved.
translation: Because the way I am now is the way all true lovers are—moody and fickle in every emotion, constant only in imagining the face of the person they love.

original: How dost thou like this tune?
translation: How do you like this song?

original: It gives a very echo to the seat Where Love is throned.
translation: It echoes poignantly in the heart.

original: Thou dost speak masterly.
translation: You speak well.

original: My life upon ’t, young though thou art, thine eye   Hath stay’d upon some favor that it loves.
translation: I'd bet my life that, young as you are, you've fallen in love with a woman before.

original: Hath it not, boy?
translation: Am I right, boy?

original: A little, by your favor.
translation: A little bit, sir.

original: What kind of woman is’t?
translation: What kind of woman is she?

original: Of your complexion.
translation: She looks something like you.

original: She is not worth thee, then. What years, i' faith?
translation: She's not worthy of you, then. How old is she?

original: About your years, my lord.
translation: About your age, my lord.

original: Too old by heaven. Let still the woman take   An elder than herself.
translation: Then she's too old, by heaven. A woman should be with a man older than she is,

original: So wears she to him,   So sways she level in her husband’s heart.
translation: so she can adapt herself to her husband and keep his love constant.

original: For, boy, however we do praise ourselves,   Our fancies are more giddy and unfirm,   More longing, wavering, sooner lost and worn,   Than women’s are.
translation: We men praise ourselves, boy, but in reality we are more fickle and inconstant in love than women are—our desires waver and disappear sooner and more frequently.

original: I think it well, my lord.
translation: I think you're right, my lord.

original: Then let thy love be younger than thyself,   Or thy affection cannot hold the bent.
translation: Then your beloved should be younger than you are, or you won't be able to maintain your feelings for her.

original: And so they are. Alas, that they are so,  To die even when they to perfection grow!
translation: So they are. It's too bad that this is how it is—beauty starts to die just as it reaches its perfection!

original: O, fellow, come, the song we had last night.—
translation: Oh, you fellow, come sing the song we heard last night.

original: Mark it, Cesario, it is old and plain;   The spinsters and the knitters in the sun   And the free maids that weave their thread with bones   Do use to chant it
translation: Listen closely to it, Cesario, it's a simple old song. The wool spinners and knitters used to sing it while they sewed, and innocent maidens recited it over their weaving.

original: . It is silly sooth,   And dallies with the innocence of love,   Like the old age.
translation: It tells the simple truth about the innocence of love, as it was in the good old days.

original: Are you ready, sir?
translation: Are you ready, sir?

original: Ay; prithee, sing.
translation: Yes; please, sing.

original: Come away, come away, death,   And in sad cypress let me be laid.   Fly away, fly away breath,   I am slain by a fair cruel maid.   My shroud of white, stuck all with yew,   O, prepare it!   My part of death, no one so true   Did share it.   Not a flower, not a flower sweet   On my black coffin let there be strown.   Not a friend, not a friend greet   My poor corpse, where my bones shall be thrown.   A thousand thousand sighs to save,   Lay me, O, where   Sad true lover never find my grave,   To weep there!
translation: Come now, come now death,And let me be laid in a cypress coffin.Fly away, fly away breath,I've been killed by a fair, cruel girl.My shroud of white, adorned with yew sprigs,Oh, prepare it for me!No one as faithful as IHas ever died like me.Throw no flowers, no sweet flowersUpon my black coffin.Let no friends, no friends seeMy poor corpse, or my scattered bones.Save your thousand sighs of mourning,And bury me, Oh, whereNo sad true lovers can find my grave,To weep there!

original: There’s for thy pains.
translation: That's for your trouble.

original: No pains, sir. I take pleasure in singing, sir.
translation: It was no trouble, sir. I take pleasure in singing, sir.

original: I’ll pay thy pleasure then.
translation: I'll pay you for your pleasure, then.

original: Truly, sir, and pleasure will be paid, one time or  another.
Give me now leave to leave thee.
translation: Allow me to let you leave now.

original: Now, the melancholy god protect thee, and the tailor  make thy doublet of changeable taffeta, for thy mind is  a very opal.
translation: May the god of melancholy watch over you, and may a tailor make you a jacket of  opal , for your mind changes like the colors of an opal.

original: I would have men of such constancy put to  sea, that their business might be everything and their  intent everywhere, for that’s it that always makes a  good voyage of nothing. Farewell.
translation: Men as changeable as you should be put out to sea, where they can make everything their business and scatter their ideas everywhere, drifting about on the changeable waves—that's how you make a good voyage out of nothing. Farewell.

original: Let all the rest give place.
translation: The rest of you can leave too.

original: Once more, Cesario,   Get thee to yond same sovereign cruelty.
translation: Once more, Cesario, go visit that supremely cruel woman.

original: Tell her my love, more noble than the world,   Prizes not quantity of dirty lands;   The parts that fortune hath bestowed upon her,   Tell her, I hold as giddily as fortune;
translation: Tell her that my love is more noble than anything else in the world, and has nothing to do with her property or the riches she has inherited.

original: But ’tis that miracle and queen of gems   That nature pranks her in attracts my soul.
translation: Tell her that the fortune I value the most is her gem-like beauty, which is priceless and attracts my helpless soul.

original: But if she cannot love you, sir?
translation: But if she cannot love you, sir?

original: I cannot be so answer’d.
translation: I cannot accept that answer.

original: Sooth, but you must.
translation: Truly, but you must.

original: Say that some lady, as perhaps there is,   Hath for your love a great a pang of heart   As you have for Olivia.
translation: Imagine a lady—who probably exists somewhere—who loves you just as passionately as you love Olivia.

original: You cannot love her.   You tell her so. Must she not then be answered?
translation: But you cannot love her, and you tell her so. Doesn't she have to accept your answer then?

original: There is no woman’s sides   Can bide the beating of so strong a passion   As love doth give my heart.
translation: There is no woman strong enough to withstand the passion of love that's in my heart.

original: No woman’s heart   So big, to hold so much. They lack retention.
translation: No woman's heart is big enough to hold so much emotion. Women can't carry too much.

original: Alas, their love may be called appetite,   No motion of the liver, but the palate,   That suffer surfeit, cloyment, and revolt;
translation: Alas, love for them is just a shallow appetite—a matter of taste, not a matter of the heart. If they try to eat too much, they get sick,

original: But mine is all as hungry as the sea,   And can digest as much.
translation: but my love is as insatiable as the sea, and can swallow just as much as the ocean.

original: Make no compare   Between that love a woman can bear me   And that I owe Olivia.
translation: Don't compare my love for Olivia to any love a woman could have for me.

original: Ay, but I know—
translation: Yes, but I know—

original: What dost thou know?
translation: What do you know?

original: Too well what love women to men may owe.   In faith, they are as true of heart as we.
translation: I know too well how strongly a woman can love a man. Really, their hearts are as true as ours are.

original: My father had a daughter loved a man   As it might be, perhaps, were I a woman,   I should your lordship.
translation: My father had a daughter who loved a man just as strongly as I might love you, if I were a woman.

original: And what’s her history?
translation: And what's her story?

original: A blank, my lord. She never told her love,   But let concealment, like a worm i' the bud,   Feed on her damask cheek.
translation: Her story is blank, my lord. She never spoke of her love, but kept her passion concealed. It tormented her from the inside, like a worm trapped inside a closed flower bud, and fed on her outer beauty until it faded.

original: She pined in thought,   And with a green and yellow melancholy   She sat like patience on a monument,   Smiling at grief.
translation: She pined away quietly and sadly, and sat like a sculpture of patience itself, smiling despite her grief.

original: Was not this love indeed?   We men may say more, swear more, but indeed   Our shows are more than will,
translation: Now wasn't this true love? We men might say more and promise more, but indeed our words are stronger than our passions.

original: for still we prove   Much in our vows, but little in our love.
translation: We are good at making vows of love, but worse at keeping them.

original: But died thy sister of her love, my boy?
translation: But did your sister die of her love, my boy?

original: I am all the daughters of my father’s house,   And all the brothers too—and yet I know not.
translation: I am all of my father's daughters, and all of his sons too—and yet I'm not certain of that.

original: Sir, shall I to this lady?
translation: Sir, should I go see this lady then?

original: Ay, that’s the theme. To her in haste. Give her this jewel. Say My love can give no place, bide no denay.
translation: Yes, that's right. Go to her quickly. Give her this jewel. Say that my love cannot yield, and cannot be denied.

original: Come thy ways, Signior Fabian.
translation: Come along, Mister Fabian.

original: Nay, I’ll come. If I lose a scruple of this sport, let  me be boiled to death with melancholy.
translation: I'm coming, don't worry. If I miss the tiniest bit of this joke, may I get boiled to death.

original: Wouldst thou not be glad to have the niggardly rascally sheep-biter come by some notable shame?
I would exult, man. You know, he brought me out o'  favor with my lady about a bear-baiting here.
To anger him, we’ll have the bear again, and we will  fool him black and blue. Shall we not, Sir Andrew?
translation: We'll bring the bear back just to make him angry then, and we'll make a fool of him until he's ruined. Won't we, Sir Andrew?

original: An we do not, it is pity of our lives.
translation: If we don't, it will be the worst mistake of our lives.

original: Here comes the little villain.
translation: Here comes the little villain.

original: How now, my metal of India?
translation: How's it going, my golden one?

original: Get you all three into the boxtree.
translation: All three of you hide in the hedge.

original: Malvolio’s coming  down this walk. He has been yonder i' the sun practising behavior to his own shadow this half hour.
translation: Malvolio's coming this way down the path. He's been over there practicing his elegant manner for the past half hour.

original: Observe him, for the love of mockery, for I know this letter will  make a contemplative idiot of him.
translation: Watch him closely, if you love mockery, because I know that this letter will turn him into a starry-eyed fool.

original: Close, in the name of jesting!
translation: Now hide, if you love jokes!

original: Lie thou there (throwing down a letter), for here comes the trout that must be caught with tickling.
translation: You lie there now , for here comes the fish that must be caught by tickling it.

original: 'Tis but fortune, all is fortune. Maria once told me  she did affect me, and I have heard herself come thus  near, that, should she fancy, it should be one of my  complexion.
translation: All is luck, only luck. Maria once told me that Lady Olivia liked me, and I've almost heard Olivia herself say that if she should love a man, he would be someone with my personality.

original: Besides, she uses me with a more exalted  respect than anyone else that follows her. What should I think on ’t?
translation: Besides, she treats me with more respect and admiration than anyone else in her service. So what should I think of all this?

original: (  aside  ) Here’s an overweening rogue!
translation: What an arrogant villain!

original: O, peace! Contemplation makes a rare  turkey-cock of him.
translation: Oh, gimme a break! When he's alone and musing to himself he acts even more like a proud peacock.

original: How he jets under his advanced  plumes!
translation: See how he struts and shows his feathers!

original: (  aside  ) 'Slight, I could so beat the rogue!
translation: By God, I'd like to beat him up!

original: (  aside  ) Peace, I say.
translation: Quiet, I say.

original: To be Count Malvolio!
translation: I could be "Count Malvolio!"

original: (  aside  ) Ah, rogue!
translation: Ah, that villain!

original: (  aside  ) Pistol him, pistol him.
(  aside  ) Peace, peace!
translation: Quiet, quiet!

original: There is example for ’t. The lady of the Strachy  married the yeoman of the wardrobe.
translation: There are other instances of such things happening. The Lady Strachy married her wardrobe assistant.

original: (  aside  ) Fie on him, Jezebel!
translation: Curse him, wicked Jezebel!

original: O, peace! Now he’s deeply in. Look how  imagination blows him.
translation: Oh, quiet! Now he's really lost in his imagination. Look how his fantasies puff him up.

original: Having been three months married to her, sitting in my  state—
translation: Imagine me after three months being married to her, sitting in my majestic chair—

original: (  aside  ) Oh, for a stone-bow, to hit him in the eye!
translation: Oh, if only I had a slingshot, to shoot him in the eye!

original: Calling my officers about me, in my branched velvet  gown, having come from a daybed, where I have left  Olivia sleeping—
translation: Calling my servants around me, dressed in my embroidered velvet gown, having just come from the sofa where I've left Olivia sleeping—

original: (  aside  ) Fire and brimstone!
translation: Bloody hell!

original: (  aside  ) O, peace, peace!
translation: hispering] Oh quiet, quiet!

original: And then to have the humor of state, and after a demure travel of regard,
translation: And then to have an expression of great authority, and to gravely survey the room

original: telling them I know my place as I  would they should do theirs, to ask for my kinsman Toby—
translation: and then tell them that I know my place, and I'd like them to know theirs. I'd ask for my cousin Toby—

original: (  aside  ) Bolts and shackles!
translation: My God!

original: (  aside  ) O peace, peace, peace! Now, now.
translation: Oh quiet, quiet, quiet! Now, now.

original: Seven of my people, with an obedient start, make out  for him.
translation: Seven of my servants obediently would go to find him.

original: I frown the while, and perchance wind up watch, or play with my—some rich jewel.
translation: I frown while I wait, and perhaps wind my watch,  or play with my—with some rich jewel  I'm wearing.

original: Toby approaches,  curtsies there to me—
translation: Toby approaches me and bows—

original: (  aside  ) Shall this fellow live?
translation: Will we let this fellow live?

original: Though our silence be drawn from us with cars,  yet peace.
translation: We must keep our silence—even though it is hard to, when he's being this offensive. Quiet.

original: I extend my hand to him thus, quenching my familiar  smile with an austere regard of control—
translation: I reach out my hand to him like so, extinguishing my usual smile and replacing it with a severe look of authority—

original: (  aside  ) And does not Toby take you a blow o' the lips  then?
translation: And doesn't Toby give you a punch in the mouth then?

original: Saying, “Cousin Toby, my fortunes having cast me on  your niece give me this prerogative of speech—”
translation: And I say, "Cousin Toby, since fortune has allowed me to marry your niece, I have the right to say this—"

original: (  aside  ) What, what?
translation: What, what?

original: “You must amend your drunkenness.”
translation: "You must give up your drinking."

original: (  aside  ) Out, scab!
translation: Out of here, you scab!

original: (  aside  ) Nay, patience, or we break the sinews of our  plot.
translation: No, be patient, or we'll ruin our plan.

original: “Besides, you waste the treasure of your time with a  foolish knight—”
translation: "And another thing—you're wasting your valuable time with that foolish knight—"

original: (  aside  ) That’s me, I warrant you.
translation: That's me, I'm sure.

original: “One Sir Andrew—”
translation: "That Sir Andrew—"

original: (  aside  ) I knew ’twas I, for many do call me fool.
translation: I knew it was me, for I've often been called foolish.

original: (  seeing the letter  ) What employment have we here?
translation: And what do we have here?

original: (  aside  ) Now is the woodcock near the gin.
translation: Now the bird approaches the snare.

original: O, peace! And the spirit of humors intimate  reading aloud to him!
translation: Oh, quiet! I hope the mood strikes him to read it out loud!

original: It is, in contempt of  question, her hand.
translation: It's her handwriting, without question.

original: (  aside  ) Her C’s, her U’s and her T’s. Why that?
translation: Her C's, her U's, and her T's. Why only mention those?

original: (  aside  ) This wins him, liver and all.
translation: This is winning him over, heart and all.

original: “Jove knows I love, But who? Lips, do not move;  No man must know.” “No man must know.” What follows? The numbers altered.  “No man must know.” If this should be thee, Malvolio?
translation: "God knows that I love,But who!Lips, do not speak;No man must know.""No man must know." But what's next? The poem's meter changes. "No man must know." What if she's writing about you, Malvolio?

original: (  aside  ) Marry, hang thee, brock!
translation: Damn, go hang yourself, you badger!

original: “I may command where I adore,  But silence, like a Lucrece knife, With bloodless stroke my heart doth gore; M.O.A.I. doth sway my life.”
translation: "I may command the one I love,But silence, like a knife,Cuts my heart with a bloodless wound.M.O.A.I. rules my life."

original: (  aside  ) A fustian riddle!
translation: An elaborate riddle!

original: (  aside  ) Excellent wench, say I.
translation: Such a clever girl, I say.

original: “M.O.A.I. doth sway my life.” Nay, but first, let me  see, let me see, let me see.
translation: "M.O.A.I. rules my life." No, but first, let me see, let me see, let me see.

original: (  aside  ) What dish o' poison has she dressed him!
translation: What a dish of poison she's prepared for him!

original: (  aside  ) And with what wing the staniel checks at it!
translation: And see how eagerly he goes to eat it!

original: “I may command where I adore.” Why, she may command me. I serve her, she is my lady. Why, this is evident to  any formal capacity. There is no obstruction in this.  And the end—what should that alphabetical position  portend? If I could make that resemble something in  me—Softly! M.O.A.I.—
(  aside  ) O, ay, make up that.—He is now at a cold scent.
translation: Oh, yes, notice that. The trail's gone cold for him.

original: Sowter will cry upon ’t for all this, though  it be as rank as a fox.
translation: He'll pick up the scent eventually, no matter how much it smells of a prank.

original: “M”—Malvolio. “M”—why, that begins my name.
translation: "M"—Malvolio. "M"—why, that's the first letter of my name.

original: Did not I say he would work it out? The cur is  excellent at faults.
translation: Didn't I say he would figure it out? This dog is excellent at tracking.

original: “M.” But then there is no consonancy in the sequel.
translation: "M." But then the next letter doesn't agree with my name.

original: That suffers under probation. “A” should follow but “O”  does.
translation: This theory doesn't stand up to the test. "A" should be next, but instead it's "O."

original: (  aside  ) And “O” shall end, I hope.
translation: And this will all end in an "O" as well, I hope—the "O" of a hangman's noose.

original: (  aside  ) Ay, or I’ll cudgel him and make him cry “O!”
translation: Yes, or else I'll beat him with a club and make him yell "O!"

original: And then “I” comes behind.
translation: And then an "I" comes last.

original: Ay, an you had any eye behind you, you might  see more detraction at your heels than fortunes before  you.
translation: Yes, and if you had an "I" in the back of your head, you might see more trouble behind you than good luck before you.

original: “M.O.A.I.” This simulation is not as the former, and  yet to crush this a little, it would bow to me, for  every one of these letters are in my name. Soft, here  follows prose.
translation: "M.O.A.I." The hidden meaning of this part isn't like the other one, but if I force it a little, it too could refer to me—for every one of these letters is in my name. Wait, there's some more prose now.

original: “If this fall into thy hand, revolve.
translation: "If this should fall into your hands, consider it well.

original: In my stars I am  above thee, but be not afraid of greatness. Some are  born great, some achieve greatness, and some have  greatness thrust upon 'em.
translation: By birth I am ranked above you, but don't be afraid of my greatness. Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon them.

original: Thy Fates open their hands.  Let thy blood and spirit embrace them. And, to inure  thyself to what thou art like to be, cast thy humble  slough and appear fresh.
translation: Your fate welcomes you. Accept it with your body and spirit. And, to prepare yourself for the upper-class life you will have soon, cast aside your lowly outer self and become a new, fresh person.

original: Be opposite with a kinsman,  surly with servants. Let thy tongue tang arguments of  state. Put thyself into the trick of singularity.
translation: Be rude to your companions, and be mean to servants. Talk loudly and often about politics, and make a habit of being unique and eccentric.

original: She  thus advises thee that sighs for thee. Remember who  commended thy yellow stockings and wished to see thee  ever cross-gartered. I say, remember.
translation: The woman who  sighs  with love for you advises you to do this. Remember who it was who complimented your yellow stockings, and asked to see you always wearing crossed laces going up your legs. Remember her, I say.

original: Go to, thou art  made, if thou desir’st to be so; if not, let me see thee a steward still, the fellow of servants, and not worthy to touch Fortune’s fingers.
translation: Now go. You are assured of becoming a gentleman, if you want to be. If not, just keep acting like a steward, a companion of servants, and not worthy to grasp the greatness before you.

original: Farewell. She that would  alter services with thee,   The Fortunate Unhappy”
translation: Farewell. Signed, one who would switch places with you and be  your  servant, The Fortunate Unfortunate"

original: Daylight and champaign discovers not more. This is  open.
translation: Daylight in an open field couldn't be clearer than this.

original: I will be proud, I will read politic authors, I  will baffle Sir Toby, I will wash off gross  acquaintance, I will be point- devise the very man.
translation: This is obvious. I will act proud, I will study politics, I will insult Sir Toby, I will rid myself of lower-class acquaintances, and I will act exactly as she asked me to.

original: I do not now fool myself, to let imagination jade me, for  every reason excites to this, that my lady loves me.
translation: I'm not fooling myself now, or letting my imagination trick me—reason points to the inevitable conclusion that my lady Olivia loves me.

original: She did commend my yellow stockings of late, she did praise my leg being cross-gartered, and in this she manifests  herself to my love, and with a kind of injunction,  drives me to these habits of her liking.
translation: She did compliment my yellow stockings lately , and she did praise my crossed laces, and in this she has proven that she loves me.

original: I thank my  stars I am happy. I will be strange, stout, in yellow  stockings, and cross-gartered, even with the swiftness  of putting on. Jove and my stars be praised! Here is yet a postscript.
translation: I thank my lucky stars. I'm so happy. I will act just as she wanted—I'll be proud and aloof, and put on my yellow stockings and crossed laces as quickly as I can. May God and my lucky stars be praised! And here's more, a postscript.

original: “Thou canst not choose but know who I am.
translation: "You have probably figured out who I am.

original: If thou  entertainest my love, let it appear in thy smiling. Thy  smiles become thee well.
translation: If you accept my love, then let me know by smiling. Your smiles look good on you.

original: Therefore in my presence still  smile, dear my sweet, I prithee.”
translation: So please smile whenever you're in my presence, my dear sweetheart."

original: Jove, I thank thee! I will smile. I will do everything  that thou wilt have me.
translation: Thank you God! I will smile for her. I'll do everything she wants me to.

original: I will not give my part of this sport for a pension of  thousands to be paid from the Sophy.
translation: I wouldn't have missed this entertainment for a pension of thousands, to be paid by the Shah of Persia.

original: I could marry this wench for this device.
translation: I could marry that Maria for coming up with this scheme.

original: So could I too.
translation: So could I.

original: And ask no other dowry with her but such another jest.
Nor I neither.
translation: Neither would I.

original: Here comes my noble gull-catcher.
translation: Here comes my noble fool-catcher.

original: Wilt thou set thy foot o' my neck?
translation: Should I kiss your feet?

original: Or o' mine either?
translation: Or should I?

original: Shall I play my freedom at tray-trip, and become thy  bondslave?
translation: Should I gamble away my freedom at dice, and become your slave?

original: I' faith, or I either?
translation: Or should I?

original: Why, thou hast put him in such a dream that when the  image of it leaves him he must run mad.
translation: Why, you've sent Malvolio into such a fantasy that he'll go mad when he learns the truth.

original: Nay, but say true, does it work upon him?
translation: No, tell me the truth, did he fall for my letter?

original: Like aqua vitae with a midwife.
If you will then see the fruits of the sport, mark his  first approach before my lady.
translation: If you want to see the real results of this joke, then watch him when he first approaches my lady.

original: He will come to her in  yellow stockings, and ’tis a color she abhors, and  cross-gartered, a fashion she detests.
translation: He'll come to her in yellow stockings—a color she hates—and with crossed laces on his legs—a fashion she despises.

original: And he will smile upon her, which will now be so unsuitable to her  disposition, being addicted to a melancholy as she i
translation: And he'll smile constantly at her, which will go completely against her current mood, as she seems addicted to melancholy lately.

original: s,  that it cannot but turn him into a notable contempt. If  you will see it, follow me.
translation: All of it together will surely make her notice him and scorn him. If you want to see this, follow me.

original: To the gates of Tartar, thou most excellent devil of  wit!
translation: I'll follow you to the deepest gates of Hell, you witty devil!

original: I’ll make one too.
translation: I'll join the group too.

original: Save thee, friend, and thy music. Dost thou live by thy tabour?
translation: God bless you, friend, and your music. Do you make your living by playing your drum?

original: No, sir, I live by the church.
translation: No, sir, I live by the church.

original: Art thou a churchman?
translation: Are you a clergyman?

original: No such matter, sir. I do live by the church; for I do live at my house, and my house doth stand by the  church.
translation: Not at all, sir. I live by the church because I live in my house, and my house is by the church.

original: So thou mayst say the king lies by a beggar if a beggar dwell near him,
translation: You may as well say then that the king sleeps with a beggar if a beggar lives near him,

original: or the church stands by thy tabor, if  thy tabor stand by the church.
translation: or that the church stands next to your drum if your drum stands next to the church.

original: You have said, sir. To see this age!
translation: You're right, sir. What a wonder this modern age is!

original: A sentence is but a cheveril glove to a good wit. How quickly the wrong  side may be turned outward!
translation: A sentence is like a supple glove for good wit—it can be turned inside out so quickly!

original: Nay, that’s certain. They that dally nicely with words  may quickly make them wanton.
translation: Yes, that's certainly true. Those who play around with words too much can quickly make them changeable and promiscuous.

original: I would therefore my sister had no name, sir.
translation: If that's so, then I wish my sister didn't have a name, sir.

original: Why, man?
translation: Why, man?

original: Why, sir, her name’s a word, and to dally with that  word might make my sister wanton.
translation: Well, sir, her name's a word, and to  play around with that word  might make my sister promiscuous.

original: But, indeed, words are very rascals since bonds disgraced them.
translation: But indeed, words have been rascals ever since people started needing  written contracts to guarantee them .

original: Thy reason, man?
translation: What's your reason for that, man?

original: Troth, sir, I can yield you none without words, and  words are grown so false, I am loath to prove reason  with them.
translation: Truly, sir, I can't give you a reason without using words, and since words have become so false and unreliable, I'm hesitant to use them for my proof.

original: I warrant thou art a merry fellow and carest for  nothing.
translation: I'll bet you're a happy fellow, without a care in the world.

original: Not so, sir, I do care for something. But in my  conscience, sir, I do not care for you.
translation: Not so, sir, I do care for something. But honestly, sir, I don't care for you.

original: If that be to  care for nothing, sir, I would it would make you  invisible.
translation: If that means that I care for nothing, sir, then you should become invisible right now—as you're  nothing .

original: Art not thou the Lady Olivia’s fool?
translation: Aren't you the Lady Olivia's fool?

original: No, indeed, sir; the Lady Olivia has no folly. She will keep no fool, sir, till she be married,
translation: No indeed, sir, the Lady Olivia has no foolishness. She won't keep a fool until she gets married.

original: and fools are  as like husbands as pilchards are to herrings; the  husband’s the bigger:
translation: Fools are to husbands as  anchovies are to sardines —husbands are the larger version.

original: I am indeed not her fool, but her  corrupter of words.
translation: I'm not her fool, just her corrupter of words.

original: I saw thee late at the Count Orsino’s.
translation: I saw you at Duke Orsino's recently.

original: Foolery, sir, does walk about the orb like the sun. It  shines everywhere.
translation: Foolishness, sir,  wanders about the earth like the sun . It's everywhere.

original: I would be sorry, sir, but the fool  should be as oft with your master as with my mistress: I think I saw your wisdom there.
translation: I'd be sorry if your master was less acquainted with foolishness than my mistress is. I think I saw you there, you wise man.

original: Nay, an thou pass upon me, I’ll no more with thee.  Hold, there’s expenses for thee.
translation: If you're just going to make fun of me, I want nothing to do with it. But wait, here's a coin for you.

original: Now Jove, in his next commodity of hair, send thee a  beard!
By my troth, I’ll tell thee, I am almost sick for one, (aside]  though I would not have it grow on my chin.    though I would not have it grow on my chin.  [To  fool]  Is thy lady within?
translation: Honestly, I'm telling you, I'm dying for one,  though I don't want it on my own chin—I'm dying for a certain man with a beard.

original: Would not a pair of these have bred, sir?
translation: If I had a pair of these coins, sir, do you think they'd have children?

original: Yes, being kept together and put to use.
I would play Lord Pandarus of Phrygia, sir, to bring a Cressida to this Troilus.
translation: I'd like to play the pimp, sir, and bring these two lovers together.

original: I understand you, sir. 'Tis well  begged.
translation: I understand you sir. You're pretty good at begging.

original: The matter, I hope, is not great, sir, begging but a  beggar. Cressida was a beggar.
translation: It's no problem for me, sir, as I'm only begging on a beggar's behalf. The famous lover  Cressida  became a beggar in her old age, they say.

original: My lady is within, sir. I will construe to them whence you come.
translation: My lady is inside, sir. I'll explain where you come from,

original: Who you are and  what you would are out of my welkin, I might say  “element,” but the word is overworn.
translation: but who you are and what you want are beyond my knowledge. I'd say I'm "not in my element," but those words are overused.

original: This fellow is wise enough to play the fool,   And to do that well craves a kind of wit.
translation: This fellow is wise enough to play the fool, and to do that well you have to be clever.

original: He must observe their mood on whom he jests,   The quality of persons, and the time,   And, like the haggard, check at every feather   That comes before his eye.
translation: He has to pay attention to the mood and status of the person he's mocking, the time, and must also pursue every target he sees.

original: This is a practise   As full of labor as a wise man’s art,   For folly that he wisely shows is fit.   But wise men, folly-fall'n, quite taint their wit.
translation: This is a skill that requires just as much work as any wise man's job, for he plays the fool very wisely. Wise men, on the other hand, ruin their reputation for intelligence when they try to play the fool.

original: Save you, gentleman.
translation: God bless you, sir.

original: And you, sir.
translation: And you, sir.

original: Dieu vous garde, monsieur.
translation: May God protect you, sir.

original: Et vous aussi. Votre serviteur!
translation: And you also. At your service!

original: I hope, sir, you are, and I am yours.
translation: I hope so, sir, and I am at your service too.

original: Will you encounter the house? My niece is desirous you  should enter, if your trade be to her.
translation: Will you come in the house? My niece wants you to, if your business is with her.

original: I am bound to your niece, sir. I mean, she is the list  of my voyage.
translation: I'm bound for your niece, sir. I mean, she's the destination of my voyage.

original: Taste your legs, sir. Put them to motion.
translation: Try your legs then sir, and put them in motion.

original: My legs do better understand me, sir, than I understand what you mean by bidding me taste my legs.
translation: My legs stand under me better than I understand you, and what you mean by "try your legs."

original: I mean, to go, sir, to enter.
translation: I mean to enter the house, sir.

original: I will answer you with gait and entrance. But we are  prevented.
translation: I'll answer you by walking in. But we've been anticipated.

original: Most excellent accomplished lady, the heavens rain  odors on you!
translation: Most excellent accomplished lady, may the heavens rain odors upon you!

original: (  aside  ) That youth’s a rare courtier. “Rain odors.”  Well.
translation: That youth's a classy fellow. "Rain odors." Nice.

original: My matter hath no voice, lady, but to your own most  pregnant and vouchsafed ear.
translation: My message can't be told to anyone, my lady. It's only for your own willing and receptive ears.

original: “Odors,” “pregnant,” and “vouchsafed.” I’ll get 'em all three all ready.
translation: [To himself) "Odors," "willing," and "receptive." I'll have to remember those.

original: Let the garden door be shut, and leave me to my  hearing.
translation: Close the garden door and let me be alone to hear this message.

original: Give me your hand, sir.
translation: Give me your hand, sir.

original: My duty, madam, and most humble service.
translation: I offer you my obedience, madam, and my most humble service.

original: What is your name?
translation: What is your name?

original: Cesario is your servant’s name, fair princess.
translation: Cesario is your servant's name, fair princess.

original: My servant, sir! 'Twas never merry world   Since lowly feigning was call’d compliment.
translation: My servant, sir! The world has gone downhill since false humility started passing for a compliment.

original: You’re servant to the Count Orsino, youth.
translation: You're Duke Orsino's servant, youth, not mine.

original: And he is yours, and his must needs be yours: Your servant’s servant is your servant, madam.
translation: But he is your servant, so all that he has is yours too. Your servant's servant is your servant, madam.

original: For him, I think not on him. For his thoughts, Would they were blanks, rather than fill’d with me.
translation: As for him, I don't think about him. And as for his thoughts, I wish that they were blank pages instead of filled with pictures of me.

original: Madam, I come to whet your gentle thoughts On his behalf.
translation: Madam, I've come on his behalf to improve your feelings towards him.

original: O, by your leave, I pray you,   I bade you never speak again of him.
translation: Oh, please, I beg you, I asked you never speak of him again.

original: But, would you undertake another suit,   I had rather hear you to solicit that   Than music from the spheres.
translation: But if you would tell me that another man loves me instead, I would rather hear that than angels singing.

original: Dear lady—
translation: Dear lady—

original: Give me leave, beseech you. I did send,   After the last enchantment you did here,   A ring in chase of you.
translation: Please, let me speak. After the magic spell you cast on me last time you were here, I sent that ring to you.

original: So did I abuse   Myself, my servant, and, I fear me, you:
translation: With that trick I degraded myself, my servant, and you, I'm afraid.

original: Under your hard construction must I sit,   To force that on you, in a shameful cunning   Which you knew none of yours.
translation: I must then accept your judgment of this act, which you probably condemn—for I forced that ring on you through shameful trickery, and without your consent.

original: What might you think?   Have you not set mine honor at the stake,   And baited it with all the unmuzzled thoughts   That tyrannous heart can think?
translation: What must you think of me? Haven't you tied my honor to a  stake like a bear , and let the hounds of your anger attack it?

original: To one of your  receiving   Enough is shown.
translation: But I've shown my situation clearly enough for someone of your intelligence to understand.

original: A cypress, not a bosom,   Hides my heart. So, let me hear you speak.
translation: My heart's on my sleeve—I can't hide my passion. So let me hear you speak.

original: I pity you.
translation: I pity you.

original: That’s a degree to love.
translation: That's a step towards love.

original: No, not a grize. For ’tis a vulgar proof That very oft we pity enemies.
translation: No, not a step. It's a common experience that we often pity our enemies.

original: Why then methinks ’tis time to smile again.   O world, how apt the poor are to be proud!
translation: Then I think it's time for me to smile again. Oh, how easy it is for the poor to be proud of something they don't have!

original: If one should be a prey, how much the better   To fall before the lion than the wolf!
translation: But if I must be defeated, then better to be defeated by a noble enemy than a lowly one.

original: The clock upbraids me with the waste of time.   Be not afraid, good youth, I will not have you.
translation: See, the clock scolds me for wasting time. Don't worry, youth, I won't keep pursuing you.

original: And yet when wit and youth is come to harvest,   Your wife is like to reap a proper man.
translation: And when you're older and wiser, your future wife will have a fine handsome husband.

original: There lies your way, due west.
translation: There's your way back home, due west.

original: Then westward ho! Grace and good disposition attend your ladyship! You’ll nothing, madam, to my lord by me?
translation: Then I'm off to the west! I wish you the best of fortune. You don't have a message for the duke?

original: Stay, I prithee, tell me what thou thinkest of me.
translation: Stay, please, and tell me what you really think of me.

original: That you do think you are not what you are.
translation: I think that you're not who you think you are.

original: If I think so, I think the same of you.
translation: If that's true, then I think the same thing of you.

original: Then think you right: I am not what I am.
translation: Then you're correct. I am not what I seem to be.

original: I would you were as I would have you be!
translation: I wish you were what I want you to be!

original: Would it be better, madam, than I am?  I wish it might, for now I am your fool.
translation: Would that be better, madam, than me being what I am? I wish that it would, for right now I'm a fool.

original: Oh, what a deal of scorn looks beautiful   In the contempt and anger of his lip!
translation: Oh, look how beautiful he is even in his anger and contempt!

original: A murderous guilt shows not itself more soon   Than love that would seem hid. Love’s night is noon.
translation: A murderer's guilt is easier to hide than feelings of love. Midday is like nighttime for love—that's how brightly passion shines.

original: Cesario, by the roses of the spring,   By maidhood, honor, truth, and everything,   I love thee so,
translation: Cesario, I swear by the roses of spring, by virginity, by honor, by truth, and by everything, that I love you. I love you so much

original: that, maugre all thy pride,   Nor wit nor reason can my passion hide.
translation: that neither my wit nor my reason can hide my passion, despite your pride.

original: Do not extort thy reasons from this clause,   For that I woo, thou therefore hast no cause,
translation: Don't draw the wrong conclusions from this, though— just because I'm wooing you doesn't mean you shouldn't woo me.

original: But rather reason thus with reason fetter.   Love sought is good, but given unsought better.
translation: Use your better logic and see that love asked for is good, but love freely given is better.

original: By innocence I swear, and by my youth   I have one heart, one bosom, and one truth,
translation: And I swear by innocence and by my own youth that I have only one heart and one love to give,

original: And that no woman has, nor never none   Shall mistress be of it, save I alone.
translation: and no woman has ever ruled them, and never will—except for myself.

original: And so adieu, good madam. Nevermore   Will I my master’s tears to you deplore.
translation: And so I'll say farewell, good madam. I'll never again try to make you pity my master's passion.

original: Yet come again, for thou perhaps mayst move  That heart, which now abhors, to like his love.
translation: But come again, for you might still convince my heart, which hates him now, to somehow accept his love.

original: No, faith, I’ll not stay a jot longer.
translation: No, really, I won't stay a moment longer.

original: Thy reason, dear venom, give thy reason.
translation: What's your reason for leaving, my bitter friend?

original: You must needs yield your reason, Sir Andrew.
translation: Yes, you must tell us your reason, Sir Andrew.

original: Marry, I saw your niece do more favors to the Count’s  servingman than ever she bestowed upon me. I saw’t i'the orchard.
translation: Well, I saw your niece Olivia treating the Duke's messenger better than she has ever treated me. I saw it in the garden.

original: Did she see thee the while, old boy? Tell me that.
translation: Did she see you at the time though, old boy? Tell me that.

original: As plain as I see you now.
translation: Yes, she saw me as plainly as I see you now.

original: This was a great argument of love in her toward you.
translation: Then that was proof that she loves you.

original: 'Slight, will you make an ass o' me?
translation: What, are trying to make a fool of me?

original: I will prove it legitimate, sir, upon the oaths of  judgment and reason.
translation: I'll prove it to be true, sir, with judgment and logic.

original: And they have been grand-jurymen since before Noah was  a sailor.
translation: And judgment and logic have been wise jury members since the time of Noah's ark.

original: She did show favor to the youth in your sight only to  exasperate you, to awake your dormouse valor, to put  fire in your heart and brimstone in your liver.
translation: She treated the youth so well while you were watching to exasperate and anger you, to wake up your meekly sleeping boldness, to fire up your passions.

original: You  should then have accosted her, and with some excellent  jests, fire-new from the mint, you should have banged  the youth into dumbness.
translation: You should have approached her that minute, whipped out some excellent jokes you invented right there on the spot, and humiliated the youth into silence.

original: This was looked for at your  hand, and this was balked.
translation: That was the opening she gave you, but you missed it.

original: The double gilt of this  opportunity you let time wash off, and you are now  sailed into the north of my lady’s opinion, where you  will hang like an icicle on a Dutchman’s beard,
translation: This was a golden opportunity for you, but you let it slip away, and now you've sailed out of the warmth of my lady's good opinion. You'll stay there like an icicle in a sailor's beard

original: unless  you do redeem it by some laudable attempt either of  valor or policy.
translation: unless you can redeem yourself to her through some noble act of bravery or politics.

original: An ’t be any way, it must be with valor, for policy I  hate. I had as lief be a Brownist as a politician.
Why, then, build me thy fortunes upon the basis of  valor. Challenge me the count’s youth to fight with him.
translation: Well then, improve your fortunes through your bravery. Challenge the duke's young servant to a fight.

original: Hurt him in eleven places. My niece shall take note of  it,
translation: Hurt him in eleven places. My niece will notice this,

original: and assure thyself, there is no love-broker in the  world can more prevail in man’s commendation with woman  than report of valor.
translation: and let me assure you, no matchmaker in the world can win you a woman's love like a reputation for bravery can.

original: There is no way but this, Sir Andrew.
translation: This is the only way, Sir Andrew.

original: Will either of you bear me a challenge to him?
translation: Will either of you deliver the message of my challenge to him?

original: Go, write it in a martial hand. Be curst and brief. It is no matter how witty, so it be eloquent and full of  invention.
translation: Go and write it down, in fierce handwriting. Be rude and brief. It doesn't need to be witty, as long as it's eloquent and original.

original: Taunt him with the license of ink.
translation: Taunt him with all the possibilities of writing.

original: If thou  “thou”-est him some thrice, it shall not be amiss; and  as many lies as will lie in thy sheet of paper, although the sheet were big enough for the bed of Ware in  England, set 'em down.
translation: Refer to him  familiarly @

original: Go, about it. Let there be gall  enough in thy ink, though thou write with a goose-pen,  no matter. About it.
translation: Go, get started now. Even if you're using an ordinary pen, you can still fill it with bitter, venomous ink. Now go ahead.

original: Where shall I find you?
translation: Where will I find you when I'm done?

original: We’ll call thee at the cubiculo. Go.
translation: We'll meet you in the little room. Now go.

original: This is a dear manikin to you, Sir Toby.
translation: This knight is a beloved puppet to you, Sir Toby.

original: I have been dear to him, lad, some two thousand strong, or so.
translation: And I've been a beloved expense to him, as he's spent two thousand or so of his ducats on me.

original: We shall have a rare letter from him: but you’ll not  deliver ’t?
translation: His letter's sure to be a work of art. But you won't deliver it, will you?

original: Never trust me, then. And by all means stir on the  youth to an answer. I think oxen and wainropes cannot  hale them together.
translation: Never trust me again if I don't. And by all means encourage the youth to answer the knight's challenge. An oxcart couldn't haul them close enough together to fight.

original: For Andrew, if he were opened and  you find so much blood in his liver as will clog the  foot of a flea, I’ll eat the rest of the anatomy.
translation: As for Andrew, if you dissected him and found enough  red blood in his liver  for even a flea to notice, I'd eat the rest of his body. He's a coward through and through.

original: And his opposite, the youth, bears in his visage no  great presage of cruelty.
translation: And his opponent, the youth, doesn't seem to have much aggression in his face either.

original: Look where the youngest wren of nine comes.
translation: Look, here comes the smallest bird of all.

original: If you desire the spleen, and will laugh yourself into  stitches, follow me.
translation: If you want to have a laughing fit, and really laugh until you split your sides, then follow me.

original: Yond gull Malvolio is turned  heathen, a very renegado. For there is no Christian that means to be saved by believing rightly can ever believe such impossible passages of grossness.
translation: That gullible Malvolio must have renounced Christianity, for no Christian who intends to go to heaven  by his faith c ould ever believe the absurd, exaggerated things like we put in that letter.

original: He’s in yellow  stockings.
translation: He's wearing yellow stockings.

original: And cross-gartered?
translation: With crossed laces?

original: Most villanously, like a pedant that keeps a school i'  the church.
translation: Yes, and they look awful—like an unfashionable village schoolteacher.

original: I have dogged him, like his murderer. He  does obey every point of the letter that I dropped to  betray him.
translation: I've been stalking him like a murderer, and he's followed every instruction I gave in that letter I dropped.

original: He does smile his face into more lines than  is in the new map with the augmentation of the Indies.
translation: He smiles so much that his face has more lines in it than a map of the  Indies .

original: You have not seen such a thing as ’tis. I can hardly  forbear hurling things at him.
translation: You've never seen anything like this. I can hardly keep from throwing things at him.

original: I know my lady will  strike him. If she do, he’ll smile and take ’t for a  great favor.
translation: I know my lady will get so annoyed she'll hit him eventually, and when she does, he'll just smile and imagine that she's flattering him.

original: Come, bring us, bring us where he is.
translation: Come, bring us, bring us where he is.

original: I would not by my will have troubled you, But, since you make your pleasure of your pains, I will no further chide you.
translation: I didn't want to trouble you, but you seem to take pleasure in enduring suffering, so I won't scold you about it anymore.

original: I could not stay behind you. My desire,   More sharp than filèd steel, did spur me forth.
translation: I couldn't stay behind. My desire to go was sharper than a knife, and it spurred me onward.

original: And not all love to see you, though so much   As might have drawn one to a longer voyage,
translation: It wasn't just love for you, though that much might have inspired a man to go on an even longer voyage.

original: But jealousy what might befall your travel,   Being skilless in these parts, which to a stranger,   Unguided and unfriended, often prove   Rough and unhospitable.
translation: I was also worried about what might happen to you in your travels, since you don't know this area, and it can be rough and inhospitable to a stranger without a guide or friend.

original: My willing love,   The rather by these arguments of fear,   Set forth in your pursuit.
translation: My willing love for you, combined with these fears for your safety, drove me to follow you.

original: My kind Antonio,   I can no other answer make but thanks,   And thanks, and ever thanks.
translation: My kind Antonio, the only answer I can give you is thanks, and thanks, and infinite thanks.

original: And oft good turns   Are shuffled off with such uncurrent pay.   But were my worth as is my conscience, firm,   You should find better dealing.
translation: Often such good deeds are only rewarded with cheap words, but if I had any wealth I would strengthen my gratitude with money.

original: What’s to do?   Shall we go see the relics of this town?
translation: Now what should we do? Should we go see the monuments of this town?

original: Tomorrow, sir. Best first go see your lodging.
translation: We'll do that tomorrow, sir. First we should find a place for you to stay.

original: I am not weary, and ’tis long to night:
translation: I'm not weary, and night is a long way away.

original: I pray you, let us satisfy our eyes   With the memorials and the things of fame   That do renown this city.
translation: Please, let's go satisfy our eyes with the sight of the memorials and statues that make this city famous.

original: Would you’d pardon me;   I do not without danger walk these streets:
translation: I hope you'll pardon me: I can't walk these streets without being in danger.

original: Once in a sea-fight 'gainst the Count his galleys   I did some service, of such note indeed,
translation: Once in a battle at sea I served on the side fighting against Duke Orsino's ships, and I distinguished myself enough that I might be recognized.

original: That were I ta'en here it would scarce be answered.
translation: If I were arrested here, they'd make me answer for my deeds.

original: Belike you slew great number of his people?
translation: Then you must have killed many of his men?

original: The offence is not of such a bloody nature;   Albeit the quality of the time and quarrel   Might well have given us bloody argument.
translation: My deeds weren't so bloody as that, though we had just cause to shed some blood over that quarrel.

original: It might have since been answered in repaying   What we took from them, which, for traffic’s sake,   Most of our city did.
translation: We could have since resolved the matter by paying reparations for the damage we did to them in battle, for the sake of maintaining our trade relations. Most of our city did.

original: Only myself stood out;   For which, if I be lapsèd in this place,   I shall pay dear.
translation: I was the only one who refused to pay anything. That's why I'll pay dearly if I should be cap here.

original: Do not then walk too open.
translation: Then don't walk around too conspicuously.

original: It doth not fit me. Hold, sir, here’s my purse.
translation: It's not a good idea for me, certainly. Wait, sir, here's my purse.

original: In the south suburbs, at the Elephant,   Is best to lodge.
translation: The best place to stay is an inn called the Elephant. It's in the suburbs to the south.

original: I will bespeak our diet,   Whiles you beguile the time and feed your knowledge   With viewing of the town. There shall you have me.
translation: I'll order our meals while you spend your time pleasantly and educate yourself by exploring the town. You can find me back at the Elephant.

original: Why I your purse?
translation: Why should I take your purse, though?

original: Haply your eye shall light upon some toy   You have desire to purchase,
translation: Just if some trinket should catch your eye and you want to buy it—

original: and your store,   I think, is not for idle markets, sir.
translation: I have the feeling that your store of money isn't large enough for useless purchases.

original: I’ll be your purse-bearer and leave you For an hour.
translation: I'll carry your purse then, and leave you for an hour.

original: To the Elephant.
translation: And meet me at the Elephant.

original: I do remember.
translation: I remember.

original: I have sent after him. He says he’ll come.   How shall I feast him? What bestow of him?   For youth is bought more oft than begged or borrow’d.   I speak too loud.
translation: [To herself]  I've sent for him. He says he'll come. What food should I give him? What gifts? For it's better to buy something than beg for it or borrow it—and it's the same with youth and love. But I'm speaking too loud.

original: (to MARIA)   Where’s Malvolio? He is sad and civil   And suits well for a servant with my fortunes.   Where is Malvolio?
translation: [To MARIA]  Where's Malvolio? He is very serious and solemn, which is appropriate for someone in mourning like I am. Where is Malvolio?

original: He’s coming, madam; but in very strange manner. He is  sure possessed, madam.
translation: He's coming, madam, but in a very strange manner. He seems crazy, madam.

original: Why, what’s the matter? Does he rave?
translation: Why, what's the matter? Is he talking nonsense?

original: No, madam, he does nothing but smile. Your ladyship  were best to have some guard about you if he come, for  sure the man is tainted in ’s wits.
translation: No, madam, he does nothing but smile. It would be best if you had a guard nearby if he comes here, for the man is surely sick in his head.

original: Go call him hither.
translation: Go call him here.

original: I am as mad as he,  If sad and merry madness equal be.
translation: I am as mad as he is, if sad madness and merry madness are equals.

original: How now, Malvolio?
translation: What's going on, Malvolio?

original: Sweet lady, ho, ho.
translation: Sweet lady, hello.

original: Smilest thou? I sent for thee upon a sad occasion.
translation: Are you smiling? I sent for you on a sad occasion.

original: Sad, lady! I could be sad. This does make some  obstruction in the blood, this cross-gartering, but what of that?
translation: Sad, my lady! I could be sad. These crossed laces do cut off the circulation in my legs a bit, but what of that?

original: If it please the eye of one, it is with me as  the very true sonnet is, “Please one, and please all.”
translation: If a certain person likes them, then it's like that poem says:  "Please one, and please all."

original: Why, how dost thou, man? What is the matter with thee?
translation: Why, what's going on, man? What is the matter with you?

original: Not black in my mind, though yellow in my legs.
translation: My legs are yellow, but I don't feel blue.

original: It did  come to his hands, and commands shall be executed. I  think we do know the sweet Roman hand.
translation: The letter came to me, and its commands must be obeyed. I think I recognized the fancy Italian handwriting.

original: Wilt thou go to bed, Malvolio?
translation: Don't you think you ought to go to bed, Malvolio?

original: To bed? “Ay, sweetheart, and I’ll come to thee.”
God comfort thee! Why dost thou smile so, and kiss thy hand so oft?
translation: For God's sake! Why are you smiling like that, and kissing your hand so often?

original: How do you, Malvolio?
translation: Are you okay, Malvolio?

original: At your request! Yes, nightingales answer daws!
translation: You think I'll answer you? Noblemen don't answer servants!

original: Why appear you with this ridiculous boldness before my  lady?
translation: Why are you acting with such ridiculous arrogance in front of my lady?

original: “Be not afraid of greatness.” 'Twas well writ.
translation: "Don't be afraid of my greatness." It was well written.

original: What meanest thou by that, Malvolio?
translation: What do you mean by that, Malvolio?

original: “Some are born great—”
translation: "Some are born great—"

original: Ha?
translation: What?

original: “Some achieve greatness—”
translation: "Some achieve greatness—"

original: What sayest thou?
translation: What did you say?

original: “And some have greatness thrust upon them.”
translation: "And some have greatness thrust upon them."

original: Heaven restore thee!
translation: May heaven restore your sanity!

original: “Remember who commended thy yellow stockings—”
translation: "Remember who it was who complimented your yellow stockings—"

original: Thy yellow stockings?
translation: Your yellow stockings?

original: “And wished to see thee cross-gartered.”
translation: "And asked to see you always wearing crossed laces going up your legs."

original: Cross-gartered?
translation: Crossed laces?

original: “Go to, thou art made, if thou desirest to be so—”
translation: "Now go. You are assured of becoming a gentleman, if you want to be—"

original: Am I made?
translation: Am I a gentleman?

original: “If not, let me see thee a servant still.”
translation: "If not, just keep acting like a servant."

original: Why, this is very midsummer madness.
translation: This is surely insanity.

original: Madam, the young gentleman of the Count Orsino’s is  returned. I could hardly entreat him back. He attends  your ladyship’s pleasure.
translation: Madam, Duke Orsino's young gentleman has returned. I had to beg him to come back, but he is here now and ready to see you when you're ready.

original: I’ll come to him.
translation: I'll go to him.

original: Good Maria, let this fellow be looked to. Where’s my  cousin Toby?
translation: Good Maria, take care of this fellow here. Where's my cousin Toby?

original: Let some of my people have a special care  of him. I would not have him miscarry for the half of my dowry.
translation: Let some of my servants take special care of Malvolio. I'd give half my wealth to keep him from harm.

original: Oh, ho! Do you come near me now? No worse man than Sir Toby to look to me. This concurs directly with the  letter.
translation: Oh ho! Do you see me now? Sir Toby himself has been told to take care of me. This fits exactly with the letter.

original: She sends him on purpose that I may appear  stubborn to him, for she incites me to that in the  letter.
translation: She sends Sir Toby to me on purpose so that I can be rude to him, just as she told me to in the letter.

original: “Cast thy humble slough,” says she. “Be opposite with a kinsman, surly with servants. Let thy tongue  tang with arguments of state. Put thyself into the trick of singularity,” and consequently sets down the manner  how:
translation: "Cast aside your lowly outer self," she said. "Be rude to your companions, and be mean to servants. Talk loudly and often about politics, and make a habit of being unique and eccentric." And then she wrote down the ways I should go about this:

original: as, a sad face, a reverend carriage, a slow tongue, in the habit of some sir of note, and so forth.
translation: I should have a solemn face and a dignified demeanor, speak slowly, dress like a distinguished gentleman, and so forth.

original: I have  limed her, but it is Jove’s doing, and Jove make me  thankful!
translation: I've  caught  her now, but it is really God's doing—and may God make me thankful!

original: And when she went away now, “Let this fellow  be looked to.” “Fellow!” Not “Malvolio,” nor after my  degree, but “fellow.”
translation: And when she went away just now, she said "take care of this fellow here." "Fellow!" Not "Malvolio," nor anything appropriate for a servant, but "fellow."

original: Why, everything adheres together,  that no dram of a scruple, no scruple of a scruple, no  obstacle, no incredulous or unsafe circumstance—what can be said?
translation: Almost "companion" or "partner." Why, everything is coming together perfectly, and not the tiniest amount of doubt, no obstacle, no incredible or unfortunate event could ruin it—what else can be said?

original: Nothing that can be can come between me and  the full prospect of my hopes. Well, Jove, not I, is the doer of this, and he is to be thanked.
translation: Nothing that exists can now come between me and the fulfillment of my hopes. Well, God is responsible for this, not me, and he is to be thanked.

original: Which way is he, in the name of sanctity?
translation: Where is he, in the name of all that's holy?

original: If all the  devils of hell be drawn in little, and Legion himself  possessed him, yet I’ll speak to him.
translation: Even if all the devils of hell are crammed together inside of him, even if a troop of demons possesses him, I still want to speak to him.

original: Here he is, here he is. How is’t with you, sir? How  is’t with you, man?
translation: Here he is, here he is. How are you, sir? How are you feeling, man?

original: Go off, I discard you. Let me enjoy my private. Go off.
translation: Go away, I cast you off. Let me enjoy my privacy. Go away.

original: Lo, how hollow the fiend speaks  within him! Did not I tell you? Sir Toby, my lady prays  you to have a care of him.
translation: Oh my, the demon speaks so loudly from within him. Didn't I tell you? Sir Toby, my lady asks you to take care of him.

original: Aha! Does she so?
translation: Aha! Does she?

original: Go to, go to! Peace, peace. We  must deal gently with him. Let me alone.
—How do you,  Malvolio? How is ’t with you? What, man, defy the devil! Consider, he’s an enemy to mankind.
translation: How are you, Malvolio? How are you feeling? Come on, man, renounce the devil! Remember, he's the enemy of mankind.

original: Do you know what you say?
translation: Do you know what you're saying?

original: La you, an you speak ill of the  devil, how he takes it at heart! Pray God, he be not  bewitched!
translation: Look, he resents it when you insult the devil! Pray to God that he's not bewitched!

original: Carry his water to the wisewoman.
translation: Get a urine sample from him and take it to the healing woman.

original: Marry, and it shall be done tomorrow morning if I  live. My lady would not lose him for more than I’ll say.
translation: Sure, I'll do it tomorrow morning, I swear. My lady would give a lot to keep from losing him.

original: How now, mistress?
translation: What's that, mistress?

original: O Lord!
translation: Oh Lord!

original: Prithee, hold thy peace. This is not the  way. Do you not see you move him? Let me alone with him.
translation: Please, keep quiet. This isn't the way to go about it. Don't you see that you're making him upset? Leave me alone with him.

original: No way but gentleness, gently, gently. The fiend is  rough and will not be roughly used.
translation: The only way to deal with him is gently, gently. The demon in him is rough, but we can't treat it roughly.

original: Why, how now, my bawcock! How dost thou,  chuck?
translation: Why, hello, my fine fellow! How are you, little chicken?

original: Sir!
translation: Sir!

original: Ay, Biddy, come with me.
translation: Yes, little chicken, come with me.

original: —What, man! 'Tis not for  gravity to play at cherry-pit with Satan. Hang him, foul collier!
translation: What, man! You're too serious to play games with Satan. Damn him, that  dirty coal miner devil!

original: Get him to say his prayers, good Sir Toby, get him to  pray.
translation: Get him to say his prayers, good Sir Toby, get him to pray.

original: My prayers, minx?
translation: My prayers, you hussy?

original: No, I warrant you, he will not  hear of godliness.
translation: No, I'm telling you, he doesn't want to hear about God.

original: Go, hang yourselves all! You are idle, shallow things.  I am not of your element. You shall know more hereafter.
translation: Go hang yourselves, all of you! You are lazy, shallow creatures. I'm made of better stuff than you. You'll learn more about that, later.

original: Is ’t possible?
translation: Is it possible?

original: If this were played upon a stage now, I could condemn  it as an improbable fiction.
translation: If this were being acted out on a stage, I would complain that it was unrealistic.

original: His very genius hath taken the infection of the device, man.
translation: He's really taken our trick to heart—it seems to have infected his very soul.

original: Nay, pursue him now, lest the device take air and  taint.
translation: No, pursue him now, before he exposes the prank and it gets ruined.

original: Why, we shall make him mad indeed.
translation: Why, we're really going to make him crazy.

original: The house will be the quieter.
translation: The house will be a calmer place for it.

original: Come, we’ll have him in a dark room and bound. My niece is already in the belief that he’s mad.
translation: Come, we'll get him into a madhouse soon enough. My niece already thinks that he's crazy.

original: We may carry it thus, for our pleasure and his penance, till our very  pastime, tired out of breath, prompt us to have mercy on him,
translation: We can take it as far as we want, punishing him and having fun, until we're tired and out of breath from laughing so hard, and then we can have mercy on him

original: at which time we will bring the device to the bar  and crown thee for a finder of madmen. But see, but see!
More matter for a May morning.
translation: Here's more material for our comedy.

original: Here’s the challenge, read it.  Warrant there’s vinegar and pepper in ’t.
translation: Here's my challenge; read it. I promise that it's feisty enough.

original: Is ’t so saucy?
translation: Is it that insulting?

original: Ay, is ’t, I warrant him. Do but read.
translation: Yes, it is, I promise. Just read it.

original: Give me.    “Youth, whatsoever thou art, thou art  but a scurvy fellow.”
translation: Give it to me.  "Youth, whatever you are, you're nothing but a filthy fellow."

original: Good, and valiant.
translation: Good, and brave.

original: “Wonder not, nor admire not in thy mind, why I  do call thee so, for I will show thee no reason for ’t.”
translation: "And don't be amazed or ask why I call you that, for I won't give you any reason for it."

original: A good note, that keeps you from the blow of the law.
translation: Good job, that vagueness will keep you from being accused of slander.

original: (reads)     “Thou comest to the lady Olivia, and in my  sight she uses thee kindly.
translation: [Reading]   "You came to the lady Olivia, and she was kind to you in front of me.

original: But thou liest in thy  throat. That is not the matter I challenge thee for.”
translation: But you lie like a dog. That's not what I'm challenging you about."

original: Very brief, and to exceeding good sense—less.
translation: Very brief, and full of good sense... or nonsense.

original: “I will waylay thee going home, where if it be  thy chance to kill me—”
translation: "I will ambush you on your way home, and if you happen to kill me there—"

original: Good.
translation: Good.

original: “Thou killest me like a rogue and a villain.”
translation: "You'll be killing me like a criminal and a villain."

original: Still you keep o' the windy side of the law. Good.
“Fare thee well, and God have mercy upon one  of our souls. He may have mercy upon mine, but my hope  is better, and so look to thyself.
translation: "Farewell then, and may God have mercy upon one of our souls. He may have mercy upon mine, but my hope of surviving is better than yours, so watch yourself.

original: Thy friend, as thou  usest him, and thy sworn enemy,   Andrew Aguecheek”
translation: Signed, your friend, if you were friendly in return, and your sworn enemy, Andrew Aguecheek"

original: If this letter move him not, his legs cannot. I’ll give ’t him.
translation: If this letter won't make him get up and fight, then his legs must not work. I'll give it to him.

original: You may have very fit occasion for ’t. He is now in  some commerce with my lady and will by and by depart.
translation: You have a very convenient opportunity for it. He's doing some business with my lady right now, and he'll be leaving sooner or later.

original: Go, Sir Andrew. Scout me for him at the corner the  orchard like a bum-baily.
translation: Go, Sir Andrew. Look for him in the corner of the garden as if you were a bounty hunter.

original: So soon as ever thou seest  him, draw, and as thou drawest, swear horrible,
translation: As soon as you see him, draw your sword, and swear horribly as you draw it.

original: for it  comes to pass oft that a terrible oath, with a  swaggering accent sharply twanged off, gives manhood  more approbation than ever proof itself would have  earned him. Away!
translation: It's often the case that a terrible swear word uttered with an arrogant tone can increase your reputation for courage better than actually fighting would. Now go!

original: Nay, let me alone for swearing.
translation: No, I can't bear to swear.

original: Now will not I deliver his letter, for the behavior of  the young gentleman gives him out to be of good capacity and breeding. His employment between his lord and my  niece confirms no less. Therefore this letter, being so  excellently ignorant, will breed no terror in the youth.
translation: Now I won't deliver this letter, for the young gentleman's behavior shows that he is noble and sensible, and his role as a messenger between his lord and my niece confirms this. Therefore this letter, which is so incredibly ignorant, won't frighten him at all

original: He will find it comes from a clodpole. But, sir, I will deliver his challenge by word of mouth, set upon  Aguecheek a notable report of valor, and drive the  gentleman (as I know his youth will aptly receive it)  into a most hideous opinion of his rage, skill, fury,  and impetuosity.
translation: . He'll know it came from a fool. But, sir, I  wil l  deliver Sir Andrew's challenge by word of mouth. I'll describe him as having a great reputation for bravery, and convince the youth that Sir Andrew is angry, courageous, and skilled with a sword—and he'll believe me because he's so young.

original: This will so fright them both that they will kill one another by the look, like cockatrices.
translation: Then they'll both be so afraid, that when they see each other they'll kill each other with just a look, like  basilisks .

original: Here he comes with your niece. Give them way till he  take leave, and presently after him.
translation: Here comes the youth with your niece. Stay away until he leaves her, and then confront him.

original: I will meditate the while upon some horrid message for  a challenge.
translation: While I wait I'll come up with some horrible message to be the challenge.

original: I have said too much unto a heart of stone   And laid mine honor too unchary on ’t.
translation: I've said too much to your heart of stone, and carelessly laid my honor and reputation on that stone.

original: There’s something in me that reproves my fault,   But such a headstrong potent fault it is   That it but mocks reproof.
translation: There's something in me that condemns my love, but that love is so willful and powerful that it ignores all condemnation.

original: With the same 'havior that your passion bears Goes on my master’s grief.
translation: My master's behavior in his passion for you is the same as yours in your passion for me.

original: Here, wear this jewel for me. 'Tis my picture.   Refuse it not. It hath no tongue to vex you.
translation: Here, wear this locket for me. My picture is inside. Don't refuse it, please. Unlike me, it has no voice to upset you with.

original: And I beseech you come again tomorrow.   What shall you ask of me that I’ll deny,   That honor, saved, may upon asking give?
translation: And I beg you to come again tomorrow. What could you ask of me that I would deny, as long as I can retain my honor in giving it?

original: Nothing but this: your true love for my master.
translation: Nothing but this: give your true love to my master.

original: How with mine honor may I give him that Which I have given to you?
translation: How could I keep my honor and  give him what I have already given to you?

original: I will acquit you.
translation: I will release you from any obligation to me.

original: Well, come again tomorrow. Fare thee well. A fiend like thee might bear my soul to hell.
translation: Well, come again tomorrow. Farewell. A devil who wore your face could lead my soul to hell.

original: Gentleman, God save thee.
translation: Hello, gentleman.

original: And you, sir.
translation: And hello to you, sir.

original: That defense thou hast, betake thee to ’t
translation: Prepare yourself with whatever fighting defenses you have.

original: . Of what  nature the wrongs are thou hast done him, I know not,  but thy intercepter, full of despite, bloody as the  hunter, attends thee at the orchard end.
translation: I don't know what you've done to insult him, but someone is full of defiance and bloodthirstiness towards you, and he waits for you at the end of the garden.

original: Dismount thy  tuck, be yare in thy preparation, for thy assailant is  quick, skillful and deadly.
translation: Draw your sword and prepare yourself swiftly, for your assailant is quick, skillful, and deadly.

original: You mistake, sir. I am sure no man hath any quarrel to  me. My remembrance is very free and clear from any image of offense done to any man.
translation: You must be mistaken, sir. I'm sure no man has any reason to quarrel with me. I can't remember ever offending anyone.

original: You’ll find it otherwise, I assure you.
translation: You'll find the truth to be otherwise, I assure you.

original: Therefore, if  you hold your life at any price, betake you to your  guard,
translation: So if you value your life at all, be on your guard,
