original: for your opposite hath in him what youth,  strength, skill, and wrath can furnish man withal.
translation: for your opponent has all the youth, strength, skill, and anger that God can give to a man.

original: I pray you, sir, what is he?
translation: Please, sir, who is he?

original: He is knight, dubbed with unhatched rapier and on  carpet consideration, but he is a devil in private  brawl.
translation: He is a knight. His sword has never been used in battle, and he was knighted through his court connections rather than his battle skill, but he's a devil when he's fighting a private duel.

original: Souls and bodies hath he divorced three, and his  incensement at this moment is so implacable that  satisfaction can be none but by pangs of death and  sepulchre.
translation: He's killed three people, and his anger is so great right now that the only thing he'll be satisfied with is seeing you dead and buried.

original: Hob, nob, is his word. “Give ’t or take ’t.”
translation: "Kill or be killed, it doesn't matter" is his motto.

original: I will return again into the house and desire some  conduct of the lady.
translation: I'll go back into the house and ask for a protective escort from the lady.

original: I am no fighter.
translation: I'm no fighter.

original: I have heard of  some kind of men that put quarrels purposely on others,  to taste their valor. Belike this is a man of that  quirk.
translation: I've heard of some men who pick fights with people on purpose, just to test their bravery. This man must have that kind of personality.

original: Sir, no. His indignation derives itself out of a very  competent injury. Therefore get you on and give him his  desire.
translation: No, sir. His fury comes from a very real insult you gave him. So go ahead and give him what he wants.

original: Back you shall not to the house, unless you  undertake that with me which with as much safety you  might answer him.
translation: You won't be allowed to go back into the house unless you want to fight  me , and if you're going to do that you might as well fight him instead.

original: Therefore on, or strip your sword  stark naked, for meddle you must, that’s certain, or  forswear to wear iron about you.
translation: So go on to the garden, or else draw your sword right now. There's no way you're going to avoid a fight today, unless you want to give up your title as a gentleman and swear that you'll never carry a sword again.

original: This is as uncivil as strange.
translation: This is as rude as it is strange.

original: I beseech you, do me  this courteous office, as to know of the knight what my  offense to him is.
translation: I beg you, please do me the favor of asking the knight how I've offended him. I

original: It is something of my negligence,  nothing of my purpose.
translation: t must be something I've done without knowing it, not on purpose.

original: I will do so. Signior Fabian, stay you by this  gentleman till my return.
translation: I will do so. Sir Fabian, stay with this gentleman until I return.

original: Pray you, sir, do you know of this matter?
translation: Please, sir, do you know anything about this matter?

original: I know the knight is incensed against you, even to a  mortal arbitrament, but nothing of the circumstance  more.
translation: I know the knight is furious with you, even to the degree of wanting a fight to the death, but I don't know any more details.

original: I beseech you, what manner of man is he?
translation: Please, what kind of man is he?

original: Nothing of that wonderful promise, to read him by his  form, as you are like to find him in the proof of his  valor.
translation: He doesn't look so great from the outside, but in fighting he always proves his bravery.

original: He is, indeed, sir, the most skillful, bloody,  and fatal opposite that you could possibly have found in any part of Illyria.
translation: Indeed, sir, he's the most skillful, bloodthirsty, and deadly opponent that you could find in all of Illyria.

original: Will you walk towards him? I will  make your peace with him if I can.
translation: Will you go see him?  I'll try to appease him for you if I can.

original: I shall be much bound to you for ’t. I am one that had rather go with sir priest than sir knight. I care not  who knows so much of my mettle.
translation: I'll be in your debt if you can do it. I'm a man who would rather deal with priests than with knights. I don't care if everyone knows that I'm not brave.

original: Why, man, he’s a very devil. I have not seen such a  firago.
translation: Why, man, he's a real devil. I've never seen such a  virago.

original: I had a pass with him, rapier, scabbard, and  all, and he gives me the stuck-in with such a mortal  motion, that it is inevitable.
translation: I fought a round with him, with real swords and all, and his thrusts and lunges are so deadly that  defeat  is inevitable.

original: And on the answer, he  pays you as surely as your feet hit the ground they step on.
translation: And when he strikes at you, he'll hit you as surely as your feet hit the ground they're standing on.

original: They say he has been fencer to the Sophy.
translation: They say that he used to fence for the Shah of Persia.

original: Pox on ’t! I’ll not meddle with him.
translation: Damn my luck! I won't mess with him.

original: Ay, but he will not now be pacified. Fabian can scarce hold him yonder.
translation: Yes, but now he can't be calmed down. Fabian can barely keep him from coming over here now.

original: Plague on ’t, an I thought he had been valiant and so  cunning in fence, I’d have seen him damned ere I’d have  challenged him.
translation: Damn it, if I'd known that he was so brave and skilled at fighting, I wouldn't have challenged him in a million years.

original: Let him let the matter slip, and I’ll  give him my horse, gray Capilet.
translation: If he'll forget the whole matter, I'll give him my gray horse Capilet.

original: I’ll make the motion. Stand here, make a good show on  ’t.   This shall end without the perdition of souls.
Marry,   I’ll ride your horse as well as I ride you.
translation: And I'll ride your horse just like I ride you.

original: I have his horse to take up the quarrel. I have persuaded him the youth’s a devil.
translation: He's offered his horse to settle the quarrel. I've persuaded him that the youth's a fighting devil.

original: He is as horribly conceited of him, and pants and looks pale, as if a bear were at his heels.
translation: The youth is just as afraid of Sir Andrew. He's pale and gasping, as if a bear were chasing him.

original: (t   o   VIOLA   )   There’s no remedy, sir; he will fight with  you for ’s oath sake.
translation: [To VIOLA]  There's nothing to be done, sir; he still wants to fight you just because he swore that he would.

original: Marry, he hath better bethought  him of his quarrel, and he finds that now scarce to be  worth talking of.
translation: But he's reconsidered his reasons for challenging you, and now realizes that they're so insignificant that they're not worth discussing.

original: Therefore, draw for the supportance of his vow. He protests he will not hurt you.
translation: So draw your sword so that he can fulfill his promise. He promises he won't hurt you.

original: Pray God defend me! A little thing would make  me tell them how much I lack of a man.
translation: May God defend me! Whatever insignificant insult I committed will now reveal just how unmanly I am.

original: Give ground, if you see him furious.
translation: Back off, if you see him get angry.

original: Come, Sir Andrew, there’s no remedy. The gentleman  will, for his honor’s sake, have one bout with you.
translation: Come, Sir Andrew, there's nothing to be done. The gentleman insists on fighting one round with you for his honor's sake.

original: He  cannot by the duello avoid it.
translation: The rules of dueling say he can't avoid it.

original: But he has promised me,  as he is a gentleman and a soldier, he will not hurt  you. Come on, to ’t.
Pray God, he keep his oath!
translation: I pray to God that he keeps his promise!

original: I do assure you, ’tis against my will.
translation: I assure you, I wish none of this was happening.

original: Put up your sword. If this young gentleman   Have done offence, I take the fault on me.
translation: Put away your sword. If this young gentleman has offended you, then let the blame pass to me.

original: If you offend him, I for him defy you.
translation: And if you've offended him, then I'll fight you on his behalf.

original: You, sir? Why, what are you?
translation: You, sir? Why, who are you?

original: One, sir, that for his love dares yet do more Than you have heard him brag to you he will.
translation: I'm his friend, sir, and I would do more to you for his sake than whatever he might have said he would .

original: Nay, if you be an undertaker, I am for you.
translation: Well, if you're someone who accepts challenges, then I'll challenge you.

original: O good Sir Toby, hold! Here come the officers.
translation: Oh good Sir Toby, stop! Here come the officers.

original: I’ll be with you anon.
translation: We'll continue this later.

original: Pray, sir, put your sword up, if you  please.
translation: Please, sir, put away your sword, please.

original: Marry, will I, sir. And for that I promised you, I’ll  be as good as my word. He will bear you easily and reins well.
translation: I will then, sir. And as for what I promised you, I'll be as good as my word. He is easy to ride, and responds well to the reins.

original: This is the man. Do thy office.
translation: This is the man. Do your duty.

original: Antonio, I arrest thee at the suit of Count Orsino.
translation: Antonio, I arrest you on the orders of Duke Orsino.

original: You do mistake me, sir.
translation: You've mistaken me for someone else, sir.

original: No, sir, no jot. I know your favor well, Though now you have no sea-cap on your head.— Take him away. He knows I know him well.
translation: No, sir, not a bit. I know your face well, even without a sailor's cap on your head. Take him away. He knows that I've recognized him.

original: I must obey.   (t   o   VIOLA   )   This comes with seeking you:   But there’s no remedy. I shall answer it
translation: I must obey.  [To VIOLA]  This happened because I was looking for you, but there's nothing to be done now. I'll answer for what I've done.

original: What will you do, now my necessity   Makes me to ask you for my purse?
translation: But what will you do, now that I am forced to ask for my purse back?

original: It grieves me   Much more for what I cannot do for you   Than what befalls myself.
translation: I feel worse about not being able to help you than I do about what's going to happen to me.

original: You stand amazed,   But be of comfort.
translation: You look confused, but don't worry about me.

original: Come, sir, away.
translation: Come, sir, let's go.

original: I must entreat of you some of that money.
translation: I must ask you for some of that money.

original: What money, sir?   For the fair kindness you have showed me here,   And part being prompted by your present trouble,   Out of my lean and low ability   I’ll lend you something.
translation: What money, sir? I'll lend you what I can to thank you for the kindness you've shown me here, and because I pity your current troubles,

original: My having is not much.   I’ll make division of my present with you.   Hold, there’s half my coffer.   (offering him money)
translation: but I don't have much. I'll divide my money with you. Here is half of all that I have.  [Offering him money]

original: Will you deny me now?   Is ’t possible that my deserts to you   Can lack persuasion?
translation: Will you really deny that you know me now? Is it possible that all I've done for you can't persuade you to help me?

original: Do not tempt my misery,   Lest that it make me so unsound a man   As to upbraid you with those kindnesses   That I have done for you.
translation: Don't make my misery even worse, or make me so angry that I list out all the kind things I've done for you.

original: I know of none,   Nor know I you by voice or any feature.
translation: I don't know of any kind thing you've done, and I don't know your voice or your face.

original: I hate ingratitude more in a man   Than lying, vainness, babbling, drunkenness,   Or any taint of vice whose strong corruption   Inhabits our frail blood—
translation: I hate an ungrateful man more than I hate lying, vanity, babbling, drunkenness, or any other sin that corrupts our frail human blood—

original: O heavens themselves!
translation: Oh God!

original: Come, sir, I pray you, go.
translation: Come on, sir, please, let's go.

original: Let me speak a little. This youth that you see here   I snatched one half out of the jaws of death,   Relieved him with such sanctity of love,
translation: Let me speak a little. This youth that you see here—I snatched him from the jaws of death and nursed him back to health with tenderness and love,

original: And to his image, which methought did promise   Most venerable worth, did I devotion.
translation: and I thought that he seemed so noble and worthy that I totally devoted myself to him.

original: What’s that to us? The time goes by. Away!
translation: What do we care about that? You're wasting time. Let's go!

original: But oh, how vile an idol proves this god!   Thou hast, Sebastian, done good feature shame.
translation: But oh, this god turned out to be a false idol! Sebastian, you have shamed your good looks.

original: In nature there’s no blemish but the mind.   None can be called deformed but the unkind.
translation: On the outside you seem perfect, but you are really a deformed monster because of your unkind soul.

original: Virtue is beauty, but the beauteous evil   Are empty trunks o'erflourished by the devil.
translation: Virtue is beauty, but someone beautiful and evil is like an empty chest decorated by the devil.

original: The man grows mad. Away with him. Come, come, sir.
translation: The man is going mad. Take him away. Come on, come on, sir.

original: Lead me on.
translation: Lead me on.

original: Methinks his words do from such passion fly,   That he believes himself. So do not I.
translation: His words are so passionate that he must believe what he's saying. But I can hardly believe it.

original: Prove true, imagination, oh, prove true,   That I, dear brother, be now ta'en for you!
translation: Please be true, imagination, oh please be true—let it be true that I've been mistaken for you, my dear brother!

original: Come hither, knight. Come hither, Fabian. We’ll whisper o'er a couplet or two of most sage saws.
translation: Come here, Sir Andrew. Come here, Fabian. We'll whisper together about some wise sayings.

original: He named Sebastian. I my brother know   Yet living in my glass.
translation: He called me Sebastian. I have seen my brother when I look in my mirror.

original: Even such and so   In favor was my brother, and he went   Still in this fashion, color, ornament,   For him I imitate.
translation: My brother looked like me, and now I'm dressed as he used to dress, in the same fashion, colors, and with the same accessories—because I imitated him in my disguise.

original: Oh, if it prove,   Tempests are kind and salt waves fresh in love!
translation: Oh, if it's true, then storms are kind and the ocean is full of love!

original: A very dishonest paltry boy, and more a coward than a  hare.
translation: What a dishonorable, puny boy, and more cowardly than a rabbit.

original: His dishonesty appears in leaving his friend here  in necessity and denying him.
translation: He shows his dishonesty in abandoning his friend in his time of need, and denying that he even knew him.

original: And for his cowardship,  ask Fabian.
translation: And as for his cowardice, ask Fabian.

original: A coward, a most devout coward, religious in it.
translation: He's a coward, a true coward, religiously devoted to his cowardice.

original: 'Slid, I’ll after him again and beat him.
translation: By God's eyelid, I'll go after him again and fight him.

original: Do, cuff him soundly, but never draw thy sword.
translation: Please do, beat him up well, but don't draw your sword.

original: An I do not—
translation: And if I don't—

original: Come, let’s see the event.
translation: Come, let's go see what will happen.

original: I dare lay any money ’twill be nothing yet.
translation: I'll bet any money that nothing will happen—still.

original: Will you make me believe that I am not sent for you?
translation: Are you trying to convince me that I wasn't sent to fetch you?

original: Go to, go to, thou art a foolish fellow. Let me be  clear of thee.
translation: Go away, go on, you're a foolish fellow. Leave me alone.

original: Well held out, i' faith.
translation: Good job keeping up this trick of yours—seriously.

original: No, I do not know you, nor I  am not sent to you by my lady, to bid you come speak  with her, nor your name is not Master Cesario, nor this  is not my nose neither.
translation: No, I  don't  know you, and my lady  didn't  send me to fetch you, and she  doesn't  want you to speak with her, and your name is  not  Master Cesario, and this isn't my nose, either.

original: I prithee, vent thy folly somewhere else. Thou know’st  not me.
translation: Please, go spout your nonsense somewhere else. You don't know me.

original: Vent my folly? He has heard that word of some great  man and now applies it to a fool. Vent my folly!
translation: Spout my nonsense? He must have heard that word used by some great man and now he applies it to a jester. Spout my nonsense!

original: I am  afraid this great lubber, the world, will prove a  cockney.
translation: This foolish world, it turns out, is an effeminate dandy.

original: I prithee now, ungird thy strangeness and tell  me what I shall vent to my lady. Shall I vent to her  that thou art coming?
translation: Now please abandon your strange behavior and tell me what I should "spout" to my lady. Should I spout to her that you're coming?

original: I prithee, foolish Greek, depart from me. There’s  money for thee.    If you tarry longer, I  shall give worse payment.
translation: Please, foolish jester, leave me alone. Here's some money for you.  If you stay longer, I'll give you something worse.

original: By my troth, thou hast an open hand. These wise men  that give fools money get themselves a good report—after fourteen years' purchase.
Now, sir, have I met you again? There’s  for you.
translation: Can this be, sir, that we meet again? Take that.

original: Why, there’s for thee, and there,  and there. Are all the people mad?
translation: Well then, take that, and that, and that. Has everyone gone mad? [Draws his dagger]

original: Hold, sir, or I’ll throw your dagger o'er the house.
This will I tell my lady straight. I would not  be in some of your coats for two pence.
translation: I'll tell my lady about this straight away. She won't like anyone attacking Cesario—I wouldn't take money to be in some of your shoes.

original: (  seizi    ng  SEBASTIAN)  Come on, sir, hold!
translation: Come on, sir, stop!

original: Nay, let him alone. I’ll go another way to work with  him.
translation: No, leave him be. I'll get him in a different way. I

original: I’ll have an action of battery against him if there be any law in Illyria.
translation: 'll sue him for assault and battery, if there's any justice and law in Illyria.

original: Though I struck him first, yet  it’s no matter for that.
translation: I struck him first, but that shouldn't matter.

original: Let go thy hand.
translation: Let me go.

original: Come, sir, I will not let you go. Come, my young  soldier, put up your iron. You are well fleshed. Come  on.
translation: Come, sir, I won't let you go yet. Come on, my young soldier, put your weapon away. You've gotten excited by a taste of battle. Come on.

original: I will be free from thee.
translation: I will get free from you!

original: What wouldst thou now? If thou darest tempt me further, draw thy sword.
translation: What will you do now? If you dare to try my patience further, then draw your sword.

original: What, what? Nay, then I must have an ounce or two of  this malapert blood from you.
translation: What, what? No, for then I'd have to spill an ounce or two of your impudent blood.

original: Hold, Toby! On thy life I charge thee, hold!
translation: Stop, Toby! I command you to stop!

original: Madam!
translation: Madam!

original: Will it be ever thus?
translation: Will it always be like this with you?

original: Ungracious wretch,   Fit for the mountains and the barbarous caves,   Where manners ne'er were preach’d!
translation: You ungrateful wretch, you are only fit to live in the mountains and caves far from civilization, where good manners are unnecessary!

original: Out of my sight!—
Be not offended, dear Cesario.—
translation: [To SEBASTIAN]  Don't be offended, dear Cesario.

original: Rudesby, be gone!
translation: @ Go away, you brute!

original: I prithee, gentle friend,   Let thy fair wisdom, not thy passion, sway   In this uncivil and unjust extent   Against thy peace.
translation: Please, gentle friend, may your wisdom, not your passion, guide you through these uncivilized actions against you.

original: Go with me to my house,   And hear thou there how many fruitless pranks   This ruffian hath botched up, that thou thereby   Mayst smile at this.
translation: Come with me to my house, and let me tell you about the many pointless practical jokes my beastly uncle has clumsily attempted, so you might come to laugh at this one.

original: Thou shalt not choose but go.   Do not deny. Beshrew his soul for me!
translation: You mustn't leave. Don't deny me. Damn that Toby's soul!

original: He started one poor heart of mine in thee.
translation: He startled my heart—my heart which lives in you.

original: What relish is in this? How runs the stream?   Or I am mad, or else this is a dream.
translation: Something strange is going on. Where is all this leading? I must be mad, or else this is a dream.

original: Let fancy still my sense in Lethe steep.   If it be thus to dream, still let me sleep!
Nay, come, I prithee. Would thou’dst be ruled by me!
translation: Now come, please. I wish you would take my advice!

original: Madam, I will.
translation: Madam, I will.

original: Oh, say so, and so be!
translation: Oh, say it, and do it too!

original: Nay, I prithee, put on this gown and this beard. Make  him believe thou art Sir Topas the curate.
translation: No, I'm telling you, put on this robe and beard. Make him believe that you're Sir Topas the priest.

original: Do it  quickly. I’ll call Sir Toby the whilst.
translation: Do it quickly. I'll call Sir Toby while you're getting dressed.

original: Well, I’ll put it on, and I will dissemble myself in  ’t, and I would I were the first that ever dissembled in such a gown.
translation: Well, I'll put it on, and I'll disguise myself in it. If only I was the first person to play the hypocrite while wearing a priest's robe.

original: I am not tall enough to become the function well, nor  lean enough to be thought a good student,
translation: I'm not tall enough to look like a real priest, nor skinny enough to look like a good student,

original: but to be said an honest man and a good housekeeper goes as fairly as  to say a careful man and a great scholar. The  competitors enter.
translation: but if you're known as an honest man and a good neighbor, then that's just as good as being dutiful and intelligent. Now here come my associates.

original: Jove bless thee, master Parson.
translation: God bless you, Mr Priest.

original: Bonos dies, Sir Toby. For, as the old hermit of Prague, that never saw pen and ink, very wittily said to a  niece of King Gorboduc, “That that is is.”
translation: Bonos dies , Sir Toby.  As the old hermit of Prague, who never learned to read or write, said very wittily to a niece of King Gorboduc,  "That which is, is."

original: So I, being  Master Parson, am Master Parson. For, what is “that” but “that,” and “is” but “is”?
translation: So if I'm Mr. Priest, then I'm Mr. Priest. For doesn't "that" just mean "that," and isn't "is" just "is?"

original: To him, Sir Topas.
translation: Go to him, Sir Topas.

original: (  disguising his voice   )  What ho, I say! Peace in this  prison!
translation: What's going on, I say! Quiet in this prison!

original: The knave counterfeits well. A good knave.
translation: The fool is good at acting. A good fool.

original: (  from within   )  Who calls there?
translation: Who's that calling?

original: Sir Topas the curate, who comes to visit Malvolio the  lunatic.
translation: Sir Topas the priest, who is here to visit Malvolio the lunatic.

original: Sir Topas, Sir Topas, good Sir Topas, go to my lady—
translation: Sir Topas, Sir Topas, good Sir Topas, please go to my lady—

original: Out, hyperbolical fiend! How vexest thou this man!  Talkest thou nothing but of ladies?
translation: Out, you enormous devil!  See how you're hurting this man! Can't you talk about anything but ladies?

original: (  aside  ) Well said, Master Parson.
translation: Well said, Mr. Priest.

original: Sir Topas, never was man thus wronged. Good Sir Topas, do not think I am mad. They have laid me here in  hideous darkness.
Fie, thou dishonest Satan! I call thee by the most  modest terms,
translation: Shame on you, dishonorable Satan! I address you with moderate language,

original: for I am one of those gentle ones that  will use the devil himself with courtesy.
translation: for I'm one of those courteous people who will be polite even to the devil himself.

original: Sayest thou  that house is dark?
translation: Did you say that this house is dark?

original: As hell, Sir Topas.
translation: Dark as hell, Sir Topas.

original: Why, it hath bay windows transparent as barricadoes,  and the clerestories toward the south-north are as  lustrous as ebony.
translation: Why, it has bay windows as transparent as walls, and the upper windows facing toward the south-north are as clear as  ebony .

original: And yet complainest thou of  obstruction?
translation: And you're complaining about darkness and a bad view?

original: I am not mad, Sir Topas. I say to you this house is  dark.
translation: I'm not crazy, Sir Topas. I tell you that this house is dark.

original: Madman, thou errest.
translation: You madman, you're wrong.

original: I say, there is no darkness but  ignorance, in which thou art more puzzled than the  Egyptians in their fog.
translation: I say that there's no darkness but ignorance, and you're more ignorant than the Egyptians during Moses' plague of fog.

original: I say, this house is as dark as ignorance, though  ignorance were as dark as hell.
translation: And I say that this house is as dark as ignorance, and ignorance is as dark as hell.

original: And I say, there was  never man thus abused.
translation: And I say that no man has ever been abused like I've been.

original: I am no more mad than you are.  Make the trial of it in any constant question.
translation: I'm no more crazy than you are. Ask me any question and I'll prove my sanity.

original: What is the opinion of Pythagoras concerning wildfowl?
translation: What did the philosopher Pythagoras believe about wild birds?

original: That the soul of our grandam might haply inhabit a  bird.
translation: That our grandmother's soul could end up inhabiting a bird.

original: What thinkest thou of his opinion?
translation: What do you think of his belief?

original: I think nobly of the soul, and no way approve his  opinion.
translation: I think that the soul is very noble, and I disagree with his belief.

original: Fare thee well. Remain thou still in darkness.
translation: Farewell then. Remain in the darkness.

original: Thou  shalt hold the opinion of Pythagoras ere I will allow of thy wits, and fear to kill a woodcock lest thou  dispossess the soul of thy grandam. Fare thee well.
translation: I won't declare you sane until you agree with Pythagoras, and fear to kill a pigeon because it might have the soul of your grandmother. Farewell.

original: Sir Topas, Sir Topas!
translation: Sir Topas, Sir Topas!

original: My most exquisite Sir Topas!
translation: Perfect, Sir Topas!

original: Nay, I am for all waters.
translation: Yes, I can play many parts.

original: Thou mightst have done this without thy beard and gown. He sees thee not.
translation: You might have done this without the robe and beard. He never saw you.

original: To him in thine own voice, and bring me word how thou  findest him. I would we were well rid of this knavery.
translation: Go talk to him with your own voice, and tell me how he's feeling. I want this foolishness to be over soon.

original: If he may be conveniently delivered, I would he were,  for I am now so far in offense with my niece that I  cannot pursue with any safety this sport to the upshot.
translation: If we can conveniently let him go, I want to do it, for I'm now in so much trouble with my niece that I can't safely pursue this prank to its conclusion.

original: Come by and by to my chamber.
translation: Come to my room in a while.

original: Hey, Robin, jolly Robin,   Tell me how thy lady does.
translation: Hey, Robin, jolly Robin,Tell me how your lady is.

original: Fool!
translation: Fool!

original: (sings) My lady is unkind, perdy.
translation: [Singing] My lady is unkind indeed.

original: Fool!
translation: Fool!

original: (sings) Alas, why is she so?
translation: [Singing] Alas, why is she like this?

original: Fool, I say!
translation: Fool, I say!

original: (sings) She loves another—Who calls, ha?
translation: [Singing] She loves another man—Who's that shouting?

original: Good fool, as ever thou wilt deserve well at my hand,  help me to a candle, and pen, ink, and paper.
translation: Good fool, I'll certainly reward you if you'll help me get a candle, a pen, ink, and paper.

original: As I am a  gentleman, I will live to be thankful to thee for ’t.
Master Malvolio?
translation: Master Malvolio?

original: Ay, good fool.
translation: Yes, good fool.

original: Alas, sir, how fell you besides your five wits?
translation: Alas, sir, how did you lose your sanity?

original: Fool, there was never a man so notoriously abused: I  am as well in my wits, Fool, as thou art.
translation: Fool, no one has ever been abused like I've been. I'm just as sane as you are, Fool.

original: But as well? Then you are mad indeed, if you be no  better in your wits than a fool.
translation: Just as sane as me? You must be crazy then, if you're no saner than a fool.

original: They have here propertied me, keep me in darkness, send ministers to me
translation: They've treated me like their property here, kept me in the darkness, sent their minions after me

original: —asses!—and do all they can to face me  out of my wits.
translation: —those asses!—and done all they could to drive me insane by pretending I was insane.

original: Advise you what you say. The minister is here.
translation: Be careful what you say. The priest is here.

original: Malvolio, Malvolio, thy wits the  heavens restore! Endeavor thyself to sleep, and leave  thy vain bibble-babble.
translation: Malvolio, Malvolio, may God restore your sanity! Try to sleep, and stop your silly babbling.

original: Sir Topas!
translation: Sir Topas!

original: Maintain no words with him, good fellow.     Who, I, sir? Not I, sir. God b' wi'  you, good Sir Topas.    Marry, amen.  [in his own voice]  I will, sir, I will.
translation: Don't try to talk to him, good fellow. [In his own voice] Who, me, sir? Not me, sir. God be with you, goodbye Sir Topas. [As Sir Topas] Amen. [In his own voice] Yes, sir, yes.

original: Fool, fool, fool, I say!
translation: Fool, fool, fool, I say!

original: Alas, sir, be patient. What say you sir? I am shent for speaking to you.
translation: Alas, sir, be patient. What do you have to say, sir? I've just been scolded for speaking to you.

original: Good fool, help me to some light and some paper. I tell thee, I am as well in my wits as any man in Illyria.
translation: Good fool, please help me find a candle and some paper. I tell you, I'm as sane as any man in Illyria.

original: Well-a-day that you were, sir.
translation: If only you were, sir.

original: By this hand, I am. Good fool, some ink, paper, and  light, and convey what I will set down to my lady.
translation: I  swear by my own hand, I am. Good fool, bring me some ink, paper, and light, and then deliver the letter I'll write to my lady.

original: It  shall advantage thee more than ever the bearing of  letter did.
translation: You'll be better rewarded for delivering this letter than you've ever been rewarded before.

original: I will help you to ’t. But tell me true, are you not  mad indeed? Or do you but counterfeit?
translation: I'll help you. But tell me the truth, are you really not crazy? Or are you just acting?

original: Believe me, I am not. I tell thee true.
translation: Believe me, I'm not crazy. I'm telling you the truth.

original: Nay, I’ll ne'er believe a madman till I see his brains. I will fetch you light, and paper, and ink.
translation: No, I'll never believe a madman until he's dead and I can see his brains. But I'll bring you a candle, and paper, and ink.

original: Fool, I’ll requite it in the highest degree. I prithee, be gone.
translation: Fool, I'll repay you for this many times over. Now please, go.

original: I am gone, sir,   And anon, sir,   I’ll be with you again,   In a trice,   Like to the old Vice,   Your need to sustain,   Who, with dagger of lath   In his rage and his wrath,   Cries “Aha,” to the devil,   Like a mad lad,   “Pare thy nails, dad,   Adieu, goodman devil.”
translation: I am going, sir,But soon, sir,I'll be with you again,In just a moment,Like the old Vice,Who helps you in your time of need,With a wooden dagger,And his rage and wrath,Who shouts "Aha" to the devil,Like a mad boy,Yelling "Trim your nails, dad,And farewell, you peasant devil."

original: This is the air, that is the glorious sun.   This pearl she gave me, I do feel ’t and see ’t,
translation: This is really the air, and that's really the glorious sun. Here's the pearl she gave me—I can feel it and see it.

original: And though ’tis wonder that enwraps me thus,   Yet ’tis not madness.
translation: And though I'm full of amazement and confusion, I'm not crazy.

original: Where’s Antonio, then?   I could not find him at the Elephant.   Yet there he was, and there I found this credit,   That he did range the town to seek me out.
translation: But where's Antonio, then? I couldn't find him at the Elephant. But he had been there before me, and they told me that he was walking about the town and looking for me.

original: His counsel now might do me golden service.
translation: His advice would be like gold to me right now.

original: For though my soul disputes well with my sense   That this may be some error, but no madness,
translation: My soul makes the same strong argument as my senses, which is that all this is some mistake, but that I'm not crazy.

original: Yet doth this accident and flood of fortune   So far exceed all instance, all discourse,   That I am ready to distrust mine eyes   And wrangle with my reason that persuades me   To any other trust but that I am mad—
translation: Yet this mistake is such a sudden flood of good fortune, which exceeds all my expectations or possibility, that it makes me distrust my own eyes and wrestle with my reason, and suggests that maybe I  am  insane

original: Or else the lady’s mad. Yet if ’twere so,   She could not sway her house, command her followers,   Take and give back affairs and their dispatch   With such a smooth, discreet, and stable bearing   As I perceive she does.
translation: —or that the lady's insane. But if that were so, she wouldn't be able to run her house, command her servants, and take care of all her business affairs in the smooth, discreet, and stable way that she does.

original: There’s something in ’t   That is deceivable. But here the lady comes.
translation: There's something deceptive going on here. But here comes the lady.

original: Blame not this haste of mine. If you mean well,   Now go with me and with this holy man   Into the chantry by.
translation: Don't blame me for being so hasty. If you mean well, then come with me and this holy priest into the little chapel over there.

original: There, before him   And underneath that consecrated roof,   Plight me the full assurance of your faith,   That my most jealous and too doubtful soul   May live at peace.
translation: There, before the priest and under that sacred roof, you can swear your everlasting love for me, make your marriage vows, and soothe my jealous and doubtful soul.

original: He shall conceal it   Whiles you are willing it shall come to note,   What time we will our celebration keep   According to my birth. What do you say?
translation: The priest will keep it a secret until you're willing for it to be made public, and then we can have a full wedding ceremony and celebration that fits my social rank. What do you say?

original: I’ll follow this good man, and go with you; And, having sworn truth, ever will be true.
translation: I'll follow this good priest, and go with you; and once I've sworn to be faithful, I'll be faithful forever.

original: Then lead the way, good father; and heavens so shine  That they may fairly note this act of mine.
translation: Then lead the way, good father; and may the sun shine brightly to recognize and bless this marriage.

original: Now, as thou lovest me, let me see his letter.
translation: Now, if you're really my friend, let me see his letter.

original: Good Master Fabian, grant me another request.
translation: Good Master Fabian, do me a favor first.

original: Anything.
translation: Anything.

original: Do not desire to see this letter.
translation: Don't ask to see this letter.

original: This is, to give a dog and in recompense desire my dog again.
translation: That request is like giving me a dog, and as payment asking for the dog back.

original: Belong you to the Lady Olivia, friends?
translation: Are you in the service of the Lady Olivia, friends?

original: Ay, sir, we are some of her trappings.
translation: Yes, sir, we are part of her entourage.

original: I know thee well. How dost thou, my good fellow?
translation: I know you well. How are you, my good fellow?

original: Truly, sir, the better for my foes and the worse for  my friends.
translation: Truly, sir, I'm better because of my enemies, and worse because of my friends.

original: Just the contrary. The better for thy friends.
translation: Don't you mean the opposite? You're better because of your friends.

original: No, sir, the worse.
translation: No, sir, I'm worse.

original: How can that be?
translation: How can that be?

original: Marry, sir, they praise me and make an ass of me, now  my foes tell me plainly I am an ass.
translation: Well, sir, my friends praise me and in so doing make a fool of me, while my enemies tell me plainly that I am a fool.

original: So that by my foes, sir I profit in the knowledge of myself, and by my  friends, I am abused.
translation: Therefore my enemies help me gain knowledge of myself, while my friends deceive me.

original: So that, conclusions to be as  kisses, if your four negatives make your two  affirmatives, why then the worse for my friends and the  better for my foes.
translation: The same rule applies to both conclusions and kisses—since four negatives make two affirmatives, I'm worse because of my friends and better because of my enemies.

original: Why, this is excellent.
translation: Why, this is excellent wordplay.

original: By my troth, sir, no—though it please you to be one of  my friends.
translation: Truly sir, don't say so—unless you want to be one of my friends.

original: Thou shalt not be the worse for me: there’s gold.
translation: You won't be worse off because of me: here's some gold.

original: But that it would be double-dealing, sir, I would you  could make it another.
translation: I wish you'd deal me another coin, sir, but then it would be double-dealing, and therefore dishonorable.

original: O, you give me ill counsel.
translation: Oh, you're giving me bad advice.

original: Put your grace in your pocket, sir, for this once, and  let your flesh and blood obey it.
translation: Put your virtue away just this once, sir, and let your human weakness take my advice.

original: Well, I will be so much a sinner, to be a  double-dealer. There’s another. (  giving a coin  )
translation: Well I'll be a sinner then, and a double-dealer. Here's another.

original: Primo, secundo, tertio is a good play, and the old  saying is, the third pays for all.
translation: Three rolls of the dice is lucky, sir, and the old saying goes "the third time's the charm."

original: The triplex, sir, is  a good tripping measure, or the bells of Saint Bennet,  sir, may put you in mind—one, two, three.
You can fool no more money out of me at this throw.
translation: You won't win any more money from me with  this  third roll of the dice.

original: If  you will let your lady know I am here to speak with her, and bring her along with you, it may awake my bounty  further.
translation: But if you'll tell your lady that I'm here to speak with her, and bring her along with you when you return, then you might wake up my generosity.

original: Marry, sir, lullaby to your bounty till I come again.
translation: Well then, sir, I'll sing a lullaby to your generosity while I'm gone, so it can nap until I return.

original: I go, sir, but I would not have you to think that my  desire of having is the sin of covetousness.
translation: I'll go now, sir, but don't think that I'm doing this just because I'm greedy—I'm more interested in the art of begging than the actual money.

original: But, as you say, sir, let your bounty take a nap, I will awake it  anon.
translation: But as you say, sir, let your generosity sleep, and I'll wake it up soon.

original: Here comes the man, sir, that did rescue me.
translation: Here comes the man who rescued me, sir.

original: That face of his I do remember well.   Yet, when I saw it last, it was besmeared   As black as Vulcan in the smoke of war.
translation: I remember that face well, though the last time I saw it it was blackened by the smoke of war.

original: A baubling vessel was he captain of,   For shallow draught and bulk unprizable,     With which such scathful grapple did he make   With the most noble bottom of our fleet,
translation: He was the captain of a small, flimsy ship, worthless because of its size—but with that pitiful boat he fought such a damaging battle against my fleet's most noble warship

original: That very envy and the tongue of loss
translation: that we had to admire him even in our bitter defeat.

original: Cried fame and honor on him.   —What’s the matter?
translation: [To the officer]  What's going on here?

original: Orsino, this is that Antonio   That took the   Phoenix   and her fraught from Candy,   And this is he that did the   Tiger   board   When your young nephew Titus lost his leg.
translation: Orsino, this is the same Antonio who took our ship the  Phoenix  and its cargo from Crete, and who boarded the  Tiger  in the battle where your young nephew Titus lost his leg.

original: Here in the streets, desperate of shame and state,   In private brabble did we apprehend him.
translation: We arrested him here in the streets, where he was recklessly brawling as if he didn't care that we were looking for him.

original: He did me kindness, sir, drew on my side,
translation: He was kind to me, sir, and drew his sword to defend me,

original: But in conclusion put strange speech upon me.   I know not what ’twas but distraction.
translation: but then he said some strange things to me. I don't know what he meant, except that he might be insane.

original: Notable pirate! Thou saltwater thief,
translation: You famous pirate! You thief of the seas,

original: What foolish boldness brought thee to their mercies,   Whom thou, in terms so bloody and so dear,   Hast made thine enemies?
translation: what foolish boldness inspired you to visit the enemies you once robbed and murdered?

original: Orsino, noble sir,   Be pleased that I shake off these names you give me.   Antonio never yet was thief or pirate,   Though, I confess, on base and ground enough,   Orsino’s enemy.
translation: Orsino, noble sir, I must deny those names you give me. I have never been a thief or a pirate, though I admit to being your enemy for good and solid reasons.

original: A witchcraft drew me hither.
translation: I am here because I've been bewitched.

original: That most ingrateful boy there by your side   From the rude sea’s enraged and foamy mouth   Did I redeem.
translation: I rescued that ungrateful boy—the one there by your side—from the rude sea's angry waves.

original: A wreck past hope he was.   His life I gave him and did thereto add   My love, without retention or restraint,   All his in dedication.
translation: He was a wreck, and seemed past hope. I saved his life and gave him my love, without reservation or restraint, and dedicated myself to him totally

original: For his sake   Did I expose myself, pure for his love,   Into the danger of this adverse town,   Drew to defend him when he was beset,
translation: . For his sake I endangered myself in this town, and purely out of love for him I drew my sword to defend him when he was being attacked.

original: Where being apprehended, his false cunning,   (Not meaning to partake with me in danger)   Taught him to face me out of his acquaintance,
translation: But when I was arrested, he decided not to endanger himself, and he used his treacherous cunning to pretend that he'd never met me before.

original: And grew a twenty-years-removed thing   While one would wink, denied me mine own purse,   Which I had recommended to his use   Not half an hour before.
translation: In the blink of an eye he became a totally different person, and he refused to give me back my own purse, which I had lent to him just half an hour before.

original: How can this be?
translation: How is this possible?

original: When came he to this town?
translation: When did he come to this town?

original: Today, my lord, and for three months before,  No interim, not a minute’s vacancy, Both day and night did we keep company.
translation: Today, my lord. For three months before that we spent every day and night together without a break.

original: Here comes the Countess. Now heaven walks on earth.
translation: Look, an angel is walking on earth—here comes the Countess.

original: But for thee, fellow. Fellow, thy words are madness:   Three months this youth hath tended upon me;   But more of that anon.
Take him  aside.
translation: Take him away.

original: What would my lord, but that he may not have,   Wherein Olivia may seem serviceable?
translation: What do you want, my lord—except for the one thing you cannot have—that I can help you with?

original: Cesario, you do not keep promise with me.
translation: Cesario, you broke your promise to me.

original: Madam?
translation: Madam?

original: Gracious Olivia—
translation: Gracious Olivia—

original: What do you say, Cesario?—Good my lord—
translation: What do you have to say for yourself, Cesario?—My lord, a moment—

original: My lord would speak. My duty hushes me.
translation: My lord wants to speak. It's my duty to be silent.

original: If it be aught to the old tune, my lord, It is as fat and fulsome to mine ear  As howling after music.
translation: If you're just going to repeat the same old things, my lord, then it will be as pleasant to my ears as hearing howling after listening to beautiful music.

original: Still so cruel?
translation: Are you still so cruel?

original: Still so constant, lord.
translation: I am still consistent, my lord.

original: What, to perverseness?
translation: Consistent in what, being horrible?

original: You, uncivil lady,   To whose ingrate and unauspicious altars   My soul the faithfull’st off'rings have breathed out   That e'er devotion tendered
translation: I have breathed from my soul the most faithful, devoted offerings possible, but they've only fallen upon your ungrateful and unwelcoming  altar , you rude lady.

original: —what shall I do?
translation: What else can I do?

original: Even what it please my lord that shall become him.
translation: Do whatever pleases you, within reason.

original: Why should I not, had I the heart to do it,   Like to the Egyptian thief at point of death,   Kill what I love?
translation: Why shouldn't I—if I had the heart to do it—kill what I love, like that Egyptian thief Thyamis who murdered the woman he loved just before he died?

original: —A savage jealousy   That sometimes savors nobly.
translation: That kind of savage jealousy sometimes seems noble.

original: But hear me this:   Since you to nonregardance cast my faith,   And that I partly know the instrument   That screws me from my true place in your favor,   Live you the marble-breasted tyrant still.
translation: But listen to me now: since you keep denying my faithful love, and since I can guess who has forced me from my rightful place in your heart, you can go on being a cold-hearted tyrant as long as you like—

original: But this your minion, whom I know you love,   And whom, by heaven I swear, I tender dearly,   Him will I tear out of that cruel eye   Where he sits crowned in his master’s spite.
translation: but I'm going to take your darling Cesario from you. I know that you love him, and I swear that I care deeply for him as well, but I must tear him away from you because his place in your heart humiliates me.

original: And I, most jocund, apt, and willingly, To do you rest, a thousand deaths would die.
translation: And I would cheerfully, readily, and willingly die a thousand deaths if it would bring you peace.

original: Where goes Cesario?
translation: Where is Cesario going?

original: After him I love   More than I love these eyes, more than my life,   More, by all mores, than e'er I shall love wife.
translation: I'm following the man I love more than I love my eyes or my life, more, far more, than I'll ever love a wife.

original: If I do feign, you witnesses above,   Punish my life for tainting of my love!
translation: If I'm lying about this, you angels above, put me to death for dishonoring my love.

original: Ay me, detested! How am I beguiled!
translation: Oh no, you scorn me! I've been tricked!

original: Who does beguile you? Who does do you wrong?
translation: Who tricked you? Who has done you wrong?

original: Hast thou forgot thyself? Is it so long?— Call forth the holy father.
translation: Have you forgotten your own actions? Has it been so long?—Call the priest who was with us earlier.

original: Come, away!
translation: Come, let's go!

original: Whither, my lord?—Cesario, husband, stay.
translation: Where are you taking him, my lord?—Cesario, my husband, stay.

original: Husband?
translation: Husband?

original: Ay, husband. Can he that deny?
translation: Yes, husband. Can he deny it?

original: Her husband, sirrah?
translation: Are you her husband, you wretch?

original: No, my lord, not I.
translation: No, my lord, I'm not.

original: Alas, it is the baseness of thy fear   That makes thee strangle thy propriety.   Fear not, Cesario.
translation: Alas, your fear is so great that it makes you disguise your true identity. But don't be afraid, Cesario.

original: Take thy fortunes up.   Be that thou know’st thou art, and then thou art   As great as that thou fear’st.
translation: Reach out and accept your good fortune. Be the person you know you are, and then you will be as powerful as the person you fear.

original: O, welcome, father!   Father, I charge thee, by thy reverence,   Here to unfold
translation: Oh, welcome, father! Father, can I respectfully ask you to explain

original: (though lately we intended   To keep in darkness what occasion now   Reveals before ’tis ripe)
translation: (though we recently wanted to hide it, the time is now ripe to reveal it)

original: what thou dost know   Hath newly passed between this youth and me.
translation: what you know has happened between this youth and me?

original: A contract of eternal bond of love,   Confirmed by mutual joinder of your hands,   Attested by the holy close of lips,   Strengthened by interchangement of your rings,
translation: You made an oath of eternal love, which was confirmed by joining hands, proved by a holy kiss, and strengthened by an exchange of rings.

original: And all the ceremony of this compact   Sealed in my function, by my testimony,
translation: I witnessed and approved all this in my official capacity as a priest.

original: Since when, my watch hath told me, toward my grave   I have traveled but two hours.
translation: All this took place only two hours ago.

original: O thou dissembling cub! What wilt thou be   When time hath sowed a grizzle on thy case?
translation: Oh, you lying little puppy! How much worse will you be when you're old and gray?

original: Or will not else thy craft so quickly grow   That thine own trip shall be thine overthrow?
translation: Or will you get so good at being crafty that your own tricks will trick you?

original: Farewell, and take her; but direct thy feet   Where thou and I henceforth may never meet.
translation: Farewell, and take her; but go somewhere where you and I will never meet again.

original: My lord, I do protest—
translation: My lord, I promise—

original: O, do not swear! Hold little faith, though thou hast too much fear.
translation: Oh, don't promise! Keep a little faith—your faith in me—even though you're so afraid.

original: For the love of God, a surgeon! Send one presently to  Sir Toby.
translation: For the love of God, someone get a doctor! Send one to Sir Toby right away.

original: What’s the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: He has broke my head across and has given Sir Toby a  bloody coxcomb too. For the love of God, your help! I  had rather than forty pound I were at home.
Who has done this, Sir Andrew?
translation: Who has done this, Sir Andrew?

original: The Count’s gentleman, one Cesario. We took him for a  coward, but he’s the very devil incardinate.
translation: That Cesario, the Duke's gentleman. We thought he was a coward, but he actually fights like the devil himself.

original: My gentleman, Cesario?
translation: My servant Cesario?

original: 'Od’s lifelings, here he is!—You broke my head for  nothing, and that that I did, I was set on to do ’t by  Sir Toby.
translation: By God, here he is!—You broke my head for no reason. I didn't do anything, and whatever I did, Sir Toby made me do.

original: Why do you speak to me? I never hurt you.
translation: Why are you saying this to me? I never hurt you.

original: You drew your sword upon me without cause,   But I bespoke you fair and hurt you not.
translation: You drew your sword against me without a good reason, but I spoke politely to you and didn't hurt you.

original: If a bloody coxcomb be a hurt, you have hurt me. I  think you set nothing by a bloody coxcomb.
translation: If a bloody head is an injury, then you've hurt me. I don't think you care at all about a bloody head.

original: Here comes Sir Toby halting. You shall hear more.
translation: Here comes Sir Toby, limping. He'll tell you more about what happened.

original: But  if he had not been in drink, he would have tickled you  othergates than he did.
translation: If he hadn't been drunk, he would have hurt you more than he did.

original: How now, gentleman? How is ’t with you?
translation: Hello, gentleman! How are you?

original: That’s all one: has hurt me, and there’s the end on ’t.     Sot, didst see Dick Surgeon, sot?
translation: It doesn't matter: he has hurt me, and that's all there is to it.  You drunken fool, have you seen Dick the surgeon?

original: Oh, he’s drunk, Sir Toby, an hour agone. His eyes were  set at eight i' the morning.
translation: Oh, he's drunk, Sir Toby, since an hour ago. He was cross eyed at eight in the morning.

original: Then he’s a rogue, and a passy-measures pavin. I hate a drunken rogue.
translation: Then he's a rogue, and I hate a drunken rogue. He spins and sways like he's doing a slow dance.

original: Away with him! Who hath made this havoc with them?
translation: Take him away! Who has caused all this trouble?

original: I’ll help you, Sir Toby, because we’ll be dressed  together.
translation: I'll help you, Sir Toby. They'll bandage us up together.

original: Will you help?—An ass-head, and a coxcomb, and a knave, a thin-faced knave, a gull!
translation: Will you help me—an ass, and a fool, and a bastard, a gullible skinny bastard?

original: Get him to bed, and let his hurt be looked to.
translation: Get him to bed, and make sure his wounds are tended to.

original: I am sorry, madam, I have hurt your kinsman,   But, had it been the brother of my blood,   I must have done no less with wit and safety.
translation: I am sorry, madam. I've hurt your relative, but I would've had to do the same thing even to my own brother, for I was acting in self-defense.

original: You throw a strange regard upon me, and by that   I do perceive it hath offended you.
translation: You're looking at me like I'm a stranger, so I can tell that I've offended you.

original: Pardon me, sweet one, even for the vows   We made each other but so late ago.
translation: Forgive me, sweet one, for the sake of the vows we made to each other so recently.

original: One face, one voice, one habit, and two persons! A natural perspective, that is and is not!
Antonio, O my dear Antonio! How have the hours racked and tortured me Since I have lost thee!
translation: Antonio, oh my dear Antonio! How time has tortured me ever since I lost you!

original: Sebastian are you?
translation: Are you Sebastian, then?

original: Fear’st thou that, Antonio?
translation: Do you doubt that, Antonio?

original: How have you made division of yourself?
translation: How have you divided yourself in two?

original: An apple, cleft in two, is not more twin   Than these two creatures. Which is Sebastian?
translation: These two people are as identical as two halves of an apple. Which is Sebastian?

original: Most wonderful!
translation: It's unbelievable!

original: Do I stand there? I never had a  brother;   Nor can there be that deity in my nature,   Of here and everywhere.
translation: Is that me standing there? I never had a brother, and I'm not a god who can be everywhere at once.

original: I had a sister,   Whom the blind waves and surges have devoured.
translation: I had a sister, but she was drowned by the cruel ocean.

original: Of charity, what kin are you to me?   What countryman? What name? What parentage?
translation: Please tell me, are you related to me? What country are you from? What is your name? Who are your parents?

original: Of Messaline. Sebastian was my father;   Such a Sebastian was my brother too,
translation: I am from Messaline. Sebastian was my father, and my brother was also named Sebastian.

original: So went he suited to his watery tomb
translation: He was dressed just like you when he drowned.

original: If spirits can assume both form and suit   You come to fright us.
translation: If ghosts can take on human forms and clothes, then you must be here to frighten us.

original: A spirit I am indeed,   But am in that dimension grossly clad   Which from the womb I did participate.
translation: I am a spirit indeed, as I have a soul. But my spirit wears the same earthly form that I've had since I was born. I

original: Were you a woman, as the rest goes even,
translation: f you were only a woman—since everything else about you fits—

original: My father had a mole upon his brow.
translation: My father had a mole on his forehead.

original: And so had mine.
translation: Mine did too.

original: And died that day when Viola from her birth Had numbered thirteen years.
translation: And he died on the day that Viola turned thirteen.

original: Oh, that record is lively in my soul!  He finished indeed his mortal act That day that made my sister thirteen years.
translation: Oh, that memory is still so vivid to me! He did indeed die on the day my sister turned thirteen.

original: If nothing lets to make us happy both   But this my masculine usurped attire,   Do not embrace me till each circumstance   Of place, time, fortune, do cohere and jump   That I am Viola.
translation: If the only thing keeping us from being happy is my deceptive masculine clothes, then don't hug me until every circumstance of place, time, and luck fit together and prove that I am Viola.

original: Which to confirm,   I’ll bring you to a captain in this town,   Where lie my maiden weeds, by whose gentle help   I was preserved to serve this noble count.
translation: To confirm this, I'll take you to a captain in this town who has been keeping my woman's clothing, and who saved my life so that I might serve this noble Duke.

original: All the occurrence of my fortune since   Hath been between this lady and this lord.
translation: Everything that's happened to me since then has involved this lady and this lord.

original: So comes it, lady, you have been mistook.   But nature to her bias drew in that.
translation: So you've been mistaken, my lady. But nature has fixed everything and drawn you to your natural orientation.  Your love for Cesario was really an inclination for someone like me.

original: You would have been contracted to a maid;
translation: You wanted to be married to a maiden,

original: Nor are you therein, by my life, deceived.   You are betrothed both to a maid and man.
translation: but you weren't actually deceived about that, given that you believed you were married to my sister.

original: Be not amazed. Right noble is his blood.
translation: Don't be shocked.  His blood is pure and noble .

original: If this be so, as yet the glass seems true,   I shall have share in this most happy wreck.
Boy, thou hast said to me a thousand times   Thou never shouldst love woman like to me.
translation: Boy, you've said to me a thousand times that you'd never love a woman like you love me.

original: And all those sayings will I overswear;
translation: Everything I said before I'll promise once again,

original: And those swearings keep as true in soul   As doth that orbèd continent the fire   That severs day from night.
translation: and I'll keep my promises in my soul like fire is kept in the sun.

original: Give me thy hand, And let me see thee in thy woman’s weeds.
translation: Give me your hand, and let me see you in your woman's clothes.

original: The captain that did bring me first on shore   Hath my maid’s garments.
translation: The captain who first brought me to shore has my woman's clothing.

original: He, upon some action,   Is now in durance at Malvolio’s suit,   A gentleman and follower of my lady’s.
translation: He has some legal charge against him, and is in prison because he's been sued by Malvolio—a gentleman and a servant of my lady's.

original: He shall enlarge him.
translation: He'll release him.

original: Fetch Malvolio hither:   And yet, alas, now I remember me,   They say, poor gentleman, he’s much distract.
translation: Bring Malvolio here—but no, now I remember, they say that the poor gentleman is mentally confused.

original: A most extracting frenzy of mine own   From my remembrance clearly banished his.
translation: My own distracting madness made me forget all about him.

original: (to FOOL)   How does he, sirrah?
translation: [To the FOOL]  How is he, fool?

original: Truly, madam, he holds Beelzebub at the staves' end as  well as a man in his case may do.
translation: Truly, madam, he keeps the devil away as well as a man in his situation can.

original: Has here writ a letter to you. I should have given ’t you today morning, but  as a madman’s epistles are no gospels, so it skills not  much when they are delivered.
translation: He's written a letter to you here. I should have given it to you this morning, but a madman's letters aren't gospel truth, so it doesn't matter too much when they're delivered.

original: Open ’t, and read it.
translation: Open it, and read it.

original: Look then to be well edified when the fool delivers the madman.    “By the Lord, madam,”—
translation: Be prepared to learn a lot now, for a fool is reciting the words of a madman.  "By God, madam,"—

original: How now? Art thou mad?
translation: What's this? Are you crazy?

original: No, madam, I do but read madness. An your ladyship will have it as it ought to be, you must allow  vox.
translation: No, madam, but I'm reading the words of craziness. And if you want things done the right way, then let me do a dramatic reading.

original: Prithee, read i' thy right wits.
translation: Please, read it like a sane person.

original: So I do, madonna. But to read his right wits is to read thus. Therefore perpend, my princess, and give ear.
translation: I will, holy lady, but even if I read this letter sanely, I'll still sound crazy. So pay attention, my princess, and listen.

original: Read it you, sirrah.
translation: You read it, sir.

original: “By the Lord, madam, you wrong me, and the world shall  know it.
translation: "By God, madam, you've wronged me, and the world will know about it.

original: Though you have put me into darkness and given  your drunken cousin rule over me, yet have I the benefit of my senses as well as your Ladyship.
translation: You've put me in a dark room and let your drunken uncle torment me, but I've still kept my sanity and am no more crazy than you are.

original: I have your own  letter that induced me to the semblance I put on, with  the which I doubt not but to do myself much right or you much shame.
translation: I have your own letter, which encouraged me to act the way I did, and with this letter I will prove that I am innocent and you are guilty.

original: Think of me as you please. I leave my duty  a little unthought of and speak out of my injury. The  madly used Malvolio.”
translation: Think of me however you want. I will leave my role as your steward and speak out about the injuries you've caused me. Signed, the madly-abused Malvolio."

original: Did he write this?
translation: Did he write this?

original: Ay, madam.
translation: Yes, madam.

original: This savors not much of distraction.
translation: This doesn't sound much like madness.

original: See him delivered, Fabian; bring him hither.
translation: Release him, Fabian, and bring him here.

original: My lord so please you, these things further thought  on,   To think me as well a sister as a wife,
translation: My lord, if you'll take into consideration what you've just seen and heard, I hope that you'll accept me as a sister-in-law instead of a wife.

original: One day shall crown the alliance on ’t, so please you,   Here at my house and at my proper cost.
translation: We can have the two weddings on the same day, if you want, here at my house, and I'll pay for everything.

original: Madam, I am most apt to embrace your offer.
translation: Madam, I'll happily accept your offer.

original: (to VIOLA)   Your master quits you, and for your service  done him,   So much against the mettle of your sex,   So far beneath your soft and tender breeding,
translation: [To VIOLA]  Your master releases you from his service. Because you served me so well, doing things that no woman, especially one of your noble birth,

original: And since you called me “master” for so long,   Here is my hand.
translation: should be expected to do, and because you called me "master" for so long, I will offer you my hand in marriage.

original: You shall from this time be   Your master’s mistress.
translation: From now on you'll be your master's mistress.

original: A sister! You are she.
translation: And you will be my sister!

original: Is this the madman?
translation: Is this the madman?

original: Ay, my lord, this same. How now, Malvolio!
translation: Yes, my lord, that's him. How are you, Malvolio?

original: Madam, you have done me wrong, Notorious wrong.
translation: Madam, you have mistreated me. Scandalously mistreated me.

original: Have I, Malvolio? No.
translation: Have I, Malvolio? No.

original: (handing a paper)     Lady, you have. Pray you, peruse that letter.   You must not now deny it is your hand.
translation: [Handing OLIVIA a paper]  Lady, you have. Please look at that letter. You can't deny that it's in your handwriting.

original: Write from it if you can, in hand or phrase;   Or say ’tis not your seal, not your invention:   You can say none of this.
translation: Try to write differently if you can, or try to say that that isn't your seal, with your design on it—you can't deny any of this.

original: Well, grant it then   And tell me, in the modesty of honor,   Why you have given me such clear lights of favor,   Bade me come smiling and cross-gartered to you,   To put on yellow stockings, and to frown   Upon Sir Toby and the lighter people?
translation: Well, admit it then and tell me, with the sincerity of an honorable person, why you gave me such clear signs of affection, telling me to come to you smiling, with crossed laces, to wear yellow stockings, and to be rude to Sir Toby and the servants?

original: And, acting this in an obedient hope,   Why have you suffered me to be imprisoned,   Kept in a dark house, visited by the priest,
translation: And when I obeyed all your commands, why did you then let me be imprisoned in a dark house, be visited by a priest—

original: And made the most notorious geck and gull   That e'er invention played on? Tell me why.
translation: and make me into the biggest fool and sucker that ever had a joke played on him? Tell me why.

original: Alas, Malvolio, this is not my writing,   Though, I confess, much like the character.
translation: Alas, Malvolio, this is not my handwriting. Though, I admit, the letters look very similar.

original: But out of question, ’tis Maria’s hand.   And now I do bethink me, it was she   First told me thou wast mad, then camest in smiling,   And in such forms which here were presupposed   Upon thee in the letter.
translation: But it's definitely Maria's handwriting.  And now that I think about it, she was the one who first told me you were crazy, and then you came in smiling and acting in the way the letter instructed you to act.

original: Prithee, be content.   This practice hath most shrewdly passed upon thee;   But when we know the grounds and authors of it,   Thou shalt be both the plaintiff and the judge   Of thine own cause.
translation: Please, don't be so upset. You've been fooled by a cruel practical joke,  but when we find out who's responsible for this, you will be the judge and jury who sentences the culprits to a punishment for their crime.

original: Good madam, hear me speak,   And let no quarrel nor no brawl to come   Taint the condition of this present hour,   Which I have wonder’d at.
translation: Good madam, let me speak, and don't let any quarreling cast a shadow over the surprised joy of these happy couples, which I have been amazed by.

original: In hope it shall not,   Most freely I confess, myself and Toby   Set this device against Malvolio here,   Upon some stubborn and uncourteous parts   We had conceived against him.
translation: To avoid any fighting, I'll confess that Toby and I were the ones who tricked Malvolio here, because of the arrogant and rude behavior we had observed in him.

original: Maria writ   The letter at Sir Toby’s great importance,   In recompense whereof he hath married her.
translation: Maria only wrote the letter at Sir Toby's urgent request, and he has rewarded her for it by marrying her.

original: How with a sportful malice it was followed,   May rather pluck on laughter than revenge,   If that the injuries be justly weighed   That have on both sides passed.
translation: The whole practical joke should inspire laughter instead of revenge, especially if we consider that both sides injured each other equally.

original: Alas, poor fool, how have they baffled  thee!
translation: Alas, you poor fool, how they've humiliated you!

translation: Cesario, come here. You'll be Cesario to me while you're still a man, but when I see you in women's clothes, then you'll be Orsino's mistress, and his love's queen.

original: When that I was and a little tiny boy,   With hey, ho, the wind and the rain,   A foolish thing was but a toy,   For the rain it raineth every day. translation: The deer that wants to mate with the lion must die in the process.

original: heart too capable   Of every line and trick of his sweet favour:

translation: Yes. You have some hint of soldier about you: let me ask you a question. Man is the enemy of virginity: how can we barricade it up against him?

translation: Keep him out.

There is none: man, sitting down before you, will undermine you and blow you up.

translation: A virgin is like a man who hangs himself, because virginity should kill itself

original: You shall not need to fear me.

translation: You came, I think, from France?

translation: Here you're about to see a countryman of yours that has served worthily.

translation: What's his name?

translation: All that she has of value is her honesty, and I don't know if even that has been examined.

translation: Alas, poor lady! It's a hard bondage to become the wife of a lord who detests you.

translation: I assume, good creature, wherever she may be, her heart is heavy. This young maid here might do her a great wrong if she wanted to.

original: How do you mean? May be the amorous count solicits her In the unlawful purpose.
translation: What do you mean? Maybe the loving count is trying to seduce her?

original: He does indeed;
translation: He is indeed.

original: And brokes with all that can in such a suit   Corrupt the tender honour of a maid:
translation: And he comes with full force on this mission to corrupt the tender honor of a virgin.

original: But she is arm'd for him and keeps her guard   In honestest defence.
translation: But she is prepared for him and keeps her guard up in honest defense.

original: The gods forbid else!
translation: The gods forbid she do otherwise!

original: So, now they come:
translation: So, now they come.

original: That is Antonio, the duke's eldest son; That, Escalus.
translation: That is Antonio, the duke's eldest son. That one's Escalus.

original: Which is the Frenchman?
translation: Which one is the Frenchman?

original: He;   That with the plume:
translation: Him. That one with the plume.

original: 'tis a most gallant fellow.   I would he loved his wife:

translation: but still, is he not a handsome man?

translation: I like his looks.

translation: It's a pity he's not honest. There's the same rogue that takes him to these places. If I were his wife, I would poison that vile rascal.

translation: Which one's he?

translation: That silly looking man in the scarves. Why is he melancholy?

translation: and, to pay you further, I'll share some advice with this virgin that will be worth hearing.

translation: We'll take your offer gratefully.

translation: If your lordship doesn't find him to be a worthless nothing, don't respect me any longer.

original: On my life, my lord, a bubble.
translation: On my life, my lord, he'll prove to be nothing but a bubble.

original: Do you think I am so far deceived in him?
translation: You really think I'm so completely deceived by him?

translation: Believe it, my lord, based on my own personal knowledge, without any ill will, but to speak of him as I would speak of a family member:

translation: and he doesn't have one good quality worthy of following your lordship.

translation: It would be best that you know him as he is. Otherwise, if you're too trusting of his virtue, which he doesn't have, he might fail you at some great and important moment.

original: I would I knew in what particular action to try him.
translation: I wish I could think of a particular way to test him.

translation: There's no better way than to let him fetch back his lost drum which we've all heard him so confidently say he'll do.

translation: I know you are valiant, and I'll support you when I speak of your soldierly ability. Farewell.

translation: I do not love speaking at length.

translation: Sure, no more than a fish loves water.

translation: Will you go see her?

translation: With all my heart, my lord.

translation: If you doubt that I'm she, I don't know how else I'll prove it to you further without ruining my whole plan.

original: and she told me,   In a sweet verbal brief, it did concern   Your highness with herself.
translation: She told me in person that it has something to do with your highness and herself.

original: Upon his many protestations to marry me   when his wife was dead, I blush to say it, he won   me.
translation: "After he told me many times that he would marry me when his wife was dead, I blush to say that I gave myself to him.

original: Now is the Count Rousillon a widower:
translation: Now the Count Rousillon is a widower.

original: his vows   are forfeited to me, and my honour's paid to him.
translation: He broke his vows to me and I've already given my honor away to him.

original: He   stole from Florence, taking no leave, and I follow   him to his country for justice:
translation: He fled from Florence without saying goodbye, and I've followed him to his country for justice.

original: grant it me, O   king!
translation: Grant me justice, oh king!

original: in you it best lies;
translation: You're the only one who can.

original: otherwise a seducer   flourishes, and a poor maid is undone.   DIANA CAPILET.
translation: Otherwise, a seducer will live happily and a poor maid will be ruined. Diana Capilet."

original: I will buy me a son-in-law in a fair, and toll for this: I'll none of him.
translation: I will buy myself a son-in-law at a fair and sell this one. I don't want anything to do with him.

original: The heavens have thought well on thee Lafeu,   To bring forth this discovery.
translation: The heavens have been kind to you, Lafeu, to reveal this information.

original: Seek these suitors:
translation: Find these people who want to speak to me.

original: Go speedily and bring again the count.
translation: Go quickly and bring the count back in.

original: I am afeard the life of Helen, lady,   Was foully snatch'd.
translation: Lady, I am afraid that Helena was the victim of foul play.

original: Now, justice on the doers!
translation: Now, may the perpetrators be brought to justice!

original: I wonder, sir, sith wives are monsters to you, And that you fly them as you swear them lordship, Yet you desire to marry.
translation: I'm surprised, sir, since wives are like monsters to you and you flee from them as soon as you make your vows to them, that you would want to marry again.

original: What woman's that?
translation: What woman is that?

original: I am, my lord, a wretched Florentine,   Derived from the ancient Capilet:
translation: I am, my lord, a wretched Florentine of the ancient Capilet family.

original: My suit, as I do understand, you know,   And therefore know how far I may be pitied.
