translation: You know why I'm here, I've been told, and therefore you know how much I deserve to be pitied.

original: I am her mother, sir, whose age and honour Both suffer under this complaint we bring, And both shall cease, without your remedy.
translation: I am her mother, sir. I'm too old for this shock and my honor has taken a hit because of this. I'll lose both my life and honor if you don't help us.

original: Come hither, count; do you know these women?
translation: Come here, count. Do you know these women?

original: My lord, I neither can nor will deny But that I know them: do they charge me further?
translation: My lord, I can't and won't deny that I know them. Do you they accuse me of anything else?

original: Why do you look so strange upon your wife?
translation: Why do you look upon your wife like you're a stranger?

original: She's none of mine, my lord.
translation: She's not my wife, my lord.

original: If you shall marry,   You give away this hand, and that is mine;
translation: If you marry someone, you'll give away your hand that belongs to me.

original: You give away heaven's vows, and those are mine;
translation: You'll give away heaven's vows and those belong to me.

original: You give away myself, which is known mine;
translation: You'll give yourself away and you are known to belong to me.

original: For I by vow am so embodied yours,
translation: For, by your vow, I am part of your body.

original: That she which marries you must marry me,   Either both or none.
translation: A woman who marries you must also then marry me. It's both of us or neither of us.

original: Your reputation comes too short for my daughter; you are no husband for her.
translation: Your reputation is much too bad to marry my daughter. You won't be marrying her.

original: My lord, this is a fond and desperate creature,   Whom sometime I have laugh'd with:
translation: My lord, this is a foolish and desperate creature who I laughed with occasionally.

original: let your highness   Lay a more noble thought upon mine honour   Than for to think that I would sink it here.
translation: I hope your highness would more nobly trust that I've been honorable than to think that I'd give my honor away to this woman.

original: Sir, for my thoughts, you have them ill to friend Till your deeds gain them: fairer prove your honour Than in my thought it lies.
translation: Sir, don't look for my thoughts to be friendly to you until your actions have earned it. Prove yourself to be more honorable than I think you are.

original: Good my lord, Ask him upon his oath, if he does think He had not my virginity.
translation: My good lord, ask him to swear that he didn't take my virginity.

original: What say'st thou to her?
translation: What do you say to her?

original: She's impudent, my lord, And was a common gamester to the camp.
translation: She's shameless, my lord, and was a common whore for the soldiers.

original: He does me wrong, my lord;
translation: He wrongs me, my lord.

original: if I were so,   He might have bought me at a common price:   Do not believe him.
translation: If I were what he says, he might have bought my love cheaply. Don't believe him.

original: O, behold this ring,   Whose high respect and rich validity   Did lack a parallel;
translation: Oh, look at this ring, that has no equal in respect and richness.

original: yet for all that   He gave it to a commoner o' the camp,   If I be one.
translation: For all that value, you think he gave it to a common army whore, if that's what you think I am?

original: He blushes, and 'tis it:
translation: He blushes and that seals the deal.

original: Of six preceding ancestors, that gem,   Conferr'd by testament to the sequent issue,   Hath it been owed and worn.
translation: For six generations, that gem, required by the wills and testaments to be passed down to the next heir, has been worn by our family.

original: This is his wife;   That ring's a thousand proofs.
translation: This is his wife. That ring gives the proof a thousand times.

original: Methought you said You saw one here in court could witness it.
translation: I thought you said you saw someone in the court who could be a witness.

original: I did, my lord, but loath am to produce So bad an instrument: his name's Parolles.
translation: I did, my lord, but I hate to produce such a bad man. His name's Parolles.

original: I saw the man to-day, if man he be.
translation: I saw the man today, if he is a man.

original: Find him, and bring him hither.
translation: Find him, and bring him here.

original: What of him?
translation: You'll believe Parolles?

original: He's quoted for a most perfidious slave,   With all the spots o' the world tax'd and debosh'd;
translation: He's known to be a lying rascal as disgraced and horrible as the worst blemishes in human history.

original: Whose nature sickens but to speak a truth.
translation: It would make him ill to tell the truth just once.

original: Am I or that or this for what he'll utter,   That will speak any thing?
translation: Are you going to make up your mind about me based on what he says when he'll say anything?

original: She hath that ring of yours.
translation: She has your ring.

original: I think she has:
translation: I thinks he does.

original: certain it is I liked her,   And boarded her i' the wanton way of youth:
translation: It's true that I liked her, and I made advances towards her like youths always do.

original: She knew her distance and did angle for me,   Madding my eagerness with her restraint,
translation: She knew how far apart we were socially and tried to win me, making me more eager by playing hard-to-get,

original: As all impediments in fancy's course   Are motives of more fancy;
translation: as all obstacles to desire tend to make the desire greater.

original: and, in fine,   Her infinite cunning, with her modern grace,   Subdued me to her rate: she got the ring;
translation: In short, her endless cunning, with her common charm, made me give her what she wanted: she got the ring.

original: And I had that which any inferior might   At market-price have bought.
translation: And I had something from her that any lower-class man could buy from her more cheaply.

original: I must be patient:
translation: I must be patient.

original: You, that have turn'd off a first so noble wife,   May justly diet me.
translation: If you've gotten rid of your first noble wife so easily, you'll obviously try to get rid of me too.

original: I pray you yet;
translation: I plead with you still.

original: Since you lack virtue, I will lose a husband;
translation: Since you have no virtue at all, I will lose a husband.

original: Send for your ring, I will return it home,   And give me mine again.
translation: Call for your ring, I'll put it back on and get out of here.

original: I have it not.
translation: I don't have it.

original: What ring was yours, I pray you?
translation: What ring belonged to you, can I ask?

original: Sir, much like The same upon your finger.
translation: Sir, a ring very similar to the one on your finger.

original: Know you this ring? this ring was his of late.
translation: You know this ring? This ring belonged to him recently.

original: And this was it I gave him, being abed.
translation: And this was the ring I gave him when we were in bed.

original: The story then goes false, you threw it him Out of a casement.
translation: This story must be false. You threw it to him out of a window.

original: I have spoke the truth.
translation: I have spoken the truth.

original: My lord, I do confess the ring was hers.
translation: My lord, I confess that the ring was hers.

original: You boggle shrewdly, every feather stars you. Is this the man you speak of?
translation: You tell lies manically, every change in the story startles you. Is this the man you mean?

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: Tell me, sirrah, but tell me true, I charge you,
translation: Tell me, sir, but tell me the truth, I command you.

original: Not fearing the displeasure of your master,
translation: Don't be afraid of making your master mad.

original: Which on your just proceeding I'll keep off,
translation: I'll deal with that if you answer honestly.

original: By him and by this woman here what know you?
translation: What do you know about him and this woman here?

original: So please your majesty, my master hath been an honourable gentleman: tricks he hath had in him, which gentlemen have.
translation: If it please your majesty, my master has been an honorable gentleman. He's only done things that gentlemen do.

original: Come, come, to the purpose: did he love this woman?
translation: Come, come, answer my question: did he love this woman?

original: Faith, sir, he did love her; but how?
translation: Well, sir, he did love her. But how did he love her?

original: How, I pray you?
translation: How, will you tell us?

original: He did love her, sir, as a gentleman loves a woman.
translation: Sir, he loved her as a gentleman loves a woman.

original: How is that?
translation: How is that?

original: He loved her, sir, and loved her not.
translation: Sir, he loved her and loved her not.

original: As thou art a knave, and no knave. What an equivocal companion is this!
translation: Just like you're a rogue and not a rogue. What a rambling companion this man is!

original: I am a poor man, and at your majesty's command.
translation: I am a poor man, and at your majesty's command.

original: He's a good drum, my lord, but a naughty orator.
translation: He beats the drum, well, my lord, but he speaks naughtily.

original: Do you know he promised me marriage?
translation: Do you know he promised me marriage?

original: Faith, I know more than I'll speak.
translation: Well, I know more than I'll say.

original: But wilt thou not speak all thou knowest?
translation: You won't say all you know?

original: Yes, so please your majesty. I did go between them,   as I said;
translation: Yes, if it please your majesty. I did go between them as I said.

original: but more than that, he loved her:
translation: Beyond that, he loved her.

original: for   indeed he was mad for her, and talked of Satan and   of Limbo and of Furies and I know not what:
translation: He was crazy for her and he talked in his passion about Satan and Limbo and the Furies and I don't know what else.

original: yet I   was in that credit with them at that time that I   knew of their going to bed, and of other motions,
translation: I was still friends with them when I knew that they had gone to bed together, and that other things had happened,

original: as promising her marriage, and things which would   derive me ill will to speak of;
translation: like him promising her marriage, and things which would make you angry to hear from me.

original: therefore I will not   speak what I know.
translation: Therefore I won't say what I know.

original: Thou hast spoken all already, unless thou canst say   they are married:
translation: You've said everything I need to know already unless you can say that they are married.

original: but thou art too fine in thy   evidence; therefore stand aside.
translation: But you are clear enough in your evidence. Therefore, stand aside.

original: Ay, my good lord.
translation: Yes, my good lord.

original: Where did you buy it? or who gave it you?
translation: Where did you buy it? Or who gave it to you?

original: It was not given me, nor I did not buy it.
translation: It was not given to me and I did not buy it.

original: Who lent it you?
translation: Who lent it to you?

original: It was not lent me neither.
translation: It wasn't lent to me either.

original: Where did you find it, then?
translation: Where did you find it, then?

original: I found it not.
translation: I didn't find it.

original: If it were yours by none of all these ways, How could you give it him?
translation: If you didn't get it any of these ways, how did you have it to give it to him?

original: I never gave it him.
translation: I never gave it to him.

original: This woman's an easy glove, my lord; she goes off and on at pleasure.
translation: This woman's like a loose glove, my lord. She slips off and on, going back and forth, without warning.

original: This ring was mine; I gave it his first wife.
translation: This ring belonged to me. I gave it to his first wife.

original: It might be yours or hers, for aught I know.
translation: It could be yours or it could be hers for all that I know.

original: Take her away; I do not like her now;
translation: Take her away. I don't like her anymore.

original: To prison with her: and away with him.
translation: Take her to prison and away with him.

original: Unless thou tell'st me where thou hadst this ring,   Thou diest within this hour.
translation: Unless you tell me where you got this ring, you'll die within the hour.

original: I'll never tell you.
translation: I'll never tell you.

original: Take her away.
translation: Take her away.

original: I'll put in bail, my liege.
translation: I'll post my bail, my lord.

original: I think thee now some common customer.
translation: Now I think you probably are a whore.

original: By Jove, if ever I knew man, 'twas you.
translation: By God, if I've ever slept with a man, it was you.

original: Wherefore hast thou accused him all this while?
translation: Why have you accused him of sleeping with you all this time then?

original: Because he's guilty, and he is not guilty:
translation: Because he's guilty and he's not guilty.

original: He knows I am no maid, and he'll swear to't;
translation: He knows I'm not a virgin and he'll swear to it.

original: I'll swear I am a maid, and he knows not.
translation: I swear I am a virgin and he doesn't know it.

original: Great king, I am no strumpet, by my life;
translation: Great king, I'm no loose woman, by my life.

original: I am either maid, or else this old man's wife.
translation: I am either a virgin, or else this old man's wife.

original: She does abuse our ears: to prison with her.
translation: She just talks nonsense to us. To prison with her.

original: Good mother, fetch my bail. Stay, royal sir:
translation: Good mother, get my bail. Hold one moment, royal sir.

original: The jeweller that owes the ring is sent for,   And he shall surety me.
translation: The jeweler that the ring came from is coming, and he will pay my bail.

original: But for this lord,   Who hath abused me, as he knows himself,   Though yet he never harm'd me, here I quit him:
translation: As for this lord, who has abused me, as he's said himself, although he's never yet harmed me, this is the last I'll say of him:

original: He knows himself my bed he hath defiled;   And at that time he got his wife with child:
translation: He knows he's defiled my bed, and when he did so, he got his wife pregnant.

original: Dead though she be, she feels her young one kick:
translation: Even though she's dead, she feels her child kick inside her.

original: So there's my riddle: one that's dead is quick:   And now behold the meaning.
translation: So there's my riddle: someone who's dead is pregnant. And now you'll see what I mean.

original: Is there no exorcist Beguiles the truer office of mine eyes? Is't real that I see?
translation: Is there no sorcerer who has bewitched me to see what my eyes present to me? Is what I see real?

original: No, my good lord; 'Tis but the shadow of a wife you see, The name and not the thing.
translation: No, my good lord. It's only the shadow of a wife you see before you. The name of wife but not the thing itself.

original: Both, both. O, pardon!
translation: Both, both. Oh, forgive me!

original: O my good lord, when I was like this maid,   I found you wondrous kind.
translation: Oh, my good lord, when I pretended to be this maid, I found you incredibly kind.

original: There is your ring;   And, look you, here's your letter;   this it says:
translation: There's your ring. And, look at this, here's your letter.  Here's what it says:

original: 'When from my finger you can get this ring   And are by me with child,' etc.
translation: "When you can get this ring from my finger and are pregnant by me, etc."

original: This is done:   Will you be mine, now you are doubly won?
translation: This is done. Will you be mine, now that I've fulfilled both conditions?

original: If she, my liege, can make me know this clearly, I'll love her dearly, ever, ever dearly.
translation: My lord, if she can explain this to me clearly, I'll love her dearly, ever, ever dearly.

original: If it appear not plain and prove untrue, Deadly divorce step between me and you! O my dear mother, do I see you living?
translation: If it's not clear and it proves untrue, then we'll instantly be separated by divorce!

original: Mine eyes smell onions; I shall weep anon:
Good Tom Drum, lend me a handkercher: so, I thank thee: wait on me home, I'll make sport with  thee: Let thy courtesies alone, they are scurvy ones.
translation: Good Tom Drum, lend me a handkerchief. There, I thank you. Come visit me at home and we'll have a fun time. Forget your manners—your manners are worthless anyway.

original: Let us from point to point this story know,   To make the even truth in pleasure flow.
translation: Tell us the story from beginning to end so that we can enjoy the whole tale.

original: The king's a beggar, now the play is done:
translation: The king now turns into a beggar since the play is over.

original: All is well ended, if this suit be won,   That you express content;
translation: All will indeed end well if you tell us you're happy with our performance.

original: which we will pay,   With strife to please you, day exceeding day:
translation: We'll do whatever we can to please you day after day.

original: Ours be your patience then, and yours our parts;
translation: Now we'll patiently listen while you perform for us:

original: Your gentle hands lend us, and take our hearts.
translation: give us your hands in applause and we'll love you for it.

original: Before we proceed any further, hear me speak.
translation: Before we go on, hear me out.

original: Speak, speak.
translation: Go ahead. Talk.

original: You are all resolved rather to die than to famish?
translation: You are all committed to fight to the death rather than die by starvation?

original: Resolved. resolved.
translation: Yes, we're committed.

original: First, you know Caius Marcius is chief enemy to the  people.
translation: First, you know Caius Marcius is the people's greatest enemy.

original: We know't, we know't.
translation: We know it!

original: Let us kill him, and we'll have corn at our own price. Is't a verdict?
translation: Let's kill him and sell corn at a price we can decide. Do we have an agreement?

original: No more talking on't; let it be done: away, away!
translation: Enough talk; let it be done: let's go!

original: One word, good citizens.
translation: Hold on: listen, good citizens.

original: We are accounted poor citizens, the patricians good.   What authority surfeits on would relieve us:
translation: We are thought of as poor and worthless, while the senators are thought of as noble. Their leftovers would be enough for us.

original: if they   would yield us but the superfluity, while it were   wholesome, we might guess they relieved us humanely;   but they think we are too dear:
translation: If they would only give us the scraps from their table, as long as it isn't spoiled, we'd think of it as generous; but they think that even this is  asking too much.

original: the leanness that   afflicts us, the object of our misery, is as an   inventory to particularise their abundance; our   sufferance is a gain to them.
translation: Our starvation, which makes us miserable, is the yardstick by which they measure their successes— they celebrate our suffering!

original: Let us revenge this with   our pikes, ere we become rakes: for the gods know I   speak this in hunger for bread, not in thirst for  revenge.
translation: Let us take revenge with our pikes, before we become as thin as they are: the gods know I say so out of hunger, not out of thirst for revenge.

original: Would you proceed especially against Caius Marcius?
translation: Should we focus our revenge on Caius Marcius?

original: Against him first: he's a very dog to the commonalty.
translation: Yes, him first: he's terrible to the common people.

original: Consider you what services he has done for his country?
translation: What about all he's done for this country?

original: Very well; and could be content to give him good report fort, but that he pays himself with being proud.
translation: It's all well and good, and he ought to be satisfied with our admiration, but instead he rubs it in our faces.

original: Nay, but speak not maliciously.
translation: Come on, don't speak rudely of him.

original: I say unto you, what he hath done famously, he did   it to that end:
translation: Listen: the things he's done for us, he's done only for the fame.

original: though soft-conscienced men can be   content to say it was for his country he did it to   please his mother and to be partly proud;
translation: Forgiving men might say he did it for his country, but really he did it only to please his mother and partly to be proud.

original: which he   is, even till the altitude of his virtue.
translation: However brave he is, it's only equal to his arrogance.

original: What he cannot help in his nature, you account a vice in him. You must in no way say he is covetous.
translation: You're condemning him for being who he is. You can't say he's greedy, after all.

original: If I must not, I need not be barren of accusations; he hath faults, with surplus, to tire in repetition.
translation: If he's not greedy, he's horrible in a hundred other ways; we'd grow exhausted listing all his faults.

original: What shouts are these? The other side o' the city is risen: why stay we prating here? to the Capitol!
translation: Where is that shouting from? Other parts of the city are in revolt already. Why are we standing here chattering? To the Capitol!

original: Come, come.
translation: Come, come!

original: Soft! who comes here?
translation: Wait! Who is that?

original: Worthy Menenius Agrippa; one that hath always loved the people.
translation: Honorable Menenius Agrippa; a man who has always had the common people's interests in mind.

original: He's one honest enough: would all the rest were so!
translation: He's an honest politician: if only the others were!

original: What work's, my countrymen, in hand? where go you With bats and clubs? The matter? speak, I pray you.
translation: What are you about to do, fellow citizens? Where are you going with these bats and clubs? What's going on? Please, tell me.

original: Our business is not unknown to the senate; they have   had inkling this fortnight what we intend to do,   which now we'll show 'em in deeds.
translation: The senate is well aware of our business; they've known for a month what we intend to do, and we'll show them now we meant it.

original: They say poor   suitors have strong breaths: they shall know we   have strong arms too.
translation: They say the poor people coming to ask for help have only a strong odor to them, but we'll show them we have strong arms too.

original: Why, masters, my good friends, mine honest neighbours, Will you undo yourselves?
translation: Sirs, good friends, honest neighbors, why? Are you trying to get yourselves killed?

original: We cannot, sir, we are undone already.
translation: That would be pointless, sir, we're already dying.

original: I tell you, friends, most charitable care   Have the patricians of you.
translation: I tell you, friends, the senators care deeply about all of you.

original: For your wants,   Your suffering in this dearth, you may as well   Strike at the heaven with your staves as lift them   Against the Roman state, whose course will on   The way it takes, cracking ten thousand curbs   Of more strong link asunder than can ever   Appear in your impediment.
translation: You may as well attack heaven with your sticks as try to fight Rome; it won't do anything to stop your starvation. Rome will go on as it always does, easily crushing ten thousand times what you can throw against it.

original: For the dearth,   The gods, not the patricians, make it, and   Your knees to them, not arms, must help.
translation: As for the lack of food, it's not the senators' fault. Begging them for help will do more good than attacking them.

original: Alack,   You are transported by calamity   Thither where more attends you, and you slander   The helms o' the state, who care for you like fathers,   When you curse them as enemies.
translation: Alas, this tragedy has driven you mad if  you think that cursing the senators, who care for you like your own parents, will make them more willing to help you.

original: Care for us! True, indeed! They ne'er cared for us   yet: suffer us to famish, and their store-houses   crammed with grain;
translation: Care for us! Yeah, right! They've never cared for us: they will let us starve while their warehouses are full of food.

original: make edicts for usury, to   support usurers; repeal daily any wholesome act   established against the rich, and provide more   piercing statutes daily, to chain up and restrain   the poor.
translation: They've supported laws which cheat us financially; every day they do more to protect the rich and hurt the poor.

original: If the wars eat us not up, they will; and   there's all the love they bear us.
translation: @ That's  how they show they love us.

original: Either you must   Confess yourselves wondrous malicious,   Or be accused of folly.
translation: Either you have to admit you're awfully cruel, or I must simply say you're wrong.

original: I shall tell you   A pretty tale: it may be you have heard it;   But, since it serves my purpose, I will venture   To stale 't a little more.
translation: Let me tell you a story. Maybe you've heard it before, but since it applies to this situation so well, allow me to tell it again.

original: Well, I'll hear it, sir: yet you must not think to fob off our disgrace with a tale: but, an 't please you, deliver.
translation: Well, I'll listen, sir: but you can't think to do away with our suffering with a story. Still, if you want, go ahead.

original: There was a time when all the body's members   Rebell'd against the belly, thus accused it:   That only like a gulf it did remain   I' the midst o' the body, idle and unactive,   Still cupboarding the viand,
translation: Once upon a time,  all the body's other parts rebelled against the belly  and accused it of being  just a bottomless pit in the middle of the body that hoards all the food.

original: never bearing   Like labour with the rest, where the other instruments   Did see and hear, devise, instruct, walk, feel,   And, mutually participate, did minister   Unto the appetite and affection common   Of the whole body. The belly answer'd—
translation: It does nothing, while all the other parts of the body have a role: they see and hear, think, speak, walk, touch, and by working together, these parts contribute to the greater good of the whole body. The belly answered—

original: Well, sir, what answer made the belly?
translation: Well, sir? What did the belly answer?

original: Sir, I shall tell you. With a kind of smile,   Which ne'er came from the lungs, but even thus—
translation: Sir, I shall tell you. With a belly laugh—the kind of laugh which never came from the lungs, but like this, see?  [He laughs deeply]

original: For, look you, I may make the belly smile   As well as speak—it tauntingly replied   To the discontented members, the mutinous parts   That envied his receipt;
translation: For look, I can make the belly laugh as well as rumble—it replied sarcastically to the other parts of the body, the parts which envied the belly's food—

original: even so most fitly   As you malign our senators for that   They are not such as you.
translation: just the way you are criticizing our senators for being different from you.

original: Your belly's answer? What!   The kingly-crowned head, the vigilant eye,   The counsellor heart, the arm our soldier,   Our steed the leg, the tongue our trumpeter.
translation: Well? What did your belly answer? The majestic head, the careful eye, the wise heart, the strong arm, the swift leg, the tongue which speaks.

original: With other muniments and petty helps   In this our fabric, if that they—
translation: With other bits and minor assistants in this our skin, if they—

original: What then? 'Fore me, this fellow speaks! What then? what then?
translation: What, then? You want to interrupt me and tell your own story? What then? What then?

original: Should by the cormorant belly be restrain'd, Who is the sink o' the body,—
translation: If all those hard-working body parts are dragged down by the greedy belly, that garbage-pit of the body—

original: Well, what then?
translation: Well, what then?

original: The former agents, if they did complain, What could the belly answer?
translation: If those other parts did complain, what could the belly possibly say in its defense?

original: I will tell you If you'll bestow a small—of what you have little— Patience awhile, you'll hear the belly's answer.
translation: I'll tell you, if you can give me just a little bit of patience—and I know you don't have much—you'll hear the belly's answer.

original: Ye're long about it.
translation: You're taking long enough.

original: Note me this, good friend;   Your most grave belly was deliberate,   Not rash like his accusers, and thus answer'd:
translation: Listen to me, my friend. The belly was was quite serious, and careful in his answer—unlike his rowdy accusers—and answered like this:

original: 'True is it, my incorporate friends,' quoth he,   'That I receive the general food at first,   Which you do live upon; and fit it is,   Because I am the store-house and the shop   Of the whole body:
translation: "It's true, friends of my body," he said, "That I receive the food we all depend on first, but of course I do: I'm the body's storage and its grocery store.

original: but, if you do remember,   I send it through the rivers of your blood,   Even to the court, the heart, to the seat o' the brain;
translation: But don't forget that I distribute nutrients into the rivers of your blood, and to the heart, and to the brain;

original: And, through the cranks and offices of man,   The strongest nerves and small inferior veins   From me receive that natural competency   Whereby they live: and though that all at once,   You, my good friends,'—this says the belly, mark me,—
translation: it is I who send that energy everywhere, into all the working parts of a man. Both the strongest nerves and the tiniest little veins get their livelihood from me. And despite all of that, you really want to say to me"—the belly says this, just to be clear—

original: Ay, sir; well, well.
translation: Sure, sir; go on.

original: 'Though all at once cannot   See what I do deliver out to each,   Yet I can make my audit up,
translation: "Though you can't all see that I am giving out to you, I can tally it up

original: that all   From me do back receive the flour of all,   And leave me but the bran.' What say you to't?
translation: and show you that you are getting the best, while I'm keeping just the leftovers for myself." What do you say to all that?

original: It was an answer: how apply you this?
translation: It was an answer, I guess, but what are you trying to say?

original: The senators of Rome are this good belly,   And you the mutinous members;
translation: The senators of Rome are this good belly, and you are the rioting body parts. Just think about what the senators really do—

original: for examine   Their counsels and their cares, digest things rightly   Touching the weal o' the common, you shall find   No public benefit which you receive   But it proceeds or comes from them to you   And no way from yourselves.
translation: think also about what the common people do— and you'll find that there's no good thing you receive that doesn't come from them.

original: What do you think,   You, the great toe of this assembly?
translation: What do you think of that, you,  big toe  of this group?

original: I the great toe! why the great toe?
translation: Why am I the big toe?

original: For that, being one o' the lowest, basest, poorest,   Of this most wise rebellion, thou go'st foremost:
translation: Well, because as one of the lowest and poorest of this most wise rebellion,  you go first.

original: Thou rascal, that art worst in blood to run,   Lead'st first to win some vantage.
translation: You, wretched man, who are the lowest-born of this whole group, are trying to gain something by leading them.

original: But make you ready your stiff bats and clubs:   Rome and her rats are at the point of battle;   The one side must have bale.
translation: Well, you'd better get your bats and clubs ready: if you rats are really going to fight Rome, one side is going to wind up hurt.

original: Hail, noble Marcius!
translation: Welcome, honorable Marcius!

original: Thanks. What's the matter, you dissentious rogues,
translation: Thanks. What's the matter, you rebellious good-for-nothings, that,

original: That, rubbing the poor itch of your opinion,   Make yourselves scabs?
translation: on the  whim of your opinions, become troublemakers  like this ?

original: We have ever your good word.
translation: You always have the nicest things to say about us.

original: He that will give good words to thee will flatter   Beneath abhorring. What would you have, you curs,   That like nor peace nor war?
translation: Anyone who would compliment you would flatter you terribly. What do you want, you dogs, that like neither peace nor war?

original: the one affrights you,   The other makes you proud. He that trusts to you,   Where he should find you lions, finds you hares;   Where foxes, geese: you are no surer, no,   Than is the coal of fire upon the ice,   Or hailstone in the sun.
translation: War scares you, peace makes you too confident in yourselves. Anyone that trusts you finds cowards where they might hope for brave men. They find idiots where they might hope for scholars. You're about as reliable as a snowball on the sun, or a coal of fire on ice.

original: Your virtue is   To make him worthy whose offence subdues him   And curse that justice did it.   Who deserves greatness   Deserves your hate; and your affections are   A sick man's appetite, who desires most that   Which would increase his evil.
translation: The only thing you're good at is celebrating criminals and then cursing justice. You hate great men because they're great, and you indulge only in vices.

original: He that depends   Upon your favours swims with fins of lead   And hews down oaks with rushes. Hang ye! Trust Ye?   With every minute you do change a mind,   And call him noble that was now your hate,   Him vile that was your garland.
translation: Anyone relying on you is trying to swim with lead weights or cut down trees with grass; they only slow themselves down. Go hang yourselves! Trust you? With every minute you change your mind: you suddenly hate someone you loved, or want to honor someone you hated just moments ago.

original: What's the matter,   That in these several places of the city   You cry against the noble senate, who,   Under the gods, keep you in awe, which else   Would feed on one another?
translation: What's your problem now, that you're up in arms against the senate around the city— the very senate whose leadership, with the blessing of the god,s keeps you from killing each other?

original: What's their seeking?
translation: What do they want?

original: For corn at their own rates; whereof, they say, The city is well stored.
translation: They're asking to buy corn at a price they would determine. They say the city has plenty of it.

original: Hang 'em! They say!
translation: Oh, let them go hang themselves!

original: They'll sit by the fire, and presume to know   What's done i' the Capitol; who's like to rise,   Who thrives and who declines; side factions   and give out   Conjectural marriages; making parties strong   And feebling such as stand not in their liking   Below their cobbled shoes.
translation: They  say? They'll sit by the fire in their homes, and presume to know what's going on in the Capitol. They think they know who's on the way up, who's succeeding and who's failing; they take sides and announce alliances, making political parties strong and weak at a whim.

original: They say there's   grain enough!   Would the nobility lay aside their ruth,   And let me use my sword, I'll make a quarry   With thousands of these quarter'd slaves, as high   As I could pick my lance.
translation: They  say there's grain enough! I wish the senate would stop being so compassionate and let me use my sword to resolve this; I'd kill these idiots and make a pile of them as high as my sword.

original: Nay, these are almost thoroughly persuaded;
translation: No, these men are almost completely persuaded to stand down.

original: For though abundantly they lack discretion,   Yet are they passing cowardly.
translation: Although they are terribly rowdy and rude, they're also terribly cowardly.

original: But, I beseech you,   What says the other troop?
translation: But what about the other rebellious groups?

original: They are dissolved: hang 'em!   They said they were an-hungry; sigh'd forth proverbs,   That hunger broke stone walls, that dogs must eat,   That meat was made for mouths, that the gods sent not   Corn for the rich men only:
translation: They've all dispersed: hang 'em! They said they were very hungry, begged using frilly, proverbial language—that hunger broke stone walls, that even dogs must eat, that meat was made for mouths, that the gods sent corn for poor as well as rich—

original: with these shreds   They vented their complainings; which being answer'd,   And a petition granted them, a strange one—   To break the heart of generosity,   And make bold power look pale—
translation: they complained with trash like this. When they were given an option— a strange option, and far too generous—

original: they threw their caps   As they would hang them on the horns o' the moon,   Shouting their emulation.
translation: they threw their hats in the air as though they meant to hang them on the  horns of the moon , shouting in celebration.

original: What is granted them?
translation: What option were they given?

original: Five tribunes to defend their vulgar wisdoms,   Of their own choice: one's Junius Brutus,   Sicinius Velutus, and I know not—   'Sdeath!
translation: Five representatives of their own choice to defend their idiotic ideas. One is Junius Brutus, Sicinius Velutus, and I don't know the rest. Forget it!

original: The rabble should have first unroof'd the city,   Ere so prevail'd with me:
translation: The mob should've destroyed the city before they ever got so much from me.

original: it will in time   Win upon power and throw forth greater themes   For insurrection's arguing.
translation: It will be a disaster, and only make more conflict in the senate.

original: This is strange.
translation: This is strange.

original: Go, get you home, you fragments!
translation: Go, get out of here, you rabble-rousers!

original: Where's Caius Marcius?
translation: Where's Caius Marcius?

original: Here: what's the matter?
translation: I'm here, what's the matter?

original: The news is, sir, the Volsces are in arms.
I am glad on 't: then we shall ha' means to vent Our musty superfluity. See, our best elders.
translation: Good! It will give us a way to get rid of this moldy excess. Here come our best senators.

original: Marcius, 'tis true that you have lately told us; The Volsces are in arms.
translation: Marcius, what you warned us about recently has come true: it looks like the Volsces are getting ready to attack.

original: They have a leader,   Tullus Aufidius, that will put you to 't.
translation: They have a leader, Tullus Aufidius, that will really give you a hard time.

original: I sin in envying his nobility,   And were I any thing but what I am,   I would wish me only he.
translation: I know I shouldn't, but I admire his strength; if I had to be anyone but myself,  I would wish to be him .

original: You have fought together.
translation: So you've fought him before?

original: Were half to half the world by the ears and he.   Upon my party, I'd revolt to make   Only my wars with him:
translation: If the whole world were at war, and he were on my side, I would change sides just to fight with him.

original: he is a lion   That I am proud to hunt.
translation: He is the only man worth fighting with.

original: Then, worthy Marcius, Attend upon Cominius to these wars.
translation: Then, worthy Marcius, go with Cominius to war.

original: It is your former promise.
translation: It is what you promised before.

original: Sir, it is;   And I am constant.
translation: Sir, it is; and I will not break my promise.

original: Titus Lartius, thou   Shalt see me once more strike at Tullus' face.   What, art thou stiff? stand'st out?
translation: Titus Lartius, you'll see me fight with Tullus once again. What's wrong, are you dead? Are you upset?

original: No, Caius Marcius; I'll lean upon one crutch and fight with t'other, Ere stay behind this business.
translation: No, Caius Marcius; I'll lean upon one crutch and fight with the other, rather than stay behind while you are fighting.

original: O, true-bred!
translation: Oh, you pure-bred Roman!

original: Your company to the Capitol; where, I know, Our greatest friends attend us.
translation: Come with me to the Capitol, where, I know, our best friends are waiting for us.

original: Lead you on. @     Follow Cominius; We must follow you; Right worthy you priority.
translation: Take us there.

original: Noble Marcius!
translation: Noble Marcius!

original: Hence to your homes; be gone!
translation: Get to your homes; be gone!

original: Nay, let them follow: The Volsces have much corn; take these rats thither To gnaw their garners. Worshipful mutiners, Your valour puts well forth: pray, follow.
translation: No, let them come along! The Volsces have plenty of corn; take these rats there to gnaw at it. Show us your bravery, you great rebels: pray, follow.

original: Was ever man so proud as is this Marcius?
translation: Has there ever been anyone as arrogant as Marcius?

original: He has no equal.
translation: No, he has no equal.

original: When we were chosen tribunes for the people,—
translation: When we were chosen as representatives for the people—

original: Mark'd you his lip and eyes?
translation: Did you see his expressions?

original: Nay. but his taunts.
translation: No, but I heard him taunt us.

original: Being moved, he will not spare to gird the gods.
translation: When he's angry, he would taunt the gods themselves.

original: Be-mock the modest moon.
translation: He'd mock the moon.

original: The present wars devour him: he is grown Too proud to be so valiant.
translation: The wars have completely ruined him: he's become too proud to be so brave.

original: Such a nature,   Tickled with good success, disdains the shadow   Which he treads on at noon:
translation: That kind of man, who has been flattered with success, looks down on everything, even his own shadow.

original: but I do wonder   His insolence can brook to be commanded   Under Cominius.
translation: I wonder if he can deal with being under Cominius's command.

original: Fame, at the which he aims,   In whom already he's well graced, can not   Better be held nor more attain'd than by   A place below the first:
translation: Actually, he's in the best position for acquiring fame—which is all he wants, and all he's ever wanted— because fame is most easily gotten as the second in command.

original: for what miscarries   Shall be the general's fault, though he perform   To the utmost of a man,
translation: The leader always has to take responsibility for what goes wrong, even if he does his best,

original: and giddy censure   Will then cry out of Marcius 'O if he   Had borne the business!'
translation: and then Maricus will cry out, "If only I had been in charge!"

original: Besides, if things go well, Opinion that so sticks on Marcius shall Of his demerits rob Cominius.
translation: Right—and then if things go well, Marcius will get all the credit Cominius deserves.

original: Come:   Half all Cominius' honours are to Marcius.   Though Marcius earned them not,
translation: Indeed: half of what Cominius does right will be attributed to Marcius even if he doesn't deserve it,

original: and all his faults   To Marcius shall be honours, though indeed   In aught he merit not.
translation: and everything Cominus does wrong will be somehow made Marcius's honors, just the same.

original: Let's hence, and hear   How the dispatch is made, and in what fashion,
translation: Lets go and hear how things are announced, and how—

original: More than his singularity, he goes   Upon this present action.
translation: beyond just his strangeness—he takes action.

original: Lets along.
translation: Let's go.

original: So, your opinion is, Aufidius, That they of Rome are entered in our counsels And know how we proceed.
translation: So, Aufidius—you think that the Romans have spies among us, and know what we're going to do?

original: Is it not yours?   What ever have been thought on in this state,   That could be brought to bodily act ere Rome   Had circumvention?
translation: Don't you? When have we ever even thought of doing something that Rome didn't attempt to counter before we had the chance to even get started?

original: 'Tis not four days gone   Since I heard thence; these are the words: I think   I have the letter here; yes, here it is.
translation: Less than four days ago, I heard from Rome—this is what they said— I have the letter here somewhere . . . yes, here it is.

original: 'They have press'd a power, but it is not known   Whether for east or west: the dearth is great;   The people mutinous;
translation: "They have sent out a battalion of soldiers, but it is not known whether they went east or west. The city's famine is serious, and the people are mutinous.

original: and it is rumour'd,   Cominius, Marcius your old enemy,   Who is of Rome worse hated than of you,   And Titus Lartius, a most valiant Roman,   These three lead on this preparation   Whither 'tis bent: most likely 'tis for you:   Consider of it.'
translation: There are rumours that three men lead the battalion: Cominius, Marcius your rival (whom Rome hates even more than they hate you), and Titus Lartius, a most valiant Roman. They are probably bound for you; be careful."

original: Our army's in the field We never yet made doubt but Rome was ready To answer us.
translation: We've never yet sent out an army unless we were ready to have Rome fight with us.

original: Nor did you think it folly   To keep your great pretences veil'd till when   They needs must show themselves;
translation: But at the same time, you've never thought it was a mistake to hide your warlike aims until the last possible second.

original: which   in the hatching,   It seem'd, appear'd to Rome.   By the discovery   We shall be shorten'd in our aim, which was   To take in many towns ere almost Rome   Should know we were afoot.
translation: This time, Rome seems to have known from the start, so that our initial plan—to conquer towns secretly, without Rome getting word— has been ruined.

original: Noble Aufidius,   Take your commission; hie you to your bands:   Let us alone to guard Corioli:
translation: Honorable Aufidius, here are your orders: go out to your soldiers, and leave us to guard the city of Corioli.

original: If they set down before 's, for the remove   Bring your army; but, I think, you'll find   They've not prepared for us.
translation: If they besiege us, come at them from behind. Still, I think you'll find that they underestimate our strength.

original: O, doubt not that;   I speak from certainties.
translation: Oh, don't doubt for a minute that they plan to besiege Corioli. I am certain of it;

original: Nay, more,   Some parcels of their power are forth already,   And only hitherward. I leave your honours.
translation: some of their forces are headed this way already. I will leave you, sirs.

original: If we and Caius Marcius chance to meet,   'Tis sworn between us we shall ever strike   Till one can do no more.
translation: If I meet Caius Marcius in battle, we have sworn to fight to the death.

original: The gods assist you!
translation: May the gods assist you!

original: And keep your honours safe!
translation: May they keep you safe, sirs!

original: Farewell.
translation: Goodbye.

original: Farewell.
translation: Goodbye.

original: Farewell.
translation: Goodbye.

original: I pray you, daughter, sing; or express yourself in a   more comfortable sort: if my son were my husband, I   should freelier rejoice in that absence wherein he   won honour than in the embracements of his bed where   he would show most love.
translation: Why don't you sing, daughter, or at least speak cheerfully? If my son Caius Marcius were my husband, as he is yours,  I would rejoice more when he is gone to win honor in battle than I would in his embrace when he would most show love.

original: When yet he was but   tender-bodied and the only son of my womb, when   youth with comeliness plucked all gaze his way, when   for a day of kings' entreaties a mother should not   sell him an hour from her beholding, I, considering   how honour would become such a person—that it was   no better than picture-like to hang by the wall—if   renown made it not stir, was pleased to let him seek   danger where he was like to find fame. To a cruel   war I sent him;
translation: When he was just a baby, my first son, so young and beautiful that he won everyone's attention and was impossible to give up even for a moment— even then, thinking of his incredible potential, I sent him willingly to a cruel war.

original: from whence he returned, his brows   bound with oak. I tell thee, daughter, I sprang not   more in joy at first hearing he was a man-child   than now in first seeing he had proved himself a man.
translation: When he returned, he had gained resolve, and had already saved the life of another man. I tell you, my daughter, I was not more happy to know that I had born a son than I was in seeing that he had  proven  himself a man.

original: But had he died in the business, madam; how then?
translation: But what if he had died in that war; how would you have felt then?

original: Then his good report should have been my son; I   therein would have found issue.
translation: Then the news of his bravery would have taken his place.

original: Hear me profess   sincerely: had I a dozen sons, each in my love   alike and none less dear than thine and my good   Marcius, I had rather had eleven die nobly for their   country than one voluptuously surfeit out of action.
translation: Listen; I'm being serious: if I had a dozen sons, each of them loved as much as I love our Marcius, I would rather have eleven die nobly for their country than one to die lazy and indulgent, doing nothing for the good of anyone.

original: Madam, the Lady Valeria is come to visit you.
translation: Madam, the Lady Valeria has arrived to visit you.

original: Beseech you, give me leave to retire myself.
translation: Please excuse me; let me go and rest in my room.

original: Indeed, you shall not.   Methinks I hear hither your husband's drum,   See him pluck Aufidius down by the hair,   As children from a bear, the Volsces shunning him:
translation: No, you may not. I can practically hear your husband's drum; I can imagine him pulling Aufidius down by his hair as a bear would kill children, the Volsces running in fear.

original: Methinks I see him stamp thus, and call thus:   'Come on, you cowards! you were got in fear,   Though you were born in Rome:'
translation: I can see him striding forward and calling out: "Come on, you cowards! You were conceived by weaklings, though you were born in Rome!"

original: his bloody brow   With his mail'd hand then wiping, forth he goes,   Like to a harvest-man that's task'd to mow   Or all or lose his hire.
translation: He wipes his bloody brow with an armored hand, and there he goes, like a farmer at harvest driven to cut all the grain or lose his job.

original: His bloody brow! O Jupiter, no blood!
translation: His bloody brow! By the gods, no blood!

original: Away, you fool! it more becomes a man   Than gilt his trophy:
translation: Get away, you fool! Blood is more appropriate to a brave man than gold in his trophy.

original: the breasts of Hecuba,   When she did suckle Hector, look'd not lovelier   Than Hector's forehead when it spit forth blood   At Grecian sword, contemning.
translation: The breasts of  Hecuba, mother of  Hector , were not more beautiful than Hector's forehead when it bled from the blow of a Greek sword.

original: Tell Valeria,   We are fit to bid her welcome.
translation: Tell Valeria we're ready to greet her.

original: Heavens bless my lord from fell Aufidius!
translation: Heaven protect my husband from the deadly Aufidius!

original: He'll beat Aufidius 'head below his knee And tread upon his neck.
translation: He'll crush Aufidius's head beneath his knee and stomp on his neck.

original: My ladies both, good day to you.
translation: My ladies, hello to you both.

original: Sweet madam.
translation: Sweet lady.

original: I am glad to see your ladyship.
translation: I am glad to see you, ma'am.

original: How do you both? you are manifest house-keepers. What are you sewing here? A fine spot, in good faith. How does your little son?
translation: How are you? You are such perfect house-wives. What are you sewing? That's a great pattern, seriously. How is your little boy?

original: I thank your ladyship; well, good madam.
translation: Thank you, ma'am. He's doing well.

original: He had rather see the swords, and hear a drum, than look upon his school-master.
translation: He would rather play with swords and hear a war drum than study.

original: O' my word, the father's son: I'll swear,'tis a   very pretty boy.
translation: Oh, my word , just like his father! I say, he's a very handsome boy.

original: O' my troth, I looked upon him o'   Wednesday half an hour together:
translation: To be honest, I was watching him Wednesday for at least half an hour:

original: has such a   confirmed countenance. I saw him run after a gilded   butterfly: and when he caught it, he let it go   again; and after it again; and over and over he   comes, and again; catched it again; or whether his   fall enraged him,
translation: he has such a bold look about him. I saw him run after a golden butterfly, and when he caught it, he let it go again, and then chased it again; over and over he comes, and again, caught it again, and then suddenly, maybe his stumble enraged him,

original: or how 'twas, he did so set his   teeth and tear it; O, I warrant it, how he mammocked   it!
translation: or maybe—I don't know why— he chomped down on the butterfly with his teeth and tore it up; Oh, I do say, how he chewed upon it!

original: One on 's father's moods.
translation: He is moody and abrupt, just like his father.

original: Indeed, la, 'tis a noble child.
translation: Indeed, it's true: he's a magnificent child.

original: Come, lay aside your stitchery; I must have you play the idle husewife with me this afternoon.
translation: Come on, enough sewing; why don't you spend the afternoon with me?

original: No, good madam; I will not out of doors.
translation: No, ma'am; I can't go out.

original: Not out of doors!
translation: You can't go out?

original: She shall, she shall.
translation: Oh, she'll go, she'll go.

original: Indeed, no, by your patience; I'll not over the threshold till my lord return from the wars.
translation: No, if you don't mind. I can't bear to leave the house until my husband gets back from the war.

original: Fie, you confine yourself most unreasonably: come, you must go visit the good lady that lies in.
translation: Ugh, you're holding yourself down for no good reason: come on, go spend the afternoon with our pregnant friend.

original: I will wish her speedy strength, and visit her with my prayers; but I cannot go thither.
translation: I wish her the best, and please send her my prayers, but I simply can't go.

original: Why, I pray you?
translation: Why not? Explain yourself.

original: 'Tis not to save labour, nor that I want love.
translation: It's not that I'm lazy, nor that I don't love her.

original: You would be another Penelope: yet, they say, all   the yarn she spun in Ulysses' absence did but fill   Ithaca full of moths.
translation: You want to be like  Penelope ? Think of the good waiting did her; they say all the yarn she spun while Ulysses was away just filled the island of Ithaca with moths.

original: Come; I would your cambric   were sensible as your finger, that you might leave   pricking it for pity. Come, you shall go with us.
translation: Come on, I wish your sewing linen could feel the pain of your needle, so that you'd leave it alone out of pity and come with us. Come on!

original: No, good madam, pardon me; indeed, I will not forth.
translation: No, ma'am, pardon me; I truly will not go.

original: In truth, la, go with me; and I'll tell you excellent news of your husband.
translation: Honestly! Come with me, and I'll give you good news of your husband.

original: O, good madam, there can be none yet.
translation: O, ma'am, there can't possibly be news yet.

original: Verily, I do not jest with you; there came news from him last night.
translation: Seriously, I'm not kidding; news from him came in just last night.

original: Indeed, madam?
translation: Really?

original: In earnest, it's true; I heard a senator speak it.   Thus it is: the Volsces have an army forth; against   whom Cominius the general is gone, with one part of   our Roman power:
translation: Yes, it's really true; I heard a senator share the news. It's this: the Volsces have sent out their army, and Cominius has gone to fight them with a part of our force.

original: your lord and Titus Lartius are set   down before their city Corioli; they nothing doubt   prevailing and to make it brief wars.
translation: Your husband and Titus Lartius are encamped in front of Corioli. They are sure to win and end this quickly.

original: This is true,   on mine honour; and so, I pray, go with us.
translation: This is all true, on my honor. So, please, don't worry and come along with us!

original: Give me excuse, good madam; I will obey you in every thing hereafter.
translation: Forgive me, ma'am. In anything other than this, I would follow your lead, but for now I just can't.

original: Let her alone, lady: as she is now, she will but disease our better mirth.
translation: Oh, leave her alone. In this mood, she'd just drag down our high spirits.

original: In troth, I think she would. Fare you well, then. Come, good sweet lady. Prithee, Virgilia, turn thy solemness out o' door. and go along with us.
translation: Yes, I think she really would. Farewell, then. Come, my good friend. Oh, once more, Virgilia, get your sad self out of the house and come along with us.

original: No, at a word, madam; indeed, I must not. I wish you much mirth.
translation: In a word, no. I just can't. I hope you have a good time, though.

original: Well, then, farewell.
translation: Well, then, farewell.

original: Yonder comes news. A wager they have met.
translation: Here comes some news. I bet our other force has begun to fight the Volsces.

original: My horse to yours, no.
translation: I bet my horse against yours they haven't.

original: 'Tis done.
translation: Done.

original: Agreed.
translation: Agreed.

original: Say, has our general met the enemy?
translation: Hey, has our general started fighting?

original: They lie in view; but have not spoke as yet.
translation: The two forces have seen each other, but haven't begun fighting yet.

original: So, the good horse is mine.
translation: So, the good horse is mine.

original: I'll buy him of you.
translation: I'll just buy him back.

original: No, I'll nor sell nor give him: lend you him I will For half a hundred years. Summon the town.
translation: No, I won't sell him or give him to you; I'll lend him to you for fifty years, though.

original: How far off lie these armies?
translation: How far away are their armies?

original: Within this mile and half.
translation: No more than a mile and a half.

original: Then shall we hear their 'larum, and they ours.
translation: Then we'll hear their trumpets, and they'll hear ours.

original: Now, Mars, I prithee, make us quick in work,   That we with smoking swords may march from hence,   To help our fielded friends!
translation: To the god of war, I pray: make our work quick, so that with we may march to help our friends in the field before our swords have even cooled from our own battle!

original: Come, blow thy blast.
translation: Go ahead, blow the trumpet.

original: Tutus Aufidius, is he within your walls?
translation: Is Tullus Aufidius in the city?

original: No, nor a man that fears you less than he, That's lesser than a little.
translation: No, nor anyone less afraid of you than he is, which is very little.

original: Hark! our drums   Are bringing forth our youth.
translation: Listen! Our drums are calling for our strong young men.

original: We'll break our walls,   Rather than they shall pound us up:
translation: We'll break our own walls rather than be locked in by you.

original: our gates,   Which yet seem shut, we, have but pinn'd with rushes;   They'll open of themselves.
translation: The gates of the city, which might seem shut in fear, we've only barricaded with grass; they'll open easily to fight you.

original: Hark you. far off! There is Aufidius; list, what work he makes Amongst your cloven army.
translation: Listen! Hear that? That's Aufidius; listen—he's killing everyone in your divided army.

original: O, they are at it!
translation: Oh, they are fighting!

original: Their noise be our instruction. Ladders, ho!
translation: Their trumpets might as well be ours, too! Put ladders to the wall!

original: They fear us not, but issue forth their city.
translation: They aren't afraid of us; instead, they're attacking.

original: Now put your shields before your hearts, and fight   With hearts more proof than shields. Advance,   brave Titus:
translation: Put your shields in front of your hearts, and fight with hearts stronger than those shields. Forward, brave Titus!

original: They do disdain us much beyond our thoughts,   Which makes me sweat with wrath.
translation: Their boldness is disdainful, which makes me sweat with wrath.

original: Come on, my fellows:   He that retires I'll take him for a Volsce,   And he shall feel mine edge.
translation: Come on, my soldiers; I'll treat anyone who takes a backward step like the enemy and promptly kill them.

original: All the contagion of the south light on you,   You shames of Rome! you herd of—
translation: May all the diseases of the south wind poison you, you shames of Rome! you herd of—

original: Boils and plagues   Plaster you o'er, that you may be abhorr'd   Further than seen and one infect another   Against the wind a mile!
translation: sores and plagues cover your whole body, that you'll be hated from even further than you can be seen, and so that you infect each other against the wind even a mile away!

original: You souls of geese,   That bear the shapes of men, how have you run   From slaves that apes would beat! Pluto and hell!
translation: You cowards, more likely to fly than fight, you have run from wretches who even apes could defeat! The devil curse you!

original: All hurt behind; backs red, and faces pale   With flight and agued fear!
translation: You've all been injured as you ran away— your backs are red with blood, and your faces white with cowardice and sickly fear!

original: Mend and charge home,   Or, by the fires of heaven, I'll leave the foe   And make my wars on you:
translation: Pull yourselves together and charge back to the fight, or by the fires of heaven, I will stop fighting the Volsces and will turn to fight you!

original: l   ook to't: come on;   If you'll stand fast, we'll beat them to their wives,   As they us to our trenches followed.
translation: Don't think I'm joking; come on! If you can stand your ground, we'll beat them home to their wives, as they beat us to our trenches.

original: So, now the gates are ope: now prove good seconds: 'Tis for the followers fortune widens them, Not for the fliers: mark me, and do the like.
translation: So, now the gates are open; this looks like a good opportunity. Luck has opened them so that we can follow the Volsces into the city, not so that they can flee. Come with me!

original: Fool-hardiness; not I.
translation: That's foolish; I'm not going in.

original: Nor I.
translation: Me neither.

original: See, they have shut him in.
translation: See, they have trapped him inside.

original: To the pot, I warrant him.
translation: He's doomed, I'm sure.

original: What is become of Marcius?
translation: What's happened to Marcius?

original: Slain, sir, doubtless.
translation: He's been killed sir, surely.

original: Following the fliers at the very heels,   With them he enters; who, upon the sudden,   Clapp'd to their gates:
translation: He followed the Volsces right into the city as they retreated, and they suddenly slammed the gates shut behind him.

original: he is himself alone,   To answer all the city.
translation: He's alone in Corioli against the entire city.

original: O noble fellow!   Who sensibly outdares his senseless sword,   And, when it bows, stands up.
translation: Oh, that brave man! Who knowingly dares more than  even his sword  would, and when it fails, he continues by force of will.

original: Thou art left, Marcius:   A carbuncle entire, as big as thou art,   Were not so rich a jewel. Thou wast a soldier   Even to Cato's wish,
translation: You've left us, Marcius. A ruby as big as a man is not worth as much as you. You were a soldier to make our ancestors jealous—

original: not fierce and terrible   Only in strokes; but, with thy grim looks and   The thunder-like percussion of thy sounds,   Thou madst thine enemies shake,
translation: not just fierce and powerful in battle, but with your fearsome looks and the thunder-like sounds of your movements, you made your enemies shake in terror,

original: as if the world   Were feverous and did tremble.
translation: as if the whole world had a fever, and trembled.

original: Look, sir.
translation: Look, sir.

original: O,'tis Marcius! Let's fetch him off, or make remain alike.
translation: Oh my god, it's Marcius! Lets rescue him, or we'll find ourselves bleeding like he is.

original: This will I carry to Rome.
translation: I'll take this back to Rome.

original: And I this.
translation: And I'll take this.

original: A murrain on't! I took this for silver.
translation: Oh, curse this! I thought this was silver.

original: See here these movers that do prize their hours   At a crack'd drachm!
translation: Look at these layabouts, who have no concern for all the time they waste!

original: Cushions, leaden spoons,   Irons of a doit, doublets that hangmen would   Bury with those that wore them, these base slaves,   Ere yet the fight be done, pack up:
translation: Cushions, lead spoons, third-rate swords, shirts that no one would ever want— these losers are plundering all of this junk before the fight is even over!

original: down with them!   And hark, what noise the general makes! To him!
translation: To hell with them! But listen, that's Cominius's trumpet! We must go to him!

original: There is the man of my soul's hate, Aufidius,   Piercing our Romans: then, valiant Titus, take   Convenient numbers to make good the city;
translation: That's where Aufidius, my worst enemy, is fighting against our men. Brave Titus, you stay here with enough men to secure the city,

original: Whilst I, with those that have the spirit, will haste   To help Cominius.
translation: and I'll take whoever is brave enough to hurry to Cominius's aid.

original: Worthy sir, thou bleed'st; Thy exercise hath been too violent for A second course of fight.
translation: But brave sir, you're bleeding! You've already done far too much fighting to turn around and go to another part of the battle.

original: Sir, praise me not;   My work hath yet not warm'd me: fare you well:
translation: Don't call me brave if that's what you'd expect of me. All that fighting has barely warmed me up; goodbye.

original: The blood I drop is rather physical   Than dangerous to me: to Aufidius thus   I will appear, and fight.
translation: My bleeding is good for me rather than dangerous. I'll face Aufidius just like this, blood and all.

original: Now the fair goddess, Fortune,   Fall deep in love with thee; and her great charms   Misguide thy opposers' swords!
translation: May Lady Luck go with you, and may she turn away the swords of your enemies!

original: Bold gentleman,   Prosperity be thy page!
translation: Brave soldier, may prosperity walk beside you!

original: Thy friend no less Than those she placeth highest! So, farewell.
translation: As much prosperity as anyone has ever won! So, goodbye.

original: Thou worthiest Marcius!
translation: That brave Marcius.

original: Go, sound thy trumpet in the market-place; Call thither all the officers o' the town, Where they shall know our mind: away!
translation: Go, blow your trumpets in the center of the city, and call its leaders together so they can hear what we have to say. Go!

original: Breathe you, my friends: well fought;   we are come off   Like Romans, neither foolish in our stands,   Nor cowardly in retire:
translation: Relax for a moment, my friends, you fought well. We've lived up to our names as Romans— neither foolish in the fight nor cowardly in stepping back from it.

original: believe me, sirs,   We shall be charged again. Whiles we have struck,   By interims and conveying gusts we have heard   The charges of our friends.
translation: Believe me, sirs, they'll charge at us again. As we've been fighting, we've heard the trumpets of our friends' fight over the wind.

original: Ye Roman gods!   Lead their successes as we wish our own,   That both our powers, with smiling   fronts encountering,   May give you thankful sacrifice.
translation: Oh, Roman gods! Give them success as we hope for our own, so that both our forces may willingly give you thankful sacrifice.

original: Thy news?
translation: What news do you have?

original: The citizens of Corioli have issued,   And given to Lartius and to Marcius battle:
translation: The citizens of Corioli have attacked the forces of [Titus] Lartius and Marcius.

original: I saw our party to their trenches driven,   And then I came away.
translation: I saw our Romans driven back to their trenches just before I left.

original: Though thou speak'st truth, Methinks thou speak'st not well. How long is't since?
translation: If you're telling the truth, it's a truth I don't much like. How long ago was this?

original: Above an hour, my lord.
translation: More than an hour, sir.

original: 'Tis not a mile; briefly we heard their drums: How couldst thou in a mile confound an hour, And bring thy news so late?
translation: They're less than a mile away; we just heard their drums. How did it take you an hour to come a mile; why are you so late?

original: Spies of the Volsces   Held me in chase, that I was forced to wheel   Three or four miles about,
translation: Spies of the Volsces chased after me, and I had to run three or four miles extra in order to lose them.

original: else had I, sir,   Half an hour since brought my report.
translation: I'd have been here a half hour ago otherwise, sir.

original: Who's yonder,   That does appear as he were flay'd?
translation: Who's that coming this way, covered in wounds?

original: O gods   He has the stamp of Marcius; and I have   Before-time seen him thus.
translation: Oh my god, it must be Marcius; I've seen him like this before.

original: Come I too late?
translation: Am I too late?

original: The shepherd knows not thunder from a tabour More than I know the sound of Marcius' tongue From every meaner man.
translation: As the shepherd can distinguish between a tambourine and thunder, I can tell that is the sound of Marcius's voice rather than any lesser man.

original: Come I too late?
translation: Am I too late?

original: Ay, if you come not in the blood of others, But mantled in your own.
translation: Ha! If that's your blood and not the blood of your enemies, then yes.

original: O, let me clip ye   In arms as sound as when I woo'd,
translation: Oh, let me wrap my arms around you like I would around a lover;

original: in heart   As merry as when our nuptial day was done,   And tapers burn'd to bedward!
translation: I'm as happy as I was the day I was married,  when the candles had burned low.

original: Flower of warriors, How is it with Titus Lartius?
translation: Greatest of warriors, how's it going with Titus Lartius in the other part of the battle?

original: As with a man busied about decrees:   Condemning some to death, and some to exile;   Ransoming him, or pitying, threatening the other;
translation: It's going about as well as with a mayor, busy with running a city: condemning some to death, and some to exile; taking ransom from some, taking pity on others, and threatening still more.

original: Holding Corioli in the name of Rome,   Even like a fawning greyhound in the leash,   To let him slip at will.
translation: He holds Corioli in the name of Rome, and the city is his like a greyhound on a leash, ready to race at his command.

original: Where is that slave Which told me they had beat you to your trenches? Where is he? call him hither.
translation: Where is that lowly messenger who told me that your force had been beaten to your trenches? Where is he? Get him over here.

original: Let him alone;   He did inform the truth:
translation: Leave him alone. He was just telling the truth.

original: but for our gentlemen,   The common file—a plague! tribunes for them!—
translation: A plague on our common soldiers! We'll have them court martialed!

original: The mouse ne'er shunn'd the cat as they did budge   From rascals worse than they.
translation: No mouse has ever fled a cat as they did flee from rascals even worse than themselves.

original: But how prevail'd you?
translation: So then how did you win?

original: Will the time serve to tell? I do not think. Where is the enemy? are you lords o' the field? If not, why cease you till you are so?
translation: Do we have time for an idle story? I don't think so. Where is the enemy? Have you won already? If not, why waste time until you have?

original: Marcius, We have at disadvantage fought and did Retire to win our purpose.
translation: Marcius, we've been fighting outnumbered, and we're regrouping now to make another go of it.

original: How lies their battle? know you on which side They have placed their men of trust?
translation: How are they organized? Do you know where they've placed their best soldiers?

original: As I guess, Marcius, Their bands i' the vaward are the Antiates, Of their best trust; o'er them Aufidius, Their very heart of hope.
translation: As far as I can tell, Marcius, the men in the front are the Antiates, their best soldiers. Aufidius, the very heart of their army, leads them.

original: I do beseech you,   By all the battles wherein we have fought,   By the blood we have shed together, by the vows   We have made to endure friends,
translation: Then I beg you: by all the battles we've fought together, by all the blood we've shed together, by our very friendship itself—

original: that you directly   Set me against Aufidius and his Antiates;
translation: send me directly against Aufidius and his Antiates,

original: And that you not delay the present, but,   Filling the air with swords advanced and darts,   We prove this very hour.
translation: and lets not waste any time, but fill the air with our swords and arrows this very hour.

original: Though I could wish   You were conducted to a gentle bath   And balms applied to, you, yet dare I never   Deny your asking:
translation: Though I wish I could have you taken to recover in a spa and have medicine given to you, I can't deny what you ask.

original: take your choice of those   That best can aid your action.
translation: Take whatever soldiers you think will be best suited to help you.

original: Those are they   That most are willing. If any such be here—   As it were sin to doubt—   that love this painting   Wherein you see me smear'd;
translation: The best soldiers are the boldest. If anyone here—dare I even doubt it— loves  the painting in which you see me smeared ;

original: if any fear   Lesser his person than an ill report;   If any think brave death outweighs bad life   And that his country's dearer than himself;
translation: if anyone fears death less than shame; if anyone thinks a brave death is better than a fearful life, and that cares more for his country than his life;

original: Let him alone, or so many so minded,   Wave thus, to express his disposition,   And follow Marcius.
translation: let that man, or however many like that are here, raise your arms to show your commitment, and follow me!

original: O, me alone! make you a sword of me?   If these shows be not outward, which of you   But is four Volsces?
translation: Oh, just me then!  Make you a sword of me?  If your enthusiasm reflects your actual boldness, each of you is worth four of the Volsces!

original: none of you but is   Able to bear against the great Aufidius   A shield as hard as his.
translation: You're all a match for the great Aufidius himself.

original: A certain number,   Though thanks to all, must I select   from all: the rest   Shall bear the business in some other fight,   As cause will be obey'd.
translation: Thanks to all of you, but I'll have to take only a few of you. The rest of you will hold your own in another fight, as the situation requires.

original: Please you to march;   And four shall quickly draw out my command,   Which men are best inclined.
translation: Lets get moving, and you four  [indicating four men]  quickly pick out the best men among you.

original: March on, my fellows: Make good this ostentation, and you shall Divide in all with us.
translation: Good luck, my friends. Make good on your enthusiasm and we'll all share the rich prizes of war!

original: So, let the ports be guarded: keep your duties,   As I have set them down. If I do send, dispatch   Those centuries to our aid:
translation: So, let the gates be guarded. Attend to the duties I've assigned to you. If I send word, send those soldiers  [pointing]  to help us.

original: the rest will serve   For a short holding: if we lose the field,   We cannot keep the town.
translation: The rest will serve to hold the city while they are away. Anyway, if we lose the battle, we'll certainly lose the town.

original: Fear not our care, sir.
translation: Don't worry about us, sir.
