original: Hence, and shut your gates upon's. Our guider, come; to the Roman camp conduct us.
translation: All right, lets go; shut the gates behind us. Come on, guide, take us to the other camp.

original: I'll fight with none but thee; for I do hate thee Worse than a promise-breaker.
We hate alike: Not Afric owns a serpent I abhor More than thy fame and envy. Fix thy foot.
translation: I hate you just as much: there's not a snake in all of Africa I hate more than you and your fame. Stand and fight!

original: Let the first budger die the other's slave, And the gods doom him after!
translation: Let the first man to budge die as the other's slave, and the gods doom him!

original: If I fly, Marcius, Holloa me like a hare.
translation: If I run, Marcius, lasso me like a hare.

original: Within these three hours, Tullus,   Alone I fought in your Corioli walls,   And made what work I pleased:
translation: Not three hours ago, Tullus, I fought alone inside Corioli, and did whatever I wanted.

original: 'tis not my blood   Wherein thou seest me mask'd; for thy revenge   Wrench up thy power to the highest.
translation: The blood you see on me is not my own, I'll tell you that— if you want revenge, you'll have to fight better than you ever have before.

original: Wert thou the Hector That was the whip of your bragg'd progeny, Thou shouldst not scape me here.
Officious, and not valiant, you have shamed me In your condemned seconds.
translation: You groveling, cowardly idiots! You've interfered in our fight and brought terrible shame on me.

original: If I should tell thee o'er this thy day's work,   Thou'ldst not believe thy deeds:
translation: If I told you again about the work you have already done today, you wouldn't believe your own deeds.

original: but I'll report it   Where senators shall mingle tears with smiles,   Where great patricians shall attend and shrug,   I' the end admire,
translation: Instead, I'll tell Rome's senators, who will laugh and cry, and the best among them will listen and shrug, but in the end they'll all admire you.

original: where ladies shall be frighted,   And, gladly quaked, hear more; where the   dull tribunes,   That, with the fusty plebeians, hate thine honours,   Shall say against their hearts
translation: Ladies will be scared and excited and will ask to hear more; the most average and the most senior men in the Senate, even if they're jealous, will say in spite of themselves:

original: 'We thank the gods   Our Rome hath such a soldier.'   Yet camest thou to a morsel of this feast,   Having fully dined before.
translation: "We thank the gods our Rome has such a soldier."  Yet all of this was just a snack for you; you ate earlier .

original: O general, Here is the steed, we the caparison: Hadst thou beheld—
Pray now, no more: my mother,   Who has a charter to extol her blood,   When she does praise me grieves me.
translation: Please, no more: even my own mother, who has more right to praise me than anyone else, grieves me when she does.

original: I have done   As you have done; that's what I can; induced   As you have been;
translation: I have done as you have done: that is, I've done my best. I have the same reasons as you:

original: that's for my country:   He that has but effected his good will   Hath overta'en mine act.
translation: that is, I love my country. Any man who has acted as well as he can has done the same as me.

original: You shall not be   The grave of your deserving; Rome must know   The value of her own:
translation: You shall not silence your own praise; Rome needs to know how valuable you are to our republic.

original: 'twere a concealment   Worse than a theft,
translation: Not to praise you would be worse than stealing your praise;

original: no less than a traducement,   To hide your doings; and to silence that,   Which, to the spire and top of praises vouch'd,   Would seem but modest:
translation: it would be nothing less than to lie about your reputation, to hide your actions.

original: therefore, I beseech you   In sign of what you are, not to reward   What you have done—   before our army hear me.
translation: Please, let me review your actions before our men, not as a reward, but simply in acknowledgement of who you are.

original: I have some wounds upon me, and they smart To hear themselves remember'd.
translation: I have some wounds upon me, and they hurt when I'm reminded of them.

original: Should they not,   Well might they fester 'gainst ingratitude,   And tent themselves with death.
translation: If they didn't, they might as well infect themselves against ingratitude and welcome death.

original: Of all the horses,   Whereof we have ta'en good and good store, of all   The treasure in this field achieved and city,   We render you the tenth,
translation: In reward, take a tenth of all the horses, and all the goods plundered from the battle and the city.

original: to be ta'en forth,   Before the common distribution, at   Your only choice.
translation: You and you alone will choose your tenth first, before the rest of us.

original: I thank you, general;   But cannot make my heart consent to take   A bribe to pay my sword:
translation: I thank you, general, but I couldn't bear to accept payment for this fighting.

original: I do refuse it;   And stand upon my common part with those   That have beheld the doing.
translation: I must refuse and stand with all the other soldiers who were there to see me fight.

original: May these same instruments, which you profane,   Never sound more!
translation: May these very trumpets, which you misuse by praising me, never blow again!

original: when drums and trumpets shall   I' the field prove flatterers, let courts and cities be   Made all of false-faced soothing!
translation: When drums and trumpets are used for flattery at war, courts and cities will be home to calm deceit!

original: When steel grows soft as the parasite's silk,   Let him be made a coverture for the wars!
translation: When our weapons grow soft as spider's silk, may that silk be like a blanket for the wars.

original: No more, I say! For that I have not wash'd   My nose that bled, or foil'd some debile wretch.—
translation: No more, I say! Merely because I haven't cleaned my bloody nose, or because I killed some foolish wretch—

original: Which, without note, here's many else have done,—   You shout me forth   In acclamations hyperbolical;   As if I loved my little should be dieted   In praises sauced with lies.
translation: which many others here have done— you shout these wild praises of me, as if I enjoyed having what little praise I am entitled to covered up with lies.

original: Too modest are you;   More cruel to your good report than grateful   To us that give you truly: by your patience,   If 'gainst yourself you be incensed,
translation: You are too modest, and your modesty only tarnishes your reputation. Please, if you truly think so little of yourself,

original: we'll put you,   Like one that means his proper harm, in manacles,   Then reason safely with you.
translation: we'll restrain you like one restrains a man who wants to hurt himself— then we can talk reasonably with you.

original: Therefore, be it known,   As to us, to all the world, that Caius Marcius   Wears this war's garland:
translation: Therefore, be it known to all the world as it is clear to us, that Caius Marcius wears  this war's garland .

original: in token of the which,   My noble steed, known to the camp, I give him,   With all his trim belonging;
translation: In token of his victory, I give him my noble steed along with his luxurious saddle and bridle, known to everyone in the camp.

original: and from this time,   For what he did before Corioli, call him,   With all the applause and clamour of the host,   CAIUS MARCIUS CORIOLANUS!
translation: From this time forward, for what he did in Corioli, let us all call him—with the applause and approval of the whole army— [shouting, as though to the whole army]  Caius Marcius Coriolanus!

original: Bear   The addition nobly ever!
translation: Bear that name nobly forever!

original: Caius Marcius Coriolanus!
translation: Caius Marcius Coriolanus!

original: I will go wash;   And when my face is fair, you shall perceive   Whether I blush or no:
translation: I will go wash, and when my face is clean, you will all see whether I blush or not.

original: howbeit, I thank you.   I mean to stride your steed, and at all times   To undercrest your good addition   To the fairness of my power.
translation: Either way, I thank you. I will try to ride your horse, and at all times to live up to the name you have given me as much as I can.

original: So, to our tent;   Where, ere we do repose us, we will write   To Rome of our success.
translation: So, to our tent, where before we rest, we will write to Rome of our success.

original: You, Titus Lartius,   Must to Corioli back: send us to Rome   The best, with whom we may articulate,   For their own good and ours.
translation: You, Titus Lartius, must return to Corioli. From there, send the best of the Volscians to Rome so that we can negotiate the terms of their surrender, for their own good and ours.

original: I shall, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: The gods begin to mock me. I, that now Refused most princely gifts, am bound to beg Of my lord general.
translation: The gods begin to mock me. I, who just refused the most lavish gifts, now have to beg something of my lord general.

original: I sometime lay here in Corioli   At a poor man's house; he used me kindly:
translation: During the fight here in Corioli I hid for a bit in a poor man's house, and he was kind to me.

original: He cried to me; I saw him prisoner;   But then Aufidius was with in my view,   And wrath o'erwhelm'd my pity:
translation: When I saw Aufidius, wrath overwhelmed whatever pity I had, and so although the man begged me to be merciful, I made him a prisoner.

original: I request you   To give my poor host freedom.
translation: Please, give my poor host his freedom.

original: O, well begg'd! Were he the butcher of my son, he should Be free as is the wind. Deliver him, Titus.
translation: O, well begged! Were he to murder my own son, he would be free as the wind. Free him, Titus.

original: Marcius, his name?
translation: Marcius, what's his name?

original: By Jupiter! forgot. I am weary; yea, my memory is tired. Have we no wine here?
Go we to our tent: The blood upon your visage dries; 'tis time It should be look'd to: come.
translation: Lets go to our tent. The blood is drying on your face; it's time we dealt with it. Come on.

original: The town is ta'en!
translation: The town has been captured!

original: 'Twill be deliver'd back on good condition.
translation: They'll let us have it back once we negotiate the terms of our surrender.

original: Condition!   I would I were a Roman; for I cannot,   Being a Volsce, be that I am.
translation: Surrender! I wish I were a Roman, because I cannot be a Volscian if men like you, talking of surrender, are Volscians.

original: Condition!   What good condition can a treaty find   I' the part that is at mercy?
translation: Surrender? What good terms can we get from a treaty when we are the ones who have lost?

original: Five times, Marcius,   I have fought with thee: so often hast thou beat me,   And wouldst do so, I think, should we encounter   As often as we eat.
translation: Five times, Marcius, I have fought with you, and five times I've lost. You'd defeat me, I think, if we were to fight as often as we eat.

original: By the elements,   If e'er again I meet him beard to beard,   He's mine, or I am his:
translation: By earth and sun, if ever again I meet him beard to beard,  he will be mine or I will be his.

original: mine emulation   Hath not that honour in't it had;
translation: Our rivalry, which so far has been fought in fair and open terms, will turn dirty:

original: for where   I thought to crush him in an equal force,   True sword to sword, I'll potch at him some way   Or wrath or craft may get him.
translation: where before I thought to beat him sword to sword, I'll do anything now; I'll thrust at him however I can. If not by wrath, I'll kill him by cleverness.

original: He's the devil.
translation: He's the devil.

original: Bolder, though not so subtle. My valour's poison'd   With only suffering stain by him;
translation: Bolder than the devil, though not as clever. My honor has been poisoned by all the times he has defeated me.

original: for him   Shall fly out of itself: nor sleep nor sanctuary,   Being naked, sick, nor fane nor Capitol,
translation: To kill him, I will sacrifice that honor and be devilish. I will kill him anywhere, at any time, honorable or not: if he is sleeping, or naked, or takes refuge in a temple or in Rome;

original: The prayers of priests nor times of sacrifice,   Embarquements all of fury, shall lift up   Their rotten privilege and custom 'gainst   My hate to Marcius:
translation: neither the prayers of priests nor their sacrifices will stop my revenge against Marcius.

original: where I find him, were it   At home, upon my brother's guard, even there,   Against the hospitable canon, would I   Wash my fierce hand in's heart.
translation: Even if I found him in my home, guarded by my own brother— even there, against all decency and hospitality, I would wash my avenging hand in his heart's blood.

original: Go you to the city;   Learn how 'tis held; and what they are that must   Be hostages for Rome.
translation: Go you to the city; find out how it's holding up, and who is being sent as hostages to Rome.

original: Will not you go?
translation: Won't you go?

original: I am attended at the cypress grove: I pray you—   'Tis south the city mills—
translation: People are waiting for me at the cypress grove. Please, find me there—it's south of the city mills—

original: bring me word thither   How the world goes, that to the pace of it   I may spur on my journey.
translation: and bring me word of how the world goes, so that the news may inspire me on my journey.

original: I shall, sir.
translation: I shall, sir.

original: The augurer tells me we shall have news to-night.
translation: The prophet tells me we will get news tonight.

original: Good or bad?
translation: Good or bad?

original: Not according to the prayer of the people, for they love not Marcius.
translation: Well, not the good news the people are praying for, since they don't like Marcius.

original: Nature teaches beasts to know their friends.
translation: Nature teaches beasts to know their friends.

original: Pray you, who does the wolf love?
translation: Tell me then, who does the wolf love?

original: The lamb.
translation: The lamb.

original: Ay, to devour him; as the hungry plebeians would the noble Marcius.
translation: Right—to devour him: as the hungry people would like to devour noble Marcius.

original: He's a lamb indeed, that baes like a bear.
translation: If he's a lamb, he's one that baas like a bear.

original: He's a bear indeed, that lives like a lamb. You two are old men: tell me one thing that I shall ask you.
translation: He's a bear that lives like a lamb. You two are old men; answer me one question.

original: Well, sir.
translation: Go ahead, sir.

original: In what enormity is Marcius poor in, that you two have not in abundance?
translation: What small flaw does Marcius have that you two do not have twice over?

original: He's poor in no one fault, but stored with all.
translation: It's not that he has one fault, but all of them.

original: Especially in pride.
translation: He has pride, especially.

original: And topping all others in boasting.
translation: And his boasting is worse than all his other flaws.

original: This is strange now: do you two know how you are censured here in the city, I mean of us o' the right-hand file? do you?
translation: Well that's weird: do you two know how you are thought of in the city, I mean by those of us in the higher class? Do you?

original: Why, how are we censured?
translation: Why, what do they say about us?

original: Because you talk of pride now,—will you not be angry?
translation: Because you're talking of pride, now—you won't be angry if I tell you, will you?

original: Well, well, sir, well.
translation: Come on, sir, come on.

original: Why, 'tis no great matter; for a very little thief of   occasion will rob you of a great deal of patience:
translation: It's no big deal.  A small occasion will rob you of a great deal of patience:

original: give your dispositions the reins, and be angry at   your pleasures; at the least if you take it as a   pleasure to you in being so.
translation: if you let your emotions lead you, you'll be angry at your pleasures if you take pleasure in being angry.

original: You blame Marcius for   being proud?
translation: You blame Marcius for being proud?

original: We do it not alone, sir.
translation: We're not the only ones who do, sir.

original: I know you can do very little alone; for your helps   are many, or else your actions would grow wondrous   single:
translation: I know you can do very little alone, for you need a lot of help, or your actions would be awfully small.

original: your abilities are too infant-like for   doing much alone.
translation: Your abilities are too much like an infant's for doing much by yourself.

original: You talk of pride: O that you   could turn your eyes toward the napes of your necks,   and make but an interior survey of your good selves!   O that you could!
translation: You talk of pride: if only you could turn your eyes inward and see yourselves! If only you could!

original: What then, sir?
translation: What would we see, sir?

original: Why, then you should discover a brace of unmeriting, proud, violent, testy magistrates, alias fools, as any in Rome.
Menenius, you are known well enough too.
translation: Menenius, there's plenty said about you too.

original: I am known to be a humorous patrician, and one that   loves a cup of hot wine with not a drop of allaying   Tiber in't; said to be something imperfect in   favouring the first complaint;
translation: I am known to be a light-hearted politician—a man who loves a mulled wine with not a drop of water in it; said to be a bit imperfect in taking the first side I hear presented;

original: hasty and tinder-like   upon too trivial motion; one that converses more   with the buttock of the night than with the forehead   of the morning:
translation: I can be hasty over small things; I stay up too late and sleep in too long;

original: what I think I utter, and spend my   malice in my breath.
translation: I say what I think and hold back no mean words.

original: Meeting two such wealsmen as   you are—I cannot call you Lycurguses—   if the drink   you give me touch my palate adversely, I make a   crooked face at it.
translation: Meeting two statesmen like you— I cannot call you politicians— if you give me a bad drink, I'll scowl at it.

original: I can't say your worships have   delivered the matter well, when I find the ass in   compound with the major part of your syllables:
translation: I can't say you two have done well if you are mixing up your head and your ass:

original: and   though I must be content to bear with those that say   you are reverend grave men, yet they lie deadly that   tell you you have good faces.
translation: and though I have to deal with those who say you are serious, great men, they are lying if they say you are pleasant to look at.

original: If you see this in   the map of my microcosm, follows it that I am known   well enough too?
translation: If you see this in my face, don't you think I know myself?

original: what barm can your bisson   conspectuities glean out of this character, if I be   known well enough too?
translation: What can your dim wits see in me, if I am known well enough too?

original: Come, sir, come, we know you well enough.
translation: Come, sir, come, we know you well enough.

original: You know neither me, yourselves nor any thing.
translation: You don't know me; you don't know anything!

original: You   are ambitious for poor knaves' caps and legs: you   wear out a good wholesome forenoon in hearing a   cause between an orange wife and a fosset-seller;
translation: You are in politics simply so men will bow to you; you will waste a whole morning listening to a dispute between a fruit seller and a liquor man,

original: and then rejourn the controversy of three pence to a   second day of audience.
translation: and then call that minor dispute back for another wasted day.

original: When you are hearing a   matter between party and party, if you chance to be   pinched with the colic, you make faces like   mummers;
translation: When you are listening to an argument between two citizens, if you let loose a fart, you twist your faces ignorantly so everyone knows;

original: set up the bloody flag against all   patience;
translation: you make war on everyone's patience,

original: and, in roaring for a chamber-pot,   dismiss the controversy bleeding the more entangled   by your hearing:
translation: and in roaring that you need to shit, dismiss disputes unfinished and even worse than when they started.

original: all the peace you make in their   cause is, calling both the parties knaves. You are   a pair of strange ones.
translation: The only thing you accomplish is to call everyone dishonest. You're a pair of strange men.

original: Come, come, you are well understood to be a perfecter giber for the table than a necessary bencher in the Capitol.
translation: Come, come, you are well known as a better comedian than a politician.

original: Our very priests must become mockers, if they shall   encounter such ridiculous subjects as you are.
translation: Our very priests must start to mock, if they encounter men as ridiculous as you.

original: When   you speak best unto the purpose, it is not worth the   wagging of your beards;
translation: When you finally do address important matters, that conversation is worse than if you'd kept quiet and simply  wagged your beards.

original: and your beards deserve not   so honourable a grave as to stuff a botcher's   cushion, or to be entombed in an ass's pack-   saddle.
translation: Your beards don't even deserve to stuff a seamstress's needle-cushion, or to stuff a donkey's saddle-pillow.

original: Yet you must be saying, Marcius is proud;   who in a cheap estimation, is worth predecessors   since Deucalion, though peradventure some of the   best of 'em were hereditary hangmen.
translation: Yet here are you are saying Marcius is proud; a man who is worth all your ancestors since  Deucalion , though probably many of them were just lowly executioners.

original: God-den to   your worships: more of your conversation would   infect my brain, being the herdsmen of the beastly   plebeians: I will be bold to take my leave of you.
translation: Good evening to you; to continue talking with you would make me dumber, you shepherds of ignorant  plebeians . I will be rude enough to leave you.

original: How now, my as fair as noble ladies,—and the moon, were she earthly, no nobler,—whither do you follow your eyes so fast?
translation: How are you, my ladies, as beautiful as you are noble—the moon set down on Earth would be no nobler—what are you looking for so urgently?

original: Honourable Menenius, my boy Marcius approaches; for the love of Juno, let's go.
translation: Honorable Menenius, my son Marcius is coming into Rome; for the love of God, let's go meet him!

original: Ha! Marcius coming home!
translation: What? Marcius is coming home?

original: Ay, worthy Menenius; and with most prosperous approbation.
translation: Yes, worthy Menenius; and with most incredible praise!

original: Take my cap, Jupiter, and I thank thee. Hoo! Marcius coming home!
translation: Take my cap, great gods, and praise be! Hoo! Marcius coming home!

original: Nay,'tis true.
translation: It's true.

original: Look, here's a letter from him: the state hath another, his wife another; and, I think, there's one at home for you.
translation: Look, here's a letter from him. Another went to the Senate, and another to his wife, and I bet there's another one at home for you.

original: I will make my very house reel tonight: a letter for me!
translation: I will make such a celebration that my very house will reel tonight: a letter for me!

original: Yes, certain, there's a letter for you; I saw't.
translation: Yes, there's certainly a letter for you: I saw it.

original: A letter for me! it gives me an estate of seven   years' health; in which time I will make a lip at   the physician:
translation: A letter for me! It will give seven years of life, at which point I will stick out my tongue at the physician.

original: the most sovereign prescription in   Galen is but empiricutic, and, to this preservative,   of no better report than a horse-drench.
translation: The most powerful medicine in  Galen  is quack medicine, and compared to this, no better than horse pills!

original: Is he   not wounded? he was wont to come home wounded.
translation: Is he not wounded? He always seems to come home wounded.

original: O, no, no, no.
translation: Oh, no, no, no.

original: O, he is wounded; I thank the gods for't.
translation: Yes, he is wounded, thank the gods.

original: So do I too, if it be not too much: brings a' victory in his pocket? the wounds become him.
translation: So long as he is not too wounded; he brings a victory with him? If so, the wounds suit him.

original: On's brows: Menenius, he comes the third time home with the oaken garland.
Has he disciplined Aufidius soundly?
translation: Has he beaten Aufidius thoroughly?

original: Titus Lartius writes, they fought together, but Aufidius got off.
translation: Titus Lartius writes that they fought together, but Aufidius escaped.

original: And 'twas time for him too, I'll warrant him that:
translation: That's just like him, I'll give him that.

original: an he had stayed by him, I would not have been so   fidiused for all the chests in Corioli, and the gold   that's in them.
translation: I'd bet all the treasure in Corioli against Aufidius ever finishing a fight with our man Marcius.

original: Is the senate possessed of this?
translation: Does the senate know yet?

original: Good ladies, let's go. Yes, yes, yes; the senate   has letters from the general, wherein he gives my   son the whole name of the war:
translation: Good ladies, let's go. Yes, yes, yes, the senate has letters from the general in which he honors my son with the name of the whole war:

original: he hath in this   action outdone his former deeds doubly
translation: my son has outdone himself this time.

original: In troth, there's wondrous things spoke of him.
translation: Honestly; they are saying wonderful things about him that are almost hard to believe.

original: Wondrous! ay, I warrant you, and not without his true purchasing.
translation: Hard to believe! Yes, I bet, but not without him really doing these things.

original: The gods grant them true!
translation: May the gods make these reports true!

original: True! pow, wow.
True! I'll be sworn they are true. Where is he wounded? @     God save your good worships! Marcius  is coming home: he has more cause to be proud. Where is  he wounded?
translation: True! I'd bet my life they're true. Where is he wounded? God save both of you! Marcius is coming home with even more reason to be proud![To the women] Where is he wounded?

original: I' the shoulder and i' the left arm there will be large cicatrices to show the people, when he shall stand for his place. He received in the repulse of Tarquin seven hurts i' the body.
One i' the neck, and two i' the thigh,—there's nine that I know.
translation: Also, he has one in the neck and two in the thigh—there are nine scars I know of.

original: He had, before this last expedition, twenty-five wounds upon him.
translation: He had, before this last battle, twenty-five wounds on him.

original: Now it's twenty-seven: every gash was an enemy's grave.
Hark! the trumpets.
translation: Listen! The trumpets!

original: These are the ushers of Marcius: before him he   carries noise, and behind him he leaves tears:
translation: They must be welcoming Marcius: he carries the sounds of trumpets with him and leaves tears behind him.

original: Death, that dark spirit, in 's nervy arm doth lie;   Which, being advanced, declines, and then men
translation: Death, that dark spirit, lies deep within his arm:  it is raised, then falls, and men die.

original: Know, Rome, that all alone Marcius did fight   Within Corioli gates:
translation: Know, Rome, that Marcius fought alone inside the gates of Corioli.

original: where he hath won,   With fame, a name to Caius Marcius; these   In honour follows Coriolanus.   Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus!
translation: There, he has won a new name to go with his fame: welcome to Rome, famed Coriolanus!

original: Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus!
translation: Welcome to Rome, famed Coriolanus!

original: No more of this; it does offend my heart: Pray now, no more.
translation: No more of this; I am embarrassed by all this. Please, no more.

original: Look, sir, your mother!
translation: Look, sir, your mother!

original: O, You have, I know, petition'd all the gods For my prosperity!
translation: Oh, you have, I know, prayed to all the gods for my success!

original: Nay, my good soldier, up;   My gentle Marcius, worthy Caius, and   By deed-achieving honour newly named,—
translation: No, my good soldier, stand up. My gentle Marcius, worthy Caius, and by your deeds newly named—

original: What is it?—   Coriolanus must I call thee?—   But O, thy wife!
translation: what is it I am supposed to call you now? Coriolanus? But oh, your wife!

original: My gracious silence, hail!
translation: My gracious silence , greetings!

original: Wouldst thou have laugh'd had I come coffin'd home,   That weep'st to see me triumph?
translation: You are crying over my victory; would you have laughed if I came home in a coffin?

original: Ay, my dear,   Such eyes the widows in Corioli wear,   And mothers that lack sons.
translation: Oh, my dear, the widows in Corioli have eyes like yours, eyes like mothers who lack sons.

original: Now, the gods crown thee!
translation: Now, the gods crown you!

original: O my sweet lady, pardon.
translation: Oh my sweet lady, forgive me.

original: I know not where to turn: O, welcome home: And welcome, general: and ye're welcome all.
translation: I don't know where to turn; oh, welcome home, and welcome general, welcome all!

original: A hundred thousand welcomes. I could weep   And I could laugh, I am light and heavy. Welcome.
translation: A hundred thousand welcomes. I could weep and I could laugh, I am light and heavy hearted. Welcome.

original: A curse begin at very root on's heart,   That is not glad to see thee!
translation: Curse anyone who is not glad to see you!

original: You are three   That Rome should dote on: yet, by the faith of men,   We have some old crab-trees here   at home that will not   Be grafted to your relish.
translation: You are three men that Rome should honor; yet, by the nature of men, we have some old grumps here at home that will not be join in our celebration.

original: Yet welcome, warriors:   We call a nettle but a nettle and   The faults of fools but folly.
translation: Nevertheless welcome, warriors. We call thorns just thorns, and the mistakes of fools just foolishness.

original: Ever right.
translation: As we should.

original: Menenius ever, ever.
translation: As we should, Menenius, as we should.

original: Give way there, and go on!
translation: Clear a way for them!

original: Your hand, and yours:   Ere in our own house I do shade my head,   The good patricians must be visited;
translation: Let me take your hand, and yours. Before I can return to our home, I must visit the good senators

original: From whom I have received not only greetings,   But with them change of honours.
translation: from whom I have had not just a letter, but also a new set of honors.

original: I have lived   To see inherited my very wishes   And the buildings of my fancy:
translation: I have lived to see my dreams made into reality.

original: only   There's one thing wanting, which I doubt not but   Our Rome will cast upon thee.
translation: There's only one thing missing,  which I have no doubt our Rome will honor you with.

original: Know, good mother, I had rather be their servant in my way, Than sway with them in theirs.
translation: Know, good mother, I had rather serve Rome my way than rule Rome in theirs.

original: On, to the Capitol!
translation: Let's go, to the Capitol!

original: All tongues speak of him, and the bleared sights   Are spectacled to see him:
translation: Everyone speaks of him, and every eye is turned to see him.

original: your prattling nurse   Into a rapture lets her baby cry   While she chats him:
translation: The gossiping nurse lets her baby cry itself into a fit while she talks about him;

original: the kitchen malkin pins   Her richest lockram 'bout her reechy neck,   Clambering the walls to eye him:
translation: the kitchen wench pins her finest blouse around her filthy neck just to climb a wall and see him from afar.

original: stalls, bulks,  windows,   Are smother'd up, leads fill'd, and ridges horsed   With variable complexions, all agreeing   In earnestness to see him:
translation: Stalls, walls, and windows are covered in people, and men of all sorts watch from hilltops to see him.

original: seld-shown flamens   Do press among the popular throngs and puff   To win a vulgar station:
translation: Seldom-seen priests press in among the crowds of common people and exhaust themselves just to get a glimpse.

original: or veil'd dames   Commit the war of white and damask in   Their nicely-gawded cheeks to the wanton spoil   Of Phoebus' burning kisses:
translation: Veiled and perfumed ladies war with their own beauty and throw themselves into the burning sun.

original: such a pother   As if that whatsoever god who leads him   Were slily crept into his human powers   And gave him graceful posture.
translation: It's such an insane commotion one might think that Coriolanus had become a kind of god.

original: On the sudden, I warrant him consul.
Then our office may, During his power, go sleep.
translation: If he gains power, we may lose all our authority.

original: He cannot temperately transport his honours From where he should begin and end, but will Lose those he hath won.
translation: But he cannot possibly maintain his cool throughout the nomination process for consul, and so he will lose whatever praise he's won.

original: In that there's comfort.
translation: In that there's comfort.

original: Doubt not   The commoners, for whom we stand,   but they   Upon their ancient malice will forget   With the least cause these his new honours,
translation: Don't doubt that the commoners we represent still hate him, and that they'll use any excuse to forget these news honors.

original: which   That he will give them make I as little question   As he is proud to do't.
translation: There's no question he'll crack, and as little question that he'll be proud to crack when he does.

original: I heard him swear,   Were he to stand for consul,
translation: I heard him swear that—were he to be nominated as consul—

original: never would he   Appear i' the market-place nor on him put   The napless vesture of humility;
translation: he would never appear in the market, nor ever lower himself to be humble;

original: Nor showing, as the manner is, his wounds   To the people, beg their stinking breaths.
translation: nor would he  show his wounds to the people  to beg for their approval.

original: 'Tis right.
translation: That's right.

original: It was his word: O, he would miss it rather Than carry it but by the suit of the gentry to him, And the desire of the nobles.
translation: That's what he said, anyway—that he would rather not be consul if it required him  to do anything but appeal to the gentry and the desires of the nobles.

original: I wish no better Than have him hold that purpose and to put it In execution.
translation: I want nothing more than for him to remain committed to that.

original: 'Tis most like he will.
translation: It's likely that he will.

original: It shall be to him then as our good wills, A sure destruction.
So it must fall out   To him or our authorities.
translation: So he'll be destroyed either by himself or by us.

original: For an end,   We must suggest the people in what hatred   He still hath held them;
translation: In order to be certain of this, we should tell the people that he still hates them;

original: that to's power he would   Have made them mules, silenced their pleaders and   Dispropertied their freedoms,
translation: that if he could've, he'd have made them slaves, silenced their representatives and stolen their freedoms.

original: holding them,   In human action and capacity,   Of no more soul nor fitness for the world   Than camels in the war,
translation: We will tell them that he holds them, in deed and spirit, to be no better than beasts in war,

original: who have their provand   Only for bearing burdens, and sore blows   For sinking under them.
translation: good only for bearing burdens and being whipped.

original: This, as you say, suggested   At some time when his soaring insolence   Shall touch the people   —
translation: And we'll suggest all this some time when his high-and-mighty attitude will have an impact on the people—

original: which time shall not want,   If he be put upon 't; and that's as easy   As to set dogs on sheep—
translation: there will be many opportunities if we goad him, and that's as easy as making a dog herd sheep.

original: will be his fire   To kindle their dry stubble; and their blaze   Shall darken him for ever.
translation: His reaction will set their beards aflame, and their fury will ruin him forever.

original: What's the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: You are sent for to the Capitol. 'Tis thought   That Marcius shall be consul:
translation: Someone in the Capitol has sent for you. There is word that Marcius will be consul;

original: I have seen the dumb men throng to see him and   The blind to bear him speak:
translation: I have seen speechless men crowd around him and blind men beg to hear him speak.

original: matrons flung gloves,   Ladies and maids their scarfs and handkerchers,   Upon him as he pass'd:
translation: Widows threw gloves, ladies and maids threw scarves and handkerchiefs upon him as he passed.

original: the nobles bended,   As to Jove's statue, and the commons made   A shower and thunder with their caps and shouts:
translation: Nobles bowed as though to a god's statue, and the commoners thundered with applause and approval.

original: I never saw the like.
translation: I've never seen anything like it.

original: Let's to the Capitol; And carry with us ears and eyes for the time, But hearts for the event.
translation: Let's go to the Capitol, and though we might act attentive to what's going on, keep our hearts set on our plan to ruin him.

original: Have with you.
translation: I'm with you.

original: Come, come, they are almost here. How many stand for consulships?
translation: Come, come, they are almost here. How many are up for the consulship?

original: Three, they say: but 'tis thought of every one Coriolanus will carry it.
translation: Three, they say, but everyone thinks Coriolanus will win it.

original: That's a brave fellow; but he's vengeance proud, and loves not the common people.
translation: He's an extraordinary fellow, but he's also so proud, and doesn't love the common people.

original: Faith, there had been many great men that have   flattered the people, who ne'er loved them;
translation: Oh come on, there have been many great men who have flattered the people but not loved them,

original: and there   be many that they have loved, they know not   wherefore:
translation: and there have been many people have loved without reason.

original: so that, if they love they know not why,   they hate upon no better a ground:
translation: Whoever they love, they don't know why, and they hate with the same ignorance:

original: therefore, for   Coriolanus neither to care whether they love or hate   him manifests the true knowledge he has in their   disposition;
translation: therefore, for Coriolanus not to care whether they love or hate him is just an example that he knows the people well,

original: and out of his noble carelessness lets   them plainly see't.
translation: and out of his nobility he lets the people plainly see that.

original: If he did not care whether he had their love or no,   he waved indifferently 'twixt doing them neither   good nor harm:
translation: If he didn't care whether they loved him or not, he'd be indifferent to them, but that's not what he does;

original: but he seeks their hate with greater   devotion than can render it him; and leaves   nothing undone that may fully discover him their   opposite.
translation: instead, he seems to seek their hate with greater devotion than he can possibly win it, and does everything he can to show how he is different from them.

original: Now, to seem to affect the malice and   displeasure of the people is as bad as that which he   dislikes, to flatter them for their love.
translation: To attract the hatred of the people is just as bad as flattering them, which he says he dislikes.

original: He hath deserved worthily of his country:
translation: He has earned much from his country,

original: and his   ascent is not by such easy degrees
translation: and his rise to power has not been easy,

original: as those who,   having been supple and courteous to the people,   bonneted, without any further deed to have them at   an into their estimation and report:
translation: as it is for those who are kind and courteous to the people, who tip their hats and then, doing nothing else, win the people's favor.

original: but he hath so   planted his honours in their eyes, and his actions   in their hearts, that for their tongues to be   silent,
translation: But Coriolanus has so demonstrated his honor that if they were to be silent

original: and not confess so much, were a kind of   ingrateful injury;
translation: it would be a kind of betrayal.

original: to report otherwise, were a   malice, that, giving itself the lie, would pluck   reproof and rebuke from every ear that heard it.
translation: To say other than that he is worthy would be a cruelty, a lie that would call for denial from everyone who heard it.

original: No more of him; he is a worthy man: make way, they are coming.
translation: No more of him; he is an admirable man: make way, they are coming.

original: Having determined of the Volsces and   To send for Titus Lartius,
translation: Now that we've decided what to do with the Volsces and are sending for Titus Lartius,

original: it remains,   As the main point of this our after-meeting,   To gratify his noble service that   Hath thus stood for his country:
translation: the remaining point of this meeting is to reward the noble service of the man who has stood for his country.

original: therefore,   please you,   Most reverend and grave elders, to desire   The present consul, and last general   In our well-found successes,
translation: Therefore, most serious elders, please allow Cominius, our current consul and recent general,

original: to report   A little of that worthy work perform'd   By Caius Marcius Coriolanus,
translation: to report a little of that worthy work performed by Caius Marcius Coriolanus,

original: whom   We met here both to thank and to remember   With honours like himself.
translation: whom we met here both to thank and to award with honors.

original: Speak, good Cominius:
translation: Speak, good Cominius.

original: Leave nothing out for length, and make us think   Rather our state's defective for requital   Than we to stretch it out.
translation: Leave nothing out; make us feel as though we do not have enough reward for him rather than that he has not done enough to earn rewards.

original: We do request your kindest ears,
translation: Masters of the people, we do request your kindest ears,

original: and after,
translation: and after, that you generously report to those you represent, the commoners, what happens here.

original: We are convented   Upon a pleasing treaty,
translation: We are brought together on a happy occasion,

original: and have hearts   Inclinable to honour and advance   The theme of our assembly.
translation: and our hearts are ready to honor and continue the theme of this discussion.

original: Which the rather   We shall be blest to do,
translation: Which we'll be better prepared to do

original: if he remember   A kinder value of the people than   He hath hereto prized them at.
translation: if Coriolanus would acknowledge that the common people are better than he's been saying they are.

original: That's off, that's off; I would you rather had been silent. Please you To hear Cominius speak?
translation: Lay off, lay off; I wish you had kept silent. Please, let's hear Cominius speak.

original: Most willingly; But yet my caution was more pertinent Than the rebuke you give it.
translation: Of course, but my hesitation is worth more than to be brushed away by you.

original: He loves your people But tie him not to be their bedfellow. Worthy Cominius, speak.
translation: He loves your people, but don't tie him down to be their lover. Worthy Cominius, speak.

original: Nay, keep your place.
translation: No, stay where you are.

original: Sit, Coriolanus; never shame to hear What you have nobly done.
translation: Sit, Coriolanus, don't be ashamed to hear about your noble deeds.

original: Your horror's pardon: I had rather have my wounds to heal again Than hear say how I got them.
translation: Pardon me, your honor. I would rather be wounded all over again than hear someone recite how I got them.

original: Sir, I hope My words disbench'd you not.
translation: Sir, I hope my words didn't upset you.

original: No, sir: yet oft,   When blows have made me stay, I fled from words.
translation: No, sir, although often when I had rather take action, people want to talk.

original: You soothed not, therefore hurt not:
translation: You did not belittle me, therefore you haven't hurt me.

original: but   your people,   I love them as they weigh.
translation: As for your common people, I love them for what they're worth.

original: Pray now, sit down.
translation: Please, sit down.

original: I had rather have one scratch my head i' the sun When the alarum were struck than idly sit To hear my nothings monster'd.
translation: I'd rather sit ignorantly in the sun while the city is attacked than sit here and hear my minor actions twisted into marvelous deeds.

original: Masters of the people,   Your multiplying spawn how can he flatter—
translation: Masters of the people, how can he flatter the masses of the people—

original: That's thousand to one good one—
translation: with one good man to a thousand others who aren't so good—

original: when you now see   He had rather venture all his limbs for honour   Than one on's ears to hear it?
translation: when you see that he had rather risk his life for honor than risk an ear to hear about it?

original: Proceed, Cominius.
translation: Go ahead, Cominius.

original: I shall lack voice: the deeds of Coriolanus   Should not be utter'd feebly.
translation: I will barely be able to tell what he has done.  The deeds of Coriolanus should not be uttered weakly.

original: It is held   That valour is the chiefest virtue, and   Most dignifies the haver:
translation: They say that bravery is the most important virtue:

original: if it be,   The man I speak of cannot in the world   Be singly counterpoised.
translation: if so, the man I speak of has no equal in the world.

original: At sixteen years,   When Tarquin made a head for Rome, he fought   Beyond the mark of others:
translation: When he was sixteen years old and Tarquin attempted to conquer Rome, he fought far behind enemy lines, beyond the reach of others.

original: our then dictator,   Whom with all praise I point at, saw him fight,
translation: Our leader at the time, who with all praise I point at, saw him fight,

original: When with his Amazonian chin he drove   The bristled lips before him:
translation: when with his  Amazonian chin  he drove grown men to flee him.

original: be bestrid   An o'er-press'd Roman and i' the consul's view   Slew three opposers: Tarquin's self he met,   And struck him on his knee:
translation: He stood over a fallen Roman and in the view of the consul, killed three men to defend him. He met Tarquin himself, and struck him on the knee.

original: in that day's feats,   When he might act the woman in the scene,   He proved best man i' the field, and for his meed   Was brow-bound with the oak.
translation: In that battle, he was so young  he could have acted the woman in the scene,  instead he proved the best man in the fight, and for his bravery was awarded the oaken garland.

original: His pupil age   Man-enter'd thus, he waxed like a sea,   And in the brunt of seventeen battles since   He lurch'd all swords of the garland.
translation: He advanced from boy to man this way, swelling like the sea, and in the midst of seventeen battles since he cheated everyone else of the garland.

original: For this last,   Before and in Corioli, let me say,   I cannot speak him home:
translation: For this last fight, just now in Corioli, let me say there is no praise sufficient.

original: he stopp'd the fliers;   And by his rare example made the coward   Turn terror into sport:
translation: He kept our men from fleeing, and by his incredible example made our cowardly men confident.

original: as weeds before   A vessel under sail, so men obey'd   And fell below his stem:
translation: As weeds bend away from a ship at sail, so men obeyed and fell beneath his force;

original: his sword, death's stamp,   Where it did mark, it took; from face to foot   He was a thing of blood, whose every motion   Was timed with dying cries:
translation: his sword was death itself: where it struck, it killed; from face to foot he was a thing of blood as in a dance, a man whose every movement was timed to dying cries .

original: alone he enter'd   The mortal gate of the city, which he painted   With shunless destiny;
translation: Alone, he entered the gates of Corioli and painted it with the blood of his victims like Fate itself;

original: aidless came off,   And with a sudden reinforcement struck   Corioli like a planet: now all's his:
translation: without aid he did this, as though suddenly strengthened, and struck Corioli like a planet. Now everything is his:

original: When, by and by, the din of war gan pierce   His ready sense; then straight his doubled spirit   Re-quicken'd what in flesh was fatigate,   And to the battle came he;
translation: when sounds of war returned him to awareness as from a trance, he braced himself and by his own power made himself alive again; he came to the battle outside the city

original: where he did   Run reeking o'er the lives of men, as if   'Twere a perpetual spoil:
translation: and ran like a war machine over the lives of men, as though it were a game, a slaughter,

original: and till we call'd   Both field and city ours, he never stood   To ease his breast with panting.
translation: and until we called both the battle and the city ours, he did not stand to take a breath.

original: Worthy man!
translation: Excellent man!

original: He cannot but with measure fit the honours Which we devise him.
translation: We must measure our honors to fit his deeds.

original: Our spoils he kick'd at,   And look'd upon things precious as they were   The common muck of the world:
translation: He kicked at the spoils of war, Corioli's treasure, and looked upon precious things as though they were the common trash of the world.

original: he covets less   Than misery itself would give;
translation: He desires less than misery gives freely,

original: rewards   His deeds with doing them, and is content   To spend the time to end it.
translation: thinks of his deeds as their own reward, and is  content to spend the time to end it.

original: He's right noble: Let him be call'd for.
translation: He is truly noble. Call him in.

original: Call Coriolanus.
translation: Call Coriolanus.

original: He doth appear.
translation: He doth appear.

original: I do owe them still My life and services.
translation: Nothing has changed: I owe them, as always, my life and service.

original: It then remains That you do speak to the people.
translation: Then the only thing left is that you speak to the people.

original: I do beseech you,   Let me o'erleap that custom,
translation: I ask you, let me skip that custom:

original: for I cannot   Put on the gown, stand naked and entreat them,   For my wounds' sake, to give their suffrage:
translation: I can't put on a beggar's gown, stand naked and plead with them to vote for me based on my scars.

original: please you   That I may pass this doing.
translation: Please, let me avoid that.

original: Sir, the people Must have their voices; neither will they bate One jot of ceremony.
translation: Sir, the people must have their say; they will not miss even a moment of ceremony.

original: Put them not to't:
translation: Don't anger them, Coriolanus.

original: Pray you, go fit you to the custom and   Take to you, as your predecessors have,
translation: Please, engage in the custom and show, as your predecessors have,

original: Your honour with your form.
translation: the honor of your body's scars.

original: It is apart That I shall blush in acting, and might well Be taken from the people.
translation: It is a part that I will blush to act, and I don't really need to do it.

original: Mark you that?
translation: Hear that?

original: To brag unto them, thus I did, and thus;
translation: To brag to them, "I did this, and this,"

original: Show them the unaching scars which I should hide,
translation: showing them old scars which I should hide,

original: As if I had received them for the hire   Of their breath only!
translation: as though I had received those scars only in order to get their votes!

original: Do not stand upon't.
translation: Don't let this one thing bother you.

original: We recommend to you, tribunes of the people,   Our purpose to them:
translation: Tribunes of the people,  present our purpose to them,

original: and to our noble consul   Wish we all joy and honour.
translation: and to our noble consul, we wish you joy and honor.

original: To Coriolanus come all joy and honour!
translation: To Coriolanus, all joy and honor!

original: You see how he intends to use the people.
translation: You see how he intends to treat the people.

original: May they perceive's intent! He will require them, As if he did contemn what he requested Should be in them to give.
translation: May they see it too! He will ask for their favor as though scornful that they could ever give him anything.

original: Come, we'll inform them Of our proceedings here: on the marketplace, I know, they do attend us.
translation: Come, let's tell them of what's happened here. The people are waiting in the marketplace for us.

original: Once, if he do require our voices, we ought not to deny him.
translation: In short, if he needs us to vouch for him, we shouldn't deny him.

original: We may, sir, if we will.
translation: We may, if we want to.

original: We have power in ourselves to do it, but it is a   power that we have no power to do;
translation: We have the authority to do it, but it is a power that is not ours to wield alone.

original: for if he show us   his wounds and tell us his deeds, we are to put our   tongues into those wounds and speak for them;
translation: If he shows us his wounds and tells us his deeds, only then are we to let those wounds inspire us to speak for him.

original: so, if   he tell us his noble deeds, we must also tell him   our noble acceptance of them.
translation: So, if he tells us his noble deeds, it's our position to nobly accept them.

original: Ingratitude is   monstrous, and for the multitude to be ingrateful,   were to make a monster of the multitude:
translation: Ingratitude is monstrous, and if the common people were to be ungrateful it would make a monster of our republic—

original: of the   which we being members, should bring ourselves to be   monstrous members.
translation: we, being members of that republic, would make monsters of ourselves.

original: And to make us no better thought of, a little help will serve; for once we stood up about the corn, he himself stuck not to call us the many-headed multitude.
translation: And it won't take much to make us seem monstrous, after all. When we protested about the corn, he certainly didn't hesitate to call us a "many-headed multitude."

original: We have been called so of many; not that our heads   are some brown, some black, some auburn, some bald,   but that our wits are so diversely coloured:
translation: We've been called that by many, even though we're clearly individuals: some of us with brown hair, some with black, auburn, or bald, and our minds equally diverse.

original: and   truly I think if all our wits were to issue out of   one skull, they would fly east, west, north, south,
translation: I truly think that even if all our minds were contained in one skull, our thoughts would fly east, west, north, south,

original: and their consent of one direct way should be at   once to all the points o' the compass.
translation: and any consent we would reach would be to all directions at once.

original: Think you so? Which way do you judge my wit would fly?
translation: You think so? Which way do you think my thoughts would fly?

original: Nay, your wit will not so soon out as another man's will;'tis strongly wedged up in a block-head, but if it were at liberty, 'twould, sure, southward.
translation: No, your thoughts won't fly out like another man's might, because of your thick head! But if your thoughts could fly, surely they'd fly south.

original: Why that way?
translation: Why that way?

original: To lose itself in a fog, where being three parts melted away with rotten dews, the fourth would return for conscience sake, to help to get thee a wife.
translation: To lose themselves in a fog, where most of them would melt away with plague, and only a fourth would return for conscience's sake to help you get a wife.

original: You are never without your tricks: you may, you may.
translation: You're never without these jokes—go on, then.

original: Are you all resolved to give your voices?
translation: Are you all ready to vote on Coriolanus?

original: But   that's no matter, the greater part carries it.
translation: But that's no matter, the majority is obvious.

original: I   say, if he would incline to the people, there was   never a worthier man.
translation: As far as I'm concerned, if Coriolanus would simply acknowledge the people, there would be no better choice for consul.

original: Here he comes, and in the gown of humility: mark his   behavior.
translation: Here he comes in  the gown of humility ; look at how he behaves.

original: We are not to stay all together, but to   come by him where he stands, by ones, by twos, and   by threes.
translation: In this ceremony, we're supposed to approach him where he stands, in groups of two or three.

original: He's to make his requests by   particulars; wherein every one of us has a single   honour,
translation: He will make his requests individually, so that every one of us has the honor

original: in giving him our own voices with our own   tongues:
translation: of giving him our votes with our own tongues.

original: therefore follow me, and I direct you how   you shall go by him.
translation: Therefore, follow me and I'll organize this.

original: Content, content.
translation: We agree.

original: O sir, you are not right: have you not known The worthiest men have done't?
translation: Oh, sir, you're not right: don't you know that the worthiest men have done this?

original: What must I say?   'I Pray, sir'—   Plague upon't!
translation: What am I going to say? "I beg you, sir"— to hell with it!

original: I cannot bring   My tongue to such a pace:—'Look, sir, my wounds!
translation: I cannot bring myself to say this kind of thing: "Look sir, my wounds!

original: I got them in my country's service, when   Some certain of your brethren roar'd and ran   From the noise of our own drums.'
translation: I got them in the service of my country, when people like you cried and ran away from the sound of our own drums."

original: O me, the gods! You must not speak of that: you must desire them To think upon you.
translation: Oh my god, you can't say that. You need to convince them to consider you.

original: Think upon me! hang 'em! I would they would forget me, like the virtues Which our divines lose by 'em.
translation: Consider me? Damn them! I wish they would forget me, like they forget every virtue we try to teach them.

original: You'll mar all: I'll leave you: pray you, speak to 'em, I pray you, In wholesome manner.
translation: You'll ruin everything. I must leave you: please, speak to them, I beg you, in a kind way.

original: Bid them wash their faces And keep their teeth clean.
translation: I'll tell them to wash their faces and keep their teeth clean.

original: So, here comes a brace.
translation: So, here comes a pair.

original: You know the cause, air, of my standing here.
translation: You know the reason, sir, I am standing here.

original: We do, sir; tell us what hath brought you to't.
translation: We do, sir, but please tell us yourself what's brought you here.

original: Mine own desert.
translation: That which I deserve.

original: Your own desert!
translation: That which you deserve?

original: Ay, but not mine own desire.
translation: Yes, but not that which I desire.

original: How not your own desire?
translation: How is it not what you desire?

original: No, sir,'twas never my desire yet to trouble the poor with begging.
translation: No, sir, I've never wanted to trouble the poor by begging.

original: You must think, if we give you any thing, we hope to gain by you.
translation: You must know that we will only give you anything if we have something to gain by you.

original: Well then, I pray, your price o' the consulship?
translation: Well then, tell me, what's the price of consulship?

original: The price is to ask it kindly.
translation: The price is simply to ask it kindly.

original: Kindly! Sir, I pray, let me ha't: I have wounds to show you, which shall be yours in private. Your good voice, sir; what say you?
You shall ha' it, worthy sir.
translation: You shall have it, worthy sir.

original: A match, sir. There's in all two worthy voices begged. I have your alms: adieu.
translation: Fair enough, sir. So that's two worthy voices begged, then. I am in your debt; good-bye.

original: But this is something odd.
translation: This sure is bizarre.

original: An 'twere to give again,—but 'tis no matter.
translation: If I could do it over—but forget it.

original: Pray you now, if it may stand with the tune of your voices that I may be consul, I have here the customary gown.
translation: Please, if it is acceptable to you that I be consul, I have the customary gown here.

original: You have deserved nobly of your country, and you have not deserved nobly.
translation: On one hand, you have been noble for you country, but you have also not been noble.

original: Your enigma?
translation: What do you mean?

original: You have been a scourge to her enemies, you have been a rod to her friends; you have not indeed loved the common people.
translation: You have been a torment to Rome's enemies and made trouble for her friends; but you have not loved the common people.

original: You should account me the more virtuous that I have   not been common in my love.
translation: You should think of me as more virtuous for not giving out my love to just anyone.

original: I will, sir, flatter my   sworn brother, the people, to earn a dearer   estimation of them;
translation: I will, sir, flatter those to whom I am devoted—that is the people—to earn their respect.

original: 'tis a condition they account   gentle: and since the wisdom of their choice is   rather to have my hat than my heart,
translation: They call this being "gentle," and since they had rather have a tip of my hat than the labor of my heart,

original: I will practise   the insinuating nod and be off to them most   counterfeitly;
translation: I will practice the nod and show deference most falsely.

original: that is, sir, I will counterfeit the   bewitchment of some popular man and give it   bountiful to the desirers.
translation: That is, sir, I will act star-struck like some normal man and serve up this performance to whoever wants it.

original: Therefore, beseech you,   I may be consul.
translation: Is this good enough for you to make me consul?

original: We hope to find you our friend; and therefore give you our voices heartily.
translation: We hope you'll be our friend, and give you our votes gladly with that in mind.

original: You have received many wounds for your country.
translation: You have received many wounds for your country.

original: I will not seal your knowledge with showing them. I will make much of your voices, and so trouble you no  further.
translation: I will not confirm your knowledge by displaying them. I am already making much of your votes, and do not want to trouble you further.

original: The gods give you joy, sir, heartily!
translation: The gods give you joy, sir, great joy!

original: Most sweet voices!
translation: These sweet voices!

original: Better it is to die, better to starve,   Than crave the hire which first we do deserve.
translation: It is better to die, better to starve, than to crave to get what we already deserve.

original: Why in this woolvish toge should I stand here,   To beg of Hob and Dick, that do appear,   Their needless vouches?
translation: Why must I stand here in this wooly, ratty toga, to beg of  Hob and Dick , or whoever shows up, their meaningless favor?

original: Custom calls me to't:   What custom wills, in all things should we do't,
translation: Because of custom; if we did everything custom called for,

original: The dust on antique time would lie unswept,   And mountainous error be too highly heapt   For truth to o'er-peer.
translation: the  dust on antique time would never be cleaned off , and we would make error after error until they piled up like mountains, too high for truth to reach.

original: Rather than fool it so,   Let the high office and the honour go   To one that would do thus.
translation: Rather than be so foolish, let the public positions and honor go to those who will be honorable!

original: I am half through;   The one part suffer'd, the other will I do.
translation: I am half finished; now that I have suffered the first half, I will suffer the other half as well.

original: Here come more voices.
translation: Here come more  voices .

original: Your voices: for your voices I have fought;   Watch'd for your voices;
translation: Your voices: for your voices I have fought; stood guard over Rome for your voices;

original: for Your voices bear   Of wounds two dozen odd; battles thrice six   I have seen and heard of;
translation: for your voices I've been wounded two dozen times or more; three times six battles I have seen and heard;

original: for your voices have   Done many things, some less, some more your voices:   Indeed I would be consul.
translation: for your voices I have done many things — some less, some more. Your voices? Indeed I would be consul.

original: He has done nobly, and cannot go without any honest man's voice.
translation: He has done nobly, and should not be denied the vote of any honest man.

original: Therefore let him be consul: the gods give him joy, and make him good friend to the people!
translation: Therefore let him be consul. The gods give him joy, and make him a good friend to the people!

original: Amen, amen. God save thee, noble consul!
translation: Amen, amen. God save you, noble consul!

original: Worthy voices!
translation: Worthy voices!

original: You have stood your limitation; and the tribunes   Endue you with the people's voice:
translation: You have done this as long as you need to, and the tribunes approve that you have the voice of the people.

original: remains   That, in the official marks invested, you   Anon do meet the senate.
translation: The only thing left for you to do is to meet with the Senate in your official robes.

original: Is this done?
translation: So it's over?

original: The custom of request you have discharged: The people do admit you, and are summon'd To meet anon, upon your approbation.
translation: You have done your duty according to the custom. The people accept you, and you are summoned to meet later, upon your approval.

original: Where? at the senate-house?
translation: Where? In the senate?

original: There, Coriolanus.
translation: Yes, Coriolanus.

original: May I change these garments?
translation: May I change these garments?

original: You may, sir.
translation: You may, sir.

original: That I'll straight do; and, knowing myself again, Repair to the senate-house.
translation: Then I'll do that right away, and once I recognize myself again, will head to the senate.

original: I'll keep you company. Will you along?
translation: I'll keep you company.  Will you come along?

original: We stay here for the people.
translation: We stay here for the people.

original: Fare you well.
translation: Good-bye.

original: He has it now, and by his looks methink 'Tis warm at 's heart.
translation: That's that—it looks to me like he found all of this heart-warming.

original: With a proud heart he wore his humble weeds. will you dismiss the people?
translation: He wore his humble robes with a proud heart. Will you dismiss the people?

original: How now, my masters! have you chose this man?
translation: What's the deal, friends? Have you chosen that man?

original: He has our voices, sir.
translation: He has our voices, sir.

original: We pray the gods he may deserve your loves.
translation: We pray to the gods he may deserve the love you give him.

original: Amen, sir: to my poor unworthy notice, He mock'd us when he begg'd our voices.
translation: Amen sir: it seemed to me, though I'm unworthy, that he mocked us when he begged for our voices.

original: Certainly He flouted us downright.
translation: Certainly. He was downright sarcastic.

original: No,'tis his kind of speech: he did not mock us.
translation: No, that's just how he talks; he did not mock us.

original: Not one amongst us, save yourself, but says He used us scornfully: he should have show'd us His marks of merit, wounds received for's country.
translation: Everyone among us but you says he used us scornfully. He should have shown us his marks of merit—the wounds he received for his country.

original: Why, so he did, I am sure.
translation: Why, surely he did.

original: No, no; no man saw 'em.
translation: No, no, no one saw them.

original: He said he had wounds, which he could show   in private;
translation: He said he had wounds, which he could show in private.

original: And with his hat, thus waving it in scorn,   'I would be consul,' says he: 'aged custom,   But by your voices, will not so permit me;
translation: [Waves hat]  And he did this with his hat, waving it scornfully. "I would be consul," he said, "but by old custom, I cannot be until I have your voices—

original: Your voices therefore.' When we granted that,   Here was 'I thank you for your voices: thank you:
translation: thus, give me your voices." When we granted them,  he was like  "I thank you for your voices, thank you:

original: Your most sweet voices: now you have left   your voices,   I have no further with you.' Was not this mockery?
translation: your most sweet voices— now you have no voices left, I have no need for you." Wasn't he mocking us?

original: Why either were you ignorant to see't, Or, seeing it, of such childish friendliness To yield your voices?
translation: You were either ignorant of it or, seeing it, why were you so childishly friendly? Why give him your voices?

original: Could you not have told him   As you were lesson'd,
translation: Could you not have told him as you were taught?

original: when he had no power,   But was a petty servant to the state,   He was your enemy,
translation: When he was powerless, just a servant to the state, he was your enemy;

original: ever spake against   Your liberties and the charters that you bear   I' the body of the weal;
translation: he always spoke out against your liberties and the rights of the people in our republic.

original: and now, arriving   A place of potency and sway o' the state,   If he should still malignantly remain   Fast foe to the plebeii,
translation: And now that he has a position of power, what if he remains a foe to the people—

original: your voices might   Be curses to yourselves? You should have said   That as his worthy deeds did claim no less   Than what he stood for,
translation: won't your voices be curses to yourselves? You should have said that just as his deeds were worth no less than what he stood for,

original: so his gracious nature   Would think upon you for your voices and   Translate his malice towards you into love,   Standing your friendly lord.
translation: so he ought to think upon your voices and change his hate for you into love, and thus be friendly to you.

original: Thus to have said,   As you were fore-advised, had touch'd his spirit   And tried his inclination;
translation: If you'd said that, as you we told you to ahead of time, you would have gotten to the core of things and seen what he was really like.

original: from him pluck'd   Either his gracious promise, which you might,   As cause had call'd you up, have held him to
translation: You'd either have gotten a gracious promise from him—which you then could have called up in the future—

original: Or else it would have gall'd his surly nature,   Which easily endures not article   Tying him to aught;
translation: or it would have been easy to see his unfriendly nature and made him furious.

original: so putting him to rage,   You should have ta'en the advantage of his choler   And pass'd him unelected.
translation: Seeing his rage, you could have taken advantage of his short temper and then let him go unelected.

original: Did you perceive   He did solicit you in free contempt   When he did need your loves,
translation: Did you see how he asked for your approval with such contempt when he needed your love?

original: and do you think   That his contempt shall not be bruising to you,   When he hath power to crush?
translation: Do you really think that his contempt will not be far, far worse when he has power and no longer needs you?

original: Why, had your bodies   No heart among you? or had you tongues to cry   Against the rectorship of judgment?
translation: Did not a single one of you have an ounce of boldness? Did no tongue cry out to guide you with good judgement?

original: Have you   Ere now denied the asker?
translation: Have you ever before denied someone who asked?

original: and now again   Of him that did not ask, but mock, bestow   Your sued-for tongues?
translation: And now, even of one who mocked instead of asking, you still bestow whatever he requests?

original: He's not confirm'd; we may deny him yet.
translation: He's not confirmed; we could still deny him.

original: And will deny him: I'll have five hundred voices of that sound.
translation: And we will deny him. I'll have five hundred voices of that.

original: I twice five hundred and their friends to piece 'em.
translation: I'll have double five hundred, and their friends alongside!

original: Get you hence instantly, and tell those friends,   They have chose a consul that will from them take   Their liberties;
translation: Then leave, instantly, and tell those friends that they have approved a consul who will take their freedoms,

original: make them of no more voice   Than dogs that are as often beat for barking   As therefore kept to do so.
translation: a man who will care less about what they have to say than about dogs beaten for barking— dogs kept just to be beaten.

original: Let them assemble,   And on a safer judgment all revoke   Your ignorant election;
translation: Assemble the people and be more reasonable: revoke this ignorant election.

original: enforce his pride,   And his old hate unto you; besides, forget not   With what contempt he wore the humble weed,
translation: Remind the people of his pride and long-standing hate for them, and don't forget the contempt with which he wore his humble toga—

original: How in his suit he scorn'd you; but your loves,   Thinking upon his services, took from you   The apprehension of his present portance,
translation: how even as he asked you for approval, he scorned you. Your good nature, thinking on his service, blinded you to the way he behaved in that moment,

original: Which most gibingly, ungravely, he did fashion   After the inveterate hate he bears you.
translation: which so reflected the deep-seated hate he has for you.

original: Lay A fault on us, your tribunes; that we laboured, No impediment between, but that you must Cast your election on him.
translation: Blame your choice on us, your representatives. Say that it was we who insisted you elect him.

original: Say, you chose him   More after our commandment than as guided   By your own true affections,
translation: Say you chose him more because we commanded it than out of your own true feelings,

original: and that your minds,   Preoccupied with what you rather must do   Than what you should,
translation: and that your minds, preoccupied with what you  had  to do rather than what you  should  do

original: made you against the grain   To voice him consul: lay the fault on us.
translation: made you go against yourselves to name him consul. Blame us.

original: Ay, spare us not. Say we read lectures to you.
translation: Right, don't leave us out of it. Say we lectured you.

original: How youngly he began to serve his country,   How long continued, and what stock he springs of,   The noble house o' the Marcians,
translation: That we reminded you how young he was when he began to serve his country, how he has done so ever since, that he comes from a strong people, the noble family of the Marcians—

original: from whence came   That Ancus Marcius, Numa's daughter's son,   Who, after great Hostilius, here was king;
translation: the family of Ancus Marcius, Numa's daughter's son, who was king of Rome after the great Hostilius,

original: Of the same house Publius and Quintus were,   That our beat water brought by conduits hither;   And   [Censorinus,]
translation: and of Publius and Quintus, who built our aqueducts; even Censorinus,

original: nobly named so,   Twice being   [by the people chosen]   censor,   Was his great ancestor.
translation: nobly named for being twice elected censor, was his great ancestor.
