original: One thus descended,   That hath beside well in his person wrought   To be set high in place,
translation: he was a man from that family, with many great qualities which make him suited for public service.

original: we did commend   To your remembrances:
translation: We commanded that you remember

original: but you have found,   Scaling his present bearing with his past,
translation: But you have realized, thinking on his behavior just now and in the past,

original: That he's your fixed enemy, and revoke   Your sudden approbation.
translation: that he is determined to be your enemy, and you take back your  sudden vote.

original: Say, you ne'er had done't—   Harp on that still—   but by our putting on;
translation: Just keep repeating that you would never have supported him unless we had demanded it.

original: And presently, when you have drawn your number,   Repair to the Capitol.
translation: So, when you have enough people, go to the Capitol.

original: We will so: almost all Repent in their election.
translation: We will do just that. Nearly everyone regrets their vote.

original: Let them go on;   This mutiny were better put in hazard,   Than stay, past doubt, for greater:
translation: Let's just let them do it. It will be better for us to take a risk and let them mutiny than to try to guarantee it ourselves.

original: If, as his nature is, he fall in rage   With their refusal, both observe and answer   The vantage of his anger.
translation: If, as usual, Coriolanus rages at their refusal, we will be there to observe and respond to that situation.

original: To the Capitol, come:   We will be there before the stream o' the people;
translation: Let's go to the Capitol. We will be there before the crowd of the people,

original: And this shall seem, as partly 'tis, their own,   Which we have goaded onward.
translation: so that this uprising which we have shaped will seem like their idea, which it partly is.

original: Tullus Aufidius then had made new head?
translation: So Tullus Aufidius had assembled a new army?

original: He had, my lord; and that it was which caused Our swifter composition.
translation: He had, my lord, which was what urged us to make our peace so quickly.

original: So then the Volsces stand but as at first, Ready, when time shall prompt them, to make road. Upon's again.
translation: So then the Volsces are back to where they started: ready, whenever the time comes, to attack us again.

original: They are worn, lord consul, so, That we shall hardly in our ages see Their banners wave again.
translation: They are so worn out, lord consul, that I can't imagine we'll see them wave their banners again in our lifetimes.

original: Saw you Aufidius?
translation: Did you see Aufidius?

original: On safe-guard he came to me; and did curse Against the Volsces, for they had so vilely Yielded the town: he is retired to Antium.
translation: He came to me in a truce, and cursed his own Volsces for so easily surrendering Corioli. He has gone back to Antium.

original: Spoke he of me?
translation: Did he speak of me?

original: He did, my lord.
translation: He did, my lord.

original: How? what?
translation: How? What?

original: How often he had met you, sword to sword;
translation: How he had often met you in battle, sword to sword;

original: That of all things upon the earth he hated   Your person most,
translation: that of all things on earth he hated you most;

original: that he would pawn his fortunes   To hopeless restitution, so he might   Be call'd your vanquisher.
translation: that he would give anything he owned, hopelessly, to be known as the one who defeated you.

original: At Antium lives he?
translation: And he lives at Antium?

original: At Antium.
translation: At Antium.

original: I wish I had a cause to seek him there, To oppose his hatred fully. Welcome home.
translation: I wish I had a reason to seek him out there, and to oppose his hatred fully.  Welcome back.

original: Behold, these are the tribunes of the people,   The tongues o' the common mouth:
translation: Look, those are the tribunes of the people, their spokespeople.

original: I do despise them;   For they do prank them in authority,   Against all noble sufferance.
translation: I do despise them, for they take on unearned authority beyond anyone's patience.

original: Pass no further.
translation: Stop here.

original: Ha! what is that?
translation: What? What is that?

original: It will be dangerous to go on: no further.
translation: It will be dangerous to go on: no further.

original: What makes this change?
translation: Why, what's changed?

original: The matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: Hath he not pass'd the noble and the common?
translation: Hasn't Coriolanus won the approval of nobles and commoners alike?

original: Cominius, no.
translation: No, Cominius.

original: Have I had children's voices?
translation: Were the people back there children, then, whose voices don't count?

original: Tribunes, give way; he shall to the market-place.
translation: Move, tribunes: Coriolanus will go to the marketplace.

original: The people are incensed against him.
translation: The people are furious with him.

original: Stop, Or all will fall in broil.
translation: Stop here, or everything will go to pieces.

original: Are these your herd?
translation: These furious people, did you herd them together?

original: Must these have voices, that can yield them now   And straight disclaim their tongues?
translation: Do we listen to these voices, which only now are gotten together and make declarations on command?

original: What are   your offices?   You being their mouths, why rule you not their teeth?
translation: What is your role in this? If you are their spokesmen, why don't you control their impulses?

original: Have you not set them on?
translation: Isn't it  you  who have put them up to this?

original: Be calm, be calm.
translation: Be calm, be calm.

original: It is a purposed thing, and grows by plot,   To curb the will of the nobility:
translation: This is intentional; it's part of their plot to weaken the authority of the senate.

original: Suffer't, and live with such as cannot rule   Nor ever will be ruled.
translation: If we don't push back, we'll not be fit to rule, nor will the people ever let themselves be ruled.

original: Call't not a plot:   The people cry you mock'd them,
translation: Don't call it a plot. The people say you mocked them,

original: and of late,   When corn was given them gratis, you repined;   Scandal'd the suppliants for the people,
translation: and that just recently, when they were given corn, you complained it was a scandal for the people to depend on the government.

original: call'd them   Time-pleasers, flatterers, foes to nobleness.
translation: You called them lazy, flatterers, the enemies of the state.

original: Why, this was known before.
translation: Why, this is old news.

original: Not to them all.
translation: Not to them all.

original: Have you inform'd them sithence?
translation: Oh, so you've informed them then?

original: How! I inform them!
translation: Who, me? I inform them?

original: You are like to do such business.
translation: You are the sort of person who would.

original: Not unlike, Each way, to better yours.
translation: I'm not unlike you, but that I'm better in every way.

original: Why then should I be consul? By yond clouds, Let me deserve so ill as you, and make me Your fellow tribune.
translation: Why then should I be consul? By heaven, let me be as lowly as you and just be a tribune instead.

original: You show too much of that   For which the people stir:
translation: You show too much pride, which the people hate.

original: if you will pass   To where you are bound, you must inquire your way,   Which you are out of, with a gentler spirit,
translation: If you want to continue on this path, you will need to ask for the people's approval more gently,

original: Or never be so noble as a consul,   Nor yoke with him for tribune.
translation: or you'll never be either consul nor tribune.

original: Let's be calm.
translation: Let's be calm.

original: The people are abused; set on. This paltering   Becomes not Rome,
translation: The people are abused; they've been put up to this. This backstabbing does not suit Rome,

original: nor has Coriolanus   Deserved this so dishonour'd rub, laid falsely   I' the plain way of his merit.
translation: nor has Coriolanus deserved this dishonorable treatment, laid against his clear merit.

original: Tell me of corn! This was my speech, and I will speak't again—
translation: Corn again? Tell me about it. Here's what I said, I'll say it again—

original: Not now, not now.
translation: Not now, not now.

original: Not in this heat, sir, now.
translation: Not in this conflict, sir, not now.

original: Now, as I live, I will. My nobler friends,   I crave their pardons:
translation: Now . As I live, I will speak now. To my noble friends, I beg your pardon.

original: For the mutable, rank-scented many, let them   Regard me as I do not flatter, and   Therein behold themselves:
translation: As for the disgusting, fickle masses, let them see me speak honestly, and in that speech see themselves.

original: I say again,   In soothing them, we nourish 'gainst our senate   The cockle of rebellion, insolence, sedition,   Which we ourselves have plough'd for, sow'd,   and scatter'd,
translation: I say again: in soothing these masses, we are merely stirring up the forces of rebellion against the senate which we ourselves  have plowed for, seeded, and tended .

original: By mingling them with us, the honour'd number,   Who lack not virtue, no, nor power, but that   Which they have given to beggars.
translation: By treating them too well, we nobles are robbed of our virtue and power by beggars.

original: Well, no more.
translation: Fine, enough.

original: No more words, we beseech you.
translation: No more words, we beg you.

original: How! no more!
translation: Oh! No more?

original: As for my country I have shed my blood,   Not fearing outward force,
translation: Just as I have shed blood for my country with no fear of opposition,

original: so shall my lungs   Coin words till their decay against those measles,   Which we disdain should tatter us, yet sought   The very way to catch them.
translation: I'll speak here until my lungs decay from an infection we have brought upon ourselves.

original: You speak o' the people, As if you were a god to punish, not A man of their infirmity.
translation: You speak of the people as if you were a vengeful god, not a mortal man like them.

original: 'Twere well We let the people know't.
translation: We'd better let the people know.

original: What, what? his choler?
translation: Know what—his fury?

original: Choler! Were I as patient as the midnight sleep, By Jove, 'twould be my mind!
translation: Fury? If I were as patient as a man asleep, by god, it would still be in my mind!

original: It is a mind That shall remain a poison where it is, Not poison any further.
translation: It is a mind that shall remain poisonous, but which we will not allow to poison others.

original: Shall remain! Hear you this Triton of the minnows? mark you His absolute 'shall'?
'Twas from the canon.
translation: It was out of line.

original: 'Shall'!   O good but most unwise patricians!
translation: "Shall!" Oh good but unwise senators!

original: why,   You grave but reckless senators, have you thus   Given Hydra here to choose an officer,
translation: Why, you serious but reckless senators, have you allowed monstrous  Hydra  here to choose a leader,

original: That with his peremptory 'shall,' being but   The horn and noise o' the monster's,
translation: that with his rude "shall," only the monster's voice,

original: wants not spirit   To say he'll turn your current in a ditch,   And make your channel his?
translation: already has the boldness to say he'll ruin your power and make your authority his?

original: If he have power   Then vail your ignorance; if none, awake   Your dangerous lenity.
translation: If he has power, then push down your ignorance; if he does not, awake from your dangerous politeness.

original: If you are learn'd,   Be not as common fools; if you are not,   Let them have cushions by you.
translation: If you are educated, don't behave like common fools; if you are not, let them sit beside you in the Senate.

original: You are plebeians,   If they be senators: and they are no less,   When, both your voices blended, the great'st taste   Most palates theirs.
translation: You are commoners, if they are senators, and if your voices are heard together, it is they who set the tastes of Rome.

original: They choose their magistrate,   And such a one as he, who puts his 'shall,'   His popular 'shall' against a graver bench   Than ever frown in Greece.
translation: They choose their leaders, and and one like this, who puts his "shall," his commoner's "shall," against a more senior group of senators than ever served in Greece.

original: By Jove himself!   It makes the consuls base: and my soul aches   To know,
translation: By god himself! This makes the consuls common, and my soul aches to know

original: when two authorities are up,   Neither supreme, how soon confusion   May enter 'twixt the gap of both and take   The one by the other.
translation: how soon a system will break down when two groups have equal authority.

original: Well, on to the market-place.
translation: Well, let's go to the market then.

original: Whoever gave that counsel, to give forth The corn o' the storehouse gratis, as 'twas used Sometime in Greece,—
translation: Whoever gave that advice, to give out the storehouse's corn for free, as they did sometimes in Greece—

original: Well, well, no more of that.
translation: Come on, come on, enough of that.

original: Though there the people had more absolute power, I say, they nourish'd disobedience, fed The ruin of the state.
translation: There in Greece, where the people had more power, they grew disobedient and brought on the ruin of the state.

original: Why, shall the people give One that speaks thus their voice?
translation: What, should the people really wish to be ruled by a man who thinks of their voices this way?

original: I'll give my reasons,   More worthier than their voices.
translation: I'll give my reasons, far better than their voices.

original: They know the corn   Was not our recompense, resting well assured   That ne'er did service for't:
translation: They know the corn was not payment to them; they know every well they did nothing to deserve it.

original: being press'd to the war,   Even when the navel of the state was touch'd,   They would not thread the gates.
translation: At war, even when the enemy was at our gates, they would not stand to fight.

original: This kind of service   Did not deserve corn gratis. Being i' the war   Their mutinies and revolts, wherein they show'd   Most valour, spoke not for them:
translation: This kind of service does not earn corn out of generosity. And in the war, they showed the most bravery in their mutinies and revolts; these did not speak well of them.

original: the accusation   Which they have often made against the senate,   All cause unborn, could never be the motive   Of our so frank donation. Well, what then?
translation: The accusations which they constantly make against the Senate, all without reason, could never be the reason behind giving them corn. So why did we?

original: How shall this bisson multitude digest   The senate's courtesy?
translation: What do you think the public has learned from this?

original: Let deeds express   What's like to be their words: 'we did request it;   We are the greater poll, and in true fear   They gave us our demands.'
translation: Here's what they are probably saying to themselves: "We asked for it, and since there are more of us, they gave in to our demands in true fear."

original: Thus we debase   The nature of our seats and make the rabble   Call our cares fears;
translation: By doing this, we  weaken our own position and make the rabble call our generosity fear.

original: which will in time   Break ope the locks o' the senate and bring in   The crows to peck the eagles.
translation: In time, this will break the senate open and bring in crows to peck the eagles.

original: Come, enough.
translation: Come on, enough.

original: Enough, with over-measure.
translation: Enough, and more than enough.

original: No, take more:   What may be sworn by, both divine and human,   Seal what I end withal!
translation: No, take more— I'm not done. By everything, both god and man, I swear it.

original: This double worship,   Where one part does disdain with cause, the other   Insult without all reason,
translation: This double worship, in which the nobles disdain the people with good reason, the people insult the nobles without any reason—

original: where gentry, title, wisdom,   Cannot conclude but by the yea and no   Of general ignorance,—
translation: in which neither rank, title, nor wisdom can act without getting a yes or no from general ignorance—

original: it must omit   Real necessities, and give way the while   To unstable slightness:
translation: it must leave out what really matters, and instead give way to instability and whims.

original: purpose so barr'd,   it follows,   Nothing is done to purpose. Therefore, beseech you,—
translation: When good work is so restricted, it follows that no good work will be done. Therefore, I beg you—

original: You that will be less fearful than discreet,   That love the fundamental part of state   More than you doubt the change on't,
translation: whoever would rather be careful than fearful, whoever loves the foundations of the state more than you doubt it is changing,

original: that prefer   A noble life before a long, and wish   To jump a body with a dangerous physic   That's sure of death without it,
translation: whoever prefers a noble life more than a long, and would revive a dying man with dangerous medicine rather than do nothing—

original: at once pluck out   The multitudinous tongue; let them not lick   The sweet which is their poison:
translation: rob the public rabble of their voices . Do not let them lick the poison which they love:

original: your dishonour   Mangles true judgment and bereaves the state   Of that integrity which should become't,
translation: to dishonor yourselves mangles good judgement and cuts off the state from that integrity it ought to have,

original: Not having the power to do the good it would,   For the in which doth control't.
translation: and those who would most benefit rob the state of the power to do good.

original: Has said enough.
translation: He's said enough.

original: Has spoken like a traitor, and shall answer As traitors do.
translation: He has spoken like a traitor, and shall answer as traitors do.

original: Thou wretch, despite o'erwhelm thee!   What should the people do with these bald tribunes?
translation: You wretch; misery o'erwhelm you! What should the people do with these shameless tribunes?

original: On whom depending, their obedience fails   To the greater bench:
translation: The more they depend on you, the less they will respect the Senate.

original: in a rebellion,   When what's not meet, but what must be, was law,   Then were they chosen:
translation: These tribunes were chosen in the midst of a rebellion, when necessity prevailed over decency.

original: in a better hour,   Let what is meet be said it must be meet,   And throw their power i' the dust.
translation: Let us now say that time has passed, and take away their power.

original: Manifest treason!
translation: That, right there—that's treason!

original: This a consul? no.
translation: Is this the behavior of a consul? No.

original: The aediles, ho!
translation: Soldiers, seize him!

original: Let him be apprehended.
translation: Let him be taken away.

original: In whose name myself   Attach thee as a traitorous innovator,
translation: As for you, I call you a plotting traitor,

original: A foe to the public weal: obey, I charge thee,   And follow to thine answer.
translation: a foe to the public good. Obey, I demand it, and go to your own trial.

original: Hence, old goat!
translation: Get out of here, you old fart!

original: Aged sir, hands off.
translation: Hands off, old man!

original: Hence, rotten thing! or I shall shake thy bones Out of thy garments.
translation: Get out here, you rotten thing, or I will shake your bones out of your clothes.

original: Help, ye citizens!
translation: Citizens, help me!

original: On both sides more respect.
translation: All of you, calm down!

original: Here's he that would take from you all your power.
translation: Here's the man who would take all your power!

original: Seize him, AEdiles!
translation: Seize him, guards!

original: Down with him! down with him!
translation: Down with him, down with him!

original: Weapons, weapons, weapons!
translation: Weapons, weapons, weapons!

original: Peace, peace, peace! Stay, hold, peace!
translation: Peace, peace, peace! Stop it! Calm down!

original: What is about to be? I am out of breath; Confusion's near; I cannot speak. You, tribunes To the people! Coriolanus, patience! Speak, good Sicinius.
translation: What is going on? I am out of breath, this is near a riot; I am not loud enough. You, tribunes to the people! Coriolanus, patience! Speak, good Sicinius.

original: Hear me, people; peace!
translation: Hear me, people; calm down!

original: Let's hear our tribune: peace Speak, speak, speak.
translation: Let's hear our tribune. Peace. Speak, speak, speak.

original: You are at point to lose your liberties: Marcius would have all from you; Marcius, Whom late you have named for consul.
Fie, fie, fie! This is the way to kindle, not to quench.
translation: No, no, no! This the way to start a fire, not to put one out.

original: To unbuild the city and to lay all flat.
translation: The way to unbuild the city and flatten it.

original: What is the city but the people?
translation: What is the city if not the people?

original: True, The people are the city.
translation: True, the people are the city

original: By the consent of all, we were establish'd The people's magistrates.
translation: By the republic's agreement, we were made the people's representatives.

original: You so remain.
translation: You still are!

original: And so are like to do.
translation: And you will continue to be.

original: That is the way to lay the city flat; To bring the roof to the foundation, And bury all, which yet distinctly ranges, In heaps and piles of ruin.
translation: That is the way to flatten the city, to bring the roof crashing down and to bury us all in heaps and piles of ruin.

original: This deserves death.
translation: He deserves to be executed.

original: Or let us stand to our authority,   Or let us lose it.
translation: Either let us stand up with our authority or we'll lose it.

original: We do here pronounce,   Upon the part o' the people, in whose power   We were elected theirs, Marcius is worthy   Of present death.
translation: We hereby pronounce, by the power of the people by whom we were elected, that Marcius deserves to be executed.

original: Therefore lay hold of him; Bear him to the rock Tarpeian, and from thence Into destruction cast him.
AEdiles, seize him!
translation: Guards, seize him!

original: Yield, Marcius, yield!
translation: Give yourself up, Marcius!

original: Hear me one word; Beseech you, tribunes, hear me but a word.
translation: Just listen, tribunes, I beg you, listen!

original: Peace, peace!
translation: Peace, peace!

original: Be that you seem, truly your   country's friend,
translation: Be what you say you are—truly your country's friend—

original: And temperately proceed to what you would   Thus violently redress.
translation: and proceed reasonably with this, rather than violently.

original: Sir, those cold ways,   That seem like prudent helps, are very poisonous   Where the disease is violent.
translation: Sir: that slow actions which might seem reasonable are actually poisonous when things are bad enough.

original: Lay hands upon him,   And bear him to the rock.
translation: Lay hands upon him, and take him to the rock.

original: No, I'll die here.    There's some  among you have beheld me fighting: Come, try upon yourselves what you have seen me.
translation: No, I'll die here.  Some of you have seen me fight. Come on, go ahead and subject yourselves to what you've seen me do to others.

original: Down with that sword! Tribunes, withdraw awhile.
translation: Put your sword away! Tribunes, just lay off a while.

original: Lay hands upon him.
translation: Capture him.

original: Help Marcius, help, You that be noble; help him, young and old!
translation: All of you who are noble, help Marcius! Young and old, help him!

original: Down with him, down with him!
translation: Down with him, down with him!

original: Go, get you to your house; be gone, away! All will be naught else.
translation: Go, go to your house, be gone, go away! We'll lose everything if we can't get rid of them.

original: Get you gone.
translation: Get out of here!

original: Stand fast; We have as many friends as enemies.
translation: Don't run! We have as many friends as enemies.

original: Sham it be put to that?
translation: Is our situation so dire that we should count our friends?

original: The gods forbid! I prithee, noble friend, home to thy house; Leave us to cure this cause.
translation: God forbid!  Please, noble friend, get home to your house; leave us to fix this.

original: For 'tis a sore upon us, You cannot tent yourself: be gone, beseech you.
translation: This is our problem; you can't cure your own disease. Go, please.

original: Come, sir, along with us.
translation: Come, sir, come along with us.

original: I would they were barbarians—as they are, Though in Rome litter'd—not Romans—as they are not, Though calved i' the porch o' the Capitol—
Be gone; Put not your worthy rage into your tongue; One time will owe another.
translation: Go, don't talk about how angry you are; we'll deal with this on another occasion.

original: On fair ground I could beat forty of them.
translation: I could beat forty of them in a fair fight.

original: I could myself   Take up a brace o' the best of them; yea, the   two tribunes:
translation: I'd be happy to beat up a bunch of the best of them— those two tribunes, particularly.

original: But now 'tis odds beyond arithmetic;   And manhood is call'd foolery, when it stands   Against a falling fabric.
translation: But this is well beyond a matter of odds, and boldness is called foolishness when it stands against a crumbling city.

original: Will you hence,   Before the tag return?
translation: Will you get out of here, before the crowd returns?

original: whose rage doth rend   Like interrupted waters and o'erbear   What they are used to bear.
translation: Their rage is like the deep sea and overwhelms them.

original: Pray you, be gone: I'll try whether my old wit be in request With those that have but little: this must be patch'd With cloth of any colour.
translation: I beg you, leave. I'll see if my old humor is still good for something with the poor. We must try everything in this situation.

original: Nay, come away.
translation: No, come on; let's go.

original: This man has marr'd his fortune.
translation: This man has ruined himself.

original: His nature is too noble for the world:   He would not flatter Neptune for his trident,
translation: He is too noble for this world. He would not flatter   Neptune  for his riches,

original: Or Jove for's power to thunder. His heart's his mouth:
translation: or  Jupiter  for thunderous power. He speaks whatever is in his heart;

original: What his breast forges, that his tongue must vent;
translation: whatever feelings he has, he can't help but declare,

original: And, being angry, does forget that ever   He heard the name of death.
translation: and when he is angry, he forgets there's such a thing as death.

original: Here's goodly work!
translation: That sounds promising!

original: I would they were abed!
translation: I wish they'd sleep this off!

original: I would they were in Tiber! What the vengeance! Could he not speak 'em fair?
translation: I wish they were underwater! What a roar from them. Couldn't Coriolanus just be polite?

original: Where is this viper That would depopulate the city and Be every man himself?
translation: Where is that viper who wants everyone in the city either dead or like himself?

original: You worthy tribunes,—
translation: My dear tribunes—

original: He shall be thrown down the Tarpeian rock   With rigorous hands:
translation: He'll be thrown down the Tarpeian rock yet!

original: he hath resisted law,
translation: He has resisted the law,

original: And therefore law shall scorn him further trial   Than the severity of the public power   Which he so sets at nought.
translation: and therefore the law will deny him any more trial than the strength of the public itself, of which he thinks so little.

original: He shall well know The noble tribunes are the people's mouths, And we their hands.
translation: He will know that the tribunes are the people's mouths, and we their hands.

original: He shall, sure on't.
translation: He will, that's for sure.

original: Sir, sir,—
translation: Sir, sir—

original: Peace!
translation: Silence!

original: Do not cry havoc, where you should but hunt With modest warrant.
translation: Do not let loose entirely, when you should still restrain yourselves.

original: Sir, how comes't that you Have holp to make this rescue?
translation: Sir, how is it that you hope to rescue this situation?

original: Hear me speak: As I do know the consul's worthiness, So can I name his faults,—
translation: Listen: just as I know the consul's worthiness, I'm well aware of his flaws.

original: Consul! what consul?
translation: Consul! What consul?

original: The consul Coriolanus.
translation: The consul Coriolanus.

original: He consul!
translation: Him? Consul?

original: No, no, no, no, no.
translation: No, no, no, no, no.

original: If, by the tribunes' leave, and yours, good people,   I may be heard, I would crave a word or two;
translation: If you, tribunes, and you, good people, will simply allow me to speak, I only need a moment or two;

original: The which shall turn you to no further harm   Than so much loss of time.
translation: my words will do far less harm to you than that which you already pursue.

original: Speak briefly then;   For we are peremptory to dispatch   This viperous traitor:
translation: Speak briefly then, for we are more than ready to be rid of this poisonous traitor.

original: to eject him hence   Were but one danger, and to keep him here   Our certain death:
translation: To throw him out of power is just a moment of danger, and to keep him here would mean our certain death.

original: therefore it is decreed   He dies to-night.
translation: Therefore, it is decided he should die tonight.

original: Now the good gods forbid   That our renowned Rome,
translation: God forbid that Rome,

original: whose gratitude   Towards her deserved children is enroll'd   In Jove's own book,
translation: which has famously done so much for her people,

original: like an unnatural dam   Should now eat up her own!
translation: should now eat up her own child!

original: He's a disease that must be cut away.
translation: He's a diseased limb that must be cut off.

original: O, he's a limb that has but a disease;   Mortal, to cut it off; to cure it, easy.
translation: Sure, then: he's Rome's diseased limb. To cut it off will kill all of Rome; to cure the disease, though, is easy.

original: What has he done to Rome that's worthy death?
translation: What has he done to Rome that makes him deserve death?

original: Killing our enemies, the blood he hath lost—   Which, I dare vouch, is more than that he hath,   By many an ounce—
translation: In killing our enemies, the blood he has lost—which I bet is more than he has left—

original: he dropp'd it for his country;   And what is left, to lose it by his country,
translation: he shed that blood for his country. Whatever's left, if Rome were to take it from him,

original: Were to us all, that do't and suffer it,   A brand to the end o' the world.
translation: it would be to all of us as though the end of the world.

original: This is clean kam.
translation: What twisted logic.

original: Merely awry: when he did love his country, It honour'd him.
translation: It's simply nonsense. When he did love his country, it honored him.

original: The service of the foot Being once gangrened, is not then respected For what before it was.
translation: The use of a diseased food is not judged equal to what it was in the past.

original: We'll hear no more.   Pursue him to his house, and pluck him thence:
translation: We'll hear no more. Chase him to his house, and pull him out of it,

original: Lest his infection, being of catching nature,   Spread further.
translation: or his infection will spread further.

original: One word more, one word.   This tiger-footed rage, when it shall find   The harm of unscann'd swiftness,
translation: One more word, one word. This wild and hasty rage will prove dangerous, and when it does,

original: will too late   Tie leaden pounds to's heels.
translation: i t will be too late to slow down.

original: Proceed by process;   Lest parties, as he is beloved, break out,   And sack great Rome with Romans.
translation: Slow down while you still can, or an opposing side will break out into conflict, and it will be Romans pillaging Rome.

original: If it were so,—
translation: So what?—

original: What do ye talk? Have we not had a taste of his obedience? Our aediles smote? ourselves resisted? Come.
translation: What are you talking about? Haven't we felt his wrath already? Our guards attacked, and us resisting? Come on.

original: Consider this: he has been bred i' the wars   Since he could draw a sword, and is ill school'd   In bolted language;
translation: Just consider: he has been a child of war since he was old enough to draw a sword, and is poorly schooled in polite language.

original: meal and bran together   He throws without distinction.
translation: He does not make fine distinctions.

original: Give me leave,   I'll go to him, and undertake to bring him   Where he shall answer, by a lawful form,   In peace, to his utmost peril.
translation: Just leave him alone; I'll go to him, and do my best to bring him to the senate so he can answer all this lawfully and without violence.

original: Noble tribunes,   It is the humane way:
translation: Noble tribunes, this is the humane way to do it.

original: the other course   Will prove too bloody, and the end of it   Unknown to the beginning.
translation: The other course of action would prove too bloody, and who knows what would come of it.

original: Noble Menenius, Be you then as the people's officer. Masters, lay down your weapons.
translation: Noble Menenius, you will then act as the people's representative. Sirs, lay down your weapons.

original: Go not home.
translation: But don't go home.

original: Meet on the market-place. We'll attend you there: Where, if you bring not Marcius, we'll proceed In our first way.
translation: Meet in the market. We'll find you there. If you do not bring Marcius, we'll go back and try the other way.

original: I'll bring him to you. @  @ Let me desire your company. He must come,  or what is worst will follow.
translation: I'll bring him to you.  Please, come with me. Coriolanus must come, or things will only get worse.

original: Pray you, let's to him.
translation: Yes, let's go.

original: Let them puff all about mine ears, present me   Death on the wheel or at wild horses' heels,
translation: Let them say what they will. They can threaten me with death on the rack or threaten to drag me behind wild horses,

original: Or pile ten hills on the Tarpeian rock,   That the precipitation might down stretch   Below the beam of sight,
translation: or pile ten hills on top of the Tarpeian cliff so that the rain stretches down out of sight,

original: yet will I still   Be thus to them.
translation: but still I will resist them.

original: You do the nobler.
translation: In doing so, you are honorable.

original: I muse my mother   Does not approve me further, who was wont   To call them woollen vassals,
translation: I wonder why my mother isn't even more proud of me. She always called the people dumb servants,

original: things created   To buy and sell with groats, to show bare heads   In congregations,
translation: machines made to buy and sell, just bodies in the room,

original: to yawn, be still and wonder,   When one but of my ordinance stood up   To speak of peace or war.
translation: which yawn and silently wonder when someone with my strength stood up to speak of peace or war.

original: I talk of you:   Why did you wish me milder?
translation: I'm talking about you: why did you urge me to calm down?

original: would you have me   False to my nature? Rather say I play   The man I am.
translation: Would you have me be someone I'm not?  Rather say I play the man I am.

original: O, sir, sir, sir, I would have had you put your power well on, Before you had worn it out.
translation: Oh, sir, sir, sir, I wish you'd actually gotten power before you'd used it up.

original: Let go.
translation: Leave off.

original: You might have been enough the man you are,   With striving less to be so;
translation: You'd be just as much the man you are if you wouldn't try so hard to be that man.

original: lesser had been   The thwartings of your dispositions,
translation: People wouldn't work so hard against you

original: if   You had not show'd them how ye were disposed   Ere they lack'd power to cross you.
translation: if you hadn't shown them how you felt while they still had the power to stop you.

original: Let them hang.
translation: To hell with them.

original: Ay, and burn too.
translation: Yeah, and let them burn, too.

original: Come, come, you have been too rough, something too rough; You must return and mend it.
translation: Come on, you have been too rude to them, far too rude; you have to go back and apologize.

original: There's no remedy; Unless, by not so doing, our good city Cleave in the midst, and perish.
translation: There's no use; except that if he doesn't, our city will divide itself in half and be destroyed.

original: Pray, be counsell'd:
translation: Please, listen:

original: I have a heart as little apt as yours,
translation: although my heart is not as strong as yours,

original: But yet a brain that leads my use of anger   To better vantage.
translation: I have a brain to guide my fury into better advantages for us.

original: Well said, noble woman?   Before he should thus stoop to the herd,
translation: Well said, noble woman. Before Coriolanus should bow to the crowd—

original: but that   The violent fit o' the time craves it as physic   For the whole state,
translation: which he should never do unless these violent times absolutely required it—

original: I would put mine armour on,   Which I can scarcely bear.
translation: I feel as though I should put my armor on, which pains me.

original: What must I do?
translation: What must I do?

original: Return to the tribunes.
translation: Return to the tribunes.

original: Well, what then? what then?
translation: Well, what then? What then?

original: Repent what you have spoke.
translation: Apologize for what you've said.

original: For them! I cannot do it to the gods; Must I then do't to them?
translation: To them? I cannot apologize to the gods, and you want me to apologize to them?

original: You are too absolute;
translation: You are too stubborn.

original: Though therein you can never be too noble,   But when extremities speak.
translation: In this you are also noble, except in bizarre situations like this.

original: I have heard you say,   Honour and policy, like unsever'd friends,   I' the war do grow together:
translation: I've heard you say before that honor and judgement become inseparable friends in the course of war.

original: grant that, and tell me,   In peace what each of them by the other lose,   That they combine not there.
translation: Think of that, and tell me how you have not lost both by failing to combine them here, in peacetime.

original: Tush, tush!
translation: Nonsense!

original: A good demand.
translation: She makes a good point.

original: If it be honour in your wars to seem   The same you are not, which, for your best ends,   You adopt your policy,
translation: If it's honorable at war to adapt yourself to your conditions,

original: how is it less or worse,   That it shall hold companionship in peace   With honour, as in war, since that to both   It stands in like request?
translation: how is it worse that you should do the same—be flexible— in a time of peace?

original: Why force you this?
translation: Why are you forcing this point?

original: Because that now it lies you on to speak   To the people; not by your own instruction,   Nor by the matter which your heart prompts you,
translation: Because the pressure is now on you to speak to the people, and to do so not the way you normally might, nor just however your heart tells you to,

original: But with such words that are but rooted in   Your tongue, though but bastards and syllables   Of no allowance to your bosom's truth.
translation: but to speak useful words, even if you don't truly believe them.

original: Now, this no more dishonours you at all   Than to take in a town with gentle words,
translation: This is no more dishonor to you than to use gentle words to capture a town

original: Which else would put you to your fortune and   The hazard of much blood.
translation: which would otherwise risk the lives of many men to capture.

original: I would dissemble with my nature where   My fortunes and my friends at stake required   I should do so in honour:
translation: If I had to be someone I wasn't when my friends and fortunes were at stake, it would be honorable for me to do so.

original: I am in this,   Your wife, your son, these senators, the nobles;
translation: In this case,  I am your wife, your son, these senators, the nobles ;

original: And you will rather show our general louts   How you can frown
translation: would you rather show the common people that you can frown

original: than spend a fawn upon 'em,   For the inheritance of their loves and safeguard   Of what that want might ruin.
translation: than just once compliment them for Rome's sake?

original: Noble lady!   Come, go with us;
translation: Noble lady! Come along with us.

original: s   peak fair: you may salve so,   Not what is dangerous present,
translation: Talk to him: if you can calm him so,  we might avoid not only the dangerous present

original: but the loss   Of what is past.
translation: but also deal with our past conflict.

original: I prithee now, my son,   Go to them, with this bonnet in thy hand;   And thus far having stretch'd it—here be with them—
translation: I beg you, my son,  [She mimics the action of humbly fidgeting with a peasant's cap]  go along with this hat in your hand, and having stretched it—do it like this—

original: Thy knee bussing the stones—   for in such business   Action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant   More learned than the ears—
translation: with your knees on the ground—for in this kind of thing, your behavior is everything, and idiots care more about what they see than what they hear—

original: waving thy head,   Which often, thus, correcting thy stout heart,   Now humble as the ripest mulberry   That will not hold the handling:
translation: shaking your head like this a few times,  as humble as the ripest mulberry  from a tree ready to be picked.

original: or say to them,   Thou art their soldier, and being bred in broils   Hast not the soft way which,
translation: Then say to them that you are a soldier in their service, and that since you grew up in the war, you're not very polite,

original: thou dost confess,   Were fit for thee to use as they to claim,
translation: which you confess is really better for this situation.

original: In asking their good loves, but thou wilt frame   Thyself, forsooth, hereafter theirs, so far   As thou hast power and person.
translation: In asking for their approval, just wilt your body like this—seriously— and say that you'll be their servant forever as long as you live.

original: This but done,   Even as she speaks, why, their hearts were yours;
translation: If you can do this, as she says, they will accept you.

original: For they have pardons, being ask'd, as free   As words to little purpose.
translation: They will freely pardon you, if you ask.

original: Prithee now,   Go, and be ruled:
translation: Please now, go and be humble,

original: although I know thou hadst rather   Follow thine enemy in a fiery gulf   Than flatter him in a bower.
translation: although I know you'd rather follow an enemy into hell than flatter him in a garden.

original: Here is Cominius.
translation: Here comes Cominius.

original: I have been i' the market-place; and, sir,'tis fit You make strong party, or defend yourself By calmness or by absence: all's in anger.
translation: I've been in the market, sir, and you'd better go either with a strong guard or defend yourself by calmness or by not going at all: they're pretty angry.

original: Only fair speech.
translation: Just be polite.

original: I think 'twill serve, if he Can thereto frame his spirit.
translation: I think that would work, if he could actually do it.

original: He must, and will Prithee now, say you will, and go about it.
translation: He must, and will. Listen: say you'll do it, and do it.

original: Must I go show them my unbarbed sconce?   Must I with base tongue give my noble heart   A lie that it must bear?
translation: I have to go bare my uncovered head to them? I have to put a lie upon my conscience?

original: Well, I will do't:
translation: Well, I'll do it.

original: Yet, were there but this single plot to lose,   This mould of Marcius, they to dust should grind it   And throw't against the wind.
translation: Yet if this were the only land for which I ever fought, let them take my body, grind it to dust, and throw it to the wind.

original: To the market-place!   You have put me now to such a part which never   I shall discharge to the life.
translation: To the market! You're insisting now I play a part which I don't know how I'll ever make believable.

original: Come, come, we'll prompt you.
translation: Come, come, we'll help you.

original: I prithee now, sweet son, as thou hast said   My praises made thee first a soldier,
translation: Please, sweet son, as you have said my praise was what made you a soldier,

original: so,   To have my praise for this, perform a part   Thou hast not done before.
translation: have my praise for this too and perform a part you've not played before.

original: Well, I must do't:   Away, my disposition, and possess me   Some harlot's spirit!
translation: Well, I guess I have to do it. Farewell, my self, and let me take on prostitute-like spirit!

original: my throat of war be turn'd,   Which quired with my drum, into a pipe   Small as an eunuch, or the virgin voice   That babies lulls asleep!
translation: I'll turn my voice of war, like a drum, into a tiny pipe like the virgin voice that would lull babies to sleep.

original: the smiles of knaves   Tent in my cheeks, and schoolboys' tears take up   The glasses of my sight!
translation: I'll smile fake smiles, and I'll cry schoolboy's tears.

original: a beggar's tongue   Make motion through my lips, and my arm'd knees,
translation: I'll speak like a beggar, and my knees,

original: Who bow'd but in my stirrup, bend like his   That hath received an alms!
translation: which until now have only bent in my stirrups, will bend like a man asking for money in the street!

original: I will not do't,   Lest I surcease to honour mine own truth   And by my body's action teach my mind   A most inherent baseness.
translation: [Having briefly considered this, he wavers]  I can't do this, or I'll have to betray my own truth and my body will teach my mind to be evil.

original: At thy choice, then:   To beg of thee, it is my more dishonour   Than thou of them.
translation: It's up to you, then. It's more dishonorable for me to beg you than for you to beg them.

original: Come all to ruin; let   Thy mother rather feel thy pride than fear   Thy dangerous stoutness,
translation: Let the world burn; let your mother be the heart of your pride rather than the victim of your foolish stubbornness,

original: for I mock at death   With as big heart as thou.
translation: for I am as invincible as you.

original: Do as thou list   Thy valiantness was mine, thou suck'dst it from me,   But owe thy pride thyself.
translation: But do whatever you want. Your bravery was mine—you sucked it from me— but your pride is your own.

original: Pray, be content:   Mother, I am going to the market-place;   Chide me no more.
translation: Enough. Mother, I am going to the market, stop scolding me.

original: I'll mountebank their loves,   Cog their hearts from them, and come home beloved   Of all the trades in Rome.
translation: I'll lie for their love, cheat their hearts from them, and come home loved by people of every profession in Rome.

original: Look, I am going:   Commend me to my wife. I'll return consul;
translation: Look, I'm going; give my best to my wife. I'll return consul

original: Or never trust to what my tongue can do   I' the way of flattery further.
translation: if my tongue has any power at all to flatter.

original: Do your will.
translation: Go ahead.

original: Away! the tribunes do attend you: arm yourself   To answer mildly;
translation: Go! The tribunes are waiting for you. Prepare to answer gently,

original: for they are prepared   With accusations, as I hear, more strong   Than are upon you yet.
translation: for they are ready with accusations, I think, even stronger than you've heard so far.

original: The word is 'mildly.' Pray you, let us go: Let them accuse me by invention, I Will answer in mine honour.
translation: Like you said, "gently." Please, lets go. Let them make up whatever they want, I'll answer honorably.

original: Ay, but mildly.
translation: Sure, but gently.

original: Well, mildly be it then. Mildly!
translation: Whatever, gently then. Gently!

original: In this point charge him home, that he affects   Tyrannical power:
translation: Let's drive this point home: he wants to be a tyrant.

original: if he evade us there,   Enforce him with his envy to the people,
translation: If he manages to evade that, lets accuse him of being greedy,

original: And that the spoil got on the Antiates   Was ne'er distributed.
translation: and say that he never distributed the spoils of war from the  Antiates.

original: What, will he come?
translation: Well, is he coming?

original: He's coming.
translation: He's coming.

original: How accompanied?
translation: Who accompanies him?

original: With old Menenius, and those senators That always favour'd him.
translation: Just old Menenius, and the senators who've always been on his side.

original: Have you a catalogue Of all the voices that we have procured Set down by the poll?
translation: Do you have a list of all the votes we've gotten?

original: I have; 'tis ready.
translation: I do, it's ready.

original: Have you collected them by tribes?
translation: And you've organized them by group?

original: I have.
translation: I have.

original: Assemble presently the people hither;   And when they bear me say 'It shall be so   I' the right and strength o' the commons,'
translation: Assemble everyone here. And when they hear me say "This is how it will be in the name and the strength of our people,"

original: be it either   For death, for fine, or banishment, then let them   If I say fine, cry 'Fine;' if death, cry 'Death.'
translation: whether I say either for death, fine, or banishment, have them yell accordingly: "Fine," if it's a fine; "Death,"

original: Insisting on the old prerogative   And power i' the truth o' the cause.
translation: if it's for death. We'll insist on the old reasons and the power of truth.

original: I shall inform them.
translation: I'll inform them.

original: And when such time they have begun to cry,   Let them not cease,
translation: And when they've begun to shout, make sure they don't stop;

original: but with a din confused   Enforce the present execution   Of what we chance to sentence.
translation: instead, make sure they wildly cheer whatever we happen to decide on.

original: Very well.
translation: Very well.

original: Make them be strong and ready for this hint, When we shall hap to give 't them.
translation: Make sure they're really ready when we give them the sign.

original: Go about it.
translation: Go to it.

original: Put him to choler straight: he hath been used   Ever to conquer, and to have his worth   Of contradiction:
translation: Lets get him angry right away. He's so used to conquering, and to seeing value only in contradiction.

original: being once chafed, he cannot   Be rein'd again to temperance; then he speaks   What's in his heart;
translation: Once we irritate him, he'll never calm down, and he'll speak what's in his heart.

original: and that is there which looks   With us to break his neck.
translation: What's in there will be what we need to break his neck.

original: Well, here he comes.
translation: All right; here he comes.

original: Calmly, I do beseech you.
translation: Calmly, please.

original: Ay, as an ostler, that for the poorest piece   Will bear the knave by the volume.
translation: Sure, like a stableboy, who will take any amount of abuse for a penny.

original: The honour'd gods   Keep Rome in safety, and the chairs of justice   Supplied with worthy men! plant love among 's!
translation: May the honored gods keep Rome safe, and positions of justice be held by worthy men! May we all love one another!

original: Throng our large temples with the shows of peace,   And not our streets with war!
translation: Fill our temples with peaceful demonstrations and our streets with war!

original: Amen, amen.
translation: Indeed, indeed.

original: A noble wish.
translation: A noble wish.

original: Draw near, ye people.
translation: Come here, people.

original: List to your tribunes. Audience: peace, I say!
translation: Listen to your tribunes. Attention: silence, I say!

original: First, hear me speak.
translation: First, hear me speak.

original: Well, say. Peace, ho!
translation: Sure, go ahead. Silence, everyone.

original: Shall I be charged no further than this present? Must all determine here?
translation: Will this be my last trial? Will everything come down to this?

original: do demand,   If you submit you to the people's voices,
translation: I insist upon it, so long as you will submit to the people's vote,

original: Allow their officers and are content   To suffer lawful censure for such faults   As shall be proved upon you?
translation: abide by their representatives, and are willing to deal with lawful condemnation for the verdict which is reached?

original: I am content.
translation: I am content with these terms.

original: Lo, citizens, he says he is content:
translation: Hear that, citizens, he says he is content!

original: The warlike service he has done, consider; think   Upon the wounds his body bears,
translation: Consider the military service he has done; think about all the wounds on his body, huge scars

original: which show   Like graves i' the holy churchyard.
translation: which look like graves in a churchyard.

original: Scratches with briers, Scars to move laughter only.
translation: Just scratches. Laughable scars, really.

original: Consider further,   That when he speaks not like a citizen,   You find him like a soldier:
translation: Take into account that when he speaks, he is speaking as a soldier.

original: do not take   His rougher accents for malicious sounds,
translation: Don't take his roughness the wrong way; he's not being cruel,

original: But, as I say, such as become a soldier,   Rather than envy you.
translation: but like I said, he's just being soldier rather than trying to pretend to be like you.

original: Well, well, no more.
translation: Good, good, enough.

original: What is the matter   That being pass'd for consul with full voice,
translation: How can it be that after I was voted in as consul with your full approval,

original: I am so dishonour'd that the very hour   You take it off again?
translation: I've fallen so far within an hour that you revoke your vote?

original: Answer to us.
translation: Answer to us.

original: Say, then: 'tis true, I ought so.
translation: Go on, then: it's true, I ought to answer to you.

original: We charge you, that you have contrived to take   From Rome all season'd office and to wind   Yourself into a power tyrannical;
translation: We charge you with attempted tyranny, with the plan to take over all of Rome's offices,

original: For which you are a traitor to the people.
translation: for which you are a traitor to the people.

original: How! traitor!
translation: What? A traitor?

original: Nay, temperately; your promise.
translation: No, gently; you promised to respond gently.

original: The fires i' the lowest hell fold-in the people!   Call me their traitor!
translation: The lowest circles of hell take in these people! You're calling me their traitor?

original: Thou injurious tribune!   Within thine eyes sat twenty thousand deaths,
translation: You ruinous tribune! If you could deal me twenty thousand deaths,

original: In thy hand clutch'd as many millions, in   Thy lying tongue both numbers,
translation: held twenty million deaths in your hand, and with your tongue could deal as many over again,

original: I would say   'Thou liest' unto thee with a voice as free   As I do pray the gods.
translation: I would say "you lie" to you with a voice as free as the one I use to pray to the gods.

original: Mark you this, people?
translation: Do you hear this, people?

original: To the rock, to the rock with him!
Peace!   We need not put new matter to his charge:
translation: Silence! We do not need to go through this again.

original: What you have seen him do and heard him speak,
translation: What you have seen him do and heard him say—

original: Beating your officers, cursing yourselves,   Opposing laws with strokes and here defying   Those whose great power must try him;
translation: beating your officers, cursing you, opposing laws with grand gestures and here defying even to be tried—

original: even this,   So criminal and in such capital kind,   Deserves the extremest death.
translation: even this, so criminal and so serious— deserves the most extreme death.

original: But since he hath Served well for Rome,—
translation: But since he has served Rome well—

original: What do you prate of service?
translation: What would you know of service?

original: I talk of that, that know it.
translation: I only speak of what I know.

original: You?
translation: You?

original: Is this the promise that you made your mother?
translation: Is this the promise that you made your mother?

original: Know, I pray you,—
translation: Listen, I beg you—

original: I know no further:   Let them pronounce the steep Tarpeian death,
translation: I know only this: let them condemn me to a steep Tarpeian death.

original: Vagabond exile, raying, pent to linger   But with a grain a day, I would not buy   Their mercy at the price of one fair word;
translation: As a vagabond exile, made to beg for grains, I would not buy a word of their mercy,

original: Nor cheque my courage for what they can give,   To have't with saying 'Good morrow.'
translation: nor stop by boldness for anything they could give me to be had with saying "Good day."

original: For that he has,   As much as in him lies, from time to time   Envied against the people,   seeking means   To pluck away their power,
translation: For crimes against the people—seeking to pluck away their power,

original: as now at last   Given hostile strokes, and that not in the presence   Of dreaded justice, but on the ministers   That do distribute it;
translation: and now at the end for his hostile blows in the presence not only of the judges but of the people themselves—

original: in the name o' the people   And in the power of us the tribunes, we,   Even from this instant, banish him our city,
translation: in the name of the people and by the power vested in us as tribunes we, from this instant onward, banish him from our city,

original: In peril of precipitation   From off the rock Tarpeian never more   To enter our Rome gates:
translation: Rome. If he ever again enters our gates, he will be thrown off the Tarpeian rock.

original: i' the people's name,   I say it shall be so.
translation: In the people's name, I say it shall be so.

original: It shall be so, it shall be so; let him away: He's banish'd, and it shall be so.
translation: It shall be so, it shall be so; let him go. He's banished, and it shall be so.

original: Hear me, my masters, and my common friends,—
translation: Hear me, sirs, and my friends, the people—

original: He's sentenced; no more hearing.
translation: His sentence has been passed; there will be no more "hearing."

original: Let me speak:   I have been consul, and can show for Rome   Her enemies' marks upon me.
translation: Let me speak. I have been consul, and can show for Rome her enemies' scars upon me.

original: I do love   My country's good with a respect more tender,   More holy and profound, than mine own life,
translation: I love my country tenderly, more profoundly than my own life,

original: My dear wife's estimate, her womb's increase,   And treasure of my loins; then if I would   Speak that,—
translation: my own dear wife, or the fruits of her very womb, my own treasured children; if I would say that—

original: We know your drift: speak what?
translation: We get it; if you would say what?

original: There's no more to be said, but he is banish'd, As enemy to the people and his country: It shall be so.
translation: There's no more to be said except that he is banished. He's an enemy to the people and his country; that's it.

original: It shall be so, it shall be so.
translation: It shall be so, it shall be so.

original: You common cry of curs! whose breath I hate   As reek o' the rotten fens,
translation: You common junkyard dogs, whose breath I hate like the reeking of a rotten swamp,

original: whose loves I prize   As the dead carcasses of unburied men   That do corrupt my air,
translation: whose love I hold equal to the bloated carcasses of unburied dead men, the stink of which corrupts my air,

original: I banish you;   And here remain with your uncertainty!
translation: I  banish  you . Remain here with your uncertainty!

original: Let every feeble rumour shake your hearts!   Your enemies, with nodding of their plumes,   Fan you into despair!
translation: Let every feeble rumor shake your hearts! May your enemies' smallest motions drive you into despair!

original: Have the power still   To banish your defenders;
translation: May you keep this power to banish your defenders,

original: till at length   Your ignorance, which finds not till it feels,   Making not reservation of yourselves,   Still your own foes,
translation: until your ignorance, with no sense of your own self-preservation,

original: deliver you as most   Abated captives to some nation   That won you without blows!
translation: delivers you as slaves to some nation who will conquer you without a single blow.

original: Despising,   For you, the city, thus I turn my back:   There is a world elsewhere.
translation: I despise Rome, for you're in it, and turn my back. There is a world elsewhere.

original: The people's enemy is gone, is gone!
translation: The people's enemy is gone; he's gone!

original: Our enemy is banish'd! he is gone! Hoo! hoo!
translation: Our enemy is banished; he is gone, hooray!

original: Go, see him out at gates, and follow him,   As he hath followed you, with all despite;
translation: Go, follow him out to the gates, and follow him, as he has followed you, with all your bitterness.

original: Give him deserved vexation. Let a guard   Attend us through the city.
translation: Give him the torment he deserves. We will have a guard take us through the city.

original: Come, come; let's see him out at gates; come. The gods preserve our noble tribunes! Come.
translation: Come, lets follow him to the gates. The gods preserve our noble tribunes! Come.

original: Come, leave your tears: a brief farewell: the beast   With many heads butts me away.
translation: Come on, stop crying. A brief farewell is enough;  the beast with many heads  butts me away.

original: Nay, mother,   Where is your ancient courage? you were used   To say extremity was the trier of spirits;
translation: Mother, no— where is your courage? You used to say that challenge was the spirit's forge,

original: That common chances common men could bear;   That when the sea was calm all boats alike   Show'd mastership in floating;
translation: that average men could bear average events, that when the sea was calm all boats were good at floating.

original: fortune's blows,   When most struck home, being gentle wounded, craves   A noble cunning:
translation: The true blows of bad luck, when they really hit home, call for more than average men.

original: you were used to load me   With precepts that would make invincible   The heart that conn'd them.
translation: You gave me all these sayings that, to believe them, would make a man invincible.

original: O heavens! O heavens!
translation: Oh, heavens! Oh, heavens!

original: Nay! prithee, woman,—
translation: Stop it, please woman—

original: Now the red pestilence strike all trades in Rome, And occupations perish!
translation: May the plague strike everyone in Rome, and all the workers perish!

original: What, what, what!   I shall be loved when I am lack'd. Nay, mother.   Resume that spirit, when you were wont to say,
translation: Hear, hear, hear! They'll miss me once I'm gone. Mother, come back to that spirit when you used to say

original: If you had been the wife of Hercules,   Six of his labours you'ld have done, and saved   Your husband so much sweat.
translation: that if you'd been the wife of  Hercules, you'd have done six of his labors  and saved your husband the trouble.

original: Cominius,   Droop not; adieu. Farewell, my wife, my mother:   I'll do well yet.
translation: Cominius, don't look so sad; good-bye. Farewell, my wife, my mother: I'll be fine.

original: Thou old and true Menenius,   Thy tears are salter than a younger man's,   And venomous to thine eyes.
translation: Old and true Menenius, your tears are saltier than a younger man's would be, and poisonous to your eyes.

original: My sometime general,   I have seen thee stem, and thou hast oft beheld   Heart-hardening spectacles;
translation: Cominius, my old general, you've often seen spectacles that would harden the heart;

original: tell these sad women   'Tis fond to wail inevitable strokes,   As 'tis to laugh at 'em.
translation: tell these sad women it's as good to laugh at fate as to cry.

original: My mother, you wot well   My hazards still have been your solace:
translation: Mother, you know well that my risks have always been your comfort,

original: and   Believe't not lightly—   though I go alone,   Like to a lonely dragon,
translation: and believe me, although I go alone like a lonely dragon—

original: that his fen   Makes fear'd and talk'd of more than seen—
translation: whose terrifying surroundings make him more feared and talked about then seen—

original: your son   Will or exceed the common or be caught   With cautelous baits and practise.
translation: your son will as always be better than average; never caught by baits or cleverness.

original: My first son.   Whither wilt thou go?
translation: My first son.

original: Take good Cominius   With thee awhile: determine on some course,
translation: Where will you go? Take good Cominius with you for a while, and choose some course.

original: More than a wild exposture to each chance   That starts i' the way before thee.
translation: Don't just go wildly toward whatever chance waits for you daily.

original: O the gods!
translation: Oh, gods!

original: I'll follow thee a month, devise with thee   Where thou shalt rest,
translation: I'll travel behind you for a month and help you figure out where you can stay,

original: that thou mayst hear of us   And we of thee:
translation: so that you can hear of us and vice versa,

original: so if the time thrust forth   A cause for thy repeal, we shall not send   O'er the vast world to seek a single man,
translation: so if by any chance this vote is reversed, we will not have to seek everywhere for a single man,

original: And lose advantage, which doth ever cool   I' the absence of the needer.
translation: and lose whatever advantage we would've had to find you when we most need you.

original: Fare ye well:   Thou hast years upon thee; and thou art too full   Of the wars' surfeits, to go rove with one   That's yet unbruised:
translation: Good-bye, no. You are old, and are too beaten up by the harshness of war to go wander with someone still unbruised;

original: bring me but out at gate.   Come, my sweet wife, my dearest mother, and   My friends of noble touch,
translation: just walk me about of the gate. Come, my sweet wife, my dearest mother, and my noble friends:

original: when I am forth,   Bid me farewell, and smile.
translation: when I go, just bid me farewell and smile.

original: I pray you, come.   While I remain above the ground, you shall   Hear from me still,
translation: Please, come. While I live, you'll hear from me,

original: and never of me aught   But what is like me formerly.
translation: and I will always be what I have always been.

original: That's worthily   As any ear can hear.
translation: That's as good as we could ever ask.

original: Come, let's not weep.
translation: Come on, let's not weep.

original: If I could shake off but one seven years   From these old arms and legs, by the good gods,   I'ld with thee every foot.
translation: If were just seven years younger, by the good gods, I'd accompany you every step of the way.

original: Give me thy hand: Come.
translation: Give me your hand; come.

original: Bid them all home; he's gone, and we'll no further. The nobility are vex'd, whom we see have sided In his behalf.
translation: Tell them all to head home. He's gone, and we're done here. The nobility, who we see have taken his side, are very upset.

original: Now we have shown our power, Let us seem humbler after it is done Than when it was a-doing.
translation: Now that we've shown them how powerful we are, let's act humbler now that it's done than while we were doing it.

original: Bid them home: Say their great enemy is gone, and they Stand in their ancient strength.
translation: Tell them to go home. Say their great enemy is gone, and they stand as strong as ever.

original: Dismiss them home.
translation: Dismiss them to their homes.

original: Here comes his mother.
translation: Here comes his mother.

original: Let's not meet her.
translation: Let's avoid her.

original: Why?
translation: Why?

original: They say she's mad.
translation: They say she's a madwoman.

original: They have ta'en note of us: keep on your way.
translation: They've seen us! Just stay calm.

original: O, ye're well met: the hoarded plague o' the gods Requite your love!
translation: Oh, am I glad to see you: may the great plagues of the gods return your love!

original: Peace, peace; be not so loud.
translation: Quiet, quiet, don't be so loud.

original: If that I could for weeping, you should hear,— Nay, and you shall hear some. @  Will you be gone?
translation: If I just went and wept, you would still hear me—and indeed, you will hear some weeping. Will you get out of here?

original: You shall stay too: I would I had the  power To say so to my husband.
translation: You shall stay—I wish I had the power to say so to my husband.

original: Are you mankind?
translation: Are you women or animals?

original: Ay, fool; is that a shame? Note but this fool.
translation: Ugh, you fool— is that a problem? Look at this fool.

original: Was not a man my father?
translation: Wasn't my father a man?

original: Hadst thou foxship   To banish him that struck more blows for Rome   Than thou hast spoken words?
translation: By what clever betrayal have you banished a man from Rome who struck more blows in our city's service than you have spoken words?

original: O blessed heavens!
translation: Oh, dear god!

original: More noble blows than ever thou wise words;   And for Rome's good.
translation: More noble blows than you've said wise words— and for Rome's good.

original: I'll tell thee what; yet go:   Nay, but thou shalt stay too:
translation: I'll tell you what: go, go on. No, but you'll stay, won't you?

original: I would my son   Were in Arabia, and thy tribe before him,   His good sword in his hand.
translation: I wish my son were  in Arabia , and your whole tribe before him with one good sword in his hand.

original: What then?
translation: What then?

original: What then! He'ld make an end of thy posterity.
translation: What then! He'd kill you and all your family.

original: Bastards and all. Good man, the wounds that he does bear for Rome!
translation: Bastards, all of them. Good man, the wounds that he bears for Rome's sake!

original: Come, come, peace.
translation: Come on, come on, calm down.

original: I would he had continued to his country As he began, and not unknit himself The noble knot he made.
translation: I wish Coriolanus had continued to serve his country the way he started, and not ruined himself.

original: I would he had.
translation: I wish he had.

original: 'I would he had'! 'Twas you incensed the rabble:
translation: "I wish he had!" It was  you  who started the riot!

original: Cats, that can judge as fitly of his worth   As I can of those mysteries which heaven   Will not have earth to know.
translation: You are cats, as fit to be the judge of Coriolanus as I am to know the mysteries of heaven which are forbidden to those on earth.

original: Pray, let us go.
translation: Please, lets go.

original: Now, pray, sir, get you gone:   You have done a brave deed.
translation: Now, please sir, get out of here. What you've done is brave indeed.

original: Ere you go, hear this:—
translation: Before you go, listen to me.

original: As far as doth the Capitol exceed   The meanest house in Rome,
translation: As much as the Capitol is better than the lowliest house in Rome—

original: so far my son—   This lady's husband here, this, do you see—
translation: that's how much my son, this lady's husband here,  here , do you see her?—

original: Whom you have banish'd, does exceed you all.
translation: whom you have banished, is better than all of you.

original: Well, well, we'll leave you.
translation: Sure, sure; we'll leave.

original: Why stay we to be baited With one that wants her wits?
translation: Why should we stand here to be yelled at by a madwoman?

original: Take my prayers with you.
translation: My prayers go with you.

original: I would the gods had nothing else to do   But to confirm my curses!
translation: I wish the gods had nothing else to do but curse them!

original: Could I meet 'em   But once a-day, it would unclog my heart   Of what lies heavy to't.
translation: If I could  meet them  just once a day, it would clear my heart of all its baggage.

original: You have told them home; And, by my troth, you have cause. You'll sup with me?
translation: You've driven them home. And my god, do you have a good reason to. Will you get dinner with me?

original: Anger's my meat; I sup upon myself,   And so shall starve with feeding.
translation: Anger's my meat; I feed upon myself, and so will starve.

original: Come, let's go:   Leave this faint puling and lament as I do,   In anger, Juno-like. Come, come, come.
translation: Come, lets go. Leave this quiet weeping and grieve the way I do, deep in fury like a god. Come, come, come.

original: Fie, fie, fie!
translation: Damn, damn, damn!

original: I know you well, sir, and you know me: your name, I think, is Adrian.
translation: I know you well, sir, and you know me: your name, I think, is Adrian.

original: It is so, sir: truly, I have forgot you.
translation: It is, sir. To be honest, though, I have forgotten your name.

original: I am a Roman; and my services are, as you are, against 'em: know you me yet?
translation: I am a Roman, but I work—as you do—against Rome. Do you still not know me?

original: Nicanor? no.
translation: Nicanor? No, it can't be you!

original: The same, sir.
translation: It is, sir.

original: You had more beard when I last saw you; but your   favour is well approved by your tongue.
translation: You had more beard when I last saw you, but your voice does sound like Nicanor's.

original: What's the   news in Rome?
translation: What's the news in Rome?

original: I have a note from the Volscian state,   to find you out there: you have well saved me a   day's journey.
translation: I have a note for you from the Volscians; it's saved me a day's journey to meet you here.

original: There hath been in Rome strange insurrections; the people against the senators, patricians, and nobles.
translation: There has been a strange insurrection in Rome: the people have risen up against the senators, patricians, and nobles.

original: Hath been! is it ended, then? Our state thinks not so: they are in a most warlike preparation, and hope to come upon them in the heat of their division.
translation: Has been! Is it over, then? The Volscians wouldn't say so: they're preparing for war, and are hoping to catch Rome in the midst of this turmoil.

original: The main blaze of it is past, but a small thing   would make it flame again:
translation: The main conflict is over, but almost anything would make it start again.

original: for the nobles receive   so to heart the banishment of that worthy   Coriolanus, that they are in a ripe aptness to take   all power from the people
translation: The nobles have really taken the banishment of worthy Coriolanus to heart, and they are on the verge of taking power from the people

original: and to pluck from them   their tribunes for ever.
translation: and robbing them of their representatives forever.

original: This lies glowing, I can   tell you, and is almost mature for the violent   breaking out.
translation: Their action lies glowing like an ember, believe me, and is  ready to burst into flame.

original: Coriolanus banished!
translation: Coriolanus has been banished?!

original: Banished, sir.
translation: Banished, sir.

original: You will be welcome with this intelligence, Nicanor.
translation: The Volscians will welcome you with this news, Nicanor.

original: The day serves well for them now.
translation: Things are good for them for now.
