original: I have heard it   said, the fittest time to corrupt a man's wife is   when she's fallen out with her husband.
translation: I've heard it said that the best time to seduce a man's wife is when she and the husband are fighting.

original: Your noble   Tullus Aufidius will appear well in these wars, his   great opposer, Coriolanus, being now in no request   of his country.
translation: Your noble Tullus Aufidius will do well in these wars now that Coriolanus, the only man strong enough to oppose him, can't be called upon by Rome.

original: He cannot choose. I am most fortunate, thus accidentally to encounter you: you have ended my business, and I will merrily accompany you home.
translation: He has no choice. It is really lucky that I've encountered you like this; my business is over now, and I'll merrily accompany you home.

original: I shall, between this and supper, tell you most strange things from Rome; all tending to the good of their adversaries. Have you an army ready, say you?
translation: Between now and supper, I'll tell you some very strange things from Rome, all of which will be good for their enemies. You have an army ready, you say?

original: A most royal one; the centurions and their charges, distinctly billeted, already in the entertainment, and to be on foot at an hour's warning.
I am joyful to hear of their readiness, and am the man, I think, that shall set them in present action. So, sir, heartily well met, and most glad of your  company.
translation: I'm glad to hear they're ready, and I think my news will send them into action. So, sir, it's great to meet you here, and I'm glad to have your company.

original: You take my part from me, sir; I have the most cause to be glad of yours.
translation: You've taken the words right out of my mouth, sir; I am the one who is glad of your company.

original: Well, let us go together.
translation: Well, let us go together.

original: A goodly city is this Antium.
translation: This Antium place is not so bad.

original: City,   'Tis I that made thy widows:
translation: [As though speaking to the city]  City, I was the one who widowed your women;

original: many an heir   Of these fair edifices 'fore my wars   Have I heard groan and drop:
translation: I killed many of the men who lived in your fair buildings.

original: then know me not,   Lest that thy wives with spits and boys with stones   In puny battle slay me.
translation: Do not know me, or your wives will spit on me and your boys will attack me with stones.

original: Save you, sir.
translation: God save you, sir.

original: And you.
translation: And you.

original: Direct me, if it be your will, Where great Aufidius lies: is he in Antium?
translation: Could you please direct me to where the great Aufidius stays? Is he in Antium?

original: He is, and feasts the nobles of the state At his house this night.
translation: He is, indeed, and is having a feast for nobles at his house tonight.

original: Which is his house, beseech you?
translation: Please tell me, which is his house?

original: This, here before you.
translation: This one, right here.

original: Thank you, sir: farewell.
translation: Thank you, sir, good-bye.

original: O world, thy slippery turns!
translation: Oh, world, your unexpected twists and turns!

original: Friends now fast sworn,   Whose double bosoms seem to wear one heart,
translation: Even now there are best friends—friends so close they seem to have the same heart;

original: Whose house, whose bed, whose meal, and exercise,   Are still together,     who twin, as 'twere, in love   Unseparable,
translation: friends whose house, whose bed, whose meal, whose hobbies are always the same,  like inseparable twins—

original: shall within this hour,   On a dissension of a doit, break out   To bitterest enmity:
translation: who within this very hour, over a tiny argument, will become the most bitter enemies.

original: so, fellest foes,   Whose passions and whose plots have broke their sleep,   To take the one the other, by some chance,
translation: In the same way, the most dire foes, men who have lost sleep planning plots to take one another by some chance,

original: Some trick not worth an egg, shall grow dear friends   And interjoin their issues.
translation: some trick worth almost nothing, will become dear friends and work together.

original: So with me:   My birth-place hate I, and my love's upon   This enemy town.
translation: S o it is with me. I hate my birthplace, and I love this enemy town.

original: I'll enter: if he slay me,   He does fair justice; if he give me way,   I'll do his country service.
translation: I'll enter Aufidius's house; if he slays me, that's fair; if he lets me stay, I'll fight on the Volscian side.

original: Wine, wine, wine! What service is here! I think our fellows are asleep.
translation: Wine, wine, wine! They want so much! It's like the other servants are asleep.

original: Where's Cotus? my master calls for him. Cotus!
translation: Where's Cotus? My master is calling for him. Cotus!

original: A goodly house: the feast smells well; but I Appear not like a guest.
translation: This place is great: the feast smells wonderful, but I'm not dressed to be a noble guest.

original: What would you have, friend? whence are you? Here's no place for you: pray, go to the door.
translation: What do you need, friend? Where did you come from? You don't belong here; please leave.

original: I have deserved no better entertainment, In being Coriolanus.
translation: I deserve no better welcome, being who I am.

original: Whence are you, sir? Has the porter his eyes in his head; that he gives entrance to such companions? Pray, get you out.
translation: Where did you come from, sir? Does the doorman even have eyes in his head, if he's letting people like you in? Please, get out.

original: Away!
translation: You get out!

original: Away! get you away.
translation: Away, get away!

original: Now thou'rt troublesome.
translation: Now you're being troublesome.

original: Are you so brave? I'll have you talked with anon.
translation: Are you really this bold? I'll get someone to take care of you in a minute.

original: What fellow's this?
translation: Who's this guy?

original: A strange one as ever I looked on: I cannot get him out of the house: prithee, call my master to him.
translation: As strange a person as I've ever seen. I can't get him out of the house. Please, call my master in to take care of him.

original: What have you to do here, fellow? Pray you, avoid the house.
translation: What are you doing here? Please, get out of this house.

original: Let me but stand; I will not hurt your hearth.
translation: Just let me stand here; I won't get in your way.

original: What are you?
translation: What's your deal?

original: A gentleman.
translation: I am a gentleman.

original: A marvellous poor one.
translation: An awfully poor one, then.

original: True, so I am.
translation: That's true enough, so I am.

original: Pray you, poor gentleman, take up some other station; here's no place for you; pray you, avoid:  come.
translation: Then please, poor gentleman, go interfere with some other house; this is no place for you.  Please, leave, come on.

original: Follow your function, go, and batten on cold bits.
What, you will not? Prithee, tell my master what a strange guest he has here.
translation: What, will you really not leave?  Go tell my master what a strange guest we have here.

original: And I shall.
translation: And I shall.

original: Where dwellest thou?
translation: Where do you live?

original: Under the canopy.
translation: Under the stars.

original: Under the canopy!
translation: Under the stars!

original: Ay.
translation: Yeah.

original: Where's that?
translation: Where's that?

original: I' the city of kites and crows.
I' the city of kites and crows! What an ass it is! Then thou dwellest with daws too?
No, I serve not thy master.
translation: No, I don't serve your master.

original: How, sir! do you meddle with my master?
translation: What?! Are you messing with my master?

original: Ay; 'tis an honester service than to meddle with thy mistress. Thou pratest, and pratest; serve with thy trencher, hence!
translation: Sure; it's more honest than screwing with your mistress. You talk and talk; go do your job, go!

original: Where is this fellow?
translation: Where is this guy?

original: Here, sir: I'ld have beaten him like a dog, but for disturbing the lords within.
translation: Here he is, sir. I would've beaten him like a dog, but I didn't want to disturb the lords feasting.

original: Whence comest thou? what wouldst thou? thy name? Why speak'st not? speak, man: what's thy name?
translation: Where have you come from? What do you want? What's your name? Why don't you speak? Speak, man: what's your name?

original: If, Tullus,
translation: If, Tullus, you do not know me yet, and seeing me, don't recognize me for who I am, then I suppose I will have to tell you.

original: What is thy name?
translation: What is your name?

original: A name unmusical to the Volscians' ears, And harsh in sound to thine.
translation: A name unmusical to the Volscian's ears, and even worse to yours.

original: Say, what's thy name?   Thou hast a grim appearance, and thy face   Bears a command in't; though thy tackle's torn.
translation: Tell me, what's your name? You have a grim look, and a commanding face, though your clothes are torn.

original: Thou show'st a noble vessel: what's thy name?
translation: You have the stature of a nobleman. What's your name?

original: Prepare thy brow to frown: know'st thou me yet?
translation: Prepare to frown—you still don't recognize me?

original: I know thee not: thy name?
translation: I do not know you. What's your name?

original: My name is Caius Marcius, who hath done   To thee particularly and to all the Volsces   Great hurt and mischief;
translation: My name is Caius Marcius, the man who has done great damage to you and to all the Volsces.

original: thereto witness may   My surname, Coriolanus:
translation: From that damage comes my surname, Coriolanus.

original: the painful service,   The extreme dangers and the drops of blood   Shed for my thankless country are requited   But with that surname;
translation: That surname is the only thing left of the painful service, extreme dangers, and all the blood I shed for my thankless country.

original: a good memory,   And witness of the malice and displeasure   Which thou shouldst bear me: only that name remains;
translation: It is a memorial to the hatred you should have for me—only that name remains.

original: The cruelty and envy of the people,   Permitted by our dastard nobles, who   Have all forsook me, hath devour'd the rest;
translation: The cruelty and envy of the common people, which our idiot nobles allowed, has devoured all of Rome.

original: And suffer'd me by the voice of slaves to be   Whoop'd out of Rome.
translation: The people yelled me out of Rome.

original: Now this extremity   Hath brought me to thy hearth; not out of hope—   Mistake me not—to save my life,
translation: This difficult situation has brought me to your home, not out of hope to save my life—don't get me wrong;

original: for if   I had fear'd death, of all the men i' the world   I would have 'voided thee,
translation: if I feared death I would have avoided you more than anyone else—

original: but in mere spite,   To be full quit of those my banishers,   Stand I before thee here.
translation: but out of spite, to fully condemn those who banished me. That's why I'm here.

original: Then if thou hast   A heart of wreak in thee,
translation: If you have a heart filled with rage,

original: that wilt revenge   Thine own particular wrongs and stop those maims   Of shame seen through thy country,
translation: and you would like to avenge the wrongs which Rome has done to your country, Volscian,

original: speed   thee straight,   And make my misery serve thy turn:   so use it   That my revengeful services may prove   As benefits to thee,
translation: take advantage of my misery: use me, in my spirit of revenge, for your own war;

original: for I will fight   Against my canker'd country with the spleen   Of all the under fiends.
translation: I will fight against my poisoned country with the rage of every devil in hell.

original: But if so be   Thou darest not this and that to prove more fortunes   Thou'rt tired,
translation: But if you don't dare to do this, and are tired of fighting,

original: then, in a word, I also am   Longer to live most weary, and present   My throat to thee and to thy ancient malice;
translation: then I must admit to you that I am also just as tired of living; here is my throat, the object of your hatred,

original: Which not to cut would show thee but a fool,   Since I have ever follow'd thee with hate,   Drawn tuns of blood out of thy country's breast,
translation: which you would be a fool not to cut—since we have always been enemies and I have spilled tons of blood from your country,

original: And cannot live but to thy shame, unless   It be to do thee service.
translation: to leave me living would only bring you shame—unless you take me into your service.

original: O Marcius, Marcius!   Each word thou hast spoke hath weeded from my heart   A root of ancient envy.
translation: Oh Marcius, Marcius! Every word you've spoken has pulled from my heart a root of ancient hatred.

original: If Jupiter   Should from yond cloud speak divine things,   And say 'Tis true,'
translation: If god himself were to speak from behind a cloud, and say "It's true!"

original: I'ld not believe them more   Than thee, all noble Marcius.
translation: I wouldn't believe him any more than you, noble Marcius.

original: Let me twine   Mine arms about that body,
translation: Let me throw my arms around that body ,

original: where against   My grained ash an hundred times hath broke   And scarr'd the moon with splinters:
translation: against which I have broke my weapon a hundred times, and scarred the moon with splinters. [Forcefully hugs Marcius]

original: here I clip   The anvil of my sword,
translation: I embrace  the anvil of my sword ,

original: and do contest   As hotly and as nobly with thy love   As ever in ambitious strength I did   Contend against thy valour.
translation: and would fight as hard for your love as I have fought against you in the past for valor.

original: Know thou first,   I loved the maid I married; never man   Sigh'd truer breath; but that I see thee here,   Thou noble thing!
translation: You must know that I loved the woman I married—no one has said a truer thing—but now that I see you here—you noble thing!—

original: more dances my rapt heart   Than when I first my wedded mistress saw   Bestride my threshold.
translation: my heart dances, entranced, more than when I first saw my bride in her dress.

original: Why, thou Mars! I tell thee,   We have a power on foot; and I had purpose   Once more to hew thy target from thy brawn,   Or lose mine arm fort:
translation: Why,  you are Mars himself ! I tell you, I have an army in the field, and if I had good reason to fight with you once more I'd give my right arm to do it.

original: thou hast beat me out   Twelve several times, and I have nightly since   Dreamt of encounters 'twixt thyself and me;
translation: You've beaten me a dozen times, and I have dreamed every night since of encounters between us:

original: We have been down together in my sleep,   Unbuckling helms, fisting each other's throat,   And waked half dead with nothing.
translation: we've been wrestling together in my sleep, unbuckling our helmets, grasping at each other's throat. Every time, I wake with nothing.

original: Worthy Marcius,   Had we no quarrel else to Rome, but that   Thou art thence banish'd, we would muster all   From twelve to seventy,
translation: Worthy Marcius, if we had no other bone to pick with Rome except that you were banished, we would muster every man between the ages of twelve and seventy,

original: and pouring war   Into the bowels of ungrateful Rome,   Like a bold flood o'er-bear.
translation: and we would pour war like boiling oil into the stomach of ungrateful Rome—like a flood we would drown her.

original: O, come, go in,   And take our friendly senators by the hands;
translation: Oh, come, go in, and shake hands with the friendly senators

original: Who now are here, taking their leaves of me,   Who am prepared against your territories,   Though not for Rome itself.
translation: who are here bidding me good luck to move against your territories, though not until now Rome itself.

original: You bless me, gods!
translation: You bless me, gods!

original: Therefore, most absolute sir, if thou wilt have   The leading of thine own revenges,
translation: Therefore, most respected sir, if you would like to lead your own revenge,

original: take   The one half of my commission; and set down—
translation: take half of the leadership with me. We can chart out—

original: As best thou art experienced, since thou know'st   Thy country's strength and weakness,—   thine own ways;
translation: since you're the best experienced—the country's strengths and weaknesses, your own strategies:

original: Whether to knock against the gates of Rome,   Or rudely visit them in parts remote,
translation: whether to knock directly on the gates of Rome, or to strike remote towns,

original: To fright them, ere destroy. But come in:   Let me commend thee first to those that shall   Say yea to thy desires.
translation: to frighten them before we destroy them. But come in, let me introduce you first to the men who will approve all of this.

original: A thousand welcomes!   And more a friend than e'er an enemy;   Yet, Marcius, that was much. Your hand: most welcome!
translation: A thousand welcomes! More a friend now than you ever were an enemy, and believe me, Marcius, you were quite an enemy. Your hand—most welcome!

original: Here's a strange alteration!
translation: Well, that's quite a change!

original: By my hand, I had thought to have strucken him with a cudgel; and yet my mind gave me his clothes made a false report of him.
translation: And to think I would've hit him with a club; but it was because his clothes made him seem different than he is.

original: What an arm he has! he turned me about with his finger and his thumb, as one would set up a top.
translation: What an arm he has! He turned me around with his finger and his thumb, like one would spin a top.

original: Nay, I knew by his face that there was something in him: he had, sir, a kind of face, methought,—I cannot tell how to term it.
He had so; looking as it were—would I were hanged, but I thought there was more in him than I could think.
translation: He had this sort of—looking like this—kill me, but I thought there was something more to him than met the eye.

original: So did I, I'll be sworn: he is simply the rarest man i' the world.
translation: So did I, I swear! He's the most marvelous man in the world.

original: I think he is: but a greater soldier than he you wot  on.
translation: I think he is, but we know of a greater soldier than him.

original: Who, my master?
translation: Who, my master Tullus Aufidius?

original: Nay, it's no matter for that.
translation: Definitely, there's no doubt about that.

original: Worth six on him.
translation: He's worth six Coriolanuses.

original: Nay, not so neither: but I take him to be the greater soldier.
translation: Well, I wouldn't say that, but I do think he's the better soldier.

original: Faith, look you, one cannot tell how to say that: for the defence of a town, our general is excellent.
translation: Listen, there's no real basis for saying that; for the defense of a town, our general is excellent.

original: Ay, and for an assault too.
translation: Yeah, and for an assault too.

original: O slaves, I can tell you news,—news, you rascals!
translation: Guys, I have news for you—news, you rascals!

original: What, what, what? let's partake.
translation: What, what, what? Tell us.

original: I would not be a Roman, of all nations; I had as lieve be a condemned man.
translation: I would rather be of any nation rather than of Rome right now; to be Roman is to be a man condemned to death.

original: Wherefore? wherefore?
translation: Why? Why?

original: Why, here's he that was wont to thwack our general, Caius Marcius.
translation: Why, here's the man that's been beating our general around, Caius Marcius.

original: Why do you say 'thwack our general '?
translation: Why do you say "beating our general around?"

original: I do not say 'thwack our general;' but he was always good enough for him.
translation: Well, not "beating him," but he was always a good match for Aufidius.

original: Come, we are fellows and friends: he was ever too hard for him; I have heard him say so himself.
translation: Come, we are friends here—Coriolanus was always too hard for Aufidius; I have heard Aufidius say so himself.

original: He was too hard for him directly, to say the troth on't: before Corioli he scotched him and notched him like a carbon ado.
An he had been cannibally given, he might have broiled and eaten him too.
translation: And had Coriolanus been into cannibalism, he might have cooked and eaten him, too.

original: But, more of thy news?
translation: But, what other news?

original: Why, he is so made on here within, as if he were son   and heir to Mars;
translation: Well, he's been welcomed as though he were the son and heir to Mars.

original: set at upper end o' the table; no   question asked him by any of the senators, but they   stand bald before him:
translation: He sits at the head of the table, and the senators question him with their caps in their hands, respectfully;

original: our general himself makes a   mistress of him:
translation: our general himself acts like his mistress.

original: sanctifies himself with's hand and   turns up the white o' the eye to his discourse.
translation: He treats the touch of his hand as holy, and devotedly listens to his every word.

original: But   the bottom of the news is that our general is cut i'   the middle and but one half of what he was   yesterday;
translation: But the big news is that our general has been cut into half of what he was yesterday,

original: for the other has half, by the entreaty   and grant of the whole table.
translation: for Coriolanus has taken half the army, at the request and approval of the whole table.

original: He'll go, he says,   and sowl the porter of Rome gates by the ears: he   will mow all down before him, and leave his passage  polled.
translation: He'll go, he says, and drag the guards of Rome's gate out by the ears. He'll mow down everything in his way, and leave wreckage in his path.

original: And he's as like to do't as any man I can imagine.
translation: And he's as able to do that as any man I can imagine.

original: Do't! he will do't; for, look you, sir, he has as   many friends as enemies;
translation: Do that!  He will do it. Look you, sir, he has as many friends as enemies.

original: which friends, sir, as it   were, durst not, look you, sir, show themselves, as   we term it, his friends whilst he's in directitude.
translation: Those friends, sir, as it were, dare not—look you sir—show themselves, as we call it, "his friends," while he's in directitude.

original: Directitude! what's that?
translation: Directitude! What's that?

original: But when they shall see, sir, his crest up again,   and the man in blood,
translation: But when they see, sir, his flag up again, and the man covered in blood,

original: they will out of their   burrows, like conies after rain, and revel all with   him.
translation: they will flee out of their burrows like rabbits after rain, and celebrate with him .

original: But when goes this forward?
translation: But when will they move out?

original: To-morrow; to-day; presently; you shall have the   drum struck up this afternoon:
translation: Tomorrow, today even, this very moment! You'll hear the drums this afternoon.

original: 'tis, as it were, a   parcel of their feast, and to be executed ere they   wipe their lips.
translation: It's practically a part of their dinner, and will be done before they wipe their lips and finish.

original: Why, then we shall have a stirring world again. This peace is nothing, but to rust iron, increase tailors, and breed ballad-makers.
translation: Why, then we'll have an exciting world again. This peace is good for nothing but to rust iron, to make tailors rich, and encourage artists.

original: Let me have war, say I; it exceeds peace as far as   day does night;
translation: Let me have war, I say. War's as much better than peace as day is better than night;

original: it's spritely, waking, audible, and   full of vent.
translation: it's energetic, awake, loud, full of energy.

original: Peace is a very apoplexy, lethargy;   mulled, deaf, sleepy, insensible; a getter of more   bastard children than war's a destroyer of men.
translation: Peace is like a coma: speechless, deaf, sleepy; more bastard children are born in peacetime than men die in war.

original: 'Tis so: and as war, in some sort, may be said to be a ravisher, so it cannot be denied but peace is a great maker of cuckolds.
Ay, and it makes men hate one another.
translation: Yeah, and it makes men hate one another.

original: Reason; because they then less need one another. The wars for my money. I hope to see Romans as cheap as Volscians. They are rising, they are rising.
translation: The reason is that, in peace, they need one another less. I'll put my money on the wars! I hope to see Romans brought down to our level.  They are rising, they are rising!

original: In, in, in, in!
translation: In, in, in, in!

original: We hear not of him, neither need we fear him;
translation: We hear no news of him, and we shouldn't fear him.

original: His remedies are tame i' the present peace   And quietness of the people, which before   Were in wild hurry.
translation: He can't do anything while the people are peaceful and quiet, when before they were rioting.

original: Here do we make his friends   Blush that the world goes well,
translation: We make his friends blush that everything is going so well;

original: who rather had,   Though they themselves did suffer by't, behold   Dissentious numbers pestering streets
translation: they would rather have crowds of dissenting people in the streets,

original: than see   Our tradesmen with in their shops and going   About their functions friendly.
translation: even if it caused them problems, than they would see our tradesmen in their shops doing their jobs happily.

original: We stood to't in good time.
translation: We did the right thing at the right time.

original: Is this Menenius?
translation: Is this Menenius?

original: 'Tis he,'tis he: O, he is grown most kind of late.
translation: It's him, it's him. Oh, he's grown very kind lately.

original: Hail sir!
translation: Hello there!

original: Hail to you both!
translation: Hello to you both!

original: Your Coriolanus   Is not much miss'd, but with his friends:
translation: No one but his friends seem to miss your Coriolanus.

original: The commonwealth doth stand, and so would do,   Were he more angry at it.
translation: The  commonwealth  stands, and would even were he more angry at it.

original: All's well; and might have been much better, if He could have temporized.
translation: All is well. It might have been much better, though, if he could have been calmed.

original: Where is he, hear you?
translation: Where is he, have you heard?

original: Nay, I hear nothing: his mother and his wife Hear nothing from him.
translation: No, I have heard nothing. His mother and his wife hear nothing from him.

original: The gods preserve you both!
translation: The gods save you both!

original: God-den, our neighbours.
translation: Good evening, neighbours.

original: God-den to you all, god-den to you all.
translation: Good evening, good evening to you all.

original: Ourselves, our wives, and children, on our knees, Are bound to pray for you both.
translation: We, and our wives and children, pray for you both on our knees.

original: Live, and thrive!
translation: Live, and thrive!

original: Farewell, kind neighbours: we wish'd Coriolanus Had loved you as we did.
translation: Farewell, kind neighbors. We wish Coriolanus had loved you as we did!

original: Now the gods keep you!
translation: Gods bless you!

original: Farewell, farewell.
translation: Good-bye, good-bye.

original: This is a happier and more comely time Than when these fellows ran about the streets, Crying confusion.
translation: People are happier and more prosperous now than when these sort of people ran around in the street, rioting.

original: Caius Marcius was   A worthy officer i' the war;
translation: Caius Marcius was a worthy officer in the war,

original: but insolent,   O'ercome with pride, ambitious past all thinking,   Self-loving,—
translation: but he was also insolent, overcome with pride, ambitious beyond imagination, self-absorbed—

original: And affecting one sole throne, Without assistance.
translation: And he desired complete power.

original: I think not so.
translation: I do not think so.

original: We should by this, to all our lamentation, If he had gone forth consul, found it so.
translation: Well, had he become consul, we would have found that he did want complete power, and then much to our dismay.

original: The gods have well prevented it, and Rome Sits safe and still without him.
translation: The gods have done well to prevent that, and Rome sits safe and sound without him.

original: Worthy tribunes,   There is a slave, whom we have put in prison,   Reports, the Volsces with two several powers   Are enter'd in the Roman territories,
translation: Worthy tribunes: there is a slave in prison reporting that the Volsces have entered Roman territories with several battalions,

original: And with the deepest malice of the war   Destroy what lies before 'em.
translation: and with the deep hatred of war, destroy everything that lies before them.

original: 'Tis Aufidius,   Who, hearing of our Marcius' banishment,   Thrusts forth his horns again into the world;
translation: It must be Aufidius. He's heard of Marcius' banishment, and now he flexes his muscles;

original: Which were inshell'd when Marcius stood for Rome,   And durst not once peep out.
translation: when Marcius stood to protect Rome, he wouldn't have dared to peep out of his hole.

original: Come, what talk you Of Marcius?
translation: What? Why are you talking about Marcius?

original: Go see this rumourer whipp'd. It cannot be The Volsces dare break with us.
translation: Go make sure this gossiping prisoner gets whipped. There's no way the Volsces would dare to fight with us.

original: Cannot be!   We have record that very well it can,   And three examples of the like have been   Within my age.
translation: No way! We have every reason to believe there is a way, and there are three examples of it within my lifetime.

original: But reason with the fellow,   Before you punish him, where he heard this,
translation: Just talk to the prisoner before you punish him. Find out where he heard this,

original: Lest you shall chance to whip your information   And beat the messenger who bids beware   Of what is to be dreaded.
translation: or you will risk losing information and beating a messenger who warns us for good reason.

original: Tell not me: I know this cannot be.
translation: Don't talk to me; I know this can't be true.

original: Not possible.
translation: It's not possible.

original: The nobles in great earnestness are going All to the senate-house: some news is come That turns their countenances.
translation: The nobles are all going to the senate with great urgency. Some news has come which made them all frown.

original: 'Tis this slave;— Go whip him, 'fore the people's eyes:—his raising; Nothing but his report.
translation: It's this prisoner!  Go whip him before their very eyes. He has nothing but this report.

original: Yes, worthy sir, The slave's report is seconded; and more, More fearful, is deliver'd.
translation: Yes, worthy sir, the slave's report has been backed up by another, and others, even more fearful, have been delivered.

original: What more fearful?
translation: What do you mean, more fearful?

original: It is spoke freely out of many mouths—   How probable I do not know—
translation: All the people are saying—I don't know if it's true—

original: that Marcius,   Join'd with Aufidius, leads a power 'gainst Rome,
translation: that Marcius has joined forces with Aufidius to lead an army against Rome,

original: And vows revenge as spacious as between   The young'st and oldest thing.
translation: vowing revenge as spacious as between the youngest and oldest things.

original: This is most likely!
Raised only, that the weaker sort may wish Good Marcius home again.
translation: This rumor has been spread only so that weak people will wish to have good Marcius home again.

original: The very trick on't.
translation: That's the trick of it.

original: This is unlikely: He and Aufidius can no more atone Than violentest contrariety.
translation: This news is unlikely. He and Aufidius could never work together, no more than the most violent opposites.

original: You are sent for to the senate:
translation: The senate sends for you.

original: A fearful army, led by Caius Marcius   Associated with Aufidius, rages   Upon our territories;
translation: A fearful army, led by Caius Marcius, who is allied with Aufidius, rages upon our territories.

original: and have already   O'erborne their way, consumed with fire, and took   What lay before them.
translation: They have already crushed everyone in their path, burned towns and villages, and took everything that lay before them.

original: O, you have made good work!
translation: Oh, look what you have done!

original: What news? what news?
translation: What's the news?

original: You have holp to ravish your own daughters and To melt the city leads upon your pates, To see your wives dishonour'd to your noses,—
translation: You have helped to rape your own daughters, to melt the city's lead roofs down onto your heads, and to see your wives raped while you watch.

original: What's the news? what's the news?
translation: What's the news? What's the news?

original: Your temples burned in their cement, and Your franchises, whereon you stood, confined Into an auger's bore.
translation: Your temples will burn on their foundations, and your freedoms, on which you so insisted, made into machinery of your own misery.

original: Pray now, your news? You have made fair work, I fear me.—Pray, your news?— If Marcius should be join'd with Volscians,—
translation: Pray now, what news? [To the TRIBUNES] You have done something terrible, I'm afraid. Please, your news? If Marcius has joined with the Volscians—

original: If!   He is their god:
translation: If! He is their god.

original: he leads them like a thing   Made by some other deity than nature,   That shapes man better;
translation: He leads them like a  thing made by some other deity than nature, that shapes man better.

original: and they follow him,   Against us brats, with no less confidence   Than boys pursuing summer butterflies,
translation: And they follow him against us, children that we are, with all the confidence of  boys pursuing summer butterflies ,

original: Or butchers killing flies.
translation: or butchers killing flies.

original: You have made good work,   You and your apron-men;
translation: You've done it now, you and your lowly laborers,

original: you that stood so up much   on the voice of occupation and   The breath of garlic-eaters!
translation: you tribunes that carried on about the votes of the working,  garlic-eating  common man!

original: He will shake Your Rome about your ears.
translation: He will, like an earthquake, shake your Rome around your ears.

original: As Hercules Did shake down mellow fruit. You have made fair work!
But is this true, sir?
translation: But is this true, sir?

original: Ay; and you'll look pale   Before you find it other.
translation: Yes, and you'll  look pale  before you find it false.

original: All the regions   Do smilingly revolt; and who resist   Are mock'd for valiant ignorance,
translation: All our territories willingly revolt against Rome, and the ones that resist are mocked for their brave stupidity

original: And perish constant fools.
translation: and then perish like fools.

original: Who is't can blame him?   Your enemies and his find something in him.
translation: And who can blame him, Coriolanus? Even your enemies find something worthy in him.

original: We are all undone, unless The noble man have mercy.
translation: We're all doomed, unless that noble Coriolanus will be merciful.

original: Who shall ask it?   The tribunes cannot do't for shame;
translation: Who can ask mercy of him? The disgraced tribunes cannot do it;

original: the people   Deserve such pity of him as the wolf   Does of the shepherds:
translation: the people deserve his pity no more than shepherds deserve the pity of a wolf.

original: for his best friends, if they   Should say 'Be good to Rome,' they charged him even   As those should do that had deserved his hate,
translation: A s for his best friends, if they tell him "be good to Rome," they're asking of him the same thing his enemies would ask,

original: And therein show'd like enemies.
translation: and so they too would show themselves to be enemies.

original: 'Tis true:   If he were putting to my house the brand   That should consume it,
translation: It's true. If he were burning my own house,

original: I have not the face   To say 'Beseech you, cease.' You have made fair hands,   You and your crafts! you have crafted fair!
translation: I don't have the right to say "Please, stop." You tribunes have made something extraordinary, you and your cleverness—you've made a clever thing indeed!

original: You have brought A trembling upon Rome, such as was never So incapable of help.
translation: You have brought a trembling upon Rome, a terror which nothing can stop.

original: Say not we brought it.
translation: Don't say we brought it.

original: How! Was it we? we loved him but, like beasts And cowardly nobles, gave way unto your clusters, Who did hoot him out o' the city.
translation: What?! Did we bring on this terror, then? We loved him, but like dumb animals and cowardly nobles, we let you and your crowds throw him out of the city.

original: But I fear   They'll roar him in again.
translation: I'm afraid they'll drag him in again.

original: Tullus Aufidius,   The second name of men, obeys his points   As if he were his officer:
translation: Tullus Aufidius, the second strongest man, obeys Coriolanus as though he were the leader.

original: desperation   Is all the policy, strength and defence,   That Rome can make against them.
translation: Desperation is the only plan, the only strength, and the only defense that Rome has left.

original: Here come the clusters.   And is Aufidius with him?
You are they   That made the air unwholesome, when you cast   Your stinking greasy caps in hooting at   Coriolanus' exile.
translation: You are to blame for poisoning the air when you threw your stinking greasy hats up, hooting and celebrating Coriolanus's exile.

original: Now he's coming;   And not a hair upon a soldier's head   Which will not prove a whip:
translation: Now he's coming back, and there's not a hair on his head which will not be like a whip for your backs.

original: as many coxcombs   As you threw caps up will he tumble down,   And pay you for your voices.
translation: He'll pay you for your voices now: as many caps as you threw up, that many heads will he cut off.

original: 'Tis no matter;   if he could burn us all into one coal,   We have deserved it.
translation: But no matter. If he could burn us all into ashes and shape us into a coal, we would deserve it.

original: Faith, we hear fearful news.
translation: Oh, that's fearful news.

original: For mine own part, When I said, banish him, I said 'twas pity.
translation: As far as I'm concerned, when I said he had to be banished, I thought it was a shame.

original: And so did I.
translation: And so did I.

original: And so did I; and, to say the truth, so did very   many of us:
translation: And so did I; to tell the truth, so did many of us.

original: that we did, we did for the best;
translation: We did it because we thought it was for the best,

original: and   though we willingly consented to his banishment, yet   it was against our will.
translation: and though we willingly agreed to his banishment, it was not what we really wanted.

original: Ye re goodly things, you voices!
translation: You're wonderful people, you voices!

original: You have made Good work, you and your cry! Shall's to the Capitol?
translation: You've gone and done it now, you and your crying! Shall we go to the Capitol?

original: O, ay, what else?
translation: Oh, yes, what else can we do?

original: Go, masters, get you home; be not dismay'd:
translation: Go, sirs, go home. Don't worry.

original: These are a side that would be glad to have   This true which they so seem to fear.
translation: Those two are actually hoping for what they seem to be afraid of.

original: Go home,   And show no sign of fear.
translation: Go home, and show no sign of fear.

original: The gods be good to us! Come, masters, let's home. I ever said we were i' the wrong when we banished him.
translation: May the gods be good to us! Come, friends, lets go home. I've always said we were making a mistake to banish him.

original: So did we all. But, come, let's home.
translation: We all did. But come on, let's go home.

original: I do not like this news.
translation: I do not like this news.

original: Nor I.
translation: Neither do I.

original: Let's to the Capitol. Would half my wealth Would buy this for a lie!
Pray, let us go.
translation: Yeah, let's go.

original: Do they still fly to the Roman?
translation: Are our men still flocking to Coriolanus?

original: I do not know what witchcraft's in him,
translation: I don't know what magic he has,

original: but   Your soldiers use him as the grace 'fore meat,   Their talk at table, and their thanks at end;
translation: but your soldiers treat him like  the prayer before a meal, their conversation over dinner, and their thanks at the meal's end.

original: And you are darken'd in this action, sir,   Even by your own.
translation: You are made to look weaker by all this sir, even in the eyes of your own men.

original: I cannot help it now,   Unless, by using means, I lame the foot   Of our design.
translation: I can't help it now without shooting myself in the foot and ruining our plans.

original: He bears himself more proudlier,   Even to my person, than I thought he would   When first I did embrace him:
translation: He carries himself more proudly, even to me, than I thought he would when I first welcomed him.

original: yet his nature   In that's no changeling; and I must excuse   What cannot be amended.
translation: But, to be fair, it's not as though he's acting any differently now than he did then, and I must excuse what can't be changed.

original: Yet I wish, sir,—   I mean for your particular,—
translation: Yet I wish, sir—I mean, for your sake—

original: you had not   Join'd in commission with him;
translation: that you hadn't given him half your authority,

original: but either   Had borne the action of yourself, or else   To him had left it solely.
translation: but either kept control to entirely yourself or given it entirely to him.

original: I understand thee well; and be thou sure,   when he shall come to his account, he knows not   What I can urge against him.
translation: I understand what you mean, and believe me, when push comes to shove, he doesn't know what I can bring to bear against him,

original: Although it seems,   And so he thinks, and is no less apparent   To the vulgar eye, that he bears all things fairly.
translation: even though it seems—and so he and others think—that everything is going well for him.

original: And shows good husbandry for the Volscian state,   Fights dragon-like, and does achieve as soon   As draw his sword;
translation: But he is taking good care of the Volscian nation, fights dragon-like, and wins battles just by drawing his sword.

original: yet he hath left undone   That which shall break his neck or hazard mine,   Whene'er we come to our account.
translation: He hasn't done anything which would break his neck or cause me to risk mine, whenever we are put to the test.

original: Sir, I beseech you, think you he'll carry Rome?
translation: Sir, tell me, do you think he'll conquer Rome?

original: All places yield to him ere he sits down;   And the nobility of Rome are his:
translation: All places surrender to him before he's done. The nobility of Rome support him;

original: The senators and patricians love him too:
translation: the senators and patricians love him too.

original: The tribunes are no soldiers; and their people   Will be as rash in the repeal, as hasty   To expel him thence.
translation: The tribunes aren't soldiers, and their people will be as quick in welcoming him back as they were hasty to get rid of him in the first place.

original: I think he'll be to Rome   As is the osprey to the fish, who takes it   By sovereignty of nature.
translation: I think he'll be to Rome like an  osprey  to a fish—he'll conquer it by his very nature.

original: First he was   A noble servant to them; but he could not   Carry his honours even:
translation: First he was a noble servant to them, but even then they wouldn't give him honor. It's hard to say why they rejected him—

original: whether 'twas pride,   Which out of daily fortune ever taints   The happy man;
translation: whether it was his pride, which taints otherwise good men;

original: whether defect of judgment,   To fail in the disposing of those chances   Which he was lord of;
translation: whether it was his poor judgement in not seizing the opportunities he was given;

original: or whether nature,   Not to be other than one thing, not moving   From the casque to the cushion,
translation: or whether it was his nature, which is to be one thing only, unable to take of a soldier's helmet and sit on a statesman's cushion,

original: but commanding peace   Even with the same austerity and garb   As he controll'd the war; but one of these—
translation: attempting to command a city at peace the way he would have commanded an army at war. Somehow, one of these—

original: As he hath spices of them all, not all,   For I dare so far free him—
translation: and he has bits of all of them, though he doesn't embody any one fully—

original: made him fear'd,   So hated, and so banish'd: but he has a merit,   To choke it in the utterance.
translation: made him so feared and so hated that they banished him. But he has other merits  so great a man will choke  attempting to utter them.

original: So our virtues   Lie in the interpretation of the time:
translation: Our virtues are subject to interpretation,

original: And power, unto itself most commendable,   Hath not a tomb so evident as a chair   To extol what it hath done.
translation: and power, which in itself seems good, is doomed to fall into a tomb as much as to be talked about.

original: One fire drives out one fire; one nail, one nail;   Rights by rights falter, strengths by strengths do  fail.   Come, let's away.
translation: [Reciting a common axiom]  "One fire drives out one fire; one nail, one nail; rights by rights falter, strengths by strengths do fail." Let's go.

original: When, Caius, Rome is thine,   Thou art poor'st of all; then shortly art thou mine.
translation: [As though to Coriolanus,]  When Rome falls, Caius, you'll be the poorest of them all. Shortly after, you'll be mine.

original: No, I'll not go: you hear what he hath said   Which was sometime his general; who loved him   In a most dear particular.
translation: No, I will not go. You've heard what he said to someone who was once his general, someone who dearly loved him.

original: He call'd me father:   But what o' that?
translation: He called me "father," but so what?

original: Go, you that banish'd him;   A mile before his tent fall down, and knee   The way into his mercy:
translation: You, who banished him, should go; fall to your knees a mile from his tent, and crawl into his mercy.

original: nay, if he coy'd   To hear Cominius speak, I'll keep at home.
translation: No, if he wouldn't hear Cominius speak, there's no use in me going.

original: He would not seem to know me.
translation: He acted as though he did not know me.

original: Do you hear?
translation: Hear that?

original: Yet one time he did call me by my name:
translation: Just once, he called me by my name.

original: I urged our old acquaintance, and the drops   That we have bled together.
translation: I reminded him of our old friendship, and the blood that we've spilled together.

original: Coriolanus   He would not answer to: forbad all names;
translation: He refused to answer to the name "Coriolanus"— in fact, he wouldn't answer to anything.

original: He was a kind of nothing, titleless,   Till he had forged himself a name o' the fire   Of burning Rome.
translation: He was a kind of nothing, as though nameless until he'd make himself a name in the fires of burning Rome.

original: Why, so: you have made good work! A pair of tribunes that have rack'd for Rome, To make coals cheap,—a noble memory!
translation: Why, there it is! You've done it now! A pair of tribunes that have destroyed Rome, and for what?—what a nice memorial you leave behind!

original: I minded him how royal 'twas to pardon   When it was less expected:
translation: I reminded him how it is noble to be merciful when mercy is least expected.

original: he replied,   It was a bare petition of a state   To one whom they had punish'd.
translation: He replied that this was a pathetic request from a country to a man it had punished.

original: Very well: Could he say less?
translation: Fair enough; what else could he say?

original: I offer'd to awaken his regard   For's private friends:
translation: I tried to remind him of his respect for his personal friends,

original: his answer to me was,   He could not stay to pick them in a pile   Of noisome musty chaff:
translation: and his answer to me was that  he could not be bothered to pick them out of a pile of stinking, rotting wheat.

original: he said 'twas folly,   For one poor grain or two, to leave unburnt,   And still to nose the offence.
translation: He said it would be a mistake to leave the grain unburnt for the sake of one poor grain or two , and thus to have to bear the stink of the rest.

original: For one poor grain or two!   I am one of those; his mother, wife, his child,   And this brave fellow too,
translation: For one poor grain or two! I am one of those; his mother, his wife, his child, and Cominius here too.

original: we are the grains:   You are the musty chaff; and you are smelt   Above the moon: we must be burnt for you.
translation: We are the grains,  [To the TRIBUNES]  you are the rotting waste, and you stink to high heaven. We will be burned because of you.

original: Nay, pray, be patient: if you refuse your aid   In this so never-needed help, yet do not   Upbraid's with our distress.
translation: No, please, be calm. If you refuse to help now, when we need help more than ever, you have no right to yell at us.

original: But, sure, if you   Would be your country's pleader,
translation: But if you would go plead to Coriolanus on behalf of your country,

original: your good tongue,   More than the instant army we can make,   Might stop our countryman.
translation: your good voice will be worth more than whatever army we can call to arms.

original: No, I'll not meddle.
translation: No, I won't interfere.

original: Pray you, go to him.
translation: Please, go to him.

original: What should I do?
translation: And what should I say?

original: Only make trial what your love can do For Rome, towards Marcius.
translation: Only ask what your love toward Marcius can do for Rome.

original: Well, and say that Marcius   Return me, as Cominius is return'd,   Unheard; what then?
translation: Sure, and what if Marcius sends me back without listening— what then?

original: But as a discontented friend, grief-shot   With his unkindness? say't be so?
translation: I'll just be crushed, a friend shot through with grief by his unkindness; is that what you want?

original: Yet your good will must have that thanks from Rome, after the measure As you intended well.
translation: But your efforts will win great thanks from Rome, simply because we know you have tried.

original: I'll undertake 't:   I think he'll hear me.
translation: I'll do it. I think he'll listen to me.

original: Yet, to bite his lip   And hum at good Cominius, much unhearts me.
translation: Yet,  to bite his lip and hum  at good Cominius—this disheartens me.

original: He was not taken well; he had not dined:
translation: Maybe he was just feeling ill, or he hadn't eaten.

original: The veins unfill'd, our blood is cold, and then   We pout upon the morning, are unapt   To give or to forgive;
translation: When we are ill or unfed, our blood is cold and then we are grumpy— then we are unlikely to be kind and forgive.

original: but when we have stuff'd   These and these conveyances of our blood   With wine and feeding,
translation: But perhaps when we are full of food and wine, and our blood runs more easily,

original: we have suppler souls   Than in our priest-like fasts:
translation: we are more easily convinced of mercy than in our  priest-like fasts .

original: therefore I'll watch him   Till he be dieted to my request,   And then I'll set upon him.
translation: Therefore, I'll wait until he's eaten to make my request, and then I'll go to ask him.

original: You know the very road into his kindness, And cannot lose your way.
translation: You know the way to his heart, and cannot fail.

original: Good faith, I'll prove him, Speed how it will. I shall ere long have knowledge Of my success.
translation: With luck, I'll get him to agree, however it goes. I guess we'll know whether I succeed very soon.

original: He'll never hear him.
translation: Coriolanus will never listen to him.

original: Not?
translation: No?

original: I tell you, he does sit in gold, his eye   Red as 'twould burn Rome;
translation: I'm telling you, he sits like a king, his eye red as though he meant to burn Rome with it,

original: and his injury   The gaoler to his pity.
translation: and absolutely without pity.

original: I kneel'd before him;   'Twas very faintly he said 'Rise;' dismiss'd me   Thus, with his speechless hand:
translation: I kneeled before him, and all he said, very faintly, was "Rise." Then he dismissed me with his hand.

original: what he would do,   He sent in writing after me; what he would not,   Bound with an oath to yield to his conditions:
translation: He sent a letter after me describing his intentions and containing his conditions for surrender.

original: So that all hope is vain.
translation: I think all hope is lost,

original: Unless his noble mother, and his wife;   Who, as I hear, mean to solicit him   For mercy to his country.
translation: although his noble mother and his wife will go, I hear, to ask for mercy.

original: Therefore, let's hence,   And with our fair entreaties haste them on.
translation: Therefore, let's go and wish them luck.

original: Stay: whence are you?
translation: Stop. Where are you from?

original: Stand, and go back.
translation: Stop where you are and go back.

original: You guard like men; 'tis well: but, by your leave, I am an officer of state, and come To speak with Coriolanus.
translation: You are bold guards, as you should be. But please, hear me out—I am a statesman, and come to speak with Coriolanus.

original: From whence?
translation: From where?

original: From Rome.
translation: From Rome.

original: You may not pass, you must return: our general Will no more hear from thence.
translation: You may not pass, and you must return. Our general will not hear anything more from Rome.

original: You'll see your Rome embraced with fire before You'll speak with Coriolanus.
translation: You'll see Rome embraced with fire before you'll speak with Coriolanus.

original: Good my friends,   If you have heard your general talk of Rome,
translation: Good friends, if you have heard your general talk about Rome,

original: And of his friends there, it is lots to blanks,   My name hath touch'd your ears it is Menenius.
translation: and of his friends there, by all odds you'll have heard him mention my name— it is Menenius.

original: Be it so; go back: the virtue of your name Is not here passable.
translation: Even so, go back. The virtue of your name does not win you passage here.

original: I tell thee, fellow,   The general is my lover:
translation: Sir, listen—the general loves me.

original: I have been   The book of his good acts, whence men have read   His name unparallel'd,
translation: I have often talked of him publicly as a man without equal;

original: haply amplified;
translation: I've sung his praises loudly.

original: For I have ever verified my friends,   Of whom he's chief,
translation: I have always spoken well of my friends—and he's my best friend—

original: with all the size that verity   Would without lapsing suffer:
translation: with all the generosity that truth would allow.

original: nay, sometimes,   Like to a bowl upon a subtle ground,   I have tumbled past the throw;
translation: Even, sometimes, like a bowler carried along with the ball,

original: and in his praise   Have almost stamp'd the leasing: therefore, fellow,   I must have leave to pass.
translation: I have praised him so much it's almost gone too far. Therefore, please, men, you must let me pass.

original: Faith, sir, if you had told as many lies in his   behalf as you have uttered words in your own,
translation: Honestly, sir, if you had lied as many times for him as you have uttered words for yourself— even then,

original: you   should not pass here; no, though it were as virtuous   to lie as to live chastely. Therefore, go back.
translation: you couldn't pass here; no, even if lying were as virtuous as to live peacefully. Therefore, go back.

original: Prithee, fellow, remember my name is Menenius, always factionary on the party of your general.
translation: Please, my good man, remember my name is Menenius; I have always been on Coriolanus's side.

original: Howsoever you have been his liar, as you say you have, I am one that, telling true under him, must say, you cannot pass. Therefore, go back.
translation: Even if you've lied on his behalf—as you say you have—I am one that, telling the truth on his behalf, must say you cannot pass. Therefore, go back.

original: Has he dined, canst thou tell? for I would not speak with him till after dinner.
translation: Has he dined, do you know? I'd rather not speak with him until after dinner.

original: You are a Roman, are you?
translation: You are a Roman, right?

original: I am, as thy general is.
translation: I am, as your general is.

original: Then you should hate Rome, as he does.
translation: Then you should hate Rome, as he does.

original: Can you,   when you have pushed out your gates the very   defender of them,
translation: When you have banished your defender

original: and, in a violent popular   ignorance, given your enemy your shield,
translation: and in a violent foolishness given your enemy your shield,

original: think to   front his revenges with the easy groans of old   women,
translation: do you really think you can stop his revenge with the groans of old women,

original: the virginal palms of your daughters, or with   the palsied intercession of such a decayed dotant as   you seem to be?
translation: the pleas of your daughters, or with whatever kind of old requests from a decaying corpse as you seem to be?

original: Can you think to blow out the   intended fire your city is ready to flame in, with   such weak breath as this?
translation: Do you think you can blow out the impending fire your city is ready to flame in with breath this weak?

original: No, you are deceived;   therefore, back to Rome, and prepare for your   execution:
translation: No, you're lying to yourself. Therefore, back to Rome, and prepare for your execution.

original: you are condemned, our general has sworn   you out of reprieve and pardon.
translation: You are condemned. Our general has sworn that you cannot be pardoned.

original: Sirrah, if thy captain knew I were here, he would use me with estimation.
Come, my captain knows you not.
translation: Come on, my captain doesn't know you.

original: I mean, thy general.
translation: Your general, I mean.

original: My general cares not for you. Back, I say, go; lest I let forth your half-pint of blood; back,—that's the utmost of your having: back.
translation: My general doesn't care about you. Back, I say, go, before I let out a half-pint of your blood. Back; that's all you're going to get from me: back!

original: Nay, but, fellow, fellow,—
translation: No, but—

original: What's the matter?
translation: What is all this?

original: Now, you companion, I'll say an errand for you:
translation: Now, buddy, I'll give you a chore:

original: You shall know now that I am in estimation; you shall   perceive that a Jack guardant cannot office me from   my son Coriolanus:
translation: now you'll know that I'm respected. You'll see that some Jack guard can't send me away from my son Coriolanus.

original: guess, but by my entertainment   with him, if thou standest not i' the state of   hanging,
translation: Just guess, by the way he treats me, if you're not going to be hanged for this,

original: or of some death more long in   spectatorship, and crueller in suffering; behold now   presently, and swoon for what's to come upon thee. @
translation: or maybe something even worse and more cruel. Watch, watch this, and try not to faint in fear about what will happen to you.

original: The glorious gods sit in hourly synod   about thy particular prosperity and love thee no worse   than thy old father Menenius does.
translation: The glorious gods are even now talking about your extraordinary prosperity, and love you just as your old father Menenius does!

original: O my son, my son!   Thou art preparing fire for us.
translation: Oh, my son, my son! You're preparing fire for us.

original: Look thee, here's water   to quench it.
translation: But look, I offer you water to quench it.

original: I was hardly moved to come to thee but,   being assured none but myself could move thee,
translation: I almost didn't come to you, but since I was told no one but me could convince you,

original: I have   been blown out of gates with sighs and conjure   thee to pardon Rome and they petitionary countrymen.
translation: I have come out of Rome's gates sighing sadly to beg you to pardon Rome, and your countrymen.

original: The good gods assuage thy wrath and turn the dregs   of it upon this varlet here—
translation: May the good gods calm your wrath, and turn what's left of it upon this evil man here—

original: this, who like a block hath denied my access to thee.
translation: [pointing to the GUARD]  who, like a stone, denied my access to you.

original: Away!
translation: Go away!

original: How! away!
translation: Wait, what? Away?

original: Wife, mother, child, I know not. My affairs   Are servanted to others:
translation: I do not know wife, mother, or child.  I am the servant of others,

original: though I owe   My revenge properly, my remission lies   In Volscian breasts.
translation: and though I too am owed revenge, my debt is with the Volscians.

original: That we have been familiar,   Ingrate forgetfulness shall poison, rather   Than pity note how much.
translation: Cruel forgetfulness shall poison any memory that you and I were once friends, rather than pity remember that friendship.

original: Therefore, be gone.   Mine ears against your suits are stronger than   Your gates against my force.
translation: Therefore, be gone. I will resist anything you have to say more strongly than Rome's gates will resist my force.

original: Yet, for I loved thee,   Take this along; I writ it for thy sake
translation: Yet, as I did love you once, take this along. I wrote it for you

original: And would have rent it. Another word, Menenius,   I will not hear thee speak.
translation: [hands MENENIUS a letter]  and otherwise would have torn it up. Menenius, do not speak another word.

original: This man, Aufidius,   Was my beloved in Rome: yet thou behold'st!
translation: This man was my beloved in Rome— but you see how I treat him!

original: You keep a constant temper.
translation: You maintain your temper.

original: Now, sir, is your name Menenius?
translation: Now, sir, is your name Menenius?

original: 'Tis a spell, you see, of much power: you know the way home again.
translation: You see Coriolanus is greatly committed to our cause. You know the way home again.

original: Do you hear how we are shent for keeping your greatness back?
translation: Do you hear how we are punished for keeping your greatness back?

original: What cause, do you think, I have to swoon?
translation: Why, exactly, do you think I will faint?

original: I neither care for the world nor your general: for   such things as you, I can scarce think there's any,   ye're so slight.
translation: I care neither for the world nor your general— as for you, I can barely even think of you, you matter so little.

original: He that hath a will to die by   himself fears it not from another:
translation: A man who wants to die fears nothing from other men.

original: let your general   do his worst.
translation: Let your general do his worst.

original: For you, be that you are, long; and   your misery increase with your age! I say to you,   as I was said to, Away!
translation: For you, stay your miserable selves, and may your misery increase with age! I say to you, as it was said to me, go away!

original: A noble fellow, I warrant him.
translation: He seems like a noble man, honestly.

original: The worthy fellow is our general: he's the rock, the oak not to be wind-shaken.
translation: The worthy man is our general. He's like a rock, an oak unshaken by the wind.

original: We will before the walls of Rome tomorrow   Set down our host.
translation: Tomorrow, we'll camp our army in front of the walls of Rome.

original: My partner in this action,   You must report to the Volscian lords, how plainly   I have borne this business.
translation: Aufidius, my partner in this war, you must report to the Volscian lords how straightforwardly I've acted.

original: Only their ends   You have respected;
translation: You've respected only the goals of the Volscians.

original: stopp'd your ears against   The general suit of Rome; never admitted   A private whisper,
translation: You plugged your ears against the general pleas of Rome, listened not even to a whisper,

original: no, not with such friends   That thought them sure of you.
translation: no, not even with friends who were certain that you would.

original: This last old man,   Whom with a crack'd heart I have sent to Rome,
translation: This last old man, whom with a broken heart I have sent back to Rome,

original: Loved me above the measure of a father;   Nay, godded me, indeed.
translation: loved me more than a father; no, he loved me as a god, even.

original: Their latest refuge   Was to send him;
translation: It was Rome's last hope to send him,

original: for whose old love I have,   Though I show'd sourly to him, once more offer'd   The first conditions, which they did refuse   And cannot now accept;
translation: and because I have such deep love for him—even though I conveyed that poorly to him—I've again offered the original conditions of surrender, which they had refused before and can't accept now.

original: to grace him only   That thought he could do more, a very little   I have yielded to:
translation: Out of respect for Menenius, who thought he could do more, I have yielded very little.

original: fresh embassies and suits,   Nor from the state nor private friends, hereafter   Will I lend ear to.
translation: No new negotiators or beggars, neither from the state nor private friends, will I listen to from now on.

original: Ha! what shout is this?   Shall I be tempted to infringe my vow   In the same time 'tis made? I will not.
translation: Huh? What are these shouts about?  [Shouting from offstage]  Will I be tempted to take back my vow the moment it's made? I will not.

original: My wife comes foremost; then the honour'd mould   Wherein this trunk was framed, and in her hand   The grandchild to her blood.
translation: My wife comes at the head of the group, and after her  the honored mold in which my body was created , and holding her hand, her grandchild.

original: But, out, affection!   All bond and privilege of nature, break!   Let it be virtuous to be obstinate.
translation: But I will not feel affection! I must break every familial bond and instinct! Let it be virtuous to be coldhearted.

original: What is that curt'sy worth? or those doves' eyes,   Which can make gods forsworn? I melt, and am not   Of stronger earth than others.
translation: What is that curtsy worth, or those dove's eyes, which would make a god break his promise? I melt, and am not made of stronger earth than other men.

original: My mother bows;   As if Olympus to a molehill should   In supplication nod:
translation: My mother bows. As if  Mount Olympus  should bow to a molehill!

original: and my young boy   Hath an aspect of intercession, which   Great nature cries 'Deny not.'
translation: My young boy has a face which seems to cry out "Don't send us away."

original: let the Volsces   Plough Rome and harrow Italy: I'll never   Be such a gosling to obey instinct,
translation: And yet let the Volsces plow Rome to the ground and destroy all of Italy. I will not be such a child to bend to instinct,

original: but stand,   As if a man were author of himself   And knew no other kin.
translation: but will stand strong, as if a man created himself wholly and had no family.

original: My lord and husband!
translation: My lord and husband!

original: These eyes are not the same I wore in Rome.
translation: These eyes are not the same I had when I was in Rome.

original: The sorrow that delivers us thus changed Makes you think so.
translation: It is the tragedy that brings us here which makes you think so.

original: Like a dull actor now,   I have forgot my part, and I am out,   Even to a full disgrace.
translation: [Breaking down]  Like a bad actor, I have forgotten my part, and I am out of character, to my complete disgrace.

original: Best of my flesh,   Forgive my tyranny; but do not say   For that 'Forgive our Romans.'
translation: Beloved, please forgive my tyranny, but do not ask me to "Forgive our Romans."

original: O, a kiss   Long as my exile, sweet as my revenge!   Now, by the jealous queen of heaven, that kiss   I carried from thee, dear;
translation: You kissed me as I was exiled, and by the jealous queen of heaven, I have carried it with me ever since

original: and my true lip   Hath virgin'd it e'er since.
translation: and touched my lips to no one else.

original: You gods! I prate,   And the most noble mother of the world   Leave unsaluted: sink, my knee, i' the earth;
translation: You gods! I'm rambling, and leave the most noble mother of the world ungreeted. My knees sink into the earth.  [He kneels]

original: O, stand up blest!   Whilst, with no softer cushion than the flint,   I kneel before thee;
translation: Oh, stand up you foolish man, while I, with no cushion but the stony ground, kneel before you,

original: and unproperly   Show duty, as mistaken all this while   Between the child and parent.
translation: and improperly show deference, as though you were the parent and I the child.

original: What is this?   Your knees to me? to your corrected son?
translation: What is this? You would kneel to me, to your son?

original: Then let the pebbles on the hungry beach   Fillip the stars;
translation: Then let the world reverse itself— let pebbles on the beach fill up the stars,

original: then let the mutinous winds   Strike the proud cedars 'gainst the fiery sun;
translation: and let the mutinous winds blow trees into the the fiery sun,

original: Murdering impossibility, to make   What cannot be, slight work.
translation: doing the impossible and making what cannot be suddenly easy.

original: Thou art my warrior; I holp to frame thee. Do you know this lady?
translation: You are my warrior. I helped to create you.  Do you know this lady?

original: The noble sister of Publicola,   The moon of Rome,
translation: The noble sister of Publicola, the pride of Roma,

original: chaste as the icicle   That's curdied by the frost from purest snow   And hangs on Dian's temple: dear Valeria!
translation: chaste as the icicle that's formed by frost from purest snow and hangs on the temple of  Diana : dear Valeria!

original: This is a poor epitome of yours, Which by the interpretation of full time May show like all yourself.
translation: This is a weaker version of you, which, in time, may come to be much like you.

original: The god of soldiers,   With the consent of supreme Jove, inform   Thy thoughts with nobleness;
translation: The god of soldiers, with the consent of the supreme God, keep my thoughts noble,

original: that thou mayst prove   To shame unvulnerable,
translation: so that I may be invulnerable to shame.

original: and stick i' the wars   Like a great sea-mark, standing every flaw,   And saving those that eye thee!
translation: Gods, keep my resolve in this war like a great  sea-mark,  standing strong against every flaw and saving those who can see you!

original: Your knee, sirrah.
translation: Kneel, boy.

original: That's my brave boy!
translation: That's my brave boy!

original: Even he, your wife, this lady, and myself, Are suitors to you.
translation: Even he, your wife, this lady, and myself, have come to beg your mercy.

original: I beseech you, peace:
translation: Please, no more; don't ask.

original: Or, if you'ld ask, remember this before:
translation: Or, if you ask, remember this:

original: The thing I have forsworn to grant may never   Be held by you denials.
translation: I have sworn not to do anything but deny you.

original: Do not bid me   Dismiss my soldiers, or capitulate   Again with Rome's mechanics:
translation: Do not ask me to dismiss my soldiers, or to submit again to Rome's laws.

original: tell me not   Wherein I seem unnatural:
translation: Do not tell me that I have gone mad;

original: desire not   To ally my rages and revenges with   Your colder reasons.
translation: do not ask me to exchange my rage and revenge with your cold reason.

original: O, no more, no more!
translation: Oh, no more, no more!

original: You have said you will not grant us any thing;
translation: You have said you will not grant us anything,

original: For we have nothing else to ask, but that   Which you deny already:
translation: for we have nothing else to ask other than what you have already denied.

original: yet we will ask;   That, if you fail in our request, the blame   May hang upon your hardness:
translation: Yet we will ask anyway, so that if you do not say yes, the blame may be solely on you.

original: therefore hear us.
translation: Therefore, hear us.

original: Aufidius, and you Volsces, mark; for we'll Hear nought from Rome in private. Your request?
translation: Aufidius, and you Volsces, listen, because I don't want to be accused of hearing anything from Rome in private.  Your request?

original: Should we be silent and not speak, our raiment   And state of bodies would bewray what life   We have led since thy exile.
translation: If we stayed silent and did not speak, our clothes and bodies alone should tell you how we've lived since your exile.

original: Think with thyself   How more unfortunate than all living women   Are we come hither:
translation: Just consider: we are the most miserable women alive,

original: since that thy sight,   which should   Make our eyes flow with joy, hearts dance   with comforts,
translation: since now that we have finally seen you again, that sight—which should make our eyes flow with joy and our hearts dance—

original: Constrains them weep and shake with fear and sorrow;
translation: instead makes us weep and shake with fear and sorrow.

original: Making the mother, wife and child to see   The son, the husband and the father tearing   His country's bowels out.
translation: We, the mother, wife, and child are forced to see the son, husband, and the father tearing the guts out of his country.

original: And to poor we   Thine enmity's most capital: thou barr'st us   Our prayers to the gods,   which is a comfort   That all but we enjoy;
translation: And to us, your hatred is even worse. You prevent us even from praying to the gods,  something which even the most wretched can do—

original: for how can we,   Alas, how can we for our country pray.   Whereto we are bound, together with thy victory,   Whereto we are bound?   alack, or we must lose   The country, our dear nurse, or else thy person,   Our comfort in the country.
translation: for how could we pray for our country, if it is to pray against you, or for you, if against our country?

original: We must find   An evident calamity, though we had   Our wish, which side should win:
translation: We see a disaster in either case:

original: for either thou   Must, as a foreign recreant, be led   With manacles thorough our streets,
translation: either you must, as a foreign monster, be led in chains through our streets,

original: or else   triumphantly tread on thy country's ruin,   And bear the palm for having bravely shed   Thy wife and children's blood.
translation: or else you will triumphantly walk through the ruins of Rome, and wear garlands for having bravely killed your wife and child.

original: For myself, son,   I purpose not to wait on fortune till   These wars determine:
translation: As for me, son, I cannot wait to see what happens.

original: if I cannot persuade thee   Rather to show a noble grace to both parts   Than seek the end of one,
translation: If I cannot persuade you to be merciful to both yourself and Rome rather than seek to destroy one,

original: thou shalt no sooner   March to assault thy country than to tread—   Trust to't, thou shalt not—   on thy mother's womb,   That brought thee to this world.
translation: you will no sooner march to attack your country than you will walk over my dead body, the very womb that brought you into this world.

original: Ay, and mine, That brought you forth this boy, to keep your name Living to time.
translation: Indeed, and mine too, the body that brought you this boy, your son, who bears your name.

original: A' shall not tread on me; I'll run away till I am bigger, but then I'll fight.
translation: You will not tread on me. I'll run away till I am bigger, but then I'll fight you.
