original: Not of a woman's tenderness to be, Requires nor child nor woman's face to see. I have sat too long.
translation: If I want to avoid being tender, I cannot see the face of a child or a woman. I have sat  and listened too long.

original: Nay, go not from us thus.
translation: No, don't go leave us like that.

original: If it were so that our request did tend   To save the Romans, thereby to destroy   The Volsces whom you serve,
translation: Were it true that we were asking you to save the Romans by destroying the Volsces,

original: you might condemn us,   As poisonous of your honour: no; our suit   Is that you reconcile them:
translation: then you might rightly condemn us for poisoning your honor, but that's not what we're asking. No, we're asking that you make a peace between them.

original: while the Volsces   May say 'This mercy we have show'd;' the Romans,   'This we received;'
translation: Then, the Volsces may say "we've shown this mercy," and the Romans may say "this mercy we have received,"

original: and each in either side   Give the all-hail to thee and cry 'Be blest   For making up this peace!'
translation: and both sides will cry out praise to you and say: "Bless you for bringing us peace!"

original: Thou know'st, great son,   The end of war's uncertain, but this certain,
translation: You know, great son, that war's outcome is uncertain, but we know this much—

original: That, if thou conquer Rome, the benefit   Which thou shalt thereby reap is such a name,   Whose repetition will be dogg'd with curses;   Whose chronicle thus writ:
translation: if you conquer Rome, all you'll get out of it will be  a name so cursed that in the history books  they'll write:

original: 'The man was noble,   But with his last attempt he wiped it out;
translation: "The man  was   noble, but with his last acts undid all his nobility;

original: Destroy'd his country, and his name remains   To the ensuing age abhorr'd.' Speak to me, son:
translation: he destroyed his own country, and his name will be hated forever." Speak to me, son.

original: Thou hast affected the fine strains of honour,   To imitate the graces of the gods;
translation: You have been at other times so honorable you seemed to imitate the gods,

original: To tear with thunder the wide cheeks o' the air,   And yet to charge thy sulphur with a bolt   That should but rive an oak. Why dost not speak?
translation: to tear open the air with thunder, and to work yourself up like lightning that would split an oak tree. Why won't you speak?

original: Think'st thou it honourable for a noble man   Still to remember wrongs?
translation: Do you think it's honorable for a noble man to hold grudges?

original: Daughter, speak you:   He cares not for your weeping.
translation: [To VIRGILIA]  Daughter, you speak— he doesn't care about your weeping.

original: Speak thou, boy:   Perhaps thy childishness will move him more   Than can our reasons.
translation: [To young MARCIUS]  You speak, boy. Perhaps your youthful voice will move him more than our reasoning.

original: There's no man in the world   More bound to 's mother; yet here he lets me prate   Like one i' the stocks.
translation: There's no man in the world more bound to his mother, but here he lets me ramble on like  a man in the stocks .

original: Thou hast never in thy life   Show'd thy dear mother any courtesy,
translation: You have never in your life shown your dear mother any courtesy,

original: When she, poor hen, fond of no second brood,   Has cluck'd thee to the wars and safely home,   Loaden with honour.
translation: when she, poor hen, fond of  no second brood , has clucked you to the wars and safely home, covered in medals.

original: Say my request's unjust,   And spurn me back: but if it be not so,   Thou art not honest; and the gods will plague thee,
translation: Say that what I'm asking is unjust, and throw me out. But if it is not unjust, than you're not being fair, and the gods will plague you

original: That thou restrain'st from me the duty which   To a mother's part belongs.
translation: for preventing me from doing the duty which a mother should.

original: He turns away:   Down, ladies; let us shame him with our knees.   To his surname Coriolanus 'longs more pride   Than pity to our prayers.
translation: He turns away. Down, ladies, let us shame him on our knees. He has more pride in that name, Coriolanus, than he has pity for our prayers.

original: Down: an end;   This is the last: so we will home to Rome,   And die among our neighbours.
translation: Down, and that's it.  [All kneel]  This is all we can do. Lets go home to Rome and die among our neighbors.

original: Nay, behold 's:   This boy, that cannot tell what he would have   But kneels and holds up bands for fellowship,
translation: No, look at this: this boy who barely knows what we are doing, kneeling and holds up his hands for friendship,

original: Does reason our petition with more strength   Than thou hast to deny 't. Come, let us go:
translation: makes our case with more strength than you can have to deny it. Come, let us go.

original: This fellow had a Volscian to his mother;   His wife is in Corioli and his child   Like him by chance.
translation: This fellow had a Volscian as his mother, his wife is in Corioli and this child just looks like him by chance.

original: Yet give us our dispatch:   I am hush'd until our city be a-fire,   And then I'll speak a little.
translation: We'll go like this— I will not speak until our city is burning, and then I'll speak a little.

original: O mother, mother!   What have you done?
translation: Oh, mother, mother! What have you done?

original: Behold, the heavens do ope,   The gods look down, and this unnatural scene   They laugh at.
translation: Behold, the heavens open up, the gods look down and laugh at this mad scene.

original: O my mother, mother! O!   You have won a happy victory to Rome;   But, for your son,—
translation: Oh my mother, mother! Oh! You have won a fortunate victory for Rome, but for your son—

original: believe it, O, believe it,   Most dangerously you have with him prevail'd,   If not most mortal to him.
translation: believe me, Oh, believe me— you have very dangerously convinced him, if not sentenced him to death.

original: But, let it come.   Aufidius, though I cannot make true wars,   I'll frame convenient peace.
translation: But, let death come. Aufidius, though I cannot make an all out war, I'll bring us a convenient peace.

original: Now, good Aufidius,   Were you in my stead, would you have heard   A mother less? or granted less, Aufidius?
translation: Now, good Aufidius, if you were in my place, would you have listened to your mother less? Or given less, Aufidius?

original: I was moved withal.
translation: I was also moved by it.

original: I dare be sworn you were:   And, sir, it is no little thing to make   Mine eyes to sweat compassion.
translation: I'd risk swearing that you were. And sir, it is no little thing to make  my eyes sweat with compassion.

original: But, good sir,   What peace you'll make, advise me: for my part,   I'll not to Rome, I'll back with you;
translation: But, good sir, tell me what peace terms you'll agree to. As for me, I'll not return to Rome, but will go back with you,

original: and pray you,   Stand to me in this cause. O mother! wife!
translation: so please, support me in making peace. Oh, mother! Wife!

original: I am glad thou hast set thy mercy and   thy honour   At difference in thee:
translation: I am glad your mercy and honor are working against each other;

original: out of that I'll work   Myself a former fortune.
translation: I'll make a fortune out of this situation.

original: Ay, by and by;   But we will drink together; and you shall bear   A better witness back than words,
translation: Yes, this is what must be. But we'll drink together first, and you'll take back a treaty to Rome,

original: which we,   On like conditions, will have counter-seal'd.
translation: which we will agree to.

original: Come, enter with us. Ladies, you deserve   To have a temple built you:
translation: Come along with us.  Ladies, you deserve to have a temple built to you.

original: all the swords   In Italy, and her confederate arms,   Could not have made this peace.
translation: All the swords in Italy, and all the other weapons too, could not have brought this peace.

original: See you yond coign o' the Capitol, yond corner-stone?
translation: Do you see that corner of the Capitol, that cornerstone?

original: Why, what of that?
translation: Why, what about it?

original: If it be possible for you to displace it with your   little finger, there is some hope the ladies of   Rome,
translation: If you can move that with your little finger, there is some hope the ladies of Rome,

original: especially his mother, may prevail with him.
translation: especially his mother, will convince Coriolanus not to attack.

original: But I say there is no hope in't: our throats are   sentenced and stay upon execution.
translation: But I say there's really no hope; we have been sentenced to death and are just waiting for the execution.

original: Is't possible that so short a time can alter the condition of a man!
translation: Is it possible that a man can change so much in so little time?

original: There is differency between a grub and a butterfly;   yet your butterfly was a grub.
translation: There is a difference between a caterpillar and a butterfly, but butterflies do start out as caterpillars.

original: This Marcius is grown   from man to dragon: he has wings; he's more than a   creeping thing.
translation: Marcius has grown from man to dragon: he has wings, he is more than  a creeping thing.

original: He loved his mother dearly.
translation: He loved his mother dearly.

original: So did he me: and he no more remembers his mother   now than an eight-year-old horse.
translation: He loved me dearly, too. He no more remembers his mother now than an old horse does.

original: The tartness   of his face sours ripe grapes: when he walks, he   moves like an engine, and the ground shrinks before   his treading:
translation: The fury of his face turns grapes sour. When he walks, he moves like a great machine, and the ground cowers before him.

original: he is able to pierce a corslet with   his eye; talks like a knell, and his hum is a   battery.
translation: He is able to pierce armor with his eyes; his voice is like a funeral bell and his very hum is an assault.

original: He sits in his state, as a thing made for   Alexander.
translation: He sits on his throne like a statue of  Alexander.

original: What he bids be done is finished with   his bidding. He wants nothing of a god but eternity   and a heaven to throne in.
translation: What he orders to be done is done by very order itself. He is a god, except that he lacks eternity and a heaven in which to rule.

original: Yes, mercy, if you report him truly.
translation: Yes, god have mercy if you are describing him truthfully.

original: I paint him in the character.
translation: I paint him just as he is.

original: Mark what mercy his   mother shall bring from him: there is no more mercy   in him than there is milk in a male tiger;
translation: Watch what mercy his mother will bring from him. There is no more mercy in him than there is milk in a male tiger.

original: that   shall our poor city find: and all this is long of   you.
translation: T hat's what our poor city will learn. And all of this is your fault.

original: The gods be good unto us!
translation: The gods be good to us!

original: No, in such a case the gods will not be good unto us. When we banished him, we respected not them; and, he returning to break our necks, they respect not  us.
translation: No, in this case the gods will not be good to us. When we banished him, we did not respect the gods, and when he returns to break our necks, the gods will not respect us.

original: Sir, if you'ld save your life, fly to your house:
translation: [To SICINIUS]  Sir, if you value your life, flee to your house.

original: The plebeians have got your fellow-tribune   And hale him up and down,
translation: The commoners have got the other tribune and are running him through the streets,

original: all swearing, if   The Roman ladies bring not comfort home,   They'll give him death by inches.
translation: all swearing that if the Roman ladies do not bring good news back, they will torture him to death.

original: What's the news?
translation: What's the news?

original: Good news, good news; the ladies have prevail'd,
translation: Good news, good news! The ladies have succeeded!

original: The Volscians are dislodged, and Marcius gone:
translation: The Volscians are packing up their camp, and Marcius has gone.

original: A merrier day did never yet greet Rome,   No, not the expulsion of the Tarquins.
translation: No happier day has ever dawned on Rome, no, not even the retreat of  the Tarquins.

original: Friend, Art thou certain this is true? is it most certain?
translation: Friend, are you certain this is true? Are you absolutely certain?

original: As certain as I know the sun is fire:
translation: As certain as I know the sun is fire.

original: Where have you lurk'd, that you make doubt of it?
translation: Where have you been, that you doubt it?

original: Ne'er through an arch so hurried the blown tide,   As the recomforted through the gates. Why, hark you!
translation: News has never flown so quickly through the city as this, straight through the front gates. Why, listen!

original: The trumpets, sackbuts, psalteries and fifes, Tabours and cymbals and the shouting Romans, Make the sun dance. Hark you!
translation: The trumpets and bugles, organs and flutes, tambourines and cymbals and the shouting Romans make the very sun dance. Listen!

original: This is good news:   I will go meet the ladies.
translation: This is good news indeed. I'll go meet the ladies.

original: This Volumnia   Is worth of consuls, senators, patricians,   A city full; of tribunes, such as you,   A sea and land full.
translation: Volumnia is worth a city full of consuls, senators, and nobles. She's worth an ocean and a continent of tribunes such as you.

original: You have pray'd well to-day:   This morning for ten thousand of your throats   I'd not have given a doit.
translation: You have prayed well today. This morning I would not have given a cent to save ten thousand of your throats.

original: Hark, how they joy!
translation: Listen to how joyful they are!

original: First, the gods bless you for your tidings; next, Accept my thankfulness.
translation: First, may the gods bless you for this news. Next, allow me to thank you.

original: Sir, we have all Great cause to give great thanks.
translation: Sir, we all have great reason to give great thanks.

original: They are near the city?
translation: The women are near the city?

original: Almost at point to enter.
translation: They are about to enter it.

original: We will meet them, And help the joy.
translation: We will meet them, and contribute to this joy.

original: Behold our patroness, the life of Rome!
translation: Behold our savior, the lifeblood of Rome!

original: Call all your tribes together, praise the gods,   And make triumphant fires; strew flowers before them:
translation: Call all the people together, praise the gods, and light all the city's ceremonial flames. Throw flowers in the streets,

original: Unshout the noise that banish'd Marcius,   Repeal him with the welcome of his mother;
translation: choke down the words that banished Marcius and replace them with the welcome of his mother.

original: Cry 'Welcome, ladies, welcome!'
translation: Cry, "Welcome, ladies, welcome!"

original: Welcome, ladies, Welcome!
translation: Welcome, ladies, welcome!

original: Go tell the lords o' the city I am here:
translation: Go tell the lords of the city that I am here.

original: Deliver them this paper: having read it,   Bid them repair to the market place;
translation: Deliver them this letter. Once they have read it, tell them to come to the market,

original: where I,   Even in theirs and in the commons' ears,   Will vouch the truth of it.
translation: where I will declare the truth of what it says to the ears of the public.

original: Him I accuse   The city ports by this hath enter'd   a   nd   Intends to appear before the people,   hoping   To purge himself with words: dispatch.
translation: Coriolanus, who I accuse in the letter, has entered the city  and intends to appear before the people  to pardon himself with words.

original: Most welcome!
translation: You're very welcome here!

original: How is it with our general?
translation: How's it going with our general?

original: Even so As with a man by his own alms empoison'd, And with his charity slain.
translation: He has poisoned himself with his own forgiveness, killed himself with his own charity.

original: Most noble sir,   If you do hold the same intent wherein   You wish'd us parties,
translation: Most noble sir, if you still want us to be your allies,

original: we'll deliver you   Of your great danger.
translation: we'll help save you from great danger.

original: Sir, I cannot tell: We must proceed as we do find the people.
translation: Sir, I don't know whether there will be danger. We will have to take things as they come and see how the people feel.

original: The people will remain uncertain whilst 'Twixt you there's difference; but the fall of either Makes the survivor heir of all.
translation: The people will be uncertain how to feel while you and Coriolanus are opposed. But if either one of you falls, the survivor will win everything.

original: I know it;   And my pretext to strike at him admits   A good construction.
translation: I know, and I have a good reason to strike at him.

original: I raised him, and I pawn'd   Mine honour for his truth:
translation: I raised him up among the Volscians, and gave up my honor for his sake.

original: who being so heighten'd,   He water'd his new plants with dews of flattery,   Seducing so my friends;
translation: Once he had power, he used flattery to win all my former friends to his side,

original: and, to this end,   He bow'd his nature, never known before   But to be rough, unswayable and free.
translation: and in this way, he made himself—always known to be rough— even more stubbornly powerful.

original: Sir, his stoutness When he did stand for consul, which he lost By lack of stooping,—
translation: Sir, his stubbornness was what cost him the Roman consulship, which he lost because he could not bow—

original: That I would have spoke of:   Being banish'd for't, he came unto my hearth;   Presented to my knife his throat:
translation: I would bring that up. He was banished for stubbornness, came to my home, and put my knife at his throat.

original: I took him;   Made him joint-servant with me; gave him way   In all his own desires;
translation: I took him in, made him equal to me, let him do whatever he desired—

original: nay, let him choose   Out of my files, his projects to accomplish,   My best and freshest men;
translation: nay, let him choose from my own plans which projects to work on with my best and freshest men.

original: served his designments   In mine own person; holp to reap the fame   Which he did end all his;
translation: I worked for him myself, and helped him to earn the fame which in the end all came to him,

original: and took some pride   To do myself this wrong: till, at the last,   I seem'd his follower, not partner,
translation: and even was proud of that, until, in the end, I was his follower and not his partner.

original: and   He waged me with his countenance, as if   I had been mercenary.
translation: e looked at me and treated me like I was just a soldier for hire.

original: So he did, my lord:   The army marvell'd at it, and, in the last,   When he had carried Rome
translation: Indeed, my lord. The army could barely believe it, and in the end, when he had conquered everything but Rome,

original: and that we look'd   For no less spoil than glory,—
translation: and we were looking forward to treasures and glory—

original: There was it:   For which my sinews shall be stretch'd upon him.
translation: That was it! For giving it up, all my muscles will strain upon him.

original: At a few drops of women's rheum, which are   As cheap as lies, he sold the blood and labour   Of our great action:
translation: For the price of a few women's tears, which are as cheap as lies, he sold the blood and labor of our great war.

original: therefore shall he die,   And I'll renew me in his fall. But, hark!
translation: Therefore, he shall die, and I'll rise as he falls. But listen!

original: Your native town you enter'd like a post, And had no welcomes home: but he returns, Splitting the air with noise.
translation: You came back to your hometown like a lowly messenger, and had no welcomes home. But he returns, and the air splits with noise.

original: And patient fools, Whose children he hath slain, their base throats tear With giving him glory.
translation: And these fools, whose children he has killed, will tear their throats apart cheering at his glory.

original: Therefore, at your vantage,   Ere he express himself, or move the people   With what he would say,
translation: Therefore, when you are ready, before he has a chance to speak or bring the people to his side,

original: let him feel your sword,   Which we will second.
translation: let him feel your sword, and we will help.

original: When he lies along,   After your way his tale pronounced shall bury   His reasons with his body.
translation: When he lies dead, you can tell the story and his reasons will be buried with his body.

original: Say no more: Here come the lords.
translation: Say no more: here come the lords.

original: You are most welcome home.
translation: Welcome home!

original: I have not deserved it. But, worthy lords, have you with heed perused What I have written to you?
translation: I have not deserved it. But, worthy lords, have you looked at what I have written to you?

original: We have.
translation: We have.

original: And grieve to hear't.   What faults he made before the last, I think   Might have found easy fines:
translation: And we grieve to hear it. Were it not for his final mistake, I think his other errors would have been forgivable.

original: but there to end   Where he was to begin and give away   The benefit of our levies,
translation: But to end where he began, and to turn our terms of peace around

original: answering us   With our own charge,   making a treaty where   There was a yielding,—   this admits no excuse.
translation: and force us into our own treaty, where it is as though he surrendered— there can be no excuse for this.

original: He approaches: you shall hear him.
translation: He's coming. You'll hear what he has to say.

original: Hail, lords! I am return'd your soldier,   No more infected with my country's love   Than when I parted hence,
translation: Honorable lords! I have returned again as your soldier, no more infected with my country's love than when I left,

original: but still subsisting   Under your great command.
translation: but still under your great command.

original: You are to know   That prosperously I have attempted and   With bloody passage led your wars even to   The gates of Rome.
translation: You must know that I successfully led the army in your wars to the very gates of Rome.

original: Our spoils we have brought home   Do more than counterpoise a full third part   The charges of the action.
translation: The spoils we brought home will pay for more than a third of the entire war.

original: We have made peace   With no less honour to the Antiates   Than shame to the Romans:
translation: We have made peace with great honor to this city and great shame for the Romans.

original: and we here deliver,   Subscribed by the consuls and patricians,   Together with the seal o' the senate, what   We have compounded on.
translation: [Holding a paper]  Here I deliver the treaty, agreed to by the consuls and the nobles and signed by the senate.

original: Read it not, noble lords; But tell the traitor, in the high'st degree He hath abused your powers.
translation: Do not read it, noble lords, but tell the traitor how he has committed high treason and abused your powers.

original: Traitor! how now!
translation: Traitor? What's going on?

original: Ay, traitor, Marcius!
translation: Yes, traitor, Marcius!

original: Marcius!
translation: Marcius?

original: Ay, Marcius, Caius Marcius: dost thou think   I'll grace thee with that robbery, thy stol'n name   Coriolanus in Corioli?
translation: Yes, Marcius! Caius Marcius. Do you think I'll honor you with that robbery, that name you stole from Corioli—Coriolanus?

original: You lords and heads o' the state, perfidiously   He has betray'd your business, and given up,
translation: You lords and heads of state, how disloyally he has betrayed us all, and given up

original: For certain drops of salt, your city Rome,   I say 'your city,' to his wife and mother;
translation: your city Rome —I say "your city"— for a few  drops of salt  from wife and mother.

original: Breaking his oath and resolution like   A twist of rotten silk,   never admitting   Counsel o' the war,
translation: He has broken his oath like he would tear a piece of rotten silk;

original: but at his nurse's tears   He whined and roar'd away your victory,
translation: at his nurse's tears he, like a complaining child, begged and sobbed away your victory.

original: That pages blush'd at him and men of heart   Look'd wondering each at other.
translation: Servants blushed to see it, and brave men looked at each other in shock.

original: Hear'st thou, Mars?
translation: Do you hear this, Mars?

original: Name not the god, thou boy of tears!
translation: Don't name the god of war, you tearful boy!

original: Ha!
translation: Ha!

original: No more.
translation: That's enough.

original: Measureless liar, thou hast made my heart   Too great for what contains it. Boy! O slave!
translation: You impossible liar, you have made my heart break even as it swells in fury. Boy! Oh, you slave.

original: Pardon me, lords, 'tis the first time that ever   I was forced to scold.
translation: Pardon me, lords, this is the first time I was ever forced to scold a man.

original: Your judgments, my grave lords,   Must give this cur the lie:   and his own notion—   Who wears my stripes impress'd upon him;
translation: Grave lords, you must use your judgements and see that this dog is lying.   He wears honors that I have earned for him,

original: that   Must bear my beating to his grave—
translation: and must remember to his grave all the times I beat him;

original: shall join   To thrust the lie unto him.
translation: these show he is lying.

original: Peace, both, and hear me speak.
translation: Peace, both of you, and listen to me.

original: Cut me to pieces, Volsces; men and lads,   Stain all your edges on me.
translation: Cut me to pieces Volsces, men and lads,  stain all your edges on me .

original: Boy! false hound!   If you have writ your annals true, 'tis there,   That, like an eagle in a dove-cote,
translation: Boy! You false hound! If you have written your histories truthfully, you'll find there, that like an eagle in a dove's nest,

original: I   Flutter'd your Volscians in Corioli:   Alone I did it. Boy!
translation: I  fluttered  your Volscians in Corioli. Alone!  I  did it! Boy!

original: Why, noble lords,   Will you be put in mind of his blind fortune,   Which was your shame,
translation: Why, noble lords, will you be brought to shame

original: by this unholy braggart,   'Fore your own eyes and ears?
translation: by this damned bragger who has won fortune by killing our people?

original: Let him die for't.
translation: Let him die for it.

original: 'Tear him to pieces.' 'Do it presently.' 'He kill'd my son.' 'My daughter.' 'He killed my cousin Marcus.' 'He killed my father.'
translation: Tear him to pieces! Do it now! He killed my son! He killed my daughter! He killed my cousin Marcus! He killed my father!

original: Peace, ho! no outrage: peace!
translation: Peace, everyone! No outrage, peace!

original: The man is noble and his fame folds-in   This orb o' the earth.
translation: This man is noble and he is famous around the world.

original: His last offences to us   Shall have judicious hearing. Stand, Aufidius,   And trouble not the peace.
translation: His crimes against us will be heard in a military trial. Stand aside, Aufidius, and don't trouble the peace.

original: O that I had him, With six Aufidiuses, or more, his tribe, To use my lawful sword!
translation: Oh that I had him, and six Aufidiuses more, on which to use my sword!

original: Insolent villain!
translation: You disrespectful villain!

original: Kill, kill, kill, kill, kill him!
translation: Kill, kill, kill, kill, kill him!

original: Hold, hold, hold, hold!
translation: Stop, stop, stop, stop!

original: My noble masters, hear me speak.
translation: My noble masters, hear me speak.

original: O Tullus,—
translation: Oh, Tullus—

original: Thou hast done a deed whereat valour will weep.
translation: You have done a deed at which all bravery weeps.

original: Tread not upon him. Masters all, be quiet; Put up your swords.
translation: Do not stand over him. Sirs, be quiet. Sheath your swords.

original: My lords, when you shall know—   as in this rage,   Provoked by him, you cannot—   the great danger   Which this man's life did owe you,
translation: My lords, when you are more aware of the great danger this man's life posed to you,

original: you'll rejoice   That he is thus cut off.
translation: you'll be glad he's dead.

original: Please it your honours   To call me to your senate,
translation: If you want to call me to the senate,

original: I'll deliver   Myself your loyal servant, or endure   Your heaviest censure.
translation: I'll go as your loyal servant, and there take your most serious condemnations.

original: Bear from hence his body; And mourn you for him: let him be regarded As the most noble corse that ever herald Did follow to his urn.
translation: Carry his body out of here, and mourn for him. Let him be regarded as the most noble corpse that bards will ever sing about.

original: His own impatience Takes from Aufidius a great part of blame. Let's make the best of it.
translation: Coriolanus did provoke Aufidius, and so takes a great part of the blame. Let's make the best of it.

original: My rage is gone;   And I am struck with sorrow. Take him up.
translation: Suddenly shocked by what he has done, and crying]  My rage is gone, and I am struck with sorrow. Pick him up.

original: Help, three o' the chiefest soldiers; I'll be one.
translation: Help, three of the strongest soldiers; I'll be one of the men who carries him.

original: Beat thou the drum, that it speak mournfully:   Trail your steel pikes.
translation: Beat the drum in a mournful way. Drag your pikes in the ground.

original: Though in this city he   Hath widow'd and unchilded many a one,   Which to this hour bewail the injury,
translation: Though he has made many widows in this city, and though many mothers still wail at their children which he killed,

original: Yet he shall have a noble memory. Assist.
translation: he will be noble in our memories. Assist me.

original: You do not meet a man but frowns:
translation: Every man you meet these days is frowning.

original: our bloods   No more obey the heavens than our courtiers   Still seem as does the king.
translation: Our bodies are in agreement with the  planetary influences  just as the courtiers's moods seem to reflect the king's.

original: But what's the matter?
translation: What's wrong?

original: His daughter, and the heir of's kingdom, whom   He purposed to his wife's sole son—a widow   That late he married—hath referr'd herself   Unto a poor but worthy gentleman:
translation: The king wanted his daughter, the only heir to his kingdom, to marry his wife's only son. By his wife, I mean a widow he recently married. But the daughter decided to marry a poor but honest man instead.

original: she's wedded;   Her husband banish'd; she imprison'd: all   Is outward sorrow; though I think the king   Be touch'd at very heart.
translation: She's married, her husband is banished, she's imprisoned: everything seems terrible. I think the king is overwhelmed with sadness.

original: None but the king?
translation: Only the king?

original: He that hath lost her too; so is the queen,   That most desired the match;
translation: So is the man who was supposed to marry her. So is the queen, who really wanted the marriage to happen.

original: but not a courtier,   Although they wear their faces to the bent   Of the king's look's, hath a heart that is not   Glad at the thing they scowl at.
translation: But all the courtiers, although they frown like the king, are secretly happy about the thing they frown at.

original: And why so?
translation: Why?

original: He that hath miss'd the princess is a thing   Too bad for bad report:
translation: The man who lost the princess is so bad it's impossible to describe him accurately.

original: and he that hath her—   I mean, that married her, alack, good man!   And therefore banish'd—is a creature such   As, to seek through the regions of the earth   For one his like, there would be something failing   In him that should compare.
translation: And the man who has her—I mean the man who married her, oh, poor good man!—and is banished because of this, is a man so good that even if you searched through the whole world for his equal, anyone you found to compare with him would still be a little less good.

original: I do not think   So fair an outward and such stuff within   Endows a man but he.
translation: I don't think any man is as attractive inside and out as he is.

original: You speak him far.
translation: You speak highly of him.

original: I do extend him, sir, within himself, Crush him together rather than unfold His measure duly.
What's his name and birth?
translation: What's his name and family?

original: I cannot delve him to the root:
translation: I don't know his whole family tree.

original: his father   Was call'd Sicilius, who did join his honour   Against the Romans with Cassibelan,   But had his titles by Tenantius whom   He served with glory and admired success,   So gain'd the sur-addition Leonatus;
translation: His father was called Sicilius. Sicilius fought against the Romans with Cassibelan, but was granted nobility under Tenantius. He served Tenantius so gloriously and was so well-known for his achievements that he was given the additional name " Leonatus ."

original: And had, besides this gentleman in question,   Two other sons, who in the wars o' the time   Died with their swords in hand; for which   their father,   Then old and fond of issue, took such sorrow   That he quit being, and his gentle lady,   Big of this gentleman our theme, deceased   As he was born.
translation: He had two other sons, in addition to this man we are talking about, who died fighting in the wars taking place at the time. Their father, who was old and fond of his children, was so sad that he died. His sensitive wife, pregnant with this man who is the theme of our conversation, died as he was born.

original: The king he takes the babe   To his protection, calls him Posthumus Leonatus,   Breeds him and makes him of his bed-chamber,   Puts to him all the learnings that his time   Could make him the receiver of;
translation: The king took the baby under his protection, called him  Posthumus  Leonatus, raised him, and made him one of his closest attendants. He gave him as much of an education as Posthumus could find time for.

original: which he took,   As we do air, fast as 'twas minister'd,   And in's spring became a harvest, lived in court—   Which rare it is to do—most praised, most loved,
translation: Posthumus took to this education as naturally as people take to air, that is, he took it in as quickly as it was given to him. He fulfilled his potential when he grew up, and lived in court—a rare thing to do—greatly praised and greatly loved.

original: A sample to the youngest, to the more mature   A glass that feated them, and to the graver   A child that guided dotards;
translation: He was an example to the youngest, to the full-grown a model for their own behavior, and seemed to  serious  observers like a child leading old people.

original: to his mistress,   For whom he now is banish'd, her own price   Proclaims how she esteem'd him and his virtue;   By her election may be truly read   What kind of man he is.
translation: As for his wife, who is the reason he is now banished, her own  excellence  shows how much she valued him and his virtue. By the fact that she chose him you can clearly understand what kind of man he is.

original: I honour him Even out of your report. But, pray you, tell me, Is she sole child to the king?
translation: I respect him just from hearing you describe him. But tell me, is she the king's only child?

original: His only child.   He had two sons: if this be worth your hearing,   Mark it:
translation: Yes, his only child. He had two sons. Pay attention, if this is something you want to hear about.

original: the eldest of them at three years old,   I' the swathing-clothes the other, from their nursery   Were stol'n, and to this hour no guess in knowledge   Which way they went.
translation: When the older one was three and the other one was still in his  swaddling clothes , they were stolen from their nursery, and to this day no one has any idea where they went.

original: How long is this ago?
translation: How long ago was this?

original: Some twenty years.
translation: About twenty years.

original: That a king's children should be so convey'd, So slackly guarded, and the search so slow, That could not trace them!
translation: How could it be that a king's children were taken in this way? And that they were so badly guarded? And that the search for them was so slow and found no trace of them?

original: Howsoe'er 'tis strange, Or that the negligence may well be laugh'd at, Yet is it true, sir.
translation: However strange it is and however much you could laugh at the incompetence, it's true, sir.

original: I do well believe you.
translation: I believe you.

original: We must forbear: here comes the gentleman, The queen, and princess.
translation: We have to stop talking: here come this man, the queen, and the princess.

original: No, be assured you shall not find me, daughter,   After the slander of most stepmothers,   Evil-eyed unto you:
translation: My daughter, you can be sure I will not scheme against you despite the lies they tell about most stepmothers.

original: you're my prisoner, but   Your gaoler shall deliver you the keys   That lock up your restraint.
translation: You're my prisoner, but although I am your jailer I will give you the keys that keep you locked in here.

original: For you, Posthumus,   So soon as I can win the offended king,   I will be known your advocate:
translation: As for you, Posthumus, as soon as I can calm the upset king, I will speak in your defense.

original: marry, yet   The fire of rage is in him, and 'twere good   You lean'd unto his sentence with what patience   Your wisdom may inform you.
translation: He is still burning with anger, and it would be best for you to go along with his sentence of banishment as patiently as you can manage.

original: Please your highness, I will from hence to-day.
translation: Yes your highness, I will leave today.

original: You know the peril.
translation: You know the risk.

original: I'll fetch a turn about the garden, pitying   The pangs of barr'd affections, though the king   Hath charged you should not speak together.
translation: I'll take a walk around the garden, since I pity how sad you are to be separated from the person you love, even though the king commanded that you should not be allowed to speak to each other.

original: O   Dissembling courtesy! How fine this tyrant   Can tickle where she wounds!
translation: What lying kindness! She's a bully who wounds you then tickles the wound.

original: My dearest husband,   I something fear my father's wrath; but nothing—   Always reserved my holy duty—what   His rage can do on me:
translation: My dear husband, I am sometimes afraid of my father's anger, but not at all—except that it is my god-given duty not to make him angry—what he could do to me because of it.

original: you must be gone;   And I shall here abide the hourly shot   Of angry eyes, not comforted to live,   But that there is this jewel in the world   That I may see again.
translation: You must go, and I will be here suffering from the glares shot at me by angry eyes. I can't bear to stay alive, except that I have this hope, as though it is a precious jewel I own, that I might see you again.

original: My queen! my mistress!   O lady, weep no more, lest I give cause   To be suspected of more tenderness   Than doth become a man.
translation: My queen! My wife! Don't cry any more, or I'll show more weakness than is proper for a man.

original: I will remain   The loyal'st husband that did e'er plight troth:
translation: I will keep being the most loyal husband who ever married anyone.

original: My residence in Rome at one Philario's,   Who to my father was a friend, to me   Known but by letter:
translation: I am staying in Rome at a man called Philario's house. He was a friend of my father's, but I have only communicated with him by writing.

original: thither write, my queen,   And with mine eyes I'll drink the words you send,   Though ink be made of gall.
translation: Send your letters there, my queen, and I'll drink the words you send me with my eyes, even though ink is made of that bitter material,  gall .

original: Be brief, I pray you: If the king come, I shall incur I know not How much of his displeasure.
translation: Keep this short, please. If the king comes, I don't know how angry at me he will be.

original: Yet I'll move him To walk this way: I never do him wrong, But he does buy my injuries, to be friends; Pays dear for my offenses.
translation: I'll convince the king to walk this way. Not only do I do him wrong, but I make him reward me for it: he doesn't know I'm the person who causes the problems he pays me to solve. He's bribing the wrongs I do to him as though they're people and he wants to make them his friends.

original: Should we be taking leave As long a term as yet we have to live, The loathness to depart would grow. Adieu!
translation: Even if we kept saying goodbye for the rest of our lives, it would keep getting harder to leave. Goodbye!

original: Nay, stay a little:   Were you but riding forth to air yourself,   Such parting were too petty.
translation: No, stay a little longer. Even if you were just going on a ride to get some air, that would not be enough of a goodbye.

original: Look here, love;   This diamond was my mother's: take it, heart;   But keep it till you woo another wife,   When Imogen is dead.
translation: Look, my love, this diamond ring was my mother's. Take it, sweetheart. Keep it only until you ask another woman to marry you, when I, Imogen, am dead.

original: How, how! another?   You gentle gods, give me but this I have,
translation: What? Another woman? Kind gods, just give me this one I have,

original: And sear up my embracements from a next   With bonds of death!
translation: and if I try to kiss another one then stop me by burning me to death!

original: Remain, remain thou here
translation: [To the ring]  Stay, stay there

original: While sense can keep it on.
translation: [To Imogen]  while I am alive enough to keep it on.

original: And, sweetest, fairest,   As I my poor self did exchange for you,   To your so infinite loss, so in our trifles   I still win of you:
translation: And, sweetest, most beautiful woman, just as I exchanged myself for you, which was such a bad bargain for you, I'm still getting a better deal in this exchange of presents.

original: for my sake wear this;   It is a manacle of love; I'll place it   Upon this fairest prisoner.
translation: Wear this for my sake. It is a handcuff  of love . I'll put it on this most beautiful of prisoners.

original: O the gods! When shall we see again?
translation: Oh gods! When will we see each other again?

original: Alack, the king!
translation: Oh no, the king!

original: Thou basest thing, avoid! hence, from my sight!
translation: You lowest of things, go away! Go, out of my sight!

original: If after this command thou fraught the court   With thy unworthiness, thou diest: away!
translation: If after being commanded to do this you still weigh the court down with your undeserving presence, you will die. Go away!

original: Thou'rt poison to my blood.
translation: You are like poison in my blood.

original: The gods protect you! And bless the good remainders of the court! I am gone.
translation: May the gods protect you! And bless those who stay in the court! I am gone.

original: There cannot be a pinch in death More sharp than this is.
translation: Death can't hurt worse than this.

original: O disloyal thing, That shouldst repair my youth, thou heap'st A year's age on me.
translation: You disloyal thing, you should make me feel young again but you make me feel a year older.

original: I beseech you, sir,   Harm not yourself with your vexation   I am senseless of your wrath;
translation: Please, sir, don't hurt yourself with your anger.

original: a touch more rare   Subdues all pangs, all fears.
translation: I can't feel it. An even worse pain overcomes all hurts, all fears.

original: Past grace? Obedience?
translation: So you are past showing me grace? Past obedience?

original: Past hope, and in despair; that way, past grace.
That mightst have had the sole son of my queen!
translation: You could have married my wife, the queen's, only son!

original: O blest, that I might not! I chose an eagle, And did avoid a puttock.
Thou took'st a beggar; wouldst have made my throne A seat for baseness.
translation: You married a beggar. You wanted to make my throne a resting-place for lowness.

original: No; I rather added A lustre to it.
translation: No, I made it shine more brightly.

original: O thou vile one!
translation: You disgusting person!

original: Sir,   It is your fault that I have loved Posthumus:
translation: Sir, it's your fault I fell in love with Posthumus.

original: You bred him as my playfellow, and he is   A man worth any woman, overbuys me   Almost the sum he pays.
translation: You brought him up to be my playmate, and he is a man who would deserve any woman. He is worth almost twice as much as me.

original: What, art thou mad?
translation: Are you crazy?

original: Almost, sir: heaven restore me!
translation: Nearly, sir. May the gods make me sane again!

original: Would I were   A neat-herd's daughter, and my Leonatus   Our neighbour shepherd's son!
translation: I wish I were a cattle-herder's daughter and that my Leonatus were the son of another cattle-herder who lived nearby!

original: Thou foolish thing!
translation: You foolish thing!

original: They were again together: you have done Not after our command. Away with her, And pen her up.
translation: They were together again. You didn't obey my order. Take her away and lock her up.

original: Beseech your patience. Peace,   Dear lady daughter, peace!
translation: Please forgive me. Calm down, dear daughter, calm down!

original: Sweet sovereign,   Leave us to ourselves; and make yourself some comfort   Out of your best advice.
translation: Dear king, leave us alone, and comfort yourself as best you can.

original: Nay, let her languish   A drop of blood a day;
translation: No, let her suffer as though she sheds a drop of blood every day

original: and, being aged,   Die of this folly!
translation: and finally, when she is old, let her die of this foolishness!

original: Fie! you must give way.
translation: Come on! You have to give up.

original: Here is your servant. How now, sir! What news?
translation: Here is your servant. Hey, sir, what's the news?

original: My lord your son drew on my master.
translation: Your son drew his sword against my master Posthumus.

original: Ha! No harm, I trust, is done?
translation: What! I hope no one was hurt?

original: There might have been,   But that my master rather play'd than fought   And had no help of anger:
translation: They could have been except that my master didn't fight back, just played around without feeling any anger.

original: they were parted   By gentlemen at hand.
translation: Some gentlemen who were nearby separated them.

original: I am very glad on't.
translation: I am very glad to hear that.

original: Your son's my father's friend; he takes his part.   To draw upon an exile!
translation: Your son is my father's friend. He defends him. Drawing his sword against an exile!

original: O brave sir!   I would they were in Afric both together;   Myself by with a needle, that I might prick   The goer-back.
translation: What a brave man!  I wish they were both in Africa together, and that I were near them with a needle, to poke whichever one retreated from the fight.

original: Why came you from your master?
translation: Why did you leave your master?

original: On his command: he would not suffer me   To bring him to the haven;
translation: On his orders. He wouldn't let me accompany him to the port.

original: left these notes   Of what commands I should be subject to,   When 't pleased you to employ me.
translation: He left these notes about what my duties should be, if you want to employ me.

original: This hath been Your faithful servant: I dare lay mine honour He will remain so.
translation: He has been a faithful servant to you. I bet my honor he will remain faithful.

original: I humbly thank your highness.
translation: Thank you, your highness.

original: Pray, walk awhile.
translation: Please, walk with me awhile.

original: About some half-hour hence,   I pray you, speak with me:
translation: Talk to me in about half an hour.

original: you shall at least   Go see my lord aboard: for this time leave me.
translation: You will at least watch my husband get on his ship. Leave me alone for now.

original: Sir, I would advise you to shift a shirt;
translation: Sir, I recommend that you change your shirt.

original: the   violence of action hath made you reek as a   sacrifice: where air comes out, air comes in:
translation: Your  violent exercise  made you stink like burned meat offered to the gods. Any place air goes out, air also goes in.

original: there's none abroad so wholesome as that you vent.
translation: There's no air anywhere as healthy as the air you give off.

original: If my shirt were bloody, then to shift it. Have I hurt  him?
translation: I would change my shirt if it had blood on it. Have I hurt him?

original: No, 'faith; not so much as his patience.
translation: No, not even his feelings.

original: Hurt him! his body's a passable carcass, if he be not hurt: it is a thoroughfare for steel, if it be not  hurt.
translation: Hurt him! If he's not hurt, he's a dead body. It's like he's a highway for swords, he's been stabbed so many times.

original: His steel was in debt; it went o' the backside the town.
translation: Cloten's sword owed someone money and sneaked around the back part of town instead of passing through it.

original: The villain would not stand me.
translation: That criminal wouldn't stand and fight me.

original: No; but he fled forward still, toward your  face.
translation: No, he kept running away by going forward, towards your face.

original: Stand you! You have land enough of your own: but he added to your having; gave you some ground.
translation: What, stand and fight you? You have plenty of your own land, but he added to what you have: he gave you some ground.

original: As many inches as you have oceans. Puppies!
translation: He gave you as many inches as you have oceans. What a silly young person!

original: I would they had not come between us.
translation: I wish they hadn't separated us.

original: So would I, till you had measured how long a fool you were upon the ground.
translation: So do I, until you fell and measured how long an idiot you were against the ground.

original: And that she should love this fellow and refuse me!
translation: How could she love this man and refuse to marry me?

original: If it be a sin to make a true election, she is damned.
translation: If it's a sin to make a good choice then she's damned.

original: Sir, as I told you always, her beauty and her brain   go not together:
translation: Sir, as I've always told you, her beauty and her brain don't match.

original: she's a good sign, but I have seen   small reflection of her wit.
translation: She looks good, but I've never seen her looks reflected in her thinking.

original: She shines not upon fools, lest the reflection should hurt her.
translation: She doesn't shine on idiots, because their reflection would hurt her.

original: Come, I'll to my chamber. Would there had been some hurt done!
translation: Well, I'll go to my room. I wish someone had gotten hurt!

original: I wish not so; unless it had been the fall of an ass, which is no great hurt.
translation: I don't, unless a donkey was knocked down, which wouldn't be so bad.

original: You'll go with us?
translation: You'll go with me?

original: I'll attend your lordship.
translation: I'll visit you later, my lord.

original: Nay, come, let's go together.
translation: No, come on, let's all go together.

original: Well, my lord.
translation: All right, my lord.

original: I would thou grew'st unto the shores o' the haven,   And question'dst every sail:
translation: I wish you had  stayed longer on shore  and asked every sail of every boat for information about Posthumus.

original: if he should write   And not have it, 'twere a paper lost,   As offer'd mercy is.
translation: If he wrote to me and I didn't get the letter it would be as bad to lose that paper as to miss an offer of mercy from someone who defeated you.

original: What was the last   That he spake to thee?
translation: What was the last thing he said to you?

original: It was his queen, his queen!
translation: It was "my queen, my queen!"

original: Then waved his handkerchief?
translation: Then he waved his handkerchief?

original: And kiss'd it, madam.
translation: And kissed it, ma'am.

original: Senseless Linen! happier therein than I! And that was all?
translation: That unfeeling piece of cloth was luckier than I am! And that was all?

original: No, madam; for so long   As he could make me with this eye or ear   Distinguish him from others, he did keep   The deck, with glove, or hat, or handkerchief,
translation: No, ma'am. For as long as I could tell him apart from the others by sight or sound, he stayed on deck waving his glove, hat, or handkerchief.

original: Still waving, as the fits and stirs of 's mind   Could best express how slow his soul sail'd on,   How swift his ship.
translation: He kept waving, as though expressing his restless mind through this action could show how slowly his soul sailed on, and how quickly his ship did.

original: Thou shouldst have made him As little as a crow, or less, ere left To after-eye him.
translation: You should have kept watching him until he seemed as small as a crow, or smaller.

original: Madam, so I did.
translation: I did, ma'am.

original: I would have broke mine eye-strings; crack'd them, but   To look upon him, till the diminution   Of space had pointed him sharp as my needle,
translation: I would have broken my eyes, let them crack, just to keep looking at him until he was so far away that he was as small as the point of one of my needles.

original: Nay, follow'd him, till he had melted from   The smallness of a gnat to air, and then   Have turn'd mine eye and wept.
translation: No, I would have looked at him until he had melted from the size of a mosquito into air, and then I would have looked away and cried.

original: But, good Pisanio,   When shall we hear from him?
translation: Good Pisanio, when will we hear from him?

original: Be assured, madam, With his next vantage.
translation: Definitely as soon as he lands somewhere, ma'am.

original: I did not take my leave of him, but had   Most pretty things to say:
translation: I didn't say goodbye to him, even though I had planned to say the prettiest things.

original: ere I could tell him   How I would think on him at certain hours   Such thoughts and such, or I could make him swear   The shes of Italy should not betray   Mine interest and his honour, or have charged him,   At the sixth hour of morn, at noon, at midnight,   To encounter me with orisons, for then   I am in heaven for him;
translation: My father came in before I could tell Posthumus I would think specific thoughts about him at specific times. And before I could make him promise not to cheat on me with Italian women, which would be bad for me and for his honor. And before I could tell him to pray for me at six in the morning, at noon, and at midnight, which would be like being in heaven with him.

original: or ere I could   Give him that parting kiss which I had set   Betwixt two charming words,
translation: And before I could give him that goodbye kiss which I had planned to give him between two charming words.

original: comes in my father   And like the tyrannous breathing of the north   Shakes all our buds from growing.
translation: My father interrupted us like the cruel north wind that kills flowers before they can grow.

original: The queen, madam, Desires your highness' company.
translation: The queen would like to see you, your highness.

original: Those things I bid you do, get them dispatch'd. I will attend the queen.
translation: Do the things I told you to do. [To the LADY] I will go see the queen.

original: Madam, I shall.
translation: I will, ma'am.

original: Believe it, sir, I have seen him in Britain: he was   then of a crescent note, expected to prove so worthy   as since he hath been allowed the name of;
translation: Believe me, sir, I have seen  him  in Britain. He was still growing up, and people expected him to become just as virtuous as they say he eventually became.

original: but I   could then have looked on him without the help of   admiration, though the catalogue of his endowments   had been tabled by his side and I to peruse him by  items.
translation: But I wasn't impressed by him, and wouldn't have been even if there had been a list of all his good qualities near him and I had to read each item on the list and consider it independently.

original: You speak of him when he was less furnished than now he is with that which makes him both without and  within.
translation: But you're talking about what he was like when he didn't yet have all the qualities, inner and outer, that he does now.

original: I have seen him in France: we had very many there could behold the sun with as firm eyes as he.
This matter of marrying his king's daughter, wherein he must be weighed rather by her value than his own, words him, I doubt not, a great deal from the matter.
translation: This business of him marrying his king's daughter makes him seem better than he is, because she's worth far more than he is and people have to judge him by her worth.

original: And then his banishment.
translation: And now he's exiled.

original: Ay, and the approbation of those that weep this   lamentable divorce under her colours are wonderfully   to extend him;
translation: Yes, and the people who cry about this separation because they're loyal to her say amazing things about him.

original: be it but to fortify her judgment,   which else an easy battery might lay flat, for   taking a beggar without less quality.
translation: This is just to make her seem wiser because otherwise you could easily criticize her for marrying a worthless beggar.

original: But how comes   it he is to sojourn with you? How creeps   acquaintance?
translation: Why is he coming to stay with you? How do you know each other?

original: His father and I were soldiers together; to whom I   have been often bound for no less than my life.
translation: His father and I were soldiers together, and he often saved my life.

original: Here comes the Briton: let him be so entertained   amongst you as suits, with gentlemen of your   knowing, to a stranger of his quality.
translation: Here comes the British man. Treat him as well as men of your class should treat such a noble stranger.

original: I beseech you all, be better known to this   gentleman; whom I commend to you as a noble friend   of mine:
translation: Please, get to know this man. You should because he's a noble friend of mine.

original: how worthy he is I will leave to appear   hereafter, rather than story him in his own hearing.
translation: Instead of bragging about how great he is in front of him, I'll let it become clear later.

original: Sir, we have known together in Orleans.
translation: Sir, we met in Orleans.

original: Since when I have been debtor to you for courtesies, which I will be ever to pay and yet pay still.
translation: And since we met you've done me many favors and I owe you a lot for that. I'll always owe you and will never be able to repay the full amount.

original: Sir, you o'er-rate my poor kindness: I was glad I   did atone my countryman and you;
translation: Sir, you're making too much of what was simple kindness. I was glad to make peace between you and my countryman.

original: it had been pity   you should have been put together with so mortal a   purpose as then each bore, upon importance of so   slight and trivial a nature.
translation: It would have been a pity if you had attacked each other in such a deadly way, which is what you wanted to do, over such an unimportant matter.

original: By your pardon, sir, I was then a young traveller;   rather shunned to go even with what I heard than in   my every action to be guided by others' experiences:
translation: You see, sir, I was not an experienced traveler then. I was stubborn and did the opposite of what people told me I should do based on their own experiences.

original: but upon my mended judgment—if I offend not to say   it is mended—my quarrel was not altogether slight.
translation: But even though I am wiser now, if I do say so myself, I don't think the argument was over an unimportant matter.

original: 'Faith, yes, to be put to the arbitrement of swords, and by such two that would by all likelihood have confounded one the other, or have fallen both.
translation: It was extreme to try to settle it by fighting with swords, especially since you would probably have hurt or killed each other.

original: Can we, with manners, ask what was the difference?
translation: Would it be rude for us to ask what the argument was about?

original: Safely, I think: 'twas a contention in public,   which may, without contradiction, suffer the report.
translation: No, it's fine. It was a public argument and so no one would think it was wrong to tell you about it.

original: It was much like an argument that fell out last   night, where each of us fell in praise of our   country mistresses;
translation: It was a lot like an argument we had last night when we all raved about our girlfriends at home.

original: this gentleman at that time   vouching—and upon warrant of bloody   affirmation—his to be more fair, virtuous, wise,   chaste, constant-qualified and less attemptable   than any the rarest of our ladies in France.
translation: This man, Posthumus, was saying that his girlfriend was more beautiful, a better person, wiser, less sexual, better in every way, and  less easy  than than even the best women in France, and he threatened to fight anyone who disagreed.

original: That lady is not now living, or this gentleman's opinion by this worn out.
translation: I'm sure that either that woman is dead or this man has changed his mind about her.

original: She holds her virtue still and I my mind.
translation: She still has all her virtues and I still have the same opinion about her.

original: You must not so far prefer her 'fore ours of Italy.
translation: But you wouldn't say she was that much better than our women here in Italy.

original: Being so far provoked as I was in France, I would abate her nothing, though I profess myself her adorer, not her friend.
translation: If I got as worked up as I did in France, I would not take away any of the things I said about her. I would add that I am her admirer, not her equal.

original: As fair and as good—a kind of hand-in-hand   comparison—had been something too fair and too good   for any lady in Britain.
translation: Even if you put her hand in hand with our women here by saying she was as beautiful and as good as they are, you would still be describing her as too beautiful and too good to be a British woman.

original: If she went before others   I have seen, as that diamond of yours outlustres   many I have beheld. I could not but believe she   excelled many:
translation: Maybe this would be true if she were better than others I have seen, just as that diamond of yours is brighter than many I have seen. Then I would have to believe that she was better than many women.

original: but I have not seen the most   precious diamond that is, nor you the lady.
translation: But I have not seen the most precious diamond that exists, and you have not seen the most precious woman who exists.

original: I praised her as I rated her: so do I my stone.
translation: I described her as I saw her then, and I would do the same thing with my diamond.

original: What do you esteem it at?
translation: How much do you think it's worth?

original: More than the world enjoys.
translation: More than is contained in the world.

original: Either your unparagoned mistress is dead, or she's outprized by a trifle.
translation: Either your unequaled lover is dead or she's worth less than a trinket.

original: You are mistaken: the one may be sold, or given,
translation: You're wrong. One of them can be sold or given away,

original: if   there were wealth enough for the purchase, or merit   for the gift: the other is not a thing for sale,   and only the gift of the gods.
translation: or it could if anyone had enough money to buy it, but the other is not a thing that's for sale, and can only be given away by the gods.

original: Which the gods have given you?
translation: Which the gods have given to you?

original: Which, by their graces, I will keep.
translation: Which, if they let me, I will keep.

original: You may wear her in title yours: but, you know,   strange fowl light upon neighbouring ponds.
translation: You are  entitled  to her now and can wear her. But, you know, unfamiliar birds land on familiar ponds.

original: Your   ring may be stolen too: so your brace of unprizable   estimations; the one is but frail and the other   casual;
translation: Your ring could be stolen, and so could your string of high opinions of her. One is weak and the other is temporary.

original: a cunning thief, or a that way accomplished   courtier, would hazard the winning both of first and  last.
translation: A clever thief, or a courtier good at that sort of thing, would take the bet that they could win both things.

original: Your Italy contains none so accomplished a courtier   to convince the honour of my mistress, if, in the   holding or loss of that, you term her frail.
translation: Your Italy doesn't hold a courtier talented enough to convince my wife to sleep with him, if you mean by saying she's "weak" that being loyal makes her weak or that she's easily convinced to be disloyal.

original: I do   nothing doubt you have store of thieves;   notwithstanding, I fear not my ring.
translation: I don't doubt that there are plenty of thieves here, but I'm not worried I'll lose my ring.

original: Let us leave here, gentlemen.
translation: Let's leave, gentlemen.

original: Sir, with all my heart. This worthy signior, I thank him, makes no stranger of me; we are familiar at  first.
translation: Gladly, sir. This good man doesn't treat me like a stranger. We're being very informal, and I thank him for that.

original: With five times so much conversation, I should get   ground of your fair mistress, make her go back, even   to the yielding,
translation: With only five times the amount of conversation we've had, I would defeat your wife and make her retreat and finally yield to me,

original: had I admittance and opportunity to  friend.
translation: if I could just get into her presence and was given the  opportunity.

original: No, no.
translation: No, no.

original: I dare thereupon pawn the moiety of my estate to   your ring; which, in my opinion, o'ervalues it   something:
translation: I'm willing to bet half of my property against your ring, which in my opinion is more than the ring is worth.

original: but I make my wager rather against your   confidence than her reputation: and, to bar your   offence herein too, I durst attempt it against any   lady in the world.
translation: It's your confidence, not her reputation, that makes me think I'll win. Don't be offended: I would try this with any woman in the world.

original: You are a great deal abused in too bold a   persuasion;
translation: You're wrong to be so sure of yourself.

original: and I doubt not you sustain what you're   worthy of by your attempt.
translation: I don't doubt that if you try to do this you'll get what you have coming to you.

original: What's that?
translation: What's that?

original: A repulse: though your attempt, as you call it, deserve more; a punishment too.
translation: A refusal. Though your "try," as you call it, deserves more: a punishment.

original: Gentlemen, enough of this: it came in too suddenly; let it die as it was born, and, I pray you, be better acquainted.
translation: Gentlemen, that's enough. This started too quickly. Let it end just as quickly, and please, make friends with each other.

original: Would I had put my estate and my neighbour's on the approbation of what I have spoke!
translation: I wish I had bet both my property and my neighbor's to prove what I said!

original: What lady would you choose to assail?
translation: What woman would you choose to harass?

original: Yours; whom in constancy you think stands so safe.
translation: Your wife, who you're so sure is loyal.

original: I will lay you ten thousand ducats to your ring,   that, commend me to the court where your lady is,   with no more advantage than the opportunity of a   second conference,
translation: If you send me with a letter of recommendation to the court where your wife is, with just one opportunity to talk to her a second time, then I bet you ten thousand  ducats  against your ring that

original: and I will bring from thence   that honour of hers which you imagine so reserved.
translation: I will take her honor, which you think is so safe, and bring it back with me.

original: I will wage against your gold, gold to it: my ring I hold dear as my finger; 'tis part of it.
translation: I'll bet you gold against your gold instead. My ring is as important to me as my finger. It's part of it.

original: You are afraid, and therein the wiser.
translation: You're afraid, and that's wise of you.

original: If you buy   ladies' flesh at a million a dram, you cannot   preserve it from tainting:
translation: Even if you buy women's bodies at a million ducats per ounce , you can't keep them from going bad.

original: but I see you have some   religion in you, that you fear.
translation: I see you're afraid of your wife as though she's your god.

original: This is but a custom in your tongue; you bear a graver purpose, I hope.
translation: That's just the way you talk. I hope you're actually more serious and don't really mean this.

original: I am the master of my speeches, and would undergo what's spoken, I swear.
translation: I'm in control of what I say, and I promise I'm willing to go through with what I've said.

original: Will you? I shall but lend my diamond till your   return: let there be covenants drawn between's:
translation: Will you? I'll just lend you my ring until you come back. Let's draw up a contract.

original: my   mistress exceeds in goodness the hugeness of your   unworthy thinking:
translation: My wife is so much better than your worthless mind can understand.

original: I dare you to this match: here's my  ring.
translation: I dare you to try this. Here's my ring.

original: I will have it no lay.
translation: I won't let this bet happen.

original: By the gods, it is one. If I bring you no   sufficient testimony that I have enjoyed the dearest   bodily part of your mistress, my ten thousand ducats   are yours;
translation: By the gods, it's a bet. If I don't bring you good enough evidence that I've taken advantage of your wife's most pleasant body part, my ten thousand ducats will be yours.

original: so is your diamond too: if I come off,   and leave her in such honour as you have trust in,   she your jewel, this your jewel, and my gold are   yours:
translation: Your diamond will be yours too. If I come back and she's still as honorable as you believe her to be now, she (your jewel), this ring (your jewel), and my gold will all be yours.

original: provided I have your commendation for my more   free entertainment.
translation: If, that is, you send a letter telling her to spend time with me.

original: I embrace these conditions; let us have articles   betwixt us. Only, thus far you shall answer:
translation: I accept these conditions. Let's draw up an agreement. I would only add that this should be your penalty:

original: if   you make your voyage upon her and give me directly   to understand you have prevailed, I am no further   your enemy; she is not worth our debate:
translation: if you try to seduce her and tell me clearly that you succeeded, I will not be your enemy any more. She will not be worth arguing about.

original: if she   remain unseduced, you not making it appear   otherwise, for your ill opinion and the assault you   have made to her chastity you shall answer me with   your sword.
translation: If you can't tell me she was seduced, I will challenge you to a sword-fight for your bad opinion of her and your attack on her loyalty.

original: Your hand; a covenant: we will have these things set   down by lawful counsel, and straight away for   Britain, lest the bargain should catch cold and   starve:
translation: Let's shake on it. It's a deal. We'll have a lawyer write these things down, and I'll head to Britain immediately  before the deal dies of a cold .

original: I will fetch my gold and have our two   wagers recorded.
translation: I'll get my gold and have our bets written down.

original: Agreed.
translation: I agree.

original: Will this hold, think you?
translation: Do you think they'll go through with this?

original: Signior Iachimo will not from it. Pray, let us follow 'em.
translation: Iachimo won't let it go. Come on, let's follow them.

original: Whiles yet the dew's on ground, gather those flowers; Make haste: who has the note of them?
translation: Pick those flowers while there's still dew on the ground. Hurry up. Who has the list of them?

original: I, madam.
translation: I do, ma'am.

original: Dispatch.
translation: Do it.

original: Now, master doctor, have you brought those drugs?
translation: Now, doctor, have you brought those drugs?

original: Pleaseth your highness, ay: here they are, madam:
translation: Yes, your highness. Here they are, ma'am.

original: But I beseech your grace, without offence,—   My conscience bids me ask—
translation: Please, don't be offended, but my conscience makes me ask this:

original: wherefore you have   Commanded of me those most poisonous compounds,   Which are the movers of a languishing death;   But though slow, deadly?
translation: why have you asked me to make these really poisonous mixtures, which cause a slow, painful, death—slow, but deadly?

original: I wonder, doctor,   Thou ask'st me such a question.
translation: I'm surprised, doctor, that you're asking me such a question.

original: Have I not been   Thy pupil long? Hast thou not learn'd me how   To make perfumes? distil? preserve? yea, so   That our great king himself doth woo me oft   For my confections?
translation: Haven't I been your student for a long time? Haven't you taught me how to make perfumes, alcohol, and preserves? Am I not so good at it that our great king himself often begs me to give him some of the things I make?

original: Having thus far proceeded,—   Unless thou think'st me devilish—is't not meet   That I did amplify my judgment in   Other conclusions?
translation: Since I've come this far in my studies, unless you think I'm evil, isn't it right for me to learn different skills?

original: I will try the forces   Of these thy compounds on such creatures as   We count not worth the hanging, but none human,
translation: I'm going to test the effects of these mixtures on animals that we don't even consider important enough to hang, but none of them will be human.

original: To try the vigour of them and apply   Allayments to their act, and by them gather   Their several virtues and effects.
translation: I'll test how strong the potions are and then try their antidotes, to understand the different effects these potions have.

original: Your highness   Shall from this practise but make hard your heart:
translation: Your highness, this test will just make you hard-hearted.

original: Besides, the seeing these effects will be   Both noisome and infectious.
translation: And seeing the effects of the poison will be both disgusting and dangerous.

original: O, content thee.
translation: Don't worry.

original: Here comes a flattering rascal; upon him   Will I first work:
translation: Here comes a sweet-talking good-for-nothing. I'll start with him.

original: he's for his master,   An enemy to my son.
How now, Pisanio!
translation: [To Pisanio]  Hey, Pisanio!

original: Doctor, your service for this time is ended;   Take your own way.
translation: [To Cornelius]  Doctor, I don't need anything else from you. Go away.

original: I do suspect you, madam; But you shall do no harm.
translation: [To himself I'm suspicious of you, ma'am. But you won't hurt anyone.

original: Hark thee, a word.
translation: Listen, I have something to tell you.

original: [Aside]   I do not like her. She doth think she has   Strange lingering poisons:
translation: [To himself]  I don't like her. She thinks she has slow, unusual poisons.

original: I do know her spirit,   And will not trust one of her malice with   A drug of such damn'd nature.
translation: I know what she's really like, and wouldn't trust someone that evil with a drug of that kind.

original: Those she has   Will stupefy and dull the sense awhile;   Which first, perchance, she'll prove on   cats and dogs,   Then afterward up higher:
translation: The ones she has will send you to sleep and dull your senses for a while. Maybe she'll try them on cats and dogs first, then on animals higher up the chain of being.

original: but there is   No danger in what show of death it makes,   More than the locking-up the spirits a time,   To be more fresh, reviving.
