translation: But although it makes you seem dead, it's not dangerous. It just shuts your mind down for a bit and you wake up energized.

original: She is fool'd   With a most false effect; and I the truer,   So to be false with her.
translation: She'll be fooled by this fake effect, and I'm being true to myself by giving her a fake.

original: No further service, doctor, Until I send for thee.
translation: I won't need anything more from you, doctor, until I send for you.

original: I humbly take my leave.
translation: Good bye.

original: Weeps she still, say'st thou? Dost thou think in time   She will not quench and let instructions enter   Where folly now possesses? Do thou work:
translation: You say she's still crying? Don't you think that, in time, she'll give in and let good advice enter her brain which is now full of silliness? Help with this.

original: When thou shalt bring me word she loves my son,   I'll tell thee on the instant thou art then   As great as is thy master, greater, for   His fortunes all lie speechless and his name   Is at last gasp:
translation: When you bring me word she's in love with my son, I'll tell you at once you're as good as your master, because his luck is so sick it can't talk and his reputation is almost dead.

original: return he cannot, nor   Continue where he is: to shift his being   Is to exchange one misery with another,
translation: He can't come back or stay where he is. For him, moving means exchanging one unpleasant situation for another.

original: And every day that comes comes to decay   A day's work in him.
translation: And at the end of every day he hasn't achieved anything except grow older.

original: What shalt thou expect,   To be depender on a thing that leans,   Who cannot be new built, nor has no friends,   So much as but to prop him?
translation: What good is it to lean on something that's fragile and can't be built up to be stronger, and has no one to hold it up? That's what it's like to depend on Posthumus.

original: Thou takest up   Thou know'st not what; but take it for thy labour:   It is a thing I made, which hath the king   Five times redeem'd from death: I do not know   What is more cordial.
translation: You don't know what you're picking up. But take it in exchange for your work. It's something I made, which saved the king from death five different times. I don't know of anything that's better for your health.

original: Nay, I prethee, take it;   It is an earnest of a further good   That I mean to thee. Tell thy mistress how   The case stands with her; do't as from thyself.
translation: No, please, take it. It's a preview of the other good deeds I will do for you. Tell your employer what her situation is. Do it as though you're just saying what you think.

original: Think what a chance thou changest on, but think   Thou hast thy mistress still, to boot, my son,   Who shall take notice of thee:
translation: Consider what good luck this is for you. You still have an employer even though you're betraying your employer. I mean, you have my son, who will show his appreciation of you.

original: I'll move the king   To any shape of thy preferment such   As thou'lt desire;
translation: I'll get the king to give you any kind of promotion you want.

original: and then myself, I chiefly,   That set thee on to this desert, am bound   To load thy merit richly. Call my women:   Think on my words.
translation: And I especially, since I'm telling you about these rewards available to you, will need to pay you everything you deserve. Call my women, and think about what I've said.

original: A sly and constant knave,   Not to be shaked;
translation: He's a sneaky and loyal good-for-nothing, and I can't get him to go away.

original: the agent for his master   And the remembrancer of her to hold   The hand-fast to her lord.
translation: He's his master's spy and he's reminding Imogen to stay loyal to her husband.

original: I have given him that   Which, if he take, shall quite unpeople her   Of liegers for her sweet,
translation: But I have given him something which, if he takes it, will kill him and so get rid of the last of her sweet-heart's minions.

original: and which she after,   Except she bend her humour, shall be assured   To taste of too.
translation: After that, if she doesn't change her mind, she'll definitely be sorry.

original: So, so: well done, well done:   The violets, cowslips, and the primroses,   Bear to my closet.
translation: Great. Well done, well done. Take the violets, the cowslips, and the primroses to my room.

original: Fare thee well, Pisanio;   Think on my words.
translation: Good-bye, Pisanio. Think about my words.

original: And shall do: But when to my good lord I prove untrue, I'll choke myself: there's all I'll do for you.
translation: I will. But if I ever betray my good master, I'll choke myself. That's the only thing I'll do for you.

original: A father cruel, and a step-dame false;   A foolish suitor to a wedded lady,   That hath her husband banish'd;—O, that husband!
translation: I have a a cruel father, a lying stepmother, a silly suitor who wants to marry a married woman whose husband is banished—Oh, what a husband!

original: My supreme crown of grief! and those repeated   Vexations of it! Had I been thief-stol'n,   As my two brothers, happy!
translation: He's the biggest reason for me to be sad! And those other annoying people make that sadness worse! If I'd been stolen like my two brothers, I would have been happy!

original: but most miserable   Is the desire that's glorious: blest be those,   How mean soe'er, that have their honest wills,   Which seasons comfort. Who may this be? Fie!
translation: Noble people who want something and don't get it are the most unhappy. People are lucky who can do what they want, however poor they are, which makes a good situation even better. Who is this? Go away!

original: Madam, a noble gentleman of Rome, Comes from my lord with letters.
translation: Ma'am, a noble man from Rome has brought letters from my master.

original: Change you, madam? The worthy Leonatus is in safety And greets your highness dearly.
translation: Did you just turn pale, ma'am? The good Leonatus is safe and greets you with love.

original: Thanks, good sir: You're kindly welcome.
translation: Thank you, sir. You're very welcome here.

original: [Aside]   All of her that is out of door most rich!   If she be furnish'd with a mind so rare,   She is alone the Arabian bird, and I   Have lost the wager.
translation: [To himself]  She's very beautiful on the outside! If her mind is as outstanding as her looks, she's as much better than other women as the phoenix is better than other birds, and I have lost my bet.

original: Boldness be my friend!   Arm me, audacity, from head to foot!   Or, like the Parthian, I shall flying fight;   Rather directly fly.
translation: I should be bold! Boldness, make me strong from head to foot! Or I'll have to shoot at her while running away, like the Parthians do. It would be better to run away at once.

original: [Reads]   'He is one of the noblest note, to whose   kindnesses I am most infinitely tied. Reflect upon   him accordingly, as you value your trust—   LEONATUS.'
translation: [Reading the letter]  "He's one of the men with the best reputations, and I owe him a lot for his kindness. So treat him well, if you want to be trusted.—Leonatus."

original: So far I read aloud:   But even the very middle of my heart   Is warm'd by the rest, and takes it thankfully.
translation: I'll only read this part aloud. The rest of it warms my whole body, even the deepest part of my heart. I am grateful for it.

original: You are as welcome, worthy sir, as I   Have words to bid you, and shall find it so   In all that I can do.
translation: You are as welcome as it's possible to be, and you'll see it's true from what I do for you.

original: Thanks, fairest lady.   What, are men mad?
translation: Thanks, most beautiful lady. Are men crazy?

original: Hath nature given them eyes   To see this vaulted arch, and the rich crop   Of sea and land, which can distinguish 'twixt   The fiery orbs above and the twinn'd stones   Upon the number'd beach?
translation: Has nature given them eyes to see the sky and the rich crops that come from the sea and the land, to tell apart the fiery stars above from the equal number of grains of sands on the crowded beach?

original: and can we not   Partition make with spectacles so precious   'Twixt fair and foul?
translation: And can we not use these amazing instruments to tell the difference between good and bad?

original: What makes your admiration?
translation: Why are you staring?

original: It cannot be i' the eye, for apes and monkeys   'Twixt two such shes would chatter this way and   Contemn with mows the other;
translation: It can't be his eyes that are bad, because even monkeys looking at two women like this would pick one by making noises at her and make faces at the other one.

original: nor i' the judgment,   For idiots in this case of favour would   Be wisely definite; nor i' the appetite;
translation: It can't be his common sense, because idiots would definitely know the right answer when deciding which was better.

original: Sluttery to such neat excellence opposed   Should make desire vomit emptiness,   Not so allured to feed.
translation: Or desire, because messiness contrasted with such neat superiority would make anyone throw up rather than desire the messy one.

original: What is the matter, trow?
translation: Come on, what's the matter?

original: The cloyed will,   That satiate yet unsatisfied desire,
translation: He's stuffed himself, he's satisfied his desire but is not satisfied,

original: that tub   Both fill'd and running, ravening first the lamb   Longs after for the garbage.
translation: he's a tub that's filled but still emptying out, he's devoured the lamb and now is hungry for garbage.

original: What, dear sir, Thus raps you? Are you well?
translation: What's wrong with you, sir? Are you well?

original: Thanks, madam; well.
translation: Thanks, ma'am. Well...

original: Beseech you, sir, desire My man's abode where I did leave him: he Is strange and peevish.
translation: Please, sir, go find my servant where I left him. He's strange and grumpy.

original: I was going, sir, To give him welcome.
translation: I was just going, sir, to welcome him.

original: Continues well my lord? His health, beseech you?
translation: How is my husband's health? Is he well?

original: Well, madam.
translation: Well, ma'am.

original: Is he disposed to mirth? I hope he is.
translation: Is he happy? I hope he is.

original: Exceeding pleasant; none a stranger there So merry and so gamesome: he is call'd The Briton reveller.
translation: He's very good company. There's no other stranger there so happy and eager to play games. He's called the British partier.

original: When he was here, He did incline to sadness, and oft-times Not knowing why.
translation: When he was here, he used to be sad a lot, and often didn't know why.

original: I never saw him sad.   There is a Frenchman his companion, one   An eminent monsieur, that, it seems, much loves   A Gallian girl at home;
translation: I never saw him be sad. He has a companion, a Frenchman, a well-known man, who is in love with a French girl back home.

original: he furnaces   The thick sighs from him, whiles the jolly Briton—   Your lord, I mean—laughs from's free lungs, cries   'O,
translation: He's always sighing like a furnace for her, while the cheerful Briton—your husband, I mean—laughs deeply, and cries out:

original: Can my sides hold, to think that man, who knows   By history, report, or his own proof,   What woman is,
translation: "Oh, I think I'll split my sides laughing, just thinking that any man who knows by history, other people's stories, or his own experience, what women are like, no

original: yea, what she cannot choose   But must be, will his free hours languish for   Assured bondage?'
translation: —what they can't help being like, would spend his free time pining for a woman who would make him her slave!"

original: Will my lord say so?
translation: My husband says that?

original: Ay, madam, with his eyes in flood with laughter:   It is a recreation to be by   And hear him mock the Frenchman.
translation: Yes, ma'am, crying with laughter. It's such fun to be near him and hear him make fun of the Frenchman.

original: But, heavens know,   Some men are much to blame.
translation: Heaven knows, some men do terrible things.

original: Not he, I hope.
translation: Not him, I hope.

original: Not he: but yet heaven's bounty towards him might   Be used more thankfully.
translation: Not him. But the gifts the gods gave him could be used better.

original: In himself, 'tis much;   In you, which I account his beyond all talents,   Whilst I am bound to wonder, I am bound   To pity too.
translation: It's terrible for him. But seeing you , who belong to him more than all the coins he owns, I have to feel amazement and pity.

original: What do you pity, sir?
translation: What do you pity, sir?

original: Two creatures heartily.
translation: Two people, with all my heart.

original: Am I one, sir? You look on me: what wreck discern you in me Deserves your pity?
translation: Am I one of them, sir? You're looking at me. What disaster do you see in me that deserves your pity?

original: Lamentable! What, To hide me from the radiant sun and solace I' the dungeon by a snuff?
translation: Horrible! How could he hide from the bright sun and find comfort in a dungeon with a candle?

original: I pray you, sir, Deliver with more openness your answers To my demands. Why do you pity me?
translation: Please, sir, answer my questions more clearly. Why do you pity me?

original: That others do—   I was about to say—enjoy your—
translation: Because other people—I was about to say—enjoy your—

original: But   It is an office of the gods to venge it,   Not mine to speak on 't.
translation: but it's the gods' job to revenge this, not mine to talk about it.

original: You do seem to know   Something of me, or what concerns me:
translation: You seem to know something about me or that has to do with me.

original: pray you,—   Since doubting things go ill often hurts more   Than to be sure they do;
translation: Please—since worrying that things have gone wrong is often worse that knowing that they have,

original: for certainties   Either are past remedies, or, timely knowing,   The remedy then born—discover to me   What both you spur and stop.
translation: and it's either too late to change something you know has happened or, knowing about it in time, you can find a way to fix it—tell me what you want to say and why you've stopped yourself from saying it.

original: Had I this cheek   To bathe my lips upon; this hand, whose touch,   Whose every touch, would force the feeler's soul   To the oath of loyalty; this object, which   Takes prisoner the wild motion of mine eye,   Fixing it only here;
translation: If I had this cheek to kiss (this hand whose touch, whose every touch, would force the person who felt it to swear an oath of loyalty) and you to look at, who capture my eye's wild movement, fixing it here on you—

original: should I, damn'd then,   Slaver with lips as common as the stairs   That mount the Capitol;
translation: If I, damned at once for it, slurped on lips as common to all as the stairs that go up to the Capitol building,

original: join gripes with hands   Made hard with hourly falsehood—falsehood, as   With labour;
translation: if I gripped hands made hard by telling lies every hour (as though telling lies were the same thing as manual labor),

original: then by-peeping in an eye   Base and unlustrous as the smoky light   That's fed with stinking tallow;
translation: if I peeped into an eye as lowly and dull as the light given off by a cheap smoky candle,

original: it were fit   That all the plagues of hell should at one time   Encounter such revolt.
translation: it would be right for all the plagues of hell to come punish me for this rebellion.

original: My lord, I fear, Has forgot Britain.
translation: I'm afraid that my husband has forgotten Britain.

original: And himself. Not I,   Inclined to this intelligence, pronounce   The beggary of his change;
translation: And himself. It's not me who's claiming that the exchange he's made is so bad it leaves him a beggar.

original: but 'tis your graces   That from my mutest conscience to my tongue   Charms this report out.
translation: It's all your good qualities that draw out this report of his activities from my conscience, which would prefer to remain silent, and make me say this out loud.

original: Let me hear no more.
translation: Don't say any more.

original: O dearest soul! your cause doth strike my heart   With pity, that doth make me sick.
translation: Oh poor thing! Your situation strikes so much pity into my heart that it makes me sick.

original: A lady   So fair, and fasten'd to an empery,   Would make the great'st king double,—
translation: A woman so beautiful, and who comes with a kingdom, would double the value of even the greatest king.

original: to be partner'd   With tomboys hired with that self-exhibition   Which your own coffers yield! with diseased ventures   That play with all infirmities for gold   Which rottenness can lend nature!
translation: But you're shared with  whores  paid with your own money!  Add to that his terrible unnatural plans to  gamble with all kinds of disgusting people for gold !

original: such boil'd stuff   As well might poison poison! Be revenged;   Or she that bore you was no queen, and you   Recoil from your great stock.
translation: These spotted people could poison poison! You should get your revenge. Or your mother was no queen, and you're letting down your noble family.

original: Revenged!   How should I be revenged? If this be true,—
translation: Revenge! How would I take my revenge? If this is true -

original: As I have such a heart that both mine ears   Must not in haste abuse—if it be true,   How should I be revenged?
translation: but I am so in love that I should not be willing to believe rumors I hear - if it's true, how would I get my revenge?

original: Should he make me   Live, like Diana's priest, betwixt cold sheets,
translation: You should think, "Is it right for him to make me live, like a nun of the goddess Diana's, lying between cold sheets?"

original: Whiles he is vaulting variable ramps,   In your despite, upon your purse?
translation: while he's  leaping over differently-sized hurdles , injuring you and your bank account?

original: Revenge it.   I dedicate myself to your sweet pleasure,   More noble than that runagate to your bed,   And will continue fast to your affection,   Still close as sure.
translation: Take your revenge. I'm available for your pleasure. I'll treat you more nobly than that runaway from your bed, and I will continue to love you, secretly and surely.

original: What, ho, Pisanio!
translation: Pisanio!

original: Let me my service tender on your lips.
translation: Let me prove my willingness to serve you by kissing you.

original: Away! I do condemn mine ears that have   So long attended thee. If thou wert honourable,   Thou wouldst have told this tale for virtue, not   For such an end thou seek'st,—as base as strange.
translation: Go away! I'm angry at my ears for listening to you for so long. If you were honorable you would have told this story for a virtuous reason, not for the kind of goal you're after—that's as low as it is strange.

original: Thou wrong'st a gentleman, who is as far   From thy report as thou from honour, and   Solicit'st here a lady that disdains   Thee and the devil alike.
translation: You're acting wrongly towards a gentleman, who is as far from doing what you describe as you are from being honorable. You're trying to sleep with a woman who rejects you like she does the devil.

original: What ho, Pisanio!   The king my father shall be made acquainted   Of thy assault:
translation: Pisanio! My father the king will be told about your assault on me.

original: if he shall think it fit,   A saucy stranger in his court to mart   As in a Romish stew and to expound   His beastly mind to us, he hath a court   He little cares for and a daughter who   He not respects at all. What, ho, Pisanio!
translation: If he thinks it's right for a rude stranger to bargain like he's in a Roman brothel and to speak his horrible mind to me, he doesn't care about his court and doesn't respect his daughter at all. Pisanio!

original: O happy Leonatus! I may say   The credit that thy lady hath of thee   Deserves thy trust, and thy most perfect goodness   Her assured credit.
translation: Oh lucky Leonatus! I can say the belief your wife has in you deserves your trust in her, and your perfect goodness deserves her strong belief.

original: Blessed live you long!   A lady to the worthiest sir that ever   Country call'd his! and you his mistress, only   For the most worthiest fit!
translation: May you remain this blessed for a long time! You're the wife of the most virtuous man who ever lived in a country! And you're a wife who only deserves the most virtuous man!

original: Give me your pardon.   I have spoke this, to know if your affiance   Were deeply rooted; and shall make your lord,   That which he is, new o'er:
translation: Forgive me. I spoke this to know if you really loved him, and this news will be so welcome to your husband that it will be as though he is made new.

original: and he is one   The truest manner'd; such a holy witch   That he enchants societies into him;   Half all men's hearts are his.
translation: He is one of the best-mannered people. He's so holy that it's like he's a witch who enchants people into spending time with him. Half of all of men's hearts belong to him.

original: You make amends.
translation: You're making up for your behavior.

original: He sits 'mongst men like a descended god:   He hath a kind of honour sets him off,   More than a mortal seeming.
translation: He's like a god on earth compared to other men. He has a kind of honor that sets him apart, which seems like something more godlike than mortal.

original: Be not angry,   Most mighty princess, that I have adventured   To try your taking a false report;
translation: Don't be angry, powerful princess, that I tried to tell you a lie. The fact that you could tell I was lying just confirms your good judgement,

original: which hath   Honour'd with confirmation your great judgment   In the election of a sir so rare,   Which you know cannot err:
translation: which was already apparent in your choice of such an excellent husband. You know your judgement is never wrong.

original: the love I bear him   Made me to fan you thus, but the gods made you,   Unlike all others, chaffless. Pray, your pardon.
translation: I was blowing on you as though to separate wheat from chaff, but unlike everyone else, the gods made you without any chaff. Please forgive me.

original: All's well, sir: take my power i' the court for yours.
translation: It's all right, sir. You'll be given all the power I have in the court.

original: My humble thanks. I had almost forgot   To entreat your grace but in a small request,   And yet of moment to, for it concerns   Your lord;
translation: Thank you. I had almost forgotten to ask you for one small thing, but it's important, because it's about your husband.

original: myself and other noble friends,   Are partners in the business.
translation: It also concerns me and some other noble friends.

original: Pray, what is't?
translation: What is it?

original: Some dozen Romans of us and your lord—   The best feather of our wing—have mingled sums   To buy a present for the emperor
translation: About twelve of us Romans and your lord—the best among us—put money together to buy a present for the emperor.

original: Which I, the factor for the rest, have done   In France:
translation: I was the agent for the others and bought it in France.

original: 'tis plate of rare device, and jewels   Of rich and exquisite form; their values great;
translation: It's silver carved with rare designs and well-shaped precious stones. They're worth a lot.

original: And I am something curious, being strange,   To have them in safe stowage: may it please you   To take them in protection?
translation: I'm a little nervous about being able to store them safely, since I'm a stranger here. Could you keep them?

original: Willingly;   And pawn mine honour for their safety:
translation: Gladly. And I bet my honor they'll be safe.

original: since   My lord hath interest in them, I will keep them   In my bedchamber.
translation: Since my husband has a stake in them, I'll keep them in my bedroom.

original: They are in a trunk,   Attended by my men:
translation: They're in a trunk, which my men have.

original: I will make bold   To send them to you, only for this night;   I must aboard to-morrow.
translation: I will send them to you, just for tonight. I have to sail back tomorrow.

original: O, no, no.
translation: Oh, no, no.

original: Yes, I beseech; or I shall short my word   By lengthening my return.
translation: Yes, please. Or I'll break my promise by coming back later than I said.

original: From Gallia   I cross'd the seas on purpose and on promise   To see your grace.
translation: I crossed the sea from  France  on purpose just to see you, because I promised I would.

original: I thank you for your pains: But not away to-morrow!
translation: Thank you for taking the trouble. But don't leave tomorrow!

original: O, I must, madam:   Therefore I shall beseech you, if you please   To greet your lord with writing, do't to-night:
translation: I have to, ma'am. Please, if you would like to write to your husband, do it tonight.

original: I have outstood my time; which is material   To the tender of our present.
translation: I have been here too long, and we need to give our present as soon as possible.

original: I will write. Send your trunk to me; it shall safe be kept, And truly yielded you. You're very welcome.
translation: I will write to him. Send your trunk to me. It will be kept safe and honestly given back to you. You're very welcome.

original: Was there ever man had such luck! when I kissed the   jack, upon an up-cast to be hit away!
translation: Was any man ever this unlucky? I even had the jack and kissed it, but then I suddenly lost!

original: I had a   hundred pound on't: and then a whoreson jackanapes   must take me up for swearing;
translation: I bet a hundred pounds on the card game. And then a rude son of a prostitute criticized me for swearing.

original: as if I borrowed mine   oaths of him and might not spend them at my pleasure.
translation: As if I borrowed my swear words from him and couldn't spend them however I wanted.

original: What got he by that? You have broke his pate with your bowl.
translation: But what did he get for that? You cracked his head with your bowl.

original: If his wit had been like him that broke it, it would have run all out.
translation: If his brains had been like the man who cracked them open, they would all have run away.

original: When a gentleman is disposed to swear, it is not for any standers-by to curtail his oaths, ha?
translation: When a man feels like swearing, it's not right for a bystander to cut short his oaths, right?

original: No my lord;
translation: No.

original: nor crop the ears of them.
translation: Or cut off the oaths' ears.

original: Whoreson dog! I give him satisfaction? Would he had been one of my rank!
translation: That dog, son of a prostitute! How dare he ask me to fight him? I wish he were in the same class as me so I could!

original: To have smelt like a fool.
translation: He would have been a stinky fool too then.

original: I am not vexed more at any thing in the earth: a   pox on't! I had rather not be so noble as I am;   they dare not fight with me, because of the queen my   mother:
translation: This annoys me more than anything on earth, darn it! I wish I weren't as noble as I am. They don't dare to fight me, because of my mother the queen.

original: every Jack-slave hath his bellyful of   fighting, and I must go up and down like a cock that   nobody can match.
translation: Any lower-class person can fight as much as he wants, and I have to walk around like a rooster that no other rooster can beat in a fight.

original: You are cock and capon too; and you crow, cock, with your comb on.
translation: You're a rooster and a chicken. And you're crowing like a foolish rooster.

original: Sayest thou?
translation: What did you say?

original: It is not fit your lordship should undertake every companion that you give offence to.
translation: It's not right for you to fight every single one of your companions who offends you.

original: No, I know that: but it is fit I should commit offence to my inferiors.
translation: No, I know that. But it's right for me to be offensive to my social inferiors.

original: Ay, it is fit for your lordship only.
translation: Yes, you're the only one who does that.

original: Why, so I say.
translation: That's what I'm saying.

original: Did you hear of a stranger that's come to court  to-night?
translation: Did you hear about a stranger who's come to court tonight?

original: A stranger, and I not know on't!
translation: What? A stranger, and I don't know about him!

original: He's a strange fellow himself, and knows it not.
translation: He's a strange man himself, and doesn't know it.

original: There's an Italian come; and, 'tis thought, one of Leonatus' friends.
translation: An Italian man has come. It's thought that he's one of Leonatus's friends.

original: Leonatus! a banished rascal; and he's another, whatsoever he be. Who told you of this stranger?
translation: Leonatus! A banished good-for-nothing. This man's the same thing, whoever he is. Who told you about him?

original: One of your lordship's pages.
translation: One of your servants.

original: Is it fit I went to look upon him? is there no derogation in't?
translation: Would it be proper for me to go look at him? Would it lower people's opinions of me?

original: You cannot derogate, my lord.
translation: You couldn't possibly lower people's opinions of you, my lord.

original: Not easily, I think.
translation: Not easily, I think.

original: You are a fool granted; therefore your issues, being foolish, do not derogate.
translation: Everyone already knows you're a fool. So, since anything you do will be foolish, it won't lower people's opinions any further.

original: Come, I'll go see this Italian: what I have lost to-day at bowls I'll win to-night of him. Come, go.
translation: All right, I'll go see this Italian man. I'll win back from him tonight the same amount of money I lost betting on lawn bowling today. Come on, let's go.

original: I'll attend your lordship.
translation: I'll meet you there.

original: That such a crafty devil as is his mother   Should yield the world this ass!
translation: How strange that a clever devil like his mother gave birth to such a fool!

original: a woman that   Bears all down with her brain; and this her son   Cannot take two from twenty, for his heart,   And leave eighteen.
translation: She's a woman who crushes everyone with her brain, and her son can't subtract two from twenty and get eighteen no matter how hard he tries

original: Alas, poor princess,   Thou divine Imogen, what thou endurest,   Betwixt a father by thy step-dame govern'd,   A mother hourly coining plots,
translation: . Poor princess, holy Imogen, you're suffering so much! You have a father ruled by your stepmother, a stepmother making up new plots every hour,

original: a wooer   More hateful than the foul expulsion is   Of thy dear husband, than that horrid act   Of the divorce he'ld make!
translation: a suitor who's worse than the horrible banishment of your dear husband, I mean who's worse than the separation he wants to cause between you and your husband!

original: The heavens hold firm   The walls of thy dear honour, keep unshaked   That temple, thy fair mind, that thou mayst stand,   To enjoy thy banish'd lord and this great land!
translation: May the gods keep your honor firm and keep you sane so that you can stay strong until you get your banished husband back and inherit this great country!

original: Who's there? my woman Helen?
translation: Who's there? Is it my attendant Helen?

original: Please you, madam
translation: Yes, ma'am.

original: What hour is it?
translation: What time is it?

original: Almost midnight, madam.
translation: Almost midnight, ma'am.

original: I have read three hours then: mine eyes are weak:   Fold down the leaf where I have left: to bed:
translation: I have read for three hours, then. My eyes are tired. Fold down the page I stopped at. I'll go to bed.

original: Take not away the taper, leave it burning;   And if thou canst awake by four o' the clock,   I prithee, call me. Sleep hath seized me wholly
translation: Don't take the candle. Leave it lit. And if you can wake up by four o'clock, please wake me. I'm so tired I'll fall asleep immediately.

original: To your protection I commend me, gods.
translation: Gods, I give myself up to your protection.

original: From fairies and the tempters of the night   Guard me, beseech ye.
translation: Save me from fairies and night-time demons, please.

original: The crickets sing, and man's o'er-labour'd sense   Repairs itself by rest.
translation: [To himself]  The crickets are singing, and people's tired-out senses are being healed by sleep.

original: Our Tarquin thus   Did softly press the rushes, ere he waken'd   The chastity he wounded.
translation: Tarquin  tiptoed over the floors this way, before he woke up his victim and raped her.

original: Cytherea,   How bravely thou becomest thy bed, fresh lily,   And whiter than the sheets! That I might touch!
translation: Aphrodite , you fresh lily, you look so beautiful on your bed and you're whiter than the sheets! I wish I could touch you!

original: But kiss; one kiss! Rubies unparagon'd,   How dearly they do't!
translation: And only kiss you—one kiss! Your lips are like the most beautiful rubies and kiss so delightfully!

original: 'Tis her breathing that   Perfumes the chamber thus: the flame o' the taper   Bows toward her, and would under-peep her lids,   To see the enclosed lights, now canopied   Under these windows, white and azure laced   With blue of heaven's own tinct.
translation: It's her breath that makes the room smell so good. The flame of the candle leans towards her and wants to look under her eyelids to see the lights closed up inside the windows of her eyes, which are white and the same blue as the sky.

original: But my design,   To note the chamber: I will write all down:
translation: But my plan is to take notes about the room. I will write everything down.

original: Such and such pictures; there the window; such   The adornment of her bed; the arras; figures,   Why, such and such; and the contents o' the story.
translation: [He starts taking notes]   There paintings, there a window, her bed is decorated in this way and has a canopy with these things embroidered on it, and what story is being told.

original: Ah, but some natural notes about her body,   Above ten thousand meaner moveables   Would testify, to enrich mine inventory.
translation: Oh, but to make my list better I should add some notes about natural marks on her body. That would be more convincing than describing ten thousand less important objects.

original: O sleep, thou ape of death, lie dull upon her!   And be her sense but as a monument,   Thus in a chapel lying! Come off, come off:
translation: Deathlike sleep, keep her lying there! May she feel as little as a carved statue lying in a church!  [To her bracelet]  Come off, come off.

original: As slippery as the Gordian knot was hard!   'Tis mine; and this will witness outwardly,   As strongly as the conscience does within,   To the madding of her lord.
translation: That was as easy as  the Gordian knot  was hard! This is mine. Seeing this, added to his own thoughts, will make her husband crazy.

original: On her left breast   A mole cinque-spotted, like the crimson drops   I' the bottom of a cowslip: here's a voucher,   Stronger than ever law could make: this secret   Will force him think I have pick'd the lock and ta'en   The treasure of her honour.
translation: On her left breast there's a mole with five spots that look like the red marks on the petals of a cowslip. This is proof stronger than you could ever find in a court of law. My knowing this secret will make him think that I've picked her lock and stolen her honor.

original: No more. To what end?   Why should I write this down, that's riveted,   Screw'd to my memory? She hath been reading late   The tale of Tereus; here the leaf's turn'd down   Where Philomel gave up.
translation: I don't need any more. What use would it be? Why would I write this down, when it's nailed into my memory? She was just reading the story of  Tereus . The page is dog-eared where Philomel was raped.

original: I have enough:   To the trunk again, and shut the spring of it.   Swift, swift, you dragons of the night, that dawning   May bare the raven's eye!
translation: I have enough proof. I'll get back to the trunk, and shut the lid. Pass quickly, quickly, night, so that it's dawn soon and the birds wake up!

original: I lodge in fear;   Though this a heavenly angel, hell is here.
translation: I'm scared lying here. Although she's an angel from heaven, this is hell.

original: One, two, three: time, time!
translation: One, two, three, strikes. It's time!

original: Fear it not, sir: I would I were so sure To win the king as I am bold her honour Will remain hers.
translation: Don't worry, sir. I wish I were as sure that the king would come around to my side as I am that she won't do anything dishonorable.

original: What means do you make to him?
translation: What are you doing to try to contact the king?

original: Not any, but abide the change of time,   Quake in the present winter's state and wish   That warmer days would come:
translation: Nothing, except wait for time to pass, like when you shiver with cold in winter and wish that warmer days would come.

original: in these sear'd hopes,   I barely gratify your love; they failing,   I must die much your debtor.
translation: That change of season, by which I mean the king changing his mind, is the only hope I have to repay your kindness. If it fails, I'll die without having repaid you fully.

original: Your very goodness and your company   O'erpays all I can do. By this, your king   Hath heard of great Augustus:
translation: Your goodness and your company are worth more than anything I can do for you. By this time, your king will have heard from great Augustus.

original: Caius Lucius   Will do's commission throughly: and I think   He'll grant the tribute, send the arrearages,
translation: Caius Lucius will do his job well. And I think the king will pay the emperor his tribute and send what he owes.

original: Or look upon our Romans, whose remembrance   Is yet fresh in their grief.
translation: Or else, he'll soon see the Romans again, and the country is still grieving over what happened last time the Romans invaded.

original: I do believe,   Statist though I am none, nor like to be,   That this will prove a war;
translation: I think, although I'm not a politician and probably never will be, that this will cause a war.

original: and you shall hear   The legions now in Gallia sooner landed   In our not-fearing Britain than have tidings   Of any penny tribute paid.
translation: It's far more likely that the Roman legions that are now in France will be sent to invade my fearless country of Britain than that any tribute will be paid.

original: Our countrymen   Are men more order'd than when Julius Caesar   Smiled at their lack of skill, but found   their courage   Worthy his frowning at:
translation: Our countrymen are more organized now than when Julius Caesar was amused at how incompetent they were but found that their courage was not so amusing.

original: their discipline,   Now mingled with their courages, will make known   To their approvers they are people such   That mend upon the world.
translation: They now combine discipline with that courage, and anyone who attacks them will see that they have improved.

original: See! Iachimo!
translation: Look! Iachimo!

original: The swiftest harts have posted you by land; And winds of all the comers kiss'd your sails, To make your vessel nimble.
translation: The fastest deer carried you over land and all the winds filled your sails to make your ship go quickly.

original: Welcome, sir.
translation: Welcome, sir.

original: I hope the briefness of your answer made The speediness of your return.
translation: I hope you came back so quickly because the answer you got from my wife was so short.

original: Your lady Is one of the fairest that I have look'd upon.
translation: Your wife is one of the most beautiful women I've seen.

original: And therewithal the best; or let her beauty Look through a casement to allure false hearts And be false with them.
translation: And also the best, or her beauty would be like a woman staring out of a window to trap disloyal hearts and betray them.

original: Here are letters for you.
translation: Here are letters for you.

original: Their tenor good, I trust.
translation: I hope they contain good news.

original: 'Tis very like.
translation: Probably.

original: Was Caius Lucius in the Britain court When you were there?
translation: Was Caius Lucius at the British court when you were there?

original: He was expected then, But not approach'd.
translation: They were expecting him, but he wasn't there yet.

original: All is well yet. Sparkles this stone as it was wont? or is't not Too dull for your good wearing?
translation: Then everything's still fine. So is this jewel as bright as it used to be? Or has it grown too dull to wear?

original: If I had lost it,   I should have lost the worth of it in gold.
translation: If I had lost it, I would only have lost its worth in gold.

original: I'll make a journey twice as far, to enjoy   A second night of such sweet shortness which   Was mine in Britain,
translation: I would travel twice as far to enjoy another night as pleasantly short as the one I had in Britain.

original: for the ring is won.
translation: Because I won the ring.

original: The stone's too hard to come by.
translation: No, it would be too hard to win this jewel.

original: Not a whit, Your lady being so easy.
translation: Not at all, since your wife is so easy.

original: Make not, sir, Your loss your sport: I hope you know that we Must not continue friends.
translation: Don't make up for your loss by messing with me. I hope you know that we're not going to be friends after this.

original: Good sir, we must,   If you keep covenant.
translation: Sir, we have to, if you keep your promise.

original: Had I not brought   The knowledge of your mistress home, I grant   We were to question further:
translation: If I hadn't slept with your wife before coming home, the deal was that we'd fight.

original: but I now   Profess myself the winner of her honour,   Together with your ring; and not the wronger   Of her or you, having proceeded but   By both your wills.
translation: But now I've said I won her and your ring. I haven't done wrong by you or her, since you both went through with this willingly.

original: If you can make't apparent   That you have tasted her in bed, my hand   And ring is yours;
translation: If you can prove that you slept with her, my friendship and my ring are yours.

original: if not, the foul opinion   You had of her pure honour gains or loses   Your sword or mine, or masterless leaves both   To who shall find them.
translation: If not, we'll fight over the fact that you had such a bad opinion of her reputation until one or the other or both of us is dead and our swords are left lying on the ground for whoever finds them.

original: Sir, my circumstances,   Being so near the truth as I will make them,   Must first induce you to believe:
translation: Sir, what I can tell you will make you believe I'm telling the truth.

original: whose strength   I will confirm with oath; which, I doubt not,   You'll give me leave to spare, when you shall find   You need it not.
translation: I will confirm my story by swearing that what I say is true. But I don't think you'll make me do that, because I'll have already convinced you.

original: Proceed.
translation: Go on.

original: First, her bedchamber,—   Where, I confess, I slept not, but profess   Had that was well worth watching—it was hang'd   With tapesty of silk and silver;
translation: First, her room. I admit I didn't sleep there, since I had such good reason to stay awake. The room was covered in tapestries made of silk and silver.

original: the story   Proud Cleopatra, when she met her Roman,   And Cydnus swell'd above the banks, or for   The press of boats or pride:
translation: They told the story of proud Cleopatra meeting her Roman lover, when the river Cydnus flooded either because of the weight of so many boats on it or because it was proud to carry them.

original: a piece of work   So bravely done, so rich, that it did strive   In workmanship and value;
translation: That was such a beautiful piece of work, so expensive looking, that it was hard to tell which was worth more, the expert design or its valuable materials.

original: which I wonder'd   Could be so rarely and exactly wrought,   Since the true life on't was—
translation: I was amazed it was so unusually and beautifully made, since it looked so lifelike—

original: This is true; And this you might have heard of here, by me, Or by some other.
translation: This is true. But you could have heard that from me, right here, or from someone else.

original: More particulars Must justify my knowledge.
translation: I must tell you more details to prove this to you.

original: So they must, Or do your honour injury.
translation: You must, or you will be dishonored.

original: The chimney   Is south the chamber, and the chimney-piece   Chaste Dian bathing:
translation: The chimney is in the south of the room, and it's carved with the virgin goddess Diana washing herself.

original: never saw I figures   So likely to report themselves: the cutter   Was as another nature, dumb;
translation: I never saw carvings that looked so alive. The person who carved them was like a second creator of the world but without the ability to make things speak.

original: outwent her,   Motion and breath left out.
translation: He made her more beautiful than she is in real life, but without the ability to move or breathe.

original: This is a thing Which you might from relation likewise reap, Being, as it is, much spoke of.
translation: That's also something you could have heard about, since it's talked about a lot.

original: The roof o' the chamber   With golden cherubins is fretted:
translation: The roof of the room is decorated with golden angels.

original: her andirons—   I had forgot them—were two winking Cupids   Of silver, each on one foot standing, nicely   Depending on their brands.
translation: The irons in her fireplace—I almost forgot them—were two sparkling silver statues of Cupid, each of them showing him standing on one foot and seeming to lean on the burning wood in the fire.

original: This is her honour!
translation: These details aren't worth as much as her honor!

original: Let it be granted you have seen all this—and praise   Be given to your remembrance—
translation: Even if you did see all these things—and you have a great memory, by the way—

original: the description   Of what is in her chamber nothing saves   The wager you have laid.
translation: describing the stuff in her room does not win the bet you made.

original: Then, if you can,
translation: Well then, assuming you can...

original: Be pale: I beg but leave to air this jewel;
translation: ...then turn pale in shock. Please give me permission to take out this jewel.

original: see!   And now 'tis up again: it must be married   To that your diamond; I'll keep them.
translation: See! Now I've put it away again. It'll get married to your diamond. I'll keep them both.

original: Jove! Once more let me behold it: is it that Which I left with her?
translation: By Jove! Let me see that again. Is that the one I left with her?

original: Sir—I thank her—that:   She stripp'd it from her arm; I see her yet;
translation: Sir, it is, and I'm thankful to her for giving it to me. She took it off her arm. It's as though I can still see her doing it.

original: Her pretty action did outsell her gift,   And yet enrich'd it too: she gave it me, and said   She prized it once.
translation: Her beautiful movement was worth more than the present, but it also made it more valuable. She gave it to me and said it used to be important to her.

original: May be she pluck'd it off To send it me.
translation: Maybe she took it off to send it to me.

original: She writes so to you, doth she?
translation: Does she write that in her letter to you?

original: O, no, no, no! 'tis true. Here, take this too;
translation: Oh, no, no, no! It's true. Here, take this too.

original: It is a basilisk unto mine eye,   Kills me to look on't.
translation: Looking at that ring is like looking a basilisk in the eye: looking at it kills me.

original: Let there be no honour   Where there is beauty; truth, where semblance; love,   Where there's another man:
translation: Beauty and honor should never go together, or truth and outward appearances, or love where there's another man.

original: the vows of women   Of no more bondage be, to where they are made,   Than they are to their virtues; which is nothing.   O, above measure false!
translation: The promises of women shouldn't be trusted any more women can be trusted to act virtuously, which is not at all. Oh, she was so horribly unfaithful!

original: Have patience, sir,   And take your ring again; 'tis not yet won:
translation: Wait, sir, and take your ring back. He hasn't won it yet.

original: It may be probable she lost it; or   Who knows if one of her women, being corrupted,   Hath stol'n it from her?
translation: She probably lost it, or maybe one of her women was convinced to steal it from her.

original: Very true;   And so, I hope, he came by't. Back my ring:
translation: That's very true. I hope that's how he got it. Give me back my ring.

original: Render to me some corporal sign about her,   More evident than this; for this was stolen.
translation: Tell me some mark on her body that's better proof than this, because this was stolen.

original: By Jupiter, I had it from her arm.
translation: I swear by Jupiter, I got it straight from her own arm.

original: Hark you, he swears; by Jupiter he swears.
translation: Listen, he swears. He swears by Jupiter.

original: 'Tis true:—nay, keep the ring—'tis true: I am sure   She would not lose it: her attendants are   All sworn and honourable:—they induced to steal it!   And by a stranger!—No, he hath enjoyed her:
translation: It's true—no, keep the ring. It's true. I'm sure she wouldn't lose it. Her attendants are all loyal and honorable. They couldn't be convinced to steal it by a stranger! No, he's slept with her.

original: The cognizance of her incontinency   Is this: she hath bought the name of whore   thus dearly.
translation: This is a sign she went out of control. All she got in return was the name "whore."

original: There, take thy hire; and all the fiends of hell   Divide themselves between you!
translation: There, take your pay. May all the devils in hell divide their punishments between you and her!

original: Sir, be patient: This is not strong enough to be believed Of one persuaded well of—
translation: Sir, wait. This isn't good enough evidence for anyone who has faith in—

original: Never talk on't; She hath been colted by him.
translation: Never talk about it. They slept together.

original: If you seek   For further satisfying, under her breast—   Worthy the pressing—lies a mole, right proud   Of that most delicate lodging:
translation: If you want more evidence, under her breast (which is worth squeezing) there's a mole, which seems proud to live there.

original: by my life,   I kiss'd it; and it gave me present hunger   To feed again, though full. You do remember   This stain upon her?
translation: I swear, I kissed it. And it made me desire her again, even though I was satisfied. You do remember this mark like a stain on her, don't you?

original: Ay, and it doth confirm   Another stain,
translation: Yes, and it confirms that she's stained in a different way.

original: as big as hell can hold,   Were there no more but it.
translation: Her sins would fill Hell up completely, even if there were no other sins in there.

original: Will you hear more?
translation: Do you want to hear more?

original: Spare your arithmetic: never count the turns; Once, and a million!
translation: That's enough math. Don't count the things you did, whether there were one or a million!

original: I'll be sworn—
translation: I promise—

original: No swearing.   If you will swear you have not done't, you lie;
translation: No promising. If you promise you didn't do it, you're lying.

original: And I will kill thee, if thou dost deny   Thou'st made me cuckold.
translation: And I'll kill you if you deny you slept with my wife.

original: I'll deny nothing.
translation: I won't deny anything.

original: O, that I had her here, to tear her limb-meal!
translation: I wish I had her here, so I could tear her apart!

original: I will go there and do't, i' the court, before   Her father. I'll do something—
translation: I'll go there and do it, in the court, in front of her father. I'll do something—

original: Quite besides   The government of patience! You have won:
translation: I can't stand this any more! You won.

original: Let's follow him, and pervert the present wrath   He hath against himself.
translation: Let's follow him, and talk him out of doing anything terrible to himself.

original: With all my heart.
translation: Absolutely.

original: Is there no way for men to be but women   Must be half-workers?
translation: Is there no way for men to be born except for women to do half the work?

original: We are all bastards;   And that most venerable man which I   Did call my father, was I know not where   When I was stamp'd; some coiner with his tools   Made me a counterfeit:
translation: We're all illegitimate. That respected man I called my father wasn't in the room when I was conceived. I was a fake made by some forger.

original: yet my mother seem'd   The Dian of that time so doth my wife   The nonpareil of this. O, vengeance, vengeance!
translation: But my mother appeared like a virgin goddess then, and my wife appears equally astounding now. Oh, revenge, revenge!

original: Me of my lawful pleasure she restrain'd   And pray'd me oft forbearance; did it with   A prudency so rosy the sweet view on't   Might well have warm'd old Saturn; that I thought her   As chaste as unsunn'd snow.
translation: She held off my sexual desires and often asked me to show restraint. She asked this with such sweet prudence that even a god would have found her attractive. I thought she was as pure as unmelted snow.

original: O, all the devils!   This yellow Iachimo, in an hour,—wast not?—   Or less,—at first?—perchance he spoke not, but,   Like a full-acorn'd boar, a German one,   Cried 'O!' and mounted;
translation: Oh, by all the devils! Unhealthy-looking Iachimo—in an hour, wasn't it? Or less, the first time they laid eyes on each other! Maybe he didn't speak, but like a wild boar cried out and mounted her.

original: found no opposition   But what he look'd for should oppose and she   Should from encounter guard.
translation: He didn't find any resistance except exactly the kind he wanted, not the kind she should have used to stop him.

original: Could I find out   The woman's part in me! For there's no motion   That tends to vice in man, but I affirm   It is the woman's part: be it lying, note it,   The woman's; flattering, hers; deceiving, hers;   Lust and rank thoughts, hers, hers; revenges, hers;
translation: I wish I could find the part of me made out of a woman! If it's lying, that's the part that's made from a woman. If it's buttering people up, it's hers. If it's deceiving people, it's hers. If it's filled with lust and disgusting thoughts, it's hers, definitely hers. If it wants revenge, it's hers.

original: Ambitions, covetings, change of prides, disdain,   Nice longing, slanders, mutability,   All faults that may be named, nay, that hell knows,   Why, hers, in part or all; but rather, all;
translation: If it's filled with ambition, jealousy, changing clothes, disrespect, ridiculous cravings, slander, changes of mind, and all sins that don't have names, no—all the sins there are in hell, then it's partly or all hers. Or actually, all.

original: For even to vice   They are not constant but are changing still   One vice, but of a minute old, for one   Not half so old as that.
translation: Women aren't even faithful to evil, because they're always changing from one sin to the next within thirty seconds.

original: I'll write against them,   Detest them, curse them: yet 'tis greater skill   In a true hate, to pray they have their will:
translation: I'll write about them, hate them, curse them. But it's a better revenge to pray that they get what they want.

original: The very devils cannot plague them better.
translation: Not even the devils themselves could be worse to them than they are to themselves.

original: Now say, what would Augustus Caesar with us?
translation: Tell us, what does August Caesar want from us?

original: When Julius Caesar, whose remembrance yet   Lives in men's eyes and will to ears and tongues   Be theme and hearing ever, was in this Britain   And conquer'd it,
translation: When Julius Caesar, who's still remembered and who will be talked about forever, got to this country of Britain and conquered it,

original: Cassibelan, thine uncle,—   Famous in Caesar's praises, no whit less   Than in his feats deserving it—for him   And his succession granted Rome a tribute,   Yearly three thousand pounds,
translation: your uncle Cassibelan, who is as famous because Caesar praised him as for anything he did to deserve that praise, granted a tribute to Rome that would be paid by him and his successors, of three thousand pounds a year.

original: which by thee lately   Is left untender'd.
translation: You haven't paid it lately.

original: And, to kill the marvel, Shall be so ever.
translation: That's not so surprising—you'll get used to that, because we're never going to pay it again.

original: There be many Caesars,   Ere such another Julius. Britain is   A world by itself;
translation: There'll have to be a lot of rulers before another one as good as Julius Caesar appears. Britain is its own world,

original: and we will nothing pay   For wearing our own noses.
translation: and we won't pay anyone anything for the right to wear our own noses.

original: That opportunity   Which then they had to take from 's, to resume   We have again.
translation: The Romans had to take our freedom by force, and now we have a chance to get it back.

original: Remember, sir, my liege,   The kings your ancestors, together with   The natural bravery of your isle, which stands   As Neptune's park, ribbed and paled in   With rocks unscalable and roaring waters,   With sands that will not bear your enemies' boats,   But suck them up to the topmast.
translation: Remember, husband, that your ancestors were kings and your island is naturally well fortified. It's like a park belonging to Neptune, the god of the sea, guarded by unclimbable rocks and roaring water and quicksand that will sink any boat up to its highest mast.

original: A kind of conquest   Caesar made here; but made not here his brag   Of 'Came' and 'saw' and 'overcame: '
translation: Caesar sort of conquered us, but he wasn't talking about us when he bragged that he "came," "saw," and "conquered."

original: with shame—   That first that ever touch'd him—he was carried   From off our coast, twice beaten; and his shipping—   Poor ignorant baubles!— upon our terrible seas,   Like egg-shells moved upon their surges, crack'd   As easily 'gainst our rocks:
translation: He felt shame for the first time when he was defeated and had to sail away—twice. His ships, like little toys, were as fragile as eggshells on our terrible seas and cracked against our rocks.

original: for joy whereof   The famed Cassibelan, who was once at point—   O giglot fortune!—to master Caesar's sword,   Made Lud's town with rejoicing fires bright   And Britons strut with courage.
translation: Famous Cassibelan, who almost defeated Caesar, and would have except that luck betrayed him, burned bright victory fires in the town of  Lud  and encouraged the Britons to be proud of being brave.

original: Come, there's no more tribute to be paid: our   kingdom is stronger than it was at that time; and,   as I said, there is no moe such Caesars:
translation: Come on, no more tribute needs to be paid. Our kingdom is stronger now than it was then, and, as I said, there are no more kings like Caesar.

original: other of   them may have crook'd noses, but to owe such   straight arms, none.
translation: Some might have crooked noses like him, but their arms aren't as powerful.

original: Son, let your mother end.
translation: Son, let your mother end this conversation.

original: We have yet many among us can gripe as hard as   Cassibelan: I do not say I am one; but I have a   hand.
translation: There are lots of us who can complain as loudly as Cassibelan. I'm not saying I'm one of them, but I do have a hand I can use to fight.

original: Why tribute? why should we pay tribute? If   Caesar can hide the sun from us with a blanket, or   put the moon in his pocket, we will pay him tribute   for light; else, sir, no more tribute, pray you now.
translation: Why tribute? Why should we pay tribute? If Caesar could hide the sun from us with a blanket, or put the moon in hist pocket, we would pay him tribute for light, but otherwise, sir, no tribute, please.

original: You must know,   Till the injurious Romans did extort   This tribute from us, we were free:
translation: You should know, we were free until the cruel Romans forced us to pay this tribute.

original: Caesar's ambition,   Which swell'd so much that it did almost stretch   The sides o' the world, against all colour here   Did put the yoke upon 's;
translation: Caesar was so ambitious that the whole world almost seemed too small for him, and he made us work for him even though that was against our natures.

original: which to shake off   Becomes a warlike people, whom we reckon   Ourselves to be.
translation: A warlike people should try to shake off oppression, and we think that's the kind of people we are.

original: We do.
translation: We do.

original: Say, then, to Caesar,   Our ancestor was that Mulmutius which   Ordain'd our laws, whose use the sword of Caesar   Hath too much mangled;
translation: So tell Caesar that our ancestor Mulmutius made laws for us, and we were forced violently by Caesar to change them.

original: whose repair and franchise   Shall, by the power we hold, be our good deed,   Though Rome be therefore angry:
translation: We'll do our best to do the right thing and go back to the old laws, even if it makes Rome angry.

original: Mulmutius made our  laws,   Who was the first of Britain which did put   His brows within a golden crown and call'd   Himself a king.
translation: Mulmutius, who made those laws, was the first man in Britain to put on a crown and call himself king.

original: I am sorry, Cymbeline,   That I am to pronounce Augustus Caesar—   Caesar, that hath more kings his servants than   Thyself domestic officers—thine enemy:
translation: I'm sorry, Cymbeline, to have to call August Caesar—who has more kings as servants than you have hired help—your enemy.

original: Receive it from me, then: war and confusion   In Caesar's name pronounce I 'gainst thee: look   For fury not to be resisted.
translation: But I have to tell you: in Caesar's name I declare war against you. You won't be able to resist our power.

original: Thus defied,   I thank thee for myself.
translation: So, although I have to declare you an enemy, I thank you for how well you've treated me.

original: Thou art welcome, Caius.   Thy Caesar knighted me; my youth I spent   Much under him; of him I gather'd honour;
translation: You're welcome, Caius. Your emperor knighted me. I spent a long time at his court when I was young, and I was honored by him.

original: Which he to seek of me again, perforce,   Behoves me keep at utterance.
translation: But now I have to say that he's trying to dishonor me.

original: I am perfect   That the Pannonians and Dalmatians for   Their liberties are now in arms; a precedent   Which not to read would show the Britons cold:   So Caesar shall not find them.
translation: I know very well that the  Pannonians and Dalmatians  are now fighting for their freedom. Not to follow their example would make us seem like we didn't care about our freedom. But we'll show Caesar that we do.

original: Let proof speak.
translation: We'll see.

original: His majesty bids you welcome. Make   pastime with us a day or two, or longer:
translation: The king welcomes you here. Stay and enjoy yourself with us for a day or two, or longer.

original: if   you seek us afterwards in other terms, you   shall find us in our salt-water girdle:
translation: If you come back for a different purpose, you'll find us buckled here in our  salt-water belt .

original: if you   beat us out of it, it is yours; if you fall in   the adventure, our crows shall fare the better   for you; and there's an end.
translation: If you can beat us out of it, it's yours. If you fail, you'll give our crows something to eat. That's all.

original: So, sir.
translation: Fine, sir.

original: I know your master's pleasure and he mine: All the remain is 'Welcome!'
translation: I know what your king wants and he knows what I want. All that's left to say is, "Welcome!"

original: How? of adultery? Wherefore write you not   What monster's her accuser?
translation: What? Accused of adultery? Why don't you mention which monster accused her?

original: Leonatus,   O master! what a strange infection   Is fall'n into thy ear! What false Italian,   As poisonous-tongued as handed, hath prevail'd   On thy too ready hearing?
translation: Oh, Leonatus! Master! What a strange idea got into your head! What lying Italian, with as much poison in his words as he has hidden in his pocket, took advantage of your gullibility?

original: Disloyal! No:   She's punish'd for her truth, and undergoes,   More goddess-like than wife-like, such assaults   As would take in some virtue.
translation: Disloyal! No, she's not. She's being punished for being loyal to you, and is standing up to their attempts to change her mind with the strength of a goddess, not of a normal wife.

original: O my master!   Thy mind to her is now as low as were   Thy fortunes.
translation: Oh my master! Your opinion of her is as low as your funds were when you married her.

original: How! that I should murder her?   Upon the love and truth and vows which I   Have made to thy command? I, her? her blood?
translation: What? He's ordering me to murder her, if I want to be true to my affection for him and to the promises I made to obey him? Me, murder her? Shed her blood?

original: If it be so to do good service, never   Let me be counted serviceable. How look I,   That I should seem to lack humanity   so much as this fact comes to?
translation: If that's called being a good servant, I never want to be one. What do I look like? Like someone who is so inhuman he could do something like this?

original: 'Do't: the letter   that I have sent her, by her own command   Shall give thee opportunity.'
translation: "Do it. The letter I sent her will make her give you the opportunity to."

original: O damn'd paper!   Black as the ink that's on thee! Senseless bauble,   Art thou a feodary for this act, and look'st   So virgin-like without?
translation: Oh, damned paper! As black-hearted as the ink on you is black! You unconscious object, how can you be part of this plot, while looking so  innocent  on the outside?

original: Lo, here she comes.   I am ignorant in what I am commanded.
translation: She's coming. I'll act like I don't know what I've been ordered to do.

original: How now, Pisanio!
translation: Hello, Pisanio!

original: Madam, here is a letter from my lord.
translation: Ma'am, here's a letter from my lord.

original: Who? thy lord? that is my lord, Leonatus!   O, learn'd indeed were that astronomer   That knew the stars as I his characters;   He'ld lay the future open.
translation: Who? Your lord? That's my lord, Leonatus! An astronomer who knew the stars as well as I know his handwriting would be very wise! He could tell the future.

original: You good gods,   Let what is here contain'd relish of love,   Of my lord's health, of his content, yet not   That we two are asunder;
translation: Good gods, make what's written in here be about love and about my husband being in good health and happy, but not happy that we're apart.

original: let that grieve him:   Some griefs are med'cinable; that is one of them,   For it doth physic love: of his content,   All but in that! Good wax, thy leave.
translation: Let that make him sad. Some sadnesses can be cured, and that is one of them. Absence makes love stronger. I hope he's happy about everything except this absence! Wax seal, let me open you.

original: Blest be   You bees that make these locks of counsel! Lovers   And men in dangerous bonds pray not alike:
translation: Bless you, you bees who make these seals that keep secrets! Lovers and men in jail don't make this same prayer.

original: Though forfeiters you cast in prison, yet   You clasp young Cupid's tables. Good news, gods!
translation: Although wax seals throw people in jail, they also keep the writings of Cupid, the god of love, secret. Please let this be good news, gods!

original: 'Justice, and your father's wrath, should he take me   in his dominion, could not be so cruel to me, as   you, O the dearest of creatures, would even renew me   with your eyes.
translation: "The justice system and your father's anger, if he captured me in his country, could not be so cruel to me, as seeing you, dearest of creatures, would not make me feel better.

original: Take notice that I am in Cambria,   at Milford-Haven: what your own love will out of   this advise you, follow. So he wishes you all   happiness, that remains loyal to his vow, and your,   increasing in love,   LEONATUS POSTHUMUS.'
translation: You should know I'm in Cambria, at Milford-Haven. You should do what your love for me tells you to do about this. Wishing you all happiness, still loyal to his wedding vow, always more in love with you, Leonatus Posthumus."

original: O, for a horse with wings! Hear'st thou, Pisanio?   He is at Milford-Haven: read, and tell me   How far 'tis thither. If one of mean affairs   May plod it in a week, why may not I   Glide thither in a day?
translation: Oh, I wish I had a horse with wings! Did you hear, Pisanio? He's at Milford-Haven. Look it up and tell me how far away that is. If someone on ordinary business can plod there in a week, why couldn't I glide there in a day?

original: Then, true Pisanio,—   Who long'st, like me, to see thy lord; who long'st,—   let me bate,-but not like me—yet long'st,   But in a fainter kind:—O, not like me;   For mine's beyond beyond—
translation: Then, honest Pisanio, since I know you're eager too to see your master, eager—but wait, not as much as I am, still eager, but less so—oh, not as eager as me, because my eagerness is beyond beyondness.

original: say, and speak thick;   Love's counsellor should fill the bores of hearing,   To the smothering of the sense—how far it is   To this same blessed Milford: and by the way   Tell me how Wales was made so happy as   To inherit such a haven:
translation: Tell me, and speak quickly. Anyone giving information to someone in love should speak so fast they can't hear. How far is it to this blessed Milford? And by the way, tell me how Wales could be so lucky to have such a town in it.

original: but first of all,   How we may steal from hence, and for the gap   That we shall make in time, from our hence-going   And our return, to excuse: but first, how get hence:
translation: But first, tell me how we can sneak away from here and how to explain the time we'll spend going there and coming back. But first, how to get away from here.

original: Why should excuse be born or e'er begot?   We'll talk of that hereafter. Prithee, speak,   How many score of miles may we well ride   'Twixt hour and hour?
translation: Why start thinking of an excuse before you've done anything you need to excuse? We'll talk about that later. Please, tell me, how many tens of miles can we ride per hour?

original: One score 'twixt sun and sun, Madam, 's enough for you:
translation: Twenty miles between sunrise and sunset, ma'am, is enough for you.

original: and too much too.
translation: Or too much.

original: Why, one that rode to's execution, man,   Could never go so slow: I have heard of   riding wagers,   Where horses have been nimbler than the sands   That run i' the clock's behalf.
translation: Someone riding to his own execution could never go that slowly. I have heard of riding bets, when horses ran more quickly than the sand falling through an hourglass.

original: But this is foolery:   Go bid my woman feign a sickness; say   She'll home to her father: and provide me presently   A riding-suit, no costlier than would fit   A franklin's housewife.
translation: But this is nonsense. Go tell my attendant to pretend she's sick. Say she's going home to her father. And then bring me a riding costume no more expensive than something a middle-class housewife would wear.

original: Madam, you're best consider.
translation: Ma'am, you should think this through.

original: I see before me, man: nor here, nor here,   Nor what ensues, but have a fog in them,   That I cannot look through.
translation: I can see in front of me. What's there, or there, or what will happen in the future, I can't see.

original: Away, I prithee;   Do as I bid thee: there's no more to say,   Accessible is none but Milford way.
translation: Go on, please. Do as I told you. There's nothing more to say, and no road to take except the one to Milford.

original: A goodly day not to keep house, with such   Whose roof's as low as ours!
translation: This is a beautiful day to get outside, especially given how low our roof is!

original: Stoop, boys; this gate   Instructs you how to adore the heavens and bows you   To a morning's holy office: the gates of monarchs   Are arch'd so high that giants may jet through   And keep their impious turbans on, without   Good morrow to the sun.
translation: Stoop, boys. This doorway teaches you how to pray by making you bow in the morning. The doorways of kings have such high arches that giants can rush through them and keep their  unholy turbans  on, without saying good morning to the sun by bowing and taking off their hats.

original: Hail, thou fair heaven!   We house i' the rock, yet use thee not so hardly   As prouder livers do.
translation: Hello, beautiful sky! We live in a rock, but we treat you better than people proud of their fancy houses do.

original: Hail, heaven!
translation: Hello, sky!

original: Hail, heaven!
translation: Hello, sky!

original: Now for our mountain sport: up to yond hill;   Your legs are young; I'll tread these flats. Consider,   When you above perceive me like a crow,   That it is place which lessens and sets off;
translation: Now, time for our mountain exercises. Go up to that hill. You have young legs. I'll stay on this plane. Think, when I seem as small as a crow from up there, that it's just context that makes you seem more or less important.

original: And you may then revolve what tales I have told you   Of courts, of princes, of the tricks in war:   This service is not service, so being done,   But being so allow'd:   to apprehend thus,   Draws us a profit from all things we see;
translation: And then think about the stories I told you about courts, about princes, about war. Nothing you do has meaning in itself, but in how people perceive it. Thinking this way makes us learn from everything we see.

original: And often, to our comfort, shall we find   The sharded beetle in a safer hold   Than is the full-wing'd eagle.
translation: We'll often be comforted by seeing a dung beetle in a safer situation than an eagle.

original: O, this life   Is nobler than attending for a cheque,   Richer than doing nothing for a bauble,   Prouder than rustling in unpaid-for silk:
translation: This life is more noble than working for pay, more enjoyable than doing nothing in return for a tiny reward, and brings you more self respect than wearing silk you can't pay for.

original: Such gain the cap of him that makes 'em fine,   Yet keeps his book uncross'd: no life to ours.
translation: People like that are bowed to by the people who make their expensive clothes, but can't pay them for their services. That's no life at all compared to ours.

original: Out of your proof you speak: we, poor unfledged,   Have never wing'd from view o' the nest, nor know not   What air's from home.
translation: We only know what you tell us. We're like poor chicks who have never flown out of sight of the nest and don't know what the air is like farther away from home.

original: Haply this life is best,   If quiet life be best; sweeter to you   That have a sharper known; well corresponding   With your stiff age:
translation: Maybe this life is the best one, if a quiet life is the best kind. It seems easier to you because you've experienced a harder kind of life. It's right for your old age.

original: but unto us it is   A cell of ignorance; travelling a-bed;   A prison for a debtor, that not dares   To stride a limit.
translation: But to us it's a place that keeps us ignorant, like we're traveling without leaving our beds, like we're in jail for debt and don't dare to break out.

original: What should we speak of   When we are old as you? when we shall hear   The rain and wind beat dark December, how,   In this our pinching cave, shall we discourse   The freezing hours away?
translation: What will we talk about when we're as old as you are? When we hear the rain and wind in dark December? Will we spend hours talking in our cold, narrow cave?

original: We have seen nothing;   We are beastly, subtle as the fox for prey,   Like warlike as the wolf for what we eat;   Our valour is to chase what flies;
translation: We have seen nothing. We are like animals, as clever as a fox looking for prey, as brave as a wolf in killing what we need to eat. We use our bravery to chase things that run away.

original: our cage   We make a quire, as doth the prison'd bird,   And sing our bondage freely.
translation: We make our cage into a choir, like captive birds, singing freely about being slaves.
