original: How you speak!   Did you but know the city's usuries   And felt them knowingly; the art o' the court   As hard to leave as keep; whose top to climb   Is certain falling, or so slippery that   The fear's as bad as falling;
translation: What are you saying? If you just knew about and had experienced the city's corruption, the craft of being in court, a craft that is as hard to give up as it is to keep doing... Advancing in court will certainly lead to disaster, or if it doesn't, the fear of a downfall is as bad as a downfall.

original: the toil o' the war,   A pain that only seems to seek out danger   I' the name of fame and honour; which dies i'   the search,   And hath as oft a slanderous epitaph   As record of fair act;
translation: Or the hard work of war—work that only leads to finding danger in the name of fame and honor, which are lost while you're looking for them. And you're just as likely to have lies written on your tombstone as a true report of your brave deeds.

original: nay, many times,   Doth ill deserve by doing well; what's worse,   Must court'sy at the censure:—
translation: No, often you get slandered for acting well. And you'll have to just bow and accept a scolding.

original: O boys, this story   The world may read in me: my body's mark'd   With Roman swords, and my report was once   First with the best of note: Cymbeline loved me,   And when a soldier was the theme, my name   Was not far off:
translation: Oh boys, I'm living proof of this story. My body is scarred by Roman swords, and I was once known as one of the best men. Cymbeline loved me, and whenever people were talking about soldiers, they would mention me.

original: then was I as a tree   Whose boughs did bend with fruit: but in one night,   A storm or robbery, call it what you will,   Shook down my mellow hangings, nay, my leaves,   And left me bare to weather.
translation: I was like a tree whose branches were full of fruit. But one night a storm or robbery, whatever you want to call it, shook down all my ripe fruit, no, more, even my leaves, and left me naked in bad weather.

original: Uncertain favour!
translation: Luck is so unpredictable!

original: My fault being nothing—as I have told you oft—   But that two villains, whose false oaths prevail'd   Before my perfect honour, swore to Cymbeline   I was confederate with the Romans:
translation: I was not at fault—as I have often told you—but two evil men, whose lying promises were trusted more than my honorable reputation, swore that I was collaborating with the Romans.

original: so   Follow'd my banishment, and this twenty years   This rock and these demesnes have been my world;   Where I have lived at honest freedom, paid   More pious debts to heaven than in all   The fore-end of my time.
translation: So I was banished, and for twenty years this rock and this land have been my whole world. I have lived here in honest freedom, and have prayed more than in all the rest of my life before.

original: But up to the mountains!   This is not hunters' language: he that strikes   The venison first shall be the lord o' the feast;   To him the other two shall minister;   And we will fear no poison, which attends   In place of greater state. I'll meet you in the  valleys.
translation: But get up to the mountains! We're not talking like hunters. Whoever hits a deer first will be named the lord of the feast and the other two will serve him. We won't be afraid of being poisoned, unlike those in nobler places. I'll meet you in the valley.

original: How hard it is to hide the sparks of nature!   These boys know little they are sons to the king;   Nor Cymbeline dreams that they are alive.
translation: It's so hard to hide people's natures! These boys have no idea they're the sons of the king, and Cymbeline has no idea they're alive.

original: They think they are mine; and though train'd   up thus meanly   I' the cave wherein they bow, their thoughts do hit   The roofs of palaces, and nature prompts them   In simple and low things to prince it much   Beyond the trick of others. This Polydore,   The heir of Cymbeline and Britain, who   The king his father call'd Guiderius,—
translation: They think they're my sons, and even though I've raised them humbly in this cave that makes them bow, their ambitions reach high enough to hit the roofs of palaces. Even when they're doing simple and low things they seem much more like princes than anyone else. Polydore, Cymbeline's and Britain's heir, was called Guiderius by his father.

original: Jove!   When on my three-foot stool I sit and tell   The warlike feats I have done, his spirits fly out   Into my story:
translation: By Jove! When I sit on my stool and tell them about the deeds I did at war, he puts himself entirely into the story.

original: say 'Thus, mine enemy fell,   And thus I set my foot on 's neck;' even then   The princely blood flows in his cheek, he sweats,   Strains his young nerves and puts himself in posture   That acts my words.
translation: When I say, "My enemy fell in this way, and I put my foot on his neck in this way," his noble blood flows into his face and he sweats and acts my words out.

original: The younger brother, Cadwal,   Once Arviragus, in as like a figure,   Strikes life into my speech and shows much more   His own conceiving.—
translation: His younger brother, Cadwal, once called Arviragus, also acts out my stories but adds his own twist to them.

original: Hark, the game is roused!   O Cymbeline! heaven and my conscience knows   Thou didst unjustly banish me: whereon,   At three and two years old, I stole these babes;
translation: Listen, they've found a deer! Oh Cymbeline! The gods and my conscience know you were wrong to banish me. So, when they were three and two years old, I stole these babies.

original: Thinking to bar thee of succession, as   Thou reft'st me of my lands. Euriphile,   Thou wast their nurse; they took thee for   their mother,   And every day do honour to her grave:
translation: I thought I would take your heirs from you, the way you took my lands. Euriphile, you were their nurse. They thought you were their mother, and visit her grave every day.

original: Myself, Belarius, that am Morgan call'd,   They take for natural father. The game is up.
translation: They think I, Belarius, now called Morgan, am their birth father.  The hunt has started.

original: Thou told'st me, when we came from horse, the place   Was near at hand: ne'er long'd my mother so   To see me first, as I have now.
translation: You told me, when we got off the horses, that we were almost there. My mother never wanted to see me as much before I was born as I want to see my husband now.

original: Pisanio! man!   Where is Posthumus? What is in thy mind,   That makes thee stare thus? Wherefore breaks that sigh   From the inward of thee?
translation: Pisanio! My man! Where is Posthumus? What is it you're thinking that makes you stare like that? Why are you sighing?

original: One, but painted thus,   Would be interpreted a thing perplex'd   Beyond self-explication: put thyself   Into a havior of less fear, ere wildness   Vanquish my staider senses.
translation: A painting of someone making that face would be described as someone helplessly confused. Look less afraid, or I'll get scared.

original: What's the matter?   Why tender'st thou that paper to me, with   A look untender? If't be summer news,   Smile to't before; if winterly, thou need'st   But keep that countenance still.
translation: What's the matter? Why are you handing me that paper with such a mean look? If it's good news, smile. If it's bad, just keep looking the way you do now.

original: My husband's hand!   That drug-damn'd Italy hath out-craftied him,   And he's at some hard point.
translation: My husband's handwriting! Poisonous Italy has done something bad to him, and he's in trouble.

original: Speak, man: thy tongue   May take off some extremity, which to read   Would be even mortal to me.
translation: Speak! You might be able to tell me bad news in a kind way that would make it seem less bad, even if reading it would kill me.

original: Please you, read; And you shall find me, wretched man, a thing The most disdain'd of fortune.
translation: Please, read this. You'll find out I'm the most unlucky man in the world.

original: [Reads]   'Thy mistress, Pisanio, hath played the   strumpet in my bed; the testimonies whereof lie   bleeding in me. I speak not out of weak surmises,   but from proof as strong as my grief and as certain   as I expect my revenge.
translation: [Reading the letter]  "Your mistress, Pisanio, was unfaithful to me. I have proof of this that is very painful to me. I'm not saying this based on weak guesswork, but based on proof as strong as my grief and as certain as my revenge.

original: That part thou, Pisanio,   must act for me, if thy faith be not tainted with   the breach of hers.
translation: You'll have to get that revenge for me, Pisanio, unless you're also betraying me along with her.

original: Let thine own hands take away   her life: I shall give thee opportunity at   Milford-Haven.
translation: Kill her with your own hands. I will give you an opportunity at Milford-Haven.

original: She hath my letter for the purpose   where, if thou fear to strike and to make me certain   it is done, thou art the pandar to her dishonour and   equally to me disloyal.'
translation: She has my letter setting this up. If you are too afraid to attack her and tell me it's been done, you're a pimp for her and as disloyal to me as she is."

original: What shall I need to draw my sword? the paper   Hath cut her throat already.
translation: I don't even need to draw my sword. This letter has already cut her throat.

original: No, 'tis slander,   Whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue   Outvenoms all the worms of Nile, whose breath   Rides on the posting winds and doth belie   All corners of the world:
translation: No, slander did, which has an edge sharper than a sword, a tongue more poisonous than all the snakes in the Nile, and a voice that rides on the winds and spreads lies to all the corners of the world.

original: kings, queens and states,   Maids, matrons, nay, the secrets of the grave   This viperous slander enters. What cheer, madam?
translation: Slander reaches kings, queens, all royals, unmarried women, wives, and even gets into graves to lie about the dead. How are you feeling, ma'am?

original: False to his bed! What is it to be false?   To lie in watch there and to think on him?   To weep 'twixt clock and clock?
translation: Unfaithful to him? What does it mean to be unfaithful? To lie awake in bed and think about him? To weep for an hour?

original: if sleep   charge nature,   To break it with a fearful dream of him   And cry myself awake? that's false to's bed, is it?
translation: If I fall asleep, to have a nightmare about him and wake up crying? Is that being unfaithful to him?

original: Alas, good lady!
translation: Poor lady!

original: I false! Thy conscience witness: Iachimo,   Thou didst accuse him of incontinency;
translation: Me, unfaithful! You should be ashamed. Iachimo, you accused him of being unfaithful.

original: Thou then look'dst like a villain; now methinks   Thy favour's good enough.
translation: You seemed like a bad man to me then, but now you seem fine.

original: Some jay of Italy   Whose mother was her painting, hath betray'd him:   Poor I am stale, a garment out of fashion;
translation: Some loose woman in Italy, who had no mother except her makeup, lied to him. I'm out of date now, like clothes that are out of fashion.

original: And, for I am richer than to hang by the walls,   I must be ripp'd:—to pieces with me!—
translation: Because I'm too expensive a piece of clothing to use to pad walls, I have to be ripped to pieces!

original: O,   Men's vows are women's traitors! All good seeming,   By thy revolt, O husband, shall be thought   Put on for villany; not born where't grows,   But worn a bait for ladies.
translation: Oh, men's promises betray women! Now, because of your betrayal, husband, all men who seem good will be assumed to be lying for some  criminal purpose, their good qualities not natural to them but just bait to catch women.

original: Good madam, hear me.
translation: Ma'am, listen to me.

original: True honest men being heard, like false Aeneas,   Were in his time thought false, and Sinon's weeping   Did scandal many a holy tear, took pity   From most true wretchedness:
translation: After Aeneas betrayed his lover, honest men were assumed to be lying.  Sinon's  fake crying slandered many people's real tears, and made people not feel pity for actual sadness.

original: so thou, Posthumus,   Wilt lay the leaven on all proper men;   Goodly and gallant shall be false and perjured   From thy great fall.
translation: You, Posthumus, will infect all honest men with your wickedness. Good, gallant men will be seen as lying and unfaithful after your terrible failure.

original: Come, fellow, be thou honest:   Do thou thy master's bidding: when thou see'st him,   A little witness my obedience:
translation: Come on, Pisanio, be a good servant and do what your master told you to. When you see him, tell him a little about how obedient I was.

original: look!   I draw the sword myself: take it, and hit   The innocent mansion of my love, my heart;
translation: Look! I'm taking out the sword myself. Take it, and hit the innocent house of of my love, my heart.

original: Fear not; 'tis empty of all things but grief;   Thy master is not there, who was indeed   The riches of it: do his bidding;
translation: Don't be afraid. It's empty of anything but sadness. Your master is not there, and he was the only treasure in it. Do as he says.

original: strike   Thou mayst be valiant in a better cause;   But now thou seem'st a coward.
translation: Stab me. You might be brave when you're asked to do something better than this, but now you seem like a coward.

original: Hence, vile instrument! Thou shalt not damn my hand.
translation: Go away, terrible object! You won't damn my hand.

original: Why, I must die;   And if I do not by thy hand, thou art   No servant of thy master's. Against self-slaughter   There is a prohibition so divine   That cravens my weak hand.
translation: I have to die. If you don't do it, you can't be called your master's servant. It's such a terrible sin to kill yourself that I'm too afraid to do it.

original: Come, here's my heart.   Something's afore't. Soft, soft! we'll no defence;   Obedient as the scabbard.
translation: Come on, here's my heart. There's something in front of it. No, wait! There should be nothing protecting it. I'm as willing to have a sword put in me as a scabbard is.

original: What is here?   The scriptures of the loyal Leonatus,   All turn'd to heresy? Away, away,   Corrupters of my faith! you shall no more   Be stomachers to my heart.
translation: What's in here? The holy writings of Leonatus, which have turned out to be unholy? Go away, go away, you're tempting me to sin! I won't  wear  you over my heart anymore!

original: Thus may poor fools   Believe false teachers: though those that   are betray'd   Do feel the treason sharply, yet the traitor   Stands in worse case of woe.
translation: Foolish people believe liars so easily. Although the people who are betrayed pay the consequences of the betrayal, the betrayer is in an even worse situation.

original: And thou, Posthumus, thou that didst set up   My disobedience 'gainst the king my father   And make me put into contempt the suits   Of princely fellows, shalt hereafter find   It is no act of common passage, but   A strain of rareness:
translation: You, Posthumus, you made me disobey the king my father and made me reject the proposals of princes of my own class. You'll find out soon enough that not everyone would do these things.

original: and I grieve myself   To think, when thou shalt be disedged by her   That now thou tirest on, how thy memory   Will then be pang'd by me.
translation: I'm sad to think that when the woman you're with now dumps you, you'll remember me and feel sad.

original: Prithee, dispatch:   The lamb entreats the butcher: where's thy knife?   Thou art too slow to do thy master's bidding,   When I desire it too.
translation: Go on, do it. The lamb is begging the butcher to kill it. Where's your knife? You're too slow to do what your master wants even though I want it too.

original: O gracious lady, Since I received command to do this business I have not slept one wink.
translation: Good lady, ever since I was ordered to do this I haven't slept a wink.

original: Do't, and to bed then.
translation: Do it, then go to bed.

original: I'll wake mine eye-balls blind first.
translation: I'd rather stay awake until I was blind.

original: Wherefore then   Didst undertake it? Why hast thou abused   So many miles with a pretence? this place?   Mine action and thine own? our horses' labour?   The time inviting thee? the perturb'd court,   For my being absent?
translation: Then why did you start this? Why did you lie to me to get me to come so many miles? To this place? Why did we do all this? Why make our horses work so hard? Why wait so long? Why let the court get upset about my absence?

original: whereunto I never   Purpose return. Why hast thou gone so far,   To be unbent when thou hast ta'en thy stand,   The elected deer before thee?
translation: I'll never go back there. Why have you gone this far, just to change your mind when you were about to do it, and your victim was in front of you like a deer you were hunting?

original: But to win time   To lose so bad employment;
translation: Just to win some time to think about how to get out of doing this terrible thing.

original: in the which   I have consider'd of a course. Good lady,   Hear me with patience.
translation: And I've thought of something in that time. Listen to me patiently.

original: Talk thy tongue weary; speak   I have heard I am a strumpet;
translation: Talk as much as you want, go on. I have read that I am a prostitute,

original: and mine ear   Therein false struck, can take no greater wound,   Nor tent to bottom that. But speak.
translation: and my ear, injured by that lie, can't be wounded any more than that, or cured. But talk.

original: Then, madam, I thought you would not back again.
translation: Then, ma'am, I thought you wouldn't go back.

original: Most like; Bringing me here to kill me.
translation: That makes sense, since you were bringing me here to kill me.

original: Not so, neither:   But if I were as wise as honest, then   My purpose would prove well.
translation: No, not at all. But if I'm as wise as I am honest, this plan will end well.

original: It cannot be   But that my master is abused:   Some villain, ay, and singular in his art.   Hath done you both this cursed injury.
translation: My master must have been lied to. Some criminal, really good at doing what he does, has told this lie about you.

original: Some Roman courtezan.
translation: Some Roman prostitute.

original: No, on my life.   I'll give but notice you are dead and send him   Some bloody sign of it;   for 'tis commanded   I should do so:
translation: No, I promise. I'll tell him you are dead and send him some blood-covered thing to prove it, because that's what he's ordered me to do.

original: you shall be miss'd at court,   And that will well confirm it.
translation: Your absence at court will be noticed, and that will make it seem true.

original: Why good fellow,   What shall I do the while? where bide? how live?
translation: My good man, what will I do in all that time? Where will I live? How will I support myself?

original: Or in my life what comfort, when I am   Dead to my husband?
translation: And how will I be able to stand my life, when my husband wants me dead?

original: If you'll back to the court—
translation: If you want to go back to the court—

original: No court, no father; nor no more ado   With that harsh, noble, simple nothing,
translation: No court, no father. And I don't want to deal anymore with that mean, noble, stupid, no one,

original: That Cloten, whose love-suit hath been to me   As fearful as a siege.
translation: Cloten, whose attempt to win me over was as terrible as being attacked.

original: If not at court, Then not in Britain must you bide.
translation: If you don't want to go back to court, you shouldn't stay in Britain.

original: Where then   Hath Britain all the sun that shines? Day, night,   Are they not but in Britain?
translation: Then where should I go? Is Britain the only place where sun shines? Is it the only place with day and night?

original: I' the world's volume   Our Britain seems as of it, but not in 't;   In a great pool a swan's nest: prithee, think   There's livers out of Britain.
translation: Compared to the whole world, Britain seems like part of it but separate from it. It's like a swan's nest in a huge lake. Please, remember there are people who live outside of Britain.

original: I am most glad   You think of other place. The ambassador,   Lucius the Roman, comes to Milford-Haven   To-morrow:
translation: I am glad you're thinking about other countries. The Roman ambassador, Lucius, is coming to Milford-Haven tomorrow.

original: now, if you could wear a mind   Dark as your fortune is, and but disguise   That which, to appear itself, must not yet be   But by self-danger, you should tread a course   Pretty and full of view;
translation: If you could be secretive given your bad situation, and wear a disguise because your real appearance could only put you in danger, you could go where you want to go safely.

original: yea, haply, near   The residence of Posthumus; so nigh at least   That though his actions were not visible, yet   Report should render him hourly to your ear   As truly as he moves.
translation: Yes, you could even end up next to where Posthumus is staying. Close enough at least that although you couldn't see him, you would hear every hour about whatever he was doing.

original: O, for such means! Though peril to my modesty, not death on't, I would adventure.
translation: What wouldn't I do for that information! This puts my reputation in danger, but it isn't necessarily deadly to it.

original: Well, then, here's the point:   You must forget to be a woman; change   Command into obedience: fear and niceness—   The handmaids of all women, or, more truly,   Woman its pretty self—into a waggish courage:
translation: Well then, here's what I recommend: you should stop being a woman, and exchange obedience for commands, fear and sensitivity (which are natural to women, or really, which are the essence of being a woman) for mischievous courage.

original: Ready in gibes, quick-answer'd, saucy and   As quarrelous as the weasel; nay, you must   Forget that rarest treasure of your cheek,   Exposing it—but, O, the harder heart!   Alack, no remedy!—to the greedy touch   Of common-kissing Titan,
translation: You should be quick to insult people and talk back. Be rude and as violent as a weasel. You should stop protecting your skin (what a terrible thing, but it's the only way!), and let the sun shine on it as it does on everyone else.

original: and forget   Your laboursome and dainty trims, wherein   You made great Juno angry.
translation: And you should give up all the work you put every day into primping, which makes the goddess Juno angry.

original: Nay, be brief I see into thy end, and am almost A man already.
translation: All right, that's enough. I see what you're getting at, and I'm already almost done becoming a man.

original: First, make yourself but like one.   Fore-thinking this, I have already fit—   'Tis in my cloak-bag—doublet, hat, hose, all   That answer to them:
translation: First, just make yourself look like one. Planning on this, I already found a jacket, hat, and pants that will fit you.  They're in my bag.

original: would you in their serving,   And with what imitation you can borrow   From youth of such a season, 'fore noble Lucius   Present yourself, desire his service, tell him   wherein you're happy,—which you'll make him know,   If that his head have ear in music,—doubtless   With joy he will embrace you, for he's honourable   And doubling that, most holy.
translation: Wearing them and acting as much like a man as you can, introduce yourself to noble Lucius, ask to be his servant, and tell him what you're good at. You can show him, if he knows anything about music. I'm sure he'll be glad to help you because he's honorable and, moreover, very religious.

original: Your means abroad,   You have me, rich; and I will never fail   Beginning nor supplyment.
translation: He'll pay for your travel abroad and I'll help with anything I can.

original: Thou art all the comfort   The gods will diet me with. Prithee, away:
translation: You're the only comfort the gods have given me now. Come on, let's go.

original: There's more to be consider'd; but we'll even   All that good time will give us:
translation: We have more to think about, but we'll set everything right as far as we can.

original: this attempt   I am soldier to, and will abide it with   A prince's courage. Away, I prithee.
translation: I will do my best at this, and I'll be as brave as a prince. Let's go, please.

original: Well, madam, we must take a short farewell,   Lest, being miss'd, I be suspected of   Your carriage from the court.
translation: Well, ma'am, I have to say good-bye for now, because if they realize I'm gone from court they'll suspect me of helping you escape.

original: My noble mistress,   Here is a box; I had it from the queen:   What's in't is precious; if you are sick at sea,   Or stomach-qualm'd at land, a dram of this   Will drive away distemper.
translation: Here's a box. I got it from the queen. What's in it is worth a lot. If you're sea-sick, or just have a stomach-ache on land, a mouthful of this will cure you.

original: To some shade,   And fit you to your manhood. May the gods   Direct you to the best!
translation: Find somewhere to hide, and become a man. May the gods protect you!

original: Amen: I thank thee.
translation: Amen. Thank you.

original: Thus far; and so farewell.
translation: That's all I have to say, so goodbye.

original: Thanks, royal sir.   My emperor hath wrote, I must from hence;
translation: Thanks, sir. My emperor wrote to me to leave.

original: And am right sorry that I must report ye   My master's enemy.
translation: I am sorry I'll have to tell him you're his enemy.

original: Our subjects, sir,   Will not endure his yoke;
translation: My subjects won't allow him to oppress us anymore.

original: and for ourself   To show less sovereignty than they, must needs   Appear unkinglike.
translation: And if I were less eager for freedom than they are, I would seem less king-like than them.

original: So, sir: I desire of you A conduct over-land to Milford-Haven. Madam, all joy befal your grace!
translation: All right, sir. I'd like to be accompanied to Milford-Haven over land. Ma'am, my best wishes to you.

original: And you!
translation: And you!

original: My lords, you are appointed for that office; The due of honour in no point omit. So farewell, noble Lucius.
translation: My lords, you're here to accompany him. Treat him well. Goodbye, noble Lucius.

original: Your hand, my lord.
translation: Let me shake your hand, my lord.

original: Receive it friendly; but from this time forth I wear it as your enemy.
translation: Shake it as a friend, but from now on my hand will be your enemy.

original: Sir, the event Is yet to name the winner: fare you well.
translation: Sir, we don't know how the fight will go yet. Goodbye.

original: Leave not the worthy Lucius, good my lords, Till he have cross'd the Severn. Happiness!
translation: Don't leave honorable Lucius, my good lords, until he has crossed the river Severn. Best wishes!

original: He goes hence frowning: but it honours us That we have given him cause.
translation: He's leaving us with a frown. It reflects well on us that we gave him a reason to frown.

original: 'Tis all the better; Your valiant Britons have their wishes in it.
translation: It's the best thing. Your subjects the brave Britons are getting what they want.

original: Lucius hath wrote already to the emperor   How it goes here. It fits us therefore ripely   Our chariots and our horsemen be in readiness:
translation: Lucius already wrote to the emperor about what happened here. So we should prepare our war chariots and cavalry.

original: The powers that he already hath in Gallia   Will soon be drawn to head, from whence he moves   His war for Britain.
translation: The emperor will summon the troops he has stationed in France. From there, he'll attack Britain.

original: 'Tis not sleepy business; But must be look'd to speedily and strongly.
translation: We can't be lazy about this, but have to act quickly and well.

original: Our expectation that it would be thus   Hath made us forward. But, my gentle queen,   Where is our daughter?
translation: I thought this would happen so I prepared for this. But, my dear queen, where is our daughter?

original: She hath not appear'd   Before the Roman, nor to us hath tender'd   The duty of the day: she looks us like   A thing more made of malice than of duty:
translation: She didn't talk to the Roman ambassador, and hasn't come to say good morning to me yet. She's become mean and forgotten her responsibilities.

original: We have noted it. Call her before us; for   We have been too slight in sufferance.
translation: I've noticed. Tell her to come see me. I've been too easygoing with her punishment.

original: Royal sir,   Since the exile of Posthumus, most retired   Hath her life been; the cure whereof, my lord,   'Tis time must do.
translation: Sir, she hasn't been around people very much since Posthumus was exiled. She needs time to get over that.

original: Beseech your majesty,   Forbear sharp speeches to her: she's a lady   So tender of rebukes that words are strokes   And strokes death to her.
translation: Please, your majesty, don't be too hard on her. She's so sensititve to criticism that criticizing her is like hitting her, and hitting her is like killing her.

original: Where is she, sir? How Can her contempt be answer'd?
translation: Where is she, sir? What can I say in response to the disrespect she shows me?

original: Please you, sir, Her chambers are all lock'd; and there's no answer That will be given to the loudest noise we make.
translation: Sir, her rooms are locked, and there was no answer even when we knocked as loudly as we could.

original: My lord, when last I went to visit her,   She pray'd me to excuse her keeping close,
translation: My lord, when I last visited her she asked me to forgive her for staying in her room.

original: Whereto constrain'd by her infirmity,   She should that duty leave unpaid to you,   Which daily she was bound to proffer:
translation: Because she's not feeling well, she said she wouldn't be able to come see you every day the way she used to.

original: this   She wish'd me to make known; but our great court   Made me to blame in memory.
translation: She wanted me to tell you this, but I was distracted by all the things happening in court and forgot.

original: Her doors lock'd? Not seen of late? Grant, heavens, that which I fear Prove false!
translation: Her doors are locked? She hasn't been seen lately? Gods, please let me be wrong about what I'm afraid has happened!

original: Son, I say, follow the king.
translation: Son, follow the king.

original: That man of hers, Pisanio, her old servant, have not seen these two days.
translation: That old servant of hers, Pisanio, hasn't been seen for two days.

original: Go, look after.
translation: Go, follow him.

original: Pisanio, thou that stand'st so for Posthumus!   He hath a drug of mine; I pray his absence   Proceed by swallowing that, for he believes   It is a thing most precious.
translation: Pisanio, you substitute for Posthumus! He has a drug of mine. I pray that he's absent from court because he drank it, believing it was a really effective medicine.

original: But for her,   Where is she gone? Haply, despair hath seized her,   Or, wing'd with fervor of her love, she's flown   To her desired Posthumus:
translation: But as for her, where is she? Maybe she's depressed, or her love has made her run away to see her beloved Posthumus.

original: gone she is   To death or to dishonour; and my end   Can make good use of either: she being down,   I have the placing of the British crown.
translation: She's gone, and is either dead or dishonored. I can work with either of those outcomes. Now she's out of the way, I decide who gets the British crown.

original: How now, my son!
translation: Well, son?

original: 'Tis certain she is fled. Go in and cheer the king: he rages; none Dare come about him.
translation: She's definitely run away. Go and comfort the king. He's furious. No one dares go near him.

original: All the better: may This night forestall him of the coming day!
translation: That's all for the best. I hope he dies tonight!

original: I love and hate her: for she's fair and royal,   And that she hath all courtly parts more exquisite   Than lady, ladies, woman;
translation: I love and hate her. She's beautiful and royal, and all her desirable parts are more beautiful than those of any lady, and ladies, any woman.

original: from every one   The best she hath, and she, of all compounded,   Outsells them all; I love her therefore:
translation: She's taken the best parts from all women, and mixing them all together is worth more than any of them. That's why I love her.

original: but   Disdaining me and throwing favours on   The low Posthumus slanders so her judgment   That what's else rare is choked;
translation: But disrespecting me and throwing herself away on low Posthumus makes her seem so brainless that all her other good qualities don't matter.

original: and in that point   I will conclude to hate her, nay, indeed,   To be revenged upon her. For when fools Shall—
translation: So for that I'll decide to hate her, no, more than that: to be revenged against her. Because when foolish people—

original: Who is here? What, are you packing, sirrah?   Come hither: ah, you precious pander!
translation: Who is here? What are you up to? Come here, you dainty pimp!

original: Villain,   Where is thy lady? In a word; or else   Thou art straightway with the fiends.
translation: You thug, where's your mistress? Tell me now, or I'll kill you and send you to hell.

original: O, good my lord!
translation: Oh, my good lord!

original: Where is thy lady? Or, by Jupiter,—   I will not ask again. Close villain,   I'll have this secret from thy heart, or rip   Thy heart to find it.
translation: Where is your mistress? Or, by Jupiter—I won't ask again. You sneaking thug, I'll get this secret out of your brain, or rip out your brain.

original: Is she with Posthumus?   From whose so many weights of baseness cannot   A dram of worth be drawn.
translation: Is she with Posthumus? He's so worthless, he doesn't have an ounce of goodness in him.

original: Alas, my lord, How can she be with him? When was she missed? He is in Rome.
translation: Unfortunately, sir, how could she be with him? How long has she been gone? He's in Rome.

original: Where is she, sir? Come nearer; No further halting: satisfy me home What is become of her.
translation: Where is she, sir? Come closer. Don't delay any more. Tell me what happened to her.

original: O, my all-worthy lord!
translation: Oh, my excellent lord!

original: All-worthy villain!   Discover where thy mistress is at once,   At the next word:
translation: You excellent thug! Tell me where your mistress is at once, with the next words you say.

original: no more of 'worthy lord!'   Speak, or thy silence on the instant is   Thy condemnation and thy death.
translation: No more of this "excellent lord" stuff! Speak, or your silence will condemn you to death.

original: Then, sir, This paper is the history of my knowledge Touching her flight.
translation: Then, sir, this paper contains everything I know about her escape.

original: Let's see't. I will pursue her Even to Augustus' throne.
translation: Let's see this. I will follow her even as far as Augustus's throne in Rome.

original: Or this, or perish. She's far enough; and what he learns by this May prove his travel, not her danger.
translation: I had no choice except to give him the letter or die. She's far enough away, and what he learns from the letter might make him travel, but won't put her in danger.

original: Hum!
translation: Hmm!

original: I'll write to my lord she's dead. O Imogen, Safe mayst thou wander, safe return again!
translation: I'll write to my master that she's dead. Oh Imogen, travel safely and come back safe!

original: Sirrah, is this letter true?
translation: Sir, is this letter real?

original: Sir, as I think.
translation: I think so, sir.

original: It is Posthumus' hand; I know't. Sirrah, if thou   wouldst not be a villain, but do me true service,   undergo those employments wherein I should have   cause to use thee with a serious industry,
translation: It's Posthumus's handwriting: I recognize it. Sir, if you don't want to be a thug anymore but instead want to be a good servant to me, do the things I tell you as well as you can.

original: that is,   what villany soe'er I bid thee do, to perform it   directly and truly, I would think thee an honest   man:
translation: I mean, whatever criminal acts I ask you to do, do immediately and well. Then I'll think you're an honest man.

original: thou shouldst neither want my means for thy   relief nor my voice for thy preferment.
translation: You'll always be able to count on my money to get you out of trouble and I'll be a character reference for you.

original: Well, my good lord.
translation: All right, my good lord.

original: Wilt thou serve me? for since patiently and   constantly thou hast stuck to the bare fortune of   that beggar Posthumus,
translation: Will you obey me? Given how patiently and loyally you stuck by that beggar Posthumus, who has no money,

original: thou canst not, in the   course of gratitude, but be a diligent follower of   mine: wilt thou serve me?
translation: you'll definitely be loyal to me. Will you obey me?

original: Sir, I will.
translation: Sir, I will.

original: Give me thy hand; here's my purse. Hast any of thy late master's garments in thy possession?
translation: Give me your hand: here's my purse. Do you have access to any of your last master's clothes?

original: I have, my lord, at my lodging, the same suit he wore when he took leave of my lady and mistress.
translation: My lord, I have in my room the outfit he wore when he said goodbye to my mistress.

original: The first service thou dost me, fetch that suit hither: let it be thy lint service; go.
translation: The first thing you'll do in my service is fetch that outfit. It'll be a laundry run. Go.

original: I shall, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: Meet thee at Milford-Haven!—I forgot to ask him one   thing; I'll remember't anon:—even there, thou   villain Posthumus, will I kill thee.
translation: "Meet you at Milford-Haven!" I forgot to ask him one thing. I'll remember what it is soon. You thug, Posthumus, I'll kill you there.

original: I would these   garments were come. She said upon a time—the   bitterness of it I now belch from my heart—that she   held the very garment of Posthumus in more respect   than my noble and natural person together with the   adornment of my qualities.
translation: I wish those clothes were here already. She said once—it was so mean it makes me belch—that she respected Posthumus's clothes more than my noble and well endowed body and all my good qualities combined.

original: With that suit upon my   back, will I ravish her: first kill him, and in her   eyes; there shall she see my valour, which will then   be a torment to her contempt.
translation: Wearing that suit, I'll rape her. First I'll kill him, while she watches. Then she'll see how brave I am, and she'll be sorry about disrespecting me.

original: He on the ground, my   speech of insultment ended on his dead body, and   when my lust hath dined,—which, as I say, to vex   her I will execute in the clothes that she so   praised,—to the court I'll knock her back, foot   her home again.
translation: With him lying on the ground, once my insulting speech to his dead body is over, and when I have satisfied my lust—which, as I said, to get back at her I'll do while wearing the clothes she was so enthusiastic about—I'll drag her back to court, kick her home.

original: She hath despised me rejoicingly,   and I'll be merry in my revenge.
translation: She was happy while insulting me, and I'll be happy to get my revenge on her.

original: Be those the garments?
translation: Are those the clothes?

original: Ay, my noble lord.
translation: Yes, my noble lord.

original: How long is't since she went to Milford-Haven?
translation: How long ago did she go to Milford-Haven?

original: She can scarce be there yet.
translation: She'll be getting there around now.

original: Bring this apparel to my chamber; that is the second   thing that I have commanded thee: the third is,   that thou wilt be a voluntary mute to my design.
translation: Bring these clothes to my room. That is the second order I've given you. The third is, that you won't say anything abut my plan.

original: Be   but duteous, and true preferment shall tender itself   to thee. My revenge is now at Milford: would I had   wings to follow it! Come, and be true.
translation: Just be obedient and I'll promote you. I'll get my revenge at Milford. I wish I had wings so I could get there more quickly. Come on, and be loyal to me.

original: Thou bid'st me to my loss: for true to thee   Were to prove false, which I will never be,   To him that is most true.
translation: You're asking me to do something self-destructive. If I'm loyal to you, I'll betray the most honest man in the world, which I'll never do.

original: To Milford go,   And find not her whom thou pursuest. Flow, flow,   You heavenly blessings, on her! This fool's speed   Be cross'd with slowness; labour be his meed!
translation: Go to Milford, and don't find the woman you're chasing. Bless her, gods! Slow this fool down, and let his only reward be to work hard!

original: I see a man's life is a tedious one:   I have tired myself, and for two nights together   Have made the ground my bed. I should be sick,   But that my resolution helps me.
translation: I see that a man's life is hard. I've tired myself out, and I slept on the ground for two nights in a row. I would have gotten sick, except that I'm determined not to.

original: Milford,   When from the mountain-top Pisanio show'd thee,   Thou wast within a ken: O Jove! I think   Foundations fly the wretched; such, I mean,   Where they should be relieved.
translation: Milford, when Pisanio showed you to me from the mountain-top, you seemed close. Oh, Jove! I think help isn't given to desperate people—I mean, the help that should be given to them.

original: Two beggars told me   I could not miss my way: will poor folks lie,   That have afflictions on them, knowing 'tis   A punishment or trial? Yes; no wonder,   When rich ones scarce tell true. To lapse in fulness   Is sorer than to lie for need, and falsehood   Is worse in kings than beggars.
translation: Two beggars told me I was on the right road. How can poor people lie when they themselves are suffering, when they know what the consequences are? No wonder, given that rich people don't tell the truth either. Sinning when you have everything you need is worse than lying to get what you need, and lying is a worse sin for kings than beggars.

original: My dear lord!   Thou art one o' the false ones. Now I think on thee,   My hunger's gone; but even before, I was   At point to sink for food.
translation: My dear husband! You're one of the liars. Now I'm thinking about you, I'm not hungry any more, even though I was about to faint from hunger.

original: But what is this?   Here is a path to't: 'tis some savage hold:   I were best not to call; I dare not call:   yet famine,   Ere clean it o'erthrow nature, makes it valiant,   Plenty and peace breeds cowards: hardness ever   Of hardiness is mother.
translation: But what's this? There's a path to it. It's some savage's hiding place. I shouldn't call out. I don't dare to call out. But starvation, before it kills you, makes you brave. Prosperity and peace make people cowards. Hardship always makes people strong.

original: Ho! who's here?   If any thing that's civil, speak; if savage,   Take or lend. Ho! No answer? Then I'll enter.
translation: Hello! Who's there? If there's anyone civilized, speak. If you're a savage, take my life or give me something to eat. Hello! No answer? Then I'll go in.

original: Best draw my sword: and if mine enemy   But fear the sword like me, he'll scarcely look on't.   Such a foe, good heavens!
translation: I'd better take out my sword. And if my enemy is as afraid of my sword as I am, he'll barely be able to look at it. Please grant me an enemy like that, gods!

original: You, Polydore, have proved best woodman and   Are master of the feast: Cadwal and I   Will play the cook and servant; 'tis our match:   The sweat of industry would dry and die,   But for the end it works to.
translation: You, Polydore, have shown yourself to be the best hunter and you will be master of the feast. Cadwal and I will play at being cooks and servants. That's what we agreed on. No one would work if they didn't get anything in return.

original: Come; our stomachs   Will make what's homely savoury: weariness   Can snore upon the flint, when resty sloth   Finds the down pillow hard.
translation: Come on, we're hungry enough to think a humble meal tastes delicious. Tired people can fall asleep on hard rock, while lazy people aren't able to sleep even on down pillows.

original: Now peace be here,   Poor house, that keep'st thyself!
translation: Now, may everything be peaceful here, in our house that's been left empty!

original: I am thoroughly weary.
translation: I'm exhausted.

original: I am weak with toil, yet strong in appetite.
translation: I'm tired from working, but hunger makes me strong.

original: There is cold meat i' the cave; we'll browse on that, Whilst what we have kill'd be cook'd.
translation: There's cold food in the cave. We'll snack on that while we cook what we killed.

original: Stay; come not in. But that it eats our victuals, I should think Here were a fairy.
translation: Wait, don't go in. If it weren't eating our food, I'd think it was a fairy.

original: What's the matter, sir?
translation: What's the matter, sir?

original: By Jupiter, an angel! or, if not, An earthly paragon! Behold divineness No elder than a boy!
translation: An angel, by Jupiter! Or, if not, something with no equal on earth! No older than a boy.

original: Good masters, harm me not:   Before I enter'd here, I call'd; and thought   To have begg'd or bought what I have took:
translation: Don't hurt me. I called out before I went in there, and wanted to beg for or buy what I took.

original: good troth,   I have stol'n nought, nor would not, though I had found   Gold strew'd i' the floor. Here's money for my meat:
translation: I promise I haven't stolen anything, and I wouldn't even if I found gold scattered over the floor. Here's money for my food.

original: I would have left it on the board so soon   As I had made my meal, and parted   With prayers for the provider.
translation: I would have left it on the table as soon as I had eaten, and would have left praying for the people who provided it.

original: Money, youth?
translation: Money, young man!

original: All gold and silver rather turn to dirt! As 'tis no better reckon'd, but of those Who worship dirty gods.
translation: Gold and silver should just turn to dirt, since it isn't worth any more than dirt except to people who worship dirty gods.

original: I see you're angry: Know, if you kill me for my fault, I should Have died had I not made it.
translation: I see you're angry. You should know, if you kill me for what I did, I would have died anyway if I hadn't done it.

original: Whither bound?
translation: Where are you heading?

original: To Milford-Haven.
translation: To Milford-Haven.

original: What's your name?
translation: What's your name?

original: Fidele, sir. I have a kinsman who   Is bound for Italy; he embark'd at Milford;
translation: Fidele , sir. A relative of mine is going to Italy. He got on a ship at Milford.

original: To whom being going, almost spent with hunger,   I am fall'n in this offence.
translation: I was going to meet him and almost died of hunger on the way.

original: Prithee, fair youth,   Think us no churls, nor measure our good minds   By this rude place we live in.
translation: Please, handsome youth, don't think we're peasants, and don't make assumptions about our characters based on this wild place we live in.

original: Well encounter'd!   'Tis almost night: you shall have better cheer   Ere you depart: and thanks to stay and eat it.   Boys, bid him welcome.
translation: Welcome! It's almost night. We'll feed you better before you leave, and we'll thank you for staying and eating. Boys, welcome him.

original: Were you a woman, youth, I should woo hard but be your groom. In honesty, I bid for you as I'd buy.
translation: If you were a woman, young man, I would try everything to get you to marry me. Really, that's what I think of you.

original: I'll make't my comfort   He is a man; I'll love him as my brother:
translation: I'll make the best of him being a man: I'll love him like he's my brother.

original: And such a welcome as I'd give to him   After long absence, such is yours: most welcome!   Be sprightly, for you fall 'mongst friends.
translation: And I'll welcome him in the same way I'd welcome my brother after he was gone a long time. You're very welcome. Cheer up, you're among friends now!

original: 'Mongst friends, If brothers.
translation: If we're like brothers, then we're definitely friends.

original: Would it had been so, that they   Had been my father's sons!
translation: I wish it were true and that they were my father's sons!

original: then had my prize   Been less, and so more equal ballasting   To thee, Posthumus.
translation: Then I wouldn't have mattered as much, and you would have seemed more like my equal, Posthumus.

original: He wrings at some distress.
translation: He's sad about something.

original: Would I could free't!
translation: I wish I could do something about it!

original: Or I, whate'er it be, What pain it cost, what danger. God's!
translation: And me, however painful and hard it was to fix it. By the gods!

original: Hark, boys.
translation: Listen, boys.

original: Great men,   That had a court no bigger than this cave,   That did attend themselves and had the virtue   Which their own conscience seal'd them—laying by   That nothing-gift of differing multitudes—   Could not out-peer these twain.
translation: Great men who had a court the size of this cave, who were their own servants and considered themselves virtuous (because the opinions everyone else has of you don't matter) couldn't be nobler than these two.

original: Pardon me, gods!   I'd change my sex to be companion with them,   Since Leonatus's false.
translation: Forgive me, gods, but I would rather be a man so I could be friends with them, especially since Leonatus is untrustworthy.

original: It shall be so.   Boys, we'll go dress our hunt. Fair youth, come in:   Discourse is heavy, fasting;
translation: Let's do that. Boys, let's prepare the meat. Handsome young man, come on in. It's hard to talk when you're hungry.

original: when we have supp'd,   We'll mannerly demand thee of thy story,   So far as thou wilt speak it.
translation: When we have eaten, we'll politely ask you for your story, as much of it as you want to tell us.

original: Pray, draw near.
translation: Please, come closer.

original: The night to the owl and morn to the lark less welcome.
translation: The night is less welcome to owls and the morning to larks than you are to us here.

original: Thanks, sir.
translation: Thank you, sir.

original: I pray, draw near.
translation: Please, come closer.

original: This is the tenor of the emperor's writ:
translation: This is what the emperor writes:

original: That since the common men are now in action   'Gainst the Pannonians and Dalmatians,   And that the legions now in Gallia are   Full weak to undertake our wars against   The fall'n-off Britons, that we do incite   The gentry to this business.
translation: that since the commoners are fighting the Pannonians and Dalmatians, and the legions now in France are too weak to fight the rebelling Britons, we should recruit the nobles to do this.

original: He creates   Lucius preconsul: and to you the tribunes,   For this immediate levy, he commends   His absolute commission. Long live Caesar!
translation: He makes Lucius preconsul, and he's ordering you tribunes to recruit people. Long live Caesar!

original: Is Lucius general of the forces?
translation: Is Lucius leading the forces?

original: Ay.
translation: Yes.

original: Remaining now in Gallia?
translation: He's still in France?

original: With those legions   Which I have spoke of, whereunto your levy   Must be supplyant:
translation: With those legions I mentioned, which you'll supplement with the people you recruit.

original: the words of your commission   Will tie you to the numbers and the time   Of their dispatch.
translation: The documents I gave you will tell you the numbers needed and when they'll leave.

original: We will discharge our duty.
translation: We'll do our duty.

original: I am near to the place where they should meet, if   Pisanio have mapped it truly. How fit his garments   serve me!
translation: I'm near the place where they're supposed to meet, if Pisanio's map is right. His clothes fit me really well!

original: Why should his mistress, who was made by   him that made the tailor, not be fit too? the   rather—saving reverence of the word—for 'tis said   a woman's fitness comes by fits.
translation: Why shouldn't his wife, who was made by the same god who made the tailor who made the clothes,  fit  me just as well? Or rather, as it were, it's said women have fits when you fit well.

original: Therein I must   play the workman. I dare speak it to myself—for it   is not vain-glory for a man and his glass to confer   in his own chamber—
translation: I will have to do some work. If I say so myself—and it's not vanity for a man to look in a mirror in his own room—

original: I mean, the lines of my body are   as well drawn as his; no less young, more strong,   not beneath him in fortunes, beyond him in the   advantage of the time, above him in birth, alike   conversant in general services, and more remarkable   in single oppositions: yet this imperceiverant   thing loves him in my despite.
translation: my body is as attractive as his. I'm as young, stronger, not less rich than he is, more powerful, more noble, able to do the same things, and better at fighting. But this dimwitted thing loves him instead of me.

original: What mortality is!   Posthumus, thy head, which now is growing upon thy   shoulders, shall within this hour be off; thy   mistress enforced; thy garments cut to pieces before   thy face: and all this done, spurn her home to her   father;
translation: Humans are such fools! Posthumus, your head, which is now growing on top of your shoulders, will come off within an hour, your wife will be raped, your clothes will be cut to pieces in front of your face, and all of this done to kick her home to her father.

original: who may haply be a little angry for my so   rough usage; but my mother, having power of his   testiness, shall turn all into my commendations. My   horse is tied up safe:
translation: He may be a little angry at me for my rough treatment of her. But my mother is able to calm him and will make him see that this reflects well on me. My horse is safely tied up.

original: out, sword, and to a sore   purpose! Fortune, put them into my hand! This is   the very description of their meeting-place; and   the fellow dares not deceive me.
translation: Out, sword, and do terrible things! Luck, give them to me! This is exactly the meeting place he described, and that fellow doesn't dare lie to me.

original: You are not well: remain here in the cave; We'll come to you after hunting.
translation: You aren't feeling well. Stay here in the cave. We'll come back to see you after hunting.

original: Brother, stay here. Are we not brothers?
translation: Brother, stay here. We're brothers, aren't we?

original: So man and man should be; But clay and clay differs in dignity, Whose dust is both alike. I am very sick.
translation: Just as men should be to each other. But some men are thought to be worth more than others, even though they're made out of the same stuff. I am very sick.

original: Go you to hunting; I'll abide with him.
translation: You go hunting. I'll stay with him.

original: So sick I am not, yet I am not well;   But not so citizen a wanton as   To seem to die ere sick: so please you, leave me;   Stick to your journal course:
translation: I'm not that sick, although I'm not well. But I won't be like a weak city person and act like I'm dying when I'm just sick. Please, leave me alone. Do what you usually do all day.

original: the breach of custom   Is breach of all. I am ill, but your being by me   Cannot amend me; society is no comfort   To one not sociable:
translation: There's nothing worse than breaking a routine. I am sick, but you staying with me won't make me better. Company is no help for someone who's antisocial.

original: I am not very sick,   Since I can reason of it. Pray you, trust me here:   I'll rob none but myself; and let me die,   Stealing so poorly.
translation: I'm not very sick, since I can talk reasonably. Please, trust me to stay here. I won't rob anyone except myself. Let me die and  steal only from myself.

original: I love thee; I have spoke it How much the quantity, the weight as much, As I do love my father.
translation: I love you. I have already told you how much, and how deeply: as much as I love my father.

original: What! how! how!
translation: What? What did you say?

original: If it be sin to say so, I yoke me   In my good brother's fault: I know not why   I love this youth;
translation: If it's a sin to say that, I'll sin too along with my brother. I don't know why I love this young man.

original: and I have heard you say,   Love's reason's without reason: the bier at door,   And a demand who is't shall die, I'd say   'My father, not this youth.'
translation: I have heard you say that the reason for love is unreasonable. If a coffin were at the door and we were told someone had to die, I'd say, "My father, not this young man."

original: [Aside]   O noble strain!   O worthiness of nature! breed of greatness!
translation: [To himself]  What a noble thing to say! They're so naturally virtuous! And high-born!

original: Cowards father cowards and base things sire base:   Nature hath meal and bran, contempt and grace.
translation: Cowards give birth to cowards and low things give birth to low things. Nature is like grain: it contains flour that you keep and bran you throw away. In the same way, there are low and high people.

original: I'm not their father; yet who this should be,   Doth miracle itself, loved before me.   'Tis the ninth hour o' the morn.
translation: I am not their father. I have no idea who this person is they love more than me.  [ To the others]  It's nine in the morning.

original: Brother, farewell.
translation: Goodbye, brother.

original: I wish ye sport.
translation: Have fun.

original: You health. So please you, sir.
translation: Get better. Let's go, sir.

original: [Aside]   These are kind creatures. Gods, what lies   I have heard!   Our courtiers say all's savage but at court:   Experience, O, thou disprovest report!
translation: [To herself]  These are kind people. I've been told such terrible lies! Our courtiers say everyone who isn't at court is a savage! But my experience shows this isn't true!

original: The imperious seas breed monsters, for the dish   Poor tributary rivers as sweet fish.   I am sick still; heart-sick. Pisanio,   I'll now taste of thy drug.
translation: The seas contain monsters, but the fish that live in little rivers taste just as good. I am still sick—sick with sadness. Pisanio, I'll try your medicine.

original: I could not stir him: He said he was gentle, but unfortunate; Dishonestly afflicted, but yet honest.
translation: I couldn't get him to tell me anything. He said he was a noble, but in a bad situation. He was in trouble, but an honest man.

original: Thus did he answer me: yet said, hereafter I might know more.
translation: He answered me in the same way. But he said I might learn more later.

original: To the field, to the field! We'll leave you for this time: go in and rest.
translation: Let's go, let's hunt! We'll leave you for now. Go inside and rest.

original: We'll not be long away.
translation: We won't be away for long.

original: Pray, be not sick, For you must be our housewife.
translation: Please, don't be sick. You have to be our housewife.

original: Well or ill, I am bound to you.
translation: Sick or healthy, we're in this together.

original: And shalt be ever.
translation: And always will be.

original: This youth, how'er distress'd, appears he hath had Good ancestors.
translation: This young man seems like he's in trouble, but like he's from a good family.

original: How angel-like he sings!
translation: He sings like an angel!

original: But his neat cookery! he cut our roots   In characters,
translation: And his cooking! He cut our root vegetables into the shapes of letters,

original: And sauced our broths, as Juno had been sick   And he her dieter.
translation: and made our soups taste so good that it was as though the goddess Juno were sick and he were in charge of feeding her.

original: Nobly he yokes   A smiling with a sigh, as if the sigh   Was that it was, for not being such a smile;
translation: Nobly, he smiles but sighs, as if the sigh was sighing because it wasn't a beautiful smile.

original: The smile mocking the sigh, that it would fly   From so divine a temple, to commix   With winds that sailors rail at.
translation: The smile makes fun of the sigh, because it flies out from its holy home in that boy to mix with winds that sailors swear at.

original: I do note That grief and patience, rooted in him both, Mingle their spurs together.
translation: I did notice that he seemed to be feeling a combination of sadness and patience, as though those feelings were plants growing together.

original: Grow, patience! And let the stinking elder, grief, untwine His perishing root with the increasing vine!
It is great morning. Come, away!— Who's there?
translation: It's midmorning. Come on, let's go—who's there?

original: I cannot find those runagates; that villain Hath mock'd me. I am faint.
translation: I can't find those runaways. That thug was lying to me. I feel faint.

original: 'Those runagates!'   Means he not us? I partly know him: 'tis   Cloten, the son o' the queen.
translation: "Those runaways!" He must mean us! I sort of know him. It's Cloten, the queen's son.

original: I fear some ambush.   I saw him not these many years, and yet   I know 'tis he. We are held as outlaws: hence!
translation: I'm worried there are people here to ambush us. I haven't seen him for years, but I know it's him. We're outlaws. Let's go!

original: He is but one: you and my brother search What companies are near: pray you, away; Let me alone with him.
translation: There's only one of him. You and my brother should look to see if there are other people here. Go, please. Leave me alone with him.

original: Soft! What are you That fly me thus? some villain mountaineers? I have heard of such. What slave art thou?
translation: Wait! Who are you, running at me like that? Some mountain-climbing bandit? I have heard of those people. What kind of slave are you?

original: A thing More slavish did I ne'er than answering A slave without a knock.
translation: I never did anything more slavish than what I'm doing right now: answering a slave without hitting him.

original: Thou art a robber, A law-breaker, a villain: yield thee, thief.
translation: You're a robber, a law-breaker, a thug. Surrender, thief.

original: To who? to thee? What art thou? Have not I   An arm as big as thine? a heart as big?
translation: To who? To you? Who are you? Don't I have an arm as strong as yours? A heart that's just as good?

original: Thy words, I grant, are bigger, for I wear not   My dagger in my mouth. Say what thou art,   Why I should yield to thee?
translation: Your words are stronger, but that's because I don't insult strangers. Tell me who you are. Why would I surrender to you?

original: Thou villain base, Know'st me not by my clothes?
translation: You low thug, don't you know who I am from my clothes?

original: No, nor thy tailor, rascal, Who is thy grandfather: he made those clothes, Which, as it seems, make thee.
translation: No, or from your tailor, you good-for-nothing, who I bet is your grandfather. He made your clothes, and it seems that your clothes make you who you are.

original: Thou precious varlet, My tailor made them not.
translation: You ridiculous criminal, my tailor didn't make them.

original: Hence, then, and thank The man that gave them thee. Thou art some fool; I am loath to beat thee.
translation: Go away, then, and go thank the man who gave them to you. You're some fool. It would be wrong to beat you up.

original: Thou injurious thief, Hear but my name, and tremble.
translation: You insulting thief, hear my name and be afraid.

original: What's thy name?
translation: What's your name?

original: Cloten, thou villain.
translation: Cloten, you thug.

original: Cloten, thou double villain, be thy name,   I cannot tremble at it:
translation: Cloten, you double thug, if that's your name, fine, but I can't be afraid of it.

original: were it Toad, or   Adder, Spider,   'Twould move me sooner.
translation: If it were Toad, or Snake, or Spider, it would be more likely to scare me.

original: To thy further fear, Nay, to thy mere confusion, thou shalt know I am son to the queen.
translation: To scare you more, to completely overwhelm you, I'll tell you I'm the queen's son.

original: I am sorry for 't; not seeming So worthy as thy birth.
translation: I'm sorry to hear it. You don't live up to your noble family.

original: Art not afeard?
translation: Aren't you afraid?

original: Those that I reverence those I fear, the wise: At fools I laugh, not fear them.
translation: I'm afraid of the people I respect, wise people. I laugh at fools—I'm not afraid of them.

original: Die the death:   When I have slain thee with my proper hand,
translation: Die, then. When I have killed you with my own hand,

original: I'll follow those that even now fled hence,   And on the gates of Lud's-town set your heads:   Yield, rustic mountaineer.
translation: I'll keep following those people who ran away just now, and I'll stick all of your heads on the gates of Lud-town. Surrender, you hillbilly.

original: No companies abroad?
translation: You didn't see any soldiers out there?

original: None in the world: you did mistake him, sure.
translation: Not a single one. You must have gotten him confused with someone else.

original: I cannot tell: long is it since I saw him,   But time hath nothing blurr'd those lines of favour   Which then he wore;
translation: I can't tell. It's a long time since I saw him, but time hasn't made me forget what he looked like.

original: the snatches in his voice,   And burst of speaking, were as his: I am absolute   'Twas very Cloten.
translation: The sound of his voice and the way he speaks in short bursts sounded like what he remembered. I'm absolutely sure it was Cloten himself.

original: In this place we left them: I wish my brother make good time with him, You say he is so fell.
translation: We left them here. I hope my brother deals with him quickly, since you say he's so dangerous.

original: Being scarce made up,   I mean, to man, he had not apprehension   Of roaring terrors;
translation: When he was barely grown up, he wasn't afraid of the most horrible danger.

original: for the effect of judgment   Is oft the cause of fear. But, see, thy brother.
translation: Having good judgement is often what makes you afraid. There's your brother.

original: This Cloten was a fool, an empty purse;   There was no money in't:
translation: This Cloten fellow was a fool, like an empty purse with no money in it.

original: not Hercules   Could have knock'd out his brains, for he had none:
translation: Even Hercules couldn't have knocked out his brains, because he didn't have any.

original: Yet I not doing this, the fool had borne   My head as I do his.
translation: But if I hadn't done this, the fool would have been carrying my head the way I'm carrying his.

original: What hast thou done?
translation: What did you do?

original: I am perfect what: cut off one Cloten's head,   Son to the queen, after his own report;
translation: I know exactly what I did: cut off some man Cloten's head, a son of the queen according to him.

original: Who call'd me traitor, mountaineer, and swore   With his own single hand he'ld take us in   Displace our heads where—thank the gods!—they grow,   And set them on Lud's-town.
translation: He called me a traitor, a mountain bandit, and promised that he himself would take our heads off the necks they grow on now (thank the gods!) and stick them on the gates of Lud's-town.

original: We are all undone.
translation: We're done for.

original: Why, worthy father, what have we to lose,   But that he swore to take, our lives?
translation: But father, what do we have to lose except what he promised he'd take, our lives?

original: The law   Protects not us: then why should we be tender   To let an arrogant piece of flesh threat us,   Play judge and executioner all himself,   For we do fear the law?
translation: The law doesn't protect us, so why should we let an arrogant lump threaten us and play at being a judge and executioner all by himself, because we're afraid of the law?

original: What company   Discover you abroad?
translation: How many soldiers did you see around here?

original: No single soul   Can we set eye on; but in all safe reason   He must have some attendants.
translation: We didn't see a single one, but we should assume he had attendants with him.

original: Though his humour   Was nothing but mutation, ay, and that   From one bad thing to worse; not frenzy, not   Absolute madness could so far have raved   To bring him here alone;
translation: Although he was unpredictable and went from one bad idea to another, it wasn't complete madness that brought him so far from court alone.

original: although perhaps   It may be heard at court that such as we   Cave here, hunt here, are outlaws, and in time   May make some stronger head;
translation: Although maybe it was said at court that people like us who live in caves here and hunt here are outlaws and could band together to be stronger.

original: the which he hearing—   As it is like him—might break out, and swear   He'ld fetch us in; yet is't not probable   To come alone, either he so undertaking,   Or they so suffering:
translation: He heard this and it's very likely that he stood up and promised he'd round us up. But it's not likely either that he would want to come alone  or that they would let him.

original: then on good ground we fear,   If we do fear this body hath a tail   More perilous than the head.
translation: We should worry  that he was the  head  of a company of dangerous soldiers.

original: Let ordinance Come as the gods foresay it: howsoe'er, My brother hath done well.
translation: Let the future go the way the gods want it to. However it goes, my brother did the right thing.

original: I had no mind To hunt this day: the boy Fidele's sickness Did make my way long forth.
translation: I didn't feel like hunting today. The boy Fidele's sickness was weighing on me all the way here.

original: With his own sword,   Which he did wave against my throat, I have ta'en   His head from him:
translation: I took his head from him with his own sword, which he waved at my throat.

original: I'll throw't into the creek   Behind our rock; and let it to the sea,   And tell the fishes he's the queen's son, Cloten:   That's all I reck.
translation: I'll throw that sword into the stream behind our cave, and let it float to the sea and tell the fish he's the queen's son, Cloten. That's all I have to say.

original: I fear 'twill be revenged: Would, Polydote, thou hadst not done't! though valour Becomes thee well enough.
translation: I'm worried they'll get their revenge for this. I wish you hadn't done this, Polydore! Though your bravery is a credit to you.

original: Would I had done't   So the revenge alone pursued me!
translation: I wish I had done it so I was the only one who would be punished!

original: Polydore,   I love thee brotherly, but envy much   Thou hast robb'd me of this deed:
translation: Polydore, I love you as a brother but I'm jealous because you robbed me of the opportunity to kill him.

original: I would revenges,   That possible strength might meet, would seek us  through   And put us to our answer.
translation: I hope they follow us looking for revenge so we can fight them.

original: Well, 'tis done:   We'll hunt no more to-day, nor seek for danger   Where there's no profit. I prithee, to our rock;
translation: Well, it's done. We won't hunt any more today, or look for danger pointlessly. Please, let's go back  to our cave.

original: You and Fidele play the cooks: I'll stay   Till hasty Polydore return, and bring him   To dinner presently.
translation: You and Fidele cook something. I'll stay here until reckless Polydore returns, and bring him home for dinner soon.

original: Poor sick Fidele!   I'll weringly to him:
translation: Poor sick Fidele! I'll hurry back to him.

original: to gain his colour   I'ld let a parish of such Clotens' blood,   And praise myself for charity.
translation: To make him look less pale I'd stab a whole parish full of fools like Cloten and be proud of my good deed.

original: O thou goddess,   Thou divine Nature, how thyself thou blazon'st   In these two princely boys!
translation: Oh you goddess, holy Nature, you show yourself so clearly in these two princely boys!

original: They are as gentle   As zephyrs blowing below the violet,   Not wagging his sweet head; and yet as rough,   Their royal blood enchafed, as the rudest wind,   That by the top doth take the mountain pine,   And make him stoop to the vale.
translation: They are as gentle as breezes blowing around a violet without shaking it, but as rough when they get angry as the strongest wind that knocks a pine down from a mountain into a valley.

original: 'Tis wonder   That an invisible instinct should frame them   To royalty unlearn'd, honour untaught,   Civility not seen from other, valour   That wildly grows in them, but yields a crop   As if it had been sow'd.
translation: It's amazing how by instinct they act like royalty, with honor that was never taught to them, politeness that is unmatched in anyone, and bravery that grows wild but grows as well as if it were deliberately planted.

original: Yet still it's strange   What Cloten's being here to us portends,   Or what his death will bring us.
translation: But I don't know what Cloten being here means for us, or what the consequences of his death will be.

original: Where's my brother?   I have sent Cloten's clotpoll down the stream,   In embassy to his mother:
translation: Where's my brother? I sent Cloten's head down the stream, with a message to his mother.

original: his body's hostage   For his return.
translation: His body stays here as a hostage to make sure he comes back.

original: My ingenious instrument! Hark, Polydore, it sounds! But what occasion Hath Cadwal now to give it motion? Hark!
translation: My instrument! Listen, Polydore, it's being played! But why has Cadwal brought it out? Listen!

original: Is he at home?
translation: Is he at home?

original: He went hence even now.
translation: He just left here.

original: What does he mean? since death of my dear'st mother   it did not speak before. All solemn things   Should answer solemn accidents.
translation: What is he doing? It hasn't been played since my dear mother died. You should only seem to be sad because something sad has happened.

original: The matter?   Triumphs for nothing and lamenting toys   Is jollity for apes and grief for boys.   Is Cadwal mad?
translation: What's going on? Celebrating over nothing and crying over nothing is happiness fit only for apes and sadness for boys. Is Cadwal crazy?

original: Look, here he comes, And brings the dire occasion in his arms Of what we blame him for.
translation: Look, here he comes, and carries in his arm the sad thing we were saying he should be responding to.

original: The bird is dead   That we have made so much on.
translation: The bird we were so fond of is dead.

original: I had rather   Have skipp'd from sixteen years of age to sixty,   To have turn'd my leaping-time into a crutch,   Than have seen this.
translation: I would rather have skipped from sixteen years old to sixty, to give up my leaping time in my youth for a crutch, than see this.

original: O sweetest, fairest lily! My brother wears thee not the one half so well As when thou grew'st thyself.
translation: Oh, sweetest, most beautiful lily! Your brother isn't wearing you half as well on his arms as you wore yourself when you were alive.

original: O melancholy!   Who ever yet could sound thy bottom? find   The ooze, to show what coast thy sluggish crare   Might easiliest harbour in?
translation: Oh, this is a bottomless sorrow! It's like a deep sea with no mud on the bottom to make you hope you were approaching a harbor with your slow sadness!

original: Thou blessed thing!   Jove knows what man thou mightst have made; but I,   Thou diedst, a most rare boy, of melancholy.   How found you him?
translation: You blessed thing! Jove knows what kind of man you would have become. But I know you died as a unique boy, of sadness. How did you find him?

original: Stark, as you see:
translation: Dead, as you see.

original: Thus smiling, as some fly hid tickled slumber,   Not as death's dart, being laugh'd at;   his   right cheek   Reposing on a cushion.
translation: Smiling like this, as though he had been tickled by a  fly while sleeping, laughing as though death's arrow had not hit him, lying on his right side.

original: Where?
translation: Where?

original: O' the floor;   His arms thus leagued:
translation: On the floor, with his arms together like this.

original: I thought he slept, and put   My clouted brogues from off my feet, whose rudeness   Answer'd my steps too loud.
translation: I thought he was sleeping, and took my heavy shoes off my feet because they made my steps too loud.

original: Why, he but sleeps:   If he be gone, he'll make his grave a bed;
