translation: He's only sleeping. If he's gone, we'll make his grave a bed.

original: With female fairies will his tomb be haunted,   And worms will not come to thee.
translation: May only female fairies haunt his tomb, so that worms won't come.

original: With fairest flowers   Whilst summer lasts and I live here, Fidele,   I'll sweeten thy sad grave:
translation: I'll decorate your sad grave with the most beautiful flowers while it's still summer and I still live here, Fidele.

original: thou shalt not lack   The flower that's like thy face, pale primrose, nor   The azured harebell, like thy veins, no, nor   The leaf of eglantine, whom not to slander,   Out-sweeten'd not thy breath:
translation: You'll have the flower that's like your face, pale primrose, and the harebell as blue as your veins, and the eglantine, which it's no slander to say is not sweeter than your breath was.

original: the ruddock would,   With charitable bill,—O bill, sore-shaming   Those rich-left heirs that let their fathers lie   Without a monument!—bring thee all this;
translation: A robin would kindly bring you all these flowers in his bill, making those heirs who inherit a lot of money and don't build a tomb for their fathers ashamed!

original: Yea, and furr'd moss besides, when flowers are none,   To winter-ground thy corse.
translation: Yes, and soft moss too, when their are no flowers, to make your body ready for winter.

original: Prithee, have done;   And do not play in wench-like words with that   Which is so serious.
translation: Please, stop talking, and don't play around with girlish words about something so serious.

original: Let us bury him,   And not protract with admiration what   Is now due debt. To the grave!
translation: Let's bury him, and not keep being amazed about something that's over and done with. To the grave!

original: Say, where shall's lay him?
translation: Where will we bury him?

original: By good Euriphile, our mother.
translation: Next to our mother, good Euriphile.

original: Be't so:   And let us, Polydore, though now our voices   Have got the mannish crack, sing him to the ground,   As once our mother;
translation: All right. And let us, Polydore, even though our voices have changed, sing goodbye to him as we did with our mother.

original: use like note and words,   Save that Euriphile must be Fidele.
translation: Let's use the same tune and words, substituting Fidele for Euriphile.

original: Cadwal,   I cannot sing: I'll weep, and word it with thee;
translation: Cadwall, I can't sing. I'll cry and talk with you.

original: For notes of sorrow out of tune are worse   Than priests and fanes that lie.
translation: But sad songs out of tune are worse than lying priests and temples.

original: We'll speak it, then.
translation: We'll say it then.

original: Great griefs, I see, medicine the less; for Cloten   Is quite forgot. He was a queen's son, boys;
translation: I see that a greater sadness makes you forget a lesser one, because Cloten has been completely forgotten. He was a queen's son, boys.

original: And though he came our enemy, remember   He was paid for that: though mean and   mighty, rotting   Together, have one dust, yet reverence,   That angel of the world, doth make distinction   Of place 'tween high and low.
translation: And although he came as our enemy, remember that he paid for that. Although high and low people rot into the same dust, still, respect for higher classes distinguishes high and low people while they are alive.

original: Our foe was princely   And though you took his life, as being our foe,   Yet bury him as a prince.
translation: Our enemy was a prince and although you took his life because he was your enemy, you should bury him in a way fitting for a prince.

original: Pray You, fetch him hither.
translation: Please, fetch him.

original: Thersites' body is as good as Ajax',   When neither are alive.
translation: Thersites's body is as good as Ajax's when they're both dead.

original: If you'll go fetch him, We'll say our song the whilst. Brother, begin.
translation: If you go fetch him, we'll say our song while you're gone. Brother, you begin.

original: Nay, Cadwal, we must lay his head to the east; My father hath a reason for't.
translation: No, Cadwal, his head has to point east. My father has some reason for that.

original: 'Tis true.
translation: It's true.

original: Come on then, and remove him.
translation: Come on then, move him.

original: So. Begin.
translation: All right. Begin.

original: Fear no more the heat o' the sun,   Nor the furious winter's rages;   Thou thy worldly task hast done,
translation: Don't fear the heat of the sun anymore Or the furious rage of winter You have finished your work in this world

original: Home art gone, and ta'en thy wages:   Golden lads and girls all must,   As chimney-sweepers, come to dust.
translation: And have gone home and collected your pay. Golden boys and girls all must, Like dandelions, turn into dust.

original: Fear no more the frown o' the great;   Thou art past the tyrant's stroke;   Care no more to clothe and eat;
translation: Don't fear the anger of important people any more, You are safe from a tyrant's punishment. Don't worry anymore about finding clothes and food.

original: To thee the reed is as the oak:   The sceptre, learning, physic, must   All follow this, and come to dust.
translation: Now sticks are the same thing as oak trees to you. Kings' power, knowledge, and medicine must All turn to dust in the same way.

original: Fear no more the lightning flash,
translation: Don't be afraid of lightning bolts.

original: Nor the all-dreaded thunder-stone;
translation: Or the thunder that everyone is afraid of.

original: Fear not slander, censure rash;
translation: Don't be afraid of slander or thoughtless criticism.

original: Thou hast finish'd joy and moan:
translation: You're through with joy and sighing.

original: All lovers young, all lovers must Consign to thee, and come to dust.
No exorciser harm thee!
translation: May no exorcist harm you!

original: Nor no witchcraft charm thee!
translation: And no witchcraft cast a spell on you!

original: Ghost unlaid forbear thee!
translation: May restless ghosts leave you alone!

original: Nothing ill come near thee!
translation: May nothing evil come near you!

original: Quiet consummation have; And renowned be thy grave!
We have done our obsequies: come, lay him down.
translation: We have finished our ceremony. Come on, set him down.

original: Here's a few flowers; but 'bout midnight, more:   The herbs that have on them cold dew o' the night   Are strewings fitt'st for graves.
translation: Here are a few flowers. We'll pick more around midnight. Plants that have cold nighttime dew on them are the most appropriate decorations for graves.

original: Upon their faces.   You were as flowers, now wither'd: even so   These herblets shall, which we upon you strew.   Come on, away: apart upon our knees.
translation: Put them on their faces. You used to be like flowers, and have wilted. These plants we are scattering on you will too. Come on, let's go. Let's pray elsewhere.

original: The ground that gave them first has them again:   Their pleasures here are past, so is their pain.
translation: The earth that they came from now holds them again. Their joys here are past, and so is their pain.

original: [Awaking]   Yes, sir, to Milford-Haven; which is   the way?—   I thank you.—By yond bush?—Pray, how far thither?
translation: [Waking up]  Yes, sir, how do I get to Milford-Haven?—Thank you.—Past that bush?—How far away is it?—

original: 'Ods pittikins! can it be six mile yet?—   I have gone all night. 'Faith, I'll lie down and sleep.   But, soft! no bedfellow!—O god s and goddesses!
translation: God, can it be another six miles?—I've walked all night. I'll lie down and sleep. But wait! Not with anyone!—Oh gods and goddesses!

original: These flowers are like the pleasures of the world;   This bloody man, the care on't. I hope I dream;   For so I thought I was a cave-keeper,   And cook to honest creatures:
translation: These flowers are like the pleasures of this world, and this bloody man is like the sadness in it. I hope I'm dreaming. I thought I lived in a cave, and was a cook for honest men.

original: but 'tis not so;   'Twas but a bolt of nothing, shot at nothing,   Which the brain makes of fumes: our very eyes   Are sometimes like our judgments, blind.
translation: But that's not true. It was a lightning bolt that came from nowhere and hit nothing, invented by my brain. People's eyes are sometimes as bad as their judgement.

original: Good faith,   I tremble stiff with fear: but if there be   Yet left in heaven as small a drop of pity   As a wren's eye, fear'd gods, a part of it!
translation: Goodness, I'm still trembling with fear. But if there is still left in heaven a drop of pity as small as a bird's eye, please give me a part of it, gods!

original: The dream's here still: even when I wake, it is   Without me, as within me; not imagined, felt.
translation: The dream's still here. Even when I wake up, it's outside me as well as inside. I can feel it, not just imagine it.

original: A headless man! The garments of Posthumus!   I know the shape of's leg: this is his hand;   His foot Mercurial; his Martial thigh;   The brawns of Hercules: but his Jovial face   Murder in heaven?—How!—'Tis gone.
translation: A headless man! Posthumus's clothes! I recognize the shape of his leg. This is his hand. His foot like  Mercury's . His thigh like  Mars's . His muscles like  Hercules's . But his Jove-like face—oh gods!—how could this be—it's gone.

original: Pisanio,   All curses madded Hecuba gave the Greeks,   And mine to boot, be darted on thee! Thou,   Conspired with that irregulous devil, Cloten,   Hast here cut off my lord. To write and read   Be henceforth treacherous! Damn'd Pisanio   Hath with his forged letters,—damn'd Pisanio—   From this most bravest vessel of the world   Struck the main-top!
translation: Pisanio, may all the curses  Hecuba  threw at the Greeks, added to mine, be thrown at you! You plotted with that strange devil, Cloten, to kill my lord in this way. May writing and reading be considered treason from now on! Damned Pisanio with his fake letters - damned Pisanio - knocked the main mast off the best ship in the world!

original: O Posthumus! alas,   Where is thy head? where's that? Ay me!   where's that?   Pisanio might have kill'd thee at the heart,   And left this head on.
translation: Oh Posthumus! Where is your head? Where is it? Where is it? Pisanio could have stabbed you in the heart and left your head on.

original: How should this be? Pisanio?   'Tis he and Cloten: malice and lucre in them   Have laid this woe here. O, 'tis pregnant, pregnant!
The drug he gave me, which he said was precious   And cordial to me, have I not found it   Murderous to the senses? That confirms it home:   This is Pisanio's deed, and Cloten's:
translation: The drug he gave me, which he said was effective and would make me feel better—didn't it knock me out? That confirms it. Pisanio did this, and Cloten!

original: O!   Give colour to my pale cheek with thy blood,   That we the horrider may seem to those   Which chance to find us: O, my lord, my lord!
translation: Oh! I'll put your blood on my pale cheek so that we seem more frightening to anyone who happens to see us. Oh, my husband, my husband!

original: To them the legions garrison'd in Gailia,   After your will, have cross'd the sea, attending   You here at Milford-Haven with your ships:
translation: The troops stationed in Gallia, as you asked, crossed the sea to meet you here in Milford-Haven with your ships.

original: They are in readiness.
translation: They're ready.

original: But what from Rome?
translation: But what have you heard from Rome?

original: The senate hath stirr'd up the confiners   And gentlemen of Italy, most willing spirits,   That promise noble service:
translation: The senate encouraged those remaining at home and the noblemen of Italy, willing fighters who will serve well.

original: and they come   Under the conduct of bold Iachimo,   Syenna's brother.
translation: They are coming under the leadership of brave Iachimo, the Duke of Siena's brother.

original: When expect you them?
translation: When do you expect them to get here?

original: With the next benefit o' the wind.
translation: When the next wind blows this way.

original: This forwardness   Makes our hopes fair. Command our present numbers   Be muster'd; bid the captains look to't.
Now, sir,   What have you dream'd of late of this war's purpose?
translation: [To the SOOTHSAYER]  Now, sir, what have you dreamed about the outcome of this war?

original: Last night the very gods show'd me a vision—   I fast and pray'd for their intelligence—thus:
translation: Last night the gods themselves showed me a vision. I had fasted and prayed for news from them.

original: I saw Jove's bird, the Roman eagle, wing'd   From the spongy south to this part of the west,   There vanish'd in the sunbeams:
translation: I saw Jove's bird, the Roman eagle, fly from the marshy south to this part of the west and vanish into the sun.

original: which portends—   Unless my sins abuse my divination—   Success to the Roman host.
translation: This means, unless my sins make me interpret this wrong, that the Roman army will win.

original: Dream often so,   And never false. Soft, ho! what trunk is here   Without his top? The ruin speaks that sometime   It was a worthy building.
translation: May you often dream that, and never be wrong about it. Wait! Whose body is here without a head? What's left of this ruined building seems to show that it was once noble.

original: How! a page!   Or dead, or sleeping on him? But dead rather;   For nature doth abhor to make his bed   With the defunct, or sleep upon the dead.   Let's see the boy's face.
translation: A page boy! Dead or sleeping? Dead probably, because it isn't natural to sleep next to or on dead people. Let's see the boy's face.

original: He's alive, my lord.
translation: He's alive, sir.

original: He'll then instruct us of this body. Young one,   Inform us of thy fortunes, for it seems   They crave to be demanded.
translation: Then he'll tell us about this body. Young one, tell us what happened to you, because it's impossible not to ask.

original: Who is this   Thou makest thy bloody pillow? Or who was he   That, otherwise than noble nature did,   Hath alter'd that good picture? What's thy interest   In this sad wreck? How came it? Who is it?   What art thou?
translation: Who is this you're using as a bloody pillow? Or who was it who did this to him so unnaturally? What do you have to do with this tragedy? How did it happen? Who is it? Who are you?

original: I am nothing: or if not,   Nothing to be were better. This was my master,   A very valiant Briton and a good,   That here by mountaineers lies slain.
translation: I'm no one, or if not, I wish I were. This was my master, a very brave and good British man, killed by mountain bandits.

original: Alas!   There is no more such masters: I may wander   From east to occident, cry out for service,   Try many, all good, serve truly, never   Find such another master.
translation: There are no more masters like this one. I could wander from east to west, calling out I wanted to serve someone, try many masters, all good, serve them well, and never find another master like this one.

original: 'Lack, good youth! Thou movest no less with thy complaining than Thy master in bleeding: say his name, good friend.
translation: Poor young man! You're making me as sad by complaining as your master is by bleeding. Tell me his name, good friend.

original: Richard du Champ.
translation: Richard du Champ.

original: If I do lie and do No harm by it, though the gods hear, I hope They'll pardon it.—Say you, sir?
translation: If I lie and don't hurt anyone by doing it, even though the gods hear, I hope they'll forgive me. What did you say, sir?

original: Thy name?
translation: What's your name?

original: Fidele, sir.
translation: Fidele, sir.

original: Thou dost approve thyself the very same:   Thy name well fits thy faith, thy faith thy name.
translation: You show yourself to be exactly what that name means: faithful. Your name fits your faithfulness well, your faithfulness fits your name.

original: Wilt take thy chance with me? I will not say   Thou shalt be so well master'd, but, be sure,   No less beloved.
translation: Will you take your chances with me? I won't say I'll be as good a master, but be sure I won't love you any less than he did.

original: The Roman emperor's letters,   Sent by a consul to me, should not sooner   Than thine own worth prefer thee: go with me.
translation: Even if the Roman emperor sent a consul to me with a letter praising you, it wouldn't make me value you any more than your own virtue does. Come with me.

original: I'll follow, sir. But first, an't please the gods,   I'll hide my master from the flies, as deep   As these poor pickaxes can dig;
translation: I'll follow you, sir. But first, if it's all right with the gods, I'll hide my master from the flies, as deep as I can dig with my hands.

original: and when   With wild wood-leaves and weeds I ha' strew'd his  grave,   And on it said a century of prayers,   Such as I can, twice o'er, I'll weep and sigh;
translation: And when I have covered his grave with wild leaves and plants I'll say a hundred prayers over it, the ones I know, twice, and cry and sigh.

original: And leaving so his service, follow you,   So please you entertain me.
translation: And leaving his employment in that way, I'll follow you if you would like to employ me.

original: Ay, good youth!   And rather father thee than master thee.   My friends,   The boy hath taught us manly duties:
translation: Good young man! I wish I were your father instead of your master. My friends, the boy has shown us how to be a man.

original: let us   Find out the prettiest daisied plot we can,   And make him with our pikes and partisans   A grave: come, arm him.
translation: Let's find the prettiest patch of daisies we can and dig him a grave with our spears and poles. Come on, give him a weapon.

original: Boy, he is preferr'd   By thee to us, and he shall be interr'd   As soldiers can. Be cheerful; wipe thine eyes   Some falls are means the happier to arise.
translation: Boy, you've given him a good recommendation and he will be buried as well as soldiers can manage. Cheer up. Wipe your eyes. Some misfortunes lead to situations that make you happier.

original: Again; and bring me word how 'tis with her.
translation: Go back, and report to me how she's feeling.

original: A fever with the absence of her son,   A madness, of which her life's in danger. Heavens,   How deeply you at once do touch me!
translation: She got feverish after her son disappeared, went crazy, and might die. Gods, you're so cruel to me all at once!

original: Imogen,   The great part of my comfort, gone; my queen   Upon a desperate bed, and in a time   When fearful wars point at me; her son gone,   So needful for this present:
translation: Imogen, my main source of comfort, is gone. My queen is sick in bed, and I'm about to go to war. Her son is necessary for that, but he's gone.

original: it strikes me, past   The hope of comfort. But for thee, fellow,   Who needs must know of her departure and   Dost seem so ignorant, we'll enforce it from thee   By a sharp torture.
translation: I don't have any hope left. You, you must know something about where she went even though you're acting ignorant. We'll get it out of you by some horrible torture.

original: Sir, my life is yours;   I humbly set it at your will;
translation: Sir, my life belongs to you. You can do whatever you want with it.

original: but, for my mistress,   I nothing know where she remains, why gone,   Nor when she purposes return. Beseech your highness,   Hold me your loyal servant.
translation: But as for my mistress, I don't know where she is, why she left, or when she plans to come back. Please, your highness, believe I'm a loyal servant to you.

original: Good my liege,   The day that she was missing he was here:   I dare be bound he's true and shall perform   All parts of his subjection loyally.
translation: Your highness, he was here the day she went missing. I promise he's honest and will do his duty loyally.

original: For Cloten,   There wants no diligence in seeking him,   And will, no doubt, be found.
translation: As for Cloten, we're doing everything we can to find him and I'm sure we will.

original: The time is troublesome.
translation: This is a hard time.

original: We'll slip you for a season; but our jealousy Does yet depend.
translation: I'll let you go for now, but you're not necessarily getting out of being punished.

original: So please your majesty,   The Roman legions, all from Gallia drawn,   Are landed on your coast,
translation: Your majesty, the Roman legions have left Gallia and landed on your coast,

original: with a supply   Of Roman gentlemen, by the senate sent.
translation: along with some Roman nobles sent by the senate.

original: Now for the counsel of my son and queen! I am amazed with matter.
translation: I wish my son and queen were here to advise me! I don't know what to do.

original: Good my liege,   Your preparation can affront no less   Than what you hear of: come more, for more   you're ready:
translation: Your highness, you were prepared for this many troops. If more arrive, you're ready for them too.

original: The want is but to put those powers in motion   That long to move.
translation: You only have to give your waiting troops their marching orders.

original: I thank you. Let's withdraw;   And meet the time as it seeks us.
translation: Thank you. Let's leave, and do what we need to.

original: We fear not   What can from Italy annoy us; but   We grieve at chances here. Away!
translation: I'm not afraid of how Italy can annoy us. But I'm sad about what's happened here. Let's go!

original: I heard no letter from my master since   I wrote him Imogen was slain: 'tis strange:   Nor hear I from my mistress who did promise   To yield me often tidings: neither know I   What is betid to Cloten; but remain   Perplex'd in all.
translation: I haven't heard anything from my master since I wrote to him that Imogen was killed. It's strange. I haven't heard from my mistress either, even though she promised to write to me often. Nor do I know what happened to Cloten. I'm puzzled about everything.

original: The heavens still must work.   Wherein I am false I am honest; not true, to be true.
translation: The gods have to work this out. By lying I'm being honest.

original: These present wars shall find I love my country,   Even to the note o' the king, or I'll fall in them.   All other doubts, by time let them be clear'd:
translation: In this coming war I will show I love my country as much as the king does, or I'll die in it. Let time answer any other questions.

original: Fortune brings in some boats that are not steer'd.
translation: Luck sometimes brings boats safely to shore that don't have anyone steering them.

original: The noise is round about us.
translation: There's noise all around us.

original: Let us from it.
translation: Let's run from it.

original: What pleasure, sir, find we in life, to lock it From action and adventure?
translation: What is the point of a life safe from fighting and adventures?

original: Nay, what hope   Have we in hiding us?
translation: And what hope do we have in being able to hide?

original: This way, the Romans   Must or for Britons slay us, or receive us   For barbarous and unnatural revolts   During their use, and slay us after.
translation: This way, either the Romans will kill us for being Britons, or use us to start a violent rebellion and kill us afterwards.

original: Sons,   We'll higher to the mountains; there secure us.
translation: Sons, let's go higher up the mountains and find a safe place there.

original: To the king's party there's no going:
translation: We can't join the king's side.

original: newness   Of Cloten's death—we being not known, not muster'd   Among the bands—may drive us to a render   Where we have lived, and so extort from's that   Which we have done,
translation: Cloten's recent death and us not being known by anyone in the army may force us to reveal where we used to live and what we did.

original: whose answer would be death   Drawn on with torture.
translation: The result would be that we would be tortured to death.

original: This is, sir, a doubt In such a time nothing becoming you, Nor satisfying us.
translation: That's a dishonorable fear for you to have, and we don't agree.

original: It is not likely   That when they hear the Roman horses neigh,   Behold their quarter'd fires, have both their eyes   And ears so cloy'd importantly as now,
translation: It isn't likely that when they can hear the Roman horses neighing, see their campfires, and have so many important things to look at and listen to,

original: That they will waste their time upon our note,   To know from whence we are.
translation: that they will waste time wondering where we came from.

original: O, I am known   Of many in the army: many years,   Though Cloten then but young, you see, not wore him   From my remembrance.
translation: Oh, many people in the army know me. After many years, although Cloten was very young then, you see, I could still recognize him.

original: And, besides, the king   Hath not deserved my service nor your loves;   Who find in my exile the want of breeding,   The certainty of this hard life;
translation: And besides, the king hasn't deserved my help or for you to love him. By exiling me he forced you to be badly raised and to live this hard life.

original: aye hopeless   To have the courtesy your cradle promised,   But to be still hot summer's tamings and   The shrinking slaves of winter.
translation: You can't have the noble training you should have by birth, but instead have to work in the heat of summer and the cold of winter.

original: Than be so   Better to cease to be. Pray, sir, to the army:   I and my brother are not known;
translation: It would be better to die than to live like that. Please sir, let's go to the army. No one knows me and my brother.

original: yourself   So out of thought, and thereto so o'ergrown,   Cannot be question'd.
translation: They've forgotten you so completely that no one will question you.

original: By this sun that shines,   I'll thither: what thing is it that I never   Did see man die! scarce ever look'd on blood,   But that of coward hares, hot goats, and venison!
translation: By the sun, I'm going. How is it that I have never seen a man die? I've hardly seen blood, except of cowardly hares, lustful goats, and deer!

original: Never bestrid a horse, save one that had   A rider like myself, who ne'er wore rowel   Nor iron on his heel!
translation: I've never ridden a horse, except one that was used to a rider like me who has  never worn a spur!

original: I am ashamed   To look upon the holy sun, to have   The benefit of his blest beams, remaining   So long a poor unknown.
translation: I am ashamed to look at the holy sun, to be given the gift of its blessed beams, while remaining unknown and poor for so long.

original: By heavens, I'll go:   If you will bless me, sir, and give me leave,   I'll take the better care,
translation: I'll go, by the gods. If you give me your blessing and permission, sir, I'll be better off,

original: but if you will not,   The hazard therefore due fall on me by   The hands of Romans!
translation: but if you don't want to, I'll take my chances fighting the Romans!

original: So say I amen.
translation: I say the same thing.

original: No reason I, since of your lives you set   So slight a valuation, should reserve   My crack'd one to more care.
translation: There's no reason for me, since you care so little about your lives, to take care of my old one.

original: Have with you, boys!   If in your country wars you chance to die,   That is my bed too, lads, an there I'll lie:   Lead, lead.
translation: Let's go, boys! If you happen to die in your country's war, then I will too. Lead on.

original: The time seems long; their blood thinks scorn, Till it fly out and show them princes born.
translation: They're impatient. Their noble blood will now reveal itself proving them to be princes.

original: Yea, bloody cloth, I'll keep thee, for I wish'd   Thou shouldst be colour'd thus. You married ones,   If each of you should take this course, how many   Must murder wives much better than themselves   For wrying but a little!
translation: Yes, bloody cloth, I'll keep you, because I wanted you to be this color. You who are married, if all of you did this, so many of you would murder wives who are much better than you just for straying a bit!

original: O Pisanio!   Every good servant does not all commands:   No bond but to do just ones.
translation: Oh Pisanio! Good servants don't obey every order. Their duty is just to obey the moral ones.

original: Gods! if you   Should have ta'en vengeance on my faults, I never   Had lived to put on this: so had you saved   The noble Imogen to repent, and struck   Me, wretch more worth your vengeance.
translation: Gods, if you had taken revenge on me for my sins, I would never has lived long enough to do this and you would have given the noble Imogen a chance to repent and punished me, who deserve it more.

original: But, alack,   You snatch some hence for little faults; that's love,   To have them fall no more: you some permit   To second ills with ills, each elder worse,   And make them dread it, to the doers' thrift.
translation: But sadly you kill some of us for small sins. That shows your love for those people, because you keep them from sinning worse. Some you allow to do evil after evil, each one worse, so that they are afraid of your revenge but can only be punished once.

original: But Imogen is your own: do your best wills,   And make me blest to obey! I am brought hither   Among the Italian gentry, and to fight   Against my lady's kingdom: 'tis enough   That, Britain, I have kill'd thy mistress; peace!   I'll give no wound to thee.
translation: But Imogen is with you now. Do what you want, and bless me for obeying you! I am brought here along with the Italian nobles, to fight against my wife's country. It's enough that I've killed your ruler, Britain. Let's be at peace! I won't attack you.

original: Therefore, good heavens,   Hear patiently my purpose: I'll disrobe me   Of these Italian weeds and suit myself   As does a Briton peasant: so I'll fight   Against the part I come with; so I'll die   For thee, O Imogen, even for whom my life   Is every breath a death;
translation: So, gods, listen to what I mean to do:  I'll take off these Italian clothes and dress like a British peasant. So I'll fight against the army I came with. And that way I'll die for you, oh Imogen, since I already feel like I'm dying for you with every breath I take.

original: and thus, unknown,   Pitied nor hated, to the face of peril   Myself I'll dedicate. Let me make men know   More valour in me than my habits show.
translation: And so, unknown, neither pitied nor hated, I'll face danger. Let me show more bravery in this than I usually do.

original: Gods, put the strength o' the Leonati in me!   To shame the guise o' the world, I will begin   The fashion, less without and more within.
translation: Gods, give me the strength of a Leonatus! To make the world feel ashamed, I'll turn the usual fashion around by making myself seem less noble on the outside and more on the inside.

original: The heaviness and guilt within my bosom   Takes off my manhood:
translation: The sadness and guilt in my heart make me less of a man.

original: I have belied a lady,   The princess of this country, and the air on't   Revengingly enfeebles me; or could this carl,   A very drudge of nature's, have subdued me   In my profession?
translation: I lied about a woman, the princess of this country, and the country's air in revenge makes me weak, or how else could this peasant, this manual laborer, be better at my job than I am?

original: Knighthoods and honours, borne   As I wear mine, are titles but of scorn.
translation: Knighthoods and honors like the ones I have are worth nothing except as insults to me.

original: If that thy gentry, Britain, go before   This lout as he exceeds our lords, the odds   Is that we scarce are men and you are gods.
translation: If your nobles, Britain, surpass this oaf in fighting even as he surpasses our own nobles, it would seem that we're barely men and you're gods.

original: Stand, stand! We have the advantage of the ground;
translation: Stand your ground! We have the advantage in this place.

original: The lane is guarded: nothing routs us but   The villany of our fears.
translation: They can't sneak up on us in this alley. Nothing is making us run away except that we are afraid.

original: Stand, stand, and fight!
translation: Stand your grounds and fight!

original: Away, boy, from the troops, and save thyself; For friends kill friends, and the disorder's such As war were hoodwink'd.
translation: Run, boy, away from the army and save yourself. Friends are killing friends and it's as much of a mess as if we were all blindfolded.

original: 'Tis their fresh supplies.
translation: It's because they just got fresh troops.

original: It is a day turn'd strangely: or betimes Let's reinforce, or fly.
translation: The day went unexpectedly. Let's reinforce the troops soon or run away.

original: Camest thou from where they made the stand?
translation: Did you come from where they made a stand?

original: I did. Though you, it seems, come from the fliers.
translation: I did. But it seems like you were one of the people who ran away.

original: I did.
translation: I was.

original: No blame be to you, sir; for all was lost,   But that the heavens fought:
translation: I don't blame you, sir, because there was no hope except that the gods fought for us.

original: the king himself   Of his wings destitute, the army broken,   And but the backs of Britons seen, all flying   Through a straight lane;
translation: The king was trapped alone, the army beaten up, and no one could see anything except the backs of Britons running away through a narrow alley.

original: the enemy full-hearted,   Lolling the tongue with slaughtering, having work   More plentiful than tools to do't, struck down   Some mortally, some slightly touch'd, some falling   Merely through fear;
translation: The enemy, rejoicing, was eager to slaughter them, with more people to kill than they had weapons to do it with. Some people were killed, some a little injured, some just fell down from fear.

original: that the straight pass was damm'd   With dead men hurt behind, and cowards living   To die with lengthen'd shame.
translation: The narrow way was dammed up with dead men hit in the back, and cowards who stayed alive to die of shame later.

original: Where was this lane?
translation: Where was this alley?

original: Close by the battle, ditch'd, and wall'd with turf;   Which gave advantage to an ancient soldier,   An honest one, I warrant; who deserved   So long a breeding as his white beard came to,   In doing this for's country:
translation: Next to the battlefield, with ditches on the sides and walls made of grass. This gave an opportunity to an ancient solder, an honest one I bet. He deserved to be made as noble as his white beard was long for doing this in the service of his country.

original: athwart the lane,   He, with two striplings-lads more like to run   The country base than to commit such slaughter   With faces fit for masks, or rather fairer   Than those for preservation cased, or shame—   Made good the passage;
translation: He, along with two young boys more likely to run races in the countryside than kill people this way, with faces attractive enough to make masks out of, or rather more beautiful than anyone whose face was made into a mask to remind people of their virtue or shame—they protected the passageway.

original: cried to those that fled,   'Our Britain s harts die flying, not our men:   To darkness fleet souls that fly backwards. Stand;   Or we are Romans and will give you that   Like beasts which you shun beastly, and may save,   But to look back in frown: stand, stand.'
translation: They called to the men running away: "British deer die while running away, not British men. The souls of people who run away go to hell. Stand your ground, or we will act like Romans and treat you like animals because you're running away like animals. You can save yourselves by just turning around and frowning. Stand your ground."

original: These three,   Three thousand confident, in act as many—   For three performers are the file when all   The rest do nothing—with this word 'Stand, stand,'   Accommodated by the place, more charming   With their own nobleness, which could have turn'd   A distaff to a lance, gilded pale looks,   Part shame, part spirit renew'd;
translation: These three were as confident as if there were three thousand of them, and had the same effect as three thousand—because three people can make a difference when no one else is doing anything. They said "stand your ground" and looked at home where they were, and convinced people by their example, which could even have turned a woman's stick for spinning wool into a spear.

original: that some,   turn'd coward   But by example—O, a sin in war,   Damn'd in the first beginners!—gan to look   The way that they did, and to grin like lions   Upon the pikes o' the hunters.
translation: They made people seem less afraid, partly because they were ashamed to and partly because their courage came back. Some people, who were acting like cowards just because everyone else was—which is a sin in war and the people who began this trend should be damned!—began to act the same as the three men and to bare their teeth like lions at hunters' spears.

original: Then began   A stop i' the chaser, a retire, anon   A rout, confusion thick; forthwith they fly   Chickens, the way which they stoop'd eagles;
translation: Then the chase ended, the enemy fell back and was defeated, and there was nothing but confusion in their ranks. Immediately they ran like chickens when before they acted like eagles.

original: slaves,   The strides they victors made: and now our cowards,   Like fragments in hard voyages, became   The life o' the need: having found the backdoor open   Of the unguarded hearts, heavens, how they wound!
translation: They went back like slaves over the space they first crossed like conquerors. And now those who were cowards at first on our side, like crumbs that save your life when you're starving on a long journey, saved the day. Finding the enemies' backs unprotected, they stabbed them to the heart!

original: Some slain before; some dying; some their friends   O'er borne i' the former wave: ten, chased by one,   Are now each one the slaughter-man of twenty:   Those that would die or ere resist are grown   The mortal bugs o' the field.
translation: They trampled over some men who had been killed before, some who were dying, some who fell over in the crowd. Before, ten men were chased by one, but those men turned around and killed twenty. The men who chose to die rather than give up became the terror of the battlefield.

original: This was strange chance A narrow lane, an old man, and two boys.
translation: This was a strange coincidence: a narrow road, an old man, and two boys.

original: Nay, do not wonder at it: you are made   Rather to wonder at the things you hear   Than to work any.
translation: No, don't be amazed. It's your nature to be amazed at things you hear about rather than do anything yourself.

original: Will you rhyme upon't,   And vent it for a mockery?
translation: Are you going to make a poem about it and act it out?

original: Here is one:   'Two boys, an old man twice a boy, a lane,   Preserved the Britons, was the Romans' bane.'
translation: Here's one: "Two boys, an old man in his second childhood, and a road saved the British and destroyed the Romans."

original: Nay, be not angry, sir.
translation: Don't be angry, sir?

original: 'Lack, to what end?   Who dares not stand his foe, I'll be his friend;
translation: Why should I? I'll be friends with anyone who doesn't dare stay and fight his enemy.

original: For if he'll do as he is made to do,   I know he'll quickly fly my friendship too.   You have put me into rhyme.
translation: Because if he does what is natural to him, I know he'll run away from my friendship too. You made me rhyme.

original: Farewell; you're angry.
translation: Goodbye: you're angry?

original: Still going?
translation: Still running away?

original: This is a lord! O noble misery,   To be i' the field, and ask 'what news?' of me!   To-day how many would have given their honours   To have saved their carcasses!
translation: That was a lord? Oh what a noble hardship, to be in the battlefield and ask me "what's going on?" Today so many chose to give up their honor to save their bodies!

original: took heel to do't,   And yet died too! I, in mine own woe charm'd,   Could not find death where I did hear him groan,   Nor feel him where he struck:
translation: They ran to do it, but died anyway! I, cloaked in my own sadness, couldn't find death even where I heard him groaning, and couldn't get hit by him even where he was striking people down.

original: being an ugly monster,   'Tis strange he hides him in fresh cups, soft beds,   Sweet words; or hath more ministers than we   That draw his knives i' the war.
translation: He's an ugly monster, so it's strange he hides in refreshing cups, soft beds, and sweet words, and has more minions than there are soldiers taking knives out to serve him in the war.

original: Well, I will find him   For being now a favourer to the Briton,   No more a Briton, I have resumed again   The part I came in: fight I will no more,   But yield me to the veriest hind that shall   Once touch my shoulder.
translation: Well, because he's on the British side, I won't be a British soldier anymore. I'll go back to the side I came here with. I won't fight any more, but surrender to the lowest soldier who just touches me on the shoulder once.

original: Great the slaughter is   Here made by the Roman; great the answer be   Britons must take.
translation: The Romans killed a lot of people here, and the Britons will punish them for it.

original: For me, my ransom's death;   On either side I come to spend my breath;   Which neither here I'll keep nor bear again,   But end it by some means for Imogen.
translation: My prize will be death. I've fought on both sides, but instead of sticking with one or the other I'll die for Imogen's sake.

original: Great Jupiter be praised! Lucius is taken. 'Tis thought the old man and his sons were angels.
translation: May great Jupiter be praised! Lucius has been captured. It's believed that the old man and his sons were angels.

original: There was a fourth man, in a silly habit, That gave the affront with them.
translation: There was a fourth man, in humble clothes, who fought with them.

original: So 'tis reported: But none of 'em can be found. Stand! who's there?
translation: I've heard that said. But none of them can be found. Stop! Who's there?

original: A Roman, Who had not now been drooping here, if seconds Had answer'd him.
translation: A Roman, who wouldn't have been stuck here if people had come to his help.

original: Lay hands on him; a dog!   A leg of Rome shall not return to tell   What crows have peck'd them here.
translation: Grab him. He's a dog! Not even a single Roman leg will make it home to report what crows pecked it here.

original: He brags   his service   As if he were of note: bring him to the king.
translation: He's bragging about his fighting as if he's important. Bring him to the king.

original: You shall not now be stol'n, you have locks upon you; So graze as you find pasture.
translation: You won't be rescued, you're locked up. So you can eat whatever you find.

original: Ay, or a stomach.
translation: Or whatever you're hungry for.

original: Most welcome, bondage! for thou art a way,   think, to liberty: yet am I better   Than one that's sick o' the gout;
translation: Welcome, slavery! You are a way to find freedom. I'm better off than someone sick with gout.

original: since he had rather   Groan so in perpetuity than be cured   By the sure physician, death, who is the key   To unbar these locks.
translation: He would prefer to suffer forever than to be cured by that talented doctor, death, the key to these locks.

original: My conscience, thou art fetter'd   More than my shanks and wrists: you good gods, give me   The penitent instrument to pick that bolt,   Then, free for ever! Is't enough I am sorry?
translation: My consciousness, you're less free than my legs and arms. Good gods, give me the pick to pick that lock, then I'll be free forever! Is it enough that I'm sorry for what I did?

original: So children temporal fathers do appease;   Gods are more full of mercy. Must I repent?   I cannot do it better than in gyves,   Desired more than constrain'd: to satisfy,   If of my freedom 'tis the main part, take   No stricter render of me than my all.
translation: That's how children get their fathers to forgive them. Gods are more merciful. Do I have to repent? I couldn't do it better than while tied up. And it's more that I want to than that I have to. As a punishment, just take everything I have from me and no more.

original: I know you are more clement than vile men,   Who of their broken debtors take a third,   A sixth, a tenth, letting them thrive again   On their abatement:
translation: I know you're kinder than disgusting humans, who take a third of what people in debt owe, or a sixth or a tenth, and leave them the rest so they can earn their money back.

original: that's not my desire:   For Imogen's dear life take mine; and though   'Tis not so dear, yet 'tis a life; you coin'd it:
translation: That's not what I want. In return for Imogen's precious life, take mine. Although it's not as precious, it's still a life. You created it.

original: 'Tween man and man they weigh not every stamp;   Though light, take pieces for the figure's sake:   You rather mine, being yours:
translation: Humans don't weigh every coin we exchange. Even if they're  lighter than they should be , we accept that they have a certain value because of the image stamped onto them. There's even more reason for you to take mine since I was created in your image.

original: and so, great powers,   If you will take this audit, take this life,   And cancel these cold bonds. O Imogen!   I'll speak to thee in silence.
translation: And so, gods, examine this financial record and cancel the loan. Oh Imogen! I'll speak to you by staying silent.

original: No more, thou thunder-master, show   Thy spite on mortal flies:   With Mars fall out, with Juno chide,   That thy adulteries   Rates and revenges.   Hath my poor boy done aught but well,   Whose face I never saw?
translation: You  thunder-god , don't punish human flies anymore. Disagree with Mars and fight with Juno who gets angry and gets her revenge for your adultery. Has my poor boy, whose face I never got to see, done anything wrong?

original: I died whilst in the womb he stay'd   Attending nature's law:
translation: I died while he was still in his mother's womb, growing naturally.

original: Whose father then, as men report   Thou orphans' father art,   Thou shouldst have been, and shielded him   From this earth-vexing smart.
translation: People say you're a father to orphans, and you should have been a father to him and protected him from this pain.

original: Lucina lent not me her aid,   But took me in my throes;
translation: Lucina  didn't help me but killed me while I was in labor.

original: That from me was Posthumus ript,   Came crying 'mongst his foes,   A thing of pity!
translation: So Posthumus was cut out of me and arrived crying surrounded by enemies, a pitiful little thing!

original: Great nature, like his ancestry, Moulded the stuff so fair, That he deserved the praise o' the world, As great Sicilius' heir.
translation: Nature and his genes made him so attractive that he deserved to be praised by the whole world as Sicilius's heir.

original: When once he was mature for man,   In Britain where was he   That could stand up his parallel;
translation: When he had grown into a man, who else in Britain was equal to him

original: Or fruitful object be   In eye of Imogen, that best   Could deem his dignity?
translation: or who else could compete with him in Imogen's affection, she who more than anyone could see how virtuous he was?

original: With marriage wherefore was he mock'd,   To be exiled, and thrown   From Leonati seat,
translation: Why was he punished for getting married, exiled and driven out of the Leonatus famiy home,

original: and cast   From her his dearest one,   Sweet Imogen?
translation: and separated from his beloved, sweet Imogen?

original: Why did you suffer Iachimo,   Slight thing of Italy,   To taint his nobler heart and brain   With needless jealosy;
translation: Why did you let Iachimo, a worthless Italian, infect his noble heart and mind with pointless jealousy?

original: And to become the geck and scorn   O' th' other's villany?
translation: And let him be duped by Iachimo's trickery?

original: For this from stiller seats we came,   Our parents and us twain,
translation: We came from more peaceful places, our parents and the two of us.

original: That striking in our country's cause   Fell bravely and were slain,   Our fealty and Tenantius' right   With honour to maintain.
translation: Fighting for our country, we fell bravely and died in battle, to show our loyalty and to win for Tenantius.

original: Like hardiment Posthumus hath   To Cymbeline perform'd:
translation: Posthumus did the same service for Cymbeline.

original: Then, Jupiter, thou king of gods,   Why hast thou thus adjourn'd   The graces for his merits due,   Being all to dolours turn'd?
translation: So, Jupiter, king of the gods, why have you put off rewarding him as he deserves, now he's in so much trouble?

original: Thy crystal window ope; look out;
translation: Open your window, look down,

original: No longer exercise   Upon a valiant race thy harsh   And potent injuries.
translation: don't punish a brave people so harshly.

original: Since, Jupiter, our son is good, Take off his miseries.
translation: Jupiter, since our son is a good person, don't let him be miserable.

original: Peep through thy marble mansion; help;
translation: Look out of your marble palace! Help!

original: Or we poor ghosts will cry   To the shining synod of the rest   Against thy deity.
translation: Or we poor ghosts will complain about you to the assembly of the rest of the gods.

original: Help, Jupiter; or we appeal, And from thy justice fly.
translation: Help, Jupiter, or we will appeal to them and give up on your justice system.

original: No more, you petty spirits of region low,   Offend our hearing; hush!
translation: Don't offend us by talking anymore, you minor spirits from below! Shh!

original: How dare you ghosts   Accuse the thunderer, whose bolt, you know,   Sky-planted batters all rebelling coasts?
translation: How dare you ghosts accuse me of these things when you know my lightning bolts shoot from the sky at all rebelling countries?

original: Poor shadows of Elysium, hence, and rest   Upon your never-withering banks of flowers:   Be not with mortal accidents opprest;   No care of yours it is; you know 'tis ours.
translation: Poor ghosts from  Elysium , go away, and rest on your hills covered in undying flowers. Don't worry about what happens on earth. It isn't any of your business, and you know it's mine.

original: Whom best I love I cross; to make my gift,   The more delay'd, delighted. Be content;   Your low-laid son our godhead will uplift:   His comforts thrive, his trials well are spent.   Our Jovial star reign'd at his birth, and in   Our temple was he married. Rise, and fade.
translation: I make trouble for the people I love best, because postponing my help makes people appreciate it more. You can be sure, my power will save your son even though he's been laid low. Things that will comfort him are being taken care of, and the things he's going through are good for him. He was born under my star, and was married in my temple. Get up and fade away.

original: He shall be lord of lady Imogen,   And happier much by his affliction made.   This tablet lay upon his breast, wherein   Our pleasure his full fortune doth confine:
translation: He will be lady Imogen's husband, and this suffering will make him happier in the end. Set this tablet on his chest, where I've set down his destiny.

original: and so, away: no further with your din   Express impatience, lest you stir up mine.   Mount, eagle, to my palace crystalline.
translation: So, go away. Don't make any more noise saying you're impatient, or I'll become impatient too. Fly up, eagle, to my crystal palace.

original: He came in thunder; his celestial breath   Was sulphurous to smell: the holy eagle   Stoop'd as to foot us:
translation: He came surrounded by thunder. His holy breath smelled like sulphur. The holy eagle stooped as though it would kick us.

original: his ascension is   More sweet than our blest fields:
translation: Seeing him fly away is more beautiful than the blessed fields we live in.

original: his royal bird   Prunes the immortal wing and cloys his beak,   As when his god is pleased.
translation: His royal bird is cleaning his immortal wing and keeping his beak shut, as he does when his god is pleased.

original: Thanks, Jupiter!
translation: Thanks, Jupiter!

original: The marble pavement closes, he is enter'd His radiant root. Away! and, to be blest, Let us with care perform his great behest.
translation: The marble roof closes: he has gone back to the bright place where he lives. Let's go! And we should do exactly as he asked so he blesses us.

original: [Waking]   Sleep, thou hast been a grandsire, and begot   A father to me; and thou hast created   A mother and two brothers: but, O scorn!   Gone! they went hence so soon as they were born:   And so I am awake.
translation: [Waking up]  Sleep, you were like a grandfather: you gave birth to a father for me, and you created a mother and two brothers. But what a terrible joke! They're gone! They vanished as quickly as they appeared. So I'm awake now.

original: Poor wretches that depend   On greatness' favour dream as I have done,   Wake and find nothing. But, alas, I swerve:   Many dream not to find, neither deserve,   And yet are steep'd in favours:
translation: Poor people who depend on the kindness of great men dream the same kinds of dreams as me, and wake up to find that they have nothing. But I'm wrong. Many don't dream about getting anything or deserve to get anything but are drowned in presents.

original: so am I,   That have this golden chance and know not why.   What fairies haunt this ground?
translation: That's true of me, since I had this wonderful dream and don't know why. What fairies haunt this place?

original: A book? O rare one!   Be not, as is our fangled world, a garment   Nobler than that it covers:
translation: [Finding the tablet]  A book! Oh, it's a beautiful one! Don't be like this unpredictable world and have a cover that looks more noble than what it's covering.

original: let thy effects   So follow, to be most unlike our courtiers,   As good as promise.
translation: Don't be like courtiers and instead be as good as you appear to be.

original: 'When as a lion's whelp shall, to himself unknown,   without seeking find, and be embraced by a piece of   tender air;
translation: "When a lion's cub, not knowing himself, finds and is embraced by a piece of soft air without looking for it,

original: and when from a stately cedar shall be   lopped branches, which, being dead many years,   shall after revive, be jointed to the old stock and   freshly grow; then shall Posthumus end his miseries,   Britain be fortunate and flourish in peace and plenty.'
translation: and when branches are cut from a noble cedar tree and, after being dead many years, come back to life and are re-attached to the old trunk and grow again, then Posthumus's sorrows will end, and Britain will be fortunate, prosperous, and peaceful."

original: 'Tis still a dream, or else such stuff as madmen   Tongue and brain not; either both or nothing;   Or senseless speaking or a speaking such   As sense cannot untie.
translation: I'm still dreaming, or this is the sort of thing crazy people say without knowing what they mean.  Either both those things, or nothing I can think of. It's either meaningless words or words that are impossible to understand.

original: Be what it is,   The action of my life is like it, which   I'll keep, if but for sympathy.
translation: Whatever this writing is, my life is like it in that it's also difficult, so I'll keep it because we're alike.

original: Come, sir, are you ready for death?
translation: Come on, sir, are you ready to die?

original: Over-roasted rather; ready long ago.
translation: I was ready long ago. Now I'm overdone.

original: Hanging is the word, sir: if you be ready for that, you are well cooked.
So, if I prove a good repast to the spectators, the dish pays the shot.
translation: Well, if I give the spectators a good meal, it's worth the trouble of killing and cooking me.

original: A heavy reckoning for you, sir. But the comfort is,   you shall be called to no more payments, fear no   more tavern-bills; which are often the sadness of   parting, as the procuring of mirth:
translation: Bad luck for you, sir. But the good news is you won't have to pay any more bills or worry about the check in bars, which often makes you sad when you leave even though you're paying to be made happy by alcohol.

original: you come in   flint for want of meat, depart reeling with too   much drink; sorry that you have paid too much, and   sorry that you are paid too much; purse and brain   both empty;
translation: You come in starving and leave staggering from drinking too much. You're sad you gave so much money, and sad that you took so much alcohol in. Your wallet and your head are both empty.

original: the brain the heavier for being too   light, the purse too light, being drawn of   heaviness:
translation: Your head is worse off for feeling light and your wallet that used to be heavier is too light.

original: of this contradiction you shall now be   quit. O, the charity of a penny cord! It sums up   thousands in a trice:
translation: You won't have to deal with this contradiction anymore. A rope you can buy for a penny is so kind! It can save you thousands of pounds at once.

original: you have no true debitor and   creditor but it; of what's past, is, and to come,   the discharge: your neck, sir, is pen, book and   counters; so the acquittance follows.
translation: It's the only one who really owes you or lends you anything. It can discharge you from the past, the present and the future. Your neck is its pen, book, and and counter. It forgives you your debt immediately.

original: I am merrier to die than thou art to live.
translation: I'm happier to die than you are to live.

original: Indeed, sir, he that sleeps feels not the   tooth-ache: but a man that were to sleep your   sleep, and a hangman to help him to bed, I think he   would change places with his officer;
translation: Yes, sir, someone who's asleep doesn't feel his toothache, but I think that someone who sleeps the kind of sleep you're going to  would gladly change places with the hangman helping him to bed.

original: for, look you,   sir, you know not which way you shall go.
translation: Because, you see, sir, you don't know which way you'r going to go, to hell or heaven.

original: Yes, indeed do I, fellow.
translation: Yes, I do.

original: Your death has eyes in 's head then; I have not seen   him so pictured:
translation: Then your grim reaper has eyes in his skull. I haven't seen him illustrated that way.

original: you must either be directed by   some that take upon them to know, or do take upon   yourself that which I am sure you do not know, or   jump the after inquiry on your own peril:
translation: You must either have been told that by people who pretend to know, or you've decided for yourself what I'm sure you don't know and chosen to skip the judgement after you die, which is risky.

original: and how   you shall speed in your journey's end, I think you'll   never return to tell one.
translation: I think you'll never come back to tell me how that will go for you.

original: I tell thee, fellow, there are none want eyes to direct them the way I am going, but such as wink and will not use them.
translation: Believe me, fellow, there's no one who can't see where I'm going except those who keep their eyes closed and refuse to use them.

original: What an infinite mock is this, that a man should   have the best use of eyes to see the way of   blindness!
translation: What a joke that is, that a man would use his eyes to see what blindness looks like.

original: I am sure hanging's the way of winking.
translation: I'm sure hanging is a way to shut your eyes.

original: Knock off his manacles; bring your prisoner to the  king.
translation: Take off his handcuffs and bring your prisoner to the king.

original: Thou bring'st good news; I am called to be made free.
translation: You bring good news. I'm being summoned to be set free.

original: I'll be hang'd then.
translation: If that's true then I'll be hanged.

original: Thou shalt be then freer than a gaoler; no bolts for  the dead.
translation: Then you will be freer than a jailor, because no locks can stop the dead.

original: Unless a man would marry a gallows and beget young   gibbets, I never saw one so prone. Yet, on my   conscience, there are verier knaves desire to live,   for all he be a Roman:
translation: Unless a man married a noose and gave birth to young nooses, I never saw anyone so likely to be hanged. But I swear there are worse criminals who want to live, even though he's a Roman.

original: and there be some of them   too that die against their wills; so should I, if I   were one. I would we were all of one mind, and one   mind good;
translation: And there are some of them who die against their wills. I would, if I were a criminal. I wish we all got along, and were all good people.

original: O, there were desolation of gaolers and   gallowses! I speak against my present profit, but   my wish hath a preferment in 't.
translation: Oh, then there would be no jobs for jailers and nooses! I'm arguing against my own profit, but I would also wish to be promoted to do something else.

original: Stand by my side, you whom the gods have made   Preservers of my throne.
translation: Stand next to me, you whom the gods aided to save my throne.

original: Woe is my heart   That the poor soldier that so richly fought,   Whose rags shamed gilded arms, whose naked breast   Stepp'd before larges of proof, cannot be found:
translation: I'm sad that the poor soldier who fought so well, whose ragged clothes made those wearing golden armor ashamed of themselves, who stepped up unprotected to fight nobles known for their skill, can't be found.

original: He shall be happy that can find him, if   Our grace can make him so.
translation: Anyone who finds him will be made happy if that's within my power.

original: I never saw   Such noble fury in so poor a thing;
translation: I never saw such a poor man show such noble fierceness.

original: Such precious deeds in one that promises nought   But beggary and poor looks.
translation: He did such amazing things for someone who looked like a beggar.

original: No tidings of him?
translation: There's no news of him?

original: He hath been search'd among the dead and living, But no trace of him.
translation: He's been searched for among those who are dead and alive, but there's no trace of him.

original: To my grief, I am The heir of his reward;
translation: Sadly, I'll have to keep his reward...

original: which I will add   To you, the liver, heart and brain of Britain,
translation: To add to yours. You three are like Britain's liver, heart, and brain.

original: By whom I grant she lives. 'Tis now the time   To ask of whence you are. Report it.
translation: Britain stays alive because of you. It's now time to ask you where you come from. Tell me.

original: Sir,   In Cambria are we born, and gentlemen:
translation: Sir, we were born in Cambria. We're gentlemen.

original: Further to boast were neither true nor modest,   Unless I add, we are honest.
translation: I can't tell you anything else while telling the truth and being humble, except that we're honest.

original: Bow your knees.   Arise my knights o' the battle:
translation: Kneel down, and when you get up you will be knights.

original: I create you   Companions to our person and will fit you   With dignities becoming your estates.
translation: I make you my companions, and I will give you titles as honorable as you are.

original: There's business in these faces. Why so sadly Greet you our victory? you look like Romans, And not o' the court of Britain.
translation: I can tell something has happened. Why do you look so sad after we won? You look like Romans, not British courtiers.

original: Hail, great king! To sour your happiness, I must report The queen is dead.
translation: Hello, great king! I have to ruin your happiness by telling you the queen is dead.

original: Who worse than a physician   Would this report become?
translation: It doesn't reflect well on a doctor to report that someone they were treating died.

original: But I consider,   By medicine life may be prolong'd, yet death   Will seize the doctor too. How ended she?
translation: But I suppose that although life can be made longer with medicine, eventually even a doctor dies. How did she die?

original: With horror, madly dying, like her life,   Which, being cruel to the world, concluded   Most cruel to herself.
translation: Horribly, dying in a frenzy like she lived her life. In that life she was cruel to everyone else, and her life ended cruelly for her.

original: What she confess'd   I will report, so please you: these her women   Can trip me, if I err; who with wet cheeks   Were present when she finish'd.
translation: I'll tell you what she confessed, if you don't mind. Her women here can cut me off if I get anything wrong. They were there, crying, when she died.

original: Prithee, say.
translation: Please, tell me.

original: First, she confess'd she never loved you, only   Affected greatness got by you, not you:
translation: First, she confessed she never love you and only desired the power she got from you, not you.

original: Married your royalty, was wife to your place;   Abhorr'd your person.
translation: She married your royalty, was a wife to your social position, but hated you.

original: She alone knew this; And, but she spoke it dying, I would not Believe her lips in opening it. Proceed.
translation: She was the only one who knew that. Except that she said it while she was dying, I wouldn't believe it even from her own mouth. Go on.

original: Your daughter, whom she bore in hand to love   With such integrity, she did confess   Was as a scorpion to her sight;
translation: She pretended to love your daughter deeply, but confessed that she actually hated her.

original: whose life,   But that her flight prevented it, she had   Ta'en off by poison.
translation: If Imogen hadn't run away, the queen would have poisoned her.

original: O most delicate fiend! Who is 't can read a woman? Is there more?
translation: What a sneaky demon! Who can know what women are actually like? Is there more?

original: More, sir, and worse. She did confess she had   For you a mortal mineral; which, being took,   Should by the minute feed on life and lingering   By inches waste you:
translation: There's more, sir, and it's worse. She confessed she had a poison prepared for you that, when you swallowed it, would make you waste away and die slowly.

original: in which time she purposed,   By watching, weeping, tendance, kissing, to   O'ercome you with her show, and in time,   When she had fitted you with her craft, to work   Her son into the adoption of the crown:
translation: She meant to stay up, cry, tend to you, kiss you, and to overcome you with her show of love. In time, when she had killed you with her poison, she would have gotten her son onto the throne.

original: But, failing of her end by his strange absence,   Grew shameless-desperate; open'd, in despite   Of heaven and men, her purposes; repented   The evils she hatch'd were not effected; so   Despairing died.
translation: But when her plan failed after he disappeared so strangely, she grew desperately shameless and admitted her plots against the gods and people, regretted that she did not succeed in doing the evil things she had planned, and died in despair.

original: Heard you all this, her women?
translation: Did you, her women, hear all of this?

original: We did, so please your highness.
translation: We did, your highness.

original: Mine eyes   Were not in fault, for she was beautiful;   Mine ears, that heard her flattery; nor my heart,   That thought her like her seeming;
translation: My eyes weren't wrong, she was beautiful. Or my ears, that heard the flattering things she said. Or my heart, that thought she was what she seemed to be.

original: it had   been vicious   To have mistrusted her: yet, O my daughter!   That it was folly in me, thou mayst say,   And prove it in thy feeling. Heaven mend all!
translation: It would have been a sin to not trust her. But oh, my daughter! You can say I was foolish, and prove it by what you went through. May the gods save us all!

original: Thou comest not, Caius, now for tribute that   The Britons have razed out, though with the loss   Of many a bold one;
translation: Caius, you're not here now for the tribute that we Britons crossed out of the account books, although at the cost of losing many brave men.

original: whose kinsmen have made suit   That their good souls may be appeased with slaughter   Of you their captives, which ourself have granted:   So think of your estate.
translation: Their relatives have asked that the dead men's souls should be put at rest by killing you, their captives. I agreed, so think about your wills.

original: Consider, sir, the chance of war: the day   Was yours by accident; had it gone with us,   We should not, when the blood was cool,   have threaten'd   Our prisoners with the sword.
translation: Sir, consider how much is up to chance in war. You won by accident. If we had won, we would not have threatened to kill our prisoners in cold blood.

original: But since the gods   Will have it thus, that nothing but our lives   May be call'd ransom, let it come: sufficeth   A Roman with a Roman's heart can suffer:
translation: But since that's the way the gods want it and we can pay no ransom except our lives, let death come. A Roman can suffer with Roman strength.

original: Augustus lives to think on't: and so much   For my peculiar care. This one thing only   I will entreat; my boy, a Briton born,   Let him be ransom'd: never master had   A page so kind, so duteous, diligent,   So tender over his occasions, true,   So feat, so nurse-like:
translation: Augustus is still alive to think about this. And so much for me. I will only ask you one thing: my boy, born a Briton—let him be ransomed. No master ever had as kind, dutiful, and hardworking a page, so gentle in doing his job, so quick, so nurse-like.

original: let his virtue join   With my request, which I make bold your highness   Cannot deny; he hath done no Briton harm,   Though he have served a Roman: save him, sir,   And spare no blood beside.
translation: Don't deny my request because I'm sure you can't deny his virtue. He hasn't harmed any Britons, although he served a Roman. Save him and no one else, sir.

original: I have surely seen him:   His favour is familiar to me. Boy,   Thou hast look'd thyself into my grace,   And art mine own.
translation: I'm sure I've seen him before. He looks familiar. Boy, you've attracted my attention and now work for me.

original: I know not why, wherefore,   To say 'live, boy:' ne'er thank thy master; live:   And ask of Cymbeline what boon thou wilt,   Fitting my bounty and thy state, I'll give it;
translation: I don't know why I'm saying "stay alive, boy." Don't thank your master for it. Stay alive, and ask Cymbeline whatever favor you want that is proper for me to give and for you to ask, and I'll grant it.

original: Yea, though thou do demand a prisoner,   The noblest ta'en.
translation: Even if you ask for a prisoner, even the noblest one captured.

original: I humbly thank your highness.
translation: Thank you, your highness.

original: I do not bid thee beg my life, good lad; And yet I know thou wilt.
translation: I'm not asking you to beg for my life, dear boy, but I know you will.

original: No, no: alack,   There's other work in hand:
translation: No, no, I'm sorry. There's something else going on.

original: I see a thing   Bitter to me as death: your life, good master,   Must shuffle for itself.
translation: I see something as terrible to me as death itself. Your life will have to take care of itself, good master.

original: The boy disdains me,   He leaves me, scorns me:
translation: The boy disrespects me. He abandons me and sneers at me.

original: briefly die their joys   That place them on the truth of girls and boys.   Why stands he so perplex'd?
translation: People who trust in the honesty of girls and boys will be disappointed. Why is he standing there looking so amazed?

original: What wouldst thou, boy?   I love thee more and more: think more and more   What's best to ask.
translation: What do you want, boy? I love you more and more. Think more and more about what you should ask for.

original: Know'st him thou look'st on? speak,   Wilt have him live? Is he thy kin? thy friend?
translation: Do you know the man you're looking at? Tell me, do you want him to live? Is he a family member? A friend?

original: He is a Roman; no more kin to me   Than I to your highness;
translation: He's a Roman. He's no closer a family member to me than I am to you, your highness.

original: who, being born your vassal,   Am something nearer.
translation: Even though I was born your subject, I am more closely related to you.

original: Wherefore eyest him so?
translation: Why are you looking at him like that?

original: I'll tell you, sir, in private, if you please To give me hearing.
translation: I'll tell you privately, if you agree to listen to me.

original: Ay, with all my heart, And lend my best attention. What's thy name?
translation: Yes, with all my heart, and I'll pay close attention. What's your name?

original: Fidele, sir.
translation: Fidele, sir.

original: Thou'rt my good youth, my page; I'll be thy master: walk with me; speak freely.
translation: You're my good young man, my page. I'll be your master. Walk with me. You can tell me anything.

original: Is not this boy revived from death?
translation: Isn't this the boy come back to life?

original: One sand another Not more resembles that sweet rosy lad Who died, and was Fidele. What think you?
translation: One grain of sand doesn't look more like another than that boy looks like the sweet attractive one who died and was Fidele. What do you think?

original: The same dead thing alive.
translation: It's the same dead person, come back to life.

original: Peace, peace! see further; he eyes us not; forbear; Creatures may be alike: were 't he, I am sure He would have spoke to us.
translation: Wait! Let's keep watching. He doesn't see us. Wait. Sometimes people look alike. If it were him, I'm sure he would have talked to us.

original: But we saw him dead.
translation: But we saw him dead.

original: Be silent; let's see further.
translation: Be quiet. Let's keep watching.

original: It is my mistress: Since she is living, let the time run on To good or bad.
translation: It's my mistress. Since she's alive, I don't care what happens.

original: Come, stand thou by our side; Make thy demand aloud.
translation: Come on, stand next to me and say what you want out loud.

original: Sir, step you forth;   Give answer to this boy, and do it freely;
translation: Sir, step forward. Answer this boy, and do it honestly,

original: Or, by our greatness and the grace of it,   Which is our honour, bitter torture shall   Winnow the truth from falsehood. On, speak to him.
translation: or by my power and what makes it great, which is my honor, you'll be tortured horribly to separate truth from lies. Go on, talk to him.

original: My boon is, that this gentleman may render Of whom he had this ring.
translation: What I ask is, for this gentleman to tell me where he got this ring.

original: What's that to him?
translation: What does that have to do with him?

original: That diamond upon your finger, say How came it yours?
translation: That diamond ring on your finger, how did you get it?

original: Thou'lt torture me to leave unspoken that Which, to be spoke, would torture thee.
translation: You're threatening to torture me if I don't say something that, when I say it, will torture you.

original: How! me?
translation: What, me?

original: I am glad to be constrain'd to utter that   Which torments me to conceal. By villany   I got this ring:
translation: I'm glad to be forced to reveal a secret that is so painful to keep. I got this ring dishonestly.

original: 'twas Leonatus' jewel;   Whom thou didst banish; and—which more may   grieve thee,   As it doth me—a nobler sir ne'er lived   'Twixt sky and ground.
translation: It was Leonatus's ring, whom you banished, and—this may make you as sad as it makes me—who is the noblest man who ever lived.

original: Wilt thou hear more, my lord?
translation: Do you want to hear more, sir?

original: All that belongs to this.
translation: Everything to do with this.

original: That paragon, thy daughter,— For whom my heart drops blood, and my false spirits Quail to remember—Give me leave; I faint.
translation: That ideal woman, your daughter—mentioning her, my heart bleeds and my lying mind cringes—I'm sorry, I feel faint.

original: My daughter! what of her? Renew thy strength: I had rather thou shouldst live while nature will Than die ere I hear more: strive, man, and speak.
translation: My daughter! What about her? Be strong. I would prefer you to live while you can than to die without telling me more. Try harder, and tell me.

original: Upon a time,—unhappy was the clock   That struck the hour!—it was in Rome,—accursed   The mansion where!—'twas at a feast,—O, would   Our viands had been poison'd, or at least   Those which I heaved to head!—the good Posthumus—   What should I say?
translation: Once—and curse the clock that struck the hour!—it was in Rome—curse the house where this happened!—it was at a feast—oh, I wish our food had been poisoned, or at least the food I threw in my mouth!—the good Posthumus—What can I say?
