original: he was too good to be   Where ill men were; and was the best of all   Amongst the rarest of good ones,—sitting sadly,   Hearing us praise our loves of Italy   For beauty that made barren the swell'd boast   Of him that best could speak, for feature, laming   The shrine of Venus, or straight-pight Minerva.
translation: He was too good to be around bad men, and he was the best of all good men—sitting sadly, hearing us say that our Italian lovers were more beautiful than even the best speaker could boast, and were more beautiful than the goddesses Venus or tall Minerva.

original: Postures beyond brief nature, for condition,   A shop of all the qualities that man   Loves woman for, besides that hook of wiving,   Fairness which strikes the eye—
translation: We were describing them as beyond anything nature could make, like they were shops filled with all the qualities that men love women for, outside the trap of marriage. Beauty that hits the eye—

original: I stand on fire: Come to the matter.
translation: I'm in suspense. Get to the point.

original: All too soon I shall,   Unless thou wouldst grieve quickly. This Posthumus,   Most like a noble lord in love and one   That had a royal lover, took his hint;
translation: I will all too soon, unless you're eager to be sad. Posthumus, like a noble lord in love, with a royal lover, took this opportunity.

original: And, not dispraising whom we praised,—therein   He was as calm as virtue—he began   His mistress' picture;
translation: Not insulting the women we praised—he was as calm as virtue itself would be—he began to describe his wife.

original: which by his tongue   being made,   And then a mind put in't, either our brags   Were crack'd of kitchen-trolls, or his description   Proved us unspeaking sots.
translation: When he described what she looked like, and then added an excellent mind to the picture, we were left sounding like we were praising ugly kitchen servants or like we were silent idiots.

original: Nay, nay, to the purpose.
translation: No, no, get to the point.

original: Your daughter's chastity—there it begins.   He spake of her, as Dian had hot dreams,   And she alone were cold:
translation: Your daughter's faithfulness—that's where it begins. He spoke of her as if even the virgin goddess Diana had wet dreams, and only his wife felt nothing sexual.

original: whereat I, wretch,   Made scruple of his praise; and wager'd with him   Pieces of gold 'gainst this which then he wore   Upon his honour'd finger, to attain   In suit the place of's bed and win this ring   By hers and mine adultery.
translation: So I, criminal that I am, doubted what he said. And I bet him gold against this ring, which he wore on his honorable finger, that I would sleep with his wife and win this ring by committing adultery with her.

original: He, true knight,   No lesser of her honour confident   Than I did truly find her, stakes this ring;   And would so, had it been a carbuncle   Of Phoebus' wheel, and might so safely, had it   Been all the worth of's car.
translation: He, a true noble, was confident that she was as honorable as I soon found out she was, and bet this ring. He would have done the same thing if it was a jewel from the wheel of the sun-god's chariot, and could have done it safely even if it had been worth the whole chariot.

original: Away to Britain   Post I in this design: well may you, sir,   Remember me at court; where I was taught   Of your chaste daughter the wide difference   'Twixt amorous and villanous.
translation: So I hurried off to Britain with this plan. You may well remember seeing me in court, where I was taught by your loyal daughter the huge difference between being in love and being wicked.

original: Being thus quench'd   Of hope, not longing, mine Italian brain   'Gan in your duller Britain operate   Most vilely; for my vantage, excellent:
translation: Losing hope but not my desire, my Italian brain began to plot cleverly in your slower country of Britain. I took advantage of people's slowness.

original: And, to be brief, my practise so prevail'd,   That I return'd with simular proof enough   To make the noble Leonatus mad,   By wounding his belief in her renown   With tokens thus, and thus; averting notes   Of chamber-hanging, pictures, this her bracelet,—   O cunning, how I got it!—
translation: To cut to the point, my plot worked well enough that I returned with enough fake proof to make noble Leonatus go crazy by hurting his trust in her honor with certain details, throwing in descriptions of wall-hangings, paintings, her bracelet here—oh, I stole it so cleverly!

original: nay, some marks   Of secret on her person, that he could not   But think her bond of chastity quite crack'd,   I having ta'en the forfeit. Whereupon—   Methinks, I see him now—
translation: Even some secret marks on her body, so that he had to believe that she had been unfaithful to him with me. So - It's like I can see him now—

original: [Advancing]   Ay, so thou dost,   Italian fiend! Ay me, most credulous fool,   Egregious murderer, thief, any thing   That's due to all the villains past, in being,   To come!
translation: [Stepping forward]  Yes, you can, you Italian devil! Gullible fool, horrible murderer, doing anything any criminal ever did, is doing, will do!

original: O, give me cord, or knife, or poison,   Some upright justicer! Thou, king, send out   For torturers ingenious: it is I   That all the abhorred things o' the earth amend   By being worse than they.
translation: Give me a rope, or a knife, or poison, some honest way to get justice! You, king, send for clever torturers! I am the thing that makes all the disgusting things on earth seem better by being worse than they are.

original: I am Posthumus,   That kill'd thy daughter:—villain-like, I lie—   That caused a lesser villain than myself,   A sacrilegious thief, to do't: the temple   Of virtue was she; yea, and she herself.   Spit, and throw stone s, cast mire upon me, set   The dogs o' the street to bay me:
translation: I am Posthumus, who killed your daughter—like a criminal, I'm lying—who made a lesser criminal, an unholy thief, do it. She was the temple of virtue, and she was herself. Spit, throw stones, throw mud on me, set the dogs in the street on me.

original: every villain   Be call'd Posthumus Leonatus; and   Be villany less than 'twas! O Imogen!   My queen, my life, my wife! O Imogen,   Imogen, Imogen!
translation: May every criminal be called Posthumus Leonatus, and may evil itself seem less bad compared to me! Oh Imogen! My queen, my life, my wife! Oh Imogen, Imogen, Imogen!

original: Peace, my lord; hear, hear—
translation: Wait, my lord. Listen, listen—

original: Shall's have a play of this? Thou scornful page, There lie thy part.
translation: Do you think this is a play? You mocking page, this is your part.

original: O, gentlemen, help!   Mine and your mistress! O, my lord Posthumus!
translation: Oh gentlemen, help! This is my mistress and your wife! Oh, my lord Posthumus!

original: You ne'er kill'd Imogen til now. Help, help!   Mine honour'd lady!
translation: You never killed Imogen until now. Help, help! My dear lady!

original: Does the world go round?
translation: Is the world spinning?

original: How come these staggers on me?
translation: What's happening to me?

original: Wake, my mistress!
translation: Wake up, mistress!

original: If this be so, the gods do mean to strike me To death with mortal joy.
translation: If this is true, the gods are trying to kill me with happiness.

original: How fares thy mistress?
translation: How is your wife?

original: O, get thee from my sight; Thou gavest me poison: dangerous fellow, hence! Breathe not where princes are.
translation: Get away from me. You gave me poison. You dangerous man, get out of here! Don't breathe in the same room as royalty.

original: The tune of Imogen!
translation: Imogen's voice!

original: Lady, The gods throw stones of sulphur on me, if That box I gave you was not thought by me A precious thing: I had it from the queen.
translation: Ma'am, throw stinking rocks at me if I didn't think that box I gave you was powerful medicine. I got it from the queen.

original: New matter still?
translation: More new information?

original: It poison'd me.
translation: It poisoned me.

original: O gods!   I left out one thing which the queen confess'd.   Which must approve thee honest:
translation: Oh gods! I left out one thing the queen confessed, which proves you to be honest.

original: 'If Pisanio   Have,' said she, 'given his mistress that confection   Which I gave him for cordial, she is served   As I would serve a rat.'
translation: She said, "If Pisanio has given his mistress that potion I told him was medicine, she's as dead as a rat drinking rat poison."

original: What's this, Comelius?
translation: What does that mean, Cornelius?

original: The queen, sir, very oft importuned me   To temper poisons for her, still pretending   The satisfaction of her knowledge only   In killing creatures vile, as cats and dogs,   Of no esteem:
translation: Sir, the queen often begged me to make poison for her, always pretending she wanted to learn by killing low creatures, like cats and dogs, that no one cared about.

original: I, dreading that her purpose   Was of more danger, did compound for her   A certain stuff, which, being ta'en, would cease   The present power of life, but in short time   All offices of nature should again   Do their due functions. Have you ta'en of it?
translation: I, worrying she actually meant to do something worse, made her a mixture that would make anyone who drank it seem dead but would after a short time make all the parts of their body work again. Did you drink any of it?

original: Most like I did, for I was dead.
translation: Probably, because I was dead.

original: My boys, There was our error.
translation: My boys, that's where we went wrong.

original: This is, sure, Fidele.
translation: This is definitely Fidele.

original: Why did you throw your wedded lady from you? Think that you are upon a rock; and now Throw me again.
translation: Why did you push your wife away from you? Pretend you're on the side of a cliff, and see if you can push me away again.

original: Hang there like a fruit, my soul, Till the tree die!
translation: My dear, you're like my soul. Hang there like you're fruit and I'm a tree until this tree dies!

original: How now, my flesh, my child! What, makest thou me a dullard in this act? Wilt thou not speak to me?
translation: My flesh and blood, my child! You're acting like I don't matter. Won't you speak to me?

original: Your blessing, sir.
translation: Give me your blessing, sir.

original: Though you did love this youth, I blame ye not: You had a motive for't.
translation: I don't blame you for loving this young man. You had a reason to.

original: My tears that fall Prove holy water on thee! Imogen, Thy mother's dead.
translation: May my tears falling on you act like holy water! Imogen, your mother's dead.

original: I am sorry for't, my lord.
translation: I'm sorry, sir.

original: O, she was nought; and long of her it was That we meet here so strangely: but her son Is gone, we know not how nor where.
translation: Oh, she was worthless. It's no thanks to her that we're meeting here so strangely. But her son is gone, and we don't know how or where.

original: My lord,   Now fear is from me, I'll speak troth. Lord Cloten,   Upon my lady's missing, came to me   With his sword drawn; foam'd at the mouth, and swore,   If I discover'd not which way she was gone,   It was my instant death
translation: My lord, now that I'm not afraid any more, I'll tell you the truth. When my mistress went missing, Lord Cloten came to me with his sword out, foamed at the mouth, and promised that I would die at once if I didn't tell him where she had gone.

original: . By accident,   had a feigned letter of my master's   Then in my pocket; which directed him   To seek her on the mountains near to Milford;
translation: By chance, I had a lying letter from my master in my pocket, which told him to look for her in the mountains near Milford.

original: Where, in a frenzy, in my master's garments,   Which he enforced from me, away he posts   With unchaste purpose and with oath to violate   My lady's honour: what became of him   I further know not.
translation: In a frenzy, wearing my masters clothes which he forced me to give him, he rode away with a sinful plan, promising to rape my mistress. I don't know anything more about what happened.

original: Let me end the story: I slew him there.
translation: Let me end the story: I killed him there.

original: Marry, the gods forfend!   I would not thy good deeds should from my lips   Pluck a bard sentence:
translation: Gods forbid! You've done good deeds—I don't want to have to order you thrown in jail.

original: prithee, valiant youth,   Deny't again.
translation: Please, brave young man, deny it.

original: I have spoke it, and I did it.
translation: I said it, and I did it.

original: He was a prince.
translation: He was a prince.

original: A most incivil one: the wrongs he did me   Were nothing prince-like; for he did provoke me   With language that would make me spurn the sea,   If it could so roar to me:
translation: A very rude one. He didn't treat me like he was a prince. He provoked me with language that would make me mad enough to kick the sea if it roared at me like that.

original: I cut off's head;   And am right glad he is not standing here   To tell this tale of mine.
translation: I cut off his head. And I am very happy he is not standing here instead of me to tell this story.

original: I am sorry for thee: By thine own tongue thou art condemn'd, and must Endure our law: thou'rt dead.
translation: I'm sorry, but you've condemned yourself by saying this and have to face your punishment under our law. You're dead.

original: That headless man I thought had been my lord.
translation: I thought that headless man was my husband.

original: Bind the offender, And take him from our presence.
translation: Tie up the criminal and take him out of my sight.

original: Stay, sir king:   This man is better than the man he slew,   As well descended as thyself;
translation: Wait, sir king. This man is nobler than the man he killed, from as good a family as you,

original: and hath   More of thee merited than a band of Clotens   Had ever scar for.
translation: and has deserved more from you than a gang of Clotens could.

original: Let his arms alone; They were not born for bondage.
translation: Leave his arms alone. They weren't born to be unfree.

original: Why, old soldier,   Wilt thou undo the worth thou art unpaid for,   By tasting of our wrath?
translation: You old soldier, do you want to undo all the good deeds I haven't paid you for yet, and make me angry?

original: How of descent   As good as we?
translation: How is he from as good a family as me?

original: In that he spake too far.
translation: He didn't really mean that.

original: And thou shalt die for't.
translation: And you'll die for that.

original: We will die all three:   But I will prove that two on's are as good   As I have given out him.
translation: All three of us will die. But I will prove that two of us are as good as I said.

original: My sons, I must,   For mine own part, unfold a dangerous speech,   Though, haply, well for you.
translation: My sons, I have to say something dangerous for me, but perhaps good for you.

original: Your danger's ours.
translation: Anything dangerous for you is dangerous for us.

original: And our good his.
translation: And anything good for us is good for you.

original: Have at it then, by leave. Thou hadst, great king, a subject who Was call'd Belarius.
translation: Well then, I'll say it. Great king, you had a subject called Belarius.

original: What of him? he is A banish'd traitor.
translation: What about him? He is a banished traitor.

original: He it is that hath Assumed this age; indeed a banish'd man; I know not how a traitor.
translation: I was him before I grew old. I was indeed banished, but I don't know what makes me a traitor.

original: Take him hence: The whole world shall not save him.
translation: Take him away. Nothing can save him.

original: Not too hot: First pay me for the nursing of thy sons; And let it be confiscate all, so soon As I have received it.
translation: Wait. First pay me for bringing up your sons, and then you can take the reward away as soon as you give it to me.

original: Nursing of my sons!
translation: Bringing up my sons!

original: I am too blunt and saucy: here's my knee:
translation: I am being too blunt and disrespectful. I'm kneeling before you.

original: Ere I arise, I will prefer my sons;   Then spare not the old father.
translation: Before I get up, I will promote my sons. Then don't show their old father any mercy.

original: Mighty sir,   These two young gentlemen, that call me father   And think they are my sons, are none of mine;   They are the issue of your loins, my liege,   And blood of your begetting.
translation: Sir, these two young men who call me father and think they are my sons are not related to me. They are your children, sir, and your own flesh and blood.

original: How! my issue!
translation: What! My children!

original: So sure as you your father's. I, old Morgan,   Am that Belarius whom you sometime banish'd:
translation: As certainly as you are your father's child. I, old Morgan, am the Belarius you banished.

original: Your pleasure was my mere offence, my punishment   Itself, and all my treason; that I suffer'd   Was all the harm I did.
translation: Your whim was my only crime, punishment, and treason. I never did anything wrong except suffer.

original: These gentle princes—   For such and so they are—these twenty years   Have I train'd up: those arts they have as I   Could put into them; my breeding was, sir, as   Your highness knows.
translation: These kind princes—because they are kind and they are princes—I brought up for twenty years. I taught them everything I could. Sir, you know what my education was.

original: Their nurse, Euriphile,   Whom for the theft I wedded, stole these children   Upon my banishment: I moved her to't,   Having received the punishment before,   For that which I did then: beaten for loyalty   Excited me to treason: their dear loss,   The more of you 'twas felt, the more it shaped   Unto my end of stealing them.
translation: Their nurse, Euriphile, stole the children when I was banished, and I married her in return for this favor. I convinced her to do it, having already been punished for the crime I committed then. Having been punished for being loyal, I decided to be a traitor. I wanted to steal them to hurt you.

original: But, gracious sir,   Here are your sons again; and I must lose   Two of the sweet'st companions in the world.
translation: But, dear sir, here are your sons back. I'm losing two of the best friends in the world.

original: The benediction of these covering heavens   Fall on their heads like dew! for they are worthy   To inlay heaven with stars.
translation: May the gods make blessings rain down on them like dew! They are virtuous enough that they should be made into constellations.

original: Thou weep'st, and speak'st.   The service that you three have done is more   Unlike than this thou tell'st.
translation: You're crying while you speak. The good deeds you did for me were more surprising than this story you're telling.

original: I lost my children:   If these be they, I know not how to wish   A pair of worthier sons.
translation: I lost my children. If these are those children, I don't think it would be possible to have two better sons.

original: Be pleased awhile.   This gentleman, whom I call Polydore,   Most worthy prince, as yours, is true Guiderius:   This gentleman, my Cadwal, Arviragus,   Your younger princely son;
translation: Wait a moment. This man I call Polydore is really your Guiderius, worthy king. This man, my Cadwal, is your younger royal son Arviragus.

original: he, sir, was lapp'd   In a most curious mantle, wrought by the hand   Of his queen mother, which for more probation   I can with ease produce.
translation: He, sir, was wrapped in a beautifully woven blanket, made by his mother the queen, which I can easily show you for more proof.

original: Guiderius had Upon his neck a mole, a sanguine star; It was a mark of wonder.
translation: Guiderius had a mole on his neck, a red star. It was an amazing thing.

original: This is he; Who hath upon him still that natural stamp: It was wise nature's end in the donation, To be his evidence now.
translation: This is him, and he still has that mark. Nature was wise in giving it to him, since now it's evidence for him.

original: O, what, am I   A mother to the birth of three? Ne'er mother   Rejoiced deliverance more.
translation: Am I a mother giving birth to three children? No mother was ever happier to deliver children.

original: Blest pray you be,   That, after this strange starting from your orbs,   may reign in them now! O Imogen,   Thou hast lost by this a kingdom.
translation: After strangely changing social classes, may you be blessed in the one you've come back to! Oh Imogen, you've lost a kingdom because of this.

original: No, my lord;   I have got two worlds by 't. O my gentle brothers,   Have we thus met?
translation: No, my lord, I have gained two whole worlds. Oh my dear brothers, have we met this way?

original: O, never say hereafter   But I am truest speaker you call'd me brother,   When I was but your sister; I you brothers,   When ye were so indeed.
translation: Never say I don't tell the truth more than you do. You called me brother although I was only your sister, but I called you brothers and that was exactly you where.

original: Did you e'er meet?
translation: Did you meet each other before?

original: Ay, my good lord.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: And at first meeting loved; Continued so, until we thought he died.
translation: And loved each other from the first, and still did until we thought he died.

original: By the queen's dram she swallow'd.
translation: Because of the queen's potion she drank.

original: O rare instinct!   When shall I hear all through? This fierce   abridgement   Hath to it circumstantial branches, which   Distinction should be rich in.
translation: What an amazing instinct! When will I hear all the details? This rough abridged version has so many side stories that I should know more about.

original: Where? how lived you?   And when came you to serve our Roman captive?   How parted with your brothers? how first met them?   Why fled you from the court? and whither?
translation: Where? How did you live? How did you come to be a servant to my Roman prisoner? How did you leave your brothers? How did you first meet them? Why did you run away from the court? And where?

original: These,   And your three motives to the battle, with   I know not how much more, should be demanded;   And all the other by-dependencies,   From chance to chance:
translation: I should ask these things, and the reason you three joined the battle, and I don't know what else. And all the other circumstances, from the beginning.

original: but nor the time nor place   Will serve our long inter'gatories.
translation: But this isn't the time or place to ask complicated questions.

original: See,   Posthumus anchors upon Imogen,   And she, like harmless lightning, throws her eye   On him, her brother, me, her master, hitting   Each object with a joy: the counterchange   Is severally in all.
translation: See, Posthumus is like a ship anchored to Imogen, and she's shooting glances like harmless lightning bolts at him, her brother, me, and her old master, hitting all of us with her joy. We all have different expressions.

original: Let's quit this ground,   And smoke the temple with our sacrifices.
translation: Let's leave, and fill the temple with smoke from our burnt offerings to the gods.

original: Thou art my brother; so we'll hold thee ever.
translation: I'll always consider you my brother.

original: You are my father too, and did relieve me, To see this gracious season.
translation: You are like another father to me and helped me survive long enough to see all this.

original: All o'erjoy'd, Save these in bonds: let them be joyful too, For they shall taste our comfort.
translation: Everyone is happy, except these people who are tied up. Let them be happy too—we'll share our joy with them.

original: My good master, I will yet do you service.
translation: My good master, I'll do you one more service.

original: Happy be you!
translation: Bless you!

original: The forlorn soldier, that so nobly fought, He would have well becomed this place, and graced The thankings of a king.
translation: That last soldier who fought so nobly: he would have been a good addition and I would have been honored to thank him.

original: I am, sir,   The soldier that did company these three   In poor beseeming; 'twas a fitment for   The purpose I then follow'd.
translation: Sir, I am the soldier who kept these three company. I was dressed humbly in accordance with the plan I had then.

original: That I was he,   Speak, Iachimo: I had you down and might   Have made you finish.
translation: Tell them that it was me, Iachimo. I knocked you to the ground and could have killed you.

original: [Kneeling]   I am down again:   But now my heavy conscience sinks my knee,   As then your force did.
translation: [Kneeling]  And now I'm on the ground again. But now it's my bad conscience making me sink to my knee, while before it was your strength.

original: Take that life, beseech you,   Which I so often owe: but your ring first;   And here the bracelet of the truest princess   That ever swore her faith.
translation: Take that life, please, that I owe you. But take your ring first. And here's the bracelet of the most honest princess who ever swore to be faithful.

original: Kneel not to me: The power that I have on you is, to spare you; The malice towards you to forgive you: live, And deal with others better.
translation: Don't kneel to me. I'll show my power over you by letting you live, and punish you by forgiving you. Live, and treat other people more honestly

original: Nobly doom'd! We'll learn our freeness of a son-in-law; Pardon's the word to all.
translation: That was a noble judgement! I'll learn forgiveness from my son-in-law. Everyone is pardoned.

original: You holp us, sir, As you did mean indeed to be our brother; Joy'd are we that you are.
translation: You helped us, sir, as if you were our brother. We're happy that you really are.

original: Your servant, princes. Good my lord of Rome,   Call forth your soothsayer:
translation: I'm your servant, princes. My good Roman lord, call for your soothsayer.

original: as I slept, methought   Great Jupiter, upon his eagle back'd,   Appear'd to me, with other spritely shows   Of mine own kindred:
translation: As I slept, I thought great Jupiter appeared to me on his eagle, along with the ghosts of my own family members.

original: when I waked, I found   This label on my bosom; whose containing   Is so from sense in hardness, that I can   Make no collection of it: let him show   His skill in the construction.
translation: When I woke, I found this document on my chest. What it says is so hard to understand that I don't have any idea what it means. He should test his skill by figuring it out.

original: Philarmonus!
translation: Philarmonus!

original: Here, my good lord.
translation: Here, my good lord.

original: Read, and declare the meaning.
translation: Read this, and tell us what it means.

original: [Reads]   'When as a lion's whelp shall, to himself   unknown, without seeking find, and be embraced by a   piece of tender air;
translation: [Reads]  "When a lion's cub, not knowing himself, finds a piece of soft air and is hugged by it without looking for it,

original: and when from a stately cedar   shall be lopped branches, which, being dead many   years, shall after revive, be jointed to the old   stock, and freshly grow;
translation: and when branches are cut from a noble cedar tree and, after being dead many years, come back to life and are re-attached to the old trunk and grow again,

original: then shall Posthumus end   his miseries, Britain be fortunate and flourish in   peace and plenty.'
translation: then Posthumus's sorrows will end, and Britain will be fortunate, prosperous, and peaceful."

original: Thou, Leonatus, art the lion's whelp;   The fit and apt construction of thy name,   Being Leonatus, doth import so much.
translation: You, Leonatus, are the lion's cub. That's what your name, Leonatus, means.

original: The piece of tender air, thy virtuous daughter,   Which we call 'mollis aer;' and 'mollis aer'   We term it 'mulier:'
translation: The piece of soft air is your virtuous daughter. The word for "woman" in Latin, "mulier," comes from "mollis aer," soft air.

original: which 'mulier' I divine   Is this most constant wife; who, even now,   Answering the letter of the oracle,   Unknown to you, unsought, were clipp'd about   With this most tender air.
translation: The "mulier" is, I think, this faithful wife. Just now, as the prophecy says, you didn't recognize her and didn't think you would find her, but you were hugged by this soft air.

original: This hath some seeming.
translation: That makes sense.

original: The lofty cedar, royal Cymbeline,   Personates thee: and thy lopp'd branches point   Thy two sons forth;
translation: The tall cedar, royal Cymbeline, stands for you. And your cut branches are your two sons

original: who, by Belarius stol'n,   For many years thought dead, are now revived,   To the majestic cedar join'd, whose issue   Promises Britain peace and plenty.
translation: who, stolen by Belarius and for many years thought to be dead, are now brought back to life and attached to the old cedar, whose children are a sign of coming peace and prosperity for Britain.

original: Well   My peace we will begin. And, Caius Lucius,   Although the victor, we submit to Caesar,   And to the Roman empire; promising   To pay our wonted tribute,
translation: Well, that peace will begin now. And, Caius Lucius, although we won, we submit to Caesar and the Roman empire and promise to pay our usual tribute.

original: from the which   We were dissuaded by our wicked queen;   Whom heavens, in justice, both on her and hers,   Have laid most heavy hand.
translation: I was convinced not to by my evil queen, who, along with her son, has been punished terribly by the gods.

original: The fingers of the powers above do tune   The harmony of this peace. The vision   Which I made known to Lucius, ere the stroke   Of this yet scarce-cold battle, at this instant   Is full accomplish'd;
translation: The gods are tuning the music of this peace. The vision I told Lucius about before this recent battle has now come true.

original: for the Roman eagle,   From south to west on wing soaring aloft,   Lessen'd herself, and in the beams o' the sun   So vanish'd:
translation: The Roman eagle, flying from south to west, has completely vanished into the sun.

original: which foreshow'd our princely eagle,   The imperial Caesar, should again unite   His favour with the radiant Cymbeline,   Which shines here in the west.
translation: This showed that our royal eagle, the emperor Caesar, would again unite with bright Cymbeline who shines here in the west.

original: Laud we the gods;   And let our crooked smokes climb to their nostrils   From our blest altars.
translation: Let us praise the gods, and burn offerings at our blessed altars until the smoke reaches their noses.

original: Publish we this peace   To all our subjects. Set we forward: let   A Roman and a British ensign wave   Friendly together: so through Lud's-town march:
translation: Announce this peace to all our subjects. Let's set out together. A Roman and a British flag will wave together like friends. March through Lud's-town

original: And in the temple of great Jupiter   Our peace we'll ratify; seal it with feasts.   Set on there! Never was a war did cease,   Ere bloody hands were wash'd, with such a peace.
translation: and we'll make our peace official in the temple of great Jupiter, then celebrate with feasts. Let's go! A war was never ended with such a peace, before the blood was even washed off the soldiers' hands.

original: Your lordship is the most patient man in loss, the most coldest that ever turned up ace.
translation: You're the best loser, you keep your cool like no one else.

original: It would make any man cold to lose.
translation: Losing would make any man feel cold.

original: But not every man patient after the noble temper of your lordship. You are most hot and furious when you  win.
translation: But it wouldn't make any man as patient as you are. You are so energetic and angry when you win.

original: Winning will put any man into courage.
translation: Winning makes any man brave.

original: If I could   get this foolish Imogen, I should have gold enough.   It's almost morning, is't not?
translation: If I could get silly Imogen to marry me, I would have enough gold. It's almost morning, isn't it?

original: Day, my lord.
translation: It's already day, my lord.

original: I would this music would come: I am advised to give her music o' mornings; they say it will penetrate.
Come on; tune: if you can penetrate her with your   fingering, so; we'll try with tongue too:
translation: Come on, play. If you can change her mind by   just playing your instruments, great. We'll try singing too .

original: if none   will do, let her remain; but I'll never give o'er.
translation: If none of it works, she can stay in there. But I'll never give up.

original: First, a very excellent good-conceited thing;   after, a wonderful sweet air, with admirable rich   words to it: and then let her consider.
translation: First, something really excellent and with fancy effects in it. Then, a wonderful sweet tune, with beautiful rich words in it. And then let her think about it.

original: Hark, hark! the lark at heaven's gate sings,   And Phoebus 'gins arise,   His steeds to water at those springs   On chaliced flowers that lies;
translation: Listen, Listen! The birds are singing at the gates of the sky   And the sun-god wakes up  To give his horses water  Cupped in flowers

original: And winking Mary-buds begin   To ope their golden eyes:
translation: And marigolds begin To open their golden eyes.

original: With every thing that pretty is,   My lady sweet, arise:   Arise, arise.
translation: Wake up, my sweet lady, Along with everything pretty: Wake up, wake up.

original: So, get you gone. If this penetrate, I will   consider your music the better:
translation: All right, go away. If this works, I'll think your music is even better than I think it is now.

original: if it do not, it is   a vice in her ears, which horse-hairs and   calves'-guts, nor the voice of unpaved eunuch to   boot, can never amend.
translation: If it doesn't, there's something wrong with her ears, and instruments made out of horse hairs and calf guts and the voices of  castrated men  can't change that.

original: Here comes the king.
translation: Here comes the king.

original: I am glad I was up so late; for that's the reason I   was up so early:
translation: I'm glad I stayed up so late, because now by staying up all night I'm up early.

original: he cannot choose but take this   service I have done fatherly.
translation: He'll be thankful for this good deed I have done and will treat me in a fatherly way.

original: Good morrow to your majesty and to my gracious mother.
translation: Good morning, your majesty and my mother.

original: Attend you here the door of our stern daughter? Will she not forth?
translation: Are you waiting here at the door for my unrelenting daughter? Is she refusing to come out?

original: I have assailed her with music, but she vouchsafes no  notice.
translation: I attacked her with music, but she hasn't responded.

original: The exile of her minion is too new;   She hath not yet forgot him:
translation: Her minion's exile is too recent. She hasn't forgotten him yet.

original: some more time   Must wear the print of his remembrance out,   And then she's yours.
translation: Some more time will erase her memory of him, and then she'll be yours.

original: You are most bound to the king,   Who lets go by no vantages that may   Prefer you to his daughter.
translation: You owe the king a lot for not letting go of any opportunity to try to get his daughter to like you.

original: Frame yourself   To orderly soliciting, and be friended   With aptness of the season; make denials   Increase your services;
translation: You should do this right and wait for the proper time. When she says no, try harder to please her.

original: so seem as if   You were inspired to do those duties which   You tender to her; that you in all obey her,
translation: Act as if you felt inspired by love to do the things you do for her and that you obey her completely,

original: Save when command to your dismission tends,   And therein you are senseless.
translation: except when she orders you to go away. In that case, you play dumb.

original: Senseless! not so.
translation: Dumb! I'm not.

original: So like you, sir, ambassadors from Rome; The one is Caius Lucius.
translation: Sir, ambassadors came from Rome. One is Caius Lucius.

original: A worthy fellow,   Albeit he comes on angry purpose now;
translation: He's a good man, even though he comes with an angry message now.

original: But that's no fault of his: we must receive him   According to the honour of his sender;   And towards himself, his goodness forespent on us,   We must extend our notice.
translation: But that's not his fault. I must treat him as well as the man who sent him deserves, and I have to pay attention to him because he has acted well towards me in the past.

original: Our dear son,   When you have given good morning to your mistress,   Attend the queen and us; we shall have need   To employ you towards this Roman. Come, our queen.
translation: Dear son, when you have said hello to your girlfriend, come find the queen and me. We will need your help with this Roman. Come, my queen.

original: If she be up, I'll speak with her; if not, Let her lie still and dream.
translation: If she's up, I'll speak to her. If not, she can keep lying down and dreaming.

original: By your leave, ho!   I Know her women are about her: what   If I do line one of their hands?
translation: Hello!  [To himself]  I know her attendants are with her. What if I bribe one of them?

original: 'Tis gold   Which buys admittance; oft it doth; yea, and makes   Diana's rangers false themselves, yield up   Their deer to the stand o' the stealer;
translation: Gold often buys you a way in, and makes even the goddess Diana's attendants deceive her and give up the deer they were tracking to a thief.

original: and 'tis gold   Which makes the true man kill'd and saves the thief;   Nay, sometime hangs both thief and true man:
translation: It's gold that leads to an honest man being killed and saves a thief. Sometimes it leads to both thief and honest man being hanged.

original: what   Can it not do and undo? I will make   One of her women lawyer to me, for   I yet not understand the case myself.
translation: What can't it do and undo? I'll make one of her women my  lawyer , because I don't completely understand the case myself.

original: By your leave.
translation: Hello!

original: Who's there that knocks?
translation: Who's knocking out there?

original: A gentleman.
translation: A gentleman.

original: No more?
translation: That's all?

original: Yes, and a gentlewoman's son.
translation: Yes, and I'm also a lady's son.

original: That's more Than some, whose tailors are as dear as yours, Can justly boast of. What's your lordship's pleasure?
translation: That's more than some people can say who go to the same expensive tailors you do. What do you want?

original: Your lady's person: is she ready?
translation: Your mistress. Is she ready?

original: Ay, To keep her chamber.
translation: Yes, to stay in her room.

original: There is gold for you; Sell me your good report.
translation: Here's gold for you. I'll pay you to say good things about me.

original: How! my good name? or to report of you What I shall think is good?—The princess!
translation: What? Are you asking me to sell my reputation? Or describe you accurately? Here's the princess!

original: Good morrow, fairest: sister, your sweet hand.
translation: Good morning, beautiful one. Sister, give me your sweet hand.

original: Good morrow, sir. You lay out too much pains   For purchasing but trouble;
translation: Good morning, sir. You're putting in too much effort for no reward.

original: the thanks I give   Is telling you that I am poor of thanks   And scarce can spare them.
translation: All I can say to thank you is that I don't have much thanks left and can hardly spare any.

original: Still, I swear I love you.
translation: Still, I promise I love you.

original: If you but said so, 'twere as deep with me:
translation: If you just said you did, it would mean the same to me.

original: If you swear still, your recompense is still   That I regard it not.
translation: If you keep promising, my answer will always be that I don't care.

original: This is no answer.
translation: That's no answer.

original: But that you shall not say I yield being silent,   I would not speak.
translation: I wouldn't speak, except that if I didn't say anything, you would say my silence meant consent.

original: I pray you, spare me: 'faith,   I shall unfold equal discourtesy   To your best kindness:
translation: Please, leave me alone. I will only pay back your kindness with rudeness.

original: one of your great knowing   Should learn, being taught, forbearance.
translation: Someone of your huge intelligence should learn to give up.

original: To leave you in your madness, 'twere my sin: I will not.
translation: It would be wrong to let you be this crazy. I won't.

original: Fools are not mad folks.
translation: Fools are not crazy.

original: Do you call me fool?
translation: Are you calling me a fool?

original: As I am mad, I do:   If you'll be patient, I'll no more be mad;   That cures us both.
translation: I'm crazy, so I did. If you agree to be patient, I won't be mad any more. So we're both cured.

original: I am much sorry, sir,   You put me to forget a lady's manners,   By being so verbal:
translation: I am really sorry, sir, that you made me forget the good manners that a lady should have by talking so much.

original: and learn now, for all,   That I, which know my heart, do here pronounce,   By the very truth of it, I care not for you,
translation: So let me announce here and now, forever, that I know my own heart and I don't care for you.

original: And am so near the lack of charity—   To accuse myself—I hate you; which I had rather   You felt than make't my boast.
translation: I'll even accuse myself of lacking charity by saying that I hate you. I wish you could understand that without my having to say it.

original: You sin against   Obedience, which you owe your father. For   The contract you pretend with that base wretch,   One bred of alms and foster'd with cold dishes,   With scraps o' the court, it is no contract, none:
translation: You're sinning by disobeying your father. The marriage you pretend to be in with that lowlife was paid for by handouts and leftovers and scraps from the court, and it isn't legally binding.

original: And though it be allow'd in meaner parties—   Yet who than he more mean?—to knit their souls,   On whom there is no more dependency   But brats and beggary, in self-figured knot;
translation: Lower-class people—but who's lower than him?—are allowed to marry for love because the only consequence for them will be brats and poverty,

original: Yet you are curb'd from that enlargement by   The consequence o' the crown, and must not soil   The precious note of it with a base slave.
translation: but you can't have that freedom because you'll inherit the crown. You can't make it dirty by marrying a lower-class slave.

original: A hilding for a livery, a squire's cloth,   A pantler, not so eminent.
translation: He's a worthless man who should be a servant or a squire or a bread-carver, not raised to such a high class.

original: Profane fellow   Wert thou the son of Jupiter and no more   But what thou art besides, thou wert too base   To be his groom:
translation: You rude man, even if you were the son of Jupiter and no better than you are now, you would be too lowly to be his servant.

original: thou wert dignified enough,   Even to the point of envy, if 'twere made   Comparative for your virtues, to be styled   The under-hangman of his kingdom, and hated   For being preferred so well.
translation: You would be honored enough, and people would envy you, given your qualities, if you were made his kingdom's hangman's assistant, and you would be hated for being promoted so high.

original: The south-fog rot him!
translation: May he rot in the fog of the south of Europe!

original: He never can meet more mischance than come   To be but named of thee.
translation: The worst thing that could happen to him is for you to just say his name.

original: His meanest garment,   That ever hath but clipp'd his body, is dearer   In my respect than all the hairs above thee,   Were they all made such men. How now, Pisanio!
translation: I care more about any piece of clothing he ever wore than as many men like you as you have hairs on your head. Pisanio!

original: 'His garment!' Now the devil—
translation: "Any piece of clothing!" The devil—

original: To Dorothy my woman hie thee presently—
translation: Go to Dorothy, my attendant—

original: 'His garment!'
translation: "Any piece of clothing!"

original: I am sprited with a fool.   Frighted, and anger'd worse:
translation: A foolish man is haunting me. I'm afraid, but more angry than afraid.

original: go bid my woman   Search for a jewel that too casually   Hath left mine arm: it was thy master's: 'shrew me,   If I would lose it for a revenue   Of any king's in Europe.
translation: Go ask my attendant to search for a bracelet that's missing from my arm. It was my husband's. I swear I wouldn't lose it for the wealth of any king in Europe.

original: I do think   I saw't this morning: confident I am   Last night 'twas on mine arm; I kiss'd it:
translation: I think I saw it this morning. I'm sure it was on my arm last night. I kissed it.

original: I hope it be not gone to tell my lord   That I kiss aught but he.
translation: I hope it hasn't gone to tell my husband that I kiss anything other than him.

original: 'Twill not be lost.
translation: It won't be lost.

original: I hope so: go and search.
translation: I hope so. Go look for it.

original: You have abused me: 'His meanest garment!'
translation: You were rude to me. "Any piece of clothing he ever wore!"

original: Ay, I said so, sir: If you will make't an action, call witness to't.
translation: Yes, sir, I said that. If you want to sue me, find a witness.

original: I will inform your father.
translation: I'll tell your father.

original: Your mother too:   She's my good lady, and will conceive, I hope,   But the worst of me.
translation: Tell your mother too. She's in charge of me, and I hope she'll just think worse of me for this.

original: So, I leave you, sir,   To the worst of discontent.
translation: I'll leave you to your anger, sir.

original: I'll be revenged: 'His meanest garment!' Well.
translation: I'll get my revenge. "Any piece of clothing!" Fine.

original: Hung be the heavens with black, yield day to night!
translation: The skies are covered with darkness, day has passed into night now!

original: Comets, importing change of times and states,   Brandish your crystal tresses in the sky,   And with them scourge the bad revolting stars   That have consented unto Henry's death!
translation: Comets, which announce change, you should move frantically through the sky and punish those that are responsible for Henry's death!

original: King Henry the Fifth, too famous to live long!   England ne'er lost a king of so much worth.
England ne'er had a king until his time.
translation: England has never had such a king before him.

original: Virtue he had, deserving to command:
translation: He was virtuous and good, a born leader.

original: His brandish'd sword did blind men with his beams:   His arms spread wider than a dragon's wings;
translation: His sword shined, its light could blind men around him. His arms were wider than a dragon's wings.

original: His sparking eyes, replete with wrathful fire,   More dazzled and drove back his enemies
translation: His bright eyes were so full of angry fire that his glare blinded and drove away his enemies.

original: Than mid-day sun fierce bent against their faces.
translation: The fire in his eyes was brighter than the sun shining in his enemies' faces at noon.

original: What should I say? his deeds exceed all speech:   He ne'er lift up his hand but conquered.
translation: What else can I say? Words don't do his actions justice. He succeeded every time he set out to do something.

original: We mourn in black: why mourn we not in blood?
translation: We mourn dressed in black, but shouldn't we mourn by  shedding blood ?

original: Henry is dead and never shall revive:
translation: Henry is dead and will never live again.

original: Upon a wooden coffin we attend,   And death's dishonourable victory   We with our stately presence glorify,
translation: We are here around a wooden coffin, honoring the dishonest victory of death over our king.

original: Like captives bound to a triumphant car.
translation: We are attached to the coffin like slaves bound to a chariot processing through the streets in triumph .

original: What! shall we curse the planets of mishap   That plotted thus our glory's overthrow?
translation: What!? Should we curse the planets that bring bad luck, because they planned to ruin our triumph?

original: Or shall we think the subtle-witted French   Conjurers and sorcerers, that afraid of him   By magic verses have contrived his end?
translation: Or should we think that it was the crafty and clever French magicians and wizards that cast magic spells on him to end his life, because they were so afraid of him?

original: He was a king bless'd of the King of kings.
translation: He was lucky because he was the best of  kings .

original: Unto the French the dreadful judgement-day   So dreadful will not be as was his sight.
translation: For the French, he was worse than the end of the world, they were so terrified to see him.

original: The battles of the Lord of hosts he fought:   The church's prayers made him so prosperous.
translation: He fought battles in the name of God and the prayers of the church made him successful.

original: The church! where is it? Had not churchmen pray'd,   His thread of life had not so soon decay'd:
translation: The church! Where is the church? Wasn't it the churchmen who  prayed  for his death?

original: None do you like but an effeminate prince,   Whom, like a school-boy, you may over-awe.
translation: Men of the church only like a weak prince who they can control as if he were a school boy.

original: Gloucester, whate'er we like, thou art protector   And lookest to command the prince and realm.
translation: Gloucester, let's consider you for a moment. You are the new king's protector and so you must guide the prince and rule the realm.

original: Thy wife is proud; she holdeth thee in awe,   More than God or religious churchmen may.
translation: Your wife is proud, she admires you more than God or churchmen might.

original: Name not religion, for thou lovest the flesh, And ne'er throughout the year to church thou go'st Except it be to pray against thy foes.
translation: Do not call on religion. You love only objects and money and sex and you only go to church during the year to pray against your enemies.

original: Cease, cease these jars and rest your minds in peace:
translation: Stop, stop these arguments, you two and relax a little.

original: Let's to the altar: heralds, wait on us:
translation: Let's get on with the funeral, messengers are waiting for us.

original: Instead of gold, we'll offer up our arms:   Since arms avail not now that Henry's dead.
translation: We will offer our weapons to the altar instead of gold, since there is no use for weapons now that Henry is dead.

original: Posterity, await for wretched years,   When at their mothers' moist eyes babes shall suck,
translation: Future generations, years of misery await you, when babies will only be fed by their mothers' tears.

original: Our isle be made a nourish of salt tears,   And none but women left to wail the dead.
translation: Our island will feed on salty tears, and only women will be left to mourn the dead.

original: Henry the Fifth, thy ghost I invocate:   Prosper this realm, keep it from civil broils,   Combat with adverse planets in the heavens!
translation: I call on your ghost, Henry the Fifth. Make this country rich and keep it free of conflict. Fight with the planets in the sky that try to prevent this!

original: A far more glorious star thy soul will make   Than Julius Caesar or bright—
translation: After all, your soul will transform into a more famous star than Julius Caesar or shining—

original: My honourable lords, health to you all!
translation: Honorable lords, I wish you all well!

original: Sad tidings bring I to you out of France,   Of loss, of slaughter and discomfiture:
translation: I bring bad news to you from France;  news of loss, killings and absolute defeat.

original: Guienne, Champagne, Rheims, Orleans,   Paris, Guysors, Poictiers, are all quite lost.
translation: We have lost Guienne, Champagne, Rheims, Orleans, Paris, Guysors, and Poictiers.

original: What say'st thou, man, before dead Henry's corse?
translation: What are you saying? And why are you saying it before the body of the dead Henry?

original: Speak softly, or the loss of those great towns   Will make him burst his lead and rise from death.
translation: Speak quietly, or else he might break out of his lead-lined coffin and rise from the dead, if he hears about the loss of those great towns.

original: Is Paris lost? is Rouen yielded up? If Henry were recall'd to life again, These news would cause him once more yield the ghost.
translation: Has Paris been lost? And did Rouen surrender? If Henry were brought back to life, that news would make him die again.

original: How were they lost? What treachery was used?
translation: How were they lost? Was treason involved?

original: No treachery; but want of men and money.
translation: No treason—there weren't enough men and we needed more money.

original: Amongst the soldiers this is muttered,   That here you maintain several factions,   And whilst a field should be dispatch'd and fought,   You are disputing of your generals:
translation: The soldiers were saying that you have opposing groups here, and instead of sending out men to fight, you are arguing about your generals.

original: One would have lingering wars with little cost;
translation: One general wants to delay the war and save money.

original: Another would fly swift, but wanteth wings;
translation: Another wants to act quickly and fly, but has no wings to do so.

original: A third thinks, without expense at all,   By guileful fair words peace may be obtain'd.
translation: A third one thinks that peace can be brought about with deceitful words and with no money spent at all.

original: Awake, awake, English nobility!   Let not sloth dim your horrors new-begot:
translation: You have to wake up, English aristocrats! Don't let your laziness cloud your vision of these new horrors.

original: Cropp'd are the flower-de-luces in your arms;   Of England's coat one half is cut away.
translation: The  flower-de-luces  are cut out of your coat of arms, so half of England's coat of arms is already gone.

original: Were our tears wanting to this funeral, These tidings would call forth their flowing tides.
translation: If we didn't cry enough at this funeral, this news will surely make us cry more.

original: Me they concern; Regent I am of France.   Give me my steeled coat. I'll fight for France.
translation: As Regent of France, I am concerned about this. Give me my armor. I'll fight for France.

original: Away with these disgraceful wailing robes!
translation: Put away these shameful mourning clothes!

original: Wounds will I lend the French instead of eyes,   To weep their intermissive miseries.
translation: I will not cry for the miseries in France but will instead fight for them and offer up my body.

original: Lords, view these letters full of bad mischance.
translation: Lords, take a look at these letters which tell of horror.

original: France is revolted from the English quite,   Except some petty towns of no import:
translation: France is rebelling against the English, other than some small towns of no importance.

original: The Dauphin Charles is crowned king of Rheims;   The Bastard of Orleans with him is join'd;
Reignier, Duke of Anjou, doth take his part;   The Duke of Alencon flieth to his side.
translation: Reignier, Duke of Anjou is also with them, and the Duke of Alencon ran to support him.

original: The Dauphin crowned king! All fly to him! O, whither shall we fly from this reproach?
translation: The Dauphin has been made king! And they all run to him! Oh, how can we escape this shame?

original: We will not fly, but to our enemies' throats. Bedford, if thou be slack, I'll fight it out.
translation: We won't run, unless we run toward the throats of our enemies. Bedford, if you're too lazy, I will fight.

original: Gloucester, why doubt'st thou of my forwardness? An army have I muster'd in my thoughts, Wherewith already France is overrun.
translation: Why do you doubt that I am ready to fight, Gloucester? In my mind, I imagine that I have already gathered an army and invaded France.

original: My gracious lords, to add to your laments,
translation: Kind lords, I bring more sad news to add to your sorrows.

original: Wherewith you now bedew King Henry's hearse,   I must inform you of a dismal fight   Betwixt the stout Lord Talbot and the French.
translation: While you were here, mourning King Henry's coffin and crying over him, there was a disastrous fight between the bold Lord Talbot and the French.

original: What! Wherein Talbot overcame? Is't so?
translation: What? And Talbot lost this fight? Is that right?

original: O, no; wherein Lord Talbot was o'erthrown:   The circumstance I'll tell you more at large.
translation: Oh no, I will tell you more about how Talbot was defeated.

original: The tenth of August last this dreadful lord,   Retiring from the siege of Orleans,   Having full scarce six thousand in his troop.
translation: On the 10th of August, this frightening man left the blockade at Orleans. He had barely 6000 soldiers.

original: By three and twenty thousand of the French   Was round encompassed and set upon.   No leisure had he to enrank his men;
translation: They were completely surrounded by 23,000 French soldiers. He couldn't put his men back into battle formation.

original: He wanted pikes to set before his archers;   Instead whereof sharp stakes pluck'd out of hedges
translation: He wanted to put pikes in the ground in front  of his archers to protect them from the enemy, but sharp spears attacked them from the hedges.

original: They pitched in the ground confusedly,   To keep the horsemen off from breaking in.
translation: So, they sank to the ground, confused, to try and keep the men on horses from breaking in.

original: More than three hours the fight continued;   Where valiant Talbot above human thought   Enacted wonders with his sword and lance:
translation: The fight continued for more than three hours, when brave Talbot, seemingly superhuman, carried out wonders with his sword and spear.

original: Hundreds he sent to hell, and none durst stand him;   Here, there, and every where, enraged he flew:
translation: He sent hundreds of men to hell and none dared to stand against him. He was flying around angrily, all over the place.

original: The French exclaim'd, the devil was in arms;   All the whole army stood agazed on him:
translation: "The devil is here!" cried the French. The whole army was looking at him, amazed.

original: His soldiers spying his undaunted spirit   A Talbot! A Talbot! Cried out amain   And rush'd into the bowels of the battle.
translation: His soldiers were carefully watching his unbreakable spirit. "Talbot! Talbot!" they cried out with all their strength and hurried to the center of the battle.

original: Here had the conquest fully been seal'd up,   If Sir John Fastolfe had not play'd the coward:
translation: This is where the battle would have ended, if John Fastolfe had not been such a coward.

original: He, being in the vaward, placed behind   With purpose to relieve and follow them,
translation: He should have followed and helped them, since he was at the front of the troops.

original: Cowardly fled, not having struck one stroke.
translation: But instead he ran away like a coward and didn't even use his sword once.

original: Hence grew the general wreck and massacre;   Enclosed were they with their enemies:
translation: This is when the real ruin and massacre started—once they were surrounded by their enemies.

original: A base Walloon, to win the Dauphin's grace,   Thrust Talbot with a spear into the back,
translation: A lowly  Walloon  wanted to win the Dauphin's favor and so he thrust his spear into Talbot's back.

original: Whom all France with their chief assembled strength   Durst not presume to look once in the face.
translation: Now all of France does not want to look Talbot in the face, not even after they have gathered all their strength.

original: Is Talbot slain?
translation: Is Talbot dead?

original: Then I will slay myself,   For living idly here in pomp and ease,   Whilst such a worthy leader, wanting aid,   Unto his dastard foemen is betray'd.
translation: Then, I will kill myself, because being lazy and living in luxurious comfort, while such a noble leader is destroyed by his cowardly enemies, is betrayal.

original: O no, he lives; but is took prisoner, And Lord Scales with him and Lord Hungerford: Most of the rest slaughter'd or took likewise.
translation: Oh, no, he lives. But he is a prisoner, along with Lord Scales and Lord Hungerford. The others were either killed or also taken prisoner.

original: His ransom there is none but I shall pay:
translation: I don't care how much I have to pay to get him out, I will pay it.

original: I'll hale the Dauphin headlong from his throne:   His crown shall be the ransom of my friend;
translation: I'll drag the Dauphin from his throne and his crown will be the price I pay to bring back my friend.

original: Four of their lords I'll change for one of ours.
translation: I will exchange four of their lords for one of ours.

original: Farewell, my masters; to my task will I;
translation: Goodbye, my lords, I need to carry out this job.

original: Bonfires in France forthwith I am to make,   To keep our great Saint George's feast withal:
translation: I will make fires in France, to celebrate our holiday— Saint George's celebration .

original: Ten thousand soldiers with me I will take,   Whose bloody deeds shall make all Europe quake.
translation: I will take 10,000 soldiers with me and their bloody actions will shake all of Europe.

original: So you had need; for Orleans is besieged;
translation: You should do that, since Orleans is surrounded.

original: The English army is grown weak and faint:
translation: The English army is becoming weak.

original: The Earl of Salisbury craveth supply,
translation: The Earl of Salisbury needs help.

original: And hardly keeps his men from mutiny,   Since they, so few, watch such a multitude.
translation: He can't stop his men from rebelling, since the few he has left have to watch such a huge army.

original: Remember, lords, your oaths to Henry sworn, Either to quell the Dauphin utterly, Or bring him in obedience to your yoke.
translation: You should remember what you swore to Henry, lords. Either we crush the Dauphin completely, or we make him our obedient slave.

original: I do remember it; and here take my leave, To go about my preparation.
translation: I remember it and am leaving now to prepare.

original: I'll to the Tower with all the haste I can, To view the artillery and munition; And then I will proclaim young Henry king.
translation: I'll go to the Tower, as fast as I can, to check out the state of our weapons. And then I will announce that young Henry is king.

original: To Eltham will I, where the young king is, Being ordain'd his special governor, And for his safety there I'll best devise.
translation: I will go to Eltham, where the young king is. I am his guardian, after all and am in charge of his safety.

original: Each hath his place and function to attend:   I am left out; for me nothing remains.
translation: Each of you has somewhere to go and something to do. I am the only one left out, there is nothing for me to do.

original: But long I will not be Jack out of office:
translation: But I will not be like someone who has been told to leave his rightful place.

original: The king from Eltham I intend to steal   And sit at chiefest stern of public weal.
translation: I am planning to steal the king from Eltham and so assume the highest position from Exeter and control the state.

original: Mars his true moving, even as in the heavens   So in the earth, to this day is not known:
translation: We still don't know the exact way in which Mars moves in the heavens or on earth.

original: Late did he shine upon the English side;   Now we are victors; upon us he smiles.
translation: Recently, he has shown favor to the English, but now we have won and he seems to smile on us.

original: What towns of any moment but we have?   At pleasure here we lie near Orleans;
translation: What important towns do we have? We are happily here near Orleans.

original: Otherwhiles the famish'd English, like pale ghosts,   Faintly besiege us one hour in a month.
translation: Otherwise the starving English, looking like pale ghosts, would surround us slowly, in their weak state.

original: They want their porridge and their fat bull-beeves:
translation: They only want to eat their porridge and beef.

original: Either they must be dieted like mules
translation: We must either feed them as if they were mules

original: And have their provender tied to their mouths
translation: and have their animal food tied close to their mouths,

original: Or piteous they will look, like drowned mice.
translation: or they will look miserable, like drowned mice.

original: Let's raise the siege: why live we idly here?
translation: Let's increase our attacks. Why are we so lazy these days?

original: Talbot is taken, whom we wont to fear:
translation: We used to be scared of Talbot, but he is captured.

original: Remaineth none but mad-brain'd Salisbury;   And he may well in fretting spend his gall,
translation: The only one left is the crazy Salisbury and he is so impatient that he will probably lose his anger.

original: Nor men nor money hath he to make war.
translation: Plus, he hasn't got any men or money to start a war.

original: Sound, sound alarum!
translation: Call our men to battle!

original: we will rush on them.
translation: We will hurry towards them.

original: Now for the honour of the forlorn French!
translation: We fight for the honor of the hopeless French!

original: Him I forgive my death that killeth me   When he sees me go back one foot or fly.
translation: I forgive whoever will kill me,  when he sees that I step one foot back and run away.

original: Who ever saw the like? What men have I! Dogs! cowards! dastards! I would ne'er have fled, But that they left me 'midst my enemies.
translation: Who has ever seen anything like this before? What kind of men do I have? Dogs! Cowards! I wouldn't have run away if they hadn't left me alone surrounded by my enemies.

original: Salisbury is a desperate homicide;   He fighteth as one weary of his life.
translation: Salisbury is a desperate murderer. He fought as if he were tired of his own life.

original: The other lords, like lions wanting food,   Do rush upon us as their hungry prey.
translation: The other lords were like lions who want food—they hurried towards us. They were the hungry lions, we were the prey.

original: Froissart, a countryman of ours, records,   England all Olivers and Rowlands bred,   During the time Edward the Third did reign.
translation: Our countryman,  Froissart , writes that England brought to life all  Olivers and Rowlands , during Edward the Third's rule.

original: More truly now may this be verified;   For none but Samsons and Goliases   It sendeth forth to skirmish.
translation: Now, we can confirm this is true, because England have sent out only  Samsons and Goliases to fight.

original: One to ten!
translation: One English man for every ten French ones!

original: Lean, raw-boned rascals! who would e'er suppose   They had such courage and audacity?
translation: Thin, skeleton-like  villains ! Who would have thought they had such courage and boldness?

original: Let's leave this town;
translation: Let's leave this town,

original: for they are hare-brain'd  slaves,
translation: because they are reckless villains.

original: And hunger will enforce them to be more eager:
translation: Hunger will make them even more eager.

original: Of old I know them;
translation: I have known them for a while.

original: rather with their teeth   The walls they'll tear down than forsake the siege.
translation: They would rather tear down the walls with their teeth than give up this attack.

original: I think, by some odd gimmors or device   Their arms are set like clocks,
translation: I think that by some mechanism or device their arms are like clocks.

original: stiff to strike on;
translation: Their arms remain firm when you hit them.

original: Else ne'er could they hold out so as they do.
translation: Otherwise, they could not last as long as they do now.

original: By my consent, we'll even let them alone.
translation: I say, let's leave them alone.

original: Be it so.
translation: Let's.

original: Where's the Prince Dauphin? I have news for him.
translation: Where is the Prince Dauphin? I have news for him.

original: Bastard of Orleans, thrice welcome to us.
translation: You're very welcome, Bastard of Orleans.

original: Methinks your looks are sad, your cheer appall'd:   Hath the late overthrow wrought this offence?
translation: I think you look sad, and your face is pale. Did our recent loss cause this?

original: Be not dismay'd, for succor is at hand:   A holy maid hither with me I bring,
translation: Don't fear! Help is on its way. I bring a holy girl with me.

original: Which by a vision sent to her from heaven   Ordained is to raise this tedious siege   And drive the English forth the bounds of France.
translation: She has been sent a vision from heaven by which God appointed her to end this battle and drive the English out of France.

original: The spirit of deep prophecy she hath,   Exceeding the nine sibyls of old Rome:   What's past and what's to come she can descry.
translation: She is a prophet, even more powerful than  the nine sibyls of old Rome  and she sees the past and the future.

original: Speak, shall I call her in? Believe my words,   For they are certain and unfallible.
translation: Tell me, should I ask her to come in? Believe the words I speak, because they are true and reliable.

original: Go, call her in.
translation: Go, tell her to come in.

original: But first, to try her skill,
translation: But let's test how good she is first.

original: Reignier, stand thou as Dauphin in my place:   Question her proudly; let thy looks be stern:
translation: Reignier, pretend that you are the Dauphin and sit in my place. Ask her proud questions and look harshly on her.

original: By this means shall we sound what skill she hath.
translation: This way, we can test her skills.

original: Fair maid, is't thou wilt do these wondrous feats?
translation: Pretty girl, is it you who will perform these miraculous actions?

original: Reignier, is't thou that thinkest to beguile me?   Where is the Dauphin?   Come, come from behind;
translation: Reignier, do you think that you can deceive me?   Where is the Dauphin?  Come, come from behind.

original: I know thee well, though never seen before.
translation: I know you well although I have never seen you before.

original: Be not amazed, there's nothing hid from me:
translation: Don't be surprised, you can't hide anything from me.

original: In private will I talk with thee apart.
translation: I will talk to you alone.

original: Stand back, you lords, and give us leave awhile.
translation: Stand back, you lords, and leave us for a while.

original: She takes upon her bravely at first dash.
translation: For her first meeting, she plays her part well.

original: Dauphin, I am by birth a shepherd's daughter,   My wit untrain'd in any kind of art.
translation: Dauphin, I am a shepherd's daughter, I am unintelligent and uneducated.

original: Heaven and our Lady gracious hath it pleased   To shine on my contemptible estate:
translation: But Heaven and the Virgin Mary have decided to shine on my low status.

original: Lo, whilst I waited on my tender lambs,   And to sun's parching heat display'd my cheeks,   God's mother deigned to appear to me   And in a vision full of majesty
translation: While I was taking care of my young lambs, and the sun's heat burned my cheeks, God's mother appeared to me in an impressive vision.

original: Will'd me to leave my base vocation   And free my country from calamity:
translation: She wanted me to leave my poor job and save my country from disaster.

original: Her aid she promised and assured success:   In complete glory she reveal'd herself;
translation: In her perfect glory, she promised me her help and said it was guaranteed that I would succeed.

original: And, whereas I was black and swart before,   With those clear rays which she infused on me   That beauty am I bless'd with which you see.
translation: I was dark and ugly before but she made me beautiful, as you can see, with her bright rays.

original: Ask me what question thou canst possible,   And I will answer unpremeditated:
translation: Ask me anything you want and I will answer it straight away.

original: My courage try by combat, if thou darest,   And thou shalt find that I exceed my sex.
translation: Test my courage in a fight, if you dare to and you will find that I am better at it than other women.

original: Resolve on this, thou shalt be fortunate,   If thou receive me for thy warlike mate.
translation: If you agree, you will be lucky, because you can have me as your  partner  in this war.

original: Thou hast astonish'd me with thy high terms:
translation: I am amazed by your well-spoken words.

original: Only this proof I'll of thy valour make,
translation: I will only test your courage in one fight with you.

original: In single combat thou shalt buckle with me,   And if thou vanquishest, thy words are true;
translation: If you overcome me and win, your words are true.

original: Otherwise I renounce all confidence.
translation: If not, you lose all my trust.

original: I am prepared:
translation: I am ready.

original: here is my keen-edged sword,   Deck'd with five flower-de-luces on each side;
translation: Here is my sharp sword, decorated with five flower-de-luces on each side.

original: The which at Touraine, in Saint Katharine's   churchyard,   Out of a great deal of old iron I chose forth.
translation: I picked this sword out of old iron at Touraine, in Saint Katherine's churchyard.

original: Then come, o' God's name; I fear no woman.
translation: Then let's do this, in God's name! I am not afraid of any woman.

original: And while I live, I'll ne'er fly from a man.
translation: And while I am alive, I will never run away from any man.

original: Stay, stay thy hands! thou art an Amazon And fightest with the sword of Deborah.
Christ's mother helps me, else I were too weak.
translation: I would be too weak without the help of the Virgin Mary.

original: Whoe'er helps thee, 'tis thou that must help me:
translation: Whoever is it that helps you, it is you that must help me.

original: Impatiently I burn with thy desire;
translation: The same urge to fight that you feel now burns in me, impatiently.

original: My heart and hands thou hast at once subdued.
translation: You have conquered my heart and my hands.

original: Excellent Pucelle, if thy name be so,
translation: You are excellent, Pucelle—if that is your name.

original: Let me thy servant and not sovereign be:
translation: Let me be your servant instead of your ruler.

original: 'Tis the French Dauphin sueth to thee thus.
translation: The French Dauphin begs you so.

original: I must not yield to any rites of love,   For my profession's sacred from above:
translation: I must not give in to love, because my purpose is blessed from the heavens.

original: When I have chased all thy foes from hence,   Then will I think upon a recompense.
translation: When I have frightened away all your enemies, then I will think about a payment.

original: Meantime look gracious on thy prostrate thrall.
translation: In the meantime, look with favor on your kneeling slave.

original: My lord, methinks, is very long in talk.
translation: I think my lord is talking too much.

original: Doubtless he shrives this woman to her smock; Else ne'er could he so long protract his speech.
translation: He must be hearing her confession and offering her forgiveness, otherwise he wouldn't speak for so long.

original: Shall we disturb him, since he keeps no mean?
translation: Should we interrupt him, since he is taking so long?

original: He may mean more than we poor men do know: These women are shrewd tempters with their tongues.
translation: He may know more than us poor men do. These women can tempt with their sharp tongues.

original: My lord, where are you? What devise you on? Shall we give over Orleans, or no?
translation: My lord, what are your intentions? What are you planning to do? Should we abandon Orleans or not?

original: Why, no, I say, distrustful recreants! Fight till the last gasp; I will be your guard.
translation: I say: "No!" you doubting cowards! You will fight until your last breath. I will be your guard.

original: What she says I'll confirm: we'll fight it out.
translation: I can confirm what she says. We will fight!

original: Assign'd am I to be the English scourge.   This night the siege assuredly I'll raise:
translation: I have been chosen to punish the English. I will start the attack tonight.

original: Expect Saint Martin's summer, halcyon days,   Since I have entered into these wars.
translation: Expect  Saint Martin's summer  and calm days, now that I have come to fight in these battles.

original: Glory is like a circle in the water,   Which never ceaseth to enlarge itself   Till by broad spreading it disperse to nought.
