translation: Also, I worry that if your thoughts were closely examined, the king, your ruler, would not be entirely excluded from the jealous cruelty of your arrogant heart.

original: Gloucester, I do defy thee. Lords, vouchsafe   To give me hearing what I shall reply.
translation: Gloucester, I dare you. Lords, listen to my reply to him.

original: If I were covetous, ambitious or perverse,   As he will have me, how am I so poor?
translation: If I were greedy, ambitious or stubborn, as he described me, why am I so poor?

original: Or how haps it I seek not to advance   Or raise myself, but keep my wonted calling?
translation: Or why do I not try to rise above my status, but instead keep my low position?

original: And for dissension, who preferreth peace   More than I do?—except I be provoked.
translation: And in a disagreement, who prefers peace more than I do—unless I am provoked?

original: No, my good lords, it is not that offends;   It is not that that hath incensed the duke:
translation: No, my good lords, this is not what offends him. It is not this that made the duke angry.

original: It is, because no one should sway but he;   No one but he should be about the king;
translation: It is because he believes no one but him should rule, no one but him should be around the king.

original: And that engenders thunder in his breast   And makes him roar these accusations forth.
translation: That's  what causes thunder in his chest and makes him scream these accusations at us.

original: But he shall know I am as good—
translation: But he shall know that I am as good—

original: As good! Thou bastard of my grandfather!
Ay, lordly sir; for what are you, I pray, But one imperious in another's throne?
translation: Yes, my lord, but what are you if not one acting like a king in someone else's throne?

original: Am I not protector, saucy priest?
translation: Am I not the protector, you insolent priest?

original: And am not I a prelate of the church?
translation: Am I not the representative of the church?

original: Yes, as an outlaw in a castle keeps And useth it to patronage his theft.
translation: Yes, you are like a criminal who lives in a castle and uses it to protect what he stole.

original: Unreverent Gloucester!
translation: You are not worthy of respect, Gloucester!

original: Thou art reverent Touching thy spiritual function, not thy life.
translation: You are worthy of respect, when it comes to your spiritual function but not your life.

original: Rome shall remedy this.
Roam thither, then.
My lord, it were your duty to forbear.
translation: My lord, it is your duty to refrain yourself.

original: Ay, see the bishop be not overborne.
translation: Yes, the bishop should not be overruled.

original: Methinks my lord should be religious And know the office that belongs to such.
translation: I think my lord should be religious and know that the office belongs to such religious persons.

original: Methinks his lordship should be humbler; it fitteth not a prelate so to plead.
translation: I think his lordship should be more modest, a priest should not beg so much.

original: Yes, when his holy state is touch'd so near.
translation: Yes, especially when his holy status is so closely concerned.

original: State holy or unhallow'd, what of that? Is not his grace protector to the king?
translation: Holy or unholy status, who cares about that? Isn't his grace the protector to the king?

original: Plantagenet, I see, must hold his tongue,   Lest it be said 'Speak, sirrah, when you should;
translation: I see that a Plantagenet must remain quiet  unless they would say "Speak, sir, when you should.

original: Must your bold verdict enter talk with lords?'
translation: Why must your daring judgement interrupt the lords' talk?"

original: Else would I have a fling at Winchester.
translation: Otherwise, I would attack Winchester with my words.

original: Uncles of Gloucester and of Winchester,   The special watchmen of our English weal,
translation: Uncles Gloucester and Winchester, you are the special men who watch over our commonwealth.

original: I would prevail, if prayers might prevail,   To join your hearts in love and amity.
translation: I would successfully persuade you, with the help of my prayers, to join your hearts in love and friendship.

original: O, what a scandal is it to our crown,   That two such noble peers as ye should jar!
translation: Oh, it is a scandal to our crown that two good lords should argue!

original: Believe me, lords, my tender years can tell   Civil dissension is a viperous worm   That gnaws the bowels of the commonwealth.
translation: Believe me, my lords, even my youth recognizes that civil disagreement is like a poisonous snake that chews the insides of the commonwealth.

original: What tumult's this?
translation: What noise is that?

original: An uproar, I dare warrant, Begun through malice of the bishop's men.
translation: I'd say it is a hubbub that began as a result of the bitterness of the bishop's men.

original: O, my good lords, and virtuous Henry,   Pity the city of London, pity us!
translation: Oh, my good lords and virtuous Henry! Feel sorry for the city of London, feel sorry for us!

original: The bishop and the Duke of Gloucester's men,   Forbidden late to carry any weapon,
translation: The bishop and the Duke of Gloucester's men, who have recently been forbidden from carrying weapons,

original: Have fill'd their pockets full of pebble stones
translation: have filled their pockets with small stones.

original: And banding themselves in contrary parts   Do pelt so fast at one another's pate
translation: They formed groups of the two opposing parties and threw the stones at each others' heads

original: That many have their giddy brains knock'd out:
translation: so that many of their mad brains were knocked out of them.

original: Our windows are broke down in every street   And we for fear compell'd to shut our shops.
translation: In every street, our windows are broken and we were so afraid of them that we had to close our shops.

original: We charge you, on allegiance to ourself, To hold your slaughtering hands and keep the peace. Pray, uncle Gloucester, mitigate this strife.
translation: We command you, based on your loyalty to us, to stop your murdering hands and to maintain peace. Please, uncle Gloucester, calm down this fight.

original: Nay, if we be forbidden stones, We'll fall to it with our teeth.
translation: No! If we are forbidden from using stones, we will fight with our own teeth!

original: Do what ye dare, we are as resolute.
translation: Do what you want! We are determined.

original: You of my household, leave this peevish broil And set this unaccustom'd fight aside.
translation: Those of you who are from my house, leave this foolish and unusual fight behind.

original: My lord, we know your grace to be a man   Just and upright;
translation: @ My lord, we know that your grace is a good fair man

original: and, for your royal birth,   Inferior to none but to his majesty:
translation: and that only the king has a higher royal birth than you do.

original: And ere that we will suffer such a prince,   So kind a father of the commonweal,   To be disgraced by an inkhorn mate,
translation: And before we allow such a prince, such a kind father to the commonwealth to be disgraced by someone of a low status,

original: We and our wives and children all will fight   And have our bodies slaughtered by thy foes.
translation: we and our wives and children will  all  fight and have ourselves killed by your enemies.

original: Ay, and the very parings of our nails Shall pitch a field when we are dead.
translation: Yes! And the trimmings of our nails will prepare a battle for us when we are dead.

original: Stay, stay, I say! And if you love me, as you say you do, Let me persuade you to forbear awhile.
translation: Stay, stay, I say! And if you love me as much as you say you do, let me persuade you to stop for a while.

original: O, how this discord doth afflict my soul!
translation: Oh, how this disorder upsets my soul!

original: Can you, my Lord of Winchester, behold   My sighs and tears and will not once relent?
translation: Lord Winchester, can you watch me sigh and cry and not soften at the sight of it?

original: Who should be pitiful, if you be not?
translation: Who will be sympathetic if not you?

original: Or who should study to prefer a peace.   If holy churchmen take delight in broils?
translation: Or who will work towards peace, if holy churchmen take pleasure in fights?

original: Yield, my lord protector; yield, Winchester;
translation: Surrender, my lord protector, and surrender Winchester.

original: Except you mean with obstinate repulse   To slay your sovereign and destroy the realm.
translation: Or do you mean to kill your king and destroy the country with your stubborn refusal?

original: You see what mischief and what murder too   Hath been enacted through your enmity;
translation: If you see what evil and murder have occurred here because of your hatred,

original: Then be at peace except ye thirst for blood.
translation: then be at peace and stop your thirst for blood.

original: He shall submit, or I will never yield.
translation: He should obey, otherwise I will never surrender.

original: Compassion on the king commands me stoop; Or I would see his heart out, ere the priest Should ever get that privilege of me.
translation: The king's kindness makes me bow. Otherwise I would keep fighting against him before the priest would have an advantage over me.

original: Behold, my Lord of Winchester,
translation: Look, my lord of Winchester,

original: the duke   Hath banish'd moody discontented fury,
translation: the duke has let go of his anger,

original: As by his smoothed brows it doth appear:
translation: as you can tell by looking at his calm expression.

original: Why look you still so stern and tragical?
translation: Why do you still look so strict and full of sorrow, though?

original: Here, Winchester, I offer thee my hand.
translation: Winchester, here. I offer you my hand.

original: Fie, uncle Beaufort!
translation: Shame on you, uncle Beaufort!

original: I have heard you preach   That malice was a great and grievous sin;
translation: I've heard you preach that evil was a great and dreadful sin

original: And will not you maintain the thing you teach,
translation: and you still won't live according to what you preach,

original: But prove a chief offender in the same?
translation: but instead turn into the sinner yourself?

original: Sweet king! the bishop hath a kindly gird. For shame, my lord of Winchester, relent! What, shall a child instruct you what to do?
Well, Duke of Gloucester, I will yield to thee; Love for thy love and hand for hand I give.
translation: Well, Duke of Gloucester, I surrender to you. I give you my hand for your hand and my love for your love.

original: Ay, but, I fear me, with a hollow heart.—
translation: Yes, but I fear that you don't mean this and do it with an empty heart.

original: See here, my friends and loving countrymen,   This token serveth for a flag of truce   Betwixt ourselves and all our followers:
translation: See, my friends and loving countrymen, this sign that represents a flag of peace between us and our followers.

original: So help me God, as I dissemble not!
translation: God help me, I am not pretending!

original: So help me God, as I intend it not!
translation: God help me, I didn't mean it!

original: O, loving uncle, kind Duke of Gloucester,
translation: Oh, loving uncle, kind Duke of Gloucester!

original: How joyful am I made by this contract!
translation: I am so happy about this agreement!

original: Away, my masters!
translation: Go away now, my masters.

original: trouble us no more;   But join in friendship,
translation: Don't make any more problems but make friends with one another,

original: as your lords have done.
translation: as your lords have done here.

original: I'll to the surgeon's.
translation: I am happy about this. I'll go to the surgeon.

original: And so will I.
translation: And so will I.

original: And I will see what physic the tavern affords.
translation: And I will see what type of medicine the pub might offer.

original: Accept this scroll, most gracious sovereign, Which in the right of Richard Plantagenet We do exhibit to your majesty.
translation: Accept this document, my most gracious king. It shows the right of Richard Plantagenet.

original: Well urged, my Lord of Warwick:
translation: Good timing, Lord of Warwick.

original: or sweet prince,   And if your grace mark every circumstance,   You have great reason to do Richard right;
translation: Sweet prince, if you consider every detail, you have good reason to treat Richard well,

original: Especially for those occasions   At Eltham Place I told your majesty.
translation: especially for those reasons I told your majesty about at  Eltham Palace .

original: And those occasions, uncle, were of force: Therefore, my loving lords, our pleasure is That Richard be restored to his blood.
translation: And those reasons, uncle, were convincing. Therefore, my loving lords, it is our pleasure that Richard shall be given his property and titles back.

original: Let Richard be restored to his blood; So shall his father's wrongs be recompensed.
translation: Let Richard have his rights back, so that his father's wrongs will be repaid.

original: As will the rest, so willeth Winchester.
translation: And all the rest, Winchester wants it that way.

original: If Richard will be true, not that alone   But all the whole inheritance I give
translation: If Richard is truthful, I will give him not only that but also all the inheritance

original: That doth belong unto the house of York,   From whence you spring by lineal descent.
translation: that rightfully belongs to the family of York, from where his bloodline began.

original: Thy humble servant vows obedience And humble service till the point of death.
translation: Your poor servant swears that he will be obedient and I offer my lowly service until the day I die.

original: Stoop then and set your knee against my foot;
translation: Bow then and put your knee against my foot.

original: And, in reguerdon of that duty done,   I gird thee with the valiant sword of York:
translation: As a reward, with this brave sword of York, I give you a title.

original: Rise Richard, like a true Plantagenet,   And rise created princely Duke of York.
translation: Richard, stand up, like a true Plantagenet and rise as the newly titled Duke of York.

original: And so thrive Richard as thy foes may fall! And as my duty springs, so perish they That grudge one thought against your majesty!
translation: And so Richard prospers while your enemies fall! And as it is my duty, so those that have even one hateful thought against your majesty will die!

original: Welcome, high prince, the mighty Duke of York!
translation: Welcome, high prince, the powerful Duke of York!

original: Perish, base prince, ignoble Duke of York!
translation: Die, lowly prince, dishonorable Duke of York!

original: Now will it best avail your majesty   To cross the seas and to be crown'd in France:
translation: Now it may be good time for your majesty to travel across the sea and be crowned in France.

original: The presence of a king engenders love   Amongst his subjects and his loyal friends,   As it disanimates his enemies.
translation: The king's presence brings about love among his people and his loyal friends,  and it discourages his enemies.

original: When Gloucester says the word, King Henry goes; For friendly counsel cuts off many foes.
translation: Wherever Gloucester will tell me to go, I will go. Friendly advice helps you get rid of many enemies.

original: Your ships already are in readiness.
translation: Your ships are ready.

original: Ay, we may march in England or in France,   Not seeing what is likely to ensue.
translation: Ah, yes, we may go to fight in England or in France, but we can't predict what will happen afterwards.

original: This late dissension grown betwixt the peers   Burns under feigned ashes of forged love   And will at last break out into a flame:
translation: This recent disagreement that has grown between the lords burns under ashes of false love and will finally turn into a flame!

original: As fester'd members rot but by degree,   Till bones and flesh and sinews fall away,   So will this base and envious discord breed.
translation: Like rotten arms and legs slowly decompose, until bones and ligaments fall apart, so this lowly and malicious disorder will spread.

original: And now I fear that fatal prophecy   Which in the time of Henry named the Fifth   Was in the mouth of every sucking babe;
translation: And now I am afraid of that the deadly prophecy which was spread around during Henry the Fifth's reign and heard from the mouth of every new born baby;

original: That Henry born at Monmouth should win all   And Henry born at Windsor lose all:
translation: that  Henry born at Monmouth  should win it all while  Henry born at Windsor  should lose it all.

original: Which is so plain that Exeter doth wish   His days may finish ere that hapless time.
translation: It is so clear that Exeter wishes that his days may end before that unlucky time.

original: These are the city gates, the gates of Rouen,
translation: These are the gates of the city Rouen,

original: Through which our policy must make a breach:
translation: through which, according to our strategy, we must make an opening to get into.

original: Take heed, be wary how you place your words;
translation: Be careful how you construct your sentences and what words you use.

original: Talk like the vulgar sort of market men   That come to gather money for their corn.
translation: Talk like the commoners, like the people at markets who come to collect money for their wheat.

original: If we have entrance, as I hope we shall,
translation: If we enter, and I really hope we do,

original: And that we find the slothful watch but weak,
translation: and if we find that the lazy guards are weak,

original: I'll by a sign give notice to our friends,   That Charles the Dauphin may encounter them.
translation: I'll give a sign to our friends that Charles the Dauphin can confront them.

original: Our sacks shall be a mean to sack the city, And we be lords and rulers over Rouen; Therefore we'll knock.
translation: Our bags will be used to attack the city and we'll be lords and rulers of Rouen. And so, I'll knock.

original: Qui est la?
translation: Who is there?

original: Paysans, pauvres gens de France; Poor market folks that come to sell their corn.
translation: Peasants, the poor people of France. Poor market people who come here to sell their wheat.

original: Enter, go in; the market bell is rung.
Now, Rouen, I'll shake thy bulwarks to the ground.
translation: Now I will destroy your walls, Rouen.

original: Saint Denis bless this happy stratagem! And once again we'll sleep secure in Rouen.
translation: Bless this happy plan, Saint Denis! And once again, we'll sleep safely in Rouen.

original: Here enter'd Pucelle and her practisants; Now she is there, how will she specify Where is the best and safest passage in?
By thrusting out a torch from yonder tower; Which, once discern'd, shows that her meaning is, No way to that, for weakness, which she enter'd.
translation: By signaling a burning torch from that tower over there, so we will recognize what she means. No entrance is as weakly guarded as the one she entered.

original: Behold, this is the happy wedding torch That joineth Rouen unto her countrymen, But burning fatal to the Talbotites!
See, noble Charles, the beacon of our friend; The burning torch in yonder turret stands.
translation: See, noble Charles, the torch of our friend! The burning torch is over there at that tower.

original: Now shine it like a comet of revenge, A prophet to the fall of all our foes!
Defer no time, delays have dangerous ends; Enter, and cry 'The Dauphin!' presently, And then do execution on the watch.
translation: Let's not waste time, wasting time has dangerous consequences. Enter the city and immediately scream "The Dauphin!" and then kill all the guards.

original: France, thou shalt rue this treason with thy tears,   If Talbot but survive thy treachery.
translation: France, you will regret this treason with your tears, if Talbot survives your betrayal.

original: Pucelle, that witch, that damned sorceress,   Hath wrought this hellish mischief unawares,
translation: The witch Pucelle, that cursed sorceress has brought this evil mischief so unexpectedly on us,

original: That hardly we escaped the pride of France.
translation: that we barely escaped the French.

original: Good morrow, gallants! want ye corn for bread?
translation: Good morning, you fine young gentlemen! Do you want wheat instead of bread?

original: I think the Duke of Burgundy will fast   Before he'll buy again at such a rate:
translation: I think the Duke of Burgundy would rather starve than buy food again at that cost.

original: 'Twas full of darnel; do you like the taste?
translation: It was full of weeds, do you like the taste of it?

original: Scoff on, vile fiend and shameless courtezan! I trust ere long to choke thee with thine own And make thee curse the harvest of that corn.
translation: Make fun of me as much as you want, you disgusting devil and shameless prostitute! Trust me, I will soon choke you with your own weapon and I'll make sure that you regret the outcome of your actions.

original: Your grace may starve perhaps before that time.
translation: Your king will starve before that will happen.

original: O, let no words, but deeds, revenge this treason!
translation: Oh, you should let actions and not words revenge this treason!

original: What will you do, good grey-beard? break a lance, And run a tilt at death within a chair?
translation: What are you going to do, good man with the grey beard? Break a spear in two and fight in a tournament with it until you die?

original: Foul fiend of France, and hag of all despite,
translation: You dirty demon from France and witch filled with hate!

original: Encompass'd with thy lustful paramours!
translation: You are surrounded by your passionate lovers!

original: Becomes it thee to taunt his valiant age   And twit with cowardice a man half dead?
translation: Do you think it's appropriate for you to mock his incredible age and insult a half dead man by talking of him being a coward?

original: Damsel, I'll have a bout with you again,   Or else let Talbot perish with this shame.
translation: Girl, I'll fight you again. If I don't then I will die of shame.

original: Are ye so hot, sir? yet, Pucelle, hold thy peace; If Talbot do but thunder, rain will follow.
God speed the parliament! who shall be the speaker?
translation: God, hurry up the parliament! Who will be the speaker?

original: Dare ye come forth and meet us in the field?
translation: Do you come forward and meet us in battle?

original: Belike your lordship takes us then for fools, To try if that our own be ours or no.
translation: It looks like your lordship thinks we are idiots! He thinks we're going to try our luck.

original: I speak not to that railing Hecate, But unto thee, Alencon, and the rest; Will ye, like soldiers, come and fight it out?
Signior, no.
translation: No, we won't, my lord.

original: Signior, hang! base muleters of France! Like peasant foot-boys do they keep the walls And dare not take up arms like gentlemen.
translation: Hang then, "my lord!" Lowly French mule-drivers! They stand near the walls like peasant boy servants and don't dare to grasp their weapons and fight like gentlemen.

original: Away, captains! let's get us from the walls;
translation: Stand back, captains! Go away from the walls!

original: For Talbot means no goodness by his looks.   God be wi' you, my lord!
translation: It looks like Talbot doesn't mean us well. God be with you, my lord!

original: we came but to tell you   That we are here.
translation: We only came to tell you that we are here.

original: And there will we be too, ere it be long,
translation: And we will be where you are, very soon.

original: Or else reproach be Talbot's greatest fame!
translation: Or otherwise Talbot will be most famous for his disgrace.

original: My vows are equal partners with thy vows.
translation: My promise is as sure as yours.

original: But, ere we go, regard this dying prince,   The valiant Duke of Bedford.
translation: But, before we go, look towards this dying prince—the brave Duke of Bedford.

original: Come, my lord,   We will bestow you in some better place,   Fitter for sickness and for crazy age.
translation: My lord, come! We will carry you to a nicer place than this; a place better suited to your sickness and your weak old age.

original: Lord Talbot, do not so dishonour me: Here will I sit before the walls of Rouen And will be partner of your weal or woe.
translation: Lord Talbot, don't dishonor me. I will sit here, on the walls of Rouen and will also swear, like you did, in the name of happiness or misery.

original: Courageous Bedford, let us now persuade you.
translation: Brave Bedford, please let us change your mind!

original: Not to be gone from hence;
translation: I won't leave this place.

original: for once I read   That stout Pendragon in his litter sick   Came to the field and vanquished his foes:
translation: I read somewhere that the strong  Pendragon  was carried onto the battle field in his sick bed and killed all his enemies.

original: Methinks I should revive the soldiers' hearts,   Because I ever found them as myself.
translation: I think that I should renew the hearts of our soldiers, because I feel so similar to them.

original: Undaunted spirit in a dying breast!
translation: The spirit coming from your dying chest is unbreakable!

original: Then be it so:
translation: Then, let it be so.

original: heavens keep old Bedford safe!
translation: Keep the old Bedford safe, heavens!

original: And now no more ado,
translation: And now, no more fuss.

original: brave Burgundy,   But gather we our forces out of hand   And set upon our boasting enemy.
translation: Brave Burgundy, let's gather our soldiers immediately and march towards our bragging enemy.

original: Whither away, Sir John Fastolfe, in such haste?
translation: Where are you going in such a hurry, Sir John Fastolfe?

original: Whither away! to save myself by flight: We are like to have the overthrow again.
translation: Which way!? I have to save myself by running away because it seems like we're about to be defeated again.

original: What! will you fly, and leave Lord Talbot?
translation: What!? You will run away and leave Lord Talbot?

original: Ay, All the Talbots in the world, to save my life!
translation: Yes. I will leave all the Talbots in the world to save my life!

original: Cowardly knight! ill fortune follow thee!
translation: That knight is such a coward! I hope bad luck follows him.

original: Now, quiet soul, depart when heaven please,   For I have seen our enemies' overthrow.
translation: Now, my quiet soul, please die when heaven tells you to,  because I have seen our enemies conquered.

original: What is the trust or strength of foolish man?
translation: What does the trust or strength of a foolish man mean?

original: They that of late were daring with their scoffs   Are glad and fain by flight to save themselves.
translation: Those who recently challenged us with their mockery are relieved and want to run away to save themselves.

original: Lost, and recover'd in a day again! This is a double honour, Burgundy: Yet heavens have glory for this victory!
translation: We have both lost and won in only one day! This is a double honor, Burgundy. But we must thank heavens for this victory!

original: Warlike and martial Talbot, Burgundy Enshrines thee in his heart and there erects Thy noble deeds as valour's monuments.
translation: Talbot—our warrior and leader—Burgundy will keep you in his heart like a saint and there will build a monument to your bravery and all your great acts.

original: Thanks, gentle duke. But where is Pucelle now?
translation: Thanks, kind duke. But where is Pucelle now?

original: I think her old familiar is asleep:
translation: I think her old trusted  spirit  is asleep.

original: Now where's the Bastard's braves, and Charles his  gleeks?
translation: Where is the laughter of the Bastard and Charles' jokes now?

original: What, all amort?
translation: What?  Are they all depressed now?

original: Rouen hangs her head for grief   That such a valiant company are fled.
translation: Rouen lowers her head in grief that such a courageous company ran away.

original: Now will we take some order in the town,
translation: Now  we  will establish order in the town .

original: Placing therein some expert officers,   And then depart to Paris to the king,
translation: We'll place some experienced officers here and then go to Paris to meet the king,

original: For there young Henry with his nobles lie.
translation: because that's where young Henry and his dukes are.

original: What wills Lord Talbot pleaseth Burgundy.
translation: Whatever Talbot wants to do, Burgundy agrees to.

original: But yet, before we go, let's not forget   The noble Duke of Bedford late deceased,
translation: But before we go, let's not forget the kind Duke of Bedford who has recently died.

original: But see his exequies fulfill'd in Rouen:
translation: Let's arrange a funeral for him here in Rouen.

original: A braver soldier never couched lance,   A gentler heart did never sway in court;
translation: A braver soldier has never risen his spear in an attack and a gentler heart never ruled over the court than he.

original: But kings and mightiest potentates must die,   For that's the end of human misery.
translation: But even kings and the most powerful rulers must die one day, as tha t's the end of human misery.

original: Dismay not, princes, at this accident,
translation: Princes, don't despair over this unpredictable event.

original: Nor grieve that Rouen is so recovered:
translation: And don't grieve that they took back Rouen.

original: Care is no cure, but rather corrosive,
translation: Caring about it won't help us, but will make it even worse,

original: For things that are not to be remedied.
translation: for the  things that have happened cannot be changed.

original: Let frantic Talbot triumph for a while   And like a peacock sweep along his tail;
translation: Let the excited Talbot celebrate his victory, like a  peacock  swinging his tail around, for a while.

original: We'll pull his plumes and take away his train,
translation: We'll tear his feathers and take away his  tail ,

original: If Dauphin and the rest will be but ruled.
translation: so long as  the Dauphin and the rest of you follow my advice.

original: We have been guided by thee hitherto, And of thy cunning had no diffidence: One sudden foil shall never breed distrust.
translation: We have been guided by you until now and have not once mistrusted your magical powers. One unexpected defeat won't make us stop believing in you.

original: Search out thy wit for secret policies, And we will make thee famous through the world.
translation: Think of some surprise strategies and we will make you famous around the world.

original: We'll set thy statue in some holy place, And have thee reverenced like a blessed saint: Employ thee then, sweet virgin, for our good.
translation: We'll put up a statue of you in some holy place. And we'll worship you like a blessed saint. Do your best, sweet virgin, for our sake.

original: Then thus it must be; this doth Joan devise:   By fair persuasions mix'd with sugar'd words
translation: Then it must be so. Joan plans to persuade the Duke of Burgundy with sweet words

original: We will entice the Duke of Burgundy   To leave the Talbot and to follow us.
translation: and convince him  to leave Talbot and follow us instead.

original: Ay, marry, sweeting, if we could do that,   France were no place for Henry's warriors;
translation: Ah, my darling! If we could do that, there would be no place for Henry's warriors in France.

original: Nor should that nation boast it so with us,   But be extirped from our provinces.
translation: And England would not show off in front of us, but instead would be removed from our provinces.

original: For ever should they be expulsed from France And not have title of an earldom here.
translation: They should be expelled from France forever and not hold any title here.

original: Your honours shall perceive how I will work To bring this matter to the wished end.
translation: Your honors will observe how I plan to carry this out until we achieve what we want.

original: Hark! by the sound of drum you may perceive Their powers are marching unto Paris-ward.
translation: Listen! That sound of the drum tells us that their armies are marching towards Paris.

original: There goes the Talbot, with his colours spread, And all the troops of English after him.
translation: There goes Talbot, carrying his flags, and all the English soldiers are following after him.

original: Now in the rearward comes the duke and his: Fortune in favour makes him lag behind. Summon a parley; we will talk with him.
translation: Now at the back comes the duke and his luck makes him fall behind, which is good for us. Ask to negotiate and we'll talk to him.

original: A parley with the Duke of Burgundy!
translation: We want to negotiate with the Duke of Burgundy!

original: Who craves a parley with the Burgundy?
translation: Who wants to negotiate with Burgundy?

original: The princely Charles of France, thy countryman.
translation: The prince Charles of France, your countryman.

original: What say'st thou, Charles? for I am marching hence.
translation: What do you have to say to me, Charles? See, I am walking towards you now.

original: Speak, Pucelle, and enchant him with thy words.
Brave Burgundy, undoubted hope of France! Stay, let thy humble handmaid speak to thee.
translation: Brave Burgundy, you are the unquestionable hope of France! Stay here and let me—your lowly servant girl speak to you.

original: Speak on; but be not over-tedious.
translation: Speak then. But don't speak too much.

original: Look on thy country, look on fertile France,
translation: Look at your country, look at fruitful France

original: And see the cities and the towns defaced   By wasting ruin of the cruel foe.
translation: and see that the cities and towns are destroyed by the destructive ruin of its cruel enemy.

original: As looks the mother on her lowly babe   When death doth close his tender dying eyes,   See, see the pining malady of France;
translation: Look at the wasting French disease as if you were a mother looking at her poor baby when death is closing his young dying eyes.

original: Behold the wounds, the most unnatural wounds,   Which thou thyself hast given her woful breast.
translation: See the wounds, the most unnatural wounds, which you yourself have given her miserable breasts.

original: O, turn thy edged sword another way;
translation: Oh, turn your sharp sword in another direction!

original: Strike those that hurt, and hurt not those that help.
translation: Attack those who hurt and don't hurt those who help.

original: One drop of blood drawn from thy country's bosom   Should grieve thee more than streams of foreign gore:
translation: One drop of blood from your country's breasts should make you more miserable than rivers of foreign blood.

original: Return thee therefore with a flood of tears,   And wash away thy country's stained spots.
translation: Return with a flood of tears and wash away the staining spots of your country.

original: Either she hath bewitch'd me with her words, Or nature makes me suddenly relent.
translation: She has either charmed me with her words or nature suddenly makes me regret everything.

original: Besides, all French and France exclaims on thee,   Doubting thy birth and lawful progeny.
translation: Also, all the French and France accuse you, they are doubting your birth and the legitimacy of your lineage.

original: Who joint'st thou with but with a lordly nation   That will not trust thee but for profit's sake?
translation: And you join a proud nation that only trusts you for the sake of profit?

original: When Talbot hath set footing once in France   And fashion'd thee that instrument of ill,
translation: Once Talbot has set up a base in France and made you into that tool of destruction,

original: Who then but English Henry will be lord   And thou be thrust out like a fugitive?
translation: who but the English Henry will be lord and you will be cast away like a refugee!

original: Call we to mind, and mark but this for proof,
translation: Let's use an example.

original: Was not the Duke of Orleans thy foe?   And was he not in England prisoner?
translation: Do you remember your enemy the Duke of Orleans? Wasn't he prisoner in England?

original: But when they heard he was thine enemy,   They set him free without his ransom paid,   In spite of Burgundy and all his friends.
translation: But when they heard that he was your enemy, they let him go and they didn't pay for his release, despite Burgundy and all his friends.

original: See, then, thou fight'st against thy countrymen   And joint'st with them will be thy slaughtermen.
translation: Can you see, then, that you fight against your countrymen, and when you join with them they will become your murderers.

original: Come, come, return; return, thou wandering lord:
translation: Come here! Come back, come back, you restless lord.

original: Charles and the rest will take thee in their arms.
translation: Charles and the others will welcome you into their arms.

original: I am vanquished;
translation: I am defeated.

original: these haughty words of hers   Have batter'd me like roaring cannon-shot,
translation: Her arrogant words have beaten me like a loud shot from a cannon.

original: And made me almost yield upon my knees.
translation: They made me almost fall down onto my knees.

original: Forgive me, country, and sweet countrymen,
translation: Forgive me, my country and my sweet countrymen!

original: And, lords, accept this hearty kind embrace:   My forces and my power of men are yours:
translation: And lords, accept this sincere kind embrace. My army is yours.

original: So farewell, Talbot; I'll no longer trust thee.
translation: So, goodbye Talbot! I don't trust you anymore.

original: Done like a Frenchman: turn, and turn again!
translation: He's like a Frenchman! He turns and then turns again.

original: Welcome, brave duke! thy friendship makes us fresh.
translation: Welcome, brave duke! Your friendship renews us.

original: And doth beget new courage in our breasts.
translation: And it makes us feel new courage in our chests.

original: Pucelle hath bravely play'd her part in this, And doth deserve a coronet of gold.
translation: Pucelle has played her part in this splendidly. She deserves a golden crown.

original: Now let us on, my lords, and join our powers, And seek how we may prejudice the foe.
translation: Let's go now, my lords. And let's combine our powers and find out how we may damage the enemy.

original: My gracious prince, and honourable peers,
translation: My kind prince, and honest lords!

original: Hearing of your arrival in this realm,   I have awhile given truce unto my wars,
translation: I have heard about your arrival in this country and so I have made peace for a while in my wars,

original: To do my duty to my sovereign:
translation: so I can pay my respects to my king.

original: In sign, whereof, this arm,
translation: I show you a sign of my respects here

original: that hath reclaim'd   To your obedience fifty fortresses,   Twelve cities and seven walled towns of strength,
translation: —this arm that regained fifty fortresses, twelve cities and seven powerful towns surrounded by a wall.

original: Beside five hundred prisoners of esteem,
translation: On top of that, we have taken five hundred prisoners of high rank.

original: Lets fall his sword before your highness' feet,
translation: I let my sword fall before your highness' feet

original: And with submissive loyalty of heart   Ascribes the glory of his conquest got   First to my God and next unto your grace.
translation: and with the obedient loyalty of my heart, I give credit first to my God and then to your grace, for the glory of my victory.

original: Is this the Lord Talbot, uncle Gloucester, That hath so long been resident in France?
translation: Uncle Gloucester, is this the Lord Talbot, that has been in France for so long?

original: Yes, if it please your majesty, my liege.
translation: Yes, if you are happy with that, my lord.

original: Welcome, brave captain and victorious lord!
translation: Brave captain and victorious lord, welcome!

original: When I was young, as yet I am not old,
translation: When I was young—not that I am old now—

original: I do remember how my father said   A stouter champion never handled sword.
translation: I remember how my father used to say  that a bolder champion had never held a sword than you.

original: Long since we were resolved of your truth,   Your faithful service and your toil in war;
translation: Ever since then, we have been convinced that this is true because of your faithful service and your efforts in war.

original: Yet never have you tasted our reward,   Or been reguerdon'd with so much as thanks,
translation: And yet you've never been rewarded, and we have never thanked you for all you've done,

original: Because till now we never saw your face:
translation: because we have never seen your face until now.

original: Therefore, stand up; and, for these good deserts,   We here create you Earl of Shrewsbury;
translation: Therefore, stand up and for these good actions, we make you Earl of Shrewsbury.

original: And in our coronation take your place.
translation: Take your place in our procession.

original: Now, sir,   to you, that were so hot at sea,
translation: Now, sir!  You were so angry when we were at sea ,

original: Disgracing of these colours that I wear   In honour of my noble Lord of York:
translation: insulting the colors of the badge that I wear in the name of my kind Lord of York.

original: Darest thou maintain the former words thou spakest?
translation: Do you stand by the words you spoke then?

original: Yes, sir; as well as you dare patronage The envious barking of your saucy tongue Against my lord the Duke of Somerset.
translation: Yes, sir, I dare as much as you dare to defend the jealous barking of your insolent tongue that spoke against my lord, the Duke of Somerset.

original: Sirrah, thy lord I honour as he is.
translation: Boy, I honor your lord for what he's worth.

original: Why, what is he? as good a man as York.
translation: Why? What is he worth? He is as good a man as York.

original: Hark ye; not so: in witness, take ye that.
translation: Listen, I don't think so. Take this from me!

original: Villain, thou know'st the law of arms is such
translation: You're a villain! You know the law of weapons here.

original: That whoso draws a sword, 'tis present death,
translation: Whoever uses a sword, must die immediately

original: Or else this blow should broach thy dearest blood.
translation: or else I would use mine and make your dearest blood flow.

original: But I'll unto his majesty, and crave   I may have liberty to venge this wrong;
translation: But I'll go to his majesty and request permission to revenge what you've done to me.

original: When thou shalt see I'll meet thee to thy cost.
translation: When you see me next, I'll repay you for this.

original: Well, miscreant, I'll be there as soon as you; And, after, meet you sooner than you would.
translation: Well, you villain! I'll be there as soon as you will. And afterwards, I'll meet you sooner than you would meet me.

original: Lord bishop, set the crown upon his head.
translation: Put the crown on his head, lord bishop.

original: God save King Henry, of that name the sixth!
translation: God save King Henry! He is the sixth one with that name.

original: Now, governor of Paris, take your oath,   That you elect no other king but him;
translation: Now, governor of Paris, make a promise, that you accept no other king but him.

original: Esteem none friends but such as are his friends,
translation: Consider no other friends but his friends

original: And none your foes but such as shall pretend   Malicious practises against his state:
translation: and your enemies should be those who plot to harm him.

original: This shall ye do, so help you righteous God!
translation: You shall do this! God be with you!

original: My gracious sovereign, as I rode from Calais,   To haste unto your coronation,
translation: I came from Calais to hurry to your coronation, my gentle king,

original: A letter was deliver'd to my hands,   Writ to your grace from the Duke of Burgundy.
translation: and I was given this letter from the Duke of Burgundy. It's addressed to you.

original: Shame to the Duke of Burgundy and thee! I vow'd, base knight, when I did meet thee next, To tear the garter from thy craven's leg,
translation: Shame on you and the Duke of Burgundy! I swore to you when I last met you, lowly knight, that I would pull off the knight's garter, that ribbon, from your coward's leg.

original: Which I have done, because unworthily   Thou wast installed in that high degree.
translation: I've done this because you don't deserve such high status.

original: Pardon me, princely Henry, and the rest
translation: Prince Henry and the rest of you, excuse me.

original: This dastard, at the battle of Patay,   When but in all I was six thousand strong
translation: During the  battle of Patay , this coward, when I was alone among six thousand men

original: And that the French were almost ten to one,
translation: and the French had a ten to one advantage,

original: Before we met or that a stroke was given,   Like to a trusty squire did run away:
translation: this  "reliable" attendant  r an away from me before we even attacked.

original: In which assault we lost twelve hundred men;   Myself and divers gentlemen beside   Were there surprised and taken prisoners
translation: In that battle we lost twelve hundred men and myself and some other gentlemen were unexpectedly taken prisoner.

original: Then judge, great lords, if I have done amiss;
translation: Great lords, judge then, if what I did was wrong

original: Or whether that such cowards ought to wear   This ornament of knighthood,
translation: and if c owards like him should be allowed to wear this symbol of knighthood.

original: yea or no.
translation: Yes or no?

original: To say the truth, this fact was infamous And ill beseeming any common man, Much more a knight, a captain and a leader.
translation: To be honest, that crime is shameful and doesn't suit any ordinary man, let alone a knight, a captain, and a leader!

original: When first this order was ordain'd, my lords,   Knights of the garter were of noble birth,
translation: When the order of the Garters was first set up, my lords, knights of that order were of noble birth,

original: Valiant and virtuous, full of haughty courage,
translation: they were virtuous and good and had courage.

original: Such as were grown to credit by the wars;   Not fearing death, nor shrinking for distress,
translation: These knights rose in honor through the wars, they weren't scared of death and they didn't run away from hardship.

original: But always resolute in most extremes.
translation: They were always determined in difficult situations.

original: He then that is not furnish'd in this sort   Doth but usurp the sacred name of knight,
translation: He, who does not possess those qualities, assumes the precious name of knight falsely.

original: Profaning this most honourable order,
translation: He pollutes this most honorable order

original: And should, if I were worthy to be judge,   Be quite degraded, like a hedge-born swain
translation: and if I could decide what to do with him, his position would be lowered, and he would become a person of very low birth

original: That doth presume to boast of gentle blood.
translation: who only thinks he can brag about his highborn blood.

original: Stain to thy countrymen, thou hear'st thy doom! Be packing, therefore, thou that wast a knight: Henceforth we banish thee, on pain of death.
translation: Do you hear the judgement? Your countrymen will be marked by this! Therefore, go pack your things. You were once a knight but now we cast you out and if you return, you'll die.

original: And now, my lord protector, view the letter Sent from our uncle Duke of Burgundy.
translation: And now, my lord protector, read the letter that the Duke of Burgundy sent us.

original: What means his grace, that he hath changed his style?   No more but, plain and bluntly, 'To the king!'
translation: What does he mean, why has he changed his form of address? Does he say nothing more than a simple "To the king?"

original: Hath he forgot he is his sovereign?
translation: Has he forgotten that Henry is his king?

original: Or doth this churlish superscription   Pretend some alteration in good will?
translation: Or does this blunt address mean that his good intentions have changed?

original: What's here?
translation: What do we have here?

original: 'I have, upon especial cause,   Moved with compassion of my country's wreck,
translation: "I have moved away from the ruin of my country,

original: Together with the pitiful complaints   Of such as your oppression feeds upon,
translation: as well as the pathetic complaints that encourage your oppression.

original: Forsaken your pernicious faction   And join'd with Charles, the rightful King of France.'
translation: I have abandoned your destructive group and joined Charles, the true King of France."

original: O monstrous treachery!
translation: Oh, this is terrible treason!

original: can this be so,   That in alliance, amity and oaths,   There should be found such false dissembling guile?
translation: How can there be such trickery among what should be unity, friendship and promises?

original: What! doth my uncle Burgundy revolt?
translation: My uncle Burgundy rebels against me?

original: He doth, my lord, and is become your foe.
translation: He does, my lord. And now he is your enemy.

original: Is that the worst this letter doth contain?
translation: Is anything worse written in this letter?

original: It is the worst, and all, my lord, he writes.
translation: That is the worst that he writes, my lord.

original: Why, then, Lord Talbot there shall talk with him And give him chastisement for this abuse. How say you, my lord? are you not content?
translation: Well, then, you will talk with him, Talbot and punish him for this betrayal. What do you say to that, my lord? Are you not happy about it?

original: Content, my liege! yes, but that I am prevented, I should have begg'd I might have been employ'd.
translation: Happy, my king! Yes! It's only that I would have liked to have begged to do what you have ordered.

original: Then gather strength and march unto him straight: Let him perceive how ill we brook his treason And what offence it is to flout his friends.
translation: Gather all your men and meet him immediately. Let him see how badly we think of his treason and how he insulted us by mocking his friends.

original: I go, my lord, in heart desiring still You may behold confusion of your foes.
translation: My lord, I am off! With all my heart I hope that you may see the destruction of your enemies.

original: Grant me the combat, gracious sovereign.
translation: My gracious king, give me permission to fight in a duel.

original: And me, my lord, grant me the combat too.
translation: My lord, grant me permission too.

original: This is my servant: hear him, noble prince.
translation: This is my servant. Listen to what he has to say, kind prince.

original: And this is mine: sweet Henry, favour him.
translation: And this is my servant. Sweet Henry, give him what he wants.

original: Be patient, lords; and give them leave to speak. Say, gentlemen, what makes you thus exclaim? And wherefore crave you combat? or with whom?
translation: Lords, be patient and let them speak. Gentlemen, tell me what makes you ask for this? And why do you want to fight or with whom do you want to fight?

original: With him, my lord; for he hath done me wrong.
translation: With him, because he has harmed me, my lord.

original: And I with him; for he hath done me wrong.
translation: And I want to fight with him, because he has harmed me.

original: What is that wrong whereof you both complain? First let me know, and then I'll answer you.
translation: What is the cause of this wrongdoing, that you both complain about? Tell me about it first and then I'll reply to your request.

original: Crossing the sea from England into France,
translation: While I was traveling across the sea from England to France,

original: This fellow here, with envious carping tongue,   Upbraided me about the rose I wear;
translation: this hateful and critical man who stands before you accused me about the rose that I wear.

original: Saying, the sanguine colour of the leaves   Did represent my master's blushing cheeks,
translation: He said that the blood-red color of the petals looked like the blushing cheeks of my master.

original: When stubbornly he did repugn the truth   About a certain question in the law   Argued betwixt the Duke of York and him;
translation: He stubbornly rejected the truth about the question of succession that had been discussed between himself and the Duke of York.

original: With other vile and ignominious terms:
translation: He used vulgar and degrading words.

original: In confutation of which rude reproach   And in defence of my lord's worthiness,   I crave the benefit of law of arms.
translation: In order to prove him wrong and to defend the name of my lord, I wish to challenge him to a duel.

original: And that is my petition, noble lord:
translation: And that's my request too, kind lord.

original: For though he seem with forged quaint conceit   To set a gloss upon his bold intent,
translation: Although he gives an attractive interpretation of his daring plan, using false and cunning rhetoric.

original: Yet know, my lord, I was provoked by him;
translation: You should know, my lord, that  I  was provoked by  him .

original: And he first took exceptions at this badge,   Pronouncing that the paleness of this flower   Bewray'd the faintness of my master's heart.
translation: He started objecting to my badge first, saying that the white color of this flower revealed my master's cowardly heart.

original: Will not this malice, Somerset, be left?
translation: Won't you stop this hate, Somerset?

original: Your private grudge, my Lord of York, will out, Though ne'er so cunningly you smother it.
translation: Your personal resentment will end, although you won't be the one who suppresses it, my Lord of York.

original: Good Lord, what madness rules in brainsick men,   When for so slight and frivolous a cause   Such factious emulations shall arise!
translation: Good lord, what kind of madness is ruling these foolish men? Why does such a small and silly argument cause this divisive rivalry!?

original: Good cousins both, of York and Somerset,   Quiet yourselves, I pray, and be at peace.
translation: My good kinsmen, York and Somerset, I ask you now to be quiet and to be at peace.

original: Let this dissension first be tried by fight, And then your highness shall command a peace.
translation: Let this disagreement be tested in a fight and then your highness can ask for peace.

original: The quarrel toucheth none but us alone; Betwixt ourselves let us decide it then.
translation: This argument doesn't concern anyone but us. We can decide it between us, then.

original: There is my pledge; accept it, Somerset.
Nay, let it rest where it began at first.
translation: No, let it remain where it was before.

original: Confirm it so, mine honourable lord.
translation: Let us do this, then, my honorable lord.

original: Confirm it so! Confounded be your strife!
translation: Let you do this!? Your argument should be destroyed!

original: And perish ye, with your audacious prate!
translation: And you should die along with your reckless chatter!

original: Presumptuous vassals, are you not ashamed   With this immodest clamorous outrage   To trouble and disturb the king and us?
translation: Aren't you ashamed, you arrogant servants, that you trouble and disturb the king and us with this shameless noisy insult?!

original: And you, my lords, methinks you do not well   To bear with their perverse objections;
translation: As for you, my lords, I don't think you should take their wicked accusations

original: Much less to take occasion from their mouths   To raise a mutiny betwixt yourselves:
translation: and definitely don't take it as an opportunity to start a fight between yourselves.

original: Let me persuade you take a better course.
translation: Let me persuade you to do something better.

original: It grieves his highness: good my lords, be friends.
translation: It makes his highness sad and so, my good lords, be friends.

original: Come hither, you that would be combatants:
translation: Come here, you that want to fight each other.

original: Henceforth I charge you, as you love our favour,   Quite to forget this quarrel and the cause.
translation: Here I order you to forget this argument and the reason for it, if you love us.

original: And you, my lords, remember where we are,
translation: And you, my lords, remember where we are.

original: In France, amongst a fickle wavering nation:
translation: We're in France at the center of a changeable and hesitant nation.

original: If they perceive dissension in our looks   And that within ourselves we disagree,
translation: If they see that we are arguing and that we can't agree among ourselves,

original: How will their grudging stomachs be provoked   To wilful disobedience, and rebel!
translation: their resentful tempers will be provoked to intentional disobedience and rebellion!

original: Beside, what infamy will there arise,   When foreign princes shall be certified
translation: Also, can you imagine what a scandal it would be abroad if foreign princes found out

original: That for a toy, a thing of no regard,   King Henry's peers and chief nobility   Destroy'd themselves, and lost the realm of France!
translation: that King Henry's lords and the highest aristocracy destroyed themselves and lost France over something so small and unimportant?

original: O, think upon the conquest of my father,   My tender years,
translation: You should remember my father's victories and my young age.

original: and let us not forego   That for a trifle that was bought with blood
translation: And let us not lose something that we bought with blood over a small argument.

original: Let me be umpire in this doubtful strife.   I see no reason, if I wear this rose,
translation: Let me be the judge in this fearful argument. I don't see why, if I wear this rose—

original: My Lord of York, I promise you, the king Prettily, methought, did play the orator.
translation: I thought that the king played the role of the public speaker rather well, my lord of York.

original: And so he did; but yet I like it not, In that he wears the badge of Somerset.
translation: Yes, he did. But I don't like that he is wearing Somerset's badge.

original: Tush, that was but his fancy, blame him not; I dare presume, sweet prince, he thought no harm.
translation: Oh, come on! He only did it on a whim. Don't blame him for it. I dare say, sweet prince, that he didn't mean harm by it.

original: An if I wist he did,—but let it rest; Other affairs must now be managed.
translation: From what I know, he did—but let's forget about that. We must manage other things now.

original: Well didst thou, Richard, to suppress thy voice;
translation: You did well, Richard, to stop speaking,

original: For, had the passions of thy heart burst out,   I fear we should have seen decipher'd there   More rancorous spite,
translation: because if the passions of your heart were to come to the surface, I am afraid it would have revealed more hateful malice

original: more furious raging broils,   Than yet can be imagined or supposed.
translation: and a fight more angry and furious than can be imagined or assumed.

original: But howsoe'er, no simple man that sees   This jarring discord of nobility,
translation: But anyway, any ordinary man who sees this disturbing conflict between the lords,

original: This shouldering of each other in the court,   This factious bandying of their favourites,
translation: this pushing of each other in court and the  competition  between their favorites,

original: But that it doth presage some ill event.
translation: can see that this will have some terrible outcome.

original: 'Tis much when sceptres are in children's hands;   But more when envy breeds unkind division;
translation: It's bad enough when children are kings, but it is even worse when jealousy creates unnatural divisions.

original: There comes the rain, there begins confusion.
translation: That one starts the rain, but this one starts destruction.

original: Go to the gates of Bourdeaux, trumpeter: Summon their general unto the wall.
translation: Trumpeter, go to the gates of Bourdeaux and call their general to the wall.

original: English John Talbot, captains, calls you forth,   Servant in arms to Harry King of England;
translation: Captains, the English John Talbot, Harry King of England's armed servant, called you here.

original: And thus he would: Open your city gates;   Be humble to us;
translation: He says to open your city gates and be respectful to us.

original: call my sovereign yours,   And do him homage as obedient subjects;
translation: Call my king your king and do him the honor as his obedient subjects,

original: And I'll withdraw me and my bloody power:
translation: and I and my blood-thirsty soldiers will pull back.

original: But, if you frown upon this proffer'd peace,   You tempt the fury of my three attendants,
translation: But if you don't accept my offer of peace, you will make my three guards here angry.

original: Lean famine, quartering steel, and climbing fire;
translation: You risk starvation, the anger of swords that can divide your body into pieces, and fire that can climb up that wall.

original: Who in a moment even with the earth   Shall lay your stately and air-braving towers,
translation: They will kill you in a moment and strike you down from those high towers,

original: If you forsake the offer of their love.
translation: if you refuse the love they offer you.

original: Thou ominous and fearful owl of death,   Our nation's terror and their bloody scourge!
translation: You predict death , our nation's terror and their bloody whips!

original: The period of thy tyranny approacheth.
translation: The end of your tyranny is almost here.

original: On us thou canst not enter but by death;
translation: You'll enter over our dead bodies.

original: For, I protest, we are well fortified   And strong enough to issue out and fight:
translation: I can tell you, we are secure behind these walls and strong enough to come forward and fight.

original: If thou retire, the Dauphin, well appointed,   Stands with the snares of war to tangle thee:
translation: If you get tired, the Dauphin will be fully equipped to catch you in his trap.

original: On either hand thee there are squadrons pitch'd,   To wall thee from the liberty of flight;
translation: There are army units drawn up in battle formation on either side of you, to prevent you from running away.

original: And no way canst thou turn thee for redress,
translation: And you can't run for help!

original: But death doth front thee with apparent spoil   And pale destruction meets thee in the face.
translation: Death is staring you in the face with a look of obvious destruction and deadly massacre.

original: Ten thousand French have ta'en the sacrament   To rive their dangerous artillery
translation: Ten thousand Frenchmen have taken  Communion  and are ready to use their dangerous weapons

original: Upon no Christian soul but English Talbot.
translation: against no other Christian soul but the English Talbot.

original: Lo, there thou stand'st, a breathing valiant man,   Of an invincible unconquer'd spirit!
translation: Look, there you stand, a breathing, fearless man who is never defeated!

original: This is the latest glory of thy praise   That I, thy enemy, due thee withal;
translation: This is the last bit of praise I—your enemy—give you.

original: For ere the glass, that now begins to run,   Finish the process of his sandy hour,
translation: Before the sand in the hourglass, that has just begun to run, ends its life when the last sand grains fall,

original: These eyes, that see thee now well coloured,   Shall see thee wither'd, bloody, pale and dead.
translation: these eyes that now see well, shall see you shrunk, bloody, white and dead.

original: Hark! hark! the Dauphin's drum, a warning bell, Sings heavy music to thy timorous soul; And mine shall ring thy dire departure out.
translation: Listen! Listen! It's the Dauphin's drum, it's the warning bell ringing to warn us of an invasion. It signs a sad tune to your fearful soul and mine shall ring for your dreadful death!

original: He fables not;
translation: He is not making this up.

original: I hear the enemy:
translation: I can hear the enemy.

original: Out, some light horsemen, and peruse their wings.
translation: Go, some horsemen, and investigate the forces at the sides of the army.

original: O, negligent and heedless discipline!
translation: Oh, what a neglectful and careless strategy!

original: How are we park'd and bounded in a pale,
translation: How is it possible that we are fenced in and confined inside!

original: A little herd of England's timorous deer,   Mazed with a yelping kennel of French curs!
translation: We're like a little flock of England's timid deer, confused by a barking pack of French dogs!

original: If we be English deer, be then in blood;
translation: If we are English deer, let's be full of their life too.

original: Not rascal-like, to fall down with a pinch,   But rather, moody-mad and desperate stags   ,
translation: Not like young, inferior deer that fall down when they are bitten,  but rather like deer wild with anger and desperation.

original: Turn on the bloody hounds with heads of steel   And make the cowards stand aloof at bay:
translation: We'll attack the bloody dogs with antlers like swords and make the cowards back off.

original: Sell every man his life as dear as mine,   And they shall find dear deer of us, my friends.
translation: Give every man his life which is as  dear  as mine and they'll find  dear  deer in us, my friends!

original: God and Saint George, Talbot and England's right,   Prosper our colours in this dangerous fight!
translation: God and  Saint George , Talbot and England's right, help us win this dangerous fight!

original: Are not the speedy scouts return'd again, That dogg'd the mighty army of the Dauphin?
translation: Have the lively guards that followed the powerful army of the Dauphin not returned yet?

original: They are return'd, my lord, and give it out   That he is march'd to Bourdeaux with his power,   To fight with Talbot:
translation: They have returned, my lord and report that he is heading to Bourdeaux with his army, to fight Talbot.

original: as he march'd along,   By your espials were discovered   Two mightier troops
translation: As he marched on, our spies discovered two bigger armies

original: than that the Dauphin led,
translation: than the one that the Dauphin is in charge of,

original: Which join'd with him and made their march for  Bourdeaux.
translation: which joined him and continued with him to Bourdeaux.

original: A plague upon that villain Somerset,   That thus delays my promised supply   Of horsemen,
translation: Curse that villain Somerset who delays my promised supply of horsemen,

original: that were levied for this siege!
translation: who are required for this attack!

original: Renowned Talbot doth expect my aid,
translation: The famous Talbot expects my help,

original: And I am lowted by a traitor villain   And cannot help the noble chevalier:
translation: and I am mocked by a treasonous villain and can't help the noble knight.

original: God comfort him in this necessity!
translation: I hope God will be his comfort when he needs it!

original: If he miscarry, farewell wars in France.
translation: If he is harmed, we can say goodbye to our victory in France.

original: Thou princely leader of our English strength,   Never so needful on the earth of France,
translation: You princely leader of our English armies, you have never been this needed in France!

original: Spur to the rescue of the noble Talbot,
translation: You should hurry to save the noble Talbot,

original: Who now is girdled with a waist of iron   And hemm'd about with grim destruction:
translation: since he is now shackled and imprisoned and surrounded by promises of horrible death.

original: To Bourdeaux, warlike duke! to Bourdeaux, York!
translation: Go to Bourdeaux, you duke warrior! York, go to Bourdeaux!

original: Else, farewell Talbot, France, and England's honour.
translation: Or otherwise, we can say goodbye to Talbot and to England's honor.

original: O God, that Somerset, who in proud heart   Doth stop my cornets, were in Talbot's place!
translation: Oh God, if only Somerset, whose pride stopped him from delivering my horsemen, was in Talbot's place!

original: So should we save a valiant gentleman   By forfeiting a traitor and a coward.
translation: Then we would save a noble gentlemen and instead lose a traitor and a coward.

original: Mad ire and wrathful fury makes me weep,   That thus we die, while remiss traitors sleep.
translation: Mad anger and incredible fury makes me cry because we will die like this, while careless traitors sleep.

original: O, send some succor to the distress'd lord!
translation: Oh, send some help to the worried lord!

original: He dies, we lose; I break my warlike word; We mourn, France smiles; we lose, they daily get; All 'long of this vile traitor Somerset.
translation: If he dies, we lose, I break the word of a soldier, we grieve, France smiles, we lose, they win....All because of this evil traitor Somerset!

original: Then God take mercy on brave Talbot's soul;   And on his son young John,
translation: Then, let God take pity on the soul of brave Talbot and also on his young son John,

original: who two hours since   I met in travel toward his warlike father!
translation: who I met two hours ago as he was traveling to see his father.

original: This seven years did not Talbot see his son;   And now they meet where both their lives are done.
translation: Talbot hasn't seen his son for  seven years  and now when they finally meet both of their lives are nearly over.

original: Alas,
translation: Ah, well!

original: what joy shall noble Talbot have   To bid his young son welcome to his grave?
translation: What joy will noble Talbot have to share with his young son when he's about to die?

original: Away! vexation almost stops my breath,
translation: Let's go! Agony almost stops me from breathing,

original: That sunder'd friends greet in the hour of death.
translation: thinking about separated relatives that meet in the hour of their death.

original: Lucy, farewell; no more my fortune can,   But curse the cause I cannot aid the man.
translation: Goodbye, Lucy. I can't do much but curse the reason I can't help the man.

original: Maine, Blois, Poictiers, and Tours, are won away,   'Long all of Somerset and his delay.
translation: Maine, Blois, Poictiers, and Tours have been conquered all because of Somerset and his inaction.

original: Thus, while the vulture of sedition   Feeds in the bosom of such great commanders,
translation: And so, while the  vulture of rebellion  eats out the hearts of these great commanders,

original: Sleeping neglection doth betray to loss   The conquest of our scarce cold conqueror,
translation: lazy neglect dishonors the conquests of our recently dead king,

original: That ever living man of memory,   Henry the Fifth:
translation: a man who will live forever in our memory —Henry the Fifth.

original: whiles they each other cross,   Lives, honours, lands and all hurry to loss.
translation: While the lords argue with each other, his life, honors, and lands all hurry to their ends.

original: It is too late; I cannot send them now:
translation: It's too late, I can't send them now.

original: This expedition was by York and Talbot   Too rashly plotted:
translation: This military action was planned too hastily by York and Talbot.

original: all our general force   Might with a sally of the very town   Be buckled with:
translation: All of our general army might be surprised by a sudden attack.

original: the over-daring Talbot   Hath sullied all his gloss of former honour   By this unheedful, desperate, wild adventure:
translation: Talbot risks too much and he has stained all the shine of his previous honor with this careless, desperate and wild move.

original: York set him on to fight and die in shame,   That, Talbot dead, great York might bear the name.
translation: York sent Talbot to go fight and die in shame, so that when Talbot is dead, great York may have his title.

original: Here is Sir William Lucy, who with me Set from our o'ermatch'd forces forth for aid.
translation: Here is Sir William Lucy. He was sent with me from our outnumbered army to ask for help.

original: How now, Sir William! whither were you sent?
translation: How is it going, Sir William? Where are you coming from?

original: Whither, my lord?
translation: Where, my lord?

original: from bought and sold Lord Talbot;   Who, ring'd about with bold adversity,   Cries out for noble York and Somerset,
translation: From the betrayed Lord Talbot, who, in his brave misfortune is crying out for noble York and Somerset

original: To beat assailing death from his weak legions:
translation: so they can conquer the death that has attacked his weak troops.

original: And whiles the honourable captain there   Drops bloody sweat from his war-wearied limbs,
translation: And while the honorable captain drops  bloody sweat  from his tired arms and legs,

original: And, in advantage lingering, looks for rescue,
translation: as he is desperately trying to hold onto his superior military position,

original: You, his false hopes, the trust of England's honour,   Keep off aloof with worthless emulation.
translation: you—his false hopes, the guardians of England's honor, stand aside due to your foolish rivalry.

original: Let not your private discord keep away   The levied succors that should lend him aid,
translation: Don't let your personal disagreement stop you from gathering military assistance to help him out.

original: While he, renowned noble gentleman,   Yields up his life unto a world of odds:
translation: While he, a famous noble gentleman, gives up his life for a huge risk,

original: Orleans the Bastard, Charles, Burgundy,   Alencon, Reignier, compass him about,   And Talbot perisheth by your default.
translation: Orleans the Bastard, Charles, Burgundy, Alencon and Reignier surround him and Talbot dies because you failed to act.

original: York set him on; York should have sent him aid.
translation: York sent him there, York should have sent him help.

original: And York as fast upon your grace exclaims; Swearing that you withhold his levied host, Collected for this expedition.
translation: And York also reacted as quickly against you, swearing that you withheld the army that was reserved for this military action.

original: York lies; he might have sent and had the horse; I owe him little duty, and less love; And take foul scorn to fawn on him by sending.
translation: York lies, he should have sent for help. I don't owe him anything—no duty and even less love. And I find it disgraceful that he didn't send for help.

original: The fraud of England, not the force of France,   Hath now entrapp'd the noble-minded Talbot:
translation: It is England that has tricked and trapped the noble Talbot, not France.

original: Never to England shall he bear his life;   But dies, betray'd to fortune by your strife.
translation: He will never return to England alive, but he dies betrayed by your argument.

original: Come, go; I will dispatch the horsemen straight: Within six hours they will be at his aid.
translation: Come, let's go! I will send the horsemen immediately. They will be at his side in six hours.

original: Too late comes rescue: he is ta'en or slain; For fly he could not, if he would have fled; And fly would Talbot never, though he might.
translation: The rescue will be too late. He is already taken or killed, because he did not run away; and he would not have even if he had been able to, because Talbot would never run away.

original: If he be dead, brave Talbot, then adieu!
translation: If he is dead, then brave Talbot goodbye!

original: His fame lives in the world, his shame in you.
translation: His fame will continue on in the world and his shame will live in you.

original: O young John Talbot!
translation: Oh, young Talbot!

original: I did send for thee   To tutor thee in stratagems of war,
translation: I sent for you so I could teach you the strategies of war,

original: That Talbot's name might be in thee revived
translation: so that the name of Talbot might be brought back to life in you

original: When sapless age and weak unable limbs   Should bring thy father to his drooping c   hair.
translation: when weak age and incapable arms and legs put your father in his grave.

original: But, O malignant and ill-boding stars!
translation: But, oh, you evil and wicked stars!

original: Now thou art come unto a feast of death,   A terrible and unavoided danger:
translation: You have now come to a celebration of death, which is a terrible danger that cannot be avoided.

original: Therefore, dear boy, mount on my swiftest horse;
translation: That's why, my dear boy, you have to get on my fastest horse

original: And I'll direct thee how thou shalt escape   By sudden flight:
translation: and I'll instruct you how on how to escape and run away.

original: come, dally not, be gone.
translation: Come, don't delay, and go!

original: Is my name Talbot?
translation: Isn't my name Talbot?

original: and am I your son?
translation: And am I not your son?

original: And shall I fly?
translation: And I should run away?

original: O if you love my mother,   Dishonour not her honourable name,
translation: Oh, if you love my mother, don't dishonor her honorable name.

original: To make a bastard and a slave of me!
translation: Don't make a bastard and a slave out of me!

original: The world will say, he is not Talbot's blood,   That basely fled when noble Talbot stood.
translation: The world will say that I am not of Talbot's blood because I ran away like a coward while noble Talbot stayed.

original: Fly, to revenge my death, if I be slain.
translation: If I am killed, you have to fly to avenge my death.
