original: He that flies so will ne'er return again.
translation: The one that runs away will never come back.

original: If we both stay, we both are sure to die.
translation: If both of us stay, we are both going to die, I'm sure of that.

original: Then let me stay; and, father, do you fly:
translation: Then let me stay and you run away, father.

original: Your loss is great, so your regard should be;
translation: The loss of you would have a devastating impact and so your self-regard should be high.

original: My worth unknown, no loss is known in me.
translation: Nobody knows what I'm worth and my loss would have no impact.

original: Upon my death the French can little boast;   In yours they will, in you all hopes are lost.
translation: The French can't boast about my death but they will with yours because all hope is lost with you.

original: Flight cannot stain the honour you have won;
translation: If you run away, it won't ruin the honor you have already earned.

original: But mine it will, that no exploit have done:
translation: But my honor would because I have done no heroic deeds.

original: You fled for vantage, everyone will swear;
translation: You ran away because of a military advantage, everyone will say so.

original: But, if I bow, they'll say it was for fear.
translation: But if I retreat, they'll say it was because I was afraid.

original: There is no hope that ever I will stay,   If the first hour I shrink and run away.
translation: I'll never stay during future battles, if in the first hour I decide to run away.

original: Here on my knee I beg mortality,   Rather than life preserved with infamy.
translation: I ask for my death, rather than for a life protected by shame.

original: Shall all thy mother's hopes lie in one tomb?
translation: Shall all your mother's hopes lie in one grave?

original: Ay, rather than I'll shame my mother's womb.
translation: Yes, rather that than if I were to shame my mother's womb.

original: Upon my blessing, I command thee go.
translation: I give you my blessings and order you to go.

original: To fight I will, but not to fly the foe.
translation: I will go to fight, but not to run away from the enemy.

original: Part of thy father may be saved in thee.
translation: Part of your father may be saved in you.

original: No part of him but will be shame in me.
translation: Every part of him would only be shameful to me.

original: Thou never hadst renown, nor canst not lose it.
translation: You've never known it, so you can't lose it.

original: Yes, your renowned name: shall flight abuse it?
translation: Yes, your famous name! Should running away dishonor it?

original: Thy father's charge shall clear thee from that stain.
translation: Your father's order shall clean you from that stain.

original: You cannot witness for me, being slain. If death be so apparent, then both fly.
translation: You can't know what I'll do, when you're dead. If death is so certain, we should both run away.

original: And leave my followers here to fight and die? My age was never tainted with such shame.
translation: And leave my men here to fight and die? I've never been marked with so much shame.

original: And shall my youth be guilty of such blame?
translation: And should my young age be guilty of that?

original: No more can I be sever'd from your side,   Than can yourself yourself in twain divide:
translation: I cannot be more separated from you than you can separate and divide yourself in two.

original: Stay, go, do what you will, the like do I;
translation: One says stay, the other says go. Do what you wish, and I'll do the same.

original: For live I will not, if my father die.
translation: I know I won't live if my father dies.

original: Then here I take my leave of thee, fair son,   Born to eclipse thy life this afternoon.
translation: Then, here I leave you my great son. I was born to extinguish your life this afternoon.

original: Come, side by side together live and die.   And soul with soul from France to heaven fly.
translation: Come, we will live and die side by side. And our souls will fly from France to heaven together.

original: Saint George and victory!
translation: Saint George and victory!

original: fight, soldiers, fight.
translation: Fight, soldiers, fight.

original: The regent hath with Talbot broke his word   And left us to the rage of France his sword.
translation: York has broken his word to me and left us to angrily fight the French.

original: Where is John Talbot?
translation: Where is my son?

original: Pause, and take thy breath;
translation: Stop for a moment and take a deep breath.

original: I gave thee life and rescued thee from death.
translation: I gave you life and saved you from death.

original: O, twice my father, twice am I thy son!
translation: Oh, you are twice my father and I am twice your son!

original: The life thou gavest me first was lost and done,   Till with thy warlike sword, despite of late,   To my determined time thou gavest new date.
translation: The life that you first gave me was lost until your warrior's sword, despite recent events, prolonged my life, which seemed to have an appointed ending.

original: When from the Dauphin's crest thy sword struck fire,   It warm'd thy father's heart with proud desire   Of bold-faced victory.
translation: When you attacked the Dauphin's helmet with your sword, it warmed your father's heart with pride for such a bold victory.

original: Then leaden age,   Quicken'd with youthful spleen and warlike rage,   Beat down Alencon,   Orleans, Burgundy,
translation: Then old age, made fast with youthful anger, defeated Alencon, Orleans, Burgundy

original: And from the pride of Gallia rescued thee.
translation: and saved you from the  best of  France.

original: The ireful bastard Orleans, that drew blood   From thee, my boy, and had the maidenhood   Of thy first fight,
translation: The enraged bastard Orleans, that took blood from you, my boy, and took the virginity of your first fight,

original: I soon encountered,   And interchanging blows
translation: I met him soon after that and we exchanged some blows.

original: I quickly shed   Some of his bastard blood; and in disgrace   Bespoke him thus;
translation: I quickly drew some of his bastard blood and insultingly told him:

original: 'Contaminated, base   And misbegotten blood I spill of thine,   Mean and right poor,
translation: "I spill your poisonous, lowly and illegitimate blood

original: for that pure blood of mine   Which thou didst force from Talbot, my brave boy:'
translation: in revenge for my pure blood which you took from Talbot, my brave son."

original: Here, purposing the Bastard to destroy,   Came in strong rescue.
translation: Then, I intended to destroy the Bastard but he was saved.

original: Speak, thy father's care,   Art thou not weary, John? how dost thou fare?
translation: Speak to me, are you not tired, John? How are you?

original: Wilt thou yet leave the battle, boy, and fly,   Now thou art seal'd the son of chivalry?
translation: Will you leave the battle, boy, or run away now that you have proven yourself to be brave?

original: Fly, to revenge my death when I am dead:
translation: Run away to avenge my death when I'm dead.

original: The help of one stands me in little stead.
translation: The help of one person doesn't really matter to me.

original: O, too much folly is it, well I wot,   To hazard all our lives in one small boat!
translation: Oh, it's too insane, I know, to gamble away our lives in one small boat.

original: If I to-day die not with Frenchmen's rage,   To-morrow I shall die with mickle age:
translation: If I don't die today from the anger of the French, tomorrow I'll die of old age.

original: By me they nothing gain an if I stay;   'Tis but the shortening of my life one day:
translation: They don't gain anything by killing me and if I stay, it only shortens my life by one day.

original: In thee thy mother dies, our household's name,
translation: Your mother dies with you, as does the name of our family.

original: My death's revenge, thy youth, and England's fame:
translation: The revenge of my death, your young age, England's fame

original: All these and more we hazard by thy stay;
translation: —we gamble all those and more away if you stay here!

original: All these are saved if thou wilt fly away.
translation: But they will all be saved if you run away.

original: The sword of Orleans hath not made me smart;
translation: I don't feel pain from the sword of Orleans.

original: These words of yours draw life-blood from my heart:
translation: It is your words that draw blood from my heart.

original: On that advantage, bought with such a shame,   To save a paltry life and slay bright fame,
translation: I would be ashamed if I saved my own life at the expense of your death and reputation.

original: Before young Talbot from old Talbot fly,   The coward horse that bears me fail and die!
translation: Before young Talbot runs from old Talbot, may the cowardly horse that takes me away fall and die!

original: And like me to the peasant boys of France,   To be shame's scorn and subject of mischance!
translation: C ompare me to the poor French boys, I will also be an object of mockery and a victim of misfortune!

original: Surely, by all the glory you have won,   An if I fly, I am not Talbot's son:
translation: Isn't it certain, by all the fame you have won, that if I run away, I'm not Talbot's son?

original: Then talk no more of flight, it is no boot;   If son to Talbot, die at Talbot's foot.
translation: So, don't talk of running away any more, it's of no use. If Talbot's son should die, he'll die by Talbot's feet.

original: Then follow thou thy desperate sire of Crete,   Thou Icarus; thy life to me is sweet:
translation: Then follow your desperate  son of Crete, your Icarus . Your life is too dear to me.

original: If thou wilt fight, fight by thy father's side;   And, commendable proved, let's die in pride.
translation: If you will fight, fight at your father's side and we'll die admirably and honorably.

original: Where is my other life? mine own is gone;
translation: Where is my other life? I have lost my own.

original: O, where's young Talbot? where is valiant John?
translation: Oh, where is young Talbot? Where is brave John?

original: Triumphant death, smear'd with captivity,   Young Talbot's valour makes me smile at thee:
translation: Victorious death, that has me in its grasp, the courage of young John makes me smile at you.

original: When he perceived me shrink and on my knee,   His bloody sword he brandish'd over me,
translation: When he saw me fall down on my knees, he waved his bloody sword over me

original: And, like a hungry lion, did commence   Rough deeds of rage and stern impatience;
translation: and like a hungry lion he started moving with violent, angry acts of rage and cruel fury.

original: But when my angry guardant stood alone,   Tendering my ruin and assail'd of none,
translation: But when my angry protector stood alone, taking care of me when I fell, he attacked nobody.

original: Dizzy-eyed fury and great rage of heart   Suddenly made him from my side to start   Into the clustering battle of the French;
translation: With dazzled eyes and a great anger of his heart he suddenly moved from me and went into the crowded French battle.

original: And in that sea of blood my boy did drench   His over-mounting spirit, and there died,   My Icarus, my blossom, in his pride.
translation: And my son drowned his over-ambitious spirit in that sea of blood and in his pride died, my  Icarus  and my blooming flower.

original: O, my dear lord, lo, where your son is borne!
translation: Oh, my dear lord, look, your son is being carried here!

original: Thou antic death, which laugh'st us here to scorn,
translation: It is grinning death, which laughs at us and mocks us here.

original: Anon, from thy insulting tyranny,   Coupled in bonds of perpetuity,   Two Talbots, winged through the lither sky,   In thy despite shall 'scape mortality.
translation: Soon, because of your insulting tyranny two Talbots will fly through the sky, joined together forever, escaping death.

original: O, thou, whose wounds become hard-favour'd death,   Speak to thy father ere thou yield thy breath!
translation: Oh you, whose wounds are mortal, speak to your father before you stop breathing!

original: Brave death by speaking, whether he will or no;
translation: Win over death by speaking, whether he wants you to or not;

original: Imagine him a Frenchman and thy foe.
translation: imagine that death is only a Frenchman and your enemy.

original: Poor boy!   he smiles, methinks, as who should say,
translation: Poor boy!  I think he smiles, as if he agreed with what I said

original: Had death been French, then death had died to-day.
translation: —if death had been French then death would have died today.

original: Come, come and lay him in his father's arms:
translation: Come, come and put him in his father's arms.

original: My spirit can no longer bear these harms.
translation: My spirit can't stand this pain any longer.

original: Soldiers, adieu! I have what I would have,
translation: Goodbye, soldiers! I have what I wanted.

original: Now my old arms are young John Talbot's grave.
translation: Now my old arms serve as a grave for young John Talbot.

original: Had York and Somerset brought rescue in, We should have found a bloody day of this.
translation: If York and Somerset brought help, this would have been a bloody day.

original: How the young whelp of Talbot's, raging-wood, Did flesh his puny sword in Frenchmen's blood!
translation: Did you see Talbot's young puppy? He was furious when he dug his inexperienced sword in Frenchmen's blood!

original: Once I encounter'd him, and thus I said:
translation: I met him once and I said to him:

original: 'Thou maiden youth, be vanquish'd by a maid:'
translation: "You are a virginal young boy, so be killed by a virgin."

original: But, with a proud majestical high scorn,   He answer'd thus:
translation: But he answered with a proud noble sneer:

original: 'Young Talbot was not born   To be the pillage of a giglot wench:'
translation: "Young Talbot wasn't born to be some whore's prey."

original: So, rushing in the bowels of the French,   He left me proudly, as unworthy fight.
translation: And then he hurried into the depths of the French, leaving me proudly as if I wasn't worth his fight.

original: Doubtless he would have made a noble knight; See, where he lies inhearsed in the arms Of the most bloody nurser of his harms!
Hew them to pieces, hack their bones asunder Whose life was England's glory, Gallia's wonder.
translation: Cut them down to pieces, break their bones apart. Their life was the glory of England and now it's the source of wonder in France.

original: O, no, forbear! for that which we have fled During the life, let us not wrong it dead.
translation: Oh, no, let it go! Let us not harm the dead, since we ran away from him when he was alive.

original: Herald, conduct me to the Dauphin's tent, To know who hath obtained the glory of the day.
translation: Messenger, take me to the Dauphin's tent, so I can find out who won today.

original: On what submissive message art thou sent?
translation: What message of surrender do you bring?

original: Submission, Dauphin! 'tis a mere French word;
translation: Surrender, Dauphin! That's exclusively a French word.

original: We English warriors wot not what it means.
translation: English warriors don't know what it means.

original: I come to know what prisoners thou hast ta'en   And to survey the bodies of the dead.
translation: I came to find out what prisoners you've taken and to examine the bodies of the dead.

original: For prisoners ask'st thou? hell our prison is. But tell me whom thou seek'st.
But where's the great Alcides of the field,
translation: Where is the great  Alcides  of the battle,

original: Valiant Lord Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury,   Created, for his rare success in arms,
translation: the brave Lord Talbot , Earl of Shrewsbury, for he was made an earl for his extraordinary success in battle,

original: Great Earl of Washford, Waterford and Valence;   Lord Talbot of Goodrig and Urchinfield,   Lord Strange of Blackmere, Lord Verdun of Alton,   Lord Cromwell of Wingfield, Lord Furnival of Sheffield,
translation: Great Earl of Washford, Waterford and Valence, Lord Talbot of Goodrig and Urchinfield, Lord Strange of Blackmere, Lord Verdun of Alton, Lord Cromwell of Wingfield, Lord Furnival of Sheffield,

original: The thrice-victorious Lord of Falconbridge;
translation: Lord of Falconbridge who won three times,

original: Knight of the noble order of Saint George,
translation: the knight of the noble order of Saint George,

original: Worthy Saint Michael and the Golden Fleece;
translation: worthy of  Saint Michael  and  the Golden Fleece ,

original: Great marshal to Henry the Sixth   Of all his wars within the realm of France?
translation: the great marshal to Henry the Sixth and all his wars in France?

original: Here is a silly stately style indeed!
translation: This is a silly stately list of titles!

original: The Turk, that two and fifty kingdoms hath,   Writes not so tedious a style as this.
translation: The Turk  who had fifty two kingdoms did not write in a style as dull as this.

original: Him that thou magnifiest with all these titles   Stinking and fly-blown lies here at our feet.
translation: The one that you describe so elaborately with all these titles is lying at your feet, stinking and rotting.

original: Is Talbot slain,
translation: Has Talbot been killed?

original: the Frenchmen's only scourge,   Your kingdom's terror and black Nemesis?
translation: He was the only weapon we had against the French, he was your country's terror and black  Nemesis .

original: O, were mine eyeballs into bullets turn'd,   That I in rage might shoot them at your faces!
translation: Oh, if only my eyeballs were turned into bullets, so I could shoot them in anger at your faces!

original: O, that I could but call these dead to life!
translation: Oh, if only I had the power to bring the dead back to life!

original: It were enough to fright the realm of France:   Were but his picture left amongst you here,   It would amaze the proudest of you all.
translation: It would be enough to scare France to have only his picture left here, it would terrify the proudest of you.

original: Give me their bodies, that I may bear them hence   And give them burial as beseems their worth.
translation: Give me their bodies, so that I may take them from here and give them the burial they deserve.

original: I think this upstart is old Talbot's ghost,   He speaks with such a proud commanding spirit.
translation: I think this arrogant person is old Talbot's ghost. He speaks in such a proud and controlling way.

original: For God's sake let him have 'em; to keep them here,   They would but stink, and putrefy the air.
translation: For God's sake, let him have the bodies. They would smell and infect the air if we kept them here.

original: Go, take their bodies hence.
translation: Go and take their bodies away.

original: I'll bear them hence; but from their ashes shall be  rear'd A phoenix that shall make all France afeard.
translation: I'll take them from here, but from their ashes will rise like a phoenix that will scare the whole of France.

original: So we be rid of them, do with 'em what thou wilt. And now to Paris, in this conquering vein: All will be ours, now bloody Talbot's slain.
translation: Now that we're rid of them, do what you want with them. And now, let's go to Paris, in this victorious fashion. Everything will be ours, now that Talbot is killed!

original: Have you perused the letters from the pope, The emperor and the Earl of Armagnac?
translation: Have you read the letters from the pope, the emperor and the Earl of Armagnac?

original: I have, my lord: and their intent is this:
translation: I have, my lord, and this is what they want:

original: They humbly sue unto your excellence   To have a godly peace concluded of   Between the realms of England and of France.
translation: they ask your excellence earnestly to settle a godly peace between the countries of England and France.

original: How doth your grace affect their motion?
translation: And are you inclined to agree with their proposal?

original: Well, my good lord; and as the only means To stop effusion of our Christian blood And 'stablish quietness on every side.
translation: Yes, I am, my good lord. It is the only way to stop the outpouring of our Christian blood and establish peace on both sides.

original: Ay, marry, uncle; for I always thought   It was both impious and unnatural
translation: Ah yes, uncle. I have always thought that it was ungodly and unnatural

original: That such immanity and bloody strife   Should reign among professors of one faith.
translation: that such barbarity and bloody fighting should rule people who hold the same faith.

original: Beside, my lord, the sooner to effect   And surer bind this knot of amity,
translation: Also, my lord, the sooner peace is established, the stronger this friendship will be.

original: The Earl of Armagnac, near knit to Charles,   A man of great authority in France,
translation: The Earl of Armagnac is closely related to Charles, he is a man of great authority in France

original: Proffers his only daughter to your grace   In marriage,
translation: and offers his only daughter to your grace in marriage.

original: with a large and sumptuous dowry.
translation: She has a large and impressive  dowry .

original: Marriage, uncle! alas, my years are young!
translation: Marriage, uncle! Ah, but I am still so young!

original: And fitter is my study and my books   Than wanton dalliance with a paramour.
translation: It is better that I spend my time studying and buried in books than fooling around with a lover.

original: Yet call the ambassador; and, as you please,   So let them have their answers every one:
translation: But call the ambassador, and have them write their answers to all the letters.

original: I shall be well content with any choice   Tends to God's glory and my country's weal.
translation: I will be happy with any choice that pleases God and my country's welfare.

original: What! is my Lord of Winchester install'd,   And call'd unto a cardinal's degree?
translation: What!? Is the Lord of Winchester inaugurated, and has he become a cardinal?

original: Then I perceive that will be verified   Henry the Fifth did sometime prophesy,
translation: Then I think what Henry the Fifth once predicted will come true:

original: 'If once he come to be a cardinal,   He'll make his cap co-equal with the crown.'
translation: "If he becomes a cardinal one day, he'll make his Cardinal's hat as powerful as the crown."

original: My lords ambassadors, your several suits   Have been consider'd and debated on.
translation: My lords ambassadors, your separate requests have been considered and debated.

original: And therefore are we certainly resolved   To draw conditions of a friendly peace;
translation: And therefore we can say for certain that we will draw up the conditions of a friendly peace,

original: Which by my Lord of Winchester we mean   Shall be transported presently to France.
translation: which shall be taken to France immediately by my Lord of Winchester.

original: And for the proffer of my lord your master,
translation: And as I was asked,

original: I have inform'd his highness so at large   As liking of the lady's virtuous gifts,
translation: I have informed his highness about the virtuous gifts of the lady,

original: Her beauty and the value of her dower,
translation: her beauty and the price of her dower

original: He doth intend she shall be England's queen.
translation: and he agreed that she shall be England's queen.

original: In argument and proof of which contract,   Bear her this jewel, pledge of my affection.
translation: As evidence of our contract bring her this jewel, as a promise of my love.

original: And so, my lord protector, see them guarded   And safely brought to Dover;
translation: And so, my lord protector, make sure they are protected and safely brought to Dover

original: where inshipp'd   Commit them to the fortune of the sea.
translation: where once they have set off, leave them to be carried by the sea.

original: Stay, my lord legate:
translation: My lord Representative, stay.

original: you shall first receive   The sum of money which I promised   Should be deliver'd to his holiness   For clothing me in these grave ornaments.
translation: You will first get the money which I promised to be delivered to his holiness the Pope in exchange for giving me these dignified robes of office.

original: I will attend upon your lordship's leisure.
translation: I will do as my lord pleases.

original: Now Winchester will not submit, I trow,   Or be inferior to the proudest peer.
translation: Now Winchester won't surrender, or be subordinate to the proudest lords, I am sure.

original: Humphrey of Gloucester, thou shalt well perceive   That, neither in birth or for authority,   The bishop will be overborne by thee:
translation: Humphrey of Gloucester, you will soon realize that the bishop won't be  overshadowed  by you, not in birth or in authority.

original: I'll either make thee stoop and bend thy knee,   Or sack this country with a mutiny.
translation: I'll make them walk over you and sink you to your knees, or else start a rebellion in this country.

original: These news, my lord, may cheer our drooping spirits: 'Tis said the stout Parisians do revolt And turn again unto the warlike French.
translation: This news, my lords, could cheer us up. It's rumored that the brave Parisians revolt and look to the French soldiers again.

original: Then march to Paris, royal Charles of France, And keep not back your powers in dalliance.
translation: Then let's go to Paris, royal Charles of France, and don't delay your troops.

original: Peace be amongst them, if they turn to us; Else, ruin combat with their palaces!
translation: If they turn to us for help, peace be with them! But if not, let ruin bring down their palaces!

original: Success unto our valiant general, And happiness to his accomplices!
translation: I wish success to our brave general and happiness to his allies!

original: What tidings send our scouts? I prithee, speak.
translation: What news do you bring, scout? I beg you, speak.

original: The English army, that divided was Into two parties, is now conjoined in one, And means to give you battle presently.
translation: The English army that was divided into two parts has now merged into one and is planning on attacking you soon.

original: Somewhat too sudden, sirs, the warning is; But we will presently provide for them.
translation: That warning seems a bit of out the blue, sirs. But we will prepare ourselves immediately anyway.

original: I trust the ghost of Talbot is not there: Now he is gone, my lord, you need not fear.
translation: I hope that Talbot's ghost isn't there. Now that he is gone, you don't have to fear him, my lord.

original: Of all base passions, fear is most accursed. Command the conquest, Charles, it shall be thine, Let Henry fret and all the world repine.
translation: Fear is the worst of all the main passions. Give us orders so we can win, Charles. Victory will be yours! Let Henry be scared of us and let all the world cry.

original: Then on, my lords; and France be fortunate!
translation: Then, off we go, my lords! Luck be with you, France!

original: The regent conquers, and the Frenchmen fly.
translation: The regent is victorious and the Frenchmen are running away.

original: Now help, ye charming spells and periapts;
translation: Now you must help, you  magic spells and amulets .

original: And ye choice spirits that admonish me   And give me signs of future accidents.
translation: And you, excellent spirits that warned me and gave me signs about the future.

original: You speedy helpers, that are substitutes Under the lordly monarch of the north, Appear and aid me in this enterprise.
translation: Quick helpers, the servants of the devil, appear to me and help me with my plan.

original: This speedy and quick appearance argues proof   Of your accustom'd diligence to me.
translation: This swift and quick appearance is proof of your familiar determination to help me.

original: Now, ye familiar spirits, that are cull'd   Out of the powerful regions under earth,
translation: Now, my familiar spirits, that have been picked from the powerful spaces under the earth,

original: Help me this once, that France may get the field.
translation: help me once more so that France will win the battle.

original: O, hold me not with silence over-long!
translation: Oh, don't leave me hanging here in this silence for too long!

original: Where I was wont to feed you with my blood,
translation: Whereas until now I was accustomed to feed you my blood,

original: I'll lop a member off and give it you   In earnest of further benefit,
translation: I'll cut off a limb and give it to you as an advance payment for a later favor,

original: So you do condescend to help me now.
translation: so that you will agree to help me now.

original: No hope to have redress? My body shall Pay recompense, if you will grant my suit.
translation: Is there no hope of assistance? My body shall compensate for it, if you'll fulfill my request.

original: Cannot my body nor blood-sacrifice   Entreat you to your wonted furtherance?
translation: Can't my body or  blood sacrifice  convince you to assist me like you usually do?

original: Then take my soul, my body, soul and all,   Before that England give the French the foil.
translation: Take my soul, my body, soul and everything, then, before England defeats the French.

original: See, they forsake me!
translation: See, they abandon me!

original: Now the time is come   That France must vail her lofty-plumed crest   And let her head fall into England's lap.
translation: Now it is time for France to lower her helmet decorated with feathers and  let her head fall into England's lap .

original: My ancient incantations are too weak,   And hell too strong for me to buckle with:
translation: My old spells are too weak and hell is too strong for me to fight against.

original: Now, France, thy glory droopeth to the dust.
translation: Now, your glory falls down into the dust, France!

original: Damsel of France, I think I have you fast:
translation: You French girl, I think I have captured you.

original: Unchain your spirits now with spelling charms   And try if they can gain your liberty.
translation: Now ask your spirits for help with conjuring spells and see if they can gain you your freedom.

original: A goodly prize, fit for the devil's grace!
translation: A great prize,  good for the devil!

original: See, how the ugly wench doth bend her brows,   As if with Circe she would change my shape!
translation: See, how the ugly girl frowns, as if she could change my shape like  Circe .

original: Changed to a worser shape thou canst not be.
translation: You can't be changed to a worse shape than you are!

original: O, Charles the Dauphin is a proper man; No shape but his can please your dainty eye.
translation: Oh, yes, Charles the Dauphin is a handsome man and you only like his shape.

original: A plaguing mischief light on Charles and thee! And may ye both be suddenly surprised By bloody hands, in sleeping on your beds!
translation: A horrible plague on Charles and you! And I hope you'll both be suddenly surprised by bloody hands, while you're asleep!

original: Fell banning hag, enchantress, hold thy tongue!
translation: Fierce cursing witch, be quiet!

original: I prithee, give me leave to curse awhile.
translation: Please, let me curse for a while.

original: Curse, miscreant, when thou comest to the stake.
translation: You can curse all you like when you are at the stake, you heretic!

original: Be what thou wilt, thou art my prisoner.
translation: Whatever you are, you are now my prisoner.

original: O fairest beauty,
translation: Oh, what a beauty you are!

original: do not fear nor fly!
translation: Don't be afraid or run away.

original: For I will touch thee but with reverent hands;
translation: I will only touch you with respectful hands.

original: I kiss these fingers for eternal peace,
translation: I kiss  these fingers  to show you I mean to be at peace with you forever.

original: And lay them gently on thy tender side.
translation: And I release your hand so that it may hang by your side.

original: Who art thou?
translation: Who are you?

original: say, that I may honour thee.
translation: Tell me so I can honor you.

original: Margaret my name, and daughter to a king, The King of Naples, whosoe'er thou art.
translation: My name is Margaret and I am the King of Naples' daughter. And who might you be?

original: An earl I am, and Suffolk am I call'd.
translation: I'm an earl and my name is Suffolk.

original: Be not offended, nature's miracle,   Thou art allotted to be ta'en by me:
translation: Don't be offended, you miracle of nature, you were destined to be taken by me.

original: So doth the swan her downy cygnets save,   Keeping them prisoner underneath her wings.
translation: I am like the swan that protects her feathery young children, keeping them prisoner under her wings.

original: Yet, if this servile usage once offend.   Go, and be free again, as Suffolk's friend.
translation: But if this treatment offends you, you are free to go and still be Suffolk's friend.

original: O, stay!
translation: Stay!

original: I have no power to let her pass;
translation: I don't have the power to let her go.

original: My hand would free her, but my heart says no
translation: My hand wants to let her go but my heart doesn't.

original: As plays the sun upon the glassy streams,   Twinkling another counterfeited beam,   So seems this gorgeous beauty to mine eyes.
translation: Like when the sun shines on the mirror-like rivers, causing another mirrored ray to twinkle, so her gorgeous beauty is like to my eyes.

original: Fain would I woo her, yet I dare not speak:
translation: I would love to flirt with her, but I am unable to speak.

original: I'll call for pen and ink, and write my mind.
translation: I'll ask for pen and paper and write down everything that's on my mind.

original: Fie, de la Pole! disable not thyself;
translation: Ah, please, de la Pole! Don't underestimate yourself.

original: Hast not a tongue? is she not here?
translation: Do you not have a tongue? Isn't she right here?

original: Wilt thou be daunted at a woman's sight?
translation: Will you be intimidated at the sight of a woman?

original: Ay, beauty's princely majesty is such,   Confounds the tongue and makes the senses rough.
translation: Yes! The power of beauty is so strong that it destroys the power of the tongue and dulls all the senses.

original: Say, Earl of Suffolk—if thy name be so— What ransom must I pay before I pass? For I perceive I am thy prisoner.
translation: Tell me, Earl of Suffolk—if that's your name—what price do I have to pay before you'll let me go? I suppose, I am your prisoner.

original: How canst thou tell she will deny thy suit, Before thou make a trial of her love?
translation: How can you know that she will deny your request before you have even tested her love?

original: Why speak'st thou not? what ransom must I pay?
translation: Why don't you speak? What price do I have to pay?

original: She's beautiful, and therefore to be woo'd; She is a woman, therefore to be won.
translation: She is so beautiful that I must flirt with her, since she is a woman and must be won over.

original: Wilt thou accept of ransom? yea, or no.
translation: Will you accept some sort of price? Yes, or no?

original: Fond man, remember that thou hast a wife; Then how can Margaret be thy paramour?
translation: Foolish man, do you forget that you have a wife? Then how can Margaret be your lover?

original: I were best to leave him, for he will not hear.
translation: I should probably leave him, since he's not listening to me.

original: There all is marr'd; there lies a cooling card.
translation: That's it, this ruins all my hopes of winning.

original: He talks at random; sure, the man is mad.
translation: He speaks very randomly. I'm sure that man is mad.

original: And yet a dispensation may be had.
translation: And yet divorce with the Pope's permission is an option.

original: And yet I would that you would answer me.
translation: And yet I'd like him to answer me!

original: I'll win this Lady Margaret. For whom? Why, for my king: tush, that's a wooden thing!
translation: I'll win this Lady Margaret. For whom? Well, for my king! Ah, what a stupid idea!

original: He talks of wood: it is some carpenter.
Yet so my fancy may be satisfied,   And peace established between these realms
translation: And yet, my infatuation would be satisfied and peace would be established between these two countries.

original: But there remains a scruple in that too;
translation: But there is a problem that stands in my way.

original: For though her father be the King of Naples,   Duke of Anjou and Maine,
translation: Although her father is the King of Naples, Duke of Anjou and Maine,

original: yet is he poor,   And our nobility will scorn the match.
translation: he is poor and the lords at court will mock this match.

original: Hear ye, captain, are you not at leisure?
It shall be so, disdain they ne'er so much. Henry is youthful and will quickly yield. Madam, I have a secret to reveal.
translation: Yes, that's how it will be, however arrogant they will be about it. Henry is young and will agree to this.

original: What though I be enthrall'd? he seems a knight, And will not any way dishonour me.
translation: What, even though I am taken captive? Well, he seems like a knight and won't disrespect me in any way.

original: Lady, vouchsafe to listen what I say.
translation: Lady, please listen to what I have to say.

original: Perhaps I shall be rescued by the French; And then I need not crave his courtesy.
translation: Maybe I'll be rescued by the French and then I don't need to hope for his kindness.

original: Sweet madam, give me a hearing in a cause—
translation: Sweet madam, please hear what I have to say about—

original: Tush, women have been captivate ere now.
translation: Ah, please, women have been taken prisoner before me.

original: Lady, wherefore talk you so?
translation: Lady, why do you talk like this?

original: I cry you mercy, 'tis but Quid for Quo.
Say, gentle princess, would you not suppose Your bondage happy, to be made a queen?
translation: Tell me, gentle princess, wouldn't you think your imprisonment is a good thing if you were made a queen?

original: To be a queen in bondage is more vile Than is a slave in base servility; For princes should be free.
translation: To be an imprisoned queen is more low than to be a slave in servitude. Princes should be free.

original: And so shall you, If happy England's royal king be free.
translation: And you will be free, if the happy royal king of England is free.

original: Why, what concerns his freedom unto me?
translation: Why should I care about his freedom? What's it to me?

original: I'll undertake to make thee Henry's queen,   To put a golden sceptre in thy hand
translation: I want to make you Henry's queen and put a golden scepter in your hand

original: And set a precious crown upon thy head,   If thou wilt condescend to be my—
translation: and a precious crown on your head, if you will agree to be my—

original: What?
translation: Your what?

original: His love.
translation: His love.

original: I am unworthy to be Henry's wife.
translation: I am not good enough to be Henry's wife.

original: No, gentle madam; I unworthy am   To woo so fair a dame to be his wife,   And have no portion in the choice myself.
translation: No, gentle madam, I am not good enough to court such a fair woman to be his wife, and have no part in the choice myself.

original: How say you, madam, are ye so content?
translation: What do you say, madam? Are you happy with that?

original: An if my father please, I am content.
translation: If my father is happy, I will be too.

original: Then call our captains and our colours forth. And, madam, at your father's castle walls We'll crave a parley, to confer with him.
translation: Then I'll call our captains and the bearers of our military flags. And we'll ask for negotiation at your father's walls, madam, so we can discuss this with him.

original: See, Reignier, see, thy daughter prisoner!
translation: See, Reignier, your daughter is a prisoner!

original: To whom?
translation: A prisoner to whom?

original: To me.
translation: To me.

original: Suffolk, what remedy? I am a soldier, and unapt to weep, Or to exclaim on fortune's fickleness.
translation: Suffolk, what can I do? I am a soldier and am unable to cry or to accuse inconstancy of fortune.

original: Yes, there is remedy enough, my lord:
translation: Yes, there is something you can do, my lord.

original: Consent, and for thy honour give consent,   Thy daughter shall be wedded to my king;
translation: Agree to allow your daughter to marry my king.

original: Whom I with pain have woo'd and won thereto;
translation: I have courted and won Margaret

original: And this her easy-held imprisonment   Hath gained thy daughter princely liberty.
translation: and this easily endured imprisonment has gained your daughter's freedom.

original: Speaks Suffolk as he thinks?
translation: Does Suffolk speak his mind?

original: Fair Margaret knows That Suffolk doth not flatter, face, or feign.
translation: Fair Margaret knows that Suffolk doesn't flatter, deceive or fake anything.

original: Upon thy princely warrant, I descend To give thee answer of thy just demand.
translation: On your princely guarantee, I will come down to give you an answer to your honorable request.

original: And here I will expect thy coming.
translation: And I wait for your arrival here.

original: Welcome, brave earl, into our territories: Command in Anjou what your honour pleases.
translation: Welcome, brave earl, into our lands! Let me know what you'd like in Anjou.

original: Thanks, Reignier, happy for so sweet a child, Fit to be made companion with a king: What answer makes your grace unto my suit?
translation: Thanks, Reignier. Would you be happy if your sweet child was made a companion to a king? What is your answer to my suggestion?

original: Since thou dost deign to woo her little worth
translation: Since you have already put in the effort to court her and the little she is worth,

original: To be the princely bride of such a lord;
translation: to be the bride of such a lord,

original: Upon condition I may quietly   Enjoy mine own, the country Maine and Anjou,
translation: I will agree on the condition that I may quietly enjoy my  territories  of Maine and Anjou,

original: Free from oppression or the stroke of war,
translation: which will be free from oppression and the attacks of war.

original: My daughter shall be Henry's, if he please.
translation: My daughter will be Henry's if he is happy with it.

original: That is her ransom; I deliver her; And those two counties I will undertake Your grace shall well and quietly enjoy.
translation: That's her price then. I will deliver her. And I'll make sure that you will quietly enjoy those two territories.

original: And I again, in Henry's royal name, As deputy unto that gracious king, Give thee her hand, for sign of plighted faith.
translation: And I, in return, in Henry's royal name, since you are the deputy of the king, give you her hand as a sign of the promise.

original: Reignier of France, I give thee kingly thanks,   Because this is in traffic of a king.
translation: Reignier of France, I thank you in the name of my king, because this is the king's business.

original: I do embrace thee, as I would embrace The Christian prince, King Henry, were he here.
translation: I embrace you like I would embrace the Christian prince, King Henry, if he were here.

original: Farewell, my lord: good wishes, praise and prayers Shall Suffolk ever have of Margaret.
translation: Goodbye, my lord. Suffolk will always have good wishes, praise and prayers from Margaret.

original: Farewell, sweet madam: but hark you, Margaret; No princely commendations to my king?
translation: Goodbye, sweet madam. But, listen, Margaret, don't you want to send any royal greetings to my king?

original: Such commendations as becomes a maid, A virgin and his servant, say to him.
translation: I send him the greetings that a girl, a virgin and his servant would send him. You can tell him that.

original: Words sweetly placed and modestly directed. But madam, I must trouble you again; No loving token to his majesty?
translation: Those words are sweetly said and worthy of your virtue. But, madam, I must ask you again: No loving keepsake for his majesty?

original: Yes, my good lord, a pure unspotted heart, Never yet taint with love, I send the king.
translation: Yes, my good lord, I send the king my pure and unstained heart, never before touched with love.

original: And this withal.
translation: And also this.

original: That for thyself: I will not so presume To send such peevish tokens to a king.
translation: That you can keep for yourself. I would not dare to send such foolish keepsakes to a king.

original: O, wert thou for myself!
translation: Oh, if only you were mine!

original: But, Suffolk, stay;
translation: But Suffolk, stop.

original: Thou mayst not wander in that labyrinth;   There Minotaurs and ugly treasons lurk.
translation: You shouldn't get lost in that  labyrinth  because that is where  Minotaurs  and ugly treasons hide.

original: Solicit Henry with her wondrous praise:
translation: Persuade Henry by praising her wonderful qualities.

original: Bethink thee on her virtues that surmount,   And natural graces that extinguish art;
translation: Remember her virtues that excel and natural graces that outdo any artifice.

original: Repeat their semblance often on the seas,
translation: Recall the image of them as you journey across the sea

original: That, when thou comest to kneel at Henry's feet,   Thou mayst bereave him of his wits with wonder.
translation: so that when you come to kneel at Henry's feet, you will deprive him of his senses with wonder.

original: Bring forth that sorceress condemn'd to burn.
translation: Bring forward the witch that has been condemned to burn.

original: Ah, Joan, this kills thy father's heart outright!
translation: Ah, Joan, this kills your father!

original: Have I sought every country far and near,
translation: I have searched every region hoping to find you

original: And, now it is my chance to find thee out,   Must I behold thy timeless cruel death?
translation: and now that I have, I must watch your early, cruel death?

original: Ah, Joan, sweet daughter Joan, I'll die with thee!
translation: Ah, Joan, my sweet daughter Joan, I'll die with you!

original: Decrepit miser! base ignoble wretch! I am descended of a gentler blood: Thou art no father nor no friend of mine.
translation: You weak miserable creature! Lowly inferior villain! I come from a nobler bloodline. You aren't my father or my friend.

original: Out, out! My lords, an please you, 'tis not so;   I did beget her, all the parish knows:
translation: No, no! My lords, if it's all right with you, it's not true. I am her father, all of the locals know that.

original: Her mother liveth yet, can testify   She was the first fruit of my bachelorship.
translation: Her mother still lives and she can prove that Joan was the first fruit of my youth.

original: Graceless! wilt thou deny thy parentage?
translation: How awkward! Will you deny where you come from?

original: This argues what her kind of life hath been, Wicked and vile; and so her death concludes.
translation: This demonstrates what kind of life she led—wicked and wretched and so her death is a fitting end.

original: Fie, Joan, that thou wilt be so obstacle!
translation: How could you be so stubborn, Joan!

original: God knows thou art a collop of my flesh;   And for thy sake have I shed many a tear:
translation: God knows that you are a part of my body and I have cried so much for your sake.

original: Deny me not, I prithee, gentle Joan.
translation: Don't deny me, I beg you, gentle Joan.

original: Peasant, avaunt! You have suborn'd this man, Of purpose to obscure my noble birth.
translation: Leave me, peasant! You have bribed this man to bring my noble birth into question.

original: 'Tis true, I gave a noble to the priest   The morn that I was wedded to her mother.
translation: It's true that I gave  a gold coin  to the priest that morning when I married her mother.

original: Kneel down and take my blessing, good my girl.
translation: Kneel down and take my blessing, my good girl.

original: Wilt thou not stoop?
translation: Won't you kneel?

original: Now cursed be the time   Of thy nativity!
translation: Then  I curse the moment you were born!

original: I would the milk   Thy mother gave thee when thou suck'dst her breast,   Had been a little ratsbane for thy sake!
translation: I wish the milk your mother gave you when you sucked her breasts had been rat poison, for your sake!

original: Or else, when thou didst keep my lambs a-field,   I wish some ravenous wolf had eaten thee!
translation: Or I wish that some hungry wolf had eaten you, while you took care of my lambs in the field.

original: Dost thou deny thy father, cursed drab?
translation: Do you deny your father, cursed whore?

original: O, burn her, burn her! hanging is too good.
translation: She deserves to burn, hanging is too kind a punishment!

original: Take her away; for she hath lived too long, To fill the world with vicious qualities.
translation: Take her away, she has already lived too long and filled the world with horrible things.

original: First, let me tell you whom you have condemn'd:
translation: First, let me tell you who you have damned here.

original: Not me begotten of a shepherd swain,
translation: Not someone who was conceived by a shepherd,

original: But issued from the progeny of kings;   Virtuous and holy;
translation: but a successor of kings, virtuous and holy,

original: chosen from above,   By inspiration of celestial grace,   To work exceeding miracles on earth.
translation: chosen from the heavens by intervention of heavenly grace to make exceptional miracles happen on earth.

original: I never had to do with wicked spirits:
translation: I had nothing to do with wicked spirits.

original: But you, that are polluted with your lusts,   Stain'd with the guiltless blood of innocents,
translation: But you, that are corrupted by your desires, stained with the  guiltless blood of innocent people ,

original: Corrupt and tainted with a thousand vices,   Because you want the grace that others have,
translation: false and contaminated with a thousand sins,

original: You judge it straight a thing impossible   To compass wonders but by help of devils.
translation: you have decided that it's an entirely impossible thing for miracles to happen unless they are done with the help of devils.

original: No, misconceived!
translation: No, wickedly created!

original: Joan of Arc hath been   A virgin from her tender infancy,   Chaste and immaculate in very thought;
translation: Joan of Arc has been a virgin ever since she was a young girl, she's been virtuous and spotless

original: Whose maiden blood, thus rigorously effused,
translation: as her  virginal blood  did so savagely pour out.

original: Will cry for vengeance at the gates of heaven.
translation: She will scream for revenge at the gates of heaven!

original: Ay, ay: away with her to execution!
translation: Yes, yes, take her away to her execution!

original: And hark ye, sirs; because she is a maid,   Spare for no faggots, let there be enow:
translation: And pay attention, sirs.  Don't spare the bundles of wood  because she is a maid. Let there be enough of it.

original: Place barrels of pitch upon the fatal stake,   That so her torture may be shortened.
translation: Put barrels of  pitch  on the stake so that her torture can be shortened.

original: Will nothing turn your unrelenting hearts?
translation: Will nothing change your unforgiving hearts?

original: Then, Joan, discover thine infirmity,   That warranteth by law to be thy privilege.
translation: Then, Joan, reveal your weakness, that legally guarantees my freedom.

original: I am with child, ye bloody homicides:
translation: I am pregnant, you bloody murderers!

original: Murder not then the fruit within my womb,   Although ye hale me to a violent death.
translation: Although you drag me to a violent death, don't murder  the fruit in my belly .

original: Now heaven forfend! the holy maid with child!
translation: Oh heaven forbid! A holy girl pregnant?!

original: The greatest miracle that e'er ye wrought: Is all your strict preciseness come to this?
translation: It's the greatest miracle that I've ever seen. How does all your strict morality come to this?

original: She and the Dauphin have been juggling: I did imagine what would be her refuge.
translation: She and the Dauphin have been having sex. I thought this would be her last resource.

original: Well, go to; we'll have no bastards live; Especially since Charles must father it.
translation: Well, we'll have no bastards here, especially since Charles should be the father to it.

original: You are deceived; my child is none of his: It was Alencon that enjoy'd my love.
translation: That's not true, my child isn't his. Alencon enjoyed my love.

original: Alencon! that notorious Machiavel! It dies, an if it had a thousand lives.
O, give me leave, I have deluded you: 'Twas neither Charles nor yet the duke I named, But Reignier, king of Naples, that prevail'd.
translation: Oh, let me go, I have lied to you! It wasn't Charles or the duke I named, but Reignier, the king of Naples that seduced me.

original: A married man! that's most intolerable.
translation: He's a married man! That's unacceptable.

original: Why, here's a girl! I think she knows not well, There were so many, whom she may accuse.
translation: Well, look at this girl! I think she doesn't know exactly who to accuse because she's slept with so many men.

original: It's sign she hath been liberal and free.
translation: It's a sign that she has been loose and promiscuous.

original: And yet, forsooth, she is a virgin pure. Strumpet, thy words condemn thy brat and thee: Use no entreaty, for it is in vain.
translation: And yet she is a pure virgin. Whore, your words damn your child and you. Don't beg any longer, there's no use.

original: Then lead me hence;
translation: Then take me away.

original: with whom I leave my curse:
translation: I leave my curse with you!

original: May never glorious sun reflex his beams   Upon the country where you make abode;
translation: May the glorious sun never shine its rays on the country where you decide to stay.

original: But darkness and the gloomy shade of death   Environ you,
translation: Darkness and the gloomy shadow of death will surround you

original: till mischief and despair   Drive you to break your necks or hang yourselves!
translation: until mischief and despair forces you to break your necks or hang yourselves!

original: Break thou in pieces and consume to ashes, Thou foul accursed minister of hell!
translation: I hope you break into pieces and are burned to ashes, you false and cursed servant of hell!

original: Lord regent, I do greet your excellence   With letters of commission from the king.
translation: Lord regent, I welcome your excellence with letters of authority to act from the king.

original: For know, my lords, the states of Christendom,   Moved with remorse of these outrageous broils,
translation: For now, the states of Christendom, moved with pity out of this excessively violent chaos,

original: Have earnestly implored a general peace   Betwixt our nation and the aspiring French;
translation: have begged for a general peace between our nation and the ambitious French.

original: And here at hand the Dauphin and his train   Approacheth, to confer about some matter.
translation: And here come the Dauphin and his company to discuss this issue.

original: Is all our travail turn'd to this effect?
translation: Is all our labor turned into this?

original: After the slaughter of so many peers,   So many captains, gentlemen and soldiers,   That in this quarrel have been overthrown
translation: After so many of our men, so many captains, gentlemen and soldiers have been killed in this battle

original: And sold their bodies for their country's benefit,
translation: and sacrificed their bodies for the good of their country,

original: Shall we at last conclude effeminate peace?
translation: should we settle it all with an unmanly peace?

original: Have we not lost most part of all the towns,   By treason, falsehood and by treachery,   Our great progenitors had conquered?
translation: Haven't we lost most of our towns which our ancestors gained through treason, falsehood and treachery?

original: O Warwick, Warwick! I foresee with grief   The utter loss of all the realm of France.
translation: Oh, Warwick, Warwick! With grief, I predict the absolute loss of France.

original: Be patient, York: if we conclude a peace, It shall be with such strict and severe covenants As little shall the Frenchmen gain thereby.
translation: Be patient, York. If we settle a peace, it will be with strict and harsh terms of agreement in which the Frenchmen will gain very little.

original: Since, lords of England, it is thus agreed   That peaceful truce shall be proclaim'd in France,
translation: Lords of England, we heard that it has been agreed that a peaceful treaty will be reached in France,

original: We come to be informed by yourselves   What the conditions of that league must be.
translation: so we have come here in person to find out the conditions of this union.

original: Speak, Winchester; for boiling choler chokes The hollow passage of my poison'd voice, By sight of these our baleful enemies.
Charles, and the rest, it is enacted thus:
translation: The decree says this, listen up  Charles  and your men:

original: That, in regard King Henry gives consent,   Of mere compassion and of lenity,
translation: That King Henry agreed, out of pure compassion and mercifulness,

original: To ease your country of distressful war,
translation: to let your country be relieved after the stressful war

original: And suffer you to breathe in fruitful peace,
translation: and will allow you to breathe in the smell of a productive peace.

original: You shall become true liegemen to his crown:
translation: You shall become faithful loyal followers to his crown.

original: And Charles, upon condition thou wilt swear   To pay him tribute,   submit thyself,
translation: And Charles, you will swear to pay him homage  and submit yourself,

original: Thou shalt be placed as viceroy under him,   And still enjoy thy regal dignity.
translation: and you will be named as a representative of the king under him, and still maintain your royal status.

original: Must he be then as shadow of himself?
translation: Must he only be a shadow of himself?

original: Adorn his temples with a coronet,
translation: Should he put a crown on his head

original: And yet, in substance and authority,   Retain but privilege of a private man?
translation: and yet have no greater authority than any private citizen?

original: This proffer is absurd and reasonless.
translation: This offer is absurd and makes no sense.

original: 'Tis known already that I am possess'd   With more than half the Gallian territories,
translation: It's known that I am already in charge of more than half of the French territories

original: And therein reverenced for their lawful king:
translation: and there I am respected as their rightful king.

original: Shall I, for lucre of the rest unvanquish'd,   Detract so much from that prerogative,
translation: Should I, in the remaining undefeated territories, deny my own rightful place

original: As to be call'd but viceroy of the whole?
translation: and instead be called merely the king's representative to the whole country?

original: No, lord ambassador, I'll rather keep   That which I have than,
translation: No, lord ambassador, I'd like to keep what I have,

original: coveting for more,   Be cast from possibility of all.
translation: rather than desire more and lose everything in the process.

original: Insulting Charles!
translation: Insulting Charles!

original: hast thou by secret means   Used intercession to obtain a league,
translation: Have you intervened in some secret way, have you tried to  create a union

original: And, now the matter grows to compromise,   Stand'st thou aloof upon comparison?
translation: and now that we are trying to reach a compromise, do you pull back and hold up the title you're being offered the one you currently hold?

original: Either accept the title thou usurp'st,   Of benefit proceeding from our king
translation: Either accept the title out of generosity from our king

original: And not of any challenge of desert,   Or we will plague thee with incessant wars.
translation: and don't talk about value, or we will destroy you with our unending wars.

original: My lord, you do not well in obstinacy   To cavil in the course of this contract:
translation: My lord, you are very stubborn to debate the terms of this contract.

original: If once it be neglected, ten to one   We shall not find like opportunity.
translation: If it is underestimated, we won't present another such opportunity, that's for sure.

original: To say the truth, it is your policy   To save your subjects from such massacre   And ruthless slaughters
translation: To tell you the truth, it is your desire to to save your people from such massacre and cruel killings,

original: as are daily seen   By our proceeding in hostility;
translation: which we have seen daily in our hatred,

original: And therefore take this compact of a truce,
translation: that makes you accept this offer of peace.

original: Although you break it when your pleasure serves.
translation: Although you'll break it when it suits you.

original: How say'st thou, Charles? shall our condition stand?
translation: What do you say, Charles?  Are you happy with our terms of agreement?

original: It shall; Only reserved, you claim no interest In any of our towns of garrison.
translation: I am, with the only exception that you will claim no interest in any of our military towns.

original: Then swear allegiance to his majesty,   As thou art knight,
translation: Then, since you are a knight, swear loyalty to his majesty,

original: never to disobey   Nor be rebellious to the crown of England,
translation: never to disobey or rebel against the English crown.

original: Thou, nor thy nobles, to the crown of England.
translation: This is applicable to both yourself and your men.

original: So, now dismiss your army when ye please:   Hang up your ensign, let your drums be still,
translation: So, now send away your army when you wish, hang up your flags, let your drums be silent.

original: For here we entertain a solemn peace.
translation: Because we have here achieved a serious peace.

original: Your wondrous rare description, noble earl,   Of beauteous Margaret hath astonish'd me:
translation: Noble earl, your wonderful description of the beautiful Margaret has astonished me.

original: Her virtues graced with external gifts   Do breed love's settled passions in my heart:
translation: Her virtues, which seem to be enhanced with her external appearance have created feelings of love and passion in my heart.

original: And like as rigor of tempestuous gusts   Provokes the mightiest hulk against the tide,
translation: And like harsh violent winds your description provokes the largest vessel floating against the tide.

original: So am I driven by breath of her renown   Either to suffer shipwreck
translation: So I am out of breath from her glory and am either going to suffer a shipwreck

original: or arrive   Where I may have fruition of her love.
translation: or arrive on shore where I may enjoy her love.

original: Tush, my good lord, this superficial tale   Is but a preface of her worthy praise;
translation: Oh please, my good lord, this shallow tale is only an introduction of the praise of her true value.

original: The chief perfections of that lovely dame   Had I sufficient skill to utter them,
translation: The greatest perfections of that lovely woman, if I had the skill,

original: Would make a volume of enticing lines,   Able to ravish any dull conceit:
translation: could make a whole book of beautiful poetry,  capable of captivating any dull imagination.

original: And, which is more, she is not so divine,   So full-replete with choice of all delights,   But with as humble lowliness of mind
translation: What's more, she is so heavenly, so full with a choice of all delights, but she has a modest and lowly state of mind.

original: She is content to be at your command;
translation: She is happy to be at your command.

original: Command, I mean, of virtuous chaste intents,   To love and honour Henry as her lord.
translation: And by that I mean she has virtuous, chaste intentions to love and honor Henry as her lord.

original: And otherwise will Henry ne'er presume. Therefore, my lord protector, give consent That Margaret may be England's royal queen.
translation: Henry wouldn't want it any other way.  Therefore, my lord protector, agree that Margaret may be the royal queen of England.

original: So should I give consent to flatter sin.
translation: I might as well agree to praise sin.

original: You know, my lord, your highness is betroth'd   Unto another lady of esteem:
translation: You know, my lord, that your king is engaged to another respectful lady.

original: How shall we then dispense with that contract,   And not deface your honour with reproach?
translation: How should we deal with that betrothal and not deform your honor in disgrace?

original: As doth a ruler with unlawful oaths;
translation: Like a ruler does with illegal promises,

original: Or one that, at a triumph having vow'd   To try his strength, forsaketh yet the lists   By reason of his adversary's odds:
translation: or one that at a  jousting tournament  swore to try his strength but abandoned the designated combat arena because he saw his opponent was more likely to win.

original: A poor earl's daughter is unequal odds,   And therefore may be broke without offence.
translation: A daughter of a poor earl is a similar case and therefore may be broken off without any damage.

original: Why, what, I pray, is Margaret more than that? Her father is no better than an earl, Although in glorious titles he excel.
translation: Well, is Margaret any more than a poor earl's daughter? Her father is no better than an earl, although he does have some worthy titles.

original: Yes, lord, her father is a king,
translation: Yes, lord, her father is a king.

original: The King of Naples and Jerusalem;   And of such great authority in France
translation: He is the King of Naples and Jerusalem and holds great sway in France.

original: As his alliance will confirm our peace   And keep the Frenchmen in allegiance.
translation: An alliance with him will confirm our peace with France and keep the Frenchmen loyal to us.

original: And so the Earl of Armagnac may do, Because he is near kinsman unto Charles.
translation: But the Earl of Armagnac may do the same because he is close to Charles.

original: Beside, his wealth doth warrant a liberal dower, Where Reignier sooner will receive than give.
translation: Also, his wealth does promise a generous dower, while Reignier would rather receive than give.

original: A dower, my lords!
translation: A dowry, my lords!

original: disgrace not so your king,   That he should be so abject, base and poor,   To choose for wealth and not for perfect love.
translation: Don't disgrace your king so much as to think that he should be so hopeless, low, and poor to choose money over perfect love.

original: Henry is able to enrich his queen   And not seek a queen to make him rich:
translation: Henry is perfectly able to give his queen money and does not need to look for one who would make him rich.

original: So worthless peasants bargain for their wives,
translation: Peasants who are worth nothing try to find their wives in such a way.

original: As market-men for oxen, sheep, or horse.
translation: They're like men in the market, selling oxen, sheep, or horse.

original: Marriage is a matter of more worth   Than to be dealt in by attorneyship;
translation: But marriage should not be dealt with in negotiations between lawyers,

original: Not whom we will, but whom his grace affects,
translation: and it's not about who we want but who his grace likes.

original: Must be companion of his nuptial bed:
translation: She will be his companion in bed, after all!

original: And therefore, lords, since he affects her most,   It most of all these reasons bindeth us,
translation: And therefore, lords, since he likes her the most, for that reason we should prefer her as well,

original: In our opinions she should be preferr'd.
translation: and so she should be our first choice.

original: For what is wedlock forced but a hell,   An age of discord and continual strife?
translation: After all, what is a forced marriage but a never ending battle?

original: Whereas the contrary bringeth bliss,   And is a pattern of celestial peace.
translation: While the opposite brings joy and is a way to heavenly peace.

original: Whom should we match with Henry, being a king,   But Margaret, that is daughter to a king?
translation: Then, who else should be matched with Henry, who is a king, than Margaret, who is the daughter of a king?

original: Her peerless feature, joined with her birth,   Approves her fit for none but for a king:
translation: Her unique physical appearance and her birth makes her perfect only for a king.

original: Her valiant courage and undaunted spirit,   More than in women commonly is seen,   Will answer our hope in issue of a king;
translation: Her brave courage and fearless spirit, which isn't usually seen in women, will be an answer to our hope of giving a child to the king.

original: For Henry, son unto a conqueror,   Is likely to beget more conquerors,
translation: Henry, a conqueror's son, is likely to breed more conquerors

original: If with a lady of so high resolve   As is fair Margaret he be link'd in love.
translation: if he is joined in union with a lady of such courage as Margaret.

original: Then yield, my lords; and here conclude with me   That Margaret shall be queen, and none but she.
translation: Give up, then, my lords and here I finish by saying that Margaret shall be queen, and no one but her.

original: Whether it be through force of your report,   My noble Lord of Suffolk,
translation: I don't know if it's because of the power of your account of her, my noble Lord of Suffolk,

original: or for that   My tender youth was never yet attaint   With any passion of inflaming love,
translation: or because my young days have never been touched with any passion of love's fire,

original: I cannot tell; but this I am assured,   I feel such sharp dissension in my breast,
translation: I can't really tell but I am sure that I feel a sharp pain in my chest.

original: Such fierce alarums both of hope and fear,   As I am sick with working of my thoughts.
translation: I feel passionate alarms of both hope and fear and it makes me sick trying to figure out my thoughts.

original: Take, therefore, shipping; post, my lord, to France;
translation: Therefore, take a ship to France, my lord, and hurry.

original: Agree to any covenants,
translation: Agree to any terms

original: and procure   That Lady Margaret do vouchsafe to come   To cross the seas to England
translation: and ensure that Lady Margaret will come across the seas to England

original: and be crown'd   King Henry's faithful and anointed queen:
translation: and here be crowned King Henry's faithful and blessed queen.

original: For your expenses and sufficient charge,   Among the people gather up a tenth.
translation: For your expenses and spending money for the journey,  collect taxes  from the people.

original: Be gone, I say; for, till you do return,   I rest perplexed with a thousand cares.
translation: Go, and until you return I will rest here puzzled by a thousand thoughts.

original: And you, good uncle, banish all offence:
translation: And you, good uncle, let go of all your hatred.

original: If you do censure me by what you were,   Not what you are,
translation: If you would judge me by your own former recklessness in your youth and not your older age,

original: I know it will excuse   This sudden execution of my will.
translation: I know you will forgive me for my sudden change.

original: And so, conduct me where, from company,   I may revolve and ruminate my grief.
translation: And so, take me where I may consider and mediate on my melancholy of love alone.

original: Ay, grief, I fear me, both at first and last.
translation: Yes, I am afraid it is the first and the last melancholy.

original: Thus Suffolk hath prevail'd;
translation: And so Suffolk has won

original: and thus he goes,
translation: and there he goes,

original: As did the youthful Paris once to Greece,   With hope to find the like event in love,
translation: like the young  Paris  once did to Greece, hoping to find the  same outcome  in love,

original: But prosper better than the Trojan did.
translation: but Suffolk will succeed better than the Trojan did.

original: Margaret shall now be queen, and rule the king;   But I will rule both her, the king and realm.
translation: Margaret will now be queen and rule the king but I will rule her, the king and the country.

original: As by your high imperial majesty   I had in charge at my depart for France,   As procurator to your excellence,   To marry Princess Margaret for your grace,
translation: I was commanded by your majesty to travel to France as your representative and arrange a marriage with Princess Margaret on your behalf.

original: So, in the famous ancient city, Tours,   In presence of the Kings of France and Sicil,   The Dukes of Orleans, Calaber, Bretagne and Alencon,   Seven earls, twelve barons and twenty reverend bishops,   I have perform'd my task and was espoused:
translation: And so in that famous ancient city  Tours —in the presence of the Kings of France and Sicily and the Dukes of Orleans, Calaber, Bretagne and Alencon, seven earls, twelve barons and twenty bishops—I carried out my task and married her  by proxy .

original: And humbly now upon my bended knee,   In sight of England and her lordly peers,   Deliver up my title in the queen   To your most gracious hands, that are the substance   Of that great shadow I did represent;
translation: And now, humbly on my knees in front of England and her lords, I turn the queen over to your gracious hands, since you are the substance of the shadow that I represented when I was abroad.

original: The happiest gift that ever marquess gave,   The fairest queen that ever king received.
translation: She is the best gift that a  marquess  has ever given anyone, and the most beautiful queen that any king has ever married.

original: Suffolk, arise. Welcome, Queen Margaret:   I can express no kinder sign of love   Than this kind kiss.
translation: Stand up, Suffolk. Welcome, Queen Margaret!  [Kisses her]  This kind kiss is the most affectionate sign of love that I can give you.

original: O Lord, that lends me life,   Lend me a heart replete with thankfulness!
translation: Oh, Lord, that gives me life, let me also have a heart full of gratitude!

original: For thou hast given me in this beauteous face   A world of earthly blessings to my soul,   If sympathy of love unite our thoughts.
translation: Because you have given my soul a whole world of earthly blessings in this beautiful face, if she and I can learn to love each other.

original: Great King of England and my gracious lord,   The mutual conference that my mind hath had,
translation: Great king of England and my good husband, I've already been in intimate conversation with you in my mind—

original: By day, by night, waking and in my dreams,   In courtly company or at my beads,
translation: I thought of you during the day and during the night, when I was awake and in my dreams, when I was with people at court or when I was praying alone.

original: With you, mine alder-liefest sovereign,   Makes me the bolder to salute my king   With ruder terms, such as my wit affords   And over-joy of heart doth minister.
translation: So after all this imagined conversation, my dear lord, I feel bold enough to greet my king in a friendly way, as my heart and mind directs me.

original: Her sight did ravish; but her grace in speech,
translation: The sight of her enchants me, but her speech is even more graceful.

original: Her words y-clad with wisdom's majesty,   Makes me from wondering fall to weeping joys;
translation: Her words, clothed with the power of wisdom, make me go from admiration to tears of joy.

original: Such is the fulness of my heart's content.   Lords, with one cheerful voice welcome my love.
translation: That's how happy I am. Lords, welcome my love with one cheerful voice.

original: Long live Queen Margaret, England's happiness!
translation: Long live Queen Margaret, England's happiness!

original: We thank you all.
translation: Thank you, everyone.

original: My lord protector, so it please your grace,   Here are the articles of contracted peace   Between our sovereign and the French king Charles,
translation: [To GLOUCESTER]  My lord  protector , if it's all right with you, here are the conditions of the peace negotiation between our king and the French king Charles.

original: For eighteen months concluded by consent.
translation: The peace will last for eighteenth months.

original: [Reads]   'Imprimis, it is agreed between the French   king Charles, and William de la Pole, Marquess of   Suffolk, ambassador for Henry King of England, that   the said Henry shall espouse the Lady Margaret,   daughter unto Reignier King of Naples, Sicilia and   Jerusalem,
translation: [Reads]  "Firstly, it is agreed between the French king Charles and William de la Pole, Marquess of Suffolk, ambassador for Henry King of England, that the said Henry shall marry the Lady Margaret, daughter of King Reignier of Naples, Sicilia and Jerusalem,

original: and crown her Queen of England ere the   thirtieth of May next ensuing. Item, that the duchy   of Anjou and the county of Maine shall be released   and delivered to the king her father'—
translation: and crown her Queen of England before the next thirtieth of May. Likewise, that the dukedom of Anjou and the county of Maine will be released from English control and given to her father the king - "

original: Uncle, how now!
translation: Uncle, what are you doing?

original: Pardon me, gracious lord; Some sudden qualm hath struck me at the heart And dimm'd mine eyes, that I can read no further.
