translation: Excuse me, my good lord. Something has suddenly made me feel sick and blurred my vision, so that I can't read any more.

original: Uncle of Winchester, I pray, read on.
translation: Please, uncle of Winchester, keep reading.

original: [Reads]   'Item, It is further agreed between them,   that the duchies of Anjou and Maine shall be   released and delivered over to the king her father,
translation: [Reads]  "Likewise, it is also agreed between them, that the dukedoms of Anjou and Maine shall be released from English control and given to her father the king,

original: and she sent over of the King of England's own   proper cost and charges, without having any dowry.'
translation: and she will be sent over at the King of England's personal cost, with no  dowry .

original: They please us well. Lord marquess, kneel down:   We here create thee the first duke of Suffolk,   And gird thee with the sword.
translation: That's fine with us. Lord marquees, kneel down. We'll make you the first duke of Suffolk, giving you a new title with our  sword .

original: Cousin of York,   We here discharge your grace from being regent   I' the parts of France, till term of eighteen months   Be full expired.
translation: Cousin  of York, we dismiss you from your post as  regent  in those territories in France, until the period of eighteenth months is over.

original: Thanks, uncle Winchester,   Gloucester, York, Buckingham, Somerset,   Salisbury, and Warwick;   We thank you all for the great favour done,   In entertainment to my princely queen.
translation: Thanks, uncle Winchester, Gloucester, York, Buckingham, Somerset, Salisbury, and Warwick. We thank you for all that you have done to welcome my royal queen.

original: Brave peers of England, pillars of the state,   To you Duke Humphrey must unload his grief,   Your grief, the common grief of all the land.
translation: Noblemen of England, since you're the leading men in this country, Duke Humphrey has to unload his grief on you—which is your grief too, and the grief of everyone in England.

original: What! Did my brother Henry spend his youth,   His valour, coin and people, in the wars?
translation: What? Didn't my brother  Henry  spend his young days, his bravery, his money, and English lives in the wars?

original: Did he so often lodge in open field,   In winter's cold and summer's parching heat,   To conquer France, his true inheritance?
translation: To conquer France, which was his birthright, didn't he so often sleep in an open field through cold winters and hot summers?

original: And did my brother Bedford toil his wits,   To keep by policy what Henry got?
translation: And didn't my brother Bedford work so hard to maintain by good politics the lands that Henry had conquered?

original: Have you yourselves, Somerset, Buckingham,   Brave York, Salisbury, and victorious Warwick,   Received deep scars in France and Normandy?
translation: Haven't you, Somerset, Buckingham, brave York, Salisbury and victorious Warwick, received deep scars fighting in France and Normandy?

original: Or hath mine uncle Beaufort and myself,   With all the learned council of the realm,   Studied so long, sat in the council-house   Early and late, debating to and fro   How France and Frenchmen might be kept in awe,
translation: Haven't my uncle Beaufort and I studied hard, with all the country's  council , sitting in the council house early and staying until late, debating back and forth how to defeat the French and keep our territories?

original: And had his highness in his infancy   Crowned in Paris in despite of foes?   And shall these labours and these honours die?
translation: And wasn't his highness crowned in Paris as a baby, against the will of his enemies? And shall all this work and all our victories be for nothing?

original: Shall Henry's conquest, Bedford's vigilance,   Your deeds of war and all our counsel die?
translation: Shall Henry's conquest, Bedford's skill in politics, your bravery in war, and all our advice be for nothing?

original: O peers of England, shameful is this league!   Fatal this marriage, cancelling your fame,   Blotting your names from books of memory,   Razing the characters of your renown,   Defacing monuments of conquer'd France,   Undoing all, as all had never been!
translation: Oh, men of England, this is a shameful union! This marriage is disastrous! It destroys your reputations, smudging your names from the history books, erasing the written records of our famous actions, disfiguring the memorials of conquered France, undoing everything as if it had never happened!

original: Nephew, what means this passionate discourse, This peroration with such circumstance? For France, 'tis ours; and we will keep it still.
translation: What does this passionate argument mean, nephew? Why all this elaborate speech? France is ours and we'll keep it.

original: Ay, uncle, we will keep it, if we can;   But now it is impossible we should:
translation: Yes, uncle, we will keep it, if we can. But now it seems impossible.

original: Suffolk, the new-made duke that rules the roast,   Hath given the duchy of Anjou and Maine   Unto the poor King Reignier, whose large style   Agrees not with the leanness of his purse.
translation: Suffolk, the new-made duke, has the power now. And he's given the dukedom of Anjou and Maine to the poor King Reignier, who doesn't have any money to back up his great title.

original: Now, by the death of Him that died for all, These counties were the keys of Normandy. But wherefore weeps Warwick, my valiant son?
translation: By Christ's death, who died for us all, these countries were our foothold in Normandy. But why do you cry, my brave son Warwick?

original: For grief that they are past recovery:   For, were there hope to conquer them again,   My sword should shed hot blood, mine eyes no tears.
translation: Because they are not going to be saved. And if there was a hope that we could conquer them again, my sword would shed hot blood and my eyes wouldn't cry.

original: Anjou and Maine! Myself did win them both;   Those provinces these arms of mine did conquer:   And are the cities, that I got with wounds,   Delivered up again with peaceful words?   Mort Dieu!
translation: Anjou and Maine! I conquered both of them! My own arms conquered those provinces. So how can those cities that I won in battle be given back with peaceful words? God's death!

original: For Suffolk's duke, may he be suffocate,   That dims the honour of this warlike isle!
translation: As for the Duke of Suffolk, who dishonors this brave island, may he be suffocated!

original: France should have torn and rent my very heart,   Before I would have yielded to this league.
translation: France would have had to tear and rip up my heart before I'd surrender to this union.

original: I never read but England's kings have had   Large sums of gold and dowries with their wives:   And our King Henry gives away his own,   To match with her that brings no vantages.
translation: I have only ever read about English kings that have gained large amounts of gold and property by marrying. And our King Henry gives away his own money to marry a woman who has nothing to her name.

original: A proper jest, and never heard before, That Suffolk should demand a whole fifteenth For costs and charges in transporting her! She should have stayed in France and starved in France, Before—
translation: It's a real joke I've never heard before, that Suffolk demands large reimbursements for the cost of transporting her here! She should have stayed in France and starved in France, before —

original: My Lord of Gloucester, now ye grow too hot: It was the pleasure of my lord the King.
translation: My Lord of Gloucester, you're too angry now. You have to remember that it was what the King wanted.

original: My Lord of Winchester, I know your mind;   'Tis not my speeches that you do mislike,   But 'tis my presence that doth trouble ye.
translation: I know what you think, my Lord of Winchester. It's not my speeches that you don't like but my presence that bothers you.

original: Rancour will out: proud prelate, in thy face   I see thy fury:
translation: Your anger will explode, proud priest. I see your rage in your face.

original: if I longer stay,   We shall begin our ancient bickerings.   Lordings, farewell; and say, when I am gone,   I prophesied France will be lost ere long.
translation: If I stay longer we'll bring up old grudges. Therefore, goodbye, my lords. And when I'm gone, say that I predicted France will be lost before long.

original: So, there goes our protector in a rage.   'Tis known to you he is mine enemy,   Nay, more, an enemy unto you all,   And no great friend, I fear me, to the king.
translation: So, there goes our protector in anger. It's known to you that he is my enemy. No, more than that. He's an enemy to all of you and no friend to the king, I'm afraid.

original: Consider, lords, he is the next of blood,   And heir apparent to the English crown:   Had Henry got an empire by his marriage,   And all the wealthy kingdoms of the west,   There's reason he should be displeased at it.
translation: Consider, lords, that he is the  next in line  and heir to the English throne. And if Henry got an empire by his marriage and all  the rich countries in the west , there is no reason we would have been unhappy about this.

original: Look to it, lords! Let not his smoothing words   Bewitch your hearts; be wise and circumspect.
translation: But be careful, lords! Don't let his flattering words enchant your hearts. Be smart and cautious.

original: What though the common people favour him,   Calling him 'Humphrey, the good Duke of   Gloucester,'   Clapping their hands, and crying with loud voice,   'Jesu maintain your royal excellence!'   With 'God preserve the good Duke Humphrey!'
translation: What does it matter that the common people like him, calling him "Humphrey, the good Duke of Gloucester", applauding him and shouting loudly: "Let Jesus keep your royal excellence!" and "God save the good Duke Humphrey!"

original: I fear me, lords, for all this flattering gloss,   He will be found a dangerous protector.
translation: I am afraid, lords, that for all his smooth words, he will turn out to be a dangerous protector.

original: Why should he, then, protect our sovereign,   He being of age to govern of himself?
translation: Why should he rule for the king, then, since the king is already old enough to rule for himself?

original: Cousin of Somerset, join you with me,   And all together, with the Duke of Suffolk,   We'll quickly hoise Duke Humphrey from his seat.
translation: Cousin of Somerset, if you support me in this and we all work together with the Duke of Suffolk, we can quickly take Duke Humphrey down from his throne.

original: This weighty business will not brook delay: I'll to the Duke of Suffolk presently.
translation: We shouldn't wait any longer when the problem is so serious. I'll go to the Duke of Suffolk immediately.

original: Cousin of Buckingham, though Humphrey's pride   And greatness of his place be grief to us,   Yet let us watch the haughty cardinal:
translation: Cousin of Buckingham, though Humphrey's pride and his great position disturbs us, we should be suspicious of the proud cardinal too.

original: His insolence is more intolerable   Than all the princes in the land beside:   If Gloucester be displaced, he'll be protector.
translation: He is more arrogant than all the nobles in this country. If Gloucester is pushed aside, the cardinal will be protector.

original: Or thou or I, Somerset, will be protector, Despite Duke Humphrey or the cardinal.
translation: Or you or I, Somerset, will be the protector, in spite of Duke Humphrey and the cardinal.

original: Pride went before, ambition follows him.   While these do labour for their own preferment,   Behoves it us to labour for the realm.
translation: The proud cardinal left before and the ambitious Buckingham and Somerset follow him. While they work for their own advancement, some of us work hard for the country.

original: I never saw but Humphrey Duke of Gloucester   Did bear him like a noble gentleman.   Oft have I seen the haughty cardinal,   More like a soldier than a man o' the church,   As stout and proud as he were lord of all,
translation: I have always seen Humphrey Duke of Gloucester behave like a noble gentleman. But I have often seen the proud cardinal looking more like a soldier than a man of the church, as arrogant and proud as if he were lord of everything.

original: Swear like a ruffian and demean himself   Unlike the ruler of a commonweal.
translation: He swears like a hooligan and does not behave like the ruler of the commonwealth.

original: Warwick, my son, the comfort of my age,   Thy deeds, thy plainness and thy housekeeping,   Hath won the greatest favour of the commons,   Excepting none but good Duke Humphrey:
translation: [To WARWICK]  Warwick, my son—who comforts me in my old age—your good behavior and open and generous nature have made you the most popular with the people, except for good Duke Humphrey.

original: And, brother York, thy acts in Ireland,   In bringing them to civil discipline,   Thy late exploits done in the heart of France,   When thou wert regent for our sovereign,   Have made thee fear'd and honour'd of the people:
translation: [To YORK]  And my brother-in-law York, your bravery in Ireland when you defeated the rebellion there, and your recent remarkable actions in the heart of France, when you were the regent for your king, have made you feared and honored by the people.

original: Join we together, for the public good,   In what we can, to bridle and suppress   The pride of Suffolk and the cardinal,   With Somerset's and Buckingham's ambition;   And, as we may, cherish Duke Humphrey's deeds,   While they do tend the profit of the land.
translation: Let's join together for the general good, and do what we can to control and rein in the pride of Suffolk and the cardinal, as well as Somerset's and Buckingham's ambition. And we'll support Duke Humphrey's actions as much as we can, while they promote the good of the country.

original: So God help Warwick, as he loves the land, And common profit of his country!
translation: So God help Warwick, since he loves the land and common good of his country!

original: And so says York, for he hath greatest cause.
translation: And York agrees, since he has the biggest reason.

original: Then let's make haste away, and look unto the main.
translation: Then let's get started and see to the most important business at hand.

original: Unto the main! O father, Maine is lost;   That Maine which by main force Warwick did win,   And would have kept so long as breath did last!
translation: Let's see to the most important business! Oh, father, Maine is lost. I won it in battle and would have kept it for as long as I breathe!

original: Main chance, father, you meant; but I meant Maine,   Which I will win from France, or else be slain.
translation: You meant the  most important business  but I meant Maine, which I will win back from France, or otherwise die trying.

original: Anjou and Maine are given to the French;   Paris is lost; the state of Normandy   Stands on a tickle point, now they are gone:   Suffolk concluded on the articles,   The peers agreed, and Henry was well pleased   To change two dukedoms for a duke's fair daughter.
translation: Anjou and Maine are given to the French; Paris is lost; we're barely hanging on to Normandy. Now that they're all gone, Suffolk decided the terms and conditions, everyone agreed, and Henry was happy enough to exchange two dukedoms for a beautiful daughter of the duke.

original: I cannot blame them all: what is't to them?   'Tis thine they give away, and not their own.   Pirates may make cheap pennyworths of their pillage   And purchase friends and give to courtezans,   Still revelling like lords till all be gone;
translation: I can't blame them all, for what's it to them? It's  your  inheritance that they give away and not their own. Pirates may exchange what they stole for virtually nothing and so buy friends and give to prostitutes, enjoying their ill-gotten gains like lords until it's all gone.

original: While as the silly owner of the goods   Weeps over them and wrings his hapless hands   And shakes his head and trembling stands aloof,   While all is shared and all is borne away,
translation: Meanwhile the helpless owner of the stolen stuff cries over it, and wrings his poor hands, and shakes his head, but stands aside and does nothing while the pirates take his property.

original: Ready to starve and dare not touch his own:   So York must sit and fret and bite his tongue,   While his own lands are bargain'd for and sold.   Methinks the realms of England, France and Ireland   Bear that proportion to my flesh and blood   As did the fatal brand Althaea burn'd   Unto the prince's heart of Calydon.
translation: He is about to starve and doesn't dare to touch what's his own. In the same way, York has to sit and fret and stay silent, while his own lands are exchanged and sold. I think that the countries of England, France and Ireland are as part of my flesh and blood as was the deadly branding iron  Althea  burned on the prince of Calydon's heart.

original: Anjou and Maine both given unto the French!   Cold news for me, for I had hope of France,   Even as I have of fertile England's soil.   A day will come when York shall claim his own;   And therefore I will take the Nevils' parts   And make a show of love to proud Duke Humphrey,
translation: Anjou and Maine are both surrendered to the French! This is sad news for me, because I had as much hope to rule France as I do to rule fertile England. A day will come when York will claim what belongs to him; and so I'll support Salisbury and Warwick and pretend to be loyal to the proud Duke Humphrey.

original: And, when I spy advantage, claim the crown,   For that's the golden mark I seek to hit:   Nor shall proud Lancaster usurp my right,   Nor hold the sceptre in his childish fist,   Nor wear the diadem upon his head,   Whose church-like humours fits not for a crown.
translation: But when I find a way, I'll claim the crown, since that's the golden target I'm aiming for. The proud  Lancaster  won't take my throne, or hold the scepter in his childish hand, or wear the crown on his head. He's too simple and religious to make a good king.

original: Then, York, be still awhile, till time do serve:   Watch thou and wake when others be asleep,   To pry into the secrets of the state;   Till Henry, surfeiting in joys of love,   With his new bride and England's dear-bought queen,   And Humphrey with the peers be fall'n at jars:
translation: Then, York, be patient for a while, until the right opportunity arises. Be on your guard and awake when others are asleep, to find out the secrets of the government—until Henry enjoys the love of his new bride and England's expensively-purchased queen too much, and until Humphrey falls out with his friends.

original: Then will I raise aloft the milk-white rose,   With whose sweet smell the air shall be perfumed;   And in my standard bear the arms of York   To grapple with the house of Lancaster;   And, force perforce, I'll make him yield the crown,   Whose bookish rule hath pull'd fair England down.
translation: Then I will raise high the  milk-white rose , whose sweet smell will perfume the air. With the banner of the house of York, I'll challenge the house of Lancaster and make the king give up his crown, with force if necessary—since his silly bookishness and bad government has dragged our beautiful England down.

original: Why droops my lord, like over-ripen'd corn,   Hanging the head at Ceres' plenteous load?   Why doth the great Duke Humphrey knit his brows,   As frowning at the favours of the world?
translation: Why does my lord droop like an over-ripened corn, hanging its head at  Ceres ' rich harvest? Why does the great Duke Humphrey frown as though he were frowning at all his good fortune?

original: Why are thine eyes fixed to the sullen earth,   Gazing on that which seems to dim thy sight?   What seest thou there? King Henry's diadem,   Enchased with all the honours of the world?
translation: Why are your eyes focused on the dull- colored ground, staring at something that seems to darken your sight? What do you see there? King Henry's crown, decorated with all the titles of the world?

original: If so, gaze on, and grovel on thy face,   Until thy head be circled with the same.   Put forth thy hand, reach at the glorious gold.   What, is't too short? I'll lengthen it with mine:
translation: If that's so, keep looking and lie face down, until your head wears the same crown. Put your hand out and reach for that glorious golden crown. What? Is your arm too short? I'll make it longer by adding mine.

original: And, having both together heaved it up,   We'll both together lift our heads to heaven,   And never more abase our sight so low   As to vouchsafe one glance unto the ground.
translation: And once we've lifted it up together, we'll lift our heads to heaven, and will never degrade ourselves again by taking a single look at the ground.

original: O Nell, sweet Nell, if thou dost love thy lord,   Banish the canker of ambitious thoughts.
translation: Oh, Nell, sweet Nell, if you love your husband, stop the infection of ambitious thoughts.

original: And may that thought, when I imagine ill   Against my king and nephew, virtuous Henry,   Be my last breathing in this mortal world!   My troublous dream this night doth make me sad.
translation: And if I ever think to plot against my king and nephew, virtuous Henry, let it be the last time I take a breath in this mortal world! Last night's troubling dream has made me sad.

original: What dream'd my lord? Tell me, and I'll requite it With sweet rehearsal of my morning's dream.
translation: What did you dream about? Tell me and I'll repay it by telling you sweetly about my morning dream.

original: Methought this staff, mine office-badge in court,   Was broke in twain; by whom I have forgot,   But, as I think, it was by the cardinal;
translation: I dreamed that this staff, my badge of office in court, was broken in two. I have forgotten who did it, but I think it was the cardinal.

original: And on the pieces of the broken wand   Were placed the heads of Edmund Duke of Somerset,   And William de la Pole, first duke of Suffolk.   This was my dream: what it doth bode, God knows.
translation: And the heads of Edmund, Duke of Somerset, and William de la Pole, first duke of Suffolk, were placed on the pieces of the broken stick. That was my dream. God knows what it means.

original: Tut, this was nothing but an argument   That he that breaks a stick of Gloucester's grove   Shall lose his head for his presumption.   But list to me, my Humphrey, my sweet duke:
translation: Oh, please, that was nothing if not evidence that anyone who challenges Gloucester in the slightest will lose his head for trying. But listen to me, my Humphrey, my sweet duke.

original: Methought I sat in seat of majesty   In the cathedral church of Westminster,   And in that chair where kings and queens are crown'd;   Where Henry and dame Margaret kneel'd to me   And on my head did set the diadem.
translation: I imagined that I sat on the royal throne in the cathedral in Westminster, and on that throne where kings and queens were crowned, Henry and Margaret knelt to me and put the crown on my head.

original: Nay, Eleanor, then must I chide outright:   Presumptuous dame, ill-nurtured Eleanor,   Art thou not second woman in the realm,   And the protector's wife, beloved of him?
translation: No, Eleanor, then I must reprimand you for this. Bold woman, ill-mannered Eleanor! Aren't you the second highest-ranked woman in the country, the protector's wife, and loved by him?

original: Hast thou not worldly pleasure at command,   Above the reach or compass of thy thought?   And wilt thou still be hammering treachery,   To tumble down thy husband and thyself   From top of honour to disgrace's feet?   Away from me, and let me hear no more!
translation: Don't you have everything in this world you could desire, beyond what you can even imagine? And will you then still be talking about treason, which would make both you and your husband fall down from the top of honor to the feet of disgrace? Get away from me and don't let me hear about that!

original: What, what, my lord! Are you so choleric   With Eleanor, for telling but her dream?
translation: But, but, my lord! Are you so angry with Eleanor only because she told you about her dream?

original: Next time I'll keep my dreams unto myself,   And not be cheque'd.
translation: I'll keep my dreams to myself next time and won't be told off for them.

original: Nay, be not angry; I am pleased again.
translation: No, don't be angry. I am all right again.

original: My lord protector, 'tis his highness' pleasure You do prepare to ride unto Saint Alban's, Where as the king and queen do mean to hawk.
I go. Come, Nell, thou wilt ride with us?
translation: I'll go. Come, Nell. You will come with us, yes?

original: Yes, my good lord, I'll follow presently.
translation: Yes, my good husband. I'll come in a moment.

original: Follow I must; I cannot go before,   While Gloucester bears this base and humble mind.   Were I a man, a duke, and next of blood,   I would remove these tedious stumbling-blocks   And smooth my way upon their headless necks;
translation: I have to follow because I can't go in front of you, while Gloucester is of this unambitious and humble mind. If I were a man, a duke, and next in line to the throne, I would remove these annoying stumbling blocks and clear my way to the crown on their headless necks.

original: And, being a woman, I will not be slack   To play my part in Fortune's pageant.   Where are you there? Sir John! Nay, fear not, man,   We are alone; here's none but thee and I.
translation: And being a woman, I won't mind playing the part that fate has prepared for us. Where are you? Sir John! No, don't be afraid, man. We are alone. There's no one here but you and me.

original: Jesus preserve your royal majesty!
translation: Jesus preserve your royal majesty!

original: What say'st thou? Majesty! I am but grace.
translation: What did you say? "Majesty?" I am only a duchess.

original: But, by the grace of God, and Hume's advice, Your grace's title shall be multiplied.
translation: But thanks to the help of God and advice from Hume, you'll have a better title.

original: What say'st thou, man? Hast thou as yet conferr'd   With Margery Jourdain, the cunning witch,   With Roger Bolingbroke, the conjurer?
translation: What are you saying, man? Have you spoken with Margery Jourdain, the skillful witch, and with Roger Bolingbroke, the magician?

original: And will they undertake to do me good?
translation: And will they help me out?

original: This they have promised, to show your highness   A spirit raised from depth of under-ground,
translation: That's what they have promised—to show your highness a spirit summoned from deep underground.

original: That shall make answer to such questions   As by your grace shall be propounded him.
translation: He will answer any questions that your grace would like to ask him.

original: It is enough; I'll think upon the questions:   When from St. Alban's we do make return,   We'll see these things effected to the full.
translation: That's all. I'll think about these questions. When I come back from St Alban's, we'll make sure this will happen.

original: Here, Hume, take this reward; make merry, man,   With thy confederates in this weighty cause.
translation: [Gives him gold]  Here, Hume, take your reward. Celebrate with your partners in this important business.

original: Hume must make merry with the duchess' gold;   Marry, and shall. But how now, Sir John Hume!   Seal up your lips, and give no words but mum:   The business asketh silent secrecy.
translation: Hume must enjoy the duchess' money! And so he will. But what's this, Sir John Hume! Close your lips and give no words, only silence. The business requires silence and secrecy.

original: Dame Eleanor gives gold to bring the witch:   Gold cannot come amiss, were she a devil.   Yet have I gold flies from another coast;   I dare not say, from the rich cardinal   And from the great and new-made Duke of Suffolk,   Yet I do find it so;
translation: Dame Eleanor gives gold so I'll bring her a witch. Gold is always useful, even if she were a devil. Yet I have gold that comes from another source. I dare not say that it's from the rich cardinal and from the great and newly-appointed Duke of Suffolk. But yes, that's right.

original: for to be plain,   They, knowing Dame Eleanor's aspiring humour,   Have hired me to undermine the duchess   And buz these conjurations in her brain.
translation: To say it simply, they—knowing the ambitious frame of Dame Eleanor's mind—have hired me to undermine the duchess and whisper these spells to her.

original: They say 'A crafty knave does need no broker;'   Yet am I Suffolk and the cardinal's broker.   Hume, if you take not heed, you shall go near   To call them both a pair of crafty knaves.
translation: They say "a cunning villain doesn't need a go-between." Yet I am a go-between for Suffolk and the cardinal. Hume, if you aren't careful, you'll come close to calling them both a pair of cunning villains.

original: Well, so it stands; and thus, I fear, at last   Hume's knavery will be the duchess' wreck,   And her attainture will be Humphrey's fall:   Sort how it will, I shall have gold for all.
translation: Well, that's how it is, and I'm afraid that at last Hume's villainy will ruin the duchess, and when she's convicted of treason, it will be the end of Humphrey. However it ends, I'll get my reward.

original: My masters, let's stand close: my lord protector will come this way by and by, and then we may deliver our supplications in the quill.
translation: Gentlemen, let's stand near one another. My lord protector will come this way soon, and then we can tell him our requests as a group.

original: Marry, the Lord protect him, for he's a good man! Jesu bless him!
translation: Yes, may the Lord protect him, since he is a good man! Jesus bless him!

original: Here a' comes, methinks, and the queen with him. I'll be the first, sure.
translation: I think he's coming now, with the queen. I have to be the first to talk to him.

original: Come back, fool; this is the Duke of Suffolk, and not my lord protector.
translation: Step back, you idiot! This is the Duke of Suffolk and not my lord protector.

original: How now, fellow! Would'st anything with me?
translation: What's this, man? What do you want from me?

original: I pray, my lord, pardon me; I took ye for my lord protector.
translation: Please, my lord, I am sorry, I thought you were the lord protector.

original: 'To my Lord Protector!' Are your supplications to his lordship? Let me see them: what is thine?
translation: "To my Lord Protector!" Do you have requests to his lordship? Let me see them. What's yours?

original: Mine is, an't please your grace, against John Goodman, my lord cardinal's man, for keeping my house, and lands, and wife and all, from me.
translation: Mine is, if it's all right with your grace, against John Goodman, the lord cardinal's servant. He has taken my house, lands, wife and everything from me.

original: Thy wife, too! That's some wrong, indeed. What's yours? What's here!
translation: Your wife as well! Something is wrong about that, for sure. What's yours? What do we have here?

original: 'Against the Duke of Suffolk, for enclosing  the commons of Melford.' How now, sir knave!
translation: "Against the Duke of Suffolk, for fencing in the communal land of Melford." What's this, you villain!

original: Alas, sir, I am but a poor petitioner of our whole  township.
translation: But, sir, I am only one poor petitioner from our whole town.

original: Against my master, Thomas Horner, for saying that the Duke of York was rightful heir to the crown.
translation: This is against my master, Thomas Horner, for saying that the Duke of York was the true heir to the crown.

original: What sayst thou? Did the Duke of York say he was rightful heir to the crown?
translation: What did you say? Did the Duke of York say that he was the true heir to the crown?

original: That my master was? No, forsooth: my master said that he was, and that the king was an usurper.
translation: That my master was the true heir? No, my master said that he was and that the king is ruling wrongfully.

original: Who is there?
translation: Who is there?

original: Take this fellow in, and send for his master with a pursuivant presently: we'll hear more of your matter before the King.
translation: Take this man inside and get his master to come immediately with a messenger. We'll hear more about your issue in front of the king.

original: And as for you, that love to be protected Under the wings of our protector's grace, Begin your suits anew, and sue to him.
translation: And as for you, since you love to be protected under our protector's wings, you can start your requests all over again and ask him.

original: Away, base cullions! Suffolk, let them go.
translation: Get out, you lowly peasants! Suffolk, send them away.

original: Come, let's be gone.
translation: Come, let's go.

original: My Lord of Suffolk, say, is this the guise,   Is this the fashion in the court of England?   Is this the government of Britain's isle,   And this the royalty of Albion's king?
translation: My Lord Suffolk, tell me, is this what happens, is this the custom in the court of England? Is this the government of the British island, and is this the royalty of  Albion 's king?

original: What shall King Henry be a pupil still   Under the surly Gloucester's governance?   Am I a queen in title and in style,   And must be made a subject to a duke?
translation: Should King Henry be a student under the teaching of the grumpy Gloucester? Am I a queen in title and mode of address, and do I have to obey a duke?

original: I tell thee, Pole, when in the city Tours   Thou ran'st a tilt in honour of my love   And stolest away the ladies' hearts of France,   I thought King Henry had resembled thee   In courage, courtship and proportion:
translation: I'm telling you,  Pole , when you took part in the tournament in the city of Tours and jousted for my love, stealing away the hearts of all the ladies of France, I thought that King Henry was like you—in courage, flirting, and looks.

original: But all his mind is bent to holiness,   To number Ave-Maries on his beads;   His champions are the prophets and apostles,   His weapons holy saws of sacred writ,   His study is his tilt-yard, and his loves   Are brazen images of canonized saints.
translation: But all he thinks about is religion and counting  Hail Marys  on his rosary. The heroes that he admires are the prophets and apostles, his weapons are holy books, his study is his tournament ground, and his loves are his bronze statues of glorified saints.

original: I would the college of the cardinals   Would choose him pope, and carry him to Rome,   And set the triple crown upon his head:   That were a state fit for his holiness.
translation: I wish that the highest council of the Catholic Church's cardinal would choose him to be a pope and take him to Rome, and set the pope's triple crown on his head. That would be an appropriate job for his holiness.

original: Madam, be patient: as I was cause Your highness came to England, so will I In England work your grace's full content.
translation: Madam, be patient. I was the reason why your highness came to England and so I will do everything here in England to please you.

original: Beside the haughty protector, have we Beaufort,   The imperious churchman, Somerset, Buckingham,   And grumbling York:
translation: In addition to the arrogant protector, we have Beaufort, the bossy churchman, Somerset, Buckingham and the sulky York.

original: and not the least of these   But can do more in England than the king.
translation: And even the least important of them can do more in England than the king.

original: And he of these that can do most of all Cannot do more in England than the Nevils: Salisbury and Warwick are no simple peers.
Not all these lords do vex me half so much   As that proud dame, the lord protector's wife.   She sweeps it through the court with troops of ladies,   More like an empress than Duke Humphrey's wife:
translation: All of these lords don't annoy me half as much as that proud woman, the lord protector's wife. She parades through the court with a group of ladies, more like an empress than Duke Humphrey's wife.

original: Strangers in court do take her for the queen:   She bears a duke's revenues on her back,   And in her heart she scorns our poverty:
translation: Foreigners in the court think she is the queen. She dresses in a magnificent style thanks to the duke's income and secretly she makes fun of me for being poor.

original: Shall I not live to be avenged on her?   Contemptuous base-born callet as she is,
translation: Shouldn't I be revenged on her? She is a contemptible lowly-born whore!

original: She vaunted 'mongst her minions t'other day,   The very train of her worst wearing gown   Was better worth than all my father's lands,   Till Suffolk gave two dukedoms for his daughter.
translation: She boasted to her friends the other day that the train of her most unfashionable dress was worth what my father's lands were, until Suffolk gave him two dukedoms for his daughter.

original: Madam, myself have limed a bush for her,   And placed a quire of such enticing birds,   That she will light to listen to the lays,   And never mount to trouble you again.
translation: Madam, I have already laid a trap and placed a group of little birds around her, so that she will fall from her nest to listen to their pretty songs, and never trouble you again.

original: So, let her rest: and, madam, list to me;   For I am bold to counsel you in this.   Although we fancy not the cardinal,   Yet must we join with him and with the lords,   Till we have brought Duke Humphrey in disgrace.
translation: So, let her go for now and listen to me, madam, because I am bold enough to advise you on this. Although we don't like the cardinal, we have to join him and his lords, until we have brought Duke Humphrey down.

original: As for the Duke of York, this late complaint   Will make but little for his benefit.   So, one by one, we'll weed them all at last,   And you yourself shall steer the happy helm.
translation: As for the Duke of York, this allegation about him being the true king we just heard will do him little good. So, one by one, we'll uproot them all, until at last you alone will rule the happy kingdom.

original: For my part, noble lords, I care not which; Or Somerset or York, all's one to me.
translation: When it comes to me, my lords, I don't really care which one—Somerset or York. They're all the same to me.

original: If York have ill demean'd himself in France, Then let him be denay'd the regentship.
translation: If York has behaved badly in France, then don't make him regent.

original: If Somerset be unworthy of the place, Let York be regent; I will yield to him.
translation: If Somerset isn't worthy of the position, then York should be regent. I'll surrender to him.

original: Whether your grace be worthy, yea or no, Dispute not that: York is the worthier.
translation: Don't discuss whether you are worthy or not. York is clearly more worthy.

original: Ambitious Warwick, let thy betters speak.
translation: Let others better than you speak, ambitious Warwick.

original: The cardinal's not my better in the field.
translation: The cardinal isn't better than me pn the battlefield.

original: All in this presence are thy betters, Warwick.
translation: Everyone around you is better than you, Warwick.

original: Warwick may live to be the best of all.
translation: Warwick could still end up to be the best of you all.

original: Peace, son! And show some reason, Buckingham, Why Somerset should be preferred in this.
translation: Calm down, son! And give us a reason, Buckingham, why Somerset should be regent instead.

original: Because the king, forsooth, will have it so.
translation: Because the king wants it that way.

original: Madam, the king is old enough himself To give his censure: these are no women's matters.
translation: Madam, the king is old enough to give us his opinion. These issues are not for women.

original: If he be old enough, what needs your grace To be protector of his excellence?
translation: If he's old enough, why does your grace need to be protector of his excellence?

original: Madam, I am protector of the realm; And, at his pleasure, will resign my place.
translation: Madam, I am the protector of this country and if he wants me to, I will resign my place.

original: Resign it then and leave thine insolence. Since thou wert king—as who is king but thou?— The commonwealth hath daily run to wreck; The Dauphin hath prevail'd beyond the seas; And all the peers and nobles of the realm Have been as bondmen to thy sovereignty.
The commons hast thou rack'd; the clergy's bags Are lank and lean with thy extortions.
translation: You have ruined the common people; the moneybags of the church are shrunken and poor because of your taxes.

original: Thy sumptuous buildings and thy wife's attire Have cost a mass of public treasury.
translation: Your luxurious buildings and your wife's dresses have cost a lot of public money.

original: Thy cruelty in execution Upon offenders, hath exceeded law, And left thee to the mercy of the law.
translation: Your cruelty when punishing offenders is beyond law and has left you to the mercy of the law.

original: Thy sale of offices and towns in France, If they were known, as the suspect is great, Would make thee quickly hop without thy head.
translation: If we knew about your selling of official positions and towns in France (since there is already suspicion about it), you'd be beheaded.

original: Give me my fan: what, minion! Can ye not?
translation: Give me my fan. What, servant? Can't you do that?

original: I cry you mercy, madam; was it you?
translation: I beg your pardon, madam. Was it you?

original: Was't I! Yea, I it was, proud Frenchwoman: Could I come near your beauty with my nails, I'd set my ten commandments in your face.
translation: Was it? Yes, it was, you proud Frenchwoman! If only I could come closer to your beautiful face with my nails, I'd scratch it with my fingernails!

original: Sweet aunt, be quiet; 'twas against her will.
translation: Sweet aunt, be quiet. She didn't mean to do it.

original: Against her will! Good king, look to't in time;   She'll hamper thee, and dandle thee like a baby:
translation: She didn't mean to do it! Good king, beware of her. She'll manipulate you and pet you like a baby.

original: Though in this place most master wear no breeches,   She shall not strike Dame Eleanor unrevenged.
translation: But although  the greatest master  in this place doesn't wear trousers, she won't slap Dame Eleanor without paying for it.

original: Lord cardinal, I will follow Eleanor,   And listen after Humphrey, how he proceeds:
translation: Lord cardinal, I'll follow Eleanor and watch out for Humphrey and what he's going to do next.

original: She's tickled now; her fume needs no spurs,   She'll gallop far enough to her destruction.
translation: She is provoked now; we don't need to make her any angrier. She'll run fast and far enough towards her own destruction.

original: Now, lords, my choler being over-blown   With walking once about the quadrangle,   I come to talk of commonwealth affairs.
translation: Now, lords, I calmed down as I walked around the quadrangle once, so I have come to talk about the government.

original: As for your spiteful false objections,   Prove them, and I lie open to the law:   But God in mercy so deal with my soul,   As I in duty love my king and country!
translation: As for your hateful, false accusations, show your proof and let the law judge my case. But God will have mercy on my soul, since God knows I love my king and country!

original: But, to the matter that we have in hand:   I say, my sovereign, York is meetest man   To be your regent in the realm of France.
translation: But, let's talk about the matter in hand. I say, my king, that York is the right man to be your regent in France.

original: Before we make election, give me leave To show some reason, of no little force, That York is most unmeet of any man.
translation: Before we make a choice, let me show you why York is the most unsuitable out of all men.

original: I'll tell thee, Suffolk, why I am unmeet:   First, for I cannot flatter thee in pride;
translation: I'll tell you why I am unsuitable, Suffolk. First of all, because my self-respect will not allow me to flatter you.

original: Next, if I be appointed for the place,   My Lord of Somerset will keep me here,   Without discharge, money, or furniture,   Till France be won into the Dauphin's hands:
translation: Next, because if I am appointed to the position, my lord of Somerset will keep me here without payment, money or military equipment, until France is won by the Dauphin.

original: Last time, I danced attendance on his will   Till Paris was besieged, famish'd, and lost.
translation: Last time I had to listen to his commands, Paris was attacked, our people starved, and the city was lost.

original: That can I witness; and a fouler fact Did never traitor in the land commit.
translation: I can bear witness to that. A traitor has never committed worse crimes.

original: Peace, headstrong Warwick!
translation: Calm yourself, stubborn Warwick!

original: Image of pride, why should I hold my peace?
translation: You're the embodiment of pride! Why should I be calm?

original: Because here is a man accused of treason: Pray God the Duke of York excuse himself!
translation: Because he is a man accused of treason. I pray God that the Duke of York excuses himself!

original: Doth any one accuse York for a traitor?
translation: Does anyone accuse York of being a traitor?

original: What mean'st thou, Suffolk; tell me, what are these?
translation: What do you mean, Suffolk? Tell me, who are these people?

original: Please it your majesty, this is the man   That doth accuse his master of high treason:
translation: Please, majesty, this  [points to PETER]  is the man that accuses his master of high treason.

original: His words were these: that Richard, Duke of York,   Was rightful heir unto the English crown   And that your majesty was a usurper.
translation: He said that Richard, Duke of York is the true heir to the English crown and that your majesty has no right to the throne.

original: Say, man, were these thy words?
translation: Is this what you said, man?

original: An't shall please your majesty, I never said nor thought any such matter: God is my witness, I am falsely accused by the villain.
translation: If it makes your majesty happy, I never said nor thought that! God is my witness that I am accused falsely by this villain.

original: By these ten bones, my lords, he did speak them to me in the garret one night, as we were scouring my Lord of York's armour.
translation: By these fingers, my lords, he said those words to me in the watch-tower one night as we were cleaning the armor of my Lord of York.

original: Base dunghill villain and mechanical,   I'll have thy head for this thy traitor's speech.
translation: Lowly foul villain, peasant! I'll have your head for your treachery.

original: I do beseech your royal majesty,   Let him have all the rigor of the law.
translation: I ask your royal majesty to punish him with all the harshness of the law.

original: Alas, my lord, hang me, if ever I spake the words.   My accuser is my 'prentice; and when I did correct   him for his fault the other day, he did vow upon his   knees he would be even with me:
translation: Ah, hang me if I have ever spoken those words, my lord. My apprentice is the one who accuses me and when I punished him for his mistake the other day, he swore on his knees that he would get even with me.

original: I have good   witness of this: therefore I beseech your majesty,   do not cast away an honest man for a villain's   accusation.
translation: I have witnesses to prove it. So I beg your majesty, don't cast away an honest man because of a villain's accusation.

original: Uncle, what shall we say to this in law?
translation: Uncle, how should we answer to this?

original: This doom, my lord, if I may judge:   Let Somerset be regent over the French,   Because in York this breeds suspicion:
translation: My advice, my lord, would be to let Somerset be the regent of France because this makes us suspicious of York.

original: And let these have a day appointed them   For single combat in convenient place,   For he hath witness of his servant's malice:   This is the law, and this Duke Humphrey's doom.
translation: Let the two of them set a date to duel in a suitable place, for he has seen how evil his servant is. This is the law and this is Duke Humphrey's sentence.

original: I humbly thank your royal majesty.
translation: I humbly thank you, your royal majesty.

original: And I accept the combat willingly.
translation: And I willingly accept the fight.

original: Alas, my lord, I cannot fight; for God's sake, pity   my case. The spite of man prevaileth against me.
translation: Ah, but my lord, I can't fight! For God's sake, take pity on my situation. The viciousness of mankind is against me.

original: O   Lord, have mercy upon me! I shall never be able to   fight a blow. O Lord, my heart!
translation: Oh, Lord, have mercy on me! I shall never be able to fight. Oh, Lord, my heart!

original: Sirrah, or you must fight, or else be hang'd.
translation: Sir, either you fight or you'll be hanged.

original: Away with them to prison; and the day of combat shall be the last of the next month. Come, Somerset, we'll see thee sent away.
translation: Take them away to prison; the day of the fight will be the last day of the next month. Come, Somerset, we'll make sure that they're sent away.

original: Come, my masters; the duchess, I tell you, expects performance of your promises.
translation: Come on, everyone! I tell you, the duchess is expecting quite a show based on what you promised her.

original: Master Hume, we are therefore provided: will her ladyship behold and hear our exorcisms?
translation: Master Hume, we are ready for that. Will her ladyship come to see and hear us summon the spirit?

original: Ay, what else? Fear you not her courage.
translation: Yes, what else would she do? Don't doubt her courage.

original: I have heard her reported to be a woman of an  invincible spirit: but it shall be convenient, Master  Hume, that you be by her aloft, while we be busy below;
translation: I have heard that she is a woman of an unbreakable spirit. But it might be good if you and her stand above us and watch, while we're busy below.

original: and so, I pray you, go, in God's name, and leave u
translation: And so please, in God's name, go and leave us.

original: Mother Jourdain, be you prostrate and grovel on the earth; John Southwell, read you; and let us to our work.
translation: Mother Jourdain, lay down on the floor and crawl on the ground. John Southwell, you read. Let's get to work.

original: Well said, my masters; and welcome all. To this gear the sooner the better.
translation: That's well said, my masters. And welcome to you all. The sooner this business is started, the better.

original: Patience, good lady; wizards know their times:
translation: Be patient, good lady. Wizards know when it's the best time.

original: Deep night, dark night, the silent of the night,   The time of night when Troy was set on fire;   The time when screech-owls cry and ban-dogs howl,   And spirits walk and ghosts break up their graves,   That time best fits the work we have in hand.
translation: Deep night, dark night, silent night, the time of night when  Troy  was set on fire, the time when  barn owls  cry and  watchdog s howl, when spirits walk and ghosts come out of their graves—that's the time that 's best for the work we are doing here.

original: Madam, sit you and fear not: whom we raise,   We will make fast within a hallow'd verge.
translation: Sit yourself down, madam, and don't be afraid. Whoever it is that we raise, we will confine them within the magic circle.

original: Adsum.
translation: I am here.

original: Asmath,   By the eternal God, whose name and power   Thou tremblest at, answer that I shall ask;
translation: Satan , answer what I ask by the eternal God, whose name and power makes you tremble.

original: For, till thou speak, thou shalt not pass from hence.
translation: Until you speak, you won't leave this place.

original: Ask what thou wilt. That I had said and done!
translation: Ask whatever you want. I wish that I had answered it and could be done with this!

original: 'First of the king: what shall  of him become?'
translation: "At first, about the king: what will happen to him?"

original: The duke yet lives that Henry shall depose; But him outlive, and die a violent death.
translation: Although the duke that Henry shall depose still lives, Henry will outlive him and he will die a violent death.

original: 'What fates await the Duke of Suffolk?'
translation: "What will happen to the Duke of Suffolk?"

original: By water shall he die, and take his end.
translation: He will die by water.

original: 'What shall befall the Duke of Somerset?'
translation: "What will happen to the Duke of Somerset?"

original: Let him shun castles;   Safer shall he be upon the sandy plains   Than where castles mounted stand.
translation: He should avoid castles. He'll be safer on the sandy lands than where castles stand on a hill.

original: Have done, for more I hardly can endure.
translation: That's all. I can't take any more.

original: Descend to darkness and the burning lake! False fiend, avoid!
translation: Go down to the darkness and the burning lake! Be gone, treacherous demon!

original: Lay hands upon these traitors and their trash.   Beldam, I think we watch'd you at an inch.
translation: Arrest these traitors and take away their rubbish. Witch, we've been watching you very closely.

original: What, madam, are you there? The king and commonweal   Are deeply indebted for this piece of pains:
translation: [To DUCHESS]  What, are you there, madam? The king and the commonwealth are very thankful to you for this trouble you have taken.

original: My lord protector will, I doubt it not,   See you well guerdon'd for these good deserts.
translation: I am sure that my lord protector will see you well rewarded for these good actions.

original: Not half so bad as thine to England's king, Injurious duke, that threatest where's no cause.
translation: My actions aren't half as bad as yours towards the king of England, you insulting duke that threatens me for no reason.

original: True, madam, none at all: what call you this?   Away with them!
translation: That's true, madam. No reason at all. What do you call all this? Take them away!

original: Let them be clapp'd up close.   And kept asunder. You, madam, shall with us.   Stafford, take her to thee.
translation: Lock them up under close guard, and make sure they're in solitary confinement. Madam, you shall come with us. Stafford, take her with you.

original: We'll see your trinkets here all forthcoming. All, away!
translation: We'll make sure that all your silly trinkets here are kept safe and ready to be shown as evidence in court. Go away, all of you!

original: Lord Buckingham, methinks, you watch'd her well:   A pretty plot, well chosen to build upon!
translation: Lord Buckingham, I think that you watched her closely enough. It's a cunning scheme, and a good foundation to build on!

original: Now, pray, my lord, let's see the devil's writ.   What have we here?
translation: Now please, my lord, let's see the what the devil has written. [Picks up paper]  What do we have here?

original: [Reads]   'The duke yet lives, that Henry shall depose;   But him outlive, and die a violent death.'   Why, this is just   'Aio te, AEacida, Romanos vincere posse.'
translation: [Reads]  "Although the duke that Henry shall depose still lives, Henry will outlive him and he will die a violent death." This is exactly like " I proclaim that you, the descendant of Aeacus, can conquer the Romans ".

original: Well, to the rest:   'Tell me what fate awaits the Duke of Suffolk?   By water shall he die, and take his end.   What shall betide the Duke of Somerset?   Let him shun castles;   Safer shall he be upon the sandy plains   Than where castles mounted stand.'
translation: Well, let's see the rest. "What will happen to the Duke of Suffolk? He shall die by water. What will happen to the Duke of Somerset? He should avoid castles. He'll be safer on the sandy lands than where castles stand on a hill."

original: Come, come, my lords;   These oracles are hardly attain'd,   And hardly understood.
translation: Come on, my lords, after all this trouble, these prophecies make no sense.

original: The king is now in progress towards Saint Alban's,   With him the husband of this lovely lady:
translation: The king is now on his way towards Saint Alban's and the husband of this lovely lady is with him.

original: Thither go these news, as fast as horse can   carry them:   A sorry breakfast for my lord protector.
translation: Let's bring them this news, as fast as horse can carry us. It will be a sad breakfast for my lord protector.

original: Your grace shall give me leave, my Lord of York, To be the post, in hope of his reward.
translation: Please, my Lord of York, let me be the messenger. I'm hoping I'll get a reward from him.

original: At your pleasure, my good lord. Who's within there, ho!
translation: As you wish, my good lord. Hey, who's there?

original: Invite my Lords of Salisbury and Warwick To sup with me to-morrow night. Away!
translation: Invite my Lords of Salisbury and Warwick to have dinner with me tomorrow night. Go!

original: Believe me, lords, for flying at the brook,   I saw not better sport these seven years' day:
translation: Believe me, lords, in seven years I haven't seen better entertainment than  hunting waterbirds by using dogs .

original: Yet, by your leave, the wind was very high;   And, ten to one, old Joan had not gone out.
translation: But the wind was very high, and I bet you  ten to one  that the old Joan hasn't been able to fly.

original: But what a point, my lord, your falcon made,   And what a pitch she flew above the rest!
translation: But your falcon flew very high, my lord, higher than anyone else!

original: To see how God in all his creatures works!   Yea, man and birds are fain of climbing high.
translation: Ah, to see how God moves all his creatures! Yes, man and birds like to climb high.

original: No marvel, an it like your majesty,   My lord protector's hawks do tower so well;
translation: No wonder, if your majesty allows me to say, that my lord protector's hawks soar so high above us.

original: They know their master loves to be aloft,   And bears his thoughts above his falcon's pitch.
translation: They know that their master loves to be above others, and that his thoughts are at the highest point the falcon can fly.

original: My lord, 'tis but a base ignoble mind That mounts no higher than a bird can soar.
translation: My lord, it's your lowly and dishonorable brain that cannot fly higher than a bird can.

original: I thought as much; he would be above the clouds.
translation: I thought as much. He wants to be above the clouds.

original: Ay, my lord cardinal? How think you by that? Were it not good your grace could fly to heaven?
translation: Yes, my lord cardinal? What do you mean by that? Wouldn't it be good if your grace could fly to heaven?

original: The treasury of everlasting joy.
translation: Heaven is the place of never-ending joy.

original: Thy heaven is on earth; thine eyes and thoughts   Beat on a crown,
translation: [To GLOUCESTER]  Your heaven is on earth; your eyes and thoughts are set on the crown.

original: the treasure of thy heart;   Pernicious protector, dangerous peer,   That smooth'st it so with king and commonweal!
translation: That's the treasure you're after, you wicked protector, dangerous man, who so smoothly flatters the king and country!

original: What, cardinal, is your priesthood grown peremptory?   Tantaene animis coelestibus irae?
translation: Cardinal, is your office suddenly all-powerful? " Is there so much anger in heavenly minds ?"

original: Churchmen so hot? Good uncle, hide such malice;   With such holiness can you do it?
translation: Are the men of church so angry? Good uncle, hide your ill will. How can a holy man behave this way?

original: No malice, sir; no more than well becomes So good a quarrel and so bad a peer.
translation: No ill will, sir. Or no more than is fit for such a good fight and such a bad man.

original: As who, my lord?
translation: Which bad man do you mean, my lord?

original: Why, as you, my lord, An't like your lordly lord-protectorship.
translation: You, my lord! If it please your lord-protectorship.

original: Why, Suffolk, England knows thine insolence.
translation: Suffolk, England knows how disrespectful you are!

original: And thy ambition, Gloucester.
translation: And England also knows how ambitious you are, Gloucester.

original: I prithee, peace, good queen, And whet not on these furious peers; For blessed are the peacemakers on earth.
translation: Please, be calm, good queen and don't encourage these enraged men. Because the ones who make peace on earth are blessed!

original: Let me be blessed for the peace I make, Against this proud protector, with my sword!
translation: Let me be blessed for the peace that I make against this proud protector—with my sword!

original: Faith, holy uncle, would 'twere come to that!
translation: Ah, holy uncle, how could it come to this?

original: Marry, when thou darest.
translation: Indeed, when you encouraged it.

original: Make up no factious numbers for the matter; In thine own person answer thy abuse.
translation: Don't bring any of your supporters into this business. You alone should be accountable for your insult to me.

original: Ay, where thou darest not peep: an if thou darest, This evening, on the east side of the grove.
translation: Yes, if you dare to show up. If you do, meet me this evening on the east side of the forest.

original: How now, my lords!
translation: What's this, my lords?

original: Believe me, cousin Gloucester,   Had not your man put up the fowl so suddenly,   We had had more sport.
translation: Believe me, cousin Gloucester, if your falconer hadn't provoked the fowl so suddenly, we would have had more fun.

original: [Aside to GLOUCESTER]   Come with  thy two-hand sword.
translation: [Whispers to GLOUCESTER]  Bring your heavy sword.

original: True, uncle.    Are ye advised? The  east side of the grove.
translation: That's true, uncle.  Do you understand? The east side of the forest.

original: I am with you.
translation: I understand.

original: Why, how now, uncle Gloucester!
translation: What's going on, uncle Gloucester?

original: Talking of hawking; nothing else, my lord.
translation: We're talking about hawking. Nothing else, my lord!

original: Now, by God's mother, priest, I'll  shave your crown for this, Or all my fence shall fail.
translation: Now, by the Virgin Mary, I'll shave your tonsure for this, or otherwise all my fencing skills shall fail me.

original: Medice, teipsum— Protector, see to't well, protect yourself.
translation: "Doctor, heal yourself." Protector, you do the same and protect yourself.

original: The winds grow high; so do your stomachs, lords.   How irksome is this music to my heart!
translation: The winds blow high and so do your tempers, lords. This music sounds out of tune in my heart!

original: When such strings jar, what hope of harmony?   I pray, my lords, let me compound this strife.
translation: When such strings sound discordant, is there any hope they'll ever be harmonious? Please, my lords, let me settle this fight.

original: What means this noise? Fellow, what miracle dost thou proclaim?
translation: What is this noise? What miracle do you mean, man?

original: A miracle! A miracle!
translation: A miracle, a miracle!

original: Come to the king and tell him what miracle.
translation: Come to the king and tell him what this miracle is.

original: Forsooth, a blind man at Saint Alban's shrine, Within this half-hour, hath received his sight; A man that ne'er saw in his life before.
Now, God be praised, that to believing souls Gives light in darkness, comfort in despair!
translation: Now we give thanks to God, he who gives light in darkness and comfort in despair to those that believe!

original: Here comes the townsmen on procession, To present your highness with the man.
translation: The men of the town have marched here to show you this man, your highness.

original: Great is his comfort in this earthly vale, Although by his sight his sin be multiplied.
translation: His comfort is great in this mortal world, although by gaining his sight, he will be subject to more temptations.

original: Stand by, my masters: bring him near the king; His highness' pleasure is to talk with him.
translation: Stand aside, my masters. Bring him close to the king. His highness would like to talk to him.

original: Good fellow, tell us here the circumstance, That we for thee may glorify the Lord. What, hast thou been long blind and now restored?
translation: Good man, tell us the details of this so that we may celebrate the Lord in your name. Have you always been blind, has your sight now been restored?

original: Born blind, an't please your grace.
translation: I was born blind, as it pleases your grace.

original: Ay, indeed, was he.
translation: Yes, he was, indeed.

original: What woman is this?
translation: Who's this woman?

original: His wife, an't like your worship.
translation: I'm his wife, your worship.

original: Hadst thou been his mother, thou couldst have better told.
translation: If you had been his mother, you would have been in a better position to say that he was blind from his birth.

original: Where wert thou born?
translation: Where were you born?

original: At Berwick in the north, an't like your grace.
Poor soul, God's goodness hath been great to thee: Let never day nor night unhallow'd pass, But still remember what the Lord hath done.
translation: You are a poor soul. God's goodness has been great to you. Let not a day or night pass without saying your prayers, but remember what the Lord has done for you.

original: Tell me, good fellow, camest thou here by chance, Or of devotion, to this holy shrine?
translation: Tell me, good man, did you come here by accident or because of your devotion to this holy place?

original: God knows, of pure devotion; being call'd   A hundred times and oftener, in my sleep,   By good Saint Alban;
translation: God knows that I came here because of pure devotion. I was called a hundred times and more, in my sleep by the good Saint Alban.

original: who said, 'Simpcox, come,   Come, offer at my shrine, and I will help thee.'
translation: He said: "Simpox, come, come, make an offering at this holy place and I will help you."

original: Most true, forsooth; and many time and oft Myself have heard a voice to call him so.
translation: That's true, really. And I have heard a voice call him that way many times.

original: What, art thou lame?
translation: Are you crippled?

original: Ay, God Almighty help me!
translation: Yes, God Almighty help me!

original: How camest thou so?
translation: How did it happen?

original: A fall off of a tree.
translation: I fell off a tree.

original: A plum-tree, master.
translation: A plum-tree, master.

original: How long hast thou been blind?
translation: How long have you been blind?

original: Born so, master.
translation: I was born that way, master.

original: What, and wouldst climb a tree?
translation: Then how could you have climbed a tree?

original: But that in all my life, when I was a youth.
translation: I've only done it that once time, when I was young.

original: Too true; and bought his climbing very dear.
translation: That's true! And the climbing has cost him dearly.

original: Mass, thou lovedst plums well, that wouldst venture so.
translation: God, you must really love plums, in order to do that.

original: Alas, good master, my wife desired some damsons, And made me climb, with danger of my life.
translation: Ah, good master, my wife wanted some of them and she made me climb, even though it was dangerous for me.

original: A subtle knave! But yet it shall not serve. Let me see thine eyes: wink now: now open them: In my opinion yet thou seest not well.
translation: You are a crafty villain! But it won't do. Let me see your eyes. Now wink. Now open then. I think that you can't see well.

original: Yes, master, clear as day, I thank God and Saint Alban.
translation: Yes I can, master. As clear as day. I thank God and Saint Alban.

original: Say'st thou me so? What colour is this cloak of?
translation: Do you say that to me? What color is this cloak?

original: Red, master; red as blood.
translation: Red, master. Red as blood.

original: Why, that's well said. What colour is my gown of?
translation: Well, that's correct. What color is my robe?

original: Black, forsooth: coal-black as jet.
Why, then, thou know'st what colour jet is of?
translation: Well, how do you know what color jet is, then?

original: And yet, I think, jet did he never see.
translation: I don't think he's ever seen jet.

original: But cloaks and gowns, before this day, a many.
translation: But he has seen many cloaks and robes before today.

original: Never, before this day, in all his life.
translation: Never before today, in all his life!

original: Tell me, sirrah, what's my name?
translation: Tell me sir, what's my name?

original: Alas, master, I know not.
translation: Ah, master, I don't know.

original: What's his name?
translation: What's his name?

original: I know not.
translation: I don't know.

original: Nor his?
translation: Or his?

original: No, indeed, master.
translation: No, indeed, master.

original: What's thine own name?
translation: What's your own name?

original: Saunder Simpcox, an if it please you, master.
translation: Saunder Simpox, if it pleases you, master.

original: Then, Saunder, sit there, the lyingest knave in   Christendom. If thou hadst been born blind, thou   mightest as well have known all our names as thus to   name the several colours we do wear.
translation: Then, Saunder, stay there, you villain who lies the most in the whole of the Christian world! If you have been born blind, you might as well have know all our names in the same way you name the several colors that we wear.

original: Sight may   distinguish of colours, but suddenly to nominate them   all, it is impossible.
translation: Sight may distinguish between colors, but to suddenly name them all is impossible!

original: My lords, Saint Alban here   hath done a miracle; and would ye not think his   cunning to be great, that could restore this cripple   to his legs again?
translation: My lords, Saint Alban here has done a miracle. Wouldn't you think that his skill is so great that he would restore this cripple his legs again?

original: O master, that you could!
translation: Oh, master, if only you could!

original: My masters of Saint Alban's, have you not beadles in your town, and things called whips?
translation: My masters of Saint Alban's, don't you have constables in your town and things called whips?

original: Yes, my lord, if it please your grace.
translation: Yes, my lord, if it pleases your grace.

original: Then send for one presently.
translation: Then send for one immediately.

original: Sirrah, go fetch the beadle hither straight.
translation: Sir, go get the constable straight away.

original: Now fetch me a stool hither by and by. Now, sirrah, if you mean to save yourself from whipping, leap me over this stool and run away.
translation: Now get me a stool immediately. Now, sir, if you want to save yourself from whipping, jump across this stool and run away.

original: Alas, master, I am not able to stand alone: You go about to torture me in vain.
translation: Ah, but master, I am not able to stand unsupported. You are about to torture me for nothing.

original: Well, sir, we must have you find your legs. Sirrah beadle, whip him till he leap over that same stool.
translation: Well, sir, we must make you find your legs. Sir constable, whip him until he jumps over that stool there.

original: I will, my lord. Come on, sirrah; off with your doublet quickly.
translation: I will, my lord. Come on, sir, take off your jacket!

original: Alas, master, what shall I do? I am not able to stand.
translation: Ah, master, what shall I do? I am not able to stand.

original: O God, seest Thou this, and bearest so long?
translation: Oh, God, can you see this and can you endure it for so long?

original: It made me laugh to see the villain run.
translation: It made me laugh to see the villain run.

original: Follow the knave; and take this drab away.
translation: Follow the villain and take this whore away.

original: Alas, sir, we did it for pure need.
translation: Ah, sir, we did it because we really needed the money.

original: Let them be whipped through every market-town, till they come to Berwick, from whence they came.
translation: Let them be whipped through every market town, until they come back to Berwick, from where they came.

original: Duke Humphrey has done a miracle to-day.
translation: Duke Humphrey has done a miracle today.

original: True; made the lame to leap and fly away.
translation: True, he made the crippled jump and run away.

original: But you have done more miracles than I; You made in a day, my lord, whole towns to fly.
What tidings with our cousin Buckingham?
translation: What's the news, cousin Buckingham?

original: Such as my heart doth tremble to unfold.   A sort of naughty persons, lewdly bent,   Under the countenance and confederacy   Of Lady Eleanor, the protector's wife,   The ringleader and head of all this rout,   Have practised dangerously against your state,
translation: My heart trembles to reveal it. A gang of wicked people bent on evil, supported by and in collusion with Lady Eleanor, the protector's wife—the leader and head of this gang—have made a dangerous plot against you.

original: Dealing with witches and with conjurers:   Whom we have apprehended in the fact;   Raising up wicked spirits from under ground,
translation: They employed witches and magicians, whom we have caught in the act, raising wicked spirits from underground.

original: Demanding of King Henry's life and death,   And other of your highness' privy-council;   As more at large your grace shall understand.
translation: They wanted to know when King Henry would die, and others from your highness' council, as your grace shall find out at length.

original: And so, my lord protector, by this means   Your lady is forthcoming yet at London.
translation: And so, my lord protector, your lady is awaiting a trial in London. This news has blunted the edge of your weapon, I think.

original: This news, I think, hath turn'd your weapon's edge;   'Tis like, my lord, you will not keep your hour.
translation: It seems like you won't come to your duel at the appointed time.

original: Ambitious churchman, leave to afflict my heart:   Sorrow and grief have vanquish'd all my powers;
translation: Ambitious churchman, stop torturing my heart. Sorrow and grief have defeated all my powers

original: And, vanquish'd as I am, I yield to thee,   Or to the meanest groom.
translation: and defeated as I am, I surrender to you or to the humblest servant.

original: O God, what mischiefs work the wicked ones, Heaping confusion on their own heads thereby!
translation: Oh God, what mischief do the wicked ones do, so that they pile up destruction on their heads by doing so!

original: Gloucester, see here the tainture of thy nest. And look thyself be faultless, thou wert best.
translation: Gloucester, this corruption in your own family. Make sure that you aren't guilty too.

original: Madam, for myself, to heaven I do appeal,   How I have loved my king and commonweal:   And, for my wife, I know not how it stands;   Sorry I am to hear what I have heard:   Noble she is,
translation: Madam, I turn to heaven to clear my name. I have loved my king and the country so much. As for my wife, I don't know how things stand; I am sorry for what I have heard, since she is noble.

original: but if she have forgot   Honour and virtue and conversed with such   As, like to pitch, defile nobility,   I banish her my bed and company
translation: But if she has forgotten about honor and virtue and has been associated with the sort of company that, like  pitch , defiles nobility, I banish her from my bed and company.

original: And give her as a prey to law and shame,   That hath dishonour'd Gloucester's honest name.
translation: I'll turn her over to the law to be punished and shamed, because she has dishonored Gloucester's honest name.

original: Well, for this night we will repose us here:   To-morrow toward London back again,   To look into this business thoroughly   And call these foul offenders to their answers
translation: Well, we will sleep here tonight. We'll head towards London again tomorrow, to look into this business properly and bring these criminals to trial.

original: And poise the cause in justice' equal scales,   Whose beam stands sure, whose rightful cause prevails.
translation: We'll put the case to justice, whose scales are evenly balanced and who always finds out what's right.

original: Now, my good Lords of Salisbury and Warwick,   Our simple supper ended, give me leave   In this close walk to satisfy myself,
translation: Now that our simple dinner is over and we're alone in this garden together, my good Lords of Salisbury and Warwick,

original: In craving your opinion of my title,   Which is infallible, to England's crown.
translation: I'd like to know your opinion of my certain title to England's crown.

original: My lord, I long to hear it at full.
translation: My lord, I long to hear more about your claim.

original: Sweet York, begin: and if thy claim be good, The Nevils are thy subjects to command.
translation: Sweet York, tell us. And if your claim is good, you can command the whole of my family.

original: Then thus:   Edward the Third, my lords, had seven sons:   The first, Edward the Black Prince, Prince of Wales;   The second, William of Hatfield, and the third,   Lionel Duke of Clarence: next to whom   Was John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster;
translation: It goes like this: Edward the Third, my lords, had seven sons. The first, Edward the Black Prince, Prince of Wales; the second was William of Hatfield, and the third was Lionel Duke of Clarence; next to whom was John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster.
