translation: Who can find a partridge in the  kite 's nest, and not assume that was how the bird died, even if the kite flew away with an clean beak? This tragedy is as suspicious as those.

original: Are you the butcher, Suffolk? Where's your knife? Is Beaufort term'd a kite? Where are his talons?
translation: Are you the killer, Suffolk? Where is your knife? Is Beaufort the kite, then? Where are his claws?

original: I wear no knife to slaughter sleeping men;   But here's a vengeful sword, rusted with ease,   That shall be scoured in his rancorous heart   That slanders me with murder's crimson badge.
translation: I don't carry a knife to murder sleeping men. But here's a vengeful sword, not often used, that will plunge into the jealous heart of the one who sullies my good name with an accusation of murder.

original: Say, if thou darest, proud Lord of Warwickshire,   That I am faulty in Duke Humphrey's death.
translation: Say, if you dare, proud Lord of Warwickshire, that I am guilty of Duke Humphrey's death.

original: What dares not Warwick, if false Suffolk dare him?
translation: What doesn't Warwick dare to do, if false Suffolk dares him?

original: He dares not calm his contumelious spirit Nor cease to be an arrogant controller, Though Suffolk dare him twenty thousand times.
translation: He doesn't dare to calm his anger, nor stop being an arrogant busybody, although Suffolk dared him twenty thousand times.

original: Madam, be still; with reverence may I say; For every word you speak in his behalf Is slander to your royal dignity.
translation: Madam, be calm. With courtesy, I may say that every word you speak on his behalf is an attack to your royal dignity.

original: Blunt-witted lord, ignoble in demeanor!   If ever lady wrong'd her lord so much,   Thy mother took into her blameful bed   Some stern untutor'd churl,
translation: You are a stupid man and lack manners! If ever a lady did such a thing to her husband, your mother took some coarse ignorant person into her bed.

original: and noble stock   Was graft with crab-tree slip; whose fruit thou art,   And never of the Nevils' noble race.
translation: Your noble family tree was  joined  by cutting a wild apple tree—you're the fruit of that, not of the Nevils' noble race!

original: But that the guilt of murder bucklers thee   And I should rob the deathsman of his fee,   Quitting thee thereby of ten thousand shames,   And that my sovereign's presence makes me mild,
translation: If you weren't made brave by your guilt, I would have killed you myself rather than let you be executed for the murder, exonerating you of ten thousand shames. But my king's presence makes me restrain myself.

original: I would, false murderous coward, on thy knee   Make thee beg pardon for thy passed speech,   And say it was thy mother that thou meant'st   That thou thyself was born in bastardy;
translation: Otherwise I would make you beg for a pardon on your knees for what you said, you false murderous coward! I would make you say that it was your mother that you meant, that you were born a bastard.

original: And after all this fearful homage done,   Give thee thy hire and send thy soul to hell,   Pernicious blood-sucker of sleeping men!
translation: And after you'd admitted all this, I'd kill you and send your soul to hell, you wicked blood-sucker of sleeping men!

original: Thou shall be waking well I shed thy blood, If from this presence thou darest go with me.
translation: You'll know you're awake when I shed your blood, if you won't go with me from this royal presence.

original: Away even now, or I will drag thee hence: Unworthy though thou art, I'll cope with thee And do some service to Duke Humphrey's ghost.
translation: Let's go away now or I will drag you away, although you are not worthy. And I'll fight with you and do some favor for Duke Humphrey's ghost.

original: What stronger breastplate than a heart untainted!   Thrice is he armed that hath his quarrel just,
translation: An innocent heart is the strongest breastplate! He is armed three times as much if his fight is justified.

original: And he but naked, though lock'd up in steel   Whose conscience with injustice is corrupted.
translation: And the man whose conscience is corrupted with injustice is naked, even if he wears his armor.

original: What noise is this?
translation: What's this noise?

original: Why, how now, lords! Your wrathful weapons drawn Here in our presence! Dare you be so bold? Why, what tumultuous clamour have we here?
translation: What's this, lords? You draw your weapons out angrily here in our presence? Do you dare to be so bold? What riotous noise did we hear?

original: The traitorous Warwick with the men of Bury Set all upon me, mighty sovereign.

[To the Commons, entering]   Sirs, stand apart;   the king shall know your mind.   Dread lord, the commons send you word by me,   Unless Lord Suffolk straight be done to death,   Or banished fair England's territories,   They will by violence tear him from your palace   And torture him with grievous lingering death.
translation: [To the commoners coming in]  Sirs, stand aside, the king will hear you out. Respected lord, the commoners send you a message from me: unless Lord Suffolk is killed straight away or banished from England, they will tear him from your palace by violence and torture him with a slow brutal death.

original: They say, by him the good Duke Humphrey died;   They say, in him they fear your highness' death;   And mere instinct of love and loyalty,   Free from a stubborn opposite intent,   As being thought to contradict your liking,   Makes them thus forward in his banishment.
translation: They say that he killed Duke Humphrey; they say that they are afraid he might kill you too. A simple instinct of love and loyalty, free from stubborn hostile intention (or any desire to oppose your wishes) makes them demand his banishment.

original: They say, in care of your most royal person,   That if your highness should intend to sleep   And charge that no man should disturb your rest   In pain of your dislike or pain of death,   Yet, notwithstanding such a strait edict,   Were there a serpent seen, with forked tongue,   That slily glided towards your majesty,   It were but necessary you were waked,
translation: They say, since they care about your royal person, that if your highness planned to sleep and ordered that no man should disturb you on pain of death—yet despite such a strict rule, if they saw a serpent with a split tongue slyly gliding towards your majesty, they would wake you up.

original: Lest, being suffer'd in that harmful slumber,   The mortal worm might make the sleep eternal;   And therefore do they cry, though you forbid,   That they will guard you, whether you will or no,   From such fell serpents as false Suffolk is,
translation: Otherwise you might keep sleeping and the poisonous snake would make that sleep last forever. And so they would shout, although you forbade it, and they will guard you, whether you want or not, from a dangerous serpent like lying Suffolk.

original: With whose envenomed and fatal sting,   Your loving uncle, twenty times his worth,   They say, is shamefully bereft of life.
translation: His poisonous and deadly sting shamefully killed your loving uncle (whose life was worth twenty times more), so they say.

original: An answer from the king, my Lord of Salisbury!
translation: We want an answer from the king, my Lord of Salisbury!

original: 'Tis like the commons, rude unpolish'd hinds,   Could send such message to their sovereign:   But you, my lord, were glad to be employ'd,   To show how quaint an orator you are:
translation: We expect those rude rough peasants to send such a message to their king. But you, my lord, were happy to be their messenger, so you can show what a skillful speaker you are.

original: But all the honour Salisbury hath won   Is, that he was the lord ambassador   Sent from a sort of tinkers to the king.
translation: But all the honor that Salisbury has won is that he was the lord ambassador a gang of  beggars and thieves  sent to the king.

original: An answer from the king, or we will all break in!
translation: We want an answer from the king, or we'll break in!

original: Go, Salisbury, and tell them all from me.   I thank them for their tender loving care;   And had I not been cited so by them,   Yet did I purpose as they do entreat;
translation: Go, Salisbury, and tell them everything from me. I thank them for their loving care for me, and even if they hadn't urged me, I was still planning to do what they propose.

original: For, sure, my thoughts do hourly prophesy   Mischance unto my state by Suffolk's means:   And therefore, by His majesty I swear,   Whose far unworthy deputy I am,   He shall not breathe infection in this air   But three days longer, on the pain of death.
translation: I predict that Suffolk means to overthrow me. And therefore, I swear by God, whose unworthy agent I am, that he shall not contaminate this air for longer than three days, on pain of death.

original: O Henry, let me plead for gentle Suffolk!
translation: Oh Henry, let me speak on kind Suffolk's behalf.

original: Ungentle queen, to call him gentle Suffolk!   No more, I say: if thou dost plead for him,   Thou wilt but add increase unto my wrath.
translation: You are an unkind queen to call him kind Suffolk! I'm not going to say anything else. If you speak for him, you will increase my anger.

original: Had I but said, I would have kept my word,   But when I swear, it is irrevocable.   If, after three days' space, thou here be'st found   On any ground that I am ruler of,   The world shall not be ransom for thy life.
translation: Had I only said it, I would have kept my word, but when I swear it, it is irreversible.  [To SUFFOLK]  If you are found on any part of the land that I rule after three days, the whole world won't be a price big enough to ransom your life.

original: Come, Warwick, come, good Warwick, go with me;   I have great matters to impart to thee.
translation: Come, Warwick; good Warwick, come with me. I have things that I want to discuss with you.

original: Mischance and sorrow go along with you!   Heart's discontent and sour affliction   Be playfellows to keep you company!
translation: Let bad luck and sorrow go away with you! Heart's discontent and sour suffering can keep you company!

original: There's two of you; the devil make a third!   And threefold vengeance tend upon your steps!
translation: There's two of you, then, and the devil will make a third one! And vengeance three times over will follow you!

original: Cease, gentle queen, these execrations, And let thy Suffolk take his heavy leave.
translation: Stop these curses, kind queen, and let your Suffolk leave sadly.

original: Fie, coward woman and soft-hearted wretch! Hast thou not spirit to curse thine enemy?
translation: Ugh, you are like a coward woman and a girl with a sensitive heart! Don't you have the courage to curse your enemy?

original: A plague upon them! Wherefore should I curse them?   Would curses kill, as doth the mandrake's groan,   I would invent as bitter-searching terms,   As curst, as harsh and horrible to hear,   Deliver'd strongly through my fixed teeth,   With full as many signs of deadly hate,   As lean-faced Envy in her loathsome cave:
translation: A plague on them! Why should I curse them? If curses could kill like a  mandrake 's shriek, I would come up with such piercing words, harsh and horrible to hear, and I would deliver them strongly through my clenched teeth, with as many signs of deadly hate as Envy in her hateful cave.

original: My tongue should stumble in mine earnest words;   Mine eyes should sparkle like the beaten flint;   Mine hair be fixed on end, as one distract;   Ay, every joint should seem to curse and ban:   And even now my burthen'd heart would break,   Should I not curse them.
translation: My tongue would stutter when I say those true words, my eyes would sparkle like the stone which gives off a spark when it is struck, and my hair would stand upright like a madman. And even now my heart would break, if I didn't curse them.

original: Poison be their drink!   Gall, worse than gall, the daintiest that they taste!   Their sweetest shade a grove of cypress trees!   Their chiefest prospect murdering basilisks!   Their softest touch as smart as lizards' sting!
translation: Let them drink poison! Bile, worse than bile, would be the most refined thing that they would taste! Their sweetest shade would be a forest of  cypress trees ! Their greatest view would be murdering basilisks! Their softest touch would be as painful as a lizard's sting!

original: Their music frightful as the serpent's hiss,   And boding screech-owls make the concert full!   All the foul terrors in dark-seated hell—
translation: Their music would be as frightening as the serpent's hiss, and ominous screeching owls would make the concert of noises complete! All the horrible terrors in dark hell—

original: Enough, sweet Suffolk; thou torment'st thyself;
translation: Enough, sweet Suffolk. You are torturing yourself.

original: And these dread curses, like the sun 'gainst glass,   Or like an overcharged gun, recoil,   And turn the force of them upon thyself.
translation: And these horrible curses, like the sun against a glass, or like an overloaded gun, recoil and turn the force on yourself.

original: You bade me ban, and will you bid me leave?   Now, by the ground that I am banish'd from,   Well could I curse away a winter's night,
translation: You told me to curse and now you tell me to stop? Now, by the ground that I am banished from, I could curse away a winter's night.

original: Though standing naked on a mountain top,   Where biting cold would never let grass grow,   And think it but a minute spent in sport.
translation: If I were standing naked on the top of the mountain, where biting cold would never allow grass to grow, I'd think it was only a minute of entertainment.

original: O, let me entreat thee cease. Give me thy hand,   That I may dew it with my mournful tears;   Nor let the rain of heaven wet this place,   To wash away my woful monuments.
translation: Oh, let me beg you to stop this. Give me your hand, so I can cover it with my mournful tears. Don't let even the holiest rain make this place wet, to wash away my sorrowful mementos.

original: O, could this kiss be printed in thy hand,   That thou mightst think upon these by the seal,   Through whom a thousand sighs are breathed for thee!   So, get thee gone, that I may know my grief;   'Tis but surmised whiles thou art standing by,   As one that surfeits thinking on a want.
translation: Oh, if this kiss could print my lips on your hand, so that you could think of the lips which breathe a thousand sighs for you! So go, so that I can know how terrible my grief is. I can only imagine it if you're still here, and I am like one that overindulges and grows sick by deprivation.

original: I will repeal thee, or, be well assured,   Adventure to be banished myself:   And banished I am, if but from thee.   Go; speak not to me; even now be gone.
translation: I will recall you from exile, or be sure that I will try to be banished as well. And I am banished from you. Go, don't speak to me, and be gone.

original: O, go not yet! Even thus two friends condemn'd   Embrace and kiss and take ten thousand leaves,   Loather a hundred times to part than die.   Yet now farewell; and farewell life with thee!
translation: Oh, don't go yet! Two condemned friends may embrace and kiss and say goodbye ten thousand times, more reluctantly than to die a hundred times. Now, goodbye! And goodbye life, with you.

original: Thus is poor Suffolk ten times banished;   Once by the king, and three times thrice by thee.   'Tis not the land I care for, wert thou thence;   A wilderness is populous enough,   So Suffolk had thy heavenly company:
translation: So poor Suffolk is banished ten times—once by the king, and nine times by you. I don't care about this land, if you are not in it. A wilderness is inhabited enough, provided that Suffolk has your heavenly company.

original: For where thou art, there is the world itself,   With every several pleasure in the world,   And where thou art not, desolation.
translation: Because where you are, there is the whole world, with all the joys of the world, and where you are not, there is desolation.

original: I can no more: live thou to joy thy life;   Myself no joy in nought but that thou livest.
translation: I can't do this anymore. Live to enjoy your life. I won't have joy in anything except in knowing that you are still alive.

original: Wither goes Vaux so fast? What news, I prithee?
translation: Why are you in a rush, Vaux? What news do you bring?

original: To signify unto his majesty   That Cardinal Beaufort is at point of death;   For suddenly a grievous sickness took him,   That makes him gasp and stare and catch the air,   Blaspheming God and cursing men on earth.
translation: To tell his majesty that Cardinal Beaufort is almost dead, because a sudden sickness took over him. It makes him gasp and stare and breath heavily, cursing God and men on earth.

original: Sometimes he talks as if Duke Humphrey's ghost   Were by his side; sometime he calls the king,   And whispers to his pillow, as to him,   The secrets of his overcharged soul;   And I am sent to tell his majesty   That even now he cries aloud for him.
translation: Sometimes he talks as if Duke Humphrey's ghost is standing by his side; sometimes he calls the king and whispers to his pillow as it were him. He confesses the secrets of his overburdened soul, and I am sent to tell his majesty that he is screaming loudly for him even at this moment.

original: Go tell this heavy message to the king.
translation: Go and give that sad message to the king.

original: Ay me! What is this world! What news are these!   But wherefore grieve I at an hour's poor loss,   Omitting Suffolk's exile, my soul's treasure?
translation: Poor me! What is this world? What sort of news is this? But why do I grieve at a loss of an old man, disregarding the exile of Suffolk, the treasure of my soul?

original: Why only, Suffolk, mourn I not for thee,   And with the southern clouds contend in tears,   Theirs for the earth's increase, mine for my sorrows?
translation: Why do I not mourn for you, Suffolk, and compete with the  southern cloud s for tears—theirs for the earth's increase, mine for sorrows?

original: Now get thee hence: the king, thou know'st, is coming;   If thou be found by me, thou art but dead.
translation: Now go away. The king, as you know, is coming, and if he found you with me, you are dead.

original: If I depart from thee, I cannot live;   And in thy sight to die, what were it else   But like a pleasant slumber in thy lap?   Here could I breathe my soul into the air,   As mild and gentle as the cradle-babe   Dying with mother's dug between its lips:
translation: If I leave you, I cannot live. And what else is it to  die  in front of you, but a pleasant sleep in your  lap ? Here I could breathe my last breath, as mild and gentle as the baby dying with mother's nipple between its lips.

original: Where, from thy sight, I should be raging mad,   And cry out for thee to close up mine eyes,   To have thee with thy lips to stop my mouth;   So shouldst thou either turn my flying soul,   Or I should breathe it so into thy body,   And then it lived in sweet Elysium.
translation: Whereas I will go mad when I'm away from you, and cry out for you to close my eyes, to have you stop my mouth with your lips. So you would return my flying soul, or I would breathe it into your body, where it would live in sweet  heaven .

original: To die by thee were but to die in jest;   From thee to die were torture more than death:   O, let me stay, befall what may befall!
translation: To die by you would not be dying at all. To die away from you is more torturous than any other death. Oh, let me stay, no matter what happens!

original: Away! Though parting be a fretful corrosive,   It is applied to a deathful wound.
translation: Go away! Although saying goodbye to you is like putting an aggravating corrosive to a deadly wound.

original: To France, sweet Suffolk: let me hear from thee;   For wheresoe'er thou art in this world's globe,   I'll have an Iris that shall find thee out.
translation: Go to France, sweet Suffolk, and let me hear from you. Because wherever you may in this world's globe, I'll have an  Iris  that shall find you.

original: I go.
translation: I am going.

original: And take my heart with thee.
translation: And take my heart with you.

original: A jewel, lock'd into the wofull'st cask   That ever did contain a thing of worth.
translation: It's like a jewel, locked in the saddest casket that never contained such a worthy thing.

original: Even as a splitted bark, so sunder we   This way fall I to death.
translation: We are split in two like a ship that's broken in half. I go to my death this way.

original: This way for me.
translation: And this way for me.

original: How fares my lord? Speak, Beaufort, to thy sovereign.
translation: How is my lord? Speak to your king, Beaufort.

original: If thou be'st death, I'll give thee England's treasure, Enough to purchase such another island, So thou wilt let me live, and feel no pain.
translation: If you were death, I'd give you England's treasure (which would be enough to buy another similar island), just so you will let me live without any pain.

original: Ah, what a sign it is of evil life, Where death's approach is seen so terrible!
translation: Ah, what does this say about your evil life, that death appears so terribly to you!

original: Beaufort, it is thy sovereign speaks to thee.
translation: Beaufort, it is your king who is speaking to you.

original: Bring me unto my trial when you will.   Died he not in his bed? Where should he die?   Can I make men live, whether they will or no?   O, torture me no more! I will confess.
translation: Bring me to your trial when you want. Didn't Gloucester die in his bed? Where else should he die? Can I make men live, whether they want or not? Oh, don't torture me! I will confess.

original: Alive again? Then show me where he is:   I'll give a thousand pound to look upon him.   He hath no eyes, the dust hath blinded them.   Comb down his hair; look, look!
translation: Is he alive again? Then show me where he is! I'll give a thousand pounds just to look at him. He doesn't have eyes, the  dust  has made him blind. Comb his hair and look, look!

original: It stands upright,   Like lime-twigs set to catch my winged soul.   Give me some drink; and bid the apothecary   Bring the strong poison that I bought of him.
translation: It stands upright, like twigs smeared with  birdlime  that are ready to catch my soul as it takes flight. Give me something to drink, and tell the apothecary to bring the strong poison that I bought from him.

original: O thou eternal Mover of the heavens.   Look with a gentle eye upon this wretch!
translation: Oh, you eternal God of heavens! Look gently on this poor man!

original: O, beat away the busy meddling fiend   That lays strong siege unto this wretch's soul.   And from his bosom purge this black despair!
translation: Oh, beat back the interfering devil that attacks this man's soul! And wash away this black despair from his heart!

original: See, how the pangs of death do make him grin!
translation: See how the pain of death makes him grimace!

original: Disturb him not; let him pass peaceably.
translation: Don't disturb him; let him die peacefully.

original: Peace to his soul, if God's good pleasure be!   Lord cardinal, if thou think'st on heaven's bliss,   Hold up thy hand, make signal of thy hope.
translation: Peace to his soul, if God wants him to have peace! Lord cardinal, if you think of heaven's bliss, hold up your hand and give a signal that you hope to be saved.

original: He dies, and makes no sign. O God, forgive him!
translation: [The CARDINAL dies]  He died without giving a sign. Oh, God, forgive him!

original: So bad a death argues a monstrous life.
translation: Such a bad death suggests he has lead a monstrous life.

original: Forbear to judge, for we are sinners all. Close up his eyes and draw the curtain close; And let us all to meditation.
translation: Don't judge him. We are all sinners. Close his eyes and draw the curtain tightly, and let us all reflect and pray.

original: The gaudy, blabbing and remorseful day   Is crept into the bosom of the sea;   And now loud-howling wolves arouse the jades   That drag the tragic melancholy night;
translation: The bright day has sunk into the depth of the sea, and now loud-howling wolves awaken the  dragons  that drag night's sad chariot.

original: Who, with their drowsy, slow and flagging wings,   Clip dead men's graves and from their misty jaws   Breathe foul contagious darkness in the air.
translation: Their drowsy, slow and dropping wings hit dead men's graves, and they breathe horrible contagious darkness into the air from their misty jaws.

original: Therefore bring forth the soldiers of our prize;   For, whilst our pinnace anchors in the Downs,   Here shall they make their ransom on the sand,   Or with their blood stain this discolour'd shore.
translation: So bring forward the soldiers from the ship we captured. While our  boat  stops in the  Downs , they will either pay their ransom here on the sand, or we'll stain this gray shore with their blood.

original: Master, this prisoner freely give I thee;   And thou that art his mate, make boot of this;   The other, Walter Whitmore, is thy share.
translation: Master, I give you this prisoner freely. And since you are his companion, take advantage of this. Walt Whitmore, the other is yours.

original: What is my ransom, master? Let me know.
translation: What is the ransom, master? Tell me.

original: A thousand crowns, or else lay down your head.
translation: A thousand crowns, or else you'll lose your head.

original: And so much shall you give, or off goes yours.
translation: And so much you will give us, or else we'll cut off your head.

original: What, think you much to pay two thousand crowns,   And bear the name and port of gentlemen?   Cut both the villains' throats; for die you shall:
translation: Do you think it's too much to pay two thousand crowns, since you bear the name and wear the clothes of gentlemen? Cut both the villain's throats, because you shall die!

original: The lives of those which we have lost in fight   Be counterpoised with such a petty sum!
translation: Such a small amount isn't worth the lives of the men we lost in battle.

original: I'll give it, sir; and therefore spare my life.
translation: I'll give it to you, sir; so spare my life!

original: And so will I and write home for it straight.
translation: And so will I; I'll write home for the money straight away.

original: I lost mine eye in laying the prize  aboard, And therefore to revenge it, shalt thou die; And so should these, if I might have my will.
translation: I lost my eye in boarding the captured ship. So to take revenge, you will die and so would all of them, if I have a say in it.

original: Be not so rash; take ransom, let him live.
translation: Don't be so harsh. Take the money and let them live.

original: Look on my George; I am a gentleman: Rate me at what thou wilt, thou shalt be paid.
And so am I; my name is Walter Whitmore. How now! Why start'st thou? What, doth death affright?
Thy name affrights me, in whose sound is death.   A cunning man did calculate my birth   And told me that by water I should die:
translation: Your name frightens me. It sounds like death in my ears. A man skilled in magic cast my horoscope and told me that I will die by water.

original: Yet let not this make thee be bloody-minded;   Thy name is Gaultier, being rightly sounded.
translation: But don't let this make you think about my death. Your name is Gaultier, if it is pronounced correctly.

original: Gaultier or Walter, which it is, I care not:   Never yet did base dishonour blur our name,   But with our sword we wiped away the blot;
translation: Gaultier or Walter, I don't care which it is. Lowly dishonor has never stained my name, because we wiped away that spot with our sword.

original: Therefore, when merchant-like I sell revenge,   Broke be my sword, my arms torn and defaced,   And I proclaim'd a coward through the world!
translation: Therefore, if I ransom prisoners like a merchant, my sword is broken, my coat of arms is torn and damaged, and I am called a coward throughout the world!

original: Stay, Whitmore; for thy prisoner is a prince, The Duke of Suffolk, William de la Pole.
translation: No more, Whitmore. Your prisoner is a nobleman—the Duke of Suffolk, William de la Pole.

original: The Duke of Suffolk muffled up in rags!
translation: The Duke of Suffolk dressed in rags!

original: Ay, but these rags are no part of the duke: Jove sometimes went disguised, and why not I?
But Jove was never slain, as thou shalt be.
translation: But Jove was never killed and you will be.

original: Obscure and lowly swain, King Henry's blood,   The honourable blood of Lancaster,   Must not be shed by such a jaded groom.   Hast thou not kiss'd thy hand and held my stirrup?   Bare-headed plodded by my foot-cloth mule   And thought thee happy when I shook my head?
translation: I nsignificant and lowly peasant, King Henry's blood—the honorable blood of Lancaster—won't be spilled by such a contemptible  servant . Have you not  kissed your hand  and held my stirrup? You walked  bare-headed  by my mule and considered yourself happy when I acknowledged you even slightly.

original: How often hast thou waited at my cup,   Fed from my trencher, kneel'd down at the board,   When I have feasted with Queen Margaret?   Remember it and let it make thee crest-fall'n,   Ay, and allay this thy abortive pride;
translation: How often have you served me drinks, acted as my taster, and bowed at my table when I was having dinner with Queen Margaret? Remember that and let it make you humble! And stop being so proud; it doesn't work for you.

original: How in our voiding lobby hast thou stood   And duly waited for my coming forth?   This hand of mine hath writ in thy behalf,   And therefore shall it charm thy riotous tongue.
translation: Remember how you used to stand in our lobby and obediently wait for my arrival? My hand has written on your behalf, so it has the right to silence your disrespectful words.

original: Speak, captain, shall I stab the forlorn swain?
translation: Speak, captain. Should I stab this wretched fellow?

original: First let my words stab him, as he hath me.
translation: First, let my words stab him, as he has just done with his.

original: Base slave, thy words are blunt and so art thou.
translation: Lowly slave, your words are as useless as you are.

original: Convey him hence and on our longboat's side Strike off his head.
translation: Take him away and cut off his head on the side of our largest boat.

original: Thou darest not, for thy own.
translation: You wouldn't dare, for fear of losing your own head.

original: Yes, Pole.
translation: Yes I would, Pole.

original: Pole?
translation: Pole?

original: Pool! Sir Pool! Lord!   Ay, kennel, puddle, sink; whose filth and dirt   Troubles the silver spring where England drinks.   Now will I dam up this thy yawning mouth   For swallowing the treasure of the realm:
translation: Pool! Sir Pool! Lord! Yes, gutter, puddle, sewer, whose filth and dirt muddies the silver spring where England drinks. Now I'll block up your gaping mouth for swallowing the treasure of the kingdom.

original: Thy lips that kiss'd the queen shall sweep the ground;   And thou that smiledst at good Duke Humphrey's death,   Against the senseless winds shalt grin in vain,   Who in contempt shall hiss at thee again:
translation: Your lips, that once kissed the queen, will feel the ground now. And you that smiled when good Duke Humphrey died will grimace in vain against the merciless winds, which will hiss at you in contempt.

original: And wedded be thou to the hags of hell,   For daring to affy a mighty lord   Unto the daughter of a worthless king,   Having neither subject, wealth, nor diadem.
translation: And you will be married to the  old women of hell , for daring to engage a  mighty lord  to the daughter of a worthless king who had neither followers, wealth, nor a crown.

original: By devilish policy art thou grown great,   And, like ambitious Sylla, overgorged   With gobbets of thy mother's bleeding heart.   By thee Anjou and Maine were sold to France,   The false revolting Normans thorough thee   Disdain to call us lord, and Picardy   Hath slain their governors, surprised our forts,   And sent the ragged soldiers wounded home.
translation: You have grown powerful by devilish tricks, and like ambitious  Sylla , you are stuffed with chunks of raw flesh from your country's bleeding heart. Anjou and Maine were sold to France because of you, your false rebellious Normans refused to call us lords because of you, and  Picardy  has killed their lords, seized our fortresses, and sent the exhausted and wounded soldiers home.

original: The princely Warwick, and the Nevils all,   Whose dreadful swords were never drawn in vain,   As hating thee, are rising up in arms:   And now the house of York, thrust from the crown   By shameful murder of a guiltless king   And lofty proud encroaching tyranny,   Burns with revenging fire
translation: The noble Warwick and all the Nevils, whose dreadful swords were never drawn senselessly, are rising up because they hate you. And now the house of York, deprived of the crown by the shameful murder of  a guiltless king  and grasping ambition, is ready for revenge.

original: ; whose hopeful colours   Advance our half-faced sun, striving to shine,   Under the which is writ 'Invitis nubibus.'
translation: Their hopeful military banners show a  half-faced sun , rising to shine, under which is written:  "in spite of clouds."

original: The commons here in Kent are up in arms:   And, to conclude, reproach and beggary   Is crept into the palace of our king.   And all by thee. Away! Convey him hence.
translation: The commoners here in Kent are ready to fight. And to conclude, disgrace and beggary have spread into the palace of our king. And this is all because of you! Away! Take him from here.

original: Drones suck not eagles' blood but rob beehives:   It is impossible that I should die   By such a lowly vassal as thyself.   Thy words move rage and not remorse in me:
translation: The non-working  male bees  don't suck eagles' blood but rob beehives. It is impossible that I'll die by the hand of such a lowly servant like you! Your words make me angry and not guilty.

original: I go of message from the queen to France;   I charge thee waft me safely cross the Channel.
translation: I'm going to carry a message from the queen to France. I demand that you carry me safely across the Channel.

original: Walter,—
translation: Walter—

original: Come, Suffolk, I must waft thee to thy death.
translation: Come, Suffolk, I must carry you to your death.

original: Gelidus timor occupat artus it is thee I fear.
translation: "Cold fear almost entirely seizes my limbs." It is you that I'm afraid of.

original: Thou shalt have cause to fear before I leave thee. What, are ye daunted now? Now will ye stoop?
translation: You'll have a reason to be afraid before I'm done with you. Are you scared now? Will you bow now?

original: My gracious lord, entreat him, speak him fair.
translation: My gracious lord, beg him. Speak courteously to him.

original: Suffolk's imperial tongue is stern and rough,   Used to command, untaught to plead for favour.   Far be it we should honour such as these   With humble suit:
translation: Suffolk's commanding tongue is strict and rough; it is used to giving commands and not used to asking for a favor. It is too much for  us  to honor someone like you with humble begging.

original: no, rather let my head   Stoop to the block than these knees bow to any   Save to the God of heaven and to my king;
translation: No, I'd rather let my head bow to the cutting block than these knees bow to anyone, apart from the God of heaven and my king.

original: And sooner dance upon a bloody pole   Than stand uncover'd to the vulgar groom.   True nobility is exempt from fear:   More can I bear than you dare execute.
translation: I would sooner dance on a bloody spike than stand  hat-less  next to this vulgar servant. True nobility is not afraid. I can take more than you dare to throw at me.

original: Hale him away, and let him talk no more.
translation: Drag him away and don't let him talk any more.

original: Come, soldiers, show what cruelty ye can,   That this my death may never be forgot!   Great men oft die by vile bezonians:
translation: Come, soldiers and show all the cruelty you can, so that my death may never be forgotten! Great men often die at the hands of lowly beggars.

original: A Roman sworder and banditto slave   Murder'd sweet Tully; Brutus' bastard hand   Stabb'd Julius Caesar; savage islanders   Pompey the Great; and Suffolk dies by pirates.
translation: A Roman assassin and bandit slave murdered the sweet  Tully ; the bastard  Brutus  stabbed Julius Caeasar; savage islanders killed  Pompey the Great.  And Suffolk will be killed by pirates.

original: And as for these whose ransom we have set, It is our pleasure one of them depart; Therefore come you with us and let him go.
translation: And as for these whose ransom we have accepted, we'll let one of you go. So  you come with us, and let him go.

original: There let his head and lifeless body lie, Until the queen his mistress bury it.
translation: We'll let his head and lifeless body lie there, until his lover the queen can bury it.

original: O barbarous and bloody spectacle!   His body will I bear unto the king:
translation: Oh, barbaric and bloody spectacle! I will take his body to the king.

original: If he revenge it not, yet will his friends;   So will the queen, that living held him dear.
translation: If he doesn't take revenge, his friends will and so will the queen that held him so dear when he was alive.

original: Come, and get thee a sword, though made of a lath; they have been up these two days.
translation: Come and get yourself a sword, even though it's made of wood. They've been rebelling these past two days.

original: They have the more need to sleep now, then.
translation: They have more reason to sleep now, then.

original: I tell thee, Jack Cade the clothier means to dress the commonwealth, and turn it, and set a new nap upon  it.
So he had need, for 'tis threadbare. Well, I say it was never merry world in England since gentlemen came  up.
translation: He really needs to, since it's worn-out. Well, I say that England has never been as good as in the old days, ever since gentlemen came into fashion.

original: O miserable age! Virtue is not regarded in  handicrafts-men.
translation: Oh, it's a miserable time! Virtue is not valued in handicraft workers.

original: The nobility think scorn to go in leather aprons.
translation: The nobility consider it lowly to wear leather aprons like working men.

original: Nay, more, the king's council are no good workmen.
translation: No, it's even worse. The king's council are not good working men.

original: True; and yet it is said, labour in thy vocation;
translation: True! And yet it is said that each man must do his own job.

original: which is as much to say as, let the magistrates be   labouring men; and therefore should we be   magistrates.
translation: Which is as much to say the magistrates should be working men. So we should be magistrates.

original: Thou hast hit it; for there's no better sign of a brave mind than a hard hand.
translation: You have hit the nail on the head, because there is no better sign of a fine mind than a hand toughened by manual labor.

original: I see them! I see them! There's Best's son, the tanner of Wingham,—
translation: I see them, I see them! There's Best's son, the craftsman of Wingham—

original: He shall have the skin of our enemies, to make dog's-leather of.
translation: He'll make gloves out of the skin of our enemies!

original: And Dick the Butcher,—
translation: And Dick the Butcher—

original: Then is sin struck down like an ox, and iniquity's throat cut like a calf.
translation: He'll shoot down sin like an ox, and cut the throat of injustice like a calf.

original: And Smith the weaver,—
translation: And Smith, the weaver—

original: Argo, their thread of life is spun.
translation: So, their fate is determined.

original: Come, come, let's fall in with them.
translation: Come, come, let's join them!

original: We John Cade, so termed of our supposed father,—
Or rather, of stealing a cade of herrings.
translation: Or rather, because he stole a barrel of herrings.

original: For our enemies shall fall before us, inspired with the spirit of putting down kings and princes, —Command silence.
translation: Our enemies will fall before us, since we're inspired to put down kings and noblemen—tell everyone to be quiet.

original: Silence!
translation: Be quiet!

original: My father was a Mortimer,—
translation: My father was a Mortimer—

original: He was an honest man, and a good bricklayer.
translation: He was an honest man, and a good bricklayer.

original: My mother a Plantagenet,—
translation: My mother a Plantagenet—

original: I knew her well; she was a midwife.
translation: I knew her well, she was a midwife.

original: My wife descended of the Lacies,—
She was, indeed, a pedler's daughter, and sold many laces.
translation: Indeed, she was a pedlar's daughter and sold many laces.

original: But now of late, not able to travel with her furred pack, she washes bucks here at home.
translation: But recently, she is not able to travel with her pedlar's pack, so she washes her laundry here at home.

original: Therefore am I of an honourable house.
translation: So I come from an honorable house.

original: Ay, by my faith, the field is honourable; and there was he borne, under a hedge, for his father had never a house but the cage.
translation: Yes, indeed, the field is honorable. In fact he was born in a field, under a hedge, since his father never had a house but only a cage.

original: Valiant I am.
translation: I am brave.

original: A' must needs; for beggary is valiant.
translation: Yes, he must be. Since being a beggar is brave.

original: I am able to endure much.
translation: I am able to endure much.

original: No question of that; for I have seen him whipped three market-days together.
translation: There is no question of that, because I have seen him whipped at the market three days in a row.

original: I fear neither sword nor fire.
translation: I am not afraid of sword or fire.

original: He need not fear the sword; for his coat is of proof.
translation: He is not afraid of the sword, because his coat is so  that it serves as an impenetrable armor.

original: But methinks he should stand in fear of fire, being burnt i' the hand for stealing of sheep.
translation: But I think that he should be afraid of fire, since he was branded on the hand for stealing sheep.

original: Be brave, then; for your captain is brave, and vows   reformation. There shall be in England seven   halfpenny loaves sold for a penny: the three-hooped   pot; shall have ten hoops and I will make it felony   to drink small beer:
translation: Be brave, then, because your captain is brave and he promises you major changes. There will be seven halfpenny loaves of bread sold for a penny in England; the  three-hooped pot shall have ten hoops;  and I will make it a crime to drink weak beer.

original: all the realm shall be in   common; and in Cheapside shall my palfrey go to   grass: and when I am king, as king I will be,—
translation: Everything in the country will be a common resource. My riding horse will go to graze on  Cheapside . And when I am king, because I  will  be king—

original: God save your majesty!
translation: God save your majesty!

original: I thank you, good people: there shall be no money;
translation: I thank you, good people. There will be no money.

original: all shall eat and drink on my score; and I will   apparel them all in one livery, that they may agree   like brothers and worship me their lord.
translation: Everyone will eat and drink on me, and I will dress them all in one uniform, so that they may get on like brothers and worship me, their lord.

original: The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers.
translation: The first thing we'll do is kill all the lawyers.

original: Nay, that I mean to do. Is not this a lamentable   thing, that of the skin of an innocent lamb should   be made parchment? That parchment, being scribbled   o'er, should undo a man?
translation: No, that's my plan. Isn't it a miserable thing, that the skin of an innocent lamb is made into parchment? And that parchment is written on and then condemns a man?

original: Some say the bee stings:   but I say, 'tis the bee's wax; for I did but seal   once to a thing, and I was never mine own man   since. How now! Who's there?
translation: Some say that the bee stings, but I say it's the bee's sealing wax, because I put my name on a document once and I haven't been my own person ever since. What's this? Who's there?

original: The clerk of Chartham: he can write and read and cast accompt.
translation: The clerk of Chartham. He can write and read and add up accounts.

original: O monstrous!
translation: Oh, how unnatural!

original: We took him setting of boys' copies.
translation: We found him preparing written exercises for schoolboys.

original: Here's a villain!
translation: Here's a villain!

original: Has a book in his pocket with red letters in't.
translation: He has a book in his pocket with the saints' days printed in red.

original: Nay, then, he is a conjurer.
translation: Ah, well, then he is a magician.

original: Nay, he can make obligations, and write court-hand.
translation: No, he can draw up legal bonds and write legal documents.

original: I am sorry for't: the man is a proper man, of mine honour; unless I find him guilty, he shall not die. Come hither, sirrah, I must examine thee: what is thy  name?
translation: I am sorry for that. The man is a fine man, by my honor. Unless I find him guilty, he won't die. Come here, sir, I must question you. What's your name?

original: Emmanuel.
They use to write it on the top of letters: 'twill go hard with you.
translation: They used to write it on the top of letters. It will be worse with you.

original: Let me alone. Dost thou use to write thy name? Or hast thou a mark to thyself, like an honest plain-dealing man?
Sir, I thank God, I have been so well brought up that I can write my name.
translation: Sir, I thank God, I have been so well brought up that I can write my name.

original: He hath confessed: away with him! He's a villain and a traitor.
translation: He has confessed it! Take him away! He's a villain and a traitor.

original: Away with him, I say! Hang him with his pen and ink-horn about his neck.
translation: Take him away, I say! Hang him with his pen and inkwell around his neck.

original: Where's our general?
translation: Where is our general?

original: Here I am, thou particular fellow.
translation: Here I am, man.

original: Fly, fly, fly! Sir Humphrey Stafford and his brother are hard by, with the king's forces.
translation: Run, run run! Sir Humphrey Stafford and his brother are close with the king's armies.

original: Stand, villain, stand, or I'll fell thee down. He shall be encountered with a man as good as himself: he is but a knight, is a'?
translation: Wait, villain, wait! Or I'll stop you. He's picking a fight with a man as good as himself. He's nothing but a knight, right?

original: No.
translation: No, nothing but a knight.

original: To equal him, I will make myself a knight presently.
translation: To match him, I'll make myself into a knight right now.

original: Rise up Sir John Mortimer.
translation: Stand up, Sir John Mortimer.

original: Now have at him!
translation: Now, let's have him!

original: Rebellious hinds, the filth and scum of Kent,   Mark'd for the gallows, lay your weapons down;
translation: Rebellious peasants, the filth and scum of Kent, ready for the gallows—put your weapons down.

original: Home to your cottages, forsake this groom:   The king is merciful, if you revolt.
translation: Go home to your cottages; abandon this servant Cade. The king will have mercy, if you surrender.

original: But angry, wrathful, and inclined to blood, If you go forward; therefore yield, or die.
translation: But if you are angry, mad, and bloodthirsty, and if you go ahead, you'll either surrender or you'll die.

original: As for these silken-coated slaves, I pass not: It is to you, good people, that I speak, Over whom, in time to come, I hope to reign; For I am rightful heir unto the crown.
translation: I don't care for these slaves with silk coats on. It is to you, good people, that I speak. I hope to rule over you in time to come, because I am the rightful heir to the crown!

original: Villain, thy father was a plasterer; And thou thyself a shearman, art thou not?
translation: Villain, your father was a plasterer. And you yourself are a man who shears wool, aren't you?

original: And Adam was a gardener.
translation: And Adam was a gardener.

original: And what of that?
translation: So what?

original: Marry, this: Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March. Married the Duke of Clarence' daughter, did he not?
translation: So this: Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March married the Duke of Clarence's daughter, didn't he?

original: Ay, sir.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: By her he had two children at one birth.
translation: He had twins with her.

original: That's false.
translation: That's not true.

original: Ay, there's the question; but I say, 'tis true:   The elder of them, being put to nurse,   Was by a beggar-woman stolen away;
translation: Yes, that's the question. But I say that it is true. The elder of them was given to the nurse to be breastfed, and the baby was stolen away by a beggar woman.

original: And, ignorant of his birth and parentage,   Became a bricklayer when he came to age:   His son am I; deny it, if you can.
translation: He didn't know about his birth or parentage and so he became a bricklayer when he grew up. I am his son. Deny it if you can.

original: Nay, 'tis too true; therefore he shall be king.
translation: No, it's too true! So he should be king.

original: Sir, he made a chimney in my father's house, and the bricks are alive at this day to testify it; therefore deny it not.
translation: Sir, he built a chimney in my father's house and the bricks are still there today to testify it. So don't deny it.

original: And will you credit this base drudge's words, That speaks he knows not what?
translation: And will you believe the words of this lowly slave that doesn't know what he is talking about?

original: Ay, marry, will we; therefore get ye gone.
translation: Yes, we will. So go away!

original: Jack Cade, the Duke of York hath taught you this.
translation: Jack Cade, the Duke of York has told you to do this.

original: [Aside]   He lies, for I invented it myself.   Go to, sirrah, tell the king from me, that, for his   father's sake,
translation: [To himself]  He's wrong, since I made it up myself.  [Aloud]  Go, sir, tell the king from me that for his father's sake—

original: Henry the Fifth, in whose time boys   went to span-counter for French crowns, I am content   he shall reign; but I'll be protector over him.
translation: Henry the Fifth, in whose time boys fought the French— I am happy that he's king. But I'll be his protector.

original: And furthermore, we'll have the Lord Say's head for selling the dukedom of Maine.
translation: And moreover, we'll have the Lord Say's head for selling the dukedom of Maine.

original: And good reason; for thereby is England mained, and   fain to go with a staff, but that my puissance holds   it up.
translation: And for good reason. Because of him, England is now maimed, obliged to walk with a staff, and only my power holds it up.

original: Fellow kings, I tell you that that Lord Say   hath gelded the commonwealth, and made it an eunuch:   and more than that, he can speak French; and   therefore he is a traitor.
translation: Fellow kings, I tell you that Lord Say has castrated the commonwealth and made it an eunuch. And worse than that, he can speak French, and therefore he is a traitor.

original: O gross and miserable ignorance!
translation: Oh, utter and pitiable ignorance!

original: Nay, answer, if you can: the Frenchmen are our   enemies;
translation: No, answer if you can. The French are our enemies.

original: go to, then, I ask but this: can he that   speaks with the tongue of an enemy be a good   counsellor, or no?
translation: You can leave after I ask you this: can someone who speaks the language of the enemy be a good counselor, or not?

original: No, no; and therefore we'll have his head.
translation: No, no; and so we'll have his head!

original: Well, seeing gentle words will not prevail, Assail them with the army of the king.
translation: Well, since peaceable words won't work, attack them with the king's army.

original: Herald, away; and throughout every town   Proclaim them traitors that are up with Cade;
translation: Messenger, go and proclaim in every town that those who are fighting alongside Cade are traitors.

original: That those which fly before the battle ends   May, even in their wives' and children's sight,   Be hang'd up for example at their doors:   And you that be the king's friends, follow me.
translation: And announce that those who try to run away before the battle ends may be hanged at their own doors as an example, even in the sight of their wives and children. All of you that fight for the king, follow me!

original: And you that love the commons, follow me.   Now show yourselves men; 'tis for liberty.   We will not leave one lord, one gentleman:
translation: And you that love the common people, follow me! Now show yourselves, men; this fight is for freedom. We won't spare one lord or one gentleman.

original: Spare none but such as go in clouted shoon;   For they are thrifty honest men, and such   As would, but that they dare not, take our parts.
translation: Don't spare anyone but people who wear patched shoes, because they are respectable honest men and would be on our side, if they dared.

original: They are all in order and march toward us.
translation: They are all in order for battle and are marching towards us!

original: But then are we in order when we are most out of order. Come, march forward.
translation: But we are most ordered when we are out of order and rebellious. Come, let's march forward!

original: Where's Dick, the butcher of Ashford?
translation: Where's Dick, the butcher of Ashford?

original: Here, sir.
translation: Here, sir.

original: They fell before thee like sheep and oxen, and thou   behavedst thyself as if thou hadst been in thine own   slaughter-house:
translation: They fell before you like sheep and oxen, and you behaved as if you had been in your own slaughter-house.

original: therefore thus will I reward thee,   the Lent shall be as long again as it is; and thou   shalt have a licence to kill for a hundred lacking   one.
translation: Therefore, I will reward you.  Lent  will be twice as long and you'll have receive a special butcher's Lent license to kill ninety-nine animals.

original: I desire no more.
translation: I want nothing more.

original: And, to speak truth, thou deservest no less. This monument of the victory will I bear;
translation: And to tell you the truth, you deserve nothing less. I'll take this memorial trophy of victory—

original: and the bodies shall be dragged at my horse' heels till I do come to London, where we will have the mayor's sword borne before us.
translation: and the bodies will be dragged behind my horse until I come to London, where we will have the mayor's sword carried before us.

original: If we mean to thrive and do good, break open the gaols and let out the prisoners.
translation: If we mean to be successful and do something good, break into the prisons and release the prisoners.

original: Fear not that, I warrant thee. Come, let's march towards London.
translation: Don't worry, I assure you I will. Come on, let's march towards London.

original: Oft have I heard that grief softens the mind,   And makes it fearful and degenerate;   Think therefore on revenge and cease to weep.
translation: I have often heard that grief softens the mind, making it deteriorate with fear. So I should think about revenge and stop crying.

original: But who can cease to weep and look on this?   Here may his head lie on my throbbing breast:   But where's the body that I should embrace?
translation: But who can stop crying and look at this? His head may lie on my heaving chest, but where is the body that I would like to embrace?

original: What answer makes your grace to the rebels' supplication?
translation: What do you say to the rebels' petition, your grace?

original: I'll send some holy bishop to entreat;   For God forbid so many simple souls   Should perish by the sword!
translation: I'll send a holy bishop to meet with them. God forbid that so many ordinary people should die violently!

original: And I myself,   Rather than bloody war shall cut them short,   Will parley with Jack Cade their general:   But stay, I'll read it over once again.
translation: Rather than let them die in a bloody war, I'll go myself to negotiate with their general Jack Cade. But wait, I'll read it over once again.

original: Ah, barbarous villains! Hath this lovely face   Ruled, like a wandering planet, over me,
translation: Oh, barbaric villains! How did this lovely face rule over me like a moving planet,

original: And could it not enforce them to relent,   That were unworthy to behold the same?
translation: but wasn't able to force them to have mercy, since they were unworthy to look at him?

original: Lord Say, Jack Cade hath sworn to have thy head.
translation: Lord Say, Jack Cade swore that he will have your head.

original: Ay, but I hope your highness shall have his.
translation: Yes, but I hope that your highness shall have his.

original: How now, madam!   Still lamenting and mourning for Suffolk's death?
translation: How are you, madam? Are you still sad and grieving Suffolk's death?

original: I fear me, love, if that I had been dead,   Thou wouldst not have mourn'd so much for me.
translation: I am afraid that if I had been dead, love, you wouldn't have grieved so much for me.

original: No, my love, I should not mourn, but die for thee.
translation: No, my love. I wouldn't have grieved, but I would have died for you.

original: How now! What news? Why comest thou in such haste?
translation: What's the news? Why are you in such a hurry?

original: The rebels are in Southwark; fly, my lord!   Jack Cade proclaims himself Lord Mortimer,   Descended from the Duke of Clarence' house,   And calls your grace usurper openly   And vows to crown himself in Westminster.
translation: The rebels are in  Southwark . Run away, my lord! Jack Cade claims that he is Lord Mortimer, descended from the Duke of Clarence's house, and he openly calls you a usurper and swears that he will crown himself in Westminster.

original: His army is a ragged multitude   Of hinds and peasants, rude and merciless:   Sir Humphrey Stafford and his brother's death   Hath given them heart and courage to proceed:
translation: His army is a weary large group of servants and peasants, rough and merciless. The deaths of Sir Humphrey Stafford and his brother have given them strength and courage to carry on.

original: All scholars, lawyers, courtiers, gentlemen,   They call false caterpillars, and intend their death.
translation: They call all scholars, lawyers, courtiers and gentlemen treacherous parasites, and plan to kill them.

original: O graceless men! They know not what they do.
translation: Oh, ignorant men! They don't know what they're doing.

original: My gracious lord, return to Killingworth, Until a power be raised to put them down.
translation: My gracious lord, return to Killingworth, until an army is put together to stop them.

original: Ah, were the Duke of Suffolk now alive, These Kentish rebels would be soon appeased!
translation: Ah, if the Duke of Suffolk were alive now, these Kentish rebels would be defeated very soon!

original: Lord Say, the traitors hate thee; Therefore away with us to Killingworth.
translation: Lord Say, the traitors hate you. So come away with us to Killingworth.

original: So might your grace's person be in danger. The sight of me is odious in their eyes; And therefore in this city will I stay And live alone as secret as I may.
translation: Then your grace might be in danger. They hate the sight of me. So I will stay in this city and go into hiding.

original: Jack Cade hath gotten London bridge:   The citizens fly and forsake their houses:
translation: Jack Cade has gotten to London bridge. The citizens are running away and abandoning their houses.

original: The rascal people, thirsting after prey,   Join with the traitor, and they jointly swear   To spoil the city and your royal court.
translation: The rabble, thirsting after their prey, has joined the traitor. They all swear to plunder the city and your royal court.

original: Then linger not, my lord, away, take horse.
translation: Then let's not stay here any longer. My lord, let's go, take a horse!

original: Come, Margaret; God, our hope, will succor us.
translation: Come, Margaret. God, our hope, will help us.

original: My hope is gone, now Suffolk is deceased.
translation: My hope is gone now that Suffolk is dead.

original: Farewell, my lord: trust not the Kentish rebels.
translation: Goodbye, my lord. Don't trust these Kentish rebels.

original: Trust nobody, for fear you be betray'd.
translation: Don't trust anyone or you may be betrayed.

original: The trust I have is in mine innocence, And therefore am I bold and resolute.
translation: I only trust my own innocence, and that's why I am brave and determined.

original: How now! Is Jack Cade slain?
translation: What's this? Is Jack Cade dead?

original: No, my lord, nor likely to be slain; for they have   won the bridge, killing all those that withstand   them:
translation: No, my lord. Nor is he likely to be killed, because they have taken over London Bridge, killing everyone who stood in their way.

original: the lord mayor craves aid of your honour from   the Tower, to defend the city from the rebels.
translation: The lord mayor requests your help from the Tower, to defend the city from the rebels.

original: Such aid as I can spare you shall command;   But I am troubled here with them myself;   The rebels have assay'd to win the Tower.
translation: I'll help as much as I can. But I am also struggling to hold them off here. The rebels are trying to conquer the Tower.

original: But get you to Smithfield, and gather head,   And thither I will send you Matthew Goffe;   Fight for your king, your country and your lives;   And so, farewell, for I must hence again.
translation: But go to Smithfield and raise an army there, and I will send  Matthew Goffe  along with you. Fight for your king, your country, and your lives. And, so goodbye. I have to go back again!

original: Now is Mortimer lord of this city. And here, sitting   upon London-stone, I charge and command that, of the   city's cost, the pissing-conduit run nothing but   claret wine this first year of our reign
translation: Now Mortimer is the lord of this city. And here, sitting on the London-stone, I command that, at the city's cost, the  water fountain  will run nothing but red wine for the whole first year of our rule.

original: . And now   henceforward it shall be treason for any that calls   me other than Lord Mortimer.
translation: And from now on, it will be treason for anyone to call me anything else but Lord Mortimer.

original: Jack Cade! Jack Cade!
translation: Jack Cade! Jack Cade!

original: Knock him down there.
translation: Knock him down!

original: If this fellow be wise, he'll never call ye Jack Cade more: I think he hath a very fair warning.
translation: If this man is wise, he'll never call you Jack Cade again. I think he's had a fair warning.

original: My lord, there's an army gathered together in Smithfield.
translation: My lord, there is an army gathered in Smithfield.

original: Come, then, let's go fight with them; but first, go and set London bridge on fire; and, if you can, burn down the Tower too. Come, let's away.
translation: Come, then and let's go fight them. But first, go and set London Bridge on fire. And if you can, burn down the Tower too. Come, let's go.

original: So, sirs: now go some and pull down the Savoy; others to the Inns of Court; down with them all.
translation: So, sirs, now let's go and pull down the Savoy. Others, go to the Inns of Court and pull them all down.

original: I have a suit unto your lordship.
Be it a lordship, thou shalt have it for that word.
translation: If it is a lordship, your request will be granted for using that word.

original: Only that the laws of England may come out of your  mouth.
translation: I request that all the laws of England come from your mouth.

original: Mass, 'twill be sore law, then; for he was thrust in the mouth with a spear, and 'tis not whole yet.
translation: It will be a painful law, then, because he was stabbed in the mouth with a spear and it's not healed yet.

original: Nay, John, it will be stinking law for his breath stinks with eating toasted cheese.
translation: No, John, it will be a stinking law because his breath stinks from eating toasted cheese.

original: I have thought upon it, it shall be so. Away, burn all the records of the realm: my mouth shall be the parliament of England.
translation: I have thought about it; it shall be so. Go and burn all the records of the kingdom. My mouth will be the parliament of England.

original: Then we are like to have biting statutes, unless his teeth be pulled out.
translation: Then we will have severe statutes, unless his teeth are pulled out.

original: And henceforward all things shall be in common.
translation: And from now on all things will be shared.

original: My lord, a prize, a prize! Here's the Lord Say,   which sold the towns in France
translation: My lord, I have a prize for you! Here is the Lord Say, who sold the towns in France.

original: ; he that made us pay   one and twenty fifteens, and one shilling to the   pound, the last subsidy.
translation: He made us pay a tax of 140 per cent, and the last taxation was one shilling to the pound.

original: Well, he shall be beheaded for it ten times. Ah,   thou say, thou serge, nay, thou buckram lord! Now   art thou within point-blank of our jurisdiction   regal. What canst thou answer to my majesty for   giving up of Normandy unto Mounsieur Basimecu, the   dauphin of France?
translation: Well, he'll be beheaded for it ten times over. Ah, you silk fabric, you woollen fabric—no, you coarse linen! Now you are within the direct range of our legal power. How can you defend yourself to my majesty for giving up Normandy to Monsieur  Basimecu , the dauphin of France?

original: Be it known unto thee by these   presence, even the presence of Lord Mortimer, that I   am the besom that must sweep the court clean of such   filth as thou art. Thou hast most traitorously   corrupted the youth of the realm in erecting a   grammar school; and whereas, before, our forefathers   had no other books but the score and the tally, thou   hast caused printing to be used, and, contrary to   the king, his crown and dignity, thou hast built a   paper-mill.
translation: Let it be known to you all in the presence of Lord Mortimer, that I am the broom that must sweep the court clean of dirt like you. You have traitorously corrupted the youth of the country by setting up a grammar school, and while our ancestors had no other books but the  score and tally  to keep accounts, you've used printing. Against the crown and dignity of the king, you have built a paper mill.

original: It will be proved to thy face that thou   hast men about thee that usually talk of a noun and   a verb, and such abominable words as no Christian   ear can endure to hear.
translation: It will be proved to your face that you have men around you that usually talk about "nouns" and "verbs" and similar abominable words than no Christian ear can dare to hear.

original: Thou hast appointed   justices of peace, to call poor men before them   about matters they were not able to answer.   Moreover, thou hast put them in prison
translation: You have appointed justices of peace, to call poor men in front of them and ask them about things they didn't understand. Moreover, you have put them in prison;

original: ; and because   they could not read, thou hast hanged them; when,   indeed, only for that cause they have been most   worthy to live. Thou dost ride in a foot-cloth, dost  thou not?
translation: and because they couldn't read, you have hanged them for the one reason why they were worthy to live. Your horse has an ornamental cloth draped over him when you ride, doesn't he?

original: What of that?
translation: And why does that matter?

original: Marry, thou oughtest not to let thy horse wear a cloak, when honester men than thou go in their hose and doublets.
translation: You shouldn't let your horse wear a cloak, when men more honest than you only wear breeches and jacket with no other garment.

original: And work in their shirt too; as myself, for example, that am a butcher.
translation: And they work in their shirt too—like myself, for example, a butcher.

original: You men of Kent,—
translation: You men of Kent—

original: What say you of Kent?
translation: What are you saying about Kent?

original: Nothing but this; 'tis 'bona terra, mala gens.'
Away with him, away with him! He speaks Latin.
translation: Take him away, take him away! He speaks Latin.

original: Hear me but speak, and bear me where you will.   Kent, in the Commentaries Caesar writ,   Is term'd the civil'st place of this isle:   Sweet is the country, because full of riches;   The people liberal, valiant, active, wealthy;   Which makes me hope you are not void of pity.
translation: Hear me speak a little and then take me wherever you like. Kent, in the Commentaries Caesar wrote, is called the most civil place on this island. The country is called sweet, because it's full of wealth. The people are called generous, brave, active and wealthy, which makes me hope you have some pity.

original: I sold not Maine, I lost not Normandy,   Yet, to recover them, would lose my life.   Justice with favour have I always done;   Prayers and tears have moved me, gifts could never.
translation: I didn't sell Maine, nor did I lose Normandy. To take them back would have killed me. I have always been compassionate when I had to carry out justice. Prayers and tears have moved me, but bribes never could.

original: When have I aught exacted at your hands,   But to maintain the king, the realm and you?   Large gifts have I bestow'd on learned clerks,   Because my book preferr'd me to the king,   And seeing ignorance is the curse of God,   Knowledge the wing wherewith we fly to heaven,
translation: When have I raised any taxes, except when it was necessary to satisfy the king, the country, and you? I have given large gifts to scholars, because the king valued me for my learning. And seeing ignorance is the curse of God, knowledge is the wing on which we fly to heaven.

original: Unless you be possess'd with devilish spirits,   You cannot but forbear to murder me:   This tongue hath parley'd unto foreign kings   For your behoof,—
translation: Unless you are possessed with evil spirits, you can't murder me. This tongue has negotiated with foreign kings for your benefit—

original: Tut, when struck'st thou one blow in the field?
translation: Please, tell me, when did you fight in the field?

original: Great men have reaching hands: oft have I struck Those that I never saw and struck them dead.
translation: Great men have hands that can reach far. I have often fought those that I never saw in person, and killed them too.

original: O monstrous coward! What, to come behind folks?
translation: Oh, you monstrous coward! Did you attack from behind?

original: These cheeks are pale for watching for your good.
translation: These cheeks are pale because I remained awake for your own good.

original: Give him a box o' the ear and that will make 'em red  again.
translation: Slap him; that will bring color to his cheeks.

original: Long sitting to determine poor men's causes Hath made me full of sickness and diseases.
translation: I've spent a long time sitting as a judge to settle poor men's cases, and it's made me sick and diseased.

original: Ye shall have a hempen caudle, then, and the help of  hatchet.
translation: You will have a hangman's rope, then, and the help of the executioner's axe.

original: Why dost thou quiver, man?
translation: Why do you shake, man?

original: The palsy, and not fear, provokes me.
translation: It is palsy and not fear that makes me shake.

original: Nay, he nods at us, as who should say, I'll be even with you: I'll see if his head will stand steadier on a pole, or no. Take him away, and behead him.
translation: No, he nods at us like one who would say, I'll be be fair with you. I'll see if his head will stand steady on a pole or not. Take him away and behead him.

original: Tell me wherein have I offended most?   Have I affected wealth or honour? Speak.   Are my chests fill'd up with extorted gold?   Is my apparel sumptuous to behold?
translation: Tell me, what have I done to offend you? Have I taken your wealth or honor? Tell me. Are my chests filled with stolen money? Do my clothes look luxurious?

original: Whom have I injured, that ye seek my death?   These hands are free from guiltless bloodshedding,   This breast from harbouring foul deceitful thoughts.   O, let me live!
translation: Whom have I hurt, that you want me dead? These hands are guiltless of shedding innocent blood. This heart is guiltless of having bad, deceitful feelings. Oh, let me live!

original: [Aside]   I feel remorse in myself with his words;   but I'll bridle it: he shall die, an it be but for   pleading so well for his life.
translation: [To himself]  I feel pity inside when he speaks. But I'll restrain it. He shall die, even if it's just for pleading for his life.

original: [Aloud.]   Away with him!  He   has a familiar under his tongue; he speaks not o'   God's name.
translation: [Aloud.]  Take him away! He has a demon under his tongue; he doesn't speak God's language.

original: It shall be done.
translation: It shall be done.

original: Ah, countrymen! If when you make your prayers, God should be so obdurate as yourselves, How would it fare with your departed souls? And therefore yet relent, and save my life.
Away with him! And do as I command ye.
translation: Take him away! And do as I ordered you.

original: The proudest peer in the realm shall not wear a head   on his shoulders, unless he pay me tribute; there   shall not a maid be married, but she shall pay to me   her maidenhead ere they have it:
translation: The proudest man in the country won't wear a head on his shoulders, unless he gives me a payment as an act of homage. A virgin won't be married before she gives me her virginity.

original: men shall hold of   me in capite; and we charge and command that their   wives be as free as heart can wish or tongue can tell.
translation: Men will hold property directly from the crown, and we charge and command that their wives will be as sexually available as a heart can wish or tongue can tell.

original: My lord, when shall we go to Cheapside and take up commodities upon our bills?
translation: My lord, when will we go to Cheapside and spear decapitated heads on our weapons?

original: Marry, presently.
translation: Soon.

original: O, brave!
translation: Oh, that's marvelous!

original: But is not this braver? Let them kiss one another,   for they loved well when they were alive. Now part   them again, lest they consult about the giving up of   some more towns in France.
translation: But isn't this even better? Let them kiss each other because they loved each other well when they were alive. Now break them apart again, lest they talk about giving up some more towns in France.

original: Soldiers, defer the   spoil of the city until night: for with these borne   before us, instead of maces, will we ride through   the streets, and at every corner have them kiss. Away!
translation: Soldiers, delay the plunder of the city until tonight. We will ride through the streets with these heads carried before us instead of staffs of office, and have them kiss at every corner. Let's go!

original: Up Fish Street! Down Saint Magnus' Corner! Kill and knock down! Throw them into Thames!
translation: Let's go up Fish Street! Down Saint Magnus' Corner! Kill and knock everything down! Throw them into the Thames!

original: What noise is this I hear? Dare any be so bold to sound retreat or parley, when I command them kill?
translation: What's that noise? Does anyone dare to sound a retreat or ask for negotiation, when I commanded them to fight?

original: Ay, here they be that dare and will disturb thee:   Know, Cade, we come ambassadors from the king   Unto the commons whom thou hast misled;
translation: Yes, we're here to dare and disturb you. Cade, you should know that we are ambassadors from the king to the commoners, whom you have misled.

original: And here pronounce free pardon to them all   That will forsake thee and go home in peace.
translation: We offer a free pardon to all of them that will abandon you and go home in peace.

original: What say ye, countrymen? Will ye relent,   And yield to mercy whilst 'tis offer'd you;   Or let a rebel lead you to your deaths?   Who loves the king and will embrace his pardon,   Fling up his cap, and say 'God save his majesty!'
translation: What do you say, countrymen? Will you stop and surrender to the mercy that is offered to you, or let a rebel lead you to your deaths? Whoever loves the king and will accept his pardon, throw your cap in the air and say "God save his majesty!"

original: Who hateth him and honours not his father,   Henry the Fifth, that made all France to quake,   Shake he his weapon at us and pass by.
translation: Whoever hates him and doesn't honor his father, Henry the Fifth—who made all of France shake—shake your weapon in defiance and pass us by.

original: God save the king! God save the king!
translation: God save the king! God save the king!

original: What, Buckingham and Clifford, are ye so brave? And   you, base peasants, do ye believe him? Will you   needs be hanged with your pardons about your necks?   Hath my sword therefore broke through London gates,   that you should leave me at the White Hart in   Southwark?
translation: Are Buckingham and Clifford so bold? And you, lowly peasants, do you believe him? Will you be hanged with your pardons around your necks? Has my sword broke through London gates so you should leave me at the  White Hart  in Southwark?
