original: I thought ye would never have given out   these arms till you had recovered your ancient   freedom: but you are all recreants and dastards,   and delight to live in slavery to the nobility.
translation: I thought you would never have given up these weapons until you have regained your ancient freedom. But you are all deserters and cowards, and want to live like slaves to the nobility.

original: Let   them break your backs with burthens, take your   houses over your heads, ravish your wives and   daughters before your faces: for me, I will make   shift for one; and so, God's curse light upon you   all!
translation: Let them break your backs with burdens, take your houses over your heads, rape your wives and daughters in front of you. I, on the other hand, will look out for myself. and so, God's curse on you all!

original: We'll follow Cade, we'll follow Cade!
translation: We'll follow Cade, we'll follow Cade!

original: Is Cade the son of Henry the Fifth,   That thus you do exclaim you'll go with him?   Will he conduct you through the heart of France,   And make the meanest of you earls and dukes?
translation: Is Cade the son of Henry the Fifth? Is that why you scream that you will follow him? Will he take you through the heart of France and make the most humble of you earls and dukes?

original: Alas, he hath no home, no place to fly to;   Nor knows he how to live but by the spoil,   Unless by robbing of your friends and us.   Were't not a shame, that whilst you live at jar,   The fearful French, whom you late vanquished,   Should make a start o'er seas and vanquish you?
translation: No, he has no home and no place to run to, and he doesn't know how to live except by plundering—stealing from your friends and us. Wouldn't it be a shame if while you're rebelling, the terrible French, whom you have recently crushed, were to suddenly invade and crush you?

original: Methinks already in this civil broil   I see them lording it in London streets,   Crying 'Villiago!' unto all they meet.   Better ten thousand base-born Cades miscarry   Than you should stoop unto a Frenchman's mercy.   To France, to France, and get what you have lost;
translation: I think that I can already see them in this civil war, taking over London streets, screaming "Foreigners!" at everyone they meet. It would be better if ten thousand lowly-born Cades should die, rather than leaving you at the mercy of the French. To France, to France, and go get what you have lost.

original: Spare England, for it is your native coast;   Henry hath money, you are strong and manly;   God on our side, doubt not of victory.
translation: Spare England, because it is your native country. Henry has money, you are strong and manly, and God is on our side, so don't doubt that we'll win.

original: A Clifford! A Clifford! We'll follow the king and  Clifford.
translation: To Clifford! To Clifford! We'll follow the king and Clifford.

original: Was ever feather so lightly blown to and fro as this   multitude? The name of Henry the Fifth hales them   to an hundred mischiefs, and makes them leave me   desolate. I see them lay their heads together to   surprise me.
translation: Was there ever a feather blown back and forth as lightly as this crowd? The name of Henry the Fifth moves them and makes them abandon me. I can see them putting their heads together to capture me.

original: My sword make way for me, for here is   no staying. In despite of the devils and hell, have   through the very middest of you?
translation: Make way for me, my sword, since I'm not staying here. In spite of the devils and hell, I'll cut my way through the middle of the crowd.

original: And heavens and   honour be witness, that no want of resolution in me.   But only my followers' base and ignominious   treasons, makes me betake me to my heels.
translation: Heavens and honor be witness that I'm running not because I'm a coward, but only because the lowly and humiliating desertion of my followers make me run away from here.

original: What, is he fled? Go some, and follow him; And he that brings his head unto the king Shall have a thousand crowns for his reward.
translation: Has he run away? Go, some of you, and follow him. Whoever brings his head to the king will have a reward of thousand crowns.

original: Follow me, soldiers: we'll devise a mean To reconcile you all unto the king.
translation: Follow me, soldiers. We'll come up with a way to reconcile you all with the king.

original: Was ever king that joy'd an earthly throne,   And could command no more content than I?   No sooner was I crept out of my cradle   But I was made a king, at nine months old.
translation: Was there ever a king that enjoyed this earthly throne and was more miserable than me? As soon as I crept out of my cradle, nine months old, I was made a king.

original: Was never subject long'd to be a king   As I do long and wish to be a subject.
translation: No commoner wants to be a king as much as I want to be a commoner.

original: Health and glad tidings to your majesty!
translation: We wish health and good news to your majesty!

original: Why, Buckingham, is the traitor Cade surprised? Or is he but retired to make him strong?
translation: Is the traitor Cade captured, Buckingham? Or has he retreated to gather his strength?

original: He is fled, my lord, and all his powers do yield; And humbly thus, with halters on their necks, Expect your highness' doom of life or death.
translation: He has escaped, my lord, and all his soldiers surrendered. With ropes around their necks, they humbly await your sentence of life or death.

original: Then, heaven, set ope thy everlasting gates,   To entertain my vows of thanks and praise!   Soldiers, this day have you redeemed your lives,   And show'd how well you love your prince and country:
translation: Then, heaven, open your everlasting gates to receive my vows of thanks and praise! Soldiers, you have redeemed your lives today and showed how well you love your king and country.

original: Continue still in this so good a mind,   And Henry, though he be infortunate,   Assure yourselves, will never be unkind:   And so, with thanks and pardon to you all,   I do dismiss you to your several countries.
translation: Carry on in this spirit and Henry, although he is unfortunate, promises you that he will never be unkind. And so I send you back to your homes, with thanks and pardon.

original: God save the king! God save the king!
translation: God save the king! God save the king!

original: Please it your grace to be advertised   The Duke of York is newly come from Ireland,   And with a puissant and a mighty power   Of gallowglasses and stout kerns   Is marching hitherward in proud array,
translation: Your grace should know that the Duke of York has just come from Ireland with a powerful and strong army of  Irish soldiers . They are marching this way, ready for a fight.

original: Thus stands my state, 'twixt Cade and York distress'd. Like to a ship that, having 'scaped a tempest, Is straightway calm'd and boarded with a pirate: But now is Cade driven back, his men dispersed; And now is York in arms to second him. I pray thee, Buckingham, go and meet him, And ask him what's the reason of these arms. Tell him I'll send Duke Edmund to the Tower; And, Somerset, we'll commit thee thither, Until his army be dismiss'd from him.
My lord, I'll yield myself to prison willingly, Or unto death, to do my country good.
translation: My lord, I surrender to go to prison willingly. Or go to my death, to do some good for my country.

original: In any case, be not too rough in terms; For he is fierce and cannot brook hard language.
translation: Either way, don't be too harsh in your choice of language. He is fierce and cannot tolerate such language.

original: I will, my lord; and doubt not so to deal As all things shall redound unto your good.
translation: I will, my lord, and don't doubt that I shall negotiate so that everything will turn out well for you.

original: Come, wife, let's in, and learn to govern better; For yet may England curse my wretched reign.
translation: Come, wife, let's go in and learn to rule better. England may curse my horrible rule up until now.

original: Fie on ambition! Fie on myself, that have a sword,   and yet am ready to famish! These five days have I   hid me in these woods and durst not peep out, for   all the country is laid for me;
translation: To hell with ambition! To hell with me, who has a sword but will starve anyway! I have been hiding in these woods for these past five days and didn't dare to come out, because the entire country is looking for me.

original: but now am I so   hungry that if I might have a lease of my life for a   thousand years I could stay no longer. Wherefore,   on a brick wall have I climbed into this garden, to   see if I can eat grass, or pick a sallet another   while, which is not amiss to cool a man's stomach   this hot weather.
translation: But now I am so hungry that even if I could stay alive for a thousand years here, I couldn't wait any longer. That's why I have climbed into this garden over a brick wall, to see if I can eat grass, or pick salad (leaves and vegetables), which is not bad to satisfy a man's appetite during this hot weather.

original: And I think this word 'sallet'   was born to do me good: for many a time, but for a   sallet, my brainpan had been cleft with a brown   bill; and many a time, when I have been dry and   bravely marching, it hath served me instead of a   quart pot to drink in; and now the word 'sallet'   must serve me to feed on.
translation: And I think that this word "salad" will do me some good. If I didn't have  it , my skull would have been cut in half by an ax. And often, when I have been thirsty and marching, I've used it as a pot to drink out of. Now the word "salad" has to be enough to feed me.

original: Lord, who would live turmoiled in the court,   And may enjoy such quiet walks as these?   This small inheritance my father left me   Contenteth me, and worth a monarchy.
translation: Who would live stressed in the court when you could enjoy such quiet walks like these? This small inheritance that my father left me makes me happy and it is worth a whole monarchy.

original: I seek not to wax great by others' waning,   Or gather wealth, I care not, with what envy:   Sufficeth that I have maintains my state   And sends the poor well pleased from my gate.
translation: I don't want to grow great by others' loss, or gather wealth, regardless of others' jealousy. It's enough that I have what I need and can send the poor from my gate with plenty of food.

original: Here's the lord of the soil come to seize me for a   stray, for entering his fee-simple without leave.   Ah, villain, thou wilt betray me, and get a thousand   crowns of the king carrying my head to him:
translation: Here is the owner of the garden who has come to catch me for trespassing, for entering his land without permission. Oh, villain, you will betray me and get a thousand crowns from the king when you carry my head to him.

original: but   I'll make thee eat iron like an ostrich, and swallow   my sword like a great pin, ere thou and I part.
translation: But I'll stab you and make you swallow my sword like an ostrich, before you and I say goodbye.

original: Why, rude companion, whatsoe'er thou be,   I know thee not; why, then, should I betray thee?
translation: Rough fellow! Whoever you are, I don't know you. Why, then, do you think that I will betray you?

original: Is't not enough to break into my garden,   And, like a thief, to come to rob my grounds,   Climbing my walls in spite of me the owner,   But thou wilt brave me with these saucy terms?
translation: Isn't it enough to break into my garden and steal from me like a thief, climbing my walls without the permission of the owner? Will you will also defy me with these rude words?

original: Brave thee! Ay, by the best blood that ever was   broached, and beard thee too. Look on me well: I   have eat no meat these five days;
translation: Defy you! Yes, by the best blood that was ever shed, I defy you! Look at me. I haven't eaten food for these last five days.

original: yet, come thou and   thy five men, and if I do not leave you all as dead   as a doornail, I pray God I may never eat grass more.
translation: Yet if you and your five servants come at me and I don't leave you as dead as a doornail, I pray to God that I never eat grass again.

original: Nay, it shall ne'er be said, while England stands,   That Alexander Iden, an esquire of Kent,   Took odds to combat a poor famish'd man.
translation: No, as long as England stands, it won't be said that Alexander Iden, a gentleman of Kent, accepted such an unequal challenge from a poor hungry man.

original: Oppose thy steadfast-gazing eyes to mine,   See if thou canst outface me with thy looks:   Set limb to limb, and thou art far the lesser;   Thy hand is but a finger to my fist,   Thy leg a stick compared with this truncheon;
translation: Look at me and see if you can defy me with your looks. Compare limb with limb and you will see that you are the weaker one. Your hand is only a finger compared to my whole fist, your leg is a stick compared to my leg.

original: My foot shall fight with all the strength thou hast;   And if mine arm be heaved in the air,   Thy grave is digg'd already in the earth.   As for words, whose greatness answers words,   Let this my sword report what speech forbears.
translation: My foot shall fight will all the strength you have and if I just raise my arm, you're as good as dead. As for words, the power of my sword answers them.

original: By my valour, the most complete champion that ever I   heard!
translation: By my bravery, you are the most accomplished fighter that I have ever heard of!

original: Steel, if thou turn the edge, or cut not out   the burly-boned clown in chines of beef ere thou   sleep in thy sheath, I beseech God on my knees thou   mayst be turned to hobnails.
translation: Sword, if you fail me and don't cut this heavily-built clown into strips of beef before you sleep in your sheath, I pray God on my knees that you may be melted down and turned into nails for boots.

original: O, I am slain! Famine and no other hath slain me:   let ten thousand devils come against me, and give me   but the ten meals I have lost, and I'll defy them   all.
translation: Oh, I'm murdered! Starvation and nothing else has killed me. Give me the ten meals that I have lost, and I could defeat ten thousand devils.

original: Wither, garden; and be henceforth a   burying-place to all that do dwell in this house,   because the unconquered soul of Cade is fled.
translation: Wither, garden, and from now on be a grave for everyone who lives in this house, because the unconquered soul of Cade is gone.

original: Is't Cade that I have slain, that monstrous traitor?   Sword, I will hollow thee for this thy deed,   And hang thee o'er my tomb when I am dead:
translation: Did I just kill the unnatural traitor Cade? Sword, I will bless you for this act and place you over my tomb when I am dead.

original: Ne'er shall this blood be wiped from thy point;   But thou shalt wear it as a herald's coat,   To emblaze the honour that thy master got.
translation: I'll never wipe off his blood, but you shall wear it like a herald's coat, to display the honor that your master has won.

original: Iden, farewell, and be proud of thy victory. Tell   Kent from me, she hath lost her best man
translation: Goodbye, Iden, and be proud of your victory. Tell Kent from me that she has lost her best man.

original: , and exhort   all the world to be cowards; for I, that never   feared any, am vanquished by famine, not by valour.
translation: Urge everyone to be cowards, because I—who has never been afraid of anyone—am now killed by starvation and not by bravery.

original: How much thou wrong'st me, heaven be my judge.   Die, damned wretch, the curse of her that bare thee;   And as I thrust thy body in with my sword,   So wish I, I might thrust thy soul to hell.
translation: Heaven will judge how you've wronged me. Die, damned man, the curse of the mother that gave birth to you. As I thrust my sword into your body, so I wish that I could send your soul to hell.

original: Hence will I drag thee headlong by the heels   Unto a dunghill which shall be thy grave,   And there cut off thy most ungracious head;   Which I will bear in triumph to the king,   Leaving thy trunk for crows to feed upon.
translation: I will drag you by the heels to a dunghill that will be your grave, and there I'll cut off your ungrateful head, which I will take triumphantly to the king, leaving the rest of your body for the crows to eat.

original: From Ireland thus comes York to claim his right,   And pluck the crown from feeble Henry's head:   Ring, bells, aloud; burn, bonfires, clear and bright,   To entertain great England's lawful king.
translation: Here comes York from Ireland to claim his right and take the crown from the head of weak Henry. Ring the bells loud and start bright bonfires to welcome great England's lawful king.

original: Ah! Sancta majestas, who would not buy thee dear?   Let them obey that know not how to rule;   This hand was made to handle naught but gold.
translation: Oh, sacred majesty, who wouldn't do anything to buy yo? Those don't know how to rule should obey instead. This hand was made to handle nothing but gold.

original: I cannot give due action to my words,   Except a sword or sceptre balance it:   A sceptre shall it have, have I a soul,   On which I'll toss the flower-de-luce of France.
translation: I can't make my words powerful enough to fit my actions, unless a sword or a scepter supports me. I'll have a scepter, that's as sure as I have a soul, on which I'll toss the  flower-de-luce  of France.

original: Whom have we here? Buckingham, to disturb me? The king hath sent him, sure: I must dissemble.
translation: Who do we have here? Does Buckingham come to disturb me? I am sure that the king has sent him. I must disguise the truth.

original: York, if thou meanest well, I greet thee well.
translation: York, I welcome you, if you mean well.

original: Humphrey of Buckingham, I accept thy greeting. Art thou a messenger, or come of pleasure?
translation: Humphrey of Buckingham, I accept your welcome. Are you a messenger, or do you come on your own initiative?

original: A messenger from Henry, our dread liege,   To know the reason of these arms in peace;   Or why thou, being a subject as I am,
translation: I am a messenger sent from Henry, our respected king, to find out why you've raised an army during peace time, and why you—since you're a subject just like me—

original: Against thy oath and true allegiance sworn,   Should raise so great a power without his leave,   Or dare to bring thy force so near the court.
translation: should do so without the king's permission and against your promise to be loyal to him. And how do you dare to bring your army so close to the court?

original: [Aside]   Scarce can I speak, my choler is so great:   O, I could hew up rocks and fight with flint,   I am so angry at these abject terms;   And now, like Ajax Telamonius,   On sheep or oxen could I spend my fury.
translation: [To himself]  I can barely speak, my anger is bubbling. Oh, I could cut down rocks and fight with a small stone; I am so angry at these insulting terms. And now, like  Ajax Telamonius,  I could slaughter a sheep or oxen to calm my anger.

original: I am far better born than is the king,   More like a king, more kingly in my thoughts:   But I must make fair weather yet a while,   Till Henry be more weak and I more strong,—
translation: I have a superior claim to the throne than the king; I am more like a king, because I have more kingly thoughts. But I must pretend to be agreeable for a while, until Henry is weaker and I am stronger.

original: Buckingham, I prithee, pardon me,   That I have given no answer all this while;   My mind was troubled with deep melancholy.   The cause why I have brought this army hither   Is to remove proud Somerset from the king,   Seditious to his grace and to the state.
translation: Buckingham, I am sorry, forgive me for not answering you for all this time. My mind is troubled with deep sadness. The reason why I have brought this army here is to remove proud Somerset's influence on the king. He is disloyal to the king and to the state.

original: That is too much presumption on thy part:   But if thy arms be to no other end,
translation: You expect too much. But if your army is here for no other reason,

original: The king hath yielded unto thy demand:   The Duke of Somerset is in the Tower.
translation: the king has agreed to your demand. The Duke of Somerset is in the Tower.

original: Upon thine honour, is he prisoner?
translation: Tell me, on your honor: is he a prisoner?

original: Upon mine honour, he is prisoner.
translation: On my honor, he is a prisoner.

original: Then, Buckingham, I do dismiss my powers.   Soldiers, I thank you all; disperse yourselves;   Meet me to-morrow in St. George's field,   You shall have pay and every thing you wish.
translation: Then, Buckingham, I will send away my army. Soldiers, thank you all, scatter yourselves. Meet me tomorrow in  St. George's field  and you'll have your wages and anything else you want.

original: And let my sovereign, virtuous Henry,   Command my eldest son, nay, all my sons,   As pledges of my fealty and love;   I'll send them all as willing as I live:   Lands, goods, horse, armour, any thing I have,   Is his to use, so Somerset may die.
translation: Ask my king, the virtuous Henry, to summon my eldest son—no, all of my sons, as pledges of my loyalty and love. I'll send them as willingly as I live. My lands, goods, horses, armor, and everything I have is his to use, provided that Somerset dies.

original: York, I commend this kind submission: We twain will go into his highness' tent.
translation: York, I praise this kind submission. We will go together to his highness' tent.

original: Buckingham, doth York intend no harm to us, That thus he marcheth with thee arm in arm?
translation: Buckingham, does York not intend harm us, since you come together arm in arm?

original: In all submission and humility York doth present himself unto your highness.
translation: York has come to your highness with submission and humility.

original: Then what intends these forces thou dost bring?
translation: Then why did you bring this army with you?

original: To heave the traitor Somerset from hence, And fight against that monstrous rebel Cade, Who since I heard to be discomfited.
translation: To take the traitor Somerset from here and fight that monstrous rebel Cade, who I have heard is now defeated.

original: If one so rude and of so mean condition   May pass into the presence of a king,   Lo, I present your grace a traitor's head,
translation: If someone so ignorant and of such low rank may come into the presence of a king, here is a traitor's head.

original: The head of Cade, whom I in combat slew.
translation: This is the head of Cade, who I killed in a one-on-one fight.

original: The head of Cade! Great God, how just art Thou! O, let me view his visage, being dead, That living wrought me such exceeding trouble. Tell me, my friend, art thou the man that slew him?
translation: The head of Cade! Great God, how just you are! Oh, let me see how he looks like now that he's dead, but caused me so much trouble when he was alive. Tell me, my friend, are you the man that killed him?

original: I was, an't like your majesty.
translation: I was, if it please your majesty.

original: How art thou call'd? And what is thy degree?
translation: What's your name and what is your rank?

original: Alexander Iden, that's my name; A poor esquire of Kent, that loves his king.
So please it you, my lord, 'twere not amiss He were created knight for his good service.
translation: If my king is happy with it, it wouldn't be out of place to make him a knight for this good service.

original: Iden, kneel down.
translation: Iden, kneel down.

original: Rise up a knight. We give thee for reward a thousand marks, And will that thou henceforth attend on us.
translation: Stand up a knight. We give you a thousand crowns as a reward and desire that you will attend on us from now on.

original: May Iden live to merit such a bounty. And never live but true unto his liege!
translation: May Iden live to be deserving of such a generosity and never live unless he is loyal to his king!

original: See, Buckingham, Somerset comes with the queen: Go, bid her hide him quickly from the duke.
translation: Buckingham, look—Somerset is coming with the queen. Go and tell her to hide him quickly from York.

original: For thousand Yorks he shall not hide his head, But boldly stand and front him to his face.
translation: He shall not hide his head even if there were thousand Yorks here, but he will bravely stand and confront him face to face.

original: How now! Is Somerset at liberty? Then, York, unloose thy long-imprison'd thoughts, And let thy tongue be equal with thy heart. Shall I endure the sight of Somerset? False king! Why hast thou broken faith with me, Knowing how hardly I can brook abuse? King did I call thee? No, thou art not king, Not fit to govern and rule multitudes, Which darest not, no, nor canst not rule a traitor. That head of thine doth not become a crown; Thy hand is made to grasp a palmer's staff, And not to grace an awful princely sceptre. That gold must round engirt these brows of mine, Whose smile and frown, like to Achilles' spear, Is able with the change to kill and cure. Here is a hand to hold a sceptre up And with the same to act controlling laws. Give place: by heaven, thou shalt rule no more O'er him whom heaven created for thy ruler.
O monstrous traitor! I arrest thee, York, Of capital treason 'gainst the king and crown; Obey, audacious traitor; kneel for grace.
translation: Oh, monstrous traitor! I arrest you, York, of capital treason against the king and the crown. Obey, audacious traitor. Kneel in front of your king.

original: Wouldst have me kneel? First let me ask of these, If they can brook I bow a knee to man. Sirrah, call in my sons to be my bail;
translation: Do you want me to kneel!? First, let me ask these attendants, if they can permit me to bow to any man. Sir, call my sons to come in and bail me out.

original: I know, ere they will have me go to ward, They'll pawn their swords for my enfranchisement.
translation: I know that before they will let me go to custody, they will bring out their swords to free me.

original: Call hither Clifford! Bid him come amain, To say if that the bastard boys of York Shall be the surety for their traitor father.
translation: Call Clifford! Tell him to come quickly to say whether the bastard boys of York shall be the assurance for their traitor father.

original: O blood-besotted Neapolitan, Outcast of Naples, England's bloody scourge! The sons of York, thy betters in their birth, Shall be their father's bail; and bane to those That for my surety will refuse the boys!
See where they come: I'll warrant they'll make it good.
translation: See where they come! I swear that they will make everything all right.

original: And here comes Clifford to deny their bail.
translation: And here comes Clifford to stop them from bailing you out.

original: Health and all happiness to my lord the king!
translation: I wish health and happiness to my lord the king!

original: I thank thee, Clifford: say, what news with thee? Nay, do not fright us with an angry look; We are thy sovereign, Clifford, kneel again; For thy mistaking so, we pardon thee.
translation: Thank you, Clifford! What's the news with you? No, don't look at so angrily. We are the king, Clifford, so kneel again. We excuse you for not doing so.

original: This is my king, York, I do not mistake; But thou mistakest me much to think I do: To Bedlam with him! Is the man grown mad?
translation: This is my king, York. I am not making a mistake. But you mistake me for thinking that I do. To the madhouse with him! Has he become mad?

original: Ay, Clifford; a bedlam and ambitious humour Makes him oppose himself against his king.
translation: Yes, Cliffors, a mad and ambitious mood makes him oppose himself against his king.

original: He is a traitor; let him to the Tower, And chop away that factious pate of his.
translation: He is a traitor, take him to the Tower and chop off his rebellious head.

original: He is arrested, but will not obey; His sons, he says, shall give their words for him.
translation: He is arrested but won't listen to us. He says that his sons will speak for him.

original: Will you not, sons?
translation: Won't you speak for me, sons?

original: Ay, noble father, if our words will serve.
translation: We will, noble father. If our words will be enough.

original: And if words will not, then our weapons shall.
translation: And if words won't be, then our weapons will.

original: Why, what a brood of traitors have we here!
translation: Ah, what a group of traitors do we have here!

original: Look in a glass, and call thy image so:   I am thy king, and thou a false-heart traitor.
translation: Look in a mirror and call yourself a traitor. I am your king and you are a disloyal traitor.

original: Call hither to the stake my two brave bears,   That with the very shaking of their chains   They may astonish these fell-lurking curs:   Bid Salisbury and Warwick come to me.
translation: Call my two brave bears to the  stake , to terrify these fierce dogs with the shaking of their chains. Tell Salisbury and Warwick to come here.

original: Are these thy bears? We'll bait thy bears to death. And manacle the bear-ward in their chains, If thou darest bring them to the baiting place.
translation: Are these your bears? We'll fight your bears until we kill them. And we'll put the bear-baiter in their chains, if you dare to bring them to the bear pit.

original: Oft have I seen a hot o'erweening cur   Run back and bite, because he was withheld;
translation: I have often seen an angry overexcited dog turn around and bite the dog handler, because he was stopped from fighting.

original: Who, being suffer'd with the bear's fell paw,   Hath clapp'd his tail between his legs and cried:   And such a piece of service will you do,   If you oppose yourselves to match Lord Warwick.
translation: The dog, hurt by the bear's savage paw, has put his tail between his legs and cried. And you'll be just like that, if you stand against Lord Warwick.

original: Hence, heap of wrath, foul indigested lump, As crooked in thy manners as thy shape!
Nay, we shall heat you thoroughly anon.
translation: No, we'll make you hot from fighting very soon.

original: Take heed, lest by your heat you burn yourselves.
translation: Be careful, unless you burn yourselves with that heat.

original: Why, Warwick, hath thy knee forgot to bow?   Old Salisbury, shame to thy silver hair,   Thou mad misleader of thy brain-sick son!   What, wilt thou on thy death-bed play the ruffian,   And seek for sorrow with thy spectacles?
translation: Why don't you kneel in front of me, Warwick? Old Salisbury, shame to your silver hair, you mad corrupter of your brain-sick son! Will you play a hooligan on your death-bed and look for sorrow with your glasses?

original: O, where is faith? O, where is loyalty?   If it be banish'd from the frosty head,   Where shall it find a harbour in the earth?   Wilt thou go dig a grave to find out war,   And shame thine honourable age with blood?
translation: Oh, where is faith? Oh, where is loyalty? If its banished from your old head, where shall it find a home anywhere in this world? Will you go and dig a grave to find war, and shame your honorable age with bloodshed?

original: Why art thou old, and want'st experience?   Or wherefore dost abuse it, if thou hast it?   For shame! In duty bend thy knee to me   That bows unto the grave with mickle age.
translation: Are you old and still lack experience? Or why do you misuse your wisdom, if you have it? Shame on you! Kneel dutifully in front of me, like old age kneels to the grave.

original: My lord, I have consider'd with myself   The title of this most renowned duke;
translation: My lord, I have considered the title of this renowned duke myself,

original: And in my conscience do repute his grace   The rightful heir to England's royal seat.
translation: and in my conscience I consider him the rightful heir to the English throne.

original: Hast thou not sworn allegiance unto me?
translation: Haven't you sworn your loyalty to me?

original: I have.
translation: I have.

original: Canst thou dispense with heaven for such an oath?
translation: Can you disregard it and swear against heaven?

original: It is great sin to swear unto a sin,   But greater sin to keep a sinful oath.
translation: It is sinful to swear to a sin. But it is even a greater sin to keen a sinful promise.

original: Who can be bound by any solemn vow   To do a murderous deed, to rob a man,   To force a spotless virgin's chastity,   To reave the orphan of his patrimony,   To wring the widow from her custom'd right,
translation: Who can be bound to any serious promise to commit a murder, to rob a man, to rape a virgin, to steal an orphan's inheritance, to steal the rights of inheritance from a widow,

original: And have no other reason for this wrong   But that he was bound by a solemn oath?
translation: and have no other reason for these crimes than that he made a promise to do so?

original: A subtle traitor needs no sophister.
translation: A cunning traitor doesn't need false logic.

original: Call Buckingham, and bid him arm himself.
translation: Call Buckingham, and tell him to arm for battle.

original: Call Buckingham, and all the friends thou hast, I am resolved for death or dignity.
translation: Call Buckingham and all the friends you have. I am determined to die or take the throne.

original: The first I warrant thee, if dreams prove true.
translation: I will give you the first, if my dreams come true.

original: You were best to go to bed and dream again, To keep thee from the tempest of the field.
translation: It would be better if you went back to bed and dreamed again, to keep yourself safe from the storm of the battlefield.

original: I am resolved to bear a greater storm   Than any thou canst conjure up to-day;
translation: I am determined to suffer a greater storm than any of you can stir up today.

original: And that I'll write upon thy burgonet,   Might I but know thee by thy household badge.
translation: And I'll write on your helmet, if I can recognize you by your family crest.

original: Now, by my father's badge, old Nevil's crest,   The rampant bear chain'd to the ragged staff,   This day I'll wear aloft my burgonet,
translation: Now, by my father's badge, old Nevil's crest—the roaring bear chained to the rough staff—I'll wear my helmet on my horse,

original: As on a mountain top the cedar shows   That keeps his leaves in spite of any storm,   Even to affright thee with the view thereof.
translation: like a cedar shows itself on a mountain top and keeps its leaves though any storm, just to frighten you with the view.

original: And from thy burgonet I'll rend thy bear And tread it under foot with all contempt, Despite the bear-ward that protects the bear.
translation: And I'll tear your bear from your helmet, and tread it under your feet with contempt, despite the bear-keeper that protects the bear.

original: And so to arms, victorious father, To quell the rebels and their complices.
translation: And so let's fight, victorious father! To kill the rebels and their accomplices.

original: Fie! Charity, for shame! Speak not in spite, For you shall sup with Jesu Christ to-night.
translation: Oh, please! That's shameful! Don't speak, because you'll have dinner with Jesus Christ tonight.

original: Foul stigmatic, that's more than thou canst tell.
translation: Foul criminal, that's more than you can say for yourself.

original: If not in heaven, you'll surely sup in hell.
translation: If I won't have dinner in heaven, I'll surely have dinner in hell!

original: Clifford of Cumberland, 'tis Warwick calls:   And if thou dost not hide thee from the bear,   Now, when the angry trumpet sounds alarum   And dead men's cries do fill the empty air,   Clifford, I say, come forth and fight with me:
translation: Clifford of Cumberland, Warwick calls you! And if you don't hide from the bear, now, when the angry trumpet calls to battle and the cries of dying men fill the empty air, then come forward and fight with me, Clifford!

original: Proud northern lord, Clifford of Cumberland,   Warwick is hoarse with calling thee to arms.
translation: You proud northern lord, Clifford of Cumberland, I'm losing my voice by calling you to fight!

original: How now, my noble lord? What, all afoot?
translation: How is it going, my noble lord? Are they all fighting?

original: The deadly-handed Clifford slew my steed,   But match to match I have encounter'd him
translation: The murderous Clifford killed my horse, but I have followed him and finally met him.

original: And made a prey for carrion kites and crows   Even of the bonny beast he loved so well.
translation: And now I've killed his horse, that he loved so much.

original: Of one or both of us the time is come.
translation: The time has come for one or both of us now.

original: Hold, Warwick, seek thee out some other chase, For I myself must hunt this deer to death.
translation: Stop, Warwick, and find some other prey for yourself. This deer is mine to kill.

original: Then, nobly, York; 'tis for a crown thou fight'st. As I intend, Clifford, to thrive to-day, It grieves my soul to leave thee unassail'd.
translation: Then I hope you fight nobly, York. You fight for a crown, after all. Since I am planning to win today, Clifford, it makes me sad to leave without attacking you.

original: What seest thou in me, York? Why dost thou pause?
translation: What do you see in me, York? Why did you stop?

original: With thy brave bearing should I be in love, But that thou art so fast mine enemy.
translation: I would admire your bravery, if you weren't my worst enemy.

original: Nor should thy prowess want praise and esteem, But that 'tis shown ignobly and in treason.
translation: Your cunning should be worthy of respect and praise, except you use your cleverness for treasonous ends.

original: So let it help me now against thy sword As I in justice and true right express it.
translation: Well, I hope my cunning helps me against your sword, since I use it for justice and what's right.

original: My soul and body on the action both!
translation: I bet my body and soul on the outcome of this fight!

original: A dreadful lay! Address thee instantly.
translation: A bad bet! Prepare yourself now!

original: La fin couronne les oeuvres.
translation: The end crowns the works.

original: Thus war hath given thee peace, for thou art still. Peace with his soul, heaven, if it be thy will!
translation: And so war has given you peace, because now you're still. Peace be with his soul, heaven, if that's your will!

original: Shame and confusion! All is on the rout;   Fear frames disorder, and disorder wounds   Where it should guard.
translation: Shame and confusion! Everything is out of control. Fear creates disorder, and disorder hurts the thing it should be protecting.

original: O war, thou son of hell,   Whom angry heavens do make their minister   Throw in the frozen bosoms of our part   Hot coals of vengeance!
translation: Oh, war, you are a son of hell. The angry heavens throw you into cold hearts to ignite a fire of revenge!

original: Let no soldier fly.   He that is truly dedicate to war   Hath no self-love, nor he that loves himself   Hath not essentially but by circumstance   The name of valour.
translation: No soldier should retreat. Whoever is truly devoted to war doesn't think about protecting himself, and whoever tries to protect himself won't ever be brave except by accident.

original: O, let the vile world end,   And the premised flames of the last day   Knit earth and heaven together!   Now let the general trumpet blow his blast,   Particularities and petty sounds   To cease!
translation: Oh, I hope the horrible world ends, and the preordained flames of the judgement day unite earth and heaven together! I wish that the trumpet sounding the end of days to all men would sound now, to stop these small and petty sounds!

original: Wast thou ordain'd, dear father,   To lose thy youth in peace, and to achieve   The silver livery of advised age,   And, in thy reverence and thy chair-days, thus   To die in ruffian battle? Even at this sight   My heart is turn'd to stone: and while 'tis mine,   It shall be stony.
translation: Was it your destiny, dear father, to lose your youth in peace, and to grow old just so you can die in this rough battle? This sight alone has turned my heart into stone, and as long as it's mine, it will be stony.

original: York not our old men spares;   No more will I their babes: tears virginal   Shall be to me even as the dew to fire,   And beauty that the tyrant oft reclaims   Shall to my flaming wrath be oil and flax.   Henceforth I will not have to do with pity:
translation: York doesn't spare our old men, so I won't spare their babies. These innocent tears will be for me like the  dew to a fire , and beauty that often subdues cruelty will be  oil and wax  to my flaming anger. From now on, I won't have pity.

original: Meet I an infant of the house of York,   Into as many gobbets will I cut it   As wild Medea young Absyrtus did:   In cruelty will I seek out my fame.   Come, thou new ruin of old Clifford's house:
translation: If I meet an infant from the house of York, I'll cut it into as many chunks of raw flesh as wild  Medea did to young Absyrtus . I'll try to become famous for cruelty. Come, you new ruin of the house of old Clifford.

original: As did AEneas old Anchises bear,   So bear I thee upon my manly shoulders;   But then AEneas bare a living load,   Nothing so heavy as these woes of mine.
translation: Like  Aeneas carried old Anchises , I'll carry you on my manly shoulders. But then again, Aeneas carried a living body, so he didn't suffer as much as I do.

original: So, lie thou there;   For underneath an alehouse' paltry sign,   The Castle in Saint Alban's, Somerset   Hath made the wizard famous in his death.
translation: So, you lie there. Because he died under a sign of a worthless pub called the Castle in Saint Alban's, Somerset has proven the  wizard's  prophecy.

original: Sword, hold thy temper; heart, be wrathful still:   Priests pray for enemies, but princes kill.
translation: Sword, stop your violence; heart, continue to be angry. Priests pray for enemies, but princes kill.

original: Away, my lord! You are slow; for shame, away!
translation: We must get away, my lord! Oh, you are slow; let's go!

original: Can we outrun the heavens? Good Margaret, stay.
translation: Can we run faster than the heavens? Good Margaret, wait.

original: What are you made of? You'll nor fight nor fly:
translation: What are you made of? You won't fight or run!

original: Now is it manhood, wisdom and defence,   To give the enemy way, and to secure us   By what we can, which can no more but fly.
translation: Now it's brave, wise, and smart to let the enemy win and to save ourselves however we can. And we can do nothing else but run!

original: If you be ta'en, we then should see the bottom   Of all our fortunes: but if we haply scape,   As well we may, if not through your neglect,
translation: If you are captured, we would hit the rock bottom of our luck. But if we manage to escape—as we may still do, if you don't slow us down—

original: We shall to London get, where you are loved   And where this breach now in our fortunes made   May readily be stopp'd.
translation: we can get to London, where you are loved and where this hole in our luck can be easily repaired.

original: But that my heart's on future mischief set,   I would speak blasphemy ere bid you fly:   But fly you must; uncurable discomfit   Reigns in the hearts of all our present parts.
translation: If I weren't afraid of hell, I would speak blasphemy before I told you to run. But you must go. Our surviving forces are undeniably defeated.

original: Away, for your relief! And we will live   To see their day and them our fortune give:   Away, my lord, away!
translation: Run away for your safety! We'll survive to see  our  victorious day and give them piece of our luck. Run, my lord, run!

original: Of Salisbury, who can report of him,   That winter lion, who in rage forgets   Aged contusions and all brush of time,   And, like a gallant in the brow of youth,   Repairs him with occasion?
translation: Who can give us any news of Salisbury? He fought like an old lion who in his anger forgets about his old age, as if he were young again.

original: This happy day   Is not itself, nor have we won one foot,   If Salisbury be lost.
translation: It's not a properly happy day, nor have we really won, if we have lost Salisbury.

original: My noble father,   Three times to-day I holp him to his horse,   Three times bestrid him;
translation: My noble father, I helped him to get up on his horse three times today, and I defended him three times from enemy soldiers.

original: thrice I led him off,   Persuaded him from any further act:   But still, where danger was, still there I met him;
translation: I led him off the battlefield three times, too, and tried to persuade him from fighting anymore. But either way, wherever there was danger, I was always with him.

original: And like rich hangings in a homely house,   So was his will in his old feeble body.   But, noble as he is, look where he comes.
translation: His fighting spirit in his old weak body was like a rich tapestry in a humble house. But speaking of the noble man, here he comes.

original: Now, by my sword, well hast thou fought to-day;   By the mass, so did we all. I thank you, Richard:   God knows how long it is I have to live;   And it hath pleased him that three times to-day   You have defended me from imminent death.
translation: Now, by my sword, you have fought well today. And so did we all! Thank you, Richard. God knows how long I have to live, and he saved me from sudden death three times today.

original: Well, lords, we have not got that which we have:   'Tis not enough our foes are this time fled,   Being opposites of such repairing nature.
translation: Well, lords, we haven't won yet.  It's not enough that our enemies have run away this time, since they are enemies who can recover swiftly.

original: I know our safety is to follow them;   For, as I hear, the king is fled to London,   To call a present court of parliament.
translation: I know the best way to keep ourselves safe is to follow them. I hear that the king has run away to London to call an immediate court of parliament.

original: Let us pursue him ere the writs go forth.   What says Lord Warwick? Shall we after them?
translation: Let's follow him before he can send the summons. What do you think, Lord Warwick? Should we go after them?

original: After them! Nay, before them, if we can.   Now, by my faith, lords, 'twas a glorious day:   Saint Alban's battle won by famous York   Shall be eternized in all age to come.
translation: After them? No, before them if we can! Now, this truly was a glorious day, lords. Saint Alban's battle was won by famous York, and it will be famous for all ages to come.

original: Sound drums and trumpets, and to London all:   And more such days as these to us befall!
translation: Sound the drums and trumpets, and let's all go to London. And let's hope we see many more days like this!

original: I wonder how the king escaped our hands.
translation: I wonder how the king escaped us.

original: While we pursued the horsemen of the north,   He slily stole away and left his men:   Whereat the great Lord of Northumberland,   Whose warlike ears could never brook retreat,   Cheer'd up the drooping army   ;
translation: While we followed the horsemen of the north, he tricked us, ran away, and left his men. After that, the great Lord of Northumberland, whose ears were used to the sounds of war and hated for his soldiers ever to retreat, encouraged his spiritless army.

original: and himself,   Lord Clifford and Lord Stafford, all abreast,   Charged our main battle's front, and breaking in   Were by the swords of common soldiers slain.
translation: He himself, Lord Clifford, and Lord Stafford, all in armor, charged at the front of our battalion. When they got through, they were killed by the swords of ordinary soldiers.

original: Lord Stafford's father, Duke of Buckingham, Is either slain or wounded dangerously; I cleft his beaver with a downright blow: That this is true, father, behold his blood.
translation: Lord Stafford's father, the Duke of Buckingham, is either killed or hurt badly. I split his helmet visor with a hit directly from above. You can see that it's true, father – look at his blood.

original: And, brother, here's the Earl of Wiltshire's blood, Whom I encounter'd as the battles join'd.
translation: And, brother, here is the Earl of Wiltshire's blood. I fought with him when the battle started.

original: Speak thou for me and tell them what I did.
translation: And you speak for me and tell them what I did.

original: Richard hath best deserved of all my sons. But is your grace dead, my Lord of Somerset?
translation: Out of all my sons, Richard deserves the most. But, are you dead, my Lord of Somerset?

original: Such hope have all the line of John of Gaunt!
Thus do I hope to shake King Henry's head.
translation: And I hope to deal similarly with King Henry's head.

original: And so do I. Victorious Prince of York,   Before I see thee seated in that throne   Which now the house of Lancaster usurps,   I vow by heaven these eyes shall never close.
translation: And so do I. Victorious Prince of York, I swear by heaven that my eyes shall never close until I see you seated in that throne, which has been stolen by the house of Lancaster.

original: This is the palace of the fearful king,   And this the regal seat: possess it, York;   For this is thine and not King Henry's heirs'.
translation: This is the palace of the frightened king, and this is the royal throne. Sit on it, York! Because it is yours and does not belong to King Henry's heirs.

original: Assist me, then, sweet Warwick, and I will; For hither we have broken in by force.
translation: Help me, then, my good Warwick, and I will, since we have already broken in by force.

original: We'll all assist you; he that flies shall die.
translation: We'll all help you out. He that runs away shall die.

original: Thanks, gentle Norfolk: stay by me, my lords; And, soldiers, stay and lodge by me this night.
translation: Thanks, noble Norfolk. Stay next to me, my lords. And soldiers, stay and settle next to me tonight.

original: And when the king comes, offer no violence, Unless he seek to thrust you out perforce.
translation: And when the king comes, don't be violent towards him, unless he tries to push you out by force.

original: The queen this day here holds her parliament, But little thinks we shall be of her council: By words or blows here let us win our right.
translation: The queen holds her parliament here today, but she doesn't know that we'll be her council. Let us win our right to the throne here—either with words or hits!

original: Arm'd as we are, let's stay within this house.
translation: Let's stay inside this house, armed as we are now.

original: The bloody parliament shall this be call'd, Unless Plantagenet, Duke of York, be king, And bashful Henry deposed, whose cowardice Hath made us by-words to our enemies.
translation: We will call it the bloody parliament, unless Plantagenet, Duke of York, is king, and shy Henry deposed. His cowardliness has made us well-known to our enemies.

original: Then leave me not, my lords; be resolute; I mean to take possession of my right.
translation: Don't leave me, then, my lords. Be bold! I am planning to claim my right.

original: Neither the king, nor he that loves him best, The proudest he that holds up Lancaster, Dares stir a wing, if Warwick shake his bells. I'll plant Plantagenet, root him up who dares: Resolve thee, Richard; claim the English crown.
My lords, look where the sturdy rebel sits,   Even in the chair of state: belike he means,   Back'd by the power of Warwick, that false peer,   To aspire unto the crown and reign as king.
translation: My lords, look where the obstinate rebel is sitting—on the throne! Perhaps he plans to take over the crown and rule as king, supported by the power of Warwick, that disloyal lord.

original: Earl of Northumberland, he slew thy father.   And thine, Lord Clifford; and you both have vow'd  revenge   On him, his sons, his favourites and his friends.
translation: Earl of Northumberland, he killed your father. And yours, Lord Clifford. And you both have sworn to take revenge on him, his sons, his acolytes, and his friends.

original: If I be not, heavens be revenged on me!
translation: If I am not avenged, heavens take revenge on me!

original: The hope thereof makes Clifford mourn in steel.
translation: In hope of that revenge, I'll wear armor instead of black mourning clothes.

original: What, shall we suffer this? let's pluck him down: My heart for anger burns; I cannot brook it.
translation: What? Shall we allow this? Let's put him in his place. My heart burns with anger and I can't endure it.

original: Be patient, gentle Earl of Westmoreland.
translation: Be patient, gentle Earl of Westmoreland.

original: Patience is for poltroons, such as he: He durst not sit there, had your father lived. My gracious lord, here in the parliament Let us assail the family of York.
translation: Patience is for cowards like him! He would not have dared to sit there if you father were alive. My gracious lord, let us attack the family of York here in the parliament.

original: Well hast thou spoken, cousin: be it so.
translation: You have spoken well, cousin. Let's do it.

original: Ah, know you not the city favours them, And they have troops of soldiers at their beck?
translation: Ah, don't you know that the citizens of London like them and that they have a group of soldiers at their command?

original: But when the duke is slain, they'll quickly fly.
translation: But when the duke is killed, they'll run away quickly.

original: F   ar be the thought of this from Henry's heart,   To make a shambles of the parliament-house!   Cousin of Exeter, frowns, words and threats   Shall be the war that Henry means to use.
translation: This couldn't be further from my thoughts. To make a slaughter-house of the parliament house!? Cousin of Exeter, I will use frowns, words and threats instead of weapons.

original: Thou factious Duke of York, descend my throne,   and kneel for grace and mercy at my feet;   I am thy sovereign.
translation: You, rebellious Duke of York, step down from my throne and kneel for grace and mercy at my feet. I am your king.

original: I am thine.
translation: No, I am yours.

original: For shame, come down: he made thee Duke of York.
translation: For shame, come down! He made you Duke of York.

original: 'Twas my inheritance, as the earldom was.
Thy father was a traitor to the crown.
translation: Your father was a traitor to the crown.

original: Exeter, thou art a traitor to the crown In following this usurping Henry.
translation: Exeter, you are a traitor to the crown because you follow Henry who usurped the throne.

original: Whom should he follow but his natural king?
translation: Whom should we follow but his rightful king?

original: True, Clifford; and that's Richard Duke of York.
translation: That's true, Clifford. And his rightful king is Richard Duke of York.

original: And shall I stand, and thou sit in my throne?
translation: So I should stand here while you sit on my throne?

original: It must and shall be so: content thyself.
translation: That must be and shall be what happens. Accept it.

original: Be Duke of Lancaster; let him be king.
translation: Be Duke of Lancaster and let him be king.

original: He is both king and Duke of Lancaster; And that the Lord of Westmoreland shall maintain.
translation: He is both king and Duke of Lancaster. The Lord of Westmoreland will stand by that.

original: And Warwick shall disprove it. You forget That we are those which chased you from the field And slew your fathers, and with colours spread March'd through the city to the palace gates.
translation: And Warwick will disagree with it. You are forgetting that we're the ones who chased you from the battlefield and killed your fathers, and marched through the city to the palace gates with military flags.

original: Yes, Warwick, I remember it to my grief; And, by his soul, thou and thy house shall rue it.
translation: Yes, Warwick. I remember it and it makes me grieve. And, I swear by my father's soul, you and your house will regret it.

original: Plantagenet, of thee and these thy sons, Thy kinsman and thy friends, I'll have more lives Than drops of blood were in my father's veins.
translation: Plantagenet, by the time I've through with you, your sons here, your kinsmen, and your friends, I'll have killed more men than there were drops of blood in my father's veins.

original: Urge it no more; lest that, instead of words, I send thee, Warwick, such a messenger As shall revenge his death before I stir.
translation: You'd better stop talking now, Warwick. Or else, instead of exchanging words, I'll send you a messenger who will revenge Westmoreland's father's death before I even move.

original: Poor Clifford! how I scorn his worthless threats!
translation: Poor Clifford! How I mock his meaningless threats!

original: Will you we show our title to the crown? If not, our swords shall plead it in the field.
translation: Do you want me to explain my claim to the throne? If not, our swords will make a case for it in the battlefield.

original: What title hast thou, traitor, to the crown?   Thy father was, as thou art, Duke of York;   Thy grandfather, Roger Mortimer, Earl of March:
translation: What title do you have, you traitor to the crown? Your father was Duke of York, just like you. Your grandfather, Roger Mortimer, was the Earl of March.

original: I am the son of Henry the Fifth,   Who made the Dauphin and the French to stoop   And seized upon their towns and provinces.
translation: I am the son of Henry V, who made the French prince  and the French people submit and he took over their towns and provinces.

original: Talk not of France, sith thou hast lost it all.
translation: Don't talk about France since you have lost all of it.

original: The lord protector lost it, and not I: When I was crown'd I was but nine months old.
translation: I didn't lose it. The Lord Protector did. I was only nine months old when I was crowned king.

original: You are old enough now, and yet, methinks, you lose. Father, tear the crown from the usurper's head.
translation: You are old enough now, and I think you're losing even now. Father, tear the crown off the usurper's head.

original: Sweet father, do so; set it on your head.
translation: Sweet father, do it. Put in on your own head.

original: Good brother, as thou lovest and honourest arms, Let's fight it out and not stand cavilling thus.
translation: Good brother, since you love and honor fighting, let's fight it out and not stand arguing here over details.

original: Sound drums and trumpets, and the king will fly.
translation: Let the drums and trumpets sound, and the king will run away.

original: Sons, peace!
translation: Sons, calm down!

original: Peace, thou! and give King Henry leave to speak.
translation: You calm down! And let King Henry speak.

original: Plantagenet shall speak first: hear him, lords; And be you silent and attentive too, For he that interrupts him shall not live.
Think'st thou that I will leave my kingly throne,   Wherein my grandsire and my father sat?   No: first shall war unpeople this my realm;
translation: Do you think that I will leave my kingly throne, where my grandfather and my father sat? No. I'd sooner let war kill everyone in my kingdom.

original: Ay, and their colours, often borne in France,   And now in England to our heart's great sorrow,   Shall be my winding-sheet. Why faint you, lords?   My title's good, and better far than his.
translation: Yes, and their military flags will be my burial sheet. Those flags were often carried in France, and now, it makes us sad to say, they're flown in England too. Why do you lose heart, lords? My claim to the throne is good and much better than his.

original: Prove it, Henry, and thou shalt be king.
translation: Prove it, Henry, and you'll be king.

original: Henry the Fourth by conquest got the crown.
translation: Henry the Fourth got the crown by conquering.

original: 'Twas by rebellion against his king.
translation: He won it in a rebellion against his king.

original: I know not what to say; my title's weak.— Tell me, may not a king adopt an heir?
translation: I don't know what to say now. My claim to the throne is indeed weak.

original: What then?
translation: And then what?

original: An if he may, then am I lawful king; For Richard, in the view of many lords, Resign'd the crown to Henry the Fourth, Whose heir my father was, and I am his.
He rose against him, being his sovereign, And made him to resign his crown perforce.
translation: Henry rose up against Richard, although Richard was his king, and forced him to give up his crown.

original: Suppose, my lords, he did it unconstrain'd, Think you 'twere prejudicial to his crown?
No; for he could not so resign his crown But that the next heir should succeed and reign.
translation: No, because he would not have willingly given up his crown except to make sure that the next rightful heir would succeed him and rule.

original: Art thou against us, Duke of Exeter?
translation: Are you against us, Duke of Exeter?

original: His is the right, and therefore pardon me.
translation: York has the better claim to the throne, and so forgive me.

original: Why whisper you, my lords, and answer not?
translation: Why do you whisper, my lords, and not answer?

original: My conscience tells me he is lawful king.
translation: My conscience tells me he is the lawful king.

original: All will revolt from me, and turn to him.
translation: Everyone will rebel against me and turn to him.

original: Plantagenet, for all the claim thou lay'st, Think not that Henry shall be so deposed.
translation: Plantagenet, although you claim that it's your right to be king, don't think that Henry will removed so easily.

original: Deposed he shall be, in despite of all.
translation: He shall be removed in spite of everything.

original: Thou art deceived: 'tis not thy southern power, Of Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, nor of Kent, Which makes thee thus presumptuous and proud, Can set the duke up in despite of me.
translation: You are mistaken. You're so presumptuous and proud about your powers in the south, but not all of them taken together—Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, and Kent—would be strong enough to put the Duke of York on the throne if I stand in his way.

original: King Henry, be thy title right or wrong, Lord Clifford vows to fight in thy defence: May that ground gape and swallow me alive, Where I shall kneel to him that slew my father!
translation: King Henry, I don't care if your claim to the throne is right or wrong. I, Lord Clifford, vow to fight to defend you. Let the ground open up and swallow me alive, if ever I kneel to the man that killed my father!

original: O Clifford, how thy words revive my heart!
translation: Oh, Clifford! Your words bring my heart back to life.

original: Henry of Lancaster, resign thy crown. What mutter you, or what conspire you, lords?
translation: Henry of Lancaster, give up your crown. What are you muttering about, or what are you conspiring, lords?

original: Do right unto this princely Duke of York, Or I will fill the house with armed men, And over the chair of state, where now he sits, Write up his title with usurping blood.
translation: Give up the throne to this noble Duke of York. If not, I will fill this Parliament House with armed soldiers, and I'll write the Duke's title  above the throne he now sits on with the blood of the usurping Henry.

original: My Lord of Warwick, hear me but one word: Let me for this my life-time reign as king.
translation: My Lord of Warwick, listen to just one word. Let me rule as king for my lifetime.

original: Confirm the crown to me and to mine heirs, And thou shalt reign in quiet while thou livest.
translation: If you leave the crown to me and my heirs after you die, we'll let you rule in peace for the rest of your life.

original: I am content: Richard Plantagenet, Enjoy the kingdom after my decease.
translation: I am satisfied. Richard Plantagenet, you can have the kingdom after my death.

original: What wrong is this unto the prince your son!
translation: You do a great wrong to your son, the prince!

original: What good is this to England and himself!
translation: But it's good for England and the king himself!

original: Base, fearful and despairing Henry!
translation: Unworthy, fearful and despairing Henry!

original: How hast thou injured both thyself and us!
translation: How you have hurt both yourself and us!

original: I cannot stay to hear these articles.
translation: I can't stay to hear the terms of agreement.

original: Nor I.
translation: Neither can I.

original: Come, cousin, let us tell the queen these news.
translation: Come, friend, and let us tell the queen these news.

original: Farewell, faint-hearted and degenerate king, In whose cold blood no spark of honour bides.
translation: Goodbye, you timid and wretched king. There is no honor at all in your weak blood.

original: Be thou a prey unto the house of York, And die in bands for this unmanly deed!
translation: I hope you'll be fall prey to the House of York and die in chains for this unmanly decision!

original: In dreadful war mayst thou be overcome, Or live in peace abandon'd and despised!
translation: I hope you'll be killed in a terrible war or else live in peace but abandoned and despised!

original: Turn this way, Henry, and regard them not.
translation: Look this way, Henry, and don't pay attention to them.

original: They seek revenge and therefore will not yield.
translation: They are looking for revenge so they won't give up.

original: Ah, Exeter!
translation: Ah, Exeter!

original: Why should you sigh, my lord?
translation: Why do you sigh, my lord?

original: Not for myself, Lord Warwick, but my son,   Whom I unnaturally shall disinherit.   But be it as it may: I here entail   The crown to thee and to thine heirs for ever;
translation: Not for myself, Lord Warwick, but for my son. I have unnaturally disinherited him. But it is what it is. I here bequeath the crown to you and to your heirs forever.

original: Conditionally, that here thou take an oath   To cease this civil war, and, whilst I live,   To honour me as thy king and sovereign,   And neither by treason nor hostility   To seek to put me down and reign thyself.
translation: Under this condition: that you swear to me here to stop this civil war and to honor me as your king while I live. And that you promise not to attempt to overthrow me and rule yourself, either by committing treason or declaring open war against me.

original: This oath I willingly take and will perform.
translation: I will gladly take this oath and keep it.

original: Long live King Henry! Plantagenet embrace him.
translation: Long live King Henry! Embrace him, Plantagenet.

original: And long live thou and these thy forward sons!
translation: And long live you and these eager sons of yours!

original: Now York and Lancaster are reconciled.
translation: Now York and Lancaster have made peace.

original: Accursed be he that seeks to make them foes!
translation: Cursed be he who tries to make them enemies!

original: Farewell, my gracious lord; I'll to my castle.
translation: Goodbye, my gracious lord. I'll go to my castle.

original: And I'll keep London with my soldiers.
translation: And I'll stay in London with my soldiers.

original: And I to Norfolk with my followers.
translation: And I'll go to Norfolk with my followers.

original: And I unto the sea from whence I came.
translation: And I'll go to the sea where I came from.

original: And I, with grief and sorrow, to the court.
translation: And I'll go to the court with my grief and sorrow.

original: Here comes the queen, whose looks bewray her anger: I'll steal away.
translation: Here comes the queen and her looks give away her anger. I'll slip away.

original: Exeter, so will I.
translation: Exeter, so will I.

original: Nay, go not from me; I will follow thee.
translation: No, don't go away from me. I will follow you.

original: Be patient, gentle queen, and I will stay.
translation: Be patient, gentle queen, and I will stay.

original: Who can be patient in such extremes?   Ah, wretched man! would I had died a maid   And never seen thee, never borne thee son,   Seeing thou hast proved so unnatural a father.
translation: Who can be patient in such extreme situations? Ah, you wretched man! I wish I had died a virgin and never had seen you or given birth to your son, now that you've proven to be such an unloving father.

original: Hath he deserved to lose his birthright thus?   Hadst thou but loved him half so well as I,   Or felt that pain which I did for him once,   Or nourish'd him as I did with my blood,   Thou wouldst have left thy dearest heart-blood there,   Rather than have that savage duke thine heir   And disinherited thine only son.
translation: Has he deserved to lose his inheritance like this? If you had loved him half as much as I do, or felt my labor pains, or nursed him with my breast milk,  you would have shed blood from your heart rather than make that barbarous duke your heir and disinherit your only son.

original: Father, you cannot disinherit me: If you be king, why should not I succeed?
translation: Father, you can't disinherit me! If you are the king, why shouldn't I be next in line for the throne?

original: Pardon me, Margaret; pardon me, sweet son: The Earl of Warwick and the duke enforced me.
translation: I am sorry, Margaret. I am sorry, my sweet son. The Earl of Warwick and the duke forced me to do it.

original: Enforced thee! art thou king, and wilt be forced?   I shame to hear thee speak. Ah, timorous wretch!   Thou hast undone thyself, thy son and me;   And given unto the house of York such head   As thou shalt reign but by their sufferance.
translation: Forced you! Are you a king who will be forced? I am ashamed to hear you speak. Ah, fearful rascal! You have ruined yourself, your son, and me. And you have given so much free rein to the house of York that now you rule with their permission.

original: To entail him and his heirs unto the crown,   What is it, but to make thy sepulchre   And creep into it far before thy time?   Warwick is chancellor and the lord of Calais;   Stern Falconbridge commands the narrow seas;   The duke is made protector of the realm;   And yet shalt thou be safe?
translation: Leaving the throne to him and his heirs can only mean that you're digging your own grave and creeping into it long before your time? Warwick is chancellor and the lord of Calais, stern Falconbridge rules over the seas, the duke is the protector of the country and yet you think you're safe?

original: such safety finds   The trembling lamb environed with wolves.   Had I been there, which am a silly woman,   The soldiers should have toss'd me on their pikes   Before I would have granted to that act.
translation: This is a safety that's like when a shaking lamb is surrounded by wolves. If I—a silly woman—had been there, the soldiers would have thrown my head on their spears before I would have made this agreement.

original: But thou preferr'st thy life before thine honour:   And seeing thou dost, I here divorce myself   Both from thy table, Henry, and thy bed,   Until that act of parliament be repeal'd   Whereby my son is disinherited.
translation: But you care more about your life than your honor. Because I have seen that now, I divorce myself from you here, both from your royal table, Henry, and from your bed, until this parliamentary act disinheriting my son is revoked.

original: The northern lords that have forsworn thy colours   Will follow mine, if once they see them spread;   And spread they shall be, to thy foul disgrace   And utter ruin of the house of York.   Thus do I leave thee. Come, son, let's away;   Our army is ready; come, we'll after them.
translation: The northern lords that have falsely sworn their loyalty to you will follow my own flag once they see it fly. And it will be flown indeed, which will disgrace you and utterly ruin the House of York.  And so I leave you with that thought. Come, son, let's go. Our army is ready. Come, we'll follow them.

original: Stay, gentle Margaret, and hear me speak.
translation: Stay, gentle Margaret, and hear me speak.

original: Thou hast spoke too much already: get thee gone.
translation: You have spoken too much already. Get lost.

original: Gentle son Edward, thou wilt stay with me?
translation: Gentle son Edward, will you stay with me?

original: Ay, to be murder'd by his enemies.
translation: Yes, to be murdered by his enemies.

original: When I return with victory from the field I'll see your grace: till then I'll follow her.
translation: When I return victorious from the battlefield, I'll come see you. Until then, I'll stick with her.

original: Come, son, away; we may not linger thus.
translation: Come, son, let's go. We can't stay here any longer.

original: Poor queen! how love to me and to her son   Hath made her break out into terms of rage!   Revenged may she be on that hateful duke,   Whose haughty spirit, winged with desire,   Will cost my crown,
translation: Poor queen! It's love for me and her son that has made her express this great rage! I hope she'll be revenged d on that hateful duke, whose arrogance, combined with desire for power, will deprive me of my crown.

original: and like an empty eagle   Tire on the flesh of me and of my son!   The loss of those three lords torments my heart:   I'll write unto them and entreat them fair.   Come, cousin you shall be the messenger.
translation: Like a hungry eagle, he will feed on the body of me and of my son! The loss of those three lords troubles me greatly. I'll write to them and plead with them to come back to me. Come, friend, you will be my messenger.

original: And I, I hope, shall reconcile them all.
translation: And I, I hope, that I can make peace between them all.

original: Brother, though I be youngest, give me leave.
translation: Brother, let me do this, even though I'm the youngest.

original: No, I can better play the orator.
translation: No, I am a better public speaker than you.

original: But I have reasons strong and forcible.
translation: But I have strong and compelling reasons to be the one.

original: Why, how now, sons and brother! At a strife? What is your quarrel? How began it first?
translation: What's going on, my sons and brother? Are you fighting? What is your argument about? What started it?

original: No quarrel, but a slight contention.
translation: It's not an argument. Just a small disagreement.

original: About what?
translation: What about?

original: About that which concerns your grace and us; The crown of England, father, which is yours.
translation: About something that concerns your grace and us—the English crown, father, which is yours.

original: Mine boy? not till King Henry be dead.
translation: Mine, boy? Not until King Henry is dead.

original: Your right depends not on his life or death.
translation: Your right to the throne doesn't depend on his life or death.

original: Now you are heir, therefore enjoy it now: By giving the house of Lancaster leave to breathe, It will outrun you, father, in the end.
translation: You're the rightful heir, so take the throne now. Father, giving the house of Lancaster time to rest and recover itself will bring you down in the end.

original: I took an oath that he should quietly reign.
translation: I took an oath that he could reign peacefully.

original: But for a kingdom any oath may be broken: I would break a thousand oaths to reign one year.
translation: But any promise can be broken for the sake of a kingdom. I would break a thousand promises if I could only rule for one year.

original: No; God forbid your grace should be forsworn.
translation: No, God forbid that your grace should break an oath.

original: I shall be, if I claim by open war.
translation: I would be breaking one, if I started an open war to claim the throne.

original: I'll prove the contrary, if you'll hear me speak.
translation: I'll prove otherwise, if you'll hear what I have to say.

original: Thou canst not, son; it is impossible.
translation: You can't, son. It's impossible.

original: An oath is of no moment, being not took   Before a true and lawful magistrate,   That hath authority over him that swears:
translation: The oath isn't binding because it wasn't sworn before a real and lawful judge who can hold you legally to your promise.

original: Henry had none, but did usurp the place;   Then, seeing 'twas he that made you to depose,   Your oath, my lord, is vain and frivolous.
translation: Henry had no such authority but forcefully took your place on the thrown. And since it was him that made you give up the crown, your promise, my lord, is silly and worthless.

original: Therefore, to arms! And, father, do but think   How sweet a thing it is to wear a crown;   Within whose circuit is Elysium   And all that poets feign of bliss and joy.
translation: Therefore, let's fight! And think about how sweet it would feel to wear a crown, father.  Paradise  can be found in the circle of a crown along with all the joy and happiness that poets imagine.

original: Why do we finger thus? I cannot rest   Until the white rose that I wear be dyed   Even in the lukewarm blood of Henry's heart.
translation: Why do we wait around? I won't rest until the  white rose  that I wear will be dyed with the cowardly blood of Henry's heart.

original: Richard, enough; I will be king, or die.   Brother, thou shalt to London presently,   And whet on Warwick to this enterprise.   Thou, Richard, shalt to the Duke of Norfolk,   And tell him privily of our intent.
translation: Richard, that's enough! I will be king or die. Brother, go to London at once and encourage Warwick to think about this. You, Richard, will go to the Duke of Norfolk and tell him about our intentions in secret.

original: You Edward, shall unto my Lord Cobham,   With whom the Kentishmen will willingly rise:   In them I trust; for they are soldiers,   Witty, courteous, liberal, full of spirit.
translation: You,  Edward, will go to Lord Cobham, who the soldiers from Kent would willingly join in rebellion. I believe in them because they are soldiers— witty, polite, generous, and full of courage.

original: While you are thus employ'd, what resteth more,   But that I seek occasion how to rise,   And yet the king not privy to my drift,   Nor any of the house of Lancaster?
