translation: While you are running these errands, what else is there for me to do but prepare for the opportunity to take power without the king or the house of Lancaster being aware of my intentions?

original: But, stay: what news? Why comest thou in such post?
translation: Wait! What's the news? Why do you come here in such a hurry?

original: The queen with all the northern earls and lords Intend here to besiege you in your castle: She is hard by with twenty thousand men; And therefore fortify your hold, my lord.
translation: The queen with all the northern earls and lords plans to attack you here in your castle. She is nearby with twenty thousand men. You should guard your fortress, my lord.

original: Ay, with my sword. What! think'st thou that we fear  them?   Edward and Richard, you shall stay with me;   My brother Montague shall post to London:
translation: Yes, I'll guard it with my sword! What, do you think that we are afraid of them? Edward and Richard, you will stay with me. I'll send my brother Montague to ride to London swiftly.

original: Let noble Warwick, Cobham, and the rest,   Whom we have left protectors of the king,   With powerful policy strengthen themselves,   And trust not simple Henry nor his oaths.
translation: Let noble Warwick, Cobham, and the others, whom we have left as protectors of the king, now protect themselves with cunning and plotting rather than trusting foolish Henry or his promises.

original: Brother, I go; I'll win them, fear it not: And thus most humbly I do take my leave.
translation: I will go, brother. I'll win them over, don't worry. And so I humbly leave you.

original: Sir John and Sir Hugh Mortimer, mine uncles, You are come to Sandal in a happy hour; The army of the queen mean to besiege us.
translation: My uncles, Sir John and Sir Hugh Mortimer, you have arrived in Sandal at a good time. The queen's army plans to attack us.

original: She shall not need; we'll meet her in the field.
translation: She won't need to. We'll meet her in the field in battle.

original: What, with five thousand men?
translation: What, with five thousand men?

original: Ay, with five hundred, father, for a need: A woman's general; what should we fear?
translation: Yes, with five hundred if we need to, father! It's a woman's army so why should we be scared?

original: I hear their drums: let's set our men in order, And issue forth and bid them battle straight.
translation: I hear their drums of war. Let's make sure our men are ready, and then we'll send them into battle straight away.

original: Five men to twenty! Though the odds be great,   I doubt not, uncle, of our victory.
translation: Five men for every twenty! Although the odds are great, I don't doubt that we'll win, uncle.

original: Many a battle have I won in France,   When as the enemy hath been ten to one:   Why should I not now have the like success?
translation: I have won many battles in France, when the enemy was ten to one. Why shouldn't I have the same success now?

original: Ah, whither shall I fly to 'scape their hands? Ah, tutor, look where bloody Clifford comes!
translation: Ah, where should I run to escape them? Tutor, look, the bloodthirsty Clifford is coming!

original: Chaplain, away! Thy priesthood saves thy life. As for the brat of this accursed duke, Whose father slew my father, he shall die.
translation: Go away, clergyman! Your holy position saves your life. And, as for the kid of this damned Duke, whose father killed my father, he will die.

original: And I, my lord, will bear him company.
translation: And I will die with him, my lord.

original: Soldiers, away with him!
translation: Soldiers, take him away!

original: Ah, Clifford, murder not this innocent child, Lest thou be hated both of God and man!
translation: Clifford, don't murder this innocent child, or you will be hated both by God and mankind!

original: How now! is he dead already? Or is it fear That makes him close his eyes? I'll open them.
translation: What's happened? Is he already dead? Or does fear make him close his eyes? I'll open them.

original: So looks the pent-up lion o'er the wretch   That trembles under his devouring paws;   And so he walks, insulting o'er his prey,   And so he comes, to rend his limbs asunder.
translation: That's just how the caged lion looks at the poor victim that shakes under the lion's hungry paws. And thats just how the lion walks, conquering his prey. And that's just how the lion comes nearer to tear his victim's limbs apart.

original: Ah, gentle Clifford, kill me with thy sword,   And not with such a cruel threatening look.   Sweet Clifford, hear me speak before I die.   I am too mean a subject for thy wrath:   Be thou revenged on men, and let me live.
translation: Ah, gentle Clifford, kill me with your sword and not with such a cruel, threatening stare. Kind Clifford, listen to what I have to say before you kill me. I am too young for your anger. Take your revenge on men, and let me live.

original: In vain thou speak'st, poor boy; my father's blood Hath stopp'd the passage where thy words should enter.
translation: You speak in vain, poor boy. Thinking about my father's death and his spilled blood has prevented your words from reaching me.

original: Then let my father's blood open it again: He is a man, and, Clifford, cope with him.
translation: Then let my father's blood make it up to you. He is a man and you can fight him instead, Clifford.

original: Had thy brethren here, their lives and thine   Were not revenge sufficient for me;   No, if I digg'd up thy forefathers' graves   And hung their rotten coffins up in chains,   It could not slake mine ire, nor ease my heart.
translation: Even if your brothers were here, killing you and killing them would not be enough of revenge for me. Even if I dug up your ancestors' graves and hung their rotting coffins up in chains, it still wouldn't calm my anger or soothe my heart.

original: The sight of any of the house of York   Is as a fury to torment my soul;   And till I root out their accursed line   And leave not one alive, I live in hell.   Therefore—
translation: Just seeing anyone from the house of York  torments  my soul. And until I destroy your whole damned family line, leaving no one alive, I continue to live in hell. That's why—

original: O, let me pray before I take my death! To thee I pray; sweet Clifford, pity me!
translation: Oh, let me pray before I die! I pray to you, kind Clifford, take pity on me!

original: Such pity as my rapier's point affords.
translation: I'll take as much pity as the blade of my sword allows me to.

original: I never did thee harm: why wilt thou slay me?
translation: I never hurt you. Why do you want to kill me?

original: Thy father hath.
translation: Your father hurt me.

original: But 'twas ere I was born.   Thou hast one son; for his sake pity me,   Lest in revenge thereof, sith God is just,   He be as miserably slain as I.
translation: But that was before I was even born. You have one son. Take pity on me for his sake, in case, since God is just, your son is killed just as horribly as I am.

original: Ah, let me live in prison all my days;   And when I give occasion of offence,   Then let me die, for now thou hast no cause.
translation: Oh, let me stay in prison for the rest of my life, and if I give you any reason to be angry with me there, then let me die. You have no reason to kill me now.

original: No cause! Thy father slew my father; therefore, die.
translation: No reason! Your father killed my father. And so, you die.

original: Di faciant laudis summa sit ista tuae!
translation: May the Gods ensure that this is the high point of your glory.

original: Plantagenet! I come, Plantagenet! And this thy son's blood cleaving to my blade Shall rust upon my weapon, till thy blood, Congeal'd with this, do make me wipe off both.
translation: Plantagenet! I am coming for you, Plantagenet! And your son's blood here, clinging to my sword, will stay rusting here until your blood mixes with his. Then I'll wipe off both your blood and his.

original: The army of the queen hath got the field:   My uncles both are slain in rescuing me;   And all my followers to the eager foe   Turn back and fly, like ships before the wind   Or lambs pursued by hunger-starved wolves.
translation: The queen's army has won. Both of my uncles died as they were rescuing me. All of my followers turned their backs to the savage enemy and ran away like ships blown away the wind or lambs chased by starving wolves.

original: My sons, God knows what hath bechanced them:   But this I know, they have demean'd themselves   Like men born to renown by life or death.
translation: Only God know what has happened to my sons. But I do know this—they have behaved like men born to be remembered as heroes whether they live or die.

original: Three times did Richard make a lane to me.   And thrice cried 'Courage, father! fight it out!'   And full as oft came Edward to my side,   With purple falchion, painted to the hilt   In blood of those that had encounter'd him:
translation: Richard tried to get to me three times, and three times he shouted, "Courage, father! Keep fighting!" And Edward came to me just as frequently, with bloodied sword, which was covered with blood of those that had fought him.

original: And when the hardiest warriors did retire,   Richard cried 'Charge! and give no foot of ground!'   And cried 'A crown, or else a glorious tomb!   A sceptre, or an earthly sepulchre!'
translation: And when the strongest warriors were falling and fleeing, Richard still shouted, "Charge! And don't let your feet touch the ground!" And he also shouted: "We'll get the crown or we'll go to our graves! A scepter or a tomb!"

original: With this, we charged again: but, out, alas!   We bodged again; as I have seen a swan   With bootless labour swim against the tide   And spend her strength with over-matching waves.
translation: Hearing this, we charged again. But, sad to say, we were overwhelmed again. It reminded me of when I once saw a swan hopelessly swimming against the tide and using up her strength to swim through waves that were much more powerful than she was.

original: Ah, hark! the fatal followers do pursue;   And I am faint and cannot fly their fury:   And were I strong, I would not shun their fury:
translation: Ah, listen! These enemies who want to kill me are after me. And I am weak and cannot escape their rage. And even if I were strong, I would not flee their rage.

original: The sands are number'd that make up my life;   Here must I stay, and here my life must end.
translation: The sands in the hourglass of my life are running out. I must stay here, and my life must end here.

original: Come, bloody Clifford, rough Northumberland, I dare your quenchless fury to more rage: I am your butt, and I abide your shot.
Yield to our mercy, proud Plantagenet.
translation: Surrender to us, proud Plantagenet!

original: Ay, to such mercy as his ruthless arm, With downright payment, show'd unto my father. Now Phaethon hath tumbled from his car, And made an evening at the noontide prick.
My ashes, as the phoenix, may bring forth   A bird that will revenge upon you all:
translation: My dead body may provoke my followers to take revenge on all of you, like a  phoenix rising from the ashes .

original: And in that hope I throw mine eyes to heaven,   Scorning whate'er you can afflict me with.   Why come you not? what! multitudes, and fear?
translation: And I prepare for death with that hope. Nothing you torment me with can bother me now. Why aren't you coming for me? What? There are more of you and yet you're afraid?

original: So cowards fight when they can fly no further; So doves do peck the falcon's piercing talons; So desperate thieves, all hopeless of their lives, Breathe out invectives 'gainst the officers.
translation: That's how cowards fight when they can no longer run away. That's how doves peck hopelessly at the falcon's piercing claws. And that's how desperate thieves, with no chance of being saved, shout out insults against the officers who arrest them.

original: O Clifford, but bethink thee once again,   And in thy thought o'er-run my former time;
translation: Oh, Clifford, use your brain once again, and think over the life I have lived.

original: And, if though canst for blushing, view this face,   And bite thy tongue, that slanders him with cowardice   Whose frown hath made thee faint and fly ere this!
translation: And, if you can do it without blushing,  look at my face and shut your mouth, rather than calling me a coward when my very frown used to make you feel weak and run away!

original: I will not bandy with thee word for word, But buckle with thee blows, twice two for one.
translation: I won't exchange insults with you back and forth, but I will have a little combat with you and strike you four times for every one time you strike me.

original: Hold, valiant Clifford! for a thousand causes I would prolong awhile the traitor's life. Wrath makes him deaf: speak thou, Northumberland.
translation: Wait, brave Clifford! I would prolong the life of this traitor a little bit longer for a thousand reasons. Anger makes Clifford deaf. Speak, Northumberland.

original: Hold, Clifford! do not honour him so much   To prick thy finger, though to wound his heart:
translation: Wait, Clifford! Don't give him the honor of letting him prick your finger in combat even if it means you get to stab him through the heart.

original: What valour were it, when a cur doth grin,   For one to thrust his hand between his teeth,   When he might spurn him with his foot away?
translation: When a dog shows its teeth, is it brave to put your hand in his mouth when you could just as easily kick him away with your foot?

original: It is war's prize to take all vantages;   And ten to one is no impeach of valour.
translation: In war, you get to take everything you can. It's not even dishonorable for ten men to attack one.

original: Ay, ay, so strives the woodcock with the gin.
translation: Yes, yes, so the stupid little bird is trying to get out of the trap.

original: So doth the cony struggle in the net.
translation: Just like a rabbit struggling to get out of the net.

original: So triumph thieves upon their conquer'd booty; So true men yield, with robbers so o'ermatch'd.
translation: And you're just like thieves enjoying the goods they've stolen. And I'm just like a real man, giving up when he knows he is outmatched by petty robbers like you.

original: What would your grace have done unto him now?
translation: What does your grace want done to him now?

original: Brave warriors, Clifford and Northumberland,   Come, make him stand upon this molehill here,   That wrought at mountains with outstretched arms,   Yet parted but the shadow with his hand.
translation: Brave warriors, Clifford and Northumberland, come! Come, make him stand on this molehill here. He reached for mountains with his outstretched arms, but he only managed to obtain the shadow of a mountain.

original: What! was it you that would be England's king?   Was't you that revell'd in our parliament,   And made a preachment of your high descent?   Where are your mess of sons to back you now?
translation: Hey! Wasn't it you who said you would be the king of England?  Wasn't it you who threw a fit in our parliament and lectured us about your important ancestors? Where is your quartet of sons now?

original: The wanton Edward, and the lusty George?   And where's that valiant crook-back prodigy,   Dicky your boy, that with his grumbling voice   Was wont to cheer his dad in mutinies?
translation: The wild Edward, and the lustful George? And where's that brave hunchbacked monster, your boy  Dicky , that cheered up his dad with his grumbly voice during the fight?

original: Or, with the rest, where is your darling Rutland?   Look, York: I stain'd this napkin with the blood   That valiant Clifford, with his rapier's point,   Made issue from the bosom of the boy;
translation: And, come to think of it, where is your darling Rutland? Look, York. I stained this napkin with the blood that brave Clifford got from your son's chest with his sword.

original: And if thine eyes can water for his death,   I give thee this to dry thy cheeks withal.   Alas poor York! but that I hate thee deadly,   I should lament thy miserable state.
translation: And if you can cry for his death, I'll offer you this napkin to dry your cheeks with. Oh, poor York! If I didn't hate you so much, I would feel sorry that you're in such bad shape.

original: I prithee, grieve, to make me merry, York.   What, hath thy fiery heart so parch'd thine entrails   That not a tear can fall for Rutland's death?
translation: I beg you, be sad in order to make me happy, York. Has your fiery heart dried up your insides so much that you can't even shed one tear for Rutland's death?

original: Why art thou patient, man? thou shouldst be mad;   And I, to make thee mad, do mock thee thus.   Stamp, rave, and fret, that I may sing and dance.
translation: Why are you so calm, man? You should be mad! And I will mock you now to make you mad. Stamp your foot, rant, and panic, so I can sing and dance.

original: Thou wouldst be fee'd, I see, to make me sport:   York cannot speak, unless he wear a crown.   A crown for York! and, lords, bow low to him:   Hold you his hands, whilst I do set it on.
translation: Oh, I see you won't humor me with  such entertainment unless you've been paid. York can't speak unless he wears a crown. A crown for York! And bow low to him, lords. Hold his hands while I place it on his head.

original: Ay, marry, sir, now looks he like a king!   Ay, this is he that took King Henry's chair,   And this is he was his adopted heir.
translation: Ah, there, sir, now he looks like a king! Yes, this is the man that took King Henry's throne and also the man who was chosen to be his heir.

original: But how is it that great Plantagenet   Is crown'd so soon, and broke his solemn oath?   As I bethink me, you should not be king   Till our King Henry had shook hands with death.
translation: But how is it possible that the great Plantagenet has crowned so quickly? How did he break his sacred promise? I thought you weren't supposed to be king until King Henry had died.

original: And will you pale your head in Henry's glory,   And rob his temples of the diadem,   Now in his life, against your holy oath?
translation: And will you wear Henry's glory, stealing the crown from off his head while he's still alive, despite your holy promise?

original: That is my office, for my father's sake.
translation: I must do the deed, for my father's sake.

original: Nay, stay; lets hear the orisons he makes.
translation: No, wait. Let's hear his prayers.

original: She-wolf of France, but worse than wolves of France,   Whose tongue more poisons than the adder's tooth!
translation: You're a French she-wolf, but worse than French wolves, since your tongue is more poisonous than the tooth of a venomous snake.

original: How ill-beseeming is it in thy sex   To triumph, like an Amazonian trull,   Upon their woes whom fortune captivates!
translation: It is so unattractive when women, like  Amazonian  whores, rejoice in the misery of men brought down by fortune.

original: But that thy face is, visor-like, unchanging,   Made impudent with use of evil deeds,   I would assay, proud queen, to make thee blush.
translation: If your face wasn't like a unchanging mask, hardened by your evil deeds, I would attempt, proud queen, to make you blush.

original: To tell thee whence thou camest, of whom derived,   Were shame enough to shame thee, wert thou not  shameless.   Thy father bears the type of King of Naples,   Of both the Sicils and Jerusalem,   Yet not so wealthy as an English yeoman.
translation: If you weren't shameless, just saying where you came from and who your ancestors are would have been enough disgrace to make you feel ashamed. Your father bears the title of the King of Naples, ruling over Sicily and Jerusalem, too, yet he is not as rich as an English landowner.

original: Hath that poor monarch taught thee to insult?   It needs not, nor it boots thee not, proud queen,   Unless the adage must be verified,   That beggars mounted run their horse to death.
translation: Has that poor king taught you to curse? It's not necessary, and it doesn't do you any good, proud queen, unless the old saying proves true that  beggars on horseback will drive their horses to death .

original: 'Tis beauty that doth oft make women proud;   But, God he knows, thy share thereof is small:   'Tis virtue that doth make them most admired;   The contrary doth make thee wonder'd at:
translation: It's usually beauty that makes women proud but God knows that your share of beauty is small. It's usually virtue that makes women admired, but it's the opposite of virtue that makes people stare at you.

original: 'Tis government that makes them seem divine;   The want thereof makes thee abominable:   Thou art as opposite to every good   As the Antipodes are unto us,   Or as the south to the septentrion.
translation: It's usually self-control that makes women seem heavenly. Your total lack of self-control makes you abominable. You are as opposite to everything that is good as people living on the other side of the world in the Antipodes  are to us, or as the south is to the  north .

original: O tiger's heart wrapt in a woman's hide!   How couldst thou drain the life-blood of the child,   To bid the father wipe his eyes withal,   And yet be seen to bear a woman's face?
translation: Oh, you have a tiger's heart wrapped in a woman's skin! How could you drain the blood of a child and make the father wipe his eyes with it, and still appear to have a woman's face?

original: Women are soft, mild, pitiful and flexible;   Thou stern, obdurate, flinty, rough, remorseless.   Bids't thou me rage? why, now thou hast thy wish:   Wouldst have me weep? why, now thou hast thy will:
translation: Women are soft, mild, compassionate and yielding. You are stern, stubborn, hard, violent and without remorse. You ask me to be angry? Well, now your wish will come true. Do you want me to cry? Well, now you'll get what you want.

original: For raging wind blows up incessant showers,   And when the rage allays, the rain begins.   These tears are my sweet Rutland's obsequies:   And every drop cries vengeance for his death,   'Gainst thee, fell Clifford, and thee, false   Frenchwoman.
translation: The raging wind blows rain showers up into the air, but when the wind calms down, the rain begins to fall. These tears are my sweet Rutland's funeral prayers, and every drop cries for vengeance for his death against you, cruel Clifford, and you, treacherous Frenchwoman.

original: Beshrew me, but his passion moves me so That hardly can I cheque my eyes from tears.
translation: Damn me, but his grief is so moving that I can hardly stop myself from crying.

original: That face of his the hungry cannibals   Would not have touch'd, would not have stain'd with  blood:   But you are more inhuman, more inexorable,   O, ten times more, than tigers of Hyrcania.
translation: Not even hungry cannibals would have touched Rutland's face or stained it with blood. But you are ten times more inhuman and more relentless than the tigers of  Hyrcania .

original: See, ruthless queen, a hapless father's tears:   This cloth thou dip'dst in blood of my sweet boy,   And I with tears do wash the blood away.
translation: See, ruthless queen, here are the tears of an unfortunate father. With these tears, I wash away the blood from this napkin that you dipped in the blood of my sweet son.

original: Keep thou the napkin, and go boast of this:   And if thou tell'st the heavy story right,   Upon my soul, the hearers will shed tears;   Yea even my foes will shed fast-falling tears,   And say 'Alas, it was a piteous deed!'
translation: You can keep the napkin and go boast of my murder. And if you tell the tragic story right, I swear that the listeners will cry. Yes, even my enemies will cry heavily and they'll say, "Oh, it was a terrible act!"

original: There, take the crown, and, with the crown, my curse;   And in thy need such comfort come to thee   As now I reap at thy too cruel hand!   Hard-hearted Clifford, take me from the world:   My soul to heaven, my blood upon your heads!
translation: Here, take the crown, and, with the crown also take my curse. I want you to have as much comfort as your too cruel hand is now giving me! Unmerciful Clifford, take me away from this world!  My soul will go to heaven and my blood will be on your hands!

original: Had he been slaughter-man to all my kin, I should not for my life but weep with him. To see how inly sorrow gripes his soul.
translation: Even if he were the murderer of all my family, I would cry with him, seeing how his soul is gripped by sorrow.

original: What, weeping-ripe, my Lord Northumberland? Think but upon the wrong he did us all, And that will quickly dry thy melting tears.
translation: What, are you on the verge of tears, my Lord Northumberland? Just think about the wrong he did to all of us, and that will quickly dry your dripping tears.

original: Here's for my oath, here's for my father's death.
translation: Here is what I promised you for killing my father.

original: And here's to right our gentle-hearted king.
translation: And this is to secure the power of our gentle-hearted king.

original: Open Thy gate of mercy, gracious God! My soul flies through these wounds to seek out Thee.
translation: Open your gates of mercy, kind God! My soul flies through these wounds to look for you!

original: Off with his head, and set it on York gates; So York may overlook the town of York.
translation: Off with his head, and put it on the gates of York, so that York's head may look over the town of York.

original: I wonder how our princely father 'scaped,   Or whether he be 'scaped away or no   From Clifford's and Northumberland's pursuit:
translation: I wonder how our father managed to escape, or if he even did escape from Clifford and Northumberland chasing after him.

original: Had he been ta'en, we should have heard the news;   Had he been slain, we should have heard the news;   Or had he 'scaped, methinks we should have heard   The happy tidings of his good escape.   How fares my brother? why is he so sad?
translation: If he were taken, we would have heard the news already. If we were killed, we would have heard the news already. Or if he escaped, I think we would have heard the happy news of his fortunate escape. Now, how are you, brother? Why are you so sad?

original: I cannot joy, until I be resolved   Where our right valiant father is become.   I saw him in the battle range about;   And watch'd him how he singled Clifford forth.
translation: I can't be happy until I am told where our brave father is. I saw him in the battle moving around, and I watched how he singled out Clifford.

original: Methought he bore him in the thickest troop   As doth a lion in a herd of neat;   Or as a bear, encompass'd round with dogs,   Who having pinch'd a few and made them cry,   The rest stand all aloof, and bark at him.
translation: I thought father placed himself in the busiest area of the battle as if he were a lion in a group of cattle. Or else like a bear, surrounded with dogs, who, once the bear has bitten a few and made them cry, stand at a distance and bark at him.

original: So fared our father with his enemies;   So fled his enemies my warlike father:   Methinks, 'tis prize enough to be his son.
translation: That's how our father dealt with our enemies. That's how our warrior father escaped his enemies. I think it's enough of a prize to be his son.

original: See how the morning opes her golden gates,   And takes her farewell of the glorious sun!   How well resembles it the prime of youth,   Trimm'd like a younker prancing to his love!
translation: See how the morning opens her golden arms, and says goodbye to the glorious sun! The morning looks very much like the peak of youth, dressed like a fashionable young man leaping towards his love!

original: Dazzle mine eyes, or do I see three suns?
translation: Are my eyes blinded by the beams, or do I see three suns?

original: Three glorious suns, each one a perfect sun;   Not separated with the racking clouds,   But sever'd in a pale clear-shining sky.
translation: Three glorious suns. Each one is a perfect sun, not just seeming to be separated by the drifting clouds but actually separate in a pale, clear sky.

original: See, see! they join, embrace, and seem to kiss,   As if they vow'd some league inviolable:   Now are they but one lamp, one light, one sun.   In this the heaven figures some event.
translation: Look, look! They come together and embrace. They look like they're kissing as if they promised to join in an indestructible union. Now they are joined together like one lamp, one light, one sun. The heavens must be predicting some event by showing this.

original: 'Tis wondrous strange, the like yet never heard of.   I think it cites us, brother, to the field,
translation: It's very strange, something that I've never heard of. I think it is calling us to the battlefield, brother.

original: That we, the sons of brave Plantagenet,   Each one already blazing by our meeds,   Should notwithstanding join our lights together   And over-shine the earth as this the world.
translation: It means that we, the sons of the brave Plantagenet, since each of is already renowned for our own individual successes, we should nevertheless join our strengths and outshine the earth just like these three suns shine over the world.

original: Whate'er it bodes, henceforward will I bear   Upon my target three fair-shining suns.
translation: Whatever it means, I will wear the image of three shining suns on my shield from now on.

original: Nay, bear three daughters: by your leave I speak it, You love the breeder better than the male.
translation: No, you should wear three daughters instead. I speak this with your permission. You love women more than men.

original: But what art thou, whose heavy looks foretell Some dreadful story hanging on thy tongue?
translation: But who are you? Your frowns predict some terrible story that you are going to tell.

original: Ah, one that was a woeful looker-on Whenas the noble Duke of York was slain, Your princely father and my loving lord!
translation: Ah, I am someone who was an unlucky bystander when the noble Duke of York was killed, your father and my beloved lord.

original: O, speak no more, for I have heard too much.
translation: Oh, stop speaking, for I have already heard too much.

original: Say how he died, for I will hear it all.
translation: Tell us how he died. I'm going to hear it all.

original: Environed he was with many foes,   And stood against them, as the hope of Troy   Against the Greeks that would have enter'd Troy.   But Hercules himself must yield to odds;
translation: He was surrounded by many enemies, and he stood against them, like when Hector stood against the Greeks that were trying to get into Troy . But even  Hercules  himself would have to surrender when outnumbered.

original: And many strokes, though with a little axe,   Hew down and fell the hardest-timber'd oak.   By many hands your father was subdued;   But only slaughter'd by the ireful arm   Of unrelenting Clifford and the queen,
translation: And even a little axe can cut down the toughest oak with many strokes.  Your father was captured by many soldiers, but he was killed only the hateful hands of the remorseless Clifford and the queen.

original: Who crown'd the gracious duke in high despite,   Laugh'd in his face; and when with grief he wept,   The ruthless queen gave him to dry his cheeks   A napkin steeped in the harmless blood   Of sweet young Rutland, by rough Clifford slain:
translation: She mockingly crowned the duke to spite him, laughed in his face, and, when he cried with grief, the cruel queen gave him a napkin to dry his cheeks that was dipped in the innocent blood of sweet, young Rutland, who rough Clifford killed.

original: And after many scorns, many foul taunts,   They took his head, and on the gates of York   They set the same; and there it doth remain,   The saddest spectacle that e'er I view'd.
translation: And after many insults, many nasty taunts, they cut off his head and put it up on the gates of York. And it's still there now. It's the saddest sight that I've ever seen.

original: Sweet Duke of York, our prop to lean upon,   Now thou art gone, we have no staff, no stay.   O Clifford, boisterous Clifford! Thou hast slain   The flower of Europe for his chivalry;
translation: Sweet Duke of York, the father we could lean on, you are now gone and we have nothing to support us. Oh, Clifford, wild Clifford! You have killed the flower of Europe for his bravery.

original: And treacherously hast thou vanquish'd him,   For hand to hand he would have vanquish'd thee.   Now my soul's palace is become a prison:
translation: You've treacherously slaughtered him, a man who would have destroyed you in hand-to-hand combat. Now my body has become a prison.

original: Ah, would she break from hence, that this my body   Might in the ground be closed up in rest!   For never henceforth shall I joy again,   Never, O never shall I see more joy!
translation: Ah, if only my soul would break away from my body so that my body could be buried in the ground! Because I'll never be happy from now on! Never, oh never, shall I experience joy again!

original: I cannot weep; for all my body's moisture   Scarce serves to quench my furnace-burning heart:
translation: I am not able to cry because all of the wetness of my body is being used to try to put out the fire of my burning heart.

original: Nor can my tongue unload my heart's great burthen;   For selfsame wind that I should speak withal   Is kindling coals that fires all my breast,   And burns me up with flames that tears would quench.
translation: I can't speak my grief either because the same air that I would speak with is lighting the fire in my chest, burning me with flames that tears would extinguish.

original: To weep is to make less the depth of grief:   Tears, then, for babes—blows and revenge for me!   Richard, I bear thy name; I'll venge thy death,   Or die renowned by attempting it.
translation: To cry is to lessen the depth of grief. Tears are for children, fighting and revenge are for me. Richard, my father, I share your name. I'll revenge your death or earn fame when I die in the attempt.

original: His name that valiant duke hath left with thee; His dukedom and his chair with me is left.
translation: That brave duke left his name with you. He left his dukedom and his power with me.

original: Nay, if thou be that princely eagle's bird, Show thy descent by gazing 'gainst the sun: For "chair and dukedom," "throne and kingdom" say; Either that is thine, or else thou wert not his.
translation: No, if you're truly a prince, show your power by looking directly into the sun without blinking like an eagle: instead of "power and dukedom," say "throne and kingdom." They rightfully belong to you, too, or else you're not our father's son.

original: How now, fair lords! What fare? What news abroad?
translation: How are you, my lords? What success have you had? Have you heard any news from abroad?

original: Great Lord of Warwick, if we should recount Our baleful news, and at each word's deliverance Stab poniards in our flesh till all were told, The words would add more anguish than the wounds. O valiant lord, the Duke of York is slain!
translation: Great lord of Warwick, if we should repeat our deadly news, and stab daggers in our flesh as each word is spoken until our speech was done, the words would be more painful than the wounds. Oh, brave lord, the Duke of York is killed!

original: O Warwick, Warwick! That Plantagenet, Which held thee dearly as his soul's redemption, Is by the stern Lord Clifford done to death.
translation: Oh, Warwick, Warwick! Plantagenet, who cared about you as much as he cared about his own soul's salvation, was killed by the cruel Clifford.

original: Ten days ago I drown'd these news in tears;   And now, to add more measure to your woes,   I come to tell you things sith then befall'n.
translation: I cried after hearing this news ten days ago. And now, to add even more to your misery, I am here to tell you what's happened since.

original: After the bloody fray at Wakefield fought,   Where your brave father breathed his latest gasp,   Tidings, as swiftly as the posts could run,   Were brought me of your loss and his depart.
translation: After the bloody battle was fought at  Wakefield , where your brave father drew his last breath, news was brought to me of your loss and his death as swiftly as the messengers could carry it.

original: I, then in London keeper of the king,   Muster'd my soldiers, gather'd flocks of friends,   And very well appointed, as I thought,   March'd toward Saint Alban's to intercept the queen,   Bearing the king in my behalf along;
translation: I was then in London, watching over the king,  so I gathered my soldiers and many friends, and well-prepared (as I thought), headed towards  Saint Alban's  to block the queen's way. I took the king with me for my own advantage.

original: For by my scouts I was advertised   That she was coming with a full intent   To dash our late decree in parliament   Touching King Henry's oath and your succession.
translation: I was warned by my spies that she was coming fully intending to overturn our recent agreement in the parliament—the one about King Henry's oath and your succession to the throne.

original: Short tale to make, we at Saint Alban's met   Our battles join'd, and both sides fiercely fought:   But whether 'twas the coldness of the king,   Who look'd full gently on his warlike queen,   That robb'd my soldiers of their heated spleen;   Or whether 'twas report of her success;   Or more than common fear of Clifford's rigour,   Who thunders to his captives blood and death,   I cannot judge   :
translation: To make a long story short,  we met at Saint Alban's, our armies crossed swords, and both sides fought fiercely. But I don't know if it was the coldness of the king, who looked gently on his warrior-like queen, that took away the fiery passion from my soldiers, or if it was the news of her success, or the general fear of cruel Clifford, who treats the ones he captures with blood and death—I can't tell what did it in the end.

original: but to conclude with truth,   Their weapons like to lightning came and went;   Our soldiers', like the night-owl's lazy flight,   Or like an idle thresher with a flail,   Fell gently down, as if they struck their friends.
translation: But to sum it all up truthfully, their weapons came and went like flashes of lightning. Our soldiers fell down gently, like the lazy flight of a night owl or a useless farmer in a wheat field,  as if they were attacking their friends and not their enemies.

original: I cheer'd them up with justice of our cause,   With promise of high pay and great rewards:   But all in vain; they had no heart to fight,   And we in them no hope to win the day;
translation: I encouraged them by reminding them about the justice we were fighting for and by promising them high pay and great rewards. But it was all in vain. They didn't have the heart to fight and we had no hope in them to win the battle.

original: So that we fled;   the king unto the queen;   Lord George your brother, Norfolk and myself,   In haste, post-haste, are come to join with you:   For in the marches here we heard you were,   Making another head to fight again.
translation: So we ran away. The king ran to the queen, while your brother Lord George, Norfolk, and myself have come quickly as we can to join you. Near the Welsh border, we heard heard that you were here, getting an army together for another fight.

original: Where is the Duke of Norfolk, gentle Warwick? And when came George from Burgundy to England?
translation: Where is the Duke of Norfolk, kind Warwick? And when did George come from Burgundy to England?

original: Some six miles off the duke is with the soldiers; And for your brother, he was lately sent From your kind aunt, Duchess of Burgundy, With aid of soldiers to this needful war.
translation: The duke and his soldiers are around six miles away. Your brother recently left your kind aunt, the Duchess of Burgundy, who gave him soldiers to help populate our depleted army.

original: 'Twas odds, belike, when valiant Warwick fled: Oft have I heard his praises in pursuit, But ne'er till now his scandal of retire.
translation: The odds must have been very unfavorable if brave Warwick ran away. I have often heard you praised for following the enemy, but I've never heard of your disgrace in fleeing until now.

original: Nor now my scandal, Richard, dost thou hear;   For thou shalt know this strong right hand of mine   Can pluck the diadem from faint Henry's head,   And wring the awful sceptre from his fist,
translation: You don't hear of my disgrace now, Richard. You will see that this strong right hand of mine can tear the crown off weak Henry's head, and wrench the staff from his fist.

original: Were he as famous and as bold in war   As he is famed for mildness, peace, and prayer.
translation: I'd do so even if he were as renowned and as brave in war as he is is famous for his mildness, peacefulness and praying.

original: I know it well, Lord Warwick; blame me not:   'Tis love I bear thy glories makes me speak.   But in this troublous time what's to be done?
translation: I know that's true, Lord Warwick. Don't blame me. It's the love that I have for your glory that makes me speak. But what should we do in these troubling times?

original: Shall we go throw away our coats of steel,   And wrap our bodies in black mourning gowns,   Numbering our Ave-Maries with our beads?
translation: Shall we go and throw away our steel armor and wear black mourning clothes, counting  Hail Marys  with our rosary  beads?

original: Or shall we on the helmets of our foes   Tell our devotion with revengeful arms?   If for the last, say ay, and to it, lords.
translation: Or, instead, should we show our devotion and count the strokes we make with our vengeful swords on the helmets of our enemies? If you think it's the latter, say yes, and let's get to it, lords!

original: Why, therefore Warwick came to seek you out;   And therefore comes my brother Montague.   Attend me, lords. The proud insulting queen,   With Clifford and the haught Northumberland,   And of their feather many more proud birds,   Have wrought the easy-melting king like wax.
translation: Well, that's why I came to look for you and that's why my brother Montague is coming. Listen to me, lords. The proud insulting queen, with Clifford and the arrogant Northumberland, and many proud folks like them, have molded this king as if he were easily melted wax.

original: He swore consent to your succession,   His oath enrolled in the parliament;   And now to London all the crew are gone,   To frustrate both his oath and what beside   May make against the house of Lancaster.
translation: He swore an oath that you would succeed him, and his promise was officially recorded in the parliament. And now all the men are going to London to overturn both his promise and anything else that can be used against the House of Lancaster.

original: Their power, I think, is thirty thousand strong:   Now, if the help of Norfolk and myself,   With all the friends that thou, brave Earl of March,   Amongst the loving Welshmen canst procure,   Will but amount to five and twenty thousand,
translation: I think they have thirty thousand soldiers. Now, if we put together the soldiers that Norfolk and I are providing, all the friends that you—brave  Earl of March —can gather from the loving Welshmen, it will only be about twenty-five thousand total.

original: Why, Via! To London will we march amain,   And once again bestride our foaming steeds,   And once again cry 'Charge upon our foes!'   But never once again turn back and fly.
translation: I say, "onward," then! We'll go straight to London, and once again ride our horses, and once again shout, "Charge at our enemies!," but we'll never again turn back and flee.

original: Ay, now methinks I hear great Warwick speak: Ne'er may he live to see a sunshine day, That cries 'Retire,' if Warwick bid him stay.
translation: Yes, now that sounds like the Warwick I know and love. I don't think a man would live to see the sun rise again if he cried, "Withdraw! once Warwick told him to stay.

original: Lord Warwick, on thy shoulder will I lean; And when thou fail'st—as God forbid the hour!— Must Edward fall, which peril heaven forfend!
translation: Lord Warwick, I will lean on your shoulder and when you fail in your mission—God forbid!—Edward will also fall, heaven forbid!

original: No longer Earl of March, but Duke of York:   The next degree is England's royal throne;   For King of England shalt thou be proclaim'd   In every borough as we pass along;
translation: You are no longer Earl of March but Duke of York! Next stop: the throne of England. You shall be named the King of England in every part of the country that we pass.

original: And he that throws not up his cap for joy   Shall for the fault make forfeit of his head.   King Edward, valiant Richard, Montague,   Stay we no longer, dreaming of renown,   But sound the trumpets, and about our task.
translation: And anyone who won't throw up his hat in joy shall lose his head for that mistake. King Edward, brave Richard, Montague, let's not stay here for much longer, only dreaming of glory. Let's sound the trumpets, and carry out our mission.

original: Then, Clifford, were thy heart as hard as steel, As thou hast shown it flinty by thy deeds, I come to pierce it, or to give thee mine.
translation: Then, Clifford, even if your heart is as hard as steel, as you have shown it to be steely by your actions, I'd come either to pierce your heart or to give you my own heart and loyalty.

original: Then strike up drums: God and Saint George for us!
How now! What news?
translation: What now? What's the news?

original: The Duke of Norfolk sends you word by me, The queen is coming with a puissant host; And craves your company for speedy counsel.
translation: The Duke of Norfolk sends me with a message for you. The queen is coming with a powerful army and he desires your company for a immediate consultation.

original: Why then it sorts, brave warriors, let's away.
translation: Well, then, things are falling into place. Brave warriors, let's go!

original: Welcome, my lord, to this brave town of York. Yonder's the head of that arch-enemy That sought to be encompass'd with your crown: Doth not the object cheer your heart, my lord?
translation: Welcome to this splendid town of York, my lord. Over there is the head of our biggest enemy that wanted to take over your crown. Doesn't it cheer you to look on it, my lord?

original: Ay, as the rocks cheer them that fear their wreck: To see this sight, it irks my very soul. Withhold revenge, dear God! 'Tis not my fault, Nor wittingly have I infringed my vow.
translation: Yes, as the rocks cheer up those that fear they'll crash on them. To see this disturbs my soul. Stop this revenge, dear God! It's not my fault and I haven't knowingly broken my oath.

original: My gracious liege, this too much lenity   And harmful pity must be laid aside.   To whom do lions cast their gentle looks?   Not to the beast that would usurp their den.
translation: My gracious lord, this harmful mildness and pity must be put to one side. At whom do lions look gently? Not the beast that wants to take over their cave.

original: Whose hand is that the forest bear doth lick?   Not his that spoils her young before her face.   Who 'scapes the lurking serpent's mortal sting?   Not he that sets his foot upon her back.
translation: Whose hand does the forest bear lick? Not the hunter that slaughters her young in front of her. Who escapes the sting of the sneaky, venomous snake? Not the man that puts his foot on her back.

original: The smallest worm will turn being trodden on,   And doves will peck in safeguard of their brood.   Ambitious York doth level at thy crown,   Thou smiling while he knit his angry brows:
translation: The smallest worm will grown violent when someone steps on it, and doves will peck to keep their littles ones safe. Ambitious York aims at your crown! You smile while he furrows his angry brows.

original: He, but a duke, would have his son a king,   And raise his issue, like a loving sire;   Thou, being a king, blest with a goodly son,   Didst yield consent to disinherit him,   Which argued thee a most unloving father.
translation: He is only a duke and wants his son to be a king! Like a loving father, he'd raise up his offspring. You, a king's who's lucky to have a fine son, agreed to disinherit him which made you look like a rather unloving father.

original: Unreasonable creatures feed their young;   And though man's face be fearful to their eyes,   Yet, in protection of their tender ones,   Who hath not seen them, even with those wings   Which sometime they have used with fearful flight,   Make war with him that climb'd unto their nest,   Offer their own lives in their young's defence?
translation: Even creatures without reason feed their young. And though they view man's face as scary, who hasn't seen them use their wings, which were meant for taking flight, to fight in protection of their young ones against any man who invades their nest? They offer their own lives in defense of their young!

original: For shame, my liege, make them your precedent!   Were it not pity that this goodly boy   Should lose his birthright by his father's fault,
translation: For shame, my king, take those creatures as an example! Wouldn't it be a pity if this fine young boy should lose his birthright because of the mistake his father made?

original: And long hereafter say unto his child,   'What my great-grandfather and his grandsire got   My careless father fondly gave away'?   Ah, what a shame were this!
translation: And, in years to come, he'll say to his own child, "That which my great-grandfather and my grand-father got, my father threw away carelessly"?  Ah, what a shame that would be!

original: Look on the boy;   And let his manly face, which promiseth   Successful fortune, steel thy melting heart   To hold thine own and leave thine own with him.
translation: Look at this boy. Let his manly face, which promises good fortune, harden your melting heart into fighting to hold your title and let him inherit it.

original: Full well hath Clifford play'd the orator,   Inferring arguments of mighty force.   But, Clifford, tell me, didst thou never hear   That things ill-got had ever bad success?
translation: Clifford has played the role of orator very well, offering powerful arguments. But, tell me Clifford, have you never heard that things wrongfully gained end up turning out badly?

original: And happy always was it for that son   Whose father for his hoarding went to hell?   I'll leave my son my virtuous deeds behind;   And would my father had left me no more!
translation: And was it always a happy ending for the son whose father went to hell for hoarding his money? My son will inherit my virtuous actions, and I wish my father left me nothing but those too!

original: For all the rest is held at such a rate   As brings a thousand-fold more care to keep   Than in possession and jot of pleasure.   Ah, cousin York! Would thy best friends did know   How it doth grieve me that thy head is here!
translation: Because the rest that I've inherited is considered to be worth so much that it brings a thousand times more troubles to hold on to than it does to possess or enjoy it. Ah, cousin York! I wish your best friends knew how grief-stricken I am that that your head is here!

original: My lord, cheer up your spirits: our foes are nigh,   And this soft courage makes your followers faint.
translation: My lord, cheer up. Our enemies are near and this lack of courage makes your followers weak.

original: You promised knighthood to our forward son:   Unsheathe your sword, and dub him presently.   Edward, kneel down.
translation: You promised our impressive son a knighthood. Unsheathe your sword and dub him a knight immediately. Edward, kneel.

original: Edward Plantagenet, arise a knight; And learn this lesson, draw thy sword in right.
translation: Edward Plantagenet, stand as a knight. And learn this lesson: only use your sword for a just cause.

original: My gracious father, by your kingly leave, I'll draw it as apparent to the crown, And in that quarrel use it to the death.
translation: My gracious father, if you allow me, I'll use my sword to fight for my right to be heir to the crown. In that fight, I'll fight with this sword to the death.

original: Why, that is spoken like a toward prince.
translation: You spoke that like a brave prince.

original: Royal commanders, be in readiness:   For with a band of thirty thousand men   Comes Warwick, backing of the Duke of York;
translation: Royal leaders, prepare yourselves. Warwick is coming with a group of thirty thousand men, supporting the Duke of York.

original: And in the towns, as they do march along,   Proclaims him king, and many fly to him:   Darraign your battle, for they are at hand.
translation: And in the towns through which they pass, they proclaim him king and many join him. Get the soldiers ready because they are nearly here.

original: I would your highness would depart the field: The queen hath best success when you are absent.
translation: I wish your highness would leave the battlefield. The queen is most successful when you're not there.

original: Ay, good my lord, and leave us to our fortune.
translation: Yes, my good lord. And leave us to our own fate.

original: Why, that's my fortune too; therefore I'll stay.
translation: But that's my fate too. So I'll stay.

original: Be it with resolution then to fight.
translation: Then let's go fight with determination.

original: My royal father, cheer these noble lords And hearten those that fight in your defence: Unsheathe your sword, good father; cry 'Saint George!'
translation: My royal father, cheer up these brave lords and encourage those that fight to defend you. Take up your sword, good father, and shout, "Saint George!"

original: Now, perjured Henry! Wilt thou kneel for grace, And set thy diadem upon my head; Or bide the mortal fortune of the field?
translation: Now, lying Henry! Will you kneel for mercy, and put your crown on my head? Or will you await your fate on the battlefield?

original: Go, rate thy minions, proud insulting boy! Becomes it thee to be thus bold in terms Before thy sovereign and thy lawful king?
translation: Go and scold your followers, you proud, insulting boy! Do you dare address your sovereign and your lawful king with these rude words?

original: I am his king, and he should bow his knee; I was adopted heir by his consent: Since when, his oath is broke; for, as I hear, You, that are king, though he do wear the crown, Have caused him, by new act of parliament, To blot out me, and put his own son in.
translation: [To QUEEN MARGARET]

original: And reason too: Who should succeed the father but the son?
translation: And there's a good reason for that too. Who should follow the father but his son?

original: Are you there, butcher? O, I cannot speak!
translation: Are you there, murderer? Oh, I cannot speak!

original: Ay, crook-back, here I stand to answer thee, Or any he the proudest of thy sort.
translation: Yes, hunchback! I am standing here to answer you or whoever's the most foolhardy of your mob.

original: 'Twas you that kill'd young Rutland, was it not?
translation: It was you who killed young Rutland, wasn't it?

original: Ay, and old York, and yet not satisfied.
translation: Yes, and I killed old York. But I'm still not satisfied.

original: For God's sake, lords, give signal to the fight.
translation: For God's sake, lords, give a signal to start the fight.

original: What say'st thou, Henry, wilt thou yield the crown?
translation: What do you say, Henry? Will you give up your crown?

original: Why, how now, long-tongued Warwick! Dare you speak? When you and I met at Saint Alban's last, Your legs did better service than your hands.
translation: Ah, how are you, you blabbing Warwick? Do you dare to speak? When we last met at Saint Alban's, you were running away instead of fighting.

original: Then 'twas my turn to fly, and now 'tis thine.
translation: Then it was my time to flee, and now it's yours.

original: You said so much before, and yet you fled.
translation: You said that before, and yet it was you who ran away.

original: 'Twas not your valour, Clifford, drove me thence.
translation: It wasn't your bravery that made me run, Clifford.

original: No, nor your manhood that durst make you stay.
translation: But your manliness didn't make you stay either.

original: Northumberland, I hold thee reverently. Break off the parley; for scarce I can refrain The execution of my big-swoln heart Upon that Clifford, that cruel child-killer.
translation: Northumberland, I respect you. End the conversation because I can barely stop my swollen heart from taking revenge upon Clifford, the cruel child-killer!

original: I slew thy father, call'st thou him a child?
translation: I killed your father. Do you call him a child?

original: Ay, like a dastard and a treacherous coward, As thou didst kill our tender brother Rutland; But ere sunset I'll make thee curse the deed.
translation: Yes, you did, like a treasonous coward, just as you killed our young brother Rutland. But I will make you regret that you did before the sun sets.

original: Have done with words, my lords, and hear me speak.
translation: Stop squabbling, my lords, and listen to me now.

original: Defy them then, or else hold close thy lips.
translation: Challenge them then, or if you won't, then keep your mouth closed.

original: I prithee, give no limits to my tongue: I am a king, and privileged to speak.
translation: Please, don't tell me what my tongue can do. I am a king and I am privileged to speak.

original: My liege, the wound that bred this meeting here Cannot be cured by words; therefore be still.
translation: My king, the wound that is the cause of this meeting can't be healed by words. Therefore, be silent.

original: Then, executioner, unsheathe thy sword: By him that made us all, I am resolved that Clifford's manhood lies upon his tongue.
translation: Then, murderer, unsheathe your sword. By God, I am convinced that Clifford's manliness exists only in his words.

original: Say, Henry, shall I have my right, or no? A thousand men have broke their fasts to-day, That ne'er shall dine unless thou yield the crown.
translation: Tell me, Henry, will I have my right to the throne or not? A thousand men had breakfast this morning, but they'll never eat dinner again if you don't give up the crown.

original: If thou deny, their blood upon thy head; For York in justice puts his armour on.
translation: If you deny him his right, their blood will be on your head. York justly puts on his armor.

original: If that be right which Warwick says is right, There is no wrong, but every thing is right.
translation: If what Warwick says is right is actually right, then there is nothing wrong in the world, but everything is right.

original: Whoever got thee, there thy mother stands; For, well I wot, thou hast thy mother's tongue.
translation: Whoever your father may be, I know it's your mother who stands over there. For I can tell you have your mother's tongue.

original: But thou art neither like thy sire nor dam; But like a foul mis-shapen stigmatic, Mark'd by the destinies to be avoided, As venom toads, or lizards' dreadful stings.
translation: But you aren't like your father or your mother. Instead, you're like a ugly, deformed monster, branded by the fates as someone who should be avoided, like poisonous toads or the stings of dreadful lizards.

original: Iron of Naples hid with English gilt, Whose father bears the title of a king,— As if a channel should be call'd the sea,— Shamest thou not, knowing whence thou art extraught, To let thy tongue detect thy base-born heart?
translation: You cheap Naples girl, disguised in English robes. Your father has the title of a king but in the same way we could also call a channel the sea. Are you not ashamed of yourself, knowing where you come from, to let your tongue reveal your lowly origins?

original: A wisp of straw were worth a thousand crowns,   To make this shameless callet know herself.   Helen of Greece was fairer far than thou,   Although thy husband may be Menelaus;   And ne'er was Agamemnon's brother wrong'd   By that false woman, as this king by thee.
translation: I'd pay a thousand crowns to make this shameless whore know herself for what she is . Helen of Greece was more beautiful than you although your husband may be Menelaus. But  Menelaus, Agamemnon's brother , was never wronged by that false woman like you have wronged this king.

original: His father revell'd in the heart of France,   And tamed the king, and made the dauphin stoop;   And had he match'd according to his state,   He might have kept that glory to this day;
translation: The king's father, Henry V, had great success in the heart of France, where he won over the king of France, and made the dauphin, the prince, bow to him too. And if this king here had married according to his station, he might have retained his father's glory until today.

original: And, in this resolution, I defy thee; Not willing any longer conference, Since thou deniest the gentle king to speak. Sound trumpets! Let our bloody colours wave! And either victory, or else a grave.
translation: And, in that spirit, I refuse to listen to you any longer since you won't let the gentle king speak. Let the trumpets sound! Let our bloody flags wave! We'll either have victory or death.

original: Stay, Edward.
translation: Stay, Edward.

original: No, wrangling woman, we'll no longer stay: These words will cost ten thousand lives this day.
translation: No, you bargaining woman. We won't stay any longer. These words will cost ten thousand soldiers their lives today.

original: Forspent with toil, as runners with a race,   I lay me down a little while to breathe;
translation: I am exhausted from all the fighting, like runners are exhausted after a race. I'll lay down a little to catch my breath.

original: For strokes received, and many blows repaid,   Have robb'd my strong-knit sinews of their strength,   And spite of spite needs must I rest awhile.
translation: The hits I received, and the ones that I gave in return, have tired out my strong muscles, and come what may, I have to rest for a while.

original: Smile, gentle heaven! Or strike, ungentle death! For this world frowns, and Edward's sun is clouded.
translation: Smile on us, kind heaven! Or strike us down, you unkind death! Because this world is frowning and the sun that represents me is clouded with darkness.

original: How now, my lord! What hap? What hope of good?
translation: What's happening, my lord? What luck? Do we have hope for a happy outcome?

original: Our hap is loss, our hope but sad despair; Our ranks are broke, and ruin follows us: What counsel give you? Whither shall we fly?
translation: Our luck is gone and our hope is only sad desperation. They got through the first row of our soldiers and so we're ruined. What advice do you give us? Where should we run?

original: Bootless is flight, they follow us with wings; And weak we are and cannot shun pursuit.
translation: Running away is pointless. They'll follow us as if they have wings. And we are weak and can't escape their pursuit.

original: Ah, Warwick, why hast thou withdrawn thyself?   Thy brother's blood the thirsty earth hath drunk,   Broach'd with the steely point of Clifford's lance;
translation: Ah, Warwick! Why have you left the fighting? The thirsty earth is now soaked with your  brother 's blood. He was pierced by Clifford's spear.

original: And in the very pangs of death he cried,   Like to a dismal clangour heard from far,   'Warwick, revenge! brother, revenge my death!'
translation: And when he was dying he shouted, as if an ominous ringing heard from far away, "Warwick, revenge me! Brother, revenge my death!"

original: So, underneath the belly of their steeds,   That stain'd their fetlocks in his smoking blood,   The noble gentleman gave up the ghost.
translation: And so, under the horse's belly, with the horse's legs stained with your brother's streaming blood, the noble gentleman died.

original: Then let the earth be drunken with our blood:   I'll kill my horse, because I will not fly.   Why stand we like soft-hearted women here,   Wailing our losses, whiles the foe doth rage;
translation: Then let the earth drown in our blood. I'll kill my horse because I will not run away. Why do we stand here like weak women, crying over what we lost, while our enemies are in a frenzy?

original: And look upon, as if the tragedy   Were play'd in jest by counterfeiting actors?
translation: Why do we look on it all as if the tragedy was only make-believe, performed by actors playing pretend?

original: Here on my knee I vow to God above,   I'll never pause again, never stand still,   Till either death hath closed these eyes of mine   Or fortune given me measure of revenge.
translation: I go down on my knee now and swear to God above that I'll never stop again, I'll never stand still, until either death closes my eyes or I get to take my revenge, if fate allows it.

original: O Warwick, I do bend my knee with thine;   And in this vow do chain my soul to thine!
translation: Oh, Warwick! I go down on my knees with you and I swear to join my soul with yours!

original: And, ere my knee rise from the earth's cold face,   I throw my hands, mine eyes, my heart to thee,   Thou setter up and plucker down of kings,   Beseeching Thee, if with Thy will it stands   That to my foes this body must be prey,   Yet that thy brazen gates of heaven may ope,   And give sweet passage to my sinful soul!
translation: And before I rise from the cold ground, I give over my hands, my eyes, and my heart to my God who establishes and removes kings.  I beg you, God, if its your will agree that my body must become prey for my enemies that your brass gates of heaven may open allow in  my sinful soul!

original: Now, lords, take leave until we meet again,   Where'er it be, in heaven or in earth.
translation: Now, lords, you can go until we meet again. Wherever that may be, in heaven or on earth.

original: Brother, give me thy hand; and, gentle Warwick, Let me embrace thee in my weary arms: I, that did never weep, now melt with woe That winter should cut off our spring-time so.
translation: Give me your hand, brother. And kind Warwick, let me embrace you with my weak arms. I that have never cried am now melting with sorrow at the fact that we should be separated so soon.

original: Away, away! Once more, sweet lords farewell.
translation: Let's go, let's go! Once more goodbye, sweet lords.

original: Yet let us all together to our troops,   And give them leave to fly that will not stay;   And call them pillars that will stand to us;
translation: Let us all go together to our soldiers and tell those who don't want to stay to run away. If they'll stand next to us and support us, we'll call them pillars.

original: And, if we thrive, promise them such rewards   As victors wear at the Olympian games:   This may plant courage in their quailing breasts;   For yet is hope of life and victory.   Forslow no longer, make we hence amain.
translation: And, if we are successful, we'll promise them rewards like the winners wear at the Olympic Games. This may give them courage in their quivering hearts since there is still hope of life and victory. Let's not delay. Let's go speedily!

original: Now, Clifford, I have singled thee alone: Suppose this arm is for the Duke of York, And this for Rutland; both bound to revenge, Wert thou environ'd with a brazen wall.
translation: Now I have isolated you away from the rest, Clifford. Let's pretend that this arm is for the Duke of York and this one is for Rutland. Both will have revenge, even if you were surrounded by a brass wall.

original: Now, Richard, I am with thee here alone:   This is the hand that stabb'd thy father York;   And this the hand that slew thy brother Rutland;
translation: Now,  I am here alone with you, Richard. This is the hand that stabbed your father York and this is the hand that killed your brother Rutland.

original: And here's the heart that triumphs in their death   And cheers these hands that slew thy sire and brother   To execute the like upon thyself;   And so, have at thee!
translation: And here's the heart that is happy because of their deaths and encourages these hands that killed your father and brother to also kill you. And so, here I come!

original: Nay Warwick, single out some other chase; For I myself will hunt this wolf to death.
translation: No, Warwick, choose some other prey. I will hunt this wolf alone until he's met his death.

original: This battle fares like to the morning's war,   When dying clouds contend with growing light,   What time the shepherd, blowing of his nails,   Can neither call it perfect day nor night.
translation: This battle is like the time between early morning and day, when fading clouds fight with the growing light. At such a time, the shepherd, warming his hands by blowing on them, can't call it completely day or night.

original: Now sways it this way, like a mighty sea   Forced by the tide to combat with the wind;   Now sways it that way, like the selfsame sea   Forced to retire by fury of the wind:
translation: Now it goes one way, like a powerful sea forced by the tide to fight with the wind. And now it inclines the other way, like that same sea forced to give up fighting because of the wind's intensity.

original: Sometime the flood prevails, and then the wind;   Now one the better, then another best;   Both tugging to be victors, breast to breast,   Yet neither conqueror nor conquered:   So is the equal poise of this fell war.
translation: Sometimes the sea wins, sometimes the wind. Now is one the better one, then the other. Both are fighting to be the winner, face to face. Yet neither is winner or loser. And that's how it is with the equal balance of this war.

original: Here on this molehill will I sit me down.   To whom God will, there be the victory!   For Margaret my queen, and Clifford too,   Have chid me from the battle; swearing both   They prosper best of all when I am thence.
translation: I will sit down here on this molehill. Whoever God wants to win, will win! My queen Margaret, and Clifford too, told me to stay away from the battle. Both said that they fight best when I am not there.

original: Would I were dead! if God's good will were so;   For what is in this world but grief and woe?   O God! methinks it were a happy life,   To be no better than a homely swain;
translation: I wish I were dead! If only God would allow it, because what's left in this world apart from grief and sorrow? Oh, God! I think life would be happy if we could all be just simple countrymen.

original: To sit upon a hill, as I do now,   To carve out dials quaintly, point by point,   Thereby to see the minutes how they run,
translation: We could sit on a hill, like I do now and carve out sundials skillfully, bit by bit, to watch the minutes as they fly by.

original: How many make the hour full complete;   How many hours bring about the day;   How many days will finish up the year;   How many years a mortal man may live.
translation: How many make one hour, how many hours make one day, how many days make one year, how many years a man can live.

original: When this is known, then to divide the times:   So many hours must I tend my flock;   So many hours must I take my rest;   So many hours must I contemplate;   So many hours must I sport myself;
translation: When we know this, we can then divide the time. I must spend this many hours taking care of the flock. I must spend this many hours thinking. I must spend this many hours enjoying myself.

original: So many days my ewes have been with young;   So many weeks ere the poor fools will ean:   So many years ere I shall shear the fleece:
translation: This many days have my sheep been pregnant. This many weeks before they give birth. This many years before I shall shear the sheep's wool.

original: So minutes, hours, days, months, and years,   Pass'd over to the end they were created,   Would bring white hairs unto a quiet grave.   Ah, what a life were this! How sweet! How lovely!
translation: And so minutes, hours, days, months and years, used in the ways they were meant for, would make us white-haired before our peaceful dying day. Ah, what a life that would be! How sweet and how lovely!

original: Gives not the hawthorn-bush a sweeter shade   To shepherds looking on their silly sheep,   Than doth a rich embroider'd canopy   To kings that fear their subjects' treachery?
translation: Doesn't the hawthorn bush give a nicer shade to shepherds looking after their sheep than a richly embroidered  canopy  in a procession does for kings who are afraid that their people may betray them?

original: O, yes, it doth; a thousand-fold it doth.   And to conclude, the shepherd's homely curds,   His cold thin drink out of his leather bottle.   His wonted sleep under a fresh tree's shade,   All which secure and sweetly he enjoys,   Is far beyond a prince's delicates,
translation: Oh, yes, it does! A thousand times nicer! And, in conclusion,  the shepherd's homemade cheese, his cold drink out of his leather bottle, his usual sleep under the shade of a fresh tree—all that he enjoys carefree and happy—are far better than luxuries belonging to a prince.

original: His viands sparkling in a golden cup,   His body couched in a curious bed,   When care, mistrust, and treason waits on him.
translation: Even if his food is sparkling in a golden cup and his body is lying in a fine bed, what is that worth when troubles, mistrust and treason are all around him?

original: Ill blows the wind that profits nobody.   This man, whom hand to hand I slew in fight,   May be possessed with some store of crowns
translation: There's nothing good about events that nobody profits from. This man, whom I killed in a hand to hand fight may have some gold coins on his body.

original: And I, that haply take them from him now,   May yet ere night yield both my life and them   To some man else, as this dead man doth me.
translation: I'll take them gladly from him now, but i may lose both my life and these coins to another man before the end of the night just as this man lost them to me.

original: Who's this? O God! It is my father's face,   Whom in this conflict I unwares have kill'd.   O heavy times, begetting such events!
translation: But who is this? Oh, God! It is the face of my father, whom I have killed in this fight, unaware of who he was. Oh, these are sad times when such things can happen!

original: From London by the king was I press'd forth;   My father, being the Earl of Warwick's man,   Came on the part of York, press'd by his master;   And I, who at his hands received my life, him   Have by my hands of life bereaved him.
translation: I came from London because the king called us to battle. My father, since he is one of the Earl of Warwick's men, came to fight for York, commanded to do so by his master. And I, who was given my life from his hands, have now taken life from him by my hands.

original: Pardon me, God, I knew not what I did!   And pardon, father, for I knew not thee!   My tears shall wipe away these bloody marks;   And no more words till they have flow'd their fill.
translation: Pardon me, God, I didn't know what I was doing! And forgive me, father, because I didn't know it was you! My tears will wash away these bloody stains and I will speak no more words until my tears have fully flowed.

original: O piteous spectacle! O bloody times!   Whiles lions war and battle for their dens,   Poor harmless lambs abide their enmity.
translation: Oh, miserable sight! Oh, these are bloody times! While lions fight one another for their dens, poor harmless lambs have to survive their conflict.

original: Weep, wretched man, I'll aid thee tear for tear;   And let our hearts and eyes, like civil war,   Be blind with tears, and break o'ercharged with grief.
translation: Weep, miserable man, I'll help you by shedding a tear for each of yours. And let our hearts and eyes be blind with tears, like this civil war itself, until our hearts and eyes break with grief.

original: Thou that so stoutly hast resisted me,   Give me thy gold, if thou hast any gold:   For I have bought it with an hundred blows.   But let me see: is this our foeman's face?
translation: You that have fought me so bravely, give me your gold now, if you have any gold. I have earned it with those hundred times I hit you. But let me see: is this the face of our enemy?

original: Ah, no, no, no, it is mine only son!   Ah, boy, if any life be left in thee,   Throw up thine eye! See, see what showers arise,   Blown with the windy tempest of my heart,   Upon thy wounds, that kill mine eye and heart!
translation: Ah, no, no, no, it's my only son! Ah, boy, if there is any life left in you, open your eyes! Look, look, at these rain showers that fall, blown by the windy tempest inside my heart, on to your wounds, wounds that poison my eye and break my heart!

original: O, pity, God, this miserable age!   What stratagems, how fell, how butcherly,   Erroneous, mutinous and unnatural,   This deadly quarrel daily doth beget!
translation: Oh, God, take pity on these miserable times! The deadly fight daily causes these violent actions that are so cruel, so bloody, so wrongful, so rebellious, and so unnatural!

original: O boy, thy father gave thee life too soon,   And hath bereft thee of thy life too late!
translation: Oh, boy, your father brought you into this world too soon and has taken you out of it too early!

original: Woe above woe! Grief more than common grief!   O that my death would stay these ruthful deeds!   O pity, pity, gentle heaven, pity!
translation: Sorrow on top of sorrow! Grief more than the usual grief! Oh, that my death could prevent these lamentable actions!

original: The red rose and the white are on his face,   The fatal colours of our striving houses:   The one his purple blood right well resembles;   The other his pale cheeks, methinks, presenteth:
translation: Oh, pity, take pity, gentle heaven, take pity! There's both the red rose and the white rose on his face, the deadly colors of the enemy houses. His purple blood looks like the red rose while it seems to me his pale cheeks look like the white rose.

original: Wither one rose, and let the other flourish;   If you contend, a thousand lives must wither.
translation: Let one rose fade away and let the other grow strong. If you fight, a thousand lives will be lost.

original: How will my mother for a father's death Take on with me and ne'er be satisfied!
translation: Imagine how my mother will deal with me to learn of my father's death—she'll never be satisfied!
