original: How will my wife for slaughter of my son Shed seas of tears and ne'er be satisfied!
translation: Imagine how my wife will shed seas worth of tears for the murder of my son—she'll never be satisfied!

original: How will the country for these woeful chances Misthink the king and not be satisfied!
translation: Imagine how the country will think badly of the king after these unfortunate circumstances—they'll never be satisfied!

original: Was ever son so rued a father's death?
translation: Has ever a son lamented a father's death so much?

original: Was ever father so bemoan'd his son?
translation: Has ever a father so wailed for his son so much?

original: Was ever king so grieved for subjects' woe? Much is your sorrow; mine ten times so much.
translation: Has ever a king grieved for his people's sorrows so much? Your sorrow is great, but mine is ten times stronger.

original: I'll bear thee hence, where I may weep my fill.
translation: I'll take you away from here to somewhere where I can weep until I can weep no more.

original: These arms of mine shall be thy winding-sheet;   My heart, sweet boy, shall be thy sepulchre,   For from my heart thine image ne'er shall go;   My sighing breast shall be thy funeral bell;
translation: My arms shall be your burial shroud! My heart, sweet boy, shall be your grave, because your image will never leave it. My sighs will be your funeral bell.

original: And so obsequious will thy father be,   Even for the loss of thee, having no more,   As Priam was for all his valiant sons.
translation: And your father will be so dutiful in performing funeral rites for your loss, since I have no more sons, just as  Priam  observed all the rituals for all of his brave sons.

original: I'll bear thee hence; and let them fight that will,   For I have murdered where I should not kill.
translation: I'll take you away from here. Let others fight if they want to, but I have murdered the very person I should never kill.

original: Sad-hearted men, much overgone with care, Here sits a king more woeful than you are.
translation: Men with sadness in their hearts, overcome with trouble: here sits a king more sorrowful than you are.

original: Fly, father, fly! For all your friends are fled, And Warwick rages like a chafed bull: Away! For death doth hold us in pursuit.
translation: Run away, father, run! All your friends have fled and Warwick is raging like an angry bull. Let's go! Death is chasing after us.

original: Mount you, my lord; towards Berwick post amain:   Edward and Richard, like a brace of greyhounds   Having the fearful flying hare in sight,
translation: Mount your horse, my lord, and ride towards Berwick as fast as you can. Edward and Richard, like a pair of greyhounds who can see the frightened fleeing rabbit in front of them ,

original: With fiery eyes sparkling for very wrath,   And bloody steel grasp'd in their ireful hands,   Are at our backs; and therefore hence amain.
translation: are right behind us, with fiery eyes sparkling in their blinding anger. They are holding bloody swords in their angry hands. So, let's go quickly!

original: Away! For vengeance comes along with them: Nay, stay not to expostulate, make speed; Or else come after: I'll away before.
translation: Let's go! They're coming for vengeance. No, don't stay to debate the matter. Hurry or otherwise follow after us. I'll go away before you.

original: Nay, take me with thee, good sweet Exeter: Not that I fear to stay, but love to go Whither the queen intends. Forward; away!
translation: No, take me with you, good, sweet Exeter. It's not that I am afraid to stay, but I want to go wherever my queen is going. Let's go—away!

original: Here burns my candle out; ay, here it dies,   Which, whiles it lasted, gave King Henry light.   O Lancaster, I fear thy overthrow   More than my body's parting with my soul!
translation: My life's candle burns out here. Yes, it dies here. While it lasted, it gave light to King Henry. Oh, Lancaster, I'm more afraid you'll be defeated than I am of death!

original: My love and fear glued many friends to thee;   And, now I fall, thy tough commixture melts.   Impairing Henry, strengthening misproud York,   The common people swarm like summer flies;   And whither fly the gnats but to the sun?
translation: Love for me, and fear of me, helped you make a lot of friends, and now, as I'm I fall, all of that is falling apart. The common people are swarming everywhere like flies in the summer—hurting Henry and strengthening the wrongfully proud York—and where do such gnats fly but to the  sun ?

original: And who shines now but Henry's enemies?   O Phoebus, hadst thou never given consent   That Phaethon should cheque thy fiery steeds,   Thy burning car never had scorch'd the earth!
translation: And aren't only Henry's enemies shining now? Oh,  Phoebus , if only you hadn't given permission to  Phaethon, allowing him to  ride your horses, your chariot would never have burned the earth!

original: And, Henry, hadst thou sway'd as kings should do,   Or as thy father and his father did,   Giving no ground unto the house of York,   They never then had sprung like summer flies;
translation: And Henry, if only you ruled like kings should do, or as your father and his father did, and hadn't made this oath to the House of York, they would never have sprung up like swarms of flies in summer.

original: I and ten thousand in this luckless realm   Had left no mourning widows for our death;   And thou this day hadst kept thy chair in peace.
translation: In this unfortunate kingdom, then, ten thousand men, I among them, wouldn't have left mourning widows grieving our deaths. And today, you'd have kept your throne entirely in peace.

original: For what doth cherish weeds but gentle air?   And what makes robbers bold but too much lenity?   Bootless are plaints, and cureless are my wounds;
translation: Isn't it gentle air that makes weeds grow? Isn't it leniency in the law that makes robbers bold? Complaints are useless, and my wounds cannot be cured.

original: No way to fly, nor strength to hold out flight:   The foe is merciless, and will not pity;   For at their hands I have deserved no pity.
translation: There is nowhere I can flee to, and I wouldn't have the strength to run either. The enemy has no mercy and won't pity me because I don't deserve pity from them.

original: The air hath got into my deadly wounds,   And much effuse of blood doth make me faint.   Come, York and Richard, Warwick and the rest;   I stabb'd your fathers' bosoms, split my breast.
translation: The air has gotten into my deadly wounds, and the loss of blood makes me weak. Come, York, Richard, Warwick and all the rest of you. I stabbed your fathers' chests, you should split open mine.

original: Now breathe we, lords: good fortune bids us pause,   And smooth the frowns of war with peaceful looks.   Some troops pursue the bloody-minded queen,
translation: Now we can breathe, lords. Our good fortune makes us stop for a while and look peacefully instead of frowning like we did while fighting. Some soldiers follow after the blood-thirsty queen.

original: That led calm Henry, though he were a king,   As doth a sail, fill'd with a fretting gust,   Command an argosy to stem the waves.   But think you, lords, that Clifford fled with them?
translation: She ruled Henry, even though he is a king, like a ship's sail, blown around with a nasty wind, steers a large merchant ship to cut through the waves. But do you think Clifford fled with them, lords?

original: No, 'tis impossible he should escape, For, though before his face I speak the words Your brother Richard mark'd him for the grave: And wheresoe'er he is, he's surely dead.
translation: No, it's impossible that he could have escaped. Your brother Richard's right in front of me, but I'll tell you that Richard wounded Clifford seriously. Wherever he may be, he is surely dead.

original: Whose soul is that which takes her heavy leave?
translation: Who is that who dies with such suffering?

original: A deadly groan, like life and death's departing.
translation: A deadly groan, like the separation between life and death.

original: See who it is: and, now the battle's ended, If friend or foe, let him be gently used.
translation: See who it is. Now that the battle is over, treat him honorably, whether he's a friend or an enemy.

original: Revoke that doom of mercy, for 'tis Clifford;   Who not contented that he lopp'd the branch   In hewing Rutland when his leaves put forth,
translation: Take back that sentence of mercy, because it's Clifford. He wasn't content to have killed the child, young Rutland, just as he'd started to grow.

original: But set his murdering knife unto the root   From whence that tender spray did sweetly spring,   I mean our princely father, Duke of York.
translation: Clifford then turned his murderous knife upon the  root from which young Rutland grew . I mean our royal father,  the Duke of York.

original: From off the gates of York fetch down the head, Your father's head, which Clifford placed there; Instead whereof let this supply the room: Measure for measure must be answered.
translation: Take the head down from off the gates of York—your father's head, which Clifford put there. Instead, let Clifford's head take its place. An eye for an eye.

original: Bring forth that fatal screech-owl to our house, That nothing sung but death to us and ours: Now death shall stop his dismal threatening sound, And his ill-boding tongue no more shall speak.
translation: Bring forward that creature who was deadly to our house, who did nothing but bring death to us and our loved ones. Now death shall stop his gloomy, threatening voice, and his ominous tongue shall speak no more.

original: I think his understanding is bereft. Speak, Clifford, dost thou know who speaks to thee? Dark cloudy death o'ershades his beams of life, And he nor sees nor hears us what we say.
translation: I think he can't perceive us anymore. Clifford, speak! Do you know who is speaking to you? Dark, cloudy death covers up the sunbeams of his life, and he neither sees us nor hears what we are saying.

original: O, would he did! And so perhaps he doth: 'Tis but his policy to counterfeit, Because he would avoid such bitter taunts Which in the time of death he gave our father.
translation: Oh, I wish he did! And maybe he does but it's his strategy to pretend because he doesn't want to hear the sort of angry taunts which he delivered to our father at the time of his death.

original: If so thou think'st, vex him with eager words.
translation: If you think so, irritate him with sharp words.

original: Clifford, ask mercy and obtain no grace.
translation: Clifford, ask for mercy and receive no grace.

original: Clifford, repent in bootless penitence.
translation: Clifford, repent with fruitless remorse.

original: Clifford, devise excuses for thy faults.
translation: Clifford, make up excuses for your crimes.

original: While we devise fell tortures for thy faults.
translation: While we think of brutal tortures for your actions.

original: Thou didst love York, and I am son to York.
translation: You loved York and I am York's son.

original: Thou pitied'st Rutland; I will pity thee.
translation: You pitied Rutland and now I will pity you.

original: Where's Captain Margaret, to fence you now?
translation: Where's Captain Margaret to protect you now?

original: They mock thee, Clifford: swear as thou wast wont.
translation: They mock you, Clifford. Swear as you used to.

original: What, not an oath? Nay, then the world goes hard   When Clifford cannot spare his friends an oath.   I know by that he's dead   ;
translation: What? Not a single curse? Wow, well the world has become a sad place when Clifford doesn't have one curse for his friends. Well, that's how we know that he's dead.

original: and, by my soul,   If this right hand would buy two hour's life,   That I in all despite might rail at him,   This hand should chop it off,
translation: By my soul, if this right hand would bring him back to life for two hours just so I could insult and taunt him, I'd cut it off.

original: and with the   issuing blood   Stifle the villain whose unstanched thirst   York and young Rutland could not satisfy.
translation: Then I'd use the blood pouring out the wound to choke this villain whose insatiable thirst for blood couldn't be satisfied by killing York and the young Rutland.

original: Ay, but he's dead: off with the traitor's head,   And rear it in the place your father's stands.   And now to London with triumphant march,   There to be crowned England's royal king:
translation: Yes, but he's dead. Off with the traitor's head and put it up in the place where your father's head is. And now let's march triumphantly to London. There you'll be crowned king of England.

original: From whence shall Warwick cut the sea to France,   And ask the Lady Bona for thy queen:   So shalt thou sinew both these lands together;
translation: From there, I'll cross the sea to France and arrange for  Lady Bona  to be your queen. That way you'll tie these two nations together.

original: And, having France thy friend, thou shalt not dread   The scatter'd foe that hopes to rise again;   For though they cannot greatly sting to hurt,   Yet look to have them buzz to offend thine ears.
translation: And, having France as an ally, you won't fear that the enemy, now dispersed but hoping to return, will ever rise again. Even though they can't do much to hurt you now, expect them to make trouble and spread rumors to offend you.

original: First will I see the coronation;   And then to Brittany I'll cross the sea,   To effect this marriage, so it please my lord.
translation: First, I will see the coronation and then I'll go to Brittany across the sea to make this marriage happen, if my lord agrees.

original: Even as thou wilt, sweet Warwick, let it be;   For in thy shoulder do I build my seat,   And never will I undertake the thing   Wherein thy counsel and consent is wanting.
translation: Just as you wish, sweet Warwick, let it happen. I build my throne relying on your support, and I will never do anything if you counsel me against it or don't give consent.

original: Richard, I will create thee Duke of Gloucester,   And George, of Clarence: Warwick, as ourself,   Shall do and undo as him pleaseth best.
translation: Richard, I will make you Duke of Gloucester and George, I'll make you Duke of Clarence. Warwick, in my name, shall do and undo whatever he wants.

original: Let me be Duke of Clarence, George of Gloucester; For Gloucester's dukedom is too ominous.
Tut, that's a foolish observation: Richard, be Duke of Gloucester. Now to London, To see these honours in possession.
translation: Oh, please, that's a silly comment: Richard, Duke of Gloucester. Now, let's go to London, so you can receive these honors.

original: Under this thick-grown brake we'll shroud ourselves; For through this laund anon the deer will come; And in this covert will we make our stand, Culling the principal of all the deer.
translation: We'll hide under this thick bush, because the deer will soon come through this clearing. We can make a hiding place from which to shoot in this concealed spot. We'll aim at the superior deer.

original: I'll stay above the hill, so both may shoot.
translation: I'll stay above the hill so that both of us can shoot.

original: That cannot be; the noise of thy cross-bow   Will scare the herd, and so my shoot is lost.   Here stand we both, and aim we at the best:
translation: That won't work. The noise of your bow will scare the herd and my shot will be pointless. Let us both stand here and aim at the best deer.

original: Here comes a man; let's stay till he be past.
translation: Look a man is coming our way. Let's not move until he's gone.

original: From Scotland am I stol'n, even of pure love,   To greet mine own land with my wishful sight.   No, Harry, Harry, 'tis no land of thine;
translation: I have snuck away from Scotland out of pure love in order to look longingly at my own land. No, Harry, Harry, it's not your land.

original: Thy place is fill'd, thy sceptre wrung from thee,   Thy balm wash'd off wherewith thou wast anointed:
translation: Your throne is filled, your scepter taken from you, the  oil  that once blessed you at your coronation has now washed away.

original: No bending knee will call thee Caesar now,   No humble suitors press to speak for right,   No, not a man comes for redress of thee;   For how can I help them, and not myself?
translation: No citizens on bended knee will call you  Caesar now. N o humble people will come to you to ask for justice. No, no one at all will come to ask for help from you. Because how can I help them when I could not help myself?

original: Ay, here's a deer whose skin's a keeper's fee: This is the quondam king; let's seize upon him.
translation: Ah, well here's a deer whose skin is worth a high price. This is the former king. Let's grab him.

original: Let me embrace thee, sour adversity, For wise men say it is the wisest course.
translation: Let me embrace you, sour misery, because wise men say that's the wisest thing to do.

original: Why linger we? Let us lay hands upon him.
translation: Why do we wait? Let's get him.

original: Forbear awhile; we'll hear a little more.
translation: Wait a while. Let's hear a little more.

original: My queen and son are gone to France for aid;   And, as I hear, the great commanding Warwick   Is thither gone, to crave the French king's sister   To wife for Edward:
translation: My queen and son have gone to France for help. I hear that the great, powerful Warwick has also gone there to ask if the French king's sister-in-law will be Edward's wife.

original: if this news be true,   Poor queen and son, your labour is but lost;   For Warwick is a subtle orator,   And Lewis a prince soon won with moving words.
translation: If this news is true, your efforts are in vain, poor queen and son, because Warwick is a persuasive speaker and Lewis is a king who is too easily won by well-spoken words.

original: By this account then Margaret may win him;   For she's a woman to be pitied much:
translation: But, then, in the same way, Margaret might convince him too, since she's a woman who can be much pitied.

original: Her sighs will make a battery in his breast;   Her tears will pierce into a marble heart;   The tiger will be mild whiles she doth mourn;   And Nero will be tainted with remorse,   To hear and see her plaints, her brinish tears.
translation: Her sighs will make an assault on his chest, her tears will pierce into his marble heart. The tiger in her will act gentle while she bewails her situation, and even Emperor  Nero  would be moved to hear and see her laments and her salty tears.

original: Ay, but she's come to beg, Warwick to give;   She, on his left side, craving aid for Henry,   He, on his right, asking a wife for Edward.   She weeps, and says her Henry is deposed;   He smiles, and says his Edward is install'd;
translation: Yes, but she's come to beg and Warwick's going to make an offer. She, one on side, comes begging for aid for Henry. Warwick, on the other side, comes asking for a wife for Edward. She weeps and says her Henry's been deposed. He smiles and says his Edward is made king.

original: That she, poor wretch, for grief can speak no more;   Whiles Warwick tells his title, smooths the wrong,   Inferreth arguments of mighty strength,   And in conclusion wins the king from her,   With promise of his sister, and what else,   To strengthen and support King Edward's place.
translation: She, the poor woman, says she can't speak anymore because of her grief while Warwick announces his title, glosses over the conflict, presents very strong arguments, and finally wins the king from her, with a promise of his sister in marriage. Besides the marriage, he'll get anything he needs to strengthen and support King Edward's power.

original: O Margaret, thus 'twill be; and thou, poor soul,   Art then forsaken, as thou went'st forlorn!
translation: Oh, Margaret, that's how it will be. And you, poor soul, will then be abandoned, as miserable leaving as when you came!

original: Say, what art thou that talk'st of kings and queens?
translation: Tell us, who are you who speaks of kings and queens?

original: More than I seem, and less than I was born to: A man at least, for less I should not be; And men may talk of kings, and why not I?
translation: More than I seem and less than I was born to be. I am a man at least, because I shouldn't be less than that. And since men may talk of kings, why shouldn't I?

original: Ay, but thou talk'st as if thou wert a king.
translation: Yes, but you speak as if you were a king.

original: Why, so I am, in mind; and that's enough.
translation: Well, I am, in my mind. And that's enough.

original: But, if thou be a king, where is thy crown?
translation: But if you are a king, where is your crown?

original: My crown is in my heart, not on my head; Not decked with diamonds and Indian stones, Nor to be seen: my crown is called content: A crown it is that seldom kings enjoy.
translation: My crown is in my heart, not on my head. It's not decorated with diamonds and Indian jewels and it can't be seen. My crown is called contentedness. It's a crown that kings don't often get to enjoy wearing.

original: Well, if you be a king crown'd with content,   Your crown content and you must be contented   To go along with us;
translation: Well, if you are a king crowned with contentedness, both your happy crown and yourself must be content to come with us.

original: for as we think,   You are the king King Edward hath deposed;   And we his subjects sworn in all allegiance   Will apprehend you as his enemy.
translation: We think that you are the king who was deposed by King Edward. We, his subjects, sworn to be faithful to him, will arrest you as his enemy.

original: But did you never swear, and break an oath?
translation: But have you never sworn and then broken the oath?

original: No, never such an oath; nor will not now.
translation: No, I've never sworn an oath like that. And I won't do it now.

original: Where did you dwell when I was King of England?
translation: Where did you live when I was King of England?

original: Here in this country, where we now remain.
translation: Here in this region, where we are now.

original: I was anointed king at nine months old; My father and my grandfather were kings, And you were sworn true subjects unto me: And tell me, then, have you not broke your oaths?
translation: I became king when I was nine months old. My father and my grandfather were kings and you were sworn to be my faithful subjects. Tell me, then, haven't you broken your oaths to me?

original: No; For we were subjects but while you were king.
translation: No, because we were loyal subjects to you while you were king.

original: Why, am I dead? Do I not breathe a man?   Ah, simple men, you know not what you swear!
translation: Well, am I dead? Am I not breathing like any man? Ah, foolish men, you don't know what you swore!

original: Look, as I blow this feather from my face,   And as the air blows it to me again,   Obeying with my wind when I do blow,   And yielding to another when it blows,   Commanded always by the greater gust;
translation: Look, I blow this feather from my face and  the air blows it back to me again. It follows my breath when I blow, and it surrenders to the wind when it blows. The feather is always commanded by the more powerful gust.

original: Such is the lightness of you common men.   But do not break your oaths; for of that sin   My mild entreaty shall not make you guilty.
translation: The fickleness of you common men is the same. But don't break your oaths. My mild plea shall not make you guilty of that sin.

original: Go where you will, the king shall be commanded;   And be you kings, command, and I'll obey.
translation: Go wherever you want and you can command the king. As if you were kings, command me and I'll obey you.

original: We are true subjects to the king, King Edward.
translation: We are faithful subjects of the king, King Edward.

original: So would you be again to Henry, If he were seated as King Edward is.
translation: And you would be again to Henry, if he was seated where King Edward sits.

original: We charge you, in God's name, and the king's, To go with us unto the officers.
translation: We order you, in God's name and the king's, to go with us to the officers.

original: In God's name, lead; your king's name be obey'd: And what God will, that let your king perform; And what he will, I humbly yield unto.
translation: In God's name, lead on. Your king's name will be obeyed. Whatever God wills, that's what your king will do. And what he wants me to do, I'll yield to him.

original: Brother of Gloucester, at Saint Alban's field   This lady's husband, Sir Richard Grey, was slain,   His lands then seized on by the conqueror:
translation: Brother Gloucester, this lady's husband, Sir Richard Grey, was killed at Saint Alban's battlefield. His lands were taken over by the enemy.

original: Her suit is now to repossess those lands;   Which we in justice cannot well deny,   Because in quarrel of the house of York   The worthy gentleman did lose his life.
translation: She now wants to make a case to get back those lands, which we cannot justly deny her, since the worthy gentleman lost his life fighting for the house of York.

original: Your highness shall do well to grant her suit; It were dishonour to deny it her.
translation: Your highness would do well to give her what she wants. It would be dishonorable to deny it to her.

original: It were no less; but yet I'll make a pause.
translation: That's true, but I'll pause before agreeing.

original: Yea, is it so? I see the lady hath a thing to grant, Before the king will grant her humble suit.
translation: Oh, is that it? I see that the lady has something she can offer him, before the king will agree to her humble request.

original: He knows the game: how true he keeps the wind!
translation: He knows how to play the game. Oh, how coyly he plots this conquest!

original: Silence!
translation: Be quiet!

original: Widow, we will consider of your suit; And come some other time to know our mind.
translation: I will consider your request, widow. Come some other time to find out what I've decided.

original: Right gracious lord, I cannot brook delay: May it please your highness to resolve me now; And what your pleasure is, shall satisfy me.
translation: My gracious lord, I can't delay finding out your answer. Would it be possible for your highness to answer me now? Whatever you decide, that will satisfy me.

original: Ay, widow? Then I'll warrant you all your lands, An if what pleases him shall pleasure you. Fight closer, or, good faith, you'll catch a blow.
translation: Yes, widow? Then I bet you that all your lands will be yours, if what pleases him will pleasure you too. She needs to fight closer to the enemy or, I'd wager, she'll get hit.

original: I fear her not, unless she chance to fall.
translation: I'm not afraid for her, unless she should chance to fall under him.

original: God forbid that! For he'll take vantages.
translation: God prevent that from happening! Because then he'll take advantage.

original: How many children hast thou, widow? Tell me.
translation: How many children do you have, widow? Tell me.

original: I think he means to beg a child of her.
translation: I think he wants to beg her to give him a child.

original: Nay, whip me then: he'll rather give her two.
translation: No, whip me if you're right about that. He'd rather give her two of his own children.

original: Three, my most gracious lord.
translation: Three, my most gracious lord.

original: You shall have four, if you'll be ruled by him.
translation: You will have four, if you'll be ruled by him.

original: 'Twere pity they should lose their father's lands.
translation: It's a shame that they should lose their father's lands.

original: Be pitiful, dread lord, and grant it then.
translation: Feel sorry for them, honorable lord, and give me the land then.

original: Lords, give us leave: I'll try this widow's wit.
translation: Lords, leave us alone. I'll test the intellect of this widow.

original: Ay, good leave have you; for you will have leave, Till youth take leave and leave you to the crutch.
translation: Yes, enjoy your privacy.  You'll take what you can get until you lose your youth and you're hobbling around on a crutch in old age.

original: Now tell me, madam, do you love your children?
translation: Now, madam, tell me, do you love your children?

original: Ay, full as dearly as I love myself.
translation: Yes, as much as I love myself.

original: And would you not do much to do them good?
translation: And wouldn't you do a lot for them?

original: To do them good, I would sustain some harm.
translation: For them, I would even undergo being hurt.

original: Then get your husband's lands, to do them good.
translation: Then get them your husband's lands to do good by them.

original: Therefore I came unto your majesty.
translation: That's why I came to your majesty.

original: I'll tell you how these lands are to be got.
translation: I'll tell you how you can get these lands.

original: So shall you bind me to your highness' service.
translation: If you can get them, I'll be your highness' faithful servant.

original: What service wilt thou do me, if I give them?
translation: What service can you do for me, if I give you the lands?

original: What you command, that rests in me to do.
translation: Whatever you command, it'll be my responsibility to carry out.

original: But you will take exceptions to my boon.
translation: But you think there are exceptions to my request.

original: No, gracious lord, except I cannot do it.
translation: No, gracious lord, unless I can't do it.

original: Ay, but thou canst do what I mean to ask.
translation: Yes, but you can do what I'm planning to ask you to do.

original: Why, then I will do what your grace commands.
translation: Well, then, I will do what your grace commands.

original: He plies her hard; and much rain wears the marble.
translation: He is working on her persistently. He's wearing down her stony exterior.

original: As red as fire! nay, then her wax must melt.
translation: He is as hot as fire! Her wax must melt under him.

original: Why stops my lord, shall I not hear my task?
translation: Why does my lord stop? Shall I not hear what I have to do?

original: An easy task; 'tis but to love a king.
translation: It's an easy job—only to love a king.

original: That's soon perform'd, because I am a subject.
translation: That can be done easily because I am one of your loyal subjects.

original: Why, then, thy husband's lands I freely give thee.
translation: Well, then, I give you back your husband's lands freely.

original: I take my leave with many thousand thanks.
translation: And I leave with a thousand thanks.

original: The match is made; she seals it with a curtsy.
translation: The match is made. She seals the deal by curtsying.

original: But stay thee, 'tis the fruits of love I mean.
translation: But wait. I'm talking about the enjoyment of love.

original: The fruits of love I mean, my loving liege.
translation: I'm also talking about the enjoyment of love, my loving lord.

original: Ay, but, I fear me, in another sense. What love, think'st thou, I sue so much to get?
translation: Yes, but I think you mean it in another sense. What kind of love, do you think, do I try so hard to get from you?

original: My love till death, my humble thanks, my prayers; That love which virtue begs and virtue grants.
translation: My love until death, my humble thanks, my prayers. A kind of love that being virtuous asks of me and being virtuous then makes me be.

original: No, by my troth, I did not mean such love.
translation: No, to tell you the truth, I didn't mean that kind of love.

original: Why, then you mean not as I thought you did.
translation: Well, then you don't mean what I thought you did.

original: But now you partly may perceive my mind.
translation: But now you may partially understand what I meant.

original: My mind will never grant what I perceive Your highness aims at, if I aim aright.
translation: My mind will never allow me to think what I imagine your highness means, if I guess correctly.

original: To tell thee plain, I aim to lie with thee.
translation: I'll say it simply then. I want to sleep with you.

original: To tell you plain, I had rather lie in prison.
translation: To say it simply, I would rather sleep in prison.

original: Why, then thou shalt not have thy husband's lands.
translation: Well, then you won't have your husband's lands.

original: Why, then mine honesty shall be my dower; For by that loss I will not purchase them.
translation: Well, then my chastity will be payment enough. No, I won't pay for these lands with my virtue.

original: Therein thou wrong'st thy children mightily.
translation: You wrong your children so much by refusing.

original: Herein your highness wrongs both them and me. But, mighty lord, this merry inclination Accords not with the sadness of my suit: Please you dismiss me either with 'ay' or 'no.'
translation: Your highness wrongs both them and me in making this demand. But, powerful king, this playful toying with me does not fit well with the seriousness of my request. Please, let me go and either tell me "yes" or "no."

original: Ay, if thou wilt say 'ay' to my request; No if thou dost say 'no' to my demand.
translation: "Yes," if you'll say "yes" to what I request. "No," if you'll say "no" to what I demand.

original: Then, no, my lord. My suit is at an end.
translation: Then, I say "no," my lord. My pleas to you are over.

original: The widow likes him not, she knits her brows.
translation: The widow doesn't like him, she's frowning.

original: He is the bluntest wooer in Christendom.
translation: He makes his sexual offer more directly than any man in the Christian world.

original: Her looks do argue her replete with modesty;   Her words do show her wit incomparable;   All her perfections challenge sovereignty:
translation: Her appearance proves that she is full of modesty. Her words show her matchless intellect. All the ways in which she seems perfect make the case for her to be queen.

original: One way or other, she is for a king;   And she shall be my love, or else my queen.
translation: One way or another, she's meant for a king's bed. And she shall be my lover, or, if not, my queen.

original: 'Tis better said than done, my gracious lord: I am a subject fit to jest withal, But far unfit to be a sovereign.
translation: That's easier said than done, my royal lord. I am a lowly subject that's only fit to joke with on this topic, but I'm certainly not fit to be a ruler.

original: Sweet widow, by my state I swear to thee I speak no more than what my soul intends; And that is, to enjoy thee for my love.
translation: Sweet widow, I swear to you, by my royal standing, that I don't say anything I don't intend to make true. That is, I'm going to to enjoy you as a lover.

original: And that is more than I will yield unto: I know I am too mean to be your queen, And yet too good to be your concubine.
translation: And that's more than I'll consent to. I know I am too poor to be your queen and yet too good to be your mistress.

original: You cavil, widow: I did mean, my queen.
translation: You're just coming up with excuses, widow. I really mean to make you my queen.

original: 'Twill grieve your grace my sons should call you  father.
translation: It will make you upset to hear my sons call you father.

original: No more than when my daughters call thee mother.   Thou art a widow, and thou hast some children;
translation: Not more than when my daughters call you mother. You are a widow and you have some children.

original: And, by God's mother, I, being but a bachelor,   Have other some: why, 'tis a happy thing   To be the father unto many sons.   Answer no more, for thou shalt be my queen.
translation: And, holy moly, even though I'm only a bachelor, I do have some other children myself. It's a happy thing to be a father to many sons. Don't say anything else since you will be my queen.

original: The ghostly father now hath done his shrift.
translation: He's like a priest who's heard her confession and granted absolution.

original: When he was made a shriver, 'twas for shift.
translation: He became like a priest to get her to sleep with him.

original: Brothers, you muse what chat we two have had.
translation: Brothers, you must be wondering what we've been talking about.

original: The widow likes it not, for she looks very sad.
translation: Whatever it was, the widow doesn't like it. She looks very sad.

original: You'll think it strange if I should marry her.
translation: You would think it's strange if I said I'm going to marry her.

original: To whom, my lord?
translation: Marry her to whom, my lord?

original: Why, Clarence, to myself.
translation: Well, Clarence, to myself.

original: That would be ten days' wonder at the least.
That's a day longer than a wonder lasts.
translation: That's one day longer than a wonder lasts.

original: By so much is the wonder in extremes.
translation: Yes, I meant that it would be extraordinary even for a wonder.

original: Well, jest on, brothers: I can tell you both Her suit is granted for her husband's lands.
translation: Well, keep joking about it, brothers. I can tell you both that I'll grant her request and return her husband's lands.

original: My gracious lord, Henry your foe is taken, And brought your prisoner to your palace gate.
translation: My gracious lord, your enemy Henry was captured and brought as your prisoner to your palace gates.

original: See that he be convey'd unto the Tower: And go we, brothers, to the man that took him, To question of his apprehension. Widow, go you along. Lords, use her honourably.
translation: Make sure that he is taken to the Tower. And let's go, brothers, to the man that captured him, so we can find out how he was taken. Widow, go along, and, lords, treat her well.

original: Ay, Edward will use women honourably.   Would he were wasted, marrow, bones and all,   That from his loins no hopeful branch may spring,   To cross me from the golden time I look for!
translation: Yes, Edward will treat women well . I wish he were consumed with disease,  in his bone marrow, bones and everything else, so that he could father no future monarchs who would prevent me from getting the crown myself!

original: And yet, between my soul's desire and me—   The lustful Edward's title buried—   Is Clarence, Henry, and his son young Edward,
translation: And yet, even once Edward's dead, Clarence, Henry, and his son young Edward, stand in my way of getting the throne too.

original: And all the unlook'd for issue of their bodies,   To take their rooms, ere I can place myself:   A cold premeditation for my purpose!
translation: Not to mention all the as-yet-unborn children they may father, who will take over for them before I can put myself on the throne. Well, this is an unfortunate thing to anticipate if I want to be king!

original: Why, then, I do but dream on sovereignty;   Like one that stands upon a promontory,   And spies a far-off shore where he would tread,   Wishing his foot were equal with his eye,
translation: Honestly, I can only dream of being the king, like a man who stands on a cliff, looking at a faraway shore where he wants to walk, wishing that his foot was already in the place he's seeing.

original: And chides the sea that sunders him from thence,   Saying, he'll lade it dry to have his way:   So do I wish the crown, being so far off;   And so I chide the means that keeps me from it;
translation: He curses the sea that keeps him so far from that land, and says that he'll drain it dry in order to get there. That's how much I want to have the crown, even though it's so far away from me, and so I curse the obstacles that keep me from obtaining it.

original: And so I say, I'll cut the causes off,   Flattering me with impossibilities.   My eye's too quick, my heart o'erweens too much,   Unless my hand and strength could equal them.
translation: And so I say that I'll murder those in my way. I am deluding myself with impossibilities. I look too far ahead, my heart presumes too much about what I am capable of, unless my hand and strength could do what my mind and heart imagine.

original: Well, say there is no kingdom then for Richard;   What other pleasure can the world afford?   I'll make my heaven in a lady's lap,   And deck my body in gay ornaments,   And witch sweet ladies with my words and looks.
translation: Well, let's say that I'll never be king. What other pleasures can the world offer me? I can enjoy women and wear lavish clothing and seduce  sweet ladies with my words and looks.

original: O miserable thought! And more unlikely   Than to accomplish twenty golden crowns!   Why, love forswore me in my mother's womb:
translation: Oh, what a hopeless idea! It's more unlikely than obtaining twenty different kingdoms! After all, love rejected me when I was in my mother's womb.

original: And, for I should not deal in her soft laws,   She did corrupt frail nature with some bribe,   To shrink mine arm up like a wither'd shrub;
translation: In order that I'd never have anything to do with love, maybe love bribed gullible nature to shrink my arm like it was a decaying bush.

original: To make an envious mountain on my back,   Where sits deformity to mock my body;   To shape my legs of an unequal size;   To disproportion me in every part,
translation: What's more, to make a disgusting mountain on my back, which makes everyone see that my body is deformed. Also, to make my legs different sizes and to make me disproportional in all my body parts.

original: Like to a chaos, or an unlick'd bear-whelp   That carries no impression like the dam.   And am I then a man to be beloved?   O monstrous fault, to harbour such a thought!
translation: I am like a shapeless mass, or like an unformed bear cub before its mother has licked into shape. And with all this, I'm supposed to be a man who's loved? Oh, it's a horrible mistake to even entertain such a thought!

original: Then, since this earth affords no joy to me,   But to command, to check, to o'erbear such   As are of better person than myself,   I'll make my heaven to dream upon the crown,
translation: Then, since this world doesn't offer me any happiness, apart from ruling, punishing, and dominating those people that have better appearances than I do, I'll make it my heaven on earth to dream about the crown.

original: And, whiles I live, to account this world but hell,   Until my mis-shaped trunk that bears this head   Be round impaled with a glorious crown.   And yet I know not how to get the crown,   For many lives stand between me and home:
translation: And, while I live, I will consider this world hell until my misshapen body will be topped by a glorious crown encircling my head. But I still don't know how to get the crown since many people stand between me and my goal.

original: And I,—like one lost in a thorny wood,   That rends the thorns and is rent with the thorns,   Seeking a way and straying from the way;   Not knowing how to find the open air,   But toiling desperately to find it out,—
translation: And I'm like someone lost in a thorny forest who pushes the thorns out of the way but is scratched by the thorns at the same time, looking for a path and straying from the path, not knowing how to find the way out, but desperately trying to find it.

original: Torment myself to catch the English crown:   And from that torment I will free myself,   Or hew my way out with a bloody axe.
translation: Just like that, I torment myself about finding a way to seize the English crown. I will free myself from that torment or I'll cut my way through with a bloody axe.

original: Why, I can smile, and murder whiles I smile,   And cry 'Content' to that which grieves my heart,   And wet my cheeks with artificial tears,   And frame my face to all occasions.
translation: After all, I can smile, and murder while I'm smiling. I can pretend that I'm happy about that which makes me sad and I can cry fake tears and put on whatever expressions are necessary for any situation.

original: I'll drown more sailors than the mermaid shall;   I'll slay more gazers than the basilisk;   I'll play the orator as well as Nestor,   Deceive more slily than Ulysses could,
translation: I'll drown more sailors than the  sirens  did, I'll kill more onlookers than the  basilisk  did. I'll persuade people with my rhetoric just like  Nestor  did, and I'll deceive them more cunningly than  Ulysses  could.

original: And, like a Sinon, take another Troy.   I can add colours to the chameleon,   Change shapes with Proteus for advantages,
translation: And, like  Sinon , I will bring down a kingdom just like he brought down Troy. I can show more different colors than a chameleon, and I can change my shape with more variety than  Proteus.

original: And set the murderous Machiavel to school.   Can I do this, and cannot get a crown?   Tut, were it farther off, I'll pluck it down.
translation: I can teach the murderous  Machiavelli  a thing or two. How can I do all of this and fail to win the   crown? Hah, even if I was further down the line of succession, I'd still win it.

original: Fair Queen of England, worthy Margaret, Sit down with us: it ill befits thy state And birth, that thou shouldst stand while Lewis doth  sit.
translation: Fair Queen of England, good Margaret: sit down next to us. It doesn't fit your position and birthright that you should stand up while I sit.

original: No, mighty King of France: now Margaret   Must strike her sail and learn awhile to serve   Where kings command. I was, I must confess,   Great Albion's queen in former golden days:
translation: No, powerful King of France. Margaret must lower herself now and learn for a while to serve where kings rule. Yes, I was, I must confess, England's queen in golden days of the past.

original: But now mischance hath trod my title down,   And with dishonour laid me on the ground;   Where I must take like seat unto my fortune,   And to my humble seat conform myself.
translation: But now misfortune has taken my title, and dishonor has forced me to the ground where I must sit. And so I'll just have to adjust to my new lowly situation.

original: Why, say, fair queen, whence springs this deep despair?
translation: Tell me, fair queen, where does this deep despair come from?

original: From such a cause as fills mine eyes with tears And stops my tongue, while heart is drown'd in cares.
translation: From a cause that makes me cry when I think about it. It's hard for me to speak about it because I'm filled to the brim with worries.

original: Whate'er it be, be thou still like thyself, And sit thee by our side:
translation: Whatever it may be, always act like a queen and sit next to me.

original: Yield not thy neck   To fortune's yoke, but let thy dauntless mind   Still ride in triumph over all mischance.
translation: Don't let fortune run wildly over you, but let your courageous mind still triumph over the bad things that happen.

original: Be plain, Queen Margaret, and tell thy grief;   It shall be eased, if France can yield relief.
translation: Be straightforward, Queen Margaret, and tell me about your grief. It shall be made easier to bear if the King of France can offer some help.

original: Those gracious words revive my drooping thoughts   And give my tongue-tied sorrows leave to speak.   Now, therefore, be it known to noble Lewis,   That Henry, sole possessor of my love,   Is of a king become a banish'd man,   And forced to live in Scotland a forlorn;
translation: Those gracious words lift my spirits and make it possible for me to speak my silent sorrows. Now, then, let it be known to noble Lewis that Henry, the only one that has my love, is no longer a king but a banished man and is forced to live as an outcast in Scotland.

original: While proud ambitious Edward Duke of York   Usurps the regal title and the seat   Of England's true-anointed lawful king.
translation: Meanwhile, arrogant, ambitious Edward, Duke of York has stolen his title and has usurped the throne of England's rightful and lawful king.

original: This is the cause that I, poor Margaret,   With this my son, Prince Edward, Henry's heir,   Am come to crave thy just and lawful aid;
translation: This is the reason why I, poor Margaret, with my son here, Prince Edward, Henry's heir, have come to ask for your just and fair help.

original: And if thou fail us, all our hope is done:   Scotland hath will to help, but cannot help;   Our people and our peers are both misled,   Our treasures seized, our soldiers put to flight,   And, as thou seest, ourselves in heavy plight.
translation: And if you won't help us, all our hope is gone. Scotland wants to help but can't help. Our people and our noble followers are all led astray. Our possessions have been taken, our soldiers forced to flee, and as you can see, we are in a sorrowful situation ourselves.

original: Renowned queen, with patience calm the storm, While we bethink a means to break it off.
translation: Famous queen, calm your grief with patience, while I think of a way to end your sadness.

original: The more we stay, the stronger grows our foe.
translation: The longer we wait here, the stronger our enemy grows.

original: The more I stay, the more I'll succor thee.
translation: The longer I pause, the more I can help you.

original: O, but impatience waiteth on true sorrow. And see where comes the breeder of my sorrow!
translation: Oh, but impatience is part of real sorrow. And look, here comes the creator of all my sorrow!

original: What's he approacheth boldly to our presence?
translation: Who is it that comes in such a bold way into the kingly presence?

original: Our Earl of Warwick, Edward's greatest friend.
translation: Our Earl of Warwick, Edward's best friend.

original: Welcome, brave Warwick! What brings thee to France?
translation: Welcome, brave Warwick! What brings you to France?

original: Ay, now begins a second storm to rise; For this is he that moves both wind and tide.
translation: Yes, now a second storm begins to rise, since this is the man who is so powerful that he can move both the wind and the tide.

original: From worthy Edward, King of Albion,   My lord and sovereign, and thy vowed friend,   I come, in kindness and unfeigned love,   First, to do greetings to thy royal person;
translation: I come from the great Edward, King of England, my lord and ruler, and your sworn friend. I come in kindness and genuine love. First, I want to greet your royal highness.

original: And then to crave a league of amity;   And lastly, to confirm that amity   With a nuptial knot, if thou vouchsafe to grant   That virtuous Lady Bona, thy fair sister,   To England's king in lawful marriage.
translation: Then, I want to ask to form an alliance of friendship. Lastly, I want to confirm that friendship with a marriage contract, if you agree to give your sister-in-law, the virtuous Lady Bona, to the King of England as his wife.

original: If that go forward, Henry's hope is done.
translation: [To herself]

original: King Lewis and Lady Bona, hear me speak,   Before you answer Warwick. His demand   Springs not from Edward's well-meant honest love,   But from deceit bred by necessity;
translation: King Lewis and Lady Bona, listen to what I have to say before you give an answer to Warwick. His request doesn't come from Edward's honest love. He's just trying to trick you because they have no other choice.

original: For how can tyrants safely govern home,   Unless abroad they purchase great alliance?   To prove him tyrant this reason may suffice,   That Henry liveth still: but were he dead,   Yet here Prince Edward stands, King Henry's son.
translation: How can usurpers safely rule at home unless they make a great alliance abroad? I can prove that he's a usurper simply by one reason: Henry still lives. But, even if he were dead, here stands Prince Edward, King Henry's son.

original: Look, therefore, Lewis, that by this league and  marriage   Thou draw not on thy danger and dishonour;   For though usurpers sway the rule awhile,   Yet heavens are just, and time suppresseth wrongs.
translation: Beware, Lewis, that you won't endanger and dishonor yourself by this union and marriage. Even though usurpers may be in power for a while, the heavens are fair, and wrongdoers will be punished in time.

original: Injurious Margaret!
translation: Offensive Margaret!

original: And why not queen?
translation: And why not "queen"?

original: Because thy father Henry did usurp; And thou no more are prince than she is queen.
translation: Because your father Henry usurped the throne, so you are no more a prince than she is a queen.

original: Then Warwick disannuls great John of Gaunt,   Which did subdue the greatest part of Spain;   And, after John of Gaunt, Henry the Fourth,   Whose wisdom was a mirror to the wisest;
translation: Then, Warwick, you ignore the great John of Gaunt, who conquered a big part of Spain. After John of Gaunt came Henry the Fourth, who was as wise as the wisest man there is.

original: And, after that wise prince, Henry the Fifth,   Who by his prowess conquered all France:   From these our Henry lineally descends.
translation: And, after that  wise prince, there was Henry V, who conquered all of France by his power. And these are the kings from whom our Henry descends.

original: Oxford, how haps it, in this smooth discourse,   You told not how Henry the Sixth hath lost   All that which Henry Fifth had gotten?   Methinks these peers of France should smile at that.
translation: Oxford, how does it happen, in this smooth-talking story, you didn't mention how Henry the Sixth lost everything that Henry the Fifth had won? I think that these noblemen of France would find that amusing.

original: But for the rest, you tell a pedigree   Of threescore and two years; a silly time   To make prescription for a kingdom's worth.
translation: But, as for all the rest, you recount a family tree of sixty-two years, which is not much time to make a long-term claim for a kingdom.

original: Why, Warwick, canst thou speak against thy liege, Whom thou obeyed'st thirty and six years, And not bewray thy treason with a blush?
translation: Can you speak against your king, Warwick—a king you obeyed for thirty-six years—and not betray your treason by blushing?

original: Can Oxford, that did ever fence the right, Now buckler falsehood with a pedigree? For shame! Leave Henry, and call Edward king.
translation: Can Oxford, who always fought for justice, now hide lies behind a family tree? Shame on you! Get over Henry and accept Edward as king.

original: Call him my king by whose injurious doom   My elder brother, the Lord Aubrey Vere,   Was done to death? And more than so, my father,   Even in the downfall of his mellow'd years,   When nature brought him to the door of death?
translation: Accept him as my king? The man who wrongfully sentenced my older brother, the  Lord Aubrey Vere, to death ? And, besides that, sentenced my father to death even though he was nearing the end of his life anyway and was declining towards death already?

original: No, Warwick, no; while life upholds this arm,   This arm upholds the house of Lancaster.
translation: No, Warwick, no. As long as I'm alive, I'll defend the house of Lancaster.

original: And I the house of York.
translation: And I will defend the house of York.

original: Queen Margaret, Prince Edward, and Oxford, Vouchsafe, at our request, to stand aside, While I use further conference with Warwick.
translation: Queen Margaret, Prince Edward and Oxford.  If you don't mind, at my request, to stand aside while I talk further with Warwick.

original: Heavens grant that Warwick's words bewitch him not!
translation: God forbid that Warwick's words charm him!

original: Now Warwick, tell me, even upon thy conscience, Is Edward your true king? For I were loath To link with him that were not lawful chosen.
translation: Warwick, tell me now, deep in your heart, is Edward your true king? Because I would hate to join with one who was not rightfully chosen.

original: Thereon I pawn my credit and mine honour.
translation: I swear it on my reputation and my honor.

original: But is he gracious in the people's eye?
translation: But is he popular with the people?

original: The more that Henry was unfortunate.
translation: He is, especially because Henry was so unpopular.

original: Then further, all dissembling set aside, Tell me for truth the measure of his love Unto our sister Bona.
translation: Then, also, just speaking honestly, tell me truthfully how much he really loves my sister-in-law Lady Bona.

original: Such it seems   As may beseem a monarch like himself.   Myself have often heard him say and swear   That this his love was an eternal plant,
translation: He loves her as much as it suits a king like himself. I have often heard him speak and swear that his love was like a plant that will never die.

original: Whereof the root was fix'd in virtue's ground,   The leaves and fruit maintain'd with beauty's sun,
translation: It will never die because the root is buried in the field of virtue and the sun of beauty shines upon the leaves and the fruit.

original: Exempt from envy, but not from disdain,   Unless the Lady Bona quit his pain.
translation: His love is free from jealousy but not from the possibility of being hurt by Lady Bona's scorn, unless she should end his pain by returning his love.

original: Now, sister, let us hear your firm resolve.
translation: Sister, we want to hear your decision now.

original: Your grant, or your denial, shall be mine:
translation: Whether you agree to this, or refuse it, I'll go along with whatever you say.

original: Then, Warwick, thus: our sister shall be Edward's;   And now forthwith shall articles be drawn   Touching the jointure that your king must make,   Which with her dowry shall be counterpoised.
translation: Then, Warwick, here's my decision: my sister-in-law will be Edward's wife. Now conditions must be drawn up to determine what your king must give us as part of the marriage settlement. Her dowry shall be equal to whatever he pays us.

original: Draw near, Queen Margaret, and be a witness   That Bona shall be wife to the English king.
translation: Come close, Queen Margaret, and act as a witness to the agreement that Lady Bona shall become the wife of the English king.

original: To Edward, but not to the English king.
translation: A wife to Edward but not to the English king.

original: Deceitful Warwick! It was thy device By this alliance to make void my suit: Before thy coming Lewis was Henry's friend.
translation: You deceitful Warwick! It was your plan to nullify my plea to King Lewis with this marriage alliance. Lewis was Henry's friend before you came here.

original: And still is friend to him and Margaret:   But if your title to the crown be weak,   As may appear by Edward's good success,   Then 'tis but reason that I be released   From giving aid which late I promised.
translation: And he is still a friend to Henry and Margaret. But if your claim to the throne is weak, as it seems to be judging from Edward's success, then it makes sense that I shouldn't have to give the help that I had recently promised.

original: Yet shall you have all kindness at my hand   That your estate requires and mine can yield.
translation: Yet you will have all the kindness you deserve from me, whatever kindness is appropriate for your position and whatever kindness I'm able to give.

original: Henry now lives in Scotland at his ease,   Where having nothing, nothing can he lose.
translation: Henry now lives in Scotland peacefully, and since he has nothing there, he has nothing to lose.

original: And as for you yourself, our quondam queen,   You have a father able to maintain you;   And better 'twere you troubled him than France.
translation: And as for you, our former queen, you have a father that is able to take care of you and it would be better if you went over to him and troubled him than troubled the King of France.

original: Peace, impudent and shameless Warwick, peace,   Proud setter up and puller down of kings!
translation: Shut up, you insolent, shameless Warwick, be quiet, proud man who establishes and removes kings!

original: I will not hence, till, with my talk and tears,   Both full of truth, I make King Lewis behold   Thy sly conveyance and thy lord's false love;   For both of you are birds of selfsame feather.
translation: I won't leave this place until with my words and tears, both of which are real, I make King Lewis recognize your cunning trickery and the falseness of your lord's love for Lady Bona. Both you and the king are made of the same stuff.

original: Warwick, this is some post to us or thee.
translation: Warwick, there is some letter for us or for you.

original: My lord ambassador, these letters are for you, Sent from your brother, Marquess Montague.
translation: My lord ambassador, these letters are for you. They are from your brother, Marquess Montague.

original: These from our king unto your majesty.
translation: These are from our king to your king.

original: And, madam, these for you; from whom I know not.
translation: And madam, these are for you. I don't know who sent them.

original: I like it well that our fair queen and mistress Smiles at her news, while Warwick frowns at his.
translation: I like that our queen is smiling at the news she's received while Warwick is frowning at the news he's received.

original: Nay, mark how Lewis stamps, as he were nettled: I hope all's for the best.
translation: No, look at how Lewis stamps his foot, as if he was irritated by something. I hope all's going to turn out well.

original: Warwick, what are thy news? And yours, fair queen?
translation: What is your news, Warwick? And yours, fair queen?

original: Mine, such as fill my heart with unhoped joys.
translation: Mine fill my heart with happiness I did not hope for.

original: Mine, full of sorrow and heart's discontent.
translation: Mine is full of sorrow and makes my heart heavy.

original: What! Has your king married the Lady Grey!   And now, to soothe your forgery and his,   Sends me a paper to persuade me patience?
translation: Madness! Has your king married the Lady Grey? And now, to smooth over your lies and his lies, he sends me a note to tell me to be calm?

original: Is this the alliance that he seeks with France?   Dare he presume to scorn us in this manner?
translation: Is this the alliance that he wants to make with France? How can he dare to insult us in this way?

original: I told your majesty as much before: This proveth Edward's love and Warwick's honesty.
translation: I warned your majesty about this before. It proves the falseness of Edward's love and Warwick's honesty.

original: King Lewis, I here protest, in sight of heaven,   And by the hope I have of heavenly bliss,   That I am clear from this misdeed of Edward's,
translation: King Lewis, I swear, in front of heaven, and by the hope that I have of going to heaven, that I am innocent when it comes to Edward's crime.

original: No more my king, for he dishonours me,   But most himself, if he could see his shame.   Did I forget that by the house of York   My father came untimely to his death?
translation: He is no longer my king because he dishonors me but he dishonors himself more, if he could only see how ashamed he should be. Did I forget that my father died prematurely because of the house of York?

original: Did I let pass the abuse done to my niece?   Did I impale him with the regal crown?   Did I put Henry from his native right?   And am I guerdon'd at the last with shame?
translation: Did I forget about what Edward tried to do to  my niece ? Did I put the royal crown on his head? Did I tear Henry off his rightful throne? And am I ultimately rewarded with shame?

original: Shame on himself! For my desert is honour:   And to repair my honour lost for him,   I here renounce him and return to Henry.
translation: Shame on him! I wanted to follow an honorable king. And to repair my honor that I lost because of him, I will abandon him and return to Henry's service.

original: Warwick, these words have turn'd my hate to love; And I forgive and quite forget old faults, And joy that thou becomest King Henry's friend.
translation: Warwick, your words have turned my hate to love. I forgive and completely forget your old mistakes, and I am happy that you have returned to be King Henry's friend.

original: So much his friend, ay, his unfeigned friend,   That, if King Lewis vouchsafe to furnish us   With some few bands of chosen soldiers,   I'll undertake to land them on our coast   And force the tyrant from his seat by war.
translation: Yes, I am so much his friend, his genuine friend, that, if King Lewis will be willing to send us with some troops of selected soldiers, I'll take them to our coast and try to force the tyrant out of his throne through war.

original: 'Tis not his new-made bride shall succor him:   And as for Clarence, as my letters tell me,   He's very likely now to fall from him,   For matching more for wanton lust than honour,   Or than for strength and safety of our country.
translation: His new bride won't be able to help him. And, when it comes to Clarence, my letters tell me that he's very likely to abandon him, because he married Lady Gray for lust and for  honor or the strength and safety of our country.

original: Dear brother, how shall Bona be revenged But by thy help to this distressed queen?
translation: Dear brother, how else can I be revenged except by your helping this distressed queen?

original: Renowned prince, how shall poor Henry live, Unless thou rescue him from foul despair?
translation: Famous prince, how can poor Henry live if you don't save him from his miserable situation?

original: My quarrel and this English queen's are one.
translation: My argument and the English queen's argument are one and the same.

original: And mine, fair lady Bona, joins with yours.
translation: And my argument, fair Lady Bona, is the same as yours too.

original: And mine with hers, and thine, and Margaret's. Therefore at last I firmly am resolved You shall have aid.
translation: And mine is the same as hers and yours and Margaret's. And so I have definitely decided to offer you help.

original: Let me give humble thanks for all at once.
translation: Let me thank you for all you'll do for us at once.

original: Then, England's messenger, return in post, And tell false Edward, thy supposed king, That Lewis of France is sending over masquers To revel it with him and his new bride: Thou seest what's past, go fear thy king withal.
translation: [To the messenger]

original: Tell him, in hope he'll prove a widower shortly, I'll wear the willow garland for his sake.
translation: [To the messenger]

original: Tell him, my mourning weeds are laid aside, And I am ready to put armour on.
translation: [To the messenger]

original: Tell him from me that he hath done me wrong, And therefore I'll uncrown him ere't be long. There's thy reward: be gone.
translation: [To the messenger]

original: But, Warwick,   Thou and Oxford, with five thousand men,   Shall cross the seas, and bid false Edward battle;
translation: Warwick, you and Oxford will cross the sea with five thousand men and challenge the false Edward to fight.

original: And, as occasion serves, this noble queen   And prince shall follow with a fresh supply.   Yet, ere thou go, but answer me one doubt,   What pledge have we of thy firm loyalty?
translation: And, when it makes sense, this noble queen and prince will follow with more reinforcements. But, before you go, answer one question: how can we be sure of your unwavering loyalty?

original: This shall assure my constant loyalty, That if our queen and this young prince agree, I'll join mine eldest daughter and my joy To him forthwith in holy wedlock bands.
translation: This will prove my eternal loyalty: if our queen and this young prince agree, I joyfully offer my eldest daughter to the prince for holy marriage.

original: Yes, I agree, and thank you for your motion.   Son Edward, she is fair and virtuous,   Therefore delay not, give thy hand to Warwick;
translation: Yes, I agree and I thank you for that suggestion. Edward, my son, she is beautiful and virtuous. Therefore, don't hesitate, and give your hand to Warwick.

original: And, with thy hand, thy faith irrevocable,   That only Warwick's daughter shall be thine.
translation: Clasping hands, swear that you'll be constant forever and you'll be faithful to Warwick's daughter.

original: Yes, I accept her, for she well deserves it; And here, to pledge my vow, I give my hand.
translation: Yes, I accept her because she deserves it. And here, as part of my vow, I give you my hand.

original: Why stay we now? These soldiers shall be levied,   And thou, Lord Bourbon, our high admiral,   Shalt waft them over with our royal fleet.
translation: What are we waiting for? These soldiers will be recruited, and you, Lord Bourbon, our High Admiral, shall convey them over the sea with our royal navy.

original: I long till Edward fall by war's mischance,   For mocking marriage with a dame of France.
translation: I can't wait until Edward falls to bad fortune in this war as punishment for toying with marriage with a French lady.

original: I came from Edward as ambassador,   But I return his sworn and mortal foe:   Matter of marriage was the charge he gave me,   But dreadful war shall answer his demand.
translation: I came as an ambassador from Edward, but I return as his sworn and deadly enemy. He told me to take care of his marriage, but he'll have war instead.

original: Had he none else to make a stale but me?   Then none but I shall turn his jest to sorrow.   I was the chief that raised him to the crown,   And I'll be chief to bring him down again:
translation: Didn't he have someone other than me to make into a laughingstock?  Well, then no one but me will turn his joke into sorrow. I was the most effective in raising him up to get the crown and I'll be the most effective in bringing him down again.

original: Not that I pity Henry's misery,   But seek revenge on Edward's mockery.
translation: I don't particularly feel bad for Henry's misery, but I must seek revenge for Edward's mockery of me.

original: Now tell me, brother Clarence, what think you Of this new marriage with the Lady Grey? Hath not our brother made a worthy choice?
translation: Now tell me, brother Clarence, what do you think of this new marriage between Edward and Lady Grey? Don't you think our brother chose well?

original: Alas, you know, 'tis far from hence to France; How could he stay till Warwick made return?
My lords, forbear this talk; here comes the king.
translation: Don't talk about this now, my lords. Here comes the king.

original: And his well-chosen bride.
translation: And his well-chosen bride.

original: I mind to tell him plainly what I think.
translation: I intend to tell him simply what I think of this.

original: Now, brother of Clarence, how like you our choice, That you stand pensive, as half malcontent?
translation: Clarence, brother, now how do you like our choice, since you're standing there looking so thoughtful as if you were partly dissatisfied?

original: As well as Lewis of France, or the Earl of Warwick, Which are so weak of courage and in judgment That they'll take no offence at our abuse.
translation: I like it as well as King Lewis of France or the Earl of Warwick, who have such little courage or sense that they surely won't be offended by this insult to them.

original: Suppose they take offence without a cause, They are but Lewis and Warwick: I am Edward, Your king and Warwick's, and must have my will.
translation: Maybe they are insulted without a reason. They are only Lewis and Warwick, after all. I am Edward, your king and Warwick's king, too. And my wishes must be fulfilled.

original: And shall have your will, because our king: Yet hasty marriage seldom proveth well.
translation: And you will have your wishes fulfilled because you're the king. Still, quick marriages rarely turn out well.

original: Yea, brother Richard, are you offended too?
translation: Okay, Richard, my brother. Are you insulted too?

original: Not I: No, God forbid that I should wish them sever'd Whom God hath join'd together; ay, and 'twere pity To sunder them that yoke so well together.
translation: Not me! No, God forbid that I would want two lovebirds joined by God to be separated. Yes, and it would be a shame to break apart a pair that goes together so well.

original: Setting your scorns and your mislike aside,   Tell me some reason why the Lady Grey   Should not become my wife and England's queen.
translation: Putting your mockery and your displeasure on one side for a moment, tell me any reason why the Lady Grey shouldn't become my wife and Queen of England.

original: And you too, Somerset and Montague,   Speak freely what you think.
translation: And you too, Somerset and Montague, tell me freely what you think.

original: Then this is mine opinion: that King Lewis Becomes your enemy, for mocking him About the marriage of the Lady Bona.
translation: Then this is my opinion: King Lewis will become your enemy because you humiliated him by not marrying Lady Bona.

original: And Warwick, doing what you gave in charge, Is now dishonoured by this new marriage.
translation: And Warwick, who was only doing what you told him to do, now feels dishonored by this new marriage.

original: What if both Lewis and Warwick be appeased By such invention as I can devise?
translation: What if both Lewis and Warwick could be calmed down by a plan that I come up with?

original: Yet, to have join'd with France in such alliance Would more have strengthen'd this our commonwealth 'Gainst foreign storms than any home-bred marriage.
translation: Yet, if we had joined with France in this alliance, it would have strengthened our kingdom against foreign enemies more than any marriage made at home could do.

original: Why, knows not Montague that of itself England is safe, if true within itself?
translation: Yes, but doesn't you know, Montague, that England can be safe alone if it stays purely English?

original: But the safer when 'tis back'd with France.
translation: But it is safer when it is supported by France.

original: 'Tis better using France than trusting France:   Let us be back'd with God and with the seas   Which He hath given for fence impregnable,
translation: It's better to use France than to trust France. Let us be supported by God and by the seas around us which he has given us as a strong defense.

original: And with their helps only defend ourselves;   In them and in ourselves our safety lies.
translation: With that help alone we can defend ourselves. Our safety relies on that help and in ourselves.

original: For this one speech Lord Hastings well deserves To have the heir of the Lord Hungerford.
translation: Lord Hastings really deserves to marry a wealthy noblewoman just for that speech alone.

original: Ay, what of that? It was my will and grant; And for this once my will shall stand for law.
translation: Oh, why do you bring that up? It was what I wanted and commanded, and what I say in this case is the law.

original: And yet methinks your grace hath not done well,   To give the heir and daughter of Lord Scales   Unto the brother of your loving bride;
translation: But I think that your grace hasn't done very well in this case to marry the heir and daughter of Lord Scales to your loving bride's brother.

original: She better would have fitted me or Clarence:   But in your bride you bury brotherhood.
translation: She would have been a better fit for me or Clarence. But you abandon your brothers for your wife.

original: Or else you would not have bestow'd the heir Of the Lord Bonville on your new wife's son, And leave your brothers to go speed elsewhere.
translation: Or otherwise you wouldn't have betrothed the daughter of Lord Bonville to your new stepson, leaving your brothers to try their luck elsewhere.

original: Alas, poor Clarence! Is it for a wife That thou art malcontent? I will provide thee.
translation: Ah, poor Clarence! Are you dissatisfied because you want a wife so badly? I will get you one.

original: In choosing for yourself, you show'd your judgment, Which being shallow, you give me leave To play the broker in mine own behalf; And to that end I shortly mind to leave you.
translation: You showed us your judgment in choosing wives when you chose one for yourself. And since that judgment was unimpressive, I'm going to ahead and play matchmaker for myself. And in order to do that, I'm planning to leave you shortly.

original: Leave me, or tarry, Edward will be king, And not be tied unto his brother's will.
translation: Leave me or stay, but I will still be king, and won't be tied to my brother's wishes.

original: My lords, before it pleased his majesty   To raise my state to title of a queen,   Do me but right, and you must all confess   That I was not ignoble of descent;
translation: My lords, even before his majesty decided to raise me up to be the queen, you'd do right by me to admit that I already was from a noble family.

original: And meaner than myself have had like fortune.   But as this title honours me and mine,   So your dislike, to whom I would be pleasing,   Doth cloud my joys with danger and with sorrow.
translation: Those of worse-born families have had my luck before me. But just as this title honors me and my family, your disapproval distracts me from my joy with thoughts of danger and sorrow because I want to please you.

original: My love, forbear to fawn upon their frowns:   What danger or what sorrow can befall thee,   So long as Edward is thy constant friend,   And their true sovereign, whom they must obey?
translation: My love, keep showing your affection for them even when they're frowning at you. What danger or tragedy can happen to you as long as I am loyal to you and serve as their ruler whom they must obey?

original: Nay, whom they shall obey, and love thee too,   Unless they seek for hatred at my hands;   Which if they do, yet will I keep thee safe,   And they shall feel the vengeance of my wrath.
translation: Yes, they will obey me and love you, unless they want me to hate them. If they do, I'll stay loyal to you and keep you safe and they will experience my vengeful wrath.

original: I hear, yet say not much, but think the more.
translation: I listen, but I don't say much, but I keep thinking.

original: Now, messenger, what letters or what news From France?
translation: Now, messenger, what letters or news do you bring from France?

original: My sovereign liege, no letters; and few words, But such as I, without your special pardon, Dare not relate.
translation: My royal lord, I bring no letters. I don't have many words either, but I don't dare to say them without your special permission.

original: Go to, we pardon thee: therefore, in brief, Tell me their words as near as thou canst guess them. What answer makes King Lewis unto our letters?
