translation: Go on, I give you permission. So, tell me quickly the words as closely as you can remember them. How does King Lewis respond to my letters?

original: At my depart, these were his very words: 'Go tell false Edward, thy supposed king, That Lewis of France is sending over masquers To revel it with him and his new bride.'
translation: When I was leaving, these were his exact words: "Go tell the false Edward, your so-called king, that Lewis of France is sending over masque performers to celebrate with him and his new bride."

original: Is Lewis so brave? Belike he thinks me Henry. But what said Lady Bona to my marriage?
translation: Is Lewis so boldly rude? Maybe he thinks I'm like Henry. But what did Lady Bona say about my marriage?

original: These were her words, utter'd with mad disdain: 'Tell him, in hope he'll prove a widower shortly, I'll wear the willow garland for his sake.'
translation: These were her words, spoken with mad anger: "Tell him I'll wear a willow garland, the sign of a lover who's been thrown aside, in hopes that he'll soon be widowed."

original: I blame not her, she could say little less; She had the wrong. But what said Henry's queen? For I have heard that she was there in place.
translation: I don't blame her because she couldn't say anything different. She was wronged. But what did Henry's queen say? Because I heard that she was there too.

original: 'Tell him,' quoth she, 'my mourning weeds are done, And I am ready to put armour on.'
translation: "Tell him," she said, "that my mourning clothes have been cast aside and I am ready to put on my armor."

original: Belike she minds to play the Amazon. But what said Warwick to these injuries?
translation: Maybe she intends to act like a wild Amazon warrior. What did Warwick say about these insults?

original: He, more incensed against your majesty Than all the rest, discharged me with these words: 'Tell him from me that he hath done me wrong, And therefore I'll uncrown him ere't be long.'
translation: He was more furious at your majesty than anyone else, and he dismissed me with these words: "Tell him from me that he has wronged me and that's why I'll take away his crown before too long."

original: Ha! durst the traitor breathe out so proud words? Well I will arm me, being thus forewarn'd: They shall have wars and pay for their presumption. But say, is Warwick friends with Margaret?
translation: Ha! Did the traitor speak these proud words? Well, I will put armor on since I've been warned. They shall have wars and pay for their boldness. But, tell me, is Warwick friends with Margaret?

original: Ay, gracious sovereign; they are so link'd in friendship That young Prince Edward marries Warwick's daughter.
translation: Yes, gracious lord, they are such close friends that the young Prince Edward will marry Warwick's daughter.

original: Belike the elder; Clarence will have the younger.
translation: Probably the older daughter. I will have the younger one.

original: Not I: My thoughts aim at a further matter; I Stay not for the love of Edward, but the crown.
translation: I won't be going with you. My thoughts are focused on something else entirely. I don't stay here for because I love Edward but because I want the crown.

original: Clarence and Somerset both gone to Warwick!   Yet am I arm'd against the worst can happen;   And haste is needful in this desperate case.
translation: Clarence and Somerset have both gone to Warwick! But I am prepared for the worst that can happen and moving quickly is necessary in this extreme situation.

original: Pembroke and Stafford, you in our behalf   Go levy men, and make prepare for war;   They are already, or quickly will be landed:   Myself in person will straight follow you.
translation: Pembroke and Stafford, go and gather men in my name, and prepare for war. They have already landed or they will be landing soon. I will follow you straight away myself.

original: But, ere I go, Hastings and Montague,   Resolve my doubt. You twain, of all the rest,   Are near to Warwick by blood and by alliance:   Tell me if you love Warwick more than me?
translation: But, before I go, Hastings and Montague, clear up something for me. Of all of them, you two are closest to Warwick by blood and friendship. Tell me, do you love Warwick more than you love me?

original: If it be so, then both depart to him;   I rather wish you foes than hollow friends:
translation: If that's the case, then you can both leave to go to him. I would rather have you as enemies than insincere friends.

original: But if you mind to hold your true obedience,   Give me assurance with some friendly vow,   That I may never have you in suspect.
translation: But if you want to be truly obedient to me, give me your word with a friendly promise so that I never need to suspect you of treachery.

original: So God help Montague as he proves true!
translation: God help me while I prove my loyalty!

original: And Hastings as he favours Edward's cause!
translation: And God help me while I fight for Edward!

original: Now, brother Richard, will you stand by us?
translation: Richard, my brother, will you stand with me?

original: Ay, in despite of all that shall withstand you.
Why, so! Then am I sure of victory. Now therefore let us hence; and lose no hour, Till we meet Warwick with his foreign power.
translation: Well, there you go! Then I am sure I'll win. Now let us go from here and let's not lose time until we find Warwick with his foreign army.

original: Trust me, my lord, all hitherto goes well; The common people by numbers swarm to us.
translation: Trust me, my lord. Everything has gone well so far. The commoners rush to support us in huge number.

original: But see where Somerset and Clarence come! Speak suddenly, my lords, are we all friends?
translation: But look at Somerset and Clarence coming! Tell us immediately, my lords—are we all friends?

original: Fear not that, my lord.
translation: Don't be worried about that, my lord.

original: Then, gentle Clarence, welcome unto Warwick;   And welcome, Somerset: I hold it cowardice   To rest mistrustful where a noble heart   Hath pawn'd an open hand in sign of love;
translation: Then, kind Clarence, welcome to Warwick, and you too, Somerset. I think it's cowardly not to trust a noble man who has pledged his love and loyalty to you and shaken hands on it.

original: Else might I think that Clarence, Edward's brother,   Were but a feigned friend to our proceedings:   But welcome, sweet Clarence; my daughter shall be  thine.
translation: Otherwise, I might think that Edward's brother Clarence was only pretending to be friendly to our side of the battle. But you are welcome, sweet Clarence and my daughter will be yours.

original: And now what rests but, in night's coverture,   Thy brother being carelessly encamp'd,   His soldiers lurking in the towns about,   And but attended by a simple guard,   We may surprise and take him at our pleasure?
translation: And now what's left for us to do but attack by cover of darkness? Since your brother's camp is not well set up, and he just has a low-key guard while his soldiers are wandering about the town, we can surprise him and capture him whenever we feel like it.

original: Our scouts have found the adventure very easy:   That as Ulysses and stout Diomede   With sleight and manhood stole to Rhesus' tents,   And brought from thence the Thracian fatal steeds,
translation: Our spies have found sneaking into Edward's camp easy. We'll be just like  Ulysses  and the bold Diomedes  in the Trojan War who snuck into Rhesus' tents with macho cunning, and stole the deadly Thracian horses.

original: So we, well cover'd with the night's black mantle,   At unawares may beat down Edward's guard   And seize himself;
translation: Just like that, covered with the dark cape of night, we'll catch them unawares, knock out Edward's guard, and capture him.

original: I say not, slaughter him,   For I intend but only to surprise him.   You that will follow me to this attempt,   Applaud the name of Henry with your leader.
translation: I don't say "kill him" because I only want to capture him. Anyone who wants to attempt this with me, shout the name of Henry with your leader.

original: Why, then, let's on our way in silent sort: For Warwick and his friends, God and Saint George!
translation: Well, then, let's go in a silent manner. For Warwick and his friends, God and Saint George!

original: Come on, my masters, each man take his stand: The king by this is set him down to sleep.
translation: Come on, gentlemen, take your positions, everyone. The king has fallen asleep in his chair by now.

original: What, will he not to bed?
translation: What, he's not sleeping in his bed?

original: Why, no; for he hath made a solemn vow Never to lie and take his natural rest Till Warwick or himself be quite suppress'd.
translation: No, he's not, because he made a solemn vow never to lie down and sleep normally until either Warwick or himself has been conquered.

original: To-morrow then belike shall be the day, If Warwick be so near as men report.
translation: Maybe tomorrow will be the day, if Warwick is as close as men report.

original: But say, I pray, what nobleman is that That with the king here resteth in his tent?
translation: But, tell me, who is the nobleman who is resting with the king here in his tent?

original: 'Tis the Lord Hastings, the king's chiefest friend.
translation: It's Lord Hastings, the king's best friend.

original: O, is it so? But why commands the king That his chief followers lodge in towns about him, While he himself keeps in the cold field?
translation: Oh, is that true? But why does the king order his closest followers to stay in towns around him while he himself sleeps on the cold ground?

original: 'Tis the more honour, because more dangerous.
translation: It's more honorable because it's more dangerous.

original: Ay, but give me worship and quietness; I like it better than a dangerous honour. If Warwick knew in what estate he stands, 'Tis to be doubted he would waken him.
translation: Yes, but I'd rather have dignity and peace. I prefer that to receiving a dangerous honor. If Warwick knew what condition the king is in, I fear he would wake him up and kill him.

original: Unless our halberds did shut up his passage.
translation: Unless our weapons could prevent him from entering.

original: Ay, wherefore else guard we his royal tent, But to defend his person from night-foes?
translation: Yes, why else would we guard his royal tent but to defend him from enemies in the night?

original: This is his tent; and see where stand his guard. Courage, my masters! Honour now or never! But follow me, and Edward shall be ours.
translation: This is his tent. Look at his guards standing there. Take courage, my men! Gain honor now or never! Follow me and Edward will be captured by us.

original: Who goes there?
translation: Who's there?

original: Stay, or thou diest!
translation: Stop, or you'll die!

original: What are they that fly there?
translation: Who is it running around here?

original: Richard and Hastings: let them go; here is The duke.
translation: Richard and Hastings, let them be. We have the duke.

original: The duke! Why, Warwick, when we parted, Thou call'dst me king.
translation: The duke! Warwick, when we said goodbye, you called me king.

original: Ay, but the case is alter'd:   When you disgraced me in my embassade,   Then I degraded you from being king,   And come now to create you Duke of York.
translation: Yes, but now the circumstances are different. When you shamed me in my ambassadorial mission, then I said you were no king of mine and now I've come to demote you to Duke of York.

original: Alas! How should you govern any kingdom,   That know not how to use ambassadors,   Nor how to be contented with one wife,
translation: Alas, how could you rule over any kingdom when you don't know how to treat ambassadors? Or how to be happy with one wife?

original: Nor how to use your brothers brotherly,   Nor how to study for the people's welfare,   Nor how to shroud yourself from enemies?
translation: Or how to treat your brothers with like brothers? Or how to work for people's well-being? or how to protect yourself from enemies?

original: Yea, brother of Clarence, are thou here too?   Nay, then I see that Edward needs must down.   Yet, Warwick, in despite of all mischance,   Of thee thyself and all thy complices,   Edward will always bear himself as king:
translation: Oh, my brother Clarence are you also here? Well, then I see  that my kingship must end. Yet, Warwick, despite the mistreatment I've received from you and all your accomplices, I'll always carry myself like a king.

original: Though fortune's malice overthrow my state,   My mind exceeds the compass of her wheel.
translation: Even though my bad fortune has dethroned me, I'm thinking about things above and beyond what fortune has in store for me.

original: Then, for his mind, be Edward England's king:
translation: Then you can stay the King of England in your thoughts.

original: But Henry now shall wear the English crown,   And be true king indeed, thou but the shadow.   My Lord of Somerset, at my request,   See that forthwith Duke Edward be convey'd   Unto my brother, Archbishop of York.
translation: But Henry shall now wear the English crown and be the true king while you'll be only a shadow of a king. Lord of Somerset, I'm requesting that you make sure that Duke Edward here is taken immediately to my brother, the Archbishop of York.

original: When I have fought with Pembroke and his fellows,   I'll follow you, and tell what answer   Lewis and the Lady Bona send to him.   Now, for a while farewell, good Duke of York.
translation: After I have fought with Pembroke and his followers, I'll follow you and tell you what message Lewis and Lady Bona have for Edward. Goodbye for a while now, good Duke of York.

original: What fates impose, that men must needs abide; It boots not to resist both wind and tide.
translation: What fate prepares for you, men must endure. It is useless to resist fate.

original: What now remains, my lords, for us to do But march to London with our soldiers?
translation: What else do we have left  to do, my lords, but to march to London with our soldiers?

original: Ay, that's the first thing that we have to do; To free King Henry from imprisonment And see him seated in the regal throne.
translation: Yes, that's the first thing we have to do in order to rescue King Henry from imprisonment and put him back on the throne.

original: Madam, what makes you in this sudden change?
translation: Madam, what's caused your sudden change of mood?

original: Why brother Rivers, are you yet to learn What late misfortune is befall'n King Edward?
translation: Rivers, my brother, haven't you heard about the recent catastrophe that has happened to King Edward?

original: What! Loss of some pitch'd battle against Warwick?
translation: What happened? Did he lose some battle against Warwick?

original: No, but the loss of his own royal person.
translation: No, but he's lost his power.

original: Then is my sovereign slain?
translation: You mean my king's been killed?

original: Ay, almost slain, for he is taken prisoner,   Either betray'd by falsehood of his guard   Or by his foe surprised at unawares:
translation: Yes, almost killed, since he has been captured and taken prisoner. He was either betrayed by the treachery of his guards or else his enemy ambushed him unexpectedly.

original: And, as I further have to understand,   Is new committed to the Bishop of York,   Fell Warwick's brother and by that our foe.
translation: And, as I also understand, he is now in the custody of the Archbishop of York, cruel Warwick's brother and, therefore, our enemy.

original: These news I must confess are full of grief; Yet, gracious madam, bear it as you may: Warwick may lose, that now hath won the day.
translation: I must admit this is miserable news. Yet, dear lady, deal with your grief as best you can. Warwick may still lose the war even though he won the battle.

original: Till then fair hope must hinder life's decay.   And I the rather wean me from despair   For love of Edward's offspring in my womb:
translation: Until then, I'll hold on to hope to delay my life falling apart. And I especially want to avoid despair because I so love Edward's child that's growing inside of me.

original: This is it that makes me bridle passion   And bear with mildness my misfortune's cross;
translation: This is what makes me hold back my emotions and bear my bad luck calmly.

original: Ay, ay, for this I draw in many a tear   And stop the rising of blood-sucking sighs,   Lest with my sighs or tears I blast or drown   King Edward's fruit, true heir to the English crown.
translation: Yes, yes, it's because of this that I will prevent myself again and again from crying a lot and I'll stop myself from sighing too. I'm afraid my sighs and tears could blow away or drown King Edward's unborn baby, the true heir to the English crown.

original: But, madam, where is Warwick then become?
translation: But, madam, where has Warwick now gone?

original: I am inform'd that he comes towards London,   To set the crown once more on Henry's head:   Guess thou the rest; King Edward's friends must down,
translation: I was told that he is coming to London to crown Henry as king again. You can guess the rest. King Edward's friends must be defeated.

original: But, to prevent the tyrant's violence,—   For trust not him that hath once broken faith,—   I'll hence forthwith unto the sanctuary,   To save at least the heir of Edward's right:
translation: But, to avoid the tyrant Edward's violence—because you should never trust someone who has once already broken a vow—I'll hide in safety , to protect Edward's rightful heir at least.

original: There shall I rest secure from force and fraud.   Come, therefore, let us fly while we may fly:   If Warwick take us we are sure to die.
translation: In a safe place, I can rest easy and not have to worry about violence or treachery. Come, then, and let us flee while we still can. If Warwick captures us, we will surely die.

original: Now, my Lord Hastings and Sir William Stanley,   Leave off to wonder why I drew you hither,   Into this chiefest thicket of the park.
translation: Now, Lord Hastings and Sir William Stanley, stop wondering why I brought you here, into the densest part of the hunting woods.

original: Thus stands the case: you know our king, my brother,   Is prisoner to the bishop here, at whose hands   He hath good usage and great liberty,   And, often but attended with weak guard,   Comes hunting this way to disport himself.
translation: Here's the situation: you know that our king, my brother, is a prisoner to the archbishop here. At his hands, he has been treated well and has been given quite a lot of freedom. And, only accompanied by weak guards, he often comes hunting this way to entertain himself.

original: I have advertised him by secret means   That if about this hour he make his way   Under the colour of his usual game,   He shall here find his friends with horse and men   To set him free from his captivity.
translation: I have told him secretly that if he came this way right about now, under the pretext of his usual hunting , he would find his friends here with horses and men that will rescue him from his prison.

original: This way, my lord; for this way lies the game.
translation: This way, my lord. The prey is over this way.

original: Nay, this way, man: see where the huntsmen stand. Now, brother of Gloucester, Lord Hastings, and the  rest, Stand you thus close, to steal the bishop's deer?
translation: No, this way, man. Can you see where the huntsmen stand? Now, brother of Gloucester, Lord Hastings and everyone else, are you hiding yourself like this so you can steal the bishop's deer?

original: Brother, the time and case requireth haste: Your horse stands ready at the park-corner.
translation: Brother, the time and circumstance presses us to do this quickly. Your horse is here, ready at the corner of the grounds.

original: But whither shall we then?
translation: But where shall we go from here?

original: To Lynn, my lord, And ship from thence to Flanders.
translation: To Lynn, my lord, and then take a ship to Flanders from there.

original: Well guess'd, believe me; for that was my meaning.
translation: [To himself]

original: Stanley, I will requite thy forwardness.
translation: Stanley, I will reward your eagerness.

original: But wherefore stay we? 'Tis no time to talk.
translation: But why are we still here? This is no time to talk!

original: Huntsman, what say'st thou? Wilt thou go along?
translation: What do you say, huntsman? Will you go with us?

original: Better do so than tarry and be hang'd.
translation: I'd rather go with you than stay behind and be hanged for letting you go.

original: Come then, away; let's ha' no more ado.
translation: Come then, let's go. Let's not waste any more time.

original: Bishop, farewell: shield thee from Warwick's frown; And pray that I may repossess the crown.
translation: Goodbye archbishop. I hope you'll be protected from Warwick's anger. Pray for me to regain the crown.

original: Master lieutenant, now that God and friends Have shaken Edward from the regal seat, And turn'd my captive state to liberty, My fear to hope, my sorrows unto joys, At our enlargement what are thy due fees?
translation: Officer, now that God and my friends have removed Edward from the throne and set me free, turning my fear to hope and sorrow into joy, what money do I owe you for the food received in prison?

original: Subjects may challenge nothing of their sovereigns; But if an humble prayer may prevail, I then crave pardon of your majesty.
translation: Subjects can't require any payment from their kings. But if you'll hear my simple prayer, then I'll ask forgiveness from your majesty.

original: For what, lieutenant? For well using me?   Nay, be thou sure I'll well requite thy kindness,   For that it made my imprisonment a pleasure;
translation: Forgiveness for what, lieutenant? For treating me well? No, you can be sure that I'll repay your kindness, because you made my imprisonment almost a pleasure.

original: Ay, such a pleasure as incaged birds   Conceive when after many moody thoughts   At last by notes of household harmony   They quite forget their loss of liberty.
translation: Yes, the kind of pleasure that caged birds begin to experience after many melancholy thoughts when, at last, by filling the house with song, they completely forget that they are not free.

original: But, Warwick, after God, thou set'st me free,   And chiefly therefore I thank God and thee;   He was the author, thou the instrument.
translation: But, Warwick, besides God, you were my chief rescuer so I particularly thank God and you. He was the creator and you carried out his will.

original: Therefore, that I may conquer fortune's spite   By living low, where fortune cannot hurt me,   And that the people of this blessed land   May not be punish'd with my thwarting stars,
translation: I want to avoid fate's hatred of me by living humbly so fortune cannot hurt me, and I want to ensure that the people of this blessed country won't get punished for my bad luck along with me.

original: Warwick, although my head still wear the crown,   I here resign my government to thee,   For thou art fortunate in all thy deeds.
translation: Therefore, Warwick, although I will still wear the crown, I turn over the running of the government to you because you are lucky in everything you do.

original: Your grace hath still been famed for virtuous;   And now may seem as wise as virtuous,   By spying and avoiding fortune's malice,   For few men rightly temper with the stars:
translation: Your grace is renowned for being virtuous and now may be as clever as he is virtuous, by foreseeing and avoiding the hate of fortune. You're clever because only a few men don't try to fight their fate.

original: Yet in this one thing let me blame your grace,   For choosing me when Clarence is in place.
translation: But let me correct your grace in this one thing: don't choose me when you have Clarence ready to rule.

original: No, Warwick, thou art worthy of the sway, To whom the heavens in thy nativity Adjudged an olive branch and laurel crown, As likely to be blest in peace and war; And therefore I yield thee my free consent.
translation: No, Warwick. You are worthy of the power. At your birth, the stars aligned to symbolize an olive branch, a symbol of peace, and a laurel crown, a symbol of victory, which meant you would blessed in peace and war alike. That's why I grant you my willing consent for you to rule.

original: And I choose Clarence only for protector.
translation: I think only Clarence should serve as Lord Protector in place of the king if the king will not rule.

original: Warwick and Clarence give me both your hands:   Now join your hands, and with your hands your hearts,   That no dissension hinder government:
translation: Warwick and Clarence, both of you give me your hands. Now join your hands together, and join your hearts together with them so that no disagreement may stand in the way of your governing.

original: I make you both protectors of this land,   While I myself will lead a private life   And in devotion spend my latter days,   To sin's rebuke and my Creator's praise.
translation: I make you both protectors of this country, while I will lead a private life myself and spend my last days in prayers, condemning sin and praising God.

original: What answers Clarence to his sovereign's will?
translation: What does Clarence say to his king's wishes?

original: That he consents, if Warwick yield consent; For on thy fortune I repose myself.
translation: That he agrees, if Warwick agrees too, because I rely on your decisions.

original: Why, then, though loath, yet must I be content:   We'll yoke together, like a double shadow   To Henry's body, and supply his place;   I mean, in bearing weight of government,   While he enjoys the honour and his ease.
translation: Well, although I am reluctant, I must be happy with it. We'll join together, like a double shadow of Henry's body and fill his place. I mean fill his place in carrying the weight of the government while he enjoys living honorably and at ease.

original: And, Clarence, now then it is more than needful   Forthwith that Edward be pronounced a traitor,   And all his lands and goods be confiscate.
translation: And, Clarence, now it is even more necessary that Edward quickly should be declared a traitor and all his lands and possessions should be confiscated.

original: What else? And that succession be determined.
translation: Obviously! And the order of succession must be determined.

original: Ay, therein Clarence shall not want his part.
translation: Yes, you'll have be high up on that list, Clarence.

original: But, with the first of all your chief affairs,   Let me entreat, for I command no more,   That Margaret your queen and my son Edward   Be sent for, to return from France with speed;
translation: For the first of your great tasks, since I have nothing else to command, let me ask that that you send for Queen Margaret and my son Edward to return quickly from France.

original: For, till I see them here, by doubtful fear   My joy of liberty is half eclipsed.
translation: Until I see them here, my joy at being free won't be complete because of my fears and doubts.

original: It shall be done, my sovereign, with all speed.
translation: It will be done as swiftly as possible, my king.

original: My Lord of Somerset, what youth is that, Of whom you seem to have so tender care?
translation: My Lord Somerset, who is that young man that you seem to care for so much?

original: My liege, it is young Henry, earl of Richmond.
translation: My lord, this is young Henry, earl of Richmond.

original: Come hither, England's hope.
translation: Come forward, hope of England's future.

original: If secret powers   Suggest but truth to my divining thoughts,   This pretty lad will prove our country's bliss.   His looks are full of peaceful majesty,   His head by nature framed to wear a crown,   His hand to wield a sceptre, and himself   Likely in time to bless a regal throne.
translation: If some secret powers bring any truth to my prophetic thoughts, this handsome boy will be our country's salvation. His looks are full of peace and majesty, his head is shaped by nature to wear a crown, his hand to hold a scepter and he himself is likely to sit in the throne soon enough.

original: Make much of him, my lords, for this is he   Must help you more than you are hurt by me.
translation: Be good to him, my lords, because you'll eventually get more help from him than you've had suffering because of me.

original: What news, my friend?
translation: What news do you bring, my friend?

original: That Edward is escaped from your brother, And fled, as he hears since, to Burgundy.
translation: Edward escaped from your brother and ran away to Burgundy, it has been said.

original: Unsavoury news! But how made he escape?
translation: Distasteful news! But how did he escape?

original: He was convey'd by Richard Duke of Gloucester   And the Lord Hastings, who attended him   In secret ambush on the forest side   And from the bishop's huntsmen rescued him;   For hunting was his daily exercise.
translation: He was stolen away secretly by Richard, Duke of Gloucester and the Lord Hastings, who waited for him in hiding on the edge of the forest. They rescued him from the archbishop's huntsmen. Edward had been hunting daily.

original: My brother was too careless of his charge. But let us hence, my sovereign, to provide A salve for any sore that may betide.
translation: My brother the archbishop was too careless with his prisoner. But let us go from here, my king, to provide healing to any injury that may occur.

original: My lord, I like not of this flight of Edward's;   For doubtless Burgundy will yield him help,   And we shall have more wars before 't be long.
translation: My lord, I don't like Edward's escaping because Burgundy will definitely offer him help, and we shall have more wars before too long.

original: As Henry's late presaging prophecy   Did glad my heart with hope of this young Richmond,   So doth my heart misgive me, in these conflicts   What may befall him, to his harm and ours:
translation: Just as Henry's recent forward-looking prophecy warmed my heart with hope of this young Richmond, so too is my heart worried about what may happen to Richmond in these battles that could hurt both him and ourselves.

original: Therefore, Lord Oxford, to prevent the worst,   Forthwith we'll send him hence to Brittany,   Till storms be past of civil enmity.
translation: Therefore, Lord Oxford, to stop the worst from hasting, we'll quickly send him over to Brittany until this civil war is over.

original: Ay, for if Edward repossess the crown, 'Tis like that Richmond with the rest shall down.
translation: Yes, because if Edwards gets the crown back, Richmond and everyone else will fall.

original: It shall be so; he shall to Brittany. Come, therefore, let's about it speedily.
translation: It shall be so, he will go to Brittany. Come, then, let's deal with it quickly.

original: Now, brother Richard, Lord Hastings, and the rest,   Yet thus far fortune maketh us amends,   And says that once more I shall interchange   My waned state for Henry's regal crown.
translation: Now brother Richard, Lord Hastings and all of you: up until these gates, fortune has been repaying what it took from me. I believe the fates will allow me to trade in my diminished position for Henry's kingly crown.

original: Well have we pass'd and now repass'd the seas   And brought desired help from Burgundy:   What then remains, we being thus arrived   From Ravenspurgh haven before the gates of York,   But that we enter, as into our dukedom?
translation: We've gone back and forth over the seas and brought the help we wanted from Burgundy. Now that we've traveled from Ravenspurgh haven and arrived in front of the gates of York, what is there to do besides enter our dukedom of York?

original: The gates made fast! Brother, I like not this; For many men that stumble at the threshold Are well foretold that danger lurks within.
translation: The gates are tightly secured. I don't like this, brother. If you stumble over the threshold of a door, it's usually an omen that there's danger lurking inside.

original: Tush, man, abodements must not now affright us: By fair or foul means we must enter in, For hither will our friends repair to us.
translation: Oh, come on, man! Omens won't scare us. We must get in by hook or by crook because our friends will rejoin us here when we're inside.

original: My liege, I'll knock once more to summon them.
translation: My lord, I'll knock one more time to call them.

original: My lords, we were forewarned of your coming, And shut the gates for safety of ourselves; For now we owe allegiance unto Henry.
translation: My lords, we were warned about you coming here, and we closed the gates to protect ourselves. Now we are loyal to Henry.

original: But, master mayor, if Henry be your king, Yet Edward at the least is Duke of York.
translation: But, mayor, if Henry is your king, then I, Edward, am still at least the Duke of York.

original: True, my good lord; I know you for no less.
translation: True, my good lord. I know that to be your title.

original: Why, and I challenge nothing but my dukedom, As being well content with that alone.
translation: Well, I'm insisting on nothing except being recognized as the duke, and I'll be perfectly happy with just that alone.

original: But when the fox hath once got in his nose, He'll soon find means to make the body follow.
translation: But once the fox has poked his nose inside the chicken coop, he'll soon figure out a way to get his whole body inside too.

original: Why, master mayor, why stand you in a doubt? Open the gates; we are King Henry's friends.
translation: Why are you hesitating, mayor? Open the gates, we are King Henry's friends.

original: Ay, say you so? The gates shall then be open'd.
translation: Oh, are you, you say? Then we'll open the gates.

original: A wise stout captain, and soon persuaded!
translation: He is a wise, brave leader to be so easily persuaded of our loyalty!

original: The good old man would fain that all were well, So 'twere not 'long of him; but being enter'd, I doubt not, I, but we shall soon persuade Both him and all his brothers unto reason.
translation: The good old man just wants the conflicts to be resolved so that he doesn't have to deal with it. But once we're in, I'm sure we shall quickly persuade him and his followers to listen to reason.

original: So, master mayor: these gates must not be shut But in the night or in the time of war. What! Fear not, man, but yield me up the keys;
translation: So, mayor, these gates should only be closed during the night or during wartime. Relax! Don't be scared—just give me the keys.

original: For Edward will defend the town and thee, And all those friends that deign to follow me.
translation: Edward will defend you, your town, and all those friends of yours that decide to follow me.

original: Brother, this is Sir John Montgomery, Our trusty friend, unless I be deceived.
translation: Brother, this is Sir John Montgomery. He is our trusted friend, unless he is deceiving me.

original: Welcome, Sir John! But why come you in arms?
translation: Welcome, Sir John! But why do you come with armed soldiers?

original: To help King Edward in his time of storm, As every loyal subject ought to do.
translation: To help King Edward in this time of crisis, as every loyal subject should.

original: Thanks, good Montgomery; but we now forget Our title to the crown and only claim Our dukedom till God please to send the rest.
translation: Thanks, good Montgomery, but I've now cast aside my claim to the throne and only declare myself the Duke of York until God chooses to give me back my kingship.

original: Then fare you well, for I will hence again: I came to serve a king and not a duke. Drummer, strike up, and let us march away.
translation: Then goodbye, because I will leave again. I came to serve a king, not a duke. Drummer, start playing, and let's march away.

original: Nay, stay, Sir John, awhile, and we'll debate By what safe means the crown may be recover'd.
translation: No, stay here a while, Sir John, and we can debate how the crown might be won back securely.

original: What talk you of debating? In few words,   If you'll not here proclaim yourself our king,   I'll leave you to your fortune and be gone   To keep them back that come to succor you:
translation: Why do you talk about debating it? Let me put it bluntly: if you won't declare yourself our king, I'll leave you to your own devices and will take away these men who have come to support you.

original: Why shall we fight, if you pretend no title?
translation: Why should we fight for you if you don't claim to have a right to the throne?

original: Why, brother, wherefore stand you on nice points?
translation: Brother, why are you quibbling over minor issues?

original: When we grow stronger, then we'll make our claim: Till then, 'tis wisdom to conceal our meaning.
translation: When my army has grown stronger, then I'll make my claim to be the rightful king. Until then, it's wise to hide my intentions.

original: Away with scrupulous wit! Now arms must rule.
translation: Enough with the overcautious overthinking! Battles must decide what happens next now.

original: And fearless minds climb soonest unto crowns. Brother, we will proclaim you out of hand: The bruit thereof will bring you many friends.
translation: And fearless men ascend most quickly the throne. Brother, we will claim your kingship immediately, and the news of that will bring you many friends.

original: Then be it as you will; for 'tis my right, And Henry but usurps the diadem.
translation: Then do what you think best. It is my right after all and Henry only usurps the crown.

original: Ay, now my sovereign speaketh like himself; And now will I be Edward's champion.
translation: Yes, now my king speaks like himself. Now I will fight for Edward.

original: Sound trumpet; Edward shall be here proclaim'd: Come, fellow-soldier, make thou proclamation.
translation: Sound the trumpet. Edward will be proclaimed king here and now. Come, soldier, you make the announcement.

original: Edward the Fourth, by the grace of God, king of England and France, and lord of Ireland, & c.
translation: Edward the Fourth, by the grace of God, you are the king of England and France, and Lord of Ireland, et cetera.

original: And whosoe'er gainsays King Edward's right, By this I challenge him to single fight.
translation: And whoever dares to to deny King Edward's right, I will challenge him to single combat.

original: Long live Edward the Fourth!
translation: Long live Edward the Fourth!

original: Thanks, brave Montgomery; and thanks unto you all:   If fortune serve me, I'll requite this kindness.   Now, for this night, let's harbour here in York;
translation: Thanks, brave Montgomery, and thanks to all of you. If luck is on my side, I'll repay your kindness. Now, let's stay here in York for tonight.

original: And when the morning sun shall raise his car   Above the border of this horizon,   We'll forward towards Warwick and his mates;   For well I wot that Henry is no soldier.
translation: And when the morning sun rises, we'll go towards Warwick and his men, because I know well that Henry is not a soldier.

original: Ah, froward Clarence! How evil it beseems thee   To flatter Henry and forsake thy brother!   Yet, as we may, we'll meet both thee and Warwick.
translation: Ah, unreasonable Clarence! How evil it seems for you to follow Henry and abandon your brother! Yes, we may meet both you and Warwick in battle.

original: Come on, brave soldiers: doubt not of the day,   And, that once gotten, doubt not of large pay.
translation: Come on, brave soldiers, do not doubt we'll have victory in battle. And, once we have it, don't doubt that you'll be paid well for it.

original: What counsel, lords? Edward from Belgia,   With hasty Germans and blunt Hollanders,
translation: What advice would you give us, lords? Edward is coming from the Netherlands with quick-tempered Germans and uncivilized Dutchmen.

original: Hath pass'd in safety through the narrow seas,   And with his troops doth march amain to London;   And many giddy people flock to him.
translation: They have passed the English Channel safely and he is marching rapidly towards London with his army. Many inconstant people join him.

original: Let's levy men, and beat him back again.
translation: Let's muster our men and let's beat him back to where he came from.

original: A little fire is quickly trodden out; Which, being suffer'd, rivers cannot quench.
translation: A little fire can be quickly extinguished. If it's allowed to grow, not even whole rivers can put it out.

original: In Warwickshire I have true-hearted friends,   Not mutinous in peace, yet bold in war;   Those will I muster up: and thou, son Clarence,   Shalt stir up in Suffolk, Norfolk, and in Kent,   The knights and gentlemen to come with thee:
translation: I have good friends in Warwickshire. They don't rebel during times of peace, and they are brave during wartime. I will recruit those followers, and you, Clarence, my son-in-law, shall convince the knights and gentlemen in Suffolk, Norfolk and Kent to come with you.

original: Thou, brother Montague, in Buckingham,   Northampton and in Leicestershire, shalt find   Men well inclined to hear what thou command'st:
translation: You, Montague, my brother, will find men in Buckingham, Northampton, and Leicestershire who will be happy to follow your command.

original: And thou, brave Oxford, wondrous well beloved,   In Oxfordshire shalt muster up thy friends.
translation: And you, brave Oxford, hugely beloved, you'll recruit your friends in Oxfordshire.

original: My sovereign, with the loving citizens,   Like to his island girt in with the ocean,   Or modest Dian circled with her nymphs,   Shall rest in London till we come to him.
translation: My king will remain in London with his supportive citizens until we come to him, like an island surrounded by the ocean, or the chaste goddess Diana su rrounded by the nymphs that waited on her.

original: Fair lords, take leave and stand not to reply.   Farewell, my sovereign.
translation: Go, fair lords and do not wait to answer me. Goodbye, my king.

original: Farewell, my Hector, and my Troy's true hope.
In sign of truth, I kiss your highness' hand.
translation: I kiss your hand as a sign of my loyalty.

original: Well-minded Clarence, be thou fortunate!
translation: Loyal Clarence, I hope you will do well!

original: Comfort, my lord; and so I take my leave.
translation: Take courage, my lord. And so I am going.

original: And thus I seal my truth, and bid adieu.
translation: And I kiss your hand in loyalty too, and say goodbye.

original: Sweet Oxford, and my loving Montague, And all at once, once more a happy farewell.
translation: Sweet Oxford and my loving Montague both leaving me at the same time. Once again I wish you a fond farewell.

original: Farewell, sweet lords: let's meet at Coventry.
translation: Goodbye, good lords. Let's meet at Coventry.

original: Here at the palace I will rest awhile. Cousin of Exeter, what thinks your lordship? Methinks the power that Edward hath in field Should not be able to encounter mine.
translation: I will stay here at the palace for a while. What do you think, Lord of Exeter? I think that the power that Edward has in the battlefield won't be able to match mine.

original: The doubt is that he will seduce the rest.
translation: The only fear is that he may persuade more soldiers to switch sides and fight for him.

original: That's not my fear; my meed hath got me fame:   I have not stopp'd mine ears to their demands,   Nor posted off their suits with slow delays;
translation: That's not what I fear. My virtue has made me famous. I haven't listening to my subjects' demands. I haven't put off listening to their petitions with long delays.

original: My pity hath been balm to heal their wounds,   My mildness hath allay'd their swelling griefs,   My mercy dried their water-flowing tears;
translation: My pity served as relief to heal their wounds, my mildness has soothed their growing griefs, my mercy dried their tears.

original: I have not been desirous of their wealth,   Nor much oppress'd them with great subsidies.   Nor forward of revenge, though they much err'd:
translation: I have never wanted their money, nor have I ever forced them to pay great taxes, nor did I ever harshly punish them even when they deserved my revenge.

original: Then why should they love Edward more than me?   No, Exeter, these graces challenge grace:   And when the lion fawns upon the lamb,   The lamb will never cease to follow him.
translation: So then why should they love Edward more than me? No, Exeter, these virtuous actions of mine will command respect and love. When the lion acts tenderly to the lamb, the lamb will never stop following him.

original: Hark, hark, my lord! What shouts are these?
translation: Listen, listen, my lord! What does this shouting mean?

original: Seize on the shame-faced Henry, bear him hence;   And once again proclaim us King of England.   You are the fount that makes small brooks to flow:
translation: Grab the bashful Henry and bring him here. Once again I proclaim myself the King of England. You are like the source from which small streams flow.

original: Now stops thy spring; my sea shall suck them dry,   And swell so much the higher by their ebb.
translation: Now your water stops flowing. The sea of my own power will make all of your streams dry up, and the sea levels of my power will only grow when yours diminishes.

original: Hence with him to the Tower; let him not speak.
translation: Take him to the Tower. Don't let him speak.

original: And, lords, towards Coventry bend we our course Where peremptory Warwick now remains: The sun shines hot; and, if we use delay, Cold biting winter mars our hoped-for hay.
Away betimes, before his forces join, And take the great-grown traitor unawares: Brave warriors, march amain towards Coventry.
translation: Away quickly, before his forces appear by surprise and steal back this great traitor. Brave warriors, march quickly towards Coventry!

original: Where is the post that came from valiant Oxford? How far hence is thy lord, mine honest fellow?
translation: Where is the messenger that came from brave Oxford? How far away is your lord, honest man?

original: By this at Dunsmore, marching hitherward.
translation: By now he'll be at Dunsmore, marching this way.

original: How far off is our brother Montague? Where is the post that came from Montague?
translation: How far away is our brother Montague? Where is the messenger that came from Montague?

original: By this at Daintry, with a puissant troop.
translation: By now he'll be at Daintry, with a powerful army.

original: Say, Somerville, what says my loving son? And, by thy guess, how nigh is Clarence now?
translation: Somerville, tell me, what does my loving son say? And can you guess how close Clarence might be now?

original: At Southam I did leave him with his forces, And do expect him here some two hours hence.
translation: I left him at Southam with his army and I am expecting him to be here in around two hours.

original: Then Clarence is at hand, I hear his drum.
translation: Then Clarence is near. I hear his army's drum.

original: It is not his, my lord; here Southam lies: The drum your honour hears marcheth from Warwick.
translation: It's not his, my lord. That's coming from the direction of Southam. The drum that you hear is coming from Warwick.

original: Who should that be? Belike, unlook'd-for friends.
translation: Who could that be? Perhaps unexpected friends.

original: They are at hand, and you shall quickly know.
translation: They are near and you'll find out soon.

original: Go, trumpet, to the walls, and sound a parle.
translation: Go, trumpeter to the walls and play a fanfare to call for negotiations.

original: See how the surly Warwick mans the wall!
translation: Look how the arrogant Warwick guards the wall!

original: O unbid spite! Is sportful Edward come? Where slept our scouts, or how are they seduced, That we could hear no news of his repair?
translation: Oh, unwelcome hate! Is lecherous Edward here? Did our spies fall asleep, or they were bribed, since they didn't bring us any news of Edward coming towards us?

original: Now, Warwick, wilt thou ope the city gates,   Speak gentle words and humbly bend thy knee,
translation: Warwick, will you open the city gates, speak kind words and bend the knee to me?

original: Call Edward king and at his hands beg mercy?   And he shall pardon thee these outrages.
translation: Will you call Edward your king and ask for mercy at his hands? If so, I will forgive you for all your crimes.

original: Nay, rather, wilt thou draw thy forces hence,   Confess who set thee up and pluck'd thee own,   Call Warwick patron and be penitent?
translation: How about instead you withdraw your armies from here, admit who got you your power and took it away, call me your past protector, and be repentant?

original: And thou shalt still remain the Duke of York.
translation: You can still be the Duke of York.

original: I thought, at least, he would have said the king; Or did he make the jest against his will?
translation: I thought at least he would have said "you can still be the king." Or was he joking against his will?

original: Is not a dukedom, sir, a goodly gift?
translation: Isn't being a duke, sir, a gift to be grateful for?

original: Ay, by my faith, for a poor earl to give: I'll do thee service for so good a gift.
translation: Yes, only a gift that a poor earl could give. I'll fight you for giving such a good gift.

original: 'Twas I that gave the kingdom to thy brother.
translation: I was the man who gave the kingdom to your brother.

original: Why then 'tis mine, if but by Warwick's gift.
translation: Well, then it belongs to me, even if only because you gave it to me.

original: Thou art no Atlas for so great a weight: And weakling, Warwick takes his gift again; And Henry is my king, Warwick his subject.
translation: You're not like Atlas, who carried the world on his shoulders, even though you once carried the weight of the country. You're a weakling and I'm taking back my gift. Henry is my king and Warwick is his faithful servant.

original: But Warwick's king is Edward's prisoner: And, gallant Warwick, do but answer this: What is the body when the head is off?
translation: But your king is now my prisoner. And, answer this question, brave Warwick: What do you call a body when the head is cut off?

original: Alas, that Warwick had no more forecast,   But, whiles he thought to steal the single ten,   The king was slily finger'd from the deck!
translation: Ah, what a shame that Warwick didn't see that coming. But while he thought to steal a only a 10 from the deck of cards, we stole a king while he wasn't looking!

original: You left poor Henry at the Bishop's palace,   And, ten to one, you'll meet him in the Tower.
translation: You left poor Henry at the Archbishop's palace and the odds are ten to one that you'll meet him in the Tower.

original: 'Tis even so; yet you are Warwick still.
translation: That's right, Warwick. Yet you still can be the Earl of Warwick.

original: Come, Warwick, take the time; kneel down, kneel down: Nay, when? Strike now, or else the iron cools.
translation: Come, Warwick. Take this opportunity. Kneel down, kneel down. If not now, when? Strike while the iron is hot.

original: I had rather chop this hand off at a blow, And with the other fling it at thy face, Than bear so low a sail, to strike to thee.
translation: I would rather chop off this hand and fling it at your face than stoop so low as to bow to you.

original: Sail how thou canst, have wind and tide thy friend,   This hand, fast wound about thy coal-black hair   Shall, whiles thy head is warm and new cut off,
translation: Good luck to you then, you'll need all the help you can get. When your head is still warm and just cut off,

original: Write in the dust this sentence with thy blood,   'Wind-changing Warwick now can change no more.'
translation: this hand, gripping your black hand tightly, will write this sentence in the dust with your blood: "Side-changing Warwick can change no more."

original: O cheerful colours! See where Oxford comes!
translation: Oh, friendly flags! Look, Oxford is coming!

original: Oxford, Oxford, for Lancaster!
translation: Oxford! Oxford for Lancaster!

original: The gates are open, let us enter too.
translation: The gates are open, let us go in too.

original: So other foes may set upon our backs. Stand we in good array; for they no doubt Will issue out again and bid us battle: If not, the city being but of small defence, We'll quickly rouse the traitors in the same.
translation: So that other enemies may attack our soldiers at the back? No, let's stand ready for battle because they will surely come out again and challenge us to fight. If not, the city is poorly fortified and we can quickly storm the walls and fight the traitors.

original: O, welcome, Oxford! For we want thy help.
translation: Oh, welcome, Oxford! We need your help.

original: Montague, Montague, for Lancaster!
translation: Montague! Montague for Lancaster!

original: Thou and thy brother both shall buy this treason Even with the dearest blood your bodies bear.
translation: You and your brother shall both pay for this treason with all the blood in your bodies.

original: The harder match'd, the greater victory: My mind presageth happy gain and conquest.
translation: The greater the enemy, the greater the victory. I predict success and triumph.

original: Somerset, Somerset, for Lancaster!
translation: Somerset! Somerset for Lancaster!

original: Two of thy name, both Dukes of Somerset, Have sold their lives unto the house of York; And thou shalt be the third if this sword hold.
translation: Two other men that had your name, both Dukes of Somerset, have been killed by the house of York. You will be the third if this sword is strong enough.

original: And lo, where George of Clarence sweeps along, Of force enough to bid his brother battle; With whom an upright zeal to right prevails More than the nature of a brother's love! Come, Clarence, come; thou wilt, if Warwick call.
translation: And look at George of Clarence coming along, with a big enough army to battle his brother. In Clarence, his passion for rightful justice is more powerful than his natural love of a brother. Come, Clarence, come. You'll come when I call you.

original: Father of Warwick, know you what this means?
translation: Warwick, father-in-law, do you know what this means?

original: Look here, I throw my infamy at thee   I will not ruinate my father's house,   Who gave his blood to lime the stones together,   And set up Lancaster.
translation: Look here, I am throwing my bad reputation at you. I won't destroy my father's house. My father gave his blood to join the stones together and build Lancaster.

original: Why, trow'st thou, Warwick,   That Clarence is so harsh, so blunt, unnatural,   To bend the fatal instruments of war   Against his brother and his lawful king?
translation: Do you really think, Warwick, that I'm so crude, so rough, and so unnatural that I'd use weapons of war against my brother and my lawful king?

original: Perhaps thou wilt object my holy oath:   To keep that oath were more impiety   Than Jephthah's, when he sacrificed his daughter.
translation: You will perhaps bring up that I made a holy oath. But to keep to that promise would be more blasphemous than when  Jephthah  kept an oath to sacrifice his daughter's life.

original: I am so sorry for my trespass made   That, to deserve well at my brother's hands,   I here proclaim myself thy mortal foe,
translation: I am so sorry for my crime here, that in order to deserve good treatment from my brother's hands, I here proclaim myself your mortal enemy.

original: With resolution, wheresoe'er I meet thee—   As I will meet thee, if thou stir abroad—   To plague thee for thy foul misleading me.
translation: I swear that wherever I find you—and I will, no matter how far you go—I'll torment you for cruelly misleading me.

original: And so, proud-hearted Warwick, I defy thee,   And to my brother turn my blushing cheeks.   Pardon me, Edward, I will make amends:
translation: And so, proud Warwick, I reject you and I turn, ashamed, to my brother. Forgive me, Edward, I will make up for it.

original: And, Richard, do not frown upon my faults,   For I will henceforth be no more unconstant.
translation: And Richard, don't hate me for my sins because I will never be unfaithful again.

original: Now welcome more, and ten times more beloved, Than if thou never hadst deserved our hate.
translation: I fully welcome you, and I love you ten times more than I would if you never had deserved my hate.

original: Welcome, good Clarence; this is brotherlike.
translation: Welcome, good Clarence. This is very brotherly of you.

original: O passing traitor, perjured and unjust!
translation: Oh, you total traitor! You've lied and acted unjustly!

original: What, Warwick, wilt thou leave the town and fight? Or shall we beat the stones about thine ears?
translation: Will you leave the town and fight, Warwick? Or shall we come in and throw stones at you?

original: Alas, I am not coop'd here for defence! I will away towards Barnet presently, And bid thee battle, Edward, if thou darest.
translation: Alas, my town is not built to defend against an army! I will go away to Barnet immediately and challenge you to a battle, Edward, if you dare to accept.

original: Yes, Warwick, Edward dares, and leads the way. Lords, to the field; Saint George and victory!
translation: Yes, Warwick, I'll dare to fight you, and I'll go ahead of you. Lords, let's go to the battlefield! For Saint George and victory!

original: So, lie thou there: die thou, and die our fear; For Warwick was a bug that fear'd us all. Now, Montague, sit fast; I seek for thee, That Warwick's bones may keep thine company.
translation: So, lie there, Warwick. Die, and our fear will die with you. Warwick was a creature that scared all of us. Now, Montague, get ready. I am looking for you, so that Warwick's bones can keep your bones company.

original: Ah, who is nigh? Come to me, friend or foe,   And tell me who is victor, York or Warwick?   Why ask I that?
translation: Ah, who is here? Come to me, whether you are a friend or an enemy and tell me who won—York or Warwick? Why do I ask that?

original: My mangled body shows,   My blood, my want of strength, my sick heart shows,   That I must yield my body to the earth   And, by my fall, the conquest to my foe.
translation: My torn body, my blood, my weakness, and my sick heart all demonstrate that I am about to die. And, when I die, my enemy will be victorious.

original: Thus yields the cedar to the axe's edge,   Whose arms gave shelter to the princely eagle,   Under whose shade the ramping lion slept,   Whose top-branch overpeer'd Jove's spreading tree   And kept low shrubs from winter's powerful wind.
translation: Just like this, the tree surrenders to the axe, a tree whose branches offered shelter to the princely eagle, under whose shade the pouncing lion slept. A tree whose top branches were taller than an oak and kept low bushes safe from the powerful winds of winter.

original: These eyes, that now are dimm'd with death's black  veil,   Have been as piercing as the mid-day sun,   To search the secret treasons of the world:
translation: The light of my eyes is dimming under the black veil of death. These eyes used to be as bright as the sun in the middle of the day, which illuminates all the secret treacheries in the world.

original: The wrinkles in my brows, now filled with blood,   Were liken'd oft to kingly sepulchres;   For who lived king, but I could dig his grave?   And who durst mine when Warwick bent his brow?
translation: My wrinkles are now filled with blood; they used to be compared to the graves of kings. Because what king could I not dig a grave for? And who would dare dig mine when I angrily furrowed my brow?

original: Lo, now my glory smear'd in dust and blood!   My parks, my walks, my manors that I had   Even now forsake me, and of all my lands   Is nothing left me but my body's length.   Why, what is pomp, rule, reign, but earth and dust?   And, live we how we can, yet die we must.
translation: Ah, now my glory is smeared with dust and blood! My parks, my garden paths, my palaces! I had it all. But they are all gone now and nothing is left of my lands but my body. What is all that pomp and circumstance, greatness and power but earth and dust? No matter how well we live, we must all die.

original: Ah, Warwick, Warwick! Wert thou as we are.   We might recover all our loss again;
translation: Ah, Warwick, Warwick! If only you were standing strong like us. We might get back what we have lost.

original: The queen from France hath brought a puissant power:   Even now we heard the news: ah, could'st thou fly!
translation: The queen has brought a powerful army from France. We have just heard the news. Ah, if only you could escape death!

original: Why, then I would not fly. Ah, Montague,   If thou be there, sweet brother, take my hand.   And with thy lips keep in my soul awhile!
translation: I wouldn't if I could. Oh, Montague, sweet friend, if you are there, take my hand. And kiss me to keep my dying soul from passing through my lips!

original: Thou lovest me not; for, brother, if thou didst,   Thy tears would wash this cold congealed blood   That glues my lips and will not let me speak.   Come quickly, Montague, or I am dead.
translation: You don't love me, because, if you did, friend, your tears would wash away this cold thick blood that makes my lips stick together and won't let me speak. Come quickly, Montague, or I'll be dead.

original: Ah, Warwick! Montague hath breathed his last;   And to the latest gasp cried out for Warwick,   And said 'Commend me to my valiant brother.'
translation: Ah, Warwick! Montague has died too. And until his last breath, he cried out for Warwick and said, "Send my love to my brave comrade."

original: And more he would have said, and more he spoke,   Which sounded like a clamour in a vault,
translation: And he would have said more and he did speak more, but it sounded like the echoes in a tomb.

original: That mought not be distinguished; but at last   I well might hear, delivered with a groan,   'O, farewell, Warwick!'
translation: We couldn't make out what he was saying, but in the end, I imagined I could hear him saying, with a groan, "Oh, goodbye, Warwick!"

original: Sweet rest his soul! Fly, lords, and save yourselves; For Warwick bids you all farewell to meet in heaven.
translation: Let my soul rest in peace! Go, lords and save yourselves. Now Warwick says goodbye to you and may we all meet in heaven.

original: Away, away, to meet the queen's great power!
translation: Let's go, let's go! Let's meet the queen's great army!

original: Thus far our fortune keeps an upward course,   And we are graced with wreaths of victory.
translation: So far, our luck has been getting better and better, and we've been winning.

original: But, in the midst of this bright-shining day,   I spy a black, suspicious, threatening cloud,   That will encounter with our glorious sun,   Ere he attain his easeful western bed:
translation: But, in the middle of this bright sunny day, I see a black, ominous, threatening cloud that will  meet our glorious sun  before it sets today.

original: I mean, my lords, those powers that the queen   Hath raised in Gallia have arrived our coast   And, as we hear, march on to fight with us.
translation: What I refer to, my lords, are those armies that the queen has recruited in France. They have arrived on our coast, and we hear that they are coming our way to fight with us.

original: A little gale will soon disperse that cloud   And blow it to the source from whence it came:
translation: A little wind will soon scatter the enemy cloud and blow it back to where it came from.

original: The very beams will dry those vapours up,   For every cloud engenders not a storm.
translation: The sun beams will vanquish those wisps, since not every cloud leads to a storm.

original: The queen is valued thirty thousand strong,   And Somerset, with Oxford fled to her:
translation: The queen's army is estimated to be thirty thousand men. Somerset and Oxford joined her too.

original: If she have time to breathe be well assured   Her faction will be full as strong as ours.
translation: If she has time to gather her strength, her army will be as strong as ours.

original: We are advertised by our loving friends   That they do hold their course toward Tewksbury:   We, having now the best at Barnet field,   Will thither straight, for willingness rids way;
translation: We are informed by our loving friends that they are going towards Tewksbury. Since we have now won at the Barnet battlefield, we'll go there immediately. Where there's a will, there's a way.

original: And, as we march, our strength will be augmented   In every county as we go along.   Strike up the drum; cry 'Courage!' and away.
translation: And, as we march, our strength will be increased in every part of the country that we pass. Start the drumming, shout "Courage!" and let's go.

original: Great lords, wise men ne'er sit and wail their loss,   But cheerly seek how to redress their harms.   What though the mast be now blown overboard,   The cable broke, the holding-anchor lost,   And half our sailors swallow'd in the flood?
translation: Great lords, wise men never sit and cry about what they've lost. They cheerfully try to figure out how to make up their losses. So, what if the mast was blown overboard, the cable broke, the anchor was lost, and half of our sailors were drowned in the flood?

original: Yet lives our pilot still. Is't meet that he   Should leave the helm and like a fearful lad   With tearful eyes add water to the sea   And give more strength to that which hath too much,   Whiles, in his moan, the ship splits on the rock,   Which industry and courage might have saved?
translation: Our captain is still alive.  Is it right that he should abandon the wheel and like a fearful little boy add water to the sea with his tears, giving more strength to the sea that has too much water already, while, as he moans, the ship is dashed to pieces on the rock when it could have been saved by hard work and courage?

original: Ah, what a shame! Ah, what a fault were this!   Say Warwick was our anchor; what of that?   And Montague our topmast; what of him?   Our slaughter'd friends the tackles; what of these?
translation: Ah, what a shame that would be! Ah, what a terrible mistake this would be! Maybe Warwick was our anchor—who cares? Maybe Montague was our sail—get over it! And our slaughtered friends were the rigging—let's move on!

original: Why, is not Oxford here another anchor?   And Somerset another goodly mast?   The friends of France our shrouds and tacklings?
translation: Isn't Oxford another anchor? Isn't Somerset another mast? Aren't our French allies our ropes?

original: And, though unskilful, why not Ned and I   For once allow'd the skilful pilot's charge?
translation: And although we don'st have much skill in battle, why shouldn't my son little Ned  and I for once be allowed to take charge as captains?

original: We will not from the helm to sit and weep,   But keep our course, though the rough wind say no,   From shelves and rocks that threaten us with wreck,   As good to chide the waves as speak them fair.
translation: We won't sit and cry at the wheel, but we'll keep to our path and avoid the rocks and dangers, even if the rough winds tries to shipwreck us. We'll do better by attacking the waves than speaking gently and sweetly about them.

original: And what is Edward but ruthless sea?   What Clarence but a quicksand of deceit?   And Richard but a ragged fatal rock?   All these the enemies to our poor bark.
translation: And isn't Edward only a merciless sea? And Clarence only a deceitful quicksand? And Richard only an uneven deadly rock? All these are the enemies of our poor ship.

original: Say you can swim; alas, 'tis but a while!   Tread on the sand; why, there you quickly sink:   Bestride the rock; the tide will wash you off,   Or else you famish; that's a threefold death.
translation: Maybe you can swim, but that will only keep you alive for a while! Step on the sand and there you will quickly sink. Sit upon the rock, the tide will wash you off, or else you will starve. That's three ways to die.

original: This speak I, lords, to let you understand,   If case some one of you would fly from us,   That there's no hoped-for mercy with the brothers   More than with ruthless waves, with sands and rocks.
translation: I speak all this, lords, to make myself clear that if one of you wants to desert us, you won't get any more mercy from those brother than you'd get from merciless waves or quicksand or rocks.

original: Why, courage then! What cannot be avoided   'Twere childish weakness to lament or fear.
translation: Take courage then! It's childish weakness to fear and cry about what you can't avoid.

original: Methinks a woman of this valiant spirit   Should, if a coward heard her speak these words,   Infuse his breast with magnanimity   And make him, naked, foil a man at arms.
translation: I think a woman with such a brave spirit as my mother has could fill a coward's fearful heart with courage with her words, inspiring him to defeat an armed man with his bare hands.

original: I speak not this as doubting any here   For did I but suspect a fearful man   He should have leave to go away betimes,   Lest in our need he might infect another   And make him of like spirit to himself.
translation: I don't say this doubting any of your bravery, because if I did suspect that any of you were fearful, I'd make you leave immediately to prevent you from infecting anyone else with your cowardice in our time of need.

original: If any such be here—as God forbid!—   Let him depart before we need his help.
translation: If that applies to anyone here—God forbid!—he should leave before we need his help.

original: Women and children of so high a courage,   And warriors faint! Why, 'twere perpetual shame.
translation: Can you believe it, incredible courage from women and children, and weakness from warriors! This shame will last forever.

original: O brave young prince! Thy famous grandfather   Doth live again in thee: long mayst thou live   To bear his image and renew his glories!
translation: Oh, brave young prince, your triumphant  grandfather, Henry the Fifth,  lives again in you. Live long and be like him, just as glorious in victory!

original: And he that will not fight for such a hope. Go home to bed, and like the owl by day, If he arise, be mock'd and wonder'd at.
translation: And anyone who won't fight for such a hope as that, go home to bed. Like an owl who is seen awake during the day, if you're a coward, you'll be mocked and treated like a strange creature.

original: Thanks, gentle Somerset; sweet Oxford, thanks.
translation: Thanks, gentle Somerset. Thanks, sweet Oxford.

original: And take his thanks that yet hath nothing else.
translation: And take thanks from me since I have nothing else yet to give.

original: Prepare you, lords, for Edward is at hand. Ready to fight; therefore be resolute.
translation: Get ready, lords. Edward is near. He is ready to fight and so be bold.

original: I thought no less: it is his policy To haste thus fast, to find us unprovided.
translation: I thought this would happen. It's his strategy to hurry so quickly and find us unprepared.

original: But he's deceived; we are in readiness.
translation: But we've got him this time because we are prepared.

original: This cheers my heart, to see your forwardness.
translation: It makes me happy to see your confidence.

original: Here pitch our battle; hence we will not budge.
translation: Let's have the battle right here. We will not move from this spot.

original: Brave followers, yonder stands the thorny wood,   Which, by the heavens' assistance and your strength,   Must by the roots be hewn up yet ere night.
translation: My brave followers! Here's this army like a thorny wood. By the help of God, and the help all of your strength, men, we will cut these men down on the field like trees in a forest before the night is over.

original: I need not add more fuel to your fire,   For well I wot ye blaze to burn them out   Give signal to the fight, and to it, lords!
translation: I don't need to add any more fuel to your fire, because I know that you're burning to tear these men down. Give the signal to fight, and go for it, lords!

original: Lords, knights, and gentlemen, what I should say   My tears gainsay; for every word I speak,   Ye see, I drink the water of mine eyes.
translation: Lords, knights, and gentlemen, my tears will contradict whatever I would say. You see, my tears drip down my cheek with every word I speak.

original: Therefore, no more but this: Henry, your sovereign,   Is prisoner to the foe; his state usurp'd,   His realm a slaughter-house, his subjects slain,   His statutes cancell'd and his treasure spent;   And yonder is the wolf that makes this spoil.
translation: Therefore, I'll say nothing else but this: Henry, your king, is our enemy's prisoner, his throne has been usurped, his country has been made a slaughter-house, his people have been killed, his laws have been spoken, and his money has been spent.

original: You fight in justice: then, in God's name, lords,   Be valiant and give signal to the fight.
translation: And over there is the wolf behind it all. You fight on the side of justice. Then, in God's name, lords, be brave and give the signal to fight.

original: Now here a period of tumultuous broils. Away with Oxford to Hames Castle straight: For Somerset, off with his guilty head. Go, bear them hence; I will not hear them speak.
translation: Now we've reached the end of all the tumultuous fighting. Take Oxford to Hames Castle immediately. As for Somerset, off with his guilty head. Go, take them away. I won't to hear them speak.

original: For my part, I'll not trouble thee with words.
translation: I will not trouble you with my words!

original: Nor I, but stoop with patience to my fortune.
translation: Nor will I. But I submit to my fate patiently.

original: So part we sadly in this troublous world, To meet with joy in sweet Jerusalem.
translation: So we say goodbye sadly in this troubled world, only to greet joy in sweet heaven.

original: Is proclamation made, that who finds Edward Shall have a high reward, and he his life?
translation: Has it been declared that whoever finds Edward will get a big reward and be allowed to live?

original: It is: and lo, where youthful Edward comes!
translation: It is. And look: here comes the young Edward!

original: Bring forth the gallant, let us hear him speak.   What! Can so young a thorn begin to prick?
translation: Bring the young man forward and let's hear him speak. What? Can such a young boy be so rude already?

original: Edward, what satisfaction canst thou make   For bearing arms, for stirring up my subjects,   And all the trouble thou hast turn'd me to?
translation: Edward, what is your excuse for bearing arms against me, stirring up my people to violence, and for all the trouble you caused me?

original: Speak like a subject, proud ambitious York!   Suppose that I am now my father's mouth;
translation: You should speak like a subject, proud ambitious Duke of York! I am representing my father.

original: Resign thy chair, and where I stand kneel thou,   Whilst I propose the selfsame words to thee,   Which traitor, thou wouldst have me answer to.
translation: Give up the throne and kneel where I stand, while I say the same words to you that you've just said to me, you traitor.

original: Ah, that thy father had been so resolved!
translation: Oh, if only your father had been so strong-willed!

original: That you might still have worn the petticoat, And ne'er have stol'n the breech from Lancaster.
translation: Then you wouldn't have been the one wearing the pants in your marriage.

original: Let Aesop fable in a winter's night; His currish riddles sort not with this place.
By heaven, brat, I'll plague ye for that word.
translation: I swear to heaven, brat, I'll attack you like the plague for saying that.

original: Ay, thou wast born to be a plague to men.
translation: Yes, you were born to be a plague for people.

original: For God's sake, take away this captive scold.
translation: For God's sake, take away this shrewish prisoner!

original: Nay, take away this scolding crookback rather.
translation: No, take away this shrewish hunchback instead.

original: Peace, wilful boy, or I will charm your tongue.
translation: Quiet, you headstrong boy, or I will silence your tongue forever.

original: Untutor'd lad, thou art too malapert.
translation: Uneducated boy, you are too impudent.

original: I know my duty; you are all undutiful:   Lascivious Edward, and thou perjured George,   And thou misshapen Dick, I tell ye all
translation: I know my duty. None of you do. Lustful Edward, and you, treacherous George, and you, deformed  Dick , I am telling you all:

original: I am your better, traitors as ye are:   And thou usurp'st my father's right and mine.
translation: I am superior to you, even though you're traitors. You have usurped the throne from me and my father.

original: Take that, thou likeness of this railer here.
translation: Take that, you mirror image of your ranting mother here.

original: Sprawl'st thou? Take that, to end thy agony.
translation: Are you still writhing? Take that, to end your agony.

original: And there's for twitting me with perjury.
translation: And here's for calling me treacherous.

original: O, kill me too!
translation: Oh, kill me too!

original: Marry, and shall.
translation: I will, gladly.

original: Hold, Richard, hold; for we have done too much.
translation: Stop, Richard, stop. We have done too much.

original: Why should she live, to fill the world with words?
translation: Why should she live and fill the world with her words?

original: What, doth she swoon? Use means for her recovery.
translation: Is she fainting? Help her recover.

original: Clarence, excuse me to the king my brother; I'll hence to London on a serious matter: Ere ye come there, be sure to hear some news.
translation: Clarence, give my excuses to my brother the king. I'm off to London because to take care of some serious business. Before you come there, wait to hear some news from me.

original: What? What?
translation: What? What?

original: The Tower, the Tower.
translation: The Tower, the Tower.
