original: O Ned, sweet Ned! Speak to thy mother, boy!   Canst thou not speak? O traitors! Murderers!   They that stabb'd Caesar shed no blood at all,   Did not offend, nor were not worthy blame,   If this foul deed were by to equal it:
translation: Oh, Ned, sweet Ned! Speak to your mother, boy! Can you not speak? Oh, traitors! Murderers! Compared to this horrible, act the men who stabbed Caesar spilled no blood at all, didn't offend anyone, and weren't deserving of blame.

original: He was a man; this, in respect, a child:   And men ne'er spend their fury on a child.   What's worse than murderer, that I may name it?   No, no, my heart will burst, and if I speak:   And I will speak, that so my heart may burst.
translation: Caesar was a man. My son, in comparison, was a child. And men never act violently towards children. What's worse than being a murderer so I can call them that? No, no, my heart will burst if I speak: I will speak so my heart can burst .

original: Butchers and villains! Bloody cannibals!   How sweet a plant have you untimely cropp'd!   You have no children, butchers! If you had,   The thought of them would have stirr'd up remorse:
translation: Butchers and villains! Bloody cannibals! You have cut short the life of this sweet boy too early. You have no children, butchers! If you did have children, the thought of them would have made you feel pity.

original: But if you ever chance to have a child,   Look in his youth to have him so cut off   As, deathmen, you have rid this sweet young prince!
translation: But if you ever do have a child, prepare to have him slaughtered in his youth just as you killers have executed this sweet young prince!

original: Away with her; go, bear her hence perforce.
translation: Take her away from here with force.

original: Nay, never bear me hence, dispatch me here, Here sheathe thy sword, I'll pardon thee my death: What, wilt thou not? Then, Clarence, do it thou.
translation: No, don't take me away from here, kill me here. Bury your sword in my body and I'll forgive you for my death. What, you won't do it? Then, Clarence, you do it.

original: By heaven, I will not do thee so much ease.
translation: By heaven, I will not give you so much comfort.

original: Good Clarence, do; sweet Clarence, do thou do it.
translation: Good Clarence, do. Sweet Clarence, please do it.

original: Didst thou not hear me swear I would not do it?
translation: Didn't you hear me swear that I wouldn't do it?

original: Ay, but thou usest to forswear thyself:   'Twas sin before, but now 'tis charity.
translation: Yes but you are used to swearing and the breaking your promise. It was a sin before, but now it is charity.

original: What, wilt thou not? Where is that devil's butcher,   Hard-favour'd Richard? Richard, where art thou?
translation: What, won't you do it? Where is that devilish slaughterer, ugly Richard? Richard, where are you?

original: Thou art not here: murder is thy alms-deed;   Petitioners for blood thou ne'er put'st back.
translation: You aren't here. Murder is your act of charity. You never turn away those who are begging for death.

original: Away, I say; I charge ye, bear her hence.
translation: I say, away! I order you, take her away from here.

original: So come to you and yours, as to this Prince!
translation: May the same happen to you and your family as it happened to this Prince!

original: Where's Richard gone?
translation: Where has Richard gone?

original: To London, all in post; and, as I guess, To make a bloody supper in the Tower.
translation: To London, in  a big hurry.  And I suspect he is going to be shedding blood in the Tower.

original: He's sudden if a thing comes in his head.   Now march we hence: discharge the common sort   With pay and thanks,
translation: He's impulsive when an idea comes into his head. Now let's go from here. Tell the common soldiers to go.  Pay them and thank them.

original: and let's away to London   And see our gentle queen how well she fares:   By this, I hope, she hath a son for me.
translation: Let's go to London and see how my gentle queen is doing. I hope that she has given birth to a son for me by now.

original: Good day, my lord. What, at your book so hard?
translation: Hello, my lord. Are you reading your book so carefully?

original: Ay, my good lord:—my lord, I should say rather; 'Tis sin to flatter; 'good' was little better: 'Good Gloucester' and 'good devil' were alike, And both preposterous; therefore, not 'good lord.'
translation: Yes, my good lord. My lord, I should rather say. It's a sin to flatter. "Good" is basically flattery. "Good Gloucester" and "good devil" are also flattery, and both nonsensical to say, so I won't say "good lord."

original: Sirrah, leave us to ourselves: we must confer.
translation: Sir, leave us alone. We must discuss something.

original: So flies the reckless shepherd from the wolf; So first the harmless sheep doth yield his fleece And next his throat unto the butcher's knife. What scene of death hath Roscius now to act?
translation: He leaves just like a careless shepherd fleeing when the wolf is near his sheep. First the harmless sheep gives up its wool to the shepherd and the next thing he knows his throat is slit by the butcher's knife. What type of death scene will be performing today?

original: Suspicion always haunts the guilty mind; The thief doth fear each bush an officer.
translation: Fearful anticipations always haunt a guilty mind. The thief thinks every bush he sees is an officer.

original: The bird that hath been limed in a bush, With trembling wings misdoubteth every bush; And I, the hapless male to one sweet bird, Have now the fatal object in my eye Where my poor young was limed, was caught and kill'd.
translation: A bird that's been trapped by a hunter in a bush approaches every bush with trembling wings. And I, the unlucky father to one sweet child, now see the hunter before me upon whose weapon my poor child was trapped, caught, and killed.

original: Why, what a peevish fool was that of Crete, That taught his son the office of a fowl! An yet, for all his wings, the fool was drown'd.

I, Daedalus; my poor boy, Icarus; Thy father, Minos, that denied our course; The sun that sear'd the wings of my sweet boy Thy brother Edward, and thyself the sea Whose envious gulf did swallow up his life. Ah, kill me with thy weapon, not with words! My breast can better brook thy dagger's point Than can my ears that tragic history. But wherefore dost thou come? Is't for my life?
translation: I am Daedalus and my poor boy is Icarus. Your father is like Minos in the story, who imprisoned them. The sun burned the wings of my sweet boy. You and your brother Edward are like the sea in the story, whose angry depths swallowed up Icarus' body. Ah, kill me with your weapon, not with your words! My chest can endure your dagger's point better than my ears can endure hearing this tragic story. But why did you come here? Did you come for my life?

original: Think'st thou I am an executioner?
translation: Do you think I am an executioner?

original: A persecutor, I am sure, thou art: If murdering innocents be executing, Why, then thou art an executioner.
translation: I'm sure you are a tormentor. If murdering innocent people is executing, then you're definitely an executioner.

original: Thy son I kill'd for his presumption.
translation: I killed your son because of his arrogance.

original: Hadst thou been kill'd when first thou didst presume,   Thou hadst not lived to kill a son of mine.
translation: If you were killed the first time you were arrogant, you wouldn't have been alive to kill my son.

original: And thus I prophesy, that many a thousand,   Which now mistrust no parcel of my fear,   And many an old man's sigh and many a widow's,   And many an orphan's water-standing eye—   Men for their sons, wives for their husbands,   And orphans for their parents timeless death—   Shall rue the hour that ever thou wast born.
translation: And so here I predict that as many as a thousand people, who now suspect no part of what I fear will happen, will curse the day that you were born with many sighs of old men and widows, many tears shed by orphans and by men for their sons, wives for their husbands, and orphans for their parents' premature deaths.

original: The owl shriek'd at thy birth,—an evil sign;   The night-crow cried, aboding luckless time;   Dogs howl'd, and hideous tempest shook down trees;   The raven rook'd her on the chimney's top,   And chattering pies in dismal discords sung.
translation: The owl shrieked when you were born. That's an evil sign. The crow cried , predicting bad fortune. Dogs howled and a horrible tempest knocked down trees. The raven cowered on the top of the chimney, and magpies sang dissonantly.

original: Thy mother felt more than a mother's pain,   And, yet brought forth less than a mother's hope,   To wit, an indigested and deformed lump,   Not like the fruit of such a goodly tree.
translation: Your mother felt more than normal labor pains, and she gave birth to less than what mothers hope for. That is to say, a shapeless and deformed lump, not like the progeny that should come from such a good lineage.

original: Teeth hadst thou in thy head when thou wast born,   To signify thou camest to bite the world:   And, if the rest be true which I have heard,   Thou camest—
translation: You had teeth in your head when you were born to show that you came to bite the world. And, if all the other stories that I heard are true, you came—

original: I'll hear no more: die, prophet in thy speech:
translation: I won't hear anymore. Die speaking, prophet!

original: For this amongst the rest, was I ordain'd.
translation: I alone was destined for this.

original: Ay, and for much more slaughter after this. God forgive my sins, and pardon thee!
translation: Yes, and for much more killing after this. May God forgive my sins and may He forgive you!

original: What, will the aspiring blood of Lancaster   Sink in the ground? I thought it would have mounted.
translation: So, will the blood of the Lancaster who wanted to be king sink in the ground? I thought it would have ascended.

original: See how my sword weeps for the poor king's death!   O, may such purple tears be alway shed   From those that wish the downfall of our house!
translation: Look how my sword drips blood like tears for the poor king's death! Oh, I hope we'll always drip tears of blood from the bodies of those who  want to destroy our house!

original: If any spark of life be yet remaining,   Down, down to hell; and say I sent thee thither:
translation: If there is any life left in you, go down, down to hell, and say that I sent you there.

original: I, that have neither pity, love, nor fear.   Indeed, 'tis true that Henry told me of;   For I have often heard my mother say   I came into the world with my legs forward:
translation: Yes, I sent you there, I, that have neither pity, love nor fear. Yes, it's true what Henry said about me. I have often heard my mother say that I came into the world with my feet first.

original: Had I not reason, think ye, to make haste,   And seek their ruin that usurp'd our right?   The midwife wonder'd and the women cried   'O, Jesus bless us, he is born with teeth!'
translation: Don't you think I had a good reason to hurry and aim to ruin those that usurped our right to the throne? The midwife was amazed and the women cried, "Oh Jesus, bless us! He was born with teeth!"

original: And so I was; which plainly signified   That I should snarl and bite and play the dog.   Then, since the heavens have shaped my body so,   Let hell make crook'd my mind to answer it.
translation: And so I was, which basically meant that I would snarl and bite and act like a dog. Then, since God in heaven has shaped my body in such way, let hell make my mind deformed to match my body.

original: I have no brother, I am like no brother;   And this word 'love,' which graybeards call divine,   Be resident in men like one another   And not in me: I am myself alone.
translation: There is no one like me. I am like no one else. And this word, "love," which wise old men call divine, can be found in men who are like one another but not in  me. I am myself alone.

original: Clarence, beware; thou keep'st me from the light:   But I will sort a pitchy day for thee;   For I will buz abroad such prophecies   That Edward shall be fearful of his life,
translation: Clarence, be careful. You're between me and the crown. But I will arrange a dark day for you. I will spread so many rumors and omens all over the world that Edward will be afraid for his life.

original: And then, to purge his fear, I'll be thy death.   King Henry and the prince his son are gone:   Clarence, thy turn is next, and then the rest,
translation: And then to get rid of his fear of you, I'll kill you, Clarence. King Henry and the prince his son are now gone. Clarence, you're next, and then the rest.

original: Counting myself but bad till I be best.   I'll throw thy body in another room   And triumph, Henry, in thy day of doom.
translation: I consider myself worth nothing until I am king. Henry, I'll throw your body in another room and celebrate this day of your death.

original: Once more we sit in England's royal throne,   Re-purchased with the blood of enemies.   What valiant foemen, like to autumn's corn,   Have we mow'd down, in tops of all their pride!
translation: We sit on the English throne once more. We bought it back with the blood of our enemies. We have gotten rid of many brave enemies, at the height of their pride, mowing them down like corn in a harvest!

original: Three Dukes of Somerset, threefold renown'd   For hardy and undoubted champions;   Two Cliffords, as the father and the son,   And two Northumberlands; two braver men   Ne'er spurr'd their coursers at the trumpet's sound;
translation: Three Dukes of Somerset, all three renowned as bold and fearless warriors. Two Cliffords, the father and the son. Two Northumberlands: two braver men have never charged their horses into battle.

original: With them, the two brave bears, Warwick and Montague,   That in their chains fetter'd the kingly lion   And made the forest tremble when they roar'd.
translation: Along with them, the two brave members of the House of Warwick—the Earl of  Warwick and Montague—who captured the king and made the forest shake when they roared.

original: Thus have we swept suspicion from our seat   And made our footstool of security.   Come hither, Bess, and let me kiss my boy.
translation: And so we have removed all potential traitors from our kingdom and we can rest in safety and security. Come to me, Bess, and let me kiss my boy.

original: Young Ned, for thee, thine uncles and myself   Have in our armours watch'd the winter's night,   Went all afoot in summer's scalding heat,   That thou mightst repossess the crown in peace;   And of our labours thou shalt reap the gain.
translation: Young Ned, it's all been for you that your uncles and myself have gone to war in the freezing winter night and marched to battle in the summer's scalding heat. All so that you may inherit the crown in peace after me, so that you can take reap the rewards of our labor.

original: I'll blast his harvest, if your head were  laid;   For yet I am not look'd on in the world.
translation: I'll spoil that plan once your head's been cut off. I am not yet well-respected in the world.

original: This shoulder was ordain'd so thick to heave;   And heave it shall some weight, or break my back:   Work thou the way,—and thou shalt execute.
translation: My hunchback was made so heavy to train me to lift weight, and I'll lift it up this weight or I'll break my back in trying. If I can come up with a plan, I'll execute it.

original: Clarence and Gloucester, love my lovely queen; And kiss your princely nephew, brothers both.
translation: My brothers, Clarence and Gloucester, love my lovely queen and kiss your nephew the prince, both of you.

original: The duty that I owe unto your majesty I seal upon the lips of this sweet babe.
translation: I will kiss the lips of this sweet baby as an oath to stay true to the duty that I owe to your majesty.

original: Thanks, noble Clarence; worthy brother, thanks.
translation: Thanks, noble Clarence. Worthy brother, thank you.

original: And, that I love the tree from whence thou  sprang'st, Witness the loving kiss I give the fruit.  To say the truth, so Judas kissed his master And cried 'all hail!' when as he meant all harm.
translation: And because I love your father, the tree from which you came, watch the loving kiss I give to you, the fruit.

original: Now am I seated as my soul delights, Having my country's peace and brothers' loves.
translation: Now I am sitting on the throne with delight, since the country is peaceful and I have the love of both my brothers.

original: What will your grace have done with Margaret? Reignier, her father, to the king of France Hath pawn'd the Sicils and Jerusalem, And hither have they sent it for her ransom.
translation: What does your grace want to do with Margaret? Her father Reignier has sold Naples and Jerusalem to the king of France, and he's offered us the money to pay her ransom.

original: Away with her, and waft her hence to France.   And now what rests but that we spend the time   With stately triumphs, mirthful comic shows,   Such as befits the pleasure of the court?
translation: Let's be done with her and send her over to France. And now what else is there to do but spend our time with stately processions celebrating our victory, joyful comic shows, whatever the court finds pleasing?

original: Sound drums and trumpets! Farewell sour annoy!   For here, I hope, begins our lasting joy.
translation: Play the drums and trumpets! Bitter trouble, goodbye! I hope that our long lasting happiness begins here.

original: My life itself, and the best heart of it,   Thanks you for this great care: I stood i' the level   Of a full-charged confederacy, and give thanks   To you that choked it.
translation: I thank you with all my heart and my life itself for this great thing you've done. I was the target of a plot that was about to be carried out and I thank you for stopping it.

original: Let be call'd before us   That gentleman of Buckingham's; in person   I'll hear him his confessions justify;
translation: Have Buckingham's servant called before me. I'll hear him speak for himself

original: And point by point the treasons of his master   He shall again relate.
translation: and he'll tell every detail of his master's treason again.

original: Nay, we must longer kneel: I am a suitor.
translation: No, I have to kneel longer. I have a request.

original: Arise, and take place by us: half your suit   Never name to us; you have half our power:
translation: Get up and sit next to me. Don't tell me half your request, since you have half my power.

original: The other moiety, ere you ask, is given;   Repeat your will and take it.
translation: I grant you the other half before you ask. Tell me your request and grant it yourself.

original: Thank your majesty.   That you would love yourself, and in that love   Not unconsider'd leave your honour,
translation: Thank you, your majesty. My request is that you love yourself and, by doing that,

original: nor   The dignity of your office, is the point   Of my petition.
translation: that you not neglect your honor or the dignity of your position.

original: Lady mine, proceed.
translation: Go on, my lady.

original: I am solicited, not by a few,   And those of true condition, that your subjects   Are in great grievance: there have been commissions   Sent down among 'em, which hath flaw'd the heart   Of all their loyalties:
translation: I am told by many people, important ones, that your subjects are unhappy.  Taxes  have been imposed on them that make them disloyal.

original: wherein, although,   My good lord cardinal, they vent reproaches   Most bitterly on you, as putter on   Of these exactions, yet the king our master—
translation: So, although, my good lord cardinal, they reproach you bitterly for convincing the king to order these taxes, not even the king our master—

original: Whose honour heaven shield from soil!—even he   escapes not   Language unmannerly, yea, such which breaks   The sides of loyalty, and almost appears   In loud rebellion.
translation: may God protect his honor!—escapes their rude criticism. The language they use is too strong for loyal subjects and almost turns into a loud rebellion.

original: Not almost appears,   It doth appear; for, upon these taxations,   The clothiers all, not able to maintain   The many to them longing, have put off   The spinsters, carders, fullers, weavers,
translation: It doesn't almost turn into that, it does. Because of these taxes, the makers of clothing can't afford to pay all those working for them and have dismissed the spinners, wool-combers, wool-cleaners, and weavers

original: who,   Unfit for other life, compell'd by hunger   And lack of other means, in desperate manner   Daring the event to the teeth, are all in uproar,   And danger serves among then!
translation: who don't have any other skills and who have become desperate from hunger and poverty. They're in an uproar, daring anyone to resist them, and they're putting us in danger!

original: Taxation!   Wherein? and what taxation?
translation: Taxes! On what? What taxes?

original: My lord cardinal,   You that are blamed for it alike with us,   Know you of this taxation?
translation: My lord cardinal, you're being blamed too. Do you know about these taxes?

original: Please you, sir,   I know but of a single part, in aught   Pertains to the state;
translation: Sir, I know only a part of state business,

original: and front but in that file   Where others tell steps with me.
translation: and I am only the most important of the many people in charge of this business.

original: No, my lord,   You know no more than others; but you frame   Things that are known alike; which are not wholesome   To those which would not know them, and yet must   Perforce be their acquaintance.
translation: No, my lord, you don't know any more than anyone else. But you cause things to happen that can be known about. These things are bad for those who don't want to know about them but have to.

original: These exactions,   Whereof my sovereign would have note, they are   Most pestilent to the bearing; and, to bear 'em,   The back is sacrifice to the load.
translation: These taxes my king wants to know about are very hard to bear. For the people trying to bear them it's like they're laborers breaking their backs to carry their loads.

original: They say   They are devised by you; or else you suffer   Too hard an exclamation.
translation: They say the taxes were your idea. Or perhaps you're being unfairly talked about.

original: Still exaction! The nature of it? in what kind, let's know, Is this exaction?
translation: Taxes again! What is this? Tell me, what are these taxes?

original: I am much too venturous   In tempting of your patience; but am bolden'd   Under your promised pardon.
translation: I'm worried about boring you, but I take courage from your promise to forgive me.

original: The subjects' grief   Comes through commissions, which compel from each   The sixth part of his substance, to be levied   Without delay;
translation: The subjects are suffering from taxes that take a sixth of each person's wealth, to be collected immediately.

original: and the pretence for this   Is named, your wars in France: this makes bold mouths:   Tongues spit their duties out, and cold hearts freeze   Allegiance in them;
translation: The excuse for this is said to be your wars in France. That makes people say bold things. People refuse to do their duties and no longer feel loyalty.

original: their curses now   Live where their prayers did: and it's come to pass,   This tractable obedience is a slave   To each incensed will.
translation: Instead of praying for you, they curse you. And now their obedience has been overpowered by their anger.

original: I would your highness   Would give it quick consideration, for   There is no primer business.
translation: I would like you to think about this, your highness, because there's nothing more important.

original: By my life, This is against our pleasure.
translation: I swear by my life, this is not what I wanted.

original: And for me,   I have no further gone in this than by   A single voice; and that not pass'd me but   By learned approbation of the judges.
translation: As for me, I haven't been any more responsible for it than a single man giving his opinion can be. And I only approved it because wise judges agreed it was a good idea.

original: If I am   Traduced by ignorant tongues, which neither know   My faculties nor person, yet will be   The chronicles of my doing, let me say   'Tis but the fate of place, and the rough brake   That virtue must go through.
translation: If I have been betrayed by ignorant people who don't know me or my good qualities but insist on reporting what I do, let me say that that's the fate of important people and the rough obstacle that virtue has to face.

original: We must not stint   Our necessary actions, in the fear   To cope malicious censurers; which ever,   As ravenous fishes, do a vessel follow   That is new-trimm'd, but benefit no further   Than vainly longing.
translation: We must do what is necessary to stop evil-minded critics. These people are like hungry sharks following a newly-loaded ship, who can do nothing but wish the boat would sink and provide them with food.

original: What we oft do best,   By sick interpreters, once weak ones, is   Not ours, or not allow'd; what worst, as oft,   Hitting a grosser quality, is cried up   For our best act.
translation: Weak interpreters say that the good things we do are either not our doing or just not true. What's worse, just as often, they choose something unpleasant about us and say it's our greatest act.

original: If we shall stand still,   In fear our motion will be mock'd or carp'd at,   We should take root here where we sit, or sit   State-statues only.
translation: If we stand still, fearing that we'll be mocked or complained about for moving, we'll grow roots where we sit and become silent trees, or just sit like powerful statues.

original: Things done well,   And with a care, exempt themselves from fear;   Things done without example, in their issue   Are to be fear'd. Have you a precedent   Of this commission?
translation: Things done well and carefully give you nothing to fear. You should fear the consequences of things that have never been done before. Do you have a precedent for this tax?

original: I believe, not any.   We must not rend our subjects from our laws,   And stick them in our will. Sixth part of each?   A trembling contribution!
translation: I don't think you have one. We must not break our own laws to make our subjects do what we want. A sixth of each one's property? That's a terrible contribution!

original: Why, we take   From every tree lop, bark, and part o' the timber;   And, though we leave it with a root, thus hack'd,   The air will drink the sap.
translation: It's like we're taking the top, the bark, and part of the stump from  every tree ! And, although we leave each one with a root once it's been hacked, the air will dry its sap.

original: To every county   Where this is question'd send our letters, with   Free pardon to each man that has denied   The force of this commission:
translation: Send a letter to every county where this tax was taken with a free pardon for every man who refused to pay this tax.

original: pray, look to't;   I put it to your care.
translation: Do it, I trust you to take care of it.

original: [To the Secretary]   Let there be letters writ to every shire,   Of the king's grace and pardon. The grieved commons   Hardly conceive of me;
translation: [To the SECRETARY]  Let there be letters written to every part of the country announcing the king's kindness and pardon. The unhappy commoners think badly of me.

original: let it be noised   That through our intercession this revokement   And pardon comes: I shall anon advise you   Further in the proceeding.
translation: Let it be said that I asked for this retraction and pardon. Then I will tell you what to do next.

original: I am sorry that the Duke of Buckingham Is run in your displeasure.
translation: I'm sorry you're unhappy with the Duke of Buckingham.

original: It grieves many:   The gentleman is learn'd, and a most rare speaker;   To nature none more bound; his training such,   That he may furnish and instruct great teachers,   And never seek for aid out of himself.
translation: Many people are. The gentleman is well-read and a very good speaker. No one has better natural qualities. He's educated enough to teach great teachers all by himself without asking for help.

original: Yet see,   When these so noble benefits shall prove   Not well disposed, the mind growing once corrupt,   They turn to vicious forms, ten times more ugly   Than ever they were fair.
translation: But see, when these noble qualities are not well put together in a man and the mind is corrupted, they turn into bad qualities, ten times uglier than they were beautiful.

original: This man so complete,   Who was enroll'd 'mongst wonders, and when we,   Almost with ravish'd listening, could not find   His hour of speech a minute;
translation: This perfect man was thought to be a wonder of nature. He could make an hour of speaking seem like a minute because we were listening in such fascination.

original: he, my lady,   Hath into monstrous habits put the graces   That once were his, and is become as black   As if besmear'd in hell.
translation: He, my lady, has put all the energy that once made him good into monstrous habits and has become as evil as if he had been smeared with hell's ashes.

original: Sit by us; you shall hear—   This was his gentleman in trust—of him   Things to strike honour sad. Bid him recount   The fore-recited practises; whereof   We cannot feel too little, hear too much.
translation: Sit next to me and you will hear things that will make an honorable person sad. This was his trusted servant. Tell him to repeat the things he told us before about Buckingham's actions. I can't feel too little or hear too much about them.

original: Stand forth, and with bold spirit relate what you, Most like a careful subject, have collected Out of the Duke of Buckingham.
translation: Stand up and bravely tell what you observed about the Duke of Buckingham, like a good subject should.

original: Speak freely.
translation: Speak freely.

original: First, it was usual with him, every day   It would infect his speech, that if the king   Should without issue die, he'll carry it so   To make the sceptre his:
translation: First, it was a habit with him, every day he would infect his speech by saying it, that if the king died without an heir, he would take power himself.

original: these very words   I've heard him utter to his son-in-law,   Lord Abergavenny; to whom by oath he menaced   Revenge upon the cardinal.
translation: I've heard him say these very words to his son-in-law, Lord Abergavenny, and he promised him he would take revenge on the cardinal.

original: Please your highness, note   This dangerous conception in this point.
translation: Please, your highness, pay attention to this dangerous idea.

original: Not friended by his wish, to your high person   His will is most malignant; and it stretches   Beyond you, to your friends.
translation: He means you harm. He wants to do evil to you, and his anger stretches beyond you, to your friends.

original: My learn'd lord cardinal, Deliver all with charity.
translation: Wise lord cardinal, speak charitably.

original: Speak on:   How grounded he his title to the crown,   Upon our fail?
translation: Go on. How did he justify his claim to the crown when I die?

original: to this point hast thou heard him   At any time speak aught?
translation: Have you heard him say anything about that point at any time?

original: He was brought to this By a vain prophecy of Nicholas Hopkins.
translation: He thought of this because of Nicholas Hopkins's meaningless prophecy.

original: What was that Hopkins?
translation: Who was Hopkins?

original: Sir, a Chartreux friar, His confessor, who fed him every minute With words of sovereignty.
How know'st thou this?
translation: How do you know this?

original: Not long before your highness sped to France,   The duke being at the Rose, within the parish   Saint Lawrence Poultney, did of me demand   What was the speech among the Londoners   Concerning the French journey:
translation: Not long before you went to France, your Highness, the duke was at the Rose in the town of Saint Lawrence Poultney. He asked me what the Londoners were saying about the French journey.

original: I replied,   Men fear'd the French would prove perfidious,   To the king's danger. Presently the duke   Said, 'twas the fear, indeed;
translation: I replied that men were afraid the French would be treacherous and harm the king. Then the duke said that this was indeed what people were afraid of,

original: and that he doubted   'Twould prove the verity of certain words   Spoke by a holy monk; 'that oft,' says he,   'Hath sent to me, wishing me to permit   John de la Car, my chaplain,   a choice hour   To hear from him a matter of some moment:
translation: and that he thought it would prove the truth of some words spoken by a holy monk. "This monk often," he said, "has written to me asking me to allow him to meet with John de la Car, my priest,  for an hour to hear about an important matter.

original: Whom after under the confession's seal   He solemnly had sworn, that what he spoke   My chaplain to no creature living,   but   To me, should utter, with demure confidence   This pausingly ensued:
translation: Under the safety of confession he said that my priest should repeat what he said to no one except me. He hesitantly said this:

original: neither the king nor's heirs,   Tell you the duke, shall prosper: bid him strive   To gain the love o' the commonalty: the duke   Shall govern England.'
translation: tell the duke that neither the king nor his heirs will prosper. Tell him to try to gain the people's affection. The duke will govern England."

original: If I know you well,   You were the duke's surveyor, and lost your office   On the complaint o' the tenants:
translation: If I recognize you, you were the duke's surveyor and lost your job because of his tenants' complaints.

original: take good heed   You charge not in your spleen a noble person   And spoil your nobler soul: I say, take heed;   Yes, heartily beseech you.
translation: Take care you don't accuse a noble person out of anger and damn your soul, which is even nobler. Watch out, I beg you.

original: Let him on. Go forward.
translation: Let him go on. Come forward.

original: On my soul, I'll speak but truth.   I told my lord the duke, by the devil's illusions   The monk might be deceived; and that 'twas dangerous  for him   To ruminate on this so far, until   It forged him some design,
translation: I swear on my soul, I'll tell the truth. I told my lord the duke that the monk might have been deceived by the devil's tricks and that it was dangerous for him to think about this so much because it would make him start thinking about a plot.

original: which, being believed,   It was much like to do: he answer'd, 'Tush,   It can do me no damage;'
translation: This was likely to happen if he believed it. He answered, "Shh, it can't do me any harm."

original: adding further,   That, had the king in his last sickness fail'd,   The cardinal's and Sir Thomas Lovell's heads   Should have gone off.
translation: He added that if the king had died of his last sickness the cardinal's and Sir Thomas Lovell's heads would have come off.

original: Ha! what, so rank? Ah ha! There's mischief in this man: canst thou say further?
translation: What! He said this so openly? Aha! That man is trouble. Can you say anything more?

original: I can, my liege.
translation: I can, my king.

original: Proceed.
translation: Go on.

original: Being at Greenwich, After your highness had reproved the duke About Sir William Blomer,—
translation: At Greenwich, when you had scolded the duke about Sir William Blomer—

original: I remember Of such a time: being my sworn servant, The duke retain'd him his. But on; what hence?
translation: I remember that. He was my servant and the duke hired him. But go on, what happened then?

original: 'If,' quoth he, 'I for this had been committed,   As, to the Tower, I thought, I would have play'd   The part my father meant to act upon   The usurper Richard;
translation: He said, "If I had been imprisoned for this in the Tower, as I thought I might be, I would have done  what my father meant to do to the usurper Richard .

original: who, being at Salisbury,   Made suit to come in's presence; which if granted,   As he made semblance of his duty, would   Have put his knife to him.'
translation: When the king was at Salisbury my father asked to be brought into his presence. If this had been allowed, he would have stabbed him as he pretended to kiss his hand.

original: A giant traitor!
translation: What a giant traitor!

original: Now, madam, may his highness live in freedom, and this man out of prison?
translation: Now, ma'am, can the king live safely if this man is not in jail?

original: God mend all!
translation: May God make all this better!

original: There's something more would out of thee; what say'st?
translation: There's something more you want to say. What is it?

original: After 'the duke his father,' with 'the knife,'   He stretch'd him, and, with one hand on his dagger,   Another spread on's breast, mounting his eyes   He did discharge a horrible oath;
translation: After he said these things about "the duke his father" and "the knife," he stretched himself out and, with one hand on his dagger and another on his chest, he rolled his eyes and let out a horrible curse.

original: whose tenor   Was,—were he evil used, he would outgo   His father by as much as a performance   Does an irresolute purpose.
translation: The gist of it was that, if he were badly treated, he would do so much better than his father: as if he were going to do what his father only sort of wished he could do.

original: There's his period,   To sheathe his knife in us. He is attach'd;   Call him to present trial: if he may   Find mercy in the law, 'tis his:
translation: That's what he wants, to stab me. He has been arrested. Call him to trial at once. If he can find any mercy for himself in the law, it's his.

original: if none,   Let him not seek 't of us: by day and night,   He's traitor to the height.
translation: If not, he won't get any from me. I swear by day and night, he's the worst of traitors.

original: Is't possible the spells of France should juggle Men into such strange mysteries?
translation: Is it possible that France could enchant men to do such strange things?

original: New customs, Though they be never so ridiculous, Nay, let 'em be unmanly, yet are follow'd.
translation: New fashions are being followed, however ridiculous or even unmanly they are.

original: As far as I see, all the good our English   Have got by the late voyage is but merely   A fit or two o' the face; but they are shrewd ones;
translation: As far as I can see, the only good thing our Englishmen got from the recent voyage was a few new facial expressions. But they're good ones.

original: For when they hold 'em, you would swear directly   Their very noses had been counsellors   To Pepin or Clotharius, they keep state so.
translation: When they put on those expressions, you would swear their noses had been counsellors to kings  Pepin or Clotharius  because they look so dignified.

original: They have all new legs, and lame ones: one would take  it, That never saw 'em pace before, the spavin Or springhalt reign'd among 'em.
translation: They have new ways of walking, and they seem lame. You would think if you had never seen them walk like that before that they had leg diseases.

original: Death! my lord, Their clothes are after such a pagan cut too, That, sure, they've worn out Christendom.
translation: For the love of God! My lord, their clothes look like pagan clothes. They don't look like Christians anymore.

original: How now! What news, Sir Thomas Lovell?
translation: Hello! What's the news, Sir Thomas Lovell?

original: Faith, my lord, I hear of none, but the new proclamation That's clapp'd upon the court-gate.
translation: Truly, my lord, I haven't heard about anything except the new proclamation that's been put up on the gate to the court.

original: What is't for?
translation: What is it for?

original: The reformation of our travell'd gallants, That fill the court with quarrels, talk, and tailors.
translation: To reform the returned travelers who fill the court with quarrels, talk, and tailors.

original: I'm glad 'tis there: now I would pray our monsieurs To think an English courtier may be wise, And never see the Louvre.
They must either,   For so run the conditions, leave those remnants   Of fool and feather that they got in France,   With all their honourable point of ignorance   Pertaining thereunto,
translation: The proclamation asks that they give up those scraps of foolish cloth and feathers they got in France along with all their pointless knowledge, or rather ignorance, about them.

original: as fights and fireworks,   Abusing better men than they can be,   Out of a foreign wisdom, renouncing clean   The faith they have in tennis, and tall stockings,
translation: They must also give up fights and fireworks and insulting better men than they can ever be for not knowing about foreign things. They must completely renounce their faithfulness to tennis and tall stockings,

original: Short blister'd breeches, and those types of travel,   And understand again like honest men;   Or pack to their old playfellows:
translation: short pants that look like they have blisters on them, and that sort of thing they picked up from traveling, and act like honest men again. Or head back to their old playmates in France.

original: there, I take it,   They may, 'cum privilegio,' wear away   The lag end of their lewdness and be laugh'd at.
translation: There, as I understand, the proclamation allows them "freely" to indulge in the rest of their foolishness and be laughed at.

original: 'Tis time to give 'em physic, their diseases Are grown so catching.
What a loss our ladies Will have of these trim vanities!
translation: The ladies will miss these neat pointless things!

original: Ay, marry,   There will be woe indeed, lords:
translation: Yes, it's true. There will be sadness about that, lords.

original: the sly whoresons   Have got a speeding trick to lay down ladies;   A French song and a fiddle has no fellow.
translation: The clever bastards have figured out a quick trick to make ladies go to bed with them. You can't compete with a French song and a  fiddle .

original: The devil fiddle 'em! I am glad they are going,   For, sure, there's no converting of 'em: now   An honest country lord, as I am, beaten   A long time out of play,
translation: May the devil fiddle them! I am glad they are going because it's impossible to change them. Now an honest country noblemen like me, who couldn't compete,

original: may bring his plainsong   And have an hour of hearing; and, by'r lady,   Held current music too.
translation: can bring my church songs and be listened to for an hour. And, by the virgin Mary, it will be considered fashionable music too.

original: Well said, Lord Sands; Your colt's tooth is not cast yet.
translation: Well said, Lord Sands. You're still a wild young colt with all its teeth.

original: No, my lord; Nor shall not, while I have a stump.
translation: Yes, my lord, and I'll keep at it while I still have a tooth in my head.

original: Sir Thomas, Whither were you a-going?
translation: Sir Thomas, where were you headed?

original: To the cardinal's: Your lordship is a guest too.
translation: To the cardinal's. You're a guest there too.

original: O, 'tis true:   This night he makes a supper, and a great one,   To many lords and ladies;
translation: Oh, it's true. Tonight he's having a dinner, a huge one, for many lords and ladies.

original: there will be   The beauty of this kingdom, I'll assure you.
translation: All the beauties in the kingdom will be there, I assure you.

original: That churchman bears a bounteous mind indeed, A hand as fruitful as the land that feeds us; His dews fall every where.
No doubt he's noble; He had a black mouth that said other of him.
translation: No doubt he's noble. Anyone who says otherwise has an evil mouth.

original: He may, my lord; has wherewithal: in him   Sparing would show a worse sin than ill doctrine:
translation: They may, my lord, and probably do. Hoarding would be a worse sin for him than a wrong belief.

original: Men of his way should be most liberal;   They are set here for examples.
translation: Men like him should be generous. They are put on this earth as examples to the rest.

original: True, they are so:   But few now give so great ones. My barge stays;   Your lordship shall along. Come, good Sir Thomas,   We shall be late else;
translation: It's true, they are. But few men now are such great examples. My barge is waiting. You'll come with me. Come, Sir Thomas, or we'll be late.

original: which I would not be,   For I was spoke to, with Sir Henry Guildford   This night to be comptrollers.
translation: I wouldn't want to be, because I was asked (along with Sir Henry Guildford) to be a master of ceremonies.

original: I am your lordship's.
translation: I'm at your service.

original: Ladies, a general welcome from his grace   Salutes ye all; this night he dedicates   To fair content and you:
translation: Ladies, the cardinal welcomes all of you. He dedicates tonight to happiness and you.

original: none here, he hopes,   In all this noble bevy, has brought with her   One care abroad;
translation: No one here, he hopes, in this troop of nobles, has brought a single sorrow with her.

original: he would have all as merry   As, first, good company, good wine, good welcome,   Can make good people. O, my lord, you're tardy:
translation: He wants everyone to be as happy as good company, good wine, and a good welcome can make good people. Oh, my lord, you're late.

original: The very thought of this fair company Clapp'd wings to me.
translation: The thought of this beautiful company made me hurry.

original: You are young, Sir Harry Guildford.
translation: You are young, Sir Harry Guildford.

original: Sir Thomas Lovell, had the cardinal   But half my lay thoughts in him, some of these   Should find a running banquet ere they rested,
translation: Sir Thomas Lovell, if the cardinal had even half my unreligious thoughts in him, some of these women would have a  quick refreshment  before they rested

original: I think would better please 'em: by my life,   They are a sweet society of fair ones.
translation: that I think would please them more than this one. I swear by my life, they're a sweet band of beauties.

original: O, that your lordship were but now confessor To one or two of these!
translation: Oh, if only you were the confessor of one or two of them!

original: I would I were; They should find easy penance.
Faith, how easy?
translation: Really? How easy?

original: As easy as a down-bed would afford it.
translation: As easy as a feather-bed would make it.

original: Sweet ladies, will it please you sit? Sir Harry,   Place you that side; I'll take the charge of this:   His grace is entering. Nay, you must not freeze;
translation: Sweet ladies, would you sit? Sir Harry, you seat this half of them. I'll be in charge of the other half. The cardinal is entering. No, don't freeze us:

original: Two women placed together makes cold weather:   My Lord Sands, you are one will keep 'em waking;   Pray, sit between these ladies.
translation: two women placed together makes cold weather. My Lord Sands, you'll keep them awake. Please, sit between these ladies.

original: By my faith,   And thank your lordship. By your leave, sweet ladies:
translation: Certainly, and thank you, your lordship. Please, sweet ladies,

original: If I chance to talk a little wild, forgive me;   I had it from my father.
translation: if I talk a little wildly, forgive me. I inherited it from my father.

original: Was he mad, sir?
translation: Was he crazy, sir?

original: O, very mad, exceeding mad, in love too: But he would bite none; just as I do now, He would kiss you twenty with a breath.
Well said, my lord.   So, now you're fairly seated.
translation: Well said my lord. So, now you're beautifully seated between two beauties.

original: Gentlemen,   The penance lies on you, if these fair ladies   Pass away frowning.
translation: Gentleman, you'll be punished if these beautiful ladies leave looking unhappy.

original: For my little cure, Let me alone.
translation: As for me, don't worry.

original: You're welcome, my fair guests: that noble lady,   Or gentleman, that is not freely merry,   Is not my friend:
translation: You're welcome, my beautiful guests. Whatever noble lady or gentleman is not happy is not my friend.

original: this, to confirm my welcome;   And to you all, good health.
translation: I drink to confirm my welcome. Good health to you all.

original: Your grace is noble: Let me have such a bowl may hold my thanks, And save me so much talking.
translation: You're noble, your grace. Let me have a cup like that to hold my thanks and I'll drink it to save so much talking.

original: My Lord Sands,   I am beholding to you: cheer your neighbours.
translation: My Lord Sands, thank you. Entertain your neighbors.

original: Ladies, you are not merry: gentlemen,   Whose fault is this?
translation: Ladies, you are not happy. Gentlemen, whose fault is this?

original: The red wine first must rise In their fair cheeks, my lord; then we shall have 'em Talk us to silence.
translation: The red wine must first flush their beautiful faces, my lord. Then they'll talk so much we'll have to be silent.

original: You are a merry gamester, My Lord Sands.
translation: You're a cheerful player, my lord Sands.

original: Yes, if I make my play. Here's to your ladyship: and pledge it, madam, For 'tis to such a thing,—
You cannot show me.
translation: You can't show me.

original: I told your grace they would talk anon.
translation: I told you they would talk soon, your grace.

original: What's that?
translation: What's that?

original: Look out there, some of ye.
translation: Some of you go look outside.

original: What warlike voice, And to what end is this? Nay, ladies, fear not; By all the laws of war you're privileged.
translation: What warlike noise was that, and what was it for? No, don't be afraid, ladies. The laws of war will protect you.

original: How now! what is't?
translation: Well? What is it?

original: A noble troop of strangers;   For so they seem: they've left their barge and landed;
translation: It seems like a noble band of strangers. They've left their barge and come to land.

original: And hither make, as great ambassadors   From foreign princes.
translation: They're heading here as great ambassadors from foreign princes.

original: Good lord chamberlain,   Go, give 'em welcome; you can speak the French tongue;
translation: Good lord chamberlain, go welcome them. You can speak French.

original: And, pray, receive 'em nobly, and conduct 'em   Into our presence, where this heaven of beauty   Shall shine at full upon them. Some attend him.
translation: And please treat them well and bring them to us, where beauty as plentiful as in heaven will shine on them. Go with him, some of you.

original: You have now a broken banquet; but we'll mend it. A good digestion to you all: and once more I shower a welcome on ye; welcome all.
translation: Your feast has been broken up, but we'll fix that. I wish all of you good digestion. I welcome you once more: welcome, all.

original: A noble company! what are their pleasures?
translation: This is a noble band! What do they want?

original: Because they speak no English, thus they pray'd   To tell your grace, that, having heard by fame   Of this so noble and so fair assembly   This night to meet here,
translation: Because they don't speak English, they asked me to tell you that, having heard rumors of this noble and beautiful crowd meeting here tonight,

original: they could do no less   Out of the great respect they bear to beauty,
translation: they had to leave their flocks because of the great respect they have for beauty.

original: But leave their flocks; and, under your fair conduct,   Crave leave to view these ladies and entreat   An hour of revels with 'em.
translation: They beg you to allow them to see these ladies and they ask for an hour of dancing with them.

original: Say, lord chamberlain, They have done my poor house grace; for which I pay 'em A thousand thanks, and pray 'em take their pleasures.
translation: Tell them, lord chamberlain, they have done an honor to my house. I give them a thousand thanks in return and ask them to do as they like.

original: The fairest hand I ever touch'd! O beauty, Till now I never knew thee!
translation: The most beautiful hand I ever touched! Oh, I never knew what beauty was until now!

original: My lord!
translation: My lord!

original: Your grace?
translation: Yes, your grace?

original: Pray, tell 'em thus much from me:   There should be one amongst 'em, by his person,   More worthy this place than myself;
translation: Please, tell them this from me: one of them should be more worthy of sitting here than me.

original: to whom,   If I but knew him, with my love and duty   I would surrender it.
translation: If I could only recognize him, I would give up this seat to him out of my love and duty.

original: I will, my lord.
translation: I will, my lord.

original: What say they?
translation: What do they say?

original: Such a one, they all confess, There is indeed; which they would have your grace Find out, and he will take it.
translation: They all confess that there is one like that. If you can find him he will take the seat.

original: Let me see, then. By all your good leaves, gentlemen; here I'll make My royal choice.
translation: Let me see, then. Allow me, gentlemen. I choose the king here.

original: Ye have found him, cardinal:
translation: You found him, cardinal.

original: You hold a fair assembly; you do well, lord: You are a churchman, or, I'll tell you, cardinal, I should judge now unhappily.
translation: You throw a beautiful party. That's a good thing, lord. If you weren't a churchman, cardinal, I can tell you I would judge you badly.

original: I am glad Your grace is grown so pleasant.
translation: I am glad you're making so many jokes, your grace.

original: My lord chamberlain, Prithee, come hither: what fair lady's that?
translation: Please, come here, my lord chamberlain. Who's that beautiful lady?

original: An't please your grace, Sir Thomas Bullen's daughter— The Viscount Rochford,—one of her highness' women.
translation: Your grace, that's Sir Thomas Bullen's daughter. He's the Viscount Rochford. She's one of the queen's ladies in waiting.

original: By heaven, she is a dainty one. Sweetheart,   I were unmannerly, to take you out,   And not to kiss you.
translation: By God, she's a pretty one. Sweetheart, I would be rude to dance with you and not kiss you.

original: A health, gentlemen!   Let it go round.
translation: Drink to her health, gentlemen! Everyone drink.

original: Sir Thomas Lovell, is the banquet ready I' the privy chamber?
translation: Sir Thomas Lovell, is the banquet in the private room ready?

original: Yes, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: Your grace, I fear, with dancing is a little heated.
translation: I'm worried you feel a little hot from dancing, your grace.

original: I fear, too much.
translation: Yes, I'm afraid I feel very hot.

original: There's fresher air, my lord, In the next chamber.
translation: There's fresher air in the next room, my lord.

original: Lead in your ladies, every one: sweet partner,   I must not yet forsake you: let's be merry:   Good my lord cardinal, I have half a dozen healths   To drink to these fair ladies,
translation: Everyone, lead in your ladies. Dear partner, I won't abandon you yet. Let's be cheerful. My good lord cardinal, I have half a dozen toasts to drink to these beautiful ladies,

original: and a measure   To lead 'em once again; and then let's dream   Who's best in favour. Let the music knock it.
translation: and I have to dance with them again. And then let's think about whom I like best. Let the music play.

original: Whither away so fast?
translation: Where are you going so fast?

original: O, God save ye! Even to the hall, to hear what shall become Of the great Duke of Buckingham.
translation: Oh, hello! To the hall to hear what will happen to the great Duke of Buckingham.

original: I'll save you That labour, sir. All's now done, but the ceremony Of bringing back the prisoner.
translation: I'll spare you that effort, sir. It's all over, except for bringing the prisoner back to jail.

original: Were you there?
translation: Were you there?

original: Yes, indeed, was I.
translation: Yes, I was.

original: Pray, speak what has happen'd.
translation: Please tell me what happened.

original: You may guess quickly what.
translation: You can easily guess.

original: Is he found guilty?
translation: Was he found guilty?

original: Yes, truly is he, and condemn'd upon't.
translation: Yes, and condemned for it.

original: I am sorry for't.
translation: I'm sorry about that.

original: So are a number more.
translation: So are many other people.

original: But, pray, how pass'd it?
translation: But tell me, how did it happen?

original: I'll tell you in a little. The great duke   Came to the bar; where to his accusations   He pleaded still not guilty and alleged   Many sharp reasons to defeat the law.
translation: I'll tell you in a few words. The great duke came to court, where he still pled not guilty to the accusations against him and made many good arguments to escape the law.

original: The king's attorney on the contrary   Urged on the examinations, proofs, confessions   Of divers witnesses; which the duke desired   To have brought viva voce to his face:
translation: But the king's lawyer brought against him the questioning, proofs, and confessions of many different witnesses. The duke asked to have them testify in front of him.

original: At which appear'd against him his surveyor;   Sir Gilbert Peck his chancellor; and John Car,   Confessor to him; with that devil-monk,   Hopkins, that made this mischief.
translation: So his surveyor appeared against him along with Sir Gilbert Peck (his chancellor), John Car (his confessor) and that devilish monk Hopkins, who caused this trouble.

original: That was he That fed him with his prophecies?
translation: He was the one who fed the duke his prophecies?

original: The same.   All these accused him strongly; which he fain   Would have flung from him, but, indeed, he could not:
translation: Yes. They all accused him strongly. He tried to deny everything but couldn't.

original: And so his peers, upon this evidence,   Have found him guilty of high treason.
translation: So his peers, seeing this evidence, found him guilty of high treason. He said a lot that was very learned to argue for his life.

original: Much   He spoke, and learnedly, for life; but all   Was either pitied in him or forgotten.
translation: But everything he said was either pitied (but not listened to) or forgotten.

original: After all this, how did he bear himself?
translation: After all this, how did he act?

original: When he was brought again to the bar, to hear   His knell rung out, his judgment, he was stirr'd   With such an agony, he sweat extremely,   And something spoke in choler, ill, and hasty:
translation: When he was brought back to the stand to hear the judgement, he was filled with such agony that he sweated a lot and spoke words angrily, badly, and hastily.

original: But he fell to himself again, and sweetly   In all the rest show'd a most noble patience.
translation: But he came back to himself and showed a noble patience for the rest of it.

original: I do not think he fears death.
translation: I do not think he fears death.

original: Sure, he does not: He never was so womanish; the cause He may a little grieve at.
translation: Surely he doesn't. He was never that womanish. He may be a little sad about the cause of his death.

original: Certainly The cardinal is the end of this.
translation: Certainly the cardinal is responsible for this.

original: 'Tis likely,   By all conjectures: first, Kildare's attainder,   Then deputy of Ireland;
translation: It's likely, and everyone thinks so. First, there's the fact that Kildare was arrested, who was then the deputy of Ireland.

original: who removed,   Earl Surrey was sent thither, and in haste too,   Lest he should help his father.
translation: Once he was removed, the Earl of Surry was sent there, and quickly too, so he couldn't help his father.

original: That trick of state Was a deep envious one.
translation: That was a sneaky, jealous trick.

original: At his return   No doubt he will requite it.
translation: No doubt he'll take his revenge for it when he returns.

original: This is noted,   And generally, whoever the king favours,   The cardinal instantly will find employment,   And far enough from court too.
translation: It has been noticed that, in general, the cardinal instantly finds a job far from court for whomever the king favors.

original: All the commons   Hate him perniciously, and, o' my conscience,   Wish him ten fathom deep:
translation: All the common people hate him and I swear they want him dead and buried.

original: this duke as much   They love and dote on; call him bounteous Buckingham,   The mirror of all courtesy;—
translation: They love this duke as much as they hate the cardinal. They call him generous Buckingham, the best example of all good qualities—

original: Stay there, sir, And see the noble ruin'd man you speak of.
translation: Stop there, sir, and look at the noble, ruined man you're talking about.

original: Let's stand close, and behold him.
translation: Let's get closer and look at him.

original: All good people,   You that thus far have come to pity me,   Hear what I say, and then go home and lose me.
translation: Good people, you who have come here to pity me, listen to what I say and then go home and forget me.

original: I have this day received a traitor's judgment,   And by that name must die: yet, heaven bear witness,   And if I have a conscience, let it sink me,   Even as the axe falls, if I be not faithful!
translation: Today I was sentenced as a traitor, and I must die as one. But, may heaven bear witness, and may my conscience sink me into the ground just as the axe is falling if I lie, I am a faithful subject!

original: The law I bear no malice for my death;   'T has done, upon the premises, but justice:   But those that sought it I could wish more Christians:   Be what they will, I heartily forgive 'em:
translation: I don't blame the law for my death. It did what was right based on the evidence. But I wish those who prosecuted me were better Christians. Whatever they are, I gladly forgive them.

original: Yet let 'em look they glory not in mischief,   Nor build their evils on the graves of great men;   For then my guiltless blood must cry against 'em.
translation: But let them be sure not to be proud of the mischief they do or kill great men to pursue their evil goals. Because then my innocent blood will accuse them.

original: For further life in this world I ne'er hope,   Nor will I sue, although the king have mercies   More than I dare make faults.
translation: I don't hope for more life in this world and I won't ask for it, although the king is able to forgive more evil deeds than I would dare do.

original: You few that loved me,   And dare be bold to weep for Buckingham,   His noble friends and fellows, whom to leave   Is only bitter to him, only dying,   Go with me, like good angels, to my end;
translation: You few who loved me and dare to weep for Buckingham, his noble friends, the only pain and death he feels is having to leave you. Go with me to my death like good angels.

original: And, as the long divorce of steel falls on me,   Make of your prayers one sweet sacrifice,   And lift my soul to heaven. Lead on, o' God's name.
translation: And, as the blade cuts me in two, offer your prayers as a sweet offering to God and lift my soul to heaven. Let's go, in God's name.

original: I do beseech your grace, for charity, If ever any malice in your heart Were hid against me, now to forgive me frankly.
translation: Please, your grace, as a kindness, forgive me if there was ever any resentment against me in your heart.

original: Sir Thomas Lovell, I as free forgive you   As I would be forgiven: I forgive all;   There cannot be those numberless offences   'Gainst me, that I cannot take peace with:
translation: Sir Thomas Lovell, I forgive you as freely as I wish to be forgiven. I forgive everything. There can't be so many crimes against me that I can't forgive them all.

original: no black envy   Shall mark my grave. Commend me to his grace;   And if he speak of Buckingham, pray, tell him   You met him half in heaven: my vows and prayers   Yet are the king's;
translation: No evil resentment will be left in me when I die. Give my best to the king. If he talks about Buckingham, please, tell him you saw him already half in heaven. My prayers are still with the king

original: and, till my soul forsake,   Shall cry for blessings on him: may he live   Longer than I have time to tell his years!
translation: and until I die I will bless him: may he live longer than I have time to count his age!

original: Ever beloved and loving may his rule be!   And when old time shall lead him to his end,   Goodness and he fill up one monument!
translation: May he be always beloved and loving! And when it's time for him to die, may he lie in the same grave as  goodness !

original: To the water side I must conduct your grace; Then give my charge up to Sir Nicholas Vaux, Who undertakes you to your end.
translation: I must lead you to the riverbank, your grace, then hand you over to Sir Nicholas Vaux, who will lead you to your death.

original: Prepare there,   The duke is coming:
translation: Prepare yourselves, the duke is coming.

original: see the barge be ready;   And fit it with such furniture as suits   The greatness of his person.
translation: Make sure the barge is ready and fill it with furniture good enough for someone that important.

original: Nay, Sir Nicholas,   Let it alone; my state now will but mock me.   When I came hither, I was lord high constable   And Duke of Buckingham; now, poor Edward Bohun:
translation: No, Sir Nicholas, leave it alone. Standing on ceremony will only mock me now. When I came here I was lord high constable and the Duke of Buckingam. Now, I'm just Edward Bohun.

original: Yet I am richer than my base accusers,   That never knew what truth meant: I now seal it;   And with that blood will make 'em one day groan for't.
translation: But I am better than my low accusers who never knew what truth was. I am now showing them. And my blood will punish them for this someday.

original: My noble father, Henry of Buckingham,   Who first raised head against usurping Richard,   Flying for succor to his servant Banister,   Being distress'd, was by that wretch betray'd,   And without trial fell; God's peace be with him!
translation: My noble father , Henry of Buckingham, who first revolted against the usurper Richard, ran for help to his servant Bannister when he was in trouble and was betrayed by that wretch and died without a trial. May he rest in peace!

original: Henry the Seventh succeeding, truly pitying   My father's loss, like a most royal prince,   Restored me to my honours, and, out of ruins,   Made my name once more noble.
translation: Henry VII succeeded to the throne and pitied the death of my father. Like a good king should, he gave me back the titles I had lost and made my name noble again.

original: Now his son,   Henry the Eighth, life, honour, name and all   That made me happy at one stroke has taken   For ever from the world. I had my trial,   And, must needs say, a noble one; which makes me,   A little happier than my wretched father:
translation: Now his son, Henry VIII, takes my life, honor, name, and everything that made me happy from this world with one stroke. I had my trial and I have to say it was a noble one. That makes me a little luckier than my poor father.

original: Yet thus far we are one in fortunes: both   Fell by our servants, by those men we loved most;   A most unnatural and faithless service!
translation: But we are the same in our fortune in this way: we were both brought down by our servants, by the men we loved most. Those were unnatural and unfaithful servants!

original: Heaven has an end in all: yet, you that hear me,   This from a dying man receive as certain:   Where you are liberal of your loves and counsels   Be sure you be not loose;
translation: God is responsible for everything. But you who listen to me, know this for sure since you hear it from a dying man. Be sure that you are not too generous with your love and your secrets.

original: for those you make friends   And give your hearts to, when they once perceive   The least rub in your fortunes, fall away   Like water from ye, never found again   But where they mean to sink ye.
translation: Because those you make your friends and give your hearts to will fall away from you like drops of water when they see the smallest misfortune ahead of you. And they will disappear forever, except when they come back to drown you.

original: All good people,   Pray for me! I must now forsake ye: the last hour   Of my long weary life is come upon me.
translation: All good people should pray for me! I must leave you now. The last hour of my long, tired life has arrived.

original: Farewell:   And when you would say something that is sad,   Speak how I fell. I have done; and God forgive me!
translation: Goodbye. And when you want to hear something sad, talk about how I died. I am done. May God forgive me!

original: O, this is full of pity! Sir, it calls, I fear, too many curses on their heads That were the authors.
translation: Oh, this is sad! I'm afraid this will damn the people who did it.

original: If the duke be guiltless,   'Tis full of woe:
translation: If the duke is innocent, this is really sad.

original: yet I can give you inkling   Of an ensuing evil, if it fall,   Greater than this.
translation: But I can give you a hint of a future evil that will be worse than this if it happens.

original: Good angels keep it from us! What may it be? You do not doubt my faith, sir?
translation: May good angels protect us from it! What can it be? You trust me to keep it secret, don't you sir?

original: This secret is so weighty, 'twill require A strong faith to conceal it.
translation: This secret is so important that it will require great strength of character to keep it secret.

original: Let me have it; I do not talk much.
translation: Let me hear it. I don't talk much.

original: I am confident,   You shall, sir:
translation: I trust you. You will hear it, sir.

original: did you not of late days hear   A buzzing of a separation   Between the king and Katharine?
translation: Did you not recently hear talk about a separation between the king and Katharine?

original: Yes, but it held not:   For when the king once heard it, out of anger   He sent command to the lord mayor straight   To stop the rumor,
translation: Yes, but it wasn't true. Because when the king heard about it, he was angry and sent an order immediately to the mayor to stop the rumor

original: and allay those tongues   That durst disperse it.
translation: and arrest the people who dared to spread it.

original: But that slander, sir,   Is found a truth now: for it grows again   Fresher than e'er it was; and held for certain   The king will venture at it.
translation: But it turns out that this lie is true now. Because the rumor has reappeared stronger than it ever was, and it's believed that the king will definitely try to get a separation.

original: Either the cardinal,   Or some about him near, have, out of malice   To the good queen, possess'd him with a scruple   That will undo her:
translation: Either the cardinal or some of his people have, out of malice against the good queen, ruined her by sowing some doubt in the king.

original: to confirm this too,   Cardinal Campeius is arrived, and lately;   As all think, for this business.
translation: What confirms the truth of this is that Cardinal Campeius has recently arrived, and everyone thinks it's about this business.

original: 'Tis the cardinal;   And merely to revenge him on the emperor   For not bestowing on him,
translation: It's the cardinal. And he's doing this just to get revenge against the emperor for not making him

original: at his asking,   The archbishopric of Toledo, this is purposed.
translation: archbishop of Toledo as he asked.

original: I think you have hit the mark: but is't not cruel That she should feel the smart of this? The cardinal Will have his will, and she must fall.
translation: I think you're right. But isn't it cruel to make her suffer for that? The cardinal will get what he wants and she will lose power.

original: 'Tis woful. We are too open here to argue this; Let's think in private more.
translation: It is sad. We shouldn't talk about this so openly. Let's consider this more in private.

original: 'My lord, the horses your lordship sent for, with   all the care I had, I saw well chosen, ridden, and   furnished.
translation: "My lord, I made sure the horses you sent for were well chosen, trained, and cared for.

original: They were young and handsome, and of the   best breed in the north. When they were ready to   set out for London, a man of my lord cardinal's, by   commission and main power, took 'em from me; with   this reason:
translation: They were young and good-looking, and of the best breed of the north. When they were ready to send to London, a servant of the cardinal's took them from me by force and with a warrant he had. He said this was the reason:

original: His master would be served before a   subject, if not before the king; which stopped our   mouths, sir.'
translation: his master had to be served before a subject, if not before the king. We couldn't say anything to that, sir."

original: I fear he will indeed: well, let him have them:   He will have all, I think.
translation: I am afraid he will be served before the king. Well, let him have them. I think he will have everything.

original: Well met, my lord chamberlain.
translation: Hello, my lord chamberlain.

original: Good day to both your graces.
translation: Good day to both of you.

original: How is the king employ'd?
translation: What is the king doing?

original: I left him private, Full of sad thoughts and troubles.
translation: I left him alone, thinking sad thoughts and feeling troubled.

original: What's the cause?
translation: Why?

original: It seems the marriage with his brother's wife Has crept too near his conscience.
translation: It seems that he's feeling guilty about his marriage to his brother's wife.

original: No, his conscience Has crept too near another lady.
translation: No, I think he's thinking about another lady.

original: 'Tis so:   This is the cardinal's doing, the king-cardinal:
translation: It's true. This is the cardinal's doing, the king-cardinal more like.

original: That blind priest, like the eldest son of fortune,   Turns what he list. The king will know him one day.
translation: That blind priest does what he wants as if he's fortune's oldest son and heir. The king will find out what he's really like someday.

original: Pray God he do! he'll never know himself else.
translation: I pray to God he does! Or he'll never understand himself.

original: How holily he works in all his business!   And with what zeal! for, now he has crack'd the league   Between us and the emperor, the queen's great nephew,
translation: He acts so religiously in everything he does! And so eagerly! Because now he has broken the alliance between us and  the emperor , the queen's powerful nephew,

original: He dives into the king's soul, and there scatters   Dangers, doubts, wringing of the conscience,   Fears, and despairs; and all these for his marriage:
translation: he messes with the king's mind and scatters dangerous thoughts, doubts, fears, and despair, and troubles his conscience. All this is about his marriage.

original: And out of all these to restore the king,   He counsels a divorce; a loss of her   That, like a jewel, has hung twenty years   About his neck, yet never lost her lustre;
translation: And to cure the king of all this he suggests a divorce. That would mean the loss of the woman who hung around his neck like a jewel for twenty years and never lost her brightness.

original: Of her that loves him with that excellence   That angels love good men with; even of her   That, when the greatest stroke of fortune falls,   Will bless the king: and is not this course pious?
translation: The loss of the woman who loves him as much as angels love good men. The woman who would still bless the king even if the worst disaster happened. Isn't this a religious thing to do?

original: Heaven keep me from such counsel! 'Tis most true   These news are every where; every tongue speaks 'em,   And every true heart weeps for't:
translation: May heaven protect me from advice like that! It's true that this news is everywhere. Everyone is saying this and every good heart weeps for it.

original: all that dare   Look into these affairs see this main end,   The French king's sister.
translation: Everyone who dares look into this affair see that he wants the king to marry the French king's sister.

original: Heaven will one day open   The king's eyes, that so long have slept upon   This bold bad man.
translation: One day God will open the king's eyes. He hasn't seen this bold, bad man as he really is for so long.

original: And free us from his slavery.
translation: And God will free us from slavery to him.

original: We had need pray,   And heartily, for our deliverance;   Or this imperious man will work us all   From princes into pages:
translation: We need to pray (and to pray strongly) for help, or this proud man will turn us from princes into servants.

original: all men's honours   Lie like one lump before him, to be fashion'd   Into what pitch he please.
translation: He does whatever he wants with men's honors.

original: For me, my lords,   I love him not, nor fear him; there's my creed:   As I am made without him, so I'll stand,   If the king please;
translation: As for me, my lord, I neither love him nor fear him. That's what I say. I'll do the best I can without his help, if the king wishes it.

original: his curses and his blessings   Touch me alike, they're breath I not believe in.   I knew him, and I know him;
