original: Which reformation must be sudden too,   My noble lords; for those that tame wild horses   Pace 'em not in their hands to make 'em gentle,   But stop their mouths with stubborn bits, and spur 'em,   Till they obey the manage.
translation: They have to be stopped at once, my noble lords. People who tame wild horses don't lead them in their hands to tame them but they put hard  bits  in their mouths and spur them until they obey commands.

original: If we suffer,   Out of our easiness and childish pity   To one man's honour, this contagious sickness,   Farewell all physic: and what follows then?
translation: If we allow this contagious sickness to go on without stopping it because we're too forgiving and childishly pity one man, medicine won't be able to help us. What then?

original: Commotions, uproars, with a general taint   Of the whole state: as, of late days, our neighbours,   The upper Germany, can dearly witness,   Yet freshly pitied in our memories.
translation: Riots, uproar, complete destruction of the whole country.  Lately our neighbor, northern Germany, has shown us what happens when heresy takes over , and we're still pitying their recent disaster.

original: My good lords, hitherto, in all the progress   Both of my life and office, I have labour'd,   And with no little study, that my teaching   And the strong course of my authority   Might go one way, and safely;
translation: My good lords, so far, in both my daily life and my job, I have worked and studied hard to make my teaching and my power lead safely to one thing.

original: and the end   Was ever, to do well: nor is there living,   I speak it with a single heart, my lords,   A man that more detests, more stirs against,   Both in his private conscience and his place,   Defacers of a public peace, than I do.
translation: This goal was always to do the right thing. There is no one alive, and I say this honestly my lords, who hates or works harder to stop people who cause public disruptions, either in his private thoughts or his public office, than I do.

original: Pray heaven, the king may never find a heart   With less allegiance in it! Men that make   Envy and crooked malice nourishment   Dare bite the best.
translation: I pray to God the king will always be surrounded by people as loyal as I am to him! Men whose lives are full of envy and evil resentment dare to attack even the best people.

original: I do beseech your lordships,   That, in this case of justice, my accusers,   Be what they will, may stand forth face to face,   And freely urge against me.
translation: I beg you, my lords, to bring my accusers (whoever they are) face to face with me to accuse me in this trial.

original: Nay, my lord, That cannot be: you are a counsellor, And, by that virtue, no man dare accuse you.
translation: No, my lord, that can't happen. You're a councilor and because of that no one dares to accuse you.

original: My lord, because we have business of more moment,   We will be short with you. 'Tis his highness' pleasure,   And our consent, for better trial of you,   From hence you be committed to the Tower;
translation: My lord, we'll hurry this along because we have more important business. The king wishes and we agree that you should be imprisoned in the Tower.

original: Where, being but a private man again,   You shall know many dare accuse you boldly,   More than, I fear, you are provided for.
translation: Then you'll be just a private citizen again and you'll find out who dares to accuse you. It'll be more people, I'm afraid, than you're ready to face.

original: Ah, my good Lord of Winchester, I thank you;   You are always my good friend; if your will pass,   I shall both find your lordship judge and juror,   You are so merciful:
translation: Ah, thank you, my good lord of Winchester. You have always been my good friend. If you do what you want, you're so merciful that you will act as both judge and jury to me.

original: I see your end;   'Tis my undoing: love and meekness, lord,   Become a churchman better than ambition:   Win straying souls with modesty again,   Cast none away.
translation: I see your goal: it's to destroy me. Love and humility are more fitting for a churchman than ambition, lord. Win back sinners by being modest: don't banish them.

original: That I shall clear myself,   Lay all the weight ye can upon my patience,   I make as little doubt, as you do conscience   In doing daily wrongs.
translation: I have less doubt that I will clear my name, whatever you make me suffer in the meantime, than you have any doubts about whether you should be doing evil things every day.

original: I could say more,   But reverence to your calling makes me modest.
translation: I could say more, but respect for your job makes me modest.

original: My lord, my lord, you are a sectary, That's the plain truth: your painted gloss discovers, To men that understand you, words and weakness.
My Lord of Winchester, you are a little,   By your good favour, too sharp;
translation: My Lord of Winchester, excuse me but you're a little too rude.

original: men so noble,   However faulty, yet should find respect   For what they have been: 'tis a cruelty   To load a falling man.
translation: Noble men, whatever their faults, should be respected for what they once were. It's cruel to kick a man when he's down.

original: Good master secretary, I cry your honour mercy; you may, worst Of all this table, say so.
translation: Secretary, I'm sorry. You have the least right of anyone here to say that.

original: Why, my lord?
translation: Why, my lord?

original: Do not I know you for a favourer Of this new sect? ye are not sound.
translation: Don't I know you're a follower of this new religion? You are not trustworthy.

original: Not sound?
translation: Not trustworthy?

original: Not sound, I say.
translation: Not trustworthy, that's what I said.

original: Would you were half so honest! Men's prayers then would seek you, not their fears.
translation: I wish you were half as honest as I am trustworthy! Then men would pray for you, not fear you.

original: I shall remember this bold language.
translation: I'll remember this arrogant language.

original: Do. Remember your bold life too.
translation: Do. Remember your arrogant life too.

original: This is too much; Forbear, for shame, my lords.
translation: This is too much. Stop this—you should be ashamed of yourselves, my lords.

original: I have done.
translation: I'm done.

original: And I.
translation: So am I.

original: Then thus for you, my lord: it stands agreed,   I take it, by all voices, that forthwith   You be convey'd to the Tower a prisoner;
translation: So as for you, my lord, I take it we've all agreed that you'll be taken immediately to the Tower as a prisoner.

original: There to remain till the king's further pleasure   Be known unto us: are you all agreed, lords?
translation: You'll stay there as a prisoner until we know what the king wants. Have you all agreed, lords?

original: We are.
translation: We have.

original: Is there no other way of mercy, But I must needs to the Tower, my lords?
translation: Is there no other way? Do I have to go to the Tower, my lords?

original: What other Would you expect? you are strangely troublesome. Let some o' the guard be ready there.
translation: What other way do you expect? You're unusually annoying. Let's have some guards in here.

original: For me? Must I go like a traitor thither?
translation: For me? Must I be led there like a traitor?

original: Receive him, And see him safe i' the Tower.
translation: Take him and put him safely in the Tower.

original: Stay, good my lords,   I have a little yet to say. Look there, my lords;
translation: Wait, my good lords, I still have a few things to say. Look here, my lords.

original: By virtue of that ring, I take my cause   Out of the gripes of cruel men, and give it   To a most noble judge, the king my master.
translation: By the power of this ring, I take my cause out of the hands of cruel men and give it to a noble judge, the king my master.

original: This is the king's ring.
translation: This is the king's ring.

original: 'Tis no counterfeit.
translation: It's not a fake.

original: 'Tis the right ring, by heaven: I told ye all, When ye first put this dangerous stone a-rolling, 'Twould fall upon ourselves.
translation: That's the ring, by heaven. I told you when you started this dangerous business that it would backfire on us.

original: Do you think, my lords, The king will suffer but the little finger Of this man to be vex'd?
translation: My lords, do you think the king will allow even this man's little finger to get hurt?

original: 'Tis now too certain: How much more is his life in value with him? Would I were fairly out on't!
translation: Now it's all too clear. His life is worth so much more to the king than his little finger! I wish I had nothing to do with this!

original: My mind gave me,   In seeking tales and informations   Against this man, whose honesty the devil   And his disciples only envy at,
translation: I was already worried, looking for stories and information against this man who's so honest that the devil and his minions can only envy him, not hurt him.

original: Ye blew the fire that burns ye: now have at ye!
translation: You're the reason I'm in trouble now, damn you!

original: Dread sovereign, how much are we bound to heaven   In daily thanks, that gave us such a prince;   Not only good and wise, but most religious:
translation: Powerful king, we're so grateful every day to God for giving us a king like you! You're not just good and wise, but very religious.

original: One that, in all obedience, makes the church   The chief aim of his honour; and, to strengthen   That holy duty, out of dear respect,
translation: You're someone who obediently works for the good of the church. And, to strengthen that holy tie between the king and the church,

original: His royal self in judgment comes to hear   The cause betwixt her and this great offender.
translation: you come yourself as a judge to hear the case between it and this terrible criminal.

original: You were ever good at sudden commendations,   Bishop of Winchester. But know, I come not   To hear such flattery now, and in my presence;   They are too thin and bare to hide offences.
translation: You were always good at sudden flattery, Bishop of Winchester. But I haven't come to be flattered to my face like that now. That flattery is too thin and bare to hide crimes behind.

original: To me you cannot reach, you play the spaniel,   And think with wagging of your tongue to win me;   But, whatsoe'er thou takest me for, I'm sure   Thou hast a cruel nature and a bloody.
translation: You can't reach me like that. You act like a dog and think wagging your tongue will win me over. But, whatever you take me for, I'm sure you have a cruel and bloody nature.

original: [To CRANMER]   Good man, sit down. Now let me see the proudest   He, that dares most, but wag his finger at thee:
translation: [To CRANMER]  Sit down, you good man. Now let me just see a man arrogant enough even just to wag his finger at you.

original: By all that's holy, he had better starve   Than but once think this place becomes thee not.
translation: By everything that's holy, he would be better off starving to death than even thinking once that you don't deserve to sit here.

original: May it please your grace,—
translation: Please, your grace—

original: No, sir, it does not please me.   I had thought I had had men of some understanding   And wisdom of my council; but I find none.   Was it discretion, lords, to let this man,   This good man,—few of you deserve that title,—
translation: No, sir, it does not please me. I thought I had men of some intelligence and wisdom on my council, but I can't see any. Was it wise, lords, to let this man, this good man—few of you deserve that title—

original: This honest man, wait like a lousy footboy   At chamber—door? and one as great as you are?   Why, what a shame was this! Did my commission   Bid ye so far forget yourselves?
translation: this honest man, wait like a lice-covered servant at the door? A man as important as you are? What a shameful thing to do! Did I give you permission to do something so unworthy of you?

original: I gave ye   Power as he was a counsellor to try him,   Not as a groom:
translation: I gave you power to try his case as a councilor, not a servant.

original: there's some of ye, I see,   More out of malice than integrity,   Would try him to the utmost, had ye mean;   Which ye shall never have while I live.
translation: There are some of you, I see, who would give him the death penalty if you could, more out of resentment than honesty. You will never be able to do that while I am alive.

original: Thus far,   My most dread sovereign, may it like your grace   To let my tongue excuse all.
translation: My extremely powerful king, please let me tell you our excuses.

original: What was purposed   Concerning his imprisonment, was rather,   If there be faith in men, meant for his trial,   And fair purgation to the world, than malice,   I'm sure, in me.
translation: We meant to imprison him more, I swear, because we needed to try him and show that we had done so fairly, than out of resentment—at least on my part, I'm sure.

original: Well, well, my lords, respect him;   Take him, and use him well, he's worthy of it.   I will say thus much for him, if a prince   May be beholding to a subject, I   Am, for his love and service, so to him.
translation: All right, my lords, respect him. Take him and treat him well—he deserves it. I will say this much for him: if a prince can owe anything to a subject, I owe him for his love and service to me.

original: Make me no more ado, but all embrace him:   Be friends, for shame, my lords! My Lord of   Canterbury,   I have a suit which you must not deny me;
translation: Don't make any more fuss, but hug him, all of you. Be friends, my lords, honestly! My Lord of Canterbury, I have a request you can't deny.

original: That is, a fair young maid that yet wants baptism,   You must be godfather, and answer for her.
translation: That is, there's a  beautiful young girl  who still needs to be baptized. You must be her godfather in the ceremony.

original: The greatest monarch now alive may glory In such an honour: how may I deserve it That am a poor and humble subject to you?
translation: The greatest king alive would be proud of this honor. How can I deserve it, when I am just a poor, humble, subject of yours?

original: Come, come, my lord, you'ld spare your spoons: you   shall have two noble partners with you; the old   Duchess of Norfolk, and Lady Marquess Dorset:
translation: Come, come, my lord, you just don't want to pay for a gift. There will be two other nobles as godparents too: the old Duchess of Norfolk and Lady Marquess Dorset.

original: will   these please you?   Once more, my Lord of Winchester, I charge you,   Embrace and love this man.
translation: Do they sound good to you? Once more, my Lord of Winchester, I command you to hug and love this man.

original: With a true heart And brother-love I do it.
translation: I do it with an honest heart and brotherly love.

original: And let heaven Witness, how dear I hold this confirmation.
translation: Let God be my witness that I am very happy about this confirmation of friendship.

original: Good man, those joyful tears show thy true heart:   The common voice, I see, is verified   Of thee, which says thus, 'Do my Lord of Canterbury   A shrewd turn, and he is your friend for ever.'
translation: Good man, your happy tears show your honesty. I see that everyone is right in saying about you, "Do a favor for my Lord of Canterbury and he will be your friend forever."

original: Come, lords, we trifle time away; I long   To have this young one made a Christian.   As I have made ye one, lords, one remain;   So I grow stronger, you more honour gain.
translation: Come on, lords, we're wasting time. I can't wait for this young one to be made a Christian. Now that I've united all of you, lords, stay that way. That'll make me stronger and you more honorable.

original: You'll leave your noise anon, ye rascals: do you take the court for Paris-garden? ye rude slaves, leave your gaping.
translation: Stop this noise now, you jerks. Do you think the court is a public amusement park? You rude slaves, shut your mouths.

original: Good master porter, I belong to the larder.
translation: Mister porter, I work in the kitchen.

original: Belong to the gallows, and be hanged, ye rogue! is   this a place to roar in? Fetch me a dozen crab-tree   staves, and strong ones:
translation: Work in a noose and be hanged, you rogue! Is this somewhere to roar? Get me a dozen wooden poles, and strong ones.

original: these are but switches to   'em. I'll scratch your heads: you must be seeing   christenings? do you look for ale and cakes here,   you rude rascals?
translation: These ones are just twigs compared to those. I'll scratch your heads. You insist on seeing baptisms? Do you expect beer and cake here, you rude jerks?

original: Pray, sir, be patient: 'tis as much impossible—   Unless we sweep 'em from the door with cannons—
translation: Please sir, calm down. It's impossible—unless we blast them away from the door with cannons—

original: To scatter 'em, as 'tis to make 'em sleep   On May-day morning; which will never be:   We may as well push against Powle's, as stir em.
translation: to make them go away, as impossible as making them sleep on  May-day morning . That will never happen. We might as well be pushing against St. Paul's cathedral, they'll be just as hard to move.

original: How got they in, and be hang'd?
translation: How did they get in, damn you?

original: Alas, I know not; how gets the tide in?
translation: I don't know. How does the tide get in?

original: You did nothing, sir.
translation: You did nothing, sir.

original: I am not Samson, nor Sir Guy, nor Colbrand,   To mow 'em down before me:
translation: I'm not a hero like  Samson or Sir Guy or Colbrand . I couldn't mow them down in front of me.

original: but if I spared any   That had a head to hit, either young or old,   He or she, cuckold or cuckold-maker,
translation: I didn't refrain from hitting anyone's head, young or old, man or woman, anyone with an unfaithful wife or anyone cheating with someone else's wife.

original: Let me ne'er hope to see a chine again   And that I would not for a cow, God save her!
translation: If I did, let me never see meat again, and I wouldn't make that bargain in exchange for a cow, God bless it!

original: I shall be with you presently, good master puppy. Keep the door close, sirrah.
translation: I'll be with you soon, mister dog. Keep the door closed, you.

original: What would you have me do?
translation: What do you want me to do?

original: What should you do, but knock 'em down by the   dozens? Is this Moorfields to muster in? or have   we some strange Indian with the great tool come to   court, the women so besiege us?
translation: What would you do except knock them down by the dozens? Is this a public field to meet in? Or do we have some strange Indian with a huge tool visiting court to make the women attack us like this?

original: Bless me, what a   fry of fornication is at door! On my Christian   conscience, this one christening will beget a   thousand; here will be father, godfather, and all  together.
translation: Bless me, what a fornicating mob is at the door! On my Christian conscience, this one baptism will cause a thousand more. Here are the future fathers and godfathers all gathered together.

original: The spoons will be the bigger, sir. There is a   fellow somewhat near the door, he should be a   brazier by his face, for, o' my conscience, twenty   of the dog-days now reign in's nose; all that stand   about him are under the line,
translation: The presents will be all the bigger, sir. There's a fellow kind of near the door. I think he's a  smith  from his face, because his face looks as hot as the dog days of summer. Everyone standing around him is in the southern hemisphere.

original: they need no other   penance: that fire-drake did I hit three times on   the head, and three times was his nose discharged   against me; he stands there, like a mortar-piece, to   blow us.
translation: They don't need to burn in hell because they're already in it. I hit that dragon three times on the head and three times his nose was discharged at me. He stands there like a bomb ready to blow us up.

original: There was a haberdasher's wife of small   wit near him, that railed upon me till her pinked   porringer fell off her head, for kindling such a   combustion in the state.
translation: There was a dumb clothes-seller's wife near him who shouted at me until her hat, which looked like a decorated bowl, fell off her head, for starting such a fire in the country.

original: I missed the meteor once,   and hit that woman; who cried out 'Clubs!' when I   might see from far some forty truncheoners draw to   her succor, which were the hope o' the Strand, where   she was quartered.
translation: I missed the meteor-like man once and hit that woman. She cried out "clubs!" and I could see about forty people with clubs run to help her. They were the best hope in  the Strand , where she was.

original: They fell on; I made good my   place: at length they came to the broom-staff to   me; I defied 'em still: when suddenly a file of   boys behind 'em, loose shot, delivered such a shower   of pebbles,
translation: They attacked. I defended myself. Finally they were hitting me and I kept defying them. Suddenly, a group of boys behind them threw such a number of pebbles

original: that I was fain to draw mine honour in,   and let 'em win the work: the devil was amongst   'em, I think, surely.
translation: that I had to let them win the battle. The devil was fighting with them, for sure.

original: These are the youths that thunder at a playhouse,   and fight for bitten apples; that no audience, but   the tribulation of Tower-hill, or the limbs of   Limehouse, their dear brothers, are able to endure.
translation: Those are the boys who make such noise at a play and fight for bitten apples. No audience except the worst ones at  Tower-hill or the similar ones at Limehouse  can stand them.

original: I have some of 'em in Limbo Patrum, and there they   are like to dance these three days; besides the   running banquet of two beadles that is to come.
translation: I have some of them locked up and they'll stay there for three days. And the noise will be worse when the officials meant to keep the peace arrive.

original: Mercy o' me, what a multitude are here!   They grow still too; from all parts they are coming,   As if we kept a fair here! Where are these porters,   These lazy knaves? Ye have made a fine hand, fellows:
translation: Lord, what a crowd is here! It's still growing, too. They're coming from everywhere as if this were a fair! Where are those porters, those lazy good-for-nothings? You've done well, fellows.

original: There's a trim rabble let in: are all these   Your faithful friends o' the suburbs? We shall have   Great store of room, no doubt, left for the ladies,   When they pass back from the christening.
translation: You've let in a nice crowd. Are these all your good friends from town? No doubt we'll have plenty of room left for the ladies when they come back from the baptism.

original: An't please   your honour,   We are but men;
translation: Your honor, we're only human.

original: and what so many may do,   Not being torn a-pieces, we have done:   An army cannot rule 'em.
translation: And we've done what two men can do without being torn to pieces. An army couldn't stop them.

original: As I live,   If the king blame me for't, I'll lay ye all   By the heels, and suddenly; and on your heads   Clap round fines for neglect: ye are lazy knaves;
translation: I swear if the king blames me for it, I'll knock you over immediately. And I'll fine you for neglecting your jobs. You're lazy good-for-nothings.

original: And here ye lie baiting of bombards, when   Ye should do service. Hark! the trumpets sound;   They're come already from the christening:
translation: You lie here drinking when you should be working. Listen! The trumpets are sounding. They've already come from the baptism.

original: Go, break among the press, and find a way out   To let the troop pass fairly; or I'll find   A Marshalsea shall hold ye play these two months.
translation: Go on, make a break in the crowd to let them pass. Or I'll find a jail to hold you for two months.

original: Make way there for the princess.
translation: Make room for the princess.

original: You great fellow, Stand close up, or I'll make your head ache.
translation: You big fellow, make room or I'll make your head ache.

original: You i' the camlet, get up o' the rail; I'll peck you o'er the pales else.
translation: You in the camel-hair cloth, get on the fence or I'll throw you over it.

original: Heaven, from thy endless goodness, send prosperous life, long, and ever happy, to the high and mighty princess of England, Elizabeth!
translation: From your endless supply of goodness, God, send a lucky, long, and happy life to the powerful princess of England, Elizabeth!

original: [Kneeling]   And to your royal grace, and the good queen,   My noble partners, and myself, thus pray:
translation: [Kneeling]  Your grace, you, the good queen, my noble fellow-godparents, and I pray in this way:

original: All comfort, joy, in this most gracious lady,   Heaven ever laid up to make parents happy,   May hourly fall upon ye!
translation: may heaven give you all the comfort and joy in this princess that ever made parents happy every hour!

original: Thank you, good lord archbishop: What is her name?
translation: Thank you, lord archbishop. What is her name?

original: Elizabeth.
translation: Elizabeth.

original: Stand up, lord.
translation: Stand up, lord.

original: With this kiss take my blessing: God protect thee! Into whose hand I give thy life.
translation: Take my blessing with this kiss. May God protect you! I trust him to keep you safe.

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: My noble gossips, ye have been too prodigal: I thank ye heartily; so shall this lady, When she has so much English.
translation: My noble friends, you have been too generous. Thank you very much. This girl will thank you too when she learns enough English.

original: Let me speak, sir,   For heaven now bids me; and the words I utter   Let none think flattery, for they'll find 'em truth.   This royal infant—heaven still move about her!—
translation: Let me speak, sir, because now God tells me to. I hope no one thinks that the words I say are flattery, because they'll find them to be true. This royal child—may God be with her always!—

original: Though in her cradle, yet now promises   Upon this land a thousand thousand blessings,   Which time shall bring to ripeness: she shall be—   But few now living can behold that goodness—
translation: although still a baby, promises to bring a thousand, thousand blessings to this country in time. She will be—few alive now will live to see this goodness—

original: A pattern to all princes living with her,   And all that shall succeed: Saba was never   More covetous of wisdom and fair virtue   Than this pure soul shall be:
translation: an example for all the kings alive then, and all to come. This pure soul will have as much wisdom and virtue as the queen of Sheba wished for.

original: all princely graces,   That mould up such a mighty piece as this is,   With all the virtues that attend the good,   Shall still be doubled on her:
translation: She'll have double all the royal qualities that go into making someone as powerful as this along with all the virtues that good people have.

original: truth shall nurse her,   Holy and heavenly thoughts still counsel her:   She shall be loved and fear'd: her own shall bless her;   Her foes shake like a field of beaten corn,   And hang their heads with sorrow: good grows with her:
translation: Truth will raise her, holy and religious thoughts will advise her always, she will be loved and feared, her family and friends will bless her, her enemies will shake in fear like a field of beaten corn and hang their heads in sorrow. Goodness will grow as she grows.

original: In her days every man shall eat in safety,   Under his own vine, what he plants; and sing   The merry songs of peace to all his neighbours:   God shall be truly known;
translation: In her life everyone will eat what he plants safely in his own field and sing the happy songs of peace to all his neighbors. God will be truly understood

original: and those about her   From her shall read the perfect ways of honour,   And by those claim their greatness, not by blood.   Nor shall this peace sleep with her:
translation: a nd those around her will learn how to be honorable from her and will be great because of that, not because they come from good families. Nor will this peace die with her.

original: but as when   The bird of wonder dies, the maiden phoenix,   Her ashes new create another heir,   As great in admiration as herself;
translation: But like when that amazing bird, the virgin  phoenix , dies,  a new heir  as amazing as she was will be born from her ashes.

original: So shall she leave her blessedness to one,   When heaven shall call her from this cloud of darkness,   Who from the sacred ashes of her honour   Shall star-like rise, as great in fame as she was,   And so stand fix'd:
translation: So someone will inherit her blessings who will rise like a star from the holy ashes of her honor and stay firmly in the sky when heaven calls her from this dark cloud, the earth.

original: peace, plenty, love, truth, terror,   That were the servants to this chosen infant,   Shall then be his, and like a vine grow to him:
translation: Peace, plenty, love, truth, terror, which served this chosen baby, will belong to him and grow on him like a vine.

original: Wherever the bright sun of heaven shall shine,   His honour and the greatness of his name   Shall be, and make new nations:
translation: Wherever the bright sun shines, his honor and the greatness of his name will be found and will create new countries.

original: he shall flourish,   And, like a mountain cedar, reach his branches   To all the plains about him: our children's children   Shall see this, and bless heaven.
translation: He will grow and, like  a tree on a mountain, reach his branches over all the plains around him. Our children's children will see this and bless God.

original: Thou speakest wonders.
translation: You say amazing things.

original: She shall be, to the happiness of England,   An aged princess; many days shall see her,   And yet no day without a deed to crown it.
translation: She will live to be an old queen and make England happy. She will live many days and do a great deed on every one.

original: Would I had known no more! but she must die,   She must, the saints must have her; yet a virgin,   A most unspotted lily shall she pass   To the ground, and all the world shall mourn her.
translation: I wish I knew nothing more! But she must die, she must, the saints must have her. Still a virgin, a pure flower, she will fall to the ground and the whole world will miss her.

original: O lord archbishop,   Thou hast made me now a man! never, before   This happy child, did I get any thing:
translation: Oh, lord archbishop, now you've made me a man! It's like I never made anything before I conceived this happy child.

original: This oracle of comfort has so pleased me,   That when I am in heaven I shall desire   To see what this child does, and praise my Maker.   I thank ye all.
translation: This comforting prophecy has pleased me so much that when I am in heaven I will want to see what this child does, and praise God. I thank you all.

original: To you, my good lord mayor,   And your good brethren, I am much beholding;   I have received much honour by your presence,   And ye shall find me thankful. Lead the way, lords:
translation: I am very thankful to you, my good lord mayor, and your good companions. You have done me a lot of honor in being here and I will repay you. Lead the way, lords.

original: Ye must all see the queen, and she must thank ye,   She will be sick else. This day, no man think   Has business at his house; for all shall stay:   This little one shall make it holiday.
translation: You must all see the queen and she must thank you or she will be sick. Today, no one should think he has to go home. Everyone will stay. It's a holiday because of this little one.

original: Good morrow, and well met. How have ye done Since last we saw in France?
translation: Good morning, and good to see you. How have you been since we last met in France?

original: I thank your grace, Healthful; and ever since a fresh admirer Of what I saw there.
translation: Thank you, sir, I've been well. And ever since I've been thinking admiringly about what I saw there.

original: An untimely ague   Stay'd me a prisoner in my chamber
translation: An unfortunate sickness kept me prisoner in my room

original: when   Those suns of glory, those two lights of men,   Met in the vale of Andren.
translation: when  those two men  as glorious and bright as suns met in the valley of Andren.

original: 'Twixt Guynes and Arde:   I was then present, saw them salute on horseback;
translation: Between Guynes and Arde. I was there and saw them greet each other on horseback. I saw them when they got off the horses.

original: Beheld them, when they lighted, how they clung   In their embracement, as they grew together;
translation: They held on to each other so hard when they hugged that it looked like they were two plants growing together.

original: Which had they, what four throned ones could have  weigh'd   Such a compounded one?
translation: If they had, those two together would have been worth more than four kings.

original: All the whole time I was my chamber's prisoner.
translation: The whole time I was stuck in my room like a prisoner.

original: Then you lost   The view of earthly glory: men might say,   Till this time pomp was single, but now married   To one above itself.
translation: Then you lost your chance to see glory on earth. It's as if all glory has been single in the past, but now it's married to glory greater than itself.

original: Each following day   Became the next day's master, till the last   Made former wonders its. To-day the French,   All clinquant, all in gold, like heathen gods,   Shone down the English;
translation: Every day was better than the one before until the last one was full of all the wonders seen before. One day the French, all clanking, all dressed in gold like heathen gods, shone brighter than the English.

original: and, to-morrow, they   Made Britain India: every man that stood   Show'd like a mine. Their dwarfish pages were   As cherubins, all guilt:
translation: The next day, the British were dressed so richly that they made Britain seem like India. Every man standing up looked like a mine because they were covered in gold. Their short pages looked like gold-covered cherubs.

original: the madams too,   Not used to toil, did almost sweat to bear   The pride upon them, that their very labour   Was to them as a painting:
translation: The ladies, too, not used to work, almost sweated to carry the beautiful things they wore, and their effort was like makeup: it made them look better.

original: now this masque   Was cried incomparable; and the ensuing night   Made it a fool and beggar.
translation: One day this display was said to be incomparable, but the next night it was made to look like the display of a fool and a beggar.

original: The two kings,   Equal in lustre, were now best, now worst,   As presence did present them; him in eye,   Still him in praise: and, being present both   'Twas said they saw but one; and no discerner   Durst wag his tongue in censure.
translation: Of the two kings, equal in brightness, one seemed better, then worse, at any moment. One looked better at one time, but the other one was praised more. When they were both present, people said they only saw one. No onlooker dared criticize anything.

original: When these suns—   For so they phrase 'em—by their heralds challenged   The noble spirits to arms, they did perform   Beyond thought's compass;
translation: When these suns, as they were called, had their announcers challenge the noblemen to fight, those nobles did better than you can imagine.

original: that former fabulous story,   Being now seen possible enough, got credit,   That Bevis was believed.
translation: The old legend of  Bevis  now seemed possible and was believed.

original: O, you go far.
translation: Oh, you're praising them highly.

original: As I belong to worship and affect   In honour honesty, the tract of every thing   Would by a good discourser lose some life,   Which action's self was tongue to.
translation: I swear by my reputation and love for honesty, the description of everything that was done there couldn't do justice to it even if it were described by a good talker.

original: All was royal;   To the disposing of it nought rebell'd.   Order gave each thing view; the office did   Distinctly his full function.
translation: Things went  perfectly.  Everything was done in good order, and the people in charge did their job well.

original: Who did guide, I mean, who set the body and the limbs Of this great sport together, as you guess?
One, certes, that promises no element In such a business.
translation: Someone you wouldn't expect to have any part in such business.

original: I pray you, who, my lord?
translation: Tell me, who, my lord?

original: All this was order'd by the good discretion Of the right reverend Cardinal of York.
translation: This was organized wisely by the honorable Cardinal of York.

original: The devil speed him! no man's pie is freed   From his ambitious finger. What had he   To do in these fierce vanities?
translation: May the devil take good care of him! He's got his ambitious finger in everyone's pie. What did he have to do with this foolish fighting?

original: I wonder   That such a keech can with his very bulk   Take up the rays o' the beneficial sun   And keep it from the earth.
translation: I'm surprised that such a lump of fat can block the rays of the kind sun with his bulk and keep them from the earth.

original: Surely, sir,   There's in him stuff that puts him to these ends;   For, being not propp'd by ancestry, whose grace   Chalks successors their way, nor call'd upon   For high feats done to the crown;
translation: Surely, sir, there's something in him that makes him want these things. He doesn't have the help of being from a good family, which guarantees succession to power, and he isn't being rewarded for brave deeds done for the king.

original: neither allied   For eminent assistants; but, spider-like,   Out of his self-drawing web, he gives us note,
translation: Nor does he have powerful allies. But, like a spider, spinning his own web for himself, he makes us notice him.

original: The force of his own merit makes his way   A gift that heaven gives for him, which buys   A place next to the king.
translation: He clears a path for himself with his own worth. It's a gift to him from God, which buys him a place next to the king.

original: I cannot tell   What heaven hath given him,—let some graver eye   Pierce into that; but I can see his pride   Peep through each part of him: whence has he that,   If not from hell?
translation: I can't tell what God has given him. Let some wiser man look into that. But I can see his pride showing in every part of him. Where did he get that, if not from hell?

original: the devil is a niggard,   Or has given all before, and he begins   A new hell in himself.
translation: The devil doesn't like to give anything away, or he's already given away everything, so the Cardinal begins a new hell inside himself.

original: Why the devil,   Upon this French going out, took he upon him,   Without the privity o' the king, to appoint   Who should attend on him?
translation: Why the devil, when this French expedition took place, did he take it upon himself to decide who would go with the king without asking him?

original: He makes up the file   Of all the gentry; for the most part such   To whom as great a charge as little honour   He meant to lay upon:
translation: He made up the list of all the nobles. Mostly it was those he meant to get a lot of money out of without giving them credit for it.

original: and his own letter,   The honourable board of council out,   Must fetch him in the papers.
translation: He sends for the money by writing a letter, without consulting the king's honorable councilors.

original: I do know   Kinsmen of mine, three at the least,
translation: I know relatives of mine, at least three,

original: that have   By this so sickened their estates,   that never   They shall abound as formerly.
translation: who because of this are in so much financial trouble that they'll never get their finances back to where they were before.

original: O, many   Have broke their backs with laying manors on 'em   For this great journey.
translation: Oh, many people have broken their backs paying for mansions for the court to stay in on this great journey.

original: What did this vanity   But minister communication of   A most poor issue?
translation: What did this foolish man do, except help this bad thing happen?

original: Grievingly I think, The peace between the French and us not values The cost that did conclude it.
translation: Sadly, I think the peace between the French and us isn't worth the money that was paid to make it.

original: Every man,   After the hideous storm that follow'd, was   A thing inspired; and, not consulting, broke   Into a general prophecy;
translation: Every man, after  the horrible storm  that followed the peace-making, was a prophet. Without thinking, they broke into a prophecy about general things:

original: That this tempest,   Dashing the garment of this peace, aboded   The sudden breach on't.
translation: that this storm, dashing against the clothes of the people making this peace, meant that it would be broken soon.

original: Which is budded out; For France hath flaw'd the league, and hath attach'd Our merchants' goods at Bourdeaux.
translation: And the peace has been broken. Because France has broken the treaty and has seized our merchants' goods at Bordeaux.

original: Is it therefore The ambassador is silenced?
translation: Is that why the ambassador has been silenced?

original: Marry, is't.
translation: Yes, it is.

original: A proper title of a peace; and purchased At a superfluous rate!
Why, all this business Our reverend cardinal carried.
translation: The respected cardinal carried out all this business.

original: Like it your grace,   The state takes notice of the private difference   Betwixt you and the cardinal.
translation: Your grace, the government notices the private quarrel between you and the cardinal.

original: I advise you—   And take it from a heart that wishes towards you   Honour and plenteous safety—that you read   The cardinal's malice and his potency   Together;
translation: I advise you—this comes from a heart that wishes you honor and safety—to consider both the cardinal's ill-will and his power.

original: to consider further that   What his high hatred would effect wants not   A minister in his power.
translation: Consider furthermore that he has all the minions he needs to do what he wants out of his powerful hatred.

original: You know his nature,   That he's revengeful, and I know his sword   Hath a sharp edge: it's long and, 't may be said,   It reaches far, and where 'twill not extend,   Thither he darts it.
translation: You know his vengeful nature and I know his sword has a sharp edge. It's long and they say it reaches far and, where it doesn't reach, he throws it.

original: Bosom up my counsel,   You'll find it wholesome. Lo, where comes that rock   That I advise your shunning.
translation: Remember my advice. You'll find that it's good. See, the  rock  I advise you to avoid is coming now.

original: The Duke of Buckingham's surveyor, ha? Where's his examination?
Here, so please you.
translation: Here, sir.

original: Is he in person ready?
translation: Is he ready to appear in person?

original: Ay, please your grace.
translation: Yes, your grace.

original: Well, we shall then know more; and Buckingham Shall lessen this big look.
translation: Well, I'll find out more. Buckingham won't look this confident soon.

original: This butcher's cur is venom-mouth'd, and I   Have not the power to muzzle him;
translation: This dog of a  butcher's son  has a poisonous bite, and I can't muzzle him.

original: therefore best   Not wake him in his slumber. A beggar's book   Outworths a noble's blood.
translation: So it's better not to wake him when he's sleeping. A beggar's pocket book is worth more than the blood of a nobleman.

original: What, are you chafed? Ask God for temperance; that's the appliance only Which your disease requires.
translation: Are you angry? Ask God to make you patient. That's what you need to be cured of this disease of anger.

original: I read in's looks   Matter against me; and his eye reviled   Me, as his abject object:
translation: I saw from how he looked at me that he has a grudge against me. His eye seemed to be disgusted by me, thinking I was a worthless thing to look at.

original: at this instant   He bores me with some trick: he's gone to the king;   I'll follow and outstare him.
translation: Right now he's plotting against me. He's gone to the king. I'll follow and glare at him.

original: Stay, my lord,   And let your reason with your choler question   What 'tis you go about: to climb steep hills   Requires slow pace at first:
translation: Wait, my lord, and think about what you're doing. You have to go slowly at first when climbing steep hills.

original: anger is like   A full-hot horse, who being allow'd his way,   Self-mettle tires him.
translation: Anger is like a horse eager to run. Allowed to do what he wants, he tires himself out.

original: Not a man in England   Can advise me like you: be to yourself   As you would to your friend.
translation: Not a single man in England can give me as good advice as you can. Act the same way toward yourself as you would to a friend, and give yourself good advice.

original: I'll to the king;   And from a mouth of honour quite cry down   This Ipswich fellow's insolence;
translation: I'll go to the king. I'll use my honorable position to insult this arrogant man from  Ipswich .

original: or proclaim   There's difference in no persons.
translation: If I don't succeed, it shows that people of different classes are equal.

original: Be advised;   Heat not a furnace for your foe so hot   That it do singe yourself: we may outrun,   By violent swiftness, that which we run at,   And lose by over-running.
translation: Think about this. Don't hurt yourself by plotting against your enemy. By running too quickly towards what you run toward, you can miss it and lose.

original: Know you not,   The fire that mounts the liquor til run o'er,   In seeming to augment it wastes it? Be advised:
translation: Don't you know that a fire that makes a pot boil over seems to increase its volume but actually wastes it? Think about this.

original: I say again, there is no English soul   More stronger to direct you than yourself,   If with the sap of reason you would quench,   Or but allay, the fire of passion.
translation: Again, there is no English man who could give you better advice than you could give yourself, if you would just be reasonable and stop being angry, or at least be less angry.

original: Sir,   I am thankful to you; and I'll go along   By your prescription: but this top-proud fellow,   Whom from the flow of gall I name not but   From sincere motions,
translation: Sir, I'm thankful to you, and I'll do what you say. But I know this arrogant man, whom I despise not because of  hot-headed anger  but for good reason,

original: by intelligence,   And proofs as clear as founts in July when   We see each grain of gravel,
translation: I know this from secret sources, with proof as clear as streams in July, when you can see every stone at the bottom.

original: I do know   To be corrupt and treasonous.
translation: to be corrupt and a traitor.

original: Say not 'treasonous.'
translation: Don't say "a traitor."

original: To the king I'll say't; and make my vouch as strong   As shore of rock. Attend. This holy fox,   Or wolf, or both,—
translation: I'll say it to the king. And I'll swear it with a promise as strong as a rock. Listen.

original: for he is equal ravenous   As he is subtle, and as prone to mischief   As able to perform't; his mind and place   Infecting one another, yea, reciprocally—
translation: This holy man is like a fox, or a wolf, or both: he is as greedy as he is sly and he's as willing to do evil as he is able to do it. His mind and his social position infect each other.

original: Only to show his pomp as well in France   As here at home, suggests the king our master   To this last costly treaty, the interview,   That swallow'd so much treasure, and like a glass   Did break i' the rinsing.
translation: He suggested this expensive alliance to the king only so he could show off as much in France as he does here at home. The meeting swallowed so much money, and like a glass it broke as it was being made.

original: Faith, and so it did.
translation: That's true, it did.

original: Pray, give me favour, sir. This cunning cardinal   The articles o' the combination drew   As himself pleased; and they were ratified   As he cried 'Thus let be':
translation: Listen, sir. This sly cardinal drew up the treaty as he pleased. It was signed when he said "Let it be this way."

original: to as much end   As give a crutch to the dead: but our count-cardinal   Has done this, and 'tis well; for worthy Wolsey,   Who cannot err, he did it.
translation: It's as useful as giving a crutch to a dead person. But our ruler the cardinal did it anyway, and that's good. Because honest Wolsey, who never makes mistakes, did it.

original: Now this follows,—   Which, as I take it, is a kind of puppy   To the old dam, treason,—Charles the emperor,   Under pretence to see the queen his aunt—
translation: Then this happened (which looks a lot like treason, as much as a dog looks like its mother).  Charles  the emperor, claiming he wanted to see  the queen his aunt

original: For 'twas indeed his colour, but he came   To whisper Wolsey,—here makes visitation:   His fears were, that the interview betwixt   England and France might, through their amity,   Breed him some prejudice;
translation: (that was his story, but he came to whisper to Wolsey) visited. He was afraid that the meeting between England and France might do him harm if they became allies.

original: for from this league   Peep'd harms that menaced him: he privily   Deals with our cardinal; and, as I trow,—   Which I do well; for I am sure the emperor   Paid ere he promised; whereby his suit was granted   Ere it was ask'd;
translation: He talked privately to our cardinal. I think (and it's something I do well) that the emperor paid before he agreed to anything. And then his request was granted before he asked.

original: but when the way was made,   And paved with gold, the emperor thus desired,   That he would please to alter the king's course,   And break the foresaid peace.
translation: But anyway, when the path had been cleared with bribes, the emperor asked the cardinal to change the king's actions and break this alliance.

original: Let the king know,   As soon he shall by me, that thus the cardinal   Does buy and sell his honour as he pleases,   And for his own advantage.
translation: The king should know, and I'll tell him, that the cardinal buys and sells his honor whenever he wants, for his own advantage.

original: I am sorry To hear this of him; and could wish he were Something mistaken in't.
translation: I am sorry to hear this about him, and I hope there's a mistake in what you say about him.

original: No, not a syllable: I do pronounce him in that very shape He shall appear in proof.
translation: No, not at all. I describe him exactly as he is, and I'll prove it.

original: Your office, sergeant; execute it.
translation: Do your job, sergeant.

original: Sir,   My lord the Duke of Buckingham, and Earl   Of Hereford, Stafford, and Northampton,
translation: My lord the Duke of Buckingham, Earl of Hereford, Stafford, and Northampton, sir,

original: I   Arrest thee of high treason, in the name   Of our most sovereign king.
translation: I arrest you for high treason in the name of our king.

original: Lo, you, my lord, The net has fall'n upon me! I shall perish Under device and practise.
translation: See, my lord, I've been caught in his trap! I'll die from his plots.

original: I am sorry   To see you ta'en from liberty, to look on   The business present:
translation: I'm sorry to see you captured and to see this happen.

original: 'tis his highness' pleasure   You shall to the Tower.
translation: The king wants you to go to the  Tower .

original: It will help me nothing   To plead mine innocence; for that dye is on me   Which makes my whitest part black.
translation: It won't help me to say I'm innocent. Even the most innocent part of me will be made to seem guilty.

original: The will of heaven   Be done in this and all things! I obey.   O my Lord Abergavenny, fare you well!
translation: May God's will be done in this and all things! I obey. Oh, lord Abergavenny, goodbye!

original: Nay, he must bear you company.   The king is pleased you shall to the Tower, till you  know How he determines further.
translation: No, he must go with you.  The king wants you to go the Tower until he decides what will happen to you.

original: As the duke said, The will of heaven be done, and the king's pleasure By me obey'd!
translation: As the duke said, may God's will be done and may I do what the king wants!

original: Here is a warrant from   The king to attach Lord Montacute;
translation: Here is a warrant from the king to arrest Lord Montacute,

original: and the bodies   Of the duke's confessor, John de la Car,   One Gilbert Perk, his chancellor—
translation: the duke's  confessor , John de la Car, and a certain Gilbert Perk, his  chancellor —

original: So, so; These are the limbs o' the plot: no more, I hope.
translation: All right. That's the end of his plot. I hope no more people will be arrested.

original: A monk o' the Chartreux.
translation: A Chartreux monk.

original: O, Nicholas Hopkins?
He.
translation: That's him.

original: My surveyor is false; the o'er-great cardinal   Hath show'd him gold; my life is spann'd already:
translation: My surveyor is a liar. The overly-powerful cardinal gave him gold. My life is already over.

original: I am the shadow of poor Buckingham,   Whose figure even this instant cloud puts on,   By darkening my clear sun. My lord, farewell.
translation: I am the shadow of poor Buckingham, and even now clouds cover me and darken the bright sun of my life. Goodbye, my lord.

original: Now, say, Chatillon, what would France with us?
translation: Tell me, Chatillon, what does the king of France want from me?

original: Thus, after greeting, speaks the King of France In my behavior to the majesty, The borrow'd majesty, of England here.
translation: After greeting you, the King of France says I should behave in this way to you, your Majesty—your borrowed Majesty—

original: A strange beginning: 'borrow'd majesty!'
translation: A strange beginning: "borrowed Majesty!"

original: Silence, good mother; hear the embassy.
translation: Be quiet, dear mother. Listen to the message.

original: Philip of France, in right and true behalf   Of thy deceased brother Geffrey's son,   Arthur Plantagenet, lays most lawful claim   To this fair island and the territories,
translation: Philip of France, on behalf of your dead brother Geffrey's son, Arthur Plantagenet, lays claim lawfully to this beautiful island and its territories:

original: To Ireland, Poictiers, Anjou, Touraine, Maine,
translation: Ireland, Poictiers, Anjou, Touraine, and Maine.

original: Desiring thee to lay aside the sword   Which sways usurpingly these several titles,   And put these same into young Arthur's hand,   Thy nephew and right royal sovereign.
translation: He asks you to give up the power you have stolen over these different places and give these territories to young Arthur, your nephew and your true king.

original: What follows if we disallow of this?
translation: What will happen if I refuse to do this?

original: The proud control of fierce and bloody war, To enforce these rights so forcibly withheld.
translation: Fierce and bloody war will force you to give back what you have stolen to the rightful owner.

original: Here have we war for war and blood for blood, Controlment for controlment: so answer France.
translation: We can return war for war, blood for blood, and force for force: give that answer to the king of France.

original: Then take my king's defiance from my mouth, The farthest limit of my embassy.
translation: Then let me express my king's willingness to fight you. That is the most I am allowed to do as ambassador.

original: Bear mine to him, and so depart in peace:
translation: Tell him the same from me, and leave peacefully.

original: Be thou as lightning in the eyes of France;   For ere thou canst report I will be there,   The thunder of my cannon shall be heard:   So hence!
translation: Shoot back like lightning to the king of France, because before you can give your report I will be there and the thunder of my cannons will be heard.  So leave!

original: Be thou the trumpet of our wrath   And sullen presage of your own decay.
translation: Be a trumpet that announces my anger and that frighteningly foretells your own destruction.

original: An honourable conduct let him have:   Pembroke, look to 't. Farewell, Chatillon.
translation: Escort him back honorably: Pembroke, take care of it. Goodbye, Chatillon.

original: What now, my son! have I not ever said   How that ambitious Constance would not cease   Till she had kindled France and all the world,   Upon the right and party of her son?
translation: What now, my son? Haven't I always said that that ambitious Constance wouldn't stop until she got France and the whole world to fight for her son's rights?

original: This might have been prevented and made whole   With very easy arguments of love,   Which now the manage of two kingdoms must   With fearful bloody issue arbitrate.
translation: This could have been prevented and the argument settled very easily by acting in a loving way, but now two kingdoms must settle the issue with a terrible and bloody fight.

original: Our strong possession and our right for us.
translation: Our strong position and the rightfulness of our cause will be on our side.

original: Your strong possession much more than your right,   Or else it must go wrong with you and me:
translation: Your strong position will help much more than the fact that you're in the right, or this might go badly for me and you.

original: So much my conscience whispers in your ear,   Which none but heaven and you and I shall hear.
translation: My conscience whispers that much in your ear, which is something no one but heaven, you, and I will hear.

original: My liege, here is the strangest controversy Come from country to be judged by you, That e'er I heard: shall I produce the men?
translation: My king, this is the strangest case I've ever heard that has come from the countryside to be judged by you. Should I bring the men forward?

original: Let them approach. Our abbeys and our priories shall pay This expedition's charge.
translation: Let them come. Our abbeys and monasteries will pay their travel costs.

original: What men are you?
translation: Who are you?

original: Your faithful subject I, a gentleman   Born in Northamptonshire and eldest son,   As I suppose, to Robert Faulconbridge,
translation: I am your faithful subject, a gentleman born in Northamptonshire and the oldest son, I believe, of Robert Faulconbridge,

original: A soldier, by the honour-giving hand   Of Coeur-de-lion knighted in the field.
translation: a soldier who was knighted on the battlefield by the honor-giving hand of  Coeur-de-lion .

original: What art thou?
translation: And who are you?

original: The son and heir to that same Faulconbridge.
translation: The son and heir to the same Faulconbridge.

original: Is that the elder, and art thou the heir? You came not of one mother then, it seems.
translation: Is he the oldest, and you're the heir? You didn't come from the same mother then, it seems.

original: Most certain of one mother, mighty king;   That is well known;
translation: Certainly from the same mother, great king; that is well known.

original: and, as I think, one father:   But for the certain knowledge of that truth   I put you o'er to heaven and to my mother:
translation: And, I think, the same father. But to know for certain that that it true, I direct you to heaven and my mother.

original: Of that I doubt, as all men's children may.
translation: I can doubt it, as all men's children can.

original: Out on thee, rude man! thou dost shame thy mother And wound her honour with this diffidence.
translation: You rude man! You shame your mother and insult her honor by doubting that.

original: I, madam? no, I have no reason for it;
translation: I, ma'am? No, I have no reason to.

original: That is my brother's plea and none of mine;   The which if he can prove, a' pops me out   At least from fair five hundred pound a year:
translation: That is my brother's argument and not mine. If he can prove it, he'll take away at least a good five hundred pounds a year from me.

original: Heaven guard my mother's honour and my land!
translation: May heaven save my mother's honor and my land.

original: A good blunt fellow. Why, being younger born, Doth he lay claim to thine inheritance?
translation: You're a good, straightforward fellow. Why, being born later, does he claim your inheritance?

original: I know not why, except to get the land.   But once he slander'd me with bastardy:
translation: I don't know why, except to get the land. But once he slandered me by saying I was a bastard.

original: But whether I be as true begot or no,   That still I lay upon my mother's head,   But that I am as well begot, my liege,—   Fair fall the bones that took the pains for me!—   Compare our faces and be judge yourself.
translation: Whether I was conceived in wedlock or not is on my mother's conscience. But that I am as well born, my king—God bless the bones that went through such labor for me!—you can compare our faces and judge for yourself.

original: If old sir Robert did beget us both   And were our father and this son like him,   O old sir Robert, father, on my knee   I give heaven thanks I was not like to thee!
translation: If old sir Robert was father to us both and this son looks like him, oh old sir Robert, father, I thank heaven on my knee that I don't look like you!

original: Why, what a madcap hath heaven lent us here!
translation: What, what a crazy person God has given us here!

original: He hath a trick of Coeur-de-lion's face; The accent of his tongue affecteth him. Do you not read some tokens of my son In the large composition of this man?
translation: His face looks like Coeur-de-lion's. The way he talks sounds like him. Do you not see some signs of my son in the whole makeup of this man?

original: Mine eye hath well examined his parts And finds them perfect Richard. Sirrah, speak, What doth move you to claim your brother's land?
translation: My eye has looked him over well and finds that he looks just like Richard. Speak, fellow, what makes you claim your brother's land?

original: Because he hath a half-face, like my father. With half that face would he have all my land: A half-faced groat five hundred pound a year!
My gracious liege, when that my father lived, Your brother did employ my father much,—
translation: Kind king, when my father was alive, your brother had a lot of jobs for my father—

original: Well, sir, by this you cannot get my land: Your tale must be how he employ'd my mother.
And once dispatch'd him in an embassy   To Germany, there with the emperor   To treat of high affairs touching that time.
translation: And once sent him as an ambassador to Germany, to negotiate with the emperor there about important matters of the time.

original: The advantage of his absence took the king   And in the mean time sojourn'd at my father's;
translation: The king took advantage of his absence and in the mean time stayed at my father's house.

original: Where how he did prevail I shame to speak,   But truth is truth: large lengths of seas and shores   Between my father and my mother lay,   As I have heard my father speak himself,   When this same lusty gentleman was got.
translation: I am ashamed to talk about what he did there, but the truth is the truth. There were long stretches of sea and land between my father and my mother, as I have heard my father himself say, when  this energetic gentlemen  was conceived.

original: Upon his death-bed he by will bequeath'd   His lands to me, and took it on his death   That this my mother's son was none of his;   And if he were, he came into the world   Full fourteen weeks before the course of time.
translation: On his death-bed he left his land to me in his will, and as he was dying he claimed that my mother's son here was not his. If he was, he came into the world a good fourteen weeks early.

original: Then, good my liege, let me have what is mine,   My father's land, as was my father's will.
translation: Then, my good king, let me have what's mine, my father's land, as my father wished.

original: Sirrah, your brother is legitimate;   Your father's wife did after wedlock bear him,   And if she did play false, the fault was hers;   Which fault lies on the hazards of all husbands   That marry wives.
translation: Sir, your brother is legitimate. Your father's wife gave birth to him after marriage and if she was unfaithful, that's her fault. That is a risk all husbands take who marry wives.

original: Tell me, how if my brother,   Who, as you say, took pains to get this son,   Had of your father claim'd this son for his?
translation: Tell me, what if my brother—who, as you say, was this son's real father—had gone to your father and claimed this boy as his son?

original: In sooth, good friend, your father might have kept   This calf bred from his cow from all the world;   In sooth he might; then, if he were my brother's,   My brother might not claim him; nor your father,   Being none of his, refuse him:
translation: Really, good friend, your father could have kept this calf his cow gave birth to secret from the world; really, he could have. Even if he were my brother's, my brother could not have claimed him.

original: this concludes;   My mother's son did get your father's heir;   Your father's heir must have your father's land.
translation: And your father never raised any suspicion about it. It follows, then, that my mother's son conceived your father's heir.  Your father's heir must have your father's land.

original: Shall then my father's will be of no force To dispossess that child which is not his?
translation: So should my father's will have no power to disinherit the child that is not his?

original: Of no more force to dispossess me, sir, Than was his will to get me, as I think.
translation: He has no more power to disinherit me than he had to conceive me, I think.

original: Whether hadst thou rather be a Faulconbridge And like thy brother, to enjoy thy land, Or the reputed son of Coeur-de-lion, Lord of thy presence and no land beside?
translation: Would you prefer to be a Faulconbridge and like your brother, so you could have your land? Or the supposed son of Coeur-de-lion, lord of your body and no land to go with it?

original: Madam, an if my brother had my shape,   And I had his, sir Robert's his, like him;
translation: Madam, if my brother looked like me and I looked like him and sir Robert,

original: And if my legs were two such riding-rods,   My arms such eel-skins stuff'd, my face so thin   That in mine ear I durst not stick a rose   Lest men should say 'Look, where three-farthings goes!'
translation: and if my legs were two whips like his, my arms stuffed eel-skins, my face so thin that I didn't dare stick a rose behind my ear for fear that men would say, "Look, there goes a  three-farthing  coin!"

original: And, to his shape, were heir to all this land,   Would I might never stir from off this place,
translation: And if, in addition to looking like him, I could be heir to all this land, I would not choose to leave this place.

original: I would give it every foot to have this face;   I would not be sir Nob in any case.
translation: I would give every foot of land to have this face. I don't want to be sir Fool, whatever happens.

original: I like thee well: wilt thou forsake thy fortune, Bequeath thy land to him and follow me? I am a soldier and now bound to France.
translation: I like you. Will you abandon your fortune, leave your land to him, and follow me? I am a soldier and now heading to France.

original: Brother, take you my land, I'll take my chance.
translation: Brother, you take my land, I'll take my chance.

original: Your face hath got five hundred pound a year,   Yet sell your face for five pence and 'tis dear.
translation: Your face has gained you five hundred pounds a year, but sell your face for five pence and it's overpriced.

original: Madam, I'll follow you unto the death.
translation: Ma'am, I'll follow you to death.

original: Nay, I would have you go before me thither.
translation: No, I would prefer you to go there ahead of me.

original: Our country manners give our betters way.
translation: It's good manners in our country to let our superiors go first.

original: What is thy name?
translation: What is your name?

original: Philip, my liege, so is my name begun, Philip, good old sir Robert's wife's eldest son.
translation: Philip, my king, that's how my name begins. Philip, good old sir Robert's wife's oldest son.

original: From henceforth bear his name whose form thou bear'st: Kneel thou down Philip, but rise more great, Arise sir Richard and Plantagenet.
translation: From now on you should have the name of the man you look like. Kneel down Philip, but get up greater, get up as Sir Richard and a Plantagenet.

original: Brother by the mother's side, give me your hand:   My father gave me honour, yours gave land.
translation: Brother on my mother's side, give me your hand: my father gave me honor, yours gave you land.

original: Now blessed be the hour, by night or day,   When I was got, sir Robert was away!
translation: Now may the hour of night or day be blessed when I was conceived and Sir Robert was away!

original: The very spirit of Plantagenet! I am thy grandam, Richard; call me so.
translation: That's the Plantagenet spirit! I am your grandmother, Richard. Call me that.

original: Madam, by chance but not by truth; what though?
translation: Ma'am, by luck and not by honor. But who cares about that?

original: Something about, a little from the right,   In at the window, or else o'er the hatch:   Who dares not stir by day must walk by night,   And have is have, however men do catch:
translation: Roundabout, a little wrong, climbing in at the window or over the roof: whoever doesn't dare go out in the daytime must walk at night, and having is having however men get it.

original: Near or far off, well won is still well shot,   And I am I, howe'er I was begot.
translation: Whether you're near or far off, winning means you shot well. And I am me, however I was conceived.

original: Brother, adieu: good fortune come to thee! For thou wast got i' the way of honesty.
translation: Brother, goodbye. May good fortune come to you! Because you were conceived honestly.

original: A foot of honour better than I was;   But many a many foot of land the worse.
translation: I'm a foot more honorable than I was, but I have lost many and many feet of land.

original: Well, now can I make any Joan a lady.
translation: Well, now I can make any girl a lady.

original: 'Good den, sir Richard!'—'God-a-mercy, fellow!'—   And if his name be George, I'll call him Peter;   For new-made honour doth forget men's names;   'Tis too respective and too sociable   For your conversion.
translation: "Good day, Sir Richard!"—"God bless you, fellow!"—And if his name is George, I'll call him Peter, because being made more honorable makes your forget men's names. Remembering people's names is too familiar and too sociable for my new self.

original: Now your traveller,   He and his toothpick at my worship's mess,   And when my knightly stomach is sufficed,   Why then I suck my teeth and catechise   My picked man of countries:
translation: I'll have a traveler eat at my noble table with his toothpick. When I have satisfied my knightly appetite, I will purse my lips and question my  picked  man about countries:

original: 'My dear sir,'   Thus, leaning on mine elbow, I begin,   'I shall beseech you'—that is question now;   And then comes answer like an Absey book:   'O sir,' says answer, 'at your best command;   At your employment; at your service, sir;'   'No, sir,' says question, 'I, sweet sir, at yours:'   And so, ere answer knows what question would,   Saving in dialogue of compliment,
translation: "My dear sir," I will begin, leaning on my elbow in this way, "I beg you"—that's me asking a question now, and then he'll answer as though he's reading out of an ABC book: "Oh sir", he says, answering, "as you command; as you wish to employ me; at your service, sir." "No sir," I say, questioning, "I, good sir, am at yours." And so, before answer knows what question was asking, we'll have a dialog full of compliments.

original: And talking of the Alps and Apennines,   The Pyrenean and the river Po,   It draws toward supper in conclusion so.
translation: And discussing the Alps and Apennines, the Pyrenees and the river Po, we'll talk until dinner.

original: But this is worshipful society   And fits the mounting spirit like myself,   For he is but a bastard to the time   That doth not smack of observation;
translation: This is good society and is right for an ambitious spirit like mine, because a man who doesn't strike you as observant is just a bastard of his time period.

original: And so am I, whether I smack or no;   And not alone in habit and device,   Exterior form, outward accoutrement,   But from the inward motion to deliver   Sweet, sweet, sweet poison for the age's tooth:
translation: And I am a bastard, whether I strike or not. You can tell not just by how he dresses and acts, his outside appearance, his exterior equipment, but from how he expresses what's inside, giving sweet sweet poison to the tooth of his age.

original: Which, though I will not practise to deceive,   Yet, to avoid deceit, I mean to learn;   For it shall strew the footsteps of my rising.
translation: Which, though I will not try to deceive people, in order to avoid deceiving them I want to learn.  Because that will be a celebration of my rise in importance, like strewing petals around myself.

original: But who comes in such haste in riding-robes?   What woman-post is this? hath she no husband   That will take pains to blow a horn before her?
translation: But who comes here so quickly, wearing a riding outfit? What post-woman is this? Doesn't she have a husband who is willing to blow a horn in front of her?

original: O me! it is my mother. How now, good lady! What brings you here to court so hastily?
translation: Oh no! It's my mother. Hello, good lady! What brings you here to court so quickly?

original: Where is that slave, thy brother? where is he, That holds in chase mine honour up and down?
translation: Where is that slave your brother? Where is he? He hunts up and down after my reputation, trying to kill it.

original: My brother Robert? old sir Robert's son? Colbrand the giant, that same mighty man? Is it sir Robert's son that you seek so?
Sir Robert's son! Ay, thou unreverend boy, Sir Robert's son: why scorn'st thou at sir Robert? He is sir Robert's son, and so art thou.
translation: Sir Robert's son! Yes, you disrespectful boy, Sir Robert's son. Why are you rejecting Sir Robert? He is Sir Robert's son, and so are you.

original: James Gurney, wilt thou give us leave awhile?
translation: James Gurney, could you leave us for a while?

original: Good leave, good Philip.
translation: Gladly, good Philip.

original: Philip! sparrow: James, There's toys abroad: anon I'll tell thee more.
Madam, I was not old sir Robert's son:   Sir Robert might have eat his part in me   Upon Good-Friday and ne'er broke his fast:
translation: Ma'am, I was not old Sir Robert's son. Sir Robert could have eaten the part of me he was responsible for on the fast day day Good-Friday without breaking his fast.

original: Sir Robert could do well: marry, to confess,   Could he get me? Sir Robert could not do it:   We know his handiwork:
translation: Sir Robert could do well. But really, tell the truth: could he conceive me? Sir Robert couldn't do it.

original: therefore, good mother,   To whom am I beholding for these limbs?   Sir Robert never holp to make this leg.
translation: We know his handiwork. So good mother, who is responsible for these limbs of mine? Sir Robert never helped make this leg.

original: Hast thou conspired with thy brother too, That for thine own gain shouldst defend mine honour? What means this scorn, thou most untoward knave?
translation: Have you plotted with your brother too, when for your own sake you should defend my honor? What does this insult mean, you rude good-for-nothing?

original: Knight, knight, good mother, Basilisco-like.   What! I am dubb'd! I have it on my shoulder.
translation: Knight, knight, good mother, like the character  Basilisco  in that play. I have been dubbed! I have it on my shoulder.

original: But, mother, I am not sir Robert's son;   I have disclaim'd sir Robert and my land;   Legitimation, name and all is gone:
translation: But, mother, I am not Sir Robert's son. I have given up my claim to Sir Robert and my land. Legitimacy my name, and all other things are gone.

original: Then, good my mother, let me know my father;   Some proper man, I hope: who was it, mother?
translation: So, my good mother, tell me who my father was. Some honorable man, I hope. Who was it, mother?

original: Hast thou denied thyself a Faulconbridge?
translation: Have you denied you are a Faulconbridge?

original: As faithfully as I deny the devil.
translation: As faithfully as I deny the devil.

original: King Richard Coeur-de-lion was thy father:   By long and vehement suit I was seduced   To make room for him in my husband's bed:
translation: King Richard Coeur-de-lion was your father. After he argued vehemently for a long time he convinced me to make room for him in my husband's bed.
