original: Heaven lay not my transgression to my charge!   Thou art the issue of my dear offence,   Which was so strongly urged past my defence.
translation: May heaven not punish me for my sin! You are the result of my dear sin, which he argued for so strongly that I couldn't defend myself.

original: Now, by this light, were I to get again,   Madam, I would not wish a better father.   Some sins do bear their privilege on earth,   And so doth yours; your fault was not your folly:
translation: I swear, ma'am, if I were going to be conceived again I couldn't wish for a better father. Some sins give you benefits on earth, and yours is one of them. You were not foolish to commit that sin.

original: Needs must you lay your heart at his dispose,   Subjected tribute to commanding love,   Against whose fury and unmatched force   The aweless lion could not wage the fight,   Nor keep his princely heart from Richard's hand.   He that perforce robs lions of their hearts   May easily win a woman's.
translation: You had to give him your heart, since you were his subject and his love commanded you. Even the lion that's not afraid of anything could not have fought again his passion and unequaled strength, or keep his royal heart out of Richard's hand. Anyone who violently robs lions of their hearts can easily win a woman's.

original: Ay, my mother,   With all my heart I thank thee for my father!   Who lives and dares but say thou didst not well   When I was got, I'll send his soul to hell.
translation: Yes, my mother, I thank you with all my heart for my father! If anyone alive dares even to say you didn't do the right thing when I was conceived, I'll send his soul to hell.

original: Come, lady, I will show thee to my kin;   And they shall say, when Richard me begot,   If thou hadst said him nay, it had been sin:   Who says it was, he lies; I say 'twas not.
translation: Come, lady, I will show you to my relatives; and they will say that if you had said no to Richard when he conceived me it would have been a sin. Whoever says it was, is lying. I say it was not.

original: Before Angiers well met, brave Austria.
translation: A pleasure to see you here in front of Angiers, brave king of Austria.

original: Arthur, that great forerunner of thy blood,   Richard, that robb'd the lion of his heart   And fought the holy wars in Palestine,   By this brave duke came early to his grave:
translation: Arthur, your great relative, Richard, who robbed the lion of his heart and fought the holy wars in Palestine, was killed young by this great duke.

original: And for amends to his posterity,   At our importance hither is he come,   To spread his colours, boy, in thy behalf,
translation: To make up for it to Richard's relative, he's come here at my request to fight on your side, boy,

original: And to rebuke the usurpation   Of thy unnatural uncle, English John:
translation: and to punish your unnatural uncle the English king John for stealing your throne.

original: Embrace him, love him, give him welcome hither.
translation: Hug him, love him, and welcome him here.

original: God shall forgive you Coeur-de-lion's death   The rather that you give his offspring life,   Shadowing their right under your wings of war:
translation: God will forgive you for Coeur-de-lion's death because you give his children life, protecting their rights by going to war.

original: I give you welcome with a powerless hand,   But with a heart full of unstained love:
translation: I welcome you with a powerless hand, but with a heart full of pure love.

original: Welcome before the gates of Angiers, duke.
translation: Welcome here to the gates of Angiers, duke.

original: A noble boy! Who would not do thee right?
translation: You're a noble boy! Who wouldn't do what was right by you?

original: Upon thy cheek lay I this zealous kiss,   As seal to this indenture of my love,
translation: I kiss you eagerly on your cheek as a seal to this contract, which I make out of love for you.

original: That to my home I will no more return,   Till Angiers and the right thou hast in France,   Together with that pale, that white-faced shore,   Whose foot spurns back the ocean's roaring tides   And coops from other lands her islanders,
translation: I won't return to my home until Angiers and what rightfully belongs to you in France, along with that pale white-faced shore whose foot kicks back the ocean's roaring waves and keeps the islanders safe from other countries

original: Even till that England, hedged in with the main,   That water-walled bulwark, still secure   And confident from foreign purposes,
translation: —until that England, I mean, hedged in by the sea, that water-walled fort, always safe and confident that it will not be harmed by foreign armies—

original: Even till that utmost corner of the west   Salute thee for her king:
translation: until even that farthest corner of the west recognizes you as its king.

original: till then, fair boy,   Will I not think of home, but follow arms.
translation: Until then, dear boy, I won't think about home, but will keep fighting.

original: O, take his mother's thanks, a widow's thanks, Till your strong hand shall help to give him strength To make a more requital to your love!
translation: Oh, his mother thanks you, a widow thanks you, until your strong hand helps give him strength to pay you back more for your love.

original: The peace of heaven is theirs that lift their swords In such a just and charitable war.
translation: Heaven's peace waits for those who fight in such a just and generous war.

original: Well then, to work:
translation: Well then, let's go to work.

original: our cannon shall be bent   Against the brows of this resisting town.
translation: Our cannons will be turned toward the walls of this resisting town.

original: Call for our chiefest men of discipline,   To cull the plots of best advantages:
translation: Call for our best soldiers to figure out how we can take the advantage.

original: We'll lay before this town our royal bones,   Wade to the market-place in Frenchmen's blood,   But we will make it subject to this boy.
translation: We'll camp our royal bones in front of this town and wade to the market-place in the blood of Frenchmen if we have to, to make it obey this boy.

original: Stay for an answer to your embassy,   Lest unadvised you stain your swords with blood:
translation: Just wait for an answer to your message, in case you stain your swords with blood unnecessarily.

original: My Lord Chatillon may from England bring,   That right in peace which here we urge in war,
translation: My Lord Chatillon might bring from England an acknowledgement of your rightful claim in peace, instead of us having to fight for it here.

original: And then we shall repent each drop of blood   That hot rash haste so indirectly shed.
translation: If that happens we will regret every drop of blood that we hurried rashly to shed before getting an answer.

original: A wonder, lady! lo, upon thy wish,   Our messenger Chatillon is arrived!
translation: What a miracle! Look, as you wished, our messenger Chatillon has arrived!

original: What England says, say briefly, gentle lord;   We coldly pause for thee; Chatillon, speak.
translation: Tell us briefly what the king of England says, kind lord. We've been waiting for you before we start fighting. Speak, Chatillon.

original: Then turn your forces from this paltry siege   And stir them up against a mightier task.
translation: Then turn your forces away from this unimportant siege and encourage them to do a more difficult task.

original: England, impatient of your just demands,   Hath put himself in arms: the adverse winds,   Whose leisure I have stay'd, have given him time   To land his legions all as soon as I;
translation: The king of England, annoyed by your just demands, has armed himself. The wind was against me and I had to wait for it to change. That gave him time to land his army at the same time I landed.

original: His marches are expedient to this town,   His forces strong, his soldiers confident.   With him along is come the mother-queen,   An Ate, stirring him to blood and strife;
translation: He marches quickly toward this town. His troops are strong, his soldiers confident. The queen mother comes with him like the goddess of disorder, encouraging him to shed blood and fight.

original: With her her niece, the Lady Blanch of Spain;   With them a bastard of the king's deceased,   And all the unsettled humours of the land,   Rash, inconsiderate, fiery voluntaries,   With ladies' faces and fierce dragons' spleens,
translation: With her is her niece, the Lady Blanch of Spain. And with them too is a bastard of the dead king, and all the restless passions of the country, foolhardy, unthinking, aggressive volunteers, with the faces of ladies and the guts of fierce dragons.

original: Have sold their fortunes at their native homes,   Bearing their birthrights proudly on their backs,   To make hazard of new fortunes here:
translation: They have sold their fortunes back home, carrying everything they own proudly on their backs to gamble for new fortunes here.

original: In brief, a braver choice of dauntless spirits   Than now the English bottoms have waft o'er   Did nearer float upon the swelling tide,   To do offence and scath in Christendom.
translation: In short, a braver set of fearless men than the English ships have carried over has never floated on the swelling sea to do harm and damage in Christian Europe.

original: The interruption of their churlish drums Cuts off more circumstance: they are at hand, To parley or to fight; therefore prepare.
translation: The interruption of their rude drums cuts off more explanation. They are close by, either to negotiate or fight. So get ready.

original: How much unlook'd for is this expedition!
translation: This attack is so unexpected!

original: By how much unexpected, by so much   We must awake endeavour for defence;
translation: However unexpected it is, we'll have to make all the more effort to defend ourselves.

original: For courage mounteth with occasion:
translation: Courage increases when you need it most.

original: Let them be welcome then: we are prepared.
translation: So let's welcome them. We are ready.

original: Peace be to France, if France in peace permit   Our just and lineal entrance to our own;
translation: May France be at peace if France allows me to enter it peacefully as its rightful owner.

original: If not, bleed France, and peace ascend to heaven,   Whiles we, God's wrathful agent, do correct   Their proud contempt that beats His peace to heaven.
translation: If not, may France bleed and peace rise up to heaven while I, God's angry representative, punish the proud disobedience that makes His peace run away to heaven.

original: Peace be to England, if that war return   From France to England, there to live in peace.
translation: May England be at peace if war returns from France to England to live there at peace.

original: England we love; and for that England's sake   With burden of our armour here we sweat.   This toil of ours should be a work of thine;
translation: I love England. For England's sake I'm sweating here in heavy armor. This work of mine should be your work too.

original: But thou from loving England art so far,   That thou hast under-wrought his lawful king,   Cut off the sequence of posterity,   Out-faced infant state and done a rape   Upon the maiden virtue of the crown.
translation: But you're so far from loving England that you undermined its lawful king, cut off his heir from his inheritance, defied a child king, and raped the virtuous virgin crown.

original: Look here upon thy brother Geffrey's face;   These eyes, these brows, were moulded out of his:   This little abstract doth contain that large   Which died in Geffrey, and the hand of time   Shall draw this brief into as huge a volume.
translation: [Points at ARTHUR]  Look here at your brother Geffrey's face; these eyes, these eyebrows, were molded out of his. This little summary contains in small the large shape of dead Geffrey, and the hand of time will draw out this brief summary into as huge a volume.

original: That Geffrey was thy elder brother born,   And this his son; England was Geffrey's right   And this is Geffrey's:
translation: Geffrey was your older brother and this is his son. England belonged to Geffrey and this is Geffrey's heir.

original: in the name of God   How comes it then that thou art call'd a king,   When living blood doth in these temples beat,   Which owe the crown that thou o'ermasterest?
translation: In the name of God, why are you called a king when this boy is alive and owns the crown you have taken from him?

original: From whom hast thou this great commission, France, To draw my answer from thy articles?
translation: Who gave you this job of forcing me to answer your questions?

original: From that supernal judge, that stirs good thoughts   In any breast of strong authority,   To look into the blots and stains of right:
translation: That heavenly judge who encourages good thoughts in anyone with power to look into crimes.

original: That judge hath made me guardian to this boy:   Under whose warrant I impeach thy wrong   And by whose help I mean to chastise it.
translation: That judge made me this boy's guardian. With a warrant from him I impeach you for your crime, and I mean to punish it with his help.

original: Alack, thou dost usurp authority.
translation: Sadly, you have no right to that power.

original: Excuse; it is to beat usurping down.
translation: Excuse my presumption, since I take it in order to punish you from stealing the power that rightfully belongs to someone else.

original: Who is it thou dost call usurper, France?
translation: Who do you say has stolen power?

original: Let me make answer; thy usurping son.
translation: Let me answer: your stealing son.

original: Out, insolent! thy bastard shall be king, That thou mayst be a queen, and cheque the world!
translation: You rude woman! Your bastard will be king so you can be a queen and tax the whole world!

original: My bed was ever to thy son as true   As thine was to thy husband; and this boy   Liker in feature to his father Geffrey   Than thou and John in manners;
translation: I was always as faithful to your son as you were to your husband. This boy looks more like his father Geffrey than you and John are alike in your manners.

original: being as like   As rain to water, or devil to his dam.   My boy a bastard!
translation: And you two are as alike as rain and water, or the devil and his mother. You call my boy a bastard!

original: By my soul, I think   His father never was so true begot:   It cannot be, an if thou wert his mother.
translation: By my soul, I think his father was not conceived as legitimately. He can't have been, if you were his mother.

original: There's a good mother, boy, that blots thy father.
translation: That's a good mother you have, boy, who insults your father.

original: There's a good grandam, boy, that would blot thee.
translation: That's a good grandmother you have, boy, who insults you.

original: Peace!
translation: Stop!

original: Hear the crier.
translation: Listen to the announcer.

original: What the devil art thou?
translation: Who the devil are you?

original: One that will play the devil, sir, with you,   An a' may catch your hide and you alone:
translation: One who wants to act like a devil with you, sir, if I can catch you and your skin alone.

original: You are the hare of whom the proverb goes,   Whose valour plucks dead lions by the beard;
translation: You are the hare in that proverb who's brave enough to pull dead lions by the beard.

original: I'll smoke your skin-coat, an I catch you right;   Sirrah, look to't; i' faith, I will, i' faith.
translation: I'll smoke you out of your skin, if I can catch you at the right time. Watch out for it, fellow. Really, I'll do it, really.

original: O, well did he become that lion's robe That did disrobe the lion of that robe!
It lies as sightly on the back of him   As great Alcides' shows upon an as   s:
translation: It looks as good on him as great Hercules's would look on a donkey.

original: But, ass, I'll take that burthen from your back,   Or lay on that shall make your shoulders crack.
translation: But, donkey, I'll take that burden off your back or throw on one that will make your shoulders crack.

original: What craker is this same that deafs our ears With this abundance of superfluous breath?
translation: Who is this croaker who deafens us with all his excessive noise?

original: Lewis, determine what we shall do straight.
translation: Lewis, decide what we will do immediately.

original: Women and fools, break off your conference.   King John, this is the very sum of all;   England and Ireland, Anjou, Touraine, Maine,   In right of Arthur do I claim of thee:
translation: Women and fools, stop talking. King John, this is the heart of the matter: on Arthur's behalf I claim from you England, Ireland, Anjou, Touraine, and Maine.

original: Wilt thou resign them and lay down thy arms?
translation: Will you hand them over and lay down your weapons?

original: My life as soon: I do defy thee, France.
translation: I would just as soon lay down my life. I defy you, king of France.

original: Arthur of Bretagne, yield thee to my hand;   And out of my dear love I'll give thee more   Than e'er the coward hand of France can win:   Submit thee, boy.
translation: Arthur of Bretagne, surrender to me and out of my dear love for you I'll give you more than the French coward can win. Surrender to me, boy.

original: Come to thy grandam, child.
translation: Come to your grandmother, child.

original: Do, child, go to it grandam, child:
translation: Do, child, go to grandma, child.

original: Give grandam kingdom, and it grandam will   Give it a plum, a cherry, and a fig:   There's a good grandam.
translation: Give grandma kingdom, and grandma will give you a plum, a cherry, and a fig. That's a good grandma.

original: Good my mother, peace! I would that I were low laid in my grave: I am not worth this coil that's made for me.
translation: Mother, stop! I wish I were dead. I'm not worth this fight I'm causing.

original: His mother shames him so, poor boy, he weeps.
translation: He's so ashamed of his mother, poor boy, he's crying.

original: Now shame upon you, whether she does or no!   His grandam's wrongs, and not his mother's shames,   Draws those heaven-moving pearls from his poor eyes,   Which heaven shall take in nature of a fee;
translation: Shame on you, whether he's ashamed of his mother or not! His grandmother's crimes, not being ashamed of his mother, draw those tears from his poor eyes that would convince even heaven, and which heaven will take as payment for fighting on his side.

original: Ay, with these crystal beads heaven shall be bribed   To do him justice and revenge on you.
translation: Yes, with these crystal tears heaven will be bribed to bring justice to him and take revenge on you.

original: Thou monstrous slanderer of heaven and earth!
translation: You monstrous slanderer of heaven and earth!

original: Thou monstrous injurer of heaven and earth!   Call not me slanderer; thou and thine usurp   The dominations, royalties and rights   Of this oppressed boy:
translation: You monstrous harmer of heaven and earth! Don't call me a slanderer. You and yours steal the power, royalty, and rights of this oppressed boy.

original: this is thy eld'st son's son,   Infortunate in nothing but in thee:
translation: This is your oldest son's son, unfortunate in nothing except being related to you.

original: Thy sins are visited in this poor child;   The canon of the law is laid on him,   Being but the second generation   Removed from thy sin-conceiving womb.
translation: This poor child is punished for your sins. The law is punishing him for being only the second generation removed from your sinful womb.

original: Bedlam, have done.
translation: You're crazy! Stop talking.

original: I have but this to say,   That he is not only plagued for her sin,   But God hath made her sin and her the plague   On this removed issue,
translation: I only have this to say: that he is not only punished for her sin, but God has made her sin and her the punishment of this child descended from her.

original: plague for her   And with her plague; her sin his injury,   Her injury the beadle to her sin,
translation: She's punished and she punishes him. Her sin harms him, and the harm she does compounds her sin.

original: All punish'd in the person of this child,   And all for her; a plague upon her!
translation: All the punishment falls on this child, and all because of her. Damn her!

original: Thou unadvised scold, I can produce A will that bars the title of thy son.
translation: You thoughtless scolder, I can show you a will that disinherits your son.

original: Ay, who doubts that? a will! a wicked will: A woman's will; a canker'd grandam's will!
translation: Yes, who doubts that? A will! A wicked will; a woman's will; a decayed grandmother's will!

original: Peace, lady! pause, or be more temperate:   It ill beseems this presence to cry aim   To these ill-tuned repetitions.
translation: Stop, lady! Stop, or be more calm. It isn't fitting to repeat these unpleasant things in this company.

original: Some trumpet summon hither to the walls   These men of Angiers: let us hear them speak   Whose title they admit, Arthur's or John's.
translation: [To a servant]  Blow a trumpet to summon the men of Angiers here to the walls. Let's hear them say whose claim they recognize, Arthur's or John's.

original: Who is it that hath warn'd us to the walls?
translation: Who is it who calls us to the walls?

original: 'Tis France, for England.
translation: It's the king of France, on behalf of the king of England.

original: England, for itself. You men of Angiers, and my loving subjects—
translation: The king of England, for myself. You men of Angiers, and my loving subjects—

original: You loving men of Angiers, Arthur's subjects, Our trumpet call'd you to this gentle parle—
translation: You loving men of Angiers, Arthur's subjects, our trumpets called you to this polite discussion—

original: For our advantage; therefore hear us first.   These flags of France, that are advanced here   Before the eye and prospect of your town,   Have hither march'd to your endamagement:
translation: For our advantage. So hear us first. These French flags camped here where you can see them have marched here to attack you.

original: The cannons have their bowels full of wrath,   And ready mounted are they to spit forth   Their iron indignation 'gainst your walls:   All preparation for a bloody siege   All merciless proceeding by these French   Confronts your city's eyes, your winking gates;
translation: The cannons are loaded with anger and stand ready to spit out their iron anger at your walls. All these things are preparations for a bloody attack. You can see for yourself all of their cruel preparations.

original: And but for our approach those sleeping stones,   That as a waist doth girdle you about,   By the compulsion of their ordinance   By this time from their fixed beds of lime   Had been dishabited, and wide havoc made   For bloody power to rush upon your peace.
translation: If I hadn't gotten here, these sleeping stones in the wall that surrounds your city like a waist would by this time have been detached by the force of the French guns from their limestone beds. In the terrible confusion, bloody violence would have attacked your peace.

original: But on the sight of us your lawful king,   Who painfully with much expedient march   Have brought a countercheque before your gates,   To save unscratch'd your city's threatened cheeks,   Behold, the French amazed vouchsafe a parle;
translation: But I, your lawful king, by marching quickly and painfully, brought an opposing army to your gates to save your threatened city's cheeks from being scratched. At the sight of me, see, the French are amazed and are willing to talk.

original: And now, instead of bullets wrapp'd in fire,   To make a shaking fever in your walls,   They shoot but calm words folded up in smoke,   To make a faithless error in your ears:
translation: And now, instead of bullets wrapped in fire that would make your walls shake with fever, they only shoot calm words covered in smoke to convince you to make a dishonorable mistake.

original: Which trust accordingly, kind citizens,   And let us in, your king, whose labour'd spirits,   Forwearied in this action of swift speed,   Crave harbourage within your city walls.
translation: Don't trust them, kind citizens, and let me, your king, exhausted by his speedy march here, beg for shelter inside your city walls.

original: When I have said, make answer to us both.   Lo, in this right hand, whose protection   Is most divinely vow'd upon the right   Of him it holds, stands young Plantagenet,   Son to the elder brother of this man,   And king o'er him and all that he enjoys:
translation: When I have spoken, answer both of us. Look, held by this right hand—which God will protect when it fights for the rights of the boy it holds—stands young Plantagenet, son of this man's older brother, and king of him and everything he owns.

original: For this down-trodden equity, we tread   In warlike march these greens before your town,   Being no further enemy to you   Than the constraint of hospitable zeal   In the relief of this oppressed child   Religiously provokes.
translation: For his ignored rights we are marching on this green land in front of your town. We're not your enemies except insofar as we have to be in our religious, kind eagerness to help this oppressed child.

original: Be pleased then   To pay that duty which you truly owe   To that owes it, namely this young prince:
translation: So agree to do what you should and obey the right person, this young prince.

original: And then our arms, like to a muzzled bear,   Save in aspect, hath all offence seal'd up;   Our cannons' malice vainly shall be spent   Against the invulnerable clouds of heaven;
translation: hen our weapons, like a muzzled bear, will not hurt you except by frightening you. Our cannons' anger will be taken out pointlessly against the clouds of heaven, which can't be harmed.

original: And with a blessed and unvex'd retire,   With unhack'd swords and helmets all unbruised,   We will bear home that lusty blood again   Which here we came to spout against your town,   And leave your children, wives and you in peace.
translation: And with a blessed and peaceful retreat, with swords not hacked and helmets not battered, we will carry back home the energetic blood which we came here to spout against your town and we will leave your children, your wives, and you in peace.

original: But if you fondly pass our proffer'd offer,   'Tis not the roundure of your old-faced walls   Can hide you from our messengers of war,   Though all these English and their discipline   Were harbour'd in their rude circumference.
translation: But if you foolishly pass up our offer, the curves of your old-faced walls can't hide you from our messengers of war, even if all these English people and their army are camped around their rough edges.

original: Then tell us, shall your city call us lord,   In that behalf which we have challenged it?   Or shall we give the signal to our rage   And stalk in blood to our possession?
translation: So tell us, will your city call this person we've threatened it for its ruler? Or will we give the signal to our anger and take the city with blood?

original: In brief, we are the king of England's subjects: For him, and in his right, we hold this town.
translation: In short, we are the king of England's subjects. We hold this town for him, defending his rights.

original: Acknowledge then the king, and let me in.
translation: So acknowledge the king and let me in.

original: That can we not; but he that proves the king, To him will we prove loyal: till that time Have we ramm'd up our gates against the world.
translation: We can't do that, but we will be loyal to whoever proves himself king. Until then we've shut our gates against the whole world.

original: Doth not the crown of England prove the king? And if not that, I bring you witnesses, Twice fifteen thousand hearts of England's breed,—
translation: Doesn't having the crown of England prove me king? And if that doesn't, I bring you witnesses: an army of thirty thousand hearts from England—

original: Bastards, and else.
translation: Bastards, and others.

original: To verify our title with their lives.
translation: To prove my title with their lives.

original: As many and as well-born bloods as those,—
translation: As many and as well-born people as those—

original: Some bastards too.
translation: Some bastards too.

original: Stand in his face to contradict his claim.
translation: Face him to contradict his claim.

original: Till you compound whose right is worthiest, We for the worthiest hold the right from both.
translation: Until you agree who has the best claim, we withhold obedience from both of you to reserve it for the worthiest.

original: Then God forgive the sin of all those souls That to their everlasting residence, Before the dew of evening fall, shall fleet, In dreadful trial of our kingdom's king!
translation: Then may God forgive the sins of all those souls that will fly to their eternal homes before evening, to be judged terribly by our kingdom's king!

original: Amen, amen! Mount, chevaliers! to arms!
translation: Amen, amen! On your horses, knight! To arms!

original: Saint George, that swinged the dragon, and e'er since Sits on his horseback at mine hostess' door, Teach us some fence!
translation: Saint George, who beat the dragon, and ever since sits on horseback on the sign at my local pub, teach us some fencing!

original: Sirrah, were I at home, At your den, sirrah, with your lioness I would set an ox-head to your lion's hide, And make a monster of you.
Peace! no more.
translation: Stop! No more of that sort of talk.

original: O tremble, for you hear the lion roar.
translation: Oh be afraid, because you hear the lion roar.

original: Up higher to the plain; where we'll set forth In best appointment all our regiments.
translation: Let's get to higher ground. There we'll put all our troops in order.

original: Speed then, to take advantage of the field.
translation: Hurry, then, to get the best part of the battlefield.

original: It shall be so; and at the other hill Command the rest to stand. God and our right!
translation: That's right. And command the rest to stand at the other hill. For God and our right!

original: You men of Angiers, open wide your gates,   And let young Arthur, Duke of Bretagne, in,   Who by the hand of France this day hath made   Much work for tears in many an English mother,   Whose sons lie scattered on the bleeding ground;
translation: Men of Angiers, open wide your gates and let in young Arthur, duke of Bretagne, who by the power of the king of France today gave many English mothers reason to cry because their sons lie scattered on the bloody ground.

original: Many a widow's husband grovelling lies,   Coldly embracing the discolour'd earth;   And victory, with little loss, doth play   Upon the dancing banners of the French,
translation: Many widows' husbands lie on the ground, passionlessly embracing the stained earth. The French have won the battle with few causalities, as you can see from their dancing banners.

original: Who are at hand, triumphantly display'd,   To enter conquerors and to proclaim   Arthur of Bretagne England's king and yours.
translation: They are waiting triumphantly nearby to enter as conquerors and to proclaim Arthur of Bretagne your and all of England's king.

original: Rejoice, you men of Angiers, ring your bells:   King John, your king and England's doth approach,   Commander of this hot malicious day:
translation: Be joyful, men of Angiers, ring your bells. King John, your and all of England's king, approaches, winner of this intense and deadly battle.

original: Their armours, that march'd hence so silver-bright,   Hither return all gilt with Frenchmen's blood;   There stuck no plume in any English crest   That is removed by a staff of France;
translation: The armors of those who marched here used to be bright silver, and they will return decorated with the blood of Frenchmen. No feather stuck in an English helmet was removed by a French spear.

original: Our colours do return in those same hands   That did display them when we first march'd forth;   And, like a troop of jolly huntsmen, come   Our lusty English, all with purpled hands,   Dyed in the dying slaughter of their foes:
translation: Our banners return in the same hands that held them when we first marched out. Our energetic Englishmen come like a band of happy hunters, with red hands dyed in the dying blood of their enemies.

original: Open your gates and gives the victors way.
translation: Open your gates and let the winners in.

original: Heralds, from off our towers we might behold,   From first to last, the onset and retire   Of both your armies; whose equality   By our best eyes cannot be censured:
translation: Heralds, we could see from our towers the charge and retreat of both your armies from beginning to end. They seemed equal even to the best observer among us.

original: Blood hath bought blood and blows have answered blows;   Strength match'd with strength, and power confronted  power:   Both are alike; and both alike we like.
translation: Blood bought blood and hits answered hits. Strength was matched with strength and power fought power. They're both equal and we like both equally.

original: One must prove greatest: while they weigh so even,   We hold our town for neither, yet for both.
translation: One must prove itself to be the greatest. While they're so evenly balanced, we must keep our town safe for neither, but for both.

original: France, hast thou yet more blood to cast away?   Say, shall the current of our right run on?
translation: France, do you have more blood to throw away? Will the tide of our right to the crown run on?

original: Whose passage, vex'd with thy impediment,   Shall leave his native channel and o'erswell   With course disturb'd even thy confining shores,
translation: If you try to block the tide, the water will leave its home river and flood violently over your shores,

original: Unless thou let his silver water keep   A peaceful progress to the ocean.
translation: unless you let its silver water keep peacefully flowing to the ocean.

original: England, thou hast not saved one drop of blood,   In this hot trial, more than we of France;   Rather, lost more.
translation: England, you haven't lost a single drop of blood less than we French have in this intense battle. Rather, you've lost more.

original: And by this hand I swear,   That sways the earth this climate overlooks,   Before we will lay down our just-borne arms,   We'll put thee down, 'gainst whom these arms we bear,
translation: And I swear, by this hand that rules all the land around here, before we put down our weapons carried in a just cause we'll put you down, against whom we carry these weapons.

original: Or add a royal number to the dead,   Gracing the scroll that tells of this war's loss   With slaughter coupled to the name of kings.
translation: Or add a royal name to the list of the dead, decorating the scroll on which the names of people lost in this war are written by adding the name of kings.

original: Ha, majesty! how high thy glory towers,   When the rich blood of kings is set on fire!
translation: Ha, royalty! You look and act so glorious when kings get angry!

original: O, now doth Death line his dead chaps with steel;   The swords of soldiers are his teeth, his fangs;   And now he feasts, mousing the flesh of men,   In undetermined differences of kings.
translation: Oh, now Death lines his dead jaws with steel. Soldiers' swords are his teeth, his fangs. And now he feasts, tearing the flesh of men, not distinguishing the difference between kings.

original: Why stand these royal fronts amazed thus?   Cry, 'havoc!' kings; back to the stained field,   You equal potents, fiery kindled spirits!
translation: Why are these royal faces staring at me blankly? Kings, shout "Go!" Go back to the blood-stained battlefield, you equal armies and angry spirits!

original: Then let confusion of one part confirm   The other's peace: till then, blows, blood and death!
translation: Then let destruction of one side secure the peace of the other. Until then, blows, blood, and death!

original: Whose party do the townsmen yet admit?
translation: Whose side are the townspeople on now?

original: Speak, citizens, for England; who's your king?
translation: Speak, citizens, for England: who's your king?

original: The king of England; when we know the king.
translation: The king of England—when we know who the king is.

original: Know him in us, that here hold up his right.
translation: Recognize me as the king, since I'm fighting for his rights here.

original: In us, that are our own great deputy And bear possession of our person here, Lord of our presence, Angiers, and of you.
translation: No, recognize me, since I do my own great work and stand here, lord of my army, Angiers, and of you.

original: A greater power than we denies all this;   And till it be undoubted, we do lock   Our former scruple in our strong-barr'd gates;
translation: A higher power than us denies all this. Until there's no dispute about it, we lock our uncertainty inside our strongly-barred gates.

original: King'd of our fears, until our fears, resolved,   Be by some certain king purged and deposed.
translation: Our fears are our kings until our fears, resolved, are gotten rid of and deposed by a definite king.

original: By heaven, these scroyles of Angiers flout you, kings,   And stand securely on their battlements,   As in a theatre, whence they gape and point   At your industrious scenes and acts of death.
translation: By heaven, these good-for-nothings of Angiers defy you, kings, and stand safely on their walls like in a theater. From there they gawp and point at your hardworking scenes and acts of death.

original: Your royal presences be ruled by me:   Do like the mutines of Jerusalem,   Be friends awhile and both conjointly bend   Your sharpest deeds of malice on this town:
translation: Take my advice, kings: follow the example of the rebels in Jerusalem. Be friends for a while and join forces to do your worst to this town.

original: By east and west let France and England mount   Their battering cannon charged to the mouths,   Till their soul-fearing clamours have brawl'd down   The flinty ribs of this contemptuous city:
translation: France and England can both point their fully charged cannons from east and west, until their terrifying sounds have knocked down the hard ribs of this disrespectful city.

original: I'ld play incessantly upon these jades,   Even till unfenced desolation   Leave them as naked as the vulgar air.
translation: I want to keep attacking these worthless people until wall-less destruction leaves them as naked as the common air.

original: That done, dissever your united strengths,   And part your mingled colours once again;   Turn face to face and bloody point to point;
translation: When that's done, stop working together and separate out your banners again, which were mingled together. Turn face to face with bloody weapons.

original: Then, in a moment, Fortune shall cull forth   Out of one side her happy minion,   To whom in favour she shall give the day,   And kiss him with a glorious victory.
translation: Then, in a moment, Fortune will choose a happy follower from one of the sides. She'll make him win and kiss him with a glorious victory.

original: How like you this wild counsel, mighty states?   Smacks it not something of the policy?
translation: How do you like this wild advice, powerful kings? Doesn't it sound like good politics?

original: Now, by the sky that hangs above our heads,   I like it well.
translation: Now, by the sky that hangs above our heads, I like it.

original: France, shall we knit our powers   And lay this Angiers even to the ground;   Then after fight who shall be king of it?
translation: France, shall we combine our forces and knock this Angiers to the ground, then afterward fight about who will be king of it?

original: An if thou hast the mettle of a king,   Being wronged as we are by this peevish town,   Turn thou the mouth of thy artillery,   As we will ours, against these saucy walls;
translation: If you have the character of a king, you won't tolerate being treated badly by this disobedient town. Turn the mouths of your cannons, as we will do with ours, against these disrespectful walls.

original: And when that we have dash'd them to the ground,   Why then defy each other and pell-mell   Make work upon ourselves, for heaven or hell.
translation: And when we have beat them to the ground, we'll defy each other and attack each other every which way, for heaven or hell.

original: Let it be so. Say, where will you assault?
translation: Very well. Where will you attack?

original: We from the west will send destruction Into this city's bosom.
translation: We will send destruction into the city's breast from the west.

original: I from the north.
translation: And I from the north.

original: Our thunder from the south Shall rain their drift of bullets on this town.
translation: Our thunder from the south will rain bullets on the town.

original: O prudent discipline! From north to south: Austria and France shoot in each other's mouth: I'll stir them to it. Come, away, away!
translation: Oh wise strategy! From north to south, Austria and France shoot in each other's faces. I'll encourage them. Come on, let's go! Let's go!

original: Hear us, great kings: vouchsafe awhile to stay,   And I shall show you peace and fair-faced league;   Win you this city without stroke or wound;
translation: Listen to us, great kings: agree to wait a while and I will show you a way to make peace and an honest alliance. Win this city without violence or wounds.

original: Rescue those breathing lives to die in beds,   That here come sacrifices for the field:   Persever not, but hear me, mighty kings.
translation: Rescue the people still breathing and alive who come here as sacrifices on this battlefield so they can die in bed later. Don't go on with this plan but listen to me, powerful kings.

original: Speak on with favour; we are bent to hear.
translation: Continue to speak. We're listening.

original: That daughter there of Spain, the Lady Blanch,   Is niece to England: look upon the years   Of Lewis the Dauphin and that lovely maid:
translation: That Spanish woman, the Lady Blanch, is a niece of the king of England. Compare the ages of Lewis the Dauphin and that beautiful virgin.

original: If lusty love should go in quest of beauty,   Where should he find it fairer than in Blanch?   If zealous love should go in search of virtue,   Where should he find it purer than in Blanch?   If love ambitious sought a match of birth,   Whose veins bound richer blood than Lady Blanch?
translation: If young love were to go looking for beauty, who is more beautiful than Blanch? If true love were to go looking for virtue, who is more pure than Blanch? If ambitious love looked for a marriage that matched its social station, who is more noble than Lady Blanch?

original: Such as she is, in beauty, virtue, birth,   Is the young Dauphin every way complete:   If not complete of, say he is not she;
translation: Just as she is perfect in beauty, virtue, and family, the young Dauphin is also complete in those things. Except not complete, because he is not her.

original: And she again wants nothing, to name want,   If want it be not that she is not he:
translation: And she also lacks nothing, except one thing, which is that she is not him.

original: He is the half part of a blessed man,   Left to be finished by such as she;   And she a fair divided excellence,   Whose fulness of perfection lies in him.
translation: He is half of a blessed man, left to be finished by someone like her. And she is half of a divided beautiful excellence, who will be fully perfect when combined with him.

original: O, two such silver currents, when they join,   Do glorify the banks that bound them in;   And two such shores to two such streams made one,   Two such controlling bounds shall you be, kings,   To these two princes, if you marry them.
translation: Two silver streams, when they join, make the banks that contain them more glorious. If you have them marry each other one stream will join two shores: you two kings will be two controlling limits to these two royals.

original: This union shall do more than battery can   To our fast-closed gates; for at this match,   With swifter spleen than powder can enforce,   The mouth of passage shall we fling wide ope,   And give you entrance:
translation: This marriage will achieve more than attacking our tightly-closed gates can. Because once this match is made, faster than gunpowder can force us to do the same thing, we will fling the passageway open and let you in.

original: but without this match,   The sea enraged is not half so deaf,   Lions more confident, mountains and rocks   More free from motion, no, not Death himself   In moral fury half so peremptory,   As we to keep this city.
translation: But without this marriage, the angry sea is not half as deaf, lions half as confident, mountains and rocks more firmly stuck, no, Death himself is not half as quick to kill in his rage as we are to defend this city.

original: Here's a stay   That shakes the rotten carcass of old Death   Out of his rags! Here's a large mouth, indeed,   That spits forth death and mountains, rocks and seas,   Talks as familiarly of roaring lions   As maids of thirteen do of puppy-dogs!
translation: That's a sentence that shakes Death's rotten corpse out of his rags! That's a big mouth that spits out death and mountains, rocks and seas, and talks as familiarly about roaring lions as thirteen-year-old girls talk about puppy dogs!

original: What cannoneer begot this lusty blood?   He speaks plain cannon fire, and smoke and bounce;   He gives the bastinado with his tongue:
translation: What gunman conceived this energetic man? He speaks cannon fire, and smoke, and bouncing. He beats you with his tongue.

original: Our ears are cudgell'd; not a word of his   But buffets better than a fist of France:   Zounds! I was never so bethump'd with words   Since I first call'd my brother's father dad.
translation: Our ears are clubbed. Every word of his hits better than a French fist. By God! I've never been so thumped with words since I first called my brother's father dad.

original: Son, list to this conjunction, make this match;   Give with our niece a dowry large enough:   For by this knot thou shalt so surely tie   Thy now unsured assurance to the crown,
translation: Son, listen to this proposal. Make this marriage happen. Give our niece a large enough dowry. By this marriage you will certainly ensure your threatened claim to the crown.

original: That yon green boy shall have no sun to ripe   The bloom that promiseth a mighty fruit.
translation: This way young Arthur won't become powerful:  he'll be like a flower that doesn't get enough sun to develop from a green bud into a fruit.

original: I see a yielding in the looks of France;   Mark, how they whisper: urge them while their souls   Are capable of this ambition,
translation: The king of France looks like he'll agree. See how they're whispering. Encourage them while they are capable of being convinced to do this,

original: Lest zeal, now melted by the windy breath   Of soft petitions, pity and remorse,   Cool and congeal again to what it was.
translation: so that anger, melted by weak begging, pity, and regret, can't cool and congeal back to what it was before.

original: Why answer not the double majesties This friendly treaty of our threaten'd town?
translation: Why don't the two kings answer this friendly proposal from our threatened town?

original: Speak England first, that hath been forward first To speak unto this city: what say you?
translation: Let England speak first, since before they've always insisted on speaking first to this city. What do you say?

original: If that the Dauphin there, thy princely son,   Can in this book of beauty read 'I love,'   Her dowry shall weigh equal with a queen:
translation: If the Dauphin there, your royal son, can read the words "I love" in this  book of beauty , her dowry will be equal to a queen's.

original: For Anjou and fair Touraine, Maine, Poictiers,   And all that we upon this side the sea,   Except this city now by us besieged,   Find liable to our crown and dignity,
translation: Anjou and beautiful Touraine, Maine, Poictiers, and everything on this side of the sea, except this city we're attacking now, that we find fitting for our power and dignity,

original: Shall gild her bridal bed and make her rich   In titles, honours and promotions,   As she in beauty, education, blood,   Holds hand with any princess of the world.
translation: will decorate her marriage bed and make her as rich in titles, honors, and rank as she is in beauty, education, family—which is to say equal to any princess in the world.

original: What say'st thou, boy? look in the lady's face.
translation: What do you say, boy? Look at the lady's face.

original: I do, my lord; and in her eye I find   A wonder, or a wondrous miracle,   The shadow of myself form'd in her eye:
translation: I am looking, my lord, and in her eye I find a wonder, or a wonderful miracle, my own shape formed in her eye.

original: Which being but the shadow of your son,   Becomes a sun and makes your son a shadow:
translation: Since this is only the shadow of your son, it becomes a sun and makes your son a shadow.

original: I do protest I never loved myself   Till now infixed I beheld myself   Drawn in the flattering table of her eye.
translation: I swear I never loved myself until I now say myself drawn on the flattering paper of her eye

original: Drawn in the flattering table of her eye!   Hang'd in the frowning wrinkle of her brow!   And quarter'd in her heart! he doth espy   Himself love's traitor:
translation: Drawn on the flattering paper of her eye! Hanged in the frowning wrinkle of her forehead! And cut into quarters her heart! He sees himself as  love's traitor .

original: this is pity now,   That hang'd and drawn and quartered, there should be   In such a love so vile a lout as he.
translation: This is a pity, that such a disgusting fool as he is should be hanged, drawn, and quartered in such a love.

original: My uncle's will in this respect is mine:   If he see aught in you that makes him like,   That any thing he sees, which moves his liking,   I can with ease translate it to my will;
translation: [To the Dauphin]  I will do what my uncle wants in this matter. If he sees anything in you that makes him like you, I can easily make myself see whatever he sees in you.

original: Or if you will, to speak more properly,   I will enforce it easily to my love.   Further I will not flatter you, my lord,   That all I see in you is worthy love,
translation: Or I mean, to speak more properly, I can force myself to love you. I won't flatter you, my lord, by saying that everything I see in you makes me love you.

original: Than this; that nothing do I see in you,   Though churlish thoughts themselves should be your  judge,   That I can find should merit any hate.
translation: But I'll say this: I can see nothing in you, although you'll have to be the judge of any bad thoughts you have, that would make me hate you.

original: What say these young ones? What say you my niece?
translation: What do these young people say? What does my niece say?

original: That she is bound in honour still to do What you in wisdom still vouchsafe to say.
translation: That it's her duty to do what you wisely say she should.

original: Speak then, prince Dauphin; can you love this lady?
translation: Then speak, prince Dauphin: can you love this lady?

original: Nay, ask me if I can refrain from love; For I do love her most unfeignedly.
translation: No, ask me if I can stop loving her, because I genuinely love her.

original: Then do I give Volquessen, Touraine, Maine,   Poictiers and Anjou, these five provinces,   With her to thee; and this addition more,   Full thirty thousand marks of English coin.
translation: Then I give the five provinces of Volquessen, Touraine, Maine, Poictiers, and Anjou to you along with her. And in addition to this, thirty thousand  marks  in English coins.

original: Philip of France, if thou be pleased withal,   Command thy son and daughter to join hands.
translation: Philip of France, if this pleases you then command your son and daughter to take each other's hands.

original: It likes us well; young princes, close your hands.
translation: It does please me. Young royals, take each other's hands.

original: And your lips too; for I am well assured That I did so when I was first assured.
translation: And kiss each other too, because I'm sure I did that when I got engaged.

original: Now, citizens of Angiers, ope your gates,   Let in that amity which you have made;   For at Saint Mary's chapel presently   The rites of marriage shall be solemnized.
translation: Now, citizens of Angiers, open your gates and let in the friendship you made. The marriage will take place soon at Saint Mary's chapel.

original: Is not the Lady Constance in this troop?   I know she is not, for this match made up   Her presence would have interrupted much:   Where is she and her son? tell me, who knows.
translation: Is the Lady Constance not in this crowd? I know she isn't, because her presence would have kept this match from being made. Where are her son and her? Tell me, if anyone knows.

original: She is sad and passionate at your highness' tent.
translation: She's back at your tent, sad and angry.

original: And, by my faith, this league that we have made   Will give her sadness very little cure.   Brother of England, how may we content   This widow lady?
translation: I bet this alliance we made won't cure her sadness. My brother of England, how can we satisfy this widowed lady?

original: In her right we came;   Which we, God knows, have turn'd another way,   To our own vantage.
translation: I came to fight for her. God knows, I have turned things to my own advantage.

original: We will heal up all;   For we'll create young Arthur Duke of Bretagne   And Earl of Richmond; and this rich fair town   We make him lord of.
translation: I will heal this all. I will make young Arthur Duke of Bretagne and Earl of Richmond and the lord of this beautiful rich town.

original: Call the Lady Constance;   Some speedy messenger bid her repair   To our solemnity:
translation: Call Lady Constance. Have some speedy messenger ask her to come to the ceremony.

original: I trust we shall,   If not fill up the measure of her will,   Yet in some measure satisfy her so   That we shall stop her exclamation.
translation: I trust that even if we don't give her everything she wants we will give her enough to stop her complaining.

original: Go we, as well as haste will suffer us,   To this unlook'd for, unprepared pomp.
translation: Let's go as quickly as we can to this ceremony, which we didn't prepare for or expect.

original: Mad world! mad kings! mad composition!   John, to stop Arthur's title in the whole,   Hath willingly departed with a part,
translation: Crazy world! Crazy kings! Crazy alliance! John, to stop Arthur's claim to the whole, willingly parted with a part.

original: And France, whose armour conscience buckled on,   Whom zeal and charity brought to the field   As God's own soldier, rounded in the ear   With that same purpose-changer, that sly devil,   That broker, that still breaks the pate of faith,   That daily break-vow,
translation: France—with armor buckled on by conscience, and who was brought to the field by eagerness and charity like the soldier of God himself—was smooth-talked by that purpose-changer, that clever devil, that middleman who always hurts faithfulness's head, that daily oath-breaker who wins from everyone.

original: he that wins of all,   Of kings, of beggars, old men, young men, maids,   Who, having no external thing to lose   But the word 'maid,' cheats the poor maid of that,
translation: It wins from kings, from beggars, old men young men, virgins—it cheats a poor virgin out of the only thing she owns, the word "virgin".

original: That smooth-faced gentleman, tickling Commodity,   Commodity, the bias of the world,   The world, who of itself is peised well,   Made to run even upon even ground,
translation: That smooth-faced gentleman is tickling Convenience, Convenience. It tilts the world one way or the other, although the world left alone is equally balanced and made to run evenly on even ground.

original: Till this advantage, this vile-drawing bias,   This sway of motion, this Commodity,   Makes it take head from all indifferency,   From all direction, purpose, course, intent:   And this same bias, this Commodity,   This bawd, this broker, this all-changing word,
translation: Until, that is, this advantage, that draws people to evil, this swaying, this Convenience, this pimp, this middleman, this word that changes everything,

original: Clapp'd on the outward eye of fickle France,   Hath drawn him from his own determined aid,   From a resolved and honourable war,   To a most base and vile-concluded peace.
translation: thrown in the eyes of the unreliable king of France, distracts him from the goal he had set, from a clear and honorable war to a cowardly and badly negotiated peace.

original: And why rail I on this Commodity?   But for because he hath not woo'd me yet:   Not that I have the power to clutch my hand,   When his fair angels would salute my palm;
translation: Why do I complain about Convenience? Because he hasn't tried to buy my affection yet. I'm sure I wouldn't have the power to close my hand when his beautiful  angels  want to greet my palm.

original: But for my hand, as unattempted yet,   Like a poor beggar, raileth on the rich.   Well, whiles I am a beggar, I will rail   And say there is no sin but to be rich;
translation: But my hand, not tested yet, complains like a poor beggar about rich people. Well, while I am a beggar, I will complain and say that being rich is the only sin.

original: And being rich, my virtue then shall be   To say there is no vice but beggary.   Since kings break faith upon commodity,   Gain, be my lord, for I will worship thee.
translation: And when I'm rich, my virtue will then be to say there is no sin but begging. Since kings break alliances when it's convenient, be my lord, Profit, and I will worship you.

original: Gone to be married! gone to swear a peace!   False blood to false blood join'd! gone to be friends!   Shall Lewis have Blanch, and Blanch those provinces?
translation: Gone to get married! Gone to make peace! Lying blood is joined to lying blood! Gone to be friends? Will Lewis have Blanch, and Blanch have those provinces?

original: It is not so; thou hast misspoke, misheard:   Be well advised, tell o'er thy tale again:   It cannot be; thou dost but say 'tis so:   I trust I may not trust thee; for thy word   Is but the vain breath of a common man:   Believe me, I do not believe thee, man;   I have a king's oath to the contrary.
translation: It isn't true. You misspoke or misheard. Be cautious, tell your story again. It can't be true, you're just saying it's true. I trust I can't trust you, because your word is just the empty sounds made by a common man. Believe me, I don't believe you, man. I have a king's oath to do the opposite of what you say.

original: Thou shalt be punish'd for thus frighting me,   For I am sick and capable of fears,   Oppress'd with wrongs and therefore full of fears,   A widow, husbandless, subject to fears,   A woman, naturally born to fears;
translation: You will be punished for frightening me in this way, because I am sick and easy to scare and I'm a woman, naturally afraid.

original: And though thou now confess thou didst but jest,   With my vex'd spirits I cannot take a truce,   But they will quake and tremble all this day.
translation: And even if you confess now that you were only joking, I can't calm my troubled mind, but it will tremble with fear all day.

original: What dost thou mean by shaking of thy head?   Why dost thou look so sadly on my son?   What means that hand upon that breast of thine?   Why holds thine eye that lamentable rheum,   Like a proud river peering o'er his bounds?   Be these sad signs confirmers of thy words?
translation: What do you mean by shaking your head? Why do you look so sadly at my son? What does that hand on your chest mean? Why is your eye crying so sadly, like a proud river swelling over its banks? Do these sad signs confirm your words?

original: Then speak again; not all thy former tale,   But this one word, whether thy tale be true.
translation: Then speak again. Don't tell the whole story again, but say this one word: whether your story is true.

original: As true as I believe you think them false That give you cause to prove my saying true.
translation: My story is as true as you think these people's promises were false.

original: O, if thou teach me to believe this sorrow,   Teach thou this sorrow how to make me die,   And let belief and life encounter so   As doth the fury of two desperate men   Which in the very meeting fall and die.
translation: Oh, if you teach me to believe this sad thing, teach this sad thing how to kill me, and let belief and life fight like two furious, desperate men who fall and die at the moment they clash together.

original: Lewis marry Blanch! O boy, then where art thou?   France friend with England, what becomes of me?
translation: Lewis is marrying Blanch! Oh, boy, then where are you? Now that France is friends with England, what will happen to me?

original: Fellow, be gone: I cannot brook thy sight:   This news hath made thee a most ugly man.
translation: Man, go away. I can't stand the sight of you. This news has made you a very ugly man.

original: What other harm have I, good lady, done, But spoke the harm that is by others done?
translation: What harm have I done, good lady, except that I told you the harm done by others?

original: Which harm within itself so heinous is As it makes harmful all that speak of it.
translation: That harm is so terrible in itself that it makes anyone who speaks of it harmful.

original: I do beseech you, madam, be content.
translation: Please, ma'am, accept what's happened.

original: If thou, that bid'st me be content, wert grim,   Ugly and slanderous to thy mother's womb,   Full of unpleasing blots and sightless stains,   Lame, foolish, crooked, swart, prodigious,   Patch'd with foul moles and eye-offending marks,   I would not care, I then would be content,   For then I should not love thee   ,
translation: [To ARTHUR]  If you who ask me to accept this were grim, ugly, and an insult to your mother's womb, full of unpleasant blots and disgusting stains, lame, foolish, misshapen, dark, monstrous, covered in ugly moles and offensive-looking marks, I wouldn't care. Then I would accept this, because then I would not love you.

original: no, nor thou   Become thy great birth nor deserve a crown.   But thou art fair, and at thy birth, dear boy,   Nature and Fortune join'd to make thee great:   Of Nature's gifts thou mayst with lilies boast,   And with the half-blown rose.
translation: No, and you wouldn't do credit to your great family or deserve the crown. But you are handsome, and at your birth, dear boy, Nature and Fortune joined together to make you great. You can compare favorably the gifts Nature gave you with lilies and half-opened roses.

original: But Fortune, O,   She is corrupted, changed and won from thee;   She adulterates hourly with thine uncle John,   And with her golden hand hath pluck'd on France   To tread down fair respect of sovereignty,   And made his majesty the bawd to theirs.   France is a bawd to Fortune and King John,   That strumpet Fortune, that usurping John!
translation: Fortune, oh, she has been corrupted, changed, and stolen from you. She's committing adultery every hour with your uncle John, and with her golden hand has encouraged the king of France to walk all over the rightful king and made him their pimp. France is a pimp to Fortune and King John. Fortune is a prostitute and John is a thief!

original: Tell me, thou fellow, is not France forsworn?   Envenom him with words, or get thee gone   And leave those woes alone which I alone   Am bound to under-bear.
translation: [To SALISBURY]  Tell me, you fellow, hasn't the king of France broken his promise? Poison him with words, or go and leave me alone to bear the sorrows I'm the only one who has to bear.

original: Pardon me, madam, I may not go without you to the kings.
translation: I'm sorry, ma'am, I can't go to the kings without you.

original: Thou mayst, thou shalt; I will not go with thee:
translation: You can and you will. I will not go with you.

original: I will instruct my sorrows to be proud;   For grief is proud and makes his owner stoop.   To me and to the state of my great grief   Let kings assemble; for my grief's so great   That no supporter but the huge firm earth   Can hold it up:
translation: I will turn my sorrow into pride. Sadness is proud and makes its owner bow to it. Let kings assemble around me and the authority of my great sadness, because my sadness is so great that no support except the huge firm earth can hold it up.

original: 'Tis true, fair daughter; and this blessed day   Ever in France shall be kept festival:
translation: It's true, beautiful daughter, and this blessed day will always be celebrated as a festival in France.

original: To solemnize this day the glorious sun   Stays in his course and plays the alchemist,   Turning with splendor of his precious eye   The meagre cloddy earth to glittering gold:
translation: To celebrate this day the glorious sun stops in its track and acts like a scientist, turning the meager muddy earth into glittering gold with the brightness of his precious eye.

original: The yearly course that brings this day about   Shall never see it but a holiday.
translation: When this day comes up every year it will always be treated as a holiday.

original: A wicked day, and not a holy day!
translation: An evil day, not a holy day!

original: What hath this day deserved? what hath it done,   That it in golden letters should be set   Among the high tides in the calendar?
translation: What has this day deserved? What has it done to be set in  golden letters  among the saint's days on the calendar?

original: Nay, rather turn this day out of the week,   This day of shame, oppression, perjury.
translation: No, instead remove this day from the week, this day of shame, oppression, lies.

original: Or, if it must stand still, let wives with child   Pray that their burthens may not fall this day,   Lest that their hopes prodigiously be cross'd:   But on this day let seamen fear no wreck;   No bargains break that are not this day made:
translation: Or, if it must remain, let pregnant wives pray not to give birth on this day, fearing that their hopes will end in disaster. May sailors not fear shipwreck except on this day. May no bargains be broken that are not made on this day.

original: This day, all things begun come to ill end,   Yea, faith itself to hollow falsehood change!
translation: May everything begun on this day end badly, yes, may faith itself change into hollow lies!

original: By heaven, lady, you shall have no cause To curse the fair proceedings of this day: Have I not pawn'd to you my majesty?
translation: By heaven, lady, you will have no reason to curse the good things that have happened today. Haven't I sold my kingship to you?

original: You have beguiled me with a counterfeit   Resembling majesty, which, being touch'd and tried,   Proves valueless: you are forsworn, forsworn;
translation: You tricked me with a fake that looked like kingship, which, being touched and tested, proved to be worthless. You broke your oath, broke your oath.

original: You came in arms to spill mine enemies' blood,   But now in arms you strengthen it with yours:   The grappling vigour and rough frown of war   Is cold in amity and painted peace,   And our oppression hath made up this league.
translation: You came armed to spill my enemies' blood, but now you strengthen it by giving someone of your blood into their arms. The fighting strength and rough frown of war can do nothing in friendship and gaudy peace, and this alliance was made by oppressing us.

original: Arm, arm, you heavens, against these perjured kings!   A widow cries; be husband to me, heavens!   Let not the hours of this ungodly day   Wear out the day in peace; but, ere sunset,   Set armed discord 'twixt these perjured kings!   Hear me, O, hear me!
translation: To arms, heaven, to fight these lying kings! A widow cries out: be a husband to me, heaven! Don't let the hours of this unholy day use up the day peacefully. But, before sunset, make these lying kings fight again! Hear me, oh hear me!

original: Lady Constance, peace!
translation: Calm down, Lady Constance!

original: War! war! no peace! peace is to me a war   O Lymoges! O Austria! thou dost shame   That bloody spoil: thou slave, thou wretch, thou  coward!   Thou little valiant, great in villany!   Thou ever strong upon the stronger side!
translation: War! War! No peace. Peace is a war to me. Oh Lymoges! Oh Austria! You shame that bloody lion skin! You slave, you weakling, you coward! You're not very brave, but very evil! You're always acting strong on the stronger side!

original: Thou Fortune's champion that dost never fight   But when her humorous ladyship is by   To teach thee safety! thou art perjured too,   And soothest up greatness.
translation: You're Fortune's fighter, and never fight except when you can be sure that  unpredictable lady  is near to guide you to safety! You're a liar too, and you flatter great men.

original: What a fool art thou,   A ramping fool, to brag and stamp and swear   Upon my party! Thou cold-blooded slave,   Hast thou not spoke like thunder on my side,   Been sworn my soldier, bidding me depend   Upon thy stars, thy fortune and thy strength,   And dost thou now fall over to my fores?
translation: What a fool you are, a roaring fool, to brag and stamp and swear on my side! You cold-blooded slave, haven't you spoken like thunder on my behalf and sworn to be my soldier, telling me to rely on your luck, your fortune, and your strength? And now you fall over in front of me?

original: Thou wear a lion's hide! doff it for shame,   And hang a calf's-skin on those recreant limbs.
translation: You wear a lion's skin! Take it off, be ashamed of yourself, and hang a calf's skin on those cowardly limbs.

original: O, that a man should speak those words to me!
translation: Oh, I wish a man had spoken those words to me—!

original: And hang a calf's-skin on those recreant limbs.
translation: And hang a calf's skin on those cowardly limbs.

original: Thou darest not say so, villain, for thy life.
translation: You don't dare say so, you good-for-nothing—you'd be dead.

original: And hang a calf's-skin on those recreant limbs.
translation: And hang a calf's skin on those cowardly limbs.

original: We like not this; thou dost forget thyself.
translation: I don't like this. Behave yourself.

original: Here comes the holy legate of the pope.
translation: Here comes the pope's holy deputy.

original: Hail, you anointed deputies of heaven!   To thee, King John, my holy errand is.
translation: Greetings, you holy deputies of God! I have a holy message for you, King John.

original: I Pandulph, of fair Milan cardinal,   And from Pope Innocent the legate here,   Do in his name religiously demand   Why thou against the church, our holy mother,   So wilfully dost spurn;
translation: I, Pandulph, cardinal of beautiful Milan, and deputy of Pope Innocent, in his name religiously ask why you're stubbornly disobeying the church, our holy mother.

original: and force perforce   Keep Stephen Langton, chosen archbishop   Of Canterbury, from that holy see?   This, in our foresaid holy father's name,   Pope Innocent, I do demand of thee.
translation: Why are you using force to stop Stephen Langton, our chosen archbishop of Canterbury, from taking up his holy office? I ask you this in the name our holy father, Pope Innocent.

original: What earthy name to interrogatories   Can task the free breath of a sacred king?   Thou canst not, cardinal, devise a name   So slight, unworthy and ridiculous,   To charge me to an answer, as the pope.
translation: What earthly authorities can question a holy king's freedom? Cardinal, you can't think of a name more unimportant, worthless, and ridiculous to tell me to do anything as the Pope's.

original: Tell him this tale; and from the mouth of England   Add thus much more, that no Italian priest   Shall tithe or toll in our dominions;
translation: Tell him this. And tell him this much more from the king of England's mouth: that no Italian priest will tax my country.

original: But as we, under heaven, are supreme head,   So under Him that great supremacy,   Where we do reign, we will alone uphold,   Without the assistance of a mortal hand:
translation: But since I, under God, am the highest leader, I will rule my great country for God without help from any mortal.

original: So tell the pope, all reverence set apart   To him and his usurp'd authority.
translation: Tell the pope that as respectfully as he and his stolen authority deserve.

original: Brother of England, you blaspheme in this.
translation: Brother, you're speaking sinfully.

original: Though you and all the kings of Christendom   Are led so grossly by this meddling priest,   Dreading the curse that money may buy out;
translation: Although you and all the Christian kings are ordered around by this meddling priest, paying him money because you're afraid of being cursed;

original: And by the merit of vile gold, dross, dust,   Purchase corrupted pardon of a man,   Who in that sale sells pardon from himself,
translation: and since with disgusting gold, scum, and dust, you buy corrupted forgiveness from a man who will not be forgiven by God for selling it;

original: Though you and all the rest so grossly led   This juggling witchcraft with revenue cherish,
translation: and although you and the rest are ordered around and love and pay for this deceitful witchcraft

original: Yet I alone, alone do me oppose   Against the pope and count his friends my foes.
translation: —I alone, alone, oppose the pope and consider his friends my enemies.

original: Then, by the lawful power that I have,   Thou shalt stand cursed and excommunicate.   And blessed shall he be that doth revolt   From his allegiance to an heretic;
translation: Then by the lawful power I have, you will be cursed and excommunicated. And anyone who rebels against you—since you're a heretic—will be blessed.

original: And meritorious shall that hand be call'd,   Canonized and worshipped as a saint,   That takes away by any secret course   Thy hateful life.
translation: And the hand that assassinates you and takes your hateful life away will be called worthy, and will be made a saint and worshiped.

original: O, lawful let it be   That I have room with Rome to curse awhile!
translation: Oh, let it be lawful for me to curse along with Rome for a while!

original: Good father cardinal, cry thou amen   To my keen curses; for without my wrong   There is no tongue hath power to curse him right.
translation: Good father cardinal, say amen to my sharp curses. Because without including a reference to the wrong he did me, no tongue has power to curse him properly.

original: There's law and warrant, lady, for my curse.
translation: Lady, there's law and reason behind my curse.

original: And for mine too: when law can do no right,   Let it be lawful that law bar no wrong:
translation: And mine too. When law can't do right, let it be legal to do wrong.

original: Law cannot give my child his kingdom here,   For he that holds his kingdom holds the law;   Therefore, since law itself is perfect wrong,   How can the law forbid my tongue to curse?
translation: Law can't give my child his kingdom, because whoever has the kingdom is in charge of the law. So, since the law itself is completely wrong, how can the law keep me from cursing?

original: Philip of France, on peril of a curse,   Let go the hand of that arch-heretic;
translation: Philip of France, you will be cursed if you don't let go of the hand of that terrible heretic

original: And raise the power of France upon his head,   Unless he do submit himself to Rome.
translation: and attack him with all the power of France, unless he submits to Rome.

original: Look'st thou pale, France? do not let go thy hand.
translation: Do you look scared, France? Don't let go.

original: Look to that, devil; lest that France repent, And by disjoining hands, hell lose a soul.
translation: Take care that he doesn't, devil. If France repents and lets go, hell will lose a soul.

original: King Philip, listen to the cardinal.
translation: King Philip, listen to the cardinal.

original: And hang a calf's-skin on his recreant limbs.
translation: And hang a calf's skin on those cowardly limbs.

original: Well, ruffian, I must pocket up these wrongs, Because—
translation: Well, you criminal, I have to pocket these insults because—

original: Your breeches best may carry them.
translation: Your pants can carry them best.

original: Philip, what say'st thou to the cardinal?
translation: Philip, what do you say to the cardinal?

original: What should he say, but as the cardinal?
translation: What should he say except to agree with the cardinal?

original: Bethink you, father; for the difference   Is purchase of a heavy curse from Rome,   Or the light loss of England for a friend:
translation: Consider, father. The options are to suffer a painful curse from Rome or the small loss of England as a friend.

original: Forego the easier.
translation: Give up what's easiest.

original: That's the curse of Rome.
translation: That's the curse of Rome.

original: O Lewis, stand fast! the devil tempts thee here In likeness of a new untrimmed bride.
translation: Oh Lewis, be strong! The devil tempts you here in the shape of a wild new bride.

original: The Lady Constance speaks not from her faith, But from her need.
translation: The Lady Constance isn't speaking according to what she believes, but what she needs.

original: O, if thou grant my need,   Which only lives but by the death of faith,   That need must needs infer this principle,   That faith would live again by death of need.
translation: Oh, if you grant that I have needs only because you betrayed and broke faith with me, you have to agree that faith would be alive again if my needs died.

original: O then, tread down my need, and faith mounts up;   Keep my need up, and faith is trodden down!
translation: So tread my needs down and faith rises up again. Keep my needs up, and faith is trampled down!
