original: This is the prison. What is he lies here?
translation: This is the prison. Who is this lying here?

original: O death, made proud with pure and princely beauty! The earth had not a hole to hide this deed.
translation: Oh death, decorated with pure and princely beauty! The earth doesn't have a hole deep enough to hide this crime.

original: Murder, as hating what himself hath done, Doth lay it open to urge on revenge.
translation: Murder, hating what it has done, lays the body in plain sight to encourage revenge.

original: Or, when he doom'd this beauty to a grave, Found it too precious-princely for a grave.
translation: Or, when it doomed this beauty to a grave, found it too precious and royal for a grave.

original: Sir Richard, what think you? have you beheld,   Or have you read or heard? or could you think?   Or do you almost think, although you see,   That you do see?
translation: Sir Richard, what do you think? Have you seen, or have you read or heard, or could you think of, or could you even almost think of—although you see it—what you see?

original: could thought, without this object,   Form such another? This is the very top,   The height, the crest, or crest unto the crest,   Of murder's arms:
translation: C ould imagination, without seeing this, imagine anything like this? This is the top, the height, the peak, the peak of the peak, of murder's coat of arms.

original: this is the bloodiest shame,   The wildest savagery, the vilest stroke,   That ever wall-eyed wrath or staring rage   Presented to the tears of soft remorse.
translation: This is the most shameful murder, the wildest savageness, the ugliest blow, that cross-eyed anger or staring rage ever gave to the tears of gentle sadness.

original: All murders past do stand excused in this:   And this, so sole and so unmatchable,   Shall give a holiness, a purity,   To the yet unbegotten sin of times;
translation: All past murders are excused by this one. This one, so unique and unmatched, will make all the sins that haven't been committed yet seem holy and pure.

original: And prove a deadly bloodshed but a jest,   Exampled by this heinous spectacle.
translation: This makes murder seem like a joke compared to this terrible display.

original: It is a damned and a bloody work; The graceless action of a heavy hand, If that it be the work of any hand.
translation: It is a damned and bloody deed, the sinful action of an evil hand—if it's the work of any hand.

original: If that it be the work of any hand!   We had a kind of light what would ensue:   It is the shameful work of Hubert's hand;   The practise and the purpose of the king:   From whose obedience I forbid my soul,
translation: If  it's the work of any hand! We thought this might happen. It is the shameful work of Hubert's hand, the plot and idea of the king I forbid myself to obey.

original: Kneeling before this ruin of sweet life,   And breathing to his breathless excellence   The incense of a vow, a holy vow,
translation: Kneeling in front of this sweet ruined life, I breathe to his breathless excellence an incense-like promise, a holy promise,

original: Never to taste the pleasures of the world,   Never to be infected with delight,   Nor conversant with ease and idleness,   Till I have set a glory to this hand,   By giving it the worship of revenge
translation: never to indulge in worldly pleasures, never to be infected with joy or familiar with comfort and rest, until I have made my hand glorious by taking holy revenge.

original: Our souls religiously confirm thy words.
translation: Our souls say amen to your words.

original: O, he is old and blushes not at death. Avaunt, thou hateful villain, get thee gone!
translation: Oh, he's old and isn't ashamed to look at death. Go, you hateful criminal, go away!

original: I am no villain.
translation: I am no criminal!

original: Must I rob the law?
translation: Do I have to rob justice of its due by executing you myself?

original: Your sword is bright, sir; put it up again.
translation: Your sword is bright, sir. Put it away again.

original: Not till I sheathe it in a murderer's skin.
translation: Not until I sheathe it in a murderer's skin.

original: Stand back, Lord Salisbury, stand back, I say;   By heaven, I think my sword's as sharp as yours:
translation: Stand back, Lord Salisbury, stand back. By God, I think my sword is as sharp of yours.

original: I would not have you, lord, forget yourself,   Nor tempt the danger of my true defence;   Lest I, by marking of your rage, forget   Your worth, your greatness and nobility.
translation: I don't want you to act badly, my lord, or tempt me to defend myself against you. Seeing you so angry, I might forget your position, power, and nobility.

original: Out, dunghill! darest thou brave a nobleman?
translation: Get out, you pile of crap! Do you dare threaten a nobleman?

original: Not for my life: but yet I dare defend My innocent life against an emperor.
translation: No, I swear by my life. But I will fight for my innocent life even against an emperor.

original: Thou art a murderer.
translation: You are a murderer.

original: Do not prove me so; Yet I am none: whose tongue soe'er speaks false, Not truly speaks; who speaks not truly, lies.
translation: Don't make me one. But I'm not. Whoever speaks that faslehood isn't telling the truth. Whoever doesn't speak the truth is lying.

original: Cut him to pieces.
translation: Cut him to pieces.

original: Keep the peace, I say.
translation: No, keep the peace.

original: Stand by, or I shall gall you, Faulconbridge.
translation: Stand back or I'll stab you, Faulconbridge.

original: Thou wert better gall the devil, Salisbury:   If thou but frown on me, or stir thy foot,   Or teach thy hasty spleen to do me shame,   I'll strike thee dead.
translation: You'd be better off stabbing the devil, Salisbury. If you just frown at me or move your foot, or rashly insult me, I'll kill you.

original: Put up thy sword betime;   Or I'll so maul you and your toasting-iron,   That you shall think the devil is come from hell.
translation: Put away your sword now, or I'll maul you and your little skewer so badly you'll think the devil has come from hell to do it.

original: What wilt thou do, renowned Faulconbridge? Second a villain and a murderer?
translation: What will you do, famous Faulconbridge? Fight for a criminal and a murderer?

original: Lord Bigot, I am none.
translation: Lord Bigot, I am not those things.

original: Who kill'd this prince?
translation: Who killed this prince?

original: 'Tis not an hour since I left him well: I honour'd him, I loved him, and will weep My date of life out for his sweet life's loss.
translation: I left him healthy less than an hour ago. I respected him, I loved him, and I will cry for the rest of my life over the loss of his sweet life.

original: Trust not those cunning waters of his eyes,   For villany is not without such rheum;   And he, long traded in it, makes it seem   Like rivers of remorse and innocency.
translation: Don't trust the deceitful tears in his eyes because criminals can cry like that. He's been doing this for a long time and can make it seem like he's crying out of sadness and innocence.

original: Away with me, all you whose souls abhor   The uncleanly savours of a slaughter-house;   For I am stifled with this smell of sin.
translation: Let's go, everyone whose soul hates the dirty smells of a slaughter-house. I am choking on this smell of sin.

original: Away toward Bury, to the Dauphin there!
translation: Let's go to Bury, to the Dauphin there!

original: There tell the king he may inquire us out.
translation: Tell the king he can find us there.

original: Here's a good world! Knew you of this fair work? Beyond the infinite and boundless reach Of mercy, if thou didst this deed of death, Art thou damn'd, Hubert.
Do but hear me, sir.
translation: Just listen to me, sir.

original: Ha! I'll tell thee what;   Thou'rt damn'd as black—nay, nothing is so black;   Thou art more deep damn'd than Prince Lucifer:
translation: Ha! I'll tell you what. You're damned as black—no, nothing is as black—you're more deeply damned than Prince Lucifer.

original: There is not yet so ugly a fiend of hell   As thou shalt be, if thou didst kill this child.
translation: There isn't a devil in hell as ugly as you will be, if you killed this child.

original: Upon my soul—
translation: By my soul—

original: If thou didst but consent   To this most cruel act, do but despair;
translation: If you only agreed to this cruel deed, despair.

original: And if thou want'st a cord, the smallest thread   That ever spider twisted from her womb   Will serve to strangle thee, a rush will be a beam   To hang thee on;
translation: And if you don't have a rope, the smallest thread a spider ever twisted from its belly will be enough to strangle you, a piece of straw will be a beam to hang you on.

original: or wouldst thou drown thyself,   Put but a little water in a spoon,   And it shall be as all the ocean,   Enough to stifle such a villain up.   I do suspect thee very grievously.
translation: Or if you want to drown yourself, just put a little water in a spoon and it will be as big as the whole ocean, enough to drown such a criminal. I strongly suspect you.

original: If I in act, consent, or sin of thought,   Be guilty of the stealing that sweet breath
translation: If in action, in agreeing to this, or by sinning in my thoughts, I'm guilty of stealing the sweet breath

original: Which was embounded in this beauteous clay,   Let hell want pains enough to torture me.   I left him well.
translation: that was bound up in this beautiful body, hell won't contain enough tortures for me. I left him healthy.

original: Go, bear him in thine arms.   I am amazed, methinks, and lose my way   Among the thorns and dangers of this world.
translation: Go, carry him in you arms. I am lost, I think, and lose my way in the thorns and dangers of this world.

original: How easy dost thou take all England up!   From forth this morsel of dead royalty,   The life, the right and truth of all this realm   Is fled to heaven;
translation: [HUBERT picks up ARTHUR's body]  How easily you pick up all of England! From this scrap of dead royalty, the life, the justice, and the truth of this whole kingdom have flown away to heaven.

original: and England now is left   To tug and scamble and to part by the teeth   The unowed interest of proud-swelling state.   Now for the bare-pick'd bone of majesty   Doth dogged war bristle his angry crest   And snarleth in the gentle eyes of peace:
translation: England is now left to tug and quarrel and bite apart the stolen power of this proud king. Now stubborn war bristles his angry fur and snarls at peace's sweet eyes over the bare bones of majesty.

original: Now powers from home and discontents at home   Meet in one line; and vast confusion waits,   As doth a raven on a sick-fall'n beast,   The imminent decay of wrested pomp.
translation: Now foreign invaders and civil war meet to fight in a single army. And terrible confusion, like a vulture on a sick animal, waits for the king's stolen power to fall apart at any moment.

original: Now happy he whose cloak and cincture can   Hold out this tempest. Bear away that child   And follow me with speed:
translation: Now anyone whose cloak and belt can hold together in this storm is happy. Carry away that child and follow me quickly.

original: I'll to the king:   A thousand businesses are brief in hand,   And heaven itself doth frown upon the land.
translation: I'll go to the king. There are a thousand things to do now and heaven itself frowns at the country.

original: Thus have I yielded up into your hand The circle of my glory.
translation: So I have given my glorious crown to you.

original: Take again From this my hand, as holding of the pope Your sovereign greatness and authority.
translation: Take it back from me, admitting that your great power and authority comes from the Pope.

original: Now keep your holy word: go meet the French,   And from his holiness use all your power   To stop their marches 'fore we are inflamed.
translation: Now keep your holy promise: go meet the French and use all the Pope's power to stop their advance before they destroy us.

original: Our discontented counties do revolt;   Our people quarrel with obedience,   Swearing allegiance and the love of soul   To stranger blood, to foreign royalty.
translation: My unhappy counties are rebelling and my people refuse to obey, swearing allegiance and love to enemies, to foreign kings.

original: This inundation of mistemper'd humour   Rests by you only to be qualified:
translation: This flood of bad emotions can only be stopped by you.

original: Then pause not; for the present time's so sick,   That present medicine must be minister'd,   Or overthrow incurable ensues.
translation: So don't wait, because this age is so sick that medicine must be given to it immediately or it will die.

original: It was my breath that blew this tempest up,   Upon your stubborn usage of the pope;
translation: My words started this storm because you were treating the Pope badly.

original: But since you are a gentle convertite,   My tongue shall hush again this storm of war   And make fair weather in your blustering land.
translation: But now that you have converted back and are obedient, my words will end this storm of war and make good weather in your wind-blown country.

original: On this Ascension-day, remember well,   Upon your oath of service to the pope,   Go I to make the French lay down their arms.
translation: Remember that on  Ascension Day , now you've sworn loyalty to the Pope today, I'm going to make the French put down their weapons.

original: Is this Ascension-day? Did not the prophet   Say that before Ascension-day at noon   My crown I should give off?
translation: Is it Ascension Day? Didn't that prophet say that I would give away my crown before Ascension Day at noon?

original: Even so I have:   I did suppose it should be on constraint:   But, heaven be thank'd, it is but voluntary.
translation: I have done that. I thought I would be forced to do it, but, thank God, it was voluntary.

original: All Kent hath yielded; nothing there holds out   But Dover castle: London hath received,   Like a kind host, the Dauphin and his powers:
translation: All of Kent has surrendered. No one there holds out except Dover Castle. London has received the Dauphin and his army like a good host.

original: Your nobles will not hear you, but are gone   To offer service to your enemy,   And wild amazement hurries up and down   The little number of your doubtful friends.
translation: Your nobles refuse to listen to you and have gone to offer their services to your enemy, and your few remaining friends are full of doubts and wild confusion.

original: Would not my lords return to me again, After they heard young Arthur was alive?
translation: My lords wouldn't come back to me after they heard young Arthur was alive?

original: They found him dead and cast into the streets, An empty casket, where the jewel of life By some damn'd hand was robb'd and ta'en away.
translation: They found him dead and thrown into the streets, an empty box from which the jewel of life was stolen and taken away by some damned hand.

original: That villain Hubert told me he did live.
translation: That criminal Hubert told me he was alive.

original: So, on my soul, he did, for aught he knew.   But wherefore do you droop? why look you sad?
translation: He did, because he thought it was true, I swear. But why are you drooping? Why do you look sad?

original: Be great in act, as you have been in thought;   Let not the world see fear and sad distrust   Govern the motion of a kingly eye:   Be stirring as the time; be fire with fire;
translation: Act greatly, just as your thoughts have been great. Don't let the world see fear and sad worry in your kingly eyes. Be as strong as the time calls for, be fire to meet fire.

original: Threaten the threatener and outface the brow   Of bragging horror: so shall inferior eyes,   That borrow their behaviors from the great,   Grow great by your example and put on   The dauntless spirit of resolution.
translation: Threaten the threatener, and stare down boastful horror in the face. Your inferiors, who copy the behavior of great men, will follow your example and become fearless and brave.

original: Away, and glister like the god of war,   When he intendeth to become the field:   Show boldness and aspiring confidence.
translation: Go, and shine like the god of war when he wants to join a battle. Show bravery and ambitious confidence.

original: What, shall they seek the lion in his den,   And fright him there? and make him tremble there?   O, let it not be said:
translation: What, can they search for the lion in his own den and frighten him there? And make him tremble there? Oh, don't let that be said of you.

original: forage, and run   To meet displeasure farther from the doors,   And grapple with him ere he comes so nigh.
translation: Go out and run to meet anger further from your doors, and wrestle with him before he comes so close.

original: The legate of the pope hath been with me,   And I have made a happy peace with him;
translation: The Pope's messenger was with me and I have made peace with him on good terms.

original: And he hath promised to dismiss the powers   Led by the Dauphin.
translation: He has promised to send away the army led by the Dauphin.

original: O inglorious league!   Shall we, upon the footing of our land,   Send fair-play orders and make compromise,   Insinuation, parley and base truce   To arms invasive?
translation: What a shameful alliance! Will we, on our own land, play fair and make compromises, agreements, discussions, and low peace with invading armies?

original: shall a beardless boy,   A cocker'd silken wanton, brave our fields,   And flesh his spirit in a warlike soil,   Mocking the air with colours idly spread,   And find no cheque?
translation: Will a beardless boy, a childish immoral brat, dare come to our fields and wave his weapons around on our ground, mocking the air with his foolishly spread banners, and not meet with any resistance?

original: Let us, my liege, to arms:   Perchance the cardinal cannot make your peace;   Or if he do, let it at least be said   They saw we had a purpose of defence.
translation: Let's go to battle, my king. Maybe the cardinal can't make peace for you. Or if he does, at least let it be said they saw we were prepared to defend ourselves.

original: Have thou the ordering of this present time.
translation: You're in charge for now.

original: Away, then, with good courage! yet, I know, Our party may well meet a prouder foe.
translation: Go bravely then! But I know our side may well meet an even prouder enemy.

original: My Lord Melun, let this be copied out,   And keep it safe for our remembrance:
translation: Lord Melun, have this copied and keep it safe for our records.

original: Return the precedent to these lords again;   That, having our fair order written down,
translation: Return the original to these lords so that we have the agreement written down.

original: Both they and we, perusing o'er these notes,   May know wherefore we took the sacrament   And keep our faiths firm and inviolable.
translation: Then both they and we, looking over these notes, will know why we swore to remain firmly faithful to each other.

original: Upon our sides it never shall be broken.   And, noble Dauphin, albeit we swear   A voluntary zeal and an unurged faith   To your proceedings;   yet believe me, prince,
translation: We will never break this agreement. And, noble Dauphin, although we swear willingly and without you asking for it, believe me, prince,

original: I am not glad that such a sore of time   Should seek a plaster by contemn'd revolt,   And heal the inveterate canker of one wound   By making many.
translation: I'm not glad that this wound we have at this time is trying to cure itself by sinfully rebelling, which heals the endless pain of one wound by making many more.

original: O, it grieves my soul,   That I must draw this metal from my side   To be a widow-maker! O, and there   Where honourable rescue and defence   Cries out upon the name of Salisbury!
translation: Oh, I'm sad to have to draw my sword to make wives into widows! Oh, and to kill exactly the people who should be able to call on me to honorably rescue and defend them!

original: But such is the infection of the time,   That, for the health and physic of our right,   We cannot deal but with the very hand   Of stern injustice and confused wrong.   And is't not pity, O my grieved friends,   That we, the sons and children of this isle,   Were born to see so sad an hour as this;
translation: But that's the infection of this age, that in order to make justice healthy we have to act with terrible injustice and confused wrongdoing. And isn't it a pity, oh my sad friends, that we, the sons and children of this island, lived to see such a sad time as this.

original: Wherein we step after a stranger march   Upon her gentle bosom, and fill up   Her enemies' ranks,—I must withdraw and weep   Upon the spot of this enforced cause,—   To grace the gentry of a land remote,   And follow unacquainted colours here?   What, here?
translation: Do we have to follow a foreigner over this island's kind breast and fight for our country's enemies—I have to go apart and cry here where we are forced to do this—to help nobles from a foreign land and follow unknown flags here? What, here?

original: O nation, that thou couldst remove!   That Neptune's arms, who clippeth thee about,   Would bear thee from the knowledge of thyself,   And grapple thee unto a pagan shore;
translation: Oh country, I wish you could go away! I wish the sea-god's arms that surround you could carry you away so you didn't know what was happening to you, and bring you to a non-Christian shore.

original: Where these two Christian armies might combine   The blood of malice in a vein of league,   And not to spend it so unneighbourly!
translation: There, these two Christian armies could forget their anger toward each other and fight together against non-Christians, rather than expressing their anger here in such an unneighborly way!

original: A noble temper dost thou show in this;   And great affections wrestling in thy bosom   Doth make an earthquake of nobility.
translation: You show a noble character in saying this, and the great emotions wrestling in your heart make a noble earthquake.

original: O, what a noble combat hast thou fought   Between compulsion and a brave respect!   Let me wipe off this honourable dew,   That silverly doth progress on thy cheeks:
translation: Oh, you've fought such a noble battle between what you were forced to do and your brave loyalty! Let me wipe away these honorable tears that flow like silver down your cheeks.

original: My heart hath melted at a lady's tears,   Being an ordinary inundation;   But this effusion of such manly drops,   This shower, blown up by tempest of the soul,   Startles mine eyes, and makes me more amazed   Than had I seen the vaulty top of heaven   Figured quite o'er with burning meteors.
translation: My heart has melted at a woman's tears, which are an ordinary occurrence. But this flow of manly tears, this rainstorm blown off from thunderstorms in your soul, startles me and makes me more amazed than I would be if I have seen the sky covered with burning meteors.

original: Lift up thy brow, renowned Salisbury,   And with a great heart heave away the storm:   Commend these waters to those baby eyes   That never saw the giant world enraged;   Nor met with fortune other than at feasts,   Full of warm blood, of mirth, of gossiping.
translation: Look up, famous Salisbury, and bravely push away the storm. Let baby eyes cry, since they've never seen the giant world get angry or had any experience other than feasts full of energy, happiness, and gossiping.

original: Come, come; for thou shalt thrust thy hand as deep   Into the purse of rich prosperity   As Lewis himself: so, nobles, shall you all,   That knit your sinews to the strength of mine.   And even there, methinks, an angel spake:
translation: Come, come. You'll get as much money out of this as Lewis himself. So will you, nobles, who put your strength behind mine. And just now, I think, an angel speaks:

original: Look, where the holy legate comes apace,   To give us warrant from the hand of heaven
translation: Look, the holy deputy is coming quickly to give us a warrant from God

original: And on our actions set the name of right   With holy breath.
translation: and to show us that the heavens approve of our actions.

original: Hail, noble prince of France!   The next is this, King John hath reconciled   Himself to Rome; his spirit is come in,   That so stood out against the holy church,   The great metropolis and see of Rome:
translation: Greetings, noble prince of France! This is the news: King John has been reconciled with Rome. He's changed his mind since the time he stood against the holy church, the great city and authority of Rome.

original: Therefore thy threatening colours now wind up;   And tame the savage spirit of wild war,   That like a lion foster'd up at hand,   It may lie gently at the foot of peace,   And be no further harmful than in show.
translation: So put away your threatening banners and calm the savage emotion of wild war that, like a lion raised as a pet, can lie gently at peace's foot and not cause any harm, although it looks dangerous.

original: Your grace shall pardon me, I will not back:   I am too high-born to be propertied,   To be a secondary at control,   Or useful serving-man and instrument,   To any sovereign state throughout the world.
translation: I'm sorry, your grace, I won't turn back. I'm too noble to obey orders, to be second in command, or to be a useful servant and tool to any state in the world.

original: Your breath first kindled the dead coal of wars   Between this chastised kingdom and myself,   And brought in matter that should feed this fire;   And now 'tis far too huge to be blown out   With that same weak wind which enkindled it.
translation: Your breath started the fire again in the dead coals of war between this punished kingdom and me and brought wood to feed this fire. Now it's far too huge to be blown out by the same weak breath that started it.

original: You taught me how to know the face of right,   Acquainted me with interest to this land,   Yea, thrust this enterprise into my heart;   And come ye now to tell me John hath made   His peace with Rome? What is that peace to me?
translation: You taught me to know what was right, showed me my right to this country, made me want to start this. And are you coming now to tell me John made his peace with Rome? What does that peace have to do with me?

original: I, by the honour of my marriage-bed,   After young Arthur, claim this land for mine;   And, now it is half-conquer'd, must I back   Because that John hath made his peace with Rome?
translation: By the honor of my marriage-bed, I claim this country as mine after young Arthur. Now it is half-conquered, must I go back because John has made his peace with Rome?

original: Am I Rome's slave? What penny hath Rome borne,   What men provided, what munition sent,   To underprop this action? Is't not I   That undergo this charge? who else but I,   And such as to my claim are liable,   Sweat in this business and maintain this war?
translation: Am I Rome's slave? What penny has Rome contributed, what men has it provided, what equipment has it sent to support this war? Wasn't I the one who paid for this? Who else except for me and those who follow me have sweated to do this business and fight this war?

original: Have I not heard these islanders shout out   'Vive le roi!' as I have bank'd their towns?   Have I not here the best cards for the game,   To win this easy match play'd for a crown?   And shall I now give o'er the yielded set?   No, no, on my soul, it never shall be said.
translation: Haven't I heard these islanders shout out "Long live the king!" as I fortified their towns? Don't I have the best cards in this game to win this easy match that we play for a crown? And should I now give up the game I've won? No, no, I swear that will never be said of me.

original: You look but on the outside of this work.
translation: You're just considering this from the outside.

original: Outside or inside, I will not return   Till my attempt so much be glorified   As to my ample hope was promised   Before I drew this gallant head of war,
translation: Outside or inside, I won't return until I win as much as was promised to me and as much as I hoped before I drew up this army.

original: And cull'd these fiery spirits from the world,   To outlook conquest and to win renown   Even in the jaws of danger and of death.
translation: I picked these brave men out of their ordinary lives to dare to conquer and to win fame in the jaws of danger and death.

original: What lusty trumpet thus doth summon us?
translation: What loud trumpet calls for us?

original: According to the fair play of the world,   Let me have audience; I am sent to speak:
translation: According to fair play, let me talk to you. I have been sent as a messenger.

original: My holy lord of Milan, from the king   I come, to learn how you have dealt for him;   And, as you answer, I do know the scope   And warrant limited unto my tongue.
translation: My holy lord of Milan, I come from the king to learn how you have negotiated for him. Depending on your answer, I know what I am allowed to say.

original: The Dauphin is too wilful-opposite, And will not temporize with my entreaties; He flatly says he'll not lay down his arms.
translation: The Dauphin is stubbornly opposing me and won't do what I beg him to. He bluntly says he won't lay down his weapons.

original: By all the blood that ever fury breathed,   The youth says well. Now hear our English king;   For thus his royalty doth speak in me.
translation: By all the blood that anger ever breathed, the young man speaks well. Now listen to our English king because I speak for him.

original: He is prepared, and reason too he should:   This apish and unmannerly approach,   This harness'd masque and unadvised revel,   This unhair'd sauciness and boyish troops,   The king doth smile at;
translation: H e is prepared, and there's good reason he should be: the king laughs at this apelike and rude approach, this costume dance with armor, this unwise game, this hairless boldness, this boyish army.

original: and is well prepared   To whip this dwarfish war, these pigmy arms,   From out the circle of his territories.
translation: He's well prepared to whip this dwarf-like war and these pygmy weapons, out of his territory.

original: That hand which had the strength, even at your door,   To cudgel you and make you take the hatch,   To dive like buckets in concealed wells,   To crouch in litter of your stable planks,   To lie like pawns lock'd up in chests and trunks,   To hug with swine, to seek sweet safety out   In vaults and prisons, and to thrill and shake   Even at the crying of your nation's crow,   Thinking his voice an armed Englishman;
translation: His hand had the strength, at your own door, to beat you and make you leap out the door, to dive like buckets into wells and hide, to crouch on your dirty stable floors, to lie like pawned objects locked up in chests and trunks, to hug pigs, to look for sweet safety in tombs and prisons, and to tremble at the cry of one of your country's crows, thinking his voice was an armed Englishman.

original: Shall that victorious hand be feebled here,   That in your chambers gave you chastisement?   No: know the gallant monarch is in arms   And like an eagle o'er his aery towers,   To souse annoyance that comes near his nest.
translation: Will the conquering hand that punished you in your own rooms be made weak here? No. You should know the brave king is armed and hovers like an eagle over his nest to get rid of annoyances that come near it.

original: And you degenerate, you ingrate revolts,   You bloody Neroes, ripping up the womb   Of your dear mother England, blush for shame;
translation: You corrupted, ungrateful rebels, you bloody tyrants  ripping up the womb  of your dear mother England, blush with shame.

original: For your own ladies and pale-visaged maids   Like Amazons come tripping after drums,   Their thimbles into armed gauntlets change,   Their needles to lances, and their gentle hearts   To fierce and bloody inclination.
translation: Your own wives and pale-faced daughters are tripping after drums like  Amazonian  warriors, changing their thimbles into armored gloves, their needles into lances, and their sweet hearts into fierce and bloody tendencies.

original: There end thy brave, and turn thy face in peace;   We grant thou canst outscold us:
translation: Stop your bragging there and get away from us unharmed. I admit you're better at scolding than I am.

original: fare thee well;   We hold our time too precious to be spent   With such a brabbler.
translation: Goodbye. My time is worth too much to be spent with such a babbler.

original: Give me leave to speak.
translation: Let me speak.

original: No, I will speak.
translation: No, I will speak.

original: We will attend to neither. Strike up the drums; and let the tongue of war Plead for our interest and our being here.
translation: I won't listen to either of you. Strike the drums, and let war's mouth announce my claim and my reason for being here.

original: Indeed your drums, being beaten, will cry out;   And so shall you, being beaten: do but start   An echo with the clamour of thy drum,   And even at hand a drum is ready braced   That shall reverberate all as loud as thine;
translation: Yes, your drums will cry out when they're beaten. And so will you, when you're beaten. Just start an echo with the sound of your drum and close by a drum is ready to echo it back just as loud.

original: Sound but another, and another shall   As loud as thine rattle the welkin's ear   And mock the deep-mouth'd thunder:
translation: Beat another, and another will rattle the sky's ear as loudly as yours and imitate loud thunder.

original: for at hand,   Not trusting to this halting legate here,   Whom he hath used rather for sport than need   Is warlike John;
translation: John is nearby, ready for war, not trusting  this clumsy deputy  he made use of because it amused him, not out of necessity.

original: and in his forehead sits   A bare-ribb'd death, whose office is this day   To feast upon whole thousands of the French.
translation: On his forehead sits a skeleton death, whose job today is to feast on thousands of the French.

original: Strike up our drums, to find this danger out.
translation: Beat our drums to find this danger.

original: And thou shalt find it, Dauphin, do not doubt.
translation: And you will find it, Dauphin, don't doubt it.

original: How goes the day with us? O, tell me, Hubert.
translation: How is the battle going? Oh, tell me, Hubert.

original: Badly, I fear. How fares your majesty?
translation: Badly, I'm afraid. How are you, your majesty?

original: This fever, that hath troubled me so long, Lies heavy on me; O, my heart is sick!
translation: This fever I've suffered from so long is weighing on me. Oh, my heart is sick!

original: My lord, your valiant kinsman, Faulconbridge, Desires your majesty to leave the field And send him word by me which way you go.
translation: My lord, your brave relative, Faulconbridge, wants you to leave the battlefield and send me back to tell him which way you're going.

original: Tell him, toward Swinstead, to the abbey there.
translation: Tell him toward Swinstead, to the abbey there.

original: Be of good comfort; for the great supply   That was expected by the Dauphin here,   Are wreck'd three nights ago on Goodwin Sands.
translation: Don't worry; the many reinforcements expected by the Dauphin here were shipwrecked three nights ago on  Goodwin Sands .

original: This news was brought to Richard but even now:   The French fight coldly, and retire themselves.
translation: Richard heard the news just now. The French aren't fighting enthusiastically and they're retreating.

original: Ay me! this tyrant fever burns me up,   And will not let me welcome this good news.
translation: Oh poor me! This tyrant of a fever burns me up and won't let me feel happy at this good news.

original: Set on toward Swinstead: to my litter straight;   Weakness possesseth me, and I am faint.
translation: Go on toward Swinstead. Take me to my stretcher. I'm overcome by weakness and feel faint.

original: I did not think the king so stored with friends.
translation: I didn't think the king had so many friends.

original: Up once again; put spirit in the French: If they miscarry, we miscarry too.
translation: Let's pick ourselves back up. Encourage the French. If they are defeated we are too.

original: That misbegotten devil, Faulconbridge, In spite of spite, alone upholds the day.
translation: That illegitimate devil Faulconbridge is winning the battle despite everything.

original: They say King John sore sick hath left the field.
translation: They say King John left the battlefield very sick.

original: Lead me to the revolts of England here.
translation: Take me to the English rebels here.

original: When we were happy we had other names.
translation: When we were happy we were called something else.

original: It is the Count Melun.
translation: It's the Count Melun.

original: Wounded to death.
translation: Fatally wounded.

original: Fly, noble English, you are bought and sold;   Unthread the rude eye of rebellion   And welcome home again discarded faith.   Seek out King John and fall before his feet;
translation: Run away, English nobles, you've made a bad bargain. Unthread rebellion's needle and welcome back your discarded loyalty. Find King John and fall to his feet.

original: For if the French be lords of this loud day,   He means to recompense the pains you take   By cutting off your heads: thus hath he sworn   And I with him, and many moe with me,   Upon the altar at Saint Edmundsbury;
translation: Because if the French prince wins this fierce battle he means to reward the work you did by cutting off your heads. He swore this, and so did I and many more people too, on the altar at Saint Edmundsbury

original: Even on that altar where we swore to you   Dear amity and everlasting love.
translation: —yes, the same altar where we swore dear friendship and eternal love to you.

original: May this be possible? may this be true?
translation: Is this possible? Is this true?

original: Have I not hideous death within my view,   Retaining but a quantity of life,   Which bleeds away, even as a form of wax   Resolveth from his figure 'gainst the fire?
translation: Am I not about to die horribly? Don't I have just a small amount of life left, which bleeds away like a wax statue losing its shape in front of a fire?

original: What in the world should make me now deceive,   Since I must lose the use of all deceit?   Why should I then be false, since it is true   That I must die here and live hence by truth?
translation: What in the world would make me lie now, since I have to give up all lying? Why would I be dishonest, since it's true I have to die here and from now on I have to just tell the truth?

original: I say again, if Lewis do win the day,   He is forsworn, if e'er those eyes of yours   Behold another day break in the east:
translation: I tell you again, if Lewis wins the battle he will break his promise to you if those eyes of yours live to see another day break in the east.

original: But even this night, whose black contagious breath   Already smokes about the burning crest   Of the old, feeble and day-wearied sun,   Even this ill night, your breathing shall expire,
translation: Or you might die tonight—the night's black unhealthy breath already smokes around the burning top of the old, weak sun worn out from day, and if you keep fighting your breathing will end.

original: Paying the fine of rated treachery   Even with a treacherous fine of all your lives,   If Lewis by your assistance win the day.
translation: You'll pay the price of costly betrayal by being betrayed and killed if Lewis wins this battle with your help.

original: Commend me to one Hubert with your king:   The love of him, and this respect besides,   For that my grandsire was an Englishman,   Awakes my conscience to confess all this.
translation: Send my love to a certain Hubert, who's with your king.  Love for him and the fact that my grandfather was an Englishman make me feel I should confess all this.

original: In lieu whereof, I pray you, bear me hence   From forth the noise and rumour of the field,   Where I may think the remnant of my thoughts   In peace, and part this body and my soul   With contemplation and devout desires.
translation: So in exchange for this, I beg you, carry me away from the noise of the battlefield to somewhere I can think my last thoughts in peace, and part my soul from this body with thoughtfulness and holy wishes.

original: We do believe thee: and beshrew my soul   But I do love the favour and the form   Of this most fair occasion, by the which   We will untread the steps of damned flight,
translation: We believe you. And damn me, I love this beautiful opportunity given to us to go back on the steps of our damned betrayal.

original: And like a bated and retired flood,   Leaving our rankness and irregular course,   Stoop low within those bounds we have o'erlook'd   And cabby run on in obedience   Even to our ocean, to our great King John.
translation: Like a flood that has ended and drawn back, we'll leave our wild and unusual course, stoop low into the restraints we've escaped from, and run on obediently to our ocean, to our great King John.

original: My arm shall give thee help to bear thee hence;   For I do see the cruel pangs of death   Right in thine eye. Away, my friends! New flight;   And happy newness, that intends old righ
translation: My arm will help to carry you away because I see you're dying. Let's go, my friends! This is a new betrayal, but a happy newness that goes back to old right actions.

original: The sun of heaven methought was loath to set,   But stay'd and made the western welkin blush,   When English measure backward their own ground   In faint retire.
translation: I thought the sun seemed reluctant to set, and instead stayed and made the western sky blush when the English retreated weakly over their own ground.

original: O, bravely came we off,   When with a volley of our needless shot,   After such bloody toil, we bid good night;
translation: We came off bravely when, shooting unnecessarily after them, we said good night after such bloody work

original: And wound our tattering colours clearly up,   Last in the field, and almost lords of it!
translation: and wrapped our ripped banners up, last on the battlefield and almost winners of it!

original: Where is my prince, the Dauphin?
translation: Where is my prince, the Dauphin?

original: Here: what news?
translation: Here: what news do you have?

original: The Count Melun is slain; the English lords   By his persuasion are again fall'n off,
translation: The Count Melun has been killed. He persuaded the English lords to desert.

original: And your supply, which you have wish'd so long,   Are cast away and sunk on Goodwin Sands.
translation: Your reinforcements that you've waited for so long have been shipwrecked and sunk on Goodwin Sands.

original: Ah, foul shrewd news! beshrew thy very heart!   I did not think to be so sad to-night   As this hath made me.
translation: Oh, terrible bad news! Damn your heart! I didn't think I'd be as sad tonight as this news made me.

original: Who was he that said   King John did fly an hour or two before   The stumbling night did part our weary powers?
translation: Who was it who said King John ran away an hour or two before our tired armies stopped fighting for the night?

original: Whoever spoke it, it is true, my lord.
translation: Whoever said it, it's true, my lord.

original: Well; keep good quarter and good care to-night: The day shall not be up so soon as I, To try the fair adventure of to-morrow.
translation: Well. Sleep well and take care tonight. The sun won't be up as soon as I am to see what luck tomorrow will bring us.

original: Who's there? speak, ho! speak quickly, or I shoot.
translation: Who's there? Speak! Speak quickly or I'll shoot.

original: A friend. What art thou?
translation: A friend. Who are you?

original: Of the part of England.
translation: I'm on the English side.

original: Whither dost thou go?
translation: Where are you going?

original: What's that to thee? why may not I demand Of thine affairs, as well as thou of mine?
translation: Why does it matter to you? Why can't I ask you about what you're doing instead of you asking me that?

original: Hubert, I think?
translation: Hubert, I think?

original: Thou hast a perfect thought:   I will upon all hazards well believe   Thou art my friend,
translation: Your guess is correct. I will guess you are my friend

original: that know'st my tongue so well.   Who art thou?
translation: since you know my voice so well. Who are you?

original: Who thou wilt: and if thou please, Thou mayst befriend me so much as to think I come one way of the Plantagenets.
translation: Whoever you want, and if you want you can consider me a friend because I am descended from the Plantagenets on one side.

original: Unkind remembrance! thou and eyeless night   Have done me shame:
translation: A cruel reminder! You and the dark night have shamed me.

original: brave soldier, pardon me,   That any accent breaking from thy tongue   Should 'scape the true acquaintance of mine ear.
translation: Brave soldier, forgive me for my ear not recognizing any sound coming from your mouth.

original: Come, come; sans compliment, what news abroad?
translation: Come on, come on. Don't bother complimenting me—what news is there?

original: Why, here walk I in the black brow of night, To find you out.
translation: I'm walking here under the black forehead of night to find you.

original: Brief, then; and what's the news?
translation: In short, then: what's the news?

original: O, my sweet sir, news fitting to the night, Black, fearful, comfortless and horrible.
translation: Oh, my dear sir, news fitting to the night, black, frightening, without comfort, and horrible.

original: Show me the very wound of this ill news: I am no woman, I'll not swoon at it.
translation: Show me the wound of this bad news. I'm not a woman, I won't faint at it.

original: The king, I fear, is poison'd by a monk:   I left him almost speechless;
translation: I'm afraid the king has been poisoned by a monk. When I left he was almost speechless.

original: and broke out   To acquaint you with this evil, that you might   The better arm you to the sudden time,   Than if you had at leisure known of this.
translation: I left to tell you about this evil deed so you could prepare yourself better for this sudden occurrence than if you learned about it later.

original: How did he take it? who did taste to him?
A monk, I tell you; a resolved villain, Whose bowels suddenly burst out: the king Yet speaks and peradventure may recover.
translation: A monk, I tell you. A resolved criminal whose guts suddenly burst out. The king is still speaking and may get better.

original: Who didst thou leave to tend his majesty?
translation: Who did you leave to take care of him?

original: Why, know you not? the lords are all come back,   And brought Prince Henry in their company;
translation: Don't you know? The lords have all come back and they brought Prince Henry with them.

original: At whose request the king hath pardon'd them,   And they are all about his majesty.
translation: At his request the king pardoned them and they are all with him.

original: Withhold thine indignation, mighty heaven,   And tempt us not to bear above our power!   I'll tell thee, Hubert, half my power this night,   Passing these flats, are taken by the tide;
translation: Hold back your anger, great heaven, and don't tempt me to act beyond my power! I'll tell you, Hubert, half my army was shipwrecked passing these rocks tonight.

original: It is too late: the life of all his blood   Is touch'd corruptibly, and his pure brain,   Which some suppose the soul's frail dwelling-house,
translation: It's too late. His blood is too infected and his pure brain, which is where some people think the soul lives,

original: Doth by the idle comments that it makes   Foretell the ending of mortality.
translation: shows that he's going to die by the meaningless comments it makes.

original: His highness yet doth speak, and holds belief   That, being brought into the open air,
translation: The king still speaks and believes that if he were brought outside,

original: It would allay the burning quality   Of that fell poison which assaileth him.
translation: the open air would calm the burning of the deadly poison that attacks him.

original: Let him be brought into the orchard here. Doth he still rage?
translation: Have him brought into the orchard here. Is he still talking crazily?

original: He is more patient Than when you left him; even now he sung.
translation: He's calmer than when you left him. He was singing just now.

original: O vanity of sickness! fierce extremes   In their continuance will not feel themselves.
translation: Oh, that's the nonsense of sickness! Fierce extremes come one after the other, without him realizing it.

original: Death, having prey'd upon the outward parts,   Leaves them invisible, and his siege is now   Against the mind, the which he pricks and wounds   With many legions of strange fantasies,   Which, in their throng and press to that last hold,   Confound themselves.
translation: Death, having preyed on the outer parts of the body, invisibly leaves them and now attacks the mind, which he stabs and wounds with many troops of strange delusions that, as they crowd and push towards that last fortress, confuse each other.

original: 'Tis strange that death   should sing.   I am the cygnet to this pale faint swan,   Who chants a doleful hymn to his own death,
translation: It's strange that death would sing. I am the  cygnet  of  this pale weak swan  that chants a sad hymn about his own death

original: And from the organ-pipe of frailty sings   His soul and body to their lasting rest.
translation: and, using his weakness as an instrument to accompany him, sings his body and soul to eternal sleep.

original: Be of good comfort, prince; for you are born To set a form upon that indigest Which he hath left so shapeless and so rude.
translation: Take comfort, prince. You were born to give shape to the shapeless and rough mess he's left behind.

original: Ay, marry, now my soul hath elbow-room;   It would not out at windows nor at doors.
translation: Oh good, now my soul has elbow-room. It wouldn't leave from windows or doors.

original: There is so hot a summer in my bosom,   That all my bowels crumble up to dust:
translation: There's so hot a summer in my chest that all my intestines crumble into dust.

original: I am a scribbled form, drawn with a pen   Upon a parchment, and against this fire   Do I shrink up.
translation: I am a scribbled shape drawn with a pen on parchment and I shrivel up in the fire.

original: How fares your majesty?
translation: How are you, your majesty?

original: Poison'd,—ill fare—dead, forsook, cast off:   And none of you will bid the winter come   To thrust his icy fingers in my maw,
translation: Poisoned—bad food—dead, abandoned, thrown away. None of you is willing to ask the winter to come shove his icy fingers in my mouth

original: Nor let my kingdom's rivers take their course   Through my burn'd bosom, nor entreat the north   To make his bleak winds kiss my parched lips   And comfort me with cold.
translation: or let my kingdom's rivers run through my burned chest or beg the north to make his cold winds kiss my dry lips and comfort me with cold.

original: I do not ask you much,   I beg cold comfort; and you are so strait   And so ingrateful, you deny me that.
translation: I don't ask you much, I beg for cold comfort. And yet you're so greedy and ungrateful that you deny me that.

original: O that there were some virtue in my tears, That might relieve you!
translation: Oh, I wish my tears were medicine that could help you!

original: The salt in them is hot.   Within me is a hell;
translation: The salt in them is hot. There's a hell inside me.

original: and there the poison   Is as a fiend confined to tyrannize   On unreprievable condemned blood.
translation: The poison is like a devil locked up in there. It's torturing my blood as if the blood were sinners in Hell who would never be forgiven by God, condemned to suffer forever.

original: O, I am scalded with my violent motion, And spleen of speed to see your majesty!
translation: Oh, I'm sweating after rushing here to see you, your majesty!

original: O cousin, thou art come to set mine eye:   The tackle of my heart is crack'd and burn'd,   And all the shrouds wherewith my life should sail   Are turned to one thread, one little hair:
translation: Oh cousin, you've come to shut my eye. The rope of my heart is cracked and burned, and all the sails of my life's boat now hang by one thread, one little hair.

original: My heart hath one poor string to stay it by,   Which holds but till thy news be uttered;   And then all this thou seest is but a clod   And module of confounded royalty.
translation: My heart has one poor string to set its course with, which will only hold until you tell your news. Then all you see here will just be a lump and a mess of disordered royalty.

original: The Dauphin is preparing hitherward,   Where heaven He knows how we shall answer him;
translation: The Dauphin is preparing to come here, where God knows we'll fight him.

original: For in a night the best part of my power,   As I upon advantage did remove,   Were in the Washes all unwarily   Devoured by the unexpected flood.
translation: Tonight I moved most of my army to a more strategic position and they were all drowned unexpectedly in the marshes.

original: You breathe these dead news in as dead an ear. My liege! my lord! but now a king, now thus.
translation: You say this dead news in an ear that's just as dead. My king! My lord! Just now he was a king, now he's this.

original: Even so must I run on, and even so stop. What surety of the world, what hope, what stay, When this was now a king, and now is clay?
translation: I too must run on like this and stop like this. What certainty is there in the world, what hope, what security, when this was a king until just before now, and now is clay?

original: Art thou gone so? I do but stay behind   To do the office for thee of revenge,   And then my soul shall wait on thee to heaven,   As it on earth hath been thy servant still.
translation: [To KING JOHN's body]  Are you gone? I only stay behind to take revenge for you; then my soul will accompany you to heaven just as it was always your servant on earth.

original: Now, now, you stars that move in your right spheres,   Where be your powers?
translation: Now, now, you nobles like stars that now move in your proper trajectories, where is your army?

original: show now your mended faiths,   And instantly return with me again,   To push destruction and perpetual shame   Out of the weak door of our fainting land.
translation: Show your new loyalty and come back with me now to push destruction and eternal shame out of the weak door of our fainting country.

original: Straight let us seek, or straight we shall be sought;   The Dauphin rages at our very heels.
translation: Let's attack immediately, or we will be attacked immediately. The Dauphin is biting at our heels.

original: It seems you know not, then, so much as we:   The Cardinal Pandulph is within at rest,
translation: It seems you don't know as much as we do, then. The Cardinal Pandulph is inside sleeping.

original: Who half an hour since came from the Dauphin,   And brings from him such offers of our peace   As we with honour and respect may take,   With purpose presently to leave this wa
translation: Half an hour ago he came from the Dauphin and brings from him offers of peace that we can accept with honor and respect. He wants to stop fighting at once.

original: He will the rather do it when he sees Ourselves well sinewed to our defence.
translation: He will do it more willingly when he sees us well-prepared to defend ourselves.

original: Nay, it is in a manner done already;   For many carriages he hath dispatch'd   To the sea-side, and put his cause and quarrel   To the disposing of the cardinal:
translation: No, in a way it's already done because he's sent most of his army to the seashore, and given his cause and demands to the cardinal to negotiate for him.

original: With whom yourself, myself and other lords,   If you think meet, this afternoon will post   To consummate this business happily.
translation: If you think it right, you and me and other lords will hurry to the cardinal this afternoon to end this business well.

original: Let it be so: and you, my noble prince, With other princes that may best be spared, Shall wait upon your father's funeral.
translation: Very well. And you, my noble prince, will attend your father's funeral along with the other noblemen we can spare most easily.

original: At Worcester must his body be interr'd; For so he will'd it.
translation: His body must be buried at Windsor; that's what he wanted.

original: Thither shall it then:   And happily may your sweet self put on   The lineal state and glory of the land!
translation: It will be taken there then. And may you yourself happily take on your inherited power over this country!

original: To whom with all submission, on my knee   I do bequeath my faithful services   And true subjection everlastingly.
translation: [Kneels]  I promise you on my knee to serve you obediently and always to be a faithful subjec

original: And the like tender of our love we make, To rest without a spot for evermore.
translation: And I make the same promise of pure love that will go on forever.

original: I have a kind soul that would give you thanks And knows not how to do it but with tears.
translation: My soul thanks you, and I'm the sort of person who doesn't know how to thank you except by crying.

original: O, let us pay the time but needful woe,   Since it hath been beforehand with our griefs.
translation: Oh, let's be as sad as we need to at this time, since it has given us a lot to be sad about.

original: This England never did, nor never shall,   Lie at the proud foot of a conqueror,   But when it first did help to wound itself.
translation: This England never did and never will lie at the foot of a proud conqueror, except when it has first helped him by wounding itself.

original: Now these her princes are come home again,   Come the three corners of the world in arms,   And we shall shock them. Nought shall make us rue,   If England to itself do rest but true.
translation: Now that its nobles have come home again, let the three corners of the world come to fight us, and we'll destroy them. Nothing will hurt us if England just stays faithful to itself.

original: Let fame, that all hunt after in their lives,   Live register'd upon our brazen tombs   And then grace us in the disgrace of death;
translation: Fame, the thing that we all want in our lives, should be engraved brazenly onto our tombs, commanding us respect even after death has destroyed us.

original: When, spite of cormorant devouring Time,   The endeavor of this present breath may buy   That honour which shall bate his scythe's keen edge   And make us heirs of all eternity.
translation: In spite of time's quick passing, the things we have done while alive can embolden us to fight honorably against death and ensure we are remembered forever.

original: Therefore, brave conquerors,—for so you are,   That war against your own affections   And the huge army of the world's desires,—   Our late edict shall strongly stand in force:
translation: Therefore, my brave  conquerors , for that is what you are, our recent agreement will be binding and help us to fight the war against our own passions and the desires of this great world.

original: Navarre shall be the wonder of the world;   Our court shall be a little Academe,   Still and contemplative in living art.
translation: Navarre  will be the wonder of the world. Our court will be like a little university, a place to stop and think about how to live our lives.

original: You three, Biron, Dumain, and Longaville,   Have sworn for three years' term to live with me   My fellow-scholars, and to keep those statutes   That are recorded in this schedule here:
translation: You three men, Biron, Dumain and Longaville, have promised to stay with me for three years as my fellow scholars, and to obey the rules that are written down in this agreement here.

original: Your oaths are pass'd; and now subscribe your names,   That his own hand may strike his honour down   That violates the smallest branch herein:
translation: Your oaths have been pledged and now you must sign your names, so that if you break even the smallest detail of this agreement, you will have lost your honor by your own hand.

original: If you are arm'd to do as sworn to do,   Subscribe to your deep oaths, and keep it too.
translation: If you are prepared to do what is written here, then sign your names and keep these promises.

original: I am resolved; 'tis but a three years' fast:
translation: I will do it; it is only three years!

original: The mind shall banquet, though the body pine:
translation: My mind will indulge in knowledge, even when my body goes hungry.

original: Fat paunches have lean pates, and dainty bits   Make rich the ribs, but bankrupt quite the wits.
translation: Fat people are stupid, and delicious things makes the stomach larger, but intelligence and wit smaller.

original: My loving lord, Dumain is mortified:
translation: My loving lord, I am embarrassed by these things.

original: The grosser manner of these world's delights   He throws upon the gross world's baser slaves:
translation: The rude nature of these worldly pleasures should be left for the lowlifes of this world, like slaves.

original: To love, to wealth, to pomp, I pine and die;   With all these living in philosophy.
translation: Let them love, indulge and do extravagant things, I will suffer and die with all the people who have chosen knowledge and wisdom instead.

original: I can but say their protestation over;
translation: Now that they have finished talking, I feel that I have to say something.

original: So much, dear liege, I have already sworn,   That is, to live and study here three years.
translation: My dear lord, I have already promised to study here with you for three years.

original: But there are other strict observances;   As, not to see a woman in that term,   Which I hope well is not enrolled there;
translation: But as to the other things which you want us to promise: to not see a woman this entire time, which I hope is not written there;

original: And one day in a week to touch no food   And but one meal on every day beside,   The which I hope is not enrolled there;
translation: to fast for one day a week and to only eat one meal every other day, which I also hope is not written there;

original: And then, to sleep but three hours in the night,   And not be seen to wink of all the day—   When I was wont to think no harm all night   And make a dark night too of half the day—   Which I hope well is not enrolled there:
translation: to only sleep for three hours every night and to not close your eyes at all during the day, when all I want is to sleep all night and for half of the day as well, I hope is not written there!

original: O, these are barren tasks, too hard to keep,   Not to see ladies, study, fast, not sleep!
translation: Oh these tasks are pointless and will be too hard to keep, not to see women, to study, and to not even eat or sleep!

original: Your oath is pass'd to pass away from these.
translation: In your oath you promise to give up these things.

original: Let me say no, my liege, an if you please: I only swore to study with your grace And stay here in your court for three years' space.
translation: Then I must say no, my lord, since I only promised to study with you and stay in your court for three years.

original: You swore to that, Biron, and to the rest.
translation: You swore to more than that Biron.

original: By yea and nay, sir, then I swore in jest. What is the end of study? let me know.
translation: Perhaps I did, sir, but I was only joking. Tell me, what is the point of this study?

original: Why, that to know, which else we should not know.
translation: Well, of course, to know things that we didn't know before.

original: Things hid and barr'd, you mean, from common sense?
translation: Are you talking about things that common sense hides and conceals from us?

original: Ay, that is study's godlike recompense.
translation: Why yes, that is the divine advantage of study.

original: Come on, then; I will swear to study so,   To know the thing I am forbid to know:
translation: Okay then, I will promise to study as you wish, and will hopefully find out the things which I am not meant to know.

original: As thus,—to study where I well may dine,   When I to feast expressly am forbid;
translation: It shall be like this: I must study where I eat, even though I am now forbidden to eat at all;

original: Or study where to meet some mistress fine,   When mistresses from common sense are hid;
translation: I must study where I could meet beautiful women, as all beautiful women are hidden from common sense.

original: Or, having sworn too hard a keeping oath,   Study to break it and not break my troth.
translation: Or, if I have committed myself to an oath which is too hard to keep, I must learn how to break it without breaking my faith.

original: If study's gain be thus and this be so,   Study knows that which yet it doth not know:   Swear me to this, and I will ne'er say no.
translation: If this is the purpose of study, then studying has a lot to learn itself! Come on then, I will swear to this oath, and I will never say no to anything.

original: These be the stops that hinder study quite And train our intellects to vain delight.
translation: These things are the obstacles that stop us from studying and tempt our minds to pointless pleasures.

original: Why, all delights are vain; but that most vain,   Which with pain purchased doth inherit pain:   As, painfully to pore upon a book   To seek the light of truth;
translation: Well aren't all pleasures pointless? Although the most pointless, the thing which requires work to get, and also comes with suffering and difficulty, is the effort required to make sense of a book to search for the truth.

original: while truth the while   Doth falsely blind the eyesight of his look:   Light seeking light doth light of light beguile:
translation: Your vision is clouded by lies and treachery;  eyes, which are searching for knowledge, often make themselves  unable to see properly .

original: So, ere you find where light in darkness lies,   Your light grows dark by losing of your eyes.
translation: So, before you can find the skill to understand obscure knowledge, you lose the ability to understand anything because your eyes no longer work.

original: Study me how to please the eye indeed   By fixing it upon a fairer eye,   Who dazzling so, that eye shall be his heed   And give him light that it was blinded by.
translation: Let me study how to please an eye instead, by giving me a beautiful woman's eye to gaze into, I will be dazzled, and that more beautiful eye will be my focus and will give me back the power to see.

original: Study is like the heaven's glorious sun   That will not be deep-search'd with saucy looks:
translation: Study is like the sun, it shouldn't be looked at with rude glances

original: Small have continual plodders ever won   Save base authority from others' books
translation: —people who constantly do dull work have never learnt much, except common material from other people's books.

original: These earthly godfathers of heaven's lights   That give a name to every fixed star   Have no more profit of their shining nights   Than those that walk and wot not what they are.
translation: The astronomers who have named every star don't get any greater benefits from the shining night sky, than the people who walk around and don't know what any of them are.

original: Too much to know is to know nought but fame;   And every godfather can give a name.
translation: People who know too much, only learn for the fame it brings them, but  anyone can have a name .

original: How well he's read, to reason against reading!
translation: How intelligent he must be, to even argue against reading!

original: Proceeded well, to stop all good proceeding!
He weeds the corn and still lets grow the weeding.
The spring is near when green geese are a-breeding.
How follows that?
translation: What is the next line?

original: Fit in his place and time.
translation: Something appropriate to its place and time.

original: In reason nothing.
translation: There is nothing in reason.

original: Something then in rhyme.
translation: Then follow with something in rhyme.

original: Biron is like an envious sneaping frost, That bites the first-born infants of the spring.
translation: Biron is like an evil, biting frost, that eats away at spring's young flowers.

original: Well, say I am; why should proud summer boast   Before the birds have any cause to sing?
translation: Well what if I am? Why should the arrogant summer show off before the birds have a reason to sing?

original: Why should I joy in any abortive birth?
translation: Why should I enjoy such an unnatural event?

original: At Christmas I no more desire a rose   Than wish a snow in May's new-fangled mirth;   But like of each thing that in season grows.
translation: When it is Christmas, I don't hope to see a rose; when it is May and the ground is covered in flowers I don't hope to see snow—I simply enjoy the things that do grow in that season.

original: So you, to study now it is too late,   Climb o'er the house to unlock the little gate.
translation: This is the same as your decision to study now,  it is completely pointless.

original: Well, sit you out: go home, Biron: adieu.
translation: Fine, don't sign the oath. Go home, Biron, see you later.

original: No, my good lord; I have sworn to stay with you:
translation: No, my good lord. I have promised to stay with you.

original: And though I have for barbarism spoke more   Than for that angel knowledge you can say,
translation: Even though I have spoken more against this study, than you have been able to in favor of this "divine knowledge,"

original: Yet confident I'll keep what I have swore   And bide the penance of each three years' day.
translation: I am confident that I will stick to this oath, and endure this punishment every day for three years.

original: Give me the paper; let me read the same;   And to the strict'st decrees I'll write my name.
translation: Come on, give me the paper. I will read these promises and then sign my name to these extreme rules.

original: How well this yielding rescues thee from shame!
translation: At least it saves you from the shame of not agreeing!

original: 'Item, That no woman shall come within a mile of my court:' Hath this been proclaimed?
translation: "The first item—that no woman will come within a mile of my court." Has this been announced?

original: Four days ago.
translation: Four days ago.

original: Let's see the penalty.
translation: Let's see what the punishment would be.

original: 'On pain of losing her tongue.' Who devised this  penalty?
translation: "She would lose her tongue." Who came up with this punishment?!

original: Marry, that did I.
translation: That was me.

original: Sweet lord, and why?
translation: Why, sweet friend?

original: To fright them hence with that dread penalty.
translation: To scare them off with such a harsh punishment.

original: A dangerous law against gentility!
translation: This is a dangerous law that goes against good manners.

original: 'Item, If any man be seen to talk with a woman   within the term of three years, he shall endure such   public shame as the rest of the court can possibly  devise.'
translation: "The next item, if any man is seen talking to a woman within these three years, then he will have to endure whatever public shame the rest of the court can come up with."

original: This article, my liege, yourself must break;   For well you know here comes in embassy   The French King's daughter with yourself to speak—
translation: My lord, you are going to have to break this rule yourself! Did you forget that the French King's daughter is coming here as an ambassador to speak with you?

original: A maid of grace and complete majesty—   About surrender up of Aquitaine   To her decrepit, sick and bedrid father:
translation: She is a lady of charm and perfect dignity, and wishes to speak with you about the possibility of giving up  Aquitaine  to her weak, sick and bed-bound father.

original: Therefore this article is made in vain,   Or vainly comes the admired Princess hither.
What say you, lords? Why, this was quite forgot.
translation: What do you think of this, lords? I had quite forgotten about it.

original: So study evermore is overshot: While it doth study to have what it would It doth forget to do the thing it should, And when it hath the thing it hunteth most, 'Tis won as towns with fire, so won, so lost.
We must of force dispense with this decree; She must lie here on mere necessity.
translation: Then it is vital for us to get rid of this rule, it is an absolute necessity that the Princess stays here.

original: Necessity will make us all forsworn   Three thousand times within this three years' space;
translation: I predict that necessity will make us all break these promises three thousand times within these three years.

original: For every man with his affects is born,   Not by might master'd but by special grace:
translation: For every man is born with his own desires, and these cannot be controlled by anyone, except God.

original: If I break faith, this word shall speak for me;   I am forsworn on 'mere necessity.'
translation: If I break any of these promises, then let it be said that I only did it out of "mere necessity."

original: So to the laws at large I write my name:
translation: With this in mind, I will sign my name to the rules that remain.

original: And he that breaks them in the least degree   Stands in attainder of eternal shame:
translation: The man that breaks any of these oaths even slightly is condemned to eternal shame.

original: Suggestions are to other as to me;   But I believe, although I seem so loath,   I am the last that will last keep his oath.
translation: I am as prone to temptations as any other man, but I believe, even though I was the most reluctant, I will be the last one to break these oaths.

original: But is there no quick recreation granted?
translation: Will we be allowed any entertainment at all?

original: Ay, that there is. Our court, you know, is haunted   With a refined traveller of Spain;   A man in all the world's new fashion planted,   That hath a mint of phrases in his brain;
translation: Of course there is. Our court, you know, is visited regularly by a stylish traveler from Spain, who always appears in the latest fashions and has a variety of witty expressions to deliver

original: One whom the music of his own vain tongue   Doth ravish like enchanting harmony;
translation: . The words he speaks are like music to me, they have a magical, enchanting quality.

original: A man of complements, whom right and wrong   Have chose as umpire of their mutiny:
This child of fancy, that Armado hight,   For interim to our studies shall relate   In high-born words the worth of many a knight   From tawny Spain lost in the world's debate.
translation: This fantastic creature,  called  Armado, will be a break from our studies, and can tell us in noble words, the achievements of many knights from sunny Spain, that have been forgotten because of all the fighting we've been doing.

original: How you delight, my lords, I know not, I;   But, I protest, I love to hear him lie   And I will use him for my minstrelsy
translation: I don't know what pleases you, my lords, but I must admit, I love hearing him  lie  and I will use him for my  entertainment .

original: Armado is a most illustrious wight, A man of fire-new words, fashion's own knight.
translation: Armado is a very renowned person, he is a man who makes up new words, and is a true knight of fashion.

original: Costard the swain and he shall be our sport; And so to study, three years is but short.
translation: The servant Costard and him will be our entertainment and we will study like this. Come on, three years isn't actually that long.

original: Which is the duke's own person?
translation: Which of you represents the Duke?

original: This, fellow: what wouldst?
translation: I do, what do you want?

original: I myself reprehend his own person, for I am his grace's farborough: but I would see his own person in flesh and blood.
This is he.
translation: I am him.

original: Signior Arme—Arme—commends you. There's villany abroad: this letter will tell you more.
Sir, the contempts thereof are as touching me.
A letter from the magnificent Armado.
translation: A letter from the magnificent Armado.

original: How low soever the matter, I hope in God for high  words.
translation: However bad the matter is, I hope to God that he speaks with good words.

original: A high hope for a low heaven: God grant us patience!
translation: Good words are a bad sort of thing to hope to God for. Instead, let's ask him to give us patience!

original: To hear? or forbear laughing?
translation: Patience to listen? Or patience to stop ourselves from laughing?

original: To hear meekly, sir, and to laugh moderately; or to forbear both.
translation: To listen patiently, sir, and only laugh a little, or to do neither of these things.

original: Well, sir, be it as the style shall give us cause to climb in the merriness.
The matter is to me, sir, as concerning Jaquenetta. The manner of it is, I was taken with the manner.
In what manner?
translation: Found in what way?

original: In manner and form following, sir; all those three:
translation: In all three of these ways sir:

original: I was seen with her in the manor-house, sitting with   her upon the form, and taken following her into the   park;
translation: I was seen with her in the manor-house, I sat with her on a bench, and was caught following her into the park.

original: which, put together, is in manner and form   following.
translation: All three of these things put together have led to my arrest.

original: Now, sir, for the manner,—it is the   manner of a man to speak to a woman: for the form,—   in some form.
