translation: Now sir, to speak about customs—it is the custom of a man to  speak to  a woman, it is a habit, in some sense.

original: For the following, sir?
translation: And what we are about to hear?

original: As it shall follow in my correction: and God defend the right!
translation: After it I will be punished, and may God defend me!

original: Will you hear this letter with attention?
translation: Will you listen to this letter carefully?

original: As we would hear an oracle.
translation: As if we were listening to a prophecy.

original: Such is the simplicity of man to hearken after the  flesh.
translation: Men are so stupid to not be able to resist women.

original: 'Great deputy, the welkin's vicegerent and sole dominator of Navarre, my soul's earth's god, and body's fostering patron.'
translation: "Great leader, the heavenly commander and only ruler of Navarre, my soul's god on earth and my body's protector."

original: Not a word of Costard yet.
translation: No mention of Costard yet.

original: 'So it is,'—
translation: "So it is..."

original: It may be so: but if he say it is so, he is, in telling true, but so.
translation: That might be true, but telling the truth isn't even worth much nowadays.

original: Peace!
translation: Peace!

original: Be to me and every man that dares not fight!
translation: Peace be to me and every man who doesn't stick up for themselves!

original: No words!
translation: Stop talking!

original: Of other men's secrets, I beseech you.
translation: I ask you to stop talking about other men's private affairs.

original: 'So it is, besieged with sable-coloured   melancholy, I did commend the black-oppressing humour   to the most wholesome physic of thy health-giving   air; and, as I am a gentleman, betook myself to   walk.
translation: "So this is what happened. I, filled with the  darkest  sadness, decided to  ease my melancholy by giving it the medicine of some fresh air, and, on my word as a gentleman, I went for a walk.

original: The time when. About the sixth hour; when   beasts most graze, birds best peck, and men sit down   to that nourishment which is called supper: so much   for the time when.
translation: At what time? Around 6pm, the time when most animals eat, most birds peck at their food, and most men sit down to enjoy their evening meal. So much for that.

original: Now for the ground which? which,   I mean, I walked upon: it is y-cleped thy park.
translation: Now you ask, what ground? What ground I walked upon. It is called the park.

original: Then   for the place where; where, I mean, I did encounter   that obscene and preposterous event, that draweth   from my snow-white pen the ebon-coloured ink, which   here thou viewest, beholdest, surveyest, or seest;
translation: Then you ask where? Where I mean, that I saw the obscene and ridiculous event, that I have been forced to write about with my white goose-quill pen and my black ink, and that you are being forced to view, witness, analyze and see?

original: but to the place where; it standeth north-north-east   and by east from the west corner of thy curious-   knotted garden:
translation: As to the place where it happened, it was somewhere in between the north and the north-east from the secret place in the west of your  complex  garden.

original: there did I see that low-spirited   swain, that base minnow of thy mirth,'—
translation: It was there that   I saw this vile servant, so small that he should be laughed at."

original: Me?
translation: Me?

original: 'that unlettered small-knowing soul,'—
translation: "That illiterate, stupid boy,"

original: Me?
translation: Me?

original: 'that shallow vassal,'—
translation: "that empty rascal,"

original: Still me?
translation: Still me?

original: 'which, as I remember, hight Costard,'—
translation: "who, if I remember, is called Costard,"

original: O, me!
translation: Oh, it is me!

original: 'sorted and consorted, contrary to thy established proclaimed edict and continent canon, which with,—O, with—but with this I passion to say wherewith,—
translation: "who associated himself with and mingled, against your fixed oath and your rules, with, oh it pains me to say who with."

original: With a wench.
translation: With a girl.

original: 'with a child of our grandmother Eve, a   female; or, for thy more sweet understanding, a   woman.
translation: "with a child of Eve, a female, or if it helps you to understand it better, a woman.

original: Him I, as my ever-esteemed duty pricks me on,   have sent to thee, to receive the meed of   punishment, by thy sweet grace's officer, Anthony   Dull;
translation: Encouraged by my sense of duty, I have sent him to you to be punished, along with your sweet grace's officer, Anthony Dull

original: a man of good repute, carriage, bearing, and   estimation.'
translation: —a man who has a good reputation, behavior, manner and opinion."

original: 'Me, an't shall please you; I am Anthony Dull.
translation: That's me, if it pleases you. I am Anthony Dull.

original: 'For Jaquenetta,—so is the weaker vessel   called which I apprehended with the aforesaid   swain,
translation: "As for Jaquenetta, as she is the weaker of the two that I caught,

original: —I keep her as a vessel of the law's fury;   and shall, at the least of thy sweet notice, bring   her to trial.
translation: I will keep her as a symbol of the law's anger and will, whenever you want me to, bring her to trial.

original: Thine, in all compliments of devoted   and heart-burning heat of duty. ADRIANO DE ARMADO.'
translation: Yours, with respects to my devoted and  burning  sense of duty. ADRIANO DE ARMADO."

original: This is not so well as I looked for, but the best that ever I heard.
translation: That is not as good a matter as I had hoped for, but it is one of the best letters that I have ever heard.

original: Ay, the best for the worst. But, sirrah, what say you to this?
translation: Yes, it is the best example of something awful. But, boy, what do you have to say for yourself?

original: Sir, I confess the wench.
translation: Sir, I admit to being with the wench.

original: Did you hear the proclamation?
translation: Did you hear the announcement?

original: I do confess much of the hearing it but little of the marking of it.
translation: I confess that I did hear it but I didn't pay much attention to it.

original: It was proclaimed a year's imprisonment, to be taken with a wench.
translation: It was announced that if you were found with a wench, you would be imprisoned for a year.

original: I was taken with none, sir: I was taken with a damsel.
Well, it was proclaimed 'damsel.'
translation: Well then, the same applies to a "damsel."

original: This was no damsel, neither, sir; she was a virgin.
translation: Then she was not a damsel either sir; she was a virgin.

original: It is so varied, too; for it was proclaimed 'virgin.'
translation: That is just the same thing expressed in different words; it also applies to "virgin."

original: If it were, I deny her virginity: I was taken with a  maid.
translation: If that's true then she is not a virgin, I was found with a maid.

original: This maid will not serve your turn, sir.
translation: This maid will not help you sir.

original: This maid will serve my turn, sir.
Sir, I will pronounce your sentence: you shall fast a week with bran and water.
translation: Sir, I will now announce your punishment. You will fast for a week with only bread and water.

original: I had rather pray a month with mutton and porridge.
translation: I would rather pray for a month with some mutton and porridge.

original: And Don Armado shall be your keeper. My Lord Biron, see him deliver'd o'er: And go we, lords, to put in practise that Which each to other hath so strongly sworn.
translation: Don Armado shall look after you. My Lord Biron, take him to his house immediately. My lords, we shall go and start to live our lives according to the promises we have made.

original: I'll lay my head to any good man's hat, These oaths and laws will prove an idle scorn. Sirrah, come on.
translation: I know for certain, these oaths and laws will prove to be pointless soon enough. Come on boy.

original: I suffer for the truth, sir; for true it is, I was   taken with Jaquenetta, and Jaquenetta is a true   girl;
translation: I will be punished for the truth sir, for it is true, I was found with Jaquenetta and she is a true girl.

original: and therefore welcome the sour cup of   prosperity!
translation: Therefore bring on my  suffering !

original: Affliction may one day smile again; and   till then, sit thee down, sorrow!
translation: My fortunes  might one day turn around and until then, be patient sadness!

original: Boy, what sign is it when a man of great spirit grows melancholy?
translation: What does it mean, Moth, when a happy man becomes melancholy?

original: A great sign, sir, that he will look sad.
translation: It simply means, sir, that he is sad.

original: Why, sadness is one and the self-same thing, dear imp.
translation: Well then sadness is always the same, dear child.

original: No, no; O Lord, sir, no.
translation: No no. Oh my Lord, sir, no.

original: How canst thou part sadness and melancholy, my tender juvenal?
translation: How can you understand sadness and melancholy, my dear boy?

original: By a familiar demonstration of the working, my tough  senor.
translation: I have often seen how it works, my tough master.

original: Why tough senor? why tough senor?
translation: Why "tough master?" Why "tough master?"

original: Why tender juvenal? why tender juvenal?
translation: Why "dear boy?" Why "dear boy?"

original: I spoke it, tender juvenal, as a congruent epitheton appertaining to thy young days, which we may nominate tender.
translation: I said it, dear boy, as a suitable description for your youth, which I consider it dear.

original: And I, tough senior, as an appertinent title to your old time, which we may name tough.
translation: And I called you my tough master, as a suitable description for your old age, which we should think of as tough.

original: Pretty and apt.
How mean you, sir? I pretty, and my saying apt? or I apt, and my saying pretty?
translation: What do you mean, sir? Am I pretty and my words appropriate or am I appropriate and my words pretty?

original: Thou pretty, because little.
translation: You are pretty because you are little.

original: Little pretty, because little. Wherefore apt?
translation: I am a little pretty, because I am little. So am I not appropriate at all?

original: And therefore apt, because quick.
translation: And indeed you are appropriate, because you are so quick.

original: Speak you this in my praise, master?
translation: Are you praising me, my master?

original: In thy condign praise.
translation: It is well deserved.

original: I will praise an eel with the same praise.
translation: An eel could be praised in the same way as you have praised me.

original: What, that an eel is ingenious?
translation: What, is an eel so clever?

original: That an eel is quick.
translation: An eel is quick.

original: I do say thou art quick in answers: thou heatest my  blood.
translation: I meant that your wit is quick! You're making my blood boil.

original: I am answered, sir.
translation: I understand now sir.

original: I love not to be crossed.
translation: I do not like being contradicted.

original: He speaks the mere contrary; crosses love not  him.
translation: That's difficult when his very words are contradictions.

original: I have promised to study three years with the duke.
translation: I have promised that I will study for three years with the Duke.

original: You may do it in an hour, sir.
translation: You could do that in an hour, sir.

original: Impossible.
translation: Impossible!

original: How many is one thrice told?
translation: What is one times three?

original: I am ill at reckoning; it fitteth the spirit of a  tapster.
translation: I am not good at calculations, that is the job of the tavern-keeper.

original: You are a gentleman and a gamester, sir.
translation: You are both a gentleman and a gambler, sir.

original: I confess both: they are both the varnish of a complete man.
Then, I am sure, you know how much the gross sum of deuce-ace amounts to.
It doth amount to one more than two.
translation: It amounts to one more than two.

original: Which the base vulgar do call three.
translation: Which the common people would call three.

original: True.
translation: True.

original: Why, sir, is this such a piece of study?
translation: Why are you undertaking this difficult task sir?

original: Now heret   is three studied, ere ye'll thrice wink:
translation: Here we have managed to work out three, before we have even blinked three times.

original: and how   easy it is to put 'years' to the word 'three,' and   study three years in two words, the dancing horse   will tell you.
translation: How easy it would be to just add the word "years" onto the end of the word "three" and there you have it, three years of study in only two words, as  the dancing horse  would tell you.

original: A most fine figure!
translation: What an excellent figure of speech!

original: To prove you a cipher.
translation: That means nothing.

original: I will hereupon confess I am in love: and as it is   base for a soldier to love, so am I in love with a   base wench.
translation: I must confess to you, Moth, that I am in love. As it is cheap of a soldier to fall in love, it is only fitting that I have fallen in love with a cheap girl.

original: If drawing my sword against the humour   of affection would deliver me from the reprobate   thought of it, I would take Desire prisoner, and   ransom him to any French courtier for a new-devised   curtsy.
translation: If I could fight against my desire to love and escape these corrupt thoughts, I would take Love as my prisoner and sell it off to the next  French attendant that bows to me .

original: I think scorn to sigh: methinks I should   outswear Cupid. Comfort, me, boy: what great men   have been in love?
translation: It is disgraceful for me to sigh with love when I should abandon Cupid for good. Comfort me, my boy—what great men have been in love before?

original: Hercules, master.
translation: Hercules has, master.

original: Most sweet Hercules! More authority, dear boy, name more; and, sweet my child, let them be men of good repute and carriage.
translation: Oh most sweet Hercules! Tell me more, dear boy, tell me more! And my sweet child, let them be men with good reputations and behavior.

original: Samson, master: he was a man of good carriage, great carriage, for he carried the town-gates on his back like a porter: and he was in love.
translation: What about Samson, master? He was a man who carried a lot of power, immense power in fact, for he carried the burden of the town-gates on his back and he was in love.

original: O well-knit Samson! strong-jointed Samson! I do   excel thee in my rapier as much as thou didst me in   carrying gates.
translation: Oh worthy Samson! Oh strong Samson! I may be better than you with my sword but you are better than me at  carrying town-gates .

original: I am in love too. Who was Samson's   love, my dear Moth?
translation: I am in love too. Who was Samson's love, my dear Moth?

original: A woman, master.
translation: A woman, Master.

original: Of what complexion?
translation: What was she like?

original: Of all the four, or the three, or the two, or one of  the four.
Tell me precisely of what complexion.
translation: Tell me precisely what she was like.

original: Of the sea-water green, sir.
translation: She was green like sea-water.

original: Is that one of the four complexions?
translation: Is that related to one of the four humors?

original: As I have read, sir; and the best of them too.
translation: That's what I've read sir, and apparently it's the best of them too.

original: Green indeed is the colour of lovers; but to have a love of that colour, methinks Samson had small reason for it. He surely affected her for her wit.
It was so, sir; for she had a green wit.
My love is most immaculate white and red.
translation: My own love is the color of purest white and red.

original: Most maculate thoughts, master, are masked under such colours.
translation: Yet dirty thoughts are hidden under these colors, master.

original: Define, define, well-educated infant.
translation: Explain what you mean, my clever child.

original: My father's wit and my mother's tongue, assist me!
translation: May my father's wit and my mother's tongue help me!

original: Sweet invocation of a child; most pretty and pathetical!
translation: Speak my child, with sweet and moving words!

original: If she be made of white and red,   Her faults will ne'er be known,   For blushing cheeks by faults are bred   And fears by pale white shown:
translation: If she is the  color of white and red ,  No-one will ever know her flaws, For cheeks blush when people make mistakes And fear makes a person turn white.

original: Then if she fear, or be to blame,   By this you shall not know,   For still her cheeks possess the same   Which native she doth owe.
translation: So even if she is scared or does something wrong, You will never know this by her face, For her cheeks will always keep the same color That they have naturally.

original: A dangerous rhyme, master, against the reason of   white and red.
translation: A dangerous poem, master, warning against a woman of white and red.

original: Is there not a ballad, boy, of the King and the Beggar?
The world was very guilty of such a ballad some three ages since: but I think now 'tis not to be found; or, if it were, it would neither serve for the writing nor the tune.
translation: There used to be a ballad on that subject a long time ago, but by now it has either been lost or, if found, would not be an acceptable subject for such a tale.

original: I will have that subject newly writ o'er, that I may example my digression by some mighty precedent. Boy, I do love that country girl that I took in the park with the rational hind Costard: she deserves well.
To be whipped; and yet a better love than my master.
translation: She deserves to be whipped more like. Although she also deserves to be loved by someone better than my master.

original: Sing, boy; my spirit grows heavy in love.
translation: Sing for me Moth, my heart burns with love.

original: And that's great marvel, loving a light wench.
translation: And that's quite incredible, when you love a fiery wench.

original: I say, sing.
translation: I said sing!

original: Forbear till this company be past.
translation: Wait until these people have gone.

original: Sir, the Duke's pleasure is, that you keep Costard   safe: and you must suffer him to take no delight   nor no penance;
translation: Sir, the Duke wants you to keep Costard safe and ensure that he has no pleasures and no punishments.

original: but a' must fast three days a week.
translation: He must fast for three days a week.

original: For this damsel, I must keep her at the park: she   is allowed for the day-woman. Fare you well.
translation: I will keep this maid at the park, she is going to be the dairy-woman. Goodbye.

original: I do betray myself with blushing. Maid!
translation: I reveal my true feelings by blushing. Maid!

original: Man.
translation: Man.

original: I will visit thee at the lodge.
translation: I will visit you at the house in the forest.

original: That's hereby.
translation: That's near here.

original: I know where it is situate.
translation: I know where it is.

original: Lord, how wise you are!
translation: Lord, you are so wise!

original: I will tell thee wonders.
translation: I will tell you wonderful things.

original: With that face?
I love thee.
translation: I love you.

original: So I heard you say.
translation: You have said that before.

original: And so, farewell.
translation: Goodbye then.

original: Fair weather after you!
translation: May the sun shine for you!

original: Come, Jaquenetta, away!
translation: Come Jaquenetta, let's go!

original: Villain, thou shalt fast for thy offences ere thou be pardoned.
translation: Villain, you will fast for your offenses before you are forgiven.

original: Well, sir, I hope, when I do it, I shall do it on a full stomach.
Thou shalt be heavily punished.
translation: You will be heavily punished.

original: I am more bound to you than your fellows, for they are but lightly rewarded.
translation: I am closer to you than your servants, for they are only lightly rewarded when I am heavily punished.

original: Take away this villain; shut him up.
translation: Take away this villain, shut him up.

original: Come, you transgressing slave; away!
translation: Come on, you misbehaving slave. Let's go!

original: Let me not be pent up, sir: I will fast, being loose.
translation: Don't let me be imprisoned sir! I can fast and be free.

original: No, sir; that were fast and loose: thou shalt to  prison.
Well, if ever I do see the merry days of desolation that I have seen, some shall see.
What shall some see?
translation: What shall people see?

original: Nay, nothing, Master Moth, but what they look upon. It is not for prisoners to be too silent in their words; and therefore I will say nothing: I thank God I have as little patience as another man; and therefore I can be quiet.
I do affect the very ground, which is base, where   her shoe, which is baser, guided by her foot, which   is basest, doth tread.
translation: I now love even the common ground where her shoe, and indeed her common foot have walked.

original: I shall be forsworn, which   is a great argument of falsehood, if I love. And   how can that be true love which is falsely   attempted?
translation: I am going to break my oath and prove myself to be a liar, if I love her. Can it be true love if it is started under false pretenses?

original: Love is a familiar; Love is a devil:   there is no evil angel but Love.
translation: Love is an evil spirit, it is a devil; Love is the only evil angel.

original: Yet was Samson so   tempted, and he had an excellent strength; yet was   Solomon so seduced, and he had a very good wit.
translation: Yet even Samson was tempted by this evil angel, and he was incredibly strong; Solomon too was seduced by love, and he was incredibly clever.

original: Cupid's butt-shaft is too hard for Hercules' club;   and therefore too much odds for a Spaniard's rapier.
translation: Cupid's arrow is even more powerful than Hercules' club and so what hope do I have with my sword?

original: The first and second cause will not serve my turn;   the passado he respects not, the duello he regards   not: his disgrace is to be called boy; but his   glory is to subdue men.
translation: He  doesn't follow any of the rules of fighting —there is no  passado , there is no  duello . He may be seen as a boy, but he has the power to destroy men.

original: Adieu, valour! rust rapier!   be still, drum! for your manager is in love; yea,   he loveth.
translation: Goodbye courage! My sword might as well rust, the war drums might as well stop sounding! For your master is in love. Yes, he is in love.

original: Assist me, some extemporal god of rhyme,   for I am sure I shall turn sonnet. Devise, wit;   write, pen; for I am for whole volumes in folio.
translation: Help me, some god of poetry, for I must now become a love poet. Think, brain; write, pen. I must write  folios  of my love.

original: Now, madam, summon up your dearest spirits:   Consider who the king your father sends,   To whom he sends, and what's his embassy:
translation: Now, madam, you must gather all of your energy and consider who the King, your father, sends you to talk to and what message you must deliver.

original: Yourself, held precious in the world's esteem,   To parley with the sole inheritor   Of all perfections that a man may owe,   Matchless Navarre;
translation: Since the world thinks so highly of you, it is only right that you have been sent to speak with the remarkable King of Navarre, a man who is said to be perfect.

original: the plea of no less weight   Than Aquitaine, a dowry for a queen.
translation: You are speaking on behalf of  your country , speak with the grace that this important message deserves.

original: Be now as prodigal of all dear grace   As Nature was in making graces dear   When she did starve the general world beside   And prodigally gave them all to you.
translation: Be as graceful as Nature intended for you to be, when she gave you all the honors and beauty of this world and left none for anyone else.

original: Good Lord Boyet, my beauty, though but mean,   Needs not the painted flourish of your praise:
translation: Good Lord Boyet, although my beauty is only moderate, that does not mean I need you to praise it so much.

original: Beauty is bought by judgement of the eye,   Not utter'd by base sale of chapmen's tongues:
translation: Beauty is something which only the eye can judge, it cannot be bought and sold in some kind of business deal.

original: I am less proud to hear you tell my worth   Than you much willing to be counted wise   In spending your wit in the praise of mine.
translation: I feel more unhappy when you describe my beauty, than you feel wise when praising me with your wit.

original: But now to task the tasker: good Boyet,   You are not ignorant, all-telling fame   Doth noise abroad,
translation: But now I will give you your task: Good Boyet, you are not stupid, you have heard the many rumors that have spread abroad.

original: Navarre hath made a vow,   Till painful study shall outwear three years,   No woman may approach his silent court:
translation: It is said that the King of Navarre has made a promise that no women are allowed to enter his silent court until he has spent three years focused on studying.

original: Therefore to's seemeth it a needful course,   Before we enter his forbidden gates,   To know his pleasure;
translation: Therefore, it seems necessary that we find out if this is true before we enter his forbidden  gates.

original: and in that behalf,   Bold of your worthiness, we single you   As our best-moving fair solicitor.
translation: That's where you come in. We've picked you to be our spokesperson, as we know you are worthy and persuasive.

original: Tell him, the daughter of the King of France,   On serious business, craving quick dispatch,   Importunes personal conference with his grace:
translation: Tell him that the daughter of the King of France needs to talk to him privately about important matters and must return to France as soon as possible.

original: Haste, signify so much; while we attend,   Like humble-visaged suitors, his high will.
translation: Go quickly and tell him this; we will wait out here to find out what he will say, like some poor and unappealing admirers.

original: Proud of employment, willingly I go.
translation: I am proud to do this task, I will willingly go now.

original: All pride is willing pride, and yours is so.
translation: If you are proud to do it, you should always be willing.

original: Who are the votaries, my loving lords, That are vow-fellows with this virtuous Duke?
translation: Who are the other men, the adoring lords, who have supposedly agreed to these same promises with our good Duke?

original: Lord Longaville is one.
translation: One of them is Lord Longaville.

original: Know you the man?
translation: Do you know this man?

original: I know him, madam: at a marriage-feast,   Between Lord Perigort and the beauteous heir   Of Jaques Falconbridge, solemnized   In Normandy, saw I this Longaville:
translation: I know him madam. I met him at a marriage ceremony in Normandy, between Lord  Perigord  and the beautiful heiress of Jacques Falconbridge.

original: A man of sovereign parts he is esteem'd;   Well fitted in arts, glorious in arms:   Nothing becomes him ill that he would well.
translation: He is said to be a man who has many excellent qualities: he is gifted in the arts, he is a strong fighter. Whatever he does he does well and he looks good doing it.

original: The only soil of his fair virtue's gloss,   If virtue's gloss will stain with any soil,   Is a sharp wit matched with too blunt a will;
translation: The only flaw on an otherwise perfect character, if every character must have a flaw, is that he has a quick wit, but he never uses it.

original: Whose edge hath power to cut, whose will still wills   It should none spare that come within his power.
translation: His wit is as sharp as a knife and could put down anyone that he talked to, if he chose to use it.

original: Some merry mocking lord, belike; is't so?
translation: He is more of a happy-go-lucky kind of lord, is that right?

original: They say so most that most his humours know.
translation: People who know his moods the best do say so.

original: Such short-lived wits do wither as they grow. Who are the rest?
translation: Such wit is short-lived and inconsequential. Who are the others?

original: The young Dumain, a well-accomplished youth,   Of all that virtue love for virtue loved:   Most power to do most harm, least knowing ill;
translation: The young Dumain, a very talented young man, but he is so innocent and virtuous that he can end up doing more harm than good, because he is so unaware of the harm that he is doing.

original: For he hath wit to make an ill shape good,   And shape to win grace though he had no wit.
translation: He is clever enough to make even a bad thing look good, and his appearance certainly makes him appealing even when his wit can't.

original: I saw him at the Duke Alencon's once;   And much too little of that good I saw   Is my report to his great worthiness.
translation: I met him at Duke  Alencon's  house once, and I admit that I didn't see enough of this talent that he is reported to have.

original: Another of these students at that time   Was there with him, if I have heard a truth.
translation: Another one of these students was there with him on that occasion, if I remember correctly.

original: Biron they call him; but a merrier man,   Within the limit of becoming mirth,   I never spent an hour's talk withal:
translation: They call him Biron and I have certainly never chatted with a man who is so amusing.

original: His eye begets occasion for his wit;   For every object that the one doth catch   The other turns to a mirth-moving jest,
translation: He finds any opportunity he can to make a witty joke; everything he sees he manages to turn into a hilarious joke,

original: Which his fair tongue, conceit's expositor,   Delivers in such apt and gracious words   That aged ears play truant at his tales
translation: which he delivers so cleverly, using such smart words that older people don't understand his hilarity

original: And younger hearings are quite ravished;   So sweet and voluble is his discourse.
translation: and young people are delighted by what they hear—so sweet and quick is his tongue!

original: God bless my ladies! are they all in love, That every one her own hath garnished With such bedecking ornaments of praise?
translation: Oh my poor ladies! You must all be in love, to describe your lords with such incredible words of praise?

original: Here comes Boyet.
translation: Here comes Boyet.

original: Now, what admittance, lord?
translation: Can we enter now, my lord?

original: Navarre had notice of your fair approach;   And he and his competitors in oath   Were all address'd to meet you, gentle lady,   Before I came.
translation: The King of Navarre was told that you were coming and  him and his partners in oath  were preparing to meet you, gentle lady, before I arrived.

original: Marry, thus much I have learnt:   He rather means to lodge you in the field,   Like one that comes here to besiege his court,   Than seek a dispensation for his oath,   To let you enter his unpeopled house.
translation: So far I have learnt this: He has decided that you will stay in the field, as if you were an army coming to attack his court, rather than go against his oath and let you enter his empty house.

original: Here comes Navarre.
translation: Here comes the King now.

original: Fair princess, welcome to the court of Navarre.
translation: Welcome to the court of Navarre, fair princess.

original: 'Fair' I give you back again; and 'welcome' I have not yet: the roof of this court is too high to be yours; and welcome to the wide fields too base to be  mine.
translation: You can take back calling me "fair," and I have not yet been welcomed into the court of Navarre. This sky is far too high to belong to you and being welcomed in these fields is far below me.

original: You shall be welcome, madam, to my court.
translation: You will be welcome, madam, to the court of Navarre.

original: I will be welcome, then: conduct me thither.
translation: If I am welcome, then lead me inside.

original: Hear me, dear lady; I have sworn an oath.
translation: Listen to me, dear lady, I have made a promise.

original: Our Lady help my lord! he'll be forsworn.
translation: Ladies, we must help my lord! He must break his promise.

original: Not for the world, fair madam, by my will.
translation: I will not break it for the world, fair madam, not of my own accord.

original: Why, will shall break it; will and nothing else.
translation: Why, in the end you shall break it of your own accord, no one else will force you to do it.

original: Your ladyship is ignorant what it is.
translation: Your ladyship does not understand our oath.

original: Were my lord so, his ignorance were wise,   Where now his knowledge must prove ignorance.
translation: Normally my lord, even in your ignorance you are wise, but now a desire for knowledge has made you act foolishly.

original: I hear your grace hath sworn out house-keeping:   Tis deadly sin to keep that oath, my lord,   And sin to break it.   But pardon me. I am too sudden-bold:
translation: I have heard that you have promised to stop welcoming guests, my lord. I must warn you, this is a dangerous promise to keep, but now it is a dangerous promise for you to break as well. But you must excuse me, I have said too much.

original: To teach a teacher ill beseemeth me.   Vouchsafe to read the purpose of my coming,   And suddenly resolve me in my suit.
translation: It is not right for me to try to teach an academic like you.  [ Giving FERDINAND a piece of paper ]  Promise to read why I have come here and answer me immediately.

original: Madam, I will, if suddenly I may.
translation: Madam, I will, right away.

original: You will the sooner, that I were away; For you'll prove perjured if you make me stay.
translation: You will want me to leave as quickly as possible, or you will end up breaking your promise if I have to stay longer.

original: Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?
Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?
translation: Did I dance with you once in Brabant?

original: I know you did.
translation: Yes you did.

original: How needless was it then to ask the question!
translation: Why did you bother asking the question then?

original: You must not be so quick.
translation: You should not be so sharp with me.

original: 'Tis 'long of you that spur me with such questions.
translation: It is only because you encourage me with such silly questions.

original: Your wit's too hot, it speeds too fast, 'twill tire.
translation: Your wit is too quick, you will get tired soon.

original: Not till it leave the rider in the mire.
What time o' day?
translation: What time is it?

original: The hour that fools should ask.
translation: A time when foolish people ask foolish questions.

original: Now fair befall your mask!
translation: Well good luck to that mask that you wear!

original: Fair fall the face it covers!
translation: May it continue to cover my pretty face!

original: And send you many lovers!
translation: And send you many lovers!

original: Amen, so you be none.
translation: As long as you're not one of them!

original: Nay, then will I be gone.
translation: I will go then.

original: Madam, your father here doth intimate   The payment of a hundred thousand crowns;   Being but the one half of an entire sum   Disbursed by my father in his wars.
translation: Madam, in this letter your father asks for the repayment of a hundred thousand crowns, which is only half of what my father lent to you in his wars!

original: But say that he or we, as neither have,   Received that sum, yet there remains unpaid   A hundred thousand more; in surety of the which,   One part of Aquitaine is bound to us,   Although not valued to the money's worth.
translation: We have never received that money from you and neither did he, yet you still owe us a hundred thousand more and until we get that, one part of Aquitaine belongs to us, although the land isn't even worth that much.

original: If then the king your father will restore   But that one half which is unsatisfied,   We will give up our right in Aquitaine,   And hold fair friendship with his majesty.
translation: If the King, your father, will give back the half which is not settled by payments, we will give up our power in Aquitaine, and maintain a good relationship with him.

original: But that, it seems, he little purposeth,
translation: But he doesn't seem to want that.

original: For here he doth demand to have repaid   A hundred thousand crowns; and not demands,   On payment of a hundred thousand crowns,   To have his title live in Aquitaine;
translation: For in this letter he claims he is entitled to the hundred thousand crowns, instead of demanding that, for this sum, he can have control over Aquitaine back.

original: Which we much rather had depart withal   And have the money by our father lent   Than Aquitaine so gelded as it is.
translation: We would much rather give up Aquitaine, as it is so separated from the rest of our land, and have the money that was lent by your father.

original: Dear Princess, were not his requests so far   From reason's yielding, your fair self should make   A yielding 'gainst some reason in my breast   And go well satisfied to France again.
translation: Dear Princess, if these requests weren't so unreasonable, then your beautiful self would be able to convince me to agree, and you could return to France happy again.

original: You do the king my father too much wrong And wrong the reputation of your name, In so unseeming to confess receipt Of that which hath so faithfully been paid.
translation: You cause offense to my father, the King, and shame your own name, in refusing to accept that you received this money from us.

original: I do protest I never heard of it; And if you prove it, I'll repay it back Or yield up Aquitaine.
translation: I maintain that I have never heard of it, but if you can prove it, I will either repay the money or I will give you back the region of Aquitaine.

original: We arrest your word. Boyet, you can produce acquittances For such a sum from special officers Of Charles his father.
translation: We will hold you to your word. Boyet, you can collect documents to prove this deal took place from some of the officers of his father Charles.

original: Satisfy me so.
translation: That would be enough to convince me.

original: So please your grace, the packet is not come Where that and other specialties are bound: To-morrow you shall have a sight of them.
translation: So be it. The package containing the contracts hasn't arrived yet but you will be able to see them tomorrow.

original: It shall suffice me: at which interview   All liberal reason I will yield unto.
translation: That will be okay—once I have seen them I will be able to respond to you in a polite and reasonable manner.

original: Meantime receive such welcome at my hand   As honour without breach of honour may   Make tender of to thy true worthiness:
translation: Until then, I hope you feel truly welcomed, as you deserve to be, but without breaking my oath.

original: You may not come, fair princess, in my gates;   But here without you shall be so received   As you shall deem yourself lodged in my heart,   Though so denied fair harbour in my house.
translation: Although you cannot come inside my gates, fair princess, you will be treated so well out here that you will feel like you are staying in my heart, even if you can't enter my house.

original: Your own good thoughts excuse me, and farewell:   To-morrow shall we visit you again.
translation: May your good thoughts excuse me and goodbye, we shall visit you again tomorrow.

original: Sweet health and fair desires consort your grace!
translation: May you have good health and happiness!

original: Thy own wish wish I thee in every place!
translation: And the same to you!

original: Lady, I will commend you to mine own heart.
translation: Lady, I will keep you in my heart.

original: Pray you, do my commendations; I would be glad to see  it.
translation: Please do, I would be happy to see what goes on in that organ of yours.

original: I would you heard it groan.
translation: I wish you could hear my pains.

original: Is the fool sick?
translation: Poor thing, are you sick?

original: Sick at the heart.
translation: Sick in the heart!

original: Alack, let it blood.
Would that do it good?
translation: Would that help?

original: My physic says 'ay.'
translation: My doctor says it will.

original: Will you prick't with your eye?
No point, with my knife.
translation: That's pointless, but I will with my knife?

original: Now, God save thy life!
translation: Oh never mind, good luck to you!

original: And yours from long living!
translation: And may you not live long with this pain!

original: I cannot stay thanksgiving.
translation: Sorry but I cannot stay to thank you.

original: Sir, I pray you, a word: what lady is that same?
translation: Sir, I have a question for you. Who is that lady?

original: The heir of Alencon, Katharine her name.
translation: That is the heir of Alencon, her name is Katharine.

original: A gallant lady. Monsieur, fare you well.
translation: A pretty lady. Monsieur, goodbye to you now.

original: I beseech you a word: what is she in the white?
translation: One quick word sir, who is that wearing white?

original: A woman sometimes, an you saw her in the light.
translation: A woman I believe, if you see her in the light.

original: Perchance light in the light. I desire her name.
translation: I want to know her name.

original: She hath but one for herself; to desire that were a  shame.
translation: She has only one name for herself, and you should not wish to have it for yourself.

original: Pray you, sir, whose daughter?
translation: Please sir, whose daughter is she?

original: Her mother's, I have heard.
translation: Her mother's, I have heard.

original: God's blessing on your beard!
translation: Come on, grow up!

original: Good sir, be not offended. She is an heir of Falconbridge.
translation: Don't be offended good sir. She is an heir of the Falconbridge family.

original: Nay, my choler is ended. She is a most sweet lady.
Not unlike, sir, that may be.
translation: That is very likely true.

original: What's her name in the cap?
translation: What is her name, the one in the hat?

original: Rosaline, by good hap.
Is she wedded or no?
translation: Is she married or not?

original: To her will, sir, or so.
translation: To her own will sir, or something like that.

original: You are welcome, sir: adieu.
translation: Thank you sir, goodbye.

original: Farewell to me, sir, and welcome to you.
translation: Goodbye to me sir, and welcome to you!

original: That last is Biron, the merry madcap lord: Not a word with him but a jest.
translation: That last lord is Biron, every word he says is some kind of joke.

original: And every jest but a word.
translation: And every joke is merely one word.

original: It was well done of you to take him at his word.
translation: You did well at fighting back against his word play.

original: I was as willing to grapple as he was to board.
translation: I was as willing to have such a fight of words, as he was to respond.

original: Two hot sheeps, marry.
And wherefore not ships? No sheep, sweet lamb, unless we feed on your lips.
translation: Why can't we be ships instead? We'll only be sheep, my sweet child, if we can kiss you.

original: You sheep, and I pasture: shall that finish the jest?
translation: If you are a sheep, then I am a field...is that the joke?

original: So you grant pasture for me.
translation: If your field is mine....

original: Not so, gentle beast: My lips are no common, though several they be.
translation: No, my gentle animal. Although my lips are parted, that does not mean they are for any common person to enjoy.

original: Belonging to whom?
translation: Who do they belong to?

original: To my fortunes and me.
translation: To my fate, and to me.

original: Good wits will be jangling; but, gentles, agree: This civil war of wits were much better used On Navarre and his book-men; for here 'tis abused.
translation: Clever people will always bicker, but come now friends, and get along. Save this battle of wits and use it on the king of Navarre and his book-loving friends; it is wasted here.

original: If my observation, which very seldom lies, By the heart's still rhetoric disclosed with eyes, Deceive me not now, Navarre is infected.
translation: If my observations are correct, which they normally are, I have seen in the king's eyes, things which his heart has tried to hide. I am certain, the king of Navarre is sick.

original: With what?
translation: With what?

original: With that which we lovers entitle affected.
translation: The thing that romantics would call being lovesick.

original: Your reason?
translation: Why do you think this?

original: Why, all his behaviors did make their retire   To the court of his eye, peeping thorough desire:
translation: Well, all of his emotions were hidden in his eyes, as his desires peeped out of them.

original: His heart, like an agate, with your print impress'd,   Proud with his form, in his eye pride express'd:
translation: His heart was like a precious stone, and it was your name that was engraved into it, and he was proud of this engraving, I could see it in his eyes!

original: His tongue, all impatient to speak and not see,   Did stumble with haste in his eyesight to be;   All senses to that sense did make their repair,   To feel only looking on fairest of fair:
translation: His tongue, desperate to speak, stumbled over his words as he looked at you. All of his senses made his way to his eye, to feel what it was like to look at the most beautiful person.

original: Methought all his senses were lock'd in his eye,   As jewels in crystal for some prince to buy;   Who, tendering their own worth from where they were  glass'd,   Did point you to buy them, along as you pass'd:
translation: I felt like I could see all of his senses in his eye, like jewels in a glass container that a prince could buy and, having offered you everything he could, did hope that you would be convinced by them, during your conversation.

original: His face's own margent did quote such amazes   That all eyes saw his eyes enchanted with gazes.
translation: His own face gave away the amazing things he felt about the Princess, as everything he saw made his eyes light up.

original: I'll give you Aquitaine and all that is his,   An you give him for my sake but one loving kiss.
translation: I'll get you Aquitaine and all that is his, all you have to do is give him one loving kiss!

original: Come to our pavilion: Boyet is disposed.
translation: Let's go to our tent, Boyet is in a silly mood.

original: But to speak that in words which his eye hath disclosed. I only have made a mouth of his eye, By adding a tongue which I know will not lie.
translation: But I am only telling you things that I have seen in his eyes; I am only telling you about true feelings that he cannot yet put into words.

original: Thou art an old love-monger and speakest skilfully.
He is Cupid's grandfather and learns news of him.
translation: He is Cupid's grandfather and finds out things from him.

translation: Do you understand what I've told you, you foolish women?

translation: No.

translation: What then, do you see?

translation: Oh yes, our cue to leave.

translation: You are too much for me to deal with.

translation: Sweet music! Go, young Moth, take this key, release Costard and bring him here quickly. I must send him to deliver a letter to my love.

original: But O,—but O,—

original: 'The hobby-horse is forgot.'
translation: "The hobby-horse is forgot."

No, master; the hobby-horse is but a colt, and your love perhaps a hackney. But have you forgot your love?
translation: No master, a hobby-horse would only be a suitable name for a young love, and your love is more of a used horse. You had almost forgotten about your love, hadn't you?

translation: I almost had.

translation: You careless student! You need to know everything about her by heart.

translation: By heart and in my heart, my boy.

translation: And indeed out of your heart, master. I will prove all three of these things to you.

translation: What will you prove?

translation: You love her  " by"   heart because your heart cannot have her; you love her  "in"   your heart, because your heart is in love with her; you love her "o ut"   of your heart because you are disheartened by the fact that you can't be with her.

original: I am all these three.
translation: I am all three of these things.

original: And three times as much more, and yet nothing at all.
translation: And even if you were nine of these things, you would still have nothing to show for it.

original: Fetch hither the swain: he must carry me a letter.
translation: Bring Costard here, I need him to deliver a letter for me.

original: A message well sympathized; a horse to be ambassador for an ass.
translation: A well thought through idea, sending that mule as a messenger for an ass.

original: Ha, ha! what sayest thou?
translation: Ha, ha! What are you saying?

original: Marry, sir, you must send the ass upon the horse, for he is very slow-gaited. But I go.
translation: I am saying sir, that you are going to send an ass to ride upon a horse, because he is as slow as an ass. But anyway, I will go and get him.

original: The way is but short: away!
translation: It's not far, off you go!

original: As swift as lead, sir.
The meaning, pretty ingenious? Is not lead a metal heavy, dull, and slow?
translation: Is this some clever joke that I don't understand? Isn't lead a metal and aren't metals heavy, dull and slow?

original: Minime, honest master; or rather, master, no.
translation: No, no, my truthful master, of course not.

original: I say lead is slow.
translation: I am telling you, lead is slow.

original: You are too swift, sir, to say so: Is that lead slow which is fired from a gun?
translation: You are too quick to say so, sir. Tell me, is lead slow when it is fired out of a gun?

original: Sweet smoke of rhetoric! He reputes me a cannon; and the bullet, that's he: I shoot thee at the swain.
translation: What a clever expression then! He thinks of me as the gun and he is the quick bullet that is flying out of it—I send you flying towards Costard!

original: Thump then and I flee.
translation: Like a bullet then, I go.

original: A most acute juvenal; voluble and free of grace! By thy favour, sweet welkin, I must sigh in thy face: Most rude melancholy, valour gives thee place. My herald is return'd.
translation: What a clever young boy, so chatty and free with his words! Oh sky, I have to sigh in your sweet air! But no, now I must be brave and ignore my sadness. Look, my messenger has returned.

original: A wonder, master! here's a costard broken in a shin.
Some enigma, some riddle: come, thy l'envoy; begin.
No egma, no riddle, no l'envoy; no salve in the mail, sir: O, sir, plantain, a plain plantain! no l'envoy, no l'envoy; no salve, sir, but a plantain!
By virtue, thou enforcest laughter; thy silly   thought my spleen;
translation: My goodness, you do make me laugh, your silly ideas hurt  my spleen ;

original: the heaving of my lungs provokes   me to ridiculous smiling.
translation: the amount my lungs have shook with laughter has forced me into silly smiling.

original: O, pardon me, my stars!
translation: Oh forgive me, my Lord!

original: Doth the inconsiderate take salve for l'envoy, and   the word l'envoy for a salve?
translation: Do ignorant people use a " salve ," a greeting as if it were a farewell, and "l'envoy" the other way round?

original: Do the wise think them other? is not l'envoy a salve?
No, page: it is an epilogue or discourse, to make plain   Some obscure precedence that hath tofore been sain.
translation: No, my boy. It is an epilogue or a speech to clear up what has happened so far.

original: I will example it:
translation: I will give you an example:

original: The fox, the ape, and the humble-bee,   Were still at odds, being but three.
translation: The fox, the ape and the bumble-bee,  Are always quarreling, as there are only three of them.

original: There's the moral. Now the l'envoy.
translation: That's the moral. Now the l'envoy would be:

original: I will add the l'envoy. Say the moral again.
translation: Let me add the l'envoy. Say the moral again.

original: The fox, the ape, and the humble-bee, Were still at odds, being but three.
Until the goose came out of door,   And stay'd the odds by adding four.
translation: Until the goose came out of the door,  And sorted the quarrel out by being the fourth member of the group.

original: Now will I begin your moral, and do you follow with   my l'envoy.
translation: Now I will say the moral again, and you can repeat my l'envoy at the end of it.

original: The fox, the ape, and the humble-bee,   Were still at odds, being but three.
translation: The fox, the ape and the bumble-bee,  Are always quarreling, as there are only three of them.

original: Until the goose came out of door, Staying the odds by adding four.
A good l'envoy, ending in the goose: would you desire more?
The boy hath sold him a bargain, a goose, that's flat.
translation: The boy has made a fool out of him, he's made him a goose that's for certain.

original: Sir, your pennyworth is good, an your goose be fat.
translation: Sir your bits were quite good and your goose is certainly fat.

original: To sell a bargain well is as cunning as fast and loose:
translation: To win your point that way is as cunning as it is unfair.

original: Let me see; a fat l'envoy; ay, that's a fat goose.
translation: Let me see, a fat epilogue, yes that's a fat goose then.

original: Come hither, come hither. How did this argument begin?
translation: Come on now, come on now. How did this argument begin anyway?

original: By saying that a costard was broken in a shin. Then call'd you for the l'envoy.
translation: Well I said that Costard had injured his shin and you asked right away for the l'envoy.

original: True, and I for a plantain: thus came your argument in; Then the boy's fat l'envoy, the goose that you bought; And he ended the market.
translation: True, and I asked for a plantain to heal my shin—here's where your argument began. Then the boy made his epilogue, you bought the goose and he ended the matter.

original: But tell me; how was there a costard broken in a shin?
translation: But tell me again, how could a head have injured its shin?

original: I will tell you sensibly.
translation: I will tell you sensibly now.

original: Thou hast no feeling of it, Moth: I will speak that  l'envoy: I Costard, running out, that was safely within, Fell over the threshold and broke my shin.
We will talk no more of this matter.
translation: Let's talk no more about this matter.

original: Till there be more matter in the shin.
translation: Not until there is pus oozing from the shin.

original: Sirrah Costard, I will enfranchise thee.
translation: Costard, sir, I am going to release you.

original: O, marry me to one Frances: I smell some l'envoy, some goose, in this.
By my sweet soul, I mean setting thee at liberty, enfreedoming thy person; thou wert immured, restrained, captivated, bound.
translation: For goodness sake, I mean I am going to give you your freedom, I am going to let you go. You were imprisoned, restrained, held as my captive and you won't be anymore.

original: True, true; and now you will be my purgation and let me loose.
translation: If this is true then I will be cleared of all of my guilt and set free?

original: I give thee thy liberty, set thee from durance; and, in lieu thereof, impose on thee nothing but this: bear this significant
translation: I give you your freedom and put an end to your imprisonment. I ask just one small thing of you in return.

original: to the country maid Jaquenetta: there is remuneration; for the best ward of mine honour is rewarding my dependents. Moth, follow.
Like the sequel, I. Signior Costard, adieu.
translation: I will follow after you. Goodbye Costard.

original: My sweet ounce of man's flesh! my incony Jew!
translation: Oh you wonderful man! My fine Jew!

original: Now will I look to his remuneration.
translation: Now I will look more closely at this "remuneration."

original: Remuneration!   O, that's the Latin word for three farthings: three   farthings—remuneration.
translation: Remuneration!  That must be the Latin word for three farthings , three farthings or  remuneration .

original: —'What's the price of this   inkle?'—'One penny.'—'No, I'll give you a   remuneration:' why, it carries it.
translation: "What is the price of this thread?" "One penny." "I'll give you a remuneration for it!" Why, it sounds good.

original: Remuneration!   why, it is a fairer name than French crown. I will   never buy and sell out of this word.
O, my good knave Costard! exceedingly well met.
translation: Oh, you rascal Costard! Am I glad to see you!

original: Pray you, sir, how much carnation ribbon may a man buy for a remuneration?
translation: Excuse me sir, how much flesh-colored ribbon can a person buy with a remuneration?

original: What is a remuneration?
translation: What is a remuneration?

original: Marry, sir, halfpenny farthing.
translation: Why, sir, it is a halfpenny farthing.

original: Why, then, three-farthing worth of silk.
translation: Well then you can buy three-farthings worth of silk.

original: I thank your worship: God be wi' you!
translation: Thank you very much sir, and god be with you!

original: Stay, slave; I must employ thee: As thou wilt win my favour, good my knave, Do one thing for me that I shall entreat.
translation: Stay for a minute, mister, I have a task for you. If you want to get in my good books, you rascal, do this one little thing for me.

original: When would you have it done, sir?
translation: When would you like me to do it sir?

original: This afternoon.
translation: This afternoon.

original: Well, I will do it, sir: fare you well.
translation: Very well, I will do it sir! Goodbye.

original: Thou knowest not what it is.
translation: You don't know what it is that I want you to do.

original: I shall know, sir, when I have done it.
translation: I shall know what it is, sir, after I have done it.

original: Why, villain, thou must know first.
translation: No, you fool, you have to know what it is first.

original: I will come to your worship to-morrow morning.
translation: Okay then, I will come and find out from you tomorrow morning.

original: It must be done this afternoon.
translation: No, it must be done this afternoon.

original: Hark, slave, it is but this:
translation: Listen, slave, I need you to do this:

translation: the Princess is coming here to hunt in the park, and with her will be a gentle lady that people call Rosaline.

original: ask for her;   And to her white hand see thou do commend   This seal'd-up counsel. There's thy guerdon; go.
translation: Ask for her and put this sealed letter into her pale hand. Here's your  guerdon , now off you go.

original: Gardon, O sweet gardon! better than remuneration, a'leven-pence farthing better: most sweet gardon! I will do it sir, in print. Gardon! Remuneration!
translation: Gardon, Oh sweet gardon! Way better than a remuneration, eleven-pence farthing better actually. Most sweet gardon! I will do it sir, just as you asked. Gardon! Remuneration!

original: And I, forsooth, in love!
translation: I cannot believe it, I am in love!

original: I, that have been love's  whip;   A very beadle to a humorous sigh;
translation: I have opposed love for so long, and tried to protect myself against its telling sighs.

original: A critic, nay, a night-watch constable;   A domineering pedant o'er the boy;   Than whom no mortal so magnificent!
translation: I have been a critic of love, or even a night-time guard against it; I have been like a controlling teacher over this boy, Cupid—is there a prouder mortal on this earth?

translation: That completely blind, stubborn boy, who is  both old and young . That giant dwarf, master Cupid, ruler of love-rhymes, the lord of crossed arms, the elected leader of sighs and groans, the chief of all those who drag their feet or moan, the prince of  women's genitals , the king of  male ones , the absolute ruler and great general of  men who judged those in love .

original: —O my little heart:—   And I to be a corporal of his field,   And wear his colours like a tumbler's hoop!   What, I! I love! I sue! I seek a wife!
translation: Oh my little heart! I have to be a soldier for love and wear the colors of love like an  acrobat's ribbons ! What, me! I now love! I want to date a woman! I am looking for a wife!

original: A woman, that is like a German clock,   Still a-repairing, ever out of frame,   And never going aright, being a watch,   But being watch'd that it may still go right!
translation: A woman that has been elaborately made like a  German clock , always needing repairs, always out of sorts, will never tell the right time. But  a small clock , as it needs to be watched all the time, always tells the right time!

original: Nay, to be perjured, which is worst of all;   And, among three, to love the worst of all;   A wightly wanton with a velvet brow,   With two pitch-balls stuck in her face for eyes;
translation: Oh, to break my oath would be the worst thing, and out of the three promises, to fall in love is the worst. A fair-skinned, promiscuous woman with a face as smooth as velvet, with two pitch-black balls stuck on her face as eyes.

original: Ay, and by heaven, one that will do the deed   Though Argus were her eunuch and her guard:
translation: Yes, and by heaven, she is someone who will have sex with me, although I have to battle  Argus  to get to her.

translation: Well I will sigh for her! I will stay awake for her! I will pray for her!

original: Go to; it is a plague   That Cupid will impose for my neglect   Of his almighty dreadful little might.
translation: Oh me, this is a sickness that Cupid has given me because I ignored his importance for so long.

original: Well, I will love, write, sigh, pray, sue and groan:   Some men must love my lady and some Joan.
translation: Well then I guess I will love, I will write, sigh, pray, court and groan; some men get to love a lady as brilliant as mine, and some must love someone of  a lower status.

original: Was that the king, that spurred his horse so hard Against the steep uprising of the hill?
translation: Did I just see the king, riding his horse fiercely, as they went up that hill?

original: I know not; but I think it was not he.
translation: I don't know, but I don't think it was him.

original: Whoe'er a' was, a' show'd a mounting mind.
translation: Well whoever it was, they seem ambitious

original: Well, lords, to-day we shall have our dispatch:   On Saturday we will return to France.
translation: . Anyway, lords, today we shall be given permission to leave, and we will return to France on Saturday.

original: Then, forester, my friend, where is the bush   That we must stand and play the murderer in?
translation: Tell me forester, where should a hunter stand when committing murder?

original: Hereby, upon the edge of yonder coppice; A stand where you may make the fairest shoot.
translation: Right here, on the edge of this green space. Stand here and you will make a beautiful shot.

original: I thank my beauty, I am fair that shoot, And thereupon thou speak'st the fairest shoot.
translation: I guess that compared to other hunters I am beautiful, and that's an advantage. It means that you can call me a beautiful shooter.

original: Pardon me, madam, for I meant not so.
translation: Sorry madam, I didn't mean it like that.

original: What, what? first praise me and again say no? O short-lived pride! Not fair? alack for woe!
translation: What sir? You are going to praise me and then take it away immediately? Oh short-lived flattery! You don't think I'm beautiful?! Oh poor me!

original: Yes, madam, fair.
translation: Madam, you are beautiful.

original: Nay, never paint me now: Where fair is not, praise cannot mend the brow. Here, good my glass, take this for telling true: Fair payment for foul words is more than due.
translation: Don't you try to flatter me now—if I am not actually beautiful then your words alone cannot change that.  Thank you for being my mirror and telling me the truth, you deserve this money even if the words are hurtful.

original: Nothing but fair is that which you inherit.
translation: You are only made up of beautiful things.

original: See see, my beauty will be saved by merit!   O heresy in fair, fit for these days!
translation: Look, my beauty can be saved by  money ! Oh it is a violation of beauty but is only too suitable these days!

original: A giving hand, though foul, shall have fair praise.
translation: A generous hand, even though it is an ugly thing, can receive a lot of praise.

original: But come, the bow: now mercy goes to kill,   And shooting well is then accounted ill.
translation: Anyway, give me the bow. Now I, in my  mercy , must kill this deer, and even if I shoot well, my shot should be considered a bad thing.

original: Thus will I save my credit in the shoot:   Not wounding, pity would not let me do't;   If wounding, then it was to show my skill,   That more for praise than purpose meant to kill.
translation: Indeed, I can save my reputation in this shoot as, if I don't hit the deer, then I can say that my pity made me miss it on purpose, or, if I do hit the deer, then I only did it to show my skill and to be praised, not because I wanted to kill it.

original: And out of question so it is sometimes,   Glory grows guilty of detested crimes,
translation: And it is undeniable that sometimes, people have to do things that they hate in order to gain the honor that they want.

original: When, for fame's sake, for praise, an outward part,   We bend to that the working of the heart;
translation: It is for the fame, for the praise, these superficial things, that we commit our hearts to this activity.

original: As I for praise alone now seek to spill   The poor deer's blood, that my heart means no ill.
translation: So I now aim to spill this poor deer's blood only for fame, not because I want to harm it at all.

original: Do not curst wives hold that self-sovereignty Only for praise sake, when they strive to be Lords o'er their lords?
translation: Don't difficult wives like to have power over their husbands, simply for the praise they will get when they boss them around?

original: Only for praise: and praise we may afford To any lady that subdues a lord.
translation: Yes, only for the praise, and indeed we give this praise to any lady that manages to get the better of her husband.

original: Here comes a member of the commonwealth.
translation: Oh look, here comes one of the common men.

original: God dig-you-den all! Pray you, which is the head lady?
translation: Good day to you all! Who is the head lady?

original: Thou shalt know her, fellow, by the rest that have no  heads.
translation: Surely you will know her, boy, by the fact that she is the only one with a head.

original: Which is the greatest lady, the highest?
translation: Okay, which of you is the greatest lady, the highest one?

original: The thickest and the tallest.
translation: The fattest and the tallest one.

original: The thickest and the tallest!
translation: The fattest and the tallest!

original: it is so; truth is truth.
translation: Of course! That must be it!

original: An your waist, mistress, were as slender as my wit,   One o' these maids' girdles for your waist should be  fit.
translation: Imagine mistress, if your waist was as small as my brain is, you would be able to fit into any of these maids' corsets!

original: Are not you the chief woman? you are the thickest here.
translation: But since you are the fattest here, does that mean that you are the woman in charge?

original: What's your will, sir? what's your will?
translation: What do you want, sir? Why are you here?

original: I have a letter from Monsieur Biron to one Lady  Rosaline.
translation: I have a letter from Monsieur Biron to one Lady Rosaline.

original: O, thy letter, thy letter! he's a good friend of mine: Stand aside, good bearer. Boyet, you can carve; Break up this capon.
translation: Oh a letter, a letter! Biron is a good friend of mine, so hand it over messenger. Boyet, you can open it—let's hear this love letter.

original: I am bound to serve. This letter is mistook, it importeth none here; It is writ to Jaquenetta.
translation: As you wish. Hang on a minute, this letter must be a mistake, it has nothing to do with anyone here. This letter is for Jaquenetta.

original: We will read it, I swear. Break the neck of the wax, and every one give ear.
'By heaven, that thou art fair, is most infallible;   true, that thou art beauteous; truth itself, that   thou art lovely.
translation: "By heaven, it is certain that you are beautiful; it is true that you are pretty and it is even more true that you are lovely.

original: More fairer than fair, beautiful   than beauteous, truer than truth itself, have   commiseration on thy heroical vassal!
translation: You are more beautiful that the word beautiful suggests, you are prettier than a pretty person, you are truer than truth itself, so have some pity on your heroic slave!

original: The   magnanimous and most illustrate king Cophetua set   eye upon the pernicious and indubitate beggar   Zenelophon; and he it was that might rightly say,   Veni, vidi, vici;
translation: Once, the great and illustrious  King Cophetua set eyes upon the fatal and undoubtable beggar Zenelophon  and right away he might have said " Veni, vidi, vici,"

original: which to annothanize in the   vulgar,—O base and obscure vulgar!—videlicet, He   came, saw, and overcame:   he came, one; saw two;   overcame, three.
translation: which to explain in common language for the common people, means, "He came, he saw, he conquered." First he came, then he saw, and then he conquered.

original: Who came? the king: why did he   come? to see: why did he see? to overcome: to   whom came he? to the beggar: what saw he? the   beggar: who overcame he? the beggar.
translation: Who came? The King! Why did he come? To see! Why did he need to see? To conquer! Who did he come to? The beggar! What did he see? The beggar! What did he  conquer ? The beggar!

original: The   conclusion is victory: on whose side? the king's.
translation: The conclusion of this is a victory—but for who? The King.

original: The captive is enriched: on whose side? the   beggar's. The catastrophe is a nuptial: on whose   side? the king's: no, or both in one, or one in   both.
translation: The prisoner has been improved, but who is the prisoner? The beggar. This ended in a marriage, but on whose side? The King's? No. Or were they both married, or married together.

original: I am the king; for so stands the comparison:   thou the beggar; for so witnesseth thy lowliness.
translation: I am the King in this story, and so you must be the beggar, because of your poverty.

original: Shall I command thy love? I may: shall I enforce   thy love? I could: shall I entreat thy love? I   will.
translation: Shall I order you to love me? I might. Shall I force you to love me? I could. Shall I ask you to love me? I will.

original: What shalt thou exchange for rags? robes;   for tittles? titles; for thyself? me.
translation: What will you get in exchange? For your rags, you will get amazing dresses; for your  pennies you will now get titles ; for yourself you will get me.

original: Thus,   expecting thy reply, I profane my lips on thy foot,   my eyes on thy picture. and my heart on thy every   part. Thine, in the dearest design of industry, ADRIANO DE ARMADO.'
translation: I am waiting for your reply. I will kiss your foot, I will stare at your picture, and will heart will constantly think of you.

original: What plume of feathers is he that indited this letter? What vane? what weathercock? did you ever hear better?
translation: What kind of show-off wrote this letter? What kind of inconstant and unreliable man is he? Have you ever heard something so ridiculous?

original: I am much deceived but I remember the style.
translation: I am convinced that I know the person who has written it.

original: Else your memory is bad, going o'er it erewhile.
translation: Well I should hope so, or your memory isn't very good—you only just read it!

original: This Armado is a Spaniard, that keeps here in court; A phantasime, a Monarcho, and one that makes sport To the prince and his bookmates.
Thou fellow, a word: Who gave thee this letter?
translation: A word, Costard. Who gave you this letter?

original: I told you; my lord.
translation: I told you—my lord.

original: To whom shouldst thou give it?
translation: Who did he tell you to give it to?

original: From my lord to my lady.
translation: He said to give it to my lady, from my lord.

original: From which lord to which lady?
translation: From which lord to which lady?

original: From my lord Biron, a good master of mine, To a lady of France that he call'd Rosaline.
translation: It came from my lord Biron, a good master of mine, to be given to a lady of France that he said was called Rosaline.

original: Thou hast mistaken his letter. Come, lords, away.
translation: You have got the wrong letter. Come, lords, let's go.

original: Here, sweet, put up this: 'twill be thine another day.
translation: Here you go, my sweet friend, keep this—it will truly be yours one day soon.

original: Who is the suitor? who is the suitor?
Shall I teach you to know?
translation: Shall I let you in on a secret?

original: Ay, my continent of beauty.
translation: Why yes, you beautiful thing.

original: Why, she that bears the bow. Finely put off!
translation: Well of course, it's the person that has the bow. Dodged that one well!

original: My lady goes to kill horns; but, if thou marry, Hang me by the neck, if horns that year miscarry. Finely put on!
Well, then, I am the shooter.
translation: Okay then, I am the shooter.

original: And who is your deer?
translation: And who will be your prey?

original: If we choose by the horns, yourself come not near. Finely put on, indeed!
You still wrangle with her, Boyet, and she strikes at the brow.
translation: You keep trying to argue with her Boyet, but she hits you right in the head.

original: But she herself is hit lower: have I hit her now?
translation: But she herself has been hit lower, in the heart, hasn't she? Have I got to her now?

original: Shall I come upon thee with an old saying, that was a man when King Pepin of France was a little boy, as touching the hit it?
So I may answer thee with one as old, that was a woman when Queen Guinover of Britain was a little wench, as touching the hit it.
Thou canst not hit it, hit it, hit it, Thou canst not hit it, my good man.
translation: You cannot hit the mark, you cannot hit the mark, You cannot hit the right thing, my good man.

original: An I cannot, cannot, cannot, An I cannot, another can.
By my troth, most pleasant: how both did fit it!
A mark marvellous well shot, for they both did hit it.
translation: A target that has been well shot, seeing as they both did hit their mark.

original: A mark! O, mark but that mark! A mark, says my lady! Let the mark have a prick in't, to mete at, if it may  be.
Wide o' the bow hand! i' faith, your hand is out.
translation: You are aiming too wide from the target! Indeed, you are out of practice.

original: Indeed, a' must shoot nearer, or he'll ne'er hit the  clout.
translation: Indeed, he should shoot from closer, or he will never hit the cloth at all.

original: An if my hand be out, then belike your hand is in.
Then will she get the upshoot by cleaving the pin.
Come, come, you talk greasily; your lips grow foul.
translation: Stop that now, don't say such indecent things—your mouth is dirty.

original: She's too hard for you at pricks, sir: challenge her to bowl.
I fear too much rubbing. Good night, my good owl.
translation: I fear the balls will rub too much. Good night, you wise thing.

original: By my soul, a swain! a most simple clown!
translation: Oh dear, what a suitor! Such a simple fellow!

original: Lord, Lord, how the ladies and I have put him down!
translation: Lord, lord, how the ladies and I have mocked him!

original: O' my troth, most sweet jests! most incony   vulgar wit!
translation: Oh my word, what hilarious jokes! What fine,  common  wit!

original: When it comes so smoothly off, so obscenely, as it   were, so fit.
translation: When it is done so well, so crudely, it seems so fitting!

original: Armado o' th' one side,—O, a most dainty man!
translation: Yet, there is also Armado, and what a particular kind of man he is!

original: To see him walk before a lady and to bear her fan!   To see him kiss his hand! and how most sweetly a'   will swear!
translation: I love seeing him walking in front of a woman, fanning her! I love seeing him kiss his own hand and swearing his love for a woman so strongly!

original: And his page o' t' other side, that handful of wit!   Ah, heavens, it is a most pathetical nit!
translation: Then there is also his page, that small clever thing! Oh heavens, he is quite a touching little guy!

original: Sola, sola!
translation: Hey there, hey there!

original: Very reverend sport, truly; and done in the testimony of a good conscience.
translation: A very good shot, really, and you did it with a clear conscience.

original: The deer was, as you know, sanguis, in blood; ripe   as the pomewater,
translation: The deer was, as you know,  in prime condition , as ripe as a juicy apple.

original: who now hangeth like a jewel in   the ear of caelo, the sky, the welkin, the heaven;   and anon falleth like a crab on the face of terra,   the soil, the land, the earth.
translation: At one moment it hung like an earring in the ear of  the sky ,  the air, the heavens , and then, a moment later it fell like a crab-apple onto the ground, the soil, the land, the earth.

original: Truly, Master Holofernes, the epithets are sweetly varied, like a scholar at the least: but, sir, I assure ye, it was a buck of the first head.
translation: Really, Master Holofernes, the variety of names you have used are lovely, similar to how a scholar would speak to say the least. However sir, I must correct you, it was a five-year-old male deer with its first antlers.

original: Sir Nathaniel, haud credo.
translation: Sir Nathaniel, haud credo.

original: 'Twas not an 'auld grey doe', 'twas a pricket.
