Most barbarous intimation!
translation: What a ridiculous announcement!

original: yet a kind of   insinuation, as it were, in via, in way, of   explication;
translation: Yet, it is a kind of suggestion, as it were,  @ a means of  symbolizing a more detailed description. @

original: facere, as it were, replication, or   rather, ostentare, to show, as it were, his   inclination, after his undressed, unpolished,   uneducated, unpruned, untrained, or rather,   unlettered, or ratherest, unconfirmed fashion, to   insert again my haud credo for a deer.
translation: To make, as it were, a reply, or rather, to show  his opinion, in the best way he can, as a  scruffy, untidy, stupid, uncontrolled, uninstructed, or rather, uneducated, or even better ignorant idiot , to swap again my  haud credo  for a deer.

original: I said the deer was not an 'auld grey doe', twas a  pricket.
translation: I just said that the deer was not an old grey doe, it was a two-year-old deer.

original: Twice-sod simplicity, his coctus! O thou monster Ignorance, how deformed dost thou look!
Sir, he hath never fed of the dainties that are bred   in a book; he hath not eat paper, as it were; he   hath not drunk ink:
translation: Sir, he has never enjoyed the treats that can be found in a book; he hasn't eaten paper, as it were; he hasn't drunk the ink.

original: his intellect is not   replenished; he is only an animal, only sensible in   the duller parts:
translation: His mind has not been filled with ideas, he is just an animal, only able to feel things physically.

original: And such barren plants are set before us, that we   thankful should be,   Which we of taste and feeling are, for those parts that   do fructify in us more than he.
translation: Remember sir, when boring people are put before us, we should be thankful, that we are full of different tastes and emotions, since those things keep developing in us, when they don't in him.

original: For as it would ill become me to be vain, indiscreet,  or a fool,   So were there a patch set on learning, to see him in a  school:
translation: For although I know I should never be vain, careless, or an idiot,  if he went to a school it would be like teaching a fool !

original: But omne bene, say I; being of an old father's mind,   Many can brook the weather that love not the wind.
translation: Anyway,  all is well , I say, if I remember what they used to think in the past,  you have to just put up with the things that you can't change.

original: You two are book-men: can you tell me by your wit What was a month old at Cain's birth, that's not five weeks old as yet?
Dictynna, goodman Dull; Dictynna, goodman Dull.
translation: That would be Dictynna my goodman Dull, that would be Dictynna.

original: What is Dictynna?
translation: What is Dictynna?

original: A title to Phoebe, to Luna, to the moon.
The moon was a month old when Adam was no more, And raught not to five weeks when he came to five-score. The allusion holds in the exchange.
translation: The moon was only a month old when Adam was the same age, and it hadn't reached five weeks old, even when Adam was a hundred! The riddle works for Adam as well.

original: 'Tis true indeed; the collusion holds in the exchange.
translation: It's true indeed, the word play still works, even when the riddle has been changed.

original: God comfort thy capacity! I say, the allusion holds in the exchange.
translation: May God help your intelligence! I said already, that the riddle works for Adam as well.

original: And I say, the pollusion holds in the exchange; for the moon is never but a month old: and I say beside that, 'twas a pricket that the Princess killed.
translation: And I say that there has been a mistake in your conversation, for the moon can never be more than a month old, and more than that, I am telling you that it was a two-year-old deer that the Princess killed.

original: Sir Nathaniel, will you hear an extemporal epitaph on the death of the deer? And, to humour the ignorant, call I the deer the princess killed a  pricket.
translation: Sir Nathaniel, would you like to hear an improvised eulogy about the death of the deer? To please the stupid listeners, I will even call the deer the Princess killed, only two-years-old.

original: Perge, good Master Holofernes, perge; so it shall please you to abrogate scurrility.
I will something affect the letter, for it argues  facility.
translation: I will focus on using alliteration, as it will help the flow of it.

original: A rare talent!
translation: He has a rare talent!

original: If a talent be a claw, look how he claws him with a talent.
translation: Only if a talent is a claw, because look at how he flatters him with his talent.

original: This is a gift that I have, simple, simple; a   foolish extravagant spirit, full of forms, figures,   shapes, objects, ideas, apprehensions, motions,   revolutions:
translation: It's a gift that I have, it's as simple as that. I am a silly, over-the top person,  full of words, figures of speech, shapes, objects outside of the mind, ideas, views, inner feelings, reflections.

original: these are begot in the ventricle of   memory, nourished in the womb of pia mater, and   delivered upon the mellowing of occasion.
translation: These are made in the depths of memory, they grow in the  outskirts of the brain , and are spoken when the time is just right.

original: But the   gift is good in those in whom it is acute, and I am   thankful for it.
translation: But a gift like this is good for a clever person, and I am thankful for it.

original: Sir, I praise the Lord for you; and so may my parishioners; for their sons are well tutored by you, and their daughters profit very greatly under you: you are a good member of the commonwealth.
Mehercle, if their sons be ingenuous, they shall want no instruction; if their daughters be capable, I will put it to them: but vir sapit qui pauca loquitur; a soul feminine saluteth us.
God give you good morrow, master Person.
Master Parson, quasi pers-on. An if one should be pierced, which is the one?
translation: She says Parson, as if the word was piers-on. If someone should be pierced, who will it be?

original: Marry, master schoolmaster, he that is likest to a  hogshead.
Piercing a hogshead! a good lustre of conceit in a tuft of earth; fire enough for a flint, pearl enough for a swine: 'tis pretty; it is well.
translation: Breaking open an ale barrel! A good moment of wit from someone so stupid, enough of a spark to light a fire, enough of a jewel to interest a villain. It is a good line.

original: Good master Parson, be so good as read me this letter: it was given me by Costard, and sent me from Don Armado: I beseech you, read it.
translation: Good master Parson, would you be so kind as to read this letter to me? It was given to me by Costard and has been sent to me from Don Armado. I beg you, please read it to me.

original: Ay, sir, and very learned.
translation: Yes sir, and you are very good at them.

original: Let me hear a staff, a stanze, a verse; lege, domine.
translation: Let's hear a paragraph of it, or a stanza, or a verse. Read, master.

original: If love make me forsworn, how shall I swear to love?
translation: If loving you will break my oath, then how can I swear on my oath that I love you?

original: Ah, never faith could hold, if not to beauty vow'd!
translation: Oh faith could never hold onto me, if I was not so attached to your beauty!

original: Though to myself forsworn, to thee I'll faithful prove:
translation: Even though I have broken the promises I made to myself, I will prove to you that I can be faithful.

original: Those thoughts to me were oaks, to thee like   osiers bow'd.
translation: The thoughts I had that I thought were as strong as oaks, under your influence they were like a bending willow tree, constantly changing.

original: Study his bias leaves and makes his book thine eyes,   Where all those pleasures live that art would   comprehend:
translation: The student now must abandon his studies and make your eyes his next book, the place where all the desires that knowledge understands live.

original: If knowledge be the mark, to know thee shall suffice;   Well learned is that tongue that well can thee commend,
translation: If knowledge is the target, then to know you should be enough to hit it — your tongue is so clever that you can praise me.

original: All ignorant that soul that sees thee without wonder;   Which is to me some praise that I thy parts admire:
translation: A person who sees you and isn't amazed is stupid, which means I must be at least a bit clever, because I admire everything about you.

original: Thy eye Jove's lightning bears, thy voice his dreadful  thunder,   Which not to anger bent, is music and sweet fire.
translation: Your eyes shine like Jupiter's lightning, your voice echoes like his dreadful thunder which, as it is not often angry, sounds like music and sweet fire.

original: Celestial as thou art, O, pardon, love, this wrong,   That sings heaven's praise with such an earthly tongue.
translation: You are so heavenly, please forgive all that I have done wrong for love, a love that praises you, a thing from heaven, with just a simple voice.

original: You find not the apostraphas, and so miss the   accent: let me supervise the canzonet.
translation: You didn't notice the apostrophes and so you have put emphasis on the wrong words, let me look at this  poem .

original: Here are   only numbers ratified; but, for the elegancy,   facility, and golden cadence of poesy, caret.
translation: Here are lines which have the  right meter  to them, but they lack elegancy, fluency, and the required flow of poetry.

original: Ovidius Naso was the man: and why, indeed, Naso,   but for smelling out the odouriferous flowers of   fancy, the jerks of invention?
translation: Ovid  was the best man at doing this, and why was his surname  Naso , why, because he could smell out the best parts of love to write about, the best witty speeches from his imagination.

original: Imitari is nothing:   so doth the hound his master, the ape his keeper,   the tired horse his rider. But, damosella virgin,   was this directed to you?
translation: Imitation is pointless, it is like comparing a dog to its master, a monkey to its keep, a tired horse to its rider. But my virgin girl, was this letter given to you?

original: Ay, sir, from one Monsieur Biron, one of the strange queen's lords.
I will overglance the superscript: 'To the   snow-white hand of the most beauteous Lady   Rosaline.'
translation: I will look again at who the letter is addressed to: "To the pure, white hand of the most beautiful Lady Rosaline."

original: I will look again on the intellect of   the letter, for the nomination of the party writing   to the person written unto: 'Your ladyship's in all   desired employment, BIRON.'
translation: I will now look again at the signature of the letter, to find the name of the person who has written it: "Yours, in any way you want me to be, BIRON."

original: Sir Nathaniel, this   Biron is one of the votaries with the king; and here   he hath framed a letter to a sequent of the stranger   queen's, which accidentally, or by the way of   progression, hath miscarried.
translation: Sir Nathaniel, this Biron is one of the lords who has sworn the oath with the king, and yet here he has written a letter to one of the foreign queen's ladies, which, either accidentally, or as a result of its journey, has failed to get to the right person.

original: Trip and go, my   sweet; deliver this paper into the royal hand of the   king: it may concern much. Stay not thy   compliment; I forgive thy duty; adieu.
translation: Get going, my sweet girl. Deliver this letter into the King's hand, it may be very important. Don't hang around to thank me, you don't need to show your appreciation. Goodbye now.

original: Good Costard, go with me. Sir, God save your life!
translation: Good Costard, come with me! Sir, God's thanks to you!

original: Have with thee, my girl.
translation: I'll go with you, my girl.

original: Sir, you have done this in the fear of God, very religiously; and, as a certain father saith,—
Sir tell me not of the father; I do fear colourable colours. But to return to the verses: did they please you, Sir Nathaniel?
Marvellous well for the pen.
translation: The handwriting was very nice.

original: I do dine to-day at the father's of a certain pupil   of mine; where, if, before repast, it shall please   you to gratify the table with a grace,
translation: I am going to have dinner today at the house of one of my student's fathers, where I hope before the meal, you will be able to say grace.

original: I will, on my   privilege I have with the parents of the foresaid   child or pupil, undertake your ben venuto;
translation: I will use the relationship that I have with the parents of this child, or pupil, to make sure that  you are welcome  for the meal.

original: where I   will prove those verses to be very unlearned,   neither savouring of poetry, wit, nor invention: I   beseech your society.
translation: When we are there, I will prove that these verses are very simple, and contain no poetry, wit, or imagination. I hope you with come with me.

original: And thank you too; for society, saith the text, is the happiness of life.
And, certes, the text most infallibly concludes it.
translation: And certainly, the text truly settles the matter.

original: Sir, I do invite you too; you shall not say me nay: pauca verba. Away! the gentles are at their game, and we will to our recreation.
translation: Sir, you are invited as well and you will not turn me down. Fewer words are best. Let's go! The lords are hunting, and now it's time for our entertainment.

original: The king he is hunting the deer; I am coursing   myself:
translation: The king is currently hunting deer, while I am  cursing myself ;

original: they have pitched a toil; I am toiling in   a pitch,—pitch that defiles: defile! a foul   word.
translation: they have laid their traps for their prey while I have been captured by that black, sticky substance of love and am now infected by it—infected!  That is a dirty word.

original: Well, set thee down, sorrow! for so they say   the fool said, and so say I, and I the fool: well   proved, wit!
translation: Anyway, be patient sadness! For this is supposedly what the fool said and now I say it too, so I must be a fool, oh well said!

original: By the Lord, this love is as mad as   Ajax: it kills sheep; it kills me, I a sheep:   well proved again o' my side!
translation: My goodness, being in love is  as mad as Ajax. It kills sheep , it kills me, oh then I must be a sheep! Well said again!

original: I will not love: if   I do, hang me; i' faith, I will not. O, but her   eye,—by this light, but for her eye, I would not   love her; yes, for her two eyes.
translation: I will not love. If I do, kill me anyway! Truthfully I cannot love. Oh, but her eye, her eye allows me to see, I wouldn't love her if not for her two eyes.

original: Well, I do nothing   in the world but lie, and lie in my throat.
translation: Oh the only thing I seem to do in this world is tell gross lies and I can feel them in my throat.

original: By   heaven, I do love: and it hath taught me to rhyme   and to be melancholy; and here is part of my rhyme,   and here my melancholy.
translation: By heaven, I do love and it has taught me how to write poetry and here is part of my poem, and here is my sadness.

original: Well, she hath one o' my   sonnets already: the clown bore it, the fool sent   it, and the lady hath it: sweet clown, sweeter   fool, sweetest lady!
translation: I've already sent her one of my sonnets, Costard that clown took it to her, I, the fool sent it and she now has it—sweet clown, s weeter fool, sweetest lady!

original: By the world, I would not care   a pin, if the other three were in.
translation: By the world I wouldn't mind at all, if the other three were in love.

original: Here comes one   with a paper: God give him grace to groan!
translation: Here comes one of the others with paper—oh please let him be groaning like I am!

original: Ay me!
translation: Why me!

original: Shot, by heaven! Proceed, sweet Cupid: thou hast thumped him with thy bird-bolt under the left pap. In faith, secrets!
translation: My goodness, he has been struck too! Carry on, sweet Cupid, you have shot him in the heart with your arrow. Let's hear what he will confess!

original: So sweet a kiss the golden sun gives not   To those fresh morning drops upon the rose,   As thy eye-beams, when their fresh rays have smote   The night of dew that on my cheeks down flows:
translation: The golden sun doesn't shine so brightly on the fresh dew of a morning rose, as your eyes do, when they look after my cheeks, covered with last night's tears.

original: Nor shines the silver moon one half so bright   Through the transparent bosom of the deep,   As doth thy face through tears of mine give light;
translation: The silver moon doesn't shine half as bright in the dead of night, as your face shines through my tears.

original: Thou shinest in every tear that I do weep:   No drop but as a coach doth carry thee;   So ridest thou triumphing in my woe.
translation: You are reflected in every tear that I weep, every drop is like a coach to carry you away, as you ride and rejoice at my sadness.

original: Do but behold the tears that swell in me,   And they thy glory through my grief will show:
translation: Just look at the tears that grow in me and know that they show your glory by the effect that it has on me.

original: But do not love thyself; then thou wilt keep   My tears for glasses, and still make me weep.
translation: Yet, don't just love yourself, since then my tears will just be like a mirror for you to look at yourself in, and I will keep crying.

original: O queen of queens! how far dost thou excel,   No thought can think, nor tongue of mortal tell.
translation: Oh queen of queens! How incredible you are cannot even be thought of, it cannot be put into words.

original: How shall she know my griefs? I'll drop the paper:   Sweet leaves, shade folly. Who is he comes here?
translation: How will you know my pains? I will give you paper, and  the leaves  will hide my silliness. Wait, who is coming?

original: What, Longaville! and reading! listen, ear.
translation: Oh, it is Longaville, and he is reading! I will listen to what he has to say.

original: Now, in thy likeness, one more fool appear!
translation: He looks as lovesick as you do, another foolish man!

original: Ay me, I am forsworn!
translation: Oh poor me, I am finished!

original: Why, he comes in like a perjure, wearing papers.
In love, I hope: sweet fellowship in shame!
translation: I hope he's in love, I could use the company!

original: One drunkard loves another of the name.
translation: One lovesick man loves another woman.

original: Am I the first that have been perjured so?
translation: Am I the first to be untruthful in this way?

original: I could put thee in comfort. Not by two that I know: Thou makest the triumviry, the corner-cap of society, The shape of Love's Tyburn that hangs up simplicity.
I fear these stubborn lines lack power to move: O sweet Maria, empress of my love! These numbers will I tear, and write in prose.
O, rhymes are guards on wanton Cupid's hose: Disfigure not his slop.
translation: Don't ruin Cupid's work.

original: This same shall go.
translation: This is what I've got so far.

original: Did not the heavenly rhetoric of thine eye,   'Gainst whom the world cannot hold argument,   Persuade my heart to this false perjury?
translation: Didn't the heavenly words that your eye speaks, words that no-one in the world can debate against, convince my heart to be dishonest in this way?

original: Vows for thee broke deserve not punishment.
translation: The vows that I have broken for you don't deserve to be punished.

original: A woman I forswore; but I will prove,   Thou being a goddess, I forswore not thee:
translation: I promised to abandon all women, but if I can prove that you are the goddess I think you are, then I have not broken any promise.

original: My vow was earthly, thou a heavenly love;   Thy grace being gain'd cures all disgrace in me.
translation: My oath was made on the earth, but you are a heavenly love, and if I can win your favor then all my disgraces will be gone.

original: Vows are but breath, and breath a vapour is:
translation: Vows are just breath and breath is like a vapor that melts away.

original: Then thou, fair sun, which on my earth dost shine,   Exhalest this vapour-vow; in thee it is:
translation: Then it is you, fair sun, that shines on my earth, evaporating this vapor and my vow, it is you who has done it.

original: If broken then, it is no fault of mine:   If by me broke, what fool is not so wise   To lose an oath to win a paradise?
translation: If the vow is broken then, it isn't my fault. If it is broken by me, then what fool wouldn't forget any oath to win a paradise?

original: This is the liver-vein, which makes flesh a deity, A green goose a goddess: pure, pure idolatry. God amend us, God amend! we are much out o' the way.
translation: This is written in the lover's style, which tries to make humans seem like gods, a silly young woman seem like a goddess. It is pure, pure glorification. God help us, God help us! Something has gone really wrong.

original: By whom shall I send this?—Company! stay.
translation: Who shall I send this poem with? There's someone here, hang on.

original: All hid, all hid; an old infant play. Like a demigod here sit I in the sky. And wretched fools' secrets heedfully o'ereye. More sacks to the mill! O heavens, I have my wish!
translation: Everyone's hiding, it's like an old childish game and I sit here like a demigod, overseeing these silly fools confess their secrets. There is more to come! Oh wonderful, I have my wish!

original: Dumain transform'd! four woodcocks in a dish!
translation: Dumain is transformed as well! Four fools in one place!

original: O most divine Kate!
translation: Oh most divine Kate!

original: O most profane coxcomb!
By heaven, the wonder in a mortal eye!
translation: By heaven, the wonder of her mortal eye.

original: By earth, she is not, corporal, there you lie.
translation: You should say "by earth" as she is human, there you have already lied.

original: Her amber hair for foul hath amber quoted.
translation: Her amber hair makes the color amber itself even look ugly.

original: An amber-colour'd raven was well noted.
As upright as the cedar.
translation: She is as upright as a cedar tree.

original: Stoop, I say; Her shoulder is with child.
As fair as day.
translation: She is as beautiful as the day.

original: Ay, as some days; but then no sun must shine.
translation: Yes, maybe she is as beautiful as the days when the sun doesn't shine.

original: O that I had my wish!
translation: Oh that I could have my love!

original: And I had mine!
translation: And I have mine!

original: And I mine too, good Lord!
translation: And I have mine as well, good Lord!

original: Amen, so I had mine: is not that a good word?
translation: So be it, if I could have mine too—isn't that good of me?

original: I would forget her; but a fever she Reigns in my blood and will remember'd be.
translation: I would try to forget her, but she has made my blood hot and so must be remembered.

original: A fever in your blood! why, then incision Would let her out in saucers: sweet misprision!
Once more I'll read the ode that I have writ.
translation: I will read the verse once more.

original: Once more I'll mark how love can vary wit.
translation: And once more I will hear how a clever man's words can change when he is in love.

original: On a day—alack the day!—
translation: On a day, oh on that day!

original: Love, whose month is ever May,   Spied a blossom passing fair   Playing in the wanton air:
translation: Love, that always comes in May, Saw a flower that was incredibly beautiful,  Playing in the shameless air.

original: Through the velvet leaves the wind,   All unseen, can passage find;   That the lover, sick to death,   Wish himself the heaven's breath.
translation: Through the softest leaves the wind, Finds a hidden pathway, So that the lover, sick to death, Will wish that he has the breath of heaven.

original: Air, quoth he, thy cheeks may blow;   Air, would I might triumph so!
translation: He says that "Air may blow on his cheeks, It would be an honor."

original: But, alack, my hand is sworn   Ne'er to pluck thee from thy thorn;
translation: But sadly I have made a promise To never pluck you from your stem.

original: Vow, alack, for youth unmeet,   Youth so apt to pluck a sweet!
translation: Curse this vow, for it is not right for a young man,  When a young man is so ready to pluck a sweet flower!

original: Do not call it sin in me,   That I am forsworn for thee;   Thou for whom Jove would swear   Juno but an Ethiope were;   And deny himself for Jove,   Turning mortal for thy love.
translation: Don't call me sinful, Even though I have sworn against you.  You, a woman that Jupiter would swear,  Was far more beautiful  than Juno, And would become a mortal to be with you.

original: This will I send, and something else more plain,   That shall express my true love's fasting pain.
translation: I will send this sonnet, and another plainer letter that will be express the pain I have from not being with her.

original: O, would the king, Biron, and Longaville,   Were lovers too!
translation: Oh I wish that the King, Biron and Longaville were lovers as well.

original: Ill, to example ill,   Would from my forehead wipe a perjured note;   For none offend where all alike do dote.
translation: If my wrongdoings could be justified by theirs, it would save me from being considered a liar, as none of us could get in trouble if we've all done the same.

original: Dumain, thy love is far from charity. That in love's grief desirest society. You may look pale, but I should blush, I know, To be o'erheard and taken napping so.
translation: Dumain, your love isn't Christian love, that looks for company in its trouble. You look pale, but it is me who should be blushing, for having listened to you from my hiding place.

original: Come, sir, you blush; as his your case is  such;
translation: Come sir, you blush because you feel exactly the same as he does.

original: You chide at him, offending twice as much;   You do not love Maria?
translation: You tell him off, but you're twice as bad as he is! Don't you love Maria?

original: Longaville   Did never sonnet for her sake compile,   Nor never lay his wreathed arms athwart   His loving bosom to keep down his heart.
translation: Longaville didn't compose a sonnet for her, or hold his arms crossed over his chest to keep his heart in its place.

original: I have been closely shrouded in this bush   And mark'd you both and for you both did blush:
translation: I have been hidden in this bush and have watched you both and felt embarrassed for both of you.

original: I heard your guilty rhymes, observed your fashion,   Saw sighs reek from you, noted well your passion:
translation: I heard your poems, I watched your behavior, I heard your sighs and noted your passions.

original: Ay me! says one; O Jove! the other cries;   One, her hairs were gold, crystal the other's eyes:
translation: "Oh me!" says one of you, "Oh Jupiter," the other one cries. For one of you, you talked about her golden hair, the other one talked about the jewels in her eyes.

original: You would for paradise break faith, and troth;
translation: You are prepared to break your vow for this paradise.

original: And Jove, for your love, would infringe an oath.
translation: And you think even Jupiter would break a promise to have your love.

original: What will Biron say when that he shall hear   Faith so infringed, which such zeal did swear?
translation: What will Biron say when he hears that your promises have been broken, when you swore to keep them with such enthusiasm?

original: How will he scorn! how will he spend his wit!   How will he triumph, leap and laugh at it!
translation: How he will scorn, how he will mock you! How he will hold it over you, laughing at your ridiculousness!

original: For all the wealth that ever I did see,   I would not have him know so much by me.
translation: For all the money I have, I would hate for him to have seem himself in the way I've seen you.

original: Now step I forth to whip hypocrisy.
translation: Now I will come forwards to stir things up even more.

original: Ah, good my liege, I pray thee, pardon me!
translation: My good lord, I pray you, forgive me!

original: Good heart, what grace hast thou, thus to reprove   These worms for loving, that art most in love?
translation: Good heart, what a privilege it is for you to be able to tell these miserable creatures off for loving, when you are the most in love out of all of them?

original: Your eyes do make no coaches; in your tears   There is no certain princess that appears;
translation: Are you telling me that your eyes aren't coaches ready to carry the Princess away, that her face doesn't appear in your tears?

original: You'll not be perjured, 'tis a hateful thing;
translation: You won't reveal that you've been dishonest too, that is not very nice.

original: Tush, none but minstrels like of sonneting!   But are you not ashamed? nay, are you not,   All three of you, to be thus much o'ershot?
translation: My goodness, you are all entertainers with your poetry! But aren't you ashamed? Are you not ashamed, all three of you, to be so wrong?

original: You found his mote; the king your mote did see;   But I a beam do find in each of three.   O, what a scene of foolery have I seen,   Of sighs, of groans, of sorrow and of teen!
translation: You saw his hypocrisy, the King saw yours, but I've seen the liar in all three of you. Oh what a scene of foolery have I witnessed, a scene filled with sighs, groans, sadness and grief!

original: O me, with what strict patience have I sat,   To see a king transformed to a gnat!
translation: Oh it has been hard for me to have the patience to watch, as I have seen a King transformed into nothing!

original: To see great Hercules whipping a gig,   And profound Solomon to tune a jig,   And Nestor play at push-pin with the boys,   And critic Timon laugh at idle toys!
translation: I have seen great Hercules off his head, serious Solomon trying to sing a song ,  Nestor  playing a game with children, and the critical  Timon  laughing at pointless games!

original: Where lies thy grief, O, tell me, good Dumain?   And gentle Longaville, where lies thy pain?   And where my liege's? all about the breast:   A caudle, ho!
translation: Where does it hurt, oh tell me, good Dumain? And gentle Longaville, where is your pain? And where is the King's? Is it deep in your chest, we must get you a  drink !

original: Too bitter is thy jest. Are we betray'd thus to thy over-view?
translation: You are too mean in your jokes. Have we been betrayed by what you have seen?

original: Not you to me, but I betray'd by you:
translation: You haven't been betrayed by me, but I have been betrayed by you.

original: I, that am honest; I, that hold it sin   To break the vow I am engaged in;
translation: I am an honest man and think it is a sin to break the vow that I have promised to keep.

original: I am betray'd, by keeping company   With men like men of inconstancy.
translation: I am betrayed by hanging out with men who are so unfaithful.

original: When shall you see me write a thing in rhyme?   Or groan for love? or spend a minute's time   In pruning me?
translation: When will you see me write something in rhyme? Or groan for love? Or spend even a minute grooming myself?

original: When shall you hear that I   Will praise a hand, a foot, a face, an eye,   A gait, a state, a brow, a breast, a waist,   A leg, a limb?
translation: When will you hear me praising a hand, a foot, a face, an eye, a way of walking, a posture, a brow, a breast, a waist, a leg, a limb?

original: Soft! whither away so fast? A true man or a thief that gallops so?
translation: Be quiet! Why do you go away so quickly?

original: I post from love: good lover, let me go.
translation: I hurry away from love. Good lover, let me go.

original: God bless the King!
translation: God bless the King!

original: What present hast thou there?
translation: What gift have you got there?

original: Some certain treason.
translation: It's definitely treason.

original: What makes treason here?
translation: What does treason have to do with it?

original: Nay, it makes nothing, sir.
translation: Treason doesn't have to do anything sir, it's just treason.

original: If it mar nothing neither, The treason and you go in peace away together.
translation: Then I don't have to let it ruin anything either. This treason and you can go away in peace together then.

original: I beseech your grace, let this letter be read: Our parson misdoubts it; 'twas treason, he said.
Biron, read it over.
translation: Biron, read it.

original: Where hadst thou it?
translation: Where did you get it?

original: Of Costard.
translation: From Costard.

original: Where hadst thou it?
translation: Costard, where did you get it?

original: Of Dun Adramadio, Dun Adramadio.
How now! what is in you? why dost thou tear it?
translation: Hey! What are you doing? Why did you tear it up?

original: A toy, my liege, a toy: your grace needs not fear it.
translation: It was nothing, my lord, nothing—your grace doesn't need to worry about it.

original: It did move him to passion, and therefore let's hear  it.
translation: It made him have a tantrum, so I think we should hear it.

original: It is Biron's writing, and here is his name.
translation: It is in Biron's writing, and look, here's his name.

original: Ah, you whoreson loggerhead! you were born to do me shame. Guilty, my lord, guilty! I confess, I confess.
translation: Oh you stupid idiot! You were born to get me in trouble. Guilty, my lord, guilty! I confess, I confess.

original: What?
translation: What do you confess?

original: That you three fools lack'd me fool to make up the  mess: He, he, and you, and you, my liege, and I, Are pick-purses in love, and we deserve to die. O, dismiss this audience, and I shall tell you more.
translation: That you three idiots needed me to make our group complete.  He, he, yes you, you, my lord, and I, are cheats for love, and we deserve to die. Oh, get rid of these two and I will tell you more.

original: Now the number is even.
translation: Now we're all square.

original: True, true; we are four. Will these turtles be gone?
Hence, sirs; away!
translation: Okay you two, time to go!

original: Walk aside the true folk, and let the traitors stay.
translation: The honest people will walk away and leave the traitors behind.

original: Sweet lords, sweet lovers, O, let us embrace!
translation: My sweet lords, sweet lovers, oh let's hug it out!

original: As true we are as flesh and blood can be:   The sea will ebb and flow, heaven show his face;
translation: Our friendship is as true and real as it can be, as true as the fact that the sea will have tides,  and heaven will show his face.

original: Young blood doth not obey an old decree:   We cannot cross the cause why we were born;   Therefore of all hands must we be forsworn.
translation: Young men cannot obey an old oath, we cannot go against our destiny, therefore we are bound to break our promises.

original: What, did these rent lines show some love of thine?
translation: What, did these lines we have been given show some love of yours?

original: Did they, quoth you?
translation: Did they, you ask!

original: Who sees the heavenly Rosaline,   That, like a rude and savage man of Inde,   At the first opening of the gorgeous east,   Bows not his vassal head and strucken blind   Kisses the base ground with obedient breast?
translation: Who has seen the heavenly Rosaline, that would not, like an ignorant and uncivilized man of India, on seeing the first light of dawn, bow his inferior head and struck blind by its light, kiss the ground with a willing heart?

original: What peremptory eagle-sighted eye   Dares look upon the heaven of her brow,   That is not blinded by her majesty?
translation: What unblinking,  strong eye  would dare to look at the heaven of her face and not be blinded by her beauty?

original: What zeal, what fury hath inspired thee now? My love, her mistress, is a gracious moon; She an attending star, scarce seen a light.
translation: What desire, what frenzy has inspired you now? My love, her mistress, is like a gracious moon whereas Rosaline is just an attending star, her light can only just be seen.

original: My eyes are then no eyes, nor I Biron:
translation: My eyes then are not eyes, and I am not Biron if what you say is true.

original: O, but for my love, day would turn to night!
translation: Oh, were it not for my love, day would turn to night!

original: Of all complexions the cull'd sovereignty   Do meet, as at a fair, in her fair cheek,   Where several worthies make one dignity,   Where nothing wants that want itself doth seek.
translation: The best parts of all complexions come together in her cheek, all different kinds of value come together to make one excellent thing, and nothing that you would want is missing.

original: Lend me the flourish of all gentle tongues,—   Fie, painted rhetoric!
translation: Give me the words of all noble tongues, I don't need rhetoric!

original: O, she needs it not:   To things of sale a seller's praise belongs,   She passes praise; then praise too short doth blot.
translation: Oh and she doesn't need it either, as a man praises the thing that he wants to sell and she surpasses all praise; any praise is not good enough to describe her!

original: A wither'd hermit, five-score winters worn,   Might shake off fifty, looking in her eye:
translation: An old hermit, worn down by fifty winters, could shake off these fifty years just by looking in her eye

original: Beauty doth varnish age, as if new-born,   And gives the crutch the cradle's infancy:
translation: —her beauty improves age, making people feel newly-born and gives old age the energy of youth.

original: O, 'tis the sun that maketh all things shine.
translation: Oh it is her, the sun, that makes all things shine!

original: By heaven, thy love is black as ebony.
Is ebony like her?
translation: Is she like ebony?

original: O wood divine!   A wife of such wood were felicity.
translation: Oh then this wood is divine! A wife of this wood would be a happy thing.

original: O, who can give an oath? where is a book?
translation: Oh who should swear to an oath?! Find me a bible.

original: That I may swear beauty doth beauty lack,   If that she learn not of her eye to look:   No face is fair that is not full so black.
translation: I want to swear on it that beauty is missing out if it doesn't learn from Rosaline's eye how to appear—there is no face so beautiful, as one that is dark.

original: O paradox! Black is the badge of hell, The hue of dungeons and the school of night; And beauty's crest becomes the heavens well.
translation: That's a contradiction! Black is a sign of hell, it is the color of dungeons and the teacher of night's darkness. It is the sun which makes the heavens more beautiful.

original: Devils soonest tempt, resembling spirits of light.
translation: The Devil can transform itself into an angel of light.

original: O, if in black my lady's brows be deck'd,   It mourns that painting and usurping hair   Should ravish doters with a false aspect;
translation: Oh, if my lady's eyebrows were painted  black like the fashion , it would show how cosmetics and false hair can tempt lovers with misleading appearances.

original: And therefore is she born to make black fair.
translation: Therefore she is born to make darkness beautiful again.

original: Her favour turns the fashion of the days,
translation: Her face completely changes, and turns around what is considered fashionable nowadays.

original: For native blood is counted painting now;   And therefore red, that would avoid dispraise,   Paints itself black, to imitate her brow.
translation: For a complexion that is naturally reddish in its color is now only used for paintings, and so women who have this complexion paint themselves black in order to be praised and to look like her.

original: To look like her are chimney-sweepers black.
And since her time are colliers counted bright.
translation: And since her, even coal miners are thought to be beautiful.

original: And Ethiopes of their sweet complexion crack.
translation: And even Ethiops boast about their sweet complexions.

original: Dark needs no candles now, for dark is light.
translation: We don't even need candles now when it is dark, because darkness has become light.

original: Your mistresses dare never come in rain, For fear their colours should be wash'd away.
translation: Your mistresses should make sure that they never go outside in the rain, because their make-up would all be washed away.

original: 'Twere good, yours did; for, sir, to tell you plain, I'll find a fairer face not wash'd to-day.
translation: Well then, it would be good if your mistress did go outside in the rain, because sir, her face could do with being washed.

original: I'll prove her fair, or talk till doomsday here.
translation: I will prove her to be beautiful, or I will talk until the end of the world.

original: No devil will fright thee then so much as she.
translation: Then on the last day of the world, she will be more frightening than any devil.

original: I never knew man hold vile stuff so dear.
translation: I never knew a man to care so much about something so cheap.

original: Look, here's thy love: my foot and her face see.
translation: Look, here's your love—you can look at my black shoe and see her face.

original: O, if the streets were paved with thine eyes, Her feet were much too dainty for such tread!
translation: Oh, even if the streets were covered with your eyes, her feet would be too elegant to walk on them!

original: O, vile! then, as she goes, what upward lies The street should see as she walk'd overhead.
translation: Oh, that's disgusting! As she walks, these eyes would have to see up her dress as she walks on them.

original: But what of this? are we not all in love?
translation: But what does this mean? Are we all in love?

original: Nothing so sure; and thereby all forsworn.
translation: Oh that is certain, and so we have all broken our oath!

original: Then leave this chat; and, good Biron, now prove Our loving lawful, and our faith not torn.
translation: Then let's stop this conversation and good Biron, use your logic to demonstrate to us that our loving is okay and our faith is not broken.

original: Ay, marry, there; some flattery for this evil.
translation: Yes indeed, do that—make this evil seem a bit better.

original: O, some authority how to proceed; Some tricks, some quillets, how to cheat the devil.
translation: Oh, give us some ideas about what we should do next—some tricks, some subtle verbal distinctions to avoid being seen as liars.

original: Some salve for perjury.
translation: Some medicine for our illness.

original: 'Tis more than need.
translation: Oh it is more than necessary.

original: Have at you, then, affection's men at arms.
translation: Here it goes then, love's warriors.

original: Consider what you first did swear unto,   To fast, to study, and to see no woman;   Flat treason 'gainst the kingly state of youth.
translation: Think about what you first promised, to fast, to study and to see no women—promising to do these things is treason against the best time of your life.

original: Say, can you fast? your stomachs are too young;   And abstinence engenders maladies.
translation: Think about it, should we fast? Our stomachs are too young and not eating could give us diseases.

original: O, we have made a vow to study, lords,   And in that vow we have forsworn our books.
translation: Also think about your promise to study, lords, and the fact that this vow has made us reject our books,

original: For when would you, my liege, or you, or you,   In leaden contemplation have found out   Such fiery numbers as the prompting eyes   Of beauty's tutors have enrich'd you with?
translation: for we wouldn't know how to write poetry without seeing a woman's beautiful face.

original: Other slow arts entirely keep the brain;   And therefore, finding barren practisers,   Scarce show a harvest of their heavy toil:
translation: Other dull or more serious kinds of learning clog up the arteries, and are done for so long and take such effort that you don't end up learning much anyway.

original: But love, first learned in a lady's eyes,   Lives not alone immured in the brain;   But, with the motion of all elements,
translation: Love is first learned in a lady's eyes, it cannot be confined simply to the mind, it lives with the winds and the storms.

original: Courses as swift as thought in every power,   And gives to every power a double power,   Above their functions and their offices.
translation: It moves as quickly as thoughts through every part of you, and gives a double force to each part it visits, above and beyond their ordinary functions.

original: It adds a precious seeing to the eye;   A lover's eyes will gaze an eagle blind;   A lover's ear will hear the lowest sound,   When the suspicious head of theft is stopp'd:
translation: It even gives a person precious eyesight, with eyes so bright they can  blind an eagle , with an ear so sharp it can hear even the quietest sound, when a thief that is listening out for the slightest noise hears nothing.

original: Love's feeling is more soft and sensible   Than are the tender horns of cockl'd snails;   Love's tongue proves dainty Bacchus gross in taste:
translation: Love's touch is softer and more sensitive than the  soft horns of a snail ; Love's tongue shows itself to have better taste than even  Bacchus .

original: For valour, is not Love a Hercules,   Still climbing trees in the Hesperides?   Subtle as Sphinx; as sweet and musical   As bright Apollo's lute, strung with his hair:
translation: For its bravery, isn't Love like Hercules, still climbing trees in the  Hesperides ? It is subtle as a  Sphinx , as sweet and musical as the sound of Apollo's lute, the strings made with Love's hair.

original: And when Love speaks, the voice of all the gods   Makes heaven drowsy with the harmony.
translation: When Love speaks, the voices of all other gods make heaven sleepy with the sound of their harmony.

original: Never durst poet touch a pen to write   Until his ink were temper'd with Love's sighs;   O, then his lines would ravish savage ears   And plant in tyrants mild humility.
translation: A poet never touches their pen unless their ink is full of Love's sighs and the lines they write have the power to please common ears and even make tyrants more humble.

original: From women's eyes this doctrine I derive:   They sparkle still the right Promethean fire;
translation: I get all of this information from women's eyes as they throw out sparks like the very fire which  Prometheus  stole from heaven.

original: They are the books, the arts, the academes,   That show, contain and nourish all the world:   Else none at all in ought proves excellent.
translation: Their eyes are the books, the arts, the schools, that reflect, embody and feed the whole world, or without them nothing in the world seems good.

original: Then fools you were these women to forswear,   Or keeping what is sworn, you will prove fools.
translation: You were fools to give up these women, and if you keep your oaths, you will still be fools.

original: For wisdom's sake, a word that all men love,   Or for love's sake, a word that loves all men,   Or for men's sake, the authors of these women,   Or women's sake, by whom we men are men,
translation: Do it for wisdom's sake, a word that all men love, do it for love's sake, a word that loves all men. Do it for men's sake, so they can write about these women, do it for women's sake, who put us on this earth.

original: Let us once lose our oaths to find ourselves,   Or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths.
translation: We must give up our oaths to find ourselves, or if we keep them we will lose ourselves completely.

original: It is religion to be thus forsworn,   For charity itself fulfills the law,   And who can sever love from charity?
translation: It is within the beliefs of our religion to change our mind, for  charity  is a part of the law, and isn't Love just loving another?

original: Saint Cupid, then! and, soldiers, to the field!
translation: For Saint Cupid then! Like soldiers, let's go to our battlefield!

original: Advance your standards, and upon them, lords; Pell-mell, down with them! but be first advised, In conflict that you get the sun of them.
translation: Hold up your flags and march with them lords. Attack them at close quarters! Be advised though, make sure that they have the sun in their eyes so that you can get the better of them.

original: Now to plain-dealing; lay these glozes by: Shall we resolve to woo these girls of France?
translation: Now let's talk simply, lay these metaphors aside. Are we determined to woo these girls of France?

original: And win them too: therefore let us devise Some entertainment for them in their tents.
translation: And we will win them too! Let's think up some entertainment for them in their tents.

original: First, from the park let us conduct them thither;
translation: First, let's lead them from the park to their tents.

original: Then homeward every man attach the hand   Of his fair mistress:
translation: Then, after that, each man can grab hold of the hand of his own, beautiful mistress.

original: in the afternoon   We will with some strange pastime solace them,   Such as the shortness of the time can shape;
translation: In the afternoon we will amuse them with some kind of new entertainment, whatever we can come up with this quickly.

original: For revels, dances, masks and merry hours   Forerun fair Love, strewing her way with flowers.
translation: For it is said that things like celebrations, dances, masks, and happy times prepare a pathway for  Love  to enter.

original: Away, away! no time shall be omitted That will betime, and may by us be fitted.
translation: Let's go! There is no time to be lost in our preparations.

original: Allons! allons!
translation: Let's go! Let's go!

original: Sow'd cockle reap'd no corn;   And justice always whirls in equal measure:   Light wenches may prove plagues to men forsworn;   If so, our copper buys no better treasure.
translation: We will get nothing but falsehoods and achieve nothing if we do not take the necessary measures to win these ladies.

original: Satis quod sufficit.
translation: Enough is enough.

original: I praise God for you, sir:
translation: I thank God for you sir,

original: your reasons at dinner   have been sharp and sententious; pleasant without   scurrility, witty without affection, audacious without   impudency, learned without opinion, and strange with-   out heresy.
translation: your remarks at dinner were clever and wise, humorous without needing vile language, witty without being snobby, confident without being immodest, learned without showing your opinion, and you mentioned unusual things without being offensive.

original: I did converse this quondam day with   a companion of the King's, who is intituled, nomi-   nated, or called, Don Adriano de Armado.
translation: I was talking about this the other day  with one of the King's companions, who is entitled, nominated, or simply called, Don Adriano de Armado.

original: Novi hominem tanquam te:
translation: I know the man like I know you .

original: his humour is lofty, his   discourse peremptory, his tongue filed, his eye   ambitious, his gait majestical, and his general   behavior vain, ridiculous, and thrasonical.
translation: His humor is proud, his speech is arrogant, his tongue is too smooth, his eye too ambitious, his walk is too grand and his general behavior is vain, ridiculous and  boastful .

original: He is   too picked, too spruce, too affected, too odd, as it   were, too peregrinate, as I may call it.
translation: He is too fussy, too fashionable, too emotional, too peculiar, or I could even say  too foreign.

original: A most singular and choice epithet.
translation: A remarkable and appropriate description.

original: He draweth out the thread of his verbosity finer   than the staple of his argument.
translation: He prolongs his argument for so long that the topic itself is forgotten.

original: I abhor such   fanatical phantasimes, such insociable and   point-devise companions;
translation: I hate such extravagant people who live in a fantasy world, companions who are unsociable and too precise.

original: such rackers of   orthography, as to speak dout, sine b, when he should   say doubt;
translation: He cares far too much about spelling, he insists on pronouncing  dout ,  without  the "b" when he should say doubt;

original: det, when he should pronounce debt,—d,   e, b, t, not d, e, t:
translation: det  when he should pronounce debt. It is  d, e, b, t,  not  d, e, t.

original: he clepeth a calf, cauf;   half, hauf; neighbour vocatur nebor; neigh   abbreviated ne.
translation: He  calls  a calf, a  cauf ,  a half,  hauf . He  calls  a neighbor, a  nebor , and even neigh he shortens to  ne .

original: This is abhominable,—which he   would call abbominable: it insinuateth me of   insanie: ne intelligis, domine? to make frantic,  lunatic.
translation: This is all  abhominable , or as he would say  abbominable . It makes me mad -  do you understand, sir?  In short, he's a lunatic.

original: Laus Deo, bone intelligo.
translation: God be praised, I understand good.

original: Bon, bon, for bene! Priscian a little scratch'd, 'twill serve.
Videsne quis venit?
translation: Do you see who is coming?

original: Video, et gaudeo.
translation: I see, and I am glad.

original: Chirrah!
Quare chirrah, not sirrah?
translation: Why does he say chirrah and not sir?

original: Men of peace, well encountered.
translation: Men of peace, it is lovely to meet you.

original: Most military sir, salutation.
translation: What a soldierly greeting, hello to you too.

original: They have been at a great feast of languages, and stolen the scraps.
translation: These men have been at a feast with people who speak many different languages, and they only remember little snippets of things that they have heard.

original: O, they have lived long on the alms-basket of words.
translation: Oh I know, these men have lived for ages, speaking only the words which other people have  rejected .

original: I marvel thy master hath not eaten thee for a word;   for thou art not so long by the head as   honorificabilitudinitatibus:
translation: I am amazed that your master hasn't tried to steal even your name, Moth, since it is a lot easier to say than " honorificabilitudinitatibus"

original: thou art easier   swallowed than a flap-dragon.
translation: —your name can be digested a lot better than  a raisin floating in burning brandy!

original: Peace! the peal begins.
translation: Hang on, their conversation is starting.

original: Monsieur, are you not lettered?
translation: Sir, are you very clever?

original: Yes, yes; he teaches boys the hornbook. What is a, b, spelt backward, with the horn on his head?
Ba, pueritia, with a horn added.
translation: It's Ba, my child, with an added horn.

original: Ba, most silly sheep with a horn. You hear his  learning.
translation: Baaaaa, you silly sheep with a horn. Did you hear his clever line?

original: Quis, quis, thou consonant?
The third of the five vowels, if you repeat them; or the fifth, if I.
translation: To the third of the five vowels, if you say them. Or to the fifth vowel, if I say them.

original: I will repeat them,—a, e, i,—
translation: Okay I will repeat them—a, e, i—

original: The sheep: the other two concludes it,—o, u.
Now, by the salt wave of the Mediterraneum, a sweet touch, a quick venue of wit! snip, snap, quick and home! it rejoiceth my intellect: true wit!
Offered by a child to an old man; which is wit-old.
What is the figure? what is the figure?
translation: What is this figure of speech? What is this figure of speech?

original: Horns.
translation: One which has horns.

original: Thou disputest like an infant: go, whip thy gig.
Lend me your horn to make one, and I will whip about your infamy manu cita.—a gig of a cuckold's horn.
An I had but one penny in the world, thou shouldst   have it to buy gingerbread:
translation: If I had even one penny in this world, I would give it to you to buy gingerbread!

original: hold, there is the very   remuneration I had of thy master, thou halfpenny   purse of wit, thou pigeon-egg of discretion.
translation: Hang on, I could give you that  remuneration  that I got from your master, you small  bundle  of wit, you  little person  of good judgement.

original: O, an   the heavens were so pleased that thou wert but my   bastard, what a joyful father wouldst thou make me!
translation: Oh, if God would even let you be my bastard son, I would be a very happy father!

original: Go to; thou hast it ad dunghill, at the fingers'   ends, as they say.
translation: Carry on, you have him at the  dunghill , at the fingers' ends, as people say.

original: O, I smell false Latin; dunghill for unguem.
translation: Oh, I smell false Latin; he uses dunghill instead of "unguem!"

original: Arts-man, preambulate, we will be singled from the barbarous. Do you not educate youth at the charge-house on the top of the mountain?
translation: You clever man, walk with me. Let's set ourselves apart from the uncultured people. Is it true that you teach young people at the school on the top of the mountain?

original: Or mons, the hill.
translation: Or on the top of the hill.

original: At your sweet pleasure, for the mountain.
I do, sans question.
translation: I do, without question.

original: Sir, it is the king's most sweet pleasure and affection to congratulate the Princess at her pavilion in the posteriors of this day, which the rude multitude call the afternoon.
The posterior of the day, most generous sir, is liable, congruent and measurable for the afternoon: the word is well culled, chose, sweet and apt, I do assure you, sir, I do assure.
translation: The later part of the day, my noble friend, is a suitable and fitting phrase to call the afternoon. The word has been well chosen, it is pleasant and appropriate, you can be sure of that sir.

original: Sir, the king is a noble gentleman, and my familiar,   I do assure ye, very good friend: for what is   inward between us, let it pass.
translation: Sir, the king is a noble gentleman, and my close friend, indeed he is a very good friend of mine; the secrets that we share will stay as secrets.

original: I do beseech thee,   remember thy courtesy; I beseech thee, apparel thy   head:
translation: I ask you to remember your place, and I ask you to put your hat back on for this.

original: and among other important and most serious   designs, and of great import indeed, too, but let   that pass:
translation: There are several urgent and serious things we could discuss, and they are important as well, but let's leave them for now.

original: for I must tell thee, it will please his   grace, by the world, sometime to lean upon my poor   shoulder, and with his royal finger, thus, dally   with my excrement, with my mustachio; but, sweet   heart, let that pass.
translation: For I must tell you the truth. The King sometimes likes to lean on my shoulder and play with the hair of my mustache with his finger, but let's say no more about that.

original: By the world, I recount no   fable: some certain special honours it pleaseth his   greatness to impart to Armado, a soldier, a man of   travel, that hath seen the world; but let that pass.
translation: I promise you, this is no lie. The King has trusted me with important and special honors, as he knows that I am a soldier and a man who has traveled and seen the world. But let's say no more about me.

original: The very all of all is,—but, sweet heart, I do   implore secrecy,
translation: Most importantly, this must be kept a secret!

original: —that the king would have me   present the princess, sweet chuck, with some   delightful ostentation, or show, or pageant, or   antique, or firework.
translation: The King wants me to present the Princess, that  sweet girl ,  with some kind of entertaining show, or spectacle, or crazy performance, or a firework display.

original: Now, understanding that the   curate and your sweet self are good at such   eruptions and sudden breaking out of mirth, as it   were, I have acquainted you withal, to the end to   crave your assistance.
translation: Now, as I know that you and Sir Nathaniel are very good at organizing sudden moments of entertainment, I have told you this, because I would like your help with it.

original: Sir, you shall present before her the Nine Worthies.
translation: Sir, you shall present her with the story of the  "Nine Worthies."

original: Sir Nathaniel, as concerning some entertainment of  time, some   show in the posterior of this day, to be rendered by   our assistants, at the king's command, and this most   gallant, illustrate, and learned gentleman, before   the princess;
translation: Sir Nathaniel, when it comes to thinking up entertainment for this time, for a show that will be performed in the afternoon, with our help, on the King's orders, and with this worthy, renowned and clever gentleman, to be performed before the Princess,

original: I say none so fit as to present the   Nine Worthies.
translation: I tell you, there is no story more suitable than that of the Nine Worthies.

original: Where will you find men worthy enough to present them?
translation: Where are you going to find men worthy enough to play these men?

original: Joshua, yourself; this gallant gentleman, Judas Maccabaeus; this swain, because of his great limb or joint, shall pass Pompey the Great; the page, Hercules,—
translation: You will play Joshua;  This brave gentleman will play Judas Maccabaeus; Costard, because he is a large boy, will pass for Pompey the Great; Moth will play Hercules.

original: Pardon, sir; error: he is not quantity enough for that Worthy's thumb: he is not so big as the end of his club.
translation: Excuse me sir, that's a mistake. Moth is not big enough to play Hercules, he wouldn't even be able to hold his club.

original: Shall I have audience? he shall present Hercules in minority: his enter and exit shall be strangling a snake; and I will have an apology for that purpose.
An excellent device! so, if any of the audience hiss, you may cry 'Well done, Hercules! now thou crushest the snake!' that is the way to make an offence gracious, though few have the grace to do it.
translation: That's an excellent plan! It also means that if anyone in the audience hisses at me, you can simply shout "Well done, Hercules! Now you have killed the snake!" That is how we can make such an offense acceptable, even though few people would have been able to think up such a clever idea!

original: For the rest of the Worthies?—
translation: What about the rest of the Worthies?

original: I will play three myself.
translation: I will play three of them myself.

original: Thrice-worthy gentleman!
translation: That makes you three times as worthy!

original: Shall I tell you a thing?
translation: Can I tell you something?

original: We attend.
translation: We are listening.

original: We will have, if this fadge not, an antic. I beseech you, follow.
translation: If this does not succeed, we will be a laughing stock. I beg you, follow me now.

original: Via, goodman Dull! thou hast spoken no word all this  while.
translation: Come on, my good Dull! You haven't said anything this whole time.

original: Nor understood none neither, sir.
translation: I haven't understood anything that's been said either.

original: Allons! we will employ thee.
translation: Let's go! You will be involved as well.

original: I'll make one in a dance, or so; or I will play On the tabour to the Worthies, and let them dance the  hay.
translation: I'll take part in one dance or something, or I could play the drum for the Worthies, while they do a country dance.

original: Most dull, honest Dull! To our sport, away!
Sweet hearts, we shall be rich ere we depart, If fairings come thus plentifully in: A lady wall'd about with diamonds! Look you what I have from the loving king.
translation: My sweet friends, we are going to be rich before we leave here, if gifts keep arriving so often. I will be a lady surrounded by jewels! Look what the loving king has sent me this time!

original: Madame, came nothing else along with that?
translation: Madam, was anything else sent with that?

original: Nothing but this! yes, as much love in rhyme As would be cramm'd up in a sheet of paper, Writ o' both sides the leaf, margent and all, That he was fain to seal on Cupid's name.
translation: Just this.  Yes, he has sent as many loving verses as he could fit onto one piece of paper. He has written on both sides, he has even written in the margins, so much so that he was forced to write his name on top of Cupid's.

original: That was the way to make his godhead wax, For he hath been five thousand years a boy.
translation: That was his way of making his name bigger, since he was and always will be a boy.

original: Ay, and a shrewd unhappy gallows too.
translation: Yes, and he has been a naughty, trouble-making boy who deserves to be hanged.

original: You'll ne'er be friends with him; a' kill'd your  sister.
He made her melancholy, sad, and heavy;   And so she died:
translation: He made her so sad and so depressed that she died.

original: had she been light, like you,   Of such a merry, nimble, stirring spirit,   She might ha' been a grandam ere she died:
translation: If she had been cheerful, and had a merry, lively and energetic spirit like you do, then she might have lived to be a grandmother.

original: And so may you; for a light heart lives long.
translation: I hope you will too, for a light heart lives a long time.

original: What's your dark meaning, mouse, of this light word?
translation: What's your hidden meaning, dear, in using the word"light?"

original: A light condition in a beauty dark.
We need more light to find your meaning out.
translation: Shed more light on the subject and we'll work out what you mean.

original: You'll mar the light by taking it in snuff; Therefore I'll darkly end the argument.
translation: You'll ruin the light by getting offended; therefore I'll end this argument and leave you in the dark.

original: Look what you do, you do it still i' the dark.
So do not you, for you are a light wench.
translation: You wouldn't need to bother, since you don't care about being indecent.

original: Indeed I weigh not you, and therefore light.
You weigh me not? O, that's you care not for me.
Great reason; for 'past cure is still past care.'
translation: For good reason, for it's not worth worrying about something which isn't going to improve.

original: Well bandied both; a set of wit well play'd. But Rosaline, you have a favour too: Who sent it? and what is it?
I would you knew:
translation: Just you wait.

original: An if my face were but as fair as yours,   My favour were as great;
translation: If my face was as beautiful as yours, my gifts would be beautiful too.

original: be witness this.
translation: Look at this!

original: Nay, I have verses too,
translation: Oh and I have verses of poetry too!

original: I thank Biron:   The numbers true; and, were the numbering too,   I were the fairest goddess on the ground:   I am compared to twenty thousand fairs.
translation: I thank Biron, the meter is correct and by his judgement, I am the most gorgeous goddess on this earth, he has compared me to twenty thousand other fair women.

original: O, he hath drawn my picture in his letter!
translation: Oh and he has also drawn a picture of me in his letter!

original: Any thing like?
translation: Does it seem accurate to you?

original: Much in the letters; nothing in the praise.
Beauteous as ink; a good conclusion.
translation: You are as pretty as ink, that's a good conclusion.

original: Fair as a text B in a copy-book.
'Ware pencils, ho! let me not die your debtor, My red dominical, my golden letter: O, that your face were not so full of O's!
A pox of that jest! and I beshrew all shrows.
translation: Curse that joke! I wish a plague on all chatty women like you.

original: But, Katharine, what was sent to you from fair Dumain?
translation: Katharine, what did the lovely Dumain send you?

original: Madam, this glove.
translation: Madam, this glove.

original: Did he not send you twain?
translation: Did he not send you two?

original: Yes, madam, and moreover Some thousand verses of a faithful lover, A huge translation of hypocrisy, Vilely compiled, profound simplicity.
translation: Yes he did, madam, and with it he sent a thousand verses of the poetry of a "faithful lover," which were a huge pack of lies, badly put together and incredibly silly.

original: This and these pearls to me sent Longaville: The letter is too long by half a mile.
translation: Longaville sent me these pearls and this letter, which is far too long.

original: I think no less. Dost thou not wish in heart The chain were longer and the letter short?
translation: I think you're right. Would it be better if the necklace was longer and the letter shorter?

original: Ay, or I would these hands might never part.
We are wise girls to mock our lovers so.
translation: We are clever girls to mock our lovers like this.

original: They are worse fools to purchase mocking so.
translation: Or they are huge fools for earning this level of mockery.

original: That same Biron I'll torture ere I go:   O that I knew he were but in by the week!
translation: I'll make Biron suffer before I go, if only I'd have known how deeply he was in love sooner!

original: How I would make him fawn and beg and seek   And wait the season and observe the times
translation: How I would make him flatter me, look for me and beg to have me, and wait until the moment that  I  want and do what seems right  to me .

original: And spend his prodigal wits in bootless rhymes   And shape his service wholly to my hests   And make him proud to make me proud that jests!
translation: I would force his incredible wit to make-up pointless rhymes for me, and would shape him to be just like  I want him to be  and make him proud to be the object of my jokes!

original: So pair-taunt-like would I o'ersway his state   That he should be my fool and I his fate.
translation: So I would rule over him with  my better hand , so that he would be my fool and I would control his fate.

original: None are so surely caught, when they are catch'd, As wit turn'd fool: folly, in wisdom hatch'd, Hath wisdom's warrant and the help of school And wit's own grace to grace a learned fool.
translation: No men can be caught so easily, as when they are charmed and their wit turns into stupidity. Stupidity comes out of wisdom, it has wisdom's approval and the help of study and the charm of wit to add to the charm of a clever fool.

original: The blood of youth burns not with such excess As gravity's revolt to wantonness.
translation: A young man's blood isn't even as uncontrollable as when serious matters become indecent.

original: Folly in fools bears not so strong a note As foolery in the wise, when wit doth dote; Since all the power thereof it doth apply To prove, by wit, worth in simplicity.
translation: Stupidity in fools isn't so offensive, as when a wise person acts stupid, and when it is noticed. Since a wise fool has thrown away his intelligence, they are forced to prove the wisdom of simple thoughts.

original: Here comes Boyet, and mirth is in his face.
translation: Here comes Boyet, and he is full of cheer.

original: O, I am stabb'd with laughter! Where's her grace?
translation: Oh, I hurt from laughing so much! Where is her grace?

original: Thy news Boyet?
translation: What's happened Boyet?

original: Prepare, madam, prepare!
translation: Get ready, madam, get ready!

original: Arm, wenches, arm! encounters mounted are   Against your peace:
translation: There are men here to disrupt your peaceful chat.

original: Love doth approach disguised,   Armed in arguments; you'll be surprised:
translation: Your lovers are about to come here in disguise, armed with words for you, you will be so surprised!

original: Muster your wits; stand in your own defence;   Or hide your heads like cowards, and fly hence.
translation: Gather up your wits ladies, prepare to defend yourselves, or hide like cowards, and run away quickly.

original: Saint Denis to Saint Cupid! What are they That charge their breath against us? say, scout, say.
Under the cool shade of a sycamore   I thought to close mine eyes some half an hour;   When, lo! to interrupt my purposed rest,
translation: I was having a nap in the shade of a sycamore tree for half an hour, when suddenly, my nap was interrupted.

original: Toward that shade I might behold addrest   The king and his companions: warily   I stole into a neighbour thicket by,
translation: I heard the King and his companions talking nearby and   I carefully hid in a bush nearby,

original: And overheard what you shall overhear,
translation: and heard them discussing what you will hear them tell you again in a minute;

original: That, by and by, disguised they will be here.
translation: that they will be here soon, in disguise.

original: Their herald is a pretty knavish page,   That well by heart hath conn'd his embassage:   Action and accent did they teach him there;
translation: Their messenger is a pretty dishonest attendant, who has learned his message off by heart, using the gestures and the vocal technique that they have taught him.

original: 'Thus must thou speak,' and 'thus thy body bear:'   And ever and anon they made a doubt   Presence majestical would put him out,
translation: They said to him, "You must speak like this," and "You must stand like this," and they kept worrying that the presence of you, your majesty might confuse him.

original: 'For,' quoth the king, 'an angel shalt thou see;   Yet fear not thou, but speak audaciously.'
translation: The King said to him, "For even though you are going to see an angel standing before you, don't be scared, but speak with courage!"

original: The boy replied, 'An angel is not evil;   I should have fear'd her had she been a devil.'
translation: The boy replied, "An angel isn't evil so why would I fear her? I would only fear her if she was a devil."

original: With that, all laugh'd and clapp'd him on the shoulder,   Making the bold wag by their praises bolder:
translation: At that remark they all laughed and patted him on the shoulder, becoming more brave by the minute and adding more and more of this bravery into their praises of you.

original: One rubb'd his elbow thus, and fleer'd and swore   A better speech was never spoke before;
translation: One of them  rubbed his elbow  like this, and grinned and stated that he didn't think there had ever been a speech as good as theirs before.

original: Another, with his finger and his thumb,   Cried, 'Via! we will do't, come what will come;'
translation: Another one of them snapped his fingers and cried, " Come on ! let's do it, no matter what happens."

original: The third he caper'd, and cried, 'All goes well;'   The fourth turn'd on the toe, and down he fell.
translation: The third Lord did a little dance and cried, "I hope everything goes well." The fourth tripped over himself and fell on the ground.

original: With that, they all did tumble on the ground,   With such a zealous laughter, so profound,   That in this spleen ridiculous appears,   To cheque their folly, passion's solemn tears.
translation: At that moment, they all fell to the ground with him, cackling with such a strong laughter, so loud, that their merriment became ridiculous and the serious emotion of passion was forced to stop their silliness.

original: But what, but what, come they to visit us?
translation: But what, but what, they have come to visit us?

original: They do, they do: and are apparell'd thus.
translation: They have, they are coming now and are dressed in this way.

original: Like Muscovites or Russians, as I guess.
translation: They are dressed like Muscovites or Russians it looks like.

original: Their purpose is to parle, to court and dance;   And every one his love-feat will advance   Unto his several mistress, which they'll know   By favours several which they did bestow.
translation: Their aim is to speak with you, to flirt and to dance, and each of them has an act of love that they will perform for their own mistress, identifying her by the presents which they gave you.

original: And will they so?
translation: Will they now?

original: the gallants shall be task'd;   For, ladies, we shall every one be mask'd;   And not a man of them shall have the grace,   Despite of suit, to see a lady's face.
translation: These men will be tested then. For ladies, we shall all wear masks, so that none of them will have the honor, even when they ask, to see our faces.

original: Hold, Rosaline, this favour thou shalt wear,   And then the king will court thee for his dear;
translation: Hang on Rosaline, you will wear this gift and then the King will flirt with you, thinking that you are me.

original: Hold, take thou this, my sweet, and give me thine,   So shall Biron take me for Rosaline.
translation: Here, take this, my sweet, and give me yours, and Biron will also think that I am Rosaline.

original: And change your favours too; so shall your loves   Woo contrary, deceived by these removes.
translation: You two swap your presents too, so that your lovers will woo the wrong women, deceived by these exchanges.

original: Come on, then; wear the favours most in sight.
translation: Come on then, let's make sure we wear these gifts in an obvious place.

original: But in this changing what is your intent?
translation: What is the point of these exchanges?

original: The effect of my intent is to cross theirs:
translation: The point of these exchanges is to trick them before they can trick us.

original: They do it but in mocking merriment;   And mock for mock is only my intent.
translation: They do it as a light bit of mockery, and mocking this mockery is my only purpose.

original: Their several counsels they unbosom shall   To loves mistook, and so be mock'd withal   Upon the next occasion that we meet,   With visages displayed, to talk and greet.
translation: They will reveal secrets to mistaken lovers, and will be mocked in front of everyone when we next meet them, at which time we will be ourselves again, ready to greet them and talk to them.

original: But shall we dance, if they desire to't?
translation: But do we dance with them, if they want us to?

original: No, to the death, we will not move a foot; Nor to their penn'd speech render we no grace, But while 'tis spoke each turn away her face.
