translation: No, we would rather die than move a foot. We will also pay no attention to the speech they have written for us, but we will turn our faces away from them instead.

original: Why, that contempt will kill the speaker's heart, And quite divorce his memory from his part.
translation: Oh wow, that disgust will upset the speaker and he will completely forget what he was going to say.

original: Therefore I do it; and I make no doubt   The rest will ne'er come in, if he be out
translation: And so I will do it, and I am certain that the rest of them will not try again, if the speaker is puzzled.

original: There's no such sport as sport by sport o'erthrown,   To make theirs ours and ours none but our own:
translation: There's no game that's better than a game which outdoes another game, making their sport our sport and letting us have our own fun as well.

original: So shall we stay, mocking intended game,   And they, well mock'd, depart away with shame.
translation: So we will stay, mocking their actions and they will run away in shame when we have done this.

original: The trumpet sounds: be mask'd; the maskers come.
translation: That's the trumpets! Put your masks on ladies, the masked men are coming.

original: All hail, the richest beauties on the earth!—
translation: All hail the richest beauties on the earth!

original: Beauties no richer than rich taffeta.
translation: Their beauties are no better than a good piece of silk.

original: A holy parcel of the fairest dames.
translation: A divine collection of the most beautiful women.

original: That ever turn'd their—backs—to mortal views!
translation: That ever turned away from mortal opinions.

original: Their eyes, villain, their eyes!
translation: Their eyes, you idiot, their eyes!

original: That ever turn'd their eyes to mortal views!—Out—
translation: That ever turned their eyes away from mortal opinions. Out!

original: True; out indeed.
translation: Yes, get out.

original: Out of your favours, heavenly spirits, vouchsafe Not to behold—
translation: Although we are not liked by you, you heavenly goddesses, promise not to look—

original: Once to behold, rogue.
translation: Promise to look at us, you rascal.

original: Once to behold with your sun-beamed eyes, —with your sun-beamed eyes—
translation: Promise to look at us with your sun-beamed eyes—with your shining, glistening eyes—

original: They will not answer to that epithet; You were best call it 'daughter-beamed eyes.'
They do not mark me, and that brings me out.
translation: They aren't paying attention to me, and that annoys me.

original: Is this your perfectness? be gone, you rogue!
translation: Is that the best that you have to say? Get out of here, you scoundrel!

original: What would these strangers? know their minds, Boyet: If they do speak our language, 'tis our will: That some plain man recount their purposes Know what they would.
translation: What do these foreign men want? Find out from them Boyet. If they speak English then we would appreciate it if one of them would tell us what they're doing here in simple language. Go, find out from them.

original: What would you with the Princess?
translation: What do you want with the Princess?

original: Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.
translation: Simply a peaceful and a friendly visit.

original: What would they, say they?
translation: What did they say they wanted?

original: Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.
translation: Simply a peaceful and a friendly visit.

original: Why, that they have; and bid them so be gone.
translation: Well, they have had that now, so tell them they can leave.

original: She says, you have it, and you may be gone.
translation: She says you have had a peaceful and friendly visit and now you may leave.

original: Say to her, we have measured many miles To tread a measure with her on this grass.
translation: Tell her that we have traveled for many miles to dance with her on this grass.

original: They say, that they have measured many a mile To tread a measure with you on this grass.
translation: They say that they have traveled for many miles to dance with you on this grass.

original: It is not so. Ask them how many inches Is in one mile: if they have measured many, The measure then of one is easily told.
translation: That's not true. Ask them how many inches there are in a mile. If they have traveled many miles, then they should at least have counted how many is in one.

original: If to come hither you have measured miles, And many miles, the princess bids you tell How many inches doth fill up one mile.
translation: If you have traveled many miles to get there, the Princess would like to know how many inches are in one mile.

original: Tell her, we measure them by weary steps.
translation: Tell her that we measured our journey by the weary steps that we took.

original: She hears herself.
translation: She heard you herself.

original: How many weary steps, Of many weary miles you have o'ergone, Are number'd in the travel of one mile?
translation: Okay then, out of the many weary miles that you have traveled, how many weary steps did you take in one mile?

original: We number nothing that we spend for you:
translation: We don't count anything that we do for you.

original: Our duty is so rich, so infinite,   That we may do it still without accompt.
translation: Our sense of duty is so strong, so limitless that we will always do it without counting.

original: Vouchsafe to show the sunshine of your face,   That we, like savages, may worship it.
translation: Promise to show us the sunshine of your face so that we can adore it, like beasts.

original: My face is but a moon, and clouded too.
translation: My face is just a reflection, and it is masked as well.

original: Blessed are clouds, to do as such clouds do! Vouchsafe, bright moon, and these thy stars, to shine, Those clouds removed, upon our watery eyne.
translation: How lucky are the masks, which cover the ladies faces, as clouds cover the sky! Be safe bright moon, and your stars will shine on our weeping eyes, once your masks have been removed.

original: O vain petitioner! beg a greater matter; Thou now request'st but moonshine in the water.
translation: Oh what a pointless wish! Ask for something more important. All you have now requested is to see the reflection of the moon in the water.

original: Then, in our measure do but vouchsafe one change. Thou bid'st me beg: this begging is not strange.
translation: Then, while we are here, just let us have one dance. You asked me to beg, and we're used to doing that.

original: Play, music, then! Nay, you must do it soon.
translation: Let the music play then! We must dance soon.

original: Not yet! no dance! Thus change I like the moon.
Will you not dance? How come you thus estranged?
translation: Why won't you dance? Why do you stay so far away from me?

original: You took the moon at full, but now she's changed.
translation: You thought that it was a full moon, but now it's already changed to something else.

original: Yet still she is the moon, and I the man. The music plays; vouchsafe some motion to it.
translation: Yet if you are still the moon, then I can be the man in the moon. The music is starting, lets organize some dancing to it.

original: Our ears vouchsafe it.
translation: Our ears can listen to it.

original: But your legs should do it.
translation: But your legs should dance to it.

original: Since you are strangers and come here by chance, We'll not be nice: take hands. We will not dance.
translation: As you are foreigners and happened to come here, we don't have to do what you want. Take my hand now, we will not dance with you.

original: Why take we hands, then?
translation: Well, why are we holding hands then?

original: Only to part friends: Curtsy, sweet hearts; and so the measure ends.
translation: Only to say goodbye as friends. Curtsy to your men, my dears, here is where the music stops.

original: More measure of this measure; be not nice.
We can afford no more at such a price.
translation: We can't let you have more just because you ask.

original: Prize you yourselves: what buys your company?
translation: Then value yourselves, what will buy us your company?

original: Your absence only.
translation: Only your absence.

original: That can never be.
translation: That will never happen.

original: Then cannot we be bought: and so, adieu; Twice to your visor, and half once to you.
translation: Well we can't be bought, so goodbye.

original: If you deny to dance, let's hold more chat.
translation: If you won't dance with me, then let's at least chat more.

original: In private, then.
translation: Okay, but in private.

original: I am best pleased with that.
translation: I am happy with that.

original: White-handed mistress, one sweet word with thee.
translation: My pale-handed mistress, let me have one word with you.

original: Honey, and milk, and sugar; there is three.
translation: Honey, milk, sugar—there, that's three words.

original: Nay then, two treys, and if you grow so nice, Metheglin, wort, and malmsey: well run, dice! There's half-a-dozen sweets.
Seventh sweet, adieu: Since you can cog, I'll play no more with you.
translation: Then here's your seventh, goodbye. Since you're a cheat, I don't want to play with you anymore.

original: One word in secret.
translation: One word in secret.

original: Let it not be sweet.
translation: As long as it's not sweet.

original: Thou grievest my gall.
Gall! bitter.
Therefore meet.
translation: Let's talk.

original: Will you vouchsafe with me to change a word?
translation: Will you give me the chance to call you by another name?

original: Name it.
translation: Name it.

original: Fair lady,—
translation: Fair lady—

original: Say you so? Fair lord,— Take that for your fair lady.
translation: Do you think so? Fair lord, take that in exchange for your "fair lady."

original: Please it you, As much in private, and I'll bid adieu.
translation: If you want to, let's talk more in private and then I'll bid you goodbye.

original: What, was your vizard made without a tongue?
translation: Sorry, does your mask not allow you to speak?

original: I know the reason, lady, why you ask.
translation: I know why you ask me that, lady.

original: O for your reason! quickly, sir; I long.
translation: Oh okay then, tell me the reason! Quickly, I can't wait to hear it.

original: You have a double tongue within your mask, And would afford my speechless vizard half.
Veal, quoth the Dutchman. Is not "veal" a calf?
A calf, fair lady!
translation: A calf, fair lady!

original: No, a fair lord calf.
Let's part the word.
translation: Can't we share the word?

original: No, I'll not be your half Take all, and wean it; it may prove an ox.
Look, how you butt yourself in these sharp mocks! Will you give horns, chaste lady? do not so.
Then die a calf, before your horns do grow.
translation: Then you should die while you're young, before your horns can grow.

original: One word in private with you, ere I die.
translation: One word in private with you then, before I die.

original: Bleat softly then; the butcher hears you cry.
translation: Talk softly then, you wouldn't want the butcher to hear you.

original: The tongues of mocking wenches are as keen   As is the razor's edge invisible,   Cutting a smaller hair than may be seen,
translation: The tongues of mocking women are as sharp as a razor, able to cut hairs that can't even be seen.

original: Above the sense of sense; so sensible   Seemeth their conference; their conceits have wings   Fleeter than arrows, bullets, wind, thought, swifter  things.
translation: Their conversations are so clever that they are more than even the senses can understand, their clever ideas come quicker than arrows, bullets, wind, thought, or even quicker things.

original: Not one word more, my maids; break off, break off.
translation: No more words, my maids. Stop talking to them now.

original: By heaven, all dry-beaten with pure scoff!
translation: My goodness, we've all been severely beaten by their mockery.

original: Farewell, mad wenches; you have simple wits.
translation: Goodbye, you mad women, your wits are quite plain.

original: Twenty adieus, my frozen Muscovits.
translation: Twenty goodbyes to you, you cold Muscovites.

original: Are these the breed of wits so wonder'd at?
translation: Are these the kind of wits that you saw earlier?

original: Tapers they are, with your sweet breaths puff'd out.
translation: They were like candles, blown out by your words.

original: Well-liking wits they have; gross, gross; fat, fat.
translation: They have large minds, that are wide and fat.

original: O poverty in wit, kingly-poor flout! Will they not, think you, hang themselves tonight? Or ever, but in vizards, show their faces? This pert Biron was out of countenance quite.
translation: Oh what a lack of wit, what feeble mockery for a King! Don't you think they might hang themselves tonight in shame? Or only show their faces when hidden behind masks? The lively Biron seemed very upset.

original: O, they were all in lamentable cases! The king was weeping-ripe for a good word.
translation: Oh they were all in sorry states! The King was ready to cry in trying to find something to say to you.

original: Biron did swear himself out of all suit.
translation: Biron swore that he had nothing left to say.

original: Dumain was at my service, and his sword: Non point, quoth I; my servant straight was mute.
translation: Dumain was under my control, and so was his sword. "No point," I said, when he didn't even say anything.

original: Lord Longaville said, I came o'er his heart; And trow you what he called me?
translation: Lord Longaville said that I had taken possession of his heart, and do you know what he called me?

original: Qualm, perhaps.
Yes, in good faith.
translation: Yes he did.

original: Go, sickness as thou art!
translation: Go, you must be a sickness!

original: Well, better wits have worn plain statute-caps. But will you hear? the king is my love sworn.
And quick Biron hath plighted faith to me.
translation: And the impatient Biron committed to loving me.

original: And Longaville was for my service born.
translation: And Longaville to being my love.

original: Dumain is mine, as sure as bark on tree.
translation: Dumain is mine, as certain as the fact that there is bark on a tree.

original: Madam, and pretty mistresses, give ear: Immediately they will again be here In their own shapes; for it can never be They will digest this harsh indignity.
translation: Madam, and pretty mistresses, listen to me. They will be back in a minute dressed as themselves again, for I know they won't be able to put up with this shame.

original: Will they return?
translation: They will come back?

original: They will, they will, God knows, And leap for joy, though they are lame with blows: Therefore change favours; and, when they repair, Blow like sweet roses in this summer air.
How blow? how blow? speak to be understood.
translation: What do you mean blossom? How can we blossom? Speak simply.

original: Fair ladies mask'd are roses in their bud; Dismask'd, their damask sweet commixture shown, Are angels vailing clouds, or roses blown.
translation: When fair ladies are masked they are like new roses, when they are unmasked and their beautiful red and white complexion is revealed, they are like angels removing clouds from the sky, or roses blossoming.

original: Avaunt, perplexity! What shall we do, If they return in their own shapes to woo?
translation: Get rid of such puzzling lines! What shall we do if they come back to woo us dressed as themselves?

original: Good madam, if by me you'll be advised,   Let's, mock them still, as well known as disguised:
translation: Good madam, if you'll let me offer some advice, I think that we should carry on mocking them, like we did when they were disguised.

original: Let us complain to them what fools were here,   Disguised like Muscovites, in shapeless gear;
translation: Let's complain to them about the idiots who have just been here, dressed as Muscovites, in shapeless clothes.

original: And wonder what they were and to what end   Their shallow shows and prologue vilely penn'd   And their rough carriage so ridiculous,   Should be presented at our tent to us.
translation: Let's tell them we were amazed by them and wondered why their superficial performance, their poorly written verses and their ridiculous behavior were presented to us in our tent.

original: Ladies, withdraw: the gallants are at hand.
translation: Ladies, withdraw, the men will be here soon.

original: Whip to our tents, as roes run o'er land.
translation: Let's dash to our tents, like deer when they run across land.

original: Fair sir, God save you! Where's the princess?
translation: Hello sir, God bless you! Where is the Princess?

original: Gone to her tent. Please it your majesty Command me any service to her thither?
translation: She's gone to her tent, would your majesty like me to ask her something?

original: That she vouchsafe me audience for one word.
translation: I would like to ask her to speak with me for just a minute.

original: I will; and so will she, I know, my lord.
translation: I will ask her, and she will come, I know it my lord.

original: This fellow pecks up wit as pigeons pease,   And utters it again when God doth please:
translation: This man eats up our wit, like a  pigeon pea , and speaks the same line again when the time is right.

original: He is wit's pedler, and retails his wares   At wakes and wassails, meetings, markets, fairs;
translation: He is a seller of wit, and makes his money at festivals and parties, meetings, markets and fairs.

original: And we that sell by gross, the Lord doth know,   Have not the grace to grace it with such show.
translation: People like him, who sell wit in large quantities, the Lord knows they don't have the ability to put on a performance like we can.

original: This gallant pins the wenches on his sleeve;   Had he been Adam, he had tempted Eve;
translation: He has complete power over women; if he had been Adam it would have been him who would have tempted Eve, not the other way around.

original: A' can carve too, and lisp: why, this is he   That kiss'd his hand away in courtesy;   This is the ape of form, monsieur the nice,
translation: He can also fail to deliver and stutter on his words. The same person who wore his hand out by kissing it so much is also a very polite man, he's Mr Nice Guy.

original: That, when he plays at tables, chides the dice   In honourable terms:
translation: He's so nice  that when he plays backgammon, he even tells the dice off politely.

original: nay, he can sing   A mean most meanly; and in ushering   Mend him who can:
translation: He can sing a  tenor  role fairly well, and when acting as an usher he lets anyone who he thinks can do better try it instead.

original: the ladies call him sweet;   The stairs, as he treads on them, kiss his feet:
translation: The ladies call him sweet, and he has climbed up the  social ladder  easily.

original: This is the flower that smiles on every one,   To show his teeth as white as whale's bone;
translation: He smiles at everyone he sees, to prove that his teeth are as white as ivory;

original: And consciences, that will not die in debt,   Pay him the due of honey-tongued Boyet.
translation: people with consciences, so as not to die in debt, pay him the honor of calling him "Sweet speaking Boyet."

original: A blister on his sweet tongue, with my heart, That put Armado's page out of his part!
translation: Let a blister grow on the tongue of the man that made Moth forget his lines!

original: See where it comes! Behavior, what wert thou Till this madman show'd thee? and what art thou now?
translation: Look, he is coming! What were good manners until Boyet showed us what they could be? And where are they now?

original: All hail, sweet madam, and fair time of day!
translation: Hail, my sweet madam, and a good day to you!

original: "Fair" in "all hail" is foul, as I conceive.
Construe my speeches better, if you may.
translation: Interpret my speeches better, if you can.

original: Then wish me better; I will give you leave.
translation: If you want me to be better than I am, then I'll just leave.

original: We came to visit you, and purpose now To lead you to our court; vouchsafe it then.
translation: We came to visit you and now would like to take you to our court. Accept this offer.

original: This field shall hold me; and so hold your vow: Nor God, nor I, delights in perjured men.
translation: I will stay in this field, so that you can stay true to your vow. Neither God nor I are a fan of liars.

original: Rebuke me not for that which you provoke: The virtue of your eye must break my oath.
translation: Don't judge me for something which you have made me do. The virtuous power of your eye must make me break my oath.

original: You nickname virtue; vice you should have spoke;   For virtue's office never breaks men's troth.
translation: You call this power I have virtuous when you should have called it evil, since something that is virtuous will never make a man break his oath.

original: Now by my maiden honour, yet as pure   As the unsullied lily, I protest,   A world of torments though I should endure,   I would not yield to be your house's guest;
translation: Now, by my maiden honor, which is still as pure as the whitest lily, I am determined that I should endure horrible things before I agree to be a guest in your house.

original: So much I hate a breaking cause to be   Of heavenly oaths, vow'd with integrity.
translation: This is how much I hate men who break the oaths that they agreed to with such integrity.

original: O, you have lived in desolation here, Unseen, unvisited, much to our shame.
translation: Oh but you have had to stay here and be lonely, unnoticed and unvisited, which is shameful to us.

original: Not so, my lord; it is not so, I swear; We have had pastimes here and pleasant game: A mess of Russians left us but of late.
translation: No it isn't my lord, I swear it isn't. We have had amusements here and pleasant games, only just now a group of four Russians left us.

original: How, madam! Russians!
translation: Really, madam! Russians?!

original: Ay, in truth, my lord; Trim gallants, full of courtship and of state.
translation: Yes, truthfully my lord. They were stylish suitors, full of manners and dignity.

original: Madam, speak true. It is not so, my lord:
translation: Madam, tell the truth, that was not the case, my lord.

original: My lady, to the manner of the days,   In courtesy gives undeserving praise.
translation: My lady is giving them praise that they don't deserve because it is polite.

original: We four indeed confronted were with four   In Russian habit:
translation: The four of us were confronted with four men in Russian clothing.

original: here they stay'd an hour,   And talk'd apace; and in that hour, my lord,   They did not bless us with one happy word.
translation: They stayed here for an hour and chattered away and in that whole hour, they didn't say anything interesting.

original: I dare not call them fools; but this I think,   When they are thirsty, fools would fain have drink.
translation: I don't want to call them fools, but I think that when they are thirsty,  it would be fools that were drinking .

original: This jest is dry to me.
translation: This joke is not amusing to me.

original: Fair gentle sweet,   Your wit makes wise things foolish:
translation: My gentle lady, you make even wise things seem silly.

original: when we greet,   With eyes best seeing, heaven's fiery eye,   By light we lose light:
translation: When we look directly at the sun with our eyes, we are blinded and can no longer see.

original: your capacity   Is of that nature that to your huge store   Wise things seem foolish and rich things but poor.
translation: You knowledge is similar to that, in the sense that when you talk wise things seem foolish and rich things seem poor.

original: This proves you wise and rich, for in my eye,—
translation: Then you must be wise and rich, for in my mind—

original: But that you take what doth to you belong, It were a fault to snatch words from my tongue.
translation: But there you take the words that I was about to say about you, it is not nice to take words from my tongue.

original: O, I am yours, and all that I possess!
translation: Oh I am all yours, and so is everything I own!

original: All the fool mine?
translation: So the whole fool is mine?

original: I cannot give you less.
translation: I can't give you any less.

original: Which of the vizards was it that you wore?
translation: Which mask did you wear?

original: Where? when? what vizard? why demand you this?
translation: Where? When? What mask? Why do you ask me this?

original: There, then, that vizard; that superfluous case That hid the worse and show'd the better face.
translation: There, then, that mask, that ridiculous covering, that hid the worst of you and showed a better face.

original: We are descried; they'll mock us now downright.
translation: We are found out! They'll mock us completely.

original: Let us confess and turn it to a jest.
translation: Let's confess and turn it into a joke.

original: Amazed, my lord? why looks your highness sad?
translation: You look bewildered my lord? Or are you sad?

original: Help, hold his brows! he'll swoon! Why look you pale? Sea-sick, I think, coming from Muscovy.
translation: Help, hold his brows! He might faint! Why do you look so pale? Perhaps you're sea-sick, having travelled all the way from Muscovy...?

original: Thus pour the stars down plagues for perjury.
translation: Therefore do whatever you want to us for our lies.

original: Can any face of brass hold longer out? Here stand I,  lady, dart thy skill at me;
translation: Can a shameless face like mine last much longer? I stand here, my lady, give me everything you've got.

original: Bruise me  with scorn, confound me with a flout;   Thrust thy sharp wit quite through my ignorance;
translation: Hurt me with your scorn, destroy me with a joke, make your sharp wit go right through my stupidity.

original: Cut me to pieces with thy keen conceit;   And I will wish thee never more to dance,   Nor never more in Russian habit wait.
translation: Cut me into pieces with your keen tongue and I will never again invite you to dance and never come to you in Russian clothing again.

original: O, never will I trust to speeches penn'd,   Nor to the motion of a schoolboy's tongue,   Nor never come in vizard to my friend,   Nor woo in rhyme, like a blind harper's song!
translation: Oh I will never rely on speeches that we have written, or trust a boy to deliver them. I will never come to my lover wearing a mask, nor woo her with rhymes like the song of a blind harper.

original: Taffeta phrases, silken terms precise,   Three-piled hyperboles, spruce affectation,   Figures pedantical;
translation: I will never use rich phrases, flattering and over-precise words, excessive exaggeration, smart affection, pedantic rhetorical devices.

original: these summer-flies   Have blown me full of maggot ostentation:
translation: The flies that come out in summer have laid their eggs on me and made me a pretentious show-off.

original: I do forswear them; and I here protest,   By this white glove;—how white the hand, God knows!—
translation: I give these things up and I promise by your white glove, how white your hand is who knows!

original: Henceforth my wooing mind shall be express'd   In russet yeas and honest kersey noes:
translation: From here on I shall only woo you in simple ways with honest, plain words.

original: And, to begin, wench,—so God help me, la!—   My love to thee is sound, sans crack or flaw.
translation: So to begin, wench, may God help me, aha! My love for you is strong, without  a crack or a flaw.

original: Sans sans, I pray you.
translation: Speak without, without, I beg of you.

original: Yet I have a trick   Of the old rage:
translation: Yet I still have a touch of my old madness.

original: bear with me, I am sick;   I'll leave it by degrees.
translation: Bear with me, I am sick, I will gradually get rid of this illness.

original: Soft, let us see:   Write, 'Lord have mercy on us' on those three;
translation: So let's see, let's write "Lord have mercy on us" on these three men.

original: They are infected; in their hearts it lies;   They have the plague, and caught it of your eyes;
translation: They are truly sick, it is deep in their hearts. They have the plague of love and caught it by looking in your eyes.

original: These lords are visited; you are not free,   For the Lord's tokens on you do I see.
translation: These lords are attacked by this illness, and you are not safe yourself, since I see you are wearing the Lord's presents.

original: No, they are free that gave these tokens to us.
translation: No, the men who gave us these presents are generous.

original: Our states are forfeit: seek not to undo us.
translation: We have stopped being honorable men already, please don't try to ruin us.

original: It is not so; for how can this be true, That you stand forfeit, being those that sue?
translation: That's not true. How can that be true that you risk being ruined, when you're the ones that started this all in the first place?

original: Peace! for I will not have to do with you.
translation: Quiet! I'll have nothing more to do with you.

original: Nor shall not, if I do as I intend.
translation: Neither will I, if I get what I want.

original: Speak for yourselves; my wit is at an end.
translation: I'm done with speaking to you, my wits are done for.

original: Teach us, sweet madam, for our rude transgression Some fair excuse.
translation: Tell us, sweet madam, what we can do to make up for our bad behavior.

original: The fairest is confession. Were not you here but even now disguised?
translation: The fairest way is by confessing. Was it you that come here before in disguise?

original: Madam, I was.
translation: Madam, it was.

original: And were you well advised?
translation: And were you in your right mind?

original: I was, fair madam.
translation: I was, fair madam.

original: When you then were here, What did you whisper in your lady's ear?
translation: When you were here before, what did you whisper in your lady's ear?

original: That more than all the world I did respect her.
translation: That more than anything else, I valued her.

original: When she shall challenge this, you will reject her.
translation: When she will lay claim to this, you will reject her.

original: Upon mine honour, no.
translation: Upon my honor, I won't.

original: Peace, peace! forbear: Your oath once broke, you force not to forswear.
translation: Peace, peace! Don't say anymore, having broken your oath once already, you won't care if you break it again.

original: Despise me, when I break this oath of mine.
translation: Hate me, if I break another oath.

original: I will: and therefore keep it. Rosaline, What did the Russian whisper in your ear?
translation: I will and therefore make sure you keep it. Rosaline, what did the Russian whisper in your ear?

original: Madam, he swore that he did hold me dear As precious eyesight, and did value me Above this world; adding thereto moreover That he would wed me, or else die my lover.
translation: Madam, he swore that I was as important to him as precious eyesight and that he valued me more than the world, adding also that he would marry me, or die my lover.

original: God give thee joy of him! the noble lord Most honourably doth unhold his word.
translation: God may you have him! This noble lord most honorably has forgotten what he promised.

original: What mean you, madam? by my life, my troth, I never swore this lady such an oath.
translation: What do you mean madam? By my life, my dear, I never swore this lady such an oath.

original: By heaven, you did; and to confirm it plain, You gave me this: but take it, sir, again.
translation: By heaven, you did and to prove it even more, you gave me this!  Take it back again sir.

original: My faith and this the princess I did give: I knew her by this jewel on her sleeve.
translation: I did give the Princess my love and this gift. I knew her by the jewel she had on her sleeve.

original: Pardon me, sir, this jewel did she wear; And Lord Biron, I thank him, is my dear. What, will you have me, or your pearl again?
translation: Excuse me sir, she was wearing my jewel. Lord Biron, thanks to you, for being my dear. What, do you want your pearl back, or will you have me instead?

original: Neither of either; I remit both twain.
translation: I'll have neither of them, I give up both of them.

original: I see the trick on't: here was a consent,   Knowing aforehand of our merriment,   To dash it like a Christmas comedy:

Some carry-tale, some please-man, some slight zany,   Some mumble-news, some trencher-knight, some Dick,   That smiles his cheek in years and knows the trick   To make my lady laugh when she's disposed,   Told our intents before;
translation: It was some kind of tell-tale, a creep, a humble assistant, a gossip, a hanger-on, a fellow who looked old with wrinkles and knows how to make my lady laugh when she wants to be merry that told you of our plan.

original: which once disclosed,   The ladies did change favours: and then we,   Following the signs, woo'd but the sign of she.
translation: Once they knew the ladies swapped their gifts and then we, following these gifts, woo'ed the lady that wore them.

original: Now, to our perjury to add more terror,   We are again forsworn, in will and error.   Much upon this it is: and might not you.
translation: Now, we have betrayed ourselves even more, and have again broken another oath, by doing this wrong. This is pretty much what has happened.

original: Forestall our sport, to make us thus untrue?
translation: Couldn't you have prevented this from happening, stopped us from breaking our oath?

original: Do not you know my lady's foot by the squier,   And laugh upon the apple of her eye?
translation: Don't you know the exact size of my lady's foot, and look pleasantly at her pupil?

original: And stand between her back, sir, and the fire,   Holding a trencher, jesting merrily?
translation: Don't you act almost as a fire screen, standing between her and the fire, ready to serve her, making jokes?

original: You put our page out: go, you are allow'd;
translation: You made Moth upset, go, you are allowed.

original: Die when you will, a smock shall be your shroud.   You leer upon me, do you? there's an eye   Wounds like a leaden sword.
translation: Whenever you die, we can bury you like the woman you are. You stare at me like that, do you? Your eye wounds about as much as a wooden sword.

original: Full merrily Hath this brave manage, this career, been run.
translation: Well done, your argument has moved at full speed, good job.

original: Lo, he is tilting straight! Peace! I have done.
translation: Oh, he is going back immediately to his witty lines. Peace, I am done with this.

original: Welcome, pure wit! thou partest a fair fray.
translation: Welcome, you witty thing! You're breaking up a good fight.

original: O Lord, sir, they would know Whether the three Worthies shall come in or no.
translation: Oh Lord sir, I was just sent to find out whether the three Worthies can come in yet or not.

original: What, are there but three?
translation: What? Are there only three of them?

original: No, sir; but it is vara fine, For every one pursents three.
translation: No sir, it is perfectly all right, it's just that each person is playing three parts.

original: And three times thrice is nine.
translation: And three times three is nine.

original: Not so, sir; under correction, sir; I hope it is not  so. You cannot beg us, sir, I can assure you, sir we know what we know: I hope, sir, three times thrice, sir,—
translation: That is not so sir, I hope it is not so. You can't take us for fools sir—I can assure you, we know what we know. I hope sir, three times three is—

original: Is not nine.
translation: Is not nine.

original: Under correction, sir, we know whereuntil it doth  amount.
translation: To correct you sir, we know what it amounts to.

original: By Jove, I always took three threes for nine.
translation: My goodness, I always thought that three threes were nine.

original: O Lord, sir, it were pity you should get your living by reckoning, sir.
translation: Oh Lord sir, it would be difficult for you if you had to make your living by doing calculations.

original: How much is it?
translation: How much is it then?

original: O Lord, sir, the parties themselves, the actors, sir, will show whereuntil it doth amount: for mine own part, I am, as they say, but to parfect one man in one poor man, Pompion the Great, sir.
translation: Oh Lord sir, the men themselves, the actors, will show you what it amounts to. For my own part, as they say, I will be a poor man playing the part of a great man, Pompion the Great, sir.

original: Art thou one of the Worthies?
translation: Are you one of the Worthies?!

original: It pleased them to think me worthy of Pompion the Great: for mine own part, I know not the degree of the Worthy, but I am to stand for him.
translation: They thought that I was worthy enough to play Pompion the Great and although I don't know the rank of this Worthy, I am happy to play him.

original: Go, bid them prepare.
translation: Go, tell them to get ready.

original: We will turn it finely off, sir; we will take some care.
translation: We will pull it off sir, we will take care we do.

original: Biron, they will shame us: let them not approach.
translation: Biron, let's not let them perform, they will shame us!

original: We are shame-proof, my lord: and tis some policy To have one show worse than the king's and his company.
translation: We are shame-proof my lord and anyway, it is a clever device to have a show that is worse than the King's and his company.

original: I say they shall not come.
translation: I am telling you, they aren't coming.

original: Nay, my good lord, let me o'errule you now:   That sport best pleases that doth least know how:
translation: No, my good lord, I'm going to overrule you now, as it is often the thing that we least expect that pleases us the most.

original: Where zeal strives to content, and the contents   Dies in the zeal of that which it presents:
translation: It is only an issue when enthusiasm tries to please, and the contents of the show get lost in the enthusiasm.

original: Their form confounded makes most form in mirth,   When great things labouring perish in their birth.
translation: This ruins what the play is actually about, but has its own reward in the fact that it makes people laugh—great things can sometimes be ruined before they even get started.

original: A right description of our sport, my lord.
translation: A good description of what we just did as Russians, my lord.

original: Anointed, I implore so much expense of thy royal sweet breath as will utter a brace of words.
translation: King, I was wondering if you would use up some of your royal, sweet breath to say a few words before the show begins.

original: Doth this man serve God?
translation: Is this man religious?

original: Why ask you?
translation: Why do you ask?

original: He speaks not like a man of God's making.
translation: He doesn't speak like a man of God.

original: That is all one, my fair, sweet, honey monarch;
translation: It's all the same to me my fair, sweet, lovely monarch.

original: for,   I protest, the schoolmaster is exceeding   fantastical; too, too vain, too too vain:
translation: Yet I have to say the schoolmaster Holofernes is incredibly imaginative, and certainly far, far too in love with himself.

original: but we   will put it, as they say, to fortuna de la guerra.
translation: But I guess we will have to leave it up to the  chance of war .

original: I wish you the peace of mind, most royal couplement!
translation: I wish you peace of mind, my royal pair!

original: Here is like to be a good presence of Worthies.
translation: You are about to see a good company of Worthies.

original: He   presents Hector of Troy; the swain, Pompey the   Great; the parish curate, Alexander; Armado's page,   Hercules; the pedant, Judas Maccabaeus:
translation: He presents Hector of Troy, Costard is Pompey the Great, the parson is Alexander the Great, Armado's attendant is Hercules and the pedantic teacher is Judas Maccabaeus.

original: And if   these four Worthies in their first show thrive,   These four will change habits, and present the other  five.
translation: If these four Worthies do well in the first show, they will change their costumes and show us the other five Worthies.

original: There is five in the first show.
translation: There are five in the first show.

original: You are deceived; 'tis not so.
translation: You are wrong, that's not true.

original: The pedant, the braggart, the hedge-priest, the fool and the boy:— Abate throw at novum, and the whole world again Cannot pick out five such, take each one in his vein.
The ship is under sail, and here she comes amain.
translation: The ship has set off, and here she comes with all speed.

original: I Pompey am,—
translation: I Pompey am—

original: You lie, you are not he.
translation: That's a lie, you are not Pompey.

original: I Pompey am,—
translation: I Pompey am—

original: With leopard's head on knee.
Well said, old mocker: I must needs be friends with thee.
translation: Well said, my good man, I should be friends with you.

original: I Pompey am, Pompey surnamed the Big—
translation: I Pompey am, with the surname of "the Big."

original: The Great.
translation: You mean "The Great."

original: It is, 'Great,' sir:—
translation: Oh yes, it is "Great" sir.

original: Pompey surnamed the Great;   That oft in field, with targe and shield, did make   my foe to sweat:
translation: Pompey's surname is "The Great," a man that was always in battle, with a shield, making his enemies scared.

original: And travelling along this coast, I here am come by  chance,   And lay my arms before the legs of this sweet lass of  France,
translation: When I was traveling along the coast, I arrived at Navarre by chance, and lay my weapons before the legs of this Princess of France.

original: If your ladyship would say, 'Thanks, Pompey,' I had  done.
translation: If your ladyship will just say "Thanks, Pompey," then my work here is done.

original: Great thanks, great Pompey.
translation: Great thanks to you, great Pompey.

original: 'Tis not so much worth; but I hope I was perfect: I made a little fault in 'Great.'
translation: It wasn't very good, but I hope I was at least word perfect. I made that small error when I forgot to say "Great."

original: My hat to a halfpenny, Pompey proves the best Worthy.
translation: I'll bet anything that Pompey ends up being the best Worthy.

original: When in the world I lived, I was the world's commander; By east, west, north, and south, I spread my conquering might: My scutcheon plain declares that I am Alisander,—
translation: When I was alive, I was the world's commander, I conquered in every direction, east, west, north and south. My coat of arms clearly shows that I am Alexander—

original: Your nose says, no, you are not for it stands too  right.
translation: Your nose would suggest that you aren't, because it is too straight for you to be Alexander the Great.

original: Your nose smells 'no' in this, most tender-smelling  knight.
The conqueror is dismay'd. Proceed, good Alexander.
translation: The conqueror is upset. Carry on, good Alexander.

original: When in the world I lived, I was the world's commander,—
translation: When I was alive, I was the world's commander—

original: Most true, 'tis right; you were so, Alisander.
translation: That's true, that's right, you were Alexander.

original: Pompey the Great,—
translation: Pompey the Great?!

original: Your servant, and Costard.
translation: Your servant sir, and also Costard.

original: Take away the conqueror, take away Alisander.
translation: Take away the conquerer, take away Alexander.

original: O, sir, you have overthrown   Alisander the conqueror!
translation: Oh sir, you have ruined Alexander the Great!

original: You will be scraped out of   the painted cloth for this:
translation: You will be taken out of the  painting  for this!

original: your lion, that holds   his poll-axe sitting on a close-stool, will be given   to Ajax: he will be the ninth Worthy.
translation: Your lion, that holds your battle axe and sits by you, will be given to  Ajax  instead—he will be the ninth Worthy!

original: A conqueror,   and afeard to speak! run away for shame, Alisander.
translation: A conquerer and yet too afraid to talk. Run away for shame, Alexander!

original: There, an't shall please you;
translation: I am sorry about that.

original: a foolish mild man; an   honest man, look you, and soon dashed.
translation: He is a silly man, an honest man mind you, but soon put to shame.

original: He is a   marvellous good neighbour, faith, and a very good   bowler:
translation: He is a very good neighbor though, and a very good bowler!

original: but, for Alisander,—alas, you see how   'tis,—a little o'erparted.
translation: But when he plays Alexander, well, you saw what happened, it was a bit too difficult for him.

original: But there are Worthies   a-coming will speak their mind in some other sort.
translation: But there are other Worthies coming who will speak their minds in other ways.

original: Great Hercules is presented by this imp,   Whose club kill'd Cerberus, that three-headed canis;
translation: @ dog .

original: And when he was a babe, a child, a shrimp,   Thus did he strangle serpents in his manus.
translation: When he was a baby, a child, a young thing, he strangled snakes with his bare  hands .

original: Quoniam he seemeth in minority,   Ergo I come with this apology.
translation: Since  he looks like a child, I therefore come to apologize.

original: Keep some state in thy exit, and vanish.
translation: Behave in a dignified manner when you exit, and now leave.

original: Judas I am,—
translation: I am Judas—

original: A Judas!
translation: A traitor!

original: Not Iscariot, sir. Judas I am, ycliped Maccabaeus.
translation: Not Judas Iscariot sir, I am called Judas Maccabaeus.

original: Judas Maccabaeus clipt is plain Judas.
translation: Judas Maccabaeus shortened is just Judas.

original: A kissing traitor. How art thou proved Judas?
Judas I am,—
translation: I am Judas—

original: The more shame for you, Judas.
translation: Shame on you Judas.

original: What mean you, sir?
translation: What do you mean sir?

original: To make Judas hang himself.
translation: To make Judas hang himself.

original: Begin, sir; you are my elder.
translation: You should hang yourself first sir, as you are my elder.

original: Well followed: Judas was hanged on an elder.
translation: A nice line, as Judas was hanged on an elder tree.

original: I will not be put out of countenance.
translation: I will not allow my face to show I am upset.

original: Because thou hast no face.
translation: Because you have no face.

original: What is this?
translation: What is this?

original: A cittern-head.
The head of a bodkin.
A Death's face in a ring.
The face of an old Roman coin, scarce seen.
translation: The face of an old Roman coin, that can barely be seen because it has worn away.

original: The pommel of Caesar's falchion.
translation: The knob at the end of Caesar's sword.

original: The carved-bone face on a flask.
Saint George's half-cheek in a brooch.
translation: The face of Saint George in profile on a brooch.

original: Ay, and in a brooch of lead.
translation: Yes, and a brooch made of lead at that.

original: Ay, and worn in the cap of a tooth-drawer. And now forward; for we have put thee in countenance.
You have put me out of countenance.
translation: Actually you have made me feel quite embarrassed and my face is blushing.

original: False; we have given thee faces.
translation: Lies! Since we've given you loads of faces to choose from!

original: But you have out-faced them all.
translation: But you have made them all shameful things.

original: An thou wert a lion, we would do so.
translation: Even if you were a lion, we would do the same.

original: Therefore, as he is an ass, let him go. And so adieu, sweet Jude! nay, why dost thou stay?
For the latter end of his name.
translation: To hear the rest of his name.

original: For the ass to the Jude; give it him:—Jud-as, away!
translation: Give the ass to the Jude, give it to him—Jude-ass away!

original: This is not generous, not gentle, not humble.
translation: That is not kind, not nice, not worthy.

original: A light for Monsieur Judas! it grows dark, he may  stumble.
Alas, poor Maccabaeus, how hath he been baited!
translation: Oh, poor Maccabaeus, how he's been mocked!

original: Hide thy head, Achilles: here comes Hector in arms.
translation: Achilles you'd better hide, here comes Hector with weapons.

original: Though my mocks come home by me, I will now be merry.
translation: Although I'll pay for my mockery later, I'll keep having fun for now.

original: Hector was but a Troyan in respect of this.
translation: Hector was a Trojan who did the same.

original: But is this Hector?
translation: But is this Hector?

original: I think Hector was not so clean-timbered.
translation: I don't think Hector was that well-built.

original: His leg is too big for Hector's.
translation: His leg is too big to be Hector's.

original: More calf, certain.
translation: He has more calf, that's for certain.

original: No; he is best endued in the small.
This cannot be Hector.
translation: This cannot be Hector.

original: He's a god or a painter; for he makes faces.
translation: He must be either a god or a painter, because he creates some interesting faces.

original: The armipotent Mars, of lances the almighty, Gave Hector a gift,—
translation: Mars, mighty in arms, with his powerful spears, gave Hector a gift.

original: A gilt nutmeg.
translation: Was it a nutmeg covered in the yolk of an egg?

original: A lemon.
translation: Was it a lemon?

original: Stuck with cloves.
translation: Filled with garlic?

original: No, cloven.
translation: No, split down the middle.

original: Peace!—
translation: Quiet!

original: The armipotent Mars, of lances the almighty   Gave Hector a gift, the heir of Ilion;
translation: Mars, mighty in arms, with his powerful spears, gave Hector, the heir of Troy, a gift.

original: A man so breathed, that certain he would fight; yea   From morn till night, out of his pavilion.
translation: He was so strong that he could fight you from morning until evening in front of his tent.

original: I am that flower,—
translation: I am that flower—

original: That mint.
translation: A mint maybe.

original: That columbine.
Sweet Lord Longaville, rein thy tongue.
translation: Sweet Lord Longaville, please watch your tongue.

original: I must rather give it the rein, for it runs against  Hector.
translation: I'm afraid I'm going to have to let it run free, since it runs after Hector.

original: Ay, and Hector's a greyhound.
translation: Yes, and Hector was very fast.

original: The sweet war-man is dead and rotten; sweet chucks, beat not the bones of the buried: when he breathed, he was a man. But I will forward with my device.
translation: The sweet warrior is long dead and gone but sweet people, do not speak badly about the dead. When he breathed he was a man. I will continue with my performance.

original: Sweet royalty, bestow on me the sense of hearing.
translation: Sweet royalty, please listen to what I have to say.

original: Speak, brave Hector: we are much delighted.
translation: Speak, brave Hector, we are delighted to hear what you have to say.

original: I do adore thy sweet grace's slipper.
translation: I love your sweet grace's shoe.

original: Loves her by the foot,—
translation: He loves her foot.

original: He may not by the yard.
translation: He isn't allowed to love three feet.

original: This Hector far surmounted Hannibal,—
translation: This Hector was even greater than Hannibal.

original: The party is gone, fellow Hector, she is gone; she is two months on her way.
translation: Fellow Hector she is pregnant, she is pregnant! She is two months along!

original: What meanest thou?
translation: What do you mean?

original: Faith, unless you play the honest Troyan, the poor wench is cast away: she's quick; the child brags in her belly already: tis yours.
translation: Faith, unless you are actually Hector, the poor girl is ruined, she is pregnant and the child is already strutting around in her belly. It's yours.

original: Dost thou infamonize me among potentates? thou shalt die.
translation: Are you trying to ruin me in front of these powerful people? You shall die for it.

original: Then shall Hector be whipped for Jaquenetta that is quick by him and hanged for Pompey that is dead by him.
translation: Hector will have to be whipped as well because Jaquenetta is pregnant by him and then he will have to be hanged for killing me, Pompey.

original: Most rare Pompey!
translation: Well said Pompey!

original: Renowned Pompey!
translation: Renowned Pompey!

original: Greater than great, great, great, great Pompey! Pompey the Huge!
translation: You are even greater than great, great, great, great Pompey! You are now Pompey the Huge!

original: Hector trembles.
translation: Hector trembles.

original: Pompey is moved. More Ates, more Ates! stir them on! stir them on!
Hector will challenge him.
translation: Hector will challenge him.

original: Ay, if a' have no man's blood in's belly than will sup a flea.
translation: Yes, but he won't be able to hurt Pompey enough to even draw enough blood to feed a flea.

original: By the north pole, I do challenge thee.
translation: I challenge you by the north pole.

original: I will not fight with a pole, like a northern man: I'll slash; I'll do it by the sword. I bepray you, let me borrow my arms again.
Room for the incensed Worthies!
translation: Make room for the angry Worthies!

original: I'll do it in my shirt.
translation: I'll fight just in my shirt.

original: Most resolute Pompey!
translation: Pompey is so determined!

original: Master, let me take you a buttonhole lower. Do you not see Pompey is uncasing for the combat? What mean you? You will lose your reputation.
translation: Master, I'll help you to take off your clothes. Do you not see that Pompey is undressing ready to fight you? What are you doing? You will ruin your reputation if you don't.

original: Gentlemen and soldiers, pardon me; I will not combat in my shirt.
translation: Gentlemen and soldiers, excuse me. I will not fight him now in my shirt.

original: You may not deny it: Pompey hath made the challenge.
translation: You can't refuse, Pompey has challenged you.

original: Sweet bloods, I both may and will.
translation: Fiery men, I both can and I will.

original: What reason have you for't?
translation: What reason do you have for doing that?

original: The naked truth of it is, I have no shirt; I go woolward for penance.
translation: The real truth of it is, I'm not wearing a shirt. I wear wool against my bare skin as punishment for my behavior.

original: True, and it was enjoined him in Rome for want of linen: since when, I'll be sworn, he wore none but a dishclout of Jaquenetta's, and that a' wears next his heart for a favour.
translation: True, and it was imposed on him in Rome because there was a lack of linen. Since then he hasn't worn anything except a dishcloth of Jaquenetta's which he wears next to his heart as a gift.

original: God save you, madam!
translation: God save you, madam!

original: Welcome, Mercade; But that thou interrupt'st our merriment.
translation: Welcome Mercade, but you have interrupted our entertainment.

original: I am sorry, madam; for the news I bring Is heavy in my tongue. The king your father—
translation: I am sorry madam, but the news I bring is hard to report. The king your father—

original: Dead, for my life!
translation: Is dead, I know it!

original: Even so; my tale is told.
translation: It is true, that's what I came here to say.

original: Worthies, away! the scene begins to cloud.
translation: Worthies, leave! The scene has become darker.

original: For mine own part, I breathe free breath. I have seen the day of wrong through the little hole of discretion, and I will right myself like a soldier.
translation: For my own part I am relieved that I can breathe the air freely. I have seen how you can be humiliated for doing bad things, and I am going to punish myself like a soldier.

original: How fares your majesty?
translation: How are you, your majesty?

original: Boyet, prepare; I will away tonight.
translation: Boyet, prepare our things, we will leave tonight.

original: Madam, not so; I do beseech you, stay.
translation: Madam, don't leave, I ask you to stay.

original: Prepare, I say. I thank you, gracious lords,   For all your fair endeavors;
translation: Prepare our things, I said. Thank you, kind lords, for everything that you have done.

original: and entreat,   Out of a new-sad soul, that you vouchsafe   In your rich wisdom to excuse or hide   The liberal opposition of our spirits,
translation: I hope, now that I am sad, that you clever men promise to excuse and overlook the great jokes we have played on you.

original: If over-boldly we have borne ourselves   In the converse of breath: your gentleness   Was guilty of it.
translation: If we have acted too boldly when speaking to you, then your kindness was responsible for it.

original: Farewell worthy lord!   A heavy heart bears not a nimble tongue:   Excuse me so, coming too short of thanks   For my great suit so easily obtain'd.
translation: Goodbye my worthy lord! A heavy heart does not lead to a witty tongue, I apologize for not being able to thank you enough due to a lack of time.

original: The extreme parts of time extremely forms   All causes to the purpose of his speed,   And often at his very loose decides   That which long process could not arbitrate:
translation: Having so little time left makes a person have to act quickly, and often in these final moments he decides the things that he has debated over for a long time.

original: And though the mourning brow of progeny   Forbid the smiling courtesy of love   The holy suit which fain it would convince,
translation: Even though the sad face of a child that has lost her father doesn't allow you to love, and marriage hardly seems like the first thing on your mind.

original: Yet, since love's argument was first on foot,   Let not the cloud of sorrow justle it   From what it purposed;
translation: Yet, since love was just getting started, don't let your sadness push it aside and ignore it,

original: since, to wail friends lost   Is not by much so wholesome-profitable   As to rejoice at friends but newly found.
translation: since it is just as important to cry for people we have lost, as it is to rejoice at people we have found.

original: I understand you not: my griefs are double.
translation: I don't understand you, I am grieving too much.

original: Honest plain words best pierce the ear of grief;   And by these badges understand the king.
translation: Honest, simple words are a better choice when someone is grieving, so I will try to explain to you what the King means.

original: For your fair sakes have we neglected time,   Play'd foul play with our oaths:
translation: For you, my beautiful ladies, we didn't pay attention to time and we broke our oaths without thinking.

original: your beauty, ladies,   Hath much deform'd us, fashioning our humours   Even to the opposed end of our intents:
translation: Your beauty, ladies, has changed us, making us act in ways that we never expected.

original: And what in us hath seem'd ridiculous,—   As love is full of unbefitting strains,   All wanton as a child, skipping and vain,
translation: The things we have done seem ridiculous, because love makes people act in ridiculous ways, like a foolish child skipping around.

original: Form'd by the eye and therefore, like the eye,   Full of strange shapes, of habits and of forms,   Varying in subjects as the eye doth roll   To every varied object in his glance:
translation: Love is made by the eye, and so, like an eye, it is full of strange shapes, strange behavior and strange appearances, changing from one person to another, just like an eye looks from one thing to another.

original: Which parti-coated presence of loose love   Put on by us, if, in your heavenly eyes,   Have misbecomed our oaths and gravities,   Those heavenly eyes, that look into these faults,   Suggested us to make.
translation: It was your heavenly eyes that led us to forget our oaths and promises in the first place, and for which we behaved in such a silly way, because we needed to love you.

original: Therefore, ladies,   Our love being yours, the error that love makes   Is likewise yours:
translation: Therefore ladies, because our love belongs to you, you are partly to blame for the mistakes we have made.

original: we to ourselves prove false,   By being once false for ever to be true   To those that make us both,—fair ladies, you:
translation: We too are liars, for going against one vow to try to make another vow for love, for you, our beautiful ladies.

original: And even that falsehood, in itself a sin,   Thus purifies itself and turns to grace.
translation: Even though we broke our vows, and that was a sin, we have redeemed ourselves and found our virtue again in you.

original: We have received your letters full of love;   Your favours, the ambassadors of love;
translation: We have received your love letter, your presents, your messengers of love.

original: And, in our maiden council, rated them   At courtship, pleasant jest and courtesy,   As bombast and as lining to the time:
translation: As a group of young women, we thought that they were no more than flirting, an enjoyable game and a way to be polite, an  extra touch  to our visit.

original: But more devout than this in our respects   Have we not been; and therefore met your loves   In their own fashion, like a merriment.
translation: But we haven't taken this whole business any more seriously than this, and therefore played along with your jokes like you did with ours, like it was a game.

original: Our letters, madam, show'd much more than jest.
translation: Our letters madam, were much more than just jokes.

original: So did our looks.
translation: Our looks were too.

original: We did not quote them so.
translation: We didn't fully notice them.

original: Now, at the latest minute of the hour, Grant us your loves.
translation: Now in this final moment, give us your loves.

original: A time, methinks, too short   To make a world-without-end bargain in.
translation: This time is too short to make a decision which is going to last forever.

original: No, no, my lord, your grace is perjured much,   Full of dear guiltiness;
translation: No, no my lord, you have broken your oath and are now full of guilt.

original: and therefore this:   If for my love, as there is no such cause,   You will do aught, this shall you do for me:
translation: I will say this though, if you will do anything for my love, though I don't see why you would, then do this for me.

original: Your oath I will not trust; but go with speed   To some forlorn and naked hermitage,   Remote from all the pleasures of the world;   There stay until the twelve celestial signs   Have brought about the annual reckoning.
translation: I won't trust your oath, but go quickly to some abandoned and unfurnished place, far away from all the pleasures of this world and stay there until a year has gone by and you have made up for what you have done.

original: If this austere insociable life   Change not your offer made in heat of blood;
translation: If this difficult and lonely lifestyle doesn't change the loving offer you have just made me;

original: If frosts and fasts, hard lodging and thin weeds   Nip not the gaudy blossoms of your love,   But that it bear this trial and last love;
translation: if the cold and the lack of food, difficult conditions and bad clothes doesn't stop your love from growing,

original: Then, at the expiration of the year,   Come challenge me,
translation: then come and find me at the end of this year, and show me that your love has stayed strong.

original: challenge me by these deserts,   And, by this virgin palm now kissing thine   I will be thine;
translation: Come and find me to get what you deserve to have, and by the hand I now kiss, I will be yours.

original: and till that instant shut   My woeful self up in a mourning house,   Raining the tears of lamentation   For the remembrance of my father's death.
translation: Until then I am going to hide myself away in mourning and weep and cry about the death of my father.

original: If this thou do deny, let our hands part,   Neither entitled in the other's heart.
translation: If you can't agree to this, let's leave it now, and agree to never be together.

original: If this, or more than this, I would deny, To flatter up these powers of mine with rest, The sudden hand of death close up mine eye! Hence ever then my heart is in thy breast.
translation: If I would not agree to this, just because it will be difficult, then I don't even deserve to live! Therefore, I will love you faithfully until then.

original: But what to me, my love? but what to me? A wife?
translation: But what's there for me, my love? What's there for me? A wife?

original: A beard, fair health, and honesty; With three-fold love I wish you all these three.
O, shall I say, I thank you, gentle wife?
translation: Then, can I say, I thank you, my sweet wife?

original: Not so, my lord; a twelvemonth and a day I'll mark no words that smooth-faced wooers say: Come when the king doth to my lady come; Then, if I have much love, I'll give you some.
translation: Not now my lord. For just over a year I will not listen to anything that men say to me in love. When the King comes to see my lady, come with him—if I have love in my heart, you can have some of it.

original: I'll serve thee true and faithfully till then.
translation: I'll be faithful to you and wait until then.

original: Yet swear not, lest ye be forsworn again.
translation: Don't swear to that, I would hate for you to break another oath.

original: What says Maria?
translation: What does Maria say?

original: At the twelvemonth's end I'll change my black gown for a faithful friend.
translation: After twelve months I will change out of my black gown, for a faithful lover.

original: I'll stay with patience; but the time is long.
translation: I'll wait with patience, but it's a long time.

original: The liker you; few taller are so young.
translation: That's more like you, you may be tall but you're also young.

original: Studies my lady? mistress, look on me; Behold the window of my heart, mine eye, What humble suit attends thy answer there: Impose some service on me for thy love.
translation: Are you deep in thought my lady? Mistress, look at me and see the love that I have for you in my eyes. What do I have to do to get an answer, tell me to do something so that you can love me.

original: Oft have I heard of you, my Lord Biron,   Before I saw you;
translation: I have heard a lot about you, my Lord Biron, and before I met you, all I knew is what I had heard from rumors and stories.

original: and the world's large tongue   Proclaims you for a man replete with mocks,   Full of comparisons and wounding flouts,   Which you on all estates will execute   That lie within the mercy of your wit.
translation: People say that you are a man who always mocks people, you are full of satire and hurtful jokes which you use on everyone you meet to destroy them with your wit.

original: To weed this wormwood from your fruitful brain,   And therewithal to win me, if you please,   Without the which I am not to be won,
translation: To get rid of this bitterness from your clever mind, and in doing so to win me, if that's what you want, as there is no other way we will be together,

original: You shall this twelvemonth term from day to day   Visit the speechless sick and still converse   With groaning wretches;
translation: you must spend the next year visiting mutes and sick people and speak with ill women.

translation: Your task is to use all of the power of your wit to try to make helpless and weak people laugh.

original: To move wild laughter in the throat of death? It cannot be; it is impossible: Mirth cannot move a soul in agony.
translation: To make people laugh when they are about to die? That's impossible I tell you, hilarity cannot affect a person who is in pain.

original: Why, that's the way to choke a gibing spirit,   Whose influence is begot of that loose grace   Which shallow laughing hearers give to fools:
translation: Why, that's how to get rid of your sarcastic nature, which seems to have the same charm as people imagine fools to have.

original: A jest's prosperity lies in the ear   Of him that hears it, never in the tongue   Of him that makes it:
translation: The success of a joke comes with how people hear it, not in how the person says it.

original: then, if sickly ears,   Deaf'd with the clamours of their own dear groans,   Will hear your idle scorns, continue then,   And I will have you and that fault withal;
translation: So, if sick ears, so fed up of the sounds of their own awful groans, will listen to your pointless jokes, carry on and you will win my love, jokes and all.

original: But if they will not, throw away that spirit,   And I shall find you empty of that fault,   Right joyful of your reformation.
translation: But if they won't listen to you, then get rid of your sarcasm, and I will think you have been cured and be pleased about how you have changed.

original: A twelvemonth! well; befall what will befall, I'll jest a twelvemonth in an hospital.
translation: Twelve months! Okay well maybe if I get injured, I could spend the year in a hospital waiting for you.

original: Ay, sweet my lord; and so I take my  leave.
translation: Yes my lord, and so I will go.

original: No, madam; we will bring you on your way.
translation: No madam, we will accompany you when you leave.

original: Our wooing doth not end like an old play; Jack hath not Jill: these ladies' courtesy Might well have made our sport a comedy.

translation: Come sir, it is only for just over a year, and then it will be over.

original: That's too long for a play.
translation: That's too long for a play.

original: Sweet majesty, vouchsafe me,—
translation: Your majesty, hear what I have to say.

original: Was not that Hector?
translation: Wasn't he Hector?

original: The worthy knight of Troy.
translation: The worthy knight of Troy.

original: I will kiss thy royal finger, and take leave.
translation: I will kiss your royal finger and leave.

translation: I will stick to my vows. I have promised Jaquenetta that I will be a farmer for three years in order to win her love.

translation: But, your highness, would you like to hear the dialogue that the two clever men created about the owl and the cuckoo? It should have come at the end of the show.

original: Call them forth quickly; we will do so.
translation: Call them here quickly, we will hear it.

original: Holla! approach.
translation: Hey! Come here.

translation: This side is Winter, this side is Spring. The first half will be performed by the owl, the other by the cuckoo. Spring, begin.

translation: When there are colorful daisies and blue violets And silver-white cuckoo flowers And yellow cuckoo-buds Covering the meadows so wonderfully,

translation: The cuckoo then, on every tree, Mocks married men, for he sings  "Cuckoo!" "Cuckoo, cuckoo!" Oh what a terrifying word, That scares the ears of married people!

original: When shepherds pipe on oaten straws   And merry larks are ploughmen's clocks,   When turtles tread, and rooks, and daws,   And maidens bleach their summer smocks
translation: When shepherds play songs on straws made out of oat, And cheerful birds wake ploughmen up in the morning. When turtle-doves mate, along with rooks and jackdaws,  And young girls dye their dresses ready for the summer.

original: The cuckoo then, on every tree,   Mocks married men; for thus sings he, Cuckoo;   Cuckoo, cuckoo: O word of fear,   Unpleasing to a married ear!
translation: The cuckoo then, on every tree,  Mocks married men, for her sings " Cuckoo !" "Cuckoo, cuckoo!" Oh what a terrifying word, That scares the ears of married people!

Escalus.

original: My lord.

original: Of government the properties to unfold,   Would seem in me to affect speech and discourse;

original: you're as pregnant in   As art and practise hath enriched any   That we remember.
translation: you have as much theory and practice as anyone I can remember.

translation: There's our commission, from which I don't want you to waver.

translation: [To an attendant]  Hey, call up Angelo; ask him to come to me.

translation: How do you think Angelo will measure up to me?

original: what think you of it?
translation: What do you think about it?

original: If any in Vienna be of worth To undergo such ample grace and honour, It is Lord Angelo.
translation: If anyone in Vienna is worthy of such plentiful grace and honor, it is Lord Angelo.

original: Look where he comes.
translation: Look, here he comes.

original: Always obedient to your grace's will, I come to know your pleasure.
Angelo,   There is a kind of character in thy life,   That to the observer doth thy history   Fully unfold.
translation: Angelo, there is a level of quality in your life that makes your whole story apparent to any observer.

original: Thyself and thy belongings   Are not thine own so proper as to waste   Thyself upon thy virtues, they on thee.
translation: Your circumstances and your very self are not exclusively your own, for you to weary yourself in becoming virtuous.

original: Heaven doth with us as we with torches do,   Not light them for themselves;
translation: Heaven does with us what we do with torches; we don't light them for their own sake.

original: for if our virtues   Did not go forth of us, 'twere all alike   As if we had them not.
translation: If our virtues didn't radiate from us, it would be as if we didn't have them.

original: Spirits are not finely touch'd   But to fine issues,
translation: Our spirits are finely created to do fine things.

original: nor Nature never lends   The smallest scruple of her excellence   But, like a thrifty goddess, she determines   Herself the glory of a creditor,
translation: Nature's a penny-pinching goddess: she won't give even the tiniest piece of greatness without figuring out how she will profit from it

original: Both thanks and use.
translation: —both from people thanking her for it, and from them using it.

translation: But I'm speaking to someone that can take on my role himself. Kneel, then, Angelo.

original: —   In our remove be thou at full ourself;
translation: [ ANGELO kneels ]   With my permission: be completely like me.

original: Mortality and mercy in Vienna   Live in thy tongue and heart:
translation: Mortality and mercy  in Vienna are at your word and in your heart.

original: old Escalus,   Though first in question, is thy secondary.   Take thy commission.
translation: Old Escalus, though my right-hand man, is second to you. Take your commission.

translation: No more side-stepping. I  carefully  considered and deliberated before I chose you, so take your role.

translation: My exit has to be so quick that I have to leave now–-we won't have time to cover some of the important matters.

original: and do look to know   What doth befall you here.
translation: And I'll want to know what's happened to you here.

original: So, fare you well;   To the hopeful execution do I leave you   Of your commissions.
translation: So, take care. I leave you to your post with the highest expectations.

original: Yet give leave, my lord, That we may bring you something on the way.
translation: My lord, may I have permission to bring you something along the way?

original: My haste may not admit it;
translation: I'm in too much of a hurry to allow it.

original: Nor need you, on mine honour, have to do   With any scruple;
translation: And I swear on my honor that I don't need you to have anything to do with any controversy.

original: your scope is as mine own   So to enforce or qualify the laws   As to your soul seems good.
translation: Your power is the same as my own; you can enforce or modify the laws as you see fit.

translation: Give me your hand: I'll leave discreetly. I love the people, but I don't like being watched all the time.

original: Though it do well, I do not relish well   Their loud applause and Aves vehement;   Nor do I think the man of safe discretion   That does affect it.
translation: Though it does good in the long run, I don't really enjoy their loud applause and shouting, "Hail!"–-and I don't know any trustworthy man that does enjoy it.

original: Once more, fare you well.
translation: Once again, take care!

original: The heavens give safety to your purposes!
translation: May the heavens keep you safe on your journey!

original: Lead forth and bring you back in happiness!
translation: May they guide you and bring you back happy!

original: I thank you. Fare you well.
translation: Thank you. Goodbye.

original: I shall desire you, sir, to give me leave   To have free speech with you;
translation: Sir, I ask you to give me permission to speak freely with you.

original: and it concerns me   To look into the bottom of my place:
translation: I want to fully understand my position:

translation: I know I have power, but I'm not sure its extent, and what it entails.

original: 'Tis so with me. Let us withdraw together, And we may soon our satisfaction have Touching that point.
translation: I agree. Let's leave together so that we can quickly reach an agreement on that point.

original: I'll wait upon your honour.
translation: I'll follow you, your Honor.

translation: If the Duke and the other dukes don't unite with the King of Hungary, then all the dukes will rebel against the king.

original: Heaven grant us its peace, but not the King of Hungary's!
translation: May heaven give us peace, but not peace with the King of Hungary!

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

translation: You sound like the hypocritical pirate, who took the Ten Commandments with him to sea, but scraped one of the commandments off.

original: "Thou shalt not steal?"
translation: "Thou shalt not steal?"

original: Ay, that he razed.
translation: Yes, he burned that one off.

original: Why, 'twas a commandment to command the captain and   all the rest from their functions:
translation: Well, it was a commandment commanding the captain and all the rest not to do their jobs!

original: they put forth   to steal.
translation: They went out to steal.
