translation: There isn't a soldier among us that, when he sits down to pray before a meal, wants to hear someone pray for peace.

original: I never heard any soldier dislike it.
translation: I've never heard a soldier say he didn't like it.

original: I believe thee; for I think thou never wast where grace was said.
translation: I believe you, since I think you've never heard someone say a prayer before.

What, in metre?
In any proportion or in any language.
translation: In any form or in any language.

original: I think, or in any religion.
translation: I think, or in any religion.

translation: Yes, why not? Grace is grace, in spite of all the controversy. For example, you're a twisted crook, in spite of all grace.

original: Well, there went but a pair of shears between us.
translation: Well, you just cut all ties between us.

original: I grant; as there may between the lists and the velvet. Thou art the list.
And thou the velvet:
translation: And you're the velvet?

original: thou art good velvet; thou'rt   a three-piled piece, I warrant thee:
translation: You're good velvet; I bet you're a three-layer piece.

translation: I'd rather be a hem of English wool than be layered the way you are, into a French velvet.

original: Do I speak   feelingly now?
translation: Am I speaking clearly enough now?

original: I think thou dost; and, indeed, with most painful   feeling of thy speech:
translation: I think you are. And, in fact, it's having a painful effect on the listeners.

original: I will, out of thine own   confession, learn to begin thy health; but, whilst I   live, forget to drink after thee.
translation: From what you've said, I'll drink to you but, while I live,  I won't drink after you .

original: I think I have done myself wrong, have I not?
translation: I feel like I've done myself wrong, haven't I?

original: Yes, that thou hast, whether thou art tainted or free.
translation: Yes, you have, whether you're sick or not.

translation: Of what, indeed?

original: Judge.
translation: Guess.

original: To three thousand dolours a year.
Ay, and more.
translation: Yes, and more.

Thou art always figuring diseases in me; but thou art full of error; I am sound.
translation: You're always accusing me of having diseases, but you're wrong; I'm solidly healthy.

original: Nay, not as one would say, healthy; but so sound as   things that are hollow:

original: thy bones are hollow;   impiety has made a feast of thee.
translation: Your  bones are hollow ! Your sin is eating you alive.

original: How now! which of your hips has the most profound  sciatica?
Well, well; there's one yonder arrested and carried to prison was worth five thousand of you all.
translation: Well, well! Someone over there was arrested and carried to prison who's worth five thousand of you all.

original: Who's that, I pray thee?
translation: Who's that, then?

original: Marry, sir, that's Claudio, Signior Claudio.
Claudio to prison? 'tis not so.
translation: Claudio's going to prison? It can't be.

original: Nay, but I know 'tis so:
translation: Unfortunately, I know it is.

original: I saw him arrested, saw   him carried away; and, which is more,
translation: I saw him arrested, saw him carried away, and—even worse—

original: within these   three days his head to be chopped off.
translation: three days from now he'll have his head chopped off.

translation: All joking aside, that can't be true. Are you sure about this?

translation: I'm too sure of it. And it's for getting Ms. Juliet pregnant.

translation: Believe me, it might be true. He promised to meet me two hours ago, and he's always kept his promises.

translation: Come on! Let's go figure out if it's true.

translation: Hello there! What news do you have?

translation: That man was carried off to prison.

original: Well; what has he done?
translation: Well? What did he do?

translation: A woman.

original: But what's his offence?
translation: But what's his offense?

What, is there a maid with child by him?

translation: What proclamation, man?

translation: And what about the ones in the city?

translation: So will all the brothels in the outskirts be pulled down?

translation: To the ground, mistress.

translation: Well, this is certainly a change in our country! What will happen to me?

translation: What can we do, Mr. Bartender? Let's go in.

translation: Man, why are you showing me to the whole world like this? Take me to prison, where I've been committed.

translation: I'm not doing it out of spite; it's Lord Angelo's special orders.

translation: Well, how are you, Claudio? Why the handcuffs?

translation: After overeating we want to fast for a while; in the same way, other kinds of excess lead us to restraint.

translation: Our human nature thirsts for evil, like rats devouring their scavenged food. And when we drink, we die.

translation: And yet, to tell you the truth, I'd rather have the indulgence of freedom than the morality of imprisonment.

translation: What was your crime, Claudio?

translation: To speak of it would be another crime

translation: Sexual immorality?

translation: Just a minute, good friend. Lucio, can I speak with you?

translation: As long as you want, if it'll do you any good. Is sex such a serious crime?

translation: But this new governor has dredged up all the old punishments which,

translation: Write to the Duke and appeal to him.

translation: I've done that, but he's nowhere to be found.

original: I prithee, Lucio, do me this kind service:   This day my sister should the cloister enter   And there receive her approbation:
translation: Please, Lucio, do this for me: today my sister is supposed to enter the  convent  and take her vows;

original: Acquaint her with the danger of my state:   Implore her, in my voice, that she make friends   To the strict deputy;   bid herself assay him:
translation: let her know what danger I'm in. Ask her to make friends with the deputy governor; ask her to win him over.

original: I have great hope in that; for in her youth   There is a prone and speechless dialect,   Such as move men;
translation: I have high hopes for that because she's young, and her honest, plain way of speaking has the power to convince men.

original: beside, she hath prosperous art   When she will play with reason and discourse,   And well she can persuade.
translation: Besides, she's usually successful when she argues or debates, and can easily persuade someone.

original: I pray she may; as well for the encouragement of the   like, which else would stand under grievous   imposition,
translation: I hope she can, both to encourage lovers that others could be horribly punished,

original: as for the enjoying of thy life,
translation: and to save your life.

original: who I   would be sorry should be thus foolishly lost at a   game of tick-tack. I'll to her.
translation: I'd be sorry to lose you over something as silly as a game of tic-tac-toe. I'll go to her.

original: I thank you, good friend Lucio.
translation: Thanks, Lucio; you're a good friend.

original: Within two hours.
translation: I'll go to her within these two hours.

original: Come, officer, away!
translation: Come on, officer, let's go!

original: No, holy father; throw away that thought;
translation: No,  holy father , don't even think of that.

original: Believe not that the dribbling dart of love   Can pierce a complete bosom.
translation: You can't believe that silly old  love  would win over a man as steadfast as me.

original: Why I desire thee   To give me secret harbour,
translation: There's a reason for my asking you for a secret hiding place

original: hath a purpose   More grave and wrinkled than the aims and ends   Of burning youth.
translation: —an old man's reason, serious reason as far from lusty youth's desires and goals as possible.

original: May your grace speak of it?
translation: Can you tell me, your Grace?

original: My holy sir, none better knows than you   How I have ever loved the life removed   And held in idle price to haunt assemblies   Where youth, and cost, and witless bravery keeps.
translation: Holy father, no one knows better than you how much I've loved living in isolation, and how little I've valued the gatherings where young people, wealth, and stupid acts of bravery take place.

original: I have deliver'd to Lord Angelo,   A man of stricture and firm abstinence,   My absolute power and place here in Vienna,
translation: I've given my absolute power and position here in Vienna to Lord Angelo, a man of upstanding discipline and strict abstinence.

original: And he supposes me travell'd to Poland;   For so I have strew'd it in the common ear,   And so it is received.
translation: He thinks I've traveled to Poland, since I've spread that rumor in public and it's come back to him.

original: Now, pious sir,   You will demand of me why I do this?
translation: Now, devout sir, do you want to know why I'm doing this?

original: Gladly, my lord.
translation: Yes, please, my lord.

original: We have strict statutes and most biting laws.
translation: We have strict statutes and extremely harsh laws.

original: The needful bits and curbs to headstrong weeds,   Which for this nineteen years we have let slip;   Even like an o'ergrown lion in a cave,   That goes not out to prey.
translation: I've let the necessary  bits  and restraints for unruly citizens slip in the last nineteen years, like an overgrown lion in a cave who doesn't go out to hunt.

original: Now, as fond fathers,   Having bound up the threatening twigs of birch,   Only to stick it in their children's sight   For terror,
translation: It's like fathers who make threatening switches out of twigs not to use them, but only to scare their children.

original: not to use, in time the rod   Becomes more mock'd than fear'd; so our decrees,   Dead to infliction, to themselves are dead;
translation: Over time, these sorts of fathers are ridiculed more than they're feared. So my decrees—which I haven't enforced—are essentially useless.

original: And liberty plucks justice by the nose;   The baby beats the nurse, and quite athwart   Goes all decorum.
translation: Freedom takes advantage of justice, the baby beats the babysitter, and all order goes to pieces.

original: It rested in your grace   To unloose this tied-up justice when you pleased:
translation: Sir, you had the power to unleash this pent-up justice whenever you wanted,

original: And it in you more dreadful would have seem'd   Than in Lord Angelo.
translation: and it would have seemed more serious coming from you than from Lord Angelo.

original: I do fear, too dreadful:   Sith 'twas my fault to give the people scope,
translation: I'm afraid it would have seemed too serious, since it was my fault to give the people such free reign.

original: 'Twould be my tyranny to strike and gall them   For what I bid them do:
translation: I would seem like a tyrant if I punished and chastised them for what I told them to do

original: for we bid this be done,   When evil deeds have their permissive pass   And not the punishment.
translation: –-since I effectively let evil deeds go unpunished.

original: Therefore indeed, my father,   I have on Angelo imposed the office;
translation: For that reason, father, I've given Angelo the job:

original: Who may, in the ambush of my name, strike home,   And yet my nature never in the fight   To do in slander.
translation: so that he can ambush them in my name and strike home without me dirtying my hands in the fight.

original: And to behold his sway,   I will, as 'twere a brother of your order,   Visit both prince and people:
translation: To keep an eye on his progress, I'll disguise myself as a friar of your order, and visit both the governor and the people.

original: therefore, I prithee,   Supply me with the habit and instruct me   How I may formally in person bear me   Like a true friar.
translation: So, will you please supply me with the  habit  and teach me how to properly act like a true friar?

original: More reasons for this action   At our more leisure shall I render you;   Only, this one: Lord Angelo is precise;
translation: I'll share more of the reasons for my actions with you soon. Here's one: Lord Angelo is precise.

original: Stands at a guard with envy; scarce confesses   That his blood flows, or that his appetite   Is more to bread than stone: hence shall we see,   If power change purpose, what our seemers be.
translation: He keeps his jealousy in check, hardly admits that he's flesh and blood or that he ever gets hungry. So we'll see if he is what he truly seems to be, or if power changes him.

original: And have you nuns no farther privileges?
translation: And you nuns don't have any other privileges?

original: Are not these large enough?
translation: Are these not enough?

original: Yes, truly; I speak not as desiring more;
translation: Yes, indeed they are. I'm not saying that I want anything more,

original: But rather wishing a more strict restraint   Upon the sisterhood, the votarists of Saint Clare.
translation: I'm actually wishing for stricter rules here in the sisterhood of the nuns of  Saint Clare .

original: Ho! Peace be in this place!
translation: Hey! Peace be in this place!

original: Who's that which calls?
translation: Who's that who's calling?

original: It is a man's voice. Gentle Isabella,   Turn you the key, and know his business of him;   You may, I may not; you are yet unsworn.
translation: It's a man's voice. Dear Isabella: you turn the key and find out what he wants. You can; I can't. You haven't taken your vows yet.

original: When you have vow'd, you must not speak with men   But in the presence of the prioress:
translation: Once you've taken your vows, you can't speak with men unless the prioress is there.

original: Then, if you speak, you must not show your face,   Or, if you show your face, you must not speak.   He calls again; I pray you, answer him.
translation: Then, if you speak, you can't show your face. Or if you show your face, you can't speak. He's calling again; please, answer him.

original: Peace and prosperity! Who is't that calls?
translation: Peace and prosperity! Who's there?

original: Hail, virgin, if you be, as those cheek-roses   Proclaim you are no less!
translation: Greetings, virgin—if you are one, since those rosy cheeks show you're nothing less!

original: Can you so stead me   As bring me to the sight of Isabella,   A novice of this place and the fair sister   To her unhappy brother Claudio?
translation: Can you help me out by bringing me to Isabella, a novice here and the pretty sister of her unlucky brother Claudio?

original: Why "her unhappy brother?" let me ask,
translation: Why "her unlucky brother?" I have to ask,

original: The rather for I now must make you know   I am that Isabella and his sister.
translation: and now I should let you know that I am Isabella, his sister.

original: Gentle and fair, your brother kindly greets you: Not to be weary with you, he's in prison.
translation: Gentle and pretty one, your brother sends his warm greetings. I don't want to beat around the bush: he's in prison.

original: Woe me! for what?
translation: Oh no! For what?

original: For that which, if myself might be his judge, He should receive his punishment in thanks: He hath got his friend with child.
translation: For that which, if I were his judge, his only punishment would be congratulations. He got his girlfriend pregnant.

original: Sir, make me not your story.
translation: Sir, you're making this up.

original: It is true.   I would not—though 'tis my familiar sin   With maids to seem the lapwing and to jest,   Tongue far from heart—play with all virgins so:
translation: It's true. Though I'm often prone to  run around  and joke with girls, not meaning what I say, I wouldn't play with all virgins that way.

original: I hold you as a thing ensky'd and sainted.
translation: To me, you're like an angel in the sky.

original: By your renouncement an immortal spirit,   And to be talk'd with in sincerity,   As with a saint.
translation: By taking your vows, you're an immortal spirit to have serious conversations with, like with a saint.

original: You do blaspheme the good in mocking me.
Do not believe it. Fewness and truth, 'tis thus:   Your brother and his lover have embraced:
translation: No, not at all! Truth be told, this is it: your brother and his girlfriend have had sex.

original: As those that feed grow full, as blossoming time   That from the seedness the bare fallow brings   To teeming foison,
translation: Just like people who eat get full and seeds at springtime grow from bare soil into blossoming plants,

original: even so her plenteous womb   Expresseth his full tilth and husbandry.
translation: her fertile womb reflects his full cultivation and  husbandry .

original: Some one with child by him? My cousin Juliet?
Is she your cousin?
translation: Is she your cousin?

original: Adoptedly; as school-maids change their names By vain though apt affection.
translation: My adopted cousin, in the way that schoolgirls change their names when they're silly and like each other.

original: She it is.
translation: She's the one.

original: O, let him marry her.
translation: Oh, let him marry her.

original: This is the point.   The duke is very strangely gone from hence;
translation: That's the point. The Duke has mysteriously left the country.

original: Bore many gentlemen, myself being one,   In hand and hope of action:
translation: He left many gentlemen behind waiting for action—myself included.

original: but we do learn   By those that know the very nerves of state,   His givings-out were of an infinite distance   From his true-meant design.
translation: But we have heard from those at the very head of the state that what happened was far from his original intentions.

original: Upon his place,   And with full line of his authority,   Governs Lord Angelo; a man whose blood   Is very snow-broth;
translation: Lord Angelo rules in the Duke's place, and with his complete authority. Angelo is a man with snow running through his veins.

original: one who never feels   The wanton stings and motions of the sense,
translation: He never feels the tugs of human emotion or the senses,

original: But doth rebate and blunt his natural edge   With profits of the mind, study and fast.
translation: but rather stifles and contains his natural inclinations with prayer, study, and fasting.

original: He—to give fear to use and liberty,   Which have for long run by the hideous law,   As mice by lions—hath pick'd out an act,
translation: To scare those of us who have gotten used to being free and doing what we please despite the horrible laws, like mice scared by lions—Angelo has picked out an act—fornication

original: Under whose heavy sense your brother's life   Falls into forfeit: he arrests him on it;   And follows close the rigour of the statute,   To make him an example.
translation: —of which your brother is convicted and sentenced cruelly to death. He arrested him for it, and is following the letter of the law closely to make an example of him.

original: All hope is gone,   Unless you have the grace by your fair prayer   To soften Angelo: and that's my pith of business   'Twixt you and your poor brother.
translation: All hope is gone, unless you're able—with your pretty face and sweet prayers—to soften Angelo. And that's the heart of my business between you and your poor brother.

original: Doth he so seek his life?
translation: Does Angelo want to take my brother's life away, just like that?

original: Has censured him Already; and, as I hear, the provost hath A warrant for his execution.
translation: Angelo's charged him already. And I've heard that the provost has a warrant for his execution.

original: Alas! what poor ability's in me To do him good?
translation: Alas! What can I possibly to do to help him?

original: Assay the power you have.
translation: Use all the power you have.

original: My power? Alas, I doubt—
translation: My power? Oh, no, I doubt—

original: Our doubts are traitors   And make us lose the good we oft might win   By fearing to attempt.
translation: Our doubts betray us. They make us lose the prize we might otherwise win by convincing us not to try.

original: Go to Lord Angelo,   And let him learn to know,
translation: Go to Lord Angelo, and make him understand:

original: when maidens sue,   Men give like gods; but when they weep and kneel,   All their petitions are as freely theirs   As they themselves would owe them.
translation: when young girls make requests, men give like gods. But when girls cry and grovel, men grant their wishes as quickly as if the men owed them in the first place.

original: I'll see what I can do.
translation: I'll see what I can do.

original: But speedily.
translation: But be quick about it.

original: I will about it straight;   No longer staying but to give the mother   Notice of my affair.
translation: I'll do it immediately; I just need a moment to tell the Mother Superior what I'm up to.

original: I humbly thank you:   Commend me to my brother: soon at night   I'll send him certain word of my success.
translation: I give you my humble thanks. Give my best to my brother. Soon, tonight, I'll let him know if I've been successful.

original: I take my leave of you.
translation: I'll leave you, then.

original: Good sir, adieu.
translation: Farewell, good sir.

original: We must not make a scarecrow of the law,
translation: We can't let the law become like a scarecrow.

original: Setting it up to fear the birds of prey,   And let it keep one shape, till custom make it   Their perch and not their terror.
translation: When a scarecrow is set up to scare away scavenger birds, it becomes such a familiar presence that the birds perch on it instead of being afraid.

original: Ay, but yet   Let us be keen, and rather cut a little,   Than fall, and bruise to death.
translation: Yes, but let's be smart, and improve it little by little so that the whole thing doesn't fall out from under us.

original: Alas, this gentleman   Whom I would save, had a most noble father!
translation: But this man who I want to save has a powerful, aristocratic father!

original: Let but your honour know,   Whom I believe to be most strait in virtue,
translation: I know you are incredibly virtuous, your Honor.

original: That, in the working of your own affections,   Had time cohered with place or place with wishing,
translation: But please just ask yourself about your own experiences with love. If you've ever been in the right place at the right time when the desire hit you,

original: Or that the resolute acting of your blood   Could have attain'd the effect of your own purpose,
translation: have you gotten carried away with feeling and fulfilled that desire?

original: Whether you had not sometime in your life   Err'd in this point which now you censure him,   And pull'd the law upon you.
translation: Haven't you ever made a mistake like the one for which you're now punishing Claudio? Imagine if the law had come down on you then.

original: 'Tis one thing to be tempted, Escalus,   Another thing to fall.
translation: Escalus, it's one thing to be tempted, but another thing entirely to fall.

original: I not deny,   The jury, passing on the prisoner's life,   May in the sworn twelve have a thief or two   Guiltier than him they try.
translation: I cannot deny that, among a jury of twelve people trying a prisoner, there might be a thief or two more guilty than the man on trial.

original: What's open made to  justice,   That justice seizes:
translation: What  justice sees , justice grabs.

original: what know the laws   That thieves do pass on thieves? 'Tis very pregnant,   The jewel that we find, we stoop and take't   Because we see it;
translation: Who knows what the code of law is among thieves? It's like how we bend down and pick up a jewel  because  we see it.

original: but what we do not see   We tread upon, and never think of it.
translation: But we walk right over the things we don't see and are never the wiser.

original: You may not so extenuate his offence   For I have had such faults;
translation: You can't excuse his crime on the grounds that I have similar faults.

original: but rather tell me,   When I, that censure him, do so offend,   Let mine own judgment pattern out my death,   And nothing come in partial. Sir, he must die.
translation: Instead, you should tell me when I, who judge him, commit that offense. My judgment on him will be the model for my own death, so nothing is done partially. Sir, he has to die.

original: Be it as your wisdom will.
translation: If you say so, sir.

original: Where is the provost?
translation: Where is the provost?

original: Here, if it like your honour.
translation: I'm here, sir.

original: See that Claudio   Be executed by nine to-morrow morning:
translation: Make sure that Claudio is executed by nine tomorrow morning.

original: Bring him his confessor, let him be prepared;   For that's the utmost of his pilgrimage.
translation: Bring the priest to him for confession and last rites, since his pilgrimage ends here.

original: [aside]   Well, heaven forgive him! and forgive us all!
translation: [To himself]  Well, heaven forgive him! And forgive us all!

original: Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall:   Some run from brakes of ice, and answer none:   And some condemned for a fault alone.
translation: Some people get ahead by sinning, and others fall on hard times for doing good. Some who commit a whole heap of crimes never have to answer for them, while others are condemned for a single mistake.

original: Come, bring them away:
translation: Come on, bring them away.

original: if these be good people in   a commonweal that do nothing but use their abuses in   common houses, I know no law: bring them away.
translation: If these people—who do nothing but raise hell in brothels—are good people, then I don't know the law. Bring them away!

original: How now, sir! What's your name? and what's the matter?
translation: What's going on, sir? What's your name? What's the matter?

original: If it Please your honour, I am the poor duke's   constable, and my name is Elbow:
translation: Begging your pardon, your Honor. I'm the poor Duke's constable, and my name is Elbow.

original: I do lean upon   justice, sir, and do bring in here before your good   honour two notorious benefactors.
translation: Sir, I depend upon justice, and bring in two notorious  benefactors  here before you.

original: Benefactors? Well; what benefactors are they? are they not malefactors?
translation: Benefactors? Well, they're benefactors, are they? Aren't they malefactors?

original: If it please your honour, I know not well what they   are:
translation: Begging your pardon, your Honor, I don't know exactly who they are.

original: but precise villains they are, that I am sure   of; and void of all profanation in the world that   good Christians ought to have.
translation: But they are downright crooks, I'm sure of that. And they lack the  profanation  that all good Christians should have.

original: This comes off well; here's a wise officer.
translation: That makes plenty of sense. This is a smart officer!

original: Go to: what quality are they of? Elbow is your name? why dost thou not speak, Elbow?
translation: Oh, enough. What are these men like? Elbow is your name, yes? Why don't you speak up, Elbow?

original: He cannot, sir; he's out at elbow.
What are you, sir?
translation: What's your profession, sir?

original: He, sir! a tapster, sir; parcel-bawd;
translation: Him, sir? He's a bartender, sir, and the servant of a brothel-keeper.

original: one that   serves a bad woman;   whose house, sir, was, as they   say, plucked down in the suburbs;
translation: He serves a bad woman whose house, sir, was, as they say, "torn down" in the outskirts of the town.

original: and now she   professes a hot-house, which, I think, is a very ill  house too.
translation: And now she claims she runs a sauna which is, I think, a very dirty place, too.

original: How know you that?
translation: How do you know that?

original: My wife, sir, whom I detest before heaven and your  honour,—
How? thy wife?
translation: What? Your wife?

original: Ay, sir; whom, I thank heaven, is an honest woman,—
translation: Yes, sir, who is, thank God, an honest woman—

original: Dost thou detest her therefore?
translation: And you "detest" her for that?

original: I say, sir, I will detest myself also, as well as   she, that this house,
translation: Yes, sir, and I'll detest myself, too, along with my wife, that that house is a brothel.

original: if it be not a bawd's house,   it is pity of her life, for it is a naughty house.
translation: If it's not a brothel, then I swear on her life that it's at least a very naughty place.

original: How dost thou know that, constable?
translation: How do you know that, constable?

original: Marry, sir, by my wife;
translation: Indeed , sir, from my wife.

original: who, if she had been a woman   cardinally given,
translation: If she had been more  virtuous ,

original: might have been accused in   fornication, adultery, and all uncleanliness there.
translation: she might have been guilty of fornication, adultery, and all sorts of trouble there.

original: By the woman's means?
translation: As a prostitute?

original: Ay, sir, by Mistress Overdone's means: but as she spit in his face, so she defied him.
translation: Yes, sir, under Mistress Overdone. But because she spit in his face, she got away.

original: Sir, if it please your honour, this is not so.
translation: Sir, begging your pardon: it's not true.

original: Prove it before these varlets here, thou honourable man; prove it.
Do you hear how he misplaces?
translation: Do you hear how he misuses his words?

original: Sir, she came in great with child; and longing,   saving your honour's reverence, for stewed prunes;
translation: Sir, she came in very pregnant, with a craving—begging your pardon, your Honor—for  stewed prunes .

original: sir, we had but two in the house, which at that very   distant time stood, as it were, in a fruit-dish, a   dish of some three-pence;
translation: Sir, we only had two in the house, which way back then were sitting in a fruit bowl, a bowl worth three pence

original: your honours have seen   such dishes; they are not China dishes, but very   good dishes,—
translation: —you've all seen the kind of dish, they're not cheap dishes, they're very good dishes—

original: Go to, go to: no matter for the dish, sir.
translation: Enough, enough! The dish isn't important, sir.

original: No, indeed, sir, not of a pin; you are therein in   the right: but to the point.
translation: Of course, sir, not at all. You're completely right there. To the point.

original: As I say, this   Mistress Elbow, being, as I say, with child, and   being great-bellied, and longing, as I said, for   prunes;
translation: Like I said, this Mrs. Elbow, who (like I said) was very pregnant and craving, like I said, prunes,

original: and having but two in the dish, as I said,   Master Froth here, this very man, having eaten the   rest, as I said, and, as I say, paying for them very   honestly;
translation: and only two being in the bowl (like I said) because Mr. Froth here, this very man, had eaten the rest (like I said), and (as I say) had paid for them up front.

original: for, as you know, Master Froth, I could   not give you three-pence again.
translation: For, as you know, Mr. Froth, I couldn't give you three pence again.

original: No, indeed.
translation: No, of course not.

original: Very well: you being then, if you be remembered, cracking the stones of the foresaid prunes,—
Ay, so I did indeed.
translation: Yes, I was doing that.

original: Why, very well;
translation: Well then, there you go.

original: I telling you then, if you be   remembered, that such a one and such a one were past   cure of the thing you wot of, unless they kept very   good diet, as I told you,—
translation: And I was telling you then, if you remember, that someone or other was past the help of medicine with the  same disease  you had, unless they kept a very good diet, as I told you—

original: All this is true.
translation: All this is true.

original: Why, very well, then,—
translation: Well, there you have it—

original: Come, you are a tedious fool: to the purpose.
translation: Enough, you're dragging on; get to the point.

original: What   was done to Elbow's wife, that he hath cause to   complain of? Come me to what was done to her.
translation: What happened to Elbow's wife that's made him so upset? Tell me what happened to her.

original: Sir, your honour cannot come to that yet.
translation: Sir, you can't jump ahead to that yet, your Honor.

original: No, sir, nor I mean it not.
translation: No, sir, I'm serious.

original: Sir, but you shall come to it, by your honour's   leave.
translation: Sir, we'll get to that, begging your Honor's pardon.

original: And, I beseech you, look into Master Froth   here, sir;
translation: And, please: look at Mr. Froth here,

original: a man of four-score pound a year; whose   father died at Hallowmas: was't not at Hallowmas,   Master Froth?
translation: a man who earns eighty pounds per year, and father Dad died on  November 1 . Wasn't it November 1, Mr. Froth?

original: All-hallond eve.
translation: October 31.

original: Why, very well; I hope here be truths.
translation: Well, that's all right. I hope that's true.

original: He, sir,   sitting, as I say, in a lower chair, sir; 'twas in   the Bunch of Grapes, where indeed you have a delight   to sit, have you not?
translation: Sir, he was sitting (as I said) in a small chair, sir. It was in living room, wasn't it, where you usually like to sit, right?

original: I have so; because it is an open room and good for  winter.
translation: That's right, because it's an open room and good for winter.

original: Why, very well, then; I hope here be truths.
translation: Well, that's all right, then. I hope that's true.

original: This will last out a night in Russia,   When nights are longest there: I'll take my leave.
translation: This story is longer than a winter night in Russia. I'm leaving now.

original: And leave you to the hearing of the cause;   Hoping you'll find good cause to whip them all.
translation: [To ESCALUS]  I'll leave you to hear the testimony, and hope you'll find a reason to whip them all.

original: I think no less. Good morrow to your lordship.
translation: I suspect I will. Goodbye, your Lordship.

original: Now, sir, come on: what was done to Elbow's wife, once  more?
translation: Now come on, sir. What happened to Elbow's wife? Once more.

original: Once, sir? there was nothing done to her once.
translation: Once, sir? There was nothing done to her "once."

original: I beseech you, sir, ask him what this man did to my  wife.
translation: Sir, I'm begging you: ask him what this man did to my wife.

original: I beseech your honour, ask me.
translation: I'm begging you, sir: ask me.

original: Well, sir; what did this gentleman to her?
translation: Well, sir, what did this gentleman do to her?

original: I beseech you, sir, look in this gentleman's face.
translation: I'll ask you, sir, to look in this man's face.

original: Good Master Froth, look upon his honour; 'tis for a   good purpose. Doth your honour mark his face?
translation: Mr. Froth, look into his eyes. It's for a good reason. Sir, can you see his face?

original: Ay, sir, very well.
translation: Yes, sir, very well.

original: Nay; I beseech you, mark it well.
translation: No, I beg you—look really hard.

original: Well, I do so.
translation: All right, I'm doing it.

original: Doth your honour see any harm in his face?
translation: Do you see any harm in his face?

original: Why, no.
translation: Well, no.

original: I'll be supposed upon a book, his face is the worst   thing about him.
translation: I'll swear on the Bible that his face is the worst thing about him.

original: Good, then; if his face be the   worst thing about him, how could Master Froth do the   constable's wife any harm? I would know that of   your honour.
translation: So, then, if his face is the worst thing about him, how could Mr. Froth hurt the constable's wife? I'm asking you, your Honor.

original: He's in the right. Constable, what say you to it?
translation: He's making sense. Constable, what do you say to that?

original: First, an it like you, the house is a respected house; next, this is a respected fellow; and his mistress is a respected woman.
By this hand, sir, his wife is a more respected person than any of us all.
Varlet, thou liest; thou liest, wicked varlet! the time has yet to come that she was ever respected with man, woman, or child.
translation: Crook, you lie, you lie, you crooked criminal!  She has yet to ever be respected with man, woman, or child.

original: Sir, she was respected with him before he married with  her.
Which is the wiser here? Justice or Iniquity? Is this true?
translation: Who's coming out on top here? Justice, or crime? Is this true?

original: O thou caitiff! O thou varlet! O thou wicked   Hannibal!
translation: Oh, you piece of trash! You crook! Oh, you evil  Hannibal !

original: I respected with her before I was married   to her! If ever I was respected with her, or she   with me, let not your worship think me the poor   duke's officer.
translation: Me, respected with her before I married her? If I was ever respected with her, or she with me, don't think for one second, sir, that I'm an officer of the Duke.

original: Prove this, thou wicked Hannibal, or   I'll have mine action of battery on thee.
translation: Prove it, you evil Hannibal, or I'll have the right to beat you up.

original: If he took you a box o' the ear, you might have your action of slander too.
translation: If he hit you in the head, you might have the right to call him some names, too.

original: Marry, I thank your good worship for it. What is't your worship's pleasure I shall do with this wicked  caitiff?
Truly, officer, because he hath some offences in him   that thou wouldst discover if thou couldst,
translation: Really, officer, since he's guilty of some crimes that you could find out if you questioned him,

original: let him   continue in his courses till thou knowest what they   are.
translation: let him keep talking until you see what they are.

original: Marry, I thank your worship for it. Thou seest, thou   wicked varlet,
translation: Of course, and thank you, sir, for that. You see what you've gotten into now, you evil crook:

original: now, what's come upon thee: thou art   to continue now, thou varlet; thou art to continue.
translation: keep talking, you crook, keep talking.

original: Where were you born, friend?
translation: Where were you born, friend?

original: Here in Vienna, sir.
translation: Here in Vienna, sir.

original: Are you of fourscore pounds a year?
translation: Do you make at least eighty pounds a year?

original: Yes, an't please you, sir.
translation: Yes, of course, sir.

original: So. What trade are you of, sir?
translation: So, what's your occupation, sir?

original: Tapster; a poor widow's tapster.
translation: Bartender. A poor widow's bartender.

original: Your mistress' name?
translation: What's your employer's name?

original: Mistress Overdone.
translation: Mistress Overdone.

original: Hath she had any more than one husband?
translation: Has she had more than one husband?

original: Nine, sir; Overdone by the last.
Nine! Come hither to me, Master Froth.   Master   Froth, I would not have you acquainted with   tapsters:
translation: Nine! Come over here, Mr. Froth. Mr. Froth, I recommend you don't make friends with any bartenders.

original: they will draw you, Master Froth, and you   will hang them. Get you gone, and let me hear no   more of you.
translation: They'll  draw you , Mr. Froth, and you'll get into trouble. Get out of here, and make sure I don't hear about you again.

original: I thank your worship. For mine own part, I never come into any room in a tap-house, but I am drawn in.
translation: Thank you, your Worship. As far as I'm concerned, I never go into any room in a pub; I'm just drawn in.

original: Well, no more of it, Master Froth: farewell.
translation: Well, that's it, then, Mr. Froth. Goodbye.

original: Come you hither to me, Master tapster. What's your name, Master tapster?
translation: Come over here, Mr. Bartender. What's your name, Mr. Bartender?

original: Pompey.
translation: Pompey.

original: What else?
translation: What else?

original: Bum, sir.
Troth, and your bum is the greatest thing about you;   so that in the beastliest sense you are Pompey the   Great.
translation: Indeed, and your bum is the greatest thing about you, so that in the most physical sense you are " Pompey the Great ."

original: Pompey, you are partly a bawd, Pompey,   howsoever you colour it in being a tapster, are you   not?
translation: Pompey: you're also a pimp, Pompey, no matter how much you spin it as being a "bartender." Aren't you?

original: come, tell me true: it shall be the better for  you.
translation: Come on, tell me the truth. It'll be easier for you.

original: Truly, sir, I am a poor fellow that would live.
translation: Really, sir, I'm just a poor man who wants to make a living.

original: How would you live, Pompey? by being a bawd? What do you think of the trade, Pompey? is it a lawful  trade?
translation: How do you make your living, Pompey? By being a pimp? What do you think of the business, Pompey? Is it a legal business?

original: If the law would allow it, sir.
translation: If the law would allow it, sir.

original: But the law will not allow it, Pompey; nor it shall not be allowed in Vienna.
translation: But the law won't allow it, Pompey. And it won't be allowed in Vienna.

original: Does your worship mean to geld and splay all the youth of the city?
No, Pompey.
translation: No, Pompey.

original: Truly, sir, in my poor opinion, they will to't then.
translation: Really, sir, in my humble opinion, then they'll get on with it.

original: If your worship will take order for the drabs and   the knaves, you need not to fear the bawds.
translation: If you, sir, will punish the sluts and the hooligans, then you won't need to worry about the pimps.

original: There are pretty orders beginning, I can tell you: it is but heading and hanging.
translation: The punishments are beginning, I can tell you: both beheading and hanging.

original: If you head and hang all that offend that way but   for ten year together,
translation: If you behead and hang everyone who has sex—even for just ten years straight

original: you'll be glad to give out a   commission for more heads: if this law hold in   Vienna ten year, I'll rent the fairest house in it   after three-pence a bay:
translation: —you'll hardly have any heads left to chop off. If this law stands in Vienna for ten years, I'll rent the nicest house in the city for three pence a month. I

original: if you live to see this   come to pass, say Pompey told you so.
translation: f you live to see this happen, say that Pompey told you so.

original: Thank you, good Pompey; and, in requital of your   prophecy, hark you: I advise you, let me not find   you before me again upon any complaint whatsoever;
translation: Thank you, Pompey. And in return for your prophecy, listen: I'll advise you not to let me find you in front of me again for any crime whatsoever-

original: no, not for dwelling where you do:
translation: -not even for living where you do.

original: if I do, Pompey,   I shall beat you to your tent, and prove a shrewd   Caesar to you;
translation: I f I do, Pompey, I'll beat you into a retreat, Pompey. And I'll turn out to be a savvy  Caesar  to you.

original: in plain dealing, Pompey, I shall   have you whipt: so, for this time, Pompey, fare you  well.
translation: To be honest, Pompey, I'll have you whipped. So, for now, Pompey, goodbye.

original: I thank your worship for your good counsel.
translation: Thank you, sir, for your good advice.

original: [aside]   but I shall follow it as the flesh and fortune shall   better determine.
translation: [To himself]  ...but as to how much I'll follow it, I'll leave it all up to luck.

original: Whip me? No, no; let carman whip his jade:   The valiant heart is not whipt out of his trade.
translation: Whip me? No, no. A man can whip his old horse, but a brave heart won't be whipped out of its business.

original: Come hither to me, Master Elbow; come hither, Master constable. How long have you been in this place of  constable?
translation: Come over here, Mr. Elbow. Come here, Mr. Constable. How long have you had the position of constable?

original: Seven year and a half, sir.
translation: Seven and a half years, sir.

original: I thought, by your readiness in the office, you had continued in it some time. You say, seven years  together?
translation: I thought you've done the job for a while, because of your obvious expertise. You said seven years all together?

original: And a half, sir.
translation: And a half, sir.

original: Alas, it hath been great pains to you. They do you   wrong to put you so oft upon 't:
translation: It's a shame; it must have been such a strain on you. They're doing you wrong by making you work for so long.

original: are there not men   in your ward sufficient to serve it?
translation: Aren't there other men in your district who'd be capable of serving?

original: Faith, sir, few of any wit in such matters:
translation: Indeed, sir, not many with a sharp enough mind for such things.

original: as they   are chosen, they are glad to choose me for them; I   do it for some piece of money, and go through with   all.
translation: Whenever they're nominated, they're glad to nominate me in their place. I take it for a little money, and go through with it all.

original: Look you bring me in the names of some six or seven, the most sufficient of your parish.
translation: Look: bring in the names of six or seven of the most capable men in your district.

original: To your worship's house, sir?
translation: To your Worship's house, sir?

original: To my house. Fare you well.
translation: To my house. Take care.

original: What's o'clock, think you?
translation: What time is it, do you think?

original: Eleven, sir.
translation: Eleven, sir.

original: I pray you home to dinner with me.
translation: Please, come to my house and have lunch with me.

original: I humbly thank you.
translation: I'm humbled; thank you.

original: It grieves me for the death of Claudio; But there's no remedy.
translation: I'm sad for Claudio's death, but there's nothing to be done.

original: Lord Angelo is severe.
translation: Lord Angelo is severe.

original: It is but needful:   Mercy is not itself, that oft looks so;
translation: It's only necessary. What often seems to be mercy isn't mercy at all.

original: Pardon is still the nurse of second woe:   But yet,—poor Claudio! There is no remedy.   Come, sir.
translation: Pardoning someone can just lead to more harm. But still—poor Claudio! There's no help for it. Come on, sir.

original: He's hearing of a cause; he will come straight I'll tell him of you.
translation: He's hearing a case, but he'll come straight from there. I'll let him know you're here.

original: Pray you, do.
translation: Please, do.

original: I'll know   His pleasure; may be he will relent.
translation: I'll see what he wants; maybe he'll back down.

original: Alas,   He hath but as offended in a dream!
translation: Alas, he's only committed a crime if we're in a dream!

original: All sects, all ages smack of this vice; and he   To die for't!
translation: All kinds, all ages are guilty of this vice, and Claudio's going to die for it?

original: Now, what's the matter. Provost?
translation: Now, what's the matter, Provost?

original: Is it your will Claudio shall die tomorrow?
translation: Do you want Claudio to die tomorrow?

original: Did not I tell thee yea? hadst thou not order? Why dost thou ask again?
translation: Didn't I tell you "yes?" Don't you have the order? Why are you asking again?

original: Lest I might be too rash:
translation: I don't want to be too hasty.

original: Under your good correction, I have seen,   When, after execution, judgment hath   Repented o'er his doom.
translation: Under your leadership, I've seen judges wish they hadn't killed a man after an execution.

original: Go to; let that be mine:
translation: Enough; let me worry about that.

original: Do you your office, or give up your place,   And you shall well be spared.
translation: Do your job, or give up your position; then you'll definitely be spared.

original: I crave your honour's pardon. What shall be done, sir, with the groaning Juliet? She's very near her hour.
translation: I beg your pardon, your Honor. Sir, what should we do about Juliet, who's pregnant? She's getting close to her due date.

original: Dispose of her To some more fitter place, and that with speed.
translation: Take her to a more appropriate place—and quickly.

original: Here is the sister of the man condemn'd Desires access to you.
translation: The sister of the condemned man is here, and wants to speak with you.

original: Hath he a sister?
translation: He has a sister?

original: Ay, my good lord; a very virtuous maid,
translation: Yes, sir: a very virtuous girl

original: And to be shortly of a sisterhood,   If not already.
translation: who's about to become a nun, if she isn't one already.

original: Well, let her be admitted.
translation: Well, let her come in.

original: See you the fornicatress be removed:
translation: Make sure the slut is taken away.

original: Let have needful, but not lavish, means;   There shall be order for't.
translation: Give her what she needs to survive, but no more. I'll provide for it.

original: God save your honour!
translation: God bless you, your Honor!

original: Stay a little while.    You're welcome:  what's your will?
translation: Stay a little while.[To ISABELLA] You're welcome here. What do you want?

original: I am a woeful suitor to your honour, Please but your honour hear me.
translation: I'm a sad petitioner, your Honor. Please, just listen to my request, your Honor.

original: Well; what's your suit?
translation: Well, what's your request?

original: There is a vice that most I do abhor,   And most desire should meet the blow of justice;
translation: There's a sin that I hate more than anything, and that I truly hope will be punished.

original: For which I would not plead, but that I must;   For which I must not plead, but that I am   At war 'twixt will and will not.
translation: I wouldn't defend it unless I had to. And I can't defend it without debating myself whether I will or won't.

original: Well; the matter?
translation: Well, what is it?

original: I have a brother is condemn'd to die: I do beseech you, let it be his fault, And not my brother.
translation: I have a brother who's condemned to die. Please, let his fault be condemned, but not him!

original: Heaven give thee moving graces!
translation: God has blessed you with the power of speaking!

original: Condemn the fault and not the actor of it?
translation: Condemn the fault and not the person who did it?

original: Why, every fault's condemn'd ere it be done:
translation: Well, every fault's condemned before it's even done.

original: Mine were the very cipher of a function,   To fine the faults whose fine stands in record,   And let go by the actor.
translation: But it would be very difficult to find faults in the record that paid their fines while the people who did the faults went free.

original: O just but severe law! I had a brother, then. Heaven keep your honour!
translation: The law is harsh, but it is just! I had a brother, in that case. God bless you, your Honor!

original: [aside to ISABELLA]   Give't not o'er so: to him   again, entreat him;
translation: [To ISABELLA so that only she can hear]  Don't give in to him so easily! Beg him. Kneel down in front of him.

original: Kneel down before him, hang upon his gown:   You are too cold; if you should need a pin,
translation: Pull on the edge of his robe. You're too cold!

original: You could not with more tame a tongue desire it:   To him, I say!
translation: If you only need a pin you could hardly ask with less conviction. Go to him, I say!

original: Must he needs die?
translation: Does he have to die?

original: Maiden, no remedy.
translation: Girl, there's no help for it.

original: Yes; I do think that you might pardon him, And neither heaven nor man grieve at the mercy.
translation: But I do think you could pardon him, and that neither God nor people would disapprove of your mercy.

original: I will not do't.
translation: I will not do it.

original: But can you, if you would?
translation: But could you, if you wanted to?

original: Look, what I will not, that I cannot do.
translation: Look: what I won't do, I can't do.

original: But might you do't, and do the world no wrong, If so your heart were touch'd with that remorse As mine is to him?
translation: But couldn't you pardon him without doing anything wrong? If so, isn't your heart filled with pity, like mine is for him?

original: He's sentenced; 'tis too late.
translation: He's sentenced to die. It's too late.

original: You are too cold.
translation: You're too cold.

original: Too late? why, no; I, that do speak a word.   May call it back again.
translation: Too late? I don't think so; when I say something, I can always take it back again.

original: Well, believe this,   No ceremony that to great ones 'longs,
translation: Well, believe this: no fancy things that powerful people have

original: Not the king's crown, nor the deputed sword,   The marshal's truncheon, nor the judge's robe,
translation: —like the king's crown, or the soldier's sword, or the police man's club, or the judge's robe—

original: Become them with one half so good a grace   As mercy does.
translation: look as good on them as mercy does.

original: If he had been as you and you as he,   You would have slipt like him; but he, like you,   Would not have been so stern.
translation: If Claudio had been you instead of himself, you would have made the same mistake. And Claudio, unlike you, wouldn't have been so strict with you if you were in his position.

original: Pray you, be gone.
translation: Please get out of here.

original: I would to heaven I had your potency,   And you were Isabel!
translation: I wish I had your power, and that you were Isabella!

original: should it then be thus?   No; I would tell what 'twere to be a judge,   And what a prisoner.
translation: Would it be the same then? No. I would say what it meant to be a judge, and what it meant to be a prisoner.

original: Ay, touch him; there's the vein.
translation: Yes, get him; that's touched a nerve.

original: Your brother is a forfeit of the law, And you but waste your words.
translation: Your brother is a prisoner of the law. You're only wasting your words.

original: Alas, alas!   Why, all the souls that were were forfeit once;   And He that might the vantage best have took   Found out the remedy.
translation: Oh no! Oh no! Well, all souls were prisoners once, and God, who could have punished them, gave them the Savior instead.

original: How would you be,   If He, which is the top of judgment, should   But judge you as you are?
translation: How would things turn out for you if God—the highest judge—judged  you  as you are?

original: O, think on that;   And mercy then will breathe within your lips,   Like man new made.
translation: Oh, think about that, and then you'll want to be merciful. You'll be like a brand new man.

original: Be you content, fair maid;   It is the law, not I condemn your brother:
translation: Calm down, pretty girl. It's the law—not me—that condemns your brother.

original: Were he my kinsman, brother, or my son,   It should be thus with him: he must die tomorrow.
translation: If he were my relative, brother, or my son, he would get the same treatment. He has to die tomorrow.

original: To-morrow! O, that's sudden! Spare him, spare him!   He's not prepared for death.
translation: Tomorrow! Oh, that's soon! Spare his life, spare his life! He's not prepared to die.

original: Even for our kitchens   We kill the fowl of season: shall we serve heaven   With less respect than we do minister   To our gross selves?
translation: Even when it comes to our own food, we only kill birds when they're in season. Should we kill a man for the sake of God's law when he doesn't deserve it—when we follow stricter regulations for our own food?

original: Good, good my lord, bethink you;   Who is it that hath died for this offence?   There's many have committed it.
translation: My good, good lord, just think: who has ever died for Claudio's offense? Many have committed it.

original: Ay, well said.
translation: Yes! Well said.

original: The law hath not been dead, though it hath slept:
translation: The law hasn't been dead, even thought it's slept.

original: Those many had not dared to do that evil,   If the first that did the edict infringe   Had answer'd for his deed:
translation: Many of them wouldn't have done what they did if the first man who broke the law would have been punished.

original: now 'tis awake   Takes note of what is done; and, like a prophet,   Looks in a glass, that shows what future evils,
translation: Now, the law is awake, and it sees what people do. Like a prophet, the law looks into a magic mirror that shows future evils

original: Either new, or by remissness new-conceived,   And so in progress to be hatch'd and born,
translation: —either new ones, or those committed by repeat offenders

original: Are now to have no successive degrees,   But, ere they live, to end.
translation: —that are being thought up and put into practice. And now they won't happen. They'll end before they begin.

original: Yet show some pity.
translation: But show some pity.

original: I show it most of all when I show justice;   For then I pity those I do not know,   Which a dismiss'd offence would after gall;
translation: I show the most pity when I'm just. Then I'm pitying people I don't know, who might be encouraged to do wrong if an offense went unpunished.

original: And do him right that, answering one foul wrong,   Lives not to act another. Be satisfied;   Your brother dies to-morrow; be content.
translation: By punishing the wrongdoer, I'm also helping him by not letting him live to commit another crime. Let it go. Your brother dies tomorrow. Be content.

original: So you must be the first that gives this sentence,   And he, that suffer's.
translation: So you have to be the first person to give this sentence, and he's the one that suffers?

original: O, it is excellent   To have a giant's strength; but it is tyrannous   To use it like a giant.
translation: It must be great to have unlimited power. But it's corrupt to use that power without limits.

original: That's well said.
translation: That's well said.

original: Could great men thunder   As Jove himself does, Jove would ne'er be quiet,
translation: If powerful men could thunder like  Jove  does, Jove would never be quiet!

original: For every pelting, petty officer   Would use his heaven for thunder;   Nothing but thunder!
translation: Every worthless officer would use his heavenly thunder—there'd be nothing but thunder!

original: Merciful Heaven,   Thou rather with thy sharp and sulphurous bolt   Split'st the unwedgeable and gnarled oak   Than the soft myrtle:
translation: Merciful God, you'd rather split the strong, old oak tree than the soft myrtle tree.

original: but man, proud man,   Drest in a little brief authority,   Most ignorant of what he's most assured,
translation: But man—proud man—with a little, brief power in his hands is ignorant of the grace that's promised him.

original: His glassy essence, like an angry ape,   Plays such fantastic tricks before high heaven   As make the angels weep; who, with our spleens,   Would all themselves laugh mortal.
translation: He mimics the essence of God like an angry ape, playing such awful tricks that the angels weep. If they had mortal bodies like us, they'd laugh themselves to death.

original: O, to him, to him, wench! he will relent; He's coming; I perceive 't.
translation: Oh, move in, move in, girl! He'll relent. He's about to give in; I can tell.

original: Pray heaven she win him!
translation: I pray to God that she wins him over!

original: We cannot weigh our brother with ourself: Great men may jest with saints; 'tis wit in them, But in the less foul profanation.
translation: We can't compare ourselves to our brothers. Great men can joke around with saints, and it seems witty. But if regular men do it, it might seem like crass profanity.

original: Thou'rt i' the right, girl; more o, that.
translation: You're in the right, girl! More of that!

original: That in the captain's but a choleric word, Which in the soldier is flat blasphemy.
translation: What sounds like a harsh word coming from a captain sounds like blasphemy coming from a soldier.

original: Art avised o' that? more on 't.
translation: Are you sure about that? Say more.

original: Why do you put these sayings upon me?
translation: Why are you saying these things to me?

original: Because authority, though it err like others,   Hath yet a kind of medicine in itself,   That skins the vice o' the top.
translation: When a man of authority makes a mistake, his power works like a kind of medicine to take the edge off his fault.

original: Go to your bosom;   Knock there, and ask your heart what it doth know   That's like my brother's fault:
translation: Look into heart, probe it, and ask yourself if you have a fault like my brother's.

original: if it confess   A natural guiltiness such as is his,   Let it not sound a thought upon your tongue   Against my brother's life.
translation: If you find that you're just as naturally guilty as he is, then don't even think of saying a single word against my brother's life.

original: [aside]   She speaks, and 'tis   Such sense, that my sense breeds with it.
translation: [To himself]  When she speaks, she makes so much  sense  that I want to sleep with her.

original: Fare you  well.
translation: [To ISABELLA]  Take care.

original: Gentle my lord, turn back.
translation: My noble lord, reverse your decision.

original: I will bethink me: come again tomorrow.
translation: I'll think about it. Come again tomorrow.

original: Hark how I'll bribe you: good my lord, turn back.
translation: Listen how I'll bribe you. My good lord, reverse your decision.

original: How! bribe me?
translation: What? Bribe me?

original: Ay, with such gifts that heaven shall share with you.
translation: Yes, with the blessings that heaven will give you.

original: You had marr'd all else.
translation: You've ruined everything else.

original: Not with fond shekels of the tested gold,   Or stones whose rates are either rich or poor   As fancy values them;
translation: Not with precious golden coins, and not with gems whose value fluctuates with market demand,

original: but with true prayers   That shall be up at heaven and enter there   Ere sun-rise,
translation: but with honest prayers that will rise to heaven and enter before sunrise.

original: prayers from preserved souls,   From fasting maids whose minds are dedicate   To nothing temporal.
translation: Prayers from pure souls, from fasting virgins whose minds are dedicated only to holy things.

original: Well; come to me to-morrow.
translation: Well, come to see me again tomorrow.

original: Go to; 'tis well; away!
translation: That's enough; all's well. Let's go!

original: Heaven keep your honour safe!
translation: May God keep you safe, your Honor!

original: Amen: For I am that way going to temptation, Where prayers cross.
translation: Amen. Since I'm on the way to temptation, I could use the prayers.

original: At what hour to-morrow Shall I attend your lordship?
translation: What time tomorrow should I come to you, your Lordship?

original: At any time 'fore noon.
translation: At any time before noon.

original: 'Save your honour!
translation: God bless you, your Honor!

original: From thee, even from thy virtue!   What's this, what's this? Is this her fault or mine?
translation: Seduced by you, actually—by your virtue! What's this, what's this? Is this her fault or mine?

original: The tempter or the tempted, who sins most?   Ha! Not she: nor doth she tempt:
translation: Who sins most: the tempter, or the tempted? Ha! Not her. She's not tempting, anyway.

original: but it is I   That, lying by the violet in the sun,   Do as the carrion does, not as the flower,   Corrupt with virtuous season.
translation: Like a dead animal lying next to a sweet-smelling flower, it's me that covers the good smells with my stink.

original: Can it be   That modesty may more betray our sense   Than woman's lightness?
translation: Is it possible that modesty is more seductive to me than loose women?

original: Having waste ground enough,   Shall we desire to raze the sanctuary   And pitch our evils there? O, fie, fie, fie!
translation: With everything I've done, am I going to corrupt a holy nun and do evil things with her? Oh, for shame, for shame!

original: What dost thou, or what art thou, Angelo?   Dost thou desire her foully for those things   That make her good?
translation: What are you doing? Who are you, Angelo? Do you want her—disgustingly—because of all the things that make her good?

original: O, let her brother live!   Thieves for their robbery have authority   When judges steal themselves.
translation: Oh, let her brother live! Thieves have an excuse for their robbery if judges steal, too.

original: What, do I love her,   That I desire to hear her speak again,   And feast upon her eyes? What is't I dream on?
translation: What? Do I love her? I want to hear her speak again, and look into her eyes! What is it I'm dreaming of?

original: O cunning enemy, that, to catch a saint,   With saints dost bait thy hook! Most dangerous   Is that temptation that doth goad us on   To sin in loving virtue:
translation: Oh, tricky devil: to catch a saint, you've baited your hook with saints. The temptation that pushes us to sin by loving virtue is very dangerous.

original: never could the strumpet,   With all her double vigour, art and nature,   Once stir my temper;
translation: With all her energy, craft, and looks, a whore could never arouse me.

original: but this virtuous maid   Subdues me quite. Even till now,   When men were fond, I smiled and wonder'd how.
translation: But this virtuous girl has gotten the better of me. Until now, when men fell in love, I smiled and wondered how.

original: Hail to you, provost! so I think you are.
translation: Greetings to you, Provost! At least I think that's who you are.

original: I am the provost. What's your will, good friar?
translation: I am the provost. How can I help you, good friar?

original: Bound by my charity and my blest order,   I come to visit the afflicted spirits   Here in the prison.
translation: Owing to my charity and the duties of my order, I've come to visit the troubled people here in the prison.

original: Do me the common right   To let me see them and to make me know   The nature of their crimes, that I may minister   To them accordingly.
translation: Do me a favor: let me see them, and tell me what their crimes were so that I can minister to them accordingly.

original: I would do more than that, if more were needful.
translation: I would do more than that if it were necessary.

original: Look, here comes one: a gentlewoman of mine,   Who, falling in the flaws of her own youth,   Hath blister'd her report:
translation: Look, her comes one: a gentlewoman who is one of my prisoners. She caved in to her own youthful desires and has ruined her reputation.

original: she is with child;   And he that got it, sentenced;
translation: She's pregnant, and the man who knocked her up is sentenced to die

original: a young man   More fit to do another such offence   Than die for this.
translation: —a young man who ought to be committing another "offense" of that kind rather than dying for it.

original: When must he die?
translation: When is he scheduled to die?

original: As I do think, to-morrow. I have provided for you: stay awhile, @     And you shall be conducted.
translation: Tomorrow, I think. I've prepared everything for you, so stay a while.  And you'll be taken care of.

original: Repent you, fair one, of the sin you carry?
translation: Pretty girl: do you repent of the sin that got you pregnant?

original: I do; and bear the shame most patiently.
translation: I do, and I'm bearing the shame most patiently.

original: I'll teach you how you shall arraign your conscience,   And try your penitence, if it be sound,
translation: I'll show you how to put your conscience on trial so that you can see if your repentance is real,

original: Or hollowly put on.
translation: or only hollow and fake.

original: I'll gladly learn.
translation: I'm happy to learn.

original: Love you the man that wrong'd you?
translation: Do you love the man that wronged you?

original: Yes, as I love the woman that wrong'd him.
So then it seems your most offenceful act Was mutually committed?
translation: So then, it seems your offensive act was mutually committed?

original: Mutually.
translation: Mutually.

original: Then was your sin of heavier kind than his.
translation: Then your sin was more serious than his was.

original: I do confess it, and repent it, father.
translation: I confess it and repent it, father.

original: 'Tis meet so, daughter: but lest you do repent,   As that the sin hath brought you to this shame,
translation: That's good, daughter. But don't only repent because the sin has caused you to be ashamed.

original: Which sorrow is always towards ourselves, not heaven,
translation: Shame is always self-centered, not God-centered.

original: Showing we would not spare heaven as we love it,   But as we stand in fear,—
translation: It shows we don't obey God because we love him, but only because we're afraid—

original: I do repent me, as it is an evil, And take the shame with joy.
translation: I repent it because it's evil, and I accept the shame joyfully.

original: There rest.   Your partner, as I hear, must die to-morrow,   And I am going with instruction to him.
translation: Rest, then. I hear your partner has to die tomorrow, and I'm going to give him his last rites.

original: Grace go with you, Benedicite!
translation: Grace be with you, and God bless you!

original: Must die to-morrow! O injurious love,   That respites me a life,
translation: He dies tomorrow! Oh, unjust love: because I'm carrying Claudio's child, my life has been spared.

original: whose very comfort   Is still a dying horror!
translation: But any comfort I gain from that turns to horror because of Claudio's death!

original: 'Tis pity of him.
translation: It's a shame about him.

original: When I would pray and think, I think and pray   To several subjects.
translation: When I want to pray and think, I end up praying and thinking about a lot of different things.

original: Heaven hath my empty words;   Whilst my invention, hearing not my tongue,   Anchors on Isabel:
translation: My empty words are directed to God, while the object of my prayers is Isabella, despite what I say.

original: Heaven in my mouth,   As if I did but only chew his name;   And in my heart the strong and swelling evil   Of my conception.
translation: "Heaven" is on my lips as if I spoke the name of "Jesus" half-heartedly. And my heart is filled with the steady, growing evil of my thoughts.

original: The state, whereon I studied   Is like a good thing, being often read,   Grown sere and tedious;
translation: I have studied government, and it is like a a good book that gets boring when you read it too many times.

original: yea, my gravity,   Wherein—let no man hear me—I take pride,   Could I with boot change for an idle plume,   Which the air beats for vain.
translation: As for my power, in which—I hope no one's listening—I take pride, I'd be happy to trade it for any boring, useless job.

original: O place, O form,   How often dost thou with thy case, thy habit,   Wrench awe from fools and tie the wiser souls   To thy false seeming!
translation: Oh, high rank! Oh, formalities! How often do your appearances and clothes impress idiots, and even corrupt smarter men so that they think they really are what they seem to be!

original: Blood, thou art blood:   Let's write good angel on the devil's horn:   'Tis not the devil's crest.
translation: I'll write "Good Angel" on my forehead, and pretend there's not devil horns growing there.

original: How now! who's there?
translation: Hello? Who's there?

original: One Isabel, a sister, desires access to you.
translation: A nun named Isabella wants to see you.

original: Teach her the way.
translation: Show her the way.

original: O heavens!   Why does my blood thus muster to my heart,   Making both it unable for itself,
translation: For goodness' sake! Why is my blood rushing to my heart—making my heart pound

original: And dispossessing all my other parts   Of necessary fitness?
translation: and depriving the rest of my body of the blood it needs?

original: So play the foolish throngs with one that swoons;   Come all to help him, and so stop the air   By which he should revive:
translation: It's like a dumb crowd around a fainting person: they all come to help him and then deprive him of the air he needs to revive.

original: and even so   The general, subject to a well-wish'd king,   Quit their own part,
translation: It's like when the subjects of a king, wishing him well, all crowd up to him;

original: and in obsequious fondness   Crowd to his presence, where their untaught love   Must needs appear offence.
translation: since they don't know how to show affection, it actually comes off as offensive.

original: How now, fair maid?
translation: How are you, beautiful girl?

original: I am come to know your pleasure.
translation: I came to find out what you've decided.

original: That you might know it, would much better please me Than to demand what 'tis. Your brother cannot live.
translation: I like that you came to "find out," instead of demanding to know. Your brother will not live.

original: Even so. Heaven keep your honour!
translation: Well, all right. God bless you, your Honor!

original: Yet may he live awhile; and, it may be, As long as you or I; yet he must die.
translation: And yet, he might live a little longer—maybe as long as you and I—and then he'll have to die.

original: Under your sentence?
translation: By your command?

original: Yea.
translation: Yes.

original: When, I beseech you? that in his reprieve, Longer or shorter, he may be so fitted That his soul sicken not.
translation: When, may I ask? Let him know how long or short his release will be, so he won't be sick with worry about it.

original: Ha! fie, these filthy vices!
translation: Ha! Shame on these dirty sins.

original: It were as good   To pardon him that hath from nature stolen   A man already made,
translation: It's as good as pardoning someone who murdered a full-grown man

original: as to remit   Their saucy sweetness that do coin heaven's image   In stamps that are forbid:
translation: to forgive those cheeky lovers who make babies before they're supposed to.

original: 'tis all as easy   Falsely to take away a life true made   As to put metal in restrained means   To make a false one.
translation: It's as easy to wrongly take away a  truly  made life as it is to have sex outside of marriage to make a false life.

original: 'Tis set down so in heaven, but not in earth.
translation: That may be the case in heaven, but not on earth.

original: Say you so? then I shall pose you quickly.   Which had you rather,
translation: Do you say so? Then I'll ask you quickly, which would you prefer:

original: that the most just law   Now took your brother's life;
translation: that your brother were killed now under the just law?

original: or, to redeem him,   Give up your body to such sweet uncleanness   As she that he hath stain'd?
translation: Or that, to save him, you would give up your body to the same sexual sin that has ruined Juliet?

original: Sir, believe this, I had rather give my body than my soul.
translation: Sir, believe this: I would rather give up my body than my soul.

original: I talk not of your soul: our compell'd sins Stand more for number than for accompt.
translation: I'm not talking about your soul. Sins that we're forced to commit don't really count.

original: How say you?
translation: What do you mean?

original: Nay, I'll not warrant that; for I can speak   Against the thing I say.
translation: No, I can't guarantee that, since I can contradict myself easily.

original: Answer to this:   I, now the voice of the recorded law,   Pronounce a sentence on your brother's life:
translation: Answer this: As the legal authority at this time, I sentence your brother to death.

original: Might there not be a charity in sin   To save this brother's life?
translation: Wouldn't it be charitable to commit a sin that might save your brother's life?

original: Please you to do't, I'll take it as a peril to my soul, It is no sin at all, but charity.
translation: If you'll do it, I'll take the spiritual consequences. It's not a sin at all; it's charity.

original: Pleased you to do't at peril of your soul, Were equal poise of sin and charity.
translation: If you'll do it in spite of the spiritual consequences, I'd say the sin and charity are about even.

original: That I do beg his life, if it be sin,
translation: Then I beg you to spare his life, if that's a sin.

original: Heaven let me bear it! you granting of my suit,   If that be sin,
translation: May God help me bear it! If your granting my request is a sin,

original: I'll make it my morn prayer   To have it added to the faults of mine,   And nothing of your answer.
translation: I'll have it added to my faults and will pray for it every morning, so that you don't have to answer for anything.

original: Nay, but hear me. Your sense pursues not mine: either you are ignorant, Or seem so craftily; and that's not good.
translation: No, listen to me. You're not understanding what I'm saying. Either you're ignorant or pretending to be ignorant, and that's not good.

original: Let me be ignorant, and in nothing good, But graciously to know I am no better.
translation: I hope to be ignorant and not good at anything, so that I always know I'm not better than anyone else.

original: Thus wisdom wishes to appear most bright   When it doth tax itself;
translation: People show their wisdom most when they hold back.

original: as these black masks   Proclaim and enshield beauty ten times louder   Than beauty could, display'd.
translation: In the same way, your nun's outfit announces and protects your beauty ten times more than your beauty could on its own, if it were visible.

original: But mark me;   To be received plain, I'll speak more gross:   Your brother is to die.
translation: But listen—to make myself clear—your brother will die.

original: So.
translation: So.

original: And his offence is so, as it appears, Accountant to the law upon that pain.
translation: The punishment for his crime is death, according to the law.

original: True.
translation: True.
