original: Admit no other way to save his life,—   As I subscribe not that, nor any other,   But in the loss of question,
translation: What if his life couldn't be spared in any possible way—since nothing else can be said on his behalf

original: —that you, his sister,   Finding yourself desired of such a person,   Whose credit with the judge, or own great place,
translation: —unless you, his sister—finding yourself desired by someone connected to the judge, or the judge himself

original: Could fetch your brother from the manacles   Of the all-building law;
translation: —could save your brother from the punishment of the supreme law?

original: and that there were   No earthly mean to save him, but that either   You must lay down the treasures of your body   To this supposed,
translation: And what if there were no way on earth to save him except sleeping with this hypothetical judge?

original: or else to let him suffer;   What would you do?
translation: Otherwise you'd have to let him suffer. What would you do?

original: As much for my poor brother as myself:
translation: I would do the same for my brother that I would do for myself.

original: That is, were I under the terms of death,   The impression of keen whips I'ld wear as rubies,   And strip myself to death,
translation: I mean, if I were sentenced to death, I'd gladly endure beating with whips, strip myself down to nothing,

original: as to a bed   That longing have been sick for, ere I'ld yield   My body up to shame.
translation: and lie sick in bed before I would surrender my body to shame.

original: Then must your brother die.
translation: Then your brother has to die.

original: And 'twere the cheaper way:
translation: And it's better that way.

original: Better it were a brother died at once,   Than that a sister, by redeeming him,   Should die for ever.
translation: It's better my brother dies immediately than that his sister—by saving him—condemned her soul to hell forever.

original: Were not you then as cruel as the sentence That you have slander'd so?
translation: Aren't you being just as harsh as the death sentence you've been criticizing?

original: Ignomy in ransom and free pardon   Are of two houses:
translation: Demanding a bribe that will cause me public shame and freely granting a pardon are two different things.

original: lawful mercy   Is nothing kin to foul redemption.
translation: Legal mercy has nothing to do with this dirty deal.

original: You seem'd of late to make the law a tyrant; And rather proved the sliding of your brother A merriment than a vice.
translation: Just a few minutes ago you seemed to think the law was too harsh, and that your brother's sin was more of a joke than a sin.

original: O, pardon me, my lord; it oft falls out,
translation: Oh, forgive me, my lord. It sometimes comes out like that.

original: To have what we would have, we speak not what we mean:   I something do excuse the thing I hate,   For his advantage that I dearly love.
translation: When we really want something, we say things we don't mean. Even though I hate premarital sex, I had to forgive this sin for my brother's sake, because I love him.

original: We are all frail.
translation: We're all weak.

original: Else let my brother die, If not a feodary, but only he Owe and succeed thy weakness.
translation: Let my brother die, then, if no one else has the same weakness. And no other man will ever commit the same "crime."

original: Nay, women are frail too.
translation: No, women are weak, too.

original: Ay, as the glasses where they view themselves;   Which are as easy broke as they make forms.
translation: It's true, we're as weak as the mirrors we use to look at ourselves; they break as easily as they reflect shapes.

original: Women! Help Heaven! men their creation mar   In profiting by them.
translation: Women! God help us! Men make the earth a worse place by having children with them.

original: Nay, call us ten times frail;   For we are soft as our complexions are,   And credulous to false prints.
translation: No, call us weak ten more times—we're as soft as the skin on our faces, and gullible, too.

original: I think it well:   And from this testimony of your own sex,
translation: I think you're right. Since you, a woman, have said so

original: —   Since I suppose we are made to be no stronger   Than faults may shake our frames,
translation: —and since I guess we can't be any stronger than the weakness of our own bodies—

original: —let me be bold;   I do arrest your words. Be that you are,   That is, a woman;
translation: I'll be bold, and take you at your word. Be what you are: a woman.

original: if you be more, you're none;
translation: I f you insist on being a nun, you're not really a woman.

original: If you be one, as you are well express'd   By all external warrants, show it now,   By putting on the destined livery.
translation: If you are a woman, as you seem to be from what I can see of your attractive body, show me now. Show me your weakness.

original: I have no tongue but one: gentle my lord, Let me entreat you speak the former language.
translation: I can only be the way that I am. My noble lord, can we please go back to talking like we were before?

original: Plainly conceive, I love you.
translation: Understand me clearly: I love you.

original: My brother did love Juliet, And you tell me that he shall die for it.
translation: My brother loved Juliet, and you're telling me he has to die for it.

original: He shall not, Isabel, if you give me love.
translation: Isabella, if you make love to me, your brother won't die.

original: I know your virtue hath a licence in't, Which seems a little fouler than it is, To pluck on others.
translation: I know you're virtuous, so I think you're just testing me—although this test seems foul.

original: Believe me, on mine honour, My words express my purpose.
translation: Believe me; I swear I mean what I say.

original: Ha! little honour to be much believed,   And most pernicious purpose! Seeming, seeming!
translation: Ha! Everyone thinks you're a good man, but you're not. And look what you've done with it! You seem, you seem!

original: I will proclaim thee, Angelo; look for't:
translation: I'll tell everyone about you, Angelo. Just wait and see.

original: Sign me a present pardon for my brother,   Or with an outstretch'd throat I'll tell the world  aloud   What man thou art.
translation: Sign a pardon for my brother immediately, or I'll tell the world at the top of my lungs just what kind of man you are.

original: Who will believe thee, Isabel?   My unsoil'd name, the austereness of my life,   My vouch against you,
translation: Who would believe you, Isabella? My perfect reputation and disciplined life will work against you.

original: and my place i' the state,   Will so your accusation overweigh,   That you shall stifle in your own report   And smell of calumny.
translation: And my place in the government will outweigh your accusation to the point that you'll be ruined by your own report, and be filled with shame.

original: I have begun,   And now I give my sensual race the rein:   Fit thy consent to my sharp appetite;
translation: Now that I've gotten going, I'll give my sexual desire free rein: give me what I'm hungry for.

original: Lay by all nicety and prolixious blushes,   That banish what they sue for; redeem thy brother   By yielding up thy body to my will;
translation: Forget all your manners and polite blushing about what your brother did; save him by giving your body up to me.

original: Or else he must not only die the death,   But thy unkindness shall his death draw out   To lingering sufferance.
translation: Or else he'll not only die—because of your unkindness he'll also be tortured beforehand, and we'll draw out his suffering.

original: Answer me to-morrow,   Or, by the affection that now guides me most,   I'll prove a tyrant to him. As for you,   Say what you can, my false o'erweighs your true.
translation: Answer me tomorrow or, I swear by the love I have for you in this moment, I'll be as harsh as I can with him. As for you, say what you want. My lie has more power than your truth.

original: To whom should I complain? Did I tell this,   Who would believe me?
translation: Who can I complain to? If I told, who would believe me?

original: O perilous mouths,   That bear in them one and the self-same tongue,   Either of condemnation or approof;
translation: Curse the men who have the power, who utter words of condemnation or forgiveness with the same tongue!

original: Bidding the law make court'sy to their will:   Hooking both right and wrong to the appetite,   To follow as it draws! I'll to my brother:
translation: They can make the law do whatever they want—doing right or wrong to feed their own appetite as it grows! I'll go to my brother.

original: Though he hath fallen by prompture of the blood,   Yet hath he in him such a mind of honour.
translation: Although he's committed a sexual sin, I still believe he's a good person.

original: That, had he twenty heads to tender down   On twenty bloody blocks, he'ld yield them up,   Before his sister should her body stoop   To such abhorr'd pollution.
translation: If he had twenty heads that he could give to be chopped off twenty times, he'd give them up before he'd let his sister stoop to such a dirty level.

original: Then, Isabel, live chaste, and, brother, die:   More than our brother is our chastity.
translation: So, Isabella: live and be a virgin. Brother: die. My virginity is worth more than my brother's life.

original: I'll tell him yet of Angelo's request,   And fit his mind to death, for his soul's rest.
translation: I'll tell him what Angelo asked, and help him prepare for death so that his soul can rest in peace.

original: So then you hope of pardon from Lord Angelo?
translation: So then you hope Lord Angelo will pardon you?

original: The miserable have no other medicine But only hope: I've hope to live, and am prepared to die.
translation: The miserable have nothing to help them except hope. I hope that I live, but I'm prepared to die.

original: Be absolute for death; either death or life   Shall thereby be the sweeter.
translation: Be completely set on death. That way, whether you live or die, it will be all the sweeter.

original: Reason thus with life:   If I do lose thee, I do lose a thing   That none but fools would keep:
translation: Just say to life, "If I lose you, I lose something that only idiots want to keep.

original: a breath thou art,   Servile to all the skyey influences,   That dost this habitation, where thou keep'st,   Hourly afflict:
translation: You're just the breath that keeps this body of mine going by the hour, under God's direction.

original: merely, thou art death's fool;   For him thou labour'st by thy flight to shun   And yet runn'st toward him still.
translation: You lose out to Death every time. You do everything you can to get away from him, but every second you get closer to Death.

original: Thou art not noble;   For all the accommodations that thou bear'st   Are nursed by baseness.
translation: You're not classy; everything that sustains you is low-down and humble.

original: Thou'rt by no means valiant;   For thou dost fear the soft and tender fork   Of a poor worm.
translation: You're not brave; you're afraid of a bee's sting.

original: Thy best of rest is sleep,   And that thou oft provokest; yet grossly fear'st   Thy death, which is no more.
translation: Sleep is the best rest, and you always want to sleep. But you're grossly afraid of death, which is basically the same thing as a long sleep.

original: Thou art not thyself;   For thou exist'st on many a thousand grains   That issue out of dust. Happy thou art not;
translation: You're not yourself; you're made of a thousand tiny particles that came from dust. You're not happy;

original: For what thou hast not, still thou strivest to get,   And what thou hast, forget'st.
translation: you want what you don't have and forget what you do have.

original: Thou art not certain;   For thy complexion shifts to strange effects,   After the moon.
translation: You're not consistent; you change your mind as often as the moon changes its shape.

original: If thou art rich, thou'rt poor;   For, like an ass whose back with ingots bows,   Thou bear's thy heavy riches but a journey,   And death unloads thee.
translation: If you're rich, you're poor, because, like a donkey carrying heavy gold on his back, you can only carry your riches in life. You will have to leave them behind when you die.

original: Friend hast thou none;   For thine own bowels, which do call thee sire,
translation: You have no friends; you're constantly cursing your own internal organs (which you supposedly command)

original: The mere effusion of thy proper loins,   Do curse the gout, serpigo, and the rheum,   For ending thee no sooner.
translation: for the gout, arthritis, and rheumatism that should have killed you sooner.

original: Thou hast nor youth nor age,   But, as it were, an after-dinner's sleep,   Dreaming on both;
translation: You're neither young nor old; you're always dreaming about the one that you're not.

original: for all thy blessed youth   Becomes as aged, and doth beg the alms   Of palsied eld;
translation: When you're young, you're like an old man who has to beg for money from older folks.

original: and when thou art old and rich,   Thou hast neither heat, affection, limb, nor beauty,   To make thy riches pleasant.
translation: And when you're old, you no longer have the desire, agility, and good looks to enjoy your wealth."

original: What's yet in this   That bears the name of life? Yet in this life   Lie hid moe thousand deaths: yet death we fear,   That makes these odds all even.
translation: So what's so good about the thing we call "life?" There's a thousand things to suffer from in life, yet it's death we fear. That makes these odds all even.

original: I humbly thank you. To sue to live, I find I seek to die; And, seeking death, find life: let it come on.
translation: I give you my humble thanks. In begging to live, I'm killing myself spiritually. Seeking death gives me eternal life. Bring it on.

original: What, ho! Peace here; grace and good company!
translation: Hey! Hello? Peace, grace, and blessings!

original: Who's there? come in: the wish deserves a welcome.
translation: Who's there? Come in. Such kind wishes deserve a welcome.

original: Dear sir, ere long I'll visit you again.
translation: Dear sir, I'll visit you again before too long.

original: Most holy sir, I thank you.
translation: Thank you, most holy sir.

original: My business is a word or two with Claudio.
translation: I want to have a word or two with Claudio.

original: And very welcome. Look, signior, here's your sister.
translation: You're welcome to. Look, sir, here's your sister.

original: Provost, a word with you.
translation: Provost, a word with you.

original: As many as you please.
translation: As many words as you please.

original: Bring me to hear them speak, where I may be concealed.
translation: Can you hide me somewhere so I can hear them speak?

original: Now, sister, what's the comfort?
translation: Now, sister, is there good news?

original: Why,   As all comforts are; most good, most good indeed.
translation: Why, as good as news can be! Very good, very good indeed.

original: Lord Angelo, having affairs to heaven,   Intends you for his swift ambassador,   Where you shall be an everlasting leiger:
translation: Lord Angelo, who is a servant of heaven, wants you to go to heaven soon as his ambassador. And you'll stay there as his representative.

original: Therefore your best appointment make with speed;   To-morrow you set on.
translation: So your exciting appointment is coming up fast; it'll be tomorrow.

original: Is there no remedy?
translation: Is there no help for it?

original: None, but such remedy as, to save a head, To cleave a heart in twain.
translation: No help, except to save your head by breaking a heart.

original: But is there any?
translation: But is there any way to avoid death?

original: Yes, brother, you may live:   There is a devilish mercy in the judge,
translation: Yes, brother. You could live. The judge has a kind of evil mercy.

original: If you'll implore it, that will free your life,   But fetter you till death.
translation: But if you ask for it, it'll save your life, but burden you until death.

original: Perpetual durance?
translation: Forever?

original: Ay, just; perpetual durance, a restraint,
translation: Yes, exactly. Forever.

original: Though all the world's vastidity you had,   To a determined scope.
translation: Even if you had the whole world, this "mercy" would keep you in a tiny piece of it.

original: But in what nature?
translation: What kind of mercy is it?

original: In such a one as, you consenting to't, Would bark your honour from that trunk you bear, And leave you naked.
translation: The kind that, if you agreed to it, would strip you of your honor and leave you naked.

original: Let me know the point.
translation: Get to the point already.

original: O, I do fear thee, Claudio; and I quake,   Lest thou a feverous life shouldst entertain,   And six or seven winters more respect   Than a perpetual honour.
translation: Oh, I'm afraid of you, Claudio. And I'm shaking just thinking of you leading a sinful life, as if you'd value six or seven years more than eternal honor.

original: Darest thou die?   The sense of death is most in apprehension;
translation: Are you afraid to die? The scariest part of death is the anticipation.

original: And the poor beetle, that we tread upon,   In corporal sufferance finds a pang as great   As when a giant dies.
translation: And the little beetle that you step on feels as much pain as a a huge giant when he dies.

original: Why give you me this shame?   Think you I can a resolution fetch   From flowery tenderness?
translation: Why are you embarrassing me like this? Do you think I can man up with all this flowery poetry?

original: If I must die,   I will encounter darkness as a bride,   And hug it in mine arms.
translation: If I have to die, I'll go into the darkness like a bride, and embrace it with my arms.

original: There spake my brother; there my father's grave   Did utter forth a voice.
translation: So said my brother. My father just spoke from beyond the grave.

original: Yes, thou must die:   Thou art too noble to conserve a life   In base appliances.
translation: Yes, you have to die. You're too good to save your life by lowering yourself.

original: This outward-sainted deputy,   Whose settled visage and deliberate word   Nips youth i' the head and follies doth emmew   As falcon doth the fowl, is yet a devil
translation: This deputy—who seems so saintly, who slaps young people upside the head with his stern face and harsh words, and snaps up mistakes the way falcons snap up birds—is a devil.

original: His filth within being cast, he would appear   A pond as deep as hell.
translation: If you could see the depth of evil inside him, it would be a pit as deep as hell.

original: The prenzie Angelo!
translation: That perfect Angelo!

original: O, 'tis the cunning livery of hell,   The damned'st body to invest and cover   In prenzie guards!
translation: Oh, it's just hell's clever scheme to dress the most accursed men up as perfect soldiers!

original: Dost thou think, Claudio?   If I would yield him my virginity,   Thou mightst be freed.
translation: What do you think, Claudio? If I gave up my virginity to him, you could be freed.

original: O heavens! it cannot be.
translation: Oh, heavens! It can't be.

original: Yes, he would give't thee, from this rank offence,   So to offend him still.
translation: Yes, he would free you, but after this horrible crime you would offend him more.

original: This night's the time   That I should do what I abhor to name,   Or else thou diest to-morrow.
translation: Tonight's when I'm supposed to do what I can't even name, or else you die tomorrow.

original: Thou shalt not do't.
translation: You shouldn't do it.

original: O, were it but my life, I'ld throw it down for your deliverance As frankly as a pin.
translation: Oh, if it were only my life, I'd give it up for your freedom as easily as a pin.

original: Thanks, dear Isabel.
translation: Thanks, dear Isabella.

original: Be ready, Claudio, for your death tomorrow.
translation: Be ready for your death tomorrow, Claudio.

original: Yes. Has he affections in him,   That thus can make him bite the law by the nose,   When he would force it?
translation: Yes. Does he have such desires in him that he's willing to break the law like that whenever he feels the urge?

original: Sure, it is no sin,   Or of the deadly seven, it is the least.
translation: Surely it's not a sin. Or, of the  deadly seven , it's the least serious.

original: Which is the least?
translation: Which is the least?

original: If it were damnable, he being so wise, Why would he for the momentary trick Be perdurably fined? O Isabel!
translation: If lust were really that bad, why would a wise man like him willingly take on the eternal consequences for a momentary thrill? Oh, Isabella!

original: What says my brother?
translation: What are you saying, brother?

original: Death is a fearful thing.
translation: Death is a scary thing.

original: And shamed life a hateful.
translation: And a life of shame is a hateful thing.

original: Ay, but to die, and go we know not where;   To lie in cold obstruction and to rot;
translation: Yes, but to die, and to go somewhere unknown, to lie in a cold grave and rot

original: This sensible warm motion to become   A kneaded clod; and the delighted spirit   To bathe in fiery floods, or to reside   In thrilling region of thick-ribbed ice;
translation: ...for my warm, thinking body to become a piece of dirt, and for my soul to go either down to fiery hell or up to the exciting icy castle of heaven.

original: To be imprison'd in the viewless winds,   And blown with restless violence round about   The pendent world;
translation: ..to be blown about violently in the winds around and around the world.

original: or to be worse than worst   Of those that lawless and incertain thought   Imagine howling: 'tis too horrible!
translation: ..or to be in worse suffering than we imagine even in our most uncensored, uncertain thoughts...it's too horrible!

original: The weariest and most loathed worldly life   That age, ache, penury and imprisonment   Can lay on nature is a paradise   To what we fear of death.
translation: The most tired, deplorable worldly life with all the age, ache, poverty, and imprisonment that nature can lay on is a paradise compared with death, which we fear.

original: Alas, alas!
translation: Oh no! Oh no!

original: Sweet sister, let me live:   What sin you do to save a brother's life,
translation: Sweet sister, let me live. Nature will be so forgiving of whatever sin you have to commit to save your brother's life,

original: Nature dispenses with the deed so far   That it becomes a virtue.
translation: that the sin will become a virtue.

original: O you beast!   O faithless coward! O dishonest wretch!   Wilt thou be made a man out of my vice?
translation: Oh, you animal! You weak coward! You lying dog! You want to save your life through my sin?

original: Is't not a kind of incest, to take life   From thine own sister's shame? What should I think?
translation: Isn't it a kind of incest to take your life from your own sister's shame? What am I supposed to think?

original: Heaven shield my mother play'd my father fair!   For such a warped slip of wilderness   Ne'er issued from his blood.
translation: I hope my mother didn't cheat on my father—but I'm sure such a deformed piece of savagery never came from his side of the family.

original: Take my defiance!   Die, perish! Might but my bending down   Reprieve thee from thy fate, it should proceed:
translation: I defy you! Die, die! If I could save you from your fate by praying, I'd do it.

original: I'll pray a thousand prayers for thy death,   No word to save thee.
translation: I'll pray a thousand prayers for your death, but not a word to save you.

original: Nay, hear me, Isabel.
translation: No, listen to me, Isabella.

original: O, fie, fie, fie!   Thy sin's not accidental, but a trade.
translation: Oh, shame on you! Your sin wasn't just an accident; it's your occupation.

original: Mercy to thee would prove itself a bawd:   'Tis best thou diest quickly.
translation: Mercy would just  help  you commit more sins. It's best you die quickly.

original: O hear me, Isabella!
translation: Oh, listen to me, Isabella!

original: Vouchsafe a word, young sister, but one word.
translation: Let me have a word with you, little sister. Just a word.

original: What is your will?
translation: What do you want?

original: Might you dispense with your leisure, I would by and   by have some speech with you:
translation: If you don't mind giving up your free time, I'd like to speak with you.

original: the satisfaction I   would require is likewise your own benefit.
translation: What I want will be to your own benefit, too.

original: I have no superfluous leisure; my stay must be stolen out of other affairs; but I will attend you  awhile.
translation: I don't have any extra free time. My visit is taking time away from other things. But I'll listen to you awhile.

original: Son, I have overheard what hath passed between you   and your sister.
translation: Son, I overheard what you and your sister said to each other.

original: Angelo had never the purpose to   corrupt her; only he hath made an essay of her   virtue to practise his judgment with the disposition   of natures:
translation: Angelo was never trying to corrupt her. He was only testing her virtue to practice his judgment of people's dispositions.

original: she, having the truth of honour in her,   hath made him that gracious denial which he is most   glad to receive.
translation: She's honorable and truthful, so she's denied him in exactly the way he wanted.

original: I am confessor to Angelo, and I   know this to be true;
translation: I'm Angelo's  confessor,  and I know this to be true.

original: therefore prepare yourself to   death: do not satisfy your resolution with hopes   that are fallible:
translation: So prepare yourself for death. Don't depend on empty hope.

original: tomorrow you must die; go to   your knees and make ready.
translation: You have to die tomorrow. Pray and get ready.

original: Let me ask my sister pardon. I am so out of love with life that I will sue to be rid of it.
translation: Tell my sister that I ask for her forgiveness. I'm hate this life so much that I'd do anything to die.

original: Hold you there: farewell.
translation: Stay there. Goodbye.

original: Provost, a word with you!
translation: Provost, a word with you!

original: What's your will, father?
translation: What do you want, father?

original: That now you are come, you will be gone. Leave me   awhile with the maid:
translation: Now that you just got here, I ask that you'll leave again. Leave me alone with the girl for a while.

original: my mind promises with my   habit no loss shall touch her by my company.
translation: You can trust me to be alone with her—I'm a monk.

original: In good time.
translation: Take your time.

original: The hand that hath made you fair hath made you good:
translation: The same God that made you beautiful has also made you good.

original: the goodness that is cheap in beauty makes beauty   brief in goodness;
translation: The little good that's in beauty means that goodness is hardly ever beautiful.

original: but grace, being the soul of   your complexion, shall keep the body of it ever   fair.
translation: But grace—which is the core of your being—will keep you beautiful forever.

original: The assault that Angelo hath made to you,   fortune hath conveyed to my understanding;
translation: I've found out about how Angelo propositioned you.

original: and, but   that frailty hath examples for his falling, I should   wonder at Angelo. How will you do to content this   substitute, and to save your brother?
translation: And if there weren't so many who've fallen before him, then I'd be surprised at Angelo. What happens if you agree to his trade and save your brother?

original: I am now going to resolve him: I had rather my   brother die by the law than my son should be   unlawfully born.
translation: I'm going to respond to him now: I'd rather my brother die legally than that my son be  born  illegitimate.

original: But, O, how much is the good duke   deceived in Angelo! I
translation: But, oh, the Duke is so wrong about Angelo!

original: f ever he return and I can   speak to him, I will open my lips in vain, or   discover his government.
translation: If the Duke ever comes back and I can speak to him, I will tell him about Angelo's government as soon as I can open my lips.

original: That shall not be much amiss: Yet, as the matter   now stands, he will avoid your accusation; he made   trial of you only.
translation: That wouldn't be a bad thing to do. And yet, as it now stands, it'd be hard to accuse Angelo, since he only propositioned you.

original: Therefore fasten your ear on my   advisings: to the love I have in doing good a   remedy presents itself.
translation: So listen to my advice: I love doing good, and I have a solution in mind.

original: I do make myself believe   that you may most uprighteously do a poor wronged   lady a merited benefit;
translation: I almost think that you could do some much-needed good for a poor, abused lady.

original: redeem your brother from   the angry law; do no stain to your own gracious   person;
translation: At the same time, you could redeem your brother from the harsh law, avoid dirtying yourself,

original: and much please the absent duke, if   peradventure he shall ever return to have hearing of   this business.
translation: and really please the Duke who isn't here—if by chance he ever comes back and has a chance to hear about all this.

original: Let me hear you speak farther. I have spirit to do anything that appears not foul in the truth of my  spirit.
translation: Please tell me more. I'm willing to do anything that doesn't seem wrong to me.

original: Virtue is bold, and goodness never fearful. Have you not heard speak of Mariana, the sister of Frederick the great soldier who miscarried at sea?
translation: Virtue is bold, and good people are never afraid. Have you ever heard of Mariana, the sister of the great soldier Frederick, who died at sea?

original: I have heard of the lady, and good words went with her  name.
translation: I've heard of her, and have heard good things attached to that name.

original: She should this Angelo have married; was affianced   to her by oath, and the nuptial appointed:
translation: She was supposed to marry this Angelo. He was engaged to her, and the wedding date was set.

original: between   which time of the contract and limit of the   solemnity, her brother Frederick was wrecked at sea,
translation: But between the engagement and the ceremony, her brother Frederick was shipwrecked,

original: having in that perished vessel the dowry of his   sister.
translation: and her dowry sunk along with the ship.

original: But mark how heavily this befell to the   poor gentlewoman: there she lost a noble and   renowned brother,
translation: But listen how terribly it worked out for the poor woman: she lost her noble, respected brother,

original: in his love toward her ever most   kind and natural; with him, the portion and sinew of   her fortune, her marriage-dowry;
translation: who was always kind and loving to her. Along with him, she lost her entire fortune and her marriage dowry.

original: with both, her   combinate husband, this well-seeming Angelo.
translation: And, along with all of that, she lost her would-be husband, this well-seeming Angelo.

original: Can this be so? did Angelo so leave her?
translation: Is this true? And did Angelo leave her like that?

original: Left her in her tears, and dried not one of them   with his comfort;
translation: He left her in tears, and he didn't stick around to comfort her.

original: swallowed his vows whole,   pretending in her discoveries of dishonour: in few,   bestowed her on her own lamentation, which she yet   wears for his sake;
translation: He went back on his vows, and made up a story about her having an affair. In short, he sent her into a period of mourning, which she's still in for his sake.

original: and he, a marble to her tears,   is washed with them, but relents not.
translation: He hasn't taken pity on her at all. He's not even sympathetic to her constant tears.

original: What a merit were it in death to take this poor maid from the world! What corruption in this life, that it will let this man live! But how out of this can she  avail?
translation: It would have been better for him to kill this poor girl, and take her out of the world! Life is horrible if it lets this man live! But how can she get out of this?

original: It is a rupture that you may easily heal: and the cure of it not only saves your brother, but keeps you from dishonour in doing it.
translation: It's a break which you could easily fix. Fixing it not only saves your brother, but keeps you from dishonoring yourself while you do it.

original: Show me how, good father.
translation: Show me how, good father.

original: This forenamed maid hath yet in her the continuance   of her first affection:
translation: T he woman I mentioned, Mariana, is still in love with Angelo.

original: his unjust unkindness, that   in all reason should have quenched her love, hath,   like an impediment in the current, made it more   violent and unruly.
translation: The wrong he did her—which, all things considered, should have ended her love—has only made it stronger and wilder, like a rock in a stream.

original: Go you to Angelo; answer his   requiring with a plausible obedience; agree with   his demands to the point;
translation: Go to Angelo. Answer his request obediently and convincingly. Agree to his demands completely.

original: only refer yourself to   this advantage, first, that your stay with him may   not be long; that the time may have all shadow and   silence in it; and the place answer to convenience.
translation: Only ask him this: that your first visit to him is short, that it stays dark and silent the entire time, and that the place is convenient.

original: This being granted in course,—and now follows   all,—we shall advise this wronged maid to stead up   your appointment, go in your place;
translation: If he grants all this—and now it all comes together—we'll get the abandoned woman to go to the appointment in your place.

original: if the encounter   acknowledge itself hereafter, it may compel him to   her recompense:
translation: If the encounter is acknowledged afterward, it might convince him to marry her.

original: and here, by this, is your brother   saved, your honour untainted, the poor Mariana   advantaged, and the corrupt deputy scaled.
translation: And with all that, your brother is saved, your reputation is clean, the poor Mariana is helped, and the corrupt deputy gets his just deserts.

original: The maid   will I frame and make fit for his attempt.
translation: I'll talk to the girl and get her ready for his attempt.

original: If you   think well to carry this as you may, the doubleness   of the benefit defends the deceit from reproof.   What think you of it?
translation: If you don't mind doing this, the benefit to everyone will make your lie inconsequential. What do you think?

original: The image of it gives me content already; and I trust it will grow to a most prosperous perfection.
translation: I feel better just imagining it. I think it will work out extremely well.

original: It lies much in your holding up. Haste you speedily   to Angelo:
translation: It all depends on how you carry it out. Go quickly to Angelo.

original: if for this night he entreat you to his   bed, give him promise of satisfaction.
translation: If he asks you to come to his bed tonight, promise him you will.

original: I will   presently to Saint Luke's: there, at the moated   grange, resides this dejected Mariana.
translation: I'll go now to St. Luke's, were poor Mariana lives at the convent.

original: At that   place call upon me; and dispatch with Angelo, that   it may be quickly.
translation: Find me there, and take care of Angelo so that it can all happen soon.

original: I thank you for this comfort. Fare you well, good  father.
translation: Thank you for your help. Take care, good father.

original: Nay, if there be no remedy for it, but that you will needs buy and sell men and women like beasts, we shall have all the world drink brown and white bastard.
O heavens! what stuff is here?
translation: Oh, heavens! What's going on here?

original: 'Twas never merry world since, of two usuries, the   merriest was put down, and the worser allowed by   order of law a furred gown to keep him warm;
translation: Things have never been right since sex and money-lending were repaid like this: the one who was just having fun was killed, and the worse one was allowed by order of the law to wear a fur coat to keep him warm

original: and   furred with fox and lamb-skins too, to signify, that   craft, being richer than innocency, stands for the  facing.
translation: —and made with fox and lamb-skins, too. This all goes to show that because the guilty are richer than the innocent, they can do whatever they want!

original: Come your way, sir. 'Bless you, good father friar.
translation: Come on, sir. Bless you, good father friar.

original: And you, good brother father. What offence hath this man made you, sir?
Marry, sir, he hath offended the law: and, sir, we   take him to be a thief too, sir;
translation: Well, sir, he's broken the law. And, sir, we think he's a thief, too, sir.

original: for we have found   upon him, sir, a strange picklock, which we have   sent to the deputy.
translation: For we found a lock-picking device with him which we sent to the deputy.

original: Fie, sirrah! a bawd, a wicked bawd!
translation: Shame on you,  sir ! You pimp, you wicked pimp!

original: The evil that thou causest to be done,   That is thy means to live.
translation: You make your living from this horrible evil.

original: Do thou but think   What 'tis to cram a maw or clothe a back   From such a filthy vice:
translation: Do you even think about what it means to put food on the table or clothes on your back by such a dirty crime?

original: say to thyself,   From their abominable and beastly touches   I drink, I eat, array myself, and live.
translation: Do you say to yourself, "from their disgusting, beastly encounters I drink, eat, clothe myself, and live?"

original: Canst thou believe thy living is a life,   So stinkingly depending? Go mend, go mend.
translation: Can you believe your living is a life that depends on such filth? Go improve yourself, improve yourself.

original: Indeed, it does stink in some sort, sir; but yet, sir, I would prove—
translation: It's true, sir. It does stink in a way. But sir, I would argue—

original: Nay, if the devil have given thee proofs for sin,   Thou wilt prove his.
translation: No, if the devil has given you arguments with which to defend sin, then you're his already.

original: Take him to prison, officer:   Correction and instruction must both work   Ere this rude beast will profit.
translation: [To an officer]  Take him to prison, officer. Correction and teaching will have to help this rude animal improve himself.

original: He must before the deputy, sir; he has given him   warning:
translation: He has to have a trial in front of the deputy, sir. The deputy has given him a warning,

original: the deputy cannot abide a whoremaster: if   he be a whoremonger, and comes before him, he were   as good go a mile on his errand.
translation: and he can't stand a pimp. If he is a pimp, and stands trial, he'd be better off doing anything else.

original: That we were all, as some would seem to be, From our faults, as faults from seeming, free!
translation: If only we were all free from our faults—as some seem to be—and that our faults weren't so apparent to others!

original: His neck will come to your waist,—a cord, sir.
I spy comfort; I cry bail. Here's a gentleman and a friend of mine.
translation: There is hope; I might get bail! Here comes a gentleman who's a friend of mine.

original: How now, noble Pompey! What, at the wheels of   Caesar? art thou led in triumph?
translation: What's going on, noble Pompey? Are you being  held prisoner ? Are you on display like a prisoner of war?

original: What, is there   none of Pygmalion's images, newly made woman, to be   had now, for putting the hand in the pocket and   extracting it clutch'd?
translation: Don't you have any  beautiful women , all dolled up and ready to reach into our pockets and rob us of all our cash?

original: What reply, ha? What   sayest thou to this tune, matter and method?
translation: What, no reply? Ha. What do you have to say about this thing and the way it's been done?

original: Is't   not drowned i' the last rain, ha? What sayest   thou, Trot? Is the world as it was, man?
translation: Shouldn't it all be over and done, huh? What do you have to say for yourself? Is the world the same as it was, man?

original: Which is   the way? Is it sad, and few words? or how? The   trick of it?
translation: How do you feel? Are you sad? Do you want to say a few words? Or anything? Tell us the gist.

original: Still thus, and thus; still worse!
translation: It just keeps going on and on and getting worse and worse!

original: How doth my dear morsel, thy mistress? Procures she still, ha?
translation: How's my sweetie pie, your mistress? Is she still pimping?

original: Troth, sir, she hath eaten up all her beef, and she is herself in the tub.
Why, 'tis good; it is the right of it;
translation: Well that's good. That's the right thing to do.

original: it must be   so: ever your fresh whore and your powdered bawd:   an unshunned consequence; it must be so. Art going   to prison, Pompey?
translation: It got to be that way. You've got to have a fresh whore and a powdered pimp. Got to embrace the consequences. Are you going to prison, Pompey?

original: Yes, faith, sir.
translation: Yes, indeed I am, sir.

original: Why, 'tis not amiss, Pompey. Farewell: go, say I sent thee thither. For debt, Pompey? or how?
For being a bawd, for being a bawd.
translation: For being a pimp, for being a pimp.

original: Well, then, imprison him: if imprisonment be the   due of a bawd, why, 'tis his right:
translation: Well, then, put him in prison. If imprisonment is the punishment for pimping, then it's right, isn't it?

original: bawd is he   doubtless, and of antiquity too; bawd-born.
translation: He's definitely a pimp, and has been one for a long time. He was born a pimp.

original: Farewell, good Pompey. Commend me to the prison,   Pompey: you will turn good husband now, Pompey; you   will keep the house.
translation: Farewell, dear Pompey. Give the prison my best wishes, Pompey. You'll be a good husband now, Pompey, and keep  house .

original: I hope, sir, your good worship will be my bail.
translation: I had hoped that you might pay my bail, your good Worship.

original: No, indeed, will I not, Pompey; it is not the wear.
translation: No I won't, Pompey. It's not meant to be.

original: I will pray, Pompey, to increase your bondage: If   you take it not patiently, why, your mettle is the   more. Adieu, trusty Pompey.
translation: I'll pray that your punishment is even worse, Pompey. And if you don't take it well, then you're even worse than I thought. Goodbye, trusty Pompey.

original: 'Bless you, friar.
translation: [To DUKE VINCENTIO]  Bless you, friar.

original: And you.
translation: And you.

original: Does Bridget paint still, Pompey, ha?
Come your ways, sir; come.
translation: Come on, sir, come on.

original: You will not bail me, then, sir?
translation: You won't bail me out, then, sir?

original: Then, Pompey, nor now. What news abroad, friar? what news?
translation: Not then, Pompey, and not now.  What's the news out there, friar? What's the news?

original: Come your ways, sir; come.
translation: Come on, sir, come on.

original: Go to kennel, Pompey; go.
What news, friar, of the duke?
translation: What the news about the Duke, friar?

original: I know none. Can you tell me of any?
translation: I don't know anything. Can you tell me anything?

original: Some say he is with the Emperor of Russia; other some, he is in Rome: but where is he, think you?
translation: Some say he's with the Emperor of Russia; others say he's in Rome. But where do you think he is?

original: I know not where; but wheresoever, I wish him well.
translation: I don't know where. But wherever he is, I wish him well.

original: It was a mad fantastical trick of him to steal from   the state, and usurp the beggary he was never born   to.
translation: What a crazy, fantastic trick for him to sneak away from the government and pretend to be a  beggar  when he's really rich.

original: Lord Angelo dukes it well in his absence; he   puts transgression to 't.
translation: Lord Angelo is doing well while the Duke is gone. He makes people answer for their crimes.

original: He does well in 't.
translation: He's doing well with it.

original: A little more lenity to lechery would do no harm in him: something too crabbed that way, friar.
translation: A little more leniency with sex wouldn't do him any harm. He's a little too uptight with that, friar.

original: It is too general a vice, and severity must cure it.
translation: It's a common fault, so you have to be harsh to put an end to it.

original: Yes, in good sooth, the vice is of a great kindred;   it is well allied:
translation: Yes, it's true, everyone seems to have a weakness for sex; it's pretty far-spread.

original: but it is impossible to extirp   it quite, friar, till eating and drinking be put   down.
translation: But it's impossible to exterminate it completely, friar. You could as easily put an end to eating and drinking.

original: They say this Angelo was not made by man and   woman after this downright way of creation: is it   true, think you?
translation: They say that Angelo wasn't conceived by a man and a woman in the usual way. Do you think that's true?

original: How should he be made, then?
translation: How would he be born, then?

original: Some report a sea-maid spawned him; some, that he   was begot between two stock-fishes.
translation: Some say a sea-nymph gave birth to him. Others say he was conceived by two dried fish.

original: But it is   certain that when he makes water his urine is   congealed ice; that I know to be true:
translation: But it's true that when he pees, his urine is pure ice. I know that's true.

original: and he is a   motion generative; that's infallible.
translation: He's a puppet without the ability to reproduce, that's undoubtable.

original: You are pleasant, sir, and speak apace.
translation: You're funny, sir, and you speak quickly.

original: Why, what a ruthless thing is this in him, for the   rebellion of a codpiece to take away the life of a   man!
translation: It's so unforgiving of him, to kill a man for a little rebellion of the  penis !

original: Would the duke that is absent have done this?
translation: Would the absent Duke have done this?

original: Ere he would have hanged a man for the getting a   hundred bastards, he would have paid for the nursing   a thousand:
translation: Before he would have hanged one man for having a hundred bastards, he would have paid to care for a thousand bastards.

original: he had some feeling of the sport: he   knew the service, and that instructed him to mercy.
translation: He knew a little about the game. He got it, and that led him to be merciful.

original: I never heard the absent duke much detected for women; he was not inclined that way.
translation: I never heard that the absent Duke was a ladies' man. He wasn't built that way.

original: O, sir, you are deceived.
translation: Oh, sir, you're wrong.

original: 'Tis not possible.
Who, not the duke? yes, your beggar of fifty; and   his use was to put a ducat in her clack-dish: the   duke had crotchets in him.
translation: Who, the Duke? He'd see a fifty-year-old  beggar  woman and put a coin in her bucket; he had his quirks.

original: He would be drunk too;   that let me inform you.
translation: And he'd get drunk, too, let me tell you.

original: You do him wrong, surely.
translation: You're definitely being too hard on him.

original: Sir, I was an inward of his. A shy fellow was the duke: and I believe I know the cause of his withdrawing.
translation: Sir, I was a good friend of his. The Duke was a shy man, and I think I know why he left.

original: What, I prithee, might be the cause?
translation: Please tell me, what might be the reason?

original: No, pardon; 'tis a secret must be locked within the   teeth and the lips:
translation: No, sorry. It's a secret and my lips are sealed.

original: but this I can let you   understand, the greater file of the subject held the   duke to be wise.
translation: But I can tell you this: most of the people thought of the Duke as a wise man.

original: Wise! why, no question but he was.
translation: Wise? Well, there's no question about it; he was—

original: A very superficial, ignorant, unweighing fellow.
translation: —a very superficial, ignorant, and impulsive man.

original: Either this is the envy in you, folly, or mistaking:
translation: Either you're jealous of him, you're stupid, or you've made a mistake.

original: the very stream of his life and the business he hath   helmed must upon a warranted need give him a better   proclamation.
translation: The quality of his life and the work he's done have to give him a better name.

original: Let him be but testimonied in his own   bringings-forth, and he shall appear to the   envious a scholar, a statesman and a soldier.
translation: Let his actions be a testament to his critics: he's a scholar, a governor, and a soldier.

original: Therefore you speak unskilfully: or if your   knowledge be more it is much darkened in your malice.
translation: You don't know what you're talking about. Or if you do know, you're lying out of bad intentions.

original: Sir, I know him, and I love him.
translation: Sir, I know him, and I love him.

original: Love talks with better knowledge, and knowledge with dearer love.
translation: Love should know better. And if you did know him, you'd speak with more love.

original: Come, sir, I know what I know.
translation: Come on, sir, I know what I know.

original: I can hardly believe that, since you know not what   you speak.
translation: I can hardly believe that, since you don't know what you're talking about.

original: But, if ever the duke return, as our   prayers are he may, let me desire you to make your   answer before him.
translation: But, if the Duke ever returns—as we hope and pray—let me ask you to tell him what you've said.

original: If it be honest you have spoke,   you have courage to maintain it: I am bound to call   upon you; and, I pray you, your name?
translation: If you've told the truth, you'll say it to his face. I'll have to call on you to do so. And, tell me, what was your name?

original: Sir, my name is Lucio; well known to the duke.
translation: Sir, my name is Lucio, and I'm familiar with the Duke.

original: He shall know you better, sir, if I may live to report you.
translation: He'll know you better soon, sir, if I live to report you.

original: I fear you not.
translation: I'm not afraid of you.

original: O, you hope the duke will return no more; or you imagine me too unhurtful an opposite. But indeed I can do you little harm; you'll forswear this again.
translation: Oh, you'd better hope the Duke will never come back, since you think I'm not someone to fear. But it's true I can't hurt you much. You'll repeat this in front of the Duke?

original: I'll be hanged first: thou art deceived in me, friar. But no more of this. Canst thou tell if Claudio die to-morrow or no?
translation: I'll be hanged first. You're wrong about me, friar. But enough of this. Can you tell me if Claudio will die tomorrow, sir?

original: Why should he die, sir?
translation: Why would he die, sir?

original: Why? For filling a bottle with a tundish. I would   the duke we talk of were returned again:
translation: Why? For sticking his pipe in the hole. I wish the Duke we were talking about would come back already.

original: the   ungenitured agent will unpeople the province with   continency; sparrows must not build in his   house-eaves, because they are lecherous.
translation: The deputy he's left in his place will reduce the population with his abstinence policy. Even the sparrows can't build nests on window-sills because they're too lustful!

original: The duke   yet would have dark deeds darkly answered; he would   never bring them to light: would he were returned!
translation: The Duke, too, would have punished serious crimes. But he would never have exposed them. I wish he were back!

original: Marry, this Claudio is condemned for untrussing.   Farewell, good friar: I prithee, pray for me.
translation: Indeed, Claudio is condemned for having sex. Goodbye, good friar. Please pray for me.

original: The   duke, I say to thee again, would eat mutton on   Fridays.
translation: The Duke, I'll tell you again, would eat meat on  Fridays .

original: He's not past it yet, and I say to thee,   he would mouth with a beggar, though she smelt brown   bread and garlic: say that I said so. Farewell.
translation: He's not too high and mighty, I'm saying, to talk with a beggar, even if she smelled like brown bread and garlic. You can tell him I said so. Goodbye.

original: No might nor greatness in mortality   Can censure 'scape;
translation: No matter how big or powerful you are, you're not immune to criticism.

original: back-wounding calumny   The whitest virtue strikes.
translation: Back-breaking rumors can ruin even the best reputation.

original: What king so strong   Can tie the gall up in the slanderous tongue?   But who comes here?
translation: Could even the strongest king stop the power of a gossiping tongue? But who's this?

original: Go; away with her to prison!
translation: Go, take her away to prison!

original: Good my lord, be good to me; your honour is accounted a merciful man; good my lord.
translation: My good lord, be good to me. I've heard that you're a merciful man, your Honor. My good lord.

original: Double and treble admonition, and still forfeit in the same kind! This would make mercy swear and play the tyrant.
translation: You were warned two, then three times. And you're still up to the same stuff! This would make even the most merciful man act like a tyrant.

original: A bawd of eleven years' continuance, may it please your honour.
translation: A bawd for eleven years straight, if you will, sir.

original: My lord, this is one Lucio's information against me.   Mistress Kate Keepdown was with child by him in the   duke's time; he promised her marriage:
translation: My lord, Lucio's the one who informed on me. Ms.  Kate Keepdown  got knocked up by him back in the Duke's day, and he promised to marry her.

original: his child   is a year and a quarter old, come Philip and Jacob:   I have kept it myself; and see how he goes about to  abuse me!
translation: His child is a year and three months old, come  May 1 . I've taken care of the child myself, and look how he goes around and rats on me!

original: That fellow is a fellow of much licence: let him be called before us. Away with her to prison! Go to; no more words.
translation: That man is way too liberal. Bring him here to us. Take her away to prison! Cut it out, don't say anything else.

original: Provost, my brother Angelo will not be altered;   Claudio must die to-morrow:
translation: Provost, my friend Angelo won't change his mind; Claudio has to die tomorrow.

original: let him be furnished   with divines, and have all charitable preparation.
translation: Send him a priest so he can have his last rites.

original: if my brother wrought by my pity, it should not be   so with him.
translation: If Angelo had listened to me take pity on him, Claudio wouldn't be going to his death.

original: So please you, this friar hath been with him, and advised him for the entertainment of death.
translation: Sir, the friar has visited him and counseled him about being prepared for death.

original: Good even, good father.
translation: Good evening, good father.

original: Bliss and goodness on you!
translation: God bless you with happiness and goodness!

original: Of whence are you?
translation: Where are you from?

original: Not of this country, though my chance is now   To use it for my time:
translation: Not from this country, though I'm here for now.

original: I am a brother   Of gracious order, late come from the See   In special business from his holiness.
translation: I'm a monk in a holy order, and came from the Vatican on a special mission from the Pope.

original: What news abroad i' the world?
translation: What's the news abroad in the world?

original: None, but that there is so great a fever on   goodness, that the dissolution of it must cure it:
translation: None, except there seems to be such a lack of goodness that the only way to change things would be if the whole generation died.

original: novelty is only in request; and it is as dangerous   to be aged in any kind of course, as it is virtuous   to be constant in any undertaking.
translation: Everyone wants something new. It's as dangerous to have done anything for very long as it is to be virtuous and trustworthy in any project.

original: There is scarce   truth enough alive to make societies secure; but   security enough to make fellowships accurst:
translation: There's hardly enough truth out there to keep society secure, but there's enough  security  to keep business corrupt.

original: much   upon this riddle runs the wisdom of the world. This   news is old enough, yet it is every day's news. I   pray you, sir, of what disposition was the duke?
translation: This is the paradox at the heart of earthly wisdom. This is old news, really. But it's the same news every day. Let me ask you, sir, what kind of person was the Duke?

original: One that, above all other strifes, contended especially to know himself.
translation: The kind of man that tried to be self-aware, above all else.

original: What pleasure was he given to?
translation: What did he like to do?

original: Rather rejoicing to see another merry, than merry at   any thing which professed to make him rejoice:
translation: He preferred to see other people happy than to do anything that would make him happy himself.

original: a   gentleman of all temperance. But leave we him to   his events, with a prayer they may prove prosperous;
translation: He was a very modest man. But we'll leave him to his own affairs, and we'll pray they turn out well.

original: and let me desire to know how you find Claudio   prepared. I am made to understand that you have   lent him visitation.
translation: Let me know if Claudio seems ready. I'm led to understand that you've been to see him.

original: He professes to have received no sinister measure   from his judge, but most willingly humbles himself   to the determination of justice:
translation: He claims he doesn't think he's been punished too harshly by the judge, and willingly humbles himself to receive justice.

original: yet had he framed   to himself, by the instruction of his frailty, many   deceiving promises of life;
translation: He had kept on hoping, in his weakness, that he had a chance to live.

original: which I by my good   leisure have discredited to him, and now is he   resolved to die.
translation: But I've taken the time to help him see it isn't possible. Now he's set to die.

original: You have paid the heavens your function, and the   prisoner the very debt of your calling.
translation: You've done God's work, helping prisoners just as you've been called to do.

original: I have   laboured for the poor gentleman to the extremest   shore of my modesty:
translation: I've done everything I can to help the poor man.

original: but my brother justice have I   found so severe, that he hath forced me to tell him   he is indeed Justice.
translation: But Angelo has been so severe that he's forced me to admit he is Justice incarnate.

original: If his own life answer the straitness of his proceeding, it shall become him well; wherein if he chance to fail, he hath sentenced himself.
translation: If Angelo's own life lives up to the strictness of his judgement, then good for him. On the other hand, if he happens to mess up, he's sentenced himself.

original: I am going to visit the prisoner. Fare you well.
translation: I'm going to visit the prisoner. Take care.

original: Peace be with you!
translation: Peace be with you!

original: He who the sword of heaven will bear   Should be as holy as severe;
translation: Anyone  who says he's dishing out God's justice should be as perfect as he is strict.

original: Pattern in himself to know,   Grace to stand, and virtue go;   More nor less to others paying   Than by self-offences weighing.
translation: He should be an example of knowledge, grace, and virtue, and he shouldn't dole out punishments greater or less than those he would give himself.

original: Shame to him whose cruel striking   Kills for faults of his own liking!   Twice treble shame on Angelo,   To weed my vice and let his grow!
translation: Shame on the cruel man who kills another for crimes he himself commits! Double, triple times the shame on Angelo, to punish another man's crime while he lets his own go!

original: O, what may man within him hide,   Though angel on the outward side!
translation: A man can hide so much when he looks like an angel from the outside!

original: How may likeness made in crimes,   Making practise on the times,   To draw with idle spiders' strings   Most ponderous and substantial things!
translation: Identical crimes in these strange times seem to be teaching us thought-provoking, substantial things! I

original: Craft against vice I must apply:   With Angelo to-night shall lie   His old betrothed but despised;
translation: have to be clever to put an end to this evil. Tonight, Angelo will sleep with Mariana, his one-time fiancée whom he abandoned.

original: So disguise shall, by the disguised,   Pay with falsehood false exacting,   And perform an old contracting.
translation: Her disguise, and she herself, will give Angelo exactly what he deserved—and make good on an old promise.

original: Take, O, take those lips away,   That so sweetly were forsworn;
translation: [Singing]    Take, oh, take those lips away That so sweetly promised you'd be faithful to me;

original: And those eyes, the break of day,   Lights that do mislead the morn:
translation: And those eyes that, like the dawn, Make you think that morning has come.

original: But my kisses bring again, bring again;   Seals of love, but sealed in vain, sealed in vain.
translation: But kiss me again and again, To prove your love, though it's all fake, all fake.

original: Break off thy song, and haste thee quick away:
translation: End your song there and go away now.

original: Here comes a man of comfort, whose advice   Hath often still'd my brawling discontent.
translation: Here comes a religious man whose advice always makes me feel better when I'm upset.

original: I cry you mercy, sir; and well could wish   You had not found me here so musical:
translation: Forgive me, sir. I wish you hadn't found me listening to music.

original: Let me excuse me, and believe me so,   My mirth it much displeased, but pleased my woe.
translation: Let me excuse myself, and please believe me: it didn't make me happy, it just made me sadder.

original: 'Tis good; though music oft hath such a charm   To make bad good, and good provoke to harm.
translation: That's all right, although music often has the power to turn bad into good, and good into bad.

original: I pray, you, tell me, hath any body inquired   for me here to-day? much upon this time have   I promised here to meet.
translation: Please tell me, has anyone asked for me here today? I promised to meet someone here at this time.

original: You have not been inquired after: I have sat here all day.
translation: No one has asked for you. I've sat here all day.

original: I do constantly believe you. The time is come even now. I shall crave your forbearance a little: may be I will call upon you anon, for some advantage to  yourself.
translation: Of course, I believe you. It's just coming to be the time now. Please wait here for a minute—I'll come back to you shortly with some news that will help you.

original: I am always bound to you.
translation: I will always follow your instructions.

original: Very well met, and well come. What is the news from this good deputy?
translation: Good to see you. And you're welcome here. What's the news from the good deputy?

original: He hath a garden circummured with brick,   Whose western side is with a vineyard back'd;
translation: [Showing him a ring of keys]  He has a garden with a brick wall around it; the western side backs up onto a vineyard.

original: And to that vineyard is a planched gate,   That makes his opening with this bigger key:
translation: To enter the vineyard, there's a gate that can be opened with this bigger key.

original: This other doth command a little door   Which from the vineyard to the garden leads;
translation: This other one opens a little door between the vineyard and the garden.

original: There have I made my promise   Upon the heavy middle of the night   To call upon him.
translation: I promised to meet him there in the middle of the night.

original: But shall you on your knowledge find this way?
translation: But do you know how to get there?

original: I have ta'en a due and wary note upon't:
translation: I was careful to remember it.

original: With whispering and most guilty diligence,   In action all of precept, he did show me   The way twice o'er.
translation: He showed me the way twice, whispering and looking guilty about everything he did.

original: Are there no other tokens Between you 'greed concerning her observance?
translation: And you didn't agree on any other details for the meeting?

original: No, none, but only a repair i' the dark;   And that I have possess'd him my most stay   Can be but brief;
translation: No, none, just that we'll meet in the dark and that I can only stay for a little while.

original: for I have made him know   I have a servant comes with me along,   That stays upon me,
translation: I told him that my servant will come with me and wait for me,

original: whose persuasion is   I come about my brother.
translation: thinking I'm visiting my brother.

original: 'Tis well borne up. I have not yet made known to Mariana A word of this. What, ho! within! come forth!
translation: That's well done. I haven't told Mariana about this yet.  Hello there! You in there, come out!

original: I pray you, be acquainted with this maid; She comes to do you good.
translation: Please be introduced. Here's a girl who's come to help you.

original: I do desire the like.
translation: That's what I hope.

original: Do you persuade yourself that I respect you?
translation: You know that I respect you, right?

original: Good friar, I know you do, and have found it.
translation: Good friar, I know you do; I've found you to be respectful.

original: Take, then, this your companion by the hand,   Who hath a story ready for your ear.
translation: Take this girl's hand, then, and listen to the story she has to tell you.

original: I shall attend your leisure: but make haste;   The vaporous night approaches.
translation: I'll wait for you. But hurry—it's nearly nightfall.

original: Will't please you walk aside?
translation: Will you come walk with me alone?

original: O place and greatness! millions of false eyes   Are stuck upon thee:
translation: Oh, rank! Oh, power! Millions of eyes are on you at all times.

original: volumes of report   Run with these false and most contrarious quests   Upon thy doings:
translation: The history books are full of misleading, misguided attempts to secure you.

original: thousand escapes of wit   Make thee the father of their idle dreams   And rack thee in their fancies.
translation: You always seem to remain out of reach, which is why you continue to fill people's dreams and take up all their waking thoughts.

original: Welcome, how agreed?
translation: Welcome back. Have you both agreed?

original: She'll take the enterprise upon her, father, If you advise it.
translation: Father, she'll do it, if you tell her to.

original: It is not my consent, But my entreaty too.
translation: I don't just agree to it, I'm asking her to do it, too.

original: Little have you to say When you depart from him, but, soft and low, "Remember now my brother."
translation: You don't have to say anything when you leave him, except whisper, "Remember my brother, now."

original: Fear me not.
translation: Don't worry.

original: Nor, gentle daughter, fear you not at all.   He is your husband on a pre-contract:
translation: And you, my daughter, don't you worry at all. He's your husband by engagement.

original: To bring you thus together, 'tis no sin,   Sith that the justice of your title to him   Doth flourish the deceit.
translation: It's not sinful for you to have sex with him. The fact that you're legally bound to him as a wife makes the trick the opposite of dishonest.

original: Come, let us go:   Our corn's to reap, for yet our tithe's to sow.
translation: Come on, let's go. It's time to put our plan into action.

original: Come hither, sirrah. Can you cut off a man's head?
translation: Come here, sir. Could you cut off a man's head?

original: If the man be a bachelor, sir, I can;
translation: I can if he's a bachelor, sir.

original: but if he be a   married man, he's his wife's head, and I can never   cut off a woman's head.
translation: But if he's a married man, he's his  wife's head , and I could never cut off a woman's head.

original: Come, sir, leave me your snatches, and yield me a   direct answer.
translation: Come on, sir, none of your jokes—give me a direct answer.

original: To-morrow morning are to die Claudio   and Barnardine. Here is in our prison a common   executioner, who in his office lacks a helper:
translation: Tomorrow morning, Claudio and Barnadine are sentenced to die. There's a common executioner here in our prison who needs a helper.

original: if   you will take it on you to assist him, it shall   redeem you from your gyves;
translation: If you'll help him, you can get out of prison early.

original: if not, you shall have   your full time of imprisonment and your deliverance   with an unpitied whipping, for you have been a   notorious bawd.
translation: If not, you'll serve your full sentence and be released with a full whipping, since you're a notorious pimp.

original: Sir, I have been an unlawful bawd time out of mind;   but yet I will be content to be a lawful hangman.
translation: Sir, I've been an illegal pimp for as long as I can remember, but I'd be happy to be a legal executioner.

original: I   would be glad to receive some instruction from my   fellow partner.
translation: It'd be helpful to receive some instructions from my fellow worker.

original: What, ho! Abhorson! Where's Abhorson, there?
Do you call, sir?
translation: Did you call me, sir?

original: Sirrah, here's a fellow will help you to-morrow in   your execution.
translation: Sir, this man will help you tomorrow with the execution.

original: If you think it meet, compound with   him by the year, and let him abide here with you;
translation: If you see fit, take him on full-time and let him live here with you.

original: if   not, use him for the present and dismiss him. He   cannot plead his estimation with you; he hath been a  bawd.
translation: If not, use him for now and then get rid of him. He can't say much for himself when it comes to his reputation; he's been a pimp.

original: A bawd, sir? fie upon him! he will discredit our  mystery.
translation: A pimp, sir? Get rid of him! He'll ruin all the mystery.

original: Go to, sir; you weigh equally; a feather will turn the scale.
translation: Enough, sir. The two of you are equally on the scale. A feather would tip it.

original: Pray, sir, by your good favour,—for surely, sir, a good favour you have, but that you have a hanging look,—do you call, sir, your occupation a mystery?
Ay, sir; a mystery
translation: Yes, sir, a mystery.

original: Painting, sir, I have heard say, is a mystery; and   your whores, sir, being members of my occupation,   using painting, do prove my occupation a mystery:
translation: Sir, I've heard that painting is a mystery. And whores, sir, who work in my occupation, paint their faces, so that makes my occupation a  mystery.

original: but what mystery there should be in hanging, if I   should be hanged, I cannot imagine.
translation: But the mystery of hanging? If I were going to be hanged, I can't imagine.

original: Sir, it is a mystery.
translation: Sir, it is a mystery.

original: Proof?
translation: Proof?

original: Every true man's apparel fits your thief: if it be   too little for your thief, your true man thinks it   big enough;
translation: Every executioner's clothes  fit  the thief. If the clothes are too small for the thief, the executioner thinks they look big enough.

original: if it be too big for your thief, your   thief thinks it little enough: so every true man's   apparel fits your thief.
translation: If they're too big for the thief, the executioner thinks they're small enough. So every executioner's clothes fit a thief.

original: Are you agreed?
translation: Have you reached an agreement?

original: Sir, I will serve him; for I do find your hangman is a more penitent trade than your bawd; he doth oftener ask forgiveness.
You, sirrah, provide your block and your axe to-morrow four o'clock.
Come on, bawd; I will instruct thee in my trade;  follow.
translation: Come on, pimp. I'll teach you my trade. Follow me.

original: I do desire to learn, sir: and I hope, if you have   occasion to use me for your own turn, you shall find   me yare;
translation: I want to learn, sir. And I hope—if you have the need to use me for longer—that you'll find I'm up to the task.

original: for truly, sir, for your kindness I owe you   a good turn.
translation: For, truly, I owe you for your kindness, sir.

original: Call hither Barnardine and Claudio.
translation: Bring Barnadine and Claudio here.

original: The one has my pity; not a jot the other, Being a murderer, though he were my brother.
translation: I pity one of them, but wouldn't pity the other one—a murderer—even if he were my own brother.

original: Look, here's the warrant, Claudio, for thy death:
translation: Look, Claudio: here's the warrant for your death.

original: 'Tis now dead midnight, and by eight to-morrow   Thou must be made immortal. Where's Barnardine?
translation: It's now exactly midnight, and by eight tomorrow you'll be on your way to the afterlife. Where's Barnadine?

original: As fast lock'd up in sleep as guiltless labour When it lies starkly in the traveller's bones: He will not wake.
translation: As fast asleep as an innocent traveler when he sleeps along the road. He won't wake up.

original: Who can do good on him? Well, go, prepare yourself.  But, hark, what noise? Heaven give your spirits comfort!
translation: What can anyone do to help him? Well, go, prepare yourself.  But wait, what's that noise? May God give you peace.

original: By and by. I hope it is some pardon or reprieve For the most gentle Claudio.
translation: Just a moment![To himself] I hope it's a pardon or reprieve for the very noble Claudio.

original: Welcome father.
translation: Welcome, father.

original: The best and wholesomest spirts of the night Envelope you, good Provost! Who call'd here of late?
translation: Bless you. I hope you're having a good night, good Provost! Who came here so late?

original: None, since the curfew rung.
translation: No one, since the last bells rung.

original: Not Isabel?
translation: Not Isabella?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: They will, then, ere't be long.
translation: They will, then, before too long.

original: What comfort is for Claudio?
translation: Is there any comfort for Claudio?

original: There's some in hope.
translation: Hope brings some comfort.

original: It is a bitter deputy.
translation: Angelo is a terrible deputy.

original: Not so, not so; his life is parallel'd   Even with the stroke and line of his great justice:
translation: Not true, not true! His life holds up to the standard of his extreme justice.

original: He doth with holy abstinence subdue   That in himself which he spurs on his power   To qualify in others:
translation: He keeps his own desires at bay with holy discipline; that's what gives him the authority to correct faults in others.

original: were he meal'd with that   Which he corrects, then were he tyrannous;   But this being so, he's just.
translation: If he were the same as the people he corrected, he'd be a tyrant. But, because of his good character, he's just.

original: [Knocking within]   Now are they come.
translation: [The sound of knocking comes from offstage]  Now they're here.

original: This is a gentle provost: seldom when   The steeled gaoler is the friend of men.
translation: This is a good provost. It's not often that a steely jailor is friendly like this.

original: [Knocking within]   How now! what noise? That spirit's possessed with haste   That wounds the unsisting postern with these strokes.
translation: [The sound of more knocking]  What now? What's that noise? Anyone who knocks that hard at the back door must be in a real hurry!

original: There he must stay until the officer Arise to let him in: he is call'd up.
translation: He'll stay there until the officer comes to let him in. His time has come.

original: Have you no countermand for Claudio yet, But he must die to-morrow?
translation: You don't have a pardon for Claudio yet? He has to die tomorrow?

original: None, sir, none.
translation: No pardon, sir, none.

original: As near the dawning, provost, as it is, You shall hear more ere morning.
translation: Although it's already near morning, Provost, you'll hear more before dawn.

original: Happily   You something know; yet I believe there comes   No countermand;
translation: I hope you know something, but I don't think there's a pardon coming.

original: no such example have we:
translation: There's no precedent for it.

original: Besides, upon the very siege of justice   Lord Angelo hath to the public ear   Profess'd the contrary.
translation: Besides, Lord Angelo has spoken against overturning justice to the public.

original: This is his lordship's man.
translation: This is his Lordship Angelo's servant.

original: And here comes Claudio's pardon.
translation: And here comes Claudio's pardon.

original: [Giving a paper]   My lord hath sent you this note; and by me this   further charge, that you swerve not from the   smallest article of it,
