original: One sin, I know, another doth provoke;   Murder's as near to lust as flame to smoke:
translation: One sin leads to another; murder is as close to lust as fire is to smoke.

original: Poison and treason are the hands of sin,   Ay, and the targets, to put off the shame:
translation: If I stick around, I'll be poisoned, or accused of treason, anything to keep me from exposing him.

original: Then, lest my lie be cropp'd to keep you clear,   By flight I'll shun the danger which I fear.
translation: So, to save myself and not expose him, I'll leave here and escape the danger I'm afraid of.

original: He hath found the meaning, for which we mean   To have his head.
translation: He's figured out the riddle, which means I'll have to kill him.

original: He must not live to trumpet forth my infamy,   Nor tell the world Antiochus doth sin   In such a loathed manner;
translation: He can't survive another day to ruin my reputation, or to tell the world the hateful sin I've committed.

original: And therefore instantly this prince must die:   For by his fall my honour must keep high.
translation: The prince must die instantly for my honor's sake.

original: Who attends us there?
translation: Who's there?

original: Doth your highness call?
translation: Did you call, sir?

original: Thaliard,   You are of our chamber, and our mind partakes   Her private actions to your secrecy;   And for your faithfulness we will advance you.
Thaliard, behold, here's poison, and here's gold;   We hate the prince of Tyre, and thou must kill him:
translation: [He pulls out a bottle of poison and a bag of gold]  Look, Thaliard, here's poison, and here's gold. I hate Pericles, Prince of Tyre, and I want you to kill him.

original: It fits thee not to ask the reason why,   Because we bid it. Say, is it done?
translation: Don't ask me why—it's because I said so. Understand?

original: My lord, 'Tis done.
translation: Sir, I understand.

original: Enough.
translation: Good.

original: Let your breath cool yourself, telling your haste.
translation: Catch your breath, please. We can tell you've come in a rush.

original: My lord, prince Pericles is fled.
translation: Sir, Prince Pericles is gone.

original: As thou   Wilt live, fly after:
translation: If you want to live, go after him!

original: and like an arrow shot   From a well-experienced archer hits the mark   His eye doth level at, so thou ne'er return
translation: Be like an arrow shot by an experienced archer— hit the target I've got my sights on, and don't come back here

original: Unless thou say 'Prince Pericles is dead.'
translation: until you can tell me that Pericles is dead.

original: My lord, If I can get him within my pistol's length, I'll make him sure enough: so, farewell to your  highness.
translation: Sir, if I can get within gunshot, I'll take him out. Goodbye, sir.

original: Thaliard, adieu!
translation: Goodbye, Thaliard!

original: Till Pericles be dead, My heart can lend no succor to my head.
translation: I won't rest until Pericles is dead.

original: Let none disturb us.—
translation: Don't let anyone come in here.

original: Why should   this change of thoughts,   The sad companion, dull-eyed melancholy,   Be my so used a guest as not an hour,   In the day's glorious walk, or peaceful night,   The tomb where grief should sleep, can breed me quiet?
translation: Why am I so changed? Why am I sad, downcast, and melancholy every hour of every day? Neither a beautiful day nor a quiet night (which should be where I put my worries to rest) can give me peace.

original: Here pleasures court mine eyes, and mine eyes shun  them,   And danger, which I fear'd, is at Antioch,   Whose aim seems far too short to hit me here:
translation: Even when I'm surrounded by things I should enjoy, I can't get rid of this fear of danger waiting for me at Antioch— but there's no way the king could reach me here!

original: Yet neither pleasure's art can joy my spirits,   Nor yet the other's distance comfort me.
translation: And yet, nothing can cheer me up, not even the reality of distance.

original: Then it is thus: the passions of the mind,   That have their first conception by mis-dread,   Have after-nourishment and life by care;   And what was first but fear what might be done,   Grows elder now and cares it be not done.
translation: That's the way the mind works: once we start worrying about something, it only gets worse and worse, until we convince ourselves that the danger is real.

original: And so with me: the great Antiochus,   'Gainst whom I am too little to contend,   Since he's so great can make his will his act,   Will think me speaking, though I swear to silence;
translation: Just like that, my fear of Antiochus, who is a much more powerful king than I am—and can put his desires into action— has been blown out of proportion. Even though I haven't said a word, he'll assume I've told his secret.

original: Nor boots it me to say I honour him.   If he suspect I may dishonour him:
translation: And it won't help for me to say I'm loyal to him, if he's already decided I'm not.

original: And what may make him blush in being known,   He'll stop the course by which it might be known;
translation: If he's determined to keep his secret under wraps, all he has to do is kill me.

original: With hostile forces he'll o'erspread the land,   And with the ostent of war will look so huge,   Amazement shall drive courage from the state;   Our men be vanquish'd ere they do resist,
translation: He'll infiltrate my country with his armies, wage war, and overthrow the government .

original: And subjects punish'd that ne'er thought offence:
translation: He'll punish my subjects, too, even though they never did anything to hurt him.

original: Which care of them, not pity of myself,
translation: I'm more worried about them than I am about myself;

original: Who am no more but as the tops of trees,   Which fence the roots they grow by and defend them,   Makes both my body pine and soul to languish,   And punish that before that he would punish.
translation: I'm just the treetops that protect the roots by which the people grow, and help defend them. It's concern for them that makes my body  sick  and my soul tired with wanting to punish Antiochus before he punishes us.

original: Joy and all comfort in your sacred breast!
translation: God bless you, sir!

original: And keep your mind, till you return to us, Peaceful and comfortable!
translation: And good luck on your journey!

original: Peace, peace, and give experience tongue.
translation: Quiet, please. Let someone who knows what he's talking about speak up.

original: They do abuse the king that flatter him:
translation: These men are just flattering you, sir, and flattery only fans the fire of sin.

original: For flattery is the bellows blows up sin;   The thing which is flatter'd, but a spark,   To which that blast gives heat and stronger glowing;
translation: When a king's fault is just a spark, flattery is the blast that gives it heat and makes it glow stronger.

original: Whereas reproof, obedient and in order,   Fits kings, as they are men, for they may err.
translation: On the other hand, wise advice is the best tool a king can make use of, since even kings make mistakes sometimes.

original: When Signior Sooth here does proclaim a peace,   He flatters you, makes war upon your life.
translation: When Mr. Yes-man over here wishes you good luck, he's flattering you and, really, threatening your life.

original: Prince, pardon me, or strike me, if you please;   I cannot be much lower than my knees.
translation: [He kneels]  Forgive me, sir. Hit me if you want. I can't get much lower than here, on my knees.

original: All leave us else; but let your cares o'erlook What shipping and what lading's in our haven, And then return to us.   @ Helicanus, thou Hast moved us: what seest thou in our looks?
translation: Everyone else leave. But take care to see what ships are coming in and out of the harbor and report back to me.Helicanus, you've got my attention. How do I look?

original: An angry brow, dread lord.
translation: You look angry, sir.

original: If there be such a dart in princes' frowns, How durst thy tongue move anger to our face?
translation: You know that kings' moods can have serious consequences, right? How dare you make me angry?

original: How dare the plants look up to heaven, from whence They have their nourishment?
translation: How dare plants grow up toward the sky, from which they receive rain and sun?

original: Thou know'st I have power To take thy life from thee.
translation: You know I have the power to kill you.

original: I have ground the axe myself; Do you but strike the blow.
translation: I sharpened the axe myself. Just strike the blow.

original: Rise, prithee, rise.   Sit down: thou art no flatterer:   I thank thee for it;
translation: Get up, please. Get up. Sit down. I'm glad you're not a flatterer.

original: and heaven forbid   That kings should let their ears hear their   faults hid!
translation: Kings shouldn't be surrounded by men who make excuses for their faults!

original: Fit counsellor and servant for a prince,   Who by thy wisdom makest a prince thy servant,   What wouldst thou have me do?
translation: You're a wise counsellor and servant fit for a prince; by your wisdom, you've made me your servant, ready to do your will. What should I do?

original: To bear with patience Such griefs as you yourself do lay upon yourself.
translation: Be patient, and don't be so hard on yourself.

original: Thou speak'st like a physician, Helicanus,   That minister'st a potion unto me   That thou wouldst tremble to receive thyself.
translation: You sound like a doctor, Helicanus, but what you're prescribing me is something you'd hardly do yourself.

original: Attend me, then: I went to Antioch,   Where as thou know'st, against the face of death,   I sought the purchase of a glorious beauty.
translation: You see, I went to Antioch where, as you know, I faced death for the chance to win a famously beautiful woman.

original: From whence an issue I might propagate,   Are arms to princes, and bring joys to subjects.
translation: I had hoped we would get married and have children together, heirs for my throne that would strengthen my rule in this country and delight my subjects.

original: Her face was to mine eye beyond all wonder;   The rest—   hark in thine ear—   as black as incest:
translation: I thought she was beautiful in person, but listen: they were committing incest.

original: Which by my knowledge found, the sinful father   Seem'd not to strike, but smooth:
translation: Once I figured it out, her sinful father didn't lash out; he suddenly became very smooth.

original: but thou   know'st this,   'Tis time to fear when tyrants seem to kiss.
translation: As you well know, it's time to be afraid  when tyrants kiss you .

original: Such fear so grew in me, I hither fled,   Under the covering of a careful night,   Who seem'd my good protector; and, being here,   Bethought me what was past, what might succeed.
translation: I ran away in the dark of night and, once I got here, thought I was safe.

original: I knew him tyrannous; and tyrants' fears   Decrease not, but grow faster than the years:
translation: I know Antiochus is a tyrant, and that he's probably getting increasingly paranoid about what I know.

original: And should he doubt it, as no doubt he doth,   That I should open to the listening air   How many worthy princes' bloods were shed,   To keep his bed of blackness unlaid ope,
translation: And if he suspects that I've told the world how he killed all of those princes, and slept with his own daughter,

original: To lop that doubt, he'll fill this land with arms,   And make pretence of wrong that I have done him:
translation: then there's no doubt that he'll invade our country on the pretense of me having offended him.

original: When all, for mine, if I may call offence,   Must feel war's blow, who spares not innocence:   Which love to all, of which thyself art one,   Who now reprovest me for it,—
translation: Then the country will be plunged into war for my so— called offense, and many innocent people will die, and everyone I love, yourself included, will blame me for it—

original: Alas, sir!
translation: Oh, sir!

original: Drew sleep out of mine eyes, blood from my cheeks,   Musings into my mind, with thousand doubts   How I might stop this tempest ere it came;
translation: I can't sleep. I'm pale and sick. I can't stop thinking about it, can't stop trying to come up with ways to stop this storm before it happens.

original: And finding little comfort to relieve them,   I thought it princely charity to grieve them.
translation: And since there's no solution, I'm just letting myself be sad about it.

original: Well, my lord, since you have given me leave to speak.   Freely will I speak. Antiochus you fear,   And justly too, I think, you fear the tyrant,   Who either by public war or private treason   Will take away your life.
translation: Well, sir, since you've given me permission to speak, I will. You're right to be afraid of Antiochus, since he'll either wage a public war or kill you privately.

original: Therefore, my lord, go travel for a while,   Till that his rage and anger be forgot,   Or till the Destinies do cut his thread of life.
translation: So, I recommend that you get away and don't come back until he either gets over his anger or  dies .

original: Your rule direct to any; if to me.   Day serves not light more faithful than I'll be.
translation: You can trust me to rule the country while you're gone; I'll be as faithful as day is to the sun.

original: I do not doubt thy faith; But should he wrong my liberties in my absence?
translation: I do trust you, but what if Antiochus attacks while I'm gone?

original: We'll mingle our bloods together in the earth, From whence we had our being and our birth.
Tyre, I now look from thee then, and to Tarsus   Intend my travel, where I'll hear from thee;   And by whose letters I'll dispose myself.
translation: Well, then, I'll leave Tyre and head to Tarsus. I'lll wait for a letter from you there.

original: The care I had and have of subjects' good   On thee I lay whose wisdom's strength can bear it.
translation: Take care of my subjects while I'm gone; I leave it up to the strength of your wisdom.

original: I'll take thy word for faith, not ask thine oath:
translation: I'll take whatever you say as truth; I won't ask you to swear, since you either mean what you say or you don't.

original: Who shuns not to break one will sure crack both:   But in our orbs we'll live so round and safe,   That time of both this truth shall ne'er convince,   Thou show'dst a subject's shine, I a true prince.
translation: We'll each do our jobs, safe and surrounded in our own spheres. Time will tell how you'll be the best subject you can be, and how I'll be the best prince.

original: So, this is Tyre, and this the court. Here must I   kill King Pericles; and if I do it not, I am sure to   be hanged at home: 'tis dangerous.
translation: So, this is Tyre, and this is the court. I'm supposed to kill King Pericles here and, if I don't do it, I'll be hanged back home. It's dangerous.

original: Well, I perceive   he was a wise fellow, and had good discretion, that,   being bid to ask what he would of the king, desired   he might know none of his secrets:
translation: Well, now I see that a man would be wise if, being told to ask for whatever he wanted from the king, said he didn't want to know any of the king's secrets.

original: now do I see he   had some reason for't; for if a king bid a man be a   villain,
translation: Now I see his reason for it: I mean, if a king tells you to be a villain,

original: he's bound by the indenture of his oath to   be one! Hush! here come the lords of Tyre.
translation: you're bound by your promise to him to be one. Quiet! Here come the lords of Tyre.

original: You shall not need, my fellow peers of Tyre,   Further to question me of your king's departure:
translation: Fellow lords of Tyre, there's no need to question me anymore about the king's departure.

original: His seal'd commission, left in trust with me,   Doth speak sufficiently he's gone to travel.
translation: He left his sealed letter of approval with me; that's enough proof for my role while he's traveling.

original: How! the king gone!
translation: What? The king's gone?

original: If further yet you will be satisfied, Why, as it were unlicensed of your loves, He would depart, I'll give some light unto you. Being at Antioch—
translation: If you're still not satisfied—since he didn't go with your permission—I'll tell you why he left. When he was at Antioch—

original: What from Antioch?
translation: What about Antioch?

original: Royal Antiochus—on what cause I know not—   Took some displeasure at him; at least he judged so:
translation: For reasons unknown to me, King Antiochus got angry at him (or at least Pericles thought so).

original: And doubting lest that he had err'd or sinn'd,   To show his sorrow, he'ld correct himself;
translation: Pericles, worried that he had offended the king, to show his remorse until he could rectify the situation,

original: So puts himself unto the shipman's toil,   With whom each minute threatens life or death.
translation: decided to sail away, despite it being dangerous on the seas.

original: Well, I perceive   I shall not be hang'd now, although I would;
translation: Well, I guess I won't be hanged now (though I almost was).

original: But since he's gone, the king's seas must please:
translation: He's gone, but the king should be happy anyway,

original: He 'scaped the land, to perish at the sea.
translation: since Pericles will probably die at sea. I'll come out of hiding.

original: I'll present myself. Peace to the lords of Tyre!
translation: Greetings, lords of Tyre!

original: Lord Thaliard from Antiochus is welcome.
translation: Welcome, Lord Thaliard of Antioch.

original: From him I come   With message unto princely Pericles;
translation: I have a message from Antiochus for Prince Pericles

original: But since my landing I have understood   Your lord has betook himself to unknown travels,   My message must return from whence it came.
translation: but, since I got here I've heard that the prince is out on some unknown travels. I guess I'll have to take my message back to where it came from.

original: We have no reason to desire it,   Commended to our master, not to us:
translation: We certainly wouldn't ask you to read it to us if it's addressed to Pericles.

original: Yet, ere you shall depart, this we desire,   As friends to Antioch, we may feast in Tyre.
translation: But please, before you leave, let's celebrate our friendship with a feast here in Tyre.

original: My Dionyza, shall we rest us here, And by relating tales of others' griefs, See if 'twill teach us to forget our own?
translation: Dionyza, should we sit down here and tell each other sad stories? Maybe that way we'll forget our own sad lives.

original: That were to blow at fire in hope to quench it;
translation: That's like blowing on a fire to try to put it out.

original: For who digs hills because they do aspire   Throws down one mountain to cast up a higher.
translation: It's like digging up a hill to stop it growing tall; you'll build a higher mountain in the process.

original: O my distressed lord, even such our griefs are;   Here they're but felt, and seen with mischief's eyes,   But like to groves, being topp'd, they higher rise.
translation: My dear, as bad as our suffering is, at least it's only felt. If someone up to no good were to take notice,  they might make things even worse.

original: O Dionyza,   Who wanteth food, and will not say he wants it,   Or can conceal his hunger till he famish?
translation: Oh, Dionyza, how can someone who's starving not beg for food? Can he pretend he's not hungry until he dies?

original: Our tongues and sorrows do sound deep   Our woes into the air; our eyes do weep,   Till tongues fetch breath that may proclaim them  louder;
translation: We should proclaim our grief loudly, cry out, weep, then shout even louder.

original: That, if heaven slumber while their creatures want,   They may awake their helps to comfort them.
translation: Then maybe the gods will wake up from their sleep, take notice of how their creatures are suffering, and help us.

original: I'll then discourse our woes, felt several years,   And wanting breath to speak help me with tears.
translation: I'll start by telling our sad story of the last few years, and you can help me by crying during the pauses.

original: I'll do my best, sir.
translation: I'll do my best, sir.

original: This Tarsus, o'er which I have the government,   A city on whom plenty held full hand,   For riches strew'd herself even in the streets;
translation: Tarsus, which I rule, was once wealthy. We had everything we wanted: the streets were strewn with riches,

original: Whose towers bore heads so high they kiss'd the clouds,   And strangers ne'er beheld but wondered at;
translation: we built towers up to the skies, and every visitor who came here was amazed.

original: Whose men and dames so jetted and adorn'd,   Like one another's glass to trim them by:
translation: Our men and women wore fine clothes and jewelry; they were like mirrors to each other's own riches.

original: Their tables were stored full, to glad the sight,   And not so much to feed on as delight;
translation: They had more than enough food on their tables.

original: All poverty was scorn'd, and pride so great,   The name of help grew odious to repeat.
translation: No one was poor. We were proud; we couldn't imagine needing help from anyone.

original: O, 'tis too true.
translation: Oh, it's too true.

original: But see what heaven can do! By this our change,   These mouths, who but of late, earth, sea, and air,   Were all too little to content and please,
translation: But look what heaven can do! At one time, the earth, sea, and air were hardly enough to content and please our mouths,

original: Although they gave their creatures in abundance,   As houses are defiled for want of use,   They are now starved for want of exercise:
translation: though they gave us all the food we needed to survive. Just as houses become run-down from lack of use, our mouths are now starved for lack of exercise.

original: Those palates who, not yet two summers younger,   Must have inventions to delight the taste,   Would now be glad of bread, and beg for it:
translation: Two years ago we looked for the best recipes to please our palates; now we'd be happy to get a crust a bread, and beg for it.

original: Those mothers who, to nousle up their babes,   Thought nought too curious, are ready now   To eat those little darlings whom they loved.
translation: Women who once happily nursed their babies would hardly think it strange that they would now want to eat them.

original: So sharp are hunger's teeth, that man and wife   Draw lots who first shall die to lengthen life:
translation: Hunger is such a grim reality that husbands and wives take bets on which of them will die first.

original: Here stands a lord, and there a lady weeping;   Here many sink, yet those which see them fall   Have scarce strength left to give them burial.   Is not this true?
translation: Look, there's a man, and there's a woman crying. Here so many are sick that, even when someone dies, no one has the strength to bury them. Isn't this true?

original: Our cheeks and hollow eyes do witness it.
translation: You can tell by our sunken cheeks and hollow eyes.

original: O, let those cities that of plenty's cup   And her prosperities so largely taste,   With their superfluous riots, hear these tears!
translation: Oh, if only the cities that have enough, who enjoy the tastes of prosperity, with their superfluous riots, would hear these tears!

original: The misery of Tarsus may be theirs.
translation: One day, they could be as miserable as Tarsus.

original: Where's the lord governor?
translation: Where's the governor?

original: Here. Speak out thy sorrows which thou bring'st in haste, For comfort is too far for us to expect.
translation: Here. Tell me the bad news that you hurried to bring us; I can't imagine it's good news you bring.

original: We have descried, upon our neighbouring shore, A portly sail of ships make hitherward.
translation: We can make out, on the opposite shore, a large group of ships sailing this way.

original: I thought as much.   One sorrow never comes but brings an heir,   That may succeed as his inheritor;
translation: I figured. It never rains but it pours; one struggle gives way to another.

original: And so in ours:
translation: It's that way with us.

original: some neighbouring nation,   Taking advantage of our misery,   Hath stuff'd these hollow vessels with their power,   To beat us down, the which are down already;
translation: Some nearby country is going to take advantage of our weakness. They've sent all these ships to kick us while we're down,

original: And make a conquest of unhappy me,   Whereas no glory's got to overcome.
translation: and conquer us in our misery, though it'll hardly be difficult for them to overcome us.

original: That's the least fear; for, by the semblance Of their white flags display'd, they bring us peace, And come to us as favourers, not as foes.
translation: I don't think so. They're flying white flags to show they come in peace. They're coming as friends rather than as foes.

original: Thou speak'st like him's untutor'd to repeat:
translation: You idiot, that doesn't mean anything!

original: Who makes the fairest show means most deceit.
translation: Those that seem to be the most kind are the most deceitful.

original: But bring they what they will and what they can,   What need we fear?
translation: But let them do what they will and what they can, why should we be afraid?

original: The ground's the lowest, and we are half way there.
translation: Our lives couldn't be more miserable than they are now; we're halfway to the ground.

original: Go tell their general we attend him here,   To know for what he comes, and whence he comes,   And what he craves.
translation: Go, tell their general he can meet us here to announce why and from where he comes, and what he wants.

original: I go, my lord.
translation: On my way, sir.

original: Welcome is peace, if he on peace consist; If wars, we are unable to resist.
translation: Peace would be great, if that's what he's here for. If it's war he wants, there's nothing we can do about it.

original: Lord governor, for so we hear you are,   Let not our ships and number of our men   Be like a beacon fired to amaze your eyes.
translation: So we hear you're the governor? Don't be so surprised by all our ships and men.

original: We have heard your miseries as far as Tyre,   And seen the desolation of your streets:
translation: We've heard about your suffering all the way in Tyre, and we've seen the destruction in your streets.

original: Nor come we to add sorrow to your tears,   But to relieve them of their heavy load;
translation: We came to help, not to make things worse.

original: And these our ships, you happily may think   Are like the Trojan horse was stuff'd within   With bloody veins, expecting overthrow,
translation: These ships might look like the  Trojan horse  (which had Greek soldiers hidden inside, bloodthirsty and ready to attack),

original: Are stored with corn to make your needy bread,   And give them life whom hunger starved half dead.
translation: but they're filled with grain to make bread, to bring all your starving people back to life.

original: The gods of Greece protect you! And we'll pray for you.
translation: May the gods of Greece protect you! And we'll pray for you.

original: Arise, I pray you, rise: We do not look for reverence, but to love, And harbourage for ourself, our ships, and men.
translation: Get up, please. I didn't come to be worshipped. All I ask is a place for myself, my ships, and my men to stay.

original: The which when any shall not gratify,   Or pay you with unthankfulness in thought,   Be it our wives, our children, or ourselves,
translation: If anyone fails to thank you, or think grateful thoughts toward you—whether it's our wives, children, or ourselves—

original: The curse of heaven and men succeed their evils!
translation: may they be cursed by heaven and punished by men!

original: Till when,—the which I hope shall ne'er be seen,—   Your grace is welcome to our town and us.
translation: Until the day someone denies you (which day we hope will never come) you're very welcome here in our town and with us.

original: Which welcome we'll accept; feast here awhile, Until our stars that frown lend us a smile.
translation: We'll accept your welcome and feast here a while, until our fortunes turn again from bad to good.

original: Yet cease your ire, you angry stars of heaven!
translation: Please, heaven, stop your wrath!

original: Wind, rain, and thunder, remember, earthly man   Is but a substance that must yield to you;   And I, as fits my nature, do obey you:
translation: Wind, rain and thunder: remember that earthly men can only yield to you and recognize that I, as an earthly man, do obey you.

original: Alas, the sea hath cast me on the rocks,   Wash'd me from shore to shore, and left me breath   Nothing to think on but ensuing death:
translation: The sea has tossed me onto the rocks, washed me from shore to shore, and left me sure of nothing but that my end is near.

original: Let it suffice the greatness of your powers   To have bereft a prince of all his fortunes;
translation: Please, let it be enough for your great powers that I, a prince, have lost everything.

original: And having thrown him from your watery grave,   Here to have death in peace is all he'll crave.
translation: Since you've thrown me out of your watery grave, all I ask is to die here in peace.

original: What, ho, Pilch!
translation: Come on, buddy!

original: Ha, come and bring away the nets!
translation: Hey, come bring the nets in!

original: What, Patch-breech, I say!
translation: What'd you say, dummy?

original: What say you, master?
translation: What did you say, master?

original: Look how thou stirrest now! come away, or I'll fetch thee with a wanion.
translation: Oh, look how fast you're moving now! Come on, then, or I'll come after you with a vengeance.

original: Faith, master, I am thinking of the poor men that were cast away before us even now.
translation: Master, I'm thinking of the poor men that were shipwrecked before us even now.

original: Alas, poor souls, it grieved my heart to hear what pitiful cries they made to us to help them, when, well-a-day, we could scarce help ourselves.
translation: Poor souls. It was heart-wrenching to hear them crying out for help when, truth be told, we could barely help ourselves.

original: Nay, master, said not I as much when I saw the   porpus how he bounced and tumbled?
translation: I told you this was coming when I saw the dolphin jumping in the waves.

original: they say   they're half fish, half flesh: a plague on them,   they ne'er come but I look to be washed.
translation: T hey say dolphins are part fish, part human . . . curse them, every time I see one I end up in a storm.

original: Master, I   marvel how the fishes live in the sea.
translation: Master, how do fish live in the sea?

original: Why, as men do a-land; the great ones eat up the   little ones:
translation: The same way men do on land: the big ones eat the little ones.

original: I can compare our rich misers to   nothing so fitly as to a whale;
translation: Whales are like rich men ,

original: a' plays and   tumbles, driving the poor fry before him, and at   last devours them all at a mouthful:
translation: they play and tumble, pushing all the little fish in front of them, then eat them up all in one gulp.

original: such whales   have I heard on o' the land, who never leave gaping   till they've swallowed the whole parish, church,   steeple, bells, and all.
translation: I've heard of whales like that on land, who won't stop until they've swallowed the whole parish, church, steeple, bells, and everything else.

original: A pretty moral.
translation: That's a nice moral.

original: But, master, if I had been the sexton, I would have been that day in the belfry.
Why, man?
translation: Why, man?

original: Because he should have swallowed me too: and when I   had been in his belly, I would have kept such a   jangling of the bells, that he should never have   left,
translation: Because, when he swallowed me, I would have made a bunch of noise in his belly. I would have jangled all the bells so much that he wouldn't have left

original: till he cast bells, steeple, church, and   parish up again. But if the good King Simonides   were of my mind,—
translation: until he vomited up all the bells, steeple, church, and parish again. If King Simonides agreed with me—

original: Simonides!
translation: Simonides!

original: We would purge the land of these drones, that rob the bee of her honey.
How from the finny subject of the sea   These fishers tell the infirmities of men;
translation: It's amazing how these fishermen have gone from talking about fish in the sea to explaining the men's weaknesses,

original: And from their watery empire recollect   All that may men approve or men detect!
translation: and how, from their watery corner of the world, they've come to understand everything that men could think of or discover.

original: Peace be at your labour, honest fishermen.
translation: Hello there, honest fishermen.

original: Honest! good fellow, what's that? If it be a day fits you, search out of the calendar, and nobody look after it.
translation: Honest? What's that mean? If you pointed to any old day on the calendar, we wouldn't know what it meant.

original: May see the sea hath cast upon your coast.
translation: As you can see, I've been shipwrecked here.

original: What a drunken knave was the sea to cast thee in our way!
translation: The sea must have been drunk if it dropped you here.

original: A man whom both the waters and the wind,   In that vast tennis-court, have made the ball   For them to play upon, entreats you pity him:
translation: I'm a man whom the waves and the wind have hit around like a tennis ball all day in gigantic tennis court of the sea. Please, have pity on me.

original: He asks of you, that never used to beg.
translation: I'm asking you, and I don't usually beg.

original: No, friend, cannot you beg? Here's them in our country Greece gets more with begging than we can do with working.
translation: You don't beg? There's a lot of people in our country, Greece, that get more from begging than we do from working.

original: Canst thou catch any fishes, then?
translation: Do you know how to catch fish?

original: I never practised it.
translation: I've never tried it.

original: Nay, then thou wilt starve, sure; for here's nothing to be got now-a-days, unless thou canst fish for't.
translation: Well, you'll starve then. There's nothing to be had these days unless you fish for it.

original: What I have been I have forgot to know;   But what I am, want teaches me to think on:
translation: I can't think about what I was before; I can only think about what I am now,

original: A man throng'd up with cold: my veins are chill,   And have no more of life than may suffice   To give my tongue that heat to ask your help;
translation: which is cold. I'm freezing down to my veins and barely have enough life left in me to warm my tongue up to ask you for help.

original: Which if you shall refuse, when I am dead,   For that I am a man, pray see me buried.
translation: Please help me, or at least, when I'm dead, make sure I get a proper burial.

original: Die quoth-a? Now gods forbid! I have a gown here;   come, put it on; keep thee warm.
translation: Did you say "die"? May the gods forbid! I have a coat here, come on, put it on, get warm.

original: Now, afore me, a   handsome fellow!
translation: Now come with me, handsome man!

original: Come, thou shalt go home,
translation: You can come home with me.

original: and   we'll have flesh for holidays, fish for   fasting-days, and moreo'er puddings and flap-jacks,   and thou shalt be welcome.
translation: We'll have  meat on holidays , fish on fasting days, and plenty of desserts and pancakes, and you're welcome to it all.

original: I thank you, sir.
translation: Thank you, sir.

original: Hark you, my friend; you said you could not beg.
translation: Hey, man, you said you wouldn't beg!

original: I did but crave.
translation: I only asked.

original: But crave! Then I'll turn craver too, and so I shall 'scape whipping.
translation: Only asked! Maybe I'll become a beggar too, and talk my way out of a whipping.

original: Why, are all your beggars whipped, then?
translation: Why? Are all beggars whipped in this country, then?

original: O, not all, my friend, not all; for if all your   beggars were whipped, I would wish no better office   than to be beadle.
translation: Oh, not all of them, my friend, not all. If all beggars were whipped, I would want no better job than to  be a beadle.

original: But, master, I'll go draw up the   net.
translation: But master, I'll go pull the nets in.

original: How well this honest mirth becomes their  labour!
translation: Joking makes their work fun!

original: Hark you, sir, do you know where ye are?
translation: Listen, sir, do you know where you are?

original: Not well.
translation: Not really.

original: Why, I'll tell you: this is called Pentapolis, and our king the good Simonides.
translation: Well, I'll tell you. This is Pentapolis, and our king is the good Simonides.

original: The good King Simonides, do you call him.
translation: The good King Simonides, huh?

original: Ay, sir; and he deserves so to be called for his peaceable reign and good government.
translation: Yes, sir, and he deserves it. He rules with peace and good government.

original: He is a happy king, since he gains from his subjects the name of good by his government. How far is his court distant from this shore?
translation: He's fortunate to have his subjects speak so highly of his government. How far is the court from where we are now?

original: Marry, sir, half a day's journey: and I'll tell   you, he hath a fair daughter, and to-morrow is her   birth-day;
translation: Well, sir, it's half a day's journey. And, by the way, he has a beautiful daughter and tomorrow is her birthday.

original: and there are princes and knights come   from all parts of the world to just and tourney for her love.
translation: Princes and knights from all over the world have come to fight in a tournament for her love.

original: Were my fortunes equal to my desires, I could wish to make one there.
translation: If my luck matched my desires, I'd try my hand at that.

original: O, sir, things must be as they may; and what a man cannot get, he may lawfully deal for—his wife's soul.
translation: Oh, Sir, things are what they are. What a man can't get, he can trade for (like his wife's soul).

original: Help, master, help! here's a fish hangs in the net,   like a poor man's right in the law; 'twill hardly   come out.
translation: Help, master, help! There's a heavy fish stuck in the net! He's as stuck as a poor man in a prison! We can't get it out.

original: Ha! bots on't, 'tis come at last, and   'tis turned to a rusty armour.
translation: Hey! Here we go! We got it out at last, and it turned into a suit of rusty armor.

original: An armour, friends! I pray you, let me see it.
translation: Armor? Let me see that.

original: Thanks, fortune, yet, that, after all my crosses,   Thou givest me somewhat to repair myself;
translation: After all the  bad luck  I've had, finally, something to help me fix myself,

original: And though it was mine own, part of my heritage,   Which my dead father did bequeath to me.   With this strict charge, even as he left his life,
translation: though it is my own, and part of my heritage: this is my armor, given to me by my dead father. Just before he died he told me,

original: 'Keep it, my Pericles; it hath been a shield   Twixt me and death;'—   and pointed to this brace;—   'For that it saved me,
translation: "Keep it, Pericles. It's kept me safe all my life," and he pointed to this brace, "It saved me.

original: keep it; in like necessity—   The which the gods protect thee from!—   may   defend thee.'
translation: Keep it. When you need it, though I hope the gods will protect you from such a situation, it will defend you."

original: It kept where I kept, I so dearly loved it;   Till the rough seas, that spare not any man,   Took it in rage, though calm'd have given't again:
translation: I've always had it with me and have always loved it. I'd never been separated from it until the storm, which doesn't spare anyone, took it in its rage. Now that it's calmed, it's given it back again.

original: I thank thee for't: my shipwreck now's no ill,   Since I have here my father's gift in's will.
translation: I thank you for it. I didn't lose much after all in the shipwreck, since I have my father's gift now.

original: What mean you, sir?
translation: What do you mean, sir?

original: To beg of you, kind friends, this coat of worth,   For it was sometime target to a king;   I know it by this mark.
translation: Friends, can I beg for you to give me this armor? I recognize the marks;

original: He loved me dearly,   And for his sake I wish the having of it;
translation: it belongs to a king who loved me, and I want to have it for his sake.

original: And that you'ld guide me to your sovereign's court,   Where with it I may appear a gentleman;
translation: Can I also ask you to lead me to the king's court? With this armor, I'll dress up like like a gentleman

original: And if that ever my low fortune's better,   I'll pay your bounties; till then rest your debtor.
translation: and, if I win and improve my bad luck, I'll pay you back for kindness. Until then, I owe you.

original: Why, wilt thou tourney for the lady?
translation: What, you're going to enter the tournament for the lady?

original: I'll show the virtue I have borne in arms.
translation: I'll show how skilled I am in battle.

original: Why, do 'e take it, and the gods give thee good on't!
translation: Well, take it, then, and may the gods bless you!

original: Ay, but hark you, my friend; 'twas we that made up   this garment through the rough seams of the waters:
translation: But listen, sir: we're the ones that pulled this armor out of the rough sea,

original: there are certain condolements, certain vails. I   hope, sir, if you thrive, you'll remember from   whence you had it.
translation: so there are certain conditions, certain respects to paid. I hope, sir, if you're successful, that you'll remember where you got it from.

original: Believe 't, I will.   By your furtherance I am clothed in steel;
translation: Believe me, I will. With your help, I have a suit of armor.

original: And, spite of all the rapture of the sea,   This jewel holds his building on my arm:
translation: In spite of what the sea did to me, I still have this valuable ring,

original: Unto thy value I will mount myself   Upon a courser, whose delightful steps   Shall make the gazer joy to see him tread.
translation: which I'll sell to buy a horse so beautiful everyone will love to see me riding him.

original: Only, my friend, I yet am unprovided   Of a pair of bases.
translation: And yet, my friends, I still need some jousting equipment.

original: We'll sure provide: thou shalt have my best gown to make thee a pair; and I'll bring thee to the court  myself.
translation: We can help you with that. We'll make sure you get a pair, and I'll bring you to court myself.

original: Then honour be but a goal to my will, This day I'll rise, or else add ill to ill.
translation: All I want is honor. It can only get better from here.

original: Are the knights ready to begin the triumph?
translation: Are the knights ready to begin the contest?

original: They are, my liege; And stay your coming to present themselves.
translation: They are, sir, and are waiting to present themselves to you.

original: Return them, we are ready; and our daughter,   In honour of whose birth these triumphs are,
translation: Bring them in; I'm ready. Since this whole thing is in honor of her birthday,

original: Sits here, like beauty's child, whom nature gat   For men to see, and seeing wonder at.
translation: my beautiful daughter,  whom Nature made for men to see , will sit here, where everyone can marvel at her.

original: It pleaseth you, my royal father, to express My commendations great, whose merit's less.
translation: Father, you like bragging about me even when I don't deserve it.

original: It's fit it should be so; for princes are   A model which heaven makes like to itself:
translation: I have to— princes are as vain as the gods.

original: As jewels lose their glory if neglected,   So princes their renowns if not respected.
translation: Just like jewels lose their shine if they're not polished, princes lose their reputations if they're not respected.

original: 'Tis now your honour, daughter, to explain   The labour of each knight in his device.
translation: Now, daughter, it's your job to explain what each knight's  emblem  means.

original: Which, to preserve mine honour, I'll perform.
translation: I'll do my best.

original: Who is the first that doth prefer himself?
translation: Who's this first knight?

original: A knight of Sparta, my renowned father;
translation: A knight from Sparta, sir.

original: And the device he bears upon his shield   Is a black Ethiope reaching at the sun   The word, 'Lux tua vita mihi.'
translation: The design on his shield shows an African man reaching toward the sun, with the motto "Your light is my life."

original: He loves you well that holds his life of you.
translation: Sounds like he loves you a lot, if you're his whole life.

original: Who is the second that presents himself?
translation: Who's the second knight?

original: A prince of Macedon, my royal father;
translation: A prince of Macedon, sir.

original: And the device he bears upon his shield   Is an arm'd knight that's conquer'd by a lady;   The motto thus, in Spanish, 'Piu por dulzura que por  fuerza.'
translation: His design shows a knight being conquered by a lady. The motto, in Spanish, is "Better by sweetness than by force."

original: And what's the third?
translation: And the third?

original: The third of Antioch; And his device, a wreath of chivalry; The word, 'Me pompae provexit apex.'
translation: The third is from Antioch. His shield shows a green wreath, with the motto, "I'll fight my way to the top."

original: What is the fourth?
translation: And the fourth?

original: A burning torch that's turned upside down; The word, 'Quod me alit, me extinguit.'
translation: A burning torch turned upside down, with the motto, "That which lights me snuffs me out."

original: Which shows that beauty hath his power and will, Which can as well inflame as it can kill.
translation: Which symbolizes that his love of beauty could as easily lead him to do great things as evil ones.

original: The fifth, an hand environed with clouds, Holding out gold that's by the touchstone tried; The motto thus, 'Sic spectanda fides.'
translation: The fifth knight's shield shows a hand emerging from clouds, holding pure gold. His motto is, "Faith should be valued this way."

original: And what's The sixth and last, the which the knight himself With such a graceful courtesy deliver'd?
translation: And what about the sixth and the last? It's very polite to go last, you know.

original: He seems to be a stranger; but his present is A wither'd branch, that's only green at top; The motto, 'In hac spe vivo.'
translation: I think he's a stranger. His shield design is a dead tree branch with only a little green at the top. The motto is, "This hope keeps me alive."

original: A pretty moral; From the dejected state wherein he is, He hopes by you his fortunes yet may flourish.
translation: That's a nice moral. It means that he's currently down and out but hopes that, by marrying you, he'll be on his way to a better fortune.

original: He had need mean better than his outward show   Can any way speak in his just commend;
translation: He'll have to do better than this to prove himself.

original: For by his rusty outside he appears   To have practised more the whipstock than the lance.
translation: His rusty armor looks less like a knight's and more like it came from a junk shop.

original: He well may be a stranger, for he comes To an honour'd triumph strangely furnished.
translation: He must be a stranger, since he showed up with such a strange outfit.

original: And on set purpose let his armour rust Until this day, to scour it in the dust.
translation: And let his armor rust until today on purpose, before he wears it in the tournament.

original: Opinion's but a fool, that makes us scan   The outward habit by the inward man.
translation: It's foolish to judge a book by its cover.

original: But stay, the knights are coming: we will withdraw   Into the gallery.
translation: Wait, the knights are coming—let's go into the stadium.

original: Knights,   To say you're welcome were superfluous.
translation: Knights, I hardly need to say how welcome you are.

original: To place upon the volume of your deeds,   As in a title-page, your worth in arms,   Were more than you expect, or more than's fit,   Since every worth in show commends itself.
translation: To write an endorsement of the book of your good deeds, like on a title page, would be more than is needed, since you've already showed your worth by doing the deeds themselves.

original: Prepare for mirth, for mirth becomes a feast:   You are princes and my guests.
translation: So, get ready to laugh, since feasts are best enjoyed with laughter. All of you princes are my guests.

original: But you, my knight and guest; To whom this wreath of victory I give, And crown you king of this day's happiness.
translation: Except for you; you're my guest. Here's a victory crown so everyone know's you're the king of the feast.

original: 'Tis more by fortune, lady, than by merit.
translation: It was more by good luck, ma'am, than by skill.

original: Call it by what you will, the day is yours;   And here, I hope, is none that envies it.
translation: Call it whatever you want; the day is yours. And I hope no one here is jealous of you.

original: In framing an artist, art hath thus decreed,   To make some good, but others to exceed;   And you are her labour'd scholar.
translation: Some artists are good, but according to the standards of art, some are excellent; you're clearly the best that art has to offer.

original: Come, queen o'   the feast,—   For, daughter, so you are,—   here take your place:
translation: [To THAISA]  Come, daughter, queen of the feast (since that's what you are), take your place.

original: Marshal the rest, as they deserve their grace.
We are honour'd much by good Simonides.
translation: You've honored us with this feast,  Simonides.

original: Your presence glads our days: honour we love; For who hates honour hates the gods above.
translation: I'm glad you're all here. I love honor; anyone who hates honor hates the gods above.

original: Sir, yonder is your place.
translation: Sir, there's your place.

original: Some other is more fit.
translation: Some other place would be better.

original: Contend not, sir; for we are gentlemen That neither in our hearts nor outward eyes Envy the great nor do the low despise.
translation: Don't argue, sir. We gentlemen don't get jealous of others with our eyes or our hearts. We neither envy the powerful nor hate the weak.

original: You are right courteous knights.
translation: You're all very kind, polite knights.

original: Sit, sir, sit.
translation: Sit, sir, sit.

original: By Jove, I wonder, that is king of thoughts, These cates resist me, she but thought upon.
translation: By Jove, king of thoughts: I can hardly eat this delicious food; I can't stop thinking about a certain girl.

original: By Juno, that is queen of marriage, All viands that I eat do seem unsavoury. Wishing him my meat. Sure, he's a gallant gentleman.
translation: By Juno, queen of marriage: everything I eat tastes bland; I only want to taste him. [To SIMONIDES] He's definitely an rich gentleman.

original: He's but a country gentleman; Has done no more than other knights have done; Has broken a staff or so; so let it pass.
translation: He's just a country gentleman. He's done no more than any other knight would do, he's broken a lance or two, so let it go.

original: To me he seems like diamond to glass.
Yon king's to me like to my father's picture,   Which tells me in that glory once he was;
translation: That king is like a picture of my own father; looking at him reminds me of how glorious he once was.

original: Had princes sit, like stars, about his throne,   And he the sun, for them to reverence;
translation: He used to have princes sit around his throne like stars, looking up to him like the  sun .

original: None that beheld him, but, like lesser lights,   Did vail their crowns to his supremacy:
translation: No one who saw him could hold a candle to his greatness; those smaller lights were outshone by his supremacy.

original: Where now his son's like a glow-worm in the night,   The which hath fire in darkness, none in light:
translation: I, his, son, am just a little firefly. You can see me at night, but I'm invisible in the day.

original: Whereby I see that Time's the king of men,   He's both their parent, and he is their grave,   And gives them what he will, not what they crave.
translation: From this, I can say that Time rules men. He raises men up and he puts them in their graves, and doesn't always give them what they want.

original: What, are you merry, knights?
translation: What are you all laughing at?

original: Who can be other in this royal presence?
translation: How could we do anything else in your royal presence?

original: Here, with a cup that's stored unto the brim,—
translation: Here, fill your cup up to the brim.

original: As you do love, fill to your mistress' lips,—   We drink this health to you.
translation: Here's a toast to your love for Thaisa and to all your health.

original: We thank your grace.
translation: We thank you, sir.

original: Yet pause awhile:   Yon knight doth sit too melancholy,
translation: [Pointing to PERICLES]  But wait: that knight looks sad,

original: As if the entertainment in our court   Had not a show might countervail his worth.   Note it not you, Thaisa?
translation: like our party isn't good enough for him. Haven't you noticed, Thaisa?

original: What is it To me, my father?
translation: What is it to me, father?

original: O, attend, my daughter:   Princes in this should live like gods above,   Who freely give to every one that comes   To honour them:
translation: Listen, daughter: princes, like the gods, should be generous to anyone who comes before them.

original: And princes not doing so are like to gnats,
translation: Stingy princes are like gnats;

original: Which make a sound, but kill'd are wonder'd at.
translation: they buzz around and everyone's glad when they're killed.

original: Therefore to make his entrance more sweet,   Here, say we drink this standing-bowl of wine to him.
translation: So, to make Pericles's stay more enjoyable, what do you say we drink a toast of this wine to him to help cheer him up?

original: Alas, my father, it befits not me   Unto a stranger knight to be so bold:
translation: Father, I can't be that forward with a strange knight.

original: He may my proffer take for an offence,   Since men take women's gifts for impudence.
translation: He might be offended by the offer, since some men take women's gifts as disrespect.

original: How! Do as I bid you, or you'll move me else.
translation: What? Do what I say, or else.

original: Now, by the gods, he could not please me  better.
translation: Now, by the gods, there's nothing that would make me happier.

original: And furthermore tell him, we desire to know of him, Of whence he is, his name and parentage.
translation: And also tell him we want to know where he came from and who his parents are.

original: The king my father, sir, has drunk to you.
translation: Sir, the king, my father, just drank a toast to you.

original: I thank him.
translation: Tell him I said thanks.

original: Wishing it so much blood unto your life.
translation: He wished you good health.

original: I thank both him and you, and pledge him freely.
translation: Thanks to him and to you. I'm honored.

original: And further he desires to know of you, Of whence you are, your name and parentage.
translation: And he also wants to know where you came from, what your name is, and who your parents are.

original: A gentleman of Tyre; my name, Pericles;
translation: I'm from Tyre. My name is Pericles.

original: My education been in arts and arms;
translation: I've been schooled in arts and in arms.

original: Who, looking for adventures in the world,   Was by the rough seas reft of ships and men,   And after shipwreck driven upon this shore.
translation: I was looking for adventure in the world when I was shipwrecked by storms, lost my men, and landed on your shore.

original: He thanks your grace; names himself Pericles,   A gentleman of Tyre,
translation: [Returning to SIMONIDES]  He said thank you, and that his name is Pericles, that he's from Tyre,

original: Who only by misfortune of the seas   Bereft of ships and men, cast on this shore.
translation: and was only shipwrecked here by chance.

original: Now, by the gods, I pity his misfortune,   And will awake him from his melancholy.
translation: Now, by the gods, I feel sorry for him and will cheer him up.

original: Come, gentlemen, we sit too long on trifles,   And waste the time, which looks for other revels.
translation: Come on, gentlemen, we're spending too much time on little things. Let's not waste time any longer; let's find another pastime.

original: Even in your armours, as you are address'd,   Will very well become a soldier's dance.
translation: Even in your armor, as you're dressed, you'll look great dancing a soldier's dance.

original: I will not have excuse, with saying this   Loud music is too harsh for ladies' heads,   Since they love men in arms as well as beds.
translation: No excuses; no one say the music is too loud for the ladies. We all know that ladies love to dance with soldiers as much as they like to get in bed with them!

original: So, this was well ask'd,'twas so well perform'd.
translation: Well, I'm glad I asked; that was a good dance.

original: Come, sir;   Here is a lady that wants breathing too:
translation: [To PERICLES]  Here, sir, this lady needs a partner, too.

original: And I have heard, you knights of Tyre   Are excellent in making ladies trip;   And that their measures are as excellent.
translation: I've heard you knights of Tyre are excellent dancers, and that you have a way of dancing with women, and that your rhythm is excellent.

original: In those that practise them they are, my lord.
translation: Those that dance might, sir.

original: O, that's as much as you would be denied Of your fair courtesy.
translation: Well, you might miss your chance if you keep talking.

original: Unclasp, unclasp:   Thanks, gentlemen, to all; all have done well.
translation: All right, break it up. Thanks, gentleman, and everyone. You all did well.

original: To PERICLES]   But you the best.
translation: [To PERICLES]  But you were the best.

original: Pages and lights, to conduct   These knights unto their several lodgings!
translation: [To ALL]  Servants, bring lamps and take these knights to their rooms!

original: Yours, sir,   We have given order to be next our own.
translation: [To PERICLES]  We've asked for you to have the best room, right next to mine.

original: I am at your grace's pleasure.
translation: Thank you, sir.

original: Princes, it is too late to talk of love;   And that's the mark I know you level at:
translation: It's too late now to talk about love (though I know that's what you're all aiming for).

original: Therefore each one betake him to his rest;   To-morrow all for speeding do their best.
translation: Everyone go to bed; we'll get to it tomorrow.

original: No, Escanes, know this of me,   Antiochus from incest lived not free:
translation: Listen, Escanes: Antiochus was committing incest,

original: For which, the most high gods not minding longer   To withhold the vengeance that they had in store,   Due to this heinous capital offence,
translation: and the most high gods couldn't contain their vengeance any longer against this most horrible of crimes.

original: Even in the height and pride of all his glory,   When he was seated in a chariot   Of an inestimable value, and his daughter with him,   A fire from heaven came and shrivell'd up   Their bodies, even to loathing;
translation: He was at the height of his glory, riding in his expensive chariot with his daughter when lightening struck from heaven, shriveling up their bodies to a disgusting, stinking mess.

original: for they so stunk,   That all those eyes adored them ere their fall   Scorn now their hand should give them burial.
translation: It was so horrible that no one who formerly adored them would stoop low enough to bury them.

original: 'Twas very strange.
translation: It was very strange.

original: And yet but justice; for though This king were great, his greatness was no guard To bar heaven's shaft, but sin had his reward.
translation: It was just, though. Even though he was a great king, his greatness couldn't shield him from heaven's wrath. His sin got its reward.

original: 'Tis very true.
translation: It's very true.

original: See, not a man in private conference Or council has respect with him but he.
translation: See, no one has private access to Pericles except for Helicanus.

original: It shall no longer grieve without reproof.
translation: We can't let this go on any longer without challenging it.

original: And cursed be he that will not second it.
translation: Anyone who's not with us is against us.

original: Follow me, then. Lord Helicane, a word.
translation: Follow me, then. Helicanus, can we have a word?

original: With me? and welcome: happy day, my lords.
translation: With me? Of course. Hello, gentlemen.

original: Know that our griefs are risen to the top, And now at length they overflow their banks.
translation: You have to understand that our grievances have piled up to the point of overflowing.

original: Your griefs! for what? wrong not your prince you love.
translation: Your grievances! Why? Don't say anything against the prince you love.

original: Wrong not yourself, then, noble Helicane;   But if the prince do live, let us salute him,   Or know what ground's made happy by his breath.
translation: Then don't say anything against yourself, Helicanus: if the prince is alive, let us see him. Otherwise just tell us where he's buried.

original: If in the world he live, we'll seek him out;   If in his grave he rest, we'll find him there;
translation: If he's alive somewhere in the world, we'll find him; if he's in his grave, we'll find him there.

original: And be resolved he lives to govern us,   Or dead, give's cause to mourn his funeral,   And leave us to our free election.
translation: Give us the right to know if he's still our rightful ruler or, if he's dead, let us mourn him with a funeral and then have an open election.

original: Whose death indeed's the strongest in our censure:   And knowing this kingdom is without a head,—   Like goodly buildings left without a roof   Soon fall to ruin,—
translation: If he is dead, and we don't have a ruler, then we would hardly want the kingdom to continue this way, like a building without a roof, a country without a king is quickly ruined.

original: your noble self,   That best know how to rule and how to reign,   We thus submit unto,—   our sovereign.
translation: With all your experience, we would look to you, and would appoint you to be our next king.

original: Live, noble Helicane!
translation: Long live Helicanus!

original: For honour's cause, forbear your suffrages:   If that you love Prince Pericles, forbear.
translation: Please, for honor's sake, no more. If you love Prince Pericles, you'll stop.

original: Take I your wish, I leap into the seas,   Where's hourly trouble for a minute's ease.
translation: I'll do as you wish: I'll set sail to find him, as dangerous as it is out there on the seas.

original: A twelvemonth longer, let me entreat you to   Forbear the absence of your king:
translation: Let me ask you to stand the absence of the king for another year.

original: If in which time expired, he not return,   I shall with aged patience bear your yoke.
translation: If I can't find the Prince within that time, I'll patiently accept your appointment.

original: But if I cannot win you to this love,   Go search like nobles, like noble subjects,   And in your search spend your adventurous worth;
translation: If you can't wait, go and look for him; show how loyal you are by your diligent searching.

original: Whom if you find, and win unto return,   You shall like diamonds sit about his crown.
translation: Then, if you find him and bring him back, he will reward you generously.

original: To wisdom he's a fool that will not yield; And since Lord Helicane enjoineth us, We with our travels will endeavour us.
translation: We'd be foolish not to give in to your wisdom. Since you told us so, we'll go about our travels like you said.

original: Then you love us, we you, and we'll clasp hands: When peers thus knit, a kingdom ever stands.
translation: We're all friends here; let's shake hands. Our kingdom is strong because we're all united.

original: Good morrow to the good Simonides.
translation: Good morning, Simonides.

original: Knights, from my daughter this I let you know,   That for this twelvemonth she'll not undertake   A married life.
translation: Gentlemen, I have to tell you that my daughter has decided not to marry for another year.

original: Her reason to herself is only known,   Which yet from her by no means can I get.
translation: Only she knows why; she won't tell me.

original: May we not get access to her, my lord?
translation: Can't we see her, sir?

original: 'Faith, by no means; she has so strictly tied   Her to her chamber, that 'tis impossible.
translation: Absolutely not; she's locked in her room and it's impossible to get her out.

original: One twelve moons more she'll wear Diana's livery;   This by the eye of Cynthia hath she vow'd   And on her virgin honour will not break it.
translation: She's sworn to remain a  virgin  for another year, and swears on her honor she won't go back on her promise.

original: Loath to bid farewell, we take our leaves.
translation: We're sad to leave, but we'll go now.

original: So,   They are well dispatch'd; now to my daughter's letter:
translation: Well, they're gone. Now about my daughter's letter . . .  [He looks at a letter]

original: She tells me here, she'd wed the stranger knight,   Or never more to view nor day nor light.
translation: She says here that she wants to marry the stranger knight, or she'll never see the light of day again.

original: 'Tis well, mistress; your choice agrees with mine;   I like that well: nay, how absolute she's in't,   Not minding whether I dislike or no!
translation: That's fine, missy; your choice is the same as mine. I really like that. It's funny how set she is in it; she doesn't care whether or not I dislike it!

original: Well, I do commend her choice;   And will no longer have it be delay'd.   Soft! here he comes: I must dissemble it.
translation: Well, I'm happy with her choice, but  I'll pretend I'm not.  Shh! Here he comes! I'll have to pretend it.

original: All fortune to the good Simonides!
translation: All blessings to you, good Simonides!

original: To you as much, sir! I am beholding to you   For your sweet music this last night:
translation: The same to you, sir! I owe you for that lovely singing last night.

original: I do   Protest my ears were never better fed   With such delightful pleasing harmony.
translation: I swear I've never heard such a great voice.

original: It is your grace's pleasure to commend; Not my desert.
translation: Thanks for the compliment, but I hardly deserve it.

original: Sir, you are music's master.
translation: You're a master of music.

original: The worst of all her scholars, my good lord.
translation: I'm the worst of all music's students, sir.

original: Let me ask you one thing: What do you think of my daughter, sir?
translation: Let me ask you a question: what do you think of my daughter, sir?

original: A most virtuous princess.
translation: She's a virtuous princess.

original: And she is fair too, is she not?
translation: And she's pretty, too, right?

original: As a fair day in summer, wondrous fair.
translation: As beautiful as a summer day; extremely beautiful.

original: Sir, my daughter thinks very well of you; Ay, so well, that you must be her master, And she will be your scholar: therefore look to it.
I am unworthy for her schoolmaster.
translation: I'm not worthy to be her teacher.

original: She thinks not so; peruse this writing else.
translation: She doesn't think so; look at this letter.

original: [Aside]   What's here?   A letter, that she loves the knight of Tyre!   'Tis the king's subtlety to have my life.
translation: [To himself, reading the letter]  What does this say? She says in this letter that she loves me! Maybe this is the king's plot to kill me?

original: O, seek not to entrap me, gracious lord,   A stranger and distressed gentleman,
translation: [To SIMONIDES]  Oh, please don't try to trap me, sir. I'm just an unlucky stranger and a gentleman in distress.

original: That never aim'd so high to love your daughter,   But bent all offices to honour her.
translation: I never wanted to marry your daughter; I just wanted to do my best to honor her.

original: Thou hast bewitch'd my daughter, and thou art A villain.
translation: You've tricked my daughter into loving you, you crook.

original: By the gods, I have not:   Never did thought of mine levy offence;
translation: I swear I haven't. I never did anything to hurt you.

original: Nor never did my actions yet commence   A deed might gain her love or your displeasure.
translation: I never wanted to win her over and never wanted to offend you.

original: Traitor, thou liest.
translation: Traitor, you lie!

original: Traitor!
translation: Traitor?

original: Ay, traitor.
translation: Yes, traitor.

original: Even in his throat—unless it be the king— That calls me traitor, I return the lie.
translation: Anyone who calls me a traitor (unless he's a king, of course) is a liar.

original: Now, by the gods, I do applaud his courage.
translation: Now, by the gods, I have to applaud his bravery.

original: My actions are as noble as my thoughts,   That never relish'd of a base descent.
translation: I've only tried to do the right thing; I haven't thought or done a single wrong thing.

original: I came unto your court for honour's cause,   And not to be a rebel to her state;
translation: I came here to compete in the tournament for honor's sake, not to commit treason.

original: And he that otherwise accounts of me,   This sword shall prove he's honour's enemy.
translation: Anyone who says otherwise will have to fight me for honor.

original: No? Here comes my daughter, she can witness it.
translation: Really? Here comes my daughter; she can prove it.

original: Then, as you are as virtuous as fair,
translation: Please, since you're as honest as you are beautiful,

original: Resolve your angry father, if my tongue   Did ere solicit, or my hand subscribe   To any syllable that made love to you.
translation: tell the truth: tell your angry father that I never said or wrote anything proclaiming my feelings to you.

original: Why, sir, say if you had, Who takes offence at that would make me glad?
translation: Well, if you did, I wouldn't be offended; I'd be glad.

original: Yea, mistress, are you so peremptory?
translation: Hey, missy, aren't you getting a little hasty?

original: I am glad on't with all my heart.—
translation: [To himself]  I'm happy about this, with all my heart.

original: I'll tame you; I'll bring you in subjection.   Will you, not having my consent,   Bestow your love and your affections   Upon a stranger?
translation: [To PERICLES and THAISA]  You'll have to listen to me; I'll make you do what I want. Would you really agree to marry a stranger without my permission?

original: who, for aught I know,   May be, nor can I think the contrary,   As great in blood as I myself.—
translation: He could be anybody, we don't even know if he's a prince.

original: Therefore hear you, mistress; either frame   Your will to mine,—   and you, sir, hear you,   Either be ruled by me, or I will make you—   Man and wife:
translation: So, listen, missy: You'll either obey me (and you, too, sir, listen to me) or I'll make you . . . man and wife!

original: Nay, come, your hands and lips must seal it too:
translation: Come on, then, hold each other's hands, kiss, and seal the deal!

original: And being join'd, I'll thus your hopes destroy;   And for a further grief,—God give you joy!—   What, are you both pleased?
translation: And, now that you're together, I'll disappoint you again, with the further condition . . . God bless you! Are you happy?

original: Yes, if you love me, sir.
translation: Of course, if you love me, sir!

original: Even as my life, or blood that fosters it.
translation: I swear on my life, with all my heart!

original: What, are you both agreed?
translation: You both feel the same way?

original: Yes, if it please your majesty.
translation: Yes, if you approve.

original: It pleaseth me so well, that I will see you wed; And then with what haste you can get you to bed.
translation: I approve so wholeheartedly that I'd like to have the wedding immediately and get you off to bed!

original: Now sleep y-slaked hath the rout;   No din but snores the house about,   Made louder by the o'er-fed breast   Of this most pompous marriage-feast.
translation: Now it's night and everyone is asleep; the only sound in the house is snoring, all the louder after being overfed at this marriage feast.

original: The cat, with eyne of burning coal,   Now crouches fore the mouse's hole;   And crickets sing at the oven's mouth,   E'er the blither for their drouth.
translation: Cats' eyes shine like burning coals as they hunt for mice, crickets chirp in the empty kitchen, and everything goes on as usual.

original: Hymen hath brought the bride to bed.   Where, by the loss of maidenhead,   A babe is moulded.
translation: Meanwhile, Pericles and Thaisa go to their  marriage bed , where, by the loss of virginity, a baby is conceived.

original: Be attent,   And time that is so briefly spent   With your fine fancies quaintly eche:
translation: Pay attention: we'll bridge a lot of action into a short amount of time with the help of your imagination.

original: What's dumb in show I'll plain with speech.
translation: It'll be silent, but I'll explain it afterward.

original: Philemon, ho!
translation: Hey, Philemon!

original: Doth my lord call?
translation: Did you call me, sir?

original: Get fire and meat for these poor men: 'T has been a turbulent and stormy night.
translation: Start a fire and get some food for these poor men. It's been a rough and stormy night.

original: I have been in many; but such a night as this, Till now, I ne'er endured.
translation: I've been in many storms, but, until now, I've never seen a night as bad as this.

original: Your master will be dead ere you return; There's nothing can be minister'd to nature That can recover him.   @ Give this to the 'pothecary, And tell me how it works.
translation: Your master will be dead before you get back; there's no way on earth to help him now. Give this to the doctor, and tell me how it works.

original: Good morrow.
translation: Good morning.

original: Good morrow to your lordship.
translation: Good morning, sir.

original: Gentlemen, Why do you stir so early?
translation: Gentleman, what are you doing up so early?

original: Sir,   Our lodgings, standing bleak upon the sea,   Shook as the earth did quake;
translation: Sir, our house, which overlooks the sea, shook in the earthquake.

original: The very principals did seem to rend,   And all-to topple: pure surprise and fear   Made me to quit the house.
translation: It seemed like the foundation itself was breaking and that the whole building would split in two! It scared us enough that we left quickly.

original: That is the cause we trouble you so early; 'Tis not our husbandry.
translation: That's why we're bothering you so early—it's not our fault.

original: O, you say well.
translation: Fair enough.

original: But I much marvel that your lordship, having   Rich tire about you, should at these early hours   Shake off the golden slumber of repose.
translation: But I'm surprised that someone as rich and well-provided as you is awake at this hour.

original: 'Tis most strange,   Nature should be so conversant with pain,   Being thereto not compell'd.
translation: It's odd that you'd want to sacrifice sleep when you don't have to.

original: I hold it ever,   Virtue and cunning were endowments greater   Than nobleness and riches:
translation: I truly believe that virtue and wisdom are more important to have than status and wealth.

original: careless heirs   May the two latter darken and expend;   But immortality attends the former.   Making a man a god.
translation: Careless children can ruin and waste the latter, but the former last forever, making humans like gods.

original: 'Tis known, I ever   Have studied physic, through which secret art,   By turning o'er authorities, I have,   Together with my practise,
translation: As everyone knows, I've studied medicine for a long time, the secrets of which I've discovered through reading old experts and through my own experience.

original: made familiar   To me and to my aid the blest infusions   That dwell in vegetives, in metals, stones;
translation: I'm now familiar with the powerful potions to be found in plants, metals, and stones.

original: And I can speak of the disturbances   That nature works, and of her cures;
translation: And I can talk about the  good and bad that Nature is capable of ,

original: which doth give me   A more content in course of true delight   Than to be thirsty after tottering honour,   Or tie my treasure up in silken bags,   To please the fool and death.
translation: all of which I enjoy this a lot more than I would trying to earn money or win other people's approval; that's totally worthless.

original: Your honour has through Ephesus pour'd forth   Your charity, and hundreds call themselves   Your creatures, who by you have been restored:
translation: Sir, you've been generous here in Ephesus. Thousands of people have been cured by you and are loyal to you.
