translation: [To LYSIMACHUS]  Can we rest and get provisions, sir, in Mytilene? We can pay you in gold for everything that we need.

original: Sir, With all my heart; and, when you come ashore, I have another suit.
translation: Sir, with all my heart. And when you come on shore, I have another request.

original: You shall prevail, Were it to woo my daughter; for it seems You have been noble towards her.
translation: The answer is "yes" if you're asking to marry my daughter. It seems you've been kind to her.

original: Sir, lend me your arm.
translation: Sir, give me your arm.

original: Come, my Marina.
translation: Come, my Marina.

original: Hail, Dian! to perform thy just command,   I here confess myself the king of Tyre;
translation: Praise Diana! I'm doing what you asked: I'll tell the whole story here. I'm the king of Tyre .

original: Who, frighted from my country, did wed   At Pentapolis the fair Thaisa.
translation: I left my country because I was afraid for my life, and married Thaisa in Pentapolis.

original: At sea in childbed died she, but brought forth   A maid-child call'd Marina; who, O goddess,   Wears yet thy silver livery.
translation: She died giving birth to our daughter, Marina, at sea. Marina is still a virgin like you, Diana!

original: She at Tarsus   Was nursed with Cleon; who at fourteen years   He sought to murder:
translation: Cleon took care of her in Tarsus, but when she was fourteen years old he tried to murder her.

original: but her better stars   Brought her to Mytilene; 'gainst whose shore   Riding, her fortunes brought the maid aboard us,
translation: Luckily, she came to Mytilene, where, when I arrived, by good fortune she was brought aboard my ship and,

original: Where, by her own most clear remembrance, she   Made known herself my daughter.
translation: by recounting her story, she made it clear she was my daughter.

original: Voice and favour! You are, you are—O royal Pericles!
translation: I recognize that voice! You're, you're—oh, Pericles!

original: What means the nun? she dies! help, gentlemen!
translation: What did that nun say? Is she dead? Help her, gentlemen!

original: Noble sir, If you have told Diana's altar true, This is your wife.
translation: Sir, if you've told the truth just now at Diana's altar, this is your wife.

original: Reverend appearer, no; I threw her overboard with these very arms.
translation: Sir, it can't be. I threw her overboard with my own hands.

original: Upon this coast, I warrant you.
translation: Near this coast, I bet.

original: 'Tis most certain.
translation: Exactly.

original: Look to the lady; O, she's but o'erjoy'd.
translation: [To the nuns]  Take care of the lady, she's just overexcited.

original: Early in blustering morn this lady was   Thrown upon this shore.
translation: [To PERICLES]  Early one morning, this woman washed up on shore.

original: I oped the coffin,   Found there rich jewels; recover'd her, and placed her   Here in Diana's temple.
translation: I opened the coffin, found some expensive jewels inside, revived her, and made her a nun here in Diana's temple.

original: May we see them?
translation: Can we see the jewels?

original: Great sir, they shall be brought you to my house, Whither I invite you. Look, Thaisa is recovered.
translation: Of course, come to my house and I'll bring them to you. Look, Thaisa woke up.

original: O, let me look!   If he be none of mine, my sanctity   Will to my sense bend no licentious ear,   But curb it, spite of seeing.
O, my lord,   Are you not Pericles? Like him you spake,   Like him you are: did you not name a tempest,   A birth, and death?
translation: Oh, sir, are you Pericles? You spoke just like him, and you look just like him . . . did you mention a storm, a birth, and a death?

original: The voice of dead Thaisa!
translation: The voice of Thaisa, who's dead!

original: That Thaisa am I, supposed dead And drown'd.
translation: I am Thaisa, who you thought was dead and drowned.

original: Immortal Dian!
translation: Immortal Diana!

original: Now I know you better. When we with tears parted Pentapolis, The king my father gave you such a ring.
translation: Now I recognize you. When we left Pentapolis, my father, the king, gave you this ring.

original: This, this: no more, you gods!
translation: This, this— no more, gods!

original: your present kindness   Makes my past miseries sports: you shall do well,   That on the touching of her lips I may   Melt and no more be seen.
translation: All this goodness makes the past pain seem like nothing. You'll do well if, when I kiss her, I melt and am never seen again!

original: O, come, be buried   A second time within these arms.
translation: Oh, come and  let me hold you .  [PERICLES and THAISA embrace]

original: My heart Leaps to be gone into my mother's bosom.
translation: My heart jumps at the thought of being able to hug my own mother.

original: Look, who kneels here! Flesh of thy flesh, Thaisa; Thy burden at the sea, and call'd Marina For she was yielded there.
Blest, and mine own!
translation: Bless you, daughter!

original: Hail, madam, and my queen!
translation: I salute you, my queen!

original: I know you not.
translation: I don't know you.

original: You have heard me say, when I did fly from Tyre,   I left behind an ancient substitute:
translation: Do you remember me saying that, when I left Tyre, I left an old friend behind?

original: Can you remember what I call'd the man?   I have named him oft.
translation: Do you remember his name? I've mentioned it many times.

original: 'Twas Helicanus then.
translation: It was Helicanus back then.

original: Still confirmation:   Embrace him, dear Thaisa; this is he.
translation: More confirmation! Give him a hug, Thaisa, this is Helicanus.

original: Now do I long to hear how you were found;   How possibly preserved; and who to thank,   Besides the gods, for this great miracle.
translation: Now I want to know how you were found, how you survived, and who I should thank (besides the gods) for this miracle.

original: Lord Cerimon, my lord; this man, Through whom the gods have shown their power; that can From first to last resolve you.
translation: Thank Lord Cerimon, dear, this man through whom the gods have shown their power. He can tell you everything from beginning to end.

original: Reverend sir,   The gods can have no mortal officer   More like a god than you.
translation: Sir, you're the nearest thing to a god that a man can be.

original: Will you deliver   How this dead queen re-lives?
translation: Can you explain how my queen came back to life?

original: I will, my lord.   Beseech you, first go with me to my house,   Where shall be shown you all was found with her;
translation: I can, sir. But first, let's go into my house, where I can show you everything we found with her.

original: How she came placed here in the temple;   No needful thing omitted.
translation: We'll explain how she came here to the temple, and we won't leave anything out.

original: Pure Dian, bless thee for thy vision! I   Will offer night-oblations to thee.
translation: Diana, bless your perfect plan! I will make a sacrifice to you tonight.

original: Thaisa,   This prince, the fair-betrothed of your daughter,   Shall marry her at Pentapolis.
translation: Thaisa, this is Lysimachus, who's engaged to your daughter and is about to marry her in Pentapolis.

original: And now,   This ornament   Makes me look dismal will I clip to form;   And what this fourteen years no razor touch'd,   To grace thy marriage-day, I'll beautify.
translation: And now, I'll shave off this long beard that I've grown for the last fourteen years. I'll look young again for your wedding day, Marina.

original: Lord Cerimon hath letters of good credit, sir, My father's dead.
translation: Lord Cerimon has received trustworthy letters saying my father's dead.

original: Heavens make a star of him! Yet there, my queen,   We'll celebrate their nuptials, and ourselves   Will in that kingdom spend our following days:
translation: May the gods bless his soul. We'll go to Pentapolis to celebrate their wedding, and we'll stay there to rule that kingdom for the rest of our lives.

original: Our son and daughter shall in Tyrus reign.
translation: Marina and Lysimachus will rule in Tyre.

original: Lord Cerimon, we do our longing stay   To hear the rest untold: sir, lead's the way.
translation: [To CERIMON]  Lord Cerimon, we'll stay here until we hear the rest of the story! Sir, lead the way.

original: Here have you seen a mighty king   His child, I wis, to incest bring;
translation: Here you've seen a king commit incest with his daughter.

original: A better prince and benign lord,   That will prove awful both in deed and word.
translation: Pericles will turn out to be a much more powerful prince and a better ruler, strong in both word and deed.

original: Be quiet then as men should be,   Till he hath pass'd necessity.
translation: But now he has to keep his mouth shut, until enough time has passed.

original: I'll show you those in troubles reign,   Losing a mite, a mountain gain.
translation: I'll show you how much trouble he had to deal with; once he got over the molehill, he ran into a mountain.

original: The good in conversation,   To whom I give my benison,   Is still at Tarsus,
translation: That good man whom I bless, Pericles, is still at Tarsus,

original: where each man   Thinks all is writ he speken can;   And, to remember what he does,   Build his statue to make him glorious:
translation: where everyone is singing his praises and the city is erecting a statue of him to remember him by—

original: But tidings to the contrary   Are brought your eyes; what need speak I?
translation: everything  seems  happy. But what you're about to see contradicts that, so what can I say?

original: Good Helicane, that stay'd at home,   Not to eat honey like a drone   From others' labours; for though he strive   To killen bad, keep good alive;   And to fulfil his prince' desire,   Sends word of all that haps in Tyre:
translation: Back at home, Helicanus has hardly been  a lazy worker bee : he's done everything the prince asked him to, and has sent news of everything happening in Tyre.

original: How Thaliard came full bent with sin   And had intent to murder him;   And that in Tarsus was not best   Longer for him to make his rest.
translation: He told Pericles how Thaliard came to murder him,  and advised him not to stay in Tarsus much longer.

original: He, doing so, put forth to seas,   Where when men been, there's seldom ease;   For now the wind begins to blow;   Thunder above and deeps below   Make such unquiet, that the ship   Should house him safe is wreck'd and split;
translation: Pericles sailed away on the sea, where men can never rest easy, and was quickly caught up in a storm. The winds blew, loud thunder was heard, and the ship that should have kept him safe was wrecked.

original: And he, good prince, having all lost,   By waves from coast to coast is tost:   All perishen of man, of pelf,   Ne aught escapen but himself;
translation: Having lost everything, Pericles was tossed by waves from coast to coast. He had  nothing and no one to keep him company, since no one else escaped alive.

original: Till fortune, tired with doing bad,   Threw him ashore, to give him glad:   And here he comes. What shall be next,   Pardon old Gower,—this longs the text.
translation: Finally, fortune got tired of ruining his life, and threw him on shore to make him happy. Here he comes. What happens next—actually, I'll shut up now.

original: Imagine Pericles arrived at Tyre,   Welcomed and settled to his own desire.
translation: Imagine Pericles gets back to Tyre, where he's welcomed back and settles down quickly.

original: His woeful queen we leave at Ephesus,   Unto Diana there a votaress.
translation: We'll leave his poor queen here at Ephesus, where she becomes a priestess of Diana.

original: Now to Marina bend your mind,   Whom our fast-growing scene must find   At Tarsus,
translation: Now back to Marina, whom our quickly-moving scene will find in Tarsus.

original: and by Cleon train'd   In music, letters; who hath gain'd   Of education all the grace,   Which makes her both the heart and place   Of general wonder.
translation: Cleon educates her in music and literature until she's the most accomplished girl around, and is admired by everyone.

original: But, alack,   That monster envy, oft the wrack   Of earned praise, Marina's life   Seeks to take off by treason's knife.
translation: Unfortunately, as often happens to those who deserve praise, a jealous person threatens to take Marina's life.

original: And in this kind hath our Cleon   One daughter, and a wench full grown,   Even ripe for marriage-rite;   this maid   Hight Philoten:
translation: Cleon has a grown daughter, Philoten, who's the right age for getting married.

original: and it is said   For certain in our story, she   Would ever with Marina be:
translation: According to our story, she and Marina were always together.

original: Be't when she weaved the sleided silk   With fingers long, small, white as milk;
translation: Whenever Marina wove silk with long, thin, white fingers,

original: Or when she would with sharp needle wound   The cambric, which she made more sound   By hurting it;
translation: or drew her sharp needle through the fabric, making it stronger with each stitch,

original: or when to the lute   She sung, and made the night-bird mute,   That still records with moan;
translation: or sang like a bird while playing the lute (which people still talk about),

original: or when   She would with rich and constant pen   Vail to her mistress Dian;
translation: or when she would write prayerful letters to her goddess, Diana,

original: still   This Philoten contends in skill   With absolute Marina:   so   With the dove of Paphos might the crow   Vie feathers white.
translation: Philoten couldn't compete with the supreme Marina.  A crow could just as well compete with a dove for whiteness.

original: Marina gets   All praises, which are paid as debts,   And not as given.
translation: Marina got all the praises; everyone felt less like they were giving compliments, and more like they owed them to her!

original: This so darks   In Philoten all graceful marks,   That Cleon's wife, with envy rare,   A present murderer does prepare   For good Marina,
translation: This hurt Philoten's reputation so much that Cleon's wife, Dionyza, hires a murderer to get Marina out of the way

original: that her daughter   Might stand peerless by this slaughter.   The sooner her vile thoughts to stead,   Lychorida, our nurse, is dead:
translation: so that Philoten could shine.  As soon as she thinks up this vile plan, Lychorida, the nurse, dies.

original: And cursed Dionyza hath   The pregnant instrument of wrath   Prest for this blow.   The unborn event   I do commend to your content:
translation: Wicked Dionyza has the murderer all prepped now for his job.  I leave what's about to happen up to you.

original: Only I carry winged time   Post on the lame feet of my rhyme;   Which never could I so convey,   Unless your thoughts went on my way.
translation: Time with its winged feet flies away while I make my rhyming speeches (which are stuck firmly on the ground). I could never make you understand unless your own imagination helps. That's where I bring you now:

original: Dionyza does appear,   With Leonine, a murderer.
translation: to Dionyza meeting with a murderer named Leonine.

original: Marina thus the brothel 'scapes, and chances   Into an honest house, our story says.
translation: So Marina escapes the brothel and, according to our story, finds some decent work.

original: She sings like one immortal, and she dances   As goddess-like to her admired lays;   Deep clerks she dumbs;
translation: She sings beautifully, dances to her songs like a goddess, amazes scholars with her wisdom,

original: and with her needle composes   Nature's own shape, of bud, bird, branch, or berry,   That even her art sisters the natural roses;   Her inkle, silk, twin with the rubied cherry:
translation: and can sew anything (a bud, a bird, a branch, or a berry) perfectly realistically. Her embroidered roses are twins to those that grow in the earth; the cherries she sews with silk and  inkle  look just like the real thing.

original: That pupils lacks she none of noble race,   Who pour their bounty on her; and her gain   She gives the cursed bawd.
translation: She teaches children of the local nobility and, when their parents pay her, she's forced to give her earnings to the Bawd, that awful woman.

original: Here we her place;   And to her father turn our thoughts again,   Where we left him, on the sea.   We there him lost;   Whence, driven before the winds, he is arrived   Here where his daughter dwells;   and on this coast   Suppose him now at anchor.
translation: We'll leave Marina here and go back to her father at sea. We lost him there, but now the winds have driven him here, where his daughter is;  he just docked.

original: The city strived   God Neptune's annual feast to keep: from whence   Lysimachus our Tyrian ship espies,   His banners sable, trimm'd with rich expense;   And to him in his barge with fervor hies.
translation: From the middle of a festival celebrating Neptune, Lysimachus sees the ship approach with fancy black sails, and rows out in his own boat to check it out.

original: In your supposing once more put your sight   Of heavy Pericles; think this his bark:   Where what is done in action, more, if might,   Shall be discover'd; please you, sit and hark.
translation: Think back to poor Pericles and imagine this is his ship. You'll like what happens next; sit and listen.

original: Thou god of this great vast, rebuke these surges,   Which wash both heaven and hell; and thou, that hast   Upon the winds command, bind them in brass,   Having call'd them from the deep!
translation: God of the sea , please stop this horrible storm, which washes over both heaven and hell. You can  control the wind ; settle them down, since you're the one who called them up.

original: O, still   Thy deafening, dreadful thunders; gently quench   Thy nimble, sulphurous flashes!
translation: Stop the deafening, terrifying thunder and halt the quick, bright lightning!

original: O, how, Lychorida,   How does my queen? Thou stormest venomously;   Wilt thou spit all thyself?
translation: Oh, Lychorida, how is the queen doing? This storm is absolutely crazy!

original: The seaman's whistle   Is as a whisper in the ears of death,   Unheard.
translation: From what the sailors are saying, we're due to die any minute now.

original: Lychorida!—   Lucina, O   Divinest patroness, and midwife gentle   To those that cry by night, convey thy deity   Aboard our dancing boat; make swift the pangs   Of my queen's travails!
translation: Lychorida— oh, Lucina, goddess of midwives and childbirth, come aboard our boat and make my wife's labor go quickly!

original: Now, Lychorida!
translation: Now, Lychorida!

original: Here is a thing too young for such a place,   Who, if it had conceit, would die, as I   Am like to do:
translation: Here's a baby far too young to be on board this ship. If she were smart, she'd die, just like I'm about to do.

original: take in your arms this piece   Of your dead queen.
translation: Here's all that's left of your dead queen.

original: How, how, Lychorida!
translation: What, what, Lychorida!

original: Patience, good sir; do not assist the storm.
translation: Don't cry, sir, we've got enough wailing with the storm going on.

original: Here's all that is left living of your queen,   A little daughter: for the sake of it,   Be manly, and take comfort.
translation: Here's all that's left alive of your queen: a little daughter. For her sake, be a man and be strong.

original: O you gods!   Why do you make us love your goodly gifts,   And snatch them straight away?
translation: Oh, you gods! Why do you give us good things that we love and then take them away?

original: We here below   Recall not what we give, and therein may   Use honour with you.
translation: Those of us on earth hardly know what to do.

original: Patience, good sir, Even for this charge.
translation: Calm down, sir—as bad as this is.

original: Now, mild may be thy life!   For a more blustrous birth had never babe:
translation: [To the baby]  May you have an easy life! No baby has ever had such a chaotic birth,

original: Quiet and gentle thy conditions!
translation: but you seem to be quiet and gentle!

original: for   Thou art the rudeliest welcome to this world   That ever was prince's child. Happy what follows!
translation: This is the worst welcome to the world that any princess has ever had. It can only go up from here!

original: Thou hast as chiding a nativity   As fire, air, water, earth, and heaven can make,   To herald thee from the womb:
translation: This is the roughest start for a newborn that fire, water, earth, and heaven could put together as you came out of the womb

original: even at the first   Thy loss is more than can thy portage quit,   With all thou canst find here. Now, the good gods   Throw their best eyes upon't!
translation: — you've lost everything before you had anything at all. May the gods take note of this and bless your future!

original: What courage, sir? God save you!
translation: Have courage, sir! God bless you!

original: Courage enough: I do not fear the flaw;   It hath done to me the worst.
translation: I have enough courage; I've never been afraid in my life (to my own injury).

original: Yet, for the love   Of this poor infant, this fresh-new sea-farer,   I would it would be quiet.
translation: But for this baby's sake, this brand-new sailor, I wish the storm would quiet down.

original: Slack the bolins there! Thou wilt not, wilt thou? Blow, and split thyself.
translation: Let the sails go slack there! Do it, why don't you! Hurry up!

original: But sea-room, an the brine and cloudy billow kiss the moon, I care not.
translation: The waves are coming in over the sides of the ship, and the clouds have covered the moon so it's completely dark! I can't do anything!

original: Sir, your queen must overboard: the sea works high, the wind is loud, and will not lie till the ship be cleared of the dead.
translation: Sir, we have to throw the queen overboard. The waves are high, the wind is loud, and this storm won't stop until the ship is cleared of the dead.

original: That's your superstition.
translation: That's your superstition.

original: Pardon us, sir; with us at sea it hath been still   observed: and we are strong in custom.
translation: Sorry, sir, it's the way things are done at sea, and we're true to tradition.

original: Therefore   briefly yield her; for she must overboard straight.
translation: Give her up quickly, because we have to throw her overboard now.

original: As you think meet. Most wretched queen!
translation: If you think it's best. Poor queen!

original: Here she lies, sir.
translation: Here she is, sir.

original: A terrible childbed hast thou had, my dear;   No light, no fire: the unfriendly elements   Forgot thee utterly:
translation: You've had a terrible experience giving birth, my dear. No light, no warmth, and a storm.

original: nor have I time   To give thee hallow'd to thy grave, but straight   Must cast thee, scarcely coffin'd, in the ooze;
translation: And I don't even have time to bury you; I have to throw you into the sea without a coffin, straight into the depths.

original: Where, for a monument upon thy bones,   And e'er-remaining lamps, the belching whale   And humming water must o'erwhelm thy corpse,   Lying with simple shells.
translation: Instead of a tombstone and lighted lamps, you'll have whales, flowing water, and simple shells.

original: O Lychorida,   Bid Nestor bring me spices, ink and paper,   My casket and my jewels;
translation: [To LYCHORIDA]  Lychorida, have Nestor bring in some spices, ink, and paper, a casket, and my jewels.

original: and bid Nicander   Bring me the satin coffer:
translation: And ask Nicander to bring me that fancy box.

original: lay the babe   Upon the pillow: hie thee, whiles I say   A priestly farewell to her: suddenly, woman.
translation: Lay the baby on that pillow, there, and go, while I say goodbye to my wife. Hurry!

original: Sir, we have a chest beneath the hatches, caulked and bitumed ready.
translation: Sir, we have a chest ready, waterproofed and sealed.

original: I thank thee. Mariner, say what coast is this?
translation: Thank you. Sailor, where are we?

original: We are near Tarsus.
translation: We're near Tarsus.

original: Thither, gentle mariner. Alter thy course for Tyre. When canst thou reach it?
translation: Let's go there, and then change course for Tyre. How soon can we get there?

original: By break of day, if the wind cease.
translation: By morning, if the wind stops.

original: O, make for Tarsus!   There will I visit Cleon, for the babe   Cannot hold out to Tyrus:
translation: Let's go to Tarsus! I'll visit Cleon, since the baby can't make it to Tyre.

original: there I'll leave it   At careful nursing. Go thy ways, good mariner:   I'll bring the body presently.
translation: I'll leave her there for them to take care of. Go about your business, sailors. I'll bring you the body now.

original: Thus time we waste, and longest leagues make short;   Sail seas in cockles, have an wish but for't;   Making, to take your imagination,   From bourn to bourn, region to region.
translation: Again, we'll sail over miles of miles of ocean as if it were nothing, hopping from country to country and region to region, by the power of your imagination.

original: By you being pardon'd, we commit no crime   To use one language in each several clime   Where our scenes seem to live.
translation: Forgive us for using the same language in all these different places where our scenes are set for the sake of simplicity.

original: I do beseech you   To learn of me, who stand i' the gaps to teach you,   The stages of our story.
translation: Now let me fill you in on what happens next, in the gaps between the parts of our story:

original: Pericles   Is now again thwarting the wayward seas,   Attended on by many a lord and knight.   To see his daughter, all his life's delight.
translation: Pericles takes to the unruly sea once again, along with many courtiers. He's coming to see his daughter, the light of his life.

original: Old Escanes, whom Helicanus late   Advanced in time to great and high estate,   Is left to govern.
translation: Old Escanes, Helicanus's friend whom he left in charge, is governing while he's gone.

original: Bear you it in mind,   Old Helicanus goes along behind.   Well-sailing ships and bounteous winds have brought   This king to Tarsus,—
translation: Keep that in mind, since Helicanus is going along with Pericles. With a sturdy ship and a good wind at his back, Pericles arrives in Tarsus.

original: think his pilot thought;   So with his steerage shall your thoughts grow on,—   To fetch his daughter home, who first is gone.
translation: Just imagine his ship and all its cargo, arriving here to take Marina home, who's gone.

original: Like motes and shadows see them move awhile;   Your ears unto your eyes I'll reconcile.
translation: Watch them move like ghosts and shadows for a while, and then I'll explain in words what you've just seen.

original: See how belief may suffer by foul show!
translation: Poor Pericles believed that fake performance!

original: This borrow'd passion stands for true old woe;   And Pericles, in sorrow all devour'd,   With sighs shot through, and biggest tears  o'ershower'd,   Leaves Tarsus and again embarks.
translation: He's really grieving, though, as if she were gone. Pericles leaves Tarsus wrecked by grief, overcome with sighs and shedding constant tears.

original: He swears   Never to wash his face, nor cut his hairs:   He puts on sackcloth, and to sea.
translation: He swears never to wash his face or cut his hair or wear anything but  black , and sets out to sea.

original: He bears   A tempest, which his mortal vessel tears,   And yet he rides it out.
translation: Another storm comes and damages the boat,  but he rides it out.

original: Now please you wit.   The epitaph is for Marina writ By wicked Dionyza.
translation: Now listen to the epitaph the wicked Dionyza wrote for Marina:

original: [Reads the inscription on MARINA's monument]   'The fairest, sweet'st, and best lies here,   Who wither'd in her spring of year.
translation: [He reads the inscription on MARINA's monument]  The sweetest, most beautiful girl lies here. She died too young, in the spring of her life.

original: She was of Tyrus the king's daughter,   On whom foul death hath made this slaughter;
translation: She was the daughter of the king of Tyre; death has taken her away from us.

original: Marina was she call'd; and at her birth,   Thetis, being proud, swallow'd some part o' the earth:
translation: Her name was Marina. At her birth, Thetis was jealous of her and swallowed a piece of the earth;

original: Therefore the earth, fearing to be o'erflow'd,   Hath Thetis' birth-child on the heavens bestow'd:
translation: the earth, afraid of being flooded, gave this watery girl back to  heaven .

original: Wherefore she does, and swears she'll never stint,   Make raging battery upon shores of flint.'
translation: That's why the sea continues to storm, barraging our shores with waves.

original: No visor does become black villany   So well as soft and tender flattery.
translation: No shady presentation could be more fitting for evil deeds than such soft, tender flattery.

original: Let Pericles believe his daughter's dead,   And bear his courses to be ordered   By Lady Fortune;
translation: Let Pericles believe his daughter's dead; he's in Fortune's hands for now.

original: while our scene must play   His daughter's woe and heavy well-a-dayIn her unholy  service.
translation: Our next scene will have to do with his daughter's misfortune and trials in an ungodly occupation.

original: Patience, then,   And think you now are all in Mytilene.
translation: Patience, then, and imagine you're all in Mytilene.

original: Now our sands are almost run;   More a little, and then dumb.
translation: Now our time is almost up; there's only a little bit left before we shut up.

original: This, my last boon, give me,   For such kindness must relieve me,   That you aptly will suppose   What pageantry, what feats, what shows,   What minstrelsy, and pretty din,   The regent made in Mytilene   To greet the king.
translation: Here's the last favor I'll ask of you: that you'll envision all the parades, performances, shows, songs, and fanfare that the governor put on in Mytilene to greet the king.

original: So he thrived,   That he is promised to be wived   To fair Marina;
translation: He succeeded in getting engaged to Marina,

original: but in no wise   Till he had done his sacrifice,   As Dian bade:
translation: but they won't be married until Pericles performs the sacrifice that Diana ordered.

original: whereto being bound,   The interim, pray you, all confound.
translation: They're headed there now; picture them going in the meantime.

original: In feather'd briefness sails are fill'd,   And wishes fall out as they're will'd.
translation: The sails fill with wind, the ship goes quickly, and everyone's wishes are fulfilled.

original: At Ephesus, the temple see,   Our king and all his company.
translation: Now see the temple in Ephesus where the king and his group are.

original: That he can hither come so soon,   Is by your fancy's thankful doom.
translation: They got there so quickly only by the power of your imagination.

original: In Antiochus and his daughter you have heard   Of monstrous lust the due and just reward:
translation: You heard about the just deserts that Antiochus and his daughter got for their monstrous actions.

original: In Pericles, his queen and daughter, seen,   Although assail'd with fortune fierce and keen,   Virtue preserved from fell destruction's blast,   Led on by heaven, and crown'd with joy at last:
translation: And you've seen how Pericles, his queen, and his daughter—despite the bad fortune life threw at them—kept their virtue safe from misfortune's attacks, trusted the gods, and are happy at last.

original: In Helicanus may you well descry   A figure of truth, of faith, of loyalty:
translation: You can see that Helicanus is an example of truth, faith, and loyalty;

original: In reverend Cerimon there well appears   The worth that learned charity aye wears:
translation: Cerimon displays how wisdom and generosity can do good in the world.

original: For wicked Cleon and his wife, when fame   Had spread their cursed deed, and honour'd name   Of Pericles, to rage the city turn,   That him and his they in his palace burn;
translation: Once the word got out about what Cleon and his wife had done, the city of Tarsus (which loved Pericles) reacted in a rage, burning them to death in their own palace.

original: The gods for murder seemed so content   To punish them; although not done, but meant.
translation: The gods punished them that way for their attempted murder— though they didn't do it, they meant it.

original: So, on your patience evermore attending,   New joy wait on you! Here our play has ending.
translation: So, thanks again for your patience, and may you be blessed! This is the end of our play.

original: Old John of Gaunt, time-honour'd Lancaster,   Hast thou, according to thy oath and band,   Brought hither Henry Hereford thy bold son,
translation: OId John of Gaunt, well-respected  Lancaster  : have you, according to your promise and duty, brought here your presumptuous son Henry Hereford

original: Here to make good the boisterous late appeal,   Which then our leisure would not let us hear,   Against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?
translation: to explain his case against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray, which at the time we didn't have time to hear?

original: I have, my liege.
Tell me, moreover, hast thou sounded him,   If he appeal the duke on ancient malice;
translation: Tell me, furthermore: have you asked him whether he accuses the duke because he has a grudge against him,

original: Or worthily, as a good subject should,   On some known ground of treachery in him?
translation: or because—like a good subject—he has reason to suspect him of disloyalty?

original: As near as I could sift him on that argument,
translation: As much as I could gather,

original: On some apparent danger seen in him   Aim'd at your highness,
translation: he accuses the duke because he thinks he poses a threat to your highness,

original: no inveterate malice.
translation: not for personal reasons.

original: Then call them to our presence;
translation: Then bring them before  us :

original: face to face,   And frowning brow to brow, ourselves will hear   The accuser and the accused freely speak   :
translation: we will hear the accuser and the accused make their case, face to face.

original: High-stomach'd are they both, and full of ire,   In rage deaf as the sea, hasty as fire.
translation: They're both proud men, full of anger, and their rage makes them too hasty and quick to take offense.

original: Many years of happy days befal My gracious sovereign, my most loving liege!
translation: May you reign many years in happiness, my gracious King, my most loving lord!

original: Each day still better other's happiness   ;
Until the heavens, envying earth's good hap,   Add an immortal title to your crown!
translation: until heaven, jealous of earth's good fortune in having such a king, gives you an immortal crown after death.

original: We thank you both: yet one but flatters us,
translation: We thank you both: yet one merely flatters us,

original: As well appeareth by the cause you come;   Namely to appeal each other of high treason.
translation: since you come to accuse one another of  high treason .

original: Cousin of Hereford, what dost thou object   Against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?
translation: Cousin of Hereford, what is your accusation against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?

original: First, heaven be the record to my speech!   In the devotion of a subject's love,   Tendering the precious safety of my prince,   And free from other misbegotten hate,   Come I appellant to this princely presence.
translation: First, let heaven witness my speech! I swear that I make this accusation as a devoted subject, concerned for the precious safety of my prince, and free from any other grudge or personal motive.

original: Now, Thomas Mowbray, do I turn to thee,   And mark my greeting well; for what I speak   My body shall make good upon this earth,   Or my divine soul answer it in heaven.
translation: Now, Thomas Mowbray, I turn to you, and listen closely; for what I speak, I'll prove true while I live, or my soul will answer for it in heaven.

original: Thou art a traitor and a miscreant,   Too good to be so and too bad to live,   Since the more fair and crystal is the sky,   The uglier seem the clouds that in it fly.
translation: You are a traitor and a villain, too good to be so and too bad to live, since the brighter and clearer the sky, the uglier it looks when clouds fill it.

original: Once more, the more to aggravate the note,   With a foul traitor's name stuff I thy throat;
translation: Once more (the more to make my point), I throw the name of "foul traitor" back down your throat;

original: And wish, so please my sovereign, ere I move,   What my tongue speaks my right drawn sword may prove.
translation: and wish—if it pleased my sovereign—that before I go, I might prove what I say with my sword.

original: Let not my cold words here accuse my zeal:
translation: Don't let my cool response make me seem less passionate.

original: 'Tis not the trial of a woman's war,   The bitter clamour of two eager tongues,   Can arbitrate this cause betwixt us twain;
translation: A war of words, like the chatter of two gossipy women, won't resolve this dispute;

original: The blood is hot that must be cool'd for this:
translation: blood must be spilled before this is over.

original: Yet can I not of such tame patience boast   As to be hush'd and nought at all to say:
translation: But I am not so patient that I can listen to these insults and say nothing in return.

original: First, the fair reverence of your highness curbs me   From giving reins and spurs to my free speech;   Which else would post until it had return'd   These terms of treason doubled down his throat.
translation: First, respect for your highness stops me from speaking freely—if I could, I wouldn't stop until I'd shoved those terms of treason back down his throat.

original: Setting aside his high blood's royalty,   And let him be no kinsman to my liege,   I do defy him, and I spit at him;   Call him a slanderous coward and a villain:
translation: Leaving aside his royal blood and pretending he's not your  cousin  I defy him, spit at him, and call him a lying coward and a villain:

original: Which to maintain I would allow him odds,   And meet him, were I tied to run afoot   Even to the frozen ridges of the Alps,   Or any other ground inhabitable,   Where ever Englishman durst set his foot.
translation: which to prove I would give him time to run, and then follow him even to the frozen mountains of the Alps, or any other inhabitable ground where an Englishman has ever set foot.

original: Mean time let this defend my loyalty,   By all my hopes, most falsely doth he lie.
translation: In the meantime, let this prove my loyalty: by everything I hold dear, he's a false liar.

original: Pale trembling coward, there I throw my gage,
translation: Pale trembling coward, there I throw my  gage   [throws glove on the ground] ,

original: Disclaiming here the kindred of the king,   And lay aside my high blood's royalty,   Which fear, not reverence, makes thee to except.
translation: abandoning here my royal blood—it's fear, not respect,  that makes you refuse to challenge me because I'm the king's cousin.

original: If guilty dread have left thee so much strength   As to take up mine honour's pawn, then stoop:
translation: If guilty fear has left you enough strength, pick it up:

original: By that and all the rites of knighthood else,   Will I make good against thee, arm to arm,   What I have spoke, or thou canst worse devise.
translation: by that and all the code of knighthood, I'll take up arms to prove that you're guilty of all I've accused you of, or worse.

original: I take it up; and by that sword I swear   Which gently laid my knighthood on my shoulder,
translation: I take it up; and by the sword that knighted me,

original: I'll answer thee in any fair degree,   Or chivalrous design of knightly trial:
translation: I'll answer you in any fair fight:

original: And when I mount, alive may I not light,   If I be traitor or unjustly fight!
translation: and when I mount my horse, may I not get down again alive, if I'm a traitor or fight unjustly!

original: What doth our cousin lay to Mowbray's charge?
translation: What crime do you accuse Mowbray of, cousin?

original: It must be great that can inherit us   So much as of a thought of ill in him.
translation: It must be very bad, if it can cause us to think any ill of him.

original: Look, what I speak, my life shall prove it true;
translation: Whatever I speak, I'll risk my life to prove it true.

original: That Mowbray hath received eight thousand nobles   In name of lendings for your highness' soldiers,   The which he hath detain'd for lewd employments,   Like a false traitor and injurious villain.
translation: Mowbray has received eight thousand gold coins as a loan to pay your highness' soldiers, which he's embezzled for his own ill ends, like a false traitor and a con man.

original: Besides I say and will in battle prove,   Or here or elsewhere to the furthest verge   That ever was survey'd by English eye,
translation: Besides I say and will in battle prove—either here or elsewhere, in the farthest place that an Englishman ever saw—

original: That all the treasons for these eighteen years   Complotted and contrived in this land   Fetch from false Mowbray their first head and spring.
translation: that Mowbray is responsible for all the treasonous plots devised in this land for the past eighteen years.

original: Further I say and further will maintain   Upon his bad life to make all this good,
translation: Furthermore, I say (and further will prove by challenging him in combat)

original: That he did plot the Duke of Gloucester's death,   Suggest his soon-believing adversaries,
translation: that he plotted the Duke of Gloucester's death by putting his easily-persuaded enemies up to it,

original: And consequently, like a traitor coward,   Sluiced out his innocent soul through streams of blood:
translation: and consequently, like a traitorous coward, parted the innocent soul from its resting place as the blood flowed out of his body.

original: Which blood, like sacrificing Abel's, cries,   Even from the tongueless caverns of the earth,   To me for justice and rough chastisement;
translation: His blood, like  Abel's , cries out to me for justice and vengeance even from the silent depths of the earth;

original: And, by the glorious worth of my descent,   This arm shall do it, or this life be spent.
translation: and, by all my ancestors, I'll do it with my two hands, or I'll die instead.

original: How high a pitch his resolution soars! Thomas of Norfolk, what say'st thou to this?
translation: His determination soars to such heights! Thomas of Norfolk, how do you respond to this?

original: O, let my sovereign turn away his face   And bid his ears a little while be deaf,
translation: Oh, I wish that my sovereign might turn away his face and be deaf for a little while,

original: Till I have told this slander of his blood,   How God and good men hate so foul a liar.
translation: until I have told this villain how God and good men hate foul liars like him.

original: Mowbray, impartial are our eyes and ears:   Were he my brother, nay, my kingdom's heir,   As he is but my father's brother's son,
translation: Mowbray, our eyes and ears are impartial. If he were my brother—no, even my son and my kingdom's heir—rather than merely my father's brother's son,

original: Now, by my sceptre's awe, I make a vow,   Such neighbour nearness to our sacred blood   Should nothing privilege him, nor partialize   The unstooping firmness of my upright soul:
translation: I vow by the power of my  sword  that such nearness to our sacred family's blood would not make me more likely to favor him, or compromise my judgment.

original: He is our subject, Mowbray; so art thou:   Free speech and fearless I to thee allow.
translation: He is our subject, Mowbray, and so are you. So I allow you to speak freely and fearlessly as well.

original: Then, Bolingbroke, as low as to thy heart,   Through the false passage of thy throat, thou liest.
translation: Then, Bolingbroke, I say that you lie from your heart through your throat.

original: Three parts of that receipt I had for Calais   Disbursed I duly to his highness' soldiers;
translation: I paid three-fourths of the money I had for Calais to his highness' soldiers;

original: The other part reserved I by consent,   For that my sovereign liege was in my debt   Upon remainder of a dear account,   Since last I went to France to fetch his queen:   Now swallow down that lie.
translation: the rest was given to me by prior agreement, since the king owed me money for my expenses when I last went to France to fetch his queen: so take back that lie.

original: For Gloucester's death,   I slew him not; but to my own disgrace   Neglected my sworn duty in that case.
translation: As for Gloucester's death, I didn't kill him; although I admit  I let down my sworn duty in that case.

original: For you, my noble Lord of Lancaster,   The honourable father to my foe   Once did I lay an ambush for your life,   A trespass that doth vex my grieved soul
translation: As for you, my noble Lord of Lancaster, the honorable father to my enemy, I once tried to kill you, an offense that now grieves my soul greatly.

original: But ere I last received the sacrament   I did confess it, and exactly begg'd   Your grace's pardon, and I hope I had it.
translation: But before I last received the sacrament, I confessed it and begged your grace's pardon, and I hope I had it.

original: This is my fault: as for the rest appeall'd,   It issues from the rancour of a villain,   A recreant and most degenerate traitor
translation: These are my crimes: as for the rest accused against me, it comes from the malice of a villain, a cowardly and violent traitor—

original: Which in myself I boldly will defend;
translation: which I'll prove with my own strength,

original: And interchangeably hurl down my gage   Upon this overweening traitor's foot,   To prove myself a loyal gentleman   Even in the best blood chamber'd in his bosom.
translation: and throw down my gage upon this proud traitor's foot, to prove myself a loyal gentleman, even in the  chamber of his body  where all his "noble" blood flows.

original: In haste whereof, most heartily I pray   Your highness to assign our trial day.
translation: So I eagerly beg your highness to set a day for our duel.

original: Wrath-kindled gentlemen, be ruled by me;   Let's purge this choler without letting blood:
translation: Angry gentlemen, obey my commands: let's purge this anger from your bodies without  letting blood .

original: This we prescribe, though no physician;   Deep malice makes too deep incision;
translation: This we prescribe, though we're no doctor; your deep rage will cut too deeply.

original: Forget, forgive; conclude and be agreed;   Our doctors say this is no month to bleed.
Good uncle, let this end where it begun;   We'll calm the Duke of Norfolk, you your son.
translation: Good uncle, let this end where it began; we'll calm the Duke of Norfolk, and you will calm your son.

original: To be a make-peace shall become my age: Throw down, my son, the Duke of Norfolk's gage.
translation: To be a peacemaker is a fitting role for me, at my age: my son, throw down the Duke of Norfolk's gage.

original: And, Norfolk, throw down his.
translation: And, Norfolk, throw down his.

original: When, Harry, when? Obedience bids I should not bid again.
translation: Harry, when will you do what I command? If you were an obedient son, I wouldn't need to ask again.

original: Norfolk, throw down, we bid; there is no boot.
translation: Norfolk, throw down, we command you; there's no point refusing.

original: Myself I throw, dread sovereign, at thy foot.
translation: My king, I throw myself at your feet.

original: My life thou shalt command, but not my shame:   The one my duty owes; but my fair name,   Despite of death that lives upon my grave,   To dark dishonour's use thou shalt not have.
translation: You have power over my life, but not my honor: it's my duty to obey you, but my good name, even if you take my life, will not be dishonored by you in death.

original: I am disgraced, impeach'd and baffled here,   Pierced to the soul with slander's venom'd spear,   The which no balm can cure but his heart-blood   Which breathed this poison.
translation: I am disgraced, insulted, and slandered here, my soul pierced with the venomous spear of lies, which no medicine can cure except the blood of the man who has poisoned me.

original: Rage must be withstood: Give me his gage: lions make leopards tame.
translation: Control your rage; give me his gage. Lions can tame leopards after all.

original: Yea, but not change his spots: take but my shame.   And I resign my gage.
translation: Yes, but the leopard won't change its spots: to take that gage from me is to take my honor.

original: My dear dear lord,   The purest treasure mortal times afford   Is spotless reputation: that away,   Men are but gilded loam or painted clay.
translation: My dear dear lord, the purest treasure of our lives is spotless reputation: without that, men are just painted clay and gilded dust.

original: A jewel in a ten-times-barr'd-up chest   Is a bold spirit in a loyal breast.
translation: A brave spirit in a loyal person is like a jewel in a chest protected by ten locks.

original: Mine honour is my life; both grow in one:   Take honour from me, and my life is done:
translation: My honor is my life; both grow together. If you take my honor from me, my life is done.

original: Then, dear my liege, mine honour let me try;   In that I live and for that will I die.
translation: Then, my dear liege, let me prove my integrity in combat: I live for my honor and will die for it.

original: Cousin, throw up your gage; do you begin.
translation: Cousin, put down your gage. Don't you start as well—

original: O, God defend my soul from such deep sin!
translation: Oh god, defend my soul from such deep sin!

original: Shall I seem crest-fall'n in my father's sight?
translation: Shall I seem humbled in my father's sight?

original: Or with pale beggar-fear impeach my height   Before this out-dared dastard?
translation: Or disgrace my high rank and look like a fearful beggar before this coward?

original: Ere my tongue   Shall wound my honour with such feeble wrong,   Or sound so base a parle, my teeth shall tear   The slavish motive of recanting fear,   And spit it bleeding in his high disgrace,   Where shame doth harbour, even in Mowbray's face.
translation: Before I lose my honor by saying those shameful words, I would bite out my tongue and spit it in Mowbray's face.

original: We were not born to sue, but to command;
translation: We were not born to beg, but to command:

original: Which since we cannot do to make you friends,   Be ready, as your lives shall answer it,   At Coventry, upon Saint Lambert's day:
translation: but since we can't force you to make peace, be ready to die for it, at Coventry, upon  Saint Lambert's day .

original: There shall your swords and lances arbitrate   The swelling difference of your settled hate:
translation: There, you can settle this dispute with swords and lances.

original: Since we can not atone you, we shall see   Justice design the victor's chivalry.
translation: Since we can't find out who's in the wrong,  let the battle determine which one of you is telling the truth .

original: Lord marshal, command our officers at arms   Be ready to direct these home alarms.
translation: Lord marshal, command our armed officers to prepare for the duel.

original: Alas, the part I had in Woodstock's blood   Doth more solicit me than your exclaims,   To stir against the butchers of his life!
translation: Oh, the part of me that shared  Woodstock's  blood makes me long for revenge on his butchers even more than your cries of pain!

original: But since correction lieth in those hands   Which made the fault that we cannot correct,
translation: But since the power to take vengeance lies in the hands of the person who's responsible (and we have no hope of getting revenge on him)

original: Put we our quarrel to the will of heaven;   Who, when they see the hours ripe on earth,   Will rain hot vengeance on offenders' heads.
translation: , we have to take it up with heaven, which, when the time comes, will make everything right again.

original: Finds brotherhood in thee no sharper spur?   Hath love in thy old blood no living fire?
translation: Don't you have anything more to say? He was your brother—is there any fire left in your old blood?

original: Edward's seven sons, whereof thyself art one,   Were as seven vials of his sacred blood,   Or seven fair branches springing from one root:
translation: You're one of  Edward's  seven sons: those sons were like seven vials of his blood or seven branches springing from one root.

original: Some of those seven are dried by nature's course,   Some of those branches by the Destinies cut;
translation: Some of these seven died naturally, some by fate;

original: But Thomas, my dear lord, my life, my Gloucester,   One vial full of Edward's sacred blood,   One flourishing branch of his most royal root,   Is crack'd, and all the precious liquor spilt,   Is hack'd down, and his summer leaves all faded,   By envy's hand and murder's bloody axe.
translation: but Thomas, my dear lord, my life, my Gloucester, one vial full of Edward's sacred blood, one fine branch of the royal root, is broken and all the precious liquid spilled, hacked down and his summer leaves all faded by the hand of envy and the bloody ax of murder.

original: Ah, Gaunt, his blood was thine! that bed, that womb,   That metal, that self-mould, that fashion'd thee   Made him a man
translation: Ah, Gaunt, his blood was yours! You were born from the same blood, the same womb; the same metal that molded you made him a man too!

original: ; and though thou livest and breathest,   Yet art thou slain in him: thou dost consent   In some large measure to thy father's death,   In that thou seest thy wretched brother die,   Who was the model of thy father's life.
translation: And although you live and breathe, you are dead in him. You have allowed your father's death, by seeing your poor brother die, who so strongly resembled his father.

original: Call it not patience, Gaunt; it is despair:
translation: Don't fool yourself by saying this is patience, Gaunt: it's despair.

original: In suffering thus thy brother to be slaughter'd,   Thou showest the naked pathway to thy life,   Teaching stern murder how to butcher thee:
translation: In allowing your brother to be slaughtered, you've shown them how to kill you:

original: That which in mean men we intitle patience   Is pale cold cowardice in noble breasts.
translation: what in poor men we call patience is just cold cowardice in noblemen.

original: What shall I say? to safeguard thine own life,   The best way is to venge my Gloucester's death.
translation: What more can I say? The best way to save yourself is to avenge my Gloucester's death.

original: God's is the quarrel; for God's substitute,   His deputy anointed in His sight,   Hath caused his death:
translation: This is God's fight; for God's substitute,  His deputy anointed in His sight, has caused his death .

original: the which if wrongfully,   Let heaven revenge; for I may never lift   An angry arm against His minister.
translation: If it was wrong, let heaven take revenge; for I will never lift an angry arm against His minister, the king.

original: Where then, alas, may I complain myself?
translation: Where then can I go for help, if not to you?

original: To God, the widow's champion and defence.
translation: To God, the champion and defender of widows.

original: Why, then, I will. Farewell, old Gaunt.
translation: Why, then, I will. Goodbye, old Gaunt.

original: Thou goest to Coventry, there to behold   Our cousin Hereford and fell Mowbray fight:
translation: You go to Coventry to see our cousin Hereford and that evil Mowbray fight:

original: O, sit my husband's wrongs on Hereford's spear,   That it may enter butcher Mowbray's breast!
translation: oh, may Hereford's spear avenge my husband by stabbing Mowbray!

original: Or, if misfortune miss the first career,   Be Mowbray's sins so heavy in his bosom,   They may break his foaming courser's back,   And throw the rider headlong in the lists,   A caitiff recreant to my cousin Hereford!
translation: Or, if he's unlucky enough to miss, I hope Mowbray's sins sit so heavy in his heart that his horse's back breaks and throws its rider to the ground, so that he becomes my cousin Hereford's wretched prisoner.

original: Farewell, old Gaunt: thy sometimes brother's wife   With her companion grief must end her life.
translation: Goodbye, old Gaunt: your dead brother's wife must end her life with grief, her only companion.

original: Sister, farewell; I must to Coventry: As much good stay with thee as go with me!
translation: Goodbye, sister; I must go to Coventry: I wish us both good fortune!

original: Yet one word more: grief boundeth where it falls,   Not with the empty hollowness, but weight:
translation: But I have one more thing to say: grief falls heavy from my mouth.

original: I take my leave before I have begun,   For sorrow ends not when it seemeth done.
translation: I leave you before I've even begun, for sorrow never ends, even when it seems done.

original: Commend me to thy brother, Edmund York.
translation: Give my good wishes to your brother, Edmund York.

original: Lo, this is all:—nay, yet depart not so;   Though this be all, do not so quickly go;   I shall remember more.
translation: This is all. But no, don't go; though that's all, don't leave so quickly; I will remember what I had to say.

original: Bid him—ah, what?—   With all good speed at Plashy visit me.
translation: Tell him—ah, what?—to visit me at Plashy as soon as he can.

original: Alack, and what shall good old York there see   But empty lodgings and unfurnish'd walls,   Unpeopled offices, untrodden stones?
translation: Oh god, what will good old York see there but empty rooms and bare walls, offices with no one to use them, stones with no one to walk on them?

original: And what hear there for welcome but my groans?   Therefore commend me; let him not come there,   To seek out sorrow that dwells every where.
translation: And what can I say to welcome him, but groans of grief? Therefore give him my good regards; tell him not to come there, to look for sorrow when grief is everywhere.

original: Desolate, desolate, will I hence and die:   The last leave of thee takes my weeping eye.
translation: I will go there, desolate, desolate, and die: I cry as I leave you for the last time.

original: My Lord Aumerle, is Harry Hereford arm'd?
translation: My Lord Aumerle, is Harry Hereford ready for battle?

original: Yea, at all points; and longs to enter in.
translation: Yes, entirely, he's eager to get on the battlefield.

original: The Duke of Norfolk, sprightfully and bold, Stays but the summons of the appellant's trumpet.
translation: The Duke of Norfolk, filled with rage, is awaiting the sound of the trumpet to summon him to battle.

original: Why, then, the champions are prepared, and stay For nothing but his majesty's approach.
translation: Why, then, the champions are prepared, so we're just waiting for his majesty.

original: Marshal, demand of yonder champion   The cause of his arrival here in arms:
translation: Marshal, ask  that champion  why he's come here bearing arms:

original: Ask him his name and orderly proceed   To swear him in the justice of his cause.
translation: have him state his name and swear that his cause is just.

original: In God's name and the king's, say who thou art   And why thou comest thus knightly clad in arms,   Against what man thou comest, and what thy quarrel:
translation: In the name of God and the king, say who you are and why you come wearing knight's armor, who you're fighting against, and why.

original: Speak truly, on thy knighthood and thy oath;   As so defend thee heaven and thy valour!
translation: Speak truthfully, by your knighthood and your pledge of loyalty. Heaven help you to defend your honor and bravery!

original: My name is Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk;
translation: My name is Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk.

original: Who hither come engaged by my oath—   Which God defend a knight should violate!—   Both to defend my loyalty and truth   To God, my king and my succeeding issue,   Against the Duke of Hereford that appeals me
translation: I come here because I made a promise—that God forbid a knight should violate!—to defend both my loyalty and truth to God, my king, and my children, against the Duke of Hereford who accuses me.

original: And, by the grace of God and this mine arm,   To prove him, in defending of myself,   A traitor to my God, my king, and me:   And as I truly fight, defend me heaven!
translation: And, by the grace of God and the strength of my own bare hands, I'll prove him (by defending myself) to be a traitor to my God, my king, and to me. And as long as I fight honestly, I call on God in heaven to defend me!

original: Marshal, ask yonder knight in arms,   Both who he is and why he cometh hither   Thus plated in habiliments of war,
translation: Marshal, ask that knight in arms both who he is and why he comes here dressed for battle.

original: And formally, according to our law,   Depose him in the justice of his cause.
translation: And formally, according to our law, ask him to explain why he thinks his accusation is justified.

original: What is thy name?
translation: What is your name?

original: and wherefore comest thou hither,   Before King Richard in his royal lists?
translation: And why do you come here before King Richard in his royal  lists ?

original: Against whom comest thou? and what's thy quarrel?   Speak like a true knight, so defend thee heaven!
translation: Whom are you here to oppose?  And what's your argument? Speak like a true knight, so help you God!

original: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby   Am I;
translation: I am Harry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby.

original: who ready here do stand in arms,   To prove, by God's grace and my body's valour,   In lists, on Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk,   That he is a traitor, foul and dangerous,   To God of heaven, King Richard and to me;
translation: I stand here ready in my armor to prove, by God's grace and my bravery on the field, that Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, is a foul and dangerous traitor to God, King Richard, and to me.

original: And as I truly fight, defend me heaven!
translation: And as long as I fight honestly, I call on God in heaven to defend me!

original: On pain of death, no person be so bold   Or daring-hardy as to touch the lists,
translation: On pain of death, no one should be so bold as to touch the king's lists

original: Except the marshal and such officers   Appointed to direct these fair designs.
translation: except the marshal and the officers in charge.

original: Lord marshal, let me kiss my sovereign's hand,   And bow my knee before his majesty:
translation: Lord marshal, let me kiss my sovereign's hand and bow my knee before his majesty.

original: For Mowbray and myself are like two men   That vow a long and weary pilgrimage;
translation: Mowbray and I are like two men about to go on a long and tiring  pilgrimage,

original: Then let us take a ceremonious leave   And loving farewell of our several friends.
translation: so let us say a loving goodbye to our friends.

original: The appellant in all duty greets your highness, And craves to kiss your hand and take his leave.
translation: The accuser greets your highness with all loyalty and respect, desiring to kiss your hand and say goodbye.

original: We will descend and fold him in our arms.
translation: We will descend and embrace him.

original: Cousin of Hereford, as thy cause is right,   So be thy fortune in this royal fight!
translation: Cousin of Hereford, if your cause is just, may you be victorious in this royal fight!

original: Farewell, my blood; which if to-day thou shed,   Lament we may, but not revenge thee dead.
translation: Farewell, my  blood ;  if that blood is shed today, we'll lament it, but we won't take revenge.

original: O let no noble eye profane a tear   For me, if I be gored with Mowbray's spear:
translation: Oh, please let me not cry if Mowbray stabs me.

original: As confident as is the falcon's flight   Against a bird, do I with Mowbray fight.
translation: I'll fight with him as confident as a  falcon  against a defenseless little bird.

original: My loving lord, I take my leave of you;   Of you, my noble cousin, Lord Aumerle;
translation: My loving lord, I say goodbye to you and to my noble cousin, Lord Aumerle.

original: Not sick, although I have to do with death,   But lusty, young, and cheerly drawing breath.
translation: I may die, but I'm not sick. No, I'm young, vigorous, and still cheerfully drawing breath.

original: Lo, as at English feasts, so I regret   The daintiest last, to make the end most sweet:   O thou, the earthly author of my blood,   Whose youthful spirit, in me regenerate,   Doth with a twofold vigour lift me up   To reach at victory above my head,   Add proof unto mine armour with thy prayers;
translation: And just as I leave the best for last at the dinner table, so do I turn to you, father, whose youthful spirit lives on in me and gives me strength in the fight to come.

original: And with thy blessings steel my lance's point,   That it may enter Mowbray's waxen coat,   And furnish new the name of John a Gaunt,   Even in the lusty havior of his son.
translation: With your blessings on my lance, may it defeat Mowbray and add new glory to the name of John of Gaunt by the deeds of his son.

original: God in thy good cause make thee prosperous!
translation: May God make you prosperous in your good cause!

original: Be swift like lightning in the execution;   And let thy blows, doubly redoubled,   Fall like amazing thunder on the casque   Of thy adverse pernicious enemy:
translation: Be swift like lightning in the fight, and let your blows fall like thunder on your evil enemy.

original: Rouse up thy youthful blood, be valiant and live.
translation: Use your youthful strength: be brave and survive.

original: Mine innocency and Saint George to thrive!
translation: Let Saint George and my innocence make me successful!

original: However God or fortune cast my lot,   There lives or dies, true to King Richard's throne,   A loyal, just and upright gentleman:
translation: Whichever way this goes, I live or die a loyal, just, and honest gentleman true to King Richard's throne.

original: Never did captive with a freer heart   Cast off his chains of bondage and embrace   His golden uncontroll'd enfranchisement,   More than my dancing soul doth celebrate   This feast of battle with mine adversary.
translation: A captive never escaped slavery with more happiness than my dancing soul feels at the prospect of doing battle with my enemy.

original: Most mighty liege, and my companion peers,   Take from my mouth the wish of happy years:
translation: Most mighty liege, and my fellow nobles, I wish you all many happy years:

original: As gentle and as jocund as to jest   Go I to fight: truth hath a quiet breast.
translation: I go to fight as peacefully and happily as if I were just heading out to play a game, for honesty sets the heart at ease.

original: Farewell, my lord: securely I espy Virtue with valour couched in thine eye. Order the trial, marshal, and begin.
translation: Goodbye, my lord: I see bravery and virtue in your eyes. Order the fight, marshal, and begin.

original: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby, Receive thy lance; and God defend the right!
translation: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby, take your weapons, and may God defend whichever of you is truly innocent!

original: Strong as a tower in hope, I cry amen.
translation: Strong as a tower in my hopes, I cry out "amen."

original: Go bear this lance to Thomas, Duke of Norfolk.
translation: Go take this lance to Thomas, Duke of Norfolk.

original: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby,   Stands here for God, his sovereign and himself,
translation: Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby, stands here for God, his sovereign and himself,

original: On pain to be found false and recreant,   To prove the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray,   A traitor to his God, his king and him;
translation: to prove the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray, a traitor to his God, his king and him, and if not to prove himself a false liar:

original: And dares him to set forward to the fight.
translation: he challenges Mowbray to fight.

original: Here standeth Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk,   On pain to be found false and recreant,   Both to defend himself and to approve   Henry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby,   To God, his sovereign and to him disloyal;
translation: Here stands Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, both to defend himself and to prove Henry of Hereford, Lancaster, and Derby, disloyal to God, his sovereign and to him, and if not to prove himself a false liar:

original: Courageously and with a free desire   Attending but the signal to begin.
translation: courageously and eagerly, he waits for the signal to begin.

original: Sound, trumpets; and set forward, combatants.
translation: Sound the trumpets, and combatants, come forward.

original: Stay, the king hath thrown his warder down.
Let them lay by their helmets and their spears,   And both return back to their chairs again:
translation: Let them both set down their helmets and their spears, return back to their chairs again

original: Withdraw with us: and let the trumpets sound   While we return these dukes what we decree.
translation: , and come inside with us. And sound the trumpets while we tell the dukes what we've decided.

original: Draw near,   And list what with our council we have done.
translation: Come close to me, and hear what we've decided to do after consulting with our advisers.

original: For that our kingdom's earth should not be soil'd   With that dear blood which it hath fostered;
translation: So that our kingdom's ground should not be soiled with the blood of its own people,

original: And for our eyes do hate the dire aspect   Of civil wounds plough'd up with neighbours' sword;
translation: because our eyes hate the sight of civil war between our subjects,

original: And for we think the eagle-winged pride   Of sky-aspiring and ambitious thoughts,   With rival-hating envy, set on you   To wake our peace,
translation: and because we think it was your pride and ambition that made you disturb our country's peace,

original: which in our country's cradle   Draws the sweet infant breath of gentle sleep;   Which so roused up with boisterous untuned drums,   With harsh resounding trumpets' dreadful bray,   And grating shock of wrathful iron arms,
translation: which had been "sleeping" undisturbed like a baby until you woke it with your trumpets and drums of war,

original: Might from our quiet confines fright fair peace   And make us wade even in our kindred's blood,
translation: frightening peace away and leaving us to wade through the blood of our own family members.

original: Therefore, we banish you our territories:   You, cousin Hereford, upon pain of life,   Till twice five summers have enrich'd our fields   Shall not regreet our fair dominions,   But tread the stranger paths of banishment.
translation: We banish you from our territories. You, cousin Hereford, upon pain of death, shall not come to our fair England again for ten years, and instead will walk the unfamiliar paths of banishment.

original: Your will be done:
translation: I must obey your will.

original: this must my comfort be,   Sun that warms you here shall shine on me;
translation: My comfort is that the sun that warms you here shall shine on me,

original: And those his golden beams to you here lent   Shall point on me and gild my banishment.
translation: and the golden beams that look down on you here will also  make my banishment more bearable .

original: Norfolk, for thee remains a heavier doom,   Which I with some unwillingness pronounce:
translation: Norfolk, there's a worse sentence for you, which I say with some regret:

original: The sly slow hours shall not determinate   The dateless limit of thy dear exile;
translation: the slow hours will not bring you any closer to ending your banishment,

original: The hopeless word of 'never to return'   Breathe I against thee, upon pain of life.
translation: for I order you never to return, upon pain of death.

original: A heavy sentence, my most sovereign liege,   And all unlook'd for from your highness' mouth:
translation: A harsh sentence, my most sovereign liege, and unfair from your highness' mouth:

original: A dearer merit, not so deep a maim   As to be cast forth in the common air,   Have I deserved at your highness' hands.
translation: I deserved a better reward from you than to be cast out of my home and into the street.

original: The language I have learn'd these forty years,   My native English, now I must forego:
translation: I must no longer speak the language I have learned these forty years, my native English,

original: And now my tongue's use is to me no more   Than an unstringed viol or a harp,   Or like a cunning instrument cased up,   Or, being open, put into his hands   That knows no touch to tune the harmony:
translation: and my tongue is now no more use to me than an unstringed violin, a harp left in a case, or an instrument put in the hands o f one who doesn't know how to play it.

original: Within my mouth you have engaol'd my tongue,   Doubly portcullis'd with my teeth and lips;
translation: You have imprisoned my tongue in my mouth, locked it up behind my teeth and lips, and now I can no longer speak.

original: And dull unfeeling barren ignorance   Is made my gaoler to attend on me.
translation: Dull emotionless ignorance is my jailer.

original: I am too old to fawn upon a nurse,   Too far in years to be a pupil now:
translation: I am too old to be a student now:

original: What is thy sentence then but speechless death,   Which robs my tongue from breathing native breath?
translation: what is your sentence then but silencing me to death by stopping my tongue from speaking its native language?

original: It boots thee not to be compassionate:
translation: It won't help you to try to make us feel sorry for you.

original: After our sentence plaining comes too late.
translation: After our sentence has been handed down, it's too late to complain.

original: Then thus I turn me from my country's light,
translation: Then thus I turn away from my country's light,

original: To dwell in solemn shades of endless night.
translation: to live in dark shades of endless night.

original: Return again, and take an oath with thee.
translation: Come back and take an oath.

original: Lay on our royal sword your banish'd hands;   Swear by the duty that you owe to God—   Our part therein we banish with yourselves—   To keep the oath that we administer:
translation: Lay your  banished hands  on our royal sword. Swear by the duty that you owe to God—your duty to us we banish with you—to keep the promise you make here today:

original: You never shall, so help you truth and God!   Embrace each other's love in banishment;   Nor never look upon each other's face;
translation: that you never shall—so help you God!—become allies in banishment, nor ever look upon each other's face;

original: Nor never write, regreet, nor reconcile   This louring tempest of your home-bred hate;   Nor never by advised purpose meet   To plot, contrive, or complot any ill   'Gainst us, our state, our subjects, or our land.
translation: nor ever write, see each other in person, or reconcile with each other; nor ever for any reason meet to plot any ill against us, our state, our subjects, or our land.

original: I swear.
translation: I swear.

original: And I, to keep all this.
translation: And I swear as well to abide by all these conditions.

original: No, Bolingbroke: if ever I were traitor,   My name be blotted from the book of life,   And I from heaven banish'd as from hence!
translation: No, Bolingbroke: if I've ever been a traitor, let my name be erased from the book of life, and I banished from heaven as I've been banished from here!

original: But what thou art, God, thou, and I do know;   And all too soon, I fear, the king shall rue.
translation: But what you are, God and I do know; and all too soon, I fear, the king will regret sparing you.

original: Farewell, my liege. Now no way can I stray;   Save back to England, all the world's my way.
translation: Goodbye, my liege. Now there's no particular way I can go; all roads are open to me, except those leading back to England.

original: Uncle, even in the glasses of thine eyes   I see thy grieved heart:
translation: Uncle, even in the mirrors of your eyes, I see the reflection of your grief.

original: thy sad aspect   Hath from the number of his banish'd years   Pluck'd four away.
translation: Based on your sad expression, I will reduce your son's banishment by four years.

original: Six frozen winter spent, Return with welcome home from banishment.
translation: After six frozen winters have passed, come home from banishment—with my welcome.

original: How long a time lies in one little word!   Four lagging winters and four wanton springs   End in a word:
translation: How long a time lies in one little word! Four long winters and four fresh springs end in a word:

original: such is the breath of kings.
translation: such is the power of a king's wishes.

original: I thank my liege, that in regard of me   He shortens four years of my son's exile:
translation: I'm thankful to my liege, that out of kindness to me he shortens four years of my son's exile:

original: But little vantage shall I reap thereby;
translation: but little good it will do me.

original: For, ere the six years that he hath to spend   Can change their moons and bring their times about   My oil-dried lamp and time-bewasted light   Shall be extinct with age and endless night;
translation: For before six years have passed, the lamp of my life will have gone out with age;

original: My inch of taper will be burnt and done,   And blindfold death not let me see my son.
