translation: my candle will have burned down, and death's blindfold will stop me from seeing my son.

original: Why uncle, thou hast many years to live.
translation: Why, uncle, you have many years to live.

original: But not a minute, king, that thou canst give:
translation: But not a minute, king, that you can give:

original: Shorten my days thou canst with sullen sorrow,   And pluck nights from me, but not lend a morrow;   Thou canst help time to furrow me with age,   But stop no wrinkle in his pilgrimage;
translation: you can shorten my days with sorrow and keep me up at night, but you can't give me a morning: you can help time to age me, but you can't stop wrinkles in their tracks:

original: Thy word is current with him for my death,   But dead, thy kingdom cannot buy my breath.
translation: your word can make me die more quickly; but once I'm dead, all your kingdom couldn't make me breathe again.

original: Thy son is banish'd upon good advice,   Whereto thy tongue a party-verdict gave:
translation: I banished your son after taking advice from good counselors, including you.

original: Why at our justice seem'st thou then to lour?
translation: Why do you complain about the justice we have done?

original: Things sweet to taste prove in digestion sour.
translation: Things that taste sweet are difficult to digest.

original: You urged me as a judge; but I had rather   You would have bid me argue like a father.
translation: You asked my opinion as a judge, but I would rather you had asked me to argue as a father

original: O, had it been a stranger, not my child,   To smooth his fault I should have been more mild:
translation: . Oh, had it been a stranger, not my child, I would have gone easier on him;

original: A partial slander sought I to avoid,   And in the sentence my own life destroy'd.
translation: I tried to avoid looking prejudiced, but destroyed my own life in the process.

original: Alas, I look'd when some of you should say,   I was too strict to make mine own away;   But you gave leave to my unwilling tongue   Against my will to do myself this wrong.
translation: I hoped that some of you would say that I was being too harsh to my own son, but you allowed me to wrong myself.

original: Cousin, farewell; and, uncle, bid him so: Six years we banish him, and he shall go.
translation: Cousin, farewell; and, uncle, say goodbye: he's banished six years, and he shall go.

original: Cousin, farewell: what presence must not know, From where you do remain let paper show.
translation: Goodbye, cousin: what you can't tell me now, write to me.

original: My lord, no leave take I; for I will ride, As far as land will let me, by your side.
translation: My lord, I won't leave you now: I'll ride to the sea with you.

original: O, to what purpose dost thou hoard thy words, That thou return'st no greeting to thy friends?
translation: Oh, why won't you respond to your friends?

original: I have too few to take my leave of you,
translation: I have too few words of thanks,

original: When the tongue's office should be prodigal   To breathe the abundant dolour of the heart.
translation: for I'm not eloquent enough to speak the pain in my heart.

original: Thy grief is but thy absence for a time.
translation: Your grief is only your absence for a time.

original: Joy absent, grief is present for that time.
translation: Without joy, there is only grief.

original: What is six winters? they are quickly gone.
translation: What's six years? They'll pass before you know it.

original: To men in joy; but grief makes one hour ten.
translation: To happy people, perhaps; but grief makes one hour feel like ten.

original: Call it a travel that thou takest for pleasure.
translation: Pretend you're taking a trip for pleasure.

original: My heart will sigh when I miscall it so, Which finds it an inforced pilgrimage.
translation: My heart will sigh when I try to think of it that way—I know it's a forced march, not a vacation.

original: The sullen passage of thy weary steps   Esteem
translation: Then think of this hard journey

original: as foil wherein thou art to set   The precious jewel of thy home return.
translation: as a jewel box where you can set the precious stone of your return home.

original: All places that the eye of heaven visits   Are to a wise man ports and happy havens.
translation: Everywhere that God can reach is a safe haven to a wise man.

original: Teach thy necessity to reason thus;   There is no virtue like necessity.
translation: Tell yourself this: there is no virtue like necessity.

original: Think not the king did banish thee,   But thou the king.
translation: Think not that the king banished you, but instead that you banished the king.

original: Woe doth the heavier sit,   Where it perceives it is but faintly borne.
translation: Woe sits heavier where it perceives weakness.

original: Go, say I sent thee forth to purchase honour   And not the king exiled thee;
translation: Go, say I sent you out to win honor and not that the king exiled you.

original: or suppose   Devouring pestilence hangs in our air   And thou art flying to a fresher clime:
translation: Or pretend there's some disease going around here and you're leaving for a healthier climate.

original: Look, what thy soul holds dear, imagine it   To lie that way thou go'st, not whence thou comest:
translation: Whatever your soul holds dear, imagine that it lies where you're going, not where you came from.

original: Suppose the singing birds musicians,   The grass whereon thou tread'st the presence strew'd,   The flowers fair ladies, and thy steps no more   Than a delightful measure or a dance;
translation: Pretend the singing birds are musicians, the grass the carpet of a royal chamber, the flowers fair ladies, and your steps no more than a dance:

original: For gnarling sorrow hath less power to bite   The man that mocks at it and sets it light.
translation: for snarling sorrow has less power to bite the man who makes light of it.

original: Come, come, my son, I'll bring thee on thy way: Had I thy youth and cause, I would not stay.
translation: Come, come, my son, I'll bring you on your way: had I your youth and cause for anger, I would not stay.

original: Then, England's ground, farewell; sweet soil, adieu;   My mother, and my nurse, that bears me yet!
translation: Then, England's ground, farewell; sweet soil, goodbye; my mother, and my nurse, that still holds me!

original: Where'er I wander, boast of this I can,   Though banish'd, yet a trueborn Englishman.
translation: Wherever I wander, even though I am banished, I can always boast that I am a native Englishman.

original: We did observe. Cousin Aumerle, How far brought you high Hereford on his way?
translation: We did observe—. Cousin Aumerle, how far did you go with mighty Hereford on his journey?

original: I brought high Hereford, if you call him so, But to the next highway, and there I left him.
translation: I brought mighty Hereford—if you call him that—just to the next highway, and left him there.

original: And say, what store of parting tears were shed?
translation: And tell me, how many tears were shed when you left him?

original: Faith, none for me;
translation: None in fact.

original: except the north-east wind,   Which then blew bitterly against our faces,   Awaked the sleeping rheum, and so by chance   Did grace our hollow parting with a tear.
translation: Except when the northeast wind blew bitterly against our faces, making our eyes water.

original: What said our cousin when you parted with him?
translation: What did our cousin say when you left him?

original: 'Farewell:'   And, for my heart disdained that my tongue   Should so profane the word,
translation: "Farewell." And, since I hated to say goodbye without meaning it,

original: that taught me craft   To counterfeit oppression of such grief   That words seem'd buried in my sorrow's grave.
translation: I pretended to be so sorry for him that I couldn't even speak.

original: Marry, would the word 'farewell' have lengthen'd hours   And added years to his short banishment,   He should have had a volume of farewells;
translation: Indeed, if the word "farewell" could lengthen hours and add years to his short banishment, I would have said volumes of "farewells."

original: But since it would not, he had none of me.
translation: But since it would not, he got no goodbye from me.

original: He is our cousin, cousin;
translation: He is our cousin,  cousin ...

original: but 'tis doubt,   When time shall call him home from banishment,   Whether our kinsman come to see his friends.
translation: But it's doubtful that he'll come visit us in a friendly way when he comes home from banishment.

original: Ourself and Bushy, Bagot here and Green   Observed his courtship to the common people;
translation: Ourself and Bushy, Bagot here and Green observed how he courted the love of the common people.

original: How he did seem to dive into their hearts   With humble and familiar courtesy,
translation: He seemed to become very popular with them by acting humble and familiar.

original: What reverence he did throw away on slaves,   Wooing poor craftsmen with the craft of smiles   And patient underbearing of his fortune,   As 'twere to banish their affects with him.
translation: He threw away his respect on slaves, wooing poor craftsmen with crafty smiles and patience in the face of his bad luck, as if he wanted to make them love him instead of me.

original: Off goes his bonnet to an oyster-wench;   A brace of draymen bid God speed him well   And had the tribute of his supple knee,   With 'Thanks, my countrymen, my loving friends;'
translation: He took his hat off for some girl selling oysters. A pair of lowly cart-drivers told him godspeed, and he bowed to them and said "Thanks, my countrymen, my loving friends,"

original: As were our England in reversion his,   And he our subjects' next degree in hope.
translation: as if all of England were his, and he were heir to the throne.

original: Well, he is gone; and with him go these thoughts.
translation: Well, he is gone, and these thoughts should go with him.

original: Now for the rebels which stand out in Ireland,   Expedient manage must be made, my liege,
translation: Now as for the situation in Ireland—we must do something to manage the rebels, my liege.

original: Ere further leisure yield them further means   For their advantage and your highness' loss.
translation: If we wait too long they’ll use the extra time to their advantage against us.

original: We will ourself in person to this war:
translation: We will go in person to this war:

original: And, for our coffers, with too great a court   And liberal largess, are grown somewhat light,   We are inforced to farm our royal realm;   The revenue whereof shall furnish us   For our affairs in hand:
translation: and since we’re a little short on funds (having spent generously on entertainment for the court and gifts for our friends), we have no choice but to  raise taxes  to fund our war.

original: if that come short,   Our substitutes at home shall have blank charters;   Whereto, when they shall know what men are rich,   They shall subscribe them for large sums of gold   And send them after to supply our wants;
translation: If that still isn’t enough, we'll order our  proxies  back home to demand large sums of gold from rich men across the kingdom, and send the money to us abroad:

original: For we will make for Ireland presently.
translation: for we will be leaving to travel to Ireland very soon.

original: Bushy, what news?
translation: Bushy, what's the news?

original: Old John of Gaunt is grievous sick, my lord,   Suddenly taken;
translation: Old John of Gaunt is deathly sick, my lord; it came on suddenly.

original: and hath sent post haste   To entreat your majesty to visit him.
translation: He has sent a message asking  your majesty to visit him.

original: Where lies he?
translation: Where is he?

original: At Ely House.
translation: At Ely House.

original: Now put it, God, in the physician's mind   To help him to his grave immediately!
translation: Well, God hopes the doctor will help him to his grave immediately!

original: The lining of his coffers shall make coats   To deck our soldiers for these Irish wars.
translation: The money in his coffers will pay for coats for our soldiers in these Irish wars.

original: Come, gentlemen, let's all go visit him:   Pray God we may make haste, and come too late!
translation: Come, gentlemen, let's all go visit him: pray God we may get there quickly, but  come too late !

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: Will the king come, that I may breathe my last In wholesome counsel to his unstaid youth?
translation: Will the king come, so that I may spend my last breath giving wholesome advice to his reckless youth?

original: Vex not yourself, nor strive not with your breath; For all in vain comes counsel to his ear.
translation: Don't upset yourself, or waste your breath: it's no use giving him advice.

original: O, but they say the tongues of dying men   Enforce attention like deep harmony:
translation: Oh, but they say people are more likely to listen to the last words of dying men:

original: Where words are scarce, they are seldom spent in vain,   For they breathe truth that breathe their words in  pain.
translation: when words are few, they rarely miss their mark, for those who speak when they're close to death are always truthful.

original: He that no more must say is listen'd more   Than they whom youth and ease have taught to glose;
translation: The person who will soon have nothing to say is listened to more than the young, who tend to ramble on and waste words;

original: More are men's ends mark'd than their lives before:   The setting sun, and music at the close,   As the last taste of sweets, is sweetest last,   Writ in remembrance more than things long past:
translation: the death of a man is more notable than his life before. Like the setting sun or the final note of a piece of music, what comes last is sweetest and most memorable.

original: Though Richard my life's counsel would not hear,   My death's sad tale may yet undeaf his ear.
translation: So although Richard would rather not hear my advice, the sad story of my death may make him listen to me.

original: No; it is stopp'd with other flattering sounds,   As praises, of whose taste the wise are fond,   Lascivious metres, to whose venom sound   The open ear of youth doth always listen;
translation: No; his ears are filled with other sounds, like  flattering praise  from his hangers-on (which the young are always happy to hear)

original: Report of fashions in proud Italy,   Whose manners still our tardy apish nation   Limps after in base imitation.
translation: and reports of Italian fashions (which our country still shamefully attempts to imitate).

original: Where doth the world thrust forth a vanity—   So it be new, there's no respect how vile—   That is not quickly buzzed into his ears?
translation: When is there some new vanity in the world—for it's novelty that matters to him, not morality—that isn't quickly buzzed into his ears?

original: Then all too late comes counsel to be heard,   Where will doth mutiny with wit's regard.
translation: Then advice comes all too late, since his desires are stronger than his willpower.

original: Direct not him whose way himself will choose:   'Tis breath thou lack'st, and that breath wilt thou  lose.
translation: Don't give advice to him, since he only does what he wants: you're already short of breath, so don't waste it on him.

original: Methinks I am a prophet new inspired   And thus expiring do foretell of him:
translation: I think I am a prophet, newly inspired, and as I die I make this prediction.

original: His rash fierce blaze of riot cannot last,   For violent fires soon burn out themselves;
translation: His bad behavior cannot last, for violent fires soon burn themselves out;

original: Small showers last long, but sudden storms are short;   He tires betimes that spurs too fast betimes;
translation: small rain showers last long, but sudden storms are short; he who rides too fast will soon exhaust himself;

original: With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder:   Light vanity, insatiate cormorant,   Consuming means, soon preys upon itself.
translation: he who eats too quickly will choke; vanity is like an insatiable vulture that feeds on itself.

original: This royal throne of kings, this scepter'd isle,   This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars,   This other Eden, demi-paradise,   This fortress built by Nature for herself   Against infection and the hand of war,
translation: This royal throne of kings, this crowned island, this land of majesty, this seat of war, this other Eden—almost paradise—this fortress built by Nature as her home against disease and invaders,

original: This happy breed of men, this little world,   This precious stone set in the silver sea,   Which serves it in the office of a wall,   Or as a moat defensive to a house,   Against the envy of less happier lands,
translation: this happy race of men, this little world, this precious stone set in the  silver sea  (which acts as a wall or a moat that defends a castle against the jealousy of less happy nations),

original: This blessed plot, this earth, this realm, this  England,   This nurse, this teeming womb of royal kings,   Fear'd by their breed and famous by their birth,   Renowned for their deeds as far from home,   For Christian service and true chivalry,   As is the sepulchre in stubborn Jewry,   Of the world's ransom, blessed Mary's Son,
translation: this blessed plot of land, this earth, this realm, this England, this  nurse , this birthplace of royal kings who are feared and respected for their ancestry, as famous for their deeds of Christian service and true chivalry as is the tomb of Jesus!

original: This land of such dear souls, this dear dear land,   Dear for her reputation through the world,
translation: This land of such dear souls, this dear dear land, beloved for her reputation through the world

original: Is now leased out, I die pronouncing it,   Like to a tenement or pelting farm:
translation: —is now rented out, I die pronouncing it, like a  tenement  or a paltry little farm.

original: England, bound in with the triumphant sea   Whose rocky shore beats back the envious siege   Of watery Neptune, is now bound in with shame,   With inky blots and rotten parchment bonds:
translation: England, surrounded by the triumphant sea, with a rocky shore that beats back the jealousy of the sea god Neptune, is now fenced in by its own shame, sealed with ink blots and rotten legal documents.

original: That England, that was wont to conquer others,   Hath made a shameful conquest of itself.
translation: The England that used to conquer others has made a shameful conquest of itself.

original: Ah, would the scandal vanish with my life,   How happy then were my ensuing death!
translation: Ah, if the scandal ended with my life, I could die happy!

original: The king is come: deal mildly with his youth;
translation: The king is here: be gentle to this youth,

original: For young hot colts being raged do rage the more.
translation: since young horses only get angrier when shouted at.

original: How fares our noble uncle, Lancaster?
translation: How are you, noble uncle Lancaster?

original: What comfort, man? how is't with aged Gaunt?
translation: Can you give us some comfort, York? How is old Gaunt?

original: O how that name befits my composition!
translation: Oh, how that name fits me!

original: Old Gaunt indeed, and gaunt in being old:   Within me grief hath kept a tedious fast;   And who abstains from meat that is not gaunt?
translation: Old Gaunt indeed, and  gaunt  in being old: grief has made me lose my appetite, and the man who doesn't eat loses weight.

original: For sleeping England long time have I watch'd;   Watching breeds leanness, leanness is all gaunt:
translation: I've stayed up late to keep an eye on sleeping England, and lack of sleep makes you thin too.

original: The pleasure that some fathers feed upon,   Is my strict fast; I mean, my children's looks;   And therein fasting, hast thou made me gaunt:
translation: And I am fasting as well of the pleasure that some fathers feed on—by which I mean the sight of my  children —and so by depriving me of that, you have  made me gaunt:

original: Gaunt am I for the grave, gaunt as a grave,   Whose hollow womb inherits nought but bones.
translation: I am gaunt for the grave, gaunt as a grave, whose hollow womb inherits nothing but bones.

original: Can sick men play so nicely with their names?
translation: Can sick men make such amusing puns on their names?

original: No, misery makes sport to mock itself:
translation: No, I joke because I'm mocking my own misery:

original: Since thou dost seek to kill my name in me,   I mock my name, great king, to flatter thee.
translation: since you have tried to kill my family name by banishing my son, I mock my name to flatter you.

original: Should dying men flatter with those that live?
translation: Should dying men flatter those that live?

original: No, no, men living flatter those that die.
translation: No, no, living men flatter those that die.

original: Thou, now a-dying, say'st thou flatterest me.
translation: But you, who are dying, say that you flatter me.

original: O, no! thou diest, though I the sicker be.
translation: Oh, no! You're dying, although I'm the sicker one.

original: I am in health, I breathe, and see thee ill.
translation: I'm healthy, I breathe, and  I see that you're sick.

original: Now He that made me knows I see thee ill;   Ill in myself to see, and in thee seeing ill.
translation: God knows I see  you  sick; my vision may not be so good anymore, but I see you are ill.

original: Thy death-bed is no lesser than thy land   Wherein thou liest in reputation sick;
translation: Your deathbed is no less than your land, where you lie with a disease of bad reputation;

original: And thou, too careless patient as thou art,   Commit'st thy anointed body to the cure   Of those physicians that first wounded thee:
translation: and you, too careless patient that you are, put your body in the hands of the  doctors who first hurt you .

original: A thousand flatterers sit within thy crown,   Whose compass is no bigger than thy head;   And yet, incaged in so small a verge,   The waste is no whit lesser than thy land.
translation: A thousand flatters sit within your crown, which is no larger than your head: and yet despite its small size, there is a sickness there that might encompass the whole country.

original: O, had thy grandsire with a prophet's eye   Seen how his son's son should destroy his sons,   From forth thy reach he would have laid thy shame,   Deposing thee before thou wert possess'd,   Which art possess'd now to depose thyself.
translation: Oh, had your grandfather been able to see the future, seeing how his grandson would destroy his own sons, he would have taken the crown out of your grasp, deposing you before you had it—and now, you are about to depose yourself.

original: Why, cousin, wert thou regent of the world,   It were a shame to let this land by lease;   But for thy world enjoying but this land,   Is it not more than shame to shame it so?
translation: Why, cousin,  if you were king of the world it would be a shame to rent out this land; but since you're only king of this country, it's even more shameful to treat it as you do.

original: Landlord of England art thou now, not king:   Thy state of law is bondslave to the law; And thou—
translation: You're just the landlord of England, not king: you rule as a slave to the  law , not by your own right; and you—

original: A lunatic lean-witted fool,   Presuming on an ague's privilege,
translation: A crazy dim-witted fool, thinking that he can presume to criticize me just because he's ill—

original: Darest with thy frozen admonition   Make pale our cheek, chasing the royal blood   With fury from his native residence.
translation: daring with his criticisms to make us turn  pale , chasing the royal blood from our cheeks.

original: Now, by my seat's right royal majesty,   Wert thou not brother to great Edward's son,   This tongue that runs so roundly in thy head   Should run thy head from thy unreverent shoulders.
translation: Now, by the royal majesty of my throne, if you weren't my father's brother, I would have your head for this.

original: O, spare me not, my brother Edward's son,   For that I was his father Edward's son;
translation: Oh, don't spare me, my  brother Edward's  son, because I'm the son of  his  father Edward ;

original: That blood already, like the pelican,   Hast thou tapp'd out and drunkenly caroused:   My brother Gloucester, plain well-meaning soul,   Whom fair befal in heaven 'mongst happy souls!
translation: you've already drained the family blood and drunkenly rolled around in it:  I mean my brother Gloucester, a plain and well-meaning soul now in heaven, sacrificed like the  pelican.

original: May be a precedent and witness good   That thou respect'st not spilling Edward's blood:
translation: That proves that you had no problem spilling your grandfather's blood before.

original: Join with the present sickness that I have;   And thy unkindness be like crooked age,   To crop at once a too long wither'd flower.
translation: Your unkindness to our family makes my sickness worse, cutting down the already-withered flower of my life.

original: Live in thy shame, but die not shame with thee!   These words hereafter thy tormentors be!
translation: Live in your shame, but shame won't die with you: you will be remembered this way! Let these words torment you from now on!

original: Convey me to my bed, then to my grave:   Love they to live that love and honour have.
translation: Take me to my bed, then to my grave: people only love to live when they have love and honor, and I have neither.

original: And let them die that age and sullens have; For both hast thou, and both become the grave.
translation: And let them die that are old and bad-tempered! For you are both, and both are appropriate for the grave.

original: I do beseech your majesty, impute his words   To wayward sickliness and age in him:
translation: I beg your majesty, know that he only spoke this way because he is old and sick.

original: He loves you, on my life, and holds you dear   As Harry Duke of Hereford, were he here.
translation: He loves you—I swear it on my life—and holds you as dear as his own son, Harry Duke of Hereford, were he here.

original: Right, you say true: as Hereford's love, so his; As theirs, so mine; and all be as it is.
My liege, old Gaunt commends him to your majesty.
translation: My liege, old Gaunt sends greetings to your majesty.

original: What says he?
translation: What does he say?

original: Nay, nothing; all is said.
translation: Nothing; he's said all he can.

original: His tongue is now a stringless instrument;   Words, life and all, old Lancaster hath spent.
translation: His tongue is now a stringless instrument; his words and his life are finished.

original: Be York the next that must be bankrupt so! Though death be poor, it ends a mortal woe.
translation: May I be next! Death is hard, but it ends the struggles of our lives.

original: The ripest fruit first falls, and so doth he;   His time is spent, our pilgrimage must be.   So much for that.
translation: The ripest fruit falls first, and so does he; his time is over, so we must carry on his absence. So much for that.

original: Now for our Irish wars:   We must supplant those rough rug-headed kerns,   Which live like venom where no venom else   But only they have privilege to live.
translation: Now for our Irish wars: we must defeat these rough woolly-headed rebels, which spread like poison,

original: And for these great affairs do ask some charge,   Towards our assistance we do seize to us   The plate, corn, revenues and moveables,   Whereof our uncle Gaunt did stand possess'd.
translation: and since we need money to fund these great affairs, we will take all of Gaunt's property, jewels, and income.

original: How long shall I be patient? ah, how long   Shall tender duty make me suffer wrong?
translation: How long shall I be patient? Ah, how long shall duty to my king make me allow wrongdoing?

original: Not Gloucester's death, nor Hereford's banishment   Not Gaunt's rebukes, nor England's private wrongs,   Nor the prevention of poor Bolingbroke   About his marriage, nor my own disgrace,   Have ever made me sour my patient cheek,   Or bend one wrinkle on my sovereign's face.
translation: Not Gloucester's death, nor Hereford's banishment, not Gaunt's criticisms, nor England's private injuries, nor poor Bolingbroke being prevented from marrying, nor my own disgrace has ever made me give a sour look or provoke one wrinkle on my sovereign's face.

original: I am the last of noble Edward's sons,   Of whom thy father, Prince of Wales, was first:   In war was never lion raged more fierce,   In peace was never gentle lamb more mild,   Than was that young and princely gentleman.
translation: I am the last of noble Edward's sons, of whom your father, Prince of Wales, was first: that young and princely gentleman was more fierce than a lion and more gentle than a lamb in peace.

original: His face thou hast, for even so look'd he,   Accomplish'd with the number of thy hours;
translation: You have his face, for he looked exactly like you at your age.

original: But when he frown'd, it was against the French   And not against his friends;
translation: But when he frowned, it was against the French and not against his friends;

original: his noble hand   Did will what he did spend and spent not that   Which his triumphant father's hand had won
translation: he spent within his means and not what his father had earned;

original: His hands were guilty of no kindred blood,   But bloody with the enemies of his kin.
translation: his hands were not stained with the blood of his family, but bloody with the enemies of his family.

original: O Richard! York is too far gone with grief,   Or else he never would compare between.
translation: Oh Richard! York is too far gone with grief, or else he never would compare the two of you.

original: Why, uncle, what's the matter?
translation: Why, uncle, what's the matter?

original: O my liege,   Pardon me, if you please; if not, I, pleased   Not to be pardon'd, am content withal.
translation: Oh my liege, pardon me, if you please; if not, I will be content not to be pardoned.

original: Seek you to seize and gripe into your hands   The royalties and rights of banish'd Hereford?   Is not Gaunt dead, and doth not Hereford live?   Was not Gaunt just, and is not Harry true?   Did not the one deserve to have an heir?   Is not his heir a well-deserving son?
translation: Will you seize and grip into your hands all the rightful inheritance of banished Hereford? Isn't Gaunt dead, and doesn't Hereford live? Was not Gaunt fair, and is not Harry loyal? Didn't Gaunt deserve to have an heir? Is not his heir a well-deserving son?

original: Take Hereford's rights away, and take from Time   His charters and his customary rights;
translation: Take Hereford's rights away, and you take away ancient customs and rights:

original: Let not to-morrow then ensue to-day;   Be not thyself; for how art thou a king   But by fair sequence and succession?
translation: tomorrow won't come after today, and you won't be yourself—for how are you a king except by  fair inheritance and succession ?

original: Now, afore God—God forbid I say true!—   If you do wrongfully seize Hereford's rights,   Call in the letters patent that he hath   By his attorneys-general to sue   His livery, and deny his offer'd homage,   You pluck a thousand dangers on your head,   You lose a thousand well-disposed hearts   And prick my tender patience, to those thoughts   Which honour and allegiance cannot think.
translation: Now, before God—God forbid my prediction comes true!—if you wrongfully seize Hereford's rights, taking away his legal right to the income and honors of the dukedom of Lancaster, you bring a thousand dangers on your head, you lose a thousand hearts that would have been well-disposed towards you, and you test my patience by bringing me to thoughts which honor and allegiance cannot allow me to think.

original: Think what you will, we seize into our hands His plate, his goods, his money and his lands.
translation: Think what you want. We'll take his jewelry, his goods, his money and his lands.

original: I'll not be by the while: my liege, farewell:
translation: I'll not stand here while you do: my liege, goodbye.

original: What will ensue hereof, there's none can tell;   But by bad courses may be understood   That their events can never fall out good.
translation: What will happen after this, no one knows, but bad courses of action never lead to good results.

original: Go, Bushy, to the Earl of Wiltshire straight:   Bid him repair to us to Ely House   To see this business.
translation: Go to the Earl of Wiltshire straight away, Bushy, and tell him to go to Ely House to see to this business.

original: To-morrow next   We will for Ireland; and 'tis time, I trow:   And we create, in absence of ourself,   Our uncle York lord governor of England;   For he is just and always loved us well.
translation: We'll go to Ireland the day after next: it's time to, I think. In our absence, we appoint our uncle York lord governor of England, for he is just and always loved us well.

original: Come on, our queen: to-morrow must we part;   Be merry, for our time of stay is short.
translation: Come on, our queen: tomorrow must we part; be merry, for our time together is short.

original: Well, lords, the Duke of Lancaster is dead.
translation: Well, lords, the Duke of Lancaster is dead.

original: And living too; for now his son is duke.
translation: And living too; for now his son is duke.

original: Barely in title, not in revenue.
translation: But only in title, not in income.

original: Richly in both, if justice had her right.
translation: He would be rich in both, if justice had its way.

original: My heart is great; but it must break with silence, Ere't be disburden'd with a liberal tongue.
translation: I have much in my heart, but  it must break with silence before I say what I think.

original: Nay, speak thy mind; and let him ne'er speak more That speaks thy words again to do thee harm!
translation: No, come out with it, and let him never speak again that betrays you by repeating what he hears!

original: Tends that thou wouldst speak to the Duke of Hereford?
translation: Would you speak on behalf of the Duke of Hereford?

original: If it be so, out with it boldly, man;   Quick is mine ear to hear of good towards him.
translation: If it be so, come out with it boldly, man; I'm eager to hear those who speak good of him.

original: No good at all that I can do for him;
translation: I can't do much good at all for him,

original: Unless you call it good to pity him,   Bereft and gelded of his patrimony.
translation: unless you call it good to pity him for having lost his inheritance.

original: Now, afore God, 'tis shame such wrongs are borne   In him, a royal prince, and many more   Of noble blood in this declining land.
translation: Now, before God, it is a shame that he, a royal prince, is wronged in this way, as are so many more of noble blood in this declining land.

original: The king is not himself, but basely led   By flatterers;
translation: The king is not himself, but directed by flatterers;

original: and what they will inform,   Merely in hate, 'gainst any of us all,   That will the king severely prosecute   'Gainst us, our lives, our children, and our heirs.
translation: and they will tell him lies about us to make him enemies to us, our lives, our children, and our heirs.

original: The commons hath he pill'd with grievous taxes,   And quite lost their hearts:
translation: He's taxed the common people so much that he has quite lost their love;

original: the nobles hath he fined   For ancient quarrels, and quite lost their hearts.
translation: he's fined the nobles too, for old quarrels, and quite lost their hearts.

original: And daily new exactions are devised,   As blanks, benevolences, and I wot not what:
translation: Every day new taxes are invented, such as  blanks ,  benevolences , and I know not what:

original: But what, o' God's name, doth become of this?
translation: but what, in God's name, will come of this?

original: Wars have not wasted it, for warr'd he hath not,   But basely yielded upon compromise   That which his noble ancestors achieved with blows:
translation: He hasn't spent it on wars, for he hasn't fought any; instead, he makes compromises when his noble ancestors would have fought on the battlefield:

original: More hath he spent in peace than they in wars.
translation: he's spent more in peace than they spent in war.

original: The Earl of Wiltshire hath the realm in farm.
The king's grown bankrupt, like a broken man.
translation: The king's grown bankrupt, like a broken man.

original: Reproach and dissolution hangeth over him.
translation: Criticism and debauchery surround him.

original: He hath not money for these Irish wars,   His burthenous taxations notwithstanding,
translation: He has no money for these Irish wars, even with all those heavy taxes,

original: But by the robbing of the banish'd duke.
translation: except by the robbing of the banished duke.

original: His noble kinsman: most degenerate king!
translation: Who is his noble cousin—most wicked king!

original: But, lords, we hear this fearful tempest sing,   Yet see no shelter to avoid the storm;   We see the wind sit sore upon our sails,
translation: But, lords, we hear this fearful tempest coming, but see no shelter in which to hide from the storm; we see the wind wreck our sails,

original: And yet we strike not, but securely perish.
translation: and if we don't strike back, we'll surely die.

original: We see the very wreck that we must suffer;
translation: We see the shipwreck that will come to us;

original: And unavoided is the danger now,   For suffering so the causes of our wreck.
translation: there's no avoiding the danger now, for we will suffer the same.

original: Not so; even through the hollow eyes of death   I spy life peering;
translation: Not so; even through the hollow eyes of death I can see life;

original: but I dare not say   How near the tidings of our comfort is.
translation: but I dare not say how close we are to finding hope.

original: Nay, let us share thy thoughts, as thou dost ours.
translation: No, let us share your thoughts, as you do ours.

original: Be confident to speak, Northumberland:   We three are but thyself;
translation: Don't be afraid to speak, Northumberland: telling us would be like telling yourself;

original: and, speaking so,   Thy words are but as thoughts; therefore, be bold.
translation: and, speaking so, your words are just like your own thoughts; come out with it, then.

original: Then thus: I have from Port le Blanc, a bay   In Brittany, received intelligence   That Harry Duke of Hereford, Rainold Lord Cobham,   That late broke from the Duke of Exeter,   His brother, Archbishop late of Canterbury,   Sir Thomas Erpingham, Sir John Ramston,   Sir John Norbery, Sir Robert Waterton and Francis  Quoint,   All these well furnish'd by the Duke of Bretagne   With eight tall ships, three thousand men of war,   Are making hither with all due expedience   And shortly mean to touch our northern shore:
translation: Then here it is: I have from Port le Blanc, a bay in Brittany, received news that Harry Duke of Hereford, Rainold Lord Cobham (that late ran away from the Duke of Exeter), his brother, Archbishop late of Canterbury, Sir Thomas Erpingham, Sir John Ramston, Sir John Norbery, Sir Robert Waterton and Francis Quoint have been given eight tall ships and three thousand men by the Duke of Bretagne, and will soon land on our northern shore.

original: Perhaps they had ere this, but that they stay   The first departing of the king for Ireland.
translation: They would have come earlier, but are waiting for the king to leave for Ireland.

original: If then we shall shake off our slavish yoke,   Imp out our drooping country's broken wing,   Redeem from broking pawn the blemish'd crown,   Wipe off the dust that hides our sceptre's gilt   And make high majesty look like itself,
translation: If you would free us from slavery, mend our country's broken wing, save the crown from pawnbroking, wipe off the dust that hides our scepter's gold,  and make high majesty look like itself again,

original: Away with me in post to Ravenspurgh;   But if you faint, as fearing to do so,   Stay and be secret, and myself will go.
translation: come away with me now to Ravenspurgh; but if you're afraid, stay and tell no one, and I'll go on my own.

original: To horse, to horse! urge doubts to them that fear.
translation: To horse, to horse! Encourage those who are afraid.

original: Hold out my horse, and I will first be there.
translation: If my horse holds out, I'll be the first there.

original: Madam, your majesty is too much sad:
translation: Madam, your majesty is sad too often:

original: You promised, when you parted with the king,   To lay aside life-harming heaviness   And entertain a cheerful disposition.
translation: you promised, when you parted with the king, to lay aside depression and be cheerful.

original: To please the king I did; to please myself   I cannot do it;
translation: To please the king I did, but to please myself I cannot do it.

original: yet I know no cause   Why I should welcome such a guest as grief,   Save bidding farewell to so sweet a guest   As my sweet Richard
translation: Yet I don't know why I welcome such a guest as grief, except because I had to say goodbye to so sweet a guest as my sweet Richard.

original: : yet again, methinks,   Some unborn sorrow, ripe in fortune's womb,   Is coming towards me, and my inward soul   With nothing trembles
translation: And yet again, I feel as if some unborn sorrow, ready to be birthed by fortune, is coming towards me, and my soul is afraid of something

original: : at some thing it grieves,   More than with parting from my lord the king.
translation: ; it grieves at something more than just my parting from the king.

original: Each substance of a grief hath twenty shadows,   Which shows like grief itself, but is not so;
translation: For each real grief there are twenty imaginary shadows, which look like grief but are not so:

original: For sorrow's eye, glazed with blinding tears,   Divides one thing entire to many objects;   Like perspectives, which rightly gazed upon   Show nothing but confusion, eyed awry   Distinguish form:
translation: for sorrow's eye, blurred with blinding tears,  divides one thing into many objects . Like a  perspective painting  (which looked at directly is a mass of confusing shapes, but looked at from an angle shows a clear form),

original: so your sweet majesty,   Looking awry upon your lord's departure,   Find shapes of grief, more than himself, to wail;
translation: you, looking from an angle at your lord's departure, find more shapes of grief to distress you.

original: Which, look'd on as it is, is nought but shadows   Of what it is not.
translation: But, looked at it is, it's nothing but unreal shadows.

original: Then, thrice-gracious queen,   More than your lord's departure weep not: more's not  seen;   Or if it be, 'tis with false sorrow's eye,   Which for things true weeps things imaginary.
translation: Then, most gracious queen, don't cry at anything more than your lord's departure: there isn't anything else, or if there is, you're seeing it with the eye of sorrow, whose tears create imaginary images.

original: It may be so; but yet my inward soul   Persuades me it is otherwise:
translation: It may be so; and yet my inward soul tells me it's not.

original: howe'er it be,   I cannot but be sad; so heavy sad   As, though on thinking on no thought I think,   Makes me with heavy nothing faint and shrink.
translation: For whatever reason, I can't help but be sad: so extremely sad that, even if I'm not thinking of anything in particular, I feel exhausted and frightened by this heavy nothing weighing on me.

original: 'Tis nothing but conceit, my gracious lady.
translation: It's nothing but your imagination, my gracious lady.

original: 'Tis nothing less: conceit is still derived   From some forefather grief;   mine is not so,
translation: It's less than even that: at least imagination has some grief at the root of it,  whereas mine has no clear cause.

original: For nothing had begot my something grief;   Or something hath the nothing that I grieve:
translation: Nothing has caused me grief about something, or something has caused me to grieve about nothing.

original: 'Tis in reversion that I do possess;   But what it is, that is not yet known; what   I cannot name; 'tis nameless woe, I wot.
translation: Something is coming towards me, something that isn't yet known; what it is I cannot name; it's a nameless sadness, I know.

original: God save your majesty! and well met, gentlemen: I hope the king is not yet shipp'd for Ireland.
translation: God save your majesty! and greetings, gentlemen: I hope the king has not left for Ireland yet.

original: Why hopest thou so? 'tis better hope he is;
translation: Why do you hope so? One had better hope he is,

original: For his designs crave haste, his haste good hope:   Then wherefore dost thou hope he is not shipp'd?
translation: for he's in a hurry, and his success against the rebels requires speed—so why do you hope he isn't gone yet?

original: That he, our hope, might have retired his power,   And driven into despair an enemy's hope,
translation: Because then he, our hope, might have brought his army here and defeated our enemy's hopes

original: Who strongly hath set footing in this land:   The banish'd Bolingbroke repeals himself,   And with uplifted arms is safe arrived   At Ravenspurgh.
translation: —for banished Bolingbroke is back in England, and is safely arrived at Ravenspurgh with an army at his back.

original: Now God in heaven forbid!
translation: Now God in heaven forbid!

original: Ah, madam, 'tis too true:
translation: Ah, madam, it's too true.

original: and that is worse,   The Lord Northumberland, his son young Henry Percy,   The Lords of Ross, Beaumond, and Willoughby,   With all their powerful friends, are fled to him.
translation: And what's worse, the Lord Northumberland, his son young Henry Percy, and the Lords of Ross, Beaumond, and Willoughby, with all their powerful friends, have gone to fight with them.

original: Why have you not proclaim'd Northumberland And all the rest revolted faction traitors?
translation: Why have you not proclaimed Northumberland and all the rest of the rebels as traitors?

original: We have: whereupon the Earl of Worcester   Hath broke his staff, resign'd his stewardship,
translation: We have: and when we did so, the Earl of Worcester broke his  staff  and resigned his stewardship,

original: And all the household servants fled with him   To Bolingbroke.
translation: and all the household servants went with him to Bolingbroke.

original: So, Green, thou art the midwife to my woe,   And Bolingbroke my sorrow's dismal heir:
translation: So, Green, you are the midwife to my sadness, and Bolingbroke is the child of my sorrow:

original: Now hath my soul brought forth her prodigy,   And I, a gasping new-deliver'd mother,   Have woe to woe, sorrow to sorrow join'd.
translation: now my soul has brought forth her offspring, and I, a gasping new mother, have joined my unborn sorrow with a real one.

original: Despair not, madam.
translation: Don't despair, madam.

original: Who shall hinder me?
translation: Who shall stop me?

original: I will despair, and be at enmity   With cozening hope:
translation: I will despair, and be an enemy to false hope:

original: he is a flatterer,   A parasite, a keeper back of death,   Who gently would dissolve the bands of life,   Which false hope lingers in extremity.
translation: he is a flatterer, a parasite, and a keeper back of death—death, which would let us end our lives gently, when hope makes up live on and suffer.

original: Here comes the Duke of York.
translation: Here comes the Duke of York.

original: With signs of war about his aged neck:
translation: He's wearing armor;

original: O, full of careful business are his looks!
translation: oh, and he looks worried!

original: Uncle, for God's sake, speak comfortable words.
translation: Uncle, for God's sake, speak comforting words.

original: Should I do so, I should belie my thoughts:
translation: If I did so, I would be lying:

original: Comfort's in heaven; and we are on the earth,   Where nothing lives but crosses, cares and grief.
translation: comfort's in heaven; and we are on the earth, where nothing lives but problems, cares and grief.

original: Your husband, he is gone to save far off,   Whilst others come to make him lose at home:
translation: Your husband went to save a far-away place, while others make him lose at home:

original: Here am I left to underprop his land,   Who, weak with age, cannot support myself:
translation: I'm here to prop him up, but weak with age, I can't even support myself.

original: Now comes the sick hour that his surfeit made;   Now shall he try his friends that flatter'd him.
translation: Now comes the sickness after his over-indulgence; now he shall test the loyalty of the friends that flattered him.

original: My lord, your son was gone before I came.
translation: My lord, your son was gone before I came.

original: He was? Why, so! go all which way it will!
translation: He was? Why, then! What will be will be!

original: The nobles they are fled, the commons they are cold,   And will, I fear, revolt on Hereford's side.
translation: The nobles are fled; the common people are cold and will, I fear, join Hereford's side.

original: My lord, I had forgot to tell your lordship, To-day, as I came by, I called there; But I shall grieve you to report the rest.
translation: My lord, I had forgot to tell your lordship. Today, on way here, I stopped there—but I will grieve you to report the rest.

original: What is't, knave?
translation: What is it, scoundrel?

original: An hour before I came, the duchess died.
translation: An hour before I came, the duchess died.

original: God for his mercy! what a tide of woes   Comes rushing on this woeful land at once!
translation: God for his mercy! What a tide of woes comes rushing on this sad land at once!

original: I know not what to do: I would to God,   So my untruth had not provoked him to it,   The king had cut off my head with my brother's.
translation: I don't know what to do: I wish to God, provided I hadn't done anything disloyal, the king had cut off my head with my brother's.

original: What, are there no posts dispatch'd for Ireland?   How shall we do for money for these wars?
translation: What, are there no messages sent to Ireland? How will we have money for these wars?

original: Gentlemen, will you go muster men?
translation: Gentlemen, will you go raise men for battle?

original: If I know how or which way to order these affairs   Thus thrust disorderly into my hands,   Never believe me.
translation: I don't  know how or which way to order the disorderly affairs that have been thrust into my hands, believe me.

original: Both are my kinsmen:   The one is my sovereign, whom both my oath   And duty bids defend; the other again   Is my kinsman, whom the king hath wrong'd,   Whom conscience and my kindred bids to right.
translation: Both are of my family: the one is my sovereign, whom both my oath and duty bids me to defend; the other is also my kinsman, who the king has wronged, and conscience and my family bids me to fight for his rights.

original: Well, somewhat we must do.
translation: Well, we have to do something.

original: The wind sits fair for news to go to Ireland,   But none returns
translation: The wind is good to send messages to Ireland, but we've heard nothing back.

original: . For us to levy power   Proportionable to the enemy   Is all unpossible.
translation: We can't raise an army the size of Bolingbroke's.

original: Besides, our nearness to the king in love Is near the hate of those love not the king.
translation: Besides, the king's enemies hate us because he loves us.

original: And that's the wavering commons:
translation: And the wavering common people are his enemies too:

original: for their love   Lies in their purses,
translation: they love their wallets,

original: and whoso empties them   By so much fills their hearts with deadly hate.
translation: and whoever takes money from them fills their hearts with deadly hate.

original: Wherein the king stands generally condemn'd.
translation: In that the king is condemned by everyone.

original: If judgement lie in them, then so do we, Because we ever have been near the king.
translation: If they have power over us, we'll be condemned too, because we've been always  near the king.

original: Well, I will for refuge straight to Bristol castle: The Earl of Wiltshire is already there.
translation: Well, I'll go to Bristol castle now for safety; the Earl of Wiltshire is already there.

original: Thither will I with you;
translation: I'll go there for you;

original: for little office   The hateful commons will perform for us,
translation: for the common people won't do anything for us,

original: Except like curs to tear us all to pieces.   Will you go along with us?
translation: except to tear us to pieces like dogs. Will you go along with us?

original: No; I will to Ireland to his majesty.
translation: No; I'll go to Ireland to his majesty.

original: Farewell: if heart's presages be not vain,   We three here art that ne'er shall meet again.
translation: Goodbye: if the heart can predict the future, the three of us will never meet again.

original: That's as York thrives to beat back Bolingbroke.
translation: Unless York succeeds in beating back Bolingbroke.

original: Alas, poor duke! the task he undertakes   Is numbering sands and drinking oceans dry:
translation: Oh, poor duke! His task is like counting the sands or drinking an ocean dry;

original: Where one on his side fights, thousands will fly.
translation: where one fights for him, thousands will fly to the other side.

original: Farewell at once, for once, for all, and ever.
translation: Goodbye at once, for once, forever.

original: Well, we may meet again.
translation: Well, we may meet again.

original: I fear me, never.
translation: I fear never.

original: How far is it, my lord, to Berkeley now?
translation: How far is it, my lord, to Berkeley now?

original: Believe me, noble lord,   I am a stranger here in Gloucestershire:   These high wild hills and rough uneven ways   Draws out our miles, and makes them wearisome,
translation: Believe me, noble lord, Gloucestershire is unknown to me: these high wild hills and rough uneven roads have made us go more slowly.

original: And yet your fair discourse hath been as sugar,   Making the hard way sweet and delectable.
translation: And yet your words have been like sugar, making the hard way sweet and delicious

original: But I bethink me what a weary way   From Ravenspurgh to Cotswold will be found   In Ross and Willoughby, wanting your company,
translation: . It will be a tiring journey from Ravenspurgh to Cotswold for Ross and Willoughby, lacking your company,

original: Which, I protest, hath very much beguiled   The tediousness and process of my travel:
translation: which, I say, has very much improved our progress.

original: But theirs is sweetened with the hope to have   The present benefit which I possess;
translation: But theirs is sweetened by the hope to have what I have;

original: And hope to joy is little less in joy   Than hope enjoy'd:
translation: and hope of future joy is almost as good as hope currently enjoyed.

original: by this the weary lords   Shall make their way seem short, as mine hath done   By sight of what I have, your noble company.
translation: So by this their journey will seem short, as mine has in your company.

original: Of much less value is my company Than your good words. But who comes here?
translation: My company is worth less than your good words. But who comes here?

original: It is my son, young Harry Percy, Sent from my brother Worcester, whencesoever. Harry, how fares your uncle?
translation: It is my son, young Harry Percy, sent by my brother Worcester, wherever he is. Harry, how is your uncle?

original: I had thought, my lord, to have learn'd his health of  you.
translation: I had thought, my lord, that I might hear about him from you.

original: Why, is he not with the queen?
translation: Why, isn't he with the queen?

original: No, my good Lord; he hath forsook the court,
translation: No, my good lord; he has left the court,

original: Broken his staff of office and dispersed   The household of the king.
translation: broken his staff of office and dispersed the king's household.

original: What was his reason? He was not so resolved when last we spake together.
translation: What was his reason? He wasn't on our side when we last spoke together.

original: Because your lordship was proclaimed traitor.
translation: Because your lordship was proclaimed a traitor.

original: But he, my lord, is gone to Ravenspurgh,   To offer service to the Duke of Hereford,
translation: But he, my lord, is gone to Ravenspurgh, to offer his service to the Duke of Hereford,

original: And sent me over by Berkeley, to discover   What power the Duke of York had levied there;
translation: and sent me over here to Berkeley, to find out how large an army the Duke of York had raised there;

original: Then with directions to repair to Ravenspurgh.
translation: then he told me to meet him in Ravenspurgh.

original: Have you forgot the Duke of Hereford, boy?
translation: Have you forgotten the Duke of Hereford, boy?

original: No, my good lord, for that is not forgot   Which ne'er I did remember:
translation: No, my good lord, for that would be to forget what I never remembered;

original: to my knowledge,   I never in my life did look on him.
translation: to my knowledge, I've never seen him in my life.

original: Then learn to know him now; this is the duke.
translation: Then learn to know him now; this is the duke.

original: My gracious lord, I tender you my service,   Such as it is, being tender, raw and young:
translation: My gracious lord, I offer you my service, such as it is, being tender, raw and young:

original: Which elder days shall ripen and confirm   To more approved service and desert.
translation: when I'm older, I'll be more worthy of it.

original: I thank thee, gentle Percy; and be sure   I count myself in nothing else so happy   As in a soul remembering my good friends;
translation: I thank you, gentle Percy; and be sure that I count myself lucky for nothing so much as my good friends.

original: And, as my fortune ripens with thy love,   It shall be still thy true love's recompense:
translation: And as my fortune improves with your love, I'll reward you well: my heart promises this,

original: My heart this covenant makes, my hand thus seals it.
translation: and a handshake seals it.

original: How far is it to Berkeley? and what stir Keeps good old York there with his men of war?
translation: How far is it to Berkeley? And what business keeps good old York there with his soldiers?

original: There stands the castle, by yon tuft of trees,   Mann'd with three hundred men, as I have heard;
translation: There stands the castle, by that patch of trees, with three hundred men defending it, as I have heard;

original: And in it are the Lords of York, Berkeley, and Seymour;   None else of name and noble estimate.
translation: and in it are the Lords of York, Berkeley, and Seymour, but no other noblemen.

original: Here come the Lords of Ross and Willoughby, Bloody with spurring, fiery-red with haste.
translation: Here come the Lords of Ross and Willoughby, their horses bloody from spurring them on and their faces red from hurrying here.

original: Welcome, my lords. I wot your love pursues   A banish'd traitor:
translation: Welcome, my lords. I know you follow a banished  traitor:

original: all my treasury   Is yet but unfelt thanks,
translation: I can only give you thanks now,

original: which more enrich'd   Shall be your love and labour's recompense.
translation: but soon you'll be rewarded for your efforts on my behalf.

original: Your presence makes us rich, most noble lord.
translation: Your presence makes us rich, most noble lord.

original: And far surmounts our labour to attain it.
translation: And is worth more than our labor to find you.

original: Evermore thanks, the exchequer of the poor;
translation: Eternal thanks, my poor-man bankers;

original: Which, till my infant fortune comes to years,   Stands for my bounty. But who comes here?
translation: this richness must stand for my reward until my infant fortune inherits his due. But who comes here?

original: It is my Lord of Berkeley, as I guess.
translation: I think it is my Lord of Berkeley.

original: My Lord of Hereford, my message is to you.
translation: My Lord of Hereford, my message is for you.

original: My lord, my answer is—to Lancaster;   And I am come to seek that name in England;
translation: My lord, my answer can only come from my Lord of  Lancaster ; I am here to seek that name in England;

original: And I must find that title in your tongue,   Before I make reply to aught you say.
translation: and you must call me by my proper title before I can reply to anything you say.

original: Mistake me not, my lord; 'tis not my meaning   To raze one title of your honour out:
translation: Don't mistake me, my lord; I didn't mean to erase one of your titles.

original: To you, my lord, I come, what lord you will,   From the most gracious regent of this land,   The Duke of York,
translation: To you, my lord, I come, whatever lord you are, from the most gracious regent of this land, the Duke of York,

original: to know what pricks you on   To take advantage of the absent time   And fright our native peace with self-born arms.
translation: to ask why you take advantage of the king's absence to frighten our natural peace with your army.

original: I shall not need transport my words by you; Here comes his grace in person. My noble uncle!
translation: I won't need to talk to him through you; here comes his grace in person. My noble uncle!

original: Show me thy humble heart, and not thy knee, Whose duty is deceiveable and false.
translation: Show me your humble heart, and not your knee; you're only pretending to be dutiful.

original: My gracious uncle—
translation: My gracious uncle—

original: Tut, tut!   Grace me no grace, nor uncle me no uncle:   I am no traitor's uncle; and that word 'grace'   In an ungracious mouth is but profane.
translation: Tut, tut! Don't "grace" me or "uncle" me: I am no traitor's uncle; and the word "grace" in an ungracious mouth is just profanity.

original: Why have those banish'd and forbidden legs   Dared once to touch a dust of England's ground?
translation: Why have those banished and forbidden feet dared once to touch a dust of England's ground?

original: But then more 'why?' why have they dared to march   So many miles upon her peaceful bosom,   Frighting her pale-faced villages with war   And ostentation of despised arms?
translation: But then more "why?" Why have they dared to march so many miles upon this peaceful land, frightening her pale-faced villages with war and display of arms?

original: Comest thou because the anointed king is hence?   Why, foolish boy, the king is left behind,   And in my loyal bosom lies his power.
translation: Do you come because the anointed king isn't here?  Why, foolish boy, the king  is  here; he appointed me his representative.

original: Were I but now the lord of such hot youth   As when brave Gaunt, thy father, and myself   Rescued the Black Prince, that young Mars of men,   From forth the ranks of many thousand French,
translation: If only I were the young lord I was when brave Gaunt, your father, and myself rescued the Black Prince, that young  Mars  of men, from many thousand French soldiers,

original: O, then how quickly should this arm of mine   Now prisoner to the palsy, chastise thee   And minister correction to thy fault!
translation: oh, then how quickly should my hand (now prisoner to the palsy) punish you for your offence!

original: My gracious uncle, let me know my fault: On what condition stands it and wherein?
translation: My gracious uncle, tell me what I've done wrong:  what law have I broken and when?

original: Even in condition of the worst degree,   In gross rebellion and detested treason:
translation: You've broken the law in the worst way possible, in shameless rebellion detested treason:

original: Thou art a banish'd man, and here art come   Before the expiration of thy time,   In braving arms against thy sovereign.
translation: you are a banished man, but you came here before the end of your banishment, bearing arms against your sovereign.

original: As I was banish'd, I was banish'd Hereford;   But as I come, I come for Lancaster.
translation: When I was banished, I was banished as Hereford; but as I come, I come for Lancaster.

original: And, noble uncle, I beseech your grace   Look on my wrongs with an indifferent eye:
translation: And, noble uncle, I ask you to be indulgent with me:

original: You are my father, for methinks in you   I see old Gaunt alive;
translation: you are my father, for I think in you I see old Gaunt alive.

original: O, then, my father,   Will you permit that I shall stand condemn'd   A wandering vagabond;
translation: Oh, then, my father, will you allow me to stand condemned as a wandering beggar,

original: my rights and royalties   Pluck'd from my arms perforce and given away   To upstart unthrifts?   Wherefore was I born?
translation: my rights and income taken from me by force and given away to upstart spendthrifts?  Why was I born?

original: If that my cousin king be King of England,   It must be granted I am Duke of Lancaster.
translation: If my cousin is King of England, it must be that I am Duke of Lancaster.

original: You have a son, Aumerle, my noble cousin;   Had you first died, and he been thus trod down,   He should have found his uncle Gaunt a father,   To rouse his wrongs and chase them to the bay.
translation: You have a son, Aumerle, my noble cousin; if you had died first, and he was treated this way, he would have found in his uncle Gaunt a father to fight for him.

original: I am denied to sue my livery here,   And yet my letters-patents give me leave:
translation: I am refused the right to wear the colors of the dukedom of Lancaster here, although I have the legal right to do so;

original: My father's goods are all distrain'd and sold,   And these and all are all amiss employ'd.
translation: my father's good are all liquidated and sold, and these and everything he owned are put to ill ends.

original: What would you have me do?
translation: What do you want me to do?

original: I am a subject,   And I challenge law: attorneys are denied me;
translation: I am a subject, and I challenge the law:

original: And therefore, personally I lay my claim   To my inheritance of free descent.
translation: I am denied attorneys, and therefore I've come here to claim my inheritance in person.

original: The noble duke hath been too much abused.
translation: The noble duke has been too much abused.

original: It stands your grace upon to do him right.
translation: Your grace is responsible for seeing justice done.

original: Base men by his endowments are made great.
translation: Low-born men enrich themselves by his property.

original: My lords of England, let me tell you this:   I have had feeling of my cousin's wrongs   And laboured all I could to do him right;
translation: My lords of England, let me tell you this: I know my cousin has been wronged, and I've done all I could to do him right.

original: But in this kind to come, in braving arms,   Be his own carver and cut out his way,
translation: But to come like this, with an army, to help himself to what he wants at the dinner table,

original: To find out right with wrong, it may not be;
translation: to do right by doing a wrong—it must not be.

original: And you that do abet him in this kind   Cherish rebellion and are rebels all.
translation: And you that help him do this are all damned rebels.

original: The noble duke hath sworn his coming is   But for his own;
translation: The noble duke has sworn his coming is just to claim his inheritance;

original: and for the right of that   We all have strongly sworn to give him aid;
translation: and to obtain that, we have all sworn to help him.

original: And let him ne'er see joy that breaks that oath!
translation: Let him never see joy that breaks that oath!

original: Well, well, I see the issue of these arms:   I cannot mend it, I must needs confess,   Because my power is weak and all ill left:
translation: Well, well, I see how it is: I can't do anything about it, I admit, because my army is weak and too small to fight.

original: But if I could, by Him that gave me life,   I would attach you all and make you stoop   Unto the sovereign mercy of the king;
translation: But if I could, by Him that gave me life, I would punish you all and make you stoop under the king's power.

original: But since I cannot, be it known to you   I do remain as neuter.
translation: But since I cannot, be it known to you, I will remain neutral.

original: So, fare you well;   Unless you please to enter in the castle   And there repose you for this night.
translation: So, go on your way; unless you'd like to enter in the castle and sleep for this night.

original: An offer, uncle, that we will accept:
translation: An offer, uncle, that we will accept:

original: But we must win your grace to go with us   To Bristol castle, which they say is held   By Bushy, Bagot and their complices,
translation: but we must persuade your grace to go with us to Bristol castle, which they say is held by Bushy, Bagot and their accomplices—

original: The caterpillars of the commonwealth,   Which I have sworn to weed and pluck away.
translation: the caterpillars of the commonwealth, which I have sworn to weed and pluck away.

original: It may be I will go with you: but yet I'll pause;   For I am loath to break our country's laws.
translation: It may be I will go with you...but I'm still reluctant to break our country's laws.

original: Nor friends nor foes, to me welcome you are:
translation: Friend or foe, it's all the same to me:

original: Things past redress are now with me past care.
translation: I can't care anymore about things that can no longer be fixed.

original: My lord of Salisbury, we have stay'd ten days,   And hardly kept our countrymen together,   And yet we hear no tidings from the king;
translation: My lord of Salisbury, we have waited ten days, and hardly kept our countrymen together, and yet we hear nothing from the king.

original: Therefore we will disperse ourselves: farewell.
translation: Therefore we will disperse the army: farewell.

original: Stay yet another day, thou trusty Welshman: The king reposeth all his confidence in thee.
translation: Stay yet another day, trusty Welshman: you're the king's last hope.

original: 'Tis thought the king is dead; we will not stay.
translation: It's thought the king is dead; we will not wait.

original: The bay-trees in our country are all wither'd   And meteors fright the fixed stars of heaven;   The pale-faced moon looks bloody on the earth   And lean-look'd prophets whisper fearful change;
translation: The bay-trees in our country are all withered, and meteors disturb the fixed stars in the sky; the pale-faced moon looks bloody on the earth; and frightened prophets whisper of fearful change.

original: Rich men look sad and ruffians dance and leap,   The one in fear to lose what they enjoy,   The other to enjoy by rage and war:
translation: Rich men look sad and poor men dance and leap, the one fearing to lose what they enjoy, the other looking forward to enjoying the spoils of war:

original: These signs forerun the death or fall of kings.
translation: these signs predict the death or fall of kings.

original: Farewell: our countrymen are gone and fled,   As well assured Richard their king is dead.
translation: Farewell, our countrymen are as surely gone as Richard is dead.

original: Ah, Richard, with the eyes of heavy mind   I see thy glory like a shooting star   Fall to the base earth from the firmament.
translation: Ah, Richard, with the eyes of a heavy heart I see your glory fall like a shooting star from the sky back down to earth.

original: Thy sun sets weeping in the lowly west,   Witnessing storms to come, woe and unrest:
translation: The sun cries as it sets in the west, seeing storms to come, sadness, and unrest.

original: Thy friends are fled to wait upon thy foes,   And crossly to thy good all fortune goes.
translation: Your friends have abandoned you to help your enemies, and all your luck is running out.

original: Bring forth these men.
translation: Bring the men out.

original: Bushy and Green, I will not vex your souls—   Since presently your souls must part your bodies—   With too much urging your pernicious lives,   For 'twere no charity;
translation: Bushy and Green, I won't bother with your souls—since they'll be parted from your body soon anyway—by telling you what an evil life you've led, since that will be no help.

original: yet, to wash your blood   From off my hands, here in the view of men   I will unfold some causes of your deaths.
translation: But to justify myself,  I will publicly explain some reasons why you must die.

original: You have misled a prince, a royal king,   A happy gentleman in blood and lineaments,   By you unhappied and disfigured clean:
translation: You have misled a prince, a royal king—a gentleman happy in his ancestry, disfigured, and made unhappy by you.

original: You have in manner with your sinful hours   Made a divorce betwixt his queen and him,   Broke the possession of a royal bed   And stain'd the beauty of a fair queen's cheeks   With tears drawn from her eyes by your foul wrongs.
translation: Your sinfulness has caused a divorce between his queen and him, since he spent his time away from the marriage bed, amusing himself with you. You have stained the queen's cheeks with tears from your awful wrongs.

original: Myself, a prince by fortune of my birth,   Near to the king in blood, and near in love   Till you did make him misinterpret me,
translation: I was myself a prince, near to the king in fortune and blood, until you made him misinterpret me,

original: Have stoop'd my neck under your injuries,   And sigh'd my English breath in foreign clouds,   Eating the bitter bread of banishment;
translation: and have stooped my neck under your crimes, sighing my English breath in foreign lands and eating the bitter bread of banishment.

original: Whilst you have fed upon my signories,   Dispark'd my parks and fell'd my forest woods,
translation: Meanwhile, you have used my seal for your own gain, ruined my land and cut down my trees,

original: From my own windows torn my household coat,   Razed out my imprese, leaving me no sign,   Save men's opinions and my living blood,   To show the world I am a gentleman.
translation: and destroyed my coat of arms in my own windows—leaving me no sign, except men's opinions and my living blood, to show the world I am a gentleman.

original: This and much more, much more than twice all this,   Condemns you to the death.
See them deliver'd over   To execution and the hand of death.
translation: See them delivered over to execution and the hand of death.

original: More welcome is the stroke of death to me Than Bolingbroke to England. Lords, farewell.
translation: The stroke of death is more welcome to me than Bolingbroke is to England. Lords, goodbye.

original: My comfort is that heaven will take our souls And plague injustice with the pains of hell.
translation: My comfort is that heaven will take our souls, and that the unjust people who do this to us will suffer in hell.

original: My Lord Northumberland, see them dispatch'd.
translation: My Lord Northumberland, see they are executed.

original: Uncle, you say the queen is at your house   ;
translation: Uncle, you say the queen is at your house;

original: For God's sake, fairly let her be entreated:
translation: for God's sake, treat her fairly.

original: Tell her I send to her my kind commends;   Take special care my greetings be deliver'd.
translation: Tell her I send her my kind regards; take special care that my greetings are delivered.

original: A gentleman of mine I have dispatch'd With letters of your love to her at large.
translation: I've sent a servant to deliver her the letters explaining your continued love and affection for her.

original: Thanks, gentle uncle.
translation: Thanks, gentle uncle.

original: Come, lords, away.   To fight with Glendower and his complices:
translation: Come, lords, let's go to fight with  Glendower  and his accomplices:

original: Awhile to work, and after holiday.
translation: we must work a while before we can take a holiday.

original: Barkloughly castle call they this at hand?
translation: Do they call this place Barkloughly castle?

original: Yea, my lord. How brooks your grace the air, After your late tossing on the breaking seas?
translation: Yes, my lord. How do you feel, now that you're on land again after that rough sea journey?

original: Needs must I like it well: I weep for joy   To stand upon my kingdom once again.
translation: I feel much better: I weep for joy to stand upon my kingdom once again.

original: Dear earth, I do salute thee with my hand,   Though rebels wound thee with their horses' hoofs:   As a long-parted mother with her child   Plays fondly with her tears and smiles in meeting,   So, weeping, smiling, greet I thee, my earth,   And do thee favours with my royal hands.
translation: Dear earth, I touch you with my hand, even as rebels wound you with their horses' hoofs: just as a mother who's been separated from her child smiles and cries when they're reunited, so I greet you, my earth, both crying and smiling, and honor you with my royal hand.

original: Feed not thy sovereign's foe, my gentle earth,   Nor with thy sweets comfort his ravenous sense;
translation: Let no food grow for your sovereign's enemies, my gentle earth, and don't give them anything to comfort them—

original: But let thy spiders, that suck up thy venom,   And heavy-gaited toads lie in their way,   Doing annoyance to the treacherous feet   Which with usurping steps do trample thee:
translation: but let your venomous spiders and toads lie in their way, biting the treacherous feet that tread on you.

original: Yield stinging nettles to mine enemies;   And when they from thy bosom pluck a flower,   Guard it, I pray thee, with a lurking adder   Whose double tongue may with a mortal touch   Throw death upon thy sovereign's enemies.
