translation: Let your plants sting them; when they pluck a flower, let there be a poisonous snake inside it whose forked tongue could kill them in an instant.

original: Mock not my senseless conjuration, lords:
translation: Don't make fun of me for talking to the ground, my lords;

original: This earth shall have a feeling and these stones   Prove armed soldiers, ere her native king   Shall falter under foul rebellion's arms.
translation: this earth will hear me and the stones themselves will rise to my defense, before her native king is defeated by rebellion.

original: Fear not, my lord: that Power that made you king   Hath power to keep you king in spite of all.
translation: Don't be afraid, my lord; God, who made you king, has the power to keep you king in spite of everything.

original: The means that heaven yields must be embraced,   And not neglected;
translation: We should make use of what heaven gives us, not ignore it;

original: else, if heaven would,   And we will not, heaven's offer we refuse,   The proffer'd means of succor and redress.
translation: otherwise, by refusing His help, we're disobeying God's will.

original: He means, my lord, that we are too remiss;
translation: He means, my lord, that we should be doing more,

original: Whilst Bolingbroke, through our security,   Grows strong and great in substance and in power.
translation: since Bolingbroke grows stronger in power and arms through our lack of opposition.

original: Discomfortable cousin! know'st thou not   That when the searching eye of heaven is hid,   Behind the globe, that lights the lower world,   Then thieves and robbers range abroad unseen   In murders and in outrage, boldly here;
translation: Silly, gloomy cousin! Don't you know that when the sun is down, thieves and robbers roam about unseen, boldly committing murders and other crimes;

original: But when from under this terrestrial ball   He fires the proud tops of the eastern pines   And darts his light through every guilty hole,   Then murders, treasons and detested sins,   The cloak of night being pluck'd from off their backs,   Stand bare and naked, trembling at themselves?
translation: but when the the sun appears again in the east, he sets the tops of trees on fire and shines a light in every dark place—then, murders, treason, and other detestable sins will show themselves for what they are, the cloak of night plucked from their backs.

original: So when this thief, this traitor, Bolingbroke,   Who all this while hath revell'd in the night   Whilst we were wandering with the antipodes,
translation: So when this thief, this traitor, Bolingbroke—who has enjoyed the night while the we, the sun, were wandering down below

original: Shall see us rising in our throne, the east,   His treasons will sit blushing in his face,   Not able to endure the sight of day,   But self-affrighted tremble at his sin.
translation: —shall see us rising in our throne, the east, his treason will not survive the light of day, and even he will tremble at his sin.

original: Not all the water in the rough rude sea   Can wash the balm off from an anointed king;
translation: Not all the water in the rough rude sea can wash the  balm  off from an anointed king;

original: The breath of worldly men cannot depose   The deputy elected by the Lord:
translation: no word from an ordinary, earthly man can depose the deputy elected by the Lord.

original: For every man that Bolingbroke hath press'd   To lift shrewd steel against our golden crown,   God for his Richard hath in heavenly pay   A glorious angel:
translation: For every man that Bolingbroke has in his army, God has a glorious angel to fight for Richard;

original: then, if angels fight,   Weak men must fall, for heaven still guards the right.
translation: and if angels fight, weak men must be defeated, for heaven still defends the what is right.

original: Welcome, my lord! how far off lies your power?
translation: Welcome, my lord! How far away is your army?

original: Nor near nor farther off, my gracious lord,   Than this weak arm:
translation: My weak arm, my gracious lord, is as close are you're going to get to an army:

original: discomfort guides my tongue   And bids me speak of nothing but despair.
translation: gloom guides my tongue and makes me speak of nothing but despair.

original: One day too late, I fear me, noble lord,   Hath clouded all thy happy days on earth:   O, call back yesterday, bid time return,   And thou shalt have twelve thousand fighting men!
translation: Returning one day too late, I'm afraid, noble lord, has ruined all your happy days on earth: oh, call back yesterday, tell time to run backwards, and you would have had twelve thousand men to fight for you!

original: To-day, to-day, unhappy day, too late,   O'erthrows thy joys, friends, fortune and thy state:
translation: But today, today, unhappy day, it's too late: your joys, friends, fortune and kingdom are lost.

original: For all the Welshmen, hearing thou wert dead.   Are gone to Bolingbroke, dispersed and fled.
translation: For all the Welshmen, hearing you were dead, have left and gone to fight for Bolingbroke.

original: Comfort, my liege; why looks your grace so pale?
translation: Take comfort, my liege; why are you so pale?

original: But now the blood of twenty thousand men   Did triumph in my face, and they are fled;
translation: Until now the blood of twenty thousand men made my cheeks red with triumph, but now they're gone;

original: And, till so much blood thither come again,   Have I not reason to look pale and dead?
translation: and until so much blood comes to me again, don't I have good reason to look pale and dead?

original: All souls that will be safe fly from my side,   For time hath set a blot upon my pride.
translation: Anyone who would be safe, leave me! For time has ruined me.

original: Comfort, my liege; remember who you are.
translation: Be calm, my liege—remember who you are.

original: I had forgot myself; am I not king?   Awake, thou coward majesty! thou sleepest.
translation: Yes, I had forgotten. Aren't I the king? Wake up, cowardly majesty!

original: Is not the king's name twenty thousand names?   Arm, arm, my name! a puny subject strikes   At thy great glory.
translation: You've been sleeping. Isn't the king's name worth twenty thousand names? Take up arms and fight for me, my name! A puny subject threatens your great glory.

original: Look not to the ground,   Ye favourites of a king: are we not high?
translation: Don't look at the ground, my friends; aren't you raised high, as favorites of a king?

original: High be our thoughts: I know my uncle York   Hath power enough to serve our turn. But who comes  here?
translation: Our thoughts should be positive too; I know my uncle York has an army large enough to fight for us. But who's here now?

original: More health and happiness betide my liege Than can my care-tuned tongue deliver him!
translation: I wish you more health and happiness, my liege, than I can give you!

original: Mine ear is open and my heart prepared;   The worst is worldly loss thou canst unfold.
translation: I'm listening and my heart is ready; the worst you can say is just loss on this earth.

original: Say, is my kingdom lost? why, 'twas my care   And what loss is it to be rid of care?
translation: Tell me, is my kingdom lost? Well, it was my responsibility; and what loss is it to be rid of a burden?

original: Strives Bolingbroke to be as great as we?   Greater he shall not be; if he serve God,   We'll serve Him too and be his fellow so:
translation: Does Bolingbroke want to take my throne? He can never be greater; if he serves God, we're both His servants.

original: Revolt our subjects? that we cannot mend;   They break their faith to God as well as us:
translation: Do our subjects rebel against us? We can't fix that, since they betray God as well as us.

original: Cry woe, destruction, ruin and decay:   The worst is death, and death will have his day.
translation: Go ahead, speak of  despair, destruction, ruin and decay: the worst is death, and death will have his day.

original: Glad am I that your highness is so arm'd   To bear the tidings of calamity.
translation: I'm glad that your highness is so prepared to handle my sad news.

original: Like an unseasonable stormy day,   Which makes the silver rivers drown their shores,   As if the world were all dissolved to tears,   So high above his limits swells the rage   Of Bolingbroke, covering your fearful land   With hard bright steel and hearts harder than steel.
translation: Bolingbroke covers your fearful land with bright steel and hearts as hard as swords, like a stormy day that makes the rivers overflow and drown their shores.

original: White-beards have arm'd their thin and hairless scalps   Against thy majesty; boys, with women's voices,   Strive to speak big and clap their female joints   In stiff unwieldy arms against thy crown:
translation: Old men have put on helmets to cover their thin and hairless scalps; boys with women's voices try to sound like tough men;

original: The very beadsmen learn to bend their bows   Of double-fatal yew against thy state;
translation: your own archers turn their bows against you;

original: Yea, distaff-women manage rusty bills   Against thy seat: both young and old rebel,   And all goes worse than I have power to tell.
translation: even washer-women are taking up rusty pikes against your throne: both young and old rebel, and everything goes worse than I have power to tell.

original: Too well, too well thou tell'st a tale so ill.
translation: You tell a sad tale too well, too well

original: Where is the Earl of Wiltshire? where is Bagot?   What is become of Bushy? where is Green?   That they have let the dangerous enemy   Measure our confines with such peaceful steps?
translation: . Where is the Earl of Wiltshire? Where is Bagot? How have Bushy and Green let the dangerous enemy come into this country without meeting any opposition?

original: If we prevail, their heads shall pay for it:   I warrant they have made peace with Bolingbroke.
translation: If we survive this, they'll pay for it with their heads: I bet they've made peace with Bolingbroke.

original: Peace have they made with him indeed, my lord.
translation: They have indeed made peace with him, my lord.

original: O villains, vipers, damn'd without redemption!   Dogs, easily won to fawn on any man!
translation: Oh villains, vipers, damn them to hell! Dogs, easily won to slobber over any man!

original: Snakes, in my heart-blood warm'd, that sting my heart!   Three Judases, each one thrice worse than Judas!
translation: Snakes, nurtured in my own blood, that now sting my heart! Three Judases, each one three times worse than Judas!

original: Would they make peace? terrible hell make war   Upon their spotted souls for this offence!
translation: They want peace? Let hell make war on their souls for this!

original: Sweet love, I see, changing his property,   Turns to the sourest and most deadly hate:
translation: I see that sweet love easily turns to the most deadly hate.

original: Again uncurse their souls; their peace is made   With heads, and not with hands;
translation: Uncurse their souls; their peace is made by losing their heads, not with a handshake;

original: those whom you curse   Have felt the worst of death's destroying wound   And lie full low, graved in the hollow ground.
translation: the men you curse are dead in the ground for you.

original: Is Bushy, Green, and the Earl of Wiltshire dead?
translation: Are Bushy, Green, and the Earl of Wiltshire dead?

original: Ay, all of them at Bristol lost their heads.
translation: Yes, all of them lost their heads at Bristol.

original: Where is the duke my father with his power?
translation: Where is the duke my father with his army?

original: No matter where; of comfort no man speak:   Let's talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;
translation: Who cares where; let no man talk of comfort. Let's talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs;

original: Make dust our paper and with rainy eyes   Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth,
translation: dust is our paper, and with our tears we'll write "sorrow" on the ground.

original: Let's choose executors and talk of wills:   And yet not so, for what can we bequeath   Save our deposed bodies to the ground?
translation: Let's  choose executors and talk of wills—but no, for what can we leave behind after we're dead, except our  deposed  body to the grave?

original: Our lands, our lives and all are Bolingbroke's,   And nothing can we call our own but death   And that small model of the barren earth   Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.
translation: Our lands, our lives and everything we have are Bolingbroke's; we have nothing to call our own but death, and the earth covering our coffin.

original: For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground   And tell sad stories of the death of kings;
translation: For God's sake, let us sit on the ground and tell sad stories of the death of kings:

original: How some have been deposed; some slain in war,   Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed;   Some poison'd by their wives: some sleeping kill'd;   All murder'd:
translation: how some have been deposed; some killed in war; some haunted by the ghosts of the kings they deposed; some poisoned by their wives: some killed while they slept—all murdered.

original: for within the hollow crown   That rounds the mortal temples of a king   Keeps Death his court
translation: For within the hollow crown that sits on the king's mortal head, Death keeps his court,

original: and there the antic sits,   Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,   Allowing him a breath, a little scene,   To monarchize, be fear'd and kill with looks,   Infusing him with self and vain conceit,
translation: and sits amusing himself, grinning at his power, allowing the king a breath, a little time, to be a monarch, be feared and kill with looks, feeling vain and self-satisfied,

original: As if this flesh which walls about our life,   Were brass impregnable,
translation: as if this thin wall of flesh were impenetrable brass.

original: and humour'd thus   Comes at the last and with a little pin   Bores through his castle wall, and farewell king!
translation: But Death comes and with a little pin breaks through his castle wall, and: farewell king!

original: Cover your heads and mock not flesh and blood   With solemn reverence: throw away respect,   Tradition, form and ceremonious duty,   For you have but mistook me all this while:
translation: Cover your heads ; such signs of respect now are just a mockery, when you know that I'm flesh and blood.  Throw away respect, tradition, all forms of royal ceremony and duty, for you have been mistaken all this while:

original: I live with bread like you, feel want,   Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus,   How can you say to me, I am a king?
translation: I live by bread like you, feel want, taste grief, need friends. Subjected like this, how can you say to me that I am a king?

original: My lord, wise men ne'er sit and wail their woes,   But presently prevent the ways to wail.
translation: My lord, wise men never sit and wail with grief, but find ways to prevent more grief.

original: To fear the foe, since fear oppresseth strength,   Gives in your weakness strength unto your foe,   And so your follies fight against yourself.
translation: If you're afraid—since fear saps your strength—you give strength to your enemy by your weakness, and so fight against yourself.

original: Fear and be slain; no worse can come to fight:   And fight and die is death destroying death;   Where fearing dying pays death servile breath.
translation: Be afraid and you'll die; there's nothing worse than coming to a fight afraid, since to be afraid of dying is to make yourself a slave to death.

original: My father hath a power; inquire of him And learn to make a body of a limb.
translation: My father has an army; ask about him and learn to make a whole body from a single limb.

original: Thou chidest me well:
translation: You speak the truth.

original: proud Bolingbroke, I come   To change blows with thee for our day of doom.
translation: Proud Bolingbroke, I come to fight with you for our day of doom.

original: This ague fit of fear is over-blown;   An easy task it is to win our own.
translation: This fit of fear was overblown; winning will be an easy task, since we're winning what belongs to us.

original: Say, Scroop, where lies our uncle with his power?   Speak sweetly, man, although thy looks be sour.
translation: Tell us, Scroop, where is our uncle with his army? Speak sweetly, man, although your looks are sour.

original: Men judge by the complexion of the sky   The state and inclination of the day:
translation: Men look at the sky and see what sort of a day it will be;

original: So may you by my dull and heavy eye,   My tongue hath but a heavier tale to say.
translation: so you can guess, by my sad and tearful eyes, that my tongue has another heavy tale to say.

original: I play the torturer, by small and small   To lengthen out the worst that must be spoken:
translation: I'm like a torturer, telling you all the bad news in small parts.

original: Your uncle York is join'd with Bolingbroke,   And all your northern castles yielded up,   And all your southern gentlemen in arms   Upon his party.
translation: Your uncle York has allied with Bolingbroke, giving up all your northern castles and all your southern army to him.

original: Thou hast said enough.
translation: You've said enough.

original: Beshrew thee, cousin, which didst lead me forth   Of that sweet way I was in to despair!
translation: I hate you, cousin, for leading me out of that sweet way to despair!

original: What say you now? what comfort have we now?   By heaven, I'll hate him everlastingly   That bids me be of comfort any more.
translation: What do you have to say now? What comfort do we have now? By heaven, I'll hate him forever that tells me to "be of comfort" anymore.

original: Go to Flint castle: there I'll pine away;   A king, woe's slave, shall kingly woe obey.
translation: I'll go to Flint castle: there I'll waste away; a king, sorrow's slave, shall obey his sorrow.

original: That power I have, discharge; and let them go   To ear the land that hath some hope to grow,   For I have none:
translation: The men that I have, let them go, to plow the earth that still has some hope to give, for I have none.

original: let no man speak again   To alter this, for counsel is but vain.
translation: Let no men try to argue with me, for advice is no use.

original: My liege, one word.
translation: My liege, one word—

original: He does me double wrong   That wounds me with the flatteries of his tongue.
translation: He wrongs me twice that wounds me with flattery.

original: Discharge my followers: let them hence away,   From Richard's night to Bolingbroke's fair day.
translation: Release my followers; let them all go free—from Richard's night to Bolingbroke's fair day.

original: So that by this intelligence we learn   The Welshmen are dispersed,
translation: So we hear that the Welshmen have  abandoned him,

original: and Salisbury   Is gone to meet the king, who lately landed   With some few private friends upon this coast.
translation: and Salisbury went to meet the king, who recently landed with a few close friends upon this coast.

original: The news is very fair and good, my lord: Richard not far from hence hath hid his head.
translation: The news is very favorable and good, my lord: Richard is hiding not far from here.

original: It would beseem the Lord Northumberland   To say 'King Richard':
translation: Lord Northumberland should be more respectful and say "King Richard";

original: alack the heavy day   When such a sacred king should hide his head.
translation: God forbid such a sacred king should have to hide.

original: Your grace mistakes; only to be brief Left I his title out.
translation: Your grace has misunderstood me; I left his title out only to be brief.

original: The time hath been,   Would you have been so brief with him,
translation: There was a time when, if you had been so brief with him,

original: he would   Have been so brief with you, to shorten you,   For taking so the head, your whole head's length
translation: he would have been so brief with you as to shorten your body by a head.

original: Mistake not, uncle, further than you should.
translation: Careful, uncle—don't misunderstand me further than you should.

original: Take not, good cousin, further than you should. Lest you mistake the heavens are o'er our heads.
translation: Don't take, good cousin, further than you should, lest you should forget that heaven watches our actions.

original: I know it, uncle, and oppose not myself Against their will. But who comes here?
translation: I know it, uncle,  and would not oppose myself against the will of heaven. But who's here now?

original: Welcome, Harry: what, will not this castle yield?
translation: Welcome, Harry: what, won't this castle surrender?

original: The castle royally is mann'd, my lord, Against thy entrance.
translation: The castle is royally defended against your entrance, my lord.

original: Royally! Why, it contains no king?
translation: Royally! Why, since it contains no king?

original: Yes, my good lord,   It doth contain a king; King Richard lies   Within the limits of yon lime and stone:
translation: Yes, my good lord, it does contain a king; King Richard is inside those lime and stone walls,

original: And with him are the Lord Aumerle, Lord Salisbury,   Sir Stephen Scroop, besides a clergyman   Of holy reverence; who, I cannot learn.
translation: and with him are the Lord Aumerle, Lord Salisbury, Sir Stephen Scroop, and a clergyman whose name I can't find out.

original: O, belike it is the Bishop of Carlisle.
translation: Oh, no doubt it is the Bishop of Carlisle.

original: Noble lords,   Go to the rude ribs of that ancient castle;   Through brazen trumpet send the breath of parley   Into his ruin'd ears, and thus deliver:
translation: Noble lords, go to the old outer walls of that ancient castle, and sound the trumpet to announce our intention to talk with him.

original: Henry Bolingbroke   On both his knees doth kiss King Richard's hand   And sends allegiance and true faith of heart   To his most royal person,
translation: Say: Henry Bolingbroke kneels to King Richard and kisses his hand, in allegiance and true good faith,

original: hither come   Even at his feet to lay my arms and power,   Provided that my banishment repeal'd   And lands restored again be freely granted:
translation: and comes here to lay my army and power at his feet—provided that my banishment be repealed and he freely returns my property to me.

original: If not, I'll use the advantage of my power   And lay the summer's dust with showers of blood   Rain'd from the wounds of slaughter'd Englishmen:
translation: If not, I'll use the advantage of my numbers to cover the summer's dust with showers of blood rained from the wounds of slaughtered Englishmen

original: The which, how far off from the mind of Bolingbroke   It is, such crimson tempest should bedrench   The fresh green lap of fair King Richard's land,   My stooping duty tenderly shall show.
translation: —although to drench fair King Richard's green land with such a scarlet storm could not be further from my intention, as this show of respect demonstrates!

original: Go, signify as much, while here we march   Upon the grassy carpet of this plain.
translation: Go, tell him that, while we march here on this grassy plain.

original: Let's march without the noise of threatening drum,   That from this castle's tatter'd battlements   Our fair appointments may be well perused.
translation: But let's march without the noise of threatening war drums, so that our offer of peace may be taken favorably from this castle's old battlements.

original: Methinks King Richard and myself should meet   With no less terror than the elements   Of fire and water, when their thundering shock   At meeting tears the cloudy cheeks of heaven.
translation: I think King Richard and I should meet with no less force than fire and water, when they thunder and bring tears to the cheek of heaven.

original: Be he the fire, I'll be the yielding water:   The rage be his, whilst on the earth I rain   My waters; on the earth, and not on him.
translation: But if he's the fire, I'll be the submissive water: he'll rage while I  rain  my waters on the earth, and not on him.

original: March on, and mark King Richard how he looks.
translation: March on, and make sure to tell me how King Richard looks.

original: See, see, King Richard doth himself appear,   As doth the blushing discontented sun   From out the fiery portal of the east,
translation: Look, look, King Richard has appeared in person, like the angry sun from the fiery portal of the east,

original: When he perceives the envious clouds are bent   To dim his glory and to stain the track   Of his bright passage to the occident.
translation: when it seems the jealous clouds intend to dim his brightness as he travels to the west.

original: Yet looks he like a king: behold, his eye,   As bright as is the eagle's, lightens forth   Controlling majesty:
translation: Yet he looks like a king: see, his eye, as bright as the eagle's, shoots majestic glances.

original: alack, alack, for woe,   That any harm should stain so fair a show!
translation: Oh, it would be a pity if any harm should come to something so fair!

original: We are amazed; and thus long have we stood   To watch the fearful bending of thy knee,
translation: We are amazed; and have waited a long time for you to kneel to us, because we thought ourself your lawful king.

original: The king of heaven forbid our lord the king   Should so with civil and uncivil arms   Be rush'd upon!
translation: God forbid that we should threaten our lord the king with such violence!

original: Thy thrice noble cousin   Harry Bolingbroke doth humbly kiss thy hand;
translation: Your noble cousin Henry Bolingbroke humbly kisses your hand,

original: And by the honourable tomb he swears,   That stands upon your royal grandsire's bones,   And by the royalties of both your bloods,   Currents that spring from one most gracious head,   And by the buried hand of warlike Gaunt,   And by the worth and honour of himself,   Comprising all that may be sworn or said,
translation: swearing by the honorable tomb of your royal grandfather—and by the royal blood that runs in both your veins, and by the hands of his father Gaunt—

original: His coming hither hath no further scope   Than for his lineal royalties and to beg   Enfranchisement immediate on his knees:
translation: that he comes here only to reclaim his righful property and to beg on his knees that you take back his banishment.

original: Which on thy royal party granted once,   His glittering arms he will commend to rust,   His barbed steeds to stables, and his heart   To faithful service of your majesty.
translation: Once he has that, he will let his glittering sword rust away, confining his horses to their stables and his heart to the faithful service of your majesty.

original: This swears he, as he is a prince, is just;   And, as I am a gentleman, I credit him.
translation: As a prince, his word is good; as I am a gentleman, I believe him.

original: Northumberland, say thus the king returns:   His noble cousin is right welcome hither;
translation: Northumberland, tell him that the king says this: his noble cousin is very welcome here,

original: And all the number of his fair demands   Shall be accomplish'd without contradiction:
translation: and all his fair demands will be accepted without contradiction.
Say this to him as graciously as you can.

original: No, good my lord; let's fight with gentle words Till time lend friends and friends their helpful  swords.
translation: No, my good lord; let's fight with gentle words, and wait it out until our friends can come to our aid with their swords.

original: O God, O God! that e'er this tongue of mine,   That laid the sentence of dread banishment   On yon proud man, should take it off again   With words of sooth!
translation: Oh God, oh God—that my tongue, which laid the sentence of banishment on this proud man, should ever take it off again with accommodating words!

original: O that I were as great   As is my grief, or lesser than my name!
translation: Oh, that I were as a great as my grief, or less than a king!

original: Or that I could forget what I have been,   Or not remember what I must be now!
translation: Or that I could forget what I have been, or not remember what I must be now!

original: Swell'st thou, proud heart? I'll give thee scope to  beat,   Since foes have scope to beat both thee and me.
translation: Do you swell, proud heart? I'll give you some room to beat, since my enemies will soon beat both you and me.

original: Northumberland comes back from Bolingbroke.
translation: Northumberland returns with a message from Bolingbroke.

original: What must the king do now? must he submit?   The king shall do it: must he be deposed?   The king shall be contented: must he lose   The name of king? o' God's name, let it go:
translation: What does the king have to do now? Must he submit? The king shall do it. Must he be deposed? The king will be satisfied. Must he lose the name of king? In God's name, let it go:

original: I'll give my jewels for a set of beads,   My gorgeous palace for a hermitage,   My gay apparel for an almsman's gown,   My figured goblets for a dish of wood,   My sceptre for a palmer's walking staff,   My subjects for a pair of carved saints   And my large kingdom for a little grave,   A little little grave, an obscure grave;
translation: I'll exchange my jewels for a set of beads, my gorgeous palace for a hermitage, my fine clothes for a beggar's gown, my engraved goblets for a wooden dish, my scepter for a pilgrim's walking staff, and my large kingdom for a little grave, a little little grave, an obscure grave.

original: Or I'll be buried in the king's highway,   Some way of common trade, where subjects' feet   May hourly trample on their sovereign's head;   For on my heart they tread now whilst I live;   And buried once, why not upon my head?
translation: Or I'll be buried in the king's highway, some common road, where the feet of my subjects can trample on their sovereigns' head—for they tread on my heart while I live, so why not on my head after I'm dead

original: Aumerle, thou weep'st, my tender-hearted cousin!   We'll make foul weather with despised tears;
translation: Aumerle, you're crying, my tender-hearted cousin! Our tears will make bad weather;

original: Our sighs and they shall lodge the summer corn,   And make a dearth in this revolting land.
translation: our sighs will tear the summer corn from its stems, making a famine in this rebellious land.

original: Or shall we play the wantons with our woes,   And make some pretty match with shedding tears?   As thus, to drop them still upon one place,   Till they have fretted us a pair of graves   Within the earth; and, therein laid,—there lies   Two kinsmen digg'd their graves with weeping eyes.
translation: Or, shall we make a game of it, dropping all our tears in one place, until they have made a pair of graves within the earth, and lie in them—there lies two kinsmen who digged their own graves with tears.

original: Would not this ill do well? Well, well, I see   I talk but idly, and you laugh at me.
translation: Wouldn't that be funny? Well, well, I see I'm just babbling, and you laugh at me.

original: My lord, in the base court he doth attend To speak with you; may it please you to come down.
translation: My lord, he waits to speak with you in the lower courtyard, if you'll come down.

original: Down, down I come; like glistering Phaethon,   Wanting the manage of unruly jades.
translation: Down, down I come, like glittering  Phaethon , unable to manage his unruly horses.

original: In the base court? Base court, where kings grow base,   To come at traitors' calls and do them grace.   In the base court? Come down? Down, court!   down, king!
translation: In the lower courtyard? Lower courtyard, where kings are made low, coming when a traitor calls and acting respectful to him. In the lower courtyard? Come down? Down, court!

original: For night-owls shriek where mounting larks   should sing.
translation: Down, king! For it's night when it should be day.

original: What says his majesty?
translation: What does his majesty say?

original: Sorrow and grief of heart   Makes him speak fondly, like a frantic man
translation: His sorrow and grief make him sound unhinged—

original: Yet he is come.
translation: but he's here.

original: Stand all apart, And show fair duty to his majesty.
translation: Everyone make way, and show respect to his majesty.

original: My gracious lord,—
translation: My gracious lord—

original: Fair cousin, you debase your princely knee   To make the base earth proud with kissing it:
translation: Fair cousin, you shouldn't shame your knee by kneeling on the ground.

original: Me rather had my heart might feel your love   Than my unpleased eye see your courtesy.
translation: I'd rather that my heart feel you love than my eye see this sign of respect.

original: Up, cousin, up; your heart is up, I know,   Thus high at least, although your knee be low.
translation: Up, cousin, up; your heart is up, I know—this high [ points to crown] at least, although your knee is low.

original: My gracious lord, I come but for mine own.
translation: My gracious lord, I come only for what belongs to me.

original: Your own is yours, and I am yours, and all.
translation: Your own is yours, and I am yours, and everything.

original: So far be mine, my most redoubted lord, As my true service shall deserve your love.
translation: Let it be mine, my most noble lord, only as my true service deserves your love.

original: Well you deserve: they well deserve to have,   That know the strong'st and surest way to get.
translation: Oh, you deserve: they deserve who know the strongest and best way to get what they want.

original: Uncle, give me your hands: nay, dry your eyes;   Tears show their love, but want their remedies.
translation: Uncle, give me your hands: no, dry your eyes; tears show their love, but won't fix anything.

original: Cousin, I am too young to be your father,   Though you are old enough to be my heir.
translation: Cousin, I am too young to be your father, though you are old enough to be my heir.

original: What you will have, I'll give, and willing too;   For do we must what force will have us do.
translation: What you want, I'll give you willingly, for we must do what force compels us to do.

original: Set on towards London, cousin, is it so?
translation: We'll go to London, cousin, isn't that so?

original: Yea, my good lord.
translation: Yes, my good lord.

original: Then I must not say no.
translation: Then I must not say no.

original: What sport shall we devise here in this garden, To drive away the heavy thought of care?
translation: What game should we play in this garden, to distract ourselves from our sad thoughts?

original: Madam, we'll play at bowls.
translation: Madam, bowling!

original: 'Twill make me think the world is full of rubs, And that my fortune rubs against the bias.
Madam, we'll dance.
translation: Madam, we'll dance.

original: My legs can keep no measure in delight,   When my poor heart no measure keeps in grief:
translation: My legs can't keep time in delight, when my poor heart can't keep time in grief.

original: Therefore, no dancing, girl; some other sport.
translation: Therefore, no dancing, girl; something else to pass the time.

original: Madam, we'll tell tales.
translation: Madam, we'll tell stories.

original: Of sorrow or of joy?
translation: Happy or sad?

original: Of either, madam.
translation: Either, madam.

original: Of neither, girl:   For of joy, being altogether wanting,   It doth remember me the more of sorrow;   Or if of grief, being altogether had,   It adds more sorrow to my want of joy:
translation: Neither, girl: for happy stories remind me of my sorrow, and sad stories add more sorrow to my already sad life.

original: For what I have I need not to repeat;   And what I want it boots not to complain.
translation: I already know I'm sad, and there's no point in complaining about my lack of happiness.

original: Madam, I'll sing.
translation: Madam, I'll sing.

original: 'Tis well that thou hast cause But thou shouldst please me better, wouldst thou weep.
translation: I'm pleased that you feel like singing, but it would please me better if you cried.

original: I could weep, madam, would it do you good.
translation: I would cry, madam, if it would do you good.

original: And I could sing, would weeping do me good, And never borrow any tear of thee.
translation: And I could sing, if crying did me any good, and you wouldn't need to cry at all.

original: But stay, here come the gardeners:   Let's step into the shadow of these trees.
translation: But wait, here come the gardeners: let's hide in the shadow of these trees.

original: My wretchedness unto a row of pins,   They'll talk of state; for every one doth so   Against a change
translation: Oh, God, I bet they'll talk about politics, for everyone does when they expect a change in government;

original: ; woe is forerun with woe.
translation: sorrow is a sign that there's more sorrow to come.

original: Go, bind thou up yon dangling apricocks,   Which, like unruly children, make their sire   Stoop with oppression of their prodigal weight:   Give some supportance to the bending twigs.
translation: Go, tie up those dangling apricots, which overburden their parent tree with their weight, like unruly children—give some support to the bending twigs.

original: Go thou, and like an executioner,   Cut off the heads of too fast growing sprays,   That look too lofty in our commonwealth:   All must be even in our government.
translation: Go and, like an executioner, cut off the heads of plants that grow too fast and too high: in our  commonwealth , this garden, we must govern fairly and make sure no plant is taller than the others.

original: You thus employ'd, I will go root away   The noisome weeds, which without profit suck   The soil's fertility from wholesome flowers.
translation: While you're busy with that, I'll pull out the  useless weeds  that suck the soil's nutrients from our healthy flowers.

original: Why should we in the compass of a pale   Keep law and form and due proportion,   Showing, as in a model, our firm estate,
translation: But why we should we govern our garden this way—making sure everything is in proportion—within these walls,

original: When our sea-walled garden, the whole land,   Is full of weeds, her fairest flowers choked up,   Her fruit-trees all upturned, her hedges ruin'd,   Her knots disorder'd and her wholesome herbs   Swarming with caterpillars?
translation: while the world outside is full of weeds, her fairest flowers unable to grow, her fruit-trees all cut down, her hedges ruined, her mazes disorganized, and her healthy herbs swarming with caterpillars?

original: Hold thy peace:   He that hath suffer'd this disorder'd spring   Hath now himself met with the fall of leaf:
translation: Be quiet: the gardener that allowed such a mess is getting what he deserves; fall is coming after spring.

original: The weeds which his broad-spreading leaves did shelter,   That seem'd in eating him to hold him up,   Are pluck'd up root and all by Bolingbroke,   I mean the Earl of Wiltshire, Bushy, Green.
translation: The weeds sheltered by the tree's leaves (parasites that seemed to hold it up by eating it) are all plucked up, root and all, by Bolingbroke—I mean the Earl of Wiltshire, Bushy, and Green.

original: What, are they dead?
translation: What, are they dead?

original: They are; and Bolingbroke   Hath seized the wasteful king.
translation: They are; and Bolingbroke has imprisoned the wasteful king.

original: O, what pity is it   That he had not so trimm'd and dress'd his land   As we this garden!
translation: Oh, it's a pity that he didn't manage his land as we take care of this garden!

original: We at time of year   Do wound the bark, the skin of our fruit-trees,   Lest, being over-proud in sap and blood,   With too much riches it confound itself:
translation: At this time of year, we harvest the sap from our fruit-trees, so they don't rot with over-sweetness;

original: Had he done so to great and growing men,   They might have lived to bear and he to taste   Their fruits of duty:
translation: if he had done the same with his nobleman, they might have lived to produce the fruits of duty.

original: superfluous branches   We lop away, that bearing boughs may live:
translation: We cut away unnecessary branches, so that the more fruitful branches can live:

original: Had he done so, himself had borne the crown,   Which waste of idle hours hath quite thrown down.
translation: if he had done so, he might still wear the crown which he has cast away by being so lazy and careless.

original: What, think you then the king shall be deposed?
translation: What, so you think the king will be deposed, then?

original: Depress'd he is already, and deposed   'Tis doubt he will be:
translation: Well, he's been cast down already, so it seems likely that he'll be deposed:

original: letters came last night   To a dear friend of the good Duke of York's,   That tell black tidings.
translation: letters came last night to a dear friend of the good Duke of York's, telling bad news.

original: O, I am press'd to death through want of speaking!
translation: Oh, I'll die if I don't reply!

original: Thou, old Adam's likeness, set to dress this garden,   How dares thy harsh rude tongue sound this unpleasing  news?
translation: You, old man—who, like Adam, are commanded to tend this garden—how dare you talk about this sad news so rudely?

original: What Eve, what serpent, hath suggested thee   To make a second fall of cursed man?
translation: What Eve, what serpent, has persuaded you to make man fall a second time?

original: Why dost thou say King Richard is deposed?   Darest thou, thou little better thing than earth,   Divine his downfall?
translation: Why do you say King Richard is deposed? Do you dare—since you're little better than dust—to predict his downfall?

original: Say, where, when, and how,   Camest thou by this ill tidings? speak, thou wretch.
translation: Say, where, when, and how you heard this news? Speak, you fool.

original: Pardon me, madam: little joy have I   To breathe this news; yet what I say is true.
translation: Forgive me, madam: I am sad to say it, but what I say is true.

original: King Richard, he is in the mighty hold   Of Bolingbroke: their fortunes both are weigh'd:   In your lord's scale is nothing but himself,   And some few vanities that make him light;
translation: King Richard is imprisoned by the powerful Bolingbroke. Weighed against each other, Richard has only himself (and his vanities make him light);

original: But in the balance of great Bolingbroke,   Besides himself, are all the English peers,   And with that odds he weighs King Richard down.
translation: on his side of the scale, Bolingbroke has, in addition to himself, all the English noblemen, and with those odds the scale tips in his favor.

original: Post you to London, and you will find it so;   I speak no more than every one doth know.
translation: If you send a letter to London to ask for news, you'll hear the same; I'm only saying what everyone already knows.

original: Nimble mischance, that art so light of foot,   Doth not thy embassage belong to me,   And am I last that knows it? O, thou think'st   To serve me last, that I may longest keep   Thy sorrow in my breast.
translation: Bad luck, do you move so quickly that I'm the last to know it? Oh, I see, you think to come to me last, so that I'll be sorry for longer.

original: Come, ladies, go,   To meet at London London's king in woe.
translation: Come ladies, go, let's meet the king at London.

original: What, was I born to this, that my sad look   Should grace the triumph of great Bolingbroke?
translation: What, was I born for this, that I should give Bolingbroke satisfaction by looking sad at his triumph?

original: Gardener, for telling me these news of woe,   Pray God the plants thou graft'st may never grow.
translation: Gardener, for telling me this sad news, I pray to God your plants may never grow.

original: Poor queen! so that thy state might be no worse,   I would my skill were subject to thy curse.
translation: Poor queen! I would take that curse, if only it would help you.

original: Here did she fall a tear; here in this place   I'll set a bank of rue, sour herb of grace:
translation: Here did she let a tear fall to the ground; so in this place I'll plant a bed of rue, a sour but noble herb.

original: Rue, even for ruth, here shortly shall be seen,   In the remembrance of a weeping queen.
translation: Soon we'll see rue here—which stands for  ruth —to remember a queen's tears.

original: This way the king will come; this is the way   To Julius Caesar's ill-erected tower,
translation: The king will come this way; this is the way to  Julius Caesar’s tower ,

original: To whose flint bosom my condemned lord   Is doom'd a prisoner by proud Bolingbroke:
translation: where my lord is condemned by proud Bolingbroke to be a prisoner.

original: Here let us rest, if this rebellious earth   Have any resting for her true king's queen.
translation: Let us rest here, if this rebellious earth can offer any rest for her true king’s queen.

original: But soft, but see, or rather do not see,   My fair rose wither:
translation: But wait, see—or rather, don’t see—my fair rose wither.

original: yet look up, behold,   That you in pity may dissolve to dew,   And wash him fresh again with true-love tears.
translation: Yet still look at him, so that you can cry in pity and wash him fresh again with true love’s tears.

original: Ah, thou, the model where old Troy did stand,   Thou map of honour, thou King Richard's tomb,   And not King Richard;
translation: Ah, you, you’re the grave where Troy once stood, the map of honor: the tomb of King Richard, not King Richard himself.

original: thou most beauteous inn,   Why should hard-favour'd grief be lodged in thee,   When triumph is become an alehouse guest?
Join not with grief, fair woman, do not so,   To make my end too sudden:
translation: Don’t be sad too, fair woman; it will bring me to my end sooner.

original: learn, good soul,   To think our former state a happy dream;   From which awaked, the truth of what we are   Shows us but this:
translation: Good soul, pretend that our old life was a happy dream that we’ve not woken up from.

original: I am sworn brother, sweet,   To grim Necessity, and he and I   Will keep a league till death.
translation: My only companion now is Necessity, sweetheart, and I’ll be with him until my death.

original: Hie thee to France   And cloister thee in some religious house:
translation: Go to France to some religious house;

original: Our holy lives must win a new world's crown,   Which our profane hours here have stricken down.
translation: we’ll find another crown in heaven, although we’ve lost the ones we had on earth.

original: What, is my Richard both in shape and mind   Transform'd and weaken'd?
translation: What, is my Richard transformed and weakened in shape and mind?

original: hath Bolingbroke deposed   Thine intellect? hath he been in thy heart?
translation: Has Bolingbroke deposed your intellect? Has he been in your heart?

original: The lion dying thrusteth forth his paw,   And wounds the earth, if nothing else, with rage   To be o'erpower'd;
translation: The dying lion hits the ground with his paw in rage;

original: and wilt thou, pupil-like,   Take thy correction mildly, kiss the rod,   And fawn on rage with base humility,
translation: will you accept these humiliations and take your punishment like this,

original: Which art a lion and a king of beasts?
translation: when you’re a lion and a king of beasts?

original: A king of beasts, indeed; if aught but beasts,   I had been still a happy king of men.
translation: A king of beasts, indeed; if they had been nothing but beasts, I would still be a happy king of men.

original: Good sometime queen, prepare thee hence for France:   Think I am dead and that even here thou takest,   As from my death-bed, thy last living leave.
translation: Good old queen, prepare to go to France: imagine that I’m dead, and that here you’re saying goodbye to me on my deathbed

original: In winter's tedious nights sit by the fire   With good old folks and let them tell thee tales   Of woeful ages long ago betid;
translation: . During long winter nights, sit by the fire with good old people and let them tell you sad stories from long ago.

original: And ere thou bid good night, to quit their griefs,   Tell thou the lamentable tale of me   And send the hearers weeping to their beds
translation: And before you say goodnight, tell them my sad story, and send them crying to their beds:

original: For why, the senseless brands will sympathize   The heavy accent of thy moving tongue   And in compassion weep the fire out;
translation: the logs themselves will weep and extinguish the fire, and some will cry in ashes,

original: And some will mourn in ashes, some coal-black,   For the deposing of a rightful king.
translation: when they hear about the deposing of a rightful king.

original: My lord, the mind of Bolingbroke is changed: You must to Pomfret, not unto the Tower. And, madam, there is order ta'en for you; With all swift speed you must away to France.
translation: My lord, Bolingbroke has changed his mind: you must go to Pomfret, not to the Tower. And madam, he’s ordered that you must go to France.

original: Northumberland, thou ladder wherewithal   The mounting Bolingbroke ascends my throne,
translation: Northumberland—the ladder with which Bolingbroke climbs to the throne

original: The time shall not be many hours of age   More than it is ere foul sin gathering head   Shalt break into corruption:
translation: —it won’t be long until things go bad between you two:

original: thou shalt think,   Though he divide the realm and give thee half,   It is too little, helping him to all;
translation: if he gives you half the kingdom, you won’t think it’s enough, since you helped give him everything.

original: And he shall think that thou, which know'st the way   To plant unrightful kings, wilt know again,   Being ne'er so little urged, another way   To pluck him headlong from the usurped throne.
translation: And he’ll be suspicious of you; since you know how to depose kings and put someone else in their place, what’s to stop you from doing it again?

original: The love of wicked men converts to fear;   That fear to hate, and hate turns one or both   To worthy danger and deserved death.
translation: The love of wicked men turns to fear, that fear to hate, and hate to danger and deserved death.

original: My guilt be on my head, and there an end. Take leave and part; for you must part forthwith.
translation: Well, on my own head be it, and that’s it. Say goodbye; you have to go now.

original: Doubly divorced! Bad men, you violate   A twofold marriage, 'twixt my crown and me,   And then betwixt me and my married wife.
translation: Doubly divorced! Bad men, you’ve broken two marriages, one between my crown and me, and then between me and and my married wife.

original: Let me unkiss the oath 'twixt thee and me;   And yet not so, for with a kiss 'twas made.
translation: Let me unkiss the oath between you and me—and yet no, since we made it with a kiss.

original: Part us, Northumberland; I toward the north,   Where shivering cold and sickness pines the clime;
translation: Separate us, Northumberland; I to the north, where there’s nothing but cold and sickness;

original: My wife to France: from whence, set forth in pomp,   She came adorned hither like sweet May,   Sent back like Hallowmas or short'st of day.
translation: my wife to France, from whence she came like the spring, sent back like the depth of winter.

original: And must we be divided? must we part?
translation: And must we be divided? Do we have to leave each other?

original: Ay, hand from hand, my love, and heart from heart.
translation: Yes, hand from hand, my love, and heart from heart.

original: Banish us both and send the king with me.
translation: Banish us both and send the king with me.

original: That were some love but little policy.
translation: That would be nice of us, but hardly politically sensible.

original: Then whither he goes, thither let me go.
translation: Then wherever he goes, let me go with him.

original: So two, together weeping, make one woe.   Weep thou for me in France, I for thee here;
translation: So the two of us will cry together. Cry for me in France, and I’ll cry for you here;

original: Better far off than near, be ne'er the near.
translation: better to be as far away from me as possible.

original: Go, count thy way with sighs; I mine with groans.
translation: Go, count your journey with sighs, I’ll count mine with groans.

original: So longest way shall have the longest moans.
translation: The longest journey will have the longest moans of grief.

original: Twice for one step I'll groan, the way being short,   And piece the way out with a heavy heart.
translation: I’ll groan twice for every step, since my journey is short, and go with a heavy heart.

original: Come, come, in wooing sorrow let's be brief,   Since, wedding it, there is such length in grief;
translation: Let’s be brief in wooing sorrow, since it will be a long marriage.

original: One kiss shall stop our mouths, and dumbly part;   Thus give I mine, and thus take I thy heart.
translation: One kiss shall stop our mouths, and we’ll leave in silence; I'll give you mine  [kisses her]  and leave with your heart.

original: Give me mine own again; 'twere no good part   To take on me to keep and kill thy heart.
translation: Give me my heart back again; I can’t be responsible for killing your heart.

original: So, now I have mine own again, be gone,   That I might strive to kill it with a groan.
translation: So, now I have my heart again, be gone, so that I can kill it with a groan.

original: We make woe wanton with this fond delay: Once more, adieu; the rest let sorrow say.
translation: We’re making a fool of sorrow with all this delaying; goodbye, once more, and let sorrow say the rest.

original: My lord, you told me you would tell the rest,
translation: My lord, you told me you would tell the rest of the story

original: When weeping made you break the story off,
translation: since crying made you stop.

original: of our two cousins coming into London.
translation: of how our two cousins came into London,

original: Where did I leave?
translation: Where was I?

original: At that sad stop, my lord,
translation: At the sad place, my lord,

original: Where rude misgovern'd hands from windows' tops   Threw dust and rubbish on King Richard's head.
translation: where people threw dust and garbage on King Richard’s head from the windows.

original: Then, as I said, the duke, great Bolingbroke,   Mounted upon a hot and fiery steed   Which his aspiring rider seem'd to know,   With slow but stately pace kept on his course,   Whilst all tongues cried 'God save thee,   Bolingbroke!'
translation: Then, as I was saying: the duke rode through the streets on a royal horse while everyone cried “God save you, Bolingbroke!”

original: You would have thought the very windows spake,   So many greedy looks of young and old   Through casements darted their desiring eyes   Upon his visage, and that all the walls   With painted imagery had said at once   'Jesu preserve thee! welcome, Bolingbroke!'
translation: You would have thought the windows themselves were speaking, since so many people, young and old, leaned out their windows to get a look at him, and that the walls were crying out “Jesus preserve you! Welcome, Bolingbroke!”

original: Whilst he, from the one side to the other turning,   Bareheaded, lower than his proud steed's neck,   Bespake them thus: 'I thank you, countrymen:'   And thus still doing, thus he pass'd along.
translation: Meanwhile, he turned his head from one to the other, taking his hat off and speaking to them like this: “I thank you, countrymen.” And doing that, he went on his way.

original: Alack, poor Richard! where rode he the whilst?
translation: Oh, poor Richard! Where did he ride?

original: As in a theatre, the eyes of men,   After a well-graced actor leaves the stage,   Are idly bent on him that enters next,   Thinking his prattle to be tedious;
translation: Just like the audience at a theater tends not to like an actor that follows the star player, thinking him to be tedious,

original: Even so, or with much more contempt, men's eyes   Did scowl on gentle Richard;
translation: men’s eyes looked at Richard with contempt;

original: no man cried 'God save  him!'   No joyful tongue gave him his welcome home:   But dust was thrown upon his sacred head:
translation: no one cried “God save him!” No one welcomed him back, but they threw dust on his sacred head:

original: Which with such gentle sorrow he shook off,   His face still combating with tears and smiles,   The badges of his grief and patience,   That had not God, for some strong purpose, steel'd   The hearts of men, they must perforce have melted   And barbarism itself have pitied him.
translation: which he shook off with such gentle sorrow, smiling and crying at the same time, that had not God (for some purpose) steeled the hearts of men against sympathy, even a barbarian might have pitied him.

original: But heaven hath a hand in these events,   To whose high will we bound our calm contents.
translation: But heaven has a hand in these things, and we must go along with God’s will.

original: To Bolingbroke are we sworn subjects now,   Whose state and honour I for aye allow.
translation: We’re all Bolingbroke’s subjects now, and I’ve sworn to be loyal to him.

original: Here comes my son Aumerle.
translation: Here comes my son Aumerle.

original: Aumerle that was;   But that is lost for being Richard's friend,   And, madam, you must call him Rutland now:
translation: He was Aumerle; but his earldom is lost for being Richard’s friend, and madam, you must call him Rutland now.

original: I am in parliament pledge for his truth   And lasting fealty to the new-made king.
translation: I will vouch for his loyalty in Parliament.

original: Welcome, my son: who are the violets now That strew the green lap of the new come spring?
Madam, I know not, nor I greatly care not: God knows I had as lief be none as one.
translation: Madam, I don’t know, and I don’t care: I would rather be nothing than one of them.

original: Well, bear you well in this new spring of time,   Lest you be cropp'd before you come to prime.
translation: Well, behave yourself in this new spring, lest you be cropped before your time.

original: What news from Oxford? hold those justs and triumphs?
translation: What’s the news from Oxford? Did they hold the jousts?

original: For aught I know, my lord, they do.
translation: For all I know, my lord, they do.

original: You will be there, I know.
translation: You will be there, I know.

original: If God prevent not, I purpose so.
translation: If God doesn’t prevent me from going, I plan to be there.

original: What seal is that, that hangs without thy bosom? Yea, look'st thou pale? let me see the writing.
translation: What’s that letter you have? Why do you look so pale? Let me see it.

original: My lord, 'tis nothing.
translation: My lord, it's nothing.

original: No matter, then, who see it; I will be satisfied; let me see the writing.
translation: Then it shouldn’t matter who sees it; I will be satisfied in this. Let me see the letter.

original: I do beseech your grace to pardon me:
translation: I ask your grace to forgive me;

original: It is a matter of small consequence,   Which for some reasons I would not have seen.
translation: it’s a letter of no importance, which for some reasons I don't want you to see.

original: Which for some reasons, sir, I mean to see. I fear, I fear,—
translation: Which for some reasons, sir, I will see. I fear, I fear—

original: What should you fear?
translation: What should you be afraid?

original: 'Tis nothing but some bond, that he is enter'd into   For gay apparel 'gainst the triumph day.
translation: It’s nothing but some receipt for his clothes on the tournament day.

original: Bound to himself! what doth he with a bond   That he is bound to?
translation: Bound to himself? Why would he have a receipt, if he hasn't paid yet?

original: Wife, thou art a fool.   Boy, let me see the writing.
translation: Wife, you’re a fool. Boy, let me see the letter.

original: I do beseech you, pardon me; I may not show it.
translation: I beg you, forgive me; I can’t show you.

original: I will be satisfied; let me see it, I say.
translation: I will be satisfied; let me see it, I order you.

original: Treason! foul treason! Villain! traitor! slave!
translation: Treason! Foul treason! Villain! Traitor! Slave!

original: What is the matter, my lord?
translation: What is the matter, my lord?

original: Ho! who is within there?
translation: Hey! Who's inside?

original: Saddle my horse. God for his mercy, what treachery is here!
translation: Saddle my horse. God have mercy, what treachery is here!

original: Why, what is it, my lord?
translation: Why, what is it, my lord?

original: Give me my boots, I say; saddle my horse.
translation: Give me my boots, I tell you; saddle my horse.

original: Now, by mine honour, by my life, by my troth,   I will appeach the villain.
translation: Now, by my honor, by my life, and by my word, I'll turn in the villain.

original: What is the matter?
translation: What's the matter?

original: Peace, foolish woman.
translation: Be quiet, foolish woman.

original: I will not peace. What is the matter, Aumerle.
translation: I will not be quiet. What is the matter, Aumerle?

original: Good mother, be content; it is no more Than my poor life must answer.
translation: Good mother, don't ask any more questions; my life will have to answer for it.

original: Thy life answer!
translation: Your life answer for it!

original: Bring me my boots: I will unto the king.
translation: Bring me my boots; I'm going to the king.

original: Strike him, Aumerle. Poor boy, thou art amazed. Hence, villain! never more come in my sight.
translation: Hit him, Aumerle. Poor boy, you’re shocked. Go away, villain! Never come into my sight again.

original: Give me my boots, I say.
translation: Give me my boots, I tell you.

original: Why, York, what wilt thou do?   Wilt thou not hide the trespass of thine own?
translation: Why, York, what will you do? Will you not hide the crime of your own child?

original: Have we more sons? or are we like to have?   Is not my teeming date drunk up with time?
translation: Do we have any other sons? Are we likely to have any more? Aren’t I too old?

original: And wilt thou pluck my fair son from mine age,   And rob me of a happy mother's name?
translation: And will you take my fair son away from me in my old age, robbing me of the name of a happy mother?

original: Is he not like thee? is he not thine own?
translation: Isn’t he like you? Isn’t he your own?

original: Thou fond mad woman,   Wilt thou conceal this dark conspiracy?
translation: You too-fond crazy woman, will you hide this dark plot?

original: A dozen of them here have ta'en the sacrament,   And interchangeably set down their hands,   To kill the king at Oxford.
translation: A dozen of them have sworn on God to kill the king at Oxford.

original: He shall be none; We'll keep him here: then what is that to him?
translation: He won’t be a part of it; we’ll keep him here. Then what is that to him?

original: Away, fond woman! were he twenty times my son, I would appeach him.
translation: Get away from me, fond woman! If he were twenty times my son, I would still turn him in.

original: Hadst thou groan'd for him   As I have done, thou wouldst be more pitiful.
translation: If you had suffered for him in childbirth as I have, you would be more sympathetic.

original: But now I know thy mind; thou dost suspect   That I have been disloyal to thy bed,   And that he is a bastard, not thy son:
translation: But now I see: you suspect that I’ve been disloyal to your bed, and that he’s a bastard, not your son.

original: Sweet York, sweet husband, be not of that mind:   He is as like thee as a man may be,   Not like to me, or any of my kin,   And yet I love him.
translation: Sweet York, sweet husband, don’t think that: he looks as much like you as any man could, not like me or my family, and yet I love him.

original: Make way, unruly woman!
translation: Get out of my way, unruly woman!

original: After, Aumerle! mount thee upon his horse;   Spur post, and get before him to the king,   And beg thy pardon ere he do accuse thee.
translation: After him, Aumerle! Get on his horse, ride fast, and get to the king before him to beg his pardon before he’s accused you.

original: I'll not be long behind; though I be old,   I doubt not but to ride as fast as York:
translation: I won’t be far behind you: although I’m old, I can ride as fast as York:

original: And never will I rise up from the ground   Till Bolingbroke have pardon'd thee. Away, be gone!
translation: I won’t rise from kneeling until Bolingbroke has pardoned you. Go now, be gone!

original: Can no man tell me of my unthrifty son?   'Tis full three months since I did see him last;
translation: Can’t anyone tell me where my wasteful son has gone? I haven’t seen him for three months;

original: If any plague hang over us, 'tis he.
translation: if we have a plague, it’s him.

original: I would to God, my lords, he might be found:
translation: I wish we could find him—

original: Inquire at London, 'mongst the taverns there,   For there, they say, he daily doth frequent,   With unrestrained loose companions,   Even such, they say, as stand in narrow lanes,   And beat our watch, and rob our passengers;
translation: ask around at London, among the taverns, for they say he spends his time there with the sort of companions who rob people in the streets,

original: Which he, young wanton and effeminate boy,   Takes on the point of honour to support   So dissolute a crew.
translation: while he, young, stupid, and effeminate boy, spends my money supporting that crew.

original: My lord, some two days since I saw the prince, And told him of those triumphs held at Oxford.
translation: My lord, I saw the prince about two days ago, and told him about the tournament happening at Oxford.

original: And what said the gallant?
translation: And what did the young man say?

original: His answer was, he would unto the stews,   And from the common'st creature pluck a glove,   And wear it as a favour;
translation: He said he would go to the slums and take a glove from a beggar, and wear it as a favor,

original: and with that   He would unhorse the lustiest challenger.
translation: and with that would defeat the champion in a joust.

original: As dissolute as desperate;
translation: Foolish and out-of-control;

original: yet through both   I see some sparks of better hope, which elder years   May happily bring forth. But who comes here?
translation: yet even so, I see some sparks of something better which might come out when he’s older. But who’s here now?

original: Where is the king?
translation: Where is the king?

original: What means our cousin, that he stares and looks So wildly?
translation: What's wrong with you—why do you look so wild?

original: God save your grace! I do beseech your majesty, To have some conference with your grace alone.
translation: God save your grace! I beg you to give me some time to talk to you alone.

original: Withdraw yourselves, and leave us here alone.
translation: Leave us alone.

original: What is the matter with our cousin now?
translation: What is the matter with our cousin now?

original: For ever may my knees grow to the earth, My tongue cleave to my roof within my mouth Unless a pardon ere I rise or speak.
translation: May my knees grow into the earth and my tongue stick to roof of my mouth, unless you pardon me before I stand up or speak.

original: Intended or committed was this fault?
translation: Did you intend to do something wrong, or did you already do it?

original: If on the first, how heinous e'er it be,   To win thy after-love I pardon thee.
translation: If it’s the first, no matter how bad it is, I’ll forgive you to make you love me from now on.

original: Then give me leave that I may turn the key, That no man enter till my tale be done.
translation: Then let me lock the door, so that no one can come in until I've explained myself.

original: Have thy desire.
translation: As you wish.

original: My liege, beware; look to thyself; Thou hast a traitor in thy presence there.
translation: (From outside the door) My liege, beware; protect yourself; you have a traitor in there with you.

original: Villain, I'll make thee safe.
translation: Villain, I know how to protect myself.

original: Stay thy revengeful hand; thou hast no cause to fear.
translation: Wait, don't draw your sword; you have no reason to be afraid.

original: Open the door, secure, foolhardy king:
translation: Open this locked door, foolish king:

original: Shall I for love speak treason to thy face?   Open the door, or I will break it open.
translation: will you make me speak in this treasonous way to you when I'm trying to protect you? Open the door, or I will break it open.

original: What is the matter, uncle?
translation: What’s the matter, uncle?

original: speak;   Recover breath; tell us how near is danger,   That we may arm us to encounter it.
translation: Speak  [wheezes] ; recover breath. Tell us how close we are to danger, so that we can protect ourselves.

original: Peruse this writing here, and thou shalt know The treason that my haste forbids me show.
translation: Read this, and you’ll know about the treason that I’m too out of breath to explain.

original: Remember, as thou read'st, thy promise pass'd:   I do repent me;
translation: Remember, as you read, what you promised me!  I’m sorry for what I did;

original: read not my name there   My heart is not confederate with my hand.
translation: don’t see my name signed there, since my hand didn’t follow my heart.

original: It was, villain, ere thy hand did set it down.
translation: Your heart was with them even before you signed this.

original: I tore it from the traitor's bosom, king;   Fear, and not love, begets his penitence:
translation: I took it from the traitor, king; fear, and not love, motivates his confession now.

original: Forget to pity him, lest thy pity prove   A serpent that will sting thee to the heart.
translation: Don’t forgive him, lest you regret your pity later when he stabs you in the back.

original: O heinous, strong and bold conspiracy   !
translation: Oh, horrible plot!

original: O loyal father of a treacherous son!
translation: Oh, loyal father of a treacherous soon!

original: Thou sheer, immaculate and silver fountain,   From when this stream through muddy passages   Hath held his current and defiled himself!
translation: You’re a clear fountain and he’s the stream that muddies your water.

original: Thy overflow of good converts to bad,   And thy abundant goodness shall excuse   This deadly blot in thy digressing son.
translation: But your overflow of goodness will redeem your son, even though he’s committed a crime punishable by death.

original: So shall my virtue be his vice's bawd;   And he shall spend mine honour with his shame,   As thriftless sons their scraping fathers' gold.
translation: My virtue will pay for his vice, then, so that he can spend my honor with his shame, like a spendthrift son who steals his father’s money.

original: Mine honour lives when his dishonour dies,   Or my shamed life in his dishonour lies:
translation: You dishonour me by letting him live:

original: Thou kill'st me in his life; giving him breath,   The traitor lives, the true man's put to death.
translation: the traitor survives, the true man dies.

original: What ho, my liege! for God's sake, let me in.
translation: Are you there, my liege? For God’s sake, let me in.

original: What shrill-voiced suppliant makes this eager cry?
translation: What shrill-voiced petitioner is shouting at us?

original: A woman, and thy aunt, great king; 'tis I. Speak with me, pity me, open the door. A beggar begs that never begg'd before.
translation: A woman, and your aunt, great king: it's me. Speak with me, take pity on me, open the door. I'm a beggar that's never begged before.

original: Our scene is alter'd from a serious thing, And now changed to 'The Beggar and the King.' My dangerous cousin, let your mother in: I know she is come to pray for your foul sin.
translation: This scene now looks less like a serious thing, and more like "The Beggar and the King." My dangerous cousin, let your mother in: I know she's come to pray that I forgive you for your crime.

original: If thou do pardon, whosoever pray,   More sins for this forgiveness prosper may.
translation: If you forgive him, whoever prays against it, bad things will come of it.

original: This fester'd joint cut off, the rest rest sound;   This let alone will all the rest confound.
translation: If you cut off this diseased limb, the rest of the body will live; but if you leave it, it will poison you.

original: O king, believe not this hard-hearted man! Love loving not itself none other can.
translation: Oh king, don't believe this hard-hearted man! He doesn't know how to love his own, so how can he love you?

original: Thou frantic woman, what dost thou make here? Shall thy old dugs once more a traitor rear?
translation: You crazy woman, what are you doing here? Shall your old breasts wean another traitor?

original: Sweet York, be patient. Hear me, gentle liege.
translation: Sweet York, shut up. Listen to me, gentle liege.

original: Rise up, good aunt.
translation: Get up, good aunt.

original: Not yet, I thee beseech:   For ever will I walk upon my knees,   And never see day that the happy sees,
translation: Not yet, I beseech you: I'll stay on my knees forever and never have a happy day in my life,

original: Till thou give joy; until thou bid me joy,   By pardoning Rutland, my transgressing boy.
translation: until you give me joy again by pardoning Rutland, my son, who has offended you.

original: Unto my mother's prayers I bend my knee.
translation: I kneel to add my pleas to my mother's.

original: Against them both my true joints bended be. Ill mayst thou thrive, if thou grant any grace!
translation: I kneel against them with my loyal joints! It won't go well for you, if you grant any forgiveness!

original: Pleads he in earnest? look upon his face;   His eyes do drop no tears, his prayers are in jest;   His words come from his mouth, ours from our breast:
translation: Do you think he really means it? Look at his face; he's not crying, his prayers are false; his words come from his mouth, but ours from our hearts.

original: He prays but faintly and would be denied;   We pray with heart and soul and all beside:
translation: He begs weakly and would rather that you not grant his request; we pray with heart and soul and everything else.

original: His weary joints would gladly rise, I know;   Our knees shall kneel till to the ground they grow:
translation: His tired joints would rather rise, I know; our knees will kneel to the ground until they take root there.

original: His prayers are full of false hypocrisy;   Ours of true zeal and deep integrity.
translation: His prayers are full of false hypocrisy; ours are full of true emotion and deep honesty.

original: Our prayers do out-pray his; then let them have   That mercy which true prayer ought to have.
translation: Our prayers out-pray his—so let us have the mercy which true prayer should receive.

original: Good aunt, stand up.
translation: Good aunt, stand up.

original: Nay, do not say, 'stand up;'   Say, 'pardon' first, and afterwards 'stand up.'
translation: No, don't say "stand up"; say "pardon" first, and "stand up" afterwards.

original: And if I were thy nurse, thy tongue to teach,   'Pardon' should be the first word of thy speech.
translation: If I were your nurse teaching you your first words, "pardon" would be the first word you knew.

original: I never long'd to hear a word till now;
translation: I never wanted to hear any word so much;

original: Say 'pardon,' king; let pity teach thee how:
translation: say "pardon," king, and let pity teach you how:

original: The word is short, but not so short as sweet;   No word like 'pardon' for kings' mouths so meet.
translation: the word is short, but short is sweet, and no word is better to hear from a king.

original: Speak it in French, king; say, 'pardonne moi.'
translation: Speak it in French, king; say, 'pardonne moi.'

original: Dost thou teach pardon pardon to destroy?
translation: Are you trying to ruin this?

original: Ah, my sour husband, my hard-hearted lord,   That set'st the word itself against the word!
translation: Oh, my bitter husband, my hard-hearted lord, to set our words against yours!

original: Speak 'pardon' as 'tis current in our land;   The chopping French we do not understand.
translation: Say "pardon" as we do it in our country; we don't understand French.

original: Thine eye begins to speak; set thy tongue there;
translation: Your eye begins to say it; may your tongue say it too;

original: Or in thy piteous heart plant thou thine ear;   That hearing how our plaints and prayers do pierce,   Pity may move thee 'pardon' to rehearse.
translation: or put your heart in your ear, so that, hearing our prayers, it might take pity on us and command your mouth to say the words.

original: Good aunt, stand up.
translation: Good aunt, stand up.

original: I do not sue to stand; Pardon is all the suit I have in hand.
translation: I don't beg to stand; I only ask for pardon.

original: I pardon him, as God shall pardon me.
translation: I pardon him, as God shall pardon me.

original: O happy vantage of a kneeling knee!
translation: Oh, happy outcome from my kneeling!

original: Yet am I sick for fear: speak it again;
translation: But I am still afraid; say it again.

original: Twice saying 'pardon' doth not pardon twain,   But makes one pardon strong.
translation: Two pardons is better than one.

original: With all my heart I pardon him.
translation: With all my heart I pardon him.

original: A god on earth thou art.
translation: You're a god on earth.

original: But for our trusty brother-in-law and the abbot,   With all the rest of that consorted crew,   Destruction straight shall dog them at the heels.
translation: But as for our trusty brother-in-law and the abbot, they'll be destroyed with the rest of the plotters.

original: Good uncle, help to order several powers   To Oxford, or where'er these traitors are:
translation: Good uncle, help us send an army to Oxford, or wherever the traitors are:
