original: They shall not live within this world, I swear,   But I will have them, if I once know where.
translation: they won't live much longer if I can help it, once we find them.

original: Uncle, farewell: and, cousin too, adieu:   Your mother well hath pray'd, and prove you true.
translation: Uncle, goodbye, and cousin too; your mother has begged well for you, so be loyal going forward.

original: Come, my old son: I pray God make thee new.
translation: Come on, my old son; I hope God makes you new.

original: Didst thou not mark the king, what words he spake,   'Have I no friend will rid me of this living fear?'
translation: Didn't you hear what the king said: "Don't I have a friend that will rid me of this living fear?"

original: Was it not so?
translation: Didn't he say so?

original: These were his very words.
translation: That's what he said.

original: 'Have I no friend?' quoth he: he spake it twice, And urged it twice together, did he not?
translation: "Don't I have a friend?" he said; he said it twice, and asked it twice, didn't he?

original: He did.
translation: He did.

original: And speaking it, he wistly look'd on me,   And who should say, 'I would thou wert the man'   That would divorce this terror from my heart;'
translation: And saying it, he looked at me as if he meant to say, "I wish you were the man to rid me of the thing that makes me afraid,"

original: Meaning the king at Pomfret. Come, let's go:   I am the king's friend, and will rid his foe.
translation: referring to the king at Pomfret. Come on, let's go; I'm the king's friend, and will destroy his enemy.

original: I have been studying how I may compare   This prison where I live unto the world:
translation: I've been thinking how I might compare my prison to the world:

original: And for because the world is populous   And here is not a creature but myself,   I cannot do it;
translation: but because the world is full of people and here there's no one but me, I can't do it.

original: yet I'll hammer it out.
translation: But I'll give it a try.

original: My brain I'll prove the female to my soul,   My soul the father; and these two beget   A generation of still-breeding thoughts,
translation: My brain will be the mother and my soul will be the father, and together they'll produce a generation of children, my thoughts.

original: And these same thoughts people this little world,   In humours like the people of this world,   For no thought is contented.
translation: Those thoughts will populate this little world—they'll have moods just like people in the real world, none of them satisfied

original: The better sort,   As thoughts of things divine, are intermix'd   With scruples and do set the word itself   Against the word:
translation: . The better sort of thoughts, thoughts of heaven, have too many doubts and make me read the Bible against itself:

original: As thus, 'Come, little ones,' and then again,   'It is as hard to come as for a camel   To thread the postern of a small needle's eye.'
translation: for example, "Come, little one" versus "It is as hard to come as for a camel to thread the eye of a small needle."

original: Thoughts tending to ambition, they do plot   Unlikely wonders;
translation: Ambitious thoughts dwell on ways to escape,

original: how these vain weak nails   May tear a passage through the flinty ribs   Of this hard world, my ragged prison walls,   And, for they cannot, die in their own pride.
translation: like tearing a passage through my rough prison walls with my weak fingernails—and since, there's no hope of escape, die before they have the chance to go any further.

original: Thoughts tending to content flatter themselves   That they are not the first of fortune's slaves,   Nor shall not be the last;
translation: Happier thoughts flatter themselves that they aren't the first people to be unlucky, and won't be the last:

original: like silly beggars   Who sitting in the stocks refuge their shame,   That many have and others must sit there;
translation: like beggars sitting in the stocks who tell themselves that many have and other will be in the same place, and

original: And in this thought they find a kind of ease,   Bearing their own misfortunes on the back   Of such as have before endured the like.
translation: in that thought find a kind of comfort, imagining others who have endured the same misfortunes.

original: Thus play I in one person many people,   And none contented:
translation: So I, in one person, play many people—none happy.

original: sometimes am I king;   Then treasons make me wish myself a beggar,   And so I am:
translation: Sometimes I'm a king; then treason makes me wish to be a beggar (and so I am);

original: then crushing penury   Persuades me I was better when a king;
translation: then crushing suffering persuades me that it was better when I was a king;

original: Then am I king'd again: and by and by   Think that I am unking'd by Bolingbroke,
translation: then I'm king again, but soon remember that Bolingbroke has taken my throne,

original: And straight am nothing:
translation: and I am nothing at all.

original: but whate'er I be,   Nor I nor any man that but man is   With nothing shall be pleased, till he be eased   With being nothing.
translation: But whatever I am, neither I nor anyone will pleased with anything, unless he's happy with  being nothing .

original: Music do I hear?
translation: Is this music that I'm hearing?

original: Ha, ha! keep time: how sour sweet music is,   When time is broke and no proportion kept!
translation: Ha, ha! Keep time: sweet music is sour when it doesn't stay on beat!

original: So is it in the music of men's lives.
translation: This is true as well in the music of men's lives.

original: And here have I the daintiness of ear   To cheque time broke in a disorder'd string;
translation: But while here I have a good enough ear to notice when time is broken in a song,

original: But for the concord of my state and time   Had not an ear to hear my true time broke.
translation: when I was king I couldn't hear my own time break.

original: I wasted time, and now doth time waste me;
translation: I wasted time, and now time  wastes  me.

original: For now hath time made me his numbering clock:   My thoughts are minutes; and with sighs they jar   Their watches on unto mine eyes, the outward watch,   Whereto my finger, like a dial's point,   Is pointing still, in cleansing them from tears.
translation: For now time itself could tell the time by me: my thoughts are minutes, my eyes are the face of the clock, and the finger that wipes the tears from them is the hand that tells us the time.

original: Now sir, the sound that tells what hour it is   Are clamorous groans, which strike upon my heart,   Which is the bell: so sighs and tears and groans   Show minutes, times, and hours:
translation: My groans are like the chimes that ring on the hour; so my sighs and tears and groans show minutes, times, and hours, like a clock.

original: but my time   Runs posting on in Bolingbroke's proud joy,   While I stand fooling here, his Jack o' the clock.
translation: But actually, Bolingbroke is in charge of my time; I'm just his  Jack of the clock .

original: This music mads me; let it sound no more;   For though it have helped madmen to their wits,   In me it seems it will make wise men mad.
translation: The music will make me go mad; stop it now. For though it's helped madmen to be sane again, it seems it will make sane men mad.

original: Yet blessing on his heart that gives it me!   For 'tis a sign of love; and love to Richard   Is a strange brooch in this all-hating world.
translation: And yet I bless the person who plays the music, since that's a sign of love; and not many people in this hateful world love me.

original: Hail, royal prince!
translation: Hail, royal prince!

original: Thanks, noble peer;   The cheapest of us is ten groats too dear.
translation: Thanks, noble lord, but you've priced me  ten groats above what I am—I'm not even a noble, let alone royal.

original: What art thou? and how comest thou hither,   Where no man never comes but that sad dog   That brings me food to make misfortune live?
translation: Who are you? And how did you get in, since no one ever comes here but the sad jailer that brings me just enough food to keep me alive?

original: I was a poor groom of thy stable, king,   When thou wert king;
translation: I was a poor groom of your stable, king—when you were king, that is—

original: who, travelling towards York,   With much ado at length have gotten leave   To look upon my sometimes royal master's face.
translation: and on my way to York I got permission to stop here and see the man who used to be my royal master.

original: O, how it yearn'd my heart when I beheld   In London streets, that coronation-day,   When Bolingbroke rode on roan Barbary,
translation: Oh, it broke my heart on coronation day to see Bolingbroke ride through the streets of London on Barbary,

original: That horse that thou so often hast bestrid,   That horse that I so carefully have dress'd!
translation: the horse that you used to ride and that I would so carefully saddle for you!

original: Rode he on Barbary? Tell me, gentle friend, How went he under him?
translation: So he rode on Barbary? Tell me, kind friend, how did the horse take to him?

original: So proudly as if he disdain'd the ground.
translation: Very proudly, as if he had contempt for the ground beneath his feet.

original: So proud that Bolingbroke was on his back!
translation: So proud that Bolingbroke was on his back!

original: That jade hath eat bread from my royal hand;   This hand hath made him proud with clapping him.
translation: That horse used to eat bread from my royal hand; he was proud when I touched him.

original: Would he not stumble? would he not fall down,   Since pride must have a fall, and break the neck   Of that proud man that did usurp his back?
translation: Why didn't he stumble? Why didn't he fall down—since pride must have a fall—so that Bolingbroke would fall break his neck?

original: Forgiveness, horse!
translation: But I forgive you, horse!

original: why do I rail on thee,   Since thou, created to be awed by man,   Wast born to bear?
translation: Why am I angry at you, since you were born to carry men on your back?

original: I was not made a horse;   And yet I bear a burthen like an ass,   Spurr'd, gall'd and tired by jouncing Bolingbroke.
translation: I was not born a horse, but I bear a burden like a donkey, spurred on and exhausted by Bolingbroke.

original: Fellow, give place; here is no longer stay.
translation: Man, go away; you can't stay here any longer.

original: If thou love me, 'tis time thou wert away.
translation: If you love me, it's time for you to go.

original: What my tongue dares not, that my heart shall say.
translation: My heart will show what I can't tell you with words.

original: My lord, will't please you to fall to?
translation: My lord, will you eat?

original: Taste of it first, as thou art wont to do.
translation: Taste it first, as you always do.

original: My lord, I dare not: Sir Pierce of Exton, who lately came from the king, commands the contrary.
translation: My lord, I don't dare; Sir Pierce of Exton, who came here on the king's orders, commands that I don't taste your food for poison.

original: The devil take Henry of Lancaster and thee! Patience is stale, and I am weary of it.
translation: You and Henry of Lancaster should both go to the devil! I'm tired of being patient.

original: Help, help, help!
translation: Help, help, help!

original: How now! what means death in this rude assault? Villain, thy own hand yields thy death's instrument.
translation: What's happening? Is death coming for me? Villain, I'll take the weapon that would kill me from your own hands.

original: Go thou, and fill another room in hell.
translation: Go and fill another room in hell.

original: That hand shall burn in never-quenching fire   That staggers thus my person.
translation: The hand that kills me will burn in hell forever.

original: Exton, thy fierce hand   Hath with the king's blood stain'd the king's own land.
translation: Exton, you've stained the land with its own king's blood.

original: Mount, mount, my soul! thy seat is up on high;   Whilst my gross flesh sinks downward, here to die.
translation: Go up to heaven, my soul! Your place is up there, while my body sinks downward to die.

original: As full of valour as of royal blood:   Both have I spill'd;
translation: He's as full of bravery as he is of royal blood—and I've killed both.

original: O would the deed were good!
translation: Oh, I wish this were a good deed!

original: For now the devil, that told me I did well,   Says that this deed is chronicled in hell.
translation: For now the devil, that told me I was doing the right thing, tells me that this is a deed of hell.

original: This dead king to the living king I'll bear   Take hence the rest, and give them burial here.
translation: I'll take this dead king to the living king;  [t o servants]  take away the rest of the bodies and bury them.

original: Kind uncle York, the latest news we hear   Is that the rebels have consumed with fire   Our town of Cicester in Gloucestershire;
translation: Kind uncle York, the latest news is that the rebels have set the town of Cicester in Gloucestershire on fire;

original: But whether they be ta'en or slain we hear not.
translation: but we don't know whether they've been captured or killed.

original: Welcome, my lord what is the news?
translation: Welcome, my lord. What's the news?

original: First, to thy sacred state wish I all happiness.
translation: First, I wish you all happiness in your sacred position.

original: The next news is, I have to London sent   The heads of Oxford, Salisbury, Blunt, and Kent:
translation: The next news is that I've sent the decapitated heads of Oxford, Salisbury, Blunt, and Kent to London;

original: The manner of their taking may appear   At large discoursed in this paper here.
translation: how I captured them is described in this paper.

original: We thank thee, gentle Percy, for thy pains; And to thy worth will add right worthy gains.
translation: We thank you, gentle Percy, for your efforts; we'll reward you well for this.

original: My lord, I have from Oxford sent to London   The heads of Brocas and Sir Bennet Seely,
translation: My lord, from Oxford I've sent the heads of Brocas and Sir Bennet Seely to London—

original: Two of the dangerous consorted traitors   That sought at Oxford thy dire overthrow.
translation: they were two of the dangerous traitors that plotted against you.

original: I'll rather be unmannerly than troublesome. You do yourself wrong, indeed, la!
translation: I'd rather be rude than cause trouble. You're not being fair to yourself, really!

original: Go your ways, and ask of Doctor Caius' house which   is the way:
translation: Get going now. Ask someone how to get to Doctor Caius's house.

original: and there dwells one Mistress Quickly,   which is in the manner of his nurse, or his dry   nurse, or his cook, or his laundry, his washer, and   his wringer.
translation: A woman named Mistress Quickly lives there, who is kind of his house-keeper, or his cook, or his laundry-maid.

original: Well, sir.
translation: Well, sir.

original: Nay, it is petter yet.
translation: No, this is a better idea.

original: Give her this letter; for it   is a 'oman that altogether's acquaintance with   Mistress Anne Page: and the letter is, to desire   and require her to solicit your master's desires to   Mistress Anne Page.
translation: Give her this letter, since she is someone who knows Mistress Anne Page well. The letter asks her to persuade Mistress Anne Page to marry your master.

original: I pray you, be gone: I will   make an end of my dinner; there's pippins and cheese to come.
translation: Please, get going. I will finish my dinner—there will be apples and cheese later on.

original: Mine host of the Garter!
translation: My host of the Garter Inn!

original: What says my bully-rook? speak scholarly and wisely.
translation: What do you have to say for yourself, you fine fellow? Speak wisely and like a scholar.

original: Truly, mine host, I must turn away some of my followers.
Discard, bully Hercules; cashier: let them wag; trot,  trot.
translation: Dismiss them, you handsome Hercules, dismiss them. Let them go their own way, trot, trot.

original: I sit at ten pounds a week.
translation: I spend ten pounds a week in rent.

original: Thou'rt an emperor, Caesar, Keisar, and Pheezar.
translation: You live like an emperor, a Caesar, a kaiser, and a  vizier .

original: I   will entertain Bardolph; he shall draw, he shall   tap: said I well, bully Hector?
translation: I'll hire Bardolph. He'll tend the bar, he'll serve the drinks. Does that sound good, handsome Hercules?

original: Do so, good mine host.
translation: Do that, good host.

original: I have spoke; let him follow.
translation: I've said I'll do it. Let him work for me.

original: Let me see thee froth and lime: I am at a word; follow.
translation: Be sure to cheat customers by leaving a large head of foam on the beer, and sweeten bad wine to disguise the taste. I mean what I say—follow me.

original: Bardolph, follow him.
translation: Bardolph, follow him.

original: A tapster is a good trade:   an old cloak makes a new jerkin; a withered   serving-man a fresh tapster.
translation: Being a bartender is a good occupation. An old cloak makes a good new jacket, and a wrinkled old servant will make a good new bartender.

original: Go; adieu.
translation: Go, good-bye.

original: It is a life that I have desired: I will thrive.
translation: It's an occupation I've always wanted to have. I'll do well.

original: O base Hungarian wight! wilt thou the spigot wield?
translation: Oh, you lowlife beggar! Will you really serve drinks?

original: He was gotten in drink: is not the humour conceited?
translation: His parents conceived him when they were drunk—isn't that some good irony?

original: I am glad I am so acquit of this tinderbox:
translation: I'm glad I got rid of of that red-faced, bad-tempered man.

original: his   thefts were too open; his filching was like an   unskilful singer; he kept not time.
translation: He made it too obvious when he was  stealing things ; as a thief, he was like a bad singer, he didn't act at the right moment.

original: The good humour is to steal at a minute's rest.
translation: The trick is to be able to steal quickly, at a moment's notice.

original: 'Convey,' the wise it call. 'Steal!' foh! a fico for the phrase!
translation: Educated people call stealing "conveying." "Steal!" Ha! I don't care for that word at all!

original: Well, sirs, I am almost out at heels.
translation: Well, boys, I'm almost bankrupt.

original: Why, then, let kibes ensue.
There is no remedy; I must cony-catch; I must shift.
translation: I can't do anything about it. I have to cheat people, I have to use my wits to get by.

original: Young ravens must have food.
translation: We have to eat somehow.

original: Which of you know Ford of this town?
translation: Does anyone know Ford, who lives in this town?

original: I ken the wight: he is of substance good.
translation: I know the man. He has a lot of money.

original: My honest lads, I will tell you what I am about.
translation: My good friends, I'll tell you what I'm about.

original: Two yards, and more.
No quips now, Pistol!
translation: No jokes now, Pistol!

original: Indeed, I am in the waist two   yards about; but I am now about no waste; I am about   thrift.
translation: In fact, my waist is six feet around, but right now I'm not going to overindulge, I'm going to be thrifty.

original: Briefly, I do mean to make love to Ford's   wife: I spy entertainment in her;
translation: In short, I plan to seduce Ford's wife. I believe she would take me up on my offer.

original: she discourses,   she carves, she gives the leer of invitation: I   can construe the action of her familiar style;
translation: Whe n she speaks, when she gestures, she seems like she's inviting me to approach her. I can interpret the meaning of her friendly actions,

original: and   the hardest voice of her behavior, to be Englished   rightly, is, 'I am Sir John Falstaff's.'
translation: and the meaning of her behavior, if you translate it into English, is, "I want Sir John Falstaff as my lover."

original: He hath studied her will, and translated her will, out of honesty into English.
The anchor is deep: will that humour pass?
translation: That's a difficult plan. Will you be able to pull it off?

original: Now, the report goes she has all the rule of her husband's purse: he hath a legion of angels.
As many devils entertain; and 'To her, boy,' say I.
translation: You should employ the same number of devils to help you—and I say, "Chase her."

original: The humour rises; it is good: humour me the angels.
translation: I see this plan taking shape. It's a good plan; go get that money.

original: I have writ me here a letter to her: and here   another to Page's wife, who even now gave me good   eyes too, examined my parts with most judicious   oeillades;
translation: I've written a letter to her, and I've written another letter to Page's wife, who also looked at me just now with lots of attention.  She looked over my whole body with an expression of desire.

original: sometimes the beam of her view gilded my   foot, sometimes my portly belly.
translation: Sometimes her gaze fell on my foot, sometimes on my plump belly.

original: Then did the sun on dunghill shine.
I thank thee for that humour.
translation: Thanks for that joke.

original: O, she did so course o'er my exteriors with such a   greedy intention, that the appetite of her eye did   seem to scorch me up like a burning-glass!
translation: Oh, she looked over my body with such a greedy look, that her hot desire seemed to burn me up like the sun shining through a piece of  glass !

original: Here's   another letter to her: she bears the purse too; she   is a region in Guiana, all gold and bounty.
translation: Here's another letter that I wrote to her. She also has control over her husband's money; she's like a region in  Guiana , full of gold and wealth.

original: I will   be cheater to them both, and they shall be   exchequers to me; they shall be my East and West   Indies, and I will trade to them both.
translation: I will be like a treasury officer to them, and they will be like  bank accounts  to me. They will be sources of wealth to me, and I will get money from both of them.

original: Go bear thou   this letter to Mistress Page; and thou this to   Mistress Ford: we will thrive, lads, we will thrive.
translation: Go take this letter to Mistress Page, and you take this letter to Mistress Ford. We will do well, boys, we will make money.

original: Shall I Sir Pandarus of Troy become, And by my side wear steel? then, Lucifer take all!
I will run no base humour: here, take the humour-letter: I will keep the havior of reputation.
translation: I won't behave dishonorably. Here, take the foolish letter. I will keep acting respectably.

original: [To ROBIN]   Hold, sirrah, bear you these letters  tightly;   Sail like my pinnace to these golden shores.
translation: [To ROBIN]  Hang on, servant, take these letters and keep them safe. Go to these women like my boat going to wealthy lands.

original: Rogues, hence, avaunt! vanish like hailstones, go;   Trudge, plod away o' the hoof; seek shelter, pack!
translation: [To PISTOL and NYM]  Scoundrels, get going, go on! Disappear like hailstones, go. Walk heavily, plod away on foot. Look for a new place to stay, get going!

original: Falstaff will learn the humour of the age,   French thrift, you rogues; myself and skirted page.
translation: I'll learn the tricks you need to get by these days. I'll save money the way the  French  do, you scoundrels. I'll only take care of myself and one well-dressed servant.

original: Let vultures gripe thy guts! for gourd and fullam  holds,   And high and low beguiles the rich and poor:
translation: I hope vultures eat your guts! False dice and loaded dice make good profits, and trick both rich and poor people.

original: Tester I'll have in pouch when thou shalt lack,   Base Phrygian Turk!
translation: I'll still have sixpence in my purse when you have nothing, you lowlife slavish  Turk!

original: I have operations which be humours of revenge.
translation: I have a plan to get revenge on him.

original: Wilt thou revenge?
translation: Will you take revenge?

original: By welkin and her star!
translation: By the sky and the star, I swear I will!

original: With wit or steel?
translation: With a clever plan, or by fighting him?

original: With both the humours, I: I will discuss the humour of this love to Page.
translation: I'll use both! I'll go and tell Page about Falstaff's plan to seduce his wife.

original: And I to Ford shall eke unfold   How Falstaff, varlet vile,
translation: And I'll tell Ford how Falstaff, that disgusting liar,

original: His dove will prove, his gold will hold,   And his soft couch defile.
translation: plans to seduce his wife, steal his gold, and contaminate his bed.

original: My humour shall not cool:
translation: My anger won't cool down.

original: I will incense Page to   deal with poison; I will possess him with   yellowness,
translation: I'll make Page so mad that he'll want to poison Falstaff, I'll make him jealous.

original: for the revolt of mine is dangerous:   that is my true humour.
translation: This rebellion of mine against Falstaff is dangerous for him: that's the mood I'm in.

original: Thou art the Mars of malecontents: I second thee; troop on.
What, John Rugby! I pray thee, go to the casement,   and see if you can see my master, Master Doctor   Caius, coming.
translation: Hey there, John Rugby! Please, go to the window and see if you can see my  master , Master Doctor Caius, coming.

original: If he do, i' faith, and find any   body in the house, here will be an old abusing of   God's patience and the king's English.
translation: If he comes and finds anyone in the house, I'm telling you, you'll hear him getting very angry and speaking very  bad English.

original: I'll go watch.
translation: I'll go keep a lookout for him.

original: Go; and we'll have a posset for't soon at night, in faith, at the latter end of a sea-coal fire.
An honest, willing, kind fellow, as ever servant   shall come in house withal, and, I warrant you, no   tell-tale nor no breed-bate:
translation: Rugby is as honest, hard-working, and kind a person as any servant could work alongside, and I bet he won't tell on us or make any trouble.

original: his worst fault is,   that he is given to prayer;
translation: The worst thing about him is that he has a habit of praying.

original: he is something peevish   that way: but nobody but has his fault;
translation: He's a bit foolish like that, but everybody has some flaw—

original: but let   that pass. Peter Simple, you say your name is?
translation: enough about that. Did you say your name was Peter Simple?

original: Ay, for fault of a better.
translation: Yes, since I don't have a better name.

original: And Master Slender's your master?
translation: And your master is Master Slender?

original: Ay, forsooth.
translation: Yes, that's true.

original: Does he not wear a great round beard, like a glover's paring-knife?
No, forsooth: he hath but a little wee face, with a little yellow beard, a Cain-coloured beard.
translation: No, in fact, he has only a tiny little face, with a little yellow beard, a yellow or reddish beard.

original: A softly-sprighted man, is he not?
translation: He's a timid person, isn't he?

original: Ay, forsooth: but he is as tall a man of his hands   as any is between this and his head;
translation: Yes, he is, but he's as brave as any other man around here.

original: he hath fought   with a warrener.
translation: He had a fight with a gamekeeper.

original: How say you? O, I should remember him: does he not hold up his head, as it were, and strut in his gait?
translation: What was that? Oh, I think I remember him. Doesn't he hold his head up high, so to speak, and strut when he walks?

original: Yes, indeed, does he.
translation: Yes, indeed, he does.

original: Well, heaven send Anne Page no worse fortune!
translation: Well, I hope Anne Page doesn't end up with anybody worse!

original: Tell   Master Parson Evans I will do what I can for your   master: Anne is a good girl, and I wish—
translation: Tell Master Parson Evans that I'll do what I can for your master. Anne's a good girl, and I wish—

original: Out, alas! here comes my master.
translation: Oh no, get out! Here comes my master.

original: We shall all be shent. Run in here, good young man; go into this closet: he will not stay long.
What, John Rugby! John! what, John, I say!
translation: Hey there, John Rugby! John! Hey, John!

original: Go, John, go inquire for my master; I doubt   he be not well, that he comes not home.
translation: Go, John, go ask about my master. I'm afraid he isn't well, since he hasn't come home.

original: [Singing]   And down, down, adown-a, & c.
translation: [Singing] And down, down, adown-a ...

original: Vat is you sing? I do not like des toys.
translation: What are you singing? I don't like these silly songs.

original: Pray you,   go and vetch me in my closet un boitier vert, a box,   a green-a box: do intend vat I speak? a green-a box.
translation: Please, go and get me a green box from my closet, a box, a green box. Do you understand what I'm saying? A green box.

original: Ay, forsooth; I'll fetch it you. @     I am glad he went not in himself: if he had  found the young man, he would have been horn-mad.
translation: Yes, I do, I'll get it for you. I'm glad he didn't go into his closet himself. If he had found the young man hiding in there, he would have gotten as mad as a bull.

original: Fe, fe, fe, fe! ma foi, il fait fort chaud. Je m'en vais a la cour—la grande affaire.
Is it this, sir?
translation: Is this the box you wanted, sir?

original: Oui; mette le au mon pocket: depeche, quickly. Vere is dat knave Rugby?
translation: Yes, put it in my pocket, hurry, quickly. Where is that rascal Rugby?

original: What, John Rugby! John!
translation: Hey there, John Rugby! John!

original: Here, sir!
translation: Here I am, sir!

original: You are John Rugby, and you are Jack Rugby. Come, take-a your rapier, and come after my heel to the  court.
'Tis ready, sir, here in the porch.
translation: It's ready to go, sir, out here in the hall.

original: By my trot, I tarry too long. Od's me!   Qu'ai-j'oublie!
translation: Honestly, I'm lingering here for too long. Oh my God! I forgot!

original: dere is some simples in my closet,   dat I vill not for the varld I shall leave behind.
translation: There are some medicines in my closet that I really don't want to leave behind.

original: Ay me, he'll find the young man here, and be mad!
translation: Oh no, he'll find the young man in the closet and get really mad!

original: O diable, diable! vat is in my closet? Villain! larron!
translation: Oh, you devil, you devil! Who is in my closet? Villain! Thief!

original: Rugby, my rapier!
translation: Rugby, get me my sword!

original: Good master, be content.
translation: Good master, stay calm.

original: Wherefore shall I be content-a?
translation: Why should I stay calm?

original: The young man is an honest man.
translation: The young man is an honest person.

original: What shall de honest man do in my closet? dere is no honest man dat shall come in my closet.
translation: What would an honest person be doing in my closet? No honest person would come into my closet.

original: I beseech you, be not so phlegmatic. Hear the truth of it: he came of an errand to me from Parson Hugh.
Vell.
translation: Well.

original: Ay, forsooth; to desire her to—
translation: Yes, really, to ask her to—

original: Peace, I pray you.
translation: Be quiet, please.

original: Peace-a your tongue. Speak-a your tale.
translation: Stop talking. [To SIMPLE] Tell me what happened.

original: To desire this honest gentlewoman, your maid, to speak a good word to Mistress Anne Page for my master in the way of marriage.
translation: I came to ask this good woman, your maid, to recommend my master to Anne Page as a potential husband.

original: This is all, indeed, la! but I'll ne'er put my finger in the fire, and need not.
translation: That's all, really! But I won't ever risk getting into trouble again by getting involved in things if I don't have to.

original: Sir Hugh send-a you? Rugby, baille me some paper. Tarry you a little-a while.
translation: Sir Hugh sent you here? Rugby, bring me some paper. Wait here for a minute.

original: [Aside to SIMPLE]   I am glad he is so quiet: if he   had been thoroughly moved, you should have heard him   so loud and so melancholy.
translation: [To SIMPLE so that only he can hear]  I'm glad he's so calm. If he had gotten really angry, you would have heard him be a lot louder and a lot more upset.

original: But notwithstanding,   man, I'll do you your master what good I can:
translation: But in any case, young man, I'll help your master as much as I can:

original: and   the very yea and the no is, the French doctor, my   master,—I may call him my master, look you, for I   keep his house; and I wash, wring, brew, bake,   scour, dress meat and drink, make the beds and do   all myself,—
translation: and the upshot is, the French doctor, my master—I can call him my master, you see, because I take care of his house, and I wash the clothes, brew beer, bake, clean the house, prepare the food and drink, make the beds and do it all by myself—

original: 'Tis a great charge to come under one body's hand.
translation: That's a lot of work for one person to do.

original: [Aside to SIMPLE]   Are you avised o' that? you   shall find it a great charge: and to be up early   and down late; but notwithstanding,
translation: [To SIMPLE so that only he can hear]  You're telling me that? You would find it to be a lot of work too: and you have to get up early and go to bed late, but anyway

original: —to tell you in   your ear; I would have no words of it,—my master   himself is in love with Mistress Anne Page:
translation: — [Motioning him closer]  I'm telling you this as a secret, I don't want you telling other people about this—my master is in love with Mistress Anne Page himself.

original: but   notwithstanding that, I know Anne's mind,—that's   neither here nor there.
translation: But in any case, I know how Anne feels—but that doesn't matter.

original: You jack'nape, give-a this letter to Sir Hugh; by   gar, it is a shallenge:
translation: You fool, give this letter to Sir Hugh—by God, it's a challenge to a duel.

original: I will cut his troat in dee   park; and I will teach a scurvy jack-a-nape priest   to meddle or make.
translation: I will cut his throat in the park, and I'll teach that good-for-nothing fool of a priest to go interfering in my business.

original: You may be gone; it is not good   you tarry here. By gar, I will cut all his two   stones; by gar, he shall not have a stone to throw   at his dog:
translation: You can get going, you shouldn't hang around here. By God, I'll cut off his testicles. By God, he won't have any left when I'm through with him.

original: Alas, he speaks but for his friend.
translation: Oh dear, he was only speaking on behalf of his friend.

original: It is no matter-a ver dat: do not you tell-a me   dat I shall have Anne Page for myself?
translation: That doesn't matter. Didn't you tell me that I would have Anne Page for myself?

original: By gar, I   vill kill de Jack priest; and I have appointed mine   host of de Jarteer to measure our weapon.
translation: By God, I'll kill that scoundrel of a priest, and I've asked the host of the Garter to be the referee for our fight.

original: By gar, I   will myself have Anne Page.
translation: By God, I'm going to have Anne Page myself.

original: Sir, the maid loves you, and all shall be well. We must give folks leave to prate: what, the goodyear!
translation: Sir, the woman loves you, and everything will turn out fine. We have to let people say foolish things. What the devil!

original: Rugby, come to the court with me.
translation: Rugby, come to the court with me.

original: By gar, if I have   not Anne Page, I shall turn your head out of my   door.
translation: By God, if I don't get Anne Page, I will fire you.

original: Follow my heels, Rugby.
translation: Follow me, Rugby.

original: You shall have An fool's-head of your own.
translation: You'll only make a fool out of yourself.

original: No, I   know Anne's mind for that: never a woman in Windsor   knows more of Anne's mind than I do;
translation: No, I know how Anne feels, in spite of what Doctor Caius says. No woman in Windsor knows Anne better than I do,

original: nor can do more   than I do with her, I thank heaven.
translation: and no one is more able to persuade her than I am, thank goodness.

original: Who's within there? ho!
translation: Who's in there? Hey!

original: Who's there, I trow! Come near the house, I pray you.
translation: Who's there, I wonder! Come near the house, please.

original: How now, good woman? how dost thou?
translation: How are you, good woman? How are you doing?

original: The better that it pleases your good worship to ask.
translation: I'm doing better since you asked me how I'm doing, you good gentleman!

original: What news? how does pretty Mistress Anne?
translation: What's the news? How is pretty Mistress Anne doing?

original: In truth, sir, and she is pretty, and honest, and gentle; and one that is your friend, I can tell you that by the way; I praise heaven for it.
translation: To tell you the truth, sir, she is pretty, and faithful, and has good manners, and she likes you, I can tell you that, by the way. I thank God for that.

original: Shall I do any good, thinkest thou? shall I not lose my suit?
translation: Do you think I'll make any progress in persuading her to marry me? Will she reject me?

original: Troth, sir, all is in his hands above: but   notwithstanding, Master Fenton, I'll be sworn on a   book, she loves you.
translation: To tell you the truth, sir, everything is in God's control. But if we put that aside, Master Fenton, I'd swear on the Bible that she loves you.

original: Have not your worship a wart   above your eye?
translation: Don't you have a wart above your eye?

original: Yes, marry, have I; what of that?
translation: Yes, in fact, I do—what about it?

original: Well, thereby hangs a tale:
translation: Well, that's that, then:

original: good faith, it is such   another Nan;
translation: Anne is such an extraordinary person.

original: but, I detest, an honest maid as ever   broke bread: we had an hour's talk of that wart. I   shall never laugh but in that maid's company!
translation: But, I  detest , she's the most faithful woman that ever lived. We talked for an hour about your wart. I never laugh except when I'm with that girl!

original: But   indeed she is given too much to allicholy and   musing: but for you—well, go to.
translation: But to tell you the truth, she's a little too much in habit of being  sad  and brooding about things, but when it comes to you—well, get going now.

original: Well, I shall see her to-day.
translation: Well, I'll see her today.

original: Hold, there's money   for thee; let me have thy voice in my behalf:
translation: Hang on, here's some money for you. Please take my side and say good things about me to her.

original: if   thou seest her before me, commend me.
translation: If you see her before I do, say something nice about me.

original: Will I? i'faith, that we will; and I will tell your   worship more of the wart the next time we have   confidence;
translation: Will I? Yes, I will, and I'll tell you more about the wart the next time we meet in private,

original: and of other wooers.
translation: and also about the other men who want to marry her.

original: Well, farewell; I am in great haste now.
translation: Well, goodbye. I'm really in a rush now.

original: Farewell to your worship.
translation: Goodbye, good gentleman.

original: Truly, an honest gentleman: but Anne loves him not; for I know Anne's mind as well as another does. Out upon't! what have I forgot?
translation: He really is a good man, but Anne doesn't love him. I know how Anne feels as well as anyone else does. Oh dear! what did I forget?

original: What, have I scaped love-letters in the holiday- time of my beauty, and am I now a subject for them? Let me see.
translation: How can it happen that I didn't get any love-letters when I was young and beautiful, but I get them now? Let me read it.

original: 'Ask me no reason why I love you; for though   Love use Reason for his physician, he admits him   not for his counsellor.
translation: "Don't ask me why I love you, because even though we use our brains to find reasons for being in love, people in love still don't listen to reason.

original: You are not young, no more   am I; go to then, there's sympathy: you are merry,   so am I; ha, ha! then there's more sympathy: you   love sack, and so do I; would you desire better   sympathy?
translation: You aren't young, but I'm not either; well then, we're alike in that way. You're merry, so am I; ha, ha! that's another way we're alike. You love  wine , and I do too; could we be any more alike?

original: Let it suffice thee, Mistress Page,—at   the least, if the love of soldier can suffice,—   that I love thee. I will not say, pity me; 'tis   not a soldier-like phrase: but I say, love me.
translation: Let it be enough, Mistress Page—at least, if a soldier's love is enough for you—just to know that I love you. I won't tell you to feel sorry for me, because that isn't something a soldier says, but I do ask you to love me.

original: By me,   Thine own true knight,   By day or night,   Or any kind of light,   With all his might   For thee to fight, JOHN FALSTAFF'
translation: From me, Your faithful knight, By day or night, Or at any time, Who will fight for you, With all his might, JOHN FALSTAFF"

original: What a Herod of Jewry is this! O wicked   world! One that is well-nigh worn to pieces with   age to show himself a young gallant!
translation: What a  bragging scoundrel  this man is! What a wicked world we live in! This man who is so old that he is almost falling apart is flirting like a young man!

original: What an   unweighed behavior hath this Flemish drunkard   picked—with the devil's name!—out of my   conversation, that he dares in this manner assay me?
translation: What did this  drunkard  see me doing that made him think—the devil must have put the idea into his head!—that he dares to write me a letter like this?

original: Why, he hath not been thrice in my company! What   should I say to him? I was then frugal of my   mirth: Heaven forgive me!
translation: Why, he hasn't met me more than three times! What should I have said to him? I didn't flirt with him too much. God forgive me!

original: Why, I'll exhibit a bill   in the parliament for the putting down of men. How   shall I be revenged on him? for revenged I will be,   as sure as his guts are made of puddings.
translation: Why, I'll demand that  Parliament  pass a law to suppress men. How can I get revenge on him? Because I'm going to get revenge on him, as sure his guts are made out of sausages!

original: Mistress Page! trust me, I was going to your house.
translation: Mistress Page! Believe me, I was just on my way to see you.

original: And, trust me, I was coming to you. You look very ill.
translation: And, believe me, I was just on my way to see you. You look unwell.

original: Nay, I'll ne'er believe that; I have to show to the  contrary.
translation: No, I don't think so, I have something to prove that I don't.

original: Faith, but you do, in my mind.
translation: But really, I think you do look unwell.

original: Well, I do then; yet I say I could show you to the contrary. O Mistress Page, give me some counsel!
translation: Fine, I look unwell then, but I still say that I could prove that I don't. O Mistress Page, give me some advice!

original: What's the matter, woman?
translation: What's the matter, woman?

original: O woman, if it were not for one trifling respect, I could come to such honour!
translation: Oh woman, if there weren't one small thing worrying me, I could acquire such a high social status!

original: Hang the trifle, woman! take the honour. What is it? dispense with trifles; what is it?
translation: Forget about the one small thing! Take the social status. What is it? Don't worry about small things, what is it?

original: If I would but go to hell for an eternal moment or so, I could be knighted.
What? thou liest! Sir Alice Ford! These knights will hack; and so thou shouldst not alter the article of thy gentry.
translation: What? You're lying! Sir Alice Ford! These knights might go around having sexual affairs, but that still doesn't mean you'd change your social status.

original: We burn daylight:
translation: We're wasting time.

original: here, read, read; perceive how I   might be knighted.
translation: Here, read, read, and see how I would be made a knight.

original: I shall think the worse of fat   men, as long as I have an eye to make difference of   men's liking: and yet he would not swear; praised   women's modesty; and gave such orderly and   well-behaved reproof to all uncomeliness, that I   would have sworn his disposition would have gone to   the truth of his words;
translation: I won't like fat men as much as other men, as long I'm able to judge men by their appearances— but still, he didn't swear, he praised the way that women aren't too sexually forward, and he criticized all inappropriate behavior with such careful, well-chosen words, that I would have sworn that his actions would correspond with his words;

original: but they do no more adhere   and keep place together than the Hundredth Psalm to   the tune of 'Green Sleeves.'
translation: but they don't  correspond at all.

original: What tempest, I trow,   threw this whale, with so many tuns of oil in his   belly, ashore at Windsor? How shall I be revenged   on him?
translation: How on earth did this fat beast end up in our town? How will I get revenge on him?

original: I think the best way were to entertain him   with hope, till the wicked fire of lust have melted   him in his own grease. Did you ever hear the like?
translation: I think the best thing to do would be to lead him on and make him think that we'll accept his offer, until we can use his sexual desire as a weapon against him. Did you ever hear of anything like this?

original: Letter for letter, but that the name of Page and   Ford differs!
translation: Word for word, these letters are exactly the same except that one has the name Page on it and the other has the name Ford!

original: To thy great comfort in this mystery   of ill opinions, here's the twin-brother of thy   letter: but let thine inherit first; for, I   protest, mine never shall.
translation: To make you feel better about Falstaff thinking, for some mysterious reason, that you are sexually promiscuous, look at my letter, which is exactly the same as yours. But you should accept his offer first, because, I swear, I never will.

original: I warrant he hath a   thousand of these letters, writ with blank space for   different names—sure, more,—and these are of the   second edition:
translation: I bet he has a thousand letters just like this, with a blank space to put in different women's names—no, more than a thousand—and he's probably given them to many women  before .

original: he will print them, out of doubt;   for he cares not what he puts into the press, when   he would put us two.
translation: He must print them, undoubtedly, because he must not care what he  publishes , since he's willing to write these letters to us.

original: I had rather be a giantess,   and lie under Mount Pelion. Well, I will find you   twenty lascivious turtles ere one chaste man.
translation: I would rather be buried under a  mountain  than accept his offer. I bet you I could find twenty unfaithful  turtledoves  before I could find one man who could control his sexual appetite.

original: Why, this is the very same; the very hand, the very words. What doth he think of us?
translation: Gosh, these are exactly the same, the same handwriting, the same words. What opinion does he have of us?

original: Nay, I know not:
translation: I have no idea.

original: it makes me almost ready to   wrangle with mine own honesty.
translation: It almost makes me doubt my own  chastity .

original: I'll entertain   myself like one that I am not acquainted withal;   for, sure, unless he know some strain in me, that I   know not myself, he would never have boarded me in this fury.
translation: I almost don't know who I am, because unless he knew something about me that I don't know myself, he would never have approached me like this.

original: 'Boarding,' call you it? I'll be sure to keep him above deck.
So will I if he come under my hatches, I'll never   to sea again. Let's be revenged on him:
translation: So will I, if he tries to come near me. I'll never put myself in harm's way again. Let's get revenge on him.

original: let's   appoint him a meeting; give him a show of comfort in   his suit and lead him on with a fine-baited delay,   till he hath pawned his horses to mine host of the  Garter.
translation: Let's set up a meeting with him, let's pretend to accept his offer and lead him on by delaying in a way that makes him even more excited, until he's pawned his horses to the host of the Garter Inn to get money to try to win us over.

original: Nay, I will consent to act any villany against him,   that may not sully the chariness of our honesty.
translation: Believe me, I'll agree to do any bad thing to him as long as it doesn't harm our own ethical integrity.

original: O,   that my husband saw this letter! it would give   eternal food to his jealousy.
translation: O, if my husband saw this letter! it would make him jealous forever.

original: Why, look where he comes; and my good man too:
translation: Look, he's coming, and my husband's coming too.

original: he's   as far from jealousy as I am from giving him cause;   and that I hope is an unmeasurable distance.
translation: He's never jealous, just like I never give him any reason to be jealous, and I hope that will always be true.

original: You are the happier woman.
translation: You're luckier than I am.

original: Let's consult together against this greasy knight. Come hither.
translation: Let's come up with a plan together to get the better of this fat knight. Come over here.

original: Well, I hope it be not so.
translation: Well, I hope it isn't true.

original: Hope is a curtal dog in some affairs: Sir John affects thy wife.
translation: Then your hope misleads you. Sir John wants to seduce your wife.

original: Why, sir, my wife is not young.
translation: Why, sir, my wife isn't young.

original: He wooes both high and low, both rich and poor,
translation: He goes after women with high social status and with low social status, both rich women and poor women.

original: Both young and old, one with another, Ford;   He loves the gallimaufry: Ford, perpend.
translation: He wants both young women and old women, he doesn't care which, Ford. He loves all kinds of women. Ford, think about this carefully.

original: Love my wife!
translation: He loves my wife!

original: With liver burning hot. Prevent, or go thou, Like Sir Actaeon he, with Ringwood at thy heels: O, odious is the name!
What name, sir?
translation: To be called what?

original: The horn, I say. Farewell.
translation: A cuckold. Goodbye.

original: Take heed, have open eye, for thieves do foot by night:   Take heed, ere summer comes or cuckoo-birds do sing.
translation: Be careful, look out, because villains will take your property when you're not looking. Take care, before someone  seduces your wife.

original: Away, Sir Corporal Nym!   Believe it, Page; he speaks sense.
translation: Let's go, Sir Corporal Nym! Believe it, Page; he's speaking the truth.

original: I will be patient; I will find out this.
translation: I'll be patient, I'll investigate this.

original: [To PAGE]   And this is true; I like not the humour   of lying. He hath wronged me in some humours: I   should have borne the humoured letter to her; but I   have a sword and it shall bite upon my necessity.
translation: [To PAGE]  What I said is true. I'm not in the habit of lying. Falstaff has mistreated me in certain ways. I was supposed to bring the letter to your wife, but I have ways of getting back at my enemies, and I'll use them when I have to.

original: He loves your wife; there's the short and the long.   My name is Corporal Nym; I speak and I avouch; 'tis   true: my name is Nym and Falstaff loves your wife.   Adieu. I love not the humour of bread and cheese,   and there's the humour of it. Adieu.
translation: Falstaff wants to seduce your wife, that's the long and the short of it. My name is Corporal Nym. I'm saying this and I promise that it's true. My name is Nym and Falstaff is after your wife. Goodbye. I don't like how little food I have  now , and that's how I feel about it. Goodbye.

original: 'The humour of it,' quoth a'! here's a fellow frights English out of his wits.
I will seek out Falstaff.
translation: I'm going to go look for Falstaff.

original: I never heard such a drawling, affecting rogue.
translation: I've never heard anyone speak so slowly and so pretentiously.

original: If I do find it: well.
translation: If I find out that what he says is true: well, then we'll see.

original: I will not believe such a Cataian, though the priest o' the town commended him for a true man.
'Twas a good sensible fellow: well.
translation: He was an honest intelligent person. Well, we'll see.

original: How now, Meg!
translation: Hey there, Meg!

original: Whither go you, George? Hark you.
translation: What are you up to, George?

original: How now, sweet Frank! why art thou melancholy?
translation: How are you doing, sweet Frank! Why do you look sad?

original: I melancholy! I am not melancholy. Get you home, go.
translation: Me, sad! I'm not sad. Go home, get going.

original: Faith, thou hast some crotchets in thy head. Now, will you go, Mistress Page?
translation: My goodness, you have some strange idea in your head. Hey, will you come with me, Mistress Page?

original: Have with you. You'll come to dinner, George.
translation: I'm coming. You'll come to dinner, George.

original: Look who comes yonder: she shall be our messenger to this paltry knight.
translation: Look who's coming. She'll take our message to that worthless knight.

original: Trust me, I thought on her: she'll fit it.
translation: Believe me, I thought of that too. She'll be just right for that.

original: You are come to see my daughter Anne?
translation: You're here to see my daughter Anne?

original: Ay, forsooth; and, I pray, how does good Mistress Anne?
translation: Yes; and, tell me, how is good Mistress Anne doing?

original: Go in with us and see: we have an hour's talk with you.
translation: Come with us and see. We'll talk to you for a while.

original: How now, Master Ford!
translation: What's going on with you, Master Ford?

original: You heard what this knave told me, did you not?
translation: You heard what that scoundrel told me, didn't you?

original: Yes: and you heard what the other told me?
translation: Yes, and you heard what the other man told me?

original: Do you think there is truth in them?
translation: Do you think they were telling the truth?

original: Hang 'em, slaves!
translation: Forget about them, those scoundrels!

original: I do not think the knight would   offer it: but these that accuse him in his intent   towards our wives are a yoke of his discarded men;
translation: I don't think the knight would try anything like that: but the men that told us about his plan are a pair of men that he just fired.

original: very rogues, now they be out of service.
translation: They're acting like scoundrels, now that they don't have work anymore.

original: Were they his men?
translation: They used to work for him?

original: Marry, were they.
translation: Indeed, they did.

original: I like it never the better for that. Does he lie at the Garter?
translation: That doesn't make me feel any better. Is Falstaff staying at the Garter Inn?

original: Ay, marry, does he. If he should intend this voyage   towards my wife, I would turn her loose to him;
translation: Yes, he is. If he tried to seduce my wife, I would set her loose on him,

original: and   what he gets more of her than sharp words, let it   lie on my head.
translation: and if she did anything other than scold him harshly, then I'd take responsibility for it.

original: I do not misdoubt my wife; but I would be loath to   turn them together. A man may be too confident:
translation: I don't mistrust my wife, but I still wouldn't want to let them be alone together. A man can trust his wife too much.

original: I   would have nothing lie on my head: I cannot be thus  satisfied.
translation: I don't want to be made a  cuckold . I can't feel as calm about it as you can.

original: Look where my ranting host of the Garter comes:
translation: Look, here comes the talkative host of the Garter Inn.

original: there is either liquor in his pate or money in his   purse when he looks so merrily.
translation: Either he's had something to drink or he's gotten some money, he looks so cheerful.

original: How now, mine host!
How now, bully-rook! thou'rt a gentleman. Cavaleiro-justice, I say!
translation: How are you doing, my fine fellow? You are a gentlemen. Oh, gallant Justice, I'm calling you!

original: I follow, mine host, I follow. Good even and   twenty, good Master Page!
translation: I'm here, my host. Good evening and I hope it will be twenty times as good, good Master Page!

original: Master Page, will you go   with us? we have sport in hand.
translation: Master Page, will you come with us? We're about to see something entertaining.

original: Tell him, cavaleiro-justice; tell him, bully-rook.
translation: Tell him about it, gallant Justice. Tell him, my fine fellow.

original: Sir, there is a fray to be fought between Sir Hugh the Welsh priest and Caius the French doctor.
translation: Sir, there's going to be a fight between Sir Hugh the Welsh priest and Caius the French doctor.

original: Good mine host o' the Garter, a word with you.
translation: Good host of the Garter, let me talk to you for a minute.

original: What sayest thou, my bully-rook?
translation: What do you want to talk about, my fine fellow?

original: [To PAGE]   Will you go with us to behold it?
translation: [To PAGE]  Will you go with us to watch the fight?

original: My   merry host hath had the measuring of their weapons;   and, I think, hath appointed them contrary places;
translation: The host will be the referee, and I think he's told them each a different place to meet—

original: for, believe me, I hear the parson is no jester.   Hark, I will tell you what our sport shall be.
translation: because, believe me, I hear the parson isn't a lightweight in a fight. Listen, I'll tell you what our trick is going to be.

original: Hast thou no suit against my knight, my guest-cavaleire?
translation: Are you sure you don't have any complaint to make about the knight staying with me, my gallant friend?

original: None, I protest: but I'll give you a pottle of burnt sack to give me recourse to him and tell him my name is Brook; only for a jest.
translation: None, I promise, but I'll give you two quarts of mulled wine if you'll bring me to him and tell him my name is Brook, just for a joke.

original: My hand, bully; thou shalt have egress and regress;   —said I well?—and thy name shall be Brook.
translation: [Giving FORD his hand to shake]  I promise, my fine fellow. You'll be able to go out and come back again—are those the  right words  to use?—and I'll say your name is Brook.

original: It is   a merry knight. Will you go, An-heires?
translation: Falstaff is a merry knight. Will you go with me, gentlemen?

original: Have with you, mine host.
translation: We'll come with you, my host.

original: I have heard the Frenchman hath good skill in his rapier.
translation: I heard the Frenchman is good at sword-fighting.

original: Tut, sir, I could have told you more.
translation: That's nothing, sir, I could have told you more than that.

original: In these times   you stand on distance, your passes, stoccadoes, and   I know not what:
translation: These days, fighters in a duel rely on having distance between them, they use  lunges, thrusts,  and I don't know what else.

original: 'tis the heart, Master Page; 'tis   here, 'tis here.
translation: That's the essential part of fighting, Master Page; it's done like this, like this.  [He gestures]

original: I have seen the time, with my long   sword I would have made you four tall fellows skip like rats.
translation: I remember when I could use my  long sword  to make you four brave men jump like rats.

original: Here, boys, here, here! shall we wag?
translation: Here, boys, here, here! Shall we go?

original: Have with you. I would rather hear them scold than  fight.
translation: Oh, if you want. I would rather hear them scold each other than have a real fight.

original: Though Page be a secure fool, an stands so firmly   on his wife's frailty, yet I cannot put off my   opinion so easily:
translation: Even though Page is a fool who trusts his wife too much, and is so confident about his wife's unreliable nature, still, I can't overcome my worries so easily.

original: she was in his company at Page's   house; and what they made there, I know not.
translation: My wife spent time with Falstaff at Page's house; and I don't know what they got up to together there.

original: Well,   I will look further into't: and I have a disguise   to sound Falstaff. If I find her honest, I lose not   my labour; if she be otherwise, 'tis labour well  bestowed.
translation: Well, I'll investigate it more: and I have a disguise that I'll use to interrogate Falstaff. If I find out that my wife is faithful, I'm not wasting my time; if she's not faithful, then my efforts were put to good use.

original: I will not lend thee a penny.
translation: I won't lend you a penny.

original: Why, then the world's mine oyster. Which I with sword will open.
translation: Well, then I'll get money from you by force.

original: Not a penny. I have been content, sir, you should   lay my countenance to pawn;
translation: Not a penny. I didn't mind that you used my good reputation to get people to  lend you money .

original: I have grated upon my   good friends for three reprieves for you and your   coach-fellow Nym; or else you had looked through   the grate, like a geminy of baboons.
translation: I bothered my friends until the officials let you and your friend Nym off the hook three times, and if I hadn't, you would have been trapped behind the bars of a prison cell like a pair of monkeys.

original: I am damned in   hell for swearing to gentlemen my friends, you were   good soldiers and tall fellows; and when Mistress   Bridget lost the handle of her fan, I took't upon   mine honour thou hadst it not.
translation: I damned my soul by swearing to friends of mine that you were good soldiers and brave men, and when Mistress Bridget lost the  handle of her fan , I swore on my honor that you hadn't stolen it.

original: Didst not thou share? hadst thou not fifteen pence?
Reason, you rogue, reason: thinkest thou I'll   endanger my soul gratis?
translation: And you had a good reason to do that, you scoundrel, you had a good reason. Do you think I'd put my soul in danger for nothing?

original: At a word, hang no more   about me, I am no gibbet for you. Go. A short knife   and a throng! To your manor of Pickt-hatch! Go.   You'll not bear a letter for me, you rogue! you   stand upon your honour!
translation: In short, don't hang around me anymore, don't try to  pin  any more of your crimes on me. Go away. Find a short knife and a crowd of people! Go to  Pickt-hatch ! Go. You won't carry a letter to someone for me, you scoundrel! You claim it's because you have so much honor.

original: Why, thou unconfinable   baseness, it is as much as I can do to keep the   terms of my honour precise: I, I, I myself   sometimes, leaving the fear of God on the left hand   and hiding mine honour in my necessity, am fain to   shuffle, to hedge and to lurch;
translation: Why, you unspeakably dishonorable person, even I sometimes have trouble keeping my honor pure. I, I, I myself sometimes, have to put aside my fear of God and sacrifice my honor when it becomes necessary. I have to cheat, use cunning, and steal,

original: and yet you, rogue,   will ensconce your rags, your cat-a-mountain   looks, your red-lattice phrases, and your   bold-beating oaths, under the shelter of your   honour! You will not do it, you!
translation: and yet you, scoundrel, try to cover up your rags, your wild looks, the words you learn at the tavern, and your brash swearing, by pretending to have honor! I won't allow it!

original: I do relent: what would thou more of man?
translation: I give up. What more could you ask of anybody?

original: Sir, here's a woman would speak with you.
translation: Sir, there's a woman here who wants to talk to you.

original: Let her approach.
translation: Tell her to come in.

original: Give your worship good morrow.
translation: Good day to you.

original: Good morrow, good wife.
Not so, an't please your worship.
translation: I'm not a wife, if you'll excuse me for saying so.

original: Good maid, then.
I'll be sworn, As my mother was, the first hour I was born.
I do believe the swearer. What with me?
translation: I believe you. What do you want?

original: Shall I vouchsafe your worship a word or two?
translation: Can I have a word with you?

original: Two thousand, fair woman: and I'll vouchsafe thee the hearing.
translation: Two thousand words, my good lady, and I'll listen.

original: There is one Mistress Ford, sir:—I pray, come a little nearer this ways:—I myself dwell with master Doctor Caius,—
translation: There's a woman named Mistress Ford, sir—Please, come a little further this way—I live with master Doctor Caius—

original: Well, on: Mistress Ford, you say,—
translation: Well, go on. Mistress Ford, you were saying—

original: Your worship says very true: I pray your worship, come a little nearer this ways.
translation: Sir, that's correct. Please, come a little further this way.

original: I warrant thee, nobody hears; mine own people, mine own people.
translation: I promise you, no one can hear us. These men are my own servants, my own servants.

original: Are they so? God bless them and make them his servants!
translation: Are they really? God bless them and may they serve God!

original: Well, Mistress Ford; what of her?
translation: Well, Mistress Ford, what about her?

original: Why, sir, she's a good creature. Lord Lord! your worship's a wanton! Well, heaven forgive you and all of us, I pray!
translation: Well, sir, she's a good person. Good lord! You are a reckless man! Well, God forgive you and everyone, I pray!

original: Mistress Ford; come, Mistress Ford,—
translation: Mistress Ford, come on, what about Mistress Ford—

original: Marry, this is the short and the long of it; you   have brought her into such a canaries as 'tis   wonderful.
translation: Well, here's the long and the short of it. You have put her into such a terrible  dilemma .

original: The best courtier of them all, when the   court lay at Windsor, could never have brought her   to such a canary. Yet there has been knights, and   lords, and gentlemen, with their coaches, I warrant   you, coach after coach, letter after letter, gift   after gift; smelling so sweetly, all musk, and so   rushling, I warrant you, in silk and gold; and in   such alligant terms; and in such wine and sugar of   the best and the fairest, that would have won any   woman's heart;
translation: The best  courtier  there was, when the court was here in Windsor, couldn't have put her into such a dilemma. But there used to be knights, and lords, and gentlemen, with their coaches, I'm telling you, coach after coach, letter after letter, gift after gift. They all smelled so sweetly, full of perfume, and wrapped, I promise you, in silk and gold, and the letters were written so elegantly and they were so flattering, saying she was the best and the prettiest woman, that any woman would have been won over by letters like that.

original: and, I warrant you, they could never   get an eye-wink of her: I had myself twenty angels   given me this morning; but I defy all angels, in   any such sort, as they say, but in the way of   honesty:
translation: And I promise you, they could never even get her to look at them: someone offered me twenty gold coins this morning. But I'm not interested in any gold coins at all, except when I can get them honestly

original: and, I warrant you, they could never get   her so much as sip on a cup with the proudest of   them all: and yet there has been earls, nay, which   is more, pensioners;
translation: —and, I'm telling you, they couldn't even get her to have a drink with the handsomest man in the bunch, and some of them were  earls , and even better, gentleman in the royal bodyguard.

original: but, I warrant you, all is one  with her.
translation: But, I'm telling you, none of that matters to her.

original: But what says she to me? be brief, my good she-Mercury.
Marry, she hath received your letter, for the which   she thanks you a thousand times;
translation: Well, she got your letter, and she thanks you a thousand times for it,

original: and she gives you   to notify that her husband will be absence from his   house between ten and eleven.
translation: and she wants me to tell you that her husband will be out of the house between ten and eleven o'clock.

original: Ten and eleven?
translation: Ten and eleven?

original: Ay, forsooth; and then you may come and see the   picture, she says, that you wot of: Master Ford,   her husband, will be from home.
translation: Yes, that's right, and then you can come over and do the thing that's on your mind. Master Ford, her husband, will be out of the house.

original: Alas! the sweet   woman leads an ill life with him: he's a very   jealousy man: she leads a very frampold life with   him, good heart.
translation: It's too bad! The sweet woman has a very unhappy life with him. He's a very jealous man. She has a very unpleasant life with him, the good lady.

original: Ten and eleven. Woman, commend me to her; I will not fail her.
translation: Ten and eleven. Woman, give her my regards. I won't fail to turn up.

original: Why, you say well. But I have another messenger to   your worship.
translation: Well, that's a nice thing to say. But I have another message for you.

original: Mistress Page hath her hearty   commendations to you too: and let me tell you in   your ear, she's as fartuous a civil modest wife, and   one, I tell you, that will not miss you morning nor   evening prayer, as any is in Windsor, whoe'er be the   other:
translation: Mistress Page sends her best wishes to you too, and let me tell you, she's a virtuous and well-behaved, chaste wife, and, I tell you, she's not someone who will miss morning or evening prayer, not more than anyone else in Windsor, anyone at all.

original: and she bade me tell your worship that her   husband is seldom from home; but she hopes there   will come a time.
translation: And she told me to tell you that her husband isn't out of the house very often, but she hopes there will be a time when he's away.

original: I never knew a woman so dote upon   a man: surely I think you have charms, la; yes, in  truth.
translation: I never knew a woman who was so fond of a man. I think you must be really charming, yes, really.

original: Not I, I assure thee: setting the attractions of my good parts aside I have no other charms.
translation: Not me, I promise you. If you ignore my sexual prowess, I don't have any other good qualities.

original: Blessing on your heart for't!
translation: Bless your heart for that!

original: But, I pray thee, tell me this: has Ford's wife and Page's wife acquainted each other how they love me?
translation: But, please, tell me this: have Ford's wife and Page's wife told each other that they love me?

original: That were a jest indeed! they have not so little   grace, I hope: that were a trick indeed!
translation: That would really be a good joke! They don't have such bad manners, I hope. That would be quite a joke!

original: but   Mistress Page would desire you to send her your   little page, of all loves: her husband has a   marvellous infection to the little page; and truly   Master Page is an honest man.
translation: But Mistress Page would like you to send her your young servant, for the sake of your love for her. Her husband has a great affection for the young servant, and Master Page is certainly a good man.

original: Never a wife in   Windsor leads a better life than she does: do what   she will, say what she will, take all, pay all, go   to bed when she list, rise when she list, all is as   she will: and truly she deserves it; for if there   be a kind woman in Windsor, she is one.
translation: No woman in Windsor leads a better life than she does. She can do what she likes, say what she likes, have what she likes, go to bed when she likes, get up when she likes, everything is the way she likes; and she deserves it, because there isn't a kinder woman in Windsor.

original: You must   send her your page; no remedy.
translation: You must send her your servant, there's no way out of it.

original: Why, I will.
translation: Well, I will.

original: Nay, but do so, then: and, look you, he may come and   go between you both;
translation: No, but really do it, and, you see, he can come and go between you both,

original: and in any case have a   nay-word, that you may know one another's mind, and   the boy never need to understand any thing; for   'tis not good that children should know any   wickedness:
translation: and he can carry codewords back and forth, so that you can communicate with each other, and the boy won't know what's going on, because it isn't good for children to know about bad behavior.

original: old folks, you know, have discretion,   as they say, and know the world.
translation: Older people, you know, have good judgment, people say, and know what the world is like.

original: Fare thee well: commend me to them both: there's my purse; I am yet thy debtor. Boy, go along with this woman.
translation: Goodbye. Send my regards to both of them. Here's some money, I'm in your debt. Boy, go with this woman.

original: This news distracts me!
translation: This news is bewildering!

original: This punk is one of Cupid's carriers:
translation: This whore carries messages of love.

original: Clap on more sails; pursue; up with your fights:   Give fire: she is my prize, or ocean whelm them all!
translation: Set the sail , chase her, get ready for battle, arm yourselves: may we lose everything if I don't catch her!

original: Sayest thou so, old Jack? go thy ways; I'll make   more of thy old body than I have done.
translation: [To himself]  What do you think about all this, old Jack? Go ahead with it. I'll make better use of my old body than I've done in the past.

original: Will they   yet look after thee? Wilt thou, after the expense   of so much money, be now a gainer?
translation: Will these women take care of you? After spending so much money, will you make a profit now?

original: Good body, I   thank thee. Let them say 'tis grossly done; so it be   fairly done, no matter.
translation: Handsome body, I thank you. People might say it's a dishonorable thing to do. I don't care, as long as it's successful.

original: Sir John, there's one Master Brook below would fain speak with you, and be acquainted with you; and hath sent your worship a morning's draught of sack.
translation: Sir John, there's a man named Master Brook downstairs who would like to meet you and talk to you, and he's sent you a drink of Spanish wine.

original: Brook is his name?
translation: His name is Brook?

original: Ay, sir.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: Call him in.
translation: Call him in.

original: Such Brooks are welcome to me, that o'erflow such   liquor.
translation: [To himself]  Anyone who buys me liquor is welcome.

original: Ah, ha! Mistress Ford and Mistress Page   have I encompassed you? go to; via!
translation: Ah, ha! Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, have I won you over? Go, go!

original: Bless you, sir!
translation: I wish you well, sir!

original: And you, sir! Would you speak with me?
translation: And you, sir! You want to talk to me?

original: I make bold to press with so little preparation upon you.
translation: I know I'm being forward, to force myself on you without giving you any prior notice.

original: You're welcome. What's your will? Give us leave,  drawer.
translation: You're welcome to talk to me. What do you want? Leave us alone, servant.

original: Sir, I am a gentleman that have spent much; my name is  Brook.
translation: Sir, I'm a man who has spent a lot of money. My name is Brook.

original: Good Master Brook, I desire more acquaintance of you.
translation: Good Master Brook, I'd like to get to know you better.

original: Good Sir John, I sue for yours: not to charge you;   for I must let you understand I think myself in   better plight for a lender than you are:
translation: Good Sir John, I'd like to get to know you better—not to ask you for money, because you should know that I think I'm in a better position to lend money than you are.

original: the which   hath something embolden'd me to this unseasoned   intrusion; for they say, if money go before, all   ways do lie open.
translation: But this makes me feel comfortable approaching you without warning, for, as people say, if you offer people money, no one will turn you away.

original: Money is a good soldier, sir, and will on.
translation: Money is very good at persuading people.

original: Troth, and I have a bag of money here troubles me:
translation: True, and I have a bag of money here that's a lot of trouble to carry around.

original: if you will help to bear it, Sir John, take all, or   half, for easing me of the carriage.
translation: If you'll help me carry it, Sir John, I'll give you all of it, or half of it, as a reward for taking this heavy burden off my hands.

original: Sir, I know not how I may deserve to be your porter.
translation: Sir, I don't know why you would give me money.

original: I will tell you, sir, if you will give me the hearing.
translation: I'll tell you, sir, if you'll listen to me.

original: Speak, good Master Brook: I shall be glad to be your servant.
translation: Tell me, Master Brook. I'll be glad to do something for you.

original: Sir, I hear you are a scholar,—I will be brief   with you,—and you have been a man long known to me,   though I had never so good means, as desire, to make   myself acquainted with you.
