translation: Sir, I hear you are an educated person—I'll come to the point quickly—I've known about you for a long time, although I've never had such a good chance as I wanted to meet you.

original: I shall discover a   thing to you, wherein I must very much lay open mine   own imperfection:
translation: I'm going to tell you something that will make me look like a very flawed person—

original: but, good Sir John, as you have   one eye upon my follies, as you hear them unfolded,   turn another into the register of your own; that I   may pass with a reproof the easier, sith you   yourself know how easy it is to be such an offender.
translation: but, good Sir John, even as you're hearing about my faults, as I'm telling you about them, please think about your own faults also, so you'll be more likely to excuse my faults, since you know yourself that it's easy to have them.

original: Very well, sir; proceed.
translation: Okay, then, go on.

original: There is a gentlewoman in this town; her husband's name is Ford.
translation: There's a gentlewoman in this town. Her husband's name is Ford.

original: Well, sir.
translation: Go on, sir.

original: I have long loved her, and, I protest to you,   bestowed much on her;
translation: I have been in love with her for a long time, and, I'm telling you, I've given her a lot of money.

original: followed her with a doting   observance; engrossed opportunities to meet her;   fee'd every slight occasion that could but niggardly   give me sight of her;
translation: I've been very attentive to her, I've tried to find a lot of opportunities to meet her, and taken advantage of every opportunity to get even a brief glimpse of her.

original: not only bought many presents   to give her, but have given largely to many to know   what she would have given;
translation: Not only have I bought her many presents, I've given presents to a lot of other people so they would tell me what gifts she would like.

original: briefly, I have pursued   her as love hath pursued me; which hath been on the   wing of all occasions.
translation: In short, I've chased her just like love has chased me—constantly.

original: But whatsoever I have   merited, either in my mind or, in my means, meed,   I am sure, I have received none; unless experience   be a jewel that I have purchased at an infinite   rate, and that hath taught me to say this:
translation: But whatever I've deserved from her, thanks either to my feelings or my gifts, she hasn't given me anything in return—unless it's the gift of learning from experience, which I've purchased at a huge cost, and the lesson is this:

original: 'Love like a shadow flies when substance love pursues;   Pursuing that that flies, and flying what pursues.'
translation: "the beloved runs away when the lover chases her; love chases what runs away from it, and it runs away from what chases it."

original: Have you received no promise of satisfaction at her  hands?
translation: She hasn't promised to satisfy you?

original: Never.
translation: Never.

original: Have you importuned her to such a purpose?
translation: Have you asked her to?

original: Never.
translation: Never.

original: Of what quality was your love, then?
translation: What kind of love do you have for her, then?

original: Like a fair house built on another man's ground;
translation: It's love for someone who already belongs to someone else.

original: so   that I have lost my edifice by mistaking the place   where I erected it.
translation: So I've wasted all my time trying to get something that wasn't available.

original: To what purpose have you unfolded this to me?
translation: Why are you telling me all this?

original: When I have told you that, I have told you all.   Some say, that though she appear honest to me, yet in   other places she enlargeth her mirth so far that   there is shrewd construction made of her.
translation: When I answer that question, then I've told you everything. Some people say that even though she seems chaste to me, she's so flirtatious with other men that some people have strong suspicions about her fidelity.

original: Now, Sir   John, here is the heart of my purpose:
translation: Now, Sir John, here's the thing I really want:

original: you are a   gentleman of excellent breeding, admirable   discourse, of great admittance, authentic in your   place and person, generally allowed for your many   war-like, court-like, and learned preparations.
translation: you're a gentleman with very good manners, you speak well, you mix with people in the highest social circles, you have authority because of your status and your appearance, and everyone agrees that you have a lot of accomplishments, in war, at court, and in your studies.

original: O, sir!
translation: O, sir!

original: Believe it, for you know it.
translation: Believe me, because you know it's true.

original: There is money; spend   it, spend it; spend more; spend all I have; only   give me so much of your time in exchange of it, as   to lay an amiable siege to the honesty of this   Ford's wife: use your art of wooing; win her to   consent to you: if any man may, you may as soon as   any.
translation: [He hands FALSTAFF money]  Here's some money; spend it, spend it, spend more than that, spend all the money I have In exchange, I want you to try and overcome Mistress Ford's chastity. Use your skills in seducing women. Get her to agree to have an affair with you. If any one can do it, you can.

original: Would it apply well to the vehemency of your   affection, that I should win what you would enjoy?
translation: Given that you love her so much, would it do you any good if I won the woman that you want for yourself?

original: Methinks you prescribe to yourself very preposterously.
translation: I think you're making an absurd request.

original: O, understand my drift. She dwells so securely on   the excellency of her honour, that the folly of my   soul dares not present itself: she is too bright to   be looked against.
translation: Oh, pay attention to my plan. She's so confident that she's perfectly chaste that I don't dare to approach her. She's too pure for me to get near her.

original: Now, could I could come to her   with any detection in my hand, my desires had   instance and argument to commend themselves: I   could drive her then from the ward of her purity,   her reputation, her marriage-vow, and a thousand   other her defences, which now are too too strongly   embattled against me.
translation: Now, if I could go to her and  accuse  her of having had an affair, then I would have a better argument for why she should give in to my desires, too—then I could convince her to stop caring about her purity, her reputation, her marriage vow, and all the other things that prevent her from giving in to me and that block me so effectively right now.

original: What say you to't, Sir John?
translation: What do you say to that plan, Sir John?

original: Master Brook, I will first make bold with your money; next, give me your hand; and last, as I am a gentleman, you shall, if you will, enjoy Ford's wife.
translation: Master Brook, first, I will freely take your money; then, give me your hand;  and finally, I promise, as a gentleman, that you will get to sleep with Ford's wife if you so desire.

original: O good sir!
translation: Oh, good sir!

original: I say you shall.
translation: I'm telling you, you will.

original: Want no money, Sir John; you shall want none.
translation: You won't be short of money, Sir John, you'll have all the money you want.

original: Want no Mistress Ford, Master Brook; you shall want   none.
translation: You won't be short of Mistress Ford, you'll have her.

original: I shall be with her, I may tell you, by her   own appointment; even as you came in to me, her   assistant or go-between parted from me:
translation: I'm going to meet her, in fact, because she has actually asked me to come and see her—just before you came in to see me, her messenger left my room.

original: I say I   shall be with her between ten and eleven; for at   that time the jealous rascally knave her husband   will be forth.
translation: I will see her between ten and eleven, because at that time, her jealous scoundrel of a husband won't be at home.

original: Come you to me at night; you shall   know how I speed.
translation: Come see me tonight and I'll tell you how things went.

original: I am blest in your acquaintance. Do you know Ford, sir?
translation: I'm very lucky to have met you. Do you know Ford, sir?

original: Hang him, poor cuckoldly knave! I know him not:   yet I wrong him to call him poor;
translation: I don't give a damn about him, that poor lowlife cuckold! I don't know him, but I shouldn't call him poor.

original: they say the   jealous wittolly knave hath masses of money; for the   which his wife seems to me well-favored. I will   use her as the key of the cuckoldly rogue's coffer;   and there's my harvest-home.
translation: People say that that jealous  willing cuckold  has tons of money, which is why I find his wife attractive. I'll use her to get access to that foolish scoundrel's money, and that will be a huge profit to me.

original: I would you knew Ford, sir, that you might avoid him if you saw him.
translation: I wish you knew Ford, sir, so that if you saw him, you could avoid him.

original: Hang him, mechanical salt-butter rogue!
translation: I don't give a damn about him, that cheap, lower-class scoundrel!

original: I will   stare him out of his wits; I will awe him with my   cudgel: it shall hang like a meteor o'er the   cuckold's horns.
translation: I'll stare him down until he's scared out of his wits. I'll frighten him with my club—it will be a bad omen for that cuckold.

original: Master Brook, thou shalt know I   will predominate over the peasant, and thou shalt   lie with his wife. Come to me soon at night.
translation: Master Brook, I will defeat this lower-class man, and you will sleep with his wife. Come see me tonight.

original: Ford's a knave, and I will aggravate his style;   thou, Master Brook, shalt know him for knave and   cuckold. Come to me soon at night.
translation: Ford's a lowlife, and I'll make it so that you can call him worse names than that. You, Master Brook, will learn that he's a lowlife and a cuckold. Come see me tonight.

original: What a damned Epicurean rascal is this! My heart is   ready to crack with impatience. Who says this is   improvident jealousy?
translation: What a damned, pleasure-seeking scoundrel this man is! I'm ready to burst with anger. Who says that I have no reason to be jealous?

original: my wife hath sent to him; the   hour is fixed; the match is made. Would any man   have thought this?
translation: My wife asked him to come see her: they picked a time; they made an appointment. Would any man have thought this would happen?

original: See the hell of having a false   woman! My bed shall be abused, my coffers   ransacked, my reputation gnawn at; and I shall not   only receive this villanous wrong, but stand under   the adoption of abominable terms, and by him that   does me this wrong.
translation: It's so terrible to have an unfaithful wife! She will sleep with another man, she will steal my money, she will ruin my reputation, and not only will she do all these terrible things to me, but I'm also being called terrible names by the man who's ruining me.

original: Terms! names! Amaimon sounds   well; Lucifer, well; Barbason, well; yet they are   devils' additions, the names of fiends: but   Cuckold! Wittol!—Cuckold! the devil himself hath   not such a name.
translation: Names! Names!  Amaimon  is a good name; Lucifer is another good name; Barbason is another good name; and they are all devils' names, the names of demons. But cuckold! willing cuckold!—Cuckold! Even the devil doesn't have such a bad name as that.

original: Page is an ass, a secure ass: he   will trust his wife; he will not be jealous. I will   rather trust a Fleming with my butter, Parson Hugh   the Welshman with my cheese, an Irishman with my   aqua-vitae bottle, or a thief to walk my ambling   gelding, than my wife with herself;
translation: Page is a fool, an overconfident fool. He trusts his wife, he won't be jealous. I'd rather trust a  Flemish  person not to eat my butter, or Parson Hugh the Welshman not to eat my cheese, or an Irishman not to drink my liquor, or a thief not to steal my horse, than to trust my wife to behave herself when she's unsupervised.

original: then she plots,   then she ruminates, then she devises; and what they   think in their hearts they may effect, they will   break their hearts but they will effect.
translation: When she's alone, she plots, she thinks, then she comes up with a plan, and women will carry out the plans they come up with. Even if it means doing themselves a lot of harm, they'll still carry out their plans.

original: God be   praised for my jealousy! Eleven o'clock the hour.   I will prevent this, detect my wife, be revenged on   Falstaff, and laugh at Page. I will about it;   better three hours too soon than a minute too late.   Fie, fie, fie! cuckold! cuckold! cuckold!
translation: Thank God I'm a jealous man! They're meeting at eleven o'clock. I'll stop this, I'll expose my wife, get revenge on Falstaff, and laugh at Page. I'll get to work. It would be better to be three hours too early than a minute too late. Ugh, ugh, ugh! Cuckold! Cuckold! Cuckold!

original: Jack Rugby!
translation: Jack Rugby!

original: Sir?
translation: What is it, sir?

original: Vat is de clock, Jack?
translation: What time is it, Jack?

original: 'Tis past the hour, sir, that Sir Hugh promised to  meet.
translation: It's past the time that Sir Hugh promised he would meet you, sir.

original: By gar, he has save his soul, dat he is no come;
translation: By God, he'll save his soul by not coming.

original: he   has pray his Pible well, dat he is no come: by gar,   Jack Rugby, he is dead already, if he be come.
translation: His prayers will be answered if he doesn't come. By God, Jack Rugby, he would end up dead if he came.

original: He is wise, sir; he knew your worship would kill him, if he came.
translation: He's smart, sir. He knows that you'd kill him if he came.

original: By gar, de herring is no dead so as I vill kill him. Take your rapier, Jack; I vill tell you how I vill kill him.
translation: By God, he'd be more dead than a dead fish when I got through with him. Take your sword, Jack, I'll tell you how I'll kill him.

original: Alas, sir, I cannot fence.
translation: Unfortunately, sir, I can't sword-fight.

original: Villany, take your rapier.
translation: You lowlife, pick up your sword.

original: Forbear; here's company.
translation: Cut it out, people are coming.

original: Bless thee, bully doctor!
translation: God bless you, my jolly doctor!

original: Save you, Master Doctor Caius!
translation: God bless you, Master Doctor Caius!

original: Now, good master doctor!
translation: Now then, good Master Doctor!

original: Give you good morrow, sir.
translation: I wish you a good day, sir.

original: Vat be all you, one, two, tree, four, come for?
translation: What have you four come for?

original: To see thee fight, to see thee foin, to see thee   traverse; to see thee here, to see thee there; to   see thee pass thy punto, thy stock, thy reverse, thy   distance, thy montant.
translation: We came to see you fight, to see you  thrust your sword , to see you move forward and backward, to see you here, to see you over there, to see you thrust with your sword point, to see your thrust, your backhand hit, your skill at keeping the right distance from your opponent, your upward thrust with your sword.

original: Is he dead, my Ethiopian? is   he dead, my Francisco? ha, bully! What says my   AEsculapius? my Galen? my heart of elder? ha! is   he dead, bully stale? is he dead?
translation: Is he dead, my Ethiopian? Is he dead, my Frenchman? Ha, my jolly fellow! What does the  doctor  say? The doctor with his  weak heart ? Ha! Is he dead, you fool? Is he dead?

original: By gar, he is de coward Jack priest of de vorld; he is not show his face.
translation: By God, he's the most cowardly scoundrel of a priest in the world. He hasn't shown up.

original: Thou art a Castalion-King-Urinal. Hector of Greece, my  boy!
I pray you, bear vitness that me have stay six or seven, two, tree hours for him, and he is no come.
translation: Please, bear witness to the fact that I have waited six or seven, two, three hours for him, and he hasn't come.

original: He is the wiser man, master doctor: he is a curer of   souls, and you a curer of bodies;
translation: He's wiser than you, master doctor. He cures souls, and you cure bodies.

original: if you should   fight, you go against the hair of your professions.   Is it not true, Master Page?
translation: If you fought each other, you'd be acting contrary to your professions. Isn't that right, Master Page?

original: Master Shallow, you have yourself been a great fighter, though now a man of peace.
Bodykins, Master Page, though I now be old and of   the peace, if I see a sword out, my finger itches to   make one.
translation: By God, Master Page, even though I'm old and peaceful now, if I see someone take out a sword, I have a strong urge to join in the fight.

original: Though we are justices and doctors and   churchmen, Master Page, we have some salt of our   youth in us; we are the sons of women, Master Page.
translation: Even though we are judges and doctors and priests, Master Page, we still have some energy left over from our youth. We're  men , after all, Master Page.

original: 'Tis true, Master Shallow.
translation: That's true, Master Shallow.

original: It will be found so, Master Page. Master Doctor   Caius, I am come to fetch you home. I am sworn of   the peace:
translation: You'll see it is true, Master Page. Master Doctor Caius, I've come to take you home. I've promised to keep the peace.

original: you have showed yourself a wise   physician, and Sir Hugh hath shown himself a wise   and patient churchman.
translation: You have shown that you are a wise doctor, and Sir Hugh has shown that he is a wise and calm priest.

original: You must go with me, master  doctor.
translation: You must come with me, Master Doctor.

original: Pardon, guest-justice. A word, Mounseur Mockwater.
Mock-vater! vat is dat?
translation: Mockwater! What does that mean?

original: Mock-water, in our English tongue, is valour, bully.
translation: Mockwater, in the English language, means bravery, my jolly fellow.

original: By gar, den, I have as mush mock-vater as de   Englishman.
translation: By God, then, I have as much mockwater as any Englishman does!

original: Scurvy jack-dog priest! by gar, me   vill cut his ears.
translation: That despicable low-bred priest! By God, I'll cut his ears.

original: He will clapper-claw thee tightly, bully.
Clapper-de-claw! vat is dat?
translation: Clapperclaw! What does that mean?

original: That is, he will make thee amends.
translation: It means, he'll make up for everything he's done to you.

original: By gar, me do look he shall clapper-de-claw me; for, by gar, me vill have it.
translation: By God, I'll make sure he clapperclaws me, because I'll make him, by God.

original: And I will provoke him to't, or let him wag.
Me tank you for dat.
translation: I thank you for that.

original: And, moreover, bully,—but first, master guest, and Master Page, and eke Cavaleiro Slender, go you through the town to Frogmore.
Sir Hugh is there, is he?
translation: Is Sir Hugh there?

original: He is there: see what humour he is in; and I will bring the doctor about by the fields. Will it do well?
translation: He is. Go see what kind of mood he's in, and I'll bring the Doctor there by taking the path around the fields. Will that work?

original: We will do it.
translation: We'll do it.

original: Adieu, good master doctor.
translation: Goodbye, good Master Doctor.

original: By gar, me vill kill de priest; for he speak for a jack-an-ape to Anne Page.
translation: By God, I'm going to kill that priest for trying to intervene with Anne Page on behalf on a complete idiot.

original: Let him die: sheathe thy impatience, throw cold   water on thy choler:
translation: Let him die. Don't be so agitated, try to cool down your anger.

original: go about the fields with me   through Frogmore: I will bring thee where Mistress   Anne Page is, at a farm-house a-feasting; and thou   shalt woo her.
translation: Come walk around the fields with me through Frogmore. I'll take you to where Anne Page is attending a party at a farmhouse, and you can  woo  her.

original: Cried I aim? said I well?
translation: Am I on the right track? Is this a good idea?

original: By gar, me dank you for dat: by gar, I love you;
translation: By God, thank you for this, by God, I love you.

original: and I shall procure-a you de good guest, de earl,   de knight, de lords, de gentlemen, my patients.
translation: I'll get high-ranking people to come stay at your inn: an earl, a knight, lords, gentlemen, and my patients.

original: For the which I will be thy adversary toward Anne Page. Said I well?
By gar, 'tis good; vell said.
translation: By God, that's great, I like what you're saying.

original: Let us wag, then.
translation: Let's go, then.

original: Come at my heels, Jack Rugby.
translation: Follow me, Jack Rugby.

original: I pray you now, good master Slender's serving-man, and friend Simple by your name, which way have you looked for Master Caius, that calls himself doctor of  physic?
translation: Good Master Slender's servant, whose name is Simple, can you please tell me where have you been looking for Master Caius, who calls himself a medical doctor?

original: Marry, sir, the pittie-ward, the park-ward, every way; old Windsor way, and every way but the town way.
I most fehemently desire you you will also look that way.
translation: I'd really like you to look near the town, too.

original: I will, sir.
translation: I will, sir.

original: 'Pless my soul, how full of chollors I am, and   trempling of mind! I shall be glad if he have   deceived me.
translation: Bless my soul, I'm so upset and agitated! I'll be glad if he has lied to me.

original: How melancholies I am! I will knog   his urinals about his knave's costard when I have   good opportunities for the ork. 'Pless my soul!
translation: I feel so dejected! I'll smack him on his dishonest head with his  urine-collecting bottles  when I get a chance. Bless my soul!

original: To shallow rivers, to whose falls   Melodious birds sings madrigals;   There will we make our peds of roses,   And a thousand fragrant posies.   To shallow—
translation: Let us go to shallow rivers   Where sweetly singing birds sing songs to the waterfalls; There we'll make beds out of roses  And a thousand sweet-smelling flowers.  Let us go—

original: Mercy on me! I have a great dispositions to cry.
translation: God have mercy on me! I feel like I'm going to cry.

original: Melodious birds sing madrigals—   When as I sat in Pabylon—
translation: Sweetly-singing birds sing songs— As when I sat in Babylon—

original: And a thousand vagram posies.   To shallow & c.
translation: And a thousand scattered flowers. Let us go...  (etc.)

original: Yonder he is coming, this way, Sir Hugh.
translation: Look, he's coming this way, Sir Hugh.

original: He's welcome.
translation: He's welcome.

original: To shallow rivers, to whose falls- Heaven prosper the right! What weapons is he?
No weapons, sir. There comes my master, Master Shallow, and another gentleman, from Frogmore, over the stile, this way.
translation: He's not bringing any weapons, sir. Here comes my master, Master Shallow, and another gentleman, from Frogmore, over the fence, this way.

original: Pray you, give me my gown; or else keep it in your  arms.
translation: Please, give me my coat; or else hold on to it.

original: How now, master Parson! Good morrow, good Sir Hugh.
translation: How are you doing, Master Parson! Good morning, good Sir Hugh.

original: Keep a gamester from the dice, and a good student   from his book, and it is wonderful.
translation: If you keep a gambler away from gambling, and a good student away from studying, you can get some surprising results.

original: Ah, sweet Anne Page!
translation: Oh, sweet Anne Page!

original: 'Save you, good Sir Hugh!
translation: God bless you, good Sir Hugh!

original: 'Pless you from his mercy sake, all of you!
translation: God bless you in his mercy, all of you!

original: What, the sword and the word! do you study them both, master parson?
translation: What, fighting and religion! Do you practice both of them, Master Parson?

original: And youthful still! in your doublet and hose this raw rheumatic day!
There is reasons and causes for it.
translation: I have a good reason for that.

original: We are come to you to do a good office, master parson.
translation: We've come to do something helpful for you, Master Parson.

original: Fery well: what is it?
translation: Very well, what is it?

original: Yonder is a most reverend gentleman, who, belike   having received wrong by some person,
translation: Over there is a very honorable gentleman who was probably treated badly by someone,

original: is at most   odds with his own gravity and patience that ever you   saw.
translation: and so he's not behaving in his usual dignified and calm way.

original: I have lived fourscore years and upward;
translation: I'm more than eighty years old,

original: I never   heard a man of his place, gravity and learning, so   wide of his own respect.
translation: and I never heard of someone with his job, dignity, and education, caring so little about his own reputation.

original: What is he?
translation: Who is he?

original: I think you know him; Master Doctor Caius, the renowned French physician.
translation: I think you know him: Master Doctor Caius, the famous French doctor.

original: Got's will, and his passion of my heart! I had as lief you would tell me of a mess of porridge.
translation: My God! I would rather you had told me where I could find some thick soup.

original: Why?
translation: Why?

original: He has no more knowledge in Hibocrates and Galen,
translation: He doesn't know anything about  medicine ,

original: —and he is a knave besides; a cowardly knave as you   would desires to be acquainted withal.
translation: and he is also a scoundrel, the most cowardly scoundrel you could ever meet.

original: I warrant you, he's the man should fight with him.
translation: I'm telling you, he would fight him.

original: O sweet Anne Page!
translation: Oh sweet Anne Page!

original: It appears so by his weapons. Keep them asunder: here comes Doctor Caius.
translation: It seems like it, judging by his weapons. Keep them apart, here comes Doctor Caius.

original: Nay, good master parson, keep in your weapon.
translation: No, good Master Parson, don't draw your sword.

original: So do you, good master doctor.
translation: And don't draw your sword either, good Master Doctor.

original: Disarm them, and let them question: let them keep their limbs whole and hack our English.
translation: Take away their weapons and let them talk to each other. Keep them from fighting with swords and let them just fight with words.

original: I pray you, let-a me speak a word with your ear. Vherefore vill you not meet-a me?
translation: Please, let me have a private word with you. [Aloud so that the others can hear] Why didn't you meet me?

original: Pray you, use your patience: in good time.
translation: Please, be calm. [Aloud so that the others can hear] I was going to come.

original: By gar, you are de coward, de Jack dog, John ape.
translation: By God, you are a coward, a dog, an ape!

original: [Aside to DOCTOR CAIUS]   Pray you let us not be   laughing-stocks to other men's humours;
translation: [To DOCTOR CAIUS so that only he can hear]  Please, let's not make fools out of ourselves so the others can laugh at us.

original: I desire you   in friendship, and I will one way or other make you  amends.
translation: I want to be friends with you, and I'll make things up to you one way or another.

original: [Aloud so that the others can hear]   I will knog your  urinals about your knave's cockscomb   for missing your  meetings and appointments.
translation: [Aloud so that the others can hear]  I will hit you in the head with your urine-collecting bottles for missing our meeting.

original: Diable! Jack Rugby,—mine host de Jarteer,—have I   not stay for him to kill him?
translation: You devil! Jack Rugby—my host of the Garter Inn—didn't I wait for him to kill him?

original: have I not, at de place   I did appoint?
translation: Wasn't I waiting at the place I said I would?

original: As I am a Christians soul now, look you, this is the   place appointed:
translation: As sure as I'm a Christian, I'm telling you, this was the place we were supposed to meet.

original: I'll be judgement by mine host of   the Garter.
translation: Ask the Host of the Garter Inn.

original: Peace, I say, Gallia and Gaul, French and Welsh, soul-curer and body-curer!
Ay, dat is very good; excellent.
translation: Yes, that's good, excellent.

original: Peace, I say! hear mine host of the Garter.
translation: Be quiet, I said! Listen to me, the Host of the Garter Inn.

original: Am I   politic? am I subtle? am I a Machiavel? Shall I   lose my doctor? no; he gives me the potions and the   motions. Shall I lose my parson, my priest, my Sir   Hugh?
translation: Am I devious? Am I crafty? Am I a  treacherous schemer ? Do I want to lose my doctor? No, he gives me medicines and helps my digestion. Do I want to lose my parson, my priest, my Sir Hugh?

original: no; he gives me the proverbs and the   no-verbs.
translation: No, he gives me verses from the Bible and  directions about what I shouldn't do.

original: Give me thy hand, terrestrial; so. Give me   thy hand, celestial; so.
translation: Give me your hand, man who cures bodies; like this. Give me your hand, man who cures souls; like this.

original: Boys of art, I have   deceived you both; I have directed you to wrong   places: your hearts are mighty, your skins are   whole, and let burnt sack be the issue.
translation: You educated men, I've tricked both of you. I sent you to the wrong places. Your hearts are brave, your bodies aren't hurt, and let's let this fight end in a drink!

original: Come, lay   their swords to pawn. Follow me, lads of peace;   follow, follow, follow.
translation: Come on, put their swords aside. Follow me, you peaceful men: follow, follow, follow.

original: Trust me, a mad host. Follow, gentlemen, follow.
translation: Believe me, he's a jubilant man! Follow, gentlemen, follow.

original: O sweet Anne Page!
translation: O sweet Anne Page!

original: Ha, do I perceive dat? have you make-a de sot of us, ha, ha?
translation: Ha, do I understand what's going on? Have you made fools out of us, ha, ha?

original: This is well; he has made us his vlouting-stog.
translation: This is just great. He's made everyone laugh at us.

original: I   desire you that we may be friends; and let us knog   our prains together to be revenge on this same   scall, scurvy cogging companion, the host of the  Garter.
translation: I want to be friends with you, and let's put our heads together to figure out how to take revenge on this scabby, dishonest, cheating scoundrel, the host of the Garter Inn.

original: By gar, with all my heart. He promise to bring me where is Anne Page; by gar, he deceive me too.
translation: By God, with all my heart. He promised to take me to Anne Page. By God, he tricked me there, too.

original: Well, I will smite his noddles. Pray you, follow.
translation: Well, I'll smack his head. Please, follow me.

original: Nay, keep your way, little gallant; you were wont to   be a follower, but now you are a leader.
translation: No, go your own way, my fine young man, You're used to being a servant, but now you're in charge.

original: Whether   had you rather lead mine eyes, or eye your master's  heels?
translation: Would you prefer to direct me, or to follow your master?

original: I had rather, forsooth, go before you like a man than follow him like a dwarf.
translation: I would rather direct you like a grown man than follow Falstaff like a young boy.

original: O, you are a flattering boy: now I see you'll be a  courtier.
Well met, Mistress Page. Whither go you?
translation: It's nice to see you, Mistress Page. Where are you going?

original: Truly, sir, to see your wife. Is she at home?
translation: Actually, to see your wife. Is she at home?

original: Ay; and as idle as she may hang together, for want   of company.
translation: Yes, and she's as bored and lonely as can be, because she doesn't have any company.

original: I think, if your husbands were dead,   you two would marry.
translation: If your husbands were dead, I think the two of you would get married.

original: Be sure of that,—two other husbands.
translation: Yes, we would—we'd marry two other men.

original: Where had you this pretty weather-cock?
translation: Where did you find this handsome young servant?

original: I cannot tell what the dickens his name is my   husband had him of.
translation: I don't remember who my husband hired him from.

original: What do you call your knight's   name, sirrah?
translation: What did you say your boss's name was, young man?

original: Sir John Falstaff.
translation: Sir John Falstaff.

original: Sir John Falstaff!
translation: Sir John Falstaff!

original: He, he; I can never hit on's name.
translation: Ha, ha, I can never remember his name.

original: There is such a   league between my good man and he! Is your wife at   home indeed?
translation: He's such good friends with my husband! Is your wife really at home?

original: Indeed she is.
translation: Yes, she is.

original: By your leave, sir: I am sick till I see her.
translation: I'll go see her with your permission. I'm dying to see her.

original: Has Page any brains? hath he any eyes? hath he any   thinking?   Sure, they sleep; he hath no use of them.
translation: Does Page have a brain? Can he see anything? Is he thinking?  I'm sure he's not using his brain or his eyes.

original: Why, this boy will carry a letter twenty mile, as   easy as a cannon will shoot point-blank twelve   score. He pieces out his wife's inclination; he   gives her folly motion and advantage: and now she's   going to my wife, and Falstaff's boy with her. A   man may hear this shower sing in the wind. And   Falstaff's boy with her!
translation: Why, this boy will carry letters between them as easily as a cannon can shoot straight for two-hundred-forty yards. Page increases his wife's sexual desire. He encourages her desire and gives her the opportunity to act on it, and now she's going to visit my wife, and Falstaff's servant is going with her.  Anyone could see that trouble is coming. And Falstaff's servant is going with her!

original: Good plots, they are laid;   and our revolted wives share damnation together.   Well; I will take him, then torture my wife, pluck   the borrowed veil of modesty from the so seeming   Mistress Page, divulge Page himself for a secure and   wilful Actaeon; and to these violent proceedings all   my neighbours shall cry aim.
translation: They're hatching plans, and our disloyal wives are planning to do this terrible thing together. Well; I'll take Falstaff by surprise, then confront my wife, then reveal how unfaithful this apparently well-behaved Mistress Page is, reveal that Page is overconfident and willing to be a cuckold, and my neighbors will applaud me for doing all these harsh things.

original: The clock gives me my cue, and my assurance bids me   search: there I shall find Falstaff:
translation: The clock tells me that it's time to go, and I'm certain that I should go search the house. I'll find Falstaff there.

original: I shall be   rather praised for this than mocked; for it is as   positive as the earth is firm that Falstaff is   there: I will go.
translation: I will be praised for acting this way, not made fun of, because it's absolutely certain that Falstaff is at my house. I will go.

original: Well met, Master Ford.
translation: It's nice to see you, Master Ford.

original: Trust me, a good knot: I have good cheer at home; and I pray you all go with me.
translation: What a fine group of people! I have good food and drink at home. Please come with me.

original: I must excuse myself, Master Ford.
translation: I'm afraid I can't come, Master Ford.

original: And so must I, sir: we have appointed to dine with Mistress Anne, and I would not break with her for more money than I'll speak of.
translation: And neither can I, sir. We have an appointment to eat with Mistress Anne, and I wouldn't miss the appointment for any amount of money.

original: We have lingered about a match between Anne Page and my cousin Slender, and this day we shall have our  answer.
translation: We have delayed in arranging a marriage between Anne Page and my cousin Slender, and we'll settle it today.

original: I hope I have your good will, father Page.
translation: I hope you support me marrying her, father Page.

original: You have, Master Slender; I stand wholly for you: but my wife, master doctor, is for you altogether.
translation: I do, Master Slender. I'm completely on your side, but my wife is on your side, Master Doctor.

original: Ay, be-gar; and de maid is love-a me: my nursh-a Quickly tell me so mush.
translation: Yes, by God, and the young lady loves me. My housekeeper Quickly told me so.

original: What say you to young Master Fenton? he capers, he   dances, he has eyes of youth, he writes verses, he   speaks holiday, he smells April and May:
translation: What do you think about young Master Fenton? He leaps and dances, he has young eyes, he writes poetry, he speaks cheerfully, he smells like spring.

original: he will   carry't, he will carry't; 'tis in his buttons; he   will carry't.
translation: He will succeed, he will succeed. Thanks to his youthful potential, he will succeed.

original: Not by my consent, I promise you.
translation: I won't agree to it, I promise you.

original: The gentleman is   of no having: he kept company with the wild prince   and Poins; he is of too high a region; he knows too   much.
translation: The gentleman has no property. He hangs out with the  wild prince and Poins ; his social status is too high; he's too sophisticated.

original: No, he shall not knit a knot in his fortunes   with the finger of my substance: if he take her,   let him take her simply; the wealth I have waits on   my consent, and my consent goes not that way.
translation: No, he won't increase his property with any of my property. If he wants to marry Anne, she won't have a dowry. I won't give her any money without my consent, and I don't consent to her marrying Fenton.

original: I beseech you heartily, some of you go home with me   to dinner:
translation: I urge you, some of you come home with me to have dinner.

original: besides your cheer, you shall have   sport; I will show you a monster. Master doctor,   you shall go;
translation: Besides good food, you'll have good entertainment—I'll show you a spectacle. Master Doctor, you'll come.

original: so shall you, Master Page; and you, Sir  Hugh.
translation: So will you, Master Page, and you, Sir Hugh.

original: Well, fare you well: we shall have the freer wooing at Master Page's.
translation: Well, good-bye.  It will be easier to woo Anne at Master Page's house.

original: Go home, John Rugby; I come anon.
translation: Go home, John Rugby. I'll come soon.

original: Farewell, my hearts: I will to my honest knight Falstaff, and drink canary with him.
translation: Good-bye, my friends. I'm going to go see that good knight Falstaff, and drink wine with him.

original: I think I shall drink in pipe wine first with him; I'll make him dance. Will you go, gentles?
translation: I think I'll make things rough for Falstaff first. I'll get him. Will you come with me, good men?

original: Have with you to see this monster.
translation: We're coming to see this spectacle.

original: What, John! What, Robert!
translation: Hey there, John! Hey there, Robert!

original: Quickly, quickly! is the buck-basket—
translation: Quickly, quickly! Is the laundry-basket—

original: I warrant. What, Robert, I say!
translation: I'm sure it is. Hey there, Robert, I'm calling you!

original: Come, come, come.
translation: Come, come, come.

original: Here, set it down.
translation: Here, put it down.

original: Give your men the charge; we must be brief.
translation: Tell the servants what they're supposed to do. We have to act quickly.

original: Marry, as I told you before, John and Robert, be   ready here hard by in the brew-house: and when I   suddenly call you, come forth, and without any pause   or staggering take this basket on your shoulders:
translation: [To the servants]  Well, like I told you before, John and Robert, be ready right over here in the  brew-house , and when I call you, come out right away, and without pausing or tripping, lift this basket up on your shoulders.

original: that done, trudge with it in all haste, and carry   it among the whitsters in Datchet-mead, and there   empty it in the muddy ditch close by the Thames side.
translation: When you've done that, go as quickly as you can, and carry it to the  launderers  in  Datchet-mead,  and when you get there, empty it into the muddy ditch near the bank of the  Thames River.

original: You will do it?
translation: You'll do that?

original: I ha' told them over and over; they lack no direction. Be gone, and come when you are called.
translation: I've told them over and over, they know what to do. Get going, and come when you're called.

original: Here comes little Robin.
translation: Here comes young Robin.

original: How now, my eyas-musket! what news with you?
My master, Sir John, is come in at your back-door, Mistress Ford, and requests your company.
translation: My master, Sir John, is at your back door, Mistress Ford, and he wants to see you.

original: You little Jack-a-Lent, have you been true to us?
translation: You little puppet, have you been loyal to us?

original: Ay, I'll be sworn.
translation: Yes, I promise.

original: My master knows not of your   being here and hath threatened to put me into   everlasting liberty if I tell you of it; for he   swears he'll turn me away.
translation: My master doesn't know that you're here and he threatened to put me out of work forever if I tell you that he's visiting here, because he swears he'll fire me.

original: Thou'rt a good boy:
translation: You're a good boy.

original: this secrecy of thine shall be   a tailor to thee and shall make thee a new doublet   and hose. I'll go hide me.
translation: If you keep our secrets, you'll get a new  set of clothes . I'll go hide.

original: Do so. Go tell thy master I am alone.
translation: Do that.  Go tell your master that I'm alone.

original: Mistress Page, remember you your cue.
I warrant thee; if I do not act it, hiss me.
translation: I promise you. If I don't do it properly, scold me.

original: Go to, then: we'll use this unwholesome humidity, this gross watery pumpion; we'll teach him to know turtles from jays.
Have I caught thee, my heavenly jewel? Why, now let   me die, for I have lived long enough:
translation: Do I finally have you, my divine beauty? Well, let me die now, because I have lived long enough.

original: this is the   period of my ambition: O this blessed hour!
translation: I couldn't want anything more than this. O what a blessed moment!

original: O sweet Sir John!
translation: Oh, sweet Sir John!

original: Mistress Ford, I cannot cog, I cannot prate,   Mistress Ford. Now shall I sin in my wish: I would   thy husband were dead:
translation: Mistress Ford, I can't lie, I can't talk idly, Mistress Ford. Now I wish something terrible—I wish your husband were dead.

original: I'll speak it before the   best lord; I would make thee my lady.
translation: I'll say it in front of anyone: I would make you my  lady.

original: I your lady, Sir John! alas, I should be a pitiful  lady!
translation: Your lady, Sir John! Oh dear, I would be a pathetic lady.

original: Let the court of France show me such another.
translation: I bet there wouldn't be another lady in the whole court of France like you.

original: I see   how thine eye would emulate the diamond:
translation: I see how your eyes would look like diamonds.

original: thou hast   the right arched beauty of the brow that becomes the   ship-tire, the tire-valiant, or any tire of   Venetian admittance.
translation: You have beautifully arched eyebrows that would look lovely with any kind of  Venetian head dress.

original: A plain kerchief, Sir John: my brows become nothing else; nor that well neither.
translation: A plain handkerchief, Sir John, that's the only thing that would look good with my eyebrows, and it wouldn't even look that good.

original: By the Lord, thou art a traitor to say so:
translation: By God, you're very unfair to yourself to say that.

original: thou   wouldst make an absolute courtier; and the firm   fixture of thy foot would give an excellent motion   to thy gait in a semi-circled farthingale.
translation: You would make a perfect courtier, and the steady way you place your feet means you would walk very well in a hoop-skirt.

original: I see   what thou wert, if Fortune thy foe were not, Nature   thy friend. Come, thou canst not hide it.
translation: I see what you would look like if you hadn't had  bad luck , given your natural beauty. Come on, you can't deny it.

original: Believe me, there is no such thing in me.
translation: Believe me, I don't have any qualities like that.

original: What made me love thee? let that persuade thee   there's something extraordinary in thee.
translation: What made me love you? My love should convince you that you have some extraordinary qualities.

original: Come, I   cannot cog and say thou art this and that, like a   many of these lisping hawthorn-buds, that come like   women in men's apparel, and smell like Bucklersbury   in simple time;
translation: Come on, I can't lie and say you are this and that, like so many of these tongue-tied perfumed young men that look like women in men's clothing, and smell like the  flower shops of London in the summer .

original: I cannot: but I love thee; none   but thee; and thou deservest it.
translation: I can't, but I love you. No one but you, and you deserve it.

original: Do not betray me, sir. I fear you love Mistress Page.
translation: Don't lie to me, sir. I'm afraid that you love Mistress Page.

original: Thou mightst as well say I love to walk by the Counter-gate, which is as hateful to me as the reek of a lime-kiln.
Well, heaven knows how I love you; and you shall one day find it.
translation: Well, God knows how much I love you, and one day you'll find out.

original: Keep in that mind; I'll deserve it.
translation: Remember that. I'll deserve it.

original: Nay, I must tell you, so you do; or else I could not be in that mind.
translation: No, I tell you, you do deserve it, or else I couldn't feel the way I do.

original: Mistress Ford, Mistress Ford! here's Mistress Page at the door, sweating and blowing and looking wildly, and would needs speak with you  presently.
translation: Mistress Ford, Mistress Ford! Mistress Page is at the door, sweating and puffing and looking alarmed, and she wants to speak with you right away.

original: She shall not see me: I will ensconce me behind the  arras.
translation: She won't see me. I'll hide behind the curtain.

original: Pray you, do so: she's a very tattling woman.
translation: Please, do that. She's very likely to gossip.

original: What's the matter? how now!
translation: What's the matter? What's going on?

original: O Mistress Ford, what have you done? You're shamed, you're overthrown, you're undone for ever!
translation: Oh, Mistress Ford, what have you done? You're disgraced, you're defeated, you're ruined forever!

original: What's the matter, good Mistress Page?
translation: What's the matter, good Mistress Page?

original: O well-a-day, Mistress Ford! having an honest man to your husband, to give him such cause of suspicion!
translation: It's awful, Mistress Ford! That you have an honest man for a husband and give him reason to distrust you!

original: What cause of suspicion?
translation: What reason to distrust me?

original: What cause of suspicion! Out pon you! how am I mistook in you!
translation: What reason to distrust you? Shame on you! I was so wrong about you!

original: Why, alas, what's the matter?
translation: Why, oh dear, what's the matter?

original: Your husband's coming hither, woman, with all the   officers in Windsor, to search for a gentleman that   he says is here now in the house by your consent, to   take an ill advantage of his assence:
translation: Your husband's coming here, woman, with all the officers in Windsor, to look for a man that he says you let into the house so you could take advantage of your husband's absence.

original: you are undone.
translation: You're ruined.

original: 'Tis not so, I hope.
translation: I hope that isn't true.

original: Pray heaven it be not so, that you have such a man   here! but 'tis most certain your husband's coming,   with half Windsor at his heels, to search for such a   one.
translation: I hope it isn't true that you do actually have a man here! But it's definitely true that your husband is coming to look for a man here, and he has half the town following him.

original: I come before to tell you. If you know   yourself clear, why, I am glad of it; but if you   have a friend here convey, convey him out.
translation: I came ahead to warn you. If you know that you're innocent, well, that's good, but if you have a lover here, get him out, get him out.

original: Be not   amazed; call all your senses to you; defend your   reputation, or bid farewell to your good life for ever.
translation: Don't be bewildered. Pull yourself together, defend your reputation, or you'll never be respectable again.

original: What shall I do? There is a gentleman my dear   friend; and I fear not mine own shame so much as his   peril:
translation: What will I do? There is a man here, my lover, and I'm not so much afraid of being disgraced myself as I'm afraid that he'll be in danger.

original: I had rather than a thousand pound he were   out of the house.
translation: I would give a thousand pounds to get him out of the house.

original: For shame! never stand 'you had rather' and 'you   had rather:'
translation: Shame on you! Don't waste time thinking about what "you would give."

original: your husband's here at hand, bethink   you of some conveyance: in the house you cannot   hide him.
translation: Your husband's close by, think of some way to get your lover out of the house. You can't hide him in the house.

original: O, how have you deceived me! Look, here   is a basket: if he be of any reasonable stature, he   may creep in here; and throw foul linen upon him, as   if it were going to bucking:
translation: Oh, how you have lied to me! Look, here's a basket. If he's not too big, your lover can hide in there, and you can throw dirty clothes on him, as if the basket were going out to the laundry.

original: or—it is whiting-time   —send him by your two men to Datchet-mead.
translation: Or—since it's bleaching time—have two of your servants take the basket to Datchet-mead.

original: He's too big to go in there. What shall I do?
translation: He's too big to fit in there. What will I do?

original: Let me see't, let me see't, O, let me see't! I'll in, I'll in. Follow your friend's counsel. I'll in.
translation: Let me see it, let me see it, O, let me see it! I'll get in, I'll get in. Take your friend's advice. I'll get in.

original: What, Sir John Falstaff! Are these your letters,  knight?
translation: What, Sir John Falstaff? Did you send me those love letters, knight?

original: I love thee. Help me away. Let me creep in here. I'll never—
translation: I love you. Help me get away. Let me get in the basket. I'll never—

original: Help to cover your master, boy. Call your men, Mistress Ford. You dissembling knight!
translation: Help to cover up your master, boy. [To MISTRESS FORD] Call your servants, Mistress Ford. You lying knight!

original: What, John! Robert! John!
translation: Hey, John! Robert! John!

original: Go take up these clothes here quickly.
translation: Take these clothes out of here quickly. Where's the basket pole?

original: Where's the   cowl-staff? look, how you drumble! Carry them to   the laundress in Datchet-meat; quickly, come.
translation: Look how you're dawdling! Carry these clothes to the launderers in Datchet-mead, quickly, go.

original: Pray you, come near: if I suspect without cause,   why then make sport at me; then let me be your jest;   I deserve it.
translation: Please, come with me. If it turns out that I have no reason to suspect my wife of infidelity, then you can make fun of me, then you can make a joke out of me—I'll deserve it.

original: How now! whither bear you this?
translation: What's going on? Where are you taking this basket?

original: To the laundress, forsooth.
translation: To the launderers.

original: Why, what have you to do whither they bear it? You were best meddle with buck-washing.
Buck! I would I could wash myself of the buck!
translation: Buck ! I wish I could wash away the suspicion that I am a buck!

original: Buck, buck, buck! Ay, buck; I warrant you, buck;   and of the season too, it shall appear.
translation: Buck, buck, buck! Yes, buck, I bet, buck, and I bet there are bucks present right now, as you'll see.

original: Gentlemen, I have dreamed to-night; I'll tell you my   dream.
translation: Gentleman, I had a dream last night. I'll tell you my dream.

original: Here, here, here be my keys: ascend my   chambers; search, seek, find out: I'll warrant   we'll unkennel the fox. Let me stop this way first.
translation: Here, here, here are my keys. Go up the stairs to my rooms, search, look. I bet we'll find something hiding there. Let me lock this door first.

original: So, now uncape.
translation: So, get him out of his hiding place now.

original: Good Master Ford, be contented: you wrong yourself too  much.
translation: Good Master Ford, restrain yourself. You're making yourself look ridiculous.

original: True, Master Page. Up, gentlemen: you shall see sport anon: follow me, gentlemen.
translation: True, Master Page. Go upstairs, gentlemen. You'll something entertaining soon. Follow me, gentlemen.

original: This is fery fantastical humours and jealousies.
translation: He's full of wild fantasies and jealousy.

original: By gar, 'tis no the fashion of France; it is not jealous in France.
translation: By God, this isn't how things are done in France. People don't get jealous like this in France.

original: Nay, follow him, gentlemen; see the issue of his  search.
translation: No, follow him, gentlemen. Let's see how this search turns out.

original: Is there not a double excellency in this?
translation: Hasn't our plot gotten two excellent results?

original: I know not which pleases me better, that my husband is deceived, or Sir John.
translation: I don't know what makes me happier, tricking my husband or tricking Sir John.

original: What a taking was he in when your husband asked who was in the basket!
translation: He was in such a panic when your husband asked who was in the basket!

original: I am half afraid he will have need of washing; so throwing him into the water will do him a benefit.
Hang him, dishonest rascal! I would all of the same strain were in the same distress.
translation: To hell with him, dishonest scoundrel! I wish all men like him had the same trick played on them.

original: I think my husband hath some special suspicion of Falstaff's being here; for I never saw him so gross in his jealousy till now.
translation: I think my husband had some particular reason for suspecting that Falstaff was here, because I've never seen him get so wildly jealous before.

original: I will lay a plot to try that; and we will yet have   more tricks with Falstaff:
translation: I'll come up with a plan to find that out, and we'll play more tricks on Falstaff.

original: his dissolute disease will   scarce obey this medicine.
translation: He is so depraved that this one trick won't cure him.

original: Shall we send that foolish carrion, Mistress   Quickly, to him, and excuse his throwing into the   water;
translation: How about we send that foolish rotten woman, Mistress Quickly, to him, to give him an excuse for throwing him into the water,

original: and give him another hope, to betray him to   another punishment?
translation: and then lead him on by setting up another meeting, so we can betray him with another punishment?

original: We will do it: let him be sent for to-morrow, eight o'clock, to have amends.
translation: Let's do it. Let's tell him that we want him to come over tomorrow at eight o'clock so we can make things up to him.

original: I cannot find him: may be the knave bragged of that he could not compass.
translation: I can't find him. Maybe that scoundrel bragged about doing something he couldn't actually accomplish.

original: Heard you that?
translation: Did you hear that?

original: You use me well, Master Ford, do you?
translation: You treat me well, Master Ford, do you?

original: Ay, I do so.
translation: Yes, I do.

original: Heaven make you better than your thoughts!
translation: I hope your behavior to me will be better than your suspicious thoughts about me!

original: Amen!
translation: Yes!

original: You do yourself mighty wrong, Master Ford.
translation: You're tormenting yourself needlessly, Master Ford.

original: Ay, ay; I must bear it.
translation: Yes, yes, I have to deal with it.

original: If there be any pody in the house, and in the chambers, and in the coffers, and in the presses, heaven forgive my sins at the day of judgment!
By gar, nor I too: there is no bodies.
translation: By God, I don't think there is. There's nobody there.

original: Fie, fie, Master Ford! are you not ashamed?
translation: Come, come, Master Ford! Aren't you ashamed?

original: What   spirit, what devil suggests this imagination?
translation: What impulse, what devil created this fantasy in your mind?

original: I   would not ha' your distemper in this kind for the   wealth of Windsor Castle.
translation: I wouldn't have your deranged temper for all the money in Windsor Castle.

original: 'Tis my fault, Master Page: I suffer for it.
translation: It's my own fault, Master Page. I suffer because of it.

original: You suffer for a pad conscience: your wife is as honest a 'omans as I will desires among five thousand, and five hundred too.
translation: You suffer from a sense of guilt. Your wife is as honest as any woman you could find among five thousand women, and even five hundred.

original: By gar, I see 'tis an honest woman.
translation: By God, I see she's an honest woman.

original: Well, I promised you a dinner. Come, come, walk in   the Park: I pray you, pardon me; I will hereafter   make known to you why I have done this.
translation: Well, I promised to give you dinner. Come, come, walk in the Park. Please, pardon my behavior. I'll tell you later why I did this.

original: Come,   wife; come, Mistress Page. I pray you, pardon me;   pray heartily, pardon me.
translation: Come on, wife, come on, Mistress Page. Please, pardon me. I'm pleading with you, pardon me.

original: Let's go in, gentlemen;
translation: Let's go inside, gentlemen.

original: but, trust me, we'll mock   him.
translation: [T o DOCTOR CAIUS and SIR HUGH EVANS] @

original: I do invite you to-morrow morning to my house   to breakfast: after, we'll a-birding together; I   have a fine hawk for the bush. Shall it be so?
translation: [To everyone]  I invite you to my house tomorrow morning for breakfast: afterwards, we'll  hunt birds  together; I have a fine hawk for driving birds into the bush. Shall we do that?

original: Any thing.
translation: Whatever you want.

original: If there is one, I shall make two in the company.
translation: If one person's going, I'll go too.

original: If dere be one or two, I shall make-a the turd.
translation: If one or two people are going, I'll be the third.

original: Pray you, go, Master Page.
translation: Please, let's go, Master Page.

original: I pray you now, remembrance tomorrow on the lousy knave, mine host.
translation: Please, remember our plan tomorrow to deal with that lousy scoundrel, the host of the Garter Inn.

original: Dat is good; by gar, with all my heart!
translation: That's a good idea, by God, with all my heart!

original: A lousy knave, to have his gibes and his mockeries!
translation: That lousy scoundrel, to turn us into jokes and mock us!

original: I see I cannot get thy father's love; Therefore no more turn me to him, sweet Nan.
Alas, how then?
translation: Oh dear, what will we do then?

original: Why, thou must be thyself.
translation: Well, you have to make your own choice.

original: He doth object I am too great of birth—,   And that, my state being gall'd with my expense,   I seek to heal it only by his wealth:
translation: He objects that my social class is too high. He's also afraid that, since I'm in trouble from spending too much, my only goal is to help myself by getting hold of his money.

original: Besides these, other bars he lays before me,   My riots past, my wild societies;   And tells me 'tis a thing impossible   I should love thee but as a property.
translation: Besides that, he also objects to my wild behavior in my youth and my wild companions, and he says that it's impossible that I could love you except as a source of income.

original: May be he tells you true.
translation: Maybe what he says is true.

original: No, heaven so speed me in my time to come!   Albeit I will confess thy father's wealth   Was the first motive that I woo'd thee, Anne:
translation: No, I swear by my future salvation in heaven! I admit that your father's money was the reason I wanted to marry you at first, Anne.

original: Yet, wooing thee, I found thee of more value   Than stamps in gold or sums in sealed bags;
translation: Still, when I started wooing you, I learned that you are worth more than gold coins or bags of money.

original: And 'tis the very riches of thyself   That now I aim at.
translation: What I want now is you, yourself.

original: Gentle Master Fenton,   Yet seek my father's love; still seek it, sir:
translation: Good Master Fenton, I'd still like to you to try and get my father's approval.

original: If opportunity and humblest suit   Cannot attain it, why, then,—hark you hither!
translation: Keep trying, sir. If you can't get his approval even if you have a good opportunity to ask and you ask very humbly, well—come back and talk to me then.

original: Break their talk, Mistress Quickly: my kinsman shall speak for himself.
translation: Interrupt their conversation, Mistress Quickly. My nephew wants to speak to her himself.

original: I'll make a shaft or a bolt on't: 'slid, 'tis but venturing.
translation: I'll speak to her one way or another. Good grief, I just have to give it a try.

original: Be not dismayed.
translation: Don't be discouraged.

original: No, she shall not dismay me: I care not for that, but that I am afeard.
translation: No, she won't discourage me. I don't care about that, except that I'm nervous.

original: Hark ye; Master Slender would speak a word with you.
translation: Hey there, Master Slender would like to speak with you.

original: I come to him.
translation: I'm coming.

original: This is my father's choice. O, what a world of vile ill-favor'd faults Looks handsome in three hundred pounds a-year!
translation: This is the man my father wants me to marry. Even someone full of repulsive flaws can seem attractive if he has an income of three hundred pounds a year!

original: And how does good Master Fenton? Pray you, a word with  you.
translation: And how are you, good Master Fenton? Please, let me speak to you for a moment.

original: She's coming; to her, coz. O boy, thou hadst a father!
translation: She's coming. Go up to her, nephew. Come on, you had a father—be a man!

original: I had a father, Mistress Anne; my uncle can tell you   good jests of him.
translation: I had a father, Mistress Anne, my uncle can tell you funny stories about him.

original: Pray you, uncle, tell Mistress   Anne the jest, how my father stole two geese out of   a pen, good uncle.
translation: Please, uncle, tell Mistress Anne that funny story about how my father stole two geese from a pen, good uncle.

original: Mistress Anne, my cousin loves you.
translation: Mistress Anne, my nephew loves you.

original: Ay, that I do; as well as I love any woman in Gloucestershire.
translation: Yes, I do, as much as I love any woman in Gloucestershire.

original: He will maintain you like a gentlewoman.
translation: He will support you financially as if you were a gentlewoman.

original: Ay, that I will, come cut and long-tail, under the degree of a squire.
He will make you a hundred and fifty pounds jointure.
Good Master Shallow, let him woo for himself.
translation: Good Master Shallow, let him speak for himself.

original: Marry, I thank you for it; I thank you for that good comfort. She calls you, coz: I'll leave you.
translation: Well now, I thank for that, I thank you for those comforting words. She wants to speak to you, nephew. I'll leave you.

original: Now, Master Slender,—
translation: Now, Master Slender—

original: Now, good Mistress Anne,—
translation: Now, good Mistress Anne—

original: What is your will?
translation: What is your will?

original: My will! 'od's heartlings, that's a pretty jest   indeed! I ne'er made my will yet, I thank heaven;
translation: My will!  By God, that's a funny thing to say! I haven't made my will yet, thank God.

original: I   am not such a sickly creature, I give heaven praise.
translation: I'm not so sick that I'm close to dying, thank God.

original: I mean, Master Slender, what would you with me?
translation: I mean, what do you want with me, Master Slender?

original: Truly, for mine own part, I would little or nothing   with you. Your father and my uncle hath made   motions:
translation: Honestly, speaking for myself, I don't want anything from you. Your father and my uncle have come up with a plan for us to marry.

original: if it be my luck, so; if not, happy man be   his dole! They can tell you how things go better   than I can:
translation: If it's my luck to marry you, I'll take it. If not, good luck to everyone! They can tell you what's going on better than I can.

original: you may ask your father; here he comes.
translation: You can ask your father, here he comes.

original: Now, Master Slender: love him, daughter Anne.   Why, how now! what does Master Fenton here?
translation: Now, Master Slender—love him, daughter Anne. Why, what's going on here? What's Master Fenton doing here?

original: You wrong me, sir, thus still to haunt my house:   I told you, sir, my daughter is disposed of.
translation: It's wrong of you to keep hanging around my house. I told you, my daughter's already engaged.

original: Nay, Master Page, be not impatient.
translation: Now, Master Page, don't get upset.

original: Good Master Fenton, come not to my child.
translation: Good Master Fenton, don't come here to see my daughter.

original: She is no match for you.
translation: She's not going to marry you.

original: Sir, will you hear me?
translation: Sir, will you listen to me?

original: No, good Master Fenton. Come, Master Shallow; come, son Slender, in. Knowing my mind, you wrong me, Master Fenton.
translation: No, good Master Fenton. Come in, son-in-law Slender, come in. Since you know my decision, your behavior is inappropriate, Master Fenton.

original: Speak to Mistress Page.
translation: Speak to Mistress Page.

original: Good Mistress Page, for that I love your daughter   In such a righteous fashion as I do,
translation: Good Mistress Page, because I love your daughter with such  honorable intentions ,

original: Perforce, against all cheques, rebukes and manners,   I must advance the colours of my love   And not retire: let me have your good will.
translation: I can't help trying to win her, in spite of restraints, disapproval, and other people's behavior. I can't back down. Please support me.

original: Good mother, do not marry me to yond fool.
I mean it not; I seek you a better husband.
translation: I don't want you to. I'm looking for a better husband for you.

original: That's my master, master doctor.
translation: That's my master, Master Doctor Caius.

original: Alas, I had rather be set quick i' the earth And bowl'd to death with turnips!
translation: Oh no, I'd rather be half-buried in the earth and have people kill me by bowling at my head with turnips!

original: Come, trouble not yourself. Good Master Fenton,   I will not be your friend nor enemy:
translation: Come on, don't get upset. Good Master Fenton, I won't decide ahead of time to work either for you or against you.

original: My daughter will I question how she loves you,   And as I find her, so am I affected.
translation: Instead, I'll ask my daughter if she loves you, and I'll go along with whatever she wants.

original: Till then farewell, sir: she must needs go in;   Her father will be angry.
translation: Until then, good-bye, sir. She has to come inside, or her father will get upset.

original: Farewell, gentle mistress: farewell, Nan.
translation: Good-bye, good lady. Good-bye, Nan.

original: This is my doing, now: 'Nay,' said I, 'will you cast away your child on a fool, and a physician? Look on Master Fenton:' this is my doing.
translation: I brought this about, you see. "No," I said, "will you throw away your child on a fool, and a doctor? Think about Master Fenton." I brought this about.

original: I thank thee; and I pray thee, once to-night Give my sweet Nan this ring: there's for thy pains.
translation: Thank you, and please, at some point tonight, give my sweet Nan this ring.  And here's something for your troubles. [He hands her money]

original: Now heaven send thee good fortune!
translation: I hope God blesses you!

original: A kind heart he hath: a woman would run through   fire and water for such a kind heart.
translation: He has a kind heart. A woman would endure any pains for a man with such a kind heart.

original: But yet I   would my master had Mistress Anne; or I would   Master Slender had her; or, in sooth, I would Master   Fenton had her;
translation: But I still wish that my master would marry Mistress Anne; or I wish that Master Slender would marry her; or, in fact, I wish Master Fenton would marry her.

original: I will do what I can for them all   three; for so I have promised, and I'll be as good   as my word; but speciously for Master Fenton.
translation: I'll do what I can to help all three of them, because I've promised to do so and I'll keep my promise, but I'll especially help Master Fenton.

original: Well,   I must of another errand to Sir John Falstaff from   my two mistresses: what a beast am I to slack it!
translation: Well, I have to take another message to Sir John Falstaff from my two mistresses. It's terrible of me to delay!

original: Bardolph, I say,—
translation: Bardolph, I say—

original: Here, sir.
translation: I'm here, sir.

original: Go fetch me a quart of sack; put a toast in't.
translation: Go get me a quart of wine, and put a piece of hot toast in it.

original: Have I lived to be carried in a basket, like a   barrow of butcher's offal, and to be thrown in the   Thames? Well, if I be served such another trick,   I'll have my brains ta'en out and buttered, and give   them to a dog for a new-year's gift.
translation: Is it possible that I could be carried in a basket like a wheelbarrow of animal entrails from the butcher, and be thrown into the Thames? Well, if anyone tries to play another trick like that on me again, I'll take out my foolish brains and  butter  them and give them to the dog as a New-Year's present.

original: The rogues   slighted me into the river with as little remorse as   they would have drowned a blind bitch's puppies,   fifteen i' the litter: and you may know by my size   that I have a kind of alacrity in sinking; if the   bottom were as deep as hell, I should down.
translation: The scoundrels dumped me into the river as carelessly as they would drown a blind dog's puppies, fifteen at once. And you can tell from how big I am that I sink quickly—no matter how deep the bottom is, I will sink down to it.

original: I had   been drowned, but that the shore was shelvy and   shallow,—a death that I abhor; for the water swells   a man; and what a thing should I have been when I   had been swelled! I should have been a mountain of  mummy.
translation: I would have been drowned, except that the river bed had a gentle slope and was shallow. I hate death by drowning because water makes a person swell up. What would I have looked like if I had swelled up! I would have been a huge corpse.

original: Here's Mistress Quickly, sir, to speak with you.
translation: Mistress Quickly is here, sir, to speak with you.

original: L   et me pour in some sack to the Thames water;
translation: Let me swallow some wine along with all the river water I swallowed,

original: for my   belly's as cold as if I had swallowed snowballs for   pills to cool the reins. Call her in.
translation: because my stomach is as cold as if I had swallowed snowballs to cool my kidneys off. Tell her to come in.

original: Come in, woman!
translation: Come in, woman!

original: By your leave; I cry you mercy: give your worship good morrow.
translation: With your permission, please pardon me. I hope you're doing well.

original: Take away these chalices. Go brew me a pottle of sack finely.
translation: Take away these small glasses. Go prepare me a half-gallon of wine so it will taste good.

original: With eggs, sir?
translation: With eggs in it, sir?

original: Simple of itself; I'll no pullet-sperm in my brewage.
translation: No, just pure wine. I don't want any chicken-offspring in my drink.

original: How now!
translation: What's the news?

original: Marry, sir, I come to your worship from Mistress Ford.
translation: Please, sir, I came here from Mistress Ford.

original: Mistress Ford! I have had ford enough; I was thrown into the ford; I have my belly full of ford.
Alas the day! good heart, that was not her fault: she does so take on with her men; they mistook their  erection.
So did I mine, to build upon a foolish woman's promise.
translation: I misunderstood mine too, believing in a foolish woman's promise.

original: Well, she laments, sir, for it, that it would yearn   your heart to see it.
translation: Well, sir, she's so sorry about it that it would break your heart if you saw her.

original: Her husband goes this morning   a-birding; she desires you once more to come to her   between eight and nine: I must carry her word   quickly: she'll make you amends, I warrant you.
translation: Her husband is out hunting birds this morning, and she wants you to come see her again between eight and nine o'clock. I have to give her your answer quickly. She'll make it up to you, I'm sure.

original: Well, I will visit her: tell her so; and bid her   think what a man is:
translation: Well, I'll visit her. Tell her that; and tell her to reflect on men's nature.

original: let her consider his frailty,   and then judge of my merit.
translation: Let her think about how easily damaged men are, and then she can judge what kind of man I am.

original: I will tell her.
translation: I'll tell her.

original: Do so. Between nine and ten, sayest thou?
translation: Do that. Between nine and ten, you said?

original: Eight and nine, sir.
translation: Between eight and nine, sir.

original: Well, be gone: I will not miss her.
translation: Well, get going. I won't miss the appointment.

original: Peace be with you, sir.
translation: I wish you a good day, sir.

original: I marvel I hear not of Master Brook; he sent me word to stay within: I like his money well. O, here he  comes.
translation: I'm surprised I haven't heard heard from Master Brook. He told me to wait for him here—I like getting money from him. Oh, here he comes.

original: Bless you, sir!
translation: God bless you, sir!

original: Now, master Brook, you come to know what hath passed between me and Ford's wife?
translation: Now, Master Brook, do you know what happened with me and Ford's wife?

original: That, indeed, Sir John, is my business.
translation: That, in fact, Sir John, is what I came to talk to you about.

original: Master Brook, I will not lie to you: I was at her house the hour she appointed me.
translation: Master Brook, I won't lie to you. I was at her house at the time she told me to meet her.

original: And sped you, sir?
translation: And did you succeed, sir?

original: Very ill-favoredly, Master Brook.
translation: Things went very badly, Master Brook.

original: How so, sir? Did she change her determination?
translation: Why's that, sir? Did she change her mind?

original: No, Master Brook; but the peaking Cornuto her   husband, Master Brook, dwelling in a continual   'larum of jealousy, comes me in the instant of our   encounter,
translation: No, Master Brook, but that sneaking cuckold her husband, Master Brook, who is always alarmed by jealousy, came in just as we were about to consummate our affair.

original: after we had embraced, kissed, protested,   and, as it were, spoke the prologue of our comedy;   and at his heels a rabble of his companions,
translation: After we had hugged, kissed, declared our love, and, so to speak, gone through all the preliminaries, he came with a crowd of friends behind him,

original: thither   provoked and instigated by his distemper, and,   forsooth, to search his house for his wife's love.
translation: who were compelled by his deranged temper to come along and search the house for his wife's lover.

original: What, while you were there?
translation: What do you mean, while you were there?

original: While I was there.
translation: While I was there.

original: And did he search for you, and could not find you?
translation: And he looked for you and he couldn't find you?

original: You shall hear. As good luck would have it, comes   in one Mistress Page;
translation: I'll tell you about it. As luck would have it, Mistress Page came in.

original: gives intelligence of Ford's   approach; and, in her invention and Ford's wife's   distraction, they conveyed me into a buck-basket.
translation: She told us that Ford was coming, and she came up with the idea, which Mistress Ford agreed to because she was so distraught, to carry me away in a laundry basket.

original: A buck-basket!
translation: A laundry basket!

original: By the Lord, a buck-basket! rammed me in with foul   shirts and smocks, socks, foul stockings, greasy   napkins;
translation: By God, a laundry basket! They crammed me in with dirty shirts and undergarments, dirty stockings, greasy napkins.

original: that, Master Brook, there was the rankest   compound of villanous smell that ever offended nostril.
