translation: That, Master Brook, was the most disgusting mix of revolting smells that ever hurt anyone's nose.

original: And how long lay you there?
translation: And how long did you lie in the basket?

original: Nay, you shall hear, Master Brook, what I have   suffered to bring this woman to evil for your good.
translation: No, I'll tell you, Master Brook, what I suffered so that I could corrupt this woman and help you out.

original: Being thus crammed in the basket, a couple of Ford's   knaves, his hinds, were called forth by their   mistress to carry me in the name of foul clothes to   Datchet-lane: they took me on their shoulders; met   the jealous knave their master in the door, who   asked them once or twice what they had in their   basket:
translation: When I was jammed into the basket, Mistress Ford called a couple of Ford's scoundrels, his servants, to carry me to Datchet-Lane and say that they were carrying a basket of dirty clothes. They laid the basket on their shoulders and ran into the jealous scoundrel their master at the door, who asked them once or twice what they had in their basket.

original: I quaked for fear, lest the lunatic knave   would have searched it; but fate, ordaining he   should be a cuckold, held his hand. Well: on went he   for a search, and away went I for foul clothes.
translation: I was shaking with fear, worrying that the insane scoundrel would search the basket, but Fate apparently decided that he was meant to be a cuckold and stopped him.  Well, he went on with the search, and I went away disguised as dirty clothes.

original: But   mark the sequel, Master Brook: I suffered the pangs   of three several deaths; first, an intolerable   fright, to be detected with a jealous rotten   bell-wether; next, to be compassed, like a good   bilbo, in the circumference of a peck, hilt to   point, heel to head; and then, to be stopped in,   like a strong distillation, with stinking clothes   that fretted in their own grease:
translation: But listen to what happened next, Master Brook. I suffered the pains of three different kinds of death. First, I was unbearably frightened, worried that I would be discovered by a jealous rotten  eunuch ; next, in the container, I was bent over double like a  sword , with my top touching my bottom and my heels touching my head; and then, I was stuffed like a cork in a wine bottle in with stinking clothes that were rotting in their own sweat.

original: think of that,—a   man of my kidney,—think of that,—that am as subject   to heat as butter; a man of continual dissolution   and thaw: it was a miracle to scape suffocation.
translation: Think about that—a man in my bodily condition—think of that—a man who is as sensitive to heat as butter, a man who is constantly melting and sweating. It was a miracle that I didn't suffocate.

original: And in the height of this bath, when I was more than   half stewed in grease, like a Dutch dish, to be   thrown into the Thames, and cooled, glowing hot,   in that surge, like a horse-shoe; think of   that,—hissing hot,—think of that, Master Brook.
translation: And when this sweat bath was at its worst, when I was half-cooked in sweat like a  Dutch dish , I was thrown into the Thames. Just as I was glowing hot, I was cooled off in the river like a  horse-shoe . Think about that—hissing hot—think about that, Master Brook.

original: In good sadness, I am sorry that for my sake you   have sufferd all this.
translation: In all seriousness, I'm sorry that you suffered all this for my sake.

original: My suit then is desperate;   you'll undertake her no more?
translation: My goal of sleeping with Mistress Ford looks like it will very difficult to accomplish. You won't try to seduce her again?

original: Master Brook, I will be thrown into Etna, as I have   been into Thames, ere I will leave her thus.
translation: Master Brook, I would rather be thrown into a volcano like I was thrown into the river, than leave things in this state.

original: Her   husband is this morning gone a-birding: I have   received from her another embassy of meeting; 'twixt   eight and nine is the hour, Master Brook.
translation: Her husband is out hunting this morning. She sent me another message to meet her. The appointment is between eight and nine, Master Brook.

original: 'Tis past eight already, sir.
translation: It's after eight already, sir.

original: Is it? I will then address me to my appointment.   Come to me at your convenient leisure, and you shall   know how I speed;
translation: Is it? I'll go to my appointment then. Come see me when it's convenient for you, and you'll hear how things went;

original: and the conclusion shall be   crowned with your enjoying her. Adieu. You shall   have her, Master Brook; Master Brook, you shall   cuckold Ford.
translation: and in the end you'll get to enjoy her. Good-bye. You'll have her, Master Brook, you'll make Ford a cuckold.

original: Hum! ha! is this a vision? is this a dream? do I   sleep? Master Ford awake! awake, Master Ford!   there's a hole made in your best coat, Master Ford.
translation: Hm! Ha! Is this just my imagination? Am I dreaming? Am I asleep! Master Ford, wake up! Wake up, Master Ford! Your reputation is ruined, Master Ford.

original: This 'tis to be married! this 'tis to have linen   and buck-baskets! Well, I will proclaim myself   what I am: I will now take the lecher; he is at my   house; he cannot 'scape me; 'tis impossible he   should;
translation: This is what it's like to be married! This is what you get for having clothes and laundry baskets! Well, I'll let everyone know what's going on. I'll catch the lustful man. He's at my house, he can't escape me, it would be impossible.

original: he cannot creep into a halfpenny purse,   nor into a pepper-box: but, lest the devil that   guides him should aid him, I will search   impossible places.
translation: He can't squeeze into a tiny coin-purse or into a box of pepper—but, in case the  devil  that directs him also helps him, I'll search places where it would be impossible for him to hide.

original: Though what I am I cannot avoid,   yet to be what I would not shall not make me tame:   if I have horns to make one mad, let the proverb go   with me: I'll be horn-mad.
translation: Although I can't avoid being a cuckold, the fact that I am a cuckold won't make me calmly accept being one. If I have horns that drive me crazy, I'll do just what the proverb says: I'll go  horn-mad .

original: Is he at Master Ford's already, think'st thou?
translation: Do you think he's already at Master Ford's?

original: Sure he is by this, or will be presently: but, truly, he is very courageous mad about his throwing into the water. Mistress Ford desires you to come  suddenly.
translation: I'm sure he is by now, or he will be soon. But I'm telling you, he is furiously angry about being thrown into the water. Mistress Ford wants you to come over immediately.

original: I'll be with her by and by; I'll but bring my young man here to school. Look, where his master comes; 'tis a playing-day, I see.
How now, Sir Hugh! no school to-day?
translation: Hello there, Sir Hugh! There's no school today?

original: No; Master Slender is let the boys leave to play.
translation: No, Master Slender's given permission for the boys to play.

original: Blessing of his heart!
translation: Bless his heart!

original: Sir Hugh, my husband says my son profits nothing in the world at his book. I pray you, ask him some questions in his accidence.
translation: Sir Hugh, my husband says our son William isn't getting any better at reading. Please, ask him some questions about his Latin grammar.

original: Come hither, William; hold up your head; come.
translation: Come here, William. Stand up straight, come on.

original: Come on, sirrah; hold up your head; answer your master, be not afraid.
translation: Come on, young man, stand up straight. Answer your master, don't be scared.

original: William, how many numbers is in nouns?
translation: William, how many kinds of nouns are there?

original: Two.
translation: Two.

original: Truly, I thought there had been one number more, because they say, ''Od's nouns.'
Peace your tattlings! What is 'fair,' William?
translation: Stop your chattering! What is "beautiful," William?

original: Pulcher.
translation: Pulcher.

original: Polecats! there are fairer things than polecats, sure.
You are a very simplicity 'oman: I pray you peace. What is 'lapis,' William?
translation: You're a very ignorant woman. I ask you to be quiet. What does "lapis" mean, William?

original: A stone.
translation: A stone.

original: And what is 'a stone,' William?
translation: And what is "a stone," William?

original: A pebble.
translation: A pebble.

original: No, it is 'lapis:' I pray you, remember in your prain.
translation: No, it's "lapis." I ask you, please, remember that in your mind.

original: Lapis.
translation: Lapis.

original: That is a good William. What is he, William, that does lend articles?
translation: That's a good boy, William. From what part of speech do we get articles?

original: Articles are borrowed of the pronoun, and be thus declined, Singulariter, nominativo, hic, haec, hoc.
Nominativo, hig, hag, hog; pray you, mark: genitivo, hujus. Well, what is your accusative case?
Accusativo, hinc.
I pray you, have your remembrance, child, accusative, hung, hang, hog.
translation: Please, remember your lessons, child, the accusative is hung, hang, hog.

original: 'Hang-hog' is Latin for bacon, I warrant you.
translation: I bet that "hang-hog" is Latin for bacon.

original: Leave your prabbles, 'oman. What is the focative case, William?
O,—vocativo, O.
Remember, William; focative is caret.
And that's a good root.
translation: A carrot is a good root.

original: 'Oman, forbear.
translation: Woman, cut it out.

original: Peace!
translation: Be quiet!

original: What is your genitive case plural, William?
Genitive case!
translation: Genitive case!

original: Ay.
translation: That's the one.

original: Genitive,—horum, harum, horum.
translation: Genitive—horum, harum, horum.

original: Vengeance of Jenny's case! fie on her! never name her, child, if she be a whore.
For shame, 'oman.
translation: Shame on you, woman.

original: You do ill to teach the child such words:
translation: It's wrong of you teach the child words like that.

original: he   teaches him to hick and to hack, which they'll do   fast enough of themselves, and to call 'horum:' fie  upon you!
translation: [To MISTRESS PAGE]  he teaches him to  hick and hack , which children learn fast enough on their own, and to say the word "horum." Shame on you!

original: 'Oman, art thou lunatics?
translation: Woman, are you crazy?

original: hast thou no   understandings for thy cases and the numbers of the   genders?
translation: Don't you understand the cases, singular and plural, and  genders ?

original: Thou art as foolish Christian creatures as   I would desires.
translation: You're the most foolish creature I have ever seen.

original: Prithee, hold thy peace.
translation: I'm telling you, be quiet.

original: Show me now, William, some declensions of your  pronouns.
translation: Tell me now, William, how to decline pronouns.

original: Forsooth, I have forgot.
translation: Actually, I've forgotten.

original: It is qui, quae, quod: if you forget your 'quies,' your 'quaes,' and your 'quods,' you must be preeches. Go your ways, and play; go.
He is a better scholar than I thought he was.
translation: He's a better scholar than I thought he was.

original: He is a good sprag memory. Farewell, Mistress Page.
translation: He has a good active memory. Goodbye, Mistress Page.

original: Adieu, good Sir Hugh.
translation: Goodbye, good Sir Hugh.

original: Get you home, boy. Come, we stay too long.
translation: Go along home, boy. Come on, we've been hanging around too long.

original: Mistress Ford, your sorrow hath eaten up my   sufferance.
translation: Mistress Ford, your sorrow has made the memory of my sufferings disappear.

original: I see you are obsequious in your love,   and I profess requital to a hair's breadth;
translation: I see that you are devoted to me, and I tell you, I feel exactly the same way.

original: not   only, Mistress Ford, in the simple   office of love, but in all the accoutrement,   complement and ceremony of it.
translation: I don't just love you, I also offer you all the trappings, compliments, and gestures that demonstrate love.

original: But are you   sure of your husband now?
translation: But are you sure that your husband's away?

original: He's a-birding, sweet Sir John.
translation: He's hunting birds, sweet Sir John.

original: What, ho, gossip Ford! what, ho!
translation: Hey there, my friend Ford! Hey there!

original: Step into the chamber, Sir John.
translation: Go into the room, Sir John.

original: How now, sweetheart! who's at home besides yourself?
translation: Hello there, my dear! Who's at home besides you?

original: Why, none but mine own people.
translation: Why, no one but my servants.

original: Indeed!
translation: Really!

original: No, certainly. @     Speak louder.
translation: Yes, really. Speak louder.

original: Truly, I am so glad you have nobody here.
translation: Really, I'm glad you have no one else here.

original: Why?
translation: Why?

original: Why, woman, your husband is in his old lunes again:   he so takes on yonder with my husband; so rails   against all married mankind;
translation: Why, woman, your husband is going crazy again. He's raving to my husband. He rants about all married people.

original: I am glad the fat knight is not here.
translation: I'm glad the fat knight isn't here.

original: Why, does he talk of him?
translation: Why, does he talk about him?

original: Of none but him; and swears he was carried out, the   last time he searched for him, in a basket;
translation: He talks about nothing but him, and he swears the fat knight was carried out of the house in a basket the last time he looked for him.

original: protests   to my husband he is now here, and hath drawn him and   the rest of their company from their sport, to make   another experiment of his suspicion:
translation: He tells my husband that the knight is here now, and he's pulled my husband and the rest of their friends away from the hunting to try and prove again that his suspicions are true.

original: but I am glad   the knight is not here; now he shall see his own  foolery.
translation: But I'm glad the knight isn't here now. Now your husband will see how foolish he is.

original: How near is he, Mistress Page?
translation: How close is he, Mistress Page?

original: Hard by; at street end; he will be here anon.
translation: Very close, he's at the end of the street. He'll be here soon.

original: I am undone! The knight is here.
translation: I'm ruined! The knight is here.

original: Why then you are utterly shamed, and he's but a dead man. What a woman are you!—Away with him, away with him! better shame than murder.
translation: Why, then, you're completely ruined, and the knight is a dead man. What kind of woman are you! Get him out of here, get him out of here! It's better that you be shamed than that he be murdered.

original: Which way should be go? how should I bestow him? Shall I put him into the basket again?
translation: How can I get him out of here? How can I get rid of him? Should I put him into the basket again?

original: No, I'll come no more i' the basket. May I not go out ere he come?
translation: No, I'm not getting into the basket again. Can't I leave before he gets here?

original: Alas, three of Master Ford's brothers watch the door with pistols, that none shall issue out; otherwise you might slip away ere he came. But what make you  here?
translation: Unfortunately, three of Master Ford's brothers are guarding the door with pistols, so that no one can leave, otherwise you could have snuck out before he got here. But what are you doing here?

original: What shall I do? I'll creep up into the chimney.
translation: What will I do? I'll sneak up the chimney.

original: There they always use to discharge their birding-pieces. Creep into the kiln-hole.
translation: They always shoot their hunting guns up the chimney to clear them out. Sneak into the entrance to the oven.

original: Where is it?
translation: Where is it?

original: He will seek there, on my word.
translation: He'll look there, I'm telling you.

original: Neither press,   coffer, chest, trunk, well, vault, but he hath an   abstract for the remembrance of such places, and   goes to them by his note:
translation: He has a system for keeping track of every cupboard, box, chest, trunk, hole, and vault, and he goes through them according to his system.

original: there is no hiding you in the house.
translation: We can't hide you in the house.

original: I'll go out then.
translation: I'll leave then.

original: If you go out in your own semblance, you die, Sir John. Unless you go out disguised—
translation: If you go out looking like yourself, you'll be killed, Sir John. Unless you leave in disguise—

original: How might we disguise him?
translation: How can we disguise him?

original: Alas the day, I know not! There is no woman's gown big enough for him otherwise he might put on a hat, a muffler and a kerchief, and so escape.
translation: Oh dear, I don't know! We don't have a woman's dress big enough for him, otherwise he could put on a hat, and a scarf over his face, and a kerchief, and escape in disguise.

original: Good hearts, devise something: any extremity rather than a mischief.
translation: Dear ladies, think of something. Anything at all would be better than a disaster.

original: My maid's aunt, the fat woman of Brentford, has a gown above.
translation: My maid's aunt, the fat woman who lives in Brentford, has a dress upstairs.

original: On my word, it will serve him; she's as big as he is: and there's her thrummed hat and her muffler too. Run up, Sir John.
translation: I'm telling you, that will work. She's as big as he is, and her fringed hat and her muffler are there too. Run upstairs, Sir John.

original: Go, go, sweet Sir John: Mistress Page and I will look some linen for your head.
translation: Go, go, sweet Sir John. Mistress Page and I will look for some linen to cover your head.

original: Quick, quick! we'll come dress you straight: put on the gown the while.
translation: Quick, quick! We'll come dress you right away. Put on the dress in the meantime.

original: I would my husband would meet him in this shape:
translation: I hope my husband meets him when he's dressed like this.

original: he   cannot abide the old woman of Brentford; he swears   she's a witch; forbade her my house and hath   threatened to beat her.
translation: He can't stand the old woman from Brentford. He swears she's a  witch , he said she's not allowed to come to the house, and he's threatened to beat her up.

original: Heaven guide him to thy husband's cudgel, and the devil guide his cudgel afterwards!
But is my husband coming?
translation: But is my husband coming?

original: Ah, in good sadness, is he; and talks of the basket too, howsoever he hath had intelligence.
translation: Seriously, he is, and he talks about the basket too. I don't know how he found out about that.

original: We'll try that; for I'll appoint my men to carry the basket again, to meet him at the door with it, as they did last time.
translation: We'll test him. I'll tell my servants to carry the basket again and run into him outside the door with it, like they did last time.

original: Nay, but he'll be here presently: let's go dress him like the witch of Brentford.
translation: No, he'll be here right away. Let's go dress Falstaff like the witch from Brentford.

original: I'll first direct my men what they shall do with the basket. Go up; I'll bring linen for him straight.
translation: First I'll tell my men what to do with the basket. Go up, I'll bring linen for him right away.

original: Hang him, dishonest varlet! we cannot misuse him  enough.   We'll leave a proof, by that which we will do,   Wives may be merry, and yet honest too:
translation: To hell with him, that dishonest scoundrel! We can't abuse him too much. We'll prove by our actions that wives can be  merry and honest  at the same time.

original: We do not act that often jest and laugh;   'Tis old, but true, Still swine eat all the draff.
translation: The people who joke and laugh aren't the people who go on to behave dishonestly. It's an old saying, but it's true, " Still waters run deep. "

original: Go, sirs, take the basket again on your shoulders: your master is hard at door; if he bid you set it down, obey him: quickly, dispatch.
translation: Go, young men, take the basket on your shoulders again. Your master is right outside the door. If he tells you to, obey him and put the basket down. Quickly, get going.

original: Come, come, take it up.
translation: Come on, come on, pick it up.

original: Pray heaven it be not full of knight again.
translation: I hope it doesn't have a knight in it this time.

original: I hope not; I had as lief bear so much lead.
translation: I hope not. I'd rather carry a basket full of lead.

original: Ay, but if it prove true, Master Page, have you any   way then to unfool me again?
translation: Yes, but if it turns out to be true, Master Page, and he has made a fool out of me, do you have any way to fix that?

original: Set down the basket,   villain! Somebody call my wife. Youth in a basket!   O you panderly rascals! there's a knot, a ging, a   pack, a conspiracy against me: now shall the devil   be shamed.
translation: Put down the basket, you lowlife! Somebody call my wife. What a lucky lover! Oh you  pandering  rascals! There's a group, a gang, a pack, a plot against me—now the devil will be shamed.

original: What, wife, I say! Come, come forth!   Behold what honest clothes you send forth to bleaching!
translation: Hey there, wife, I'm talking to you! Come out, come out! Let's see what innocent clothes you were sending to the laundry!

original: Why, this passes, Master Ford; you are not to go loose any longer; you must be pinioned.
translation: Why, this goes beyond all the limits of acceptable behavior, Master Ford. You can't be allowed to run around loose any longer, you should be put in a straitjacket.

original: Why, this is lunatics! this is mad as a mad dog!
translation: Why, this is crazy! He's as mad as a mad dog!

original: Indeed, Master Ford, this is not well, indeed.
translation: Really, Master Ford, this isn't acceptable, it really isn't.

original: So say I too, sir.
translation: I agree, sir, it's not.

original: Come hither, Mistress Ford; Mistress Ford the honest woman, the modest wife, the virtuous creature, that hath the jealous fool to her husband! I suspect without cause, mistress, do I?
translation: Come here, Mistress Ford. Mistress Ford the honest wife, the modest wife, the virtuous person, whose husband is a jealous fool! I'm suspicious for no good reason, mistress, am I?

original: Heaven be my witness you do, if you suspect me in any dishonesty.
translation: I swear to God that you are, if you suspect that I'm unfaithful.

original: Well said, brazen-face! hold it out. Come forth,  sirrah!
translation: Well said, you brazen women, you stick to your story! Come out, sir!

original: This passes!
translation: This goes beyond all limits of good behavior!

original: Are you not ashamed? let the clothes alone.
translation: Aren't you ashamed of yourself? Leave the clothes alone.

original: I shall find you anon.
translation: I'll find you soon.

original: 'Tis unreasonable! Will you take up your wife's clothes? Come away.
translation: This is unreasonable! Will you go through your wife's clothes? Cut it out.

original: Empty the basket, I say!
translation: I demand you empty the basket!

original: Why, man, why?
translation: Why, man, why?

original: Master Page, as I am a man, there was one conveyed   out of my house yesterday in this basket: why may   not he be there again?
translation: Master Page, as sure as I'm a man, I'm sure that someone was carried out of my house yesterday in this basket. Why shouldn't he be in there again?

original: In my house I am sure he is:   my intelligence is true; my jealousy is reasonable.   Pluck me out all the linen.
translation: I know that he's in my house, my information is accurate. It's reasonable of me to be jealous. Pull out all the linen.

original: If you find a man there, he shall die a flea's death.
translation: Anyone hiding in there must be really tiny.

original: Here's no man.
translation: There's no one in here.

original: By my fidelity, this is not well, Master Ford; this wrongs you.
translation: By my faith, this isn't acceptable, Master Ford. Your behavior reflects very badly on you.

original: Master Ford, you must pray, and not follow the imaginations of your own heart: this is jealousies.
translation: Master Ford, you should pray and ignore the fantasies in your brain. This is just jealousy.

original: Well, he's not here I seek for.
translation: Well, the person I'm looking for isn't here.

original: No, nor nowhere else but in your brain.
translation: No, and he's not anywhere else except in your brain.

original: Help to search my house this one time. If I find   not what I seek, show no colour for my extremity; let   me for ever be your table-sport;
translation: Help me search the house one more time. If I don't find what I'm looking for, if I don't give you any evidence for why I should be so passionately jealous, then let me be a laughing-stock for you forever.

original: let them say of   me, 'As jealous as Ford, that searched a hollow   walnut for his wife's leman.' Satisfy me once more;   once more search with me.
translation: Let them say things like, "Since he was as jealous as Ford, that looked for his wife's lover in a  hollow walnut."  Bear with me one more time, search the house with me one more time.

original: What, ho, Mistress Page! come you and the old woman down; my husband will come into the chamber.
translation: Hey there, Mistress Page! You and the old woman should come downstairs, my husband is coming into the bedroom.

original: Old woman! what old woman's that?
translation: Old woman! Who is that old woman?

original: Nay, it is my maid's aunt of Brentford.
translation: It's my maid's aunt from Brentford.

original: A witch, a quean, an old cozening quean! Have I not   forbid her my house? She comes of errands, does   she?
translation: A witch, a  hussy , an old cheating hussy! Haven't I forbid her to come into my house? She comes on an errand, does she?

original: We are simple men; we do not know what's   brought to pass under the profession of   fortune-telling.
translation: We're just foolish men, we don't know what women get up to when they pretend to be telling fortunes.

original: She works by charms, by spells,   by the figure, and such daubery as this is, beyond   our element we know nothing. Come down, you witch,   you hag, you; come down, I say!
translation: She uses charms, spells, voodoo dolls, and other tricks that we can't understand and don't know anything about. Come downstairs, you witch, you hag, you. Come downstairs, I say!

original: Nay, good, sweet husband! Good gentlemen, let him not strike the old woman.
translation: No, good, sweet husband! Good gentlemen, don't let him hit the old woman.

original: Come, Mother Prat; come, give me your hand.
translation: Come on, Mother Prat.  Come, give me your hand.

original: I'll prat her.
Out of my door, you witch, you hag, you baggage, you polecat, you runyon! out, out! I'll conjure you, I'll fortune-tell you.
translation: Get out the door, you witch, you hag, you old bag, you hussy, you lying old woman! Out, out! I'll cast spells on you, I'll tell your fortune.

original: Are you not ashamed? I think you have killed the poor woman.
translation: Aren't you ashamed of yourself? I think you have killed the old woman.

original: Nay, he will do it. 'Tis a goodly credit for you.
translation: No, he's going to kill her.  Well, this certainly makes you look good!

original: Hang her, witch!
translation: To hell with this witch!

original: By the yea and no, I think the 'oman is a witch indeed: I like not when a 'oman has a great peard; I spy a great peard under his muffler.
Will you follow, gentlemen? I beseech you, follow; see but the issue of my jealousy: if I cry out thus upon no trail, never trust me when I open again.
translation: Will you come with me, gentlemen? I ask you, please come with me. See what the outcome of my jealousy is. If it turns out that there's no reason for me to be jealous, never listen to me again.

original: Let's obey his humour a little further: come, gentlemen.
translation: Let's humor him a little longer. Come on, gentlemen.

original: Trust me, he beat him most pitifully.
translation: Good lord, it was pitiful how much he beat him up.

original: Nay, by the mass, that he did not; he beat him most unpitifully, methought.
translation: No, I swear, it wasn't. He didn't have any pity, in my opinion.

original: I'll have the cudgel hallowed and hung o'er the altar; it hath done meritorious service.
What think you? may we, with the warrant of womanhood and the witness of a good conscience, pursue him with any further revenge?
The spirit of wantonness is, sure, scared out of   him:
translation: I'm sure that his lust has been driven out of him by now.

original: if the devil have him not in fee-simple, with   fine and recovery, he will never, I think, in the   way of waste, attempt us again.
translation: Unless the devil has completely possessed him, he won't ever try to  ruin  us again.

original: Shall we tell our husbands how we have served him?
translation: Should we tell our husbands about the tricks we played on him?

original: Yes, by all means; if it be but to scrape the   figures out of your husband's brains.
translation: Yes, by all means—at the very least, to get rid of your husband's jealous suspicions.

original: If they can   find in their hearts the poor unvirtuous fat knight   shall be any further afflicted, we two will still be   the ministers.
translation: If they want to torment the poor badly-behaved fat knight any more, we'll still help them do it.

original: I'll warrant they'll have him publicly shamed: and methinks there would be no period to the jest, should he not be publicly shamed.
translation: I bet they'll want him humiliated in public, and I think there wouldn't be a fitting conclusion to this plot unless he were publicly humiliated.

original: Come, to the forge with it then; shape it: I would not have things cool.
Sir, the Germans desire to have three of your horses: the duke himself will be to-morrow at court, and they are going to meet him.
translation: Sir, the Germans would like to use three of your horses. The duke will be at court tomorrow, and they're going there to see him.

original: What duke should that be comes so secretly? I hear not of him in the court. Let me speak with the gentlemen: they speak English?
translation: Who is this duke who's coming so secretly? I didn't hear anything about him at court. Let me speak with the gentlemen. Do they speak English?

original: Ay, sir; I'll call them to you.
translation: Yes, sir. I'll call them in to see you.

original: They shall have my horses; but I'll make them pay;   I'll sauce them:
translation: They can have my horses, but I'll make them pay, I'll make them pay a lot.

original: they have had my house a week at   command; I have turned away my other guests: they   must come off; I'll sauce them. Come.
translation: They've taken over my house for the last week so that I had to turn away other guests. They need to pay up—I'll make them pay a lot. Let's go.

original: 'Tis one of the best discretions of a 'oman as ever I did look upon.
translation: This is one of the cleverest plots that I've ever known a woman to come up with.

original: And did he send you both these letters at an instant?
translation: And he sent you both those letters at the same time?

original: Within a quarter of an hour.
translation: Within fifteen minutes of each other.

original: Pardon me, wife. Henceforth do what thou wilt;   I rather will suspect the sun with cold   Than thee with wantonness:
translation: Forgive me, wife. From now on, do what you like. I'll sooner suspect that the sun is cold than suspect that you are unfaithful.

original: now doth thy honour stand   In him that was of late an heretic,   As firm as faith.
translation: I used to  distrust  you, but now I trust you completely.

original: 'Tis well, 'tis well; no more:   Be not as extreme in submission   As in offence.
translation: That's enough, that's enough, no more. Don't go overboard in asking forgiveness from your wife the same way you went overboard in offending her.

original: But let our plot go forward: let our wives   Yet once again, to make us public sport,   Appoint a meeting with this old fat fellow,   Where we may take him and disgrace him for it.
translation: But let's put our plan into action. For a good joke in front of the whole town, let's have our wives make another appointment to meet with this old fat man, so we can catch him and disgrace him.

original: There is no better way than that they spoke of.
translation: There's no better plan than the one they described to us.

original: How? to send him word they'll meet him in the park at midnight? Fie, fie! he'll never come.
translation: What? Tell him him they'll meet him in the park at midnight? No, no! He'll never come.

original: You say he has been thrown in the rivers and has   been grievously peaten as an old 'oman:
translation: You said he's been thrown into the river and beaten terribly when he was dressed as an old women.

original: methinks   there should be terrors in him that he should not   come; methinks his flesh is punished, he shall have   no desires.
translation: I think he'll be so traumatized by now that he won't come. I think his body has suffered so much that he can't have any more sexual desire left in him.

original: So think I too.
translation: I agree.

original: Devise but how you'll use him when he comes, And let us two devise to bring him thither.
translation: Just figure out what you'll do to him when he comes, and let the two of us figure out how to get him there.

original: There is an old tale goes that Herne the hunter,   Sometime a keeper here in Windsor forest,   Doth all the winter-time, at still midnight,   Walk round about an oak,
translation: There's an old story that  Herne the hunter , who used to be a gamekeeper here in Windsor forest, walks around an oak at the quiet hour of midnight all winter.

original: with great ragg'd horns;   And there he blasts the tree and takes the cattle   And makes milch-kine yield blood and shakes a chain   In a most hideous and dreadful manner:
translation: He has big jagged horns and he strikes the trees with disease and casts spells on the cattle and makes the dairy cows give blood instead of milk and shakes a chain in the most terrible and frightening way.

original: You have heard of such a spirit, and well you know   The superstitious idle-headed eld   Received and did deliver to our age   This tale of Herne the hunter for a truth.
translation: You've heard stories about a spirit like that, and you know very well that superstitious, foolish people in the old days heard this story of Herne the hunter and passed it on to us as a true fact.

original: Why, yet there want not many that do fear In deep of night to walk by this Herne's oak: But what of this?
translation: Why, there are still plenty of people who are afraid to walk by Herne's oak late at night. But what does that matter?

original: Marry, this is our device; That Falstaff at that oak shall meet with us.
Well, let it not be doubted but he'll come: And in this shape when you have brought him thither, What shall be done with him? what is your plot?
translation: Well, let's assume he'll come. And when you've brought Falstaff to the oak disguised as Herne the hunter, what will we do to him? What's your idea?

original: That likewise have we thought upon, and thus:   Nan Page my daughter and my little son   And three or four more of their growth we'll dress   Like urchins, ouphes and fairies, green and white,   With rounds of waxen tapers on their heads,   And rattles in their hands:
translation: We've thought about that too, and here's our idea. We'll get my daughter Nan Page and my young son and three or four more children their age, and we'll dress them up in green and white like goblins, elvish children, and elves, with crowns of wax candles on their heads, and rattles in their hands.

original: upon a sudden,   As Falstaff, she and I, are newly met,   Let them from forth a sawpit rush at once   With some diffused song:
translation: And right when Mistress Ford and I meet Falstaff, they should immediately rush out of a pit singing some incoherent song.

original: upon their sight,   We two in great amazedness will fly:   Then let them all encircle him about   And, fairy-like, to-pinch the unclean knight,
translation: When we see them, we'll run away in fright, and then they should circle the dirty old knight and pinch him the way fairies are supposed to do,

original: And ask him why, that hour of fairy revel,   In their so sacred paths he dares to tread   In shape profane.
translation: and ask him why he dares to intrude his foul body into their sacred paths at the hour when fairies are out  dancing .

original: And till he tell the truth, Let the supposed fairies pinch him sound And burn him with their tapers.
translation: And until he tells the truth, the so-called fairies should pinch him hard and burn him with their candles.

original: The truth being known, We'll all present ourselves, dis-horn the spirit, And mock him home to Windsor.
translation: Then when he's confessed the truth, we'll all reveal ourselves, take off his horns, and make fun of him the whole way home to Windsor.

original: The children must Be practised well to this, or they'll ne'er do't.
translation: The children should practice this, or they'll never get it right.

original: I will teach the children their behaviors; and I will be like a jack-an-apes also, to burn the knight with my taber.
translation: I'll teach the children what to do, and I'll dress up like a mischievous monkey, so I can burn the knight with my candle.

original: That will be excellent. I'll go and buy them vizards.
translation: That's an excellent idea. I'll go and buy them masks.

original: My Nan shall be the queen of all the fairies, Finely attired in a robe of white.
translation: My Anne will be the queen of the fairies, finely dressed in a white gown.

original: That silk will I go buy.
translation: I'll go buy the silk for that.

original: And in that time Shall Master Slender steal my Nan away And marry her at Eton. Go send to Falstaff straight.
translation: And while all this is going on, Master Slender will sneak away with my Nan and marry her at Eton.  Go send a message to Falstaff right away.

original: Nay I'll to him again in name of Brook He'll tell me all his purpose: sure, he'll come.
translation: No, I'll go see him disguised as Master Brook. He'll tell me all about his plans. I'm sure of it, he'll come.

original: Fear not you that. Go get us properties And tricking for our fairies.
translation: Don't worry about that. Go get us the props and costumes for our fairies.

original: Let us about it: it is admirable pleasures and fery honest knaveries.
translation: Let's get going. It's an admirable joke and a very well-intentioned trick.

original: Go, Mistress Ford, Send quickly to Sir John, to know his mind.
translation: Go, Mistress Ford, send a message to Sir John to find out what he's thinking.

original: I'll to the doctor: he hath my good will,   And none but he, to marry with Nan Page.
translation: I'll go see the doctor. He has my support, and I won't let anyone but him marry Nan Page.

original: That Slender, though well landed, is an idiot;   And he my husband best of all affects.
translation: That man Slender is an idiot, despite the fact that he has a lot of land, and he's the one my husband favors most.

original: The doctor is well money'd, and his friends   Potent at court: he, none but he, shall have her,   Though twenty thousand worthier come to crave her.
translation: The doctor also has a lot of money and powerful friends at court. He, no one but he, will have her, even if twenty thousand worthier people came to ask for her.

original: What wouldst thou have, boor? what: thick-skin? speak, breathe, discuss; brief, short, quick, snap.
translation: What do you want, you buffoon? What is it, you stupid man? Speak, breathe, talk. Be brief, short, quick, snappy.

original: Marry, sir, I come to speak with Sir John Falstaff from Master Slender.
translation: Well, sir, I have a message for Sir John Falstaff from Master Slender.

original: There's his chamber, his house, his castle, his   standing-bed and truckle-bed;
translation: There's his bedroom, his house, his castle, his full-size bed and his camp bed.

original: 'tis painted about   with the story of the Prodigal, fresh and new.
translation: It's freshly painted with the story of the  Prodigal Son.

original: Go   knock and call; hell speak like an Anthropophaginian   unto thee: knock, I say.
translation: Go knock on the door and call him. He'll talk to you like a  cannibal . Knock, I'm telling you.

original: There's an old woman, a fat woman, gone up into his   chamber:
translation: There's an old woman, a fat woman, who just went into his room.

original: I'll be so bold as stay, sir, till she come   down; I come to speak with her, indeed.
translation: I'll invite myself to stay, if I may, until she comes downstairs. I'd like to speak with her, in fact.

original: Ha! a fat woman! the knight may be robbed: I'll   call. Bully knight! bully Sir John! speak from   thy lungs military: art thou there?
translation: Ha! A fat woman! The knight might get robbed. I'll call him. My fine knight! My bold Sir John! Speak with your soldier's lungs: are you there?

original: it is thine   host, thine Ephesian, calls.
translation: It's your host, your  drinking companion , calling you.

original: How now, mine host!
translation: How are you, my host?

original: Here's a Bohemian-Tartar tarries the coming down of   thy fat woman. Let her descend, bully, let her   descend;
translation: There's a vagabond gypsy here waiting for the fat woman to come downstairs. Let her come down, my fine fellow, let her come down.

original: my chambers are honourable: fie! privacy?   fie!
translation: I keep a respectable inn—shame on your secret intrigues!

original: There was, mine host, an old fat woman even now with me; but she's gone.
translation: There was an old fat woman with me just now, my host, but she's gone.

original: Pray you, sir, was't not the wise woman of Brentford?
Ay, marry, was it, mussel-shell: what would you with  her?
translation: Yes, in fact, it was, you empty-headed young man. What did you want with her?

original: My master, sir, Master Slender, sent to her, seeing   her go through the streets, to know, sir, whether   one Nym, sir,
translation: My master, sir, Master Slender, saw her going through the streets and he wanted to ask her whether a man named Nym,

original: that beguiled him of a chain, had the   chain or no.
translation: who stole a chain from him, has the chain or not.

original: I spake with the old woman about it.
translation: I talked to the old woman about that.

original: And what says she, I pray, sir?
translation: And what did she say, sir?

original: Marry, she says that the very same man that beguiled Master Slender of his chain cozened him of it.
translation: Well, she says the same man that stole Master Slender's chain also cheated him out of it.

original: I would I could have spoken with the woman herself; I had other things to have spoken with her too from him.
translation: I wish I could have spoken with the woman myself. There were other things I would have liked to ask her.

original: What are they? let us know.
translation: Like what? Tell me.

original: Ay, come; quick.
translation: Yes, come on, quickly.

original: I may not conceal them, sir.
Conceal them, or thou diest.
translation: Conceal them, or die.

original: Why, sir, they were nothing but about Mistress Anne Page; to know if it were my master's fortune to have her or no.
translation: Well, sir, it wasn't about anything except Mistress Anne Page. I wanted to ask if my master will end up marrying her or not.

original: 'Tis, 'tis his fortune.
translation: Yes, yes, he will.

original: What, sir?
translation: He will what, sir?

original: To have her, or no. Go; say the woman told me so.
translation: He will either marry her or not. Go, tell him the woman told me so.

original: May I be bold to say so, sir?
translation: May I be so bold as to tell him that, sir?

original: Ay, sir; like who more bold.
translation: Yes, sir. No one could be bolder than you.

original: I thank your worship: I shall make my master glad with these tidings.
translation: Thank you, sir. I'll make my master happy with this good news.

original: Thou art clerkly, thou art clerkly, Sir John. Was there a wise woman with thee?
translation: You are wise, you are wise, Sir John. Was there a witch with you?

original: Ay, that there was, mine host;
translation: Yes, there was, my host.

original: one that hath taught   me more wit than ever I learned before in my life;   and I paid nothing for it neither, but was paid for   my learning.
translation: She taught me more than I had ever learned before in my life, and I didn't pay anything for this knowledge either, but instead I got a  reward  for learning.

original: Out, alas, sir! cozenage, mere cozenage!
translation: Oh no, sir! Cheating, flat-out cheating!

original: Where be my horses? speak well of them, varletto.
translation: Where are my horses? Tell me some good news about them, you scoundrel.

original: Run away with the cozeners;
translation: They ran away with the cheaters.

original: for so soon as I came   beyond Eton, they threw me off from behind one of   them, in a slough of mire; and set spurs and away,   like three German devils, three Doctor Faustuses.
translation: As soon as I passed Eton, they threw me off the horse into a swamp of mud, and they spurred the horses to ride away like three German devils, like three  Doctor Faustuses.

original: They are gone but to meet the duke, villain: do not say they be fled; Germans are honest men.
translation: They've only gone to meet the duke, scoundrel, don't say they fled. Germans are honest people.

original: Where is mine host?
translation: Where is the host?

original: What is the matter, sir?
translation: What's the matter, sir?

original: Have a care of your entertainments: there is a   friend of mine come to town tells me there is three   cozen-germans that has cozened all the hosts of   Readins, of Maidenhead, of Colebrook, of horses and   money.
translation: Be careful about your guests. A friend of mine who just arrived in town told me about three cheating Germans who have cheated all the hosts out of horses and money, in  Readins, Maidenhead, and Colebrook .

original: I tell you for good will, look you: you   are wise and full of gibes and vlouting-stocks, and   'tis not convenient you should be cozened. Fare you  well.
translation: I'm looking out for you, you know. You're smart and full of fun and jokes, and it isn't right for you to be cheated. Take care.

original: Vere is mine host de Jarteer?
translation: Where is the host of the Garter?

original: Here, master doctor, in perplexity and doubtful  dilemma.
translation: Here, Master Doctor, confused and in a messy situation.

original: I cannot tell vat is dat: but it is tell-a me dat   you make grand preparation for a duke de Jamany:
translation: I'm not sure what you mean by that, but someone told me that you were making big preparations to welcome a German duke.

original: by   my trot, dere is no duke dat the court is know to   come. I tell you for good vill: adieu.
translation: I know for a fact that the court isn't expecting any duke. I'm telling you this to help you out. Goodbye.

original: Hue and cry, villain, go! Assist me, knight. I am undone! Fly, run, hue and cry, villain! I am undone!
translation: Raise the alarm, scoundrel, go! Help me, knight, I'm ruined! Run, run, raise the alarm, scoundrel! I'm ruined!

original: I would all the world might be cozened; for I have   been cozened and beaten too.
translation: I wish everyone would be tricked, since I've been tricked and beaten up also.

original: If it should come to   the ear of the court, how I have been transformed   and how my transformation hath been washed and   cudgelled, they would melt me out of my fat drop by   drop and liquor fishermen's boots with me;
translation: If anyone at court heard how I disguised myself  twice , and how I was dunked in the river and beaten with a stick while I was disguised, they would laugh at me until my fat melted out of me like boot-grease.

original: I warrant   they would whip me with their fine wits till I were   as crest-fallen as a dried pear.
translation: I bet they would make fun of me with their wonderful wit until I shriveled up like a dried pear.

original: I never prospered   since I forswore myself at primero. Well, if my   wind were but long enough to say my prayers, I would  repent.
translation: I've never done well in life since I started cheating at cards. Well, if I had enough breath to pray, I would apologize to God for the bad things I've done.

original: Now, whence come you?
translation: Now, where did you come from?

original: From the two parties, forsooth.
translation: From the two women, in fact.

original: The devil take one party and his dam the other! and   so they shall be both bestowed.
translation: Let them both go to hell! And then they'll both get what they deserve.

original: I have suffered more   for their sakes, more than the villanous inconstancy   of man's disposition is able to bear.
translation: I've suffered more because of them than a man's unstable nature is able to put up with.

original: Mistress Ford, good heart,   is beaten black and blue, that you cannot see a   white spot about her.
translation: Mistress Ford, that dear woman, was beaten black and blue so that you can't see a spot of white skin on her.

original: What tellest thou me of black and blue? I was   beaten myself into all the colours of the rainbow;   and I was like to be apprehended for the witch of   Brentford:
translation: Why are you talking to me about black and blue? I was beaten until I was all the colors of the rainbow, and I was almost arrested for being the witch of Brentford.

original: but that my admirable dexterity of wit,   my counterfeiting the action of an old woman,   delivered me, the knave constable had set me i' the   stocks, i' the common stocks, for a witch.
translation: If it hadn't been for my admirably quick wit, and my ability to imitate the behavior of an old woman, the rascally policeman would have put me in the  stocks , the public stocks, for being a witch.

original: Sir, let me speak with you in your chamber: you   shall hear how things go; and, I warrant, to your   content.
translation: Sir, let me talk to you in your room. I'll tell you how things are going, and I bet you'll like what you hear.

original: Here is a letter will say somewhat. Good   hearts, what ado here is to bring you together!   Sure, one of you does not serve heaven well, that   you are so crossed.
translation: Here's a letter that will explain things. My dears, it's so much trouble to get you together! I'm sure that one of you must be a great sinner, since God keeps punishing you.

original: Come up into my chamber.
translation: Come up to my room.

original: Master Fenton, talk not to me; my mind is heavy: I will give over all.
translation: Master Fenton, don't talk to me, I'm feeling very low. I'm going to give up on everything.

original: Yet hear me speak. Assist me in my purpose, And, as I am a gentleman, I'll give thee A hundred pound in gold more than your loss.
translation: Just listen to me. Help me carry out my plan, and I promise, on my word as a gentleman, that I'll give you a hundred pounds more than you lost, in gold.

original: I will hear you, Master Fenton; and I will at the least keep your counsel.
translation: I'll listen to you, Master Fenton. At the very least I'll keep what you say a secret.

original: From time to time I have acquainted you   With the dear love I bear to fair Anne Page;   Who mutually hath answer'd my affection,   So far forth as herself might be her chooser,   Even to my wish:
translation: From time to time I've told you about how much I love Anne Page. She loves me in return, insofar as she can choose her own husband, just the way I would want.

original: I have a letter from her   Of such contents as you will wonder at;   The mirth whereof so larded with my matter,   That neither singly can be manifested,   Without the show of both;
translation: I've received a letter from her that said some things that will surprise you. The humorous material in it was so mixed up with the serious material that you couldn't look at one without looking at the other.

original: fat Falstaff   Hath a great scene: the image of the jest   I'll show you here at large. Hark, good mine host.
translation: There's a description of a big scene involving fat Falstaff— I'll show you the whole description of the joke. Pay attention, my good host.

original: To-night at Herne's oak, just 'twixt twelve and one,   Must my sweet Nan present the Fairy Queen;   The purpose why, is here: in which disguise,   While other jests are something rank on foot,   Her father hath commanded her to slip   Away with Slender and with him at Eton   Immediately to marry: she hath consented:
translation: Tonight at Herne's oak, just between midnight and one o'clock, my sweet Nan is supposed to dress up as the Fairy Queen—she explains why here. While she's disguised, and while lots of other pranks are happening at the same time, her father has ordered her to sneak away with Slender and go with him to Eton to be married immediately. She agreed to this.

original: Now, sir,   Her mother, ever strong against that match   And firm for Doctor Caius, hath appointed   That he shall likewise shuffle her away,   While other sports are tasking of their minds,   And at the deanery, where a priest attends,   Straight marry her: to this her mother's plot   She seemingly obedient likewise hath   Made promise to the doctor.
translation: Now, sir, her mother, who strongly opposes Anne's marriage to Slender and is determined that she will marry Doctor Caius, has ordered her to sneak away in the same way with Doctor Caius while everyone is distracted, and to go to the deanery where a priest will be waiting to marry them. Anne also agreed to her mother's plot and promised to marry the doctor.

original: Now, thus it rests:   Her father means she shall be all in white,   And in that habit, when Slender sees his time   To take her by the hand and bid her go,   She shall go with him:
translation: Now, here's how things stand. Her father's plan is that she'll be dressed all in white, so Slender will recognize her; when Slender sees an opportunity to take her hand, she'll go with him.

original: her mother hath intended,   The better to denote her to the doctor,   For they must all be mask'd and vizarded,   That quaint in green she shall be loose enrobed,   With ribands pendent, flaring 'bout her head;
translation: Because they will all be wearing masks, her mother also planned a way for the doctor to recognize her: Anne will be elegantly dressed in loose green clothes with hanging ribbons flying around her head.

original: And when the doctor spies his vantage ripe,   To pinch her by the hand, and, on that token,   The maid hath given consent to go with him.
translation: And the doctor, when he spots a good opportunity, is supposed to pinch her hand, and Anne said she will leave with him when she gets that signal.

original: Which means she to deceive, father or mother?
translation: Who is she intending to trick, her father or her mother?

original: Both, my good host, to go along with me:   And here it rests,
translation: Both, my good host, so she can go with me. Here's the plan.

original: that you'll procure the vicar   To stay for me at church 'twixt twelve and one,   And, in the lawful name of marrying,   To give our hearts united ceremony.
translation: You'll get the vicar to wait for me at the church between midnight and one o'clock so he can unite us in legal marriage.

original: Well, husband your device; I'll to the vicar: Bring you the maid, you shall not lack a priest.
translation: Well, execute your plan carefully. I'll go to the vicar. You bring the woman, and I'll make sure you have a priest.

original: So shall I evermore be bound to thee; Besides, I'll make a present recompense.
translation: I will be in your debt forever—and I will also give you a reward immediately.

original: Prithee, no more prattling; go. I'll hold. This is   the third time; I hope good luck lies in odd   numbers.
translation: Please, no more chattering, go. I'll keep the appointment. This is the third time—I hope the third try will turn out to be the lucky one.

original: Away I go. They say there is divinity in   odd numbers, either in nativity, chance, or death.  Away!
translation: Get going. They say there's magical power in odd numbers when it comes to birth, luck, or death. Get going!

original: I'll provide you a chain; and I'll do what I can to get you a pair of horns.
Away, I say; time wears: hold up your head, and mince.
translation: Get going, I say, it's getting late. Hold your head up and strut.

original: How now, Master Brook! Master Brook, the matter   will be known to-night, or never.
translation: Hello there, Master Brook! Master Brook, things will come to a conclusion tonight, or else they never will.

original: Be you in the   Park about midnight, at Herne's oak, and you shall   see wonders.
translation: Be in the Park around midnight, at Herne's oak, and you'll see things that will astonish you.

original: Went you not to her yesterday, sir, as you told me you had appointed?
translation: Didn't you go see her yesterday, sir, like you told me you had planned?

original: I went to her, Master Brook, as you see, like a poor   old man: but I came from her, Master Brook, like a   poor old woman.
translation: I did go to see her, Master Brook, dressed like I am now, like a poor old man, but when I left her, Master Brook, I was dressed like a poor old woman.

original: That same knave Ford, her husband,   hath the finest mad devil of jealousy in him,   Master Brook, that ever governed frenzy. I will tell   you:
translation: That scoundrel Ford, her husband, had the greatest fit of jealousy, Master Brook, that ever drove someone crazy. I'll tell you what happened.

original: he beat me grievously, in the shape of a   woman; for in the shape of man, Master Brook, I fear   not Goliath with a weaver's beam; because I know   also life is a shuttle.
translation: He beat me up terribly while I was disguised as a woman—but when I'm dressed as a man, Master Brook, even the strongest  man  with the largest spear doesn't scare me, for I know that life is short.

original: I am in haste; go along   with me: I'll tell you all, Master Brook. Since I   plucked geese, played truant and whipped top, I knew   not what 'twas to be beaten till lately.
translation: I'm in a hurry, come with me, I'll tell you everything, Master Brook. Since I I was a child playing pranks, skipping school and spinning a top, I have never been beaten like that until now.

original: Follow   me: I'll tell you strange things of this knave   Ford, on whom to-night I will be revenged, and I   will deliver his wife into your hand. Follow.   Strange things in hand, Master Brook! Follow.
translation: Follow me. I'll tell you some extraordinary things about this scoundrel Ford, who I'm going to take revenge on tonight, and I'll get you access to his wife. Follow me. Extraordinary things are about to happen, Master Brook! Follow me.

original: Come, come; we'll couch i' the castle-ditch till we   see the light of our fairies.
translation: Come on, come on. We'll lie in the ditch near the castle until we see the light from our fairies.

original: Remember, son Slender,   my daughter.
translation: Son-in-law Slender, don't forget about my daughter.

original: Ay, forsooth; I have spoke with her and we have a   nay-word how to know one another:
translation: Yes, indeed. I've talked to her and we have a password so we'll recognize each other:

original: I come to her in   white, and cry 'mum;' she cries 'budget;' and by   that we know one another.
translation: she'll be wearing white, I'll come to her and say, "mum," she'll say "budget," and that's how we'll recognize each other.

original: That's good too: but what needs either your 'mum'   or her 'budget?'
translation: That's a good idea, too, but why do you need to say "mum," and why does she need to say "budget"?

original: the white will decipher her well   enough. It hath struck ten o'clock.
translation: You'll recognize her because she'll be wearing white. The clock has struck ten o'clock.

original: The night is dark; light and spirits will become it   well. Heaven prosper our sport!
translation: It's a dark night, a fitting night for candles and fairies. May God give us good luck carrying out our plot!

original: No man means evil   but the devil, and we shall know him by his horns.   Let's away; follow me.
translation: No one intends to do anything evil except the devil, and we'll recognize him by his  horns . Let's go, follow me.

original: Master doctor, my daughter is in green: when you   see your time, take her by the band, away with her   to the deanery, and dispatch it quickly.
translation: Master Doctor, my daughter will be wearing green. When you see a good opportunity, take her by the hand, lead her away to the  dean's house , and get the marriage over with quickly.

original: Go before   into the Park: we two must go together.
translation: Go into the Park ahead of us: the two of us have to go in together.

original: I know vat I have to do. Adieu.
translation: I know what I need to do. Good-bye.

original: Fare you well, sir.
translation: Good luck, sir.

original: My husband will not rejoice so much at the abuse of   Falstaff as he will chafe at the doctor's marrying   my daughter: but 'tis no matter;
translation: My husband won't be as happy at our tricking Falstaff as he'll be upset about the doctor marrying his daughter, but it doesn't matter.

original: better a little   chiding than a great deal of heart-break.
translation: It's better to be scolded a little than to endure a big catastrophe.

original: Where is Nan now and her troop of fairies, and the Welsh devil Hugh?
translation: Where is Nan right now and her group of fairies, and the Sir Hugh, the Welsh devil?

original: They are all couched in a pit hard by Herne's oak,   with obscured lights;
translation: They're all lying in a pit right near Herne's oak, with their candles hidden.

translation: Do I look like a hunter, ha? Do I talk like Herne the hunter? Why, now, Cupid must have a conscience; he's finally making up for the trouble he's caused. Since I'm a genuine wood-spirit, I welcome you to the woods!

translation: Oh no, what was that noise?

translation: What could this be?

translation: y ou  orphans  controlled by destiny, a ttend to your tasks and your jobs.  Crier Hobgoblin, sound the  call  of the fairies.

translation: Elves, listen for your names. Be quiet, you little things.  Cricket, leap to the fireplaces of Windsor:

translation: wherever you find  unraked  fires or unswept hearths, pinch the maids there until they are blue as blueberries.

translation: Our radiant queen hates lazy maids and neglect.

translation: These are fairies—whoever speaks to them dies. I'll close my eyes and lie down and hide. No human must look at them.

translation: Where's Bede?  [A boy steps forward]  Go, and when you find a maid  who says her prayers three times before she goes to bed. S timulate her imagination

translation: s o that she sleeps as soundly as an innocent baby.

translation: Get to work, get to work.  Elves, go through  Windsor Castle , inside and outside.  Sprinkle good luck, elves, in every royal room s o that the castle will stand until the end of time i n a condition that is fitting for the dignity of the place, s o it will be worthy of the owner, and the owner will be worthy of it.

translation: Clean the various  ceremonial pews in Windsor Chapel w ith ointment and cleansing flowers.  Let each lovely seat, coat of arms, each crest, a nd all the  banners of loyalty  be forever blessed!

translation: And, meadow-fairies, be sure to sing each night, i n a ring resembling the  Garter's  circle.  Create a green image  more fresh and fertile than the field itself.

translation: And write " Let evil things happen to the person who thinks evil things ," u sing emerald tufts and purple, blue, and white flowers.  Let there be a garter made of sapphire, pearl, and detailed embroidery b uckled below the knee of each worthy,  loyal  knight.

translation: Fairies use flowers to write their messages.  Go away, scatter—but don't forget that at one o'clock, w e'll do our usual dance  a round the oak of Herne the hunter.

translation: Please, take hands, line up in order, and we'll use twenty glow-worms for our lanterns to guide our dances around the tree.

translation: But wait, I smell a mortal man.

translation: God protect me from that Welsh fairy so he doesn't turn me into a piece of cheese!

translation: You disgusting worm, you were destined for evil things since you were born.

translation: Touch his finger with fire as a test. If he's chaste, the flame will recede and it won't hurt him.

translation: Let's see, will his finger catch fire?

translation: He's corrupt, corrupt, and he has sinful desires!  S urround him, fairies. Sing a scornful song, a nd as you dance, pinch him in time with the music.

translation: [Singing] Down with sinful ideas! Down with lust and indulgence!  Lust is nothing better than a consuming passion, Fueled  by unchaste desire, That begins in the heart and that increases More and more as thoughts stimulate it.

translation: Pinch him, fairies, everyone; Pinch him for his evil deeds; Pinch him, and burn him, and turn him around, Until the candles and starlight and moonlight are gone.

translation: No, don't try to escape. I think we've caught you in the act now. Is being Herne the hunter the only thing that will satisfy you?

translation: Please, come on, let's not keep the joke going any longer. So, good Sir John, what do you think of the Windsor wives now?

translation: Do you see these horns, husband? Don't these handsome  horns  belong more in the forest than in the town?

translation: Now, sir, who's a cuckold now? Master Brook, Falstaff's a scoundrel, a cuckolded scoundrel. Here are his horns, Master Brook.

translation: And, Master Brook, Falstaff hasn't  gotten anything  that belongs to Ford except Ford's laundry basket, stick, and twenty pounds in cash, which needs to be paid back to Master Brook; his horses have been seized as security for the money, Master Brook.

translation: Sir John, we've had bad luck. We were never able to arrange a meeting.

translation: I'll never have you as my lover again, but I'll always think of you as my  deer .

translation: I begin to see that you've made an ass out of me.

original: Ay, and an ox too: both the proofs are extant.
And these are not fairies? I was three or four   times in the thought they were not fairies:
translation: And these aren't fairies? I thought three or four times that they might not be fairies.

translation: And yet my sense of guilt, and the bewilderment of my senses, turned a foolish idea into a firm belief that they were actually fairies, in spite of all rhyme and reason.

translation: See how even a smart man can be made into  laughingstock  when he sets his mind to bad actions!

translation: Sir John Falstaff, serve God and abandon your sexual desires, and then the fairies won't pinch you.

translation: Well said, fairy Hugh.

translation: And I ask you to stop being jealous.

Have I laid my brain in the sun and dried it, that   it wants matter to prevent so gross o'erreaching as   this?
translation: Have I ruined my brain so that I can't even thwart plots as overblown as this one?

translation: Have I been fooled by a Welsh goat? Will I wear a woolen  fool's cap ? I ought to choke on a piece of toasted cheese.

translation: This isn't the way to be better. Your belly is all butter.

translation: "This" and "butter!"  To think that I should live to be mocked by someone who speaks such terrible English!

translation: This is enough to put an end to all lust and late-night sexual encounters throughout the country.

translation: A fat, vain man?

translation: Old, cold, wrinkled, and with gross guts?

translation: And who lies like the devil?

translation: And who is as wicked as his wife?

translation: Well, I'm your object of mockery. You have an advantage over me. I'm defeated, I can't offer any comebacks to this Welshman's taunts.

translation: I've been  unbelievably foolish . Say whatever you like about me.

translation: Well, sir, we'll bring you to Windsor, to a certain Master Brook, whom you've cheated out of money and for whom you were going to arrange a sexual affair.

translation: Still, be cheerful, knight. You'll have a hot restorative drink at my house tonight, and when we get there, you can laugh at my wife, who's laughing at you right now.

original: tell her   Master Slender hath married her daughter.
translation: You can tell her that Master Slender has married her daughter.

translation: Wise men wouldn't be so sure about that. As sure as Anne Page is my daughter, she's Doctor Caius's wife by now.

translation: Hello there! Hey, father Page!

translation: Son, how are you? How are you, son? Have you settled everything?

translation: Settled! I'll let the highest-ranking person in Gloucester know about it. I'd rather be hanged than keep quiet.

translation: Know about what, son?

translation: Do you really need to tell me that? I think I did take the wrong person when I mistook a boy for a girl.

translation: If I had gotten married to him, I wouldn't have slept with him, even though he was wearing women's clothing.

translation: Why, this is because of your own foolishness. Didn't I tell you how to recognize my daughter by her clothes?

translation: I went up to the person in white, and said "mum," and she said "budget," just like Anne and I had arranged to do.

translation: And still, it wasn't Anne, it was a stableboy.

translation: Why, didn't you take the person wearing green?

translation: Yes, by God, and it was a boy. By God, I'll make enough noise to wake up all of Windsor.

translation: This is strange. Who got the right Anne?

translation: I'm worried. Here comes Master Fenton.

translation: Hello there, Master Fenton!

translation: Forgive me, good father! My good mother, forgive me!

translation: Now, young lady, how did it happen that you didn't go with Master Slender?

translation: Why didn't you go with Master Doctor, young lady?

translation: You're confusing her. Listen to what really happened. You would have forced her, in the most shameful way, into a marriage where there was no equality of love between the partners.

translation: The truth is that she and I, who have been engaged a long time, are now joined together so firmly that nothing can separate us.

translation: The sin she committed is a  holy one . And our deception doesn't count as an evil plot, as disobedience, or as lack of dutifulness,

translation: since by deceiving you, she avoided the thousand  godless , cursed hours that a forced marriage would have resulted in.

translation: Don't be bewildered; there's nothing you can do about it. When it comes to love, heaven is in charge of what happens. You can use money to get land, but accident and chance determine who gets a wife.

translation: Well, what can we do? Fenton, may God give you joy! If we can't avoid something, we must embrace it.

translation: Well, I won't complain any further. Master Fenton, may God give you many, many happy days!

translation: Good husband, let's all go home and laugh about these jokes around a big fire, Sir John and everyone.

translation: Let's do that. Sir John, you'll end up keeping the promise that you made to Master Brook, because tonight he will, in fact, sleep with Mistress Ford.

original: Good day, sir.
translation: Hello.

translation: It's good to see you.

translation: It's been a while. How is everything in your world?

original: It wears, sir, as it grows.
translation: Up and down, up and down.

original: Ay, that's well known:   But what particular rarity?
translation: So they say. But how weird is this—have you ever seen anything like it?

translation: Look at how amazing wealth and generosity are, how they can summon all these people to attend to them.

translation: I know this merchant.

original: I know them both; th' other's a jeweller.
translation: I know both of them. The other one is a jeweler.

original: O, 'tis a worthy lord.
Nay, that's most fix'd.
translation: Definitely.

original: A most incomparable man, breathed, as it were, To an untirable and continuate goodness: He passes.
translation: There's no one like him, almost born to be forever generous. He exceeds everyone else.

original: I have a jewel here—
translation: I have a jewel right here—

original: O, pray, let's see't: for the Lord Timon, sir?
translation: Oh please, let's see it. Is it for the Lord Timon?

original: If he will touch the estimate: but, for that—
translation: If he will pay the price. But for that—

original: 'When we for recompense have   praised the vile,
translation: "When we write poetry praising bad things for money,

translation: it ruins the better verse that rightly supports good things."

original: 'Tis a good form.
translation: It's beautiful.

original: And rich: here is a water, look ye.
translation: And expensive from the looks of it. Look at how it shines!

original: You are rapt, sir, in some work, some dedication To the great lord.
translation: You are captivated by some task, writing a poetic dedication to Lord Timon.

original: A thing slipp'd idly from me.   Our poesy is as a gum, which oozes   From whence 'tis nourish'd:
translation: Something slipped my mind. Poetry is like sap that oozes from the tree it gets its nutrients from.

original: the fire i' the flint   Shows not till it be struck; our gentle flame   Provokes itself and like the current flies   Each bound it chafes. What have you there?
translation: The spark that illuminates in the  flint  does not reveal itself until the flint is hit with something, but our gentle flame lights itself up and runs like a current over every surface it touches. What is that right there?

original: A picture, sir. When comes your book forth?
translation: A portrait. When will your book be published?

original: Upon the heels of my presentment, sir. Let's see your piece.
translation: After I have presented my poem to Timon. Let me see your painting.

original: 'Tis a good piece.
translation: It's nice.

original: So 'tis: this comes off well and excellent.
translation: Yes, it looks well made.

original: Indifferent.
translation: It's not bad.

original: Admirable: how this grace   Speaks his own standing!
translation: It is incredible how its beauty reflects the dignity of its  subject ! Look at the intelligence that twinkles in the eye!

original: what a mental power   This eye shoots forth! how big imagination   Moves in this lip! to the dumbness of the gesture   One might interpret.
translation: There is a certain imagination that moves in its lip! Even though the painting is silent I feel like I could understand what the man is saying.

original: It is a pretty mocking of the life. Here is a touch; is't good?
translation: It is a pretty good imitation of life. Here is a nice touch, do you like it?

original: I will say of it, It tutors nature: artificial strife Lives in these touches, livelier than life.
How this lord is follow'd!
translation: Look at all the people following the lord!

original: The senators of Athens: happy man!
translation: They're Senators of Athens. How lucky is he!

original: Look, more!
translation: And more too!

original: You see this confluence, this great flood   of visitors.   I have, in this rough work, shaped out a man,   Whom this beneath world doth embrace and hug   With amplest entertainment:
translation: @ earthly world.

original: my free drift   Halts not particularly, but moves itself   In a wide sea of wax:
translation: I do not mean to represent particular people, but work in generalities as if my  tablet were an entire sea of wax .

original: no levell'd malice   Infects one comma in the course I hold;   But flies an eagle flight, bold and forth on,   Leaving no tract behind.
translation: Personal grudges do not affect even the smallest details of my writing. My creative process flies forth, strong as an eagle in flight, and leaves no trace of its earthly inspirations.

original: How shall I understand you?
I will unbolt to you.   You see how all conditions, how all minds,   As well of glib and slippery creatures as   Of grave and austere quality, tender down   Their services to Lord Timon:
translation: I will unlock the meaning for you. Notice how people of all types and temperaments, whether smooth-talking and self-interested or serious and truthful, offer their services to Lord Timon.

original: his large fortune   Upon his good and gracious nature hanging   Subdues and properties to his love and tendance   All sorts of hearts; yea, from the glass-faced  flatterer   To Apemantus, that few things loves better   Than to abhor himself:
translation: His immense wealth and his kind and gracious nature overwhelm people, and buy him the approval of all sorts of people eager to love and attend him, from the flatterer whose face mirrors the wishes of his counterpart, to  Apemantus , who loves nothing more than hating himself.

original: even he drops down   The knee before him, and returns in peace   Most rich in Timon's nod.
translation: Even he bows down on his knees to Timon, and leaves peacefully after receiving Timon's approval.

original: I saw them speak together.
translation: I did see them speaking to one another.

original: Sir, I have upon a high and pleasant hill   Feign'd Fortune to be throned: the base o' the mount   Is rank'd with all deserts, all kind of natures,   That labour on the bosom of this sphere   To propagate their states:
translation: I have written down here that the goddess  Fortune  is sitting high atop her throne on a beautiful hill. The base of the mountain is surrounded by men of all stations, all dispositions, all trying their hardest to get richer while on earth.
