translation: Women, probably. But men too, because they are men themselves. What would you do with the world if you were all-powerful, Apemantus?

original: Give it the beasts, to be rid of the men.
translation: Give it to the animals and get rid of all men.

original: Wouldst thou have thyself fall in the confusion of men, and remain a beast with the beasts?
translation: Would you fall with the rest of the men and remain an animal?

original: Ay, Timon.
translation: Yes, Timon.

original: A beastly ambition, which the gods grant thee t'   attain to! If thou wert the lion, the fox would   beguile thee; if thou wert the lamb, the fox would   eat three:
translation: What a beastly thing for the gods to have you wish! If you were a lion, the fox would trick you; if you were a lamb, the fox would deceive three of you;

original: if thou wert the fox, the lion would   suspect thee, when peradventure thou wert accused by   the ass: if thou wert the ass, thy dulness would   torment thee, and still thou livedst but as a   breakfast to the wolf:
translation: if you were a fox, the lion would be suspicious of you when you were accused by the donkey; if you were a donkey, your stupidity would torment you, and you would only be the breakfast of the wolf;

original: if thou wert the wolf, thy   greediness would afflict thee, and oft thou shouldst   hazard thy life for thy dinner: wert thou the   unicorn, pride and wrath would confound thee and   make thine own self the conquest of thy fury:
translation: if you were a wolf, your greed would plague you, and you would have to risk your life just for dinner; if you were a unicorn, pride and anger would end you and when in your anger you rammed your horn and got stuck in a tree;

original: wert   thou a bear, thou wouldst be killed by the horse:   wert thou a horse, thou wouldst be seized by the   leopard: wert thou a leopard, thou wert german to   the lion and the spots of thy kindred were jurors on   thy life:
translation: if you were a bear, you would be killed by the horse; if you were a horse; you would be attacked by the leopard; if you were a leopard, you would be related to the lion and the crimes of your relatives would condemn you to death.

original: all thy safety were remotion and thy   defence absence. What beast couldst thou be, that   were not subject to a beast? and what a beast art   thou already, that seest not thy loss in   transformation!
translation: Your only safety would lie in leaving one place for another, so what beast could you be that you would not fall prey to some other beast? What kind of animal are you already that you cannot see what you would lose in changing into an animal!?

original: If thou couldst please me with speaking to me, thou mightst have hit upon it here: the commonwealth of Athens is become a forest of beasts.
translation: If your speech could ever please me, it would be these observations. The state of Athens has become a forest of beasts.

original: How has the ass broke the wall, that thou art out of  the city?
translation: How? Has a donkey broken down the wall, so you find yourself outside the city?

original: Yonder comes a poet and a painter: the plague of   company light upon thee!
translation: Look, here comes a poet and a painter. I hope you catch the plague of their company!

original: I will fear to catch it   and give way: when I know not what else to do, I'll   see thee again.
translation: For fear of catching it I'll leave now. I'll see you again when I have nothing better to do.

original: When there is nothing living but thee, thou shalt be welcome. I had rather be a beggar's dog than Apemantus.
translation: When you're the last man on earth, you'll be welcome here. I would rather be a beggar's dog than you.

original: Thou art the cap of all the fools alive.
translation: You are the captain of all fools.

original: Would thou wert clean enough to spit upon!
translation: I wish you were clean enough to spit on.

original: A plague on thee! thou art too bad to curse.
translation: Get bit! You aren't even good enough to curse.

original: All villains that do stand by thee are pure.
translation: Villains look good in your company.

original: There is no leprosy but what thou speak'st.
translation: Your speech is worse than leprosy.

original: If I name thee. I'll beat thee, but I should infect my hands.
translation: When I say your name. I'll beat you up, if only touching you wouldn't infect my hands!

original: I would my tongue could rot them off!
translation: I wish my tongue could rot them off!

original: Away, thou issue of a mangy dog! Choler does kill me that thou art alive; I swound to see thee.
translation: Get away, you son of a bitch! Your life makes me angry enough to die. I swoon just looking at you!

original: Would thou wouldst burst!
translation: Maybe you'll explode!

original: Away, Thou tedious rogue! I am sorry I shall lose A stone by thee.
translation: Get away you dumb peasant! It's sad I have to waste a stone on you.

original: Beast!
translation: Beast!

original: Slave!
translation: Slave!

original: Toad!
translation: Toad!

original: Rogue, rogue, rogue!   I am sick of this false world, and will love nought   But even the mere necessities upon 't.
translation: You worthless, worthless man! I am sick of this lying world and will not love anything but the most basic necessities.

original: Then, Timon, presently prepare thy grave;   Lie where the light foam the sea may beat   Thy grave-stone daily:
translation: So, Timon, prepare your own grave, lie down here where the light foam of the sea might lap against your grave stone every single day.

original: make thine epitaph,   That death in me at others' lives may laugh.
translation: Make your own epitaph, so my death will laugh at the lives of others.

original: O thou sweet king-killer, and dear divorce   'Twixt natural son and sire! thou bright defiler   Of Hymen's purest bed! thou valiant Mars!
translation: Oh you sweet little king-killer, which can set even a son and father at odds!  You that can defile the bed of Hymen like Mars !

original: Thou ever young, fresh, loved and delicate wooer,   Whose blush doth thaw the consecrated snow   That lies on Dian's lap!
translation: You forever young, fresh, beloved, and delicate wooer, that can ruin the  chastity of Diana  with just a blush!

original: thou visible god,   That solder'st close impossibilities,   And makest them kiss! that speak'st with   every tongue,   To every purpose!
translation: You beautiful god, which can sew together impossible events and make them kiss! That can speak in every language and for any purpose!

original: O thou touch of hearts!   Think, thy slave man rebels, and by thy virtue   Set them into confounding odds, that beasts   May have the world in empire!
translation: You tester of hearts, that think your slave man rebels against you and, with your power, set him at odds with himself so that beasts may rule the world!

original: Would 'twere so! But not till I am dead. I'll say thou'st gold: Thou wilt be throng'd to shortly.
translation: If only it were so! But not until I am dead. I'll say to gold that it will be rushed to before long.

original: Throng'd to!
translation: Rushed to!?

original: Ay.
translation: Yes.

original: Thy back, I prithee.
translation: Show me your back and leave.

original: Live, and love thy misery.
translation: May you live in misery and love it too.

original: Long live so, and so die.
translation: May you live long and miserable too, then die.

original: I am quit. Moe things like men! Eat, Timon, and abhor them.
translation: I am rid of him, and yet more men! Hate them, Timon, and eat your food.

original: Where should he have this gold? It is some poor   fragment, some slender sort of his remainder:
translation: Where could his gold be? It is the last scrap of his life of wealth.

original: the   mere want of gold, and the falling-from of his   friends, drove him into this melancholy.
translation: It was the mere desire for gold and the betrayal of his friends which drove him to this depression.

original: It is noised he hath a mass of treasure.
translation: I have heard he has a huge treasure.

original: Let us make the assay upon him: if he care not for't, he will supply us easily; if he covetously reserve it, how shall's get it?
translation: Let's test that. If he doesn't care about it, he'll give it to us without a care. If he covets it, how will we get it?

original: True; for he bears it not about him, 'tis hid.
translation: That's a good question, because he doesn't have it with him. It's hidden.

original: Is not this he?
translation: Is that not him?

original: Where?
translation: Where?

original: 'Tis his description.
translation: That's what he's supposed to look like.

original: He; I know him.
translation: Him? I recognize him.

original: Save thee, Timon.
translation: God bless you, Timon?

original: Now, thieves?
translation: What do you want, thieves?

original: Soldiers, not thieves.
translation: We're soldiers, not thieves.

original: Both too; and women's sons.
translation: Both, and women's sons too.

original: We are not thieves, but men that much do want.
translation: We are not thieves, just poor men.

original: Your greatest want is, you want much of meat.   Why should you want?
translation: The greatest thing you lack is brought about by your great desire to eat a lot—why else would you feel poor?

original: Behold, the earth hath roots;   Within this mile break forth a hundred springs;   The oaks bear mast, the briers scarlet hips;
translation: Look here, the earth has roots, and within a mile are a hundred springs. The oaks have nuts, the briers red berries.

original: The bounteous housewife, nature, on each bush   Lays her full mess before you. Want! why want?
translation: Nature is a generous housewife, who gives a great meal on each bush. Poor! How could you feel poor?

original: We cannot live on grass, on berries, water, As beasts and birds and fishes.
translation: We are not animals, birds, nor fish. We cannot live on just grass, berries, and water.

original: Nor on the beasts themselves, the birds, and fishes;   You must eat men.
translation: No you cannot even live on animals like birds and fish yourselves. You must eat men.

original: Yet thanks I must you con   That you are thieves profess'd, that you work not   In holier shapes: for there is boundless theft   In limited professions.
translation: Though I ought to thank you for at least being honest thieves who do not hide behind some more respectable disguise, for there is thievery in other professions as well.

original: Rascal thieves,   Here's gold. Go, suck the subtle blood o' the grape,   Till the high fever seethe your blood to froth,   And so 'scape hanging: trust not the physician;   His antidotes are poison, and he slays   Moe than you rob:
translation: Here's some gold, you dirty thieves. Go now and drink all the wine you can until you catch a deadly fever that makes your blood foam. Do not trust the doctor, though, because his cures are poisonous and he kills men even more often than you rob them, taking both money and lives.

original: take wealth and lives together;   Do villany, do, since you protest to do't,   Like workmen. I'll example you with thievery.
translation: Wreak havoc as your occupation dictates,  and like one being instructed in his occupation, I'll give you good examples of thieves.

original: The sun's a thief, and with his great attraction   Robs the vast sea: the moon's an arrant thief,   And her pale fire she snatches from the sun:   The sea's a thief, whose liquid surge resolves   The moon into salt tears: the earth's a thief,   That feeds and breeds by a composture stolen   From general excrement   :
translation: The sun is a thief for robbing water from the vast sea; the moon is a thief for snatching light off the sun; the sea is a thief as its tides surge forth, dissolve the moon into salty tears; the earth is a thief as it steals and feeds off the manure of animals.

original: each thing's a thief:   The laws, your curb and whip, in their rough power   Have uncheque'd theft. Love not yourselves: away,   Rob one another. There's more gold.
translation: Everything is a thief, from the laws to its enforcement, which use their unlimited power to steal. And do not make yourselves the exception, go away and rob one another. Here's some more gold.

original: Cut throats:   All that you meet are thieves: to Athens go,   Break open shops; nothing can you steal,   But thieves do lose it: steal no less for this   I give you; and gold confound you howsoe'er! Amen.
translation: Go cut some throats, because everyone you meet is a thief. Go to Athens, pillage shops, because nothing you steal will not come from a thief's pocket. Do not steal any less because I'm giving you this, more gold, which I hope may curse you! Amen.

original: Has almost charmed me from my profession, by persuading me to it.
translation: He almost makes me want to give up my profession by talking me into it.

original: 'Tis in the malice of mankind that he thus advises us; not to have us thrive in our mystery.
translation: His hatred of mankind is what gives us advice, not his concern for our craft.

original: I'll believe him as an enemy, and give over my trade.
translation: I'd trust him about as much as my enemy and just give up thieving altogether.

original: Let us first see peace in Athens: there is no time so miserable but a man may be true.
translation: Let's at least wait until the war is over. There is no worse time to be honest than a war.

original: O you gods!   Is yond despised and ruinous man my lord?   Full of decay and failing? O monument   And wonder of good deeds evilly bestow'd!
translation: Good god! Is that hateful man in tatters, looking so down and out, really my lord? Oh he is a memorial of what happens when good deeds are received ungratefully!

original: What an alteration of honour   Has desperate want made!   What viler thing upon the earth than friends   Who can bring noblest minds to basest ends!
translation: Poverty has made such a remarkable change to his honorable appearance! How vile his friends were to bring down such a great man!

original: How rarely does it meet with this time's guise,   When man was wish'd to love his enemies!   Grant I may ever love, and rather woo   Those that would mischief me than those that do!
translation: It really shows the accuracy of that saying, "Love your enemies!" I would indeed much rather love those who wish me harm to my face than those who pretend to be my friends and stab me in the back.

original: Has caught me in his eye: I will present   My honest grief unto him; and, as my lord,   Still serve him with my life. My dearest master!
translation: He has seen me, and I will show him how much I grieve for him, and how I promise still to serve him. My fine master!

original: Away! what art thou?
translation: Go away! Who are you?

original: Have you forgot me, sir?
translation: Have you forgotten who I am?

original: Why dost ask that? I have forgot all men; Then, if thou grant'st thou'rt a man, I have forgot  thee.
translation: Why bother asking that? I have forgotten all men. If you agree that you are indeed a man, then I have forgotten you too.

original: An honest poor servant of yours.
translation: I was your poor and loyal servant.

original: Then I know thee not: I never had honest man about me, I; all I kept were knaves, to serve in meat to villains.
translation: Then I definitely do not know you, because I never had an honest man around me. All those I kept around me were liars, because I wanted to serve meat to villains.

original: The gods are witness, Ne'er did poor steward wear a truer grief For his undone lord than mine eyes for you.
translation: The gods know that there has never been an assistant racked with sadness for his lord the way I am looking at you.

original: What, dost thou weep? Come nearer. Then I   love thee,   Because thou art a woman,
translation: What, are you crying? Come closer. I do love you, now, because these tears show you to be a woman.

original: and disclaim'st   Flinty mankind; whose eyes do never give   But thorough lust and laughter.
translation: You give up your manhood, because no man's eyes ever did tear up, except for lust or laughter.

original: Pity's sleeping:   Strange times, that weep with laughing, not with  weeping!
translation: Pity may as well be asleep, for these are strange times, in which people weep for laughter and not in sadness.

original: I beg of you to know me, good my lord, To accept my grief and whilst this poor wealth lasts To entertain me as your steward still.
translation: I beg you, please recognize me, my good lord. That way you can accept my sadness and let me serve as your assistant while this bad luck continues.

original: Had I a steward   So true, so just, and now so comfortable?   It almost turns my dangerous nature mild.   Let me behold thy face. Surely, this man   Was born of woman.
translation: Did I really have an assistant so honest, fair, and comforting? It almost cures me of my dangerous and violent thoughts. Let me see your face: you are definitely a man born of a woman.

original: Forgive my general and exceptless rashness,   You perpetual-sober gods! I do proclaim   One honest man—mistake me not—but one;   No more, I pray,—and he's a steward.   How fain would I have hated all mankind!
translation: Forgive me gods, for assuming the worst of all men. I admit now that there is one honest man, only one. No more, I swear—and he's just an assistant. How I dared to hate all of mankind!

original: And thou redeem'st thyself: but all, save thee,   I fell with curses.   Methinks thou art more honest now than wise;   For, by oppressing and betraying me,   Thou mightst have sooner got another service:
translation: You do redeem yourself, but the rest I did lay flat with insults. I think you are more honest than wise, because you might have been better off betraying me.

original: For many so arrive at second masters,   Upon their first lord's neck.
translation: Many do have second masters at the expense of their first.

original: But tell me true—   For I must ever doubt, though ne'er so sure—   Is not thy kindness subtle, covetous,   If not a usuring kindness, and, as rich men deal gifts,   Expecting in return twenty for one?
translation: But tell me, please, is your kindness not a subtle, greedy, and self-serving kind of kindness, which hopes to get what it gives twenty-to-one?

original: No, my most worthy master; in whose breast   Doubt and suspect, alas, are placed too late:   You should have fear'd false times when you did feast:   Suspect still comes where an estate is least.
translation: No, master, in whom doubt and suspicion have taken hold too late. You should have feared lies when you threw feasts with your wealth, but your suspicion comes when you are most poor.

original: That which I show, heaven knows, is merely love,   Duty and zeal to your unmatched mind,   Care of your food and living;
translation: What I show you is true love, duty, and enthusiasm for your outstanding mind, along with care for your wellbeing.

original: and, believe it,   My most honour'd lord,   For any benefit that points to me,   Either in hope or present, I'ld exchange   For this one wish, that you had power and wealth   To requite me, by making rich yourself.
translation: Believe me, my lord, that any advantage I could gain now I would exchange for one wish: that you had the power and wealth to make yourself rich. That would be the return for my admiration.

original: Look thee, 'tis so! Thou singly honest man,   Here, take: the gods out of my misery   Have sent thee treasure.
translation: Look here, it is true! You uniquely honest man, take this. The gods have given you a gift out of my misery.

original: Go, live rich and happy;   But thus condition'd: thou shalt build from men;   Hate all, curse all, show charity to none,
translation: Go be rich and happy, but under one condition: you take advantage of other men, hate all of them, curse all of them, and show charity to none of them.

original: But let the famish'd flesh slide from the bone,   Ere thou relieve the beggar; give to dogs   What thou deny'st to men; let prisons swallow 'em,   Debts wither 'em to nothing;
translation: Let the starving flesh slide off the bones of a beggar before you give him any money. Give to dogs what you do not give to men, whom you should let go to prison in debt.

original: be men like   blasted woods,   And may diseases lick up their false bloods!   And so farewell and thrive.
translation: Let men be like dying woods, with diseases eating at their lying blood. Live this way, and goodbye.

original: O, let me stay, And comfort you, my master.
translation: Let me stay and comfort you, master.

original: If thou hatest curses, Stay not; fly, whilst thou art blest and free: Ne'er see thou man, and let me ne'er see thee.
translation: If you hate to be insulted, do not stay. Go away, and while you are blessed and free, never meet with another man, and never let me see you here again.

original: As I took note of the place, it cannot be far where he abides.
translation: As I recall, he can't be far from here.

original: What's to be thought of him? does the rumour hold for true, that he's so full of gold?
translation: What do you think? Do you think it's true that he's got a hidden stash of gold?

original: Certain: Alcibiades reports it; Phrynia and   Timandra had gold of him:
translation: Definitely. Alcibiades says so, and Phrynia and Timandra got gold from him.

original: he likewise enriched poor   straggling soldiers with great quantity: 'tis said   he gave unto his steward a mighty sum.
translation: He also gave the poor soldiers a ton. I also heard he gave his assistant a lot too.

original: Then this breaking of his has been but a try for his  friends.
translation: So his bankruptcy has just been a test for his friends.

original: Nothing else: you shall see him a palm in Athens   again, and flourish with the highest.
translation: It can't be anything else. You'll see him high and mighty in Athens again, to be sure.

original: Therefore   'tis not amiss we tender our loves to him, in this   supposed distress of his:
translation: For that reason it's not crazy to appeal to him in his supposed distress.

original: it will show honestly in   us; and is very likely to load our purposes with   what they travail for, if it be a just true report   that goes of his having.
translation: It'll look good for us, and it is likely to end in us receiving what the others got, if it is in fact true that he has money.

original: What have you now to present unto him?
translation: What do you have to give to him?

original: Nothing at this time but my visitation: only I will promise him an excellent piece.
translation: Nothing but my presence for now. I will promise him an excellent work of art.

original: I must serve him so too, tell him of an intent that's coming toward him.
translation: Me too, and to promise him something in the future.

original: Good as the best. Promising is the very air o' the   time: it opens the eyes of expectation:   performance is ever the duller for his act;
translation: Good idea. Promises are all the rage right now. They open the door for expectation, whereas actions themselves are merely done once they happen.

original: and,   but in the plainer and simpler kind of people, the   deed of saying is quite out of use. To promise is   most courtly and fashionable:
translation: With the exception of the plainer and simpler sort, the fulfillment of promises has gone out of fashion. But still promising itself is current and stylish.

original: performance is a kind   of will or testament which argues a great sickness   in his judgment that makes it.
translation: The actual doing of the thing is a kind of statement that shows a lack of judgment in the person who made the promise in the first place.

original: Excellent workman! thou canst not paint a man so bad as is thyself.
translation: What an artist! You couldn't paint a man worse than yourself.

original: I am thinking what I shall say I have provided for   him: it must be a personating of himself;
translation: I am thinking about what I will say I have brought him. It must be some kind of portrait of himself,

original: a satire   against the softness of prosperity, with a discovery   of the infinite flatteries that follow youth and  opulency.
translation: maybe a satire about the flightiness of wealth, with an exposition about the many flatteries that youth and opulence brings with it.

original: Must thou needs stand for a villain in thine own work? wilt thou whip thine own faults in other men? Do so, I have gold for thee.
translation: Do you really need to model a villain in your work? Would you chastise your own vices in other men? Do it, and I've got gold for you.

original: Nay, let's seek him: Then do we sin against our own estate, When we may profit meet, and come too late.
translation: Let's go look for him. We would do wrong to our own prosperity if we were to arrive to late to such an opportunity.

original: True; When the day serves, before black-corner'd night, Find what thou want'st by free and offer'd light. Come.
translation: For sure. Before night falls, we ought to find what is offered freely in the light of day. Follow me.

original: I'll meet you at the turn. What a   god's gold,   That he is worshipp'd in a baser temple   Than where swine feed!
translation: I'll play your own little game. What a magnificent god is gold, that it is worshipped in a place grosser than a pigpen.

original: 'Tis thou that rigg'st the bark and plough'st the foam,   Settlest admired reverence in a slave:
translation: It is the thing that rigs the ship and sets it on its journey, the thing that makes a slave honor his master.

original: To thee be worship! and thy saints for aye   Be crown'd with plagues that thee alone obey!   Fit I meet them.
translation: May people continue to worship it! May its disciples forever be chased with its own unique plagues. It's about time to talk to them.

original: Hail, worthy Timon!
translation: Hey, Timon!

original: Our late noble master!
translation: Our great master!

original: Have I once lived to see two honest men?
translation: Have I ever seen two such honest men?

original: Sir,   Having often of your open bounty tasted,   Hearing you were retired, your friends fall'n off,   Whose thankless natures—O abhorred spirits!—   Not all the whips of heaven are large enough:
translation: Sir, after having received so many of your gifts, and then hearing you were retired, abandoned by friends so ungrateful that all the whips of heaven are not large enough to punish them.

original: What! to you,   Whose star-like nobleness gave life and influence   To their whole being! I am rapt and cannot cover   The monstrous bulk of this ingratitude   With any size of words.
translation: Incredible! To you, whose stellar generosity gave life to them! It drives me mad, and I cannot conceive of any way to describe this level of ingratitude.

original: Let it go naked, men may see't the better: You that are honest, by being what you are, Make them best seen and known.
translation: Let it go. Some men might be more optimistic. Your truthfulness, your being what you proclaim to be, make ungrateful men more noticeable.

original: He and myself Have travail'd in the great shower of your gifts, And sweetly felt it.
translation: He and I have triumphed in the great shower of your gifts and enjoyed it so much!

original: Ay, you are honest men.
translation: Yes, you are honest men.

original: We are hither come to offer you our service.
translation: We have come to offer you our service.

original: Most honest men! Why, how shall I requite you? Can you eat roots, and drink cold water? no.
translation: Such honest men! How could I ever repay you? Can you eat roots or drink cold water? No.

original: What we can do, we'll do, to do you service.
translation: We'll do what we can for you.

original: Ye're honest men: ye've heard that I have gold; I am sure you have: speak truth; ye're honest men.
translation: You are both honest men and have heard that I have gold. I am sure that you have. Tell me the truth, honest men.

original: So it is said, my noble lord; but therefore Came not my friend nor I.
translation: We have heard that. But that is not why we've come.

original: Good honest men! Thou draw'st a counterfeit Best in all Athens: thou'rt, indeed, the best; Thou counterfeit'st most lively.
translation: Good honest men! You draw the best portrait in all of Athens. Yes, you are the best, your counterfeits are the most lifelike.

original: So, so, my lord.
translation: So it is, my lord.

original: E'en so, sir, as I say.
translation: Yes, it is as I said.

original: And, for thy fiction,   Why, thy verse swells with stuff so fine and smooth   That thou art even natural in thine art.
translation: And as for your fiction, the lines swell with material so fine and smooth that your art comes to equal nature.

original: But, for all this, my honest-natured friends,   I must needs say you have a little fault:   Marry, 'tis not monstrous in you, neither wish I   You take much pains to mend.
translation: But in spite of all this, my truthful friends, I must say that you do have one vice. It's not such a bad thing, and you shouldn't try too hard to fix it.

original: Beseech your honour To make it known to us.
translation: Please, Timon, tell us what it is.

original: You'll take it ill.
translation: You won't like it.

original: Most thankfully, my lord.
translation: We'll appreciate it, my lord.

original: Will you, indeed?
translation: Will you really?

original: Doubt it not, worthy lord.
translation: Definitely.

original: There's never a one of you but trusts a knave, That mightily deceives you.
translation: Both of you are too trustful of scoundrels who wish to deceive you.

original: Do we, my lord?
translation: Are we really?

original: Ay, and you hear him cog, see him dissemble,   Know his gross patchery, love him, feed him,   Keep in your bosom:
translation: Definitely. You hear him cheat, see him pretend, and watch him commit crimes, and all the while you love him, feed him, and keep him close,

original: yet remain assured   That he's a made-up villain.
translation: knowing full well that he's a total villain.

original: I know none such, my lord.
translation: I know no one like this.

original: Nor I.
translation: Me neither.

original: Look you, I love you well; I'll give you gold,   Rid me these villains from your companies:
translation: Hey, guys, I like you a lot. I'll give you some gold, and in return you may rid the world of some evil men.

original: Hang them or stab them, drown them in a draught,   Confound them by some course, and come to me,   I'll give you gold enough.
translation: Hang them, stab them, drown them in a toilet, I don't care. Get rid of them some way, and then come to me and I'll give you even more gold.

original: Name them, my lord, let's know them.
translation: Name your enemies, Timon, we'd like to know.

original: You that way and you this, but two in company;   Each man apart, all single and alone,   Yet an arch-villain keeps him company.
translation: You, that man, and you the other, each of you still in the company of the other. Each of you is single and alone when apart from the other, but now an enemy keeps you company.

original: If where thou art two villains shall not be,   Come not near him.
translation: If you promise to rid the world of villains, do not go near the other guy.

original: If thou wouldst not reside   But where one villain is, then him abandon.
translation: If you swear you will not stand where one villain is, abandon him.

original: Hence, pack! there's gold; you came for gold, ye  slaves:
translation: So go away! Here's the gold you came for, you slaves.

original: You have work'd for me; there's payment for you: hence!
translation: Here's payment for the work you owe me. Now go!

original: You are an alchemist; make gold of that. Out, rascal dogs!
translation: You make gold from metal. Here, make gold from this! Get out of here you dogs!

original: It is in vain that you would speak with Timon;
translation: It's useless to speak with Timon.

original: For he is set so only to himself   That nothing but himself which looks like man   Is friendly with him.
translation: He only trusts himself, and nobody that looks anything like a man appears friendly to him.

original: Bring us to his cave: It is our part and promise to the Athenians To speak with Timon.
translation: Bring us to the cave. We promised the Athenians we would speak to Timon.

original: At all times alike   Men are not still the same: 'twas time and griefs   That framed him thus:
translation: Men are not the same all the time. It was time and sadness that made him this way.

original: time, with his fairer hand,   Offering the fortunes of his former days,   The former man may make him. Bring us to him,   And chance it as it may.
translation: Time presents to him the riches of his former days, the opportunity to become the man he was. Bring us to to him and we'll take our chances.

original: Here is his cave.   Peace and content be here! Lord Timon! Timon!   Look out, and speak to friends:
translation: Here is his cave. We come in peace and friendship! Timon! Timon! Come out and speak to two friends.

original: the Athenians,   By two of their most reverend senate, greet thee:   Speak to them, noble Timon.
translation: The Athenians send their best to you in two honored senators. Speak to them, Timon.

original: Thou sun, that comfort'st, burn! Speak, and   be hang'd:
translation: You, sun which comforts the world, burn them! Speak to me and then be hanged!

original: For each true word, a blister! and each false   Be as cauterizing to the root o' the tongue,   Consuming it with speaking!
translation: Because each true word must to you be like a blister, and each lie burn you to the root of your tongue, eating it away with your own talk!

original: Worthy Timon,—
translation: Great Timon—

original: Of none but such as you, and you of Timon.
translation: Great to no one but those like yourself, and you but to Timon.

original: The senators of Athens greet thee, Timon.
translation: The Senators of Athens send their regards.

original: I thank them; and would send them back the plague, Could I but catch it for them.
translation: I thank them, and would send them a disease if only I could catch it for them.

original: O, forget   What we are sorry for ourselves in thee.
translation: Forget the things that have happened to you, which we are very sorry for.

original: The senators with one consent of love   Entreat thee back to Athens;
translation: The senators unanimously agreed to ask you to come back to Athens.

original: who have thought   On special dignities, which vacant lie   For thy best use and wearing.
translation: There are many honors there, totally ready for you to take up.

original: They confess   Toward thee forgetfulness too general, gross:
translation: They admit they had were too quick to forget your good deeds,

original: Which now the public body, which doth seldom   Play the recanter, feeling in itself   A lack of Timon's aid, hath sense withal   Of its own fail, restraining aid to Timon;
translation: which they take back now that you have stopped aiding them, knowing full well that it is their fault for not extending their hands to you in your time of need.

original: And send forth us, to make their sorrow'd render,   Together with a recompense more fruitful   Than their offence can weigh down by the dram;
translation: They sent us to tell you about our sadness, along with a repayment greater than their crime could possibly weigh on you.

original: Ay, even such heaps and sums of love and wealth   As shall to thee blot out what wrongs were theirs   And write in thee the figures of their love,   Ever to read them thine.
translation: Indeed they promise such heaps of wealth and friendship that it should make you entirely forget how they wronged you, feeling within yourself instead such sentiments of love that you will always consider them your friends.

original: You witch me in it;   Surprise me to the very brink of tears:
translation: You cast a spell on me. You've beaten me to the brink of tears,

original: Lend me a fool's heart and a woman's eyes,   And I'll beweep these comforts, worthy senators.
translation: giving me a fool's heart and a woman's eyes, crying before these comforting words.

original: Therefore, so please thee to return with us   And of our Athens, thine and ours, to take   The captainship,
translation: So come back with us to Athens, a city yours as well as ours, to become a captain.

original: thou shalt be met with thanks,   Allow'd with absolute power and thy good name   Live with authority:
translation: You will be met with thanks and allowed absolute power and authority to your name.

original: so soon we shall drive back   Of Alcibiades the approaches wild,   Who, like a boar too savage, doth root up   His country's peace.
translation: Soon enough we will drive back Alcibiades and his wild attacks. He is like a savage boar, rooting up the peace in his own country.

original: And shakes his threatening sword Against the walls of Athens.
translation: He threatens the walls of Athens with his own sword.

original: Therefore, Timon,—
translation: So Timon—

original: Well, sir, I will; therefore, I will, sir; thus:   If Alcibiades kill my countrymen,   Let Alcibiades know this of Timon,   That Timon cares not.
translation: I will say this. If Alcibiades wants to kill my fellow citizens, let Alcibiades know that Timon does not care.

original: But if be sack fair Athens,   And take our goodly aged men by the beards,   Giving our holy virgins to the stain   Of contumelious, beastly, mad-brain'd war,
translation: But if he wants to pillage Athens, grabbing old men by the beards and sacrificing holy virgins to the horrors of war,

original: Then let him know, and tell him Timon speaks it,   In pity of our aged and our youth,   I cannot choose but tell him, that I care not,   And let him take't at worst;
translation: then let him know that even as I pity the old and the young, I cannot help but say still that I do not care if he does his worst.

original: for their knives care not,   While you have throats to answer: for myself,   There's not a whittle in the unruly camp   But I do prize it at my love before   The reverend'st throat in Athens.
translation: Their blades do not care that your throats suffer the consequences of their actions. And as for me, I put the smallest switchblade in their rebel barracks before the most honored throat in all of Athens.

original: So I leave you   To the protection of the prosperous gods,   As thieves to keepers.
translation: I leave you to the protection of the gods, the way I might leave thieves to their jailers.

original: Stay not, all's in vain.
translation: Let's go. It's hopeless.

original: Why, I was writing of my epitaph;   it will be seen to-morrow:
translation: I was writing the epitaph for my tombstone, which will be seen tomorrow.

original: my long sickness   Of health and living now begins to mend,   And nothing brings me all things.
translation: My blight of health and and living well is now being cured, and death will bring everything with it.

original: Go, live still;   Be Alcibiades your plague, you his,   And last so long enough!
translation: Go and keep living. Let Alcibiades be your blight, and you his. Live that way as long as you can!

original: We speak in vain.
translation: It's useless.

original: But yet I love my country, and am not One that rejoices in the common wreck, As common bruit doth put it.
translation: I do love my country, and contrary to what rumors may say, am not glad to see total destruction.

original: That's well spoke.
translation: Well said.

original: Commend me to my loving countrymen,—
translation: Give my best to my fellow Athenians—

original: These words become your lips as they pass thorough them.
translation: These words do the person who speaks them justice.

original: And enter in our ears like great triumphers In their applauding gates.
translation: And enter our ears like trumpeters celebrating at the gates.

original: Commend me to them,   And tell them that, to ease them of their griefs,   Their fears of hostile strokes,
translation: Give them my best, and tell them that, to ease their sadness, their fear of war,

original: their aches, losses,   Their pangs of love, with other incident throes   That nature's fragile vessel doth sustain   In life's uncertain voyage, I will some kindness do  them:
translation: their pains, their losses, their pangs of love, and all the other difficulties common to life, I send some kindness their way.

original: I'll teach them to prevent wild Alcibiades' wrath.
translation: I'll teach them how to defend themselves against the wild Alcibiades's wrath.

original: I like this well; he will return again.
translation: This sounds good. He will return soon enough.

original: I have a tree, which grows here in my close,   That mine own use invites me to cut down,   And shortly must I fell it:
translation: I have a tree that grows around here that I need to cut down, and I need to do that soon.

original: tell my friends,   Tell Athens, in the sequence of degree   From high to low throughout,
translation: Tell my friends in Athens of all stations that whoever wants to stop these pains

original: that whoso please   To stop affliction, let him take his haste,   Come hither, ere my tree hath felt the axe,   And hang himself.   I pray you, do my greeting.
translation: should hurry here before my my axe touches the tree, so that they might hang themselves. Please, send those regards.

original: Trouble him no further; thus you still shall find him.
translation: Stop bothering him. You will find him this way again.

original: Come not to me again: but say to Athens,   Timon hath made his everlasting mansion   Upon the beached verge of the salt flood;   Who once a day with his embossed froth   The turbulent surge shall cover:
translation: Don't come back, and instead tell all of Athens that Timon has built his house on the shore, and everyday will cover himself with the surging foam of the sea.

original: thither come,   And let my grave-stone be your oracle.   Lips, let sour words go by and language end:   What is amiss plague and infection mend!
translation: Tell them to come here and let my grave-stone be their guide. Oh lips, let these harsh words fall from you and be your last, let everything wrong with the world be healed by ravaging diseases!

original: Graves only be men's works and death their gain!   Sun, hide thy beams! Timon hath done his reign.
translation: Graves are just another of men's works, and death another of their benefits! Go away, sun! Timon has finished his time on earth.

original: His discontents are unremoveably Coupled to nature.
translation: His sadness is now a part of himself.

original: Our hope in him is dead: let us return, And strain what other means is left unto us In our dear peril.
translation: He's hopeless. Let's go back and try whatever else we can do to save ourselves.

original: It requires swift foot.
translation: We need to hurry.

original: Thou hast painfully discover'd: are his files As full as thy report?
translation: You have retrieved information at great cost. Does he have as many troops as you say?

original: I have spoke the least: Besides, his expedition promises Present approach.
translation: My estimate is conservative. Plus, he approaches at a great speed.

original: We stand much hazard, if they bring not Timon.
translation: We are in great danger if the others do not bring Timon with them.

original: I met a courier, one mine ancient friend;   Whom, though in general part we were opposed,   Yet our old love made a particular force,   And made us speak like friends:
translation: I met with a messenger friend of mine who, despite having argued with me in public, held a strong love for me and approached me like the old friend he is.

original: this man was riding   From Alcibiades to Timon's cave,   With letters of entreaty, which imported   His fellowship i' the cause against your city,   In part for his sake moved.
translation: He was riding from Alcibiades to Timon with letters hoping he would join the cause against Athens, which was inspired partly by his poor treatment here.

original: Here come our brothers.
translation: Here come our fellow Senators.

original: No talk of Timon, nothing of him expect.
translation: Let's not talk about Timon. We can't expect any help from him.

original: The enemies' drum is heard, and fearful scouring   Doth choke the air with dust: in, and prepare:   Ours is the fall, I fear; our foes the snare.
translation: The drum of the enemy armies can be heard in the city, and their marching lifts dust into the air. We fall right into the enemies' trap.

original: By all description this should be the place.   Who's here? speak, ho! No answer! What is this?
translation: This looks like the place as it was described to me. Who's there? Speak up! No Answer! What is going on?

original: Timon is dead, who hath outstretch'd his span:   Some beast rear'd this; there does not live a man.   Dead, sure; and this his grave.
translation: Timon has reached his final days. He is dead. Some horrible animal must have done this, for all men seem beasts to me now. He is definitely dead, and there is his grave.

original: What's on this tomb   I cannot read; the character I'll take with wax:
translation: I cannot read what's written on his tomb.  I'll use wax to mold out the lettering.

original: Our captain hath in every figure skill,   An aged interpreter, though young in days:   Before proud Athens he's set down by this,   Whose fall the mark of his ambition is.
translation: My captain can read any kind of lettering, for despite being young he's an experienced interpreter. In front of Athens the man whose ambition was his downfall is set down by these words.

original: Sound to this coward and lascivious town Our terrible approach.
translation: Make sure this cowardly and dirty town hears our troops approach.

original: Till now you have gone on and fill'd the time   With all licentious measure, making your wills   The scope of justice;
translation: Previously, you filled your days by using your own power unchecked, making your own personal desires equivalent with justice.

original: till now myself and such   As slept within the shadow of your power   Have wander'd with our traversed arms and breathed   Our sufferance vainly:
translation: Before now I and people like me slept in the shadow of your power, walking about with folded arms and voicing our opinions only in vain.

original: now the time is flush,   When crouching marrow in the bearer strong   Cries of itself 'No more:'
translation: Now is the time for action, when the bones of those bowing down to you finally cry out, "No more!"

original: now breathless wrong   Shall sit and pant in your great chairs of ease,   And pursy insolence shall break his wind   With fear and horrid flight.
translation: Now those supposed wrongdoers, voiceless then, will have the opportunity to sit in your positions of power. And those who were supposedly ill-mannered during your time shall be able to say and do whatever they like.

original: Noble and young,   When thy first griefs were but a mere conceit,   Ere thou hadst power or we had cause of fear,
translation: Young, honorable, Alcibiades, when your grievances were just an idea, before you had any power and we had any fear of it,

original: We sent to thee, to give thy rages balm,   To wipe out our ingratitude with loves   Above their quantity.
translation: we sent assistance to you to apologize for our ingratitude with endless admiration.

original: So did we woo   Transformed Timon to our city's love   By humble message and by promised means:
translation: And we also tried to reach out to Timon and express our city's love for him with a message of humility and promised riches.

original: We were not all unkind, nor all deserve   The common stroke of war.
translation: We were not unkind, and we do not deserve to fall to war.

original: These walls of ours   Were not erected by their hands from whom   You have received your griefs;
translation: These walls of ours were not built by the people who insulted you,

original: nor are they such   That these great towers, trophies and schools   should fall   For private faults in them.
translation: nor were they people that deserve their work to fall for the faults of others.

original: Nor are they living   Who were the motives that you first went out;   Shame that they wanted cunning, in excess   Hath broke their hearts.
translation: The people who banished you are no longer living. Their shame at their actions broke their hearts.

original: March, noble lord,   Into our city with thy banners spread:   By decimation, and a tithed death—
translation: March into our city with your banners, Alcibiades,

original: If thy revenges hunger for that food   Which nature loathes—take thou the destined tenth,   And by the hazard of the spotted die   Let die the spotted.
translation: and if in an unnatural hunger for revenge you'd like to kill one tenth of the entire city, let those unfortunate enough to have gotten such a bad turn of the  dice die  for all the rest.

original: All have not offended;   For those that were, it is not square to take   On those that are, revenges: crimes, like lands,   Are not inherited.
translation: It is not everyone's fault that you are offended. It is not fair to avenge yourself on those that are here now for those who offended you then. Crimes should not be inherited like the land.

original: Then, dear countryman,   Bring in thy ranks, but leave without thy rage:   Spare thy Athenian cradle and those kin   Which in the bluster of thy wrath must fall   With those that have offended:
translation: Dear countrymen, bring in your army, but leave without your anger. Spare your hometown of Athens and those people who in your wrath you might otherwise kill.

original: like a shepherd,   Approach the fold and cull the infected forth,   But kill not all together.
translation: Be like a shepherd and approach the herd and separate the infected parts of it. Do not kill everyone.

original: What thou wilt, Thou rather shalt enforce it with thy smile Than hew to't with thy sword.
translation: Whatever you want, enforce it with mercy and not with violence.

original: Set but thy foot   Against our rampired gates, and they shall ope;
translation: Set your foot against the ramped-up walls and they will open,

original: So thou wilt send thy gentle heart before,   To say thou'lt enter friendly.
translation: but you should tell us before you come in peace.

original: Throw thy glove,   Or any token of thine honour else,   That thou wilt use the wars as thy redress   And not as our confusion,
translation: Throw your  gauntlet down , but do it so that you may use your army to redress the wrongs done to you, and not to destroy everyone here.

original: all thy powers   Shall make their harbour in our town, till we   Have seal'd thy full desire.
translation: You can put your entire force here peacefully until you get what you want.

original: Then there's my glove;   Descend, and open your uncharged ports:
translation: There's my glove, then. Descend now and open your gates.

original: Those enemies of Timon's and mine own   Whom you yourselves shall set out for reproof   Fall and no more:
translation: Those who were enemies of Timon and me you will hand over. They, and no one else, will die.

original: and, to atone your fears   With my more noble meaning, not a man   Shall pass his quarter, or offend the stream   Of regular justice in your city's bounds,
translation: And to calm your fear of me, no man of mine shall go beyond an assigned area, or disturb the peace within the city.

original: But shall be render'd to your public laws   At heaviest answer.
translation: If they do they will have to answer to harsh punishment.

original: 'Tis most nobly spoken.
translation: Well said.

original: Descend, and keep your words.
translation: Descend and do what you have promised.

original: My noble general, Timon is dead;   Entomb'd upon the very hem o' the sea;
translation: My noble general, Timon is dead. His grave lies on the shore,

original: And on his grave-stone this insculpture, which   With wax I brought away, whose soft impression   Interprets for my poor ignorance.
translation: and on that tombstone there is this epitaph, which I brought here on wax which will show you what I cannot in ignorance.

original: 'Here lies a   wretched corse, of wretched soul bereft:   Seek not my name: a plague consume you wicked   caitiffs left!
translation: "Here lies a poor corpse and a poor, disturbed soul. Do not look for my name, and may a disease strike all you remaining cowards!

original: Here lie I, Timon; who, alive, all living men did hate:   Pass by and curse thy fill, but pass and stay   not here thy gait.'
translation: Here I lie, Timon, who when alive all living men hated. Pass here and insult me to your heart's content, but go and do not stay here too long."

original: These well express in thee thy latter spirits:
translation: These words describe you in the depression of your later life.

original: Though thou abhorr'dst in us our human griefs,   Scorn'dst our brain's flow and those our   droplets which   From niggard nature fall, yet rich conceit   Taught thee to make vast Neptune weep for aye   On thy low grave, on faults forgiven.
translation: Though you hated our human grievances, scorned our tears which from our sad dispositions fell, still your ingenious mind taught you to make the god of the sea cry for you on your low grave, on your forgiven faults.

original: Dead   Is noble Timon: of whose memory   Hereafter more.
translation: The noble Timon is dead, who will be remembered from now on.

original: Bring me into your city,   And I will use the olive with my sword,   Make war breed peace, make peace stint war, make each   Prescribe to other as each other's leech.   Let our drums strike.
translation: Bring me into your city, and I will combine peace with war. I will make war end in peace, then make peace stop war, as if each were the doctors curing the other.  Strike the drums.

original: Noble patricians, patrons of my right,   Defend the justice of my cause with arms,   And, countrymen, my loving followers,   Plead my successive title with your swords:
translation: Noble  patricians , since you support my right to rule, defend my just cause with weapons.  And countrymen, my loyal followers, fight for my inheritance with your swords:

original: I am his first-born son, that was the last   That wore the imperial diadem of Rome;   Then let my father's honours live in me,   Nor wrong mine age with this indignity.
translation: I am the first-born son of the last emperor, so let me take the crown and don't make me lower myself to ask for it.

original: Romans, friends, followers, favorers of my right,   If ever Bassianus, Caesar's son,   Were gracious in the eyes of royal Rome,
translation: Romans, friends, followers, supporters of my right to rule—if Bassianus,  Caesar's son , ever had a good reputation in the eyes of royal Rome,

original: Keep then this passage to the Capitol   And suffer not dishonour to approach   The imperial seat, to virtue consecrate,   To justice, continence and nobility;
translation: then block this man's path. Don't let dishonor approach the imperial throne, where there should be only virtue, justice, restraint, and nobility.

original: But let desert in pure election shine,   And, Romans, fight for freedom in your choice.
translation: Instead, elect someone who deserves it, and Romans, fight for your right to freely choose your own emperor.

original: Princes, that strive by factions and by friends   Ambitiously for rule and empery,   Know that the people of Rome,
translation: Ambitious princes, fighting each other to become emperor! The people of Rome,

original: for whom we stand   A special party, have, by common voice,   In election for the Roman empery,   Chosen Andronicus, surnamed Pius   For many good and great deserts to Rome:   A nobler man, a braver warrior,   Lives not this day within the city walls:
translation: whom I have been elected to represent, have voted and chosen Andronicus—called "Andronicus Pius" for all his great deeds,  since there's no nobler man or braver warrior in all of Rome—as their new emperor.

original: He by the senate is accit'd home   From weary wars against the barbarous Goths;   That, with his sons, a terror to our foes,   Hath yoked a nation strong, train'd up in arms.
translation: The Senate has summoned him home from the war against the barbaric  Goths . With his sons, he defeated a strong nation that trains its warriors from their birth.

original: Ten years are spent since first he undertook   This cause of Rome and chastised with arms   Our enemies' pride: five times he hath return'd   Bleeding to Rome, bearing his valiant sons   In coffins from the field;
translation:
It’s been ten years since he first went to war and punished our enemies' pride with his weapons; he’s come
back five times, bearing the dead bodies of his brave sons.

original: And now at last, laden with horror's spoils,   Returns the good Andronicus to Rome,   Renowned Titus, flourishing in arms.
translation: And now at last, bringing prizes won during war, the famous Titus Andronicus returns to Rome in triumph.

original: Let us entreat, by honour of his name,   Whom worthily you would have now succeed.   And in the Capitol and senate's right,   Whom you pretend to honour and adore,
translation:
Let us ask you—out of
respect for the late emperor, the Capitol, and the Senate, which you claim to
honor—

original: That you withdraw you and abate your strength;   Dismiss your followers and, as suitors should,   Plead your deserts in peace and humbleness.
translation:
that you back down, dismiss your followers, and make your case peacefully
and humbly.

original: Marcus Andronicus, so I do ally   In thy uprightness and integrity,
translation: Marcus Andronicus, I have much respect for your honesty and integrity.

original: And so I love and honour thee and thine,   Thy noble brother Titus and his sons,   And her to whom my thoughts are humbled all,   Gracious Lavinia, Rome's rich ornament,
translation: And I have so much love and honor for you and your family—your noble brother Titus and his sons, and lovely Lavinia, the object of my affections—

original: That I will here dismiss my loving friends,   And to my fortunes and the people's favor   Commit my cause in balance to be weigh'd.
translation: that I will dismiss my followers, and let the people decide my fate.

original: Friends, that have been thus forward in my right,   I thank you all and here dismiss you all,
translation: Friends and supporters: I thank you and dismiss you all,

original: And to the love and favor of my country   Commit myself, my person and the cause.
translation: relying only on the love and respect of my country to judge my cause.

original: Rome, be as just and gracious unto me As I am confident and kind to thee. Open the gates, and let me in.
translation: Rome, be as fair and gracious to me as I’ve been straightforward and kind to you. Open the gates, and let me in.

original: Tribunes, and me, a poor competitor.
translation: Tribunes, let me—a poor competitor—in, too.

original: Romans, make way: the good Andronicus.   Patron of virtue, Rome's best champion,   Successful in the battles that he fights,
translation: Romans, make way: the good Andronicus, model of virtue, Rome’s best champion, victorious in battle,

original: With honour and with fortune is return'd   From where he circumscribed with his sword,   And brought to yoke, the enemies of Rome.
translation: returns from the wars with honor and good fortune, having defeated and captured our enemies.

original: Hail, Rome, victorious in thy mourning weeds!   Lo, as the bark, that hath discharged her fraught,   Returns with precious jading to the bay   From whence at first she weigh'd her anchorage,   Cometh Andronicus, bound with laurel boughs,
translation: Hail Rome, victorious even in your mourning clothes! Like the ship returned home with treasures from abroad, Andronicus comes crowned with laurels of victory,

original: To re-salute his country with his tears,   Tears of true joy for his return to Rome.
translation: to re-salute his country with tears—tears of true joy—for his return.

original: Thou great defender of this Capitol,   Stand gracious to the rites that we intend!
translation: Jupiter Capitolinus , defender of the city, accept our offering!

original: Romans, of five and twenty valiant sons,   Half of the number that King Priam had,   Behold the poor remains, alive and dead!
translation: Romans, these men are all that’s left of my twenty-five sons (half the number that  King Priam  had). Look at them!

original: These that survive let Rome reward with love;   These that I bring unto their latest home,   With burial amongst their ancestors:
translation: The ones who are still alive deserve your love and gratitude; the ones who are dead I will bury with their ancestors.

original: Here Goths have given me leave to sheathe my sword.   Titus, unkind and careless of thine own,
translation: Here, for once, I’m putting down my sword. Titus, you've been unkind and careless to your own children.

original: Why suffer'st thou thy sons, unburied yet,   To hover on the dreadful shore of Styx?   Make way to lay them by their brethren.
translation: Why do you allow your unburied sons to remain on the shores of the  Styx ? Make way, so that I can bury them with their brothers.

original: Give us the proudest prisoner of the Goths,   That we may hew his limbs, and on a pile   Ad manes fratrum sacrifice his flesh,   Before this earthy prison of their bones;
translation: Give us the highest-ranking Goth prisoner, so that we can cut his limbs and for the spirits of our brothers sacrifice him in front of this tomb:

original: That so the shadows be not unappeased,   Nor we disturb'd with prodigies on earth.
translation: that way their spirits will be at rest and they won't haunt us.

original: I give him you, the noblest that survives, The eldest son of this distressed queen.
translation: I give you the noblest of my prisoners, the eldest son of this defeated queen.

original: Stay, Roman brethren! Gracious conqueror,   Victorious Titus, rue the tears I shed,   A mother's tears in passion for her son:
translation: Stop, Roman friends! Gracious conqueror, victorious Titus, pity the tears I shed, for they’re a mother’s tears for her son.

original: And if thy sons were ever dear to thee,   O, think my son to be as dear to me!
translation: If you ever loved your sons, imagine that I love my son just as much!

original: Sufficeth not that we are brought to Rome,   To beautify thy triumphs and return,   Captive to thee and to thy Roman yoke,
translation: Isn’t it enough that we’re brought to Rome, to add to your triumph, as your prisoners?

original: But must my sons be slaughter'd in the streets,   For valiant doings in their country's cause?   O, if to fight for king and commonweal   Were piety in thine, it is in these.
translation: Do you also have to slaughter my sons in the streets, just because they fought to protect their homeland? If your sons were brave to fight for their country, then mine were as well.

original: Andronicus, stain not thy tomb with blood:   Wilt thou draw near the nature of the gods?
translation: Andronicus, don’t stain your tomb with blood: don’t you want to be like a god?

original: Draw near them then in being merciful:   Sweet mercy is nobility's true badge:   Thrice noble Titus, spare my first-born son.
translation: Be like a god in being merciful, for sweet mercy is the truest sign of nobility. Noble Titus, let my first-born son live.

original: Patient yourself, madam, and pardon me.   These are their brethren, whom you Goths beheld   Alive and dead, and for their brethren slain   Religiously they ask a sacrifice:
translation: Calm yourself, madam, and forgive me. These are their brothers, who you saw alive and dead, and for their dead brothers they ask a religious sacrifice.

original: To this your son is mark'd, and die he must,   To appease their groaning shadows that are gone.
translation: Your son must die, to satisfy the ghosts of the dead.

original: Away with him! and make a fire straight; And with our swords, upon a pile of wood, Let's hew his limbs till they be clean consumed.
translation: Take him away! And build a fire: let’s cut him to pieces with our swords on a pile of wood, until he’s consumed by the flames.

original: O cruel, irreligious piety!
translation: Oh, cruel, irreligious faith!

original: Was ever Scythia half so barbarous?
Oppose not Scythia to ambitious Rome.   Alarbus goes to rest; and we survive   To tremble under Titus' threatening looks.
translation: Ambitious Rome is no better than Scythia. Alarbus is dead, and we live only as Titus’s prisoners.

original: Then, madam, stand resolved, but hope withal   The self-same gods that arm'd the Queen of Troy   With opportunity of sharp revenge   Upon the Thracian tyrant in his tent,
translation: Then, madam, prepare for death. But don’t give up hope that the gods —who gave the Queen of Troy opportunity to  take revenge on the Thracian tyrant  in his tent—

original: May favor Tamora, the Queen of Goths—   When Goths were Goths and Tamora was queen—   To quit the bloody wrongs upon her foes.
translation: might favor Tamora, the Queen of Goths (when you were still queen and we were still Goths, that is) to give them what they deserve.

original: See, lord and father, how we have perform'd   Our Roman rites: Alarbus' limbs are lopp'd,   And entrails feed the sacrificing fire,   Whose smoke, like incense, doth perfume the sky.
translation: See, lord and father, how we’ve done our Roman sacrifice: Alarbus's limbs are cut off and his innards feed the fire as the smoke perfumes the sky.

original: Remaineth nought, but to inter our brethren,   And with loud 'larums welcome them to Rome.
translation: There's nothing else to do but bury our brothers and welcome them to Rome with celebration.

original: Let it be so; and let Andronicus Make this his latest farewell to their souls.
translation: Let it be so, but first Andronicus will say a last goodbye to their souls.

original: In peace and honour rest you here, my sons;   Rome's readiest champions, repose you here in rest,   Secure from worldly chances and mishaps!
translation: Rest in peace and honor here, my sons: you were always ready to serve Rome, so rest here safe from any more suffering.

original: Here lurks no treason, here no envy swells,   Here grow no damned grudges; here are no storms,   No noise, but silence and eternal sleep:   In peace and honour rest you here, my sons!
translation: Here there’s no treason, no jealousy, no grudges. Here are no storms, no noise, but just silence and eternal sleep: rest in peace and honor here, my sons!

original: In peace and honour live Lord Titus long;   My noble lord and father, live in fame!
translation: Lord Titus, my noble lord and father, may you live forever in peace, honor, and good reputation!

original: Lo, at this tomb my tributary tears   I render, for my brethren's obsequies;
translation: I cry at this tomb for my brothers,

original: And at thy feet I kneel, with tears of joy,   Shed on the earth, for thy return to Rome:
translation: and I kneel at your feet with tears of joy for your return to Rome.

original: O, bless me here with thy victorious hand,   Whose fortunes Rome's best citizens applaud!
translation: Oh, bless me with your victorious hand, applauded by Rome’s best citizens!

original: Kind Rome, that hast thus lovingly reserved   The cordial of mine age to glad my heart!
translation: Kind Rome, you have given me this sweet medicine to make my heart happy again.

original: Lavinia, live; outlive thy father's days,   And fame's eternal date, for virtue's praise!
translation: Lavinia, live: outlive your father, and may everyone remember your virtue after you’re gone.

original: Long live Lord Titus, my beloved brother, Gracious triumpher in the eyes of Rome!
translation: Long live Lord Titus, my beloved brother, gracious victor in the eyes of Rome!

original: Thanks, gentle tribune, noble brother Marcus.
translation: Thanks, kind tribune, noble brother Marcus.

original: And welcome, nephews, from successful wars,   You that survive, and you that sleep in fame!   Fair lords, your fortunes are alike in all,   That in your country's service drew your swords:
translation: And welcome, nephews, from successful wars—both you who survived and you that died. Lords, everyone who fought for his country is equal in our eyes.

original: But safer triumph is this funeral pomp,   That hath aspired to Solon's happiness   And triumphs over chance in honour's bed.
translation: Your dead sons' funeral is a greater triumph than the happiness we who survive enjoy, for they have achieved the honor and security  Solon  praised.

original: Titus Andronicus, the people of Rome,   Whose friend in justice thou hast ever been,   Send thee by me, their tribune and their trust,   This palliament of white and spotless hue;
translation: But Titus Andronicus, the people of Rome—you’ve always been their friend—have sent me, their tribune, to give you this white  palliament

original: And name thee in election for the empire,   With these our late-deceased emperor's sons:   Be candidatus then, and put it on,   And help to set a head on headless Rome.
translation: and tell you that they have elected you as their emperor. Be  candidatus  with the sons of our late emperor, then, and put it on, helping to set a head on  headless Rome .

original: A better head her glorious body fits   Than his that shakes for age and feebleness:   What should I don this robe, and trouble you?
translation: Her glorious body could do with a better head, one that doesn’t shake with age and weakness. Why should I put on this robe, and trouble you?

original: Be chosen with proclamations to-day,   To-morrow yield up rule, resign my life,   And set abroad new business for you all?
translation: If you choose me today, tomorrow I’ll die, and you’ll have to go about the whole business again.

original: Rome, I have been thy soldier forty years,   And led my country's strength successfully,   And buried one and twenty valiant sons,   Knighted in field, slain manfully in arms,   In right and service of their noble country:
translation: Rome, I have been your soldier for forty years, led my country's army successfully, and buried twenty-one brave sons, killed fighting for their country.

original: Give me a staff of honour for mine age,   But not a sceptre to control the world:   Upright he held it, lords, that held it last.
translation: Give me a staff of honor in my old age, but not a scepter to control the world: the last one who held it was stronger than I am.

original: Titus, thou shalt obtain and ask the empery.
translation: Titus, you will be emperor if you ask for it.

original: Proud and ambitious tribune, canst thou tell?
translation: Proud and ambitious tribune, how can you tell?

original: Patience, Prince Saturninus.
translation: Calm down, Prince Saturninus.

original: Romans, do me right:   Patricians, draw your swords: and sheathe them not   Till Saturninus be Rome's emperor.
translation: Romans, do the right thing: patricians, draw your swords, and don’t put them away until Saturninus is Rome’s emperor.

original: Andronicus, would thou wert shipp'd to hell,   Rather than rob me of the people's hearts!
translation: Andronicus, I’d rather you were shipped to hell than steal the people’s love from me!

original: Proud Saturnine, interrupter of the good That noble-minded Titus means to thee!
translation: Proud Saturnine, you’re getting in your own way—Titus is trying to do you a favor!

original: Content thee, prince; I will restore to thee The people's hearts, and wean them from themselves.
translation: It will be all right, prince; I’ll make the people love you again.

original: Andronicus, I do not flatter thee,   But honour thee, and will do till I die:
translation: Andronicus, I say without flattery that I respect you, and will do so until I die.

original: My faction if thou strengthen with thy friends,   I will most thankful be; and thanks to men   Of noble minds is honourable meed.
translation: If you give me your support, I’ll be thankful to you; and thanks is good food for honorable men.

original: People of Rome, and people's tribunes here, I ask your voices and your suffrages: Will you bestow them friendly on Andronicus?
translation: People of Rome, and their representatives here, I ask for your voices and your votes: will you let Andronicus choose the next emperor?

original: To gratify the good Andronicus, And gratulate his safe return to Rome, The people will accept whom he admits.
translation: To please the good Andronicus, and celebrate his safe return to Rome, the people will accept whom he recommends.

original: Tribunes, I thank you: and this suit I make,   That you create your emperor's eldest son,   Lord Saturnine;
translation: Tribunes, thank you: I ask you to elect the emperor's eldest son, Lord Saturnine.

original: whose virtues will, I hope,   Reflect on Rome as Titan's rays on earth,   And ripen justice in this commonweal:
translation: I hope his virtues will shine on Rome like the sun, ripening justice in our country.

original: Then, if you will elect by my advice,   Crown him and say 'Long live our emperor!'
translation: So if you will elect him on my recommendation, crown him and say "Long live our emperor!"

original: With voices and applause of every sort,   Patricians and plebeians, we create   Lord Saturninus Rome's great emperor,
translation: With the voices of us all—patricians and  plebeians —we elect Lord Saturninus as Rome's great emperor,

original: And say 'Long live our Emperor Saturnine!'
translation: and say "Long live our Emperor Saturnine!"

original: Titus Andronicus, for thy favors done   To us in our election this day,   I give thee thanks in part of thy deserts,   And will with deeds requite thy gentleness:
translation: Titus Andronicus, I thank you for the favor you’ve done me, and in return will show my gratitude with actions.

original: And, for an onset, Titus, to advance   Thy name and honourable family,   Lavinia will I make my empress,   Rome's royal mistress, mistress of my heart,   And in the sacred Pantheon her espouse:
translation: To bring your family up in the world, I’ll marry your daughter Lavinia in the holy  Pantheon  and make her Rome’s empress and mistress of my heart.

original: Tell me, Andronicus, doth this motion please thee?
translation: Tell me, Andronicus, does this please you?

original: It doth, my worthy lord; and in this match   I hold me highly honour'd of your grace:
translation: It does, my worthy lord; you honor me with this match.

original: And here in sight of Rome to Saturnine,   King and commander of our commonweal,   The wide world's emperor, do I consecrate   My sword, my chariot and my prisoners;
translation: And here in front of all Rome, I give to you my sword, my chariot, and my prisoners,

original: Presents well worthy Rome's imperial lord:   Receive them then, the tribute that I owe,   Mine honour's ensigns humbled at thy feet.
translation: presents worthy of Rome’s imperial lord: take them then, as the tribute I owe you.

original: Thanks, noble Titus, father of my life!   How proud I am of thee and of thy gifts   Rome shall record,
translation: Thanks, noble Titus, father of my life! Rome will know how proud I am of you and your gifts,

original: and when I do forget   The least of these unspeakable deserts,   Romans, forget your fealty to me.
translation: and when I forget the least of them, Romans, forget your loyalty to me.

original: [To TAMORA]   Now, madam, are you prisoner to   an emperor;
translation: [To TAMORA]  Now, madam, you're the prisoner of an emperor;

original: To him that, for your honour and your state,   Will use you nobly and your followers.
translation: out of respect for your honor and rank, he'll treat you and your followers well.

original: A goodly lady, trust me; of the hue   That I would choose, were I to choose anew.   Clear up, fair queen, that cloudy countenance:
translation: A lovely lady, trust me; of the sort that I would choose, if I could choose again. Don't make that sad face, beautiful queen:

original: Though chance of war hath wrought this change of cheer,   Thou comest not to be made a scorn in Rome:   Princely shall be thy usage every way.
translation: although you've been defeated in war, you aren't in Rome to be humiliated. You'll be treated like a queen in every way.

original: Rest on my word, and let not discontent   Daunt all your hopes: madam, he comforts you   Can make you greater than the Queen of Goths.
translation: Trust me, and don't let grief blight your hopes: madam, the man that comforts you can make you greater than the Queen of Goths.

original: Lavinia, you are not displeased with this?
translation: Lavinia, aren't you angry about this?

original: Not I, my lord; sith true nobility Warrants these words in princely courtesy.
translation: Not I, my lord; a king should speak nobly and courteously.

original: Thanks, sweet Lavinia. Romans, let us go; Ransomless here we set our prisoners free: Proclaim our honours, lords, with trump and drum.
translation: Thanks, sweet Lavinia. Romans, let us go; we set these prisoners free without ransom. Celebrate our honor, lords, with trumpets and drums.

original: Lord Titus, by your leave, this maid is mine.
translation: Lord Titus, with all due respect, this girl is mine.

original: How, sir! are you in earnest then, my lord?
translation: How could this be, sir? Are you serious, my lord?

original: Ay, noble Titus; and resolved withal To do myself this reason and this right.
translation: Yes, noble Titus; and I'm prepared to fight for her.

original: 'Suum cuique' is our Roman justice: This prince in justice seizeth but his own.
translation: "To each his own" is our Roman law; this prince takes what is his by right.

original: And that he will, and shall, if Lucius live.
translation: And that he will, and shall, if Lucius is alive to fight for it.

original: Traitors, avaunt! Where is the emperor's guard? Treason, my lord! Lavinia is surprised!
translation: Traitors, stop! Where are the emperor's guards? Treason, my lord! Lavinia is taken!

original: Surprised! by whom?
translation: Taken! By whom?

original: By him that justly may Bear his betroth'd from all the world away.
translation: By her betrothed, who can justly take her away from all the world.

original: Brothers, help to convey her hence away, And with my sword I'll keep this door safe.
translation: Brothers, help me take her away, and I'll guard this door with my sword.
