original: Follow, my lord, and I'll soon bring her back.
translation: Come with me, my lord, and I'll bring her back soon.

original: My lord, you pass not here.
translation: My lord, you can't pass me.

original: What, villain boy! Barr'st me my way in Rome?
translation: What, stupid boy! You stand in my way in Rome?

original: Help, Lucius, help!
translation: Help, Lucius, help!

original: My lord, you are unjust, and, more than so, In wrongful quarrel you have slain your son.
translation: My lord, you are wrong, and, more than that, you've killed your own son.

original: Nor thou, nor he, are any sons of mine; My sons would never so dishonour me: Traitor, restore Lavinia to the emperor.
translation: He's no son of mine, and nor are you: my sons would never dishonor me like this. Traitor, give Lavinia to the emperor.

original: Dead, if you will; but not to be his wife, That is another's lawful promised love.
translation: I'll give her to you dead, if you want; but she'll never be his wife. She is lawfully betrothed to another.

original: No, Titus, no; the emperor needs her not,   Nor her, nor thee, nor any of thy stock:
translation: No, Titus, no; the emperor doesn't need her, nor you, nor any of your family.

original: I'll trust, by leisure, him that mocks me once;   Thee never, nor thy traitorous haughty sons,   Confederates all thus to dishonour me.
translation: I might learn to trust a man again after he made fun of me once; but I'll never trust you, nor your traitorous and proud sons, since you all planned together to dishonor me.

original: Was there none else in Rome to make a stale,   But Saturnine? Full well, Andronicus,   Agree these deeds with that proud brag of thine,   That said'st I begg'd the empire at thy hands.
translation: Wasn't there anyone else in Rome that you could mock other than Saturnine? This stunt perfectly matches your ridiculous brag that I begged you to give me the empire.

original: O monstrous! what reproachful words are these?
translation: Oh, monstrous! Why are you saying these cruel things to me?

original: But go thy ways; go, give that changing piece   To him that flourish'd for her with his sword   A valiant son-in-law thou shalt enjoy;
translation: But go away; go give your silly daughter to the man who waved his sword around for her. You'll have a brave son-in-law,

original: One fit to bandy with thy lawless sons,   To ruffle in the commonwealth of Rome.
translation: one fit to squabble with your law-breaking sons, disturbing the peace in Rome.

original: These words are razors to my wounded heart.
translation: These words cut my wounded heart like knives.

original: And therefore, lovely Tamora, queen of Goths,   That like the stately Phoebe 'mongst her nymphs   Dost overshine the gallant'st dames of Rome,
translation: And so, lovely Tamora, Queen of Goths—that, like  Phoebe  among her nymphs, outshines all the loveliest women of Rome—

original: If thou be pleased with this my sudden choice,   Behold, I choose thee, Tamora, for my bride,   And will create thee empress of Rome,   Speak, Queen of Goths, dost thou applaud my choice?
translation: if you accept my sudden proposal, I choose you, Tamora, for my wife, and will make you empress of Rome. Say something, Queen of Goths, do you approve of my choice?

original: And here I swear by all the Roman gods,   Sith priest and holy water are so near   And tapers burn so bright and every thing   In readiness for Hymenaeus stand,
translation: And I promise by all the Roman gods, since we have the priest, the holy water, and the candles here already,

original: I will not re-salute the streets of Rome,   Or climb my palace, till from forth this place   I lead espoused my bride along with me.
translation: I won't go out into the streets of Rome or to my palace until we're married.

original: And here, in sight of heaven, to Rome I swear,   If Saturnine advance the Queen of Goths,
translation: And here, by heaven, I swear to Rome that if Saturnine marries the Queen of Goths,

original: She will a handmaid be to his desires,   A loving nurse, a mother to his youth.
translation: she will be a servant to his desires, a loving nurse, and a mother to his youth.

original: Ascend, fair queen, Pantheon. Lords, accompany   Your noble emperor and his lovely bride,   Sent by the heavens for Prince Saturnine,
translation: Come up, my fair queen, and let's go to the  Pantheon . Lords, come with your noble emperor and his lovely bride, sent from heaven to Prince Saturnine,

original: Whose wisdom hath her fortune conquered:   There shall we consummate our spousal rites.
translation: who has wisely looked past her misfortune—there we will be married.

original: I am not bid to wait upon this bride. Titus, when wert thou wont to walk alone, Dishonour'd thus, and challenged of wrongs?
translation: I am not asked to go with them. Titus, when was the last time you walked alone, dishonored and accused of doing wrong?

original: O Titus, see, O, see what thou hast done! In a bad quarrel slain a virtuous son.
translation: Oh, Titus, see, oh, see what you have done! In a rash fight you've killed a virtuous son.

original: No, foolish tribune, no; no son of mine,   Nor thou, nor these, confederates in the deed   That hath dishonour'd all our family;
translation: No, foolish tribune, no; he was no son of mine, nor are you, nor these, who participated in dishonoring our family.

original: Unworthy brother, and unworthy sons!
translation: Unworthy brother, and unworthy sons!

original: But let us give him burial, as becomes; Give Mutius burial with our brethren.
translation: But at least let us bury him, as we should; give Mutius burial with our brothers.

original: Traitors, away! he rests not in this tomb:   This monument five hundred years hath stood,   Which I have sumptuously re-edified:
translation: Traitors, go away! He won't rest in this tomb: this monument has stood for five hundred years, and I have restored it at great expense,

original: Here none but soldiers and Rome's servitors   Repose in fame; none basely slain in brawls:   Bury him where you can; he comes not here.
translation: and only Rome's soldiers and servants are buried here in here, not those killed in low street fights. Bury him wherever you want, since he won't be buried here.

original: My lord, this is impiety in you: My nephew Mutius' deeds do plead for him He must be buried with his brethren.
translation: My lord, this is not fair. My nephew Mutius did something honorable; he must be buried with his brothers.

original: And shall, or him we will accompany.
translation: And he shall, or we'll go with him to the grave.

original: 'And shall!' what villain was it that spake that word?
translation: "And shall!" What villain said that?

original: He that would vouch it in any place but here.
translation: He that would fight for it in any place less holy than here.

original: What, would you bury him in my despite?
translation: What, would you bury him here without my permission?

original: No, noble Titus, but entreat of thee To pardon Mutius and to bury him.
translation: No, noble Titus, but we beg you to pardon Mutius and bury him.

original: Marcus, even thou hast struck upon my crest,   And, with these boys, mine honour thou hast wounded:
translation: Marcus, even you are against me; and with these boys, you've wounded my honor.

original: My foes I do repute you every one;   So, trouble me no more, but get you gone.
translation: You're all my enemies, so don't bother me anymore, but go away.

original: He is not with himself; let us withdraw.
translation: He is not himself; let's go.

original: Not I, till Mutius' bones be buried.
translation: I won't go until we've buried Mutius.

original: Brother, for in that name doth nature plead,—
translation: Brother, for that word reminds you of the natural ties between us—

original: Father, and in that name doth nature speak,—
translation: Father, and in that word nature speaks too—

original: Speak thou no more, if all the rest will speed.
translation: Don't say anything else, if this is going where I think it is.

original: Renowned Titus, more than half my soul,—
translation: Famous Titus, more than half my soul—

original: Dear father, soul and substance of us all,—
translation: Dear father, soul and body of us all—

original: Suffer thy brother Marcus to inter   His noble nephew here in virtue's nest,   That died in honour and Lavinia's cause.
translation: Let your brother Marcus bury his noble nephew here with honor, since he died for Lavinia's cause.

original: Thou art a Roman; be not barbarous:   The Greeks upon advice did bury Ajax   That slew himself; and wise Laertes' son   Did graciously plead for his funerals:
translation: You are a Roman; don't be uncivilized.  The Greeks buried Ajax , although he killed himself, after wise  Laertes's son  begged for a funeral:

original: Let not young Mutius, then, that was thy joy   Be barr'd his entrance here.
translation: so don't let young Mutius, who you loved, be prevented from joining his brothers.

original: Rise, Marcus, rise.   The dismall'st day is this that e'er I saw,   To be dishonour'd by my sons in Rome!
translation: Get up, Marcus, get up. This is the saddest day I ever saw, to be dishonored by my sons in Rome!

original: Well, bury him, and bury me the next.
translation: Well, bury him, and bury me next.

original: There lie thy bones, sweet Mutius, with thy friends, Till we with trophies do adorn thy tomb.
translation: Lie there, sweet Mutius, with your friends, until we cover your tomb with trophies won in battle.

original: No man shed tears for noble Mutius; He lives in fame that died in virtue's cause.
translation: Let no one cry for noble Mutius, since the person who dies fighting for what's right will live forever in memory.

original: My lord, to step out of these dreary dumps, How comes it that the subtle Queen of Goths Is of a sudden thus advanced in Rome?
translation: My lord, to leave these sad thoughts behind: how did it happen that the clever Queen of Goths is suddenly our empress?

original: I know not, Marcus; but I know it is,   Whether by device or no, the heavens can tell:
translation: I don't know, Marcus; but I know it's happened, and whether by some trickery or not, only the heavens can tell.

original: Is she not then beholding to the man   That brought her for this high good turn so far?   Yes, and will nobly him remunerate.
translation: But shouldn't she feel grateful to the man who has raised her so high? Yes, and she'll respond in kind.

original: So, Bassianus, you have play'd your prize: God give you joy, sir, of your gallant bride!
translation: So, Bassianus, you have won your prize. God make you happy with your lovely bride!

original: And you of yours, my lord! I say no more, Nor wish no less; and so, I take my leave.
translation: And you with yours, my lord! I have nothing else to say, and don't wish you any less, so I'll go now.

original: Traitor, if Rome have law or we have power, Thou and thy faction shall repent this rape.
translation: Traitor, if there's law in Rome or if we have power, you and your brothers will regret this rape.

original: Rape, call you it, my lord, to seize my own,   My truth-betrothed love and now my wife?
translation: You call it rape, my lord, to take my own, my true love and fiancee and now my wife?

original: But let the laws of Rome determine all;   Meanwhile I am possess'd of that is mine.
translation: But let the law of Rome take its course; in the meantime, I have what is mine.

original: 'Tis good, sir: you are very short with us; But, if we live, we'll be as sharp with you.
translation: All right, sir, you are very rude to us. But, if we live, you might find that I can be as sharp with you.

original: My lord, what I have done, as best I may,   Answer I must and shall do with my life.   Only thus much I give your grace to know:
translation: My lord, I'll answer for what I've done, with my life if I must. But I'll just say this:

original: By all the duties that I owe to Rome,   This noble gentleman, Lord Titus here,   Is in opinion and in honour wrong'd;
translation: I swear by my duty to Rome that this noble gentleman, Lord Titus here, has suffered a wrong at your hands.

original: That in the rescue of Lavinia   With his own hand did slay his youngest son,   In zeal to you and highly moved to wrath   To be controll'd in that he frankly gave:
translation: In the rescue of Lavinia, he killed his youngest son out of loyalty to you and in anger at being forced to go back on his word.

original: Receive him, then, to favor, Saturnine,   That hath express'd himself in all his deeds   A father and a friend to thee and Rome.
translation: Favor him, then, Saturnine, since he's proven himself in everything he does to be a father and friend to you and Rome.

original: Prince Bassianus, leave to plead my deeds:   'Tis thou and those that have dishonour'd me.
translation: Prince Bassianus, I can defend myself without your help; it's you and your friends who have dishonored me.

original: Rome and the righteous heavens be my judge,   How I have loved and honour'd Saturnine!
translation: Rome and heaven above know my love and loyalty to Saturnine!

original: My worthy lord, if ever Tamora   Were gracious in those princely eyes of thine,   Then hear me speak in indifferently for all;
translation: My worthy lord, if you ever loved Tamora, then let me speak as a neutral party.

original: And at my suit, sweet, pardon what is past.
translation: At my request, sweetheart, forgive what's in the past.

original: What, madam! be dishonour'd openly, And basely put it up without revenge?
translation: What, madam! Can I put up with these insults?

original: Not so, my lord; the gods of Rome forfend   I should be author to dishonour you!
translation: Of course not, my lord; the gods of Rome forbid that I would urge you to do anything dishonorable!

original: But on mine honour dare I undertake   For good Lord Titus' innocence in all;   Whose fury not dissembled speaks his griefs:
translation: But I vouch for good Lord Titus's innocence in everything; you can see his grief on his face.

original: Then, at my suit, look graciously on him;   Lose not so noble a friend on vain suppose,   Nor with sour looks afflict his gentle heart.
translation: Then, at my request, forgive him. Don't lose a noble friend out of suspicion, or hurt his soft heart with angry looks.

original: [Aside to SATURNINUS]   be won at last;   Dissemble all your griefs and discontents:   You are but newly planted in your throne;
translation: [So only SATURNINUS can hear]  Listen to me: hide what you're feeling. You just took the throne—

original: Lest, then, the people, and patricians too,   Upon a just survey, take Titus' part,   And so supplant you for ingratitude,
translation: so, unless you want the people and patricians to take Titus's side, and unseat you for not being grateful to him

original: Which Rome reputes to be a heinous sin,   Yield at entreats; and then let me alone:   I'll find a day to massacre them all   And raze their faction and their family,
translation: (and Romans hate ingratitude), forgive him. And then let me work: I'll find a day to kill them all. I'll destroy their faction and family,

original: The cruel father and his traitorous sons,   To whom I sued for my dear son's life,
translation: the cruel father and his traitorous sons—to whom I begged for my son's life.

original: And make them know what 'tis to let a queen   Kneel in the streets and beg for grace in vain.
translation: I'll make them know what happens to those who let a queen kneel in the streets and beg in vain.

original: [Aloud]   Come, come, sweet emperor; come, Andronicus;
translation: [To all]  Come, come, sweet emperor; come, Andronicus.

original: Take up this good old man, and cheer the heart   That dies in tempest of thy angry frown.
translation: Raise up this good old man, and cheer him up, since he's miserable when you frown at him.

original: Rise, Titus, rise; my empress hath prevail'd.
translation: Rise, Titus, rise; my empress has convinced me.

original: I thank your majesty, and her, my lord: These words, these looks, infuse new life in me.
translation: I thank your majesty, and her, my lord. These words and looks of forgiveness give new life to me.

original: Titus, I am incorporate in Rome,   A Roman now adopted happily,   And must advise the emperor for his good.
translation: Titus, I am now a Roman, and must give the emperor good advice.

original: This day all quarrels die, Andronicus;   And let it be mine honour, good my lord,   That I have reconciled your friends and you.
translation: Let's forget all our past quarrels today, Andronicus; and let it be my chief accomplishment that I've brought you all back together.

original: For you, Prince Bassianus, I have pass'd   My word and promise to the emperor,   That you will be more mild and tractable.
translation: For you, Prince Bassianus, I have promised the emperor that you'll be more mild and obedient in the future.

original: And fear not lords, and you, Lavinia;   By my advice, all humbled on your knees,   You shall ask pardon of his majesty.
translation: And don't be afraid, lords, and you, Lavinia: take my advice, kneel down, and ask his majesty for forgiveness.

original: We do, and vow to heaven and to his highness, That what we did was mildly as we might, Tendering our sister's honour and our own.
translation: We do, and promise heaven and his highness, that we were as moderate as we could be, when our sister's honor and our own was at stake.

original: That, on mine honour, here I do protest.
translation: I vow that too, on my honor.

original: Away, and talk not; trouble us no more.
translation: Go away, and be quiet; don't bother us anymore.

original: Nay, nay, sweet emperor, we must all be friends: The tribune and his nephews kneel for grace; I will not be denied: sweet heart, look back.
translation: No, no, sweet emperor; we must all be friends. The tribune and his nephews kneel for forgiveness. I won't be denied: sweetheart, look at them.

original: Marcus, for thy sake and thy brother's here,   And at my lovely Tamora's entreats,   I do remit these young men's heinous faults:
translation: Marcus, for the sake of you and your brother, and because Tamora begs me, I forgive these young men's crimes against me.

original: Stand up.   Lavinia, though you left me like a churl,   I found a friend, and sure as death I swore   I would not part a bachelor from the priest.
translation: Stand up. Lavinia, though you left me harshly, I would not have found my love if you hadn't: I swore that I wouldn't walk away from the priest without a wife.

original: Come, if the emperor's court can feast two brides,   You are my guest, Lavinia, and your friends.   This day shall be a love-day, Tamora.
translation: Come, if the emperor's court will celebrate two brides, you'll be my guest, Lavinia, and your family. This day will be a love-day, Tamora.

original: To-morrow, an it please your majesty To hunt the panther and the hart with me, With horn and hound we'll give your grace bonjour.
translation: Tomorrow, if your majesty likes, we can go hunting for panther and deer. We'll wake you with the sounds of our dogs and horns.

original: Be it so, Titus, and gramercy too.
translation: We will come, Titus, and many thanks to you.

original: Now climbeth Tamora Olympus' top,   Safe out of fortune's shot; and sits aloft,   Secure of thunder's crack or lightning flash;   Advanced above pale envy's threatening reach.
translation: So now Tamora is as high as  Olympus , safe from misfortune and jealousy. She's safe from both thunder's crack and lightning's flash,  having ascended farther than envy can reach.

original: As when the golden sun salutes the morn,   And, having gilt the ocean with his beams,   Gallops the zodiac in his glistering coach,   And overlooks the highest-peering hills;   So Tamora:
translation: She's like the golden sun that greets the morning, and, having crowned the ocean with its beams, gallops across the sky in a glittering coach and looks down on even the highest hills.

original: Upon her wit doth earthly honour wait,   And virtue stoops and trembles at her frown.
translation: Honorable and virtuous men wait for her words, and tremble when she frowns.

original: Then, Aaron, arm thy heart, and fit thy thoughts,   To mount aloft with thy imperial mistress,   And mount her pitch, whom thou in triumph long   Hast prisoner held,
translation: Then, Aaron, arm your heart and make your thoughts fit to go to the top with your imperial mistress—since she's been your prisoner in love for a long time,

original: fetter'd in amorous chains   And faster bound to Aaron's charming eyes   Than is Prometheus tied to Caucasus.
translation: bound to you with tighter chains that  Prometheus  was tied to that rock in the Caucasus.

original: Away with slavish weeds and servile thoughts!   I will be bright, and shine in pearl and gold,   To wait upon this new-made empress.
translation: Cast away poor clothing and low thoughts! I will be bright, shining in pearl and gold, when I serve this new-made empress.

original: To wait, said I? to wanton with this queen,   This goddess, this Semiramis, this nymph,   This siren, that will charm Rome's Saturnine,   And see his shipwreck and his commonweal's.
translation: Did I say serve? I meant that I'll play with this queen, this goddess, this  Semiramis , this nymph, this  siren , that will charm Rome's Saturnine, and lead him to his ruin.

original: Holloa! what storm is this?
translation: But what's all this noise?

original: Chiron, thy years want wit, thy wit wants edge, And manners, to intrude where I am graced; And may, for aught thou know'st, affected be.
translation: Chiron, you're young and stupid, and you don't have what it takes to get in my way and intrude where I'm welcome.

original: Demetrius, thou dost over-ween in all;   And so in this, to bear me down with braves.
translation: Demetrius, you've always been arrogant, and it's no different in this.

original: 'Tis not the difference of a year or two   Makes me less gracious or thee more fortunate:
translation: You're only a year or two older than me, and that doesn't make you any better.

original: I am as able and as fit as thou   To serve, and to deserve my mistress' grace;   And that my sword upon thee shall approve,   And plead my passions for Lavinia's love.
translation: I'm as fit as you to serve my mistress and make her love me. And I'll prove it with my sword, to show how much I want Lavinia's love.

original: Clubs, clubs! these lovers will not keep the peace.
translation: I'll have to call the guards; these lovers will start fighting each other soon.

original: Why, boy, although our mother, unadvised,   Gave you a dancing-rapier by your side,   Are you so desperate grown, to threat your friends?
translation: Why, boy, ever since our mother gave you a toy sword you've been desperate to start brandishing it around.

original: Go to; have your lath glued within your sheath   Till you know better how to handle it.
translation: Give it to me; I'll glue it to its sheath until you know how to handle it.

original: Meanwhile, sir, with the little skill I have, Full well shalt thou perceive how much I dare.
translation: Before that, sir, I'll use the little skill I have to show you how ready I am to use it.

original: Ay, boy, grow ye so brave?
translation: What, boy, are you so brave now?

original: [   Coming forward]   Why, how now, lords!   So near the emperor's palace dare you draw,   And maintain such a quarrel openly?
translation: [Coming forward]  What's this, lords? How can you openly draw your swords so close to the emperor's palace?

original: Full well I wot the ground of all this grudge:   I would not for a million of gold   The cause were known to them it most concerns;
translation: I know why you're fighting: I wouldn't take a million gold coins to let them know why.

original: Nor would your noble mother for much more   Be so dishonour'd in the court of Rome.   For shame, put up.
translation: Your noble mother wouldn't take so much more to let you dishonor her in Rome. For God's sake, put your swords away.

original: Not I, till I have sheathed   My rapier in his bosom
translation: I won't, not until I've stabbed him

original: and withal   Thrust these reproachful speeches down his throat   That he hath breathed in my dishonour here.
translation: and thrown his insulting words back down his throat.

original: For that I am prepared and full resolved. Foul-spoken coward, that thunder'st with thy tongue, And with thy weapon nothing darest perform!
translation: I'm prepared for that. You coward, talking about what you don't dare to do yourself!

original: Away, I say!   Now, by the gods that warlike Goths adore,   This petty brabble will undo us all.
translation: Put it away, I say! This stupid fight will ruin us all.

original: Why, lords, and think you not how dangerous   It is to jet upon a prince's right?
translation: Lords, haven't you thought how dangerous it is to try to seduce a prince's wife?

original: What, is Lavinia then become so loose,   Or Bassianus so degenerate,   That for her love such quarrels may be broach'd   Without controlment, justice, or revenge?
translation: Is Lavinia so loose, or Bassianus so corrupt, that you can fight over her love without bringing disaster on your heads?

original: Young lords, beware! and should the empress know   This discord's ground, the music would not please.
translation: Young lords, watch yourselves! If the empress knew about this, she wouldn't be happy.

original: I care not, I, knew she and all the world: I love Lavinia more than all the world.
translation: I don't care if she or anyone else knows it: I love Lavinia more than all the world.

original: Youngling, learn thou to make some meaner choice: Lavinia is thine elder brother's hope.
translation: Young man, choose someone else: Lavinia is your elder brother's choice.

original: Why, are ye mad? or know ye not, in Rome   How furious and impatient they be,   And cannot brook competitors in love?
translation: What, are you crazy? Don't you know how jealous Romans are of their competitors in love?

original: I tell you, lords, you do but plot your deaths   By this device.
translation: I tell you, lords, you're going to get yourselves killed.

original: Aaron, a thousand deaths Would I propose to achieve her whom I love.
translation: Aaron, I'd die a thousand times to have her.

original: To achieve her! how?
translation: To have her! How?

original: Why makest thou it so strange?   She is a woman, therefore may be woo'd;   She is a woman, therefore may be won;   She is Lavinia, therefore must be loved.
translation: Why do you sound so surprised? She is a woman, so can be wooed; she's a woman, and so can be won; she is Lavinia, so she must be loved.

original: What, man! more water glideth by the mill   Than wots the miller of; and easy it is   Of a cut loaf to steal a shive, we know:
translation: You know what I mean, man: more water goes by the mill than the miller knows about, and it's a simple thing to steal a slice of a loaf of bread.

original: Though Bassianus be the emperor's brother.   Better than he have worn Vulcan's badge.
translation: Bassianus is the emperor's brother, but greater men that him have been cheated on by their wives.

original: Ay, and as good as Saturninus may.
translation: True—even a man as great as Saturninus can be cheated.

original: Then why should he despair that knows to court it   With words, fair looks and liberality?
translation: Then, it should be no problem for a man who knows how to flirt with a woman, seeming generous and charming.

original: What, hast not thou full often struck a doe,   And borne her cleanly by the keeper's nose?
translation: What, haven't you often killed a deer right under her owner's nose?

original: Why, then, it seems, some certain snatch or so Would serve your turns.
Ay, so the turn were served.
translation: Yes, if that would do it.

original: Aaron, thou hast hit it.
translation: Aaron, you're right on point there.

original: Would you had hit it too!   Then should not we be tired with this ado.
translation: I wish you were as sharp! Then we wouldn't be making all this fuss.

original: Why, hark ye, hark ye! and are you such fools   To square for this? would it offend you, then   That both should speed?
translation: Why—listen to me!—are you fighting each other over her? Would you be offended if you both succeeded?

original: Faith, not me.
translation: No, not me.

original: Nor me, so I were one.
translation: Nor I, as long as I got what I wanted.

original: For shame, be friends, and join for that you jar:   'Tis policy and stratagem must do   That you affect; and so must you resolve,   That what you cannot as you would achieve,   You must perforce accomplish as you may.
translation: Well, then why don't you work together: if you want her, you'll need a plan. You must decide that if you can't have it as you would ideally want, then you will have it however you can.

original: Take this of me: Lucrece was not more chaste   Than this Lavinia, Bassianus' love.
translation: Take my word for it: Lavinia, Bassianus's love, is as chaste as  Lucrece .

original: A speedier course than lingering languishment   Must we pursue, and I have found the path.
translation: We have to find a quicker way than trying to persuade her, since that will never work, and I have just the path in mind.

original: My lords, a solemn hunting is in hand;   There will the lovely Roman ladies troop:   The forest walks are wide and spacious;
translation: My lords, tomorrow we're all going hunting, and the lovely Roman ladies will come along: the forest paths are wide and spacious,

original: And many unfrequented plots there are   Fitted by kind for rape and villany:
translation: and there are many isolated places fit for rape and other crimes.

original: Single you thither then this dainty doe,   And strike her home by force, if not by words:   This way, or not at all, stand you in hope.
translation: Bring this pretty doe there alone, and take her by force, if not by words: this is your only hope.

original: Come, come, our empress, with her sacred wit   To villany and vengeance consecrate,   Will we acquaint with all that we intend;
translation: Come on, and let's tell our empress our villainous and vengeful plans; all her energy is devoted to revenge.

original: And she shall file our engines with advice,   That will not suffer you to square yourselves,   But to your wishes' height advance you both.
translation: She will  improve on our plans  with her advice, and will make sure you don't mess up those plans by fighting amongst yourselves. You'll both get what you want.

original: The emperor's court is like the house of Fame,   The palace full of tongues, of eyes, and ears:   The woods are ruthless, dreadful, deaf, and dull;
translation: The emperor's palace is as full of tongues, eyes, and ears as the  House of Fame ; you'll have no privacy there. But the woods are pitiless, dreadful, and hear nothing;

original: There speak, and strike, brave boys, and take   your turns;   There serve your lusts, shadow'd from heaven's eye,   And revel in Lavinia's treasury.
translation: that's where you can do what you want, brave boys, and take your turns with Lavinia. There you can satisfy your lusts in the shadows, where heaven can't see, and enjoy the treasures of her body.

original: Thy counsel, lad, smells of no cowardice.
translation: Your advice is good, friend.

original: Sit fas aut nefas, till I find the stream To cool this heat, a charm to calm these fits. Per Styga, per manes vehor.
translation: Whether it's right or wrong, I must have her: until I find the stream to cool my heat, or some medicine to calm me down, I live in hell.

original: The hunt is up, the morn is bright and grey,   The fields are fragrant and the woods are green:
translation: It's time to hunt—the morning is bright and gray, the fields are sweet-smelling, and the trees are in bloom.

original: Uncouple here and let us make a bay   And wake the emperor and his lovely bride   And rouse the prince and ring a hunter's peal,   That all the court may echo with the noise.
translation: Let's separate here and make some noise to wake up the emperor and his lovely bride; we'll make enough sound to wake up the prince too, and the whole court.

original: Sons, let it be your charge, as it is ours,   To attend the emperor's person carefully:
translation: Sons, make sure you watch the emperor carefully, as I will.

original: I have been troubled in my sleep this night,   But dawning day new comfort hath inspired.
translation: I had a bad night's sleep, but felt better when I woke up.

original: Many good morrows to your majesty; Madam, to you as many and as good: I promised your grace a hunter's peal.
translation: Good morning, your majesty; and madam, good morning to you, too. I promised that I would wake you up with the sound of the hunt.

original: And you have rung it lustily, my lord; Somewhat too early for new-married ladies.
translation: And you have made quite a noise, my lord—somewhat too early for ladies who just got married.

original: Lavinia, how say you?
translation: Lavinia, what do you think?

original: I say, no; I have been broad awake two hours and more.
translation: I disagree; I've been awake for more than two hours already.

original: Come on, then; horse and chariots let us have, And to our sport. @  Madam, now shall ye see Our Roman hunting.
translation: Come on, then; let's get our horses and chariots and begin the hunt. Madam, now you'll see our Roman hunting.

original: I have dogs, my lord, Will rouse the proudest panther in the chase, And climb the highest promontory top.
translation: I have dogs, my lord, that can outrun the proudest panther in the chase, and climb the highest tops of the mountains.

original: And I have horse will follow where the game Makes way, and run like swallows o'er the plain.
translation: And I have horses that will follow wherever the prey goes, flying like swallows over the open field.

original: Chiron, we hunt not, we, with horse nor hound, But hope to pluck a dainty doe to ground.
translation: Chiron, we don't hunt with horses or dogs—but hope to catch a dainty doe, nonetheless.

original: He that had wit would think that I had none,   To bury so much gold under a tree,   And never after to inherit it.
translation: A smart man would think it's stupid to bury so much gold under a tree and never use it.

original: Let him that thinks of me so abjectly   Know that this gold must coin a stratagem,
translation: But I would tell him that I do this for a plot:

original: Which, cunningly effected, will beget   A very excellent piece of villany:   And so repose, sweet gold, for their unrest
translation: which, when it comes to pass, will make for some excellent wickedness. So rest there, sweet gold, and cause unrest.

original: That have their alms out of the empress' chest.
translation: and take revenge on the empress's enemies.

original: My lovely Aaron, wherefore look'st thou sad,   When every thing doth make a gleeful boast?
translation: My lovely Aaron, why do you look sad when everything is so beautiful?

original: The birds chant melody on every bush,   The snake lies rolled in the cheerful sun,   The green leaves quiver with the cooling wind   And make a chequer'd shadow on the ground:
translation: The birds are singing, the snake sleeps under the cheerful sun, and the green leaves enjoy the cooling wind, which makes a shadow on the ground.

original: Under their sweet shade, Aaron, let us sit,   And, whilst the babbling echo mocks the hounds,   Replying shrilly to the well-tuned horns,   As if a double hunt were heard at once,   Let us sit down and mark their yelping noise;
translation: Let's sit down in the shade, Aaron, and while sounds of the noisy hunt move through the wood, the echoes replying to the horns' call as if two hunts were happening at once, we'll stay here and listen.

original: And, after conflict such as was supposed   The wandering prince and Dido once enjoy'd,   When with a happy storm they were surprised   And curtain'd with a counsel-keeping cave,
translation: We'll be like  Dido and her wandering prince , who took shelter in a cave during a storm. I can imagine what they go up to in there, all alone.

original: We may, each wreathed in the other's arms,   Our pastimes done, possess a golden slumber;   Whiles hounds and horns and sweet melodious birds   Be unto us as is a nurse's song   Of lullaby to bring her babe asleep   .
translation: After our lovers' sport, we'll have a glorious nap. As we rest in each other's arms, the sounds of the hunt and the songs of sweet birds will lull us to sleep.

original: Madam, though Venus govern your desires,   Saturn is dominator over mine:
translation: Madam, while the goddess Venus makes you think of love, the god Saturn makes me think of destruction and death.

original: What signifies my deadly-standing eye,   My silence and my cloudy melancholy,   My fleece of woolly hair that now uncurls   Even as an adder when she doth unroll   To do some fatal execution?
translation: My angry looks, my silence, my sad mood, and my hair that uncurls like a snake uncoiling itself to strike,

original: No, madam, these are no venereal signs:   Vengeance is in my heart, death in my hand,   Blood and revenge are hammering in my head.
translation: have nothing to do with sexual desire.  Instead, they show that I'm planning to take vengeance: revenge and blood are all I can think of.

original: Hark Tamora, the empress of my soul,   Which never hopes more heaven than rests in thee,   This is the day of doom for Bassianus:
translation: Listen, Tamora—empress of my soul, since I don't hope for salvation after death—Bassianus will die today.

original: His Philomel must lose her tongue to-day,   Thy sons make pillage of her chastity   And wash their hands in Bassianus' blood.
translation: His  Philomel  must lose her tongue, for your sons plan to rape her and wash their hands in his blood.

original: Seest thou this letter? take it up, I pray thee,   And give the king this fatal plotted scroll.
translation: See this letter?  [Gives it to her]  Take it, and give it to the king.

original: Now question me no more; we are espied;   Here comes a parcel of our hopeful booty,   Which dreads not yet their lives' destruction.
translation: Don't ask me anymore; someone has seen us. Here come our victims, although they don't know it yet.

original: Ah, my sweet Moor, sweeter to me than life!
No more, great empress; Bassianus comes: Be cross with him; and I'll go fetch thy sons To back thy quarrels, whatsoe'er they be.
translation: No more, great empress; Bassianus is here. Find some reason to argue with him; meanwhile, I'll go get your sons so they can take revenge for you.

original: Who have we here? Rome's royal empress,   Unfurnish'd of her well-beseeming troop?
translation: Who have we here? Rome's royal empress, all alone with no servants?

original: Or is it Dian, habited like her,   Who hath abandoned her holy groves   To see the general hunting in this forest?
translation: Or is it the goddess  Diana  who has left her holy groves to come see the hunt?

original: Saucy controller of our private steps!   Had I the power that some say Dian had,   Thy temples should be planted presently   With horns, as was Actaeon's;
translation: How dare you intrude on me like this! If I had Diana's powers, I'd put horns on your head like  Actaeon's ,

original: and the hounds   Should drive upon thy new-transformed limbs,   Unmannerly intruder as thou art!
translation: and let the dogs tear you to pieces for disturbing my privacy!

original: Under your patience, gentle empress,   'Tis thought you have a goodly gift in horning;   And to be doubted that your Moor and you   Are singled forth to try experiments:
translation: Oh, but gentle empress, we know you have a talent for  horning . And I'm sure you and your Moor are here together:

original: Jove shield your husband from his hounds to-day!   'Tis pity they should take him for a stag.
translation: I hope your husband's dogs don't take him for a stag.

original: Believe me, queen, your swarth Cimmerian   Doth make your honour of his body's hue,   Spotted, detested, and abominable.
translation: Believe me, queen, your swarthy  Cimmerian  is turning you as black as him, disgusting and hateful.

original: Why are you sequester'd from all your train,   Dismounted from your snow-white goodly steed.
translation: Why did you sneak away from all your servants, get off your snowy white horse,

original: And wander'd hither to an obscure plot,   Accompanied but with a barbarous Moor,   If foul desire had not conducted you?
translation: and wander to this isolated forest clearing, accompanied only by a barbaric Moor—if your foul desires didn't bring you here?

original: And, being intercepted in your sport,   Great reason that my noble lord be rated   For sauciness.
translation: And, since we've caught you in the act, my noble lord has good reason to talk to you like this.

original: I pray you, let us hence,   And let her joy her raven-colour'd love;   This valley fits the purpose passing well.
translation: [To BASSIANUS]  Let's go, and let her enjoy her raven-colored lover; this ugly valley is perfect for her purposes.

original: The king my brother shall have note of this.
translation: The king, my brother, will know about this.

original: Ay, for these slips have made him noted long: Good king, to be so mightily abused!
translation: Yes, for people have noticed that you keep slipping away. The good king has been tricked one too many times!

original: Why have I patience to endure all this?
translation: Why do I have the patience to listen to you?

original: How now, dear sovereign, and our gracious mother! Why doth your highness look so pale and wan?
translation: What's the matter, dear queen and beloved mother? Why do you look so pale?

original: Have I not reason, think you, to look pale?   These two have 'ticed me hither to this place:   A barren detested vale, you see it is;
translation: Don't you think I have reason to look pale? These two lured me to this isolated valley—a foul place, as you can see,

original: The trees, though summer, yet forlorn and lean,   O'ercome with moss and baleful mistletoe:   Here never shines the sun; here nothing breeds,   Unless the nightly owl or fatal raven:
translation: where the trees are bare even in the summer, covered in moss and  mistletoe , where the sun never shines and nothing lives but owls and ravens—

original: And when they show'd me this abhorred pit,   They told me, here, at dead time of the night,   A thousand fiends, a thousand hissing snakes,   Ten thousand swelling toads, as many urchins,
translation: and showed me this horrible pit in the ground. They told me that, at night, it's filled with a thousand demons, snakes toads, and goblins,

original: Would make such fearful and confused cries   As any mortal body hearing it   Should straight fall mad, or else die suddenly.
translation: who make such awful noise that anyone hearing it would go mad or fall dead.

original: No sooner had they told this hellish tale,   But straight they told me they would bind me here   Unto the body of a dismal yew,   And leave me to this miserable death:
translation: No sooner had they said this, but they added that they would tie me here to a tree and leave me to a miserable death.

original: And then they call'd me foul adulteress,   Lascivious Goth, and all the bitterest terms   That ever ear did hear to such effect:
translation: Then they called me a foul adulteress, lustful Goth, and all the worst insults you've ever heard.

original: And, had you not by wondrous fortune come,   This vengeance on me had they executed.   Revenge it, as you love your mother's life,   Or be ye not henceforth call'd my children.
translation: If you hadn't come to rescue me, they would have killed me. Take revenge, as you love your mother, or never call yourself my children again.

original: This is a witness that I am thy son.
translation: I'll show you that I'm your son.

original: And this for me, struck home to show my strength.
translation: And take this, too, to show my strength.

original: Ay, come, Semiramis, nay, barbarous Tamora, For no name fits thy nature but thy own!
Give me thy poniard; you shall know, my boys Your mother's hand shall right your mother's wrong.
translation: Give me your knife; you'll see, my boys, that your mother's own hand will take revenge.

original: Stay, madam; here is more belongs to her;   First thrash the corn, then after burn the straw:
translation: Stop, madam; we have more plans for her. Don't burn the straw until you've  thrashed the corn .

original: This minion stood upon her chastity,   Upon her nuptial vow, her loyalty,   And with that painted hope braves your mightiness:   And shall she carry this unto her grave?
translation: This girl acts like a chaste lady and puts herself above you, parading her faithfulness in her marriage; do you want her to die with that satisfaction?

original: An if she do, I would I were an eunuch. Drag hence her husband to some secret hole, And make his dead trunk pillow to our lust.
But when ye have the honey ye desire, Let not this wasp outlive, us both to sting.
translation: But when you have the honey you want, don't let the wasp live to sting us.

original: I warrant you, madam, we wil l make that sure. Come, mistress, now perforce we will enjoy That nice-preserved honesty of yours.
translation: I promise you, madam, we'll make sure of that. Come, mistress, now we'll enjoy that "honesty" of yours that you're so anxious to preserve.

original: O Tamora! thou bear'st a woman's face,—
translation: Oh, Tamora! You have the face of a woman—

original: I will not hear her speak; away with her!
translation: I will not listen to her speak; take her away!

original: Sweet lords, entreat her hear me but a word.
translation: Sweet lords, just let me say one thing to her.

original: Listen, fair madam: let it be your glory To see her tears; but be your heart to them As unrelenting flint to drops of rain.
translation: Listen, dear madam; it's your glory to see her cry. Let her tears fall like rain on your heart of stone.

original: When did the tiger's young ones teach the dam?   O, do not learn her wrath; she taught it thee;
translation: Since when did the tiger's cubs teach their mother? Oh, don't teach her how to be angry; she taught you how—

original: The milk thou suck'dst from her did turn to marble;   Even at thy teat thou hadst thy tyranny.   Yet every mother breeds not sons alike:
translation: the milk you sucked from her turned to marble, and even at her breast you learned cruelty. But not every mother breeds the same sons—

original: [To CHIRON]   Do thou entreat her show a woman pity.
translation: [To CHIRON]  Beg her to show me a woman's pity.

original: What, wouldst thou have me prove myself a bastard?
translation: What, and show myself a bastard? I'm my mother's son.

original: 'Tis true; the raven doth not hatch a lark:   Yet have I heard,—O, could I find it now!—
translation: It's true; a raven can't give birth to a lark.  But I’ve heard—oh, if only this could happen now!—

original: The lion moved with pity did endure   To have his princely paws pared all away:   Some say that ravens foster forlorn children,
translation: that the lion has cut off his claws for pity, and that ravens have cared for orphaned children

original: The whilst their own birds famish in their nests:   O, be to me, though thy hard heart say no,   Nothing so kind, but something pitiful!
translation: while their own birds starved in their nests. Oh, be to me—although your hard heart says no—if not as kind, then at least a bit merciful!

original: I know not what it means; away with her!
translation: I don't know what she means; take her away!

original: O, let me teach thee! for my father's sake,
translation: Oh, let me explain myself! For my father’s sake—

original: That gave thee life,   when well he might have   slain thee,   Be not obdurate, open thy deaf ears.
translation: since he didn’t kill you when he might have done so—listen to me.

original: Hadst thou in person ne'er offended me,   Even for his sake am I pitiless.
translation: Even if you had never offended me yourself (which you have), I’m merciless for his sake.

original: Remember, boys, I pour'd forth tears in vain,   To save your brother from the sacrifice;   But fierce Andronicus would not relent;
translation: Remember, boys, how I begged and cried in vain to save your brother from the sacrifice, but fierce Andronicus would not show pity.

original: Therefore, away with her, and use her as you will,   The worse to her, the better loved of me.
translation: So take her away, and do whatever you want with her: the worse you treat her, the more I’ll love you.

original: O Tamora, be call'd a gentle queen,   And with thine own hands kill me in this place!
translation: Oh, Tamora, be a gentle queen, and kill me with your own hands in this place!

original: For 'tis not life that I have begg'd so long;   Poor I was slain when Bassianus died.
translation: For it isn’t my life that I’ve been begging for—I was killed when Bassianus died.

original: What begg'st thou, then? fond woman, let me go.
translation: What are you asking for, then? Stupid girl, let me go.

original: 'Tis present death I beg; and one thing more   That womanhood denies my tongue to tell:   O, keep me from their worse than killing lust,
translation: It's death now that I beg for—and one thing more, that I can barely speak for modesty's sake. Oh, keep me from their lust, which is worse than killing me,

original: And tumble me into some loathsome pit,   Where never man's eye may behold my body:   Do this, and be a charitable murderer.
translation: and throw me into some loathsome pit where no one will ever see my body. Do this, and be a charitable murderer.

original: So should I rob my sweet sons of their fee: No, let them satisfy their lust on thee.
translation: But if I did that, I would rob my sweet sons of their reward. No, I'll let them satisfy their lust with you.

original: Away! for thou hast stay'd us here too long.
translation: Come on! You've kept us here too long.

original: No grace? no womanhood? Ah, beastly creature! The blot and enemy to our general name! Confusion fall—
translation: No pity? No womanhood? Oh, foul creature, a blot on the name of all women! May you—

original: Nay, then I'll stop your mouth. Bring thou her husband: This is the hole where Aaron bid us hide him.
translation: No, then I'll stop you from talking anymore. Bring her husband's body; this is the hole where Aaron told us to throw him.

original: Farewell, my sons: see that you make her sure.   Ne'er let my heart know merry cheer indeed,   Till all the Andronici be made away.
translation: Goodbye, my sons; make sure she isn't a threat to us. I'll never be happy until all the Andronici family are dead.

original: Now will I hence to seek my lovely Moor,   And let my spleenful sons this trull deflow'r.
translation: Now I'll go find my lovely Moor, and let my angry sons enjoy their prize.

original: Come on, my lords, the better foot before: Straight will I bring you to the loathsome pit Where I espied the panther fast asleep.
translation: Come on, my lords, quickly: I'll bring you to the foul pit where I saw a panther fast asleep.

original: My sight is very dull, whate'er it bodes.
translation: My eyelids are very heavy, whatever that means.

original: And mine, I promise you; were't not for shame, Well could I leave our sport to sleep awhile.
translation: And mine, too; if I weren't embarrassed to do so, I would stop hunting and sleep for a bit.

original: What art thou fall'n? What subtle hole is this,   Whose mouth is cover'd with rude-growing briers,   Upon whose leaves are drops of new-shed blood   As fresh as morning dew distill'd on flowers?
translation: Where have you fallen? What sort of hole is this, covered in branches with blood on their leaves like the morning dew on flowers?

original: A very fatal place it seems to me.   Speak, brother, hast thou hurt thee with the fall?
translation: It seems like a very deadly place to me. Tell me, brother, did you hurt yourself when you fell?

original: O brother, with the dismall'st object hurt That ever eye with sight made heart lament!
translation: Oh, brother, I've seen something that hurt me worse than anything  I've seen before!

original: Now will I fetch the king to find them here, That he thereby may give a likely guess How these were they that made away his brother.
translation: Now I'll bring the king, who, when he finds them here, will assume that they killed his brother.

original: Why dost not comfort me, and help me out From this unhallowed and blood-stained hole?
translation: Why don't you help me out of this horrible blood-stained hole?

original: I am surprised with an uncouth fear; A chilling sweat o'er-runs my trembling joints: My heart suspects more than mine eye can see.
translation: I am paralyzed with fear; I feel a cold sweat all over my body, and my heart suspects more than I can see at the moment.

original: To prove thou hast a true-divining heart, Aaron and thou look down into this den, And see a fearful sight of blood and death.
translation: You're right to be afraid: if you and Aaron look into this hole, you'll see blood and death.

original: Aaron is gone; and my compassionate heart   Will not permit mine eyes once to behold   The thing whereat it trembles by surmise;
translation: Aaron is gone; I'm afraid to look at the thing I fear.

original: O, tell me how it is; for ne'er till now   Was I a child to fear I know not what.
translation: Oh, tell me when you see; before now I was never so childish as to fear something I couldn't see.

original: Lord Bassianus lies embrewed here, All on a heap, like to a slaughter'd lamb, In this detested, dark, blood-drinking pit.
translation: Lord Bassianus lies here like a slaughtered lamb, in this horrible, dark, blood-soaked pit.

original: If it be dark, how dost thou know 'tis he?
translation: If it's dark, how do you know it's him?

original: Upon his bloody finger he doth wear   A precious ring, that lightens all the hole,   Which, like a taper in some monument,
translation: He wears a ring on his bloody finger that lights the hole like a flaming candle in a tomb,

original: Doth shine upon the dead man's earthy cheeks,   And shows the ragged entrails of the pit:
translation: shining on his cheeks and showing the disgusting insides of the pit.

original: So pale did shine the moon on Pyramus   When he by night lay bathed in maiden blood.   O brother, help me with thy fainting hand—
translation: The moon shined like that on  Pyramus , covered in a maiden's blood at night. Oh, brother, help me out of here with your weak hand—

original: If fear hath made thee faint, as me it hath—   Out of this fell devouring receptacle,   As hateful as Cocytus' misty mouth.
translation: if fear has made you weak too, as it has me—so that I can get out of this foul hole, as horrible as the mouth of  Cocytus .

original: Reach me thy hand, that I may help thee out;   Or, wanting strength to do thee so much good,
translation: Give me your hand, so that I can help you. Or, if I don't have the strength to lift you out,

original: I may be pluck'd into the swallowing womb   Of this deep pit, poor Bassianus' grave.   I have no strength to pluck thee to the brink.
translation: I'll fall into this pit (this womb that swallows instead of giving life and has become Bassianus's grave) with you. I don't have enough strength to pull you to the top.

original: Nor I no strength to climb without thy help.
translation: And I don't have the strength to climb without your help.

original: Thy hand once more; I will not loose again, Till thou art here aloft, or I below: Thou canst not come to me: I come to thee.
translation: Give me your hand again; I won't let go until you're up here or I'm down there. You can't come to me—I'll come to you.

original: Along with me: I'll see what hole is here,   And what he is that now is leap'd into it.
translation: Come follow me; I'll see what kind of hole this is, and who just leaped into it.

original: Say who art thou that lately didst descend   Into this gaping hollow of the earth?
translation: [Calling down into the hole]  Who are you down there, who just jumped in?

original: The unhappy son of old Andronicus: Brought hither in a most unlucky hour, To find thy brother Bassianus dead.
translation: The unlucky son of old Andronicus, who stumbling on this hole has found the dead body of your brother Bassianus.

original: My brother dead! I know thou dost but jest:
translation: My brother dead! I know you must be joking—

original: He and his lady both are at the lodge   Upon the north side of this pleasant chase;   'Tis not an hour since I left him there.
translation: he and his wife are both back at the lodge on the north side of the forest; I saw them an hour ago.

original: We know not where you left him all alive; But, out, alas! here have we found him dead.
translation: We don't know where you left him alive. But out here—God forbid—we found him dead.

original: Where is my lord the king?
translation: Where is my lord, the king?

original: Here, Tamora, though grieved with killing grief.
translation: Here, Tamora, although greatly distressed.

original: Where is thy brother Bassianus?
translation: Where is your brother Bassianus?

original: Now to the bottom dost thou search my wound: Poor Bassianus here lies murdered.
translation: Now you've hit on the subject of my suffering: poor  Bassianus lies in this hole, murdered.

original: Then all too late I bring this fatal writ,   The complot of this timeless tragedy;
translation: Then I'm too late in showing you this letter, which reveals the whole plot!

original: And wonder greatly that man's face can fold   In pleasing smiles such murderous tyranny.
translation: I'm shocked that people can smile and be so murderous.

original: [Reads]   'An if we miss to meet him handsomely—   Sweet huntsman, Bassianus 'tis we mean—   Do thou so much as dig the grave for him:
translation: [Reads]  "And if we fail to meet him on the hunt—meaning Bassianus—just dig the grave for him:

original: Thou know'st our meaning. Look for thy reward   Among the nettles at the elder-tree   Which overshades the mouth of that same pit   Where we decreed to bury Bassianus.
translation: you understand us. Your money is buried by the elder-tree near the same pit where we decided to bury Bassianus.

original: Do this, and purchase us thy lasting friends.'
translation: If you do this, we'll be your friends for life."

original: O Tamora! was ever heard the like?   This is the pit, and this the elder-tree.
translation: [To TAMORA]  Oh, Tamora! Have you ever heard anything like this? This is the pit, and this is the elder-tree.

original: Look, sirs, if you can find the huntsman out   That should have murdered Bassianus here.
translation: [To servants]  Find the hunter that planned to murder Bassianus here!

original: My gracious lord, here is the bag of gold.
translation: My gracious lord, here's the bag of gold.

original: [To TITUS]   Two of thy whelps, fell curs of   bloody kind,   Have here bereft my brother of his life.
translation: [To TITUS]  Two of your sons, bloody dogs, have killed my brother here.

original: Sirs, drag them from the pit unto the prison:   There let them bide until we have devised   Some never-heard-of torturing pain for them.
translation: Drag them from the pit and put them in prison, and leave them there until I've invented some previously unheard-of torture for them.

original: What, are they in this pit? O wondrous thing! How easily murder is discovered!
translation: What, are they in this pit? Oh, it's amazing how easy it is to solve murders!

original: High emperor, upon my feeble knee   I beg this boon, with tears not lightly shed,
translation: Mighty emperor, I beg on my knees with tears not easily shed.

original: That this fell fault of my accursed sons,   Accursed if the fault be proved in them,—
translation: If this foul crime of my cursed sons—cursed if they're guilty of it—

original: If it be proved! you see it is apparent. Who found this letter? Tamora, was it you?
translation: If  they're guilty! It's obvious that they are. Who found this letter? Tamora, was it you?

original: Andronicus himself did take it up.
translation: Andronicus himself found it in the woods.

original: I did, my lord: yet let me be their bail;   For, by my father's reverend tomb,
translation: I did, my lord. But let me bail them, and by my father's honored grave,

original: I vow   They shall be ready at your highness' will   To answer their suspicion with their lives.
translation: I promise I'll produce them for the trial.

original: Thou shalt not bail them: see thou follow me.   Some bring the murder'd body, some the murderers:   Let them not speak a word; the guilt is plain;
translation: You won't bail them; follow me. Someone bring the dead body, and someone bring the murderers. Don't let them speak; their guilt is obvious.

original: For, by my soul, were there worse end than death,   That end upon them should be executed.
translation: By God, if there were some worse fate than death, I'd punish them that way.

original: Andronicus, I will entreat the king; Fear not thy sons; they shall do well enough.
translation: Andronicus, I'll advocate for you with the king. Don't worry for your sons; they'll be all right.

original: Come, Lucius, come; stay not to talk with them.
translation: Come, Lucius; don't stay to talk with them.

original: So, now go tell, an if thy tongue can speak, Who 'twas that cut thy tongue and ravish'd thee.
translation: So, now go try to tell what happened—if your tongue can speak, say who cut out your tongue and raped you.

original: Write down thy mind, bewray thy meaning so, An if thy stumps will let thee play the scribe.
translation: Write it down and explain yourself that way—if you can write with those stumps.

original: See, how with signs and tokens she can scrowl.
translation: See, she can say what she means by gesturing at us.

original: Go home, call for sweet water, wash thy hands.
translation: Go home, ask for sweet water to wash your hands.

original: She hath no tongue to call, nor hands to wash; And so let's leave her to her silent walks.
translation: She has no tongue to speak and no hands to wash, so let's leave her to walk alone in silence.

original: An 'twere my case, I should go hang myself.
translation: If it were me, I'd hang myself.

original: If thou hadst hands to help thee knit the cord.
translation: If you had hands to help you tie the knot.

original: Who is this? my niece, that flies away so fast!   Cousin, a word; where is your husband?   If I do dream, would all my wealth would wake me!
translation: Who is this?  [Sees LAVINIA]  My niece, running away from me so fast! Cousin, wait; where's your husband? If I'm dreaming, I would give everything I own to wake up from this nightmare!

original: If I do wake, some planet strike me down,   That I may slumber in eternal sleep!
translation: And if I did wake up, I'd want to die rather than see this.

original: Speak, gentle niece, what stern ungentle hands   Have lopp'd and hew'd and made thy body bare   Of her two branches, those sweet ornaments,   Whose circling shadows kings have sought to sleep in,
translation: Tell me, sweet niece, who has cut off those two branches, your arms, which kings have desired to sleep in,

original: And might not gain so great a happiness   As have thy love? Why dost not speak to me?
translation: and thought there could be no greater happiness than to have your love? Why don't you speak to me?

original: Alas, a crimson river of warm blood,   Like to a bubbling fountain stirr'd with wind,   Doth rise and fall between thy rosed lips,   Coming and going with thy honey breath.
translation: Oh, a red river of blood falls from your lips like a fountain, stirred by the wind of your sweet breath.

original: But, sure, some Tereus hath deflowered thee,   And, lest thou shouldst detect him, cut thy tongue.   Ah, now thou turn'st away thy face for shame!
translation: Surely some  Tereus  has raped you, and, to stop you from naming him, has cut out your tongue. Ah, now you turn away your face, ashamed,

original: And, notwithstanding all this loss of blood,   As from a conduit with three issuing spouts,   Yet do thy cheeks look red as Titan's face   Blushing to be encountered with a cloud.
translation: and you blush—although you've lost so much blood already from three different spouts. Your cheeks are as red as the sun, that blushes when hidden by a cloud.

original: Shall I speak for thee? shall I say 'tis so?   O, that I knew thy heart; and knew the beast,   That I might rail at him, to ease my mind!
translation: Can I speak for you? Can I say that I have it right? Oh, I wish I knew what was in your heart—and that I knew the beast who did this, so that I could vent my rage at him.

original: Sorrow concealed, like an oven stopp'd,   Doth burn the heart to cinders where it is.   Fair Philomela, she but lost her tongue,   And in a tedious sampler sew'd her mind:
translation: Unexpressed sorrow burns the heart to ashes. Fair Philomela just lost her tongue, and sewed a picture of what was done to her;

original: But, lovely niece, that mean is cut from thee;   A craftier Tereus, cousin, hast thou met,   And he hath cut those pretty fingers off,   That could have better sew'd than Philomel.
translation: but, lovely niece, that method won't work for you, since a more cunning Tereus has cut off those pretty fingers that could have sewed better than Philomel.

original: O, had the monster seen those lily hands   Tremble, like aspen-leaves, upon a lute,   And make the silken strings delight to kiss them,   He would not then have touch'd them for his life!
translation: Oh, if the monster had seen those white hands play the  lute  and make the strings themselves want to kiss them, he would not have touched them were his life at stake!

original: Or, had he heard the heavenly harmony   Which that sweet tongue hath made,   He would have dropp'd his knife, and fell asleep   As Cerberus at the Thracian poet's feet.
translation: Or if he'd heard the sweet music of your voice, he would have dropped his knife and fallen asleep like  Cerberus at the feet of the Thracian poet .

original: Come, let us go, and make thy father blind;   For such a sight will blind a father's eye:   One hour's storm will drown the fragrant meads;
translation: Come with me, let's find your father, and make him blind—for such a sight would blind any father's eye with tears. An hour of rain can drown a meadow;

original: What will whole months of tears thy father's eyes?   Do not draw back, for we will mourn with thee   O, could our mourning ease thy misery!
translation: what will whole months of tears do to your father's eyes? Don't move away, but come with me, for we'll mourn with you. Oh, if only our mourning could ease your misery!

original: Hear me, grave fathers! noble tribunes, stay!   For pity of mine age, whose youth was spent   In dangerous wars, whilst you securely slept;
translation: Listen to me, respected men! Noble tribunes, wait! Take pity on me—for my lost youth, which I spent in dangerous wars while you slept securely at home;

original: For all my blood in Rome's great quarrel shed;   For all the frosty nights that I have watch'd;   And for these bitter tears, which now you see   Filling the aged wrinkles in my cheeks;
translation: for all the blood I’ve spilled for Rome; for all the cold nights when I stayed up guarding the camp; for the bitter tears that now run down my wrinkled cheeks—

original: Be pitiful to my condemned sons,   Whose souls are not corrupted as 'tis thought.
translation: and have mercy on my sons, who are more innocent than you think.

original: For two and twenty sons I never wept,   Because they died in honour's lofty bed.
translation: I never cried for my twenty-two sons who died before, because they died with honor.

original: For these, these, tribunes, in the dust I write   My heart's deep languor and my soul's sad tears:   Let my tears stanch the earth's dry appetite;
translation: But for these sons, tribunes, I cry so that my tears write my sorrow in the dust, quenching the earth’s thirst.

original: My sons' sweet blood will make it shame and blush.   O earth, I will befriend thee more with rain,   That shall distil from these two ancient urns,   Than youthful April shall with all his showers:
translation: The sweet blood of my sons will make it blush with shame. Oh earth, if you refuse to drink the blood of my dear sons, I’ll give you more rain from my ancient eyes than you ever got in April.

original: In summer's drought I'll drop upon thee still;   In winter with warm tears I'll melt the snow   And keep eternal spring-time on thy face,   So thou refuse to drink my dear sons' blood.
translation: In the drought of summer I’ll rain on you still, and in winter I’ll melt the snow with my warm tears and make it eternally spring, if you refuse to drink my dear sons' blood.

original: O reverend tribunes! O gentle, aged men!   Unbind my sons, reverse the doom of death;
translation: Oh, powerful tribunes! Oh, merciful old men! Release my sons, take back the sentence of death,

original: And let me say, that never wept before,   My tears are now prevailing orators.
translation: and let me say—a man who never cried before—that my tears moved you.

original: O noble father, you lament in vain: The tribunes hear you not; no man is by; And you recount your sorrows to a stone.
translation: Oh, noble father, there’s no point going on like this, for the tribunes can’t hear. No one is here, and you’re only talking to the stones.

original: Ah, Lucius, for thy brothers let me plead. Grave tribunes, once more I entreat of you,—
translation: Ah, Lucius, let me plead for your brothers. Honorable tribunes, I beg you once again—

original: My gracious lord, no tribune hears you speak.
translation: My gracious lord, none of the tribunes can hear you.

original: Why, tis no matter, man; if they did hear,   They would not mark me, or if they did mark,   They would not pity me, yet plead I must;
translation: Why, it doesn't matter if they hear me, man, for they wouldn’t listen to me—or if they did listen, they wouldn’t have mercy. But I have to beg nonetheless.

original: Therefore I tell my sorrows to the stones;   Who, though they cannot answer my distress,   Yet in some sort they are better than the tribunes,   For that they will not intercept my tale:
translation: So I tell my sorrows to the stones, which—although they can’t answer me—in some ways are better than the tribunes. For they don’t interrupt my story;

original: When I do weep, they humbly at my feet   Receive my tears and seem to weep with me;   And, were they but attired in grave weeds,   Rome could afford no tribune like to these.
translation: when I cry, they seem to cry with me, as my tears trickle down the stones. If they were dressed in mourning clothes, there would be no better tribunes in Rome.

original: A stone is soft as wax,—tribunes more hard than stones;   A stone is silent, and offendeth not,   And tribunes with their tongues doom men to death.
translation: A stone is soft as wax, when tribunes are harder than stones. A stone is silent, and never offends, while tribunes doom men to death when they speak.

original: But wherefore stand'st thou with thy weapon drawn?
translation: But why are you standing with your weapon drawn?

original: To rescue my two brothers from their death: For which attempt the judges have pronounced My everlasting doom of banishment.
translation: To rescue my two brothers from their death sentence—and for that, the judges have banished me from Rome for life.

original: O happy man! they have befriended thee.   Why, foolish Lucius, dost thou not perceive   That Rome is but a wilderness of tigers?
translation: Oh, happy man! They’ve done you a favor—foolish Lucius, don’t you see that Rome is just a wilderness of tigers?

original: Tigers must prey, and Rome affords no prey   But me and mine: how happy art thou, then,   From these devourers to be banished!
translation: Tigers must kill, and there’s no better prey than me and my family. You’re fortunate, then, to be banished from this place.

original: But who comes with our brother Marcus here?
translation: But who comes here with my brother Marcus?

original: Titus, prepare thy aged eyes to weep; Or, if not so, thy noble heart to break: I bring consuming sorrow to thine age.
translation: Titus, prepare your eyes to weep; or, if you don't cry, for your noble heart to break. I bring all-consuming sorrow to you in your old age.

original: Will it consume me? let me see it, then.
translation: Will sorrow consume me? Let me see it, then.

original: This was thy daughter.
translation: This was your daughter.

original: Why, Marcus, so she is.
translation: Why, Marcus, so she is.

original: Ay me, this object kills me!
translation: Oh, this sight kills me!

original: Faint-hearted boy, arise, and look upon her.   Speak, Lavinia, what accursed hand   Hath made thee handless in thy father's sight?
translation: Faint-hearted boy, get up and look at her. Speak, Lavinia, and tell us what hand has made you handless?

original: What fool hath added water to the sea,   Or brought a faggot to bright-burning Troy?
translation: What fool has added water to the sea, or brought another torch to burning Troy?

original: My grief was at the height before thou camest,   And now like Nilus, it disdaineth bounds.   Give me a sword, I'll chop off my hands too;
translation: For my grief was already at its height before you came, and now like  Nilus , overflows all bounds. Give me a sword and I’ll chop off my hands too,

original: For they have fought for Rome, and all in vain;   And they have nursed this woe, in feeding life;   In bootless prayer have they been held up,   And they have served me to effectless use:
translation: for they have fought for Rome in vain and kept me alive to suffer; I’ve held them up in prayer, and they’ve been no use at all.

original: Now all the service I require of them   Is that the one will help to cut the other.
translation: So now all I ask is that one will do me the favor of cutting off the other.

original: 'Tis well, Lavinia, that thou hast no hands;   For hands, to do Rome service, are but vain.
translation: It’s good that you have no hands, Lavinia, since hands are useless in doing any service for Rome.

original: Speak, gentle sister, who hath martyr'd thee?
translation: Tell us, sweet sister: who did this to you?

original: O, that delightful engine of her thoughts   That blabb'd them with such pleasing eloquence,   Is torn from forth that pretty hollow cage,
translation: Oh, her tongue—that spoke her thoughts so pleasingly—is torn from her mouth,

original: Where, like a sweet melodious bird, it sung   Sweet varied notes, enchanting every ear!
translation: where it sung like a sweet songbird in a pretty cage, enchanting everyone!

original: O, say thou for her, who hath done this deed?
translation: Oh, then speak for her—who did this?

original: O, thus I found her, straying in the park, Seeking to hide herself, as doth the deer That hath received some unrecuring wound.
translation: She was already like this when I found her. She was wandering in the park trying to hide herself, like a deer that’s received a death wound.

original: It was my deer; and he that wounded her   Hath hurt me more than had he killed me dead:
translation: It was my deer, and whoever wounded her has hurt me worse than if he’d killed me.

original: For now I stand as one upon a rock   Environed with a wilderness of sea,   Who marks the waxing tide grow wave by wave,   Expecting ever when some envious surge   Will in his brinish bowels swallow him.
translation: It’s as if I’m standing on a rock surrounded by the sea, watching the tide surge and expecting that each wave will be the one that drowns me.

original: This way to death my wretched sons are gone;   Here stands my other son, a banished man,   And here my brother, weeping at my woes.
translation: My poor sons are sent to death; my other son is banished; my brother cries for our misfortune.

original: But that which gives my soul the greatest spurn,   Is dear Lavinia, dearer than my soul.
translation: But dear Lavinia—more precious than my soul—gives me the greatest suffering.

original: Had I but seen thy picture in this plight,   It would have madded me: what shall I do   Now I behold thy lively body so?
translation: If I had just seen a picture of you like this, I would have gone mad; what can I do now that I see it in real life?

original: Thou hast no hands, to wipe away thy tears:   Nor tongue, to tell me who hath martyr'd thee:   Thy husband he is dead: and for his death   Thy brothers are condemn'd, and dead by this.
translation: You have no hands to wipe away your tears or tongue to tell me who did this to you; your husband is dead, and your brothers are condemned to death for killing him.

original: Look, Marcus! ah, son Lucius, look on her!   When I did name her brothers, then fresh tears   Stood on her cheeks, as doth the honey-dew   Upon a gather'd lily almost wither'd.
translation: Look, Marcus! Oh, Lucius, look at her! When I mentioned her brothers, new tears appeared on her cheeks like honeydew on an almost-withered flower.

original: Perchance she weeps because they kill'd her husband; Perchance because she knows them innocent.
translation: Perhaps she cries because they killed her husband, or perhaps because she knows they’re innocent.

original: If they did kill thy husband, then be joyful   Because the law hath ta'en revenge on them.   No, no, they would not do so foul a deed;   Witness the sorrow that their sister makes.
translation: If they did kill your husband, then you should be pleased that they’ve been brought to justice. But no, no, they wouldn’t do something so awful; look how sad their sister looks.

original: Gentle Lavinia, let me kiss thy lips.   Or make some sign how I may do thee ease:
translation: Sweet Lavinia, let me kiss your lips. Or give some sign to tell me how I can help:

original: Shall thy good uncle, and thy brother Lucius,   And thou, and I, sit round about some fountain,   Looking all downwards to behold our cheeks   How they are stain'd, as meadows, yet not dry,   With miry slime left on them by a flood?
translation: should your uncle, your brother Lucius, and I sit around a fountain and weep, so that we see the reflection of our tear-streaked cheeks,  like a meadow streaked with slime after a flood?

original: And in the fountain shall we gaze so long   Till the fresh taste be taken from that clearness,   And made a brine-pit with our bitter tears?
translation: And should we look into the fountain so long that its fresh water turns salty from our tears?
