original: Or shall we cut away our hands, like thine?   Or shall we bite our tongues, and in dumb shows   Pass the remainder of our hateful days?
translation: Or should we cut off out own hands, like yours? Or should we stop speaking, and spend the rest of our hateful lives miming at each other?

original: What shall we do? let us, that have our tongues,   Plot some deuce of further misery,   To make us wonder'd at in time to come.
translation: What should we do? Let those of us that still have our tongues plan how to be so miserable that future ages will marvel at us.

original: Sweet father, cease your tears; for, at your grief, See how my wretched sister sobs and weeps.
translation: Sweet father, stop crying; for, seeing you cry, look how my poor sister sobs and weeps.

original: Patience, dear niece. Good Titus, dry thine eyes.
translation: Calm yourself, dear niece. Good Titus, dry your eyes.

original: Ah, Marcus, Marcus! brother, well I wot Thy napkin cannot drink a tear of mine, For thou, poor man, hast drown'd it with thine own.
translation: Oh, Marcus, Marcus! Brother, I know that your handkerchief can’t dry my tears, since it’s already so wet with your own.

original: Ah, my Lavinia, I will wipe thy cheeks.
translation: Oh, my Lavinia, I’ll wipe your cheeks.

original: Mark, Marcus, mark! I understand her signs:   Had she a tongue to speak, now would she say   That to her brother which I said to thee:
translation: Look, Marcus, look! I understand her signs—if she could talk, she’d say to your brother what I just said to you:

original: His napkin, with his true tears all bewet,   Can do no service on her sorrowful cheeks.
translation: his handkerchief, also soaked in his tears, won’t help her sad cheeks.

original: O, what a sympathy of woe is this,   As far from help as Limbo is from bliss!
translation: Oh, this is a fellowship of suffering, as far from help as  Limbo  is from heaven!

original: Titus Andronicus, my lord the emperor   Sends thee this word,—that, if thou love thy sons,   Let Marcus, Lucius, or thyself, old Titus,
translation: Titus Andronicus, my lord the emperor sends a message—if you love your sons, you, Marcus, Lucius,

original: Or any one of you, chop off your hand,   And send it to the king: he for the same   Will send thee hither both thy sons alive;   And that shall be the ransom for their fault.
translation: or any of your family should chop off your hand and send it to the king. With that ransom for their crime, he’ll send both your sons back to you alive.

original: O gracious emperor! O gentle Aaron!   Did ever raven sing so like a lark,   That gives sweet tidings of the sun's uprise?
translation: Oh, generous emperor! Oh, sweet Aaron! Has a raven ever sounded so much like a lark that sings at sunrise?

original: With all my heart, I'll send the emperor My hand:   Good Aaron, wilt thou help to chop it off?
translation: With all my heart, I’ll send the emperor my hand; good Aaron, will you help chop it off?

original: Stay, father! for that noble hand of thine,   That hath thrown down so many enemies,   Shall not be sent: my hand will serve the turn:
translation: Wait, father! Your noble hand—that has defeated so many enemies—shouldn’t be sent. My hand will serve the purpose.

original: My youth can better spare my blood than you;   And therefore mine shall save my brothers' lives.
translation: I’m young and can spare the loss of blood more easily, and so my hand should save my brothers’ lives.

original: Which of your hands hath not defended Rome,   And rear'd aloft the bloody battle-axe,   Writing destruction on the enemy's castle?
translation: Which of your hands hasn’t defended Rome, wielding a bloody battle axe and wreaking destruction on the enemy’s castle?

original: O, none of both but are of high desert:   My hand hath been but idle;
translation: Oh, both are deserving. My hand has been merely idle;

original: let it serve   To ransom my two nephews from their death;   Then have I kept it to a worthy end.
translation: if it ransoms my two nephews from their death, then it’s done something useful.

original: Nay, come, agree whose hand shall go along, For fear they die before their pardon come.
translation: Come on, figure out whose hand should be sent, lest they die before their pardon comes.

original: My hand shall go.
translation: My hand will go.

original: By heaven, it shall not go!
translation: By God, it won't go!

original: Sirs, strive no more: such wither'd herbs as these Are meet for plucking up, and therefore mine.
translation: Sirs, stop fighting; my hands are like withered herbs that need to be plucked out of the garden. So we’ll send one of mine.

original: Sweet father, if I shall be thought thy son, Let me redeem my brothers both from death.
translation: Dear father, if I’m ever worthy to be called your son, let me save my brothers from death.

original: And, for our father's sake and mother's care, Now let me show a brother's love to thee.
translation: And, now for the sake of our parents, let me show you a brother’s love.

original: Agree between you; I will spare my hand.
translation: All right, I'll spare my hand; you two figure it out.

original: Then I'll go fetch an axe.
translation: Then I'll go get an axe.

original: But I will use the axe.
translation: But I'll be the one to use it.

original: Come hither, Aaron; I'll deceive them both: Lend me thy hand, and I will give thee mine.
translation: Come quickly, Aaron; I'll deceive them both. Lend me your hand, and I'll give you mine.

original: [Aside]   If that be call'd deceit, I will be honest,   And never, whilst I live, deceive men so:
translation: [To himself]  If this is called lying, then I’ll be honest, and never lie to men like this as long as I live.

original: But I'll deceive you in another sort,   And that you'll say, ere half an hour pass.
translation: But I’ll trick you another way, as you’ll see less than half an hour from now.

original: Now stay your strife: what shall be is dispatch'd.   Good Aaron, give his majesty my hand:
translation: Now stop fighting: what’s done is done. Good Aaron, give his majesty my hand.

original: Tell him it was a hand that warded him   From thousand dangers; bid him bury it   More hath it merited; that let it have.
translation: Tell him it was a hand that defended him from a thousand dangers; ask him to bury it, since it deserved more than this.

original: As for my sons, say I account of them   As jewels purchased at an easy price;   And yet dear too, because I bought mine own.
translation: As for my sons, say I think of this as a good exchange, jewels for a cheap price—although precious, too, since I’ve bought back  my own .

original: I go, Andronicus: and for thy hand   Look by and by to have thy sons with thee.
translation: I’ll go, Andronicus; and in exchange for your hand, you’ll soon have your sons with you.

original: [Aside]     Their heads, I mean. O, how this villany   Doth fat me with the very thoughts of it!
translation: [To himself]  Their heads, I mean. Oh, the very thought of this villainy delights me even before I’ve done it!

original: Let fools do good, and fair men call for grace.   Aaron will have his soul black like his face.
translation: Let fools do good deeds, and fair men call for mercy. Aaron will have his soul as black as his face.

original: O, here I lift this one hand up to heaven,   And bow this feeble ruin to the earth:
translation: Oh, now I lift my one hand up to pray to heaven, and kneel on the ground with my feeble body:

original: If any power pities wretched tears,   To that I call!
translation: if any power pities the tears of the miserable, I call on that!

original: [To LAVINIA]   What, wilt thou kneel with me?   Do, then, dear heart; for heaven shall hear our  prayers;
translation: [To LAVINIA]  What, will you kneel with me? Do then, dear heart, for heaven will hear our prayers:

original: Or with our sighs we'll breathe the welkin dim,   And stain the sun with fog, as sometime clouds   When they do hug him in their melting bosoms.
translation: we’ll break the dim sky with our sighs and stain the sun with the fog of our tears, as when it’s overshadowed by rain clouds.

original: O brother, speak with possibilities, And do not break into these deep extremes.
translation: Oh, brother, be rational and don’t break into these fits of extreme passion.

original: Is not my sorrow deep, having no bottom? Then be my passions bottomless with them.
translation: Isn’t my sorrow deep, since there’s no end to it? Then let my passions be bottomless as well.

original: But yet let reason govern thy lament.
translation: But still, let reason govern your sorrow.

original: If there were reason for these miseries,   Then into limits could I bind my woes:   When heaven doth weep, doth not the earth o'erflow?
translation: If there were anything reasonable about these miseries, then I could bind my grief within reasonable limits. When heaven weeps, doesn’t the earth overflow with rain?

original: If the winds rage, doth not the sea wax mad,   Threatening the welkin with his big-swoln face?   And wilt thou have a reason for this coil?
translation: If the winds blow hard, don’t the waves get higher, threatening the swollen face of the sky? And would you like me to tell you the reason for this storm?

original: I am the sea; hark, how her sighs do blow!   She is the weeping welkin, I the earth:   Then must my sea be moved with her sighs;
translation: I am the sea; see how Lavinia’s sighs blow. She is the weeping sky, and I’m the earth. My sea must be moved with her sighs,

original: Then must my earth with her continual tears   Become a deluge, overflow'd and drown'd;   For why my bowels cannot hide her woes,   But like a drunkard must I vomit them.
translation: and my earth must drown with her continual tears. I can’t hide her sorrow in my bowels, but must vomit it up like a drunken man.

original: Then give me leave, for losers will have leave   To ease their stomachs with their bitter tongues.
translation: Then give me permission, for losers must give relief to their stomachs by talking bitterly.

original: Worthy Andronicus, ill art thou repaid   For that good hand thou sent'st the emperor.   Here are the heads of thy two noble sons;
translation: Worthy Andronicus, you’ve gotten a poor reward for the good hand you sent the emperor. Here are the heads of your two noble sons,

original: And here's thy hand, in scorn to thee sent back;   Thy griefs their sports, thy resolution mock'd;
translation: and here’s your hand, sent back to you in contempt; your sorrow is a joke to them, and your sacrifice is mocked.

original: That woe is me to think upon thy woes   More than remembrance of my father's death.
translation: It’s worse for me to think of what you’ve suffered than remembering the death of my own father.

original: Now let hot AEtna cool in Sicily,   And be my heart an ever-burning hell!   These miseries are more than may be borne.
translation: Now let hot  Etna  cool in Sicily, and let my heart burn like hell forever! These miseries are too much to bear.

original: To weep with them that weep doth ease some deal;   But sorrow flouted at is double death.
translation: To cry with those who cry does some help, but to mock sorrow is like dying twice.

original: Ah, that this sight should make so deep a wound,   And yet detested life not shrink thereat!
translation: Ah, how can I still be alive after this sight has made such a deep wound in me?

original: That ever death should let life bear his name,   Where life hath no more interest but to breathe!
translation: Oh, life is no more than a living death, when the only thing that tells us we're still alive is that we breathe in and out.

original: Alas, poor heart, that kiss is comfortless As frozen water to a starved snake.
translation: Oh, poor heart, that kiss can’t give any more comfort than frozen water to a starved snake.

original: When will this fearful slumber have an end?
translation: When will we wake up from this horrible dream?

original: Now, farewell, flattery: die, Andronicus;   Thou dost not slumber: see, thy two sons' heads,   Thy warlike hand, thy mangled daughter here:
translation: Now I’ll speak plainly. Die, Andronicus, for you’re not asleep. Look at your two sons’ heads, your brave hand, your mangled daughter here,

original: Thy other banish'd son, with this dear sight   Struck pale and bloodless; and thy brother, I,   Even like a stony image, cold and numb.
translation: your other banished son struck pale with the sight, your brother—me—like a stone, cold and numb.

original: Ah, now no more will I control thy griefs:   Rend off thy silver hair, thy other hand   Gnawing with thy teeth;
translation: Oh, now I won’t try to calm you down; tear off your silver hair, bite your one remaining hand with your teeth,

original: and be this dismal sight   The closing up of our most wretched eyes;   Now is a time to storm; why art thou still?
translation: and let this sad sight kill us here. Now is the time to despair; why are you so quiet?

original: Ha, ha, ha!
translation: Ha, ha, ha!

original: Why dost thou laugh? it fits not with this hour.
translation: Why are you laughing? It doesn't fit the mood.

original: Why, I have not another tear to shed:   Besides, this sorrow is an enemy,   And would usurp upon my watery eyes   And make them blind with tributary tears:
translation: Why, I don’t have another tear to shed. Besides, this sorrow is an enemy, which would make my eyes weak by blinding them with tears—

original: Then which way shall I find Revenge's cave?   For these two heads do seem to speak to me,
translation: how will I find Revenge’s cave then? For these two heads seem to speak to me,

original: And threat me I shall never come to bliss   Till all these mischiefs be return'd again   Even in their throats that have committed them.
translation: threatening that I’ll never be happy again until I take revenge by returning all these offenses in kind, back down the throats of those who have wronged us.

original: You heavy people, circle me about,   That I may turn me to each one of you,   And swear unto my soul to right your wrongs.   The vow is made.
translation: Come, let’s see what I have to do. You sad people, circle around me, so that I can turn to each of you and swear on my soul to take revenge on your behalf. The vow is made.

original: Come, brother, take a head;   And in this hand the other I will bear.
translation: [To MARCUS]  Come, brother, take a head, and in this hand I’ll carry the other.

original: Lavinia, thou shalt be employ'd: these arms!   Bear thou my hand, sweet wench, between thy teeth.
translation: [To LAVINIA]  Lavinia, you’ll have a job too—these arms! Carry my hand between your teeth, sweet girl.

original: As for thee, boy, go get thee from my sight;   Thou art an exile, and thou must not stay:
translation: [To LUCIUS]  As for you, boy, get out of my sight; you’re banished, and must not stay.

original: Hie to the Goths, and raise an army there:   And, if you love me, as I think you do,   Let's kiss and part, for we have much to do.
translation: Go to the Goths and raise an army there, and if you love me—as I think you do—let’s kiss and say goodbye, for we have much to do.

original: Farewell Andronicus, my noble father,   The wofull'st man that ever lived in Rome:   Farewell, proud Rome; till Lucius come again,
translation: Goodbye, Andronicus, my noble father and the saddest man that ever lived in Rome. Goodbye, proud Rome. Until Lucius comes again,

original: He leaves his pledges dearer than his life:   Farewell, Lavinia, my noble sister;   O, would thou wert as thou tofore hast been!
translation: he leaves behind a promise to return, dearer than his life. Farewell, Lavinia, my noble sister: oh, if only you were like you were before!

original: But now nor Lucius nor Lavinia lives   But in oblivion and hateful griefs.   If Lucius live, he will requite your wrongs;
translation: But now neither Lucius nor Lavinia lives, except in grief and despair. As long as Lucius lives, he will fight for justice for you,

original: And make proud Saturnine and his empress   Beg at the gates, like Tarquin and his queen.
translation: and make proud Saturnine and his empress beg at the gates like  Tarquin and his queen .

original: Now will I to the Goths, and raise a power,   To be revenged on Rome and Saturnine.
translation: Now I’ll go to the Goths, and raise an army to take revenge on Rome and Saturnine.

original: So, so; now sit: and look you eat no more   Than will preserve just so much strength in us   As will revenge these bitter woes of ours.
translation: There, there. Sit down. And make sure you eat no more than will keep us alive long enough to take revenge on our enemies.

original: Marcus, unknit that sorrow-wreathen knot:   Thy niece and I, poor creatures, want our hands,   And cannot passionate our tenfold grief   With folded arms.
translation: Marcus, unfold your arms: your niece and I, poor creatures, lack hands and can’t show ten times more sadness by standing like that.

original: This poor right hand of mine   Is left to tyrannize upon my breast;
translation: Instead, I have to beat my breast with my poor remaining right hand.

original: Who, when my heart, all mad with misery,   Beats in this hollow prison of my flesh,   Then thus I thump it down.
translation: My heart beats in the hollow prison of my body, enraged with misery, and I thump it down.

original: [To LAVINIA]   Thou map of woe, that thus dost talk in signs!   When thy poor heart beats with outrageous beating,   Thou canst not strike it thus to make it still.
translation: [To LAVINIA]  You  map of grief , talking in sign language! When your poor heart beats fast, you can’t strike your chest to make it quiet.

original: Wound it with sighing, girl, kill it with groans;   Or get some little knife between thy teeth,   And just against thy heart make thou a hole;
translation: Try sighing, my girl, or kill it with groans. Or take a little knife between your teeth and make a hole against your heart,

original: That all the tears that thy poor eyes let fall   May run into that sink, and soaking in   Drown the lamenting fool in sea-salt tears.
translation: so all the tears that fall from your poor eyes may run in and drown it.

original: Fie, brother, fie! teach her not thus to lay Such violent hands upon her tender life.
translation: Brother, stop! Don’t tell her how to lay violent hands on herself.

original: How now! has sorrow made thee dote already?   Why, Marcus, no man should be mad but I.   What violent hands can she lay on her life?
translation: Oh! Has sorrow already made you mad? Why, Marcus, no man should be mad but me. What violent hands can she lay on her life?

original: Ah, wherefore dost thou urge the name of hands;   To bid AEneas tell the tale twice o'er,   How Troy was burnt and he made miserable?
translation: Why do you use the word “hands?” That’s like asking Aeneas to tell the story again of how Troy was burnt and he lost everything.

original: O, handle not the theme, to talk of hands,   Lest we remember still that we have none.
translation: Oh, don’t say anything about hands, lest we remember that we don’t have any.

original: Fie, fie, how franticly I square my talk,   As if we should forget we had no hands,   If Marcus did not name the word of hands!
translation: Ha, but I’m talking foolishly—as if we could forget we have no hands, just because Marcus didn’t mention it!

original: Come, let's fall to; and, gentle girl, eat this:   Here is no drink! Hark, Marcus, what she says;   I can interpret all her martyr'd signs;
translation: Come, let’s eat. And gentle girl, eat this—what, you won’t drink? Hear what she says, Marcus; I can interpret all her signs.

original: She says she drinks no other drink but tears,   Brew'd with her sorrow, mesh'd upon her cheeks:
translation: She says she’ll drink nothing but the tears on her cheeks, brewed with her sorrow.

original: Speechless complainer, I will learn thy thought;   In thy dumb action will I be as perfect   As begging hermits in their holy prayers:
translation: [To LAVINIA]  Speechless victim, I will learn your thoughts; your silent actions will be as clear in meaning to me as the prayers of hermits.

original: Thou shalt not sigh, nor hold thy stumps to heaven,   Nor wink, nor nod, nor kneel, nor make a sign,
translation: You won’t sigh, or hold your stumps to heaven, or wink, or nod, or kneel, or make a sign

original: But I of these will wrest an alphabet   And by still practise learn to know thy meaning.
translation: without me understanding you: I’ll make an alphabet of these actions, and I’ll learn to know what you mean.

original: Good grandsire, leave these bitter deep laments: Make my aunt merry with some pleasing tale.
translation: Good grandfather, stop this bitter sadness; make my aunt laugh with some pleasing story.

original: Alas, the tender boy, in passion moved, Doth weep to see his grandsire's heaviness.
translation: Oh, the sweet boy, moved by compassion, cries to see his grandfather’s grief.

original: Peace, tender sapling; thou art made of tears, And tears will quickly melt thy life away.
translation: Calm down, innocent boy; you are made of tears, and tears will melt away your life.

original: What dost thou strike at, Marcus, with thy knife?
translation: What do you strike at with your knife, Marcus?

original: At that that I have kill'd, my lord; a fly.
translation: I struck at a fly, my lord, which I killed.

original: Out on thee, murderer! thou kill'st my heart;   Mine eyes are cloy'd with view of tyranny:
translation: Get out, murderer! You kill my heart; my eyes are filled with tears at seeing this cruelty.

original: A deed of death done on the innocent   Becomes not Titus' brother: get thee gone:   I see thou art not for my company.
translation: The murder of the innocent doesn’t become Titus’s brother; get out, since I see you aren’t fit for my company.

original: Alas, my lord, I have but kill'd a fly.
translation: My lord, I've only killed a fly.

original: But how, if that fly had a father and mother?   How would he hang his slender gilded wings,   And buzz lamenting doings in the air!
translation: But what if that fly had a father and mother? He would fly on his slender golden wings, buzzing sad songs in the air!

original: Poor harmless fly,   That, with his pretty buzzing melody,   Came here to make us merry! and thou hast   kill'd him.
translation: Poor harmless fly, that, with his pretty buzzing song, came here to make us happy! And you have killed him.

original: Pardon me, sir; it was a black ill-favor'd fly, Like to the empress' Moor; therefore I kill'd him.
translation: Forgive me, sir; it was a black ugly fly that looked like the empress’s Moor, which was why I killed him.

original: O, O, O,   Then pardon me for reprehending thee,   For thou hast done a charitable deed.
translation: Oh, oh, oh, then forgive me for attaching you, for you’ve done a good deed.

original: Give me thy knife, I will insult on him;   Flattering myself, as if it were the Moor   Come hither purposely to poison me.—
translation: Give me your knife, and I’ll butcher him, pretending it’s the Moor come here to poison me.  [Stabs the fly.]

original: There's for thyself, and that's for Tamora.   Ah, sirrah!
translation: Here’s for you, and that’s for Tamora. Ah, bastard!

original: Yet, I think, we are not brought so low,   But that between us we can kill a fly   That comes in likeness of a coal-black Moor.
translation: At least we’re not so low; between us we can still kill a fly that looks like a coal-black Moor.

original: Alas, poor man! grief has so wrought on him, He takes false shadows for true substances.
translation: Oh, poor man! He is so grief-stricken that he imagines shadows are the real thing.

original: Come, take away. Lavinia, go with me:   I'll to thy closet; and go read with thee   Sad stories chanced in the times of old.
translation: Come, let’s go. Lavinia, come with me; I’ll go to your room and read sad stories of old times with you.

original: Come, boy, and go with me: thy sight is young,   And thou shalt read when mine begin to dazzle.
translation: [To LUCIUS]  Come with me, too, boy; your young eyes can read when my own begin to fade.

original: Help, grandsire, help! my aunt Lavinia   Follows me every where, I know not why:
translation: Help, grandfather, help! My aunt Lavinia follows me everywhere, but I don’t know why.

original: Good uncle Marcus, see how swift she comes.   Alas, sweet aunt, I know not what you mean.
translation: Uncle Marcus, see how quickly she comes after me. Oh, sweet aunt, I don’t know what you mean.

original: Stand by me, Lucius; do not fear thine aunt.
translation: Stand by me, Lucius; don't be afraid of your aunt.

original: She loves thee, boy, too well to do thee harm.
translation: She loves you too much to hurt you, boy.

original: Ay, when my father was in Rome she did.
translation: Yes, when my father was in Rome she did.

original: What means my niece Lavinia by these signs?
translation: What does my niece Lavinia mean by this sign language?

original: Fear her not, Lucius: somewhat doth she mean:   See, Lucius, see how much she makes of thee:   Somewhither would she have thee go with her.
translation: Don’t be afraid of her, Lucius; she means something. See, Lucius, how much she loves you; she wants you to go somewhere with her.

original: Ah, boy, Cornelia never with more care   Read to her sons than she hath read to thee   Sweet poetry and Tully's Orator.
translation: Oh, boy,  Cornelia  never read to her sons with so much care as Lavinia reads you sweet poetry and  Tully’s Orator.

original: Canst thou not guess wherefore she plies thee thus?
translation: Can't you guess what she wants from you?

original: My lord, I know not, I, nor can I guess,   Unless some fit or frenzy do possess her:   For I have heard my grandsire say full oft,
translation: My lord, I don’t know and I can’t guess. Unless she’s suffering from some fit or madness, f or I’ve often heard my grandfather say

original: Extremity of griefs would make men mad;   And I have read that Hecuba of Troy   Ran mad through sorrow: that made me to fear;
translation: that extreme grief makes people mad, and I’ve read that  Hecuba of Troy  went mad from sorrow. That made me afraid—

original: Although, my lord, I know my noble aunt   Loves me as dear as e'er my mother did,   And would not, but in fury, fright my youth:
translation: although, my lord, I know my noble aunt loves me as dearly as my mother ever did, and would only in madness have ever frightened me—

original: Which made me down to throw my books, and fly—   Causeless, perhaps. But pardon me, sweet aunt:
translation: and I threw down my books and ran, but perhaps for no reason. Forgive me, sweet aunt;

original: And, madam, if my uncle Marcus go,   I will most willingly attend your ladyship.
translation: and madam, if my uncle Marcus comes with us, I’ll gladly go with you.

original: Lucius, I will.
translation: Lucius, I will.

original: How now, Lavinia! Marcus, what means this?   Some book there is that she desires to see.   Which is it, girl, of these? Open them, boy.
translation: What are you doing, Lavinia? Marcus, what does this mean? She wants to see one of these books. Which book? Open them, boy.

original: But thou art deeper read, and better skill'd   Come, and take choice of all my library,
translation: [To LAVINIA]  You’re a better reader than me—come and take any book from my library,

original: And so beguile thy sorrow, till the heavens   Reveal the damn'd contriver of this deed.   Why lifts she up her arms in sequence thus?
translation: and so distract yourself from your sorrow until the heavens reveal who did this to you. Why does she lift her arms up twice?

original: I think she means that there was more than one Confederate in the fact: ay, more there was; Or else to heaven she heaves them for revenge.
translation: I think she means that there was more than one who did this; yes, there was more than one. Unless she’s praying to heaven for revenge.

original: Lucius, what book is that she tosseth so?
translation: Lucius, which book is she searching through so frantically?

original: Grandsire, 'tis Ovid's Metamorphoses; My mother gave it me.
translation: Grandfather, it's Ovid's Metamorphoses; my mother gave it to me.

original: For love of her that's gone, Perhaps she cull'd it from among the rest.
translation: Perhaps she chose it for love of Lucius's mother.

original: Soft! see how busily she turns the leaves!
translation: Look! See how quickly she turns the pages.

original: What would she find? Lavinia, shall I read?
translation: What is she looking for? Lavinia, do you want me to read?

original: This is the tragic tale of Philomel,   And treats of Tereus' treason and his rape:   And rape, I fear, was root of thine annoy.
translation: This is the tragic story of Philomel, who was raped by Tereus—and rape, I fear, was what happened to you.

original: See, brother, see; note how she quotes the leaves.
translation: See, brother, see; look how she's pointing to particular passages.

original: Lavinia, wert thou thus surprised, sweet girl,   Ravish'd and wrong'd, as Philomela was,   Forced in the ruthless, vast, and gloomy woods? See,  see!
translation: Lavinia, were you attacked, sweet girl, raped as Philomel was in the silent, vast, and gloomy woods? Of course, of course!

original: Ay, such a place there is, where we did hunt—   O, had we never, never hunted there!—
translation: Yes, there is a place like that, the wood where we hunted—oh, I wish we had never, never hunted there!—

original: Pattern'd by that the poet here describes,   By nature made for murders and for rapes.
translation: just like the one described by Ovid, made by nature for murder and rape.

original: O, why should nature build so foul a den, Unless the gods delight in tragedies?
translation: Oh, why would nature create such a foul place, unless the gods take delight in our suffering?

original: Give signs, sweet girl, for here are none   but friends,   What Roman lord it was durst do the deed:
translation: Give signs, sweet girl, for everyone here is your friend: what Roman lord is responsible?

original: Or slunk not Saturnine, as Tarquin erst,   That left the camp to sin in Lucrece' bed?
translation: Was it Saturnine—like  Tarquin , who left the camp to attack Lucrece?

original: Sit down, sweet niece: brother, sit down by me.   Apollo, Pallas, Jove, or Mercury,   Inspire me, that I may this treason find!
translation: Sit down, sweet niece: brother, sit down by me. May  Apollo, Pallas, Jove, or Mercury  inspire me, so that I can find some way to expose the criminal!

original: My lord, look here: look here, Lavinia:   This sandy plot is plain;
translation: My lord, look; look at this, Lavinia. This is a plain plot of sand;

original: guide, if thou canst   This after me, when I have writ my name   Without the help of any hand at all.
translation: if I take this stick, I can write my name without any hands at all. If you can, do what I did.

original: Cursed be that heart that forced us to this shift!   Write thou good niece; and here display, at last,   What God will have discover'd for revenge;
translation: Curses on the heart that forced us to this method! Write, good niece; and tell us, at last, what God wants to be known so that we can take revenge.

original: Heaven guide thy pen to print thy sorrows plain,   That we may know the traitors and the truth!
translation: Heaven will guide your pen to show what happened, so that we may know the traitors and the truth!

original: O, do ye read, my lord, what she hath writ? 'Stuprum. Chiron. Demetrius.'
translation: Oh, do you read, my lord, what she’s written? "Rape. Chiron. Demetrius."

original: What, what! the lustful sons of Tamora Performers of this heinous, bloody deed?
translation: What, what! The lustful sons of Tamora did this horrible, bloody crime?

original: Magni Dominator poli, Tam lentus audis scelera? tam lentus vides?
translation: Magni Dominator poli, Tam lentus audis scelera? tam lentus vides?

original: O, calm thee, gentle lord; although I know   There is enough written upon this earth   To stir a mutiny in the mildest thoughts   And arm the minds of infants to exclaims.
translation: Oh, calm yourself, gentle lord—although I know there’s enough written here on the ground to enrage even the mildest person, and make children exclaim with anger.

original: My lord, kneel down with me; Lavinia, kneel;   And kneel, sweet boy, the Roman Hector's hope;
translation: My lord, kneel down with me; Lavinia, kneel; and kneel, sweet boy, who we hope will grow up to be the Roman  Hector .

original: And swear with me, as, with the woful fere   And father of that chaste dishonour'd dame,   Lord Junius Brutus sware for Lucrece' rape,
translation: Swear with me—as Lucrece’s father,  Lord Junius Brutus , swore after her rape—

original: That we will prosecute by good advice   Mortal revenge upon these traitorous Goths,   And see their blood, or die with this reproach.
translation: that we will take mortal revenge on these traitorous Goths. We’ll see them bleed, or we’ll die instead.

original: 'Tis sure enough, an you knew how.   But if you hunt these bear-whelps, then beware:
translation: Certainly we will, if we can. But if you hunt these bear cubs, then beware;

original: The dam will wake; and, if she wind you once,   She's with the lion deeply still in league,   And lulls him whilst she playeth on her back,   And when he sleeps will she do what she list.
translation: their mother will wake, and if she sees you once, she’ll set the lion on you—for she lulls him to sleep while she plays on her back, and while he sleeps she'll do what she wants.

original: You are a young huntsman, Marcus; let it alone;   And, come, I will go get a leaf of brass,   And with a gad of steel will write these words,   And lay it by:
translation: You’re not much of a huntsman, Marcus; leave it alone. And come, I’ll go get  a sheet of brass , and with a steel pen I’ll write these words and lay it aside:

original: the angry northern wind   Will blow these sands, like Sibyl's leaves, abroad,   And where's your lesson, then?
translation: the angry northern wind will blow these sands through the air like  Sibyl’s leaves .

original: Boy, what say you?
translation: [To YOUNG LUCIUS]  And what do you have to say for yourself, boy?

original: I say, my lord, that if I were a man, Their mother's bed-chamber should not be safe For these bad bondmen to the yoke of Rome.
translation: I say, my lord, that if I were a man, these slaves wouldn’t be safe in their mother’s bedroom.

original: Ay, that's my boy! thy father hath full oft For his ungrateful country done the like.
translation: Yes, that’s my boy! Your father has often done the same for his ungrateful country.

original: And, uncle, so will I, an if I live.
translation: And so will I, uncle, if I live long enough.

original: Come, go with me into mine armoury;   Lucius, I'll fit thee; and withal, my boy,
translation: Come, go with me to my armory; Lucius, I’ll fit you with armor,

original: Shalt carry from me to the empress' sons   Presents that I intend to send them both:   Come, come; thou'lt do thy message, wilt thou not?
translation: and you’ll go to the empress’s sons dressed like that, carrying presents from me. Come, come—you’ll take the message for me, won’t you?

original: Ay, with my dagger in their bosoms, grandsire.
translation: Yes, by stabbing them in their hearts, grandfather.

original: No, boy, not so; I'll teach thee another course.   Lavinia, come. Marcus, look to my house:
translation: No, boy, not that; I’ll teach you another way. Lavinia, come. Marcus, take care of my house while I’m gone;

original: Lucius and I'll go brave it at the court:   Ay, marry, will we, sir; and we'll be waited on.
translation: Lucius and I will go make a spectacle of ourselves at court. Yes, indeed we will, sir; and they’ll pay attention.

original: O heavens, can you hear a good man groan,   And not relent, or not compassion him?
translation: Oh, heavens, can you hear a good man groan, and not stop these sufferings, or take pity on him?

original: Marcus, attend him in his ecstasy,   That hath more scars of sorrow in his heart   Than foemen's marks upon his batter'd shield;
translation: Marcus, care for him in his madness, since he now has more scars of sorrow on his heart than marks of the enemy on his battered shield.

original: But yet so just that he will not revenge.   Revenge, ye heavens, for old Andronicus!
translation: And yet he’s so attached to justice that he won’t take revenge. So take revenge for old Andronicus, heavens!

original: Demetrius, here's the son of Lucius; He hath some message to deliver us.
translation: Look, Demetrius, here's the son of Lucius—and he's got some message to give us.

original: Ay, some mad message from his mad grandfather.
translation: Yes, some mad message from his mad grandfather.

original: My lords, with all the humbleness I may,   I greet your honours from Andronicus.
translation: My lords, I bring greetings from Andronicus with all the humility I can.

original: [Aside]     And pray the Roman gods confound you both!
translation: [To himself]  And I pray the Roman gods punish you both!

original: Gramercy, lovely Lucius: what's the news?
translation: Thanks, lovely Lucius; what's the news?

original: [Aside]   That you are both decipher'd, that's the news,   For villains mark'd with rape.—
translation: [To himself]  That we've found you out, that's the news, and know that you're rapists.

original: May it please you,   My grandsire, well advised, hath sent by me   The goodliest weapons of his armoury   To gratify your honourable youth,
translation: [To CHIRON and DEMETRIUS]  With all respect, my grandfather has sent me to bring you the best weapons from his armory to amuse your honorable youth,

original: The hope of Rome; for so he bade me say;   And so I do, and with his gifts present   Your lordships,
translation: for you are the hope of Rome. He told me to tell you that, and so I do. And I present you these gifts, your lordships,

original: that, whenever you have need,   You may be armed and appointed well:   And so I leave you both:
translation: so that you can always be armed whenever you need to—and with that, I'll go.

original: [Aside]   like bloody villains.
translation: [To himself]  Armed like murderous villains, that is.

original: What's here? A scroll; and written round about?   Let's see;
translation: [Looks at weapon]  What's this? A scroll tied around? Let's see.

original: [Reads]   'Integer vitae, scelerisque purus,   Non eget Mauri jaculis, nec arcu.'
translation: [Reads]   "Integer vitae, scelerisque purus, / Non eget Mauri jaculis, nec arcu."

original: O, 'tis a verse in Horace; I know it well: I read it in the grammar long ago.
[Aside]   Now, what a thing it is to be an ass!   Here's no sound jest! the old man hath found their  guilt;
translation: [To himself]  Ha, what an ass! This is no joke—the old man knows that they're guilty,

original: And sends them weapons wrapped about with lines,   That wound, beyond their feeling, to the quick.   But were our witty empress well afoot,
translation: and sends them weapons wrapped with words that wound them, although they don't pick up on it. But if our sly empress were here,

original: She would applaud Andronicus' conceit:   But let her rest in her unrest awhile.
translation: she would applaud Andronicus's cleverness. But we'll leave her be for a while, since she's unwell.

original: And now, young lords, was't not a happy star   Led us to Rome, strangers, and more than so,   Captives, to be advanced to this height?
translation: [To CHIRON and DEMETRIUS]  And now, young lords—wasn't it lucky that we came to Rome, since we arrived as foreigners and captives and now have so much power?

original: It did me good, before the palace gate   To brave the tribune in his brother's hearing.
translation: It pleased me to have a go at Marcus Andronicus at the palace gate in front of his brother.

original: But me more good, to see so great a lord Basely insinuate and send us gifts.
translation: And I love to see this great lord bow to us and send us gifts.

original: Had he not reason, Lord Demetrius? Did you not use his daughter very friendly?
translation: Doesn't he have reason, Lord Demetrius? Didn't you treat his daughter in a very friendly way?

original: I would we had a thousand Roman dames At such a bay, by turn to serve our lust.
translation: I wish we had a thousand Roman ladies like that, to take turns serving our lust.

original: A charitable wish and full of love.
translation: A kind and loving wish.

original: Here lacks but your mother for to say amen.
translation: We just miss your mother to say "amen."

original: And that would she for twenty thousand more.
translation: And she would wish we had twenty thousand more.

original: Come, let us go; and pray to all the gods For our beloved mother in her pains.
translation: Come, let's go and pray to all the gods for your beloved mother in her labor pains.

original: Pray to the devils; the gods have given us  over.
translation: Pray to the devils; the gods have given up on us.

original: Why do the emperor's trumpets flourish thus?
translation: Why do the emperor's trumpets make that sound?

original: Belike, for joy the emperor hath a son.
translation: Probably because the emperor has a son.

original: Soft! who comes here?
translation: Look! Who's that?

original: Good morr ow, lords: O, tell me, did you see Aaron the Moor?
translation: Good morning, lords; oh, tell me, have you seen Aaron the Moor?

original: Well, more or less, or ne'er a whit at all, Here Aaron is; and what with Aaron now?
translation: Well, they've seen me more or less, or they never saw me at all—here's Aaron. What do you want with him?

original: O gentle Aaron, we are all undone! Now help, or woe betide thee evermore!
translation: Oh, gentle Aaron, we're all ruined! Help, or we'll be miserable forever!

original: Why, what a caterwauling dost thou keep! What dost thou wrap and fumble in thine arms?
translation: Why do you scream and cry like that? What's that bundle in your arms?

original: O, that which I would hide from heaven's eye, Our empress' shame, and stately Rome's disgrace! She is deliver'd, lords; she is deliver'd.
To whom?
translation: To whom?

original: I mean, she is brought a-bed.
translation: I mean, she's had a child.

original: Well, God give her good rest! What hath he sent her?
translation: Well, God give her a good rest afterwards! What sort of child has he given her?

original: A devil.
translation: A devil.

original: Why, then she is the devil's dam; a joyful issue.
translation: Why, then she's the devil's mother; a happy birth.

original: A joyless, dismal, black, and sorrowful issue:   Here is the babe, as loathsome as a toad   Amongst the fairest breeders of our clime:
translation: It's a joyless, sad, and black child: here's the baby, as disgusting as a toad among the fairest ladies of our land.

original: The empress sends it thee, thy stamp, thy seal,   And bids thee christen it with thy dagger's point.
translation: The empress sends it to you—for it looks exactly like you—and orders you to kill it with your dagger.

original: 'Zounds, ye whore! is black so base a hue? Sweet blowse, you are a beauteous blossom, sure.
translation: By God, you whore! Is black so terrible a color? Sweetheart, you are a beautiful flower, you are.

original: Villain, what hast thou done?
translation: Villain, what have you done?

original: That which thou canst not undo.
translation: That which you can't undo.

original: Thou hast undone our mother.
translation: You have undone our mother.

original: Villain, I have done thy mother.
translation: Villain, I have done your mother.

original: And therein, hellish dog, thou hast undone. Woe to her chance, and damn'd her loathed choice! Accursed the offspring of so foul a fiend!
translation: And in doing that, hellish dog, you've undone her. Oh, let her good luck come to an end, and damn her disgusting choice! Curses on the offspring of such a foul devil!

original: It shall not live.
translation: It shall not live.

original: It shall not die.
translation: It shall not die.

original: Aaron, it must; the mother wills it so.
translation: Aaron, it must; the mother orders it.

original: What, must it, nurse? then let no man but I Do execution on my flesh and blood.
translation: What, it has to die, nurse? Then let no one but me kill my own flesh and blood.

original: I'll broach the tadpole on my rapier's point: Nurse, give it me; my sword shall soon dispatch it.
translation: I'll stab the tadpole with the point of my blade; nurse, give it to me. My sword will soon get rid of it.

original: Sooner this sword shall plough thy bowels up.
translation: Before you do that, this sword will tear out your bowels.

original: Stay, murderous villains! will you kill your brother?   Now, by the burning tapers of the sky,   That shone so brightly when this boy was got,
translation: Stop, murderous villains! Will you kill your brother? Now, by the light of the stars that shone so brightly when this boy was conceived,

original: He dies upon my scimitar's sharp point   That touches this my first-born son and heir!
translation: I'll kill whoever touches this child, my first-born son and heir!

original: I tell you, younglings, not Enceladus,   With all his threatening band of Typhon's brood,   Nor great Alcides, nor the god of war,   Shall seize this prey out of his father's hands.
translation: I tell you, boys,  Enceladus and all of Typhon's offspring , or  Alcides , or the god of war couldn't take this prey from his father's hands.

original: What, what, ye sanguine, shallow-hearted boys!   Ye white-limed walls! ye alehouse painted signs!
translation: What, what, you stupid, shallow boys! You white-washed walls! You painted alehouse signs!

original: Coal-black is better than another hue,   In that it scorns to bear another hue;
translation: Coal-black is better than any other color, because it will never bear another hue:

original: For all the water in the ocean   Can never turn the swan's black legs to white,   Although she lave them hourly in the flood.
translation: all the water in the ocean can never turn the swan's black legs to white, even if she bathed them hourly in the flood.

original: Tell the empress from me, I am of age   To keep mine own, excuse it how she can.
translation: Tell the empress from me that I'm old enough to keep my own child, whatever excuse she must make for it.

original: Wilt thou betray thy noble mistress thus?
translation: Will you betray your noble mistress like this?

original: My mistress is my mistress; this myself,   The vigour and the picture of my youth:   This before all the world do I prefer;
translation: My mistress is my mistress; this child is me, the picture of how I was a child. I prefer this to all the world,

original: This maugre all the world will I keep safe,   Or some of you shall smoke for it in Rome.
translation: and despite everything I will keep it safe—or all Rome will burn.

original: By this our mother is forever shamed.
translation: Our mother will be forever shamed by this.

original: Rome will despise her for this foul escape.
translation: Rome will hate her if this foul thing lives.

original: The emperor, in his rage, will doom her death.
translation: The emperor, in his anger, will condemn her to death.

original: I blush to think upon this ignomy.
translation: I can't stand to think of this humiliation.

original: Why, there's the privilege your beauty bears:   Fie, treacherous hue, that will betray with blushing   The close enacts and counsels of the heart!
translation: Why, that's because you're white: your treacherous color so easily betrays what you're thinking, since you blush so easily!

original: Here's a young lad framed of another leer:   Look, how the black slave smiles upon the father,   As who should say 'Old lad, I am thine own.'
translation: But this young boy has another kind of complexion. Look how the black slave smiles on his father, as if to say "old boy, I'm yours."

original: He is your brother, lords, sensibly fed   Of that self-blood that first gave life to you,   And from that womb where you imprison'd were   He is enfranchised and come to light:
translation: He's your brother, lords, fed from the same blood that first gave you life, and from the womb where you were imprisoned he has emerged, too, and come to the light.

original: Nay, he is your brother by the surer side,   Although my seal be stamped in his face.
translation: No, he is your brother, certainly, although he looks like me.

original: Aaron, what shall I say unto the empress?
translation: Aaron, what should I tell the empress?

original: Advise thee, Aaron, what is to be done, And we will all subscribe to thy advice: Save thou the child, so we may all be safe.
translation: Advise us what we should do, Aaron, and we'll take your advice. Save the child so that we can all be safe.

original: Then sit we down, and let us all consult. My son and I will have the wind of you: Keep there: now talk at pleasure of your safety.
translation: Then let's sit down and think. My son and I will have some space—stay over there. Stay there; now feel free to make a plan.

original: How many women saw this child of his?
translation: How many women saw his child?

original: Why, so, brave lords! when we join in league,   I am a lamb: but if you brave the Moor,   The chafed boar, the mountain lioness,
translation: Ah, see, brave lords! When we're working together, I'm like a lamb; but when you cross me, the boar, the mountain lioness,

original: The ocean swells not so as Aaron storms.   But say, again; how many saw the child?
translation: and the ocean are not so powerful as Aaron in rage. But tell us, again; how many have seen the child?

original: Cornelia the midwife and myself; And no one else but the deliver'd empress.
translation: Cornelia the midwife, me, and no one else but the empress.

original: The empress, the midwife, and yourself: Two may keep counsel when the third's away: Go to the empress, tell her this I said.
translation: The empress, the midwife, and you: two can be silent when the third's gone. Go to the empress and tell her that.

original: Weke, weke! so cries a pig prepared to the spit.
translation: Ha! She cries like a pig prepared to be roasted.

original: What mean'st thou, Aaron? wherefore didst thou this?
translation: What are you doing, Aaron? Why did you do this?

original: O Lord, sir, 'tis a deed of policy:   Shall she live to betray this guilt of ours,   A long-tongued babbling gossip? no, lords, no:   And now be it known to you my full intent.
translation: Oh, Lord, sir, for strategy. Should this babbling gossip live to tell the tale? No, lords, no—and now let me tell you my full plan.

original: Not far, one Muli lives, my countryman;   His wife but yesternight was brought to bed;   His child is like to her, fair as you are:
translation: One of my countrymen, Muli, lives not too far from here. Yesterday night his wife gave birth to a child like her, as fair-skinned as you.

original: Go pack with him, and give the mother gold,   And tell them both the circumstance of all;
translation: Go to him, give the mother money, and tell them the situation:

original: And how by this their child shall be advanced,   And be received for the emperor's heir,   And substituted in the place of mine,   To calm this tempest whirling in the court;
translation: if they give us their child, it shall become the emperor's heir and take the place of mine, to calm this storm in the court

original: And let the emperor dandle him for his own.   Hark ye, lords; ye see I have given her physic,
translation: and let the emperor have his son. Listen, lords, you see I have given her medicine—

original: And you must needs bestow her funeral;   The fields are near, and you are gallant grooms:   This done, see that you take no longer days,
translation: And you have to take care of the funeral; bury her in the fields nearby, for you're noble gentlemen. Once you're done with that, hurry up

original: But send the midwife presently to me.   The midwife and the nurse well made away,   Then let the ladies tattle what they please.
translation: and send the midwife to me. Once I've taken care of the midwife and the nurse, then the ladies can gossip all they want.

original: Aaron, I see thou wilt not trust the air With secrets.
translation: Aaron, I see you wouldn't trust the air with your secrets.

original: For this care of Tamora, Herself and hers are highly bound to thee.
translation: For this favor to our mother, we're very grateful to you.

original: Now to the Goths, as swift as swallow flies;   There to dispose this treasure in mine arms,   And secretly to greet the empress' friends.
translation: Now, swift as a sparrow, I'll go to the Goths, to leave this treasure in my arms and secretly greet the empress's friends.

original: Come on, you thick lipp'd slave, I'll bear you hence;   For it is you that puts us to our shifts:
translation: [To the baby]  Come on, you thick-lipped slave, I'll take you there, for it's you that's caused all this mess.

original: I'll make you feed on berries and on roots,   And feed on curds and whey, and suck the goat,   And cabin in a cave, and bring you up   To be a warrior, and command a camp.
translation: I'll feed you with berries and roots, and curds and whey. You'll nurse from the goat, and live in a cave, and I'll bring you up to be a great warrior and command a camp.

original: Come, Marcus; come, kinsmen; this is the way.
translation: Come on, Marcus, come; kinsmen, this is the way.

original: Sir boy, now let me see your archery;   Look ye draw home enough, and 'tis there straight.   Terras Astraea reliquit:
translation: [To Young LUCIUS]  Sir boy, now let me see your archery; make sure you draw home and shoot straight.  Terras Astraea reliquit :

original: Be you remember'd, Marcus, she's gone, she's fled.   Sirs, take you to your tools. You, cousins, shall   Go sound the ocean, and cast your nets;
translation: remember it. Marcus, justice is gone, she ran away. Sirs, pick up your weapons. You, cousins, will go around the ocean and cast your nets;

original: Happily you may catch her in the sea;   Yet there's as little justice as at land:   No; Publius and Sempronius, you must do it;
translation: perhaps you can catch her in the sea. But there’s just as little justice there as on land—so never mind. No, Publius and Sempronius, you must do it;

original: 'Tis you must dig with mattock and with spade,   And pierce the inmost centre of the earth:   Then, when you come to Pluto's region,
translation: dig with a fork and spade until you get to the center of the Earth. Then, when you get to Pluto’s underworld,

original: I pray you, deliver him this petition;   Tell him, it is for justice and for aid,   And that it comes from old Andronicus,   Shaken with sorrows in ungrateful Rome.
translation: give him this petition. Tell him I ask for justice and for help, and that it comes from old Andronicus, who suffers in ungrateful Rome.

original: Ah, Rome! Well, well; I made thee miserable   What time I threw the people's suffrages   On him that thus doth tyrannize o'er me.
translation: Oh, Rome! Well, I made you miserable when I threw the people’s votes on the tyrant Saturninus.

original: Go, get you gone; and pray be careful all,   And leave you not a man-of-war unsearch'd:
translation: Go, go away; and be careful everyone, and don't let a ship get by without searching it.

original: This wicked emperor may have shipp'd her hence;   And, kinsmen, then we may go pipe for justice.
translation: This wicked emperor may have had her shipped her away. And then, kinsmen, we're searching for justice in vain.

original: O Publius, is not this a heavy case, To see thy noble uncle thus distract?
translation: Oh, Publius, isn’t this distressing, to see your noble uncle so mad?

original: Therefore, my lord, it highly us concerns   By day and night to attend him carefully,
translation: And for that reason, my lord, we make sure to watch him all day and night,

original: And feed his humour kindly as we may,   Till time beget some careful remedy.
translation: and take care of him as best we can, until perhaps time will heal him.

original: Kinsmen, his sorrows are past remedy.   Join with the Goths; and with revengeful war   Take wreak on Rome for this ingratitude,
translation: Kinsmen, his sorrows are past fixing. Join the Goths, and by going to war take revenge on Rome for this ingratitude,

original: And vengeance on the traitor Saturnine.
translation: and on the traitor Saturnine.

original: Publius, how now! how now, my masters! What, have you met with her?
translation: Publius, how are you? How are you, my masters? What, have you found her?

original: No, my good lord; but Pluto sends you word,   If you will have Revenge from hell, you shall:
translation: No, my good lord; but Pluto says that you will have revenge from hell, if you ask for it.

original: Marry, for Justice, she is so employ'd,   He thinks, with Jove in heaven, or somewhere else,   So that perforce you must needs stay a time.
translation: He thinks that Justice is busy with Jove in heaven, or somewhere else, so you need to wait a bit.

original: He doth me wrong to feed me with delays.   I'll dive into the burning lake below,   And pull her out of Acheron by the heels.
translation: It’s wrong to make me wait. I’ll dive into the burning lake in the underworld, and pull her out of  Acheron  by the heels.

original: Marcus, we are but shrubs, no cedars we   No big-boned men framed of the Cyclops' size;
translation: Marcus, we’re just shrubs, not cedars, not big-boned men like the  cyclops .

original: But metal, Marcus, steel to the very back,   Yet wrung with wrongs more than our backs can bear:   And, sith there's no justice in earth nor hell,
translation: We’re just metal and steel, Marcus, and yet we’ve had more wrongs done to us than our backs can bear. And, since there’s no justice in earth or hell,

original: We will solicit heaven and move the gods   To send down Justice for to wreak our wrongs.   Come, to this gear. You are a good archer, Marcus;
translation: we’ll pray to heaven and move the gods to send down Justice to right our wrongs. Come, let’s do it. You are a good archer, Marcus.

original: 'Ad Jovem,' that's for you: here, 'Ad Apollinem:'   'Ad Martem,' that's for myself:   Here, boy, to Pallas: here, to Mercury:   To Saturn, Caius, not to Saturnine;
translation: "To Jove," that's for you; here, "To Apollo"; "To Mars," that's for me. Here, boy, to Pallas; here, to Mercury; to Saturn; Caius. Not to Saturnine

original: You were as good to shoot against the wind.   To it, boy! Marcus, loose when I bid.   Of my word, I have written to effect;   There's not a god left unsolicited.
translation: —you might as well shoot against the wind. Get to it, boy! Marcus, let your arrow fly when I tell you. I swear I’ve written to every god for justice.

original: Kinsmen, shoot all your shafts into the court: We will afflict the emperor in his pride.
translation: Kinsmen, shoot all your arrows at the palace; we’ll annoy the prideful emperor.

original: Now, masters, draw.
translation: Now, masters, draw.

original: O, well said, Lucius! Good boy, in Virgo's lap; give it Pallas.
My lord, I aim a mile beyond the moon; Your letter is with Jupiter by this.
translation: My lord, I aim a mile beyond the moon; I've sent your letter to Jupiter.

original: Ha, ha! Publius, Publius, what hast thou done? See, see, thou hast shot off one of Taurus' horns.
This was the sport, my lord: when Publius shot,   The Bull, being gall'd, gave Aries such a knock   That down fell both the Ram's horns in the court;
translation: This was the game, my lord; when Publius shot his arrow, Taurus butted heads with  Aries , and both the ram’s horns fell down into the court.

original: And who should find them but the empress' villain?   She laugh'd, and told the Moor he should not choose   But give them to his master for a present.
translation: And who should find them but the empress's villain? She laughed, and told the Moor he should  give them to the emperor  as a present.

original: Why, there it goes: God give his lordship joy!
translation: Why, there they go: God give joy to his lordship!

original: News, news from heaven! Marcus, the post is come. Sirrah, what tidings? have you any letters? Shall I have justice? what says Jupiter?
translation: News, news from heaven! Marcus, the post is come. Man, what do you hear? Do you have any letters for me? Will we have justice? What does Jupiter say?

original: O, the gibbet-maker! he says that he hath taken them down again, for the man must not be hanged till the next week.
But what says Jupiter, I ask thee?
translation: But what does Jupiter say, I ask you?

original: Alas, sir, I know not Jupiter; I never drank with him in all my life.
translation: Sorry, sir, I don’t know Jupiter; I’ve never had a drink with him in my life.

original: Why, villain, art not thou the carrier?
translation: But villain, aren't you the messenger?

original: Ay, of my pigeons, sir; nothing else.
translation: Yes, I carry pigeons, sir—nothing else.

original: Why, didst thou not come from heaven?
translation: Why, didn't you come from heaven?

original: From heaven! alas, sir, I never came there God   forbid I should be so bold to press to heaven in my   young days.
translation: From heaven! Oh, sir, I’ve never been there. God forbid I should barge into heaven when I’m still so young.

original: Why, I am going with my pigeons to the   tribunal plebs, to take up a matter of brawl   betwixt my uncle and one of the emperial's men.
translation: Why, I’m going with my pigeons to the tribune of the plebs, to deal with a fight between my uncle and one of the emperor’s soldiers.

original: Why, sir, that is as fit as can be to serve for   your oration;
translation: [To TITUS]  Why, sir, this is the perfect messenger for your speech.

original: and let him deliver the pigeons to   the emperor from you.
translation: Let him take the pigeons to the emperor from you.

original: Tell me, can you deliver an oration to the emperor with a grace?
Nay, truly, sir, I could never say grace in all my  life.
translation: No, truly, sir, I've never said grace in my life.

original: Sirrah, come hither: make no more ado,   But give your pigeons to the emperor:   By me thou shalt have justice at his hands.
translation: Man, come here; don’t say anything else, but just bring your pigeons to the emperor; you’ll get justice from him, for my sake.

original: Hold, hold; meanwhile here's money for thy charges.   Give me pen and ink. Sirrah, can you with a grace   deliver a supplication?
translation: Wait, wait; here’s money for your trouble. Give me pen and ink. Man, can you deliver a petition gracefully?

original: Ay, sir.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: Then here is a supplication for you. And when you   come to him, at the first approach you must kneel,   then kiss his foot, then deliver up your pigeons,
translation: Then here is a petition for you. And when you come to him, you must first kneel, then kiss his foot, then give him your pigeons,

original: and   then look for your reward. I'll be at hand, sir; see   you do it bravely.
translation: and then wait for your reward. I'll be close by, sir; make sure you do it well.

original: I warrant you, sir, let me alone.
translation: Leave it to me, sir.

original: Sirrah, hast thou a knife? come, let me see it.   Here, Marcus, fold it in the oration;   For thou hast made it like an humble suppliant.
translation: Do you have a knife? Come, give it to me. Here, Marcus, fold it in the letter, for you’ve made it look like a humble petition.

original: And when thou hast given it the emperor,   Knock at my door, and tell me what he says.
translation: And when he’s given it to the emperor, knock at my door, and tell me what he says.

original: God be with you, sir; I will.
translation: God be with you, sir; I will.

original: Come, Marcus, let us go. Publius, follow me.
translation: Come, Marcus, let's go. Publius, follow me.

original: Why, lords, what wrongs are these! was ever seen   An emperor in Rome thus overborne,   Troubled, confronted thus; and, for the extent   Of equal justice, used in such contempt?
translation: Why, lords, this is an outrage! Has there ever been a Roman emperor oppressed, disobeyed, and troubled like this—and treated with such contempt, simply for enforcing the law?

original: My lords, you know, as know the mightful gods,   However these disturbers of our peace   Buzz in the people's ears, there nought hath pass'd,   But even with law, against the willful sons   Of old Andronicus.
translation: My lords, you and the mighty gods know that whatever these disturbers of the peace say, buzzing like bees in the common people's ears, that what happened to old Andronicus's sons was just and legal.

original: And what an if   His sorrows have so overwhelm'd his wits,   Shall we be thus afflicted in his wreaks,   His fits, his frenzy, and his bitterness?
translation: And so what if he's gone crazy? Do we have to deal with the consequences of his fits and bitterness?

original: And now he writes to heaven for his redress:   See, here's to Jove, and this to Mercury;   This to Apollo; this to the god of war;   Sweet scrolls to fly about the streets of Rome!
translation: And now he writes to heaven for justice. See  [shows arrows] , here's to Jove, and this one's to Mercury; to Apollo, to the god of war . . . and these papers are scattered throughout the streets of Rome!

original: What's this but libelling against the senate,   And blazoning our injustice every where?   A goodly humour, is it not, my lords?
translation: Isn't this  libel  against the Senate, accusing us of injustice everywhere? Good ammunition, my lords,

original: As who would say, in Rome no justice were.   But if I live, his feigned ecstasies   Shall be no shelter to these outrages:
translation: for those would say there's no justice in Rome. But if I live, his pretended madness won't protect him—

original: But he and his shall know that justice lives   In Saturninus' health, whom, if she sleep,   He'll so awake as she in fury shall   Cut off the proud'st conspirator that lives.
translation: he and his family will know that justice lives as long as Saturninus is here, and if  she  sleeps, he'll wake her and set her on them in fury.

original: My gracious lord, my lovely Saturnine,   Lord of my life, commander of my thoughts,   Calm thee, and bear the faults of Titus' age,
translation: My gracious lord, my lovely Saturnine, lord of my life, commander of my thoughts: calm yourself. Remember that Titus is old;

original: The effects of sorrow for his valiant sons,   Whose loss hath pierced him deep and scarr'd his heart;
translation: his grief for his sons has pierced him deeply and scarred his heart.

original: And rather comfort his distressed plight   Than prosecute the meanest or the best   For these contempts.
translation: Comfort him in his distress instead of prosecuting the greatest or least member of his family for this.

original: [Aside]   Why, thus it shall become   High-witted Tamora to gloze with all:
translation: [To herself]  Well, it's clever to pretend to defend him like this.

original: But, Titus, I have touched thee to the quick,   Thy life-blood out: if Aaron now be wise,   Then is all safe, the anchor's in the port.
translation: But Titus, I've got you, and I've spilled your life-blood. if Aaron's plan goes smoothly, then we're almost there.

original: How now, good fellow! wouldst thou speak with us?
translation: Hello, good man! Do you want to speak with us?

original: Yea, forsooth, an your mistership be emperial.
translation: Yes, indeed, if you're an imperial lady.

original: Empress I am, but yonder sits the emperor.
translation: I'm the empress, but the emperor is there.

original: 'Tis he. God and Saint Stephen give you good den: I have brought you a letter and a couple of pigeons  here.
translation: It's him. God and Saint Stephen give you good evening; I've brought you a letter and a couple of pigeons.

original: Go, take him away, and hang him presently.
translation: Go, take him away, and hang him immediately.

original: How much money must I have?
translation: How much money do I get?

original: Come, sirrah, you must be hanged.
translation: Go on, man, you must be hanged.

original: Hanged! by'r lady, then I have brought up a neck to a fair end.
translation: Hanged! By our Lady, then I've come to a good end.

original: Despiteful and intolerable wrongs!   Shall I endure this monstrous villany?   I know from whence this same device proceeds:   May this be borne?—
translation: Spiteful and intolerable treatment! How can I endure this monstrous behavior? I know where this came from—can I bear this?

original: as if his traitorous sons,   That died by law for murder of our brother,   Have by my means been butcher'd wrongfully!
translation: He acts as if his traitorous sons, that died lawfully for murdering my brother, have been unjustly killed by me!

original: Go, drag the villain hither by the hair;   Nor age nor honour shall shape privilege:   For this proud mock I'll be thy slaughterman;
translation: Go, drag the villain here by his hair; I won't go any easier on him because he's old and honored in battle. For this proud mockery I'll kill him,

original: Sly frantic wretch, that holp'st to make me great,   In hope thyself should govern Rome and me.
translation: the crafty, crazy bastard, who helped to give me the throne hoping he could take control of Rome and me.

original: What news with thee, AEmilius?
translation: What do you have to report, Aemilius?

original: Arm, arm, my lord;—Rome never had more cause.   The Goths have gather'd head; and with a power   high-resolved men, bent to the spoil,   They hither march amain,
translation: Raise an army, my lord—Rome has never been under attack like this before. The Goths have arrived with an army of soldiers intent on sacking the city.

original: under conduct   Of Lucius, son to old Andronicus;   Who threats, in course of this revenge, to do   As much as ever Coriolanus did.
translation: They come here under the command of Lucius, old Andronicus's son, who threatens to take as much revenge as  Coriolanus  ever did.

original: Is warlike Lucius general of the Goths?   These tidings nip me, and I hang the head   As flowers with frost or grass beat down with storms:
translation: Fierce warrior Lucius is general of the Goths? This news nips me like a flower covered in frost or grass beaten down with storms.

original: Ay, now begin our sorrows to approach:   'Tis he the common people love so much;
translation: Yes, now our sorrow comes; the common people love him.

original: Myself hath often over-heard them say,   When I have walked like a private man,   That Lucius' banishment was wrongfully,   And they have wish'd that Lucius were their emperor.
translation: When I've disguised myself and walked through the streets, I've often heard them say that Lucius was wrongfully banished, and that they wish he were their emperor.

original: Why should you fear? is not your city strong?
translation: Why should you be afraid? Doesn't the city have strong defenses?

original: Ay, but the citizens favor Lucius, And will revolt from me to succor him.
translation: Yes, but the citizens prefer Lucius, and will rebel against me to support him.

original: King, be thy thoughts imperious, like thy name.   Is the sun dimm'd, that gnats do fly in it?
translation: King, your thoughts should be as imperial as your name. Is the sun dimmed when gnats fly in it?

original: The eagle suffers little birds to sing,   And is not careful what they mean thereby,   Knowing that with the shadow of his wings   He can at pleasure stint their melody:
translation: The eagle doesn't mind when little birds sing, since he knows he can shut them up whenever he wants—

original: Even so mayst thou the giddy men of Rome.   Then cheer thy spirit : for know, thou emperor,   I will enchant the old Andronicus   With words more sweet, and yet more dangerous,
translation: so can you with the silly citizens of Rome. Then cheer up, emperor. For I will enchant the old Andronicus with words sweeter and more dangerous

original: Than baits to fish, or honey-stalks to sheep,   When as the one is wounded with the bait,   The other rotted with delicious feed.
translation: than baits to fish or stalks of honeysuckle to sheep, when they're wounded with the bait or poisoned with delicious food.

original: But he will not entreat his son for us.
translation: But he won't beg his son to stop the attack.

original: If Tamora entreat him, then he will:   For I can smooth and fill his aged ear   With golden promises;
translation: If Tamora asks him, then he will. For I can smooth things over and fill his ear with golden promises.

original: that, were his heart   Almost impregnable, his old ears deaf,   Yet should both ear and heart obey my tongue.
translation: Even if his heart were hard as stone and his old ears deaf, both his heart and his ears would obey my words.

original: [To AEMILIUS]     Go thou before, be our ambassador:
translation: [To AEMILIUS]  You, go ahead of me and be our ambassador.

original: Say that the emperor requests a parley   Of warlike Lucius, and appoint the meeting   Even at his father's house, the old Andronicus.
translation: Tell Lucius that the emperor requests a meeting with him at the house of his father, old Andronicus.

original: AEmilius, do this message honourably: And if he stand on hostage for his safety, Bid him demand what pledge will please him best.
translation: Aemilius, take care with this message. If he asks for some proof that we won't harm him, ask him what we can do to show we're in good faith.

original: Your bidding shall I do effectually.
translation: I'll deliver the message as well as I can.

original: Now will I to that old Andronicus;   And temper him with all the art I have,   To pluck proud Lucius from the warlike Goths.
translation: Now I'll go to old Andronicus and deal with him with all the cunning I have, to get him to bring proud Lucius here from the warrior Goths.

original: And now, sweet emperor, be blithe again,   And bury all thy fear in my devices.
translation: And now, sweet emperor, be cheerful again, and don't be afraid, since I'm taking care of it.

original: Then go successantly, and plead to him.
translation: Then go now and talk to him.

original: Approved warriors, and my faithful friends,   I have received letters from great Rome,   Which signify what hate they bear their emperor   And how desirous of our sight they are.
translation: Faithful friends and proven warriors, I've received letters from Rome telling me how much they hate the emperor and how eagerly they look forward to our arrival.

original: Therefore, great lords, be, as your titles witness,   Imperious and impatient of your wrongs,   And wherein Rome hath done you any scath,   Let him make treble satisfaction.
translation: So, great lords who are impatient with the wrongs done to you, however Rome has hurt you, make sure you repay it threefold.

original: Brave slip, sprung from the great Andronicus,   Whose name was once our terror, now our comfort;
translation: Brave son of great Andronicus—whose name once terrorized us and now comforts us,

original: Whose high exploits and honourable deeds   Ingrateful Rome requites with foul contempt,   Be bold in us:
translation: and whose honorable service to Rome has been badly repaid—you can count on us.

original: we'll follow where thou lead'st,   Like stinging bees in hottest summer's day   Led by their master to the flowered fields,   And be avenged on cursed Tamora.
translation: We'll go where you lead us, like stinging bees led by the beekeeper to a field of flowers, and take revenge on cursed Tamora.

original: And as he saith, so say we all with him.
translation: Everything he says, we say with him.

original: I humbly thank him, and I thank you all. But who comes here, led by a lusty Goth?
translation: I thank him humbly, and I thank all of you, too. But who's that, led by a Goth warrior?

original: Renowned Lucius, from our troops I stray'd   To gaze upon a ruinous monastery;   And, as I earnestly did fix mine eye   Upon the wasted building, suddenly   I heard a child cry underneath a wall.
translation: Famous Lucius, I went ahead of the army to see a ruined monastery, and as I looked at the building, I heard a baby cry underneath a wall.

original: I made unto the noise; when soon I heard   The crying babe controll'd with this discourse:   'Peace, tawny slave, half me and half thy dam!
translation: I followed the noise to its source, and heard someone shushing the baby by saying, "Be quiet, brown slave, half me and half your mother!

original: Did not thy hue bewray whose brat thou art,   Had nature lent thee but thy mother's look,   Villain, thou mightst have been an emperor:
translation: The color of your skin betrayed who your father was; if nature had made you look like your mother, you might have been an emperor.

original: But where the bull and cow are both milk-white,   They never do beget a coal-black calf.   Peace, villain, peace!'—even thus he rates   the babe,—
translation: But when the bull and cow are both milk-white, they don't breed a coal-black calf. Be quiet, villain, be quiet!"—so he said to the baby—

original: 'For I must bear thee to a trusty Goth;   Who, when he knows thou art the empress' babe,   Will hold thee dearly for thy mother's sake.'
translation: "Since I have to take you to a trustworthy Goth, who, when he knows that you're the empress's child, will take good care of you for your mother's sake."

original: With this, my weapon drawn, I rush'd upon him,   Surprised him suddenly, and brought him hither,   To use as you think needful of the man.
translation: When I heard this, I rushed at him with my weapon drawn, took him prisoner, and bought him here to do with as you see fit.

original: O worthy Goth, this is the incarnate devil   That robb'd Andronicus of his good hand;   This is the pearl that pleased your empress' eye,
translation: Oh, many thanks, Goth, for this is the devil incarnate who robbed Andronicus of his good hand. This is the pearl that pleased the eye of your empress,

original: And here's the base fruit of his burning lust.   Say, wall-eyed slave, whither wouldst thou convey   This growing image of thy fiend-like face?
translation: and this child is the fruit of his burning lust. Tell us, slave, what should we do with this growing image of your devil-like face?

original: Why dost not speak? what, deaf? not a word?   A halter, soldiers! hang him on this tree.   And by his side his fruit of bastardy.
translation: Why don't you say anything? What, are you deaf? Not a word? Come on, soldiers! Hang him on this tree, and hang the fruit of his adulterous affair next to him.

original: Touch not the boy; he is of royal blood.
