translation: Don't touch the boy; he is of royal blood.

original: Too like the sire for ever being good.   First hang the child, that he may see it sprawl;
translation: But he's too like the father to ever be good. First hang the child so he can see it die,

original: A sight to vex the father's soul withal.   Get me a ladder.
translation: which is a sight that will distress a father's soul. Get me a ladder.

original: Lucius, save the child,   And bear it from me to the empress.   If thou do this, I'll show thee wondrous things,   That highly may advantage thee to hear:
translation: Lucius, save the child, and bring it to the empress from me. If you do this, I'll show you marvelous things that will be to your advantage to hear.

original: If thou wilt not, befall what may befall,   I'll speak no more but 'Vengeance rot you all!'
translation: If you don't, whatever happens, I'll say nothing more but "revenge rot you all!"

original: Say on: an if it please me which thou speak'st Thy child shall live, and I will see it nourish'd.
translation: Say what you have to say: if I'm pleased with what you say, your child will live and I'll see it taken care of.

original: An if it please thee! why, assure thee, Lucius,   'Twill vex thy soul to hear what I shall speak;
translation: If it please you! Why, I assure you, Lucius, you'll be enraged when you hear what I have to say,

original: For I must talk of murders, rapes and massacres,   Acts of black night, abominable deeds,   Complots of mischief, treason, villanies   Ruthful to hear, yet piteously perform'd:
translation: for I'll reveal murders, rapes, and massacres; acts committed under cover of night; horrible deeds; treasonous plots; and villainous deeds which would make you have pity when you hear them, but were performed without pity.

original: And this shall all be buried by my death,   Unless thou swear to me my child shall live.
translation: And all this will be buried with me when I die, unless you promise to me that my child will live.

original: Tell on thy mind; I say thy child shall live.
translation: Tell what you know. I promise that your child will live.

original: Swear that he shall, and then I will begin.
translation: Swear that he will, and then I'll talk.

original: Who should I swear by? thou believest no god: That granted, how canst thou believe an oath?
translation: What can I swear? You don't believe in any gods; if that's true, then how can you believe an oath?

original: What if I do not? as, indeed, I do not;   Yet, for I know thou art religious   And hast a thing within thee called conscience,
translation: So what if I don't? Indeed, I don't—but I know you're religious and have a thing called "conscience,"

original: With twenty popish tricks and ceremonies,   Which I have seen thee careful to observe,   Therefore I urge thy oath;
translation: and I've seen you perform twenty  popish  rituals and ceremonies, which you're always careful to observe. So that's why I make you swear,

original: for that I know   An idiot holds his bauble for a god   And keeps the oath which by that god he swears,   To that I'll urge him:
translation: since I know that an idiot treats a toy like a god and keeps the promise he swears by that god.

original: therefore thou shalt vow   By that same god, what god soe'er it be,   That thou adorest and hast in reverence,   To save my boy, to nourish and bring him up;   Or else I will discover nought to thee.
translation: So you will swear by that god—whatever god it is that you worship—to save my boy, take care of him, and raise him, or else I won't tell you anything.

original: Even by my god I swear to thee I will.
translation: By my god, I swear to you that I will.

original: First know thou, I begot him on the empress.
translation: The first thing you should know is that his mother is the empress.

original: O most insatiate and luxurious woman!
translation: Oh, insatiable and lustful woman!

original: Tut, Lucius, this was but a deed of charity   To that which thou shalt hear of me anon.
translation: Oh, Lucius, that was a charitable deed compared to what you'll hear from me soon.

original: 'Twas her two sons that murder'd Bassianus;   They cut thy sister's tongue and ravish'd her   And cut her hands and trimm'd her as thou saw'st.
translation: It was her sons that murdered Bassianus, and they were the ones who raped your sister, cut out her tongue, and cut her hands and  trimmed  her as you saw.

original: O detestable villain! call'st thou that trimming?
translation: Oh, horrible villain! You call that trimming?

original: Why, she was wash'd and cut and trimm'd, and 'twas Trim sport for them that had the doing of it.
translation: Why, yes, she was washed and cut and trimmed, and it was good fun for those who did it.

original: O barbarous, beastly villains, like thyself!
translation: Oh, barbaric animals, just like you!

original: Indeed, I was their tutor to instruct them:   That codding spirit had they from their mother,   As sure a card as ever won the set;
translation: Indeed, I was the one who told them to do it—they got their cunning from their mother, like a trump card that always wins the match.

original: That bloody mind, I think, they learn'd of me,   As true a dog as ever fought at head.   Well, let my deeds be witness of my worth.
translation: But their violence, I think, they learned from me, like a dog that goes for the bull's head. Well, my deeds will show what I'm made of.

original: I train'd thy brethren to that guileful hole   Where the dead corpse of Bassianus lay:   I wrote the letter that thy father found   And hid the gold within the letter mention'd,   Confederate with the queen and her two sons:
translation: Plotting with the queen and her two sons, I lured your brothers to the hole where Bassianus's dead body lay; I wrote the letter that your father found and hid the gold mentioned in the letter, in league with the queen and her sons.

original: And what not done, that thou hast cause to rue,   Wherein I had no stroke of mischief in it?   I play'd the cheater for thy father's hand,
translation: What has happened that made you suffer that I wasn't involved with in some way? I cheated your father out of his hand,

original: And, when I had it, drew myself apart   And almost broke my heart with extreme laughter:
translation: and when I had it, I broke down with laughter as soon as I was out of your sight.

original: I pry'd me through the crevice of a wall   When, for his hand, he had his two sons' heads;   Beheld his tears, and laugh'd so heartily,   That both mine eyes were rainy like to his :
translation: When he got his two sons' heads in exchange for his hand, I saw his tears from a hiding spot in the wall and laughed so hard that I cried too.

original: And when I told the empress of this sport,   She swooned almost at my pleasing tale,   And for my tidings gave me twenty kisses.
translation: When I told the empress this funny story, she almost fainted with pleasure, and as a reward gave me twenty kisses.

original: What, canst thou say all this, and never blush?
translation: What, can you say all this and not blush with shame?

original: Ay, like a black dog, as the saying is.
Art thou not sorry for these heinous deeds?
translation: Aren't you sorry for these horrible crimes?

original: Ay, that I had not done a thousand more.   Even now I curse the day—and yet, I think,   Few come within the compass of my curse,—
translation: Yes, I'm sorry that I didn't do a thousand more. Even now I curse the day—although there haven't been many such days, I admit—

original: Wherein I did not some notorious ill,   As kill a man, or else devise his death,   Ravish a maid, or plot the way to do it,
translation: when I didn't do some horrible thing like kill a man (or else plot his death), rape a girl (or plot some way to do it),

original: Accuse some innocent and forswear myself,   Set deadly enmity between two friends,   Make poor men's cattle break their necks;
translation: accuse some innocent person, swear, make two friends hate each other, break the neck of poor cattle,

original: Set fire on barns and hay-stacks in the night,   And bid the owners quench them with their tears.   Oft have I digg'd up dead men from their graves,
translation: or set barns and hay-stacks on fire and tell the owners to put out the flames with their tears. I've often dug up dead men from their graves

original: And set them upright at their dear friends' doors,   Even when their sorrows almost were forgot;   And on their skins, as on the bark of trees,   Have with my knife carved in Roman letters,
translation: and set them standing up at the doors of their dear friends—who had begun to get over their grief—and used my knife to write on their skins, as on the bark of trees,

original: 'Let not your sorrow die, though I am dead.'   Tut, I have done a thousand dreadful things   As willingly as one would kill a fly,
translation: "Don't let your sorrow die, although I'm dead." Ha, I've done a thousand awful things as easily as one would kill a fly,

original: And nothing grieves me heartily indeed   But that I cannot do ten thousand more.
translation: and nothing makes me sadder than not being able to do ten thousand more.

original: Bring down the devil; for he must not die So sweet a death as hanging presently.
translation: Cut the devil down; he doesn't deserve such an easy death as hanging.

original: If there be devils, would I were a devil,   To live and burn in everlasting fire,
translation: If there are devils, I wish I were one, and could live and burn forever in fire—

original: So I might have your company in hell,   But to torment you with my bitter tongue!
translation: so that I could see you in hell, and continue to torment you with my bitter words!

original: Sirs, stop his mouth, and let him speak no more.
translation: Sirs, shut him up, and don't let him say anything else.

original: My lord, there is a messenger from Rome Desires to be admitted to your presence.
translation: My lords, a messenger from Rome is here asking to see you.

original: Let him come near.
translation: Let him come in.

original: Welcome, AEmilius what's the news from Rome?
translation: Welcome, Aemilius. What's happening in Rome?

original: Lord Lucius, and you princes of the Goths,   The Roman emperor greets you all by me;   And, for he understands you are in arms,
translation: Lord Lucius and princes of the Goths, the Roman emperor sends his greetings. He understands that you are here with an army,

original: He craves a parley at your father's house,   Willing you to demand your hostages,   And they shall be immediately deliver'd.
translation: and asks to meet with you at your father's house—if you ask for hostages to ensure your safety, they'll be immediately sent to you.

original: What says our general?
translation: How does our general respond?

original: AEmilius, let the emperor give his pledges Unto my father and my uncle Marcus, And we will come. March away.
translation: Aemilius, if the emperor gives these promises to my father and my uncle Marcus, we'll come. Let's march away.

original: Thus, in this strange and sad habiliment,   I will encounter with Andronicus,   And say I am Revenge, sent from below   To join with him and right his heinous wrongs.
translation: So, I’ll go to Titus dressed in this strange costume, and tell him I am Revenge, sent from below to help him right his terrible wrongs.

original: Knock at his study, where, they say, he keeps,   To ruminate strange plots of dire revenge;   Tell him Revenge is come to join with him,   And work confusion on his enemies.
translation: I’ll knock at the door to his study—which is where he spends most of his time, they say, plotting ways to take revenge—and tell him Revenge has come to help him destroy his enemies.

original: Who doth molest my contemplation?   Is it your trick to make me ope the door,   That so my sad decrees may fly away,   And all my study be to no effect?
translation: Who’s bothering me? Are you trying to make me open the door, so that I’ll lose my resolve and all my work will come to nothing?

original: You are deceived: for what I mean to do   See here in bloody lines I have set down;   And what is written shall be executed.
translation: You’re wrong if you think that will happen—for I’ve written my plan on this paper in blood, and what is written will be done.

original: Titus, I am come to talk with thee.
translation: Titus, I've come to talk with you.

original: No, not a word; how can I grace my talk, Wanting a hand to give it action? Thou hast the odds of me; therefore no more.
If thou didst know me, thou wouldest talk with me.
translation: If you knew who I was, you'd talk to me.

original: I am not mad; I know thee well enough:   Witness this wretched stump, witness these crimson  lines;   Witness these trenches made by grief and care,
translation: I’m not crazy; I know who you are. By my poor stump, these lines of blood, these lines of grief on my face,

original: Witness the tiring day and heavy night;   Witness all sorrow, that I know thee well   For our proud empress, mighty Tamora:   Is not thy coming for my other hand?
translation: my exhausted days and heavy nights, and all my suffering, I know that you’re our proud empress, mighty Tamora. Have you come for my other hand?

original: Know, thou sad man, I am not Tamora;   She is thy enemy, and I thy friend:
translation: You sad man, I’m not Tamora. She’s your enemy, and I’m your friend.

original: I am Revenge: sent from the infernal kingdom,   To ease the gnawing vulture of thy mind,   By working wreakful vengeance on thy foes.
translation: I am Revenge, sent from hell to ease your mind, vulture-like in the way it gnaws at you, by taking bloody vengeance on your enemies.

original: Come down, and welcome me to this world's light;   Confer with me of murder and of death:
translation: Come down, and welcome me to this world; talk to me about murder and death.

original: There's not a hollow cave or lurking-place,   No vast obscurity or misty vale,   Where bloody murder or detested rape   Can couch for fear, but I will find them out;
translation: There isn’t a hollow cave, secret hideaway, obscure place, or misty valley where they can hide that I won’t find them.

original: And in their ears tell them my dreadful name,   Revenge, which makes the foul offender quake.
translation: I’ll whisper  “Revenge" in their ears, and the criminals will quake with fear.

original: Art thou Revenge? and art thou sent to me, To be a torment to mine enemies?
translation: Are you Revenge? And have you been sent to me to torture my enemies?

original: I am; therefore come down, and welcome me.
translation: I am; so come down and welcome me.

original: Do me some service, ere I come to thee.   Lo, by thy side where Rape and Murder stands;   Now give me some surance that thou art Revenge,   Stab them, or tear them on thy chariot-wheels;
translation: Do something for me before I come to you. I see that Rape and Murder stand by your side; to prove that you really are Revenge, stab them or crush them under the wheels of your chariot.

original: And then I'll come and be thy waggoner,   And whirl along with thee about the globe.
translation: Then I’ll come and be your charioteer, and travel with you around the globe.

original: Provide thee two proper palfreys, black as jet,   To hale thy vengeful waggon swift away,   And find out murderers in their guilty caves:
translation: I’ll give you two black horses to pull your wagon of revenge as you find the murderers in their guilty caves;

original: And when thy car is loaden with their heads,   I will dismount, and by the waggon-wheel   Trot, like a servile footman, all day long,
translation: and when the cart is loaded with their heads, I’ll dismount and trot alongside your wheel like a slavish footman all day long,

original: Even from Hyperion's rising in the east   Until his very downfall in the sea:
translation: from when the sun rises in the east until it falls into the sea.

original: And day by day I'll do this heavy task,   So thou destroy Rapine and Murder there.
translation: And I’ll do this hard task every day, if you destroy Rape and Murder there.

original: These are my ministers, and come with me.
translation: These are my agents, and come with me wherever I go.

original: Are these thy ministers? what are they call'd?
translation: Are these your agents? What are their names?

original: Rapine and Murder; therefore called so, Cause they take vengeance of such kind of men.
translation: They’re called Rape and Murder because they take revenge on rapists and murderers.

original: Good Lord, how like the empress' sons they are!   And you, the empress! but we worldly men   Have miserable, mad, mistaking eyes.
translation: Good Lord, they look a lot like the empress’s sons! And you look like the empress! But we mortal men have miserable, mad eyes that are easy to deceive.

original: O sweet Revenge, now do I come to thee;   And, if one arm's embracement will content thee,   I will embrace thee in it by and by.
translation: Oh, sweet Revenge, now I’ll come to you; and, if you can be happy with a one-armed embrace, I’ll embrace you soon.

original: This closing with him fits his lunacy   Whate'er I forge to feed his brain-sick fits,   Do you uphold and maintain in your speeches,   For now he firmly takes me for Revenge;
translation: [To CHIRON and DEMETRIUS]  Since he’s crazy, I’ll just keep agreeing with him. Whatever I come up with, just support my story in whatever you say—for now he thinks I’m Revenge.

original: And, being credulous in this mad thought,   I'll make him send for Lucius his son;
translation: And, since he’ll be easy to deceive now, I’ll make him bring his son Lucius to his house.

original: And, whilst I at a banquet hold him sure,   I'll find some cunning practise out of hand,   To scatter and disperse the giddy Goths,
translation: And during the banquet, I’ll find some cunning way to destroy the Goth army,

original: Or, at the least, make them his enemies.   See, here he comes, and I must ply my theme.
translation: or at least to make them turn against him. Look, here he comes; I have to keep this up.

original: Long have I been forlorn, and all for thee:   Welcome, dread Fury, to my woful house:   Rapine and Murder, you are welcome too.
translation: I’ve been waiting for you for a long time. Welcome to my sad house, dreaded  Fury ; Rape and Murder, you’re welcome here, too.

original: How like the empress and her sons you are!   Well are you fitted, had you but a Moor:   Could not all hell afford you such a devil?
translation: You look so much like the empress and her sons! You would look even more like them if you had a Moor with you—couldn’t you find such a devil in hell?

original: For well I wot the empress never wags   But in her company there is a Moor;   And, would you represent our queen aright,
translation: For I know that the empress doesn’t go anywhere without a Moor, and if you’re trying to look like her,

original: It were convenient you had such a devil:   But welcome, as you are. What shall we do?
translation: it would be convenient to have a devil like that. But you’re welcome just as you are. What should we do?

original: What wouldst thou have us do, Andronicus?
translation: What do you want us to do, Andronicus?

original: Show me a murderer, I'll deal with him.
translation: Show me a murderer, I'll deal with him.

original: Show me a villain that hath done a rape, And I am sent to be revenged on him.
translation: Show me a villain that's raped someone, and I'm here to take revenge on him.

original: Show me a thousand that have done thee wrong, And I will be revenged on them all.
translation: If you show me a thousand people who have wronged you, I'll take revenge on all of them.

original: Look round about the wicked streets of Rome;   And when thou find'st a man that's like thyself.   Good Murder, stab him; he's a murderer.
translation: Look around the wicked streets of Rome, and when you find a man that looks like you, good Murder, stab him, for he’s a murderer.

original: Go thou with him; and when it is thy hap   To find another that is like to thee,   Good Rapine, stab him; he's a ravisher.
translation: Go with him, good Rape, and when you find someone who looks like you, stab him, for he’s a rapist.

original: Go thou with them; and in the emperor's court   There is a queen, attended by a Moor;   Well mayst thou know her by thy own proportion,   for up and down she doth resemble thee:
translation: [To TAMORA]  Go with them, and in the emperor’s court there’s a queen served by a Moor—you’ll recognize her, since she looks exactly like you.

original: I pray thee, do on them some violent death;   They have been violent to me and mine.
translation: I beg you, give them both a violent death, for they’ve been violent to me and my family.

original: Well hast thou lesson'd us; this shall we do.   But would it please thee, good Andronicus,   To send for Lucius, thy thrice-valiant son,
translation: You’ve told us well; we’ll do it. But wouldn’t it be nice, good Andronicus, to send a message to your brave son Lucius—

original: Who leads towards Rome a band of warlike Goths,   And bid him come and banquet at thy house;   When he is here, even at thy solemn feast,
translation: who is coming towards Rome with an army of Goths—and invite him to come for a banquet at your house? And when he’s here at this feast,

original: I will bring in the empress and her sons,   The emperor himself and all thy foes;
translation: I’ll bring the empress and her sons, the emperor himself, and all your enemies.

original: And at thy mercy shalt they stoop and kneel,   And on them shalt thou ease thy angry heart.   What says Andronicus to this device?
translation: They’ll kneel before you and beg for mercy, and you can do what you want with them. What do you think of this plan?

original: Marcus, my brother! 'tis sad Titus calls.
translation: Marcus, my brother! Sad Titus is calling for you.

original: Go, gentle Marcus, to thy nephew Lucius;   Thou shalt inquire him out among the Goths:   Bid him repair to me, and bring with him   Some of the chiefest princes of the Goths;
translation: Go to your nephew Lucius, gentle Marcus, and tell him to come to my house, bringing some of the Goth princes with him.

original: Bid him encamp his soldiers where they are:   Tell him the emperor and the empress too   Feast at my house, and he shall feast with them.
translation: Ask him to leave his army where they are; tell him the emperor and the empress are also coming for a banquet at my house, and he’ll feast with them.

original: This do thou for my love; and so let him,   As he regards his aged father's life.
translation: Do this out of love for me, and tell him to come out of love and respect for his old father.

original: This will I do, and soon return again.
translation: I'll do it, and return soon.

original: Now will I hence about thy business, And take my ministers along with me.
translation: Now I’ll go and take revenge for you, bringing my agents with me.

original: Nay, nay, let Rape and Murder stay with me; Or else I'll call my brother back again, And cleave to no revenge but Lucius.
translation: No, no, let Rape and Murder stay with me. Or else I’ll call my brother back again, and I’ll count on Lucius to take revenge for me.

original: [Aside to her sons]   What say you, boys? will you   bide with him,   Whiles I go tell my lord the emperor   How I have govern'd our determined jest?
translation: [To her sons, so that only they can hear]  What do you think, boys? Will you stay with him while I go tell my husband the emperor how I’ve handled this new joke?

original: Yield to his humour, smooth and speak him fair,   And tarry with him till I turn again.
translation: Play along, be nice, and stay with him until I return again.

original: I know them all, though they suppose me mad, And will o'erreach them in their own devices: A pair of cursed hell-hounds and their dam!
translation: I know who they are, although they think I’m crazy. I’ll beat them at their own game, this pair of cursed hell-dogs and their mother!

original: Madam, depart at pleasure; leave us here.
translation: Madam, go whenever you want; leave us here.

original: Farewell, Andronicus: Revenge now goes To lay a complot to betray thy foes.
translation: Goodbye, Andronicus; Revenge is going now to lay a plot against your enemies.

original: I know thou dost; and, sweet Revenge, farewell.
translation: I know you are. Sweet Revenge, goodbye.

original: Tell us, old man, how shall we be employ'd?
translation: Tell us, old man, what should we do?

original: Tut, I have work enough for you to do. Publius, come hither, Caius, and Valentine!
translation: Oh, I have enough work for you to do. Publius, Caius, and Valentine, come here!

original: What is your will?
translation: What do you want us to do?

original: Know you these two?
translation: Do you know these two?

original: The empress' sons, I take them, Chiron and Demetrius.
translation: They're the empress's sons, Chiron and Demetrius.

original: Fie, Publius, fie! thou art too much deceived;   The one is Murder, Rape is the other's name;   And therefore bind them, gentle Publius.
translation: Oh, Publius, you’re wrong. One is Murder, and the other’s name is Rape. So put them in chains, gentle Publius;

original: Caius and Valentine, lay hands on them.   Oft have you heard me wish for such an hour,
translation: restrain them, Caius and Valentine. You’ve often heard me wish for this moment,

original: And now I find it; therefore bind them sure,   And stop their mouths, if they begin to cry.
translation: and now it’s here, so make sure they’re bound tightly. Gag them if they start to cry out.

original: Villains, forbear! we are the empress' sons.
translation: Stop, villains! We are the empress's sons.

original: And therefore do we what we are commanded. Stop close their mouths, let them not speak a word. Is he sure bound? look that you bind them fast.
translation: And so we’ll do what we’re told. Gag them, don’t let them speak a word. Is he tightly bound? Make sure they can’t escape.

original: Come, come, Lavinia; look, thy foes are bound.   Sirs, stop their mouths, let them not speak to me;   But let them hear what fearful words I utter.   O villains, Chiron and Demetrius!
translation: Come, come, Lavinia; see, your enemies are in chains. Men, stop them from talking, I don’t want to hear it. But I want them to hear every word I say. Oh villains, Chiron and Demetrius!

original: Here stands the spring whom you have stain'd with mud,   This goodly summer with your winter mix'd.
translation: Here is the fountain you’ve stained with mud, the lovely summer you’ve mixed with your winter.

original: You kill'd her husband, and for that vile fault   Two of her brothers were condemn'd to death,   My hand cut off and made a merry jest;
translation: You killed her husband, and for that vile crime two of her brothers were condemned to death, and my hand was cut off and made into a joke.

original: Both her sweet hands, her tongue, and that more dear   Than hands or tongue, her spotless chastity,   Inhuman traitors, you constrain'd and forced.
translation: You cut off her sweet hands and her tongue. And worse than that, inhuman traitors, you took something from her more precious than hands or tongue—you raped her.

original: What would you say, if I should let you speak?   Villains, for shame you could not beg for grace.   Hark, wretches! how I mean to martyr you.
translation: What would you say, if I let you speak? Villains, you’d be ashamed to beg for mercy. Listen, miserable criminals! This is how I mean to kill you.

original: This one hand yet is left to cut your throats,   Whilst that Lavinia 'tween her stumps doth hold   The basin that receives your guilty blood.
translation: I still have one hand left to cut your throats, while Lavinia holds between her stumps the basin that will receive your guilty blood.

original: You know your mother means to feast with me,   And calls herself Revenge, and thinks me mad:
translation: You know that your mother means to dine with me, and calls herself Revenge, and thinks that I’m crazy.

original: Hark, villains! I will grind your bones to dust   And with your blood and it I'll make a paste,
translation: Listen, villains! I’ll grind your bones to dust, and with your blood and that dust I’ll make a paste,

original: And of the paste a coffin I will rear   And make two pasties of your shameful heads,   And bid that strumpet, your unhallow'd dam,   Like to the earth swallow her own increase.
translation: and of that paste I’ll make two pies out of your shameful heads. And then I’ll tell that whore, your unholy mother, to eat you and swallow her own children.

original: This is the feast that I have bid her to,   And this the banquet she shall surfeit on;
translation: This is the feast I’ve prepared for her, and this is the food she’ll eat.

original: For worse than Philomel you used my daughter,   And worse than Progne I will be revenged:   And now prepare your throats. Lavinia, come,
translation: For you treated my daughter worse than Philomel, and I’ll be revenged worse than  Progne . And now prepare your throats. Lavinia, come,

original: Receive the blood: and when that they are dead,   Let me go grind their bones to powder small   And with this hateful liquor temper it;
translation: catch the blood. And when they’re dead, I’ll go grind their bones to a fine powder, and mix it with their hateful blood.

original: And in that paste let their vile heads be baked.   Come, come, be every one officious   To make this banquet;
translation: And then their vile heads will be baked in that paste. Come, come, everyone do your part in preparing this banquet,

original: which I wish may prove   More stern and bloody than the Centaurs' feast.
translation: which I hope will be more bloody and cruel than the  Centaurs' feast .

original: So, now bring them in, for I'll play the cook,   And see them ready 'gainst their mother comes.
translation: So, now bring them in, for I’ll be the cook, and make sure they’re ready for when their mother comes.

original: Uncle Marcus, since it is my father's mind That I repair to Rome, I am content.
translation: Uncle Marcus, since my father wants me to come back to Rome, I’ll do it.

original: And ours with thine, befall what fortune will.
translation: And we're with you, whatever happens.

original: Good uncle, take you in this barbarous Moor,   This ravenous tiger, this accursed devil;
translation: Good uncle, take this barbaric Moor as your prisoner—he's a hungry tiger, a cursed devil.

original: Let him receive no sustenance, fetter him   Till he be brought unto the empress' face,   For testimony of her foul proceedings:
translation: Don’t feed him, but keep him in chains until he’s brought before the empress, to prove what she’s done.

original: And see the ambush of our friends be strong;   I fear the emperor means no good to us.
translation: And make sure our army is close by; I’m afraid the emperor plans to betray us.

original: Some devil whisper curses in mine ear, And prompt me, that my tongue may utter forth The venomous malice of my swelling heart!
translation: May some devil whisper curses in my ear and give me the words, so that I can say all the venomous things that are in my heart!

original: Away, inhuman dog! unhallow'd slave! Sirs, help our uncle to convey him in.
The trumpets show the emperor is at hand.
translation: The trumpets show that the emperor is here.

original: What, hath the firmament more suns than one?
translation: What, is there more than one sun in the sky?

original: What boots it thee to call thyself a sun?
translation: What's the point of calling yourself a sun?

original: Rome's emperor, and nephew, break the parle;   These quarrels must be quietly debated.
translation: Rome's emperor, and nephew, stop it; these differences must be discussed quietly.

original: The feast is ready, which the careful Titus   Hath ordain'd to an honourable end,
translation: The feast is ready, which Titus has carefully prepared to make peace between you,

original: For peace, for love, for league, and good to Rome:   Please you, therefore, draw nigh, and take your places.
translation: and to bring love, fellowship, and honor to Rome. So please come and take your places at the table.

original: Marcus, we will.
translation: Marcus, we will.

original: Welcome, my gracious lord; welcome, dread queen;   Welcome, ye warlike Goths; welcome, Lucius;
translation: Welcome, my gracious lord; welcome, mighty queen. Welcome, warrior Goths; welcome Lucius;

original: And welcome, all: although the cheer be poor,   'Twill fill your stomachs; please you eat of it.
translation: welcome to everyone. Although the food is modest, it will fill your stomachs, so please eat it.

original: Why art thou thus attired, Andronicus?
translation: Why are you dressed like that, Andronicus?

original: Because I would be sure to have all well, To entertain your highness and your empress.
translation: Because I wanted to make sure that everything was perfect for you and your wife.

original: We are beholding to you, good Andronicus.
translation: We're grateful to you, Andronicus.

original: An if your highness knew my heart, you were.   My lord the emperor, resolve me this:
translation: If you knew what's in my heart, you would be. My lord, give me your opinion on this.

original: Was it well done of rash Virginius   To slay his daughter with his own right hand,   Because she was enforced, stain'd, and deflower'd?
translation: Was it a good choice for quick-tempered  Virginius  to kill his daughter with his own hands, because she had been raped?

original: It was, Andronicus.
translation: It was, Andronicus.

original: Your reason, mighty lord?
translation: Why do you think so, mighty lord?

original: Because the girl should not survive her shame, And by her presence still renew his sorrows.
translation: Because the girl shouldn't live any longer after having been dishonored, and by staying alive she reminds him of his grief.

original: A reason mighty, strong, and effectual;   A pattern, precedent, and lively warrant,
translation: You make a strong case and give me a pattern to follow.

original: For me, most wretched, to perform the like.   Die, die, Lavinia, and thy shame with thee;
translation: I'll follow that miserable example. Die, die, Lavinia, and let your shame die with you—

original: And, with thy shame, thy father's sorrow die!
translation: and with that shame, may your father's grief die as well!

original: What hast thou done, unnatural and unkind?
translation: Who have you done? This is cruel and unnatural!

original: Kill'd her, for whom my tears have made me blind.   I am as woful as Virginius was,
translation: I've killed the girl who made my eyes blind with tears. I am as miserable as Virginius,

original: And have a thousand times more cause than he   To do this outrage: and it now is done.
translation: and have a thousand times more cause than him to do this horrible thing. And now it's done.

original: What, was she ravish'd? tell who did the deed.
translation: What, was she raped? Tell us who did it.

original: Will't please you eat? will't please your highness feed?
translation: Will you eat? Will it please your highness to enjoy the food?

original: Why hast thou slain thine only daughter thus?
translation: Why have you killed your only daughter like this?

original: Not I; 'twas Chiron and Demetrius: They ravish'd her, and cut away her tongue; And they, 'twas they, that did her all this wrong.
translation: It wasn't me. It was Chiron and Demetrius; they raped her and cut out her tongue, and so they're responsible for all this.

original: Go fetch them hither to us presently.
translation: Go bring them here now.

original: Why, there they are both, baked in that pie;   Whereof their mother daintily hath fed,   Eating the flesh that she herself hath bred.
translation: Why, they're both here, baked in that pie. Their mother has been daintily eating the flesh of her own children.

original: 'Tis true, 'tis true; witness my knife's sharp point.
translation: It's true, it's true; I'll prove it with my sharp knife.

original: Die, frantic wretch, for this accursed deed!
translation: Die, madman, for this murder!

original: Can the son's eye behold his father bleed? There's meed for meed, death for a deadly deed!
translation: Can a son watch his father bleed and do nothing? You'll die for this!

original: You sad-faced men, people and sons of Rome,   By uproar sever'd, like a flight of fowl   Scatter'd by winds and high tempestuous gusts,
translation: You sad-looking men, people, and sons of Rome—torn apart by conflict, scattered like a flock of birds in the wind—

original: O, let me teach you how to knit again   This scatter'd corn into one mutual sheaf,   These broken limbs again into one body;
translation: we'll show you how to put this broken body back together again, how to put the scattered corn back into its sheaf.

original: Lest Rome herself be bane unto herself,   And she whom mighty kingdoms court'sy to,   Like a forlorn and desperate castaway,   Do shameful execution on herself.
translation: If we don't, Rome will be a curse to herself. The empire that once defeated many mighty kingdoms will, like a pitiful and desperate person shipwrecked on an island, collapse.

original: But if my frosty signs and chaps of age,   Grave witnesses of true experience,   Cannot induce you to attend my words,
translation: But if white hair and wrinkles (the signs of experience) can't convince you to listen to me—

original: [To Lucius]   Speak, Rome's dear friend, as erst our ancestor,   When with his solemn tongue he did discourse   To love-sick Dido's sad attending ear
translation: [To LUCIUS]  then speak, Rome's good friend. Speak as eloquently as Aeneas when he told lovesick Dido

original: The story of that baleful burning night   When subtle Greeks surprised King Priam's Troy,   Tell us what Sinon hath bewitch'd our ears,
translation: about the fall of Troy—that destructive, burning night when the Greeks surprised King Priam's city. Tell us what  Sinon  has betrayed us,

original: Or who hath brought the fatal engine in   That gives our Troy, our Rome, the civil wound.
translation: or who brought in the Trojan horse that has caused civil war in Rome.

original: My heart is not compact of flint nor steel;   Nor can I utter all our bitter grief,   But floods of tears will drown my oratory,
translation: My heart isn't made of flint or steel, and I can't talk about all our suffering without crying—

original: And break my utterance, even in the time   When it should move you to attend me most,   Lending your kind commiseration.
translation: so I'll have to stop talking, even when you should listen most closely to what I have to say.

original: Here is a captain, let him tell the tale;   Your hearts will throb and weep to hear him speak.
translation: Here's your captain: let him explain everything. Your hearts will throb and cry when you hear him.

original: Then, noble auditory, be it known to you,   That cursed Chiron and Demetrius   Were they that murdered our emperor's brother;   And they it were that ravished our sister:
translation: Then, noble listeners, you should all know that it was Chiron and Demetrius who murdered our emperor's brother and raped our sister.

original: For their fell faults our brothers were beheaded;   Our father's tears despised, and basely cozen'd   Of that true hand that fought Rome's quarrel out,   And sent her enemies unto the grave.
translation: For their foul crimes our brothers were beheaded, and my father's tears were mocked and his hand—the hand which has fought so many battles for Rome and sent her enemies to the grave—cut off as a joke.

original: Lastly, myself unkindly banished,   The gates shut on me, and turn'd weeping out,   To beg relief among Rome's enemies:
translation: Lastly, I was unkindly banished from Rome. The gates shut on me and I turned away crying, and went to seek help from Rome's enemies.

original: Who drown'd their enmity in my true tears.   And oped their arms to embrace me as a friend.
translation: They drowned their hatred for Rome in my own honest tears and treated me as their friend.

original: I am the turned forth, be it known to you,   That have preserved her welfare in my blood;   And from her bosom took the enemy's point,   Sheathing the steel in my adventurous body.
translation: I'm the one who was turned away and yet I have saved Rome with my own blood, turning the knife's point away from her and allowing it to pierce my own body.

original: Alas, you know I am no vaunter, I;   My scars can witness, dumb although they are,   That my report is just and full of truth.
translation: Oh, you know that I'm no boaster; my scars (although they're silent) can prove that what I say is fair and honest.

original: But, soft! methinks I do digress too much,   Citing my worthless praise: O, pardon me;   For when no friends are by, men praise themselves.
translation: But wait! I think I'm talking too much in praise of myself. Forgive me, for people praise themselves when friends aren't around to do it for them.

original: Now is my turn to speak. Behold this child:
translation: Now it's my turn to speak. Look at this child:

original: Of this was Tamora delivered;   The issue of an irreligious Moor,   Chief architect and plotter of these woes:
translation: This is the son of Tamora and a corrupt Moor, who was responsible for plotting all these crimes.

original: The villain is alive in Titus' house,   And as he is, to witness this is true.
translation: The villain is a prisoner in Titus's house; we've kept him to alive to prove it.

original: Now judge what cause had Titus to revenge   These wrongs, unspeakable, past patience,   Or more than any living man could bear.
translation: Now you see how many reasons Titus had to take revenge—these crimes against him were unspeakable, past endurance, more than any living man could bear.

original: Now you have heard the truth, what say you, Romans?   Have we done aught amiss,—show us wherein,   And, from the place where you behold us now,
translation: Now that you've heard the truth, what do you say, Romans? Have we done anything we shouldn't have? If we have, tell us so,

original: The poor remainder of Andronici   Will, hand in hand, all headlong cast us down.   And on the ragged stones beat forth our brains,   And make a mutual closure of our house.
translation: and the poor remains of the Andronici family will throw ourselves off the walls of our house, hand in hand, and crack our skulls on the stones below.

original: Speak, Romans, speak; and if you say we shall,   Lo, hand in hand, Lucius and I will fall.
translation: Speak, Romans, speak: if that's what you want us to do, Lucius and I will fall hand in hand.

original: Come, come, thou reverend man of Rome,   And bring our emperor gently in thy hand,
translation: Come, come, you respected elder of Rome, and take our emperor gently by the hand.

original: Lucius our emperor; for well I know   The common voice do cry it shall be so.
translation: I mean our emperor Lucius; for I know that the common people want him to take the throne.

original: Lucius, all hail, Rome's royal emperor!
translation: All hail Lucius, Rome's royal emperor!

original: Go, go into old Titus' sorrowful house,
translation: Go, go into old Titus's sad house,

original: [To Attendants]     And hither hale that misbelieving Moor,
translation: [To servants]  And bring that atheist Moor here,

original: To be adjudged some direful slaughtering death,   As punishment for his most wicked life.
translation: so that we can condemn him to some horrible death as punishment for his evil life.

original: Lucius, all hail, Rome's gracious governor!
translation: All hail, Lucius, Rome's gracious governor!

original: Thanks, gentle Romans: may I govern so,   To heal Rome's harms, and wipe away her woe!
translation: Thanks, gentle Romans; I hope that I'll govern graciously, to heal Rome's wounds and suffering.

original: But, gentle people, give me aim awhile,   For nature puts me to a heavy task:   Stand all aloof:
translation: But, gentle people, give me a moment to mourn my father. Everyone stand aside.

original: but, uncle, draw you near,   To shed obsequious tears upon this trunk.   O, take this warm kiss on thy pale cold lips,
translation: But uncle, come closer, to cry with me on this body. Oh, take this warm kiss on your pale cold lips.

original: These sorrowful drops upon thy blood-stain'd face, The last true duties of thy noble son!
translation: These sad drops on your blood-stained face are the last marks of respect and love from your noble son!

original: Tear for tear, and loving kiss for kiss,   Thy brother Marcus tenders on thy lips:
translation: Your brother Marcus, too, gives you tears and a kiss.

original: O were the sum of these that I should pay   Countless and infinite, yet would I pay them!
translation: If I could give you an infinite number of both, I would!

original: Come hither, boy; come, come, and learn of us   To melt in showers: thy grandsire loved thee well:
translation: Come here, son; come, come, and show us how to cry. Your grandfather loved you very much.

original: Many a time he danced thee on his knee,   Sung thee asleep, his loving breast thy pillow:
translation: He would often bounce you on his knee, or sing to you until you fell asleep on his chest;

original: Many a matter hath he told to thee,   Meet and agreeing with thine infancy;
translation: he told you many things that were fit for you to know when you were a child.

original: In that respect, then, like a loving child,   Shed yet some small drops from thy tender spring,   Because kind nature doth require it so:
translation: Like a loving child, then, shed some tears, since kind nature requires it.

original: Friends should associate friends in grief and woe:   Bid him farewell; commit him to the grave;   Do him that kindness, and take leave of him.
translation: Friends should be together in times of grief and sorrow. Say goodbye before we bury him. Do that kindness, and then leave him in peace.

original: O grandsire, grandsire! even with all my heart   Would I were dead, so you did live again!
translation: Oh, grandfather, grandfather! I wish I were dead, so that you could live again!

original: O Lord, I cannot speak to him for weeping;   My tears will choke me, if I ope my mouth.
translation: Oh, God, I can't talk through my tears; they'll choke me if I open my mouth.

original: You sad Andronici, have done with woes: Give sentence on this execrable wretch, That hath been breeder of these dire events.
translation: You sad family, stop your mourning to pass judgment on the evil man who is responsible for all this suffering.

original: Set him breast-deep in earth, and famish him;   There let him stand, and rave, and cry for food;
translation: Bury him up the chest in the ground, and starve him. Let him stand there, and scream, and cry for food;

original: If any one relieves or pities him,   For the offence he dies. This is our doom:   Some stay to see him fasten'd in the earth.
translation: if anyone gives him anything or takes pity on him, they'll die for it. This is my judgment; someone make sure he's buried in the ground.

original: O, why should wrath be mute, and fury dumb?   I am no baby, I, that with base prayers   I should repent the evils I have done:
translation: Oh, why should I be silent when I'm so angry? I'm no baby that will pray and ask forgiveness for the evil things I've done.

original: Ten thousand worse than ever yet I did   Would I perform, if I might have my will;   If one good deed in all my life I did,   I do repent it from my very soul.
translation: I'd do ten thousand worse things, if I could. If I ever did one good thing in all my life, I regret it from my very soul.

original: Some loving friends convey the emperor hence,   And give him burial in his father's grave:
translation: Loving friends, some of you take the emperor away and bury him in his father's grave.

original: My father and Lavinia shall forthwith   Be closed in our household's monument.
translation: My father and Lavinia will immediately be buried in our family tomb.

original: As for that heinous tiger, Tamora,   No funeral rite, nor man in mourning weeds,   No mournful bell shall ring her burial;
translation: But as for that vicious tiger, Tamora, there will be no ceremony, no mourners, no bell, no funeral.

original: But throw her forth to beasts and birds of prey:   Her life was beast-like, and devoid of pity;   And, being so, shall have like want of pity.
translation: Throw her body out as prey for beasts and vultures; her life was beast-like and she had no pity, so she won't get any from us.

original: See justice done on Aaron, that damn'd Moor,   By whom our heavy haps had their beginning:
translation: Make sure justice is done on Aaron, that damned Moor, who is responsible for all of this.

original: Then, afterwards, to order well the state,   That like events may ne'er it ruinate.
translation: And after that, I'll reform the government, so that such horrible events won't ever happen again and destroy our country.

original: Call here my varlet; I'll unarm again:
translation: Come here servant, I'll take off my armour again.

original: Why should I war without the walls of Troy,   That find such cruel battle here within?
translation: Why should I go outside Troy's walls to fight, when I have to fight such a cruel battle within them?

original: Each Trojan that is master of his heart,   Let him to field; Troilus, alas! hath none.
translation: Every Trojan that still is in control of his heart should go and fight, but I have lost mine!

original: Will this gear ne'er be mended?
translation: Will this problem never be solved?

original: The Greeks are strong and skilful to their strength,   Fierce to their skill and to their fierceness valiant;
translation: The Greeks are strong, and they are also skillful, fierce, and brave.

original: But I am weaker than a woman's tear,   Tamer than sleep, fonder than ignorance,   Less valiant than the virgin in the night   And skilless as unpractised infancy.
translation: I am weaker than the sobbing of a woman, more tame than sleep, more foolish than ignorance, less brave than a virgin in the night, and less skilled than untrained infancy itself.

original: Well, I have told you enough of this:
translation: I have given you enough advice on this matter.

original: for my part,   I'll not meddle nor make no further.
translation: I will not involve myself any more than I have.

original: He that will   have a cake out of the wheat must needs tarry the  grinding.
translation: If you want to bake a cake you have to be persistent enough to  grind  the wheat into flour.

original: Have I not tarried?
translation: Have I not been persistent?

original: Ay, the grinding; but you must tarry the bolting.
translation: Yes, you've been persistent enough to grind the flour, but you must also be persistent enough to sift the flour.

original: Have I not tarried?
translation: Have I not been persistent?

original: Ay, the bolting, but you must tarry the leavening.
translation: Yes, you've sifted the flour, but you must also be patient enough to let the the cake rise.

original: Still have I tarried.
translation: Even this have I endured.

original: Ay, to the leavening;
translation: Yes, up to the rising of the cake.

original: but here's yet in the word   'hereafter' the kneading, the making of the cake, the   heating of the oven and the baking;
translation: But there is always more to be done, the kneading of the dough, the making of the cake, the heating of the oven, and the baking of the cake itself.

original: nay, you must   stay the cooling too, or you may chance to burn your  lips.
translation: You must also wait for the cooling of the cake too, or you may burn your lips.

original: Patience herself, what goddess e'er she be,   Doth lesser blench at sufferance than I do.
translation: Patience personified, whatever kind of goddess she is, is able to endure less suffering than me.

original: At Priam's royal table do I sit;   And when fair Cressid comes into my thoughts,—
translation: I sit at  King Priam 's  royal table , but when beautiful Cressida comes into my thoughts...

original: So, traitor! 'When she comes!' When is she thence?
translation: No! "When Cressida comes" is a treacherous phrase. For when is she not in my thoughts?

original: Well, she looked yesternight fairer than ever I saw her look, or any woman else.
translation: Well, she was prettier last night than I ever saw her or any other woman look.

original: I was about to tell thee:—
translation: I was going to tell you this:

original: when my heart,   As wedged with a sigh, would rive in twain,
translation: my heart felt as if it was being forced apart by a sigh, as if it was going to split in two.

original: Lest Hector or my father should perceive me,   I have, as when the sun doth light a storm,   Buried this sigh in wrinkle of a smile:
translation: But in order that Hector or my father did not see what I was feeling, I disguised my sigh with a smile, like when the sun lights up a storm.

original: But sorrow, that is couch'd in seeming gladness,   Is like that mirth fate turns to sudden sadness.
translation: But the sorrow that is disguised by the appearance of happiness is just as false as the joy that suddenly turns into sadness.

original: An her hair were not somewhat darker than Helen's—
translation: If Cressida's hair wasn't quite a bit darker than Helen's ...

original: well, go to—there were no more comparison between   the women:
translation: well, never mind... she would be in a different league to Helen.

original: but, for my part, she is my kinswoman;
translation: But, as for me, she is family to me.

original: I   would not, as they term it, praise her:
translation: I wouldn't want to, as they say, praise her.

original: but I would   somebody had heard her talk yesterday, as I did.
translation: But I wish someone else had heard her talk yesterday.

original: I   will not dispraise your sister Cassandra's wit, but—
translation: And I'm not trying to say your sister Cassandra's not clever, but Cressida is even cleverer...

original: O Pandarus! I tell thee, Pandarus,—
translation: Oh Pandarus! I'm telling you, Pandarus!

original: When I do tell thee, there my hopes lie drown'd,   Reply not in how many fathoms deep   They lie indrench'd.
translation: When I tell you how my hope for success have sunk, do not go on to tell me how deep they are!

original: I tell thee I am mad   In Cressid's love: thou answer'st 'she is fair;'
translation: I tell you I am madly in love with Cressida, and you reply that "she is beautiful".

original: Pour'st in the open ulcer of my heart   Her eyes, her hair, her cheek, her gait, her voice,   Handlest in thy discourse
translation: You pour into the open wound of my heart her eyes, her hair, her cheek, her step, her voice, when you talk about them.

original: , O, that her hand,   In whose comparison all whites are ink,   Writing their own reproach,
translation: Oh, that hand of hers, which is so white it makes all other whites seem like ink, ink writing its own failure to be as white as her.

original: to whose soft seizure   The cygnet's down is harsh and spirit of sense   Hard as the palm of ploughman:
translation: Her hand is so soft that it makes a young swan's feathers seem as rough as the hands of a farm laborer.

original: this thou tell'st me,   As true thou tell'st me, when I say I love her;
translation: You tell me these things, and no less truly do I say that I love her.

original: But, saying thus, instead of oil and balm,   Thou lay'st in every gash that love hath given me   The knife that made it.
translation: Speaking like this you don't heal my wounds with oil and balm, you stick the same knife that made the wounds into every one of them.

original: I speak no more than truth.
translation: I only say what is true.

original: Thou dost not speak so much.
translation: You can't describe all of her virtues.

original: Faith, I'll not meddle in't. Let her be as she is: if she be fair, 'tis the better for her; an she be not, she has the mends in her own hands.
translation: Honestly, I will not meddle in your problem anymore. Leave her alone, I say. If she is beautiful, good for her. If she isn't, she can sort it out herself.

original: Good Pandarus, how now, Pandarus!
translation: Don't be so hasty, good Pandarus!

original: I have had my labour for my travail; ill-thought on of   her and ill-thought on of you;
translation: I have had no reward for my hard work, which makes both you and her think badly of me.

original: gone between and   between, but small thanks for my labour.
translation: I have gone between and between you two, but nothing for my hard work.

original: What, art thou angry, Pandarus? what, with me?
translation: Are you angry with me, Pandarus? Surely not with me?

original: Because she's kin to me, therefore she's not so fair   as Helen:
translation: I say she's not as beautiful as Helen out of modesty, because Cressida is family to me.

original: an she were not kin to me, she would be as   fair on Friday as Helen is on Sunday.
translation: If she weren't my relative, she'd beat Helen any day of the week.

original: But what care   I? I care not an she were a black-a-moor; 'tis all one  to me.
translation: But why should I care? I don't care if she is an  African , it's all the same to me.

original: Say I she is not fair?
I do not care whether you do or no.
translation: I don't care if you do or not.

original: She's a fool to   stay behind her father;
translation: She's a fool to wait behind her father.

original: let her to the Greeks; and so   I'll tell her the next time I see her:
translation: Send her to the Greeks I say, and that's what I'll say to her next time I see her.

original: for my part,   I'll meddle nor make no more i' the matter.
translation: I'm finished with this whole affair.

original: Pandarus,—
translation: Pandarus...

original: Not I.
translation: It's nothing to do with me.

original: Sweet Pandarus,—
translation: Sweet Pandarus...

original: Pray you, speak no more to me: I will leave all as I found it, and there an end.
Peace, you ungracious clamours!
translation: Be quiet, awful noises!

original: peace, rude sounds!
translation: Be quiet, unpleasant sounds!

original: Fools on both sides!
translation: Both sides of this war are fools!

original: Helen must needs be fair,   When with your blood you daily paint her thus.
translation: Helen has to have a  beautiful  face if her blush is painted on with your blood.

original: I cannot fight upon this argument;   It is too starved a subject for my sword.
translation: I cannot fight for this cause, it is a weak reason for me to draw my sword.

original: But Pandarus,—O gods, how do you plague me!
translation: But Pandarus... Oh gods, you disturb me!

original: I cannot come to Cressid but by Pandar;   And he's as tetchy to be woo'd to woo.
translation: I cannot meet Cressida without Pandarus's help, but he is as difficult to persuade to court Cressida as she is difficult to be courted.

original: As she is stubborn-chaste against all suit.   Tell me, Apollo, for thy Daphne's love,   What Cressid is, what Pandar, and what we?
translation: Tell me, Apollo, how should I understand Cressida, Pandarus and  myself?

original: Her bed is India; there she lies, a pearl:
translation: Cressida's bed is like  India , and she is like its jewel.

original: Between our Ilium and where she resides,   Let it be call'd the wild and wandering flood,   Ourself the merchant, and this sailing Pandar   Our doubtful hope, our convoy and our bark.
translation: The distance between my home and hers is like a vast ocean, and like a  merchant  I must invest my wealth in a risky venture, with Pandarus as my ship.

original: How now, Prince Troilus! wherefore not afield?
translation: Hello, Prince Troilus! Why haven't you gone to battle?

original: Because not there: this woman's answer sorts, For womanish it is to be from thence. What news, AEneas, from the field to-day?
That Paris is returned home and hurt.
translation: That Paris has come back with an injury.

original: By whom, AEneas?
translation: Who injured him, Aeneas?

original: Troilus, by Menelaus.
translation: Menelaus, Troilus.

original: Let Paris bleed; 'tis but a scar to scorn; Paris is gored with Menelaus' horn.
Hark, what good sport is out of town to-day!
Better at home, if 'would I might' were 'may.' But to the sport abroad: are you bound thither?
translation: There would be sport inside the walls if I had what I wanted. But talking about the sport outside, are you going out to fight?

original: In all swift haste.
translation: As quickly as I can.

original: Come, go we then together.
translation: Come, let's both go.

original: Who were those went by?
translation: Who were those people that passed?

original: Queen Hecuba and Helen.
translation: Queen Hecuba and Helen.

original: And whither go they?
translation: And where are they going?

original: Up to the eastern tower,   Whose height commands as subject all the vale,   To see the battle.
translation: They are going to watch the battle from the top of the eastern tower, from where you can see the land outside the city, where the battle is happening.

original: Hector, whose patience   Is, as a virtue, fix'd, to-day was moved:
translation: Even Hector, whose patience never fails, was angry today.

original: He chid Andromache and struck his armourer,
translation: He scolded Andromache and hit his armorer.

original: And, like as there were husbandry in war,   Before the sun rose he was harness'd light,
translation: Like a farmer, he was prepared to go into the battlefield before the dawn.

original: And to the field goes he; where every flower   Did, as a prophet, weep what it foresaw   In Hector's wrath.
translation: He went into the field that was wet with dew, and every flower he passed wept, anticipating the lives that he would take.

original: What was his cause of anger?
translation: Why was Hector so angry?

original: The noise goes, this: there is among the Greeks A lord of Trojan blood, nephew to Hector; They call him Ajax.
translation: Rumor is that a soldier with Trojan ancestry named Ajax, a nephew of Hector's, has joined the Greek army.

original: Good; and what of him?
translation: Okay, so why is that a problem?

original: They say he is a very man per se, And stands alone.
translation: People say Ajax is an incredible soldier, and stands out.

original: So do all men, unless they are drunk, sick, or have no  legs.
translation: All men may stand unless they are sick, drunk or have no legs.

original: This man, lady, hath robbed many beasts of their   particular additions;
translation: This man is like a mix of beasts, my lady;

original: he is as valiant as the lion,   churlish as the bear, slow as the elephant:
translation: he is as brave as a lion, as cruel as a bear, and as slow as an elephant.

original: a man   into whom nature hath so crowded humours that his   valour is crushed into folly, his folly sauced with   discretion:
translation: He is a man who has so many characteristics that his bravery has become foolishness, and his foolishness is mixed with some wisdom.

original: there is no man hath a virtue that he   hath not a glimpse of, nor any man an attaint but he   carries some stain of it:
translation: There is no virtue that he doesn't have some of, and no flaw that he doesn't carry in some way.

original: he is melancholy without   cause, and merry against the hair:
translation: He is sad without a reason, and happy when others are sad.

original: he hath the   joints of every thing, but everything so out of joint   that he is a gouty Briareus, many hands and no use,   or purblind Argus, all eyes and no sight.
translation: He contains something of everything but everything is so confused in him that he is like Briareus whose many hands were useless or Argus whose many eyes were all blind.

original: But how should this man, that makes me smile, make Hector angry?
translation: But why does this man, who sounds funny to me, make Hector angry?

original: They say he yesterday coped Hector in the battle and struck him down, the disdain and shame whereof hath ever since kept Hector fasting and waking.
translation: Rumor is that yesterday he fought Hector and knocked him down. Ever since that, the anger and shame has stopped Hector from eating or sleeping.

original: Who comes here?
translation: Who's coming now?

original: Madam, your uncle Pandarus.
translation: Madam, that is your uncle Pandarus.

original: Hector's a gallant man.
translation: Hector is a brave man.

original: As may be in the world, lady.
translation: As brave as any man in the world.

original: What's that? what's that?
translation: What was that? What was that?

original: Good morrow, uncle Pandarus.
translation: Good morning uncle Pandarus.

original: Good morrow, cousin Cressid: what do you talk of? Good morrow, Alexander. How do you, cousin? When were you at Ilium?
translation: Good morning cousin Cressida, what are you talking about? Good morning Alexander. How are you, cousin? Since when were you in Ilium?

original: This morning, uncle.
translation: This morning, uncle.

original: What were you talking of when I came? Was Hector armed and gone ere ye came to Ilium? Helen was not up, was she?
translation: What were you talking about when I arrived? Had Hector woken up and left before you came to Ilium? Helen wasn't awake was she?

original: Hector was gone, but Helen was not up.
translation: Hector has gone, but Helen wasn't awake.

original: Even so: Hector was stirring early.
translation: Ah I see, Hector got up early.

original: That were we talking of, and of his anger.
translation: That was what we were talking about, that and his anger.

original: Was he angry?
translation: Was he angry?

original: So he says here.
translation: That's what Alexander told me.

original: True, he was so:
translation: This is true, Hector was angry.

original: I know the cause too:
translation: I know the reason as well.

original: he'll lay   about him to-day, I can tell them that:
translation: Hector will attack everyone around him, I can say that.

original: and there's   Troilus will not come far behind him:
translation: And Troilus will not be far behind him.

original: let them take   heed of Troilus, I can tell them that too.
translation: The Greeks should beware of Troilus, I could say that too.

original: What, is he angry too?
translation: What? Is Troilus angry as well?

original: Who, Troilus? Troilus is the better man of the two.
translation: Who, Troilus? Troilus is the better man of the two.

original: O Jupiter! there's no comparison.
translation: By Jupiter, you cannot compare the two men.

original: What, not between Troilus and Hector? Do you know a man if you see him?
translation: What? No comparison between Troilus and Hector? Are you not able to recognize a man if you see him.

original: Ay, if I ever saw him before and knew him.
Well, I say Troilus is Troilus.
Then you say as I say; for, I am sure, he is not  Hector.
No, nor Hector is not Troilus in some degrees.
translation: You're right he is not Hector, neither does Hector have the same qualities as Troilus in some ways.

original: 'Tis just to each of them; he is himself.
translation: This is fair to both of them: they are both themselves.

original: Himself! Alas, poor Troilus! I would he were.
translation: "Himself!" If only! Poor Troilus, I wish he were himself.

original: So he is.
translation: He is himself.

original: Condition, I had gone barefoot to India.
translation: As likely as me walking to India without shoes.

original: He is not Hector.
translation: He is not Hector.

original: Himself! no, he's not himself:
translation: Himself! No, he's not himself.

original: would a' were   himself!
translation: I wish he would be himself.

original: Well, the gods are above; time must friend   or end:
translation: Oh Gods, time must either help Troilus to recover or end him.

original: well, Troilus, well: I would my heart were   in her body.
translation: Oh, why could my heart not be in her body.

original: No, Hector is not a better man than  Troilus.
translation: No, Hector is not a better man than Troilus.

original: Excuse me.
He is elder.
translation: He is older.

original: Pardon me, pardon me.
translation: Pardon?

original: Th' other's not come to't; you shall tell me another tale, when th' other's come to't. Hector shall not have his wit this year.
translation: Troilus hasn't fully come of age. You will have a different view when Troilus he has come of age. By the end of the year Hector will not have the intelligence of Troilus.

original: He shall not need it, if he have his own.
translation: Hector will not need Troilus's intelligence, if he has his own.

original: Nor his qualities.
translation: Hector will not be able to match Troilus's qualities.

original: No matter.
translation: It wouldn't matter.

original: Nor his beauty.
translation: Troilus will be the more beautiful.

original: 'Twould not become him; his own's better.
translation: Hector would look silly, since his beauty is better than Troilus's.

original: You have no judgment, niece:
translation: You have no judgement, niece.

original: Helen   herself swore th' other day, that Troilus, for   a brown favour—for so 'tis, I must confess,—   not brown neither,—
translation: The other day,  Helen herself swore that Troilus , even though he is a little dark, which I have to admit he is, although not really that dark...

original: No, but brown.
translation: No, he has dark skin.

original: 'Faith, to say truth, brown and not brown.
translation: In truth, it is dark but not that dark.

original: To say the truth, true and not true.
translation: In truth, true and not true.

original: She praised his complexion above Paris.
translation: Helen praised Troilus's complexion more than she praised Paris's complexion.

original: Why, Paris hath colour enough.
translation: I see, Paris has a good enough color.

original: So he has.
translation: This is true.

original: Then Troilus should have too much:
translation: Then Troilus has too much colour.

original: if she praised   him above, his complexion is higher than his;
translation: If Helen praised Troilus's complexion above Paris, then his complexion is darker than Paris's.

original: he   having colour enough, and the other higher, is too   flaming a praise for a good complexion.
translation: Since Paris has just enough color, it is not a compliment to say that Troilus has more color than Paris.

original: I had as   lief Helen's golden tongue had commended Troilus for   a copper nose.
translation: I would rather Helen said Troilus had a  red nose .

original: I swear to you. I think Helen loves him better than  Paris.
translation: I promise, I think Helen prefers Troilus to Paris.

original: Then she's a merry Greek indeed.
translation: Then Helen is truly promiscuous.

original: Nay, I am sure she does. She came to him th' other day into the compassed window,—and, you know, he has not past three or four hairs on his chin,—
translation: I am quite sure she does prefer Troilus to Paris. They met in privacy the other day, and you know, he has not more than three or four hairs on his chin.

original: Indeed, a tapster's arithmetic may soon bring his particulars therein to a total.
translation: Even a barmaid could add them up.

original: Why, he is very young: and yet will he, within three pound, lift as much as his brother Hector.
translation: That is because he is very young, and yet he can lift as heavy a weight as his brother Hector... give or take three pounds.

original: Is he so young a man and so old a lifter?
But to prove to you that Helen loves him: she came and puts me her white hand to his cloven chin—
translation: But, as proof that Helen loves him, she came and put her white hand on his split chin.

original: Juno have mercy! how came it cloven?
translation: Oh God! Why is it split?

original: Why, you know 'tis dimpled: I think his smiling becomes him better than any man in all Phrygia.
translation: You know full well it has a dimple. I think he smiles better than any man in all of Phrygia.

original: O, he smiles valiantly.
translation: Oh, he smiles well.

original: Does he not?
translation: Right?

original: O yes, an 'twere a cloud in autumn.
translation: Yes, like a rain cloud in autumn.

original: Why, go to, then: but to prove to you that Helen loves Troilus,—
translation: Oh shut up, but look, to prove to you that Helen loves Troilus...

original: Troilus will stand to the proof, if you'll prove it so.
Troilus! why, he esteems her no more than I esteem an addle egg.
translation: Troilus! Why, Troilus doesn't think better of her than I think of a rotten egg.

original: If you love an addle egg as well as you love an idle head, you would eat chickens i' the shell.
translation: If you loved rotten eggs as much as you love stupidity, you would eat nothing else.

original: I cannot choose but laugh, to think how she tickled his chin: indeed, she has a marvellous white hand, I must needs confess,—
translation: I have to laugh when I think of how Helen touched Troilus's chin. She has such a beautifully white hand, I must say...

original: Without the rack.
And she takes upon her to spy a white hair on his chin.
translation: And she happens to see a white hair on his chin.

original: Alas, poor chin! many a wart is richer.
translation: Poor chin, that has less hair than most warts.

original: But there was such laughing! Queen Hecuba laughed that her eyes ran o'er.
translation: It was such a funny sight that Queen Hecuba wept with laughing.

original: With mill-stones.
And Cassandra laughed.
translation: Cassandra also laughed.

original: But there was more temperate fire under the pot of her eyes: did her eyes run o'er too?
translation: She rarely laughs, did she weep as well?

original: And Hector laughed.
translation: Hector also laughed.

original: At what was all this laughing?
translation: Why were these people laughing at all?

original: Marry, at the white hair that Helen spied on Troilus'  chin.
translation: Well, at the white hair that Helen had seen on Troilus's chin.

original: An't had been a green hair, I should have laughed too.
translation: If it was a green hair I might have laughed too.

original: They laughed not so much at the hair as at his pretty  answer.
translation: They weren't laughing at the hair, they laughed at his clever response.

original: What was his answer?
translation: What was his response?

original: Quoth she, 'Here's but two and fifty hairs on your chin, and one of them is white.
translation: She said: "There are only fifty two hairs on your chin, but one of them is white."

original: This is her question.
translation: That's what Helen said, not what Troilus said.

original: That's true; make no question of that.
translation: True, I don't doubt that.

original: 'Two and   fifty hairs' quoth he, 'and one white: that white   hair is my father, and all the rest are his sons.'
translation: "Fifty two hairs," he said, "and one is white? That white hair is my father, and all the rest are his sons."

original: 'Jupiter!' quoth she, 'which of these hairs is Paris,   my husband?'
translation: "Jupiter!" she said, "which of these hairs is Paris, my husband?"

original: 'The forked one,' quoth he, 'pluck't   out, and give it him.'
translation: "The split one," he said, "pull it out and give it to him."

original: But there was such laughing!
translation: Oh and there was so much laughter.

original: and Helen so blushed, an Paris so chafed, and all the   rest so laughed, that it passed.
translation: And Helen blushed, and Paris was so angry, and all the others laughed, and so it ended.

original: So let it now; for it has been while going by.
translation: Please let it stay ended, that story took ages.

original: Well, cousin. I told you a thing yesterday; think on't.
translation: Right, cousin. I told you something yesterday, think about it.

original: So I do.
translation: I am thinking about it.

original: I'll be sworn 'tis true; he will weep you, an 'twere a man born in April.
And I'll spring up in his tears, an 'twere a nettle against May.
Hark! they are coming from the field: shall we stand up here, and see them as they pass toward Ilium? good niece, do, sweet niece Cressida.
translation: Listen, the soldiers are coming back from the battlefield. Let's stand up here and watch as they pass towards Troy? Be good and join me, Cressida my niece.

original: At your pleasure.
translation: I'll do whatever you like.

original: Here, here, here's an excellent place; here we may see most bravely: I'll tell you them all by their names as they pass by; but mark Troilus above the rest.
translation: Here, here, this place will do. We will see them well from here. I'll point them all out as they pass, but watch for Troilus in particular.

original: Speak not so loud.
translation: Don't talk so loudly.

original: That's AEneas: is not that a brave man? he's one of the flowers of Troy, I can tell you: but mark Troilus; you shall see anon.
translation: That's Aeneas. Isn't he a brave man? He's one of the best soldiers of Troy, I promise, but wait, Troilus will come soon.

original: Who's that?
translation: Who's that?

original: That's Antenor: he has a shrewd wit, I can tell you;
translation: That's Antenor. He is very clever, I promise.

original: and he's a man good enough, he's one o' the soundest   judgments in whosoever, and a proper man of person.
translation: He's a good soldier too, an excellent judge, and a noble man.

original: When comes Troilus? I'll show you Troilus anon:
translation: Where's Troilus? I'll point out Troilus soon.

original: if   he see me, you shall see him nod at me.
translation: If he sees me he'll nod at me.

original: Will he give you the nod?
translation: Will he give you the nod?

original: You shall see.
translation: You'll see it.

original: If he do, the rich shall have more.
That's Hector, that, that, look you, that; there's a   fellow   !
translation: Look, there, that's Hector, he is a brave man!

original: Go thy way, Hector! There's a brave man,   niece.
translation: Go on Hector! He's a brave man, niece.

original: O brave Hector! Look how he looks! there's   a countenance! is't not a brave man?
translation: Oh brave Hector! Look at his physique! Look at his face! Isn't he a brave man?

original: O, a brave man!
translation: Oh, he is definitely a brave man!

original: Is a' not?
translation: Isn't he?

original: it does a man's heart good.
translation: It makes me proud to see him.

original: Look you   what hacks are on his helmet!
translation: Look at those gashes on his helmet!

original: look you yonder, do   you see? look you there: there's no jesting;
translation: Do you see them? You see that, you can't fake those gashes.

original: there's laying on, take't off who will, as they say:
