translation: I'm laying on the praise thick, but if anyone can do better, as they say, let them try.

original: there be hacks!
translation: Look at those gashes!

original: Be those with swords?
translation: Are they from swords?

original: Swords! any thing, he cares not; an the devil come to him, it's all one: by God's lid, it does one's heart good. Yonder comes Paris, yonder comes Paris.
translation: Swords or anything else, he wouldn't care if the devil attacked him, he can handle anything. By God, it makes my heart good to look at him. Look, there's Paris.

original: Look ye yonder, niece; is't not a gallant man too,   is't not?
translation: Look over there niece, isn't he also an impressive man?

original: Why, this is brave now. Who said he came   hurt home to-day?
translation: He is looking strong. Didn't somebody say he was injured today?

original: he's not hurt: why, this will do   Helen's heart good now, ha!
translation: He's not hurt at all! I am sure Helen will be overjoyed.

original: Would I could see   Troilus now! You shall see Troilus anon.
translation: I wish I could see Troilus. You'll see him soon.

original: Who's that?
translation: Who's he?

original: That's Helenus. I marvel where Troilus is. That's Helenus. I think he went not forth to-day. That's  Helenus.
translation: That's Helenus. I wonder where Troilus is. That's Helenus. I'm not sure he went out to fight today. That's Helenus.

original: Can Helenus fight, uncle?
translation: Is Helenus a good fighter, uncle?

original: Helenus? no. Yes, he'll fight indifferent well. I marvel where Troilus is. Hark! do you not hear the people cry 'Troilus'? Helenus is a priest.
translation: Helenus? Oh, sure, he fights well enough. I do wonder where Troilus is though. Listen! Can't you hear the people shouting "Troilus?" Helenus is a priest.

original: What sneaking fellow comes yonder?
translation: Who is that skulking man over there?

original: Where? yonder? that's Deiphobus. 'Tis Troilus! there's a man, niece! Hem! Brave Troilus! the prince of chivalry!
translation: Where? Over there? That's Deiphobus. Oh that is Troilus! What a man, niece! Wow! Brave Troilus, a prince of chivalry!

original: Peace, for shame, peace!
translation: Be quiet uncle, you're being embarrassing.

original: Mark him; note him. O brave Troilus!
translation: Pay attention, look at him. Oh brave Troilus!

original: Look well upon   him, niece: look you how his sword is bloodied, and   his helm more hacked than Hector's, and how he looks,   and how he goes!
translation: Observe him, niece! Do you see how sword is covered in blood, and his helmet has more gashes than Hector's did, and how proudly he walks!

original: O admirable youth! he ne'er saw   three and twenty.
translation: Oh what a shining example for young men, and he isn't even twenty three!

original: Go thy way, Troilus, go thy way!   Had I a sister were a grace, or a daughter a goddess,   he should take his choice.
translation: Go on Troilus, go on! If I had the perfect sister, or a goddess of a daughter, he could choose between them!

original: O admirable man! Paris?   Paris is dirt to him; and, I warrant, Helen, to   change, would give an eye to boot.
translation: Oh what a man! Paris? Paris is dirt compared to him. I am sure Helen would give anything to have Troilus instead of Paris.

original: Here come more.
translation: More soldiers are coming.

original: Asses, fools, dolts! chaff and bran, chaff and bran!
translation: Asses, fools, idiots!

original: porridge after meat!
translation: They are like eating porridge after meat.

original: I could live and die i' the   eyes of Troilus.
translation: I would be happy having only seen Troilus.

original: Ne'er look, ne'er look: the eagles   are gone: crows and daws, crows and daws!
translation: Oh don't look at these men, they are lesser men, like crows instead of eagles.

original: I had   rather be such a man as Troilus than Agamemnon and   all Greece.
translation: I would rather be Troilus than Agamemnon or any other Greek.

original: There is among the Greeks Achilles, a better man than  Troilus.
translation: Among the Greeks there is Achilles, who is a better man than Troilus.

original: Achilles! a drayman, a porter, a very camel.
translation: Achilles! Pah, Achilles is a cart-driver, a servant, a camel of a man.

original: Well, well.
translation: If you say so.

original: 'Well, well!' why, have you any discretion?
translation: "If I say so!" What, are you a great judge now?

original: have   you any eyes? Do you know what a man is?
translation: Do you have eyes? Do you have any idea what makes a good man?

original: Is not   birth, beauty, good shape, discourse, manhood,   learning, gentleness, virtue, youth, liberality,   and such like, the spice and salt that season a man?
translation: Is it not parentage, beauty, a good figure, witty conversation, manliness, education, gentleness, strength, youth, generosity, and such virtues that are like spice and salt, the seasoning of a great man?

original: Ay, a minced man: and then to be baked with no date in the pie, for then the man's date's out.
translation: Ha, that would make an unmanly man, who has all the ingredients except for the most important one.

original: You are such a woman! one knows not at what ward you lie.
Upon my back, to defend my belly; upon my wit, to   defend my wiles; upon my secrecy, to defend mine   honesty; my mask, to defend my beauty; and you, to   defend all these:
translation: I would  lie  on my back to defend my  belly , I would rely on my wit to defend my desires, I would lie secretly to defend my honor, wear a mask to defend my beauty, and beat you down to defend these virtues.

original: and at all these wards I lie, at a   thousand watches.
translation: I will always guard myself in these ways.

original: Say one of your watches.
translation: Say one of your prayers for protection.

original: Nay, I'll watch you for that; and that's one of the   chiefest of them too:
translation: Don't ask me to talk about protection. I will make sure that you do not betray me by talking, which is one of the most important kinds of protection.

original: if I cannot ward what I would   not have hit, I can watch you for telling how I took   the blow;
translation: If I cannot protect myself from being seduced, I can at least make sure you don't go around telling everyone!

original: unless it swell past hiding, and then it's   past watching.
translation: Unless it swells past the point where I can hide it, but in that case nothing can be done.

original: You are such another!
Sir, my lord would instantly speak with you.
translation: Sir, my lord wants to speak to you urgently.

original: Where?
translation: Where?

original: At your own house; there he unarms him.
translation: At your house, he is removing his armor there.

original: Good boy, tell him I come.
translation: Good boy, tell him I am coming.

original: I doubt he be hurt. Fare ye well, good niece.
translation: I fear he will be hurt. Good bye, niece.

original: Adieu, uncle.
translation: Goodbye, uncle.

original: I'll be with you, niece, by and by.
translation: I shall see you shortly.

original: To bring, uncle?
translation: Why?

original: Ay, a token from Troilus.
translation: To give you a gift from Troilus.

original: By the same token, you are a bawd.
Words, vows, gifts, tears, and love's full sacrifice,   He offers in another's enterprise;
translation: All these things he does, he does for another man.

original: But more in Troilus thousand fold I see   Than in the glass of Pandar's praise may be;   Yet hold I off.
translation: I see a thousand times more in Troilus than Pandarus can praise, but still I don't admit it.

original: Women are angels, wooing:   Things won are done; joy's soul lies in the doing.
translation: When a man woos a woman he treats her like an angel, and then takes her for granted when he has won her, the happy part is being wooed.

original: That she beloved knows nought that knows not this:   Men prize the thing ungain'd more than it is:   That she was never yet that ever knew   Love got so sweet as when desire did sue.
translation: Any woman who has been in loved will know this: men value what they haven't had more than is worth. No woman is better off than when a man is trying to please her.

original: Therefore this maxim out of love I teach:   Achievement is command; ungain'd, beseech:
translation: I like to use this saying: when a man has a woman he controls her, but until then he must try to please her.

original: Then though my heart's content firm love doth bear,   Nothing of that shall from mine eyes appear.
translation: Because of this, although in my heart I love him desperately, I shall not show him my love.

original: Princes,   What grief hath set the jaundice on your cheeks?
translation: Princes, what sadness has made you look so pale?

original: The ample proposition that hope makes   In all designs begun on earth below   Fails in the promised largeness:
translation: All human projects fall short of what they promise to achieve.

original: cheques and disasters   Grow in the veins of actions highest rear'd,   As knots, by the conflux of meeting sap,   Infect the sound pine and divert his grain   Tortive and errant from his course of growth.
translation: You should always expect obstacles even in the greatest undertakings.

original: Nor, princes, is it matter new to us   That we come short of our suppose so far   That after seven years' siege yet Troy walls stand;   Sith every action that hath gone before,   Whereof we have record, trial did draw   Bias and thwart, not answering the aim,   And that unbodied figure of the thought   That gave't surmised shape.
translation: Nor should it come as a surprise that after seven years Troy's walls still stand, since we have been testing many ways of breaking the siege and each has met firm resistance.

original: Why then, you princes,   Do you with cheeks abash'd behold our works,   And call them shames?
translation: Why, then, do you great men feel so ashamed of our attempts, and look down like you are failures?

original: which are indeed nought else   But the protractive trials of great Jove   To find persistive constancy in men:   The fineness of which metal is not found   In fortune's love; for then the bold and coward,   The wise and fool, the artist and unread,   The hard and soft seem all affined and kin:
translation: Our attempts aren't failures, we are just being tested by Jove, who does not give great men an easy time or else everyone would appear to be a great man.

original: But, in the wind and tempest of her frown,   Distinction, with a broad and powerful fan,   Puffing at all, winnows the light away;   And what hath mass or matter, by itself   Lies rich in virtue and unmingled.
translation: Rather Jove throws great men into a storm and tosses them, so that they can prove their greatness!

original: With due observance of thy godlike seat,   Great Agamemnon, Nestor shall apply   Thy latest words.
translation: With due respect to your office, great Agamemnon, I Nestor shall continue your words.

original: In the reproof of chance   Lies the true proof of men: the sea being smooth,   How many shallow bauble boats dare sail   Upon her patient breast, making their way   With those of nobler bulk!
translation: Only dire circumstances prove the greatness of a soldier. After all, anyone is willing to go to sea on a calm day.

original: But let the ruffian Boreas once enrage   The gentle Thetis, and anon behold   The strong-ribb'd bark through liquid mountains cut,   Bounding between the two moist elements,   Like Perseus' horse:
translation: But if the Gods stir up a great storm, only mighty vessels will sail between the earth and the sky and appear godlike by doing so.

original: where's then the saucy boat   Whose weak untimber'd sides but even now   Co-rivall'd greatness?
translation: The smaller boats are not out in weather like this, are they?

original: Either to harbour fled,   Or made a toast for Neptune.
translation: No, they flee to their harbors and beg Neptune to show them mercy.

original: Even so   Doth valour's show and valour's worth divide   In storms of fortune; for in her ray and brightness   The herd hath more annoyance by the breeze   Than by the tiger; but when the splitting wind   Makes flexible the knees of knotted oaks,   And flies fled under shade, why, then the thing of  courage   As roused with rage with rage doth sympathize,   And with an accent tuned in selfsame key   Retorts to chiding fortune.
translation: Great men aren't encouraged by timid quests, but excel when they are tested by misfortune, their ferocity mirroring the storms they face.

original: Agamemnon,   Thou great commander, nerve and bone of Greece,   Heart of our numbers, soul and only spirit.
translation: Great Agamemnon, mighty commander and example of Greek strength .

original: In whom the tempers and the minds of all   Should be shut up
translation: We all must give you our opinions.

original: , hear what Ulysses speaks.   Besides the applause and approbation To which,
translation: It is proper that we all find strength in your words, although please hear me. As well as praising you both for...

original: most mighty for thy place and sway,
translation: being a mighty and respected king...

original: And thou most reverend for thy stretch'd-out life   I give to both your speeches,   which were such   As Agamemnon and the hand of Greece   Should hold up high in brass,
translation: You are respected for being so old, and I want to voice my agreement with your speeches.  The words you spoke deserved to be held in high esteem by Agamemnon and the leadership of Greece.

original: and such again   As venerable Nestor, hatch'd in silver,   Should with a bond of air, strong as the axle-tree   On which heaven rides, knit all the Greekish ears   To his experienced tongue,
translation: And similarly, your words should be seen as great wisdom by all Greeks, as you are so wise and knowledgeable, Nestor.

original: yet let it please both,   Thou great, and wise, to hear Ulysses speak.
translation: But, even so, please listen great man and wise man, to my speech.

original: Speak, prince of Ithaca;
translation: You may speak, Ithacan prince.

original: and be't of less expect   That matter needless, of importless burden,   Divide thy lips, than we are confident,   When rank Thersites opes his mastic jaws,
translation: You should know that I am confident you will not speak like Thersites, who is disgusting and harsh in his speech.

original: We shall hear music, wit and oracle
translation: From you we will hear beauty, intelligence and wisdom.

original: Troy, yet upon his basis, had been down,   And the great Hector's sword had lack'd a master,   But for these instances.
translation: Troy would have been razed and Hector would be dead if it were not for the following reasons.

original: The specialty of rule hath been neglected:   And, look, how many Grecian tents do stand   Hollow upon this plain, so many hollow factions.
translation: Military rank has not been respected enough. However many Greeks we send from our camp, we gain no advantage. There are too many empty tents in the camp and too many different factions.

original: When that the general is not like the hive   To whom the foragers shall all repair,   What honey is expected?
translation: Would you expect to get honey from a hive in which the bees are not all working to one common purpose?

original: Degree being vizarded,   The unworthiest shows as fairly in the mask.
translation: If the rank has been hidden, the lowest seems not worse than the best.

original: The heavens themselves, the planets and this centre   Observe degree, priority and place,   Insisture, course, proportion, season, form,   Office and custom, in all line of order;   And therefore is the glorious planet Sol   In noble eminence enthroned and sphered   Amidst the other;   whose medicinable eye   Corrects the ill aspects of planets evil,   And posts, like the commandment of a king,   Sans cheque to good and bad:
translation: Even the planets show a respect for order, standing in a line before the glorious sun that sits in the best place in the sky. The sun is like a king whose gaze corrects the bad potential of the planets, which would otherwise become disordered.

original: but when the planets   In evil mixture to disorder wander,   What plagues and what portents! what mutiny!   What raging of the sea! shaking of earth!   Commotion in the winds! frights, changes, horrors,   Divert and crack, rend and deracinate   The unity and married calm of states   Quite from their fixure!
translation: When the planets wander they bring with them plagues, mutinies, tempests, earthquakes, raging storms and other terrifying events.

original: O, when degree is shaked,   Which is the ladder to all high designs,   Then enterprise is sick! How could communities,   Degrees in schools and brotherhoods in cities,   Peaceful commerce from dividable shores,   The primogenitive and due of birth,   Prerogative of age, crowns, sceptres, laurels,   But by degree, stand in authentic place?
translation: When rank, which is key to all great plans, is not respected, there can be no success. How could any community, from schools or guilds in cities, or ports by the sea, or siblings dividing an inheritance, or any monarchy survive without proper respect for rank?

original: Take but degree away, untune that string,   And, hark, what discord follows! each thing meets   In mere oppugnancy: the bounded waters   Should lift their bosoms higher than the shores   And make a sop of all this solid globe:
translation: If you ignore rank, it is like you take the instrument of society out of tune, and you are guaranteed a disharmony. Everything will fall out of place, and we will face an apocalypse.

original: Strength should be lord of imbecility,   And the rude son should strike his father dead:   Force should be right; or rather, right and wrong,   Between whose endless jar justice resides,   Should lose their names, and so should justice too.   Then every thing includes itself in power,   Power into will, will into appetite;   And appetite, an universal wolf,   So doubly seconded with will and power,   Must make perforce an universal prey,   And last eat up himself.
translation: There would be lawlessness, where men rule by might alone and morality is ignored. Justice would be lost as the powerful do as they please, and chaos, like an all-consuming wolf, would turn all humanity into its prey.

original: Great Agamemnon,   This chaos, when degree is suffocate,   Follows the choking.   And this neglection of degree it is   That by a pace goes backward, with a purpose   It hath to climb.
translation: If proper respect for rank is ignored, great Agamemnon, then this chaos must follow. A lack of respect for rank can spread from the top to the bottom of an army.

original: The general's disdain'd   By him one step below, he by the next,   That next by him beneath; so every step,   Exampled by the first pace that is sick   Of his superior, grows to an envious fever   Of pale and bloodless emulation:
translation: First the second-in-command loses respect for his general, then his men lose respect for him, and their men for them as they learn to disrespect duty from their masters.

original: And 'tis this fever that keeps Troy on foot,   Not her own sinews. To end a tale of length,   Troy in our weakness stands, not in her strength.
translation: A lack of respect grows like a great sickness of envy, and it is this sickness that keeps Troy from falling to us, not Troy's own strength. Troy is still standing, not because of its strength, but because of our weakness.

original: Most wisely hath Ulysses here discover'd The fever whereof all our power is sick.
translation: Ulysses has very wisely revealed the cause of our weakness.

original: The nature of the sickness found, Ulysses, What is the remedy?
translation: If this is our sickness, Ulysses, what is our cure?

original: The great Achilles, whom opinion crowns   The sinew and the forehand of our host,   Having his ear full of his airy fame,   Grows dainty of his worth, and in his tent   Lies mocking our designs:
translation: Achilles, who is considered our best soldier, has been made complacent by his fame, and sits in his tent refusing to aid our plans.

original: with him Patroclus   Upon a lazy bed the livelong day   Breaks scurril jests;   And with ridiculous and awkward action,   Which, slanderer, he imitation calls,   He pageants us.
translation: He lies there all day with Patroclus laughing disobediently, and Patroclus impersonates us in the most rude way.

original: Sometime, great Agamemnon,   Thy topless deputation he puts on,   And, like a strutting player, whose conceit   Lies in his hamstring, and doth think it rich   To hear the wooden dialogue and sound   'Twixt his stretch'd footing and the scaffoldage,—   Such to-be-pitied and o'er-wrested seeming   He acts thy greatness in:
translation: Sometimes, great Agamemnon, he pretends to be you. Like a prancing actor, who loves nothing more than the sound of his own voice, and with none of your genius, he mimics your greatness pitiably and poorly.

original: and when he speaks,   'Tis like a chime a-mending; with terms unsquared,   Which, from the tongue of roaring Typhon dropp'd   Would seem hyperboles. At this fusty stuff   The large Achilles, on his press'd bed lolling,   From his deep chest laughs out a loud applause;   Cries
translation: . Lying on his bed, the great Achilles laughs heartily at this ridiculous impersonation, and says:

original: 'Excellent! 'tis Agamemnon just.   Now play me Nestor; hem, and stroke thy beard,   As he being drest to some oration.'
translation: "Excellent, this is just like Agamemnon. Now pretend to be Nestor, say ahem and stroke your beard, and dress like you were going to speak to the king."

original: That's done, as near as the extremest ends   Of parallels, as like as Vulcan and his wife:   Yet god Achilles still cries 'Excellent!   'Tis Nestor right. Now play him me, Patroclus,   Arming to answer in a night alarm.'
translation: When Patroclus does this, even though he gets the part totally wrong, the  god-like  Achilles shouts out "Excellent, this is just like Nestor. Now, Patroclus, pretend to be Nestor if he thinks we are being ambushed at night."

original: And then, forsooth, the faint defects of age   Must be the scene of mirth; to cough and spit,   And, with a palsy-fumbling on his gorget,   Shake in and out the rivet:
translation: With this instruction, your old age is made fun of, and Patroclus pretends to cough, spit, fumble like an old man, and shake with fear.

original: and at this sport   Sir Valour dies; cries 'O, enough, Patroclus;   Or give me ribs of steel! I shall split all   In pleasure of my spleen.'
translation: At this depiction  Sir Valor  cannot control his laughter, saying: "Oh, that is enough, Patroclus. My ribs ache from laughing, and if I laugh anymore I will split in two from it."

original: And in this fashion,   All our abilities, gifts, natures, shapes,   Severals and generals of grace exact,   Achievements, plots, orders, preventions,   Excitements to the field, or speech for truce,   Success or loss, what is or is not, serves   As stuff for these two to make paradoxes.
translation: And in this way all of our abilities, strengths, appearances, general and specific parts of our character, our achievements, plans, orders, commandments, eagerness for battle or discussion of peace is mocked by those two.

original: And in the imitation of these twain—   Who, as Ulysses says, opinion crowns   With an imperial voice—many are infect.
translation: By these two men's mockery, two men who you rightly say are perceived to be our best soldiers, are many other soldiers  infected .

original: Ajax is grown self-will'd, and bears his head   In such a rein, in full as proud a place   As broad Achilles; keeps his tent like him;
translation: Ajax refuses to follow orders, and, having grown as proud as Achilles, also refuses to leave his tent.

original: Makes factious feasts; rails on our state of war,   Bold as an oracle,
translation: He makes the same slanders as Achilles, speaks poorly of our chances as if he was an oracle.

original: and sets Thersites,   A slave whose gall coins slanders like a mint,   To match us in comparisons with dirt,   To weaken and discredit our exposure,   How rank soever rounded in with danger.
translation: And he has Thersites, a slave who produces slanders like a mint makes coins, mimic us with cheap comparisons, and leaves us undefended.

original: They tax our policy, and call it cowardice,   Count wisdom as no member of the war,   Forestall prescience, and esteem no act   But that of hand:
translation: They say our careful planning is only done to avoid fighting, they say we do not show any wisdom in how we fight this war, ignore our plans, and say that nothing but swordsmanship is worthy of men.

original: the still and mental parts,   That do contrive how many hands shall strike,   When fitness calls them on, and know by measure   Of their observant toil the enemies' weight,—   Why, this hath not a finger's dignity:
translation: Whilst we consider our army's numbers, tactics, timing, and enemies, they say that this has no dignity at all.

original: They call this bed-work, mappery, closet-war;   So that the ram that batters down the wall,   For the great swing and rudeness of his poise,   They place before his hand that made the engine,   Or those that with the fineness of their souls   By reason guide his execution.
translation: They call us armchair generals. It is like saying that the battering ram, because it hits hard, deserves all the credit, and refusing to acknowledge the engineer who created it or the commander who deployed it.

original: Let this be granted, and Achilles' horse Makes many Thetis' sons.
translation: If this is how they behave Achilles's horse is worth much more than him.

original: What trumpet? look, Menelaus.
translation: What? A trumpet? Look Menelaus.

original: From Troy.
translation: Men are coming from Troy.

original: What would you 'fore our tent?
translation: Why are you stood before our tent?

original: Is this great Agamemnon's tent, I pray you?
Even this.
translation: It is.

original: May one, that is a herald and a prince, Do a fair message to his kingly ears?
translation: May I, as a messenger and as a prince, deliver a message to the king?

original: With surety stronger than Achilles' arm 'Fore all the Greekish heads, which with one voice Call Agamemnon head and general.
translation: You certainly may. Announce your message before the Greek commanders loyal to Agamemnon.

original: Fair leave and large security. How may A stranger to those most imperial looks Know them from eyes of other mortals?
translation: You are kind and generous. How should I know which of these men are the princes?

original: How!
translation: What?

original: Ay;   I ask, that I might waken reverence,   And bid the cheek be ready with a blush   Modest as morning when she coldly eyes   The youthful Phoebus:
translation: Yes, I ask so that I may show them proper respect and work out in advance who to treat with blushing respect:

original: Which is that god in office, guiding men?   Which is the high and mighty Agamemnon?
translation: who is the divine king? Who is the high and mighty Agamemnon?

original: This Trojan scorns us; or the men of Troy Are ceremonious courtiers.
translation: This Trojan either mocks us, or the Trojans are very polite courtiers.

original: Courtiers as free, as debonair, unarm'd,   As bending angels; that's their fame in peace:
translation: As ambassadors we are polite, courteous, and as friendly as bowing angels, this is how we are known in peace-times.

original: But when they would seem soldiers, they have galls,   Good arms, strong joints, true swords; and,   Jove's accord,   Nothing so full of heart.
translation: However, as soldiers, Trojans are strong willed, able-bodied, capable, and skilled with swords, and, by Jove, show no love or mercy.

original: But peace, AEneas,   Peace, Trojan; lay thy finger on thy lips!   The worthiness of praise distains his worth,   If that the praised himself bring the praise forth:
translation: But I should not talk like this, it is immodest to praise yourself.

original: But what the repining enemy commends,   That breath fame blows; that praise, sole sure,   transcends.
translation: The only worthy praise comes reluctantly from our enemies.

original: Sir, you of Troy, call you yourself AEneas?
translation: Sir, Trojan, are you Aeneas?

original: Ay, Greek, that is my name.
translation: Yes, Greek, that is my name.

original: What's your affair I pray you?
translation: Why are you here?

original: Sir, pardon; 'tis for Agamemnon's ears.
translation: Sir, I may not say, I must speak only to Agamemnon.

original: He hears naught privately that comes from Troy.
translation: No news arrives from Troy that he does not hear.

original: Nor I from Troy come not to whisper him: I bring a trumpet to awake his ear, To set his sense on the attentive bent, And then to speak.
translation: I do not come to whisper privately with him, rather I will wake him with my trumpet, and then I will speak to him.

original: Speak frankly as the wind;
translation: Speak then.

original: It is not Agamemnon's sleeping hour:   That thou shalt know. Trojan, he is awake,   He tells thee so himself.
translation: Agamemnon isn't asleep,  in fact he is telling you this himself .

original: Trumpet, blow loud,
translation: Be loud trumpet.

original: Send thy brass voice through all these lazy tents;   And every Greek of mettle, let him know,   What Troy means fairly shall be spoke aloud.
translation: Wake the Greek tents, so that any worthy Greek might know what the Trojan king would say.

original: We have, great Agamemnon, here in Troy   A prince call'd Hector,—Priam is his father,—   Who in this dull and long-continued truce   Is rusty grown: he bade me take a trumpet,   And to this purpose speak.
translation: In Troy, great Agamemnon, there is a prince called Hector, the son of Priam, who is growing rusty in this long truce. He told me to take this trumpet and to say this:

original: Kings, princes, lords!   If there be one among the fair'st of Greece   That holds his honour higher than his ease,   That seeks his praise more than he fears his peril,   That knows his valour, and knows not his fear,   That loves his mistress more than in confession,   With truant vows to her own lips he loves,   And dare avow her beauty and her worth   In other arms than hers,—to him this challenge.
translation: "Kings, princes, lords! If there is anyone among the best of the Greeks who values his honor more than an easy life, who seeks glory more than he fears death, that is is brave and unafraid, who is willing to actually defend his mistress's honor rather than merely promise to do so, and will fight for her, I have this challenge for such a man.

original: Hector, in view of Trojans and of Greeks,   Shall make it good, or do his best to do it,   He hath a lady, wiser, fairer, truer,   Than ever Greek did compass in his arms,
translation: Hector, in front of both Trojans and Greeks, shall prove that he has a wiser, more beautiful, and more truer lady than any Greek has ever had.

original: And will to-morrow with his trumpet call   Midway between your tents and walls of Troy,   To rouse a Grecian that is true in love:
translation: Tomorrow he will sound this trumpet as he stands halfway between your tents and our walls, hoping to wake a chivalrous Greek.

original: If any come, Hector shall honour him;   If none, he'll say in Troy when he retires,   The Grecian dames are sunburnt and not worth   The splinter of a lance. Even so much.
translation: If any Greek like this comes, Hector shall fight him honorably. If no such many comes, when he returns to Troy he shall say that Grecian women are sunburned and worthless." This is his message.

original: This shall be told our lovers, Lord AEneas;
translation: Our soldiers in love shall be told this, lord Aeneas.

original: If none of them have soul in such a kind,   We left them all at home:
translation: If none of them are brave enough to come forward, we must have left the brave Greeks at home.

original: but we are soldiers;   And may that soldier a mere recreant prove,   That means not, hath not, or is not in love!
translation: But listen, we are soldiers, and a soldier is worthless if he is not in love!

original: If then one is, or hath, or means to be,   That one meets Hector; if none else, I am he.
translation: If one of them accepts your challenge he will meet Hector. If none will, I will volunteer myself.

original: Tell him of Nestor, one that was a man   When Hector's grandsire suck'd:
translation: Deliver him a message from Nestor, who was a man when Hector's grandfather was being breast-fed.

original: he is old now;   But if there be not in our Grecian host   One noble man that hath one spark of fire,   To answer for his love, tell him from me   I'll hide my silver beard in a gold beaver   And in my vantbrace put this wither'd brawn,   And meeting him will tell him that my lady   Was fairer than his grandam and as chaste   As may be in the world:
translation: He is old now but if there is not one man in the Greek army whose heart is filled with the passion to fight for his love, tell Hector from me that I will hide my white beard in a golden helmet and in my armor hide these withered muscles, and when I meet him I will tell him that my lady was fairer than his grandmother and as chaste as anyone in the world.

original: his youth in flood,   I'll prove this truth with my three drops of blood.
translation: I'll challenge him in his prime with the little life that is left to me.

original: Now heavens forbid such scarcity of youth!
translation: Heaven forbid such a lack of young, eager men.

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: Fair Lord AEneas, let me touch your hand;   To our pavilion shall I lead you, sir.
translation: Fair lord Aeneas, give me your hand, that I may guide you to my tent.

original: Achilles shall have word of this intent;   So shall each lord of Greece, from tent to tent:
translation: Achilles will hear about this challenge, as will every Greek lord.

original: Yourself shall feast with us before you go   And find the welcome of a noble foe.
translation: You must feast with us before you go, and be the guest of your worthy enemy.

original: Nestor!
translation: Nestor!

original: What says Ulysses?
translation: What are you thinking, Ulysses?

original: I have a young conception in my brain; Be you my time to bring it to some shape.
translation: I've just had an idea, help me to develop it.

original: What is't?
translation: What is it?

original: This 'tis:   Blunt wedges rive hard knots: the seeded pride   That hath to this maturity blown up   In rank Achilles must or now be cropp'd,
translation: It is this, the pride that has grown hugely in Achilles must be dealt with now.

original: Or, shedding, breed a nursery of like evil,   To overbulk us all.
translation: If we ignore it, it will cause lots of problems and ruin us all.

original: Well, and how?
translation: I agree, but how?

original: This challenge that the gallant Hector sends, However it is spread in general name, Relates in purpose only to Achilles.
translation: Although the brave, young Hector offered this challenge to everyone he intended it only for Achilles.

original: The purpose is perspicuous even as substance,   Whose grossness little characters sum up:
translation: That is so obvious it may as well have been said in the message.

original: And, in the publication, make no strain,   But that Achilles, were his brain as barren   As banks of Libya,—though, Apollo knows,   'Tis dry enough,—will, with great speed of judgment,   Ay, with celerity, find Hector's purpose   Pointing on him.
translation: Even if Achilles was a moron - and lord knows he is not very clever - he will quickly figure out that Hector's purpose is to engage him.

original: And wake him to the answer, think you?
translation: And do you think he will rise to the challenge?

original: Yes, 'tis most meet: whom may you else oppose,   That can from Hector bring his honour off,   If not Achilles?
translation: Yes, it is almost certain, who else could possibly defeat Hector apart from Achilles?

original: Though't be a sportful combat,   Yet in the trial much opinion dwells;   For here the Trojans taste our dear'st repute   With their finest palate: and trust to me, Ulysses,   Our imputation shall be oddly poised   In this wild action;
translation: Although it is not a major battle much honor hangs in the balance, as the Trojans will send their best against ours, our ability shall be greatly judged.

original: for the success,   Although particular, shall give a scantling   Of good or bad unto the general;
translation: Victory, although the fight is only between two men, shall reflect either for better or for worse upon the whole army.

original: And in such indexes, although small pricks   To their subsequent volumes, there is seen   The baby figure of the giant mass   Of things to come at large.
translation: And this small demonstration shall be used to predict future battles and even the war as a whole.

original: It is supposed   He that meets Hector issues from our choice   And choice, being mutual act of all our souls,   Makes merit her election, and doth boil,   As 'twere from us all, a man distill'd   Out of our virtues; who miscarrying,   What heart receives from hence the conquering part,   To steel a strong opinion to themselves?
translation: We must assume that the person who meets Hector is our choice, and they will only deserve selection if they are our very best, because the victorious side would gain such a boost to their morale.

original: Which entertain'd, limbs are his instruments,   In no less working than are swords and bows   Directive by the limbs.
translation: Bolstered by strong morale, soldiers fight better and harder, like their weapons are extensions of their arms.

original: Give pardon to my speech:   Therefore 'tis meet Achilles meet not Hector.
translation: Allow me to suggest something: it is because of what you have said that Achilles should not meet Hector.

original: Let us, like merchants, show our foulest wares,   And think, perchance, they'll sell; if not,   The lustre of the better yet to show,   Shall show the better.
translation: Let us, like merchants, show our worst merchandise in the hope that that it will sell. If it doesn't sell, our best will seem even better when it is compared to the first.

original: Do not consent   That ever Hector and Achilles meet;   For both our honour and our shame in this   Are dogg'd with two strange followers.
translation: Do not allow Hector and Achilles to fight. Both our victory and defeat will be determined by the two strange followers of this fight.

original: I see them not with my old eyes: what are they?
translation: I do not know who these strange followers are, what are you talking about?

original: What glory our Achilles shares from Hector,   Were he not proud, we all should share with him:
translation: If Achilles were not so proud, the glory he would take from defeating Hector would be shared between us all.

original: But he already is too insolent;   And we were better parch in Afric sun   Than in the pride and salt scorn of his eyes,   Should he 'scape Hector fair:
translation: But he is too insolent already, and we would suffer his pride and scorn if he defeats Hector.

original: if he were foil'd,   Why then, we did our main opinion crush   In taint of our best man.
translation: If he were beaten, then our reputation would be crushed alongside our best soldier.

original: No, make a lottery;   And, by device, let blockish Ajax draw   The sort to fight with Hector: among ourselves   Give him allowance for the better man;
translation: No, I think we should  hold a lottery  and make sure that by some underhand method the brutish Ajax has the ticket to fight Hector.  We and the other generals should all pretend that Ajax is the best soldier we have.

original: For that will physic the great Myrmidon   Who broils in loud applause, and make him fall   His crest that prouder than blue Iris bends.
translation: This will cure our other champion of his pride, Achilles is too used to being praised and it is time for him to feel passed over.

original: If the dull brainless Ajax come safe off,   We'll dress him up in voices: if he fail,   Yet go we under our opinion still   That we have better men.
translation: If the idiot Ajax wins, we'll praise him as our greatest hero, and if he doesn't succeed we will say we still have better soldiers.

original: But, hit or miss,   Our project's life this shape of sense assumes:   Ajax employ'd plucks down Achilles' plumes.
translation: But either way our main victory will be having Ajax humble Achilles.

original: Ulysses,   Now I begin to relish thy advice;
translation: Ulysses, I am starting to appreciate your plan.

original: And I will give a taste of it forthwith   To Agamemnon: go we to him straight.
translation: I'll go and tell Agamemnon about it. Let's go there together immediately.

original: Two curs shall tame each other: pride alone   Must tarre the mastiffs on, as 'twere their bone.
translation: We'll have our two troublesome  dogs  solve each other, their pride will be the bone that the two dogs fight over.

original: Thersites!
translation: Thersites!

original: Agamemnon, how if he had boils? full, all over, generally?
Thersites!
translation: Thersites!

original: And those boils did run? say so: did not the general run then? were not that a botchy core?
Dog!
translation: You dog!

original: Then would come some matter from him; I see none now.
Thou bitch-wolf's son, canst thou not hear?
translation: You son of a bitch, are you ignoring me?

original: Feel, then.
translation: If you won't listen to me, I'll beat my meaning into you.

original: The plague of Greece upon thee, thou mongrel beef-witted lord!
Speak then, thou vinewedst leaven, speak: I will beat thee into handsomeness.
I shall sooner rail thee into wit and holiness: but,   I think, thy horse will sooner con an oration than   thou learn a prayer without book   .
translation: It would be easier for me to talk you into being clever and righteous, but it's more likely your horse will deliver a speech that you will be able to recite a prayer by heart.

original: Thou canst strike,   canst thou? a red murrain o' thy jade's tricks!
translation: You can hit things can you? A plague on your  pathetic  actions.

original: Toadstool, learn me the proclamation.
Dost thou think I have no sense, thou strikest me thus?
translation: Do you think I have no feelings? Is that why you hit me like this?

original: The proclamation!
translation: Read the proclamation!

original: Thou art proclaimed a fool, I think.
Do not, porpentine, do not: my fingers itch.
translation: Do not push me, little satirist, my hands are itching to beat you again.

original: I would thou didst itch from head to foot and I had   the scratching of thee;   I would make thee the   loathsomest scab in Greece.
translation: I wish you itched from head to toe and that it was my job to scratch you, I'd scratch you until you were the most disgusting scab in Greece.

original: When thou art forth in   the incursions, thou strikest as slow as another.
translation: When you are actually out in the battlefield you are no quicker to engage than anyone else.

original: I say, the proclamation!
translation: I am telling you, read the proclamation!

original: Thou grumblest and railest every hour on Achilles, and thou art as full of envy at his greatness as Cerberus is at Proserpine's beauty, ay, that thou barkest at him.
Mistress Thersites!
Thou shouldest strike him.
translation: You should hit Achilles.

original: Cobloaf!
translation: Worthless creature!

original: He would pun thee into shivers with his fist, as a sailor breaks a biscuit.
You whoreson cur!
translation: You son of a whore!

original: Do, do.
translation: Oh go ahead.

original: Thou stool for a witch!
translation: You toadstool!

original: Ay, do, do; thou sodden-witted lord! thou hast no   more brain than I have in mine elbows;
translation: Go on, you brutish lump. You have less intellect in your head than I have in my elbows.

original: an assinego   may tutor thee: thou scurvy-valiant ass! thou art   here but to thrash Trojans; and thou art bought and   sold among those of any wit, like a barbarian slave.
translation: A small donkey is brighter than you, you mock-brave ass! You are only here to beat Trojans, traded like a slave by brighter men than you.

original: If thou use to beat me, I will begin at thy heel, and   tell what thou art by inches, thou thing of no   bowels, thou!
translation: Hit me again and I'll tell you exactly what you're worth, you gutless wretch, from bottom to top.

original: You dog!
translation: You dog!

original: You scurvy lord!
translation: You worthless lord!

original: You cur!
translation: You worthless creature!

original: Mars his idiot! do, rudeness; do, camel; do, do.
translation: Brainless brawler, go ahead idiot, go on, you camel, go on.

original: Why, how now, Ajax! wherefore do you thus? How now, Thersites! what's the matter, man?
translation: Woah there, Ajax! Why are you hitting him? Why, Thersites, what is wrong?

original: You see him there, do you?
translation: You see that man, yes?

original: Ay; what's the matter?
translation: Yes, what is the problem.

original: Nay, look upon him.
translation: Look at him.

original: So I do: what's the matter?
translation: I am, what is the problem?

original: Nay, but regard him well.
translation: No, really look at him.

original: 'Well!' why, I do so.
translation: Well, I am looking at him.

original: But yet you look not well upon him; for whosoever you take him to be, he is Ajax.
I know that, fool.
Ay, but that fool knows not himself.
Therefore I beat thee.
Lo, lo, lo, lo, what modicums of wit he utters! his   evasions have ears thus long.
translation: Oh look here, what small pieces of wit come out of his mouth! He has the wit of a donkey.

original: I have bobbed his   brain more than he has beat my bones: I will buy   nine sparrows for a penny, and his pia mater is not   worth the nineth part of a sparrow.
translation: I have made him look like a fool more than he has beaten me physically. If I buy nine sparrows for a penny I could not buy a ninth of a sparrow with all his wit.

original: This lord,   Achilles, Ajax, who wears his wit in his belly and   his guts in his head, I'll tell you what I say of   him.
translation: This man Ajax, Achilles, has no thoughts beyond basic impulses. I'll tell you what I think of him.

original: What?
translation: What do you think of him?

original: I say, this Ajax—
translation: I think this Ajax...

original: Nay, good Ajax.
translation: Be gentle, good Ajax.

original: Has not so much wit—
translation: Has not got enough wit.

original: Nay, I must hold you.
translation: Leave it Thersites.

original: As will stop the eye of Helen's needle, for whom he comes to fight.
translation: To fill the eye of Helen's needle, who is the only reason he was brought here.

original: Peace, fool!
translation: Be silent, fool.

original: I would have peace and quietness, but the fool will not: he there: that he: look you there.
translation: I would happily live in peace and quiet, but the fool will not, he is the fool, look at him.

original: O thou damned cur! I shall—
translation: Oh you cursed wretch! I shall...

original: Will you set your wit to a fool's?
translation: Will you set your wit against that of a fool?

original: No, I warrant you; for a fool's will shame it.
translation: I doubt he will, because my wit will make him look stupid again.

original: Good words, Thersites.
translation: Good one, Thersites.

original: What's the quarrel?
translation: Why are you arguing?

original: I bade the vile owl go learn me the tenor of the proclamation, and he rails upon me.
translation: I asked the stupid creature to tell me what the proclamation said, and he started insulting me.

original: I serve thee not.
translation: I am not your servant.

original: Well, go to, go to.
translation: Well then, go away, begone.

original: I serve here voluntarily.
translation: I serve in the army as a volunteer.

original: Your last service was sufferance, 'twas not voluntary: no man is beaten voluntary: Ajax was here the voluntary, and you as under an impress.
E'en so; a great deal of your wit, too, lies in your   sinews, or else there be liars.
translation: Even so. If most of your intelligence does not reside in your muscles, then people were lying about you.

original: Hector have a great   catch, if he knock out either of your brains: a'   were as good crack a fusty nut with no kernel.
translation: If Hector cracks open either of your heads it would be like cracking open a nut to find nothing inside

original: What, with me too, Thersites?
translation: Are you mocking me too now, Thersites?

original: There's Ulysses and old Nestor, whose wit was mouldy ere your grandsires had nails on their toes, yoke you like draught-oxen and make you plough up the wars.
translation: Ulysses and old Nestor, whose wit was mouldy by the time your grandfathers had toenails, are still able to get you two to be like ploughmen for their wars.

original: What, what?
translation: Pardon?

original: Yes, good sooth: to, Achilles! to, Ajax! to!
translation: Oh yes, hya Achilles, hya hya Ajax.

original: I shall cut out your tongue.
translation: I shall cut out your tongue.

original: 'Tis no matter! I shall speak as much as thou afterwards.
translation: It doesn't matter, afterwards I'll still speak as much sense as you.

original: No more words, Thersites; peace!
translation: Okay stop now Thersites, be silent.

original: I will hold my peace when Achilles' brach bids me,  shall I?
translation: I'll be silent on the orders of Achilles's bitch, shall I?

original: There's for you, Patroclus.
translation: That's what you get for helping him, Patroclus.

original: I will see you hanged, like clotpoles, ere I come any more to your tents: I will keep where there is wit stirring and leave the faction of fools.
translation: I'll never come to your tent again unless it is to see you thickheads hanged. I will go where there is more wit and leave you fools behind.

original: A good riddance.
translation: Good riddance.

original: Marry, this, sir, is proclaim'd through all our host:   That Hector, by the fifth hour of the sun,   Will with a trumpet 'twixt our tents and Troy   To-morrow morning call some knight to arms   That hath a stomach;
translation: ndeed, Ajax this is what was proclaimed through our camp: Hector, five hours after sunrise tomorrow, will come with a trumpet to the ground between our tents and Troy and call out to fight him any knights who are brave enough, and whoever dares...

original: and such a one that dare   Maintain—I know not what: 'tis trash. Farewell.
translation: whatever, it doesn't matter, the whole thing is trash. Goodbye.

original: Farewell. Who shall answer him?
translation: Goodbye, who shall fight him?

original: I know not: 'tis put to lottery; otherwise He knew his man.
translation: I don't know, it will be a matter of chance, otherwise his opponent would be obvious.

original: O, meaning you. I will go learn more of it.
translation: Oh, you mean yourself. I will go find out more.

original: After so many hours, lives, speeches spent,   Thus once again says Nestor from the Greeks:
translation: Even after all the time, lives, and messages that have gone by Nestor still sends the message from the Greeks:

original: 'Deliver Helen, and all damage else—   As honour, loss of time, travail, expense,   Wounds, friends, and what else dear that is consumed   In hot digestion of this cormorant war—   Shall be struck off.'
translation: "Deliver Helen, and all other damage, all honor, wasted time, effort, money, wounds, friends, and whatever else that is wasted in this war, shall be forgotten."

original: Hector, what say you to't?
translation: Hector, what do you think of this?

original: Though no man lesser fears the Greeks than I   As far as toucheth my particular,   Yet, dread Priam,   There is no lady of more softer bowels,   More spongy to suck in the sense of fear,   More ready to cry out   'Who knows what follows?'   Than Hector is:
translation: Although no one is less afraid of the Greeks than I am regarding the chance of being killed, yet, powerful Priam, there is no compassionate or concerned woman more eager to cry out "How will this end?" than I am.

original: the wound of peace is surety,   Surety secure; but modest doubt is call'd   The beacon of the wise, the tent that searches   To the bottom of the worst.
translation: Peace is dangerous because it makes us complacent in our security. A little doubt is known as the beacon of the wise, it is like a surgical  probe  that searches a wound.

original: Let Helen go:   Since the first sword was drawn about this question,   Every tithe soul, 'mongst many thousand dismes,   Hath been as dear as Helen;
translation: Helen leave, since we first begun this battle, every  sacrificed  soul, each of the many thousands, has been as important as Helen's.

original: I mean, of ours:   If we have lost so many tenths of ours,   To guard a thing not ours nor worth to us,   Had it our name, the value of one ten,   What merit's in that reason which denies   The yielding of her up?
translation: I mean the souls of our soldiers, not the Greeks. If we have lost so many men guarding something that is not Trojan nor worth as much to us a Trojan life, why shouldn't we just hand her over?

original: Fie, fie, my brother!   Weigh you the worth and honour of a king   So great as our dread father in a scale   Of common ounces?
translation: Away, away, brother! Do you value the king's honor as lowly as common soldier's lives?

original: will you with counters sum   The past proportion of his infinite?   And buckle in a waist most fathomless   With spans and inches so diminutive   As fears and reasons?
translation: Are you going to try to count out his infinite worth with the worthless lives of soldiers? Are you going to let down the infinite respect he is due for petty concerns and fears?

original: fie, for godly shame!
translation: Away, this shame is unbearable!

original: No marvel, though you bite so sharp at reasons,   You are so empty of them.
translation: It is no wonder you are so dismissive of concern and reason, you are empty of such things.

original: Should not our father   Bear the great sway of his affairs with reasons,   Because your speech hath none that tells him so?
translation: Shouldn't our father rely on reasons to make his judgments, seeing as you have nothing reasonable to say?

original: You are for dreams and slumbers, brother priest;   You fur your gloves with reason.
translation: You only care about dreaming and sleeping, priest and brother of mine. You invent reasons for living comfortably.

original: Here are   your reasons:   You know an enemy intends you harm;   You know a sword employ'd is perilous,   And reason flies the object of all harm:
translation: Here are those reasons: You know an enemy wants to hurt you, you know fighting them is risky, and that logically you should avoid being hurt.

original: Who marvels then, when Helenus beholds   A Grecian and his sword, if he do set   The very wings of reason to his heels   And fly like chidden Mercury from Jove,   Or like a star disorb'd?
translation: Who is surprised then that when Helenus sees a Greek with a sword, he uses reason as an excuse to run away like a shooting star or Mercury the messenger god away from Jupiter?

original: Nay, if we talk of reason,   Let's shut our gates and sleep: manhood and honour   Should have hare-hearts, would they but fat   their thoughts   With this cramm'd reason:
translation: No, if we only care about logic let's close the gates and go to sleep. Brave and honorable people would live in fear if they allowed reason to govern them.

original: reason and respect   Make livers pale and lustihood deject.
translation: Reason and logic make men into impotent cowards.

original: Brother, she is not worth what she doth cost The holding.
translation: Brother, Helen is not worth the price of keeping her.

original: What is aught, but as 'tis valued?
But value dwells not in particular will;   It holds his estimate and dignity   As well wherein 'tis precious of itself   As in the prizer:
translation: B ut value isn't decided by one man's will, value exists in the object as well as the person who desires it.

original: 'tis mad idolatry   To make the service greater than the god   And the will dotes that is attributive   To what infectiously itself affects,   Without some image of the affected merit.
translation: It is mad idolatry to give more in sacrifice than the god is worth, and the desire that is too strong is like a sickness when it cannot see the object's true worth.

original: I take to-day a wife, and my election   Is led on in the conduct of my will;   My will enkindled by mine eyes and ears,   Two traded pilots 'twixt the dangerous shores   Of will and judgment:
translation: If I get married today, my choice was decided by my will. My will is kindled by my eyes and ears, which are like sea-captains navigating a narrow passage between the two dangerous shores of desire and good judgement.

original: how may I avoid,   Although my will distaste what it elected,   The wife I chose? there can be no evasion   To blench from this and to stand firm by honour:
translation: How could I choose as a wife anyone other than the person I desired? There is no honorable way to turn away from choosing the person you desire once you desire them.

original: We turn not back the silks upon the merchant,   When we have soil'd them, nor the remainder viands   We do not throw in unrespective sieve,   Because we now are full.
translation: We don't return silks to the merchant we bought them from once we have made them dirty, nor do we throw away our food stores when we are full .

original: It was thought meet   Paris should do some vengeance on the Greeks:   Your breath of full consent bellied his sails;   The seas and winds, old wranglers, took a truce   And did him service:
translation: We all thought it was appropriate that Paris takes revenge upon the Greeks, your voices were like a wind of consent that blew his ship to Greece, the seas and winds even helped him on his way.

original: he touch'd the ports desired,   And for an old aunt whom the Greeks held captive,   He brought a Grecian queen, whose youth and freshness   Wrinkles Apollo's, and makes stale the morning.
translation: He got to his destination, and because the Greeks held one of his old aunts captive, he stole the Greek queen, who is more youthful than Apollo and who makes the morning seem old.

original: Why keep we her? the Grecians keep our aunt:   Is she worth keeping? why, she is a pearl,   Whose price hath launch'd above a thousand ships,   And turn'd crown'd kings to merchants.
translation: Why do we keep her? Because the Greeks keep our aunt. Is Helen worth keeping? She a pearl, so valuable that the Greeks launched over a thousand ships to get her back, making settled kings into merchants who would risk everything on the water.

original: If you'll avouch 'twas wisdom Paris went—   As you must needs, for you all cried 'Go, go,'—   If you'll confess he brought home noble prize—   As you must needs, for you all clapp'd your hands   And cried 'Inestimable!'—why do you now   The issue of your proper wisdoms rate,   And do a deed that fortune never did,   Beggar the estimation which you prized   Richer than sea and land?
translation: If you admit that it was wise Paris went, which you must because you all told him to go; if you admit he brought home a prize worth having, which you must because you all clapped and called his prize unbelievable; why do you now question what you once thought was wise, and do something never before done, question the value of something that was once worth more than the world?

original: O, theft most base,   That we have stol'n what we do fear to keep!   But, thieves, unworthy of a thing so stol'n,   That in their country did them that disgrace,   We fear to warrant in our native place!
translation: Oh it was a stupid theft if we stole something we are too afraid to keep! Even more ridiculous, we are thieves unworthy of such a thing, that are willing to disgrace the Greeks in Greece, but are afraid of our treasure when we are back home.

original: Cry, Trojans, cry!
translation: Cry, Trojans, cry!

original: What noise? what shriek is this?
translation: What is that noise? Who is screaming?

original: 'Tis our mad sister, I do know her voice.
translation: It is our mad sister, I recognize her voice.

original: Cry, Trojans!
translation: Cry, Trojans!

original: It is Cassandra.
translation: It is Cassandra.

original: Cry, Trojans, cry! lend me ten thousand eyes, And I will fill them with prophetic tears.
translation: Cry, Trojans, cry! Give me ten thousand eyes, and I will have them all weep for what will happen.

original: Peace, sister, peace!
translation: Be quiet, sister, calm down!

original: Virgins and boys, mid-age and wrinkled eld,   Soft infancy, that nothing canst but cry,   Add to my clamours!
translation: Virgins and boys, the middle-aged and the wrinkled elderly, young children that can do nothing but cry, join me in moaning!

original: let us pay betimes   A moiety of that mass of moan to come.   Cry, Trojans, cry! practise your eyes with tears!   Troy must not be, nor goodly Ilion stand;   Our firebrand brother, Paris, burns us all.
translation: Let us begin early to pay off the debt of tears we will have. Cry, Trojans, cry! Get your eyes used to tears! Troy will be destroyed, and Ilium will fall. Our hot-headed brother Paris will be the ruin of us all.

original: Cry, Trojans, cry! a Helen and a woe:   Cry, cry! Troy burns, or else let Helen go.
translation: Cry Trojans, cry! Cry because of Helen and misery! Troy will burn if Helen is not let go.

original: Now, youthful Troilus, do not these high strains   Of divination in our sister work   Some touches of remorse?
translation: Now, young Troilus, do our sister's prophecies not make you doubt yourself?

original: or is your blood   So madly hot that no discourse of reason,   Nor fear of bad success in a bad cause,   Can qualify the same?
translation: Or are you so madly excited that no amount of reason, nor fear of defeat or moral wrong-doing, can make you change your mind?

original: Why, brother Hector,   We may not think the justness of each act   Such and no other than event doth form it,   Nor once deject the courage of our minds,   Because Cassandra's mad:
translation: Brother Hector, we mustn't decide what is right or wrong only from the results nor stop being brave just because Cassandra is mad.

original: her brain-sick raptures   Cannot distaste the goodness of a quarrel   Which hath our several honours all engaged   To make it gracious.
translation: Her unhinged prophecies don't change the morality of a cause that we all fighting for properly.

original: For my private part,   I am no more touch'd than all Priam's sons:   And Jove forbid there should be done amongst us   Such things as might offend the weakest spleen   To fight for and maintain!
translation: Personally, I am no more passionate than any of Priam's sons, and God forbid we would fight for anything that any of us are too afraid to fight for and win!

original: Else might the world convince of levity   As well my undertakings as your counsels:   But I attest the gods, your full consent   Gave wings to my propension and cut off   All fears attending on so dire a project.
translation: Otherwise the world will think your wisdom and my actions were worthless, but I swear that it was your agreement that made me hurry to ignore my fears and embark on my dangerous task.

original: For what, alas, can these my single arms?   What Propugnation is in one man's valour,   To stand the push and enmity of those   This quarrel would excite?
translation: I couldn't have done all this on my own. How could I have started this war on my own?

original: Yet, I protest,   Were I alone to pass the difficulties   And had as ample power as I have will,   Paris should ne'er retract what he hath done,   Nor faint in the pursuit.
translation: Yet even without your support if I had as much strength as I have will power I wouldn't do anything differently and would continue the war.

original: Paris, you speak   Like one besotted on your sweet delights:
translation: Paris you are speaking like a man who is drunk on their delight.

original: You have the honey still, but these the gall;   So to be valiant is no praise at all.
translation: You have the sweetness of Helen, and these men have the bitterness of war, so it is hardly brave of you to want to continue.

original: Sir, I propose not merely to myself   The pleasures such a beauty brings with it;   But I would have the soil of her fair rape   Wiped off, in honourable keeping her.
translation: Sir, I'm not only concerned with the pleasures I take from her beauty, but would rather our actions be proved honorable by us keeping her.

original: What treason were it to the ransack'd queen,   Disgrace to your great worths and shame to me,   Now to deliver her possession up   On terms of base compulsion!
translation: It would be a kind of treason to Helen, disgraceful for you all, and shameful for me, to give her up because of shameful obligation!

original: Can it be   That so degenerate a strain as this   Should once set footing in your generous bosoms?
translation: Surely such cowardly thoughts would never enter your gracious minds?

original: There's not the meanest spirit on our party   Without a heart to dare or sword to draw   When Helen is defended, nor none so noble   Whose life were ill bestow'd or death unfamed   Where Helen is the subject;
translation: There is no creature so pathetic on our side that they do not have the heart or sword to defend Helen, nor is there anyone so worthy that they would be shamed by dying for Helen.

original: then, I say,   Well may we fight for her whom, we know well,   The world's large spaces cannot parallel.
translation: I say it is a proper thing to fight for someone who is without comparison throughout the world.

original: Paris and Troilus, you have both said well,   And on the cause and question now in hand   Have glozed, but superficially: not much   Unlike young men, whom Aristotle thought   Unfit to hear moral philosophy:
translation: Paris and Troilus you have both given good speeches even if they were superficial, like the young men who Aristotle thought were unfit to be part of moral debates.

original: The reasons you allege do more conduce   To the hot passion of distemper'd blood   Than to make up a free determination   'Twixt right and wrong, for pleasure and revenge   Have ears more deaf than adders to the voice   Of any true decision.
translation: The reasons you give are full of passion rather than an unbiased decision between right and wrong, after all pleasure and revenge are deaf, like a snake is, to logic.

original: Nature craves   All dues be render'd to their owners: now,   What nearer debt in all humanity   Than wife is to the husband?
translation: Nature demands that all debts are settled, and what debt could be greater than a wife being kept from her husband?

original: If this law   Of nature be corrupted through affection,   And that great minds, of partial indulgence   To their benumbed wills, resist the same,   There is a law in each well-order'd nation   To curb those raging appetites that are   Most disobedient and refractory.
translation: If natural law is upset by a man's lust, and great minds resist natural law because of their weak will, there are  laws in each nation to stop those whose appetites cannot be controlled .

original: If Helen then be wife to Sparta's king,   As it is known she is, these moral laws   Of nature and of nations speak aloud   To have her back return'd: thus to persist   In doing wrong extenuates not wrong,   But makes it much more heavy.
translation: If Helen is the wife of Menelaus, as we all know she is, the moral laws of nature and society say that she must be returned. To continue doing an immoral act does not make it better but worse.

original: Hector's opinion   Is this in way of truth; yet ne'ertheless,   My spritely brethren, I propend to you   In resolution to keep Helen still,   For 'tis a cause that hath no mean dependance   Upon our joint and several dignities.
translation: This is my honest opinion, but nonetheless, my youthful brothers, I feel like agreeing that we keep Helen, because it would reflect so badly on us if we did not.

original: Why, there you touch'd the life of our design:   Were it not glory that we more affected   Than the performance of our heaving spleens,   I would not wish a drop of Trojan blood   Spent more in her defence.
translation: That's exactly what I was trying to say, if there was no glory in carrying on the fight I wouldn't want another drop of Trojan blood to be spilled in her defense.

original: But, worthy Hector,   She is a theme of honour and renown,   A spur to valiant and magnanimous deeds,   Whose present courage may beat down our foes,   And fame in time to come canonize us;
translation: But, worthy Hector, she is a legendary prize, proof of our excellence and bravery, and if we are courageous enough to defeat our enemies we will become famous heroes.

original: For, I presume, brave Hector would not lose   So rich advantage of a promised glory   As smiles upon the forehead of this action   For the wide world's revenue.
translation: I presume brave Hector would not give up this promise of fame for all the wealth in the world.

original: I am yours,   You valiant offspring of great Priamus.
translation: I will help you, brave son of Priam.

original: I have a roisting challenge sent amongst   The dun and factious nobles of the Greeks   Will strike amazement to their drowsy spirits:
translation: I have sent a rousing challenge to the slow and in-fighting Greek nobility that will rouse them.

original: I was advertised their great general slept,   Whilst emulation in the army crept:   This, I presume, will wake him.
translation: I was told that their great champion, Achilles, refused to fight, whilst the others sought to imitate him. I presume that my challenge will wake him.

original: How now, Thersites! what lost in the labyrinth of   thy fury! Shall the elephant Ajax carry it thus?
translation: Oh Thersites! What, are you stuck in a maze of your own hate? Will the elephant Ajax win over you like this?

original: He   beats me, and I rail at him: O, worthy satisfaction!   would it were otherwise; that I could beat him,   whilst he railed at me.
translation: He hits me and I insult him,  oh that's a worthy payback!  I wish it were the other way around, and I could hit him whilst he shouted at me.

original: 'Sfoot, I'll learn to   conjure and raise devils, but I'll see some issue of   my spiteful execrations.
translation: God's foot, if I have to learn magic and how to conjure demons I will do it, to make my hatred productive.

original: Then there's Achilles, a   rare enginer! If Troy be not taken till these two   undermine it, the walls will stand till they fall of   themselves.
translation: Then there's Achilles,  a strange sapper . If Troy isn't taken by these two, it won't be until the walls fall over on their own.

original: O thou great thunder-darter of Olympus,   forget that thou art Jove, the king of gods and,   Mercury, lose all the serpentine craft of thy   caduceus, if ye take not that little, little less   than little wit from them that they have!
translation: Oh Jupiter give up your thunderbolts, and Mercury give up your  medicine , if you don't take the last of Ajax and Achilles' pathetic wit from them.

original: which   short-armed ignorance itself knows is so abundant   scarce, it will not in circumvention deliver a fly   from a spider, without drawing their massy irons and   cutting the web.
translation: Those stupid creatures couldn't think of a way of saving a fly from a spider without drawing their swords and cutting the web apart.

original: After this, the vengeance on the   whole camp! or rather, the bone-ache! for that,   methinks, is the curse dependent on those that war   for a placket.
translation: After these two, I'd put a plague on the whole camp! Or I'd make their  bones ache , a suitable curse for those that go to war over a  woman .

original: I have said my prayers and devil Envy   say Amen. What ho! my Lord Achilles!
translation: I have said my prayers and now only need the devil of Envy to agree. What's this, my lord Achilles.

original: Who's there? Thersites! Good Thersites, come in and  rail.
translation: Who's there? Thersites! Oh good, come in and start complaining.

original: If I could have remembered a gilt counterfeit, thou   wouldst not have slipped out of my contemplation: but   it is no matter; thyself upon thyself!
translation: If my memory  was able to remember a gilded fake you would not have left my prayers: but it's not important. Be true to yourself!

original: The common   curse of mankind, folly and ignorance, be thine in   great revenue! heaven bless thee from a tutor, and   discipline come not near thee!
translation: May you be kept wealthy by the common failings of mankind, stupidity and ignorance. May the gods give you the wisdom of a tutor, and you never experience punishment.

original: Let thy blood be thy   direction till thy death! then if she that lays thee   out says thou art a fair corse, I'll be sworn and   sworn upon't she never shrouded any but lazars.   Amen. Where's Achilles?
translation: Be guided by your passions until you die, and if the woman who prepares your body when you die calls you beautiful, then I was a liar and swore that she never prepared anyone who wasn't a leper. Amen. Where's Achilles?

original: What, art thou devout? wast thou in prayer?
translation: What, are you devout? Were you praying?

original: Ay: the heavens hear me!
translation: Yes, may the heavens hear me!

original: Who's there?
translation: Who's there?

original: Thersites, my lord.
translation: Thersites, my lord.

original: Where, where? Art thou come? why, my cheese, my digestion, why hast thou not served thyself in to my table so many meals? Come, what's Agamemnon?
Thy commander, Achilles. Then tell me, Patroclus, what's Achilles?
translation: He is your commander, Achilles. Now tell me, Patroclus, what's Achilles?

original: Thy lord, Thersites: then tell me, I pray thee, what's thyself?
translation: He is your lord, Thersites. Now tell me, please, what are you?

original: Thy knower, Patroclus: then tell me, Patroclus, what art thou?
translation: I am the one who understands you, Patroclus. Now tell me, Patroclus, what are you?

original: Thou mayst tell that knowest.
translation: You can tell me if you know me.

original: O, tell, tell.
translation: Tell him, tell him.

original: I'll decline the whole question. Agamemnon commands Achilles; Achilles is my lord; I am Patroclus' knower, and Patroclus is a fool.
translation: I'll begin from the beginning. Agamemnon commands Achilles, Achilles is my lord, I am Patroclus's knower, and Patroclus is a fool.

original: You rascal!
translation: You rascal!

original: Peace, fool! I have not done.
translation: Be quiet, fool! I am not finished.

original: He is a privileged man. Proceed, Thersites.
Agamemnon is a fool; Achilles is a fool; Thersites is a fool, and, as aforesaid, Patroclus is a fool.
translation: Agamemnon is a fool, Achilles is a fool, Thersites is a fool, and as I have already said, Patroclus is a fool.

original: Derive this; come.
translation: How did you figure this out, then?

original: Agamemnon is a fool to offer to command Achilles;   Achilles is a fool to be commanded of Agamemnon;
translation: Agamemnon is a fool to try and command Achilles. Achilles is a fool because he is commanded by Agamemnon.

original: Thersites is a fool to serve such a fool, and   Patroclus is a fool positive.
translation: Thersites is a fool because he serves such a fool. And Patroclus is definitely a fool.

original: Why am I a fool?
translation: Why am I a fool?

original: Make that demand of the prover. It suffices me thou art. Look you, who comes here?
Patroclus, I'll speak with nobody. Come in with me, Thersites.
translation: Patroclus I do not want to speak to anyone, come into the tent Thersites.

original: Here is such patchery, such juggling and such   knavery!
translation: These are good tricks and traps.

original: all the argument is a cuckold and a   whore; a good quarrel to draw emulous factions   and bleed to death upon.
translation: My argument was a baseless show, a clever argument that will make these men argue and fight to the death.

original: Now, the dry serpigo on   the subject! and war and lechery confound all!
translation: Now, a  plague  on the subject! Let war and greed ensnare everyone!

original: Where is Achilles?
translation: Where is Achilles?

original: Within his tent; but ill disposed, my lord.
translation: He's in the tent, but he's ill, my lord.

original: Let it be known to him that we are here.   He shent our messengers; and we lay by   Our appertainments, visiting of him:
translation: Let him know we are here. He has shamefully turned away our messengers, and we are willing to forget our rank by visiting him.

original: Let him be told so; lest perchance he think   We dare not move the question of our place,   Or know not what we are.
translation: Tell him this so that he does not think we aren't willing to pull rank on him or that we do not know our power.

original: I shall say so to him.
translation: I will tell him this.

original: We saw him at the opening of his tent: He is not sick.
translation: We saw him at the entrance of his tent so he can't be sick.

original: Yes, lion-sick, sick of proud heart: you may call it melancholy, if you will favour the man; but, by my head, 'tis pride: but why, why? let him show us the cause. A word, my lord.
translation: He's got the sickness of a lion, he's sick from pride. If you want to make him feel better call it sadness. But I know it is pride. But why is he proud? Let him show us a reason for his pride. A word with you, my lord.

original: What moves Ajax thus to bay at him?
translation: Why is Ajax so angry at Achilles?

original: Achilles hath inveigled his fool from him.
translation: Achilles has taken his fool from him.

original: Who, Thersites?
translation: Who do you mean, Thersites?

original: He.
translation: Yes.

original: Then will Ajax lack matter, if he have lost his  argument.
translation: Ajax probably has nothing to think about, without Thersites to argue with.
