original: No, you see, he is his argument that has his argument, Achilles.
translation: No, the fool takes his argument from his keeper. So now Achilles has become Thersites's argument.

original: All the better; their fraction is more our wish than their faction: but it was a strong composure a fool could disunite.
The amity that wisdom knits not, folly may easily untie. Here comes Patroclus.
translation: A friendship that isn't wise can be easily broken by folly. Patroclus is coming back.

original: No Achilles with him.
translation: Without Achilles.

original: The elephant hath joints, but none for courtesy: his legs are legs for necessity, not for flexure.
Achilles bids me say, he is much sorry,   If any thing more than your sport and pleasure   Did move your greatness and this noble state   To call upon him;
translation: Achilles asked me to say that he is very sorry if you had any serious business to come all this way to him.

original: he hopes it is no other   But for your health and your digestion sake,   And after-dinner's breath.
translation: He hopes you only came this way as part of a leisurely walk after dinner.

original: Hear you, Patroclus:   We are too well acquainted with these answers:   But his evasion, wing'd thus swift with scorn,   Cannot outfly our apprehensions.
translation: Listen, Patroclus, we know these responses very well. But his desire to avoid us, sent with such scorn, can't escape our notice.

original: Much attribute he hath, and much the reason   Why we ascribe it to him; yet all his virtues,   Not virtuously on his own part beheld,   Do in our eyes begin to lose their gloss,   Yea, like fair fruit in an unwholesome dish,   Are like to rot untasted.
translation: He has a great reputation, and it is well deserved, but all his virtues begin to seem less impressive to us if he does nothing, just as fresh fruit placed in a rotten meal won't be eaten.

original: Go and tell him,   We come to speak with him; and you shall not sin,   If you do say we think him over-proud   And under-honest, in self-assumption greater   Than in the note of judgment;
translation: Go and tell him we want to speak to him, and don't be afraid to tell him we think he has grown too proud and dishonest. He thinks he is better than he is.

original: and worthier   than himself   Here tend the savage strangeness he puts on,   Disguise the holy strength of their command,   And underwrite in an observing kind   His humorous predominance;   yea, watch   His pettish lunes, his ebbs, his flows, as if   The passage and whole carriage of this action   Rode on his tide.
translation: Tell him that while he acts aloof a better man is waiting outside, a man who is pretending not to be a divine king, a man who is willingly waiting for him to get off his high horse. I am watching his sulking and pathetic self-assured demeanor.

original: Go tell him this, and add,   That if he overhold his price so much,   We'll none of him; but let him, like an engine   Not portable, lie under this report:
translation: Go, and tell him these things, and say that if he thinks too much of himself we will not see him, but rather we will let him lie here like a siege engine without wheels and place a note outside his tent:

original: 'Bring action hither, this cannot go to war:   A stirring dwarf we do allowance give   Before a sleeping giant.' Tell him so.
translation: "Unless the fighting comes here, this engine cannot go to war, we would rather take an active dwarf than a sleeping giant." Tell him this.

original: I shall; and bring his answer presently.
translation: I will, and I will tell you what he says as soon as possible.

original: In second voice we'll not be satisfied; We come to speak with him. Ulysses, enter you.
translation: I don't want to speak to a middle man, we will come in too. Ulysses, go in.

original: What is he more than another?
translation: Is he better than anyone else?

original: No more than what he thinks he is.
translation: He thinks he is.

original: Is he so much? Do you not think he thinks himself a better man than I am?
translation: And is he as good as he thinks he is? Do you think he thinks he is better than me?

original: No question.
translation: Undoubtedly.

original: Will you subscribe his thought, and say he is?
translation: Do you agree with him, and think he is better than me?

original: No, noble Ajax; you are as strong, as valiant, as wise, no less noble, much more gentle, and altogether more tractable.
translation: No, noble Ajax, you are as strong, valiant, wise, noble, and more gentle than he, and much more easily ordered to do things.

original: Why should a man be proud? How doth pride grow? I know not what pride is.
translation: Why is anyone proud? Where does pride come from? I don't even know what pride is.

original: Your mind is the clearer, Ajax, and your virtues the   fairer. He that is proud eats up himself:
translation: Your smarter and more virtuous for being that way, Ajax, proud men tarnish themselves.

original: pride is   his own glass, his own trumpet, his own chronicle;
translation: Pride is like a mirror to itself, its own trumpet, and its own biography.

original: and whatever praises itself but in the deed, devours   the deed in the praise.
translation: Anything that honors itself except by acting well ruins the action.

original: I do hate a proud man, as I hate the engendering of  toads.
Yet he loves himself: is't not strange?
translation: Yet he is a proud man, what does that imply?

original: Achilles will not to the field to-morrow.
translation: Achilles will not fight tomorrow.

original: What's his excuse?
translation: What's his excuse?

original: He doth rely on none, But carries on the stream of his dispose Without observance or respect of any, In will peculiar and in self-admission.
translation: He doesn't have one, but carries on acting as he has been without respect for anyone else, solely on his own authority.

original: Why will he not upon our fair request Untent his person and share the air with us?
translation: Why won't he, when we have so politely asked him, leave his tent and talk with us?

original: Things small as nothing, for request's sake only,   He makes important:
translation: He pretends trivial requests are important, purely because they are asked of him.

original: possess'd he is with greatness,   And speaks not to himself but with a pride   That quarrels at self-breath: imagined worth   Holds in his blood such swoln and hot discourse   That 'twixt his mental and his active parts   Kingdom'd Achilles in commotion rages   And batters down himself:
translation: He is so certain of his greatness he is not even satisfied with his own praises of himself, his sense of self worth has such a grip on him that the mental landscape of Achilles is in a state of civil war.

original: what should I say?   He is so plaguy proud that the death-tokens of it   Cry 'No recovery.'
translation: What else is there to say? He is so sickeningly proud that his symptoms cry out: "No recovery is possible."

original: Let Ajax go to him. Dear lord, go you and greet him in his tent: 'Tis said he holds you well, and will be led At your request a little from himself.
translation: Let Ajax go to see him. Dear lord, go and greet him in his tent, it is said that he respects you, and will at your request be persuaded to make some small change in his behaviour.

original: O Agamemnon, let it not be so!   We'll consecrate the steps that Ajax makes   When they go from Achilles:
translation: Oh Agamemnon, don't let that happen! We should treasure every step that Ajax takes away from Achilles.

original: shall the proud lord   That bastes his arrogance with his own seam   And never suffers matter of the world   Enter his thoughts, save such as do revolve   And ruminate himself, shall he be worshipp'd   Of that we hold an idol more than he?
translation: The proud lord that stews in his arrogant pride and is incapable of thinking about anyone other than himself shouldn't be given the honor of a visit from a man we worship more than himself.

original: No, this thrice worthy and right valiant lord   Must not so stale his palm, nobly acquired;   Nor, by my will, assubjugate his merit,   As amply titled as Achilles is,   By going to Achilles:
translation: No this very worthy and truly valiant lord must not have his deserved honor sullied. Nor would I want to see his merit, that is as great as Achilles's, treated as worse by making him go to Achilles.

original: That were to enlard his fat already pride   And add more coals to Cancer when he burns   With entertaining great Hyperion.
translation: That would be like pumping up his already massive ego or throwing fuel into a mid-summer sun of pride.

original: This lord go to him! Jupiter forbid,   And say in thunder 'Achilles go to him.'
translation: That Ajax should go to him? May Jupiter forbid it and shout down with thunder "Achilles go him."

original: O, this is well; he rubs the vein of him.
translation: Oh this is excellent, Ulysses is playing Ajax perfectly.

original: And how his silence drinks up this applause!
translation: Look at how he silently enjoys this applause.

original: If I go to him, with my armed fist I'll pash him o'er  the face.
translation: If I go to him, I'll smash him in the face with my armored fist.

original: O, no, you shall not go.
translation: Oh no, you mustn't go in.

original: An a' be proud with me, I'll pheeze his pride: Let me go to him.
translation: If he is proud to me, I'll sort his pride out. Let me go to him.

original: Not for the worth that hangs upon our quarrel.
translation: Not for all the honor of defeating Troy.

original: A paltry, insolent fellow!
translation: He is a small, insolent man.

original: How he describes himself!
translation: Ajax could be describing himself!

original: Can he not be sociable?
translation: Is it so much for him to come out?

original: The raven chides blackness.
translation: The pot is calling the kettle black.

original: I'll let his humours blood.
He will be the physician that should be the patient.
translation: He should be the patient, but wants to be the doctor.

original: An all men were o' my mind,—
translation: If all men thought like me...

original: Wit would be out of fashion.
translation: Being witty would no longer be in fashion.

original: A' should not bear it so, a' should eat swords first: shall pride carry it?
An 'twould, you'ld carry half.
translation: If it was allowed to win it'd half be your fault.

original: A' would have ten shares.
translation: He would have ten portions of pride.

original: I will knead him; I'll make him supple.
He's not yet through warm: force him with praises: pour in, pour in; his ambition is dry.
translation: He's not ambitious enough yet, stuff him with more praise, go, go, he's not ready.

original: My lord, you feed too much on this  dislike.
translation: My lord you let Achilles's snubbing of you play too heavily on your mind.

original: Our noble general, do not do so.
translation: Noble general, do not think about it.

original: You must prepare to fight without Achilles.
translation: You must prepare for the battle with Hector without Achilles.

original: Why, 'tis this naming of him does him harm. Here is a man—but 'tis before his face; I will be silent.
translation: Saying Achilles's name is upsetting Agamemnon. Here is a man who could be our champion... but I should not discuss this whilst he is here, I will be silent.

original: Wherefore should you so? He is not emulous, as Achilles is.
translation: Why shouldn't you speak of it? Ajax isn't as proud as Achilles is.

original: Know the whole world, he is as valiant.
translation: But the whole world knows he is as brave.

original: A whoreson dog, that shall pelter thus with us! Would he were a Trojan!
translation: That son of a bitch, how dare he swindle us like this? I wish he were a Trojan.

original: What a vice were it in Ajax now,—
translation: How terrible would it be if Ajax now...

original: If he were proud,—
translation: If he were proud...

original: Or covetous of praise,—
translation: Or sought after praise...

original: Ay, or surly borne,—
translation: Yes, or if he was aloof...

original: Or strange, or self-affected!
translation: Or refused to be sociable.

original: Thank the heavens, lord, thou art of sweet composure;   Praise him that got thee, she that gave thee suck:   Famed be thy tutor, and thy parts of nature   Thrice famed, beyond all erudition:
translation: Thank heavens, lord Ajax, that you are such a great man, and may the gods bless your father and mother! Your education must have been magnificent, but no education could teach you to be as great as you naturally are.

original: But he that disciplined thy arms to fight,   Let Mars divide eternity in twain,   And give him half: and, for thy vigour,   Bull-bearing Milo his addition yield   To sinewy Ajax.
translation: The man who taught you to fight should be blessed by  Mars , even the mighty athlete  Milo   seems weak next to Ajax.

original: I will not praise thy wisdom,   Which, like a bourn, a pale, a shore, confines   Thy spacious and dilated parts: here's Nestor;   Instructed by the antiquary times,   He must, he is, he cannot but be wise:
translation: I cannot praise the wisdom which  disciplines  your body, but might compare it to Nestor, who is so old that must be wise.

original: Put pardon, father Nestor, were your days   As green as Ajax' and your brain so temper'd,   You should not have the eminence of him,   But be as Ajax.
translation: I'm sorry  father  Nestor, but I think if you were as young as Ajax, your natural wit would not exceed his, but would be its equal.

original: Shall I call you father?
translation: Will you be my father and mentor?

original: Ay, my good son.
Be ruled by him, Lord Ajax.
translation: Follow his directions, lord Ajax.

original: There is no tarrying here; the hart Achilles   Keeps thicket   .
translation: We shouldn't wait around here, the unsociable Achilles won't come into the open.

original: Please it our great general   To call together all his state of war;   Fresh kings are come to Troy:
translation: If it pleases our great general we should call together the war council as more Greek kings have arrived to help us.

original: to-morrow   We must with all our main of power stand fast:   And here's a lord,—come knights from east to west,   And cull their flower, Ajax shall cope the best.
translation: Tomorrow morning we should assemble the men on the field of battle. Even if all of the knights in the world came here, and we had our choice of them all, Ajax will perform best.

original: Go we to council. Let Achilles sleep: Light boats sail swift, though greater hulks draw deep.
Friend, you! pray you, a word: do not you follow the young Lord Paris?
Ay, sir, when he goes before me.
You depend upon him, I mean?
translation: He provides your livelihood, I mean?

original: Sir, I do depend upon the lord.
You depend upon a noble gentleman; I must needs praise him.
translation: You are provided for by a noble gentleman, who deserves praise.

original: The lord be praised!
You know me, do you not?
translation: You know who I am, right?

original: Faith, sir, superficially.
translation: Honestly, sir, only vaguely.

original: Friend, know me better; I am the Lord Pandarus.
translation: Friend, we should know each other better. I am the lord Pandarus.

original: I hope I shall know your honour better.
I do desire it.
translation: I hope so.

original: You are in the state of grace.
Grace! not so, friend: honour and lordship are my  titles.
What music is this?
translation: What is this music?

original: I do but partly know, sir: it is music in parts.
Know you the musicians?
translation: Do you know the musicians?

original: Wholly, sir.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: Who play they to?
translation: Who are they playing for?

original: To the hearers, sir.
translation: They are playing to the people that are listening, sir.

original: At whose pleasure, friend
translation: For whose pleasure, friend?

original: At mine, sir, and theirs that love music.
translation: Well it pleases me, sir, and anyone else that loves music.

original: Command, I mean, friend.
translation: Not "pleasure," I meant "command," friend.

original: Who shall I command, sir?
translation: Who will I command, sir?

original: Friend, we understand not one another: I am too courtly and thou art too cunning. At whose request do these men play?
That's to 't indeed, sir: marry, sir, at the request   of Paris my lord, who's there in person;
translation: That's it, sir. To tell you the truth, sir, they play because Paris asked them to. He's there listening to them now.

original: with him,   the mortal Venus, the heart-blood of beauty, love's   invisible soul,—
translation: With him, the human  Venus , the real expression of ideal beauty, love itself...

original: Who, my cousin Cressida?
translation: You mean my cousin Cressida?

original: No, sir, Helen: could you not find out that by her attributes?
translation: No, sir, I mean Helen. Could you not tell by my description?

original: It should seem, fellow, that thou hast not seen the   Lady Cressida.
translation: You've clearly not seen Lady Cressida,  man .

original: I come to speak with Paris from the   Prince Troilus: I will make a complimental assault   upon him, for my business seethes.
translation: I am here to speak with Paris on behalf of Prince Troilus, I will go on a  charm offensive  as my  business with him is boiling hot .

original: Sodden business! there's a stewed phrase indeed!
translation: Is your business wet? Your language itself is over-cooked.

original: Fair be to you, my lord, and to all this fair   company!
translation: I hope you and your companions are all well, my lord!

original: fair desires, in all fair measure,   fairly guide them! especially to you, fair queen!   fair thoughts be your fair pillow!
translation: I hope you are are not troubled by your thoughts, especially you beautiful queen, may you rest easily.

original: Dear lord, you are full of fair words.
You speak your fair pleasure, sweet queen. Fair prince, here is good broken music.
You have broke it, cousin: and, by my life, you   shall make it whole again;
translation: Well it is in pieces, cousin, now that you have broken it up. I swear it shall be up to you to make it whole again

original: you shall piece it out   with a piece of your performance. Nell, he is full   of harmony.
translation: with a piece of performance of your own. My love, he is full of  sweet sounds .

original: Truly, lady, no.
translation: Honestly, my lady, I'm not.

original: O, sir,—
translation: Oh, but sir do sing for us...

original: Rude, in sooth; in good sooth, very rude.
translation: Honestly, I am a very bad singer.

original: Well said, my lord! well, you say so in fits.
translation: You speak well, my lord, speaking with such a rhythm.

original: I have business to my lord, dear queen. My lord, will you vouchsafe me a word?
translation: I have business with Paris, dear queen. My lord could I have a word with you?

original: Nay, this shall not hedge us out: we'll hear you sing, certainly.
Well, sweet queen. you are pleasant with me. But, marry, thus, my lord: my dear lord and most esteemed friend, your brother Troilus,—
translation: Sweet queen, you are trying to wind me up aren't you? But listen to this, lord Paris, your brother Troilus, my lord and most esteemed friend...

original: My Lord Pandarus; honey-sweet lord,—
Go to, sweet queen, to go:—commends himself most affectionately to you,—
You shall not bob us out of our melody: if you do, our melancholy upon your head!
translation: You won't cheat me out of a song. If you do I shan't forgive you!

original: Sweet queen, sweet queen! that's a sweet queen, i'  faith.
translation: Sweet queen, sweet queen! Please don't be upset with me, I beg you.

original: And to make a sweet lady sad is a sour offence.
Nay, that shall not serve your turn; that shall not,   in truth, la.
translation: No, that won't work, it really won't. No, I don't care for such words, no and no.

original: Nay, I care not for such words; no,   no. And, my lord, he desires you, that if the king   call for him at supper, you will make his excuse.
translation: Anyway, Troilus wants you to excuse him if the king asks to see him at supper, and asks that you would give an excuse for him.

original: My Lord Pandarus,—
translation: My lord Pandarus...

original: What says my sweet queen, my very very sweet queen?
translation: What is it my sweet queen, my very very sweet queen?

original: What exploit's in hand? where sups he to-night?
translation: What is he up to, where will he be eating tonight?

original: Nay, but, my lord,—
translation: No, my lord listen to me...

original: What says my sweet queen? My cousin will fall out with you. You must not know where he sups.
I'll lay my life, with my disposer Cressida.
translation: I'll bet my life Cressida's stolen him away from my company.

original: No, no, no such matter; you are wide: come, your disposer is sick.
Well, I'll make excuse.
translation: Sure, I'll make an excuse for him.

original: Ay, good my lord. Why should you say Cressida? no, your poor disposer's sick.
translation: Ah, thank you my lord. Why did you think it was Cressida? It couldn't be her, because she's ill.

original: I spy.
You spy! what do you spy? Come, give me an instrument. Now, sweet queen.
Why, this is kindly done.
translation: Oh, suddenly you are very keen to play.

original: My niece is horribly in love with a thing you have, sweet queen.
She shall have it, my lord, if it be not my lord Paris.
translation: Whatever she wants I am sure she'll have it, so long as it isn't Paris.

original: He! no, she'll none of him; they two are twain.
translation: Ah she doesn't want anything to do with him, those two are so different.

original: Falling in, after falling out, may make them three.
Come, come, I'll hear no more of this; I'll sing you a song now.
translation: Oh be civil, I'll hear no more of this. I'll sing a song for you now.

original: Ay, ay, prithee now. By my troth, sweet lord, thou hast a fine forehead.
translation: Yes, yes, play now. Honestly, sweet lord, you do look so handsome and smart.

original: Ay, you may, you may.
Let thy song be love: this love will undo us all. O Cupid, Cupid, Cupid!
translation: Sing a love song. Love will be the ruin of us all. Oh, Cupid, Cupid, Cupid.

original: Love! ay, that it shall, i' faith.
Ay, good now, love, love, nothing but love.
translation: Ah wonderful, sing about nothing but love, love, love.

original: In good troth, it begins so.
translation: Truly I will, and now I begin.

original: Love, love, nothing but love, still more!   For, O, love's bow   Shoots buck and doe:
translation: Love, love, nothing but love, even now! Because, oh, love's bow Shoots  buck and doe .

original: The shaft confounds,   Not that it wounds,   But tickles still the sore.
translation: The  arrow  confuses, But doesn't hurt, It tickles the wound.

original: These lovers cry Oh! oh! they die!   Yet that which seems the wound to kill,   Doth turn oh! oh! to ha! ha! he!   So dying love lives still:
translation: The lovers cry "Oh! Oh!  I am dying !" But the arrow that seems to pierce  the wound , Turns moaning into laughter, Letting the dying lovers live on:

original: Oh! oh! a while, but ha! ha! ha!   Oh! oh! groans out for ha! ha! ha!   Heigh-ho!
translation: At first they moan, then they laugh, And those that moan long to laugh. So it is!

original: In love, i' faith, to the very tip of the nose.
translation: This is love alright, summed up perfectly.

original: He eats nothing but doves, love, and that breeds hot   blood.
translation: Love eats nothing but doves, and that causes a hotness in the blood.

original: Hot blood begets hot thoughts, and hot   thoughts beget hot deeds, and hot deeds is love.
translation: Hot blood leads to passionate thoughts. Passionate thoughts cause lustful actions. And lustful actions are love.

original: Is this the generation of love? hot blood, hot   thoughts, and hot deeds?
translation: Is this really where love comes from? Hot blood, heated thoughts, and lustful actions?

original: Why, they are vipers:   is love a generation of vipers? Sweet lord, who's   a-field to-day?
translation: These things sound like a can of worms. Is love a can of worms? Sweet lord, who is out on the battlefield today?

original: Hector, Deiphobus, Helenus, Antenor, and all the   gallantry of Troy:
translation: Hector, Deiphobus, Helenus, Antenor, and all the knights of Troy.

original: I would fain have armed to-day,   but my Nell would not have it so. How chance my   brother Troilus went not?
translation: I was eager to go out today, but my sweetheart wouldn't let me. How come my brother Troilus didn't go out?

original: He hangs the lip at something: you know all, Lord  Pandarus.
translation: He's keeping tight-lipped, I'm sure you know why, Lord Pandarus.

original: Not I, honey-sweet queen. I long to hear how they sped to-day. You'll remember your brother's excuse?
translation: I don't, sweet queen. I wonder how the battle has gone today. Remember to excuse Troilus from dinner?

original: To a hair.
translation: I will excuse his whole body.

original: Farewell, sweet queen.
translation: Goodbye, sweet queen.

original: Commend me to your niece.
translation: Say hello to your niece for me.

original: I will, sweet queen.
translation: I will, sweet queen.

original: They're come from field: let us to Priam's hall,   To greet the warriors.
translation: They are leaving the battlefield. Let's go to Priam's hall to greet the soldiers.

original: Sweet Helen, I must woo you   To help unarm our Hector: his stubborn buckles,   With these your white enchanting fingers touch'd,   Shall more obey than to the edge of steel   Or force of Greekish sinews;
translation: Sweet Helen, would you mind helping Hector out of his armor, your delicate white hands will open the buckles on his armor more easily than any weapon or Greek would.

original: you shall do more   Than all the island kings,—disarm great Hector.
translation: Go do something no Greek king has done, disarm great Hector.

original: 'Twill make us proud to be his servant, Paris;
translation: I'd be glad to help him, Paris.

original: Yea, what he shall receive of us in duty   Gives us more palm in beauty than we have,
translation: Doing him this service will enhance my beauty.

original: Yea, overshines ourself.
translation: Yes the act of service will outshine my beautiful self.

original: Sweet, above thought I love thee.
translation: Sweetheart, I love you more than I can say.

original: How now! where's thy master? at my cousin Cressida's?
translation: Hey! Where's your master? Is he at my cousin Cressida's house?

original: No, sir; he stays for you to conduct him thither.
translation: No sir, he is waiting for you to take him there.

original: O, here he comes.
translation: Oh, here he comes.

original: How now, how now!
translation: Hi, how's it going?

original: Sirrah, walk off.
translation: Servant, you may leave.

original: Have you seen my cousin?
translation: Have you seen my cousin?

original: No, Pandarus: I stalk about her door,   Like a strange soul upon the Stygian banks   Staying for waftage.
translation: No, Pandarus. I wait outside her door like a lost soul waiting to be taken across the river Styx.

original: O, be thou my Charon,   And give me swift transportance to those fields   Where I may wallow in the lily-beds   Proposed for the deserver!
translation: Oh, be my  Charon , and take me to the paradise where deserving people lie on beds of lilies.

original: O gentle Pandarus,   From Cupid's shoulder pluck his painted wings   And fly with me to Cressid!
translation: Oh gentle Pandarus, carry me like Cupid to Cressida!

original: Walk here i' the orchard, I'll bring her straight.
translation: Wait here in this orchard, I'll bring her over soon.

original: I am giddy; expectation whirls me round.   The imaginary relish is so sweet   That it enchants my sense:
translation: I am giddy, and dizzy with excitement. Thoughts of her enchant my senses.

original: what will it be,   When that the watery palate tastes indeed   Love's thrice repured nectar? death, I fear me,   Swooning destruction, or some joy too fine,   Too subtle-potent, tuned too sharp in sweetness,   For the capacity of my ruder powers:
translation: What is it going to be like to taste love? I fear it would kill me or knock me out, or that some great joy, whose strength and sweetness I couldn't handle, would overpower me.

original: I fear it much; and I do fear besides,   That I shall lose distinction in my joys;   As doth a battle, when they charge on heaps   The enemy flying.
translation: I worry that all the things that make me happy will become totally indistinguishable, like a heap of bodies in a battle.

original: She's making her ready, she'll come straight: you   must be witty now.
translation: She's getting ready, she will soon come here, so pull yourself together.

original: She does so blush, and fetches   her wind so short, as if she were frayed with a   sprite: I'll fetch her.
translation: She's flustered and blushing and doesn't know how to feel, I'll bring her out.

original: It is the prettiest   villain: she fetches her breath as short as a   new-ta'en sparrow.
translation: She's a pretty sight, she is short of breath, like a bird that has just been caught.

original: Even such a passion doth embrace my bosom:
translation: I feel the same.

original: My heart beats thicker than a feverous pulse;
translation: My heart is beating like a drum,

original: And all my powers do their bestowing lose,   Like vassalage at unawares encountering   The eye of majesty.
translation: and I can barely contain myself, I feel so unprepared.

original: Come, come, what need you blush? shame's a baby.
translation: Hey now, why are you blushing? Shame is for children.

original: Here she is now: swear the oaths now to her that   you have sworn to me.
translation: Here she is, tell her all those feelings you told me.

original: What, are you gone again?   you must be watched ere you be made tame, must you?   Come your ways, come your ways; an you draw backward,   we'll put you i' the fills.
translation: What's this, are you going away? Do I have to guard over you while you're  tamed ? Come along, come along, if you try and run off, I'll have to hold you still.

original: Why do you not speak to   her? Come, draw this curtain, and let's see your   picture.
translation: Why aren't you saying anything? Come, let's take off this veil and see your face.

original: Alas the day, how loath you are to offend   daylight! an 'twere dark, you'ld close sooner.   So, so; rub on, and kiss the mistress.
translation: Oh my, you shouldn't hide your face from the sun,  I'm sure you'd be more open in the dark . Go on, go on,  start the game, kiss her .

original: How now!   a kiss in fee-farm! build there, carpenter; the air   is sweet. Nay, you shall fight your hearts out ere   I part you. The falcon as the tercel, for all the   ducks i' the river: go to, go to.
translation: Woah there, a kiss without an end. This is going well and love is in the air. You'll soon be a couple.  She is as keen as he is , go on, go on.

original: You have bereft me of all words, lady.
translation: You've left me speechless, lady.

original: Words pay no debts, give her deeds: but she'll   bereave you o' the deeds too, if she call your   activity in question.
translation: Actions speak louder than words, and she'll have your actions too, given half a chance.

original: What, billing again? Here's   'In witness whereof the parties interchangeably'—   Come in, come in: I'll go get a fire.
translation: Hah,  kissing  again? The debate seems to be going well with both sides in agreement... come on in, I'll get a fire going.

original: Will you walk in, my lord?
translation: Will you go inside, my lord?

original: O Cressida, how often have I wished me thus!
translation: Oh Cressida, I have so often wished you would call me that!

original: Wished, my lord! The gods grant,—O my lord!
What should they grant? what makes this pretty abruption? What too curious dreg espies my sweet lady in the fountain of our love?
More dregs than water, if my fears have eyes.
translation: There's more dirt than water, if my fears are correct.

original: Fears make devils of cherubims; they never see truly.
translation: Fear makes good things seem bad, it hides the truth.

original: Blind fear, that seeing reason leads, finds safer footing than blind reason stumbling without fear: to fear the worst oft cures the worse.
translation: Blind fear, following reason, takes a safer path than blind reason stumbling ahead without fear. Expecting the worst often prevents it from happening.

original: O, let my lady apprehend no fear: in all Cupid's pageant there is presented no monster.
Nor nothing monstrous neither?
translation: Not only no monsters, but nothing monstrous at all?

original: Nothing, but our undertakings; when we vow to weep   seas, live in fire, eat rocks, tame tigers; thinking   it harder for our mistress to devise imposition   enough than for us to undergo any difficulty imposed.
translation: Nothing is monstrous except for our promises: when we claim that we could weep seas, live in fire, eat rocks or tame tigers, because we assume that it would be more difficult for our mistresses to ask something that we would not do.

original: This is the monstruosity in love, lady, that the will   is infinite and the execution confined, that the   desire is boundless and the act a slave to limit.
translation: This is the thing that is monstrous about love, my lady, that our will-power is greater than our abilities. Our desire is great but our abilities are limited.

original: They say all lovers swear more performance than they   are able and yet reserve an ability that they never   perform, vowing more than the perfection often and   discharging less than the tenth part of one.
translation: They say that all lovers promise more than they can do but don't do everything that they can, promising ten times what they can do and doing only a tenth of it.

original: They   that have the voice of lions and the act of hares,   are they not monsters?
translation: Isn't it monstrous that they can speak like lions but only act like hares?

original: Are there such? such are not we: praise us as we   are tasted, allow us as we prove; our head shall go   bare till merit crown it:
translation: Do such people exist? We are not like that. Speak of us as you find us, let us prove ourselves. We won't congratulate ourselves until we deserve it.

original: no perfection in reversion   shall have a praise in present: we will not name   desert before his birth, and, being born, his addition   shall be humble.
translation: Nor will we promise things that will happen in the future, but only look to the here and now. We won't claim a virtue before it is demonstrated, and when it has been we will admit it humbly.

original: Few words to fair faith: Troilus   shall be such to Cressid as what envy can say worst   shall be a mock for his truth, and what truth can   speak truest not truer than Troilus.
translation: A few words are enough to swear loyalty. Troilus will be so true to Cressida that Envy itself will not be able to mock him, except for being true. Troilus will be as true as Truth itself.

original: Will you walk in, my lord?
translation: Will you go inside, my lord?

original: What, blushing still? have you not done talking yet?
translation: You're still blushing? Have you not finished talking?

original: Well, uncle, what folly I commit, I dedicate to you.
translation: Uncle, if I talk too much I must have learnt that from you.

original: I thank you for that: if my lord get a boy of you, you'll give him me. Be true to my lord: if he flinch, chide me for it.
You know now your hostages; your uncle's word and my firm faith.
translation: Well now you have two hostages: your uncle's promise and my oath of loyalty.

original: Nay, I'll give my word for her too: our kindred,   though they be long ere they are wooed, they are   constant being won:
translation: No, I'll vouch for her to you as well. Members of my family, although they take a lot of time to be seduced, are faithful when they are won.

original: they are burs, I can tell you;   they'll stick where they are thrown.
translation: Like a dart they stick where they land, I swear.

original: Boldness comes to me now, and brings me heart. Prince Troilus, I have loved you night and day For many weary months.
translation: I feel bold and confident now. Prince Troilus, I have loved you desperately for many long months.

original: Why was my Cressid then so hard to win?
translation: Why were you so hard to win over then?

original: Hard to seem won: but I was won, my lord,   With the first glance that ever—pardon me—   If I confess much, you will play the tyrant.
translation: Hard to be won over only in appearance. I was won, my lord, by the first glance that I ever ... I'm sorry. If I say too much you'll be able to take advantage of me.

original: I love you now; but not, till now, so much   But I might master it: in faith, I lie;   My thoughts were like unbridled children, grown   Too headstrong for their mother.
translation: I love you now. But before now I loved you and was able to control it. Oh, that's not true, my thoughts about you were like naughty children that had become too confident to obey their mother.

original: See, we fools!   Why have I blabb'd? who shall be true to us,   When we are so unsecret to ourselves?   But, though I loved you well, I woo'd you not;   And yet, good faith, I wish'd myself a man,   Or that we women had men's privilege   Of speaking first.
translation: Oh we are such  idiots ! Why have I spoken so openly? Who would be honest to someone who is so bad at keeping their own secrets? Even though I loved you, I didn't pursue you. But I did wish that I were a man,  or that women had the male privilege of being able to approach the men that they liked .

original: Sweet, bid me hold my tongue,   For in this rapture I shall surely speak   The thing I shall repent.
translation: Sweetheart, tell me to be quiet, because in this elated state of mind I will say something I'll regret.

original: See, see, your silence,   Cunning in dumbness, from my weakness draws   My very soul of counsel! stop my mouth.
translation: Oh you aren't saying anything, it is a trick to make me talk so that in my weakness I give up all of my judgment. Kiss me to stop me talking!

original: And shall, albeit sweet music issues thence.
translation: As you wish.

original: Pretty, i' faith.
translation: How cute.

original: My lord, I do beseech you, pardon me;   'Twas not my purpose, thus to beg a kiss:   I am ashamed.
translation: My lord, I'm so sorry, I didn't mean to seem like I was begging for a kiss. Oh I am ashamed of myself.

original: O heavens! what have I done?   For this time will I take my leave, my lord.
translation: Oh heavens! What have I done? I think I should leave for now, my lord.

original: Your leave, sweet Cressid!
translation: You have to leave, sweet Cressida?

original: Leave! an you take leave till to-morrow morning,—
translation: Leave? If you go anywhere before tomorrow morning...

original: Pray you, content you.
translation: Please, don't argue.

original: What offends you, lady?
translation: What is upsetting you, lady?

original: Sir, mine own company.
translation: My own behavior, sir.

original: You cannot shun yourself.
translation: You can't leave yourself.

original: Let me go and try:   I have a kind of self resides with you;   But an unkind self, that itself will leave,   To be another's fool.
translation: Let me try to. I have a kind of self that lives with you, and an unnatural self that will betray itself and become someone else's fool.

original: I would be gone:   Where is my wit? I know not what I speak.
translation: I want to leave. Where has my mind gone? I don't know what I'm saying.

original: Well know they what they speak that speak so wisely.
translation: No one speaks as well as you without knowing what they are saying.

original: Perchance, my lord, I show more craft than love;   And fell so roundly to a large confession,   To angle for your thoughts:
translation: Maybe I am just pretending to be in love, my lord. And faked my confession of love to lower your guard.

original: but you are wise,   Or else you love not, for to be wise and love   Exceeds man's might; that dwells with gods above.
translation: But I couldn't fool you, or you can't truly love me, because to be wise and in love at the same time is more than a man is capable of. Only the gods can do that.

original: O that I thought it could be in a woman—   As, if it can, I will presume in you—   To feed for aye her lamp and flames of love;   To keep her constancy in plight and youth,   Outliving beauty's outward, with a mind   That doth renew swifter than blood decays!
translation: If I believed that a woman could keep her love burning forever, and to remain faithful, and to maintain a clear mind after the end of her beauty, then I would believe that you were capable of it.

original: Or that persuasion could but thus convince me,   That my integrity and truth to you   Might be affronted with the match and weight   Of such a winnow'd purity in love;   How were I then uplifted!
translation: Or if I could be convinced that my own integrity and truth could be matched with another equal to it, I would be overjoyed!

original: but, alas!   I am as true as truth's simplicity   And simpler than the infancy of truth.
translation: But alas, I am as true as truth, and I am more straightforward than truth in its own infancy.

original: In that I'll war with you.
translation: I'd argue against that.

original: O virtuous fight,   When right with right wars who shall be most right!   True swains in love shall in the world to come   Approve their truths by Troilus:
translation: Well it would be a virtuous argument, when one truthful person argues with another about who is most true. In the future when young men want to prove their honesty they will call themselves Troilus.

original: when their rhymes,   Full of protest, of oath and big compare,   Want similes, truth tired with iteration,   As true as steel, as plantage to the moon,   As sun to day, as turtle to her mate,   As iron to adamant, as earth to the centre,   Yet, after all comparisons of truth,   As truth's authentic author to be cited,   'As true as Troilus' shall crown up the verse,   And sanctify the numbers.
translation: When they write poems about love, full of claims, promises and grand comparisons, and run out of imagery after using every trick in the book they will say at last that they are "as true as Troilus," a phrase that will prove their love.

original: Prophet may you be!   If I be false, or swerve a hair from truth,   When time is old and hath forgot itself,   When waterdrops have worn the stones of Troy,   And blind oblivion swallow'd cities up,   And mighty states characterless are grated   To dusty nothing, yet let memory,   From false to false, among false maids in love,   Upbraid my falsehood!
translation: I hope that you will be shown to be a prophet!  If I am unfaithful, or in any way stray from loyalty, I hope that future generations, when the rain has worn away the stones of Troy, and entire cities have been forgotten, and whole states disappear into nothing, still use my name for those women who are unfaithful in love!

original: when they've said 'as false   As air, as water, wind, or sandy earth,   As fox to lamb, as wolf to heifer's calf,   Pard to the hind, or stepdame to her son,'   'Yea,' let them say, to stick the heart of falsehood,   'As false as Cressid.'
translation: When they've said "as false as air, as water, the wind, or the sandy earth, as false a fox is to a lamb, or as a wolf is to a cow, or hunter to a deer, or step mother to her son," at that point let them get right to the heart of falseness and say they are "as false as Cressida."

original: Go to, a bargain made: seal it, seal it; I'll be the   witness.
translation: Go for it, that sounds like a deal. Seal the deal, and I will be your witness.

original: Here I hold your hand, here my cousin's.   If ever you prove false one to another, since I have   taken such pains to bring you together, let all   pitiful goers-between be called to the world's end   after my name; call them all Pandars;
translation: Now I am holding your hand, and yours. If you are ever unfaithful to each other, let all go-betweens be forever called by my name. Call them Pandars.

original: let all   constant men be Troiluses, all false women Cressids,   and all brokers-between Pandars! say, amen.
translation: Let all faithful men be called Troilus, all unfaithful women be called Cressida, and all match-makers be called Pander! Say, amen!

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: Amen.
translation: Amen.

original: Amen. Whereupon I will show you a chamber with a   bed; which bed, because it shall not speak of your   pretty encounters, press it to death:
translation: Amen. Now we have agreed that I will show you to a room with a bed. Don't worry about the bed, which it can't tell anyone what it sees, smother it until it dies.

original: away!   And Cupid grant all tongue-tied maidens here   Bed, chamber, Pandar to provide this gear!
translation: Go! May Cupid give all confused young women the gifts of a bed, a room, and a  pander  to help them along!

original: Now, princes, for the service I have done you,   The advantage of the time prompts me aloud   To call for recompense.
translation: Now, princes, the time has come for me to ask you for a reward for the service I have done for you.

original: Appear it to your mind   That, through the sight I bear in things to love,   I have abandon'd Troy, left my possession,   Incurr'd a traitor's name;
translation: Remember that, because I can see into the  future , I have left Troy, leaving behind all my possessions and deserving a traitor.

original: exposed myself,   From certain and possess'd conveniences,   To doubtful fortunes; sequestering from me all   That time, acquaintance, custom and condition   Made tame and most familiar to my nature,
translation: I have risked my comfortable and stable life. I have given up all the time, friends, and good-standing that I had.

original: And here, to do you service, am become   As new into the world, strange, unacquainted:
translation: Because I wanted to help you I have come here, as if I was new to the world.

original: I do beseech you, as in way of taste,   To give me now a little benefit,   Out of those many register'd in promise,   Which, you say, live to come in my behalf.
translation: I ask you to show me now a small part of the reward  that you promised me.

original: What wouldst thou of us, Trojan? make demand.
translation: What would you like, Trojan? Ask for it.

original: You have a Trojan prisoner, call'd Antenor,   Yesterday took: Troy holds him very dear.
translation: You have a Trojan prisoner called Antenor, who you captured yesterday. Troy values him very highly.

original: Oft have you—often have you thanks therefore—   Desired my Cressid in right great exchange,   Whom Troy hath still denied:
translation: You have often asked Troy to release my  Cressida  in hostage exchanges, which I thank you for, but you have had no luck.

original: but this Antenor,   I know, is such a wrest in their affairs   That their negotiations all must slack,   Wanting his manage;
translation: Now I know that Antenor, who is so important to their leadership that their discussions must be slack without his management.

original: and they will almost   Give us a prince of blood, a son of Priam,   In change of him:
translation: I reckon they would almost give us one of the royal princes, one of King Priam's sons, in return for Antenor.

original: let him be sent, great princes,   And he shall buy my daughter; and her presence   Shall quite strike off all service I have done,   In most accepted pain.
translation: Let him go back, great princes, in return for my daughter. Her presence would be payment enough for all the service I have done for you, despite the hardships it has brought upon me.

original: Let Diomedes bear him,   And bring us Cressid hither:
translation: Let Diomedes hand over Antenor, and bring Cressida here.

original: Calchas shall have   What he requests of us.
translation: Calchas will get what he wants.

original: Good Diomed,   Furnish you fairly for this interchange:   Withal bring word if Hector will to-morrow   Be answer'd in his challenge: Ajax is ready.
translation: Good Diomedes, dress well for this exchange, and tell them that if Hector is still willing to go through with his challenge that Ajax is ready.

original: This shall I undertake; and 'tis a burden Which I am proud to bear.
translation: I'll do this, I am honored that I can be of service.

original: Achilles stands i' the entrance of his tent:   Please it our general to pass strangely by him,   As if he were forgot;
translation: Achilles is standing in the entrance of his tent. If you please general, you should walk past him and treat him like a stranger, as if you had completely forgotten him.

original: and, princes all,   Lay negligent and loose regard upon him:   I will come last.
translation: And, fellow princes, I suggest you also pay no attention to him. I will walk behind everyone else.

original: 'Tis like he'll question me   Why such unplausive eyes are bent on him:   If so, I have derision medicinable,   To use between your strangeness and his pride,   Which his own will shall have desire to drink:
translation: It is likely he will ask me why no one recognizes him. And if he does this, I will provide a bitter-sweet medicine, and advise him on how to fix his reputation, a medicine he'll willingly take.

original: It may be good: pride hath no other glass   To show itself but pride, for supple knees   Feed arrogance and are the proud man's fees.
translation: It will do him good. Only pride can be a lesson for pride, and our previous attempts to bow to Achilles only made him more proud.

original: We'll execute your purpose, and put on   A form of strangeness as we pass along:
translation: We'll do as you say, and deliberately pretend not to notice him as we walk by.

original: So do each lord, and either greet him not,   Or else disdainfully, which shall shake him more   Than if not look'd on. I will lead the way.
translation: Each lord should do this, and don't greet him unless you do so disdainfully, which will upset him even more than if he were ignored. I will go first.

original: What, comes the general to speak with me? You know my mind, I'll fight no more 'gainst Troy.
translation: What, does the general come to speak with me? You know my decision, I won't fight against Troy anymore.

original: What says Achilles? would he aught with us?
translation: What is Achilles saying? Does he want to talk with me?

original: Would you, my lord, aught with the general?
translation: Do you want to say something to the general, my lord?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: Nothing, my lord.
translation: He has nothing to say, my lord.

original: The better.
translation: Excellent.

original: Good day, good day.
translation: Hello, good day.

original: How do you? how do you?
translation: How are you? How are you?

original: What, does the cuckold scorn me?
How now, Patroclus!
translation: Hello, Patroclus!

original: Good morrow, Ajax.
translation: Good morning, Ajax.

original: Ha?
translation: Huh?

original: Good morrow.
translation: Good morning.

original: Ay, and good next day too.
translation: Yeah, have a good week.

original: What mean these fellows? Know they not Achilles?
translation: What is wrong with these people? Don't they know me?

original: They pass by strangely: they were used to bend To send their smiles before them to Achilles; To come as humbly as they used to creep To holy altars.
translation: They pass by like they don't know you. They used to bow before you and smile when they came to Achilles, as humble as when they go to pray.

original: What, am I poor of late?
translation: What, have I lost my reputation?

original: 'Tis certain, greatness, once fall'n out with fortune,   Must fall out with men too: what the declined is   He shall as soon read in the eyes of others   As feel in his own fall;
translation: When great men lose their good fortune they also lose all the respect of their fellow man. The newly unfortunate man reads his fall in the eyes of other people.

original: for men, like butterflies,   Show not their mealy wings but to the summer,   And not a man, for being simply man,   Hath any honour, but honour for those honours   That are without him, as place, riches, favour,   Prizes of accident as oft as merit:
translation: In that respect people are like butterflies who only show their wings during the summer: men show respect only to those who appear honorable on their outside, even if their successes were by accident rather than merit.

original: Which when they fall, as being slippery standers,   The love that lean'd on them as slippery too,   Do one pluck down another and together   Die in the fall.
translation: And when a great man falls the love that other people have shown to him falls too, the one bringing down the other so they both die.

original: But 'tis not so with me:   Fortune and I are friends: I do enjoy   At ample point all that I did possess,   Save these men's looks; who do, methinks, find out   Something not worth in me such rich beholding   As they have often given.
translation: But it won't be like this with me, good fortune is my friend. I still have all the strengths I used to have, except these men's attentions. I think these men have seen something in me that they don't respect as much as they used to.

original: Here is Ulysses;   I'll interrupt his reading.   How now Ulysses!
translation: Ulysses is coming, I'll interrupt his reading.  [To ULYSSES]  How's it going, Ulysses!

original: Now, great Thetis' son!
translation: Hello, great son of Thetis.

original: What are you reading?
translation: What are you reading?

original: A strange fellow here   Writes me:
translation: A strange man tells me:

original: 'That man, how dearly ever parted,   How much in having, or without or in,   Cannot make boast to have that which he hath,   Nor feels not what he owes, but by reflection;   As when his virtues shining upon others   Heat them and they retort that heat again   To the first giver.'
translation: "That no man, no matter how naturally talented, rich, or in favor with the king, can boast of what he has nor understand what his duty is except by seeing how other people treat him. Virtues warm the people around them, and that heat is then reflected back."

original: This is not strange, Ulysses.   The beauty that is borne here in the face   The bearer knows not, but commends itself   To others' eyes;
translation: That is not strange, Ulysses. Someone with a beautiful face wouldn't know it unless other people tell them.

original: nor doth the eye itself,   That most pure spirit of sense, behold itself,   Not going from itself; but eye to eye opposed   Salutes each other with each other's form;
translation: And an eye, our greatest natural tool, cannot see itself except by looking at something reflective, or gazing at another person's eye.

original: For speculation turns not to itself,   Till it hath travell'd and is mirror'd there   Where it may see itself. This is not strange at all.
translation: Sight only happens when we look away, and the image comes back to us . There is nothing unusual about what the man says.

original: I do not strain at the position,—   It is familiar,—but at the author's drift;
translation: I'm not calling his argument strange, it is a common idea, but I wonder what he means by it.

original: Who, in his circumstance, expressly proves   That no man is the lord of any thing,   Though in and of him there be much consisting,   Till he communicate his parts to others:
translation: He argues cleverly that no one really possesses any quality, no matter how there is in him, until they have demonstrate it to others.

original: Nor doth he of himself know them for aught   Till he behold them form'd in the applause   Where they're extended;
translation: He also shows that we cannot know anything of ourselves except through other people's applause.

original: who, like an arch,   reverberates   The voice again, or, like a gate of steel   Fronting the sun, receives and renders back   His figure and his heat.
translation: We only can only judge ourselves through the reflection of our actions, like an echo in a tunnel, or a steel gate that receives the sun and shines it back.

original: I was much wrapt in this;   And apprehended here immediately   The unknown Ajax.   Heavens, what a man is there! a very horse,   That has he knows not what.
translation: I have been very interested in this, and was immediately reminded of Ajax. By heaven, what kind of man is he? He's like a horse that doesn't know how he is being exploited.

original: Nature, what things there  are   Most abject in regard and dear in use!   What things again most dear in the esteem   And poor in worth!
translation: By nature , there are some creatures that are hated but useful, and others that we value highly but have no use!

original: Now shall we see to-morrow—   An act that very chance doth throw upon him—   Ajax renown'd.
translation: Tomorrow we'll all see an opportunity that pure luck has given him. Can you imagine Ajax being a hero?

original: O heavens, what some men do,   While some men leave to do!   How some men creep in skittish fortune's hall,   Whiles others play the idiots in her eyes!
translation: Oh heavens, it is amazing what opportunities some men will take and others will leave.  Some men skulk around and avoid greatness even though luck is on their side, whilst others act like fools to try to become famous.

original: How one man eats into another's pride,   While pride is fasting in his wantonness!   To see these Grecian lords!—
translation: The second man, although he is less worthy, steals the fame that should be the first man's. You should see the Greek lords!

original: why, even already   They clap the lubber Ajax on the shoulder,   As if his foot were on brave Hector's breast   And great Troy shrieking.
translation: They are already patting the idiot on his back and cheering him as if he had already triumphed over Hector and made great Troy shriek.

original: I do believe it; for they pass'd by me As misers do by beggars, neither gave to me Good word nor look: what, are my deeds forgot?
translation: I know, they all walked past me earlier and looked at me like I was a beggar, saying nothing and not even looking at me. Are my deeds already forgotten?

original: Time hath, my lord, a wallet at his back,   Wherein he puts alms for oblivion,   A great-sized monster of ingratitudes:   Those scraps are good deeds past; which are devour'd   As fast as they are made, forgot as soon   As done:
translation: As time passes all our actions are forgotten. Go od deeds only last a moment and then become worthless.

original: perseverance, dear my lord,   Keeps honour bright: to have done is to hang   Quite out of fashion, like a rusty mail   In monumental mockery.
translation: Only perseverance, my lord, keeps honor fresh and bright. To have  done  something is to be always out of fashion, like a rusty suit of armor.

original: Take the instant way;   For honour travels in a strait so narrow,   Where one but goes abreast: keep then the path;   For emulation hath a thousand sons   That one by one pursue:
translation: Take the most direct route, because honor always takes a path that is straight and narrow: keep on the path as there are always a thousand other men running after, one by one.

original: if you give way,   Or hedge aside from the direct forthright,   Like to an enter'd tide, they all rush by   And leave you hindmost;
translation: Give them any room, or step aside, they'll rush past you in an instant and leave you behind.

original: Or like a gallant horse fall'n in first rank,   Lie there for pavement to the abject rear,   O'er-run and trampled on:
translation: It is like a horse who falls at the front of the battle, and is run past and trampled on by those who come from behind.

original: then what they do in present,   Though less than yours in past, must o'ertop yours;   For time is like a fashionable host   That slightly shakes his parting guest by the hand,   And with his arms outstretch'd, as he would fly,   Grasps in the comer: welcome ever smiles,   And farewell goes out sighing.
translation: A success made now is worth much more than a past success, even if it is a lesser success, yes. Time is like a fashionable host who quickly says goodbye to his parting guest before embracing the next guest coming in: you are welcome when you show up but not when you leave.

original: O, let not   virtue seek   Remuneration for the thing it was;   For beauty, wit,   High birth, vigour of bone, desert in service,   Love, friendship, charity, are subjects all   To envious and calumniating time.   One touch of nature makes the whole world kin,   That all with one consent praise new-born gawds,   Though they are made and moulded of things past,   And give to dust that is a little gilt   More laud than gilt o'er-dusted.
translation: Virtues like honor, intellect, beauty, and so on, shouldn't ask to be respected for what they were but for what they are.  People only value new things, even when their old possessions are better made.

original: The present eye praises the present object.   Then marvel not, thou great and complete man,   That all the Greeks begin to worship Ajax;   Since things in motion sooner catch the eye   Than what not stirs.
translation: Someone in the present only praises things that are in the present: so you shouldn't be surprised that all the Greek lords are starting to cheer for Ajax, as he is still active.

original: The cry went once on thee,   And still it might, and yet it may again,   If thou wouldst not entomb thyself alive   And case thy reputation in thy tent;
translation: They once cheered for you, and still could cheer for you again, if you stopped burying yourself in your tent and thinking about how great you were.

original: Whose glorious deeds, but in these fields of late,   Made emulous missions 'mongst the gods themselves   And drave great Mars to faction.
translation: Especially since you were so great that the gods themselves had to enter the field of battle, even Mars !

original: Of this my privacy I have strong reasons.
translation: I have good reasons for not coming out.

original: But 'gainst your privacy   The reasons are more potent and heroical:
translation: Well, there are better and more heroic reasons for you to come out.

original: 'Tis known, Achilles, that you are in love   With one of Priam's daughters.
translation: It is well known that you are in love with one of Priam's daughters, Achilles.

original: Ha! known!
translation: Hah, what do you mean?

original: Is that a wonder?   The providence that's in a watchful state   Knows almost every grain of Plutus' gold,   Finds bottom in the uncomprehensive deeps,   Keeps place with thought and almost, like the gods,   Does thoughts unveil in their dumb cradles.
translation: Are you surprised? Nothing escapes the notice of a good government, even the affairs of the gods can not be kept private from their spies, and thoughts can be understood before they are spoken.

original: There is a mystery—with whom relation   Durst never meddle—in the soul of state;   Which hath an operation more divine   Than breath or pen can give expressure to:
translation: There is a kind of government knowledge that is never spoken of, and that is more godly than I could ever express in words.

original: All the commerce that you have had with Troy   As perfectly is ours as yours, my lord;   And better would it fit Achilles much   To throw down Hector than Polyxena:
translation: Every message you have sent over to Troy is as well known to us as it is to you, my lord, and I think it would be far more fitting that you  wrestle Hector than Polyxena .

original: But it must grieve young Pyrrhus now at home,   When fame shall in our islands sound her trump,   And all the Greekish girls shall tripping sing,   'Great Hector's sister did Achilles win,   But our great Ajax bravely beat down him.'
translation: It will be embarrassing for your son, Pyrrhus, back in Greece, when the news comes in and all the Greek girls start singing: "Achilles won great Hector's sister, But our great Ajax bravely slayed Hector."

original: Farewell, my lord: I as your lover speak;   The fool slides o'er the ice that you should break.
translation: Goodbye, my lord, speaking as your good friend I have to say, the fool is taking what should be yours.

original: To this effect, Achilles, have I moved you:   A woman impudent and mannish grown   Is not more loathed than an effeminate man   In time of action.
translation: I have told you this before, Achilles. An angry woman who acts like a man is better than a man who acts like a woman when it's time to fight.

original: I stand condemn'd for this;   They think my little stomach to the war   And your great love to me restrains you thus:
translation: I am getting the blame for this, as everyone thinks that because I don't want to fight and you don't want to leave me you won't fight as well

original: Sweet, rouse yourself; and the weak wanton Cupid   Shall from your neck unloose his amorous fold,   And, like a dew-drop from the lion's mane,   Be shook to air.
translation: . Sweetheart, get up, and matters of love will fall from you like sweat from a lion's mane.

original: Shall Ajax fight with Hector?
translation: Will Ajax fight Hector?

original: Ay, and perhaps receive much honour by him.
translation: Yes, and maybe become famous for defeating him.

original: I see my reputation is at stake My fame is shrewdly gored.
translation: My reputation is at stake, my good name has been attacked.

original: O, then, beware;   Those wounds heal ill that men do give themselves:
translation: Then be cautious, the damage we do to ourselves is the hardest to heal.

original: Omission to do what is necessary   Seals a commission to a blank of danger;
translation: Refusing to do what you have to guarantees a bad result.

original: And danger, like an ague, subtly taints   Even then when we sit idly in the sun.
translation: And danger is always just around the corner, even when we are idle.

original: Go call Thersites hither, sweet Patroclus:
translation: Go and fetch Thersites, sweet Patroclus.

original: I'll send the fool to Ajax and desire him   To invite the Trojan lords after the combat   To see us here unarm'd:
translation: I'll send the fool to Ajax and tell him to invite the Trojan lords here after the fight to meet us here without our weapons.

original: I have a woman's longing,   An appetite that I am sick withal,   To see great Hector in his weeds of peace,   To talk with him and to behold his visage,   Even to my full of view.
translation: I am sick with love, and desperate to talk with Hector away from the battlefield.

original: A labour saved!
translation: You won't have to bother fetching Thersites.

original: A wonder!
translation: There is an incredible sight!

original: What?
translation: What?

original: Ajax goes up and down the field, asking for himself.
How so?
translation: Why?

original: He must fight singly to-morrow with Hector, and is so prophetically proud of an heroical cudgelling that he raves in saying nothing.
How can that be?
translation: How is that possible?

original: Why, he stalks up and down like a peacock,—a stride   and a stand: ruminates like an hostess that hath no   arithmetic but her brain to set down her reckoning:
translation: Oh he is walking around like a peacock, taking a step then standing still, and posing like a barmaid who can't count up the bill.

original: bites his lip with a politic regard, as who should   say 'There were wit in this head, an 'twould out;'   and so there is, but it lies as coldly in him as fire   in a flint, which will not show without knocking.
translation: He bites his lip and looks contemplative, like a man who has all the answers but wont say them, but the only way you'd get anything out of his head is by knocking his brains out!

original: The man's undone forever; for if Hector break not his   neck i' the combat, he'll break 't himself in   vain-glory.
translation: He can't win, because if Hector doesn't kill him, his vanity would.

original: He knows not me: I said 'Good morrow,   Ajax;' and he replies 'Thanks, Agamemnon.'
translation: He didn't even recognize me earlier: I said "Good morning Ajax," and he replied "Thanks, Agamemnon."

original: What think   you of this man that takes me for the general? He's   grown a very land-fish, language-less, a monster.
translation: What kind of man would think I am the general? He's like a walking goldfish or some kind of language-less monster.

original: A plague of opinion! a man may wear it on both   sides, like a leather jerkin.
translation: Reputation is ridiculous. Man can wear it one way or another, like a leather waistcoat.

original: Thou must be my ambassador to him, Thersites.
translation: I want you to tell him something from me, Thersites.

original: Who, I? why, he'll answer nobody; he professes not   answering: speaking is for beggars   ;   he wears his   tongue in's arms.
translation: Me? He won't speak to anyone, it's like a motto to him: speaking is for beggars.  He only talks through his fighting.

original: I will put on his presence: let   Patroclus make demands to me, you shall see the   pageant of Ajax.
translation: I will show you what he's like, tell Patroclus to give me your message, and you'll see how ridiculous Ajax looks.

original: To him, Patroclus; tell him I humbly desire the   valiant Ajax to invite the most valorous Hector   to come unarmed to my tent,
translation: Go on Patroclus, tell him I humbly desire that the valiant Ajax would invite the valorous Hector to come unarmed to my tent,

original: and to procure   safe-conduct for his person of the magnanimous   and most illustrious six-or-seven-times-honoured   captain-general of the Grecian army, Agamemnon,   et cetera. Do this.
translation: and to ask the very brave Agamemnon not to harm my guests, et cetera. Say that.

original: Jove bless great Ajax!
translation: Jupiter bless the great Ajax!

original: Hum!
translation: Hmm!

original: I come from the worthy Achilles,—
translation: I have come on behalf of the worthy Achilles...

original: Ha!
translation: Ha!

original: Who most humbly desires you to invite Hector to his  tent,—
translation: Who very humbly asks you to invite Hector to his tent...

original: Hum!
translation: Hmm!

original: And to procure safe-conduct from Agamemnon.
translation: And to get a guarantee of safety from Agamemnon.

original: Agamemnon!
translation: Agamemnon!

original: Ay, my lord.
translation: Yes, my lord.

original: Ha!
translation: Ha!

original: What say you to't?
translation: What is your reply?

original: God b' wi' you, with all my heart.
translation: God bless you with all my heart.

original: Your answer, sir.
translation: Your response, sir?

original: If to-morrow be a fair day, by eleven o'clock it will go one way or other: howsoever, he shall pay for me ere he has me.
translation: Tomorrow's battle, if it happens, will have been decided by eleven o'clock. And whatever happens I shall make sure he is hurt before either of us wins.

original: Your answer, sir.
translation: Your response, sir?

original: Fare you well, with all my heart.
translation: A warm goodbye.

original: Why, but he is not in this tune, is he?
translation: Surely he isn't really like this?

original: No, but he's out o' tune thus. What music will be in   him when Hector has knocked out his brains, I know   not;
translation: Oh,  but he is . I don't know what sense will be in him when Hector has dashed out his brains,

original: but, I am sure, none, unless the fiddler Apollo   get his sinews to make catlings on.
translation: but it would take  Apollo  to make him understand.

original: Come, thou shalt bear a letter to him straight.
translation: Come here, I want you to deliver a letter to him.

original: Let me bear another to his horse; for that's the more capable creature.
translation: I should take it to his horse, his horse is more sensible.

original: My mind is troubled, like a fountain stirr'd; And I myself see not the bottom of it.
translation: This is all very troubling, and I don't know how the future will play out.

original: Would the fountain of your mind were clear again, that I might water an ass at it! I had rather be a tick in a sheep than such a valiant ignorance.
translation: Stupid man! I'd rather be an insect than this arrogant fool.

original: See, ho! who is that there?
translation: Look there! Who is that?

original: It is the Lord AEneas.
translation: It's the lord Aeneas.

original: Is the prince there in person?
translation: Are you the Prince himself?

original: Had I so good occasion to lie long   As you, prince Paris, nothing but heavenly business   Should rob my bed-mate of my company.
translation: If I had as good a reason not to get out of bed as you, prince Paris, nothing but prayer would get me to leave my wife alone.

original: That's my mind too. Good morrow, Lord AEneas.
translation: I agree. Good morning, Lord Aeneas.

original: A valiant Greek, AEneas,—take his hand,—
translation: A brave Greek, Aeneas, greet him!

original: Witness the process of your speech, wherein   You told how Diomed, a whole week by days,   Did haunt you in the field.
translation: You told me he has been finding you out on the battle field all week and never leaving you alone, and here he is again!

original: Health to you, valiant sir,   During all question of the gentle truce;
translation: I hope you are well, valiant sir, for at least as long as we have this truce.

original: But when I meet you arm'd, as black defiance   As heart can think or courage execute.
translation: But when we begin fighting again, I'll make sure I see you dead.

original: The one and other Diomed embraces.
translation: Greetings to both of you.

original: Our bloods are now in calm; and, so long, health!
translation: We aren't enemies at the moment, so for now I hope you are well!

original: But when contention and occasion meet,   By Jove, I'll play the hunter for thy life   With all my force, pursuit and policy.
translation: But when we start fighting again, by Jupiter, I'll try to kill you with all my strength, skill, and intelligence.

original: And thou shalt hunt a lion, that will fly   With his face backward.
translation: It will be like you are hunting a lion, one that will run from you facing towards you.

original: In humane gentleness,   Welcome to Troy! now, by Anchises' life,   Welcome, indeed!
translation: But now I greet you as a human, welcome to Troy! Now, on my father's life, welcome!

original: By Venus' hand I swear,   No man alive can love in such a sort   The thing he means to kill more excellently.
translation: By Venus my mother's hand I promise, that no one has ever loved a person they intend to kill as much as I do now.

original: We sympathize: Jove, let AEneas live,   If to my sword his fate be not the glory,   A thousand complete courses of the sun!
translation: I feel the same. Jupiter, let Aeneas live a thousand years, unless I kill him myself.

original: But, in mine emulous honour, let him die,   With every joint a wound, and that to-morrow!
translation: But, let him die bloody and broken tomorrow, all for the sake of my honor.

original: We know each other well.
translation: We understand each other well.

original: We do; and long to know each other worse.
This is the most despiteful gentle greeting, The noblest hateful love, that e'er I heard of. What business, lord, so early?
translation: This is the most violent and polite greeting I have ever heard of, with the most noble and hateful love. Why are you up so early, lord?

original: I was sent for to the king; but why, I know not.
translation: I was told to come to the king, but I don't know why.

original: His purpose meets you: 'twas to bring this Greek   To Calchas' house, and there to render him,   For the enfreed Antenor, the fair Cressid:
translation: I can tell you why he sent for you. He wants you to bring this Greek to Calchas's house, and when you are there to give him the beautiful Cressida for the freedom of Antenor.

original: That I assure you: Troilus had rather Troy were borne to Greece Than Cressid borne from Troy.
translation: I am certain you are right, Troilus would rather we gave Troy to Greece than Cressida to the Greeks.

original: There is no help; The bitter disposition of the time Will have it so. On, lord; we'll follow you.
translation: It can't be helped, this bitter time demands that it must be so. Go, lord, we'll follow you.

original: Good morrow, all.
translation: Goodbye everyone.

original: And tell me, noble Diomed, faith, tell me true, Even in the soul of sound good-fellowship, Who, in your thoughts, merits fair Helen best, Myself or Menelaus?
translation: Tell me honestly, noble Diomedes, given this spirit of friendship, who most deserves to have the beautiful Helen, myself or Menelaus?

original: Both alike: He merits well to have her, that doth seek her, Not making any scruple of her soilure, With such a hell of pain and world of charge, And you as well to keep her, that defend her, Not palating the taste of her dishonour, With such a costly loss of wealth and friends: He, like a puling cuckold, would drink up The lees and dregs of a flat tamed piece; You, like a lecher, out of whorish loins Are pleased to breed out your inheritors: Both merits poised, each weighs nor less nor more; But he as he, the heavier for a whore.
You are too bitter to your countrywoman.
translation: You're too unkind towards your countrywoman.

original: She's bitter to her country: hear me, Paris: For every false drop in her bawdy veins A Grecian's life hath sunk; for every scruple Of her contaminated carrion weight, A Trojan hath been slain: since she could speak, She hath not given so many good words breath As for her Greeks and Trojans suffer'd death.
translation: Trust me, Paris, she's been too unkind to her country. A Greek has died for every worthless drop of blood in her unfaithful veins. And a Trojan has died for every gram of her festering flesh. She hasn't spoken as many pleasant things as Trojans and Greeks died for her.

original: Fair Diomed, you do as chapmen do, Dispraise the thing that you desire to buy: But we in silence hold this virtue well, We'll but commend what we intend to sell. Here lies our way.
