translation: Fair Diomedes, just like a trader you are insulting the thing you want to buy, so it will be cheaper. But I won't defend her, as I have no desire to sell her. Come this way please.

original: Dear, trouble not yourself: the morn is cold.
Then, sweet my lord, I'll call mine uncle down; He shall unbolt the gates.
translation: Then I'll have my uncle open the gates, my lord.

original: Trouble him not;   To bed, to bed:
translation: Don't trouble him, go to bed, go to bed.

original: sleep kill those pretty eyes,   And give as soft attachment to thy senses   As infants' empty of all thought!
translation: Let sleep close your beautiful eyes, and rest peacefully.

original: Good morrow, then.
translation: Goodbye, then.

original: I prithee now, to bed.
translation: I beg you, go to sleep.

original: Are you a-weary of me?
translation: Are you tired of me?

original: O Cressida! but that the busy day, Waked by the lark, hath roused the ribald crows, And dreaming night will hide our joys no longer, I would not from thee.
translation: Oh Cressida! If it was still night and day hadn't broken, I'd stay with you.

original: Night hath been too brief.
translation: Night has been too short.

original: Beshrew the witch!
translation: Curse  the witch !

original: with venomous wights she stays   As tediously as hell, but flies the grasps of love   With wings more momentary-swift than thought.
translation: If you have troubled sleep she seems to last forever, but if you are holding your lover she barely lasts long enough to realize.

original: You will catch cold, and curse me.
translation: You'll catch a cold and hate me, if you stay out at this time of day.

original: Prithee, tarry:
translation: I beg you, stay.

original: You men will never tarry.   O foolish Cressid!
translation: You men never stick around. Oh foolish Cressida!

original: I might have still held off,   And then you would have tarried. Hark!   there's one up.
translation: If I hadn't given in to you you might have stayed. Listen! Someone's nearby.

original: What, 's all the doors open here?
translation: What, why are all the doors open?

original: It is your uncle.
translation: It is your uncle.

original: A pestilence on him! now will he be mocking: I shall have such a life!
translation: Curse him. He's going to start mocking me again. I'll never hear the end of this!

original: How now, how now! how go maidenheads? Here, you maid! where's my cousin Cressid?
Go hang yourself, you naughty mocking uncle! You bring me to do, and then you flout me too.
translation: Go hang yourself, naughty mocking uncle! You go about making me do something, and then you laugh at me for it as well.

original: To do what? to do what? let her say what: what have I brought you to do?
Come, come, beshrew your heart! you'll ne'er be good, Nor suffer others.
translation: Oh behave, have some decency! You'll never live a good life, nor allow others to live good lives.

original: Ha! ha! Alas, poor wretch! ah, poor capocchia!   hast not slept to-night?
translation: Ha ha! Alas, poor wretch! Ah, poor  thing . Haven't you slept last night?

original: would he not, a naughty   man, let it sleep? a bugbear take him!
translation: Would the naughty boy not let the thing sleep?  Oh what a naughty man!

original: Did not I tell you? Would he were knock'd i' the head!
translation: What did I say he would be like? I wish someone would knock him out.

original: Who's that at door? good uncle, go and see. My lord, come you again into my chamber: You smile and mock me, as if I meant naughtily.
translation: Who's at the door? Good uncle, go and see.  My lord, come back into my bedroom. Why are you smiling? Oh, not like that!

original: Ha, ha!
translation: Haha.

original: Come, you are deceived, I think of no such thing.
translation: Come on, you're wrong, I'm not thinking about that.

original: How earnestly they knock! Pray you, come in: I would not for half Troy have you seen here.
translation: They are knocking so loudly! Please, come in. I don't want anyone to know you are here.

original: Who's there? what's the matter? will you beat down the door? How now! what's the matter?
translation: Who's there? What's the matter? You're going to break the door down! What's the matter?

original: Good morrow, lord, good morrow.
translation: Good morning, lord, good morning.

original: Who's there? my Lord AEneas! By my troth, I knew you not: what news with you so early?
translation: Who's there? My lord Aeneas! I honestly, didn't recognize you. What's wrong that means you come here so early in the day?

original: Is not Prince Troilus here?
translation: Is Prince Troilus here?

original: Here! what should he do here?
translation: Here? Why would he be here?

original: Come, he is here, my lord; do not deny him: It doth import him much to speak with me.
translation: Look, he's obviously here, don't deny it. It's important he speaks to me.

original: Is he here, say you? 'tis more than I know, I'll be sworn: for my own part, I came in late. What should he do here?
translation: You say he's here? Oh, well, I wouldn't know, honestly. I only came back recently. Why would he be here?

original: Who!—nay, then:
translation: You mean "who" should he be doing here!

original: come, come, you'll do him wrong   ere you're ware: you'll be so true to him, to be   false to him:
translation: No, come on then. You'll hurt him if you're not careful. You're covering for him, but betraying him.

original: do not you know of him, but yet go   fetch him hither; go.
translation: I don't care if you know he is here, go get him. Now.

original: How now! what's the matter?
translation: Hey, what's the matter?

original: My lord, I scarce have leisure to salute you,   My matter is so rash:
translation: My lord, I hardly have time to say hello, my business is so important.

original: there is at hand   Paris your brother, and Deiphobus,   The Grecian Diomed, and our Antenor   Deliver'd to us;
translation: Outside the house are your brother Paris, Deiphobus, the Greek Diomedes and the Trojan Antenor, who has been returned to us.

original: and for him forthwith,   Ere the first sacrifice, within this hour,   We must give up to Diomedes' hand   The Lady Cressida.
translation: And in return for Antenor, before we even go to prayer, right now, we must give up Lady Cressida to Diomedes.

original: Is it so concluded?
translation: This has been decided?

original: By Priam and the general state of Troy: They are at hand and ready to effect it.
translation: By Priam and the politicians of Troy, they are outside ready to make it happen.

original: How my achievements mock me! I will go meet them: and, my Lord AEneas, We met by chance; you did not find me here.
translation: My success has turned to despair! I will go and meet them, my lord Aeneas, I'll pretend to have just been passing by, don't say you saw me here.

original: Good, good, my lord; the secrets of nature Have not more gift in taciturnity.
translation: Yes, my lord. No one is more discrete than me.

original: Is't possible? no sooner got but lost? The devil   take Antenor! the young prince will go mad:
translation: Is it possible? No sooner got than it is lost? I'd give Antenor to the devil! The young prince will go mad,

original: a   plague upon Antenor! I would they had broke's neck!
translation: I hope a plague takes Antenor! I wish the Greeks had broken his neck!

original: How now! what's the matter? who was here?
translation: Hey, what's the matter? Who was here?

original: Ah, ah!
translation: Ah, ah!

original: Why sigh you so profoundly? where's my lord? gone! Tell me, sweet uncle, what's the matter?
translation: Why are you sighing so deeply? Where's my lord? He's gone! Tell me, sweet uncle, what's the matter?

original: Would I were as deep under the earth as I am above!
translation: I wish I were dead!

original: O the gods! what's the matter?
translation: Oh gods! What's the matter!

original: Prithee, get thee in: would thou hadst ne'er been born! I knew thou wouldst be his death. O, poor gentleman! A plague upon Antenor!
translation: I beg you, go inside, I wish you had never been born! I knew you'd be the thing that kills him. Oh, poor gentleman! A plague upon Antenor!

original: Good uncle, I beseech you, on my knees! beseech you, what's the matter?
translation: Good uncle, I beg you, on my knees, I beg you, what's happened?

original: Thou must be gone, wench, thou must be gone; thou   art changed for Antenor:
translation: You must go,  girl , you must be gone, you are going to be traded in return for Antenor.

original: thou must to thy father,   and be gone from Troilus: 'twill be his death;   'twill be his bane; he cannot bear it.
translation: You must go to your father and away from Troilus. It will be his death, his torture, the one thing he couldn't possibly bear.

original: O you immortal gods! I will not go.
translation: Oh gods! I will not go.

original: Thou must.
translation: You have to.

original: I will not, uncle: I have forgot my father;   I know no touch of consanguinity;   No kin no love, no blood, no soul so near me   As the sweet Troilus.
translation: I will not, uncle. I have broken relations with my father, and don't recognize him as my family. He is not my relative, I feel no love for him, I am not of his blood, and there is no soul worth so much to me as that of Troilus.

original: O you gods divine!   Make Cressid's name the very crown of falsehood,   If ever she leave Troilus!
translation: Oh divine gods! Make my name a common by-word for infidelity if I ever leave Troilus!

original: Time, force, and death,   Do to this body what extremes you can;   But the strong base and building of my love   Is as the very centre of the earth,   Drawing all things to it.
translation: Oh Time, Force, and Death: do whatever you can to me, my love for Troilus is stronger than the gravity that holds us on the earth.

original: I'll go in and weep,—
translation: I'll go into my room to cry...

original: Do, do.
translation: Do, do.

original: Tear my bright hair and scratch my praised cheeks, Crack my clear voice with sobs and break my heart With sounding Troilus. I will not go from Troy.
translation: I'll tear out my hair and scratch at my cheeks, scream until my throat hurts, and break my heart crying Troilus's name. I will not leave Troy.

original: It is great morning, and the hour prefix'd   Of her delivery to this valiant Greek   Comes fast upon.
translation: It is late in the morning, and nearly time we give her to this brave Greek.

original: Good my brother Troilus,   Tell you the lady what she is to do,   And haste her to the purpose.
translation: Good brother Troilus, go tell the lady what she has to do, and tell her to be swift.

original: Walk into her house;   I'll bring her to the Grecian presently:
translation: Go into her house, I'll bring her to the Greek immediately,

original: And to his hand when I deliver her,   Think it an altar, and thy brother Troilus
translation: and when I hand her over to him, I will think of it as a marriage ceremony.

original: A priest there offering to it his own heart.
translation: Like a priest, except I will give away my own heart.

original: I know what 'tis to love; And would, as I shall pity, I could help! Please you walk in, my lords.
translation: I know what it is to love, and wish I could help him. Please go in, my lords.

original: Be moderate, be moderate.
translation: Be reasonable, be reasonable.

original: Why tell you me of moderation?   The grief is fine, full, perfect, that I taste,   And violenteth in a sense as strong   As that which causeth it:
translation: Why are you telling me to be reasonable? This grief is totally appropriate and exactly as violent as the reason that causes it!

original: how can I moderate it?   If I could temporize with my affection,   Or brew it to a weak and colder palate,   The like allayment could I give my grief.
translation: How can I be more reasonable that this?  If I could make it less painful, or water down my love, it would also be an appropriate cure for my grief .

original: My love admits no qualifying dross;   No more my grief, in such a precious loss.
translation: My love can't be diluted, nor can my grief, when what I am losing is so precious to me.

original: Here, here, here he comes.
translation: He is coming.

original: Ah, sweet ducks!
translation: Oh, such a sweet couple.

original: O Troilus! Troilus!
translation: Oh Troilus! Troilus!

original: What a pair of spectacles is here!   Let me embrace too.
translation: These two are an extraordinary sight! Let me embrace you too.

original: 'O heart,' as the goodly saying is,   '—O heart, heavy heart,   Why sigh'st thou without breaking?   where he answers again,   'Because thou canst not ease thy smart   By friendship nor by speaking.'
translation: "Oh heart," as the great saying goes, "... oh heavy, heavy heart,  Why do you sigh without  breaking ?" and the heart replies: "Because you cannot ease your pain, with company or words."

original: There was never a truer rhyme.
translation: There has never been a better saying.

original: Let us cast away   nothing, for we may live to have need of such a   verse: we see it, we see it. How now, lambs?
translation: Let us never forget anything, for one day we might need a saying like this. How are you, lambs?

original: Cressid, I love thee in so strain'd a purity,   That the bless'd gods,
translation: Cressida, I love you so purely that the divine gods are taking you away from me,

original: as angry with my fancy,   More bright in zeal than the devotion which   Cold lips blow to their deities, take thee from me.
translation: as they are angry that my devotion to you is stronger and more passionate than my devotion to them.

original: Have the gods envy?
translation: Are the gods envious of me?

original: Ay, ay, ay, ay; 'tis too plain a case.
translation: Yes, yes, yes, yes. That is too obvious a question.

original: And is it true that I must go from Troy?
translation: And is it also true that I must leave Troy?

original: A hateful truth.
translation: A hateful truth.

original: What, and from Troilus too?
translation: And must I leave Troilus too?

original: From Troy and Troilus.
translation: You have to leave Troy and Troilus.

original: Is it possible?
translation: How can it be?

original: And suddenly; where injury of chance   Puts back leave-taking, justles roughly by   All time of pause, rudely beguiles our lips   Of all rejoindure, forcibly prevents   Our lock'd embrasures,
translation: And our bad luck is splitting us up suddenly. It stops us saying goodbye, pushes past our moment of hesitation, rudely  prevents our lips from meeting , and stops us from embracing each other.

original: strangles our dear vows   Even in the birth of our own labouring breath:
translation: It strangles our promises to each other when they have only just been born.

original: We two, that with so many thousand sighs   Did buy each other, must poorly sell ourselves   With the rude brevity and discharge of one.
translation: Even though we spent so many thousands of sighs winning each other, we now lose each other spending  only one sigh .

original: Injurious time now with a robber's haste   Crams his rich thievery up, he knows not how:
translation: Time is hasty like a thief, bundling up his stolen object without knowing how valuable it is.

original: As many farewells as be stars in heaven,   With distinct breath and consign'd kisses to them,   He fumbles up into a loose adieu,
translation: What is as valuable as the stars in heaven, with so much breath and kisses devoted to each one, he bundles up into a brief goodbye.

original: And scants us with a single famish'd kiss,   Distasted with the salt of broken tears.
translation: He allows us only a brief kiss, ruined by our salty tears.

original: My lord, is the lady ready?
translation: My lord, is the lady ready to leave?

original: Hark! you are call'd: some say the Genius so   Cries 'come' to him that instantly must die.
translation: Listen! They are calling you. Some people say that a guardian spirit shouts "come" to a man who is about to die.

original: Bid them have patience; she shall come anon.
translation: Tell them to be patient, she will come soon.

original: Where are my tears? rain, to lay this wind, or my heart will be blown up by the root.
translation: Why am I not crying? I feel like I need to cry or my heart will be torn out.

original: I must then to the Grecians?
translation: I have go to the Greeks, then?

original: No remedy.
translation: There is no way of stopping it.

original: A woful Cressid 'mongst the merry Greeks! When shall we see again?
translation: I will be a sad Cressida among happy Greeks. When will we meet again?

original: Hear me, my love: be thou but true of heart,—
translation: Listen to me, my love. If you are just true to your heart...

original: I true! how now! what wicked deem is this?
translation: Are you questioning my truth? How come? What an evil judgment on me is that?

original: Nay, we must use expostulation kindly,   For it is parting from us:
translation: No, we must  protest  gently, as we don't have much time.

original: I speak not 'be thou true,' as fearing thee,   For I will throw my glove to Death himself,   That there's no maculation in thy heart:
translation: I'm not saying "be true to me" because I fear that you won't be. I would duel with Death himself to prove that there is no stain of infidelity in your heart.

original: But 'be thou true,' say I, to fashion in   My sequent protestation; be thou true,   And I will see thee.
translation: But I say "if you are true" so that I can add "then we will see each other again."

original: O, you shall be exposed, my lord, to dangers As infinite as imminent! but I'll be true.
translation: Oh, you will face dangers, my lord, as immediate as they are infinite! But I will be true to you.

original: And I'll grow friend with danger. Wear this sleeve.
translation: I will befriend danger. Wear this sleeve.

original: And you this glove. When shall I see you?
translation: Wear this glove.  When will I see you?

original: I will corrupt the Grecian sentinels, To give thee nightly visitation. But yet be true.
translation: I'll bribe the Greek guards, so that I can see you at night. Just be true to me.

original: O heavens! 'be true' again!
translation: Oh heavens. He's telling me to "be true," again!

original: Hear while I speak it, love:   The Grecian youths are full of quality;   They're loving, well composed with gifts of nature,   Flowing and swelling o'er with arts and exercise:
translation: Listen, love. Young Greek men are full of good qualities: they're loving, well put together, fluent in their education and swollen from exercise.

original: How novelty may move, and parts with person,   Alas, a kind of godly jealousy—
translation: The way that this new situation could persuade you, and touch certain parts of you, I'm afraid that a kind of  godly jealousy ...

original: Which, I beseech you, call a virtuous sin—   Makes me afeard.
translation: Which I hope you can consider a virtuous sin... Makes me afraid.

original: O heavens! you love me not.
translation: Oh heavens! You don't love me.

original: Die I a villain, then!   In this I do not call your faith in question   So mainly as my merit:
translation: Then I would die a villain! I am not questioning your loyalty so much as my own merit.

original: I cannot sing,   Nor heel the high lavolt, nor sweeten talk,   Nor play at subtle games;
translation: I cannot sing or dance the  "volta,"  I don't  sweeten my speech , and I'm not manipulative.

original: fair virtues all,   To which the Grecians are most prompt and pregnant:
translation: These are the good virtues that the Greeks are all good at and full of.

original: But I can tell that in each grace of these   There lurks a still and dumb-discoursive devil   That tempts most cunningly: but be not tempted.
translation: And in each of their talents there will be a tempting devil. But don't be tempted.

original: Do you think I will?
translation: Do you think I will be?

original: No.   But something may be done that we will not:
translation: No. But sometimes things happen against our  will ,

original: And sometimes we are devils to ourselves,   When we will tempt the frailty of our powers,   Presuming on their changeful potency.
translation: and sometimes we are devils to ourselves if we assume that our power to resist temptation will not change.

original: Nay, good my lord,—
translation: No, my good lord...

original: Come, kiss; and let us part.
translation: Come, kiss me, and let us go outside.

original: Brother Troilus!
translation: Brother Troilus!

original: Good brother, come you hither; And bring AEneas and the Grecian with you.
translation: Good brother, come here, and bring Aeneas and the Greek with you.

original: My lord, will you be true?
translation: My lord, will you be true?

original: Who, I? alas, it is my vice, my fault:   Whiles others fish with craft for great opinion,   I with great truth catch mere simplicity;
translation: Who me? Alas, my fault, my vice, is that I must be true. Other people are very artful in fishing for a good reputation, but with my great honesty the only thing I can catch is a reputation for being simple.

original: Whilst some with cunning gild their copper crowns,   With truth and plainness I do wear mine bare.
translation: Other people gild copper crowns with cunning, I wear my crown bare, expressing only truth and plainness.

original: Fear not my truth: the moral of my wit   Is 'plain and true;' there's all the reach of it.
translation: Don't worry about me being loyal: my motto has always been "plain and honest," and that's all there is to it.

original: Welcome, Sir Diomed! here is the lady   Which for Antenor we deliver you:
translation: Welcome, Sir Diomedes! Here is the lady which we must give you in return for Antenor.

original: At the port, lord, I'll give her to thy hand,   And by the way possess thee what she is.   Entreat her fair;
translation: I'll give you her hand at the gate, lord, and from there you will possess what she is. Treat her as fairly as she is fair.

original: and, by my soul, fair Greek,   If e'er thou stand at mercy of my sword,   Name Cressida and thy life shall be as safe   As Priam is in Ilion.
translation: I promise you, good Greek, that if you are ever at the mercy of my sword in battle, you just have to say her name and your life will be as safe as Troy.

original: Fair Lady Cressid,   So please you, save the thanks this prince expects:   The lustre in your eye, heaven in your cheek,   Pleads your fair usage;
translation: Fair lady Cressida, you don't need to thank this prince: the spark in your eye and your blushing cheek demand that I treat you fairly.

original: and to Diomed   You shall be mistress, and command him wholly.
translation: You shall be mistress to Diomede , and command me wholly.

original: Grecian, thou dost not use me courteously,   To shame the zeal of my petition to thee   In praising her:
translation: Greek, you are not to treat me courteously, by insulting my genuine request that you keep her safe and praising her yourself.

original: I tell thee, lord of Greece,   She is as far high-soaring o'er thy praises   As thou unworthy to be call'd her servant.
translation: I'm telling you, Greek lord, she flies above your praises and you are unworthy of being her servant.

original: I charge thee use her well, even for my charge;   For, by the dreadful Pluto, if thou dost not,   Though the great bulk Achilles be thy guard,   I'll cut thy throat.
translation: I charge you to treat her well, and do it because I charge you to do it. If you do not do it, even if the huge Achilles were protecting you, by  Pluto,  I will cut your throat.

original: O, be not moved, Prince Troilus:   Let me be privileged by my place and message,   To be a speaker free;
translation: Oh don't get upset, Prince Troilus. The privilege of being a messenger and a noble means that I can speak freely.

original: when I am hence   I'll answer to my lust: and know you, lord,   I'll nothing do on charge:
translation: When I am away from here  I'll do as I please , and I don't do anything because I am charged to.

original: to her own worth   She shall be prized; but that you say 'be't so,'   I'll speak it in my spirit and honour, 'no.'
translation: She will be prized well because of her worth. But if you tell me to treat her well, then on my honor and with all my heart I'll tell you "No."

original: Come, to the port.
translation: Let us go to the gate.

original: I'll tell thee, Diomed,   This brave shall oft make thee to hide thy head.
translation: This insult, Diomedes, will make you flee me on the battlefield.

original: Lady, give me your hand, and, as we walk,   To our own selves bend we our needful talk.
translation: Lady, give me your hand, and as we walk to the gate we'll talk between us only.

original: Hark! Hector's trumpet.
translation: Listen, it is Hector's trumpet.

original: How have we spent this morning! The prince must think me tardy and remiss, That swore to ride before him to the field.
translation: How has the morning already passed? The prince must think I am late and neglectful, since I promised to ride out to the battlefield before him.

original: 'Tis Troilus' fault: come, come, to field with him.
translation: It's Troilus's fault. Come, let's go to the battle with him.

original: Let us make ready straight.
translation: We should go immediately.

original: Yea, with a bridegroom's fresh alacrity,   Let us address to tend on Hector's heels:
translation: Yes, let's follow Hector with the speed of a bridegroom who is full of joy.

original: The glory of our Troy doth this day lie   On his fair worth and single chivalry.
translation: The glory of Troy all depends today on his strength and chivalry.

original: Here art thou in appointment fresh and fair,   Anticipating time with starting courage.
translation: You are here fresh and ready, waiting bravely for the time to fight.

original: Give with thy trumpet a loud note to Troy,   Thou dreadful Ajax;
translation: Blow your trumpet loudly to give a message to Troy, terrifying Ajax,

original: that the appalled air   May pierce the head of the great combatant   And hale him hither.
translation: that the awful sound might assault his ears and bring him here.

original: Thou, trumpet, there's my purse.   Now crack thy lungs, and split thy brazen pipe:
translation: You, trumpeter, here is my money. Now blow as hard as you can.

original: Blow, villain, till thy sphered bias cheek   Outswell the colic of puff'd Aquilon:
translation: Blow, man, until you cheeks are more full of air than the entire sky.

original: Come, stretch thy chest and let thy eyes spout blood;   Thou blow'st for Hector.
translation: Now puff out your chest and play until your eyes cry blood. You are blowing to Hector.

original: No trumpet answers.
translation: There is no reply.

original: 'Tis but early days.
translation: It's not been long enough.

original: Is not yond Diomed, with Calchas' daughter?
translation: Isn't that Diomedes with Calchas's daughter?

original: 'Tis he, I ken the manner of his gait; He rises on the toe: that spirit of his In aspiration lifts him from the earth.
translation: It is him, I recognize the way he walks. He has a spring in his step, and his spirit seems to lift him above the ground.

original: Is this the Lady Cressid?
translation: Is this the lady Cressida?

original: Even she.
translation: It is her.

original: Most dearly welcome to the Greeks, sweet lady.
translation: Welcome to the Greek camp, sweet lady.

original: Our general doth salute you with a kiss.
translation: Our general greets you with a kiss.

original: Yet is the kindness but particular; 'Twere better she were kiss'd in general.
And very courtly counsel: I'll begin. So much for Nestor.
translation: That's good advice, I'll begin. This is from Nestor.

original: I'll take what winter from your lips, fair lady: Achilles bids you welcome.
translation: I'll warm your lips, fair lady. Achilles welcomes you.

original: I had good argument for kissing once.
But that's no argument for kissing now; For this popp'd Paris in his hardiment, And parted thus you and your argument.
translation: But that's no reason for kissing now. Paris thrust himself in, with his boldness, and separated you from your reason.

original: O deadly gall, and theme of all our scorns! For which we lose our heads to gild his horns.
The first was Menelaus' kiss; this, mine: Patroclus kisses you.
translation: The first kiss I give you is from Menelaus. This one is your kiss from Patroclus.

original: O, this is trim!
translation: Oh, good one.

original: Paris and I kiss evermore for him.
translation: Paris and I do all his kissing for him.

original: I'll have my kiss, sir. Lady, by your leave.
translation: I'll have my kiss, sir. Lady, if you don't mind.

original: In kissing, do you render or receive?
translation: Do you give a kiss or take one?

original: I'll make my match to live, The kiss you take is better than you give; Therefore no kiss.
I'll give you boot, I'll give you three for one.
translation: I'll give you a profit, I'll kiss you three times in return for one kiss from you.

original: You're an odd man; give even or give none.
An odd man, lady! every man is odd.
translation: An odd man? Lady, every man is just one person.

original: No, Paris is not; for you know 'tis true, That you are odd, and he is even with you.
translation: No, Paris isn't, and you know that because of him you are alone and he has got even with you.

original: You fillip me o' the head.
No, I'll be sworn.
translation: I don't think it was me that hurt your head.

original: It were no match, your nail against his horn. May I, sweet lady, beg a kiss of you?
You may.
translation: You may.

original: I do desire it.
translation: I wish to.

original: Why, beg, then.
translation: Go on, then, beg.

original: Why then for Venus' sake, give me a kiss, When Helen is a maid again, and his.
I am your debtor, claim it when 'tis due.
Never's my day, and then a kiss of you.
translation: Then I'll never have a kiss from you.

original: Lady, a word: I'll bring you to your father.
translation: Lady, may I talk with you. I will bring you to your father.

original: A woman of quick sense.
translation: She's a quick-witted woman.

original: Fie, fie upon her!   There's language in her eye, her cheek, her lip,   Nay, her foot speaks;
translation: Bah, sod her! There's wit in her eyes, cheeks, lips, even her foot is witty.

original: her wanton spirits look out   At every joint and motive of her body.
translation: Her promiscuous spirits pour out of every joint and limb of her body.

original: O, these encounterers, so glib of tongue,   That give accosting welcome ere it comes,   And wide unclasp the tables of their thoughts   To every ticklish reader!
translation: Oh, these confident women, so clever with their tongue, they show what they really want to anyone willing to take her up on it!

original: set them down   For sluttish spoils of opportunity   And daughters of the game.
translation: Consider her either an easy prize to be won by anyone bold enough to try or a prostitute.

original: The Trojans' trumpet.
translation: The Trojans' trumpet.

original: Yonder comes the troop.
translation: Here come their soldiers.

original: Hail, all you state of Greece! what shall be done   To him that victory commands?
translation: Greetings to you, Greek rulers. How will the winner be rewarded?

original: or do you purpose   A victor shall be known? will you the knights   Shall to the edge of all extremity   Pursue each other, or shall be divided   By any voice or order of the field?
translation: Or how do you intend that the victory be decided? Do you want the knights to fight to the death, or should they be stopped by a referee?

original: Hector bade ask.
translation: Hector told me to ask you.

original: Which way would Hector have it?
translation: What conditions does Hector want?

original: He cares not; he'll obey conditions.
translation: He doesn't care, he'll obey any conditions.

original: 'Tis done like Hector; but securely done, A little proudly, and great deal misprizing The knight opposed.
translation: This is how Hector speaks, confidently, a little proudly, and greatly underestimating his opponent.

original: If not Achilles, sir, What is your name?
translation: Who are you, if you aren't Achilles?

original: If not Achilles, nothing.
translation: If I'm not Achilles, I am nothing.

original: Therefore Achilles: but, whate'er, know this:   In the extremity of great and little,   Valour and pride excel themselves in Hector;
translation: Therefore Achilles, or whoever you are, listen: there is great braveness and little pride in Hector.

original: The one almost as infinite as all,   The other blank as nothing. Weigh him well,   And that which looks like pride is courtesy.
translation: The first is almost infinite, the other almost nothing. If you look at him you'll see that when he seems proud, he is actually being polite.

original: This Ajax is half made of Hector's blood:   In love whereof, half Hector stays at home;   Half heart, half hand, half Hector comes to seek   This blended knight, half Trojan and half Greek.
translation: Ajax is a relative of Hector, and so their blood is half the same. Because of this, half of Hector comes to fight. And with only half of his heart, and one of his hands, Hector comes to fight  this half-Trojan, half-Greek knight .

original: A maiden battle, then? O, I perceive you.
translation: This won't be a fight to the death then? I see.

original: Here is Sir Diomed. Go, gentle knight,   Stand by our Ajax:
translation: This is Sir Diomedes. Go, noble knight, and stand with Ajax.

original: as you and Lord AEneas   Consent upon the order of their fight,   So be it;
translation: Whatever terms you and Lord Aeneas agree to shall be the rules for the battle.

original: either to the uttermost,   Or else a breath: the combatants being kin   Half stints their strife before their strokes begin.
translation: Let it be either to death or just a sporting fight, if the combatants are related they won't be able to hate each other fully.

original: They are opposed already.
translation: They are already prepared to fight.

original: What Trojan is that same that looks so heavy?
translation: Who is that Trojan who looks so sad?

original: The youngest son of Priam, a true knight,   Not yet mature, yet matchless, firm of word,   Speaking in deeds and deedless in his tongue;
translation: The youngest son of king Priam, a good knight, not yet fully grown up, but still an unequaled knight: an honest man, who speaks with actions not words.

original: Not soon provoked nor being provoked soon calm'd:   His heart and hand both open and both free;
translation: It's hard to make him angry, and hard to calm him down when he is angry, but he is generous with both his love and his possessions.

original: For what he has he gives, what thinks he shows;   Yet gives he not till judgment guide his bounty,   Nor dignifies an impure thought with breath;
translation: Whatever he has he shares, and whatever he thinks he shows, but only to people who he should be generous towards, and he would never be so dishonorable as to say anything inappropriate.

original: Manly as Hector, but more dangerous;   For Hector in his blaze of wrath subscribes   To tender objects, but he in heat of action   Is more vindicative than jealous love:
translation: He is as manly as Hector but more dangerous. For while Hector can be expected to show mercy even when he is angry, when he is in the heat of the fight, this knight is even more vengeful than a jealous lover.

original: They call him Troilus, and on him erect   A second hope, as fairly built as Hector.
translation: He is called Troilus, and the Trojans see him as a second hope, as well built as Hector.

original: Thus says AEneas; one that knows the youth   Even to his inches, and with private soul   Did in great Ilion thus translate him to me.
translation: This is what Aeneas said to me in private when I visited Troy, and he knows the young man very well.

original: They are in action.
translation: They are fighting.

original: Now, Ajax, hold thine own!
translation: Come on Ajax, defend yourself.

original: Hector, thou sleep'st; Awake thee!
translation: Hector you are fighting as if you're asleep, wake up!

original: His blows are well disposed: there, Ajax!
translation: His attacks are well aimed, good shot, Ajax!

original: You must no more.
translation: You must stop fighting.

original: Princes, enough, so please you.
translation: Princes, please stop.

original: I am not warm yet; let us fight again.
translation: I haven't even broken a sweat, let's fight again.

original: As Hector pleases.
translation: If Hector is happy to continue...

original: Why, then will I no more:   Thou art, great lord, my father's sister's son,   A cousin-german to great Priam's seed;
translation: Then I will stop here: you are, great lord, my father's sister's son, and the first cousin to all of Priam's sons.

original: The obligation of our blood forbids   A gory emulation 'twixt us twain:
translation: Because we are family we are not allowed to kill each other.

original: Were thy commixtion Greek and Trojan so   That thou couldst say 'This hand is Grecian all,   And this is Trojan; the sinews of this leg   All Greek, and this all Troy; my mother's blood   Runs on the dexter cheek, and this sinister   Bounds in my father's;' by Jove multipotent,   Thou shouldst not bear from me a Greekish member   Wherein my sword had not impressure made   Of our rank feud:
translation: If it were possible to separate your Greek and Trojan parts so that you could say: "This hand is all Greek, and this one is Trojan, the muscles in this leg are all Greek, and this one is Trojan, my Trojan mother's blood is in my right cheek, and the  left  cheek is made of my father's Greek blood," then, I swear by Jove, you would not leave this fight with a Greek limb on your body.

original: but the just gods gainsay   That any drop thou borrow'dst from thy mother,   My sacred aunt, should by my mortal sword   Be drain'd!
translation: But the gods forbid that I use my sword to spill any of your mother's, my sacred aunt's, blood!

original: Let me embrace thee, Ajax:   By him that thunders, thou hast lusty arms;   Hector would have them fall upon him thus:   Cousin, all honour to thee!
translation: Let me embrace you, Ajax, by Jove, you have strong arms and I'd rather they embraced me than fought me. All honor to you, cousin!

original: I thank thee, Hector   Thou art too gentle and too free a man:
translation: Thank you Hector, you are too generous and gentle.

original: I came to kill thee, cousin, and bear hence   A great addition earned in thy death.
translation: I came to kill you, cousin, and gain honor from you dying.

original: Not Neoptolemus so mirable,   On whose bright crest Fame with her loud'st Oyes   Cries 'This is he,'
translation: Not even the great Achilles, who Fame herself declares is her favourite

original: could promise to himself   A thought of added honour torn from Hector.
translation: , could expect to have that honor.

original: There is expectance here from both the sides, What further you will do.
translation: Both sides wait for your answer about what you will do.

original: We'll answer it; The issue is embracement: Ajax, farewell.
translation: We'll give you this answer: the outcome of this fight is an embrace. Ajax, goodbye.

original: If I might in entreaties find success—   As seld I have the chance—
translation: Maybe I can have more success with my words, something I rarely get a chance to do.

original: I would desire   My famous cousin to our Grecian tents.
translation: I invite my famous cousin to the Greek camp.

original: 'Tis Agamemnon's wish, and great Achilles Doth long to see unarm'd the valiant Hector.
translation: It is Agamemnon's wish, and great Achilles wants to see the valiant Hector without his weapons.

original: AEneas, call my brother Troilus to me,   And signify this loving interview   To the expecters of our Trojan part;
translation: Aeneas, go bring Troilus to me, and tell the Trojans who expect me to come back that I am going to meet the Greeks and that they may go home.

original: Desire them home. Give me thy hand, my cousin;   I will go eat with thee and see your knights.
translation: Give me your hand, cousin, I will eat with you and meet your knights.

original: Great Agamemnon comes to meet us here.
translation: Great Agamemnon is coming to meet us here.

original: The worthiest of them tell me name by name;
translation: Tell me the names of the most important people.

original: But for Achilles, mine own searching eyes   Shall find him by his large and portly size.
translation: Except for Achilles, I'll recognize him from his large build.

original: Worthy of arms! as welcome as to one   That would be rid of such an enemy;
translation: Brave fighters! You are welcome here, even though we would be glad to be rid of such an enemy.

original: But that's no welcome: understand more clear,   What's past and what's to come is strew'd with husks   And formless ruin of oblivion;
translation: But that's no welcome. Understand me clearly, our past and future are full of skeletons and total destruction.

original: But in this extant moment, faith and troth,   Strain'd purely from all hollow bias-drawing,   Bids thee, with most divine integrity,   From heart of very heart, great Hector, welcome.
translation: But this moment allows you to be welcomed, great Hector, honestly and faithfully, free of any prejudice, with the most divine fair dealing.

original: I thank thee, most imperious Agamemnon.
translation: Thank you, imperial Agamemnon.

original: My well-famed lord of Troy, no less to you.
translation: I welcome you as well, famous Trojan lord.

original: Let me confirm my princely brother's greeting: You brace of warlike brothers, welcome hither.
translation: I'd like to welcome you as well, warrior brothers, you are welcome here.

original: Who must we answer?
translation: Who are you, may I ask?

original: The noble Menelaus.
translation: The noble Menelaus.

original: O, you, my lord? by Mars his gauntlet, thanks!
translation: Oh it's you? Many thanks, by Mars!

original: Mock not, that I affect the untraded oath;   Your quondam wife swears still by Venus' glove:   She's well, but bade me not commend her to you.
translation: Don't be upset that I don't pass on best wishes from your ex-wife, but she told me not to .

original: Name her not now, sir; she's a deadly theme.
O, pardon; I offend.
translation: Oh, excuse me. I'm offending you.

original: I have, thou gallant Trojan, seen thee oft   Labouring for destiny make cruel way   Through ranks of Greekish youth, and I have seen thee,   As hot as Perseus, spur thy Phrygian steed,   Despising many forfeits and subduements,   When thou hast hung thy advanced sword i' the air,   Not letting it decline on the declined,
translation: I have,  gallant  Trojan, often seen you doing Death's job and cruelly cutting a path through ranks of young Greek soldiers, and I have seen you, as hot as  Perseus , riding your warhorse showing your scorn for those soldiers who beg for mercy, holding your sword in the air rather than letting it fall on the fallen.

original: That I have said to some my standers by   'Lo, Jupiter is yonder, dealing life!'
translation: And I have said to some other observers: "Look, Jupiter himself has come, deciding who should live and who should die!"

original: And I have seen thee pause and take thy breath,   When that a ring of Greeks have hemm'd thee in,   Like an Olympian wrestling:
translation: And I have seen you pause and catch your breath, when you have been surrounded by a ring of Greek soldiers, like a wrestler entering the ring.

original: this have I seen;   But this thy countenance, still lock'd in steel,   I never saw till now.
translation: This I have seen but until now I never saw your face without a helmet on.

original: I knew thy grandsire,   And once fought with him: he was a soldier good;   But, by great Mars, the captain of us all,   Never saw like thee.
translation: I knew your grandfather, and once fought  with  him. He was a good soldier, but by  Mars, the captain of us all , I never saw anyone like you before.

original: Let an old man embrace thee;   And, worthy warrior, welcome to our tents.
translation: Let an old man embrace you, and welcome you to our tents, worthy warrior.

original: 'Tis the old Nestor.
translation: This is old Nestor.

original: Let me embrace thee, good old chronicle, That hast so long walk'd hand in hand with time: Most reverend Nestor, I am glad to clasp thee.
translation: Let me embrace you, wise old story-teller, that has lived a very long life. Respect-worthy Nestor, I am glad to hold you in my arms.

original: I would my arms could match thee in contention, As they contend with thee in courtesy.
translation: I wish my arms were as strong as yours, I cannot hold you so tightly.

original: I would they could.
translation: I wish they could.

original: Ha! By this white beard, I'ld fight with thee to-morrow. Well, welcome, welcome! I have seen the time.
translation: Ha! By my white beard, I would fight with you tomorrow if I could. Well, welcome, welcome! I cannot believe I have lived to see this.

original: I wonder now how yonder city stands When we have here her base and pillar by us.
translation: I wonder how Troy is still standing without you standing there to hold her up.

original: I know your favour, Lord Ulysses, well.
translation: I know your face well, Lord Ulysses.

original: Ah, sir, there's many a Greek and Trojan dead,   Since first I saw yourself and Diomed   In Ilion, on your Greekish embassy.
translation: Ah, sir, many Greeks and Trojans have died since I last saw you and Diomedes in Troy as ambassadors.

original: Sir, I foretold you then what would ensue:
translation: Sir I told you then what would happen.

original: My prophecy is but half his journey yet;
translation: My prophecy has only been half fulfilled, though.

original: For yonder walls, that pertly front your town,   Yond towers, whose wanton tops do buss the clouds,   Must kiss their own feet.
translation: For those walls over there, that hold up your town so shamelessly, and those towers, which so lustfully kiss the clouds, will kiss their own feet when they fall.

original: I must not believe you:   There they stand yet, and modestly I think,   The fall of every Phrygian stone will cost   A drop of Grecian blood:
translation: I can't believe your visions will come true. Troy's walls are still standing, and they look modest to me. Every stone that falls from our walls will cost a drop of Greek blood.

original: the end crowns all,   And that old common arbitrator, Time,   Will one day end it.
translation: The end is the conclusion of everything, and time will be the judge of everyone.

original: So to him we leave it.   Most gentle and most valiant Hector, welcome:
translation: Then we will leave it to him. Most gentle and valiant Hector, welcome.

original: After the general, I beseech you next   To feast with me and see me at my tent.
translation: After you have visited the general, I ask that you will come and eat with me at my tent.

original: I shall forestall thee, Lord Ulysses, thou!
translation: I shall interrupt you there, lord Ulysses!

original: Now, Hector, I have fed mine eyes on thee;   I have with exact view perused thee, Hector,   And quoted joint by joint.
translation: Now, Hector, I have feasted my eyes on you. I have seen you very well indeed, Hector, and considered every joint.

original: Is this Achilles?
translation: Is this Achilles?

original: I am Achilles.
translation: I am Achilles.

original: Stand fair, I pray thee: let me look on thee.
translation: Stand still, please. Let me look at you.

original: Behold thy fill.
translation: Take your fill of looking.

original: Nay, I have done already.
Thou art too brief: I will the second time, As I would buy thee, view thee limb by limb.
translation: You are too quick. I'd like to see you a second time, so that I will know what to do with you.

original: O, like a book of sport thou'lt read me o'er;
translation: Oh, you'll read me like a hunting book will you?

original: But there's more in me than thou understand'st.   Why dost thou so oppress me with thine eye?
translation: There's more inside me than you understand. Why are you glaring at me like this?

original: Tell me, you heavens, in which part of his body   Shall I destroy him?
translation: Tell me, heavens, how I should destroy him?

original: whether there, or there, or there?   That I may give the local wound a name   And make distinct the very breach whereout   Hector's great spirit flew: answer me, heavens!
translation: Should I attack there, or there, or there? I need to know so that I may name the place where I wound him,  and can know the breach out of which Hector's great spirit flew. Answer me, heavens!

original: It would discredit the blest gods, proud man,   To answer such a question: stand again:
translation: It would be dishonorable for the blessed gods to answer, proud man. Stand up again.

original: Think'st thou to catch my life so pleasantly   As to prenominate in nice conjecture   Where thou wilt hit me dead?
translation: You think it will be so easy to speculate in advance where you will strike me dead?

original: I tell thee, yea.
translation: I think so, yes.

original: Wert thou an oracle to tell me so,   I'd not believe thee.
translation: If you were an oracle and thought so, I would not believe you.

original: Henceforth guard thee well;   For I'll not kill thee there, nor there, nor there;   But, by the forge that stithied Mars his helm,   I'll kill thee every where, yea, o'er and o'er.
translation: From now on protect yourself well. For I won't kill you there, nor there, nor there. But, I swear by Mars, I'll kill you everywhere, yes, over and over again.

original: You wisest Grecians, pardon me this brag;   His insolence draws folly from my lips;   But I'll endeavour deeds to match these words,   Or may I never—
translation: Wise Greeks, forgive me for boasting like this, I'll make sure I carry out what I have said or I'll never...

original: Do not chafe thee, cousin:   And you, Achilles, let these threats alone,   Till accident or purpose bring you to't:
translation: Don't get angry cousin. And you, Achilles, stop making threats, until by accident or intention you may do it.

original: You may have every day enough of Hector   If you have stomach;
translation: You can spend every day fighting Hector as much you want, if you have the stomach for it.

original: the general state, I fear,   Can scarce entreat you to be odd with him.
translation: The generals, I suspect, cannot encourage you enough to triumph over him.

original: I pray you, let us see you in the field: We have had pelting wars, since you refused The Grecians' cause.
translation: I beg you, come find me on the battlefield. We've been play-fighting since you stopped fighting.

original: Dost thou entreat me, Hector? To-morrow do I meet thee, fell as death; To-night all friends.
translation: Are you asking me to do that for you, Hector? Tomorrow I will find you, as terrifying as death. Tonight we are friends.

original: Thy hand upon that match.
translation: I'll shake to that.

original: First, all you peers of Greece, go to my tent;   There in the full convive we:
translation: First, all of you brave men, go to my tent. There we shall feast together,

original: afterwards,   As Hector's leisure and your bounties shall   Concur together, severally entreat him.
translation: and afterwards you can all meet Hector when you want.

original: Beat loud the tabourines, let the trumpets blow,   That this great soldier may his welcome know.
translation: Beat the tambourines, play the trumpets, so that this great soldier knows how welcome he is.

original: My Lord Ulysses, tell me, I beseech you, In what place of the field doth Calchas keep?
translation: Lord Ulysses, please tell me where Calchas is staying?

original: At Menelaus' tent, most princely Troilus:   There Diomed doth feast with him to-night;
translation: He is in Menelaus's tent, Prince Troilus. Diomedes is feasting with him there tonight.

original: Who neither looks upon the heaven nor earth,   But gives all gaze and bent of amorous view   On the fair Cressid.
translation: He is unable to look up or down, but only has loving eyes for the fair Cressida.

original: Shall sweet lord, be bound to you so much, After we part from Agamemnon's tent, To bring me thither?
translation: Would you be so kind as to take me there after we leave Agamemnon's tent?

original: You shall command me, sir.   As gentle tell me, of what honour was   This Cressida in Troy?
translation: If you wish, sir. Would you mind telling me what Cressida's reputation was like when she was in Troy.

original: Had she no lover there   That wails her absence?
translation: Did she not have a lover there who misses her?

original: O, sir, to such as boasting show their scars   A mock is due.
translation: Oh, sir, those who boast by showing their scars deserve to be mocked.

original: Will you walk on, my lord?   She was beloved, she loved;
translation: Will you go ahead, lord?  [To himself.]  She was beloved, she used to love.

original: she is, and doth:   But still sweet love is food for fortune's tooth.
translation: She is loved, and she loves. But sweet love is the food of  fortune .

original: I'll heat his blood with Greekish wine to-night, Which with my scimitar I'll cool to-morrow. Patroclus, let us feast him to the height.
Here comes Thersites.
translation: Here comes Thersites.

original: How now, thou core of envy! Thou crusty batch of nature, what's the news?
translation: Hey there, you heart of envy! You ugly misfit, what's the news?

original: Why, thou picture of what thou seemest, and idol of idiot worshippers, here's a letter for thee.
translation: That you are what you look like, an idol for people who worship idiots. Here's a letter for you.

original: From whence, fragment?
translation: Who from, worm?

original: Why, thou full dish of fool, from Troy.
Who keeps the tent now?
translation: Who is staying in their tent now?

original: The surgeon's box, or the patient's wound.
Well said, adversity! and what need these tricks?
translation: Very clever, always understanding the opposite of what I'm saying! Are your tricks useful?

original: Prithee, be silent, boy; I profit not by thy talk: thou art thought to be Achilles' male varlet.
translation: Please, stop talking, boy. I don't gain anything from talking to you. You are thought to be Achilles's boy-lover.

original: Male varlet, you rogue! what's that?
translation: Boy-lover, you rogue! What did you say?

original: Why, his masculine whore.
translation: Why, his male prostitute.

original: Now, the rotten diseases   of the south, the guts-griping, ruptures, catarrhs,   loads o' gravel i' the back, lethargies, cold   palsies, raw eyes, dirt-rotten livers, wheezing   lungs, bladders full of imposthume, sciaticas,   limekilns i' the palm, incurable bone-ache, and the   rivelled fee-simple of the tetter, take and take   again such preposterous discoveries!
translation: Now I will call you syphilis, gut-ache, lesions, mucus, gall-stones, tiredness, fevers, sore eyes, bladders full of abcesses, liver disease, boils, gall-stones, skin-diseases, ringworm, accept these many unacceptable truths!

original: Why thou damnable box of envy, thou, what meanest thou to curse thus?
translation: Oh you evil, box of envy. What do you mean by cursing like this?

original: Do I curse thee?
Why no, you ruinous butt, you whoreson indistinguishable cur, no.
translation: No, you hateful arse, you son of a whore, you malformed wretch, no.

original: No! why art thou then exasperate, thou idle   immaterial skein of sleave-silk, thou green sarcenet   flap for a sore eye, thou tassel of a prodigal's   purse, thou?
translation: No? Then why are you so angry, you idle fabric decoration, you pampered  eye-patch , you ornament, you?

original: Ah, how the poor world is pestered   with such waterflies, diminutives of nature!
translation: Ah the whole world is filled with leeches like you.

original: Out, gall!
translation: Get out, you blister!

original: Finch-egg!
translation: You finch-egg!

original: My sweet Patroclus, I am thwarted quite   From my great purpose in to-morrow's battle.
translation: My sweet Patroclus, I can't carry on with my plan to go to battle tomorrow.

original: Here is a letter from Queen Hecuba,   A token from her daughter, my fair love,   Both taxing me and gaging me to keep   An oath that I have sworn.
translation: This is a letter from Queen Hecuba, and has a message from her daughter, whom I love, which is making me promise not to break an oath I have sworn.

original: I will not break it:   Fall Greeks; fail fame; honour or go or stay;   My major vow lies here, this I'll obey.
translation: I can't break my oath even if it means the Greeks losing or my losing my fame.

original: Come, come, Thersites, help to trim my tent:   This night in banqueting must all be spent.   Away, Patroclus!
translation: The only vow I care about is this, and I'll obey it. Come, come, Thersites, tidy up my tent, we will spend this night banqueting. Let's go Patroclus!

original: With too much blood and too little brain, these two   may run mad; but, if with too much brain and too   little blood they do, I'll be a curer of madmen.
translation: With too much passion and too little brain, these two will go mad. But if they do go mad with too much thinking and too little courage, I will be considered a curer of madmen

original: Here's Agamemnon, an honest fellow enough and one   that loves quails; but he has not so much brain as   earwax:
translation: . Here comes Agamemnon, an honest man and one that loves eating  quails . But he doesn't have as much brain as he does earwax.

original: and the goodly transformation of Jupiter   there, his brother, the bull,—the primitive statue,   and oblique memorial of cuckolds; a thrifty   shoeing-horn in a chain, hanging at his brother's   leg,—
translation: And the walking embodiment of Jupiter stood next to him, his bull-like brother, the original model and monument to all cuckolds, is a coward, like a tool hanging from his brother's belt...

original: to what form but that he is, should wit larded   with malice and malice forced with wit turn him to?
translation: What worse shape could an angry god make you into?

original: To an ass, were nothing; he is both ass and ox: to   an ox, were nothing; he is both ox and ass. To be a   dog, a mule, a cat, a fitchew, a toad, a lizard, an   owl, a puttock, or a herring without a roe, I would   not care; but to be Menelaus, I would conspire   against destiny.
translation: If he were turned into an ass or an ox that would be fine, because he is already both. If were turned into a dog, a mule, a cat, a polecat, a toad, a lizard, an owl, a hawk, or a worthless fish, I wouldn't care, but I would do anything to avoid being turned into Menelaus.

original: Ask me not, what I would be, if I   were not Thersites; for I care not to be the louse   of a lazar, so I were not Menelaus! Hey-day!   spirits and fires!
translation: Don't ask me what I would be if I wasn't myself, because I would be perfectly happy as a louse or a leper, anything but Menelaus! Look at that, they are caring torches!

original: We go wrong, we go wrong.
translation: We've gone the wrong way, we've gone the wrong way.

original: No, yonder 'tis; There, where we see the lights.
translation: No it is this way, there, where the light is.

original: I trouble you.
translation: I've asked too much of you.

original: No, not a whit.
translation: No, not at all.

original: Here comes himself to guide you.
translation: Here he comes to show us the way.

original: Welcome, brave Hector; welcome, princes all.
translation: Welcome, brave Hector, welcome everyone.

original: So now, fair prince of Troy, I bid good night. Ajax commands the guard to tend on you.
translation: Well, now I will say goodnight, fair prince of Troy. Ajax will tell the guard to look after you.

original: Thanks and good night to the Greeks' general.
translation: Thanks and goodnight, Greek general.

original: Good night, my lord.
translation: Goodnight, my lord.

original: Good night, sweet lord Menelaus.
translation: Goodnight, sweet lord Menelaus.

original: Sweet draught: 'sweet' quoth 'a! sweet sink, sweet sewer.
translation: That's a "sweet" thing to say! "Sweet" like a drain, "sweet" like a sewer.

original: Good night and welcome, both at once, to those That go or tarry.
translation: Goodnight or welcome, if you are coming or going.

original: Good night.
translation: Goodnight.

original: Old Nestor tarries; and you too, Diomed, Keep Hector company an hour or two.
translation: Old Nestor is staying here, and you too, Diomedes, come in and keep Hector company with me.

original: I cannot, lord; I have important business, The tide whereof is now. Good night, great Hector.
translation: I can't, lord, I have important business that must be seen to at once. Goodnight, great Hector.

original: Give me your hand.
translation: Give me your hand.

original: Follow his torch; he goes to Calchas' tent: I'll keep you company.
translation: Aside to TROILUS] Follow his torch, he's going to Calchas's tent: I'll come with you.

original: Sweet sir, you honour me.
translation: Sweet sir, you honour me.

original: And so, good night.
translation: And so, good night.

original: Come, come, enter my tent.
translation: Come this way, enter my tent.

original: That same Diomed's a false-hearted rogue, a most   unjust knave; I will no more trust him when he leers   than I will a serpent when he hisses:
translation: That Diomedes is a false-hearted rogue, and an unjust fool. I don't trust him when he looks at me anymore than I do when a snake hisses at me.

original: he will spend   his mouth, and promise, like Brabbler the hound:
translation: He is always promising so much and never delivers, like a hound running away from the scent.

original: but when he performs, astronomers foretell it; it   is prodigious, there will come some change; the sun   borrows of the moon, when Diomed keeps his   word.
translation: If he is ever actually honest astronomers see it as a sign from the gods, it is such a rare event: the sun will take its light from the moon before Diomede keeps his word.

original: I will rather leave to see Hector, than   not to dog him: they say he keeps a Trojan   drab, and uses the traitor Calchas' tent: I'll   after.
translation: I'll leave Hector rather than stop following him. Apparently he has a Trojan mistress, and keeps her in Calchas's tent, I'll follow them.

original: Nothing but lechery! all incontinent varlets!
translation: I'll have nothing but lechery and easy women!

original: What, are you up here, ho? speak.
translation: Hey, is anyone awake in there? Speak.

original: Who calls?
translation: Who is asking?

original: Calchas, I think. Where's your daughter?
translation: I think that is Calchas. Where's you daughter?

original: She comes to you.
translation: She is coming out to meet you.

original: Stand where the torch may not discover us.
translation: Stand in the shadows, away from the light.

original: Cressid comes forth to him.
translation: Cressida is coming out to him.

original: How now, my charge!
Now, my sweet guardian! Hark, a word with you.
translation: Oh, my sweet guardian! Listen, I want to tell you something.

original: Yea, so familiar!
translation: She's acting so familiar with him!

original: She will sing any man at first sight.
And any man may sing her, if he can take her cliff; she's noted.
Will you remember?
translation: Will you remember?

original: Remember! yes.
translation: Of course I will remember.

original: Nay, but do, then; And let your mind be coupled with your words.
translation: Well, make sure you do, and prove what you say with actions.

original: What should she remember?
translation: What has he asked her to remember?

original: List.
translation: Listen.

original: Sweet honey Greek, tempt me no more to folly.
Roguery!
translation: What kind of poor behavior is this?

original: Nay, then,—
translation: No, then...

original: I'll tell you what,—
translation: I'll tell you what...

original: Foh, foh! come, tell a pin: you are forsworn.
translation: Bah! Tell me nothing. You are promised to someone else.

original: In faith, I cannot: what would you have me do?
translation: Honestly, I can't. What would you have me do?

original: A juggling trick,—to be secretly open.
translation: A clever thing to say... one that shows her to be secretly open.

original: What did you swear you would bestow on me?
translation: What did you promise you'd give to me?

original: I prithee, do not hold me to mine oath; Bid me do any thing but that, sweet Greek.
translation: I beg you, don't make me do what I promised. Ask me anything other than that, sweet Greek.

original: Good night.
translation: Goodnight.

original: Hold, patience!
translation: How can I endure this?

original: How now, Trojan!
translation: Quiet, Trojan!

original: Diomed,—
translation: Diomedes...

original: No, no, good night: I'll be your fool no more.
translation: No, no, goodnight. I'm not going to be your fool anymore.

original: Thy better must.
translation: You better had.

original: Hark, one word in your ear.
translation: Listen, let me say one thing into your ear.

original: O plague and madness!
translation: Oh plague and madness!

original: You are moved, prince;
translation: You are upset, prince.

original: let us depart, I pray you,   Lest your displeasure should enlarge itself   To wrathful terms:
translation: Let's go, I beg you, in case your anger makes you violent.

original: this place is dangerous;   The time right deadly; I beseech you, go.
translation: This is a dangerous place and a deadly time for you to be here. I beg you, go.

original: Behold, I pray you!
translation: Look, I beg you.

original: Nay, good my lord, go off: You flow to great distraction; come, my lord.
translation: No, my lord, leave. You are going insane, come, my lord.

original: I pray thee, stay.
translation: I beg you, stay.

original: You have not patience; come.
translation: You don't have the patience, come.

original: I pray you, stay; by hell and all hell's torments I will not speak a word!
translation: I beg you, stay. No matter what torture I see I won't say a word.

original: And so, good night.
translation: And so, goodnight.

original: Nay, but you part in anger.
translation: No, you are still angry.

original: Doth that grieve thee? O wither'd truth!
translation: Does that bother you? Oh your truth has died!

original: Why, how now, lord!
translation: Woah, lord!

original: By Jove, I will be patient.
translation: By Jupiter, I will be patient.

original: Guardian!—why, Greek!
translation: Guardian... oh, Greek!

original: Foh, foh! adieu; you palter.
translation: Pah, pah, goodbye, you time waster.

original: In faith, I do not: come hither once again.
translation: Honestly, I am not wasting your time. Come here again.

original: You shake, my lord, at something: will you go? You will break out.
translation: You are shaking, my lord, will you leave here? You are going to blow your cover.

original: She strokes his cheek!
translation: She is stroking his cheek.

original: Come, come.
translation: Come, come.

original: Nay, stay; by Jove, I will not speak a word:
translation: No, stay, by Jupiter, I won't say a word.

original: There is between my will and all offences   A guard of patience:
translation: My patience will stop me from saying or doing anything dangerous.

original: stay a little while.
translation: Let's stay a little longer.

original: How the devil Luxury, with his fat rump and potato-finger, tickles these together! Fry, lechery,  fry!
But will you, then?
translation: So you will then?

original: In faith, I will, la; never trust me else.
translation: Honestly I will, ha. If I don't then never believe me again.

original: Give me some token for the surety of it.
I'll fetch you one.
translation: I'll fetch you one.

original: You have sworn patience.
translation: You have promised to be patient.

original: Fear me not, sweet lord; I will not be myself, nor have cognition Of what I feel: I am all patience.
translation: Don't worry about me, sweet lord. I will pretend I am not me and put my emotions aside. I can be patient.

original: Now the pledge; now, now, now!
translation: Here's her promise. Now, now, now.

original: Here, Diomed, keep this sleeve.
translation: Here, Diomedes, keep this sleeve.

original: O beauty! where is thy faith?
translation: Oh beauty! Where is your loyalty?

original: My lord,—
translation: My lord...

original: I will be patient; outwardly I will.
translation: I will be patient, or at least I won't move.

original: You look upon that sleeve; behold it well. He loved me—O false wench!—Give't me again.
translation: You look at that sleeve, take good care of it. He loved me... oh you unfaithful girl... give it back to me.

original: Whose was't?
translation: Whose was it?

original: It is no matter, now I have't again. I will not meet with you to-morrow night: I prithee, Diomed, visit me no more.
translation: It doesn't matter, I want it back. I won't meet with you tomorrow night, I beg you, Diomedes, don't visit me again.

original: Now she sharpens: well said, whetstone!
I shall have it.
translation: I'll have it.

original: What, this?
translation: What, this?

original: Ay, that.
translation: Yes, that.

original: O, all you gods! O pretty, pretty pledge!
translation: Oh, all you gods! Oh, pretty gift!

original: Thy master now lies thinking in his bed   Of thee and me, and sighs, and takes my glove,   And gives memorial dainty kisses to it,   As I kiss thee.
translation: The person who gave you to me is lying in his bed now, thinking of his gift and me, and sighing. He will be taking my glove, and kisses it to remember me, just as I kiss you now.

original: Nay, do not snatch it from me;   He that takes that doth take my heart withal.
translation: No, don't take it from me! The person who takes that from me steals my heart itself.

original: I had your heart before, this follows it.
translation: I have already won your heart, so this token comes afterwards.

original: I did swear patience.
translation: I swore patience.

original: You shall not have it, Diomed; faith, you shall not; I'll give you something else.
translation: You won't have it, Diomedes. I swear, you won't. I'll give you something else.

original: I will have this: whose was it?
translation: I will have this. Whose was it?

original: It is no matter.
translation: It doesn't matter.

original: Come, tell me whose it was.
translation: Come, tell me, whose was it.

original: 'Twas one's that loved me better than you will. But, now you have it, take it.
translation: It belonged to someone that loved me better than you will. But now you have it, keep it.

original: Whose was it?
translation: Whose was it?

original: By all Diana's waiting-women yond, And by herself, I will not tell you whose.
To-morrow will I wear it on my helm, And grieve his spirit that dares not challenge it.
translation: Tomorrow I will wear this on my helmet, and see if he comes forward.

original: Wert thou the devil, and worest it on thy horn, It should be challenged.
translation: If you were the devil himself, and wore it on your horns, I would still come and fight you.

original: Well, well, 'tis done, 'tis past: and yet it is not; I will not keep my word.
translation: Right, it is done, it is over. But no, it's not, I won't keep my word.

original: Why, then, farewell; Thou never shalt mock Diomed again.
translation: Okay then, goodbye, you'll never see me again.

original: You shall not go: one cannot speak a word, But it straight starts you.
translation: You mustn't go. I can't say anything without you running off.

original: I do not like this fooling.
translation: I'm getting bored of this.

original: Nor I, by Pluto: but that that likes not you pleases me best.
translation: Nor me, by Pluto. But I am glad you are upset.

original: What, shall I come? the hour?
translation: Well, should I come when we agreed? Same time?

original: Ay, come:—O Jove!—do come:—I shall be plagued.
translation: Yes, come. Oh Jupiter! Do come. I will be cursed.

original: Farewell till then.
translation: Goodbye until then.

original: Good night: I prithee, come.
translation: Goodnight. I beg you, come tomorrow.

original: Troilus, farewell! one eye yet looks on thee   But with my heart the other eye doth see.
translation: Goodbye Troilus. Part of me still belongs to you, but another part of me cannot help itself.

original: Ah, poor our sex! this fault in us I find,   The error of our eye directs our mind:
translation: Ah, women are so weak! I think our fault is that we use our eyes to make decisions not our brains!

original: What error leads must err; O, then conclude   Minds sway'd by eyes are full of turpitude.
translation: People who are only guided by bad judgments, must do bad things. Oh, brains that are lead by eyes are full of bad thoughts.

original: A proof of strength she could not publish more, Unless she said "My mind is now turn'd whore."
translation: She couldn't sum herself up better, unless she said "My mind has become a whore."

original: All's done, my lord.
translation: It's over, my lord.

original: It is.
translation: It is.

original: Why stay we, then?
translation: Why are we still here, then.

original: To make a recordation to my soul   Of every syllable that here was spoke.
translation: To make a record in my soul of everything that was said here.

original: But if I tell how these two did co-act,   Shall I not lie in publishing a truth?
translation: Although these two are so deceitful together, that if I spoke the truth everything I said would be dishonest.

original: Sith yet there is a credence in my heart,   An esperance so obstinately strong,   That doth invert the attest of eyes and ears,   As if those organs had deceptious functions,   Created only to calumniate.
translation: Although there is still some trust in my heart and some hope so stubbornly strong, that it turns upside down what my eyes and ears have seen, as if those organs had been created only to make up lies.

original: Was Cressid here?
translation: Was Cressida here?

original: I cannot conjure, Trojan.
translation: I can't perform magic, Trojan, I couldn't fake all the things you saw.

original: She was not, sure.
translation: Surely she wasn't here.

original: Most sure she was.
translation: She definitely was.

original: Why, my negation hath no taste of madness.
translation: I don't think I have gone mad, she wasn't.

original: Nor mine, my lord: Cressid was here but now.
translation: I definitely haven't gone mad, Cressida was just here.

original: Let it not be believed for womanhood!   Think, we had mothers;
translation: For the sake of womankind, let this not be believed! Since we ourselves had mothers.

original: do not give advantage   To stubborn critics, apt, without a theme,   For depravation, to square the general sex   By Cressid's rule:
translation: Don't let the stubborn critics of women, who don't have an example of their depravation, blame their sex by Cressida's example.

original: rather think this not Cressid.
translation: It is better not to think this was Cressida.

original: What hath she done, prince, that can soil our mothers?
translation: What has she done, prince, that would be an insult to our mothers?

original: Nothing at all, unless that this were she.
translation: Nothing at all, unless that was her.

original: Will he swagger himself out on's own eyes?
translation: Will he convince himself out of it, despite all he's seen?

original: This she? no, this is Diomed's Cressida:   If beauty have a soul, this is not she;
translation: This, her? No, this is Diomedes's Cressida. If beauty has a soul, this is not her.

original: If souls guide vows, if vows be sanctimonies,   If sanctimony be the gods' delight,   If there be rule in unity itself,   This is not she.
translation: If souls guide promises, if promises are sacred, if being sacred is what the gods care about, if there is any justice in the world, that was not her.

original: O madness of discourse,   That cause sets up with and against itself!   Bi-fold authority!
translation: Oh mad talking, that argues against itself! A duplicitous judgment!

original: where reason can revolt   Without perdition, and loss assume all reason   Without revolt: this is, and is not, Cressid.
translation: Why won't my logic let her be and not be Cressida.

original: Within my soul there doth conduce a fight   Of this strange nature that a thing inseparate   Divides more wider than the sky and earth,   And yet the spacious breadth of this division   Admits no orifex for a point as subtle   As Ariachne's broken woof to enter.
Instance, O instance! strong as Pluto's gates;
translation: With one important exception!

original: Cressid is mine, tied with the bonds of heaven:   Instance, O instance! strong as heaven itself;   The bonds of heaven are slipp'd, dissolved, and loosed;   And with another knot, five-finger-tied,   The fractions of her faith, orts of her love,   The fragments, scraps, the bits and greasy relics   Of her o'er-eaten faith, are bound to Diomed.
translation: At once Cressida is mine and tied to me by heaven, and at the same time those ties have broken and she has tied another knot to Diomedes with her unfaithful dishonesty.

original: May worthy Troilus be half attach'd With that which here his passion doth express?
translation: Can the worthy Troilus really be as angry as he seems?

original: He'll tickle it for his concupy.
O Cressid! O false Cressid! false, false, false! Let all untruths stand by thy stained name, And they'll seem glorious.
translation: Oh Cressida! Oh false Cressida. False, false, false! Let all lies be given your name, that way they'll seem glorious.

original: O, contain yourself Your passion draws ears hither.
translation: Oh, be patient, your anger is drawing attention to us.

original: I have been seeking you this hour, my lord: Hector, by this, is arming him in Troy; Ajax, your guard, stays to conduct you home.
translation: I have been looking for you for an hour, my lord. Hector is getting ready for war in Troy, and Ajax, your guard, is getting ready to walk you home.

original: Have with you, prince. My courteous lord, adieu. Farewell, revolted fair! and, Diomed, Stand fast, and wear a castle on thy head!
translation: I'll come with you, prince. Courteous lord, goodbye. Farewell, ugly beauty! And, Diomedes stand up tall, you'll need a strong helmet to protect you!

original: I'll bring you to the gates.
translation: I'll show you to the gates.

original: Accept distracted thanks.
