translation: Please forgive me for not thanking you well enough, I am overwhelmed.

original: Would I could meet that rogue Diomed! I would   croak like a raven; I would bode, I would bode.
translation: I wish I could wait outside Diomedes's tent like an omen of bad luck.

original: Patroclus will give me any thing for the   intelligence of this whore: the parrot will not   do more for an almond than he for a commodious drab.
translation: I know, Patroclus would give me anything for information of such a woman as this. A parrot will not do more for an almond as he will do for easy women.

original: Lechery, lechery; still, wars and lechery; nothing   else holds fashion: a burning devil take them!
translation: Lechery, lechery, more wars and lechery! Nothing else is so fashionable at the moment. I  hope a devil takes the lot of them .

original: When was my lord so much ungently temper'd, To stop his ears against admonishment? Unarm, unarm, and do not fight to-day.
translation: Since when have you been so angry, husband, that you won't listen to my advice? Take off your armor, put down your weapons, and don't go out to fight today.

original: You train me to offend you; get you in: By all the everlasting gods, I'll go!
translation: You're provoking me want to upset you. Go back inside, by all the gods, I swear I will go out and fight.

original: My dreams will, sure, prove ominous to the day.
No more, I say.
translation: Stop speaking, enough.

original: Where is my brother Hector?
translation: Where is my brother Hector?

original: Here, sister; arm'd, and bloody in intent.
translation: Here he is, sister, in his armor and intent on fighting.

original: Consort with me in loud and dear petition,   Pursue we him on knees;
translation: Join my loud and clear pleas, let's follow him on our knees.

original: for I have dream'd   Of bloody turbulence, and this whole night   Hath nothing been but shapes and forms of slaughter.
translation: I have had dreams of a bloody disaster, for the whole night, nothing but dreams about different kinds of slaughter.

original: O, 'tis true.
translation: Oh, it is true.

original: Ho! bid my trumpet sound!
translation: Ha! Tell them to blow my trumpet!

original: No notes of sally, for the heavens, sweet brother.
translation: For heaven's sake, don't make any suggestion that you will go out there, sweet brother.

original: Be gone, I say: the gods have heard me swear.
translation: Go away, I say. The gods have heard my promise.

original: The gods are deaf to hot and peevish vows: They are polluted offerings, more abhorr'd Than spotted livers in the sacrifice.
O, be persuaded! do not count it holy   To hurt by being just:
translation: Oh, listen to her! Don't think it is holy to let yourself be injured for being just.

original: it is as lawful,   For we would give much, to use violent thefts,   And rob in the behalf of charity.
translation: It is as holy as stealing for the purpose of charity.

original: It is the purpose that makes strong the vow; But vows to every purpose must not hold: Unarm, sweet Hector.
translation: It is only the reason behind a promise that makes it justified. Any old promise does not need to be binding. Disarm, sweet Hector.

original: Hold you still, I say;
translation: Stop there, I said.

original: Mine honour keeps the weather of my fate:   Life every man holds dear;
translation: My honor is more important to me than my destiny.

original: but the brave man   Holds honour far more precious-dear than life.
translation: Every man values his life, but a brave man values his honor far more.

original: How now, young man! mean'st thou to fight to-day?
translation: Hello there, young man! Are you planning to fight today?

original: Cassandra, call my father to persuade.
translation: Cassandra, bring my father here to help persuade them.

original: No, faith, young Troilus; doff thy harness, youth;
translation: No, honestly, young Troilus, take off your armor, young man.

original: I am to-day i' the vein of chivalry:   Let grow thy sinews till their knots be strong,   And tempt not yet the brushes of the war.
translation: I am going out today as a knight should. You should let your young body grow older, don't take the risks of war yet.

original: Unarm thee, go, and doubt thou not, brave boy,   I'll stand to-day for thee and me and Troy.
translation: Disarm yourself and go, and don't doubt, brave boy, I'll fight hard enough today for you, me and all of Troy.

original: Brother, you have a vice of mercy in you, Which better fits a lion than a man.
What vice is that, good Troilus? chide me for it.
translation: What inappropriate mercy have I shown, good Troilus? Tell me off for it.

original: When many times the captive Grecian falls, Even in the fan and wind of your fair sword, You bid them rise, and live.
translation: Many times when a Greek soldier was defenseless in front of your sword, and you let them get up and live.

original: O,'tis fair play.
translation: Oh, this is just fair play.

original: Fool's play, by heaven, Hector.
translation: This is how idiots fight, by heaven, Hector.

original: How now! how now!
translation: Woah, woah.

original: For the love of all the gods,   Let's leave the hermit pity with our mothers,   And when we have our armours buckled on,
translation: For the love of all the gods, leave your pity at home with our mothers, when we are armed,

original: The venom'd vengeance ride upon our swords,   Spur them to ruthful work, rein them from ruth.
translation: we carry vengeance in our swords, and we must use them to do sad work, without becoming sad about it.

original: Fie, savage, fie!
translation: No, savage, you're wrong!

original: Hector, then 'tis wars.
translation: Hector, this is a war.

original: Troilus, I would not have you fight to-day.
translation: Troilus, I don't want you to fight today.

original: Who should withhold me?   Not fate, obedience, nor the hand of Mars   Beckoning with fiery truncheon my retire;
translation: What is going to stop me? Fate won't, nor would obedience, nor the hand of Mars if he used a burning weapon to make me go back.

original: Not Priamus and Hecuba on knees,   Their eyes o'ergalled with recourse of tears;
translation: Not my father or mother begging on their knees and their eyes full of tears.

original: Not you, my brother, with your true sword drawn,   Opposed to hinder me, should stop my way,   But by my ruin.
translation: Not you, brother, if you drew your sword to fight me, unless you managed to kill me first.

original: Lay hold upon him, Priam, hold him fast:   He is thy crutch;
translation: Grab him, Priam, hold him still. He is like your crutch, he supports you.

original: now if thou lose thy stay,   Thou on him leaning, and all Troy on thee,   Fall all together.
translation: Now if you let him go all of Troy will fall down with you.

original: Come, Hector, come, go back:   Thy wife hath dream'd; thy mother hath had visions;
translation: Come, Hector, go back inside. Your wife has dreamed, your mother has had visions,

original: Cassandra doth foresee; and I myself   Am like a prophet suddenly enrapt   To tell thee that this day is ominous:
translation: Cassandra foresees, and even I feel like a prophet and feel inspired to tell you that today is ominous.

original: Therefore, come back.
translation: Therefore, come back inside.

original: AEneas is a-field;   And I do stand engaged to many Greeks,
translation: Aeneas has gone to battle. And I have promised myself to many Greeks,

original: Even in the faith of valour, to appear   This morning to them.
translation: bound with a oath of bravery, to go out there this morning.

original: Ay, but thou shalt not go.
translation: Yes, but you should not go.

original: I must not break my faith.   You know me dutiful;
translation: I must not break my promise. You know that I am honest.

original: therefore, dear sir,   Let me not shame respect;
translation: Therefore, dear sir, don't make me disrespect you by ignoring you.

original: but give me leave   To take that course by your consent and voice,   Which you do here forbid me, royal Priam.
translation: Allow me to go out with your blessing, royal Priam.

original: O Priam, yield not to him!
translation: Oh Priam, don't let him go!

original: Do not, dear father.
translation: Don't, dear father.

original: Andromache, I am offended with you: Upon the love you bear me, get you in.
translation: Andromache, I'm upset with you. If you love me, go inside.

original: This foolish, dreaming, superstitious girl Makes all these bodements.
translation: This foolish, dreaming, superstitious girl is the person making all these bad predictions.

original: O, farewell, dear Hector!   Look, how thou diest! look, how thy eye turns pale!
translation: Oh, goodbye, dear Hector! I can see you dying! I can see your eyes turning pale!

original: Look, how thy wounds do bleed at many vents!   Hark, how Troy roars! how Hecuba cries out!
translation: I can see blood pouring from your many wounds! I can hear Troy screaming! I can hear  Hecuba  crying!

original: How poor Andromache shrills her dolours forth!   Behold, distraction, frenzy and amazement,   Like witless antics, one another meet,   And all cry, Hector! Hector's dead! O Hector!
translation: Your wife, Andromache, is screaming with grief! I see confusion, hatred, shock, and awful things all coming for you! Everyone will scream: "Hector! Hector's dead! Oh Hector!"

original: Away! away!
translation: Go away, go away!

original: Farewell: yet, soft! Hector! take my leave: Thou dost thyself and all our Troy deceive.
translation: Goodbye, still living Hector! Let me go, you are going to ruin yourself and all of Troy.

original: You are amazed, my liege, at her exclaim:
translation: You are in shock, my liege, at what she has said.

original: Go in and cheer the town: we'll forth and fight,   Do deeds worth praise and tell you them at night.
translation: Go in and make the town happy, we'll go out and fight, and perform great deeds that we can tell you about tonight.

original: Farewell: the gods with safety stand about thee!
translation: Goodbye. May the gods watch over you.

original: They are at it, hark! Proud Diomed, believe, I come to lose my arm, or win my sleeve.
translation: The men outside are fighting, listen! Proud Diomedes believe me that I will either lose my arm or regain my sleeve!

original: Do you hear, my lord? do you hear?
translation: Have you heard, my lord? Have you head?

original: What now?
translation: What is it?

original: Here's a letter come from yond poor girl.
translation: A letter has come from the poor girl.

original: Let me read.
translation: Let me read it.

original: A whoreson tisick, a whoreson rascally tisick so   troubles me, and the foolish fortune of this girl;
translation: A  terrible cough , a really awful cough is troubling me, and the fortunes of this girl.

original: and what one thing, what another, that I shall   leave you one o' these days:
translation: What is true of one thing is true of the other: I will leave you one of these days.

original: and I have a rheum   in mine eyes too, and such an ache in my bones   that, unless a man were cursed, I cannot tell what   to think on't.
translation: My eyes are rheumatic, and my bones ache so much. I must be cursed, because I cannot thing what else I might have.

original: What says she there?
translation: What does she say in the letter?

original: Words, words, mere words, no matter from the heart: The effect doth operate another way.
translation: Words, only words, nothing meaningful. What she says and the truth aren't the same.

original: Go, wind, to wind, there turn and change together. My love with words and errors still she feeds; But edifies another with her deeds.
translation: Scatter and dance in the wind. She still feeds my love for her with her words, but loves another person with her actions.

original: Now they are clapper-clawing one another; I'll go   look on.
translation: Now the two armies are fighting hard, I'll watch them.

original: That dissembling abominable varlet Diomed,   has got that same scurvy doting foolish young knave's   sleeve of Troy there in his helm:
translation: That lying, detestable crook Diomedes has got the equally awful young Trojan's sleeve on his helmet.

original: I would fain see   them meet; that that same young Trojan ass, that   loves the whore there, might send that Greekish   whore-masterly villain, with the sleeve, back to the   dissembling luxurious drab, of a sleeveless errand.
translation: Oh I would love to see them fighting and see the young Trojan that loves the whore send the whoring Greek villain to the lying and unfaithful girl without any sleeves at all.

original: O' the t'other side, the policy of those crafty   swearing rascals, that stale old mouse-eaten dry   cheese, Nestor, and that same dog-fox, Ulysses, is   not proved worthy a blackberry:
translation: On the other side of the battlefield, the tactics of the old mouse Nestor and foxhound Ulysses are as worthless as a blackberry.

original: they set me up, in   policy, that mongrel cur, Ajax, against that dog of   as bad a kind, Achilles: and now is the cur Ajax   prouder than the cur Achilles, and will not arm   to-day;
translation: They had made me set up Ajax against Achilles, but now Ajax is even prouder than Achilles and won't fight today either.

original: whereupon the Grecians begin to proclaim   barbarism, and policy grows into an ill opinion.   Soft! here comes sleeve, and t'other.
translation: Soon the whole Greek army will be uncontrollable, but I must keep quiet, here comes the knight with the sleeve and the other man.

original: Fly not; for shouldst thou take the river Styx, I would swim after.
translation: Don't flee me. Even if you were crossing the river Styx, I would swim after you.

original: Thou dost miscall retire:
translation: You are wrong to say I'm retreating:

original: I do not fly, but advantageous care   Withdrew me from the odds of multitude:
translation: I wasn't fleeing, bu being careful to withdraw from a place where I was outnumbered, alone in a crowd.

original: Have at thee!
translation: Defend yourself!

original: Hold thy whore, Grecian!—now for thy whore, Trojan!—now the sleeve, now the sleeve!
translation: Defend your whore, Greek! Fight for your whore, Trojan! Now fight for the sleeve! The sleeve!

original: What art thou, Greek? art thou for Hector's match? Art thou of blood and honour?
translation: Who are you, Greek? Are you able to fight Hector? Are you brave and noble?

original: No, no, I am a rascal; a scurvy railing knave: a very filthy rogue.
translation: No, no, I am not a brave man, I am just a sick, unpleasant creature, a dirty rogue.

original: I do believe thee: live.
translation: I believe you, you may live.

original: God-a-mercy, that thou wilt believe me; but a   plague break thy neck for frightening me!
translation: God bless you for believing me, but curse you for scaring me!

original: What's   become of the wenching rogues? I think they have   swallowed one another:
translation: What's happened to the whoring thugs? Maybe they have eaten each other up,

original: I would laugh at that   miracle: yet, in a sort, lechery eats itself.   I'll seek them.
translation: that would be a hilarious sight, although I suppose lust and greed do consume the people they meet. I'll find them.

original: Go, go, my servant, take thou Troilus' horse;   Present the fair steed to my lady Cressid:
translation: Go, go, servant, take Troilus's horse and show it to my lady Cressida.

original: Fellow, commend my service to her beauty;   Tell her I have chastised the amorous Trojan,   And am her knight by proof.
translation: My man, tell the beautiful lady that she is mine, tell her I beat her Trojan lover, and I am now her knight because of this.

original: I go, my lord.
translation: I will go now, my lord.

original: Renew, renew! The fierce Polydamas   Hath beat down Menon: bastard Margarelon   Hath Doreus prisoner,   And stands colossus-wise, waving his beam,   Upon the pashed corpses of the kings   Epistrophus and Cedius:
translation: Rally! Rally! The fierce Polydamas has beaten Menon, Margarelon the bastard has Doreus prisoner and stands over him like the Colossus of Rhodes, waving this sword over the broken bodies of the kings Epistrophus and Cedius.

original: Polyxenes is slain,   Amphimachus and Thoas deadly hurt,   Patroclus ta'en or slain, and Palamedes   Sore hurt and bruised:
translation: Polyxenes is dead, Amphimachus and Thoas are fatally wounded, Patroclus has been taken prisoner or killed, and Palamedes has been badly beaten. Their cavalry are terrifying our soldiers.

original: the dreadful Sagittary   Appals our numbers: haste we, Diomed,   To reinforcement, or we perish all.
translation: We must hurry, Diomedes, to reinforce our soldiers, or all of us will die.

original: Go, bear Patroclus' body to Achilles;   And bid the snail-paced Ajax arm for shame.
translation: Go, show Patroclus's body to Achilles, and tell Ajax to arm himself.

original: There is a thousand Hectors in the field:   Now here he fights on Galathe his horse,   And there lacks work; anon he's there afoot,   And there they fly or die, like scaled sculls   Before the belching whale;
translation: It is as if there are a thousand Hectors out there today, you see him one moment fighting on Galathe his horse, and the next moment he is fighting on foot where our soldiers either flee or are killed like schools of small fish before a hungry whale.

original: then is he yonder,   And there the strawy Greeks, ripe for his edge,   Fall down before him, like the mower's swath:
translation: Then you'll see him over there,  harvesting Greeks like they were wheat .

original: Here, there, and every where, he leaves and takes,   Dexterity so obeying appetite   That what he will he does, and does so much   That proof is call'd impossibility.
translation: He appears here, there, and everywhere and decides who shall live and who shall die. His skill is perfectly matched to his desire to kill, so much so that he can do anything he wants, and he is doing so much that proof of it would be called impossibility.

original: O, courage, courage, princes! great Achilles   Is arming, weeping, cursing, vowing vengeance:
translation: Be brave, be brave, princes! Great Achilles is arming himself, weepings, cursing, and promising revenge.

original: Patroclus' wounds have roused his drowsy blood,   Together with his mangled Myrmidons,   That noseless, handless, hack'd and chipp'd, come to  him,   Crying on Hector.
translation: Patroclus's wounds have awoken his sleepy rage, and he is rallying his  Myrmidons  many of whom have been horribly injured and all of them wanting to kill Hector.

original: Ajax hath lost a friend   And foams at mouth, and he is arm'd and at it,   Roaring for Troilus, who hath done to-day   Mad and fantastic execution,
translation: One of Ajax's friends has died, and he is now foaming at the mouth with anger, because of this he has armed himself and come out to find Troilus, who has killed a great many people today.

original: Engaging and redeeming of himself   With such a careless force and forceless care   As if that luck, in very spite of cunning,   Bade him win all.
translation: Troilus has been reckless in engaging our soldiers and even when the odds almost guaranteed his death, he simply kills them and moves on as if luck itself was on his side.

original: Troilus! thou coward Troilus!
translation: Troilus! You are a coward Troilus!

original: Ay, there, there.
translation: Yes, over there, over there.

original: So, so, we draw together.
translation: We are pulling together now.

original: Where is this Hector?   Come, come, thou boy-queller, show thy face;
translation: Where is Hector? Come here boy-killer, show yourself.

original: Know what it is to meet Achilles angry:   Hector? where's Hector? I will none but Hector.
translation: You will learn what it is like to meet me when I am angry. Hector? Where's Hector? I won't deal with anyone except Hector.

original: Troilus, thou coward Troilus, show thy head!
translation: Troilus, you coward Troilus, show yourself!

original: Troilus, I say! where's Troilus?
translation: Troilus, I say! Where's Troilus?

original: What wouldst thou?
translation: What do you want with him?

original: I would correct him.
Were I the general, thou shouldst have my office Ere that correction. Troilus, I say! what, Troilus!
translation: You aren't taking the pleasure of killing him away from me. Troilus, I say! Where are you, Troilus!

original: O traitor Diomed! turn thy false face, thou traitor, And pay thy life thou owest me for my horse!
translation: Oh it is the traitor Diomedes! Turn your deceitful face towards me, you traitor, and die for stealing my horse!

original: Ha, art thou there?
translation: Ha, where are you?

original: I'll fight with him alone: stand, Diomed.
translation: I want to fight him alone, stand back Diomedes.

original: He is my prize; I will not look upon.
translation: I have the right to kill him, I won't just be a spectator.

original: Come, both you cogging Greeks; have at you both!
translation: Come, both of you cheating Greeks, I'll fight you both!

original: Yea, Troilus? O, well fought, my youngest brother!
translation: Is that Troilus? Oh, you fight well youngest brother!

original: Now do I see thee, ha! have at thee, Hector!
translation: Now I see you, ha! Defend yourself, Hector!

original: Pause, if thou wilt.
I do disdain thy courtesy, proud Trojan:
translation: I disdain your courtesy, proud Trojan.

original: Be happy that my arms are out of use:
translation: You should be glad that I am out of practice.

original: My rest and negligence befriends thee now,   But thou anon shalt hear of me again;   Till when, go seek thy fortune.
translation: My rest and recent refusal to fight has given you the advantage, but I will find you another time, until then go and do what you want.

original: Fare thee well: I would have been much more a fresher man, Had I expected thee. How now, my brother!
translation: Goodbye, I wouldn't have let myself be so tired if I knew I would have to fight you. What's this, here's my brother!

original: Ajax hath ta'en AEneas: shall it be?
translation: Ajax has captured Aeneas, should we allow him to do this?

original: No, by the flame of yonder glorious heaven,   He shall not carry him:
translation: No, by the sun, he won't be allowed to capture him.

original: I'll be ta'en too,   Or bring him off:
translation: I'll either be captured as well, or I'll set Aeneas free.

original: fate, hear me what I say!   I reck not though I end my life to-day.
translation: Fate, hear what I am saying! I don't care if I die today.

original: Stand, stand, thou Greek; thou art a goodly mark:
translation: Stand and fight me, you Greek. You are a worthy target.

original: No? wilt thou not? I like thy armour well;   I'll frush it and unlock the rivets all,   But I'll be master of it:
translation: No? You won't fight me? I like your armor, I'll hack at it and take it to pieces, so that I can keep it for myself.

original: wilt thou not,   beast, abide?   Why, then fly on, I'll hunt thee for thy hide.
translation: Won't you fight me, you beast? Why then keep running away, and  I'll hunt you for your hide .

original: Come here about me, you my Myrmidons;
translation: Gather around me, my Myrmidons, and listen to what I say.

original: Mark what I say. Attend me where I wheel:   Strike not a stroke, but keep yourselves in breath:   And when I have the bloody Hector found,   Empale him with your weapons round about;
translation: Form up behind me and follow me as I turn, don't attack anyone but instead keep yourselves ready, and when I have found the bloodied Hector,  surround him with your weapons and kill him fiercely .

original: In fellest manner execute your aims.   Follow me, sirs, and my proceedings eye:   It is decreed Hector the great must die.
translation: Follow me, men, and watch where I go. I demand that the great Hector must die.

original: The cuckold and the cuckold-maker are at it.
translation: The cuckold and the man who made him a cuckold are fighting each other.

original: Now,   bull! now, dog! 'Loo, Paris, 'loo! now my double-   henned sparrow! 'loo, Paris, 'loo!
translation: Attack him, bull! Attack him, dog! Go, Paris, go!  Fight .  Go, Paris, go!

original: The bull has the   game: ware horns, ho!
translation: The bull can fight, watch out for his horns, woah!

original: Turn, slave, and fight.
What art thou?
translation: Who are you?

original: A bastard son of Priam's.
translation: One of Priam's bastards.

original: I am a bastard too; I love bastards: I am a bastard   begot, bastard instructed, bastard in mind, bastard   in valour, in every thing illegitimate.
translation: I am a  bastard  too, I love bastards. I am a bastard by parentage, educated by a bastard, a bastard in my thoughts, when I fight I fight like a bastard, and am illegitimate in every way.

original: One bear will   not bite another, and wherefore should one bastard?
translation: Bears  don't eat each other, so why would two bastards?

original: Take heed, the quarrel's most ominous to us: if the   son of a whore fight for a whore, he tempts judgment:   farewell, bastard.
translation: Listen, two children with whores for mothers shouldn't fight, because we might be brothers, and then we would be guilty of killing a relative. Goodbye, bastard.

original: The devil take thee, coward!
translation: Curse you, coward.

original: Most putrefied core, so fair without,   Thy goodly armour thus hath cost thy life.
translation: Cowardly man, so beautiful on the outside, your beautiful armor has cost you your life.

original: Now is my day's work done; I'll take good breath:   Rest, sword; thou hast thy fill of blood and death.
translation: Now I am able to finish for the day, and rest well. Take a rest, sword, you have had enough blood and death today.

original: Look, Hector, how the sun begins to set;   How ugly night comes breathing at his heels:
translation: Look how the sun begins to  set , Hector. Now  night  is pursuing him.

original: Even with the vail and darking of the sun,   To close the day up, Hector's life is done.
translation: Just as a dark shadow is coming over the earth, Hector's life is over.

original: I am unarm'd; forego this vantage, Greek.
translation: I have disarmed, don't take advantage like this, Greek.

original: Strike, fellows, strike; this is the man I seek.
translation: Attack, men, attack. This is the man I have been hunting.

original: So, Ilion, fall thou next! now, Troy, sink down!
translation: Now, Troy, you will fall next. Fall, Troy, now!

original: Here lies thy heart, thy sinews, and thy bone.
translation: Here's your heart, strength and support.

original: On, Myrmidons, and cry you all amain,   'Achilles hath the mighty Hector slain.'
translation: Carry on, Myrmidons, and cry out that "Achilles has killed the mighty Hector."

original: Hark! a retire upon our Grecian part.
translation: Listen, are the Greeks retreating?

original: The Trojan trumpets sound the like, my lord.
translation: The Trojan trumpets are doing the same thing as ours, my lord.

original: The dragon wing of night o'erspreads the earth,   And, stickler-like, the armies separates.
translation: A s night comes our armies stop fighting.

original: My half-supp'd sword, that frankly would have fed,   Pleased with this dainty bait, thus goes to bed.
translation: My sword has only just begun to drink blood, and it would have liked to be fed, but it can go to bed happy at having killed this man.

original: Come, tie his body to my horse's tail; Along the field I will the Trojan trail.
translation: Come, tie his body to my horse's tail, I'll drag the Trojan through the battlefield.

original: Hark! hark! what shout is that?
translation: Listen! Listen! Who is shouting like that?

original: Peace, drums!
translation: Drums, stop playing!

original: Achilles! Achilles! Hector's slain! Achilles.
translation: Achilles! Achilles! Hector's slain! Achilles!

original: The bruit is, Hector's slain, and by Achilles.
translation: The message is that Hector's slain, and by Achilles.

original: If it be so, yet bragless let it be; Great Hector was a man as good as he.
translation: If that's true he shouldn't boast about it. Great Hector was as good a man as Achilles.

original: March patiently along: let one be sent   To pray Achilles see us at our tent.
translation: Let's carry on walking back, send someone to ask Achilles to see us in our tent.

original: If in his death the gods have us befriended,   Great Troy is ours, and our sharp wars are ended.
translation: If the gods have let Hector die then Troy is ours and these awful wars will be over.

original: Stand, ho! yet are we masters of the field: Never go home; here starve we out the night.
translation: Keep fighting! We are winning the battle. Never return home, we'll fight throughout the night.

original: Hector is slain.
translation: Hector is dead.

original: Hector! the gods forbid!
translation: Hector! Oh gods, don't let it be true!

original: He's dead; and at the murderer's horse's tail,   In beastly sort, dragg'd through the shameful field.
translation: He's dead, and he is being dragged through the shameful battlefield from his killer's horse's tail like an animal.

original: Frown on, you heavens, effect your rage with speed!   Sit, gods, upon your thrones, and smile at Troy!
translation: Be angry at this, gods, and smite them! Oh gods, sitting on your thrones, and smile on Troy!

original: I say, at once let your brief plagues be mercy,   And linger not our sure destructions on!
translation: Put us out of our misery, and don't prolong our destruction!

original: My lord, you do discomfort all the host!
translation: My lord, you are upsetting our army.

original: You understand me not that tell me so:   I do not speak of flight, of fear, of death,   But dare all imminence that gods and men   Address their dangers in.
translation: You don't understand me, I'm not saying we should run away, or be afraid, or that we will die, but I challenge all imminent dangers from gods and men that they are preparing for me.

original: Hector is gone:   Who shall tell Priam so, or Hecuba?   Let him that will a screech-owl aye be call'd,   Go in to Troy, and say there, Hector's dead:
translation: Hector is dead, and who is going to tell Priam or Hecuba? Send someone who is prepared to tell this ominous news go to Troy and tell them that Hector is dead.

original: There is a word will Priam turn to stone;   Make wells and Niobes of the maids and wives,   Cold statues of the youth, and, in a word,   Scare Troy out of itself.
translation: That word will make Priam turn to stone, that will make young women and wives turn into  wells of tears , and, with that one sentence, scare Troy out of its senses.

original: But, march away:   Hector is dead; there is no more to say.   Stay yet. You vile abominable tents,   Thus proudly pitched upon our Phrygian plains,   Let Titan rise as early as he dare,   I'll through and through you!
translation: Go, march away, Hector is dead, there's nothing else to say. But you hateful tents that are pitched proudly outside our city, you can stay.

original: and, thou great-sized  coward,   No space of earth shall sunder our two hates:   I'll haunt thee like a wicked conscience still,   That mouldeth goblins swift as frenzy's thoughts.
translation: Let the sun rise early tomorrow, because I will run you through with my sword! And you,  huge coward , there is no distance that shall stop me hating you. I'll haunt you like a bad conscience that created goblins as quick as frenzied thoughts.

original: Strike a free march to Troy! with comfort go:   Hope of revenge shall hide our inward woe.
translation: March quickly into Troy, and go with the comfort: hope of revenge will hide our inner sorrow.

original: But hear you, hear you!
translation: Listen, listen!

original: Hence, broker-lackey! ignomy and shame Pursue thy life, and live aye with thy name!
translation: Go away, you middleman! May dishonor and shame follow you for the rest of your life, and may your name always mean "pimp."

original: A goodly medicine for my aching bones! O world!   world! world! thus is the poor agent despised!
translation: Oh, this is a good medicine for my aching bones! Oh world! World! World! In this way the poor servant is hated!

original: O traitors and bawds, how earnestly are you set   a-work, and how ill requited! why should our   endeavour be so loved and the performance so loathed?
translation: Oh traitors and matchmakers, how honestly are you made to work, and how badly are you rewarded? Why should people love what we make possible, but hate us when we do it?

original: what verse for it? what instance for it? Let me see:
translation: What poem can describe this What argument can I used to object to this? Let me see:

original: Full merrily the humble-bee doth sing,   Till he hath lost his honey and his sting;   And being once subdued in armed tail,   Sweet honey and sweet notes together fail.
translation: The  bumble bee  sings very merrily, Until he has lost his  honey and his sting . And when his weapon has been subdued, His sweet praise and happy words are spent.

original: Good traders in the flesh, set this in your   painted cloths.   As many as be here of pander's hall,   Your eyes, half out, weep out at Pandar's fall;
translation: Men who trade in flesh, make pictures out of this: "As many people here are in  Pandar's house , even though your eyes are  half-gone , you should still cry for Pandarus's sad fate.

original: Or if you cannot weep, yet give some groans,   Though not for me, yet for your aching bones.   Brethren and sisters of the hold-door trade,   Some two months hence my will shall here be made:
translation: If you cannot weep, groan instead, and if not for me then for your  aching bones ."  Brothers and sisters  of the prostitution business,  two months from now I'll die and my will  will  be read .

original: It should be now, but that my fear is this,   Some galled goose of Winchester would hiss:
translation: I would put it on now, but I am worried that some bitter  Winchester goose  would shout at me.

original: Till then I'll sweat and seek about for eases,   And at that time bequeathe you my diseases.
translation: Until then I will try to find something to help ease my symptoms, and at that time I will let you inherit my diseases.

original: Cease to persuade, my loving Proteus:
translation: Stop trying to convince me, enamored Proteus!

original: Home-keeping youth have ever homely wits.
translation: Young people who always stay at home are very dull.

original: Were't not affection chains thy tender days   To the sweet glances of thy honour'd love,
translation: If love didn't keep you here—chaining you to your beloved's sweet looks—

original: I rather would entreat thy company   To see the wonders of the world abroad,
translation: I would ask you to join me, so you can see the wonders of the world abroad.

original: Than, living dully sluggardized at home,
translation: That's better than to live in a dull way, being lazy at home

original: Wear out thy youth with shapeless idleness.
translation: and wasting your youth by doing nothing.

original: But since thou lovest, love still and thrive therein,   Even as I would when I to love begin.
translation: But since you're in love, continue to love and let your love grow. I'll do the same when I fall in love.

original: Wilt thou be gone?   Sweet Valentine, adieu!
translation: Are you going, then?  Sweet Valentine, goodbye!

original: Think on thy Proteus, when thou haply seest   Some rare note-worthy object in thy travel:
translation: Don't forget your Proteus, when you happen upon some special, remarkable object on your travels.

original: Wish me partaker in thy happiness   When thou dost meet good hap;
translation: Let me be a part of your happiness,  when you stumble upon good luck.

original: and in thy danger,   If ever danger do environ thee,   Commend thy grievance to my holy prayers,   For I will be thy beadsman, Valentine.
translation: And when you are in danger—if you ever are surrounded by trouble—direct your unhappiness to me, and I will pray for you, Valentine.

original: And on a love-book pray for my success?
Upon some book I love I'll pray for thee.
translation: I swear I'll pray for you, on some book I love.

original: That's on some shallow story of deep love: How young Leander cross'd the Hellespont.
That's a deep story of a deeper love: For he was more than over shoes in love.
translation: That's a deep story of even a deeper love, since he was head over heels in love.

original: 'Tis true; for you are over boots in love, And yet you never swum the Hellespont.
translation: That's true. You, though, are head over boots in love, and yet you have never swum to Hellespont.

original: Over the boots? Nay, give me not the boots.
translation: I am head over boots in love? No, don't make fun of me.

original: No, I will not, for it boots thee not.
translation: No, I won't, because it doesn't help me in any way.

original: What?
translation: What do you mean?

original: To be in love, where scorn is bought with groans;   Coy looks with heart-sore sighs;   one fading moment's  mirth   With twenty watchful, weary, tedious nights:
translation: To be in love means to court rejection with moans; provoke  disdainful looks with sorrowful sighs; and exchange  one disappearing moment of happiness for twenty wakeful, tired, and exhausted nights.

original: If haply won, perhaps a hapless gain;   If lost, why then a grievous labour won;
translation: If love is won by luck, perhaps it's an unlucky gain.  If love is lost, then it was good for nothing except sadness and toil.

original: However, but a folly bought with wit,   Or else a wit by folly vanquished.
translation: No matter the situation, love is merely foolishness bought with wisdom—or otherwise wisdom crushed by foolishness.

original: So, by your circumstance, you call me fool.
translation: So, judging from this elaborate speech, you're calling me a fool.

original: So, by your circumstance, I fear you'll prove.
translation: So, judging from your situation, I'm afraid you are a fool.

original: 'Tis love you cavil at: I am not Love.
Love is your master, for he masters you:
translation: Love is your master and he has power over you.

original: And he that is so yoked by a fool,   Methinks, should not be chronicled for wise.
translation: And I think we should not consider anyone wise who is totally controlled by a fool.

original: Yet writers say,
translation: Yet writers say that

original: as in the sweetest bud   The eating canker dwells,
translation: the worm survives by feeding off the sweetest bud, destroying the whole plant.

original: so eating love   Inhabits in the finest wits of all.
translation: So consuming love makes one live in the best sense of them all.

original: And writers say, as the most forward bud   Is eaten by the canker ere it blow,
translation: And writers also say that—as the worm eats the most tender bud before it blooms—

original: Even so by love the young and tender wit   Is turn'd to folly,
translation: so too does love turn young and vulnerable wit into foolishness.

original: blasting in the bud,   Losing his verdure even in the prime   And all the fair effects of future hopes.
translation: With love wearing down the bud,  wit  loses its green freshness, even in its prime—and along with it all the promise of future hopes.

original: But wherefore waste I time to counsel thee,   That art a votary to fond desire?
translation: But why am I wasting my time here, advising you—a devoted worshiper to foolish desire?

original: Once more adieu!   My father at the road   Expects my coming, there to see me shipp'd   .
translation: Once more, goodbye!  My father expects my arrival at the harbor, where I will board a ship.

original: And thither will I bring thee, Valentine.
translation: I'll take you there, Valentine.

original: Sweet Proteus, no;   now let us take our leave.   To Milan let me hear from thee by letters
translation: No, kind Proteus.  Let's say goodbye now. W rite me letters when I'm in Milan.

original: Of thy success in love, and what news else   Betideth here in absence of thy friend;
translation: Write to me about your success in love, and other news while your friend is gone.

original: And likewise will visit thee with mine.
translation: And my letters will be similarly full of news.

original: All happiness bechance to thee in Milan!
translation: I hope only that you'll find only happiness in Milan!

original: As much to you at home! And so, farewell.
translation: And I hope you will only have happiness here at home! And so, goodbye.

original: He after honour hunts, I after love:
translation: He pursues  honor , and I pursue love.

original: He leaves his friends to dignify them more,   I leave myself, my friends and all, for love.
translation: He leaves his friends to  honor  them more. And I abandon myself, my friends, and everything—all for the sake of love.

original: Thou, Julia, thou hast metamorphosed me,
translation: Julia, you have changed me completely.

original: Made me neglect my studies,   lose my time,   War with good counsel,   set the world at nought;   Made wit with musing weak,   heart sick with thought.
translation: You've   made me neglect my studies;  waste my time;  combat good advice;  think nothing of the world; exhaust my wits with wondering;  and sicken my heart with thinking!

original: Sir Proteus, save you! Saw you my master?
translation: God save you, Sir Proteus! Have you seen my master Valentine?

original: But now he parted hence, to embark for Milan.
translation: He just left here, to set off for Milan.

original: Twenty to one then he is shipp'd already, And I have play'd the sheep in losing him.
Indeed, a sheep doth very often stray, An if the shepherd be a while away.
translation: Indeed, a sheep wanders very often, if the shepherd is away for a while.

original: You conclude that my master is a shepherd, then, and I a sheep?
translation: You agree that my master is a shepherd, then? And I am a sheep?

original: I do.
translation: I do.

original: Why then, my horns are his horns, whether I wake or  sleep.
translation: Well then, since he owns me, my horns belong to him—whether I am awake or asleep.

original: A silly answer and fitting well a sheep.
translation: That's a silly answer, suitable for a sheep.

original: This proves me still a sheep.
translation: This proves that I am still a sheep.

original: True; and thy master a shepherd.
translation: True, and your master is a shepherd.

original: Nay, that I can deny by a circumstance.
translation: No, I can deny that with a logical argument.

original: It shall go hard but I'll prove it by another.
translation: Well, it may be a challenge, but I can prove it by another argument.

original: The shepherd seeks the sheep,   and not the sheep the   shepherd;
translation: The shepherd looks for the sheep; the sheep doesn't look for its shepherd.

original: but I seek my master,   and my master seeks   not me:   therefore I am no sheep.
translation: But  I  look for my master, and my master does not look for me. That's why I'm  not  a sheep.

original: The sheep for fodder follow the shepherd;
translation: The sheep will follow the shepherd because the shepherd is the one who feeds the sheep.

original: the   shepherd for food follows not the sheep:
translation: The shepherd doesn't follow the sheep to be fed.

original: thou for   wages followest thy master;   thy master for wages   follows not thee:
translation: You follow your master because he pays you. Y our master does not follow you, because you don't pay him.

original: therefore thou art a sheep.
translation: That's why you  are  a sheep.

original: Such another proof will make me cry 'baa.'
translation: Such an explanation makes me want to say "baa."

original: But, dost thou hear? Gavest thou my letter to Julia?
translation: But tell me: did you give my letter to Julia?

original: Ay sir:   I, a lost mutton,   gave your letter to her,   a laced mutton,
translation: Yes sir.  I, a lost sheep,  gave your letter to her,  @ .

original: and she, a laced mutton,   gave me, a   lost mutton, nothing for my labour.
translation: And she, this prostitute,  gave me, a lost sheep, nothing for my work.

original: Here's too small a pasture for such store of muttons.
translation: This field is not big enough for such a great quantity of sheep.

original: If the ground be overcharged, you were best stick her.
Nay: in that you are astray, 'twere best pound you.
Nay, sir, less than a pound shall serve me for carrying your letter.
You mistake; I mean the pound,—a pinfold.
translation: You are mistaken. I mean the pound—an animal pen.

original: From a pound to a pin?   Fold it over and over,
translation: From a pound to a  pin ?   Multiply and fold it  over and over,

original: 'Tis threefold too little for carrying a letter to   your lover.
translation: and it's three times too little for carrying a letter to your lover.

original: But what said she?
translation: But what did she say?

original: Ay.
translation: Yes.

original: Nod—Ay—why, that's noddy.
You mistook, sir; I say, she did nod: and you ask me if she did nod; and I say, 'Ay.'
translation: You misunderstood me, sir. I am saying that she nodded. And you asked me if she nodded, and I said: "Yes."

original: And that set together is noddy.
translation: Everything you just said makes you an ever bigger fool.

original: Now you have taken the pains to set it together, take it for your pains.
translation: Now that you have taken trouble to put it together, have it as a reward for the trouble you have taken.

original: No, no; you shall have it for bearing the letter.
translation: No, no. You will take it for bringing the letter to her.

original: Well, I perceive I must be fain to bear with you.
translation: Well, it looks like I must be obliged to put up with you.

original: Why sir, how do you bear with me?
translation: How do you put up with me, sir?

original: Marry, sir, the letter, very orderly; having nothing but the word 'noddy' for my pains.
Beshrew me, but you have a quick wit.
translation: The devil take me, you are quick-witted!

original: And yet it cannot overtake your slow purse.
translation: And yet my wit cannot be quicker than your hesitation to pay me.

original: Come come, open the matter in brief: what said she?
translation: Come, come: reveal the information. What did she say?

original: Open your purse, that the money and the matter may be both at once delivered.
translation: Open your purse, so that the money and the information can be delivered both at once.

original: Well, sir, here is for your pains. What said she?
translation: Well, sir, here is for your trouble.  What did she say?

original: Truly, sir, I think you'll hardly win her.
translation: Really, sir, I think you won't be able to win her that easily.

original: Why, couldst thou perceive so much from her?
translation: How could you understand so much from her?

original: Sir, I could perceive nothing at all from her;   no,   not so much as a ducat for delivering your letter:
translation: Sir, I received nothing from her at all.  No, I did not even get a gold coin from her for delivering your letter.

original: and being so hard to me that brought your mind,   I   fear she'll prove as hard to you in telling your   mind.
translation: And since she was so hard on me—the person who only conveyed your feelings to her— I am afraid she will be as hard on you when you tell her about your feelings yourself.

original: Give her no token but stones;   for she's as   hard as steel.
translation: Don't give her any gifts but  jewels ,  since she is as hard as steel.

original: What said she? Nothing?
translation: What did she say? Nothing?

original: No, not so much as 'Take this for thy pains.'
translation: No, not as much as "Take this for your troubles."

original: To   testify your bounty, I thank you,   you have testerned   me   ;
translation: I  tip  my hat to you for your generosity, since you've given me a tip.

original: in requital whereof,   henceforth carry your   letters yourself   : and so, sir, I'll commend you to my  master.
translation: And in return for my good word, y ou should carry your letters yourself.  And so sir, I'll speak well of you to my master.

original: Go, go, be gone, to save your ship from wreck,
translation: Go, go! Go away to save your ship from a shipwreck—

original: Which cannot perish having thee aboard,   Being destined to a drier death on shore.
translation: it can't sink as long as you're on board, because you're destined to hang. You'll have a drier death on shore.

original: I must go send some better messenger:
translation: I must go and send a better messenger.

original: I fear my Julia would not deign my lines,   Receiving them from such a worthless post.
translation: I am afraid my Julia won't accept my letter  if she receives it from such a worthless idiot.

original: But say, Lucetta, now we are alone, Wouldst thou then counsel me to fall in love?
translation: Now that we're alone, tell me, Lucetta: would you advise me to fall in love?

original: Ay, madam, so you stumble not unheedfully.
translation: Yes, madam. Provided that you won't have sex carelessly.

original: Of all the fair resort of gentlemen   That every day with parle encounter me,
translation: Out of the group of  beautiful gentlemen that talk to me every day ,

original: In thy opinion   which   is worthiest love?
translation: which man do you think  deserves my love the most ?

original: Please you repeat their names, I'll show my mind According to my shallow simple skill.
translation: Could you please repeat their names? I'll reveal what I think as my shallow, simple skill allows.

original: What think'st thou of the fair Sir Eglamour?
translation: What do you think of the handsome Sir Eglamour?

original: As of a knight well-spoken, neat and fine; But, were I you, he never should be mine.
translation: For a knight, he's well-spoken, elegant, and refined. But if I were you, I'd never have him.

original: What think'st thou of the rich Mercatio?
translation: What do you think of the rich Mercatio?

original: Well of his wealth; but of himself, so so.
translation: I think well of his money. But him? I think he's just so-so.

original: What think'st thou of the gentle Proteus?
translation: What do you think of the noble Proteus?

original: Lord, Lord! To see what folly reigns in us!
translation: Oh God, oh God! We are ruled by such foolishness.

original: How now! What means this passion at his name?
translation: What? Why such an outburst of passion at the sound of his name?

original: Pardon, dear madam:
translation: Excuse me, dear madam.

original: 'tis a passing shame
translation: It's very shameful

original: That I,   unworthy body as I am,
translation: for an unworthy person like myself

original: Should censure thus on lovely gentlemen.
translation: to  pass judgment in this way on lovely gentlemen like him.

original: Why not on Proteus, as of all the rest?
translation: Why not judge Proteus like we have judged all the others?

original: Then thus: of many good I think him best.
translation: Well, it's like this: I think he is the best one of them all.

original: Your reason?
translation: Why do you think that?

original: I have no other, but a woman's reason; I think him so because I think him so.
translation: My reasoning is simply a woman's reasoning. I think he is the best simply because I think he is.

original: And wouldst thou have me cast my love on him?
translation: And would you have me give my love to him?

original: Ay, if you thought your love not cast away.
translation: Yes, if you thought your love wouldn't be wasted on him.

original: Why he, of all the rest, hath never moved me.
translation: It's interesting that, out of all of them, he has never wooed me.

original: Yet he, of all the rest, I think, best loves ye.
translation: Yet I think that, out of all of them, he loves you the most.

original: His little speaking shows his love but small.
translation: He gives very few words on the subject; this shows his love is small.

original: Fire that's closest kept burns most of all.
translation: Fire that's the closest to us burns the hottest.

original: They do not love that do not show their love.
translation: You can't love if you don't show your love.

original: O, they love least that let men know their love.
translation: Oh, those who let men know about their love are the ones who love the least.

original: I would I knew his mind.
translation: If only I knew what he's thinking.

original: Peruse this paper, madam.
translation: Read this paper here, madam.

original: 'To Julia.' Say, from whom?
translation: It says "To Julia." Tell me, who is this from?

original: That the contents will show.
translation: The contents of the letter will reveal that.

original: Say, say, who gave it thee?
translation: Tell me, tell me, who gave it to you?

original: Valentine's page;   and sent, I think, from Proteus.   He would have given it you;
translation: Valentine's servant.  And I think it was sent from Proteus.   He would have given it to you himself.

original: but I, being in the way,   Did in your name receive it:   pardon the   fault I pray.
translation: But since I happened to meet him,  I took the letter on your behalf.  I am sorry if I did the wrong thing.

original: Now, by my modesty,     a goodly broker!   Dare you presume to harbour wanton lines?   To whisper and conspire against my youth?
translation: I swear by my modesty that you're a good intermediary!  Do you dare to presume to hang onto this passionate letter?  To whisper and conspire against my young age?

original: Now, trust me, 'tis an office of great worth   And you an officer fit for the place.   Or else return no more into my sight.
translation: Now, trust me, it's a powerful position,  and you should be up for the challenge. If not , then don't come to me again.

original: To plead for love deserves more fee than hate.
translation: To ask for love deserves a greater reward than to ask for hate.

original: Will ye be gone?
translation: Will you leave?

original: That you may ruminate.
translation: Yes, to give you some time to think about it.

original: And yet I would I had o'erlooked the letter:   It were a shame to call her back again   And pray her to a fault for which I chid her.
translation: And yet, I wish I had read that letter!  It would be a shame to call her back again,  and beg her to carry out the mistake that I just scolded her for doing.

original: What a fool is she,   that knows I am a maid,   And would not force the letter to my view!
translation: She is such a fool!   She knows that I am a young girl,  and still she would not force me to read the letter!

original: Since maids,   in modesty, say 'no' to that   Which they would have the profferer construe 'ay.'
translation: Young modest women say "no" when they want the hearer to understand they mean "yes."

original: Fie, fie, how wayward is this foolish love   That,   like a testy babe,   will scratch the nurse   And presently all humbled kiss the rod!
translation: Ugh! This foolish love is so unreasonable that— like an irritable child—it  will scratch its nurse and then immediately be obedient!

original: How churlishly I chid Lucetta hence,   When willingly I would have had her here!
translation: How roughly have I treated Lucetta there , when I would have wanted to have her here!

original: How angerly I taught my brow to frown,   When inward joy enforced my heart to smile!
translation: How angrily I made myself frown,  when an inside joy has made my heart smile!

original: My penance is to call Lucetta back   And ask remission for my folly past.   What ho! Lucetta!
translation: I can only call Lucetta back to make up for it  and to ask for her forgiveness for my recent foolishness.  [To LUCETTA]  Hello, Lucetta!

original: What would your ladyship?
translation: What would you like, your Ladyship?

original: Is't near dinner-time?
translation: Is it almost time for dinner?

original: I would it were, That you might kill your stomach on your meat And not upon your maid.
What is't that you took up so gingerly?
translation: What did you just pick up so carefully?

original: Nothing.
translation: Nothing.

original: Why didst thou stoop, then?
translation: Why did you stoop down, then?

original: To take a paper up that I let fall.
translation: To pick up a paper that I dropped.

original: And is that paper nothing?
translation: And that paper is nothing?

original: Nothing concerning me.
translation: Nothing that concerns me.

original: Then let it lie for those that it concerns.
translation: Let it lie there for the people it's meant for.

original: Madam, it will not lie where it concerns Unless it have a false interpeter.
translation: Madam, I won't let it lie here, in case someone who it's not meant for intercepts the letter.

original: Some love of yours hath writ to you in rhyme.
translation: Some lover of yours has written you a love poem.

original: That I might sing it, madam, to a tune. Give me a note: your ladyship can set.
translation: So I may sing it to a melody, madam. Give me a starting note, your Ladyship, so this letter can be set to music.

original: As little by such toys as may be possible. Best sing it to the tune of 'Light o' love.'
It is too heavy for so light a tune.
translation: Its content is too serious for such a light melody.

original: Heavy! Belike it hath some burden then?
translation: Serious! Maybe it carries a heavy burden, then?

original: Ay, and melodious were it, would you sing it.
translation: Yes. And if it were melodious, you'd sing it.

original: And why not you?
translation: And why wouldn't you?

original: I cannot reach so high.
Let's see your song. How now, minion!
translation: Let me see your song! Come on, you minx!

original: Keep tune there still, so you will sing it out: And yet methinks I do not like this tune.
translation: Keep the melody going so you can finish the song. Although I don't like this melody.

original: You do not?
translation: You don't?

original: No, madam; it is too sharp.
translation: No, madam. It's too sharp.

original: You, minion, are too saucy.
translation: You are too bold, minx.

original: Nay, now you are too flat   And mar the concord with too harsh a descant:
translation: No, you are too  blunt   and spoil the harmony with a variation that's too harsh.

original: There wanteth but a mean to fill your song.
translation: Your song should be filled with  @

original: The mean is drown'd with your unruly bass.
Indeed, I bid the base for Proteus.
translation: Yes, I am pretending to sing the male part as Proteus would.

original: This babble shall not henceforth trouble me. Here is a coil with protestation!
translation: I won't let this nonsense trouble me anymore. I'll make a fuss with this declaration of love!

original: Go get you gone, and let the papers lie: You would be fingering them, to anger me.
She makes it strange; but she would be best pleased To be so anger'd with another letter.
translation: She pretends she doesn't care. But she would feel so happy to get angry over another letter.

original: Nay, would I were so anger'd with the same!   O hateful hands, to tear such loving words!
translation: Ah, I wish I actually felt angry about the letter!  Oh, hateful hands, you tore up such loving words!

original: Injurious wasps, to feed on such sweet honey   And kill the bees that yield it with your stings!
translation: Harmful wasps , to feed on such sweet honey and use your sting to kill the bees that give it up!

original: I'll kiss each several paper for amends.   Look, here is writ 'kind Julia.'   Unkind Julia!
translation: I'll kiss each scrap of the torn-up paper to make up for it.  Look, here "kind Julia" is written.  Cruel Julia!

original: As in revenge of thy ingratitude,   I throw thy name against the bruising stones,   Trampling contemptuously on thy disdain.
translation: As if in revenge for your ungratefulness, I throw your name down on these harmful stones. And I  trample scornfully all over your disdain.

original: And here is writ 'love-wounded Proteus.'   Poor wounded name!   My bosom as a bed   Shall lodge thee till thy wound be thoroughly heal'd;   And thus I search it with a sovereign kiss.
translation: And here "love-wounded Proteus" is written.  Poor, wounded name!  I shall keep the scrap of paper with your name on it near my heart,  and so place a healing kiss on it.

original: But twice or thrice was 'Proteus' written down.   Be calm, good wind, blow not a word away   Till I have found each letter in the letter,
translation: Two or three times "Proteus" is written down.  Be calm, good wind, don't blow away a word of this,

original: Except mine own name: that some whirlwind bear   Unto a ragged fearful-hanging rock   And throw it thence into the raging sea!
translation: until I have found each letter in this letter. Except for my own name: you can carry that off in a whirlwind to a rugged scary cliff, and throw it from there into the raging sea!

original: Lo, here in one line is his name twice writ,   'Poor forlorn Proteus, passionate Proteus,   To the sweet Julia:'   that I'll tear away.
translation: Look, here in one line his name is written twice. "Poor, helpless Proteus, passionate Proteus, to the sweet Julia."  I will tear that away.

original: And yet I will not, sith so prettily   He couples it to his complaining names.   Thus will I fold them one on another:   Now kiss, embrace, contend, do what you will.
translation: No wait, I won't, since he links my name so nicely to his lamenting name.  So, I will  fold them  on one another.   Now kiss, embrace, grapple, and do what you want.

original: Madam, Dinner is ready, and your father stays.
translation: Madam: dinner is ready and your father is waiting.

original: Well, let us go.
translation: Well, let's go.

original: What, shall these papers lie like tell-tales here?
translation: What? Will these papers just lie here then? Like sources of gossip?

original: If you respect them, best to take them up.
translation: If you value them, you should pick them up.

original: Nay, I was taken up for laying them down: Yet here they shall not lie, for catching cold.
translation: No, I was told off for dropping them. Yet they shouldn't lie here, or they'll catch a cold.

original: I see you have a month's mind to them.
translation: I see you like them.

original: Ay, madam, you may say what sights you see; I see things too, although you judge I wink.
translation: Yes, madam, you can call it like you see it. I also see things, although I pretend that my eyes are closed.

original: Come, come; will't please you go?
translation: Come, come. Will you please go?

original: Tell me, Panthino, what sad talk was that Wherewith my brother held you in the cloister?
translation: Tell me, Panthino: what were you talking about so seriously with my brother in the cloister?

original: 'Twas of his nephew Proteus, your son.
translation: It was about his nephew Proteus—your son.

original: Why, what of him?
translation: What about him?

original: He wonder'd that your lordship   Would suffer him to spend his youth at home,   While other men, of slender reputation,   Put forth their sons to seek preferment out:
translation: He was wondering why you had him spend his young days at home while other men—of less significant status—send their sons into the world.

original: Some to the wars, to try their fortune there;   Some to discover islands far away;   Some to the studious universities.
translation: Some go to the wars, to try their luck there; some go to discover islands far away; some go to study at universities.

original: For any or for all these exercises,   He said that Proteus your son was meet,   And did request me to importune you   To let him spend his time no more at home,
translation: He said that Proteus is fit for any and all of these tasks, and he asked me to urge you to not have him spend any more time at home.

original: Which would be great impeachment to his age,   In having known no travel in his youth.
translation: That would be a great discredit to him when he's older, since he wouldn't have traveled in his younger days.

original: Nor need'st thou much importune me to that   Whereon this month I have been hammering.
translation: And you don't need to urge me to do what I've already been thinking about doing all month.

original: I have consider'd well his loss of time   And how he cannot be a perfect man,   Not being tried and tutor'd in the world:
translation: I have considered how he's losing time, and how he can't be a fully-experienced man if he isn't tested and tutored abroad.

original: Experience is by industry achieved   And perfected by the swift course of time.
translation: Experience is achieved by activity, and perfected by the quick passing of time.

original: Then tell me, whither were I best to send him?
translation: So, where do you think I should send him?

original: I think your lordship is not ignorant How his companion, youthful Valentine, Attends the emperor in his royal court.
translation: I think your Lordship is aware that Proteus' friend—the young Valentine—is waiting on the Duke of Milan in his royal court.

original: I know it well.
translation: I know about that.

original: 'Twere good, I think, your lordship sent him thither:   There shall he practise tilts and tournaments,   Hear sweet discourse, converse with noblemen.
translation: I think it would be good to send him there, your Lordship.  There, he can take part in jousts and tournaments; hear elegant conversation; and speak with noblemen.

original: And be in eye of every exercise   Worthy his youth and nobleness of birth.
translation: And he can see for himself every task worthy of his youth and noble social status.

original: I like thy counsel; well hast thou advised:   And that thou mayst perceive how well I like it,   The execution of it shall make known.
translation: I like your advice; you have given a good recommendation.  And you can see just how much I liked your counsel; I will make it happen.

original: Even with the speediest expedition   I will dispatch him to the emperor's court.
translation: I will send him to the emperor's court with the fastest haste.

original: To-morrow, may it please you, Don Alphonso,   With other gentlemen of good esteem,
translation: Don Alphonso, let him go tomorrow, if you like.  He can go with other respected gentlemen

original: Are journeying to salute the emperor   And to commend their service to his will.
translation: who are already planning to travel there in order to pay their respects to the emperor, and to commit their services to him.

original: Good company; with them shall Proteus go: And, in good time! Now will we break with him.
translation: Good company! Proteus will go with them. And just at the right moment! I will tell him now.

original: Sweet love! Sweet lines! Sweet life!
translation: Sweet love! Sweet lines! Sweet life!

original: Here is her hand, the agent of her heart;
translation: Here is her handwriting—her heart's representative.

original: Here is her oath for love, her honour's pawn.
translation: Here is her promise of love—her honor's pledge.

original: O, that our fathers would applaud our loves,   To seal our happiness with their consents!   O heavenly Julia!
translation: Oh, I hope that our fathers will be happy with our love, and accept our happiness by approving our relationship.   Oh, heavenly Julia!

original: How now! What letter are you reading there?
translation: What's all this? What letter are you reading?

original: May't please your lordship, 'tis a word or two   Of commendations sent from Valentine,
translation: If it's all right with your Lordship, it's a word or two of greeting sent from Valentine,

original: Deliver'd by a friend that came from him.
translation: delivered by one of his friends who came from him.

original: Lend me the letter; let me see what news.
translation: Give me the letter. Let me see what news it brings.

original: There is no news, my lord,
translation: There is no news, my lord!

original: but that he writes   How happily he lives, how well beloved   And daily graced by the emperor;
translation: He only writes how happily he lives in Milan; how he is well-loved; and how the emperor shows Valentine his favor every day.

original: Wishing me with him, partner of his fortune.
translation: He wishes I were there with him, to share in his good fortune.

original: And how stand you affected to his wish?
translation: And what do you think of his wish?

original: As one relying on your lordship's will And not depending on his friendly wish.
translation: I rely on what you tell me to do, your Lordship. I don't depend upon his friendly wish.

original: My will is something sorted with his wish.   Muse not that I thus suddenly proceed;   For what I will, I will, and there an end.
translation: My wish is somewhat in agreement with his wish.  Don't wonder why I decided so suddenly. Because I will have what I want—and that's that.

original: I am resolved that thou shalt spend some time   With Valentinus in the emperor's court:
translation: I have decided that you will spend some time with Valentine in the emperor's court.

original: What maintenance he from his friends receives,   Like exhibition thou shalt have from me.
translation: I'll give you the same amount of money that he gets for  allowance from his relatives.

original: To-morrow be in readiness to go:   Excuse it not, for I am peremptory.
translation: Be ready to go tomorrow. Make no excuses, because it's already decided.

original: My lord, I cannot be so soon provided: Please you, deliberate a day or two.
translation: My lord, I can't be ready that soon. Please, let me have a day or two more.

original: Look, what thou want'st shall be sent after thee:
translation: Look, anything you're missing will be sent to you after you go.

original: No more of stay!   To-morrow thou must go.
translation: No further talk of lingering around here!  You must go tomorrow.

original: Come on, Panthino: you shall be employ'd   To hasten on his expedition.
translation: [To PANTHINO]  Come on, Panthino. You will make sure that this expedition is hastened.

original: Thus have I shunn'd the fire for fear of burning,   And drench'd me in the sea, where I am drown'd.
translation: And so I have avoided the fire, because I was afraid I'd burn. And I avoided being drenched in the sea, where I would drown.

original: I fear'd to show my father Julia's letter,   Lest he should take exceptions to my love;   And with the vantage of mine own excuse   Hath he excepted most against my love.
translation: I was scared to show Julia's letter to my father because he would have made objections to my love. And with the benefit of my own excuse about Valentine sending me this letter, my father has caused the greatest obstacle to my love.

original: O, how this spring of love resembleth   The uncertain glory of an April day,   Which now shows all the beauty of the sun,   And by and by a cloud takes all away!
translation: Oh, how similar is this spring of love to the uncertain weather of a beautiful April day! Days in April can be gloriously sunny—until a cloud comes along to take all of that beauty away.

original: Sir Proteus, your father calls for you: He is in haste; therefore, I pray you to go.
translation: Sir Proteus, your father is calling for you. He is in a hurry, so please go now.

original: Why, this it is: my heart accords thereto, And yet a thousand times it answers 'no.'
translation: This is it! My heart agrees to the journey, and yet it answers "no" a thousand times over.

original: Sir, your glove.
translation: Sir, your glove.

original: Not mine; my gloves are on.
Why, then, this may be yours, for this is but one.
translation: Well, then, this one may be yours—because this is only one.

original: Ha! Let me see: ay, give it me, it's mine:
translation: Ha! Let me see! Yes, give it to me. It's mine.

original: Sweet ornament that decks a thing divine!   Ah, Silvia, Silvia!
translation: Sweet item of clothing that adorns a heavenly thing! Ah, Silvia, Silvia!

original: Madam Silvia! Madam Silvia!
translation: Madam Silvia! Madam Silvia!

original: How now, sirrah?
She is not within hearing, sir.
translation: She's not within earshot, sir.

original: Why, sir, who bade you call her?
translation: Who asked you to call her, sir?

original: Your worship, sir; or else I mistook.
translation: Your Worship, sir. Or else I misunderstood you.

original: Well, you'll still be too forward.
translation: Well, you'll always be too hasty.

original: And yet I was last chidden for being too slow.
translation: And yet, last time I was told off for being too slow.

original: Go to, sir: tell me, do you know Madam Silvia?
translation: Oh, that's enough, sir! Tell me, do you know Madam Silvia?

original: She that your worship loves?
translation: Is that the lady whom your Worship loves?

original: Why, how know you that I am in love?
translation: Oh, but how do you know that I'm in love?

original: to walk alone, like one that had   the pestilence; to sigh, like a school-boy that had   lost his A B C; to weep, like a young wench that had   buried her grandam;
translation: to walk alone, like someone that has the  plague ; to sigh, like a school boy that has forgotten the alphabet; to cry, like a young girl that buried her grandmother;

original: to fast, like one that takes   diet; to watch like one that fears robbing; to   speak puling, like a beggar at Hallowmas.
translation: to fast, like someone on a diet; to remain awake, as if worried about being robbed; to whine like a  beggar on All Saints' Day .

original: You were   wont, when you laughed, to crow like a cock; when you   walked, to walk like one of the lions;
translation: Before you fell in love, when you laughed, you crowed like a rooster; when you walked, you walked like a lion;

original: when you   fasted, it was presently after dinner; when you   looked sadly, it was for want of money:
translation: and when you didn't eat, it was because you'd just finished your dinner; when you looked sad, it was because you didn't have money.

original: and now you   are metamorphosed with a mistress, that, when I look   on you, I can hardly think you my master   .
translation: And now you've changed so much because of your mistress, that, when I look at you, I can hardly think that you are my master.

original: Are all these things perceived in me?
translation: Can you spot all these changes in me?

original: They are all perceived without ye.
translation: They are easy to see all around you.

original: Without me? They cannot.
translation: They're visible all around me? They can't be.

original: Without you? Nay, that's certain, for, without you   were so simple, none else would:
translation: All around you? Yes, for sure, because if you could simply hide the signs of love, nobody would perceive them.

original: but you are so   without these follies, that these follies are within   you and shine through you like the water in an   urinal,
translation: But you are so madly in love, inside and out, that all of the symptoms of love shine through you like urine in a doctor's test cup,

original: that not an eye that sees you but is a   physician to comment on your malady.
translation: and anyone who just looks at you can diagnose your illness as if they were a physician.

original: But tell me, dost thou know my lady Silvia?
translation: Tell me, though: do you know my lady Silvia?

original: She that you gaze on so as she sits at supper?
translation: Is she the one that you stare at when she is having dinner?

original: Hast thou observed that? Even she, I mean.
translation: Have you noticed that? I mean, yes, that's her.

original: Why, sir, I know her not.
translation: Well, sir, I don't know her.

original: Dost thou know her by my gazing on her, and yet knowest her not?
translation: So, you know her by my staring at her—and yet you don't know her?

original: Is she not hard-favoured, sir?
translation: Isn't she ugly, sir?

original: Not so fair, boy, as well-favoured.
translation: Not so beautiful, boy, as she is attractive.

original: Sir, I know that well enough.
translation: Sir, I know that.

original: What dost thou know?
translation: What do you know?

original: That she is not so fair as, of you, well-favoured.
I mean that her beauty is exquisite, but her favour  infinite.
translation: I mean that her beauty is rare, but her charm is never-ending.

original: That's because the one is painted and the other out of all count.
How painted? And how out of count?
translation: What do you mean, "artificial?" And how  is it "beyond calculation?"

original: Marry, sir, so painted, to make her fair, that no man counts of her beauty.
translation: Well, sir, she's so artificial, to make herself beautiful, that no man values her beauty.

original: How esteemest thou me? I account of her beauty.
translation: Do you think nothing of my judgment, then? I value her beauty.

original: You never saw her since she was deformed.
translation: You haven't seen her since she was disfigured.

original: How long hath she been deformed?
translation: How long has she been disfigured?

original: Ever since you loved her.
translation: Ever since you fell in love with her.

original: I have loved her ever since I saw her; and still I see her beautiful.
translation: I have loved her ever since I saw her. And she is still beautiful in my eyes.

original: If you love her, you cannot see her.
translation: You can't see her if you love her.

original: Why?
translation: Why?

original: Because Love is blind. O, that you had mine eyes;
translation: Because  Love  is blind. Oh, if only you had my eyes!

original: or your own eyes had the lights they were wont to   have when you chid at Sir Proteus for going   ungartered!
translation: Or if your own eyes had the clear-sighted ability they used to have when you told Sir Proteus off for being disheveled!

original: What should I see then?
translation: What would I see then?

original: Your own present folly and her passing deformity:   for he, being in love, could not see to garter his   hose,
translation: Your own foolishness and her extreme deformity.  Because Proteus—who is in love—at least made himself presentable by putting on his pants properly. A

original: and you, being in love, cannot see to put on your hose.
translation: nd you—also blindly in love—can't even do that.

original: Belike, boy, then, you are in love; for last morning you could not see to wipe my shoes.
translation: In that case, boy, you are in love. Because yesterday morning, you couldn't see well enough to clean my shoes.

original: T   rue, sir; I was in love with my bed:
translation: That's true, sir. I was in love with my bed.

original: I thank you,   you swinged me for my love, which makes me the   bolder to chide you for yours.
