translation: Then I am satisfied. And once again, I'll regard you as an honest man. He who is not satisfied with someone else's repentance is not of heaven or of earth. For repentance pleases both people on earth, and also God.

original: By penitence the Eternal's wrath's appeased:   And, that my love may appear plain and free,   All that was mine in Silvia I give thee.
translation: Repentance calms God's anger. And to prove that my friendship can be honest and generous, I give you my claim to Silvia.

original: O me unhappy!
translation: Oh, I am unhappy!

original: Look to the boy.
translation: Take care of that boy.

original: Why, boy! Why, wag! How now! What's the matter? Look up; speak.
translation: Boy! Come on, boy! What's the matter? Look up and speak.

original: O good sir, my master charged me to deliver a ring to Madam Silvia, which, out of my neglect, was never  done.
translation: Oh, good sir. My master instructed me to deliver a ring to Madam Silvia, which I forgot to do.

original: Where is that ring, boy?
translation: Where is that ring, boy?

original: Here 'tis; this is it.
translation: Here it is.

original: How! Let me see: Why, this is the ring I gave to Julia.
translation: Let me see. But this is the ring I gave to Julia!

original: O, cry you mercy, sir, I have mistook: This is the ring you sent to Silvia.
translation: Oh, forgive me sir. I have made a mistake. This is the ring you sent to Silvia.

original: But how camest thou by this ring? At my depart I gave this unto Julia.
translation: But how is it that you have this ring? I gave it to Julia when we said goodbye.

original: And Julia herself did give it me; And Julia herself hath brought it hither.
translation: And Julia herself gave it to me. And Julia herself has brought it here.

original: How! Julia!
translation: Julia?! Is that you?

original: Behold her that gave aim to all thy oaths,   And entertain'd 'em deeply in her heart.   How oft hast thou with perjury cleft the root!
translation: Look at me, the women who was once the object of all your promises. I received them deeply in my heart. How often have you split the bottom of my heart when you broke a promise!

original: O Proteus, let this habit make thee blush!   Be thou ashamed that I have took upon me   Such an immodest raiment, if shame live   In a disguise of love:
It is the lesser blot, modesty finds,   Women to change their shapes than men their minds.
translation: It's much more appropriate and a lesser fault for women to be deceptive in their appearance than for men to be deceptive in their love.

original: Than men their minds! 'Tis true.   O heaven! Were man   But constant, he were perfect.
translation: Than for men to be unfaithful! That's true. Oh heaven! If only man could be faithful, then he would be perfect.

original: That one error   Fills him with faults; makes him run through all the  sins:
translation: Because one mistake fills him with faults, he commits so many sins.

original: Inconstancy falls off ere it begins.
translation: Being unfaithful gets old very fast.

original: What is in Silvia's face, but I may spy   More fresh in Julia's with a constant eye?
translation: What is in Silvia's face, that I can't see more clearly in Julia's with faithful eyes?

original: Come, come, a hand from either:   Let me be blest to make this happy close;
translation: Come, come, give me your hands. Let me be blessed to make a happy end to this.

original: 'Twere pity two such friends should be long foes.
translation: It would be a pity if two friends like you should be enemies.

original: Bear witness, Heaven, I have my wish for ever.
translation: Heaven, be my witness. I will keep my wish forever.

original: And I mine.
translation: And I will keep mine.

original: A prize, a prize, a prize!
translation: A prize, a prize, a prize!

original: Forbear, forbear, I say! It is my lord the duke. Your grace is welcome to a man disgraced, Banished Valentine.
translation: Stop, stop, I say! It is my lord, the Duke. It is I, a dishonored man—the banished Valentine—who welcomes Your Grace.

original: Sir Valentine!
translation: Sir Valentine!

original: Yonder is Silvia; and Silvia's mine.
translation: There's Silvia, and Silvia is mine.

original: Turio, give back, or else embrace thy death;   Come not within the measure of my wrath;   Do not name Silvia thine; if once again,   Verona shall not hold thee.
translation: Turio, move back, or else accept your death. Don't come close to the range of my anger. Do not call Silvia yours. If you do that once more, Verona won't protect you.

original: Here she stands;   Take but possession of her with a touch:   I dare thee but to breathe upon my love.
translation: Here she is. Go ahead, try to only touch her and take her as your own; I  dare  you to do so much as  breathe  on my love.

original: Sir Valentine, I care not for her, I;   I hold him but a fool that will endanger   His body for a girl that loves him not:
translation: Sir Valentine, I don't care about her. I think a man would be foolish to put his body in danger for a girl that doesn't love him.

original: I claim her not, and therefore she is thine.
translation: I don't call her mine, and therefore she is yours.

original: The more degenerate and base art thou,   To make such means for her as thou hast done   And leave her on such slight conditions.
translation: [To TURIO]  You are all the more degenerate and lowly, because you went to such lengths to win her, and then just left her based on such insubstantial grounds.

original: Now, by the honour of my ancestry,   I do applaud thy spirit, Valentine,   And think thee worthy of an empress' love:
translation: Now, by the honor of my ancestry, I congratulate your spirit, Valentine. And I think you are worthy of an empress' love.

original: Know then, I here forget all former griefs,   Cancel all grudge, repeal thee home again,   Plead a new state in thy unrivall'd merit,   To which I thus subscribe:
translation: Know that I will now forget all previous trouble, cancel all hatred, and allow you to return to your home again. Ask for a new set of circumstances based on your unquestionable merit, and I'll agree to them.

original: Sir Valentine,   Thou art a gentleman and well derived;   Take thou thy Silvia, for thou hast deserved her.
translation: Sir Valentine, you are a gentleman. Take Silvia, because you have earned her.

original: I thank your grace; the gift hath made me happy.
translation: Thank you, your Grace. The gift has made me happy.

original: I now beseech you, for your daughter's sake,   To grant one boom that I shall ask of you.
translation: I now ask you—for your daughter's sake—to do me one more favor.

original: I grant it, for thine own, whate'er it be.
translation: I'll grant your request, whatever it may be.

original: These banish'd men that I have kept withal   Are men endued with worthy qualities:
translation: These banished men that I have lived with have some valuable qualities.

original: Forgive them what they have committed here   And let them be recall'd from their exile:
translation: Forgive them for what they have done here, and let them return home from their exile.

original: They are reformed, civil, full of good   And fit for great employment, worthy lord.
translation: They are reformed, civil, full of goodness, and ready to do you great service, noble Lord.

original: Thou hast prevail'd; I pardon them and thee:   Dispose of them as thou know'st their deserts.
translation: You have convinced me. I pardon them, and I pardon you. Make arrangements for them in accordance with what they deserve.

original: Come, let us go: we will include all jars   With triumphs, mirth and rare solemnity.
translation: Come, let's go. We will bring this all to an end with festivities, joy, and a marvelous celebration.

original: And, as we walk along, I dare be bold With our discourse to make your grace to smile. What think you of this page, my lord?
translation: And as we walk along, I will dare to be bold with our conversation—so I can make your Grace smile.  What do you think of this boy, my lord?

original: I think the boy hath grace in him; he blushes.
translation: I think the boy is charming. He blushes.

original: I warrant you, my lord, more grace than boy.
translation: I guarantee, my lord, that this person is more beautiful and charming than this person is a boy.

original: What mean you by that saying?
translation: What do you mean by that?

original: Please you, I'll tell you as we pass along,   That you will wonder what hath fortuned.
Come, Proteus; 'tis your penance but to hear   The story of your loves discovered:
translation: Come, Proteus. Your punishment will be to listen to the story of your discovered love.

original: That done, our day of marriage shall be yours;   One feast, one house, one mutual happiness.
translation: When that's done, our wedding day will also be yours. One feast, one house, and one mutual happiness.

original: If you shall chance, Camillo, to visit Bohemia, on   the like occasion whereon my services are now on   foot,
translation: Camillo, if, in your duties as a servant to the king, you ever happen to visit Bohemia (as I'm visiting Sicily now),

original: you shall see, as I have said, great   difference betwixt our Bohemia and your Sicilia.
translation: you'll see how different our two countries are.

original: I think, this coming summer, the King of Sicilia means to pay Bohemia the visitation which he justly  owes him.
translation: I think the King of Sicily is planning to visit the King of Bohemia this coming summer (as he should).

original: Wherein our entertainment shall shame us we will be justified in our loves; for indeed—
translation: The parties we throw might not be much to be proud of, but we make up for it with heart! Seriously—

original: Beseech you—
translation: Oh, come on—

original: Verily, I speak it in the freedom of my knowledge:
translation: No, really, I'm being honest—

original: we cannot with such magnificence—in so rare—I know not  what to say.
translation: we can't compete with such over-the-top, such amazing— I don't even know what to say.

original: We will give you sleepy drinks, that your  senses, unintelligent of our insufficience, may, though  they cannot praise us, as little accuse us.
translation: We'll have to spike your drinks so that you get really groggy and won't be able to compliment  or  criticize our party.

original: You pay a great deal too dear for what's given freely.
translation: You don't have to pay us back for anything; everything we give is a gift.

original: Believe me, I speak as my understanding instructs me and as mine honesty puts it to utterance.
translation: I'm only saying what I know to be true. I'm being completely honest with you.

original: Sicilia cannot show himself over-kind to Bohemia.
translation: It would be impossible for the King of Sicily to be too kind to the King of Bohemia.

original: They were trained together in their childhoods; and   there rooted betwixt them then such an affection,   which cannot choose but branch now.
translation: They went to school together when they were kids and became really close, though, naturally, they've  grown apart  since.

original: Since their   more mature dignities and royal necessities made   separation of their society,
translation: Once they reached adulthood and were crowned as kings, they had to attend to business in their respective countries.

original: their encounters,   though not personal, have been royally attorneyed   with interchange of gifts, letters, loving   embassies;
translation: Though they haven't been able to meet in person, they've exchanged gifts and letters and have sent servants on their behalf.

original: that they have seemed to be together,   though absent, shook hands, as over a vast, and   embraced, as it were, from the ends of opposed   winds.
translation: They haven't really been together, of course, but it's as if they were shaking hands or hugging from opposite sides of the globe.

original: The heavens continue their loves!
translation: God bless their friendship!

original: I think there is not in the world either malice or   matter to alter it.
translation: I don't think anything in the world could change it.

original: You have an unspeakable   comfort of your young prince Mamillius:
translation: You're so lucky to have your young prince, Mamillius.

original: it is a   gentleman of the greatest promise that ever came   into my note.
translation: He's the most promising kid I've ever met.

original: I very well agree with you in the hopes of him:
translation: I couldn't agree with you more; I have high expectations for him.

original: it   is a gallant child; one that indeed physics the   subject, makes old hearts fresh:
translation: He's a great kid—like chicken soup for the soul, he keeps us old folks young.

original: they that went on   crutches ere he was born desire yet their life to   see him a man.
translation: The Sicilians who were old and in  wheelchairs  before he was even born are hoping they live to see him grow up.

original: Would they else be content to die?
translation: Otherwise, would they be happy to die?

original: Yes; if there were no other excuse why they should desire to live.
translation: Yes, if they had nothing else to live for.

original: If the king had no son, they would desire to live on crutches till he had one.
translation: If the king didn't have a son, they would want to hang onto life in their wheelchairs until he did!

original: Nine changes of the watery star hath been   The shepherd's note since we have left our throne   Without a burthen:
translation: It's been nine months since I left my throne in Bohemia without a care in the world.

original: time as long again   Would be filled up, my brother, with our thanks;
translation: I'd be happy to stay another nine months, brother, except that I would owe you forever.

original: And yet we should, for perpetuity,   Go hence in debt: and therefore, like a cipher,
translation: All I can repay you with are my thanks!

original: Yet standing in rich place, I multiply   With one 'We thank you' many thousands more   That go before it.
translation: That being said, I'll have to multiply my single "thank you" into many thousands more.

original: Stay your thanks a while; And pay them when you part.
translation: Oh, stop thanking me. You can "pay" me when you leave.

original: Sir, that's to-morrow.
translation: I'm leaving tomorrow, sir.

original: I am question'd by my fears, of what may chance   Or breed upon our absence;
translation: I'm worried about what might have happened in Bohemia while I've been gone—

original: that may blow   No sneaking winds at home, to make us say   'This is put forth too truly:'
translation: unfavorable winds may be blowing, if you know what I mean.

original: besides, I have stay'd   To tire your royalty.
translation: Besides, I've over-stayed my welcome here and I've worn you out.

original: We are tougher, brother, Than you can put us to't.
translation: I'm tougher than you give me credit for!

original: No longer stay.
translation: I can't stay any longer.

original: One seven-night longer.
translation: Just one more week?

original: Very sooth, to-morrow.
translation: Really, tomorrow.

original: We'll part the time between's then; and in that I'll no gainsaying.
translation: We'll say goodbye in a week, and after that I won't argue any more.

original: Press me not, beseech you, so.
translation: Please, stop pushing me.

original: There is no tongue that moves, none, none i' the world,   So soon as yours could win me: so it should now,   Were there necessity in your request, although   'Twere needful I denied it.
translation: There is no one in the whole world better at convincing me to do things than you. And now, if you really needed me, you would have almost won me over—except that I'd still have to say "no."

original: My affairs   Do even drag me homeward: which to hinder   Were in your love a whip to me;
translation: Duty calls and I have to go home. If you keep me here, you'll only be hurting me in the long run;

original: my stay   To you a charge and trouble: to save both,   Farewell, our brother.
translation: if I stay, I'll only be a burden to your hospitality. So if I leave, it's a win-win! Goodbye, brother.

original: Tongue-tied, our queen? speak you.
translation: Hermione, are you tongue-tied? Say something!

original: I had thought, sir, to have held my peace until   You have drawn oaths from him not to stay.
translation: Sir, I'd planned to stay quiet until you'd pushed him to the point of swearing not to stay.

original: You, sir,   Charge him too coldly. Tell him, you are sure   All in Bohemia's well; this satisfaction   The by-gone day proclaim'd:
translation: You're too hard on him. Tell him everything in Bohemia's fine—we heard good news yesterday.

original: say this to him,   He's beat from his best ward.
translation: If you tell him that, he's lost his best reason for leaving.

original: Well said, Hermione.
translation: Well said, Hermione.

original: To tell, he longs to see his son, were strong:   But let him say so then, and let him go;
translation: Of course, that he misses his son is a good excuse. If he says that, we'll let him go.

original: But let him swear so, and he shall not stay,   We'll thwack him hence with distaffs.
translation: And if he  swears  that, we'll not only let him go, we'll chase him out the door with  frying pans !

original: Yet of your royal presence I'll adventure   The borrow of a week. When at Bohemia   You take my lord, I'll give him my commission   To let him there a month behind the gest   Prefix'd for's parting:
translation: Despite that, I'll still beg your royal self to stay another week. When my husband goes to Bohemia I'll give him permission to stay there a month past the agreed-upon departure date—

original: yet, good deed, Leontes,   I love thee not a jar o' the clock behind   What lady-she her lord.
translation: and, Leontes, you know I love you not one bit less than any woman loves her husband.

original: You'll stay?
translation: Will you stay?

original: No, madam.
translation: No, ma'am.

original: Nay, but you will?
translation: Oh, please, won't you?

original: I may not, verily.
translation: Truly, I can't.

original: Verily!   You put me off with limber vows; but I,   Though you would seek t'unsphere the   stars with oaths,   Should yet say 'Sir, no going.'
translation: "Truly!" You can keep putting me off with promises, but even if you swore by all the stars in the sky, I'd still say, "Sir, you're staying."

original: Verily,   You shall not go. A lady's 'Verily' is   As potent as a lord's. Will you go yet?
translation: Truly, you can't leave—a woman's "truly" is as strong as a man's. Are you still intent on leaving?

original: Force me to keep you as a prisoner,   Not like a guest; so you shall pay your fees   When you depart, and save your thanks.
translation: You'll force me to keep you as a prisoner rather than as a guest. Instead of thanking me, you'll have to  pay your fees  when you leave.

original: How say you?   My prisoner? or my guest? by your dread 'Verily,'   One of them you shall be.
translation: What do you say to that? Will you be my prisoner, or my  guest ? Judging by your oh-so-serious "truly," you'll have to be one of them.

original: Your guest, then, madam: To be your prisoner should import offending; Which is for me less easy to commit Than you to punish.
translation: I'll be your guest, then. For me to be your prisoner would imply that I'd committed some crime against you. It'd be harder for me to do that than it would be for you to punish me.

original: Not your gaoler, then, But your kind hostess. Come, I'll question you Of my lord's tricks and yours when you were boys: You were pretty lordings then?
translation: Then I'm not your jailer; I'm your kind hostess. Come on, I'll ask you all about your and my husband's shenanigans back when you were kids. You were cute little kings-to-be back then, weren't you?

original: We were, fair queen, Two lads that thought there was no more behind But such a day to-morrow as to-day, And to be boy eternal.
translation: We were two kids who lived like there was no tomorrow, and thought we'd be boys forever.

original: Was not my lord The verier wag o' the two?
translation: And wasn't my husband the bigger troublemaker out of you two?

original: We were as twinn'd lambs that did frisk i' the sun,   And bleat the one at the other:
translation: We were like two lambs that frolicked in the sunshine and bleated to each other;

original: what we changed   Was innocence for innocence; we knew not   The doctrine of ill-doing, nor dream'd   That any did.
translation: we were completely innocent and knew nothing about evil. We couldn't even comprehend evil.

original: Had we pursued that life,   And our weak spirits ne'er been higher rear'd   With stronger blood, we should have answer'd heaven   Boldly 'not guilty;' the imposition clear'd   Hereditary ours.
translation: If we'd stayed like that, and we'd never had to grow up, we could have gone to heaven and  honestly told God that we'd never sinned .

original: By this we gather You have tripp'd since.
O my most sacred lady!
translation: Oh, you virtuous woman!

original: Temptations have since then been born to's; for   In those unfledged days was my wife a girl;
translation: We have definitely come across temptation since then. But back in those days, my wife was still a young girl,

original: Your precious self had then not cross'd the eyes   Of my young play-fellow.
translation: and you hadn't yet caught my young playmate's eye.

original: Grace to boot!
translation: And wasn't that lucky!

original: Of this make no conclusion, lest you say   Your queen and I are devils:
translation: Please, don't finish your story. Next you're going to say that your queen and I are devils.

original: yet go on;   The offences we have made you do we'll answer,   If you first sinn'd with us and that with us   You did continue fault and that you slipp'd not   With any but with us.
translation: Actually, keep going—we'll admit to being the cause of your  sin  as long as  you  admit you sinned with us for the first time and swear you haven't sinned with anyone else since.

original: Is he won yet?
translation: Have you convinced him yet?

original: He'll stay my lord.
translation: He'll stay, sweetheart.

original: At my request he would not. Hermione, my dearest, thou never spokest To better purpose.
translation: He wouldn't when I asked! Hermione, you've never spoken better.

original: Never?
translation: Never?

original: Never, but once.
translation: Never, except once.

original: What! have I twice said well? when was't before?
translation: What? Have I said the right thing twice? When was the first time?

original: I prithee tell me; cram's with praise, and make's   As fat as tame things:
translation: Please tell me. Butter me up with praise 'til I'm as fat as a  pig for the slaughter .

original: one good deed dying tongueless   Slaughters a thousand waiting upon that.
translation: If you don't compliment a good deed, you'll stop that person from doing a thousand more good things that person might have done.

original: Our praises are our wages:
translation: Your compliments are my reward.

original: you may ride's   With one soft kiss a thousand furlongs ere   With spur we beat an acre.   But to the goal:   My last good deed was to entreat his stay:   What was my first?
translation: For a single kiss, you can ride me for a mile before you'd have to kick me with your spurs. Back to the point: if my most recent accomplishment was convincing him to stay, what was the first one?

original: it has an elder sister,   Or I mistake you: O, would her name were Grace!
translation: This accomplishment must have a sister, unless I misunderstood you. If only her name were " Grace !"

original: But once before I spoke to the purpose: when?   Nay, let me have't; I long.
translation: There was another time I said something good? What was it? Please tell me; I'm dying to know.

original: Why, that was when   Three crabbed months had sour'd themselves to death,   Ere I could make thee open thy white hand   And clap thyself my love:
translation: Obviously that was when, after three long, bitter months, I convinced you to give me your hand in marriage.

original: then didst thou utter   'I am yours for ever.'
translation: At that moment, you said, "I am yours forever."

original: 'Tis grace indeed. Why, lo you now, I have spoke to the purpose twice: The one for ever earn'd a royal husband; The other for some while a friend.
Too hot, too hot!   To mingle friendship far is mingling bloods.
translation: Too far, too far! Friendships that get too close always end with the "friends" having sex.

original: I have   tremor cordis   on me: my heart dances;   But not for joy; not joy. This entertainment   May a free face put on, derive a liberty   From heartiness, from bounty, fertile bosom,   And well become the agent; 't may, I grant;
translation: I'm having a heart attack. My heart is racing, but not with excitement—definitely not. They might as well be relaxed and open with each other here at the party, and blame it on the plentiful food and drink.

original: But to be paddling palms and pinching fingers,   As now they are, and making practised smiles,   As in a looking-glass, and then to sigh, as 'twere   The mort o' the deer;
translation: But holding hands and linking fingers, and smiling stupidly at each other and sighing as if they were having an orgasm—

original: O, that is entertainment   My bosom likes not, nor my brows!
translation: that kind of "party" hurts my heart and  my head .

original: Mamillius,   Art thou my boy?
translation: Mamillius, are you my son?

original: Ay, my good lord.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: I' fecks!   Why, that's my bawcock. What, hast   smutch'd thy nose?
translation: Goodness gracious! There's my little chickadee. Is that some dirt on your nose?

original: They say it is a copy out of mine. Come, captain,   We must be neat; not neat, but cleanly, captain:
translation: They say it looks just like mine. Come on, buddy, we should be part of the same herd.

original: And yet the steer, the heifer and the calf   Are all call'd neat.—
translation: Did you know that a  bull, a cow, and a calf are called a herd ?

original: Still virginalling   Upon his palm!—
translation: Still holding his hand!

original: How now, you wanton calf!   Art thou my calf?
translation: Well, my silly little calf. Are you my calf?

original: Yes, if you will, my lord.
translation: Yes, of course, sir.

original: Thou want'st a rough pash and the shoots that I have,   To be full like me: yet they say we are   Almost as like as eggs; women say so,
translation: You'll need a beard and  some horns  if you want to be just like me! They say we're two peas in a pod—well, women say so,

original: That will say anything but were they false   As o'er-dyed blacks, as wind, as waters, false   As dice are to be wish'd by one that fixes   No bourn 'twixt his and mine, yet were it true   To say this boy were like me.
translation: and they'd say anything. Women are as fake as dyed-blonde hair, as stable as wind, as solid as water, as fair as loaded dice—and yet, it's true that this boy looks like me.

original: Come, sir page,   Look on me with your welkin eye: sweet villain!   Most dear'st! my collop! Can thy dam?—may't be?—
translation: Come here, buddy, look at me with your dreamy eyes! You precious thing! My dear! My son! Could your mother—can it be?

original: Affection! thy intention stabs the centre:   Thou dost make possible things not so held,   Communicatest with dreams;—how can this be?—
translation: I'm going crazy ! Madness is making me think this, making me believe impossible things, making nightmares a reality. How can this be?

original: With what's unreal thou coactive art,   And fellow'st nothing: then 'tis very credent   Thou mayst co-join with something; and thou dost,   And that beyond commission, and I find it,   And that to the infection of my brains   And hardening of my brows.
translation: Madness and unreality together make nothing, so it makes sense that it would hook up with something, and it does, beyond compare, and I'm there already—so much so that my brain is sick and horns are sprouting out of my head!

original: What means Sicilia?
translation: Is Leontes all right?

original: He something seems unsettled.
translation: He seems a little upset.

original: How, my lord! What cheer? how is't with you, best brother?
translation: Hey, are you all right? How are you, brother?

original: You look as if you held a brow of much distraction Are you moved, my lord?
No, in good earnest.
translation: No, really, I'm fine.

original: How sometimes nature will betray its folly,   Its tenderness, and make itself a pastime   To harder bosoms!
translation: See how our bodies give us away, giving other people a chance to laugh at us!

original: Looking on the lines   Of my boy's face, methoughts I did recoil   Twenty-three years, and saw myself unbreech'd,   In my green velvet coat, my dagger muzzled,   Lest it should bite its master, and so prove,   As ornaments oft do, too dangerous:
translation: Just now, looking at my son's face, I went back in time twenty-three years and saw myself back  before I wore pants , in my green velvet coat, with a blunt practice  sword  (it was blunt so that I didn't cut myself, since that kind of toy is dangerous when you're a kid).

original: How like, methought, I then was to this kernel,   This squash, this gentleman.
translation: Back then I was so much like this kid.

original: Mine honest friend,   Will you take eggs for money?
translation: Buddy, would you let yourself be robbed?

original: No, my lord, I'll fight.
translation: No, sir, I'll fight.

original: You will! why, happy man be's dole! My brother, Are you so fond of your young prince as we Do seem to be of ours?
translation: You will? Well, lucky me!  Brother, do you love your son as much as I seem to love mine?

original: If at home, sir,   He's all my exercise, my mirth, my matter,   Now my sworn friend and then mine enemy,   My parasite, my soldier, statesman, all:
translation: When I'm at home I spend all my time playing, laughing, and working with him. He's my friend and my enemy, my shadow, my soldier, my little king-in-training.

original: He makes a July's day short as December,   And with his varying childness cures in me   Thoughts that would thick my blood.
translation: He makes the days fly by and his crazy antics keep me from taking myself too seriously.

original: So stands this squire   Officed with me: we two will walk, my lord,   And leave you to your graver steps.
translation: It's the same with me and my son. Well, Mamillius and I will walk along and leave you two to more serious business.

original: Hermione,   How thou lovest us, show in our brother's welcome;
translation: Hermione, you can show your love for me by giving Polixenes a warm welcome.

original: Let what is dear in Sicily be cheap:   Next to thyself and my young rover, he's   Apparent to my heart.
translation: Let him have what is expensive in Sicily for a small price. Next to you and our son, he's the person I care about the most.

original: If you would seek us, We are yours i' the garden: shall's attend you there?
translation: If you need us, we'll be in the garden. Should we wait for you there?

original: To your own bents dispose you: you'll be found,   Be you beneath the sky.
translation: Do whatever you want. I'll find you as long as you're underneath the sky.

original: I am angling now,   Though you perceive me not how I give line.   Go to, go to!
translation: I'm reeling them in now, even if you can't see my fishing line. Oh, come on!

original: How she holds up the neb, the bill to him!   And arms her with the boldness of a wife   To her allowing husband!
translation: Look how she holds up her mouth, her lips to him! As confidently as if he were her own husband!  [

original: Gone already!   Inch-thick, knee-deep, o'er head and   ears a fork'd one!
translation: There they go! I'm in thick and deep, over my head, and horns are sprouting above my ears!

original: Go, play, boy, play: thy mother plays, and I   Play too, but so disgraced a part, whose issue   Will hiss me to my grave: contempt and clamour   Will be my knell. Go, play, boy, play.
translation: Go play, boy—play! Your mother's playing, and I play such a horrible part that its reviews will put me in my grave; booing and hissing will be the last thing I hear.

original: There have been,   Or I am much deceived, cuckolds ere now;   And many a man there is, even at this present,   Now while I speak this, holds his wife by the arm,   That little thinks she has been sluiced in's absence   And his pond fish'd by his next neighbour, by   Sir Smile, his neighbour:
translation: Unless I'm mistaken, plenty of men have been cheated on by their wives before now. There may even be a man here, as I'm speaking, holding his wife by the arm not knowing she slept with someone else while he was gone. Little does he know that his neighbor (you know the one, Mr. Smiley) stuck his fishing rod in that pond while he was out of town.

original: nay, there's comfort in't   Whiles other men have gates and those gates open'd,   As mine, against their will. Should all despair   That have revolted wives, the tenth of mankind   Would hang themselves.
translation: It's actually comforting to know that I'm not alone in having something taken from me against my will. If all men who've been cheated on gave up on themselves, ten percent of the male population would hang themselves.

original: Physic for't there is none;   It is a bawdy planet, that will strike   Where 'tis predominant; and 'tis powerful, think it,   From east, west, north and south: be it concluded,   No barricado for a belly; know't;
translation: There's no solution to it. We live on a raunchy planet and the raunchiness can strike at any time (and powerfully, believe you me) from the east, west, north, or south.

original: It will let in and out the enemy   With bag and baggage: many thousand on's   Have the disease, and feel't not.
translation: It'll let the enemy in and out with bag and baggage. Thousands of us suffer from this and have no idea.

original: How now, boy!
translation: What's up, son?

original: I am like you, they say.
translation: They say I'm like you.

original: Why that's some comfort. What, Camillo there?
translation: Well, that's comforting.  Hey, Camillo, is that you?

original: Ay, my good lord.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: Go play, Mamillius; thou'rt an honest man.   @ Camillo, this great sir will yet stay longer.
translation: Mamillius, go play. That's a good boy. Camillo, this all-important man has decided to stay longer.

original: You had much ado to make his anchor hold: When you cast out, it still came home.
translation: You worked hard to make him stay. As hard as you tried, he insisted he had to get home.

original: Didst note it?
translation: Did you notice that?

original: He would not stay at your petitions: made His business more material.
translation: He wouldn't stay when you asked. It's like the more you pushed, the more he was convinced his business was more important.

original: Didst perceive it? @     They're here with me already, whispering,  rounding 'Sicilia is a so-forth:' 'tis far gone, When I shall gust it last. How came't, Camillo, That he did stay?
translation: Did you pick up on that? They're all gossiping about me already, whispering, "Leontes is such-and-such." It'll be too late by the time I hear about it. Camillo, why did he finally decide to stay?

original: At the good queen's entreaty.
translation: Because the good queen asked.

original: At the queen's be't: 'good' should be pertinent   But, so it is, it is not.
translation: The queen, huh? Whether or not she's "good" is up for debate.

original: Was this taken   By any understanding pate but thine?
translation: Did anyone else notice this besides you?

original: For thy conceit is soaking, will draw in   More than the common blocks: not noted, is't,   But of the finer natures? by some severals   Of head-piece extraordinary?
translation: I mean, you're pretty intelligent, but idiots wouldn't pick up on that, right?

original: lower messes   Perchance are to this business purblind? say.
translation: It would have escaped the average person—they'd be totally blind to the matter. What do you say to that?

original: Business, my lord! I think most understand Bohemia stays here longer.
translation: The matter, sir! I think most people can understand the fact that Polixenes is staying here longer.

original: Ha!
translation: Ha!

original: Stays here longer.
translation: He's staying here longer.

original: Ay, but why?
translation: Yes, but why?

original: To satisfy your highness and the entreaties Of our most gracious mistress.
translation: To satisfy you and because of your lovely wife's invitation.

original: Satisfy!   The entreaties of your mistress! satisfy!   Let that suffice.
translation: "Satisfy!" "Satisfy" my wife's invitation! That says it all.

original: I have trusted thee, Camillo,   With all the nearest things to my heart, as well   My chamber-councils, wherein, priest-like, thou   Hast cleansed my bosom, I from thee departed   Thy penitent reform'd:
translation: I've trusted you, Camillo, with my darkest secrets. I've confessed my soul to you as if you were a priest, and you've cleared my conscience and helped me to be a better man.

original: but we have been   Deceived in thy integrity, deceived   In that which seems so.
translation: But now I see I was wrong about you. I thought you were a good man, but you're not!

original: Be it forbid, my lord!
translation: That can't be, sir!

original: To bide upon't, thou art not honest, or,   If thou inclinest that way, thou art a coward,   Which hoxes honesty behind, restraining   From course required;
translation: To be clear: you're a liar. You're a coward who  shrinks away from honesty  and who's afraid to do the right thing.

original: or else thou must be counted   A servant grafted in my serious trust   And therein negligent;
translation: You're either a servant who won my trust only so you could betray me,

original: or else a fool   That seest a game play'd home, the rich stake drawn,   And takest it all for jest.
translation: or an idiot who sees what's going on and, for his own gain, pretends it's all a joke.

original: My gracious lord,   I may be negligent, foolish and fearful;   In every one of these no man is free,   But that his negligence, his folly, fear,   Among the infinite doings of the world,   Sometime puts forth.
translation: Sir, I may be careless, stupid, and afraid, but nobody's perfect. Carelessness, stupidity, and fear are just part of being in the world; you can't avoid them.

original: In your affairs, my lord,   If ever I were wilful-negligent,   It was my folly; if industriously   I play'd the fool, it was my negligence,   Not weighing well the end;
translation: As long as I've worked for you, sir, any time I messed up, it was because I was stupid. If I acted stupidly, it's because I made a mistake and didn't think it through.

original: if ever fearful   To do a thing, where I the issue doubted,   Where of the execution did cry out   Against the non-performance, 'twas a fear   Which oft infects the wisest:   these, my lord,   Are such allow'd infirmities that honesty   Is never free of.
translation: I f I were ever so afraid to do something, so afraid I couldn't control the consequences that I wasn't able to carry it out, well, that's a fear even the smartest people have to deal with.

original: But, beseech your grace,   Be plainer with me; let me know my trespass   By its own visage: if I then deny it,   'Tis none of mine.
translation: But, sir, I'm begging you to be straight with me. Tell me to my face how I messed up. If I deny it, then you'd better believe I didn't do it.

original: Ha' not you seen, Camillo—   But that's past doubt, you have, or your eye-glass   Is thicker than a cuckold's horn,
translation: Camillo, haven't you seen (but you must have, unless your glasses are as thick as a  cuckold's horn )

original: —or heard,—   For to a vision so apparent rumour   Cannot be mute,—or thought,—for cogitation   Resides not in that man that does not think,—   My wife is slippery?
translation: or heard (since something so obvious must have started rumors) or thought (for only someone incapable of thinking wouldn't have thought of this) that my wife is unfaithful?

original: If thou wilt confess,   Or else be impudently negative,   To have nor eyes nor ears nor thought, then say   My wife's a hobby-horse, deserves a name   As rank as any flax-wench that puts to   Before her troth-plight: say't and justify't.
translation: Unless you're planning to say "no" or you're willing to claim that you're blind, deaf, and dumb, admit that my wife's a slut who deserves every name you'd call a corner prostitute. Just say it and swear by it.

original: I would not be a stander-by to hear   My sovereign mistress clouded so, without   My present vengeance taken:
translation: I'd hate to even be a bystander overhearing someone talk about Hermione that way—I'd have to fight them.

original: 'shrew my heart,   You never spoke what did become you less   Than this; which to reiterate were sin   As deep as that, though true.
translation: For goodness' sake, you've never said anything that made you look as badly as you do now. Just to repeat what you said would be a crime, even if it  were  true.

original: Is whispering nothing?   Is leaning cheek to cheek? is meeting noses?   Kissing with inside lip? stopping the career   Of laughing with a sigh?
translation: Is whispering nothing? Leaning against each other, touching cheeks? Rubbing noses? French-kissing? Laughing until you can't breathe?

original: —a note infallible   Of breaking honesty—horsing foot on foot?   Skulking in corners?
translation: Here's one you can't ignore—playing footsie? Hiding in corners?

original: wishing clocks more swift?   Hours, minutes? noon, midnight? and all eyes   Blind with the pin and web but theirs, theirs only,   That would unseen be wicked? is this nothing?
translation: Counting down the minutes and hours until midnight, when, while all eyes but theirs are closed in sleep, they might be  wicked  in secret? Is all that nothing?

original: Why, then the world and all that's in't is nothing;   The covering sky is nothing; Bohemia nothing;   My wife is nothing; nor nothing have these nothings,   If this be nothing.
translation: Well, then, the world and everything in it is nothing, the universe is nothing, Bohemia is nothing, my wife is nothing, and everything I'm saying is nothing, if this is "nothing."

original: Good my lord, be cured Of this diseased opinion, and betimes; For 'tis most dangerous.
translation: Sir, please stop believing this sick lie, and soon; it's really dangerous.

original: Say it be, 'tis true.
translation: Say that it's true.

original: No, no, my lord.
translation: No, no, sir.

original: It is; you lie, you lie:   I say thou liest, Camillo, and I hate thee,
translation: It is! You lie! You lie! I say you lie, Camillo, and I hate you.

original: Pronounce thee a gross lout, a mindless slave,   Or else a hovering temporizer, that   Canst with thine eyes at once see good and evil,   Inclining to them both:
translation: You're a disgusting lowlife, a mindless slave, or maybe just a two-faced liar who can pay lip-service to good while really doing evil.

original: were my wife's liver   Infected as her life, she would not live   The running of one glass.
translation: If my wife's  liver  were as diseased as her whole life is, she'd drop dead in an instant.

original: Who does infect her?
translation: Who infected her?

original: Why, he that wears her like a medal, hanging   About his neck, Bohemia:
translation: Um, the guy who's carrying her around like a trophy—Polixenes!

original: who, if I   Had servants true about me, that bare eyes   To see alike mine honour as their profits,   Their own particular thrifts, they would do that   Which should undo more doing:
translation: And if I had loyal servants working for me, that kept an eye out for my reputation instead of just for their own profit and gain, they would do what needs to be done to end all this.

original: ay, and thou,   His cupbearer,—whom I from meaner form   Have benched and reared to worship, who mayst see   Plainly as heaven sees earth and earth sees heaven,   How I am galled,—
translation: Yeah, you heard me. You, his  cupbearer  (don't forget, by the way, that I helped you get out of poverty and make a life for yourself, though you're clearly ungrateful), you who see clearly how wronged I am,

original: mightst bespice a cup,   To give mine enemy a lasting wink;   Which draught to me were cordial.
translation: should poison him. Put him to sleep for good—that would be the best medicine for me.

original: Sir, my lord,   I could do this, and that with no rash potion,   But with a lingering dram that should not work   Maliciously like poison:
translation: Sir, I'm capable of doing that, and I wouldn't use any fast-acting poison. I'd use something slow, that'd drift him off the sleep so that he wouldn't feel a thing.

original: but I cannot   Believe this crack to be in my dread mistress,   So sovereignly being honourable.   I have loved thee,—
translation: But I can't believe Hermione would do this; she's always been so good. I've been loyal to you—

original: Make that thy question, and go rot!
translation: Just stop there, and go to hell!

original: Dost think I am so muddy, so unsettled,   To appoint myself in this vexation, sully   The purity and whiteness of my sheets,   Which to preserve is sleep, which being spotted   Is goads, thorns, nettles, tails of wasps,
translation: Do you think I'm so crazy and confused that I would make this up? Do you think I would destroy my own reputation and my marriage, just to welcome all the pain and difficulty that will come of that?

original: Give scandal to the blood o' the prince my son,   Who I do think is mine and love as mine,   Without ripe moving to't? Would I do this?   Could man so blench?
translation: Do you really think I would just bastardize my son (who I think is mine and who I love as my own) without a good reason? Would I do that? Would any man have the guts to do that?

original: I must believe you, sir:   I do; and will fetch off Bohemia for't;   Provided that, when he's removed, your highness   Will take again your queen as yours at first,   Even for your son's sake;
translation: Sir, I have to believe you. I do. I'll take Bohemia out as long as, once he's gone, you'll take the queen back immediately for your son's sake

original: and thereby for sealing   The injury of tongues in courts and kingdoms   Known and allied to yours.
translation: and to stop any potential gossip from spreading to our allies' courts and countries at large.

original: Thou dost advise me Even so as I mine own course have set down: I'll give no blemish to her honour, none.
translation: You're telling me to do exactly what I had already decided to do myself. I won't ruin Hermione's reputation, not at all.

original: My lord,   Go then; and with a countenance as clear   As friendship wears at feasts, keep with Bohemia   And with your queen.
translation: Well, sir, then you should put on a happy face and go back to have dinner with Polixenes and Hermione.

original: I am his cupbearer:   If from me he have wholesome beverage,   Account me not your servant.
translation: I'm his cupbearer. If he drinks an un-poisoned beverage, then I'm out of a job.

original: This is all: Do't and thou hast the one half of my heart; Do't not, thou split'st thine own.
translation: That's it. Do it and I'll love you forever. If you don't do it, you're signing your own death warrant.

original: I'll do't, my lord.
translation: I'll do it, sir.

original: I will seem friendly, as thou hast advised me.
translation: And I'll put on a happy face, like you told me.

original: O miserable lady! But, for me,   What case stand I in?
translation: Poor Hermione! But what am I supposed to do?

original: I must be the poisoner   Of good Polixenes; and my ground to do't   Is the obedience to a master, one   Who in rebellion with himself will have   All that are his so too.
translation: If I do my job of serving Leontes, then I have to poison Polixenes (who's innocent). Leontes is messed up in the head and wants everyone else to be miserable, too.

original: To do this deed,   Promotion follows.
translation: If I do this, he'll promote me.

original: If I could find example   Of thousands that had struck anointed kings   And flourish'd after, I'ld not do't;
translation: But, wait—even if I could look through the history books and find thousands of men who'd killed kings and done well afterward, I still wouldn't do it.

original: but since   Nor brass nor stone nor parchment bears not one,   Let villany itself forswear't.
translation: And, in fact, since not a single record would tell you such a story, it's obvious how wrong this is in every way.

original: I must   Forsake the court: to do't, or no, is certain   To me a break-neck. Happy star, reign now!   Here comes Bohemia.
translation: I have to get out of here. Whether I do it or not, I'll be hanged. Man, I could use some luck right about now! Here comes Polixenes.

original: This is strange: methinks My favour here begins to warp. Not speak? Good day, Camillo.
translation: This is weird, I think I'm starting to be less popular here. Why isn't he saying anything? Hello, Camillo.

original: Hail, most royal sir!
translation: Greetings, sir!

original: What is the news i' the court?
translation: What's new at court?

original: None rare, my lord.
translation: Nothing special, sir.

original: The king hath on him such a countenance   As he had lost some province and a region   Loved as he loves himself:
translation: The king has the face of someone who's just lost a much-loved territory in wartime.

original: even now I met him   With customary compliment;
translation: Just now I saw him and greeted him as always.

original: when he,   Wafting his eyes to the contrary and falling   A lip of much contempt, speeds from me and   So leaves me to consider what is breeding   That changeth thus his manners.
translation: He looked down at the floor, muttered to himself, and ran away, leaving me wondering what's going on that would so totally change his behavior.

original: I dare not know, my lord.
translation: I'm afraid to know, sir.

original: How! dare not! do not. Do you know, and dare not?   Be intelligent to me: 'tis thereabouts;   For, to yourself, what you do know, you must.   And cannot say, you dare not.
translation: Afraid? Do you know, but are afraid of what you know? Share your knowledge; it's in there somewhere, you must know. You can't just stand there and say, "I'm afraid to know."

original: Good Camillo,   Your changed complexions are to me a mirror   Which shows me mine changed too;
translation: Camillo, your face is as white as I imagine mine is right now. I'm realizing this must have something to do with me.

original: for I must be   A party in this alteration, finding   Myself thus alter'd with 't.
translation: Something has changed forever for me, hasn't it?

original: There is a sickness Which puts some of us in distemper, but I cannot name the disease; and it is caught Of you that yet are well.
translation: There's a sickness affecting some of us, but I don't know what to call the disease. And, even though you're well, you're the one who's contagious.

original: How! caught of me!   Make me not sighted like the basilisk:   I have look'd on thousands, who have sped the better   By my regard, but kill'd none so.
translation: What? I'm contagious? Don't talk about me like I'm a  basilisk ; I've looked at thousands of people, and they've been fine. I've never killed anyone just by sight.

original: Camillo,—   As you are certainly a gentleman, thereto   Clerk-like experienced, which no less adorns   Our gentry than our parents' noble names,   In whose success we are gentle,—
translation: Camillo, I know you're a good guy, and experienced in your job, which is as much a credit to you as a fancy last name is to royalty.

original: I beseech you,   If you know aught which does behove my knowledge   Thereof to be inform'd, imprison't not   In ignorant concealment.
translation: I'm begging you, if you know anything that I should know, please don't keep it from me.

original: I may not answer.
translation: I can't say.

original: A sickness caught of me, and yet I well!   I must be answer'd.
translation: I'm contagious, even though I'm not sick? You have to explain.

original: Dost thou hear, Camillo,   I conjure thee, by all the parts of man   Which honour does acknowledge, whereof the least   Is not this suit of mine, that thou declare   What incidency thou dost guess of harm   Is creeping toward me;
translation: Listen, Camillo, I demand, if you're honorable and you believe me to be, too, that you tell me what horrible things are coming my way.

original: how far off, how near;   Which way to be prevented, if to be;   If not, how best to bear it.
translation: Tell me how far off they are (or how close at hand). Tell me how to avoid it or, if I can't, how to deal with it.

original: Sir, I will tell you; Since I am charged in honour and by him That I think honourable: therefore mark my counsel, Which must be even as swiftly follow'd as I mean to utter it, or both yourself and me Cry lost, and so good night!
translation: Sir, I'll tell you, since you're bringing honor into this. Listen closely and do exactly what I say as soon as I say it, otherwise you and I are both done for!

original: On, good Camillo.
translation: Go on, Camillo.

original: I am appointed him to murder you.
translation: He ordered me to murder you.

original: By whom, Camillo?
translation: Who ordered you, Camillo?

original: By the king.
translation: The king.

original: For what?
translation: Why?

original: He thinks, nay, with all confidence he swears, As he had seen't or been an instrument To vice you to't, that you have touch'd his queen Forbiddenly.
translation: He thinks—actually, he swears as confidently as if he saw you do it or told you to do it himself—that you're having a secret affair with Hermione.

original: O, then my best blood turn   To an infected jelly and my name   Be yoked with his that did betray the Best!
translation: Well, then I might as well be dying of cancer and be named  Judas Iscariot .

original: Turn then my freshest reputation to   A savour that may strike the dullest nostril   Where I arrive,
translation: My reputation is ruined. From now on, I'll stink of this. I'll walk into a room and everyone will complain about the stench.

original: and my approach be shunn'd,   Nay, hated too, worse than the great'st infection   That e'er was heard or read!
translation: I'll be shunned and hated more than the worst epidemic in the history of the world.

original: Swear his thought over   By each particular star in heaven and   By all their influences, you may as well   Forbid the sea for to obey the moon   As or by oath remove or counsel shake   The fabric of his folly,
translation: You could swear by every star in the sky and you could force the tides to stop ebbing and flowing before you could convince him that what he now believes isn't true.

original: whose foundation   Is piled upon his faith and will continue   The standing of his body.
translation: He's built it up in his mind so much now that he'll defend it with his life.

original: How should this grow?
translation: How did this happen?

original: I know not: but I am sure 'tis safer to   Avoid what's grown than question how 'tis born.
translation: I don't know, but it's probably safer to get out of the way than it is to stand around and debate about how it got started.

original: If therefore you dare trust my honesty,   That lies enclosed in this trunk which you   Shall bear along impawn'd, away to-night!   Your followers I will whisper to the business,   And will by twos and threes at several posterns   Clear them o' the city.
translation: If you trust me, pack your things and leave tonight. I'll whisper the plan to your servants and we'll leave the city in groups of two or three, all by different gates.

original: For myself, I'll put   My fortunes to your service, which are here   By this discovery lost. Be not uncertain;   For, by the honour of my parents, I   Have utter'd truth:
translation: From this point on, I offer my services to you, considering I'll be dead if I'm found here after you're gone. I swear on my parents' lives that everything I've told you is true.

original: which if you seek to prove,   I dare not stand by; nor shall you be safer   Than one condemn'd by the king's own mouth, thereon   His execution sworn.
translation: If you want to test it on Leontes, you better believe I won't stick around—you'll be as condemned to die as a criminal sitting on death row.

original: I do believe thee:   I saw his heart in 's face. Give me thy hand:
translation: I believe you; the look on his face said it all. Give me your hand:

original: Be pilot to me and thy places shall   Still neighbour mine. My ships are ready and   My people did expect my hence departure   Two days ago.
translation: if you lead me out of here, you can continue to work for me as my servant. My ships are ready and my people are, too, because they had expected to leave two days ago.

original: This jealousy   Is for a precious creature: as she's rare,   Must it be great, and as his person's mighty,   Must it be violent, and as he does conceive   He is dishonour'd by a man which ever   Profess'd to him, why, his revenges must   In that be made more bitter.
translation: Leontes is jealous of a very special woman and, because she's so special, his jealousy is intense; because he's a powerful king, his jealousy will be violent, too, and because he thinks he's been betrayed by his best friend, his revenge will be horrific.

original: Fear o'ershades me:   Good expedition be my friend, and comfort   The gracious queen, part of his theme, but nothing   Of his ill-ta'en suspicion!
translation: I'm paralyzed with fear. Let's hope we have a safe journey out and that the queen doesn't become a victim, too, of his delusions.

original: Come, Camillo;   I will respect thee as a father if   Thou bear'st my life off hence: let us avoid.
translation: Come on, Camillo. I'll love you as much as I love my own father if you can get me out of here alive. Let's go.

original: It is in mine authority to command The keys of all the posterns: please your highness To take the urgent hour. Come, sir, away.
translation: I have the power to tell the gatekeepers to unlock the gates whenever I want, so just let me know when you think we should leave. Come on, sir, let's go.

original: Take the boy to you: he so troubles me, 'Tis past enduring.
translation: Take Mamillius with you. He's wearing me out; I can't deal with him anymore.

original: Come, my gracious lord, Shall I be your playfellow?
translation: Come here, little man. Will you play with me?

original: No, I'll none of you.
translation: No, I don't want you.

original: Why, my sweet lord?
translation: Why not, little man?

original: You'll kiss me hard and speak to me as if I were a baby still. I love you better.
translation: You'll kiss me too hard and talk to me like I'm still a baby.  I love you better.

original: And why so, my lord?
translation: And why's that, sir?

original: Not for because Your brows are blacker; yet black brows, they say, Become some women best, so that there be not Too much hair there, but in a semicircle Or a half-moon made with a pen.
translation: Not because your eyebrows are dark, although they say dark eyebrows look good on some women. It's better if you pluck them in a semi-circle, or draw a half-moon shape with a pen.

original: Who taught you this?
translation: Who taught you this?

original: I learnt it out of women's faces. Pray now What colour are your eyebrows?
translation: I learned it from women's faces. I have a question: what color are your eyebrows?

original: Blue, my lord.
translation: Blue, sir.

original: Nay, that's a mock: I have seen a lady's nose That has been blue, but not her eyebrows.
translation: No, you're joking. I've seen a lady's nose that was blue, but never her eyebrows.

original: Hark ye; The queen your mother rounds apace: we shall Present our services to a fine new prince One of these days; and then you'ld wanton with us, If we would have you.
translation: Listen, your mother is coming over. Pretty soon we'll have a new prince to take care of, and then you'll wish we'd play with you more.

original: She is spread of late Into a goodly bulk: good time encounter her!
translation: She's looking really pregnant all of a sudden. She'll go into labor soon!

original: What wisdom stirs amongst you? Come, sir, now I am for you again: pray you, sit by us, And tell 's a tale.
translation: What are you all talking about?  Come here, Mamillius, I'm ready to deal with you again. Come on, come sit by me and tell me a story.

original: Merry or sad shall't be?
translation: A happy story, or a sad story?

original: As merry as you will.
translation: As happy as you want it to be.

original: A sad tale's best for winter: I have one Of sprites and goblins.
Let's have that, good sir. Come on, sit down: come on, and do your best To fright me with your sprites; you're powerful at it.
translation: Let's hear it, then. Come on, sit down, come on. And do your best to scare me with your ghosts—you're very good at that.

original: There was a man—
translation: "There was a man—

original: Nay, come, sit down; then on.
translation: No, come and sit down. Now go on.

original: Dwelt by a churchyard: I will tell it softly; Yond crickets shall not hear it.
translation: —who lived by a church." I'll whisper it so quietly that the crickets out there won't be able to hear it.

original: Come on, then, And give't me in mine ear.
translation: Come on, then, and whisper it in my ear.

original: Was he met there? his train? Camillo with him?
translation: Did you find him? His servants? Was Camillo with him?

original: Behind the tuft of pines I met them; never Saw I men scour so on their way: I eyed them Even to their ships.
translation: I saw them while I was hiding behind a cluster of pine trees. I never saw men hurry away so quickly. I watched them go all the way to their ships.

original: How blest am I   In my just censure, in my true opinion!   Alack, for lesser knowledge! how accursed   In being so blest!
translation: I am so blessed—I knew it; I was right. If only I knew less! This blessing is a curse!

original: There may be in the cup   A spider steep'd, and one may drink, depart,   And yet partake no venom, for his knowledge   Is not infected:
translation: If someone has a cup with a  poisonous spider  hiding in it, he can drink and not be poisoned because his knowledge isn't infected.

original: but if one present   The abhorr'd ingredient to his eye, make known   How he hath drunk, he cracks his gorge, his sides,   With violent hefts. I have drunk,   and seen the spider.
translation: But if you pull the spider out of the cup, show it to him, and explain that he just drank poison, he'll start vomiting. I have drunk, and seen the spider.

original: Camillo was his help in this, his pander:   There is a plot against my life, my crown;   All's true that is mistrusted: that false villain   Whom I employ'd was pre-employ'd by him:
translation: Camillo was his accomplice; they're planning to kill me and take over my throne. Everything I suspected turned out to be true. That dirty liar—who worked for me— was a double agent working for Polixenes.

original: He has discover'd my design, and I   Remain a pinch'd thing; yea, a very trick   For them to play at will.
translation: He figured out what I knew, but I'm still in their clutches and they're still playing me for a fool.

original: How came the posterns   So easily open?
translation: How were they able to open the gates?

original: By his great authority; Which often hath no less prevail'd than so On your command.
translation: Camillo had the power to open them—he's done it many times at your command.

original: I know't too well. Give me the boy: I am glad you did not nurse him: Though he does bear some signs of me, yet you Have too much blood in him.
translation: Ah, I knew that. Give me the boy. I'm glad you didn't breastfeed him. Even though he looks kind of like me, you have too many of your genes in him already.

original: What is this? sport?
translation: Is this a joke?

original: Bear the boy hence; he shall not come about her; Away with him! and let her sport herself With that she's big with; for 'tis Polixenes Has made thee swell thus.
translation: Take Mamillius away. He's not allowed to be around her anymore. Take him away! She can entertain herself with the guy that knocked her up.[To HERMIONE]  I know it was Polixenes that got you pregnant.

original: But I'ld say he had not, And I'll be sworn you would believe my saying, Howe'er you lean to the nayward.
translation: But I say it wasn't him, and I am sure you will believe me, even if you were inclined to think otherwise .

original: You, my lords,   Look on her, mark her well; be but about   To say 'she is a goodly lady,' and   The justice of your hearts will thereto add   'Tis pity she's not honest, honourable:'
translation: All right, men, take a good look at her. I know what you're thinking: "She's an attractive woman, but it's too bad that she's a liar and a cheater."

original: Praise her but for this her without-door form,   Which on my faith deserves high speech, and straight   The shrug, the hum or ha, these petty brands   That calumny doth use—O, I am out—   That mercy does, for calumny will sear   Virtue itself:
translation: You can compliment her outer beauty, sure—I mean, she deserves that! But then you have to admit that liars use their good looks to manipulate others into thinking they're good people!

original: these shrugs, these hums and ha's,   When you have said 'she's goodly,' come between   Ere you can say 'she's honest:' but be 't known,   From him that has most cause to grieve it should be,   She's an adulteress.
translation: Your shrugs and your "hmms" show you're hesitant to say "she's honest," right? Everybody believe me; I'm the the real victim. She's having an affair.

original: Should a villain say so, The most replenish'd villain in the world, He were as much more villain: you, my lord, Do but mistake.
translation: If the worst villain in the world said that, he'd be twice as evil just for saying so. But you—you've only made a mistake.

original: You have mistook, my lady,   Polixenes for Leontes: O thou thing!
translation: You've  made the mistake, sweetheart: mistaking Polixenes for Leontes. You monster!

original: Which I'll not call a creature of thy place,   Lest barbarism, making me the precedent,   Should a like language use to all degrees   And mannerly distinguishment leave out   Betwixt the prince and beggar:
translation: I can't call you a queen anymore, because if I did, the word "queen" would cease to mean anything. You might as well call a beggar a queen.

original: I have said   She's an adulteress; I have said with whom:   More, she's a traitor and Camillo is   A federary with her,
translation: I've said it: she's having an affair, and I said with whom. On top of that, she's a traitor and Camillo is in cahoots with her.

original: and one that knows   What she should shame to know herself   But with her most vile principal, that she's   A bed-swerver, even as bad as those   That vulgars give bold'st titles, ay, and privy   To this their late escape.
translation: He knew all about the dirty deeds she and Polixenes got up to. He knew she was a whore and he knew all about their plan to escape.

original: No, by my life.   Privy to none of this.
translation: No; I swear on my life. There was nothing to know.

original: How will this grieve you,   When you shall come to clearer knowledge, that   You thus have publish'd me!
translation: You'll regret this when you come to your senses—you'll regret the things you've said about me!

original: Gentle my lord,   You scarce can right me throughly then to say   You did mistake.
translation: Sweetheart, you can almost totally fix this now if you admit you made a mistake.

original: No; if I mistake In those foundations which I build upon, The centre is not big enough to bear A school-boy's top. Away with her! to prison! He who shall speak for her is afar off guilty But that he speaks.
translation: No. If the foundation of everything I believe turns out to be fake, the whole thing will collapse.  Take her away to the prison! Anyone who tries to defend her is guilty, too.

original: There's some ill planet reigns:   I must be patient till the heavens look   With an aspect more favourable.
translation: There's some kind of evil in the air. I'll have to be patient until this all clears up.

original: Good my lords,   I am not prone to weeping, as our sex   Commonly are; the want of which vain dew   Perchance shall dry your pities:
translation: Listen, everyone: unlike most women, I'm not one to cry, and the fact that I'm not shedding a tear might lead you not to pity me.

original: but I have   That honourable grief lodged here which burns   Worse than tears drown:
translation: But I promise you that my heart is hurting more right now than tears could show.

original: beseech you all, my lords,   With thoughts so qualified as your charities   Shall best instruct you, measure me; and so   The king's will be perform'd!
translation: I'm begging you, all of you, to think clearly, see me clearly, and help the king to do the right thing!

original: Shall I be heard?
translation: Is anyone listening to me?

original: Who is't that goes with me? Beseech your highness,   My women may be with me; for you see   My plight requires it.
translation: Who's coming with me? Begging your pardon, Leontes, but I need some women to come with me on account of the pregnancy.

original: Do not weep, good fools;   There is no cause: when you shall know your mistress   Has deserved prison, then abound in tears   As I come out: this action I now go on   Is for my better grace.
translation: Don't cry; there's no reason to cry. You can cry if and when you find out that I actually deserve to be in prison. What's happening here is only a chance for me to demonstrate  grace .

original: Adieu, my lord:   I never wish'd to see you sorry; now   I trust I shall.
translation: Goodbye, sir. I never hoped to see you regret something; now I'm sure I will.

original: My women, come; you have leave.
translation: Ladies, come on, you have permission.

original: Go, do our bidding; hence!
translation: Go, do what I say! Get out!

original: Beseech your highness, call the queen again.
translation: Please, sir, tell the queen to come back.

original: Be certain what you do, sir, lest your justice Prove violence; in the which three great ones suffer, Yourself, your queen, your son.
translation: You'd better be sure of what you're doing, sir, or what you think is "justice" will devolve into violence that only causes you, your queen, and your son to suffer.

original: For her, my lord, I dare my life lay down and will do't, sir, Please you to accept it, that the queen is spotless I' the eyes of heaven and to you; I mean, In this which you accuse her.
translation: Sir, I swear on my life that the queen is innocent; I'd even die to defend it if you'd accept my sacrifice. I mean, she's innocent of what you've accused her.

original: If it prove   She's otherwise, I'll keep my stables where   I lodge my wife;
translation: If it turns out otherwise, I'll make my wife sleep in the stable.

original: I'll go in couples with her;   Than when I feel and see her no farther trust her;
translation: I'll rig her to my carriage and won't trust her any farther than I can throw her.

original: For every inch of woman in the world,   Ay, every dram of woman's flesh is false, If she be.
translation: I mean, if Hermione's a cheater, then every atom of every woman in the world is, too.

original: Hold your peaces.
translation: Everyone shut up.

original: Good my lord,—
translation: Sir—

original: It is for you we speak, not for ourselves:   You are abused and by some putter-on   That will be damn'd for't; would I knew the villain,   I would land-damn him.
translation: We're speaking for your sake, not ours. You've clearly been manipulated by some crook, and we'll punish him for it. I wish I knew the guy; I would ruin his life.

original: Be she honour-flaw'd,   I have three daughters; the eldest is eleven   The second and the third, nine, and some five;   If this prove true, they'll pay for't:
translation: If Hermione's corrupt . . .  I have three daughters . The oldest is eleven, the younger two are nine and five. If this turns out to be true, they'll pay for it.

original: by mine honour,   I'll geld 'em all; fourteen they shall not see,   To bring false generations: they are co-heirs;
translation: I swear I'll neuter all of them. They'll never hit puberty and they'll never give birth to their own bastard children. Keep in mind, they're supposed to inherit my money and everything equally.

original: And I had rather glib myself than they   Should not produce fair issue.
translation: I'd rather castrate myself than see them unable to have their own families.

original: Cease; no more. You smell this business with a sense as cold As is a dead man's nose: but I do see't and feel't As you feel doing thus; and see withal The instruments that feel.
If it be so, We need no grave to bury honesty: There's not a grain of it the face to sweeten Of the whole dungy earth.
translation: If that's true, then we shouldn't have to do away with truth altogether. Right now it's like truth has disappeared from the face of the earth.

original: What! lack I credit?
translation: What, you don't believe me?

original: I had rather you did lack than I, my lord, Upon this ground; and more it would content me To have her honour true than your suspicion, Be blamed for't how you might.
translation: I'd prefer not to believe you, sir, on this issue. I'd rather see Hermione defended, no matter how you might be blamed for starting things.

original: Why, what need we   Commune with you of this, but rather follow   Our forceful instigation?
translation: Well, what do I need you guys for? I can carry out the investigation myself.

original: Our prerogative   Calls not your counsels, but our natural goodness   Imparts this;
translation: I don't ask your opinions because I want them; I ask because I'm a generous guy.

original: which if you, or stupefied   Or seeming so in skill, cannot or will not   Relish a truth like us, inform yourselves   We need no more of your advice:
translation: If you're too idiotic and inept to realize the truth like I have, then I guess I don't need your advice anymore.

original: the matter,   The loss, the gain, the ordering on't, is all   Properly ours.
translation: The accusation, the execution, and the stakes are all mine.

original: And I wish, my liege, You had only in your silent judgment tried it, Without more overture.
translation: And I wish, sir, that you'd thought this out in your head and never said it aloud.

original: How could that be?   Either thou art most ignorant by age,   Or thou wert born a fool.
translation: Why would you say that? Either you're the most ignorant old man I've ever met or you were born an idiot.

original: Camillo's flight,   Added to their familiarity,   Which was as gross as ever touch'd conjecture,   That lack'd sight only, nought for approbation   But only seeing, all other circumstances   Made up to the deed, doth push on this proceeding:
translation: The fact that Camillo ran away, on top of Hermione and Polixenes' disgusting hook-ups (even if we didn't see them, we have all the evidence except the visual proof), on top of everything else, makes putting Hermione on trial absolutely necessary.

original: Yet, for a greater confirmation,   For in an act of this importance 'twere   Most piteous to be wild, I have dispatch'd in post   To sacred Delphos, to Apollo's temple,   Cleomenes and Dion, whom you know   Of stuff'd sufficiency:
translation: It would be wrong to go about something this serious haphazardly, so I've sent my servants Cleomenes and Dion (you know them; they're good guys) to Delphos, to Apollo's temple.

original: now from the oracle   They will bring all; whose spiritual counsel had,   Shall stop or spur me. Have I done well?
translation: They'll bring back a prophecy from the  oracle  that will settle everything, for good or bad. How did I do?

original: Well done, my lord.
translation: Well done, sir.

original: Though I am satisfied and need no more   Than what I know, yet shall the oracle   Give rest to the minds of others, such as he   Whose ignorant credulity will not   Come up to the truth.
translation: Though I'm satisfied and don't need to know anything more than I already know, the oracle will put other people's minds at ease, especially those ignorant nonbelievers who can't stomach the truth.

original: So have we thought it good   From our free person she should be confined,   Lest that the treachery of the two fled hence   Be left her to perform.
translation: I decided it was a good idea to keep Hermione in prison so that she didn't try to escape like Polixenes and Camillo.

original: Come, follow us;   We are to speak in public; for this business   Will raise us all.
translation: Come on, follow me. I'm going to speak publicly, since news of this ordeal is bound to have spread.

original: To laughter, as I take it, If the good truth were known.
translation: And everyone's laughing at him and at us, if truth be told.

original: The keeper of the prison, call to him; let him have knowledge who I am. @  @ Good lady, No court in Europe is too good for thee; What dost thou then in prison? @  @ Now, good sir, You know me, do you not?
translation: Tell the jailer to come in here. Tell him who I am. [Muttering to herself] Oh, Hermione, you're good enough for any court in Europe. What are you doing in a prison? [The gentleman comes back in with the JAILER]Now, sir, you know who I am, right?

original: For a worthy lady And one whom much I honour.
translation: I know your reputation, and I have a lot of respect for you.

original: Pray you then, Conduct me to the queen.
translation: Well then, please take me to the queen.

original: I may not, madam: To the contrary I have express commandment.
translation: I can't, ma'am. I have orders to do exactly the opposite.

original: Here's ado, To lock up honesty and honour from The access of gentle visitors! Is't lawful, pray you, To see her women? any of them? Emilia?
