translation: Well, isn't that something: locking up an innocent woman and keeping her from friendly visitors. Am I allowed to see any of her servants? Emilia?

original: So please you, madam, To put apart these your attendants, I Shall bring Emilia forth.
translation: If you'll get rid of your servants, ma'am, I can bring Emilia out.

original: I pray now, call her. Withdraw yourselves.
translation: All right, then, call her.  You may all leave.

original: And, madam, I must be present at your conference.
translation: And, ma'am, I'll have to stay in the room to monitor your conversation.

original: Well, be't so, prithee.  @  @ Here's such ado to make no stain a stain As passes colouring. @  @ Dear gentlewoman, How fares our gracious lady?
translation: Well, so be it, then.  [To herself] This is a lot of hullabaloo to make an innocent woman look guilty. [The JAILER comes back in with EMILIA][To EMILIA] How's Hermione doing?

original: As well as one so great and so forlorn May hold together: on her frights and griefs, Which never tender lady hath born greater, She is something before her time deliver'd.
translation: As well as a queen with so many reasons to grieve can be expected to do. Poor thing—because of the stress, she went into labor early.

original: A boy?
translation: A boy?

original: A daughter, and a goodly babe, Lusty and like to live: the queen receives Much comfort in't; says 'My poor prisoner, I am innocent as you.'
I dare be sworn   These dangerous unsafe lunes i' the king,   beshrew them!
translation: I swear—damn the king's crazy delusions!

original: He must be told on't, and he shall: the office   Becomes a woman best; I'll take't upon me:
translation: We have to tell him about the baby. We will. It's a woman's job and I'll do it myself.

original: If I prove honey-mouth'd let my tongue blister   And never to my red-look'd anger be   The trumpet any more.
translation: I won't have many nice things to say to him, I can guarantee you.

original: Pray you, Emilia,   Commend my best obedience to the queen:
translation: Emilia, please tell the queen that I'm completely at her service.

original: If she dares trust me with her little babe,   I'll show't the king and undertake to be   Her advocate to the loud'st.
translation: If she'll trust me with her tiny newborn, I'll show it to the king and will advocate for her to the best of my ability.

original: We do not know   How he may soften at the sight o' the child:   The silence often of pure innocence   Persuades when speaking fails.
translation: It's hard to say how he'll react—he may be touched when he sees her. Sometimes the silent testimony of pure innocence can persuade when words fail.

original: Most worthy madam,   Your honour and your goodness is so evident   That your free undertaking cannot miss   A thriving issue:
translation: Ma'am, you're so obviously good and virtuous that I can't imagine you not succeeding.

original: there is no lady living   So meet for this great errand.
translation: There's no better woman for this job.

original: Please your ladyship   To visit the next room, I'll presently   Acquaint the queen of your most noble offer;
translation: I'll go into the next room and tell the queen your plan.

original: Who but to-day hammer'd of this design,   But durst not tempt a minister of honour,   Lest she should be denied.
translation: Though she only gave birth today, she's afraid to ask them to take the baby out of this prison. If they deny her request, who knows—they might kill the child.

original: Tell her, Emilia. I'll use that tongue I have: if wit flow from't As boldness from my bosom, let 't not be doubted I shall do good.
translation: Tell her, Emilia. I'll use my gift of speech. If I can be as articulate as I am bold, then I'll do well.

original: Now be you blest for it! I'll to the queen: please you, come something nearer.
translation: And God bless you for that! I'll go to the queen. But please, come closer.

original: Madam, if't please the queen to send the babe, I know not what I shall incur to pass it, Having no warrant.
translation: Ma'am, if the queen agrees to send the baby, I don't think I can allow it. I don't have a warrant.

original: You need not fear it, sir: This child was prisoner to the womb and is By law and process of great nature thence Freed and enfranchised, not a party to The anger of the king nor guilty of, If any be, the trespass of the queen.
translation: There's nothing to worry about, sir. The baby was imprisoned in the womb, but she's been freed by natural law. She's not under any accusations from the king, and she can't possibly be guilty of anything the queen did.

original: I do believe it.
translation: I'll buy that.

original: Do not you fear: upon mine honour, I will stand betwixt you and danger.
translation: Don't worry. I swear I'll keep you out of trouble.

original: Nor night nor day no rest: it is but weakness   To bear the matter thus; mere weakness.
translation: Night and day I get no rest. I'm handling this the way I am because I'm weak, just weak.

original: If   The cause were not in being,—part o' the cause,   She the adulteress;
translation: If only the problem weren't her as a person—I can't isolate the problem or cut it out, because it's  her ; she's unfaithful.

original: for the harlot king   Is quite beyond mine arm, out of the blank   And level of my brain, plot-proof;
translation: Polixenes is beyond my reach, out of sight and out of mind, irrelevant.

original: but she   I can hook to me: say that she were gone,   Given to the fire, a moiety of my rest   Might come to me again. Who's there?
translation: But Hermione is here and within my power. If she died, say, in a fire, I might be able to sleep at night. Who's there?

original: My lord?
translation: Yes, sir?

original: How does the boy?
translation: How's Mamillius doing?

original: He took good rest to-night; 'Tis hoped his sickness is discharged.
translation: He slept well tonight. We're hoping he's gotten through his illness.

original: To see his nobleness!   Conceiving the dishonour of his mother,
translation: It's hard to see him like this! He got sick when he realized his mother is disgraced.

original: He straight declined, droop'd, took it deeply,   Fasten'd and fix'd the shame on't in himself,   Threw off his spirit, his appetite, his sleep,   And downright languish'd.
translation: He took it hard, as if her shame were his own personal burden. He stopped smiling, eating, and sleeping and then became bedridden.

original: Leave me solely: go,   See how he fares.
translation: Leave me alone; go see how he's doing.  [The SERVANT leaves]

original: Fie, fie! no thought of him:   The thought of my revenges that way   Recoil upon me:
translation: Shame on you! Don't think about Polixenes— you can't take revenge on him now without putting yourself in danger.

original: in himself too mighty,   And in his parties, his alliance; let him be   Until a time may serve:
translation: He's too powerful; he has too many friends and allies. Leave him alone until the right moment.

original: for present vengeance,   Take it on her. Camillo and Polixenes   Laugh at me, make their pastime at my sorrow:
translation: Right now, just take your revenge on Hermione. Camillo and Polixenes are laughing at me; my suffering is a huge joke to them.

original: They should not laugh if I could reach them, nor   Shall she within my power.
translation: They wouldn't be laughing if I could get to them—and she definitely won't, since she's within my power.

original: You must not enter.
translation: You can't come in here.

original: Nay, rather, good my lords, be second to me: Fear you his tyrannous passion more, alas, Than the queen's life? a gracious innocent soul, More free than he is jealous.
That's enough.
translation: That's enough.

original: Madam, he hath not slept tonight; commanded None should come at him.
translation: Ma'am, he hasn't slept tonight, and he demanded that no one be allowed into his room.

original: Not so hot, good sir:   I come to bring him sleep.
translation: Not so fast, sir; I came to help him get to sleep.

original: 'Tis such as you,   That creep like shadows by him and do sigh   At each his needless heavings, such as you   Nourish the cause of his awaking:
translation: It's people like you, yes-men who encourage his delusional fantasies, that are keeping him awake.

original: I   Do come with words as medicinal as true,   Honest as either, to purge him of that humour   That presses him from sleep.
translation: I came to tell him something so true that it'll work like medicine—my honesty will cure the disease that keeps him from sleeping.

original: What noise there, ho?
translation: Hey, what's that noise?

original: No noise, my lord; but needful conference About some gossips for your highness.
How! Away with that audacious lady! Antigonus, I charged thee that she should not come about me: I knew she would.
translation: What? Get this ridiculous woman out of here.  Antigonus, I told you not to let her get to me. I knew she would.

original: I told her so, my lord, On your displeasure's peril and on mine, She should not visit you.
translation: Sir, I told her not to come near you, and explained that you (and I) would both be angry with her if she did.

original: What, canst not rule her?
translation: Oh, so you're not the boss of her?

original: From all dishonesty he can: in this, Unless he take the course that you have done, Commit me for committing honour, trust it, He shall not rule me.
translation: He can tell me not to do something that's wrong, but right now I'm doing the right thing. Unless he follows your example and locks me up for doing good, he can't be the boss of me.

original: La you now, you hear: When she will take the rein I let her run; But she'll not stumble.
Good my liege, I come;   And, I beseech you, hear me, who profess   Myself your loyal servant, your physician,   Your most obedient counsellor,
translation: Sir, I came to ask you to listen to me as your loyal servant, your doctor, your obedient advisor.

original: yet that dare   Less appear so in comforting your evils,   Than such as most seem yours:
translation: I came because I'm bold enough (unlike your other servants, doctors, and advisors) to call you out on your evil actions.

original: I say, I come   From your good queen.
translation: I come on behalf of your good queen.

original: Good queen!
translation: "Good" queen?

original: Good queen, my lord, Good queen; I say good queen; And would by combat make her good, so were I A man, the worst about you.
Force her hence.
translation: Get her out of here!

original: Let him that makes but trifles of his eyes First hand me: on mine own accord I'll off; But first I'll do my errand. The good queen, For she is good, hath brought you forth a daughter; Here 'tis; commends it to your blessing.
translation: If you want your eyes scratched out, then come at me. I'll leave on my own, but first I have to do what I came for. The good queen (because she is good) has given birth to your daughter. Here she is, now give her your blessing.

original: Out! A mankind witch! Hence with her, out o' door: A most intelligencing bawd!
translation: Get out! You manly witch! Take her away, out the door! That damn busybody!

original: Not so: I am as ignorant in that as you In so entitling me, and no less honest Than you are mad; which is enough, I'll warrant, As this world goes, to pass for honest.
translation: Nah, none of those names suits me at all. I'm as honest as you are crazy and, all things considered, that's honest enough for anyone.

original: Traitors! Will you not push her out? Give her the bastard. Thou dotard! thou art woman-tired, unroosted By thy dame Partlet here. Take up the bastard; Take't up, I say; give't to thy crone.
translation: Traitors! Why aren't you forcing her out? Give her the bastard.[To ANTIGONUS] You old fart! Your wife is the boss of you, you're completely whipped! Pick up the bastard. I said pick it up! Give it to your hag of a wife.

original: For ever Unvenerable be thy hands, if thou Takest up the princess by that forced baseness Which he has put upon't!
translation: If you so much as touch the princess in response to his disgusting words, your hands will be cursed forever.

original: So I would you did; then 'twere past all doubt You'ld call your children yours.
translation: I wish you feared your wife, too. Then you'd know your children are yours beyond all reasonable doubt.

original: A nest of traitors!
translation: This place is full of traitors!

original: I am none, by this good light.
translation: I'm no traitor, sir, I swear.

original: Nor I, nor any   But one that's here, and that's himself,
translation: Neither am I, and neither is anyone here except for you, Leontes.

original: for he   The sacred honour of himself, his queen's,   His hopeful son's, his babe's, betrays to slander,   Whose sting is sharper than the sword's;
translation: You're a traitor to yourself, your honor, your queen, your son and heir, and your newborn baby. You've betrayed them all to gossip and rumor, causing a kind of pain that's worse than the physical.

original: and will not—   For, as the case now stands, it is a curse   He cannot be compell'd to't—once remove   The root of his opinion, which is rotten   As ever oak or stone was sound.
translation: At this time, we can't convince him to stop unless we remove the root of the issue: the completely false idea that's rotted his brain.

original: A callat   Of boundless tongue,
translation: Here's a slut who doesn't know when to shut up,

original: who late hath beat her husband   And now baits me! This brat is none of mine;   It is the issue of Polixenes:
translation: who just beat her husband and is now trying to trick me! This brat is not mine, it's Polixenes's.

original: Hence with it, and together with the dam   Commit them to the fire!
translation: Get it out of here, and throw it and the  bitch  into the fire!

original: It is yours;   And, might we lay the old proverb to your charge,   So like you, 'tis the worse.
translation: She  is  yours and, as the saying goes, she's like you to a fault.

original: Behold, my lords,   Although the print be little, the whole matter   And copy of the father, eye, nose, lip,   The trick of's frown, his forehead, nay, the valley,   The pretty dimples of his chin and cheek,   His smiles,   The very mould and frame of hand, nail, finger:
translation: Behold, gentlemen. Though she might be a  smaller version , she's an exact copy of her father: eyes, nose, mouth, his usual frown, his forehead, the cheek and chin dimples, his smile, the exact shape of his hand, fingers, and nails.

original: And thou, good goddess Nature, which hast made it   So like to him that got it, if thou hast   The ordering of the mind too, 'mongst all colours   No yellow in't, lest she suspect, as he does,   Her children not her husband's!
translation: Hermione's given birth to her husband's mini-me, and I guarantee you she has no doubt that her children are Leontes's!

original: Hang all the husbands That cannot do that feat, you'll leave yourself Hardly one subject.
translation: If you hang all the husbands who can't keep their wives quiet, you won't have any subjects left.

original: Once more, take her hence.
translation: For the last time, get her out of here!

original: A most unworthy and unnatural lord Can do no more.
translation: A king as despicable and unfit to rule as you can't do much more.

original: I'll ha' thee burnt.
translation: I'll have you burned to death.

original: I care not:   It is an heretic that makes the fire,   Not she which burns in't.
translation: I don't care. In that case, the  heretic  would be the one making the fire, not the one burning in it!

original: I'll not call you tyrant;   But this most cruel usage of your queen,   Not able to produce more accusation   Than your own weak-hinged fancy, something savours   Of tyranny
translation: I'll stop short of calling you a  tyrant , but this cruel treatment of your queen on the basis of nothing more than your unsupported fantasy definitely tastes like tyranny.

original: and will ignoble make you,   Yea, scandalous to the world.
translation: The world will see you as horrible and scandalous from here on out.

original: On your allegiance, Out of the chamber with her! Were I a tyrant, Where were her life? she durst not call me so, If she did know me one. Away with her!
translation: If you're loyal to me, you better get her out of this room! If I were a tyrant, she would be dead by now. She wouldn't dare to call me that if she actually thought I were one. Take her away!

original: I pray you, do not push me; I'll be gone.
translation: Please, don't push me, I'll leave.

original: Look to your babe, my lord; 'tis yours:   Jove send her   A better guiding spirit!
translation: Sir, take care of you child—since she is yours. May God send her a guardian angel!

original: What needs these hands?   You, that are thus so tender o'er his follies,   Will never do him good, not one of you.
translation: Get your hands off me! All of you that are coddling his idiotic behavior: you won't do him any good, not one of you.

original: Thou, traitor, hast set on thy wife to this.   My child? away with't!
translation: You traitor, you told your wife to do this.  My  child? Get it out of here!

original: Even thou, that hast   A heart so tender o'er it, take it hence   And see it instantly consumed with fire;
translation: Since you seem to care so much about it: take it away and watch it burn.

original: Even thou and none but thou. Take it up straight:   Within this hour bring me word 'tis done,   And by good testimony, or I'll seize thy life,   With what thou else call'st thine.
translation: I want it to be you and no one else.  Do it immediately, and come back within an hour to confirm you've done it. If you're not honest with me about it, I'll execute you and your entire family.

original: If thou refuse   And wilt encounter with my wrath, say so;   The bastard brains with these my proper hands   Shall I dash out.
translation: If you refuse, you'll have my anger to deal with, plus I'll dash its bastard brains out with my own two hands.

original: Go, take it to the fire;   For thou set'st on thy wife.
translation: Go! Take it to the fire as punishment for what you've made your wife do.

original: I did not, sir: These lords, my noble fellows, if they please, Can clear me in't.
translation: Sir, I didn't do anything. These gentlemen are my friends and can vouch for me.

original: We can: my royal liege, He is not guilty of her coming hither.
translation: We can, your majesty. It's not his fault that she came here.

original: You're liars all.
translation: You're all liars.

original: Beseech your highness, give us better credit:
translation: Please, your highness, give us more credit than that.

original: We have always truly served you, and beseech you   So to esteem of us, and on our knees we beg,   As recompense of our dear services   Past and to come, that you do change this purpose,
translation: We've always served you faithfully. We're begging you on our knees: in recognition of our past and future service to you, listen to us and stop what you're doing right now.

original: Which being so horrible, so bloody, must   Lead on to some foul issue: we all kneel.
translation: It's too horrible, too bloody—and it's going to end badly. Watch us kneel.  [All the gentlemen kneel to LEONTES]

original: I am a feather for each wind that blows:   Shall I live on to see this bastard kneel   And call me father?
translation: You think my mind will be changed that easily, like a feather carried on the wind? Do you expect me to wait around until this bastard can kneel and call me "father?"

original: better burn it now   Than curse it then. But be it; let it live.   It shall not neither.
translation: It's better to burn it now than to deal with it then. But fine, let it live. I'll neither burn it nor keep it.

original: You, sir, come you hither;   You that have been so tenderly officious   With Lady Margery, your midwife there,   To save this bastard's life,—for 'tis a bastard,   So sure as this beard's grey,
translation: You! You've been in cahoots with the Wicked Witch, your wife, to save this bastard's life (and it is a bastard, as sure as my beard is gray).

original: —what will you adventure   To save this brat's life?
translation: What are you willing to do to save this brat's life?

original: Any thing, my lord, That my ability may undergo And nobleness impose: at least thus much: I'll pawn the little blood which I have left To save the innocent: any thing possible.
translation: Anything, sir, that I'm capable of doing. I'll lay down my life to save the innocent. I'll do anything that's possible.

original: It shall be possible. Swear by this sword Thou wilt perform my bidding.
translation: Oh, it will be possible. Swear by my sword that you'll do what I say.

original: I will, my lord.
translation: I will, sir.

original: Mark and perform it, see'st thou! for the fail   Of any point in't shall not only be   Death to thyself but to thy lewd-tongued wife,   Whom for this time we pardon.
translation: Listen closely and do exactly what I tell you. If you fail at any point, it means death for not only you, but for your horrible wife (who, at least for now, I forgive).

original: We enjoin thee,   As thou art liege-man to us, that thou carry   This female bastard hence and that thou bear it   To some remote and desert place quite out   Of our dominions, and that there thou leave it,   Without more mercy, to its own protection   And favour of the climate.
translation: I command you as my subject to carry this bastard to some deserted place far away from this country. Leave it there, to the mercy of the elements.

original: As by strange fortune   It came to us, I do in justice charge thee,   On thy soul's peril and thy body's torture,   That thou commend it strangely to some place   Where chance may nurse or end it. Take it up.
translation: It appeared in my life by a stroke of bad luck. Therefore, I command that you, on pain of damnation and death, leave it up to luck whether it lives or dies. Now pick it up.

original: I swear to do this, though a present death   Had been more merciful.
translation: I'll swear to do this, though it would have been more merciful to just kill it.

original: Come on, poor babe:   Some powerful spirit instruct the kites and ravens   To be thy nurses! Wolves and bears, they say   Casting their savageness aside have done   Like offices of pity.
translation: Come on, poor baby. May a guardian angel protect you from vicious animals. They say that wolves and bears sometimes take pity on human babies on nurse them, too.

original: Sir, be prosperous   In more than this deed does require!
translation: Sir, good luck to you.

original: And blessing   Against this cruelty fight on thy side,   Poor thing, condemn'd to loss!
translation: I hope you're protected from everything horrible, you poor thing, even though you're condemned to be  lost .

original: No, I'll not rear Another's issue.
translation: Nope, I won't raise someone else's kid.

original: Please your highness, posts From those you sent to the oracle are come An hour since: Cleomenes and Dion, Being well arrived from Delphos, are both landed, Hasting to the court.
translation: Your highness? We just got news that the messengers you sent to Delphos are almost back. Cleomenes and Dion just got to the shore and are on their way to court.

original: So please you, sir, their speed Hath been beyond account.
translation: Sir, they've been much speedier than expected.

original: Twenty-three days   They have been absent: 'tis good speed; foretells   The great Apollo suddenly will have   The truth of this appear.
translation: They've been gone for twenty-three days; they've made good time. That bodes well for the truth Apollo will give us soon.

original: Prepare you, lords;   Summon a session, that we may arraign   Our most disloyal lady,
translation: Men, get ready for a special meeting so that we can have a trial for Hermione.

original: for, as she hath   Been publicly accused, so shall she have   A just and open trial.
translation: Since I've accused her publicly, she should have a just and open trial.

original: While she lives   My heart will be a burthen to me. Leave me,   And think upon my bidding.
translation: As long as she lives, it'll weigh on my heart. Now leave me alone, and go carry out my orders.

original: The climate's delicate, the air most sweet, Fertile the isle, the temple much surpassing The common praise it bears.
translation: The weather's fantastic, the air is fresh, the island is lush, and the temple is even more beautiful than everyone says it is.

original: I shall report, For most it caught me, the celestial habits, Methinks I so should term them, and the reverence Of the grave wearers. O, the sacrifice! How ceremonious, solemn and unearthly It was i' the offering!
translation: I'll talk about the thing that impressed me the most: the super-spiritual lifestyle (that's how I'd describe it, anyway) and discipline of the priests.

original: But of all, the burst And the ear-deafening voice o' the oracle, Kin to Jove's thunder, so surprised my sense That I was nothing.
translation: The best part was the blast of the oracle's ear-defeaning voice; it was like thunder! I was scared senseless. I felt tiny and insignificant.

original: If the event o' the journey Prove as successful to the queen,—O be't so!— As it hath been to us rare, pleasant, speedy, The time is worth the use on't.
translation: Hopefully the reading of the prophecy is as successful as our journey (for the queen's sake). It was a great, enjoyable, quick trip, but we can only hope it was worth the time.

original: Great Apollo Turn all to the best! These proclamations, So forcing faults upon Hermione, I little like.
The violent carriage of it   Will clear or end the business:
translation: Leontes's violent way of going about it all is about to come to an end.

original: when the oracle,   Thus by Apollo's great divine seal'd up,   Shall the contents discover, something rare   Even then will rush to knowledge.
translation: When we read the oracle's prophecy, sealed and endorsed by Apollo, we'll find out the truth.

original: Go: fresh horses!   And gracious be the issue!
translation: Let's get fresh horses! Let's hope the oracle has something good to say!

original: This sessions, to our great grief we pronounce,   Even pushes 'gainst our heart:
translation: My extreme grief notwithstanding, I hereby pronounce this trial open. It pulls at my heart strings; really, it does:

original: the party tried   The daughter of a king, our wife, and one   Of us too much beloved.
translation: the party tried here today is both the daughter of a king and my beloved wife.

original: Let us be clear'd   Of being tyrannous, since we so openly   Proceed in justice, which shall have due course,   Even to the guilt or the purgation.
translation: In doing this, it should be clear that I'm not a tyrant; I'm proceeding openly in the due course of justice, whether it leads to a "guilty" sentence or an "innocent" one.

original: Produce the prisoner.
translation: Bring in the prisoner.

original: It is his highness' pleasure that the queen Appear in person here in court. Silence!
translation: The king has ordered that the queen appear at court in person. Silence!

original: Read the indictment.

Hermione, queen to the worthy   Leontes, king of Sicilia, thou art here accused and   arraigned of high treason, in committing adultery   with Polixenes, king of Bohemia, and conspiring   with Camillo to take away the life of our sovereign   lord the king, thy royal husband:
translation: Hermione, Queen of Sicily and wife of King Leontes: you are here accused and called to account for high treason, for committing  adultery  with Polixenes, King of Bohemia, and conspiring with Camillo to assassinate your husband the king.

original: the pretence   whereof being by circumstances partly laid open,   thou, Hermione, contrary to the faith and allegiance   of a true subject, didst counsel and aid them, for   their better safety, to fly away by night.
translation: By nature of the circumstances, you are also charged with aiding and abetting the fugitives to their escape, which violates the trust and duty of a true subject.

original: Since what I am to say must be but that   Which contradicts my accusation and   The testimony on my part no other   But what comes from myself, it shall scarce boot me   To say 'not guilty:'
translation: Since what I'm about to say can only be a rejection of my accusations, and the only testimony this court will hear on my behalf is my own, it's hardly worth it for me to say "not guilty."

original: mine integrity   Being counted falsehood, shall, as I express it,   Be so received.
translation: Since you've already decided I'm a liar, you'll only interpret my words as lies.

original: But thus: if powers divine   Behold our human actions, as they do,   I doubt not then but innocence shall make   False accusation blush and tyranny   Tremble at patience.
translation: But listen: if God watches over us, as he does, then I'm sure that  innocence will triumph over false accusations, and that patience will defeat tyranny .

original: You, my lord, best know,   Who least will seem to do so, my past life   Hath been as continent, as chaste, as true,   As I am now unhappy;
translation: You should know better than anyone (though, at the moment, you seem to know the least) how pure and faithful I've been my entire life.

original: which is more   Than history can pattern, though devised   And play'd to take spectators.
translation: No falsified history can change that, no matter how well it's fabricated and performed for spectators.

original: For behold me   A fellow of the royal bed (which owe   A moiety of the throne), a great king's daughter,   The mother to a hopeful prince, here standing   To prate and talk for life and honour 'fore   Who please to come and hear.
translation: Look at me: I'm the king's wife (making me half of the royal government), the daughter of a powerful king, the mother of a young prince, and I'm standing here babbling on to defend my life and reputation to any old person who'll come and listen.

original: For life, I prize it   As I weigh grief, which I would spare: for honour,   'Tis a derivative from me to mine,   And only that I stand for.
translation: Honestly? My life is about as precious to me as my grief, which I'd rather not have to bear. I care about my reputation because it affects my children's future; that's the only reason I stand here now.

original: I appeal   To your own conscience, sir, before Polixenes   Came to your court, how I was in your grace,   How merited to be so;
translation: Sir, I appeal to your own conscience. Remember how much you loved me—and how much I deserved it—before Polixenes came to your court.

original: since he came,   With what encounter so uncurrent I   Have strain'd to appear thus:
translation: Since he came, I've only tried to remain worthy of your love.

original: i   f one jot beyond   The bound of honour, or in act or will   That way inclining, harden'd be the hearts   Of all that hear me, and my near'st of kin   Cry fie upon my grave!
translation: If I've done a single thing outside the demands of duty, either in thought or deed, then everyone who hears me can hate me and my own family can curse my grave!

original: I ne'er heard yet That any of these bolder vices wanted Less impudence to gainsay what they did Than to perform it first.
translation: It's hardly uncommon for someone who committed such heinous offenses to deny them later.

original: That's true enough; Through 'tis a saying, sir, not due to me.
translation: That may be true of people who've actually done such things; it has nothing to do with me.

original: You will not own it.
translation: So you won't admit it?

original: More than mistress of   Which comes to me in name of fault, I must not   At all acknowledge.
translation: I can't admit to things that I haven't done.

original: For Polixenes,   With whom I am accused, I do confess   I loved him as in honour he required,   With such a kind of love as might become   A lady like me, with a love even such,   So and no other, as yourself commanded:
translation: As far as Polixenes is concerned, I can only confess that I loved him as much as I should, with the kind of love that a woman in my position should give—the kind of love that you, yourself, commanded that I show.

original: Which not to have done I think had been in me   Both disobedience and ingratitude   To you and toward your friend, whose love had spoke,   Even since it could speak, from an infant, freely   That it was yours.
translation: If I hadn't cared for him, I would have been disobedient to you and inhospitable toward your friend. I mean, you've loved Polixenes since before you could speak, since you were a baby, and he's always loved you back.

original: Now, for conspiracy,   I know not how it tastes; though it be dish'd   For me to try how: all I know of it   Is that Camillo was an honest man;
translation: As for conspiracy: I've never tasted it, despite the fact that you keep serving it to me on a plate.  All I know is that Camillo was an honest man.

original: And why he left your court, the gods themselves,   Wotting no more than I, are ignorant.
translation: God only knows why he left your court; I have no idea.

original: You knew of his departure, as you know What you have underta'en to do in's absence.
translation: You knew he was planning to leave, and you very well know what you've been working on in his absence.

original: Sir, You speak a language that I understand not: My life stands in the level of your dreams, Which I'll lay down.
translation: You're speaking a language that I don't understand. It's as if my life were being made up by your dreams; I'll lay down what life I have now.

original: Your actions are my dreams;   You had a bastard by Polixenes,   And I but dream'd it.
translation: Your actions are my dreams! Oh, so you had Polixenes's bastard, and I just dreamed it?

original: As you were past all shame,—   Those of your fact are so—so past all truth:
translation: Like all of your kind, you're past shame, past truth.

original: Which to deny concerns more than avails; for as   Thy brat hath been cast out, like to itself,   No father owning it,—
translation: Denying your crimes only proves you've committed them. The brat is gone, on its own now, since no father will claim it—

original: which is, indeed,   More criminal in thee than it,—so thou   Shalt feel our justice, in whose easiest passage   Look for no less than death.
translation: though that's more your fault than the brat's. Now  you'll  feel my justice. Expect nothing less than a death sentence.

original: Sir, spare your threats:   The bug which you would fright me with I seek.   To me can life be no commodity:
translation: You can save your threats. Death doesn't scare me; death is what I'm after. Life holds nothing for me now.

original: The crown and comfort of my life, your favour,   I do give lost; for I do feel it gone,   But know not how it went.
translation: Your love, the light of my life? I've given up on that—it's gone, although I don't know where or why it went.

original: My second joy   And first-fruits of my body, from his presence   I am barr'd, like one infectious.
translation: My second blessing, my firstborn son? I'm barred from seeing him as if I had a contagious disease.

original: My third comfort   Starr'd most unluckily, is from my breast,   The innocent milk in its most innocent mouth,   Haled out to murder:   myself on every post   Proclaimed a strumpet: with immodest hatred   The child-bed privilege denied, which 'longs   To women of all fashion;
translation: My third blessing, my poor daughter, was ripped from my breast, the innocent milk still in her innocent mouth, and hauled out to be murdered.   I've been publicized as a whore on every street-corner, was denied the normal hospital care for women who've just given birth,

original: l   astly, hurried   Here to this place, i' the open air, before   I have got strength of limit.
translation: and, finally, was rushed to this place—in the open air—before I'd even gotten my strength back.

original: Now, my liege,   Tell me what blessings I have here alive,   That I should fear to die? Therefore proceed.
translation: So,  my king : tell me what blessings I have to live for, that would make me afraid to die? Therefore, carry on.

original: But yet hear this: mistake me not; no life,   I prize it not a straw, but for mine honour,   Which I would free, if I shall be condemn'd   Upon surmises, all proofs sleeping else   But what your jealousies awake, I tell you   'Tis rigor and not law.
translation: But hear this, and don't misunderstand me: I don't value my own life at all, but my reputation—that I would clear. If I'm going to be condemned on your suspicions alone, with no proof except whatever your jealous mind has come up with, well—that is injustice, not law.

original: Your honours all,   I do refer me to the oracle:   Apollo be my judge!
translation: Gentlemen, I defer to the oracle. May Apollo be my judge!

original: This your request Is altogether just: therefore bring forth, And in Apollos name, his oracle.
translation: Your request is perfectly reasonable. In Apollo's name, bring forth the oracle.

original: The Emperor of Russia was my father: O that he were alive, and here beholding His daughter's trial! that he did but see The flatness of my misery, yet with eyes Of pity, not revenge!

You here shall swear upon this sword of justice,   That you, Cleomenes and Dion, have   Been both at Delphos, and from thence have brought   The seal'd-up oracle, by the hand deliver'd   Of great Apollo's priest;
translation: Swear on this sword of justice that you, Cleomenes and Dion, have been to Delphos and have brought back the sealed oracle delivered to you by Apollo's priest.

original: and that, since then,   You have not dared to break the holy seal   Nor read the secrets in't.
translation: Swear that, since then, you have neither broken the holy seal nor read the secrets inside.

original: All this we swear.
translation: We swear to all of this.

original: Break up the seals and read.
translation: Break the seal and read it.

original: Hermione is chaste; Polixenes blameless; Camillo a true subject; Leontes a jealous tyrant; his innocent babe truly begotten; and the king shall live without an heir, if that which is lost be not found.
translation: Hermione is virtuous,Polixenes is blameless,Camillo is a loyal subject,Leontes is a jealous tyrant,The baby is his biological daughter,And the king will have no heirUntil he finds that which is lost.

original: Now blessed be the great Apollo!
translation: Bless you, Apollo!

original: Praised!
translation: Praise Apollo!

original: Hast thou read truth?
translation: Have you read the truth?

original: Ay, my lord; even so As it is here set down.
translation: Yes, sir. Exactly as it's written down.

original: There is no truth at all i' the oracle: The sessions shall proceed: this is mere falsehood.
translation: The oracle is complete garbage. The trial will proceed. This is a pack of lies.

original: My lord the king, the king!
translation: Sir, the king, the king!

original: What is the business?
translation: What's going on here?

original: O sir, I shall be hated to report it! The prince your son, with mere conceit and fear Of the queen's speed, is gone.
translation: Oh sir, please don't shoot the messenger. The prince, your son, out of worrying so much about his mother, is gone.

original: How! gone!
translation: What do you mean, "gone?"

original: Is dead.
translation: He's dead.

original: Apollo's angry; and the heavens themselves Do strike at my injustice. @  @ How now there!
translation: Apollo is angry. The heavens themselves are punishing me for my injustice.  Look out!

original: This news is mortal to the queen: look down And see what death is doing.
translation: This news has killed the queen. Look down and see what death is doing!

original: Take her hence:   Her heart is but o'ercharged; she will recover:
translation: Take her away. Her heart is just a little strained; she'll recover.

original: I have too much believed mine own suspicion:   Beseech you, tenderly apply to her   Some remedies for life.
translation: I put too much stock in my own suspicions. Please, take care of her, get her some medicine.

original: Apollo, pardon   My great profaneness 'gainst thine oracle!   I'll reconcile me to Polixenes,   New woo my queen, recall the good Camillo,   Whom I proclaim a man of truth, of mercy;
translation: Apollo, please forgive my blasphemy against your oracle! I'll make up with Polixenes, win my wife over again, bring Camillo back since I know now that he's a good guy.

original: For, being transported by my jealousies   To bloody thoughts and to revenge, I chose   Camillo for the minister to poison   My friend Polixenes:
translation: I was too carried away with my jealousy and got caught up with bloody thoughts of revenge. I told Camillo to poison my friend Polixenes,

original: which had been done,   But that the good mind of Camillo tardied   My swift command, though I with death and with   Reward did threaten and encourage him,
translation: which would have happened if Camillo hadn't questioned my command (even though I threatened him with death if he didn't obey).

original: Not doing 't and being done: he, most humane   And fill'd with honour, to my kingly guest   Unclasp'd my practise, quit his fortunes here,   Which you knew great, and to the hazard   Of all encertainties himself commended,   No richer than his honour:
translation: He admirably told Polixenes what I had planned, then gave up his comfortable position here to help Polixenes get away. He risked everything to do what was right.

original: how he glisters   Thorough my rust! and how his pity   Does my deeds make the blacker!
translation: His goodness glitters through my dark intentions, making my actions look even more dark by contrast!

original: Woe the while! O, cut my lace, lest my heart, cracking it, Break too.
What fit is this, good lady?
translation: What's the matter with you, ma'am?

original: What studied torments, tyrant, hast for me?   What wheels? racks? fires? what flaying? boiling?   In leads or oils?
translation: You tyrant, what tortures do you have in store for me? Stretch me on the rack? Burn me at the stake? Boil me in oil?

original: what old or newer torture   Must I receive, whose every word deserves   To taste of thy most worst?
translation: What range of old and new punishments will I receive for cursing you the way you deserve?

original: Thy tyranny   Together working with thy jealousies,   Fancies too weak for boys, too green and idle   For girls of nine, O, think what they have done   And then run mad indeed, stark mad!
translation: Your tyranny and your jealous fantasies, which were more immature than young boys' passing thoughts and more useless then nine-year-old girls' daydreams—well, just consider what your fantasies have done! If you can get your head around it, you'll really go crazy now!

original: for all   Thy by-gone fooleries were but spices of it.   That thou betray'dst Polixenes,'twas nothing;   That did but show thee, of a fool, inconstant   And damnable ingrateful:
translation: Everything you've done was just a byproduct of that. You betrayed Polixenes, but that was nothing; it just proved you were flaky and a damned ungrateful idiot.

original: nor was't much,   Thou wouldst have poison'd good Camillo's honour,   To have him kill a king: poor trespasses,   More monstrous standing by:
translation: It wasn't so bad, either, that you wrecked Camillo's life by trying to force him to kill a king. Those were small offenses compared to what came next.

original: whereof I reckon   The casting forth to crows thy baby-daughter   To be or none or little; though a devil   Would have shed water out of fire ere done't:
translation: You abandoned your daughter to the wilderness: that's not such a big deal (though even the devil himself wouldn't have done it).

original: Nor is't directly laid to thee, the death   Of the young prince, whose honourable thoughts,   Thoughts high for one so tender, cleft the heart   That could conceive a gross and foolish sire   Blemish'd his gracious dam:
translation: And really, it's not your fault that the sensitive, young prince died of a broken heart, from disbelief that his disgusting, foolish father would destroy his beloved mother.

original: this is not, no,   Laid to thy answer: but the last,—O lords,   When I have said, cry 'woe!' the queen, the queen,   The sweet'st, dear'st creature's dead,   and vengeance for't   Not dropp'd down yet.
translation: No, sir. You don't have to answer for any of this. But this most recent thing (and, gentleman, prepare to cry out as soon as you hear it): the queen, the queen, the sweetest, dearest creature is dead, and vengeance for it remains to be seen.

original: The higher powers forbid!
translation: God forbid!

original: I say she's dead; I'll swear't. If word nor oath   Prevail not, go and see:
translation: I said she's dead; I'll swear it. If you don't believe me, go and see for yourself.

original: if you can bring   Tincture or lustre in her lip, her eye,   Heat outwardly or breath within, I'll serve you   As I would do the gods.
translation: If you can bring the color back to her cheeks, open her eyes, or get her breathing again, it would be a miracle.

original: But, O thou tyrant!   Do not repent these things, for they are heavier   Than all thy woes can stir; therefore betake thee   To nothing but despair.
translation: You tyrant! Don't you dare  repent  what you've done. These crimes couldn't be offset even if you mustered every ounce of remorse in your body. From now on, your whole life should be nothing but misery.

original: A thousand knees   Ten thousand years together, naked, fasting,   Upon a barren mountain and still winter   In storm perpetual, could not move the gods   To look that way thou wert.
translation: A thousand people praying naked and fasting on a mountain in a perpetual winter storm for ten thousand years could not convince the gods to have mercy on you.

original: Go on, go on Thou canst not speak too much; I have deserved All tongues to talk their bitterest.
translation: Go on; go on. It's impossible for you to say too much. I deserve the most bitter words anyone can offer.

original: Say no more: Howe'er the business goes, you have made fault I' the boldness of your speech.
translation: Say no more. Whatever's happened, you overstepped your boundaries in making that speech.

original: I am sorry for't:   All faults I make, when I shall come to know them,   I do repent.
translation: I'm sorry for that. Any faults that come to my attention, I'm sure I'll repent for.

original: Alas! I have show'd too much   The rashness of a woman: he is touch'd   To the noble heart.
translation: Well, well. Just call me a  classic, over-emotional woman ; I've hurt the king's feelings.

original: What's gone and what's past help   Should be past grief: do not receive affliction   At my petition;
translation: Don't cry over what's in the past and can't be helped. And don't be upset only because I told you to—I'd rather you punished me for reminding you of what you forgot.

original: I beseech you, rather   Let me be punish'd, that have minded you   Of what you should forget. Now, good my liege   Sir, royal sir, forgive a foolish woman:   The love I bore your queen—lo, fool again!—
translation: Now sir, forgive me for speaking so harshly. I loved your queen so much—oops, I did it again!

original: I'll speak of her no more, nor of your children;   I'll not remember you of my own lord,   Who is lost too: take your patience to you,   And I'll say nothing.
translation: I won't talk about her anymore, or about your children, or about my husband, Antigonus, who is lost, too. Beg your pardon; I won't say a word.

original: Thou didst speak but well   When most the truth; which I receive much better   Than to be pitied of thee.
translation: No, you said the right thing; you spoke the truth. I welcome it, actually, more than I would welcome your pity.

original: Prithee, bring me   To the dead bodies of my queen and son:   One grave shall be for both: upon them shall   The causes of their death appear, unto   Our shame perpetual.
translation: Please, show me the dead bodies of my wife and son. I'll make them a double grave, and, as a mark of my shame, will write on their gravestones how and why they died.

original: Once a day I'll visit   The chapel where they lie, and tears shed there   Shall be my recreation: so long as nature   Will bear up with this exercise, so long   I daily vow to use it.
translation: I'll visit the chapel where they're buried every day and will spend all my time crying over them. I'll do this for as long as I live.

original: Come and lead me   Unto these sorrows.
translation: Lead  me to my heartbreak.

original: Thou art perfect then, our ship hath touch'd upon The deserts of Bohemia?
translation: So you're sure we've arrived in Bohemia?

original: Ay, my lord: and fear   We have landed in ill time:
translation: Yes, sir, and I'm afraid we've arrived at a bad time.

original: the skies look grimly   And threaten present blusters.
translation: The skies look dark, which means it's about to storm.

original: In my conscience,   The heavens with that we have in hand are angry   And frown upon's.
translation: In my opinion, the gods are angry at us and are punishing us.

original: Their sacred wills be done! Go, get aboard; Look to thy bark: I'll not be long before I call upon thee.
translation: May the gods' will be done! Get back on board the boat; I'll be back in a minute.

original: Make your best haste, and go not Too far i' the land: 'tis like to be loud weather; Besides, this place is famous for the creatures Of prey that keep upon't.
translation: Hurry as fast as you can, and don't go too far inland—this storm looks bad. Besides, this place is famous for its man-eating animals.

original: Go thou away: I'll follow instantly.
translation: Go on; I'll be right behind you.

original: I am glad at heart To be so rid o' the business.
translation: I'll be glad to get this over with.

original: Come, poor babe:   I have heard, but not believed,   the spirits o' the dead   May walk again:
translation: Come here, poor baby. I've heard (but haven't believed) stories about spirits of the dead walking the earth.

original: i   f such thing be, thy mother   Appear'd to me last night, for ne'er was dream   So like a waking.
translation: If these things do happen, then your mother appeared to me last night in a dream that was so real, it felt like I was awake.

original: To me comes a creature,   Sometimes her head on one side, some another;
translation: Something walked toward me, moving its head from side to side.

original: I never saw a vessel of like sorrow,   So fill'd and so becoming:
translation: I've never seen anything so sad and so completely beautiful.

original: in pure white robes,   Like very sanctity, she did approach   My cabin where I lay; thrice bow'd before me,   And gasping to begin some speech, her eyes   Became two spouts: the fury spent, anon   Did this break-from her:
translation: In pure white robes, like a goddess, she walked toward the place where I was sleeping. She bowed three times, gasping as she tried to speak. Crying with rage, she finally burst out,

original: 'Good Antigonus,   Since fate, against thy better disposition,   Hath made thy person for the thrower-out   Of my poor babe, according to thine oath,   Places remote enough are in Bohemia,   There weep and leave it crying; and, for the babe   Is counted lost for ever, Perdita,   I prithee, call't.
translation: "Antigonus, you have the bad luck to be disposing of my baby far away in Bohemia. Shed a tear as you leave her there. Since she's lost forever, you should call her 'Perdita.'

original: For this ungentle business   Put on thee by my lord, thou ne'er shalt see   Thy wife Paulina more.' And so, with shrieks   She melted into air.
translation: And for what my husband has made you do, you'll never see your wife, Paulina, again." Then, shrieking, she disappeared into thin air.

original: Affrighted much,   I did in time collect myself and thought   This was so and no slumber. Dreams are toys:   Yet for this once, yea, superstitiously,   I will be squared by this.
translation: Terrified, it took me a while to collect myself, and I wasn't sure if it was a dream or not. Usually I don't put much stock in dreams, but this one I'd swear by superstitiously.

original: I do believe   Hermione hath suffer'd death, and that   Apollo would, this being indeed the issue   Of King Polixenes, it should here be laid,   Either for life or death, upon the earth   Of its right father.
translation: I believe that Hermione died, and that Apollo wants this baby (who must be King Polixenes's daughter) to be laid here on its father's land, to either live or die.

original: Blossom, speed thee well!   There lie, and there thy character: there these;   Which may, if fortune please, both breed thee, pretty,   And still rest thine.
translation: Good luck! There you are, and there's the story of your identity. If you make it, these things might help you.

original: The storm begins; poor wretch,   That for thy mother's fault art thus exposed   To loss and what may follow! Weep I cannot,   But my heart bleeds; and most accursed am I   To be by oath enjoin'd to this.
translation: The storm is beginning! Poor brat, you're out in the elements thanks to your mother's mistake, and who knows what will happen! I can't cry, but my heart is bleeding and I'm damned for getting tangled up in this.

original: Farewell!   The day frowns more and more: thou'rt like to have   A lullaby too rough: I never saw   The heavens so dim by day. A savage clamour!   Well may I get aboard!
translation: Goodbye! It's getting darker and darker. I'm afraid the lullaby you're about to get will be a little on the rough side; I've never seen the sky so black in the daytime. The thunder, the lightning! I need to get aboard the ship!

original: This is the chase:   I am gone for ever.
translation: Well, this is it: I'm gone forever.

original: I would there were no age between sixteen and   three-and-twenty, or that youth would sleep out the   rest; for there is nothing in the between but   getting wenches with child, wronging the ancientry,   stealing, fighting—
translation: I wish  we could go straight from sixteen to twenty-three, or that we could put our lives on pause in between those ages. Ya don't get up to much at that age except knocking girls up, embarrassing your old folks, stealing, fighting—

original: Hark you now! Would any but   these boiled brains of nineteen and two-and-twenty   hunt this weather? They have scared away two of my   best sheep, which I fear the wolf will sooner find   than the master:
translation: Well, whadaya know! Only no-good youngsters would be out in this weather! They've scared away two of my best sheep, and I'll be darned if the wolves don't find them before I do.

original: if any where I have them, 'tis by   the seaside, browsing of ivy. Good luck, an't be thy   will what have we here! Mercy on 's, a barne a very   pretty barne! A boy or a child, I wonder?
translation: If they're anywhere to be found, it's down by the sea, grazing on some weeds . . .  [He looks into the basket ]  Lord have mercy, it's a baby, a very pretty little baby! Is it a boy or a girl, I wonder?

original: A   pretty one; a very pretty one: sure, some 'scape:   though I am not bookish, yet I can read   waiting-gentlewoman in the 'scape.
translation: Ah, it's a pretty one, you're a very pretty one, aren't you, with a pretty face. I may not be all that smart, but I can tell from your face your mama's a high-class lady.

original: This has been   some stair-work, some trunk-work, some   behind-door-work: they were warmer that got this   than the poor thing is here. I'll take it up for   pity:
translation: This has been some  back-room , behind-closed-doors, under-the-covers business, huh, by two people who were hotter and heavier than you are now! You poor thing, come here.

original: yet I'll tarry till my son come; he hallooed   but even now. Whoa, ho, hoa!
translation: I'll hold on 'til my son comes; I thought I heard him just now—Hey there!

original: Hilloa, loa!
translation: Howdy-hey!

original: What, art so near? If thou'lt see a thing to talk on when thou art dead and rotten, come hither. What ailest thou, man?
translation: What're you doing up here? If you wanna see the darnedest thing you ever did see, get yourself over here! What's the matter with you, boy?

original: I have seen two such sights, by sea and by land! but I am not to say it is a sea, for it is now the sky: betwixt the firmament and it you cannot thrust a bodkin's point.
translation: I've seen two unbelievable things, one in the sea and one on land! But now I don't know what's the sea and what's the sky; everything's all mixed up in this storm.

original: Why, boy, how is it?
translation: What in the world do you mean, boy?

original: I would you did but see how it chafes, how it rages,   how it takes up the shore! but that's not the   point. O, the most piteous cry of the poor souls!
translation: If only you could see how the water is roiling and raging all the way up the beach—but that's not the point! The pitiful cries of people who are doomed!

original: sometimes to see 'em, and not to see 'em; now the   ship boring the moon with her main-mast, and anon   swallowed with yest and froth, as you'ld thrust a   cork into a hogshead.
translation: I could see 'em, and then I couldn't as the ship went up and down, to and fro, pushed around in the waves like you'd push a cork into a keg of beer.

original: And then for the   land-service, to see how the bear tore out his   shoulder-bone; how he cried to me for help and said   his name was Antigonus, a nobleman.
translation: And then on land, if you'd seen how the bear tore his arm out of its socket, and heard how he cried to me for help and said his name was Antigonus, a gentleman.

original: But to make an   end of the ship, to see how the sea flap-dragoned   it: but, first, how the poor souls roared, and the   sea mocked them; and how the poor gentleman roared   and the bear mocked him, both roaring louder than   the sea or weather.
translation: But back to the ship: if you'd seen how the sea gobbled them up, and the people screamed, and the sea laughed at them, and how the poor man screamed and the bear laughed at him, both screaming louder than the sea or the storm.

original: Name of mercy, when was this, boy?
translation: Bless my soul. When was this, boy?

original: Now, now: I have not winked since I saw these sights: the men are not yet cold under water, nor the bear half dined on the gentleman: he's at it now.
translation: Now, now! I've barely blinked since I saw it all. The men have hardly sunk to the ocean floor yet and the bear hasn't finished eating the gentleman; he's at it now.

original: Would I had been by, to have helped the old man!
translation: I wish I would have been there to have helped the old man!

original: I would you had been by the ship side, to have helped her: there your charity would have lacked  footing.
translation: I wish you would have been alongside the ship, to have helped it, too, though that would have been pretty difficult.

original: Heavy matters! heavy matters! but look thee here,   boy. Now bless thyself: thou mettest with things   dying, I with things newborn.
translation: That's heavy stuff! Heavy stuff! But lookee here, boy. Cross your heart—you came across the dying, and I came across something that's newborn.

original: Here's a sight for   thee; look thee, a bearing-cloth for a squire's   child!
translation: Here's a sight for you: look, a blanket for a gentleman's baby!

original: look thee here; take up, take up, boy;   open't. So, let's see: it was told me I should be   rich by the fairies. This is some changeling:   open't. What's within, boy?
translation: Lookee here, pick it up now, pick it up, boy, and open it! So, let's see: I've got an idea the  fairies  have made me rich. This is a changeling—open it. What's it say, boy?

original: You're a made old man: if the sins of your youth are forgiven you, you're well to live. Gold! all gold!
translation: Your fortune is made, old man. Someone must have forgiven the sins of your youth; now you're set for life. Gold! All gold!

original: This is fairy gold, boy, and 'twill prove so: up with't, keep it close: home, home, the next way. We are lucky, boy; and to be so still requires nothing but secrecy. Let my sheep go: come, good boy, the next way home.
translation: This is fairy gold, boy, you'll see! Hold on to it tight. Let's get on home now. We are lucky, boy, and to hold on to our luck we need to keep this under wraps. Let the sheep go. Let's get on home now, boy!

original: Go you the next way with your findings. I'll go see if the bear be gone from the gentleman and how much he hath eaten: they are never curst but when they are hungry: if there be any of him left, I'll bury it.
translation: Go on ahead with your findings. I'll go and see if the bear is gone and, if there's anything left of the gentleman, I'll bury it.

original: That's a good deed. If thou mayest discern by that which is left of him what he is, fetch me to the sight of him.
translation: That's a good thing to do. If you can tell from what's left who he is and where he's from, bring me there to see him.

original: Marry, will I; and you shall help to put him i' the  ground.
translation: Yes, sir, I will, and you can help me bury him.

original: 'Tis a lucky day, boy, and we'll do good deeds on't.
translation: We're lucky today, boy. Let's give thanks by doing good.

original: I pray thee, good Camillo, be no more importunate: 'tis a sickness denying thee any thing; a death to grant this.
translation: Please, Camillo, don't pester me. Though it's hard to deny you anything, it would be the death of you if I said "yes."

original: It is fifteen years since I saw my country: though   I have for the most part been aired abroad, I   desire to lay my bones there.
translation: I haven't been home in fifteen years. I've been away for so long, but I do want to die and be buried there.

original: Besides, the penitent   king, my master, hath sent for me;
translation: Besides, the remorseful king, my former boss, has asked me to come.

original: to whose feeling   sorrows I might be some allay, or I o'erween to   think so, which is another spur to my departure.
translation: I might be able to ease his suffering, which is just another reason I want to go.

original: As thou lovest me, Camillo, wipe not out the rest of   thy services by leaving me now: the need I have of   thee thine own goodness hath made; better not to   have had thee than thus to want thee:
translation: Camillo, if you're loyal to me, you wouldn't think of leaving me now; I need your services especially (and, since I've been spoiled with a servant as effective as you, I can hardly settle for someone else).

original: thou, having   made me businesses which none without thee can   sufficiently manage, must either stay to execute   them thyself or take away with thee the very   services thou hast done;
translation: Plus, you've built industries for me here that no one but you can take care of, so you either need to stay here to do it yourself, or take your projects with you.

original: which if I have not enough   considered, as too much I cannot, to be more   thankful to thee shall be my study, and my profit   therein the heaping friendships.
translation: I can never thank you enough for all the work you've done—and for your friendship.

original: Of that fatal   country, Sicilia, prithee speak no more; whose very   naming punishes me with the remembrance of that   penitent, as thou callest him, and reconciled king,   my brother; whose loss of his most precious queen   and children are even now to be afresh lamented.
translation: Please, don't talk about Sicily anymore. The name alone dredges up bad memories of that "remorseful" king (as you call him), my friend, and the loss of his wife and children, which we should be mourning even now.

original: Say to me, when sawest thou the Prince Florizel, my   son? Kings are no less unhappy, their issue not   being gracious, than they are in losing them when   they have approved their virtues.
translation: Anyway, when did you last see my son, Prince Florizel? It's just as bad for a king to misplace a good son as to have a bad one at hand.

original: Sir, it is three days since I saw the prince. What his happier affairs may be, are to me unknown: but I have missingly noted, he is of late much retired from court and is less frequent to his princely exercises than formerly he hath appeared.
translation: Sir, I haven't seen the prince for three days. I'm not sure what he's up to, but I have noticed that he's been away from court a lot and that he's been neglecting his princely duties more than usual.

original: I have considered so much, Camillo, and with some   care; so far that I have eyes under my service which   look upon his removedness;
translation: I've noticed, too, Camillo—so much so that I have people watching him for me wherever he goes.

original: from whom I have this   intelligence, that he is seldom from the house of a   most homely shepherd;
translation: They've reported that he's spending most of his time at a poor shepherd's house.

original: a man, they say, that from   very nothing, and beyond the imagination of his   neighbours, is grown into an unspeakable estate.
translation: They tell me that some time ago the shepherd suddenly went from rags to riches, to the complete shock of his neighbors.

original: I have heard, sir, of such a man, who hath a daughter of most rare note: the report of her is extended more than can be thought to begin from such a  cottage.
translation: I've heard of this guy, sir, and that he has a very beautiful daughter. By all reports, she's far beyond what you'd expect from such circumstances.

original: That's likewise part of my intelligence; but, I   fear, the angle that plucks our son thither.
translation: I've heard that, too, and I'm afraid you've put your finger on the bait that's lured my son away.

original: Thou   shalt accompany us to the place; where we will, not   appearing what we are, have some question with the   shepherd;
translation: You'll come with me to the place, where we'll disguise ourselves and question the shepherd.

original: from whose simplicity I think it not   uneasy to get the cause of my son's resort thither.
translation: Since he's probably not all that bright, it won't be difficult to get the story of my son's shenanigans out of him.

original: Prithee, be my present partner in this business, and   lay aside the thoughts of Sicilia.
translation: Please forget about Sicily and come help me with this.

original: I willingly obey your command.
translation: I'm happy to do as you say.

original: My best Camillo! We must disguise ourselves.
translation: Atta boy, Camillo! Let's put on disguises.

original: When daffodils begin to peer,   With heigh! the doxy over the dale,   Why, then comes in the sweet o' the year;   For the red blood reigns in the winter's pale.
translation: When  daffodils begin to bloom, (Say "hey!") roll around in the grass with your lover Since spring, the best time of the year, is here, After a winter of waiting and wanting.

original: The white sheet bleaching on the hedge,   With heigh! the sweet birds, O, how they sing!   Doth set my pugging tooth on edge;   For a quart of ale is a dish for a king.
translation: The clean white sheets hanging out to dry (Say "hey!") and the birds' beautiful singing Have me hankering for a hook-up. I'm no snob—an  ugly girl  satisfies as much as any other.

original: The lark, that tirra-lyra chants,   With heigh! with heigh! the thrush and the jay,   Are summer songs for me and my aunts,   While we lie tumbling in the hay.
translation: The  lark  that chirps, "tweet, tweet!" (Say "hey!" Say "hey!"), the thrush, and the blue jay Are the perfect soundtrack for me and my ladies, While we get down in the hay.

original: I have served Prince Florizel and in my time wore  three-pile; but now I am out of service:
translation: I served Prince Florizel back in the day and used to wear a fancy suit, but now I'm out of a job.

original: But shall I go mourn for that, my dear?   The pale moon shines by night:   And when I wander here and there,   I then do most go right.
translation: But  am I crying over that, sweetheart? The moon shines in the night: Its light guides me as I wander around after-hours At which time I (mostly) do good.

original: If tinkers may have leave to live,   And bear the sow-skin budget,   Then my account I well may, give,   And in the stocks avouch it.
translation: If we tolerate handymen Who live on a piss-poor budget Then I might as well "fix" my income. I'll pay for it with jail time if I have to.

original: My traffic is sheets; when the kite builds, look to  lesser linen.
translation: I'm in the sheets business . If you see a hawk like me swooping in, you better get out your  second-best linens .

original: My father named me Autolycus; who being,  as I am, littered under Mercury, was likewise a  snapper-up of unconsidered trifles.
translation: My father named me " Autolycus ." Like me, he was destined to be a thief, and, like me, he spent his time snapping up overlooked goodies.

original: With die and drab I  purchased this caparison, and my revenue is the silly  cheat. Gallows and knock are too powerful on the  highway:
translation: I paid for this outfit by pimping—not to mention the additional profit of cheap booty. The threats of jail and death are pretty real out here on the street.

original: beating and hanging are terrors to me: for the  life to come, I sleep out the thought of it.
translation: I live in constant fear of being beaten or hanged, and I can't even think  about the afterlife ! I drink to forget about it.

original: A prize! a  prize!
translation: Ah, here's a treat!

original: Let me see: every 'leven wether tods; every tod yields pound and odd shilling; fifteen hundred shorn. what comes the wool to?
translation: Let's see: every sheep yields eleven pounds of wool, every pound of wool is worth a dollar and a penny, and we've shaved fifteen hundred sheep. How much does that make us?

original: If the springe hold, the cock's mine.
translation: If I do this right, I'll catch him.

original: I cannot do't without counters. Let me see; what am   I to buy for our sheep-shearing feast?
translation: I can't do it without a calculator. Let's see: what do I need to buy for the  sheep-shearing  party?

original: Three pound   of sugar, five pound of currants, rice,—what will   this sister of mine do with rice? But my father   hath made her mistress of the feast, and she lays it   on.
translation: Three pounds of sugar, five pounds of grapes, rice—no idea what my sister needs rice for, but my dad set her up as the debutante of the party, and she's in charge.

original: She hath made me four and twenty nose-gays for   the shearers, three-man-song-men all, and very good   ones; but they are most of them means and bases;
translation: She made bouquets for all twenty-four of the men who'll shave the sheep tonight. They're all decent guys, but they're rascals.

original: but   one puritan amongst them, and he sings psalms to   horn-pipes. I must have saffron to colour the warden   pies; mace; dates?—none, that's out of my note;
translation: There's only one  religious guy  out of all of them, and he's really strange. I need some spices for the pies, herbs . . . dates? No, not dates.

original: nutmegs, seven; a race or two of ginger, but that I   may beg; four pound of prunes, and as many of   raisins o' the sun.
translation: Some nutmeg, a bit of ginger (but I could get that from a friend), four pounds of prunes, and tons of raisins.

original: O that ever I was born!
translation: Oh, woe is me!

original: I' the name of me—
translation: What in the world?

original: O, help me, help me! pluck but off these rags; and then, death, death!
translation: Oh, help me, help me! Get these rags off me, so I can die in peace!

original: Alack, poor soul! thou hast need of more rags to lay on thee, rather than have these off.
translation: You poor thing! In that case, you need clothes to be buried in, not for what's left of your clothes to be taken away.

original: O sir, the loathsomeness of them offends me more than the stripes I have received, which are mighty ones and millions.
translation: Man, these ugly rags hurt me more than the millions of punches and kicks I just received.

original: Alas, poor man! a million of beating may come to a great matter.
translation: Oh, poor man! A million punches and kicks can do a lot of damage.

original: I am robbed, sir, and beaten; my money and apparel ta'en from me, and these detestable things put upon me.
translation: I've been beaten and robbed. My money and clothes were stolen, and then they threw these rags on me.

original: What, by a horseman, or a footman?
translation: Was it someone on horseback, or walking?

original: A footman, sweet sir, a footman.
translation: Walking, my friend, walking.

original: Indeed, he should be a footman by the garments he has left with thee: if this be a horseman's coat, it hath seen very hot service. Lend me thy hand, I'll help thee: come, lend me thy hand.
translation: That makes sense—someone rich enough to ride a horse wouldn't have been wearing rags like this. Give me your hand, I'll help you up. Give me your hand.

original: O, good sir, tenderly, O!
translation: Oh, thank you, sir—carefully, ow!

original: Alas, poor soul!
translation: Ah, poor thing!

original: O, good sir, softly, good sir! I fear, sir, my shoulder-blade is out.
translation: Oh, man, carefully! I think I've broken my shoulder blade.

original: How now! canst stand?
translation: Really? Can you stand?

original: Softly, dear sir; good sir, softly. You ha' done me a charitable office.
translation: Carefully, my friend, very carefully . . . [The shepherd's son lifts AUTOLYCUS to his feet] You've really helped me out.

original: Dost lack any money? I have a little money for thee.
translation: Do you need money? I can give you a little money.

original: No, good sweet sir; no, I beseech you, sir: I have a kinsman not past three quarters of a mile hence, unto whom I was going; I shall there have money, or any thing I want: offer me no money, I pray you; that kills my heart.
translation: No! My dear friend, no, please. My uncle lives under a mile away, and I was just heading there. I can get some money and anything else I need there. Please, don't offer me any money, I can't bear that.

original: What manner of fellow was he that robbed you?
translation: What kind of guy was it that robbed you?

original: A fellow, sir, that I have known to go about with troll-my-dames; I knew him once a servant of the prince: I cannot tell, good sir, for which of his virtues it was, but he was certainly whipped out of the court.
His vices, you would say; there's no virtue whipped out of the court: they cherish it to make it stay there; and yet it will no more but abide.
translation: You mean his vices, right? There's no virtue that would get you kicked out of court. They could use virtue there, considering they have none.

original: Vices, I would say, sir. I know this man well:
translation: Vices, yes, that's what I meant. I know this guy well:

original: he   hath been since an ape-bearer; then a   process-server, a bailiff; then he compassed a   motion of the Prodigal Son, and married a tinker's   wife within a mile where my land and living lies;
translation: he was an odd-jobs guy, then a police officer, then he  wasted all his money for a while , and then he married a handyman's wife about a mile away from where I live now.

original: and, having flown over many knavish professions, he   settled only in rogue: some call him Autolycus.
translation: He's tried his hand at several questionable professions and has now settled on being a criminal. Some call him Autolycus.

original: Out upon him! prig, for my life, prig: he haunts wakes, fairs and bear-baitings.
Very true, sir; he, sir, he; that's the rogue that put me into this apparel.
translation: That's true. He's the crook that put me in this outfit.

original: Not a more cowardly rogue in all Bohemia: if you had but looked big and spit at him, he'ld have run.
translation: He's the most cowardly criminal in the entire country. If you just shouted and looked intimidating, you'd scare him away.

original: I must confess to you, sir, I am no fighter: I am false of heart that way; and that he knew, I warrant him.
translation: I have to admit, I'm not a fighter—my heart's too weak. I'll bet he knew that.

original: How do you now?
translation: How are you feeling now?

original: Sweet sir, much better than I was; I can stand and walk: I will even take my leave of you, and pace softly towards my kinsman's.
translation: Much better than I was, my friend. I can stand and walk; I'll even say goodbye and make my way toward my uncle's house.

original: Shall I bring thee on the way?
translation: Do you want me to come with you?

original: No, good-faced sir; no, sweet sir.
translation: No, you sweet, caring man, you.

original: Then fare thee well: I must go buy spices for our sheep-shearing.
translation: Goodbye, then. I have to go buy spices for our sheep-shearing.

original: Prosper you, sweet sir! @  @ Your purse is not hot enough to purchase your spice. I'll be with you at your sheep-shearing too: if I make not this cheat bring out another and the shearers prove sheep, let me be unrolled and my name put in the book of virtue!    Jog on, jog on, the foot-path way, And merrily hent the stile-a: A merry heart goes all the day, Your sad tires in a mile-a.
translation: God bless you, my friend! You don't have enough money in your wallet to purchase those spices. I'll be at the sheep-shearing, too. I pulled off this trick and I'm about to make the shearers my next victims. If I can't pull it off (as if that were possible), I'll trade my wicked ways for good deeds![Singing] Run along, run along the dirt pathAnd jump right over the cattle-guardA smile can go on all dayBut a frown only lasts for a mile.

original: These your unusual weeds to each part of you   Do give a life:
translation: This costume looks good on you!

original: no shepherdess, but Flora   Peering in April's front.
This your sheep-shearing   Is as a meeting of the petty gods,   And you the queen on't.
translation: This sheep-shearing festival is a meeting of the gods, and you're the queen of all of them.

original: Sir, my gracious lord,   To chide at your extremes it not becomes me:
