translation: Sweetheart, I hate to correct your over-exaggerations—

original: O, pardon, that I name them! Your high self,   The gracious mark o' the land, you have obscured   With a swain's wearing, and me, poor lowly maid,   Most goddess-like prank'd up:
translation: please forgive me for pointing them out. Though you've disguised yourself as a shepherd, you're still the prince of our country and I'm only a poor peasant girl playing dress-up.

original: but that our feasts   In every mess have folly and the feeders   Digest it with a custom, I should blush   To see you so attired, sworn, I think,   To show myself a glass.
translation: If it weren't the kind of party where everyone will be looking a little silly, I'd be embarrassed for you to be dressed the way you are, and I could hardly look in a mirror.

original: I bless the time When my good falcon made her flight across Thy father's ground.
translation: I'm thankful for the day my falcon landed on your father's farm.

original: Now Jove afford you cause!   To me the difference forges dread;
translation: May God keep you safe here! I'm afraid of the consequences;

original: your greatness   Hath not been used to fear. Even now I tremble   To think your father, by some accident,   Should pass this way as you did:
translation: you've been sheltered enough to not know what fear is. I'm terrified of what would happen if your dad showed up here by chance the way that you did.

original: O, the Fates!   How would he look, to see his work so noble   Vilely bound up? What would he say?
translation: Oh, just imagine! What would he think of his royal son being engaged to someone like me? What would he say?

original: Or how   Should I, in these my borrow'd flaunts, behold   The sternness of his presence?
translation: And how would I, in this ridiculous outfit, respond to his anger?

original: Apprehend   Nothing but jollity.
translation: All I want you to think about is having a good time!

original: The gods themselves,   Humbling their deities to love, have taken   The shapes of beasts upon them:
translation: You know,  the gods  turned themselves into animals for the sake of love:

original: Jupiter   Became a bull, and bellow'd; the green Neptune   A ram, and bleated; and the fire-robed god,   Golden Apollo, a poor humble swain,   As I seem now.
translation: Jupiter became a bull, Neptune became a ram, and the sun god, Apollo, became a shepherd just like I am now.

original: Their transformations   Were never for a piece of beauty rarer,   Nor in a way so chaste, since my desires   Run not before mine honour, nor my lusts   Burn hotter than my faith.
translation: And their transformations weren't for girls as beautiful as you. Or as pure—since, you know, I'm not trying to move too quickly here. My commitment to you goes beyond physical desire.

original: O, but, sir,   Your resolution cannot hold, when 'tis   Opposed, as it must be, by the power of the king:
translation: But it will be hard for you to maintain that when the king is against you.

original: One of these two must be necessities,   Which then will speak, that you must   change this purpose,   Or I my life.
translation: One of two things will have to happen: you'll stop pursuing me, or I'll become a different person.

original: Thou dearest Perdita,   With these forced thoughts, I prithee, darken not   The mirth o' the feast.
translation: Perdita, please don't ruin the party by worrying.

original: Or I'll be thine, my fair,   Or not my father's. For I cannot be   Mine own, nor any thing to any, if   I be not thine.
translation: I belong to you, sweetheart, not my father. I'm nothing to myself and the world if I don't have you—

original: To this I am most constant,   Though destiny say no.
translation: I swear I mean it, despite all the odds.

original: Be merry, gentle;   Strangle such thoughts as these with any thing   That you behold the while.
translation: Be happy, relax, and get rid of all these negative thoughts.

original: Your guests are coming:   Lift up your countenance, as it were the day   Of celebration of that nuptial which   We two have sworn shall come.
translation: Your guests are coming! Smile like today's the wedding day we've been planning.

original: O lady Fortune, Stand you auspicious!
translation: I hope Lady Luck is on our side!

original: See, your guests approach: Address yourself to entertain them sprightly, And let's be red with mirth.
translation: Look, your guests are coming. Try to have fun with them; let's all have a good time.

original: Fie, daughter! when my old wife lived, upon   This day she was both pantler, butler, cook,   Both dame and servant;
translation: Shame on you, daughter! When your mother was alive, she was a jack-of-all-trades on the day of the festival.

original: welcomed all, served all;   Would sing her song and dance her turn; now here,   At upper end o' the table, now i' the middle;   On his shoulder, and his; her face o' fire   With labour and the thing she took to quench it,   She would to each one sip.
translation: She welcomed everyone, served everyone, sang and danced—she was at one end of the table, then the other, serving this man and that man, sweating from working so hard and drinking all the while.

original: You are retired,   As if you were a feasted one and not   The hostess of the meeting:
translation: Meanwhile, you're relaxing as if you were a guest and not the host!

original: pray you, bid   These unknown friends to's welcome; for it is   A way to make us better friends, more known.
translation: Please welcome these strangers. I hope we can get to know them better.

original: Come, quench your blushes and present yourself   That which you are, mistress o' the feast:
translation: All right, stop blushing and introduce yourself; you're the queen of the feast.

original: come on,   And bid us welcome to your sheep-shearing,   As your good flock shall prosper.
translation: Come on, and welcome everyone to the sheep-shearing so that we can start enjoying ourselves.

original: Sir, welcome: It is my father's will I should take on me The hostess-ship o' the day. @     You're welcome, sir. Give me those flowers there, Dorcas. Reverend sirs, For you there's rosemary and rue; these keep Seeming and savour all the winter long: Grace and remembrance be to you both, And welcome to our shearing!
translation: Welcome, sir. My father has asked me to play hostess today.[To CAMILLO] You're welcome, too, sir. [To DORCAS] Give me those flowers, Dorcas . . .[To POLIXENES and CAMILLO] Gentlemen, here are some herbs for you that will stay green all winter long; rosemary and rue are a gift to symbolize grace and remembrance. And welcome to our shearing!

original: Shepherdess, A fair one are you—well you fit our ages With flowers of winter.
translation: You are beautiful, shepherdess. And we see what you did there—you gave us winter flowers because we're old!

original: Sir, the year growing ancient,   Not yet on summer's death, nor on the birth   Of trembling winter,
translation: Since it's spring, sir—summer's not over yet and winter hasn't come—

original: the fairest   flowers o' the season   Are our carnations and streak'd gillyvors,
translation: the prettiest flowers blooming at the moment are carnations and multicolor  gillyvors ,

original: Which some call nature's bastards: of that kind   Our rustic garden's barren; and I care not   To get slips of them.
translation: which some people call "nature's bastards." We don't grow those here, and I'm not a big fan.

original: Wherefore, gentle maiden, Do you neglect them?
translation: Why don't you care for them?

original: For I have heard it said There is an art which in their piedness shares With great creating nature.
Say there be;   Yet nature is made better by no mean   But nature makes that mean:
translation: Maybe you're right, but humans can't create anything in nature that doesn't already have the potential to exist;

original: so, over that art   Which you say adds to nature, is an art   That nature makes.
translation: the "engineering" that you say is contrary to nature is actually enabled by nature itself.

original: You see, sweet maid, we marry   A gentler scion to the wildest stock,   And make conceive a bark of baser kind   By bud of nobler race:
translation: You see, sweetheart, if we  graft  a purebred plant to a weed, we can make the weed produce a beautiful flower.

original: this is an art   Which does mend nature, change it rather, but   The art itself is nature.
translation: This is "engineering" that improves nature, but the engineering itself is all natural.

original: So it is.
translation: I suppose you're right.

original: Then make your garden rich in gillyvors, And do not call them bastards.
translation: Then you should grow lots of gillyvors and stop calling them "bastards."

original: I'll not put   The dibble in earth to set one slip of them;
translation: I won't plant a single one.

original: No more than were I painted I would wish   This youth should say 'twere well and only therefore   Desire to breed by me.
translation: It'd be the same if my boyfriend only thought I was beautiful after I put on  heavy make-up .

original: Here's flowers for you;   Hot lavender, mints, savoury, marjoram;   The marigold, that goes to bed wi' the sun   And with him rises weeping:
translation: Here are flowers for you that close at night and open in the day to receive the sunshine.

original: these are flowers   Of middle summer, and I think they are given   To men of middle age. You're very welcome.
translation: As midsummer flowers, they're the perfect gift for middle-aged men. You're very welcome here.

original: I should leave grazing, were I of your flock, And only live by gazing.
translation: If I were one of your sheep, I wouldn't need to graze on grass—I could live just by gazing at your beautiful face.

original: Out, alas!   You'd be so lean, that blasts of January   Would blow you through and through.
translation: Oh, stop it! You'd starve to death in that case.

original: Now, my fair'st friend,   I would I had some flowers o' the spring that might   Become your time of day; and yours, and yours,   That wear upon your virgin branches yet   Your maidenheads growing:
translation: Now, my dear: if only I had some spring flowers for you and for my friends. Spring flowers are fitting for  young virgins .

original: O Proserpina,   For the flowers now, that frighted thou let'st fall   From Dis's waggon!
translation: I wish I had the flowers the  spring goddess  threw away when she was carted off to the underworld!

original: daffodils,   That come before the swallow dares, and take   The winds of March with beauty;
translation: I wish I had daffodils (the earliest spring flowers),

original: violets dim,   But sweeter than the lids of Juno's eyes   Or Cytherea's breath;
translation: violets (so dark and sweet),

original: pale primroses   That die unmarried, ere they can behold   Bright Phoebus in his strength—a malady   Most incident to maids;
translation: primroses (that die when kissed by the sun),

original: bold oxlips and   The crown imperial; lilies of all kinds,   The flower-de-luce being one!
translation: oxlips (the royal flowers), and every kind of lily, including the fleur-de-lis!

original: O, these I lack,   To make you garlands of, and my sweet friend,   To strew him o'er and o'er!
translation: Unfortunately I don't have any of these to make a flower-crown for you, or to throw on top of you!

original: What, like a corse?
No, like a bank for love to lie and play on;   Not like a corse;
translation: No, like a grassy hill for lovers to roll around on, not like a dead body!

original: or if, not to be buried,   But quick and in mine arms.
translation: Your body's not anywhere close to being buried, unless you mean buried in my arms.

original: Come, take your flowers:   Methinks I play as I have seen them do   In Whitsun pastorals:
translation: Come on, take your flowers. I feel like I'm acting in a community play;

original: sure this robe of mine   Does change my disposition.
translation: it's like this costume has totally changed my personality.

original: What you do   Still betters what is done. When you speak, sweet.   I'ld have you do it ever:
translation: Everything you do is even more wonderful than what you did before. My darling, I can't get enough of your voice; I could listen to you talk forever.

original: when you sing,   I'ld have you buy and sell so, so give alms,   Pray so; and, for the ordering your affairs,   To sing them too:
translation: Your singing is like charity for my poor soul, and makes me want to sing, too.

original: when you do dance, I wish you   A wave o' the sea, that you might ever do   Nothing but that; move still, still so,   And own no other function:
translation: When you dance, I don't want you to stop, I want you to keep moving so gracefully forever.

original: each your doing,   So singular in each particular,   Crowns what you are doing in the present deed,   That all your acts are queens.
translation: Everything you do—in exactly the way you do it—makes you even more perfect than you already are.

original: O Doricles, Your praises are too large: but that your youth, And the true blood which peepeth fairly through't, Do plainly give you out an unstain'd shepherd, With wisdom I might fear, my Doricles, You woo'd me the false way.
I think you have As little skill to fear as I have purpose To put you to't. But come; our dance, I pray: Your hand, my Perdita: so turtles pair, That never mean to part.
translation: You have nothing to be afraid of as far as that's concerned. Come on, let's dance. Give my your hand, Perdita, and never let go.

original: I'll swear for 'em.
translation: I'll swear to that.

original: This is the prettiest low-born lass that ever Ran on the green-sward: nothing she does or seems But smacks of something greater than herself, Too noble for this place.
translation: She's the prettiest peasant girl I've ever seen. Everything she does is graceful. She's too noble for this place.

original: He tells her something That makes her blood look out: good sooth, she is The queen of curds and cream.
translation: He's telling her something that makes her blush. Just look how fair her skin is!

original: Come on, strike up!
translation: Come on, start the music!

original: Mopsa must be your mistress: marry, garlic, To mend her kissing with!
Now, in good time!
translation: Hey, cut that out!

original: Not a word, a word; we stand upon our manners. Come, strike up!
translation: I won't say a word; I'll be perfectly polite. Come on, start the music!

original: Pray, good shepherd, what fair swain is this Which dances with your daughter?
translation: Hey, shepherd: who's the young guy dancing with your daughter?

original: They call him Doricles; and boasts himself   To have a worthy feeding: but I have it   Upon his own report and I believe it;   He looks like sooth.
translation: His name is Doricles. He says he owns a prosperous farm, and I believe it, considering how handsome and well-dressed he is.

original: He says he loves my daughter:   I think so too; for never gazed the moon   Upon the water as he'll stand and read   As 'twere my daughter's eyes:
translation: He says he's in love with my daughter, and I think it's true. To be blunt,  the way he stares at her  completely gives it away!

original: and, to be plain.   I think there is not half a kiss to choose   Who loves another best.
translation: You'd be hard pressed to say which one loves the other more.

original: She dances featly.
translation: She's a great dancer.

original: So she does any thing; though I report it, That should be silent: if young Doricles Do light upon her, she shall bring him that Which he not dreams of.
O master, if you did but hear the pedlar at the   door, you would never dance again after a tabour and   pipe; no, the bagpipe could not move you:
translation: Sir, there's a traveling salesman at the door who can play the drums and the flute better than anyone I've ever seen.

original: he sings   several tunes faster than you'll tell money; he   utters them as he had eaten ballads and all men's   ears grew to his tunes.
translation: He knows all sorts of songs—he can sing any ballad you can think of.

original: He could never come better; he shall come in. I love a ballad but even too well, if it be doleful matter merrily set down, or a very pleasant thing indeed and sung lamentably.
translation: Perfect timing, let him in! I love ballads more than I should: happy ones, sad ones, and even happy ones sung sadly.

original: He hath songs for man or woman, of all sizes; no   milliner can so fit his customers with gloves:
translation: He has songs for men and women of all shapes and sizes. He can fit a song to a crowd better than a tailor can fit a suit to your body.

original: he   has the prettiest love-songs for maids; so without   bawdry, which is strange; with such delicate   burthens of dildos and fadings, 'jump her and thump   her;' and where some stretch-mouthed rascal would,   as it were, mean mischief and break a foul gap into   the matter, he makes the maid to answer 'Whoop, do me   no harm, good man;' puts him off, slights him, with   'Whoop, do me no harm, good man.'
translation: He has love songs for the ladies (and they're not dirty, none of that funny business your average street musician puts into his songs).

original: This is a brave fellow.
translation: This guy has some serious guts.

original: Believe me, thou talkest of an admirable conceited fellow. Has he any unbraided wares?
translation: Believe me, you've already sold us on this guy. Is he selling anything else?

original: He hath ribbons of an the colours i' the rainbow;   points more than all the lawyers in Bohemia can   learnedly handle,   though they come to him by the   gross: inkles, caddisses, cambrics, lawns:
translation: He has ribbons of every color in the rainbow, more pens than anyone could ever use in a lifetime, ink, and all kinds of fabrics

original: why, he   sings 'em over as they were gods or goddesses; you   would think a smock were a she-angel, he so chants   to the sleeve-hand and the work about the square on't.
translation: (and he absolutely raves about the workmanship of the weavers).

original: Prithee bring him in; and let him approach singing.
translation: Please bring him in, and have him sing on the way.

original: Forewarn him that he use no scurrilous words in's  tunes.
translation: And please ask him not to use any inappropriate language in his songs.

original: You have of these pedlars, that have more in them than you'ld think, sister.
translation: These traveling salesmen sometimes have more to them than you might think, sis.

original: Ay, good brother, or go about to think.
translation: Yes, brother, more than I want to think about.

original: Lawn as white as driven snow;   Cyprus black as e'er was crow;
translation: Linen  as white as snow, Cotton black as a crow,

original: Gloves as sweet as damask roses;   Masks for faces and for noses;
translation: Sweet-smelling gloves, Masks for your face,

original: Bugle bracelet, necklace amber,   Perfume for a lady's chamber;
translation: Beaded bracelets, gemstone necklaces, Perfume for ladies' bedrooms,

original: Golden quoifs and stomachers,   For my lads to give their dears:
translation: Golden hairpieces and belts For young men to give their girlfriends,

original: Pins and poking-sticks of steel,   What maids lack from head to heel:
translation: Steel pins and clips For ladies that need them:

original: Come buy of me, come; come buy, come buy;   Buy lads, or else your lasses cry: Come buy.
translation: Come buy from me; come buy, come buy, Boys, buy up, or your girlfriends will be sad. Come buy!

original: If I were not in love with Mopsa, thou shouldst take no money of me; but being enthralled as I am, it will also be the bondage of certain ribbons and gloves.
translation: If I weren't in love with Mopsa, I wouldn't spend any money, but since I am in love, I'll have to buy some ribbons and gloves.

original: I was promised them against the feast; but they come not too late now.
translation: You promised to get them for me before the feast, but they're just as good now.

original: He hath promised you more than that, or there be liars.
He hath paid you all he promised you; may be, he has paid you more, which will shame you to give him again.
Is there no manners left among maids? will they   wear their plackets where they should bear their   faces?
translation: Do you ladies have no manners? Is this how you treat each other?

original: Is there not milking-time, when you are   going to bed, or kiln-hole, to whistle off these   secrets, but you must be tittle-tattling before all   our guests?
translation: Isn't there some other place where you could call each other names, instead of doing it here in front of all our guests?

original: 'tis well they are whispering: clamour   your tongues, and not a word more.
translation: Now everyone's whispering about you. Please shut up; don't say anything else.

original: I have done. Come, you promised me a tawdry-lace and a pair of sweet gloves.
translation: I'm through. Come on, you promised me some lace and a pair of pretty gloves.

original: Have I not told thee how I was cozened by the way and lost all my money?
translation: Didn't I tell you how I was tricked and lost all my money?

original: And indeed, sir, there are cozeners abroad; therefore it behoves men to be wary.
translation: Sir, it's true that there are tricksters out there, so it's always smart to be aware.

original: Fear not thou, man, thou shalt lose nothing here.
translation: Don't worry; you're in no danger here.

original: I hope so, sir; for I have about me many parcels of  charge.
translation: I hope not, considering how much merchandise I have with me.

original: What hast here? ballads?
translation: What do you have here? Ballads?

original: Pray now, buy some: I love a ballad in print o' life, for then we are sure they are true.
translation: Aw, please buy some! I love a printed ballad, since if they're printed they must be true.

original: Here's one to a very doleful tune, how a usurer's wife was brought to bed of twenty money-bags at a burthen and how she longed to eat adders' heads and toads carbonadoed.
Is it true, think you?
translation: Do you think it's true?

original: Very true, and but a month old.
translation: Very true, and only a month old.

original: Bless me from marrying a usurer!
translation: I'll never marry a banker!

original: Here's the midwife's name to't, one Mistress Tale-porter, and five or six honest wives that were present. Why should I carry lies abroad?
translation: Look: the midwife, Mrs. Rumor, signed her name to prove it, along with five or six eyewitnesses. Why would I sell lies?

original: Pray you now, buy it.
translation: Please buy it.

original: Come on, lay it by: and let's first see moe ballads; we'll buy the other things anon.
translation: All right, set it aside, but let's look through more ballads first. We'll buy the other things later.

original: Here's another ballad of a fish, that appeared upon   the coast on Wednesday the four-score of April,   forty thousand fathom above water,
translation: Here's another ballad about a fish that washed up on the coast on Wednesday, April twenty-fourth, miles away from the water,

original: and sung this   ballad against the hard hearts of maids:
translation: and sung this ballad to warn cold-hearted girls.

original: it was   thought she was a woman and was turned into a cold   fish for she would not exchange flesh with one that   loved her:
translation: People thought she was a woman who'd been turned into a fish for not having sex with her boyfriend.

original: the ballad is very pitiful and as true.
translation: The ballad is both sad and true.

original: Is it true too, think you?
translation: Is it really true?

original: Five justices' hands at it, and witnesses more than my pack will hold.
translation: Five judges verified it, and there were countless witnesses.

original: Lay it by too: another.
translation: Put that one aside. Another.

original: This is a merry ballad, but a very pretty one.
translation: This is a funny ballad, but it's pretty, too.

original: Let's have some merry ones.
translation: Let's have some funny ones!

original: Why, this is a passing merry one and goes to the tune of 'Two maids wooing a man:' there's scarce a maid westward but she sings it; 'tis in request, I can tell you.
We can both sing it: if thou'lt bear a part, thou shalt hear; 'tis in three parts.
translation: We can both sing it.[To AUTOLYCUS] If you'll take a part, we can do it, since it has three parts.

original: We had the tune on't a month ago.
translation: We learned the tune of it a month ago.

original: I can bear my part; you must know 'tis my occupation; have at it with you.
translation: I can sing my part; it's my job, of course. Let's sing.

original: Get you hence, for I must go Where it fits not you to know.
Whither?
translation: Where?

original: O, whither?
translation: Oh, where?

original: Whither?
translation: Where?

original: It becomes thy oath full well, Thou to me thy secrets tell.
Me too, let me go thither.
translation: Me too; let's go there together.

original: Or thou goest to the orange or mill.
translation: Are you going to the forest, or the town?

original: If to either, thou dost ill.
translation: Whichever it is, it's a mistake.

original: Neither.
translation: Neither.

original: What, neither?
translation: What do you mean, "neither?"

original: Neither.
translation: Neither.

original: Thou hast sworn my love to be.
translation: You said you'd be my boyfriend.

original: Thou hast sworn it more to me: Then whither goest? say, whither?
We'll have this song out anon by ourselves:
translation: Well, we can finish this song by ourselves later on.

original: my   father and the gentlemen are in sad talk, and we'll   not trouble them.
translation: My father and the gentlemen are having a serious discussion and we won't bother them.

original: Come, bring away thy pack after   me. Wenches, I'll buy for you both. Pedlar, let's   have the first choice. Follow me, girls.
translation: Come on, bring your merchandise and follow me. Ladies, I'll buy something for both of you. Give them their first choice. Follow me, girls.

original: Will you buy any tape,   Or lace for your cape,
translation: Do you want to buy any ribbons Or lace to decorate your coat,

original: My dainty duck, my dear-a?   Any silk, any thread,
translation: My beautiful girl, my dear? Any silk, any thread,

original: Any toys for your head,   Of the new'st and finest, finest wear-a?
translation: Any hats or bows for your hair Of the newest and best there is?

original: Come to the pedlar;   Money's a medler.   That doth utter all men's ware-a.
translation: Come to the traveling salesman. Money makes the world go 'round And it's with money that men buy everything.

original: Master, there is three carters, three shepherds,   three neat-herds, three swine-herds, that have made   themselves all men of hair,
translation: Sir, there are three wagon-makers, three shepherds, three cowboys, and three pig-herders outside dressed up as  satyrs .

original: they call themselves   Saltiers, and they have a dance which the wenches   say is a gallimaufry of gambols, because they are   not in't;
translation: They call themselves "The Wits" and say they have a dance to perform, but the girls are saying its a load of garbage.

original: but they themselves are o' the mind, if it   be not too rough for some that know little but   bowling, it will please plentifully.
translation: But the men say that, if people aren't easily offended, they'll enjoy the performance.

original: Away! we'll none on 't: here has been too much homely foolery already. I know, sir, we weary you.
translation: Tell them to go away! We won't have it. There's been enough shenanigans here already. Sir, I know you're getting tired of us.

original: You weary those that refresh us: pray, let's see these four threes of herdsmen.
translation: No, this is the kind of thing we like! Come on, let in this group of men.

original: One three of them, by their own report, sir, hath danced before the king; and not the worst of the three but jumps twelve foot and a half by the squier.
translation: Three of them claim to have danced for the king, but they're all liars.

original: Leave your prating: since these good men are pleased, let them come in; but quickly now.
translation: Oh, cut it out. If these men are all right with it, we'll let them in. Go quickly!

original: Why, they stay at door, sir.
translation: They're waiting at the door, sir.

original: How now, fair shepherd!   Your heart is full of something that does take   Your mind from feasting.
translation: Hello there, handsome shepherd! You're distracted by love and not too focused on this party, huh?

original: Sooth, when I was young   And handed love as you do, I was wont   To load my she with knacks:
translation: I'll tell you, when I was your age, I was a sucker for buying gifts for my girlfriend.

original: I would have ransack'd   The pedlar's silken treasury and have pour'd it   To her acceptance; you have let him go   And nothing marted with him.
translation: I would have bought every piece of silk from the traveling salesman if it would have won her over, but you've let him go without buying a single thing.

original: If your lass   Interpretation should abuse and call this   Your lack of love or bounty, you were straited   For a reply, at least if you make a care   Of happy holding her.
translation: If your girlfriend interpreted this as a lack of love on your part, you'd be hard-pressed to convince her that you really care.

original: Old sir, I know   She prizes not such trifles as these are:
translation: Sir, she doesn't care about stuff like that.

original: The gifts she looks from me are pack'd and lock'd   Up in my heart; which I have given already,   But not deliver'd.
translation: The gifts she expects from me are the ones that come from the heart,  and I've  given those to her already, though I haven't delivered them .

original: O, hear me breathe my life   Before this ancient sir, who, it should seem,   Hath sometime loved!
translation: You must have had some experience with love, sir, at your age . . . let me explain how much I love her.

original: I take thy hand, this hand,   As soft as dove's down and as white as it,   Or Ethiopian's tooth, or the fann'd   snow that's bolted   By the northern blasts twice o'er.
translation: Watch me take her hand — her soft, pure white hand .

original: What follows this? How prettily the young swain seems to wash The hand was fair before! I have put you out: But to your protestation; let me hear What you profess.
translation: What comes next? This young shepherd speaks beautifully about a beautiful woman. I'd written you off but, since you ask, I'll listen.

original: Do, and be witness to 't.
translation: Listen, and be a witness.

original: And this my neighbour too?
translation: And my friend, too?

original: And he, and more   Than he, and men, the earth, the heavens, and all:
translation: Sure—him, everyone, the earth, and the heavens.

original: That, were I crown'd the most imperial monarch,   Thereof most worthy, were I the fairest youth   That ever made eye swerve, had force and knowledge   More than was ever man's, I would not prize them   Without her love;
translation: Even if I were king of the whole world, the most handsome man alive, and wiser than anyone in history, it wouldn't matter without her love.

original: for her employ them all;   Commend them and condemn them to her service   Or to their own perdition.
translation: Everything I do, I do for her. I put my gifts and my faults into her hands, for better or worse.

original: Fairly offer'd.
translation: Fair enough.

original: This shows a sound affection.
translation: It sounds like you really love her.

original: But, my daughter, Say you the like to him?
translation: Perdita, do you feel the same way about him?

original: I cannot speak So well, nothing so well; no, nor mean better: By the pattern of mine own thoughts I cut out The purity of his.
translation: I can't speak as well as he does; not at all, and my words' meaning couldn't be better than his. But our thoughts are one and the same.

original: Take hands, a bargain! And, friends unknown, you shall bear witness to 't: I give my daughter to him, and will make Her portion equal his.
translation: Take each other's hands; let's make a wedding contract!  Our new friends will be our witnesses. I give my daughter to him in marriage, and will give them equal parts of my fortune.

original: O, that must be   I' the virtue of your daughter:
translation: The only fortune I need is your beautiful daughter;

original: one being dead,   I shall have more than you can dream of yet;
translation: when my father dies, I will have more money than you've ever dreamed of.

original: Enough then for your wonder. But, come on,   Contract us 'fore these witnesses.
translation: But, come on, let's swear to our contract before these witnesses.

original: Come, your hand; And, daughter, yours.
translation: Give me your hand. And, Perdita, give me yours.

original: Soft, swain, awhile, beseech you; Have you a father?
I have: but what of him?
translation: I do. What about him?

original: Knows he of this?
translation: Does he know about this?

original: He neither does nor shall.
translation: He doesn't and he never will.

original: Methinks a father   Is at the nuptial of his son a guest   That best becomes the table.
translation: I think fathers are usually important guests at their sons' weddings.

original: Pray you once more,   Is not your father grown incapable   Of reasonable affairs? is he not stupid   With age and altering rheums?
translation: Another question: has your father gone senile? Is he ancient and in poor health?

original: can he speak? hear?   Know man from man? dispute his own estate?
translation: Can he speak? Hear? Recognize people? Take care of his property?

original: Lies he not bed-rid? and again does nothing   But what he did being childish?
translation: Is he bedridden? Is he basically like a child again?

original: No, good sir; He has his health and ampler strength indeed Than most have of his age.
translation: No, sir. He's healthy and stronger than most men at his age.

original: By my white beard,   You offer him, if this be so, a wrong   Something unfilial:
translation: Well, then, you're a terrible son for not inviting him to your wedding.

original: reason my son   Should choose himself a wife, but as good reason   The father, all whose joy is nothing else   But fair posterity, should hold some counsel   In such a business.
translation: If my son were choosing a wife, I'd have a say in it, considering the future of my family is at stake.

original: I yield all this; But for some other reasons, my grave sir, Which 'tis not fit you know, I not acquaint My father of this business.
translation: That's all true. But for some other reasons, sir, which you don't know, I can't tell my father about this.

original: Let him know't.
translation: Tell him.

original: He shall not.
translation: I can't.

original: Prithee, let him.
translation: Please, let him know.

original: No, he must not.
translation: No, he can't know.

original: Let him, my son: he shall not need to grieve At knowing of thy choice.
translation: Let him know, son. There's no reason he would disapprove your choice.

original: Come, come, he must not. Mark our contract.
translation: I'm serious; he can't know. Let's sign the contract.

original: Mark your divorce, young sir,
translation: Sign your divorce, sir—

original: Whom son I dare not call; thou art too base   To be acknowledged: thou a sceptre's heir,
translation: I can hardly call you my son now; I wouldn't stoop down to your level.

original: That thus affect'st a sheep-hook!
translation: Look at you, a prince, dressed up with a shepherd's staff!

original: Thou old traitor,   I am sorry that by hanging thee I can   But shorten thy life one week.
translation: You old traitor, it's too bad that by hanging you I won't be shortening your life that much.

original: And thou, fresh piece   Of excellent witchcraft, who of force must know   The royal fool thou copest with,—
translation: And you, you witch, as if you don't know that you're meddling with a prince.

original: O, my heart!
translation: Oh, my heart!

original: I'll have thy beauty scratch'd with briers, and made   More homely than thy state.
translation: I'll have your beautiful face scratched with thorns until you're uglier than your ugly poverty.

original: For thee, fond boy,   If I may ever know thou dost but sigh   That thou no more shalt see this knack, as never   I mean thou shalt, we'll bar thee from succession;   Not hold thee of our blood, no, not our kin,   Far than Deucalion off: mark thou my words:   Follow us to the court.
translation: And you, lover boy, if you so much as sigh over not seeing this slut again, you'll never inherit the throne and, what's more, I'll disown you as my son. You'll be out of the family forever, mark my words. Follow me back to court.

original: Thou churl, for this time,   Though full of our displeasure, yet we free thee   From the dead blow of it.
translation: This time you're off the hook, though I am not at all pleased.

original: And you, enchantment.—   Worthy enough a herdsman: yea, him too,   That makes himself, but for our honour therein,   Unworthy thee,—
translation: And you, you witch! Your tricks might be good enough for a shepherd, but not for my son.

original: if ever henceforth thou   These rural latches to his entrance open,   Or hoop his body more with thy embraces,   I will devise a death as cruel for thee   As thou art tender to't.
translation: If you ever let him through your gates again, or lay a hand on him, I'll think up the cruelest, most painful possible death for you.

original: Even here undone!   I was not much afeard; for once or twice   I was about to speak and tell him plainly,   The selfsame sun that shines upon his court   Hides not his visage from our cottage but   Looks on alike.
translation: Ruined, at the last minute! I wasn't afraid, though. I was about to tell him that the same sun that shines in court shines here at our cottage, looking down on us equally.

original: Will't please you, sir, be gone?   I told you what would come of this: beseech you,   Of your own state take care: this dream of mine,—   Being now awake, I'll queen it no inch farther,   But milk my ewes and weep.
translation: Will you go, then? I told you what would come of this. Please, remember that you are a prince. It was all a dream. Now I'm awake, and I won't imagine I'm a queen anymore. I'll just go back to my sheep and cry.

original: Why, how now, father! Speak ere thou diest.
translation: What do you say for yourself, shepherd? Speak or you die.

original: I cannot speak, nor think   Nor dare to know that which I know.
translation: I can't speak; I can't think or wrap my head around what I know now.

original: O sir!   You have undone a man of fourscore three,   That thought to fill his grave in quiet, yea,   To die upon the bed my father died,   To lie close by his honest bones:
translation: Sir, you've ruined an eighty-three-year-old man who only wanted to die in peace on the same bed where his father passed away, and to be buried near him.

original: but now   Some hangman must put on my shroud and lay me   Where no priest shovels in dust.
translation: Now some executioner will bury me, alone.

original: O cursed wretch,   That knew'st this was the prince,   and wouldst adventure   To mingle faith with him!
translation: How dare you continue to play around with him, knowing he was the prince?

original: Undone! undone!   If I might die within this hour, I have lived   To die when I desire.
translation: Ruined! Ruined! If I die within the hour, I'll be glad to be out of my misery.

original: Why look you so upon me?   I am but sorry, not afeard; delay'd,   But nothing alter'd:
translation: Why are you looking at me like that? I'm sorry this happened, but I'm not afraid. This delays me, but doesn't change me.

original: what I was, I am;
translation: I am who I was before.

original: More straining on for plucking back, not following   My leash unwillingly.
translation: This setback makes me want to marry Perdita even more.

original: Gracious my lord,   You know your father's temper:
translation: Sir, you know your father has a temper.

original: at this time   He will allow no speech, which I do guess   You do not purpose to him; and as hardly   Will he endure your sight as yet, I fear:
translation: He doesn't want to hear from you right now, so I don't suggest you try it. He probably doesn't want to see you, either.

original: Then, till the fury of his highness settle,   Come not before him.
translation: Stay away from him until his anger dies down.

original: I not purpose it. I think, Camillo?
Even he, my lord.
translation: That's me, sir.

original: How often have I told you 'twould be thus! How often said, my dignity would last But till 'twere known!
translation: I've told you so many times that this would happen! I've been saying that I'd be ruined as soon as we were found out!

original: It cannot fail but by   The violation of my faith; and then   Let nature crush the sides o' the earth together   And mar the seeds within!
translation: You could only be ruined if I left you, but that will never happen!

original: Lift up thy looks:   From my succession wipe me, father; I   Am heir to my affection.
translation: Chin up! My father can disown me;  I have my love to sustain me .

original: Be advised.
translation: You should think this through . . .

original: I am, and by my fancy: if my reason Will thereto be obedient, I have reason; If not, my senses, better pleased with madness, Do bid it welcome.
translation: I have, and I know what I'm doing—following my heart. Call me crazy; if I'm crazy, I embrace it.

original: This is desperate, sir.
translation: This is irresponsible, sir.

original: So call it: but it does fulfil my vow;   I needs must think it honesty.
translation: Maybe so, but it's keeping my promise and therefore it's the right thing to do.

original: Camillo,   Not for Bohemia, nor the pomp that may   Be thereat glean'd, for all the sun sees or   The close earth wombs or the profound sea hides   In unknown fathoms, will I break my oath   To this my fair beloved:
translation: Camillo, I wouldn't break my vow to Perdita, not for the whole country, the sun, the earth, and the sea.

original: therefore, I pray you,   As you have ever been my father's honour'd friend,
translation: So, as my father's friend,

original: When he shall miss me,—as, in faith, I mean not   To see him any more,—
translation: when he realizes he misses me (since, by the way, I won't be seeing him anymore).

original: cast your good counsels   Upon his passion;
translation: please put in a good word for me

original: let myself and fortune   Tug for the time to come.
translation: Maybe I'll come back onto his good side in the future.

original: This you may know   And so deliver, I am put to sea   With her whom here I cannot hold on shore;   And most opportune to our need I have   A vessel rides fast by, but not prepared   For this design.
translation: You can let him know that Perdita and I are sailing away on a ship I have nearby (which is lucky, though I had it ready for something else).

original: What course I mean to hold   Shall nothing benefit your knowledge, nor   Concern me the reporting.
translation: I won't tell you where we're going, though.

original: O my lord! I would your spirit were easier for advice, Or stronger for your need.
translation: Oh, sir, I wish you would listen to my advice; you might need it.

original: Hark, Perdita @  @ I'll hear you by and by.
translation: Perdita, come here.  [To CAMILLO] I'll listen to you in a minute.

original: He's irremoveable,   Resolved for flight.
translation: I can't change his mind; he's decided to leave.

original: Now were I happy, if   His going I could frame to serve my turn,   Save him from danger, do him love and honour,
translation: I could make this work to my advantage and keep him safe, all the while being loyal to him and to Polixenes.

original: Purchase the sight again of dear Sicilia   And that unhappy king, my master, whom   I so much thirst to see.
translation: This could be my chance to see Leontes again, who I've wanted to see so much.

original: Now, good Camillo; I am so fraught with curious business that I leave out ceremony.
translation: Now, Camillo: I've been so caught up with all this that I've been rude.

original: Sir, I think You have heard of my poor services, i' the love That I have borne your father?
translation: Sir, I think you're familiar with my reputation for service through the work I've done for your father.

original: Very nobly Have you deserved: it is my father's music To speak your deeds, not little of his care To have them recompensed as thought on.
translation: Of course; he speaks very highly of you, and is always rewarding you for a job well done.

original: Well, my lord,   If you may please to think I love the king   And through him what is nearest to him, which is   Your gracious self, embrace but my direction:
translation: Well, sir, since you know I've served your father well, it follows that I would serve just as well the person he loves the most (that is, you). Hear me out:

original: If your more ponderous and settled project   May suffer alteration, on mine honour,   I'll point you where you shall have such receiving   As shall become your highness;
translation: if you encounter any difficulties on your journey, I can tell you where to go,

original: where you may   Enjoy your mistress, from the whom, I see,   There's no disjunction to be made, but by—   As heavens forefend!—your ruin; marry her,
translation: where to take Perdita (since it's clear you don't want to be separated from her, unless some sort of catastrophe got in your way), and where to marry her.

original: And, with my best endeavours in your absence,   Your discontenting father strive to qualify   And bring him up to liking.
translation: And, while you're gone, I can try to win your father over for you.

original: How, Camillo, May this, almost a miracle, be done? That I may call thee something more than man And after that trust to thee.
translation: Camillo, that would basically be a miracle, but how can we do it? You would be a superhero and I'd never doubt you again.

original: Have you thought on A place whereto you'll go?
translation: Have you thought about where you'll go?

original: Not any yet: But as the unthought-on accident is guilty To what we wildly do, so we profess Ourselves to be the slaves of chance and flies Of every wind that blows.
translation: Nowhere yet, but since this was all unplanned, we're flying by the seat of our pants here.

original: Then list to me:   This follows, if you will not change your purpose   But undergo this flight, make for Sicilia,
translation: Then, listen to me: If you're determined to leave the country, go to Sicily,

original: And there present yourself and your fair princess,   For so I see she must be, 'fore Leontes:   She shall be habited as it becomes   The partner of your bed.
translation: introduce yourself, and call your bride a princess. If she's going to visit Leontes's court, it's only fitting that she be dressed as your royal wife should.

original: Methinks I see   Leontes opening his free arms and weeping   His welcomes forth; asks thee the son forgiveness,   As 'twere i' the father's person;
translation: I can imagine Leontes greeting you with a hug, crying as he asks your forgiveness as if you were your own father.

original: kisses the hands   Of your fresh princess; o'er and o'er divides him   'Twixt his unkindness and his kindness; the one   He chides to hell and bids the other grow   Faster than thought or time.
translation: He'll kiss your princess's hands. His kindness will be a complete departure from the cruelty you've heard about in the past. He's over that now; he's kicked his evil ways to hell and has been nurturing his better qualities all these years.

original: Worthy Camillo, What colour for my visitation shall I Hold up before him?
translation: But Camillo, what reason for visiting can I make up?

original: Sent by the king your father   To greet him and to give him comforts.
translation: Say your father sent you to greet him and to bring him gifts.

original: Sir,   The manner of your bearing towards him, with   What you as from your father shall deliver,   Things known betwixt us three, I'll write you down:
translation: I'll write down some instructions for how to behave toward him and will pack all the gifts you'll deliver on your father's behalf.

original: The which shall point you forth at every sitting   What you must say; that he shall not perceive   But that you have your father's bosom there   And speak his very heart.
translation: All of it will support your story: that you've come to make peace between him and your father.

original: I am bound to you: There is some sap in this.
translation: I'll do exactly as you say. This makes a lot of sense.

original: A cause more promising   Than a wild dedication of yourselves   To unpath'd waters, undream'd shores, most certain   To miseries enough; no hope to help you,   But as you shake off one to take another;   Nothing so certain as your anchors, who   Do their best office, if they can but stay you   Where you'll be loath to be:
translation: It's a better reason, at least, than your completely haphazard journey overseas with no plan, no trajectory, and no help, with no company but each other. Take care of each other.

original: besides you know   Prosperity's the very bond of love,   Whose fresh complexion and whose heart together   Affliction alters.
translation: A heart full of love can make even the worst places bearable, and can bring a smile to your face even in the midst of suffering.

original: One of these is true: I think affliction may subdue the cheek, But not take in the mind.
Yea, say you so? There shall not at your father's house these seven years Be born another such.
translation: Oh, you think so? You're one-in-a-million, shepherd girl.

original: My good Camillo, She is as forward of her breeding as She is i' the rear our birth.
translation: Camillo, she's so far beyond her lower-class origins; she's basically as noble as you and I.

original: I cannot say 'tis pity She lacks instructions, for she seems a mistress To most that teach.
translation: I would say "it's too bad she hasn't had an education," but she seems more capable than most teachers I know.

original: Your pardon, sir; for this I'll blush you thanks.
translation: I beg your pardon, sir. I'm embarrassed, but thank you.

original: My prettiest Perdita!   But O, the thorns we stand upon!
translation: My beautiful Perdita! But we're in a sticky situation.

original: Camillo,   Preserver of my father, now of me,   The medicine of our house, how shall we do?
translation: Camillo, you've rescued my father and now me; you're a life-saver. What should we do?

original: We are not furnish'd like Bohemia's son,   Nor shall appear in Sicilia.
translation: I don't have the clothes and facilities I normally travel with as the prince of Bohemia, and I won't be able to get those things in Sicily.

original: My lord,   Fear none of this: I think you know my fortunes   Do all lie there:
translation: Sir, don't worry. As you know, I have a lot of connections there.

original: it shall be so my care   To have you royally appointed as if   The scene you play were mine.
translation: I can make sure you're provided for, as surely as if I were there myself.

original: For instance, sir,   That you may know you shall not want, one word.
translation: For example, sir—if I can ease your mind, talk with me for a moment.

original: Ha, ha! what a fool Honesty is! and Trust, his   sworn brother, a very simple gentleman!
translation: Ha, ha! Honest men are idiots, and people who trust me are just plain stupid.

original: I have sold   all my trumpery; not a counterfeit stone, not a   ribbon, glass, pomander, brooch, table-book, ballad,   knife, tape, glove, shoe-tie, bracelet, horn-ring,   to keep my pack from fasting:
translation: I've sold all my junk. I don't have a single fake gem, ribbon, mirror, perfume, jewelry, book, ballad, knife, belt, glove, shoelace, bracelet, or ring left in my bag.

original: they throng who   should buy first, as if my trinkets had been   hallowed and brought a benediction to the buyer:   by which means I saw whose purse was best in   picture; and what I saw, to my good use I   remembered.
translation: They all swarmed to be the first to buy, as if my stuff were some kind of holy charm. I took note of where they kept their wallets and remembered that for later.

original: My clown, who wants but something to   be a reasonable man, grew so in love with the   wenches' song, that he would not stir his pettitoes   till he had both tune and words;
translation: The shepherd's son (he's not all that bright, by the way) was so impressed with the girls' song that he wouldn't budge until he learned the tune and the words.

original: which so drew the   rest of the herd to me that all their other senses   stuck in ears: you might have pinched a placket, it   was senseless;
translation: That was the best advertisement, since it sent all the others running to me to get the song for themselves. There was nothing you could do; everyone was singing this god-awful song, non-stop.

original: 'twas nothing to geld a codpiece of a   purse; I could have filed keys off that hung in   chains: no hearing, no feeling, but my sir's song,   and admiring the nothing of it. So that in this   time of lethargy I picked and cut most of their   festival purses;
translation: While they were all lying around, I took the opportunity to pick their pockets and rifled through most of their purses.

original: and had not the old man come in   with a whoo-bub against his daughter and the king's   son and scared my choughs from the chaff, I had not   left a purse alive in the whole army.
translation: If that old man hadn't come in and raised a ruckus about the shepherd's daughter and the prince, scaring everyone away, I wouldn't have left a single penny in anyone's wallet.

original: Nay, but my letters, by this means being there So soon as you arrive, shall clear that doubt.
translation: No, my letters will get there before you arrive and will clear up any doubt.

original: And those that you'll procure from King Leontes—
translation: And the letters you'll get from King Leontes—

original: Shall satisfy your father.
translation: —will satisfy your father.

original: Happy be you! All that you speak shows fair.
translation: Thank you! You're so generous.

original: Who have we here? @     We'll make an instrument of this, omit Nothing may give us aid.
translation: Who have we here? [To FLORIZEL and PERDITA] We'll make use of this; we can't overlook anything that might help us.

original: If they have overheard me now, why, hanging.
translation: If they just overheard me, I'm dead.

original: How now, good fellow! why shakest thou so? Fear not, man; here's no harm intended to thee.
translation: Hello, sir! Why are you shaking? Don't be afraid; no one's going to hurt you.

original: I am a poor fellow, sir.
translation: I'm a poor man, sir.

original: Why, be so still; here's nobody will steal that from   thee:
translation: Calm down, no one here is going to steal from you.

original: yet for the outside of thy poverty we must   make an exchange; therefore discase thee instantly,   —thou must think there's a necessity in't,—and   change garments with this gentleman:
translation: However, we would like to trade you for your poor man's clothes, so get undressed (it's necessary, you see) and change clothes with this gentleman.

original: though the   pennyworth on his side be the worst, yet hold thee,   there's some boot.
translation: Though Florizel's getting the worst end of the deal already, we'll give you some money, too.

original: I am a poor fellow, sir. @  @ I know ye well enough.
translation: I'm a poor fellow, sir. I know exactly who you are.

original: Nay, prithee, dispatch: the gentleman is half flayed already.
translation: Come on, now, get your clothes off. Florizel's half-stripped already.

original: Are you in earnest, sir? @  @ I smell the trick on't.
translation: Are you serious, sir? This must be a trick.

original: Dispatch, I prithee.
translation: Get on with it, please.

original: Indeed, I have had earnest: but I cannot with conscience take it.
translation: Ah, I can see you're serious, but I can't take your clothes in good conscience.

original: Unbuckle, unbuckle.
translation: Unbuckle, unbuckle.

original: Fortunate mistress,—let my prophecy   Come home to ye!—
translation: Perdita, I hope  my plan  works out for your sake!

original: you must retire yourself   Into some covert: take your sweetheart's hat   And pluck it o'er your brows, muffle your face,   Dismantle you, and, as you can,
translation: You need to hide yourself for the time being. Take Florizel's hat and cover your face, change your clothes,

original: disliken   The truth of your own seeming; that you may—   For I do fear eyes over—to shipboard   Get undescried.
translation: and disguise yourself as much as possible. I'm afraid you're being watched, and you need to get onboard the ship undetected.

original: I see the play so lies That I must bear a part.
translation: I guess I'll play the part I've been given.

original: No remedy. Have you done there?
translation: There's nothing we can do about it.  Are you all dressed?

original: Should I now meet my father, He would not call me son.
translation: My own father wouldn't recognize me now.

original: Nay, you shall have no hat. @  @ Come, lady, come. Farewell, my friend.
translation: No, you don't need a hat.  Come on, Perdita. [To AUTOLYCUS] Goodbye, friend.

original: Adieu, sir.
translation: Goodbye, sir.

original: O Perdita, what have we twain forgot! Pray you, a word.
translation: Perdita, are we forgetting anything? Let's talk.

original: What I do next, shall be to tell the king   Of this escape and whither they are bound;
translation: Next I'll tell the king they escaped and where they're headed.

original: Wherein my hope is I shall so prevail   To force him after: in whose company   I shall review Sicilia, for whose sight   I have a woman's longing.
translation: I'm hoping he'll go after them and that I'll get to come along to see my beloved country, Sicily.

original: Fortune speed us! Thus we set on, Camillo, to the sea-side.
translation: I pray we have a quick journey! Camillo, we're off to the seaside.

original: The swifter speed the better.
translation: The quicker the better.

original: I understand the business, I hear it: to have an   open ear, a quick eye, and a nimble hand, is   necessary for a cut-purse; a good nose is requisite   also, to smell out work for the other senses.
translation: I see what's going on here. As a pickpocket, it's necessary to have an open ear, quick eye, fast hand—and a good nose, too, so you can smell out the good places to steal.

original: I see   this is the time that the unjust man doth thrive.   What an exchange had this been without boot! What   a boot is here with this exchange!
translation: This is a great time to be a criminal. He just traded me fancy clothes for my rags; I gained everything, and he gained nothing!

original: Sure the gods do   this year connive at us, and we may do any thing   extempore. The prince himself is about a piece of   iniquity, stealing away from his father with his   clog at his heels:
translation: The gods have clearly given me permission to do whatever I want now. The prince himself is up to no good, running away from his father with his whore in tow.

original: if I thought it were a piece of   honesty to acquaint the king withal, I would not   do't: I hold it the more knavery to conceal it;   and therein am I constant to my profession.
translation: Even if it were a good deed to tell the king, I wouldn't do it. I think it's more crafty to keep it a secret, and since I'm a crook, I'll do just that.

original: Aside, aside; here is more matter for a hot brain: every lane's end, every shop, church, session, hanging, yields a careful man work.
translation: But wait, there's more work to be done. Every street, store, church, meeting, and funeral can turn into an opportunity if you're savvy.

original: See, see; what a man you are now! There is no other way but to tell the king she's a changeling and none of your flesh and blood.
Nay, but hear me.
translation: No, listen to me.

original: Nay, but hear me.
translation: No, listen to me.

original: Go to, then.
translation: Go on, then.

original: She being none of your flesh and blood, your flesh   and blood has not offended the king; and so your   flesh and blood is not to be punished by him.
translation: Since she's not actually part of your family, your family hasn't offended the king, and your family can't be punished by him.

original: Show   those things you found about her, those secret   things, all but what she has with her:
translation: Show him the things you found with her—all the things that you kept secret all these years (except for whatever she took with her).

original: this being   done, let the law go whistle: I warrant you.
translation: Then, the law can have nothing to do with us, I promise you.

original: I will tell the king all, every word, yea, and his   son's pranks too;
translation: I'll tell the king everything, every word. And I'll tell him about Florizel's tricks, too.

original: who, I may say, is no honest man,   neither to his father nor to me, to go about to make   me the king's brother-in-law.
translation: He hasn't been very truthful to his father or to me, considering he was about to make me a king's brother-in-law.

original: Indeed, brother-in-law was the farthest off you could have been to him and then your blood had been the dearer by I know how much an ounce.
translation: If they had actually gotten married and you were his brother-in-law by now, he'd hate you even more, and the price on your head would be even higher.

original: Very wisely, puppies!
translation: Very smart, boys!

original: Well, let us to the king: there is that in this fardel will make him scratch his beard.
translation: Well, let's go to the king. The stuff in this bag will give him something to think about.

original: I know not what impediment this complaint may be to the flight of my master.
translation: I'm not sure how this will get in the way of Florizel's departure.

original: Pray heartily he be at palace.
translation: Let's hope he's at the palace.

original: Though I am not naturally honest, I am so sometimes by chance: let me pocket up my pedlar's  excrement.  @     How now, rustics! whither  are you bound?
translation: I'm not naturally an honest man, but sometimes I'm honest by accident. I need to take off this traveling salesman disguise. [AUTOLYCUS takes off his fake beard and speaks to the shepherds] Hello, peasants! Where are you going?

original: To the palace, an it like your worship.
Your affairs there, what, with whom, the condition of that fardel, the place of your dwelling, your names, your ages, of what having, breeding, and any thing that is fitting to be known, discover.
translation: Tell me what business you have there, and with whom. Tell me what's in that bag, where you live, your names, your ages, how much money you have, who your parents are, and anything else that I should know.

original: We are but plain fellows, sir.
translation: We're simple people, sir.

original: A lie; you are rough and hairy. Let me have no lying: it becomes none but tradesmen, and they often give us soldiers the lie: but we pay them for it with stamped coin, not stabbing steel; therefore they do not give us the lie.
Your worship had like to have given us one, if you had not taken yourself with the manner.
translation: It seemed like you were going to try to expose us for lying, but you've just revealed that you're the liar.

original: Are you a courtier, an't like you, sir?
translation: Are you a courtier or not, sir?

original: Whether it like me or no, I am a courtier. Seest   thou not the air of the court in these enfoldings?
translation: Whether I like it or not, I'm a courtier. Can't you see my courtly clothes?

original: hath not my gait in it the measure of the court?   receives not thy nose court-odor from me?
translation: Don't I walk like a courtier? Smell like one?

original: reflect I   not on thy baseness court-contempt?
translation: Look down my nose at you like one?

original: Thinkest thou,   for that I insinuate, or toaze from thee thy   business, I am therefore no courtier?
translation: Just because I'm asking you questions, you think I'm not a courtier?

original: I am courtier   cap-a-pe; and one that will either push on or pluck   back thy business there: whereupon I command thee to   open thy affair.
translation: I'm a courtier from head to toe and I have the power to help you to court or to stop you right there. For that reason I command you to tell me everything.

original: My business, sir, is to the king.
translation: I have some business with the king, sir.

original: What advocate hast thou to him?
translation: And who is pleading your case to him?

original: I know not, an't like you.
translation: I don't know, sir.

original: Advocate's the court-word for a pheasant: say you have none.
translation: "Advocate" is court-speak for "pheasant;" say you don't have one.

original: None, sir; I have no pheasant, cock nor hen.
translation: None, sir. I have no pheasant, male or female.

original: How blessed are we that are not simple men! Yet nature might have made me as these are, Therefore I will not disdain.
translation: Thank God I'm not an idiot! But, since there but for the grace of God go I, I won't look down on them.

original: This cannot be but a great courtier.
translation: He must be a really important courtier.

original: His garments are rich, but he wears them not handsomely.
translation: His clothes are fancy, but he's not wearing them elegantly.

original: He seems to be the more noble in being fantastical: a great man, I'll warrant; I know by the picking on's teeth.
translation: The fact that he's a little crazy makes him seem even more noble. I could spot it a mile away.

original: The fardel there? what's i' the fardel? Wherefore that box?
translation: What about the bag? What's in the bag? And why the box?

original: Sir, there lies such secrets in this fardel and box, which none must know but the king; and which he shall know within this hour, if I may come to the speech of him.
translation: Sir, there are secrets in this bag and this box which are for the king alone. If I get the chance to speak to him, he'll know within the hour.

original: Age, thou hast lost thy labour.
translation: Old man, you're out of luck.

original: Why, sir?
translation: Why, sir?

original: The king is not at the palace; he is gone aboard a new ship to purge melancholy and air himself: for, if thou beest capable of things serious, thou must know the king is full of grief.
translation: The king is not at the palace. He went aboard a new ship to escape his sadness. Understand? The king is grieving.

original: So 'tis said, sir; about his son, that should have married a shepherd's daughter.
translation: I've heard, sir, that he's grieving his son who almost married a shepherd's daughter.

original: If that shepherd be not in hand-fast, let him fly: the curses he shall have, the tortures he shall feel, will break the back of man, the heart of monster.
translation: If that shepherd isn't in jail already, he better run for it. The punishment he faces will be enough to break any man.

original: Think you so, sir?
translation: Do you think so, sir?

original: Not he alone shall suffer what wit can make heavy   and vengeance bitter; but those that are germane to   him, though removed fifty times, shall all come   under the hangman:
translation: He'll suffer horribly, but so will his family and everyone within fifty degrees of relation to him. They'll all be hanged;

original: which though it be great pity,   yet it is necessary. An old sheep-whistling rogue a   ram-tender, to offer to have his daughter come into   grace!
translation: it's a pity, but it's necessary. Can you believe some old shepherd was grooming his daughter to catch a prince?

original: Some say he shall be stoned; but that death   is too soft for him, say I draw our throne into a   sheep-cote! all deaths are too few, the sharpest too  easy.
translation: Some say he'll be stoned to death, but I say that's too lenient for someone who almost ruined our prince! No punishment is too harsh for him.

original: Has the old man e'er a son, sir, do you hear. an't like you, sir?
translation: Have you heard anything about the old man having a son, sir? If it please you, sir?

original: He has a son, who shall be flayed alive; then   'nointed over with honey, set on the head of a   wasp's nest; then stand till he be three quarters   and a dram dead;
translation: Oh, he has a son. He'll be skinned alive, drizzled in honey, thrown into a wasp's nest, and forced to stay there until he's nearly dead.

original: then recovered again with   aqua-vitae or some other hot infusion; then, raw as   he is, and in the hottest day prognostication   proclaims, shall be be set against a brick-wall, the   sun looking with a southward eye upon him, where he   is to behold him with flies blown to death.
translation: Then they'll wake him up with a shot of whisky and stand him, raw flesh and all, on top of a brick wall to be baked in the sun and eaten by flies.

original: But what   talk we of these traitorly rascals, whose miseries   are to be smiled at, their offences being so   capital? Tell me, for you seem to be honest plain   men, what you have to the king:
translation: But why are we talking about these backstabbing traitors? We should be thankful they're going to be put to death for their crimes! Since you seem to be humble peasants, tell me what you're bringing to the king.

original: being something   gently considered, I'll bring you where he is   aboard, tender your persons to his presence,   whisper him in your behalfs; and if it be in man   besides the king to effect your suits, here is man   shall do it.
translation: If it's worth his attention, I'll bring you aboard his ship and introduce you to him with a kind recommendation. If there's anyone besides the king who can help you, it's me.

original: He seems to be of great authority:
translation: He seems to have a lot of power.

original: close with him,   give him gold; and though authority be a stubborn   bear, yet he is oft led by the nose with gold: show   the inside of your purse to the outside of his hand,   and no more ado.
translation: Let's make friends with him and give him a little money. You can control even power with money; give him a few coins and see how easy everything becomes.

original: Remember 'stoned,' and 'flayed alive.'
translation: Remember he said we're condemned to be "stoned to death" and "skinned alive!"

original: An't please you, sir, to undertake the business for us, here is that gold I have: I'll make it as much more and leave this young man in pawn till I bring it  you.
translation: If it please you to help us, sir, please take this money. I can give more afterward—as much as you like—and you can keep this young man as collateral until I do.

original: After I have done what I promised?
translation: After I have done what I promised?

original: Ay, sir.
translation: Yes, sir.

original: Well, give me the moiety. Are you a party in this  business?
translation: Well, give me that part of it. Are you a part of this business?

original: In some sort, sir: but though my case be a pitiful one, I hope I shall not be flayed out of it.
translation: Sort of, sir. Even though my share is small, I hope I won't be skinned out of it.

original: O, that's the case of the shepherd's son: hang him, he'll be made an example.
translation: Oh, that's the punishment for the shepherd's son. Forget about him! They'll make an example out of him.

original: Comfort, good comfort!
translation: Isn't that comforting?

original: We must to the king and show   our strange sights: he must know 'tis none of your   daughter nor my sister; we are gone else.
translation: We need to see the king and show him our secret stuff. He needs to know that she's neither your daughter nor my sister, otherwise we're dead.

original: Sir, I   will give you as much as this old man does when the   business is performed, and remain, as he says, your   pawn till it be brought you.
translation: Sir, I'll give you as much money as this old man did after the business is done. And you can hold on to me as collateral in the meantime.

original: I will trust you. Walk before toward the sea-side; go on the right hand: I will but look upon the hedge and follow you.
translation: I trust you. Walk down to the sea; I'll follow you from behind.

original: We are blest in this man, as I may say, even blest.
translation: We are blessed to have met this man. Very blessed.

original: Let's before as he bids us: he was provided to do us  good.
translation: Let's get going and do what he says. God sent him to help us.

original: If I had a mind to be honest, I see Fortune would   not suffer me: she drops booties in my mouth. I am   courted now with a double occasion, gold and a means   to do the prince my master good;
translation: If I were a good man, maybe I'd make even more money than I do as a criminal. Now I have a two-for-one deal: money and a chance to do Florizel, my former master, some good.

original: which who knows how   that may turn back to my advancement? I will bring   these two moles, these blind ones, aboard him:
translation: Who knows how I can work this to my advantage? I'll bring these two idiots aboard to Polixenes.

original: if he   think it fit to shore them again and that the   complaint they have to the king concerns him   nothing, let him call me rogue for being so far   officious; for I am proof against that title and   what shame else belongs to't.
translation: If he kicks them back to shore and their reason for seeing him turns out to be bogus, the worst that can happen is that he calls me "crook" (which doesn't offend me, since I've earned that title!).

original: To him will I present   them: there may be matter in it.
translation: I'll present them to Polixenes; it may turn out to be something after all.

original: Sir, you have done enough, and have perform'd   A saint-like sorrow:
translation: Sir, you've done enough; you've grieved enough. You've redeemed every one of your sins.

original: no fault could you make,   Which you have not redeem'd; indeed, paid down   More penitence than done trespass:
translation: You've done more  penitence  than you did wrong.

original: at the last,   Do as the heavens have done, forget your evil;   With them forgive yourself.
translation: For the last time: do what God does. Forget what your evil actions and forgive yourself.

original: Whilst I remember   Her and her virtues, I cannot forget   My blemishes in them,
translation: As long as I  remember  her, I can't forget my mistakes.

original: and so still think of   The wrong I did myself; which was so much,   That heirless it hath made my kingdom and   Destroy'd the sweet'st companion that e'er man   Bred his hopes out of.
translation: I still think about how badly I messed up, leaving my kingdom without a prince and myself without a wife.

original: True, too true, my lord: If, one by one, you wedded all the world, Or from the all that are took something good, To make a perfect woman, she you kill'd Would be unparallel'd.
translation: Too true, too true, sir. No woman alive compares to the woman you killed.

original: I think so. Kill'd!   She I kill'd! I did so: but thou strikest me   Sorely, to say I did; it is as bitter   Upon thy tongue as in my thought:
translation: I think you're right. Killed? The woman I killed? It's true, but it hurts to hear you say that. It hurts to think that.

original: now, good now,   Say so but seldom.
translation: Please, don't say it often.

original: Not at all, good lady: You might have spoken a thousand things that would Have done the time more benefit and graced Your kindness better.
translation: Ma'am, please stop. Anything you could possibly say would be better than that.

original: You are one of those Would have him wed again.
translation: You're one of those men who want him to marry again.

original: If you would not so,   You pity not the state, nor the remembrance   Of his most sovereign name; consider little   What dangers, by his highness' fail of issue,   May drop upon his kingdom and devour   Incertain lookers on.
translation: If you're against him marrying, you're not thinking realistically about our country or the fact that Leontes needs  an heir to his royal name . Consider what will happen if he dies without an heir—the kingdom will descend into warfare.

original: What were more holy   Than to rejoice the former queen is well?   What holier than, for royalty's repair,   For present comfort and for future good,   To bless the bed of majesty again   With a sweet fellow to't?
translation: We should thank God Hermione is in heaven now. Only good could come of a new queen: companionship for Leontes and the possibility of future princes and princesses.

original: There is none worthy,   Respecting her that's gone. Besides, the gods   Will have fulfill'd their secret purposes;   For has not the divine Apollo said,   Is't not the tenor of his oracle,   That King Leontes shall not have an heir   Till his lost child be found?
translation: No one but Hermione herself deserves that role. Besides, the gods intended this: didn't Apollo's oracle say that King Leontes would not have an heir until his lost child was found?

original: which that it shall,   Is all as monstrous to our human reason   As my Antigonus to break his grave   And come again to me; who, on my life,   Did perish with the infant.
translation: It's about as likely that baby will return as it is that Antigonus, my husband (who died with it) will come back to life.

original: 'Tis your counsel   My lord should to the heavens be contrary,   Oppose against their wills.
translation: You're advising the king to go against the gods' will.

original: Care not for issue;   The crown will find an heir:
translation: Don't worry about having children; you'll find someone to inherit the throne.

original: great Alexander   Left his to the worthiest; so his successor   Was like to be the best.
translation: Alexander the Great didn't have children, so he left his to whoever was most worthy. That worked out fine for him.

original: Good Paulina,   Who hast the memory of Hermione,   I know, in honour,
