translation: Paulina, you keep Hermione's memory alive.

original: O, that ever I   Had squared me to thy counsel! then, even now,   I might have look'd upon my queen's full eyes,   Have taken treasure from her lips—
translation: I wish I would have listened to you before! If I had, I might be looking into my queen's eyes at this very moment. I might be kissing her precious lips—

original: And left them More rich for what they yielded.
translation: Her lips were precious, and you should consider yourself lucky they ever kissed you.

original: Thou speak'st truth.   No more such wives; therefore, no wife:
translation: You speak the truth. I won't marry again, since there's no one else like Hermione.

original: one worse,   And better used, would make her sainted spirit   Again possess her corpse, and on this stage,   Where we're offenders now, appear soul-vex'd,   And begin, 'Why to me?'
translation: If I married someone less wonderful than Hermione, yet treated that second wife better than I treated my first, I can only imagine Hermione's ghost would possess her body and come back to haunt me, asking "Why are you doing this to me?"

original: Had she such power, She had just cause.
translation: If she had that power, she'd be justified in doing so.

original: She had; and would incense me To murder her I married.
translation: She would, and she'd force me to murder my new wife.

original: I should so.
translation: I should think so.

original: Were I the ghost that walk'd, I'ld bid you mark   Her eye,   a   nd tell me for what dull part in't   You chose her;
translation: If I were Hermione's ghost, I'd make you look your new wife in the eye.   I'd ask you to tell me why you chose her.

original: then I'ld shriek, that even your ears   Should rift to hear me; and the words that follow'd   Should be 'Remember mine.'
translation: Then I'd shriek loud enough to burst your eardrums, and say, "Remember me."

original: Stars, stars, And all eyes else dead coals! Fear thou no wife; I'll have no wife, Paulina.
translation: No eyes are as beautiful as hers were. Don't be afraid of me marrying a wife, Paulina; I won't marry a new wife.

original: Will you swear Never to marry but by my free leave?
translation: Will you swear never to marry unless I give you permission?

original: Never, Paulina; so be blest my spirit!
translation: Never, Paulina, God bless my soul!

original: Then, good my lords, bear witness to his oath.
translation: Then, gentlemen, bear witness to his promise.

original: You tempt him over-much.
translation: You're playing to his weakness.

original: Unless another, As like Hermione as is her picture, Affront his eye.
translation: He won't marry again unless another woman, the spitting image of Hermione, crosses his eye.

original: Good madam,—
translation: Ma'am—

original: I have done.
translation: I'm done.

original: Yet, if my lord will marry,—if you will, sir,   No remedy, but you will,—give me the office   To choose you a queen:
translation: Yet, if you do intend to marry, sir, and won't be stopped, give me the right to choose your new queen.

original: she shall not be so young   As was your former; but she shall be such   As, walk'd your first queen's ghost,   it should take joy   To see her in your arms.
translation: She won't be as young as your first one, but she'll be someone that Hermione's ghost would be happy to see you with.

original: My true Paulina, We shall not marry till thou bid'st us.
translation: Paulina, I won't marry until you tell me.

original: That Shall be when your first queen's again in breath; Never till then.
translation: That will be when your first queen breathes again, and not a moment sooner.

original: One that gives out himself Prince Florizel, Son of Polixenes, with his princess, she The fairest I have yet beheld, desires access To your high presence.
translation: A man calling himself Prince Florizel, son of Polixenes, is here with a beautiful princess. He's asked to see you.

original: What with him? he comes not Like to his father's greatness: his approach, So out of circumstance and sudden, tells us 'Tis not a visitation framed, but forced By need and accident. What train?
translation: What is he doing here? He's not arriving with his father's usual style. This can't be planned—he must have been forced to visit suddenly by some accident. Who did he bring with him?

original: But few, And those but mean.
translation: Very few people, and most of them are peasants.

original: His princess, say you, with him?
translation: Did you say he has his princess with him?

original: Ay, the most peerless piece of earth, I think, That e'er the sun shone bright on.
translation: Yes, the most beautiful woman I think I've ever seen.

original: O Hermione,   As every present time doth boast itself   Above a better gone, so must thy grave   Give way to what's seen now!
translation: Oh, Hermione, every new woman makes men forget the old ones.

original: Sir, you yourself   Have said and writ so, but your writing now   Is colder than that theme, 'She had not been,   Nor was not to be equall'd;'—thus your verse   Flow'd with her beauty once: 'tis shrewdly ebb'd,   To say you have seen a better.
translation: Sir, you yourself have said and written that "Hermione was not, and will not be matched." Considering how you used to rave about her beauty, you're doing her a disservice now to say you've seen someone more beautiful.

original: Pardon, madam:   The one I have almost forgot,—your pardon,—
translation: I'm sorry, ma'am. I'd almost forgotten Hermione.

original: The other, when she has obtain'd your eye,   Will have your tongue too.
translation: When you see this princess, though, you'll want to praise her, too.

original: This is a creature,   Would she begin a sect, might quench the zeal   Of all professors else, make proselytes   Of who she but bid follow.
translation: She's like a goddess who converts everyone who sees her to the religion of worshipping her.

original: How! not women?
translation: Really? Women, too?

original: Women will love her, that she is a woman More worth than any man; men, that she is The rarest of all women.
translation: Women will love her for being more worth their love than men. Men will love her because she's the most special woman that ever was.

original: Go, Cleomenes; Yourself, assisted with your honour'd friends, Bring them to our embracement. Still, 'tis strange  He thus should steal upon us.
translation: Go, Cleomenes. You and some of these gentleman should welcome them on my behalf. Still, it's strange for Florizel to surprise us like this.

original: Had our prince, Jewel of children, seen this hour, he had pair'd Well with this lord: there was not full a month Between their births.
translation: If Mamillius had lived to see this day, he'd be Florizel's age. They were born about a month apart.

original: Prithee, no more; cease; thou know'st   He dies to me again when talk'd of: sure,   When I shall see this gentleman, thy speeches   Will bring me to consider that which may   Unfurnish me of reason. They are come.
translation: Please, no more—stop. You know that hearing that is like seeing him die all over again. But your words will keep me in check when I see this young man. Here they come.

original: Your mother was most true to wedlock, prince;   For she did print your royal father off,   Conceiving you:
translation: Florizel, your mother should be proud: you look exactly  like  your father did when he was your age.

original: were I but twenty-one,   Your father's image is so hit in you,   His very air, that I should call you brother,   As I did him, and speak of something wildly   By us perform'd before.
translation: So much so that I'm tempted to call you "brother," like I used to call him, and to start chatting with you about some wild escapades the two of us got up to!

original: Most dearly welcome!   And your fair princess,—goddess!—O, alas!   I lost a couple, that 'twixt heaven and earth   Might thus have stood begetting wonder as   You, gracious couple, do: and then I lost—
translation: You are very welcome here. And your beautiful princess—she's like a goddess! Oh, I lost two children some time ago that would have been as wonderful to behold as you two are now. I lost—

original: All mine own folly—the society,   Amity too, of your brave father, whom,   Though bearing misery, I desire my life   Once more to look on him.
translation: due to my own stupidity—your father's friendship, too. I'd do anything to see him again, no matter how painful it might be.

original: By his command   Have I here touch'd Sicilia and from him   Give you all greetings that a king, at friend,   Can send his brother:
translation: I'm here in Sicily by his command. He's asked me to greet you not just as a king, but as a friend and brother.

original: and, but infirmity   Which waits upon worn times hath something seized   His wish'd ability, he had himself   The lands and waters 'twixt your throne and his   Measured to look upon you;
translation: Though he wanted to come, he was held back by some unavoidable issues at home.

original: whom he loves—   He bade me say so—more than all the sceptres   And those that bear them living.
translation: He asked me to tell you that he loves you more than all the thrones and all the kings in the world.

original: O my brother,   Good gentleman! the wrongs I have done thee stir   Afresh within me, and these thy offices,   So rarely kind, are as interpreters   Of my behind-hand slackness.
translation: Oh, my brother! I'm thinking through the wrong I did you all over again; your friendly message only makes me feel more guilty.

original: Welcome hither,   As is the spring to the earth.
translation: Y ou two are as welcome as spring is on earth.

original: And hath he too   Exposed this paragon to the fearful usage,   At least ungentle, of the dreadful Neptune,   To greet a man not worth her pains, much less   The adventure of her person?
translation: And has Polixenes put this beautiful girl through a long, uncomfortable boat journey just to see me, who's hardly worth the trouble?

original: Good my lord, She came from Libya.
Where the warlike Smalus, That noble honour'd lord, is fear'd and loved?
translation: Where King Smalus rules, feared and loved by all?

original: Most royal sir, from thence; from him, whose daughter   His tears proclaim'd his, parting with her: thence,   A prosperous south-wind friendly, we have cross'd,   To execute the charge my father gave me   For visiting your highness:
translation: Exactly, sir. He was sad to part with her, his daughter, and we've just come from there to follow my father's instructions to visit you.

original: my best train   I have from your Sicilian shores dismiss'd;   Who for Bohemia bend, to signify   Not only my success in Libya, sir,   But my arrival and my wife's in safety   Here where we are.
translation: I didn't bring my gentlemen and servants here—I sent them back to Bohemia to tell everyone about our marriage, and that my wife and I have arrived safely here.

original: The blessed gods   Purge all infection from our air whilst you   Do climate here!
translation: I hope you have a happy and healthy stay here!

original: You have a holy father,   A graceful gentleman; against whose person,   So sacred as it is, I have done sin:
translation: Your father is a righteous man, and I've sinned against him.

original: For which the heavens, taking angry note,   Have left me issueless; and your father's blest,   As he from heaven merits it, with you   Worthy his goodness.
translation: As a punishment, the gods have left me without any children of my own. Your father is blessed to have you!

original: What might I have been,   Might I a son and daughter now have look'd on,   Such goodly things as you!
translation: I would be blessed, too, if I had a son and daughter like you two with me now!

original: Most noble sir,   That which I shall report will bear no credit,   Were not the proof so nigh.
translation: Sir, you'll hardly believe this, but you have to because the one who sent me is about to arrive:

original: Please you, great sir,   Bohemia greets you from himself by me;   Desires you to attach his son,
translation: Polixenes sends you his greetings. He asks that you hold his son here—

original: who has—   His dignity and duty both cast off—   Fled from his father, from his hopes, and with   A shepherd's daughter.
translation: you see, his son ran away from his father and his responsibilities with a shepherd's daughter.

original: Where's Bohemia? speak.
translation: Tell me, where's Polixenes?

original: Here in your city; I now came from him:   I speak amazedly; and it becomes   My marvel and my message.
translation: Here in your city; I just came from him. And (it may seem crazy . . . I can hardly believe it myself)

original: To your court   Whiles he was hastening, in the chase, it seems,   Of this fair couple, meets he on the way   The father of this seeming lady and   Her brother, having both their country quitted   With this young prince.
translation: while Polixenes was on his way to your court, chasing this young couple, he ran into this girl's father and brother, who have also fled the country.

original: Camillo has betray'd me; Whose honour and whose honesty till now Endured all weathers.
translation: Camillo has betrayed me, though he's always been loyal and honest before now.

original: Lay't so to his charge: He's with the king your father.
translation: You can tell him yourself; he's with your father, the king.

original: Who? Camillo?
translation: Who, Camillo?

original: Camillo, sir; I spake with him; who now   Has these poor men in question.
translation: Camillo, sir. I spoke with him and with the shepherds.

original: Never saw I   Wretches so quake: they kneel, they kiss the earth;   Forswear themselves as often as they speak:   Bohemia stops his ears, and threatens them   With divers deaths in death.
translation: I've never seen men so afraid: they kneel, kiss the ground, and swear every time they speak. Polixenes can hardly listen to them; he keeps threatening them with death.

original: O my poor father! The heaven sets spies upon us, will not have Our contract celebrated.
translation: Oh, my poor father! The spies have found us, and now we won't get to celebrate our wedding.

original: You are married?
translation: Aren't you married?

original: We are not, sir, nor are we like to be; The stars, I see, will kiss the valleys first: The odds for high and low's alike.
My lord, Is this the daughter of a king?
translation: Sir, is she a princess?

original: She is, When once she is my wife.
translation: She will be, once she's my wife.

original: That 'once' I see by your good father's speed Will come on very slowly. I am sorry, Most sorry, you have broken from his liking Where you were tied in duty, and as sorry Your choice is not so rich in worth as beauty, That you might well enjoy her.
translation: That "once" isn't likely to come to pass now that your father's on his way. I'm very sorry to hear that you're at odds with your father; you should be obedient to him. And I'm sorry, too, that you won't be able to enjoy this girl, since her station in life does not match her beauty.

original: Dear, look up:   Though Fortune, visible an enemy,   Should chase us with my father, power no jot   Hath she to change our loves.
translation: Chin up, sweetheart. Nothing that my father does can change the love we have for each other.

original: Beseech you, sir,   Remember since you owed no more to time   Than I do now: with thought of such affections,   Step forth mine advocate; at your request   My father will grant precious things as trifles.
translation: Sir, I beg you—think of what you were like when you were my age and in love. Defend me to my father. If you ask, he'll give you an expensive gift as quickly as if it were a cheap one.

original: Would he do so, I'ld beg your precious mistress, Which he counts but a trifle.
translation: If he'd really do anything, I'd ask him to give me your girlfriend, who he clearly doesn't care for.

original: Sir, my liege, Your eye hath too much youth in't: not a month 'Fore your queen died, she was more worth such gazes Than what you look on now.
translation: Sir? My lord! The way you're looking at her is hardly appropriate. Your queen, before she died, was much more beautiful than the girl you see now.

original: I thought of her, Even in these looks I made. @  But your petition Is yet unanswer'd. I will to your father: Your honour not o'erthrown by your desires, I am friend to them and you: upon which errand I now go toward him; therefore follow me And mark what way I make: come, good my lord.
translation: I was thinking of her even while I looked at this young girl. I haven't answered your question. I will speak to your father. Your love hasn't compromised your duties as prince; I support you and your actions. I'll go to him now; come with me and watch what I do. Come, sir.

original: Beseech you, sir, were you present at this relation?
translation: And, sir, were you there when all this was said?

original: I was by at the opening of the fardel, heard the old shepherd deliver the manner how he found it: whereupon, after a little amazedness, we were all commanded out of the chamber; only this methought I heard the shepherd say, he found the child.
translation: I was there when they opened the bag, heard the old shepherd explain how he found it, and that's when, after a moment of shock, we were all told to leave. But I thought I heard the shepherd say that he found the child.

original: I would most gladly know the issue of it.
translation: I'd love to know what happened next.

original: I make a broken delivery of the business; but the   changes I perceived in the king and Camillo were   very notes of admiration:
translation: I'm not telling the story very well, but the king and Camillo seemed happy to see each other.

original: they seemed almost, with   staring on one another, to tear the cases of their   eyes; there was speech in their dumbness, language   in their very gesture; they looked as they had heard   of a world ransomed, or one destroyed: a notable   passion of wonder appeared in them;
translation: They stared at each other so intensely it seemed like their eyes would pop out of their heads. They could hardly speak, but they said it all in their hugs and gestures. They looked like they'd seen the world rebuilt—or destroyed. They were filled with wonder.

original: but the wisest   beholder, that knew no more but seeing, could not   say if the importance were joy or sorrow; but in the   extremity of the one, it must needs be.
translation: But no one who was watching could tell if they were joyful, or sad. It was the extreme version of one of those two.

original: Here comes a gentleman that haply knows more.   The news, Rogero?
translation: Here comes another gentleman who probably knows more. What's the news, Rogero?

original: Nothing but bonfires: the oracle is fulfilled; the king's daughter is found: such a deal of wonder is broken out within this hour that ballad-makers cannot be able to express it. @  @ Here comes the Lady Paulina's steward: he can deliver you more. How goes it now, sir? this news which is called true is so like an old tale, that the verity of it is in strong suspicion: has the king found his heir?
translation: Nothing but sensations! The oracle is fulfilled, the king's daughter is found. So many wonderful things have happened in the last hour that even ballad-writers won't be able to express it. Here comes Lady Paulina's servant; he can tell you more. [To the THIRD GENTLEMAN] How are you, sir? This news sounds so much like a fairytale that it can hardly be true. Has the king found his heir?

original: Most true, if ever truth were pregnant by   circumstance: that which you hear you'll swear you   see, there is such unity in the proofs.
translation: It's really true, if we can believe the circumstances. You might have to see the evidence to believe it:

original: The mantle   of Queen Hermione's, her jewel about the neck of it,   the letters of Antigonus found with it which they   know to be his character, the majesty of the   creature in resemblance of the mother, the affection   of nobleness which nature shows above her breeding,
translation: Hermione's scarf, her necklace, letters in Antigonus's handwriting, the girl's resemblance to her mother, her obvious nobility which proves she's not a shepherdess . . .

original: and many other evidences proclaim her with all   certainty to be the king's daughter. Did you see   the meeting of the two kings?
translation: all this and more proves that she's the king's daughter. Did you see the meeting of the two kings?

original: No.
translation: No.

original: Then have you lost a sight, which was to be seen,   cannot be spoken of. There might you have beheld one   joy crown another, so and in such manner that it   seemed sorrow wept to take leave of them, for their   joy waded in tears.
translation: You missed a sight to be seen; I can't really explain it in words. They were so overjoyed that both of them were moved to tears.

original: There was casting up of eyes,   holding up of hands, with countenances of such   distraction that they were to be known by garment,   not by favour.
translation: They looked up to heaven and held each other's hands. They looked so much alike that we could only tell them apart by their clothes!

original: Our king, being ready to leap out of   himself for joy of his found daughter, as if that   joy were now become a loss, cries 'O, thy mother,   thy mother!'
translation: Leontes—who was about to leap out of his skin, he was so happy he found his daughter—cries out, "Oh, your mother, your mother!" as if the joy made his grief new, too.

original: then asks Bohemia forgiveness; then   embraces his son-in-law; then again worries he his   daughter with clipping her; now he thanks the old   shepherd, which stands by like a weather-bitten   conduit of many kings' reigns.
translation: He asked Polixenes for forgiveness, then hugged his new son-in-law, then hugged his daughter again, then thanked the old shepherd who stood by like an old watchman.

original: I never heard of such   another encounter, which lames report to follow it   and undoes description to do it.
translation: I have never heard of anything like it. No report can fully sum it up. Description doesn't do it justice.

original: What, pray you, became of Antigonus, that carried hence the child?
translation: What happened to Antigonus, who carried the baby to Bohemia?

original: Like an old tale still, which will have matter to   rehearse, though credit be asleep and not an ear   open.
translation: That's like something out of a fairytale, too, which you won't believe no matter how many times I tell it.

original: He was torn to pieces with a bear: this   avouches the shepherd's son;
translation: He was torn to pieces by a bear, according to the shepherd's son.

original: who has not only his   innocence, which seems much, to justify him, but a   handkerchief and rings of his that Paulina knows.
translation: We should believe him because he's fairly stupid, but also because he had some handkerchiefs and rings of Antigonus' that Paulina recognized.

original: What became of his bark and his followers?
translation: What happened to his ship and his servants?

original: Wrecked the same instant of their master's death and   in the view of the shepherd: so that all the   instruments which aided to expose the child were   even then lost when it was found.
translation: The shepherd saw them wreck at the same instant that Antigonus died, so everything that brought the child to them disappeared at the moment she was found.

original: But O, the noble   combat that 'twixt joy and sorrow was fought in   Paulina! She had one eye declined for the loss of   her husband, another elevated that the oracle was   fulfilled:
translation: But poor Paulina—she was torn between joy and grief! She was crying for her husband, but rejoicing that the oracle was fulfilled.

original: she lifted the princess from the earth,   and so locks her in embracing, as if she would pin   her to her heart that she might no more be in danger   of losing.
translation: She kept hugging the princess, as if she would hold her to her heart forever so that she'd never be lost again.

original: The dignity of this act was worth the audience of kings and princes; for by such was it acted.
translation: Kings and princes could have watched a play like that, considering kings and princes were the actors.

original: One of the prettiest touches of all and that which   angled for mine eyes, caught the water though not   the fish,
translation: One of the most beautiful parts of it ( it brought tears to my eyes )

original: was when, at the relation of the queen's   death, with the manner how she came to't bravely   confessed and lamented by the king,   how   attentiveness wounded his daughter; till, from one   sign of dolour to another, she did, with an 'Alas,'   I would fain say, bleed tears,
translation: was when the king explained how the queen died, and the poor princess listened to the whole thing, crying, saying "Oh, no!" and practically bleeding tears.

original: for I am sure my   heart wept blood. Who was most marble there changed   colour; some swooned, all sorrowed: if all the world   could have seen 't, the woe had been universal.
translation: I think my heart wept blood. Even the most unemotional people there nearly fainted, and everyone cried. If the whole world had seen it, the sadness would have been universal.

original: Are they returned to the court?
translation: Did they go back to the court?

original: No: the princess hearing of her mother's statue,   which is in the keeping of Paulina,—
translation: No, because the princess just heard about the statue of her mother, which Paulina has.

original: a piece many   years in doing and now newly performed by that rare   Italian master, Julio Romano, who, had he himself   eternity and could put breath into his work, would   beguile Nature of her custom, so perfectly he is her   ape:
translation: It's been in the works for years and was just finished by Julio Romano, the Italian master, whose sculptures are incredibly lifelike.

original: he so near to Hermione hath done Hermione that   they say one would speak to her and stand in hope of   answer: thither with all greediness of affection   are they gone, and there they intend to sup.
translation: His "Hermione" statue looks so much like her that you'd be tempted to speak to it and wait for an answer. They've all hurried to see the statue, and they're planning to have dinner there.

original: I thought she had some great matter there in hand; for she hath privately twice or thrice a day, ever since the death of Hermione, visited that removed house. Shall we thither and with our company piece the rejoicing?
translation: I thought she must have some important business in that isolated house, since she's visited it alone two or three times a day every day since Hermione's death. Should we head that way and join the celebration?

original: Who would be thence that has the benefit of access? every wink of an eye some new grace will be born: our absence makes us unthrifty to our knowledge. Let's along.
translation: Would anyone say "no" to that? Something incredible happens every time you blink! The longer we stay here, the less we'll see. Let's go.

original: Now, had I not the dash of my former life in me,   would preferment drop on my head. I brought the old   man and his son aboard the prince:
translation: If I weren't a thief, I'd be getting a promotion right about now. I brought the old man and his son onboard the prince's ship.

original: told him I heard   them talk of a fardel and I know not what: but he   at that time, overfond of the shepherd's daughter,   so he then took her to be, who began to be much   sea-sick, and himself little better, extremity of   weather continuing,
translation: I told him what I'd heard about the bag and whatnot, but he was too busy worrying about the shepherd's daughter (as he thought she was then), who was sea-sick, and then he got sea-sick, too because of the storm.

original: this mystery remained   undiscovered. But 'tis all one to me; for had I   been the finder out of this secret, it would not   have relished among my other discredits.
translation: So the mystery remained unsolved. But it's all the same to me; if I'd figured out this secret, it wouldn't have matched up very well with my other crimes.

original: Here come those I have done good to against my will,   and already appearing in the blossoms of their fortune.
translation: Here come the guys I helped against my will, already decked out in their new, fancy clothes.

original: Come, boy; I am past moe children, but thy sons and daughters will be all gentlemen born.
translation: My son, I won't be having any more children, but your sons and daughters will all be born gentlemen and women.

original: You are well met, sir. You denied to fight with me   this other day, because I was no gentleman born.
translation: Good to see you, sir. You chose not to fight with me the other day because I wasn't a gentleman.

original: See you these clothes? say you see them not and   think me still no gentleman born:
translation: See these clothes? Can you look at these and still think I wasn't born a gentleman?

original: you were best say   these robes are not gentlemen born: give me the   lie, do, and try whether I am not now a gentleman born.
translation: You might as well say these clothes weren't born gentlemen! Call me a liar. Tell me I wasn't born a gentleman.

original: I know you are now, sir, a gentleman born.
translation: I know you are now, sir, born a gentleman.

original: Ay, and have been so any time these four hours.
translation: Yep, I was born a gentleman about four hours ago!

original: And so have I, boy.
translation: Me, too, son.

original: So you have: but I was a gentleman born before my   father; for the king's son took me by the hand, and   called me brother;
translation: That's true, but I was born a gentleman before my father. You see, the king's son took me by the hand, called me "Brother,"

original: and then the two kings called my   father brother; and then the prince my brother and   the princess my sister called my father father;   and   so we wept,
translation: and then the two kings called my father "Brother." And then the prince my brother and the princess my sister called my father "Father," and we all cried.

original: and there was the first gentleman-like   tears that ever we shed.
translation: Those were the first gentlemanly tears that we ever cried.

original: We may live, son, to shed many more.
translation: We may live, son, to cry many more.

original: Ay; or else 'twere hard luck, being in so preposterous estate as we are.
translation: If we don't live to cry again, that'll be bad luck, considering how good we have it now.

original: I humbly beseech you, sir, to pardon me all the faults I have committed to your worship and to give me your good report to the prince my master.
translation: I am very sorry, sir, for all the wrong I've done you, sir. Please report good things about me to the prince my master.

original: Prithee, son, do; for we must be gentle, now we are gentlemen.
translation: You should do it, son. We should be "gentle" now that we're gentlemen.

original: Thou wilt amend thy life?
translation: You'll change your ways?

original: Ay, an it like your good worship.
translation: Of course, sir, if you like.

original: Give me thy hand: I will swear to the prince thou art as honest a true fellow as any is in Bohemia.
translation: Let's shake hands.  I'll swear to the prince that you're as honest and loyal as any man in Bohemia.

original: You may say it, but not swear it.
translation: You can say it, but don't swear it.

original: Not swear it, now I am a gentleman? Let boors and franklins say it, I'll swear it.
translation: I can't swear it, now that I'm a gentleman? If the peasants and the middle class can swear, I can swear, too.

original: How if it be false, son?
translation: But what if it's not true, son?

original: If it be ne'er so false, a true gentleman may swear   it in the behalf of his friend:
translation: If you believe it should be true, a true gentleman can swear it on behalf of his friend.

original: and I'll swear to   the prince thou art a tall fellow of thy hands and   that thou wilt not be drunk;
translation: I'lI swear to the prince that you're hardworking and not likely to get drunk,

original: but I know thou art no   tall fellow of thy hands and that thou wilt be   drunk:
translation: but I know you're not hardworking and very likely to get drunk.

original: but I'll swear it, and I would thou wouldst   be a tall fellow of thy hands.
translation: So I hope that, when I do swear it, you'll make a better effort to be hardworking and not a drunk.

original: I will prove so, sir, to my power.
translation: I'll try to live up to that, sir, to the best of my ability.

original: Ay, by any means prove a tall fellow: if I do not   wonder how thou darest venture to be drunk, not   being a tall fellow, trust me not.
translation: Yes, and please try to work hard (although it's fine by me if you get a little drunk once in a while).

original: Hark! the kings   and the princes, our kindred, are going to see the   queen's picture. Come, follow us: we'll be thy   good masters.
translation: But wait! The kings and the prince (our new family) are going to see the queen's statue. Come on and follow us. We'll take care of you.

original: O grave and good Paulina, the great comfort That I have had of thee!
translation: Paulina, you've comforted me so much.

original: What, sovereign sir,   I did not well I meant well. All my services   You have paid home:
translation: If there's anything I didn't do correctly, know that I meant to do it better. You've repaid me for everything,

original: but that you have vouchsafed,   With your crown'd brother and these your contracted   Heirs of your kingdoms, my poor house to visit,   It is a surplus of your grace, which never   My life may last to answer.
translation: and now you, Polixenes, Perdita, and Florizel have come to visit my little house. It's extremely gracious for you to be here, and I can never thank you enough.

original: O Paulina,   We honour you with trouble:
translation: Oh, Paulina, you know I'd do anything for you.

original: but we came   To see the statue of our queen: your gallery   Have we pass'd through, not without much content   In many singularities;
translation: But I came to see the statue of my queen. But I've passed through your entire gallery—which was great, and all—

original: but we saw not   That which my daughter came to look upon,   The statue of her mother.
translation: without my daughter seeing the statue of her mother that she came to see.

original: As she lived peerless,   So her dead likeness, I do well believe,   Excels whatever yet you look'd upon   Or hand of man hath done;
translation: When Hermione was alive, no one was as beautiful as she was. It's the same with her statue; I'm sure you've never seen another man-made thing that's as perfect.

original: therefore I keep it   Lonely, apart. But here it is: prepare   To see the life as lively mock'd as ever   Still sleep mock'd death:
translation: That's why I keep it hidden here. Here it is; get ready to see that which is to life as sleep is to death—the closest you can come without being the actual thing.

original: behold, and say 'tis well.
translation: Take a look, and tell me what you think.

original: Her natural posture!
translation: Exactly the way she used to stand!

original: Chide me, dear stone, that I may say indeed   Thou art Hermione; or rather, thou art she   In thy not chiding, for she was as tender   As infancy and grace.
translation: Statue, if you would reprimand me, I'd say you were the real Hermione. Actually, you're more like her because you're not reprimanding me, considering she was as sweet as a baby and as gentle as grace itself.

original: But yet, Paulina,   Hermione was not so much wrinkled, nothing   So aged as this seems.
translation: But, Paulina, Hermione didn't have that many wrinkles. She wasn't as old as this statue seems.

original: O, not by much.
translation: Not nearly as old.

original: So much the more our carver's excellence; Which lets go by some sixteen years and makes her As she lived now.
translation: That's the sculptor's skill: he made her look like she would if she lived now, sixteen years later.

original: As now she might have done,   So much to my good comfort, as it is   Now piercing to my soul.
translation: And she might have done so; seeing it makes me happy but fills me with guilt, too.

original: O, thus she stood,   Even with such life of majesty, warm life,   As now it coldly stands, when first I woo'd her!
translation: She looked just like this when I first fell in love with her, though she was warm and living, not cold and made of stone.

original: I am ashamed: does not the stone rebuke me   For being more stone than it?
translation: I'm ashamed. Is the statue reprimanding me for being more stony and cold-hearted than it?

original: O royal piece,   There's magic in thy majesty, which has   My evils conjured to remembrance and   From thy admiring daughter took the spirits,   Standing like stone with thee.
translation: My queen, your magic has conjured up all the crimes I committed against you and your daughter, making me think neither of you could ever forgive me.

original: And give me leave, And do not say 'tis superstition, that I kneel and then implore her blessing. Lady, Dear queen, that ended when I but began, Give me that hand of yours to kiss.
translation: Call me superstitious, but I'm going to kneel and ask for her blessing. Ma'am, you died just when I was born. Let me kiss your hand. [PERDITA moves to kiss HERMIONE's hand]

original: O, patience! The statue is but newly fix'd, the colour's Not dry.
translation: Oh, wait! The statue was just painted and it's not dry yet.

original: My lord, your sorrow was too sore laid on,   Which sixteen winters cannot blow away,
translation: Sir, you had a lot to grieve for, but sixteen  years  should have helped ease that pain.

original: So many summers dry; scarce any joy   Did ever so long live; no sorrow   But kill'd itself much sooner.
translation: Few joys last that long, and any other sorrow would have fizzled out long before now.

original: Dear my brother, Let him that was the cause of this have power To take off so much grief from you as he Will piece up in himself.
translation: My brother, I wish I could bear some of that grief for you.

original: Indeed, my lord, If I had thought the sight of my poor image Would thus have wrought you,—for the stone is mine— I'ld not have show'd it.
translation: Sir, if I knew my statue would make you so upset—since it belongs to me—I wouldn't have showed it to you.

original: Do not draw the curtain.
translation: Don't close the curtain.

original: No longer shall you gaze on't, lest your fancy May think anon it moves.
translation: You shouldn't look at it anymore, or you'll start to hallucinate that it's moving.

original: Let be, let be. Would I were dead, but that, methinks, already— What was he that did make it? See, my lord, Would you not deem it breathed? and that those veins Did verily bear blood?
translation: Let it be, let it be. I wish I were dead. Except . . . I think . . . already . . . who made this?  Look, doesn't it look like it's breathing? Doesn't it look like those veins have blood running through them?

original: Masterly done: The very life seems warm upon her lip.
translation: It's very well done. She looks almost alive.

original: The fixture of her eye has motion in't, As we are mock'd with art.
translation: Her eyes almost look like they're moving; this art is too realistic.

original: I'll draw the curtain: My lord's almost so far transported that He'll think anon it lives.
translation: I'll close the curtain. The king is so carried away, next he'll think that it lives.

original: O sweet Paulina, Make me to think so twenty years together! No settled senses of the world can match The pleasure of that madness. Let't alone.
I am sorry, sir, I have thus far stirr'd you: but I could afflict you farther.
translation: Sir, I'm sorry I've gotten you so worked up. But I could go one step further.

original: Do, Paulina; For this affliction has a taste as sweet As any cordial comfort. Still, methinks, There is an air comes from her: what fine chisel Could ever yet cut breath? Let no man mock me, For I will kiss her.
translation: Do it, Paulina. This suffering is sweet to me.  It looks like she's breathing. What artist could sculpt breath? No one make fun of me; I'm going to kiss her.

original: Good my lord, forbear: The ruddiness upon her lip is wet; You'll mar it if you kiss it, stain your own With oily painting. Shall I draw the curtain?
translation: Sir, restrain yourself. The red paint on her lips is wet. You'll smudge it if you kiss it, and you'll get oil paint on your own face. Should I close the curtain?

original: No, not these twenty years.
translation: No, never.

original: So long could I Stand by, a looker on.
translation: I could stand here forever, too, just looking.

original: Either forbear,   Quit presently the chapel, or resolve you   For more amazement.
translation: Either restrain yourself, leave the chapel, or get ready for more amazement.

original: If you can behold it,   I'll make the statue move indeed, descend   And take you by the hand;
translation: If you can handle it, I'll make the statue move, walk down, and take you by the hand.

original: but then you'll think—   Which I protest against—   I am assisted   By wicked powers.
translation: But I'm afraid you'll think I'm a witch using  black magic .

original: What you can make her do, I am content to look on: what to speak, I am content to hear; for 'tis as easy To make her speak as move.
translation: I'll watch anything you can make her do. I'll listen to anything you can make her say. Surely it's as easy to make her speak as it is to make her move?

original: It is required You do awake your faith. Then all stand still; On: those that think it is unlawful business I am about, let them depart.
translation: You need to have faith. Everyone stand still. And anyone who thinks I'm doing something I shouldn't can leave.

original: Proceed: No foot shall stir.
translation: Proceed. No one will leave.

original: 'Tis time; descend; be stone no more; approach;   Strike all that look upon with marvel.
translation: It's time, come down. Don't be a statue anymore. Come to us and you'll amaze all of us who are watching.

original: Come,   I'll fill your grave up: stir, nay, come away,   Bequeath to death your numbness, for from him   Dear life redeems you.
translation: Come, I'll close your grave. Move! Come on, now, forget death and come back to life.

original: You perceive she stirs:
translation: Look, she's moving.

original: Start not; her actions shall be holy as   You hear my spell is lawful:
translation: Don't be afraid! Everything she does is as safe as my spell, like I told you.

original: do not shun her   Until you see her die again; for then   You kill her double.
translation: Don't reject her until you see her die again, or you'll be killing her a second time.

original: Nay, present your hand:   When she was young you woo'd her; now in age   Is she become the suitor?
translation: No, give her your hand. You won her over when she was young. Now that you're old, is she the one who has to win you?

original: O, she's warm!  If this be magic, let it be an art Lawful as eating.
translation: Wow, she's warm! If this is from your magic spell, your magic should be considered an art as natural as eating.

original: She embraces him.
translation: She's hugging him.

original: She hangs about his neck: If she pertain to life let her speak too.
translation: She's hanging on his neck. If she's so lifelike, she should speak, too.

original: Ay, and make't manifest where she has lived, Or how stolen from the dead.
translation: Yes, and tell us where she's been living, or how she's come back from the dead.

original: That she is living,   Were it but told you, should be hooted at   Like an old tale:
translation: If I just told you she was alive, you would write it off as an  old fairytale .

original: but it appears she lives,   Though yet she speak not. Mark a little while.
translation: But even though she hasn't spoken, it certainly looks like she's living. Wait a minute.

original: Please you to interpose, fair madam: kneel   And pray your mother's blessing.
translation: Speak to her, ma'am. Kneel and ask for your mother's blessing.

original: Turn, good lady;   Our Perdita is found.
translation: Turn around, my lady. Our  Perdita  is found.

original: You gods, look down   And from your sacred vials pour your graces   Upon my daughter's head!
translation: God bless you, daughter.

original: Tell me, mine own.   Where hast thou been preserved? where lived? how found   Thy father's court?
translation: Tell me, sweetheart: how did you escape? Where did you live? How did you get back to your father's court?

original: for thou shalt hear that I,   Knowing by Paulina that the oracle   Gave hope thou wast in being, have preserved   Myself to see the issue.
translation: You should know: Paulina told me that the oracle gave us hope that you were still alive. I kept myself going just to see you.

original: There's time enough for that;   Lest they desire upon this push to trouble   Your joys with like relation. Go together,   You precious winners all; your exultation   Partake to every one.
translation: There's plenty of time for that and to tell all our stories. Go on, all of you lucky people! Go to the feast.

original: I, an old turtle,   Will wing me to some wither'd bough and there   My mate, that's never to be found again,   Lament till I am lost.
translation: Meanwhile, I'll find some lonely place to mourn my husband until I die.

original: O, peace, Paulina!   Thou shouldst a husband take by my consent,   As I by thine a wife:
translation: Oh hush, Paulina. I'll give you a husband, since you gave me a wife.

original: this is a match,   And made between's by vows.
translation: She and I have just been married again by exchanging our promises.

original: Thou hast found mine;   But how, is to be question'd; for I saw her,   As I thought, dead, and have in vain said many   A prayer upon her grave. I'll not seek far—   For him, I partly know his mind—   to find thee   An honourable husband.
translation: You found her, and I have no idea how, since I was sure I saw her die and I prayed at her grave for years. I won't have to look far to find a husband for you.

original: Come, Camillo,   And take her by the hand, whose worth and honesty   Is richly noted and here justified   By us, a pair of kings.
translation: Come on, Camillo, and take her by the hand. Polixenes and I can vouch for him as a valuable, trustworthy man.

original: Let's from this place.   What! look upon my brother: both your pardons,   That e'er I put between your holy looks   My ill suspicion.
translation: Let's leave this place. But first, take a look at my brother, Polixenes. Both of you, please forgive me for ever being suspicious of your friendship.

original: This is your son-in-law,   And son unto the king, who, heavens directing,   Is troth-plight to your daughter.
translation: This is your son-in-law, Polixenes's son, who's engaged to your daughter.

original: Good Paulina,   Lead us from hence, where we may leisurely   Each one demand an answer to his part   Perform'd in this wide gap of time since first   We were dissever'd: hastily lead away.
translation: Paulina, lead us out of here. We'll take all the time in the world asking each other what we've been up to in the many years since we were all separated. Quickly, lead the way!

original: I, that please some, try all, both joy and terror   Of good and bad, that makes and unfolds error,   Now take upon me, in the name of Time,   To use my wings.

translation: They'll sing about your disgrace in the days to come.

original: 'But if thou yield, I rest thy secret friend:
translation: "But if you say 'yes' to me, I'll be a friend to you, and I'll keep the secret.

original: The fault unknown is as a thought unacted;
translation: No one will know; it'll be like it never happened.

original: A little harm done to a great good end   For lawful policy remains enacted.
translation: The little wrong will be made right in the long run, since it'll lead to a good end.

original: The poisonous simple sometimes is compacted   In a pure compound;
translation: Sometimes a little poison is mixed in with something safe to drink.

original: being so applied,   His venom in effect is purified.
translation: The mixture effectively purifies the poison, rendering it harmless.

original: 'Then, for thy husband and thy children's sake,   Tender my suit:
translation: "So, for your husband and your children's sake, give in to me.

original: bequeath not to their lot   The shame that from them no device can take,   The blemish that will never be forgot;
translation: Don't saddle them with shame they'll never be able to get rid of, or with a dark mark on their record that can't be erased.

original: Worse than a slavish wipe or birth-hour's blot:
translation: For them, it'd be worse than being born with a birthmark or deformity,

original: For marks descried in men's nativity   Are nature's faults, not their own infamy.'
translation: since the marks we're born with are nature's fault, not our own."

original: Here with a cockatrice' dead-killing eye   He rouseth up himself and makes a pause;
translation: Like a  monster  that kills you just by looking at you, he got up and paused.

original: While she, the picture of pure piety,   Like a white hind under the gripe's sharp claws,   Pleads,
translation: Meanwhile she, like a perfect saint, or like a white deer in a vulture's claws, begged him.

original: in a wilderness where are no laws,   To the rough beast that knows no gentle right,
translation: But there are no laws in the wild, and he was an animal that didn't care about being polite;

original: Nor aught obeys but his foul appetite.
translation: he obeyed nothing but his own disgusting appetite.

original: But when a black-faced cloud the world doth threat,   In his dim mist the aspiring mountains hiding,
translation: Despite his foul impatience, he waited to hear her speak. He was like a dark cloud in the sky that hides even the tallest mountains in a dim mist.

original: From earth's dark womb some gentle gust doth get,   Which blows these pitchy vapours from their bidding,   Hindering their present fall by this dividing;
translation: From the depths of the earth, a gentle wind could blow such a cloud away, keeping it from raining on the ground below.

original: So his unhallow'd haste her words delays,   And moody Pluto winks while Orpheus plays.
Yet, foul night-waking cat, he doth but dally,   While in his hold-fast foot the weak mouse panteth:
translation: But, like a nocturnal cat that's pounced on a mouse, he was only lingering.

original: Her sad behavior feeds his vulture folly,   A swallowing gulf that even in plenty wanteth:
translation: Her fed off her sadness.

original: His ear her prayers admits, but his heart granteth   No penetrable entrance to her plaining:
translation: He listened to her prayers, but he didn't really entertain her requests.

original: Tears harden lust, though marble wear with raining.
translation: Unlike marble—which erodes with rain—lust grows harder with tears.

original: Her pity-pleading eyes are sadly fix'd   In the remorseless wrinkles of his face;
translation: Her eyes, begging for pity, were fixed sadly on his remorseless, wrinkled face.

original: Her modest eloquence with sighs is mix'd,   Which to her oratory adds more grace.
translation: She sighed as she spoke, which increased the overall effect of her eloquence.

original: She puts the period often from his place;
translation: At time she could hardly finish a sentence—

original: And midst the sentence so her accent breaks,   That twice she doth begin ere once she speaks.
translation: her voice would break off in the middle. She stopped and started twice before she was able to speak.

original: She conjures him by high almighty Jove,   By knighthood, gentry, and sweet friendship's oath,   By her untimely tears,
translation: In the name of the powerful god  Jove , knights, the aristocracy, friendship, her own tears, her husband's love,

original: her husband's love,   By holy human law, and common troth,
translation: holy human law, and common decency,

original: By heaven and earth, and all the power of both,
translation: in the name of heaven and earth and the combined power of both:

original: That to his borrow'd bed he make retire,   And stoop to honour, not to foul desire.
translation: she asked him to go back to his bed, and to do the right thing rather than caving into his perverted desires.

original: Quoth she, 'Reward not hospitality   With such black payment as thou hast pretended;
translation: She said, "Don't reward my hospitality with the horrible crimes you've described.

original: Mud not the fountain that gave drink to thee;
translation: Don't bite the hand that feeds you.

original: Mar not the thing that cannot be amended;
translation: Don't break something you can't fix.

original: End thy ill aim before thy shoot be ended;
translation: Stop aiming for this target before you shoot.

original: He is no woodman that doth bend his bow   To strike a poor unseasonable doe.
translation: A man who kills a poor deer out of season is hardly an accomplished hunter.

original: 'My husband is thy friend; for his sake spare me:
translation: "My husband is your friend. Spare me for his sake.

original: Thyself art mighty; for thine own sake leave me:   Myself a weakling; do not then ensnare me:
translation: You yourself are powerful. Leave me for your own sake. I'm weak, so don't trap me.

original: Thou look'st not like deceit; do not deceive me.
translation: You don't look like a liar, so don't lie to me.

original: My sighs, like whirlwinds, labour hence to heave thee:
translation: I'm sighing because that's all I can do to make you leave.

original: If ever man were moved with woman moans,   Be moved with my tears, my sighs, my groans:
translation: If it's possible for a man to be moved by what a woman does, let my tears, sighs, and groans move you.

original: 'All which together, like a troubled ocean,   Beat at thy rocky and wreck-threatening heart,
translation: "All these together are like a  stormy sea  beating against your rocky heart, which threatens to shipwreck me.

original: To soften it with their continual motion;   For stones dissolved to water do convert.
translation: My tears are meant to soften you, like waves soften rocks and, eventually, turn them into water.

original: O, if no harder than a stone thou art,   Melt at my tears, and be compassionate!
translation: Are you harder than stone? Let my tears move you! Be compassionate!

original: Soft pity enters at an iron gate.
translation: Although you're tough, I believe you can still feel pity.

original: 'In Tarquin's likeness I did entertain thee:   Hast thou put on his shape to do him shame?
translation: "I welcomed you as I would Tarquin himself. Why would you disrespect him this way?

original: To all the host of heaven I complain me,   Thou wrong'st his honour, wound'st his princely name.
translation: I'll pray to the gods, saying you betrayed him and dishonored his royal name.

original: Thou art not what thou seem'st;
translation: You're not what you seem.

original: and if the same,   Thou seem'st not what thou art, a god, a king;
translation: If you are what you seem, that you're seeming like something you're not. You should be a god, a king.

original: For kings like gods should govern everything.
translation: Kings, like gods, are supposed to rule  over everything.

original: 'How will thy shame be seeded in thine age,   When thus thy vices bud before thy spring!
translation: "If you're this bad as a young man, imagine how terrible you'll be when you're old!

original: If in thy hope thou darest do such outrage,   What darest thou not when once thou art a king?
translation: And if you'd do something this outrageous when you're only a prince, what will you do when you're a king?

original: O, be remember'd, no outrageous thing   From vassal actors can be wiped away;
translation: Don't forget: if common people's sins can't be wiped away,

original: Then kings' misdeeds cannot be hid in clay.
translation: then kings can't hide theirs, either.

original: 'This deed will make thee only loved for fear;   But happy monarchs still are fear'd for love:
translation: "If you do this, people will be afraid of you, but the best monarchs are loved, not just feared.

original: With foul offenders thou perforce must bear,   When they in thee the like offences prove:
translation: Once people find out what you've done, they might become the worst kind of criminals, too-

original: If but for fear of this, thy will remove;
translation: -or they might take you out of office because they're afraid that might happen.

original: For princes are the glass, the school, the book,   Where subjects' eyes do learn, do read, do look.
translation: You see,  princes  are like a mirror, a school, and a book in which subjects look, learn, and read how they're supposed to act.

original: 'And wilt thou be the school where Lust shall learn?   Must he in thee read lectures of such shame?
translation: "And do you want to be setting an example of following lust? Do you want people to follow your shameful lead?

original: Wilt thou be glass wherein it shall discern   Authority for sin, warrant for blame,
translation: Are you going to be the mirror in which criminals look, finding an excuse for sin and blame?

original: To privilege dishonour in thy name?
translation: Do you want them to commit crimes in your name?

original: Thou back'st reproach against long-living laud,   And makest fair reputation but a bawd.
translation: You're giving up what could have been a lifetime of praise. Your reputation will become a joke.

original: 'Hast thou command? by him that gave it thee,   From a pure heart command thy rebel will:
translation: "Aren't you powerful? In the king's name, keep your rebellious heart  in check .

original: Draw not thy sword to guard iniquity,   For it was lent thee all that brood to kill.
translation: Don't use your sword to defend something that's wrong; you got it to triumph over evil.

original: Thy princely office how canst thou fulfil,   When, pattern'd by thy fault, foul sin may say,   He learn'd to sin, and thou didst teach the way?
translation: How can you be a good prince if you're giving people license to commit the worst sins, and teaching them how to do it?

original: 'Think but how vile a spectacle it were,   To view thy present trespass in another.
translation: "Think about how revolted you'd be if you saw someone else making the same gross  mistake .

original: Men's faults do seldom to themselves appear;   Their own transgressions partially they smother:
translation: Men usually can't see their own faults; they hide them from themselves.

original: This guilt would seem death-worthy in thy brother.
translation: You'd put another man to death for this.

original: O, how are they wrapp'd in with infamies   That from their own misdeeds askance their eyes!
translation: You're setting yourself up for trouble by refusing to recognize your own evil!

original: 'To thee, to thee, my heaved-up hands appeal,   Not to seducing lust, thy rash relier:
translation: "I beg you, I beg you, with my hands raised: don't rape me.

original: I sue for exiled majesty's repeal;   Let him return, and flattering thoughts retire:
translation: I appeal to the  royal sensibility  that you left at the door. Bring it back, and you won't want to do this anymore

original: His true respect will prison false desire,   And wipe the dim mist from thy doting eyne,   That thou shalt see thy state and pity mine.'
translation: . The respect you owe me will put this desire to rest, help you to see yourself clearly, and force you to pity me."

original: 'Have done,' quoth he: 'my uncontrolled tide   Turns not, but swells the higher by this let.
translation: "Enough," he said. "My uncontrollable desire isn't going away; it's getting stronger with all this talking.

original: Small lights are soon blown out, huge fires abide,   And with the wind in greater fury fret:
translation: You can blow out a small light, but huge fires remain and grow larger when the wind blows.

original: The petty streams that pay a daily debt   To their salt sovereign, with their fresh falls' haste   Add to his flow, but alter not his taste.'
translation: The tiny streams that flow into the sea might add water, but they don't change the salty taste."

original: 'Thou art,' quoth she, 'a sea, a sovereign king;   And, lo, there falls into thy boundless flood   Black lust, dishonour, shame, misgoverning,   Who seek to stain the ocean of thy blood.
translation: She said, "You're a royal king. You're like a sea whose waters are polluted with lust, dishonor, shame, and wrongdoing.

original: If all these petty ills shall change thy good,
translation: If you commit this 'petty' crime, it'll cancel out everything that's good about you.

original: Thy sea within a puddle's womb is hearsed,   And not the puddle in thy sea dispersed.
translation: This puddle will swallow up your sea, instead of the puddle getting lost in it.

original: 'So shall these slaves be king, and thou their slave;   Thou nobly base, they basely dignified;
translation: "If you do this, your actions will define you. You'll be a slave to them. You'll be stooping down to their level.

original: Thou their fair life, and they thy fouler grave:   Thou loathed in their shame, they in thy pride:
translation: You'll give these thoughts life, and they'll be the death of you. You'll be hated for and ashamed of what you did, and you'll hate yourself for being prideful enough to do it.

original: The lesser thing should not the greater hide;
translation: A great man like you shouldn't be defined by something like this.

original: The cedar stoops not to the base shrub's foot,   But low shrubs wither at the cedar's root.
translation: A tree doesn't reach down to where a bush grows, does it? No. Bushes shrivel up at the foot of a tree.

original: 'So let thy thoughts, low vassals to thy state'—
translation: "So, get control of your ugly thoughts—"

original: No more,' quoth he; 'by heaven, I will not hear thee:
translation: "No more," he said, "I swear I won't listen to you.

original: Yield to my love; if not, enforced hate,   Instead of love's coy touch, shall rudely tear thee;
translation: Either give into my love or prepare yourself, because instead of caressing you lovingly and gently, I'll forcefully tear you up.

original: That done, despitefully I mean to bear thee   Unto the base bed of some rascal groom,   To be thy partner in this shameful doom.'
translation: After that, I intend to take your body to the some low-level servant's bed, to make him share your sad fate."

original: This said, he sets his foot upon the light,
translation: Having said that, he knocked the candle over with his foot.

original: For light and lust are deadly enemies:   Shame folded up in blind concealing night,   When most unseen, then most doth tyrannize.
translation: Lust can't survive in the light, but it thrives in the concealing darkness of night, when atrocious things go unseen.

original: The wolf hath seized his prey, the poor lamb cries;   Till with her own white fleece her voice controll'd   Entombs her outcry in her lips' sweet fold:
translation: The wolf had seized his prey. The poor lamb screamed, but he stuffed her own white sheet between her lips to silence her.

original: For with the nightly linen that she wears   He pens her piteous clamours in her head;
translation: He  used her own bed sheets to keep her from saying what she thought,

original: Cooling his hot face in the chastest tears   That ever modest eyes with sorrow shed.
translation: and placed his hot face against hers, wet with the most innocent  tears  that modest eyes ever shed.

original: O, that prone lust should stain so pure a bed!
translation: How terrible for such a pure girl to be raped!

original: The spots whereof could weeping purify,   Her tears should drop on them perpetually.
translation: If she could undo his crime by crying, her tears would have washed it all away.

original: But she hath lost a dearer thing than life,   And he hath won what he would lose again:
translation: She lost something more valuable than life itself, and he got something he regretted.

original: This forced league doth force a further strife;   This momentary joy breeds months of pain;
translation: The rape led to further trouble. His momentary satisfaction caused months of pain.

original: This hot desire converts to cold disdain:   Pure Chastity is rifled of her store,
translation: His hot desire turned into cold hatred. Lucrece was robbed of her sexual modesty,

original: And Lust, the thief, far poorer than before.
translation: and Tarquin, the thief, was poorer than before.

original: Look, as the full-fed hound or gorged hawk,   Unapt for tender smell or speedy flight,
translation: Just like a well-fed dog or a stuffed hawk—unable to smell well or fly quickly—

original: Make slow pursuit, or altogether balk   The prey wherein by nature they delight;   So surfeit-taking Tarquin fares this night:
translation: will pursue their desired prey lazily or even reject it entirely, Tarquin took more than his fill that night.

original: His taste delicious, in digestion souring,   Devours his will, that lived by foul devouring.
translation: He thought she tasted good at first, but he quickly got indigestion. Now that he'd gotten what he wanted, he regretted doing it.

original: O, deeper sin than bottomless conceit   Can comprehend in still imagination!
translation: Oh, it's a worse sin than anyone could imagine in their wildest dreams!

original: Drunken Desire must vomit his receipt,   Ere he can see his own abomination.
translation: Tarquin was drunk with desire, but now he'd rather throw up than see the horrible thing he'd just done.

original: While Lust is in his pride, no exclamation   Can curb his heat or rein his rash desire,
translation: When his lust was burning, nothing could cool him off or rein him in—

original: Till like a jade Self-will himself doth tire.
translation: not until he got tired of his own depravity.

original: And then with lank and lean discolour'd cheek,   With heavy eye, knit brow, and strengthless pace,
translation: His face was pale and drawn. With narrowed eyes, he frowned and lost all his strength.

original: Feeble Desire, all recreant, poor, and meek,   Like to a bankrupt beggar wails his case:
translation: After desire left him, he was like a poor, feeble, bankrupt beggar trying to make excuses.

original: The flesh being proud, Desire doth fight with Grace,   For there it revels;
translation: He was a proud man, so once his desire had its way and started to wane, he had to deal with the consequences.

original: and when that decays,   The guilty rebel for remission prays.
translation: Feeling guilty, he started praying for forgiveness.

original: So fares it with this faultful lord of Rome,
translation: That's how it was with the criminal prince of Rome.

original: Who this accomplishment so hotly chased;   For now against himself he sounds this doom,   That through the length of times he stands disgraced:
translation: After pursuing this moment so passionately, he realized his own impending doom, knowing that in a very short time he'd be in disgrace.

original: Besides, his soul's fair temple is defaced;
translation: Besides, he damned his eternal soul.

original: To whose weak ruins muster troops of cares,   To ask the spotted princess how she fares.
translation: Trying to salvage what decency he had left, he asked the ravished princess how she was doing.

original: She says, her subjects with foul insurrection   Have batter'd down her consecrated wall,   And by their mortal fault brought in subjection   Her immortality,
translation: She said she'd lost control of her emotions and her own body was rebelling against her,

original: and made her thrall   To living death and pain perpetual:
translation: having betrayed her to death and unending pain.

original: Which in her prescience she controlled still,   But her foresight could not forestall their will.
translation: While she was in her right mind she could stay  calm , she said, but wasn't sure she'd be able to much longer.

original: Even in this thought through the dark night he  stealeth,   A captive victor that hath lost in gain;
translation: He stole away through the darkness still thinking about what she said. Though he'd gotten what he wanted, he'd lost something, too.

original: Bearing away the wound that nothing healeth,   The scar that will, despite of cure, remain;
translation: He was marked by a cut that would never heal, a scar that would stay with him despite attempts to cure it.

original: Leaving his spoil perplex'd in greater pain.
translation: He left his victim to deal with worse pain.

original: She bears the load of lust he left behind,   And he the burden of a guilty mind.
translation: She was left to deal with the consequences of the rape; all he had to deal with was his guilty mind.

original: He like a thievish dog creeps sadly thence;
translation: He crept away sadly, like a dog that steals scraps from the table.

original: She like a wearied lamb lies panting there;
translation: She lay there, panting, like a tired lamb.

original: He scowls and hates himself for his offence;
translation: He frowned, hating himself for his crime.

original: She, desperate, with her nails her flesh doth tear;
translation: She desperately scratched her face with her nails.

original: He faintly flies, sneaking with guilty fear;
translation: He walked quickly and quietly, sneaking, guilty and afraid.

original: She stays, exclaiming on the direful night;
translation: She stayed, wishing that night had never happened.

original: He runs, and chides his vanish'd, loathed delight.
translation: He ran, regretting and hating his pleasure.

original: He thence departs a heavy convertite;
translation: He left her room like a serious convert.

original: She there remains a hopeless castaway;
translation: She remained there like a hopeless castaway.

original: He in his speed looks for the morning light;
translation: He wanted morning to come quickly.

original: She prays she never may behold the day,
translation: She hoped the day would never come.

original: 'For day,' quoth she, 'nights scapes doth open lay,
translation: She said, "In the daytime, everyone will  find out  what happened tonight,

original: And my true eyes have never practised how   To cloak offences with a cunning brow.
translation: since I don't know how to lie and pretend that nothing happened.

original: 'They think not but that every eye can see   The same disgrace which they themselves behold;
translation: "I feel like everyone else can see in my eyes the disgrace I see in myself.

original: And therefore would they still in darkness be,   To have their unseen sin remain untold;
translation: I wish I could shut my eyes forever so that no one would ever find out about my sin.

original: For they their guilt with weeping will unfold,
translation: I'll give away my guilt by crying,

original: And grave, like water that doth eat in steel,   Upon my cheeks what helpless shame I feel.'
translation: and my tears will cut into my cheeks like water erodes steel, showing the shame I feel."

original: Here she exclaims against repose and rest,   And bids her eyes hereafter still be blind.
translation: Though she didn't want to lie down and sleep any more, she kept her eyes shut, wishing she were blind.

original: She wakes her heart by beating on her breast,   And bids it leap from thence, where it may find   Some purer chest to close so pure a mind.
translation: As her heart pounded, she wished it would jump out of her chest and go find a purer body to live in, one as pure as she wished she was.

original: Frantic with grief thus breathes she forth her spite   Against the unseen secrecy of night:
translation: Frantic and grieving, she shouted angrily into the dark secrecy of the night:

original: 'O comfort-killing Night, image of hell!   Dim register and notary of shame!
translation: "Damn this  night , it's ruined me! The darkness kept anyone from noticing my shame!

original: Black stage for tragedies and murders fell!   Vast sin-concealing chaos! nurse of blame!
translation: Its chaos concealed my sin! It let this happen!

original: Blind muffled bawd! dark harbour for defame!
translation: Blind, silent night! Reputations are lost in the darkness!

original: Grim cave of death! whispering conspirator   With close-tongued treason and the ravisher!
translation: Death creeps in! The night was in cahoots with that lying, treacherous rapist!

original: 'O hateful, vaporous, and foggy Night!
translation: "I hate you, you foggy, misty night!

original: Since thou art guilty of my cureless crime,   Muster thy mists to meet the eastern light,
translation: Since I blame you for this unforgivable crime, now I'm asking you to keep it dark—don't allow the sun to rise.

original: Make war against proportion'd course of time;
translation: Fight against the natural progression of time.

original: Or if thou wilt permit the sun to climb   His wonted height, yet ere he go to bed,   Knit poisonous clouds about his golden head.
translation: Or, if you're going to let the sun rise in the sky, cover him with clouds all throughout the day.

original: 'With rotten damps ravish the morning air;
translation: "Keep the morning air damp.

original: Let their exhaled unwholesome breaths make sick   The life of purity, the supreme fair,   Ere he arrive his weary noon-tide prick;
translation: Let your breath be unhealthy winds, and make the day sick. Ruin what might have been a pure, beautiful day before it even gets to noon.

original: And let thy misty vapours march so thick,   That in their smoky ranks his smother'd light   May set at noon and make perpetual night.
translation: Lay a thick fog over everything to smother the sun's life, so that it sets at noon and makes the whole day night.

original: 'Were Tarquin Night, as he is but Night's child,   The silver-shining queen he would distain;   Her twinkling handmaids too, by him defiled,
translation: "Tarquin is a man of the night. If he could, he'd rape the  night  itself, ravishing the bright, silver moon and all the stars.

original: Through Night's black bosom should not peep again:   So should I have co-partners in my pain;
translation: He'd make them so dirty that they wouldn't be able to shine in the dark of night ever again. Then I'd have someone to share my pain.

original: And fellowship in woe doth woe assuage,   As palmers' chat makes short their pilgrimage.
translation: Misery loves company as much as people on a journey like to pass the time by chatting.

original: 'Where now I have no one to blush with me,   To cross their arms and hang their heads with mine,   To mask their brows and hide their infamy;
translation: "But instead I'm alone now. There's no one to blush with me, no one to cross their arms and hang their heads with me, no one else covering their faces to hide their shame.

original: But I alone alone must sit and pine,   Seasoning the earth with showers of silver brine,
translation: I'm alone, all alone, to sit and cry, covering the earth with showers of tears,

original: Mingling my talk with tears, my grief with groans,   Poor wasting monuments of lasting moans.
translation: talking and crying, grieving and groaning. And yet the cries I'm able to make can't do justice to my sadness, which will never end.

original: 'O Night, thou furnace of foul-reeking smoke,
translation: "This night is an oven filled with stinky smoke.

original: Let not the jealous Day behold that face   Which underneath thy black all-hiding cloak   Immodestly lies martyr'd with disgrace!
translation: Night, don't let the light of day see my face—I'm hiding in your blackness, lying here immodestly, like a disgraceful martyr.

original: Keep still possession of thy gloomy place,
translation: Stay where you are—

original: That all the faults which in thy reign are made   May likewise be sepulchred in thy shade!
translation: keep it gloomy so that all the crimes committed in the night can stay buried in the darkness.

original: 'Make me not object to the tell-tale Day!
translation: "Don't make me face the light of day!

original: The light will show, character'd in my brow,   The story of sweet chastity's decay,   The impious breach of holy wedlock vow:
translation: The light will reveal the whole story of my rape—and of my broken  marriage vows —that's written in my face.

original: Yea the illiterate, that know not how   To cipher what is writ in learned books,   Will quote my loathsome trespass in my looks.
translation: Even illiterate people who've never learned to read in their lives will be able to take one look and me and understand my awful crime.

original: 'The nurse, to still her child, will tell my story,   And fright her crying babe with Tarquin's name;
translation: "Nannies will tell my story to their children. They'll scare them with Tarquin's name.

original: The orator, to deck his oratory,   Will couple my reproach to Tarquin's shame;
translation: Politicians will use mine and Tarquin's shame as an anecdote in their speeches.

original: Feast-finding minstrels, tuning my defame,   Will tie the hearers to attend each line,   How Tarquin wronged me, I Collatine.
translation: Musicians at feasts will sing about my disgrace. They'll have their listeners hanging on every line as they tell how Tarquin wronged me, and how I wronged Collatine in turn.

original: 'Let my good name, that senseless reputation,   For Collatine's dear love be kept unspotted:
translation: "Let my name and my innocent reputation stay clean for Collatine's sake.

original: If that be made a theme for disputation,   The branches of another root are rotted,
translation: If my name is ruined, so is Collatine's, since we're necessarily connected.

original: And undeserved reproach to him allotted   That is as clear from this attaint of mine   As I, ere this, was pure to Collatine.
translation: He doesn't deserve that. He's as free of blame now as I was before this, when I was faithful to him.

original: 'O unseen shame! invisible disgrace!   O unfelt sore! crest-wounding, private scar!
translation: "Oh, my unseen shame and invisible disgrace! My new hurt, my wounded heart, my private scar!

original: Reproach is stamp'd in Collatinus' face,   And Tarquin's eye may read the mot afar,
