translation: Her cheeks were pale now from worrying.

original: He hath no power to ask her how she fares:
translation: He didn't have the strength to ask her how she was doing.

original: Both stood, like old acquaintance in a trance,   Met far from home, wondering each other's chance.
translation: Both of them stood in a trance, like two old acquaintances who run into each other far away from home and can't believe it.

original: At last he takes her by the bloodless hand,   And thus begins: 'What uncouth ill event   Hath thee befall'n, that thou dost trembling stand?
translation: At last, he grasped her bloodless hand and said, "Has something horrible happened to you? Why are you trembling like that?

original: Sweet love, what spite hath thy fair colour spent?   Why art thou thus attired in discontent?
translation: Sweetheart, why are you so pale? Why are you wearing mourning clothes?

original: Unmask, dear dear, this moody heaviness,   And tell thy grief, that we may give redress.'
translation: My dear, tell us why you're upset. Tell us why you're crying, so that we can make it better."

original: Three times with sighs she gives her sorrow fire,   Ere once she can discharge one word of woe:
translation: She sighed three times, getting rid of her sadness before she could say a single sad word.

original: At length address'd to answer his desire,   She modestly prepares to let them know   Her honour is ta'en prisoner by the foe;
translation: When she was finally ready to answer his question, she gathered her courage to tell them she'd been  raped  and ruined.

original: While Collatine and his consorted lords   With sad attention long to hear her words.
translation: Sad and attentive, Collatine and his friends waited for a long time to hear what she would say.

original: And now this pale swan in her watery nest   Begins the sad dirge of her certain ending;
translation: Like a pale  swan  in her watery nest, she began the sad song of her impending death.

original: 'Few words,' quoth she, 'Shall fit the trespass best,   Where no excuse can give the fault amending:
translation: She said, "It's better to keep my speech short in regards to this crime, since no excuse can undo what's been done.

original: In me moe woes than words are now depending;
translation: I have more sorrow than I have words to explain,

original: And my laments would be drawn out too long,   To tell them all with one poor tired tongue.
translation: so it would take way too long for me to tell you all my grievances myself.

original: 'Then be this all the task it hath to say:   Dear husband, in the interest of thy bed   A stranger came,
translation: "So suffice it to say this: My dear husband, a man came looking to take your place in our bed.

original: and on that pillow lay   Where thou was wont to rest thy weary head;
translation: He wanted to lay his head on your very own pillow.

original: And what wrong else may be imagined   By foul enforcement might be done to me,
translation: Anything else you might imagine was forced on me—

original: From that, alas, thy Lucrece is not free.
translation: well, all that happened to me, your Lucrece.

original: 'For in the dreadful dead of dark midnight,   With shining falchion in my chamber came   A creeping creature, with a flaming light,
translation: "A creature crept into my room in the dark of midnight, a shining sword by his side and a flaming candle in his hand.

original: And softly cried 'Awake, thou Roman dame,   And entertain my love;
translation: He whispered, 'Wake up, Roman lady, and make love to me!

original: else lasting shame   On thee and thine this night I will inflict,   If thou my love's desire do contradict.
translation: Otherwise, if you reject my desire, I'll ruin your life and your family members' lives tonight.

original: ' 'For some hard-favour'd groom of thine,' quoth he,   'Unless thou yoke thy liking to my will,   I'll murder straight,
translation: "'Unless you do what I say,' he said, 'I'll murder some low-down servant of yours.

original: and then I'll slaughter thee   And swear I found you where you did fulfil   The loathsome act of lust,
translation: Then I'll kill you and swear I found you having sex with him.

original: and so did kill   The lechers in their deed:
translation: I'll say I killed you in the act,

original: this act will be   My fame and thy perpetual infamy.'
translation: and for that, I'll be renowned as a hero forever, and you'll be the villain.'

original: 'With this, I did begin to start and cry;   And then against my heart he sets his sword,
translation: "With that, I started to shake and cry. He pointed his sword at my heart,

original: Swearing, unless I took all patiently,   I should not live to speak another word;
translation: swearing I wouldn't live to speak another word unless I obeyed him patiently.

original: So should my shame still rest upon record,   And never be forgot in mighty Rome   Th' adulterate death of Lucrece and her groom.
translation: If I fought back, my reputation would be ruined forever. Throughout all Rome, no one would ever forget the death of Lucrece and her servant in adultery.

original: 'Mine enemy was strong, my poor self weak,   And far the weaker with so strong a fear:
translation: "My enemy was strong and I was weak—even weaker than usual because I was so afraid.

original: My bloody judge forbade my tongue to speak;   No rightful plea might plead for justice there:
translation: My  would-be murderer  told me not to speak. I couldn't plead for justice the way that I wanted to.

original: His scarlet lust came evidence to swear   That my poor beauty had purloin'd his eyes;
translation: He said his lust was so strong because my poor beauty had caught his eye.

original: And when the judge is robb'd the prisoner dies.
translation: He said that if he didn't get what he wanted, I would die.

original: 'O, teach me how to make mine own excuse!
translation: "I wish I could make excuses for myself!

original: Or at the least this refuge let me find;   Though my gross blood be stain'd with this abuse,   Immaculate and spotless is my mind;
translation: Although my body is dirty after this assault, I can at least take comfort in the fact that my mind is immaculate and spotless.

original: That was not forced; that never was inclined   To accessary yieldings,
translation: My mind wasn't raped. My mind has never been forced to do something it didn't want to do.

original: but still pure   Doth in her poison'd closet yet endure.'
translation: It's still pure inside my dirty body."

original: Lo, here, the hopeless merchant of this loss,   With head declined, and voice damm'd up with woe,
translation: Her husband—who had lost something, too—hung his head, a lump in his throat.

original: With sad set eyes, and wretched arms across,   From lips new-waxen pale begins to blow
translation: His eyes were sad, his wretched arms were crossed, and his pale lips let out his breath, as if he were about to say something.

original: The grief away that stops his answer so:
translation: But he was so upset that he couldn't speak.

original: But, wretched as he is, he strives in vain;   What he breathes out his breath drinks up again.
translation: When he breathed out, he could only breathe back in again.

original: As through an arch the violent roaring tide   Outruns the eye that doth behold his haste,
translation: His sadness was like the roaring tide of a river when a dam is raised:

original: Yet in the eddy boundeth in his pride   Back to the strait that forced him on so fast;
translation: it pushed him forward, but there was a counter-current that pushed him back again.

original: In rage sent out, recall'd in rage, being past:
translation: He started with intensity, and intensely stopped.

original: Even so his sighs, his sorrows, make a saw,   To push grief on, and back the same grief draw.
translation: His sighs and tears pushed his grief on, but then drew that same grief back in.

original: Which speechless woe of his poor she attendeth,   And his untimely frenzy thus awaketh:
translation: She watched his speechless sadness, suddenly shouting out,

original: 'Dear lord, thy sorrow to my sorrow lendeth   Another power; no flood by raining slaketh.
translation: "My dear, your sadness is making me even sadder—rain doesn't put an end to a flood.

original: My woe too sensible thy passion maketh   More feeling-painful:
translation: I'm too sensitive to your emotions, and this is making it all more painful.

original: let it then suffice   To drown one woe, one pair of weeping eyes.
translation: Let me do the crying; let me bear it all.

original: 'And for my sake, when I might charm thee so,   For she that was thy Lucrece, now attend me:
translation: "Listen to me, for my sake—or for the sake of the woman I once was, when I could charm you.

original: Be suddenly revenged on my foe,   Thine, mine, his own:
translation: Take revenge on my enemy immediately. He's your enemy, my enemy, and his own enemy.

original: suppose thou dost defend me   From what is past:
translation: Pretend you're defending me from what already happened.

original: the help that thou shalt lend me   Comes all too late, yet let the traitor die;
translation: Even though your help is too late, kill him anyway.

original: For sparing justice feeds iniquity.
translation: That justice will put an end to my shame.

original: 'But ere I name him, you fair lords,' quoth she,   Speaking to those that came with Collatine,
translation: "But before I tell you his name, sirs," she said, speaking to the men who came with Collatine.

original: 'Shall plight your honourable faiths to me,   With swift pursuit to venge this wrong of mine;
translation: "All of you need to swear to me.  Swear  that you'll avenge this crime against me as quickly as possible.

original: For 'tis a meritorious fair design   To chase injustice with revengeful arms:
translation: It's an honorable task, taking revenge and putting an end to injustice.

original: Knights, by their oaths, should right poor ladies'  harms.'
translation: By trade, soldiers should protect poor ladies from harm."

original: At this request, with noble disposition   Each present lord began to promise aid,
translation: At her request, each of the men nobly promised to help her.

original: As bound in knighthood to her imposition,   Longing to hear the hateful foe bewray'd.
translation: Now bound to her by an oath, these soldiers longed to hear the enemy's name.

original: But she, that yet her sad task hath not said,   The protestation stops.
translation: But even before she had said it, she started to argue with herself.

original: 'O, speak, ' quoth she,   'How may this forced stain be wiped from me?
translation: She said, "Oh, but how can I ever make myself clean again after this dirty crime?

original: 'What is the quality of mine offence,   Being constrain'd with dreadful circumstance?
translation: "How serious is my offense, considering that I was forced under dreadful circumstances?

original: May my pure mind with the foul act dispense,   My low-declined honour to advance?
translation: Can the purity of my mind cancel out the dirty deed? Can it save my ruined reputation?

original: May any terms acquit me from this chance?
translation: Can anything redeem me from this charge?

original: The poison'd fountain clears itself again;   And why not I from this compelled stain?'
translation: A polluted fountain eventually gets clear again, so why can't I rid myself of this forced corruption?"

original: With this, they all at once began to say,   Her body's stain her mind untainted clears;
translation: At once they all rushed to tell her that her pure mind did purify her soiled body.

original: While with a joyless smile she turns away   The face
translation: But as she turned away with a joyless smile,

original: , that map which deep impression bears   Of hard misfortune, carved in it with tears.
translation: tears were running down her cheeks. Her face was like a map, and the tear-tracks were the roads worn in during her hardship.

original: 'No, no,' quoth she, 'no dame, hereafter living,   By my excuse shall claim excuse's giving.'
translation: "No, no," she said, "no woman who lives through such a thing can excuse herself."

original: Here with a sigh, as if her heart would break,   She throws forth Tarquin's name;
translation: She sighed as if her heart would break, and then said Tarquin's name.

original: 'He, he,' she says,   But more than 'he' her poor tongue could not speak;
translation: She said, "He—" but she couldn't say more than that.

original: Till after many accents and delays,   Untimely breathings, sick and short assays,
translation: She stuttered and stopped, breathing sick, short, heavy breaths.

original: She utters this, 'He, he, fair lords, 'tis he,   That guides this hand to give this wound to me.'
translation: Then she said, "He, sirs. It was he that did this to me."

original: Even here she sheathed in her harmless breast   A harmful knife,
translation: At that moment, she plunged a sharp knife into her innocent chest and killed herself.

original: that thence her soul unsheathed:   That blow did bail it from the deep unrest   Of that polluted prison where it breathed:
translation: She freed her  soul  from its deep unrest inside her polluted body.

original: Her contrite sighs unto the clouds bequeath'd   Her winged sprite,
translation: Her remorseful sighs blew her soul on wings up to heaven.

original: and through her wounds doth fly   Life's lasting date from cancell'd destiny.
translation: By wounding herself, she freed herself from her fate.

original: Stone-still, astonish'd with this deadly deed,   Stood Collatine and all his lordly crew;
translation: Collatine and all his noble friends stood stock-still, astonished by her suicide.

original: Till Lucrece' father, that beholds her bleed,   Himself on her self-slaughter'd body threw;
translation: Lucrece's father watched her bleed and then threw himself on her murdered body.

original: And from the purple fountain Brutus drew   The murderous knife,
translation: Brutus pulled the knife out of her chest.

original: and, as it left the place,   Her blood, in poor revenge, held it in chase;
translation: As it came out, her blood gushed after it.

original: And bubbling from her breast, it doth divide   In two slow rivers, that the crimson blood   Circles her body in on every side,
translation: Bubbling out of her chest, her blood flowed in two rivers over each side of her body, encircling her with crimson blood.

original: Who, like a late-sack'd island, vastly stood   Bare and unpeopled in this fearful flood.
translation: She looked like a conquered island standing bare and unpopulated in the middle of the terrifying flood.

original: Some of her blood still pure and red remain'd,
translation: Some of her blood still looked pure and red.

original: And some look'd black, and that false Tarquin stain'd.
translation: Some of it looked black—that was the blood stained by the treacherous Tarquin.

original: About the mourning and congealed face   Of that black blood a watery rigol goes,   Which seems to weep upon the tainted place:
translation: A ripple of that black blood flowed over her sad, frozen face, which seemed like it was still crying over her pollution.

original: And ever since, as pitying Lucrece' woes,   Corrupted blood some watery token shows;
translation: Ever since—as if blood itself pitied Lucrece's fate—corrupted blood turns black,

original: And blood untainted still doth red abide,   Blushing at that which is so putrified.
translation: while pure blood stays red, blushing at the putrified black blood next to it.

original: 'Daughter, dear daughter,' old Lucretius cries,   'That life was mine which thou hast here deprived.
translation: Old Lucretius cried, "My dear daughter, you've killed me, too.

original: If in the child the father's image lies,   Where shall I live now Lucrece is unlived?
translation: A child is a part of her father, so how can I go on living now that Lucrece is dead?

original: Thou wast not to this end from me derived.
translation: It wasn't supposed to end this way.

original: If children predecease progenitors,   We are their offspring, and they none of ours.
translation: If children die before their parents, it makes us into their children, instead of them being ours.

original: 'Poor broken glass, I often did behold   In thy sweet semblance my old age new born;
translation: "My darling  daughter , when I looked at you I saw so much of my younger self; it was like looking in a mirror.

original: But now that fresh fair mirror, dim and old,   Shows me a bare-boned death by time out-worn:
translation: But now when I look at you, you're not fresh and beautiful anymore; you're dark and old, and all I can see is bare-boned death before its time.

original: O, from thy cheeks my image thou hast torn,
translation: You don't look like me anymore!

original: And shivered all the beauty of my glass,   That I no more can see what once I was!
translation: You're no longer my mirror! I can't look at your beauty and see myself as I once was!

original: 'O time, cease thou thy course and last no longer,   If they surcease to be that should survive.
translation: "Time should stop right where it is—and never begin again—since someone has died who should have survived.

original: Shall rotten death make conquest of the stronger   And leave the faltering feeble souls alive?
translation: How can death kill the strong and leave the old, feeble folks alive?

original: The old bees die, the young possess their hive:
translation: When old bees die, young bees take over the hive.

original: Then live, sweet Lucrece, live again and see   Thy father die, and not thy father thee!'
translation: So come back to life, sweet Lucrece! Come back to life so that you can see your father die, not the other way around!"

original: By this, starts Collatine as from a dream,   And bids Lucretius give his sorrow place;
translation: Hearing that, Collatine shook himself as if he were waking up from a dream. He asked Lucretius to trade places with him,

original: And then in key-cold Lucrece' bleeding stream   He falls, and bathes the pale fear in his face,
translation: and then fell himself into the bloody stream around Lucrece's cold body. He covered his pale, fearful face with her blood.

original: And counterfeits to die with her a space;
translation: He acted like he wanted to die with her.

original: Till manly shame bids him possess his breath   And live to be revenged on her death.
translation: Then his manly pride forced him to breathe normally again and to live to avenge her death.

original: The deep vexation of his inward soul   Hath served a dumb arrest upon his tongue;
translation: His deep internal struggle left him tongue-tied.

original: Who, mad that sorrow should his use control,   Or keep him from heart-easing words so long,   Begins to talk;
translation: He started to talk, angry that he was overcome by his grief and that he couldn't find comforting words to say.

original: but through his lips do throng   Weak words,
translation: But his lips got caught on his words.

original: so thick come in his poor heart's aid,   That no man could distinguish what he said.
translation: He couldn't express his poor heart, considering no one could understand what he said.

original: Yet sometime 'Tarquin' was pronounced plain,   But through his teeth, as if the name he tore.
translation: They could clearly make out the word "Tarquin," but he said it through his teeth like he was tearing it.

original: This windy tempest, till it blow up rain,   Held back his sorrow's tide, to make it more;
translation: There was a windy storm inside him, keeping his grief pent up until it would overflow and make his tears start flowing.

original: At last it rains, and busy winds give o'er:
translation: Finally it rained, and the winds stopped.

original: Then son and father weep with equal strife   Who should weep most, for daughter or for wife.
translation: So Collatine and Lucretius wept together. It was impossible to tell who grieved more: the one who had lost a daughter, or the one who had lost a wife.

original: The one doth call her his, the other his,   Yet neither may possess the claim they lay.
translation: Each of them had a claim to her, but there was nothing worth having for either of them anymore.

original: The father says 'She's mine.'
translation: Her father said, "She's mine."

original: 'O, mine she is,'   Replies her husband: 'do not take away   My sorrow's interest;
translation: Her husband replied, "Oh, but she's mine. Don't take away the object of my grief.

original: let no mourner say   He weeps for her, for she was only mine,   And only must be wail'd by Collatine.'
translation: Don't let anyone else mourn for her. She's mine, and only I, Collatine, will mourn her."

original: 'O,' quoth Lucretius,' I did give that life   Which she too early and too late hath spill'd.'
translation: Lucretius said, "But I gave her life—although she's ended it too soon."

original: 'Woe, woe,' quoth Collatine, 'she was my wife,
translation: "Oh, no!" said Collatine, "She was my wife.

original: I owed her, and 'tis mine that she hath kill'd.'
translation: That's what I called her. It's my wife that's been killed."

original: 'My daughter' and 'my wife' with clamours fill'd   The dispersed air,
translation: Cries of "my daughter" and "my wife" filled the air.

original: who, holding Lucrece' life,   Answer'd their cries, 'my daughter' and 'my wife.'
translation: Each of them valued Lucrece's life and wanted the rights to her body, so they continued to cry out, "my daughter" and "my wife."

original: Brutus, who pluck'd the knife from Lucrece' side,   Seeing such emulation in their woe,   Began to clothe his wit in state and pride,
translation: Brutus  (who pulled the knife out of Lucrece's chest) saw their equal grief and started to prepare an elegant speech.

original: Burying in Lucrece' wound his folly's show.
translation: Lucrece's death was his opportunity to stop acting like an idiot.

original: He with the Romans was esteemed so   As silly-jeering idiots are with kings,   For sportive words and uttering foolish things:
translation: He had a reputation with his fellow Romans for telling funny jokes and saying stupid things, like silly court jesters do with kings.

original: But now he throws that shallow habit by,   Wherein deep policy did him disguise;
translation: But he put all that shallow stuff aside now, a serious look on his face.

original: And arm'd his long-hid wits advisedly,   To cheque the tears in Collatinus' eyes.
translation: He showed the intelligence he'd been hiding for so long. He made use of it now to help Collatine stop crying.

original: 'Thou wronged lord of Rome,' quoth he, 'arise:
translation: "You've been wronged, sir," he said. "Get up!

original: Let my unsounded self, supposed a fool,   Now set thy long-experienced wit to school.
translation: Everyone thinks I'm dumb, but I'm about teach you—the wiser man—something new.

original: 'Why, Collatine, is woe the cure for woe?   Do wounds help wounds, or grief help grievous deeds?
translation: "Collatine, can sadness cure sadness? Does hurt help hurt? Does grief undo terrible deeds?

original: Is it revenge to give thyself a blow   For his foul act by whom thy fair wife bleeds?
translation: Would it really be taking revenge on Tarquin to kill yourself after the rape that killed your wife?

original: Such childish humour from weak minds proceeds:
translation: Such childish thoughts are for weaker men than you.

original: Thy wretched wife mistook the matter so,   To slay herself, that should have slain her foe.
translation: Your poor wife was mistaken. Instead of killing herself, she should have killed Tarquin.

original: 'Courageous Roman, do not steep thy heart   In such relenting dew of lamentations;
translation: "Brave Roman, give your heart a break and stop crying.

original: But kneel with me and help to bear thy part,   To rouse our Roman gods with invocations,   That they will suffer these abominations,   Since Rome herself in them doth stand disgraced,
translation: Instead, you can kneel with me and do your part: pray that our Roman gods will help us avenge these crimes,  since Rome itself is disgraced by them.

original: By our strong arms from forth her fair streets chased.
translation: We'll chase the guilty man out of Rome's streets with our swords.

original: 'Now, by the Capitol that we adore,
translation: "I swear by our respected Roman government;

original: And by this chaste blood so unjustly stain'd,
translation: by Lucrece, a modest woman who was unjustly killed;

original: By heaven's fair sun that breeds the fat earth's store,
translation: by the beautiful sun in the sky that makes plants grow in the earth;

original: By all our country rights in Rome maintain'd,
translation: by all our rights as citizens of Rome;

original: And by chaste Lucrece' soul that late complain'd   Her wrongs to us,
translation: by sweet Lucrece's soul that only just told us what happened to her;

original: and by this bloody knife,   We will revenge the death of this true wife.'
translation: and by this bloody knife: we will take revenge for this faithful wife's death."

original: This said, he struck his hand upon his breast,   And kiss'd the fatal knife, to end his vow;
translation: That said, he placed his hand over his heart, and kissed the fatal knife to seal his promise.

original: And to his protestation urged the rest,
translation: He urged the others to do the same.

original: Who, wondering at him, did his words allow:
translation: Wondering at him, they did as he said.

original: Then jointly to the ground their knees they bow;
translation: They knelt together at the same time.

original: And that deep vow, which Brutus made before,   He doth again repeat, and that they swore.
translation: Brutus repeated his serious promise again, and they all swore to it.

original: When they had sworn to this advised doom,   They did conclude to bear dead Lucrece thence;
translation: When they had sworn to to carry out this revenge, they decided to take Lucrece's body with them to Rome.

original: To show her bleeding body thorough Rome,   And so to publish Tarquin's foul offence:
translation: They would show her bleeding body throughout the city to proclaim Tarquin's disgusting crime.

original: Which being done with speedy diligence,   The Romans plausibly did give consent   To Tarquin's everlasting banishment.
translation: After they did that, the Romans quickly and faithfully agreed to banish Tarquin forever.

original: I KNOW not how I shall offend in dedicating my  unpolished lines to your lordship, nor how the world  will censure me for choosing so strong a prop to support so weak a burden only,
translation: I'm not sure if I'll offend you by dedicating my less-than-perfect poetry to you, sir, or if the world will criticize me for choosing someone as powerful as you to validate my pathetic creation.

original: if your honour seem but pleased, I account myself highly praised, and vow to take  advantage of all idle hours, till I have honoured you  with some graver labour.
translation: But if you're happy, sir, I'll feel like I've been successful—and I'll promise to use all my free time working until I can write a more serious poem to dedicate to you.

original: But if the first heir of my  invention prove deformed, I shall be sorry it had so  noble a god-father, and never after ear so barren a  land, for fear it yield me still so bad a harvest.
translation: But if my first-ever poem turns out to be bad, I'll regret dedicating it to you and won't  try again , since I'll be afraid of producing another embarrassing poem.

original: I  leave it to your honourable survey,
translation: I leave it to up to your judgment. You can decide if it's worthy of you or not.

original: and your honour to  your heart's content; which I wish may always answer  your own wish and the world's hopeful expectation.
translation: Of course, I hope that the poem fulfills your heart's desires and that it can live up to the world's hopeful expectations.

original: EVEN as the sun with purple-colour'd face   Had ta'en his last leave of the weeping morn,
translation: The sun was purple on that rainy morning. Just as it disappeared behind a cloud,

original: Rose-cheek'd Adonis hied him to the chase;   Hunting he loved, but love he laugh'd to scorn;
translation: rosy-cheeked Adonis went out hunting. He loved hunting, but he laughed in the face of love.

original: Sick-thoughted Venus makes amain unto him,   And like a bold-faced suitor 'gins to woo him.
translation: Lovesick over him,  Venus  followed him as fast as she could. She started talking sweetly to him, and as boldly as a lover would.

original: 'Thrice-fairer than myself,' thus she began,   'The field's chief flower, sweet above compare,
translation: "You're three times as pretty as I am," she began, "the prettiest  flower  in the field, and sweeter than anything in the world.

original: Stain to all nymphs, more lovely than a man,   More white and red than doves or roses are;
translation: You put fairies to shame. You're lovelier than any man alive. Your skin is whiter than a dove's, and your blushing cheeks are redder than roses.

original: Nature that made thee, with herself at strife,   Saith that the world hath ending with thy life.
translation: You're the most perfect creature Mother Nature ever made, and she'll never make another one like you.

original: 'Vouchsafe, thou wonder, to alight thy steed,   And rein his proud head to the saddle-bow;
translation: "Hey, handsome, would you be so kind as to get down off your horse and tie his reins to the horn of the saddle?

original: If thou wilt deign this favour, for thy meed   A thousand honey secrets shalt thou know:
translation: If you'll do as I ask, I'll reward you by telling you a thousand secrets as sweet as honey.

original: Here come and sit, where never serpent hisses,   And being set, I'll smother thee with kisses;
translation: Come here and sit by me, where snakes can never bite you. Once you're here, I'll cover you with kisses.

original: 'And yet not cloy thy lips with loathed satiety,   But rather famish them amid their plenty,
translation: "But I won't overload your lips with too much kissing. I'll make you long for more even as we kiss.

original: Making them red and pale with fresh variety,
translation: I'll change it up—first your lips will be red, and then pale again.

original: Ten kisses short as one, one long as twenty:
translation: I'll give you ten quick kisses—all together as long as one normal kiss. Then I'll give you one long kiss as long as twenty quick kisses.

original: A summer's day will seem an hour but short,   Being wasted in such time-beguiling sport.'
translation: When you have such a fun way to pass the time, a summer's day seems to go by in an hour."

original: With this she seizeth on his sweating palm,   The precedent of pith and livelihood,
translation: As she said that, she grabbed his sweating hand. It pulsed with all the life in his body.

original: And trembling in her passion, calls it balm,   Earth's sovereign salve to do a goddess good:
translation: Trembling and passionate, she said his hand was sweet medicine, the best medicine on Earth that a goddess could ask for.

original: Being so enraged, desire doth lend her force   Courageously to pluck him from his horse.
translation: As she got more aroused, she worked up the courage to pull him down from his horse.

original: Over one arm the lusty courser's rein,   Under her other was the tender boy,
translation: She threw the horse's reins over one arm and held the young boy under the other.

original: Who blush'd and pouted in a dull disdain,   With leaden appetite, unapt to toy;
translation: He blushed and pouted disapprovingly. He wasn't aroused at all—he didn't want to play.

original: She red and hot as coals of glowing fire,   He red for shame, but frosty in desire.
translation: She was  red-hot  with passion; he was red because he was embarrassed, but he didn't desire her at all.

original: The studded bridle on a ragged bough   Nimbly she fastens:—O, how quick is love!—
translation: She nimbly fastened the horse to a tree branch. Love moves quickly!

original: The steed is stalled up, and even now   To tie the rider she begins to prove:
translation: Now that the horse was tied, she attempted to tie the rider, too.

original: Backward she push'd him, as she would be thrust,
translation: She pushed him backward just the way she hoped he would thrust into her.

original: And govern'd him in strength, though not in lust.
translation: Her strength made it easy to throw him around physically, but she couldn't make him want her.

original: So soon was she along as he was down,   Each leaning on their elbows and their hips:
translation: She laid down beside him. Each of them leaned on their elbows and hips.

original: Now doth she stroke his cheek, now doth he frown,   And 'gins to chide, but soon she stops his lips;
translation: When she stroked his cheek, he frowned. He started to say something, but she kissed his lips to stop him.

original: And kissing speaks, with lustful language broken,   'If thou wilt chide, thy lips shall never open.'
translation: As they kissed, she said, between kisses, "if you're going to argue with me, you'll never open your lips again."

original: He burns with bashful shame:
translation: He blushed,  embarrassed .

original: she with her tears   Doth quench the maiden burning of his cheeks;
translation: As she started to cry, her tears fell on his burning, innocent face.

original: Then with her windy sighs and golden hairs   To fan and blow them dry again she seeks:
translation: Then she dried his tears with a deep sigh and a toss of her blonde hair.

original: He saith she is immodest, blames her 'miss;   What follows more she murders with a kiss.
translation: He said she was being too forward, and that what she was doing was wrong. She shut him up again by kissing him.

original: Even as an empty eagle, sharp by fast,   Tires with her beak on feathers, flesh and bone,
translation: She was like a hungry  eagle  on the prowl: an eagle will catch a bird, pluck its feather out with its beak, and then tear the flesh away from the bone.

original: Shaking her wings, devouring all in haste,   Till either gorge be stuff'd or prey be gone;
translation: It'll flap its wings, eating as quickly as it can until it's full or there's no prey left to eat.

original: Even so she kissed his brow, his cheek, his chin,   And where she ends she doth anew begin.
translation: She kissed his forehead, his cheeks, and his chin like that, and then started all over again at the beginning.

original: Forced to content, but never to obey,
translation: He was forced to take it, but he didn't respond.

original: Panting he lies and breatheth in her face;
translation: He lay there, panting and breathing in her face.

original: She feedeth on the steam as on a prey,   And calls it heavenly moisture, air of grace;
translation: She breathed in his breath, saying it smelled heavenly and felt delightful.

original: Wishing her cheeks were gardens full of flowers,   So they were dew'd with such distilling showers.
translation: She said that if her cheeks were flowers, the moisture his breath left on them would make them grow better than any rain could.

original: Look, how a bird lies tangled in a net,   So fasten'd in her arms Adonis lies;
translation: Adonis was trapped in her arms like a bird tangled in a net.

original: Pure shame and awed resistance made him fret,   Which bred more beauty in his angry eyes:
translation: His angry eyes looked even more beautiful as he struggled against her—ashamed, innocent, and resistant.

original: Rain added to a river that is rank   Perforce will force it overflow the bank.
translation: Since he was already handsome, anything added to his face only made him  more so .

original: Still she entreats, and prettily entreats,   For to a pretty ear she tunes her tale;
translation: She kept asking this handsome boy—and asking nicely.

original: Still is he sullen, still he lours and frets,   'Twixt crimson shame and anger ashy-pale:
translation: He remained cold, frowning and pushing her away. His face was alternately flushed with embarrassment and pale with anger.

original: Being red, she loves him best; and being white,   Her best is better'd with a more delight.
translation: She loved him best when he was red—but then she loved him even more when he grew pale again.

original: Look how he can, she cannot choose but love;
translation: With a face like that, she couldn't help but love him.

original: And by her fair immortal hand she swears,   From his soft bosom never to remove,
translation: She swore she would never take her beautiful, immortal hands off his soft chest.

original: Till he take truce with her contending tears,   Which long have rain'd, making her cheeks all wet;
translation: That is, unless he would give in to her pleading tears (which had been going on for a long time, leaving her cheeks all wet)

original: And one sweet kiss shall pay this countless debt.
translation: and repay her with a single kiss.

original: Upon this promise did he raise his chin,
translation: When she promised that, he raised his chin—

original: Like a dive-dapper peering through a wave,   Who, being look'd on, ducks as quickly in;
translation: like a heron peeking his head out from a wave, and diving back in as soon as he realizes he's been seen.

original: So offers he to give what she did crave;
translation: He acted like he was going to give Venus what she wanted,

original: But when her lips were ready for his pay,   He winks, and turns his lips another way.
translation: but when she puckered her lips, he blinked and turned his lips away.

original: Never did passenger in summer's heat   More thirst for drink than she for this good turn.
translation: A traveler on a hot summer day wouldn't have longed for water as much as Venus longed for his kiss.

original: Her help she sees, but help she cannot get;
translation: She saw his lips, but couldn't make them kiss her.

original: She bathes in water, yet her fire must burn:
translation: Her cheeks were wet with tears, but her desire burned in her heart.

original: 'O, pity,' 'gan she cry, 'flint-hearted boy!   'Tis but a kiss I beg; why art thou coy?
translation: "Take pity on me," she cried, "you hard-hearted boy! All I want is a kiss, why are you being so coy?

original: 'I have been woo'd, as I entreat thee now,   Even by the stern and direful god of war,
translation: "The serious, terrifying  god of war  flirted with me the way I'm flirting with you now.

original: Whose sinewy neck in battle ne'er did bow,   Who conquers where he comes in every jar;
translation: He's never been defeated in battle; he conquers everyone he fights.

original: Yet hath he been my captive and my slave,   And begg'd for that which thou unask'd shalt have.
translation: And yet, I've made him my captive and my slave. I've made him beg for what I'd give you without asking.

original: 'Over my altars hath he hung his lance,   His batter'd shield, his uncontrolled crest,
translation: "He's  hung his sword , battered shield, and helmet over my bed.

original: And for my sake hath learn'd to sport and dance,   To toy, to wanton, dally, smile and jest,
translation: He's learned to play games, dance, fool around, waste time, relax, smile, and joke for my sake.

original: Scorning his churlish drum and ensign red,   Making my arms his field, his tent my bed.
translation: He's put aside his war drum and battle cry, making my arms his battlefield and my bed his tent instead.

original: 'Thus he that overruled I oversway'd,
translation: "So I overcame the most powerful of the gods.

original: Leading him prisoner in a red-rose chain:
translation: I made him my prisoner and bound him in chains of red roses.

original: Strong-tempered steel his stronger strength obey'd,   Yet was he servile to my coy disdain.
translation: Although he could defeat the strongest steel swords with his strength, he gave into my flirtatious tricks.

original: O, be not proud, nor brag not of thy might,   For mastering her that foil'd the god of fight!
translation: Don't be so proud! Don't think you're tough for defeating the goddess who trumped the god of war!

original: 'Touch but my lips with those fair lips of thine,—
translation: "Just touch my lips with your pretty lips.

original: Though mine be not so fair, yet are they red—   The kiss shall be thine own as well as mine.
translation: Mine aren't as pretty as yours, but at least they're red—you'll enjoy the kiss as much as I will.

original: What seest thou in the ground? hold up thy head:
translation: What are you looking at on the ground? Hold your head up;

original: Look in mine eye-balls, there thy beauty lies;
translation: look me in the eye. Your eyes are your most beautiful feature.

original: Then why not lips on lips, since eyes in eyes?
translation: If we kiss with lips on lips, why not with eyes on eyes?

original: 'Art thou ashamed to kiss? then wink again,   And I will wink;
translation: "Are you too embarrassed to kiss me? Then close your eyes again, and I'll close mine, too.

original: so shall the day seem night;   Love keeps his revels where they are but twain;
translation: We can pretend it's nighttime. Lovers usually meet in the dark of night.

original: Be bold to play, our sport is not in sight:
translation: So kiss me; no one can see us!

original: These blue-vein'd violets whereon we lean   Never can blab, nor know not what we mean.
translation: The blue-and-purple violets over there won't blab—they don't know what we're up to.

original: 'The tender spring upon thy tempting lip   Shows thee unripe; yet mayst thou well be tasted:
translation: "I can tell by the wispy hairs above your lip that you're not a man yet, but you're not too young for love.

original: Make use of time, let not advantage slip;   Beauty within itself should not be wasted:
translation: Seize the day ; don't let time pass you by. Beauty in and of itself shouldn't be wasted.

original: Fair flowers that are not gather'd in their prime   Rot and consume themselves in little time.
translation: If you don't gather pretty flowers when they're blooming, they rot and decay quickly.

original: 'Were I hard-favour'd, foul, or wrinkled-old,   Ill-nurtured, crooked, churlish, harsh in voice,
translation: "If I were ugly, gross, wrinkly, old, starving, hunchbacked, rude, harsh-voiced,

original: O'erworn, despised, rheumatic and cold,
translation: over-worked, hated, diseased, cold,

original: Thick-sighted, barren, lean and lacking juice,   Then mightst thou pause,   for then I were not for thee
translation: blind, barren, thin, or dry, you might have good reason to hesitate.  Then I wouldn't be worthy of you.

original: But having no defects, why dost abhor me?
translation: But I'm perfect, so why are you rejecting me?

original: 'Thou canst not see one wrinkle in my brow;   Mine eyes are gray and bright and quick in turning:
translation: "There's not a single wrinkle in my forehead. My eyes are gray, bright, and can move quickly.

original: My beauty as the spring doth yearly grow,
translation: I get more beautiful with every passing year.

original: My flesh is soft and plump, my marrow burning;
translation: My skin is soft, my body is plump, and my bones are healthy.

original: My smooth moist hand, were it with thy hand felt,   Would in thy palm dissolve, or seem to melt.
translation: If you would touch it, my smooth, moist hand would dissolve in your hand, or seem to melt.

original: 'Bid me discourse, I will enchant thine ear,
translation: "Let me talk for a while—I'll entertain you.

original: Or, like a fairy, trip upon the green,
translation: Or let me dance on the grass like a fairy.

original: Or, like a nymph, with long dishevell'd hair,   Dance on the sands, and yet no footing seen:
translation: Or let me fly above the sand—my hair flowing like a water spirit's, my feet never touching the ground.

original: Love is a spirit all compact of fire,   Not gross to sink, but light, and will aspire.
translation: The burning power of love doesn't weigh us down; it makes us lighter, and makes us feel like we can do anything.

original: 'Witness this primrose bank whereon I lie;
translation: "Look, see these primroses I'm lying on?

original: These forceless flowers like sturdy trees support me;
translation: These  weak flowers  support me as if they were sturdy trees.

original: Two strengthless doves will draw me through the sky,   From morn till night, even where I list to sport me:
translation: Two tiny doves can drag me across the sky, and fly me anywhere I want, from morning until night.

original: Is love so light, sweet boy, and may it be   That thou shouldst think it heavy unto thee?
translation: Love is so light, sweet boy. So why do you think it's such a burden?

original: 'Is thine own heart to thine own face affected?
translation: "Are you in love with your own face?

original: Can thy right hand seize love upon thy left?
translation: Can your right hand make love to your left?

original: Then woo thyself, be of thyself rejected,   Steal thine own freedom and complain on theft.
translation: Then flirt with yourself and be rejected by yourself. You can still be free from love, but then you'll be robbing yourself.

original: Narcissus so himself himself forsook,   And died to kiss his shadow in the brook.
translation: Narcissus  fell in love with himself, too, and he died trying to kiss his own reflection in a stream.

original: 'Torches are made to light, jewels to wear,   Dainties to taste,
translation: "Candles are supposed to be lit, jewelry is supposed to be worn, desserts are made to be tasted,

original: f   resh beauty for the use,   Herbs for their smell, and sappy plants to bear:
translation: flowers are supposed to be picked, herbs are meant to be smelled, trees are made to bear fruit.

original: Things growing to themselves are growth's abuse:
translation: Things are supposed to be used for their purposes.

original: Seeds spring from seeds and beauty breedeth beauty;
translation: Seeds are planted and produce more seeds. Beauty breeds beauty.

original: Thou wast begot; to get it is thy duty.
translation: Someone conceived you, so it's your duty to conceive a child of your own.

original: 'Upon the earth's increase why shouldst thou feed,   Unless the earth with thy increase be fed?
translation: "Why should you consume everything the earth produces without producing something to give back to it?

original: By law of nature thou art bound to breed,   That thine may live when thou thyself art dead;
translation: According to the laws of nature, you're supposed to procreate so that your children can live on after you're dead.

original: And so, in spite of death, thou dost survive,   In that thy likeness still is left alive.'
translation: That way, even when you die, you live on in your surviving  children ."

original: By this the love-sick queen began to sweat,
translation: After saying all that, the love-sick goddess started to sweat.

original: For where they lay the shadow had forsook them,   And Titan, tired in the mid-day heat,
translation: There was no shade where they were lying, and the  sun  was directly overhead in the midday heat.

original: With burning eye did hotly overlook them;   Wishing Adonis had his team to guide,
translation: The sun-god, Titan, wished Adonis would trade places with him, so that Adonis would pull the sun across the sky in his chariot

original: So he were like him and by Venus' side.
translation: and Titan could lie down next to Venus instead.

original: And now Adonis, with a lazy spright,   And with a heavy, dark, disliking eye,
translation: Adonis was starting to get bored. His eyes grew heavy and dark, indicating how unhappy he was.

original: His louring brows o'erwhelming his fair sight,   Like misty vapours when they blot the sky,
translation: He furrowed his brow low over his eyes, like  clouds  darkening the sky.

original: Souring his cheeks cries 'Fie, no more of love!   The sun doth burn my face: I must remove.'
translation: He pouted and cried, "stop! Stop talking about love! The sun is burning my face. I need to leave."

original: 'Ay me,' quoth Venus, 'young, and so unkind?
translation: "Oh dear," said Venus, "how can someone so young be so unkind?

original: What bare excuses makest thou to be gone!
translation: You're making up such lame excuses to leave!

original: I'll sigh celestial breath, whose gentle wind   Shall cool the heat of this descending sun:
translation: If I breathe my heavenly breath, it'll cool down the heat of the sun.

original: I'll make a shadow for thee of my hairs;   If they burn too, I'll quench them with my tears.
translation: I can make a shady spot for you underneath my hair. If the sun starts to burn my hair, I'll put the fire out with my tears.

original: 'The sun that shines from heaven shines but warm,
translation: "When the sun shines from the sky, obviously it's warm.

original: And, lo, I lie between that sun and thee:
translation: But look—I'm lying between the sun and you.

original: The heat I have from thence doth little harm,   Thine eye darts forth the fire that burneth me;
translation: The sun's heat doesn't hurt me at all; it's your  eyes  that set my heart on fire.

original: And were I not immortal, life were done   Between this heavenly and earthly sun.
translation: If I weren't immortal, I'd be a goner, caught between the sun and you.

original: 'Art thou obdurate, flinty, hard as steel,
translation: "Are you really so tough, like a rock? Hard as steel?

original: Nay, more than flint, for stone at rain relenteth?
translation: No, you're harder than rock—rock erodes in the rain!

original: Art thou a woman's son, and canst not feel   What 'tis to love?
translation: Didn't you have a mother—don't you know what love is?

original: how want of love tormenteth?
translation: Don't you know how hard it is to be deprived of love?

original: O, had thy mother borne so hard a mind,   She had not brought forth thee, but died unkind.
translation: If your mother was as tough as you, she wouldn't have given birth to you; she would have died instead.

original: 'What am I, that thou shouldst contemn me this?
translation: "Who am I for you to insult me this way?

original: Or what great danger dwells upon my suit?
translation: What are you afraid will happen if you give into me?

original: What were thy lips the worse for one poor kiss?
translation: Would your lips be that much worse off if they gave me a single kiss?

original: Speak, fair; but speak fair words, or else be mute:
translation: Say something sweet. Only sweet things; otherwise be quiet.

original: Give me one kiss, I'll give it thee again,   And one for interest, if thou wilt have twain.
translation: Give me one kiss, and I'll kiss you back. And I'll kiss you again if you want another one.

original: 'Fie, lifeless picture, cold and senseless stone,
translation: "You're a lifeless picture; a cold, unfeeling stone;

original: Well-painted idol,
translation: a painted statue;

original: image dun and dead,
translation: a dull, dead image;

original: Statue contenting but the eye alone,
translation: a work of art made to please the eye.

original: Thing like a man, but of no woman bred!
translation: You look like a man, but you can't be human!

original: Thou art no man, though of a man's complexion,   For men will kiss even by their own direction.'
translation: You're not a man, even though you look like one. Men kiss women of their own accord."

original: This said, impatience chokes her pleading tongue,
translation: That said, she was overcome with impatience and got tongue-tied.

original: And swelling passion doth provoke a pause;   Red cheeks and fiery eyes blaze forth he wrong;
translation: Her intense emotion forced her to stop talking. He looked angry with his red cheeks and fiery eyes.

original: Being judge in love, she cannot right her cause:
translation: Even though Venus was the goddess of love, she couldn't help her cause.

original: And now she weeps, and now she fain would speak,   And now her sobs do her intendments break.
translation: She cried, then tried to speak, then started to sob again in the middle of her sentence.

original: Sometimes she shakes her head and then his hand,   Now gazeth she on him, now on the ground;
translation: She would shake her head, then pull on his hand. She'd gaze at him, then at the ground.

original: Sometimes her arms infold him like a band:   She would, he will not in her arms be bound;
translation: She'd fold her arms around him, then,

original: And when from thence he struggles to be gone,   She locks her lily fingers one in one.
translation: when he struggled to get away and finally escaped, she'd lace her white fingers together.

original: 'Fondling,' she saith, 'since I have hemm'd thee here   Within the circuit of this ivory pale,   I'll be a park, and thou shalt be my deer;
translation: "Darling," she said, "since my white arms circle around you like a fence, I'll be a park, and you can be my  deer .

original: Feed where thou wilt, on mountain or in dale:
translation: You can nibble wherever you want: in the mountains, or in the valleys.

original: Graze on my lips; and if those hills be dry,   Stray lower, where the pleasant fountains lie.
translation: Graze on my lips. If my lips are dry, look lower, where the pleasant fountains are.

original: 'Within this limit is relief enough,
translation: "You have everything you need within this fence:

original: Sweet bottom-grass and high delightful plain,
translation: sweet grass in the valleys; high, delightful plains up top;

original: Round rising hillocks, brakes obscure and rough,   To shelter thee from tempest and from rain
translation: round, rising  hills;  dark clumps of bush to shelter you from the wind and the rain.

original: Then be my deer, since I am such a park;
translation: Be my deer, then, since I'm your park.

original: No dog shall rouse thee, though a thousand bark.'
translation: No dog will ever catch you, even if a thousand tried."

original: At this Adonis smiles as in disdain,
translation: Adonis smiled condescendingly at that.

original: That in each cheek appears a pretty dimple:   Love made those hollows,
translation: A pretty dimple showed in each cheek—if only his cheeks were dimpling for love.

original: if himself were slain,   He might be buried in a tomb so simple;
translation: A lover can only hope to be buried in  a grave as perfect as that dimple ;

original: Foreknowing well, if there he came to lie,   Why, there Love lived and there he could not die.
translation: he would know that, when he was buried there, love was all around and could never die.

original: These lovely caves, these round enchanting pits,   Open'd their mouths to swallow Venus' liking.
translation: Venus fell in love with those lovely caves, those round, enchanting holes; they swallowed her up.

original: Being mad before, how doth she now for wits?   Struck dead at first, what needs a second striking?
translation: She was crazy in love before, so where was she now? If you're dead after the first strike, do you really need to be struck again?

original: Poor queen of love, in thine own law forlorn,
translation: Poor goddess of love—she was beat at her own game!

original: To love a cheek that smiles at thee in scorn!
translation: She was in love with a dimple that only showed when he was rejecting her.

original: Now which way shall she turn? what shall she say?   Her words are done,
translation: Where could she turn? What could she say? She had no words left.

original: her woes are more increasing;   The time is spent, her object will away,
translation: Her suffering was getting worse, but she'd tried her best. Her object was trying to leave,

original: And from her twining arms doth urge releasing.
translation: straining against her arms around him.

original: Pity,' she cries, 'some favour, some remorse!'   Away he springs and hasteth to his horse.
translation: "Have pity on me," she cried, "show me some love, take it back!" But he jumped out of her arms and ran over to his horse.

original: But, lo, from forth a copse that neighbors by,   A breeding jennet, lusty, young and proud,
translation: But just then, a female  horse  came out from behind some nearby trees. She was young, attractive, energetic, and ready to breed.

original: Adonis' trampling courser doth espy,   And forth she rushes, snorts and neighs aloud:
translation: Adonis' horse saw her. She rushed over to him, snorted, and neighed.

original: The strong-neck'd steed, being tied unto a tree,   Breaketh his rein, and to her straight goes he.
translation: Adonis' strong-necked horse, still tied to the tree, broke his reins and went straight to her.

original: Imperiously he leaps, he neighs, he bounds,
translation: He leapt up impressively, neighed, and ran.

original: And now his woven girths he breaks asunder;
translation: He broke his saddle from off his back

original: The bearing earth with his hard hoof he wounds,   Whose hollow womb resounds like heaven's thunder;
translation: and pawed the earth hard with his hoof. His hoof in the dirt made a loud, echoing sound like thunder.

original: The iron bit he crusheth 'tween his teeth,   Controlling what he was controlled with.
translation: He crushed the iron bit with his teeth,  controlling  what was used to control him.

original: His ears up-prick'd;
translation: He pricked his ears up.

original: his braided hanging mane   Upon his compass'd crest now stand on end;
translation: His braided mane didn't hang down anymore; it stood straight up on his head.

original: His nostrils drink the air, and forth again,   As from a furnace, vapours doth he send:
translation: His nostrils flared and he breathed out heavily again and again, his breath like steam blowing out of a furnace.

original: His eye, which scornfully glisters like fire,   Shows his hot courage and his high desire.
translation: His eyes were shining as bright as fire, showing how hot with desire he was, and how far he'd go to get what he wanted.

original: Sometime he trots, as if he told the steps,   With gentle majesty and modest pride;
translation: He trotted gently, majestically, and modestly as if he were counting his steps.

original: Anon he rears upright, curvets and leaps,   As who should say 'Lo, thus my strength is tried,
translation: Then he reared up on his hind legs, and jumped with his back legs into the air as if to say, "look how strong I am!

original: And this I do to captivate the eye   Of the fair breeder that is standing by.'
translation: I'm doing all this to catch the eye of the pretty horse standing over there."

original: What recketh he his rider's angry stir,   His flattering 'Holla,' or his 'Stand, I say?'
translation: Does he care now that his angry rider is shouting, "hey" and "stay there?"

original: What cares he now for curb or pricking spur?
translation: Does he care about his whips and spurs?

original: For rich caparisons or trapping gay?
translation: About fancy harnesses or bright-colored ribbons?

original: He sees his love, and nothing else he sees,   For nothing else with his proud sight agrees.
translation: He can't see anything but his love; nothing else is worth looking at to him.

original: Look, when a painter would surpass the life,   In limning out a well-proportion'd steed,
translation: It was as if a  painter  had set out to draw an ideal horse that would put real horses to shame—drawing out the right proportions,

original: His art with nature's workmanship at strife,   As if the dead the living should exceed;
translation: painting him to his best ability, as if a work of art could be better than life.

original: So did this horse excel a common one   In shape, in courage, colour, pace and bone.
translation: In just the same way, that horse's body, spirit, color, speed, and form excelled all other horses.

original: Round-hoof'd, short-jointed, fetlocks shag and long,
translation: Round hooves; short joints; long, shaggy  fetlocks ;

original: Broad breast, full eye, small head and nostril wide,
translation: a broad chest; full eyes; a small head; wide nostrils;

original: High crest, short ears, straight legs and passing  strong,
translation: a high forehead; straight legs; exceptional strength;

original: Thin mane, thick tail, broad buttock, tender hide:
translation: a thin mane; thick tail; broad buttocks; and a soft hide:

original: Look, what a horse should have he did not lack,   Save a proud rider on so proud a back.
translation: this horse lacked nothing except a handsome rider on his back to match his handsome self.

original: Sometime he scuds far off and there he stares;
translation: He would scurry off and stand far away, staring.

original: Anon he starts at stirring of a feather;   To bid the wind a base he now prepares,
translation: Then he'd start at the smallest thing. He was ready to chase the wind,

original: And whether he run or fly they know not whether;
translation: whether he had to run or fly to do it.

original: For through his mane and tail the high wind sings,   Fanning the hairs, who wave like feather'd wings.
translation: The wind ran through his mane and tail, fanning the hair out like feathery wings.

original: He looks upon his love and neighs unto her;   She answers him as if she knew his mind:
translation: He looked at his love and neighed to her. She answered him as if she could read his mind.

original: Being proud, as females are, to see him woo her,
translation: Like all females, she got prideful when he started flirting with her.

original: She puts on outward strangeness, seems unkind,   Spurns at his love and scorns the heat he feels,
translation: She started acting cold and rude, rejecting his love and mocking his passion,

original: Beating his kind embracements with her heels.
translation: kicking him away when he tried to get close.

original: Then, like a melancholy malcontent,   He veils his tail that, like a falling plume,   Cool shadow to his melting buttock lent:
translation: Then, as if he were depressed, he curled his tail over his backside, shading it like an umbrella.

original: He stamps and bites the poor flies in his fume.
translation: He stamped and bit the flies in his tail.

original: His love, perceiving how he is enraged,   Grew kinder, and his fury was assuaged.
translation: His love could see how angry he was and started acting more kindly; his anger went away.

original: His testy master goeth about to take him;
translation: His grumpy master went to grab him

original: When, lo, the unback'd breeder, full of fear,
translation: when, all of a sudden, the female horse spooked.

original: Jealous of catching, swiftly doth forsake him,   With her the horse, and left Adonis there:
translation: Not wanting to lose her, Adonis'  horse  abandoned him and ran after her, leaving Adonis behind.

original: As they were mad, unto the wood they hie them,   Out-stripping crows that strive to over-fly them.
translation: They ran into the woods like crazy horses, running faster than the crows could fly in the air above them.

original: All swoln with chafing, down Adonis sits,   Banning his boisterous and unruly beast:
translation: Filled with anger, Adonis sat down, berating his energetic, misbehaving animal.

original: And now the happy season once more fits,   That love-sick Love by pleading may be blest;
translation: It was a good time then for lovesick Venus to make a more successful attempt at love.

original: For lovers say, the heart hath treble wrong   When it is barr'd the aidance of the tongue.
translation: Lovers say that your heart is most in pain when it can't find the words to articulate what it feels.

original: An oven that is stopp'd, or river stay'd,   Burneth more hotly, swelleth with more rage:
translation: When you stop an oven, it burns hotter; when you dam a river, it swells higher.

original: So of concealed sorrow may be said;
translation: It's the same when you try to keep sadness bottled up.

original: Free vent of words love's fire doth assuage;
translation: Love makes you want to speak up.

original: But when the heart's attorney once is mute,   The client breaks, as desperate in his suit.
translation: When you're silent, the  words  will break out of you because you start to get desperate.

original: He sees her coming, and begins to glow,   Even as a dying coal revives with wind,
translation: He saw her coming and started to get angry, like a dying coal that flames up in the wind.

original: And with his bonnet hides his angry brow;   Looks on the dull earth with disturbed mind,
translation: He pulled his hat down over his face and looked down at the ground, angry and disturbed.

original: Taking no notice that she is so nigh,   For all askance he holds her in his eye.
translation: He didn't look at her as she drew closer. He looked everywhere but at her.

original: O, what a sight it was, wistly to view   How she came stealing to the wayward boy!
translation: It was a sight to see how she came creeping over to the escaping boy!

original: To note the fighting conflict of her hue,   How white and red each other did destroy!
translation: It was strange to see how her face blushed and grew pale!

original: But now her cheek was pale, and by and by   It flash'd forth fire, as lightning from the sky.
translation: Her cheek was pale, but a few seconds later it would blush again, as quickly as lightning in the sky.

original: Now was she just before him as he sat,   And like a lowly lover down she kneels;
translation: She reached the place where he was sitting,  and knelt down like a humble lover.

original: With one fair hand she heaveth up his hat,   Her other tender hand his fair cheek feels:
translation: She pulled his hat up with one hand, and felt his soft cheek with her other hand.

original: His tenderer cheek receives her soft hand's print,   As apt as new-fall'n snow takes any dint.
translation: His soft cheek, like freshly-fallen snow, felt the imprint of her soft hand on it.

original: O, what a war of looks was then between them!
translation: There was a war of looks between the two of them.

original: Her eyes petitioners to his eyes suing;   His eyes saw her eyes as they had not seen them;
translation: She looked into his eyes, pleading, begging. He looked into hers like he couldn't see them.

original: Her eyes woo'd still, his eyes disdain'd the wooing:
translation: Her eyes flirted with him; his eyes rejected her flirting.

original: And all this dumb play had his acts made plain   With tears, which, chorus-like, her eyes did rain.
translation: Their silent looks gave way to an abundance of tears, which rained down from her eyes to explain her sadness.

original: Full gently now she takes him by the hand,
translation: She took him gently by the hand, encasing his  white hand  in her white one.

original: A lily prison'd in a gaol of snow,
translation: It was like a lily covered in snow,

original: Or ivory in an alabaster band;   So white a friend engirts so white a foe:
translation: or ivory wrapped in alabaster; that's how white their two hands were.

original: This beauteous combat, wilful and unwilling,   Show'd like two silver doves that sit a-billing.
translation: This beautiful battle between her and him—the willing and the unwilling—was like two silver  doves  pecking at each other.

original: Once more the engine of her thoughts began:
translation: She started to speak again, saying,

original: 'O fairest mover on this mortal round,   Would thou wert as I am, and I a man,
translation: "you're the most handsome man that ever walked the earth! If you were a woman and I were a man,

original: My heart all whole as thine, thy heart my wound;
translation: and you were the lovesick one instead of me,

original: For one sweet look thy help I would assure thee,   Though nothing but my body's bane would cure thee!'
translation: I'd help you out with an encouraging look, knowing nothing except that my body would cure you!"

original: 'Give me my hand,' saith he, 'why dost thou feel it?'
translation: "Let go of my hand," he said, "why are you holding it?"

original: 'Give me my heart,' saith she, 'and thou shalt have it:
translation: "Let go of my heart," she said, "and you can have your hand back.

original: O, give it me, lest thy hard heart do steel it,
translation: Oh, give it back to me, or your heart will harden mine!

original: And being steel'd, soft sighs can never grave it:
translation: And once it's hardened, I'll never be able to fall in love again,

original: Then love's deep groans I never shall regard,   Because Adonis' heart hath made mine hard.'
translation: not even for the sweetest lover, because Adonis' heart will have made mine hard."

original: 'For shame,' he cries, 'let go, and let me go;
translation: "Shame on you," he cried, "let me go, let me go!

original: My day's delight is past, my horse is gone,   And 'tis your fault I am bereft him so:
translation: I'm tired of this, my horse is gone, and it's your fault that I lost him. Get out of here.

original: I pray you hence, and leave me here alone;
translation: Please leave me alone.

original: For all my mind, my thought, my busy care,   Is how to get my palfrey from the mare.'
translation: All I can think about or care about right now is getting my horse back from that mare."

original: Thus she replies: 'Thy palfrey, as he should,   Welcomes the warm approach of sweet desire:
translation: She replied, "your horse is giving into the heat of love (as he should).

original: Affection is a coal that must be cool'd;   Else, suffer'd, it will set the heart on fire:
translation: You have to give desire what it wants; otherwise, if you let it burn, it'll set your heart on fire.

original: The sea hath bounds, but deep desire hath none;   Therefore no marvel though thy horse be gone.
translation: The sea has limits, but deep desire knows no bounds. Don't be surprised your horse is gone.

original: 'How like a jade he stood, tied to the tree,   Servilely master'd with a leathern rein!
translation: "He stood there  tied  with a leather rein to the tree like an old nag.

original: But when he saw his love, his youth's fair fee,
translation: But when he saw the female horse, he fell in love with her.

original: He held such petty bondage in disdain;
translation: He didn't care about being tied up then.

original: Throwing the base thong from his bending crest,   Enfranchising his mouth, his back, his breast.
translation: He threw off his burdens, freeing his head, mouth, back, and chest.

original: 'Who sees his true-love in her naked bed,   Teaching the sheets a whiter hue than white,
translation: "Is it possible for a man to see his fair-skinned true love lying naked on the bedsheets,

original: But, when his glutton eye so full hath fed,   His other agents aim at like delight?
translation: and just be content with looking? Don't other parts of your body want to be satisfied?

original: Who is so faint, that dare not be so bold   To touch the fire, the weather being cold?
translation: Who's afraid to go after what they want when they want it?

original: 'Let me excuse thy courser, gentle boy;
translation: "I'm apologizing for your horse, silly boy.

original: And learn of him, I heartily beseech thee,   To take advantage on presented joy;
translation: You should learn from him. I'm telling you: take advantage of the opportunity in front of you.

original: Though I were dumb, yet his proceedings teach thee;
translation: Putting what I've said aside, you can still learn from his actions.

original: O, learn to love;
translation: Learn to love!

original: the lesson is but plain,   And once made perfect, never lost again.'
translation: The lesson is simple and, once you learn it, you never forget it."

original: 'I know not love,' quoth he, 'nor will not know it,
translation: "I don't know anything about love," he said, "and I never want to.

original: Unless it be a boar, and then I chase it;
translation: All I care about is hunting boars.

original: 'Tis much to borrow, and I will not owe it;
translation: It sounds like a lot of work that I'm not willing to put in.

original: My love to love is love but to disgrace it;
translation: All I can say about love is that I love to reject it.

original: For I have heard it is a life in death,
translation: I've heard it doesn't last very long anyway,

original: That laughs and weeps, and all but with a breath.
translation: and that it makes you have mood swings so that you're laughing one minute and crying the next.

original: 'Who wears a garment shapeless and unfinish'd?   Who plucks the bud before one leaf put forth?
translation: " Who  wears a shirt before they're done sewing it? Who picks a flower before a single leaf has sprouted?

original: If springing things be any jot diminish'd,   They wither in their prime, prove nothing worth:
translation: If you ruin something while it's still growing, you never get to see what it could have become.

original: The colt that's back'd and burden'd being young   Loseth his pride and never waxeth strong.
translation: If you break a  horse  in and teach it to obey commands when it's young, it loses its spirit and never gets big and strong.

original: 'You hurt my hand with wringing; let us part,
translation: "You're hurting my hand by pulling on it so much—let me go.

original: And leave this idle theme, this bootless chat:
translation: Forget this nonsense. Forget all this useless chat.

original: Remove your siege from my unyielding heart;   To love's alarms it will not ope the gate:
translation: Stop  trying to get me to fall in love with you; I'm not interested.

original: Dismiss your vows, your feigned tears, your flattery;   For where a heart is hard they make no battery.'
translation: Quit your promises, your fake tears, and your flattery. I'm not going to give in to you."

original: 'What! canst thou talk?' quoth she, 'hast thou a  tongue?
translation: "What! What are you saying?" she said, "can you really be saying this?

original: O, would thou hadst not, or I had no hearing!
translation: I wish you couldn't speak at all! I wish I were deaf!

original: Thy mermaid's voice hath done me double wrong;
translation: You've hurt me two times over: you lured me in with your siren song;

original: I had my load before, now press'd with bearing:
translation: made me fall in love with you (which was bad enough); and then rejected me.

original: Melodious discord, heavenly tune harshsounding,
translation: Your looks are like a sweet melody, but your words are harsh and dissonant.

original: Ear's deep-sweet music, and heart's deep-sore wounding.
translation: Seeing and hearing you at the same time is music to the ear, but a deep wound to the heart.

original: 'Had I no eyes but ears, my ears would love   That inward beauty and invisible;
translation: "If I had ears and no eyes, my ears would love your internal, invisible beauty.

original: Or were I deaf, thy outward parts would move   Each part in me that were but sensible:
translation: Or if I had no ears, then I'd fall head over heels in love with your external attractiveness.

original: Though neither eyes nor ears, to hear nor see,   Yet should I be in love by touching thee.
translation: And if I didn't have eyes or ears and couldn't see or hear, I'd still fall in love with you through touch alone.

original: 'Say, that the sense of feeling were bereft me,   And that I could not see, nor hear, nor touch,   And nothing but the very smell were left me,
translation: "If I lost my sense of touch—if I couldn't see, hear, or touch, and all I had left was smell—

original: Yet would my love to thee be still as much;
translation: I'd still love you just as much.

original: For from the stillitory of thy face excelling   Comes breath perfumed that breedeth love by   smelling.
translation: You see, the pores of your face produce a sweet smell that would make anyone fall in love with you just by smelling.

original: 'But, O, what banquet wert thou to the taste,
translation: "And if I could only taste you, it'd be as delicious as a feast!

original: Being nurse and feeder of the other four!   Would they not wish the feast might ever last,
translation: The taste of you alone would make up for all my other lost senses. I'd never want the feast to end.

original: And bid Suspicion double-lock the door,   Lest Jealousy, that sour unwelcome guest,   Should, by his stealing in, disturb the feast?'
translation: I wouldn't mind giving up my other senses, in fact, because sight, hearing, touch, and smell might be jealous! If I had all my senses, it'd disturb the feast of taste!"

original: Once more the ruby-colour'd portal open'd,   Which to his speech did honey passage yield;
translation: He opened the red, gaping door of his mouth again as if to say something sweet.

original: Like a red morn, that ever yet betoken'd   Wreck to the seaman, tempest to the field,
translation: His mouth was like the red morning sun that tells sailors that storms are coming; farmers that the crops will be ruined;

original: Sorrow to shepherds, woe unto the birds,   Gusts and foul flaws to herdmen and to herds.
translation: shepherds that they'll lose their flocks; birds that they'll have trouble flying; and cowboys and cows that they'll have strong winds to deal with.

original: This ill presage advisedly she marketh:
translation: She took note of this bad omen.

original: Even as the wind is hush'd before it raineth,   Or as the wolf doth grin before he barketh,
translation: Like the way the wind blows before it rains; or the way a wolf grins before it barks;

original: Or as the berry breaks before it staineth,   Or like the deadly bullet of a gun,
translation: or the way a berry breaks before its juice leaks out; or the way a gun goes off before its deadly bullet strikes,

original: His meaning struck her ere his words begun.
translation: she knew exactly what he was about to say even before he started.

original: And at his look she flatly falleth down,   For looks kill love and love by looks reviveth;
translation: When she saw his face, she fell down flat. Looks can kill when you're in love; and loving looks are the only thing that can set you right again.

original: A smile recures the wounding of a frown;
translation: A smile  cancels  out all the harm that a frown does.

original: But blessed bankrupt, that by love so thriveth!
translation: But even when you have nothing to go on, you're blessed to be so in love!

original: The silly boy, believing she is dead,   Claps her pale cheek, till clapping makes it red;
translation: Thinking she was dead, the silly boy slapped her pale cheek until he made it red again.

original: And all amazed brake off his late intent,
translation: He stopped what he'd been saying.

original: For sharply he did think to reprehend her,   Which cunning love did wittily prevent:
translation: He had intended to reject her once and for all, but her clever trick prevented him from doing so.
