original: Fair fall the wit that can so well defend her!
translation: She was pretty smart to think of that!

original: For on the grass she lies as she were slain,   Till his breath breatheth life in her again.
translation: She lay there in the grass as if she were dead until his breath brought her to life again.

original: He wrings her nose, he strikes her on the cheeks,   He bends her fingers, holds her pulses hard,
translation: He pinched her nose, slapped her cheeks, bent her fingers, felt her pulse,

original: He chafes her lips; a thousand ways he seeks   To mend the hurt that his unkindness marr'd:
translation: brushed her lips—he tried a thousand different things to undo how he'd hurt her.

original: He kisses her;   and she, by her good will,   Will never rise, so he will kiss her still.
translation: Then he kissed her. As far a she was concerned, she would never get up as long as he would keep on kissing her.

original: The night of sorrow now is turn'd to day:
translation: All her sadness went away; she was happy now.

original: Her two blue windows faintly she up-heaveth,   Like the fair sun, when in his fresh array   He cheers the morn and all the earth relieveth;
translation: She opened her two blue  eyes,  shining at him like the sun when it rises in the early morning, waking the earth.

original: And as the bright sun glorifies the sky,   So is her face illumined with her eye;
translation: Her face brightened when her eyes opened, just like when the sun illuminates the sky.

original: Whose beams upon his hairless face are fix'd,   As if from thence they borrow'd all their shine.
translation: Her eyes were fixed on his hairless face as if they got all their energy from him.

original: Were never four such lamps together mix'd,
translation: Four such exceptional eyes have never been in the same place at the same time before or since.

original: Had not his clouded with his brow's repine;
translation: His eyes were overshadowed by his frowning eyebrows,

original: But hers, which through the crystal tears gave light,   Shone like the moon in water seen by night.
translation: but her eyes shone through her tears like the moon reflected in water at night.

original: 'O, where am I?' quoth she, 'in earth or heaven,   Or in the ocean drench'd, or in the fire?
translation: "Where am I?" she said, "on earth, in heaven, drowning in the ocean, burning in fire?

original: What hour is this? or morn or weary even?   Do I delight to die, or life desire?
translation: What time is it? Is it morning, or evening? Do I want to die, or live?

original: But now I lived, and life was death's annoy;   But now I died, and death was lively joy.
translation: Just a few seconds ago, I was alive and couldn't dream of dying, but then I died and I really enjoyed it.

original: 'O, thou didst kill me: kill me once again:
translation: "Oh, you  killed  me! Kill me again.

original: Thy eyes' shrewd tutor, that hard heart of thine,   Hath taught them scornful tricks and such disdain
translation: You're hard-hearted; you've been giving me rude, hateful, condescending  looks.

original: That they have murder'd this poor heart of mine;
translation: You've broken my poor heart.

original: And these mine eyes, true leaders to their queen,   But for thy piteous lips no more had seen.
translation: As for me—I can usually control myself. If I hadn't seen your luscious lips I wouldn't be in this mess.

original: 'Long may they kiss each other, for this cure!
translation: "Kiss me again, and again—you're bringing me back to life!

original: O, never let their crimson liveries wear!
translation: Never stop kissing me with your luscious red lips!

original: And as they last, their verdure still endure,   To drive infection from the dangerous year!
translation: As long as your fresh, young lips are around, the world will be free from disease all year round!

original: That the star-gazers, having writ on death,   May say, the plague is banish'd by thy breath.
translation: Astronomers who foretold an epidemic will have to change their statements, saying the disease has been cured by your breath.

original: 'Pure lips, sweet seals in my soft lips imprinted,   What bargains may I make, still to be sealing?
translation: "How can I keep the sweet, soft seal of your lips  pressing  against mine forever?

original: To sell myself I can be well contented,   So thou wilt buy and pay and use good dealing;
translation: What deal do I have to make with you? I'd be happy to sell my soul—as long as you'd buy it and treat it nicely.

original: Which purchase if thou make, for fear of slips   Set thy seal-manual on my wax-red lips.
translation: If you buy my soul, you'll have to mark me as yours by setting the seal of your lips on mine.

original: 'A thousand kisses buys my heart from me;   And pay them at thy leisure, one by one.
translation: "You can buy my heart for a thousand kisses. You can pay at your leisure, one by one.

original: What is ten hundred touches unto thee?   Are they not quickly told and quickly gone?
translation: What would a thousand kisses cost you? They're over and done with quickly.

original: Say, for non-payment that the debt should double,   Is twenty hundred kisses such a trouble?'
translation: And, if you didn't pay me and your debt doubled, would two thousand kisses really be so much trouble?"

original: 'Fair queen,' quoth he, 'if any love you owe me,   Measure my strangeness with my unripe years:
translation: "Beautiful queen" he said, "if you really love me, you'll have to understand that I'm shy because I'm young.

original: Before I know myself, seek not to know me;
translation: Don't try to have sex with me before I'm a man.

original: No fisher but the ungrown fry forbears:   The mellow plum doth fall, the green sticks fast,   Or being early pluck'd is sour to taste.
translation: Fishermen don't reel in minnows. Unripe, green plums are sour-tasting when they're picked too early.

original: 'Look, the world's comforter, with weary gait,   His day's hot task hath ended in the west;
translation: "Look, the sun is slowly setting in the west.

original: The owl, night's herald, shrieks, ''Tis very late;'
translation: You can tell it's nighttime because the owl is hooting, 'it's very late!'

original: The sheep are gone to fold, birds to their nest,
translation: The sheep have gone back to their pasture; the birds are asleep in their nests.

original: And coal-black clouds that shadow heaven's light   Do summon us to part and bid good night.
translation: The sky is growing dark. It's time to go our separate ways and say good night.

original: 'Now let me say 'Good night,' and so say you;   If you will say so, you shall have a kiss.'
translation: "Now I'll say 'good night,' and then you. If you say it, I'll give you a kiss."

original: 'Good night,' quoth she, and, ere he says 'Adieu,'   The honey fee of parting tender'd is:
translation: "Good night," she said. Before he said "goodbye," he kissed her sweetly.

original: Her arms do lend his neck a sweet embrace;   Incorporate then they seem; face grows to face.
translation: She threw her arms around his neck. They seemed to become one person, their faces pressed together.

original: Till, breathless, he disjoin'd, and backward drew   The heavenly moisture, that sweet coral mouth,   Whose precious taste her thirsty lips well knew,
translation: Breathless, he pulled back and drew his sweet, moist, pink mouth away—robbing her thirsty lips of their precious taste.

original: Whereon they surfeit, yet complain on drouth:
translation: Even when she was kissing him, she complained she wasn't getting enough.

original: He with her plenty press'd, she faint with dearth   Their lips together glued, fall to the earth.
translation: When he gave her what she wanted, she pulled him to the ground, wanting more.

original: Now quick desire hath caught the yielding prey,   And glutton-like she feeds, yet never filleth;
translation: Now she had her desired prey within her clutches. She kissed him again and again, like a hungry person who's never full.

original: Her lips are conquerors, his lips obey,
translation: Her lips were conquerors; his lips obeyed,

original: Paying what ransom the insulter willeth;
translation: giving her whatever she demanded.

original: Whose vulture thought doth pitch the price so high,   That she will draw his lips' rich treasure dry:
translation: She set the price (in kisses) so high that she was bound to rob his lips of all they could give.

original: And having felt the sweetness of the spoil,   With blindfold fury she begins to forage;
translation: Having glimpsed the  treasure  he had to offer, she furiously began to look for more.

original: Her face doth reek and smoke, her blood doth boil,
translation: Her face grew hot, her blood boiled,

original: And careless lust stirs up a desperate courage,
translation: and her strong desire made her bold.

original: Planting oblivion,
translation: She forgot herself.

original: beating reason back,
translation: She pushed her better judgment aside,

original: Forgetting shame's pure blush and honour's wrack.
translation: forgetting his innocence and the importance of preserving reputation.

original: Hot, faint, and weary, with her hard embracing,
translation: He was hot, weak, and tired from her aggressive fondling.

original: Like a wild bird being tamed with too much handling,
translation: He was like a wild bird tamed by a keeper;

original: Or as the fleet-foot roe that's tired with chasing,   Or like the froward infant still'd with dandling,
translation: or a speedy deer that gets tired of being chased; or a whining baby that quiets down after being rocked.

original: He now obeys, and now no more resisteth,
translation: Now he obeyed her. He didn't resist anymore.

original: While she takes all she can, not all she listeth.
translation: She took everything she could, but not everything she wanted.

original: What wax so frozen but dissolves with tempering,   And yields at last to every light impression?
translation: Even frozen wax becomes soft when you melt it, and retains the shape of every object you press into it.

original: Things out of hope are compass'd oft with venturing,   Chiefly in love, whose leave exceeds commission:
translation: We often try to achieve things that are impossible to get, especially in love.

original: Affection faints not like a pale-faced coward,   But then woos best when most his choice is froward.
translation: When we're in love, we aren't afraid to go the extra mile. We work the hardest for love when our lover plays hard to get.

original: When he did frown, O, had she then gave over,   Such nectar from his lips she had not suck'd.
translation: Even when he frowned, she kept going—she'd already tasted the sweetness of his lips and couldn't stop.

original: Foul words and frowns must not repel a lover;
translation: Angry words and frowns can't stop a lover.

original: What though the rose have prickles, yet 'tis pluck'd:
translation: We still pick roses even though they have thorns;

original: Were beauty under twenty locks kept fast,   Yet love breaks through and picks them all at last.
translation: in the same way, a lover pushes through all the obstacles that keep him from enjoying his beautiful lover.

original: For pity now she can no more detain him;
translation: She felt bad for him and didn't want to keep him any longer.

original: The poor fool prays her that he may depart:   She is resolved no longer to restrain him;
translation: The poor boy begged her to let him leave, and she decided not to hold him down anymore.

original: Bids him farewell, and look well to her heart,
translation: She said goodbye, and asked him to be careful with her heart,

original: The which, by Cupid's bow she doth protest,   He carries thence incaged in his breast.
translation: which she  swore  he carried with him wherever he went.

original: 'Sweet boy,' she says, 'this night I'll waste in  sorrow,   For my sick heart commands mine eyes to watch.
translation: "Sweet boy," she said, "tonight I'll be overcome with grief—I'm lovesick over you.

original: Tell me, Love's master, shall we meet to-morrow?   Say, shall we? shall we? wilt thou make the match?'
translation: My darling, tell me: what time should we meet up tomorrow? Can we? Will you meet me?"

original: He tells her, no; to-morrow he intends   To hunt the boar with certain of his friends.
translation: He told her he couldn't because he already had plans to hunt boars with some of his friends.

original: 'The boar!' quoth she; whereat a sudden pale,   Like lawn being spread upon the blushing rose,   Usurps her cheek;
translation: "Hunting!" she said, her cheeks suddenly getting as pale as white cotton fabric being thrown over a rose.

original: she trembles at his tale,   And on his neck her yoking arms she throws:
translation: She trembled at his words and threw her arms around his neck.

original: She sinketh down, still hanging by his neck,   He on her belly falls, she on her back.
translation: She sank down, still hanging onto his neck. She fell on her back, and he fell on her stomach.

original: Now is she in the very lists of love,   Her champion mounted for the hot encounter:
translation: She finally had him where she wanted,  mounted  on top of her and ready to get hot and heavy.

original: All is imaginary she doth prove,   He will not manage her, although he mount her;
translation: But she could only play it out in her mind: he wouldn't make love to her, even though he was on top of her.

original: That worse than Tantalus' is her annoy,   To clip Elysium and to lack her joy.
translation: She was being  tortured —what she wanted was right there, but she couldn't get it.

original: Even as poor birds, deceived with painted grapes,   Do surfeit by the eye and pine the maw,
translation: She was overcome with how much she wanted him, like a poor bird that thinks fake grapes are real

original: Even so she languisheth in her mishaps,   As those poor birds that helpless berries saw.
translation: and, seeing what looks like food, starves to death.

original: The warm effects which she in him finds missing   She seeks to kindle with continual kissing.
translation: She tried to get him aroused by kissing him over and over.

original: But all in vain; good queen, it will not be:   She hath assay'd as much as may be proved;
translation: But it was all in vain; for the poor goddess it was not meant to be. She had tried as much as she could.

original: Her pleading hath deserved a greater fee;
translation: She should have had better luck with him.

original: She's Love, she loves, and yet she is not loved.
translation: She was the goddess of love, she was in love with him, and yet he didn't love her back.

original: 'Fie, fie,' he says, 'you crush me; let me go;   You have no reason to withhold me so.'
translation: "Shame on you," he said, "you're crushing me! Let me go. There's no reason for you to hold me like this."

original: 'Thou hadst been gone,' quoth she, 'sweet boy, ere  this,   But that thou told'st me thou wouldst hunt the boar.
translation: "I would have let you leave already, sweet boy," she said, "except that you told me you had to go hunting tomorrow.

original: O, be advised! thou know'st not what it is   With javelin's point a churlish swine to gore,
translation: Oh, be careful! You don't know how awful and dangerous it is to stab a boar with a spear.

original: Whose tushes never sheathed he whetteth still,   Like to a mortal butcher bent to kill.
translation: Even after you stab him, he'll keep swinging his tusks, like an angry butcher on a mission to kill.

original: 'On his bow-back he hath a battle set   Of bristly pikes, that ever threat his foes;
translation: "His curved back is full of bristly hairs that are dangerous, too.

original: His eyes, like glow-worms, shine when he doth fret;
translation: His eyes shine like fireflies when he's angry.

original: His snout digs sepulchres where'er he goes;
translation: He digs deep holes with his snout wherever he goes.

original: Being moved, he strikes whate'er is in his way,   And whom he strikes his cruel tushes slay.
translation: When he's riled up, he'll knock down anything in his way. He kills anything he touches with his tusks.

original: 'His brawny sides, with hairy bristles arm'd,
translation: "His thick flanks are covered in hairy bristles, too,

original: Are better proof than thy spear's point can enter;
translation: which repel the point of a spear so that you can't wound him.

original: His short thick neck cannot be easily harm'd;   Being ireful, on the lion he will venture:
translation: It's difficult to cut his short, thick neck. When he's angry, he'll even fight a lion.

original: The thorny brambles and embracing bushes,   As fearful of him, part, through whom he rushes.
translation: Even the thorns, brambles, and thick bushes are afraid of him as he runs and crashes through them.

original: 'Alas, he nought esteems that face of thine,   To which Love's eyes pay tributary gazes;
translation: "He doesn't care at all about your pretty face, or about how much I love you.

original: Nor thy soft hands, sweet lips and crystal eyne,
translation: He doesn't care about your soft hands, sweet lips, and sparkling eyes.

original: Whose full perfection all the world amazes;
translation: He doesn't care that you're the most perfect boy in the entire world.

original: But having thee at vantage,—wondrous dread!—
translation: Once he sets his sight on you, watch out!

original: Would root these beauties as he roots the mead.
translation: He'll destroy your beautiful body as easily as he tramples over the dirt.

original: 'O, let him keep his loathsome cabin still;   Beauty hath nought to do with such foul fiends:
translation: "Oh, leave him alone in the forest. A beautiful boy like you shouldn't have anything to do with such disgusting creatures.

original: Come not within his danger by thy will;
translation: Don't put yourself in danger on purpose;

original: They that thrive well take counsel of their friends.
translation: you'd do well to take my advice.

original: When thou didst name the boar, not to dissemble,   I fear'd thy fortune, and my joints did tremble.
translation: No joke—when I heard you say 'boar,' I was afraid for you, and I started shaking.

original: 'Didst thou not mark my face? was it not white?
translation: "Didn't you see my face? Wasn't it white?

original: Saw'st thou not signs of fear lurk in mine eye?
translation: Didn't you see the fear in my eyes?

original: Grew I not faint? and fell I not downright?
translation: Didn't I faint? Didn't I fall down?

original: Within my bosom, whereon thou dost lie,   My boding heart pants, beats, and takes no rest,
translation: My heart is pounding in my chest—you can feel it. It won't stop.

original: But, like an earthquake, shakes thee on my breast.
translation: It's shaking you like an earthquake as you lay there on top of it.

original: '   For where Love reigns, disturbing Jealousy   Doth call himself Affection's sentinel;
translation: "When we're in love, we get jealous easily.

original: Gives false alarms, suggesteth mutiny,
translation: Jealousy  makes us quick to panic, even when it's a false alarm.

original: And in a peaceful hour doth cry 'Kill, kill!'
translation: Even in low-stakes situations, our jealous hearts can make us go immediately to thinking, 'kill, kill!'

original: Distempering gentle Love in his desire,   As air and water do abate the fire.
translation: Jealousy offsets the desires of love in the same way that air and water put out fire.

original: 'This sour informer, this bate-breeding spy,
translation: "Jealousy is a tattle-tale, a double-crossing spy,

original: This canker that eats up Love's tender spring,
translation: a worm that eats up love when it's just blossomed.

original: This carry-tale, dissentious Jealousy,   That sometime true news, sometime false doth bring,
translation: Jealousy gossips and causes conflict, sometimes bringing true news and sometimes fake news.

original: Knocks at my heat and whispers in mine ear   That if I love thee, I thy death should fear:
translation: Jealousy is what's making my heart pound. It's whispering in my ear telling me that, if I love you, I should be afraid of your death.

original: 'And more than so, presenteth to mine eye   The picture of an angry-chafing boar,
translation: "Because I'm so jealous for you, I can see an angry, charging boar in my mind's eye.

original: Under whose sharp fangs on his back doth lie   An image like thyself, all stain'd with gore;
translation: I can imagine that, underneath his sharp fangs, you're lying on your back, stained with blood.

original: Whose blood upon the fresh flowers being shed   Doth make them droop with grief and hang the head.
translation: Your blood is falling onto the fresh flowers underneath, making them droop and hang their heads with grief.

original: 'What should I do, seeing thee so indeed,   That tremble at the imagination?
translation: "What am I supposed to do when I see you that way? My own imagination is making me tremble.

original: The thought of it doth make my faint heart bleed,
translation: The thought of it is making my heart weak.

original: And fear doth teach it divination:
translation: Fear is making me see the future.

original: I prophesy thy death, my living sorrow,   If thou encounter with the boar to-morrow.
translation: If you hunt the boar tomorrow, I prophesy that you will die and that I will live, grieving for you.

original: 'But if thou needs wilt hunt, be ruled by me;
translation: "If you have to go hunting, then do as I say:

original: Uncouple at the timorous flying hare,   Or at the fox which lives by subtlety,   Or at the roe which no encounter dare:
translation: hunt skittish, scurrying rabbits, or sneaky foxes, or elusive deer.

original: Pursue these fearful creatures o'er the downs,   And on thy well-breath'd horse keep with thy hounds.
translation: Pursue any of these easily-hunted animals, and stay put on your sturdy horse while your dogs do the work.

original: 'And when thou hast on foot the purblind hare,
translation: "And when you're chasing a practically blind  rabbit ,

original: Mark the poor wretch, to overshoot his troubles   How he outruns the wind and with what care   He cranks and crosses with a thousand doubles:
translation: watch how the poor thing works as hard as he can to outrun you, and how he criss-crosses and doubles back,

original: The many musets through the which he goes   Are like a labyrinth to amaze his foes.
translation: squeezing through gaps in fences to confuse you and tire you out.

original: 'Sometime he runs among a flock of sheep,   To make the cunning hounds mistake their smell,
translation: "He'll run through a flock of sheep to make the dogs lose the scent.

original: And sometime where earth-delving conies keep,   To stop the loud pursuers in their yell,
translation: Then he'll burrow down underground where the moles are, so that the dogs can't follow him.

original: And sometime sorteth with a herd of deer:   Danger deviseth shifts; wit waits on fear:
translation: Then he'll hide with a herd of deer. Necessity is the mother of invention; danger forces us to be clever.

original: 'For there his smell with others being mingled,   The hot scent-snuffing hounds are driven to doubt,
translation: "You see, when his scent mingles with other scents, the sniffing dogs aren't able to follow him anymore.

original: Ceasing their clamorous cry till they have singled   With much ado the cold fault cleanly out;   Then do they spend their mouths:
translation: They stop barking until they can find the trail again—then they sound the alarm.

original: Echo replies,   As if another chase were in the skies.
translation: Their barks echo, as if a second hunt were going on up in the sky.

original: 'By this, poor Wat, far off upon a hill,   Stands on his hinder legs with listening ear,   To harken if his foes pursue him still:
translation: "The poor rabbit, far away on a hill, hears the barks. He stands up on his hind legs, straining his ears and trying to figure out if his enemies are still pursuing him.

original: Anon their loud alarums he doth hear;
translation: When he hears their loud alarms,

original: And now his grief may be compared well   To one sore sick that hears the passing-bell.
translation: he's as depressed as a sick man who hears the ringing of the death knell.

original: 'Then shalt thou see the dew-bedabbled wretch   Turn, and return, indenting with the way;
translation: "Then you'll see the rabbit covered in dew going back and forth, mixing up his trail.

original: Each envious brier his weary legs doth scratch,
translation: The briars scratch his tired legs.

original: Each shadow makes him stop, each murmur stay:
translation: He's afraid of every shadow and every sound.

original: For misery is trodden on by many,   And being low never relieved by any.
translation: For you see, the miserable are victimized by many others, and the lowest of the low never receive help from anyone.

original: 'Lie quietly, and hear a little more;
translation: "Lie quietly and listen to a little more.

original: Nay, do not struggle, for thou shalt not rise:   To make thee hate the hunting of the boar,   Unlike myself thou hear'st me moralize,
translation: No, don't fight me! Then I'll never let you up. It's unlike me to lecture like this, but I'm trying to convince you not to go hunting for boars.

original: Applying this to that, and so to so;   For love can comment upon every woe.
translation: I'm putting this speech together because I'm in love with you and have a vested interest.

original: 'Where did I leave?'
translation: "Where was I?"

original: 'No matter where,' quoth he,   'Leave me, and then the story aptly ends:   The night is spent.'
translation: "It doesn't matter," he said, "let me go. End your story there. The night is over."

original: 'Why, what of that?' quoth she.
translation: "What does that matter?" she said.

original: 'I am,' quoth he, 'expected of my friends;   And now 'tis dark,
translation: "My friends are expecting me," he said, "and it's getting dark.

original: and going I shall fall.'
translation: I need to go, even if I am going to die the way you say."

original: 'In night,' quoth she, 'desire sees best of all
translation: She replied, "The best sex happens in the dark...

original: 'But if thou fall, O, then imagine this,
translation: "...but if you are injured in the hunt, then imagine this:

original: The earth, in love with thee, thy footing trips,   And all is but to rob thee of a kiss.
translation: the  earth  is in love with you, so it trips you to try and get you to kiss it.

original: Rich preys make true men thieves;
translation: The promise of riches will make even an honest man a thief.

original: so do thy lips   Make modest Dian cloudy and forlorn,
translation: In the same way, your lips would make a  modest virgin  fall in love with you

original: Lest she should steal a kiss and die forsworn.
translation: to the point where she'd die just to get a single kiss from you.

original: 'Now of this dark night I perceive the reason:   Cynthia for shame obscures her silver shine,
translation: "Now I can see why this night is so dark. The moon is covering her silvery face because she's embarrassed that you're more beautiful than she is.

original: Till forging Nature be condemn'd of treason,   For stealing moulds from heaven that were divine;   Wherein she framed thee in high heaven's despite,   To shame the sun by day and her by night.
translation: Mother Nature should be condemned for treason for making you so beautiful as to put the moon and the sun to shame.

original: 'And therefore hath she bribed the Destinies   To cross the curious workmanship of nature,
translation: "You see, the moon has bribed the  Fates  to work against Mother Nature.

original: To mingle beauty with infirmities,   And pure perfection with impure defeature,
translation: That way, beauty eventually succumbs to ugliness, and pure perfection is always mixed with deformity.

original: Making it subject to the tyranny   Of mad mischances and much misery;
translation: For that reason, the most  beautiful people  are subject to oppression, bad luck, and misery.

original: 'As burning fevers, agues pale and faint,
translation: "They suffer from burning fevers, shivers,

original: Life-poisoning pestilence and frenzies wood,
translation: poisonous insect bites, mental illness,

original: The marrow-eating sickness, whose attaint   Disorder breeds by heating of the blood:
translation: bone cancer, blood disease,

original: Surfeits, imposthumes, grief, and damn'd despair,
translation: swelling, tumors, grief, and damned despair.

original: Swear nature's death for framing thee so fair.
translation: These are the curses that counteract the fact that Mother Nature made you beautiful.

original: 'And not the least of all these maladies   But in one minute's fight brings beauty under:
translation: "Any one of these diseases would ruin someone's beauty instantly.

original: Both favour, savour, hue and qualities,   Whereat the impartial gazer late did wonder,   Are on the sudden wasted,
translation: Good looks, forms, colors, and qualities that might have impressed you one minute are gone the next.

original: thaw'd and done,   As mountain-snow melts with the midday sun.
translation: They're erased, vanishing as fast as mountain snow that melts in the midday sun.

original: 'Therefore, despite of fruitless chastity,   Love-lacking vestals and self-loving nuns,
translation: "So you see, nuns and virgins that take a vow of chastity  are being  wasteful.

original: That on the earth would breed a scarcity   And barren dearth of daughters and of sons,   Be prodigal:
translation: They're depriving the earth of daughters and sons that might have been born—they're wasting their fertility.

original: the lamp that burns by night   Dries up his oil to lend the world his light.
translation: When a lamp burns at night, it uses up its oil to provide light.

original: 'What is thy body but a swallowing grave
translation: "Your body is just a wide-open  grave ,

original: Seeming to bury that posterity   Which by the rights of time thou needs must have,
translation: burying the children which you're bound to have in due time.

original: If thou destroy them not in dark obscurity?
translation: Why would you prevent your children from being born?

original: If so, the world will hold thee in disdain,   Sith in thy pride so fair a hope is slain.
translation: If you did, the world would hate you. You would have withheld a blessing from the world on account of your pride.

original: 'So in thyself thyself art made away;
translation: "By preventing your future children from being born, you'd be annihilating yourself—

original: A mischief worse than civil home-bred strife,   Or theirs whose desperate hands themselves do slay,   Or butcher-sire that reaves his son of life.
translation: it's a worse crime than civil war, or suicide, or a man who kills his own son.

original: Foul-cankering rust the hidden treasure frets,   But gold that's put to use more gold begets.'
translation: Rust eats away at precious metals, but gold that's invested produces more gold after a while."

original: 'Nay, then,' quoth Adon, 'you will fall again   Into your idle over-handled theme:
translation: "Oh, stop," said Adonis, "you're just saying the same thing over and over again.

original: The kiss I gave you is bestow'd in vain,
translation: It was pointless for me to kiss you,

original: And all in vain you strive against the stream;
translation: and it's pointless for you to fight this uphill battle.

original: For, by this black-faced night, desire's foul nurse,   Your treatise makes me like you worse and worse.
translation: The way you're going on in the dark of night and trying to convince me to have sex with you is making me like you less and less.

original: 'If love have lent you twenty thousand tongues,   And every tongue more moving than your own,
translation: "If you had twenty thousand tongues and each of them talked even more convincingly than you do—

original: Bewitching like the wanton mermaid's songs,
translation: and if each of them was as bewitching as a mermaid song—

original: Yet from mine ear the tempting tune is blown
translation: I still wouldn't listen.

original: For know, my heart stands armed in mine ear,   And will not let a false sound enter there;
translation: You have to understand that I'm not interested—nothing you can say is going to change my heart.

original: 'Lest the deceiving harmony should run   Into the quiet closure of my breast;
translation: "I wouldn't let a single one of your words disturb the quiet of my hard heart.

original: And then my little heart were quite undone,   In his bedchamber to be barr'd of rest.
translation: Otherwise, my little  heart  would have no peace; he wouldn't be able to sleep in his own bed, that is, my chest.

original: No, lady, no; my heart longs not to groan,   But soundly sleeps, while now it sleeps alone.
translation: No ma'am, my heart's not interested in love. It prefers to sleep—and sleep alone.

original: 'What have you urged that I cannot reprove?
translation: "I've pushed back against everything you've asked.

original: The path is smooth that leadeth on to danger:
translation: The road to hell is paved with good intentions.

original: I hate not love, but your device in love,   That lends embracements unto every stranger.
translation: I don't hate love, I just  hate  the way you're going about it. I hate the way you're willing to sleep with any random stranger.

original: You do it for increase: O strange excuse,   When reason is the bawd to lust's abuse!
translation: You say you're doing it for posterity, but that's a strange excuse to justify your own lust!

original: 'Call it not love, for Love to heaven is fled,   Since sweating Lust on earth usurp'd his name;
translation: "Don't call it 'love.' Love is a higher thing than the bodily lust you've shown me today.

original: Under whose simple semblance he hath fed   Upon fresh beauty, blotting it with blame;
translation: It's easy to call it 'love' when you just want to taste my fresh beauty and soil my reputation.

original: Which the hot tyrant stains and soon bereaves,   As caterpillars do the tender leaves.
translation: You're happy to have sex and then leave me behind, like a leaf that's been munched by caterpillars.

original: 'Love comforteth like sunshine after rain,   But Lust's effect is tempest after sun;
translation: "Love is soothing, like sunshine after a rainstorm. But lust is the opposite—it's like a storm after the sun.

original: Love's gentle spring doth always fresh remain,   Lust's winter comes ere summer half be done;
translation: Love is fresh and gentle like the spring; lust gets old quickly, like an early winter.

original: Love surfeits not, Lust like a glutton dies;
translation: You can never have too much love; lust is always excessive.

original: Love is all truth, Lust full of forged lies.
translation: Love is pure truth; lust is built on lies.

original: 'More I could tell, but more I dare not say;
translation: "I could say more, but I won't.

original: The text is old, the orator too green.
translation: It's an old story and I'm too young to tell it.

original: Therefore, in sadness, now I will away;
translation: I'll leave now.

original: My face is full of shame, my heart of teen:
translation: As you can tell by my face, I'm sad and ashamed, and my heart hurts.

original: Mine ears, that to your wanton talk attended,   Do burn themselves for having so offended.'
translation: My ears are burning from all the offensive things you've said to me today."

original: With this, he breaketh from the sweet embrace,   Of those fair arms which bound him to her breast,
translation: With that, he broke free of her arms, which had held him pinned to her chest.

original: And homeward through the dark laund runs apace;   Leaves Love upon her back deeply distress'd.
translation: He ran homeward through the darkness, leaving Venus lying there, deeply distressed.

original: Look, how a bright star shooteth from the sky,   So glides he in the night from Venus' eye.
translation: He glided away from Venus in the night like a shooting star, streaking across the sky.

original: Which after him she darts, as one on shore   Gazing upon a late-embarked friend,
translation: She watched him go the way someone standing onshore watches a friend depart on a ship—

original: Till the wild waves will have him seen no more,
translation: keeping sight of him until the waves swallow him up,

original: Whose ridges with the meeting clouds contend:
translation: and the ship disappears on the horizon.

original: So did the merciless and pitchy night   Fold in the object that did feed her sight.
translation: So, too, did the merciless darkness of the night make it hard for her to see Adonis.

original: Whereat amazed, as one that unaware   Hath dropp'd a precious jewel in the flood,
translation: She was stunned, like someone who accidentally dropped a precious jewel in the water;

original: Or stonish'd as night-wanderers often are,   Their light blown out in some mistrustful wood,
translation: or like a sleepwalker suddenly woken up in the woods, their candle blown out in the darkness.

original: Even so confounded in the dark she lay,   Having lost the fair discovery of her way.
translation: She was lying there, confused, and didn't know which way to go.

original: And now she beats her heart, whereat it groans,
translation: She pounded on her chest and groaned—

original: That all the neighbour caves, as seeming troubled,   Make verbal repetition of her moans;
translation: the sound echoing for miles around as if the whole world were as upset as she was.

original: Passion on passion deeply is redoubled:
translation: Her passion was doubled as the echo repeated it.

original: 'Ay me!' she cries, and twenty times 'Woe, woe!'   And twenty echoes twenty times cry so.
translation: "Poor me!" she cried. She said, "the tragedy, the tragedy" twenty times, and then twenty echoes followed.

original: She marking them begins a wailing note   And sings extemporally a woeful ditty;
translation: Noticing the echoes, she wailed and then started to sing an improvised, sad tune.

original: How love makes young men thrall and old men dote;
translation: She sang about how love holds young men captive and makes old men silly;

original: How love is wise in folly, foolish-witty:
translation: she sang about how love is blind and foolish.

original: Her heavy anthem still concludes in woe,   And still the choir of echoes answer so.
translation: She concluded her heavy song sadly, the choir of echoes continuing on.

original: Her song was tedious and outwore the night,
translation: Her song was long; it went on all night.

original: For lovers' hours are long, though seeming short:
translation: Lovers lose track of time and don't realize how quickly the hours go by.

original: If pleased themselves, others, they think, delight   In such-like circumstance, with suchlike sport:
translation: Lovers assume that other people will be delighted by their own happiness,

original: Their copious stories oftentimes begun   End without audience and are never done.
translation: so they tend to tell long, boring stories that are never done—and no one listens.

original: For who hath she to spend the night withal   But idle sounds resembling parasites,
translation: The annoying sound of the echoes was her only company that night,

original: Like shrill-tongued tapsters answering every call,   Soothing the humour of fantastic wits?
translation: shouting back to her like a bartender shouting down a rowdy group of customers.

original: She says ''Tis so:' they answer all ''Tis so;'   And would say after her, if she said 'No.'
translation: Whether she said, "that's the way it is," or "no, it isn't," the echoes would repeat it.

original: Lo, here the gentle lark, weary of rest,
translation: A little bird who was tired of sleeping

original: From his moist cabinet mounts up on high,   And wakes the morning,
translation: scurried out of his nest, which was damp with dew, and chirped to announce that morning had come.

original: from whose silver breast   The sun ariseth in his majesty;
translation: The sun rose in its majesty,

original: Who doth the world so gloriously behold   That cedar-tops and hills seem burnish'd gold.
translation: making the whole world—the treetops, the hills—look as if they were made of gold.

original: Venus salutes him with this fair good-morrow:
translation: Venus saluted the  sun-god  and said good morning,

original: 'O thou clear god, and patron of all light,
translation: continuing,  "you bright god, you're the god of all light.

original: From whom each lamp and shining star doth borrow   The beauteous influence that makes him bright,
translation: Every candle and shining star has you to thank for the beautiful light that makes them bright.

original: There lives a son that suck'd an earthly mother,   May lend thee light, as thou dost lend to other.'
translation: And yet, there's a man on earth who's brighter than you, if you can believe it!"

original: This said, she hasteth to a myrtle grove,
translation: Having said that, she ran over to a group of myrtle trees,

original: Musing the morning is so much o'erworn,   And yet she hears no tidings of her love:
translation: thinking how late in the morning it was getting. And yet, she couldn't hear Adonis coming.

original: She hearkens for his hounds and for his horn:
translation: She listened to see if she could hear his dogs or his hunting horn.

original: Anon she hears them chant it lustily,   And all in haste she coasteth to the cry.
translation: Suddenly, she heard the loud trumpet and went as quickly as she could toward the sound.

original: And as she runs, the bushes in the way   Some catch her by the neck,
translation: As she ran, the bushes on the way grazed her neck,

original: some kiss her face,   Some twine about her thigh to make her stay:
translation: slashed at her face, and wrapped around her legs to try and stop her.

original: She wildly breaketh from their strict embrace,
translation: She wildly broke free of them,

original: Like a milch doe, whose swelling dugs do ache,   Hasting to feed her fawn hid in some brake.
translation: like a  deer  whose teats are full of milk, running away to feed her fawn, hidden in the grass.

original: By this, she hears the hounds are at a bay;
translation: And then she heard the dogs coming closer.

original: Whereat she starts, like one that spies an adder   Wreathed up in fatal folds just in his way,
translation: She was startled, like someone who spots a  snake  curled up in the grass

original: The fear whereof doth make him shake and shudder;
translation: and shakes and shudders in fear.

original: Even so the timorous yelping of the hounds   Appals her senses and her spirit confounds.
translation: The dogs' barking frightened her, overcoming her senses and rendering her motionless.

original: For now she knows it is no gentle chase,
translation: She then realized Adonis wasn't hunting something small;

original: But the blunt boar, rough bear, or lion proud,   Because the cry remaineth in one place,
translation: it was a strong boar, a rough bear, or a proud lion. She could tell because the shouts were coming from one place,

original: Where fearfully the dogs exclaim aloud:
translation: as were the dogs' scared barks.

original: Finding their enemy to be so curst,   They all strain courtesy who shall cope him first.
translation: Knowing they had cornered their enemy, all of them fought to see who could kill him first.

original: This dismal cry rings sadly in her ear,   Through which it enters to surprise her heart;
translation: The dogs' ominous barks rang in her ears and troubled her heart.

original: Who, overcome by doubt and bloodless fear,
translation: Overcome by doubt and fear,

original: With cold-pale weakness numbs each feeling part:
translation: each part of Venus' body started to go weak and numb; she couldn't feel anything.

original: Like soldiers, when their captain once doth yield,   They basely fly and dare not stay the field.
translation: Her body parts were like cowardly soldiers that run away from the battlefield as soon as their captain surrenders.

original: Thus stands she in a trembling ecstasy;
translation: She stood there trembling and out of her mind.

original: Till, cheering up her senses all dismay'd,   She tells them 'tis a causeless fantasy,   And childish error, that they are afraid;
translation: But then she told herself she was being childish; that it was just her imagination; and that her senses were mistaken on account of her being afraid.

original: Bids them leave quaking, bids them fear no more:—   And with that word she spied the hunted boar,
translation: She told her body to stop shaking and to not be afraid. And just then she spotted the hunted boar...

original: Whose frothy mouth, bepainted all with red,   Like milk and blood being mingled both together,
translation: ...his mouth foaming, blood spilling out of it, mixing red and white together.

original: A second fear through all her sinews spread,
translation: A second, terrified thought coursed through her entire body.

original: Which madly hurries her she knows not whither:   This way runs, and now she will no further,
translation: She ran crazily; she didn't know where. She ran one way and then, when she couldn't go any further,

original: But back retires to rate the boar for murther.
translation: went back again to charge the boar with murder.

original: A thousand spleens bear her a thousand ways;
translation: She wanted to go every direction at once.

original: She treads the path that she untreads again;   Her more than haste is mated with delays,
translation: She went down one path and then back again; she hurried, and then she lagged.

original: Like the proceedings of a drunken brain,   Full of respects, yet nought at all respecting;
translation: She moved like a drunk person's brain, which thinks a hundred different thoughts but doesn't think through any one of them entirely;

original: In hand with all things, nought at all effecting.
translation: or that talks about acting but never makes a move.

original: Here kennell'd in a brake she finds a hound,   And asks the weary caitiff for his master,
translation: She found a dog hiding in the bushes and asked the poor thing where his master was.

original: And there another licking of his wound,   'Gainst venom'd sores the only sovereign plaster;
translation: He licked his wound, the only way a dog knows how to heal a poisoned cut.

original: And here she meets another sadly scowling,   To whom she speaks, and he replies with howling.
translation: Then she saw another dog scowling sadly. She spoke to him and he replied by howling.

original: When he hath ceased his ill-resounding noise,   Another flap-mouth'd mourner, black and grim,   Against the welkin volleys out his voice;
translation: When he had stopped making that horrible racket, a black, serious dog with a flappy mouth howled up to the sky.

original: Another and another answer him,
translation: Another dog, and then another, answered him.

original: Clapping their proud tails to the ground below,   Shaking their scratch'd ears, bleeding as they go.
translation: They beat their tails on the ground and shook their scratched ears, bleeding the whole time.

original: Look, how the world's poor people are amazed   At apparitions, signs and prodigies,
translation: Poor people all over the world are impressed by omens, signs, and superstitions.

original: Whereon with fearful eyes they long have gazed,   Infusing them with dreadful prophecies;
translation: They love to talk about them and believe they're significant, as if they can tell the future.

original: So she at these sad signs draws up her breath   And sighing it again, exclaims on Death.
translation: In the same way, Venus looked at all these sad signs and breathed in deeply. Breathing out again, she shouted out, cursing  Death .

original: 'Hard-favour'd tyrant, ugly, meagre, lean,   Hateful divorce of love,'—thus chides she Death,—
translation: She said to  Death,  "you misshapen, ugly, tiny, thin, hateful opposite of love.

original: 'Grim-grinning ghost, earth's worm, what dost thou mean   To stifle beauty and to steal his breath,
translation: You skeletal ghost, you earthworm, what are doing? Why would you put an end to his beauty? Why would you stop him from breathing?

original: Who when he lived, his breath and beauty set   Gloss on the rose, smell to the violet?
translation: When he was alive, his breath and his beauty could make a rose look prettier and a violet smell better.

original: 'If he be dead,—O no, it cannot be,
translation: "If he is dead—oh, no, it can't be!

original: Seeing his beauty, thou shouldst strike at it:—
translation: You couldn't have killed him, once you knew how beautiful he was!

original: O yes, it may; thou hast no eyes to see,   But hatefully at random dost thou hit.
translation: And yet, it can be, can't it? You have no eyes to see; you hatefully  hit  people at random.

original: Thy mark is feeble age, but thy false dart   Mistakes that aim and cleaves an infant's heart.
translation: You aim for sick, old people, but sometimes you miss and kill a baby instead.

original: 'Hadst thou but bid beware, then he had spoke,   And, hearing him, thy power had lost his power.
translation: "If you had only just given him a warning, then he would have talked back to you and you would have stopped in your tracks.

original: The Destinies will curse thee for this stroke;   They bid thee crop a weed, thou pluck'st a flower:
translation: The Fates will curse you for killing him. They told you to kill an old person, but you killed a  young  one.

original: Love's golden arrow at him should have fled,   And not Death's ebon dart, to strike dead.
translation: He should be falling in love at his age, not falling down dead!

original: 'Dost thou drink tears, that thou provokest such  weeping?
translation: "Do you feed off of tears? Is that why you're making me cry so much?

original: What may a heavy groan advantage thee?
translation: What do you want with a heavy groan?

original: Why hast thou cast into eternal sleeping   Those eyes that taught all other eyes to see?
translation: Why would you close his eyes forever, considering his eyes taught all other eyes how to see?

original: Now Nature cares not for thy mortal vigour,   Since her best work is ruin'd with thy rigour.'
translation: There's nothing left for Mother Nature to be proud of in this world, now that you've shot down her best work."

original: Here overcome, as one full of despair,
translation: She was overwhelmed by despair at this point.

original: She vail'd her eyelids, who, like sluices, stopt   The crystal tide that from her two cheeks fair
translation: She closed her eyes; her eyelids worked like a dam, stopping the tide of her tears from reaching her two, fair cheeks,

original: In the sweet channel of her bosom dropt;
translation: and from dripping onto her breasts.

original: But through the flood-gates breaks the silver rain,   And with his strong course opens them again.
translation: But then the tears broke through the flood-gates, and she was forced to open them again.

original: O, how her eyes and tears did lend and borrow!
translation: Her eyes and her tears were indistinguishable!

original: Her eyes seen in the tears, tears in her eye;
translation: Her eyes were filled with tears and tears were in her eyes.

original: Both crystals, where they view'd each other's sorrow,   Sorrow that friendly sighs sought still to dry;
translation: Her eyes and her tears were both like mirrors reflecting their sadness back at each other—a sadness that no amount of sighs could exhaust.

original: But like a stormy day, now wind, now rain,   Sighs dry her cheeks, tears make them wet again.
translation: It was like a stormy day: first wind, then rain. First tears made her cheeks wet, then sighs dried them again.

original: Variable passions throng her constant woe,   As striving who should best become her grief;
translation: She felt many different kinds of grief at that moment, as if she weren't sure what to feel or how to  express it.

original: All entertain'd, each passion labours so,   That every present sorrow seemeth chief,   But none is best:
translation: Each kind of sadness felt the most pressing when she felt it, but no single one fully dominated.

original: then join they all together,   Like many clouds consulting for foul weather.
translation: All her sadnesses joined together, then, like dark clouds overhead that make for bad weather.

original: By this, far off she hears some huntsman hollo;   A nurse's song ne'er pleased her babe so well:
translation: Then she heard a hunter shouting from far away. She had never been so happy to hear something in her life.

original: The dire imagination she did follow   This sound of hope doth labour to expel;
translation: The sound made her hopeful again, expelling her darkest imaginings.

original: For now reviving joy bids her rejoice,   And flatters her it is Adonis' voice.
translation: She was overjoyed now, thinking she'd heard Adonis' voice.

original: Whereat her tears began to turn their tide,   Being prison'd in her eye like pearls in glass;
translation: Her tears stopped falling. They were trapped in her eyes like pearls suspended in glass.

original: Yet sometimes falls an orient drop beside,   Which her cheek melts,
translation: One tear trailed down her left cheek,

original: as scorning it should pass,   To wash the foul face of the sluttish ground,   Who is but drunken when she seemeth drown'd.
translation: where it disappeared on her flushed, red skin—as if her skin couldn't bear to allow the tears to the pass all the way down her face to make it wet all over.

original: O hard-believing love, how strange it seems   Not to believe, and yet too credulous!
translation: Poor Venus, she couldn't believe he was dead, and yet she completely believed it!

original: Thy weal and woe are both of them extremes;   Despair and hope makes thee ridiculous:
translation: Her greatest hope and her greatest fear were two extremes. Her quick jumps from despair to hope made her ridiculous—

original: The one doth flatter thee in thoughts unlikely,   In likely thoughts the other kills thee quickly.
translation: the one thought made her happy (though it was unlikely he was alive), and the other, more probable thought nearly killed her.

original: Now she unweaves the web that she hath wrought;
translation: She convinced herself that she was wrong—

original: Adonis lives, and Death is not to blame;
translation: that Adonis was alive and that Death was not to blame.

original: It was not she that call'd him, all-to naught:   Now she adds honours to his hateful name;
translation: She had no reason to call on Death; it was pointless. Then she praised Death's hateful name,

original: She clepes him king of graves and grave for kings,   Imperious supreme of all mortal things.
translation: calling him the king of graves and the grave for kings, the god who ruled over all mortal things.

original: 'No, no,' quoth she, 'sweet Death, I did but jest;
translation: "No, no," she said, "dear Death, I was only joking!

original: Yet pardon me I felt a kind of fear   When as I met the boar, that bloody beast,   Which knows no pity, but is still severe;
translation: Forgive me, I was afraid when I saw the boar—that violent, pitiless, aggressive animal.

original: Then, gentle shadow,—truth I must confess,—   I rail'd on thee, fearing my love's decease.
translation: So, sweet ghost, I have to admit that I criticized you because I was afraid my love was dead.

original: ''Tis not my fault: the boar provoked my tongue;
translation: "It's not my fault. The boar made me talk that way.

original: Be wreak'd on him, invisible commander;   'Tis he, foul creature, that hath done thee wrong;
translation: Punish the boar, Death. That disgusting creature is the one that's done you wrong.

original: I did but act, he's author of thy slander:
translation: I only reacted; he's the cause of my criticism.

original: Grief hath two tongues, and never woman yet   Could rule them both without ten women's wit.'
translation: People can't control what they say when they're grieving. No woman in the history of the world could control her tongue when she was in mourning, even if she had the willpower of ten women put together."

original: Thus hoping that Adonis is alive,   Her rash suspect she doth extenuate;
translation: Still hoping that Adonis was alive, she continued flattering Death.

original: And that his beauty may the better thrive,   With Death she humbly doth insinuate;
translation: She begged Death to let the beautiful boy live.

original: Tells him of trophies, statues, tombs, and stories   His victories, his triumphs and his glories.
translation: She complimented  Death  on his trophies, statues, tombs, and all the stories of his victories, triumphs, and his glories.

original: 'O Jove,' quoth she, 'how much a fool was I   To be of such a weak and silly mind
translation: "Goodness," she said, "I was such an idiot—and so weak-minded—

original: To wail his death who lives and must not die   Till mutual overthrow of mortal kind!
translation: to mourn the death of someone who was alive and who will never die until the end of mankind!

original: For he being dead, with him is beauty slain,   And, beauty dead, black chaos comes again.
translation: For you see, if he's dead, then that's the end of beauty. And without beauty, the universe will descend back into chaos.

original: 'Fie, fie, fond love,
translation: "Shame on my foolish heart.

original: thou art so full of fear   As one with treasure laden, hemm'd thieves;
translation: I'm as afraid as a person carrying treasure who's being followed by thieves.

original: Trifles, unwitnessed with eye or ear,   Thy coward heart with false bethinking grieves.'
translation: The tiniest sight or sound sets my cowardly heart thinking all kinds of things that aren't true."

original: Even at this word she hears a merry horn,   Whereat she leaps that was but late forlorn.
translation: As she said that, she heard a hunting horn. She jumped into the air, even though she was downcast only a moment ago.

original: As falcon to the lure, away she flies;
translation: She flew away like a falcon following its prey.

original: The grass stoops not, she treads on it so light;
translation: She ran so quickly that she didn't even trample the grass.

original: And in her haste unfortunately spies   The foul boar's conquest on her fair delight;
translation: As she ran, sadly she saw what the evil boar had done to her beloved boy.

original: Which seen, her eyes, as murder'd with the view,   Like stars ashamed of day, themselves withdrew;
translation: When she saw him, her eyes were  murdered  by the sight. She closed her eyes, like stars dimming when day dawns...

original: Or, as the snail, whose tender horns being hit,   Shrinks backward in his shelly cave with pain,
translation: ...or like a  snail  that shrinks back into his cave of a shell when you touch his eye stalks—fleeing the pain—

original: And there, all smother'd up, in shade doth sit,   Long after fearing to creep forth again;
translation: and stays there all hidden away in the darkness, even after he's stopped being afraid to creep forward again.

original: So, at his bloody view, her eyes are fled   Into the deep dark cabins of her head:
translation: Like the snail, when Venus saw Adonis lying there, bloody, her eyes flew back into the dark recesses of her skull.

original: Where they resign their office and their light   To the disposing of her troubled brain;
translation: There, her eyes refused to see anymore, and refused to relay any images to her  brain.

original: Who bids them still consort with ugly night,   And never wound the heart with looks again;
translation: Her brain told her eyes to stay there in the darkness and never to take in heartbreaking sights ever again.

original: Who like a king perplexed in his throne,   By their suggestion gives a deadly groan,
translation: Her heart, like a king sitting, confused, on his throne, groaned when he was mentioned by the brain.

original: Whereat each tributary subject quakes;
translation: Then every bone in her body shook like an earthquake.

original: As when the wind, imprison'd in the ground,   Struggling for passage, earth's foundation shakes,
translation: It was like when the wind—funneled underground and struggling to get out—shakes the earth above,

original: Which with cold terror doth men's minds confound.
translation: terrifying and confusing mankind.

original: This mutiny each part doth so surprise   That from their dark beds once more leap her eyes;
translation: Her shaking body so surprised her that her eyes opened once again.

original: And, being open'd, threw unwilling light   Upon the wide wound that the boar had trench'd   In his soft flank;
translation: And, being open, her eyes could see the wide wound the boar had cut in Adonis' soft thigh.

original: whose wonted lily white   With purple tears, that his wound wept, was drench'd:
translation: His lily white skin was covered with the purple tears shed by his wound.

original: No flower was nigh, no grass, herb, leaf, or weed,   But stole his blood and seem'd with him to bleed.
translation: All the flowers, grass, herbs, leaves, and weeds nearby were covered in his blood, and seemed to bleed with him.

original: This solemn sympathy poor Venus noteth;
translation: Venus observed the plants' apparent sympathy.

original: Over one shoulder doth she hang her head;   Dumbly she passions, franticly she doteth;   She thinks he could not die, he is not dead:
translation: She leaned her head against her shoulder. She gestured silently and touched him frantically, thinking he couldn't die—he couldn't be dead!

original: Her voice is stopt, her joints forget to bow;
translation: She couldn't speak. She couldn't move.

original: Her eyes are mad that they have wept til now.
translation: She felt she was silly for crying before that moment.

original: Upon his hurt she looks so steadfastly,   That her sight dazzling makes the wound seem three;
translation: She looked steadily at the spot where he'd been hurt. It overwhelmed her sight, making her think she could see  three wounds .

original: And then she reprehends her mangling eye,   That makes more gashes where no breach should be:
translation: Then she corrected her blurry vision, which was inventing gashes where there were none.

original: His face seems twain, each several limb is doubled;
translation: She thought she saw two faces, four arms, and four legs.

original: For oft the eye mistakes, the brain being troubled.
translation: When you're upset, your eyes often make mistakes.

original: 'My tongue cannot express my grief for one,   And yet,' quoth she, 'behold two Adons dead!
translation: "I can't even express my grief for one Adonis, and look! Here's two dead Adonises," she said.

original: My sighs are blown away, my salt tears gone,   Mine eyes are turn'd to fire, my heart to lead:
translation: "I can't sigh anymore; my salty tears are all gone. My eyes have turned into fire and my heart has turned into lead.

original: Heavy heart's lead, melt at mine eyes' red fire!   So shall I die by drops of hot desire.
translation: I wish I could melt my hard heart with the fire coming from my eyes! Then I could kill myself, being consumed by my own desire.

original: 'Alas, poor world, what treasure hast thou lost!
translation: "The world has lost such a treasure!

original: What face remains alive that's worth the viewing?
translation: Is there anyone alive who can compare to him?

original: Whose tongue is music now?
translation: Anyone with a voice as sweet?

original: what canst thou boast   Of things long since, or any thing ensuing?
translation: Could anyone ever beat him, in the past or in the days to come?

original: The flowers are sweet, their colours fresh and trim;   But true-sweet beauty lived and died with him.
translation: The flowers may be pretty with their fresh, bright colors, but since he embodied true beauty, beauty died with him, too.

original: 'Bonnet nor veil henceforth no creature wear!   Nor sun nor wind will ever strive to kiss you:
translation: "No one needs to wear hats or veils anymore! The  sun  and the wind are gone.

original: Having no fair to lose, you need not fear;
translation: Since you can't get sunburned anymore, you don't have to be afraid.

original: The sun doth scorn you and the wind doth hiss you:
translation: The sun is laughing at you, and the wind is hissing at you.

original: But when Adonis lived, sun and sharp air   Lurk'd like two thieves, to rob him of his fair:
translation: But when Adonis was alive, the sun and the air were jealous of him and wanted to make him less handsome so that he couldn't compete with them.

original: 'And therefore would he put his bonnet on,   Under whose brim the gaudy sun would peep;
translation: "So Adonis would have to wear a hat. The sun would peek over the brim of the hat,

original: The wind would blow it off   and, being gone,   Play with his locks:
translation: but then the wind would blow it off  and play with Adonis' hair.

original: then would Adonis weep;
translation: Then Adonis would cry.

original: And straight, in pity of his tender years,   They both would strive who first should dry his tears.
translation: At once, the sun and the air would take pity on the young boy, and the two of them would compete to comfort him first.

original: 'To see his face the lion walk'd along   Behind some hedge, because he would not fear him;
translation: "Lions had to hide in the bushes to see his face, because Adonis wasn't afraid of them.

original: To recreate himself when he hath sung,   The tiger would be tame and gently hear him;
translation: Tigers would sit tamely and gently to listen to him entertain himself by singing. When he spoke,

original: If he had spoke, the wolf would leave his prey   And never fright the silly lamb that day.
translation: he could convince wolves to leave their prey, and to even put off scaring sheep for a day.

original: 'When he beheld his shadow in the brook,   The fishes spread on it their golden gills;
translation: "When he saw his reflection in a stream, fish would swim through and try to touch it.

original: When he was by, the birds such pleasure took,   That some would sing, some other in their bills   Would bring him mulberries and ripe-red cherries;
translation: When he was nearby, birds would sing to him or carry in their beaks mulberries and ripe, red cherries for him.

original: He fed them with his sight, they him with berries.
translation: They loved to look at him, so they'd bring him berries in return.

original: 'But this foul, grim, and urchin-snouted boar,   Whose downward eye still looketh for a grave,
translation: "But this gross, evil, long-nosed boar with his downward facing eyes couldn't appreciate Adonis' beauty—

original: Ne'er saw the beauteous livery that he wore;   Witness the entertainment that he gave:
translation: he never saw what he looked like and he never heard his sweet voice.

original: If he did see his face, why then I know   He thought to kiss him, and hath kill'd him so.
translation: If he did see his face, then maybe he accidentally killed him because he was trying to kiss  him .

original: ''Tis true, 'tis true; thus was Adonis slain:   He ran upon the boar with his sharp spear,
translation: "Ah, yes—this is how Adonis was killed: he hit the boar with his sharp spear,

original: Who did not whet his teeth at him again,   But by a kiss thought to persuade him there;
translation: and the boar, instead of pursuing him with his teeth, thought he could kiss Adonis and make him stop hunting him.

original: And nuzzling in his flank, the loving swine   Sheathed unaware the tusk in his soft groin.
translation: Nuzzling into his flank, the sweet pig accidentally thrust his tusk into Adonis' thigh.

original: 'Had I been tooth'd like him, I must confess,   With kissing him I should have kill'd him first;
translation: "I have to admit: if I had tusks like the boar, I would have killed Adonis when I tried to kiss him.

original: But he is dead, and never did he bless   My youth with his; the more am I accurst.'
translation: But he's dead. I never got the chance to make love to him, and I regret that."

original: With this, she falleth in the place she stood,   And stains her face with his congealed blood.
translation: With that, she fell down where she stood and rubbed her face in his congealed blood.

original: She looks upon his lips, and they are pale;   She takes him by the hand, and that is cold;
translation: She looked at his pale lips. She held his cold hand.

original: She whispers in his ears a heavy tale,   As if they heard the woeful words she told;
translation: She whispered a sad story in his ear as if he could hear the words she said.

original: She lifts the coffer-lids that close his eyes,   Where, lo, two lamps, burnt out, in darkness lies;
translation: She lifted his eyelids, but his   eyes  were burned out, filled with darkness, not light.

original: Two glasses, where herself herself beheld   A thousand times, and now no more reflect;
translation: She'd seen her own reflection in those eyes a thousand times, but they didn't reflect anymore.

original: Their virtue lost, wherein they late excell'd,   And every beauty robb'd of his effect:
translation: They had lost all the beauty they once had, and the world was short of beauty now because of it.

original: 'Wonder of time,' quoth she, 'this is my spite,   That, thou being dead, the day should yet be light.
translation: "It's strange how it's still daytime," she said, "and that it's still light outside, even though you're dead.

original: 'Since thou art dead, lo, here I prophesy:   Sorrow on love hereafter shall attend:
translation: "Since you're dead, I prophesy that lovers forever afterward will have trouble.

original: It shall be waited on with jealousy,   Find sweet beginning, but unsavoury end,
translation: They'll be jealous of each other. They'll enjoy the honeymoon phase, and then get tired of each other and break up.

original: Ne'er settled equally, but high or low,   That all love's pleasure shall not match his woe.
translation: Love and trouble will always be together; one can't exist without the other. They'll never be equal, either—the good parts of being in love will never equal the bad.

original: 'It shall be fickle, false and full of fraud,
translation: "Love will be flighty, double-crossing, and full of deception.

original: Bud and be blasted in a breathing-while;   The bottom poison, and the top o'erstraw'd
translation: Just when it sprouts and blossoms, the roots will be poisoned.

original: With sweets that shall the truest sight beguile:
translation: Just when couples are starting to enjoy love's sweet fruits, love will be snatched away from them.

original: The strongest body shall it make most weak,   Strike the wise dumb and teach the fool to speak.
translation: Love will make the strongest man weak, make the wise man dumb, and teach the stupid man to speak.

original: 'It shall be sparing and too full of riot,
translation: "Love will happen infrequently, and will cause conflict when it does arrive.

original: Teaching decrepit age to tread the measures;   The staring ruffian shall it keep in quiet,
translation: Love will teach old men to act young again. It will make the boldest scoundrel shut his mouth.

original: Pluck down the rich, enrich the poor with treasures;
translation: It will make the rich poor and the poor rich.

original: It shall be raging-mad and silly-mild,   Make the young old, the old become a child.
translation: It will be absolutely crazy and sweet and mild. It will make young men old, and old men become children again.

original: 'It shall suspect where is no cause of fear;   It shall not fear where it should most mistrust;
translation: "Love will be jealous when there's no reason to be. It will be comfortable when it should be afraid.

original: It shall be merciful and too severe,   And most deceiving when it seems most just;
translation: It will be both too forgiving and too harsh, and the most fake when it seems the most real.

original: Perverse it shall be where it shows most toward,   Put fear to valour, courage to the coward.
translation: It will be hard to get when you want it most. It will make courageous men cowardly and cowards courageous.

original: 'It shall be cause of war and dire events,
translation: "Love will cause wars and catastrophes.

original: And set dissension 'twixt the son and sire;   Subject and servile to all discontents,   As dry combustious matter is to fire:
translation: It will make sons and fathers fight one another. It will instigate countless conflicts, like dry kindling starts fires.

original: Sith in his prime Death doth my love destroy,   They that love best their loves shall not enjoy.'
translation: Since Death killed my love before his time, lovers until the end of time won't be allowed to enjoy the best part of their love."

original: By this, the boy that by her side lay kill'd   Was melted like a vapour from her sight,
translation: After she said that, the dead boy by her side evaporated into thin air.

original: And in his blood that on the ground lay spill'd,   A purple flower sprung up, chequer'd with white,
translation: And in the place where his blood lay spilled on the ground, a purple  flower  with spots of white sprang up.

original: Resembling well his pale cheeks and the blood   Which in round drops upon their whiteness stood.
translation: It resembled his pale cheeks, with their blushing spots in the middle of his white skin.

original: She bows her head, the new-sprung flower to smell,   Comparing it to her Adonis' breath,
translation: She bowed her head to smell the newly-grown flower, comparing it to her Adonis' breath.

original: And says, within her bosom it shall dwell,   Since he himself is reft from her by death:
translation: She said she would carry it by her heart always, since death took him away from her.

original: She crops the stalk, and in the breach appears   Green dropping sap, which she compares to tears
translation: She cut the stalk. Green sap oozed out of the end, which she compared to tears.

original: 'Poor flower,' quoth she, 'this was thy fathers guise—   Sweet issue of a more sweet-smelling sire—
translation: "Poor  flower ," she said, "your father cried like that. You're the sweet son of an even sweeter-smelling father.

original: For every little grief to wet his eyes:
translation: He would cry for every little thing.

original: To grow unto himself was his desire,   And so 'tis thine;
translation: He wanted to grow up to be a man, and so do you.

original: but know, it is as good   To wither in my breast as in his blood.
translation: But you should know that it's as good to wither here, next to my heart, as it is to grow here in his blood.

original: 'Here was thy father's bed, here in my breast;   Thou art the next of blood, and 'tis thy right:
translation: "Your father laid his head here, on my chest. You're his heir, so it's your place, now.

original: Lo, in this hollow cradle take thy rest,   My throbbing heart shall rock thee day and night:
translation: Look, rest yourself in the hollow cradle between my breasts. My throbbing heart will rock you day and night.

original: There shall not be one minute in an hour   Wherein I will not kiss my sweet love's flower.'
translation: I'll kiss my sweet love's flower every minute of every hour."

original: Thus weary of the world, away she hies,   And yokes her silver doves;
translation: Weary of the world now, she called her silver doves to take her away.

original: by whose swift aid   Their mistress mounted through the empty skies   In her light chariot quickly is convey'd;
translation: With their speedy help, she rose into the empty sky in her light chariot.

original: Holding their course to Paphos, where their queen   Means to immure herself and not be seen.
translation: They set their course for  Paphos , where Venus intended to hide, and never be seen again.
